0001.name: A. Caglar Tas
0001.bio: Tas is an Assistant Professor at the University of Tennessee, Knoxville, investigating the cognitive and neural mechanisms that maintain visual stability across saccadic eye movements. Their research explores transsaccadic perception and updating, specifically examining how the brain integrates information from disparate fixations into an internal representation. Utilizing behavioral psychophysics, eye-tracking technology, and functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS), Tas studies the functional relationship between visual working memory and oculomotor control. Their recent work focuses on the temporal dynamics of attention and the interaction between peripheral and foveal vision during naturalistic viewing tasks.
0001.research_direction: Dr. Tas has recently been investigating the dynamic interplay between eye movements, visual working memory, and attentional control. Their recent work explores how the visual system maintains stability and retains feature information across saccades, focusing on visual field asymmetries and the prioritization of saccade targets in naturalistic scenes. Additionally, they are examining how the contents of memory modulate oculomotor execution, such as saccade curvature, and how experimental task design impacts our ability to utilize negative search templates to ignore distractors. Furthermore, they have been evaluating the ecological validity of foundational research paradigms by investigating whether the use of artificial fixation points generalizes to real-world visual behavior.

0002.name: A. Mike Burton
0002.bio: A. Mike Burton is a Professor of Psychology at the University of York where they research the cognitive and perceptual mechanisms of face recognition. Burton examines the familiarity effect, specifically investigating why the human visual system recognizes known individuals across variable conditions while often failing with unfamiliar faces. Their research methodologies combine experimental psychology and computational modeling to determine how stable identity representations emerge from variable visual inputs. Burton also applies this research to forensic and security contexts and co-developed the Glasgow Face Matching Test (GFMT) to assess person identification in fields such as policing and passport control.
0002.research_direction: Dr. Burton's recent work explores the multidimensional nature of face perception, investigating the perceptual, computational, and neural mechanisms that govern how we process familiar versus unfamiliar faces. They have recently been examining how the visual system isolates identity-diagnostic information from ambient image variation, such as changes in viewpoint or lighting, using principal components analysis and behavioral tasks to pinpoint the critical image dimensions required for human and computer face recognition. In applied visual search contexts, their research investigates face matching in complex real-world environments like CCTV footage, testing how exposure to within-person variability across multiple target photos influences search efficiency. Additionally, they are probing the theoretical boundaries of human visual expertise by exploring individual differences in face processing and seeking to establish continuous neural markers that track varying degrees of face familiarity.

papers.title: A narrow band of image dimensions is critical for face recognition.
papers.abstract: A key challenge in human and computer face recognition is to differentiate information that is diagnostic for identity from other sources of image variation. Here, we used a combined computational and behavioural approach to reveal critical image dimensions for face recognition. Behavioural data were collected using a sorting and matching task with unfamiliar faces and a recognition task with familiar faces. Principal components analysis was used to reveal the dimensions across which the shape and texture of faces in these tasks varied. We then asked which image dimensions were able to predict behavioural performance across these tasks. We found that the ability to predict behavioural responses in the unfamiliar face tasks increased when the early PCA dimensions (i.e. those accounting for most variance) of shape and texture were removed from the analysis. Image similarity also predicted the output of a computer model of face recognition, but again only when the early image dimensions were removed from the analysis. Finally, we found that recognition of familiar faces increased when the early image dimensions were removed, decreased when intermediate dimensions were removed, but then returned to baseline recognition when only later dimensions were removed. Together, these findings suggest that early image dimensions reflect ambient changes, such as changes in viewpoint or lighting, that do not contribute to face recognition. However, there is a narrow band of image dimensions for shape and texture that are critical for the recognition of identity in humans and computer models of face recognition.

papers.title: A neural measure of the degree of face familiarity

papers.authors: D. White, A. Burton

papers.title: Face search in CCTV surveillance
papers.abstract: We present a series of experiments on visual search in a highly complex environment, security closed-circuit television (CCTV). Using real surveillance footage from a large city transport hub, we ask viewers to search for target individuals. Search targets are presented in a number of ways, using naturally occurring images including their passports and photo ID, social media and custody images/videos. Our aim is to establish general principles for search efficiency within this realistic context. Across four studies we find that providing multiple photos of the search target consistently improves performance. Three different photos of the target, taken at different times, give substantial performance improvements by comparison to a single target. By contrast, providing targets in moving videos or with biographical context does not lead to improvements in search accuracy. We discuss the multiple-image advantage in relation to a growing understanding of the importance of within-person variability in face recognition.
papers.authors: M. Mileva, A. Burton

papers.title: Are We Face Experts?
papers.authors: A. Young, A. Burton

0004.name: Aaron Schurger
0004.main_research_area: cognitive neuroscience of volition and consciousness
0004.bio: Aaron Schurger is a cognitive neuroscientist at Chapman University who examines the neural mechanisms underlying voluntary action and conscious perception. Schurger’s research on the readiness potential introduced a stochastic accumulator model to demonstrate that pre-movement neural buildup can be explained by subthreshold fluctuations in brain activity rather than a pre-determined intention to act. Their work also investigates the distinction between conscious and non-conscious processing, utilizing computational modeling and neuroimaging to identify neural signatures of subjective experience, such as the stability and reproducibility of cortical activity. Schurger's methodology integrates behavioral psychophysics, machine learning, and electrophysiology to investigate the interface between neural dynamics and human agency.
0004.research_direction: Dr. Schurger has recently been investigating the neural and cognitive mechanisms underlying voluntary movement and the conscious intention to act. Their recent work explores the precise nature of the Readiness Potential—a classic pre-motor EEG signal—using novel probe-based paradigms and computational modeling to test whether it reflects true awareness of motor preparation or simply metacognitive access to stochastic neural accumulation. In parallel, they are utilizing spiking neural networks to examine how these slow-ramping pre-motor signals might naturally emerge from spontaneous brain fluctuations rather than deliberate planning. Additionally, their research critically evaluates classic paradigms for measuring the exact timing of conscious intent and probes the theoretical and empirical criteria for determining whether an agent is perceptually conscious of specific information relevant to an upcoming action.

papers.title: Probing for intentions: The early readiness potential does not reflect awareness of motor preparation
papers.abstract: Voluntary actions are typically preceded by the Readiness Potential (RP), a negative midfrontal EEG deflection that begins ∼2 seconds before movement. What cognitive and neural process the RP reflects and how it relates to conscious intention remain unclear due to conflicting findings. We investigated the neural basis and cognitive significance of the RP in a novel probe-based paradigm. Contrary to prior reports, we found that pre-probe RP buildups were not related to reported awareness of motor preparation. Computational modeling suggested that the best explanation for these results is via metacognitive access to stochastic accumulation. Reported preparation was also related to beta desynchronization over contralateral motor cortex shortly before probe onset. We conclude that the RP may be metacognitively accessible in response to external task demands but does not reflect the onset of a conscious intention. We discuss implications of these findings for voluntary action initiation and intention awareness. Highlights We investigate the mechanisms underlying voluntary action initiation in a new probe paradigm. Contrary to prior results, the readiness does not reflect reported awareness of motor preparation. Computational modeling supports stochastic accumulation over linear ballistic accumulation and classic RP models. Reported awareness of motor preparation may emerge from metacognitive access to stochastic accumulation. Time-frequency analysis suggests reported awareness may also relate to pre-probe beta desynchronization.
papers.authors: Jake Gavenas, Aaron Schurger, U. Maoz

papers.title: Corrigendum to “What is the intention to move and when does it occur?” [Neurosci. Biobehav. Rev. 151 (2023) 105199]
papers.authors: A. Triggiani, Gabriel Kreiman, Cara Lewis, U. Maoz, Alfred Mele, L. Mudrik, A. Roskies, Aaron Schurger, M. Hallett

papers.title: What is the Intention to Move and When Does it Occur?
papers.abstract: In 1983 Benjamin Libet and colleagues published a paper apparently challenging the view that the conscious intention to move precedes the brain's preparation for movement. The experiment initiated debates about the nature of intention, the neurophysiology of movement, and philosophical and legal understanding of free will and moral responsibility. Here we review the concept of "conscious intention" and attempts to measure its timing. Scalp electroencephalographic activity prior to movement, the Bereitschaftspotential, clearly begins prior to the reported onset of conscious intent. However, the interpretation of this finding remains controversial. Numerous studies show that the Libet method for determining intent, W time, is not accurate and may be misleading. We conclude that intention has many different aspects, and although we now understand much more about how the brain makes movements, identifying the time of conscious intention is still elusive.
papers.authors: A. Triggiani, Gabriel Kreiman, Cara Lewis, U. Maoz, A. Mele, L. Mudrik, A. Roskies, Aaron Schurger, M. Hallett

papers.title: Slow ramping emerges from spontaneous fluctuations in spiking neural networks
papers.authors: Jake Gavenas, Ueli Rutishauser, Aaron Schurger, U. Maoz

papers.title: How can we determine whether or not an agent is conscious of a bit of information relevant to an action?
papers.abstract: Determining whether or not an agent is conscious of a bit of information relevant to action requires first that we can determine if an agent is conscious of a given bit of information, which by itself is challenging. In addition, we have to be able to tag that bit of information as being “relevant to action.” This chapter reviews some of the neuroscience and philosophy behind perceptual “content consciousness” and some of the key considerations involved in measuring neural information and determining its subjective status. One of those key considerations is determining (or deciding) what qualifies a bit of information as relevant to action. The chapter proposes a hypothetical empirical approach to the question posed which remains an open and active research question.
papers.authors: L. Mudrik, Aaron Schurger

0005.name: Aaron Seitz
0005.department: Department of Psychology; Department of Physical Therapy, Movement and Rehabilitation Sciences; Department of Art + Design
0005.lab_name: Brain Game Center for Mental Fitness and Well-being
0005.bio: Aaron Seitz is a Professor of Psychology and Director of the Brain Game Center at Northeastern University, investigating the mechanisms of brain plasticity and cognitive training. Seitz's research focuses on how the human brain solves the stability-plasticity dilemma, specifically examining the roles of reinforcement, attention, and multisensory integration in driving perceptual learning. Utilizing a methodology that combines computational neuroscience, human psychophysics, and neuroimaging, Seitz develops and validates gamified ambulatory tools designed to enhance sensory and cognitive function across populations ranging from athletes to individuals with neurodegenerative deficits.
0005.research_direction: Dr. Seitz's recent work explores both the methodological advancement of psychophysical assessment and the design of perceptual and cognitive training protocols. They have recently been investigating how to use machine learning and nonparametric Bayesian active learning to rapidly and accurately estimate contrast sensitivity functions for both research and clinical applications. Their research also spans vision rehabilitation and cognitive aging, examining novel training protocols to induce a preferred retinal locus in patients with central scotomas and advocating for standardized, interoperable methodologies across cognitive training interventions. Additionally, they are exploring the gamification of behavioral testing across sensory modalities, investigating whether video game features can improve measures of spatial release from masking to better capture real-world auditory difficulties in diverse clinical populations.

papers.title: Contrast Response Function Estimation with Nonparametric Bayesian Active Learning
papers.abstract: Multidimensional psychometric functions can typically be estimated nonparametrically for greater accuracy or parametrically for greater efficiency. By recasting the estimation problem from regression to classification, however, powerful machine learning tools can be leveraged to improve both accuracy and efficiency simultaneously. Contrast Sensitivity Functions (CSFs) are behaviorally estimated curves that provide insight into both peripheral and central visual function. They are impractically long to be used in many clinical workflows without compromises of some sort, however, such as sampling only a few spatial frequencies or making strong assumptions about the shape of the function. This paper describes the development of the Machine Learning Contrast Response Function (MLCRF) estimator, which quantifies the expected probability of success in performing a contrast detection or discrimination task. A machine learning CSF can then be derived from the MLCRF. Using simulated eyes created from canonical CSF curves and actual human contrast response data, the accuracy and efficiency of the MLCSF was evaluated in order to determine its potential utility for research and clinical applications. With stimuli selected randomly, the MLCSF estimator converged toward ground truth. With optimal stimulus selection via Bayesian active learning, convergence was about an order of magnitude faster, requiring only tens of stimuli to achieve reasonable estimates. Inclusion of an informative prior provided no discernible advantage to the estimator as configured. The MLCSF exhibits performance characteristics on par with state-of-the-art CSF estimators and therefore should be explored further to uncover its full potential.
papers.authors: D. Marticorena, Q. W. Wong, J. Browning, K. Wilbur, S. Jayakumar, P. Davey, A. Seitz, J. Gardner, D. Barbour

papers.title: Scotoma awareness: a novel protocol to induce fast development of a Preferred retinal locus (PRL) in patients with central vision loss
papers.authors: Marcello Maniglia, Jason Vice, Kristina M. Visscher, A. Seitz

papers.title: Gamified spatial release from masking and relationships with self-reported auditory difficulties
papers.abstract: Many individuals with and without hearing loss, including those with a history of traumatic brain injury (TBI), often report difficulties understanding speech in noise that are not well predicted by common behavioral measures. Recent work in the gamification of behavioral auditory tasks has led to the development of measures that aim to better mimic the demands of real-world auditory environments through the use of video game features that engage and motivate the user. This study examined the effects of gamification on a spatial release from masking (SRM) task in 37 adults who ranged in age, hearing sensitivity, and history of TBI. Participants completed a gamified and non-gamified version of the SRM task on an iPad using the Portable Automatic Rapid Testing (PART) application. Regression models were used to assess whether gamification had an effect on SRM and whether participant age, hearing sensitivity, or history of TBI differentially impacted results. This study was also designed to determine whether performance on the gamified SRM task was predictive of self-reported auditory difficulties that were measured using three hearing health questionnaires. Results of this work will have important implications for the development of clinically useful gamified tasks that better replicate real-world auditory environments. [R01DC018166, VA CDA1 RX003187]
papers.venue: Journal of the Acoustical Society of America
papers.authors: Tess K. Koerner, Karen Garcia, L. Charney, Vanja Pešić, Nicole Dean, Laura Coco, William J. Bologna, G. C. Stecker, A. Seitz, F. Gallun

papers.title: Nonparametric Bayesian Estimation of Contrast Sensitivity Functions
papers.authors: D. Barbour, D. Marticorena, Shohaib Shaffiey, Quinn Wai Wong, K. Wilbur, S. Jayakumar, P. Davey, Jacob R Gardner, A. Seitz

papers.title: Improving comparability across cognitive training trials for brain aging: A focus on interoperability
papers.abstract: Cognitive training may promote healthy brain aging and prevent dementia, but results from individual studies are inconsistent. There are disagreements on how to evaluate cognitive training interventions between clinical and basic scientists. Individual labs typically create their own assessment and training materials, leading to difficulties reproducing methods. Here, we advocate for improved interoperability: the exchange and cooperative development of a consensus for cognitive training design, analysis, and result interpretation. We outline five guiding principles for improving interoperability: (i) design interoperability, developing standard design and analysis models; (ii) material interoperability, promoting sharing of materials; (iii) interoperability incentives; (iv) privacy and security norms, ensuring adherence to accepted ethical standards; and (v) interpretability prioritization, encouraging a shared focus on neurobiological mechanisms to improve clinical relevance. Improving interoperability will allow us to develop scientifically optimized, clinically useful cognitive training programs to slow/prevent brain aging.
papers.authors: Adam Turnbull, A. Seitz, F. Lin

0007.name: Adam Reeves
0007.bio: Adam Reeves is a Professor Emeritus of Psychology at Northeastern University whose research examines the mechanisms of human visual perception, including color constancy, iconic memory, and stereoscopic depth. Reeves utilizes psychophysical methodologies and computational modeling to study how visual attention modulates perception and how the brain processes phenomena such as synesthesia and crowding. Their recent work focuses on the short-term retention of depth and the effects of environmental lighting conditions on visual adaptation and phenomenal contrast.
0007.research_direction: Dr. Reeves's recent work explores a diverse array of psychophysical and computational questions across early visual processing and higher-order perception. They have recently been examining color and luminance mechanisms, critically evaluating the methodological assumptions of common color constancy metrics and investigating how extreme light adaptation modulates subjective contrast and monocular depth cues. In the domains of spatial and quantitative vision, their research explores how the spatial extent and feature-selective tuning of peripheral crowding change during transient shifts of attention, while also modeling whether human numerosity estimation is fundamentally driven by early-stage integrated contrast energy rather than discrete object counting. Additionally, they are investigating the boundary between sensory imagery and social cognition by studying a rare form of synesthesia to determine how perceived "people-colors" map onto high-level personality traits.

papers.title: Five problems with color constancy metrics: discussion
papers.abstract: This critical discussion evaluates pervasive methodological deficiencies in current color constancy summary statistics. Five specific problematic areas are identified: the choice of metric (Brunswick ratio versus Color Constancy Index), the presumed independence of chromaticity from luminance, the influence of random matching behaviors on resulting indices, constraints imposed by the bounded nature of color space, and the significant cognitive reliance on memory within asymmetric matching paradigms. Reeves argues that typical indices frequently conflate illuminant estimation with compensation efficiency, which complicates the isolation of the underlying neural constancy mechanisms.
papers.venue: Journal of the Optical Society of America A
papers.authors: Adam Reeves

papers.title: Environmental Lighting Conditions, Phenomenal Contrast, and the Conscious Perception of Near and Far
papers.abstract: This study examines how light adaptation levels—ranging across darkness, daylight, and rod-saturated bright light—modulate subjective contrast, assimilation, and monocular depth perception in achromatic ON–OFF pathways. Psychophysical experiments employing computer-controlled two-alternative forced-choice (2AFC) procedures revealed that lighting conditions significantly alter the effectiveness of luminance contrast as a depth cue. Notably, physically brighter pattern regions were no longer consistently perceived as nearer under extreme bright light or daylight adaptation, suggesting that environmental lighting impacts the entire hierarchy of brain processing from the distal retina to higher-level cortical integration for 3D scenic interpretation.
papers.authors: Birgitta Dresp-Langley, Adam J. Reeves

papers.title: Synesthetic Colors Associated with Personality
papers.abstract: The stability and psychological associations of 'people-colors' were investigated in a rare synesthete (DR) through controlled trials with strangers viewed in silence or during brief verbal interactions. Utilizing the ten-item personality inventory (TIPI), the study found that DR’s synesthetic hues were robust over time and highly correlated with the Extraversion dimension (r = 0.74), while correlations with other Big Five traits remained weak. These findings imply that synesthetic concurrents can be shaped by social learning and high-level personality attributions, demonstrating a complex interplay between sensory imagery and social cognition.
papers.authors: Catherine Craver-Lemley, Caroline Dillon, Amanda McGraw, Adam Reeves

papers.title: Crowding expands and is less sensitive to target-flanker differences during a shift of visual attention
papers.abstract: This research explores the spatial dynamics of peripheral visual crowding during transient shifts of spatial attention. By utilizing orientation discrimination of Gabor targets flanked by varied distractors, the study demonstrates that the spatial extent of the crowding zone significantly expands during the attentional shift. Furthermore, the typical feature-based tuning—whereby crowding is reduced by target-flanker dissimilarity—is markedly attenuated. These results indicate a substantial reduction in spatial resolution and a failure of feature-selective suppression during the active relocation of the attentional focus across the visual field.
papers.authors: Jeff Nador, Adam Reeves

papers.title: Numerosity depends on normalized contrast energy: Review and square-root law model
papers.abstract: Perceived numerosity is proposed to be a function of integrated contrast energy (CE) rather than discrete item counts. This paper introduces a square-root law model of normalized CE to explain systematic biases in human number estimation. The model demonstrates that numerosity estimation is primarily driven by the square root of CE, normalized by contrast amplitude, which accounts for the 'weak-outnumber-strong' (WOS) illusion and other contrast-dependent distortions. The findings suggest that early-stage energy-based filters in the visual system provide the primary input for numerosity computation before higher-level object segmentation occur.
papers.authors: Quan Lei, Adam Reeves

0008.name: Adam S Greenberg
0008.lab_name: Sensory Neuroscience, Attention, & Perception Laboratory (SNAP Lab)
0008.bio: Adam S. Greenberg is an Associate Professor in the Joint Department of Biomedical Engineering at the Medical College of Wisconsin and Marquette University and directs the Sensory Neuroscience, Attention, & Perception (SNAP) Laboratory. Greenberg’s research investigates the neural mechanisms of attentional control and object perception using a multi-modal approach that includes functional MRI, psychophysics, and computational modeling. Their work examines how behavioral goals influence sensory processing in both visual and auditory systems, focusing on the sources and targets of attentional selection. Additionally, Greenberg explores the identification of neurological biomarkers for cognitive decline resulting from aging, hearing loss, and clinical interventions such as chemotherapy.
0008.research_direction: Dr. Greenberg’s recent work explores the neural mechanisms of attentional selection and object perception across multiple modalities. Investigating the architecture of these cognitive systems, they have recently been asking whether the "spotlight" of attention operates as a universal, amodal computation across diverse sensory and motor topographic brain maps. Within the visual domain, their research employs fMRI and psychophysics to examine object-based attention—specifically shift direction anisotropy—to understand how the deployment of spatial attention is fundamentally constrained by horizontal and vertical visual field meridians. Expanding beyond vision, their recent work also investigates the cortical networks responsible for auditory scene analysis, alongside clinically oriented, cross-modal research assessing how hearing loss and cochlear implants impact broader spatial and temporal attentional networks in older adults.

papers.title: Impact of Hearing Loss and Cochlear Implantation on Attentional Selection in Older Adults
papers.abstract: This study employed the non-auditory, visual Attentional Network Test (ANT) to evaluate the efficiency of the three-network model of attention—comprising alerting, orienting, and executive control—in geriatric populations across three groups: normal hearing (NH) controls, cochlear implant (CI) candidates, and established CI users. The investigation tested the information degradation hypothesis, specifically examining whether auditory rehabilitation via CI facilitates the release of higher-order cognitive resources to restore attentional selection performance to levels comparable with NH individuals. Results demonstrated that older adults with hearing loss utilized spatial orienting cues more extensively while exhibiting a marked deficit in the utilization of temporal alerting cues relative to controls. No significant differences in executive control were identified among groups, and the transition from candidate to CI user did not yield a significant restoration of attentional selection dynamics within the observed timeframe (6–12 months post-activation).
papers.authors: Michael S. Harris, Gennadiy Gurariy, Shannon Walsh, Kristin Kozlowski, Samiah Ziadeh, Sarah Mleziva, Adam S. Greenberg

papers.title: Anisotropic object-based shifts of attention arise from unequal influences of visual field meridians on neural attention gradients
papers.abstract: The neural mechanisms underlying the object-based shift direction anisotropy (SDA)—a behavioral phenomenon where horizontal attention reorienting within an object is more efficient than vertical reorienting—were investigated using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI). BOLD signals were measured in retinotopic visual cortex as participants shifted attention between target locations within an L-shaped object that crossed visual field meridians. The study evaluated the hypothesis that the SDA originates from the differential partitioning of attentional resources by horizontal and vertical meridian boundaries. Experimental findings revealed that the SDA is primarily generated when the vertical meridian acts as a functional barrier to the spread of object-based attention, particularly when the object vertex is positioned in the upper-left quadrant. These data suggest that the geometry of neural attention gradients is fundamentally constrained by the topographic organization of visual field meridians.
papers.authors: David H. Hughes, Adam J. Barnas, Adam S. Greenberg

papers.title: Are neuronal mechanisms of attention universal across human sensory and motor brain maps?
papers.abstract: This review investigates whether a singular, universal neural mechanism for attentional selection is implemented consistently across the diverse topographic maps of the human sensory and motor systems. The authors introduce a methodological framework based on population attentional receptive fields (pARFs) to enable a quantitative, voxel-wise comparison of attentional mechanisms across different modalities. By reviewing existing literature on visual, auditory, and motor attention, the paper explores the interaction between top-down frontoparietal control networks and local cortical representations. The central inquiry focuses on whether the 'spotlight' of attention is an amodal computational operation applied uniformly to any available map or if selection mechanisms are intrinsically specialized and distinct for each sensory and motor domain.
papers.authors: Edgar A. DeYoe, Wendy Huddleston, Adam S. Greenberg

papers.title: The object-based shift direction anisotropy is modulated by the horizontal visual field meridian
papers.abstract: This research explored the behavioral constraints governing the reallocation of object-based attention (OBA), specifically focusing on the shift direction anisotropy (SDA), where horizontal shifts between object parts are significantly faster than vertical shifts. Through a series of psychophysical experiments involving variations in target location and object orientation, the study investigated whether the SDA is dependent on the visual field meridians. Results indicated that the SDA magnitude is significantly modulated by the horizontal meridian, with shifts crossing this boundary showing distinct efficiency profiles compared to those that do not. Furthermore, manipulating the local feature contrast of the horizontal meridian altered the SDA, providing evidence that the efficiency of object-based attentional deployment is contingent upon the structural and perceptual salience of visual field boundaries.
papers.authors: Adam J. Barnas, Adam S. Greenberg

papers.title: Neuroimaging evidence for the direct role of auditory scene analysis in object perception
papers.abstract: The neural substrates mediating Auditory Scene Analysis (ASA) and the formation of auditory objects were examined using fMRI and Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA). Participants performed musicality judgments on stochastic pure-tone sequences and manipulated versions where low-level acoustic features (timbre and amplitude) were altered to disrupt grouping. RSA was applied to ROI-based functional profiles to correlate neural patterns with behavioral musicality ratings and low-level feature models. The analysis identified two partially overlapping networks: a low-level ASA network near the primary auditory cortex that processed acoustic feature changes, and a high-level perceptual network, primarily within the right intraparietal sulcus (IPS), that correlated with the subjective experience of musicality. These findings provide evidence for the role of the right IPS in transforming acoustic signals into stable auditory objects based on high-level organizational principles.
papers.authors: Gennadiy Gurariy, Richard Randall, Adam S. Greenberg

0009.name: Adam W. Kiefer
0009.institution: University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill
0009.department: Department of Exercise and Sport Science
0009.lab_name: Simulation, Training, Analytics and Rehabilitation (STAR) Heel Performance Laboratory
0009.bio: Adam W. Kiefer is an Assistant Professor at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, where Kiefer co-directs the STAR Heel Performance Laboratory and holds an appointment in the Human Movement Science Curriculum. Kiefer’s research applies a complex systems approach to sports performance and injury prevention by integrating immersive technologies like virtual reality and mobile eye-tracking with artificial intelligence to model human behavior. Kiefer focuses on the digital transformation of athletic training, utilizing nonlinear dynamics and machine learning to analyze the 'vision-in-action' loop and develop personalized interventions for elite athletes and clinical populations. This work involves the automation of perceptual-cognitive data analysis for application within the fields of digital health and behavioral dynamics.
0009.research_direction: Dr. Kiefer’s recent work explores human motor control and visuomotor behavior through the lens of complex dynamical systems, particularly in naturalistic athletic environments. They have recently been investigating "vision-in-action" using mobile eye-tracking and virtual reality, applying explainable machine learning to gaze metrics—such as the quiet eye period—to predict basketball shot outcomes and design gaze-contingent training platforms. Beyond visual control, their research also examines how movement coordination adapts to external constraints, utilizing nonlinear metrics to track lower-limb kinematics under heavy physical loads and to map how team rowing synchronization shifts under varying doses of temporal stress. Ultimately, their work combines ecological validity with system-level modeling to identify dynamic markers of skill acquisition, athletic resilience, and injury susceptibility.

papers.title: Beyond Body Weight: The Influence of Artificial Load on Lower-Limb Joint-Specific Landing Kinematics and Coordination Dynamics
papers.abstract: This investigation characterizes the influence of artificial mass increments on lower-extremity kinematic profiles and coordination dynamics during jump-landing tasks. Grounded in a complex adaptive systems framework, the study evaluates joint-specific kinematics and inter-segmental coordination patterns (via vector coding or analogous metrics) under varying load conditions. The researchers assess how the addition of weighted vests modulates attractor states and landing variability, identifying potential biomechanical markers of reduced system flexibility and increased injury susceptibility in high-load operational or athletic contexts. Findings support transition from reductionist component analysis to dynamic system-level modeling for quantifying athlete and warfighter resiliency.
papers.venue: Nonlinear Dynamics, Psychology, and Life Sciences
papers.authors: Dominic Willoughby, Jeffrey A. Turner, Darin A. Padua, Adam W. Kiefer

papers.title: The Utility of Head-Mounted Eye Gaze Tracking for Vision-in-Action Assessments to Enhance Skill Acquisition and Sport Performance: A Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, and Threats Analysis
papers.abstract: This paper provides a technical SWOT (Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, and Threats) analysis of head-mounted eye-tracking systems for in situ assessments of vision-in-action. The analysis highlights the enhanced ecological validity afforded by recording gaze behavior within natural performance environments compared to laboratory settings. Conversely, the authors detail technical constraints including diminished tracking fidelity resulting from eye morphology or physiological interference (e.g., squinting, lens fogging). The discussion outlines opportunities for personalized skill acquisition through gaze-contingent feedback and identifies significant threats posed by high data-processing latencies and the intensive requirements for manual gaze-motor synchronization and video stream coding.
papers.venue: Journal of Motor Learning and Development
papers.authors: Nikki Aitcheson-Huehn, Adam W. Kiefer

papers.title: Predicting Basketball Shot Outcome From Visuomotor Control Data Using Explainable Machine Learning
papers.abstract: This study evaluates the predictive utility of visuomotor control variables in determining basketball shot outcomes (make vs. miss) through explainable machine learning models. Using data from twelve athletes wearing mobile eye-tracking glasses during 200 shots from six locations, the authors trained and tested standard and conditional inference decision trees and random forest classifiers. Eight features were modeled, including shot location, arm extension timing, and quiet eye (QE) metrics (onset, offset, and duration). The models successfully predicted makers and misses with moderate-to-high accuracy, identifying relative QE duration as the most influential feature, with a success threshold identified at relative durations exceeding 18.4%.
papers.venue: Journal of Sport and Exercise Psychology
papers.authors: Nikki Aitcheson-Huehn, Ryan MacPherson, Derek Panchuk, Adam W. Kiefer

papers.title: Integration of Eye-Tracking Technology in Virtual Reality Applications for Basketball Training: A Mixed Methods Needs Assessment
papers.abstract: Applying a user-centered mixed-methods design, this study identifies and prioritizes design requirements for the integration of eye-tracking (ET) within virtual reality (VR) basketball training platforms. The researchers utilized semi-structured interviews and focus groups with coaching experts to inform a requirements questionnaire administered to student-athletes. The resulting integrated framework defines six critical domains for system development: immersive technical-tactical visualization, interactive decision-making scenarios, gaze-contingent performance indicators, real-time visual feedback, learning support functionality, and implementation readiness. The study establishes a foundational design blueprint for future high-fidelity VR-ET prototypes that support skill acquisition in team sports.
papers.venue: Journal of Coaching and Sports Science
papers.authors: Nikki Aitcheson-Huehn, Adam W. Kiefer

papers.title: How does motor performance change with increasing stress doses? A tutorial on dose-response profiles applied to crew rowing
papers.abstract: This tutorial operationalizes the biological framework of hormesis to model the relationship between stress dosage and human motor performance. Using crew rowing as an experimental exemplar, the authors model how inter-agent coordination and system-level dynamics respond to varying doses of temporal stress (defined by race target times). The paper provides a methodological roadmap for calculating stress parameters a priori and utilizing nonlinear metrics to identify U-shaped or inverted J-shaped dose-response profiles. The analysis demonstrates how moderate stressors facilitate the emergence of stable coordination patterns (eustress), whereas excessive stress magnitudes induce system-level phase transitions toward coordination breakdown (distress), offering a framework for optimizing athletic resilience training.
papers.authors: Yannick Hill, Laura S. Cuijpers, Paula L. Silva, Ruud den Hartigh, Adam W. Kiefer

0011.name: Adrian G. Palacios
0011.department: Instituto de Neurociencia, Facultad de Ciencias
0011.bio: Adrian G. Palacios is a Full Professor at the Universidad de Valparaíso and a principal investigator at the Centro Interdisciplinario de Neurociencia de Valparaíso (CINV). Palacios utilizes multielectrode electrophysiology and patch-clamp techniques to investigate retinal physiology and the mechanisms of the neural code. Their research examines the intersection of sensory biology and neurodegeneration, specifically how aging and Alzheimer’s disease affect synaptic plasticity and visual processing in transgenic and natural models. Additionally, Palacios incorporates computational modeling and complexity science to analyze neuronal population dynamics and inform the development of gene-based therapeutic interventions for nervous system repair.
0011.research_direction: Dr. Palacios’s recent work investigates the cellular and network-level mechanisms underlying neurodegeneration, with a particular focus on how aging and Alzheimer’s disease alter synaptic stability and neural circuitry. To identify accessible biomarkers for cognitive decline, they have recently been utilizing multielectrode arrays and micro-electroretinography to measure retinal ganglion cell output and signal complexity in transgenic disease models. Alongside this experimental work, their research explores novel computational clustering methods for detecting synchronous neuronal ensembles to better understand population coding and functional units in early visual processing. Additionally, they are examining deeper cognitive pathways by evaluating hippocampal GABAergic integrity in aging rodents and testing targeted gene therapies—specifically those modulating the unfolded protein response via XBP1 transcription factors—to preserve synaptic plasticity and mitigate endoplasmic reticulum stress.

papers.title: Cognitive Resilience in Aging Degus is Linked to CA3 Hippocampal GABAergic Integrity
papers.abstract: Maintaining cognitive function throughout the aging process is a critical neuroscientific challenge. This study utilizes the Octodon degus, a long-lived rodent model of sporadic Alzheimer’s disease, to investigate the relationship between hippocampal circuitry and cognitive trajectory. Using behavioral paradigms (Novel Object Recognition, Open Field, and Burrowing Test) alongside multielectrode array (MEA) electrophysiology, we categorized aged animals into groups with preserved (Good Burrowers, GB) versus impaired (Bad Burrowers, BB) cognition. We found that GB animals exhibited robust hippocampal activity, particularly within the CA3 region, a critical locus for pattern completion and memory encoding. In contrast, BB individuals showed significant reductions in spontaneous activity and synchronized firing. Pharmacological disinhibition of GABAergic systems revealed that preserved inhibitory tone in CA3 is fundamental for network stability and disinhibition-induced recruitment of recurrent excitatory circuits. These results demonstrate that the integrity of the hippocampal GABAergic system, specifically in the CA3 hub, is a primary determinant of cognitive resilience in natural aging.
papers.authors: Cristóbal Ibaceta-González, David Neira, Nicolás M. Ardiles, Nicol Baeza-Araya, Alfredo Kirkwood, Pablo Moya, Adrián G. Palacios

papers.title: XBP1s as a Therapeutic Target to Preserve Retinal Function During Aging and Neurodegeneration
papers.abstract: The loss of physiological complexity and multiscale coordination is a recognized hallmark of neurodegenerative diseases. This research investigates the neuroprotective potential of the unfolded protein response (UPR) transcription factor XBP1s in maintaining retinal integrity during aging and Alzheimer’s-related pathology. We utilized micro-electroretinography with multielectrode arrays (MEAs) to record retinal output in response to chirp and white noise stimuli across wild-type (WT), TgXBP1s, 5xFAD, and TgXBP1s/5xFAD mouse models. Retinal signal dynamics were quantified using multiscale entropy (MSE) and stimulus-response wavelet coherence (Wcoh). Findings revealed that while WT and 5xFAD mice showed significant age-related declines in signal complexity and coherence, sustained neuronal XBP1s expression effectively preserved these electrophysiological markers in adult mice. These results position XBP1s as a viable therapeutic target for protecting neural circuitry and support the use of noninvasive retinal complexity measures as scalable biomarkers for evaluating neuroprotective efficacy.
papers.authors: Leonel E. Medina, Joel Barría, Max Chacón, Maximiliano Orellana, Daniela Ponce, David Neira, Francisco Miqueles, Claudia Duran-Aniotz, Joaquín Araya-Arriagada, Bruno Cerda, Sergio T. Ferreira, Claudio Hetz, Adrian G. Palacios

papers.title: A General and Accurate Method for Neuronal Ensemble Detection in Spiking Neural Networks
papers.abstract: This study introduces an automated and scalable methodology for identifying neuronal ensembles within large populations of spiking neurons. The approach leverages similarity-based clustering of population activity vectors to detect synchronous activation patterns while allowing individual neurons to participate in multiple overlapping ensembles. The method minimizes the need for extensive parameter tuning and enhances computational efficiency relative to previous iterations. We validated the tool using synthetic spike trains across varied simulation parameters and applied it to experimental data derived from multielectrode array (MEA) recordings of retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) under simple visual stimulation. Analysis of the RGC data revealed structured, stimuli-evoked ensembles intermixed with spontaneous and sporadic activities, supporting the hypothesis that early visual system processing is organized into distinct functional units. A graphical user interface (GUI) is provided to facilitate broader community application for analyzing high-dimensional neural recordings.
papers.authors: Rubén Herzog-Amunátegui, Soraya Mora, Garance Prada, Jean-Gabriel Minonzio, Maria Jose Escobar, Rodrigo Cofre, Adrián G. Palacios

papers.title: Synaptic Function and Dysfunction: New Frontiers in CNS Disorders
papers.abstract: Central nervous system (CNS) disorders, including Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s, and multiple sclerosis, are characterized by diverse etiologies but share common themes of synaptic failure and impaired neural plasticity. This work reviews recent advances in understanding how synaptic communication, encompassing both spontaneous and action potential-evoked neurotransmission, is compromised in neurodegenerative and neurodevelopmental contexts. We explore the roles of amyloid-beta aggregation and tau hyperphosphorylation in disrupting the proteostasis network, mitochondrial health, and ionic homeostasis, which collectively lead to synaptic scaling imbalances and neuronal loss. Particular emphasis is placed on the regulatory role of the unfolded protein response (UPR) and transcription factors like XBP1 in mitigating ER stress. We propose that restoring neural plasticity through interventions such as environmental enrichment and targeted gene therapies is essential for functional recovery, moving beyond symptomatic treatments toward addressing fundamental underlying pathologies.
papers.authors: Feyza Şule Aslan, Daymara Mercerón-Martínez, Cristóbal Ibaceta-González, Claudia Salazar, Adrian G. Palacios

papers.title: Optimized adeno-associated vector to deliver the unfolded protein response transcription factor XBP1s into the hippocampus ameliorates Alzheimer's disease features in mouse models
papers.abstract: Endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress and subsequent proteostasis impairment are hallmarks of Alzheimer's disease (AD). This study reports the development and optimization of an adeno-associated virus (AAV) vector specifically designed to deliver the active form of the transcription factor XBP1 (XBP1s) to hippocampal neurons. We tested this gene therapy approach in transgenic mouse models of AD, assessing its impact on disease-related phenotypes. Results demonstrate that hippocampal XBP1s overexpression significantly enhances synaptic function and resilience, mitigating Aβ-induced cognitive deficits. Biochemical analysis confirms that the vector effectively engages the UPR signaling pathway, improving protein folding capacity and reducing toxic aggregate accumulation. This optimized AAV-XBP1s construct represents a promising gene therapy strategy to bolster the brain's buffering capacity against neurodegeneration, potentially slowing the clinical progression of Alzheimer's disease.
papers.authors: Claudio Hetz, Mei Li Diaz, Diego Arriagada, Giovanni Tamburini, Natalia Poblete, Alvaro Ardiles, David Neira, Denisse Sepulveda, Gabriela Martinez, Els Henckaerts, Julie Tordo, Sergio T. Ferreira, Adrian G. Palacios

0012.name: Adrian Nestor
0012.bio: Adrian Nestor is an Associate Professor at the University of Toronto Scarborough and the director of the Neurocomputational Vision Lab. Their research investigates the neural mechanisms of face and object recognition by integrating neuroimaging techniques, such as fMRI and EEG, with computational modeling and machine learning. Nestor conducts work in neural decoding and image reconstruction, developing algorithms to visualize mental representations from brain activity. Their research program examines the relationship between physical image properties and the structural organization of neural representations within the high-level visual cortex.
0012.research_direction: Dr. Nestor has recently been combining high-density EEG decoding and GAN-based image reconstruction to investigate the visual and neural templates underlying human face perception. Their recent work explores how dynamic facial expressions are encoded in the brain—specifically looking for continuous, anticipatory neural dynamics—and probes how internal mental models of emotion are influenced by both mnemonic recall and individual personality traits. Additionally, they are investigating the representational structure of the Other-Race Effect, utilizing computational tools to visualize and quantify the distinct visual distortions and temporal processing differences between same- and other-race faces. Finally, Dr. Nestor's research delves into mental representations of the self, decoupling objective appearance from subjective beliefs to understand the cognitive biases inherent in how we visualize our own faces.

papers.title: Evidence for dimensional representations and anticipatory dynamics in facial expression perception
papers.abstract: This investigation leverages high-density electroencephalography (EEG) and behavioral similarity measures to elucidate the neurocomputational architecture subserving the processing of dynamic facial expressions. Utilizing multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) and spatiotemporal image reconstruction, the study interrogates whether neural representations align with discrete emotion categories or continuous dimensions of valence and arousal. Findings indicate that multidimensional information is encoded with high temporal precision, manifesting distinct anticipatory dynamics in which neural states proactively represent upcoming transitions in expressive content. These results suggest a predictive, dimensional framework for the cortical representation of dynamic socio-emotional signals.
papers.authors: Tyler Roberts, Yong Zhong Liang, Gerald C. Cupchik, Jonathan S. Cant, Adrian Nestor

papers.title: Unraveling other-race face perception with GAN-based image reconstruction
papers.abstract: The current research employs a GAN-based image reconstruction framework, specifically utilizing StyleGAN2, to investigate the representational underpinnings of the Other-Race Effect (ORE). By projecting behavioral similarity ratings of same-race and other-race faces into a disentangled latent space, the authors synthesized high-fidelity visualizations of internal face templates. The study identifies a significant deficit in the visual fidelity of other-race representations and uncovers a systematic age bias, wherein reconstructed faces from other-race categories are perceived as significantly younger than the target stimuli. This methodology establishes a novel computational tool for quantifying the visual content of perceptual biases within the human face space.
papers.authors: Moaz Shoura, Dirk B. Walther, Adrian Nestor

papers.title: Revealing the neural representations underlying other-race face perception
papers.abstract: This study utilizes EEG-based neural decoding and image reconstruction to probe the neural and representational structure of the other-race effect (ORE) in East Asian and Caucasian cohorts. By analyzing temporally-cumulative occipitotemporal signals, the researchers demonstrate that within-race face decoding significantly outperforms between-race decoding, mirroring behavioral performance indices of ORE. The application of neural-based image reconstruction successfully recovered the specific visual features of same-race versus other-race representations, highlighting the relative homogeneity and reduced discriminability of the latter. The temporal analysis reveals an extensive window of significance (130–600 ms) during which the neural representation of racial and identity-based information is dynamically processed.
papers.authors: Moaz Shoura, Yong Z. Liang, Marco A. Sama, Arijit De, Adrian Nestor

papers.title: Perception and memory-based representations of facial emotions: Associations with personality functioning, affective states and recognition abilities
papers.abstract: This work explores the psychological and cognitive determinants of internal facial emotion representations using a behaviorally-driven image reconstruction paradigm. The study characterizes the visual structure of emotional templates derived from both online perception and mnemonic recall. By relating reconstruction fidelity to psychometric indices, the authors demonstrate that internal models of emotion are significantly modulated by individual differences in personality functioning, particularly borderline personality traits, and transient affective states. These results suggest that social-emotional representations in the human brain are not solely driven by sensory input but are dynamically shaped by stable cognitive traits and fluctuating psychological contexts.
papers.authors: Chi-Hsun Chang, Nataliya Drobotenko, Anthony C. Ruocco, Andy C.H. Lee, Adrian Nestor

papers.title: The Self as an Image: Appearance and Belief in Visual Representations of One's Own Face
papers.abstract: Self-face representations are examined to determine their visual structure and fidelity using a combination of psychophysical similarity judgments and StyleGAN2-based computational modeling. The study aims to decouple the relative contributions of objective appearance and subjective self-beliefs in the formation of mental self-images. By reconstructing self-face percepts from both perceptual and memory-based data, the investigation reveals significant levels of visual accuracy and consistency across different representational formats. Furthermore, it identifies specific visual distortions in self-images that correlate with self-attractiveness ratings and other self-referential traits, providing a computational framework for understanding the cognitive biases inherent in self-perception.
papers.authors: Arijit De, Shawn Liu, Kinkini Monaragala, Moaz Shoura, William A. Cunningham, Adrian Nestor

0013.name: Aihua Chen
0013.department: Institute of Brain Functional Genomics, School of Life Sciences
0013.bio: Aihua Chen is a Professor at East China Normal University and heads the Laboratory of Sensation and Action within the Institute of Brain Functional Genomics. Chen’s research investigates the neural mechanisms of multisensory integration, specifically how visual and vestibular cues combine to support self-motion perception and spatial navigation. Through single-unit electrophysiological recordings in macaque monkeys and 3D virtual reality behavioral tasks, they examine the functional properties of cortical regions including the MSTd, VPS, and STPp. Chen’s work also explores the principles of multisensory decision-making, the impact of stimulus history on perception (serial dependence), and the hierarchical control of learned saccade sequences in the prefrontal and parietal cortices.
0013.research_direction: Dr. Chen has recently been investigating the neural computations underlying multisensory perception, 3D vision, and oculomotor control in the primate brain. Using macaque electrophysiology, causal manipulations, and computational modeling, their recent work explores how cortical areas like VIP and VPS integrate optic flow with vestibular signals or static form cues to optimize self-motion and heading estimates. They are also examining how higher-level visual regions represent 3D spatial geometry, specifically investigating neural tuning to surface slant and tilt defined by binocular disparity. Furthermore, their research probes the motor domain by dissecting the hierarchical roles of the fronto-parietal network—namely the DLPFC and LIP—in the initiation and execution of learned saccade sequences.

papers.title: Distinct role of primate DLPFC and LIP in hierarchical control of learned saccade sequences
papers.abstract: This study characterizes the hierarchical neurocomputational architecture of learned saccade sequences in macaque monkeys, delineating functional specializations between the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) and lateral intraparietal cortex (LIP). Utilizing extracellular single-unit recordings during the execution of heterogeneous oculomotor sequences, the authors demonstrate that DLPFC neurons predominantly encode sequence-level initiation signals, while LIP neurons facilitate transitions at the subsequence level. Causal manipulations via microstimulation and reversible pharmacological inactivation reveal that DLPFC disruption selectively increases sequence initiation latency, whereas LIP interference significantly impairs execution accuracy and subsequence switching, establishing afronto-parietal axis for motor hierarchy management.
papers.authors: Qingjun Wang, Binchao Shi, Jing Jia, Jingyu Hu, Haoran Li, Xin Jin, Aihua Chen

papers.title: The visual representation of 3D orientation in macaque areas STPp and VPS
papers.abstract: Employing binocularly disparate random dot stereograms to simulate three-dimensional (3D) planar orientations defined by slant and tilt, this research investigates the neural representation of 3D spatial geometry in the macaque superior temporal polysensory (STPp) and visual posterior sylvian (VPS) areas. Electrophysiological results indicate that STPp neurons maintain invariant tuning for surface orientation irrespective of motion-induced depth cues, supporting a stable perceptual coordinate system. Conversely, VPS neurons exhibit dynamic response dependencies between slant, tilt, and disparity parameters, suggesting that VPS processes 3D spatial information within a fluid, multisensory-integrated framework heavily influenced by optic flow inputs.
papers.authors: Rong Wang, Bin Zhao, Aihua Chen

papers.title: Optimizing self-motion perception: a control theory perspective on vestibular–visual integration and adaptive mechanisms
papers.abstract: Synthesizing behavioral, neurophysiological, and computational findings from primate research, this review examines the optimization strategies employed by the brain to construct accurate self-motion representations from optic flow and vestibular inputs. Utilizing a control-theory framework, the authors discuss the neural implementation of reliability-weighted cue integration, non-linear divisive normalization, and multisensory plasticity. The discussion focuses on how cortical networks in areas such as MSTd, PIVC, and VIP dynamically recalibrate to minimize sensory conflict, providing a comprehensive theoretical model for spatial navigation and the potential pathophysiology of sensory integration disorders.
papers.authors: Fu Zeng, Rong Wang, Aihua Chen

papers.title: The influence of form on motion signal processing in the ventral intraparietal area of macaque monkeys
papers.abstract: This study explores the neural interaction between global form cues, presented as Glass patterns, and motion signals within the macaque ventral intraparietal area (VIP) during heading perception. Through single-unit recordings in response to motion-only, form-only, and bimodal stimuli, the authors find that VIP neurons—while lacking intrinsic orientation tuning to static form—exhibit significantly modulated heading sensitivity when form and motion signals are combined with spatial offsets. This integration follows distinct temporal dynamics, where form-driven modulation becomes most robust during the late phase of stimulation (1000–2000 ms), indicating that form information provides a delayed constraint to refine heading estimates derived from optic flow.
papers.authors: Lingqi Kong, Fu Zeng, Yingying Zhang, Li Li, Aihua Chen

papers.title: The computational rules of cross-modality suppression in the visual posterior sylvian area (VPS)
papers.abstract: Using macaque neurophysiology and computational modeling, the authors investigate bimodal integration in the visual posterior sylvian area (VPS) during combined visual (optic flow) and vestibular translation. The study identifies robust cross-modality suppression in VPS neurons, where bimodal responses are subadditive compared to unisensory responses. By applying a divisive normalization framework, the authors demonstrate that this suppression follows specific non-linear computational rules that differ from the integration patterns in the dorsal medial superior temporal area (MSTd). The findings suggest that VPS prioritizes specific sensory channels via competitive normalization to maintain dynamic range or avoid redundancy during self-motion processing.
papers.authors: Bin Zhao, Rong Wang, Zhihua Zhu, Qianli Yang, Aihua Chen

0017.name: Alan Stocker
0017.bio: Alan A. Stocker is a Professor of Psychology at the University of Pennsylvania who investigates the computational principles of human visual perception and decision-making. Stocker’s laboratory uses psychophysical experiments and probabilistic modeling to study how sensory information is integrated with prior beliefs and environmental statistics. Stocker focuses on the distinction between objective expectations shaped by the natural environment and subjective expectations influenced by previous perceptual choices. Their work characterizes the brain as an optimal inference engine, developing quantitative models that explain the relationships between perceptual bias and discriminability.
0017.research_direction: Dr. Stocker has recently been investigating how the visual system optimizes sensory encoding and inference to navigate statistically complex environments. Their recent work explores a wide array of perceptual phenomena—including the tilt illusion, sensory adaptation, ensemble perception, and optic flow heading—using a combination of psychophysics, functional MRI, and predictive neural networks. Specifically, they are studying how neural coding resources are dynamically reallocated in response to recent stimulus histories, spatial contexts, and ensemble statistics, and whether these adaptive shifts can be captured by efficient Bayesian observer models. Furthermore, they are examining how latent sensory representations are jointly processed with high-level categorical identities during holistic inference, and how these optimal percepts map onto motor actions to produce observed behavioral biases.

papers.title: A linear perception-action mapping accounts for response range-dependent biases in heading estimation from optic flow
papers.abstract: This study addresses the systematic variability in human heading estimation biases observed across prior psychophysical research. The authors introduce a normative framework that extends the efficient Bayesian observer model by incorporating a post-perceptual, linear perception-action mapping. In this model, the latent perceptual estimate is scaled by a factor that depends monotonically on the stimulus response range available to the observer. By fitting the model to experimental data across various cursor movement ranges, the researchers demonstrate that conflicting bias patterns (e.g., center-repulsive vs. peripheral-repulsive biases) are parsimoniously explained by differences in the mapping from an optimal Bayesian percept to a motor probe response rather than inherent differences in perceptual encoding. The findings suggest that human heading perception follows efficient Bayesian principles and underscore the necessity of modeling post-sensory transformations in psychophysical task analysis.
papers.authors: Qi Sun, Ling-Hao Xu, Alan A. Stocker

papers.title: The tilt illusion arises from an efficient reallocation of neural coding resources at the contextual boundary
papers.abstract: The authors provide a comprehensive, normative account of the tilt illusion by integrating psychophysical measurements with functional MRI (fMRI) data. They demonstrate that oriented contextual surrounds induce a dynamic reallocation of neural encoding precision, characterized by an increase in Fisher information (FI) for orientations proximal to the surround orientation. This shift in encoding resources is localized to cortical regions representing the center-surround boundary and increases in magnitude along the ventral visual hierarchy. By utilizing a Bayesian observer model where efficient coding jointly constrains the likelihood function and the prior distribution, the study shows that neural measures of encoding precision are sufficient to quantitatively predict the characteristic repulsive biases and increased estimation variance of the tilt illusion. The results suggest that the illusion reflects an adaptive coding strategy that optimizes representation according to the surround-conditioned statistics of orientation in natural scenes.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS)
papers.authors: Ling-Qi Zhang, Jiang Mao, Geoffrey K. Aguirre, Alan A. Stocker

papers.title: Adaptation optimizes sensory encoding for future stimuli
papers.abstract: This research tests the hypothesis that sensory adaptation is a proactive process that reconfigures encoding resources to optimize the representation of expected future stimuli. The authors quantified human orientation discrimination thresholds under various adaptation conditions and extracted sensory encoding accuracy using an information-theoretic analysis. They found that adaptation leads to a reallocation of coding capacity such that Fisher information peaks at the mean orientation of the adaptor, which aligns with the predicted temporal statistics of retinal input in natural environments. This proactive adjustment strategy was corroborated through analysis of a predictive recurrent neural network (PredNet) trained on natural scene videos, which exhibited congruent shifts in encoding precision. The findings suggest that adaptation-induced changes in neural response characteristics serve to prepare the visual system for incoming stimuli based on recent statistical history.
papers.authors: Jiang Mao, Constantin A. Rothkopf, Alan A. Stocker

papers.title: Sensory perception is a holistic inference process
papers.abstract: Challenging the reductionist view that perception reflects a single-feature estimate, the authors propose a holistic inference framework where the visual system jointly computes posterior distributions over both low-level features (e.g., orientation) and high-level categorical identities (e.g., cardinal vs. oblique). They introduce a holistic matching model for method-of-adjustment tasks, assuming that subjects report an estimate that optimally matches the test stimulus across all representational levels by minimizing a global loss function. Validation against multiple psychophysical datasets demonstrates that the model accurately predicts ubiquitous categorical biases in orientation and color perception and outperforms traditional Bayesian models both qualitatively and quantitatively. The results suggest that categorical effects are a natural consequence of optimal inference across a representational hierarchy.
papers.authors: Jiang Mao, Alan A. Stocker

papers.title: Efficient sensory encoding predicts robust averaging
papers.abstract: The authors investigate the neural and computational principles underlying robust averaging in ensemble perception, where observers assign non-uniform weights to items in a stimulus set. They show that robust averaging—specifically the overweighting of inlying items relative to the ensemble mean—naturally emerges from an optimal integration process when sensory encoding is constrained by efficient coding principles that adapt to the ensemble statistics. The study develops a hierarchical Bayesian observer model with likelihood functions shaped by the adaptive allocation of coding resources. The model accurately fits existing psychophysical datasets across different feature domains, predicting both decision accuracy and the non-uniform weighting profiles. These results suggest that the visual system establishes efficient sensory representations on rapid timescales to optimize information transfer for ensemble decision-making.
papers.authors: Long Ni, Alan A. Stocker

0018.name: Alasdair Clarke
0018.bio: Alasdair D. F. Clarke is a Senior Lecturer in the Department of Psychology at the University of Essex and is affiliated with the Centre for Brain Science. Clarke’s research integrates computational modeling, Bayesian inference, and signal detection theory to investigate how humans perceive complex visual scenes and make foraging decisions. Their work examines eye-movement biases, individual differences in visual search strategies, and the role of texture regularity and symmetry in scene analysis. Additionally, Clarke has developed standardized open-source task batteries for assessing visual performance in naturalistic environments.
0018.research_direction: Dr. Clarke's recent work explores the computational and behavioral mechanisms underlying continuous spatial decision-making, with a strong focus on generating predictive models of trial-by-trial target selection sequences during visual foraging. They have recently been investigating what drives these complex scanpaths—such as the potential influence of target scarcity—and whether human observers navigating spatial choice dilemmas can be trained to adopt optimal decision rules or if they persist in suboptimal heuristic exploration. In tandem with these behavioral investigations, Dr. Clarke is actively developing novel methodological and statistical frameworks for experimental vision science. Their recent methodological work includes designing a two-step psychophysical procedure to measure subjective visual discomfort while mitigating criterion artifacts, as well as applying Bayesian asymptotic regression to repeated-measures paradigms to capture dynamic learning trajectories rather than relying on static summary statistics.

papers.title: EXPRESS: Variable and sub-optimal responses to a choice problem persist despite experience with a simple and effective decision rule
papers.abstract: Human decision-making in focus-divide dilemmas is typically characterized by substantial inter-individual variability and pervasive suboptimality. This investigation assesses whether providing experiential exposure to a normative, rational decision rule leads observers to spontaneously adopt it in unconstrained choice settings. Participants selected their physical standing position when attempting to throw beanbags into one of two hoop targets (Experiments 1A–1C) or chose an initial fixation location prior to detecting a discrimination target that could appear in one of two spatially separated boxes (Experiment 2). The normative solution dictates that when targets are close together, positioning near the midpoint maximizes success, whereas when targets are widely separated, dedicating effort exclusively to one target optimizes performance. Although structured nudge interventions successfully prompted participants to implement optimal choices during exposure blocks, observers immediately reverted to their prior suboptimal, idiosyncratic strategies once unconstrained choice was reinstated. Experiments 3A and 3B further show that observers can reliably follow the rational decision rule when directly instructed to do so—producing substantial performance gains—yet they fail to retain it spontaneously. Drawing on reinforcement learning principles from comparative psychology, these findings indicate that persistent behavioral variability may serve as a default heuristic that prevents rigid rule-following at the cost of trial-by-trial exploration.
papers.authors: Amelia Hunt, Warren R. G. James, Josephine Reuther, Melissa Spilioti, Alasdair Clarke

papers.title: FoMo: A unifying theory of visual foraging
papers.abstract: Visual foraging generates a continuous, rich sequence of spatial decisions at the interface of perceptual processing, attention, and motor planning, yet conventional quantitative analyses have relied on fragmented summary statistics. Expanding upon earlier generative models that formulated foraging as random sampling without replacement, this work presents FoMo v2, an integrated computational model designed to predict target-by-target selection sequences in spatial foraging tasks. The updated framework incorporates structured spatial and directional mechanics—including circular von Mises distributions to capture horizontal scanning and grid-following habits—alongside latent proximity, selection inertia, and category preferences. When evaluated across multiple empirical datasets spanning both feature and conjunction visual foraging, the generative model achieves approximately 50% accuracy in predicting the exact subsequent target selection across trials (where chance is below 12%). Furthermore, posterior predictions derived from FoMo account for observed individual differences across standard metrics, including run length distributions, switch rates, and inter-target Euclidean distances, establishing a comprehensive and unified framework for computational foraging research.
papers.authors: Alasdair D. F. Clarke, Anna E. Hughes

papers.title: Measuring visual discomfort — a novel two-step method for reducing criterion effects when measuring subjective responses
papers.abstract: The quantification of visual discomfort has long been hindered by the subjective nature of the percept, the absence of an objective ground truth, and substantial inter-observer criterion differences in psychophysical scaling. Furthermore, long laboratory calibration paradigms are ill-suited for testing diverse or clinical cohorts in ecologically valid settings. Here, a two-step response procedure is developed to mitigate criterion artifacts while maintaining high data collection efficiency: participants first provide a binary determination of discomfort presence, which is subsequently used to calibrate and scale their continuous magnitude estimations. This method was deployed to test two competing physiological accounts of visual discomfort: cortical hyperexcitability induced by spatial frequency (stripe thickness) and ambiguous motion signals elicited by phase modulation wavelength (stripe undulation). Bayesian multilevel models confirmed that both spatial frequency and phase modulation significantly modulate discomfort judgments across both controlled laboratory displays (N = 34) and naturalistic field testing (N = 47), demonstrating that the two-step protocol effectively minimizes criterion contamination in subjective vision research.
papers.authors: Alasdair D. F. Clarke, Louise O'Hare, Paul B. Hibbard

papers.title: Learn more from your data with asymptotic regression
papers.abstract: In behavioral sciences and visual psychophysics, repeated-measures paradigms are commonly condensed into summary measures of central tendency, treating successive trials as independent and stationary observations while discarding dynamic temporal structure. This paper demonstrates the application of three-parameter asymptotic regression to repeated-measures data, parameterizing behavioral trajectories via an initial baseline origin, a monotonic learning rate parameter, and a terminal asymptotic performance level. Each parameter affords concrete theoretical meaning concerning baseline task capability, ecological validity, and cognitive performance ceilings. Through re-analyses of published psychophysical datasets alongside a new visual search experiment, the authors show how Bayesian nonlinear mixed-effects models implemented via tools such as brms capture both within-trial micro-dynamics and across-trial learning functions. The framework provides a principled method for distinguishing early practice artifacts from true asymptotic competence, informs optimal trial count selection, and offers a robust statistical alternative to arbitrary trial exclusion in perceptual research.
papers.authors: Alasdair D. F. Clarke, Amelia R. Hunt

papers.title: The effect of target scarcity on visual foraging
papers.abstract: In visual foraging paradigms, target selection is governed by competing factors including spatial proximity, priming history, and explicit target value. However, whether foragers exhibit an intrinsic selection bias toward rarer targets—as posited by commodity theory and implicit value frameworks—remains unresolved. Observers completed feature and conjunction foraging tasks in which the prevalence ratio between two target classes was manipulated across balanced and scarce conditions, without introducing explicit differential point values or monetary incentives. Behavioral scanpaths were modeled using a four-parameter Bayesian generative foraging architecture that decomposes item selection into latent proximity weighting, target-run repetition biases, and category preferences. Model parameter estimates and empirical trajectory analyses revealed no systematic bias toward selecting scarce items over abundant ones. Instead, selection dynamics were dominated by local proximity and persistent run behaviors, demonstrating that scarcity alone does not confer implicit subjective utility in multi-target human visual foraging.
papers.authors: A. E. Hughes, H. R. Statham, A. D. F. Clarke

0019.name: Alejandro Lleras
