0019.bio: Alejandro Lleras is a Professor in the Department of Psychology at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign and the Beckman Institute, where they co-direct the Vision Lab. Their research investigates the computational and cognitive mechanisms underlying human visual attention and awareness, focusing on the role of parallel peripheral vision in guiding goal-directed search. Utilizing a multimodal approach that integrates psychophysics, eye-tracking, and EEG, Lleras developed theoretical frameworks such as the Target Contrast Signal Theory to explain how visual features are processed and filtered during scene analysis. Their current work examines the temporal dynamics of attention and the factors that drive distractibility and attentional lapses over sustained periods.
0019.research_direction: Dr. Lleras has recently been investigating the cognitive architectures and mechanisms that underlie visual search and distractor rejection in complex environments. Their recent work explores how the visual system utilizes multiple target features—whether configuring multiple colors within a single dimension or combining color and shape in conjunction searches—to guide attention through heterogeneous displays. By leveraging behavioral experiments, eye-tracking, and computational frameworks like drift-diffusion modeling, they are probing whether classic search bottlenecks stem from inherent feature-binding constraints or from the use of hierarchical, parallel-sequential rejection strategies. Furthermore, they are examining the roots of individual variability in difficult, camouflaged search tasks to uncover how latent factors like perceptual evidence accumulation and strategic decision cautiousness independently shape observer performance.

papers.title: Color–color feature guidance in visual search
papers.abstract: This research examines the mechanisms by which multiple distinct color features within a single dimension (e.g., center-surround configurations) guide visual search. Through a series of experiments, the authors demonstrate that observers can learn and strategically employ a two-color, location-bound search template. Computational modeling comparisons reveal that this guidance operates via a parallel-sequential rejection architecture. In heterogeneous displays, the visual system prioritizes one target-defining color feature to filter a subset of distractors through peripheral vision before utilizing the second color feature to reject the remaining items, suggesting that multi-feature guidance within a dimension is executed hierarchically rather than through simultaneous integration.
papers.authors: Yiwen Wang, Simona Buetti, Andrea Yaoyun Cui, Alejandro Lleras

papers.title: Evaluating the contribution of parallel processing of color and shape in a conjunction search task
papers.abstract: The study employs a behavioral-computational framework to determine if the increased difficulty of conjunction search (e.g., color and shape) arises from feature-binding constraints or the architecture of distractor rejection. By measuring logarithmic search slopes in homogeneous feature searches and applying these parameters to heterogeneous conjunction displays, the authors test various cognitive architectures. A model-comparison approach identifies the winning model as one involving a hierarchical, parallel-sequential rejection mechanism where distractors are rejected based on a single defining feature first. The findings indicate that the constraints on conjunction search performance are better explained by strategic distractor rejection rates rather than inherent limitations in parallel feature integration or peripheral pooling.
papers.authors: Andrea Yaoyun Cui, Simona Buetti, Zoe Jing Xu, Alejandro Lleras

papers.title: Skills and cautiousness predict performance in difficult search
papers.abstract: This paper investigates individual variability in performance during difficult visual search tasks, such as finding camouflaged targets. Using eye-tracking and drift-diffusion modeling (DDM), the authors dissociate two orthogonal latent factors: Search Skill and Cautiousness. Search Skill reflects the rate of evidence accumulation and the efficiency of distractor rejection, correlating with both faster reaction times and higher accuracy. Conversely, Cautiousness represents the decision threshold adopted by the observer, where higher caution increases reaction times without necessarily improving the rate of information extraction. The results suggest that individual differences in complex search are driven by a combination of inherent perceptual efficiency and strategic conservative biases.
papers.authors: Zoe Jing Xu, Simona Buetti, Ying Xia, Alejandro Lleras

0020.name: Alessandro Farini
0020.bio: Alessandro Farini is a senior researcher and physicist at the National Institute of Optics (CNR-INO) in Florence and directs the Visual Optics Lab (ViOLa). Farini’s research investigates the intersection of applied psychophysics, visual ergonomics, and lighting science, focusing on how ophthalmic optics and environmental illumination affect human perception. They study blue-blocking filters, colorimetry, and the visual performance of patients with macular degeneration using eye-tracking methodologies and behavioral research techniques. Farini also serves as a contract professor at the University of Florence, where they teach courses in geometrical and physical optics.
0020.research_direction: Dr. Farini has recently been investigating how variations in spectral input—whether due to illumination changes, physiological anomalies, or species differences—affect visual perception and performance. In the realm of human color vision, their recent work explores mechanisms of cortical color constancy and illuminant estimation by using psychophysical tasks to assess how individuals with congenital red-green color vision deficiencies resolve the ambiguous "Dress" illusion. They have also been examining spatial vision and longitudinal chromatic aberration, measuring how monochromatic yellow light impacts visual acuity and contrast sensitivity across different age groups, while concurrently applying equine dichromatic vision models to quantify how horses perceive obstacle contrast during show jumping. Finally, their interdisciplinary scholarship extends into the history of physical optics, integrating refractive parameters with archival analysis to trace the technological evolution of early ophthalmic lenses in thirteenth-century Florence.

papers.title: Perception of The Dress for different color vision anomalies
papers.abstract: This study investigates the bistable perception of the 'The Dress' chromatic illusion in individuals with congenital color vision deficiencies (CVD), specifically comparing protan and deutan genotypes with normal trichromats. Utilizing color-matching tasks and categorical scaling, the research evaluates how the reduction in dimensionality of chromatic signals affects the resolution of visual ambiguity and the subsequent estimation of the illuminant. The results delineate the extent to which the blue-yellow and red-green pathways contribute to the stability of the illusion, providing evidence for the role of prior illumination assumptions in cortical color constancy mechanisms despite degraded retinal input.
papers.venue: Nuovo Cimento della Societa Italiana di Fisica C
papers.authors: Daniela Ducci, Elisabetta Baldanzi, Massimo Gurioli, Paolo Antonino Grasso, Federico Tommasi, Alessandro Farini

papers.title: Visual acuity and contrast sensitivity under monochromatic yellow light
papers.abstract: The research quantifies the psychophysical impact of narrowband yellow illumination (peak wavelength ~590 nm) on primary visual metrics, including visual acuity (VA) and the contrast sensitivity function (CSF). Subjects were tested under controlled monochromatic and broadband white light conditions to assess the contribution of longitudinal chromatic aberration (LCA) to retinal image degradation. Findings indicate that monochromatic yellow light effectively mitigates LCA-induced blur, maintaining VA stability while significantly enhancing contrast sensitivity at high spatial frequencies, which suggests its efficacy in optimizing visual performance for low-vision patients and specialized industrial environments.
papers.venue: Nuovo Cimento della Societa Italiana di Fisica C
papers.authors: Elisabetta Baldanzi, Paolo Antonino Grasso, Claudio Gori, Massimo Gurioli, Federico Tommasi, Alessandro Farini

papers.title: Florence and the history of glasses: between fake news and technological progress
papers.abstract: This multidisciplinary paper provides a technical and historiographical review of the development of ophthalmic lenses in late 13th-century Florence. By integrating principles of physical optics—such as the evolution of glass refractive indices and manufacturing tolerances—with archival historical analysis, the authors deconstruct common misconceptions regarding the invention of spectacles. The study evaluates the transition from beryl 'reading stones' to framed lenses, highlighting the role of the Italian National Institute of Optics in clarifying the timeline of optical innovation and its socioeconomic impact on early vision correction technology.
papers.venue: Nuovo Cimento della Societa Italiana di Fisica C
papers.authors: Elisabetta Baldanzi, Alessandro Farini

papers.title: A leap in the dark! How understanding horses' color perception improves their performance and welfare in show jumping
papers.abstract: Applying equine dichromatic vision models to sport science, this study examines how the visual system of horses (Equus ferus caballus) influences obstacle detection and navigation during show jumping. The authors calculate chromatic (ΔE) and luminance contrast ratios between jump barriers and typical arena backgrounds, identifying specific color combinations that facilitate or hinder detection for dichromatic observers. The findings demonstrate that evidence-based course design, optimized for equine spectral sensitivity, can significantly reduce jump refusal rates and associated animal stress, advocating for new color standards in equestrian competitions to enhance both performance and animal welfare.
papers.authors: Alessia Fava, Alessandro Farini

papers.title: Visual acuity and contrast sensitivity under monochromatic yellow light (Preprint)
papers.abstract: This preprint presents a systematic evaluation of spatial vision performance under narrowband spectral conditions. By measuring the contrast sensitivity function across a range of spatial frequencies (1.5 to 18 cycles per degree), the researchers identify the psychophysical benefits of monochromatic yellow light (589 nm) in reducing the eye's chromatic defocus. The study includes a comparative analysis of visual thresholds between young and elderly populations, characterizing how age-related changes in ocular media and neural processing interact with monochromatic illumination to influence the detection and recognition of high-spatial-frequency stimuli.
papers.authors: E. Baldanzi, P. A. Grasso, C. Gori, M. Gurioli, F. Tommasi, A. Farini

0021.name: Alessio Fracasso
0021.bio: Alessio Fracasso is a neuroscientist who investigates the neurophysiology of sensory-motor and visual systems, focusing on the interface between sensory stimulation, action, and perception. Fracasso utilizes ultra-high field functional magnetic resonance imaging (7T fMRI) and psychophysical modeling to map the topographic organization of the human brain at a mesoscopic scale. Their research examines population receptive field (pRF) properties and laminar-specific BOLD responses in the visual cortex. In addition to fundamental systems neuroscience, Fracasso applies these neuroimaging and computational methods to study the neural substrates of clinical conditions, including schizophrenia, congenital chiasmal malformations, and strabismus.
0021.research_direction: Dr. Fracasso has recently been investigating a diverse range of topics spanning cortical organization, oculomotor dynamics, and clinical neuroimaging. Their recent work explores the topographical mapping of the human brain using functional MRI and population receptive field modeling to understand how mid-level object dimensions are spatially arranged in the visual association cortex, as well as how visual spatial parameters undergo cross-modal reorganization within the deprived auditory cortex of congenitally deaf individuals. In the domain of active vision, they are studying the temporal dynamics of saccadic inhibition to determine how high-level image content modulates reflexive oculomotor programming and microsaccade generation. Additionally, they are utilizing structural and resting-state MRI to investigate stage-specific neural biomarkers across the psychosis spectrum, specifically evaluating choroid plexus morphology and graph-theoretical measures of hippocampal functional connectivity in early-stage psychosis and schizophrenia.

papers.title: The Neural Organization of Visual Information in the Auditory Cortex of the Congenitally Deaf
papers.abstract: This study investigates the degree of cross-modal cortical reorganization in the primary auditory cortex (AC) of congenitally deaf individuals by mapping its response to low-level visual spatial parameters. Utilizing functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) combined with population receptive field (pRF) modeling, the researchers characterize the topographic properties of visual activity within the AC. The findings demonstrate that the sensory-deprived AC in deaf subjects, but not in hearing controls, exhibits robust visual responses primarily mediated through negative BOLD signals (cross-modal deactivations). These deactivation-based maps reveal systematic spatial tuning for polar angle and eccentricity, with receptive fields characterized by large sizes and a preference for near-foveal regions, predominantly in the right hemisphere. The results suggest that deactivation-driven spatial coding constitutes a distinct mechanism for large-scale sensory plasticity following early visual deprivation.
papers.authors: Zohar Tal, Joana Sayal, Fang Fang, Yanchao Bi, Jorge Almeida, Alessio Fracasso

papers.title: Contentopic mapping in ventral and dorsal association cortex: The topographical organization of manipulable object information
papers.abstract: This research explores the hypothesis that mid-level object-related dimensions are organized topographically within human association cortex, a principle termed 'contentopy.' Using high-resolution functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and population receptive field (pRF) modeling, the authors measured neural tuning to specific action-based and manipulable object dimensions. The study identifies distinct and stable topographical maps in both ventral and dorsal occipital association cortices that encode object-specific information in a linear spatial progression across the cortical surface. These contentopic maps are shown to exist independently of eccentricity-based mapping, suggesting that topographical organization is a widespread strategy for managing high-dimensional object knowledge in association cortex, potentially optimized to reduce metabolic costs and facilitate rapid information readouts for stimulus discrimination.
papers.authors: Jorge Almeida, Stephanie Kristensen, Zohar Tal, Alessio Fracasso

papers.title: Altered functional connectivity of the hippocampus in cortico-subcortical networks in early-stage and emerging psychosis
papers.abstract: This investigation examines hippocampal functional connectivity (FC) and network topology as markers of illness stage in early-stage and emerging psychosis. Resting-state fMRI (rs-fMRI) data were analyzed from cohorts of individuals at clinical high-risk for psychosis (CHR-P), patients with first-episode psychosis (FEP), and healthy controls. Applying graph-theoretical analysis, the study assesses hippocampal centrality and network segregation/integration. Results indicate a significant reduction in FC between the hippocampus and the inferior frontal cortex in both CHR-P and FEP individuals. Furthermore, the FEP group exhibited uniquely lower hippocampal centrality and increased network segregation compared to the CHR-P group. These findings suggest that hippocampal-frontal network disruptions are present early in the psychosis spectrum, and that graph-based metrics of hippocampal influence can differentiate between stages of early-stage psychosis.
papers.venue: European Archives of Psychiatry and Clinical Neuroscience
papers.authors: Gina Brunner, Ruchika Gajwani, Joachim Gross, Andrew Gumley, Rajeev Krishnadas, Stephen M. Lawrie, Matthias Schwannauer, Frauke Schultze-Lutter, Peter J. Uhlhaas, Alessio Fracasso

papers.title: Choroid plexus morphology in schizophrenia and early-stage psychosis: A cross-sectional study
papers.abstract: The study evaluates whether morphological alterations in the choroid plexus (CP) represent a stage-specific biomarker of the psychosis spectrum. Using 3-Tesla magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and automated Gaussian mixture model (GMM) segmentation, the researchers quantified CP volumes in clinical high-risk (CHR-P), first-episode psychosis (FEP), and chronic schizophrenia (SCZ) participants. While initial analyses revealed increased CP volumes in the schizophrenia group, this effect was found to be fully mediated by total ventricular volume. No specific CP volumetric differences were identified in the CHR-P or FEP groups. The findings suggest that CP enlargement in schizophrenia is a secondary correlate of global ventricular expansion rather than a primary, stage-specific marker of early psychosis pathology.
papers.authors: Gina Brunner, Ruchika Gajwani, Joachim Gross, Andrew Gumley, Rosanne H. Timmerman, Rebecca Taylor, Rajeev Krishnadas, Stephen M. Lawrie, Matthias Schwannauer, Frauke Schultze-Lutter, Peter J. Uhlhaas, Alessio Fracasso

papers.title: Saccadic “inhibition” unveils the late influence of image content on oculomotor programming
papers.abstract: This study characterizes the temporal dynamics of oculomotor control by examining how high-level image content (faces versus noise) modulates saccadic inhibition (SI)—the transient reduction in saccade frequency following a task-irrelevant visual event. Utilizing a gaze-contingent paradigm to measure visually guided saccades and microsaccades, the authors demonstrate that while the onset of SI (~90 ms) is stimulus-independent and reflexive, the duration and recovery of the inhibitory dip are content-dependent. Face stimuli resulted in a prolonged reduction in eye movement frequency compared to noise stimuli. Additionally, both stimulus types induced a significant reduction in saccadic amplitude without altering peak velocity for early saccades. The results suggest that while early reflexive gating is content-agnostic, a delayed signal conveying high-level image information modulates the later stages of the oculomotor inhibitory response.
papers.authors: Rebecca Taylor, Antimo Buonocore, Alessio Fracasso

0022.name: Alex Martin
0022.bio: Alex Martin is a Senior Investigator and Chief of the Section on Cognitive Neuropsychology at the National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH). Martin’s research program investigates the neural architecture of semantic memory, specifically how conceptual knowledge about objects is grounded in the sensory and motor systems of the brain. Utilizing neuroimaging techniques such as functional MRI and magnetoencephalography (MEG), they explore the representation of category-specific knowledge and how these circuits are modified by learning and experience. Their work also examines the neural mechanisms underlying social interaction and communication in typically developing individuals and those with autism spectrum disorders.
0022.research_direction: Dr. Martin has recently been investigating the neural architecture underlying how the human brain organizes complex semantic knowledge, sensory representations, and whole-brain functional networks. Their recent work explores the perception and evaluation of food cues, using high-resolution fMRI and multivariate pattern analysis to uncover how distinct prefrontal and limbic networks evaluate healthfulness versus hedonics, and to test whether the gustatory cortex utilizes a common neural code for actively imagined and visually inferred tastes. Beyond sensory inference, they are also studying the hierarchical organization of semantic memory by mapping the taxonomic structure of abstract concepts and using simultaneous fMRI-EEG to probe the oscillatory and hemodynamic mechanisms of repetition suppression during visual object naming. Additionally, Dr. Martin's research investigates resting-state network topography in clinical populations, applying connectivity-based whole-brain parcellation to examine functional differentiation and subcortical-cortical integration in high-functioning individuals with autism spectrum disorder.

papers.title: Automatic engagement of limbic and prefrontal networks in response to food images reflects distinct information about food hedonics and inhibitory control
papers.abstract: Using Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA) and high-resolution functional MRI, this study investigated the neural architecture of food perception and evaluation. A data-driven clustering approach identified two dissociable sub-networks: a Prefrontal network (comprising fronto-parietal regions such as the IFG, mFG, and Pre-SMA) and a Limbic network (comprising the mid-insula, orbitofrontal cortex, amygdala, and ventral striatum). Multivariate patterns in the Prefrontal network encoded information regarding food healthfulness and were sensitive to inhibitory control and self-regulation judgments, while the Limbic network predominantly represented hedonic value. These results suggest that food cues automatically activate competing neural signals within opponent networks to guide eating behavior.
papers.authors: Jason A. Avery, Madeline Carrington, John E. Ingeholm, Valerie Darcey, W. Kyle Simmons, Kevin D. Hall, Alex Martin

papers.title: A functional parcellation of the whole brain in high-functioning individuals with autism spectrum disorder reveals atypical patterns of network organization
papers.abstract: This research provides a comprehensive whole-brain functional parcellation of the autism spectrum disorder (ASD) connectome using high-temporal signal-to-noise ratio (tSNR) resting-state fMRI. Connectivity-based mapping revealed three primary atypicalities in the ASD group compared to matched typically developing controls: a reduction in the spatial stability of whole-brain connectivity patterns within multiple functional networks, a significant failure of functional differentiation into subnetworks within the cerebellum, subcortex, and hippocampus, and aberrant integration of these subcortical structures with the neocortex. These findings suggest that disrupted network topography and subcortical-cortical decoupling are fundamental characteristics of brain organization in high-functioning individuals with ASD.
papers.authors: Andrew S. Persichetti, Jiayu Shao, Stephen J. Gotts, Alex Martin

papers.title: Repetition-related reductions in neural activity support improved behavior through increases in oscillatory power
papers.abstract: Utilizing simultaneous 7-Tesla fMRI-EEG during a visual object naming task, the authors examined the neural mechanisms underlying repetition priming and repetition suppression (RS). Stimulus repetition led to more rapid increases and earlier resolution of oscillatory power across a wide frequency range (theta to gamma) in task-engaged frontal and ventral occipitotemporal regions exhibiting fMRI RS. Specifically, gamma-band power changes were robustly correlated with individual differences in behavioral priming and fMRI-defined suppression in the left inferior frontal gyrus. These results provide multimodal evidence for a hybrid neural model of priming where reduced BOLD responses reflect enhanced processing efficiency and synchronized neural dynamics.
papers.authors: Adrian W. Gilmore, Leonardo Claudino, Cassandra M. Levesque, Anna M. Agron, Peter J. Molfese, Vinai Roopchansingh, Michael D. Rugg, Stephen J. Gotts, Alex Martin

papers.title: Taxonomic structure in a set of abstract concepts
papers.abstract: This study mapped the categorical organization of abstract knowledge using non-verbal similarity judgments and cross-validated clustering analyses of 50 abstract nouns. The results identified five robust taxonomic categories representing emotional states, quantities, mental attributes, and social interactions, indicating that abstract concepts share a hierarchical organization similar to concrete objects. Automatic semantic priming experiments further validated these clusters, demonstrating that data-driven categories provide a more accurate reflection of internal mental representations than traditional categories derived from explicit human ratings along predetermined semantic dimensions.
papers.authors: Andrew S. Persichetti, Jiayu Shao, Joseph M. Denning, Stephen J. Gotts, Alex Martin

papers.title: A common neural code for representing imagined and inferred tastes
papers.abstract: Using high-field fMRI and cross-task multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA), the researchers tested whether primary gustatory cortex represents taste quality through top-down cognitive processes. Neural activity patterns in the dorsal mid-insula were found to be quality-specific for basic tastes (sweet, salty, and sour) and were reliably similar across tasks involving active mental imagery and the visual perception of food images (inferred taste). The finding that these representational patterns are interchangeable suggests a common neural code for taste quality in primary sensory cortex that is automatically engaged by both explicit imagery and visual inference.
papers.authors: Jason A. Avery, Madeline Carrington, Alex Martin

0023.name: Alex S. Baldwin
0023.bio: Alex S. Baldwin is an Assistant Professor at McGill University and a Junior Scientist in the Brain Repair and Integrative Neuroscience (BRaIN) program at the RI-MUHC. Baldwin’s research investigates the mechanisms of human visual perception by combining psychophysical experiments with mathematical and computational modeling of neural processing. Their work focuses on spatial vision, specifically how the brain integrates local features into global contours and textures, as well as the dynamics of binocular vision and stereopsis in both healthy aging and clinical populations such as those with amblyopia.
0023.research_direction: Dr. Baldwin’s recent work investigates the psychophysical and computational mechanisms underlying visual deficits in amblyopia, with a focus on spatial vision and binocular processing. They have recently been exploring how the visual system encodes spatial form by employing physiologically-inspired scrambling algorithms to simulate neural disorganization, testing how these simulated cortical and subcortical errors impact letter identification in both typical and amblyopic vision. Their recent research also explores interocular interactions by evaluating novel dichoptic testing paradigms to quantify the specific roles of surround and overlay suppression in amblyopic binocular imbalance. Additionally, Dr. Baldwin investigates the mechanisms limiting amblyopic stereopsis, utilizing disparity noise-masking paradigms and linear amplifier modeling to parse whether depth perception deficits stem from elevated internal neural noise or impaired processing efficiency.

papers.title: Amblyopic binocular imbalance quantified by the dichoptic contrast ordering test and dichoptic letters test
papers.abstract: In amblyopia, abnormal interocular interactions lead to significant ocular dominance of the fellow eye, largely driven by suppressive mechanisms that include both overlay and surround components. This study evaluates a novel clinical tool, the Dichoptic Contrast Ordering Test (DiCOT), designed to quantify surround suppression through an interocular contrast scaling paradigm. In a cohort of adult amblyopes (strabismic and anisometropic) and normally sighted controls, DiCOT results were compared against the Dichoptic Letters Test (DLT), which measures overlay suppression. Both psychophysical assessments demonstrated high test-retest reliability and revealed a significant degree of suppression in amblyopes that correlated strongly with monocular visual acuity and stereoacuity deficits. The findings suggest that amblyopic suppression is spatially extensive and that DiCOT provides a robust, clinically applicable metric for tracking binocular imbalance.
papers.authors: Alexandre Reynaud, Marie-Céline Lorenzini, Robert K. Koenekoop, Robert F. Hess, Alex S. Baldwin

papers.title: The amblyopic acuity deficit: impact on the identification of letters distorted by spatial scrambling algorithms
papers.abstract: The impairment of optotype acuity in the amblyopic eye typically exceeds the levels predicted by the grating detection cut-off frequency, a phenomenon hypothesized to involve neural disorganization or spatial scrambling in cortical projections. We employed a physiologically-inspired algorithm to generate spatially scrambled bandpass letters, simulating either 'cortical scrambling' at the output of V1 simple cells or 'subcortical scrambling' of subunits. Psychophysical identification efficiency was measured in amblyopic and control participants, equating stimuli across eyes by normalizing for contrast or preferred spatial scale. While group-level identification in bandpass noise was less efficient in the amblyopic eye, significant efficiency differences in scrambling were observed only when participants were partitioned by stereopsis ability. Distinctive mistake patterns in the amblyopic eye correlated with acuity deficits, indicating that scrambled stimuli interrogate a functional component of amblyopia distinct from contrast-noise masking.
papers.authors: Raffles X. Zhu, Robert F. Hess, Alex S. Baldwin

papers.title: Human visual performance for identifying letters affected by physiologically-inspired scrambling
papers.abstract: In human vision, retinal inputs undergo hierarchical transformations that may introduce spatial precision errors through incorrect or convergent projections. We investigated the impact of two types of physiologically-inspired spatial scrambling—subcortical (input to V1 simple cells) and cortical (output from simple cells)—on a letter identification task. Using a decomposition and resynthesis algorithm with log-Gabor wavelets, we benchmarked human performance against Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and template-matching models. Human observers exhibited greater resilience to subcortical scrambling than to cortical scrambling. Comparison of confusion matrices revealed that human strategies align more closely with CNNs than simple template matching, suggesting that the visual system employs flexible identification mechanisms and that the subcortical stage may be a primary locus for the accumulation of spatial noise in the visual hierarchy.
papers.authors: Xingqi R. Zhu, Robert F. Hess, Alex S. Baldwin

papers.title: Amblyopic stereo vision is efficient but noisy
papers.abstract: The mechanisms limiting stereopsis in amblyopia remain poorly understood, as clinical tests often lack the quantitative precision to distinguish between input noise and processing efficiency. We utilized a disparity noise-masking paradigm to investigate stereoacuity in 29 amblyopic and 17 control participants using a random-dot 'odd-one-out' detection task. By applying the Linear Amplifier Model (LAM), we partitioned performance into equivalent internal noise and processing efficiency. Results showed that the factor-of-two difference in median stereoacuity between amblyopes (103 arcsec) and controls (56 arcsec) was driven primarily by elevated equivalent internal disparity noise (238 vs 135 arcsec), with no significant difference in efficiency. Multiple linear regression confirmed that internal noise accounted for 46% of the variance in amblyopic stereoacuity, suggesting that reduced signal quality at the input stage, rather than defective computation, is the primary limiting factor.
papers.authors: Sara Alarcon Carrillo, Robert F. Hess, Yu Mao, Jiawei Zhou, Alex S. Baldwin

0024.name: Alex White
0024.bio: Alex L. White is a cognitive neuroscientist and Assistant Professor whose research investigates the computational and neural mechanisms of visual perception, selective attention, and word recognition. White’s work focuses on the limitations of processing capacity during reading, employing methodologies such as behavioral psychophysics, eye-tracking, and functional MRI. Their research examines the functional properties of the visual word form area (VWFA), specifically how its activity is modulated by task-specific demands and top-down feedback from language regions. Currently, White explores the spatial and temporal bottlenecks that constrain the recognition of multiple words and how these constraints influence reading development.
0024.research_direction: Dr. White has recently been investigating the visual and neural mechanisms underlying reading, with a specific focus on the capacity limits of visual word recognition. Using dual-task psychophysical paradigms, their recent work explores the behavioral boundaries of the serial processing bottleneck, examining how parallel lexical access is influenced by spatial position in the visual field, sub-lexical feature integration, and higher-level linguistic grouping into compound words. In tandem with behavioral methods, they use fMRI to examine how the cortical reading circuitry processes multiple concurrent written inputs. Within this neural domain, they are investigating how bottom-up stimulus selectivity in the visual word form area is reshaped by top-down linguistic effort, and whether simultaneous word presentation drives resource competition at early orthographic versus deeper lexical-semantic stages.

papers.title: Serial processing of two words becomes parallel when they combine to form a known compound word
papers.abstract: This study investigated the constraints of the serial bottleneck in lexical access by determining whether processing capacity limits can be bypassed when multiple orthographic inputs form a single conceptual unit. Using a dual-task psychophysical paradigm with brief, masked stimuli, participants categorized word pairs that were either semantically unrelated or constituents of a familiar compound word (e.g., "sea" and "food"). While unrelated word pairs yielded performance deficits and stimulus processing trade-offs consistent with an all-or-none serial processing model, the accuracy for compound word constituents significantly exceeded serial predictions. The results indicate that the visual system can achieve parallel lexical access when individual word identities are integrated into a single higher-level linguistic representation, suggesting that the serial bottleneck in reading is not an absolute architectural constraint.
papers.authors: Amritha Anupindi, Liana R. Eisler, Mariam U. Latif, Vassiki S. Chauhan, Alex L. White

papers.title: Simultaneous cortical responses to multiple written words
papers.abstract: Using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and a simultaneous suppression paradigm, this research examined how the neural reading circuitry processes multiple concurrent linguistic inputs. Participants were presented with rapid sequences containing varying numbers of English words and pseudo-letters in both sequential and simultaneous configurations. While BOLD responses in reading-selective regions—including the left mid-occipitotemporal sulcus and inferior frontal sulcus—scaled linearly with the number of words, simultaneous presentation did not evoke significant response suppression compared to sequential presentation. However, the sensitivity of ventral temporal text-selective regions to the lexical frequencies of both words was markedly attenuated during simultaneous presentation. These findings suggest that while orthographic encoding may proceed in parallel without mutual suppression, competition for limited resources occurs at a deeper stage of lexical-semantic analysis.
papers.authors: Vassiki S. Chauhan, Krystal McCook, Mariam Latif, Alex L. White

papers.title: Reading Reshapes Stimulus Selectivity in the Visual Word Form Area
papers.abstract: This fMRI study disentangled the roles of bottom-up sensory selectivity and top-down linguistic modulation in the visual word form area (VWFA). By precisely localizing word-responsive regions in 16 adults, the researchers measured BOLD activity during lexical decision, font color detection, and fixation-monitoring tasks using English words, pseudowords, and unfamiliar character strings. The results demonstrated that while the VWFA exhibits baseline selectivity for familiar orthography even when ignored, its response magnitudes and functional connectivity with the left frontal language network are selectively enhanced only during active linguistic processing. These findings support a hybrid model of VWFA function where inherent stimulus selectivity is dynamically reshaped by voluntary linguistic effort and feedback from higher-level language systems.
papers.authors: Vassiki S. Chauhan, Krystal C. McCook, Alex L. White

papers.title: Parallel processing of written words as a function of visual field position
papers.abstract: This study characterized the spatial topography of parallel word recognition using a dual-task psychophysical paradigm to map the boundaries of the serial bottleneck across the visual field. By manipulating the eccentricity and horizontal/vertical alignment of briefly presented word pairs, the researchers identified the retinal positions that support parallel lexical access. Although recognition was found to be strictly serial for vertical arrangements and larger eccentricities, parallel processing was supported within a narrow horizontal span near the fovea, particularly when one word was fixated and the other appeared in the right visual field. The findings provide a quantitative assessment of individual differences in processing capacity and identify the specific spatial configurations that facilitate parallel word recognition during naturalistic reading.
papers.authors: Kimya Firoozan, Amritha Anupindi, Alex L. White

papers.title: Severe processing capacity limits for sub-lexical features of letter strings
papers.abstract: To identify the locus of the serial bottleneck in visual word recognition, this study investigated whether processing limits arise at a sub-lexical or phonological stage. Using a dual-task behavioral paradigm, participants performed judgments on vowel presence (sub-lexical letter identification) or pronounceability (phonological decoding) for pairs of masked character strings. In both experiments, the substantial cost of dividing attention and the presence of significant trial-by-trial stimulus processing trade-offs strongly supported an all-or-none serial processing model. The results indicate that the bottleneck preventing parallel word recognition is situated early in the processing stream, specifically at the level of integrating visual features into orthographic identities or during the identification of constituent letters.
papers.authors: Maya Campbell, Nicole Oppenheimer, Alex L. White

0025.name: Alexander C. Schütz
0025.bio: Alexander C. Schütz is a Professor of Experimental Psychology at Philipps-Universität Marburg and investigates the bidirectional interaction between visual perception and eye movements. Their research explores how the brain maintains a stable representation of the environment despite frequent saccadic interruptions and sensory gaps like the blind spot. Schütz combines psychophysics, high-speed eye tracking, EEG, and computational modeling to examine the optimization of oculomotor control for task-relevant information gathering. Their work includes studies on trans-saccadic integration, smooth pursuit eye movements, and the integration of salience and value signals in sensorimotor learning.
0025.research_direction: Dr. Schütz has recently been investigating how the brain handles sensory uncertainty and missing information, focusing heavily on metacognition and perceptual completion. Their recent work explores how observers assess their own perceptual inferences, probing metacognitive confidence judgments during tasks involving visual modal and amodal occlusion, auditory filling-in, and time-constrained visual search. To understand how the visual system actively samples ambiguous information, they are using behavioral paradigms to determine whether the oculomotor system preferentially directs saccades toward physiological blind spots to resolve uncertainty. Additionally, they are utilizing electroencephalography to characterize the neural correlates of scene processing, specifically examining how the visual system leverages structural priors to estimate object numerosity when targets are partially occluded.

papers.title: Low confidence for perceptual completion of partially occluded objects
papers.abstract: This study examines the metacognitive assessment of filled-in visual information in distal gaps, specifically focusing on modal and amodal completion of occluded objects. Using a Vernier discrimination task, the researchers compared confidence judgments across four conditions: full stimulus, physical gap, modal completion, and amodal completion. While proximal gaps (e.g., the blind spot) often lead to overconfidence in filled-in information, the results demonstrated that confidence for completed objects was significantly lower than for intact stimuli and comparable to stimuli containing explicit physical gaps. These findings suggest that metacognitive certainty is highly sensitive to the nature of the perceptual inference, distinguishing between proximal scotoma filling-in and distal occlusion completion.
papers.authors: Cemre Baykan, Pascal Mamassian, Alexander C. Schütz

papers.title: Eye movements do not preferentially test inferences in the blind spot
papers.abstract: This research investigates whether the oculomotor system treats perceptual inferences at the physiological blind spot as regions of high uncertainty worthy of active exploration. In a monocular visual search paradigm, the authors tested if saccades are preferentially directed toward the blind spot compared to control monocular and binocular regions. The results indicated that observers do not exhibit an intrinsic oculomotor bias toward the blind spot when target locations are randomized. A preference for the blind spot only emerged under blocked viewing conditions, indicating a learned contextual strategy rather than a hardwired prioritization of filled-in information gain. These findings suggest that gaze control operates based on global scene context rather than local idiosyncratic sensory gaps.
papers.authors: Cemre Baykan, Alexander C. Schütz

papers.title: Electroencephalographic Responses to the Number of Objects in Partially Occluded and Uncovered Scenes
papers.abstract: This investigation utilizes electroencephalography (EEG) to characterize the neural correlates of object quantification in complex scenes requiring perceptual completion. The study compared ERP components (P1, N1, P2) and spectral activity between scenes where objects were either fully visible or partially occluded. The findings revealed that early visual components are modulated by both the total number of items and the presence of occlusion, indicating that scene schemata and top-down models facilitate the representation of global scene properties like numerosity. This suggests that the visual system integrates local sensory fragments into a coherent numerical estimate by leveraging structural priors to resolve spatial ambiguity caused by environmental occlusion.
papers.authors: Cemre Baykan, Alexander C. Schütz

papers.title: Confidence in auditory perceptual completion
papers.abstract: The authors explored the metacognitive monitoring of auditory filling-in (the continuity illusion) to determine if it produces biases similar to those in visual filling-in at retinal scotomata. Participants judged the continuity of interrupted tones masked by noise and provided confidence ratings or performed forced-choice comparisons. Metacognitive analysis revealed a significant presence-absence asymmetry: listeners were consistently more confident in identifying physical gaps (discontinuities) than in judging filled-in tones as continuous. Unlike visual filling-in, where observers are often overconfident in their inferences, auditory filled-in stimuli do not elicit higher subjective trust, suggesting that the metacognitive signatures of perceptual completion are modality-specific and depend on different internal signal distributions.
papers.authors: Cemre Baykan, Pascal Mamassian, Alexander C. Schütz

papers.title: Confidence in incomplete visual search
papers.abstract: This study examines the determinants of decision confidence during visual search under temporal constraints. Using 1/f noise backgrounds, the researchers measured how gaze-target distance and target visibility influence presence-absence decisions and subjective confidence. Results showed that hit rates decline significantly as minimum gaze-target distance increases, with performance reaching chance levels beyond 2-3 degrees of eccentricity. Confidence judgments were found to be a joint function of foveal target visibility and the estimated probability of having overlooked the target during exploration. This indicates that observers effectively calibrate their confidence based on their own oculomotor coverage and the quality of sampled sensory information, allowing for an internal estimate of search reliability.
papers.authors: Hui Men, Alexander C. Schütz

0027.name: Alfredo Spagna
0027.bio: Alfredo Spagna is a researcher at Columbia University and serves as the Director of Undergraduate Studies in Neuroscience and Behavior. Spagna’s research investigates the psychological and neural mechanisms of attention, perception, and visual mental imagery, focusing on the distinction between internally generated mental representations and sensory-driven perception. Utilizing 7-T fMRI, MEG, and EEG, they have identified a heterarchical architecture for mental imagery centered on the left fusiform imagery node. Their current work examines the interactions between crossmodal attention and consciousness, as well as the application of neuroscientific findings to interdisciplinary fields like implicit bias and theatrical performance.
0027.research_direction: Dr. Spagna has recently been investigating the neurocognitive architecture underlying internal visual representations and goal-directed behavior. Their recent work explores the shared and distinct mechanisms between visual mental imagery and perception across various semantic domains, utilizing behavioral psychophysics, trial-by-trial vividness tracking, and machine learning to probe how the brain generates internal visual experiences of features like colors, faces, and spatial layouts. A key focus of this research involves mapping the cortical networks of color processing and imagery with ultra-high field fMRI and neuropsychological data, specifically testing whether mental imagery relies on specialized high-level hubs in the ventral temporal cortex rather than simply running early visual areas in reverse. In parallel, they are examining the structural and functional intersections of attention, working memory, and executive control, synthesizing multimodal neuroimaging, brain stimulation, and clinical lesion data to map the core frontoparietal assemblies that support flexible cognition.

papers.title: Probing the Imaginable: Shared and Distinct Processes Between Imagery and Perception Across Semantic Domains
papers.abstract: This study investigates whether visual mental imagery (VMI) and perception utilize shared neurocognitive mechanisms across five distinct semantic categories: Colors, Faces, Letters, Maps, and Shapes. By developing and validating the English version of the Battery for Imagery and Perception (eBIP), the authors assessed 75 typical imagers on measures of performance accuracy, reaction times, and trial-by-trial subjective vividness. Findings indicate significant domain-specific performance differences in Color, Face, and Map categories, while correlations in performance metrics between modalities suggest common high-level semantic representations. Unsupervised machine learning revealed a latent space of four clusters, suggesting that VMI and perception are grounded in a modality-independent semantic code. Furthermore, the results demonstrate that trial-by-trial vividness ratings are superior to global vividness questionnaires in predicting actual behavioral performance.
papers.authors: Zixin Liu, Tengyu Song, Chloe Jeanne Lambert, Kassey Chang, Kezia Chuaqui, Natalie Baer, Rachel Frank, Jianghao Liu, Paolo Bartolomeo, Alfredo Spagna

papers.title: Colors in the mind's eye
papers.abstract: This review synthesizes neuropsychological and neuroimaging evidence to elucidate the cortical architecture of color processing and imagery, challenging the classical hierarchical 'perception in reverse' model. The authors highlight case studies of patients with cerebral achromatopsia and bilateral occipito-temporal lesions who maintain intact color imagery despite perceptual deficits. Integrating ultra-high field 7T fMRI data, they argue that color imagery is mediated by a specialized domain-general hub in the left fusiform gyrus (the Fusiform Imagery Node, FIN) and anterior color-biased regions in the ventral temporal cortex, rather than early visual areas (V1–V3). The article establishes the functional independence of color imagery from naming and perceptual experience, underscoring the critical role of high-level temporal regions in generating conscious internal representations.
papers.authors: Paolo Bartolomeo, Jianghao Liu, Alfredo Spagna

papers.title: Same, Same but Different? A Multi-Method Review of the Processes Underlying Executive Control
papers.abstract: This review evaluates the complex relationships between attention, working memory, and executive control, which are often treated as separate but highly interactive cognitive functions. By analyzing longitudinal data from clinical lesion studies, invasive and non-invasive multimodal neuroimaging, and brain stimulation, the authors seek to identify the core neural assemblies supporting goal-directed behavior. The paper proposes a lower-dimensional framework to characterize the functional and anatomical overlap of these processes, emphasizing the role of the frontoparietal control network in coordinating flexible behavior. The synthesis aims to provide a comprehensive anatomo-functional model with testable hypotheses to improve clinical interventions for dysexecutive syndromes.
papers.authors: Monica N. Toba, Tal Seidel Malkinson, Henrietta Howells, Melissa-Ann Mackie, Alfredo Spagna

0028.name: Alice J. O'Toole
0028.institution: The University of Texas at Dallas
0028.department: School of Behavioral and Brain Sciences
0028.bio: Alice J. O'Toole is a Professor and holder of the Aage and Margareta Møller Endowed Chair, conducting research that integrates psychology, computer science, and neuroscience to examine human and machine perception of faces and bodies. O'Toole's work utilizes deep convolutional neural networks (DCNNs) and machine learning to model high-level visual representations, comparing algorithmic performance with human expertise in forensic face identification. They use methodologies such as psychophysics and functional neuroimaging to investigate how identity, gender, and viewpoint are encoded within neural populations and computational architectures. Recent investigations by O'Toole focus on the robustness of face representations in real-world viewing conditions and the potential biases inherent in automated recognition systems.
0028.research_direction: Dr. O'Toole's recent work explores the intersection of biological and artificial vision, focusing on the mechanisms underlying human face and body identification. They have recently been investigating the latent representational spaces of deep neural networks to understand how these models process spatial facial configurations, implicitly extract demographic traits like gender, and perform long-term person re-identification across challenging viewpoint and clothing changes. Additionally, their research develops rigorous psychophysical instruments to measure visual expertise phenomena like the other-race effect without response bias, and examines the statistical and psychological conditions required to optimize human-machine collaboration in high-stakes recognition tasks.

papers.title: Unlocking the power of partnership: How humans and machines can work together to improve face recognition
papers.abstract: This study examines the computational and psychological conditions under which human-machine collaboration optimizes face identification accuracy. The researchers propose the Proximal Accuracy Rule (PAR), which suggests that the efficacy of statistical fusion between two agents—human or machine—is inversely related to the difference in their baseline performance levels. By analyzing data from forensic experts and untrained individuals alongside state-of-the-art algorithms, the authors identify a substantial 'critical fusion zone' where combining a human reviewer with a superior algorithm still enhances overall system performance. The work provides an evidence-based framework for intelligent human-AI integration, utilizing graph matching theory to optimize partnerships and minimize the impact of individual human errors on high-stakes identification tasks.
papers.authors: P. Jonathon Phillips, Géraldine Jeckeln, Carina A. Hahn, Amy N. Yates, P. C. Fontana, Alice J. O'Toole

papers.title: Constructing a cross-race face identity triad test
papers.abstract: The authors introduce the Cross-Race Face Identity Triad (CR-FIT) test, a rigorous diagnostic instrument designed to measure the other-race effect (ORE) while eliminating the confound of response bias. Unlike traditional matching tasks, the CR-FIT employs image triads—consisting of two images of a target identity and one foil—forcing a 3-alternative choice that standardizes the decision criterion across observers. To ensure that performance disparities reflect perceptual expertise rather than stimulus variance, the researchers utilized deep convolutional neural network (DCNN) similarity scores and human pilot data to match the difficulty of African American and Caucasian face sets. Findings confirm a robust ORE across diverse populations, establishing the test as a suitable metric for assessing face matching proficiency in both forensic and research contexts.
papers.authors: Géraldine Jeckeln, Alice J. O'Toole

papers.title: The Early Bird Identifies the Worm: You Can't Beat a Head Start in Long-Term Body Re-ID (ECHO-BID)
papers.abstract: This research investigates the transferability of vision foundation models (VFMs) to the problem of long-term person re-identification (re-id) in unconstrained environments characterized by viewpoint variance, clothing changes, and distance. The authors evaluate four prominent VFMs (CLIP, DINOv2, AIMv2, and EVA-02) and demonstrate that domain-specific fine-tuning of these large-scale backbones allows them to significantly outperform traditional specialized re-id models. The proposed ECHO-BID (Eva Clothes-Change from Hidden Objects - Body IDentification) model, based on the EVA-02 Large architecture, demonstrates superior robustness to occlusion and environmental covariates. Ablation studies reveal that the scale of pretraining and the complexity of the transfer learning protocol are the primary drivers of this performance advantage in identifying people across temporal gaps.
papers.authors: Thomas M. Metz, Matthew Q. Hill, Alice J. O'Toole

papers.title: Dissecting human body representations in deep networks trained for person identification
papers.abstract: This paper provides a granular analysis of the latent representational structures within deep neural networks optimized for long-term body identification. By probing the embeddings of four distinct architectures (including Vision Transformers and CNNs) trained on millions of person images, the authors show that these models implicitly extract facial identity features and encode social categories like gender despite lacking explicit supervision for these traits. Furthermore, image-based covariates such as viewpoint (yaw) and source dataset origin are found to be linearly decodable from the embeddings. Critically, the study demonstrates that identity verification accuracy can be enhanced by performing comparisons within specific principal component subspaces, effectively filtering out noise-related variance without necessitating model retraining.
papers.venue: arXiv preprint / 19th IEEE International Conference on Face and Gesture Recognition
papers.authors: Thomas M. Metz, Matthew Q. Hill, Blake Myers, Veda Nandan Gandi, Rahul Chilakapati, Alice J. O'Toole

papers.title: Deep convolutional neural networks are sensitive to face configuration
papers.abstract: The study investigates whether deep convolutional neural networks (DCNNs) trained for face identification utilize configural information (the spatial arrangement of features) similar to the human visual system. Using a diagnostic paradigm that independently manipulates facial features (e.g., swapping eyes) and facial configuration (e.g., altering inter-ocular distance), the researchers quantified the resulting representational shifts in DCNN embedding space. While both feature and configural changes significantly altered the networks' outputs, sensitivity to configural information was found to increase significantly across hierarchical layers, far exceeding the sensitivity of low-level pixel representations. These findings suggest that DCNNs emerge as robust models of human-like configural processing, reconciliating computational efficiency with biological principles of face expertise.
papers.authors: Virginia E. Strehle, Natalie K. Bendiksen, Alice J. O'Toole

0029.name: Alisa Baron
0029.lab_name: Processing and Acquisition of Language in Multilinguals (PALM) Laboratory
0029.bio: Alisa Baron is an Associate Professor at the University of Rhode Island and directs the Processing and Acquisition of Language in Multilinguals (PALM) Laboratory. Baron’s research investigates the neurocognitive mechanisms underlying first and second language acquisition, focusing on bilingual grammar and literacy development in neurotypical and language-disordered populations. Utilizing a multi-modal approach including eye-tracking, electroencephalography (EEG), and functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS), Baron examines how cross-linguistic influences shape language processing and audio-visual integration. Their work aims to advance evidence-based assessment and intervention strategies for culturally and linguistically diverse children and individuals with neurodevelopmental disorders.
0029.research_direction: Dr. Baron has recently been investigating the neurocognitive and oculomotor mechanisms that support language processing, reading acquisition, and speech perception across diverse populations. Their recent work explores real-time linguistic processing using eye-tracking, specifically examining how rapid naming automaticity relates to gaze behavior during early reading and how bilingual children use grammatical gender cues to guide visual attention during word recognition. They are also utilizing neurophysiological methods, such as ERPs and fNIRS, to probe how neural discrimination of speech sounds predicts reading fluency and how dual-language exposure shapes the cortical networks underlying morphosyntactic processing. Furthermore, Dr. Baron is extending these behavioral paradigms into clinical interventions, investigating whether digital training applications that direct visual attention toward facial articulators can successfully support audiovisual speech integration in young adults with autism.

papers.title: Rapid Automatized Naming (RAN) and Word Reading Fluency in Early School-Aged Children: A Pilot Eye-Tracking Study
papers.abstract: While rapid automatized naming (RAN) is an established clinical predictor of word reading fluency, the oculomotor mechanisms subserving this relationship in emergent readers remain poorly understood. This investigation evaluated whether behavioral alphanumeric RAN performance (rapid letter naming [RLN] and rapid digit naming [RDN]) predicted gaze metrics across discrete temporal stages of local word reading. Thirty-three English-speaking early school-aged children (ages 6–8) completed standardized RAN assessments and an eye-tracking paradigm during oral sentence reading containing embedded target words. Dependent oculomotor measures indexed early (first fixation duration), intermediate (regression path duration), and late (total word reading time) processing stages. Linear mixed-effects regression demonstrated that RLN and RDN exclusively accounted for significant variance in regression path duration, such that faster naming speed was associated with shorter regressive durations from the target words. Neither early nor late fixation durations were reliably predicted by RAN scores. These findings indicate that RAN automaticity uniquely indexes intermediate oculomotor processing during word identification, suggesting that slower naming speeds reflect bottlenecks in the real-time integration of visual-orthographic and phonological representations.
papers.authors: Alisa Baron, Alexia Martins, Gavino Puggioni, Vanessa Harwood

papers.title: Using the Listening2Faces App with Three Young Adults with Autism: A Feasibility Study
papers.abstract: Individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) frequently exhibit atypical audiovisual speech integration alongside significant communication challenges. This pilot investigation assessed the feasibility, usability, and clinical implementation of Listening2Faces (L2F)—a specialized digital training application engineered to reinforce audiovisual speech perception by targeting gaze toward visible articulatory dynamics (mouth and jaw movements). Three young adults with ASD and complex communication needs completed baseline evaluations followed by multi-session computerized training using L2F within an educational setting. Individualized behavioral adaptations and behavioral supports, including cognitive picture rehearsal and token reinforcement, were implemented to maintain engagement and mitigate task-related distress. Feasibility was indexed via compliance, session completion rates, and progression through hierarchically structured perceptual difficulty tiers. All three participants successfully executed the baseline auditory noise assessment (ANA) and completed eight or more difficulty levels within the application, with one participant finishing the entire intervention protocol. Although individual trajectories and engagement profiles differed, the findings demonstrate the feasibility of application-based audiovisual speech perception training paired with tailored behavioral supports for autistic individuals with complex communication profiles.
papers.authors: Alisa Baron, Vanessa Harwood, Cooper Woodard, Kaitlyn Anderson, Barbara Fernandes, Jessica Sullivan, Julia Irwin

papers.title: Grammatical gender in spoken word recognition in school-age Spanish monolingual and Spanish–English bilingual children
papers.abstract: This study investigated the online processing of grammatical gender during auditory word recognition in Spanish-speaking school-aged children with varying degrees of cumulative English language exposure. Using a visual world eye-tracking paradigm with a four-alternative forced-choice visual display, children heard gender-marked definite articles followed by target nouns under conditions where distractor objects had either matching or mismatching grammatical gender, as well as grammatical versus ungrammatical article-noun pairings. Cluster-based permutation analyses were applied to fixations across the article and noun acoustic intervals. Results revealed robust lexical facilitation effects across all participants during the noun interval, alongside pronounced processing disruption and delayed target fixations during ungrammatical article-noun presentations. Furthermore, cumulative English exposure and chronological age significantly modulated gaze distributions: children with higher English exposure showed reduced overall fixations to target nouns, whereas older children demonstrated elevated target fixation rates. Additionally, lower English exposure was associated with an interaction between target noun gender (masculine vs. feminine) and competitor condition, with heightened target fixations in different-gender contexts for masculine items. These findings demonstrate that bilingual children preserve syntactic gender congruency constraints during auditory recognition, while exposure profile modulates the efficiency of lexical retrieval.
papers.authors: Alisa Baron, Katrina Connell, Daniel Kleinman, Lisa M. Bedore, Zenzi M. Griffin

papers.title: Event Related Potentials to Native Speech Contrasts Predicts Word Reading Abilities in Early School-Aged Children
papers.abstract: Fine-grained phonemic discrimination provides a neurobiological scaffolding for phoneme-grapheme correspondence and fluent word decoding; however, the precise electrophysiological dynamics linking phonological tuning to reading acquisition require clarification. This study examined auditory event-related potentials (ERPs) elicited in 33 typically developing monolingual English-speaking children aged 6 to 8 years within an auditory oddball paradigm presenting native English (/ba/ vs. /da/) and nonnative Spanish (/ba/ vs. dental /da/) consonant-vowel contrast pairs. Evoked responses were recorded over bilateral temporal and frontocentral electrode sites to determine discrimination-related components (acoustic change complex and late discriminative negativity). Standardized behavioral assessments of reading accuracy and rate were administered concurrently. Electrophysiological results indicated robust discrimination responses to native phonetic contrasts that significantly correlated with standardized single-word and pseudoword reading fluency measures. In contrast, neural sensitivity to nonnative acoustic tokens did not account for variance in English word decoding performance. These findings indicate that neuroplastic perceptual narrowing specifically optimized for native phonological categories directly supports the orthographic-phonological integration requisite for developing literacy skills.
papers.authors: Vanessa Harwood, Adrian Garcia-Sierra, Raphael Dias, Emily Jelfs, Alisa Baron

papers.title: Neural Correlates of Morphosyntactic Processing in Spanish–English Bilingual Children: A Functional Near-Infrared Spectroscopy Study
papers.abstract: Dual-language exposure fundamentally shapes neural specialization for morphosyntactic computation during childhood. This study employed functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) to delineate the cortical substrates of English grammatical processing in school-age Spanish–English bilingual children (ages 6–10), examining how age of acquisition, chronological age, and relative language usage modulate hemodynamic activity. Children listened to grammatical and ungrammatical English sentences manipulating early-acquired (present progressive -ing) and late-acquired (past tense -ed and third-person singular -s) morphosyntactic morphemes while optical absorption was recorded over bilateral inferior frontal gyri (IFG) and superior temporal gyri (STG). Bilateral frontal and temporal engagement emerged during syntactic violation detection, with greater oxy-hemoglobin (HbO) increases in left anterior cortical regions for morphosyntactic anomalies. Moreover, chronological age and greater current English exposure predicted pronounced left-lateralized IFG recruitment for later-acquired grammatical morphemes, whereas early-acquired morphemes engaged bilateral peri-sylvian networks across age cohorts. The findings demonstrate that neurodevelopmental specialization for second-language morphology is non-uniform across syntactic forms and dynamically mediated by cumulative and current environmental language input.
papers.venue: Journal of Speech, Language, and Hearing Research
papers.authors: Alisa Baron, Neelima Wagley, Xiaosu Hu, Ioulia Kovelman

0030.name: Allison B. Sekuler
0030.department: Department of Psychology; Department of Psychology, Neuroscience & Behaviour
0030.bio: Allison B. Sekuler holds the Sandra A. Rotman Chair in Cognitive Neuroscience, specializing in vision science and the neuroscience of aging. Their research employs psychophysical, electrophysiological (EEG), and neuroimaging (fMRI) methodologies to examine the neural mechanisms of visual perception, including face processing, motion perception, and perceptual learning. Sekuler’s work has documented functional brain plasticity, illustrating how the aging brain undergoes compensatory changes to maintain performance levels during physiological decline. Currently, Sekuler directs translational initiatives focused on developing neurotechnological interventions and biomarkers for the detection and treatment of dementia and age-related cognitive impairment.
0030.research_direction: Dr. Sekuler has recently been investigating the perceptual and cognitive mechanisms underlying age-related changes in vision, with a strong focus on face processing. Their recent work explores the specific sources of older adults' face discrimination deficits by modeling internal noise and calculation efficiency through external noise masking and double-pass consistency paradigms, as well as by probing spatial sampling strategies via gaze-contingent fixation tracking. Beyond basic visual processing, they are also examining the broader intersection of perception and memory, utilizing psychophysical techniques like multidimensional scaling to quantify how sensory declines influence cognitive outcomes and neural compensation. Extending their research into applied neurotechnology, they have recently been developing transformer-based deep learning architectures designed to leverage extended temporal context for robust, automated EEG seizure detection in clinical and home-monitoring environments.

papers.title: The Effect of Fixation Location on Face Perception in Younger and Older Adults
papers.abstract: This psychophysical investigation examined how constrained fixation positions—on the forehead, eyes, nose, or mouth—modulate face identity perception across the adult lifespan. Utilizing both off-face and on-face gaze-contingent paradigms, the study characterized inter-individual and age-related variations in fixation strategies. While older adults naturally displayed a downward shift in fixation patterns compared to younger adults, restricting gaze to highly diagnostic regions like the eye and nose significantly attenuated age-related performance deficits. The findings suggest that suboptimal sampling strategies contribute to age-related declines in face processing and that directing gaze to specific feature-rich regions can enhance identification accuracy in older populations.
papers.authors: Eric Cui, Farhan Vaheed, Matthew Clark, Björn Herrmann, Allison Sekuler

papers.title: Contribution of internal noise and calculation efficiency to face discrimination deficits in older adults
papers.abstract: This study quantified the underlying mechanisms of age-related face discrimination impairments by assessing the relative roles of internal noise and calculation efficiency. Using an external noise masking framework and a double-pass response consistency paradigm, the researchers estimated the equivalent input noise and calculation efficiency (k-parameter) in younger and older adults. Results from Experiment 1 demonstrated that older adults exhibit significantly higher equivalent input noise and lower calculation efficiency compared to younger controls. Experiment 2 revealed no significant age differences in the internal-to-external noise ratio, indicating that declines in face identification are primarily driven by reduced efficiency in sampling diagnostic information and increased additive internal noise rather than changes in multiplicative noise levels.
papers.authors: Sarah E. Creighton, Patrick J. Bennett, Allison B. Sekuler

papers.title: Perceptual Attributes in Memory Research
papers.abstract: This comprehensive chapter evaluates the intersection of perception and memory, emphasizing the critical importance of stimulus control and perceptual attribute scaling in experimental memory paradigms. The authors advocate for a stimulus-oriented approach, demonstrating how psychophysical measurements like multidimensional scaling (MDS) can establish similarity spaces that predict memory performance. The work further explores how age-related changes in sensory systems—such as reduced contrast sensitivity and visual acuity—impact cognitive outcomes, and discusses the bidirectional compensatory mechanisms where older brains reorganize neural networks to support perceptual tasks using memory-related regions like the hippocampus.
papers.venue: The Oxford Handbook of Human Memory
papers.authors: Robert Sekuler, Allison B. Sekuler

papers.title: LookAroundNet: Extending Temporal Context with Transformers for Clinically Viable EEG Seizure Detection
papers.abstract: In this paper, a novel transformer-based architecture named LookAroundNet is introduced to enhance the clinical viability of automated epileptic seizure detection in long-term electroencephalography (EEG). Addressing the limitations of small datasets and narrow temporal windows in existing models, LookAroundNet leverages extended temporal context and a diverse training set comprising clinical and home-monitoring recordings (including data from 6,029 subjects). The model generalizes across various recording conditions and achieves high segment-based specificity (99.62%) and accuracy, demonstrating that integrated temporal context and model ensembling are essential for robust seizure detection in unconstrained, real-world monitoring environments.
papers.authors: Ali Hashemi, Lou Pino, Graeme Moffat, Allison B. Sekuler

0031.name: Allison M Mckendrick
0031.department: Discipline of Optometry, School of Allied Health
0031.bio: Allison M. McKendrick is the Lions Eye Institute UWA Chair in Optometry Research and a Professorial Fellow at the University of Melbourne, specializing in the field of visual neuroscience. McKendrick's research program investigates the mechanisms of visual processing in healthy aging and pathological conditions such as glaucoma, migraine, and visual snow syndrome. They employ a multi-disciplinary methodology that integrates clinical psychophysics, human electrophysiology, and high-resolution ocular and brain imaging to develop diagnostic tests and monitor disease progression. Their current work focuses on translating these findings into applications, particularly regarding how vision loss impacts daily activities such as night-time driving performance.
0031.research_direction: Dr. McKendrick has recently been investigating the functional consequences and clinical assessment of glaucoma, exploring whether the disease differentially impacts ON and OFF retinocortical contrast pathways during visual search, while also developing dynamic perimetry algorithms to personalize macular and peripheral visual field testing. Their recent work examines real-world visual performance in low-luminance environments, utilizing psychophysical motion thresholds and simulated driving tasks to understand night-time hazard recognition and how specific binocular visual field defects impair low-light daily activities. Additionally, they are employing qualitative research to identify the clinical and psychosocial barriers that patients with dementia face when accessing primary vision care, aiming to establish more adaptive clinical testing protocols for this vulnerable population.

papers.title: Association between vision-related difficulties in low light levels and visual fields in glaucoma
papers.abstract: This cross-sectional investigation quantified the correlation between patient-reported visual impairment in low-luminance environments and the severity of binocular 24-2 visual field (VF) loss in primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG). Utilizing the Low Luminance Questionnaire (LLQ) and binocularly integrated visual fields (IVF) synthesized from monocular sensitivities via the best-location method, piecewise linear regression was employed to identify functional breakpoints. Findings demonstrated that log-transformed composite LLQ scores declined significantly at IVF mean sensitivities below 21.7 dB and total deviation values less than -6.3 dB. Regional analysis indicated that defects in the inferior IVF were uniquely associated with increased difficulties in low-light tasks, particularly night driving, even after adjusting for age, gender, lens status, and visual acuity.
papers.authors: Maanasi Mahalingam, Jason Charng, Vanessa T S Tang, Bill Morgan, Geoffrey Chan, Andrew Turpin, Allison M McKendrick

papers.title: Breaking down barriers to accessing dementia-friendly eyecare
papers.abstract: This qualitative study explored the clinical and psychosocial barriers preventing patients with Alzheimer’s disease and related dementias from accessing effective primary eyecare. Through semi-structured interviews with people living with dementia, family caregivers, and optometrists, researchers utilized framework analysis to produce an integrated perspective on the diagnostic and management pipeline. Five primary themes were established: the high value of vision for maintaining independence, the heterogeneous impact of dementia on traditional visual function testing, the necessity of adaptive clinical protocols, the characteristics of a supportive eye-test experience, and significant deficiencies in specialized dementia education for optometrists. The results suggest that targeted professional training and proactive diagnostic disclosure are essential for providing equitable vision care in this population.
papers.authors: Marianne Piano, Bao Nguyen, Jeanette Conrick, Lynette Joubert, Allison M McKendrick

papers.title: Visual motion perception and driving hazard visibility at night-time
papers.abstract: This investigation probed the functional association between psychophysical motion processing and hazard recognition performance under mesopic driving conditions. Seventy licensed drivers, including those with ocular pathologies, were evaluated on a battery of motion tasks: minimum displacement thresholds (Dmin), drifting Gabor velocity/contrast sensitivity, and motion surround suppression. Hazard recognition speed was quantified using a validated computer-based Night-time Hazard Visibility Test (NHVT). Multivariate regression models revealed that Dmin was the sole independent predictor of hazard response latency when adjusted for conventional chart-based visual acuity and contrast sensitivity.
