These findings indicate that the neural mechanisms underlying small-displacement motion detection are critical for identifying moving hazards in low-light environments and may serve as a functional biomarker for night driving safety.
papers.authors: Catherine Kennon, Joanne M. Wood, Philippe F. Lacherez, Alex A. Black, David Cuda, Emily Henry, Allison M McKendrick

papers.title: Contrast increment and decrement processing measured using visual search in established glaucoma
papers.abstract: This study tested whether the progression of glaucomatous visual field loss differentially impacts the ON and OFF retinocortical pathways, which process contrast increments and decrements, respectively. Fifty-one participants with established glaucoma and 25 controls performed psychophysical search tasks targeting incremental and decremental stimuli. Analysis revealed that while overall search response times increased significantly as a function of visual field mean deviation (MD), the rates of performance decline for increment and decrement processing were statistically equivalent. Furthermore, individuals with central-involving perimetric defects were markedly slower than those with central-sparing loss. These findings do not support the hypothesis of selective OFF retinal ganglion cell (RGC) vulnerability in humans, suggesting instead that glaucoma exerts a balanced impact on both ON and OFF contrast-processing channels.
papers.authors: Vanessa Thien Sze Tang, Andrew Turpin, William Huxley Morgan, Geoffrey Chan, Allison Maree McKendrick

papers.title: Personalizing the Transition From 24-2 to 10-2 Visual Field Testing Using ARREST – A Simulation Study
papers.abstract: This simulation-based study evaluated the A10 algorithm, a variant of the Australian Reduced Range Extended Spatial Test (ARREST), designed to dynamically integrate high-density 10-2 macular test locations into standard 24-2 perimetric grids. Utilizing a longitudinal dataset of 126 glaucomatous eyes, the A10 strategy was compared against the standard ZEST 24-2 procedure. The A10 approach successfully prioritized macular sampling in eyes with central damage without increasing total presentation counts or compromising the detection of peripheral field progression. The results demonstrate that personalized perimetry enables higher spatial resolution in individually relevant macular areas without neglecting the more peripheral visual field, potentially improving the clinical identification of central glaucomatous change.
papers.authors: Andrew Turpin, William H. Morgan, Allison M. McKendrick

0032.name: Alon Hafri
0032.department: Department of Linguistics and Cognitive Science
0032.bio: Alon Hafri is an Assistant Professor in the Department of Linguistics and Cognitive Science at the University of Delaware and the director of the Perception and Language (PAL) Lab. Hafri’s research focuses on the interface between vision and language, specifically investigating how the visual system extracts abstract relational structures—such as event roles and spatial configurations—from visual scenes. Utilizing psychophysics, functional MRI, and psycholinguistic techniques, they explore whether visual representations share a common compositional format with linguistic structures. Hafri’s work has demonstrated that relational information is processed rapidly and automatically, suggesting that perception provides structured content to higher-level cognitive systems.
0032.research_direction: Dr. Hafri has recently been investigating how the visual system extracts abstract, structured representations from the environment to inform higher-order cognition. Their recent work explores the psychophysics of visual compositionality, asking how relational properties—such as the physical "fitting" of object parts or the hierarchical roles of "figure" and "reference" items in a scene—govern fundamental processes like numerosity estimation and the temporal dynamics of scene processing. Bridging vision with language and development, they are also examining how perceptual event structures, like agents acting on patients, map onto linguistic syntax using artificial language learning and prelinguistic infant research. Finally, their research extends into high-level social vision, investigating the phenomenon of "moral thin-slicing" to understand how observers extract complex character impressions from extremely brief visual glimpses of others.

papers.title: Part–whole effects in visual number estimation
papers.abstract: This study investigates the fundamental 'units' of visual numerosity estimation, specifically whether the approximate number system (ANS) operates on discrete, bounded individuals or potential composite wholes. Through a series of four psychophysical experiments, we demonstrate that perceived numerosity is significantly reduced in displays where 'puzzle-piece' stimuli are geometrically combinable (i.e., they can form a unified whole through a 'fitting' relation) compared to matched displays of non-combinable pieces. This effect persisted despite explicit training to count individual components and was robust to low-level visual controls. Our findings suggest that the visual system automatically integrates object parts into potential wholes based on relational properties before extracting numerical magnitude, indicating that relational 'fitting' is a core principle of perceptual unit formation.
papers.authors: Chenxiao Guan, David Schwitzgebel, Chaz Firestone, Alon Hafri

papers.title: The psychophysics of compositionality: Relational scene perception occurs in a canonical order
papers.abstract: We explore the temporal dynamics of visual compositionality, testing the hypothesis that the mind constructs relational scene representations (e.g., 'vase on table') in a systematic, canonical order. Drawing on cognitive linguistic distinctions between 'figure' and 'reference' objects, we use five experiments to show that relational scene perception is significantly faster and more accurate when reference objects (typically larger, more stable entities that exert physical control) are processed before figure objects. This 'reference-first' advantage emerges rapidly (within 100 ms of stimulus onset) and persists in purely visual tasks devoid of linguistic descriptors. The results suggest that the 'syntax' of visual composition follows abstract structural principles shared with natural language, where entities are integrated into relational hierarchies according to their specific roles.
papers.authors: Zekun Sun, Chaz Firestone, Alon Hafri

papers.title: Moral thin-slicing: Forming moral impressions from a brief glance
papers.abstract: This research examines 'moral thin-slicing'—the capacity to extract moral-character evaluations from extremely brief visual exposures to others. Across multiple experiments, we show that observers can form reliable impressions of an individual’s moral traits from rapid, incidental glimpses. These spontaneous judgments exhibit high degrees of consensus and accurately reflect long-term moral evaluations made under deliberative conditions. Our findings indicate that morality-relevant social information is processed rapidly and automatically by the perceptual system, suggesting that high-level moral cognition is deeply rooted in sophisticated perceptual mechanisms that categorize social agents based on subtle visual cues.
papers.venue: The Journal of Experimental Social Psychology
papers.authors: Julian De Freitas, Alon Hafri

papers.title: Constraints on syntactic-conceptual mapping: the learnability of 'inverse verbs'
papers.abstract: This work characterizes the constraints governing the mapping between linguistic syntax and conceptual event representations. We specifically investigate the learnability of 'inverse verbs'—hypothetical lexical items that systematically map the Patient of a causal event to the syntactic Subject position and the Agent to the Object position. Using an artificial language learning paradigm, we demonstrate that human learners exhibit a robust bias toward canonical Agent-as-Subject mappings, finding inverse verbs significantly more difficult to acquire. These results suggest that the space of possible human languages is constrained by innate conceptual structures that privilege certain thematic-to-syntactic correspondences, providing empirical support for the conceptual nativist framework of language development.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the 50th Annual Penn Linguistics Conference
papers.authors: Tyler Knowlton, Alon Hafri

papers.title: The origins of structured thought in the mind
papers.abstract: This dispatch evaluates recent developmental evidence concerning the prelinguistic foundations of the 'language of thought' (LoT). Reviewing findings that seven-month-old infants can represent abstract relational structures—such as distinguishing between 'A chasing B' and 'B chasing A'—before acquiring linguistic syntax, I argue that these capabilities suggest a representational format characterized by role-filler independence and compositionality. These results imply that the ability to entertain structured, propositional thoughts is an inherent property of human core knowledge systems, likely implemented by perceptual mechanisms that extract abstract relational categories from the visual environment prior to the onset of language.
papers.authors: Alon Hafri

0033.name: Alon Zivony
0033.bio: Alon Zivony is a cognitive neuroscientist and Lecturer at the University of Sheffield whose research examines the temporal dynamics of selective attention and its role in object perception. Zivony developed the "diachronic" framework of attention, which characterizes attentional selection as a process unfolding through "attentional episodes" that regulate the encoding of sensory data into working memory. Their work employs behavioral psychophysics and electrophysiological methods (EEG/ERP) to dissociate the effects of category-based expectations from attentional engagement. Prior to joining Sheffield, Zivony completed a PhD at Tel-Aviv University and conducted postdoctoral research at Birkbeck, University of London, under Newton and Marie-Curie fellowships.
0033.research_direction: Dr. Zivony's recent work primarily explores the temporal dynamics of visual selective attention and working memory, frequently utilizing rapid serial visual presentation (RSVP) paradigms to isolate these mechanisms. They have recently been investigating how top-down factors, such as probabilistic expectations and long-term memory familiarity, influence working memory encoding independently of spatial attention, alongside examining how attention coordinates feature binding across rapid intervals to prevent temporal illusory conjunctions. Additionally, their research seeks to establish robust psychometric tools for measuring individual differences in the speed of attentional engagement by analyzing distractor intrusion rates. Finally, branching beyond visual cognition, Dr. Zivony also examines clinical biases, specifically investigating how societal stereotypes regarding bisexual individuals impact psychotherapists' diagnostic evaluations.

papers.title: Long-term memory speeds encoding, independently of attention
papers.abstract: This study tested whether the accelerated working memory (WM) consolidation observed for familiar items relies on an attention-independent long-term memory (LTM) template-matching mechanism rather than increased attentional priority. Observers completed a rapid serial visual presentation (RSVP) task using an invariant shape cue to select target letters presented in either English or Hebrew to native English and native Hebrew speakers. Experiments 1 and 2 demonstrated a significant accuracy advantage for familiar native-language targets over non-native targets. In Experiment 2, peripheral distractors were introduced to elicit an attentional blink (AB); while target familiarity boosted identification accuracy, familiar and unfamiliar peripheral distractors triggered AB effects of identical magnitude, confirming equivalent capacity to capture spatial attention. Experiment 3 blocked the target alphabet and showed that the familiarity benefit persisted, ruling out response bias toward native orthography. These findings demonstrate that preexisting LTM representations facilitate the rate of WM consolidation via template matching independently of selective attention.
papers.authors: Abigail Wyllie, Claudia C. von Bastian, Alon Zivony

papers.title: Measuring individual differences in the speed of attention using the distractor intrusion task
papers.abstract: Assessing individual differences in the temporal speed of attention is hindered by the low reliability and non-attentional latency confounds typical of reaction-time metrics in visual search. This investigation examined the psychometric viability of post-target distractor intrusion (DI) frequencies within the rapid serial visual presentation (RSVP) paradigm as an index of attentional engagement speed. Across three experiments reanalyzing and extending RSVP datasets, DI rates exhibited high internal consistency and 1-year test–retest reliability exceeding r = .90, achievable even with brief testing durations (~5 minutes). Furthermore, DI rates selectively correlated with external measures tied to attentional processing speed, while exhibiting divergent validity through absent or negligible correlations with executive attentional control, reading fluency, and attentional blink magnitudes. The distractor intrusion paradigm thus offers an efficient, robust, and psychometrically sound instrument for evaluating individual variation in the latency of transient visual attention.
papers.authors: Alon Zivony, Claudia C. von Bastian, Rachel Pye

papers.title: A dissociation between the effects of expectations and attention in selective visual processing
papers.abstract: Whether probabilistic expectation modulates sensory perception directly or solely via selective attention remains heavily debated due to methodological difficulties in isolating the two mechanisms. Here, expectations and selective visual attention were experimentally decoupled within an RSVP paradigm. Observers searched for targets demarcated by low-level physical cues (color or shape) while probabilistic expectations regarding alphanumeric category (letters vs. digits) were systematically varied across four experiments (N = 60). Category-level expectations failed to interact with or modulate selective attentional allocation, exerting their influence exclusively during downstream working memory encoding stages. Control analyses ruled out intertrial repetition priming and decision-level response bias. These findings provide empirical support for models positing that expectation and selective attention operate as dissociable cognitive mechanisms, demonstrating direct, attention-independent impacts of expectation on visual representation.
papers.authors: Alon Zivony, Martin Eimer

papers.title: Attention and feature binding in the temporal domain
papers.abstract: While illusory conjunctions in the spatial domain have been extensively characterized, the mechanisms governing feature binding across rapid temporal intervals remain unresolved. This study examined the involvement of selective attention in temporal feature integration and the consequences of attentional engagement latency. Participants monitored an RSVP stream to identify a cued target and reported both its hue and alphanumeric identity. Erroneous feature conjunctions across time were prevalent. Crucially, when participants committed an intrusion error by reporting the identity of an adjacent distractor instead of the target, they exhibited a concurrent increase in the likelihood of reporting that specific distractor's color. This inter-feature dependency was robust both within single participants and across individual variations. The results indicate that the temporal window demarcated by attentional engagement coordinates the co-binding of transient visual features, aligning with a diachronic model of visual attention.
papers.authors: Alon Zivony, Martin Eimer

papers.title: Bisexual stereotypes in clinical evaluation
papers.abstract: This research investigates whether psychotherapists' clinical judgments are influenced by prevailing societal stereotypes concerning bisexual individuals, specifically the notions that they are inherently confused or psychologically immature. Utilizing multiple regression analysis, the study assessed how evaluations of diagnostic issues in hypothetical bisexual clients correlate with therapists' adherence to these identity-based stereotypes. Results indicate that psychotherapists frequently endorse stereotypical beliefs similar to those held by the general public, regardless of their personal acquaintance with bisexual individuals. The findings suggest that these biases significantly skew clinical evaluations, potentially leading to inaccurate diagnoses and compromised therapeutic outcomes for bisexual clients.
papers.venue: Psychology of Sexual Orientation and Gender Diversity
papers.authors: Ori Ferster, Alon Zivony

0038.name: Anastasia Kiyonaga
0038.bio: Anastasia Kiyonaga is an Assistant Professor in the Department of Cognitive Science at the University of California, San Diego. Kiyonaga’s research investigates the neural mechanisms underlying the interaction between working memory, attention, and action, focusing on how the brain maintains goal-directed representations amidst environmental distractions. They employ a multi-modal methodology including functional MRI, transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), and oculomotor tracking to probe the competition between internal maintenance and external processing. Their work seeks to delineate the strategic control processes that manage these representational overlaps and their consequences for human behavior.
0038.research_direction: Dr. Kiyonaga has recently been investigating how visual working memory operates as a highly dynamic, goal-oriented process that extends outward into the peripheral nervous system. Their recent work explores how ocular signals, such as pupil size variations reflecting remembered brightness and the precise reinstatement of encoding gaze scanpaths, serve as active signatures of visual maintenance. Using methods like eye-tracking, stylus-tracking, and representational similarity analysis, they are examining how these peripheral sensorimotor traces flexibly adapt to shifting task demands, such as changes in the anticipated motor response format or whether a task prioritizes granular visual details over broad semantic categories. Ultimately, they are working to uncover how top-down behavioral priorities, prospective action plans, and individual differences in subjective mental imagery dynamically modulate the way the nervous system allocates and sustains transient mental representations.

papers.title: Windows to the goal: Pupillary working memory signatures prospectively adapt to task demands
papers.abstract: This research investigates the functional properties of the pupillary working memory (WM) response, specifically evaluating its generalizability to naturalistic scene stimuli and its flexibility in response to prospective behavioral goals. Utilizing natural images that varied in brightness, the study manipulated whether participants maintained a visual representation (visual detail) or a semantic one (category) during the WM delay. Results demonstrated that pupil size reflected the remembered brightness of the scene—a content-specific pupillary signature—but this effect was selectively observed when the task prioritized visual maintenance strategies. These findings indicate that the pupillary WM signal is not a passive sensory echo but a goal-dependent signature that adaptively recruits early sensorimotor pathways according to the intended use of the stored information.
papers.authors: Yueying Dong, Yun-chen Hung, Connie Xie, Anastasia Kiyonaga

papers.title: Flexible gaze reinstatement during working memory for natural scenes
papers.abstract: This study characterizes the functional role of gaze reinstatement—the retracing of visual scanpaths from encoding—during the maintenance of natural scene information in working memory (WM). By integrating eye-tracking with time-resolved representational similarity analysis (RSA) and convolutional neural network (CNN) modeling, the research assessed whether delay-period gaze patterns carry specific visual content and respond to behavioral priority. The distinctive gaze-based representations of scene features were significantly more robust when task demands emphasized visual detail over semantic categorization. Furthermore, these content-specific patterns increased in anticipation of the memory probe. The evidence suggests that gaze reinstatement is a flexible maintenance mechanism that adaptively adjusts to the required granularity and priority of stored representations.
papers.authors: Yueying Dong, Yun Hung, Lana Gaspariani, Anastasia Kiyonaga

papers.title: Flexible Working Memory in the Peripheral Nervous System
papers.abstract: This investigation examines whether working memory (WM) representations are adaptively distributed across peripheral sensors and effectors to optimize behavioral outcomes. In a delayed orientation recall task with two distinct response formats (line-drawing and wheel-adjustment), the study employed stylus- and eye-tracking to decode remembered features from delay-period motor inflections. Results showed that remembered orientations were decodable from both gaze and hand movements, with the decoding strength in each peripheral system modulated by the task-relevant response mode: gaze patterns carried more information for wheel-adjustments, while hand movements were more informative for line-drawings. These findings provide evidence that WM content is flexibly allocated across the nervous system to optimize peripheral activity according to specific behavioral demands.
papers.authors: Sihan Yang, Yueying Dong, Anastasia Kiyonaga

papers.title: Beyond Routine Maintenance: Current Trends in Working Memory Research
papers.abstract: This review synthesizes the contemporary landscape of working memory (WM) research, framing WM as an evolving construct that functions as a dynamic, goal-oriented process. The authors highlight four prominent research trajectories: (1) the cross-modal characterization of WM function across sensory modalities; (2) the intrinsic malleability of WM representations based on context and prospective actions; (3) the enduring challenge of how multi-item information is structured and integrated; and (4) the functional overlap between WM and cognitive faculties traditionally viewed as distinct, such as attention. The synthesis delineates how multi-modal neuroscientific tools and modern theoretical frameworks are redefining our understanding of the neural architectures and computational principles that support transient mental representation.
papers.authors: Kirsten C S Adam, Laura-Isabelle Klatt, Jacob A Miller, Marlene Rösner, Keisuke Fukuda, Anastasia Kiyonaga

papers.title: Ocular working memory signals are flexible to behavioral priority and subjective imagery strength
papers.abstract: This study investigated the sensitivity of ocular signals—specifically pupil size and gaze position—to the task-relevance and behavioral priority of content held in working memory (WM). Across two experiments using retroactive cues to manipulate item priority, the researchers found that task-evoked pupil dilations reflected the remembered brightness of items (pupillary WM effect) only when they were assigned high behavioral priority via reliable cues. Additionally, the magnitude of this pupillary WM signal correlated with individual variation in self-reported subjective visual imagery strength (VVIQ). These results demonstrate that peripheral ocular signals are functional signatures of the internal prioritized state of WM content and are flexibly modulated by both top-down attentional goals and individual cognitive traits.
papers.authors: Yueying Dong, Anastasia Kiyonaga

0039.name: Andrea Facoetti
0039.bio: Andrea Facoetti is an Associate Professor of Psychobiology and Physiological Psychology at the University of Padua and directs the Developmental Cognitive Neuroscience (De.Co.Ne.) Lab. Facoetti’s research investigates the psychobiological foundations of neurodevelopmental disorders, specifically the causal role of visuo-spatial and multisensory attention in reading and numerical acquisition. Their findings indicate that attentional deficits often precede and predict dyslexia, challenging strictly phonological theories. Experimental methodologies utilized by Facoetti include longitudinal behavioral studies, non-invasive brain stimulation, and the application of action video games as a remediation tool for cognitive and academic enhancement.
0039.research_direction: Dr. Facoetti’s recent work explores the foundational role of visual and temporal attention mechanisms across a variety of clinical and neurodevelopmental conditions. A major focus of their research investigates how visuo-spatial and temporal attention relate to developmental dyslexia, examining the efficacy of interventions like action video game training and posterior parietal neuromodulation alongside tests of the placebo effect in treatments like flickering lenses. They have also recently been probing non-spatial temporal attention deficits in patients with left spatial neglect by utilizing attentional blink paradigms to evaluate broader dorsal stream dysfunction. Furthermore, their developmental work tracks early attentional precursors to autism in infants, using spatial cueing and saccadic latencies to assess how visual reorienting efficiency might predict future socio-communicative behaviors.

papers.title: Flickering lenses enhance reading performance through placebo effect
papers.abstract: The researchers investigated the role of positive expectations (placebo effect) in the perceived efficacy of flickering glass treatments for developmental dyslexia (DD). Utilizing a double-blind, within-subjects design with 49 children with DD and 48 typical adults, they compared active flickering, sham (powered off), and sham with an induced positive expectancy. Results revealed that inducing positive expectations significantly improved word reading accuracy in both children with DD and adult poor readers, with effect sizes comparable to established remediation programs. Conversely, typical readers exhibited gains primarily in pseudoword decoding speed. The study concludes that placebo-driven improvements are a critical confounding factor in dyslexia interventions and that actual flickering may slightly impair word-specific recognition while facilitating sub-lexical decoding.
papers.authors: Sandro Franceschini, Giovanna Puccio, Sara Bertoni, Sara Mascheretti, Andrea Cappellini, Simone Gori, Andrea Facoetti

papers.title: Infants’ reorienting efficiency depends on parental autistic traits and predicts future socio-communicative behaviors
papers.abstract: This prospective longitudinal study investigated the developmental trajectory of stimulus-driven attention and its link to socio-communicative outcomes and parental broader autism phenotype (BAP). Saccadic latencies during an attentional cueing task were recorded in 71 8-month-old infants to quantify reorienting efficiency. Infants of parents reporting high subclinical autistic traits (HPT) exhibited significantly slower reorienting speeds ("sluggish reorienting"). Crucially, this early deficit in the right-hemisphere ventral attention network's ability to disengage and shift focus predicted poorer socio-communicative performance at 21 months. These results provide evidence for a transgenerational and early-emerging attentional precursor to social cognition deficits in autism spectrum conditions.
papers.authors: Luca Ronconi, Chiara Cantiani, Valentina Riva, Laura Franchin, Roberta Bettoni, Simone Gori, Herman Bulf, Eloisa Valenza, Andrea Facoetti

papers.title: Action video games and posterior parietal cortex neuromodulation enhance both attention and reading in adults with developmental dyslexia
papers.abstract: In this double-blind randomized controlled trial, the researchers tested whether high-frequency transcranial random noise stimulation (hf-tRNS) over the bilateral posterior parietal cortex (PPC) could augment the benefits of action video game (AVG) training in adults with developmental dyslexia. Twenty participants underwent 15 hours of AVG training with either active or sham hf-tRNS. The group receiving active stimulation showed significant enhancements in word text reading, pseudoword decoding, and temporal attention (as evidenced by a reduced attentional blink). Concurrent EEG measurements revealed increased P300 amplitudes during the attentional task, indicating that PPC neuromodulation facilitates the rapid deployment of attention required for efficient orthographic and phonological processing.
papers.authors: Sara Bertoni, Sandro Franceschini, Martina Mancarella, Giovanna Puccio, Luca Ronconi, Gianluca Marsicano, Simone Gori, Gianluca Campana, Andrea Facoetti

papers.title: The engagement of temporal attention in left spatial neglect
papers.abstract: This study examined the integrity of non-spatial temporal attention in patients with left spatial neglect (LSN) using the attentional blink (AB) paradigm. Centrally presented visual stimuli were used to measure the "dwell time" required to process sequential targets. Neglect patients, regardless of specific lesion site (parietal, frontal, or basal ganglia), demonstrated an abnormally severe and prolonged AB compared to healthy controls and non-neglect stroke patients. Their awareness of the second target remained diminished for a duration approximately three times longer than that of controls. These findings demonstrate that a core, non-spatial temporal attention impairment—linked to a broader dysfunction in the dorsal stream—is a fundamental component of the neglect syndrome.
papers.authors: Simone Gori, Milena Peverelli, Sara Bertoni, Milena Ruffino, Luca Ronconi, Franco Molteni, Andrea Facoetti

papers.title: Action Video Games Training in Children with Developmental Dyslexia: A Meta-Analysis
papers.abstract: This meta-analysis synthesized results from nine experimental studies (n=238) evaluating the efficacy of action video game (AVG) training as a remediation tool for children with developmental dyslexia (aged 5–15). Utilizing Hedge’s g to quantify effect sizes, the analysis focused on transfer effects from purely attentional training to reading and phonological skills. The meta-analysis found significant positive effects on both near-transfer measures (visual-spatial attention and attentional control) and far-transfer outcomes (reading speed and sublexical decoding). The results reinforce the causal link between visuo-attentional mechanisms and reading acquisition and support the integration of game-based, non-linguistic interventions into traditional dyslexia rehabilitation programs.
papers.authors: Giovanna Puccio, Giulia Gazzi, Sara Bertoni, Sandro Franceschini, Martina Mancarella, Simone Gori, Lucia Ronconi, Andrea Facoetti

0040.name: Andreas Hierlemann
0040.department: Department of Biosystems Science and Engineering (D-BSSE)
0040.bio: Andreas Hierlemann is a Professor of Biosystems Engineering at ETH Zurich, conducting research at the interface of microelectronics and neuroscience. Hierlemann’s work focuses on the development of CMOS-based high-density microelectrode arrays (HD-MEAs) for the recording and stimulation of electrogenic cells, including neurons and retinal circuits. Their laboratory uses these platforms to examine neuronal network dynamics, subcellular signaling such as axonal action potential propagation, and the visual processing mechanisms of the human retina. This research integrates microfluidic systems and bioelectronics to investigate neurophysiology and provide tools for pharmaceutical testing and systems biology.
0040.research_direction: Dr. Hierlemann has recently been developing advanced bioelectronic and microfluidic platforms to monitor living tissues at exceptionally high spatial and temporal resolutions. Their recent work explores the engineering of high-density microelectrode arrays and integrated organ-on-a-chip devices to non-invasively track the electrophysiology and physical health of complex 3D cell cultures. Utilizing these sophisticated sensors, they are investigating fundamental neural network dynamics, specifically mapping how the delicate balance of excitatory and inhibitory synaptic inputs orchestrates recurrent spiking in cortical circuits. Beyond the nervous system, they are also designing specialized microfluidic chambers to study three-dimensional epithelial barrier models, enabling the real-time electrical profiling and high-resolution imaging of human airway tissues during dynamic bacterial infections.

papers.title: Advances in large-scale electrophysiology with high-density microelectrode arrays
papers.abstract: This tutorial review provides a comprehensive analysis of recent advancements in CMOS high-density microelectrode array (HD-MEA) technology, emphasizing hardware architectures and their applications in characterizing electrogenic cell phenotypes. We discuss various chip design strategies, including reconfigurable switch matrices and fixed-channel readout circuits, which enable spatiotemporal sampling of bioelectric signals at scales ranging from subcellular compartments to large-scale networks. The article further surveys the integration of HD-MEAs with multimodal sensing modalities, such as impedance spectroscopy and electrochemical detection, and reviews sophisticated data analysis methodologies like automated spike sorting and functional connectivity inference used in neurodevelopmental research, stem cell biology, and drug screening.
papers.authors: Manuel Schröter, Fernando Cardes, Cat-Vu H. Bui, Lorenzo Davide Dodi, Tobias Gänswein, Julian Bartram, Lorenca Sadiraj, Philipp Hornauer, Sreedhar Kumar, Maria Pascual-Garcia, Andreas Hierlemann

papers.title: Seamless integration of CMOS microsensors into open microfluidic systems
papers.abstract: We describe the development and validation of a microphysiological platform that integrates a multifunctional 0.18 μm CMOS microelectrode array (MEA) into an open microfluidic hanging-drop system. The integrated chip features two reconfigurable 1024-electrode arrays designed for simultaneous extracellular recording, current/voltage-controlled electrical stimulation, and label-free electrochemical impedance spectroscopy. We demonstrated the device's utility by performing longitudinal electrophysiological monitoring and impedance-based viability assessment of human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC)-derived cardiac microtissues. Furthermore, the platform enabled the amperometric detection of biochemical analytes, including hydrogen peroxide and epinephrine, while maintaining 3D tissue architectures at the air–liquid interface.
papers.authors: Raziyeh Bounik, Alex E. Landolt, Jihyun Lee, Vijay Viswam, Fernando Cardes, Mario M. Modena, Andreas Hierlemann

papers.title: Parallel reconstruction of the excitatory and inhibitory inputs received by single neurons reveals the synaptic basis of recurrent spiking
papers.abstract: The study presents a novel regression-based framework for the simultaneous reconstruction of excitatory and inhibitory synaptic inputs to individual neurons during spontaneous recurrent network activity. By combining high-density microelectrode array (HD-MEA) recordings of whole-network spiking with parallel whole-cell patch-clamp measurements in rat cortical cultures, we quantified the contribution of individual presynaptic partner cells to postsynaptic potentials. Our results demonstrate that postsynaptic spiking frequently coincides with rapid escalations in the excitation-inhibition (E/I) ratio, primarily driven by network-modulated bidirectional changes in synaptic inhibition. We identify that a minority of highly connected inhibitory hub neurons play a critical role in orchestrating these spiking dynamics and maintaining network stability.
papers.authors: Julian Bartram, Felix Franke, Sreedhar Saseendran Kumar, Andreas Hierlemann

papers.title: Transwell-Based Microfluidic Platform for High-Resolution Imaging of Airway Tissues
papers.abstract: We introduce a microphysiological system designed to bridge the gap between traditional Transwell culturing and high-resolution live-cell imaging of 3D human airway models. The platform utilizes a plastics-based microfluidic device that enables the seamless transition between a physiological air-liquid interface (ALI) for tissue maturation and a liquid-liquid interface (LLI) for immersion-based high-spatiotemporal-resolution imaging. Using this platform, we continuously monitored the real-time dynamics of Pseudomonas aeruginosa infections in human stem-cell-derived bronchial epithelial tissues. The system allowed for the visualization of bacterial colonization, goblet-cell-mediated invasion, and the subsequent degradation of the epithelial barrier, providing a robust tool for studying respiratory pathogenesis and evaluating antibiotic efficacy.
papers.authors: Amanzhol Kurmashev, Julia A. Boos, Benoît-Joseph Laventie, A. Leoni Swart, Rosmarie Sütterlin, Tobias Junne, Urs Jenal, Andreas Hierlemann

papers.title: Microfluidic Platform for Real-Time Impedance Profiling of Transwell-Based Barrier Models
papers.abstract: This paper presents a microfluidic device incorporating integrated microfabricated electrodes for the continuous, non-invasive assessment of tissue barrier integrity in Transwell-based systems. By applying dynamic microfluidic flow and performing real-time impedance profiling, we addressed the limitations of conventional invasive permeability assays and endpoint-only transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) measurements. The platform's sensitivity was validated by tracking the gradual degradation of upper-airway tissue barriers under liquid-liquid interface stress. The ability to monitor barrier tightness with high temporal resolution and localized spatial accuracy makes this platform a valuable tool for toxicity testing and the investigation of disease-induced barrier disruption in organ-on-chip models.
papers.authors: Amber Bultena, Amanzhol Kurmashev, Julia A Boos, Wei Wei, Mario M Modena, Fernando Cardes, Andreas Hierlemann

0041.name: Andreas Keil
0041.lab_name: Laboratory for Brain, Body, and Behavior
0041.bio: Andreas Keil is a Professor of Psychology at the University of Florida, where they direct the Laboratory for Brain, Body, and Behavior. Keil’s research examines the neurobiological mechanisms through which human sensation and perception adapt to motivational and emotional states to facilitate survival and well-being. Using dense-array electroencephalography (EEG), steady-state visual evoked potentials (ssVEPs), and simultaneous EEG-fMRI, Keil investigates how aversive learning and threat expectancy modulate neural gain in the visual cortex. They also focus on developing and validating signal processing methods for characterizing oscillatory brain dynamics and establishing international guidelines for electrophysiological research.
0041.research_direction: Dr. Keil's recent work explores the neurophysiological mechanisms underlying visual attention and affective processing, frequently utilizing steady-state visual evoked potentials (ssVEPs) to track how the human brain allocates sensory resources. They have recently been investigating representational competition between spatially and temporally overlapping targets and distractors, as well as mapping the distinct temporal dynamics of early visual discrimination versus autonomic generalization during prolonged fear learning. Beyond traditional experimental paradigms, their research assesses the validity of novel stimuli in affective neuroscience, specifically comparing early visuocortical and evaluative responses to AI-generated versus naturalistic emotional images. Furthermore, Dr. Keil is advancing human electroencephalography (EEG) methodologies by evaluating the reliability of mass univariate statistical frameworks and developing deep generative AI models designed to predict individual-level neural responses to complex visual and semantic concepts.

papers.title: Comparing Methods for Mass Univariate Analyses of Human EEG: Empirical Data and Simulations
papers.abstract: This methodological investigation assesses the performance and validity of various mass univariate statistical frameworks applied to scalp-recorded human electroencephalography (EEG) data. Utilizing both empirical datasets and Monte Carlo simulations, the researchers evaluate the sensitivity, specificity, and family-wise error rate control of common techniques, including Cluster-Based Permutation Testing (CBPT), Threshold-Free Cluster Enhancement (TFCE), and False Discovery Rate (FDR) corrections. The study characterizes how these methods manage varying signal-to-noise ratios, temporal autocorrelations, and spatial dependencies within neural time series. Results provide evidence-based recommendations for standardizing EEG analysis pipelines to optimize the detection of true neurophysiological effects while minimizing Type I errors in high-density sensor arrays.
papers.authors: Anna-Lena Tebbe, Christian Panitz, Andreas Keil

papers.title: Emotional Responses to Naturalistic and AI-generated Affective Pictures: A Systematic Comparison
papers.abstract: This study systematically compares cortical and autonomic reactions to affectively charged images sourced from established naturalistic databases versus those synthesized using generative artificial intelligence. By recording steady-state visual evoked potentials (ssVEPs), skin conductance responses, and subjective ratings of valence and arousal, the authors examine whether AI-generated stimuli reliably recruit the same motivational systems—defense and appetitive—as traditional photographic stimuli. The findings quantify the extent to which synthetic imagery facilitates early visuocortical gain and late evaluative processing, addressing the validity of utilizing generative AI in affective neuroscience research and personalized psychological paradigms.
papers.authors: Faith Gilbert, Fan Yang, Ethan Smith, Mingzhou Ding, Ruogu Fang, Andreas Keil

papers.title: Representational Competition of Spatially and Temporally Overlapped Target and Distractor
papers.abstract: The research explores the neurophysiological mechanisms of sensory competition within the human visual system when targets and distractors exhibit high spatial and temporal overlap. Utilizing a frequency-tagging paradigm (ssVEPs) to isolate the neural processing of concurrent stimuli, the study identifies a biphasic temporal profile of resource allocation. Specifically, results indicate that an initial period of feedforward facilitation is followed by significant competitive suppression of distractor representations in early visual cortex. Comparisons with formal models of divisive normalization suggest that the observed competitive interactions are driven by an interplay of bottom-up stimulus salience and top-down attentional prioritization, providing insights into how the brain adjudicates between competing sensory inputs in complex environments.
papers.authors: Katherine McCain, Wendel Matthew Friedl, Gilles Pourtois, Faisal Mushtaq, Yuri Pavlov, Andreas Keil

papers.title: Concept2Brain: An AI model for predicting subject-level neurophysiological responses to text and pictures
papers.abstract: This work introduces Concept2Brain, a deep generative architecture designed to predict individual-level EEG responses to complex semantic content across visual and linguistic modalities. The model integrates Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP) embeddings to represent conceptual space and a conditional Variational Autoencoder (cVAE) to map these representations onto the latent space of neurophysiological dynamics. By training on a large-scale corpus of affective responses, the model successfully reconstructs canonical event-related potential (ERP) components, such as the N170 and the Late Positive Potential (LPP), without explicit supervision. The model demonstrates significant generalization ability across novel stimuli and participants, establishing a predictive framework for simulating human brain activity in response to varied conceptual information.
papers.authors: Alejandro Santos-Mayo, Faith Gilbert, Arash Mirifar, Anna-Lena Tebbe, Ruogu Fang, Mingzhou Ding, Andreas Keil

papers.title: Neurophysiological and Autonomic Dynamics of Threat Processing during Sustained Social Fear Generalization
papers.abstract: This study investigates the longitudinal dynamics of aversive generalization using facial identities across several hundred trials to simulate prolonged social engagement. By recording steady-state visual evoked potentials (ssVEPs), alpha-band power, and pupillary dilation, the researchers tracked the evolution of neural tuning functions from initial conditioning to sustained learning. The results show that while early learning is marked by sharpened visuocortical discrimination—where sensory resources are selectively deployed to the conditioned threat (CS+)—prolonged exposure leads to a divergence: autonomic measures exhibit broad generalization, whereas sensory cortical representations maintain or increase their sharpening. These findings suggest that the human brain implements distinct temporal dynamics for sensory-level discrimination versus higher-order motivational generalization in social fear contexts.
papers.authors: Jourdan J. Pouliot, Richard T. Ward, Caitlin M. Traiser, Payton Chiasson, Faith E. Gilbert, Andreas Keil

0042.name: Andrew B. Leber
0042.bio: Andrew B. Leber is a Professor of Psychology at The Ohio State University and serves as the Director of the Center for Cognitive & Brain Sciences. Leber’s research investigates the mechanisms of cognitive control, focusing on how the brain selects, updates, and modulates behavioral strategies in response to varying environmental demands. They utilize a multi-methodological approach, including functional MRI, electroencephalography, and eye-tracking, to examine the neural predictors of fluctuations in attentional focus and flexibility. Their recent work characterizes individual differences in attentional strategy and explores the factors that influence optimal performance in adaptive visual search tasks.
0042.research_direction: Dr. Leber has recently been investigating how individuals strategically manage their limited cognitive resources during visual search and working memory tasks. Their recent work explores the factors driving robust individual differences in attentional control, using choice-based paradigms to ask whether suboptimal visual search behaviors stem from fixed feature biases or a strategic desire to avoid cognitive effort. They are also examining the mechanisms of proactive distractor suppression, specifically testing how rapidly the visual system learns to ignore salient singletons and whether environmental contexts, like background scenes, can implicitly cue global suppressive states. Furthermore, Dr. Leber is studying strategy optimization during visual working memory encoding, testing how individuals leverage abstract grouping cues—such as illusory Kanizsa figures—and make dynamic decisions about which target subsets to memorize to overcome strict capacity limitations.

papers.title: What Distinguishes Optimal Visual Searchers? Evidence From a Probe Procedure
papers.abstract: Individual variance in attentional control strategy choice, as measured by the Adaptive Choice Visual Search (ACVS) paradigm, remains poorly characterized. This research contrasts a feature-based predisposition account against a flexible strategic choice model. Employing a probe procedure to quantify attentional allocation to specific display properties, Experiment 1 revealed that individuals who proactively attended to numerosity subset information—a feature essential for the optimal search strategy—showed significantly higher search optimality. Experiment 2 demonstrated that this relationship was contingent on task relevance; when subset information was rendered non-diagnostic for performance, the link between feature attention and search optimality was abolished. Experiment 3 showed that incentivizing attention to subset properties yielded modest improvements in optimality, suggesting that search suboptimality is driven by a strategic avoidance of the cognitive effort associated with subset-based enumeration rather than fixed attentional biases.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
papers.authors: Tianyu Zhang, Andrew B. Leber

papers.title: Learned distractor rejection: robust but surprisingly rapid
papers.abstract: This series of experiments investigates the acquisition rate and robustness of learned distractor suppression within the human visual system. While long-term experience with frequent distractors is known to reduce interference, the specific learning curves associated with this process remain under-characterized. The authors demonstrate that proactive suppression of salient singleton distractors is established within a remarkably small number of exposures, indicating a highly efficient mechanism for updating attentional priority maps based on environmental regularities. This learned distractor rejection proved robust against changes in target identity and task demands, suggesting a flexible, goal-directed control mechanism. The results support a model where the cognitive system rapidly extracts statistical regularities of irrelevant information to proactively dampen saliency signals and minimize attentional capture.
papers.authors: Ilana Savelson, Christopher Hauck, Mei-Ching Lien, Eric Ruthruff, Andrew B. Leber

papers.title: Assessing individual differences in grouping strategy in visual working memory
papers.abstract: This research investigates the relationship between visual working memory (WM) capacity and the strategic utilization of grouping cues to mitigate storage limitations. Employing an orientation change detection task, the authors manipulated the presence of Kanizsa illusory figures—a high-level grouping cue—against randomly oriented inducer arrays. While a general memory benefit was observed for Kanizsa-grouped items, the magnitude of this benefit varied significantly across individuals and was positively correlated with independently assessed WM capacity. Experiment 2 demonstrated that the Kanizsa benefit persisted even under sequential presentation conditions that precluded low-level sensory grouping, suggesting the application of abstract encoding rules. These findings suggest that high-capacity individuals are better equipped to leverage high-level knowledge and strategic grouping to optimize the representation of information within the highly constrained visual WM system.
papers.authors: Yin-Ting Lin, Andrew B. Leber

papers.title: Individual variation in encoding strategy optimization in visual working memory: Evidence from a change detection task
papers.abstract: The current study investigates whether individual differences in visual working memory (WM) performance are attributable to strategy optimization during encoding. Using a novel paradigm where participants could choose between red or blue targets within displays of varying color-subset numerosities, the authors measured the frequency of optimal (small-subset) encoding choices. The results demonstrated substantial individual differences in strategy use, with a significant proportion of participants employing suboptimal encoding tactics. Longitudinal analysis of trial-by-trial behavior indicated that many individuals experienced sudden improvements in strategy optimality, suggesting the discovery of the optimal rule (insight). A large-scale replication (Experiment 5) identified a modest positive correlation between independently measured WM capacity and strategy optimality. These results indicate that WM performance is not merely a reflection of fixed storage capacity but is significantly influenced by the strategic management of limited cognitive resources.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
papers.authors: Yin-Ting Lin, Andrew B. Leber

papers.title: Contextual cues can be used to predict the likelihood of and reduce interference from salient distractors
papers.abstract: The study examines the capacity of the attentional system to implicitly learn context-specific probabilities of distractor occurrence. Using a visual search task where forest or city background scenes served as contextual cues, the authors manipulated the likelihood of a salient color singleton distractor appearing. The findings revealed that distractor-induced interference was significantly reduced in contexts associated with a high probability of distractor presence compared to low-probability contexts. Crucially, this modulation occurred even though the color and location of the distractor were unpredictable on any given trial. These results suggest that contextual information can be used to dynamically tune the gain of global suppressive mechanisms. The authors conclude that implicit learning of environmental statistics allows the cognitive system to flexibly adapt its suppressive state to anticipated levels of distraction.
papers.authors: Jeff Moher, Andrew B. Leber

0043.name: Andrew Hollingworth
0043.department: Department of Psychological and Brain Sciences
0043.bio: Andrew Hollingworth is a Professor at the University of Iowa. Hollingworth’s research investigates the cognitive architecture of scene perception, focusing on the mechanisms of visual working memory and attentional guidance. Their work explores how visual information is accumulated and integrated across saccadic eye movements to form representations of natural environments. By employing eye-tracking and behavioral paradigms, Hollingworth examines the roles of categorical learning and statistical regularities in directing visual search and the interaction between short-term and long-term memory systems in sustaining visual continuity.
0043.research_direction: Dr. Hollingworth has recently been investigating the intersecting mechanisms of visual working memory (VWM), long-term memory, and attentional control during visual search. Their recent work explores how different sources of attentional guidance—such as goal-driven feature templates, selection history, and bottom-up physical saliency—interact to prioritize spatial locations on a common priority map. Using a combination of behavioral redundancy-gain paradigms, oculomotor orienting, and EEG markers of attention like the N2pc and Pd components, they are probing how the visual system utilizes negative templates (knowing what to ignore), specifically testing whether these templates rely on direct feature suppression or indirect spatial recoding. Additionally, they are examining the fundamental architecture of these guiding memory representations by asking whether features in VWM are maintained as integrated objects or separate entities, and whether inter-trial priming relies strictly on implicit mechanisms or explicitly retrievable memory traces.

papers.title: Dissociations and interactions between attention guidance from negative templates maintained in visual working memory and long-term memory
papers.abstract: This study contrasts negative attentional templates derived from long-term memory (LTM) and visual working memory (VWM) to determine their underlying implementation mechanisms. LTM-based negative templates are typically characterized by proactive suppression of distractor features during the earliest stages of visual search. However, evidence for similar proactive implementation of VWM-based negative templates has been inconsistent. Across multiple experiments, the authors observed several dissociations between these two sources of guidance in oculomotor orienting, including differences in initial guidance polarity, the latency of initial orienting responses, and the temporal patterns of guidance throughout the search trial. While both forms of guidance can operate simultaneously when specifying different sets of items, VWM-based biases were found to dominate in competitive conditions, suggesting that online attentional sets effectively overshadow learned biases in priority map computations.
papers.authors: Aditya Prakash, Andrew Hollingworth

papers.title: Template-Based and Saliency-Driven Attentional Control Converge to Coactivate on a Common, Spatially Organized Priority Map
papers.abstract: The authors investigate the interaction between template-based guidance (matching known target attributes) and saliency-driven guidance (physical stimulus salience) using a redundancy-gain paradigm. They contrast coactive mechanisms, where both sources of control converge on a common priority signal, against noncoactive mechanisms (either architecturally separate or temporally sequential). By analyzing response time distributions for redundant-target trials, the study identifies robust violations of the race model inequality (RMI), a finding unique to coactive processing. Critically, these RMI violations were only observed when redundant features appeared at the same spatial location, indicating that guidance signals from distinct sources are integrated on a common, spatially organized priority map to determine attentional priority.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
papers.authors: Zexuan Niu, J. Toby Mordkoff, Andrew Hollingworth

papers.title: Are selection history effects limited to implicit forms of memory? Evidence from inter-trial repetition
papers.abstract: Selection history effects, such as intertrial priming, are traditionally categorized as implicit memory phenomena that influence attention independently of strategic control. This research investigates whether the memory representations driving these effects are available for explicit retrieval. In categorical search tasks involving real-world objects, the authors observed reliable repetition advantages for target location and color within categories. Subsequent surprise memory tests revealed that participants could reliably report the properties of the target from the immediately preceding trial and the most recent targets found in diverse categories. These findings suggest that selection history effects are supported by memory representations that can be explicitly retrieved and reported, challenging the traditional implicit classification of these guidance mechanisms.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
papers.authors: Ariel M. Kershner, Andrew Hollingworth

papers.title: Reappearing sensory input guides visual working memory prioritization
papers.abstract: This study examines the prioritization of items held in visual working memory (VWM) and how this process is influenced by reappearing sensory information. Using a variant of the redundant feature reviewing paradigm, the authors investigated whether features from multiple objects are maintained as integrated units or separate entities. The experiments probed the incidental and strategic guidance of attention from VWM content during a retention-interval search task. The results showed that while reappearing sensory input can effectively prioritize specific VWM representations, the magnitude of attention guidance did not increase when multiple features from the same object matched the target, supporting a feature-based rather than object-based architecture for VWM-guided attention.
papers.authors: Daniel D. Thayer, Brett Bahle, Andrew Hollingworth

papers.title: Attentional Guidance From Negative Templates in Visual Working Memory is Implemented Indirectly via Spatial Recoding
papers.abstract: This research investigates the mechanism by which negative feature templates (information about what to ignore) guide attention away from distractors. Competing theories suggest either a direct suppressive signal for the cued feature or an indirect mechanism involving the selection of all non-matching features or spatial recoding. The authors test these accounts by measuring oculomotor orienting and EEG correlates of attention (such as the N2pc and Pd components). The findings reveal that when observers are cued to avoid a specific feature value maintained in VWM, the resulting attentional bias is not proactive suppression of that feature. Instead, the results support a spatial recoding account where negative templates are converted into positive spatial templates, indicating a fundamental limitation in the direct suppressive capabilities of VWM-based attentional control.
papers.authors: Aditya Prakash, Andrew Hollingworth

0044.name: Andrew Lovett
0044.department: Navy Center for Applied Research in Artificial Intelligence (NCARAI)
0044.bio: Andrew Lovett is a computer scientist at the U.S. Naval Research Laboratory working at the intersection of cognitive science and artificial intelligence. Lovett's research involves developing computational models of visual perception and spatial reasoning, specifically examining how analogical mapping and qualitative spatial representations facilitate problem-solving. They model performance on visual intelligence assessments, such as Raven’s Progressive Matrices, by simulating the encoding of topological relations and abstract spatial structures. Lovett’s methodologies include the creation of software systems that integrate attention-driven processing with structure-mapping engines to generate high-level descriptions of visual scenes.
0044.research_direction: Dr. Lovett's recent work explores the cognitive mechanisms underlying intention attribution in dynamic visual scenes, specifically focusing on how human observers detect pursuit or chasing behaviors among multiple moving agents. They have recently been utilizing novel experimental paradigms alongside attention-based computational models, such as the ARCADIA architecture, to investigate chasing subtlety, examining how deviations from a direct pursuit trajectory and varying set sizes impact an observer's reaction times and detection accuracy. Through these simulations and behavioral experiments, they are investigating whether chase detection relies on the strategic, top-down projection of spatial attention rather than functioning as a strictly low-level perceptual process. Additionally, their research spans broader cognitive learning architectures, expanding Locally Bayesian frameworks to understand how humans perform exemplar-based categorization using continuous rather than discrete visual features. By integrating Bayesian inference with structural representations, Dr. Lovett is examining the underlying mechanisms that allow human observers to flexibly generalize from specific visual instances to broader conceptual categories.

papers.title: Model Predictions and Implications for Chasing Subtlety
papers.abstract: This research evaluates an attention-based computational model of chase detection, where observers must distinguish between agents engaged in pursuit and those moving independently. Specifically, the study investigates the cognitive mechanism of 'chasing subtlety'—the degree to which a pursuer can deviate from a direct, heat-seeking trajectory toward its target without being detected. By conducting simulations prior to empirical data collection, the authors generated preregistered predictions regarding reaction times and accuracy across varying set sizes and levels of subtlety. The findings suggest that human observers utilize strategic spatial attention to track potential trajectories and that deviations from optimal paths significantly influence the temporal dynamics of intention attribution.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the 23rd International Conference on Cognitive Modelling (ICCM 2025)
papers.authors: Maria Kon, Sangeet Khemlani, Gregory Francis, Andrew Lovett

papers.title: Measuring and Modeling Pursuit Detection in Dynamic Visual Scenes
papers.abstract: This paper presents a novel experimental paradigm and computational theory to account for human performance in detecting pursuit within busy, dynamic environments. The authors developed a cognitive model using the ARCADIA architecture that mimics human behavior by tracking trajectories and scanning for pursuit candidates. Results indicate that while humans are generally accurate, they commit systematic errors when distractors move parallel to a target for brief durations. The model successfully replicates these human error patterns and reaction time latencies, which increase with set size and are consistently higher for 'pursuit absent' trials. The study characterizes chase detection as a strategic projection of spatial attention rather than a simple low-level perceptual process.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the 46th Annual Conference of the Cognitive Science Society (CogSci 2024)
papers.authors: Maria Kon, Sangeet Khemlani, Andrew Lovett

papers.title: Extending the Locally Bayesian Learning Model to Exemplar-Based Categorization with Continuous Features
papers.abstract: The authors propose an expansion of the Locally Bayesian learning framework to accommodate exemplar-based categorization tasks involving continuous rather than discrete features. The model integrates Bayesian inference with structural representations to simulate how humans learn to group novel stimuli into categories. By applying the model to standard categorization benchmarks, the researchers demonstrate that local evidence accumulation allows for more flexible and human-like generalization compared to traditional global models. The paper discusses the implications for cognitive architectures and the role of relational representations in the transition from specific instances to broader conceptual categories.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the 46th Annual Conference of the Cognitive Science Society (CogSci 2024)
papers.authors: Maria Kon, Sangeet Khemlani, Andrew Lovett

0045.name: Andrew Mienaltowski
0045.bio: Andrew Mienaltowski is a Professor in the Department of Psychological Sciences at Western Kentucky University and directs the Lifespan Social Cognition Lab. Mienaltowski's research investigates the intersection of cognitive aging and social cognition, specifically examining how adult development influences the visual recognition and categorization of emotional facial expressions. Utilizing a methodological framework that incorporates behavioral tasks and electrophysiological measures such as event-related potentials (ERPs), they explore the impact of emotional intensity and valence on attention and decision-making. Their work also extends to everyday problem-solving and social judgment processes across the adult lifespan.
0045.research_direction: Dr. Mienaltowski's recent work explores how different populations extract and interpret emotional information from complex visual stimuli. They have recently been investigating how younger and older adults process face-pareidolia images, specifically asking whether the lexical sophistication used to describe these illusory facial expressions is driven more by the observer's age or by the configural ambiguity of the image itself. In a distinct but related line of research, their recent work examines emotion recognition in young adults with autism spectrum disorder, testing how integrating extra-facial visual cues like body posture and environmental scenes influences emotional identification compared to viewing isolated faces. Across these studies, they are probing how stimulus-driven factors—such as ecologically valid scene contexts and image ambiguity—interact with observer characteristics to shape high-level affective judgments.

papers.title: Emotion labelling varies with lexical complexity more than age in face pareidolia images
papers.abstract: This study examines how observers verbally label the emotional expressions they perceive in face-pareidolia stimuli (objects and patterns perceived as having emotional faces), and asks whether the sophistication of the emotion vocabulary used depends more on the complexity of the eliciting image or on the age of the observer. Younger and older adults viewed pareidolia images varying in configural ambiguity and generated free-response emotion labels, which were coded for lexical/semantic complexity (e.g., basic versus more nuanced or differentiated emotion terms). Lexical complexity of emotion labels tracked stimulus-driven complexity of the pareidolia image more strongly than it tracked participant age, suggesting that image-level ambiguity constrains the granularity of emotional interpretation across the adult lifespan. Age-related differences in labelling sophistication were comparatively modest once image complexity was accounted for. The findings extend prior work from the authors' lab on age and emotion perception by showing that pareidolia stimuli can be used to dissociate stimulus-driven and observer-driven sources of variability in emotion language, and argue against a simple age-deficit account of emotion-label complexity.
papers.authors: Andrew Mienaltowski, Ellie Knapp, Brooke A. Lowe, Bailey Pruetz, J. Farley Norman

papers.title: Young Adults with Autism May Possess Typical-Level Skills in Identifying Emotions from Person-in-Context Images
papers.abstract: This quantitative investigation evaluated whether the integration of extra-facial cues, specifically bodily posture and environmental context (e.g., a person in a retail setting), facilitates emotion identification in young adults diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder (ASD). While prior research suggests universal deficits in facial emotion recognition for individuals with ASD, this study utilized author-developed stimuli representing head-only, whole-body, and person-in-context conditions. Results indicated that participants with ASD (Mage = 19.47) exhibited significantly higher identification accuracy for emotions like fear, anger, disgust, and sadness when stimuli were presented as whole bodies within a relevant situational context compared to isolated head or body visuals. Furthermore, no significant performance differences were observed between the ASD group and neurotypical controls (Mage = 19.73) in the context-rich condition, suggesting that individuals with ASD may effectively leverage multi-channel visual information to compensate for facial processing difficulties in ecologically valid scenarios.
papers.authors: Nathan T. Kline, Fran C. Blumberg, Alyssa Minton, Andrew Mienaltowski

0047.name: Anna C. Nobre
0047.bio: Anna C. Nobre is the Wu Tsai Professor of Psychology at Yale University and Director of the Center for Neurocognition and Behavior, having previously led the Oxford Centre for Human Brain Activity at the University of Oxford. Their research examines the neural systems supporting human cognition, specifically investigating how the brain prioritizes and selects information from sensory streams and memory to guide perception and action. By integrating neuroimaging techniques such as MEG, EEG, and fMRI with psychophysical methods, Nobre maps the dynamic regulatory mechanisms of the human brain and their impairment in neurodegenerative diseases.
0047.research_direction: Dr. Nobre's recent work explores the mechanisms by which implicit learning and internal memory representations proactively guide visual attention. They have recently been investigating how human observers leverage spatiotemporal regularities during dynamic visual search tasks, exploring how this predictive capacity operates across the adult lifespan and how multiday statistical learning relates to traits like mood instability. Additionally, Dr. Nobre is examining how attention shifts between external perceptual processing and internal mnemonic domains. By employing techniques like high-resolution eye-tracking of microsaccades and multivariate pattern analysis of MEG data, their research tests whether selecting information from spatial working memory, long-term memory, and the current sensory environment relies on shared or dissociable neural and oculomotor dynamics.

papers.title: Implicit learning across varying temporal scales in individuals with and without mood instability
papers.abstract: The study utilized ten weeks of high-frequency digital remote monitoring to investigate the longitudinal relationship between mood instability and the implicit acquisition of contextual regularities. Participants were categorized into cohorts with high or low mood instability based on Mood Disorder Questionnaire scores and daily mood ratings. While within-session learning facilitation on a contextual cueing task was preserved across groups, individuals characterized by high mood instability exhibited significantly shallower learning slopes for spatial regularities spanning multiple days. The results demonstrate that while rapid, session-specific implicit learning remains intact, the capacity to integrate and utilize environmental statistical structures across extended temporal scales is specifically compromised in populations prone to affective lability.
papers.authors: L.Z. Atkinson, N. Zokaei, P. Panchal, N. Nelissen, K.E.A. Saunders, M.F.S. Rushworth, D. Darby, J.R. Geddes, C.J. Harmer, P.J. Harrison, A.C. Nobre

papers.title: Age-invariant benefits of spatiotemporal predictions amidst distraction during dynamic visual search
papers.abstract: This research evaluated the capacity for older and younger adults to utilize environmental regularities to guide attention within a dynamic visual search paradigm. Targets and distractors transitioned in visibility over time, with spatiotemporal regularities allowing for the proactive prediction of target locations and appearance times. While advanced age was associated with global performance decrements and heightened sensitivity to distracting elements, the benefits derived from spatiotemporal predictions were robustly preserved across the adult lifespan. Critically, these predictive benefits were only statistically significant under conditions of high distraction across all age groups, suggesting a functional dissociation between the age-related decline of top-down goal-directed control and the preservation of learning-driven proactive attentional guidance.
papers.authors: Nir Shalev, Sage Boettcher, Anna C. Nobre

papers.title: Focusing attention in working and long-term memory through dissociable mechanisms
papers.abstract: The study implemented a novel experimental framework to compare the mechanisms by which attentional orienting facilitates retrieval in spatial working memory (WM) versus long-term memory (LTM) and influences concurrent perceptual processing. Retrospective cues prioritized representations at different memory timescales, followed by either a memory-guided report or a perceptual discrimination task. Findings revealed that while attentional prioritization improved performance for both systems, the effects were more robust in WM. Oculomotor analysis via high-resolution eye-tracking identified significant gaze-bias patterns and microsaccadic shifts correlated with attention in WM that were notably absent for LTM. Furthermore, perceptual enhancements for stimuli at attended locations were consistently observed for WM but occurred less reliably for LTM, indicating that internal selection across these memory systems relies on at least partially dissociable cognitive and neural processes.
papers.authors: Dongyu Gong, Dejan Draschkow, Anna C. Nobre

papers.title: Spatiotemporal predictions guide attention throughout the adult lifespan
papers.abstract: Addressing the limitations of static visual-search designs, this study utilized a dynamic search task to investigate the ability of adults to learn and apply spatiotemporal regularities for proactive attentional guidance. Participants identified targets embedded within dynamic structures that afforded the anticipation of relevant information across time and space. Behavioral results and eye-movement recordings demonstrated that spatiotemporal regularities drive effective attentional selection through the acquisition of robust long-term environmental representations. These mechanisms were found to be invariant across age groups, indicating that the ability to leverage complex environmental structures for proactive selection remains resilient throughout adulthood, even as general cognitive processing speed and fluid resources decline.
papers.authors: Nir Shalev, Sage E.P. Boettcher, Anna C. Nobre

papers.title: Neural dynamics of shifting attention between perception and working-memory contents
papers.abstract: Using magnetoencephalography (MEG) and multivariate pattern analysis, the researchers characterized the neural signatures associated with transitioning attention within and between the external sensory environment and internal working-memory representations. Participants performed a task in which sequential cues guided focus to either upcoming visual stimuli or stored mnemonic content. Decoding revealed broadly distributed and highly dynamic neural patterns that distinguished shifts within domains from those crossing the perception-memory boundary. Notably, cross-domain shifts did not require an intermediate processing stage or impose delays on the lateralization of 8-12 Hz alpha activity, a canonical index of spatial reorienting. The results suggest that neural states associated with a previous domain linger and bias subsequent selection rather than engaging a discrete switching mechanism.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS)
papers.authors: Daniela Gresch, Sage E.P. Boettcher, Chetan Gohil, Freek van Ede, Anna C. Nobre

0048.name: Anna Grubert
0048.bio: Anna Grubert is a Professor of Psychology at Durham University whose research examines the neurocognitive mechanisms of visual selective attention and working memory. Utilizing behavioral experiments in conjunction with electrophysiological techniques such as EEG and event-related potentials (ERPs), specifically the N2pc and CDA components, Grubert investigates how memory-based target representations, or attentional templates, guide the selection of information in complex visual environments. Their research explores the temporal dynamics and capacity limits of top-down control, including the ability of the human brain to activate multiple attentional templates and select multiple targets in parallel.
0048.research_direction: Dr. Grubert's recent work explores the mechanisms of top-down attentional guidance in visual search, using electrophysiological markers like the N1pc and N2pc components to track the real-time temporal dynamics of target selection. They have recently been investigating the representational capacity and processing costs of maintaining multiple concurrent attentional templates, examining whether attention is guided by independent features or bound objects during conjunction search, and comparing the parallel processing efficiency of feature-based versus spatial-location templates. Additionally, their research probes the preparatory activation of these templates—often using rapid serial probe presentation—to determine whether target switch costs arise from delayed template reconfiguration or lingering proactive interference.
