Finally, they are exploring how spatial statistical learning influences search behavior, specifically asking how high-probability spatial regularities might accelerate early attentional deployment at the level of initial visual-cortical processing.

papers.title: Temporal acceleration drives the probability cueing effect in visual search: Evidence for early attentional deployment (N1pc) at high-probability locations
papers.abstract: Spatial probability regularities are known to bias visual search, accelerating the localization of targets appearing at high-probability locations relative to low-probability locations. In this electrophysiological investigation, the mechanisms underlying this probability cueing effect were examined by tracking the temporal dynamics of early lateralized event-related potential (ERP) components. Electrophysiological recordings revealed that spatial statistical learning directly modulates the speed of attentional deployment, eliciting an early posterior contralateral negativity (N1pc) over extrastriate visual areas for targets presented at frequent locations. Rather than relying entirely on post-selective processing differences or sustained baseline shifts, the search advantage is primarily driven by temporal acceleration in attentional orienting, establishing that statistical spatial regularities facilitate early target selection at the level of initial visual-cortical processing.
papers.authors: Dirk Kerzel, Anna Grubert

papers.title: The Guidance of Attentional Selectivity in Visual Search Is Always Feature‐Based: Behavioral and Electrophysiological Evidence From Feature and Conjunction Search Tasks
papers.abstract: While attentional guidance in visual search is traditionally conceptualized as feature-based, it has remained controversial whether attentional templates can encode bound, object-based representations when targets are defined by feature conjunctions. Here, behavioral measures (balanced integration scores, reaction times, error rates) and ERP markers—specifically target-elicited N2pc and preparatory contralateral delay activity (CDA)—were compared across single-feature search (color or shape) and conjunction search tasks under low (one target) and high (two targets) working memory load. Increasing template load in the feature tasks delayed and attenuated target N2pcs by approximately 11 ms, reflecting mutual inhibitory competition among concurrently active feature templates. In conjunction search, early attentional selection remained strictly feature-driven: distractor items partially matching one target attribute elicited reliable N2pc components, and load costs mirrored those observed in isolated feature search. These results indicate that attentional selection templates do not maintain integrated holistic object representations during conjunction search; rather, top-down attentional guidance is mediated exclusively through independent, feature-specific control settings.
papers.authors: Ziyi Wang, Mikel Jimenez, Martin Eimer, Anna Grubert

papers.title: The capacity limitations of multiple‐template visual search during task preparation and target selection
papers.abstract: To determine the representational capacity and processing costs of concurrent attentional templates, this study investigated single-color and three-color visual search using behavioral and event-related potential measures. The time course of preparatory template activation was monitored in real time using the rapid serial probe presentation (RSPP) paradigm, measuring N2pc amplitudes elicited by task-irrelevant color singleton probes presented every 200 ms during the inter-search interval. In Experiment 1, where three target colors rotated in a predictable cyclic sequence (ABCABC), N2pcs were elicited exclusively by probes matching the upcoming relevant target color, demonstrating single-template activation during predictable transitions. In Experiment 2, where target color identity varied randomly across trials, probes matching any of the three target colors evoked reliable N2pc components, verifying that observers can activate at least three feature-specific templates simultaneously. However, concurrent activation incurred severe capacity-related costs: target-elicited N2pc components were substantially attenuated and delayed, accompanied by marked behavioral performance decrements, reflecting mutual inhibitory interactions among co-active templates during attentional guidance and focal selection.
papers.authors: Anna Grubert, Ziyi Wang, Ella Williams, Mikel Jimenez, Roger Remington, Martin Eimer

papers.title: Attentional templates for target features versus locations
papers.abstract: Visual search can be guided by mental representations specifying target features (knowing what to look for) or target locations (knowing where to look). This study tested whether spatial attentional templates operate with similar functional efficiency and parallel capacity as feature-based templates. Observers performed visual search under low memory load (one cued target feature or location) and high memory load (two cued target features or locations) while reaction times, error rates, and lateralized N2pc components (220–320 ms window at PO7/PO8) were acquired. Target selection in the color task demonstrated characteristic parallel guidance under high load, accompanied by small N2pc latency delays (~16 ms). Strikingly, the location task produced an analogous electrophysiological and behavioral profile, with high load delaying N2pc onset by 11 ms without disrupting target localization. These converging metrics demonstrate that spatial location templates can be activated simultaneously in visual working memory to direct attention across multiple loci with efficiency comparable to feature-based selection settings.
papers.authors: Mikel Jimenez, Ziyi Wang, Anna Grubert

papers.title: Target switch costs in visual search arise during the preparatory activation of target templates
papers.abstract: Switching between different task sets incurs behavioral performance decrements, but whether switch costs between visual search targets originate from preparatory template reconfiguration or lingering proactive interference remains unresolved. Observers searched for one of two color-defined targets alternating in predictable sequences every two trials (AABB; Experiment 1) or every four trials (Experiment 2). The real-time preparatory dynamics of attentional templates were tracked via N2pc components elicited by streams of task-irrelevant color singleton probes appearing every 200 ms during the inter-display interval. On target repetition trials, N2pcs to relevant target-color probes emerged from 800 ms prior to search display onset, reflecting robust preparatory template activation. On target switch trials, however, probe N2pcs were significantly delayed, appearing only immediately prior to display onset. Probes matching the alternative, currently irrelevant target color failed to elicit N2pcs on both switch and repeat trials, indicating an absence of template inertia. These electrophysiological findings demonstrate that target switch costs in visual search stem directly from temporal delays in the preparatory activation and reconfiguration of attentional templates.
papers.authors: Anna Grubert, Ziyi Wang, Martin Eimer

0049.name: Anna Kosovicheva
0049.bio: Anna Kosovicheva is an Assistant Professor at the University of Toronto Mississauga and co-directs the Applied Perception & Psychophysics LaboratorY (APPLY). Kosovicheva’s research uses psychophysical methodologies and eye-tracking technology to investigate mechanisms of visual localization, spatial vision, and binocular perception. They study how the visual system updates representations of object location and characterize individual differences in sensory processing. Their work also examines the application of vision science to digital readability and the clinical assessment of disorders such as amblyopia and strabismus.
0049.research_direction: Dr. Kosovicheva's recent work explores a diverse range of mechanisms underlying visual search, peripheral perception, and binocular integration. In the domain of visual attention and memory, they have recently been investigating the low prevalence effect in both abstract similarity-guided tasks and naturalistic driving scenarios, while also using massive datasets to probe the distinct psychophysical components of item memorability during hybrid search. Their research also examines the spatial architecture of peripheral vision by questioning how idiosyncratic spatial localization biases and metric irregularities map onto individual differences in visual crowding. Additionally, Dr. Kosovicheva is studying binocular vision in both typical and amblyopic populations, specifically evaluating how interocular temporal phase offsets and luminance contrast imbalances interact during dichoptic motion tasks.

papers.title: Intact Perceptual Interactions of Interocular Temporal Phase and Contrast Disparities in Amblyopia
papers.abstract: This study evaluated whether binocular visual integration in amblyopia can be enhanced by combining interocular temporal phase disparities and interocular luminance contrast imbalances. Amblyopic observers (n = 12) and age-matched controls (n = 12) performed a dichoptic apparent motion direction discrimination task using periodic luminance flicker. Stimuli introduced interocular temporal phase shifts ranging between -80° and +80° relative to a canonical 90° quadrature phase offset across three interocular contrast conditions: 50%-50%, 70%-30%, and 85%-15% (with higher contrast presented to the amblyopic eye, or a randomly chosen eye in controls). Both cohorts exhibited broad temporal tuning for dichoptic flicker integration. Under contrast-balanced baseline conditions, direction discrimination accuracy reached its peak near a negligible phase delay (-0.3°). When an 85%-15% contrast disparity was applied, overall discrimination accuracy declined and optimal integration shifted by 28.6° toward a leading delay in the lower-contrast eye. These data demonstrate that temporal phase offsets and contrast imbalances interact predictably and preserve equivalent dynamics across both amblyopic visual systems and typical controls.
papers.authors: Anna Kosovicheva, Zain Ahmed, Nikhil Chaudhry, Brooke Lim, Peter J. Bex, Emily K. Wiecek, Eric D. Gaier

papers.title: Reducing the low prevalence effect: Does similarity search translate to binary decisions?
papers.abstract: The low prevalence effect (LPE) constitutes an elevated miss rate for infrequent targets during visual search tasks, predominantly driven by conservative shifts in decision criteria rather than decrements in sensory discriminability. The authors evaluated whether structuring visual search around an explicit similarity-based selection step could mitigate the LPE when followed by a definitive binary classification. Observers conducted a two-stage visual search paradigm: they first selected the display element possessing the highest visual similarity to a designated target template, followed immediately by an explicit binary decision regarding whether that candidate item was a true target or a distractor. Although similarity-guided ranking decreased initial scanning omissions, the subsequent binary decision stage remained vulnerable to the classic criterion shift associated with low target prevalence. These findings demonstrate that similarity-based visual search strategies do not abolish criterion-driven miss errors once discrete target-presence determinations are required.
papers.authors: Graeme Gillies, Anna Kosovicheva

papers.title: What can 9 million trials tell us about memorability in a hybrid search task?
papers.abstract: Hybrid visual search paradigms require observers to search visual displays for multiple prospective targets held concurrently in visual and semantic memory. Drawing upon an extensive dataset exceeding 9 million trials from an online gamified visual search task, this investigation quantified item-level memorability metrics and dissociated their functional components. Specifically, performance was decomposed into 'hittability'—the probability of accurately identifying an item when it belongs to the active target memory set—and 'rejectability'—the efficiency with which an item is rejected when absent from the memory set. Hittability and rejectability emerged as largely orthogonal, separable psychophysical dimensions that remained consistent across individual participant cohorts, practice levels, and chronological age. Item rejectability served as a strong determinant of reaction times when searching through arrays of non-target items, whereas hittability showed a markedly weaker correlation with response latency.
papers.authors: Dyllan D. Simpson, Jeremy M. Wolfe, Anna Kosovicheva

papers.title: Spatial variability in localization biases predicts crowding performance
papers.abstract: Human observers manifest stable, idiosyncratic spatial mislocalizations when estimating the coordinates of static targets presented in peripheral vision. This study investigated whether these idiosyncratic spatial representations modulate visual crowding zones, which constrain peripheral object recognition. Psychophysical thresholds were evaluated across 12 isoeccentric polar angles at 8° eccentricity to measure critical spacing in an orientation discrimination task (flanked vs. unflanked stimuli) alongside perceived spatial separation between pairs of Gaussian luminance patches. Marked angular heterogeneity in both crowding extent and perceived separation was observed across observers and visual field meridians. Critically, local spatial variability and compression in subjective localization biases predicted the geographic profile of crowding thresholds around the visual field, indicating that early metric irregularities in spatial retinotopic representations directly contribute to individual differences in peripheral crowding limits.
papers.authors: Zainab Haseeb, Benjamin Wolfe, Anna Kosovicheva

papers.title: Taking prevalence effects on the road: Rare hazards are often missed
papers.abstract: In visual search literature, targets presented at low base rates are missed at disproportionately high rates due to conservative criterion shifts. Across five experiments, the authors assessed whether this low prevalence effect generalizes to naturalistic, dynamic scene perception within vehicular driving contexts. Observers observed brief (333 ms) dynamic video sequences from the Road Hazard Stimuli corpus and provided rapid categorical classifications of whether each scenario contained an imminent roadway hazard requiring evasive action. Across manipulated hazard prevalence conditions (ranging from 10% to 50%), hazards appearing at low prevalence were missed more than twice as frequently as identical events shown under high-prevalence regimes. Signal detection theoretic analyses established that this performance degradation reflected a systematic conservative adjustment in decision criterion (c) while perceptual sensitivity (d') remained stable, confirming that low prevalence poses a significant cognitive vulnerability during dynamic hazard detection.
papers.authors: Anna Kosovicheva, Jeremy M. Wolfe, Benjamin Wolfe

0050.name: Anna Ma-Wyatt
0050.bio: Anna Ma-Wyatt is a Professor in the School of Psychology at the University of Adelaide and directs the Active Vision Lab. Ma-Wyatt’s research investigates the mechanisms of sensorimotor integration, specifically focusing on how visual information is utilized to plan and execute eye and hand movements. Using behavioral psychophysics and motion analysis, they explore the temporal and spatial dynamics of attentional deployment and how these processes are altered by healthy aging and clinical visual field loss. Ma-Wyatt's current work also examines human-autonomy teaming, applying principles of active vision and human performance to the design and optimization of human-AI interfaces and autonomous systems.
0050.research_direction: Dr. Ma-Wyatt has recently been investigating how the human visuomotor system compensates for temporal delays and stochastic jitter during continuous manual tracking. Their recent work explores the underlying mechanisms of predictive control and reactive error correction by measuring eye and hand kinematics as participants perform visually guided pursuit under constant and abruptly shifting cursor feedback latencies. Broadening this focus on latency and spatial visualization, they are also examining applied sensorimotor challenges in extreme environments. Specifically, they are evaluating how extended reality interfaces can optimize teleoperation, supervisory control, and situational awareness to support human-robot collaboration during lunar construction.

papers.title: The impact of varying cursor latency on visuomotor tracking
papers.abstract: The human visuomotor system typically compensates for intrinsic sensorimotor latencies to bind visual inputs with motor commands during precision tracking; however, this capacity is strained when movement feedback is subject to temporal delay or stochastic jitter. This investigation evaluated the operational thresholds where feedback latency impedes continuous manual tracking to delineate the constraints governing predictive control and error correction. Participants completed visually guided pursuit across curvilinear trajectories while ocular kinematics and cursor coordinates were simultaneously recorded under varied feedback latency parameters. Cursor position was sampled throughout each trial to compute input-to-display latency, cursor velocity dynamics, and spatial cursor–target error. In the initial experiment, cursor latency was held constant per trial across six magnitudes ranging from 0 to 300 ms. Velocity spectral power analyses showed that elevated latencies suppressed smooth pursuit submovements into lower frequency bands interspersed with sporadic, high-frequency corrective adjustments, whereas lower latencies preserved continuous tracking profiles. In the second experiment, discrete, unannounced step-changes in cursor latency were introduced mid-trial. Abrupt latency increases provoked larger instantaneous positional errors and compensatory submovement frequency, whereas sudden latency reductions prompted rapid attenuation of spatial error and swift restoration of kinematic smoothness. These adjustments demonstrate the visuomotor controller's capacity for rapid recalibration under variable feedback timing, indicating that predictive and reactive error-correction pathways adapt dynamically as a function of latency magnitude.
papers.authors: Lucy J. Turner, Steven D. Wiederman, Jessica L. O'Rielly, Anna Ma-Wyatt

papers.title: Impact of extended reality on human-robot collaboration in lunar design & construction: A systematic review
papers.abstract: This systematic review employs PRISMA methodology to evaluate the efficacy of extended reality (XR) interfaces—including virtual, augmented, and mixed reality—in facilitating human-robot collaboration (HRC) for lunar infrastructure development. The synthesis analyzes current technological frameworks for teleoperation and supervisory control, focusing on how XR-mediated sensory feedback and spatial information visualization mitigate the challenges of extreme lunar environments, such as low gravity and latency. The study establishes performance metrics for situational awareness and mission safety, identifying critical gaps in existing HRC paradigms for off-earth construction and proposing integrated XR design principles to optimize human-robot teaming efficiency.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the International Astronautical Congress (IAC)
papers.authors: Albert Rajkumar, Amit Srivastava, Edward Palmer, Anna Ma-Wyatt

0051.name: Anna Schubö
0051.bio: Anna Schubö is a Professor of Psychology at Philipps University Marburg and directs the Cognitive Neuroscience of Perception and Action research group. Schubö's research investigates the neurocognitive mechanisms of visual attention, focusing on how internal goals, selection history, and environmental salience guide information processing. They employ a multi-modal approach combining behavioral psychophysics, eye tracking, and electroencephalography (EEG) to examine electrophysiological markers such as the N2pc and PD components. Their recent work explores the integration of action intentions and motor planning into attentional control systems and the maintenance of task-relevant representations in visual working memory.
0051.research_direction: Dr. Schubö has recently been investigating the dynamic mechanisms of visual attention, focusing on how top-down goals, capacity limits, and prior experiences shape target selection and distractor suppression. Their recent work explores a broad range of factors that modulate visual search, utilizing behavioral paradigms, motion-tracking, and lateralized electrophysiological markers like the N2pc, Pd, and SPCN. Specifically, they are examining how spatial attention and multi-target foraging behaviors are biased by anticipated cognitive effort, concurrent working memory demands, and prospective motor intentions. Additionally, they are studying how selection history, such as the prior semantic categorization of real-world objects, and feature-based expectations drive the proactive and reactive neural inhibition of irrelevant distractors.

papers.title: Picking the right piece: Action intentions shape visual search and action planning in human multi-target-foraging
papers.abstract: This research investigates the modulation of visual foraging behavior by subsequent motor demands, utilizing a multi-target search paradigm where participants were required to collect items to assemble specific virtual configurations. Using motion-tracking and behavioral metrics, the study demonstrates that action intentions—specifically the requirement to build particular structures—dynamically bias target selection and the spatiotemporal organization of search paths. Findings indicate that foraging is not merely a perceptual-cognitive process of item maximization but is deeply integrated with action planning, where prospective motor goals influence the prioritization of visual features and the efficiency of target acquisition sequences in a task-dependent manner.
papers.authors: David A. Kuhn, Jan Tünnermann, Anna Schubö

papers.title: Effort expectation and strategic cue use in visual search
papers.abstract: The study examines how the anticipated cognitive effort associated with upcoming task difficulty influences the strategic utilization of positive (target-defining) and negative (distractor-defining) cues in a visual search task. Employing Bayesian multilevel modeling of response times, the authors found that the facilitatory effects of positive cues scale with task difficulty, being more pronounced when search effort is high. Conversely, negative cues failed to provide reliable benefits regardless of effort expectations. The results suggest a robust interaction between effort expectation and task difficulty, indicating that observers prioritize the processing of facilitatory information over inhibitory information when adapting to high-demand environments.
papers.authors: Sizhu Han, Jan Tünnermann, Sara Katharina Hornung, Anna Schubö

papers.title: Neural evidence for feature-based distractor Inhibition
papers.abstract: This electrophysiological investigation addresses the mechanisms of proactive and reactive distractor suppression in visual search. By recording event-related potentials (ERPs) in a paradigm with fixed versus mixed search templates, the study isolates the P<sub>D</sub> (distractor-evoked positivity) component to track inhibitory processes. The findings provide evidence for feature-based inhibition, demonstrating that when distractor features are predictable, the brain implements a proactive suppression mechanism that reduces the attentional capture (indexed by the N2pc component) of irrelevant singletons. This neural evidence supports the existence of a 'signal suppression' mechanism that can be tuned to specific distractor features to facilitate efficient target selection.
papers.authors: Ann-Kathrin A. Hanne, Sizhu Han, Anna Schubö

papers.title: Complex trade-offs in a dual-target visual search task are indexed by lateralised ERP components
papers.abstract: This study explores the neural and behavioral trade-offs involved in performing simultaneous visual search and perceptual discrimination tasks. Utilizing lateralized ERP components, specifically the N2pc (attentional selection) and SPCN (working memory maintenance), the researchers measured the allocation of processing resources when participants had to find a target while maintaining or discriminating another item. The data reveal that performance costs in dual-task scenarios are reflected in the attenuation of these lateralized neural markers, suggesting a finite capacity for spatial selection and maintenance that requires dynamic weighting between search and secondary task demands.
papers.authors: Dion T. Henare, Jan Tünnermann, Imke Wagner, Alexander C. Schütz, Anna Schubö

papers.title: Distracted by objects: The impact of earlier semantic categorization
papers.abstract: The research investigates how prior semantic learning and associative history influence subsequent attentional capture by complex real-world objects. Participants first performed a semantic categorization task involving different object categories (e.g., tools, vehicles, fruits, vegetables) before engaging in a visual search task where these objects appeared as distractors. The results show that objects from previously categorized groups exerted a stronger attentional bias, slowing search for a neutral shape target. This suggests that the history of semantic processing induces a long-term change in the attentional priority of object categories, even when those categories are currently task-irrelevant, highlighting the role of selection history in shaping the saliency of semantic information.
papers.authors: Yunyun Mu, Jan Tünnermann, Anna Schubö

0052.name: Anne B Sereno
0052.department: Department of Psychological Sciences and Weldon School of Biomedical Engineering
0052.bio: Anne B. Sereno is a Professor of Psychological Sciences and Biomedical Engineering at Purdue University, where Sereno investigates the physiological mechanisms of visual attention, short-term memory, and eye movements. Their research combines behavioral psychophysics, extracellular recordings, and computational modeling to examine how cortical pathways process sensorimotor and cognitive information. A portion of Sereno’s work involves translational neuroscience, specifically the development of eye-tracking and sensorimotor technologies as biomarkers for neurological disorders. These tools are designed to assist in the diagnosis and monitoring of conditions such as traumatic brain injury, Parkinson’s disease, and autism spectrum disorder.
0052.research_direction: Dr. Sereno has recently been investigating the computational principles underlying the functional modularity of the visual system, using convolutional neural networks to re-evaluate the classic dual-stream hypothesis. Their recent work explores whether segregated, multi-branch neural architectures optimize the simultaneous recognition of distinct visual attributes and examines how different attribute-based maps might computationally constrain the binding problem in complex scenes. In parallel with these deep learning approaches, they have been revisiting foundational psychophysical experiments on pre-attentive texture segmentation, combining large-scale behavioral testing with biologically plausible models of visual grouping and feature salience. Broadening their methodological scope, Dr. Sereno is also studying age-related motor function, using wearable inertial sensors and machine learning classifiers to isolate kinematic biomarkers of physiological tremors and movement initiation delays.

papers.title: Understanding Cortical Streams from a Computational Perspective
papers.abstract: This review re-evaluates the classical dual-stream hypothesis of visual processing, which distinguishes between ventral 'what' and dorsal 'where' pathways, through the framework of computational modeling. Utilizing feed-forward convolutional neural networks (CNNs), the authors demonstrate that while shape and spatial information may be present in both streams, they are independently constructed and differently retained according to the specific task goals of each pathway. The research highlights the computational advantages of segregation, showing that two-pathway architectures achieve higher testing accuracy and greater learning efficiency than single-pathway networks, particularly as scene complexity and the number of visual objects increase. The study concludes that specialized pathways are necessary for optimal object recognition and localization and discusses how these segregated sub-pathways address the binding problem in complex visual scenes.
papers.authors: Zhixian Han, Anne B. Sereno

papers.title: Exploring neural architectures for simultaneously recognizing multiple visual attributes
papers.abstract: In this study, the authors investigate whether the computational advantage of segregated neural architectures extends to the simultaneous recognition of various visual attributes such as luminance, orientation, identity, and location. By training multi-branch convolutional neural networks on diverse combinations of these attributes, the simulations reveal that segregated pathways consistently outperform single-pathway models across all tested conditions. This performance gap increases as the number of classes within an attribute grows or as the task requires finer discrimination. The findings suggest that specialization into specialized sub-streams is a fundamental strategy for maximizing learning efficiency in the primate visual system, providing a computational justification for the functional modularity observed in higher visual processing areas.
papers.authors: Zhixian Han, Anne B. Sereno

papers.title: A spatial map: a propitious choice for constraining the binding problem
papers.abstract: This computational study addresses the 'binding problem'—the mechanism by which the brain correctly associates multiple features of an object—by evaluating the efficacy of different attribute-based maps within two-pathway neural networks. The authors compared networks constrained by identity, luminance, orientation, and location maps during multi-attribute recognition tasks. Results demonstrate that a location-based spatial map consistently yields superior accuracy in correctly binding features to their respective objects compared to other attribute maps, even when the pathways are not explicitly trained for spatial recognition. These findings align with neurophysiological evidence of pervasive retinotopic organization in the visual cortex, suggesting that spatial maps provide a robust computational constraint for maintaining object integrity in complex visual environments.
papers.authors: Zhixian Han, Anne B. Sereno

papers.title: A machine-learning method isolating changes in wrist kinematics that identify age-related changes in arm movement
papers.abstract: The research employs wearable inertial measurement units (IMUs) and machine learning classifiers to isolate and identify age-related changes in motor function and wrist kinematics. Data from younger and older adults performing postural and pronation-supination tasks were analyzed using frequency decomposition and Support Vector Machines (SVM). Kinematic analysis identified significant differences in physiological tremor amplitudes within the 9–13 Hz range, which reliably distinguished older from younger participants. Furthermore, older adults exhibited a 71 ms delay in movement initiation during active tasks. The SVM classifier achieved an AUROC of 0.86 and 89% accuracy in identifying age groups based on simple kinematic variables, demonstrating that low-cost, non-invasive sensors can provide sensitive objective biomarkers for age-related motor slowing and physiological tremors.
papers.authors: Aditya Shanghavi, Daniel Larranaga, Rhutuja Patil, Elizabeth M. Frazier, Satyajit Ambike, Bradley S. Duerstock, Anne B. Sereno

papers.title: Replicability in texture segmentation: Beck's (1966) classic experiments revisited
papers.abstract: This study provides a large-scale psychophysical replication of Jacob Beck's (1966) foundational experiments on texture segmentation, which established that local orientation differences are more salient cues for segregation than complex shape differences (e.g., T vs. L). The authors utilized a large participant pool to confirm the robust nature of Beck's original findings and extended the research by applying a biologically plausible computational model of visual grouping and selection. The model successfully explains the experimental results through the mechanisms of top-down selection and bottom-up feature salience, emphasizing the role of early visual cortical selectivities in spontaneous scene segmentation. The work reinforces the validity of orientation-based accounts of pre-attentive texture processing while providing a modern computational framework for understanding these classic perceptual phenomena.
papers.authors: Maria Kon, Anne B. Sereno

0053.name: Anne Churchland
0053.department: Department of Neurobiology, David Geffen School of Medicine
0053.bio: Anne Churchland investigates the neural circuitry governing perceptual decision-making and the integration of information across multiple sensory modalities. Churchland's research utilizes large-scale neural recordings and optogenetic manipulations in rodents to examine how cortical and subcortical populations represent evidence and guide actions. A focus of their work involves characterizing the impact of spontaneous and task-related movements on neural activity, revealing that behavioral motifs often dominate signals in sensory processing areas. As a founding member of the International Brain Laboratory, they also develop standardized, collaborative frameworks to map brain-wide computations during cognitive tasks.
0053.research_direction: Dr. Churchland has recently been investigating the large-scale neural dynamics underlying perceptual decision-making, with a particular focus on how internal cognitive states and uninstructed spontaneous movements shape cortical activity. Utilizing widefield calcium imaging in behaving mice, their recent work explores how specific regions track trial history and prior expectations, and how these retrospective cognitive signals intermingle with the profound neural variance driven by ongoing postural adjustments. They are also examining how these integrated sensorimotor dynamics shift under different conditions, such as natural transitions between engaged and disengaged behavioral states, or in genetic mouse models of autism where the integration of prior beliefs with current sensory evidence is disrupted. Broadly, their research seeks to refine models of cognitive flexibility by clarifying how both innate physical behaviors and the learning process itself influence neural representations during complex sensory tasks.

papers.title: Spontaneous movements and their relationship to neural activity fluctuate with latent engagement states
papers.abstract: This study characterizes the impact of internal cognitive state transitions, specifically between engaged and disengaged states, on cortex-wide neural dynamics in mice performing auditory decisions. Utilizing widefield calcium imaging and linear encoding models, the researchers found that while trial-averaged neural activity remains stable across states, single-trial variance increases substantially during disengagement. This elevated variability is not due to a change in the frequency of movements, but rather a change in their temporal structure: uninstructed, spontaneous movements become decoupled from task events and more idiosyncratic when animals are disengaged. The findings suggest that the timing of spontaneous behaviors serves as an embodied signature of latent engagement states that significantly shapes neural activity variability.
papers.authors: Chaoqun Yin, Maxwell D. Melin, Gabriel Rojas-Bowe, Xiaonan Richard Sun, João Couto, Steven Gluf, Alex Kostiuk, Simon Musall, Anne K. Churchland

papers.title: Altered Use of Prior Expectations and Modified Neural Dynamics in a Mouse Model of Autism
papers.abstract: The authors investigate how genetic perturbations linked to autism spectrum disorder (ASD) disrupt the integration of prior beliefs with current sensory evidence during decision-making. Focusing on Neurexin1α (Nrxn1α) loss-of-function mice, the study utilizes widefield calcium imaging during a visually guided task. Nrxn1α KO mice exhibited an underutilization of block-based priors and significantly slower updating of choices following feedback. Cortically, these mice showed elevated and increasingly correlated activity across all task epochs, regardless of whether the period was sensory or motor-related. A larger fraction of neural variance in KO mice was explained by movement variables, indicating a shift toward motor-dominated dynamics and a corresponding deficit in the synaptic mechanisms required for flexible prior utilization.
papers.authors: M. Felicia Davatolhagh, Joao Couto, Maxwell Melin, Anne K. Churchland

papers.title: Anterior cingulate cortex mixes retrospective cognitive signals and ongoing movement signatures during decision-making
papers.abstract: This research examines how the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) tracks behavioral history during self-initiated perceptual decisions in static environments. Using large-scale calcium imaging in freely moving mice, the study demonstrates that ACC neurons exhibit nonlinear mixed selectivity for previous choices and outcomes, effectively maintaining a stable internal record of trial history over multiple seconds. These historical signals are distinct from and account for a separable component of neural activity compared to ongoing postural and movement signatures. The trial history representation in ACC was found to be low-dimensional, conserved across different subjects, and independent of behavioral biases, suggesting that the ACC serves as a shared monitoring hub for integrating past actions into current decision strategies.
papers.authors: Lukas T. Oesch, Makenna C. Thomas, Davis Sandberg, João Couto, Anne K. Churchland

papers.title: From innate to instructed: A new look at perceptual decision-making
papers.abstract: This comprehensive review synthesizes recent findings on the neural mechanisms of perceptual decision-making, with a focus on the distinction between tasks leveraging spontaneous, innate behaviors and those requiring extensive training to link stimuli with abstract choices. The authors highlight the significant role that uninstructed, spontaneous movements play in driving neural variability, even in highly trained subjects. They argue that traditional models often fail to account for the impact of movement on cortical dynamics. The paper advocates for experimental paradigms that incorporate the learning process itself, suggesting that understanding how task features influence the speed and success of decision rule acquisition is critical for developing more accurate models of sensorimotor integration and cognitive flexibility.
papers.authors: Lukas T. Oesch, Michael B. Ryan, Anne K. Churchland

0054.name: Anthony Cate
0054.bio: Anthony Cate is a cognitive neuroscientist investigating the mechanisms of human visual perception and their integration with higher cognitive functions such as numeracy. Cate’s research employs functional MRI, psychophysics, and computational modeling to examine the neural representation of 3D shapes, focusing on how the brain differentiates between concave and convex geometry within the ventral and dorsal streams. The Cate lab explores pattern recognition in stochastic visual fields and evaluates the limitations of deep learning architectures in depicting numerical object consistency. Cate has contributed to the anatomical and functional mapping of human visual cortical fields using high-resolution neuroimaging analysis.
0054.research_direction: Dr. Cate's recent work explores the cognitive and sensorimotor mechanisms underlying mathematical embodiment, focusing on how physical interactions with objects shape abstract reasoning. Using year-long constructivist teaching experiments, they have recently been investigating the relationship between a student's internal mental operations—such as units-coordination—and the physical affordances of specific educational manipulatives like linking cubes and Cuisenaire rods. Ultimately, their research seeks to model how distinct sensorimotor actions are interiorized into higher-level cognitive representations to facilitate the development of algebraic generalization.

papers.title: The (activity-)effect of manipulatives on algebraic generalizations: a constructivist teaching experiment
papers.abstract: This research utilizes a year-long constructivist teaching experiment involving sixth-grade participants to investigate the cognitive mechanisms through which physical manipulatives facilitate the development of algebraic generalizations. The study specifically analyzes the interaction between students' interiorized multiplicative structures (units-coordination stages) and the physical affordances of Cuisenaire rods versus linking cubes. Results indicate that the efficacy of manipulatives is constrained by the degree of alignment between the tool's physical properties and the student's internal mental operations. Linking cubes, which enable the physical enactment of discrete units of one, supported significant transitions to generalized arithmetic, whereas Cuisenaire rods initially failed to elicit such changes until students had already mastered generalizations through discrete unit activity. These findings provide evidence for a neuro-educational model of mathematical embodiment, suggesting that the construction of algebra as generalized arithmetic is mediated by the interiorization of specific sensorimotor actions into higher-level mental operations.
papers.authors: Karen Zwanch, Brooke Mullins, Anderson Norton, Catherine Ulrich, Martha Ann Bell, Anthony Cate

0055.name: Anthony M Norcia
0055.bio: Anthony M. Norcia is a Professor (Research) of Psychology at Stanford University where they investigate the mechanisms of visual development and the neural basis of perception. Norcia utilizes high-density electroencephalography (EEG) and steady-state visual evoked potentials (SSVEP) to measure cortical responses to spatial and temporal visual stimuli. By integrating EEG source imaging with functional MRI, Norcia maps the dynamics of visual processing in human infants and adults to understand both normal maturation and the pathophysiology of developmental disorders like strabismus, amblyopia, and glaucoma.
0055.research_direction: Dr. Norcia has recently been using high-density EEG and steady-state visual evoked potentials (SSVEPs) to map the functional organization and clinical vulnerabilities of distinct neural pathways in the human visual system. A major focus of their recent work explores the mechanisms of binocular depth perception, examining how independent cortical channels for absolute and relative disparity differ in their sensitivity to contrast and blur, as well as how these mechanisms mature along distinct developmental timelines from infancy to childhood. In parallel, they are investigating the visual system's ON and OFF pathways—responsible for processing luminance increments and decrements—using frequency-tagged sawtooth waveforms. By isolating these parallel systems, Dr. Norcia aims to understand their fundamental spatial asymmetries across the upper and lower visual fields and evaluate their diagnostic utility as electrophysiological biomarkers for detecting glaucomatous damage.

papers.title: Glaucoma Classification Through SSVEP-Derived ON- and OFF-Pathway Features
papers.abstract: The research evaluates the diagnostic efficacy of feature-based classification for glaucoma using steady-state visually evoked potentials (SSVEPs) biased toward ON (luminance increment) and OFF (luminance decrement) pathways. Utilizing 128-channel EEG recordings from a large cohort of 98 glaucoma patients and 71 age-matched controls, the study employs sawtooth temporal waveforms to isolate pathway-specific responses. Spectral decomposition via recursive least squares (RLS) filters was used to extract amplitude and phase components from the 2.73 Hz stimulation frequency. Findings indicate that classification models, including logistic regression and random forest classifiers, achieve moderate predictive accuracy (AUC ~0.7), with signal phase features providing superior diagnostic separation compared to amplitude. Notably, features derived from the OFF-pathway showed enhanced sensitivity in distinguishing glaucomatous eyes, supporting the hypothesis of preferential damage to decremental pathways in the disease.
papers.authors: Martin T. W. Scott, Hui Xu, Alexandra Yakovleva, Robert Tibshirani, Jeffrey L. Goldberg, Anthony M. Norcia

papers.title: Development of human binocular vision: An electrophysiological perspective
papers.abstract: This comprehensive review synthesizes several decades of research into the maturation of human binocular vision, specifically utilizing Visual Evoked Potentials (VEPs) to track neural development. It details the transition from early binocular summation (monocular-to-binocular amplitude ratios) to more sophisticated indices of binocular interaction, such as dichoptic masking and intermodulation. The review highlights a striking developmental dissociation where absolute disparity sensitivity matures rapidly within the first 6 months of life, while the processing of relative disparity—essential for global depth structure and fine stereopsis—remains highly immature until beyond 5 years of age. The author discusses these findings in the context of extrastriate cortical maturation and the computational requirements for extracting complex depth relationships from monocular inputs.
papers.authors: Anthony M. Norcia

papers.title: Visual Field Asymmetries in Responses to ON and OFF Pathway Biasing Stimuli
papers.abstract: This study investigates how cortical responses to luminance increments and decrements vary across the human visual field using high-density EEG. Using frequency tagging and sawtooth modulation (3 Hz and 3.75 Hz) to bias neural activity toward ON or OFF pathways, the researchers simultaneously measured contrast response functions in the upper and lower visual fields. Results demonstrate that responses to luminance decrements (OFF pathway) are consistently larger than those for increments (ON pathway), with this effect being significantly more pronounced in the lower visual field. In the upper visual field, the OFF pathway exhibited reduced saturation and higher inter-subject variability. These asymmetries suggest that the balance of ON and OFF pathway processing is non-uniformly distributed across retinotopic space, likely reflecting adaptation to the asymmetric statistics of natural visual environments.
papers.authors: Martin Timothy Wilkinson Scott, Alexandra Yakovleva, Anthony Matthew Norcia

papers.title: Two Disparity Channels in Human Visual Cortex With Different Contrast and Blur Sensitivity
papers.abstract: By employing steady-state visually evoked potentials (SSVEPs) and dynamic random dot stereograms (DRDSs), this study characterizes the contrast and blur sensitivity of distinct disparity-selective subsystems in the human visual cortex. Two stimulus configurations—a disparity plane (absolute disparity) and a 0.5 cpd disparity grating (relative disparity)—were modulated at 2 Hz. The first harmonic of the disparity grating response was highly sensitive to both contrast reduction and Gaussian blur, aligning with the properties of behavioral stereoacuity mechanisms tuned to high spatial frequencies. In contrast, the second harmonic of the disparity plane response exhibited higher contrast sensitivity and robustness to blur, suggesting a separate mechanism driven by lower monocular spatial frequencies and selective for absolute disparity. These results confirm the existence of independent cortical channels for absolute and relative disparity with distinct spatiotemporal and monocular tuning profiles.
papers.authors: Milena Kaestner, Yulan D. Chen, Caroline Clement, Alex Hodges, Anthony M. Norcia

0056.name: Antimo Buonocore
0056.department: Department of Educational, Psychological and Communication Sciences
0056.lab_name: Experimental Psychology and Cognitive Neuroscience Laboratory
0056.bio: Buonocore is an Associate Professor at Suor Orsola Benincasa University and directs the research program in Visual Cognition and Eye Movements. Their research investigates the neural and behavioral mechanisms of oculomotor control, focusing on saccadic inhibition and the interference of visual transients on spatial remapping. Utilizing high-resolution eye tracking, EEG, and transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), Buonocore examines the role of the superior colliculus and brainstem in sensorimotor integration and target selection. Their work also encompasses the study of oculomotor dynamics in Parkinson's disease and the influence of joint attention on visual processing.
0056.research_direction: Dr. Buonocore has recently been investigating the intricate links between visual processing and oculomotor control. Their recent work explores the temporal dynamics of saccadic inhibition, probing how and when transient visual events—ranging from simple flashes during naturalistic viewing to high-level semantic stimuli like faces—interrupt ongoing eye movements and influence late-stage motor reprogramming. In tandem with these behavioral approaches, they are mapping the functional architecture of the human oculomotor system, utilizing 7T fMRI to measure population receptive fields and spatial tuning along the intraparietal sulcus during memory-guided saccades. Broadening their focus on visual perception, they are also examining the mechanisms of face recognition, specifically asking how spatial frequencies, stimulus orientation, and familiarity interact during coarse-to-fine visual integration.

papers.title: Sustained dynamics of saccadic inhibition and adaptive oculomotor responses during continuous exploration
papers.abstract: Primates navigate complex visual environments through a continuous cycle of saccadic eye movements. External sensory transients can momentarily interrupt this process via saccadic inhibition (SI), characterized by a reflexive drop in saccade frequency followed by a motor rebound. While SI is well-documented in trial-based experiments, its behavior during ongoing, naturalistic viewing remains under-explored. Using an eye-tracking paradigm involving repeated, task-irrelevant visual flashes during free exploration, this study identifies a dissociation between the inhibitory and rebound phases of the oculomotor response. Results demonstrate that reflexive inhibition remains remarkably stable across repeated stimulation, whereas the subsequent rebound phase—reflecting motor re-engagement and reprogramming—exhibits significant habituation. This decoupling suggests that early sensory gating and late motor execution are mediated by distinct neurophysiological pathways, potentially localized in the brainstem omnipause neurons and superior colliculus/cortical motor areas, respectively.
papers.authors: Celeste Cafaro, Giovanni Cirillo, Giovanna Vermiglio, Carlo Cavaliere, Alessio Fracasso, Antimo Buonocore

papers.title: The Influence of Spatial Frequencies, Orientation and Familiarity on Face Stimuli Integration
papers.abstract: Human face perception relies on a coarse-to-fine integration process where low spatial frequency (LSF) signals provide a global template for more detailed high spatial frequency (HSF) information. This study investigates the interplay between spatial frequencies, stimulus orientation (upright vs. inverted), and familiarity using a sequential matching task. Leveraging the face inversion effect, the experiments reveal that face integration is highly contingent on image familiarity and orientation. For familiar faces, matching accuracy was significantly enhanced when HSF probes were mapped onto HSF templates in congruent conditions; however, under incongruent conditions, mapping LSF probes onto HSF templates proved more effective, specifically for upright faces. In contrast, unfamiliar face processing was primarily sensitive to spatial frequency congruency regardless of the template's frequency content. These findings challenge the traditional hierarchical template model and suggest a flexible, task-dependent encoding strategy for integrating spatial information in face recognition.
papers.authors: Maria Cuomo, Giovanni Federico, Alessio Fracasso, Antimo Buonocore

papers.title: Mapping memory-guided saccade population receptive fields reveals principles of cortical organization along the human intraparietal sulcus
papers.abstract: The human intraparietal sulcus (IPS) is a critical hub for oculomotor planning and coordinate transformations. Using ultra-high-field functional magnetic resonance imaging (7T fMRI) and a memory-guided saccade paradigm, this research maps the population receptive fields (pRFs) of neurons involved in oculomotor control. The study identifies a series of topographic maps along the IPS that exhibit systematic shifts in receptive field size and spatial tuning from posterior to anterior regions. Crucially, the findings reveal that these cortical areas maintain a consistent contralateral bias and represent a full range of saccadic amplitudes, including small-scale movements. The results provide a detailed account of the functional architecture of the human oculomotor priority maps and suggest that IPS organization supports a seamless integration of sensory signals into motor vectors across multiple reference frames.
papers.authors: Alessio Fracasso, Jasper Fabius, Katarina Moravkova, Antimo Buonocore

papers.title: Saccadic “inhibition” unveils the late influence of image content on oculomotor programming
papers.abstract: The timing at which complex image content, such as facial information, impacts the oculomotor system remains a subject of neuroscientific debate. This study utilizes the phenomenon of saccadic inhibition (SI)—the rapid suppression of saccades by visual transients—to probe the stage of motor programming affected by high-level visual features. In a series of experiments, participants performed saccadic tasks where task-irrelevant faces or scrambled stimuli were presented. While the initial onset of saccadic inhibition (the express inhibitory component) was identical for both face and control stimuli, significant modulations in the late inhibitory phase and the subsequent motor rebound were observed exclusively for face stimuli. Quantitative analysis of saccade kinematics showed that while low-level properties determine the initial reflexive suppression, the semantic content of the image influences oculomotor output only at later stages, likely reflecting feedback from higher-order ventral stream areas to midbrain motor gating circuits.
papers.authors: Rebecca Taylor, Antimo Buonocore, Alessio Fracasso

0059.name: Arash Afraz
0059.department: National Institute of Mental Health, Laboratory of Neuropsychology
0059.lab_name: Unit on Neurons, Circuits and Behavior (UNCB)
0059.main_research_area: Neural mechanisms of visual object recognition
0059.bio: Arash Afraz is a Principal Investigator at the National Institute of Mental Health and leads the Unit on Neurons, Circuits and Behavior. Afraz researches the causal links between neural activity in the ventral visual stream, particularly the inferior temporal cortex, and the behavioral outcomes of object recognition. By integrating visual psychophysics with single-unit recording, optogenetics, and microstimulation in non-human primates, they aim to map how high-level cortical areas shape subjective visual perception. Recent work by Afraz on "perceptography" focuses on quantifying the hallucinatory percepts induced by neural perturbation to provide data for the development of visual prosthetics.
0059.research_direction: Dr. Afraz has recently been investigating the neural mechanisms of high-level visual perception and object categorization in the macaque temporal cortex. Their recent work explores how spatial frequency selectivity shapes hierarchical category representations and population coding within the inferior temporal (IT) cortex. They are also probing the causal role of the ventral stream in perception and behavior by utilizing pharmacological inactivation of face patches to study naturalistic oculomotor control, and by combining behavioral optogenetics with machine learning to reconstruct the subjective visual hallucinations induced by cortical stimulation. To facilitate these advanced neurophysiological paradigms, they are concurrently developing novel methodological tools, such as personalized, 3D-printed non-invasive head immobilization systems for awake behaving non-human primates.

papers.title: 3D-printable non-invasive head immobilization system for non-human primates
papers.abstract: The researchers present a novel, custom-designed non-invasive head immobilization system (NHIS) for macaque monkeys, utilizing 3D printing technology to overcome the clinical complications associated with traditional surgically implanted headposts. The system's design is driven by subject-specific CT or MRI scans processed through the FLoRIN and Blender software pipelines to create personalized helmets. Quantitative validation in behaving macaques demonstrated that the NHIS maintains fixational precision and accuracy (0.23° and 0.47°, respectively) comparable to invasive alternatives, while facilitating voluntary animal engagement and reducing the risk of bone necrosis or infection during high-resolution eye tracking and neurophysiological recordings.
papers.authors: Elia Shahbazi, Drew Nguyen, Tyler Swedan, Timothy Ma, Rosa Lafer-Sousa, Alvin Dinh, Reza Azadi, Amy M Ryan, Arash Afraz

papers.title: The spatial frequency representation predicts category coding in the inferior temporal cortex
papers.abstract: This study investigates the relationship between single-neuron spatial frequency (SF) selectivity and population-level category coding in the macaque inferotemporal (IT) cortex. Through extracellular recordings using SF-filtered stimuli, the authors identified a coarse-to-fine temporal progression, where the preferred spatial frequency of IT neurons shifts from low to high during the visual response. While SF and category representations appear dissociated at the single-neuron level, the study demonstrates that a neuron's SF response profile can predict its contribution to category decoding at the population level, with high-SF-preferring neurons exhibiting the most robust classification performance for face stimuli.
papers.authors: Ramin Toosi, Behnam Karami, Roxana Koushki, Farideh Shakerian, Jalaledin Noroozi, Ehsan Rezayat, Abdol-Hossein Vahabie, Mohammad Ali Akhaee, Mohammad-Reza A Dehaqani, Arash Afraz

papers.title: The impact of spatial frequency on hierarchical category representation in macaque temporal cortex
papers.abstract: The researchers examined how the spatial frequency (SF) of visual stimuli modulates the hierarchical representation of objects (superordinate, mid-level, and subordinate) within the macaque inferior temporal cortex and superior temporal sulcus. Utilizing rapid serial visual presentation (RSVP) of bandpass-filtered images, they found that mid-level category representations (e.g., faces vs. bodies) are relatively invariant to SF changes. In contrast, superordinate categorization (animate vs. inanimate) relied heavily on high-SF (HSF) information, while subordinate-level identity discrimination required the integration of both low and high SF components, suggesting that the ventral stream utilizes distinct spectral channels for different levels of categorical abstraction.
papers.authors: Esmaeil Farhang, Ramin Toosi, Behnam Karami, Roxana Koushki, Narges Kheirkhah, Farideh Shakerian, Jalaledin Noroozi, Ehsan Rezayat, Abdol-Hossein Vahabie, Mohammad-Reza A Dehaqani, Arash Afraz

papers.title: Perceptography unveils the causal contribution of inferior temporal cortex to visual perception
papers.abstract: The authors introduce 'perceptography,' a method that combines machine learning with high-throughput behavioral optogenetics to reconstruct stimulation-induced visual hallucinations. By stimulating the macaque inferotemporal (IT) cortex while concurrently presenting image perturbations, the researchers identified specific visual distortions, termed 'perceptograms,' that monkeys could not distinguish from actual cortical stimulation. The results demonstrate that the subjective content and magnitude of these induced percepts are highly dependent on the anatomical location of the stimulation, the intensity of the signal, and the specific visual context provided by concurrent external sensory input.
papers.authors: Elia Shahbazi, Timothy Ma, Martin Pernuš, Walter Scheirer, Arash Afraz

papers.title: Inactivation of face-selective neurons alters eye movements when free viewing faces
papers.abstract: This research establishes a causal link between high-level visual representations in the inferotemporal (IT) cortex and the control of the oculomotor system during naturalistic viewing. By utilizing muscimol-induced pharmacological inactivation of fMRI-localized face patches in macaques, the researchers observed significant changes in eye movement patterns during the free viewing of faces. Monkeys exhibited a specific neglect of facial features, primarily the eyes, located in the visual hemifield contralateral to the inactivated hemisphere. The findings indicate that the neural activity of face-selective neurons in the ventral stream is an essential component of the causal chain that steers gaze toward behaviorally relevant facial attributes.
papers.authors: Reza Azadi, Emily Lopez, Jessica Taubert, Allison Patterson, Arash Afraz

0060.name: Arathy Kartha
0060.department: Department of Biological and Vision Sciences
0060.lab_name: Multisensory Integration in Visual Impairment Lab
0060.bio: Arathy Kartha is an Assistant Professor at the SUNY College of Optometry. Kartha's research focuses on functional vision enhancement through multisensory integration and rehabilitation technologies. Their work utilizes virtual reality and real-world assessments to evaluate visual ability and develop training protocols for individuals with ultra-low vision and those using visual neuroprostheses. Kartha investigates how auditory and haptic cues supplement prosthetic vision to assist with navigation and object recognition. As a recipient of the NIH K99/R00 Pathway to Independence Award, they examine the intersection of psychophysics and clinical ophthalmology to evaluate vision restoration therapies.
0060.research_direction: Dr. Kartha has recently been developing and validating objective assessments of functional vision for individuals with profound visual impairment and retinal prostheses. Their recent work explores using virtual and augmented reality platforms to standardize the measurement of visuomotor coordination, spatial localization, and motion discrimination under strictly controlled luminance and contrast conditions. In addition to evaluating how effectively different commercial augmented reality devices enhance visual acuity across diverse lighting environments, they are investigating the discrepancies between subjective patient self-reports and objective behavioral performance. Furthermore, their research tests whether integrating gamification into these rigorous psychophysical assessments can reduce cognitive fatigue and improve sustained attention for patients participating in longitudinal vision restoration trials.

papers.title: Comparison of visual function analysis of people with low vision using three different models of augmented reality devices
papers.abstract: This prospective investigation evaluates the relative efficacy of three head-mounted augmented reality (AR) systems—Ziru, IrisVision, and NuEyes-Pro3—in enhancing functional vision for individuals with moderate-to-severe low vision (VA > 20/60). Distance visual acuity was assessed across four photometric conditions: high luminance high contrast (HLHC), high luminance low contrast (HLLC), low luminance high contrast (LLHC), and low luminance low contrast (LLLC). Findings indicate that Ziru and IrisVision significantly improve distance visual acuity and contrast sensitivity across varied illumination settings, whereas NuEyes demonstrated more localized improvements. The study also quantifies performance in near visual acuity, depth perception, and indoor navigation, providing a comparative performance matrix to guide the clinical prescription of electronic vision enhancement systems based on individual pathology-driven visual deficits.
papers.authors: Sarika Gopalakrishnan, Arathy Kartha, Ronald Schuchard, Donald Fletcher

papers.title: Measuring visually guided motor performance in ultra low vision using virtual reality
papers.abstract: The authors present the development and psychometric calibration of 'Wilmer VRH,' a virtual reality-based toolkit designed to quantify visuomotor coordination in the ultra-low vision (ULV) population (visual acuity ≤ 20/1600). Fifty-five distinct task items encompassing reaching, grasping, stacking, and sorting were implemented in a VR headset to standardize environmental parameters. Using a polytomous Rasch model (method of successive dichotomizations), the study analyzed performance data from 33 ULV participants and 20 normally-sighted controls under simulated ULV conditions. The Wilmer VRH exhibited high unidimensionality and reliability (item reliability = 0.94; person reliability = 0.91), establishing a robust, portable outcome measure for clinical trials involving retinal prostheses, gene therapy, and optogenetics.
papers.authors: Arathy Kartha, Roksana Sadeghi, Chris Bradley, Brittnee Livingston, Chau Tran, Will Gee, Gislin Dagnelie

papers.title: Self-Reported Visual Ability Versus Task Performance in Individuals With Ultra-Low Vision
papers.abstract: This study examines the concordance between patient-reported difficulty and objective functional performance in individuals with ultra-low vision (ULV). Matching activities were selected from the Ultra-Low Vision Visual Functioning Questionnaire (ULV-VFQ) and the virtual reality-based Wilmer VRI performance test. Using Rasch analysis and latent variable signal detection theory to estimate person ability and item difficulty, the researchers found only a modest correlation between self-reported measures and actual task execution (r² = 0.36 for person measures). These results highlight a significant divergence between subjective perception and objective capacity, emphasizing the necessity of standardized performance-based metrics over self-reports in assessing the efficacy of vision restoration interventions.
papers.authors: Arathy Kartha, Ravnit Kaur Singh, Chris Bradley, Gislin Dagnelie

papers.title: Measuring visual information gathering in individuals with ultra low vision using virtual reality
papers.abstract: The research details the validation of a virtual reality (VR) assessment module tailored for visual information gathering—specifically spatial localization and motion discrimination—in patients with profound visual impairment. Nineteen task-based scenarios were rendered in a VR headset to maintain precise control over stimulus luminance, contrast, and eccentricity. Through latent variable analysis grounded in signal detection theory, the study calibrated item difficulty and participant ability in a cohort of ULV individuals. The findings demonstrate that VR platforms can effectively mitigate the variability of real-world environmental lighting, providing a standardized and sensitive tool for longitudinal monitoring of functional vision in prosthetic and biological vision restoration research.
papers.authors: Arathy Kartha, Roksana Sadeghi, Chris Bradley, Chau Tran, Will Gee, Gislin Dagnelie

papers.title: Gamification Enhances User Engagement and Task Performance in Prosthetic Vision Testing
papers.abstract: This study explores the impact of gamification on the psychophysical assessment of retinal prosthesis users, aiming to mitigate the cognitive fatigue associated with traditional testing paradigms. Three Argus II implantees performed circle localization and motion direction discrimination tasks in both standard clinical and gamified VR formats. The gamified versions incorporated scoring systems, ambient audio, and affective feedback while maintaining identical visual stimulus parameters. Results indicated that gamification significantly enhanced localization accuracy and reduced angular error, alongside improved participant-reported enjoyment and sustained attention. However, performance gains were task-specific, with no significant improvement observed in motion discrimination, suggesting that engagement-aware adaptive difficulty tools can improve the scalability of at-home prosthetic rehabilitation.
papers.authors: Lily M. Turkstra, Byron Johnson, Arathy Kartha, Chris Bradley, Roksana Sadeghi, Gislin Dagnelie, Michael Beyeler

0062.name: Arthur G Shapiro
0062.department: Department of Psychology and Department of Computer Science
0062.lab_name: Laboratory for the Study of Perception, Reality, and Illusion (SPRI)
0062.bio: Arthur G. Shapiro studies visual perception and neuroscience, focusing on the mechanisms underlying color perception, motion, and low-light vision. Shapiro uses visual illusions to investigate the computational and physiological processes that connect physical stimuli to sensory experience. Their research involves developing models of spatial and temporal contrast to explain phenomena such as lightness constancy and the peripheral-foveal processing gap. Shapiro has received multiple awards from the Best Illusion of the Year Contest and serves as the co-editor of the Oxford Compendium of Visual Illusions.
0062.research_direction: Dr. Shapiro has recently been investigating the computational and neural mechanisms underlying visual perception, utilizing both novel and classic illusions to probe how the brain processes lightness, motion, and depth. Their recent work explores the architecture of brightness and contrast processing, combining large-scale psychophysics with factor analysis to uncover latent mechanisms across different lightness illusions, while also using steady-state visual evoked potentials (SSVEPs) to separate the cortical temporal dynamics of luminance and spatial contrast modulation. Additionally, they are examining how the visual system synthesizes global shapes from local signals by observing the continuous perpetual rotation of illusory contours and Kanizsa figures when driven by ambiguous edge motions. Finally, Dr. Shapiro is investigating binocular temporal dynamics in spatial computing, utilizing hybrid-motion psychophysical tasks to quantify how asymmetric luminance and contrast influence interocular delays and drive the Pulfrich effect in virtual reality environments.

papers.title: Relationships among lightness illusions uncovered by analyses of individual differences
papers.abstract: Conventional validation of lightness perception models typically assesses their ability to predict individual illusion signs, presupposing inter-stimulus independence. This study evaluates correlations across various lightness illusions—including White's effect, assimilation, and simultaneous contrast—using exploratory factor analysis (EFA) on data from large-scale psychophysical experiments. We identify three distinct underlying factors (assimilation, contrast, and White's effect), demonstrating that specific neural mechanisms likely drive broad clusters of illusory phenomena. Our findings reveal that prevalent spatial-filtering and early-vision models exhibit systematic biases toward specific illusory factors, suggesting that model evaluation should transition from individual illusions to these identified latent factors.
papers.authors: Yuki Kobayashi, Arthur G. Shapiro

papers.title: Perpetual rotation of real and illusory shapes
papers.abstract: This research investigates the synthesis of global shape from local motion signals by integrating edge motion illusions with Kanizsa figures. Although local edges in the display signal ambiguous linear trajectories (horizontal or vertical), the global illusory square is perceived as undergoing continuous rotation. This emergent rotational motion persists even when the stimulus is defined only by illusory contours, indicating the robustness of rigid global shape priors in visual processing. Variants involving temporal phase manipulation and amodal completion further characterize the conditions under which global context redirects local motion, revealing a bistable interaction where attention modulates the dominance of local vs. global perceptual modes.
papers.authors: Yuki Kobayashi, Arthur G. Shapiro

papers.title: The Pulfrich Effect in Virtual Reality
papers.abstract: We examine the magnitude of the Pulfrich effect—a depth misperception resulting from interocular temporal delays—within virtual reality (VR) systems. By utilizing a double-helix hybrid-motion stimulus, we characterize the influence of global luminance and local contrast on perceived depth. We report a novel finding that low-reflectance (dark) stimuli accentuate the Pulfrich effect more significantly than high-reflectance (bright) stimuli, a result linked to the asymmetric temporal dynamics of VR displays. Experimental data were successfully captured via power law models, providing quantitative constraints for mitigating or leveraging depth distortions in spatial computing environments and asymmetric lighting designs.
papers.authors: Anthony LoPrete, Alexander M Gokan, Arthur G Shapiro

papers.title: Separation of luminance and contrast modulation in steady-state visual evoked potentials
papers.abstract: This study employs steady-state visual evoked potentials (SSVEPs) to investigate the neural differentiation between luminance modulation and spatial contrast modulation. By using a 'contrast asynchrony' paradigm that pairs synchronous disk luminance changes with asynchronous disk-surround contrast signals, we recorded occipital cortical activity during sinusoidal flicker. The results demonstrate that the early visual system maintains distinct neural pathways for processing brightness and contrast information at lower temporal frequencies. However, at higher frequencies and contrast levels, these signals interact to form complex responses that deviate from linear predictions. The findings support interocular normalization models as the basis for combining contrast and luminance signals.
papers.authors: Laysa Hedjar, Jasna Martinovic, Søren K Andersen, Arthur G Shapiro

0065.name: Aude Oliva
0065.department: Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL)
0065.bio: Aude Oliva is a Senior Research Scientist at the MIT Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL) and the Director of Strategic Industry Engagement at the MIT Schwarzman College of Computing. Their research integrates human perception, computer vision, and cognitive neuroscience to model how the human brain encodes, processes, and remembers complex visual scenes. Oliva’s work involves research on image memorability, the development of "hybrid images," and the use of deep neural networks to map spatiotemporal brain dynamics. They also direct the MIT-IBM Watson AI Lab and lead initiatives focused on the intersection of natural and artificial intelligence.
0065.research_direction: Dr. Oliva has recently been investigating how complex visual experiences are processed in the brain and how computational models can decode or augment human perception. A major focus of their recent work explores scalable frameworks for neural decoding, utilizing large-scale fMRI dataset aggregation and generative diffusion models to reconstruct dynamic videos directly from brain activity. In parallel, they are studying the spatiotemporal neural dynamics of visual memorability, using MEG-fMRI fusion to map exactly when and where the brain prioritizes highly memorable images across the ventral stream. Beyond fundamental neural representations, Dr. Oliva is also examining applied visual cognition by testing human susceptibility to deepfakes under ecologically valid browsing conditions and developing AI-assisted visual interventions to improve forgery detection.

papers.title: MOSAIC: A scalable framework for fMRI dataset aggregation and modeling of human vision
papers.abstract: To overcome the statistical power and stimulus diversity limitations of individual fMRI datasets, the authors develop MOSAIC (Meta-Organized Stimuli And fMRI Imaging data for Computational modeling), a framework that aggregates eight large-scale vision fMRI repositories. The resulting corpus contains data from 93 subjects and 430,007 fMRI-stimulus pairs across 162,839 unique stimuli. By implementing a standardized preprocessing pipeline and rigorous cross-dataset train-test splits to mitigate leakage, the framework enables the joint training of brain-optimized encoding models across subjects and datasets. Empirical results demonstrate that aggregating perceptually diverse stimulus sets significantly improves decoding accuracy and stability, allowing for the successful recovery of subject-specific category-selective regions through in silico functional localizer experiments performed on the resulting digital twin models.
papers.authors: Benjamin Lahner, Mayukh Deb, N. Apurva Ratan Murty, Aude Oliva

papers.title: Brain Netflix: Scaling Data to Reconstruct Videos from Brain Activity
papers.abstract: The researchers propose a scalable framework for reconstructing dynamic visual experiences from human brain activity, addressing the challenge posed by the high dimensionality of video and the low temporal resolution of fMRI. The system utilizes a three-stage training pipeline: first, a masked brain modeling (MBM) phase for representational learning of fMRI signals; second, a regression phase to map brain representations to visual and semantic conditioning vectors; and third, a synthesis phase using a latent video diffusion model. By scaling both stimulus variety and the number of participants, the model achieves state-of-the-art results in pixel-level and semantic video reconstruction. The findings suggest that large-scale neural data enables generative models to accurately read out temporal visual percepts from blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) signals.
papers.authors: Camilo Luciano Fosco, Benjamin Lahner, Bowen Pan, Alex Andonian, Emilie L. Josephs, Alex Lascelles, Aude Oliva

papers.title: Visual perception of highly memorable images is mediated by a distributed network of ventral visual regions that enable a late memorability response
