papers.abstract: This study delineates the spatiotemporal neural dynamics of image memorability—an intrinsic property that determines recall consistency across observers. Using MEG-fMRI fusion, the authors identify a memorability-sensitive cortical signature that emerges approximately 300 ms post-stimulus onset. Comparison between semantically matched high-memorability and low-memorability images reveals increased neural responses in the early visual cortex (EVC), inferior temporal cortex, fusiform gyrus, and lateral occipital cortex for memorable stimuli. The results indicate that memorability is represented after high-level feature processing in visual regions and is subsequently reflected in medial temporal lobe (MTL) memory structures. This evidence supports a levels-of-processing theory, where highly memorable images undergo more extensive perceptual processing that facilitates their encoding into memory.
papers.authors: Benjamin Lahner, Yalda Mohsenzadeh, Caitlin Mullin, Aude Oliva

papers.title: A Systematic Comparison of fMRI-to-video Reconstruction Techniques
papers.abstract: The authors conduct a comprehensive evaluation of neural-to-stimulus reconstruction methods, focusing on the synthesis of dynamic visual content from fMRI data. As generative architectures and large-scale neural datasets become more prevalent, the study systematically benchmarks various strategies, including direct latent space mapping and conditional video diffusion models. Quality of reconstruction is quantified using a suite of structural metrics (e.g., SSIM) and semantic metrics (e.g., CLIP-score). The analysis highlights the relative efficacy of different generative backbones and investigates how data scale and stimulus diversity influence reconstruction fidelity. These benchmarks establish optimal practices for decoding dynamic mental percepts and provide a technical foundation for future brain-computer vision interfaces.
papers.authors: Camilo Fosco, Benjamin Lahner, Bowen Pan, Alex Andonian, Emilie Josephs, Alex Lascelles, Aude Oliva

papers.title: Effects of Browsing Conditions and Visual Alert Design on Human Susceptibility to Deepfakes
papers.abstract: To evaluate human vulnerability to deepfake misinformation, the authors examine detection performance under ecologically valid browsing conditions: low prevalence, brief presentation, degraded video quality, and divided attention. Online experiments reveal that these factors significantly impair human detection sensitivity (d') relative to laboratory baselines. To address this vulnerability, the study introduces 'Deepfake Caricatures,' a visual alert system that utilizes a semi-supervised Artifact Attention module to magnify subtle motion artifacts in forgeries. Results demonstrate that artifact magnification significantly enhances human detection rates and subjective confidence. Furthermore, users are more likely to integrate AI-assisted feedback when presented with caricatured artifacts than with traditional text-based warnings, suggesting superior outcomes for human-AI teaming in misinformation mitigation.
papers.venue: Journal of Online Trust and Safety
papers.authors: Emilie Josephs, Camilo Fosco, Aude Oliva

0066.name: Austin Roorda
0066.department: School of Optometry and Vision Science
0066.bio: Austin Roorda researches vision science, utilizing adaptive optics technologies to image and stimulate the human retina at a cellular scale. Roorda mapped the human trichromatic cone mosaic and developed the Adaptive Optics Scanning Laser Ophthalmoscope (AOSLO) for high-resolution retinal research. Their research combines optical engineering and neuroscience to study how the optics of the eye and the spatial arrangement of photoreceptors influence visual perception. This work also examines how these physiological factors are affected by the presence of retinal disease.
0066.research_direction: Dr. Roorda has recently been leveraging high-resolution adaptive optics imaging—such as AOSLO and phase-sensitive OCT—to probe the functional and structural limits of human vision down to the level of single photoreceptors, including measuring phototransduction-linked cellular deformations via optoretinography. Their recent work explores the interplay between fine oculomotor behavior and perception, specifically investigating how the visual system processes relative motion during fixational drift and how microsaccades are used to spatially and temporally optimize high-resolution sampling at the fovea. They are also investigating clinical adaptations to central vision loss by mapping the photoreceptor integrity and fixational stability of eccentric preferred retinal loci in patients with macular disease. Additionally, their research spans computational optics, involving the development of wide-field schematic eye models to examine how peripheral wavefront aberrations might influence the progression of myopia.

papers.title: A discontinuity in motion perception during fixational drift
papers.abstract: The human visual system demonstrates an exquisite capacity for relative motion detection, often exceeding the spatial sampling limits of foveal cones. However, this study identifies a specific perceptual failure during fixational drift: stimuli programmed to move in a direction consistent with retinal slip appear remarkably stable, even when the slip magnitude is significantly amplified. Utilizing an adaptive optics scanning light ophthalmoscope (AOSLO) for precise gaze-contingent stimulus delivery, we characterized the perceptual transition from stability to motion. We observed a sharp discontinuity in perception; motion is readily detectable in directions incongruent with drift, but undergoes systematic suppression when aligned with the direction of retinal slip. This effect is contingent upon the presence of world-fixed retinal image background content within approximately 4° of the target, suggesting the visual system integrates local retinal context to distinguish self-generated slip from exogenous motion, effectively recalibrating the perceived coordinate frame.
papers.authors: Josephine C. D'Angelo, Pavan Tiruveedhula, Raymond J. Weber, David W. Arathorn, Jorge Otero-Millan, Austin Roorda

papers.title: Optoretinography with actively stabilized adaptive optics optical coherence tomography
papers.abstract: Optoretinography (ORG) facilitates non-invasive functional evaluation of retinal physiology by quantifying nanometer-scale phototransduction-linked deformations in photoreceptor outer segments (OS). A primary challenge in phase-sensitive adaptive optics optical coherence tomography (AOOCT) is the decorrelation and noise introduced by fixational eye motion. We present an active stabilization method integrating an adaptive optics scanning light ophthalmoscope (AOSLO) for high-speed (960 Hz) retinal tracking to dynamically guide the AOOCT probe beam. This system enables real-time motion compensation, allowing for phase-sensitive ORG acquisition at 100 kHz from targeted foveal cones with minimal post-processing. We demonstrate the system's utility by performing spectral classification of individual photoreceptors based on their differential OS expansion kinetics following monochromatic stimulation and validate these results against traditional offline registration methods.
papers.authors: Jason H. Wong, Shangbang Luo, Zohreh Hosseinaee, Fabio Feroldi, Austin Roorda

papers.title: High Resolution Imaging and Fixation Analysis of Eccentric Preferred Retinal Loci in Macular Diseases
papers.abstract: This study characterizes the preferred retinal locus (PRL) structure and fixational stability in eyes with macular atrophy resulting from diverse etiologies, including congenital rubella and Stargardt disease. Utilizing multimodal high-resolution imaging—comprising AOSLO, SD-OCT, swept-source OCT angiography (OCT-A), and microperimetry—we evaluated the relationship between retinal structural integrity and fixation behavior. Despite the presence of intact, more sensitive cones at greater eccentricities, participants consistently localized the PRL within 0.44 to 1.92 degrees of the anatomic foveola. These PRL regions exhibited hyporeflective cones in confocal AOSLO and disrupted inner-segment/outer-segment (IS/OS) junctions on OCT. Fixation stability in these eccentric fixators was comparable to patients with retinitis pigmentosa. Our findings indicate that foveal proximity is prioritized over photoreceptor integrity and local sensitivity in the establishment of a new PRL during central vision loss.
papers.authors: Olubayo U Kolawole, Ethan Bensinger, Jessica Wong, Nicholas Rinella, Katharina G Foote, Hao Zhou, Ruikang K Wang, Jacque L Duncan, Austin Roorda

papers.title: The Optimal Retinal Locus for High-Resolution Vision in Space and Time
papers.abstract: Human oculomotor behavior exhibits quasi-deterministic dynamics in the temporal and spatial domains during demanding foveal resolution tasks, characterized by an attenuation of microsaccade frequency immediately preceding stimulus onset. Using an AOSLO to project stimuli and track retinal position, we analyzed how fixational drift and microsaccades coordinate to direct anticipated visual inputs toward a discrete preferred retinal locus (PRL). We demonstrate that the PRL corresponds to the retinal position yielding optimal visual acuity, even when this location is spatially offset from the anatomical center of the fovea (the locus of peak cone density). Psychophysical performance reaches an asymptote only when the interval between the final microsaccade and stimulus presentation exceeds 400 ms, suggesting a temporal threshold for retinal image stabilization required for maximal sampling. These results reveal a highly evolved, involuntary oculomotor strategy that optimizes gaze direction to maintain resolution at the physiological limits of the foveolar mosaic.
papers.authors: Josselin Gautier, Norick R Bowers, Martin S Banks, Austin Roorda

papers.title: Wide-field optical eye models for emmetropic and myopic eyes
papers.abstract: We developed wide-field schematic optical eye models for emmetropic and myopic populations that incorporate individualized anatomical biometry and reproduce measured ocular wavefront aberrations across a ±40° horizontal by ±25° vertical visual field. Most conventional models focus on paraxial optics, failing to capture the peripheral image quality relevant to peripheral defocus and its role in myopia progression. By optimizing ocular refracting surfaces and retinal shape to minimize root mean square (RMS) wavefront error relative to population data, our models account for both foveal and peripheral aberrations, including the characteristic oblate retinal shape (Q > 0). We validated these models against Seidel aberration theory and chromatic aberration expectations. The resulting framework provides a robust computational tool for investigating the effects of peripheral image quality on myopia and for the design of wide-field ophthalmic corrections.
papers.authors: G. D. Hastings, Pavan Tiruveedhula, Austin Roorda

0067.name: Avniel Ghuman
0067.bio: Avniel Ghuman is an Associate Professor of Neurological Surgery specializing in the neural mechanisms of high-level visual and social perception. Ghuman’s research integrates invasive intracranial EEG (iEEG) and non-invasive magnetoencephalography (MEG) with computational techniques, including machine learning and network analysis, to map the spatiotemporal dynamics of information flow in the brain. This work examines the representation of faces and objects within real-world contexts, utilizing deep learning models to reconstruct visual experiences from neural activity. Currently, their research explores real-world neurodynamics to understand how brain states and transitions support behavior during natural social interactions.
0067.research_direction: Dr. Ghuman has recently been investigating the neural mechanisms of naturalistic visual perception and continuous human behavior using multi-day intracranial EEG recordings. Their recent work explores how the brain processes complex, real-world visual information, probing both the encoding of dynamic facial features during unscripted social interactions and the spatiotemporal gradients of neural timescales within the ventral temporal cortex. Beyond specific visual and category-selective processes, they are also examining long-term cortical network dynamics, applying machine learning and dynamical systems theory to understand how continuous high-gamma activity reflects broad behavioral contexts over hours and days. By moving beyond isolated trial-based tasks, their research ultimately seeks to map the continuous trajectory of human neurocognitive states, investigating how cortical networks navigate between stable functional configurations and rapid chaotic transitions during everyday life.

papers.title: Neural encoding of real world face perception
papers.abstract: The neural mechanisms underlying social perception in unconstrained environments remain largely opaque. In this study, multi-electrode intracranial EEG was recorded from human subjects during spontaneous, unscripted interactions with friends and family. By parameterizing face identity, pose, motion, and expression using computer vision and state-space models, the authors developed a bidirectional latent neuro-perceptual model. This model successfully reconstructed movies of observed faces from neural activity and predicted brain dynamics from facial features. The results identified a critical network for real-world social vision spanning the occipital, temporal, and parietal cortices, often termed the 'third visual stream.' Furthermore, neural tuning was found to be sharply focused on deviations from a neutral expression prototype, following a neural Weber’s law for facial expressions that was validated by subsequent psychophysical experiments.
papers.authors: Arish Alreja, Michael J. Ward, Lisa S. Parker, R. Mark Richardson, Louis-Philippe Morency, Taylor J. Abel, Avniel Singh Ghuman

papers.title: Spatiotemporal dynamics of human high gamma discriminate naturalistic behavioral states
papers.abstract: Standard neuroscientific paradigms typically rely on repeated trial-based tasks to isolate cognitive functions, often overlooking the continuous neural dynamics that govern naturalistic behavior. This study utilized 3–12 days of continuous intracranial recordings (ECoG and sEEG) in 20 patients to investigate the neural correlates of unstructured real-world activities. Applying machine learning and graph-theoretic analyses to high-gamma band (70-150 Hz) activity, the researchers demonstrated that spatiotemporal patterns of neural synchronization and power reliably discriminate between broad behavioral states (e.g., socializing, device usage, and rest). The findings reveal that slow-varying mean activity and inter-electrode covariance are highly predictive of situational context, suggesting that human cortical networks transition between stable states that correspond to meaningful physiological and behavioral periods in everyday life.
papers.authors: Maxwell Wang, Max G'Sell, James F. Castellano, R. Mark Richardson, Avniel Ghuman

papers.title: Interacting ventral temporal gradients of timescales and functional connectivity and their relationships to visual behavior
papers.abstract: The functional specialization of the ventral temporal cortex (VTC) is organized along complex anatomical and physiological gradients. This study investigated the relationship between intrinsic neural timescales (measured via the temporal autocorrelation of high-frequency broadband activity) and long-range functional connectivity along category-selective VTC regions. Using intracranial EEG, the authors identified two interacting gradients: an increasing posterior-to-anterior gradient of neural timescales and a corresponding gradient in functional connectivity to association versus sensory-motor regions. Specifically, areas with longer intrinsic processing windows exhibited stronger connectivity to transmodal networks and lower category discriminability. These interactions predicted participant reaction times during visual tasks, suggesting that the intersection of local dynamics and global network integration defines the computational roles of VTC sub-regions in object recognition and decision-making.
papers.authors: Matthew J. Boring, R. Mark Richardson, Avniel Singh Ghuman

papers.title: A week in the life of the human brain: stable states punctuated by chaotic transitions
papers.abstract: Human neurocognitive states, such as arousal and engagement in natural activities, fluctuate over hours in the real world. To capture these dynamics, the researchers analyzed long-term continuous multi-electrode intracranial recordings from patients over several days. By integrating deep recurrent neural networks with Koopman dynamical systems theory, they mapped the trajectory of brain network configurations into a low-dimensional hourglass-shaped manifold. The dynamics were characterized by stable states punctuated by rapid, chaotic neural fluctuations during behavioral transitions. A central attractor on this manifold corresponded to the default mode network (DMN), acting as a stabilizing equilibrium. These results suggest that the brain balances stability and flexibility by utilizing chaotic exploration to transition between stable configurations anchored by homeostatic-like network hubs.
papers.authors: Maxwell Wang, Max G'Sell, James F. Castellano, R. Mark Richardson, Avniel Ghuman

0070.name: Barbara Shinn-Cunningham
0070.department: Neuroscience Institute, Mellon College of Science, Psychology, Biomedical Engineering, Electrical and Computer Engineering
0070.bio: Barbara Shinn-Cunningham serves as the Glen de Vries Dean of the Mellon College of Science and was the founding director of the Neuroscience Institute at Carnegie Mellon University. Shinn-Cunningham’s research focuses on the neural mechanisms underlying auditory scene analysis, specifically how the brain extracts meaning from complex acoustic environments like the 'cocktail party' scenario. Utilizing a combination of psychophysics, neuroimaging (EEG, MEG, fMRI), and computational modeling, they investigate how top-down attention and spatial hearing facilitate the selection of specific sound objects. Their work also explores the intersection of auditory and visual attention and the impact of hidden hearing deficits on cognitive performance.
0070.research_direction: Dr. Shinn-Cunningham has recently been investigating the mechanisms of auditory selective attention and scene analysis, focusing on how listeners maintain focus on target sound streams amidst complex or degraded acoustic environments. Their recent work extensively explores the "interruption effect," using behavioral recall paradigms to examine how unpredictable, salient distractor sounds disrupt top-down spatial attention and working memory under varying conditions, including simulated acoustic reverberation, altered temporal predictability, and differing talker identities. To uncover the neurophysiological locus of these top-down processes, they are also employing EEG to determine whether selective attention to target melodies modulates neural responses at early subcortical brainstem stages or primarily in higher-level cortical areas. Furthermore, their research investigates the perceptual building blocks of auditory object formation, specifically testing how the degraded spectral resolution characteristic of cochlear implants affects a listener's ability to group discrete sound features into coherent streams using temporal coherence cues.

papers.title: Distinct talkers combat catastrophic failures of spatial attention due to interruption
papers.abstract: This study employs a syllable-sequence recall paradigm to investigate how the task-irrelevant feature of talker identity influences the temporal buildup of spatial selective attention and its robustness to stochastic interruptions. Participants identified sequences of syllables originating from specific spatial locations amidst competing distractors. The experiments examined whether distinct talker voices (as opposed to identical voices) facilitate stream segregation and mitigate the disruption caused by unpredictable, novel acoustic interrupters. Quantitative findings demonstrated that talker-based object formation significantly enhanced recall accuracy and attenuated the 'catastrophic' performance decline following interrupters, even though talker identity was orthogonal to the spatial task requirements. Conversely, discontinuities in talker identity were found to impair the progressive optimization of attentional focus and reduce syllable recall performance.
papers.authors: Wusheng Liang, Abigail L. Noyce, Christopher A. Brown, Barbara G. Shinn-Cunningham

papers.title: Reverberation exacerbates effects of interruption on auditory spatial selective attention
papers.abstract: Across five online behavioral experiments, this research evaluates the interaction between acoustic reverberation and unpredictable interruptions during a spatialized syllable recall task. The study contrasts two competing hypotheses: whether reverberation decreases interrupter salience by blurring onsets or compounds disruption by increasing overall cognitive load and task difficulty. Listeners reported syllables from a target stream in both pseudo-anechoic and reverberant simulated environments. Results indicated that interrupters consistently impaired recall, with the most pronounced decrement occurring for the syllable immediately succeeding the interruption. Critically, this interruption-driven performance impairment was significantly larger in reverberant conditions compared to anechoic settings, suggesting that reverberation compounds the disruptive effects of salient auditory events on top-down attentional maintenance.
papers.authors: Victoria Figarola, Wusheng Liang, Sahil Luthra, Christopher Brown, Barbara Shinn-Cunningham

papers.title: Attention to Pseudo-Tone Melodies Enhances Cortical but Not Brainstem Responses in Humans
papers.abstract: This study investigates the neurophysiological locus of top-down auditory selective attention by simultaneously recording cortical and subcortical (brainstem) signals using electroencephalography (EEG). Participants attended to one of two interleaved pseudo-tone melodies presented to opposite ears. The methodology employed established EEG paradigms to extract auditory brainstem responses (ABRs) to individual pulses within the melodic sequences. Analysis revealed robust attentional modulation of cortical-evoked potentials, reflecting prioritized processing of the attended stream. However, no significant attentional modulation was detected in the brainstem responses, suggesting that while selective attention enhances the cortical representation of complex melodic stimuli, these effects do not extend to the early, subcortical stages of the human auditory pathway.
papers.authors: Victoria Figarola, Yunshu Li, Adam Tierney, Fred Dick, Abigail Noyce, Ross K Maddox, Barbara Shinn-Cunningham

papers.title: Cat-astrophic update: What makes an interrupter more disruptive?
papers.abstract: This research characterizes the 'interruption effect'—the decrease in accuracy for target sequence recall caused by salient, task-irrelevant auditory events—during a spatial attention task. Through four online behavioral experiments, the investigators manipulated the novelty of the interrupter, the working memory (WM) load (defined by target sequence length), and the temporal predictability of the interruption. Participants reported syllable sequences from a cued hemifield while ignoring a distractor stream and interrupters. Findings indicated that interrupter novelty did not modulate the effect, as unfamiliar and repeated interrupters were equally disruptive. However, increasing sequence length significantly exacerbated the disruption of the target syllable following the interrupter, and unpredictable interrupters caused greater performance deficits than those with high temporal predictability. These results suggest that interrupters disrupt both top-down attentional control and WM maintenance.
papers.venue: The Journal of the Acoustical Society of America
papers.authors: Wusheng Liang, Christopher A. Brown, Abigail L. Noyce, Barbara G. Shinn-Cunningham

papers.title: Impact of Reduced Spectral Resolution on Temporal-Coherence-Based Auditory Scene Analysis
papers.abstract: This study examines the role of spectral resolution in facilitating auditory scene analysis through the mechanism of temporal coherence. Listeners performed a segregation task involving complex acoustic scenes where streams were defined by the temporal correlation of their components. The spectral resolution was systematically manipulated to simulate the degraded inputs experienced by cochlear implant users. Results demonstrated that reducing spectral resolution significantly impairs the ability to utilize temporal coherence as a cue for stream segregation, even when the temporal information itself remains intact. This finding suggests that precise spectral-place representation is critical for integrating features across frequency channels into coherent auditory objects, and that spectral degradation contributes to the challenges faced by hearing-impaired listeners in complex acoustic environments.
papers.venue: The Journal of the Acoustical Society of America
papers.authors: Vibha Viswanathan, Michael G. Heinz, Barbara G. Shinn-Cunningham

0071.name: Barry Giesbrecht
0071.bio: Barry Giesbrecht is a Professor at UC Santa Barbara and the director of the UCSB Attention Lab, focusing on the neural and cognitive mechanisms of selective information processing. Their research utilizes a multimodal empirical approach, combining functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), electroencephalography (EEG), and psychophysical methods to study how attention interacts with memory and perception. Giesbrecht investigates the relationship between global physiological states, such as physical exercise, and the modulation of attentional control and sensory sensitivity. Additionally, their research explores the translational application of these findings to human performance and decision-making in complex environments.
0071.research_direction: Dr. Giesbrecht's recent work explores the behavioral and neural mechanisms underlying sustained attention and cognitive control across various environmental contexts. They have recently been investigating the dynamics of attentional lapses and the vigilance decrement, using Signal Detection Theory and electrophysiological markers like the P300 to determine whether performance drops reflect true perceptual decoupling or mere shifts in decision criteria. Their research also examines the temporal dynamics of these cognitive fluctuations, specifically quantifying the speed at which the attentional system can reorient to task demands following a behavioral lapse. Additionally, Dr. Giesbrecht applies these neurocognitive methods to broader domains, employing event-related potentials to study semantic integration within augmented reality environments and conducting meta-analytic research to evaluate how acute physical activity modulates executive function.

papers.title: Beyond detection rate: understanding the vigilance decrement using signal detection theory
papers.abstract: This theoretical perspective re-evaluates the vigilance decrement—the progressive decline in performance during sustained attention tasks—through the application of Signal Detection Theory (SDT). The authors challenge the conventional reliance on detection rates, which fail to distinguish between fundamental changes in sensory sensitivity (d') and strategic shifts in decision criteria (c). By analyzing performance in the Continuous Temporal Expectancy Task (CTET) relative to classical paradigms, the study argues that the observed performance drop often reflects an adaptive adjustment in response bias rather than a depletion of cognitive resources. The framework emphasizes the necessity of utilizing SDT parameters to clarify whether behavioral lapses stem from attenuated perceptual processing or altered decision-making thresholds.
papers.authors: Henri Etel Skinner, Barry Giesbrecht

papers.title: Perceptual decoupling in the sustained attention to response task is likely: comment on Bedi, Russell, & Helton (2024)
papers.abstract: This commentary contests the recently proposed claim that perceptual decoupling—the internal disengagement of attention from external sensory inputs—is an unlikely occurrence during the Sustained Attention to Response Task (SART). The authors revisit established electrophysiological and behavioral evidence demonstrating that attentional lapses in the SART are associated with attenuated P300 event-related potential (ERP) amplitudes and significant impairments in subsequent memory encoding. They argue that these markers provide robust evidence for the decoupling of cognitive resources from external task demands. The paper advocates for the validity of commission errors as behavioral proxies for mind-wandering and supports the use of real-time monitoring to characterize fluctuations in attentional engagement.
papers.authors: Shivang Shelat, Barry Giesbrecht

papers.title: Electrophysiological evidence for differential semantic processing of words and objects presented in augmented reality
papers.abstract: This study employed event-related potentials (ERPs) to investigate semantic integration in augmented reality (AR) environments. Participants engaged in a semantic congruence task where they evaluated pairings of digital word labels and physical or virtual objects. Electrophysiological data revealed that semantically incongruent pairs elicited a reliable N400 component, indicating that the brain performs conceptual mismatch detection for AR-integrated stimuli. However, the study found that the N400 morphology and latency varied depending on whether the object was physical or a synthetic digital overlay, suggesting that while the core semantic processing network is engaged, the integration of virtual content into real-world contexts involves distinct neural processing steps for digital information.
papers.authors: Tom Bullock, Emily Machniak, You-Jin Kim, Jordan Garrett, Madhav Viswesvaran, Julia Ram, Tobias Höllerer, Barry Giesbrecht

papers.title: Rapid Reorienting of Attention to Task Demands Following Lapses of Sustained Attention
papers.abstract: This research quantifies the temporal dynamics of attentional recovery after a failure in sustained attention. Utilizing a modified Sustained Attention to Response Task (SART) designed to capture corrective motor behaviors, the study examined the speed and frequency with which participants reorient attention following a lapse. Quantitative analysis showed that individuals can recover task-relevant focus with surprising speed, often executing corrective responses within approximately 200 ms of an error. This recovery is faster than simple target detection latencies, indicating that the attentional system possesses a highly efficient, high-speed reorientation mechanism that allows for the rapid restoration of goal-directed control following spontaneous fluctuations in attention.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
papers.authors: Shivang Shelat, Barry Giesbrecht

papers.title: A systematic review and Bayesian meta-analysis provide evidence for an effect of acute physical activity on cognition in young adults
papers.abstract: This comprehensive meta-analysis synthesized 651 effect sizes from 113 studies to evaluate the influence of single acute bouts of physical exercise on cognitive performance in healthy adults. Employing a Bayesian hierarchical model, the research found a small but statistically credible beneficial effect of exercise on cognition (g = 0.13), with the most pronounced improvements observed in executive function tasks related to working memory and inhibitory control. The analysis also identified critical moderators, demonstrating that vigorous intensities and shorter durations (under 30 minutes), particularly during cycling and high-intensity interval training (HIIT), produced more consistent cognitive enhancements than prolonged, low-intensity aerobic protocols.
papers.authors: Jordan Garrett, Carly Chak, Tom Bullock, Barry Giesbrecht

0072.name: Barry J Richmond
0072.lab_name: Section on Neural Coding and Computation
0072.bio: Barry J. Richmond is a senior researcher at the National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH) and serves as the Principal Investigator of the Section on Neural Coding and Computation. Their research investigates the neural mechanisms underlying visual information processing, focusing on how primate brain circuits encode, categorize, and store visual stimuli. This work specifically examines the functional roles of the inferior temporal cortex subregions, TE and TEO, in visual recognition and categorization learning using rhesus monkey models. Methodologically, Richmond’s laboratory integrates multi-electrode recordings, behavioral paradigms, and computational modeling with tools such as PET imaging and chemogenetic modulations to analyze the information-carrying capacity of neural population dynamics.
0072.research_direction: Dr. Richmond's recent work explores the functional architecture of the primate ventral visual stream and how specific temporal lobe circuits support high-level vision and learning. They have recently been investigating whether visual processing is strictly hierarchical, using selective lesions in macaques to evaluate how areas TEO and TE interact to subserve image categorization and recognition memory. Additionally, their research probes the distinct roles of inferior temporal regions in perceptual decision-making, combining focal lesions with drift-diffusion computational modeling to understand how area TE and the rhinal cortex differentially control speed-accuracy trade-offs. Beyond pure visual processing, they are also examining how these sensory representations interface with motivational networks, utilizing chemogenetic disconnection approaches to determine how specific rhinal-striatal anatomical projections mediate the acquisition of novel visual stimulus-reward associations.

papers.title: Chemogenetic Disruption of Monkey Perirhinal Neurons Projecting to the Rostromedial Caudate Impairs Associative Learning
papers.abstract: This study employs a chemogenetic disconnection approach to investigate the functional necessity of the anatomical projection from the rhinal cortex (Rh) to the rostromedial caudate (rmCD) in visual stimulus-reward association. By combining a unilateral surgical lesion of Rh with contralateral expression of the inhibitory DREADD hM4Di (delivered via a retrograde glycoprotein-E-pseudotyped lentivirus injected into the rmCD), the researchers selectively interrupted Layer 5 perirhinal neurons projecting to the striatum. Behavioral assessment using a multi-reward schedule task revealed that systemic administration of the DREADD agonist deschloroclozapine (DCZ) specifically impaired the acquisition of novel stimulus-reward associations while leaving the application of previously learned associations largely intact. These findings suggest that the Rh-rmCD circuit is essential for the initial encoding of motivational significance to visual cues but not for the retrieval or maintenance of established values.
papers.authors: Wenliang Wang, Mark A. G. Eldridge, Tsuyoshi Setogawa, Spencer Webster-Bass, Nanami Miyazaki, Jonah E. Pearl, Jeih-San Liow, Walter Lerchner, Bing Li, Janita N. Turchi, Sanjay Telu, Sridhar Goud Nerella, Phelix Rodriguez, Robert B. Innis, Victor W. Pike, Bruno B. Averbeck, Barry J. Richmond

papers.title: Dissociation between area TE and rhinal cortex in accuracy vs. speed of visual categorization in rhesus monkeys
papers.abstract: The authors investigate the differential contributions of inferior temporal area TE and the adjacent rhinal cortex to the speed and accuracy of visual categorization under ethologically relevant temporal constraints. Macaque monkeys with bilateral area TE lesions or bilateral rhinal cortex lesions were tested on a task requiring categorization of briefly presented morphed images. The results demonstrate a double dissociation: bilateral removal of area TE significantly decreased categorization accuracy without affecting decision speed, whereas bilateral rhinal cortex lesions preserved categorization accuracy but significantly slowed reaction times. Computational modeling using a Generalized Drift-Diffusion Model (GDDM) with collapsing boundaries indicated that while evidence accumulation rates (drift rate) remained constant across groups, rhinal lesions resulted in slower collapsing decision bounds, effectively delaying the termination of the decision process.
papers.authors: Bing Li, Kaleb Lowe, Samarth Chandra, Gang Chen, Mark A. G. Eldridge, Barry J. Richmond

papers.title: Is Visual Processing in Primates Strictly Hierarchical?
papers.abstract: In this full-length research contribution to the Advances in Cognitive Neurodynamics series, the authors evaluate the classical serial feed-forward model of the ventral visual stream. Utilizing evidence from selective bilateral lesions of areas TEO and TE in rhesus monkeys, the paper examines how image processing for categorization and recognition memory is distributed across the temporal lobe. The findings challenge the strict hierarchical assumption that visual information must pass through intermediate stages like TEO to reach TE for high-level object recognition. The authors propose a more complex architecture involving parallel pathways and task-dependent recruitment of temporal subregions, suggesting that the functional organization of the ventral stream is more flexible than previously described in strictly serial computational models.
papers.authors: Mark A. G. Eldridge, Samarth Chandra, Barry J. Richmond

0073.name: Bas Rokers
0073.department: Department of Psychology; Center for Neural Science
0073.bio: Bas Rokers is a Professor of Psychology and the Director of the Center for Brain and Health at New York University Abu Dhabi. Rokers investigates the neural mechanisms of three-dimensional visual perception, specifically focusing on how the brain integrates motion and depth cues to construct a representation of the environment. Utilizing a combination of behavioral psychophysics, neuroimaging (fMRI and tractography), and computational modeling, they explore the transformation of sensory signals into perceptual states. Their research also addresses practical applications in health and technology, including the treatment of amblyopia and the optimization of virtual reality systems to mitigate motion sickness and improve immersive experiences.
0073.research_direction: Dr. Rokers has recently been investigating the neural mechanisms underlying binocular vision and 3D motion processing in the human brain. Using functional MRI, population receptive field mapping, and multivariate decoding, their recent work explores how early visual areas integrate monocular inputs and how specific extrastriate regions, such as the hMT+ complex and area FST, utilize perspective and stereoscopic depth cues to represent motion in three dimensions. Beyond basic visual neuroscience, they are leveraging multimodal structural and diffusion MRI to examine microstructural white matter changes, such as quantifying tract-specific lesion burdens to predict clinical disability in multiple sclerosis. Additionally, their team is establishing large-scale, open-access neuroimaging and visual psychophysics datasets to build foundational normative brain health baselines for historically underrepresented Middle Eastern populations.

papers.title: The ASPIRE Research Institute Brain Health Dataset: Building a Foundation for Brain Health Research in the United Arab Emirates
papers.abstract: This study details the establishment of the first large-scale normative neuroimaging repository tailored to the United Arab Emirates (UAE) population, aimed at addressing the scarcity of controlled brain health data in the Middle East and North Africa (MENA). The protocol implements a comprehensive multimodal imaging battery, including high-resolution T1-weighted structural MRI, diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) for microstructural assessment, resting-state functional MRI (rs-fMRI) for connectivity analysis, and arterial spin labeling (ASL) for cerebral blood flow measurement. Psychophysical evaluations emphasize visual function through metrics such as ETDRS visual acuity, Pelli-Robson contrast sensitivity, and Randot stereoacuity, alongside VR-based perimetry. This initial release provides open-access data for a cohort of 41 participants, accompanied by standardized preprocessing pipelines to facilitate regional and global comparative neuroscience research.
papers.authors: Abdalla Z. Mohamed, Ameen Qadi, Amna Dogar, Amal Salah, Aisha Hamkari, Dana Alkalali, Gul Begum, Haidee J. Paterson, Kartik K. Sreenivasan, Milos Ljubisavljevic, Osama Abdullah, Omnia Hassanin, Puti Wen, Rawand Benour, Soumen Mohanty, Yvonne Valles, Bas Rokers

papers.title: Functional localization of visual motion area FST in humans
papers.abstract: The human homolog of the macaque fundus of the superior temporal sulcus (FST) has been difficult to delineate due to its proximity to the hMT+ complex. Here, researchers evaluated functional localizers to distinguish putative FST (pFST) from hMT and MST using 2D and 3D motion stimuli alongside population receptive field (pRF) mapping. Results revealed a distinct area localized anterior and inferior to hMT/MST that exhibited selective activation for coherent 3D motion (stereomotion) over 2D retinal motion. This functional localization was further validated through measures of motion opponency and T1-weighted signal intensity (myelination), which demonstrated that pFST possesses unique structural and functional properties consistent with its specialized role in processing complex motion signals such as structure-from-motion and looming.
papers.authors: Puti Wen, Rania Ezzo, Lowell W. Thompson, Ari Rosenberg, Michael S. Landy, Bas Rokers

papers.title: Single-trial fMRI decoding of 3D motion with stereoscopic and perspective cues
papers.abstract: This investigation utilized multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) to decode 3D motion direction (toward vs. away) from single-trial BOLD responses in the human visual cortex, specifically focusing on the hMT+ complex sub-regions (MT, MST, and FST). By manipulating stereoscopic and perspective cues, the study found that MT exhibits superior decoding accuracy for perspective-driven motion, whereas FST demonstrates a specialization for stereoscopic depth cues. Quantitative analysis revealed that decoding in V1 and MST was largely driven by retinotopic biases, while MT and FST representations were more robust to such confounds. Furthermore, individual variance in stereoscopic proficiency correlated specifically with FST decoding performance, and control experiments established that FST activity is uniquely influenced by the perceptual experience of 3D motion rather than just low-level binocular disparity.
papers.authors: Puti Wen, Lowell W. Thompson, Ari Rosenberg, Michael S. Landy, Bas Rokers

papers.title: Integrating Visual Input from Both Eyes: Binocular Retinotopic Organization based on Monocular Input
papers.abstract: To investigate the neural mechanisms of binocular integration, this study compared population receptive field (pRF) properties under monocular and binocular stimulation across the visual hierarchy (V1–hV4 and TO1). While binocular stimulation elicited greater BOLD response amplitudes, the summation was subadditive, consistent with neural normalization models. Notably, binocular input resulted in a significant increase in pRF size specifically in V1, a finding that was not observed in higher extrastriate areas. This expansion is mathematically consistent with models of monocular pRF center mismatches within a single voxel, suggesting that binocular representations in early visual cortex are formed by the integration of slightly offset monocular inputs rather than a simple linear combination of signals.
papers.authors: Abdalla Z. Mohamed, Omnia Hassanin, Rania Ezzo, Alessio Fracasso, Jonathan A. Winawer, Bas Rokers

papers.title: Quantitative evaluation of lesion load in multiple sclerosis using multimodal MR
papers.abstract: This research addresses the clinico-radiological paradox in Multiple Sclerosis (MS) by proposing a tract-based approach to lesion analysis that integrates spatial localization with microstructural composition. Using multimodal 3T MRI—including FLAIR, T1 mapping, magnetization transfer ratio (MTR), and diffusion tensor imaging (DTI)—the study quantified lesion burden within specific white matter tracts instead of broad anatomical regions. Findings indicate that lesion metrics filtered through functionally critical tracts (e.g., occipitoparietal or corticospinal) are significantly better predictors of Expanded Disability Status Scale (EDSS) scores and cognitive impairment than total lesion volume. Specifically, tract-based T1 values and fractional anisotropy (FA) provided high accuracy in stratifying relapsing-remitting patients into stable versus progressive risk categories (AUC = 0.90), offering a more precise biomarker for individualized disease monitoring.
papers.authors: Puti Wen, Osama Abdullah, Lev Brylev, Victor Bryukhov, Dana Alkalali, Mariya Matrosova, Bas Rokers

0074.name: Bei Xiao
0074.bio: Xiao is a Provost Associate Professor at American University and the Associate Director of the Institute for IDEAS, specializing in the intersection of neuroscience and machine learning. Xiao’s research investigates how the human visual system estimates the physical and functional properties of objects, with an emphasis on material perception and 3D shape recognition. Utilizing a methodology that combines human psychophysics, computer graphics, and deep learning, they develop computational models to simulate human-like perception and modify computer vision algorithms. Their current work focuses on bridging vision and language in material cognition, as well as employing virtual reality and EEG decoding to study multisensory and neural representations of material properties.
0074.research_direction: Dr. Xiao has recently been pursuing two distinct lines of research, spanning human material perception and applied machine learning in biomedicine. In the visual domain, their recent work explores the link between visual processing and semantic categorization by combining generative image synthesis, human psychophysics, and unsupervised learning to test how visual similarity judgments of ambiguous materials align with verbal descriptions. Concurrently, they are developing multimodal large language models to predict clinical trial outcomes and regulatory phase transitions. In this biomedical work, they aim to forecast trial success by extracting predictive cross-modal correlations from diverse data streams, investigating how raw clinical protocol narratives interact with structural drug representations and historical records.

papers.title: Probing the link between vision and language in material perception using psychophysics and unsupervised learning
papers.abstract: This study investigates the relationship between the visual processing of materials and their semantic categorization using a dual-modality framework. Utilizing StyleGAN-based deep generative models, we synthesized a high-fidelity 'Space of Morphable Material Appearance' encompassing well-defined categories (e.g., soap, rock, toy) and their interpolated, ambiguous intermediates. Through psychophysical experiments, we compared human visual similarity judgments with free-form verbal descriptions. Results demonstrated a moderate but significant alignment between the visual and linguistic pathways at the categorical level. However, a novel unsupervised representation alignment method revealed fundamental structural asymmetries at the image-to-image level, particularly for ambiguous stimuli where visual nuances were not captured by verbal descriptors. These findings suggest that while language reflects common semantic dimensions, the human visual system preserves fine-grained diagnostic features of material properties that linguistic labels overlook, highlighting the necessity of integrating multi-modal representations in computational models of material perception.
papers.authors: Chenxi Liao, Masataka Sawayama, Bei Xiao

papers.title: CTP-LLM: Clinical Trial Phase Transition Prediction Using Large Language Models
papers.abstract: We present CTP-LLM, a novel Large Language Model (LLM)-based framework for Clinical Trial Outcome Prediction (CTOP), specifically targeting the prediction of transitions between clinical trial phases. The model utilizes a fine-tuned GPT-3.5 Turbo architecture to process raw clinical trial protocol narratives from ClinicalTrials.gov without the need for manual feature engineering. Along with the model, we introduce the PhaseTransition (PT) dataset, a large-scale benchmark for phase transition analysis. CTP-LLM achieves an accuracy of 67% across all transition phases and a significantly higher accuracy of 75% for the critical transition from Phase III to FDA approval. The framework outperforms traditional BERT-based classifiers and demonstrates that deep-learning-based analysis of technical trial protocols can effectively identify predictive latent patterns in clinical outcomes, providing a scalable tool for pharmaceutical development and resource management.
papers.venue: 2024 IEEE International Conference on Bioinformatics and Biomedicine (BIBM)
papers.authors: Michael Reinisch, Jianfeng He, Chenxi Liao, Sauleh Siddiqui, Bei Xiao

papers.title: Multimodal Clinical Trial Outcome Prediction with Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Drug development faces high failure rates and substantial costs due to unpredictable phase transitions. We propose a multimodal prediction framework that leverages Large Language Models to analyze diverse data streams, including drug molecular representations, trial protocol narratives, and historical clinical data. By integrating heterogeneous biomedical signals, the model seeks to identify cross-modal correlations that indicate success or failure in clinical trials. We evaluate the system on a retrospective cohort of over 100,000 completed trials (1976–2024), finding that the integration of semantic protocol data with structural drug information yields superior predictive performance compared to unimodal baselines. The results underscore the utility of instruction-tuned LLMs in capturing the complex interplay between biochemical efficacy and regulatory trial design.
papers.authors: Michael Reinisch, Jianfeng He, Chenxi Liao, Sauleh Ahmad Siddiqui, Bei Xiao

0075.name: Ben D. Sawyer
0075.department: Department of Industrial Engineering and Management Systems
0075.bio: Ben D. Sawyer is an applied neuroscientist and human factors engineer focusing on the optimization of information flow within human-machine systems. Sawyer’s research integrates vision science, neurophysiology, and mathematical modeling to investigate cognitive workload, digital readability, and human performance in environments such as driving and defense. As the director of LabX and The Readability Consortium, Sawyer develops algorithms and personalized typographic systems intended to facilitate information acquisition and address distraction in digital interfaces.
0075.research_direction: Dr. Sawyer has recently been investigating the intersection of human factors, artificial intelligence, and visual ergonomics to understand how emerging technologies impact cognitive performance and digital agency. A major focus of their recent work explores applied reading research, specifically measuring how low-level typographic manipulations—such as typeface style and character spacing—influence children's reading speed and comprehension in pursuit of personalized digital reading environments. In tandem with this, they are evaluating the utility of Large Language Models in education, using behavioral metrics to test how accurately AI can simplify texts and generate reading materials compared to human-authored baselines. Broadening their focus on human-AI interaction, Dr. Sawyer is also examining the socio-technical and ethical dimensions of "Human Digital Twins," probing the intellectual property challenges, cybersecurity vulnerabilities, and labor implications associated with deploying high-fidelity digital replicas of individuals.

papers.title: Evaluating GenAI for Simplifying Texts for Education: Improving Accuracy and Consistency for Enhanced Readability
papers.abstract: This study assesses the performance of Large Language Models (LLMs) and specialized multi-agent architectures in performing automated text simplification for educational purposes. Sixty informational passages were reduced from a twelfth-grade baseline to fourth, sixth, and eighth-grade levels using diverse models and prompting techniques. Evaluation was conducted through a generalized metric framework that measured grade-level target accuracy, word count modulation, and semantic consistency (quantified via keyword and key phrase preservation). Statistical analysis via regression models and t-tests revealed significant performance variance across models and target levels, highlighting current architectural limitations in balancing linguistic complexity reduction with the preservation of informational fidelity.
papers.authors: Stephanie L. Day, Jacapo Cirica, Steven R. Clapp, Veronika Penkova, Amy E. Giroux, Abbey Banta, Catherine Bordeau, Poojitha Mutteneni, Ben D. Sawyer

papers.title: Sex worker human digital twins and intellectual property: on collaborative futures for sex thinkers, technologists, and lawyers
papers.abstract: This interdisciplinary research investigates the legal and socio-technical implications of generative AI-driven 'Human Digital Twins' (HDTs) in the adult industry. HDTs are high-fidelity digital replicas that simulate the personality, appearance, and behavioral traits of specific individuals by leveraging aggregated 'digital exhaust.' Utilizing a pragmatist feminist framework, the authors analyze the systematic marginalization of adult content creators within current copyright and IP regimes. The paper proposes a sex worker–AI collaborative model aimed at protecting creators' agency and ownership over their digital replicas, advocating for legal and technological shifts to secure their livelihoods against algorithmic displacement and labor exploitation.
papers.authors: Yvette Butler, Chibundo Egwuatu, Matthew Canham, Ben D. Sawyer

papers.title: The Influence of Format Readability on Children's Reading Speed and Comprehension
papers.abstract: This research explores whether typographic format readability gains observed in adults generalize to children. Fifty-one elementary students (grades 3–5) were tested across 11 passages manipulated by eight typefaces (four serif, four sans-serif) and three character-spacing levels. Analysis using linear mixed-effects modeling indicated that Roboto and Arial fonts significantly optimized reading speed at the group level. Individuated analysis demonstrated substantial gains in words-per-minute (WPM) when students read in their personalized 'fit' formats compared to their 'clash' formats. Crucially, no speed-accuracy tradeoffs were found in comprehension metrics, supporting the transition toward personalized digital reading environments in educational technology to enhance individual student outcomes.
papers.authors: Stephanie L. Day, Nilsu Atilgan, Amy E. Giroux, Ben D. Sawyer

papers.title: Humanizing AI in Education: A Readability Comparison of LLM and Human-Created Educational Content
papers.abstract: This study compares the readability and perceived quality of educational materials authored by humans versus those generated by Large Language Models (LLMs). Researchers used ChatGPT-3.5 to create 300-word eighth-grade level passages and compared them to human-expert-written content using metrics of reading speed, comprehension accuracy, and qualitative ratings for familiarity, interest, and quality. Linear mixed-effects models showed that AI-generated passages were read more efficiently and resulted in higher comprehension scores and perceived quality ratings than the human baseline. The results suggest that LLMs can author highly consistent and effective educational content, providing a scalable solution for creating personalized reading materials.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the Human Factors and Ergonomics Society Annual Meeting
papers.authors: Md Mamunur Rashid, Nilsu Atilgan, Jonathan Dobres, Stephanie Day, Veronika Penkova, Mert Küçük, Steven R. Clapp, Ben D. Sawyer

papers.title: Human Digital Twins: The Promise and Peril
papers.abstract: This paper presents a human factors analysis of 'Human Digital Twins' (HDTs), high-fidelity digital replicas that mirror individual biological, cognitive, and behavioral states. The authors define the current HDT technological landscape and discuss applications in augmenting human performance, personalized medicine, and cybersecurity. The analysis focuses on critical security vulnerabilities and ethical dilemmas, including social engineering through malicious twins and the potential loss of individual digital agency. Integrating human factors principles, the work proposes a design framework aimed at ensuring the deployment of trustworthy HDT systems while mitigating the risks associated with AI-driven human replication.
papers.venue: 15th International Conference on Applied Human Factors and Ergonomics (AHFE 2024)
papers.authors: Matthew Canham, Ben D. Sawyer

0076.name: Benjamin Balas
0076.bio: Benjamin Balas is a Professor of Psychology at North Dakota State University, specializing in high-level vision and the mechanisms underlying face and object recognition. After earning their Ph.D. from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in Brain and Cognitive Science, Balas completed post-doctoral training at Children’s Hospital Boston. Their research employs event-related potentials (ERPs) and psychophysical methods to investigate how the human visual system leverages natural image statistics and category-specific features for recognition. Balas’ current work explores visual development, the perception of ensemble statistics in textures, and the phenomenon of face pareidolia across the lifespan.
0076.research_direction: Dr. Balas has recently been investigating the visual and neural mechanisms underlying face and object representation across typical, clinical, and degraded viewing conditions. Their recent work explores the low-level and cortical drivers of face perception, using transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) to probe the causal mechanisms of the face inversion effect in extrastriate cortex, and testing how spectral power and orientation energy influence face pareidolia in noise. They are also examining how visual and cognitive limitations impact social perception, using simulated cataracts to study novel face learning and employing the Bubbles paradigm to map the specific facial features observers with eating disorder symptoms use for emotion recognition. Furthermore, their research investigates the nature of visual memory and mental imagery by analyzing the mid-level image statistics of memory-based drawings produced by individuals with aphantasia.

papers.title: The impact of simulated cataract on face learning
papers.abstract: Cataracts represent a prevalent visual impairment that significantly degrades contrast sensitivity and spatial resolution, thereby constraining both intermediate and higher-level visual processing. This study utilized cataract simulation goggles to investigate how impaired vision—and its subsequent restoration—affects the acquisition of novel face representations. Observers performed a face learning task under varying conditions of visual quality during both the learning and test phases. The results characterize the extent to which changes in visual input quality, whether negative (onset) or positive (restoration), modulate the efficacy of novel face identity encoding and the subsequent recognition of learned versus unlearned facial stimuli.
papers.authors: Abuk Akech, Benjamin Balas

papers.title: Face pareidolia is sensitive to spectral power and orientation energy
papers.abstract: The human visual system demonstrates a refined sensitivity to statistical regularities in natural images, including the 1/f power-spectrum fall-off coefficient and category-specific biases such as the horizontal contrast energy preference for face recognition. This research investigated the sensitivity of face pareidolia to these properties using an unconstrained detection task and fractal noise stimuli. Experiment 1 revealed that fractal noise with steeper spectral fall-off coefficients (favoring coarser image structures) yielded significantly lower rates of pareidolic face detection. Experiment 2 demonstrated that bandpass orientation filtering in either the horizontal or vertical domain reduced pareidolia rates compared to isotropic images, suggesting that pareidolic face detection relies on broadband visual information across multiple low-level channels rather than specific orientation biases typically observed in veridical face recognition.
papers.authors: Benjamin Balas

papers.title: Mid-level Characteristics of Drawings Made by Observers with Aphantasia
papers.abstract: Individuals with aphantasia report a profound deficit or complete absence of voluntary mental imagery. While prior analyses of the Aphantasia Drawing Database indicated specific impairments in object-level visual memory alongside spared scene-level accuracy, the underlying visual feature distributions remained unexplored. This study examined the mid-level image statistics of line drawings produced from memory versus direct observation. Analysis revealed distinct differences in simpler visual feature distributions between aphantasic individuals and controls, particularly when relying on image recall. These findings provide objective indices of the condition and further characterize the nature of visual encoding and representational complexity in aphantasia.
papers.authors: Benjamin Balas

papers.title: Is visual information use during facial emotion recognition related to eating disorder symptoms in college-aged men and women? An experimental study
papers.abstract: Deficits in facial emotion recognition have been identified across various eating disorders (EDs), but the specific visual information supporting these judgments remains poorly understood. This study examined ED symptom severity as a function of emotion categorization strategies using the Bubbles task, a visual cognition paradigm that reveals which image regions drive classification. College-aged participants completed an emotion categorization task while their ED symptomatology was assessed via standardized questionnaires. The results provide insights into how individuals with higher ED symptom severity weigh specific facial features during emotion processing, moving beyond simple accuracy metrics to characterize the qualitative nature of social-perceptual biases in disordered eating.
papers.authors: Ilya Nudnou, Katherine sarah Duggan, Lauren Schaefer, Benjamin Balas

papers.title: The role of lateral occipital face and object areas in the face inversion effect
papers.abstract: Face inversion typically impairs discrimination more severely than it does for other object categories, a phenomenon often attributed to a shift from face-specific to general object recognition mechanisms. This study tested the causal necessity of the right occipital face area (rOFA) and the right lateral occipital area (rLO) for upright and inverted face matching using transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS). TMS delivered over the rOFA disrupted the discrimination of both upright and inverted faces, whereas TMS over the rLO impaired only inverted face discrimination. These findings provide causal evidence that while upright faces are processed via face-specific mechanisms, inverted faces recruit a combination of face-specific and object-specific mechanisms in the extrastriate cortex, consistent with an early-stage feature processing role for the OFA.
papers.authors: Allie Geiger, Benjamin Balas

0077.name: Benjamin de Haas
0077.department: Department of Psychology and Sports Science
0077.bio: Benjamin de Haas is a Research Professor of Experimental Psychology at Justus Liebig University Giessen and the head of the Indivisual Lab. De Haas investigates individual differences in human gaze behavior and the impact of visual salience on neural representations in the visual cortex. Their research utilizes eye-tracking, functional MRI, and computational modeling to examine the intersection of low-level visual features and high-level semantic dimensions such as faces and social cues. De Haas characterizes how individual viewing patterns generalize across time and stimuli, including their influence on subjective perception and social interactions.
0077.research_direction: Dr. de Haas has recently been investigating how idiosyncratic gaze patterns during naturalistic viewing shape human perception, cognition, and cortical activity. Their recent work explores the downstream consequences of individual visual sampling strategies, examining how unique oculomotor priorities influence trait-based face evaluation, structure verbal scene descriptions, and drive divergent fMRI responses across the visual cortex. To robustly quantify active vision, they are developing novel, object-based algorithms to categorize functional fixations in complex environments and are utilizing large-scale cross-sectional datasets to trace the protracted lifespan development of basic oculomotor biases and semantic salience. Ultimately, they seek to understand how individualized oculomotor behavior acts as an active perceptual filter that constructs our subjective experience of faces, scenes, and the broader visual world.

papers.title: Detection, Inspection, Return: An Object-Based Classification and Metric of Fixations in Complex Scenes
papers.abstract: The spatiotemporal dynamics of human gaze in complex environments are typically analyzed using pixel-based heatmaps or string-based scan-paths, which often overlook the functional context of visual objects. We introduce an object-based algorithm that categorizes fixations into three functional classes: Detection (D) for the initial foveation of a scene object; Inspection (I) for subsequent fixations on the same object; and Return (R) for revisits to previously sampled objects. Re-analysis of extensive eye-tracking datasets revealed that these fixation classes exhibit distinct spatial regularities and higher intra-observer consistency compared to inter-class comparisons. We observe a systematic shift from exploratory (D) to exploitative (I and R) viewing modes over trial duration. This framework provides a computationally efficient and biologically plausible metric for quantifying gaze patterns across static and dynamic naturalistic stimuli.
papers.authors: Marcel Linka, Benjamin de Haas

papers.title: Where You Look Is What You Get: Individual Fixation Height Predicts Biases in Face Perception
papers.abstract: Idiosyncratic preferences for foveating specific facial features (e.g., eyes vs. mouth) are highly stable across individuals, yet their impact on high-level face processing is poorly defined. We tested the hypothesis that individual gaze strategies act as an active perceptual filter, biasing social and trait-based impressions. By mapping naturalistic fixation behavior to multi-dimensional perceptual ratings (valence, arousal, trustworthiness, dominance, and attractiveness), we show that an observer’s habitual foveation proximity to eyes, nose, or mouth predicts the degree to which their whole-face impressions align with ratings of isolated features. In a binary choice paradigm using face images with conflicting top-bottom feature manipulations, eye-lookers versus mouth-lookers demonstrated divergent trustworthiness biases. These findings demonstrate that individualized oculomotor sampling systematically shapes the subjective internal representation of facial identity.
papers.authors: Zeynep Ceyda Demirkan, Maximilian Davide Broda, Benjamin de Haas

papers.title: Protracted development of gaze behaviour
papers.abstract: The ontogenetic development of natural scene viewing was analyzed using a large-scale cross-sectional dataset (n = 6,720; ages 5–72). We demonstrate that active vision undergoes a protracted maturation process spanning nearly two decades, refuting previous claims of early-onset adult-like gaze patterns. Semantic salience for social features continues to evolve through late adolescence, while text-directed salience increases until the third decade of life. Basic oculomotor biases, including central fixation tendencies and horizontal meridian preferences, develop throughout adolescence in parallel with the maturation of the visual cortex and spatial sensitivity. As individuals mature, exploratory behavior increases and fixation patterns converge from idiosyncratic to canonical distributions. These results suggest that adult-like gaze mechanisms are the product of long-term developmental refinement and cortical plasticity.
papers.authors: Marcel Linka, Harun Karimpur, Benjamin de Haas

papers.title: Individual gaze predicts individual scene descriptions
papers.abstract: This study investigates whether idiosyncratic visual sampling strategies lead to divergent subjective interpretations of identical complex scenes. We analyzed free-viewing gaze data and unconstrained verbal descriptions provided by observers for a set of natural images. Pairwise dissimilarities in gaze patterns were found to significantly predict pairwise dissimilarities in the lexical content (nouns, verbs, and adjectives) of scene descriptions. In particular, individual biases toward fixating specific semantic categories, such as text and persons, predicted the frequency of corresponding semantic references in the observers' reports, even when generalized to out-of-sample images. These findings provide empirical evidence that the subjective 'internal version' of the world is shaped by individual oculomotor priorities, establishing a quantitative link between active vision and cognitive representation.
papers.authors: Diana Kollenda, Anna-Sophia Reher, Benjamin de Haas

papers.title: Individual gaze shapes diverging neural representations
papers.abstract: Complex visual scenes evoke diverse patterns of gaze across observers, but it remains unclear how these idiosyncratic eye movements impact the consistency of neural representations. Using fMRI and hyperalignment techniques, we compared cortical responses during free-viewing and central fixation of identical movie stimuli. While free-viewing significantly enhanced BOLD signal amplitudes in early visual (V1) and inferior temporal (IT) regions, it simultaneously led to a dramatic decrease in cross-brain decoding accuracy compared to a fixed-fixation condition. Pairwise differences in spatial gaze distributions and semantic salience priorities predicted the degree of representational divergence in V1 and IT, respectively. Our results indicate that individual gaze actively sculpts idiosyncratic neural representations, suggesting that shared representational spaces in the human visual system are constrained by observer-specific sampling strategies.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS)
papers.authors: Petra Borovska, Benjamin de Haas

0078.name: Benjamin Peters
0078.bio: Benjamin Peters is a Lecturer in Computational Cognitive Science at the University of Edinburgh and a fellow of the Generative AI Laboratory. Their research integrates cognitive science, neuroscience, and artificial intelligence to investigate how humans and machines perceive structure and relations within complex, dynamic environments. Peters specializes in developing brain-computational neural network models that serve as mechanistic explanations for human behavior, eye movements, and neural data. Awarded a UKRI Future Leaders Fellowship, Peters previously held research positions at the University of Glasgow and Columbia University focusing on the intersection of generative and discriminative computations in vision.
0078.research_direction: Dr. Peters' recent work explores the computational mechanisms and neural constraints underlying visual perception and cognition. They have recently been investigating how to uncover the specific algorithms driving neural systems by analyzing transfer learning profiles in artificial networks, alongside theoretical work examining how the primate brain might integrate feedforward discriminative processing with top-down generative models during vision. In parallel, their empirical research probes the neural basis of visual working memory capacity, using MEG and multivariate pattern analysis to track the precision of orientation representations during whole-report tasks. Furthermore, Dr. Peters is actively engaged in meta-science, evaluating how structured adversarial collaborations can help researchers systematically resolve entrenched theoretical disputes across cognitive computational neuroscience.

papers.title: Using Transfer Learning to Identify a Neural System's Algorithm
papers.abstract: Standard behavior-based and parts-based analytical methods often fail to differentiate between distinct algorithms that produce equivalent input-output mappings. This study proposes identifying a neural system's algorithm by its transfer learning profile, which quantifies the relative efficiency with which it learns novel mappings. Using artificial neural networks (ANNs), we performed six experiments across three task domains: a linear algebraic task, 2D image classification, and 3D nonlinear image classification. We demonstrate that the transfer learning profile effectively recovers the system's original algorithm even when standard behavioral metrics and activation/weight-based analyses fail to reveal these mechanistic differences. We conclude that this framework provides a robust foundation for attributing specific algorithms to neural systems in cognitive science and machine learning.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the Annual Meeting of the Cognitive Science Society (CogSci)
papers.authors: John Morrison, Nikolaus Kriegeskorte, Benjamin Peters

papers.title: Neural correlates of working memory precision
papers.abstract: The neuronal basis of capacity limitations in working memory (WM) remains a central question in cognitive neuroscience. Unlike standard paradigms that probe a single item, we employed a whole-report task requiring participants to memorize one, two, or four orientations of Gabor gratings and sequentially report them with accompanying confidence ratings. We recorded neural activity using magnetoencephalography (MEG) and utilized beamforming for source-level estimation. Applying multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) across the cortical surface, we found that activity patterns in posterior cortical regions significantly predicted the aggregated precision of orientation reports (a composite metric of confidence and error). This predictive capability was strongest during the encoding phase and persisted until report. These results suggest that WM capacity is fundamentally limited by the precision of initial stimulus processing in early sensory and posterior regions, supporting the sensory recruitment hypothesis.
papers.authors: Philipp Deutsch, Cora Fischer, Jochen Kaiser, Christoph Bledowski, Benjamin Peters

papers.title: Generative adversarial collaborations: A new model of scientific discourse
papers.abstract: Scientific progress theoretically relies on the falsification and refinement of competing hypotheses, yet empirical research in cognitive and neural sciences is often fragmented into insular paradigms with disjoint terminologies and methodologies. To overcome theoretical entrenchment and generational stagnation, adversarial collaborations bring proponents of conflicting theories together to systematically contrast opposing views. Building on this principle, the Cognitive Computational Neuroscience (CCN) community instituted the Generative Adversarial Collaboration (GAC) framework in 2020. Over its initial five-year implementation involving 17 collaborative teams and exceeding 100 participating researchers, the initiative facilitated structured debates, open workshops, and co-authored perspectives spanning major controversies in brain and cognitive sciences. This perspective outlines the operational design, structural incentives, and practical lessons gained from facilitating GACs, emphasizing methodological harmonization, shared conceptual lexicons, and transparent dispute resolution as a replicable paradigm for scientific discourse across disciplines.
papers.authors: Benjamin Peters, Gunnar Blohm, Ralf M. Haefner, Leyla Isik, Nikolaus Kriegeskorte, Jennifer S. Lieberman, Carlos R. Ponce, Gemma Roig, Megan A. K. Peters

papers.title: How does the primate brain combine generative and discriminative computations in vision?
papers.abstract: Visual perception can be framed as an inferential challenge, conventionally addressed through two competing paradigms across biological neuroscience and computer vision. The feedforward discriminative paradigm posits direct inference via hierarchical, bottom-up transformations that progressively filter sensory nuisance variation to produce linearly separable representations tailored for downstream motor control and cognition. Conversely, the analysis-by-synthesis or generative paradigm conceptualizes perception as Helmholtzian inference, wherein sensory inputs are evaluated through the iterative inversion of an internal generative model of the causal physical world via top-down predictive comparisons against sensory evidence. This perspective, authored by proponents across both camps, examines the conceptual divergence and substantial computational overlap between both models, showing that attributes such as recurrence, sampling, and feedback are not exclusively tied to generative approaches. The authors synthesize psychophysical, neurophysiological, and computational evidence indicating that primate visual cortex likely executes an unidentified hybrid algorithm combining rapid bottom-up feature extraction with top-down generative error-correction, and outline an empirical roadmap to quantitatively arbitrate and integrate these competing computational accounts.
papers.authors: Benjamin Peters, James J. DiCarlo, Todd M. Gureckis, Ralf M. Haefner, Leyla Isik, Joshua B. Tenenbaum, Talia Konkle, Thomas Naselaris, Kimberly Stachenfeld, Zenna Tavares, Doris Y. Tsao, Ilker Yildirim, Nikolaus Kriegeskorte

0079.name: Benjamin van Buren
0079.bio: Benjamin van Buren is an Assistant Professor of Psychology at The New School for Social Research and directs the NSSR Perception Lab. van Buren’s research uses psychophysical methodologies to investigate how the visual system recovers properties such as animacy, intentionality, and physical forces from dynamic environmental input.
