They have conducted studies on the perception of agency in simple geometric shapes and developed the "Blindfold Test" to distinguish perceptual effects from higher-level cognitive judgments. Their research program also examines the intersection of vision science with aesthetics, intuitive physics, and social cognition.
0079.research_direction: Dr. van Buren has recently been investigating how high-level cognitive domains—such as intuitive physics, social categorization, and affect—interface with core visual processes like spatial attention and memory. Their recent work explores the mechanistic drivers of attentional allocation, testing whether spatial attention is reflexively guided by internal physical models of friction or by an object's central positioning during ensemble quantity judgments. Additionally, they are studying the visual basis of emotion and aesthetics by employing computational evolutionary algorithms to synthesize specific low-level features that trigger affective responses, and by using a novel "attentional transplant" paradigm to determine if replayed gaze scanpaths causally dictate a viewer's aesthetic preferences. Finally, their research probes the fidelity of visual representations, asking whether memory for continuous facial attributes like age operates over precise physical metrics or is systematically biased by abstract social categories.

papers.title: Remembering facial age: Assimilation in memory toward categories of 'Young' and 'Old'
papers.abstract: This research examines how social categorization (age) influences the fidelity of visual representations in memory. Utilizing a matching-from-memory paradigm, the investigators demonstrate a robust assimilation bias toward prototypal category centers: observers systematically reconstructed 30-year-old faces as younger and 60-year-old faces as older. This memory distortion was found to be invariant across target gender, race, and the observer's own age, and it generalized across different identities. These findings suggest that visual memory for age operates over abstract categorical representations (e.g., 'Young' or 'Old' prototypical centers) rather than precise, veridical exemplars, with social categories actively shaping the metrics of facial memory.
papers.authors: Didi Dunin, Joan Danielle K. Ongchoco, Benjamin van Buren

papers.title: Rotating objects cue spatial attention via the perception of frictive surface contact
papers.abstract: This study identifies a novel attentional cueing effect driven by internal models of intuitive physics, specifically the force of friction. Experimental results show that isolated rotating stimuli (e.g., clockwise-rotating disks) reflexively shift spatial attention to locations congruent with predicted translation assuming frictive contact with a floor. This rotational cueing is significantly modulated by environmental context: the effect is amplified by contact with a visible floor, abolished when contact is absent, and inverted when contact occurs with a 'ceiling'. These findings indicate that the visual hierarchy rapidly integrates kinematic cues and surface-contact information to deploy attention toward the probable future states of objects.
papers.authors: Hong B. Nguyen, Benjamin van Buren

papers.title: Attentional dynamics drive aesthetic preferences for scenes: Evidence from 'attentional transplants'
papers.abstract: This paper investigates the causal relationship between visual attention patterns and individual aesthetic preferences using a novel 'attentional transplant' methodology. By programmatically replaying the gaze patterns (scanpaths) of one observer (donor) to another (recipient), the study demonstrated that recipients consistently attributed higher aesthetic value to scenes when viewing them via the attention filters of donors who liked the images compared to those who disliked them. The results provide evidence that aesthetic evaluation is computed over the specific spatio-temporal features selected by attention, and that inter-observer preference variance is largely explained by differences in attentional deployment.
papers.authors: Hong B. Nguyen, Benjamin van Buren

papers.title: Appealing, disgusting and threatening visual features determined using an evolutionary algorithm
papers.abstract: This research utilizes a computational evolutionary algorithm to programmatically synthesize and isolate visual features associated with three distinct affective responses: appeal, disgust, and threat. The study maps how the resulting evolved visual configurations—characterized by specific color distributions, textures, and geometric arrangements—capture and sustain spatial attention. The findings identify unique attentional 'fingerprints' for each affective category, demonstrating that the visual system prioritizes ecologically and emotionally significant information through reflexive processing channels that operate independently of high-level task goals.
papers.authors: Hong B. Nguyen, Benjamin van Buren

papers.title: Center of attention: Spatial position affects quantity judgments and preference for groups of objects
papers.abstract: This study explores the 'center of attention' bias in the context of ensemble perception and evaluative preference. Across several experiments, the authors tested whether the spatial positioning of objects within a display influences numerical estimation (subitizing and estimation) and aesthetic preference. The results reveal that items located at the spatial center of a visual field are prioritized for processing and given higher weight in global computations, leading to systematic overestimation of central quantity and an aesthetic bias toward central items. The findings suggest that spatial arrangement significantly modulates the weights assigned to elements during the integration of scene-level properties.
papers.authors: Hong B. Nguyen, Benjamin van Buren

0080.name: Benjamin Wolfe
0080.bio: Benjamin Wolfe is an Assistant Professor whose research examines the mechanisms of visual information acquisition in complex, naturalistic environments. Wolfe utilizes driving as a tool to investigate questions in vision science, specifically focusing on scene perception, peripheral vision, and the consequences of attentional failures in real-world tasks. Their methodology bridges visual psychophysics and human factors, employing eye-tracking and computational approaches to address road safety and digital readability. Currently, their work explores how the visual system integrates information across the visual field to support situational awareness and decision-making.
0080.research_direction: Wolfe investigates the cognitive and perceptual mechanisms underlying scene gist perception and hazard detection in dynamic, high-stakes environments. They employ psychophysical paradigms, including staircase procedures and multi-alternative forced-choice tasks, to quantify temporal detection thresholds and examine how visual degradations like optical blur disproportionately affect the perception of vulnerable road users. Their research program interrogates the interaction between bottom-up visual cues—such as retinal motion and scene context—and top-down cognitive biases, specifically probing how the low prevalence effect and decisional criterion shifts modulate the detection of rare, dangerous stimuli. Furthermore, Wolfe uses naturalistic video datasets to investigate the parameters of anticipatory processing, seeking to characterize how observers integrate temporal and pictorial information to generate predictive models of complex, evolving scenes.

papers.title: Seeing the truck, but missing the cyclist: effects of blur on duration thresholds for road hazard detection
papers.abstract: This study quantified the impact of simulated optical blur on viewing duration thresholds for hazard detection in dynamic driving environments. Using annotated dashcam footage, we estimated detection thresholds for younger and older adults through a staircase procedure that varied stimulus duration to maintain 80% accuracy. Both age groups exhibited significantly elevated duration thresholds under blurred conditions compared to clear vision. Critically, the increment in duration threshold necessitated by blur was disproportionately larger for non-vehicular hazards, such as pedestrians and cyclists, than for larger vehicular hazards like cars or trucks. These findings suggest that age-related visual degradation or uncorrected refractive errors specifically impair the rapid detection of the most vulnerable road users, highlighting the necessity of considering hazard category in driver safety assessments.
papers.authors: Silvia Guidi, Anna Kosovicheva, Benjamin Wolfe

papers.title: Highly dangerous road hazards are not immune from the low prevalence effect
papers.abstract: The low prevalence effect (LPE)—the tendency to miss targets when they appear rarely—poses a significant risk in safety-critical domains like driving. We investigated whether the perceived dangerousness of a road hazard modulates the magnitude of the LPE. Observers performed a hazard detection task using naturalistic dashcam clips previously rated for hazardousness on a continuous scale. While overall detectability increased monotonically with the hazardousness rating, the LPE remained robust across all levels of perceived danger. Observers were significantly more likely to miss highly dangerous hazards (e.g., animals or vehicles in the driver's path) when their prevalence was low compared to when they were common. These results are consistent with a decisional criterion shift account of the LPE and demonstrate that the high stakes of missing a dangerous hazard are insufficient to override the cognitive biases induced by target rarity.
papers.authors: Jiali Song, Benjamin Wolfe

papers.title: Road Hazard Stimuli: Annotated naturalistic road videos for studying hazard detection and scene perception
papers.abstract: This paper presents the Road Hazard Stimuli (RHS) dataset, a validated collection of 270 naturalistic dashcam video excerpts (2 seconds each) designed for vision research in dynamic environments. The dataset contains 180 hazard clips and 90 non-hazard clips, featuring diverse road users, lighting conditions, and traffic scenarios. Each clip is annotated with spatial hazard location, precise onset timing, and perceived dangerousness ratings obtained from a cohort of 48 independent raters. We validated the dataset using psychophysical experiments assessing hazard detection and localization performance under time pressure. The RHS dataset provides a standardized tool for investigating scene gist perception, visual search at low prevalence, and the temporal dynamics of driver awareness in complex, real-world scenes.
papers.authors: Jiali Song, Anna Kosovicheva, Benjamin Wolfe

papers.title: Predicting natural road scenes: Effects of motion, stereoscopic depth, and scene context
papers.abstract: Anticipatory processing is critical for safe navigation, yet the visual cues that support the prediction of dynamic scenes are poorly understood. We factorially manipulated motion (video vs. still image), scene context (urban vs. highway), and stereoscopic depth to examine their roles in road scene prediction. Participants viewed 2s dashcam previews and indicated the expected appearance of the scene 2s later in a 5-alternative forced choice task. Prediction accuracy was significantly higher for video previews than for still images and for urban roads than for highways, indicating that both retinal motion and scene content contribute to predictive models. Surprisingly, the addition of stereoscopic depth cues did not enhance prediction performance over monocular depth cues, suggesting that drivers primarily rely on pictorial and motion-based information for medium-term scene forecasting.
papers.authors: Jiali Song, Ginnie Wee, Benjamin Wolfe

0081.name: Bevil Conway
0081.lab_name: Section on Perception, Cognition, and Action
0081.bio: Bevil Conway is a Senior Investigator at the National Eye Institute and leads the Section on Perception, Cognition, and Action. Conway’s research investigates how the brain transforms physical sensory signals into perceptions and cognitive categories, using color as a model system to bridge physiology and psychology. Utilizing electrophysiology, functional MRI, and psychophysics in both humans and macaques, they have characterized the parallel processing organization of the inferior temporal cortex. Conway has also established links between neural representation and the linguistic categorization of color.
0081.research_direction: Dr. Conway's recent work explores the neural and cognitive mechanisms of color vision, tracing how early sensory signals are transformed into high-level perceptual, semantic, and categorical representations. Using fMRI and behavioral paradigms in macaques, they have recently been investigating how retinotopic visual areas are functionally parcellated by tuning to color and spatial frequency, and how downstream regions integrate distinct features like color and shape to encode abstract object concepts. In human subjects, their research employs time-resolved MEG to map the rapid temporal dynamics of color processing, probing the transition from early cone-opponent encoding to the later emergence of subjective hue spaces. Additionally, they are examining the broader cognitive and cultural dimensions of vision by testing whether consensus color categorization requires linguistic scaffolding, and by analyzing how the chromatic statistics of artistic paintings manipulate visual cues for object recognition.

papers.title: The origin of color categories
papers.abstract: This investigation addresses the role of linguistic scaffolds in the formation of color concepts by determining if macaque monkeys exhibit consensus color categorization. Despite sharing homologous retinal circuitry and subcortical pathways with humans, macaques lack language, providing a critical test for the innateness of color categories. Utilizing a match-to-sample behavioral paradigm and computational simulations to account for potential non-uniformities in CIELUV color space, the study demonstrates that humans possess robust consensus categories while macaques do not. Although one monkey developed a private category, the absence of group-level consensus suggests that universal color concepts are not hard-wired products of visual encoding but likely emerge through language or other human-specific cognitive mechanisms.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS)
papers.authors: Daniel J. Garside, Audrey L. Y. Chang, Hannah M. Selwyn, Bevil R. Conway

papers.title: Color and Spatial Frequency Provide Functional Signatures of Retinotopic Visual Areas
papers.abstract: The functional specialization of retinotopic visual areas (V1, V2, V3, V4, V3a, and MT) in the macaque was characterized using fMRI and a novel data-driven Sparse Supervised Embedding (SSE) analysis. By measuring voxel-wise responses to chromatic and achromatic gratings across varying spatial frequencies and saturations, the researchers identified stimulus-feature combinations that distinguish cortical parcels parcellated by eccentricity and hemifield. Findings reveal systematic functional signatures: posterior areas (V1) are differentiated from anterior areas (V4) by sensitivity to high spatial frequency and specific chromatic contrasts, while ventral parcels are distinguished from dorsal ones by differential tuning to colors that modulate all three cone types. These signatures provide a functional map that helps resolve organizational differences between human and non-human primate visual cortex.
papers.authors: Spencer R. Loggia, Stuart J. Duffield, Kurt Braunlich, Bevil R. Conway

papers.title: The representation of object concepts across the brain
papers.abstract: This study maps the neural representation of concrete object concepts in macaque monkeys trained for years on specific color-shape primitives. Using whole-brain fMRI searchlight analysis, the researchers identified areas capable of cross-feature decoding, where the representation of one concept feature (e.g., color) could be predicted by its associated partner (e.g., shape). Unlike retinotopic cortex, which maintains independent feature maps, the temporal pole (TP), anterior inferior temporal cortex (aIT), and prefrontal cortex (PFC) showed robust cross-feature decoding. TP and aIT response patterns specifically mirrored the geometric structure of color space, suggesting they store the semantic content of object concepts, while PFC activity was uniquely predictive of behavioral task errors, linking conceptual knowledge to action.
papers.authors: Spencer R. Loggia, Helen E. Feibes, Stuart Duffield, Karthik Kasi, Bevil R. Conway

papers.title: From color encoding to color perception: The temporal dynamics of color vision in the human brain
papers.abstract: The temporal evolution of color representations was investigated using time-resolved magnetoencephalography (MEG) in human observers. The study employs multivariate pattern analysis to track the transformation from early retinal-like cone-opponent signals to late-stage perceptual color categories. Results reveal that low-level chromatic features (e.g., L-M and S-cone directions) are decoded rapidly, peaking around 100ms, while representations corresponding to phenomenological hue and categorical boundaries emerge later, around 200-300ms. This coarse-to-fine dynamic suggests that the brain initially encodes color according to the physical properties of light before reformatting these signals into a perceptually stable and behaviorally relevant geometry consistent with subjective color space.
papers.authors: Lina Teichmann, Ka Chun Lam, Amaia Benitez-Andonegui, Sebastian Montesinos, Daniel Garside, Bevil R. Conway

papers.title: The color of fruits in photographs and still life paintings
papers.abstract: This research analyzes the chromatic statistics of fruits as depicted in thousands of naturalistic photographs and artistic still-life paintings to explore the relationship between object color and artistic choice. The study demonstrates that while fruit colors in both media are distinct from natural scene backgrounds and cluster along the daylight axis, artists systematically shift chromaticities in paintings to enhance saliency. Specifically, still-life fruits exhibit higher saturation and greater chromatic contrast relative to their backgrounds than those in photographs. These findings suggest that artistic representations act as 'super-normal' stimuli that amplify the neural features the visual system prioritizes for object identification, reflecting a cognitive bias towards color as a diagnostic cue for fruit recognition.
papers.authors: Thorsten Hansen, Bevil R. Conway

0082.name: Bianca M. van Kemenade
0082.lab_name: Systems Neuroscience of Action and Perception (SNAP) Lab
0082.main_research_area: systems neuroscience of action and perception
0082.bio: Bianca M. van Kemenade is a neuroscientist who leads the Systems Neuroscience of Action and Perception (SNAP) Lab at Justus Liebig University Giessen. Van Kemenade’s research examines how voluntary actions modulate sensory perception, specifically investigating the neural mechanisms that differentiate between self-generated and externally generated stimuli. They utilize functional MRI (fMRI), transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), and psychophysics to examine the roles of predictive coding and multisensory integration in agency and perception. Their work also addresses clinical neuroscience, investigating how disruptions in these predictive mechanisms contribute to altered perception in schizophrenia spectrum disorders.
0082.research_direction: Dr. van Kemenade has recently been investigating how voluntary motor actions influence sensory processing and perception in the early visual cortex. Their recent work explores competing theoretical frameworks of action-based prediction, testing whether the visual system anticipates the sensory consequences of movements through mechanisms like sensory suppression, representational sharpening, or neural pre-activation. To evaluate these models, they employ high-resolution fMRI, combining univariate BOLD analysis and multivariate pattern decoding to observe V1 activity during orientation discrimination tasks. By comparing neural responses to visual gratings that are either actively self-generated or passively viewed, Dr. van Kemenade seeks to understand exactly how motor signals modulate visual representations from the preparatory phase through to stimulus onset.

papers.title: The effects of action-based predictions in early visual cortex
papers.abstract: This neuroimaging investigation evaluates how voluntary motor activity influences neural processing and perception of contingent sensory outcomes in the primary visual cortex (V1). The study contrasts four theoretical frameworks: the classical forward model (proposing sensory suppression), pre-activation (predictive baseline shifts), sharpening (increased representational precision), and opposing processes (pre-activation followed by distinct interaction mechanisms). Using high-resolution functional MRI combined with both univariate BOLD signal analysis and multivariate pattern decoding, the researchers examined V1 activity during a preparatory window and subsequent orientation discrimination of gratings. Results revealed that the orientation of predicted stimuli could be decoded from early visual areas at levels exceeding chance before stimulus onset, supporting pre-activation across both active and passive conditions. Crucially, self-generated stimuli elicited enhanced BOLD amplitudes compared to passively presented stimuli, a finding that contradicts the neural suppression predicted by standard forward models and supports an additive or enhancement mechanism during self-initiated perception. Decoding precision did not significantly differ between active and passive conditions, providing no evidence for neural sharpening.
papers.authors: Bianca M. van Kemenade, Lars F. Muckli

0083.name: Bilge Sayim
0083.bio: Bilge Sayim is a vision scientist and CNRS researcher at the University of Lille and the University of Bern who investigates mechanisms of visual information selection and compression. Sayim’s research involves the discovery and characterization of redundancy masking, a phenomenon where the visual system reduces the number of perceived items in repeating peripheral patterns. Utilizing psychophysical methodologies and appearance-based modeling, they explore how perceptual grouping, visual crowding, and prior knowledge shape conscious experience. Sayim’s current work connects neuroscience and art to develop empirical methods for studying the subjective quality of visual appearance.
0083.research_direction: Dr. Sayim has recently been investigating the structural limits and organizational mechanisms of human visual perception, with a particular emphasis on spatial integration in peripheral vision. Their recent work extensively explores redundancy masking—the phenomenon where observers systematically underreport the number of items in repeating peripheral patterns—using psychophysical numerosity tasks and attentional cueing to determine how this visual compression interacts with spatial attention, grouping, and segmentation. In a related vein, they are examining how fundamental spatial inhomogeneities, such as radial-tangential anisotropies in the visual field, influence the perceived numerosity of peripheral item ensembles. Beyond peripheral limitations, their research also investigates dynamic object processing, probing human temporal sensitivity to facial sequences to understand how temporal order judgments are modulated by spatial orientation and top-down semantic contexts like speech.

papers.title: Compression of visual information in redundancy masking follows grouping and segmentation
papers.abstract: The human visual system employs strategies to manage perceptual overload by organizing inputs through grouping and segmentation. A key phenomenon, redundancy masking (RM), involves the systematic underreporting of items in repeating peripheral patterns, such as perceiving only two lines when three are presented. This study investigated whether RM occurs before or after these organizational processes. Using briefly presented arrays of 3–5 vertical lines with varying contrast polarities (uniform, alternating, or segmented), observers reported the number of items and their specific features. Results indicated that RM was present across all conditions but was significantly constrained by stimulus organization: masking occurred primarily within segmented subgroups of identical items. The preservation of global features, such as ordinal contrast ratios and stimulus edges even during masking, suggests that RM functions as a feature-preserving compression mechanism that operates on the products of visual grouping and segmentation.
papers.authors: Sabrina Hansmann-Roth, Wolf Harmening, Bilge Sayim

papers.title: Attention in redundancy masking
papers.abstract: Peripheral vision is severely limited by crowding and low resolution, and recently, by redundancy masking (RM)—the underestimation of item numerosity in repetitive patterns. This study assessed whether RM results from limited attentional resources. Participants performed a numerosity task on peripheral line arrays under three attentional conditions: single cue, double cue, and no cue. While attentional cueing improved overall discrimination performance (reporting numbers closer to the actual count), RM persisted across all cueing conditions. Even with a single cue maximizing attention to the target array, observers continued to report fewer items than were physically presented. These findings demonstrate that while attention modulates the precision of peripheral representations, it does not alleviate RM, suggesting that RM is a fundamental structural limit of the visual system rather than an effect of inattentional blindness or insufficient resource allocation.
papers.authors: Fazilet Zeynep Yildirim-Keles, Daniel R. Coates, Bilge Sayim

papers.title: The radial–tangential anisotropy of numerosity perception
papers.abstract: The human visual field is characterized by significant inhomogeneities, particularly the radial-tangential anisotropy where items arranged radially (along the axis from the fovea) interfere more than those arranged tangentially. This study investigated whether this spatial anisotropy modulates the perceived numerosity of peripheral item clouds. In a series of experiments, observers estimated the number of discs in displays where spatial arrangements were biased toward either radial or tangential configurations. Estimates were significantly lower for radial compared to tangential displays, an effect that persisted even when global distributions and mixed contrast polarities were used. These results indicate that the topology of peripheral vision, specifically the spatial integration limits observed in crowding and redundancy masking, fundamental determines the perceived numerosity of ensembles, challenging the idea of a purely independent 'number sense'.
papers.authors: Li L-Miao, Bert Reynvoet, Bilge Sayim

papers.title: The effect of processing partial information in dynamic face perception
papers.abstract: While face perception research typically focuses on static, holistic representations, faces in natural environments are dynamic stimuli containing critical temporal information. This study investigated human sensitivity to facial dynamics by measuring temporal order judgments of face sequences. Across experiments using upright and inverted faces, as well as scenarios with and without congruent speech, results showed that temporal sensitivity was significantly higher for upright faces. This indicates that dynamic information is processed more efficiently when presented in a canonical orientation. Furthermore, language comprehension enhanced temporal order sensitivity, suggesting that the integration of facial dynamics is modulated by top-down semantic context. The findings highlight that dynamic face perception relies on a complex interplay between partial temporal information and holistic spatial frameworks, with superior performance for biologically relevant, upright configurations.
papers.authors: Nihan Alp, Gülce Lale, Ceren Saglam, Bilge Sayim

0084.name: Billy Hammond
0084.bio: Hammond’s research examines the intersection of nutrition, vision science, and neuroscience, focusing on how dietary factors influence the central nervous system across the human lifespan. They specialize in the study of macular carotenoids, specifically lutein and zeaxanthin, and utilize psychophysical methods such as heterochromatic flicker photometry to measure macular pigment optical density and its role in neuroprotection. Hammond’s work employs behavioral and neuroimaging techniques, including critical flicker fusion, to assess visual processing speed as a biomarker for cognitive health and to investigate preventive approaches for age-related neurodegenerative diseases like dementia. Additionally, their research covers infant visual development and the optimization of visual performance in sports.
0084.research_direction: Dr. Hammond has recently been investigating how retinal filtering impacts spatial vision, specifically exploring the role of macular pigment in mitigating intraocular and atmospheric short-wavelength light scatter. Using psychophysical tasks like grating detection and two-point resolution, their recent work examines how individual differences in macular pigment optical density affect visual range through simulated blue haze and influence fine spatial resolution across the visible spectrum. In a distinct line of research, they have also been studying motion constancy by developing novel protocols to measure the lower threshold of motion—the minimum speed required to perceive directionality. By employing these paradigms alongside random dot kinematograms, Dr. Hammond tests how slow-velocity motion detection is influenced by fluctuating ambient spectral illuminants and veiling glare stress. Furthermore, their recent scholarship includes theoretical work on the historical foundations of perceptual psychology, examining Isaac Newton's early conceptualization of color as an internal neural percept rather than an objective property of light.

papers.title: Properly Speaking, Sir Isaac Newton Was the First Perceptual Psychologist and, Therefore, the First Psychologist
papers.abstract: This theoretical inquiry re-evaluates Isaac Newton’s contributions to the behavioral sciences, contending that his conceptualization of color as an internal percept rather than an objective property of light establishes him as the progenitor of perceptual psychology. The authors argue that Newton’s insights into chromatic perception—which anticipate modern neuroscience’s focus on internal neural interpretation—predate the formal 19th-century inception of the discipline by figures like Wundt and Helmholtz. By examining phenomena such as color constancy and simultaneous contrast through a Newtonian lens, the paper asserts that his unifying principles regarding the brain’s construction of perceptual reality are as fundamental to the study of psychology as Darwinian evolution is to biology.
papers.authors: Billy R. Wooten, Billy R. Hammond

papers.title: The relationship between the macular carotenoids and simulated visual range
papers.abstract: Testing the visibility hypothesis, this investigation examines whether macular pigment (MP) improves long-distance visual range by filtering blue haze—short-wavelength dominant atmospheric scatter that degrades target contrast. Fifty-eight healthy young adults were tasked with detecting sinusoidal gratings of varying spatial frequencies (3, 7.5, and 15 cpd) through simulated blue haze of increasing intensity. Higher macular pigment optical density (MPOD) was significantly associated with a greater tolerance for blue haze before losing visibility of the 3-cpd and 7.5-cpd gratings, though no significant effect was observed at 15 cpd. These data support the role of retinal xanthophylls in extending visual range for low-to-mid spatial frequency targets by attenuating the veiling luminance of short-wave light scatter.
papers.authors: Cameron J. Wysocky, Jacob B. Harth, Lisa M. Renzi-Hammond, Billy R. Hammond Jr.

papers.title: The influence of macular pigment on the fine spatial resolution of light of varying wavelengths
papers.abstract: This study investigates the impact of foveal macular pigment optical density (MPOD) on high-frequency spatial vision across the visible spectrum, specifically examining its role in mitigating intraocular light scatter. Sixty participants underwent MPOD quantification via heterochromatic flicker photometry and performed a two-point resolution task under monochromatic and broadband lighting. Results demonstrated a significant negative correlation between MPOD and resolution thresholds primarily at shorter wavelengths (420–540 nm), where individuals in the highest MPOD quartile exhibited 31–38% superior spatial resolution compared to the lowest quartile. These findings indicate that macular pigments selectively enhance fine resolution by absorbing short-wavelength light most susceptible to scatter, thereby improving visual function in sub-optimal lighting environments.
papers.authors: Yaw Buabeng, Billy R. Hammond

papers.title: The Constancy of Perceived Motion Under Different Spectral Conditions
papers.abstract: This research assesses the robustness of motion perception—specifically the lower threshold of motion (LTM)—against variations in the spectral composition of ambient illumination. Utilizing a random dot kinematogram (RDK) paradigm and a hybrid optical bench, sixty healthy adults were tested under different filtered light conditions emulating daylight across short-, medium-, and long-wave bands, as well as under glare stress. Despite substantial alterations in the spectral illuminant and the presence of veiling glare, motion detection thresholds remained remarkably stable. The findings provide empirical evidence for motion constancy, suggesting that the visual system employs adaptive mechanisms to maintain invariant motion perception, effectively isolating object movement from fluctuating environmental optical factors.
papers.authors: Jeffrey Nightingale, James M. Brown, Billy R. Hammond, Jr.

papers.title: A Novel Characterization of the Lower Threshold of Motion
papers.abstract: Addressing the methodological gap in quantifying slow-velocity motion detection, this paper introduces and validates a specialized protocol for measuring the lower threshold of motion (LTM). While high-velocity limits are well-documented, the LTM—the minimum speed required to perceive directionality—is critical for understanding visual processing under low-signal conditions. The authors detail a custom psychophysical paradigm and describe its implementation using high-precision optical controls. Validation across diverse observer groups highlights the system’s sensitivity to individual differences in neural processing speed and its potential as a tool for evaluating the efficacy of visual interventions, such as nutritional supplements or filtering lenses, on dynamic visual performance.
papers.authors: Jacob B. Harth, Lisa M. Renzi-Hammond, Cameron J. Wysocky, Spencer F. Smith, Billy R. Hammond, Jr.

0085.name: Blaire Dube
0085.bio: Dube is an Assistant Professor at Memorial University of Newfoundland whose research investigates the reciprocal interactions between visual attention and working memory systems. Utilizing a multi-methodological approach that includes behavioral psychophysics, computational modeling, eye tracking, and functional MRI, Dube examines the cognitive filters that prioritize behaviorally relevant information while mitigating sensory competition. Their work includes the development of the Filter Disruption Theory, which characterizes how salient or unexpected environmental distractors interfere with attentional filtering and memory representations. Dube’s research aims to provide a mechanistic understanding of how humans navigate complex visual environments through flexible attentional control.
0085.research_direction: Dr. Dube's recent work explores the dynamic intersection of visual working memory (VWM) and attentional control, investigating how the visual system prioritizes targets and mitigates distraction. They have recently been examining the mechanisms of learned spatial suppression using search-probe and continuous report paradigms, specifically asking whether the suppression of frequent distractors operates proactively or reactively and how it protects target fidelity in memory. Their research also probes the functional states and capacity limits of VWM, testing whether memory items become more vulnerable to visual interference while being actively manipulated and assessing the extent to which observers can flexibly distribute memory resources across multiple concurrent levels of priority. Ultimately, Dr. Dube is working to integrate these distinct phenomena by theoretically modeling both external visual selection and internal memory maintenance as a unified, multi-level system of dynamic weights and balances.

papers.title: Items in visual working memory are more susceptible to visual interference while in-use
papers.abstract: Traditional models of visual working memory (VWM) suggest that once information is encoded, it is shielded from external perceptual interference during the maintenance phase. However, these models are typically based on tasks where memory items are held in a static state. This study investigates whether VWM representations remain vulnerable when they are in an 'active' state—specifically when they are being mentally manipulated or prepared for action. Utilizing an orientation recall task with retroactive cueing, the authors demonstrated that salient visual distractors significantly impaired recall precision when they appeared during the phase where the item was being actively manipulated. In contrast, no interference was observed when distractors appeared after the manipulation phase but before the test. These results indicate that the functional state of a VWM representation determines its susceptibility to disruption, with 'in-use' items being significantly more fragile than those in a passive maintenance state.
papers.authors: Eva Lout, Julie D. Golomb, Blaire Dube

papers.title: Learned spatial suppression is not always proactive
papers.abstract: Learned spatial suppression allows observers to minimize attentional capture by distractors that frequently appear in specific locations. While prevailing theories suggest this suppression is implemented proactively (pre-stimulus), evidence for its temporal dynamics has been limited by traditional response-time metrics. This study employed a novel search-probe paradigm to index the spatial distribution of attention at search onset. Across two experiments, the authors replicated the behavioral benefits of learned suppression but found that probe discrimination accuracy was not reduced—and in some cases was enhanced—at the high-probability distractor location. These findings suggest that the suppressed location is initially selected for processing before being reactively inhibited, challenging the assumption that learned statistical regularities necessarily lead to proactive neural suppression of space.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
papers.authors: Seah Chang, Blaire Dube, Julie D. Golomb, Andrew B. Leber

papers.title: Attention as a multi-level system of weights and balances
papers.abstract: This theoretical review proposes a framework for understanding attentional selection as a dynamic system of weights and balances that operates across multiple processing levels. The authors argue against a rigid top-down/bottom-up dichotomy, instead describing how priorities are weighted based on current goals, physical stimulus salience, and selection history. The framework explicitly integrates external selective attention with internal attention (the prioritization of items within working memory). It details how these weights can be dynamically adjusted or, in the case of distraction, temporarily reversed—leading to errors like memory intrusions. By conceptualizing attention as a tiered system resolving competition through a shared priority map, the review provides a unified account of how the brain maintains focus in complex environments while remaining sensitive to unexpected but relevant events.
papers.authors: William Narhi-Martinez, Blaire Dube, Julie D. Golomb

papers.title: Suppression of a salient distractor protects the processing of target features
papers.abstract: Salient distractors are known to impair search efficiency, but their impact on the fidelity of target representations in working memory is less clear. This research investigated whether learned spatial suppression of a frequent distractor location prevents 'feature errors,' such as misreporting distractor attributes or losing target precision. Using a continuous orientation report task, the authors found that distractors significantly increased swap errors and reduced recall precision on low-probability trials. Crucially, when the distractor appeared in a predictable, high-probability location, these feature-based interference effects were significantly reduced. The findings demonstrate that experience-driven spatial suppression provides a protective benefit for feature processing, effectively gating irrelevant information to preserve the representational integrity of task-relevant items in visual working memory.
papers.authors: William Narhi-Martinez, Blaire Dube, Jiageng Chen, Andrew B. Leber, Julie D. Golomb

papers.title: Limitations on flexible allocation of visual short-term memory resources with multiple levels of goal-directed attentional prioritization
papers.abstract: Contemporary theories of visual short-term memory (VSTM) propose that resources are continuous and can be flexibly distributed according to an item's priority. This study used a continuous report task and simultaneous probabilistic spatial cues to test the limits of this flexibility, specifically whether observers can prioritize items across three distinct levels of importance. While group-level data showed that memory precision generally increased with probe probability, Bayesian individual-differences analyses revealed that only a small subset of participants could successfully maintain more than two priority levels. The results suggest that while VSTM resource allocation is theoretically continuous, there are significant practical constraints on the complexity of the attentional control settings that can be concurrently implemented, potentially limited by executive control or memory capacity itself.
papers.authors: Holly Lockhart, Blaire Dube, Kevin J. MacDonald, Naseem Al-Aidroos, Stephen M. Emrich

0090.name: Brad Wyble
0090.bio: Brad Wyble is a Professor of Psychology at Pennsylvania State University who researches the cognitive and neural architecture of visual awareness, temporal attention, and memory consolidation. Their work integrates behavioral psychophysics and electrophysiological (EEG) recordings with neurocomputational modeling to examine how the brain constructs reportable mental representations from transient visual input. Wyble conducts research on the attentional blink and attribute amnesia and developed the 'Simultaneous Type, Serial Token' (STST) model of temporal attention. Additionally, Wyble is a co-founder of Neuromatch Academy and works on the advancement of global, open-source computational neuroscience education.
0090.research_direction: Dr. Wyble's recent work investigates the intersection of attention and visual working memory, exploring how robust representations are formed—or lost—when observers do not explicitly intend to encode their surroundings. Using attribute amnesia paradigms and surprise recall-by-drawing tasks, they are examining how stimulus-intrinsic memorability and transient attentional deployment affect incidental memory consolidation during both simple tasks and naturalistic visual search. Alongside this behavioral work, they have recently been evaluating the theoretical and computational architectures underlying temporal visual attention, specifically probing capacity limits like the attentional blink using electrophysiological markers and formal modeling. Furthermore, their recent research bridges human cognition and artificial intelligence by investigating whether applying biologically inspired mechanisms, such as spatiotemporal continuity and spatial context, to self-supervised contrastive learning can yield more robust machine vision systems.

papers.title: Memorability effects emerge in incidental visual working memory
papers.abstract: This research utilizes an attribute amnesia paradigm to investigate the degree to which stimulus-intrinsic memorability modulates incidental encoding within visual working memory (VWM). Across multiple experiments involving faces and scenes, the authors demonstrate that high-memorability targets are reported in surprise trials with significantly higher accuracy (44.8% for faces; 41.6% for scenes) compared to forgettable stimuli (23.5% for faces; 27.1% for scenes). Critically, follow-up control experiments indicate that this memorability advantage is not attributable to enhanced attentional capture by memorable items or differences in target-foil perceptual contrast. These findings suggest that intrinsic memorability acts as a primary facilitator of memory consolidation even in the absence of intentional encoding strategies, indicating that VWM representations are sensitive to stimulus-centered properties independently of attentional filters.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
papers.authors: Joyce Tam, Taryn Green, Ryan E. O'Donnell, Brad Wyble

papers.title: Surprise! Draw the scene: Visual recall reveals poor incidental working memory following visual search in natural scenes
papers.abstract: Utilizing a recall-by-drawing methodology, this study assesses the fidelity of incidental working memory following a target localization task within complex natural scenes. In a series of surprise trials, participants were asked to depict the features of a target or the surrounding scene context immediately after locating them. Despite successful search performance, participants exhibited profound failures in recall, frequently failing to depict diagnostic attributes or contextual layout. Control experiments demonstrated that this failure was not a product of interference from the drawing task itself. The results provide empirical evidence that the deployment of attention during naturalistic visual search is often transient and does not necessitate the consolidation of a reportable representation into a durable working memory trace, thereby extending the phenomenon of attribute amnesia to complex environments.
papers.authors: Nicolás Cárdenas-Miller, Ryan E. O'Donnell, Joyce Tam, Brad Wyble

papers.title: (Temporal) Visual attention NOT in crisis
papers.abstract: This article challenges the narrative of a theoretical crisis in visual attention research by synthesizing mechanistic evidence from the study of temporal selection. Focusing on the attentional blink (AB) phenomenon, the authors integrate behavioral data, neurocomputational models (e.g., the STST model), and electrophysiological markers like the N2pc and P3 components to argue that observed selection failures reflect robust, evolved bottlenecks in information processing. They contend that AB effects cannot be explained by peripheral vision or task-generic interference and argue that abandoning attentional constructs would impede vision science. The authors emphasize the necessity of formal modeling to understand the functional architecture of temporal capacity limits and defend the maturity and progress of current attention theories.
papers.authors: Paul E. Dux, Roberto Dell'Acqua, Brad Wyble

papers.title: Hopfield and Hinton's neural network revolution and the future of AI
papers.abstract: This perspective reviews the foundational impact of Hopfield and Hinton's neural network architectures on artificial intelligence and psychological modeling. The authors discuss how recurrent dynamics for associative memory and backpropagation-based learning formed the scaffold for modern deep learning. They advocate for a paradigm shift in AI development that incorporates biologically inspired mechanisms, such as discrete memory consolidation stages and temporal attention windows, to improve the generalization and robustness of machine vision. By bridging the gap between human developmental psychology and neural network design, the authors suggest that cognitively grounded architectures can address current limitations in artificial intelligence efficiency.
papers.authors: James Z. Wang, Brad Wyble

papers.title: Incorporating simulated spatial context information improves the effectiveness of contrastive learning models
papers.abstract: The authors introduce Environmental Spatial Similarity (ESS), a self-supervised contrastive learning framework that leverages the spatiotemporal continuity of an agent's path through photorealistic simulated environments. By defining positive training pairs based on spatial proximity during exploration, ESS provides a similarity signal grounded in the autocorrelated visual statistics typical of biological learning. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that ESS achieves nearly 15% greater accuracy on downstream tasks compared to standard instance discrimination methods. The research suggests that incorporating historical spatial context facilitates the acquisition of robust categorical representations, particularly in agents operating in unfamiliar or constrained environments, highlighting the efficiency of environmentally informed self-supervision over independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) sampling.
papers.authors: Lizhen Zhu, James Z. Wang, Wonseuk Lee, Brad Wyble

0091.name: Bradford Z. Mahon
0091.department: Department of Psychology and the Neuroscience Institute
0091.bio: Bradford Mahon is a cognitive neuroscientist who investigates how the human brain organizes and represents object concepts and their associated motor and linguistic information. Utilizing functional MRI and behavioral studies, Mahon examines how visual input is transformed into conceptual knowledge to guide object-directed actions and naming. Their research involves studying patients with focal brain injuries from stroke or tumors, including translational work that utilizes awake brain mapping during neurosurgery to map language and motor functions. This approach facilitates causal tests of the neurocognitive organization of the ventral and dorsal visual pathways and has led to the development of surgical decision-support tools for preserving cognitive functions.
0091.research_direction: Dr. Mahon’s recent work explores the large-scale functional organization of the human brain, spanning both the basic neuroscience of object-directed action and the clinical dynamics of neurological injury. Bridging vision and motor systems, they have recently been investigating how the brain represents manipulable objects, using fMRI encoding models to map kinematic features in the parietal cortex and voxel-based lesion mapping to test whether dorsal action networks causally influence category-selective visual areas in the ventral stream. In parallel clinical research, they are examining systemic neural reorganization and vulnerability, utilizing resting-state fMRI and machine learning to probe how unilateral gliomas alter functional connectivity networks in the contralesional hemisphere. Furthermore, their recent work investigates predictive models of cortical topography and biomechanics, applying magnetic resonance elastography to study physical strain patterns in traumatic brain injury and refining intraoperative electrical stimulation to map critical language networks during awake neurosurgery.

papers.title: Causal parametric language mapping with electrical stimulation during awake neurosurgery
papers.abstract: This study employs intraoperative direct electrical stimulation (DES) to delineate language-sensitive cortical architecture during awake craniotomies. By systematically manipulating the physical parameters of cortical perturbation—specifically timing, duration, and onset latencies relative to linguistic task phases (e.g., picture naming and word reading)—the researchers demonstrate that these variables significantly modulate behavioral outcomes. Meta-analysis of granular performance data reveals that subtle variations in the mapping protocol, previously categorized as non-diagnostic noise, provide statistically meaningful signals regarding the underlying functional topography. This parametric framework facilitates the development of high-fidelity predictive models of individual brain organization, potentially optimizing the trade-off between maximal tumor cytoreduction and the preservation of critical language networks.
papers.authors: J. Raouf Belkhir, W. Tecumseh Fitch, Frank E. Garcea, Benjamin L. Chernoff, Max H. Sims, Eduardo Navarrete, Sam Haber, David A. Paul, Susan O. Smith, Webster H. Pilcher, Bradford Z. Mahon

papers.title: Left-hemisphere glioma drives systematic patterns of contralesional functional connectivity
papers.abstract: This research utilizes machine learning to evaluate the systemic impact of unilateral left-hemisphere gliomas on the contralesional functional connectome. Analyzing resting-state functional MRI data from a cohort of 48 glioma patients and 107 neurotypical controls, the study demonstrates that focal tumors induce consistent, predictable alterations in right-hemisphere (RH) functional connectivity patterns. Support vector machine (SVM) classifiers successfully distinguished patients from controls (89% accuracy) and identified clinically relevant molecular subtypes, such as isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH) mutation status (78% accuracy). Crucially, the patterns of RH connectivity were found to be predictive of the spatial coordinates of left-hemisphere lesions, particularly those involving the parietal lobe. These findings provide empirical support for large-scale functional reorganization and highlight the potential for using contralesional connectivity as a biomarker for disease progression and neural plasticity.
papers.authors: Emma Strawderman, Frank E. Garcea, Madalina E. Tivarus, Steven P. Meyers, Adnan A. Hirad, William M. Burns, Kevin A. Walter, Tyler Schmidt, Webster H. Pilcher, Bradford Z. Mahon

papers.title: Object-directed action representations are componentially built in parietal cortex
papers.abstract: The human inferior parietal lobule is a critical substrate for the visuomotor representations necessary for functional object manipulation. This study investigates the componential nature of these representations within the supramarginal gyrus (SMG). Using functional MRI and a linear encoding model, the researchers demonstrate that neural activity in the SMG during object processing can be accurately predicted by a set of empirically defined kinematic synergies. The kinematic encoding model outperformed several control visual models—including deep convolutional neural networks (AlexNet, ResNet50, VGG16) and behavioral visual similarity metrics—in accounting for SMG variance. Furthermore, the amplitude of neural responses in the SMG was specifically modulated by the functional 'centrality' of manipulation to an object's identity, independent of low-level visual features. These results suggest that the SMG processes complex object-directed actions through the productive combination of a closed set of kinematic building blocks.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS)
papers.authors: Leyla Roksan Caglar, Jon Walbrin, Emefa Akwayena, Jorge Almeida, Bradford Z. Mahon

papers.title: Visual processing of manipulable objects in the ventral stream is modulated by inputs from parietal action systems
papers.abstract: This study addresses the causal influence of dorsal visual pathway action systems on category-selective representations in the ventral temporal cortex (VTC). Utilizing Voxel-based Lesion-Activity Mapping (VLAM) in a sample of 109 neurosurgical patients with heterogeneous left-hemisphere lesions, the researchers show that damage to specific parietal structures—namely the anterior intraparietal sulcus and the supramarginal gyrus—causes a significant reduction in neural responses to tools in the medial fusiform gyrus. Contrastingly, parietal lesions did not modulate responses to non-manipulable categories such as places. Diffusion MRI connectometry further identified the descending portion of the left arcuate fasciculus as the primary white matter pathway mediating these dorsal-to-ventral interactions. These results demonstrate that the functional profile of the ventral stream is modulated by trans-cortical inputs from parietal action systems, supporting a model where motor-relevant information shapes visual object processing.
papers.authors: Frank E. Garcea, Emma L. Strawderman, William Burns, Matthew Cotroneo, Steven P. Meyers, Tyler Schmidt, Kevin A. Walter, Webster H. Pilcher, Bradford Z. Mahon

papers.title: Strain concentration drives the anatomical distribution of injury in acute and chronic traumatic brain injury
papers.abstract: Tissue damage resulting from mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI) is known to concentrate in specific neuroanatomical loci, including the midbrain, cerebellum, and mesial temporal lobe. This study tests the hypothesis that these injury patterns are driven by the biomechanical susceptibility of different brain regions to strain loading. Using Magnetic Resonance Elastography (MRE) in healthy controls, the researchers developed whole-brain biomechanical vulnerability maps based on in vivo rheological properties. These maps were validated against a prospective cohort of mTBI patients using diffusion MRI collected at acute, sub-acute, and chronic intervals. The results demonstrate that regions exhibiting high strain concentration under MRE are the primary sites of structural injury as measured by diffusion MR. Decomposing the biomechanical drivers, the study shows that increased strain is caused by both disproportionate energy arrival at high-strain structures and the failure of those structures to effectively dissipate energy, establishing a causal mechanism for the anatomy of mTBI.
papers.authors: Adnan A. Hirad, Doran Mix, Arun Venkataraman, Steven P. Meyers, Bradford Z. Mahon

0092.name: Bradley Duchaine
0092.department: Department of Psychological and Brain Sciences
0092.bio: Duchaine is a Professor and Chair of the Department of Psychological and Brain Sciences at Dartmouth College, where they investigate the cognitive and neural foundations of social perception. Their research focuses on the functional architecture of face processing, using neuropsychology, psychophysics, and neuroimaging to study conditions such as prosopagnosia and prosopometamorphopsia. Duchaine co-developed the Cambridge Face Memory Test and characterized the heritability and developmental trajectories of face recognition abilities. Their current research aims to map the broader network of category-selective visual areas and identify specific neural deficits associated with impaired social perception.
0092.research_direction: Dr. Duchaine's recent work explores the cognitive and neural architectures of high-level visual processing, primarily through the lens of face perception disorders like developmental prosopagnosia and prosopometamorphopsia (PMO). They have recently been investigating the severe facial distortions experienced by individuals with PMO, using extensive psychophysics, broad stimulus databases, and novel digital warping protocols to visualize subjective perceptions and test whether occipitotemporal representations are strictly face-specific or domain-general. Additionally, their recent research examines the neural mechanisms underlying developmental prosopagnosia by using functional MRI population receptive field (pRF) mapping to probe spatial integration in ventral face-selective cortex. They are also evaluating the diagnostic boundaries of face blindness within large behavioral cohorts, specifically looking at how common clinical exclusion criteria and neurodevelopmental comorbidities impact the classification of high-level visual impairments.

papers.title: The first comprehensive case study of early-emerging prosopometamorphopsia
papers.abstract: This longitudinal investigation characterizes a 15-year-old male participant (Zed) presenting with lifelong, dynamic prosopometamorphopsia (PMO) and comorbid developmental prosopagnosia. Through extensive psychophysical testing using a variety of object categories (faces, hands, cars) and reference frames, the authors demonstrate that the participant's facial distortions—including feature rotation, drooping, and expansion—are strictly face-specific and independent of viewpoint or visual field location. Neuroimaging results revealed attenuated face-selectivity in right posterior face-selective regions, and diffusion tensor imaging indicated reduced white matter integrity within the left inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus (IFOF). This case serves as a unique neuropsychological proof for the independence of identity recognition systems and the mechanisms supporting holistic face gestalt perception.
papers.authors: Sydney Fortner, Antônio Mello, Daniel G. Stehr, Chandana Kodiweera, Heejung Jung, Krzysztof Bujarski, Tor Wager, Bradley Duchaine

papers.title: Developmental prosopagnosics have normal spatial integration in posterior ventral face-selective regions
papers.abstract: This large-scale functional MRI study (N=40) critically evaluates the hypothesis that restricted spatial integration and abnormally small population receptive fields (pRFs) in face-selective cortex underlie the deficits in developmental prosopagnosia (DP). Using high-contrast, dynamic visual localizers and the latest pRF mapping techniques, the researchers quantified pRF size, eccentricity scaling, and visual field coverage in core ventral face areas (FFA, OFA) and intermediate visual regions (hV4, VO1). Contrary to previous findings, DPs and controls exhibited statistically comparable pRF properties and spatial organization across the visual processing hierarchy. These results suggest that DP recognition impairments do not arise from a fundamental failure of spatial integration in the ventral stream, necessitating a re-evaluation of current computational models of face blindness.
papers.authors: Daniel A. Stehr, Yiyuan Zhang, Anusha Patgiri, Alexis Kidder, Kendrick Kay, Bradley Duchaine

papers.title: Improving diagnosis of developmental prosopagnosia: The role of exclusion criteria
papers.abstract: Investigating diagnostic heterogeneity within a sample of 1479 self-referred individuals, this study explores how the application of common exclusion criteria—specifically mid-level visual deficits and autism-spectrum traits—impacts the prevalence and classification of developmental prosopagnosia (DP). Using objective measures of face memory (CFMT, FFT) and subjective indices (PI20), the authors demonstrate that approximately 7–11% of DPs exhibit intermediate visual impairments and 14–21% present with significant autism-spectrum comorbidities. The data highlight the limitations of existing categorical diagnostic frameworks and advocate for a multidimensional approach that acknowledges the continuous nature of high-level visual impairment and its diverse neurological co-occurrences.
papers.authors: Tirta Susilo, Bradley Duchaine

papers.title: Facial distortions as a critical test for models of the organization of visual function
papers.abstract: This contribution utilizes neuropsychological data from individuals with prosopometamorphopsia (PMO) to test the validity of contemporary models of the organization of the human occipitotemporal cortex (OTC). By systematically exposing five PMO participants to naturalistic stimuli across 510 object categories (the THINGS database), the authors found that in two of the five cases, visual distortions were elicited exclusively by faces, with no distortions reported for over 1,000 non-face stimuli. These findings provide strong empirical evidence for the existence of face-specific processing modules and challenge theoretical frameworks that propose distributed, graded, or domain-general representations of high-level visual objects in the human brain.
papers.authors: Antônio Mello, Bradley Duchaine

papers.title: Visualising facial distortions in prosopometamorphopsia
papers.abstract: This clinical picture study reports a rare case of a 58-year-old male with prosopometamorphopsia (PMO) whose severe facial distortions—described as grotesque and 'demonic'—occurred only during live, face-to-face interactions while being absent when viewing two-dimensional images. Exploiting this context-dependent dissociation, the researchers employed a feedback-driven digital manipulation protocol where the patient viewed a person in real life while simultaneously viewing an on-screen photograph of the same person. The photograph was digitally warped until it achieved a photorealistic match to the patient's subjective live perception. This study presents the first validated, photorealistic visualizations of PMO distortions, emphasizing that high-level visual gestalts can be influenced by the presence of interpersonal cues and stimulus dimensionality.
papers.authors: Antônio Mello, Daniel Stehr, Krzysztof Bujarski, Bradley Duchaine

0094.name: Brett Fajen
0094.bio: Brett Fajen is a Professor of Cognitive Science and Associate Dean at Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute and the director of the Perception and Action Lab. Fajen's research examines the visual control of locomotion and perceptual-motor learning through immersive virtual reality and motion capture to study human navigation in complex environments. They apply ecological and dynamical systems frameworks to investigate tasks such as obstacle avoidance, target interception, and high-speed steering. This work incorporates computational modeling to explore the neural mechanisms of motion perception, specifically linking brain areas like MT and MSTd to the processing of optic flow during self-motion.
0094.research_direction: Dr. Fajen has recently been investigating how humans use visual information to prospectively control high-speed steering and navigation through complex environments. Their recent work explores the coordination of gaze and motor action during simulated drone piloting tasks that require avoiding obstacles and traversing sequential waypoints in cluttered, forest-like settings. Specifically, they are studying how trajectory planning and speed control are influenced by the spatial layout of upcoming goals, restricted lookahead distances, and the specific action capabilities or sluggishness of the vehicle being flown. By tracking eye movements and manipulating these physical and visual constraints, they are examining the mechanisms underlying affordance-based control to understand how actors dynamically distribute their visual sampling between upcoming target paths and nearby hazards.

papers.title: Visual control of steering through multiple waypoints
papers.abstract: This study examines the informational basis of anticipatory steering control when navigating through sequential constraints. Subjects performed a simulated drone-piloting task requiring them to traverse a series of three gates. The experiments tested three specific hypotheses: treating waypoints in isolation, a weighted combination of attractors, and matching a constant-curvature path through upcoming waypoints. Results demonstrated that trajectories between initial gates were systematically modulated by the spatial layout (distance and angle) of subsequent waypoints. This behavior was significantly influenced by the agent's action capabilities; sluggish vehicle dynamics prompted earlier steering adjustments to maintain a smooth path, whereas increased agility allowed for more direct approaches. These findings suggest that human steering is characterized by an affordance-based control strategy where actors adapt their current path to remain within their movement capabilities relative to upcoming constraints.
papers.authors: A. J. Jansen, Brett R. Fajen

papers.title: Coordination of gaze and action during high-speed steering and obstacle avoidance
papers.abstract: The research investigates how skilled actors coordinate visual sampling and motor control during high-speed navigation in cluttered environments lacking explicit paths. Experienced first-person view (FPV) drone pilots navigated a simulated forest-like racecourse while their gaze and steering were recorded. Contrary to models of steering that assume a tight coupling between gaze and the intended path, results showed that gaze frequently fell on nearby obstacles and environmental surfaces rather than exclusively on waypoints or paths. Despite this distributed sampling, pilots successfully maintained high speeds, traversed waypoints, and avoided collisions. In tasks involving sequential hoops, pilots adapted their approach to the immediate hoop based on the relative position of the subsequent one. The study provides evidence that high-speed steering utilizes a flexible coordination of gaze to sample information about environmental constraints and upcoming goals, challenging existing accounts of path-centered gaze strategies.
papers.authors: Nathaniel V. Powell, Xavier Marshall, Gabriel J. Diaz, Brett R. Fajen

papers.title: Prospective control of steering through multiple waypoints
papers.abstract: This investigation addresses the role of lookahead distance in the visual control of high-speed steering through sequential goals. Participants performed a simulated drone-flying task through a forest-like environment with gates placed at irregular intervals. By manipulating the visibility of upcoming gates, the study assessed how information beyond the immediate target affects steering and speed control. Results indicated that participants consistently approached the current gate in a manner that anticipated the angular position of the next gate, provided that the lookahead distance was at least 1.5 path segments. When vision was restricted to the immediate waypoint, flight paths became longer and travel speeds were both slower and more variable. The findings demonstrate that human steering control is prospective, utilizing information about future constraints to optimize trajectories and maintain task performance, even in actors without extensive specialized experience in high-speed maneuvering.
papers.authors: A. J. Jansen, Brett R. Fajen

0095.name: Brian A. Anderson
0095.bio: Brian A. Anderson is a Professor at Texas A&M University and the Director of the Human Imaging Facility, specializing in the cognitive neuroscience of attention. Anderson identified the phenomenon of value-driven attentional capture, in which stimuli associated with reward involuntarily attract attention even when they are task-irrelevant. Their research utilizes human psychophysics, functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), and eye-tracking to investigate how selection history and motivational factors influence visual processing. This work includes applications for understanding the mechanisms underlying addiction and psychopathology.
0095.research_direction: Dr. Anderson has recently been investigating how past experiences—such as statistical regularities, aversive conditioning, and cumulative selection history—shape the strategic control of visual attention. Their recent work explores whether learned associations and state anxiety modulate deliberate target choices in adaptive choice visual search tasks, as well as whether high-probability features actively enhance working memory encoding or merely induce response biases during attribute amnesia paradigms. Additionally, they are probing the cognitive costs of distractor suppression, combining visual search with grip-force tasks to assess the subjective mental effort required to inhibit physically salient stimuli. To better capture these phenomena, Dr. Anderson is also evaluating the psychometric properties of attention tasks, specifically testing whether eye-tracking metrics of oculomotor capture can provide more reliable measures of individual differences in learning-dependent distractor suppression than traditional response-time data.

papers.title: Reliably measuring learning-dependent distractor suppression with eye tracking
papers.abstract: This research evaluates the psychometric properties of various metrics for learning-dependent distractor suppression, addressing the reliability crisis in behavioral cognitive tasks where response time (RT)-based measures frequently exhibit poor internal consistency and test-retest stability. Across three independent datasets, the authors compared oculomotor capture (defined by the frequency of distractor fixations) and target fixation latencies. Results indicate that oculomotor measures provide significantly superior split-half reliability relative to RT-based metrics, with reliability coefficients reaching levels suitable for the study of individual differences in attentional control. Furthermore, the study identifies that oculomotor reliability is enhanced in older adults, suggesting that eye-tracking parameters may circumvent the confounds associated with age-related increases in RT variability.
papers.authors: Andy J. Kim, Laurent Gregoire, Brian A. Anderson

papers.title: Aversive conditioning, anxiety, and the strategic control of attention
papers.abstract: The study investigates how aversive conditioning influences the strategic control of attention, specifically the deliberate choice of search targets. Participants were trained to associate a specific color with an aversive outcome (CS+) and another with a neutral outcome (CS-) before completing an Adaptive Choice Visual Search (ACVS) task. In the test phase, participants could choose to report the target in either the CS+ or CS- color. Findings revealed a systematic bias away from the CS+ target, which induced suboptimal search behavior in several conditions. Critically, state anxiety modulated this effect: higher levels of anxiety were associated with a paradoxically increased tendency to select the CS+ target, suggesting that anxiety shifts attentional strategies in ways that can override direct avoidance tendencies in choice-based selection.
papers.authors: David S. Lee, Andrew Clement, Laurent Gregoire, Brian A. Anderson

papers.title: Signal suppression makes search less effortful
papers.abstract: This investigation probes the relationship between the active suppression of physically salient distractors and the subjective mental effort required during visual search. While the signal suppression hypothesis posits that top-down inhibitory mechanisms can preempt attentional capture by salient-but-irrelevant stimuli, the cognitive cost of such suppression is debated. Using a paradigm that equates physical effort (e.g., grip force) to the avoidance of specific search displays, the researchers assessed observer preferences for ignoring high- versus low-salience distractors. Participants consistently exerted more physical effort to obtain search displays with high-salience distractors, which are suppressed more efficiently and thus facilitate faster target detection. This suggests that the subjective effort of search is determined by overall search efficiency rather than the recruitment of suppressive control, as observers prefer conditions where distractors are most successfully suppressed.
papers.authors: Brad T. Stilwell, Brian A. Anderson

papers.title: Statistical regularities bias memory decisions without enhancing working memory encoding: Insights from attribute amnesia
papers.abstract: Employing the attribute amnesia paradigm, this study examines whether statistical regularities in target features lead to enhanced working memory (WM) encoding or merely induce response biases. In three experiments, participants identified target locations where certain color attributes appeared with high probability. Surprise trials probing target color revealed that while participants were more accurate when targets matched high-probability colors, this effect was driven by a systematic response bias toward the frequent color rather than a more robust memory trace. The prioritization of high-probability features occurred even when those features were task-irrelevant and physically salient. These findings indicate that while the visual system implicitly extracts summary statistics and uses them to prioritize attention and bias subsequent decisions, these regularities do not automatically facilitate the transition of information into working memory in the absence of explicit task demands.
papers.authors: Niya Yan, Richard Jiang, Brian A. Anderson

papers.title: Selection history and the strategic control of attention
papers.abstract: This research explores the impact of selection history—the cumulative effect of prior attentional orienting—on the strategic and deliberate control of visual selection. Using the Adaptive Choice Visual Search (ACVS) task, the authors manipulated the frequency of target colors during a training phase to establish a selection history. Results demonstrate that a history of frequently selecting a specific feature biases participants to continue selecting that feature in a subsequent test phase, even when doing so becomes the less optimal (more effortful) strategy. This selection-history effect indicates that the strategic control of attention is not purely governed by goal-directed optimization or current task demands, but is significantly constrained by past experience, paralleling the involuntary capture effects documented in previous literature.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
papers.authors: Andy J. Kim, David S. Lee, Jeesu D. Grindell, Brian A. Anderson

0096.name: Brian Keane
0096.bio: Brian P. Keane is an Assistant Professor at the University of Rochester whose research examines the computational and neural basis of visual perception in healthy and clinical populations. Utilizing behavioral psychophysics, functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), and eye-tracking, Keane specializes in mid-level visual processes such as contour interpolation, perceptual organization, and shape completion. Their recent work focuses on identifying neural biomarkers for psychotic disorders by characterizing functional dysconnectivity within large-scale visual and somatomotor networks. These investigations aim to link specific visual processing deficits to the underlying pathophysiology and clinical progression of schizophrenia and related spectrum disorders.
0096.research_direction: Dr. Keane has recently been investigating the visual and neural mechanisms underlying neuropsychiatric and neurological conditions to identify accessible clinical biomarkers.
