Their recent fMRI work explores large-scale functional network disruptions in psychosis and schizophrenia, specifically probing thalamo-cortical dysconnectivity in visual and somatomotor networks alongside whole-brain inter-individual heterogeneity. They are also examining behavioral predictive processing in schizophrenia by investigating how resistance to top-down visual priors, such as the depth-inversion illusion, relates to specific clinical symptoms like hallucinations. Broadening their focus to other populations and methodological rigor, their recent work explores whether retinal imaging and electrophysiology can track subclinical neurotrauma from repetitive head impacts in athletes, while also testing how uncorrected minor refractive errors might mimic perceptual grouping deficits during contour integration tasks.

papers.title: Functional dysconnectivity of visual and somatomotor networks yields a simple and robust biomarker for psychosis
papers.abstract: While psychosis has been linked to thalamo-cortical hyperconnectivity and cortico-cortical hypoconnectivity across sensory networks, the network specificity, susceptibility to clinical confounds, and diagnostic biomarker potential of these disruptions have remained unresolved. Utilizing resting-state functional MRI data from the Human Connectome Early Psychosis Project (54 healthy controls and 105 patients with affective or non-affective early psychosis), resting-state functional connectivity (RSFC) matrices across 718 regions were estimated using regularized partial correlation within a multimodal cortical parcellation. Both patient cohorts showed prominent cortico-cortical hypoconnectivity and thalamo-cortical hyperconnectivity selectively in the secondary visual (visual2) and somatomotor networks, while the primary visual and auditory networks remained unaffected. Combining these equal and opposing alterations yielded a composite 'somato-visual' biomarker that distinguished patients from controls with a large effect size (t(136.2) = 6.9, p = 2e-10, Hedges' g = 1.05). This biomarker was evident in antipsychotic-naive individuals, invariant to psychiatric comorbidities, motion, stress, and demographics, and demonstrated moderate test-retest reliability (ICC = 0.62) in five-minute scans. It achieved an AUC of 0.79 under leave-one-site-out cross-validation, enhanced diagnostic classification when combined with neurocognitive testing, and successfully differentiated chronic schizophrenia patients from both healthy individuals and clinical ADHD controls across two independent datasets.
papers.authors: Brian P. Keane, Yonatan T. Abrham, Michael W. Cole, Brent A. Johnson, Boyang Hu, Carrisa V. Cocuzza

papers.title: Correcting visual acuity beyond 20/20 improves contour element detection and integration: A cautionary tale for studies of special populations
papers.abstract: Visual perception and psychophysics protocols typically require participants to exhibit standard normal or corrected-to-normal visual acuity (20/20 Snellen fraction or better), operating under the assumption that sub-threshold optical variation within this range has negligible behavioral impact. This study tested whether correcting subtle refractive errors beyond 20/20 alters performance on elementary and intermediate contour processing tasks. Healthy young adults with uncorrected visual acuity of 20/20 or better completed two tasks under both habitual uncorrected and fully optimized refractive conditions: a collinear facilitation task measuring contrast detection thresholds for a central Gabor patch flanked by collinear or orthogonal elements at 4 and 10 cycles/degree, and a contour integration task requiring discrimination of closed contours embedded in field distractors. Optimal optical correction significantly decreased contrast thresholds during collinear facilitation—producing pronounced enhancements for high spatial frequency targets (10 cpd)—and improved closed contour integration accuracy. These findings reveal that standard visual acuity screening is insufficient to prevent optical confounds and demonstrate that minor uncorrected refractive errors can mimic perceptual grouping deficits in neuropsychiatric cohorts.
papers.authors: Brian P. Keane, Steven M. Silverstein, Thomas V. Papathomas, Bart Krekelberg

papers.title: Hallucinations and the depth-inversion illusion in schizophrenia
papers.abstract: Schizophrenia is consistently associated with resistance to the depth-inversion illusion (DII), a phenomenon wherein physically concave 3D visual targets (such as faces or hollow masks) are perceived as convex due to the modulation of sensory input by top-down perceptual priors. However, the exact psychopathological dimensions associated with DII resistance have not been fully clarified. In a clinical cohort of patients with schizophrenia evaluated across inpatient and outpatient care levels, susceptibility to depth inversion was measured using 3D concave face and scene stimuli with either realistic texture or uniform beige coloring across multiple viewing conditions. Correlation analyses between illusion susceptibility indices and Brief Psychiatric Rating Scale (BPRS) symptom dimensions revealed that DII resistance was selectively and significantly associated with hallucination severity, rather than delusion severity or overall positive symptom totals. These findings support predictive processing accounts indicating that hallucinations involve an aberrant imbalance between sensory precision and prior expectations in sensory cortex.
papers.authors: Judy L. Thompson, Steven M. Silverstein, Thomas V. Papathomas, Brian P. Keane

papers.title: Increased whole-brain functional heterogeneity in psychosis during rest and task
papers.abstract: While group-level connectomic differences in psychosis are well documented, whether functional brain network organization displays heightened inter-individual heterogeneity across the psychosis spectrum remains poorly characterized. Using data from the Human Connectome Early Psychosis Project (54 healthy controls, 81 non-affective psychosis, 24 affective psychosis) and validation data from the UCLA Consortium for Neuropsychiatric Phenomics, whole-brain functional connectivity (FC) matrices and task activations during a spatial working memory task were derived across 718 parcels. Cross-subject heterogeneity was computed as the average Pearson correlation distance between an individual's FC or activation pattern and all other cohort members. Early psychosis patients—both affective and non-affective—demonstrated significantly higher whole-brain functional heterogeneity than healthy controls during both rest and cognitive task execution (ps < 0.001, Hedges' g > 0.74), spanning up to seven functional networks. This increased heterogeneity was replicated in chronic schizophrenia when compared to healthy controls and an ADHD clinical comparison group. Critically, isolated connection weights and localized parcel-wise task activations were not more variable in patients, indicating that elevated heterogeneity reflects idiosyncratic, large-scale macroscale network reorganizations.
papers.authors: Brian P. Keane, Yonatan T. Abrham, Luke J. Hearne, Howard Bi, Boyang Hu

papers.title: Football-related concussions and head impacts are associated with changes in retinal structure and signaling
papers.abstract: Subconcussive head impacts and concussions from contact sports can induce persistent microstructural neurotrauma, yet accessible biomarkers for early detection remain limited. Given that the retina provides a direct anatomical window into the central nervous system, this investigation examined structural and functional retinal alterations in collegiate football athletes with varying histories of head trauma compared to non-contact controls. Macular ganglion cell-inner plexiform layer (GCIPL) and retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL) thicknesses were measured using spectral-domain optical coherence tomography (OCT), while retinal electrophysiological processing was quantified across photopic and scotopic conditions using full-field electroretinography (ffERG). Contact athletes exposed to repetitive impacts displayed significant alterations in retinal layer thicknesses and distinct shifts in ERG waveform amplitudes and latency kinetics relative to non-contact peers. These results indicate that non-invasive structural and electrophysiological retinal assays can capture subclinical central nervous system neurotrauma and axo-glial injury linked to repetitive sports head impacts.
papers.authors: Steven M. Silverstein, J. Atlas, M. A. Young, L. Bertolace, I. Juskiewicz, K. Merchant-Borna, S. Dermady, Y. Abrham, K. Green, J. Bazarian, R. S. Ramchandran, Brian P. Keane

0098.name: Brian Odegaard
0098.bio: Brian Odegaard is an Assistant Professor in the Department of Psychology at the University of Florida and directs the Perception, Attention, and Consciousness (PAC) Laboratory. Odegaard’s research characterizes the behavioral, computational, and neural correlates of subjective experience, focusing on how the brain constructs awareness in the visual periphery. Through the integration of psychophysics, functional MRI, and computational modeling, Odegaard investigates how metacognitive biases and attentional mechanisms shape perceptual decision-making. Their recent work explores reality monitoring, multisensory integration, and the development of web-based tools for reproducible vision science.
0098.research_direction: Dr. Odegaard's recent work investigates the neural and computational mechanisms underlying visual mental imagery, object representation, and perceptual decision-making. They have recently been using functional neuroimaging, multivariate decoding, and network analysis to explore how multidimensional object similarity is mapped across human and artificial systems, and to test heterarchical models of how the parietal and visual cortices generate internal visual experiences. Additionally, their research examines target detection and perceptual decisions in the visual periphery, utilizing eye-tracking within immersive virtual reality to study these phenomena under highly naturalistic conditions. Finally, Dr. Odegaard explores the role of metacognition across these domains, investigating human confidence-accuracy relationships during ecological visual tasks and evaluating how psychophysical principles of metacognitive sensitivity can be applied to artificial intelligence to optimize human-AI collaborative decision-making.

papers.title: Assessing psychological, neural and AI-based representational geometries across multiple similarity properties
papers.abstract: This research investigates the multidimensional nature of object similarity by mapping psychological, neural, and AI-based representational spaces across eight diverse properties, including objective features (e.g., color, shape) and subjective appraisals (e.g., affect). Utilizing large-scale pairwise similarity ratings for 280 objects and fMRI-based representational similarity analysis (RSA) in 80 participants, the study identified three primary mental geometries: one for general object features, another for affective evaluations, and a third for color. Neural patterns in the prefrontal and visual cortices significantly aligned with feature-based ratings, while affective geometries were found to influence visual cortex representations unexpectedly. AI models optimized for task-specific properties demonstrated high alignment with human behavioral and neural matrices, suggesting that similarity is a multidimensional construct shaped by regional neural variability and specific modeling strategies.
papers.authors: Johan Alejandro Gamba, Vincent Taschereau-Dumouchel, Megan A. K. Peters, Brian Odegaard

papers.title: Internal World Models as Imagination Networks in Cognitive Agents
papers.abstract: This study examines the computational role of imagination as an interface for accessing internal world models (IWMs), rather than purely for reward maximization. Using psychological network analysis based on vividness reports from human populations and large language models (LLMs), the authors constructed 'imagination networks' to evaluate internal representations. Human networks displayed significant structural coherence, characterized by strong correlations between local centrality measures (strength, closeness, and expected influence) and robust clustering. Conversely, LLM-derived networks lacked these structural invariants across various prompting and memory conditions, indicating a fundamental divergence in how human and artificial agents represent internally generated environmental states. The work introduces a quantitative framework for comparing internally-generated representations across biological and artificial cognitive agents.
papers.authors: Saurabh Ranjan, Brian Odegaard

papers.title: Metacognitive sensitivity: The key to calibrating trust and optimal decision-making with AI
papers.abstract: Applying principles from human perceptual psychophysics, the authors argue that metacognitive sensitivity—the ability of a system to assign confidence scores that accurately distinguish its correct from incorrect predictions—is essential for optimizing human-AI collaboration. The study introduces a theoretical framework for evaluating how AI confidence reports influence joint decision outcomes. Analytical findings demonstrate that an AI system with lower absolute predictive accuracy but higher metacognitive sensitivity can enable human collaborators to achieve superior joint performance compared to a more accurate but poorly calibrated model. This highlights that trust calibration and the weighting of advice in hybrid settings are critically dependent on the reliability of the AI’s self-evaluative signals.
papers.authors: Doyeon Lee, Joseph Pruitt, Tianyu Zhou, Jing Du, Brian Odegaard

papers.title: Towards the study of perceptual decision-making in peripheral vision with virtual reality
papers.abstract: This investigation utilizes immersive virtual reality (VR) to evaluate perceptual decision-making in the visual periphery under naturalistic, high-stakes conditions. Participants performed target detection tasks while navigating dynamic virtual environments, allowing for the analysis of detection sensitivity, false alarm rates, and metacognitive confidence across varying eccentricities. The results indicate that peripheral vision in ecological contexts is susceptible to specific error patterns and inconsistent confidence-accuracy relationships that are often overlooked in traditional laboratory paradigms using simplified stimuli. The paper provides methodological recommendations for integrating eye-tracking in VR vision research and discusses the trade-offs between experimental control and ecological validity in naturalistic target detection and visual search tasks.
papers.authors: Doyeon Lee, Tianyu Zhou, Jing Du, Brian Odegaard

papers.title: Heterarchy or hierarchy? Insights from a new model of visual imagination
papers.abstract: The authors propose a novel neural model of visual mental imagery (VMI) that challenges conventional reverse-hierarchy frameworks by positing a heterarchical organization. Integrating fMRI, multivariate decoding, encoding models, and eye-tracking, the study reveals that stimulus-specific orientation representations during imagery originate in the parietal cortex and are more robust there than in early visual areas (V1–V3), reversing the pattern typically observed during external perception. These findings establish the parietal cortex as a domain-general hub for content-specific imagery and offer a neural mechanism for differentiating between subjectively internal (imagined) and external (perceived) experiences by modulating representations at distinct nodes of the cortical hierarchy.
papers.authors: Saurabh Ranjan, Brian Odegaard

0099.name: Brian Scholl
0099.bio: Scholl is a Professor of Psychology at Yale University and Director of the Yale Perception & Cognition Lab, where they study the mechanisms of human vision. Scholl’s research characterizes visual awareness through phenomena such as inattentional blindness and defines how the mind represents objects and events across time and space. A focus of their work involves "visual intelligence," specifically how the visual system extracts concepts like causality, agency, and intuitive physics. Scholl employs computer-based psychophysical experiments and behavioral methods to investigate how perception provides a structure for higher-level thought. Currently, they are examining the interactions between perception and memory and how visual processing categorizes dynamic events.
0099.research_direction: Dr. Scholl has recently been investigating how the mind extracts high-level structural properties and abstract categories from diverse visual and social stimuli. Their recent work explores dynamic event perception, using spatial reproduction paradigms to test how observers spontaneously represent concepts like "unfinishedness" or abstract action categories ("visual verbs") to organize spatial memory. In the realms of motion and social vision, they are studying how observers infer complex states from sparse information, employing reverse correlation to map the subtle facial cues that signal attentiveness, and utilizing point-light displays to probe the extraction of material properties from inanimate, non-rigid motion. Additionally, their research spans into high-level cognition by exploring how classical psychophysical techniques, such as magnitude estimation, can be adapted to resolve deep-seated measurement artifacts in moral judgment tasks.

papers.title: Dynamic categorical memory distortion from 'visual verbs'
papers.abstract: Visual perception is not restricted to low-level feature extraction but encompasses the spontaneous representation of abstract 'event types' (e.g., swinging vs. tossing), which function as 'visual verbs.' This research demonstrates that these categorical event representations induce adaptive, dynamic memory distortions predicated on the distinct future states predicted by the event context. Using a psychophysical position-reproduction paradigm, the study found that spatial memory for terminal coordinates was systematically biased by the categorical event structure; specifically, swinging events—which are physically constrained—exhibited significantly less horizontal motion extrapolation than tossing events. These effects were robust against task-irrelevance and resistant to verbal interference, indicating that the visual system inherently utilizes categorical event models to constrain and update mental representations of dynamic environments.
papers.authors: Huichao Ji, Brian J. Scholl

papers.title: How to show that a cruel prank is worse than a war crime: Shifting scales and missing benchmarks in the study of moral judgment
papers.abstract: While moral judgment is a primary focus of cognitive science, its quantitative assessment often relies on unanchored scales (e.g., Likert or Visual Analog Scales) that are susceptible to idiosyncratic shifts in internal standards. This study highlights the extremity of this measurement error through nine experiments showing that observers paradoxically judge a cruel prank involving social humiliation as being equal in immorality to, or even worse than, a war crime involving lethal violence when using unanchored scales. This measurement anomaly was resolved using magnitude estimation—a psychophysical method employing an explicit, invariant moral benchmark. Furthermore, re-analyzing the phenomenon of 'moral luck' via magnitude estimation yielded results diametrically opposed to those obtained with Likert scales. These findings emphasize the necessity of incorporating psychophysical principles into moral cognition research to ensure the representational validity of behavioral metrics.
papers.authors: Vladimir Chituc, Molly J. Crockett, Brian J. Scholl

papers.title: The spontaneous prioritization of 'unfinishedness' in perception: A visual Zeigarnik effect
papers.abstract: The Zeigarnik effect—the preferential mnemonic encoding of interrupted tasks—is traditionally attributed to high-level motivational states or goal-directed processing. Here, we identify a 'visual Zeigarnik effect' that operates spontaneously within the visual hierarchy, independent of high-level task goals. Across four experiments using a path-tracing paradigm, observers reproduced the spatial coordinates of probes appearing on paths that either reached a terminal point or remained visually 'unfinished.' Despite the completion status being task-irrelevant, spatial reproduction was significantly more precise on unfinished trials. This prioritization of unfinishedness was robust when controlling for low-level visual features and generalized across varied display types. These findings suggest that the visual system inherently extracts 'unfinishedness' as a structural property of event representations, facilitating the spontaneous prioritization of incomplete information even in the absence of explicit motivational or social drivers.
papers.authors: Joan Danielle K. Ongchoco, Kimberly W. Wong, Brian J. Scholl

papers.title: Attending to attention: Reverse correlation reveals subtle cues to attentiveness in others' faces
papers.abstract: The capacity to infer others' attentional states from facial cues is a fundamental social-perceptual process. This study utilized reverse correlation—a data-driven psychophysical method—to reconstruct the internal representations underlying perceived attentiveness. Observers differentiated between base faces manipulated with stochastic noise to identify the most 'attentive' exemplar. Quantitative analysis of the resulting classification images and facial landmarks demonstrated that perceived attentiveness is mediated by a complex configuration of cues: while primary determinants included direct eye gaze and pupillary dilation, non-obvious features such as reduced mouth aperture were also diagnostic. These results show that the visual system utilizes a multidimensional set of facial regularities to track the cognitive states of others, illustrating that attention functions not only as a selector for perception but also as a salient object of social representation itself.
papers.authors: Clara Colombatto, Brian J. Scholl

papers.title: Dynamic point-light cloths generate rich percepts beyond biology
papers.abstract: Biological motion perception, exemplified by point-light walkers (PLWs), is frequently cited as a paradigmatic case of domain-specific visual processing. This study challenges this view by demonstrating that non-biological dynamic point-light cloths (PLCs)—representing the motion of flexible surfaces like waving ribbons—elicit similarly rich and robust structural percepts. Through 13 preregistered experiments, we show that PLCs emerge spontaneously in the presence of dynamic noise, depend on global cohesive relative motion rather than local point kinematics, and persist in limited-lifetime dot displays. Furthermore, these displays convey secondary material properties such as stiffness. These results indicate that the visual system’s capacity for recovering complex structure from sparse, dynamic information is a generalized architectural feature of motion processing, extending the scope of high-level motion perception beyond the biological domain to include inanimate non-rigid materials.
papers.authors: Merve Erdogan, Wenyan Bi, Ilker Yildirim, Brian J. Scholl

0100.name: Brigitte Röder
0100.bio: Brigitte Röder is a Professor of Biological Psychology and Neuropsychology at the University of Hamburg, where they investigate the mechanisms of experience-dependent neuroplasticity and multisensory integration in the human brain. Their research explores sensitive periods of development and the extent of functional and structural brain adaptation following sensory deprivation, such as congenital blindness. Using behavioral testing, electroencephalography (EEG), and functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), Röder examines how early sensory experiences shape neural representations and crossmodal plasticity. Through collaboration with the LV Prasad Eye Institute in India, Röder studies cohorts of individuals who have undergone sight-restoration surgery to analyze the limitations and potential of adult brain plasticity.
0100.research_direction: Dr. Röder has recently been investigating how early visual experience shapes the long-term development and plasticity of the human brain, primarily studying individuals who have had their sight restored after a period of dense congenital cataracts. Their recent work employs a multimodal approach—including diffusion-weighted imaging, fMRI, EEG, and magnetic resonance spectroscopy—to examine the structural, functional, and neurochemical footprints of early visual deprivation. Specifically, they are exploring how a lack of early vision impacts the microstructural recovery of white matter pathways, the trial-by-trial temporal stability of visual cortical responses, shifts in the excitatory/inhibitory balance of the visual cortex, and the cross-modal reorganization of category-selective object representations in the ventral visual stream. Additionally, their broader behavioral research investigates the mechanisms of multisensory integration, probing how audiovisual spatial learning and long-term cross-modal recalibration influence phenomena like the ventriloquism aftereffect and the enhancement of sound localization.

papers.title: Individuals born with congenital cataracts exhibit both persisting impairment and considerable recovery of white matter microstructure after sight restoration
papers.abstract: The present study employed diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) to investigate the microstructural integrity of white matter (WM) in individuals who underwent surgical sight restoration following a period of dense bilateral congenital cataracts (CC group, n=18). Fractional anisotropy (FA) and mean diffusivity (MD) were quantified in visual pathways and compared with age-matched sighted controls. The results revealed a significant reduction in FA and an increase in MD within the optic radiations of CC individuals, indicating a lasting microstructural footprint of early visual deprivation. Crucially, however, FA values in these tracts were positively correlated with the duration of sight restoration, suggesting that the adult human brain retains significant structural plasticity. These findings provide evidence for a dual developmental trajectory where early sensitive periods determine basic WM architecture while subsequent sensory experience permits partial microstructural recovery.
papers.authors: Jordan D. Hassett, Cordula Hölig, Sunitha Lingareddy, Ramesh Kekunnaya, Brigitte Röder

papers.title: Visual and Auditory Object Representations in Ventral Visual Cortex After Restoring Sight in Humans
papers.abstract: This functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) study investigated the organization of visual and auditory category-selective representations (faces, scenes, body parts, and objects) in the ventral occipital temporal cortex (VOTC) of adults who had experienced a transient period of congenital blindness. Compared to normally sighted controls, the sight-recovery group displayed a marked attenuation of face-selective responses, whereas scene-selective activity remained robust. A representational similarity analysis (RSA) and cross-modal decoding approach demonstrated a double dissociation: only the sight-recovery group exhibited significant decoding of visual categories from auditory object representations in the VOTC, whereas only controls exhibited the reverse. The data suggest that early visual experience is a prerequisite for typical face-selective neural architecture and that cross-modal recruitment of the visual cortex following blindness might facilitate, rather than hinder, visual functional recovery after sight is restored.
papers.authors: Katarzyna Rączy, Madita Linke, Job van den Hurk, Carolin Heitmann, Maria J. S. Guerreiro, Minye Zhan, Ramesh Kekunnaya, Rainer Goebel, Brigitte Röder

papers.title: The Temporal Stability of Visual Cortical Processing in Humans Depends on Early Experience
papers.abstract: Proper neural circuit function depends on precisely timed temporal orchestration, yet the role of early postnatal vision in shaping the temporal stability of the human visual system remains poorly understood. Using electroencephalography (EEG), we assessed the trial-by-trial temporal variability of cortical responses in individuals who recovered sight after dense bilateral congenital cataracts. The CC group displayed significantly higher inter-trial variability (lower phase coherence) in visual-evoked oscillatory activity across the visual hierarchy, even though the absolute oscillatory strength was preserved. This temporal instability was absent in individuals with late-onset developmental cataracts, indicating that the development of stable, intricately timed visual cortical dynamics requires adequate early visual experience. We suggest that cascading timing deficits throughout the visual hierarchy constitute a primary neural mechanism underlying the incomplete visual recovery observed after congenital deprivation.
papers.authors: Suddha Sourav, Max Emanuel Feucht, Ramesh Kekunnaya, Brigitte Röder

papers.title: Altered visual cortex excitatory/inhibitory ratio following transient congenital visual deprivation in humans
papers.abstract: We investigated the visual cortex excitatory/inhibitory (E/I) balance in 10 sight-restored individuals with a history of dense bilateral congenital cataracts using 3T Magnetic Resonance Spectroscopy (MRS) and electroencephalography (EEG). CC individuals exhibited a significantly lower Glx (Glutamate/Glutamine) to GABA+ (Gamma-Aminobutyric Acid) concentration ratio compared to age-matched sighted controls. Electrophysiologically, this was reflected in a higher intercept and a steeper aperiodic slope of the EEG power spectrum at occipital sites. Within the CC group, a lower Glx/GABA+ ratio was predictive of superior visual acuity. These findings suggest that congenital blindness leads to a permanent shift in the visual cortex E/I balance, likely resulting from homeostatic plasticity mechanisms that increase inhibition to compensate for an atypical baseline level of excitation established during the period of deprivation.
papers.authors: Rashi Pant, Kabilan Pitchaimuthu, José P. Ossandón, Idris Shareef, Sunitha Lingareddy, Jürgen Finsterbusch, Ramesh Kekunnaya, Brigitte Röder

papers.title: Higher Order Visual Location Learning Does Not Explain Multisensory Enhancement of Sound Localization (Reply to Vroomen and Stekelenburg)
papers.abstract: This study addresses recent critiques regarding the mechanisms of multisensory enhancement (ME) of sound localization and the ventriloquism aftereffect (VAE). Specifically, it evaluates whether ME could be attributed to higher-order learning of visual stimulus locations. We conducted a control experiment where participants localized sounds before and after unimodal visual exposure. No significant reduction in auditory localization errors was found, indicating that unimodal spatial learning cannot explain the ME observed after audiovisual stimulation. These results confirm the dissociation between ME and VAE, demonstrating that while VAE is sensitive to high temporal stimulation frequencies (10 Hz), ME is not. This dissociation suggests that the two effects are mediated by independent neural mechanisms of multisensory integration and long-term cross-modal recalibration.
papers.authors: Patrick Bruns, Hubert R. Dinse, Brigitte Röder

0101.name: Bruno Olshausen
0101.department: Helen Wills Neuroscience Institute and School of Optometry
0101.bio: Bruno Olshausen is a professor at UC Berkeley and the director of the Redwood Center for Theoretical Neuroscience, where they develop mathematical models to explain the principles of biological vision. Olshausen’s work on sparse coding demonstrates how simple-cell receptive field properties in the primary visual cortex emerge from efficient coding principles applied to natural image statistics. Their research utilizes Bayesian inference and probabilistic modeling to investigate how the brain constructs stable 3D representations from high-dimensional, dynamic sensory input. Currently, their laboratory focuses on hierarchical cortical models, neural representations of 3D scenes, and the development of NeuroAI hardware that mimics the brain's analog and asynchronous computing strategies.
0101.research_direction: Dr. Olshausen has recently been investigating the computational principles underlying both sensory processing and higher-level cognitive mapping using normative models and high-dimensional vector representations. In the domain of early vision, their recent work explores how the efficient and sparse coding of spatiochromatic natural scenes drives the organization of retinal cone pooling and the psychological emergence of universal color categories. To understand spatial navigation and memory, they are using Vector Symbolic Architectures to examine how algebraic operations, such as vector binding and modular residue systems, might account for compositional cognitive maps and grid cell phenomena in the entorhinal-hippocampal network. Additionally, they are investigating the computational mechanisms of scene analysis by combining convolutional sparse coding with resonator networks to model how the visual system might factorize complex sensory inputs into distinct object identities and poses.

papers.title: Emergence of strategic cone weighting from efficient coding of spatiochromatic natural images
papers.abstract: An efficient coding model is developed to determine how populations of retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) optimally pool signals from the retinal cone mosaic. By maximizing information transfer through the optic nerve subject to metabolic, wiring, and noise constraints, the model predicts that linear-nonlinear RGCs adapt their spatial weighting to the L- and M-cone topography. This strategic weighting produces strong L-M cone-opponency, surpassing the efficiency of random sampling and providing a normative account for retinal circuit organization based on the statistics of spatiochromatic natural scenes.
papers.venue: Journal of the Optical Society of America A
papers.authors: Alexander Belsten, Bruno A. Olshausen

papers.title: Sparse coding of chromatic natural images recovers universals in color naming and unique hues
papers.abstract: Sparse coding models are applied to the LMS cone activation distributions derived from calibrated natural images to investigate the statistical origins of color perception. The study finds that learned basis vectors align with universal color categories identified by the World Color Survey and replicate key psychophysical features of unique hues, including mutual exclusivity between red-green and blue-yellow channels. These results suggest that color appearance and naming categories emerge as an efficient representation of the sparse statistical structure inherent in spatiochromatic sensory input.
papers.authors: Alexander Belsten, Paxon Frady, Bruno Olshausen

papers.title: Computing with residue numbers in high-dimensional representation
papers.abstract: A theoretical framework is proposed for high-capacity spatial representation using a Residue Number System (RNS) implemented via high-dimensional, complex-valued vectors in a Vector Symbolic Architecture (VSA). The model demonstrates that encoding position through modular residues enables superlinear scaling of the coding range and supports robust error-correcting attractor dynamics. This provides a computational account of grid cell modularity in the entorhinal cortex and suggests a general mechanism for representing and operating on numerical data with logarithmic resource scaling.
papers.authors: Christopher J. Kymn, Denis Kleyko, E. Paxon Frady, Connor Bybee, Pentti Kanerva, Friedrich T. Sommer, Bruno A. Olshausen

papers.title: Binding in hippocampal-entorhinal circuits enables compositionality in cognitive maps
papers.abstract: This study introduces a normative model of hippocampal-entorhinal interaction where vector binding operations enable the formation of compositional cognitive maps. By binding spatial representations with context and sensory cues, the model achieves a similarity-preserving encoding that supports flexible navigation and episodic memory. The architecture utilizes a modular attractor network to maintain self-consistency across different residues, explaining the emergence of hexagonal grid fields and remapping phenomena in the hippocampal formation through an algebraic framework of distributed representations.
papers.venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS)
papers.authors: Christopher J. Kymn, Sonia Mazelet, Anthony Hitchcock Thomas, Denis Kleyko, Edward Paxon Frady, Friedrich Sommer, Bruno A. Olshausen

papers.title: Compositional Factorization of Visual Scenes with Convolutional Sparse Coding and Resonator Networks
papers.abstract: A neuromorphic scene analysis system is presented that integrates convolutional sparse coding (CSC) with resonator networks to perform compositional factorization. CSC extracts latent feature representations from visual input, which are then encoded as high-dimensional vectors. The resonator network iteratively decomposes these vectors to simultaneously infer object identities and poses. This approach increases representation capacity and mitigates combinatorial collisions in the search space, demonstrating an effective solution for scene parsing and visual recognition tasks using VSA principles.
papers.authors: Christopher J. Kymn, Sonia Mazelet, Annabel Ng, Denis Kleyko, Bruno A. Olshausen

0102.name: Bruno Rossion
0102.department: CNRS Ingénierie moléculaire, cellulaire et physiopathologie (IMoPA); Service de Neurologie; Service de Neurochirurgie
0102.bio: Bruno Rossion is a Research Director at the CNRS and Université de Lorraine specializing in the neuro-functional mechanisms of human face recognition and categorization. Rossion conducts research on the N170 electrophysiological component and case studies on acquired prosopagnosia to examine holistic face perception and the specialized nature of face processing in the human brain. Their methodology integrates multi-modal techniques including scalp EEG, functional MRI, and direct intracerebral recordings (sEEG) in patients with epilepsy. Rossion also applies fast periodic visual stimulation (FPVS), or frequency-tagging, as a tool for quantifying category-selective responses across the ventral occipito-temporal cortex in neurotypical and clinical populations.
0102.research_direction: Dr. Rossion has recently been investigating the neural mechanisms and spatiotemporal dynamics of human visual recognition, with a primary focus on face processing. Using large-scale intracranial recordings across the ventral occipito-temporal cortex, their research explores whether category-selective neural responses operate hierarchically and probes the localized circuitry driving phenomena like face pareidolia. They are also developing implicit frequency-tagging EEG paradigms and naturalistic behavioral tasks—validated in prosopagnosic patients—to assess how the visual system automatically generalizes face identities across highly variable real-world viewpoints. Furthermore, their recent multimodal work pairs concurrent fMRI and single-unit recordings to interrogate the fundamental physiological relationship between BOLD signal fluctuations and underlying excitatory or inhibitory neuronal spiking in the human association cortex.

papers.title: A tight relationship between BOLD fMRI activation/deactivation and increase/decrease in single neuron responses in human association cortex
papers.abstract: This neurophysiological investigation addresses the coupling between Blood-Oxygen-Level-Dependent (BOLD) hemodynamic signals and cellular activity in the human association cortex. Using a frequency-tagging paradigm, the authors recorded single-unit (SU) activity and fMRI concurrently in the fusiform gyrus (FG) of patients undergoing epilepsy monitoring. They identified face-selective neurons in the lateral FG, where BOLD signals increased, and the medial FG, where BOLD signals decreased. The study demonstrates a precise correspondence where BOLD activations reflect selective increases in neuronal firing rates, while BOLD deactivations in the medial FG correlate with active suppressions of baseline spiking. Both excitatory and inhibitory neuronal responses occurred with similar mean onset latencies (~120 ms), providing robust evidence for a direct link between the direction of BOLD modulation and the sign of the underlying neural firing rate changes in the human brain.
papers.authors: Marie-Alphée Laurent, Corentin Jacques, Xiaoqian Yan, Pauline Jurczynski, Sophie Colnat-Coulbois, Louis Maillard, Steven Le Cam, Radu Ranta, Benoit R Cottereau, Laurent Koessler, Jacques Jonas, Bruno Rossion

papers.title: Concurrent category-selective neural activity across the ventral occipito-temporal cortex supports a non-hierarchical view of human visual recognition
papers.abstract: This large-scale electrophysiological study evaluates the hierarchical organization of the human ventral visual stream using intracerebral recordings from 140 participants. By measuring category-selective responses to natural images across more than 11,000 recording sites, the authors characterized the spatiotemporal dynamics of high-frequency broadband gamma activity. While a postero-anterior gradient of increasing face-selectivity (abstraction) was observed along the ventral occipito-temporal cortex (VOTC), the onset and peak of these responses were largely concurrent (starting at approximately 100 ms) across posterior and anterior regions. The finding of simultaneous, correlated activity across 90 mm of cortical territory challenges traditional models of sequential processing stages and suggests a more integrated, non-hierarchical network for visual object recognition.
papers.authors: Corentin Jacques, Jacques Jonas, Sophie Colnat-Coulbois, Bruno Rossion

papers.title: The neural basis of face pareidolia with human intracerebral recordings
papers.abstract: The study explores the neurobiological mechanisms of face pareidolia by recording direct neural activity from the ventral occipito-temporal cortex (VOTC) in 44 participants. Using a frequency-tagging oddball paradigm, the researchers contrasted neural responses to biological faces, facelike objects (pareidolic stimuli), and non-face objects. Results indicate that face-selective responses to pareidolic stimuli are distributed across the same regions as biological face responses, including the previously under-sampled anterior temporal lobe. Despite lower response amplitudes compared to real faces, 89% of facelike object-selective contacts overlapped with human face-selective contacts and exhibited identical onset latencies. These findings suggest that face pareidolia is mediated by the primary face-categorization circuitry rather than through high-level cognitive feedback or distinct specialized regions.
papers.authors: Begüm Cerrahoğlu, Corentin Jacques, Diane Rekow, Jacques Jonas, Sophie Colnat-Coulbois, Stephanie Caharel, Arnaud Leleu, Bruno Rossion

papers.title: A simple behavioral evaluation test of human face identity recognition with natural images validated with the case of prosopagnosia PS
papers.abstract: This research develops and validates two streamlined behavioral instruments for assessing human face identity recognition (FIR) using naturalistic, 'ambient' images that incorporate variations in lighting, pose, and expression. The first test utilizes a three-alternative forced-choice (3AFC) familiarity selection task for famous identities, while the second employs an identity matching task with upright and inverted orientations. Validation data from neurotypical adults showed near-ceiling accuracy and clear face-inversion effects. Critically, testing the well-characterized brain-damaged patient PS revealed profound deficits in face-based identity tasks despite preserved performance with written names. These results confirm the tests' sensitivity and specificity for clinical and experimental evaluation of face-selective recognition impairments.
papers.authors: Angélique Volfart, Caroline Michel, Bruno Rossion

papers.title: A robust neural index of automatic generalization across variable natural views of familiar face identities
papers.abstract: This study introduces an implicit electrophysiological marker for the brain's capacity to generalize identity across diverse naturalistic views of familiar faces. Using scalp EEG and a fast periodic visual stimulation (FPVS) adaptation paradigm, participants viewed 6 Hz sequences of natural face images. Every second stimulus involved an identity change (3 Hz), occurring within an adaptation context. The results revealed a robust neural response at the 3 Hz change frequency over the right occipito-temporal cortex, specifically reflecting the detection of identity change despite significant variability in head orientation, expression, and lighting. This neural signature provides an objective, task-independent measure of face identity recognition that circumvents response biases and explicit decision-making processes inherent in traditional behavioral tasks.
papers.authors: Justine David, Laurent Koessler, Bruno Rossion

0104.name: Carlos Ponce
0104.department: Department of Neurobiology, Harvard Medical School
0104.bio: Carlos Ponce is an Assistant Professor of Neurobiology who investigates the neural mechanisms of visual recognition and perception. Ponce's laboratory uses electrophysiological recordings in rhesus macaques and deep learning frameworks, including generative adversarial networks and convolutional neural networks, to identify visual features encoded by neurons in the cortical hierarchy. Through closed-loop experimental designs, Ponce extracts data from the brain to characterize the internal models the primate visual system uses to interpret complex, naturalistic scenes. This approach links biological vision and artificial intelligence to refine automated recognition technologies and determine how sensory signals become cognitive representations.
0104.research_direction: Dr. Ponce has recently been investigating the computational principles and feature selectivity that govern primate visual recognition across the cortical hierarchy. Their recent work explores how neurons spanning the ventral stream and prefrontal cortex encode complex natural scenes, using multi-electrode arrays paired with closed-loop generative networks to map whether specific brain regions prioritize local textures, ethologically relevant animal features, or global object configurations. Additionally, they are extensively probing the alignment between the biological visual system and artificial neural networks (ANNs). In this computational domain, they are examining how structural inductive biases and the functional segregation of positive and negative signals shape feature representations, and evaluating whether current deep learning models adequately capture the dynamic representational landscape of the macaque brain.

papers.title: Brain feature maps reveal progressive animal-feature representations in the ventral stream
papers.abstract: Primate visual recognition is hypothesized to rely on object-centric representations, but cortical neurons may instead follow organizational principles based on generic features across textures and environments. This study utilized multielectrode arrays to record from V1/V2, V4, and posterior inferotemporal (PIT) cortex, employing an unsupervised heatmap approach to characterize local operations within natural scenes. We discovered that while foveal populations across the hierarchy respond to entire scenes, their activity focuses on salient subregions within object contours. Notably, there is a progressive increase in selectivity for animal-related features, such as faces and limbs, along the visual hierarchy. This trend was consistent with biological tuning but diverged from various artificial neural network architectures, suggesting that the monkey ventral stream is fundamentally organized to prioritize ethologically relevant local animal features over general object configurations.
papers.authors: Zhanqi Zhang, Till S. Hartmann, Richard T. Born, Margaret S. Livingstone, Carlos R. Ponce

papers.title: Structure as an inductive bias for brain–model alignment
papers.abstract: The alignment between artificial neural networks (ANNs) and the biological visual system remains a central challenge in computational neuroscience. Recent evidence suggests that standard convolutional architectures exhibit inherent alignment with cortical representations even before task-specific training. This work evaluates how structural constraints in deep learning models serve as inductive biases that facilitate this alignment. We argue that the architectural regularities of ANNs, such as spatial locality and weight sharing, mirror the fundamental organizational principles of the primate ventral stream. These structural properties may be more critical for achieving brain-like representations than the specific objectives of the training tasks themselves, suggesting that future models should prioritize biological architectural constraints to improve their fidelity as digital twins of the visual cortex.
papers.authors: Binxu Wang, Carlos R. Ponce

papers.title: Functional segregation of inputs in artificial neural networks for vision
papers.abstract: Biological and artificial intelligence systems both utilize signed inputs, yet the role of inhibitory signals in high-level visual representations like the inferotemporal (IT) cortex is poorly understood. This study investigated how ImageNet-trained artificial neural networks (ANNs) and macaque IT neurons segregate learned representations into positive and negative weights. By employing gradient-based feature visualization and ablation of weight polarities, we found that ReLU-based ANNs segregate object and foreground information into positive weights, while background and contextual information are primarily encoded in negative weights. This segregation was found to be dependent on signal rectification, as Tanh-based networks failed to maintain this distinction. Similar results obtained when modeling primate neuronal responses suggest that signal rectification and inhibitory mechanisms are critical for shaping feature selectivity in the primate ventral stream.
papers.authors: Giordano Ramos-Traslosheros, Carlos R. Ponce

papers.title: A concentration of visual cortex-like neurons in prefrontal cortex
papers.abstract: While visual recognition is primarily attributed to the ventral stream, recent evidence suggests that the ventrolateral prefrontal cortex (vlPFC) plays a significant role in visual processing. This study investigated whether vlPFC neurons possess sensory properties comparable to the visual cortex, such as receptive fields, image selectivity, and the ability to guide the synthesis of highly activating stimuli through generative networks. By recording from vlPFC sites in monkeys, we identified a subpopulation of neurons that exhibit stable visual encoding of world statistics. These neurons appear to be anatomically clustered, consistent with functional organization identified via fMRI. The findings suggest that stable visual representations in the vlPFC may provide the necessary foundation for the integration of sensory and cognitive processes across the brain.
papers.authors: Olivia Rose, Carlos R. Ponce

papers.title: Neural Dynamics of Object Manifold Alignment in the Ventral Stream
papers.abstract: Primate ventral stream neurons respond to an immense landscape of natural images, yet the principles governing their alignment with generative image manifolds are unclear. This study used a closed-loop evolutionary algorithm to optimize stimuli from two generative networks: DeePSim, which parameterizes local image patterns, and BigGAN, which emphasizes object identity and configurational nuisance variables. We recorded from multi-electrode arrays in V1, V4, and posterior IT (PIT) of macaque monkeys. While V1 and V4 neurons showed stronger alignment with the local pattern-based DeePSim manifold, PIT neurons demonstrated comparable alignment to both textural and object-centric manifolds. Crucially, object-like responses in PIT emerged later than texture-driven responses, suggesting that global configurational selectivity requires additional processing. These results indicate that the primate visual system aligns to a representational space that current artificial models do not fully capture.
papers.authors: Binxu Wang, Carlos R. Ponce

0105.name: Carolina Diaz-Piedra
0105.department: Department of Methodology of Behavioral Sciences
0105.bio: Carolina Diaz-Piedra is an Associate Professor at the University of Granada and co-director of the Neuroergonomics and Operator Performance Lab. Diaz-Piedra’s research examines the intersection of sleep health, cognitive load, and human performance in settings such as aviation, surgery, and military operations. They employ neurophysiological indices—including EEG power spectrum analysis, gaze entropy, and thermal imaging—to quantify mental workload and fatigue in operators. This work focuses on developing behavioral interventions and monitoring tools to address safety and efficiency in complex human-machine systems.
0105.research_direction: Dr. Diaz-Piedra's recent work explores applied visual cognition and human factors, investigating how operators process information and maintain alertness in complex, high-stakes environments. They have recently been using driving simulators and oculomotor tracking to examine how visual guidance interventions, such as photoluminescent road markings, influence drivers' visual search strategies and gaze entropy during low-visibility navigation. In parallel, their research evaluates cognitive fatigue and physiological arousal in extreme operational settings by longitudinally monitoring biomarkers like saccadic peak velocity and intraocular pressure among military crews working demanding rotating shifts. Broadening their focus to the future of transportation, they are also utilizing qualitative methods to investigate how engineers and policymakers prioritize practical ethical, legal, and socio-political values during the design and deployment of automated vehicles.

papers.title: The influence of photoluminescent road markings on driver's stationary gaze entropy: a driving simulation study
papers.abstract: This investigation utilized a semi-dynamic driving simulator to evaluate how photoluminescent road markings (PRMs) affect visual search strategies and situational awareness during nighttime curve navigation. The study assessed stationary gaze entropy (SGE) across six rural highway scenarios, manipulating PRM color (green vs. red) and marking width. High-fidelity oculomotor tracking revealed that green PRMs significantly reduced gaze entropy compared to unlit white retroreflective markings, indicating more deterministic and less random visual scanning patterns. Drivers also maintained greater lateral distances from the road edge when curves were delineated with green smart markings. These findings suggest that PRMs enhance driver guidance by reducing visual uncertainty and exploration complexity, aligning with the principles of self-explaining road design to prevent roadway departure events in low-visibility conditions.
papers.authors: Leandro L. Di Stasi, Francesco Angioi, Juan de Oña, Rocío de Oña, Carolina Diaz-Piedra

papers.title: Monitoring arousal levels among a warship crew: shift- and time of day-variations of saccadic velocity
papers.abstract: This study evaluated the physiological arousal and cognitive state of a warship crew operating under a demanding rotating shift schedule over a ten-day period. Using saccadic peak velocity (SV) as an objective biomarker of neural activation, researchers monitored crewmembers before and after morning, evening, and night shifts. Additional metrics included intraocular pressure (IOP), psychomotor vigilance test (PVT) performance, and subjective workload ratings. Results demonstrated that SV and IOP significantly decreased following all shifts, with the most pronounced reductions occurring during the night shift, corresponding to the lowest levels of objective alertness and the highest fatigue. The study confirms SV as a sensitive and viable longitudinal metric for real-time monitoring of operator status in high-stakes military maritime environments, where sleep restriction and circadian disruption pose critical risks to operational safety.
papers.authors: Leandro L. Di Stasi, Jesús Vera, Beatriz Redondo, Ignacio Grueiro Méndez, Jaime J. Mas Esquerdo, Eduardo A. Gómez Quijano, Carolina Díaz-Piedra

papers.title: Ethical and legal challenges of automated driving: The prioritization of socio-political values
papers.abstract: This paper reports a qualitative, stakeholder-based investigation into how ethical and legal trade-offs in automated-vehicle design and deployment are actually prioritized by the people who must implement them, moving away from the trolley-problem framing that dominates the automated-driving ethics literature. Through workshops, semi-structured interviews, and focus groups with a diverse set of experts and stakeholders (engineers, policymakers, legal scholars), the authors elicited which socio-political values (e.g., safety, privacy, liability, equitable access, transparency) are weighted most heavily in everyday design and regulatory decisions rather than in rare extreme-harm scenarios. The results indicate that day-to-day ethical and legal concerns are dominated by mundane trade-offs—such as data governance, accountability attribution, and infrastructure equity—rather than by the moral-dilemma scenarios emphasized in prior theoretical work. The authors argue that automated-driving policy frameworks should be built around this empirically observed prioritization of socio-political values rather than around idealized dilemma cases.
papers.authors: Carolina Diaz-Piedra, Belén Liedo, Miguel Núñez de Prado-Gordillo, M. Jesús Caurcel, Leandro L. Di Stasi

0106.name: Caroline Blais
0106.department: Département de psychoéducation et de psychologie
0106.lab_name: Laboratoire de perception visuelle et sociale (LPVS)
0106.bio: Caroline Blais is a Professor at the Université du Québec en Outaouais and holds the Canada Research Chair in Cognitive and Social Vision. Blais’s research investigates how sociocultural environments modulate visual processes, focusing on face recognition and the decoding of social signals such as pain and emotion. Using psychophysical methods including the Bubbles and Reverse Correlation techniques, Blais explores cultural variability in visual strategies to identify the mechanisms underlying human social perception.
0106.research_direction: Dr. Blais has recently been investigating how humans perceive and process emotional facial expressions, focusing on how visual perception intersects with individual psychological differences. Their recent work explores the perceptual mechanisms of pain assessment by using reverse correlation psychophysical paradigms to visualize observers' internal templates of pain expressions and assess how these expectations overlap with other negative affective states. Additionally, they are investigating how a parent's own psychosocial history, such as clinical depression or childhood maltreatment, influences their behavioral and physiological processing of children's emotional signals. To understand these intergenerational effects, they combine facial decoding tasks with measures of autonomic reactivity and spontaneous facial mimicry, seeking to uncover how early trauma alters the sensorimotor and visual processing of socially relevant cues.

papers.title: Childhood maltreatment influences parental mimicry of children's emotional facial expressions
papers.abstract: This research explored the long-term impact of early developmental trauma on the sensorimotor resonance mechanisms of parents. Spontaneous facial mimicry was quantified in 57 parents utilizing FaceReader-automated electromyo-graphic proxies while they performed a children's facial emotion recognition task. Path analysis of the Childhood Trauma Questionnaire (CTQ) data demonstrated that distinct forms of maltreatment exert heterogeneous effects on mimicry: a history of physical abuse was associated with an augmentation of anger expressions, whereas physical neglect correlated with diminished anger but heightened disgust responses. Furthermore, emotional and sexual abuse predicted attenuated mimicry of sadness. These findings suggest that childhood maltreatment induces a recalibration of the automatic mirroring systems essential for parental sensitivity and intergenerational social bonding.
papers.authors: Annie Bérubé, Rachel Pétrin, Maélie Boudreault, Gabrielle Marcotte-Beaumier, Caroline Blais

papers.title: Is It Pain, Anger, Disgust, or Sadness? Individual Differences in Expectations of Pain Facial Expressions
papers.abstract: This study utilized a reverse correlation psychophysical paradigm to characterize the mental representations (expectations) of pain facial expressions and assess their perceptual distinctiveness. By quantifying the overlap between observers' internal pain templates and the six basic emotions, the authors found that expectations for pain frequently integrate facial features characteristic of anger, disgust, and sadness. K-means clustering analysis of ratings from an independent group of observers identified three distinct participant profiles defined by heterogeneous internal expectations. These results indicate that individual variability in the visual content of internal representations modulates the systematic confusion between pain and other negative affective states, highlighting a perceptual basis for clinical inaccuracies in pain assessment.
papers.authors: Arianne Richer, Francis Gingras, Marie-Pier Plouffe-Demers, Daniel Fiset, Caroline Blais

papers.title: Parental depression moderates the relationship between childhood maltreatment and the recognition of children expressions of emotions
papers.abstract: Using morphed facial stimuli from the CAFE database, this study investigated the interaction between parental depression and childhood maltreatment history on the accuracy of decoding pediatric emotional signals. Analysis of 52 parents revealed that depressive symptoms, measured via the BSI-18, significantly moderate the impact of early adversity on emotion recognition. Specifically, among parents with no history of childhood maltreatment, elevated depressive symptoms were associated with a significant reduction in recognition accuracy, particularly for sadness. Conversely, parents with severe maltreatment histories exhibited relatively consistent recognition performance across varying levels of depression. These results suggest that the cognitive and perceptual deficits typically associated with MDD are modulated by the presence of early-life trauma, necessitating tailored interventions for specific parental profiles.
papers.authors: Annie Bérubé, Rachel Pétrin, Caroline Blais

papers.title: Maternal childhood emotional abuse increases cardiovascular responses to children's emotional facial expressions
papers.abstract: This investigation quantified the autonomic reactivity of 104 mothers to children's facial expressions by analyzing heart rate variability (HRV) as a proxy for parasympathetic and sympathetic balance. While the sample exhibited two distinct cardiovascular profiles (HRV increases vs. decreases), the results indicated that a higher severity of reported childhood emotional abuse (CEA) specifically predicted a pattern of cardiovascular hyperreactivity when perceiving emotional cues in children. This hyperarousal response suggests that early emotional trauma may sensitize maternal physiological systems to child-rearing-relevant visual stimuli. Such maladaptive cardiovascular responses could potentially interfere with the homeostatic regulation required for adequate parental responsiveness, contributing to the cycle of intergenerational maltreatment.
papers.authors: Rachel Pétrin, Annie Bérubé, Émilie St-Pierre, Caroline Blais

papers.title: The Relationship Between the Ability to Infer Another's Pain and the Expectations Regarding the Appearance of Pain Facial Expressions: Investigation of the Role of Visual Perception
papers.abstract: This research explored the perceptual mechanisms underlying individual differences in pain inference through the visualization of internal templates. Utilizing a data-driven reverse correlation method on 142 participants, the study estimated the visual quality and featural specificity of observers' mental representations of pain. The findings revealed that both the sensitivity to subtle pain variations and the direction of estimation biases are significantly predicted by the visual parameters of these internal expectations. These visual contributions were found to be independent of traditional psychosocial predictors such as empathy and personality traits. The results provide evidence that inaccuracies in social pain assessment are partially attributable to suboptimal visual representations, offering a novel target for improving clinical pain evaluation reliability.
papers.authors: Alexandra Lévesque-Lacasse, Marie-Claude Desjardins, Daniel Fiset, Isabelle Charbonneau, Stéphanie Cormier, Caroline Blais

0107.name: Caroline E. Robertson
0107.department: Department of Psychological and Brain Sciences
0107.bio: Robertson is a cognitive neuroscientist who investigates the computational and neural mechanisms of visual perception, spatial memory, and neurodiversity. Their research identifies atypical GABAergic signaling and altered binocular rivalry dynamics as biomarkers of visual processing in autism. Robertson’s methodology integrates high-field fMRI, magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS), and eye-tracking with naturalistic experiments conducted in virtual reality. Their current research focuses on the interface between the visual and memory systems, exploring how the brain leverages prior knowledge and mnemonic representations to construct subjective visual experiences.
0107.research_direction: Dr. Robertson's recent work explores the functional and anatomical intersection of scene perception and spatial memory systems in the human brain. Using high-resolution fMRI and population receptive field mapping, they have recently been investigating the role of retinotopic coding in organizing the push-pull dynamics between externally oriented visual attention networks and internally oriented memory hubs, including the default mode network and the hippocampus. Their research maps the precise functional topography of these pathways to examine how adjacent scene perception and place memory areas manage the exchange between immediate sensory input and top-down mnemonic recall. Additionally, they are employing immersive virtual reality to study active vision, specifically questioning how long-term spatial memories of panoramic environments generate proactive predictions to guide perceptual processing across naturalistic head movements.

papers.title: Relating Scene Memory and Perception Activity to Functional Properties, Networks, and Landmarks of Posterior Cerebral Cortex—A Probabilistic Atlas
papers.abstract: This study characterizes the functional neuroanatomy of the human scene-processing network by evaluating the spatial distribution of place memory areas (PMAs) and scene perception areas (SPAs) across three independent fMRI datasets (n=44). Results reveal a highly reproducible anterior displacement of PMAs relative to SPAs on the lateral, ventral, and medial surfaces of the posterior cerebral cortex. Functionally, PMAs are situated at a transitional zone at the boundary between the externally oriented dorsal attention network and the internally oriented default mode network, serving as inflection points between unimodal sensory and transmodal apical regions. While SPAs significantly overlap with retinotopic visual maps, PMAs are consistently located anterior to mapped visual cortex. This research provides a validated probabilistic atlas of these regions, establishing an organizational framework where specialized mnemonic and perceptual areas are adjacently positioned to support spatial navigation.
papers.authors: Adam Steel, Deepasri Prasad, Brenda D. Garcia, Caroline E. Robertson

papers.title: Memory-based predictions prime perceptual judgments across head turns in immersive, real-world scenes
papers.abstract: This investigation examines whether long-term memory representations of panoramic environments facilitate perceptual processing during active vision. Utilizing head-mounted virtual reality (VR) and a spatial priming paradigm across four experiments (n=101), we demonstrate that reaction times for perceptual judgments are significantly reduced when observers are primed with a studied scene view that predicts the upcoming target's spatiotopic position. This priming effect is contingent on environment familiarity, occurs specifically in the direction of planned head turns, and exclusively benefits targets presented in their anticipated spatial locations. These findings suggest that the human brain leverages long-term memory of panoramic spaces to generate proactive predictions that bridge discrete views, thereby supporting efficient interaction and a seamless visual experience during large-scale motor actions.
papers.authors: Anna Mynick, Adam Steel, Adithi Jayaraman, Thomas L. Botch, Allie Burrows, Caroline E. Robertson

papers.title: Retinotopic coding organizes the interaction between internally and externally oriented brain networks
papers.abstract: The functional relationship between the internally oriented default network (DN) and externally oriented dorsal attention networks (dATNs) is traditionally viewed as globally antagonistic. This study utilizes high-resolution 7T fMRI and individualized population receptive field (pRF) mapping to show that this opponent dynamic is structured by an underlying retinotopic code. While spontaneous activity between the DN and dATN appears uncorrelated at the network level, voxel-wise functional coupling is significantly modulated by shared visual field preferences. Voxels across these networks with similar pRF coordinates exhibit stronger anti-correlation compared to those with divergent preferences. This retinotopically grounded architecture persists across DN subnetworks and integrates with domain-specific functional preferences, revealing that a shared spatial coordinate system coordinates the interaction between large-scale networks to balance internal cognition and external perception.
papers.authors: Adam Steel, Peter A. Angeli, Edward H. Silson, Caroline E. Robertson

papers.title: Positive and Negative Retinotopic Codes in the Human Hippocampus
papers.abstract: As a central hub for sensory-mnemonic integration, the hippocampus is theorized to occupy the apex of the visual processing hierarchy. Using precision 7T fMRI and voxel-wise population receptive field (pRF) mapping, we identify a bivalent retinotopic code within the human hippocampus consisting of both positive (activation-based) and negative (suppression-based) visual field tuning. The proportion of negative pRFs increases along the perceptual-mnemonic hierarchy, mirroring organizational principles observed in the cortical default network. Furthermore, hippocampal regions with opposite pRF valences demonstrate intrinsic push-pull dynamics characterized by anti-correlated activity. These findings provide evidence that retinotopic grounding is a fundamental property of hippocampal organization, facilitating the integration of discrete visual inputs with integrated mnemonic representations.
papers.authors: Peter A. Angeli, Adam Steel, Edward H. Silson, Caroline E. Robertson

papers.title: A retinotopic code structures the interaction between perception and memory systems
papers.abstract: High-level visual memory regions have traditionally been assumed to represent information using abstract, amodal neural codes. This study uses functional MRI to demonstrate that category-selective place memory areas (PMAs) at the cortical apex exhibit robust negative (inverted) retinotopic tuning. This negative tuning is functionally coupled with the standard positive retinotopic coding found in adjacent scene perception areas (SPAs), establishing a bivalent coordination mechanism. During perception, sensory drive activates SPAs while simultaneously suppressing PMAs in a spatially selective manner; this relationship reverses during top-down mnemonic recall. These results show that a shared retinotopic coordinate system scaffolds the antagonistic interaction between perceptual and mnemonic neural systems, providing a fundamental organizing principle for the dynamic exchange of information across the cortical hierarchy.
papers.authors: Adam Steel, Edward H. Silson, Brenda D. Garcia, Caroline E. Robertson

0108.name: Catherine L. Reed
0108.bio: Catherine L. Reed is a cognitive neuroscientist whose research investigates the multisensory integration of bodily, visual, and tactile information to understand how the motor system modulates perception and attention. Reed’s work focuses on the embodied attention framework, employing behavioral psychophysics and high-density electroencephalography (EEG) to examine how peripersonal space and body posture prioritize visual processing. They utilize event-related potentials (ERPs) and oscillatory analysis to characterize the neural mechanisms of action observation, social cognition, and the influence of aging on cognitive control. Current research directions for Reed involve dissociating the perceptual and motor correlates of mu-alpha and beta rhythms during emotional action simulation.
0108.research_direction: Dr. Reed’s recent work explores the intersection of cognitive electrophysiology, individual differences, and social perception. Using EEG and event-related potentials (ERPs) such as the mismatch negativity and error-related negativity, they investigate how traits like procrastination, anxiety, and impulsivity alter early sensory prediction errors and performance monitoring. They have also recently been investigating cognitive aging, examining whether working memory capacity accounts for age-related shifts in neural indices of attention and semantic processing. Finally, their research examines the perception of social cues, ranging from methodological studies on how aperiodic brain activity impacts the measurement of sensorimotor mu suppression during action observation, to behavioral experiments testing how observers hierarchically integrate visual signals from facial expressions and body posture to judge a target's emotion, threat, and status.

papers.title: Procrastination and anxiety aspects of self-control predict individual differences in the mismatch negativity (MMN)
papers.abstract: This study investigated the relationship between self-report measures of self-control and the mismatch negativity (MMN), an event-related potential (ERP) reflecting pre-attentive sensory memory and prediction error. Utilizing a large cohort (N = 246) and a passive auditory oddball paradigm, researchers evaluated six self-control dimensions: effortful control, perfectionism, impulsiveness, procrastination, perceived stress, and anxiety. Results from multiple regression analyses indicated that procrastination and trait anxiety were significant independent predictors of MMN amplitude, with higher levels of these traits associating with larger (more negative) MMNs. These findings suggest that self-control failures may be rooted in an innate temperamental hyper-reactivity to environmental change, where larger prediction errors signal a failure of top-down mechanisms to modulate reactive sensory processing.
papers.authors: Chandlyr M. Denaro, Alan A. Hartley, Jane W. Couperus, Cindy M. Bukach, Catherine L. Reed

papers.title: The cognitive instability aspect of impulsivity predicts the ERN: An ERP study
papers.abstract: This research assessed whether multidimensional facets of impulsivity, as measured by the Barratt Impulsiveness Scale (BIS-11), correlate with the error-related negativity (ERN), a medial prefrontal signal of performance monitoring. Participants performed a flanker task while high-density EEG was recorded. Regression analyses revealed that specifically the 'cognitive instability' subscale—reflecting subjective experiences of rapid or uncontrolled thoughts—predicted significantly reduced ERN amplitudes. Interestingly, total BIS-11 scores and other subscales like motor impulsiveness were not predictive of the ERN. The results indicate that cognitive instability may uniquely influence the motivational salience of errors or the neural efficiency of the error-monitoring system, potentially contributing to the behavioral dysregulation characteristic of impulsive phenotypes.
papers.authors: Folly Folivi, Chandlyr M. Denaro, Alan A. Hartley, Cindy M. Bukach, Jane W. Couperus, Catherine L. Reed

papers.title: Complex span measures of working memory do not mediate the effects of age on the P3 and N400 ERPs
papers.abstract: This study examined the degree to which age-related differences in working memory (WM) capacity, measured through operation, reading, and symmetry complex span tasks, account for variance in the P3 (visual oddball) and N400 (word-pair judgment) ERP components. Comparing younger adults (18–23 years) and older adults (69–89 years), the researchers observed significant age-related declines in complex span performance alongside reduced ERP amplitudes and delayed latencies. Crucially, mediation and regression analyses demonstrated that WM span scores did not significantly correlate with P3 or N400 metrics in either group, nor did they mediate age-associated ERP changes. These results suggest that the attentional control processes indexed by the P3 and N400 reflect cognitive resources distinct from the storage-plus-processing constraints captured by complex span tasks.
papers.authors: Jasmin Joshi, Chandlyr M. Denaro, Alan A. Hartley, Catherine L. Reed

papers.title: Aperiodic activity masks sensorimotor mu suppression during human action observation
papers.abstract: Investigating the neural substrates of social perception, this study utilized 128-channel EEG (N = 109) to evaluate the impact of aperiodic (1/f) spectral activity on the measurement of sensorimotor mu rhythm (8–14 Hz) suppression during action execution (AE) and action observation (AO). Standard Fourier analysis revealed robust mu suppression for AE but failed to reach significance for AO, suggesting that aperiodic shifts may confound oscillatory power estimates. Following the application of spectral parameterization to isolate periodic from aperiodic components, significant mu suppression was successfully recovered for AO over central electrodes.
