These results indicate that aperiodic activity contributes to the observed variability in mirror neuron system indices and emphasize the necessity of accounting for non-oscillatory signal components in cognitive electrophysiology.
papers.authors: Alison M. Harris, Chandlyr M. Denaro, Catherine L. Reed

papers.title: Relative contributions of the face and body to social judgements: emotion, threat and status
papers.abstract: This study explored the hierarchical integration of nonverbal signals across facial expressions (anger/fear), body posture (expanded/contracted), and sagittal lean (forward/backward) during social judgments of emotion, threat, and status. Across two experiments, facial anger was found to be the dominant predictor for all judgment types, while expanded body posture and forward lean specifically modulated threat and status perceptions. A critical manipulation involving facial obscuration revealed a significant increase in the weighting of body-related channels for all social assessments. The findings demonstrate that while facial cues provide primary diagnostic information, body channels contribute differentially based on the nature of the social judgment and assume compensatory importance when facial information is unavailable.
papers.authors: Brittany R. Vincente, Daniel N. McIntosh, Catherine L. Reed

0109.name: Cathleen M. Moore
0109.department: Department of Psychological and Brain Sciences
0109.bio: Cathleen M. Moore is a Professor and Starch Faculty Fellow at the University of Iowa and directs the Iowa Attention and Perception Lab. Moore’s research investigates mid-level visual processes, focusing on how the brain transforms retinal images into representations of objects and surfaces through mechanisms like figure-ground assignment and object correspondence. Utilizing psychophysical methodologies such as eye-tracking, virtual reality, and response-time analysis, Moore explores the interface between perception, attention, and cognitive control. Their current projects also extend to applied domains, examining attentional failures in environments such as lifeguarding and medical image interpretation.
0109.research_direction: Dr. Moore's recent work explores how the visual system constructs spatial and object representations to guide perception, oculomotor control, and motor action. Specifically, they have recently been investigating the mechanisms of saccadic targeting, asking whether the eyes orient toward spatially extended or partially occluded objects based on low-level 2D retinal boundaries, top-down goals, or mid-level computations like amodal surface completion. Their research also probes the limits of these mid-level organizational processes across the visual field, examining whether mechanisms like grouping and surface completion alleviate visual crowding or operate effectively in peripheral vision. Additionally, they are investigating how spatial representations interface with motor systems, utilizing immersive virtual reality to determine how 3D reachability and action affordances influence stimulus-response compatibility.

papers.title: Simon says “stay in touch”: Reachability moderates the effect of irrelevant spatial congruence
papers.abstract: The Simon effect demonstrates that manual reaction times and decision accuracy are optimized when the spatial location of a stimulus corresponds to the responding effector, even when spatial position is completely irrelevant to the non-spatial judgment task. To determine whether the spatial representation driving this stimulus-response compatibility reflects the potential for motor interaction within a 3D environment, this study evaluated the Simon effect across reachable and unreachable distances in immersive virtual reality. By systematically matching retinal image size and visual viewing angles across participant groups, visual confounding factors were eliminated. Results demonstrated that the magnitude of the Simon effect was substantially larger for stimuli presented at reachable distances than at unreachable distances, with the congruency effect on reaction time decreasing by approximately two-thirds in extrapersonal space. Because this reachability moderation persisted across equivalent image-size and viewing-angle conditions, the findings indicate that task-irrelevant spatial coding is computed over representations sensitive to action affordances and potential motor interaction rather than purely two-dimensional retinotopic coordinates.
papers.authors: Michael L. Paavola, J. Toby Mordkoff, Cathleen M. Moore

papers.title: Saccades to spatially extended objects: The roles of observer goals and part-structure cues in determining within-object landing position
papers.abstract: Saccadic targeting of spatially extended objects must translate complex object structures into discrete two-dimensional oculomotor vectors. While previous work has identified a default landing bias toward an object's center of area (COA), task-relevant features often reside away from the centroid and frequently align with discrete structural sub-parts. In Experiment 1, participants performed a multi-object visual search task requiring fine perceptual discriminations on spatially extended stimuli. Within-object saccade endpoints were systematically modulated by both strategic knowledge of target-discriminator positions and bottom-up part-structure segmentation defined by contour concavities. In Experiment 2, an unconstrained reactive orienting task to abruptly onset isolated objects eliminated the strategic goal-directed shift but preserved the part-segmentation bias, demonstrating that the structural bias is driven principally by physical stimulus geometry. Critically, these influences interacted additively with the baseline COA bias, producing maximal strategic targeting when the task-relevant zone aligned with a distinct structural part boundary. The results indicate that within-object saccadic landing sites are determined by the joint interplay of top-down task goals, part-level perceptual segmentation, and default center-of-area computations.
papers.authors: Andrew Hollingworth, Cathleen M. Moore

papers.title: Perceptual organization is limited in peripheral vision: Evidence from configural superiority
papers.abstract: Perceptual organization encompasses the mid-level visual operations that abstract three-dimensional scene geometry, depth stratification, and material properties from retinal inputs, serving as the necessary precursor to object perception. While extensively documented at central fixation, the degree to which these processes operate across the visual periphery remains uncertain. Utilizing the diagnostic configural superiority effect (CSE)—quantified via balanced integration scores (BIS)—this study investigated four distinct grouping mechanisms: amodal surface completion, 3D shape from 2D contour geometry, photometric transparency/surface scission, and shape from closure. Stimuli were cortical-magnification scaled to control for peripheral acuity loss. Centrally presented stimuli yielded robust CSEs across all four grouping categories, confirming intact mid-level perceptual parsing. Conversely, presenting identical size-scaled configurations in the periphery produced complete abolishment of CSE advantages; instead, performance deteriorated in composite arrays due to typical visual crowding. These findings provide empirical support for the hypothesis that peripheral vision fails to engage mid-level perceptual organization, consistent with central-peripheral dichotomy frameworks positing that peripheral representations are unorganized and texture-like rather than object-based.
papers.authors: Cathleen M. Moore, Qingzi Zheng, Yelda Semizer

papers.title: Saccades to partially occluded objects: Perceptual completion mediates oculomotor control
papers.abstract: Visual oculomotor orienting directs the fovea toward items of interest across cluttered visual scenes, but whether the saccadic system targets locations derived purely from low-level retinotopic image boundaries (image-based hypothesis) or from mid-level surfaces representing 3D spatial layout (object-based hypothesis) is an open question. Saccadic landing distributions were recorded while observers executed naturalistic visual searches across arrays containing complete circles, partially occluded circles, or unoccluded partial circles matched for 2D image contours. In Experiment 1, initial saccades targeting partially occluded objects systematically landed toward the center of area of the perceptually completed object rather than the centroid of the visible 2D image fragments. Experiment 2 demonstrated that this completion-dependent oculomotor bias persisted even when task constraints rendered landing on the visible fragment strategically advantageous. Experiment 3 established that this spatial landing deviation was not produced by image-level contrast artifacts caused by the presence of occluders. These findings show that oculomotor control routines are computed over mid-level representations that incorporate amodal surface completion rather than superficial, explicit retinal image configurations.
papers.authors: Michael L. Paavola, Andrew Hollingworth, Cathleen M. Moore

papers.title: Limited midlevel mediation of visual crowding: Surface completion fails to support uncrowding
papers.abstract: Visual crowding is characterized by impaired identification of peripheral target objects when surrounded by nearby flankers. While standard pooling models account for crowding through early, local loss of image details, the phenomenon of 'uncrowding'—where adding flanking elements or lengthening flankers restores target discriminability—has been widely cited as evidence that mid-level perceptual grouping protects targets from interference. To assess whether uncrowding is mediated by mid-level surface representation or early image-level feature distributions, this study tested whether amodal surface completion can produce uncrowding when low-level image attributes are held constant. Vernier offset discrimination was assessed with flanking line arrays featuring collinear gaps, supplemented by inducing notched discs (Pacmen) positioned to induce perceptual completion of continuous flankers occluded by subjective surface bars. While physical elongation of flankers produced robust uncrowding, introducing gaps abolished the effect, and inducing amodal surface completion across those gaps failed to attenuate crowding. These findings demonstrate that surface completion cues do not alleviate crowding, suggesting that reported uncrowding phenomena reflect image-level filtering and line terminator interactions rather than mid-level object representations.
papers.authors: Cathleen M. Moore, Qingzi Zheng

0110.name: Chai-Youn Kim
0110.bio: Chai-Youn Kim is a Professor at Korea University specializing in the cognitive neuroscience of perception, with a focus on visual awareness and binocular rivalry. Kim's research employs psychophysical methods and brain imaging to investigate how the brain resolves visual ambiguity and how multisensory inputs, such as auditory and motor information, modulate perceptual selection. Kim has published research on the mechanisms of synesthesia and neuroaesthetics, exploring how factors like familiarity and cross-modal correspondences influence aesthetic preference and conscious experience. Their recent work examines the interplay between sensory modalities in bistable perception, including the impact of musical congruence and action-based feedback on visual dominance.
0110.research_direction: Dr. Kim’s recent work explores the interplay between multisensory integration, conscious awareness, and visual experience. They have recently been investigating how auditory and tactile signals interact with visual processing—even when visual targets are suppressed using paradigms like continuous flash suppression and binocular rivalry—to understand whether crossmodal binding and motion adaptation can occur pre-consciously or be guided by prior conscious experience. Beyond these fundamental sensory mechanisms, their research extends into both applied and high-level visual cognition. Specifically, they are tracking the behavioral and physiological development of cybersickness during prolonged augmented reality exposure, and examining how different types of practical or theoretical art expertise modulate aesthetic preferences for fundamental 3D shape features like curvature.

papers.title: Visuotactile object processing in binocular rivalry: The role of shape congruence, voluntary action, and spatial colocalization
papers.abstract: This study employed three-dimensional (3D) objects to investigate how visuotactile integration facilitates perceptual disambiguation during binocular rivalry. Across four experiments, the researchers manipulated shape congruence in the curvature dimension using mathematically generated 'spiky' and 'round' stimuli. The study tested the effects of voluntary action by comparing active palm exploration of 3D-printed objects with passive tactile stimulation, while spatial colocalization was manipulated through the use of video recordings as visual targets to provide bodily cues of hand-object contact. Results indicated that tactile shape congruence significantly promoted the dominance of the corresponding visual percept. This crossmodal influence was most robust when visuotactile colocalization was encouraged, suggesting that sensory integration of complex 3D features is critically modulated by spatial and motoric context during naturalistic object recognition.
papers.authors: Seyoon Song, Haeji Shin, Chai-Youn Kim

papers.title: Type of art expertise matters: Practical experts show a greater curvature preference for 3D shapes than theoretical experts
papers.abstract: This research investigated whether aesthetic preference for curvature in 3D shapes is modulated by different types of art expertise. The study compared three groups: practical experts (artists), theoretical experts (art historians and critics), and non-experts. Participants evaluated 3D-rendered shapes that varied parametrically in curvature. While non-experts generally preferred curved forms over angular ones, this preference was significantly more pronounced in the practical expert group than in the theoretical expert group. These findings suggest that the nature of an individual's interaction with art—whether through creative physical practice or analytic theoretical study—shapes the degree of aesthetic valuation for fundamental visual properties like curvature.
papers.venue: Psychology of Aesthetics, Creativity, and the Arts
papers.authors: Jiwon Song, Chai-Youn Kim

papers.title: Cybersickness in Augmented Reality: Subjective and physiological changes with the course of prolonged exposure
papers.abstract: This study evaluated the temporal development and physiological characteristics of cybersickness induced by Augmented Reality (AR) environments. Participants were exposed to racing game videos through an AR device for 30-minute sessions across two movement speed conditions. The researchers integrated subjective data from the Simulator Sickness Questionnaire (SSQ), behavioral metrics of response time, and physiological signals including heart rate variability (ECG) and respiration patterns (RSP). The results demonstrated that cybersickness symptoms accumulated linearly with exposure duration, manifesting most clearly in subjective reports and significantly slowed behavioral responses. Eye-related symptoms were identified as the primary drivers of this accumulation, while movement speed had a negligible effect. Furthermore, individuals with previous AR exposure reported lower levels of discomfort, indicating that familiarity can mitigate AR-induced sickness.
papers.authors: Zion Park, Seyoon Song, Subin Jeon, Yuyeon Jung, Yeha Cha, Jiyoung Oh, Minsung Jin, Chai-Youn Kim

papers.title: Audiovisual interactions outside of visual awareness during motion adaptation
papers.abstract: To determine whether multisensory integration can occur in the absence of conscious visual awareness, the researchers utilized a continuous flash suppression (CFS) paradigm to render translational visual motion perceptually invisible during a period of adaptation. Concurrently, participants were presented with auditory motion that was either congruent or incongruent in velocity (direction and speed) with the suppressed visual motion. The strength of the resulting visual motion aftereffect (MAE) was used as a metric for processing potency. The results showed that congruent auditory motion significantly strengthened the MAE produced by the invisible visual motion compared to incongruent or stationary auditory conditions. These findings provide evidence that auditory signals can impact visual neural processing at early, pre-conscious stages, indicating that the human brain integrates crossmodal velocity signals even when one modality is suppressed from awareness.
papers.authors: Minsun Park, Randolph Blake, Chai-Youn Kim

papers.title: Prior conscious experience modulates the impact of audiovisual temporal correspondence on unconscious visual processing
papers.abstract: The study investigated the extent to which top-down modulation from prior conscious awareness influences the integration of multisensory signals that are currently suppressed from awareness. Observers were first exposed to conscious trials where the temporal correspondence between auditory beeps and visual flashes was explicitly manipulated. Subsequently, they performed a detection task on visual stimuli suppressed by continuous flash suppression. The researchers found that the impact of auditory temporal cues on the breakthrough of visual stimuli into awareness was significantly modulated by the preceding conscious experience of audiovisual synchrony. This suggests that the mechanisms governing unconscious multisensory binding are not purely bottom-up but are instead dynamically recalibrated by recent conscious representations of crossmodal temporal structure.
papers.authors: Hyun-Woong Kim, Minsun Park, Yune Sang Lee, Chai-Youn Kim

0111.name: Chaipat Chunharas
0111.bio: Chaipat Chunharas is a clinician-scientist whose research examines the neural mechanisms underlying visual perception and working memory, focusing on how the brain maintains sensory information during distraction. Chunharas utilizes psychophysical techniques, neuroimaging (fMRI, EEG), and computational modeling to investigate the representational geometry and topographic organization of the human visual cortex. Their work characterizes visual working memory distortions and the coexistence of sensory and mnemonic signals in early visual areas. Chunharas applies these cognitive and computational frameworks to clinical neurology to study the pathological mechanisms of neuropsychiatric and neurodegenerative conditions, such as mild cognitive impairment.
0111.research_direction: Dr. Chunharas has recently been investigating the neural mechanisms of feature-based attention, using fMRI and multivariate pattern analysis to understand how attentional templates for distinct ranges of color are dynamically instantiated in the early visual cortex. Alongside this fundamental visual neuroscience research, their recent work explores computational clinical neurology by applying unsupervised machine learning to item-level cognitive screening scores to subtype mild cognitive impairment and predict an individual's longitudinal progression to dementia. Additionally, they are examining the neurobiological markers of depression, utilizing multimodal neuroimaging such as resting-state fMRI and magnetic resonance spectroscopy to probe prefrontal-hippocampal connectivity and GABAergic signaling. Across these distinct topics, their lab integrates psychophysics, advanced neuroimaging, and data-driven computational models to characterize both healthy sensory processing and the trajectories of clinical cognitive and psychiatric decline.

papers.title: Predicting mild cognitive impairment and dementia progression using MoCA score-based subtyping and cognitive decline cascade analysis with unsupervised machine learning
papers.abstract: This research assesses the efficacy of unsupervised machine learning for the phenotypic categorization of Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI) and the prediction of its progression toward clinical dementia. Leveraging longitudinal Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) datasets, the investigators executed a cognitive decline cascade analysis to characterize discrete trajectories of neurocognitive deterioration. The study identifies specific MoCA sub-score clusters that exhibit differential risks for dementia conversion, suggesting that item-level granularity in cognitive screening tools provides superior prognostic utility compared to global aggregate scores for early risk stratification in memory clinics.
papers.authors: Dhup Bhukdee, Akarin Hiransuthikul, Sira Sriswasdi, Chaipat Chunharas

papers.title: Depression and the prefrontal-hippocampal pathway - A multimodal neuroimaging study in transgender women
papers.abstract: This investigation utilized a multimodal neuroimaging framework to explore the neurobiological markers of depression within the prefrontal-hippocampal circuitry of a Thai transgender cohort. Combining magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS) and resting-state functional MRI (fMRI), the authors quantified hippocampal gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) concentrations and prefrontal functional connectivity. Quantitative analysis revealed that higher depressive symptom severity, measured by PHQ-9, was significantly associated with attenuated hippocampal GABA levels and reduced fractional amplitude of low-frequency fluctuations (fALFF) in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC). These findings suggest that GABAergic inhibitory signaling within the hippocampal-prefrontal circuit plays a pivotal role in the pathophysiology of depression in this demographic.
papers.authors: Setthanan Jarukasemkit, Karen M Tam, Seksan Yoadsanit, Ty Easley, Hailey Modi, Lyn Stahl, Adun Kampaengtip, Thanissara Chansakul, Rena Janamnuaysook, Akarin Hiransuthikul, Chaipat Chunharas, Janine D Bijsterbosch

papers.title: Predicting dementia conversion using montreal cognitive assessment score-based mild cognitive impairment subtyping and cognitive decline cascade analysis with unsupervised machine learning
papers.abstract: This study establishes a computational pipeline using unsupervised learning algorithms to address the clinical heterogeneity of Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI). By applying cascade analysis to item-level responses of the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA), the research delineates distinct cognitive profiles and maps their respective longitudinal conversion rates to Alzheimer's disease. The findings demonstrate that data-driven subtyping based on specific cognitive domain deficits enables more precise identification of individuals at high risk for imminent cognitive decline, supporting the clinical implementation of machine learning for personalized dementia risk assessment.
papers.authors: Dhup Bhukdee, Akarin Hiransuthikul, Sira Sriswasdi, Chaipat Chunharas

papers.title: Zooming in and out: Selective attention modulates color signals in early visual cortex for narrow and broad ranges of task-relevant features
papers.abstract: This neuroimaging study examines the neural mechanisms underlying feature-based attention (FBA) when observers must select varying ranges of color values. Utilizing multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) of fMRI data, the authors investigated how attentional templates are instantiated in the human early visual cortex (EVC). The research reveals that selective attention proactively modulates neural representations of color signals, demonstrating that EVC can flexibly represent both narrow, highly-specific color values and broader ranges of task-relevant features. The results suggest that the precision of attentional templates in early sensory areas is dynamically adjusted based on behavioral demands, facilitating the prioritization of relevant sensory inputs in complex environments.
papers.authors: Mert Ozkan, Viola Störmer, Chaipat Chunharas

0112.name: Chaoxiong Ye
0112.department: Department of Psychology, Faculty of Education and Psychology
0112.bio: Chaoxiong Ye is an Academy Research Fellow and Principal Investigator at the University of Jyväskylä, where they lead research on the cognitive and neural mechanisms of visual working memory (VWM). Ye's work utilizes electroencephalography (EEG) and event-related potentials (ERP)—specifically the contralateral delay activity (CDA) component—alongside MEG and fMRI to investigate how attentional resources are allocated during VWM consolidation and maintenance. Ye examines how emotional valence, stimulus complexity, and individual differences in memory capacity influence the filtering of irrelevant information and the precision of stored representations. Their current research focus includes the spatio-temporal dynamics of memory processes and the interactions between long-term image memorability and short-term visual storage.
0112.research_direction: Dr. Ye has recently been investigating the temporal dynamics and resource limits of visual working memory, focusing specifically on how internal attention acts upon stored representations. Using a variety of behavioral retro-cue paradigms, their recent work explores the speed at which distinct features like color or orientation can be prioritized, and examines whether focusing on a specific item or dimension necessitates the active suppression of unattended information. They are also examining the spatial resolution of internal attention to determine how prioritizing a cued target impacts the maintenance of physically proximal versus distal uncued items. Additionally, Dr. Ye combines continuous recall tasks and electrophysiological markers like contralateral delay activity (CDA) to probe how stimulus encoding duration, perceptual redundancy, and stage-specific distractors dynamically modulate memory load across early and late maintenance phases.

papers.title: Early or late distractions hurt working memory differently depending on how long you look
papers.abstract: This study investigates the interplay between stimulus encoding duration and the susceptibility of visual working memory (VWM) to stage-specific interference. Utilizing a combination of continuous recall and change detection paradigms, the authors demonstrate that distractors presented during the encoding phase only significantly impair performance under brief presentation durations or high-precision task constraints. In contrast, delay-stage distractions consistently degrade memory representations regardless of the initial consolidation time. The results further reveal that while increased encoding time enhances resistance to heterogeneous distractors, homogeneous distractors (sharing categorical features with targets) exert persistent interference. These findings suggest that distinct suppressive mechanisms govern the filtering of distractors during encoding versus maintenance stages.
papers.authors: Guofang Ren, Ruyi Liu, Lijing Guo, Penglan Liu, Dan Nie, Jinru Chen, Chaoxiong Ye

papers.title: All identical objects reduce memory load at the late maintenance stage in working memory
papers.abstract: Using the contralateral delay activity (CDA) as an electrophysiological marker of visual working memory (VWM) storage, this research examines whether perceptual organization through stimulus identity reduces the consumption of memory resources. While behavioral data showed enhanced accuracy for arrays with identical orientations (all-same condition), ERP analyses revealed that CDA amplitudes remained undifferentiated across conditions during the early maintenance phase. However, a significant reduction in late-stage CDA amplitude was observed exclusively for the all-same condition compared to partial-redundancy or all-different displays. The findings indicate that the cognitive benefit of identical objects emerges during late-stage maintenance rather than early consolidation, highlighting that the reduction of VWM load through redundancy requires complete stimulus repetition and late-phase processing.
papers.authors: Lijing Guo, Hyung-Bum Park, Guofang Ren, Penglan Liu, Ruyi Liu, Dan Nie, Chaoxiong Ye

papers.title: Color first, space next, orientation last: A temporal comparison of retro-cue effects in visual working memory
papers.abstract: This study directly compares the efficacy and temporal dynamics of spatial versus feature-based (color, orientation) retro-cues in visual working memory. Through four experiments systematically varying cue-probe delays, the authors identified a processing speed hierarchy: color retro-cues elicited the most rapid and robust retro-cue benefits (RCBs), manifesting even at minimal delays (50 ms), followed by spatial cues at 200 ms. Orientation-based cues were found to be the least effective, requiring significantly longer delays (over 500 ms) and explicit task requirements for dual-feature encoding to produce measurable benefits. These results challenge models assuming uniform attentional selection across visual dimensions and suggest that feature-specific constraints dictate the speed and efficiency of internal attentional allocation.
papers.authors: Lijing Guo, Dan Nie, Penglan Liu, Lingcong Zhang, Chaoxiong Ye

papers.title: The modulatory mechanism of spatial distance on the role of internal attention in unattended working memory representations
papers.abstract: This study examines the 'attentional spatial proximity effect' in visual working memory (VWM) to determine how the selective prioritization of a cued item influences the maintenance of proximal versus distal uncued items. Employing a lateralized change detection task with retro-cues, the researchers manipulated the spatial separation between cued and uncued representations. Behavioral results demonstrated that the magnitude of memory decline for uncued items increased monotonically as a function of their spatial distance from the cued item. This graded performance suggests that internal attention operates via a spatially-contiguous gradient, where representations physically closer to the focus of attention are partially insulated from the costs typically associated with selective filtering or removal in VWM.
papers.authors: Qiang Liu, Lijing Guo, Jie Wang, Dan Nie, Chaoxiong Ye

papers.title: Dimension-based retro-cue benefit in working memory does not require unfocused dimension removal
papers.abstract: The authors investigated whether the dimension-based retro-cue benefit (RCB) in visual working memory (VWM) is contingent upon the removal of task-irrelevant feature dimensions. Using a double-cue paradigm with colored, oriented bars, the study tested if an initially uncued dimension (e.g., color) could be re-accessed following a second, valid retro-cue. The results showed that memory performance for the initially unfocused dimension was not only maintained but could be significantly enhanced by the subsequent cue. This demonstrates that dimension-based RCB does not require the active expulsion of irrelevant features from VWM; instead, unfocused dimensions are retained in a passive state and remain available for re-prioritization through internal attention shifts.
papers.authors: Ruyi Liu, Lijing Guo, Xiaoshu Lin, Dan Nie, Piia Astikainen, Chaoxiong Ye

0113.name: Charles E. Connor
0113.bio: Charles E. Connor is a Professor of Neuroscience and the Director of the Zanvyl Krieger Mind/Brain Institute at Johns Hopkins University. Connor’s research focuses on the neural algorithms that transform two-dimensional retinal images into three-dimensional representations of objects and environments. Through the study of population coding in the ventral visual pathway, specifically areas V4 and the inferotemporal cortex, their laboratory has identified how the brain encodes complex geometric configurations and structural relationships. Connor’s current work explores the integration of biological vision principles into deep neural networks and the development of neural coding strategies for visual prosthetics.
0113.research_direction: Dr. Connor has recently been investigating how the primate ventral visual stream transforms basic retinal inputs into rich representations of 2D planar and 3D volumetric shape. Using extracellular recordings in macaque inferotemporal (IT) cortex, their recent work explores the coding strategies underlying learned object recognition, specifically testing whether extensive visual training drives neurons to encode holistic global objects or multi-part configurations that support robust perception during partial occlusion. Additionally, they are studying the neural mechanisms of spatial constancy by recording IT responses during whole-body tilts to determine how visual, vestibular, and somatosensory cues are integrated to anchor object representations in an allocentric, gravity-based reference frame rather than a retinotopic one. Broadly, their research seeks to map the overarching computational objectives of the ventral pathway, examining how intermediate and high-level visual areas achieve necessary data compression, explicit population coding, and representational invariance across physical transformations.

papers.title: How Shape Perception Works, in Two Dimensions and Three Dimensions
papers.abstract: A synthesis of empirical discoveries across the primate ventral visual processing hierarchy resolves how retinal afferents are transformed into rich structural representations underlying 2D planar and 3D volumetric shape perception. This review organizes ventral pathway computations around three essential computational objectives: extreme data compression to facilitate transmission through limited axonal bottlenecks and long-term consolidation in memory networks, explicit population coding to ensure high-level geometric features are linearly decodable by downstream cognitive and motor control centers, and representational invariance to preserve perceptual stability across substantial transformations in retinal perspective, illumination, and scale. We outline how the progressive cascade of receptive field properties across intermediate and late ventral cortex—spanning areas V1, V2, V4, and inferotemporal (IT) cortex—mechanistically satisfies these tripartite constraints, establishing a unified neural foundation for how primates compute continuous, high-fidelity structural shape.
papers.authors: Kristina J. Nielsen, Charles E. Connor

papers.title: An inferotemporal coding strategy robust to partial object occlusion
papers.abstract: Ventral stream visual coding is marked by hierarchical compression and increasing response sparseness, transitioning from local contour orientations in primary visual cortex (V1) to localized 2D/3D shape primitives in V4, and ultimately converging on complex multipart configurations in anterior inferotemporal cortex (AIT). Whether extensive visual familiarity drives this hierarchical trajectory to its logical extreme—yielding units dedicated exclusively to unique global objects—remains unresolved. To test this hypothesis, rhesus macaques were trained over several weeks on a delayed match-to-sample paradigm to categorize eight stylized, letter-like geometric stimuli, reaching >80% discrimination accuracy. Extracellular recordings in AIT revealed pronounced learning-induced enhancement in tuning for constituent multipart configurations characteristic of the trained symbols. Crucially, however, single units did not exhibit exclusive selectivity for intact, unique letters; instead, firing rates generalized robustly to novel, unlearned geometric constructs possessing the same sub-configurations. Although sub-maximal in terms of strict population sparseness, this multi-fragment configuration code provides an optimal trade-off for natural vision, offering intrinsic fault-tolerance against partial occlusion by allowing distinct subsets of diagnostic features to independently trigger robust whole-object classification.
papers.authors: Andrew Cheng, Sach Sokol, Charles E Connor

papers.title: Object representation in a gravitational reference frame
papers.abstract: During lateral head roll, ocular counter-rolling compensates for less than 20% of rotational displacement, exposing the retina to image rotations spanning up to 180°, despite an enduring perceptual stability of environmental objects. Investigating the neurophysiological mechanisms mediating this rotational invariance, single-unit recordings were conducted in macaque anterior inferotemporal (IT) cortex while animals performed fixation during ±25° lateral whole-body tilts, generating an approximately 40° shift in retinal orientation. Among neurons exhibiting defined 3D object orientation preferences, 63% preserved their tuning within an allocentric, gravity-referenced coordinate system rather than an egocentric retinotopic frame. Experiments modulating multisensory and contextual inputs demonstrated that this gravitational alignment relies jointly on visual scene context (such as ground-plane orientation) as well as vestibular and somatosensory signals. Constructing an internal gravitational reference frame at the terminal stage of the ventral processing stream provides not only perceptual compensation for viewer posture but also the essential mechanical coordinate space required for intuitive physical reasoning regarding equilibrium, stability, and dynamics in terrestrial environments.
papers.authors: Alexandriya M X Emonds, Ramanujan Srinath, Kristina J Nielsen, Charles E Connor

0114.name: Chaz Firestone
0114.department: Department of Psychological and Brain Sciences
0114.bio: Chaz Firestone is an Associate Professor at Johns Hopkins University and directs the Perception & Mind Laboratory. Their research investigates the interface between visual perception and higher-level cognition, focusing on the functional architecture of the mind and the degree to which what is seen is influenced by what is known. Firestone’s work evaluates the evidence for top-down effects of cognition on perception and includes the study of topics such as the perception of absences, physical intuitions, and the representation of objects and events. They employ a multi-methodological approach involving psychophysics, computational modeling, and philosophical analysis to characterize the mechanisms of human vision.
0114.research_direction: Dr. Firestone has recently been investigating the foundational mechanisms and high-level abstractions of human visual perception. Their recent work explores how the mind isolates abstract structure from basic sensory features, using techniques like diffusion-generated "visual anagrams" and deep-learning benchmarks to probe whether the visual system automatically decouples artistic style from semantic content, or relational roles (like containment) from specific objects. They are also testing the boundaries of intuitive physical reasoning by tasking observers with predicting the mechanical properties of complex topological structures like knots. Additionally, they are evaluating the evolutionary and cultural origins of core perceptual biases, synthesizing cross-species and ecological data to determine whether phenomena like the Müller-Lyer illusion stem from developmental exposure to built environments or from universal computational constraints.

papers.title: The psychophysics of style
papers.abstract: Stylistic representation—the capacity to decouple an object’s representational form from its semantic content—is explored as a foundational cognitive and perceptual operation. Across ten psychophysical experiments employing naturalistic and synthetic stimuli, the researchers identify key signatures of style processing: perceptual tuning to stylistic parameters, representational constancy over stylistic shifts, and the mental rendering of novel objects in specific styles. Computational benchmarking with deep-learning-based object recognition models demonstrates a significant alignment between human stylistic similarity judgments and model-based representations, supporting the hypothesis that the visual system automatically parses representational style from object content through an autonomous parsing mechanism.
papers.authors: Tal Boger, Chaz Firestone

papers.title: Visual anagrams reveal high-level effects with 'identical' stimuli
papers.abstract: This study addresses the challenge of isolating high-level perceptual effects from lower-level visual covariates by utilizing 'visual anagrams'—diffusion-generated multi-view optical illusions that change their high-level interpretation (e.g., from a rabbit to an elephant) upon rotation. Using canonical real-world size as a case study, five experiments demonstrate that high-level perceptual phenomena, such as aesthetic preference for size-congruent depictions, persist even when comparing physically identical image statistics across different orientations. These findings establish that high-level semantic categories engage perceptual processing independently of low-level visual footprints and introduce a rigorous methodology for dissociating high-level cognition from low-level sensory features.
papers.authors: Tal Boger, Chaz Firestone

papers.title: Is visual perception WEIRD? The Müller-Lyer illusion and the Cultural Byproduct Hypothesis
papers.abstract: The authors challenge the long-standing Cultural Byproduct Hypothesis, which attributes susceptibility to the Müller-Lyer illusion to developmental exposure to 'carpentered' environments. By synthesizing evidence from comparative psychophysics (confirming susceptibility in diverse non-human species), natural scene statistics (demonstrating the illusion's presence in non-built ecologies), and sensory restoration studies (showing immediate susceptibility in congenitally blind individuals upon sight recovery), the paper argues that the illusion arises from fundamental, universal constraints of visual processing. The work concludes that apparent cross-cultural variations are better explained by ecological variability and species-wide perceptual invariants rather than culturally evolved byproducts.
papers.authors: Dorsa Amir, Chaz Firestone

papers.title: Tangled physics: Knots strain intuitive physical reasoning
papers.abstract: While human intuitive physics is often characterized by robust internal simulations, the perception of knots reveals a critical blind spot in this cognitive capacity. Across several experiments, naive observers failed to accurately predict the mechanical strength or physical behavior of various knot configurations, even when provided with high-resolution imagery or explicit structural diagrams. These results indicate that the visual system's capacity for physical scene understanding—potentially mediated by an internal physics engine—is unable to successfully compute the complex topological and frictional interactions inherent in self-entangled flexible objects, defining a novel boundary for theories of physical scene understanding and scene modeling.
papers.authors: Sholei Croom, Chaz Firestone

papers.title: A Phone in a Basket Looks Like a Knife in a Cup: Role-Filler Independence in Visual Processing
papers.abstract: This research investigates whether the cognitive principle of role-filler independence—the capacity to represent relational roles (e.g., container) separately from their constituents (e.g., basket)—is an intrinsic feature of automatic visual processing. Utilizing a visual matching paradigm with time-limited stimulus presentation, the study finds that human observers exhibit systematic 'relational confusions' between distinct object pairs that share identical relational structures. These confusions persist across controls for low-level image features and suggest that the visual system extracts abstract relational roles independently of object identity, providing evidence for a compositional, language-of-thought architecture within the perceptual system.
papers.authors: Alon Hafri, Michael F. Bonner, Barbara Landau, Chaz Firestone

0116.name: Cheryl Olman
0116.lab_name: Olman Laboratory for Imaging and Vision
0116.bio: Cheryl Olman is a researcher at the University of Minnesota specializing in high-resolution functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and visual neuroscience. Olman utilizes ultra-high-field (7T) imaging and visual psychophysics to investigate how the human brain processes local image features to construct global representations of scenes and objects. Their research explores the laminar organization of the early visual cortex to differentiate between feedforward and feedback computations while examining biophysical links between BOLD signal dynamics and excitatory/inhibitory neural activity. Olman also investigates clinical applications, focusing on how visual perceptual context and neural connectivity are altered in individuals with psychotic disorders.
0116.research_direction: Dr. Olman's recent work explores how spatial context and top-down signals shape neural representations within the human visual system. Using ultra-high-resolution 7T fMRI, they have recently been investigating the depth-resolved laminar profiles of contextual modulation in primary visual cortex to disentangle the specific lateral and feedback pathways underlying surround suppression and figure-ground segregation. In parallel, their research examines the mechanistic basis of perceptual deficits in the schizophrenia spectrum, combining psychophysics and neuroimaging to test whether impaired contrast suppression arises from local gain control anomalies in early visual cortex or from disrupted priors in higher-order areas like the lateral occipital complex. Finally, they are investigating the computational relationship between perception and mental imagery, characterizing how stimulus-evoked neural patterns are mathematically transformed and dimensionally compressed during internal visualization.

papers.title: A transformation from vision to imagery in the human brain
papers.abstract: The relationship between mental imagery and visual perception remains a fundamental question in systems neuroscience. This study proposes that the divergence between stimulus-evoked activity during vision and reinstated activity during imagery can be characterized by an 'imagery transformation' within a hierarchical generative network. Utilizing two high-resolution 7T fMRI datasets, the researchers estimated these transformations across various visual regions. The findings reveal that imagery activity patterns are not merely attenuated versions of visual patterns but represent complex mathematical mappings. In early visual cortex, these transformations effectively halve the dimensionality of the active representation and reorient the principal dimensions. Consequently, while imagery reconstructions share coarse features with vision, they occupy a distinct subspace in the neural activation manifold and explain only a fraction of the variance of visual activity.
papers.authors: Thomas Naselaris, Cheryl A. Olman

papers.title: Orientation-tuned surround suppression exhibits a unique laminar signature in human primary visual cortex
papers.abstract: Visual perception is significantly influenced by spatial context, which modifies the neural code in the primary visual cortex (V1) through feedback and lateral connections. This study employed ultra-high-resolution (0.6 mm) 7T fMRI to investigate the laminar-specific blood-oxygenation-level-dependent (BOLD) profiles of orientation-tuned surround suppression (OTSS) and figure-ground modulation (FGM). By manipulating the relative phase and orientation of annular surrounds, the researchers isolated these contextual effects. Results indicate that FGM elicits robust modulation in both superficial and deep cortical layers. In contrast, OTSS showed a distinct laminar signature characterized by its absence in the deeper layers, suggesting that long-range lateral inhibitions and feedforward-aligned mechanisms drive this suppression differently than top-down figure-ground signals.
papers.authors: Joseph H. Emerson, Karen Navarro, Cheryl A. Olman

papers.title: Orientation-dependent contextual modulation of contrast in schizophrenia
papers.abstract: Impairments in contrast surround suppression are a hallmark of psychotic disorders, yet the specific role of stimulus orientation in this deficit remains debated. This study assessed contrast discrimination thresholds in participants with schizophrenia compared to healthy controls across varying relative orientations of center and surround gratings. The research found that the characteristic reduction in suppression among patients was highly orientation-dependent; differences were most pronounced when target and surround orientations were orthogonal or obliquely related, while iso-oriented conditions showed similar suppression levels across groups. These results suggest that the neurophysiological dysfunction in schizophrenia is specific to the mechanisms of untuned gain control rather than tuned lateral inhibition, and that these effects may be further moderated by individual variations in visual acuity.
papers.authors: Victor J. Pokorny, Scott R. Sponheim, Cheryl A. Olman

papers.title: Different contextual modulation mechanisms exhibit distinct laminar profiles in human primary visual cortex
papers.abstract: This investigation seeks to clarify the independent contributions of lateral and feedback pathways to the contextual modulation of neural responses in human V1. Using sub-millimeter line-scanning fMRI at 7T, the study measured depth-resolved BOLD activity during tasks requiring the integration of local image features with broad spatial contexts. The researchers found that while both types of connectivity shape V1 representations, feedback-driven signals (such as those during scene segmentation) target the outer and inner-most layers, whereas lateral connections involved in basic feature suppression exhibit a more localized laminar footprint. The results provide non-invasive evidence for the participation of distinct intracortical microcircuits in specific visual contextual phenomena, bridging animal electrophysiology with human functional neuroimaging.
papers.authors: Joseph Emerson, Karen Navarro, Cheryl A. Olman

papers.title: Perceptual deficits in psychosis: The role of higher level visual areas and prior knowledge
papers.abstract: Perceptual distortions in psychosis are often attributed to an imbalance between sensory input and internal priors. This study explored whether these deficits originate in the early visual cortex or are mediated by higher-level regions such as the lateral occipital complex (LOC). Using a combination of 7T fMRI and behavioral psychophysics, the researchers examined center-surround contrast processing in a transdiagnostic sample. While V1 responses showed minimal differences between groups, significant anomalies were observed in the LOC, where surround suppression was weakened in people with psychotic psychopathology. These findings suggest that higher-order visual regions fail to provide necessary contextual modulation, leading to the characteristic perceptual fragmentation and failures in scene organization observed in the schizophrenia spectrum.
papers.authors: Anh Pham, Scott R. Sponheim, Cheryl A. Olman

0117.name: Chia-Huei Tseng
0117.bio: Chia-Huei Tseng is an Associate Professor who integrates psychophysics, neurophysiology, and computational modeling to investigate human cognitive functions. Tseng’s work focuses on the mechanisms of visual attention, implicit learning, and interpersonal nonverbal communication. They utilize methodologies such as steady-state visual evoked potentials (SSVEP) and EEG to map neural synchrony and "team flow" states. Research topics also include infant development, the creation of digital biomarkers for detecting cognitive decline, and the study of humanness recognition in robotic motion and human-computer interaction.
0117.research_direction: Dr. Tseng has recently been investigating how humans extract meaningful patterns from complex multisensory environments across developmental, cultural, and neural levels. Their recent work explores how preverbal infants acquire abstract rules, specifically testing whether early cognitive development requires explicit social cues or if contingent multisensory feedback and basic crossmodal correspondences—such as linking auditory pitch with spatial height—are sufficient. In the domain of biological motion, they are examining the perceptual and kinematic determinants of "humanness," utilizing point-light animations and developing new 3D motion-capture databases to study how intent and emotion are decoded across different cultures. Furthermore, Dr. Tseng is probing the neurophysiological foundations of these local-to-global visual transformations, evaluating how specific cortical architectures might give rise to emergent Gestalt phenomena like contour integration and the recognition of biological forms.

papers.title: Social and communicative not a prerequisite: Preverbal infants learn an abstract rule only from congruent audiovisual dynamic pitch–height patterns
papers.abstract: This study evaluates whether the capacity of preverbal infants to extract abstract rules from temporal sequences is gated by high-level crossmodal correspondences in non-social contexts. Using a habituation paradigm, 8- to 10-month-old infants were exposed to audiovisual stimuli where vertical movement (upward or downward) was either semantically congruent with pitch changes (ascending or descending tones) or incongruent. The experimental results demonstrate that abstract rule learning is significantly robust when stimuli follow established crossmodal correspondences but is markedly attenuated under incongruent conditions. These findings suggest that multisensory integration mechanisms, rather than social or communicative cues alone, provide the essential scaffolding for early abstract pattern recognition.
papers.authors: Hiu Mei Chow, Yuen Ki Ma, Chia-huei Tseng

papers.title: What Makes a Movement Human‐Like?
papers.abstract: This research investigates the perceptual determinants of 'humanness' in biological motion by analyzing the encoding and decoding of intent through body action. Professional performers were recruited to execute movements across diverse emotional and social scenarios, which were captured and rendered as dynamic point-light animations. Naïve observers assessed these animations to identify specific movement characteristics that trigger humanness perception. The results reveal that (1) observers can accurately distinguish human intent from motion alone, (2) Japanese participants exhibit a specific advantage in detecting negative emotional expressions compared to non-Japanese cohorts, and (3) there is near-perfect accuracy in identifying friendliness versus hostility. The study highlights the role of cultural variance and low-level kinematic features in shaping the high-level attribution of humanness to artificial agents.
papers.authors: Xiaoyue Yang, Miao Cheng, Ken Fujiwara, Yoshifumi Kitamura, Satoshi Shioiri, Chiahuei Tseng

papers.title: Social elements are not a must for preverbal infants' learning in an interactive environment
papers.abstract: This study examines the role of social interaction versus interactive contingency in the development of infant learning capabilities. By utilizing a multi-modal interactive environment, the researchers tested whether 8- to 10-month-old infants require social agents to learn abstract regularities or if the mere presence of contingent feedback is sufficient. The data indicate that infants effectively acquire abstract rules through non-social but contingently interactive stimuli. These results challenge traditional theories that prioritize social-communicative signals as the primary drivers of early cognitive development, suggesting instead that the fundamental mechanism is rooted in the detection of contingent multisensory patterns within the environment.
papers.authors: Yuen Ki Ma, Hiu-Mei Chow, Jaclyn Yeung, Anna Wing Yee Ho, Chia-huei Tseng

papers.title: Toward an Asian-based bodily movement database for emotional communication
papers.abstract: To address the Western-centric bias in existing nonverbal communication resources, this paper presents the development of a comprehensive bodily motion database focused on Asian performers. Utilizing 3D motion capture technology with 57 retroreflective markers, the researchers recorded seven basic emotional expressions across personalized scenarios from Japanese and Taiwanese performers. Validation through human recognition tasks shows that emotion discrimination accuracy is comparable to established Western databases. This resource enables the analysis of cultural nuances in affective bodily expression and provides a benchmark for evaluating Spatio-Temporal Graph Convolutional Networks (ST-GCN) in cross-cultural emotion recognition tasks.
papers.authors: Miao Cheng, Chia-huei Tseng, Ken Fujiwara, Shoi Higashiyama, Abby Weng, Yoshifumi Kitamura

papers.title: Gestalt neurons and emergent properties in visual perception: A novel concept for the transformation from local to global processing
papers.abstract: This article proposes a neurophysiological framework to account for the classic Gestalt 'Laws of Seeing' by introducing the concept of Gestalt neurons. The authors review existing evidence for long-range interactions in the visual cortex that mediate the transformation of local sensory inputs into global, emergent percepts. Key phenomena analyzed include border ownership, contour integration, and the perception of biological motion. The paper argues that these emergent properties arise from specific neuronal architectures that sum responses from feature-selective units and enhance them via feedback projections. This concept bridges the gap between psychophysical observations of global Gestalten and the localized receptive field properties of early visual processing.
papers.authors: Lothar Spillmann, Li-Chuan Hsu, Wei Wang, Chien-Chung Chen, Chun-I Yeh, Chia-Huei Tseng

0119.name: Chien-Chung Chen
0119.bio: Chien-Chung Chen is a Distinguished Professor at National Taiwan University and directs the Visual Neuroscience Laboratory. Their research utilizes a multidisciplinary approach combining psychophysical experiments, functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), and computational modeling to investigate human visual processing. Chen’s work focuses on contrast discrimination, lateral inhibitory interactions in the primary visual cortex, and the neural representation of complex forms such as faces and symmetry. Currently, they examine the integration of spatial information and the role of feedback mechanisms in visual attention and object identification.
0119.research_direction: Dr. Chen's recent work spans psychophysics, oculomotor behavior, and computational modeling to investigate both the behavioral and neural mechanisms of visual processing. They have recently been examining the role of eye movements in resolving perceptual ambiguity, tracking how focal attention, local saliency, and gaze shifts influence perceptual reversals when viewing bistable figures. Their recent research also explores visual field asymmetries in word recognition, mapping how eccentricity, spatial location, and stimulus contrast interact during the identification of Chinese characters to probe the spatial constraints of cortical magnification. Furthermore, at the intersection of artificial intelligence and neuroimaging, Dr. Chen and their team are developing novel dataset-wise attribution methods for deep neural networks, applying these computational tools to large-scale fMRI datasets to estimate population receptive fields and map complex feature representations across the human visual cortex.

papers.title: Eye-movement patterns for perceiving bistable figures
papers.abstract: This psychophysical investigation evaluates the relationship between oculomotor behavior and the perception of bistable stimuli, such as the duck/rabbit figure and the Necker cube. By recording eye-fixation patterns alongside perceptual reversals, the study demonstrates that gaze location significantly modulates the likelihood of a specific percept. Specifically, the findings show that fixation shifts across different regions of interest (ROIs) occur prior to perceptual reversals, indicating that focal attention at specific image features drives the switch. The researchers also test the role of inhibition of return (IOR) and demonstrate that removing local saliency via masking increases reversal frequency, supporting a model where gaze shifts diminish responses at current fixations to facilitate new perceptual interpretations.
papers.authors: Yi-Hsuan Hsu, Chien-Chung Chen

papers.title: Visual field asymmetries in visual word form identification
papers.abstract: This study maps visual acuity thresholds for identifying visual word forms (VWFs) across 21 locations in the visual field, ranging from foveal to 8° eccentricities, using traditional Chinese characters. The authors identify significant performance heterogeneities, specifically observing horizontal-vertical anisotropy (HVA)—where identification is superior along the horizontal compared to the vertical meridian—and vertical meridian asymmetry (VMA), where performance is better in the lower than the upper vertical meridian. By manipulating character contrast (10% to 80%), the study quantifies how contrast modulation interacts with eccentricity-dependent resolution limits. The results are analyzed in the context of the cortical magnification factor (M), suggesting that regional differences in word form processing are tied to the anatomical spacing of neural units in the visual cortex.
papers.authors: Li-Ting Tsai, Kuo-Meng Liao, Chiun-Ho Hou, Yuh Jang, Chien-Chung Chen

papers.title: Integrated Gradient Correlation: a Dataset-wise Attribution Method
papers.abstract: The authors propose Integrated Gradient Correlation (IGC), a novel attribution method designed to enhance the interpretability of deep learning models at the dataset level rather than individual instances. Standard attribution methods often struggle with stable localization of information across large datasets. IGC addresses this by correlating dataset-wise attribution patterns with model prediction scores, enabling a direct summation over specific input components for region-specific analysis. The method is validated on neuroimaging data using the Natural Scenes Dataset (NSD), where IGC is employed to map image feature representations in the human visual cortex and estimate the receptive fields of neural populations. Results demonstrate that IGC effectively reveals model strategies that are physiologically coherent with the functional architecture of the brain.
papers.authors: Pierre Lelièvre, Chien-Chung Chen

0121.name: Chris Baker
0121.bio: Chris I. Baker is a Senior Investigator and Chief of the Unit on Learning and Plasticity within the Laboratory of Brain and Cognition at the National Institute of Mental Health. Baker’s research examines the neural mechanisms of object recognition and the ways in which experience and learning reshape cortical representations in the adult brain. Utilizing high-resolution functional MRI and behavioral psychophysics, they investigate how the human brain processes complex stimuli such as faces, scenes, and words. Baker’s work also explores the extent of cortical reorganization following sensory loss or neural damage to study the brain's adaptive capacity throughout life.
0121.research_direction: Dr. Baker's recent work explores the intersection of high-level visual processing, object representation, and episodic memory retrieval. They have recently been using time-resolved MEG and large-scale image databases to map the temporal dynamics of multidimensional object properties, investigating how the brain transitions from visual to conceptual representations. Using fMRI, their research also examines how prior physical interactions with real-world objects and the category-specific recall of people, places, and things organize neural representations across the ventral temporal and medial parietal cortices. Furthermore, Dr. Baker is investigating the mechanistic links between oculomotor behavior—specifically gaze reinstatement—and neural reactivation during narrative memory recall, while simultaneously testing the replicability and efficacy of non-invasive brain stimulation techniques for modulating global visual motion processing.

papers.title: Dynamic representation of multidimensional object properties in the human brain
papers.abstract: Using time-resolved magnetoencephalography (MEG), neural response dynamics were recorded in four participants viewing over 27,000 unique natural images from the THINGS database (1,854 object concepts). Evoked signals were modeled using a data-driven similarity embedding derived from 4.7 million behavioral triplet judgments to delineate the temporal evolution of multidimensional object representations. Results demonstrated that every behaviorally-derived object dimension was significantly reflected in the time-resolved neural signal. Two distinct temporal profiles were identified: early, participant-stable peaks occurring at approximately 125 ms, primarily associated with visual object properties, and slower-rising, participant-variable peaks at approximately 300 ms, corresponding to conceptual and semantic dimensions. These findings reveal a transition from robust stimulus-driven visual coding to more idiosyncratic conceptual processing within the first few hundred milliseconds of the visual response.
papers.authors: Lina Teichmann, Martin N. Hebart, Chris I. Baker

papers.title: Brief Encounters with Real Objects Modulate the Medial Parietal But Not Occipitotemporal Cortex
papers.abstract: This study investigated the impact of real-world manual exploration of everyday objects on the neural representation of their 2D photographic images using fMRI (n=40). Participants manually explored a subset of 3D objects prior to a scanning session where they viewed photographs of both explored and unexplored items. Multivariate pattern analysis and univariate GLMs revealed that while object-responsive regions in the lateral occipital (LO) and ventral temporal cortex (VTC) contained robust, transformation-invariant visual representations of individual objects, these representations were not modulated by prior real-world physical experience. In contrast, spontaneous recognition of explored objects drove significantly increased BOLD activation in the medial parietal (MP) and posterior cingulate (PC) cortex. These results suggest a functional dissociation in the human brain between the coding of an object’s visual appearance in the occipitotemporal cortex and the experience-driven associations represented in medial parietal structures.
papers.authors: Susan G. Wardle, Beth Rispoli, Vinai Roopchansingh, Chris I. Baker

papers.title: No facilitatory effects of transcranial random noise stimulation on motion processing: A registered report
papers.abstract: This registered report evaluated the proposed facilitatory effects of high-frequency transcranial random noise stimulation (hf-tRNS) over the human middle temporal complex (hMT+) on contralateral global motion processing. In a within-subject experimental design, hf-tRNS (100–640 Hz) was compared against sham stimulation and hf-tRNS to the forehead during a global motion discrimination task. Psychophysical results and statistical comparisons across conditions indicated no significant performance improvement or specific contralateral facilitation under hf-tRNS. The failure to replicate previous findings suggests that the modulatory impact of tRNS on visual motion processing is not robust to protocol adjustments. The study emphasizes the critical need for clearly demonstrated efficacy and replicability in non-invasive brain stimulation research for both basic science and clinical applications.
papers.authors: Grace Edwards, Ryan Ruhde, Mica B. Carroll, Chris I. Baker

papers.title: Neural and behavioral reinstatement jointly reflect retrieval of narrative events
papers.abstract: The relationship between gaze reinstatement and neural reactivation was explored during episodic memory retrieval of continuous narrative movie events. Using fMRI, deep-learning-based gaze prediction (derived from the MReye signal), and natural language modeling of spoken recall, the study tested whether these phenomena are linked by a common retrieval process. Gaze patterns during recall were found to be event-specific, robust across individuals, and generalized from movie viewing to recall, adhering to the same principles as neural activity. Hidden Markov Models (HMM) confirmed that viewing behavior is recapitulated during memory retrieval. Furthermore, gaze-dependent neural activity showed substantial overlap across perception and recall tasks. These results suggest that episodic retrieval engages the same oculomotor and perceptual mechanisms that guide vision, reflecting fundamental constraints within the functional organization of the memory system.
papers.authors: Matthias Nau, Austin Greene, Hannah Tarder-Stoll, Juan Antonio Lossio-Ventura, Francisco Pereira, Janice Chen, Christopher Baldassano, Chris I. Baker

papers.title: Distributed Cortical Regions for the Recall of People, Places, and Objects
papers.abstract: Investigated the functional organization of the human medial parietal cortex (MPC) during memory recall to determine if it mirrors the category-selective medial-lateral axis (faces, objects, scenes) of the ventral temporal cortex (VTC). fMRI data were aggregated across three independent experiments involving the recall of people, places, and objects. While place-recall effects (localizing to the angular gyrus, frontal eye fields, and peripheral early visual cortex) and people-recall effects (right posterior superior temporal sulcus) replicated prior findings, no evidence was found for a dedicated object-recall subregion within the MPC comparable to the object-selectivity found in VTC. Instead, object-recall effects were distributed outside the MPC, primarily in the vicinity of the left supramarginal gyrus. The data indicate that MPC organization is dominated by representations of people and places rather than mirroring the full categorical spectrum of the ventral visual stream.
papers.authors: Alexis Kidder, Edward H. Silson, Matthias Nau, Chris I. Baker

0122.name: Christian H. Poth
0122.bio: Christian H. Poth is a Professor of General Psychology whose research examines the functional links between visual perception, attention, and oculomotor control. Poth investigates how internal states such as urgency and phasic alertness modulate cognitive control, demonstrating that high-pressure situations can prompt stimulus-driven actions that override goal-directed behavior. Using high-resolution eye-tracking, pupillometry, and computational modeling, Poth develops experimental assessments for basic vision science and clinical neuropsychology. This research includes the application of head-mounted displays for diagnostic processing.
0122.research_direction: Dr. Poth's recent work explores how transient states of arousal, alertness, and time pressure modulate human perception, action, and cognitive control. They have recently been utilizing forced-response paradigms across various conflict scenarios—such as flanker, Stroop, and Simon tasks—to investigate how high urgency interacts with stimulus processing asymmetries to trigger reflexive actions that temporarily bypass goal-directed control. In tandem with this empirical research, their theoretical work seeks to build a mechanistic architecture for phasic alertness, examining how non-specific warning signals alter perceptual thresholds and processing speeds. Additionally, they are investigating the psychometrics of momentary subjective states, validating tools like the Relaxation State Questionnaire to continuously track and differentiate the distinct low-arousal experiences of relaxation and sleepiness during cognitively taxing tasks and behavioral interventions.

papers.title: Measuring the Moment – Short-Term Relaxation Effects and the Relaxation State Questionnaire
papers.abstract: The present study validated the Relaxation State Questionnaire (RSQ) as a psychometric instrument for quantifying momentary changes in subjective mental states. Across three distinct experimental designs involving progressive muscle relaxation (PMR) and cognitively taxing conditions such as the Stroop task, the RSQ was evaluated for its sensitivity to intervention efficacy and task-induced arousal shifts. Results demonstrated that the RSQ reliably tracks state-level fluctuations in relaxation and sleepiness across varying levels of manipulation intensity. These findings establish the questionnaire as a sensitive tool for moment-to-moment assessment in clinical interventions and experimental psychophysiology.
papers.authors: Sarah Steghaus, Christian H. Poth

papers.title: Urgency overpowers cognitive control by amplifying cognitive processing asymmetries
papers.abstract: Applying the forced-response paradigm, we investigated whether the disruption of cognitive control under high urgency is contingent upon inherent processing asymmetries between stimulus features. Experiments utilized Eriksen flanker tasks with color and letter stimuli, where stimulus-onset asynchronies (SOAs) were manipulated to induce temporal processing gaps. The results revealed that while urgency typically facilitates rapid responding, it leads to a performance drop below chance level specifically when processing asymmetries exist. These findings suggest that urgency-driven dominance of behavior is not a universal impairment of control but rather an amplification of early-onset cognitive conflicts where stimulus-driven information reaches the threshold for action before goal-directed processing is complete.
papers.authors: Anika Krause, Christian H. Poth

papers.title: Urgency enforces stimulus-driven action across spatial and numerical cognitive control tasks
papers.abstract: This research examined the generalizability of the urgency-induced breakdown of cognitive control using the tachometric function approach. The paradigm was extended beyond traditional arrow stimuli to include word-based Spatial Stroop, Numerical Stroop, and Simon tasks. Across all three modalities, high urgency—quantified as short or negative raw processing times (rPT)—consistently resulted in error rates significantly exceeding chance level in incongruent trials. The consistent emergence of this pattern indicates that various types of conflicting stimulus information can trigger reflexive, stimulus-driven responses that temporarily bypass or overpower goal-directed cognitive control mechanisms.
papers.authors: Anika Krause, Christian H. Poth

papers.title: Readiness for Perception and Action: Towards a More Mechanistic Understanding of Phasic Alertness
papers.abstract: This theoretical review addresses the lack of a mechanistic architecture for phasic alertness, the transient state of physiological readiness elicited by non-specific warning stimuli. Although empirical data confirms that alerting enhances processing speeds and lowers perceptual thresholds, the precise cognitive mechanisms remain poorly understood. The article identifies core challenges, including the functional dissociation of alerting from spatial orienting and the potential role of temporal expectation. By synthesizing evidence from computational modeling and neurophysiology, the paper delineates paths for developing more mechanistic theories of how warning-induced arousal modulates the speed and precision of human perception and action.
papers.authors: Christian H. Poth

papers.title: Feeling tired versus feeling relaxed: Two faces of low physiological arousal
papers.abstract: The intricate relationship between sleepiness and relaxation was examined through a meta-analysis of datasets utilizing the Relaxation State Questionnaire (RSQ). While both states are characterized by low physiological arousal, the study investigated whether they reflect a single continuum or distinct psychological constructs. Pre-intervention analysis revealed a robust negative correlation between momentary sleepiness and relaxation scores. This quantitative dissociation demonstrates that subjective experiences of being relaxed versus being tired are qualitatively distinct, implying that they represent independent underlying constructs that may be affected differently by behavioral interventions.
papers.authors: Sarah Steghaus, Christian H. Poth

0123.name: Christian Vater
0123.bio: Christian Vater is an Assistant Professor at the University of Bern and leads the Peripheral Vision Group within the Institute of Sport Science. Vater’s research characterizes the functionality of peripheral vision in high-demand, time-constrained environments such as competitive sports, driving, and aviation. They utilize experimental methodologies including eye-tracking, behavioral analysis, and virtual reality to investigate mechanisms like gaze anchoring, multiple object tracking, and the integration of foveal and peripheral information. Recent research contributions focus on the ecological validity of perceptual-cognitive training tools and the cognitive trade-offs involved in visual information pick-up during dynamic motor tasks.
0123.research_direction: Dr. Vater's recent work explores how human observers extract and utilize visual information to make decisions in dynamic, naturalistic environments, primarily leveraging virtual reality paradigms. They have recently been investigating visual processing in high-speed sports, specifically asking how peripheral eccentricity, visual crowding, and task representativeness affect the decision-making and action responses of basketball and soccer players, as well as how viewing angles and distances influence referee judgments. Through immersive displays and motion tracking, their research tests whether classic psychophysical phenomena—such as peripheral crowding and foveal gaze-anchoring strategies—generalize from controlled laboratory conditions to complex, real-world athletic tasks. Beyond sports, Dr. Vater also studies spatial cognition and visual search, using mobile eye-tracking in complex virtual indoor spaces to understand how gaze allocation and architectural features influence efficient wayfinding and the development of cognitive maps.

papers.title: Soccer players' ability to use peripheral vision is affected by viewing angles but not crowding
papers.abstract: This study tests how well experienced soccer defenders can extract task-relevant information from peripheral vision during a dynamic, sport-specific overrun-detection task simulated in virtual reality. Twenty-two central defenders/midfielders with at least five years of experience viewed 3-vs-3 counter-attack sequences from a central-defender's first-person perspective while eccentricity between a directly attended opponent and a peripheral wing striker was systematically varied, and visual crowding among peripheral elements was manipulated independently. Increasing peripheral eccentricity monotonically reduced detection accuracy and slowed response times, replicating classic eccentricity effects on peripheral vision.
