However, contrary to predictions derived from crowding research using static, artificial stimuli, the presence of nearby flanking elements (crowding) did not impair performance, likely because the dynamic, sport-specific display and the players' freedom to shift gaze reduced the influence of crowding relative to controlled psychophysical paradigms. The findings suggest that classic laboratory crowding effects generalize only partially to naturalistic, dynamic sport scenes, and that eccentricity remains the dominant constraint on peripheral information pickup in soccer.
papers.authors: Christian Vater, Sarah Pinchuk, Bojan Vukojević

papers.title: Don't get lost in the mall! Characteristics of efficient wayfinding and gaze behavior
papers.abstract: This study investigates what gaze and navigational strategies distinguish efficient from inefficient wayfinding in a complex, multi-level indoor environment. Sixty-eight participants navigated a virtual-reality model of a large, four-floor shopping mall to locate ten different shops, later revisited four of them, and afterward produced three-dimensional sketch maps of the environment; mobile eye-tracking recorded gaze behavior throughout. The visibility of navigational goals and the width of connecting corridors were manipulated to assess their effects on wayfinding performance, cognitive load, and the fidelity of the resulting spatial sketch maps. Gaze patterns shifted systematically over the course of a search, with more exploratory scanning early in a route and more goal-directed fixations as participants neared a target, and efficient navigators showed more consistent allocation of gaze to structurally informative landmarks. Higher goal visibility and wider corridors improved objective wayfinding performance and reduced subjective cognitive load, and better wayfinding performance was associated with more accurate and complete sketch maps, linking overt visual sampling strategies during navigation to the quality of the resulting cognitive map.
papers.authors: Christian Vater, Panos Mavros, Jiayan Zhao, Cécile Abati, Christoph Hölscher

papers.title: That was a foul! How viewing angles, viewing distances, and visualization methods influence football referees' decision-making
papers.abstract: This study experimentally isolates the effects of a referee's viewing position and the medium used to present a play on the accuracy and confidence of foul-detection judgments in football (soccer). Foul and no-foul situations were captured with markerless motion tracking and re-rendered as virtual-reality animations, allowing the same situation to be viewed from three controlled viewing angles and distances, and presented either as the VR animation or as standard video. Ten experienced football referees judged whether a foul had occurred under each combination of viewing condition. Overall decision accuracy was not significantly affected by viewing angle or viewing distance, indicating that referees can extract the relevant kinematic information for foul judgments across a range of vantage points. However, referees' subjective certainty in their decisions declined as viewing distance increased, and the visualization method (VR animation versus video) selectively affected the detection of simulation (diving) but not other foul judgments. The results suggest that referee positioning guidelines should focus more on preserving decision confidence than on accuracy per se, and that VR-based training may be a valid substitute for video for most refereeing decisions except detecting simulated fouls.
papers.venue: German Journal of Exercise and Sport Research
papers.authors: Christian Vater, Urs Schnyder, Daniel Müller

papers.title: Viewing angle, skill level and task representativeness affect response times in basketball defence
papers.abstract: This study provides the first experimentally controlled test of peripheral-vision use during basketball defense using sport-specific stimuli, large peripheral eccentricities (up to 90° left/right), first-person perspective, and natural whole-body action responses, rather than the artificial static displays typical of prior crowding and peripheral-vision research. High- and low-skilled basketball players stood in a CAVE virtual-reality/motion-tracking environment and responded to four video-based task variants of increasing representativeness: a simple reaction-time task without crowding (attackers only), a simple reaction-time task with crowding (attackers plus defenders), a choice-reaction-time passing task, and a full game-simulation task. Across all four tasks, response times increased systematically with peripheral eccentricity. A crowding cost from nearby defenders was observed only in the simple reaction-time task with crowding, while expertise-related advantages for skilled over less-skilled players emerged only in the more representative choice-reaction and game-simulation tasks. The dissociation between where eccentricity, crowding, and skill effects emerge indicates that task representativeness fundamentally changes which perceptual-motor constraints govern peripheral-vision-guided decisions in sport.
papers.authors: Christian Vater

papers.title: The role of peripheral vision during decision-making in dynamic viewing sequences
papers.abstract: This study examines the effects of task pressure and viewing eccentricity on visual search strategies and decision-making performance in dynamic, first-person basketball defensive scenarios. Using immersive head-mounted displays (HMDs), 4v4 play sequences were presented where experienced players monitored a ball-carrier while reacting to peripheral opponents cutting toward the basket at varying eccentricities (up to 90°). To simulate realistic cognitive demands, a secondary auditory counting task was employed. Results demonstrate that response accuracy and latency are significantly impaired at higher viewing eccentricities, despite players allocating over 50% of their fixations to the periphery. The findings support the 'visual pivot' or 'gaze anchor' strategy, where foveal vision is used to periodically update information captured by peripheral vision, rather than relying on peripheral processing alone. Increased pressure improved performance on the secondary task through higher mental effort but did not significantly alter primary gaze behavior or decision-making accuracy.
papers.authors: Brady S. DeCouto, Brad Fawver, Joe L. Thomas, A. Mark Williams, Christian Vater

0124.name: Christian Wallraven
0124.bio: Christian Wallraven is a Professor at Korea University whose research synthesizes computer vision, computer graphics, and cognitive neuroscience to investigate the computational principles of human perception. Wallraven’s work utilizes immersive extended reality (XR) environments and neuroimaging modalities like fMRI and EEG to explore processes such as social face recognition, multisensory integration of vision and touch, and decision-making in high-risk scenarios. By comparing human cognitive strategies with machine learning models, Wallraven develops frameworks for human-AI alignment and creates biologically inspired artificial systems for use in robotics, computer animation, and clinical applications.
0124.research_direction: Dr. Wallraven's recent work explores multimodal human perception and cognition across applied visual, social, and somatosensory domains. They have recently been investigating the alignment between human visual attention and artificial intelligence saliency during driving accident anticipation, utilizing eye-tracking in virtual reality to compare machine feature maps against human spatial-temporal priors. In related human-factors research, they are modeling emergency decision-making in semi-automated driving environments by combining real-time physiological arousal metrics with psychological personality traits. Their recent work also extends to the neural and affective mechanisms of social perception, using the rubber hand illusion to test whether mechanical thermal probes can evoke the same body-ownership responses as interpersonal touch, and employing fMRI multivoxel pattern analysis to chart how the aging brain decodes dynamic facial expressions.

papers.title: Mind the Gap: Quantifying and Aligning Human-AI Visual Attention for Accident Anticipation
papers.abstract: This research investigates the divergence between human visual strategies and artificial intelligence (AI) saliency during the predictive task of accident anticipation in dynamic driving environments. We quantify 'attentional misalignment' by comparing the gaze behavior of human observers against the feature maps of Vision-Language Models (VLMs) and traditional convolutional networks. Our analysis reveals that AI systems frequently exhibit 'shortcut learning,' prioritizing spurious background cues and temporal artifacts, whereas humans consistently focus on dynamic, high-risk objects at the roadway center. We introduce a gaze-guided supervision framework that aligns machine saliency with human attention priors, utilizing rank correlation metrics such as Kendall’s tau to evaluate improvement. Results demonstrate that human-AI alignment significantly enhances predictive robustness and model explainability in safety-critical scenarios.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the 40th AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence (AAAI)
papers.authors: Hoe Sung Ryu, Christian Wallraven

papers.title: Seeing What Matters: Attentional (Mis-) Alignment Between Humans and AI in VR-Simulated Prediction of Driving Accidents
papers.abstract: We examine the congruence between human visual attention and AI-generated saliency maps during critical decision-making intervals in a virtual reality (VR)-simulated driving environment. Participants navigated a fork in the road requiring split-second choices between fatal and safe trajectories to capture ecological eye-tracking data. The study compares human fixation sequences against the attention distributions of deep learning models tasked with accident prediction. Findings highlight a persistent dissociation: although AI models achieve high predictive accuracy, they rely on visual strategies that diverge from human processing, often neglecting peripheral hazards. We quantify these discrepancies using Kendall’s tau and Spearman rank correlation across five distinct temporal segments (T5 to T1) leading to the event, providing a basis for aligning machine attention with human-centered safety priors.
papers.venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics (TVCG)
papers.authors: Hoe Sung Ryu, Uijong Ju, Christian Wallraven

papers.title: Who decides? Modeling emergency decision-making in conditionally automated driving from personality traits and heart rate
papers.abstract: This study develops a computational framework for predicting driver decision-making during emergency take-over transitions in Level 3 conditionally automated vehicles. By integrating real-time physiological markers—specifically heart rate variability (HRV) as a proxy for autonomic nervous system arousal—with stable psychological profiles derived from the Big Five personality traits, we model emergency responses in high-risk simulations. Our results show that higher levels of neuroticism and lower conscientiousness correlate with prolonged reaction times and suboptimal steering interventions. Furthermore, pre-event sympathetic activation was identified as a significant predictor of successful collision avoidance. The proposed model demonstrates the feasibility of utilizing multimodal physiological and trait-based sensing to personalize Advanced Driver Assistance Systems (ADAS) for safety-critical take-over scenarios.
papers.venue: Transportation Research Part F: Traffic Psychology and Behaviour
papers.authors: Uijong Ju, Hoesung Ryu, Christian Wallraven

papers.title: Can impersonal touch replace interpersonal touch? An investigation using the rubber hand illusion
papers.abstract: We investigate whether non-human tactile stimulation can replicate the pleasantness and subjective illusion of body ownership associated with interpersonal touch. Using the rubber hand illusion (RHI) paradigm, we compared human tactile interaction (flat hand) with impersonal touch delivered via a computer-controlled thermal probe maintained at physiological skin temperature (32°C). Both modalities employed C-tactile (CT) optimal speeds of 3 cm/s. Analysis of pleasantness ratings and RHI strength scores in a within-participants design (N=45) revealed no significant difference between human and impersonal touch conditions. Bayesian analysis supported the null hypothesis, suggesting that replicating the physical parameters (temperature and velocity) of socio-emotional touch is sufficient to evoke body-ownership illusions and affective responses regardless of the source. Individual differences in the Need-For-Touch (NFT) scale did not significantly modulate these effects.
papers.authors: Jaehyoung Bae, Christian Wallraven

papers.title: Charting Decodability of Dynamic Facial Expressions in Young and Old Adults: Similarities and Differences
papers.abstract: This study employs whole-brain fMRI and multivoxel pattern analysis (MVPA) to examine how the aging brain processes complex, dynamic emotional and conversational facial expressions. We utilized a searchlight decoding paradigm across two cohorts of younger and older adults (N=77) to identify brain regions encoding the affective content of dynamic signals. A robust bootstrapped conjunction analysis identified the right insula as a common region for successful expression decoding in both age groups, confirming its stable role in dynamic social perception across the lifespan. However, age-related differences emerged in secondary regions, with younger adults showing enhanced decodability in the fusiform face area (FFA), posterior superior temporal sulcus (pSTS), and medial prefrontal cortex. These findings highlight the preservation of core affective decoding circuits in the insula despite shifts in broader specialized neural engagement during social-cognitive aging.
papers.authors: Dilara Derya, Christian Wallraven

0125.name: Christian Windischberger
0125.department: Center for Medical Physics and Biomedical Engineering
0125.bio: Christian Windischberger is an Associate Professor of Medical Physics at the Medical University of Vienna and directs research on functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) technologies. Windischberger’s methodology involves high-resolution ultra-high-field (7T) imaging and the development of concurrent transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) and fMRI systems to map and modulate human brain networks. Within vision science, Windischberger utilizes population receptive field (pRF) mapping to study the functional organization of the visual cortex and investigate retinotopic changes associated with macular and retinal diseases. Their research characterizes brain connectivity and state-dependency to develop personalized, image-guided neurostimulation protocols for clinical applications.
0125.research_direction: Dr. Windischberger has recently been developing advanced computational tools and imaging frameworks to improve the precision, speed, and reliability of non-invasive brain mapping and neuromodulation techniques. To optimize targeted brain stimulation, they are investigating real-time motion compensation algorithms that dynamically adjust repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) dosing to account for head movement, while also building simulation frameworks to accurately monitor focal acoustic pressure fields during transcranial ultrasound stimulation (TUS). Additionally, their recent work explores methods to drastically accelerate the mapping of the visual system's retinotopic organization by designing a GPU-empowered, non-iterative algorithm for large-scale population receptive field (pRF) estimation in fMRI.

papers.title: Reducing target E-field variability in repetitive TMS through online motion compensation
papers.abstract: The efficacy of repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) for treating major depressive disorder depends heavily on precise targeting and consistent dosing, yet small movements during extended protocols often degrade target engagement by shifting the coil. This investigation quantified motion-induced electric field (E-field) fluctuations across 200 clinical sessions and introduces a real-time compensation algorithm that dynamically adjusts stimulator output based on continuous neuronavigational tracking. By interpolating precomputed E-fields, the method significantly reduced intra-session E-field coefficient of variation by 41% and inter-session variability by 74%, providing a computationally efficient solution for enhancing the reliability of therapeutic neuromodulation in patients prone to motion.
papers.authors: Sarah Grosshagauer, Michael Woletz, Marlen Becher, Jonas Björklund, Frank Padberg, Daniel Keeser, Lucia Bulubas, Christian Windischberger

papers.title: GEM-pRF: GPU-empowered mapping of population receptive fields for large-scale fMRI analysis
papers.abstract: Population receptive field (pRF) mapping is essential for characterizing the human visual system's retinotopic organization, but its clinical and large-scale utility has been restricted by the heavy computational burden of iterative parameter fitting. We present GEM-pRF (GPU-Empowered Mapping of pRF), which reformulates the General Linear Model (GLM) framework by orthogonalizing the design matrix to permit direct, non-iterative derivative calculation. This mathematical optimization, coupled with GPU acceleration, enables a dramatic reduction in computation time—by over three orders of magnitude—while maintaining high precision and accuracy. Benchmarked against established software, this scalable workflow facilitates the high-resolution analysis of massive neuroimaging datasets and complex pRF models.
papers.authors: Siddharth Mittal, Michael Woletz, David Linhardt, Christian Windischberger

papers.title: Computational framework for simulating magnetic resonance acoustic radiation force imaging (MR-ARFI) maps
papers.abstract: The development of transcranial ultrasound stimulation (TUS) requires accurate focal monitoring to ensure safe and effective neurostimulation, often through magnetic resonance acoustic radiation force imaging (MR-ARFI). This study introduces a novel computational framework for generating synthetic MR-ARFI maps by modeling the interaction between acoustic pressure fields and MR phase encoding. The framework allows for the systematic validation of displacement estimation algorithms and the optimization of imaging parameters under varying signal-to-noise ratios. By simulating the effects of steering and beam-focusing on the MR phase signal, this tool provides a robust basis for the online assessment of TUS focal zones in human applications.
papers.authors: Bernardo Campilho, Shota Hodono, Michael Woletz, Holger Hewener, Steffen Tretbar, David Norris, Christian Windischberger

0126.name: Christoph Bledowski
0126.bio: Christoph Bledowski is an apl. Professor at the Institute of Medical Psychology, Goethe University Frankfurt, where they investigate the functional and neuronal architecture of human working memory. Bledowski’s research utilizes a multimodal approach, combining behavioral psychophysics with fMRI, EEG, and MEG to delineate the neural systems responsible for mnemonic operations such as selection, updating, and feature binding. They have demonstrated the neuroanatomical dissociation between attentional focusing and mnemonic retrieval within frontoparietal and sensory networks. Bledowski’s current research programs focus on the neural representation of feature bindings in visual and auditory domains, the mechanisms of serial dependence across memory episodes, and the impact of cognitive interference on memory precision.
0126.research_direction: Dr. Bledowski’s recent work explores the behavioral and neural mechanisms of working memory, with a strong focus on how mental representations are influenced by temporal context and attentional priority. Using behavioral delayed-estimation paradigms and magnetoencephalography with multivariate inverted encoding models, they have recently been investigating serial dependence to determine how task demands drive attractive biases toward previous stimuli across trials and repulsive biases between concurrent items within a single trial. Their research also examines how the prioritization of currently versus future-relevant items in visual working memory interacts with memory load to modulate sensory precision and susceptibility to external distractors. Furthermore, they are extending these questions to auditory working memory, applying multivariate pattern analysis to neuroimaging data to decode how internal attention targets and prioritizes distinct mnemonic features across different sensory modalities.

papers.title: Distinct mechanisms for serial dependence within and across trials in visual working memory
papers.abstract: This study evaluates whether attractive serial dependence observed across trials and repulsive biases within trials in visual working memory (VWM) stem from shared or dissociable mechanisms. Using a delayed-estimation task with motion-direction stimuli, the researchers quantified bias for pairs of immediately consecutive items. Findings demonstrate a consistent attractive shift toward features from previous trials but a robust repulsive shift between concurrently maintained items within a single trial. The results suggest that while between-trial attraction serves to stabilize representations over longer intervals, within-trial repulsion reflects active competitive mechanisms that sharpen individual memory traces in the face of interference, supporting a dual-mechanism account of serial dependence in VWM.
papers.authors: Stefan Czoschke, Cora Fischer, Julia Beitner, Christoph Bledowski

papers.title: Effects of visual working memory load and item priority on susceptibility to distraction and memory accuracy
papers.abstract: The investigation explores how memory load and attentional prioritization interact to determine susceptibility to external distraction and the precision of maintained representations in visual working memory (VWM). Using a dual-task paradigm where participants performed a flanker task during VWM retention, the study manipulated the load of currently relevant (CR) and future-relevant (FR) items. Quantitative results indicated that increasing CR load significantly reduced the impact of distractor interference but simultaneously degraded memory precision. In contrast, increasing FR load had negligible effects on both distraction and precision. These findings support a model where CR and FR items are stored in functionally distinct states, with only prioritized CR items competing for sensory-perceptual resources and providing protection against distractors.
papers.authors: Hasan Gunduz, Turan Gunduz, Jan W. de Fockert, Christoph Bledowski

papers.title: A direct neural signature of serial dependence in working memory
papers.abstract: While behavioral reports exhibit an attractive bias toward previous stimuli (serial dependence), identifying a direct neural correlate has proven challenging, with previous research often showing repulsive adaptation. This study utilized magnetoencephalography (MEG) and multivariate inverted encoding models to reconstruct motion-direction representations during a visual working memory task. Reconstructions of currently remembered features showed an attractive shift toward the target direction of the preceding trial, specifically during the post-encoding retro-cue delay period. This neural shift directly predicted single-trial behavioral report errors. The results provide the first evidence for a neural signature of serial dependence and suggest that attractive biases emerge at late processing stages, likely during the readout or reactivation of memory traces rather than during initial sensory encoding.
papers.authors: Cora Fischer, Jochen Kaiser, Christoph Bledowski

papers.title: The impact of task measurements on sequential dependence in visual working memory
papers.abstract: This research examines how the specific requirements of the measurement task influence the magnitude and direction of serial dependence in visual working memory. By contrasting different response methods and stimulus durations, the study demonstrates that the typically observed attractive bias toward previous stimuli is sensitive to the temporal and task-related context of the report. The findings indicate that serial dependence is not a fixed sensory phenomenon but is modulated by the mnemonic and decision-making demands imposed on the observer. The study highlights that the interaction between successive stimulus representations depends significantly on the behavioral relevance of the preceding trial's features and the specific action required for their report.
papers.authors: Stefan Czoschke, Cora Fischer, Julia Beitner, Jochen Kaiser, Christoph Bledowski

papers.title: Information-based decoding of memory-driven attention in auditory working memory
papers.abstract: The study investigates the neural representation of task-relevant features in auditory working memory (AWM) and their role in guiding internal attention. Using multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) of neuroimaging data, the researchers decoded the contents of AWM during a delay period where participants had to prioritize specific sound features (e.g., pitch or location). Above-chance decoding was achieved in both primary auditory regions and higher-order frontoparietal areas. The results show that internally directed attention in AWM utilizes a distributed information-based coding scheme similar to that found in visual working memory, suggesting a modality-independent mechanism for the attentional prioritization of mnemonic contents.
papers.authors: Stefan Czoschke, Cora Fischer, Christoph Bledowski

0127.name: Christopher DiMattina
0127.bio: Christopher DiMattina is a Professor of Psychology at Florida Gulf Coast University and directs the Computational Perception Laboratory. DiMattina’s research investigates the information processing mechanisms of biological sensory systems, focusing on mid-level vision, perceptual organization, and the neural basis of visual aesthetics and discomfort. They employ a methodology that integrates psychophysical experiments with computational modeling and machine learning to analyze how the visual system classifies natural image features. This research includes distinguishing shadows from surface boundaries and segmenting complex textures.
0127.research_direction: Dr. DiMattina has recently been investigating the mid-level visual mechanisms underlying scene parsing and texture perception, particularly how human observers use local achromatic cues like boundary sharpness, luminance, and texture modulation to categorize image patches as object occlusions, cast shadows, or uniform surfaces. Their recent work also explores the spatial mechanisms of second-order texture segmentation, using psychophysical summation experiments to compare sensitivity to density-defined versus feature-defined boundaries as a way to test early-pooling against canonical late-pooling Filter-Rectify-Filter architectures. Additionally, they have been examining the evolutionary and computational basis of visual discomfort and trypophobia, measuring behavioral aversion to clustered patterns and dermatological lesions to determine whether these aversive responses are driven by low-level image statistics—such as deviations from 1/f spatial frequency spectra—or by high-level material appraisals related to pathogen avoidance.

papers.title: Local cues enable classification of image patches as surfaces, object boundaries, or illumination changes
papers.abstract: Parsing natural scenes into surfaces requires identifying luminance edges and inferring whether their physical origin is an object occlusion, a cast shadow, or surface material pigmentation. Although image-computable neural networks (such as filter-rectify-filter architectures) trained on natural images demonstrate that boundary sharpness and texture cues can distinguish occlusions from shadows, whether biological vision exploits these specific local achromatic cues remained unverified. Here, human classification behavior was measured using synthetic edge patches generated by quilting together natural textures, enabling independent parametric manipulation of luminance modulation, boundary sharpness (penumbral blur), and texture modulation across five stimulus sets. Observers trained with feedback on natural patches subsequently categorized synthetic patches into occlusions, shadows, or uniform textures. Psychophysical data revealed prominent nonlinear interactions among cues: for sharp step edges, increasing luminance modulation decreased texture classifications while increasing occlusion classifications, whereas for blurred edges, increased luminance modulation systematically drove shadow classifications. Boundary sharpness strongly governed edge classification under non-zero luminance modulation, suppressing shadow classifications and increasing occlusion categorizations, while texture modulation exerted negligible effects except across sharp boundaries with zero luminance modulation. Multinomial logistic regression models accurately fit and generalized across behavioral datasets, demonstrating that human visual categorization exploits the identical local achromatic cues utilized by computational vision models.
papers.authors: Christopher DiMattina, Eden E. Sterk, Madelyn G. Arena, Francesca E. Monteferrante

papers.title: A comparison of density-based and feature-based texture boundary segmentation
papers.abstract: The spatial density of micropattern elements constitutes a fundamental visual dimension that can support texture segmentation in the absence of luminance steps. Psychophysical segmentation thresholds were compared for two classes of second-order texture boundaries constructed from complementary pairs of micropatterns (such as orthogonal Gabor patches or opposite-polarity difference-of-Gaussian filters): (1) feature boundaries, which hold total micropattern count constant across opposite sides while modulating the relative proportion of each micropattern species, and (2) density boundaries, which vary the total number of micropatterns across the boundary while matching the species ratio within each side. Contrary to canonical late-pooling Filter-Rectify-Filter (FRF) architectures, which process distinct micropattern-tuned first-order channels via separate second-stage spatial filters prior to pooling and thus predict identical thresholds, human observers exhibited significantly lower segmentation thresholds for density-defined boundaries than for feature-defined boundaries. In summation experiments where two single-species density boundaries were superimposed, combining them in-phase to generate a compound density boundary produced sensitivity consistent with probability summation across channels. Conversely, superimposing them in opposite phase to form a compound feature boundary impaired performance below single-channel baselines. These findings indicate that density-based texture boundary detection operates via distinct early-pooling visual mechanisms that integrate across multiple first-order spatial filter varieties rather than relying on channel-specific second-order processing.
papers.authors: Christopher DiMattina

papers.title: Effects of luminance, texture and blur on classification of image patches as changes in material or illumination
papers.abstract: This research investigates how human observers utilize local achromatic cues—specifically luminance modulation, texture modulation, and boundary sharpness—to categorize image patches as either object boundaries (occlusions), shadow edges (illumination changes), or uniform surfaces. By parametric manipulation of synthetic edge stimuli quilted from natural textures, the study reveals strong interactions between these cues in determining perceptual categorization. Increased boundary sharpness was found to significantly increase the probability of occlusion classification in the presence of luminance modulation, whereas blurred boundaries favored shadow classification. Texture modulation showed selective importance, primarily influencing judgments for sharp edges lacking luminance contrast. Behavioral data were accurately modeled using multinomial logistic regression, confirming that human scene parsing mechanisms rely on the same diagnostic achromatic statistics as optimized machine learning models for edge classification.
papers.authors: Eden E. Sterk, Madelyn G. Arena, Christopher DiMattina

papers.title: Trypophobia, skin disease, and the visual discomfort of natural textures
papers.abstract: Trypophobia denotes the aversive emotional response and visual discomfort experienced by certain individuals when viewing clustered arrays of holes or circular geometric patterns. A prominent evolutionary account posits that this aversion constitutes an adaptation of the behavioral immune system directed toward avoiding ectoparasitic infestation and infectious dermatological pathologies. This investigation evaluated the skin-disease avoidance hypothesis by quantifying discomfort ratings across natural textures, trypophobic stimuli, and dermatological lesion imagery in participants stratified into trypophobic and non-trypophobic cohorts via the Trypophobia Questionnaire (TQ). Both cohorts exhibited congruent ordinal discomfort hierarchies across image types, with dermatological pathologies evoking maximal discomfort, followed by trypophobic patterns, and natural textures producing minimal aversion. Observers with trypophobia displayed elevated discomfort ratings across all stimulus sets, with the largest between-group divergence occurring for trypophobic and cutaneous disease stimuli. Furthermore, standard low-level image statistical metrics, including spatial frequency power spectra and deviations from 1/f spectral profiles, proved to be poor predictors of visual discomfort in natural textures and significantly under-predicted the intense aversion evoked by trypophobic and infectious imagery. These results support the skin-disease avoidance hypothesis, demonstrating that trypophobia reflects pathogen-avoidance mechanisms operating via high-level surface and material property appraisals rather than low-level early visual filter over-activation.
papers.authors: Christopher DiMattina, R. Nathan Pipitone, Martin R. Renteria, Kriston J. Ryan

0128.name: Christopher L. Striemer
0128.main_research_area: cognitive neuroscience of attention and visuomotor control
0128.bio: Christopher L. Striemer is a Professor at MacEwan University and an adjunct faculty member within the Neuroscience and Mental Health Institute at the University of Alberta. Striemer’s research examines the neural mechanisms of visual attention, perception, and visuomotor control in both healthy populations and neurological patients. Utilizing techniques such as kinematic analysis, eye tracking, fMRI, and non-invasive brain stimulation, they investigate how brain damage to the parietal lobe and cerebellum affects spatial awareness and motor coordination. A portion of their work evaluates the efficacy of prism adaptation as a rehabilitative tool for patients with spatial neglect.
0128.research_direction: Dr. Striemer has recently been investigating the neural and cognitive mechanisms underlying visuomotor control, spatial attention, and sensorimotor adaptation. Their recent work explores the dynamics of prism adaptation, specifically testing whether congruency between the adapted hand and the direction of visual shift modulates both basic motor recalibration and higher-order perceptual spatial biases. Additionally, they are examining the dorsal stream's "automatic pilot" for online reach control, seeking to understand how individual differences in executive function influence a person's ability to suppress reflexive trajectory corrections to displaced visual targets. Finally, Dr. Striemer's clinical research assesses the cerebellum's role in these broader processes by mapping how localized cerebellar strokes disrupt the longitudinal recovery of reach kinematics and investigating whether unilateral cerebellar damage can induce subclinical hemispatial neglect.

papers.title: The influence of prism adaptation on spatial biases is not dependent on which hand is used to adapt
papers.abstract: Prism adaptation (PA) inducing rightward visual displacement reliably ameliorates symptoms of hemispatial neglect, whereas leftward PA induces neglect-like spatial biases in healthy cohorts. Recent work documents a sensorimotor congruency effect, characterized by amplified prism aftereffects when the adapting limb corresponds with the direction of prismatic optical shift (e.g., left hand paired with leftward displacement) compared to incongruent pairings. The present study investigated whether this congruency effect extends beyond motor realignment to modulate attentional and perceptual spatial biases. Healthy adult participants (n = 52) completed manual line bisection and landmark judgment paradigms prior to and following leftward PA administered with either the ipsilateral left (congruent) or contralateral right (incongruent) hand across counterbalanced testing sessions. Open-loop straight-ahead pointing and closed-loop washout pointing corroborated the sensorimotor congruency effect, demonstrating significantly larger aftereffects under congruent conditions. Although leftward PA successfully elicited the predicted overall rightward shift in spatial attention across both line bisection and landmark measures, no significant congruency effects were observed on either attentional metric. These results indicate that while sensorimotor realignment demonstrates effector-displacement congruency constraints, the propagation of adaptation to higher-order spatial representations occurs independently of the adapted limb.
papers.authors: Sophia A. Slade, Jasmine Kowalewski, Dana Cobzas, Christopher L. Striemer

papers.title: “Automatic” online reach corrections are associated with individual differences in executive function
papers.abstract: Posterior parietal networks within the dorsal visual stream mediate rapid online trajectory adjustments to abrupt target displacements. This 'automatic pilot' can function outside perceptual awareness and persists even counter to explicit instructions to suppress corrections. This investigation examined whether individual differences in executive function and response inhibition modulate the suppression of these reflexive updates. Healthy adults (n = 80) completed touchscreen automatic pilot paradigms under two conditions: a 'Correct' condition requiring online trajectory steering toward displaced targets, and an 'Ignore' condition requiring participants to suppress modifications and reach strictly to the initial target locus. Participants also performed the Sustained Attention to Response Task (SART) and completed self-report psychometric inventories indexing cognitive failures (CFQ), adult ADHD symptomatology (ASRS), and global executive dysfunction (BRIEF-A). Kinematic analyses confirmed that while participants corrected significantly less frequently in the Ignore compared to the Correct condition, unintended corrections remained prevalent. Crucially, the incidence of these automatic, unintended corrections during Ignore trials correlated significantly with elevated scores on the ASRS, CFQ, and BRIEF-A, whereas no association emerged with SART commission errors or response times. These findings indicate that automatic pilot task susceptibility reflects self-reported cognitive control capabilities and may serve as an objective visuomotor metric of executive function.
papers.authors: Branden T. Otte, Christopher L. Striemer

papers.title: Direction of visual shift and hand congruency enhance spatial realignment during visuomotor adaptation
papers.abstract: Although prism adaptation (PA) provides an established model of sensorimotor plasticity in response to visual perturbations, the interaction between effector laterality and the spatial vector of optical displacement has remained underexplored. Given that sensory feedback and motor command signals cross to distinct cerebral and cerebellar structures, adaptation was hypothesized to be amplified when the optical deviation and effector share intrahemispheric circuitry. In Experiment 1, re-examination of open-loop pointing data from healthy adults (n = 17) exposed to 17° leftward or rightward displacing prisms with either the left or right hand revealed a significant congruency effect: straight-ahead pointing (SAP) aftereffects were markedly greater when the adapting limb matched the direction of visual shift (e.g., left hand adapting to leftward displacement) relative to incongruent pairings. Experiment 2 replicated this congruency-dependent amplification of proprioceptive realignment in an independent cohort of neurotypical adults (n = 25). These findings indicate that sensorimotor recalibration is selectively heightened when visual error signals and motor effectors recruit congruent intrahemispheric networks within the ipsilateral cerebellum and contralateral cerebral hemisphere.
papers.authors: Christopher L. Striemer, Adam Morrill

papers.title: Assessment and recovery of visually guided reaching deficits following cerebellar stroke
papers.abstract: The cerebellum plays an integral role in coordinating the kinematics and temporal dynamics of visually guided reaching (VGR). To determine the nature of reach kinematic impairments and their longitudinal resolution, 12 patients with isolated cerebellar stroke were tracked at acute baseline (~2 weeks post-stroke) and at 6, 12, and 24 weeks post-injury. Testing incorporated neuropsychological batteries, clinical motor exams, and an unassisted planar reaching paradigm across eight radial targets using the Kinarm exoskeleton. Relative to normative Kinarm metrics (n = 307), 6 of the 12 patients displayed significant multi-parametric kinematic impairments at baseline, displaying disruptions across both feedforward trajectory formation and feedback-driven corrective phases. Among clinical tests, consistent deficits were observed only on the Purdue Pegboard Test (PPT; 9/12 patients) and the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA; 6/11 patients). By week 24, baseline-impaired individuals showed significant functional restitution on both Kinarm kinematic measures and the PPT. Lesion overlap analysis mapped maximum shared damage in 5 of 12 patients (42% overlap) to right lobule IX and Crus II, whereas lesion subtraction between baseline-impaired and unimpaired subgroups localized reaching deficits specifically to right lobule VIII (40% overlap), supporting a role for distinct cerebellar regions in feedforward and feedback visuomotor control.
papers.authors: Chella M. Robles, Britt Anderson, Sean P. Dukelow, Christopher L. Striemer

papers.title: Left Cerebellar Lesions may be Associated with an Increase in Spatial Neglect-like Symptoms
papers.abstract: Contralateral cerebro-cerebellar connectivity suggests functional lateralization within the cerebellum that mirrors neocortical organization, implicating the left cerebellar hemisphere in visuospatial processing and the right in linguistic operations. Grounded in a cerebro-cerebellar disconnection framework, this study investigated whether unilateral cerebellar injury produces subclinical manifestations of spatial neglect. Retrospective screening data across manual line bisection, cancellation, and figure copying batteries were evaluated in 20 patients with isolated unilateral cerebellar infarcts. Patients presenting with left cerebellar lesions (n = 9) exhibited a significant increase in contralesional omissions on the left side of cancellation arrays compared to normative reference standards, whereas right cerebellar patients (n = 11) demonstrated no asymmetric visual inattention. Voxel overlap mapping revealed that Crus II (78% overlap), alongside lobules VII and IX (66% overlap), formed the common anatomical locus of injury among left cerebellar cases exhibiting attentional biases. These findings demonstrate that left cerebellar damage can disrupt contralateral fronto-parietal attention networks, yielding subclinical neglect-like spatial biases.
papers.authors: Ryan Verbitsky, Britt Anderson, James Danckert, Sean P. Dukelow, Christopher L. Striemer

0129.name: Christopher Tyler
0129.bio: Christopher Tyler is a visual neuroscientist who invented the random-dot autostereogram and conducted research on human stereoscopic depth perception. As the Head of the Brain Imaging Center at the Smith-Kettlewell Eye Research Institute, Tyler utilizes psychophysics, functional MRI (fMRI), and electroretinography to investigate the neural processing of symmetry, motion, and 3D form. Their current research focuses on characterizing oculomotor deficits and photophobia in patients with traumatic brain injury, as well as developing computational models of the visual hierarchy. Tyler also studies the intersection of vision science and Renaissance art, exploring topics such as the perspective geometry and ocular health of historical artists.
0129.research_direction: Dr. Tyler has recently been investigating a diverse array of phenomena spanning visual psychophysics, computational modeling, and cognitive neuroscience. Their recent work explores the fundamental mechanisms of visual integration, utilizing psychophysical paradigms to examine spatial summation in central motion detection and to determine how the human visual system extracts global stereoscopic 3D structure from traveling longitudinal waves. In the realm of computational vision, they are probing whether the hierarchical layers of deep neural networks can serve as valid functional models for mirror-symmetry processing in higher-order areas like the lateral occipital complex. Additionally, they are mapping cross-modal neuroplasticity by using fMRI to track how the human motion area (hMT+) reorganizes following kinesthetic training in individuals with severe low vision, while separately conducting behavioral studies to operationalize mindfulness as a distinct, somatically centered attentional stance.

papers.title: Evidence that Attentional Stance Shift is Learned Rapidly, Reliably Induces Mindfulness, and Constitutes a Distinctive Marker of Cognitive Process
papers.abstract: This research operationalizes mindfulness as a distinct attentional stance, specifically defined by the felt somatic location of the ego-center or 'seat of attention.' Across multiple experimental cohorts including meditation-naive subjects and MBSR practitioners, brief instruction (≤1 hour) in a diffuse abdominal attentional stance was evaluated. Quantitative assessments using the Perceived Stress Scale (PSS-10) and Experience of Mindfulness Questionnaire (EMQ) demonstrated that these specific attentional shifts reliably induce physiological and psychological states characteristic of advanced meditation. The findings suggest that the somatic self-regulation of attentional self-location provides a precise behavioral marker and a rapid mechanism for accessing meditative cognitive resources, mirroring the efficacy of established long-term mindfulness-based interventions.
papers.authors: Glenn Hartelius, Lora T. Likova, Daniel D. Haldeman, Marie Sester, John Elfers, Christopher W. Tyler

papers.title: Pulfrich's stereo curtain
papers.abstract: This study examines the visual perception of travelling longitudinal waves, a novel class of stimuli generated from a phased array of vertical sinusoidal oscillations. While longitudinal waves are fundamental in physical acoustics, their visual processing as an emergent global motion phenomenon remains largely unexplored. By implementation of a progressive temporal phase lag across a spatial array of vertical lines, the authors demonstrate the perception of dynamic regions of compression and rarefaction. Psychophysical data indicate that these waves support the integration of first-order local motion into complex higher-order percepts, including the generation of stereoscopic 3D surface corrugations through temporal delays or binocular disparity. The results elucidate how the visual system extracts global spatial structure from periodic motion dynamics.
papers.authors: Stuart M. Anstis, Joshua A. Solomon, Christopher W. Tyler

papers.title: Training-induced Reorganization of the Cross-modal Connectivity of the Human Motion Area in Severe Low Vision
papers.abstract: This investigation delineates the longitudinal reorganization of the cortical navigation network following specialized Cognitive-Kinesthetic Memory-Drawing training in individuals with severe low vision. Utilizing Granger causality analysis on functional MRI data, the study reveals a fundamental transformation in the connectivity profile of the human motion complex (hMT+). Pre-training connectivity was characterized by top-down inputs from sensorimotor regions (pre- and post-central cortices). Post-training analysis showed that hMT+ was repurposed as a central conduit, relaying prefrontal executive control signals to the medial navigational network and the amodal-spatial 'sketchpad' in the primary visual cortex (V1). These findings demonstrate the capacity for rapid, task-dependent neuroplastic reorganization to integrate kinesthetic feedback into global spatial representations in the absence of high-resolution form vision.
papers.authors: Lora T. Likova, Kristyo N. Mineff, Zhangziyi Zhou, Michael Liang, Christopher W. Tyler

papers.title: The canonical deep neural network as a model for human symmetry processing
papers.abstract: This work evaluates the emergence of mirror-symmetry selectivity within hierarchical Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) pre-trained on naturalistic scene statistics. By challenging the models with random-dot patterns across varying axes of symmetry, the researchers demonstrate that while early convolutional layers exhibit negligible symmetry coding, discriminability peaks at the first fully connected layer (FC6). This layer is proposed as a functional homologue to the human lateral occipital complex (LOC) based on its global processing characteristics. The results support the hypothesis that feedforward architectures can develop gestalt-like symmetry processing and a degree of polarity blindness congruent with human neurobiology through the implicit learning of environmental regularities.
papers.authors: Yoram S. Bonneh, Christopher W. Tyler

papers.title: Spatial summation for motion detection
papers.abstract: Utilizing a psychophysical summation paradigm, the researchers characterized the spatial integration mechanisms underlying the detection of motion-defined targets in central vision. Velocity thresholds were measured against varying levels of external Gaussian motion noise as a function of target diameter. The resulting threshold-versus-diameter functions displayed a non-monotonic 'swoosh' profile, with a sensitivity minimum occurring at approximately 2 degrees of visual angle. Computational modeling indicates that the observed summation properties are best characterized by a sparse sampling mechanism that compares stimulus velocity profiles against a restricted set of difference-of-Gaussian (DoG) templates. This model provides a superior account of biological motion detection efficiency compared to continuous or theoretically ideal observer integration strategies.
papers.authors: Joshua A. Solomon, Fintan Nagle, Christopher W. Tyler

0130.name: Chuan Hou
0130.bio: Chuan Hou, MD, PhD, is an Associate Scientist at the Smith-Kettlewell Eye Research Institute who researches binocular vision processing and the neural basis of amblyopia and strabismus. As a pediatric ophthalmologist, Hou utilizes VEP, fMRI-informed EEG source-imaging, and psychophysics to study interocular suppression. Their work investigates how selective visual attention influences sensory eye dominance and explores dichoptic attention-based therapies to restore visual function. Hou’s research on the role of top-down attentional influences in amblyopic suppression is supported by the National Eye Institute.
0130.research_direction: Dr. Hou has recently been investigating the mechanisms of binocular rivalry and interocular suppression in both typical observers and clinical populations with amblyopia and strabismus. Using psychophysical paradigms with dichoptically presented stimuli, their recent work explores how sensory eye dominance and perceptual suppression are modulated by low-level image features—such as spatial scale and contrast—as well as by top-down voluntary attention. To better quantify these deficits, they are also developing novel behavioral protocols that measure suppression across both amblyopia and strabismus without relying on traditional interocular contrast adjustments. Furthermore, Dr. Hou is actively examining the therapeutic potential of dichoptic, attention-based perceptual learning tasks, using fMRI and psychophysics to map how this training drives functional plasticity across the visual cortex and recovers contrast sensitivity in adult amblyopes.

papers.title: Effects of stimulus size and contrast on binocular rivalry in adults with anisometropic amblyopia
papers.abstract: This psychophysical investigation examined how stimulus dimensions and interocular contrast ratios govern binocular rivalry dynamics in adult observers with anisometropic amblyopia relative to visually normal controls. Conflicting orthogonal grating stimuli of varying spatial extents and contrast levels were dichoptically presented to quantify reversal rates, perceptual phase durations, and proportions of exclusive versus mixed percepts. In individuals with anisometropic amblyopia, binocular rivalry alternations were profoundly disrupted at small stimulus diameters, characterized by severe perceptual suppression of the amblyopic eye and heightened proportions of incomplete reversals and mixed percepts. Incrementally scaling the stimulus area or increasing physical contrast delivered to the amblyopic eye partially rescued perceptual dominance and alternation frequencies, demonstrating that interocular suppression in anisometropia is constrained by both spatial-scale summation and luminance-contrast normalization mechanisms.
papers.authors: Chuan Hou, Junxian Rao

papers.title: Attentional Eye Selection Affects Perception During Binocular Rivalry
papers.abstract: This study evaluated how voluntary attentional eye selection modulates sensory eye dominance across different spatial stimulus scales during binocular rivalry. Normal-vision observers viewed dichoptic orthogonal gratings across five stimulus sizes (1°, 2.5°, 5°, 10°, and 15°) under passive viewing and under an instructed condition where top-down attention was selectively deployed to the non-sighting eye (as determined via the hole-in-the-card sighting test). Behavioral tracking quantified alternation occurrence rates, phase durations, and proportions of monocular versus mixed percepts. Under baseline viewing, the sighting eye showed pronounced perceptual dominance across all metrics. Selectively directing attention to the non-sighting eye shifted sensory eye dominance in its favor, with the maximal attentional modulation effect occurring at the 5° stimulus size. In contrast, the relative prevalence of mixed percepts was invariant to attentional deployment across all stimulus sizes, demonstrating that voluntary attentional eye selection dynamically shifts ocular dominance without altering binocular integration states.
papers.authors: Zhangziyi Zhou, Chuan Hou

papers.title: Visual Cortical Function Changes After Perceptual Learning with Dichoptic Attention Tasks in Adults with Amblyopia: A Case Study Evaluated Using fMRI
papers.abstract: To clarify how visual perceptual learning modulates functional responses within the human visual cortex, blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) was acquired before and after training in seven adult observers with amblyopia. Training comprised two months of biweekly dichoptic sessions engaging high-attention-demand visual search and target-counting tasks designed to engage frontoparietal networks (e.g., intraparietal sulcus) while bypassing primary visual cortex (V1) low-level feature training. Retinotopic regions of interest—including striate cortex (V1) and extrastriate areas (V2, V3, V3A, and hV4)—were analyzed alongside psychophysical measures of visual acuity and stereoacuity. Observers with anisometropic amblyopia demonstrated widespread BOLD signal enhancements across all retinotopic areas alongside significant visual acuity and stereopsis gains. In contrast, strabismic amblyopes exhibited robust cortical functional recovery selectively in individuals who realized substantial behavioral visual recovery. Across all participants, the magnitude of V1 functional enhancement was significantly correlated with visual acuity and stereoacuity improvements, indicating that top-down attentional perceptual learning drives plasticity across both early sensory and higher-order cortical processing stages.
papers.authors: Chuan Hou, Zhangziyi Zhou, Ismet Joan Uner, Spero C. Nicholas

papers.title: A new approach to measure interocular suppression in amblyopia and strabismus
papers.abstract: Interocular suppression depth in amblyopia is traditionally quantified by establishing a contrast 'balance point,' which measures the contrast increment required in the amblyopic eye to match the perceptual salience of the fellow eye. This paradigm fails in strabismus without amblyopia, where contrast sensitivity in the non-fixating eye remains normal or superior. This methodological paper introduces an alternative psychophysical protocol to measure interocular suppression across both amblyopia and strabismus without adjusting interocular contrast balance. The paradigm presents stimuli of equal physical contrast to each eye through a stereoscope and contrasts perceptual performance between monocular and dichoptic viewing states. Interocular suppression is operationalized as the perceptual omission or discrimination failure of a target presented to the amblyopic or non-preferred eye when competing stimuli are concurrently introduced to the fellow eye during an orientation discrimination paradigm.
papers.authors: Chuan Hou

papers.title: Improvement of Contrast Sensitivity in Adults with Amblyopia through Dichoptic Attention Task Training
papers.abstract: This study tested whether perceptual learning mediated by dichoptic attention tasks could remediate contrast sensitivity deficits in mature amblyopic vision. Twelve adults with amblyopia (six anisometropic and six strabismic; aged 22–66 years) completed eight weeks of biweekly training sessions using a mirror stereoscope. Stimuli required participants to quickly locate and count high-contrast suprathreshold Gabor patches in the amblyopic eye amidst simultaneously presented distractors in the fellow eye, eliminating dependence on threshold-level spatial frequency or contrast discrimination. Contrast response functions and contrast sensitivity thresholds (defined at the 75% correct orientation discrimination threshold) of the amblyopic eye were tracked psychophysically before and after intervention. Following training, 10 of 12 participants demonstrated significant contrast sensitivity gains, with a mean overall increase of 31.73% (p < 0.01). The degree of contrast sensitivity improvement significantly correlated with the reduction in attentional allocation bias toward the fellow eye (rho = 0.55, p = 0.04), with comparable recovery across anisometropic and strabismic subgroups.
papers.venue: Journal of Clinical and Experimental Ophthalmology
papers.authors: Gabriela Acevedo Munares, Ismet Joan Uner, Chuan Hou

0131.name: Chujun Lin
0131.bio: Chujun Lin examines the mechanisms, structures, and behavioral consequences of human person perception. By integrating computational tools such as deep neural networks with neuroscientific methods like single-neuron recording and fMRI, Lin investigates how individuals form social impressions from complex visual cues, including faces and naturalistic videos. Their work characterizes the high-dimensional nature of trait inferences and explores how these social judgments bias decision-making in real-world contexts such as politics and the legal system.
0131.research_direction: Dr. Lin's recent work explores the high-dimensional, computational nature of social cognition and person perception in naturalistic environments. They have recently been investigating how humans form trait inferences from complex video stimuli, utilizing computational feature extraction to determine which specific visual cues—such as body posture, clothing, or facial structure—drive real-world social judgments. Their research also employs network modeling to test whether classic low-dimensional social phenomena, like the halo effect, emerge as architectural artifacts when perceivers process highly constrained inputs like static faces. Additionally, they are adapting multivariate tools like Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA) for social cognition research and utilizing Large Language Models to study how stereotype representations dynamically shift across different situations, perceivers, and intersectional identities.

papers.title: Network models reveal high-dimensional social inferences in naturalistic settings beyond latent construct models
papers.abstract: Traditional social cognition research posits that trait inferences are governed by a sparse set of latent dimensions, such as warmth and competence. We tested the high-dimensional properties of social inferences across two pre-registered studies using computationally sampled naturalistic videos and U.S. representative participants (Study 1, N = 1,598). While cross-validation indicated that 25 latent dimensions explained only 15% of the data variance, a sparse network model capturing unique, unreducible correlations between inferences provided a superior fit. These network models further elucidated the dynamics of naturalistic impressions, demonstrating how inferences co-occur and evolve from concrete observations to abstract social judgments over time.
papers.authors: Junsong Lu, Chujun Lin

papers.title: A Tutorial on Representational Similarity Analysis for Research in Social Cognition
papers.abstract: Representational similarity analysis (RSA) is a versatile multivariate technique for comparing representational structures across diverse data modalities, such as neuroimaging and behavioral ratings, by projecting them into a common similarity space. Despite its utility in quantifying relationships between complex, high-dimensional measures with incomparable units, existing tutorials are primarily tailored for neuroscience applications. This tutorial provides an accessible introduction to RSA for social cognition researchers, evaluating its methodological strengths and limitations relative to other multivariate approaches. We present commented R and Python implementations and demonstrate RSA's application through two case studies relevant to the study of social representational structures.
papers.authors: Sally Y. Xie, Ruoying Zheng, Eric Hehman, Chujun Lin

papers.title: Small-World Minds Create the Illusion of Low-Dimensional Social Cognition Under Constrained Stimuli
papers.abstract: While naturalistic social cognition exhibits high dimensionality, traditional paradigms using constrained stimuli (e.g., group labels, static faces) frequently reveal low-dimensional structures. We propose a network-based reconciliation: social inferences are mentally represented as a growing network with small-world properties. In this architecture, nodes are highly interconnected such that limited activation from constrained inputs propagates rapidly across the network, generating spurious covariation that mimics low-dimensional latent factors. Through mathematical proof and simulations, we demonstrate that these dimensions are emergent artifacts of stimulus limitations rather than functional psychological primitives, effectively accounting for the halo effect and other classic low-dimensional phenomena.
papers.authors: Junsong Lu, Chujun Lin

papers.title: The paradox of trait impressions in naturalistic contexts: rich information, sparse predictive cues
papers.abstract: In naturalistic person perception, humans are presented with a wealth of visual and contextual information, yet the specific informational drivers of trait impressions remain poorly understood. We utilized computational tools to quantify multidimensional cues (facial, bodily, clothing, and environmental) from 444 naturalistic videos. Across large-scale studies (N = 3,734), we observed that despite the availability of rich information, people rely on a sparse subset of predictive cues to form trait impressions. Notably, perceivers prioritized controllable cues—such as body posture and clothing—over uncontrollable facial structural features. These findings suggest that the human mind leverages learned co-occurrence structures to simplify information processing in naturalistic social environments.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the Annual Meeting of the Cognitive Science Society
papers.authors: Ruoying Zheng, Chujun Lin

papers.title: Stereotypes at the intersection of perceivers, situations, and categories: analyzing stereotypes from storytelling using natural language processing
papers.abstract: Stereotypes are typically investigated as a function of static group labels, yet they are situated in complex social contexts. We conducted two pre-registered studies (N = 1,721) where participants generated free-form stories about how 9 social groups are perceived across 6 representative situations and 30 intersectional identities. Applying large language models (LLMs) to analyze narrative content, we found that stereotypes exhibit significant variability across both perceivers and situations. Intersectional analyses revealed asymmetric integration effects and dominance effects (e.g., Asian identity dominating other crossed-categories), suggesting that individual experiences and situational norms interact with category representativeness to shape stereotype content in the real world.
papers.authors: Yilin Wang, Chujun Lin

0132.name: Chunyue Teng
0132.bio: Chunyue Teng is the Dennis and Charlot Nelson Singleton Assistant Professor of Cognitive Neuroscience at Lawrence University and directs the Visual Memory & Cognition Lab. Teng’s research investigates the neural mechanisms governing the interaction between visual perception and working memory, focusing on how top-down cognitive control resolves representational conflicts. They utilize a multi-modal approach integrating high-resolution electroencephalography (EEG), psychophysics, and computational modeling to examine oscillatory neural dynamics and flexible coding schemes. This work explores how the brain maintains sensory information over time and the extent to which mnemonic representations overlap with early perceptual processing.
0132.research_direction: Dr. Teng's recent work explores the dynamic interplay between visual working memory and concurrent visual perception. Using a combination of psychophysics, EEG, fMRI, and computational modeling, they have recently been investigating how the cognitive system resolves processing conflict when internal mnemonic representations overlap with external sensory inputs. Their research specifically probes how proactive and reactive cognitive control mechanisms are rapidly updated on a trial-by-trial basis to mitigate this bidirectional interference. Additionally, Dr. Teng is examining the neural and temporal architecture of memory maintenance, testing how early visual and parietal cortices divide the labor of storing stimulus "content" versus situational "context," and investigating whether working memory traces retain a persistent sensory format across extended temporal delays.

papers.title: Temporal Dynamics and Representational Consequences of the Control of Processing Conflict between Visual Working Memory and Visual Perception
papers.abstract: Visual working memory (WM) frequently interfaces with concurrent perceptual operations. When representational overlap induces processing conflict, cognitive control mechanisms must be deployed to attenuate bidirectional interference. In this electroencephalography (EEG) study, human observers completed a dual-task paradigm requiring perceptual orientation discrimination while concurrently retaining an oriented stimulus in WM. Employing a Bayesian feedback control model (FCM), trial-wise fluctuations were decomposed into distinct proactive (preparatory) and reactive (reflexive) control processes. Pre-stimulus preparatory control scaled with anticipated conflict and was electrophysiologically indexed by frontal midline theta-band (4–7 Hz) power. Upon presentation of the perceptual discriminandum, reflexive control was recruited proportionally to conflict prediction error. When an incongruent discriminandum appeared unexpectedly, reactive control suppressed its neural representation, as evidenced by below-baseline multivariate inverted encoding model (IEM) reconstruction fidelity; this stimulus suppression subsequently produced an inverted (repulsive) serial dependence bias in WM recall on the following trial. These findings demonstrate the dynamic coordination of proactive preparation and reactive suppression in adjudicating representational competition between visual perception and mnemonic maintenance.
papers.authors: Chunyue Teng, Jacqueline M. Fulvio, Mattia Pietrelli, Jiefeng Jiang, Bradley R. Postle

papers.title: Proactive control CAN be updated on a trial-by-trial basis
papers.abstract: This research addresses the mechanistic distinction between proactive and reactive modes of cognitive control within the domain of visual working memory (WM) and perception interactions. Contrary to traditional accounts that characterize proactive control as a stable, list-level strategic bias adjusted over long timescales, this work provides evidence that preparatory control states are updated at a trial-by-trial resolution. Utilizing behavioral data and computational modeling, the authors demonstrate that control prediction errors (PEs)—representing the discrepancy between expected and observed conflict—dynamically reconfigure the level of preparatory control for subsequent trials. The findings suggest that the mental coordination between internal mnemonic representations and external sensory inputs is governed by a reinforcement learning-based control architecture capable of rapid, flexible updates to mitigate processing interference.
papers.authors: Brad Postle, Chunyue Teng

papers.title: Investigating the Roles of the Visual and Parietal Cortex in Representing Content versus Context in Visual Working Memory
papers.abstract: The binding of stimulus identity (content) to trial-specific situational variables (context) is critical for effective working memory (WM) maintenance. Prior fMRI research using dual-serial retrocueing (DSR) with oriented gratings revealed that item content was maintained in early visual cortex (EVC), whereas spatial context was tracked in the intraparietal sulcus (IPS), with unprioritized memory items (UMIs) undergoing priority-dependent representational transformation relative to prioritized memory items (PMIs). In this registered report, fMRI was acquired in 24 healthy participants performing a DSR task in which spatial position served as the probed content and grating orientation served as task-relevant context. We evaluated three alternative frameworks: a domain-dependent account, a functional account (content vs. context regardless of feature space), and a hybrid account wherein IPS indexes contextual variables across domains while preserving content sensitivity. Inverted encoding models (IEMs) revealed that delay-period activity in EVC supported functional predictions, demonstrating robust priority-modulated coding of spatial location (content) without decodable orientation (context) profiles. Conversely, IPS delay-period signals matched the hybrid model, actively tracking location content alongside prioritized orientation context. Exploratory analyses in IPS further demonstrated univariate BOLD sensitivity to parametric modulations in content and context load that predicted behavioral precision, underscoring the dissociable functional contributions of sensory and posterior parietal areas in structuring WM representations.
papers.authors: Chunyue Teng, Bradley R. Postle

papers.title: Assessing the interaction between working memory and perception through time
papers.abstract: Visual working memory (VWM) maintenance directly modulates concurrent visual discrimination, reflecting shared representational substrates in posterior perceptual cortices. However, the temporal stability of this sensory recruitment remains debated: mnemonic traces may persist continuously as sensory-like codes or be converted into abstract, categorical formats over extended delays. Here, we manipulated the inter-stimulus interval (ISI) separating memory encoding from an intermediate perceptual discrimination task to dissociate temporal decay within sensory representations from abstract recoding models. Observers encoded simple visual features (color or orientation) into VWM before performing fine-grained same/different psychophysical judgments. Task-relevant features maintained across retention intervals systematically shifted perceptual discrimination thresholds for up to 4 s, demonstrating that sensory-level tuning profiles remain functionally active across time rather than converting to non-sensory codes. In contrast, task-irrelevant dimensions of the memory item exerted only brief, rapidly decaying interference on perceptual judgments. Concurrently, perceptual comparisons introduced an attractive report bias into mnemonic representations that increased monotonically across retention intervals. These results demonstrate the persistent sensory nature of prioritized visual working memory representations throughout extended maintenance periods.
papers.authors: Chunyue Teng, Simon M. Kaplan, Sarah Shomstein, Dwight J. Kravitz

0133.name: Cindy Xiong Bearfield
0133.bio: Cindy Xiong Bearfield is an Assistant Professor in the School of Interactive Computing at Georgia Tech, where they study the intersection of cognitive psychology, vision science, and human-computer interaction. Xiong Bearfield’s research investigates the perceptual and cognitive processes underlying data interpretation, focusing on how visual design choices influence decision-making, trust, and the mitigation of cognitive biases. They use empirical methodologies to map vision science mechanisms—such as ensemble coding, top-down salience, and visual search—to graphical perception tasks to develop visualization systems. Xiong Bearfield is a recipient of an NSF CAREER award and a founding leader of the VISxVISION initiative, which connects the visualization and vision science research communities.
0133.research_direction: Dr. Xiong Bearfield has recently been investigating the perceptual and cognitive mechanisms underlying how humans interact with data visualizations. Their recent work explores how fundamental visual processes—such as visual search, spatial attention, and ensemble coding—map onto complex graphical tasks, and how a viewer's individual visualization literacy drives distinct scanpath behaviors. Beyond core visual processing, they are developing psychometric scales and scalable crowdsourcing methods to measure higher-level cognitive phenomena, asking how specific chart affordances bias semantic takeaways and how readers establish trust in visual data. Additionally, their research actively tests whether Large Language Models can serve as valid behavioral proxies for human observers by probing the alignment between AI-generated data insights and human interpretative biases.

papers.title: Tell Me Without Telling Me: Two-Way Prediction of Visualization Literacy and Visual Attention
papers.abstract: This research investigates the integration of individual differences into the design of effective data visualizations by examining the interplay between visual literacy and attentional behavior. Utilizing a large-scale user study (N=235) across multiple literacy assessments including mini-VLAT, CALVI, and SGL, the authors characterize distinct scanpath patterns: individuals with high literacy scores demonstrate concentrated attentional focus on task-relevant features, whereas lower-scoring individuals exhibit more dispersed exploratory behavior. The study introduces two novel computational frameworks: Lit2Sal, a literacy-aware saliency model that outperforms traditional benchmarks in predicting observer attention, and Sal2Lit, which predicts visualization literacy levels with 86% accuracy based on a single attention map. These models facilitate personalized visual data communication by calibrating design based on estimated user expertise.
papers.venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
papers.authors: Minsuk Chang, Yao Wang, Huichen Will Wang, Yuanhong Zhou, Andreas Bulling, Cindy Xiong Bearfield

papers.title: Write, Rank, or Rate: Comparing Methods for Studying Visualization Affordances
papers.abstract: Visualization affordances denote how specific graphical design choices bias the semantic takeaways of readers. While traditionally measured through resource-intensive free-response crowdsourcing, this paper evaluates more scalable elicitation methodologies: visualization ranking, conclusion ranking, and salience rating. Through empirical comparisons across line charts, dot plots, and heatmaps, the authors demonstrate that while no individual method perfectly mirrors free-response results, combined ranking and rating strategies provide a robust proxy for identifying chart-level affordances at scale. Additionally, the paper presents a case study using GPT-4o, revealing that while Large Language Models can effectively perform salience rating, they diverge significantly from human interpretative biases in ranking tasks, suggesting limitations in their use as autonomous proxies for visualization research.
papers.venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
papers.authors: Chase Stokes, Kylie Lin, Cindy Xiong Bearfield

papers.title: Bridging Network Science and Vision Science: Mapping Perceptual Mechanisms to Network Visualization Tasks
papers.abstract: Despite the prevalence of network visualizations in modeling complex relational data, their graphical perception remains understudied relative to conventional charts. This work addresses the research gap by proposing a theoretical framework that maps five core perceptual mechanisms—visual search, attention, ensemble coding, perceptual organization, and object recognition—to standard network analytical tasks. By systematically applying this framework to re-evaluate four previous empirical studies, the authors identify critical perceptual bottlenecks in node-link diagram interpretation.
