The paper outlines a roadmap for future research, advocating for the integration of vision science principles to optimize the layout and encoding of network data to better align with human cognitive constraints.
papers.venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
papers.authors: S. Sandra Bae, Kyle R. Cave, Carsten Görg, Paul Rosen, Danielle Albers Szafir, Cindy Xiong Bearfield

papers.title: Do You “Trust” This Visualization? An Inventory to Measure Trust in Visualizations
papers.abstract: Trust is a fundamental yet inconsistently measured construct in visual data communication. This paper employs a bottom-up, data-driven approach to operationalize the reader's perspective of trust in visualizations. Through a broad compilation of trust statements and subsequent exploratory factor analysis (EFA), the authors identify three primary dimensions of the construct: information credibility, comprehensibility, and usability. Based on these factors, they developed and validated an eight-item standardized inventory, comprising four core items for measuring visualization-specific trust and four items to control for baseline trust disposition. The inventory's reliability was confirmed via McDonald’s omega, and its criterion validity was established through trust-based investment games with real-world stakes, providing a validated instrument for future empirical research in human-data interaction.
papers.venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
papers.authors: Huichen Will Wang, Kylie Lin, Andrew Cohen, Ryan Kennedy, Zach Zwald, Carolina Nobre, Cindy Xiong Bearfield

papers.title: How Aligned are Human Chart Takeaways and LLM Predictions? A Case Study on Bar Charts with Varying Layouts
papers.abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed to automate data insights, this study critically evaluates the alignment between LLM-generated takeaways and human interpretations of bar charts. The authors systematically vary chart layouts and compare the resulting takeaways for factual accuracy, semantic diversity, and attention to specific data points. The results indicate that state-of-the-art LLMs often fail to replicate human-like interpretative patterns, frequently missing nuanced trends or focusing on different data comparisons than human readers. The findings highlight significant limitations in using current LLMs for zero-shot visualization interpretation and emphasize the necessity for better-calibrated models that account for the visual and semantic hierarchies inherent in graphical representations.
papers.venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
papers.authors: Huichen Will Wang, Jane Hoffswell, Sao Myat Thazin Thane, Victor S. Bursztyn, Cindy Xiong Bearfield

0134.name: Claus-Christian Carbon
0134.department: Department of General Psychology and Methodology
0134.bio: Claus-Christian Carbon is the Chair of General Psychology and Methodology at the University of Bamberg and serves as the Dean of the Faculty of Human Sciences. Carbon’s research focuses on empirical aesthetics, the cognitive mechanisms of face processing, and the temporal dynamics of aesthetic appreciation and innovation acceptance. Carbon employs experimental psychophysics, eye-tracking, and multidimensional scaling to investigate perceptual phenomena ranging from optical illusions to haptic design. Carbon is the editor-in-chief of the journal Art & Perception and the founder of the international EPÆG research network.
0134.research_direction: Dr. Carbon's recent work explores a remarkably diverse array of topics spanning cognitive psychology, applied sensory perception, and macro-level industry transitions. In the realm of visual and cognitive processing, they are investigating how artistic framing alters the "art mode" of perception, specifically testing how different contexts and labels influence viewers' moral evaluations of depicted behaviors. Their research also extends into applied sensory science, utilizing continuous evaluation procedures to track the dynamic, moment-to-moment subjective appraisal of acoustic soundscapes in electric vehicles. Furthermore, they have recently been applying qualitative and mixed-methods approaches to map complex organizational and socio-economic systems, investigating cultural trajectories in high-end gastronomy, the role of transformational leadership in digital servitization, and the structural architecture of green hydrogen energy initiatives.

papers.title: Art for art's sake? The influence of art framing and context on the evaluation of immoral behaviour
papers.abstract: This research investigates the cognitive modulation of moral evaluation within the 'art mode' of processing, specifically examining how artistic framing (gallery vs. computer-generated context) affects the appraisal of depicted immoral behavior. Utilizing an experimental paradigm to contrast identical stimuli across differing labels, the study demonstrates that art status enables a qualitative shift in processing, allowing viewers to decouple depictions from conventional automated evaluative heuristics and socio-moral scripts. The findings suggest that artistic context serves as a primary catalyst for art-specific processing, facilitating an ethical dialogue disentangled from strict categorical judgments.
papers.authors: Itay Goetz, Lara Bernhardt, Friederike Margareta Karg, Alexander (Sasha) Pastukhov, Claus-Christian Carbon

papers.title: Envisioning the Future of Fine Dining: Insights from a Multi-Methods Study in Germany
papers.abstract: Utilizing a qualitatively driven mixed-methods approach, this study delineates long-term structural and cultural trajectories in high-end gastronomy within the German sector. The methodology integrates an inductive media content analysis with ten semi-structured expert interviews conducted with prominent figures in the field, employing Mayring's inductive category development for thematic clustering. By isolating pre-pandemic data (2018–2019) to exclude transitory pandemic effects, the analysis identifies a paradigm shift toward sustainability-oriented restaurant concepts characterized by regionalism, narrative-driven experiences, and the integration of emerging societal values into the architecture of fine dining.
papers.authors: Yana Subbotina-Dubinski, Claus-Christian Carbon

papers.title: The role of transformational leadership in navigating digital servitization
papers.abstract: This study maps the global research landscape of leadership in the context of digital transformation and servitization through a comprehensive bibliometric analysis of 1,147 publications indexed in the Scopus database (2015–2024). The analysis identifies key research hotspots and emerging themes, characterizing transformational leadership as a critical enabler for aligning digital strategies with organizational goals, mitigating institutional resistance, and facilitating the transition to holistic, data-driven service models. The findings emphasize the necessity of transformational leadership in exploiting big data analytics to establish competitive advantages in the digital age.
papers.authors: Florian Tagscherer, Claus-Christian Carbon

papers.title: Developing the architecture and characteristics for a green hydrogen ecosystem to effectively accelerate the energy transition: a contribution to innovation leadership
papers.abstract: Adopting an exploratory mixed-methods design, this research investigate the structural architecture and role characteristics of the Green Hydrogen Ecosystem (GHE) to accelerate decarbonization efforts under the Paris Agreement. The study involved 22 semi-structured expert interviews and a subsequent focus group discussion with 24 participants to validate practical insights. Qualitative content analysis identified five primary actor segments (equipment/service providers, governments/authorities, the hydrogen market, consumers, and expert councils). A key finding highlights the subjective perception of low return on investment (ROI) as a significant barrier to joint value creation and sustainable transition within the ecosystem.
papers.authors: Daniel Schwappach, Werner G. Faix, Jens Mergenthaler, Claus-Christian Carbon

papers.title: Unfolding dynamics in the perception of interior vehicle acoustics via continuous evaluation procedure (CEP)
papers.abstract: This study employs the Continuous Evaluation Procedure (CEP) to analyze the dynamic subjective appraisal of evolving soundscapes in electrified vehicles (EVs), specifically during acceleration run-ups. The research builds on previous findings of a significant negative correlation (τ = −0.32, p < 0.001) between the perceptibility of e-powertrain noise and overall qualitative impressions. By utilizing CEP, the authors demonstrate how participants continuously assess the quality of non-stationary acoustic signals, identifying temporal dynamics that single-value ratings fail to capture. The findings underscore the importance of dynamic refinement in e-NVH (Noise, Vibration, and Harshness) engineering to meet driver expectations for premium acoustic profiles.
papers.authors: Mara Münder, Gregor-Johannes Müller, Marius H. Raab, Claus-Christian Carbon

0135.name: Clayton E Curtis
0135.bio: Clayton E. Curtis is a Professor of Psychology and Neural Science at New York University who investigates the neural architecture of spatial working memory and cognitive control. Curtis focuses on the functional role of persistent neural activity within the frontoparietal cortex and how these signals mediate the integration of perception, attention, and motor planning. Utilizing a multi-modal approach including high-resolution fMRI, intracranial recordings (iEEG/ECoG), and computational modeling, their work characterizes the topographical organization of priority maps and the circuit-level dynamics that support goal-directed behavior. Additionally, Curtis examines how disruptions in these cognitive control mechanisms contribute to the pathophysiology of psychiatric disorders like schizophrenia.
0135.research_direction: Dr. Curtis has recently been investigating the neural architecture underlying spatial working memory and motor planning across the human cortical hierarchy. Their recent work explores how the brain flexibly allocates resources to prioritize mnemonic information, using fMRI and inverted encoding models to test whether this prioritization operates via population-level gain modulation. They are also examining the spatiotemporal dynamics of top-down control, mapping how memory drift and goal-directed signals propagate from the prefrontal and frontoparietal cortices down to early visual areas. Furthermore, they are probing the structure and necessity of these spatial representations, employing multivariate decoding to test if movement goals for saccades and reaches are stored in an abstract, effector-general format, while using targeted TMS-EEG to evaluate the causal role of the primary visual cortex in preserving high-fidelity visual working memory.

papers.title: Dynamics of working memory drift and information flow across the cortical hierarchy
papers.abstract: The researchers employed time-resolved fMRI decoding to characterize the spatiotemporal evolution of spatial working memory (WM) representations across the human cortical hierarchy during a memory-guided saccade task. By quantifying the directional drift of decoded neural signals toward behavioral report errors, the study found that behaviorally predictive mnemonic drift manifests earliest in higher-order dorsal visual and parietal areas (V3AB and IPS0) before propagating to the primary visual cortex (V1). Connectivity analysis indicated that feedback signals from these high-level topographic maps scale the precision of representations in early sensory areas, suggesting that persistent activity in the frontoparietal cortex drives the maintenance of high-fidelity mnemonic information via top-down information flow.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS)
papers.authors: Hsin-Hung Li, Wei Ji Ma, Clayton E. Curtis

papers.title: Effector general representation of movement goals in human frontal and parietal cortex
papers.abstract: This study addressed whether movement goal representations in the human frontoparietal cortex are effector-specific or maintained in an abstract, effector-general format. Using high-resolution fMRI and a delayed-response paradigm involving saccades and reaches, the authors applied multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) to topographic maps in the frontal eye fields (FEF) and intraparietal sulcus (IPS). The results demonstrated that spatial movement goals could be decoded across effectors, with neural patterns for planned reaches successfully classifying the locations of planned saccades. These findings indicate that the cortical architecture for motor planning utilizes an abstract mnemonic format to represent movement goals, facilitating the flexible translation of spatial information into diverse motor outputs.
papers.authors: Ziyi Duan, Margaret H. Evans, Benjamin Lawrence, Clayton E. Curtis

papers.title: Neural mechanisms of resource allocation in working memory
papers.abstract: To investigate the neural substrates of flexible resource allocation in working memory, the researchers utilized fMRI and inverted encoding models (IEMs) to reconstruct feature-selective mnemonic representations of oriented gratings. Using a two-item delayed-match-to-sample task with priority cues, they observed that behavioral prioritization was associated with a selective increase in the gain of neural population responses for the cued item across the visual and parietal hierarchy. This gain modulation, rather than a change in tuning width, predicted the precision of subsequent memory reports. The results suggest that the brain implements working memory prioritization by scaling the gain of population-level representations to optimize the fidelity of goal-relevant information.
papers.authors: Hsin-Hung Li, Thomas C. Sprague, Aspen Yoo, Wei Ji Ma, Clayton E. Curtis

papers.title: Perturbing human V1 degrades the fidelity of visual working memory
papers.abstract: This study provided causal evidence for the functional necessity of the primary visual cortex (V1) in maintaining high-fidelity visual working memory (WM). Using a combined TMS-EEG approach, the researchers applied rhythmic transcranial magnetic stimulation to retinotopically defined areas of V1 during the delay period of a spatial WM task. Physiological verification via EEG confirmed the local efficacy of the perturbation. Behavioral results demonstrated that V1 disruption significantly increased the error (decreased fidelity) of memory-guided saccades specifically for targets in the affected portion of the visual field. These findings establish that V1 activity is essential for the precise maintenance of visual representations required for goal-directed behavior.
papers.authors: Max Dake, Clayton E. Curtis

papers.title: Prioritizing working memory resources depends on the prefrontal cortex
papers.abstract: This research examined the role of the prefrontal cortex (PFC) in the flexible allocation of resources to items in working memory. Participants performed a spatial WM task with varying priority cues while undergoing fMRI. The study found that priority-dependent improvements in memory precision were reflected in the amplitude of persistent activity and the quality of spatial reconstructions in the PFC. Analysis of effective connectivity and voxel-wise modeling indicated that the PFC exerts top-down influence over sensory areas to bias representations according to task goals. The results suggest that the PFC is a critical node for the goal-directed prioritization of mnemonic information through the modulation of lower-level representations.
papers.authors: Gabrielle E. Hallenbeck, Nathan Tardiff, Thomas C. Sprague, Clayton E. Curtis

0136.name: Clayton Hickey
0136.bio: Clayton Hickey is an Associate Professor at the University of Birmingham and directs the Motivated Cognition Lab within the Centre for Human Brain Health. Hickey's research utilizes multimodal neuroimaging techniques, including fMRI, EEG, and MEG, alongside eye-tracking and pharmacological challenges to investigate how reward, reinforcement learning, and statistical regularities modulate visual attention. Their work examines incentive salience and the neural mechanisms of distractor suppression, employing electrophysiological analyses to characterize how the brain prioritizes environmental stimuli. Current research focuses on the intersection of object-based attention and reward feedback to understand the resolution of representational ambiguity in complex naturalistic scenes.
0136.research_direction: Dr. Hickey has recently been investigating the neural mechanisms that bridge visual selective attention, reward processing, and sensorimotor control. Their recent work explores how spatial attention mediates the translation of low-level perceptual inputs into high-level conceptual representations, and how visual selection is dynamically shaped by both structural object boundaries and learned reward associations. Beyond visual prioritization, they are studying the continuous interplay between sensory feedback and motor execution. Specifically, they use high-density EEG and force-control paradigms to examine how distinct neural oscillations coordinate real-time motor error correction, and how motivational incentives interact with visual and proprioceptive signals to optimize fine motor precision.

papers.title: Neural mechanisms for the attention-mediated propagation of conceptual information in the human brain
papers.abstract: The transition from perceptual input to conceptual representation is a fundamental aspect of adaptive cognition, yet the role of selective attention in this propagation is not well-defined. Using machine learning of high-density EEG and concurrently recorded EEG/fMRI, we identified the spatiotemporal characteristics of the neural network that abstracts semantic information from attended stimuli. We discovered that natural variance in the amplitude of the N2pc—an event-related potential (ERP) marker of spatial selection—predicts the quality of subsequent semantic category information carried by the neural signal. This attention-mediated propagation occurs within a discrete network comprising the prefrontal cortex, posterior parietal cortex, and anterior insular cortex. Our findings suggest that selective attention acts as a critical mechanism for the translation of low-level visual data into high-level conceptual codes suitable for semantics and action planning.
papers.authors: David Acunzo, Damiano Grignolio, Clayton Hickey

papers.title: How visual and proprioceptive feedback mediate the effect of monetary incentive on motor precision
papers.abstract: Motivational incentives are known to enhance motor performance, but the sensory pathways through which these effects are mediated remain unclear. This research utilized an isometric force control task across two experiments to determine how visual and proprioceptive feedback interact with monetary rewards. In the first experiment, incentives improved motor precision only in the presence of continuous visual feedback, suggesting that rewards primarily optimize feedback-based corrective cycles. In the second experiment, simplifying target representations to be more distinct through somatosensation and proprioception allowed incentives to enhance performance even without visual feedback. These results demonstrate that the impact of motivation on fine motor control is constrained by the availability and quality of sensory representations, whether derived from visual or proprioceptive modalities.
papers.authors: Nicholas Menghi, Giorgio Coricelli, Clayton Hickey

papers.title: Neural Mechanisms of Object Prioritization in Vision
papers.abstract: The theory of object-based attention suggests that the selection of an object part leads to the automatic prioritization of the entire object. However, recent behavioral challenges have argued that these effects might be artifacts of hemifield anisotropies or visual clutter. To test the validity of object-based prioritization, we recorded EEG during a cueing task involving task-irrelevant object boundaries. We analyzed two indices of attentional deployment: lateralized alpha oscillations and the anterior directional attentional negativity (ADAN). Our findings show that both the ADAN and alpha power lateralization are modulated by the orientation of irrelevant rectangle stimuli, independently of spatial cueing or hemifield location. These results provide neurophysiological evidence that object boundaries exert a direct influence on the spatial deployment of human visual attention, supporting the prioritization of objects as integrated structural units.
papers.authors: Damiano Grignolio, Sreenivasan Meyyappan, Joy J. Geng, George R. Mangun, Clayton Hickey

papers.title: Object-based attention is accentuated by object reward association
papers.abstract: While reward history is known to bias spatial and feature-based selection, its interaction with object-based attentional control is poorly understood. Across four experiments, we examined whether associating monetary rewards with specific objects modulates the strength of object-based prioritization. Participants performed a visual search task where specific rectangles were characterized by reward associations. Results indicated that reward significantly accentuated object-based selection; specifically, cued selection on a rewarded object led to greater prioritization of other locations on that object compared to neutral objects. This effect persisted during extinction and was not driven by the strategic utility of the reward. Our findings suggest that reward associations strengthen the attentional templates of objects, facilitating more robust information gathering from locations residing on reward-associated structural units.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
papers.authors: Damiano Grignolio, David J. Acunzo, Clayton Hickey

papers.title: Neural Oscillations Coordinate Continuous Error Correction During Force Control
papers.abstract: Precise motor control requires the brain to continuously monitor performance and execute feedback-based corrections. In this study, we used high-density EEG and an isometric force control task to identify the oscillatory dynamics supporting real-time error correction. We observed that the presence of continuous visual feedback led to ~6 Hz rhythmic fluctuations in behavior, indicative of active correction loops. These behavioral rhythms were mirrored in the power of theta, alpha, and beta oscillations, which tracked the moment-to-moment variance in force production. When feedback was removed, performance decayed linearly and these neural signatures were markedly reduced. The results suggest that distinct neural frequency bands coordinate a dynamic feedback system that monitors deviations and updates motor commands to maintain stability in a closed-loop control fashion.
papers.authors: Nicholas Menghi, Elio Balestrieri, Damiano Grignolio, Giorgio Coricelli, Clayton Hickey

0137.name: Colin Clifford
0137.bio: Colin Clifford is a Professor at UNSW Sydney who researches the computational and neural mechanisms of human vision. Clifford examines how the visual system employs contextual information and sensory adaptation to encode features including orientation, motion, color, and social cues such as eye gaze. Using psychophysical techniques, neuroimaging, and computational modeling, they investigate the relationship between neural processing and visual awareness. Their research includes the study of gaze perception and the integration of social signals within the human brain.
0137.research_direction: Dr. Clifford has recently been investigating how spatial, temporal, and historical contexts shape visual perception across both low-level features and high-level forms. Their recent work explores the mechanisms of serial dependence in orientation perception, specifically testing how trial-by-trial feedback, perceptual uncertainty, and decisional confidence modulate history-driven biases toward previous stimuli or responses. In higher-level vision, they are probing the phenomenon of face pareidolia by using synthetic visual noise to determine the minimal stimulus requirements—such as 1/f spatial statistics and bilateral symmetry—that trigger animacy detection and drive subsequent social trait attributions like age and gender. Additionally, their research examines contextual modulation in biological motion, isolating how spatial flankers and temporal adaptation exert contrasting assimilative and repulsive effects on the perceived walking direction of point-light figures.

papers.title: Image primitives supporting perception of animate forms
papers.abstract: This study investigates the minimal stimulus requirements for triggering face pareidolia and other animate form perceptions by manipulating natural scene statistics and symmetry. Observers viewed synthetic noise patterns with varying spatiotemporal spectral characteristics. Results demonstrated that patterns mimicking the statistics of natural scenes (1/f spatiotemporal spectra) maximized pareidolic reporting. Vertical symmetry significantly enhanced the perception of animate agents, with faces being the primary category, but also including animals and mythical creatures. These findings suggest that the human visual system's template for animacy detection is tuned to the regularities of the natural environment and favors bilateral symmetry.
papers.authors: Lindsay M. Peterson, Kritika Sarna, Branka Spehar, Colin W. G. Clifford

papers.title: Effects of perceptual and decisional uncertainty on serial dependence in orientation perception
papers.abstract: The research explored whether serial dependence in orientation perception is modulated by uncertainty in the preceding 'inducer' trial, specifically decoupling perceptual accuracy from decisional confidence. Participants performed orientation reproductions on Gabor patches where signal-to-noise ratios (SNR) and levels of positive evidence were independently manipulated. While serial dependence was robustly increased by target trial uncertainty (low SNR or low confidence), no modulation of the bias was observed as a function of inducer trial uncertainty or confidence. These results indicate that serial dependence does not originate from biases toward previous decisional states but is likely localized to sensory or early representational stages of visual processing.
papers.authors: Zoë Little, Colin W. G. Clifford

papers.title: The effects of feedback and task accuracy in serial dependence to orientation
papers.abstract: The study examined how response feedback and task accuracy modulate assimilative serial dependence in orientation perception. Participants reproduced Gabor orientations while receiving either informative (correct/incorrect) or random trial-by-trial feedback. Significant positive biases toward both the previous stimulus and the response were observed only following positive feedback. On trials where the previous response was incorrect, the serial dependence effect was confined to the previous response itself rather than the stimulus orientation. These findings suggest that the internal representation driving history effects is better captured by the previous decision than the external stimulus on error trials, and that feedback post-perceptually regulates these dependencies.
papers.authors: Zoë Little, Colin W. G. Clifford

papers.title: Facing your expectations: Perceived characteristics of illusory faces in symmetrical visual noise
papers.abstract: This paper investigates the social trait attributions (e.g., gender, age, emotion) associated with face pareidolia to determine if they reflect top-down selection biases or intrinsic perceptual heuristics. By utilizing synthetic visual noise patterns to provide a 'context-free' stimulus set, the authors compared trait attributions in pareidolic noise versus natural objects. Results indicated that illusory faces perceived in synthetic patterns were characterized by specific social profiles, appearing significantly older and angrier than faces found in objects, alongside a robust male gender bias. These findings provide evidence that the social categorization of ambiguous stimuli is driven by systematic perceptual and cognitive biases rather than purely semantic associations with object images.
papers.authors: Lindsay M. Peterson, Kritika Sarna, Branka Spehar, Colin W. G. Clifford

papers.title: Effect of spatial context on perceived walking direction
papers.abstract: This research investigated spatial and temporal contextual modulation in biological motion by measuring perceived walking direction in point-light walkers. Spatial contextual effects were assessed by placing flanker walkers alongside a central target, while temporal effects were measured via adaptation. Results demonstrated that spatial context exerts an assimilative (attractive) effect, where the target's perceived direction is biased toward the flankers, contrasting with the repulsive aftereffects of temporal adaptation. The spatial attraction showed broad angular tuning with a peak at approximately 30° flanker deviation. These findings implicate dissociable neural mechanisms for spatial and temporal contextual processing that nevertheless appear to operate on a shared population of sensory channels coding for walking direction.
papers.authors: Chang Chen, W. Paul Boyce, Colin J. Palmer, Colin W. G. Clifford

0138.name: Cong Yu
0138.department: School of Psychological and Cognitive Sciences
0138.bio: Cong Yu is a Professor at the School of Psychological and Cognitive Sciences at Peking University and a Principal Investigator at the IDG/McGovern Institute for Brain Research. Yu’s research utilizes psychophysical and neuroimaging techniques to investigate the mechanisms of visual perceptual learning and brain plasticity in humans and non-human primates. Yu developed the 'double training' and 'Training-Plus-Exposure' (TPE) paradigms, which challenge theories of early cortical learning specificity. Their current research involves using two-photon calcium imaging to map population-level neuronal responses in the macaque visual cortex and translating perceptual learning principles into clinical treatments for amblyopia.
0138.research_direction: Dr. Yu has recently been investigating the functional architecture and population-level coding dynamics of the primary visual cortex, alongside distinct behavioral work on human time perception. Using cellular-resolution two-photon calcium imaging and computational decoding in awake macaques, their recent work explores the representational geometry of V1 to probe how neural ensembles multiplex basic visual features and to re-examine classic topographical theories like the "ice-cube" model. Within this physiological domain, they are also examining how visual context and awareness shape sensory encoding, specifically testing the orientation-specificity of surround modulation and evaluating how continuous flash suppression impacts the information density required for stimulus reconstruction. In a parallel line of psychophysical research, Dr. Yu investigates subsecond temporal processing, utilizing double-training paradigms to determine whether human interval discrimination is strictly bound to localized neural populations or governed by abstract, interval-invariant representations.

papers.title: Orthogonal neural geometry of orientation, spatial frequency, and ocular dominance in macaque V1
papers.abstract: Applying Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to high-dimensional population responses recorded via two-photon calcium imaging in awake macaque V1, this research demonstrates that the representational geometry for orientation, spatial frequency, and ocular dominance is near-orthogonal. Although cellular-resolution anatomical maps on the cortical surface do not exhibit consistent spatial orthogonality, the neuronal ensemble activity resides within a manifold where feature axes are decoupled. Computational modeling suggests that this latent orthogonal structure is vital for maintaining feature separability and robust decoding, indicating that population-level representational geometry, rather than physical modularity, serves as the organizing principle for multiplexing stimulus features in the primary visual cortex.
papers.authors: Xin Wang, Sheng-Hui Zhang, Shi-Ming Tang, Cong Yu

papers.title: Continuous flashing suppression of V1 responses and the perceptual consequences revealed via two-photon calcium imaging and transformer modeling
papers.abstract: This study employs cellular-resolution two-photon imaging in awake macaques to evaluate how continuous flash suppression (CFS) modulates V1 neuronal activity. The data reveal that a dynamic masker presented to one eye significantly attenuates orientation-selective responses across V1, particularly in masker-eye-preferring and binocular neurons. By utilizing a cross-attention transformer model to decode population activity, the investigators found that while coarse orientation signals persist, the suppression severely degrades the information density required for stimulus reconstruction. These results suggest that V1 serves as a physiological bottleneck under CFS, where the reduction in orientation information density precludes high-level visual processing and conscious awareness.
papers.authors: Cai-Xia Chen, Xin Wang, Dan-Qing Jiang, Shi-Ming Tang, Cong Yu

papers.title: Surround modulation is predominantly orientation-unspecific in macaque V1
papers.abstract: Using large-scale two-photon calcium imaging in awake, fixating macaques, the researchers investigated whether surround modulation in V1 is orientation-selective. While traditional theories emphasize iso-orientation suppression, population-level analysis revealed that surround modulation is predominantly orientation-unspecific. An iso-oriented surround was found to induce a general gain reduction across the entire orientation-tuned population rather than specifically targeting iso-oriented channels. Similarly, cross-oriented surrounds were shown to scale up population responses globally. These findings support a model where V1 surround modulation acts as a population-wide gain control mechanism to optimize the dynamic range and encoding efficiency of the neuronal ensemble.
papers.authors: Xing-Nan Zhao, Sheng-Hui Zhang, Shi-Ming Tang, Cong Yu

papers.title: Testing Hubel and Wiesel’s “ice-cube” model of functional maps at cellular resolution in macaque V1
papers.abstract: This research re-examines the classic 'ice-cube' model of V1 organization using single-cell resolution two-photon imaging in the superficial layers of macaque V1. By mapping orientation and ocular dominance (OD) across thousands of identified neurons, the study quantified the geometric relationships between their functional gradients. The results show that intersection angles among these maps are nearly uniformly distributed at the cellular level, contradicting the predicted systematic orthogonality of the modular ice-cube model. While pixel-based smoothing produced weak trends toward orthogonality consistent with previous low-resolution studies, these patterns did not accurately represent the raw cellular architecture, suggesting a more flexible and heterogeneous organization of the primate visual cortex.
papers.authors: Sheng-Hui Zhang, Shi-Ming Tang, Cong Yu

papers.title: Double training reveals an interval-invariant subsecond temporal structure in the brain
papers.abstract: To determine if subsecond time perception is governed by an abstract, interval-invariant representation, the investigators utilized a double training protocol in a temporal interval discrimination (TID) task. While TID learning is traditionally highly specific to the trained interval, the study found that practicing TID at one base interval (e.g., 100 ms) while simultaneously performing a secondary, independent task at a transfer interval (e.g., 200 ms) enabled a complete transfer of learning. These psychophysical results provide evidence for a supramodal and conceptual representation of subsecond time in the brain that is not strictly bound to the specific neural populations activated by a single duration, highlighting the generalizability of temporal skills through targeted training protocols.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
papers.authors: Shu-Chen Guan, Ying-Zi Xiong, Cong Yu

0139.name: Corey Bohil
0139.department: Department of Humanities, Social Sciences, and Communication
0139.bio: Corey Bohil is a cognitive neuroscientist and Professor of Psychology who researches the mechanisms of human categorization and decision-making. Bohil’s work utilizes computational modeling, immersive virtual and mixed-reality environments, and physiological assessments to examine how individuals classify environmental stimuli and perform in operational settings. Their research addresses the distinction between rule-based and information-integration category learning systems. Currently, Bohil employs functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) to monitor cortical activity during cognitive tasks and human-technology interactions.
0139.research_direction: Dr. Bohil has recently been investigating how distinct cognitive states and learning mechanisms manifest in continuous behavioral and oculomotor metrics. Their recent work explores objective methods for quantifying spatial presence in virtual reality by using rhythmic finger tapping kinematics and neural network classifiers to track dynamic attentional resource allocation during immersive experiences. Additionally, they are investigating how different category learning architectures—specifically explicit rule-based versus implicit information-integration systems—guide categorical visual search. By combining eye tracking with decision-bound computational modeling, Dr. Bohil examines how these dual learning pathways independently constrain search efficiency, initial saccade trajectories, and target dwell times.

papers.title: Finger Tapping as a Behavioral Indicator of Presence in VR
papers.abstract: Subjective post-trial questionnaires remain the dominant methodology for evaluating spatial presence in virtual environments (VEs), whereas physiological markers often exhibit inconsistent reliability. To assess continuous behavioral tracking of presence over time, this investigation evaluated rhythmic finger tapping as an index of dynamic attentional resource allocation. Participants wearing sensor-equipped data gloves performed motor tapping at a specified pace during two distinct virtual reality experiences: a virtual plank height manipulation (elevated vs. ground-level conditions) and 360-degree vs. 90-degree immersive video displays. Positional timeseries profiles of finger kinematics—including inter-tap interval dynamics, autocorrelation, and power spectral density—were used to train a neural network classifier. The classifier achieved an 80% accuracy rate in differentiating high- from low-presence states across both task environments, establishing motor timing disruption under secondary-task constraints as an objective, continuous behavioral marker of immersion.
papers.authors: Sean Hinkle, Shayna Soares, Corey Bohil

papers.title: Explicit and implicit category learning in categorical visual search
papers.abstract: Although categorical visual search is frequently studied using naturalistic objects whose cognitive representational structures are ill-defined, category learning frameworks dissociate classification into explicit rule-based systems relying on hypothesis testing and working memory, and implicit information-integration systems mediated by procedural striatal networks. This study assessed how these dual learning systems guide and constrain visual search using parametric sinusoidal grating stimuli. Following acquisition under either rule-based or information-integration demands, participants executed categorical visual search while eye tracking was monitored. Quantitative decision-bound computational modeling verified strategy implementation across acquisition and transfer phases. Implicit category learning facilitated faster overall search responses and reduced target dwell duration relative to rule-based learning. Furthermore, participants who successfully generalized the category structure demonstrated robust search guidance, with implicit learners exhibiting a significantly greater proportion of initial saccades directly fixating the target, demonstrating distinct oculomotor and behavioral signatures between dual categorization architectures.
papers.authors: Corey J. Bohil, Ashley Phelps, Mark B. Neider, Joseph Schmidt

0140.name: Cory Miller
0140.bio: Cory T. Miller is a Professor of Psychology at the University of California, San Diego, and directs research on the neurobiology of natural primate behaviors. Miller’s work utilizes marmoset monkeys to investigate the neural mechanisms of active vision and vocal communication, employing wireless electrophysiology and head-mounted eye-tracking in freely moving animals. By moving beyond head-restrained experimental paradigms, their lab explores how cortical circuits in the visual and frontal systems integrate perceptual, motor, and social information during tasks such as prey pursuit and antiphonal calling. Miller's research aims to elucidate how the primate brain evolved to process complex, dynamic stimuli in the environments found in the natural world.
0140.research_direction: Dr. Miller's recent work explores the neural and behavioral foundations of naturalistic social and perceptual behaviors in freely moving marmoset monkeys. To study active vision, they have recently been pairing novel wireless electrophysiology with head-mounted eye-tracking to investigate how natural locomotion and gaze shifts structure neural dynamics in the primary visual cortex. Beyond the visual system, their research investigates the neurobiology of complex communication, probing how the frontal and anterior cingulate cortices encode vocal turn-taking and resolve the auditory cocktail party problem during dynamic acoustic exchanges. Broadening this ethological approach, they are also examining how transient physiological states and ecological resource constraints flexibly modulate prosocial decision-making and cooperative behaviors.

papers.title: Ecological factors affecting prosociality in marmoset monkeys
papers.abstract: This study characterizes the impact of transient physiological and ecological variables on the prosocial tendencies of common marmosets (Callithrix jacchus). By systematically manipulating food divisibility and time since food access (TSFA), the authors observed that larger, divisible food portions significantly promoted unsolicited food-sharing and cooperative interactions. Conversely, acute hunger states (increased TSFA) shifted behavioral outcomes toward individualistic feeding. These findings demonstrate that primate prosociality is not a fixed trait but a flexible decision-making process modulated by immediate resource constraints and internal physiological states.
papers.authors: Anand R. Mysorekar, Anushka Vispute, Cory Miller

papers.title: Active gaze behavior organizes V1 activity in freely-moving marmosets
papers.abstract: Using head-mounted eye-tracking and wireless electrophysiology in freely-moving marmosets, this work investigates how naturalistic gaze behavior structures activity in the primary visual cortex (V1). The results show a robust temporal organization of V1 neural ensembles, characterized by significant suppression during rapid gaze shifts followed by a vision-dependent enhancement during subsequent fixations. These gaze-locked dynamics were largely abolished in complete darkness, indicating that active sensing and the resulting retinal dynamics—rather than non-visual motor signals—primary structure cortical processing during natural exploration.
papers.authors: Jingwen Li, Vikram Pal Singh, Jude F. Mitchell, Alexander C. Huk, Cory T. Miller

papers.title: Primate ACC encodes natural vocal interactions in a 'cocktail party'
papers.abstract: This research investigates the neurobiological basis of the 'cocktail party problem' (CPP) within the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) of marmosets. Recording from area 24 during vocal exchanges in a noisy colony environment, the authors found that single neurons selectively encode the vocalizations of a specific conversational partner while segregating them from background conspecific calls. This selectivity persists even during acoustic overlap, a critical requirement for resolving the CPP. Furthermore, ACC neurons track conversational dynamics by encoding turn-taking structures, identifying this region as a key substrate for social monitoring in complex acoustic environments.
papers.authors: Arthur Lefevre, Vikram Pal Singh, Timothy J. Tyree, Jingwen Li, Jean-René Duhamel, Cory T. Miller

papers.title: Active vision in freely moving marmosets using head-mounted eye tracking
papers.abstract: The authors introduce CEREBRO (Chair-free Eye-Recording using Backpack mounted micROcontrollers), a wireless system designed to quantify eye and head movements in small, freely moving primates. The study reveals that natural locomotion is associated with elevated saccadic speeds and an increase in vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR) gain. Despite the increased motor activity during movement, gaze behavior remains more predictable and stable in freely moving conditions compared to traditional head-fixed paradigms. This suggests that the primate visual system possesses specialized visuo-motor adaptations to maintain stable, high-resolution foveal vision during ethologically relevant active behaviors.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS)
papers.authors: Vikram Pal Singh, Jingwen Li, Kana Dawson, Jude F. Mitchell, Cory T. Miller

papers.title: Representing the dynamics of natural marmoset vocal behaviors in frontal cortex
papers.abstract: This study employs a model-based Generalized Linear Model (GLM) framework to analyze the activity of single neurons in the marmoset prefrontal and premotor cortex during natural vocal conversations. The analysis identifies distinct functional clusters of neurons that represent sensory (hearing calls), motor (producing calls), and internal social states. Crucially, these functional representations are distributed across an anatomically heterogeneous landscape in the frontal lobe, rather than mapping to established cortical subfields. These findings suggest a distributed functional architecture for the myriad neural mechanisms required to support complex, natural social signaling in primates.
papers.authors: Jingwen Li, Mikio C. Aoi, Cory T. Miller

0142.name: Cristina de la Malla
0142.department: Department of Cognition, Development and Psychology of Education
0142.lab_name: Vision and Control of Action Group (VISCA)
0142.bio: Cristina de la Malla is an Assistant Professor at the University of Barcelona and a member of the Vision and Control of Action Group. De la Malla’s research examines the sensorimotor integration of visual and proprioceptive information, specifically how the brain processes temporal delays and predictive signals to execute interceptive actions. They use methodologies such as psychophysics, eye-tracking, and virtual reality to study the relationship between saccadic eye movements and velocity judgments. Their work further investigates the temporal dynamics of foveal and peripheral processing during ocular fixation and the role of these processes in saccade planning and change localization.
0142.research_direction: Dr. de la Malla has recently been exploring the intricate links between visual processing, continuous sensorimotor control, and action decision-making. Their recent work investigates how prior sensory history influences online motor control during manual interception, and how spatial target geometry dictates the balance of implicit adaptation versus explicit strategies during visuomotor learning. In more naturalistic contexts, they use immersive virtual reality paradigms to examine how task-irrelevant environmental variability impacts metacognitive confidence, gaze behavior, and movement kinematics during complex whole-body actions like street crossing. Additionally, their research spans foundational visual encoding and oculomotor dynamics, investigating the contrasting temporal profiles of foveal and peripheral sensitivity during individual fixations as well as evaluating psychophysical contrast sensitivity in individuals with schizophrenia.

papers.title: Serial dependence in goal-directed interceptive hand movements
papers.abstract: This study investigates how recent sensory history influences continuous sensorimotor control during manual interception. Observers executed an interception task where each trial presented sequential targets: an initial prior target moving at 5 or 15 cm/s, followed by a probe target moving at 10 cm/s in either the congruent or incongruent direction. Interception conditions manipulated motor engagement by requiring participants either to intercept both targets or to passively observe the prior before intercepting the probe. Active interception of the prior induced direction-dependent serial dependencies: probe interception errors exhibited an attractive bias for congruent movement directions and a repulsive bias for opposing directions, whereas passive observation elicited no significant modulation. Analysis of hand velocity profiles and concomitant oculomotor dynamics demonstrated an early attractive sensory bias that decayed across the movement trajectory as real-time sensory evidence was continuously acquired to guide online feedback control.
papers.authors: Cristian Muñoz-Puelman, Alexander Goettker, Cristina de la Malla

papers.title: Scene variability affects action decisions, confidence and behaviour dynamics
papers.abstract: This work explores how task-irrelevant environmental variability influences action decisions, subjective confidence, sensory sampling, and motor execution within an immersive virtual reality street-crossing paradigm. Observers judged their confidence in successfully crossing or decided whether to actively cross while facing six oncoming vehicles under varying levels of velocity dispersion. Elevated scene variability decreased crossing attempt frequencies and reduced confidence reports while significantly prolonging crossing initiation latencies. Participants compensated for these delayed onsets by executing crossing trajectories with increased movement velocity, preserving task performance. Furthermore, oculomotor recordings revealed that high-confidence decisions and crossing initiations were characterized by accelerated information acquisition and faster subsequent gaze disengagement, showing that environmental variability alters both metacognitive evaluations and execution dynamics.
papers.authors: David Aguilar-Lleyda, Antonio González-Del Pozo, Joan López-Moliner, Cristina de la Malla

papers.title: Target configuration determines how and what we learn during sensorimotor adaptation
papers.abstract: This study examines how spatial target geometry dictates learning mechanisms and coordinate frame representations during sensorimotor adaptation. Human participants completed reaching tasks under visuomotor gain perturbations (0.7× or 1.3× display scaling) across two spatial configurations: an Extent Group trained on multiple reach amplitudes along a single vector, and an Angular Group trained on fixed amplitudes across multiple angular directions. In no-feedback aftereffect assays designed to isolate implicit adaptation from cognitive strategies, the Angular Group demonstrated substantially greater implicit aftereffects, whereas the Extent Group relied predominantly on explicit re-aiming. Generalization trials to unperturbed targets revealed distinct learned models: the Angular Group acquired an extrinsic translation rule generalizing across directions but failing across amplitudes, whereas the Extent Group captured a true multiplicative gain rule that generalized to untrained amplitudes but not across spatial directions.
papers.authors: Pamela Villavicencio, Jonathan S. Tsay, Cristina de la Malla

papers.title: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis on Contrast Sensitivity in Schizophrenia
papers.abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis synthesizes visual contrast sensitivity measurements across individuals with schizophrenia relative to healthy controls. Compiling psychophysical detection thresholds across spatial and temporal frequencies from clinical studies, the meta-analysis established a pronounced deficit in contrast sensitivity among patients with schizophrenia (Hedges' g = 0.64; 95% CI: 0.40–0.88). Meta-regression indicated that stimulus duration (comparing transient ~30 ms and sustained 500 ms presentations) did not significantly moderate effect magnitudes. However, elevated antipsychotic medication dosage correlated with enhanced threshold impairment. The analysis confirms generalized degradation in early contrast encoding pathways in schizophrenia while discussing how task-unrelated attentional lapses may contribute to observed psychophysical sensitivity reductions.
papers.authors: Daniel Linares, Aster Joostens, Cristina de la Malla

papers.title: Different temporal dynamics of foveal and peripheral visual processing during fixation
papers.abstract: This study analyzes the temporal dynamics of visual sensitivity across the fovea and periphery throughout the course of ocular fixations. Utilizing dual-Purkinje-style high-precision eye tracking to ensure fixation stability, observers performed an orientation transient localization task wherein target bars flashed at varying intervals post-fixation onset within foveal, peripheral, or combined retinotopic locations. Transient localization accuracy in the visual periphery exhibited monotonic improvement as fixation elapsed over time, whereas foveal localization performance remained uniform across the entire fixation epoch. This temporal dissociation persisted when foveal and peripheral regions were simultaneously attended without dual-task interference, demonstrating that extrafoveal visual processing is selectively amplified late in fixation, likely facilitating target selection and spatial programming for subsequent saccades.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Cristina de la Malla, Martina Poletti

0143.name: Curtis L. Baker Jr.
0143.bio: Baker is a professor at McGill University investigating the low-level neural mechanisms of human visual perception, specifically figure-ground segregation and depth perception. Their laboratory explores how the early visual system extracts information from natural scenes through cues such as contrast, texture, and non-Fourier motion. Through the integration of human psychophysics, single-unit electrophysiology, and computational modeling, Baker examines how cortical neurons integrate subcortical inputs to represent complex spatial structures. Recent research focuses on developing machine learning-based receptive field models and examining the laminar organization of visual signals in the primary visual cortex.
0143.research_direction: Dr. Baker has recently been developing advanced computational encoding models to better characterize receptive fields and response dynamics in the early visual cortex. Their recent work explores how customized convolutional neural network architectures can unify the modeling of phase-sensitive simple cells and phase-invariant complex cells into a single continuous framework. In parallel, they are investigating the mechanisms underlying trial-to-trial neuronal response variability, utilizing local field potentials and multi-unit activity to model how dynamic fluctuations in internal cortical states interact with stimulus-driven visual signals. Beyond neurophysiology and modeling, Dr. Baker also conducts human psychophysical experiments to probe second-order visual processing, specifically examining how luminance masking and chromatic contrast modulation stimuli can be used to isolate and assess the functional integrity of the magnocellular pathway.

papers.title: Cortical state contributions to neuronal response variability in the early visual cortex: A system identification approach
papers.abstract: The responses of individual neurons in the primary visual cortex (V1) to identical visual stimuli exhibit significant trial-to-trial variability, which is often dismissed as noise. This study challenges that view by demonstrating that much of this variability is driven by dynamic fluctuations in the brain's internal state. We developed a multi-pathway convolutional neural network (CNN) model that integrates a stimulus-driven pathway with a state-driven pathway. The latter utilizes indicators of cortical state fluctuations derived from simultaneously recorded local field potentials (LFPs) and multi-unit activity (MUA) in the vicinity of the target neuron. Using single-unit recordings from cat areas 17 and 18, we show that this integrated model significantly outperforms stimulus-only encoding models in predicting spiking activity. The predictive improvement was found to be heterogeneous across the population, with neurons exhibiting the highest intrinsic response variability benefiting most from the inclusion of internal state indicators. Furthermore, we identified neuron-specific temporal filters for LFP frequency bands, illustrating how different neurons are uniquely coupled to distinct aspects of population dynamics.
papers.authors: Jinani Sooriyaarachchi, Chang'an A. Zhan, Curtis L. Baker Jr.

papers.title: Estimating receptive fields of simple and complex cells in early visual cortex: A convolutional neural network model with parameterized rectification
papers.abstract: Characterizing the receptive fields (RFs) of early visual cortex neurons is complicated by the distinct behaviors of phase-sensitive simple cells and phase-invariant complex cells. While simple cells are well-modeled by linear-nonlinear (LN) systems, complex cells require more sophisticated hierarchical architectures to account for their nonlinear integration of subunit inputs. We present a compact CNN encoding model that employs a parameterized rectified linear unit (PReLU) to bridge the gap between simple and complex cell modeling. The architecture consists of a primary spatiotemporal filter, a PReLU nonlinearity with a single learnable gain parameter for negative inputs, and a two-dimensional Gaussian spatial map. The PReLU parameter serves as a continuous metric of phase invariance, allowing the model to smoothly transition between an LN structure for simple cells and a subunit-summation structure for complex cells. Applying this model to neurons in cat areas 17 and 18, we demonstrate high predictive performance for both natural image responses and sinewave grating tuning curves. Our results show that complex cells are intrinsically less reliable than simple cells, but noise ceiling analysis reveals that our model captures a comparable proportion of the explainable variance in both types.
papers.authors: Philippe Nguyen, Jinani Sooriyaarachchi, Qianyu Huang, Curtis L. Baker Jr.

papers.title: Impaired perception of isoluminant contrast modulation stimuli: Evidence for a magnocellular pathway mechanism
papers.abstract: Nonlinear responses to contrast modulation (CM) stimuli—where a high-frequency carrier's contrast is varied by a low-frequency envelope—have been hypothesized to originate from Y-like retinal ganglion cells within the magnocellular pathway. To investigate the dependency of CM processing on this pathway, we conducted human psychophysical experiments comparing motion direction discrimination and detection for achromatic (yellow-black) and chromatic (red-green) CM stimuli. We utilized luminance masking noise to selectively interfere with luminance-driven motion mechanisms. Our findings indicate that perception of chromatic CMs is significantly more susceptible to luminance masking than achromatic CMs. While envelope motion discrimination for achromatic stimuli was robust even under high noise conditions, performance for chromatic stimuli was severely degraded. Notably, detection of the chromatic modulator remained relatively intact despite the failure of motion discrimination, suggesting that chromatic aberrations may provide spurious luminance signals that facilitate detection but not directional judging. These results support the hypothesis that second-order CM envelope motion is predominantly processed by nonlinearities within the retino-geniculate magnocellular pathway, suggesting CM stimuli as a viable tool for assessing magnocellular integrity in clinical contexts.
papers.authors: Ana L. Ramirez, Anna Shakhgildian, Ari Rosenberg, Curtis L. Baker Jr.

0144.name: Daniel Baker
0144.bio: Daniel Hart Baker is a vision scientist who investigates sensory perception with a focus on human binocular and spatial vision. Baker’s research integrates psychophysics, electrophysiology (EEG and MEG), neuroimaging (fMRI), and computational modeling to examine how the brain combines signals across the eyes and over time. Their work on amblyopia demonstrates that binocular combination is possible in affected individuals, providing data for the development of clinical treatments. Baker has also developed technical resources for the field, including the textbook "Research Methods Using R" and statistical frameworks for power analysis and periodic data in neuroscience.
0144.research_direction: Dr. Baker’s recent work explores the computational rules and neural dynamics underlying sensory integration and visual cognition. They have recently been investigating how the nervous system combines signals and deploys gain control, using psychophysics and physiological measures to model contrast processing via steady-state visually evoked potentials (SSVEPs), binocular integration within the autonomic pupillary light response, and analogous sensory summation mechanisms in vibrotactile perception. Additionally, their research utilizes multivariate pattern analysis of EEG data to decode the temporal processing stages of complex perceptual and cognitive phenomena. Specifically, they are probing the neural correlates of the uncanny valley effect when observers view artificial faces, as well as examining how the cortical deployment of spatial attention is modulated by repetitive motor behaviors like "stimming."

papers.title: Neural correlates of the deployment of spatial attention, and their modulation by repetitive movements
papers.abstract: This research investigates the electrophysiological signatures of spatial attention and their potential modulation by repetitive stereotypies, commonly referred to as 'stimming'. Utilizing multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) of high-density EEG data, the study decodes the locus of attended spatial coordinates (left versus right hemifield) during a modified Posner cueing paradigm. Behavioral results indicate that while stimming movements—typically associated with autism and ADHD—induce a significant increase in absolute reaction times, they do not disrupt the fundamental efficacy of the attentional orienting mechanism or the classic congruency effect. Neural decoding accuracy remained robust across conditions, suggesting that the cortical implementation of spatial attention deployment is preserved during the execution of repetitive motor behaviors, providing evidence against the assumption that stimming necessarily indicates a state of sensory or attentional distraction.
papers.authors: Cameron Smith, Daniel H. Baker

papers.title: Measuring contrast processing in the visual system using the steady state visually evoked potential (SSVEP)
papers.abstract: This study presents a methodology for the objective quantification of contrast response functions (CRFs) in the human visual system using steady-state visually evoked potentials (SSVEPs). By applying periodic luminance modulations at specific temporal frequencies and performing frequency-domain analysis, the authors derive the non-linear contrast transducer functions that characterize early visual processing. The experiments demonstrate that SSVEP-based CRFs are sensitive to both excitatory and suppressive binocular interactions, providing a quantitative framework for assessing the gain control mechanisms that maintain perceptual constancy. The findings validate the use of SSVEP as a diagnostic tool for identifying specific deficits in contrast processing, particularly in the context of amblyopia and other conditions marked by atypical interocular normalization.
papers.authors: Alex R. Wade, Daniel H. Baker

papers.title: Neural correlates of the uncanny valley effect for robots and hyper-realistic masks
papers.abstract: The uncanny valley hypothesis posits that artificial entities that closely, but imperfectly, mimic human appearance elicit a distinct sense of psychological unease. This paper characterizes the neural correlates of this effect using EEG-based multivariate pattern classification to compare human faces with androids, mechanical robots, and silicone masks. While traditional univariate ERP analyses failed to detect significant differences, multivariate decoding identified two critical temporal windows of above-chance classification. An early component (100–200 ms) is hypothesized to reflect low-level encoding of structural visual discrepancies, whereas a later component (approximately 600 ms) appears to correlate with top-down evaluative processes and the subjective experience of eeriness. These results suggest that the uncanny valley effect is mediated by a late-stage categorization conflict following initial image processing.
papers.authors: Shona Fitzpatrick, Rae Yule Kim, Ailish K. Byrne, Alex Headley, Jet G. Sanders, Helen Petrie, Rob Jenkins, Daniel H. Baker

papers.title: Binocular combination in the autonomic nervous system
papers.abstract: While binocular integration in the visual cortex is well-documented, the rules governing signal combination in subcortical autonomic pathways are less understood. This study employs pupillometry and a binocular multiprimary display system to investigate how light signals from the two eyes are combined to regulate pupil diameter. Using silent substitution to isolate the L-M cone, S-cone, melanopsin, and light flux pathways, the authors demonstrate that binocular combination algorithms are pathway-specific. Light flux and S-cone responses exhibited strong binocular facilitation with minimal interocular suppression, whereas the L-M pathway showed evidence of binocular inhibition. Computational modeling using a hierarchical Bayesian framework reveals that the autonomic pupillary response operates under a distinct set of binocular gain control rules compared to the primary perceptual pathways in the visual cortex.
papers.authors: Federico G. Segala, Aurelio Bruno, Joel T. Martin, Anisa Y. Morsi, Alex R. Wade, Daniel H. Baker

papers.title: Signal combination in vibration perception
papers.abstract: This research utilizes psychophysical threshold measurements and EEG-based somatosensory evoked potentials (SEPs) to evaluate the mechanisms of vibrotactile signal combination across multiple digits. The study tests whether the integration of somatosensory inputs follows the suppressive gain control and summation rules typical of the visual and auditory systems. Discrimination thresholds for 26 Hz vibrations revealed a classic 'dipper' pattern, and increasing the number of stimulated fingers resulted in a weak improvement in sensitivity and a sub-linear increase in SEP amplitudes. Computational modeling indicates that tactile integration involves a unique balance of probability summation and inter-channel suppression, suggesting a specialized architecture for somatosensory signal combination that is functionally distinct from the binocular normalization models used in vision science.
papers.authors: Shasha Wei, Alex R. Wade, Catherine E. J. Preston, Daniel H. Baker

0145.name: Daniel D. Dilks
0145.bio: Daniel D. Dilks is an Associate Professor at Emory University, where their research explores the functional organization, development, and plasticity of the human visual cortex. Dilks investigates specialized cortical regions for processing scenes, faces, and objects, as well as how these systems emerge in childhood and reorganize following brain damage or sensory loss in adulthood. Using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), and psychophysics, Dilks characterizes the neural mechanisms underlying visually guided navigation and categorization. Their recent studies examine the protracted development of scene-selective regions and the distinct cognitive systems involved in navigating environments versus recognizing places.
0145.research_direction: Dr. Dilks has recently been investigating the functional architecture and developmental trajectories of human spatial navigation systems. Using pediatric fMRI, multivoxel pattern analysis, and computational modeling, their recent work explores how distinct cortical networks support different navigational modes, contrasting map-based spatial memory in the retrosplenial complex with visually guided navigation in the occipital place area. Specifically, they are examining the timeline of these neural representations in young children to understand why landmark location encoding and scene categorization emerge early, whereas mechanisms for active navigation—such as processing left-right orientation, "walking" visual motion, and cortical signal-to-noise ratios—undergo protracted development. Additionally, they are mapping the broader dorsal stream network by investigating a newly identified scene-selective region in the superior parietal lobule and its role in processing first-person ego-motion.

papers.title: Two cortical navigation systems and their differential development
papers.abstract: This research investigates the ontogeny of two neuroanatomically and functionally distinct cortical navigation systems: the occipital place area (OPA), implicated in visually-guided navigation, and the retrosplenial complex (RSC), specialized for map-based navigation. Utilizing functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) adaptation in pediatric cohorts aged 5 and 8 years, we quantified the neural representation of sense (left-right orientation), a spatial feature critical to both navigational modes in adults. Our results demonstrated that while the RSC represents sense information as early as age 5, exhibiting adult-like representational fidelity, the OPA fails to represent left-right information in 5-year-olds and only reaches functional maturity by age 8. These findings provide empirical evidence for a developmental dissociation between these systems, suggesting that map-based navigation infrastructure (RSC) matures significantly earlier than the infrastructure for visually-guided navigation (OPA).
papers.authors: Rebecca J. Rennert, Daniel D. Dilks

papers.title: Early development of navigationally relevant location information in the retrosplenial complex
papers.abstract: Map-based navigation depends on the cortical encoding of landmarks and their relative spatial positions, a process primarily mediated by the retrosplenial complex (RSC). Using fMRI multivoxel pattern analysis (MVPA) and a 'Tiny Town' virtual paradigm, we investigated whether RSC location representations emerge early in childhood or follow a protracted developmental course. Our findings indicate that by age 5, the RSC represents the specific spatial locations of individual landmarks rather than their categorical identities—a functional profile that contrasts with the parahippocampal place area (PPA), which represents category but not location. Furthermore, the fidelity of these neural representations in the RSC was significantly correlated with behavioral performance on a location-judgment task. These data challenge the prevailing view that map-based navigation develops late, suggesting instead that the fundamental neural architecture for landmark-based spatial memory is established early in development.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS)
papers.authors: Yaelan Jung, Daniel D. Dilks

papers.title: A scene-selective region in the superior parietal lobule for visually guided navigation
papers.abstract: This study identifies and characterizes a novel scene-selective region within the human superior parietal lobule (SPL) and elucidates its role in visually guided navigation. Through a series of fMRI experiments, we confirmed that the SPL exhibits robust scene selectivity across both static and dynamic visual inputs. Further representational characterization revealed that the SPL, similar to the occipital place area (OPA), processes first-person perspective ego-motion and sense (left-right) information within scenes. Resting-state functional connectivity analysis indicated a preferential integration between the SPL and the OPA relative to other scene-selective cortical modules. Moreover, task-based fMRI demonstrated significantly elevated SPL engagement during active navigation tasks compared to scene categorization. Collectively, these results suggest that the SPL is a critical component of the dorsal stream system supporting navigation through the immediately visible environment.
papers.authors: Hee Kyung Yoon, Yaelan Jung, Andrew S. Persichetti, Daniel D. Dilks

papers.title: Signal and Noise Together Explain the Prolonged Development of Visually-Guided Navigation Compared to Scene Categorization: A Novel Computational Approach
papers.abstract: Human visual development displays a significant temporal gap between the early maturation of scene categorization (recognizing place types) and the later emergence of visually-guided navigation (maneuvering through environments). We addressed this discrepancy using a neurocomputational framework to analyze behavioral and fMRI data across development. Our modeling demonstrates that the protracted maturation of navigation is driven by a lower signal-to-noise ratio in the dorsal stream (e.g., OPA) relative to the ventral stream (e.g., PPA). Specifically, navigation-selective regions exhibit both weaker signal strength (less robust feature encoding) and higher internal noise during childhood relative to adulthood. This computational approach provides a mechanistic explanation for the behavioral lag, highlighting differential signal and noise maturation trajectories across the cortical pathways supporting navigation and categorization.
papers.authors: Zvi Shapiro, Alexander Weigard, Daniel D. Dilks

papers.title: “Walking selectivity” in the occipital place area in 8-year-olds, not 5-year-olds
papers.abstract: The occipital place area (OPA) is a cortical module specialized for visually-guided navigation, particularly for processing visual information relevant to walking. This study investigated the developmental timeline of 'walking selectivity'—the preferential neural response to locomotion-consistent visual motion—in 5-year-olds, 8-year-olds, and adults. Using fMRI, we found that the OPA in 8-year-olds and adults displays robust walking selectivity, responding significantly more to walking videos than to crawling, flying, or scrambled controls. In contrast, the OPA in 5-year-olds exhibited no such selectivity. These findings reveal that while behavioral walking occurs early, the cortical mechanisms for processing visual information during walking undergo a protracted development, maturing only around age 8. This supports the hypothesis that the visually-guided navigation system matures significantly later than other high-level visual systems, such as scene categorization.
papers.authors: Yaelan Jung, Debbie Hsu, Daniel D. Dilks

0146.name: Daniel Denman
0146.institution: University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus
0146.bio: Daniel Denman is an Assistant Professor in the Department of Physiology and Biophysics at the University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus, where they investigate the neural circuit dynamics underlying visual representation and perception. Denman’s research employs high-density extracellular electrophysiology, quantitative psychophysics, and physiological circuit-tracing to study how populations of neurons in the primary visual cortex (V1) interact with subcortical and cortical partners. By integrating optogenetic manipulations and computational modeling, their laboratory probes the causal relationships between large-scale neural population activity and sensory behavior across various timescales. Denman previously served as a scientist at the Allen Institute for Brain Science, where they contributed to the development and implementation of neuroengineering tools, including Neuropixels technology, for systems neuroscience research.
0146.research_direction: Dr. Denman has recently been investigating sensory coding and neural population dynamics in the mouse early visual system, specifically examining how spectral and luminance information is transformed between the thalamus and primary visual cortex. Their recent work explores how chromatic features are encoded across these areas, using simultaneous high-density Neuropixels recordings to probe how separable, high-dimensional population codes emerge from individual neurons with mixed selectivity. In parallel, they are developing novel hardware and spatial recording paradigms to map the precise physiological effects of intracranial electrical microstimulation on awake cortical circuits. By combining custom open-source current routers with 3D multi-probe arrays, Dr. Denman is characterizing how localized electrical currents propagate through the neocortex, recruit specific interneuron and pyramidal cell classes, and relate to behavioral perception.

papers.title: A bioelectric router for adaptive isochronous neurostimulation enables multipolar bioelectric stimulation from a single source
papers.abstract: The authors present the Bioelectric Router for Adaptive Isochronous Neurostimulation (BRAINS) board, an open-source hardware interface designed to extend the capabilities of standard monophasic and biphasic stimulators. Multipolar intracranial electrical brain stimulation (iEBS) offers theoretical advantages over conventional bipolar paradigms, yet remains technically inaccessible due to high costs and proprietary constraints. The BRAINS board utilizes a microcontroller-driven switching matrix that enables dynamic reassignment of anodal, cathodal, grounded, or high-impedance states across 16 channels with sub-millisecond switching latencies. Bench-top characterization demonstrated that the router maintains signal isolation and low noise profiles (RMS error < 1.5%) comparable to baseline stimulator performance. In vivo validation in mouse primary visual cortex (V1) using high-density Neuropixels probes confirmed that the system can execute high-frequency (up to 600 Hz) temporal multiplexing of current, allowing for the generation of complex current fields from a single source without introducing residual stimulation artifacts.
