This modular tool facilitates the exploration of current steering and multipolar stimulation patterns in systems neuroscience.
papers.authors: Eashan Sahai, Jordan Hickman, Daniel J Denman

papers.title: Neural population dynamics of direct electrical stimulation of neocortex
papers.abstract: This study employs a novel 3D recording paradigm to characterize how intracranial electrical microstimulation (ICMS) recruits neural populations in the awake mouse neocortex. Utilizing three orthogonally oriented Neuropixels 1.0 probes surrounding a 16-channel stimulating electrode, the authors measured extracellular potentials and single-unit activity with high spatial and temporal resolution. Findings indicate that the evoked potential propagates asymmetrically and scales sub-linearly with current amplitude, influenced by local anatomical heterogeneity. At the cellular level, only a small fraction (<5%) of neurons within the spatial extent of the evoked potential are directly activated. Fast-spiking (FS) interneurons are recruited with higher probability and nearer to the electrode source than pyramidal neurons, which exhibit anisotropic activation patterns. While sparse direct activation triggers widespread indirect modulation affecting over 50% of the local population at high intensities, behavioral experiments reveal that mice exhibit limited sensitivity to single-pulse ICMS, with detection performance failing to scale with stimulation amplitude. These results suggest that the neural code for ICMS-driven perception is constrained by sparse direct recruitment and significant population-level non-linearities.
papers.authors: Jordan L. Hickman, Grant Hughes, Eashan Sahai, Moriah Miles, Daniel J. Denman

papers.title: Separable neural population representations are constructed from mixed single neuron selectivity in the mouse early visual system
papers.abstract: The authors investigate the transformation of spectral and luminance information within the thalamocortical visual pathway of the mouse. By performing simultaneous high-density recordings in the dorsal lateral geniculate nucleus (dLGN) and primary visual cortex (V1) using Neuropixels probes, they quantified neuronal selectivity to opsin-specific luminance (M and S cone contrasts) and hue. Contrary to hierarchical models predicting a transition from mixed to categorical representations, single-neuron spectral tuning was found to be uniformly distributed in both areas, indicating a pervasive mixed selectivity. Using self-supervised latent embedding (CEBRA) and multi-output Support Vector Regression (SVR) decoding, they demonstrate that while individual neurons exhibit broad tuning, the population as a whole maintains high-dimensional, separable representations of chromatic and luminance variables. The results reveal that high-fidelity decoding of sensory features is achieved through the integration of distributed, non-categorical signals, suggesting that the early visual system employs a population-based coding strategy to preserve information across processing stages.
papers.authors: Juan Santiago Moreno, Nicholas Garcia, Daniel J Denman

0147.name: Daniel Fiset
0147.department: Département de psychoéducation et de psychologie
0147.lab_name: Laboratoire de perception visuelle et sociale (LPVS)
0147.bio: Daniel Fiset is a Professor at the Université du Québec en Outaouais and co-director of the Social and Visual Perception Laboratory. Fiset’s research examines the neurocognitive mechanisms involved in recognizing faces, facial expressions, and written language through psychophysical techniques like the Bubbles method and reverse correlation. By integrating electrophysiological recordings (EEG/ERP), Fiset investigates how low-level visual properties, such as spatial frequencies and orientations, modulate the extraction of diagnostic information. Their work addresses neurotypical visual processing and clinical conditions like prosopagnosia and dyslexia, while also evaluating the impact of social factors such as the other-race effect.
0147.research_direction: Dr. Fiset's recent work explores the perceptual mechanisms and cognitive biases underlying visual processing, social cognition, and decision-making. In the domain of face perception, they have recently been investigating the psychophysical drivers of individual face recognition abilities by contrasting part-based and holistic processing, as well as examining the spatial frequency tuning profiles necessary for categorizing basic facial expressions. Their research also employs reverse correlation paradigms to map observers' internal visual representations of pain faces, probing how individual expectations and mental prototypes might contribute to systemic biases in pain assessment across different demographics. Beyond high-level vision, they are exploring ecological perceptual judgments by assessing how extreme verbal aggression affects the pitch-calling decisions of Major League Baseball umpires, while additionally developing new statistical tools, such as local decorrelation techniques, to improve confidence interval estimation in non-stationary time-series data like EEG.

papers.title: Part-based processing, but not holistic processing, predicts individual differences in face recognition abilities
papers.abstract: This study employs a psychophysical paradigm to evaluate the predictive validity of part-based and holistic processing for face processing ability (FPA). Defining holistic processing as the perceptual integration efficiency of multiple facial parts and part-based processing as the efficiency in identifying isolated components, the researchers used a battery of tasks (N = 64) to measure individual differences. Multiple linear regression analyses revealed that part-based efficiency was a robust predictor of FPA variance, whereas perceptual integration (holistic processing) showed no significant predictive relationship. These results suggest that feature-level encoding, rather than structural integration, is the primary driver of individual variations in face recognition.
papers.authors: Pierre-Louis Audette, Laurianne Côté, Caroline Blais, Justin Duncan, Francis Gingras, Daniel Fiset

papers.title: Facial expression categorization predominantly relies on mid-spatial frequencies
papers.abstract: While previous research has debated the relative importance of low versus high spatial frequencies (SF) in emotion perception, the specific bands optimal for identifying basic facial expressions have remained unclear. This study utilizes two complementary psychophysical methods—a data-driven approach and a naturalistic distance-simulation task—to establish SF tuning profiles for basic emotions. Results demonstrate that categorization performance is highest at viewing distances corresponding to mid-range spatial frequencies (~6–13 cycles per face) and declines sharply when this information is unavailable. The findings highlight that mid-SF content is diagnostic across various expressions and suggest that its exclusion in prior studies may have led to an incomplete understanding of the visual mechanisms underlying expression recognition.
papers.authors: Isabelle Charbonneau, Justin Duncan, Caroline Blais, Joël Guérette, Marie-Pier Plouffe-Demers, Fraser Smith, Daniel Fiset

papers.title: Verbal Aggressions Against Major League Baseball Umpires Affect Their Decision Making
papers.abstract: Using a large-scale ecological dataset from Major League Baseball (N = 153,255 pitches), this study assesses the impact of extreme verbal aggression—proxied by player or coach ejections—on the subsequent decision-making of home-plate umpires. The analysis reveals a significant bias following ejections: umpires were less likely to call strikes for the team that resorted to verbal abuse and more likely to call strikes for the opposing team. Statistical controls for compensation effects suggest that verbal aggression may paradoxically confer a strategic advantage by subconsciously influencing official judgments in favor of the complaining team, challenging the assumption that such behavior is purely detrimental to the aggressor's interests.
papers.authors: Joël Guérette, Caroline Blais, Daniel Fiset

papers.title: Local decorrelation for error bars in time series
papers.abstract: Confidence intervals in within-subject designs often rely on the assumption of stationary correlation across all measurement pairs. However, in time-series and electroencephalographic (EEG) data, correlations typically vanish as the temporal distance between points increases. This paper introduces a novel decorrelation technique based on local correlation assumptions. By adjusting the width of error bars using a weighted average correlation within a specific temporal radius, the method provides more precise estimates of uncertainty for contiguous data points. The authors demonstrate the utility of this local decorrelation approach using fMRI and ERP datasets, showing it effectively preserves precision in noisy temporal data without overestimating global dependencies.
papers.authors: Denis Cousineau, Anthony Proulx, Annabelle Potvin-Pilon, Daniel Fiset

papers.title: The Relationship Between the Ability to Infer Another’s Pain and the Expectations Regarding the Appearance of Pain Facial Expressions: Investigation of the Role of Visual Perception
papers.abstract: This study investigates the perceptual factors contributing to the systemic underestimation of pain in others. Utilizing a reverse correlation paradigm, the researchers estimated the internal visual representations of pain expressions in both Black and White faces among Western and African observers. The results identified three distinct clusters of participants with varying expectations regarding the appearance of pain. A significant finding was the overlap between expectations of pain and other negative affective states like anger and disgust, suggesting that individual differences in these mental prototypes may impact the ability to accurately distinguish pain from other emotions, potentially leading to biased caregiving and clinical outcomes.
papers.authors: Ariane Lévesque-Lacasse, Marie-Claude Desjardins, Daniel Fiset, Isabelle Charbonneau, Stéphanie Cormier, Caroline Blais

0148.name: Daniel Kaiser
0148.department: Department of Mathematics and Computer Science
0148.bio: Daniel Kaiser is the Professor of Neural Computation at Justus Liebig University Giessen and directs the Neural Computation Group. Their research investigates how the human brain represents and integrates objects within structured, real-world scenes, focusing on the role of statistical regularities and top-down feedback mechanisms. Kaiser employs a multimodal approach combining functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), electroencephalography (EEG), and deep neural network modeling to explore these processes. Their work characterizes the rhythmic neural dynamics, such as alpha and beta oscillations, that support the construction of adaptive visual representations for naturalistic behavior.
0148.research_direction: Dr. Kaiser has recently been investigating how the brain constructs coherent representations of the natural visual world, spanning from the neural dynamics of spatiotemporal integration to the computational basis of aesthetic appreciation. Using multivariate EEG decoding, their recent work explores how distinct neural rhythms—specifically alpha and gamma bands—encode visual contents and route feedforward versus feedback signals to build seamless percepts from fragmented inputs. Alongside these mechanistic studies of scene perception, they employ Representational Similarity Analysis to examine how an observer’s personal experience with environmental regularities alters the neural coding of natural environments. Finally, they are investigating the cognitive and neural foundations of visual aesthetics, combining eye-tracking, fMRI, and Deep Neural Networks to ask whether shared inter-subject gaze dynamics and computationally efficient spatial integration can predict human aesthetic judgments of images and cinematic stimuli.

papers.title: Shared gaze reflects shared aesthetic experiences
papers.abstract: The researchers employed naturalistic cinematic stimuli to investigate whether inter-subject synchronization of gaze patterns serves as a robust predictor of shared aesthetic evaluations. Utilizing eye-tracking and continuous moment-to-moment aesthetic ratings, the study applied inter-subject correlation (ISC) analyses to relate attentional selection with aesthetic appreciation. The results demonstrate that similarities in gaze fixations significantly predict similarities in beauty ratings across individuals, suggesting that collective visual engagement with specific scene features is a necessary prerequisite for aligned aesthetic experiences.
papers.authors: Mustafa Alperen Ekinci, Daniel Kaiser

papers.title: Enhanced and idiosyncratic neural representations of personally typical scenes
papers.abstract: This study characterizes how the brain's internal models of environmental regularities influence the neural representation of natural scenes. Using EEG and Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA), the authors compared neural coding for scenes that were personally typical versus atypical for individual observers. The findings reveal that personally typical scenes exhibit enhanced representational strength and increased idiosyncratic variability in higher-level visual processing stages, while low-level feature coding (modeled by early layers of Deep Neural Networks) remains relatively invariant to personal typicality.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences
papers.authors: Gongting Wang, Lixiang Chen, Radoslaw Martin Cichy, Daniel Kaiser

papers.title: Representational shifts from feedforward to feedback rhythms index phenomenological integration in naturalistic vision
papers.abstract: To determine the cortical mechanisms of spatiotemporal integration, the authors manipulated the coherence of video segments presented across visual hemifields. Using multivariate spectral decoding of EEG signals, they identified a systematic shift in the dominant rhythmic channel: while incoherent stimuli were represented through gamma-band feedforward activity, phenomenologically integrated (coherent) perception was indexed by a shift to alpha-frequency feedback. This evidence characterizes alpha-band dynamics as the primary vehicle for the top-down construction of seamless percepts from fragmented inputs.
papers.authors: Lixiang Chen, Radoslaw Martin Cichy, Daniel Kaiser

papers.title: Decoding the rhythmic representation and communication of visual contents
papers.abstract: This opinion article proposes a framework in which rhythmic neural activity (alpha, beta, and gamma) serves a specialized function in encoding and transmitting specific visual contents. By reviewing evidence from multivariate decoding of oscillatory signals, the authors argue that stimulus-specific information is readable from distinct frequency bands. They specifically highlight the role of alpha-frequency rhythms in mediating content-specific feedback, allowing for a dissociation of feedforward and feedback information flows in the visual hierarchy.
papers.authors: Rico Stecher, Radoslaw Martin Cichy, Daniel Kaiser

papers.title: Integrative processing in artificial and biological vision predicts the perceived beauty of natural images
papers.abstract: This research examines whether the perceived beauty of natural scenes is linked to spatial integration—a computational process that aggregates discrete image features into efficient, holistic representations. By comparing human aesthetic judgments with Deep Neural Network (DNN) models and fMRI data, the authors found that increased integrative processing (linked to larger receptive field aggregation) significantly predicts higher beauty ratings. This suggests that aesthetic pleasure is a byproduct of the visual system's preference for computationally efficient, more 'fluent' scene representations.
papers.authors: Sanjeev Nara, Daniel Kaiser

0149.name: Daniel Linares
0149.department: Department of Cognition, Development and Educational Psychology
0149.lab_name: Vision and Control of Action Group (VISCA)
0149.bio: Daniel Linares is a Serra Húnter Fellow and researcher at the Universitat de Barcelona, affiliated with the Vision and Control of Action (VISCA) group and the Institute of Neurosciences. Their research utilizes visual psychophysics, computational modeling, and clinical neuroscience to examine how the brain processes sensory information and reaches decisions within the context of psychiatric disorders. Linares focuses on differentiating sensory deficits from decisional biases to identify biomarkers for glutamatergic dysfunction in conditions such as schizophrenia and anti-NMDAR encephalitis. Additionally, they developed technical tools for the field, including StimuliApp for mobile psychophysical testing and the R package 'quickpsy' for fitting and comparing psychometric functions.
0149.research_direction: Dr. Linares has recently been investigating the computational and behavioral mechanisms underlying visual contrast perception in both healthy and clinical populations. Their recent work explores how physical stimulus intensity maps onto internal sensory representations, using a combination of subjective magnitude estimation tasks and objective discrimination paradigms to model signal-dependent internal noise and sensory transducer functions. In parallel, they are also examining low-level perceptual abnormalities in psychiatric disorders by synthesizing literature on visual contrast sensitivity in schizophrenia. Within this clinical domain, they evaluate how methodological variables—such as antipsychotic medication dosage, visual acuity confounds, and unmodeled attentional lapses during psychometric fitting—might influence or artificially inflate assessments of sensory impairment.

papers.title: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis on Contrast Sensitivity in Schizophrenia
papers.abstract: Investigating low-level perceptual abnormalities in psychiatric disorders offers critical traction on disrupted neural and computational architectures. While impaired visual contrast sensitivity is widely cited as a hallmark sensory deficit in schizophrenia, existing findings across disparate spatial and temporal frequencies have not been systematically synthesized. Following PRISMA protocols, a systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis was conducted across 46 studies comparing individuals diagnosed with schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder to healthy control cohorts, with 43 investigations specifically evaluating chronic cohorts. Chronic schizophrenia was associated with a robust reduction in contrast sensitivity (pooled Hedges' g = 0.74, 95% CI: [0.55, 0.93], p = 8.2 × 10⁻¹⁰), accompanied by marked between-study heterogeneity. Meta-regression revealed that the magnitude of contrast impairment scaled positively with antipsychotic dosage quantified via chlorpromazine equivalents, indicating medication effects may significantly mediate observed sensory decrements. Crucially, none of the synthesized studies parametrically estimated or controlled for attentional lapses during psychometric fitting, leaving unresolved the degree to which non-sensory lapse rates artifactually inflate detection thresholds. Furthermore, comprehensive visual acuity assessments were performed in only two studies, confounding inferences regarding spatial frequency dependence and the selective vulnerability of magnocellular versus parvocellular pathways.
papers.authors: Daniel Linares, Aster Joostens, Cristina de la Malla

papers.title: Subjective ratings reveal Poisson-like noise underlying perception
papers.abstract: A foundational pursuit of sensory neuroscience is elucidating the mapping between physical stimulus intensity and internal perceptual representation. Traditional psychophysics relies heavily on discrimination sensitivity (such as two-alternative forced-choice tasks), but discrimination thresholds inherently conflate the derivative of the sensory transducer function (signal gain) with the amplitude of trial-to-trial internal noise, leaving the noise distribution underdetermined. Examining human contrast perception, this investigation establishes that the trial-by-trial response variability of numeric magnitude estimations directly exposes this internal sensory noise. Concurrently modeling empirical response means and variances revealed an internal representation governed by an asymmetric sigmoidal transducer function paired with signal-dependent, Poisson-like internal noise scaling with the square root of the internal response. Remarkably, this internal representation derived exclusively from magnitude estimations quantitatively predicted objective contrast discrimination sensitivity curves and thresholds across varying pedestal contrast levels without any free fitting parameters. This unified framework accounts for both the expansive low-contrast pedestal effect and compressive suprathreshold Weber-like behavior, demonstrating that a singular stochastic internal representation underpins both subjective appearance ratings and objective psychophysical discriminability.
papers.authors: Cristina Rodríguez-Arribas, Joan López-Moliner, Daniel Linares

0150.name: Daniel R Coates
0150.bio: Daniel R. Coates is an Assistant Professor at the University of Houston College of Optometry whose research examines spatial vision, letter recognition, and peripheral perception. Using psychophysical methods and computational modeling, Coates investigates visual crowding and its impact on reading and appearance. After earning a PhD in Vision Science from the University of California, Berkeley in 2015, Coates completed postdoctoral fellowships in Belgium and Switzerland before joining the Houston faculty in 2017. Their work focuses on stereopsis, color vision, and the development of open-source tools for psychophysical experimentation.
0150.research_direction: Dr. Coates has recently been investigating the psychophysical properties of spatial and color vision, with a particular focus on how distinct retinal pathways pool visual information. Their recent work explores spatial summation across the central visual field using stimuli modulated along the cardinal axes of DKL color space, employing both human psychophysics and computational probability summation models to understand how critical areas of summation relate to the receptive field sizes of magnocellular, parvocellular, and koniocellular ganglion cells. Translating these basic visual mechanisms into clinical tools, they are developing and validating a novel localized chromatic perimeter to evaluate its potential as a functional biomarker for detecting early neurodegenerative retinal changes in individuals with type 2 diabetes. Additionally, Dr. Coates has been examining stereoscopic depth mechanisms in virtual reality environments, specifically probing how target and background texture spatial frequencies interact to influence relative distance discrimination.

papers.title: Characterizing chromatic sensitivity across the central visual field in those with and without type 2 diabetes
papers.abstract: This study quantified local chromatic contrast detection thresholds at 20 discrete retinal locations within the central 10° of the visual field using a novel color perimetry paradigm based on the cardinal axes of the DKL color space. A cohort consisting of individuals with glucose dysfunction (HbA1c > 5.6%) and age-matched controls was evaluated. Linear mixed-effects modeling revealed that average chromatic contrast detection thresholds were significantly elevated in the glucose dysfunction group compared to controls. A significant interaction was observed between retinal location and metabolic status for the 'red' (+L-M) condition. The results suggest that localized chromatic perimetry can detect functional neurodegenerative changes in the retina that occur prior to the manifestation of clinical vascular signs in diabetic retinopathy.
papers.authors: Christopher S. Wu, Bismark Owusu-Afriyie, Julia S. Benoit, Daniel R. Coates

papers.title: Probability summation model of spatial pooling within the cardinal axes of DKL color space
papers.abstract: The spatial extent of visual pooling was investigated by measuring critical areas of summation for stimuli modulating along the cardinal axes of DKL color space across eccentricities of 5°, 10°, 15°, and 20°. A computational model incorporating convolutional filtering, downsampling layers, and probability summation was developed to reproduce human psychophysical spatial summation functions. The model successfully simulated the characteristic bilinear shape of these functions, with the slope of partial summation governed by the probability summation exponent (averaging 4.0 for achromatic, 1.6 for parvocellular, and ~3.0 for koniocellular mechanisms). The findings indicate that critical areas of spatial summation correspond to the receptive field sizes of underlying retinal ganglion cell classes, with parvocellular mechanisms displaying distinct linear pooling characteristics compared to the discrete summation areas of magnocellular and koniocellular pathways.
papers.authors: Christopher S. Wu, Daniel R. Coates

papers.title: Repeatability of a novel chromatic perimeter in a cohort of people with and without glucose dysfunction
papers.abstract: This research evaluated the test-retest reliability and diagnostic sensitivity of a custom-developed color perimeter designed to measure localized chromatic thresholds. Measurements were taken for five color conditions (achromatic, red, green, blue, and yellow) across multiple visits. The device demonstrated high repeatability in healthy control subjects. In participants with type 2 diabetes or prediabetes, repeatability remained stable, though a trend toward increased thresholds (worsening performance) was noted in individuals with longer disease duration or higher HbA1c levels. The perimeter's ability to reliably detect subtle elevations in chromatic thresholds across the posterior pole suggests its utility as a functional biomarker for early-stage diabetic eye disease prior to the development of overt retinopathy.
papers.authors: Bismark Owusu-Afriyie, Christopher S. Wu, Liam Burhans, Daniel R. Coates

papers.title: The effect of target and background texture on relative depth discrimination in a virtual environment
papers.abstract: The role of texture spatial frequency (SF) in facilitating distance discrimination was examined within a virtual reality (VR) framework using bandpass-filtered noise patterns. Observers performed a relative depth discrimination task for targets presented at 3m against a background at 6m. Experimental results showed that distance thresholds were significantly reduced when targets were rendered with mid-spatial frequency textures, which provided the most effective depth cues. Conversely, targets lacking texture presented against textured backgrounds resulted in substantial performance degradation. The study concludes that stereoscopic depth mechanisms integrate SF information globally across the visual scene, and the interaction between target and background textures is a critical factor for optimizing immersive depth perception in virtual environments.
papers.authors: Wei Hau Lew, Daniel R. Coates

papers.title: Characteristics of spatial summation in the magnocellular, parvocellular, and koniocellular pathways
papers.abstract: Spatial summation properties were characterized for targeted visual pathways across the central 20° of the visual field using chromatic modulations in DKL color space. Psychophysical measurements identified distinct summation regimes for different cell classes: complete spatial summation was consistently found for magnocellular and koniocellular pathways across all eccentricities. However, the parvocellular (+L-M and -L-M) pathway exhibited a unique linear summation profile without a detectable critical area within the range of stimulus sizes tested. An anatomically motivated model of receptive field pooling using probability summation was proposed, demonstrating that the observed critical areas are consistent with the dendritic field extents of specific retinal ganglion cell types, thereby linking functional psychophysical findings to underlying retinal neurobiology.
papers.authors: Christopher S. Wu, Daniel R. Coates

0151.name: Daniel Schneider
0151.institution: Leibniz Research Centre for Working Environment and Human Factors
0151.bio: Daniel Schneider is a cognitive neuroscientist and head of the Information Processing research group at the Leibniz Research Centre for Working Environment and Human Factors (IfADo). Schneider’s research focuses on the neural mechanisms of selective information processing, specifically examining how working memory acts as an interface between perception and goal-directed action. Utilizing electrophysiological techniques such as EEG and time-frequency analysis of alpha and beta oscillations, they investigate the roles of target enhancement and distractor suppression in maintaining mental representations. Additionally, Schneider’s work explores the impact of aging and environmental stressors, such as task interruptions, on cognitive resource allocation and performance.
0151.research_direction: Dr. Schneider's recent work explores the neurocognitive mechanisms that control attention within visual working memory and how these processes interact with other systems, such as motor planning and long-term memory. Using visual retro-cue paradigms paired with EEG to track specific oscillatory markers like alpha and beta suppression, they investigate how top-down attentional selection prioritizes internal memory representations and protects them from sensory interference. Their research spans several distinct phenomena, asking whether active processing in a temporary memory buffer can strengthen long-term memory traces and how planned motor actions modulate the gating of visual working memory. Additionally, they have recently been investigating cognitive flexibility in the face of task interruptions, examining how self-determined resumption timing alters the neural dynamics of attentional reorienting and working memory performance in both healthy and aging populations.

papers.title: Older adults benefit more from flexibility when dealing with task interruptions: Electrophysiological evidence from a working memory task
papers.abstract: This study explored age-related changes in cognitive flexibility when managing task interruptions. Specifically, it investigated whether providing participants with self-determined timing for resuming a primary task—compared to fixed short or long intervals—mitigates the performance deficits typically observed in older adults. Using a visual retroactive working memory paradigm and electroencephalography (EEG), results indicated that older adults (65–75 years) experienced significant performance gains and a restoration of posterior alpha suppression (a neural marker for the focused retrieval of task-relevant information) when allowed to resume tasks flexibly. These findings suggest that flexibility in resumption timing can compensate for age-related declines in attentional control mechanisms following interruptions.
papers.authors: Stephan Getzmann, Soner Ülkü, Edmund Wascher, Daniel Schneider

papers.title: Motor control processes moderate visual working memory gating
papers.abstract: This research examined the bidirectional interaction between motor control processes and the gating mechanisms of visual working memory (WM). Through a delayed match-to-sample color task where the response hand was cued during encoding, the study tested how planned actions influence susceptibility to sensory interference. Findings demonstrated that when a secondary interference task required the same hand as the planned WM report, task-irrelevant sensory input significantly biased the stored memory representations, leading to an attraction bias toward interfering colors. This breakdown of the WM gate was associated with modulations in mid-frontal theta power, which functioned as a reactive control signal to mitigate the impact of sensory interference on maintenance.
papers.authors: Şahcan Özdemir, Eren Günseli, Daniel Schneider

papers.title: Processing in working memory boosts long-term memory representations and their retrieval
papers.abstract: The study investigated whether the selective processing of information within working memory (WM) can modify and strengthen existing long-term memory (LTM) traces. Utilizing a three-phase paradigm involving initial LTM encoding of object-location associations followed by a WM retro-cuing phase, researchers assessed final LTM retrieval accuracy. Behavioral evidence and cross-phase EEG decoding revealed that both attentional prioritization and probe-based testing within the WM task significantly enhanced subsequent LTM retrieval. The results suggest that WM serves as an active interface for the dynamic updating and reinforcement of long-term representations through neural reinstatement mechanisms rather than merely acting as a passive temporary buffer.
papers.authors: Melinda Sabo, Daniel Schneider

papers.title: EEG Correlates of Cognitive Dynamics in Task Resumption After Interruptions: The Impact of Available Time and Flexibility
papers.abstract: This study utilized a visual working memory (WM) retro-cue task to analyze the neuro-cognitive mechanisms underlying the resumption of primary tasks following interruptions. It specifically focused on how the duration of the resumption phase and the flexibility of its timing modulate attentional reorienting. EEG analysis revealed that longer resumption intervals and self-determined (flexible) timing were associated with significantly stronger beta-band suppression during the transition back to the primary task. These oscillatory shifts are interpreted as markers of more efficient disengagement from the interrupting task and facilitated refocusing of the attentional spotlight on relevant WM contents, ultimately leading to improved behavioral performance.
papers.authors: Soner Ülkü, Stephan Getzmann, Edmund Wascher, Daniel Schneider

papers.title: The neural basis of attentional selection in goal-directed memory retrieval
papers.abstract: The investigation explored whether the reactivation of specific long-term memory (LTM) contents is mediated by the same attentional selection mechanisms used for external sensory perception. Participants performed an episodic memory task where cues indicated the relevance of specific associations previously learned during an encoding phase. Results showed that selective cuing led to faster reaction times and increased subjective confidence during retrieval. Electrophysiological data indicated that goal-directed LTM retrieval is characterized by lateralized alpha power modulations and posterior contralateral negativity, suggesting that top-down attentional selection acts as a fundamental mechanism for prioritizing task-relevant internal representations during memory reactivation.
papers.authors: Melinda Sabo, Edmund Wascher, Daniel Schneider

0153.name: Daphne Bavelier
0153.department: Faculty of Psychology and Educational Sciences
0153.bio: Daphné Bavelier is a cognitive neuroscientist and Professor at the University of Geneva, where they direct the Brain and Learning Lab at Campus Biotech. Bavelier investigates the mechanisms of human brain plasticity and learning, focusing on how the brain adapts to experiences such as deafness or training with digital media. Bavelier’s research indicates that action video games can serve as tools to enhance visual attention, perception, and spatial cognition. Utilizing fMRI, psychophysics, and eye-tracking, Bavelier currently identifies factors that promote learning and the transfer of cognitive skills across different domains.
0153.research_direction: Dr. Bavelier has recently been investigating how digital environments and video games can be leveraged to both measure and enhance human cognition. Their recent work explores the design of custom "serious games" equipped with dynamic difficulty adjustment to trace problem-solving heuristics, spatial pathfinding, and executive function development in children, while also evaluating whether domain-general action gaming interventions can transfer to specific impairments like poor reading skills. Beyond cognitive training, they are probing the clinical boundaries of digital consumption by testing whether psychological traits and mental health markers predict Internet Gaming Disorder more accurately than raw screen time. Finally, Dr. Bavelier is examining the fundamental psychometrics of cognitive assessment, using drift-diffusion modeling to resolve reliability issues and speed-accuracy trade-offs in how executive functions are traditionally measured.

papers.title: Digital Tools for Reading Success: Meta-analyses of Digital Interventions
papers.abstract: This multilevel meta-analysis, utilizing robust variance estimation (RVE) across 56 studies, evaluates the efficacy of digital interventions—specifically computer and tablet games—on reading performance in individuals under 15 years old. The research differentiates between poor readers and typically-developing school readers, moderating for linguistic factors such as language transparency and syllabic complexity. Findings indicate that while domain-specific literacy tools demonstrate medium effect sizes (g = 0.433) for poor readers and modest gains for general readers, domain-general cognitive training (e.g., action-based mechanisms) only provides significant transfer for the poor reading cohort. The results support the 'learning-to-learn' framework as a primary mechanism for overcoming literacy impairments through adaptive digital engagement.
papers.authors: Angela Pasqualotto, Emma G. Cunningham, Claire Holman, Benoit Bediou, Daphne Bavelier

papers.title: Tik-Tik: A Video Game for the Study of Search in Problem Solving
papers.abstract: The authors introduce 'Tik-Tik,' an experimentally-controlled serious game designed to operationalize the study of human search strategies and pathfinding within discrete problem-solving spaces. The game’s architecture enables the titration of difficulty through two primary structural variables: the minimum optimal solution path length and the size of the truncated search space. Across three validation studies measuring optimality, search efficiency, and the impact of incentivization, the authors demonstrate that Tik-Tik effectively captures inter-individual differences in look-ahead depth and search policy. These results establish the game as a valid platform for studying complex cognitive heuristics in ecologically-valid, yet highly-controllable, digital environments.
papers.venue: Serious Games (JCSG 2025), Lecture Notes in Computer Science
papers.authors: Cvetomir M. Dimov, Daphne Bavelier

papers.title: Modeling Skill Progression in Children Through Novel Multidimensional Probabilistic DDA
papers.abstract: This paper presents a novel methodological framework for tracking and optimizing cognitive skill acquisition through a multidimensional probabilistic Dynamic Difficulty Adjustment (DDA) system. Integrated into a customized video game, the probabilistic DDA algorithm utilizes real-time performance metrics to dynamically scale task demands across multiple executive function sub-domains simultaneously. By applying latent learning models to data from a cohort of children, the authors demonstrate that the system successfully navigates the learner's zone of proximal development, maintaining engagement while providing precise, granular assessments of developmental progression. The research underscores the potential of DDA as a tool for personalized cognitive intervention and continuous behavioral monitoring.
papers.venue: Serious Games (JCSG 2025), Lecture Notes in Computer Science
papers.authors: Angela Pasqualotto, Marios Fanourakis, Zeno Menestrina, Benoit Bediou, Daphne Bavelier

papers.title: Going beyond video game consumption when considering Internet Gaming Disorder
papers.abstract: This investigation evaluates the diagnostic validity of cumulative screen time as a primary metric for Internet Gaming Disorder (IGD) among League of Legends players. Utilizing objective tracking of playtime metrics and re-initiation latency (quantified as 'come-back-fast' behavior) across two independent cohorts, the authors perform regression analyses to dissociate consumption volume from psychological markers. The findings reveal that mental health factors (depression and anxiety scores) and specific personality traits are superior predictors of IGD symptoms compared to raw gaming duration. The results challenge current policy frameworks that prioritize quantitative time limits and advocate for a more holistic clinical assessment of digital well-being that considers mental health comorbidities.
papers.authors: Sezen Cekic, Benoît Bediou, Sophia Achab, Michael Rich, C. Shawn Green, Daphné Bavelier

papers.title: In search of better practice in executive functions assessment: Methodological issues and potential solutions
papers.abstract: This methodological critique addresses systemic measurement challenges in the structural modeling of executive functions (EF). Utilizing the EZ-diffusion model for drift diffusion modeling (DDM) and confirmatory factor analysis (CFA), the authors evaluate the psychometric properties of 'single scores' (high-conflict trials) versus 'difference scores' (calculated as the performance delta between congruent and incongruent trials). Through recursive bootstrapping and latent variable modeling on a developmental sample, the study demonstrates that drift rates derived from single-score models exhibit superior convergence, fit indices, and factor loadings, effectively mitigating the speed-accuracy trade-off and reliability issues inherent in traditional subtraction-based metrics.
papers.authors: Marc Yangüez, Benoit Bediou, Julien Chanal, Daphne Bavelier

0154.name: Daryl Fougnie
0154.bio: Daryl Fougnie is an Associate Professor of Psychology at New York University Abu Dhabi and the director of the Fougnie Lab. Fougnie’s research examines the structural and capacity limitations of human visual perception, attention, and working memory, focusing on how these systems interact to represent environmental information. They utilize psychophysics and computational modeling alongside neuroimaging techniques such as fMRI to characterize the precision and format of visual representations. Recent projects explore the neural mechanisms underlying internal selection from memory and external attentional selection, as well as trade-offs between the quantity and quality of stored visual information.
0154.research_direction: Dr. Fougnie has recently been investigating the flexible allocation and representational structure of working memory, using methods like transcranial magnetic stimulation and Bayesian modeling to probe how the prefrontal cortex manages the prioritization of memory items. Their recent work explores how active control operations, such as intentional forgetting and de-prioritization, affect the representational precision of remaining mnemonic content. Additionally, they are examining the architectural constraints of visual memory by testing the robustness of object-based feature integration and investigating how internal color category prototypes interact codependently with contextual inter-item repulsion. Expanding beyond visual research, Dr. Fougnie is also adapting continuous circular reproduction paradigms to study auditory working memory, exploring whether feature-space distortions reflect domain-general mnemonic properties.

papers.title: Not All Forgetting Is Equal: Active forgetting has selective benefits in working memory
papers.abstract: This study utilizes a novel 'forget' cue paradigm to isolate the consequences of active de-prioritization in working memory (WM). While previous research often confounded forgetting with prioritization, the authors disentangle these processes by providing cues to drop specific items without increasing the testing probability of others. The results demonstrate that active forgetting significantly enhances the precision of remaining items; however, these benefits are selectively distributed toward neutral, non-prioritized memoranda rather than items designated for high-priority maintenance. These findings suggest that intentional forgetting is an effortful cognitive operation that selectively offloads items to optimize the representational quality of secondary mnemonic contents.
papers.authors: Ying Zhou, Daryl Fougnie

papers.title: Prioritizing working memory resources depends on prefrontal cortex
papers.abstract: The authors investigated the causal role of the lateral prefrontal cortex (PFC) in controlling the allocation of limited working memory (WM) resources. Using a prioritization task combined with transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) and Bayesian modeling, the study tested how neural perturbations impact the fidelity of high- versus low-priority items. TMS applied to the retinotopically-defined superior precentral sulcus—but not the intraparietal sulcus—disrupted the balance of resource allocation, leading to a counterintuitive improvement in memory for low-priority items. These findings provide causal support for models where the lateral PFC serves as a control hub for the flexible prioritization of WM content rather than a primary storage site for visual features.
papers.authors: Ying Zhou, Clayton E. Curtis, Kartik Sreenivasan, Daryl Fougnie

papers.title: Introducing ART: a new method of testing auditory memory with circular reproduction tasks
papers.abstract: The authors describe the Auditory Reproduction Task (ART), a novel psychophysical methodology utilizing Shepard tones to investigate auditory working memory (AWM) using a circular feature space. By adapting continuous reproduction paradigms previously restricted to the visual domain, the researchers quantified precision and bias in auditory representations. Computational modeling revealed that AWM exhibits repulsion and attraction biases based on the proximity of items in feature space, mirroring visual mnemonic distortions. These findings establish that such representational constraints are domain-general rather than modality-specific, validating ART as a tool for studying cross-modal mnemonic properties.
papers.authors: Aytac Karabay, Rob Nijenkamp, Anastasios Sarampalis, Daryl Fougnie

papers.title: Color category and inter-item interaction influence color working memory codependently
papers.abstract: This research examines the interaction between internal category prototypes and contextual inter-item interactions in biasing color working memory (WM). By requiring participants to maintain two color items, the study demonstrates that memory reports shift toward or away from category-specific prototypes while being simultaneously repelled by concurrent distractors held in WM. Critically, the magnitude and direction of these biases are not additive but flexible, interacting codependently based on the specific color category. The results indicate that mnemonic distortions arise from an integrated processing hierarchy where long-term category knowledge and short-term normalization effects co-determine the fidelity of visual representations.
papers.authors: Mengdan Sun, Daryl Fougnie

papers.title: Robust object-based encoding in visual working memory
papers.abstract: This study investigates whether object-based encoding (OBE)—the mandatory integration of constituent features into visual working memory (VWM) upon selection—is a robust or task-dependent phenomenon. Using an irrelevant-change distraction paradigm, the researchers examined whether changes in task-irrelevant feature dimensions consistently interfere with the maintenance of target features. Across multiple experiments controlling for attentional allocation and feature similarity, the interference from task-irrelevant changes remained consistent. This persistence provides strong evidence for the robust nature of OBE and suggests that integrated objects, rather than independent feature-dimensions, serve as the primary units of selection in VWM.
papers.authors: Mengdan Sun, Mengsi Xu, Xuemin Zhang, Daryl Fougnie

0158.name: David Alais
0158.bio: David Alais is a Professor of Experimental Psychology at the University of Sydney, specializing in the neural mechanisms of visual and multisensory perception. Alais investigates how the brain resolves sensory ambiguity and integrates cross-modal information, focusing on the ventriloquist effect, binocular rivalry, and perceptual suppression. Recent work by Alais examines face pareidolia and serial dependence to determine how temporal context and specialized neural templates bias human awareness. Utilizing psychophysical techniques, computational modeling, and functional neuroimaging, Alais maps the spatiotemporal dynamics of consciousness and sensory integration.
0158.research_direction: Dr. Alais has recently been investigating the dynamic interplay between action, multisensory integration, and visual processing, with a major focus on how active locomotion influences perception. Using immersive virtual reality, mobile EEG, and eye-tracking, their recent work explores how the biomechanical rhythms of the human gait cycle modulate audio-visual synchrony judgments, cortical oscillations, and saccadic eye movements. Additionally, they are examining the computational mechanisms underlying multisensory spatial and temporal estimation, utilizing novel continuous-tracking paradigms and Bayesian modeling to probe how the brain resolves sensory reliability and modality-specific priors during audiovisual integration. Finally, their research investigates the mechanisms of interocular suppression, testing whether low-level local motion features or high-level holistic processing dictate the visibility of biological motion stimuli in continuous flash suppression paradigms.

papers.title: Perception of Audio-Visual Synchrony is Modulated by Walking Speed and Step-Cycle Phase
papers.abstract: This study investigates the influence of locomotion dynamics on multisensory temporal integration by assessing audio-visual (AV) synchrony perception during active walking. Using a virtual reality (VR) paradigm, observers performed synchrony judgements while walking at natural and reduced speeds. Psychophysical results demonstrated that temporal sensitivity for AV synchrony is significantly attenuated during slow walking compared to natural gaits, as evidenced by increased reaction times and wider synchrony windows. Furthermore, the probability of perceiving synchrony was found to be quadratically modulated across the stride cycle, with peak sensitivity occurring during the swing phase and significant reductions aligned with the stance phase and footfall. These findings suggest that the temporal constraints of the gait cycle extend beyond unisensory detection to modulate supra-threshold multisensory timing judgements.
papers.authors: Gabriel Clouston, Matthew J. Davidson, David Alais

papers.title: Sensory reliability takes priority over the central tendency effect in temporal and spatial estimation
papers.abstract: This research examines the interaction between Bayesian central tendency effects and sensory reliability in a multisensory context. Utilizing interleaved auditory and visual trials for spatial and temporal estimation, the study tested whether the brain employs a generalized (supra-modal) prior or modality-specific priors. Bayesian modeling of the psychophysical data confirmed that perceptual estimates are governed by modality-specific priors rather than a supra-modal average. Estimates in the less reliable modality (audition for space, vision for time) were systematically pulled toward the prior of the dominant modality, while the dominant modality's estimates remained stable. The results indicate that the brain prioritizes sensory reliability over a global regression toward the mean, favoring a modality-specific Bayesian integration strategy.
papers.authors: Alessia Tonelli, Cameron K. Phan, David Alais

papers.title: Local motion governs visibility and suppression of biological motion in continuous flash suppression
papers.abstract: The study probes the levels of visual processing involved in interocular suppression by comparing the suppression depth of biological motion (BM) stimuli against various motion controls using a tracking continuous flash suppression (tCFS) paradigm. Suppression depth was quantified as the contrast difference between breakthrough (bCFS) and resuppression (reCFS) thresholds. Results revealed that disrupting high-level semantic information through inversion or rotation of the BM figure did not significantly alter suppression depth. Conversely, manipulations of low-level local motion features were found to modulate the strength of interocular suppression. These findings support the local-precedence hypothesis, suggesting that the mechanisms of continuous flash suppression are primarily driven by low-level motion integration rather than high-level semantic or holistic processing.
papers.authors: William Swann, Matthew J. Davidson, Gabriel Clouston, David Alais

papers.title: Continuous tracking of audiovisual motion
papers.abstract: A novel 'continuous-tracking' psychophysical technique is introduced to efficiently assess audiovisual motion integration and the ventriloquist effect. Participants tracked the position of stimuli moving in random walks across visual, auditory, and audiovisual (congruent and incongruent) conditions for 60-second intervals. The primary metrics extracted were tracking lag and visual dominance weights. The data demonstrated a robust visual dominance in motion perception; visual information consistently interfered with auditory localization, even when visual reliability was experimentally attenuated. The continuous tracking paradigm provided a high-resolution measurement of the spatiotemporal processing delays (lag) between sensory modalities, confirming vision's authoritative role in the spatial perception of multisensory motion.
papers.authors: Alessia Tonelli, David Burr, Monica Gori, David Alais

papers.title: The speed and phase of locomotion dictate saccade probability and simultaneous low-frequency power spectra
papers.abstract: This study characterizes the temporal coordination between human locomotor rhythms and visuomotor behavior using simultaneous eye tracking and mobile electroencephalography (EEG) in an immersive virtual environment. Analysis of eye-movement behavior revealed that the probability of saccade initiation is rhythmically entrained to the stride cycle, with peak frequency phase-locked to the period immediately following heel-strike. Concurrently, time-frequency analysis of the EEG data showed that theta and alpha-band oscillatory power were significantly modulated by the step-cycle phase. These results demonstrate that the biomechanical demands of gait impose a rhythmic temporal structure on both the initiation of saccadic eye movements and the underlying cortical dynamics, suggesting that gait phase is a critical covariate in active-observer neuroimaging research.
papers.authors: Lydia Barnes, Matthew J. Davidson, David Alais

0159.name: David Brainard
0159.bio: David Brainard is the RRL Professor of Psychology at the University of Pennsylvania and investigates the computational and neural mechanisms of human visual perception. Their research focuses on color constancy and the process by which the visual system estimates stable object properties from light signals incident on the retina. Brainard utilizes a framework combining psychophysical experiments with image-computable modeling to study early visual encoding and the role of the retinal cone mosaic. Brainard also developed the Psychophysics Toolbox and serves as a co-editor of the Annual Review of Vision Science.
0159.research_direction: Dr. Brainard has recently been investigating visual processing mechanisms across multiple stages of the visual hierarchy, from retinal circuitry to high-level perception. Their recent work explores spatial and chromatic vision by developing image-computable, anatomically constrained models of the primate retinal ganglion cell mosaic and mapping human color discrimination thresholds using data-efficient, adaptive psychophysical procedures. Beyond early vision, they are also examining how cortical neural populations segregate task-relevant object features from complex visual backgrounds by combining monkey V4 neurophysiology with human psychophysics. Furthermore, their research extends into computational imaging, where they are utilizing diffusion probabilistic models to optimize sampling and reconstruction techniques for high-dimensional natural images.

papers.title: Temporal dynamics of human color processing measured using a continuous tracking task
papers.abstract: The authors utilize a continuous tracking paradigm to investigate the temporal latencies inherent in human chromatic processing. Observers tracked chromatic Gabor targets undergoing random-walk trajectories within the LS cone contrast plane, and tracking lag was quantified by determining the peak of the cross-correlation between target and observer velocity vectors. The results demonstrate that tracking lag decreases monotonically with increasing stimulus contrast across diverse chromatic directions. A computational model was developed to link tracking performance with 2-interval forced-choice (2IFC) detection thresholds measured in the same subjects; the model indicates that elliptical isoperformance contours for both tracking and detection exhibit nearly identical orientations and shapes, suggesting that both behaviors are supported by a common underlying representation of chromatic contrast.
papers.authors: Michael A. Barnett, Benjamin M. Chin, Geoffrey K. Aguirre, Johannes Burge, David H. Brainard

papers.title: Orthogonal neural representations support perceptual judgements of natural stimuli
papers.abstract: This study employs monkey neurophysiology and human psychophysics to test the hypothesis that the visual system utilizes orthogonal neural population representations to segregate task-relevant object features from task-irrelevant background variations. Naturalistic stimuli with parametrically controllable dimensions were generated using computer graphics, and neuronal responses were recorded from visual area V4. The findings reveal that the neural representation of object position in V4 is approximately orthogonal to the representations of several background features (e.g., rotation, depth, and luminance). Correspondingly, human observers demonstrated the ability to judge object position with high precision, largely unaffected by variations in the task-irrelevant background elements. These results provide empirical support for the theory that orthogonal subspace coding enables stable perception in complex, naturalistic environments.
papers.authors: Ramanujan Srinath, Amy M. Ni, Claire Marucci, Marlene R. Cohen, David H. Brainard

papers.title: Generalized Compressed Sensing for Image Reconstruction with Diffusion Probabilistic Models
papers.abstract: This paper addresses the optimization of linear measurement strategies for high-dimensional signal reconstruction by leveraging the advanced statistical priors embedded in diffusion probabilistic models. The authors propose a framework for jointly optimizing a measurement matrix and a denoiser-guided diffusion reconstruction algorithm, referred to as Optimal Linear Measurement (OLM). Unlike traditional methods such as Principal Component Analysis (PCA) or random compressed sensing projections which rely on simpler statistical assumptions, OLM learns measurements that are specifically tailored to the rich, non-linear structures of natural images. Experimental results on both synthetic and natural image datasets show that the OLM framework significantly outperforms standard linear measurement techniques, particularly when the optimization is targeted toward minimizing perceptual reconstruction loss.
papers.authors: Ling-Qi Zhang, Zahra Kadkhodaie, Eero P. Simoncelli, David H. Brainard

papers.title: Comprehensive characterization of human color discrimination thresholds
papers.abstract: To circumvent the 'psychophysical curse of dimensionality' in mapping the three-dimensional color space, the authors developed a data-efficient framework for characterizing human color discrimination thresholds in the isoluminant plane. The approach combines a 3AFC oddity task with a novel semi-parametric Wishart Process Psychophysical Model (WPPM) that assumes internal noise varies smoothly across the stimulus space. Stimulus selection was optimized using a non-parametric adaptive trial-placement procedure (AEPsych), allowing for a comprehensive mapping of the psychometric field with only approximately 6,000 trials per participant. The resulting model allows for the analytical readout of discrimination performance for any arbitrary stimulus pair and was validated against hold-out probe functions, providing a foundational resource for benchmarking mechanistic models of color processing.
papers.authors: Fangfang Hong, Ruby Bouhassira, Jason Chow, Craig Sanders, Michael Shvartsman, Phillip Guan, Alex H. Williams, David H. Brainard

papers.title: An image-computable, spatio-chromatic RF model of the midget RGC mosaic across the retina
papers.abstract: This work introduces a novel computational framework that synthesizes image-computable mosaics of linear spatio-chromatic receptive fields (RFs) for ON midget retinal ganglion cells (mRGCs) across the primate retina. The model rigorously incorporates anatomical constraints (cone and mRGC densities), neurophysiological data, and human optical quality measurements (wavefront aberrations). By simulating physiological experiments in both in vivo and in vitro conditions, the authors demonstrate that the model reproduces known spatio-chromatic tuning and spatial contrast sensitivity properties. The framework enables researchers to explore how different RF organization strategies—such as the specific pooling of cone signals into the RF center and surround—affect visual performance across the visual field, serving as a tool for connecting early visual circuitry to psychophysical behavior.
papers.authors: Nicolas P. Cottaris, Brian A. Wandell, David H. Brainard

0160.name: David E Osher
0160.bio: Osher is an Assistant Professor at The Ohio State University whose research examines the intersection of brain connectivity, functional specialization, and behavior through computational modeling. Their work utilizes machine learning and multimodal neuroimaging, such as functional and diffusion MRI, to develop 'connectivity fingerprints' that predict individualized neural responses and task-evoked activation. Osher investigates how connectivity patterns constrain information processing to understand the development of specialized regions for attention and high-level visual perception. Their research also extends to predicting cognitive outcomes and identifying neural markers for developmental disorders like dyslexia.
0160.research_direction: Dr. Osher's recent work explores the fundamental relationship between the brain's intrinsic architecture and its functional specialization, utilizing predictive modeling to localize high-level visual areas and broader cognitive networks solely from individualized resting-state functional connectivity. They have also recently been investigating the neurobiological consequences of binocular vision disorders, using fMRI and diffusion-weighted imaging to map structural and functional disruptions within the oculomotor vergence and frontoparietal attention networks of patients with idiopathic and concussion-related convergence insufficiency. Additionally, their research probes the computational origins of higher-order visual perception by employing novel behavioral paradigms and deep convolutional neural networks. Through this approach, they are testing whether holistic processing is genuinely unique to face perception or if it is a domain-general computation driven fundamentally by configural spatial arrangements.

papers.title: Connectivity and function are coupled across cognitive domains throughout the brain
papers.abstract: This study comprehensively evaluates the foundational hypothesis that the functional specialization of cortical regions is fundamentally determined by their extrinsic connectivity profiles. Utilizing high-resolution data from the Human Connectome Project (n = 1,018), the authors implemented ridge regression models to quantify the association between individualized resting-state functional connectivity (rs-fMRI) and task-evoked activation maps across 33 distinct cognitive domains, synthesized via the NeuroQuery meta-analytic framework. The findings reveal a robust and ubiquitous structure-function coupling across the entire brain, with the highest predictive fidelity observed in higher-order, domain-general systems compared to primary sensory regions. These results provide significant evidence for connectivity as a universal organizational principle of neural function and establish a normative reference for future research focused on individualized predictive modeling of brain activity.
papers.authors: Kelly J. Hiersche, Zeynep M. Saygin, David E. Osher

papers.title: Neural substrates of the oculomotor vergence network for concussion-related convergence insufficiency within the CONCUSS study
papers.abstract: This clinical neuroimaging study investigates the structural and functional correlates of convergence insufficiency (CI) in individuals following mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI). CI is an oculomotor impairment characterized by exophoria and reduced near-point convergence, which frequently impairs reading performance post-concussion. By examining patients from the CONCUSS cohort, the researchers analyzed white matter microstructural integrity and functional connectivity within the oculomotor vergence network. The analysis identified specific disruptions in the arcuate fasciculus and other associative white matter tracts, demonstrating that symptomatic post-concussive CI is associated with objective alterations in the neural pathways linking cortical vergence centers to brainstem motor nuclei. These findings offer potential biomarkers for assessing oculomotor recovery and the downstream neural consequences of concussion-related visual dysfunction.
papers.authors: Yuxuan Zeng, Tamara S. Oechslin, Douglas E. Widmer, David E. Osher

papers.title: Isolated Configuration: Holistic Processing Beyond the Realm of Faces
papers.abstract: This research challenges the domain-specific view of holistic processing as a mechanism exclusive to face perception. The authors developed novel, abstract stimuli designed to isolate configural information (the spatial arrangement of components) from featural information to test whether configural properties alone can drive holistic effects. Across four hallmark behavioral tasks—inversion, misalignment, part-whole, and composite effects—the study found that configural stimuli elicited robust holistic processing markers even with minimal training, whereas featural controls did not. Furthermore, deep convolutional neural networks (DCNNs) trained on these configural datasets exhibited human-like holistic processing patterns. The results suggest that holistic processing is a domain-general visual computation emerging from configural architectures, providing a computational framework for the origins of specialized face-selective systems.
papers.authors: Yuxuan Zeng, Zitong Lu, Ren E. Hentz, David E. Osher

papers.title: Predicting high-level visual areas in the absence of task fMRI
papers.abstract: The identification of category-selective functional regions of interest (fROIs) typically requires task-based fMRI localizers, which can be logistically challenging or costly. This paper introduces a method for predicting individualized fROIs in the ventral visual stream—including areas selective for faces, scenes, objects, and bodies—using only resting-state functional connectivity data. By training connectivity fingerprinting models on a large-scale dataset (HCP), the authors demonstrate that an individual’s unique connectome provides sufficient topographic information to accurately localize fROIs for high-level vision, as well as for language, motor, and working memory domains. This connectivity-based approach offers a precise and efficient alternative for functional mapping, particularly in clinical or pediatric populations where task compliance is limited.
papers.authors: M. Fiona Molloy, Zeynep M. Saygin, David E. Osher

papers.title: Neural consequences of symptomatic convergence insufficiency: A small sample study
papers.abstract: This study explores the neurobiological impact of symptomatic convergence insufficiency (CI), a common binocular vision disorder that manifests as exophoria and impaired convergence during near-work tasks. Utilizing fMRI and diffusion-weighted imaging in a cohort of symptomatic individuals, the researchers investigated how CI-related oculomotor deficits influence higher-order visual and cognitive networks. The results identified reduced functional recruitment in frontoparietal attention networks and microstructural alterations in white matter pathways during reading and visual search tasks. These findings suggest that the consequences of symptomatic CI extend beyond oculomotor discomfort, potentially affecting attentional allocation and reading efficiency by disrupting the neural circuits responsible for coordinating binocular input and cognitive processing.
papers.authors: Yuxuan Zeng, Tamara S. Oechslin, Douglas E. Widmer, Marjean T. Kulp, Nicklaus Fogt, Andrew Toole, Steven Manning, David E. Osher

0161.name: David Fitzpatrick
0161.institution: Max Planck Florida Institute for Neuroscience
0161.department: Functional Architecture and Development of Cerebral Cortex
0161.bio: Fitzpatrick is the Scientific Director and CEO of the Max Planck Florida Institute for Neuroscience, where their research examines the functional architecture and maturation of neural circuits in the primary visual cortex. Their work utilizes in vivo two-photon calcium imaging and anatomical tracing to identify how stimulus features such as orientation and motion are represented within the synaptic architecture of dendritic spines and population-level networks. A focus of Fitzpatrick’s research involves the 'nature-nurture' transform, specifically how early spontaneous activity establishes modular networks that are refined by visual experience to achieve binocular alignment. Previously a professor at Duke University, Fitzpatrick investigated the principles of intracortical connectivity and the role of experience-dependent plasticity in sensory processing.
0161.research_direction: Dr. Fitzpatrick has recently been investigating the developmental mechanisms that establish functional architecture and reliable sensory representations in the visual cortex. Their recent work explores how spontaneous pre-vision activity, such as retinal waves, interacts with self-organizing recurrent networks to build the initial scaffold for modular orientation maps. Furthermore, they are examining how early visual experience drives the integration of feedforward inputs with recurrent cortical dynamics to support mature center-surround contextual modulation and stable stimulus discriminability. Broadening their scope beyond early cortical development, they are also probing the evolution of hierarchical form vision, using high-density electrophysiology in tree shrews to map the emergence of complex feature selectivity and face representations along the ventral visual pathway.

papers.title: Development of coherent cortical responses reflects increased discriminability of feedforward inputs and their alignment with recurrent circuits
papers.abstract: The transition from immature cortical networks to reliable sensory representations requires the transformation of stimulus-driven inputs into consistent activity patterns. In the primary visual cortex (V1), layer 4 (L4) neurons provide feedforward drive to functional modules in layer 2/3 (L2/3) that are linked by strong recurrent interactions. Using longitudinal in vivo calcium imaging and electrophysiology in ferrets, this study finds that in visually naive animals, coactivity between L4 and L2/3 lacks orientation specificity, resulting in high trial-to-trial variability and poor stimulus discriminability. This state arises from low orientation selectivity in L4 and a misalignment between feedforward and recurrent circuit interactions. Following visual experience, L4 orientation discriminability increases and feedforward inputs align with L2/3 recurrent dynamics, as confirmed by whole-cell subthreshold recordings and computational modeling. This developmental alignment is essential for the emergence of reliable, modular representations characterized by interlaminar temporal coherence.
papers.authors: Augusto Abel Lempel, Sigrid Trägenap, Clara Tepohl, Matthias Kaschube, David Fitzpatrick

papers.title: Retinal waves reveal axial biases in modular patterns of cortical activity that predict future orientation preferences
papers.abstract: The formation of functional modular networks in the visual cortex is guided by spontaneous activity prior to sensory experience. This study utilizes chronic widefield and two-photon calcium imaging in neonatal tree shrews to track cortical activity before and after eye opening. The authors identified retinal-driven spontaneous waves in the immature cortex that exhibit modular structures specific to the topographic axis of the wavefront. These waves recruit neuronal populations into elongated correlated networks whose axial biases strikingly correspond to the orientation preference maps that emerge after the onset of vision. These results indicate that the structural and functional scaffold for modular orientation maps is established by retinal activity patterns well before the maturation of visually driven responses.
papers.authors: Alexandra Gribizis, David Fitzpatrick

papers.title: Self-organization of modular activity in immature cortical networks
papers.abstract: In the early stages of cortical development, spontaneous activity is organized into distributed modular patterns that serve as a precursor to mature columnar architecture. This study tests whether these structured patterns emerge through a self-organizing recurrent network mechanism involving local excitation and lateral inhibition (LE/LI). By combining widefield calcium imaging with optogenetic manipulations in juvenile ferrets prior to eye opening, the researchers find that the spatiotemporal dynamics of spontaneous events align with LE/LI model predictions. Specifically, local cortical interactions are sufficient to generate the millimeter-scale correlations and modular architecture observed in the absence of sensory input, demonstrating that the fundamental functional organization of the cortex arises through dynamic self-organization of early synaptic circuits.
papers.authors: Augusto Abel Lempel, Sigrid Trägenap, Clara Tepohl, Matthias Kaschube, David Fitzpatrick

papers.title: Contextual modulation emerges by integrating feedforward and recurrent network dynamics in primary visual cortex
papers.abstract: Mature sensory processing in the primary visual cortex involves contextual modulation, where neuronal responses to a stimulus in the receptive field center are influenced by the surrounding visual environment. This study investigates the developmental emergence of these contextual interactions using chronic imaging and computational modeling in the ferret model. The authors find that early stimulus-evoked responses lack the refined center-surround suppression and orientation-specific modulation found in adults. The transition to mature contextual processing depends on the developmental integration of feedforward inputs with the large-scale recurrent network dynamics of the superficial layers. As feedforward and recurrent interactions align, the network develops the capacity to integrate global stimulus information, facilitating scene segmentation and efficient sensory coding.
papers.authors: Sigrid Trägenap, Clara Tepohl, Matthias Kaschube, David Fitzpatrick

papers.title: A multispecies perspective on the evolution of form vision
papers.abstract: Hierarchical representation is a fundamental principle of object recognition in both biological and artificial neural networks. This research uses high-throughput electrophysiological recordings with Neuropixels probes to characterize the ventral visual pathway of the tree shrew, a close relative of primates. The findings reveal that the tree shrew visual system exhibits a primate-like functional hierarchy, with area V2 neurons showing progressively larger receptive fields, increased response latencies, and enhanced selectivity for complex features compared to V1. Notably, the tree shrew area V2 supports a complete representation of object space and contains face-selective neurons, mirroring functions of the primate inferotemporal cortex. These results suggest that hierarchical strategies for processing form and object identity are conserved across highly visual mammalian species.
papers.authors: Frank F. Lanfranchi, Madineh Sedigh-Sarvestani, Juliane Jaepel, David Fitzpatrick

0162.name: DAVID LEOPOLD
0162.lab_name: Section on Cognitive Neurophysiology and Imaging (SCNI)
0162.bio: David Leopold investigates the large-scale neural architecture underlying visual perception, specifically how the primate brain constructs a stable interpretation of the environment. Leopold’s research integrates high-field functional MRI with laminar-specific electrophysiology and pharmacological perturbations to study thalamocortical interactions and the neural correlates of conscious visibility. Their work on bistable perception demonstrates how sensory cortical activity reflects subjective states rather than mere physical stimuli. Current research directions for Leopold include the neurodevelopment of social perception circuits and the processing of dynamic, naturalistic visual scenes.
0162.research_direction: Dr. Leopold has recently been investigating the neural mechanisms of primate visual perception, advocating for a shift toward studying cortical dynamics during active, naturalistic visual behavior. Their recent work explores how established functional networks, such as fMRI-defined cortical face patches, process complex perceptual phenomena like face pareidolia at the single-unit level. To probe these local circuits in awake macaques and marmosets, they are developing advanced physiological and genetic tools, including targeted fetal viral injections for laminar-specific gene expression and novel "lennula" microprisms for chronic endoscopic calcium imaging in visual cortex. Additionally, Dr. Leopold utilizes ultra-high-resolution diffusion MRI to track gray matter myelin density, aiming to link underlying microstructural architecture to the fluid, highly integrated neural representations that support everyday vision.
