papers.title: An implanted lennula approach to measure neural Ca²⁺ responses in the awake marmoset visual cortex
papers.abstract: The study introduces the 'lennula' (lens-cannula), an integrated microprism and viral injection system designed for chronic endoscopic calcium imaging in the marmoset. Using a head-mounted miniscope in awake subjects, the researchers achieved stable GCaMP-mediated longitudinal tracking of visual responses in extrastriate areas V3 and MT over multiple weeks. Neuronal populations monitored via this method exhibited diverse tuning to naturalistic stimuli and movies, with functionally distinct cells found to be spatially intermixed within the local cortical architecture. This surgical and technical advancement facilitates the study of primate cortical dynamics and functional organization during active vision with cellular resolution.
papers.authors: Soo Hyun Park, Stephany A. Nti, Madeline Marcelle, Elena M. Esch, Kuan Hong Wang, Afonso C. Silva, David A. Leopold

papers.title: Face pareidolia minimally engages macaque face selective neurons
papers.abstract: This investigation quantified single-unit activity in four fMRI-defined macaque face-selective regions—the anterior medial (AM), anterior fundus (AF), prefrontal orbital (PO), and perirhinal cortex (PRh) face patches—during the presentation of face pareidolia stimuli (objects perceived as faces). Despite behavioral evidence that macaques perceive such illusory faces, population-level neural responses in these patches for pareidolia-evoking objects were significantly lower than those for authentic macaque faces and comparable to matched control objects. These findings indicate that neurons within the established cortical face network are primarily specialized for the analysis of realistic facial features rather than the high-level configuration responsible for the pareidolia illusion, which likely involves neural mechanisms outside these specific patches.
papers.authors: Kenji W. Koyano, Jessica Taubert, William Robison, Elena N. Waidmann, David A. Leopold

papers.title: Targeted gene transfer into developmentally defined cell populations of the primate brain
papers.abstract: The researchers present a method for introducing transgenes across the primate cerebral cortex using ultrasound-guided fetal intracerebroventricular viral injections (FIVI). By systematically modulating the gestational timing of injections and selecting specific recombinant adeno-associated virus (rAAV) serotypes and promoters, the authors achieved widespread, long-lasting, and laminar-specific expression in the cortex. The study demonstrates the platform's versatility through Cre-dependent neuronal targeting, CRISPR-based gene editing, and labeling of distal somatosensory and retinal pathways, providing a powerful, minimally invasive tool for investigating primate brain development and implementing experimental or translational genetic interventions.
papers.authors: Ana Rita Ribeiro Gomes, Natalie Hamel, Surjeet Mastwal, Naim Wright, David C. Ide, Christopher T. Richie, Ted B. Usdin, Kuan Hong Wang, David A. Leopold

papers.title: Diffusion kurtosis imaging, MAP-MRI and NODDI selectively track gray matter myelin density in the primate cerebral cortex
papers.abstract: This study evaluates higher-order diffusion MRI parameters—specifically Mean Diffusion Kurtosis (MK), the Neurite Density Index (NDI) from NODDI, and the Non-Gaussian (NG) parameter from MAP-MRI—for their efficacy in characterizing gray matter microstructure. Through ultra-high-resolution ex-vivo dMRI and histological validation in marmoset brains, the authors demonstrated that these advanced metrics, unlike standard Diffusion Tensor Imaging (DTI) measures such as Fractional Anisotropy (FA), exhibit high sensitivity and specificity for tracking regional and laminar variations in myelin density. These results suggest that higher-order diffusion parameters can serve as precise, non-invasive biomarkers for investigating cortical organization and evaluating diseases that differentially impact myelinated and non-myelinated compartments.
papers.authors: Colin Reveley, Frank Q. Ye, David A. Leopold

papers.title: The big mixup: Neural representation during natural modes of primate visual behavior
papers.abstract: This review critiques traditional reductionist approaches to visual neurophysiology, which historically emphasized hierarchical stimulus encoding and modular functional segregation under highly controlled paradigms. Drawing on recent electrophysiological and fMRI evidence from macaques engaged in natural visual behavior, the author argues for a 'big mixup' in neural representation, where cortical responses are highly dynamic, non-linear, and influenced by active behavioral sampling. The paper suggests that conventional representationalist models fail to account for the fluid and integrated manner in which the primate brain processes its surroundings, advocating for more naturalistic experimental frameworks to uncover how the brain supports daily visual experience.
papers.authors: David A. Leopold

0164.name: David Melcher
0164.lab_name: Perception and Active Cognition Lab (PAC Lab)
0164.bio: Melcher investigates how the human brain constructs a stable and continuous subjective experience from dynamic sensory input during active behavior. Their research characterizes trans-saccadic perception and the role of neural oscillations and temporal binding windows in organizing perception, attention, and action. Utilizing a multimodal approach including fMRI, EEG, MEG, and eye-tracking, Melcher explores the neural underpinnings of predictive remapping and how perception interacts with memory and motor control. Their work also examines individual differences in temporal and spatial processing across the lifespan and within clinical populations, such as those with autism, ADHD, and dyslexia.
0164.research_direction: Dr. Melcher's recent work explores the neural and computational mechanisms underlying temporal perception, predictive processing, and visual stability. Using high-density EEG and psychophysics, they are investigating how rhythmic alpha-band oscillations and aperiodic neural dynamics collectively shape the visual temporal integration window, continuous sensory encoding, and our reliance on recent perceptual history. Their research also utilizes hierarchical modeling to examine how the weighting of incoming sensory evidence versus internal perceptual priors shifts across neurodivergent populations, specifically along the ADHD, autism, and schizotypy continuums. Additionally, they have recently been developing target-centric computational frameworks, such as steerable autoencoder models, to probe how the visual system achieves trans-saccadic feature stability and spatial remapping across rapid eye movements.

papers.title: Oscillatory and aperiodic neural dynamics shape temporal perception and weighting of perceptual priors in ADHD profiles
papers.abstract: This neurophysiological investigation explores the mechanisms underlying atypical temporal perception in ADHD, which is typically characterized by a compressed subjective sense of time. The researchers integrated a sustained visual temporal integration task with resting-state electroencephalography (EEG) to determine the respective roles of rhythmic alpha-band activity and non-rhythmic aperiodic (1/f) dynamics. Findings indicate that elevated ADHD traits are significantly associated with a higher individual alpha frequency (IAF) and a shallower aperiodic slope, reflecting increased neural noise. Structural equation and mediation modeling revealed that shifts in IAF specifically mediate the reduction in temporal integration thresholds observed in ADHD, whereas the aperiodic component modulates the strength of history-dependent perceptual biases. These results suggest a bifurcated neural architecture where periodic sampling speed and aperiodic excitation/inhibition balance independently contribute to temporal processing anomalies in neurodivergent populations.
papers.authors: Gianluca Marsicano, Michele Deodato, David Melcher

papers.title: Alpha oscillations and aperiodic neural dynamics jointly predict visual temporal resolution, confidence, and dependence on prior experience
papers.abstract: The present study evaluates the synergistic influence of alpha-band rhythms and aperiodic 1/f neural dynamics on the temporal resolution of human vision. Utilizing a psychophysical paradigm involving flicker-induced integration and segregation of gratings, the authors measured temporal integration windows (TIW) alongside resting-state EEG metrics. The results demonstrate that faster individual alpha frequencies (IAF) are predictive of narrower TIWs and increased subjective metacognitive confidence, consistent with the hypothesis that alpha oscillations establish the temporal frames for discrete sensory sampling. Furthermore, steeper aperiodic slopes (reflecting a higher inhibition-to-excitation ratio) were found to enhance perceptual precision and mitigate serial dependence on previous stimuli. These findings highlight that visual temporal acuity and the weighting of perceptual history are co-determined by the speed of rhythmic sampling and the global state of neural noise.
papers.authors: Gianluca Marsicano, Michele Deodato, David Melcher

papers.title: Steerable autoencoders underlying remapping, spatiotopy, and visual stability
papers.abstract: This paper proposes a computational framework for trans-saccadic visual stability based on target-centric remapping rather than traditional global spatiotopic maps. The authors introduce a 'steerable autoencoder' model to explain how the brain maintains feature correspondence across rapid eye movements. In this model, attended object identities are linked to their feature coordinates in early visual areas through a neural network that predictively shifts feature activity to the post-saccadic retinotopic location. This steerable mechanism allows for the integration of pre-saccadic preview information with post-saccadic foveal input, accounting for experimental findings of spatiotopy and trans-saccadic feature persistence without requiring an explicit world-coordinate representation. The model provides a parsimonious account of how the visual system achieves perceptual continuity across the discontinuous inputs generated by saccades.
papers.authors: Patrick Cavanagh, David Melcher

papers.title: Phase-Dependent EEG Decoding of Continuous Visual Stimuli
papers.abstract: This study examines the rhythmic gating hypothesis by investigating whether the neural representation of sustained visual input is modulated by the phase of ongoing alpha oscillations. Using high-density EEG and multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA), the researchers tracked the decodability of continuous visual stimuli over time. Decoding accuracy was found to be a non-linear function of the instantaneous alpha phase (8–13 Hz), with classification performance significantly peaking at specific oscillatory phases, particularly around the 180° offset. These results demonstrate that information throughput in the visual system is rhythmically gated by intrinsic neural cycles, influencing how continuous sensory streams are encoded and maintained in the brain's internal representations even in the absence of discrete event onsets.
papers.authors: Michele Deodato, David Melcher

papers.title: Atypical weighting of sensory evidence and priors in causality perception along the autism–schizotypy continuum
papers.abstract: This research utilizes hierarchical computational modeling and a collision-event psychophysical task to investigate individual differences in causal inference. The study assesses how observers integrate sensory-driven signals (temporal lag precision) with prior-driven expectations (serial dependence on previous trials) to perceive causality. Participants were stratified along the autism-schizotypy spectrum to examine neurocognitive styles of predictive processing. Results revealed that autism-related traits were associated with a 'sensory-driven' style, characterized by high weighting of physical timing and high sensory precision. In contrast, schizotypal traits were linked to a 'prior-driven' style, showing a stronger reliance on perceptual history and internal expectations. These findings suggest that individual variability in causality perception reflects fundamental differences in how the brain weights new sensory evidence against internal models of the world.
papers.authors: Gianluca Marsicano, David Melcher

0165.name: David Soto
0165.institution: Basque Center on Cognition, Brain and Language
0165.bio: David Soto is an Ikerbasque Research Professor who directs the Consciousness Group at the BCBL, where they investigate the neurobiological boundaries between conscious and non-conscious cognitive processes. Soto's research integrates psychophysics, functional neuroimaging, and computational modeling to examine how information influences perceptual selection, working memory, and metacognition. Their work on unconscious working memory employs functional MRI decoded neurofeedback (fMRI-DecNef) to non-invasively manipulate brain states and evaluate changes in behavior and subjective experience. Soto's laboratory extends these investigations to typical and atypical populations with the objective of translating findings into neurocognitive interventions for learning and clinical disorders.
0165.research_direction: Dr. Soto’s recent work investigates the neural architecture underlying conscious and unconscious perception, exploring phenomena like how humans extract statistical visual summaries of complex scenes without explicit awareness. By combining functional MRI, representational similarity analysis, and computational models from deep learning, they are examining how high-level features—spanning subliminal visual stimuli, abstract social concepts, and semantic object knowledge—are mapped across distributed brain networks. Their research also explores how these categorical brain representations reorganize and specialize to maintain cognitive performance during healthy aging. Additionally, they have recently been developing co-adaptive machine learning techniques for real-time fMRI decoded neurofeedback, aiming to improve the precision with which participants can self-modulate specific multivariate neural states.

papers.title: Enhancing fMRI Decoded Neurofeedback with Co-adaptive Training: Simulation and Proof-of-principle Evidence
papers.abstract: The efficacy of fMRI-based decoded neurofeedback (DecNef) is frequently undermined by the inability of participants to reliably self-induce target multivariate brain activity patterns, a failure often attributed to non-stationarity and distributional shifts between the initial decoder training and the subsequent neurofeedback sessions. This study proposes a co-adaptation framework utilizing an adaptive machine learning algorithm that iteratively updates the decoder in real-time based on trial-wise predictions during the neurofeedback loop. Initial simulations using historical DecNef datasets demonstrated that co-adaptation significantly improves induction performance, while drift analysis confirmed the longitudinal stability of the adaptive classifier. Real-time fMRI experiments provided proof-of-principle evidence that co-adaptive training enhances the precision of neural state induction, offering a robust methodological advancement for the non-invasive modulation of specific neural representations in clinical and basic research.
papers.authors: Najmeddine Abdennour, Pedro Margolles, David Soto

papers.title: Brain Representation in Conscious and Unconscious Vision
papers.abstract: To elucidate the neural mechanisms underlying the representation of visual stimuli across the threshold of awareness, this study integrated high-precision functional MRI with representational similarity analysis (RSA) based on deep convolutional neural network (CNN) architectures. Hierarchical features from hidden layers of computer vision models (e.g., VGGNet, ResNet50) were mapped to brain activity patterns in the ventral visual stream and fronto-parietal networks. The results indicated that computer vision models effectively predicted voxel-wise activity for both conscious and unconscious contents, even in subjects exhibiting null d' perceptual sensitivity. Notably, the preservation of robust representations in fronto-parietal regions for subliminal stimuli challenges Global Neuronal Workspace theories regarding the broadcasting of conscious information and instead corroborates higher-order theories of consciousness which emphasize the role of these regions in generating meta-representations.
papers.authors: Ning Mei, David Soto

papers.title: Enhanced generalization and specialization of brain representations of semantic knowledge in healthy aging
papers.abstract: Semantic cognition is relatively preserved in healthy aging, possibly due to large-scale network reconfigurations and neural dedifferentiation. This study employed multivariate pattern classification and model-based RSA to investigate how aging affects the neural representation of animacy (living vs. non-living word concepts). Analysis of fMRI data revealed that older adults exhibit increased neural similarity across semantic categories, aligning with the neural dedifferentiation hypothesis that posits a loss of category specificity with age. Crucially, this was accompanied by a concurrent increase in the dissimilarity of item-specific conceptual representations within each category. These divergent patterns of increased generalization across categories and enhanced specialization at the item level suggest a compensatory mechanism utilizing a more efficient, sparse coding scheme to maintain semantic performance despite age-related reductions in neural resources.
papers.authors: Pedro Margolles, David Soto

papers.title: Characterising the role of awareness in ensemble perception
papers.abstract: The computation of ensemble representations—efficient statistical summaries of complex visual scenes—is often assumed to be pre-attentive or automatic, yet the necessity of visual awareness remains a subject of debate. Using a bias-free two-interval forced-choice (2IFC) psychophysical paradigm, we dissociated sensitivity to ensemble properties (e.g., mean emotional valence) from the conscious detection of task-relevant features. We show that participants can reliably discriminate ensemble-level summaries even when they are unable to explicitly detect the features defining the ensemble. Computational modeling of Type-1 and Type-2 drift rates further suggests that awareness-related processing lags behind the categorization mechanisms supporting ensemble perception. These results provide evidence for 'ensemble blindsight,' indicating that high-level visual summaries can be extracted and maintained in the absence of conscious access.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
papers.authors: Patxi Elosegi, Ning Mei, David Soto

papers.title: Brain-wide representation of social knowledge
papers.abstract: Understanding the neural architecture that maps dimensions of social concepts is critical for models of social cognition. In this fMRI study, participants engaged in mental simulation of experiences associated with personality traits varying across affect (affective vs. non-affective) and social desirability (desirable vs. undesirable). Multivariate searchlight decoding identified distributed representations for both dimensions within the superior temporal lobe, precuneus, and core nodes of the Default Mode Network (DMN), including the medial prefrontal and cingulate cortices. Decoding accuracy was significantly higher for social desirability than for affect. Furthermore, RSA revealed that representational spaces from deep language models significantly predicted neural activity in bilateral anterior temporal lobes. The findings suggest a brain-wide system for social knowledge grounded in DMN-mediated multimodal simulation and language-based semantic preprocessing.
papers.authors: Daniel Alcalá-López, Ning Mei, Pedro Margolles, David Soto

0166.name: David Souto
0166.department: School of Psychology and Vision Sciences
0166.bio: David Souto is a vision scientist whose research focuses on the mechanisms of dynamic vision and the control of eye movements, specifically how humans process motion and select task-relevant information during smooth pursuit and saccades. Souto utilizes eye-tracking and psychophysical methods to investigate visuo-motor learning, adaptation, and visual stability in dynamic environments. Their work explores applied domains such as the development of gaze-controlled assistive communication technologies and the study of pedestrian visual sampling for road safety. Souto leads the VisuoMotor Lab and coordinates the Vision Science Research Group at the University of Leicester.
0166.research_direction: Dr. Souto's recent work investigates how the visual system maintains stability during voluntary eye movements, specifically focusing on how the brain suppresses reflexive optokinetic responses to self-induced background motion. By manipulating the contrast of background motion signals during smooth pursuit, they have recently been testing competing computational models—such as sensory attenuation and visuomotor gain modulation—to understand how the visual system selectively filters this reafferent visual information. In addition to this fundamental sensorimotor research, their recent work explores the applied and clinical utility of eye-gaze systems in augmentative and alternative communication. Using qualitative methods, they are examining how assistive technology professionals interpret diagnostic feedback tools, such as heatmaps and calibration scores, to make clinical inferences about the cognitive and visual capabilities of users with complex disabilities.

papers.title: Multiple mechanisms of response suppression to self-induced sensation during pursuit eye movements
papers.abstract: The visual system encounter significant challenges in discriminating self-induced reafferent motion from objective movement in the environment during eye movements. This study investigates the mechanisms regulating the suppression of reflexive optokinetic responses to background retinal flow during voluntary smooth pursuit. By manipulating the contrast of brief background motion signals, the researchers evaluated two competing hypotheses: a visuomotor gain modulation model (proportional suppression across contrasts) and a sensory attenuation model (contrast threshold elevation). The findings revealed that neither individual account fully explained the ocular tracking data. Instead, most observers were best characterized by a model incorporating contrast-dependent gating—where suppression is maximized for high-contrast, salient signals—combined with either visuomotor or contrast gain modulation. This gating mechanism likely represents an environmental adaptation that ensures visuomotor stability during pursuit by selectively suppressing conflicting salient reafference.
papers.authors: Omar Bachtoula, Mel Ellul Miraval, Ignacio Serrano-Pedraza, David Souto

papers.title: Suppression of optokinesis in the reafferent direction during pursuit eye movements
papers.abstract: This work explores the cancellation of optokinetic nystagmus and ocular tracking responses triggered by the retinal flow of a textured background during smooth pursuit eye movements. To determine whether this suppression is mediated by sensory attenuation or visuomotor gain changes, the authors varied the contrast of background perturbations. Quantitative analysis demonstrated that ocular responses to motion in the reafferent direction are suppressed more effectively as contrast increases, a result inconsistent with simple linear suppression models. The data support a contrast-dependent gating mechanism that prioritizes the suppression of the most salient reafferent signals to maintain stable pursuit of the intended target. This mechanism suggests a specialized adaptation to environmental statistics that promotes visual stability by selectively filtering self-induced motion information based on signal strength.
papers.authors: Omar Bachtoula, Melanie Ellul Miraval, Ignacio Serrano-Pedraza, David Souto

papers.title: Use of eye-gaze technology feedback by assistive technology professionals: findings from a thematic analysis
papers.abstract: This study investigates how assistive technology professionals utilize feedback tools provided by eye-gaze systems to support clinical decision-making for users with complex disabilities. Employing a qualitative thematic analysis and focus group methodology, the research explores the perceptions and practices of two groups: professionals involved in system assessment and provision, and those providing ongoing support. The analysis identifies a critical gap between the design of current feedback tools (e.g., heatmaps, calibration scores) and the clinical inferences professionals draw regarding a user's cognitive and visual status. Results indicate that many tools are perceived as 'black boxes,' providing problem identification without actionable solutions or validated diagnostic metrics. The study calls for the development of multi-level feedback interfaces that differentiate between the needs of end-users and professionals to enhance the effectiveness of gaze-based augmentative and alternative communication.
papers.authors: Tom Griffiths, Simon Judge, David Souto

0167.name: David Watson
0167.bio: David M. Watson is a vision neuroscientist at the University of York specializing in the functional architecture of high-level visual systems. Their research integrates functional MRI, transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), and behavioral psychophysics to delineate the neural substrates of scene perception and social face processing. Watson examines how the human brain represents dynamic facial behaviors and the organizational principles of object and scene recognition. Their current work investigates the connectivity and functional specialization of the lateral and ventral visual pathways in processing complex social information.
0167.research_direction: Dr. Watson has recently been investigating the organizing principles of high-level visual cognition, exploring how the brain and artificial neural networks represent complex stimuli like faces and natural objects. Their recent work characterizes the functional and structural connectivity of the scene-selective network, examining whether intrinsic resting-state dynamics can reliably predict individual differences in spatial memory and navigation behavior. Using a combination of naturalistic fMRI, deep convolutional neural networks, and large-scale data-driven modeling, they probe phenomena such as view-symmetric face processing and the topographical mapping of latent object dimensions. Alongside these cognitive questions, Dr. Watson critically evaluates standard neuroimaging methodologies, investigating whether widely used techniques for extracting functional connectivity gradients might be capturing spatial preprocessing artifacts rather than true cortical architecture.

papers.title: Functional Connectivity of the Scene Processing Network at Rest Does Not Reliably Predict Human Behavior on Scene Processing Tasks
papers.abstract: This study evaluated whether interindividual variations in resting-state functional connectivity (RSFC) within the human scene-selective network correlate with cognitive performance in scene recognition, spatial memory, and navigation. Utilizing a large-scale public dataset (N=217), the researchers measured functional connectivity among core regions including the occipital place area (OPA), parahippocampal place area (PPA), and retrosplenial complex (RSC). While the analysis successfully replicated the known posterior–anterior connectivity bias within the network, the results failed to show any consistent associations between intrinsic network connectivity and behavioral task scores. These findings suggest that resting-state dynamics may not sufficiently reflect the neural substrates of scene perception and navigation, highlighting the potential necessity for task-based or naturalistic fMRI designs to uncover the neural basis of these behavioral traits.
papers.authors: David M. Watson, Timothy J. Andrews

papers.title: A data-driven analysis of the perceptual and neural responses to natural objects reveals organising principles of human visual cognition
papers.abstract: The authors employed a data-driven approach to investigate the functional organization of the human visual cortex using 720 object concepts from the THINGS initiative. By applying Partial Least Squares Regression (PLSR) to link 66 perceptual stimulus dimensions with whole-brain fMRI responses, they identified five latent components that accurately predicted neural activity across both low- and high-level visual areas. These components revealed smooth, graded topographic representations and captured essential object properties such as animacy, real-world size, and category. Because these identified dimensions did not align simply with traditional categorical models, the study suggests that the visual brain's organization is primarily driven by the statistical properties of objects encountered in the natural world.
papers.authors: David M. Watson, Timothy J. Andrews

papers.title: View-symmetric representations of faces in human and artificial neural networks
papers.abstract: This investigation explored how the human visual system and deep convolutional neural networks (DCNNs) represent facial identity across varying viewpoints. The study specifically focused on the emergence of 'view-symmetric' representations, in which mirror-symmetric views (e.g., -45° and +45°) are processed as more similar to each other than to other views. Using fMRI and computational modeling, the researchers demonstrated that view-symmetry is a prominent organizational feature in the later stages of the ventral visual stream and in the deeper layers of identity-trained DCNNs. These results indicate that view-symmetry serves as an important intermediate computational step in achieving viewpoint-invariant face recognition.
papers.authors: Xun Zhu, David M. Watson, Daniel Rogers, Timothy J. Andrews

papers.title: Mapping the functional and structural connectivity of the scene network
papers.abstract: Combining resting-state fMRI, naturalistic viewing fMRI (using 'Game of Thrones' stimuli), and diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI), this research characterized the extrinsic connectivity of the core scene-selective network. The analysis revealed a robust posterior–anterior connectivity bias: posterior scene regions (OPA and posterior PPA) showed preferential functional and structural links to early visual and posterior parietal regions, whereas anterior regions (RSC and anterior PPA) exhibited stronger connectivity with mnemonic and default mode network areas. The findings support a hierarchical organization within the scene network, where posterior regions are primarily involved in representing egocentric visual features and anterior regions support higher-level memory-based scene processing.
papers.authors: David M. Watson, Timothy J. Andrews

papers.title: Connectopic mapping techniques do not reflect functional gradients in the brain
papers.abstract: This methodological study critically examines 'connectopic mapping,' a technique used to identify functional gradients (e.g., retinotopy) from fMRI connectivity data. The researchers generated synthetic datasets of Gaussian white noise and processed them using standard fMRI pipelines, including spatial smoothing and interpolation across coordinate spaces. They found that these common preprocessing steps introduce spatial autocorrelations that generate illusory connectopic gradients, which closely resemble real biological maps such as eccentricity and polar angle. The study warns that many gradients reported in the connectivity literature may be artifacts of data processing rather than true reflections of the brain's functional architecture.
papers.authors: David M. Watson, Timothy J. Andrews

0168.name: David Whitney
0168.lab_name: Whitney Lab for Perception and Action
0168.bio: Whitney is a Professor of Psychology and Vision Science at the University of California, Berkeley, where they direct the Whitney Lab for Perception and Action and serve as the Faculty Director of the Cognitive Science program. Whitney’s research investigates the neural and psychological mechanisms that enable stable visual perception, focusing on how the brain integrates information across space and time to overcome internal processing delays and environmental clutter. Their work involves the study of serial dependence, ensemble perception, and visual crowding, employing a multimodal approach that includes psychophysics, functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), and transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS). Whitney’s current work explores the limits of object recognition in dynamic scenes and the idiosyncratic spatial biases that influence human visuomotor control.
0168.research_direction: Dr. Whitney has recently been investigating how the human brain processes continuous, dynamic information over time, with a major focus on how observers integrate facial expressions and situational context to infer the emotions of others. Their recent work explores these affective inferences using large-scale, naturalistic video datasets and continuous psychophysical tracking to examine individual differences in cue-combination strategies and idiosyncratic biases in emotional recollection. In addition to high-level social perception, they are studying the role of temporal history in visual processing, specifically investigating how the strength of serial dependence and predictive templates fluctuates to shift perception between sensory-driven and prior-driven modes. Finally, their research extends these questions of temporal context into motor control, testing whether sequential dependencies and variability in goal-directed reaching are driven by Bayesian inference or the dynamic resource reallocation of efficient coding.

papers.title: Integration of affective cues in context-rich and dynamic scenes varies across individuals
papers.abstract: Observers must integrate facial expressions and background context to perform affective inferences in dynamic social environments. We modeled the computational architecture of this integration by comparing observers' continuous valence and arousal judgments against Bayesian and heuristic frameworks. Using a large-scale psychophysical dataset (n = 944) derived from naturalistic video clips, we evaluated whether the visual system weights cues based on their reliability (inverse variance) or employs a simple averaging strategy. While population-level behavior was effectively modeled by Bayesian integration, we identified profound idiosyncratic variance in individual integration strategies. Some observers functioned as near-optimal Bayesian integrators, whereas others utilized heuristic biases that failed to account for cue ambiguity. These findings reveal that the capacity to optimally combine social cues is a highly variable trait that may underlie individual differences in social-cognitive attunement.
papers.authors: Jefferson Ortega, Yuki Murai, David Whitney

papers.title: Continuous affect tracking reveals that overestimation during the recollection of affect is idiosyncratic and stable
papers.abstract: Retrospective summaries of affective experiences are critical for decision-making, yet these recollections are subject to systematic biases. We quantified this bias using a continuous psychophysical tracking method where participants rated the valence and arousal of movie characters in real-time followed by a retrospective summary rating post-viewing. Our analysis revealed a robust overestimation bias, with participants recalling affect as significantly more intense than their integrated moment-to-moment ratings indicated. Crucially, this overestimation was highly idiosyncratic but stable within individuals across multiple sessions and generalized across heterogeneous affective content. These results suggest that recollective overestimation is a robust, trait-like characteristic of the social-perceptual system, reflecting a stable bias in how individuals represent and summarize their affective history.
papers.authors: Jefferson Ortega, David Whitney

papers.title: Sequential effects in reaching reveal efficient coding in motor planning
papers.abstract: Efficient coding theory, which proposes that neural systems maximize information transmission by tuning to environmental statistics, remains poorly understood in the context of motor control. We investigated sequential dependencies in goal-directed reaching tasks within unpredictable environments to test whether motor planning follows Bayesian inference or efficient coding principles. Contrary to Bayesian models predicting attractive biases toward prior targets, reaching trajectories exhibited repulsive sequential biases where movements deviated away from recent reaches. Furthermore, motor variability was significantly reduced when successive reach angles were similar. These results align with a resource-reallocation framework consistent with efficient coding, suggesting that the motor system dynamically adapts its internal representations to short-term movement history to optimize behavioral precision within finite encoding capacities.
papers.authors: Tianhe Wang, Yifan Fang, David Whitney

papers.title: Dynamic predictive templates in perception
papers.abstract: Perceptual inference is theorized to fluctuate between an 'external mode,' driven by sensory input, and an 'internal mode,' dominated by prior experiences. Using a psychophysical orientation reproduction task, we demonstrate that the strength of serial dependence alternates over minute-long durations. During the internal mode, perceptual reports are strongly attracted toward the orientation of preceding stimuli, resulting in an increased rate of false alarms that match history-dependent templates. These findings indicate that the visual system's reliance on prior information to maintain perceptual stability is a non-stationary process, with periodic shifts into internal processing modes causing transient failures of veridical inference where predictive templates override incoming sensory evidence.
papers.authors: Veith Weilnhammer, Yuki Murai, David Whitney

papers.title: VEATIC: Video-based Emotion and Affect Tracking in Context Dataset
papers.abstract: The 'emotion aperture problem' posits that isolated facial expressions are often insufficient to specify affect without situational context. We present the Video-based Emotion and Affect Tracking in Context (VEATIC) dataset, a large-scale resource comprising over 100 hours of naturalistic movie data with continuous valence and arousal annotations. By employing masking paradigms to isolate facial and contextual cues, we established human performance baselines for inferential emotion tracking. Benchmarking state-of-the-art computer vision architectures on VEATIC revealed a substantial performance gap compared to humans, particularly in scenarios where facial features are obscured or ambiguous. This dataset facilitates the development of context-aware affective computing models that mimic the human ability to integrate spatial and temporal cues for robust social perception.
papers.venue: WACV (IEEE/CVF Winter Conference on Applications of Computer Vision)
papers.authors: Zhihang Ren, Jefferson Ortega, Yifan Wang, Zhimin Chen, Yunhui Guo, Stella X. Yu, David Whitney

0169.name: Delwin Lindsey
0169.bio: Delwin T. Lindsey is a Professor of Psychology at The Ohio State University, Mansfield, where they study the neural and cognitive underpinnings of human color vision. Lindsey integrates molecular genetics, psychophysics, and functional neuroimaging (fMRI) to examine chromatic processing and the development of color perception in infants. Their research includes computational analyses of the World Color Survey to investigate universal motifs and cross-cultural diversity in color naming systems. Lindsey also examines how linguistic categories and environmental factors affect color appearance and discrimination across global populations.
0169.research_direction: Dr. Lindsey has recently been exploring the cognitive, linguistic, and evolutionary foundations of color categorization and communication. Their recent work investigates how different species and cultures partition color space, using match-to-sample paradigms in primates and unconstrained sorting tasks across diverse human languages to test whether color categories are evolutionarily conserved or shaped by semantic enculturation. To understand how color is used in practice, they are employing interactive behavioral games to evaluate information-theoretic models of communicative efficiency and color term evolution. Beyond lexical categorization, they are also examining crossmodal perception by studying how auditory properties like musical timbre systematically map onto visual dimensions such as lightness and saturation. Finally, to support these varied empirical investigations, Dr. Lindsey is working to spectrophotometrically calibrate legacy physical color palettes, aligning historical stimuli with modern international colorimetric standards to enable rigorous cross-laboratory synthesis.

papers.title: Bridging Color Standards: Aligning the Color‐Aid System with the International Commission on Illumination (CIE) and the Munsell Book of Color Coordinates
papers.abstract: Cross-study synthesis in color naming and categorization research is frequently hindered by discrepancies among the physical color palettes deployed across laboratories. Although the Munsell Book of Color (MBC) remains the dominant framework, numerous empirical investigations utilize the accessible Color-aid Corporation (CAC) system, specifically either the legacy 220-swatch Standard Set (CAC-220, used between 1948 and 1989) or the 314-swatch Full Set (CAC-314, released in 1989). To enable rigorous calibration and cross-corpus interoperability, spectrophotometric measurements of 65 swatches from the CAC-220 set and 67 swatches from the CAC-314 set were conducted across two independent laboratories under standardized CIE D65 illumination. Tristimulus colorimetric values were characterized across CIE xyY, CIELAB (L*a*b*), and CIELCh representations, and visual alignments to the World Color Survey (WCS) palette were systematically mapped. Swatches from CAC-220 and CAC-314 demonstrated strong overall photometric correspondence, displaying an average CIE 1976 Euclidean color difference (ΔE*ab) of 3.62, with only six specific swatches exhibiting marked divergence. Visual matching mapped 55 of 67 CAC-314 swatches directly into the WCS grid, while inter-laboratory measurement agreement was consistently high (ΔE*ab = 2.70–4.26). Notably, the newly measured coordinates deviated substantially from previously reported CAC metrics (ΔE*ab = 11.67–12.70), likely reflecting batch formulation drift, physical pigment aging, or divergent measurement geometries. Standard conversion matrices are provided to facilitate cross-system comparisons in cognitive color science.
papers.authors: Domicele Jonauskaite, Delwin T. Lindsey

papers.title: Human and primate categorical understanding of color
papers.abstract: This commentary critically examines recent comparative investigations assessing whether categorical perception of chromatic stimuli represents an evolutionarily conserved neurobiological mechanism or an emergent product of linguistic enculturation. In evaluating match-to-sample paradigms applied to non-human primates and adult humans (such as Garside et al.), the authors evaluate behavioral evidence for categorical color partitioning. While human observers demonstrate distinct categorical boundaries for orange, pink, green, and blue, macaque monkeys show minimal evidence for categorical perception; only a single macaque displayed a localized memory bias around pea-green, a category unobserved in human consensus data. Furthermore, the human categories observed in the match-to-sample paradigm failed to capture fundamental universal categories, notably red and yellow, which are ubiquitous across the 110 unwritten languages cataloged in the World Color Survey (WCS). This selective omission likely arises from methodological constraints: the stimulus array was confined to desaturated, high-lightness swatches (Munsell Value ~7.5), and task contingencies diverged because monkeys received trial-by-trial reinforcement whereas human observers did not. Testing broader gamuts with varied saturation and identical feedback structures is crucial to delineate how sensory opponency and lexical categories interact across primate lineages.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Delwin T. Lindsey, Angela M. Brown

papers.title: Color and tone color: audiovisual crossmodal correspondences with musical instrument timbre
papers.abstract: This study investigates the systematic relationships between auditory timbre and visual color by exploring crossmodal semantic correspondences. In two experiments, participants listened to musical recordings, provided semantic ratings on twelve crossmodal descriptors, and matched the auditory stimuli with specific colors from a calibrated palette. Results indicated that timbral brightness and pitch register significantly predicted the lightness and saturation of matched colors. High-pitched and brighter timbres were consistently associated with lighter, more saturated colors, while darker and lower-sounding timbres were matched with darker, less saturated ones. These findings demonstrate that timbre-color associations are not arbitrary but are mediated by shared semantic dimensions such as brightness and warmth, supporting the existence of universal crossmodal mappings between sound and color.
papers.authors: Lindsey Reymore, Delwin T. Lindsey

papers.title: Color sorting and color term evolution
papers.abstract: Prior investigations by Boster suggested that unconstrained pile-sorting of chromatic stimuli recapitulates the evolutionary sequence of basic color terms formalized in the Kay and McDaniel model, implying that both pile partition behavior and lexical evolution reflect shared underlying cognitive representations of color space. To test this hypothesis against alternative perceptual optimization frameworks, three behavioral experiments examined multi-level color sorting (ranging from 2 to 6 partitions) in English speakers and Somali speakers. Across conditions, stimulus sets varied sample cardinality (25, 30, or 145 calibrated swatches) and distribution across color space (spanning uniform hue cycles, widely separated hue-lightness arrays, and dense high-chroma gamuts). The resulting empirical cluster topologies, extracted via spectral clustering and k-means algorithms, were benchmarked against Kay and McDaniel’s developmental stages as well as mathematically optimal partitions derived by maximizing Regier’s well-formedness statistic using Particle Swarm Optimization. The empirical grouping structures consistently failed to align with the developmental stages of color lexicon evolution or with well-formedness configurations governed purely by perceptual similarity. These findings indicate that spontaneous sorting does not recapitulate linguistic evolution or optimal perceptual packaging, revealing complex interactions between semantic constraints and idiosyncratic task strategies.
papers.authors: Delwin T. Lindsey, Angela M. Brown, Aimee N. Violette, Ryan Lange, Prutha S. Deshpande

papers.title: The color communication game
papers.abstract: Information-theoretic models often infer communicative efficiency in color naming directly from unconstrained naming datasets under the assumption that receivers perform stochastic uniform sampling across all exemplars sharing a given label. To test this assumption behaviorally, 70 English-speaking dyads and 63 Somali-speaking dyads performed the Color Communication Game, an interactive paradigm where a sender designates 30 calibrated Munsell samples using natural language, and a decoupled receiver attempts to identify the intended physical sample. Although Somali senders utilized a reduced color term vocabulary relative to English speakers, interpersonal Mutual Information (MI) metrics calculated strictly from naming distributions remained significantly suboptimal across both language cohorts and failed to improve with sender communicative experience. However, actual receiver choice behavior showed that participants achieved substantially higher rates of exactly correct sample identification than predicted by naming-derived Monte Carlo simulations (up to 1.9-fold higher). This performance discrepancy arose because receivers systematically rejected uniform random sampling, instead selecting focal samples situated near the perceptual centroids of their internal category distributions, and comprehended synonymous lexical variants not actively produced by individual senders. These empirical results demonstrate that conventional information-theoretic naming metrics fundamentally underestimate human categorical understanding and semantic competence in communicative color exchange.
papers.authors: Angela M. Brown, Delwin T. Lindsey

0170.name: Denis G Pelli
0170.department: Department of Psychology and Center for Neural Science
0170.bio: Denis G. Pelli is a Professor of Psychology and Neural Science at New York University, specializing in the psychophysics of object recognition and visual perception. Pelli's research explores the phenomenon of "crowding," which they characterize as the failure of feature binding when objects are spaced too closely for individual recognition. Pelli developed the Pelli-Robson Contrast Sensitivity Chart for clinical vision testing and the Psychtoolbox software for visual stimulus presentation. Their current work employs feature-counting techniques and neuroimaging to investigate how cortical map sizes, particularly in area V4, relate to psychophysical spacing limits in humans.
0170.research_direction: Dr. Pelli has recently been investigating the psychophysics of subjective evaluation, particularly focusing on the mechanisms and individual differences underlying aesthetic judgments across visual, auditory, and typographic stimuli. Their recent work explores how aesthetic preference interacts with ergonomic utility, such as reading comfort in fonts, and examines the degree to which factors like observer empathy or stimulus properties drive consensus versus contention in beauty ratings. In the domain of perceptual decision-making, they are also benchmarking the temporal dynamics of object recognition, utilizing speed-accuracy tradeoff paradigms to compare human visual processing against deep convolutional neural networks. To support these diverse behavioral inquiries, Dr. Pelli has been developing open-source methodological tools for remote psychophysics, including web-based platforms that use smartphone microphones to calibrate consumer audio equipment for rigorous online data collection.

papers.title: Empathy strengthens beauty
papers.abstract: This research quantifies the extent to which individual empathy levels moderate the aesthetic and emotional appraisal of visual and auditory stimuli. Utilizing linear mixed-effects modeling and path analysis on a sample of 307 participants, the study evaluates the relationship between cognitive and affective empathy and the perceived beauty and valence of art images, nature photography, and musical excerpts. The findings indicate that higher-empathy observers report significantly elevated beauty ratings and perceive greater emotional intensity (both happiness and sadness) in the presented stimuli. The results suggest that empathy acts as a key moderator that strengthens the positive correlation between perceived stimulus emotion and felt beauty, with particularly pronounced effects in the auditory domain compared to static imagery.
papers.authors: Anna Bruns, Denis G. Pelli

papers.title: EasyEyes: Online hearing research using speakers calibrated by phones
papers.abstract: To enable rigorous psychoacoustic data collection in uncontrolled remote environments, this paper introduces an extension to the open-source EasyEyes web platform that allows for the calibration of consumer loudspeakers using a participant's smartphone microphone. The system employs cross-correlation of recorded signals with 1000 Hz sine waves or Maximum Length Sequences (MLS) to estimate the playback system's dynamic range and frequency response. By systematically accounting for ambient background noise and transducer-specific harmonic distortion, the method achieves a calibration measurement error of approximately 0.6 dB. This framework facilitates standardized auditory stimulus presentation for web-based research, effectively bridging the gap between laboratory and home testing conditions.
papers.authors: Ivan Vican, Hugo De Moraes, Chongjun Liao, Nathnael H. Tsegaye, William O'Gara, Jasper Inamoto, Denis G. Pelli

papers.title: The relationship between beauty and comfort in fonts
papers.abstract: This psychophysical study investigates the degree of alignment between aesthetic preference and ergonomic utility in typography. Using a large-scale online rating task, the authors measured perceived beauty and reading comfort across various font categories, including minimalist and ornate styles. Linear mixed-effects models reveal that while beauty and comfort generally exhibit a positive correlation at the aggregate level, there are significant individual differences; for certain observers, the attributes are strongly negatively correlated. The study demonstrates that an individual's latent preference for minimalism and their sensitivity to specific font features (e.g., serifs) predict the magnitude and direction of the beauty-comfort relationship, suggesting that aesthetic and functional appraisals are deeply integrated.
papers.authors: Maria Pombo, Minjung Kim, Denis G. Pelli

papers.title: Benchmarking the speed–accuracy tradeoff in object recognition by humans and neural networks
papers.abstract: This study benchmarks the temporal dynamics of object recognition in human observers and deep convolutional neural networks (DCNNs) using a 16-class subset of ImageNet. By employing a response-signal paradigm, the researchers measured accuracy as a function of processing duration (from 0 to 1000 ms) to generate speed-accuracy tradeoff (SAT) curves. While DCNNs often achieved higher asymptotic accuracy, their SAT curves exhibited significant structural differences from human performance, particularly in the initial rise and saturation trajectories. These findings suggest that current feed-forward artificial architectures fail to replicate the recurrent or iterative computations underlying human perceptual decision-making, highlighting a temporal divergence between biological and artificial vision.
papers.authors: Ajay Subramanian, Sara Price, Omkar Kumbhar, Elena Sizikova, Najib J. Majaj, Denis G. Pelli

papers.title: Consensus and contention in beauty judgment
papers.abstract: This research utilizes the 'beauty quartet' methodology to investigate the statistical properties of agreement and disagreement in aesthetic evaluations. By curating stimulus sets with specific mean beauty ratings and inter-participant variance, the authors tested whether observers could accurately predict group consensus (typicality) and disagreement (contention). The data reveal that while humans are adept at estimating the mean beauty of a stimulus, they consistently fail to predict the variance of those judgments. The finding that beauty variance is heterogeneous across stimuli suggests that aesthetic disagreement is not merely stochastic noise but a structured result of specific stimulus properties that elicit divergent individual responses, challenging universalist theories of beauty.
papers.authors: Maria Pombo, Aleksandra Igdalova, Denis G. Pelli

0171.name: Denise Hsien Wu
0171.bio: Denise Hsien Wu is a professor and former director at the Graduate Institute of Cognitive Neuroscience at National Central University, conducting research on the neurobiological foundations of human communication and cognition. Wu’s work utilizes behavioral experiments and neuroimaging techniques, including fMRI, MEG, and ERP, to investigate the mechanisms of statistical learning, bilingualism, and Chinese character recognition. Their research also includes neuroaesthetics, examining the computational principles and neural substrates involved in the perception of visual stimuli such as calligraphy and faces. Wu is a fellow of both the Psychonomic Society and the Association for Psychological Science and currently serves as the director of the Joint Research Centre for Language and Human Complexity.
0171.research_direction: Dr. Wu has recently been investigating the neural and cognitive mechanisms underlying statistical learning, language processing, and healthy aging. Their recent work explores how individuals extract and adapt to hidden environmental regularities, using EEG and behavioral paradigms to contrast temporal and motor sequence learning with the spatial positional learning crucial for reading visual orthography. In parallel, they are investigating the functional architecture of language by utilizing non-invasive transcranial light stimulation to probe how targeted frontal brain areas support complex syntactic processing in Mandarin speakers. Furthermore, their research employs machine learning on structural MRI and behavioral data to generate modality-specific "brain age" metrics, aiming to quantify how distinct neuroanatomical and executive functions are maintained or decline across the adult lifespan.

papers.title: Transcranial photobiomodulation on the left inferior frontal gyrus enhances Mandarin Chinese L1 and L2 complex sentence processing performance
papers.abstract: This research employed transcranial photobiomodulation (tPBM) using an 808-nm near-infrared laser targeting the left inferior frontal gyrus (LIFG) to modulate the neural processing of complex syntactic structures in Mandarin Chinese. In a series of experiments involving both native (L1) and second-language (L2) speakers, the application of tPBM significantly improved comprehension accuracy and reduced processing latencies specifically for object-extracted relative clauses (ORCs), which impose higher integration costs than subject-extracted relative clauses (SRCs). The findings demonstrate that non-invasive cortical stimulation of the LIFG can mitigate the computational demands associated with syntactic filler-gap dependency resolution, highlighting the functional role of the Broca's area-equivalent in Mandarin sentence processing across different proficiency levels.
papers.authors: Mingchuan Yang, Yang Liu, Zhaoqian Yue, Harry Luyao Chen, Denise Hsien Wu

papers.title: Modality-specific machine learning for brain and cognitive age prediction in healthy adults
papers.abstract: To quantify brain and cognitive maintenance across the adult lifespan, this study utilized regularized regression models (Elastic Net) to predict chronological age from distinct data modalities in a large cohort of 423 healthy Chinese adults (ages 19–80). The models leveraged structural MRI (gray matter volume), behavioral assessments (executive function and memory), and task-based neuroimaging features. Results indicated that while all modalities could reliably predict chronological age, modality-specific age gaps (the difference between predicted and actual age) captured divergent aspects of the aging process. Specifically, neuroanatomical markers selected by machine learning (ranging from 37 to 68 regions) showed limited overlap with behavioral predictors, suggesting that structural preservation and cognitive performance reflect partially independent trajectories of biological aging.
papers.authors: Erik Chih-Hung Chang, Pin-Wei Chen, Denise Hsien Wu

papers.title: Distinct neural mechanisms for temporal and spatial positional statistical learning: Behavioral and neurophysiological evidence
papers.abstract: The study investigated the cognitive and neural dissociation between statistical learning (SL) based on temporal regularities (sequential order) versus spatial regularities (relative position). Utilizing a novel positional statistical learning (PSL) paradigm, event-related potentials (ERPs) and behavioral metrics were recorded as participants extracted structural dependencies from visual stimuli. Findings revealed that sensitivity to spatial positional regularity—a critical foundation for logographic orthography—is subserved by distinct neurophysiological signatures compared to temporal SL. The N400 component served as a robust index for online segmentation and extraction of regularities, with high learners exhibiting earlier and more pronounced effects. The results provide support for a multi-component model of domain-general statistical learning that is differentially recruited during literacy acquisition across varying orthographic systems.
papers.authors: Andhika Renaldi, Yi-Syuan Huang, Ovid Jyh-Lang Tzeng, Denise Hsien Wu

papers.title: Rule-learning and rule-switching flexibility in motor sequence learning
papers.abstract: This study addressed the interplay between statistical rule-learning and rule-switching flexibility in dynamic environments using a modified serial reaction time (SRT) task. Participants were exposed to motor sequences where rules (Structure 1) naturally emerged and were subsequently replaced by new patterns (Structure 2). The research quantified individual differences in the sensitivity to emerging regularities and the speed of adaptation to rule changes. Quantitative analysis demonstrated that robust rule-learning does not necessarily predict high rule-switching flexibility; rather, successful learners are characterized by a specific ability to suppress previously learned dependencies when input statistics shift. These findings suggest that metacontrol over statistical learning involves dissociable mechanisms for extraction and revision of sequential expectations.
papers.authors: Yi-Syuan Huang, Ovid Jyh-Lang Tzeng, Denise Hsien Wu

papers.title: Brain and cognitive maintenance can be quantified via machine learning–derived age metrics
papers.abstract: Leveraging a multi-modal dataset of healthy adults, this paper investigates how machine-learning-derived 'brain age' and 'cognitive age' serve as sensitive biomarkers for age-related decline. By training modality-specific regularized regression models, the researchers identified neuroanatomical and behavioral features that best estimate chronological age. The study specifically highlights the predictive value of frontal-parietal integrity and executive control metrics. The divergence between modality-specific predicted ages was used to operationalize 'maintenance,' revealing that individuals with 'younger' brain metrics relative to their chronological age also exhibited preserved performance on complex cognitive tasks. This research advances the use of individualized aging metrics in clinical and cognitive neuroscience to detect early deviations from healthy aging trajectories.
papers.authors: Pin-Wei Chen, Erik Chih-Hung Chang, Denise Hsien Wu

0172.name: Dennis Levi
0172.department: Herbert Wertheim School of Optometry and Vision Science
0172.bio: Dennis M. Levi is a vision scientist at UC Berkeley who researches the neural basis of amblyopia and the development of spatial vision. Levi’s research investigates how the adult brain retains plasticity to improve visual function through perceptual learning and video-game-based therapies. Using psychophysics, fMRI, and computational modeling, Levi’s laboratory examines the mechanisms of visual crowding and binocular depth perception to inform clinical treatments for developmental vision disorders.
0172.research_direction: Dr. Levi's recent work explores the sensory and motor mechanisms underlying developmental binocular vision disorders, such as amblyopia and strabismus, and evaluates novel approaches for sensory restoration. Specifically, their research investigates the efficacy of modern digital interventions—including 3D virtual reality platforms and action video games—as perceptual learning tools designed to improve stereopsis and visual acuity in both pediatric and adult patients. In addition to comparing these interactive therapeutics against conventional occlusion therapy, they are examining the fundamental psychophysics of binocularity, such as whether training-induced stereoscopic improvements arise from enhanced binocular precision or an altered depth bias. Furthermore, they are utilizing tools like binocular eye tracking and random dot stereograms to probe the overarching breakdown of binocular integration, questioning how motor anomalies in fusional vergence relate to sensory deficits in depth perception.

papers.title: Recovery of depth perception in adults with abnormal binocular vision
papers.abstract: This investigation assesses the longitudinal efficacy and computational mechanisms of stereovision rehabilitation in adults presenting with developmental binocular vision deficits, including strabismus, anisometropia, and amblyopia. Utilizing a 3D virtual reality (VR) training platform, participants completed 30 home-based sessions targeting stereoacuity, interocular suppressive dynamics, and vergence alignment through depth-cue scaffolding. Comprehensive psychophysical and clinical assessments post-intervention revealed statistically significant reductions in stereoacuity thresholds for a majority of the cohort. Although binocular balance and alignment metrics displayed higher inter-subject variability, the findings suggest that VR-mediated perceptual learning can successfully leverage neural plasticity for sensory restoration in the mature visual system.
papers.authors: Jian Ding, Michelle Y. Ma, Hilary H. Lu, Benjamin T. Backus, Dennis M. Levi

papers.title: Emerging therapies for improving stereoacuity in amblyopia: A systematic review and meta-analysis
papers.abstract: This systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis aggregates data from 26 clinical studies to quantify the efficacy of contemporary binocular interventions—specifically virtual reality, interactive video games, and 3D films—in the treatment of stereo-deficiency associated with amblyopia and strabismus. The analysis identified a significant pooled mean improvement in stereoacuity of 0.26 log arcsec, equivalent to a 1.82-fold increase. Although these modern digital interventions yielded substantial within-group functional gains, the comparative analysis found that they do not demonstrate a consistent statistically significant superiority over conventional monocular occlusion therapy, emphasizing the need for continued refinement and objective adherence monitoring in these modalities.
papers.authors: Laura Asensio-Jurado, Marc Argilés, Lluïsa Quevedo-Junyent, Dennis M. Levi

papers.title: Vergence anomalies are associated with impaired stereopsis in amblyopia
papers.abstract: This study examines the neuro-functional relationship between fusional vergence and stereopsis in individuals with amblyopia and strabismus compared to neurotypical controls. Based on the premise that absolute disparity serves as the common substrate for both disparity-driven vergence and relative disparity processing, the researchers used binocular eye tracking and random dot stereograms to measure vergence gains and stereoacuity across the central 20° of the visual field. Findings demonstrated that impaired stereopsis was significantly correlated with anomalous vergence responses to small-diameter stimuli (4°), with no evidence of double dissociation. The results support the theory that a generalized breakdown in binocular integrative mechanisms underlies both the sensory (stereopsis) and motor (vergence) deficits in these populations.
papers.authors: Preeti Verghese, Adrien Chopin, Ângela Gomes-Tomaz, Noelia G. Alcalde, Dennis M. Levi

papers.title: Efficacy of patching combined with action video games in amblyopic children aged 4–10 years: A randomised clinical trial
papers.abstract: This prospective randomized clinical trial evaluated the therapeutic benefit of integrating child-friendly action video games (AVG) with monocular occlusion compared to passive occlusion (PO) alone in 28 children with anisometropic or strabismic amblyopia. Following a 42-hour treatment period, the AVG group demonstrated a significantly greater and more rapid recovery of best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) in the amblyopic eye (0.18 logMAR vs. 0.06 logMAR in the PO group) and achieved these gains with significantly shorter time constants (65.6 h vs. 154.6 h). While stereoacuity gains did not significantly differ between the interventions, the results establish that integrating engaging visuomotor tasks into occlusion protocols enhances both the magnitude and efficiency of acuity restoration in pediatric patients.
papers.authors: Laura Asensio-Jurado, Marc Argilés, Valldeflors Vinuela-Navarro, Lluïsa Quevedo-Junyent, Dennis M. Levi

papers.title: Playing stereoscopic video games enhances the precision but not the accuracy of depth perception
papers.abstract: This research sought to determine whether the stereoscopic gains associated with playing 3D action video games result from a reduction in the disparity pedestal (depth bias) or an enhancement of binocular precision (thresholds). Longitudinal measurements of depth detection thresholds and subjective depth biases were obtained using random dot stereograms from 21 healthy adults before and after 40 hours of stereoscopic gaming. The experimental results demonstrated a significant enhancement in stereoacuity thresholds without a concomitant change in subjective depth bias. These findings argue against the reduction of a disparity pedestal as the primary mechanism for game-induced stereoscopic improvement, highlighting instead an optimization of the visual system's sensitivity to binocular disparities.
papers.authors: Roger W. Li, Betty Z. Li, Sandy W. Chat, Dennis M. Levi

0173.name: Derek Arnold
0173.bio: Arnold is a Professor at the University of Queensland's School of Psychology, specializing in the neural and computational foundations of human perceptual experience. Their research investigates how the brain transforms sensory inputs into conscious awareness, focusing on predictive coding, temporal perception, and the mechanisms of visual imagery. Utilizing psychophysical paradigms and electroencephalography (EEG), Arnold explores individual differences in visualization, such as aphantasia, and the neural correlates of confidence in sensory decisions. Their work addresses how the brain predicts environmental changes and integrates multisensory information to guide motor planning.
0173.research_direction: Dr. Arnold's recent work explores the interplay between predictive processing, mental imagery, and visual perception. They have recently been investigating the cognitive and physiological underpinnings of mental imagery and aphantasia, utilizing psychophysical surveys and pupillometry to assess whether top-down visual generation can be reliably indexed by autonomic responses. In parallel, their research examines how predictive mechanisms operate across the visual system, using EEG oddball paradigms to map how event probabilities differentially impact early sensory versus late cognitive neural components. Furthermore, they are studying how predictive neural processes influence dynamic spatial vision and action, leveraging motion-based phenomena like the twinkle-goes illusion to probe whether positional extrapolation is driven by early perceptual mechanisms or later decisional biases affecting motor planning.

papers.title: The Twinkle-Goes illusion impacts motor planning, and is likely perceptual in origin
papers.abstract: This study investigated the 'twinkle-goes' effect—a phenomenon where the perceived terminal position of a moving stimulus overshoots its physical vanishing point when presented against a dynamic noise background—to determine its influence on motor planning. The researchers found that the illusory positional shift develops over approximately 120 ms post-disappearance and is modulated by the phase of pre-vanishing neural theta oscillations. Because the illusion directly biased the trajectory of motor responses, the findings suggest that the displacement originates from early-stage predictive perceptual mechanisms rather than late-stage decisional biases or report errors.
papers.authors: Blake William Saurels, Benjamin R. Jilek, Derek Henry Arnold

papers.title: Imagery modulates the pupillary response, but this does not reliably index differences in imagery vividness
papers.abstract: The study examined whether the imagery-induced pupillary light response (PLR)—the constriction or dilation of the pupil when imagining bright versus dark scenes—could serve as a physiological index for individual differences in mental imagery vividness. While the results confirmed that voluntary imagery significantly modulates pupil diameter in a luminance-consistent manner, the magnitude of this effect did not correlate with subjective vividness scores (VVIQ) across the participant sample. These data indicate that while mental imagery utilizes shared neural pathways with sensory perception to drive autonomic responses, the PLR is not a reliable trait-level biomarker for distinguishing visualization ability or diagnosing aphantasia.
papers.authors: Daniel Gardner, Blake W. Saurels, Derek Henry Arnold

papers.title: Vividness of mental imagery is a broad trait measure of internally generated visual experiences
papers.abstract: Utilizing a large-scale psychophysical survey, this research evaluated whether subjective vividness ratings serve as a robust trait measure for the propensity to generate internal visual experiences. The findings demonstrate that simple vividness scores are highly predictive of a wide range of phenomena, including the resolution of voluntary mental images, the frequency of involuntary visualizations, and the clarity of visual dreams. The study argues that vividness is a stable, quantifiable trait that can be efficiently measured with single-item ratings, and suggests a conceptual refinement of visual aphantasia to differentiate between a total lack of pictorial representation and the presence of faint, non-visualized representations.
papers.authors: D. Sam Schwarzkopf, Xinran A. Yu, Ecem Altan, Loren N. Bouyer, Blake W. Saurels, Elizabeth Pellicano, Derek Henry Arnold

papers.title: Deep Aphantasia: a visual brain with minimal influence from priors or inhibitory feedback?
papers.abstract: This article explores the cognitive architecture of 'deep aphantasia,' a condition defined by the complete absence of both voluntary visual imagery and an inner voice. The authors hypothesize that this phenotype reflects a visual system characterized by significantly attenuated top-down inhibitory feedback and a minimal reliance on predictive priors. Psychophysical data are discussed suggesting that deep aphantasics exhibit unique patterns in spatial extrapolation and integration tasks, potentially indicating a mode of sensory processing that is more veridical and less susceptible to the generative 'filling-in' processes typical of the neurotypical mind's eye.
papers.authors: Loren N. Bouyer, Derek H. Arnold

papers.title: Event Probabilities Have a Different Impact on Early and Late Electroencephalographic Measures Regarded as Metrics of Prediction
papers.abstract: Using an active visual oddball paradigm, the researchers dissociated the impact of conditional event probabilities from repetitive sensory stimulation on early and late ERP components. The results revealed that the late-latency P300 component is highly sensitive to fluctuations in conditional probability, with larger amplitudes observed for less likely events. Conversely, the early-latency P1 component remained invariant to probability shifts and was instead modulated by goal-directed attention linked to target proximity. These findings support a functional segregation within the predictive coding hierarchy between early sensory registration and later, probability-based cognitive evidence accumulation.
papers.authors: Blake W. Saurels, Alan Johnston, Kielan Yarrow, Derek H. Arnold

0174.name: Diane M. Beck
0174.bio: Beck is a Professor and Head of the Department of Psychology at the University of Illinois, Urbana-Champaign, where they investigate the neural and cognitive constraints of visual representation. Their research characterizes how top-down mechanisms like attention and real-world statistical regularities modulate activity in the visual cortex to facilitate scene category recognition and object awareness. Employing functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), electroencephalography (EEG), and transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), Beck explores the limits of human visual processing and the role of neural oscillations in conscious perception. Recent investigations in their lab also utilize deep neural networks to model the features that define representative exemplars of scene categories.
0174.research_direction: Dr. Beck has recently been investigating how the visual system leverages learned environmental statistics and intrinsic image properties to shape perception and conscious awareness. Their recent work explores how real-world regularities, such as highly typical scene exemplars, influence visual processing across multiple levels, from pre-attentive neural responses measured via ERPs to susceptibility in sustained inattentional blindness paradigms. In a related vein, they are examining how inherent image memorability impacts early perceptual detection thresholds using psychophysics and deep convolutional neural networks. Additionally, their research probes the fundamental neural architecture of visual consciousness, utilizing combined TMS and Event-Related Optical Signal (EROS) imaging to test whether recurrent feedback to the primary visual cortex (V1) is strictly necessary for the emergence of visual awareness.

papers.title: What makes good exemplars of a scene category good? Evidence from deep neural nets
papers.abstract: This study employs behavioral psychophysics, functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), and deep convolutional neural networks (DCNNs) to explore the neural and computational mechanisms underlying the processing advantage for representative scene exemplars. The authors demonstrate that 'good' exemplars—scenes that are highly representative of their category—are detected and categorized with higher sensitivity and faster reaction times than 'bad' exemplars. Multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) of fMRI data revealed that these statistically regular stimuli evoke more distinct category representations in the parahippocampal place area (PPA), retrosplenial cortex (RSC), and primary visual cortex (V1).
