The findings suggest that the visual system utilizes learned environmental regularities as internal predictions, facilitating the categorization process by minimizing prediction error for typical inputs.
papers.authors: Pei-Ling Yang, Diane M. Beck

papers.title: Real-world Statistical Regularity Impacts Inattentional Blindness
papers.abstract: This research investigates whether the brain's sensitivity to real-world statistical regularities—patterns of typicality and probability learned over a lifetime—influences the likelihood of stimuli reaching conscious awareness. Utilizing a sustained inattentional blindness paradigm across two large-scale experiments, the authors compared noticing rates for unexpected stimuli that were either probable (statistically regular) or improbable (statistically irregular) within their environmental context. The results indicate significantly higher rates of inattentional blindness for improbable scenes. This suggests that the visual system's predictive mechanisms prioritize stimuli that conform to internal models of the world, thereby modulating the probability that an item will successfully capture attention and enter conscious perception.
papers.authors: Ling Lee Chong, Diane M. Beck

papers.title: Highly Memorable Images Are More Readily Perceived
papers.abstract: This investigation examines the relationship between image memorability, an intrinsic property of visual stimuli, and the efficiency of early perceptual processing. Using an intact/scrambled discrimination task and an adaptive staircase procedure, the authors quantified the minimum presentation duration required for reliable detection of scenes varying in memorability. Across multiple experiments, highly memorable images were found to have significantly lower detection thresholds than low-memorability images. The researchers argue that memorable stimuli are processed more efficiently because they more closely align with stored, memory-based perceptual templates, thereby facilitating more rapid template matching during the initial stages of visual recognition.
papers.authors: Will Deng, Kara D. Federmeier, Diane M. Beck

papers.title: The Brain's Sensitivity to Real-world Statistical Regularity Does Not Require Full Attention
papers.abstract: This study assesses whether the neural mechanisms that utilize real-world statistical regularities to facilitate visual processing require focused attention. Using event-related potentials (ERPs), specifically the N300 component associated with high-level perceptual template matching, the authors recorded brain activity during a dual-task paradigm. Participants were presented with scene-object pairs that varied in category representativeness while simultaneously performing a demanding secondary task to manipulate attentional load. The N300 amplitude was systematically modulated by representativeness (exemplar goodness) regardless of the level of attentional load. These results provide evidence that the visual system's predictive modeling based on environmental regularities is a robust, pre-attentive process that can occur even when cognitive resources are diverted.
papers.authors: Evan G. Center, Kara D. Federmeier, Diane M. Beck

papers.title: Bypassing input to V1 in visual awareness: A TMS-EROS investigation
papers.abstract: This research utilizes a multimodal approach combining transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) and Event-Related Optical Signal (EROS) imaging to determine if recurrent feedback to the primary visual cortex (V1) is a prerequisite for conscious visual experience. By applying single-pulse TMS over the posterior parietal cortex (PPC) to induce phosphenes, the authors bypassed the traditional retino-geniculo-striate pathway. EROS data showed that awareness of induced phosphenes was associated with activity in the PPC at approximately 50 ms and subsequent activation in the cuneus and early visual cortex (V1/V2) at 140 ms. The presence of awareness-related signatures in both dorsal and early ventral regions, even when the initial V1 input sweep was bypassed, supports interactive models of consciousness where recurrent loops of activity are necessary for the emergence of awareness.
papers.authors: Ramisha S. Knight, Tao Chen, Evan G. Center, Gabriele Gratton, Monica Fabiani, Silvia Savazzi, Chiara Mazzi, Diane M. Beck

0175.name: Dicle Dövencioğlu
0175.bio: Nahide Dicle Dövencioğlu is an Associate Professor at Middle East Technical University and directs the Sensory Processes Lab. Dövencioğlu’s research investigates the computational and neural underpinnings of 3D vision and material perception, specifically examining how properties like softness and transparency are derived from specular motion, shading, and binocular disparity. Integrating psychophysics, fMRI, and computer graphics, they explore the interaction between active exploration and multisensory integration, including the role of linguistic sound symbolism in shaping perceptual experiences.
0175.research_direction: Dr. Dövencioğlu has recently been investigating the multidimensional perception of material properties, focusing specifically on how distinct dimensions of softness—such as deformability, viscosity, and granularity—are represented across diverse sensory and cognitive systems. Their recent work explores how visual estimates of these material attributes are dynamically modulated by cross-modal cues, using behavioral congruency tasks to determine if observing specific exploratory hand kinematics biases visual softness judgments. Furthermore, they are examining the intersection of multimodal material perception and language, utilizing semantic differential ratings to investigate how Turkish sound symbolism and onomatopoeia selectively influence the visual representation of objects and surfaces. Additionally, they are studying how the lexical categorization of haptic exploratory actions is inherently driven by the multidimensional perceptual space of the materials being manipulated.

papers.title: Visual softness perception can be manipulated through exploratory procedures
papers.abstract: While softness perception in visual and tactile modalities spans multiple distinct perceptual dimensions—including compliance/deformability, granularity, viscosity/fluidity, and surface softness—active haptic exploration typically engages diagnostic exploratory procedures (EPs) specialized for gathering specific sensory cues. This study investigated whether visual perception of material softness can be top-down modulated by observing exploratory hand kinematics. Observers judged material attributes from dynamic displays featuring deformable, viscous, granular, and surface-soft stimuli manipulated via congruent versus non-congruent exploratory procedures. Quantitative rating analyses demonstrated that observed manual interaction dynamics systematically bias visual softness judgments along specific perceptual dimensions, indicating that visual material estimation is actively constrained by sensorimotor exploration schemas.
papers.authors: Fatma Kılıç, Dicle Dövencioğlu

papers.title: Selectively manipulating softness perception of materials through sound symbolism
papers.abstract: Auditory-haptic cross-modal correspondences are prominently represented in language through sound-symbolic and onomatopoeic descriptors. In this investigation, the latent perceptual structure of material softness in Turkish was first extracted via semantic differential ratings across 40 material video clips and 29 sensory descriptors, yielding principal components corresponding to deformability, viscosity, surface softness, and granularity. A parallel rating experiment evaluated 47 Turkish onomatopoeic words against 31 sensory adjectives, recovering congruent dimensions for viscosity, granularity, and surface softness. Observers subsequently evaluated material videos presented synchronously with spoken onomatopoeic words under congruent and incongruent audiovisual conditions. The results revealed that dimension-congruent sound-symbolic cues selectively enhanced perceived softness ratings along target dimensions while incongruent sound symbolism systematically degraded them, demonstrating selective, feature-level cross-modal modulation of visual material representation by linguistic phonology.
papers.authors: Hamza Nalbantoğlu, Beyza Melis Hazır, Dicle N. Dövencioğlu

papers.title: Dokunsal Yumuşaklık Algısına İlişkin Bir İnceleme
papers.abstract: This review evaluates the multidimensional taxonomy of tactile softness perception, moving beyond classical psychophysical and mechanical models that reduce softness to a unidimensional measure of compliance (i.e., physical displacement under applied normal indentation forces). Integrating empirical findings from psychophysics, semantic differential scaling, and kinematic tracking, the authors synthesize evidence establishing four distinct perceptual dimensions of haptic softness: deformability, viscosity, granularity, and surface softness. The review details how human exploratory procedures (EPs)—including lateral rubbing, applied pressure, two-handed containment, and contour following—are dynamically tuned to optimize mechanoreceptive and kinesthetic feedback for each dimension, highlighting translational implications for affective haptics, tactile displays, and autonomous robotic manipulation.
papers.venue: Ankara Üniversitesi Dil ve Tarih-Coğrafya Fakültesi Dergisi
papers.authors: Müge Cavdan, Dicle Dövencioğlu

papers.title: Keşifsel El Hareketlerinin Türkçe Adlandırılmasında Dokunsal Malzeme Algısının Rolü
papers.abstract: Haptic exploration relies on stereotypical manual exploration schemas termed exploratory procedures (EPs), which have primarily been classified within English-language research frameworks. This study investigates the lexical categorization of EPs in Turkish and assesses whether verb choices are modulated by the perceptual softness dimensions of the explored materials. Twenty-eight native Turkish speakers participated in a free-naming task viewing video recordings of 37 material-EP interaction pairings representing distinct softness dimensions (e.g., surface softness, viscosity, granularity, and compliance). Lexical and semantic frequency analyses showed that generated action verbs systematically differentiate along the underlying physical and perceptual material properties, establishing that linguistic action descriptors are closely coupled to multidimensional haptic perceptual spaces.
papers.venue: Ankara Üniversitesi Dil ve Tarih-Coğrafya Fakültesi Dergisi
papers.authors: Gamze Yıldız, Dicle Dövencioğlu

papers.title: Ses Sembolizmi ve Nesne Algısı İlişkisine Dair Bir İnceleme
papers.abstract: This review addresses cross-modal sound symbolism and its functional relationship to physical object and surface perception. Moving beyond conventional acoustic-geometric associations—such as the Bouba/Kiki effect relating higher acoustic frequencies to sharp angularity and lower frequencies to rounded contours, as well as vowel frequency mappings to physical scale—the article examines how sound-symbolic structures convey complex material attributes. Focusing on the extensive onomatopoeic system of Turkish, the paper synthesizes evidence illustrating how vocal mimesis encodes mechanical and tactile properties such as granularity, liquidity, and surface friction, providing a theoretical framework for cross-sensory translation between auditory phonetics and multimodal material perception.
papers.venue: Avrasya Sosyal ve Ekonomi Araştırmaları Dergisi
papers.authors: Dicle Dövencioğlu

0176.name: Dimitris Samaras
0176.main_research_area: computer vision and computational behavioral science
0176.bio: Dimitris Samaras is the SUNY Empire Innovation Professor at Stony Brook University and the Director of the Computer Vision Lab. Their research involves developing physical and statistical models to interpret complex visual data, focusing on the interaction between 3D geometry and illumination for motion estimation and augmented reality. Samaras applies machine learning to human modeling, including the analysis of facial expressions, biometrics, and multimodal neuroimaging data such as fMRI and eye-tracking. Their work in computational pathology involves the design of foundational models for large-scale medical image analysis and diagnostic precision.
0176.research_direction: Dr. Samaras has recently been developing advanced generative models to tackle diverse challenges in human-centric personalization and large-scale image synthesis. Their recent work explores how to efficiently construct and animate high-fidelity 3D human avatars, investigating techniques like tensor-decomposed 3D Gaussian Splatting and low-rank adaptation to capture identity-specific details and complex deformations from minimal video data. In parallel, they are addressing the intricacies of generating massive, gigapixel-scale images—such as digital histopathology slides and remote sensing maps—by designing continuous-space and multi-scale diffusion models that preserve global structural coherence across different zoom levels. Additionally, their research investigates individual human visual attention, probing how to model and predict personalized eye-tracking scanpaths for novel subjects using only a handful of examples.

papers.title: LoRAvatar: Low-Rank Head Avatar Personalization with Registers
papers.abstract: The authors propose LoRAvatar, a framework for personalizing generic head avatar generation models using low-rank adaptation. Generic models often fail to capture subject-specific high-frequency details because they prioritize general domain priors. Standard low-rank adaptation (LoRA) remains insufficient for recovering fine identity-specific features. To address this, the authors introduce a Register Module that enhances LoRA by storing and re-purposing identity information in a learnable 3D feature space. This module is applied to the intermediate layers of a pre-trained model and utilizes dense DINOv2 features to provide localized learning signals. The Register Module operates during the adaptation phase and is not required for inference, ensuring parameter efficiency. Experimental results on a novel dataset featuring individuals with distinctive facial traits, such as wrinkles and tattoos, demonstrate that LoRAvatar significantly outperforms current personalization methods in both quantitative fidelity and qualitative detail recovery.
papers.authors: Sai Tanmay Reddy Chakkera, Aggelina Chatziagapi, Md Moniruzzaman, Chen-Ping Yu, Yi-Hsuan Tsai, Dimitris Samaras

papers.title: Few-shot Personalized Scanpath Prediction
papers.abstract: This paper introduces the task of Few-shot Personalized Scanpath Prediction (FS-PSP) to mitigate the data-intensive requirements of existing gaze prediction models. The authors propose a method that adapts to unseen individuals using only a minimal support set of scanpath examples without requiring test-time fine-tuning. The architecture utilizes a novel Subject-Embedding Network (SE-Net) to encode individualized attention traits into a distinct latent space. By decoupling the subject embedding from the sequential scanpath prediction process, the model learns a representation that maximizes inter-subject discriminability and intra-subject consistency. The final prediction model is conditioned on these embeddings to generate personalized scanpaths. Evaluation on several eye-tracking benchmarks shows that the proposed SE-Net achieves superior adaptability to new subjects compared to standard fine-tuning approaches, establishing a new state-of-the-art for few-shot gaze behavior modeling.
papers.authors: Ruoyu Xue, Jingyi Xu, Sounak Mondal, Hieu Le, Gregory J. Zelinsky, Minh Hoai, Dimitris Samaras

papers.title: ZoomLDM: Latent Diffusion Model for multi-scale image generation
papers.abstract: The authors present ZoomLDM, a latent diffusion model designed to overcome the limitations of patch-based generative methods in gigapixel imaging domains such as digital histopathology. Traditional patch-based diffusion models fail to capture global tissue architecture and long-range spatial dependencies. ZoomLDM addresses this by incorporating a magnification-aware conditioning mechanism based on self-supervised learning (SSL) embeddings, allowing for consistent image synthesis across multiple zoom levels. The framework enables the generation of contextually accurate samples at varying scales, from high-resolution cell details to low-magnification whole-slide thumbnails. The multi-scale latent space also facilitates computationally tractable synthesis of large images up to 4096 x 4096 pixels. Benchmarking on histopathology and satellite imagery datasets indicates that ZoomLDM achieves state-of-the-art Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) scores across all scales and provides effective multi-scale feature representations for downstream multiple instance learning (MIL) tasks.
papers.authors: Srikar Yellapragada, Alexandros Graikos, Kostas Triaridis, Prateek Prasanna, Rajarsi R. Gupta, Joel H. Saltz, Dimitris Samaras

papers.title: ∞-Brush: Controllable Large Image Synthesis with Diffusion Models in Infinite Dimensions
papers.abstract: This research introduces ∞-Brush, a conditional diffusion model formulated in infinite-dimensional function space to synthesize high-resolution images while preserving global structural coherence. Traditional finite-dimensional diffusion models are constrained by the resolution of their training data, and patch-based methods often lose long-range context. ∞-Brush represents images as continuous functions over coordinate space and utilizes a cross-attention neural operator to incorporate domain-specific conditioning signals. This approach allows the model to scale to arbitrary resolutions, such as 4096 x 4096, even when trained only on small pixel subsets. The authors demonstrate the efficacy of ∞-Brush in synthesizing complex, large-scale imagery for digital pathology and remote sensing. The model effectively bridges the gap between local detail and global structure, outperforming state-of-the-art finite-dimensional and patch-based diffusion models in scalability and structural fidelity.
papers.authors: Minh-Quan Le, Alexandros Graikos, Srikar Yellapragada, Rajarsi R. Gupta, Joel Saltz, Dimitris Samaras

papers.title: MIGS: Multi-Identity Gaussian Splatting via Tensor Decomposition
papers.abstract: The authors propose Multi-Identity Gaussian Splatting (MIGS), a novel 3D human avatar representation that learns a unified model for multiple identities from monocular video data. Unlike existing 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) methods that require expensive per-identity optimization, MIGS constructs a high-order tensor containing the 3DGS parameters for all training subjects. By imposing a low-rank structure and applying CANDECOMP/PARAFAC (CP) tensor decomposition, the framework factorizes shared and identity-specific deformations into a parameter-efficient unified network. This multilinear modeling approach enables the transfer of information across identities, resulting in more robust animation under challenging, out-of-distribution poses. Experimental results show that MIGS significantly reduces the total number of parameters compared to individual models while maintaining high-fidelity synthesis. Furthermore, the model demonstrates the ability to generalize to novel identities through an efficient few-shot adaptation process.
papers.authors: Aggelina Chatziagapi, Grigorios G. Chrysos, Dimitris Samaras

0178.name: Dirk Bernhardt-Walther
0178.bio: Dirk Bernhardt-Walther is a Professor in the Department of Psychology at the University of Toronto and a Senior Member of the IEEE. Bernhardt-Walther’s research investigates the neural and computational foundations of high-level sensory perception, specifically how humans represent and categorize complex real-world scenes. By combining functional neuroimaging, psychophysics, and eye tracking with computer vision and machine learning, Bernhardt-Walther identifies mid-level visual features—such as contours and symmetry—that facilitate scene recognition and aesthetic preferences. Their work also includes the development of computational tools like the Mid-level Vision Toolbox to model how structural image properties influence human cognition and neural representations.
0178.research_direction: Dr. Bernhardt-Walther has recently been investigating the neural and computational mechanisms underlying visual aesthetics and high-level scene perception. Their recent work explores the biological roots of aesthetic preference, combining fMRI and artificial neural networks to test whether aesthetic liking acts as a heuristic for metabolic efficiency in visual cortices, while also mapping how geometric versus subjective perceptions of architectural curvature are distinctly encoded across the visual hierarchy. Broadening this focus on value-based sensory processing, they are also probing how aesthetic evaluation and reward-circuit engagement differ across neurodiverse populations. In the domain of spatial and category perception, their research examines the functional organization of high-level vision, using psychophysics to test whether rapid scene recognition genuinely relies on a privileged pathway for global ensemble statistics, and mapping population receptive fields to uncover how visual scale gradients in the medial temporal lobe support specialization for scenes versus faces.

papers.title: Less is more: Aesthetic liking is inversely related to metabolic expense by the visual system
papers.abstract: This study investigates the metabolic efficiency hypothesis of visual aesthetics using both artificial neural network modeling and human neuroimaging. Using a VGG19 architecture pretrained for object and scene recognition, the researchers demonstrated that images with higher aesthetic preference ratings consistently evoked sparser neural activity and lower metabolic costs (proxied by the total number of active neurons). This relationship was absent in randomly initialized networks. Subsequent fMRI experiments confirmed this inverse correlation in the human brain, showing that BOLD signal magnitude in early visual regions (V1, V2, V4) and high-level category-selective areas—specifically the Parahippocampal Place Area (PPA), Occipital Place Area (OPA), and Fusiform Face Area (FFA)—is negatively associated with subjective aesthetic liking. The findings suggest that aesthetic pleasure acts as an energy-conserving affect heuristic, reward-signaling visual stimuli that are metabolically efficient for the brain to process.
papers.authors: Yikai Tang, William A. Cunningham, Dirk B. Walther

papers.title: No evidence for a privileged role of global ensemble statistics in rapid scene perception: A registered replication attempt
papers.abstract: This research presents a pre-registered replication of experiments asserting that global ensemble statistics (structureless texture information) are prioritized by the visual system for rapid scene perception compared to object perception. Utilizing a content-priming paradigm across multiple psychophysical experiments, the authors tested whether preserving only summary statistical information would selectively facilitate scene categorization. The results failed to replicate the purported 'global advantage' for scenes; instead, participants did not exhibit a privileged processing pathway for global properties over local structural features during rapid visual categorization. The study concludes that scene recognition does not rely on a unique, gist-first mechanism for ensemble statistics but rather follows a multi-scale processing pathway similar to that of object recognition.
papers.authors: Jiongtian Guo, Jay Pratt, Dirk B. Walther

papers.title: Neural dissociation between computational and perceived measures of curvature
papers.abstract: To determine how the brain encodes curvature during aesthetic evaluation, this study reanalyzed fMRI data of participants making beauty judgments and approach-avoidance decisions regarding architectural scenes. The analysis revealed a significant neural dissociation: activity in the early visual cortex (V2-V3, BA 17) corresponds to computational curvature (geometrically extracted contour properties) regardless of the specific task or decision context. In contrast, the fusiform gyrus (BA 37) demonstrates sensitivity to perceived curvature—the subjective human judgment of curvilinearity—only when participants are actively engaged in aesthetic evaluation. These results demonstrate that while the low-level visual system tracks geometric invariants, higher-order cortical regions integrate subjective perceptual qualities to drive the hedonic appraisal of complex environments.
papers.authors: Oshin Vartanian, Delaram Farzanfar, Enric Munar, Martin Skov, Gregor Hayn-Leichsenring, Pik Ki Ho, Dirk B. Walther

papers.title: Aesthetic processing in neurodiverse populations
papers.abstract: This systematic review evaluates the neurobiological mechanisms of aesthetic preference through the lens of neurodiversity, expanding the field beyond traditional neuropsychological lesion studies to include psychotic disorders, anhedonia, depression, anxiety, and autism. The authors identify stable patterns of aesthetic bias across these populations and map them to dysfunctions within the mesocorticolimbic reward circuit, frontolimbic connectivity, and the default mode network (DMN). By synthesizing evidence across perceptual, emotional, and evaluative levels of cognition, the review proposes that specific symptomatologies modulate the neural architecture of value-based sensory processing. The paper argues that including neurodiverse populations is critical for developing a comprehensive theory of how the brain derives meaning and pleasure from visual information.
papers.authors: Zach Buck, Everan Michalchyshyn, Amna Nishat, Mikayla Lisi, Yichen Huang, Hanyu Liu, Arina Makarenka, Charles Puttcharnun Plyngam, Abigail Windle, Zhen Yang, Dirk B. Walther

papers.title: Organization of pRF size along the AP axis of the hippocampus and adjacent medial temporal cortex is related to specialization for scenes versus faces
papers.abstract: This study employs population receptive field (pRF) mapping to investigate the topographic and functional organization of the human medial temporal lobe (MTL). The researchers discovered a prominent gradient of pRF sizes along the anterior-posterior (AP) axis of the hippocampus, where anterior regions exhibit significantly larger receptive fields compared to the posterior sections. This scaling of visual sensitivity aligns with a gradient of category specialization: the larger pRFs in the anterior MTL correspond to areas specialized for global scene processing, while the smaller pRFs in the posterior MTL correspond to areas specialized for faces and fine-grained visual details. These findings establish that pRF scaling is a fundamental organizational principle linking the granularity of visual representations to high-level cognitive specialization for scenes and objects across the hippocampal-parahippocampal axis.
papers.authors: Charlotte A. Leferink, Jordan DeKraker, Iva K. Brunec, Stefan Köhler, Morris Moscovitch, Dirk B. Walther

papers.title: Population receptive field size does not correspond to spatial frequency processing in scene-selective cortex
papers.abstract: This study employs high-resolution population receptive field (pRF) mapping and multivoxel pattern analysis (MVPA) to investigate the functional organization of the parahippocampal place area (PPA) and occipital place area (OPA). While both regions exhibit a significant anterior-posterior pRF size gradient, decoding of scene categories from spatial frequency-filtered imagery reveals a preference pattern that contradicts the expected pRF-spatial frequency correspondence observed in early visual cortex (V1). Specifically, anterior subregions with larger pRFs do not demonstrate the predicted bias toward low-spatial-frequency gist; instead, preferred scene feature representations undergo hierarchical transformations that decouple pRF size from spatial frequency selectivity in high-level visual areas, challenging the assumption that scene-selective cortex primarily processes coarse-grained global features.
papers.authors: Charlotte A. Leferink, Claudia Damiano, Dirk B. Walther

papers.title: Contours drive distinct orientation selectivity in the human visual system
papers.abstract: This research evaluates whether orientation processing in natural scenes is dominated by filter-based orientation energy or structural contours. Psychophysical experiments requiring average orientation judgments of natural scene patches demonstrate a consistent perceptual bias toward contour-based estimates, particularly when these estimates diverge from steerable pyramid filter outputs. Model-based fMRI analysis of responses from the Natural Scenes Dataset further indicates that models prioritizing contour structure better explain neural activity patterns and identify discrete orientation preferences throughout the visual cortex. These findings suggest that the human visual system extracts boundary-defining contours to encode scene orientation, rather than relying on oriented spatial frequency energy as proposed by standard filter-bank models.
papers.authors: Seohee Han, Dirk B. Walther

papers.title: Attention to complex scene features
papers.abstract: Using visual search paradigms with stimuli systematically sampled from a parametric space of high-level features via generative adversarial networks (GANs), this work evaluates the generalizability of Feature Integration Theory (FIT) and Guided Search (GS) to complex scene properties. Search performance for features such as indoor lighting and texture was found to be consistently inefficient, as evidenced by significant set size effects, suggesting that these high-level scene features are not preattentive and require selective attention for processing. However, the finding that feature search was significantly more efficient than conjunction search indicates that these ecologically valid properties still facilitate attentional guidance in a manner consistent with the GS model, suggesting a hierarchical extension of search mechanisms to functionally meaningful scene attributes.
papers.authors: Gaeun Son, Michael L. Mack, Dirk B. Walther

0179.name: Dirk Kerzel
0179.department: Psychology Department, Faculty of Psychology and Educational Sciences
0179.bio: Dirk Kerzel is a Full Professor of Cognitive Psychology who researches the mechanisms of attentional selectivity and their integration with visual working memory and oculomotor control. Kerzel’s work utilizes psychophysical paradigms and electrophysiological markers, such as the N2pc and Pd components, to investigate how stimulus saliency and top-down goals influence the selection or suppression of visual information. They study the capacity limits of the cognitive system and how distractors interfere with the execution of hand and eye movements. Currently, their research focuses on the precision of representations in visual working memory and the spatial anisotropies that affect distractor interference in complex visual search tasks.
0179.research_direction: Dr. Kerzel has recently been investigating the dynamic interplay between visual working memory, top-down goals, and bottom-up salience in guiding visual attention. Their recent work explores how memory representations structure perceptual selection, using eye-tracking and dual-target search paradigms to test whether multiple prioritized and accessory working memory templates can simultaneously guide attention and bias oculomotor capture. They are also using delayed continuous recall paradigms to examine the limits of cognitive control, specifically asking if top-down pre- and retro-cues can override the influence of stimulus-driven physical salience on memory precision. Furthermore, they have been employing high-density electroencephalography to track lateralized event-related potentials, such as the N2pc and Pd, to study how attentional templates are optimally tuned away from distractor features and how evolutionary threats involuntarily capture spatial attention.

papers.title: Electrophysiological evidence for the optimal tuning of attention
papers.abstract: This study utilizes high-density electroencephalography to evaluate the optimal tuning theory, which proposes that internal search templates are strategically shifted away from nontarget features to maximize the signal-to-noise ratio during visual search. By analyzing event-related potential (ERP) components associated with attentional orienting and selection, specifically the N1pc and N2pc, the research demonstrates that attentional priority is biased toward cue features that deviate from nontarget values in color space. The results provide robust evidence that search goals are dynamically tuned to enhance target-distractor discriminability, while ruling out alternative explanations such as sensory adaptation or rapid disengagement from the cue.
papers.authors: Dirk Kerzel

papers.title: Persistent Effects of Salience in Visual Working Memory: Limits of Cue-Driven Guidance
papers.abstract: The research investigates the extent to which top-down attentional control can modulate the influence of stimulus-driven salience on visual working memory (VWM) precision. Across four experiments using a delayed continuous recall paradigm, the authors employed spatial and feature-based pre-cues and retro-cues to manipulate the priority of items with varying physical salience (e.g., flickering or orientation contrast). Although valid cues successfully enhanced overall memory performance, they were unable to eliminate the recall precision advantage for highly salient items. These findings suggest that salience-driven prioritization is established during the initial encoding phase and remains resistant to subsequent top-down reprioritization efforts within the VWM system.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
papers.authors: Martin Constant, Dirk Kerzel

papers.title: Some animal specific fears are more specific than others: Evidence from attention and emotion measures
papers.abstract: This investigation tests the threat-capture hypothesis by examining how evolutionary fear-relevant stimuli, such as snakes and spiders, affect attentional prioritization during visual search. By combining behavioral search performance metrics with electrophysiological recordings of the N2pc (attentional selection) and Pd (distractor suppression) components, the study evaluates the neural basis of interference from threatening distractors. The results indicate that fear-related stimuli capture attention more effectively than neutral distractors, leading to increased behavioral interference. The findings suggest that the human attentional system exhibits heightened sensitivity to specific classes of threat, with the magnitude of capture varying across different types of fear-relevant animals.
papers.authors: Nicolas Burra, Coralie Pittet, Caroline Barras, Dirk Kerzel

papers.title: Effects of Retro-cue Reliability on Visual Working Memory and Attentional Template Efficiency in Visual Search
papers.abstract: This study adjudicates between the state-based model, which assumes visual working memory (VWM) can only focus on a single attentional template, and the resource hypothesis, which allows for parallel activation of multiple templates. In a combined search and memory task, the researchers manipulated the reliability of retro-cues while participants maintained two items in VWM for a dual-target search. The results show that memory precision and search efficiency covary with cue reliability, indicating that VWM resources are distributed flexibly according to task expectations. This provides evidence for the resource hypothesis, suggesting that multiple templates can concurrently guide search with efficiency levels determined by the allocation of limited resources.
papers.authors: Alexandre Fortuna, Martin Constant, Dirk Kerzel

papers.title: Quantifying the Attentional Impact of Working Memory Matching Targets and Distractors
papers.abstract: This study examines the degree to which different types of representations in visual working memory (VWM)—namely prioritized and accessory items—interact with perceptual selection. Across several experiments using eye-tracking (first fixation positions) and reaction time measures, the researchers quantified the magnitude of attentional capture by distractors that matched the content of VWM. The findings reveal that even task-irrelevant accessory representations in memory can automatically bias oculomotor selection, although the effect is significantly more robust for prioritized search templates. These results argue for a model where multiple VWM representations simultaneously interact with the attentional system, albeit with varying degrees of priority.
papers.authors: Alexandre Fortuna, Martin Constant, Dirk Kerzel

0180.name: Dirk van Moorselaar
0180.department: Department of Experimental and Applied Psychology
0180.lab_name: Institute for Brain and Behavior Amsterdam (IBBA)
0180.bio: Dirk van Moorselaar is a cognitive neuroscientist specializing in the neural mechanisms of visual attention, working memory, and distractor suppression. Van Moorselaar’s research utilizes time-resolved EEG decoding, alpha-band oscillation analysis, and psychophysics to investigate how the brain uses prior expectations and statistical learning to manage sensory selection. Their work provides evidence for the existence of proactive distractor templates and characterizes the dynamic trade-offs between storage and selection within the visual working memory system. Van Moorselaar also explores the reflexive shifts of the attentional 'zoom lens' and the role of retinotopic coordinates in suppressing interference from the environment.
0180.research_direction: Dr. van Moorselaar's recent work explores how the visual system relies on implicit statistical learning to dynamically adjust the attentional priority map based on environmental regularities. Specifically, they have recently been investigating whether learned spatial suppression can counteract involuntary attentional capture by highly salient affective distractors, such as stimuli that are inherently frightening or have acquired aversive value through fear conditioning. In addition to attentional filtering, their research examines the neural dynamics of perceptual prediction, using time-resolved EEG decoding to probe whether the brain generates anticipatory, sensory-like representations of expected visual events even when those stimuli are omitted. Finally, they are exploring whether these implicit learning mechanisms extend beyond sensory processing to the motor system by testing how visual spatial priors might automatically guide the preparation of specific manual responses.

papers.title: Suppression of fear-conditioned stimuli
papers.abstract: This study demonstrates that attentional suppression acquired through statistical learning extends to stimuli that have gained aversive significance via classical conditioning. Human participants were initially trained to suppress a specific color singleton distractor by exposing them to its frequent appearance at a high-probability location (HPL). Following this incidental learning phase, the distractor color was paired with electrical shocks to establish fear conditioning. Behavioral results indicated that while fear-conditioned stimuli (CS+) typically captured attention more strongly than neutral stimuli at low-probability locations, they remained subject to significant suppression at the HPL. These findings suggest that the visual priority map, once modified by statistical regularities, can implement a 'blanket' proactive inhibition that counteracts both physical salience and acquired threat value, challenging models that posit fear-driven attentional capture is inflexible.
papers.authors: Jan Theeuwes, Jonna van Doorn, Dirk van Moorselaar

papers.title: Learning to Suppress What I Fear
papers.abstract: The research investigated whether involuntary attentional capture by inherently fear-inducing objects can be mitigated through the implicit learning of environmental regularities. Observers performed a visual search task involving neutral shape targets and singleton distractors. The distractors initially consisted of neutral images (leaves) that appeared more frequently at a specific spatial location, allowing for the development of learned spatial suppression. Subsequently, the distractor set was expanded to include threatening images (spiders) and butterfly images. Participants with high spider fear exhibited significantly greater attentional capture by spiders at low-probability locations. Crucially, this capture was reliably attenuated when spiders appeared at the high-probability distractor location. These results indicate that statistical learning dynamically adjusts the weights of the attentional priority map to proactively suppress locations likely to contain distracting information, even when those distractors possess significant affective salience.
papers.authors: Jan Theeuwes, Dirk van Moorselaar

papers.title: Neural representations of predicted events: Evidence from time-resolved EEG decoding
papers.abstract: Using multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) on high-temporal-resolution EEG data, this study examined the neural dynamics of anticipated sensory events. Human participants learned a fixed spatial sequence of dots (A-B-C-D) where each position predicted the next. Decoding performance using an independent pattern estimator revealed that the brain represents anticipated future stimulus positions even when they are critically omitted from the sequence. This predictive activation occurred at the expected moment in time and recruited similar neural representations as actual sensory input. The results provide evidence for dynamic, trial-to-trial weight adjustments within the spatial priority map, demonstrating that statistical learning enables the visual system to generate sensory-like representations of anticipated events ahead of afferent input.
papers.authors: Ai-Su Li, Jan Theeuwes, Dirk van Moorselaar

papers.title: Statistical Learning of Motor Preparation
papers.abstract: This study investigated whether implicit statistical learning extends beyond the selection of target and distractor locations to the preparation of specific motor responses. Using a modified additional singleton task, the researchers introduced a contingency where the spatial location of the target singleton predicted the likelihood of a specific finger response (e.g., right index vs. middle finger). Behavioral data revealed that participants were significantly faster to respond when the required motor action matched the learned response-location contingency, despite the target's shape (the actual task-relevant feature) being randomized. Post-experiment interviews indicated that this learning occurred without explicit awareness of the underlying regularities. The findings suggest that the brain automatically integrates sensory and motor regularities into event files, facilitating motor preparation based on spatial priors.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
papers.authors: Jan Theeuwes, Changrun Huang, Christian Frings, Dirk van Moorselaar

0181.name: Dobromir Rahnev
0181.bio: Dobromir Rahnev is an Associate Professor at the Georgia Institute of Technology whose research investigates the computational and neural foundations of perceptual decision-making and metacognition. They utilize a methodology combining psychophysics, functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), and transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), including simultaneous TMS-fMRI protocols to establish causal brain-behavior relationships. Rahnev's work focuses on why human perception is often suboptimal, developing mathematical models based on signal detection theory and Bayesian inference to explain the divergence between objective performance and subjective confidence. Additionally, Rahnev coordinated the creation of the Confidence Database to facilitate large-scale collaborative research and open science in the field.
0181.research_direction: Dr. Rahnev’s recent work explores the computational, neural, and methodological foundations of perceptual decision-making and metacognition. They have recently been investigating how to disentangle early sensory processing from higher-level decisional biases, utilizing computational frameworks like the drift-diffusion model alongside visual illusions and purely cognitive tasks. In the domain of metacognition, their research critically evaluates the validity and reliability of prevalent behavioral metrics while also probing whether automatic multisensory integration is governed by objective signal reliability or a subject's internal sense of confidence. Additionally, they are using fMRI pattern analysis to explore neural degeneracy, examining whether identical perceptual decisions are driven by invariant brain states or multiple distinct activation motifs.

papers.title: Signatures proposed to index perceptual effects emerge in a purely cognitive task
papers.abstract: This study empirically evaluates the validity of behavioral markers—such as specific drift-diffusion model (DDM) parameter shifts and the positioning of confidence and reaction time (RT) distribution peaks—previously proposed as diagnostic signatures for distinguishing perceptual from decisional effects. Utilizing a numerical distribution-matching task designed to involve purely cognitive processing (manipulating prior beliefs and rewards), the authors tested whether these supposed perceptual signatures could be replicated in the absence of sensory manipulations. The results demonstrate that both DDM drift-rate biases and shifts in confidence/RT distribution peaks occur under purely cognitive influences, identical to patterns previously attributed exclusively to sensory processing. These findings indicate that these behavioral metrics lack the specificity required to dissociate perceptual and decisional mechanisms, challenging several current methodological frameworks in perceptual decision-making research.
papers.authors: Sixing Chen, Michaela Bocheva, Dobromir Rahnev

papers.title: Multiple brain activation patterns for the same task
papers.abstract: This investigation employs multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) and unsupervised clustering of fMRI data to examine whether a single cognitive task is subserved by an invariant neural activation pattern or if degenerate neural states exist. Participants performed a perceptual decision-making task while cortical activity was monitored over multiple sessions. The researchers identified multiple, distinct, and stable activation motifs that are functionally equivalent in achieving task performance but differ substantially in their underlying neural topography. These patterns were found to be stable within individuals and associated with specific fluctuations in internal decision variables. The results support a many-to-one mapping between brain states and cognitive outcomes, suggesting that neural degeneracy allows diverse functional architectures to subserve identical cognitive processes, thereby complicating the search for universal neural correlates.
papers.authors: Joxhens Nakuci, Jiwon Yeon, Jung-Hee Kim, Sung-Phil Kim, Dobromir Rahnev

papers.title: Automatic multisensory integration follows subjective confidence rather than objective performance
papers.abstract: This research explores the computational principles of multisensory fusion, specifically testing whether the integration of visual and auditory spatial cues is governed by objective signal reliability (inverse variance) or by internal subjective confidence. Through a series of cross-modal spatial localization experiments and hierarchical Bayesian modeling, the authors analyzed how trial-by-trial variability in sensory precision and metacognitive confidence influenced integration weights. The results revealed that subjective confidence ratings were a superior predictor of multisensory cue weighting compared to objective reliability measures. This indicates that the neural mechanisms responsible for automatic sensory integration utilize internal metacognitive signals as a heuristic proxy for cue reliability, providing a mechanism for adaptive perception even when external statistical properties are not directly accessible to the observer.
papers.authors: Yi Gao, Kai Xue, Brian Odegaard, Dobromir Rahnev

papers.title: A comprehensive assessment of current methods for measuring metacognition
papers.abstract: This study provides a large-scale empirical assessment of 17 distinct metrics used to quantify metacognitive ability, including the M-ratio (meta-d'/d'), meta-d', and the area under the type-2 ROC curve. Utilizing a massive psychophysical dataset, the author evaluates these measures across the psychometric dimensions of validity, estimation precision, and reliability. The findings indicate that while most measures are generally valid, many exhibit problematic dependencies on first-order task performance (d') and response criteria. Furthermore, the analysis reveals a dissociation between split-half reliability, which was consistently high, and test-retest reliability, which was low for several common metrics, suggesting that these measures may be sensitive to transient states rather than stable traits. The study concludes with a framework for selecting metacognitive measures based on specific experimental goals and data constraints.
papers.authors: Dobromir Rahnev

papers.title: Dynamics of sensory and decisional biases in perceptual decision making: Insights from the face distortion illusion
papers.abstract: The Flashed Face Distortion Effect (FFDE) was utilized as a paradigm to dissociate sensory from decisional components of bias within the framework of the drift-diffusion model (DDM). By modeling choice and reaction time (RT) data from an orientation-discrimination task, the authors investigated how these two forms of bias interact and evolve as a function of stimulus evidence. The results demonstrate that the FFDE is driven by an interplay between a constant sensory offset—reflecting a stable distortion of the input—and a stimulus-dependent decisional bias, reflecting a shift in the response criterion. Specifically, the decisional bias was significantly more pronounced at lower levels of sensory evidence where uncertainty is higher, while the sensory bias remained invariant. These results provide a mechanistic account of how illusory perception emerges from both early sensory distortions and flexible decisional strategies.
papers.authors: Yi Gao, Sixing Chen, Dobromir Rahnev

0182.name: Domenica Bueti
0182.bio: Domenica Bueti is a Full Professor of Cognitive Neuroscience at the International School for Advanced Studies (SISSA) and directs the Time Perception Lab. Bueti’s research examines the neural mechanisms of temporal cognition and magnitude processing, focusing on how the brain encodes and integrates dimensions such as time, space, and numerosity. This work includes the identification of chronotopic maps—topographic representations of time in the supplementary motor area and parietal cortex—using ultra-high field functional magnetic resonance imaging (7T fMRI). Bueti integrates psychophysics, neuroimaging, and transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) to characterize the functional architecture of the human timing system.
0182.research_direction: Dr. Bueti’s recent work explores the neural and cognitive mechanisms underlying visual time perception, specifically focusing on how the human brain encodes sub-second durations. Using ultra-high field 7T fMRI and population receptive field modeling, they are mapping the cortical hierarchy of interval timing to understand how representations of duration transition from being tightly coupled with spatial location in early visual areas to abstract, space-invariant codes in frontal regions. Their research also investigates how temporal perception interacts with other sensory and motor systems, utilizing psychophysics and EEG to probe how dynamic visual features like speed bias duration estimates and how motor planning during goal-directed actions actively distorts subjective time. Additionally, they have recently been examining how the brain processes more complex temporal sequences, using sensorimotor tapping tasks to delineate how local and global regularity violations impact rhythm reproduction across different sensory modalities.

papers.title: Evolution of visual time throughout goal driven action learning
papers.abstract: This research utilizes a multimodal approach—incorporating behavioral metrics, electroencephalography (EEG), and Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA)—to investigate the dynamic interplay between time perception and goal-directed action learning. Participants engaged in a dual-task involving manual reaching and sub-second duration estimation. The findings reveal that subjective time expands during the motor preparation phase preceding action onset, an effect that intensifies over trials as motor plans are optimized and action latency decreases. RSA results demonstrate that actions influence timing through two distinct, independent mechanisms: the specificity of motor planning recalibrates how duration information is encoded into neural timekeeping circuits as stimuli unfold, whereas general motor anticipation and engagement modulate the post-stimulus readout (decoding) of temporal evidence. These results suggest that perceptual time is not a passive sensory product but is actively constructed and fine-tuned by motor control systems during skill acquisition.
papers.authors: Nicola Binetti, Federico Mancinelli, Marco Zanon, Domenica Bueti

papers.title: The interaction of speed and time in biasing the perception of dynamically changing visual inputs
papers.abstract: This study addresses the sensory-driven nature of visual time perception by examining how non-temporal stimulus features, specifically speed, bias the estimation of duration in dynamically changing visual environments. Using psychophysical discrimination tasks, the authors measured points of subjective equality (PSEs) and just-noticeable differences (JNDs) for stimuli where duration and speed were systematically varied. The results demonstrate significant perceptual distortions of time induced by speed modulations, revealing an asymmetry in how the brain integrates temporal and non-temporal magnitudes. These findings support a modality-specific mechanism of interval timing where duration estimation is intrinsically linked to the neural dynamics of the primary sensory input, rather than relying on a centralized, magnitude-independent clock.
papers.authors: Francesca Iris Bellotti, Domenica Bueti

papers.title: Defining a functional hierarchy of millisecond time: from visual stimulus processing to duration perception
papers.abstract: Using ultra-high field (7T) functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging and neural population receptive field (pRF) modeling, this study maps the functional hierarchy of visual duration processing across the human cortex. The authors estimated unimodal tuning to sub-second durations across anatomically defined regions. Results reveal the existence of well-defined chronotopic maps in the parietal and premotor cortices and the caudal supplementary motor area (SMA), where neuronal preferences correlate with behavioral discrimination boundaries. Conversely, more categorical and subjective representations were observed in the insula and inferior frontal cortex. Distinct patterns of inter-regional correlation in duration preferences suggest a transition from sensory-bound duration encoding for task-related goals to abstract, subjective representations for perceptual decision-making, providing a comprehensive framework for the neural circuits of visual timing.
papers.authors: Valeria Centanino, Gianfranco Fortunato, Domenica Bueti

papers.title: The neural link between stimulus duration and spatial location in the human visual hierarchy
papers.abstract: This study employs 7T fMRI and neuronal-based modeling to characterize the integration of spatial and temporal information along the human dorsal visual stream. The authors identified a functional transition in duration coding: in early visual areas (V1-V2), neural responses to duration are monotonic and spatially dependent, intrinsically linked to the stimulus's spatial location. Along the hierarchy, particularly in the intraparietal sulcus (IPS), neuronal populations emerge that are selective to both space and time, with linked topographic organizations. In the frontal cortex, the representation of time becomes unimodal and spatially invariant. These findings characterize a cortical gradient from a coupled space-time sensory code in posterior areas to an independent, abstract representation of duration in higher-order regions, highlighting how early sensory interactions shape the final perception of visual duration.
papers.authors: Valeria Centanino, Gianfranco Fortunato, Domenica Bueti

papers.title: Global and Local Deviance Effects in the Processing of Temporal Patterns
papers.abstract: This research investigates how the human brain processes temporal sequences by analyzing the impact of regularity violations at both the local level (individual intervals) and the global level (the overall sequence structure). Through three synchronization-continuation tapping experiments using visual and auditory patterns of varying complexity, the authors assessed reproduction precision and bias. The results show that reproduction of simple sequences is predominantly affected by local interval violations. In contrast, global structural violations significantly impair the reproduction of complex visual patterns. These effects are partially mediated by rescaling and central tendency biases in the reproduced patterns. The findings indicate that the processing of temporal patterns involves a weighted integration of interval-based and structure-based mechanisms that are sensitive to both sensory modality and structural complexity.
papers.venue: Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Dunia Giomo, Romain Brasselet, Gianfranco Fortunato, Domenica Bueti

0183.name: Dominique Lamy
0183.bio: Dominique Lamy is a Professor of Psychology at Tel Aviv University and directs the Visual Cognition Lab. Lamy’s research examines the determinants of attentional priority, exploring how stimulus-driven salience, goal-directed targets, and implicit memory factors like priming of pop-out interact to guide selection. Lamy developed the Priority Accumulation Framework (PAF) to characterize the temporal dynamics and evidence accumulation involved in attentional deployment. Using behavioral psychophysics and event-related potentials (ERPs), they investigate the functional boundaries between conscious and unconscious vision, as well as the role of spatial and object-based mechanisms in perception.
0183.research_direction: Dr. Lamy has recently been investigating the mechanisms that guide visual attention, focusing heavily on how selection history and statistical learning shape spatial priority maps. Their recent work explores intertrial phenomena like priming of pop-out and priming of location, asking whether these attention biases act proactively to shift baseline priority or reactively following stimulus onset. By employing visual search, spatial-cueing, and probe-identification paradigms, they are dissecting whether task-irrelevant features fail to guide attention due to encoding deficits or priority-map integration failures, while also testing the flexibility of automatic spatial biases under different top-down task demands. Additionally, Dr. Lamy explores the boundary between conscious and unconscious visual processing, using masked liminal-prime paradigms to determine whether objective metrics like forced-choice discrimination are systematically contaminated by unconscious information when compared to subjective reports of awareness.

papers.title: Statistical Learning of Target Location Guides Attention Proactively
papers.abstract: The researchers investigated target-location probability learning (LPL) to determine whether selection history-driven biases manifest as proactive shifts in attentional priority or as reactive changes occurring only after stimulus onset. Utilizing a hybrid visual search and probe identification paradigm, they indexed the distribution of covert attention by analyzing letter-report accuracy at various display coordinates. Findings from both the learning and extinction phases revealed that participants prioritized high-probability locations even on probe trials where no search target appeared, supporting the hypothesis that LPL-mediated selection history guides attention proactively by adjusting the baseline activation levels within the spatial priority map.
papers.authors: Aidai Golan, Aniruddha Ramgir, Dominique Lamy

papers.title: How Inflexible Is the Attentional Bias Toward Recently Selected Locations?
papers.abstract: This work re-evaluates the flexibility of the priming-of-location (PoL) effect, questioning whether the observed bias toward previously selected coordinates is an automatic, context-invariant enhancement of priority. By systematically manipulating search difficulty and task-set context within a probe-based framework, the authors assessed the extent to which PoL persists across varying strategic demands. The results indicate that while the spatial and temporal parameters of PoL are sensitive to top-down modulation and changes in search context, the core bias remains significant across disparate conditions, suggesting that selecting an object automatically updates the spatial priority map in a manner that is highly persistent and resistant to override.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
papers.authors: Daniel Toledano, Dominique Lamy

papers.title: When Irrelevant-Feature Priming Fails: Encoding Failure or Failure to Guide Attention?
papers.abstract: This study investigates the mechanisms underlying the frequent failure of irrelevant-feature priming in visual search tasks. The researchers tested the 'no-encoding' account, which assumes that task-irrelevant features are not processed, against the 'attention-guidance failure' account, which posits that while encoded, these features are not successfully integrated into the priority map for selection guidance. By measuring intertrial priming effects alongside feature-response binding (S-R) effects, the authors demonstrated that irrelevant features are reliably encoded and associated with responses despite failing to speed search times, thereby validating the attention-guidance failure account and suggesting that encoding does not guarantee attentional guidance.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
papers.authors: Daniel Toledano, Nitzan Micher, Dominique Lamy

papers.title: Priming of pop-out in the spatial-cueing paradigm
papers.abstract: This investigation assesses the priority-map account of priming-of-popout (PoP) using a spatial-cueing paradigm to adjudicate between priority-based and response-based accounts of intertrial effects. The authors tested whether selecting a target feature consistently increases the attentional priority of that feature in subsequent displays, thereby modulating cue-validity effects. Experimental results showed that well-replicated contingent-capture effects typically associated with target-defining features were abolished when target and nontarget colors swapped between trials. The findings suggest that selection history does not simply boost a fixed feature-based priority signal but rather modulates the weights of attentional control sets in a context-sensitive manner.
papers.authors: Dirk Kerzel, Dominique Lamy

papers.title: Unconscious Processing Contaminates Objective Measures of Conscious Perception: Evidence From the Liminal Prime Paradigm
papers.abstract: This study evaluates the claim that forced-choice discrimination provides a valid objective measure of conscious perception by examining potential contamination from unconscious processing. Using a masked response-priming paradigm with words presented at the subjective threshold of awareness (liminal primes), the researchers compared the time courses of priming effects for 'unseen' and 'seen' stimuli across the reaction-time distribution. Findings indicated that response priming for primes rated as invisible occurred only on the fastest trials—a hallmark of unconscious processing—whereas primes rated as visible exhibited sustained effects. The presence of above-chance discrimination for subjectively unseen primes, despite these unique time courses, suggests that objective measures of consciousness are systematically contaminated by unconscious information, favoring subjective reports as a more accurate index of awareness.
papers.authors: Nitzan Micher, Diana Mazenko, Dominique Lamy

0184.name: Dora Hermes
0184.department: Department of Physiology and Biomedical Engineering
0184.bio: Hermes is an Associate Professor at the Mayo Clinic who investigates neurophysiological signals to identify biomarkers for neurological diseases and develop neuroprosthetics. Their research integrates multimodal imaging techniques, such as fMRI and intracranial EEG, with computational modeling to characterize brain network dynamics. Hermes examines how human visual and motor systems respond to sensory inputs and electrical stimulation to inform the development of therapeutic devices. This work connects fundamental neuroscience with clinical application through collaborations with neurosurgeons and neurologists to treat conditions like epilepsy.
0184.research_direction: Dr. Hermes's recent work explores the electrophysiological dynamics of the human brain, utilizing high-resolution intracranial recordings to bridge fundamental visual neuroscience and clinical neuromodulation. Specifically, they have recently been investigating how the human ventral temporal cortex integrates bottom-up sensory features, such as image contrast, with top-down cognitive task demands by examining distinct high- and low-frequency neural signals. Additionally, their research maps the effective connectivity of large-scale thalamocortical networks, probing how electrical stimulation of visual-associative subregions like the pulvinar propagates through the cortex and alters neural excitability in patients with drug-resistant epilepsy. To support these functional mapping efforts, they are also developing standardized, open-source computational pipelines and optimized data-referencing strategies to reliably isolate true brain stimulation-evoked potentials from hardware artifacts.

papers.title: Thalamic Stimulation Induced Changes in Network Connectivity and Excitability in Epilepsy
papers.abstract: This investigation utilized intracranial stereotactic EEG (sEEG) and single-pulse electrical stimulation (SPES) to evaluate the modulation of large-scale thalamocortical networks in ten subjects with drug-resistant epilepsy. By analyzing brain stimulation-evoked potentials (BSEPs) before and after repetitive 145 Hz thalamic deep brain stimulation (DBS), the authors quantified changes in effective connectivity and excitability. Findings demonstrated that prolonged DBS trials (>1.5 hours) induced significant suppression of BSEP amplitudes in functionally connected cortical regions, with the degree of modulation correlating with baseline connectivity strength. In contrast, shorter stimulation intervals primarily suppressed interictal epileptiform discharge (IED) rates in the seizure network without persistent BSEP attenuation. These results establish BSEPs as dynamic electrophysiological biomarkers for monitoring target engagement and network-level plasticity across acute and subacute timescales in clinical neuromodulation.
papers.authors: Nicholas M. Gregg, Gabriela Ojeda Valencia, Tereza Pridalova, Harvey Huang, Vaclav Kremen, Brian N. Lundstrom, Jamie J. Van Gompel, Kai J. Miller, Gregory A. Worrell, Dora Hermes

papers.title: ER-detect: A pipeline for robust detection of early evoked responses in BIDS-iEEG electrical stimulation data
papers.abstract: The authors introduce ER-detect, an open-source computational framework designed for the automated and standardized detection of early brain stimulation-evoked potentials (BSEPs) in intracranial EEG (iEEG) datasets following BIDS architecture. The pipeline facilitates the identification of primary N1 components in cortico-cortical evoked potentials (CCEPs) by implementing optimized artifact rejection, re-referencing, and feature-based detection algorithms. Specifically, it employs temporal-spectral decomposition to differentiate genuine neural responses from hardware-related stimulation artifacts. Validation on clinical sEEG recordings from epilepsy patients demonstrates that ER-detect enhances the robustness and reproducibility of mapping effective connectivity, supporting the precise localization of the epileptogenic zone and the optimization of neurostimulation paradigms.
papers.authors: Max A. van den Boom, Nicholas M. Gregg, Gabriela Ojeda Valencia, Brian N. Lundstrom, Kai J. Miller, D. van Blooijs, G. J. M. Huiskamp, F. S. S. Leijten, G. A. Worrell, Dora Hermes

papers.title: Human pulvinar stimulation engages select cortical pathways in epilepsy
papers.abstract: Using stereotactic EEG (sEEG) in 12 patients undergoing evaluation for drug-resistant epilepsy, this study maps the causal effective connectivity of the human pulvinar nucleus using single-pulse electrical stimulation (SPES). The researchers identified distinct topographical projection motifs: lateral pulvinar (PuL) stimulation selectively drove responses in striate and prestriate (V1-V2) and extrastriate visual areas, whereas ventromedial pulvinar (vPuM) stimulation preferentially engaged the lateral temporal neocortex. Furthermore, dorsomedial pulvinar (dPuM) stimulation elicited significant responses within the intraparietal sulcus (IPS). These findings demonstrate that electrical stimulation of discrete pulvinar subregions influences specific cortical networks, suggesting that subregion-specific targeting could enhance the efficacy of deep brain stimulation for managing seizures in posterior quadrant and temporal lobe epilepsies.
papers.authors: Jordan A. Bilderbeek, Nicholas M. Gregg, Maria Guadalupe Yanez-Ramos, Harvey Huang, Morgan Montoya, Peter Brunner, Jon T. Willie, Jamie J. Van Gompel, Gregory A. Worrell, Kai J. Miller, Dora Hermes

papers.title: Dissociating stimulus encoding and task demands in ECoG responses from human visual cortex
papers.abstract: This study dissociates the neural signatures of sensory encoding and cognitive modulation in the human ventral temporal cortex (VTC) using high-resolution electrocorticography (ECoG). By varying stimulus contrast and task requirements (fixation versus categorization), the authors characterized two independent neurophysiological signals: high-frequency broadband (HFB) activity (>70 Hz) and low-frequency band (LFB) oscillations (8-28 Hz). HFB responses tracked sensory image contrast with high fidelity before being modulated by task demands approximately 200 ms after stimulus onset. In contrast, LFB oscillations were insensitive to image contrast but exhibited robust suppression proportional to cognitive task demands. These findings suggest that HFB activity serves as a primary site for integrating sensory and task-related information, while LFB suppression reflects the release of inhibitory control to facilitate task-relevant processing in visual pathways.
papers.authors: Zeeshan Qadir, Harvey Huang, Müge Özker, Daniel Yoshor, Michael S. Beauchamp, Kendrick Kay, Dora Hermes

papers.title: Proper reference selection and re-referencing to mitigate bias in single pulse electrical stimulation data
papers.abstract: This methodological study evaluates the influence of intracranial EEG recording references on the quantification of brain stimulation-evoked potentials (BSEPs) used to map effective connectivity. Leveraging clinical sEEG data, the authors demonstrate that hardware references located near active neural populations or stimulation sites can introduce significant signal contamination, potentially leading to false-positive connectivity inferences. The study proposes a data-driven re-referencing strategy that identifies and mitigates reference-induced artifacts by maximizing signal independence. Validation across multiple stimulation runs confirms that this approach improves the similarity of evoked responses between sessions and clarifies the interpretation of connectivity maps. The results underscore the necessity of optimized referencing protocols for accurate electrophysiological network characterization and individualized neuromodulation therapy.
papers.authors: Harvey Huang, Joshua A. Adkinson, Michael A. Jensen, Mohammed Hasen, Isabel A. Danstrom, Kelly R. Bijanki, Nicholas M. Gregg, Kai J. Miller, Sameer A. Sheth, Dora Hermes

0186.name: Dwight J. Kravitz
0186.bio: Dwight J. Kravitz is an Associate Professor at George Washington University and a Program Director at the National Science Foundation. Kravitz researches the relationship between neuroanatomy, experience, and neural representations, specifically focusing on the functional organization of the ventral and dorsal visual pathways. Using multivariate fMRI analysis, behavioral psychophysics, and data-driven computational modeling, they explore how the brain represents visual objects, scenes, and social concepts. Kravitz’s work addresses the intersection of perceptual processing and working memory to develop a convergent understanding of vision across humans, animal models, and patient populations.
0186.research_direction: Dr. Kravitz's recent work spans empirical investigations of spatial vision and broader theoretical frameworks for understanding large-scale functional neuroanatomy. In their empirical research, they have recently been investigating how stable spatial representations and egocentric distance estimates rapidly emerge from pictorial cues in natural scenes, testing how these percepts generalize across distinct tasks, viewing durations, and individual observers. Concurrently, their recent theoretical work explores the underlying architecture of the primate visual system, critically re-evaluating the classic two-pathway model to examine how the ventral and dorsal streams might operate as highly interconnected, recurrent networks rather than strictly independent systems. Broadening this system-level perspective, Dr. Kravitz is also exploring new methodological frameworks for cognitive neuroscience, focusing on how multitask experimental designs and tests of generalization can map neural activity to dynamic task demands rather than existing psychological taxonomies.

papers.title: Distance perception in natural scene images generalize across individuals, tasks, and viewing time
papers.abstract: The mechanisms underlying spatial perception in naturalistic environments are obscured by the multitude of available depth cues. This study presents a series of preregistered behavioral experiments that quantify scene-specific spatial representations by demonstrating their generalization across distinct tasks, viewing durations, and independent observers. Participants estimated or discriminated egocentric distances to target objects in 156 natural scene images presented for durations ranging from 125 to 1,000 ms. Results indicate that even single-exposure estimates show systematic scene-specific biases that reliably predict the performance of different participants on orthogonal spatial tasks. Quantitative analysis reveals that pictorial features, specifically the perceived extent of the ground plane, account for these systematic deviations. These findings provide evidence for a highly tuned, rapid processing mechanism that integrates pictorial information into stable distance percepts during natural scene perception.
papers.authors: Prachi Mahableshwarkar, Lindsay Houck, John Philbeck, Dwight Kravitz

papers.title: Insights from the Evolving Model of Two Cortical Visual Pathways
papers.abstract: This review provides a critical evaluation of the dual cortical pathways framework, which has served as a foundational model in visual neuroscience for over four decades. While the original proposal posited a strict functional and anatomical bifurcation into independent 'what' (ventral) and 'where/how' (dorsal) streams, contemporary evidence suggests a more complex architecture. We synthesize recent neuroanatomical and physiological data to show that the primate visual system is better described as a pair of highly recurrent, interconnected heterarchies. These pathways exhibit extensive cross-talk and project to a heterogeneous set of cortical and subcortical targets, allowing for the flexible integration of information required for diverse behavioral goals. Despite the limitations of early simplifying assumptions, we argue that the core principle of grounding behavior and physiological response in neuroanatomy remains the most productive path for understanding visual function.
papers.authors: Chris Baker, Dwight Kravitz

papers.title: Centering cognitive neuroscience on task demands and generalization
papers.abstract: Current theories in cognitive neuroscience frequently rely on a priori psychological taxonomies to map neural activity to mental states, a process that may constrain the discovery of new, biologically grounded concepts. We propose an alternative theoretical and empirical framework that centers on the quantification of task demands—constraints that emerge from the dynamic interaction between an agent’s goals, sensory input, and behavior. We argue that these demands jointly determine the resulting neural and mental states across various spatiotemporal scales. By utilizing multitask experimental designs, dense sampling, and formal tests of generalization across tasks and data modalities, this framework facilitates the empirical discovery of concepts unconstrained by existing psychological labels. This approach moves the field toward an action-oriented, integrated view of the brain that explains commonalities in physiological responses as a product of shared task-level requirements.
papers.authors: Matthias Nau, Alexandra C. Schmid, Simon M. Kaplan, Chris I. Baker, Dwight J. Kravitz

papers.title: From Cells to Circuits, from Vision to Cognition, from Monkeys to Humans: Leslie Ungerleider's Pioneering Neuroscience
papers.abstract: This article serves as a comprehensive retrospective on the scientific legacy of Leslie Ungerleider, specifically focusing on her instrumental role in defining the functional neuroanatomy of the primate visual system. We review the progression of her research from early systematic lesion studies and tract-tracing in non-human primates to the application of functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) in humans. Central to this work was the identification of the diverging ventral and dorsal pathways and the subsequent expansion of these circuits to include regions involved in social perception, attention, and memory.
