We highlight how her insistence on rigorous anatomical grounding provided the necessary infrastructure for contemporary theories of object recognition and spatial vision. The review underscores the continuing relevance of her methodological approach—bridging scales from local circuits to global networks—in shaping modern systems neuroscience.
papers.authors: Chris I. Baker, Dwight J. Kravitz

0188.name: E. J. Green
0188.department: Department of Philosophy; Department of Psychological and Brain Sciences
0188.main_research_area: philosophy of perception and cognitive science
0188.bio: Green is the Miller Associate Professor at Johns Hopkins University, where they hold a primary appointment in the Department of Philosophy and a secondary appointment in the Department of Psychological and Brain Sciences. Green’s research examines the intersection of philosophy of mind and vision science, specifically investigating the nature of perceptual representation and the architectural boundary between perception and higher-level cognition. Their work addresses topics including shape constancy, multisensory object perception, and the compositionality of visual formats. Green integrates empirical findings from psychophysics and perceptual psychology with philosophical analysis to model how the mind segments and interprets sensory input.
0188.research_direction: Dr. Green’s recent work explores the foundational architecture of perceptual representation, investigating how sensory systems construct, abstract, and categorize visual information. They have recently been examining the boundary between perception and higher-order cognition by asking whether constructive processes like amodal completion rely on mental imagery, and whether early perceptual categorization, such as infant color discrimination, intrinsically requires conceptual content. Their research also investigates the mechanics of perceptual abstraction, specifically how the visual hierarchy translates highly precise, determinate sensory inputs into broader categorical judgments. Additionally, they are exploring how these representational formats operate across and within domains, examining the cross-modal transfer of shape information between sight and touch in newly sighted individuals, and how visual systems distinguish between viewpoint-dependent perspectival shifts and objective representational errors.

papers.title: Reconsidering the Role of Imagery in Perception
papers.abstract: This article interrogates the 'Constitutive View' of mental imagery, which asserts that imagery provides critical representational components for constructive perceptual processes, such as the filling-in of occluded visual regions. The authors argue that the expansive taxonomical definition of imagery underlying this view—categorizing any perceptual processing detached from immediate sensory input as imagery—fails to demarcate a psychologically unified kind. Through an analysis of amodal completion, the paper demonstrates that such phenomena are more parsimoniously explained as intrinsic, stimulus-driven constructive capacities of the perceptual system rather than mnemonic or imagery-driven augmentations. Consequently, the authors conclude that perception is best understood as an autonomous constructive process that does not routinely integrate imagery-based constituents.
papers.authors: Kevin J. Lande, E. J. Green

papers.title: Perceptual Abstraction
papers.abstract: The paper investigates the computational transition from highly determinate perceptual representations (e.g., precise chromatic coordinates or exact geometric curvatures) to the abstract contents of immediate perceptual judgments (e.g., 'red' or generic object types). The authors articulate a theoretical framework distinguishing between implicit and explicit perceptual abstraction. They formulate a novel empirical criterion to dissociate these two modalities of abstraction and explore its significance for the 'richness' debate regarding perceptual content. Furthermore, they outline the implications of this distinction for the interplay between innate representational systems and conceptual categorization, proposing that explicit abstraction involves the deployment of concepts while implicit abstraction remains a non-conceptual feature of the visual hierarchy.
papers.authors: Mason Westfall, E. J. Green

papers.title: Perceptual Categorization and Perceptual Concepts
papers.abstract: This work evaluates the thesis of 'Conceptualism'—the claim that at least some perceptual representations possess conceptual content—against recent empirical challenges. Specifically, it addresses the argument that infant categorical perception of color occurs in the absence of color concepts, thereby necessitating a non-conceptual representational format for color categories. The author critically examines this inferential leap by analyzing the structural and functional requirements for concept deployment in early development. He argues that the existence of categorical discrimination in infants does not definitively preclude a conceptualist account, provided one recognizes the specific architectural roles that concepts play in the hierarchical organization of the perceptual system.
papers.authors: E. J. Green

papers.title: Newly Sighted Perceivers and the Relation Between Sight and Touch
papers.abstract: Drawing on empirical data from 'Project Prakash' and other studies of individuals treated for congenital cataracts, this paper investigates the cross-modal transfer of shape and spatial information between vision and haptics. It addresses Molyneux's Question by examining whether human perception utilizes a common, amodal representational format for spatial geometry or if cross-modal correspondence requires the acquisition of associative mappings between disparate, modality-specific formats. By evaluating the performance of newly sighted perceivers in shape-matching tasks, the author argues that the data constrain the extent to which spatial properties are 'rationally connected' across modalities. The findings are used to constrain theories regarding the format and informational encapsulation of sensory systems.
papers.authors: E. J. Green

papers.title: Hill on Perceptual Relativity and Perceptual Error
papers.abstract: This article provides a critical analysis of Christopher Hill’s theoretical framework concerning the contents of perceptual experience, specifically the distinction between 'perceptual relativity'—variation in appearance due to perspectival shifts—and 'perceptual error'—the misrepresentation of distal properties. The author explores how these categories relate to contemporary representationalist theories, which posit that perceptual states represent mind-independent properties. The article argues that the syntactic structure of perceptual representations must account for perspectival features to maintain the distinction between viewpoint-dependent appearance and objective inaccuracy. These distinctions are assessed against empirical evidence from vision science regarding viewpoint-invariant object recognition.
papers.authors: E. J. Green

0190.name: Edward Awh
0190.bio: Awh is a Professor of Psychology at the University of Chicago and co-directs the Awh/Vogel Lab, which focuses on the cognitive neuroscience of attention and memory. Their research characterizes the architectural and neural constraints of visual working memory, specifically investigating why storage is limited to a small number of individuated items. Utilizing electroencephalography (EEG) to track alpha-band oscillations and functional neuroimaging (fMRI), Awh explores the functional overlap between spatial selective attention and online memory maintenance. Their work employs multivariate decoding and computational modeling to differentiate between spatial orienting and object-based storage while examining content-independent pointer systems in the human cortex.
0190.research_direction: Dr. Awh's recent work explores the neural architecture and capacity limits of human working memory (WM) using EEG and multivariate decoding techniques. They have recently been investigating whether WM relies on a domain-general indexing system by looking for load-tracking neural signals that remain consistent across disparate visual features and distinct sensory modalities. Additionally, their research probes how WM intersects with other core cognitive systems, testing the functional boundaries between spatial attention and WM encoding, and examining whether the memory advantage for meaningful real-world objects stems from expanded online storage capacity or long-term memory contributions. Finally, they are exploring the dynamic nature of spatial working memory by utilizing alpha-band activity to track how representations are formatted when they are initially encoded versus when they are actively mentally updated in response to new information.

papers.title: Contributions from Long-Term Memory Explain Superior Visual Working Memory Performance with Meaningful Objects
papers.abstract: Claims that semantic knowledge increases working memory (WM) storage capacity are often based on paradigms that compare trial-unique real-world objects with a restricted set of repeated simple features, a design that confounds meaningfulness with proactive interference (PI). In a series of experiments, we demonstrate that equating PI levels across stimulus types eliminates the performance benefit for meaningful objects. Hierarchical Bayesian dual-process signal detection modeling indicated that the advantage for trial-unique stimuli was selectively mediated by increased long-term memory (LTM) familiarity rather than expanded recollection-based WM storage. Furthermore, contralateral delay activity (CDA)—a sustained electrophysiological index of active storage—showed that while trial-unique objects improved behavioral accuracy, they did not increase the number of stored items, as evidenced by equivalent CDA slopes and plateaus for objects and colors. These results suggest that superior memory for meaningful objects reflects enhanced LTM contributions under low-interference conditions rather than an expansion of the online WM storage limit.
papers.authors: Hyung-Bum Park, Edward Awh

papers.title: Neural evidence for modality-independent storage in working memory
papers.abstract: While classical theories distinguish between modality-specific storage buffers, recent evidence points toward a domain-general neural signal that tracks the number of items maintained in working memory (WM). Using multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) of EEG activity across two experiments, we identified an item-based load signature that generalizes across visual and auditory modalities. We dissociated parallel but distinct neural signals that independently track stimulus modality, the number of items stored in WM (modality-independent load), and the focus of spatial attention. These load signals enabled precise cross-modal decoding, where models trained on one sensory modality successfully decoded set sizes in the other. We propose that these signals reflect the operation of a spatiotemporal 'pointer' system that binds item tokens to their respective contexts, providing a modality-independent mechanism for tracking the contents of online thoughts.
papers.authors: Darius Suplica, Henry M. Jones, Gisella K. Diaz, John P. Veillette, Howard C. Nusbaum, Edward Awh

papers.title: Cortically Disparate Visual Features Evoke Content-Independent Load Signals during Storage in Working Memory
papers.abstract: Working memory (WM) capacity is thought to be constrained by an item-based limit mediated by a general-purpose pointer system, yet most neural evidence for load-tracking signals is limited to single-modality or single-feature experiments. Here, we used EEG to determine whether neural signatures of memory load are independent of the specific visual features being stored. By independently manipulating item count across cortically disparate features (color and orientation), we identified multivariate neural patterns that track the total number of individuated items regardless of their featural content. These load-dependent signals were dissociable from stimulus-specific patterns and generalized across different feature types. The findings support a pointer-based model of WM storage, where a content-independent indexing system binds representations to a spatial coordinate system to maintain item distinctiveness and access.
papers.authors: Henry M. Jones, William S. Thyer, David Suplica, Edward Awh

papers.title: Electroencephalogram Decoding Reveals Distinct Processes for Directing Spatial Attention and Encoding Into Working Memory
papers.abstract: The degree of functional overlap between spatial attention and working memory (WM) encoding is a matter of ongoing debate, with some accounts suggesting they are indistinguishable operations. We employed multivariate decoding of EEG signatures to test whether the neural signatures of attending to a location and encoding items into WM are dissociable. By independently manipulating the number of memory items and the spatial extent (breadth and position) of covert attention, we identified distinct neural signatures for each process. Neural markers of spatial attention tracked the parameters of the attended region but were insensitive to the number of individuated items encoded. Conversely, multivariate decoding of the number of items in WM remained unaffected by variations in the spatial extent of attention. These results demonstrate that spatial attention and WM encoding are mediated by separate neural operations, challenging the identity hypothesis of attention and memory.
papers.authors: Henry M. Jones, Gisella K. Diaz, William X. Q. Ngiam, Edward Awh

papers.title: Encoded and updated spatial working memories share a common representational format in alpha activity
papers.abstract: Working memory (WM) must dynamically update its contents as environmental demands shift, yet it remains unclear whether the representational format of updated memories matches that of initially encoded information. We used alpha-band activity (8–12 Hz) in the EEG to reconstruct the spatial contents of WM as participants mentally updated remembered locations in response to auditory cues. Inverted encoding models (IEMs) precisely tracked both the initially encoded positions and the transformed locations following mental updating. Cross-training analyses revealed a robust generalization of the alpha-band reconstructions between encoded and updated states, indicating a common representational format. Furthermore, the temporal dynamics of these alpha-band updates predicted individual differences in reaction times and saccade latencies. These findings demonstrate that alpha activity serves as a consistent vehicle for both the static maintenance and the active transformation of spatial information in human WM.
papers.authors: Eren Günseli, Joshua J. Foster, David W. Sutterer, Lara Todorova, Edward K. Vogel, Edward Awh

0191.name: Edward F Ester
0191.department: Department of Psychology and Institute for Neuroscience
0191.bio: Edward F. Ester investigates the neural architectures and computational principles that support visual working memory and selective attention. Their research integrates behavioral psychophysics with neuroimaging methods, including fMRI and EEG, to reconstruct and track mnemonic representations across the human cortex. Ester examines how the brain maintains information in the absence of sensory input and how these representations are transformed into motor plans to guide goal-directed behavior. Their current projects explore the factors determining individual differences in cognitive efficiency and the impact of neural competition on memory integrity.
0191.research_direction: Dr. Ester has recently been investigating the neural and behavioral mechanisms underlying working memory, attention, and decision-making, focusing on how internal representations are maintained, selected, and transformed into actions. Their recent work explores how the brain resolves competition between goal-driven and stimulus-driven factors within internal working memory, and how neural evidence accumulation operates when decisions are based on newly learned abstract rules rather than direct sensory input. Using high-temporal-resolution EEG and paired-pulse transcranial magnetic stimulation, they are examining the distributed nature of memory networks to test the sensory recruitment hypothesis and probe how bidirectional cortical traveling waves route information between visual and frontal areas. Additionally, they have been employing sophisticated oculomotor tracking to investigate whether human gaze dynamics can decode not just the physical properties of remembered stimuli, but also their abstract categorical meaning during memory-guided tasks.

papers.title: Neural Measures of Human Decision Making Track Evidence Accumulation in Learned Space
papers.abstract: The mechanisms of neural evidence accumulation, primarily indexed by the centro-parietal positivity (CPP) in human EEG, have typically been evaluated using evidence directly available in the sensorium or retrieved from long-term memory. This study addressed whether these mechanisms extend to decisions based on computed evidence derived from newly learned representational transformations. Participants classified oriented visual stimuli into discrete categories defined by an arbitrary, experimenter-imposed boundary while scalp EEG was recorded. Findings indicated that CPP buildup rates scaled monotonically with category coherence (the angular distance from the boundary) and were significantly correlated with computational drift rates from a diffusion model. These results demonstrate that the brain's decision machinery operates identically over evidence regardless of whether it is sampled from the environment or constructed through learned rules, establishing the domain-generality and representational flexibility of decision signals.
papers.authors: Arianna Thoksakis, Edward F. Ester

papers.title: Distinct Cortical and Oculomotor Dynamics During Endogenous–Exogenous Competition in Working Memory
papers.abstract: While the competition between goal-driven (endogenous) and stimulus-driven (exogenous) factors is well-characterized in the domain of external attention, its manifestation in the selection of internal working memory (WM) representations remains poorly understood. Using high-temporal resolution EEG and gaze tracking, this research investigated how internal selection is resolved when task-relevant goals and salient distractors are in conflict. The data revealed that competition between endogenous and exogenous mechanisms significantly delayed the selection of task-relevant WM content by several hundred milliseconds. However, unlike external attention, this internal competition did not prompt the erroneous selection of task-irrelevant representations. These results highlight a fundamental divergence in the operational principles of internal versus external selective attention.
papers.authors: Dayana Valdez, Edward F. Ester

papers.title: Human eye movements track stimulus meaning
papers.abstract: Emerging research has demonstrated that gaze position can provide a readout of the physical properties of items stored in working memory, such as their location or orientation. This study tested whether the oculomotor system also encodes the abstract categorical identity of remembered stimuli. Across three experiments using rule-based categorization, the researchers showed that the categorical meaning of a stimulus could be reliably decoded from subtle variations in human gaze records, independent of its sensory features. This decoding was specific to trials where categorization was performed accurately and vanished when participants processed stimuli without classifying them. These findings provide novel evidence that human gaze behavior tracks abstract decision states and the behavioral relevance of mnemonic content.
papers.authors: Ali Caron, Edward F. Ester

papers.title: Traveling waves link human visual and frontal cortex during working memory–guided behavior
papers.abstract: While the sensory recruitment model suggests that working memory (WM) content is maintained in sensory neural populations, the mechanism for communicating this information to motor areas for response production remains unknown. This study utilized image-based EEG analyses to identify bidirectional cortical traveling waves during the control of memory-guided behaviors. A low-frequency (theta) feedforward wave propagating from occipital to frontal regions was found to emerge during the initiation of action, with a latency that predicted inter-individual differences in response time. Conversely, a higher-frequency (beta) feedback wave propagating from frontal to occipital regions emerged following response termination. These waves were absent when participants prepared but did not execute an action, implicating traveling waves as a key physiological substrate for routing information across the cortical hierarchy during memory-guided tasks.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS)
papers.authors: Canhuang Luo, Edward F. Ester

papers.title: Advancing working memory research through cortico-cortical transcranial magnetic stimulation
papers.abstract: The neural basis of working memory (WM) maintenance is increasingly viewed through a distributed systems lens rather than a purely modular one, yet causal evidence for the role of early sensory areas remains highly debated. This perspective article advocates for the implementation of cortico-cortical transcranial magnetic stimulation (ccPAS) as a tool to interrogate the functional interactions within WM networks. By delivering paired pulses to manipulate the connectivity between early visual cortex and higher-order regions like the intraparietal sulcus, researchers can causally test the sensory recruitment hypothesis. The article discusses current barriers to implementing these dual-coil TMS designs and outlines how they can be used to resolve competing theories of memory storage and representational flexibility.
papers.authors: Phivos Phylactou, Nikos Konstantinou, Edward F. Ester

0192.name: Edward K. Vogel
0192.bio: Edward K. Vogel is a Professor of Psychology at the University of Chicago and a member of the Grossman Institute for Neuroscience. Vogel’s research focuses on the neurophysiological mechanisms underlying visual attention and working memory, specifically identifying the biological and cognitive factors that limit the capacity to maintain information in an active state. Using electrophysiological techniques such as EEG and event-related potentials, Vogel utilized the contralateral delay activity (CDA) as a neural index of memory load. Their work explores how individual differences in these neural signatures predict cognitive performance and how these mechanisms are affected by various neurological and psychiatric conditions.
0192.research_direction: Dr. Vogel has recently been investigating the structural architecture of visual working memory (VWM) and its continuous interactions with attentional control and long-term memory (LTM). Their recent work explores how the visual system individuates objects, testing theoretical models wherein dynamic multiple-object tracking and static VWM rely on a shared "pointer" system of spatiotemporal indices that governs scene segmentation and item-based neural load. Using large-scale behavioral assessments and whole-report paradigms, they are also examining whether trait-level individual differences in VWM capacity fundamentally constrain the encoding of high-fidelity LTM representations, such as source and recognition memory, across varied conditions of repeated exposure and learning. Furthermore, they are studying the specific behavioral and temporal signatures that emerge at the VWM-LTM interface, investigating how explicit repetition might enable the cognitive system to rapidly recruit mnemonic chunks to bypass active storage bottlenecks.

papers.title: Item-based Parsing of Dynamic Scenes in a Combined Attentional Tracking and Working Memory Task
papers.abstract: This research explores the common structural constraints governing multiple-object tracking (MOT) and visual working memory (WM) by integrating these paradigms into a unified behavioral protocol. The study tests whether the performance bottlenecks in tracking dynamic targets and maintaining static representations originate from a shared item-based parsing mechanism. Utilizing a whole-report WM measure after an MOT interval, the authors found that visual scenes are segmented into discrete, individuated units that are prioritized for both tracking and storage. These findings suggest that individual differences in these cognitive domains are linked through a foundational parsing operation that segments the visual field into tokens for ongoing processing.
papers.authors: Piotr P. Styrkowiec, William X. Q. Ngiam, Will Epstein, Ron Gneezy, Henry M. Jones, Edward Awh, Edward K. Vogel

papers.title: Individual Differences in Working Memory and Attentional Control Continue to Predict Memory Performance Despite Extensive Learning
papers.abstract: This investigation examines the longitudinal stability of trait-level working memory (WM) and attentional control (AC) as predictors of long-term memory (LTM) accuracy across repeated exposures. Using source memory paradigms with object sequences and word pairs, the authors evaluated whether the initial predictive power of WM/AC traits diminishes as participants achieve task proficiency. Across five experiments, results consistently showed that individual variances in WM/AC robustly predict LTM accuracy even after significant learning and repetition. These findings support a 'stable demands' model, suggesting that repetitive practice and the development of retrieval expertise do not eliminate the fundamental requirement for active WM and AC resources in high-fidelity memory tasks.
papers.authors: Chong Zhao, Edward K. Vogel

papers.title: Working memory needs pointers
papers.abstract: The authors propose a refined theoretical framework for working memory (WM), arguing that prevailing neuroscientific definitions focused on stimulus-specific feature maintenance are insufficient. They introduce a 'pointer' system essential for contextual binding, where spatiotemporal indices (pointers) facilitate object individuation by linking representations to their external environment. The model posits that these content-independent pointers generate the item-based neural load signals typically observed in contralateral delay activity (CDA). This pointer-based architecture provides a mechanism for understanding WM's role as a critical gateway for the encoding and consolidation of information into episodic long-term memory.
papers.authors: Edward Awh, Edward K. Vogel

papers.title: Working memory and attentional control abilities predict individual differences in visual long-term memory tasks
papers.abstract: This study addresses the debated relationship between working memory (WM) and different forms of visual long-term memory (LTM), specifically evaluating whether individual differences in WM and attentional control (AC) predict recognition memory as effectively as source memory. Through large-scale behavioral experiments (N = 841), the researchers demonstrated that WM/AC traits are robust and consistent predictors of recognition memory performance. The results indicate that recognition and source memory are highly correlated across individuals, except under conditions of rapid stimulus presentation that exceed WM encoding resolution, suggesting that both memory types rely on a unified set of attentional and storage mechanisms for establishing durable LTM representations.
papers.authors: Chong Zhao, Edward K. Vogel

papers.title: Behavioral Signatures of the Rapid Recruitment of Long-Term Memory to Overcome Working Memory Capacity Limits
papers.abstract: This research characterizes the interaction between visual working memory (VWM) and long-term memory (LTM) when processing redundant visual arrays. While incidental repetitions often fail to improve VWM performance, the authors used a whole-report paradigm to test if explicit, intentional repetitions allow for the rapid recruitment of LTM resources. They found that even a single explicit repetition yielded robust performance gains beyond typical VWM capacity limits. A distinct response-time signature—characterized by inter-item slowing during the initial phase of retrieval—suggests the formation and recruitment of mnemonic chunks in LTM to bypass the inherent storage bottlenecks of active VWM.
papers.authors: Kirsten C. S. Adam, Chong Zhao, Edward K. Vogel

0193.name: Eero P. Simoncelli
0193.bio: Eero P. Simoncelli is a Silver Professor at New York University and the director of the Center for Computational Neuroscience at the Flatiron Institute. Simoncelli develops computational models at the intersection of mathematics, engineering, and neuroscience to characterize the representation of visual information in biological and artificial systems. Their work includes research on natural image statistics, multiscale image transforms such as the steerable pyramid, and the SSIM index for image quality assessment. Currently, Simoncelli investigates the geometric structure of neural representations and population coding principles to analyze how the brain processes complex visual scenes.
0193.research_direction: Dr. Simoncelli has recently been investigating the statistical and geometric structures of natural images to advance both generative modeling and our understanding of biological visual representations. Their recent work explores novel density estimation frameworks, utilizing dual score matching and blind denoising diffusion models to precisely characterize natural image manifolds and derive unsupervised perceptual distance metrics. Furthermore, they are probing the alignment between computational models and biological vision by analyzing local representational geometries through Fisher Information to identify "principal distortions" that distinguish different neural networks. They are also developing biologically-inspired self-supervised learning objectives, specifically investigating how "straightening" the temporal trajectories of natural video sequences can yield highly robust and predictable neural embeddings.

papers.title: Blind denoising diffusion models and the blessings of dimensionality
papers.abstract: This work provides a rigorous theoretical and empirical analysis of generative diffusion models using blind denoisers that lack explicit noise amplitude conditioning. The authors prove that these blind denoising diffusion models (BDDMs) automatically track an implicit noise schedule during the reverse process, provided the data distribution possesses low intrinsic dimensionality. They demonstrate that BDDMs can accurately sample from the target distribution in polynomial time relative to the intrinsic dimension. Empirically, BDDMs are shown to produce higher-quality samples than non-blind models by correcting the mismatch between true image noise residuals and pre-defined noise schedules.
papers.authors: Zahra Kadkhodaie, Aram-Alexandre Pooladian, Sinho Chewi, Eero P. Simoncelli

papers.title: Learning a distance measure from the information-estimation geometry of data
papers.abstract: The authors introduce the Information-Estimation Metric (IEM), an unsupervised distance measure derived from the geometric structure of signal probability densities. Grounded in the I-MMSE relationship and Tweedie’s formula, the IEM relates log-probability to the errors of an optimal denoiser across varying noise scales. Geometrically, the metric compares score vector fields of blurred signal densities. The paper proves that the IEM is a valid global distance metric and derives a local Riemannian second-order approximation. When learned on ImageNet, the IEM achieves performance competitive with supervised perceptual metrics in predicting human quality judgments.
papers.authors: Guy Ohayon, Pierre-Etienne H. Fiquet, Florentin Guth, Jona Ballé, Eero P. Simoncelli

papers.title: Learning normalized image densities via dual score matching
papers.abstract: This paper presents a framework for learning normalized energy-based models (EBMs) by modifying score-network architectures to compute scalar energies while retaining inductive biases. While standard score-matching optimizes the gradient of the log-density with respect to the input, it does not constrain the absolute density level. The authors introduce a secondary objective based on the gradient with respect to the noise level, ensuring the learned energy is consistent and normalized. This dual-matching approach enables exact density estimation and reveals that natural image manifolds possess significant geometric regularities beyond simple dimensionality reduction.
papers.venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS)
papers.authors: Florentin Guth, Zahra Kadkhodaie, Eero P. Simoncelli

papers.title: Discriminating image representations with principal distortions
papers.abstract: This research introduces a framework for comparing neural and artificial image representations by analyzing their local geometries through the Fisher Information Matrix (FIM). The FIM serves as a substrate for characterizing representational sensitivity to local stimulus perturbations. The authors define 'principal distortions'—orthogonal stimulus changes that maximize model response variance—to differentiate representations that exhibit similar global structures. This methodology allows for the identification of specific visual features where models diverge, providing a high-resolution metric for evaluating how well computational models align with biological visual representations.
papers.authors: Jenelle Feather, David Lipshutz, Sarah E. Harvey, Alex H. Williams, Eero P. Simoncelli

papers.title: Learning predictable and robust neural representations by straightening image sequences
papers.abstract: Inspired by the observation that the primate visual system 'straightens' temporal trajectories of natural videos, the authors propose a self-supervised learning objective that incentivizes representational straightness. The objective promotes neural embeddings that follow linear paths over time, allowing for prediction via linear extrapolation. The authors demonstrate that these straightened representations effectively factorize geometric, photometric, and semantic attributes. Furthermore, representations learned through this straightening principle exhibit significantly greater robustness to noise and adversarial perturbations compared to standard self-supervised methods optimized for augmentation invariance.
papers.venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS)
papers.authors: Xueyan Niu, Cristina Savin, Eero P. Simoncelli

0196.name: Elisha Merriam
0196.bio: Elisha P. Merriam heads the Computational Neuroimaging and Perception Team within the Laboratory of Brain and Cognition at the National Institute of Mental Health. Their research program focuses on characterizing how the human brain represents and maintains visual information through high-resolution functional MRI and image-computable encoding models. By applying linear systems analysis and population-level modeling, Merriam investigates the stability of sensory representations in the primary visual cortex and the mechanisms underlying spatial vision. This work includes examining representational drift over long timescales and developing computational frameworks to improve the interpretability of neuroimaging measurements.
0196.research_direction: Dr. Merriam has recently been investigating the neural computations and coordinate systems that allow the brain to construct stable visual representations of the world. Their recent work explores spatial perception and motion processing, using EEG head-tilt paradigms to untangle retinocentric from allocentric reference frames, and fMRI to isolate the neural substrates of illusory versus physical trajectories in the double-drift illusion. Additionally, they are examining the nature of top-down modulations in the human early visual cortex, seeking to determine whether these signals are driven by object-specific feedback or generalized task difficulty and arousal. Across multiple methodological approaches, they also investigate the fundamental mechanisms of orientation selectivity, utilizing lesion patient studies to assess the pulvinar's role in V1-independent visual plasticity, and employing image-computable models to probe how population-level orientation maps might emerge in the mouse superior colliculus.

papers.title: Orientation Maps in Mouse Superior Colliculus Explained by Population Model of Non-Orientation Selective Neurons
papers.abstract: In this study, the authors employ image-computable population modeling to address recent empirical findings of radial orientation preference maps in the mouse superficial superior colliculus (sSC), which appear to contradict the computational invariance observed in primates. By constructing a model based on circular-symmetric, center-surround receptive fields (RFs) typical of lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) neurons, they demonstrate that measured orientation selectivity is an emergent population property. The results show that these maps are critically dependent on the interaction between neural spatial frequency tuning and the vignetting effects introduced by stimulus apertures. This computational framework suggests that the apparent orientation tuning in mouse SC does not necessitate de novo orientation-selective circuitry but is consistent with stimulus-invariant RF mechanisms previously established in primate research.
papers.authors: Austin Kuo, Justin L. Gardner, Elisha P. Merriam

papers.title: Visual representations in the human brain rely on a reference frame that is in between allocentric and retinocentric coordinates
papers.abstract: This investigation utilized electroencephalography (EEG) and a 45° head-tilt paradigm to delineate the coordinate systems used by the human brain to represent visual orientation during sensory processing and working memory. By dissociating retinocentric (eye-centered) and allocentric (world-centered) frames, the authors employed multivariate decoding to track the stability of orientation tuning across postural changes. The data revealed that neural representations of orientation were neither purely retinocentric nor purely allocentric throughout the trial duration. Instead, the findings supported a hybrid reference frame where orientation tuning partially shifted with head orientation. These results provide the first human neurophysiological evidence that the brain maintains intermediate spatial coordinates to bridge the gap between initial retinal encoding and stable environmental perception.
papers.authors: Maria V. Servetnik, Noah J. Steinberg, Zvi N. Roth, Elisha P. Merriam

papers.title: Responses in human early visual cortex are more sensitive to task difficulty than object category
papers.abstract: The research re-examines high-level modulation in the early visual cortex (EVC) to determine whether such activity reflects object-specific feedback or generalized task-related responses (TRRs). Using 7T BOLD fMRI and an object discrimination task, the authors demonstrated that EVC signals were highly sensitive to task difficulty and arousal-linked fluctuations but lacked categorical information. While multivariate pattern analysis successfully decoded object category from the lateral occipital complex (LOC), EVC activity remained entrained to task timing and covaried with physiological markers of engagement like pupil size. These findings challenge the prevalent view that V1 activity predominantly encodes category-specific information from downstream areas, suggesting instead that many apparent high-level modulations are driven by the internal state of the observer during task performance.
papers.authors: June Hee Kim, Cassie Joynes, Grace Edwards, Chris I. Baker, Elisha P. Merriam

papers.title: Patients with V1 damage exhibit increased orientation decoding in hMT+, but only if pulvinar is intact
papers.abstract: This study investigates the neural pathways supporting visual plasticity in patients with chronic cortically induced blindness. Leveraging fMRI-based orientation decoding, the authors assessed selectivity in extrastriate area hMT+ across patients with various primary visual cortex (V1) or thalamic lesions. The results showed that in a patient with extensive V1 damage, the ipsilesional hMT+ could decode orientation information for stimuli presented within the blind field, a property not observed in healthy controls. However, this orientation selectivity was absent in a patient with combined V1 and pulvinar damage, despite hMT+ remaining visually responsive. The findings suggest that orientation tuning in hMT+ can emerge through V1-independent circuits involving the pulvinar, highlighting the critical role of subcortical-extrastriate pathways in supporting residual vision following cortical insult.
papers.authors: Bing Li, Tina T. Liu, Matthew R. Cavanaugh, Helena P. Bachmann, Berkeley K. Fahrenthold, Shruti Japee, Krystel R. Huxlin, Elisha P. Merriam

papers.title: Brain representations of motion and position in the double-drift illusion
papers.abstract: The investigation probes the neural mechanisms underlying the double-drift illusion, where internal Gabor motion biases the perceived trajectory of an object. Using fMRI and computational decoding, the authors decoupled the physical retinal path from the perceived spatiotopic path via smooth pursuit eye movements. While signals in early visual cortex (V1–V3) primarily reflected retinotopic coordinates, activity in extrastriate area hMT+ exclusively represented the illusory motion path. This decoding of the illusory trajectory remained robust even when spatial attention was diverted by a secondary task at fixation. These results provide significant evidence that hMT+ integrates retinal and extraretinal signals to encode the perceived spatial location of moving stimuli, serving as a neural substrate for spatiotopic stability in human vision.
papers.authors: Noah J. Steinberg, Zvi N. Roth, J. Anthony Movshon, Elisha Merriam

0197.name: Elissa L. Newport
0197.bio: Elissa L. Newport is the Director of the Center for Brain Plasticity and Recovery and a Professor of Neurology at Georgetown University. Newport’s research involves the 'less is more' hypothesis, which posits that children's cognitive limitations facilitate the acquisition of complex linguistic structures. They conduct research on statistical learning in language and visual domains to examine how infants and adults extract patterns from environmental input. Newport’s current work focuses on the Pediatric Stroke Research Project, using neuroimaging to investigate how the developing brain reorganizes language functions following early-life neurological injury.
0197.research_direction: Dr. Newport's recent work explores the functional and structural development of the human language system, with a particular focus on profound neuroplasticity following early brain injury. Using neuroimaging methods like fMRI and diffusion tensor imaging, they are investigating how language-related white matter tracts mature in typically developing infants and how specialized regions—including the visual word form area—reorganize to the right hemisphere after left-hemisphere perinatal strokes. Their neuroplasticity research specifically probes whether the brain maintains fundamental architectural constraints, such as spatially segregating basic sentence comprehension from emotional prosody, even when forced into large-scale cortical remapping. Alongside this neurobiological focus, they have recently been using behavioral artificial language paradigms to examine typical language acquisition, asking how children leverage statistical and distributional cues in their input to deduce productive grammatical rules.

papers.title: 6-To-8 Year-Old Children Adjust Their Linguistic Generalizations Based on Distributional Cues
papers.abstract: This study examines how children (ages 6–8) utilize distributional evidence from linguistic input to calibrate the scope of their grammatical generalizations. While children are known to regularize inconsistent patterns, the specific cues that signal whether a pattern is a productive rule versus a lexically restricted exception remain debated. Using an artificial language learning paradigm, we manipulated the type frequency and Zipfian distribution of novel words following a specific pluralization rule. Results indicate that children are sensitive to the frequency and variability of the input, adjusting their propensity for categorical generalization based on whether the distributional cues satisfied computational thresholds for rule induction. These findings support a model of language acquisition where statistical learning mechanisms interact with formal constraints on productivity to govern the development of the mental grammar.
papers.authors: Kathryn D. Schuler, Patricia A. Reeder, Heidi Getz, Kathryn Kissinger, Richard N. Aslin, Elissa L. Newport

papers.title: Right-Lateralization of the Visual Word Form Area after Left-Hemisphere Perinatal Stroke
papers.abstract: In literate adults, visual word form processing is characteristically lateralized to the left posterior fusiform gyrus, known as the visual word form area (VWFA). This study investigates whether the lateralization of the VWFA is intrinsically biased to the left hemisphere (LH) or if it follows the lateralization of the broader language network. We used fMRI to examine adolescents and young adults who sustained large perinatal strokes to the left perisylvian cortex, resulting in a complete reorganization of language to the right hemisphere (RH). Compared to neurologically healthy controls, stroke participants showed a mirror-symmetric, right-lateralized response to pseudowords in the right fusiform gyrus. This reorganization occurred despite the presence of intact tissue in the LH normally occupied by the VWFA, which responded typically to non-linguistic stimuli. These findings provide definitive evidence that VWFA lateralization is driven by co-localization with the frontotemporal language system and highlight the dramatic equipotentiality of the hemispheres for specialized cognitive functions early in development.
papers.authors: Anna Seydell-Greenwald, Natalya Vladyko, Catherine E. Chambers, William D. Gaillard, Barbara Landau, Elissa L. Newport

papers.title: Assessing the Early Lateralization of White Matter in the Infant Language Network
papers.abstract: Neural language development involves the structural maturation of frontal and temporal centers and their interconnecting white matter tracts. While leftward asymmetry of the arcuate fasciculus (AF) and uncinate fasciculus (UF) is established in adults, the developmental timing of this lateralization is unknown. We analyzed longitudinal diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) data from 114 typically developing infants (0–24 months) to characterize microstructural (FA, MD) and macrostructural trajectories of the AF, UF, and corticospinal tract (CST). Linear mixed-effects modeling revealed rapid age-related maturation in all pathways. However, unlike the adult pattern of broad left-lateralization, no significant hemispheric asymmetries in maturation rates or microstructural indices were observed in infants, with the exception of higher streamline counts in the right UF. These results suggest that the structural lateralization of the language network is not present at birth but emerges during childhood, potentially as a consequence of cortical specialization and accumulated language experience.
papers.authors: Madeline Marcelle, Venkata Sita Priyanka Illapani, William D. Gaillard, Elissa L. Newport

papers.title: Functional partitioning of sentence processing and emotional prosody in the right perisylvian cortex after perinatal stroke
papers.abstract: The typical adult brain segregates sentence processing (LH) and emotional prosody (RH) into different hemispheres. After perinatal stroke to the LH, the RH must support both functions. We used fMRI to evaluate the spatial organization and overlap of sentence comprehension and emotional prosody in the RH of individuals with LH perinatal stroke compared to healthy siblings. Participants performed blocks of forward speech versus reverse speech (sentence processing) and emotional versus neutral prosody. In stroke participants, both functions were successfully lateralized to the RH. Critically, we found significantly less activation overlap in the RH for these two functions than would be predicted by a simple mirror-reflection of the typical LH/RH maps. This suggests that the segregation of sentence-level and suprasegmental processing is a fundamental constraint on the functional architecture of the language system, maintained even during large-scale neural reorganization.
papers.authors: Kelly C. Martin, Anna Seydell-Greenwald, Peter E. Turkeltaub, Catherine E. Chambers, William D. Gaillard, Elissa L. Newport

0198.name: Elkan G. Akyürek
0198.bio: Elkan G. Akyürek is a Professor of Cognitive Neuroscience and Chair of the Department of Experimental Psychology at the University of Groningen. Akyürek's research focuses on the mechanisms of temporal integration, visual attention, and human working memory, specifically exploring how the brain parses and integrates rapid sensory input into coherent perceptual events. Utilizing a combination of electroencephalography (EEG), psychophysics, and neurocomputational modeling, they investigate the neural dynamics of memory maintenance, including the characterization of activity-silent states. Their recent work examines the adaptive nature of temporal processing and the role of oscillatory activity in attentional prioritization.
0198.research_direction: Dr. Akyürek's recent work explores the neural and cognitive mechanisms underlying visual working memory, temporal integration, and executive control. Utilizing EEG multivariate pattern analysis alongside visual impulse-perturbation paradigms, they have recently been investigating how specific features like color and spatial frequency are maintained in and reactivated from "activity-silent" working memory states. Their research also examines the temporal dynamics of visual processing, using continuous neural decoding to track how predictive information influences processing speed during visual temporal integration tasks. Additionally, they are probing the flexibility of cognition through behavioral modeling, exploring whether working memory forgetting rates adaptively tune to environmental probabilities, as well as testing the acute impacts of dietary interventions like cocoa flavanols on conflict monitoring and response inhibition.

papers.title: Acute effects of cocoa flavanols on cognitive control and response inhibition
papers.abstract: This study employed a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover design to evaluate the acute impact of high-flavanol cocoa (415 mg and 623 mg) on executive control mechanisms. Healthy young adult participants performed a battery of cognitive tasks, including the Flanker, Simon, and Go/No-go paradigms, to measure conflict monitoring, interference resolution, and motor response inhibition. Utilizing (Generalized) Linear Mixed Model analysis to account for fixed effects and random slopes, the researchers found that acute consumption of cocoa flavanols did not significantly enhance reaction times, accuracy, or commission/omission error rates across any of the tasks. Furthermore, exploratory analyses indicated that covariates such as gender and body mass index did not modulate these outcomes, suggesting that acute flavanol intake does not provide a robust benefit to cognitive control or response inhibition in this population.
papers.authors: Ahmet Altinok, Monica Moruzzi, Elkan G. Akyürek

papers.title: Behaviorally Irrelevant Feature Matching Increases Neural and Behavioral Working Memory Readout
papers.abstract: The investigation explored the neural substrates of working memory (WM) readout by manipulating the physical overlap between behaviorally irrelevant features of memoranda and subsequent external perturbations. Utilizing an impulse-perturbation paradigm with EEG and Mahalanobis-distance-based multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA), the study tested whether the neural impulse response is patterned by the task-specific WM network. Results demonstrated that matching task-irrelevant spatial frequencies between the memory item and the visual impulse significantly enhanced the decodability of orientation-specific neural representations. Behaviorally, matching the probe stimulus to the memorandum's spatial frequency resulted in accelerated reaction times during recall. These findings indicate that impulse-evoked signals directly interact with maintained WM traces through shared feature-specific neural codes, facilitating more efficient readout even across non-target feature dimensions.
papers.authors: Aytaç Karabay, Michael J. Wolff, Veera Ruuskanen, Elkan G. Akyürek

papers.title: Variable Processing Shifts during Perceptual Acceleration: Evidence from Temporal Integration
papers.abstract: This research utilized multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) of EEG data to track the temporal dynamics of perceptual acceleration during visual temporal integration. Using a 'missing element' task requiring the integration of two successive stimulus displays, the authors quantified the latency of stimulus-driven neural representations to determine how predictive information facilitates processing. The study revealed that perceptual acceleration is a nonlinear phenomenon: facilitatory shifts in processing speed were maximal at intermediate stages (approximately 200 ms post-stimulus) but diminished at later cognitive stages (approximately 400 ms). These results suggest that the time gained from temporal prediction during integration is not uniformly preserved across the perceptual-cognitive hierarchy, reflecting a dynamic and variable processing shift within the brain's representational chain.
papers.authors: Michael J. Wolff, Elkan G. Akyürek

papers.title: Adaptive forgetting speed in working memory
papers.abstract: Challenging the view of working memory (WM) decay as a fixed constraint, this study investigated whether the rate of forgetting is adaptively tuned to the temporal structure of the environment. In a series of delayed-estimation experiments, the researchers manipulated the probing hazard—the probability that a memory item would be required at a specific time point. Modeling recall precision and the probability of target response through a standard mixture model, the results showed that participants implicitly accelerated their forgetting rate when the likelihood of needing the information decreased more rapidly over time. The fast and flexible nature of these adaptations, occurring even when participants could not explicitly report the task contingencies, suggests that WM utilizes implicit statistical learning to optimize resource allocation by strategically discarding information that is statistically likely to have become irrelevant.
papers.authors: Joost de Jong, Sophia A. Wilhelm, Elkan G. Akyürek

papers.title: Maintenance of color memoranda in activity-quiescent working memory states: Evidence from impulse perturbation
papers.abstract: This study applied an impulse-perturbation method to investigate whether intrinsically non-spatial memoranda, such as color, are maintained in 'activity-silent' neural states. EEG data from a retro-cue delayed match-to-sample task were analyzed using multivariate decoding to compare cued (task-relevant) and uncued (task-irrelevant) items. While oscillatory activity in the alpha band primarily tracked cued memoranda—reflecting attentional prioritization—the visual impulse stimulus successfully reactivated both cued and uncued color representations. This finding contrasts with earlier reports on spatial orientations, where uncued items were often not decodable via impulse, suggesting that color information exhibits distinct representational resilience in quiescent synaptic states. The outcomes provide evidence for the generality of activity-silent storage mechanisms across diverse visual feature domains beyond those with spatial or orientation properties.
papers.authors: Güven Kandemir, Sophia A. Wilhelm, Nikolai Axmacher, Elkan G. Akyürek

0199.name: Ella Striem-Amit
0199.bio: Ella Striem-Amit is an Assistant Professor of Neuroscience at Georgetown University Medical Center and directs the Sensory and Motor Plasticity (SAMP) Lab. Striem-Amit’s research investigates the relationship between innate brain organization and experience-dependent plasticity in individuals with early-onset sensory or motor deprivation, such as those born blind, deaf, or without hands. Using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and behavioral psychophysics, they study how the brain maintains task-specific and topographical organization without typical sensory input or motor effectors. Their research characterizes compensatory cross-modal plasticity to inform the development of sensory aids and motor prostheses through the study of neural adaptability.
0199.research_direction: Dr. Striem-Amit's recent work explores the boundaries of cortical plasticity and functional brain organization in individuals with congenital sensory or motor deprivation. Using fMRI and multivariate decoding, they have recently been investigating how people born without hands repurpose sensorimotor cortices for compensatory foot use, and whether higher-level motor regions encode abstract action goals regardless of the specific effector used. In parallel, their research examines the neural consequences of congenital blindness and deafness by probing how deprived visual and auditory cortices establish altered functional connectivity networks. Rather than focusing solely on group-level patterns, they are tracking longitudinal stability and inter-individual variability to determine whether cross-modal plasticity produces flexible, task-dependent adaptations or stable, idiosyncratic neural "fingerprints" unique to each person's developmental trajectory.

papers.title: From Hands to Feet: Experience-Driven Plasticity in Secondary Somatosensory Cortex in People Born without Hands
papers.abstract: This study characterizes the neuroplastic reorganization of the secondary somatosensory cortex (SII) in individuals with congenital upper-limb dysplasia (IDs) who utilize their feet for manual-compensatory tasks. Using task-based fMRI and resting-state functional connectivity (RSFC) analyses, the researchers demonstrate that foot-related motor execution and sensory stimulation drive selective activation within the former hand-selective territory of the left SII in IDs, significantly exceeding the activations observed in typically developed (TD) controls. This foot selectivity in SII cannot be attributed to intrinsic organizational biases (e.g., latent somatotopy), as the hand-selective area in TD controls shows a secondary preference for the shoulder rather than the foot. Furthermore, RSFC data reveals altered coupling between SII and primary sensorimotor regions specifically in IDs. These findings suggest a hierarchical organization of cortical plasticity where reorganization in the primary somatosensory cortex (SI) remains constrained by somatotopic principles, while SII reflects functionally dependent, experience-driven adaptation to lifelong motor demands.
papers.authors: Zhiqing Deng, Florencia Martinez-Addiego, Yuqi Liu, Ella Striem-Amit

papers.title: Action-type mapping principles extend beyond evolutionarily conserved actions, even in people born without hands
papers.abstract: The research investigates whether motor association areas generalize action representations across different effectors for evolutionarily recent tool-use actions, contrasting with evolutionarily conserved actions like reaching and grasping. Using fMRI in typically developed (TD) individuals and those born without hands (IDs), the study employed univariate analyses, multivariate decoding (MVPA), and temporal signal dynamics to identify effector-independent neural architectures. While primary sensorimotor regions (M1/S1) exhibited high fidelity for concrete, body-part-specific encoding (e.g., hand vs. foot), higher-level regions in the dorsal tool-use network—specifically the left dorsal premotor cortex (PMd) and superior parietal lobule (SPL)—encoded abstract action goals regardless of whether the action was performed with the hand or the foot. Crucially, this action-type organization emerged in IDs despite the total absence of manual experience, suggesting that the hierarchical division between body-centric and action-centric representation is a fundamental organizational principle not dictated by evolutionary recency or typical sensorimotor input.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS)
papers.authors: Florencia Martinez-Addiego, Yuqi Liu, Kyungji Moon, Elizabeth Shytle, Lénia Amaral, Caroline O’Brien, Sriparna Sen, Maximilian Riesenhuber, Jody C. Culham, Ella Striem-Amit

papers.title: Unraveling the impact of congenital deafness on individual brain organization
papers.abstract: This study examines how congenital auditory deprivation and the timing of language acquisition influence inter-individual variability in brain network organization. Analyzing functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data from congenitally deaf individuals (including native signers and delayed signers) and hearing controls, the authors quantified inter-subject variability in functional connectivity (FC) originating from the deprived auditory cortex (AC). The findings reveal a significant increase in FC variability among deaf individuals, particularly within regions that undergo cross-modal reorganization and language-processing networks. This heightened variability was not significantly attenuated by early language exposure, as it persisted in native signers. The results demonstrate that sensory experience exerts a critical stabilizing influence on typical brain development, and its absence triggers a diversification of neural connectivity patterns, suggesting that cortical plasticity manifests through highly idiosyncratic, rather than uniform, organizational outcomes across individuals.
papers.authors: Lénia Amaral, Xiaosha Wang, Yanchao Bi, Ella Striem-Amit

papers.title: Can individual differences explain brain plasticity in blindness?
papers.abstract: In this theoretical review, the author addresses the long-standing debate regarding the functional role of the early visual cortex (EVC) in individuals with congenital blindness, which has been shown to participate in an heterogeneous array of tasks including language, memory, and executive control. Striem-Amit proposes that the apparent lack of a singular, group-level explanation for EVC recruitment can be resolved by considering substantial inter-individual variability in neural plasticity. The article argues that individual developmental trajectories and environmental experiences drive the formation of stable, idiosyncratic connectivity 'fingerprints.' By adopting a precision-neuroscience framework that shifts focus from group-averaged patterns to individual-specific functional architectures, the field may reconcile disparate findings and improve the efficacy of personalized rehabilitative and sensory restoration technologies.
papers.authors: Ella Striem-Amit

papers.title: Longitudinal stability of individual brain plasticity patterns in blindness
papers.abstract: This longitudinal fMRI study assesses the temporal stability of reorganized functional connectivity (FC) patterns in the primary visual cortex (V1) of congenitally blind individuals over a two-year period. By comparing repeatedly sampled FC profiles across various cognitive states (resting-state vs. task-driven), the researchers tested whether the role of blind V1 is transiently task-flexible or longitudinally consistent. Results show that V1-FC patterns are highly unique to each individual and remain remarkably stable over time, irrespective of the specific task being performed. Multivariate pattern analysis successfully decoded individual identity from these connectivity profiles with high accuracy. These findings indicate that while visual deprivation leads to diverse plasticity outcomes across the blind population, the resulting functional connectivity of V1 forms a stable individual fingerprint, challenging the hypothesis that blind V1 operates as a highly flexible, task-dependent station within the multiple-demand system.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS)
papers.authors: Lénia Amaral, Peyton Thomas, Amir Amedi, Ella Striem-Amit

0200.name: Emanuela Bricolo
0200.bio: Emanuela Bricolo is a Full Professor at the University of Milano-Bicocca who researches the cognitive mechanisms of visual attention, perception, and oculomotor control. Bricolo utilizes psychophysical techniques and eye-tracking to investigate phenomena such as visual crowding, reading patterns, and the spatial representation of numbers along a mental number line. Their work has explored the neurological basis of spatial neglect and the efficacy of neuromodulation techniques, including TMS and tRNS, in cognitive performance. Additionally, Bricolo examines the psychology of virtual environments, focusing on user learning in the metaverse and the realism of computer-generated faces.
0200.research_direction: Dr. Bricolo has recently been investigating the mechanisms of selective visuospatial attention, with a particular focus on how implicit statistical learning reshapes the center-surround inhibitory profile of the attentional focus during visual search. Their recent work translates these fundamental cognitive processes to dynamic, real-world tasks utilizing immersive virtual reality driving simulators. In this applied domain, they examine how target-distractor similarity and contextual expectations influence proactive distractor suppression, braking latency, and lane-keeping precision. Additionally, they are exploring the ecological validity of computer-generated faces as experimental stimuli, testing how rendering realism and observer familiarity modulate social evaluation and the "uncanny valley" effect.

papers.title: Prepared for the expected but unready for the unexpected: Unmet distractor expectations slow braking responsiveness but improve lane-keeping precision in a virtual driving simulation
papers.abstract: The orchestration of cognitive control during driving is essential for managing sensory complexity and navigating the external environment. This study utilized an immersive driving simulator to examine how distractor expectations modulate behavioral outcomes. Using an adaptation of the Distractor Context Manipulation (DCM) paradigm, participants performed a detection task while navigating a virtual environment. Results demonstrated a distinct trade-off between reaction efficiency and control precision: specifically, unmet distractor expectations (the presentation of distractors in low-frequency contexts) resulted in significant braking latencies but improved lane-keeping stability. These findings suggest that proactive distractor suppression mechanisms, once engaged, entail specific behavioral costs and benefits depending on the predictability of the distractor context.
papers.authors: Andrea Massironi, Marco A. Petilli, Carlotta Lega, Simone Fontana, Emanuela Bricolo

papers.title: Statistical learning re-shapes the center-surround inhibition of the visuo-spatial attentional focus
papers.abstract: To optimize signal-to-noise ratios during goal-directed visual search, the neurocognitive system projects a 'center-surround inhibition' profile, characterized by a suppressed inhibitory ring around the focus of attention. This research investigated whether implicit statistical learning of spatial contingencies can reconfigure this fundamental inhibitory architecture. By manipulating color singleton spatial frequencies, the study showed that statistical learning significantly reshapes the attentional focus, transitioning the standard center-surround profile into a non-linear gradient. Notably, this reconfiguration was spatially asymmetric and temporally dynamic, emerging exclusively within manipulated visual quadrants. These results indicate that the topography of spatial attention is not fixed but undergoes adaptive plastic changes based on learned environmental regularities.
papers.authors: Andrea Massironi, Carlotta Lega, Luca Ronconi, Emanuela Bricolo

papers.title: Statistical learning adaptively adjusts the visuospatial attentional focus under highly uncertain search contexts
papers.abstract: Visual attention mechanisms must flexibly adapt to environmental uncertainty to ensure efficient target selection. This study explored how statistical learning (SL) modulates the spatial profile of the attentional focus—specifically its central enhancement and surrounding inhibitory zone—under conditions of high contextual uncertainty. Utilizing psychophysical probes within a visual search paradigm, the researchers examined the effects of varying spatial contingencies on the excitability of the attentional focus. The findings revealed that statistical learning adaptively recalibrates the focus of attention, even when search contexts are highly unpredictable, suggesting that implicit learning mechanisms provide a robust framework for spatial prioritization and distractor suppression in complex visual scenes.
papers.authors: Andrea Massironi, Giulia Spinelli, Carlotta Lega, Emanuela Bricolo

papers.title: Using computer-generated faces in experimental psychology: The role of realism and exposure
papers.abstract: The increasing use of computer-generated (CG) faces in psychological research necessitates a rigorous evaluation of their ecological validity and the potential influence of the 'uncanny valley' effect. This study investigated how the perceived realism of CG stimuli and prior observer exposure modulate social and cognitive responses. Participants performed recognition and affinity tasks involving faces across a spectrum of human-likeness. The results indicated that while higher realism generally improves affinity, specific imperfections can trigger the uncanny valley effect, leading to negative evaluative biases. Crucially, the data demonstrated that repeated exposure to virtual avatars significantly attenuates these eerie feelings, suggesting that the suitability of CG faces as stand-ins for human faces is contingent upon both the fidelity of the rendering and the observer's familiarity with artificial agents.
papers.authors: Anna Flavia Di Natale, Stefania La Rocca, Matilde Ellen Simonetti, Emanuela Bricolo

papers.title: A protocol to evaluate the impact of visual distractors on driving attention using a virtual reality simulator
papers.abstract: The authors propose a standardized experimental protocol for evaluating the interference caused by visual distractors during driving using Virtual Reality (VR). The protocol manipulates distractor-target similarity to assess selective attention and cognitive load. Validated through behavioral metrics such as lane deviation and reaction time, the framework provides a safer and more reproducible alternative to real-world driving studies for investigating attentional lapses and testing attention-enhancing strategies in a controlled environment.
papers.authors: Simone Fontana, Andrea Massironi, Marco Petilli, Carlotta Lega, Emanuela Bricolo

0201.name: Emily A Cooper
0201.bio: Emily A. Cooper is an Associate Professor at the University of California, Berkeley, where they direct the Perceptual Reality Lab and hold a membership in the Helen Wills Neuroscience Institute. Cooper’s research investigates the computational mechanisms of human visual perception, with an emphasis on how the brain processes three-dimensional information and depth cues in natural environments. By combining psychophysical experiments with computational modeling and natural scene statistics, Cooper examines the principles of visual encoding to inform the design of augmented reality, virtual reality, and assistive vision technologies. Their work focuses on the intersection of biological vision and digital display engineering for applications in clinical vision care and immersive graphics.
0201.research_direction: Dr. Cooper has recently been investigating how the visual system encodes 3D space and motion, using computational modeling to explore how neural tuning for disparity and speed in the dorsal stream adapts to the statistical regularities of natural scenes. Their recent work also explores the psychophysics of binocular vision, examining how low-level depth cues compete with higher-level cognitive priors about familiar object shapes when observers are subjected to interocular retinal distortions. In clinical domains, they are studying the interplay of sensory noise and perceptual priors in impaired visual systems, utilizing Bayesian frameworks to characterize idiosyncratic motion misperceptions in individuals with low vision. Furthermore, Dr. Cooper investigates the applied perceptual consequences of dichoptic viewing, measuring how interocular contrast differences in augmented reality displays influence visual appearance and drive artifacts like luster and binocular rivalry.

papers.title: Statistical regularities in natural scenes that support figure-ground segregation by neural populations
papers.abstract: This study evaluates the ecological basis of neural response biases in area MT by analyzing the statistical regularities of motion and distance in natural scenes. The authors demonstrate that figural objects exhibit systematically higher retinal speeds and greater motion coherence compared to ground regions, properties that are also correlated with closer absolute distances. Using a neural population model, they show that the faster-speed and near-distance biases observed in MT neurons effectively prioritize the representation of visual figures, especially when multiple stimulus components occupy the same receptive field. These results provide a normative framework for figure-ground segregation based on the brain's adaptation to the spatiotemporal statistics of the natural environment.
papers.authors: Clara T. Friedman, Minqi Wang, Thomas Yerxa, Bryce A. Arseneau, Xin Huang, Emily A. Cooper

papers.title: Transformations of sensory information in the brain suggest changing criteria for optimality
papers.abstract: The researchers apply a Fisher Information framework to investigate how sensory optimization objectives transform across the primate dorsal visual stream. By analyzing binocular disparity tuning curves in areas V1, V2, and MT and comparing them to environmental disparity statistics, they identify a shift from maximizing mutual information in early stages to optimizing for perceptual discrimination at higher stages. Specifically, V1 and V2 representations are consistent with information preservation, while MT population responses are biased toward larger disparities to support fine-scale depth discrimination. This finding suggests that sensory hierarchies are shaped by a systematic transition in computational goals rather than a uniform efficiency criterion.
papers.authors: Tyler S. Manning, Emma Alexander, Bruce G. Cumming, Gregory C. DeAngelis, Xin Huang, Emily A. Cooper

papers.title: How small changes to one eye's retinal image can transform the perceived shape of a very familiar object
papers.abstract: This research investigates the perceptual robustness of familiar objects to interocular image distortions, finding that small differences in retinal magnification can induce significant shape misperceptions even for highly known items like mobile phones. Utilizing psychophysical tasks to measure perceived slant and shape under horizontal, vertical, and uniform magnification, the authors demonstrate that shape distortions are lawfully predicted by the induced binocular disparity cues to object pose. The results imply that the visual system's reliance on depth cues is sufficiently strong to override prior knowledge of an object's physical geometry, highlighting fundamental constraints in the integration of 3D sensory signals and cognitive expectations.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS)
papers.authors: Iona R. McLean, Emily A. Cooper

papers.title: A Paradigm for Characterizing Motion Misperception in People with Typical Vision and Low Vision
papers.abstract: The authors present a psychophysical paradigm for assessing motion perception in populations with visual impairments, such as reduced acuity and contrast sensitivity. Using a moving tilted rhombus stimulus, they observed that neurotypical observers consistently display direction biases that align with a Bayesian model of noisy sensory encoding. However, individuals with low vision exhibited a wide range of idiosyncratic response patterns, including non-Bayesian and unbiased percepts. These results highlight the complex interplay between sensory noise and perceptual priors in impaired visual systems and emphasize the need for individualized assessments in clinical vision science and rehabilitative technology design.
papers.authors: Benjamin M. Chin, Minqi Wang, Loganne T. Mikkelsen, Clara T. Friedman, Connie J. Ng, Marlena A. Chu, Emily A. Cooper

papers.title: The effect of interocular contrast differences on the appearance of augmented reality imagery
papers.abstract: This paper quantifies the perceptual consequences of interocular contrast disparities that frequently occur in augmented reality (AR) display hardware. Through a series of experiments, the researchers measured five key dimensions of visual appearance—including luster, rivalry, and depth artifacts—when eyes were presented with dichoptic stimuli. The findings establish that significant contrast imbalances trigger detrimental artifacts and that monocular AR systems often produce worse subjective experiences than binocular systems with moderate contrast differences. The study provides critical empirical thresholds for radiometric display design, aimed at minimizing discomfort and preserving image quality in near-eye XR devices.
papers.authors: Minqi Wang, Jian Ding, Dennis M. Levi, Emily A. Cooper

0202.name: Emily D Grossman
0202.bio: Emily D. Grossman is a visual neuroscientist at the University of California, Irvine, where they investigate the neural mechanisms of biological motion perception. Grossman utilizes functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), and electroencephalography (EEG) to map the cortical networks involved in integrating form and motion signals. Their research characterizes regions within the superior temporal sulcus (STS) and ventral temporal cortex that process animate movement and social cues. The Grossman laboratory currently explores how feature-based attention and perceptual learning modulate the sensitivity and invariant coding of these visual brain areas.
