0202.research_direction: Dr. Grossman has recently been investigating the neural mechanisms underlying high-level visual and social cognition, focusing on how the brain extracts social meaning, animacy, and intention from dynamic visual inputs. Their recent work explores how regions within the social-perceptual and action observation networks—such as the superior temporal sulcus (STS)—encode interactivity from sparse kinematic cues like moving shapes, and how top-down attention modulates the neural representations of complex human actions. To probe these questions, they are utilizing fMRI, representational similarity analysis, and computational modeling to map the representational continuum between intuitive physics and social intentionality, while also evaluating the methodological efficacy of different cortical atlases for capturing social cognitive states in functional neuroimaging. Additionally, their research extends into cross-modal plasticity, examining how the developmental timing of visual deprivation in early versus late blindness influences the sensory processing of non-visual emotional cues like speech prosody.

papers.title: Neural Representations of Social Interactivity: A Perceptual and Language Model Analysis
papers.abstract: This study examines how the human visual system encodes social interactivity from sparse animations through a combination of fMRI and computational modeling. Using Heider-Simmel style animations, the researchers embedded human behavioral descriptions into semantic vectors using large language models. They evaluated whether neural activity in key nodes of the social-perceptual network—specifically the posterior superior temporal sulcus (pSTS), temporoparietal junction (TPJ), and medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC)—is driven by explicit animacy features or by the underlying perceptual dynamics of interactivity. The findings demonstrate that neural representations in these regions are robustly predicted by models of implied interactivity and goal-directedness, even in the absence of explicit bodily or facial cues, suggesting that social attribution is grounded in low-level kinematic properties.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the Annual Meeting of the Cognitive Science Society
papers.authors: Sajjad Torabian, John A. Pyles, Hongjing Lu, Emily D. Grossman

papers.title: Top-down modulation of visual action perception: distinct task effects in the action observation network
papers.abstract: The Action Observation Network (AON), comprising the posterior superior temporal sulcus (pSTS), posterior parietal cortex, and premotor areas, is traditionally associated with the bottom-up processing of biological motion. This experiment utilizes fMRI and model-based representational similarity analysis (RSA) to investigate how top-down attention modulates action representations. Participants observed video vignettes of human pushing actions while attending to specific features such as the actor, effector, or target. Multivariate pattern decoding and RSA revealed that attentional state significantly warped neural representations across the AON. Specifically, task-based models provided the best fit for neural similarity structures in all ROIs, with distinct attentional demands uniquely sharpening neural tuning for task-relevant action categories in a region-specific manner.
papers.authors: Aslı Eroğlu, Burcu A. Urgen, Emily D. Grossman

papers.title: A quantitative comparison of atlas parcellations on the human superior temporal sulcus
papers.abstract: The superior temporal sulcus (STS) exhibits significant functional heterogeneity, making it a challenge for standardized ROI definition in neuroimaging. This study evaluates the effectiveness of four popular cortical atlases (including Glasser, Gordon, and Schaefer) in replacing functional localizers for social cognitive tasks. Using fMRI data from six distinct social tasks, the researchers applied SVM classification to STS activation patterns dimensionally reduced by these atlases. The results indicate that while all atlases maintained high classification accuracy, the mean activation within parcels was the most effective metric for the right STS. Surprisingly, even random null-atlases achieved high performance, leading to the conclusion that the STS represents social cognitive states through a coarse-grained topography that is captured by various granular parcellation schemes.
papers.authors: Brandon C. Hackney, John A. Pyles, Emily D. Grossman

papers.title: Neural Representations that Reveal a Unified Continuum between Physical and Social Events
papers.abstract: This research investigates the neural mechanisms that bridge intuitive physics and social perception. Utilizing a rapid event-related fMRI design, the study presented participants with animations of moving shapes that systematically varied in their violation of physical laws and their degree of intentionality. Searchlight representational similarity analysis (RSA) was used to map brain regions responding to these dynamic variations. The findings reveal that while the intraparietal sulcus (IPS) and early visual cortex predominantly encode physical features and violations, the posterior superior temporal sulcus (pSTS) and temporoparietal junction (TPJ) are tuned to intentionality and social interactivity. These results suggest that the brain maintains a unified representational continuum that facilitates the transition from perceiving purely physical events to interpreting social interactions.
papers.authors: Sajjad Torabian, John A. Pyles, Yujia Peng, Hongjing Lu, Emily D. Grossman

papers.title: "Love looks not with the eyes": supranormal processing of emotional speech in individuals with late-blindness versus preserved processing in individuals with congenital-blindness
papers.abstract: This study explores experience-dependent plasticity in the processing of emotional speech among blind individuals. Using a cross-sectional design, the researchers compared the ability of congenitally blind, late-blind, and sighted individuals to decode emotional prosody and semantic content in spoken language. Contrary to the sensory compensation hypothesis, which predicts across-the-board enhancement, the results showed that supranormal processing of emotional cues was specifically present in individuals with late-onset blindness. In contrast, congenitally blind individuals showed preserved but not enhanced performance. The findings suggest that the timing of visual deprivation determines the degree and nature of cognitive reorganization, with the retention of early visual experience potentially acting as a scaffold for heightened sensitivity to non-visual social and emotional signals.
papers.authors: Boaz M. Ben-David, Karen Arcos, Susanne M. Jaeggi, Emily D. Grossman

0206.name: Eren Günseli
0206.bio: Eren Günseli is an Assistant Professor of Psychology at Sabancı University and the director of the Memory, Attention, & Cognitive Control (MACC) Lab. Their research investigates the bidirectional relationship between attention and memory, specifically examining how attentional templates are maintained in working memory and the processes driving the reactivation of long-term memory. Günseli utilizes electroencephalography (EEG) to track contralateral delay activity and alpha oscillations, alongside fMRI and eye-tracking. Their recent work focuses on the neural dissociation between selective attention and storage, as well as the cognitive mechanisms underlying event segmentation in episodic memory.
0206.research_direction: Dr. Günseli has recently been investigating the cognitive and neural mechanisms that structure and retrieve episodic memories. Their recent work explores how continuous experience is segmented into distinct memory traces, specifically testing the relative contributions of prediction errors versus contextual shifts in forming event boundaries. Using a combination of behavioral paradigms and EEG techniques like multivariate pattern analysis, they are also examining the temporal dynamics of memory reactivation to understand how environmental changes or abstract task rules bring stored representations back into active working memory. Additionally, they are probing the executive demands of the retrieval process itself, employing dual-task designs to evaluate how divided attention differentially impacts the initial search for memories versus the subsequent monitoring of retrieved content.

papers.title: Prediction error is out of context: the dominance of contextual stability in structuring episodic memories
papers.abstract: This study evaluates the relative importance of prediction error (PE) versus contextual stability in the formation of event boundaries within episodic memory. Utilizing a sequence-learning paradigm, the authors manipulated expectancy violations (PE) and background environmental shifts (context) to quantify their respective impacts on memory segmentation. Behavioral indices demonstrate that event boundaries are primarily anchored by contextual changes, with PE exerting a negligible effect on the overall structural organization of episodic traces. These findings suggest that contextual continuity serves as the dominant scaffolding for episodic encoding, challenging the sufficiency of PE as the primary driver for delineating experiential events.
papers.authors: Berna Güler, Fatih Serin, Eren Günseli

papers.title: Effects of context changes on memory reactivation
papers.abstract: The authors utilized human electroencephalography (EEG) to investigate the neurophysiological triggers mediating the transition of long-term memory (LTM) representations into an active working memory (WM) state. By tracking the contralateral delay activity (CDA) as an index of WM storage, the study demonstrates that a change in the spatial or task-relevant context triggers a resurgence of the CDA, indicating the selective reactivation of LTM content into WM. This resurgence was dissociated from lateralized alpha-band suppression, which tracked spatial attention independently. The results identify context shifts as a critical gating mechanism for the dynamic re-recruitment of WM resources for established LTM representations.
papers.authors: Şahcan Özdemir, Yağmur Damla Şentürk, Nursima Ünver, Can Demircan, Christian N. L. Olivers, Tobias Egner, Eren Günseli

papers.title: The reactivation of task rules triggers the reactivation of task-relevant items
papers.abstract: This research explores the hierarchical control of memory retrieval by examining whether task-set reactivation facilitates the retrieval of specific item-level content. Employing time-resolved multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) on EEG data, the researchers monitored the neural signatures of rules and stimuli during memory-guided tasks. The findings reveal that the neural reactivation of abstract task rules precedes and significantly predicts the subsequent reactivation of task-relevant item features. This temporal and functional sequence supports a top-down hierarchical model of cognitive control where rule representations gate the selection of subordinate episodic features into the focus of attention.
papers.authors: Yağmur Damla Şentürk, Nursima Ünver, Can Demircan, Tobias Egner, Eren Günseli

papers.title: Prediction error and event segmentation in episodic memory
papers.abstract: This review synthesizes existing neurocomputational and empirical evidence regarding the role of prediction error (PE) in the temporal segmentation of episodic memory. Evaluating the framework of Event Segmentation Theory (EST), the authors analyze how mismatch signals detected in the hippocampus and midbrain facilitate the updating of internal event models. The review proposes an integrated model where PE serves as a signal for the detection of change, while the global continuity of contextual features determines the ultimate architectural boundaries of episodic events. The synthesis reconciles disparate findings on PE-driven segmentation by emphasizing the interaction between local surprise and global stability.
papers.authors: Sophie Nolden, Gözem Turan, Berna Güler, Eren Günseli

papers.title: How does divided attention hinder different stages of episodic memory retrieval?
papers.abstract: The study delineates the cognitive resource requirements across distinct stages of episodic memory retrieval: the initial search for memory traces and the subsequent post-retrieval monitoring of retrieved content. Utilizing a dual-task paradigm, participants performed a secondary task either during retrieval cue presentation or the decision-making phase. Behavioral results show that divided attention (DA) significantly impairs retrieval accuracy and increases reaction times primarily during the search phase. This selective vulnerability suggests that the retrieval search process is an effortful, executive-demanding operation, whereas post-retrieval monitoring is relatively more autonomous and resilient to concurrent cognitive load.
papers.authors: Nursima Ataseven, Nursima Ünver, Eren Günseli

0207.name: Erez Freud
0207.bio: Erez Freud is an Associate Professor at York University who researches the cognitive and neural mechanisms underlying object recognition and the visuomotor control of actions. Utilizing functional MRI, psychophysics, and hand-movement tracking, Freud’s work investigates the functional organization and development of the ventral and dorsal visual pathways. This research program examines how visual representations emerge in childhood, evolve throughout the lifespan, and are affected by brain damage or aging. Freud’s research focuses on the interface between perception and action, specifically regarding how the brain processes three-dimensional structural information.
0207.research_direction: Dr. Freud has recently been investigating the functional architecture of the dorsal and ventral visual streams, focusing particularly on the classic dissociation between vision-for-action and vision-for-perception. Their recent work explores how this functional segregation, alongside manual specialization and visuomotor control, operates differently in autistic adults and is modulated across the lifespan during healthy aging. To probe these mechanisms, they contrast perceptual estimations of visual illusions against grasping kinematics, utilizing both traditional laboratory psychophysics and naturalistic object manipulation tracked via markerless pose estimation. Additionally, Dr. Freud is examining the intersection of 3D spatial processing and attention, using fMRI to determine whether shape-selective networks in both visual pathways operate independently of top-down attention, and deploying spatial cueing paradigms to test how perceived depth influences the allocation of attentional resources.

papers.title: Reduced Dissociation Between Perception and Action in Autistic Individuals
papers.abstract: The 'reduced specialization' account of autism posits that typical functional segregation within cortical networks is diminished. This study examined the integrity of the perception-action dissociation—a hallmark of the primate visual system—by assessing grasping kinematics and perceptual estimation in autistic and non-autistic adults. Across two experiments utilizing the Ponzo illusion and stimulus history effects, non-autistic participants exhibited the expected dissociation: contextual and historical cues modulated perceptual estimations while sparing the visuomotor control of grasping. In contrast, autistic participants demonstrated susceptibility to these contextual modulations in both perception and action tasks. These findings provide empirical evidence that neurodevelopmental alterations in autism are associated with a reduction in the functional segregation between the ventral and dorsal visual pathways.
papers.venue: Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders
papers.authors: Zoha Ahmad, Bat-Sheva Hadad, Yarden Mazuz, Tzvi Ganel, Erez Freud

papers.title: Preserved perception-action dissociation but altered visuomotor behaviours in healthy aging
papers.abstract: The two visual pathways hypothesis suggests that vision-for-perception and vision-for-action are mediated by distinct neural substrates. This research investigates how healthy aging modulates this functional dissociation. Younger and older adults completed perceptual estimation and manual grasping tasks for objects positioned on a Ponzo illusion. While older adults displayed age-related decrements in movement kinematics and an increased reliance on local surface context during action planning, the fundamental dissociation between systems was maintained. Perceptual estimations in both groups were significantly biased by the illusion, whereas grasping apertures remained primarily tuned to the physical dimensions of the targets, suggesting that the core functional architecture of the dorsal and ventral streams is largely preserved across the adult lifespan.
papers.authors: Felicia Tassone, Zoha Ahmad, Tzvi Ganel, Erez Freud

papers.title: Reduced Hand Specialization and Idiosyncratic Visuomotor Strategies in Autism During Naturalistic Object Manipulation
papers.abstract: Atypical hemispheric lateralization is a proposed biomarker for autism spectrum disorder (ASD). We investigated this through a naturalistic LEGO-assembly task, employing markerless pose estimation to analyze the kinematics of manual actions. Despite being classified as right-handed by standard questionnaires, autistic adults exhibited significantly reduced behavioral hand specialization, characterized by a lower proportion of right-hand grasps and fewer contralateral reaches compared to neurotypical controls. Furthermore, autistic participants displayed higher movement idiosyncrasy and a spatial preference for objects in immediate proximity. These results suggest that the motor difficulties observed in autism may stem from reduced cortical specialization for visuomotor control, leading to the adoption of idiosyncratic strategies during dynamic object manipulation.
papers.authors: Emily Fewster, Bat-Sheva Hadad, Erez Freud

papers.title: Perceived depth modulates allocation of attention
papers.abstract: The close advantage effect (CAE) characterizes the preferential processing of stimuli in proximal space, yet the underlying attentional mechanisms remain poorly understood. This study utilized Posner cueing and Egly-Driver paradigms on 3D surfaces defined by pictorial depth cues to determine how perceived proximity modulates the allocation of spatial attention. We observed that participants were more accurate and efficient when shifting attention within and toward perceived close surfaces. Critically, a reduced Posner effect for closer targets suggests that attentional resources are more effectively utilized in near space. These results indicate that the attentional priority map is inherently depth-aware, prioritizing proximal regions for interaction independently of their retinal image size.
papers.authors: Tasfia Ahsan, Laurie M. Wilcox, Erez Freud

papers.title: The large-scale organization of shape processing in the ventral and dorsal pathways is dissociable from attention
papers.abstract: While the dorsal visual pathway is traditionally associated with visuomotor control, recent research suggests it also facilitates object perception. This study investigated whether dorsal shape sensitivity is independent of top-down attentional focus. Using fMRI and a parametric box-scrambling paradigm, we measured BOLD responses to novel 3D shapes across varying levels of image degradation while participants attended either to the object or to background color. Univariate and multivariate analyses revealed that the large-scale organization of shape selectivity—including shape-sensitivity gradients along the posterior-anterior axis—was preserved across both pathways regardless of the focus of attention. These findings support the conclusion that shape processing is a fundamental, distributed cortical property that is functionally dissociable from top-down attentional mechanisms.
papers.authors: Yael Goldstein-Marcusohn, Rahaf Asaad, Leen Asaad, Erez Freud

0208.name: Erich Graf
0208.bio: Erich Graf is an Associate Professor in Experimental Psychology at the University of Southampton, where they have been a faculty member since 2004. Graf earned a PhD in Vision Science from the University of California, Berkeley, focusing on how humans integrate sensory inputs with learned priors to construct internal 3D models of the world. Their research utilizes psychophysics, computational modeling, and virtual reality to investigate scene perception, multisensory integration, and the statistical regularities of natural environments. Currently, Graf studies the dynamics of spatial and semantic processing in real-world scenes and the mechanisms of decision-making in complex visual environments.
0208.research_direction: Dr. Graf has recently been investigating human depth perception in complex, real-world environments by using psychophysical experiments to assess how visual cues like binocular disparity, elevation priors, and color contribute to distance judgments. Their recent work explores how these biological depth estimation mechanisms compare to contemporary computer vision architectures, such as deep neural networks, when processing ecological scene statistics across brief presentation durations. Beyond traditional visual psychophysics, they are designing experimental paradigms that utilize immersive virtual reality to induce and longitudinally measure complex, durable psychological states like nostalgia. Furthermore, Dr. Graf's applied research examines advanced cognitive frameworks for automation, assessing how the integration of large language models, knowledge graphs, and traditional ontologies can optimize human-robot collaboration and robotic adaptability in dynamic industrial environments.

papers.title: Virtual-reality induced nostalgia: duration and psychological benefits
papers.abstract: This study investigated the efficacy of a novel nostalgia induction paradigm utilizing immersive virtual reality (VR). In a series of experiments, the authors compared a newly developed Virtual Reality Task (VRT) against the conventional Event Reflection Task (ERT). Initial validation through psychometric assessments demonstrated that the VR-based environment successfully elicited heightened levels of state nostalgia and associated psychological benefits—such as increased social connectedness and self-esteem—relative to control conditions. Subsequent longitudinal analysis using five repeated measurements at 5-minute intervals revealed that while the ERT-induced effects decayed rapidly, the augmented VRT maintained significantly higher levels of felt nostalgia over time. Although the VRT did not statistically outperform the ERT in the magnitude of immediate psychological benefit, the findings establish VR as a robust and durable medium for inducing complex emotional states in experimental settings.
papers.authors: İrem Yılmaz-Özdemir, Constantine Sedikides, Tim Wildschut, Erich Graf

papers.title: From ontologies to knowledge augmented large language models for automation: a decision-making guidance for achieving human–robot collaboration in Industry 5.0
papers.abstract: The transition toward Industry 5.0 necessitates advanced human-centric cognitive frameworks for industrial automation. This research evaluates the integration of Large Language Models (LLMs), ontologies, and knowledge graphs within robotic systems to facilitate seamless human-robot collaboration (HRC). The authors propose a structured decision-making taxonomy to guide the selection of appropriate Natural Language Processing (NLP) and knowledge representation techniques based on task dependency and environmental complexity. Through a comparative analysis across various industrial use cases, the study demonstrates how LLMs can enhance robotic adaptability and reasoning in dynamic manufacturing environments, while emphasizing the continuing utility of traditional ontologies in resource-constrained or low-dependency sectors. The framework serves as a roadmap for developing resilient, flexible robotic architectures that prioritize human-centric interaction and task generalizability.
papers.authors: John Oyekan, Christopher Turner, Michael Bax, Erich Graf

papers.title: Depth estimation in real-world scenes
papers.abstract: Human depth perception in complex environments was investigated using the Southampton-York Natural Scenes (SYNS) dataset, focusing on the relative contributions of binocular disparity, elevation, and chromatic cues. Across four psychophysical experiments, participants performed ordinal and ratio depth judgments on briefly presented (17–267 ms) outdoor scenes. Results indicated a pervasive reliance on an elevation prior, where stimuli higher in the visual field were consistently perceived as more distant. Manipulations of image color (natural, inverted, and greyscale) revealed that while humans remain highly accurate across varied conditions, deep neural networks (DNNs) and K-nearest neighbor regression models fail to match human performance, particularly when elevation cues are absent or presentation durations are extended. These findings suggest that biological depth estimation incorporates ecological scene statistics and cues that are not yet fully modeled by contemporary computer vision architectures.
papers.authors: Michaela Trescakova, Wendy Adams, Matthew Anderson, James Elder, Erich Graf

0209.name: Erik Blaser
0209.bio: Erik Blaser is a Professor of Psychology at the University of Massachusetts Boston, where they lead the Human Vision Lab and direct the Developmental and Brain Sciences program. Blaser's research utilizes psychophysical and pupillometric methodologies to investigate the mechanisms of visual attention, object tracking in feature-space, and perceptual learning. Their work examines the developmental trajectory of visual cognition, including the study of iconic memory in infants and the underlying mechanisms of enhanced visual search in individuals with Autism Spectrum Disorder. This research aims to characterize how the human visual system prioritizes and integrates sensory information to guide behavior and task performance.
0209.research_direction: Dr. Blaser has recently been investigating the dynamic allocation of visual memory resources, exploring how individuals balance internal mnemonic storage with active perceptual sampling of the external environment. Their recent work examines this "sampling-remembering trade-off" from a developmental perspective, utilizing interactive behavioral paradigms to test how young children strategically adjust their reliance on working memory versus external aids when those external resources become unreliable. Additionally, they are probing the architecture of visual long-term memory for complex naturalistic spaces by using continuous-report delayed estimation tasks to measure recall accuracy and precision for sequential scenes along a continuous walking route. Finally, Dr. Blaser is also examining the cognitive mechanisms underlying category induction, employing forced-choice psychophysical designs to determine whether the classic learning benefits of interleaved study schedules reflect genuine improvements in perceptual memory rather than simple response biases.

papers.title: Testing the interleaving effect without response bias: A forced-choice reevaluation of Kornell and Bjork (2008)
papers.abstract: In category induction, the canonical interleaving effect demonstrated by Kornell and Bjork (2008) showed that alternating exemplars of target categories during study facilitates superior inductive generalization compared to blocked schedules. However, standard identification protocols that present single test probes inherently confound mnemonic discriminability with criterion shifts and response biases, meaning that observed effect sizes could represent artifacts of decision strategies. To resolve this interpretive challenge, an online direct replication of Kornell and Bjork's Experiment 1A was conducted (N = 288), alongside a critical conceptual replication replacing the identification format with an n-alternative forced-choice (2AFC) design (N = 276) to isolate memory strength free of criterion bias. The 2AFC procedure revealed a robust interleaving benefit (t(275) = 7.19, p < .001, dz = 0.43, 95% CI [0.32, 0.55]) comparable in magnitude to that obtained in the standard identification task. These findings demonstrate that category interleaving advantages reflect genuine mnemonic differences in perceptual classification rather than response bias confounds.
papers.authors: Jamie Donenfeld, Zsuzsa Kaldy, Erik Blaser

papers.title: How attention and working memory work together in the pursuit of goals: The development of the sampling-remembering trade-off
papers.abstract: Traditional psychophysical investigations into visual working memory and attention have typically constrained participants to maximum-effort paradigms with static, isolated stimuli, leaving unaddressed how cognitive control dynamically manages resources to serve real-world behavioral goals. This theoretical framework advances an ecological, resource-rational approach focused on the sampling-remembering trade-off: the adaptive equilibrium struck between harvesting information from the external visual environment through active sampling (e.g., saccades, head movements) and maintaining representations within internal working memory buffers. Grounded in economic principles of cognitive effort, a dynamic feedback model is proposed in which an individual balances the subjective cost of querying external sources against the metabolic and cognitive load of internal mnemonic storage. The model generates three developmental predictions: (1) individual children seek an equilibrium between perceptual sampling and internal maintenance effort; (2) age-dependent increases in working memory capacity and executive control drive a strategic shift favoring greater internal storage; and (3) older children exhibit enhanced flexibility to re-calibrate trade-offs across shifting task structures.
papers.authors: Erik Blaser, Zsuzsa Kaldy

papers.title: My Tablet's About to Go Dead! 5- to 6-year-old Children Adjust Their Cognitive Strategies Depending on Whether An External Resource is Reliably Available
papers.abstract: While extensive research highlights adults' propensity to offload cognitive burden onto external artifacts, the impact of external store reliability on young children's strategic trade-offs remains poorly understood. In a preregistered experiment employing a touchscreen 'Shopping Game', 5- to 6-year-old children (N = 37) retrieved target items from a virtual grocery store using a shopping list, where storefront and list could only be inspected alternately via active toggling. The reliability of the external aid was manipulated across conditions: the list remained predictably accessible in the reliable condition, whereas participants were led to believe the list might disappear in the unreliable condition. When the external store was reliable, children exhibited greater offloading, characterized by more frequent visits of shorter dwell time and fewer items retrieved per excursion. When list access was made uncertain, children adapted by expanding study duration and maintaining more items in working memory per visit. Children also identified the reliable condition as easier and reported greater subjective preference for it, demonstrating that preschool-aged children strategically calibrate internal cognitive investment according to external resource reliability.
papers.authors: Yibiao Liang, Zsuzsa Kaldy, Erik Blaser

papers.title: The Accuracy and Precision of Memory for Natural Scenes: A Walk in the Park
papers.abstract: Quantifying the accuracy and precision of natural scene memory has been hampered by the absence of metric stimulus spaces that capture naturalistic image topologies. This study exploited the continuous, metric topology of natural navigation by generating continuous video loops of outdoor 90-meter walking circuits recorded at 6 frames per second, yielding 360 ordered scenes separated by approximately 0.25 meters. In a delayed estimation, continuous report paradigm, participants viewed a target scene extracted from a circuit and localized its position using a 360-frame continuous response wheel. Memory performance was highly accurate and exhibited no systematic directional bias, indicating an absence of net boundary extension or contraction along the route trajectory. Mnemonic precision was systematically structured by environmental similarity: circuits with higher self-similarity—indexed by the spatial half-life of the Multiscale Structural Similarity (MS-SSIM) metric—yielded significantly higher recall precision, demonstrating a demand-dependent similarity advantage in visual long-term memory for complex naturalistic spaces.
papers.venue: Open Mind: Discoveries in Cognitive Science
papers.authors: Leo Westebbe, Yibiao Liang, Erik Blaser

0210.name: Erik Chihhung Chang
0210.bio: Erik Chihhung Chang is an Associate Professor who integrates behavioral experimentation with neuroimaging techniques, such as functional MRI and electroencephalography (EEG), to investigate the relationship between human motor control and higher-order cognition. Chang’s research examines cognitive aging, focusing on how motor skill learning and inhibitory functions change across the lifespan and under the influence of physical exercise. They utilize information theory and machine learning to develop predictive databases for monitoring cognitive decline. Chang also employs task scenarios, such as simulated battlefield environments, to study brain responses in ecologically valid settings.
0210.research_direction: Dr. Chang's recent work explores the cognitive and behavioral architectures underlying spatial navigation and motor control. In the domain of spatial cognition, they are using virtual reality paradigms to investigate how individuals construct cognitive maps, specifically examining how the structural scale of environmental cues—such as global versus local landmarks—distinctly guides human wayfinding. Additionally, their research applies frameworks from information theory, including metrics like entropy and mutual information, to evaluate motor task complexity and assess the efficiency of neuro-motor processing capacity. They have also recently been probing the theoretical functional equivalence between motor imagery and actual motor execution, utilizing response repetition paradigms to test whether offline mental simulations share the exact same motoric representations as physical movements.

papers.title: Differential contributions of global and local object landmarks in human wayfinding behavior
papers.abstract: This study investigates the distinct roles of global and local environmental landmarks in human spatial navigation and survey-level representation. Using virtual reality navigation paradigms, the research quantifies how individuals utilize landmarks of varying spatial hierarchies to maintain orientation and perform pointing tasks. The results demonstrate that global landmarks serve as a primary reference for establishing allocentric cognitive maps and directional orientation, while local landmarks are predominantly leveraged for waypoint-specific route decisions. These findings suggest a hierarchical organization in human spatial cognition where structural scale dictates the functional utility of environmental cues in wayfinding.
papers.authors: Wei-Jou Lin, Erik C. Chang

papers.title: The Application of Information Theory in Studying Motor Control
papers.abstract: This work applies information theoretic frameworks to the quantification of human motor control and learning processes. By employing metrics such as entropy and mutual information, the researchers provide a standardized method for assessing the complexity of motor tasks and the efficiency of neuro-motor responses. The research specifically examines the scaling of information processing capacity across different task difficulties and age groups, facilitating cross-functional comparisons between motor performance and higher-order cognitive domains. The application of these quantitative measures offers a robust alternative to traditional behavioral metrics in analyzing the neuro-cognitive foundations of motor coordination.
papers.venue: Cognitive and Neural Foundations of Chinese Reading
papers.authors: Hsin-Ping Tien, Erik C. Chang

papers.title: Inequivalent and uncorrelated response priming in motor imagery and execution
papers.abstract: This research re-evaluates the functional equivalence hypothesis between motor imagery (MI) and motor execution (ME) through a response repetition paradigm designed to circumvent the subjectivity of self-reporting. By analyzing prime-probe repetition effects, the study demonstrates that while both MI and ME elicit response priming, the magnitude of these effects is significantly different between the two modes. Furthermore, a lack of correlation in repetition effects across the conditions suggests that the motoric representations for imagery and execution are functionally distinguishable. These results challenge the prevailing view that MI involves a complete offline simulation of the motoric processes used in actual execution.
papers.authors: Hsin-Ping Tien, Erik C. Chang

0213.name: Eva Wiese
0213.department: Institut für Psychologie und Arbeitswissenschaft, Fachgebiet Kognitionspsychologie und kognitive Ergonomie
0213.bio: Wiese is a social neuroscientist and cognitive psychologist whose research investigates the cognitive and neural mechanisms underlying mind perception and social interaction with artificial agents. Their work employs EEG/ERP, eye-tracking, and computational modeling to study how ascribing intentionality to robots modulates visual attention, working memory, and trust. Wiese currently directs projects exploring the neural correlates of trust in human-AI teaming and the design of robots that trigger human social-cognitive processing.
0213.research_direction: Dr. Wiese's recent work explores the cognitive and perceptual mechanisms underlying human-robot interaction, investigating the conditions under which non-human agents trigger specialized social processing. Using the face inversion paradigm, they have recently been examining the boundaries of holistic face perception, testing how both bottom-up structural fidelity and top-down motives for social connection influence whether robot faces are processed configurally. Their research also spans shared visuospatial attention, utilizing Multiple Object Tracking and Level-1 perspective-taking paradigms to probe how human observers spontaneously compute the visual fields of artificial agents and allocate attentional effort based on an entity's implied social presence. Additionally, they investigate how the social framing of robotic partners—such as collaborative versus competitive contexts—modulates higher-level human decision-making and risk calibration in joint tasks.

papers.title: Risk-Taking Behavior in Human-Robot Teams: Collaboration vs. Competition
papers.abstract: This pre-registered study investigates the modulation of human risk-taking behavior in social human-robot interaction (sHRI) using a modified Balloon Analogue Risk Task (BART). Participants interacted with a humanoid NAO robot in either collaborative or competitive frames. Findings indicate that social presence per se enhances risk-taking relative to baseline (solo) performance. However, competitive interaction facilitated the adoption of near-optimal strategies and higher utility, whereas collaboration increased risk propensity without equivalent performance gains. These results demonstrate that the social framing of robotic agents significantly impacts decision-making and risk calibration in joint tasks.
papers.authors: Jairo Pérez-Osorio, Eva Wiese

papers.title: Taken at Face Value: Do Robots Trigger Face-Typical Processing?
papers.abstract: Using the face inversion paradigm across three experiments, this research delineates the perceptual boundaries for triggering holistic face processing in robotic agents. The research quantifies the inversion effect as an index of configural processing. Results show that robot faces typically fail to engage specialized social brain networks; however, holistic processing is elicited when robot faces incorporate a critical density of human configurations (e.g., three or four human-like features). This suggests that high-fidelity configural design is a prerequisite for activating the social-cognitive mechanisms necessary for rapid inferences about identity and intention.
papers.authors: Ali Momen, Tobias Feldmann-Wüstefeld, Kurt Hugenberg, Eva Wiese

papers.title: Play fair: Humans prefer an equal division of labor in a joint multiple object tracking task
papers.abstract: This study examines the psychological constraints on labor division in joint Multiple Object Tracking (MOT) tasks. Participants were empowered to decide the allocation of attentional tracking load between themselves and a partner (human or computer). Results revealed a robust preference for an equal 50/50 division when collaborating with a human partner, reflecting established social fairness norms in dyadic joint action. Conversely, when the partner was a computer algorithm, participants significantly offloaded a greater proportion of the task, indicating that fairness expectations are agent-dependent and that humans adopt different cognitive strategies when delegating effort to non-human entities.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the Annual Meeting of the Cognitive Science Society (CogSci 2025)
papers.authors: Basil Wahn, Eva Wiese

papers.title: Humans take the visuospatial perspective of robots and objects that imply social presence
papers.abstract: This research explored the boundaries of spontaneous visual perspective taking (VPT) in response to non-human agents. Using a Level-1 VPT task, the study tested whether humans spontaneously calculate the visual field of robots and inanimate objects that imply social agency. The findings indicate that both humanoids and simple objects, when framed as having social presence, can trigger perspective-taking mechanisms, suggesting that implied sociality rather than biological appearance is the primary driver for the reflexive calculation of another's perspective.
papers.authors: Basil Wahn, Eva Wiese

papers.title: Social perception of robots is shaped by beliefs about their minds
papers.abstract: This research investigates how internal social connection motives modulate the holistic processing of humanoid robot faces. Utilizing the face inversion paradigm, the study demonstrated that individuals with a high need for social connection processed robot faces configurally, showing a significant inversion effect similar to that seen with human faces. This effect was markedly attenuated in individuals with low social connection motives. The findings support a top-down model of mind perception, where perceiver-centric motives can effectively override bottom-up perceptual cues to engage social-cognitive processing for non-human agents.
papers.authors: Ali Momen, Kurt Hugenberg, Eva Wiese

0215.name: Fabian Soto
0215.bio: Fabian A. Soto is an Associate Professor of Psychology at Florida International University and director of the Computational Cognitive Neuroscience Lab. Soto’s research examines the neural and computational mechanisms of learning and generalization, specifically focusing on how categorization training and visual representations influence one another. Through the integration of behavioral psychophysics, computational modeling, and neuroimaging techniques such as fMRI and EEG, Soto tests theories concerning object and face perception. Their work employs multidimensional signal detection theory and General Recognition Theory to investigate the independence of stimulus dimensions and the origins of perception biases.
0215.research_direction: Dr. Soto has recently been investigating the perceptual architecture of visual and cognitive processing, frequently utilizing multidimensional signal detection frameworks like General Recognition Theory. Their recent work extensively explores face perception, employing reverse correlation and parametrically controlled 3D stimuli to investigate whether structural dimensions—such as identity, emotional expression, static shape, and dynamic motion—are encoded independently or integrated holistically. Beyond complex object recognition, they are also investigating how psychophysical paradigms can be leveraged to mathematically disambiguate distinct neural population encoding mechanisms, exploring how behavioral threshold patterns map onto specific tuning and gain changes in the visual system. Additionally, their recent work extends these rigorous measurement frameworks into the cognitive domain, exploring how phenomenal states like tip-of-the-tongue and feeling-of-knowing relate to the metacognitive sensitivity of confidence monitoring during semantic memory retrieval.

papers.title: Shape information used for face identity and expression recognition is highly versatile and context specific
papers.abstract: This study employed reverse correlation within an anatomically-interpretable face shape space to delineate the specific features diagnostic for identity and emotional expression recognition. By estimating internal templates (mental representations) across diverse tasks—including face shape detection, identity matching, and familiarity categorization—the authors observed that recognition relies on fine-grained shape perturbations distributed globally across the facial structure rather than localized features. Critically, these representations exhibited significant context-specificity; the encoding of identity was found to be contingent upon the specific emotional expression displayed, while the representation of expression was modulated by face identity. These findings emphasize the dynamic adaptability of visual encoding mechanisms and challenge static models of facial representation.
papers.authors: Emily Renae Martin, Jason S. Hays, Fabian A. Soto

papers.title: Tip-of-the-Tongue and Feeling-of-Knowing Experiences Enhance Metacognitive Sensitivity of Confidence Evaluation of Semantic Memory
papers.abstract: The authors applied General Recognition Theory (GRT)—a multidimensional signal detection framework—to investigate the relationship between metacognitive states (tip-of-the-tongue, TOT; and feeling-of-knowing, FOK) and the precision of confidence monitoring in semantic memory. Across two experiments requiring the recall of celebrity names and general knowledge, participants provided confidence ratings for recognition decisions following retrieval failures. By constructing sensitivity-vs-metacognition curves, the researchers quantified how the strength of the subjective TOT/FOK experience influenced metacognitive sensitivity. The results provided the first evidence that these phenomenal states are associated with a quantitative enhancement in the sensitivity of confidence evaluations, suggesting that the signal underlying TOT/FOK states provides diagnostic information that facilitates more accurate metacognitive monitoring.
papers.authors: Ali Pournaghdali, Bennett L. Schwartz, Fabian A. Soto

papers.title: Leveraging Psychophysics to Infer the Mechanisms of Encoding Change in Vision
papers.abstract: This research investigates the identifiability of distinct neural population encoding mechanisms through the analysis of psychophysical thresholds. Utilizing computational simulations, the authors modeled eight mechanisms of representational change—including specific/nonspecific gain and tuning, specific suppression, and inward/outward tuning shifts—to examine their impact on Threshold-versus-Noise (TvN) and Threshold-versus-Stimulus (TvS) functions. The analysis demonstrated that most of these mechanisms generate dissociable qualitative patterns in psychometric data, with the exception of specific gain and specific tuning. Consequently, the paper argues that psychophysical paradigms can serve as critical constraints for neuroimaging studies utilizing inverted encoding models (IEM), as they allow researchers to disambiguate between neural mechanisms that may otherwise appear identical in population-level neuroimaging reconstructions.
papers.authors: Jason S. Hays, Fabian A. Soto

papers.title: Multidimensional signal detection modeling reveals Gestalt-like perceptual integration of face emotion and identity
papers.abstract: To resolve conflicting evidence regarding the independence of facial identity and emotional expression processing, the authors utilized high-fidelity 3D computer-generated faces and the General Recognition Theory (GRT) framework. The study effectively decoupled perceptual and decisional components of processing across twelve distinct experimental groups. Contrary to models proposing parallel, independent pathways, the results revealed consistent and significant violations of perceptual independence. These robust interaction effects suggest a Gestalt-like perceptual integration where the encoding of one facial dimension is fundamentally influenced by the state of the other. The findings represent substantial evidence for holistic face processing as defined by formal multidimensional signal detection standards, challenging the notion of strictly autonomous processing of invariant (identity) and changeable (expression) facial cues.
papers.authors: S. Sanaz Hosseini, Fabian A. Soto

papers.title: Face shape and motion are perceptually separable: Support for a revised model of face processing
papers.abstract: This study provides a psychophysical test of the theoretical proposal that face shape and face motion are processed via separate, parallel neural streams. Using 3D-modeled facial stimuli to precisely control shape and motion parameters and calibrate dimensional discriminability, the researchers applied General Recognition Theory (GRT) to evaluate their perceptual independence. The results supported the hypothesis of perceptual separability, indicating that the human visual system encodes static shape information and dynamic motion cues as independent dimensions. While decisional interactions were observed, the core perceptual encoding of these features remained autonomous, providing empirical psychophysical validation for contemporary dual-pathway models of facial information processing.
papers.authors: Emily Renae Martin, Jason S. Hays, Fabian A. Soto

0216.name: Fang Fang
0216.department: School of Psychological and Cognitive Sciences
0216.lab_name: Lab of Vision and Cognitive Neuroscience
0216.bio: Fang is a Professor of Brain and Cognitive Sciences and Vice President at Peking University, where they also serve as a Principal Investigator at the IDG/McGovern Institute for Brain Research. Their research investigates the neural mechanisms underlying visual perception, attention, and consciousness by integrating high-resolution fMRI, psychophysics, and transcranial electrical stimulation. Fang’s work includes the study of visual perceptual learning, cortical plasticity, and the representation of objects and faces in the human visual cortex. Their current research directions involve investigating neural prediction errors in visual reasoning and the role of subcortical nuclei in feature-based attentional control.
0216.research_direction: Dr. Fang has recently been investigating the neural mechanisms and temporal dynamics underlying visual perception and learning, alongside the representational alignment between biological and artificial neural networks. Their recent work explores the high-resolution time course of brain plasticity and wakeful sensory consolidation during visual perceptual learning, utilizing MEG, MR spectroscopy, and frequency-specific visual stimulation to probe functional changes in the early visual cortex. Additionally, they are investigating the spatiotemporal evolution of ensemble perception to determine how the human visual system computes statistical summaries from complex orientation arrays. Expanding into neuro-AI intersections, their research also evaluates how neural hierarchies in the human brain compare to artificial systems, probing human visual pathways against deep convolutional neural networks during dynamic action recognition and comparing intracranial recordings with large language models to map syntactic encoding.

papers.title: Hierarchical Frequency Tagging Probe (HFTP): A Unified Approach to Investigate Syntactic Structure Representations in Large Language Models and the Human Brain
papers.abstract: This study introduces the Hierarchical Frequency Tagging Probe (HFTP), a novel frequency-domain analytical framework designed to identify discrete neural components in both Large Language Models (LLMs) and the human brain (via intracranial recordings) that encode hierarchical syntactic structures. By applying this methodology to models including GPT-2, Gemma, and the Llama series, researchers demonstrated that artificial neural networks process syntax across layers in a manner that mirrors human brain processing hierarchies. Using representational similarity analysis (RSA), the study identified a significant alignment between LLM-based syntactic representations and neural activity in the left hemisphere, specifically within cortical regions traditionally associated with language processing. The findings provide a unified metric for comparing mechanistic syntax encoding across biological and artificial systems.
papers.venue: The Thirty-ninth Annual Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS)
papers.authors: Jingmin An, Yilong Song, Ruolin Yang, Nai Ding, Lingxi Lu, Yuxuan Wang, Wei Wang, Chu Zhuang, Qian Wang, Fang Fang

papers.title: Frequency-dependent photic modulation of wakeful consolidation in visual learning
papers.abstract: This research investigates the modulation of wakeful consolidation in visual learning through repetitive visual stimulation (RVS) at specific temporal frequencies. Utilizing an orientation discrimination task (ODT), the study demonstrates that 10-Hz flickering grating RVS significantly enhances subsequent perceptual performance, whereas 1-Hz RVS induces a performance impairment. These effects were absent when training was omitted or when non-patterned uniform disks were utilized, suggesting the modulation is specific to early-stage sensory consolidation. Neurophysiological data from event-related potentials (ERPs) and magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS) revealed that RVS-facilitated consolidation is characterized by enhanced N1 amplitudes and an elevated glutamate/GABA (excitation/inhibition) ratio in the early visual cortex (EVC). These findings implicate LTP-like synaptic plasticity as the underlying mechanism for the frequency-dependent photic modulation of learning consolidation during wakefulness.
papers.authors: Xin-Yue Yang, Chuyue Zhao, Zhentao Zuo, Aming Li, Huan Luo, Qing He, Fang Fang

papers.title: Time Course of Orientation Ensemble Representation in the Human Brain
papers.abstract: The study explores the neural mechanisms of orientation ensemble perception, specifically investigating whether the brain represents summary statistics through specialized processes or simple summation of individual item representations. Utilizing magnetoencephalography (MEG) and frequency-tagging EEG, the researchers employed multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) and inverted encoding models (IEM) to track the temporal evolution of orientation representations. Results indicate that a robust representation of the orientation ensemble emerges approximately 370 ms post-stimulus, predominantly localized within early visual areas. Crucially, IEM analysis showed that the ensemble representation is distinct from the linear summation of component orientations and is significantly correlated with individual behavioral reports of perceived average orientation. These findings suggest a gradual, specialized computational process in the human visual cortex that achieves accurate statistical summaries of complex visual scenes.
papers.authors: Xizi Gong, Tao He, Qian Wang, Junshi Lu, Fang Fang

papers.title: Human Visual Pathways for Action Recognition versus Deep Convolutional Neural Networks: Representation Correspondence in Late but Not Early Layers
papers.abstract: This study evaluates the representational alignment between human visual pathways and two-stream deep convolutional neural networks (DCNNs) during the recognition of human actions in video sequences. Using fMRI-based decoding and representational similarity analysis (RSA), researchers compared neural responses across ventral and dorsal pathways with network activations in DCNN layers. The results demonstrate that, unlike the hierarchical alignment observed in static object categorization, DCNNs do not exhibit hierarchical representation correspondence with the human brain for dynamic action recognition. Discrepancies were particularly evident in early visual layers, though later DCNN layers showed greater representational similarity to the human visual cortex. These patterns persisted across both photorealistic avatars and point-light biological motion displays, indicating fundamental differences in how artificial and biological systems encode dynamic, multi-pathway visual information.
papers.authors: Yujia Peng, Xizi Gong, Hongjing Lu, Fang Fang

papers.title: Time courses of brain plasticity underpinning visual motion perceptual learning
papers.abstract: This research utilizes magnetoencephalography (MEG) to characterize the high-resolution temporal sequence of neural changes induced by visual motion perceptual learning (VPL). Human participants were trained on a motion direction discrimination task, and MEG source reconstruction was applied to quantify plasticity in the early visual cortex (EVC) and V3A. The study found that VPL significantly increased neural selectivity and enhanced response amplitudes within the EVC. Furthermore, learning strengthened the feedforward connectivity from EVC to V3A, a change that manifested rapidly between 78 and 104 ms after stimulus onset. Subsequent neural modifications in response amplitude and selectivity occurred between 160 and 230 ms, correlating significantly with behavioral improvements in discrimination accuracy. The findings suggest that VPL modifies the visual hierarchy through both early-stage feedforward enhancement and later-stage refinement of neural representations.
papers.authors: Yongqian Song, Qian Wang, Fang Fang

0217.name: Faran Sabeti
0217.department: Discipline of Optometry, Faculty of Health
0217.bio: Faran Sabeti is an Associate Professor of Optometry and Vision Science at the University of Canberra. Sabeti’s research focuses on developing objective functional tests for the early detection of retinal and neurological diseases. They specialize in multifocal pupillographic objective perimetry (mfPOP), employing this technology to identify physiological biomarkers in conditions such as diabetic retinopathy, age-related macular degeneration, and multiple sclerosis. Sabeti’s work explores the integration of subjective and objective perimetric measures to characterize neural damage and investigates interventions, including stochastic resonance and ocular therapeutics, to alter visual function.
0217.research_direction: Dr. Sabeti’s recent work spans clinical diagnostics, retinal pharmacology, and patient health communication. They have recently been investigating novel functional biomarkers for diabetic eye disease, specifically evaluating whether multifocal pupillographic objective perimetry can map subclinical neuroretinal impairment and track longitudinal functional changes in diabetic macular edema more effectively than conventional subjective visual field testing. Alongside this focus on functional topography, their recent work explores retinal dopaminergic physiology by using multifocal electroretinography and optical coherence tomography to assess how topical levodopa administration influences retinal structure and function in young adults. Broadening their focus to clinical public health, Dr. Sabeti is also examining the accessibility of eye care information by evaluating the readability, understandability, and practical actionability of diabetic retinopathy patient education materials designed for Indigenous and general populations.

papers.title: Understandability and actionability of patient education materials for diabetic retinopathy among indigenous and general populations
papers.abstract: This study evaluated the quality, readability, understandability, and actionability of online patient education materials (PEMs) addressing diabetic retinopathy (DR), contrasting resources tailored for Indigenous Australian populations against those designed for the broader community. A systematic search identified 540 educational resources, of which 54 met the predetermined inclusion criteria across printable and audiovisual modalities. Evaluated via the Patient Education Materials Assessment Tool (PEMAT), Indigenous-targeted PEMs attained superior mean understandability scores (80%) compared to general population materials (75%). However, actionability scores were uniformly compromised across all formats: printable resources achieved mean actionability scores of 42% for the general cohort and 53% for Indigenous resources, whereas audiovisual formats demonstrated marked deficits at 29%. These data indicate that while current DR patient education resources generally communicate disease concepts comprehensibly, they substantially lack structured, stepwise instructions necessary to guide self-management and adherence to sight-preserving interventions.
papers.authors: Kam Chun Ho, Falicia Tay, Caitlin Quan, Faran Sabeti

papers.title: Retinal Function in Young Adults Following Topical Application of Levodopa to the Eye
papers.abstract: Dysregulation of the retinal dopaminergic system has been implicated in ocular pathologies including myopia. This randomized, double-masked, placebo-controlled phase I clinical trial assessed whether localized topical administration of levodopa/carbidopa drops alters human retinal structure or functional topography. Twenty-nine healthy male volunteers aged 18 to 30 years received daily unilateral administration of either a low dose (1.4 μmol levodopa / 0.34 μmol carbidopa per day, n = 14) or high dose (2.7 μmol levodopa / 0.68 μmol carbidopa per day, n = 15) for 28 days, while the contralateral eye received vehicle placebo. Testing at baseline, cessation of treatment (4 weeks), and 4 months post-treatment included high- and low-contrast visual acuity, 44-zone Matrix frequency-doubling perimetry, regional multifocal electroretinography (mfERG), and optical coherence tomography (OCT) macular thickness maps, complemented by rabbit pharmacokinetic analysis. A minor, statistically significant increase in mfERG ring 5 response amplitude and localized macular thinning appeared in low-dose eyes (p < 0.05), but these remained within physiologic limits and lacked clinical relevance; no significant perturbations occurred in high-dose eyes. Pharmacokinetics demonstrated rapid clearance within 4 hours without systemic blood accumulation, verifying the safety and retinal tolerability of topical levodopa/carbidopa formulations.
papers.authors: Faran Sabeti, Kate Thomson, Ted Maddess, Cindy Karouta, Myra Leung, Nicola Anstice, Tina Jong, Regan Ashby

papers.title: Discriminating early-stage diabetic retinopathy with subjective and objective perimetry
papers.abstract: To establish sensitive functional biomarkers capable of resolving subclinical neuroretinal impairment prior to manifest microvascular pathology, this cross-sectional study compared multifocal pupillographic objective perimetry (mfPOP) with conventional subjective automated perimetry (SAP) in type 2 diabetes mellitus (PwT2D). Subjects classified with either no diabetic retinopathy (noDR) or mild-to-moderate non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy (mmDR) underwent bilateral testing using two mfPOP configurations—the macular OFA15 (±15°) and wide-field OFA30 (±30°) variants—alongside 24-2 Matrix frequency-doubling technology and 24-2 Short-Wavelength Automated Perimetry (SWAP). Five out of eight mfPOP global indices (mean defects and pattern standard deviations) successfully discriminated noDR from mmDR eyes (p ≤ 0.02), whereas none of the corresponding SAP metrics revealed statistically significant separation. Region-specific mfPOP mapping highlighted significant peripheral hypersensitivity and response delays in mmDR, with localized distribution excluding generalized autonomic pupillary neuropathy. Discriminative power reached high diagnostic utility (AUROCs up to 0.86), confirming that mfPOP-derived response latencies and amplitude deviations serve as robust surrogate endpoints for identifying early diabetic retinal neurodegeneration.
papers.authors: Faran Sabeti, Joshua P. van Kleef, Rakesh M. Iyer, Corinne F. Carle, Christopher J. Nolan, Rong Hui Chia, Ted Maddess

papers.title: Objective perimetry identifies regional functional progression and recovery in mild Diabetic Macular Oedema
papers.abstract: This prospective longitudinal investigation monitored neuroretinal structural and functional dynamics over a 27-month period in type 2 diabetic patients presenting with mild, non-central-involving diabetic macular oedema (DMO) versus non-DMO diabetic controls. Sixteen participants (32 eyes; 10 presenting with baseline DMO) underwent longitudinal evaluation producing 94 visits, which included Early Treatment Diabetic Retinopathy Study (ETDRS) grading, posterior-pole optical coherence tomography (OCT; 64-region grid), 10–2 Matrix subjective perimetry, and objectiveFIELD Analyser (OFA) mfPOP 30° and 60° paradigms assessing per-region sensitivity and response latency. Structural and functional metrics were mapped to an identical 44-region topographic layout. Eyes with baseline DMO showed significant mean central thickness reduction from 237 ± 25 μm to 234.2 ± 26.7 μm (p < 0.05), which correlated with localized functional recovery toward normative OFA sensitivities and latency profiles (all p < 0.021), whereas non-DMO eyes demonstrated progressive structural thickening from 250.7 ± 24.4 μm to 255.7 ± 20.6 μm (p < 0.05). Matrix perimetry detected significant longitudinal changes in only sparse regions restricted to the central 8°, whereas mfPOP revealed comprehensive regional progression and recovery across wide visual fields, underscoring its utility as an objective functional monitor of DMO progression.
papers.authors: Faran Sabeti, Bhim B. Rai, Josh P. van Kleef, Emilie M. F. Rohan, Corinne F. Carle, Richard C. Barry, Rohan W. Essex, Christopher J. Nolan, Ted Maddess

0218.name: Felix Franke
0218.institution: Institute of Molecular and Clinical Ophthalmology Basel
0218.department: Faculty of Science, University of Basel; Department of Biosystems Science and Engineering, ETH Zurich
0218.bio: Franke is an Assistant Professor at the University of Basel and leads the Quantitative Visual Physiology Group at the Institute of Molecular and Clinical Ophthalmology Basel, with a continuing affiliation at ETH Zurich. Franke's research focuses on the computational principles of retinal processing, specifically investigating how distinct retinal ganglion cell types encode visual information to support oculomotor feedback loops and the optokinetic reflex. Utilizing high-density microelectrode arrays and signal processing, they develop phenomenological and digital twin models of retinal circuitry to explain how the visual system stabilizes images and synchronizes signal arrival times across varying axonal lengths. This work combines computational neuroscience and experimental physiology to study the position-dependent nature of retinal computation and the functional properties of the human fovea.
0218.research_direction: Dr. Franke’s recent work explores the neurophysiology of early visual processing alongside the development of novel neurotechnology. To improve neural characterization, they have recently been developing new computational frameworks using reverse correlation and random moving objects to rapidly map multidimensional receptive fields across the visual pathway. Their physiological research also investigates how mice and humans process ambiguous visual motion—specifically the aperture problem—by tracking how local edge cues propagate from the retina to downstream nuclei to drive reflexive gaze stabilization. Furthermore, their recent work examines the biophysics of signal timing in the human fovea, utilizing high-density microelectrode arrays to understand how variations in retinal ganglion cell axon morphology regulate conduction velocities across varying intraretinal path lengths. Beyond sensory biology, they are also engineering tamper-resistant CMOS sensors that integrate extracellular electrophysiological recording with real-time, on-chip cryptographic hashing to ensure the provenance of raw scientific data.

papers.title: Rapid estimation of receptive fields across stages of the early visual system
papers.abstract: Neural receptive-field mapping in large-scale neuronal ensembles is constrained by practical experimental durations, as conventional probe stimuli like binary white-noise checkerboards paired with spike-triggered averaging (WN/STA) often fail to drive sufficient firing in neurons exhibiting non-linear or structured feature tuning. To overcome this limitation, the authors developed reverse correlation against stimulus elements (RCASE), a framework designed for structured stimuli that are represented by the presence or absence of discrete stimulus features per frame. Implementing this framework via random moving objects (RMO), the method was benchmarked against WN/STA, spike-triggered covariance, and spatially correlated stimuli across multiple stages of early visual circuitry—including mouse retina, nucleus of the optic tract, superior colliculus, primary visual cortex, and primate retina. RMO/RCASE evoked substantially stronger and more reproducible spiking activity, reliably mapping receptive fields across a significantly greater proportion of neurons in a fraction of standard recording durations for both direction-selective and non-direction-selective populations, while concurrently extracting multi-dimensional velocity, directional, and chromatic tuning profiles.
papers.authors: Marc Büttner, Matej Znidaric, Roland Diggelmann, Federica Bianca Rosselli, Annalisa Bucci, Andreas Hierlemann, Felix Franke

papers.title: Mice and humans use ambiguous local motion to stabilize gaze
papers.abstract: Visual motion sensors in the periphery capture local contour displacements within restricted receptive fields, yielding directional ambiguity known as the aperture problem. To investigate whether reflexive oculomotor systems resolve this aperture ambiguity or execute directly upon ambiguous local motion cues, sensorimotor transmission was tracked from retinal ganglion cells through the pretectal nucleus of the optic tract (NOT) to downstream compensatory eye movements in mice and humans. Presenting geometric objects where 1D edge orientation is decoupled from true 2D translational vectors demonstrated that NOT neuron directional tuning shifts systematically toward local edge contours rather than tracking global object trajectories, a property replicated by linear spatial integration of retinal inputs. This local motion bias reliably propagated to optokinetic reflex behavior: vertical motion of tilted contours induced pronounced horizontal compensatory eye movements in both mice and humans (with human bias exacerbating under central foveal scotomas), demonstrating that gaze stabilization relies on a conserved, computationally direct heuristic rather than explicit global motion reconstruction.
papers.authors: Federica Bianca Rosselli, Marc Büttner, Annalisa Bucci, Felix Franke

papers.title: In-sensor cryptographic signature generation for linking a physical process and an immutable digital entity
papers.abstract: The growing capability of generative deep learning to synthesize realistic digital media undermines confidence in recorded observational and scientific data. To establish intrinsic provenance and tamper-resistance at the direct point of signal acquisition, this study presents a sensor chip architecture that monolithically couples physical signal detection with cryptographic verification circuits. Fabricated using 180-nm complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor (CMOS) processing, the device directly incorporates continuous hardware-level hashing units and public-key cryptographic signature engines on-chip with voltage-sensing electrodes. The system generates asymmetric cryptographic signatures of measured extracellular field potentials from cardiac myocytes in real time, binding physical measurement events to tamper-evident cryptographic hashes verifiable on public distributed ledgers before potential software-level manipulation can occur.
papers.authors: Fernando Cardes, Sebastian Bürgel, Xinyue Yuan, Qianchen Yu, Arianna Rubino, Jihyun Lee, Raziyeh Bounik, Vijay Viswam, Andreas Hierlemann, Felix Franke

papers.title: Synchronization of visual perception within the human fovea
papers.abstract: In the primate fovea centralis, anatomical specialization displaces inner retinal layers from the central umbo, forcing unmyelinated axons from temporal retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) into long, curved trajectories around the foveal depression while nasal axons project straight to the optic disc. Despite these stark disparities in intraretinal path length, human visual perception and reaction times triggered by single-cone photostimulation remain uniform across the central visual field. Using subcellular-resolution high-density microelectrode arrays (HD-MEAs) on ex vivo human retinal tissue paired with transmission electron microscopy and biophysical pathway modeling, action potential conduction velocities were found to vary systematically with path length: temporal foveal axons maintain larger cross-sectional calibers and exhibit conduction speeds exceeding those of nasal counterparts by over 40%. This biological compensation equalizes transmission delays to millisecond precision, revealing an intraretinal structural adaptation that synchronizes sensory signal arrival at the optic disc before brain processing.
papers.authors: Annalisa Bucci, Marc Büttner, Niklas Domdei, Federica B. Rosselli, Matej Znidaric, Julian Bartram, Tobias Gänswein, Roland Diggelmann, Martina De Gennaro, Cameron S. Cowan, Wolf Harmening, Andreas Hierlemann, Botond Roska, Felix Franke

papers.title: Action potential propagation speed compensates for traveling distance in the human retina
papers.abstract: The axons of human retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) are unmyelinated and exhibit low conduction velocities, posing a significant challenge for the brain to integrate visual signals from across the retina synchronously. By combining HD-MEA recordings, electron microscopy, and mathematical modeling, the researchers quantified how axonal propagation speeds vary as a function of eccentricity and soma location. The study found that conduction speeds are spatially heterogeneous and increase with axonal length, particularly in the foveal region. A mathematical model of the retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL) demonstrates that these speed adjustments compensate for variations in intraretinal path length, thereby minimizing temporal dispersion of visual information arriving at the optic nerve. This preprint provides the underlying neurophysiological evidence for the structural compensation mechanism that ensures temporal coherence in the human visual field before signals even reach the lateral geniculate nucleus or primary visual cortex.
papers.authors: Annalisa Bucci, Marc Büttner, Niklas Domdei, Federica Bianca Rosselli, Matej Znidaric, Roland Diggelmann, Martina De Gennaro, Cameron S. Cowan, Wolf Harmening, Andreas Hierlemann, Botond Roska, Felix Franke

0219.name: Filip Děchtěrenko
0219.department: Department of Cognitive Psychology, Institute of Psychology
0219.bio: Filip Děchtěrenko is the head of the Department of Cognitive Psychology at the Institute of Psychology of the Czech Academy of Sciences. Their research investigates the cognitive mechanisms underlying visual memory, attention, and perception, focusing on how humans process and retain information from complex natural scenes. Děchtěrenko utilizes a methodology combining behavioral experiments and eye-tracking with computational techniques, such as convolutional neural networks, to model image similarity and predict recognition performance. Their recent work explores the role of typicality in visual recognition and the limits of detail retention in visual long-term memory.
0219.research_direction: Dr. Děchtěrenko's recent work bridges fundamental questions about visual memory capacity with the cognitive dynamics of human-AI interaction. In the visual domain, they have recently been investigating the limits of long-term memory fidelity for complex scenes, using repeated recognition probes and surprise drawing tasks to explore how spatial granularity is retained and how artistic expertise might alter free recall mechanisms. Concurrently, their research examines how users integrate Large Language Models into creative problem-solving and academic writing, employing process-mining techniques to map iterative prompting strategies and human-AI dialogue. Across these applied AI studies, they are particularly focused on the metacognitive vulnerabilities of using generative tools, actively questioning how AI assistance influences users' epistemic beliefs, cognitive load, and their ability to accurately calibrate self-evaluations and monitor information reliability.

papers.title: Low detail retention in visual memory despite focused effort
papers.abstract: The research investigated whether intensive encoding of a restricted number of complex scenes could mitigate the limitations typically observed in high-fidelity recognition for visual details. The authors implemented a novel experimental design incorporating repeated memory probes for specific image segments to track mnemonic decay and long-term retention. Results indicated that despite high intentional focus and extended study time, participants failed to achieve high-accuracy detail-oriented memory. While observers reliably identified presented content and novel foils, they exhibited a pronounced failure to reject distractors sampled from unseen parts of previously studied photographs, suggesting that visual long-term memory representations for scenes lack sufficient granularity to exclude semantically and perceptually similar distractors.
papers.authors: Filip Děchtěrenko, Jiří Lukavský, Petr Adámek

papers.title: Visual free recall and recognition in art students and laypeople
papers.abstract: This study compared the visual memory capacities of art students and laypeople through a combination of surprise drawing tasks and recognition tests. While recognition memory performance was comparable across both groups, art students demonstrated significantly superior visual free recall. Analysis of memory-based drawings revealed that artists produced higher-quality representations with greater fidelity to the original spatial and object information.
