At the individual level, the quality of a participant's drawing was a significant predictor of their recognition accuracy, indicating that artistic expertise facilitates the encoding and subsequent retrieval of detailed visual representations from long-term memory.
papers.authors: Filip Děchtěrenko, Wilma A. Bainbridge, Jiří Lukavský

papers.title: Prompting for creative problem-solving: A process-mining study
papers.abstract: The researchers employed qualitative interaction analysis and process-mining techniques (specifically heuristics miner) to investigate how university students utilize Large Language Models (LLMs) to solve complex, ill-defined problems. The study identified specific prompting strategies, such as providing elaborated context, defining clear evaluation criteria, and offering iterative feedback, as significant correlates of higher problem-solving performance (quality, elaboration, and originality). High-performing students engaged in intensive, iterative human-AI regulation characterized by dialogue and monitoring, whereas low-performing students primarily used the AI as a static information resource. These findings underscore the necessity of active metacognitive regulation in optimizing the outcomes of generative AI-assisted creative workflows.
papers.authors: Marek Urban, Jiří Lukavský, Cyril Brom, Veronika Hein, Filip Švácha, Filip Děchtěrenko, Kamila Urban

papers.title: “ChatGPT can make mistakes. Check important info.” Epistemic beliefs and metacognitive accuracy in students’ integration of ChatGPT content into academic writing
papers.abstract: The study examined the integration of correct and incorrect information from expert-written versus ChatGPT-generated articles into student academic writing, focusing on the role of epistemic beliefs and metacognitive accuracy. In a preregistered experiment, participants evaluated the reliability of source materials while completing a writing task. Results indicated that students often treated ChatGPT as an epistemic authority despite the presence of factual inaccuracies and hallucinations. The findings revealed that students' metacognitive accuracy in identifying erroneous information was significantly lower when assisted by AI, highlighting a critical vulnerability in hybrid human-AI academic collaboration and the need for enhanced digital literacy and verification strategies.
papers.authors: Marek Urban, Cyril Brom, Jiří Lukavský, Filip Děchtěrenko, Veronika Hein, Filip Švácha, Petra Kmoníčková, Kamila Urban

papers.title: ChatGPT improves creative problem-solving performance in university students: An experimental study
papers.abstract: In a preregistered experimental study, the authors assessed the impact of Large Language Models (LLMs) on complex creative problem-solving tasks among university students. Participants utilized ChatGPT 3.5 to resolve ill-defined design challenges, with outcomes evaluated for quality, originality, and elaboration. AI assistance significantly improved performance across all creativity metrics (effect sizes d = 0.55 to 0.69) while reducing perceived task difficulty and cognitive load. However, the study observed that AI support did not enhance metacognitive calibration, as participants frequently overestimated their performance when using the tool. The results suggest that while LLMs provide powerful cognitive scaffolding for ideation, they may simultaneously impede accurate self-evaluation of problem-solving efficacy.
papers.authors: Marek Urban, Filip Děchtěrenko, Jiří Lukavský, Veronika Hrabalová, Filip Svacha, Cyril Brom, Kamila Urban

0220.name: Frank Bremmer
0220.bio: Bremmer investigates the neural mechanisms underlying multisensory spatial and motion perception, focusing on how visual processing is modulated by eye movements such as saccades. Their work integrates single-cell recordings and EEG in animal models with fMRI, behavioral psychophysics, and computational modeling in humans to decode the integration of visual, tactile, and vestibular signals. A focus of this research involves characterizing the neural dynamics of perisaccadic perception and self-motion (heading) encoding in the primate brain. Bremmer also collaborates on clinical studies to investigate disturbances in motion processing and balance control in patients with neurological and psychiatric disorders, including Parkinson’s disease.
0220.research_direction: Dr. Bremmer has recently been investigating how the primate visual system processes 3D space, coordinates complex eye movements, and integrates cues for self-motion. Their recent work explores the underlying neural and behavioral mechanisms of 3D vision, combining macaque electrophysiology to examine gaze-invariant depth coding in the ventral intraparietal area with human behavioral studies probing the potential dissociation between saccade and vergence initiation. In the domain of spatial navigation, they are utilizing optic flow paradigms and newly developed multimodal virtual reality datasets to assess how active eye movements and head tracking influence visual path integration and distance perception. Finally, Dr. Bremmer is also leveraging their expertise in movement tracking for clinical applications, developing explainable machine learning frameworks to detect subtle, high-frequency postural sway abnormalities in individuals with Parkinson's disease.

papers.title: Dissociate triggering of conjunctive and disjunctive eye movements
papers.abstract: The study examines the coordination of saccadic (version) and vergence eye movements during gaze shifts in 3D space. Utilizing the Size-Latency effect to modulate saccade initiation, the researchers measured eye movement responses to ring targets with varying vertical offsets and binocular disparities. The results revealed that saccade latencies are sensitive to target eccentricity and hemifield but remain unaffected by disparity, whereas vergence latencies depend on disparity parameters rather than spatial position. The absence of correlation between these latencies and the differing skewness of their probability distributions suggest that version and vergence are triggered by independent neural mechanisms.
papers.authors: Baptiste Caziot, Frank Bremmer

papers.title: Coding of egocentric distance in the macaque ventral intraparietal area
papers.abstract: This research investigates the gaze invariance of 3D spatial representations within the macaque ventral intraparietal area (VIP). By recording single-unit activity while varying vergence angles and disparity-based depth, the authors demonstrate that VIP neurons maintain robust egocentric distance encoding across different eye positions. Disparity-tuning curves were found to shift in accordance with vergence, supporting a gaze-invariant reference frame. Furthermore, the results show that visual motion direction selectivity in VIP is multiplexed with distance information and remains stable despite changes in binocular disparity or ocular vergence.
papers.authors: Baptiste Caziot, Sadra Fathkhani, Frank Bremmer

papers.title: Sway frequencies may predict postural instability in Parkinson's disease: a novel convolutional neural network approach
papers.abstract: The authors present a machine learning framework for the objective detection of postural impairments in individuals with early-to-mid stage Parkinson's disease (PD). Center of pressure (COP) and center of mass (COM) trajectories were transformed into time-frequency spectrograms using wavelet decomposition and subsequently processed by a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN). The model achieved perfect classification performance (100% accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity) in distinguishing PD patients from healthy age-matched controls. Explainable AI analysis via GradCAM revealed that the most discriminative features were concentrated in the high-frequency bands of the postural sway signal, highlighting their predictive value for balance deficits.
papers.authors: David Engel, R. Stefan Greulich, Alberto Parola, Kaleb Vinehout, Justus Student, Josefine Waldthaler, Lars Timmermann, Frank Bremmer

papers.title: Path integration from optic flow and the role of eye movements
papers.abstract: This study evaluates the influence of voluntary eye movements on the accuracy of visual path integration during simulated self-motion. Participants performed a distance discrimination task using optic flow stimuli under four conditions: free-viewing, central fixation, and restricted gaze windows. Using generalized linear mixed-effects models to analyze behavioral responses and eye-tracking data, the researchers found that although cumulative eye-movement amplitudes correlated with travel distance, the discrimination accuracy was not significantly improved by free eye movements compared to fixation. These results suggest that standard fixation-based experimental paradigms do not fundamentally bias the assessment of self-motion-based distance perception.
papers.authors: Renate Reisenegger, Frank Bremmer

papers.title: Comprehensive VR dataset for machine learning: Head- and eye-centred video and positional data
papers.abstract: This article describes a multimodal dataset designed for developing and benchmarking machine learning models in virtual reality (VR) environments. The data includes high-resolution video streams from head-mounted display (HMD) cameras, providing both ego-centric and eye-centered perspectives. These recordings are synchronized with 6-degree-of-freedom (6-DOF) head tracking and eye-tracking positional data (gaze vectors and pupil positions) from human subjects performing a visual search task across diverse virtual scenes. The dataset serves as a resource for researching gaze prediction, egomotion estimation, and human-computer interaction in immersive systems.
papers.authors: Alexander Kreß, Markus Lappe, Frank Bremmer

0221.name: Frank H. Durgin
0221.bio: Frank H. Durgin is the Elizabeth and Sumner Hayward Professor of Psychology and social sciences at Swarthmore College, where they investigate the mechanisms underlying human spatial representation and figurative language. Durgin's research focuses on systematic distortions in the perception of locomotor space and slant, employing high-fidelity virtual reality and perceptuo-motor calibration tasks to study how the visual system optimizes information for action. Additionally, Durgin utilizes psycholinguistic methods, including eye-tracking and event-related potentials (ERPs), to explore the cognitive processing of metaphors and their role in implicit bias. Their work provides evidence for coding strategies that prioritize functional efficiency over geometric accuracy, which challenges theories of embodied perception.
0221.research_direction: Dr. Durgin's recent work spans diverse topics across visual perception and cognitive linguistics. In vision science, their recent work explores the mechanisms underlying numerosity perception and spatial distortions, specifically investigating how figure-ground segmentation, stereopsis, and implied occlusion drive subset underestimation illusions in multi-color displays. They have also recently been using immersive virtual reality to examine how internal gravitational reference frames govern the exaggerated perception of angular elevation in 3D space. Beyond vision, they are investigating the semantic and affective dimensions of language, employing implicit measures to test how figurative language conveys emotional depth and whether grammatical gender subtly shapes the conceptualization of inanimate objects.

papers.title: Change blindness, subset segmentation, and the perceptual underestimation of subset numerosity
papers.abstract: This study characterizes the precision and systematic biases in the human perceptual estimation of color-defined subsets within heterochromatic dot arrays. While humans can simultaneously evaluate multiple subsets, the authors document a reliable underestimation of foregrounded dots (e.g., light gray among white) when presented on medium-gray backgrounds. Across six experiments employing color-change detection paradigms (change blindness), the research tests the hypothesis that these biases stem from incomplete figure-ground segmentation. Results indicate that accurate subset estimation is contingent upon resistance to foreground selection; specifically, even when stereoscopic depth cues are provided, foregrounded dots remain more susceptible to color change detection failures. The findings suggest that the perceptual underestimation of mixed-color supersets can be modeled as the integration of a significantly underestimated foreground with a relatively accurate background estimate.
papers.authors: Katelyn Becker, Eliana Dellinger, Frank H. Durgin

papers.title: Figurative language is (implicitly) more dynamic and emotionally deeper than literal language
papers.abstract: Two experiments utilized a data-driven implicit semantic differential method paired with principal component analysis (PCA) to investigate the latent affective dimensions distinguishing figurative language from literal counterparts. In the first study, metaphoric narratives were found to differ significantly from literal controls along three distinct PCA-derived dimensions—specifically scoring higher on 'Dynamism' and 'Depth'—even when explicit valence norming showed no differences. The second study replicated these findings at the level of individual words used in metaphors and similes. These results suggest that figurative language conveys enhanced affective resonance and emotional complexity compared to literal renderings, supporting neuroimaging evidence of stronger emotional engagement with metaphoric text.
papers.authors: Tshering Yanzom Dorji, Frank H. Durgin

papers.title: A conceptual replication of an implicit test of grammatical gender effects on inanimate concepts
papers.abstract: This research presents two preregistered conceptual replications of Konishi’s (1993) seminal work regarding the Whorfian hypothesis that grammatical gender influences the connotative semantics of inanimate concepts. Using the potency dimension of the semantic differential method as an implicit measure, the authors tested bilingual native speakers of German and Spanish, as well as a control group of monolingual English speakers. The first study examined whether native grammatical gender affected potency ratings when tested in a second language (English), while the second used native-language testing. In both experiments, Bayesian analysis strongly favored the null hypothesis, providing robust evidence against the claim that arbitrary linguistic gender markings modulate the implicit conceptualization of inanimate objects.
papers.authors: Devyani Mahajan, Frank H. Durgin

papers.title: Implied occlusion and subset underestimation contribute to the weak-outnumber-strong numerosity illusion
papers.abstract: The authors investigate the mechanisic basis of the 'weak-outnumber-strong' (WOS) illusion, wherein low-contrast dots appear more numerous than high-contrast dots in intermixed displays. Four experiments involving 712 participants evaluate two proposed principles: (1) general subset underestimation in multi-color mixtures and (2) a filling-in process where low-contrast (gray) dots are perceived as being partially occluded by high-contrast (white) dots. By manipulating pictorial occlusion cues and binocular stereopsis, the researchers demonstrate that the illusion is abolished if the lower-contrast dots are depicted as the foreground, but remains robust when they are depicted as the background. The study concludes that the WOS effect results from a combination of segmentation-driven subset underestimation and perceptual completion of implied occluded regions.
papers.authors: Eliana G. Dellinger, Katelyn M. Becker, Frank H. Durgin

papers.title: Default reference frames for angular expansion in the perception of visual direction
papers.abstract: Perceived angular elevation relative to the horizon is typically exaggerated by a gain factor of approximately 1.5, a phenomenon known as the scale expansion hypothesis. This study investigates whether this exaggeration persists in the absence of visual gravitational cues. Using immersive virtual environments (VE) and supine observers looking straight up, five experiments utilized magnitude estimation and psychometric matching to internal standards. The results indicate that the 1.5 gain for elevation is maintained even in nearly featureless VEs. Furthermore, supine observers showed similar exaggeration for azimuthal judgments, suggesting that when targets are viewed along the gravitational vertical, the brain defaults to an elevation-based scaling frame. This implies that the internal gravitational reference frame serves as the primary default for angular expansion in 3D space.
papers.authors: Prince U. D. Tardeh, Crystal Xu, Frank H. Durgin

0222.name: Frank Tong
0222.bio: Frank Tong investigates the neural foundations of visual perception, attentional selection, and object recognition using high-resolution 7-Tesla fMRI, visual psychophysics, and computational modeling. Tong applied multivariate pattern classification to decode subjective mental states and the contents of visual working memory from early cortical activity. Their research examines how early visual areas contribute to conscious awareness and the maintenance of information in the absence of physical stimuli. Currently, Tong compares biological perception with convolutional neural networks to model visual processing and robustness.
0222.research_direction: Dr. Tong has recently been investigating the computational principles underlying robust visual perception, frequently comparing human behavioral and neural data against deep neural network models. Their recent work explores how developmentally realistic constraints—such as visual noise or image blur—shape object recognition in both humans and artificial networks, while also evaluating the degree of nonlinear complexity necessary to accurately model primary visual cortex. In parallel, they are using fMRI and multivariate pattern analysis to understand how the visual hierarchy constructs stable representations from ambiguous or incomplete retinal input. Specifically, they have been probing phenomena like amodal completion during partial occlusion and the emergence of form-invariant motion perception to map where and how these robust representations are constructed across early and higher-order cortical areas.

papers.title: Emergence of form-independent direction selectivity in human V3A and MT+
papers.abstract: This fMRI study investigated the neural progression from form-dependent to form-invariant motion representations in the human visual hierarchy. Utilizing multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) and linear decoding, the researchers examined direction-selective activity for two distinct motion types: drifting sinusoidal gratings and random dots. While early visual areas (V1, V2) exhibited robust direction selectivity for each stimulus individually, they failed to generalize across motion types, indicating that their responses are primarily driven by local orientation-motion contingencies. In contrast, higher-order dorsal areas V3A and MT+ demonstrated significant cross-stimulus generalization for both linear and spiral motion trajectories. These findings reveal that form-invariant motion selectivity, essential for overcoming the aperture problem and achieving robust motion perception, emerges predominantly in specialized regions of the dorsal stream.
papers.authors: Sang Wook Hong, Frank Tong

papers.title: Category-specific perceptual learning of robust object recognition modelled using deep neural networks
papers.abstract: This study examines the computational and behavioral underpinnings of noise robustness in object recognition through the lens of perceptual learning. Human participants and convolutional neural networks (CNNs) were trained to identify objects from animate and inanimate categories embedded in varying levels of Gaussian noise. Behavioral results indicated that humans acquire category-specific improvements in robustness, whereas standard pre-trained CNNs initially displayed more category-general gains. However, when CNN models were pre-tuned to match human-level baseline accuracy, they replicated the human pattern of category-specific refinement. A layer-wise susceptibility analysis using Pearson correlation metrics showed that category-general robustness to signal-to-noise ratio (SSNR) fluctuations emerged in early layers, while category-specific enhancements were localized in deeper layers, suggesting a hierarchical organization of learned robustness.
papers.authors: Hojin Jang, Frank Tong

papers.title: Convolutional neural network models applied to neuronal responses in macaque V1 reveal limited nonlinear processing
papers.abstract: The research re-evaluates the prevailing view that deep, multi-layered nonlinear computations are necessary to predict the complex response properties of macaque V1 neurons. By systematically comparing standard CNN architectures (e.g., VGG-19) with simpler models, the authors discovered that the high predictive performance of deeper layers often results from non-computational factors, specifically the scaling of input image dimensions relative to unit receptive field sizes. When controlling for these variables, a modified version of AlexNet featuring significantly fewer nonlinear stages was found to be sufficient to account for V1 activity. Further analysis using Gabor pyramid models and tests for contrast saturation and normalization confirmed that relatively shallow hierarchical processing can effectively model V1 responses, indicating that the perceived necessity for deep nonlinear models in primary visual cortex may be overstated.
papers.authors: Hui-Yuan Miao, Frank Tong

papers.title: Improved modeling of human vision by incorporating robustness to blur in convolutional neural networks
papers.abstract: Standard convolutional neural networks (CNNs) exhibit severe vulnerability to image blur, a phenomenon pervasive in natural human vision due to peripheral resolution limits and optical defocus. This paper demonstrates that incorporating a 'developmental diet' of blurry images during training—or providing specific blur-augmentation—results in CNN models that are significantly more aligned with human behavioral and neural data. Blur-trained networks demonstrated superior performance in predicting fMRI representational similarity matrices (RSM) across the visual hierarchy (V1 through VOT) and exhibited a robust shape bias, contrasting with the texture-bias of standard models. These results suggest that the pervasive blur encountered during biological development acts as a critical constraint that encourages the learning of more generalized, robust, and human-like visual representations.
papers.authors: Hojin Jang, Frank Tong

papers.title: Evidence of strong amodal completion in both early and high-level visual cortices
papers.abstract: Amodal completion allows the visual system to represent the complete geometry of objects despite partial occlusion, but the cortical locus of these completed features remains contentious. Using high-resolution fMRI and multivoxel activity pattern analysis, this study mapped the representation of occluded object parts in human observers. The data revealed that information concerning the shape of occluded regions is decodable as early as V1, as well as in intermediate areas V2, V3, and V4, and high-level object-selective regions (LO, pFs). The finding of completion-related signals in primary visual cortex supports the hypothesis that amodal completion involves an active, feedback-driven reconstruction of missing features at early retinotopic sites, rather than being solely a result of high-level semantic or symbolic inference.
papers.authors: David D. Coggan, Frank Tong

0223.name: Frans Verstraten
0223.bio: Frans Verstraten is the McCaughey Chair of Psychology at the University of Sydney and a researcher in the fields of vision science and experimental psychology. Verstraten’s research focuses on the mechanisms underlying visual perception, including perceptual adaptation, motion perception, and the temporal limits of visual attention. They utilize psychophysical methodologies and immersive virtual reality to investigate how the brain processes and calibrates sensory signals within dynamic environments. Recent work by Verstraten examines the intersection of sensorimotor performance and rhythmic bodily states, specifically exploring how locomotion phases modulate visual detection accuracy.
0223.research_direction: Dr. Verstraten has recently been investigating the history, culture, and future trajectory of the vision science community. Their recent work explores the sociology of perception research, specifically examining how informal, face-to-face academic environments influence the synthesis of complex psychophysical data and new neuroscientific paradigms. Additionally, they have been documenting the historical foundations of visual neuroscience by analyzing the academic legacy of pioneering figures in the field. Through these historical and cultural perspectives, Dr. Verstraten highlights the foundational development of multi-vectorial motion processing frameworks, the evolution of computational modeling, and the enduring impact of multidisciplinary mentorship on the study of biological motion perception.

papers.title: The coffee room and the future of perception research
papers.abstract: This article provides a critical analysis of the diminishing role of informal academic environments—symbolized by the 'coffee room'—in the contemporary landscape of perception research. The author argues that the synthesis of complex psychophysical data and the advancement of neuroscientific paradigms rely heavily on spontaneous, face-to-face discourse among specialists. The paper posits that the current trend toward remote work and digital isolation threatens the serendipitous exchange of ideas that historically catalyzed major breakthroughs in visual perception, and calls for a re-prioritization of communal physical spaces to maintain the intellectual vitality of the field.
papers.authors: Frans A J Verstraten

papers.title: Obituary: Wim van de Grind (23 April 1936-14 July 2024)
papers.abstract: This commemorative article provides a comprehensive overview of the academic contributions and legacy of Professor Wim van de Grind, a pioneering figure in the fields of visual neuroscience and neuro-ethology. The text details his rigorous development of the multi-vectorial motion processing framework and the physiological foundations of natural intelligence. It underscores his influential role at Utrecht University, where his multidisciplinary approach to psychophysics and computational modeling shaped the careers of numerous prominent vision scientists, highlighting his lasting impact on the study of biological motion perception and sensory-motor coordination.
papers.authors: Frans Verstraten

0224.name: Freek van Ede
0224.department: Department of Experimental and Applied Psychology
0224.bio: Freek van Ede is an Associate Professor at Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam and the Principal Investigator of the Proactive Brain Lab. Van Ede's research investigates how the human brain selectively prioritizes and retains sensory information in working memory to guide prospective goal-directed behavior. Utilizing a combination of electroencephalography (EEG), high-resolution eye-tracking—specifically microsaccadic analysis—and virtual reality, they explore the neural dynamics of internal attention and anticipation. Their work focuses on the functional links between mnemonic representations, motor planning, and temporal expectations within a proactive perspective of cognition.
0224.research_direction: Dr. van Ede has recently been investigating the dynamic interplay between visual working memory, covert spatial attention, and motor planning. Their recent work explores how fixational eye movements, such as microsaccades, relate to internal attentional states across shifting and maintenance phases, utilizing simultaneous oculometrics and EEG to untangle oculomotor activity from neural markers of spatial selection like the N2pc. They are also examining the temporal coordination of attention during visual search, specifically questioning how the brain concurrently aligns internal search goals in memory with the selection of external sensory targets. Additionally, their research probes how varying levels of environmental cue certainty influence the anticipatory prioritization of visual representations versus subsequent motor programs.

papers.title: Proactive visual and motor prioritization differentially scale with cue reliability
papers.abstract: The investigation addressed how varying levels of environmental cue certainty (100%, 80%, and 60% reliability) modulate the proactive prioritization of visual representations and their associated motor plans in working memory (WM). Using high-density EEG in human volunteers, we independently tracked the neural dynamics of visual and motor selection by measuring posterior alpha-band (8–12 Hz) lateralization and central mu/beta-band (8–30 Hz) lateralization, respectively. Results revealed a striking dissociation: while visual prioritization remained robust in amplitude and timing across all reliability levels, motor prioritization scaled significantly with cue certainty, showing delayed onsets and diminished amplitudes as reliability decreased. This suggests that the anticipatory deployment of motor programs is more susceptible to environmental volatility and follows a more cautious strategy than the prioritization of the guiding sensory representations.
papers.authors: Sisi Wang, Freek van Ede

papers.title: Microsaccades track shifting but not necessarily maintaining covert visual-spatial attention
papers.abstract: This study evaluated whether fixational eye movements reliably track internal states of covert spatial attention across different functional stages. Using an orientation change detection paradigm with precise oculometric monitoring, we isolated the initial shift of attention to a cued location from the subsequent period of attentional maintenance. We demonstrate that directional biases in microsaccades robustly reflect the dynamic process of shifting attention, but these biases notably diminish during sustained maintenance, even when behavioral metrics confirm continued attentional focusing on the target. These findings indicate that the oculomotor system is primarily coupled to the redeployment of attention rather than its stable maintenance, suggesting that microsaccade directionality is a selective marker for attentional orienting.
papers.authors: Anna M. van Harmelen, Freek van Ede

papers.title: Concurrent selection of internal goals and external sensations during visual search
papers.abstract: We investigated the temporal coordination between the selection of internal search goals in working memory and external search targets in the environment. Using a novel search paradigm and multivariate decoding of EEG signals and fixational gaze, we challenged the serial-processing hypothesis which posits that internal and external attention must take turns. Our data provide evidence that internal and external selection processes can proceed concurrently, supported by largely non-overlapping neural activity patterns. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these processes can be effectively executed even when attention is directed to diametrically opposite spatial locations in mind and in the world, revealing an unexpected degree of flexibility in the simultaneous management of internal and external attentional resources.
papers.authors: Baiwei Liu, Freek van Ede

papers.title: Microsaccades strongly modulate but do not directly cause the EEG N2pc marker of spatial attention
papers.abstract: The N2pc is a canonical lateralized EEG event-related potential associated with covert spatial selection, but its relationship with fixational eye movements has remained controversial. By combining simultaneous eye-tracking and scalp EEG, we analyzed the N2pc amplitude as a function of microsaccade presence and direction. We found that while microsaccades in the direction of the attended stimulus profoundly enhance the N2pc and microsaccades away from it can abolish it, a statistically significant N2pc is still present in trials entirely devoid of microsaccades. This dissociation proves that the N2pc is not a direct artifact of oculomotor activity or retinal displacement, but rather a neural signature of spatial selection that is significantly modulated by, yet functionally distinct from, the oculomotor execution of microsaccades.
papers.authors: Baiwei Liu, Shuai Kong, Freek van Ede

papers.title: Looking into Working Memory to Verify Potential Search Targets
papers.abstract: Visual search requires a continuous comparison between sensory inputs and internal templates. We leveraged a recently identified gaze-based marker of internal visual focusing to track the internal inspection process during the confirmation or dismissal of potential search targets. We show that human participants 'look back' into the spatial layout of working memory when encountering external stimuli that match the search goal's features. This mnemonic verification process was slower than perceptual verification and was specifically associated with increased frontal midline theta (4–8 Hz) activity. These results establish internal verification as a core, measurable component of visual search and demonstrate how the brain dynamically samples from memory to guide external behavior.
papers.authors: Sisi Wang, Freek van Ede

0225.name: Frédéric Gosselin
0225.bio: Frédéric Gosselin is a Professor in the Department of Psychology at the Université de Montréal and the Co-director of CerebrUM. Gosselin developed the 'Bubbles' method, a psychophysical technique used to isolate and identify the specific visual information humans utilize during recognition and categorization tasks. Their research integrates psychophysics, cognitive neuroscience, and computational modeling—including EEG, fMRI, and machine learning—to decode mental representations. This work investigates the neural correlates of individual differences in face and object perception.
0225.research_direction: Dr. Gosselin has recently been investigating high-level visual representation, with a particular emphasis on the psychophysics of face perception and mental imagery. Their recent work explores the underlying mechanisms of face processing, using reverse correlation to map idiosyncratic internal templates of facial expressions and testing the relative contributions of local feature extraction versus holistic integration in human face identification. They are also examining the functional overlap between sensory perception and mental imagery by measuring psychophysical adaptation aftereffects induced by internally visualizing specific face identities. Broadening their scope to whole-brain neural dynamics, Dr. Gosselin is mapping the spatiotemporal trajectory of natural scene processing through the data-driven fusion of large-scale EEG and fMRI datasets. Additionally, they have been developing accessible methodological tools for the wider vision science community, such as a rapid psychophysical procedure to estimate screen gamma and precisely control stimulus luminance during uncalibrated web-based experiments.

papers.title: Is it pain, anger, disgust, or sadness? Individual differences in expectations of pain facial expressions
papers.abstract: The authors conducted five online experiments (total N = 956) utilizing computer-generated facial stimuli to characterize the internal templates observers associate with the expression of pain. Using reverse correlation and data-driven clustering, they identified three distinct subgroups of participants with unique internal representations of pain facial expressions. A key finding was that pain representations frequently overlap with the facial features diagnostic of anger, disgust, and sadness, suggesting that the common miscategorization of pain is rooted in suboptimal and idiosyncratic mental models of affective states. The study concludes that both movement intensity and individual differences in these mental expectations significantly modulate the perception and subsequent assessment of pain signals.
papers.authors: Arianne Richer, Francis Gingras, Marie-Pier Plouffe-Demers, Daniel Fiset, Caroline Blais, Frédéric Gosselin

papers.title: Does perceptual integration efficiency predict face identification skills?
papers.abstract: The researchers investigated whether the efficiency of integrating visual information across multiple facial features predicts individual differences in face identification ability. Using a psychophysical paradigm that independently measures part-based recognition efficiency and holistic integration (defined as the performance gain when multiple parts are combined), they assessed a cohort of neurotypical observers. Multiple regression analysis demonstrated that while part-based processing efficiency is a robust predictor of face identification skill, perceptual integration efficiency does not significantly correlate with overall performance. These results challenge classical holistic theories by suggesting that idiosyncratic expertise in face recognition is primarily driven by the precision of local feature extraction rather than global integration mechanisms.
papers.authors: Francis Gingras, Daniel Fiset, Marie-Pier Plouffe-Demers, Amanda Estéphan, Michel N’Guiamba, Dan Sun, Ye Zhang, Frédéric Gosselin

papers.title: Neural activity resolved in space and time through fusion of large-scale EEG and fMRI datasets
papers.abstract: To overcome the temporal limitations of fMRI and the spatial limitations of EEG, the authors developed a data-driven 'EEG-to-fMRI' mapping technique. Leveraging the Natural Scenes Dataset (NSD), they employed fractional ridge regression to predict voxelwise fMRI activity from high-density EEG channel amplitudes at specific time points. This fusion method yielded a full spatiotemporal trajectory of natural scene processing in the human brain, revealing initial feedforward activity in the early visual cortex that subsequently propagated through ventral and dorsal streams. The results demonstrate that neural activity peaks in accuracy in parietal regions approximately 300 ms post-stimulus, providing a voxel-level empirical source reconstruction of the visual processing stream.
papers.authors: Ian Charest, Peter Brotherwood, Mathias Salvas-Hebert, Kendrick Kay, Frédéric Gosselin

papers.title: Linearizing Screen Gamma for Precise Psychophysical Online Studies in Less Than 5 Minutes
papers.abstract: Vision scientists face significant challenges in controlling stimulus luminance during web-based experiments due to uncalibrated participant displays. The authors propose and validate a rapid psychophysical task to estimate screen Gamma by matching the perceived brightness of uniform squares to flanker stimuli alternating between two luminance levels. By measuring perceived brightness at 31 luminance points, researchers can generate a luminance lookup table to correct stimuli in real-time. Validation with remote participants via the Pack & Go platform demonstrated high test-retest reliability and linear model fits (average R² = 0.999), confirming that this three-minute procedure enables precise luminance control for online psychophysics.
papers.authors: Francis Gingras, Alex Cousineau, Daniel Fiset, Caroline Blais, Frédéric Gosselin

papers.title: Aftereffects following adaptation to face mental images
papers.abstract: This study employs a psychophysiological adaptation paradigm to investigate the degree of overlap between mental imagery and visual perception. Participants were trained to imagine specific face identities (Face A or Face B) and were subsequently tested on their ability to categorize morph levels between the two. The authors observed significant shifts in the categorization psychometric function depending on which face was imagined, indicating that mental imagery can induce adaptation aftereffects similar to those produced by physical stimuli. These findings suggest that mental imagery recruits high-level visual representations in the brain, including those in face-selective cortical areas, and provides a tool for quantifying individual differences in imagery vividness.
papers.authors: Mathias Salvas-Hébert, Vincent Taschereau-Dumouchel, Ian Charest, Frédéric Gosselin

0226.name: Fuat Balci
0226.bio: Fuat Balci is a Professor of Biological Sciences at the University of Manitoba who studies the computational and neural mechanisms of interval timing and decision-making. Balci's research integrates empirical psychophysics with theoretical modeling to analyze how humans and animals perform temporal risk assessments and maximize reward rates. Through methodologies such as optogenetics, transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS), and drift-diffusion modeling, Balci investigates the role of the nigrostriatal dopamine system in temporal control. They also examine how these cognitive functions are affected by aging and neuropsychiatric disorders.
0226.research_direction: Dr. Balci's recent work explores the computational and neural mechanisms of interval timing and metacognition across both human and rodent models. Using techniques like optogenetics and operant conditioning, they have recently been investigating how midbrain dopamine circuits modulate subjective time and how mice extrapolate temporal magnitudes across spatial frameworks. They are also examining the foundational forms of awareness by probing whether rodents can metacognitively monitor the accuracy of their own time-based motor actions. Additionally, in human subjects, Dr. Balci employs psychophysical paradigms and drift-diffusion modeling to study how spatial layouts influence our confidence in perceiving asynchronous events, and how perceptual evidence integration and metacognitive monitoring differ in individuals with subclinical obsessive-compulsive traits.

papers.title: Mice extrapolate temporal information based on previously learned spatiotemporal mappings: An asymmetrical case
papers.abstract: This research investigates the computational capacity of rodents to perform temporal extrapolation using isomorphic magnitude representations within a spatial framework. Mice were conditioned on a spatiotemporal mapping where two distinct intervals (10 s and 30 s) were paired with specific reward hoppers in a five-choice apparatus. Probing novel spatial locations revealed a directionally constrained extrapolation effect; specifically, timing was extended at a location forward of the 30-s site, whereas no backward extrapolation was observed for the 10-s site. These results indicate that murine temporal processing utilizes spatially-indexed memory architectures that are subject to inherent directional asymmetries in magnitude computation.
papers.authors: Ezgi Gür, Yalçın A. Duyan, Pınar Toptaş, Fuat Balcı

papers.title: Midbrain Dopamine Warps Subjective Time via Threshold Setting But Not Clock Speed
papers.abstract: Utilizing optogenetic modulation of tyrosine hydroxylase-positive (TH+) neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta, this study investigates the mechanistic contribution of nigrostriatal dopamine to interval timing. A drift-diffusion-timing model was employed to dissociate effects on temporal integration rate from decision threshold shifts. Experimental upregulation and downregulation of dopamine via optogenetic stimulation or inhibition resulted in corresponding bidirectional shifts in interval production times. Computational analysis determined that these behavioral changes were exclusively accounted for by alterations in the temporal decision threshold (temporal caution), rather than changes in clock speed (integration rate), thereby clarifying the role of dopamine as a modulator of the timing criterion.
papers.authors: Alihan Erdağı, Ezgi Gür, Fuat Balcı

papers.title: Perceptual decision making and metacognition in relation to obsessive-compulsive traits
papers.abstract: The research investigates the relationship between subclinical obsessive-compulsive (OC) symptoms and metacognitive monitoring using a constant-difficulty 2-AFC perceptual discrimination task. Applying Hierarchical Meta-d' modeling and Drift-Diffusion Modeling (DDM), the authors found that individuals with elevated OC traits paradoxically exhibited higher metacognitive efficiency (meta-d'/d'). However, first-order performance analysis via DDM revealed significantly reduced perceptual evidence integration efficiency (drift rate) and lower decision thresholds (caution). Furthermore, these individuals demonstrated diminished post-error slowing and lower overall confidence, suggesting that while metacognitive monitoring capacity is preserved or enhanced, the integration of this information for adaptive behavioral regulation is impaired.
papers.authors: Anıl Şafak Kaçar, Fuat Balcı

papers.title: A rudimentary form of time-dependent awareness in mice
papers.abstract: This work identifies a foundational form of time-dependent awareness in rodents, characterized by the ability to distinguish whether a motor output was governed by temporal control. In a lever-pressing task with a minimum duration requirement, reward expectancy was measured through nose-poke vigor as a proxy for confidence. Mice displayed significantly higher anticipatory responding following accurate productions compared to trials involving threshold failures (underproductions). This pattern suggests that mice possess a metacognitive mechanism capable of monitoring the state of temporal control, providing a behavioral index of internal awareness regarding the success or failure of time-based action planning.
papers.authors: Alexa Minary, Ezgi Gür, Fuat Balcı

papers.title: Asymmetrical monitoring of subjective asynchronies: a metacognitive generalized STEARC effect
papers.abstract: This study explores the metacognitive monitoring of simultaneity perception using Temporal Order Judgment (TOJ) tasks combined with subjective confidence ratings. Across four experiments, confidence was found to reliably scale with the absolute magnitude of the Stimulus Onset Asynchrony (SOA). However, the precision of this error monitoring was asymmetrically distributed, manifesting only for 'left-first' and 'bottom-first' stimulus configurations. These findings extend the Spatial-Temporal Association of Response Codes (STEARC) effect into the metacognitive domain, suggesting that the monitoring of subjective asynchronies is modulated by the spatial layout of temporal events.
papers.authors: Tutku Öztel, Martin Wiener, Fuat Balcı

0227.name: Fulvio Domini
0227.department: Department of Cognitive, Linguistic and Psychological Sciences
0227.bio: Fulvio Domini is a vision scientist who investigates how the human visual system extracts 3D information from retinal images to facilitate motor interactions with the environment. Their research addresses probabilistic inference models of depth-cue integration, proposing deterministic frameworks such as the Intrinsic Constraint (IC) and Vector Sum models to explain systematic perceptual biases. By combining computational modeling with psychophysical experiments and virtual reality, Domini examines the adaptive mapping between visual perception and motor actions like reaching and grasping.
0227.research_direction: Dr. Domini has recently been investigating the intricate relationship between 3D visual perception, intuitive physics, and visually guided action. Their recent work explores how internalized Newtonian priors—specifically Earth’s gravity and conservation of momentum—are integrated into the sensorimotor system to constrain predictions about projectile trajectories and anticipatory motor planning. In the domain of 3D depth and shape perception, they are testing standard probabilistic models of sensory integration by examining how pictorial shading interacts with binocular disparity, while also utilizing visuomotor adaptation paradigms to probe whether systematic spatial biases reflect true perceptual distortions. Furthermore, their research investigates the classical dissociation between vision-for-perception and vision-for-action by manipulating online visual and haptic feedback during grasping tasks to determine what drives motor deviations from Weber’s law.

papers.title: Relational dynamics inform predictive motor planning and perception
papers.abstract: This study demonstrates that the human sensorimotor system integrates internalized principles of conservation of momentum into both anticipatory motor planning and explicit perceptual weight judgments. Utilizing a hybrid virtual-reality/real-object paradigm with high-precision motion tracking, the authors observed that participants' lift forces were systematically modulated by the collision kinematics—specifically mass ratios and coefficients of restitution—of visually identical spheres observed in VR movies. These collision cues also induced a robust dynamic weight illusion, where objects were perceived as significantly heavier when the inferred mass from relational motion increased. These findings indicate that intuitive physical constraints are directly encoded within the representations mediating vision and action, rather than relying solely on static visual features or heuristic strategies.
papers.authors: Abdul-Rahim Deeb, Fulvio Domini

papers.title: Sensorimotor adaptation reveals systematic biases in 3D perception
papers.abstract: Addressing the controversy over whether biases in 3D spatial judgments reflect inherent perceptual distortions or experimental measurement confounds, this research employs a visuomotor adaptation framework. The study leverages the fact that adaptation is driven by discrepancies between visual depth estimates and haptic feedback. In a within-subject experiment (N=24), subjects grasped virtual 3D objects containing varied depth cues. The resulting adaptation effects and persistent aftereffects demonstrated that planned grip sizes, which are governed by visual depth estimates, consistently overestimated physical depth. This systematic bias intensified in the presence of multiple redundant depth cues. The results provide evidence that both perception and visually guided actions are influenced by distorted 3D representations and propose that sensorimotor adaptation serves as an objective tool for quantifying perceptual biases.
papers.authors: Chaeeun Lim, Dhanraj Vishwanath, Fulvio Domini

papers.title: Weak overcomes strong in sensory integration: shading warps the disparity field
papers.abstract: Prevailing models of sensory integration, such as Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE), suggest that depth cues are combined according to their relative statistical reliability, implying that highly reliable binocular disparity should typically dominate less reliable pictorial cues. In contrast, this study presents three within-subject experiments where pictorial shading significantly overrides disparity, warping the perceived 3D surface in a manner that contradicts standard reliability-based weighting and cue-vetoing accounts. The results indicate that the shading cue exerts a disproportionate influence through a form of non-probabilistic cue cooperation, where shading interacts with and effectively 'warps' the disparity field. These findings challenge the universality of the MLE principle in human 3D shape perception.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences
papers.authors: Celine Aubuchon, Jovan Kemp, Dhanraj Vishwanath, Fulvio Domini

papers.title: Sensory feedback modulates Weber’s law of both perception and action
papers.abstract: While perceptual estimates typically adhere to Weber's law, where noise scales with stimulus intensity, visually guided actions like grasping often appear to violate this principle. This study investigates whether such violations arise from dissociated visual streams or from the adaptive influence of sensory feedback on motor output. By manipulating the availability of online visual and haptic feedback, the researchers found that response variability adheres to Weber's law during pantomime grasping (no feedback) but deviates when sensory feedback is available to guide the action. The results suggest that the absence of Weber's law in motor tasks is a product of error correction and adaptive motor mapping driven by sensory feedback, rather than distinct visual processing for action and perception.
papers.authors: Ailin Deng, Evan Cesanek, Fulvio Domini

papers.title: Embeddedness of Earth’s gravity in visual perception
papers.abstract: This study investigates whether the visual system utilizes an internalized prior of Earth's gravity (1g) to constrain the perception of 3D projectile motion. Participants predicted the landing locations of objects launched under various simulated gravitational conditions while heuristic cues, such as representational momentum and online tracking, were strictly controlled. Perceptual judgments were significantly biased by the gravity manipulation, with non-terrestrial gravity conditions (e.g., simulated Mercury or Jupiter gravity) leading to systematic depth overestimations or underestimations consistent with a 1g prior. These findings suggest that the brain integrates Newtonian physical constants into its internal models of dynamic 3D events, enabling the prediction of an object's future location from limited visual information.
papers.authors: Abdul-Rahim Deeb, Fulvio Domini

0228.name: Fumiko Hoeft
0228.lab_name: Laboratory for Learning Engineering and Neural Systems (brainLENS)
0228.bio: Hoeft is a developmental cognitive neuroscientist and psychiatrist who investigates the neurobiological mechanisms underlying learning disabilities, specifically dyslexia and literacy acquisition. Their methodology integrates multimodal neuroimaging—including functional MRI and diffusion tensor imaging—with machine learning and genetic analysis to map brain maturation and predict individual learning outcomes. Hoeft conducts research on the 'Neural Noise Hypothesis' and investigates the intergenerational transmission of brain networks as well as the role of socio-emotional resilience in academic success. Currently, Hoeft serves as the Director of the UConn Brain Imaging Research Center and leads the brainLENS laboratory, focusing on translating neuroscientific findings into early identification tools and personalized educational interventions.
0228.research_direction: Dr. Hoeft has recently been investigating the neurobiological and developmental foundations of reading, learning, and overall cognitive health. Their recent work employs diverse methodologies—ranging from machine learning models of functional connectivity to systematic reviews of event-related potentials (ERPs)—to track the neurodevelopmental maturity of reading networks and identify electrophysiological biomarkers for orthographic and phonological processing. To understand the etiological pathways of learning differences, they are exploring how perinatal stressors like prematurity alter brain development, while also modeling how atypical auditory neural entrainment and neural noise contribute to developmental dyslexia. Beyond literacy, Dr. Hoeft's research extends into affective neuroscience, mapping the structural and functional MRI correlates of emotional well-being to better understand the distributed brain networks underlying reward processing and interoception.

papers.title: Human neural correlates of emotional well-being (EWB): a preliminary systematic review and meta-analysis of MRI studies based on a recent consensus definition
papers.abstract: The investigators conducted a PRISMA-compliant systematic review and meta-analysis to delineate the neuroanatomical and functional substrates of emotional well-being (EWB) using structural and functional MRI. Meta-analytic synthesis revealed that task-dependent fMRI studies involving incentive and reward processing consistently identified the left pallidum as a primary region of interest. Conversely, task-independent metrics, including resting-state functional connectivity and structural morphology, implicated the right superior temporal gyrus and insula, suggesting that EWB involves a distributed architecture supporting interoceptive processing and social cognitive mechanisms.
papers.authors: Jie Luo, Celinene M Lay, Caroline G Richter, Adam Turnbull, Fabio Richlan, Crystal L Park, Fumiko Hoeft

papers.title: Event-related potentials in the “Triangle” framework of reading and developmental dyslexia: a systematic review
papers.abstract: This systematic review utilizes the connectionist “Triangle” framework—encompassing orthographic, phonological, and semantic processing—to synthesize event-related potential (ERP) research on developmental dyslexia. The authors examined 56 studies to identify electrophysiological biomarkers associated with cognitive-linguistic nodes. Results indicate that individuals with reading disabilities demonstrate significant atypicality in ERP components linked to orthographic (N170) and phonological processing, whereas findings for semantic processing (N400) remain less conclusive. The review advocates for enhanced methodological rigor and transparency to resolve discrepancies across the literature and facilitate reproducible biomarkers for literacy disorders.
papers.authors: Silvia Siu-Yin Clement-Lam, Oliver Lasnick, Brianna Kinnie, Ayan Mitra, Cheryl Lyon, Devin Kearns, Fumiko Hoeft

papers.title: Modeling differences in neurodevelopmental maturity of the reading network using support vector regression on functional connectivity data
papers.abstract: The researchers employed a machine learning approach, specifically support vector regression (SVR), to estimate 'brain-age' maturity based on functional connectivity (FC) within the reading network and whole-brain connectomes. The results demonstrated that FC-based models accurately predict chronological age, but that reading proficiency significantly modulates the 'brain-age gap' (BAG). Specifically, poor readers exhibited an underestimated brain age, suggesting delayed neurodevelopmental maturation, while advanced readers displayed overestimated brain age. Feature importance analysis highlighted the primary role of the default mode network (DMN) and frontoparietal control systems in predicting developmental maturity.
papers.authors: Oliver HM Lasnick, Jie Luo, Brianna Kinnie, Shaan Kamal, Spencer Low, Natasza Marrouch, Fumiko Hoeft

papers.title: Perinatal influences on academic achievement and the developing brain: a scoping systematic review
papers.abstract: In this scoping review, the authors synthesize findings from 47 studies investigating the impact of perinatal insults—predominantly prematurity and prenatal alcohol exposure—on academic outcomes and neurodevelopment. The review maps how these early environmental factors disrupt developmental programming, leading to quantifiable deficits in reading and mathematical achievement. Neuroimaging evidence suggests that such perinatal stressors result in broad, non-canonical functional activation patterns during academic tasks and significant structural alterations in regions critical for long-term cognitive and educational success.
papers.authors: Deborah Schneider, Florence Bouhali, Caroline G Richter, Robert Costache, Claudia Costache, Kaitlyn Kirchhoffer, Ved Sheth, Ibo MacDonald, Fumiko Hoeft

papers.title: Sensory temporal sampling in time: an integrated model of the TSF and neural noise hypothesis as an etiological pathway for dyslexia
papers.abstract: The authors present a theoretical synthesis of the Temporal Sampling Framework (TSF) and the neural noise hypothesis to provide a unified etiological model of developmental dyslexia. This model posits that reading impairment arises from a confluence of atypical low-frequency neural entrainment to the acoustic structure of speech and elevated levels of stochastic neural variability. By integrating these two perspectives, the paper characterizes a neurobiological pathway from genetic susceptibility to the manifestation of phonological processing deficits and reading disability.
papers.authors: Oliver H M Lasnick, Fumiko Hoeft

0229.name: Gabriel J. Diaz
0229.department: Chester F. Carlson Center for Imaging Science
0229.bio: Gabriel J. Diaz is an Associate Professor in the Chester F. Carlson Center for Imaging Science at the Rochester Institute of Technology and directs the Perception for Movement (PerForM) Lab. Diaz's research focuses on the intersection of vision and motor control, specifically investigating how visual information guides complex actions like navigation and object interception using immersive virtual reality and motion capture. Their current projects include developing neuro-rehabilitation methods for stroke-induced cortical blindness and using deep learning to improve eye-tracking systems through synthetic data generation. Diaz maintains research collaborations with the University of Rochester's Center for Visual Science to study the behavioral impacts of vision loss.
0229.research_direction: Dr. Diaz’s recent work explores how humans process complex visual motion for perception and action within virtual reality environments. They have recently been investigating the visuomotor mechanisms underlying steering behavior by manipulating optic flow density and assessing how navigation and gaze dynamics are altered by healthy aging, unilateral cortical blindness, and simulated gaze-contingent visual field loss. In addition to active locomotion, their research examines whether multisensory audio-visual training can facilitate low-level visual perceptual learning during difficult peripheral global motion tasks. To support these immersive experimental paradigms, they are also evaluating how deep learning architectures can be leveraged to improve the robustness and downstream precision of eye-tracking algorithms inside VR headsets.

papers.title: Multisensory stimuli facilitate low-level perceptual learning on a difficult global motion task in virtual reality
papers.abstract: The study investigates the efficacy of inducing visual perceptual learning (VPL) within a peripheral, 4-alternative forced-choice (4AFC) global direction discrimination task utilizing head-mounted virtual reality. Participants were trained over a 10-day period on a high-difficulty motion integration stimulus located at 10° eccentricity. The experimental design compared a unimodal visual training group with an audio-visual (AV) group provided with a pulsed white-noise auditory cue that spatially simulated motion directions congruent with the horizontal visual component. Results demonstrated significant learning and spatial transfer to untrained retinotopic locations in both cohorts. Crucially, the AV group exhibited a superior performance benefit and accelerated learning rates, an advantage that persisted into unisensory post-tests where auditory cues were omitted, suggesting that multisensory integration enhances the robustness of low-level visual plasticity.
papers.authors: Catherine A. Fromm, Ross K. Maddox, Melissa J. Polonenko, Krystel R. Huxlin, Gabriel J. Diaz

papers.title: Steering in the presence of a gaze-contingent occlusion over a quarter of the visual field
papers.abstract: This research examines the hypothesis that steering biases observed in patients with cortical blindness (CB) result directly from the loss of visual information within the blind hemifield. Using a gaze-contingent display in a virtual reality steering environment, visually-healthy participants were subjected to quadrant-based occluding masks that spared foveal vision. The study sought to determine whether healthy drivers would replicate the asymmetric lane-positioning biases characteristic of left-sided CB patients (who typically bias away from their blind field). Findings indicate that healthy participants with simulated visual field deficits did not exhibit the steering biases seen in clinical CB populations. These results suggest that CB-related steering behavior is not a mere consequence of instantaneous information omission but likely arises from complex, long-term neuroplastic adaptations or compensatory motor strategies.
papers.authors: Arianna Giguere, Matthew Cavanaugh, Krystel R. Huxlin, Duje Tadin, Brett R. Fajen, Gabriel J. Diaz

papers.title: The effect of unilateral cortical blindness on lane position and gaze behavior in a virtual reality steering task
papers.abstract: This longitudinal assessment investigated how cortically-induced blindness (CB) affects the processing and integration of optic flow for navigation control. Steering behavior and gaze dynamics were analyzed in 21 CB drivers (11 left-sided, 10 right-sided deficits) and age-matched controls navigating a virtual winding road. Optic flow quality was manipulated by varying environmental texture density across low, medium, and high levels. While right-sided CB patients maintained steering profiles comparable to controls, left-sided CB patients exhibited significant lane position biases and were markedly less sensitive to variations in optic flow density and turn direction. This asymmetry suggests a lateralized disruption in the motion processing networks essential for steering control, indicating that left-hemifield CB leads to a systematic under-weighting of optic flow in the motor control loop.
papers.authors: Arianna Giguere, Matthew Cavanaugh, Krystel R. Huxlin, Duje Tadin, Brett R. Fajen, Gabriel J. Diaz

papers.title: Optic flow density modulates corner-cutting in a virtual steering task for younger and older adults
papers.abstract: The researchers investigated the potential contribution of age-related detriments in optic flow processing to steering performance using a virtual reality winding-road paradigm. Seventeen younger (mean age 21.1) and thirteen older adults (mean age 57.3) were tasked with maintaining a central lane position while environmental texture density was systematically manipulated to vary the quality of optic flow information. Quantitative analysis revealed that both age groups exhibited 'corner-cutting' behavior, which was significantly modulated by the density of proximal motion cues (rotational flow). However, no significant interaction was found between age and optic flow density, and exploratory gaze analysis showed no age-related differences in visual sampling strategies. The findings imply that the visuomotor mechanisms for steering based on naturalistic optic flow remain functionally preserved across the healthy aging lifespan.
papers.authors: Arianna Giguere, Krystel R. Huxlin, Duje Tadin, Brett R. Fajen, Gabriel J. Diaz

papers.title: Using Deep Learning to Increase Eye-Tracking Robustness, Accuracy, and Precision in Virtual Reality
papers.abstract: This study provides a technical evaluation of deep learning-based semantic segmentation for eye-feature tracking in head-mounted virtual reality systems. Recognizing the limitations of traditional computer vision in handling environmental reflections and occlusions, the authors benchmark several contemporary machine learning (ML) architectures against conventional feature-based and 3D model-based gaze estimation algorithms. Rather than relying solely on pixel-level segmentation metrics like mIoU, the paper assesses performance via downstream gaze metrics, including angular accuracy, precision, and data drop-out rates. The results demonstrate that while ML models significantly improve feature tracking robustness in diverse environments, their impact on the final gaze coordinate estimate varies depending on the underlying geometric model used for gaze calculation.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Computer Graphics and Interactive Techniques
papers.authors: Kevin Barkevich, Reynold Bailey, Gabriel J. Diaz

0230.name: Galit Yovel
0230.bio: Professor Galit Yovel researches the cognitive and neural architecture of high-level vision, specifically the mechanisms underlying face and person recognition. Yovel’s laboratory employs a multidisciplinary approach combining behavioral psychophysics, functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), and eye-tracking to investigate how perceptual, cognitive, and social systems integrate. A portion of their current work utilizes deep neural networks (DNNs) as computational models to contrast human visual processing with machine learning algorithms, aiming to characterize the representations of facial features and body identity. Through these methodologies, Yovel explores the functional organization of the face-selective cortex and the factors that enable recognition of familiar individuals.
0230.research_direction: Dr. Yovel’s recent work explores the computational and developmental mechanisms underlying human face recognition, using deep neural networks to investigate how specific visual training diets and continuous learning shape view-invariant representations. They have also recently been investigating the neural basis of real-world person perception, utilizing fMRI to examine how face- and body-selective cortical regions interact to achieve clutter-tolerant, holistic representations of people in complex scenes. Furthermore, their research uses intracranial EEG and multimodal artificial intelligence networks to disentangle the relative contributions of strictly visual versus abstract semantic information in the high-level visual cortex. By comparing these neural and computational representations, they are actively probing how visual and conceptual features differentially support the active perception versus mental recall of familiar faces and objects.

papers.title: A developmentally inspired computational model of face recognition that learns continuously through generative memory replay
papers.abstract: This study introduces a novel computational framework designed to bridge the architectural and ecological discrepancies between standard deep convolutional neural networks (DCNNs) and the human infant's ontogeny of face recognition. Unlike conventional models that utilize static batch training on expansive datasets with high within-identity variance, the proposed architecture employs a continuous learning paradigm utilizing generative memory replay. The system integrates three primary modules: an identity-encoding DCNN (Embedder), a generative Autoencoder, and a Long-Term Memory component. By simulating the gradual, low-variance visual exposure characteristic of early development—focusing on a limited number of caregivers—the model demonstrates high-fidelity identity classification and robustness against catastrophic forgetting. Quantitative results indicate that this biologically-constrained model achieves recognition performance parity with batch-trained DCNNs while better approximating the developmental trajectory of human face-space formation.
papers.authors: Naphtali Abudarham, Galit Yovel

papers.title: Concurrent emergence of view invariance, sensitivity to critical features, and identity face classification through visual experience: Insights from deep learning algorithms
papers.abstract: We utilized deep learning architectures to investigate the specific visual experience parameters required for the simultaneous development of view-invariant representations and sensitivity to diagnostic facial features. By systematically manipulating the network's training diet—specifically the balance between within-identity variability (multiple views per person) and between-identity diversity (total unique identities)—we assessed impact on identity verification performance and sensitivity to human-validated critical features. Our computational findings demonstrate that high-performance face recognition and view invariance do not emerge from raw image exposure alone but are contingent upon a training diet that replicates the high within-identity variability found in real-life experience. This suggests a shared representational basis where the emergence of sensitivity to identity-diagnostic features and view invariance are intrinsically coupled during the optimization of the face recognition system.
papers.authors: Mandy Rosemblaum, Nitzan Guy, Idan Grosbard, Libi Kliger, Naphtali Abudarham, Galit Yovel

papers.title: High-level visual cortex representations are organized along visual rather than abstract principles
papers.abstract: This research addresses the controversial hypothesis that high-level visual cortex is organized according to abstract semantic or linguistic principles, as suggested by the predictive success of Large Language Models (LLMs) in modeling neural responses. Utilizing intracranial EEG (iEEG) recordings from human ventral temporal and fronto-parietal regions, we contrasted representational similarity structures across three input modalities: raw images, visual-textual descriptions (depicting pictorial content), and abstract-textual descriptions (conceptual/biographical data). Results from representational similarity analysis (RSA) show that while both visual and visual-textual representations accurately predict the neural response relational structure in high-level visual areas, abstract-textual embeddings show significantly lower alignment and fail to explain unique neural variance. These findings indicate that the observed vision-language alignment in human visual cortex is primarily driven by visually-grounded language rather than abstract conceptual organization.
papers.authors: Adva Shoham, Rotem Broday-Dvir, Rafael Malach, Galit Yovel

papers.title: Face- and body-selective brain regions enable clutter-tolerant representations of the face, body, and whole person
papers.abstract: We investigated the neural mechanisms by which the primate visual system maintains robust representations of persons within complex, cluttered environments. Using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and a multi-stimulus paradigm, we measured neural responses to faces and bodies presented in isolation versus within cluttered scenes. Our results demonstrate that while early visual areas are significantly compromised by background clutter, high-level category-selective regions—specifically the fusiform face area (FFA) and extrastriate body area (EBA)—exhibit substantial clutter tolerance. Furthermore, we found that the presence of a body enhances the representation of a face within clutter (and vice versa), suggesting that interactions between adjacent face- and body-selective cortical modules facilitate the segregation of person-related signals from environmental noise. This synergy suggests a specialized cortical mechanism for holistic person perception that is optimized for real-world visual complexity.
papers.authors: Libi Kliger, Galit Yovel

papers.title: Using deep neural networks to disentangle visual and semantic information in human perception and memory
papers.abstract: This study employs a tripartite deep neural network (DNN) framework—consisting of vision-trained DCNNs, text-trained LLMs, and multimodal CLIP models—to computationally dissociate the visual and semantic constituents of human mental representations for familiar categories. By applying these models to behavioral data from perception and memory tasks, we quantified the relative contribution of each component to face and object recognition. Findings reveal a significant asymmetry: visual features dominate representational structures during active perception, whereas semantic/conceptual features show a significantly higher contribution during mental recall. Critically, we identified a unique, integrated visual-semantic component that is not captured by unimodal models alone, but is essential for both perception and memory. This suggests a representational shift where the high-dimensional visual details of perception are condensed into socially and semantically grounded identity concepts in memory.
papers.authors: Adva Shoham, Idan Daniel Grosbard, Or Patashnik, Daniel Cohen-Or, Galit Yovel

0231.name: Garikoitz Lerma-Usabiaga
0231.institution: Basque Center on Cognition, Brain and Language
0231.bio: Garikoitz Lerma-Usabiaga is an Ikerbasque Research Fellow and Associate Group Leader at the Basque Center on Cognition, Brain and Language (BCBL). Lerma-Usabiaga’s research examines the neurobiological foundations of vision and literacy, focusing on the functional and structural architecture of the ventral occipitotemporal cortex. They utilize multimodal neuroimaging methodologies, including functional, quantitative, and diffusion MRI, alongside computational modeling techniques such as population receptive field (pRF) mapping. Their work also involves the development of reproducible software tools for automated tractography and the characterization of spatiotemporal dynamics within the human visual system across the lifespan.
0231.research_direction: Dr. Lerma-Usabiaga has recently been investigating the structural and functional architecture of the human visual and language networks, with a particular focus on optimizing advanced neuroimaging methodologies. Their recent work explores how specialized cortical regions, such as the visual word form area, integrate bottom-up retinotopic spatial signals with top-down lexical feedback by developing novel hybrid fMRI paradigms. Additionally, they are probing methodological artifacts in visual field mapping, systematically evaluating how preprocessing choices—such as projecting fMRI data from volumetric to cortical surface spaces—impact population receptive field (pRF) estimates in the fovea. Beyond functional gray matter mapping, their research also extends to structural connectivity, where they have been building open-source, containerized diffusion MRI pipelines designed to extract highly reproducible microstructural profiles along white matter pathways.

papers.title: Design and Validation of a Hybrid Stimulus fMRI Paradigm for Simultaneous Retinotopy and Mapping of Reading-Selective Visual Cortex
papers.abstract: Reading selectively recruits specialized cortical subregions within the ventral occipitotemporal cortex (vOTC), notably the visual word form area (VWFA). Interactive models of reading postulate that these functional responses arise from bidirectional exchanges between bottom-up sensory visual inputs and top-down linguistic feedback. However, resolving the visual field organization of these regions remains challenging because high-level category selectivity confounds purely retinotopic spatial signals. In this dense-sampling functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) study (n = 11, ten sessions per participant), the authors investigated the visual field architecture of the cortical reading network using population receptive field (pRF) modeling and functional localizers. First, they systematically evaluated the influence of stimulus frequency, bar width, and element size (FWS) across multiple sessions to identify configurations that optimize the test-retest reliability of pRF eccentricity shifts observed for word and false-font stimuli relative to standard checkerboard carriers. Second, they developed and validated an innovative Word-Center (WC) hybrid paradigm designed to decouple sweeping spatial mapping carriers (moving checkerboard bars) from central lexical processing (continuous streams of words or false fonts at fixation).
