Results demonstrated that the hybrid WC design preserved stimulus equivalence, successfully isolating bottom-up retinotopic sweeps from top-down lexical influences and delivering simultaneous, highly reproducible characterizations of reading-selective functional clusters and retinotopic field maps within individual brains.
papers.authors: Miguel Martinez-Zaldivar, Yongning Lei, Garikoitz Lerma-Usabiaga

papers.title: Biases in Volumetric Versus Surface Analyses in Population Receptive Field Mapping
papers.abstract: Population receptive field (pRF) mapping with functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) provides quantitative models that link visual field coordinates to discrete anatomical loci across visual cortex. A standard preprocessing step involves projecting 3D volumetric functional data onto reconstructed 2D cortical surfaces, an operation that typically causes spatial upsampling. Using containerized analysis pipelines, this investigation assessed systematic biases in pRF parameter estimation introduced by surface versus volumetric computational spaces. The authors identified a marked and consistent overestimation of pRF coverage in the central foveal visual field when functional data underwent upsampling onto the cortical surface relative to native volumetric processing, an artifact conserved across early visual areas V1, V2, and V3. Systematic empirical and synthetic simulations revealed that this foveal coverage bias is primarily driven by cortical magnification—the pronounced nonlinear decrease in cortical representation per degree of visual angle as eccentricity increases—alongside secondary contributions from increased contrast-to-noise ratio due to surface averaging. These findings emphasize the necessity of accounting for space-representation artifacts when evaluating visual field coverage and when interpreting cross-study comparisons across divergent preprocessing pipelines.
papers.authors: David Linhardt, Michael Woletz, Pedro M. Paz-Alonso, Christian Windischberger, Garikoitz Lerma-Usabiaga

papers.title: Reproducible Tract Profiles 2 (RTP2) suite, from diffusion MRI acquisition to clinical practice and research
papers.abstract: Diffusion-weighted MRI (dMRI) tractography provides a critical, noninvasive window into white matter bundle architecture and microstructural tissue properties in vivo; however, the extreme sensitivity of dMRI pipelines to parameter configurations and execution environments severely compromises scientific reproducibility and clinical utility. To resolve this challenge, the authors introduce Reproducible Tract Profiles 2 (RTP2), an end-to-end, containerized neuroinformatics software suite engineered to transform raw diffusion datasets into standardized, highly reproducible along-tract microstructural profiles. RTP2 encapsulates automated preprocessing, anatomical parcellation, region-of-interest (ROI) definition, tractography fiber tracking, and along-tract tractometry into self-contained Docker and Singularity modules structured around Brain Imaging Data Structure (BIDS) specifications. The pipeline supports versatile anatomically curated ROI delineations, handles multiple diffusion modeling frameworks (from basic diffusion tensor metrics to advanced multi-shell reconstructions), and quantifies tissue indices such as fractional anisotropy and mean diffusivity along tract nodes. Comprehensive validation across test-retest acquisitions and multisite cohorts demonstrated high repeatability, robust parameter management, and sensitive tracking of white matter pathways, establishing an open-source tool bridging reproducible computational neuroanatomy and clinical investigations.
papers.authors: Garikoitz Lerma-Usabiaga, Mengxing Liu, Pedro M. Paz-Alonso, Brian A. Wandell

0232.name: Gene Brewer
0232.bio: Gene Brewer is a Professor of Psychology and a faculty member of the Neuroscience Graduate Program at the University of California, Riverside, where they direct the Memory and Attention Control Laboratory. Their research focuses on the cognitive and neural mechanisms underlying individual differences in working memory, sustained attention, and episodic memory retrieval. Utilizing a multi-methodological approach that includes behavioral experiments, computational modeling, and neuroimaging techniques such as EEG and neurostimulation, Brewer investigates how attention control influences performance in both theoretical and high-stakes applied contexts. Brewer’s work receives support from federal agencies including DARPA and the Air Force Office of Scientific Research and includes collaborations with the Department of Defense on personnel assessment and cognitive enhancement.
0232.research_direction: Dr. Brewer has recently been investigating the cognitive and neural mechanisms underlying attention, memory, and arousal. Their recent work explores the locus coeruleus-norepinephrine (LC-NE) system's role in sustained attention, utilizing techniques like pupillometry and transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) to probe how neuromodulatory dynamics affect sensory processing and vigilance. In the domain of learning and metacognition, they are examining how episodic encoding is impacted by mind-wandering thought probes, as well as how individuals use the ease of memory retrieval as a metacognitive heuristic to judge the subjective importance of information. Additionally, Dr. Brewer utilizes large-scale individual differences modeling to deconstruct working memory capacity, testing how subcomponents like attentional control and secondary memory interact to predict higher-order cognitive abilities such as fluid intelligence.

papers.title: The role of the LC-NE system in attention: From cells, to systems, to sensory-motor control
papers.abstract: This comprehensive review synthesizes cross-disciplinary evidence from molecular, cellular, and systems neuroscience to delineate the locus coeruleus-norepinephrine (LC-NE) system's regulation of attentional control. We characterize the neurophysiological implications of tonic and phasic LC firing regimes on neural signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and subsequent behavioral outcomes. The evidence is evaluated through three principal theoretical frameworks: the Adaptive Gain Theory (AGT) of task engagement, the Network Reset Hypothesis (NRH) of circuit reconfiguration, and the Glutamate Amplifies NE Effects (GANE) model of local signal enhancement. We integrate findings from animal models, human neuroimaging, and pupillometry to discuss the LC-NE system’s influence on sensory processing and executive function, while addressing its role in individual differences and neurodegenerative decline.
papers.authors: Alexis S. Torres, Matthew K. Robison, Gene A. Brewer

papers.title: The Impact of Thought Probes and Other Encoding Interruptions on Memory
papers.abstract: This research evaluates the potential reactivity of mind-wandering assessments by examining whether the insertion of thought probes during encoding disrupts episodic memory performance. Utilizing a paradigm where participants studied word lists interrupted by mind-wandering probes, mathematical distractors, or silent interstimulus intervals, the study tracked retrieval outcomes and temporal dynamics. While specific serial-position effects were observed on items immediately contiguous to the interruptions, results confirmed that thought probes do not significantly impair overall memory accuracy or the temporal structure of episodic retrieval. These findings suggest that thought probes introduce minimal systematic bias, supporting their use as a non-reactive measure of attentional fluctuations during mnemonic encoding.
papers.authors: Dillon H. Murphy, Gene Brewer

papers.title: Memory accessibility as a cue for perceived importance
papers.abstract: We investigate the metacognitive heuristic wherein mnemonic accessibility informs subjective evaluations of information significance. Across multiple experiments, participants completed recall and recognition tests followed by importance ratings for scientific theories. The data revealed a robust accessibility bias: successfully recalled items were consistently judged as more important than forgotten ones, and 'feelings of knowing' positively correlated with importance judgments even in the absence of successful retrieval. Crucially, this bias was significantly attenuated when memory was assessed via recognition, which reduces retrieval effort. These results indicate that individuals utilize the phenomenological ease of mnemonic access as a cue to infer the inherent value and importance of information.
papers.authors: Dillon H. Murphy, Aikaterini Stefanidi, Gene A. Brewer

papers.title: The influence of transcranial direct current stimulation to the trigeminal nerve on attention and arousal
papers.abstract: This study tested whether transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) targeting the trigeminal nerve modulates locus coeruleus (LC) activity and improves sustained attention. We monitored pretrial and stimulus-evoked pupil diameters as physiological indices of LC-mediated arousal during a vigilance task while applying anodal, cathodal, or sham stimulation over the frontal bone and mastoid. Although the results replicated standard time-on-task deteriorations in behavioral performance and pupillary responses, we found no significant main effects of tDCS on pupillary dynamics, self-reported attention states, or task accuracy. These findings fail to support the hypothesis that transcutaneous stimulation of the trigeminal pathway effectively engages LC-driven arousal mechanisms or enhances attentional vigilance in humans.
papers.authors: Alexis S. Torres, Matthew K. Robison, Samuel M. McClure, Gene A. Brewer

papers.title: What makes working memory work? A multifaceted account of the predictive power of working memory capacity
papers.abstract: In a large-scale individual differences investigation (N = 974), we adjudicated between single-process and multifaceted accounts of working memory capacity’s (WMC) predictive utility for higher-order cognition. Using structural equation modeling, we tested whether attention control (AC), primary memory (PM), and secondary memory (SM) mediated the shared variance between WMC and measures of fluid intelligence and reading comprehension. The results supported a multifaceted model, demonstrating that no single ability could independently account for WMC's relationship with higher-order cognition. This architectural effect was robust across different operationalizations of WMC, including complex span and n-back tasks, suggesting that WMC's predictive power emerges from the coordinated function of multiple distinct cognitive mechanisms.
papers.authors: Matthew K. Robison, Ashley L. Miller, Elizabeth A. Wiemers, Derek M. Ellis, Nash Unsworth, Thomas S. Redick, Gene A. Brewer

0233.name: Geoffrey K Aguirre
0233.bio: Geoffrey Karl Aguirre is a neurologist and cognitive neuroscientist at the University of Pennsylvania whose research focuses on the functional organization of the human visual cortex. Utilizing BOLD fMRI and non-invasive neuroimaging, Aguirre investigates how the brain represents visual information and how these processes are disrupted by neurologic and ophthalmologic diseases. Their work encompasses the methodological refinement of imaging techniques, the study of melanopsin-mediated visual pathways, and the characterization of neural population coding for object and facial recognition. Aguirre also examines the plasticity of the visual system in response to blindness and conditions such as migraine, bridging basic vision science with clinical behavioral neurology.
0233.research_direction: Dr. Aguirre has recently been investigating visual and sensory processing spanning basic cortical mapping, clinical sensory disorders, and translational disease models. Their recent work explores how the visual hierarchy processes temporal sensitivity to achromatic and chromatic flicker by utilizing fMRI and silent substitution stimuli. In clinical populations, they are examining sensory hypersensitivity and the "visual diet" of patients with migraine, deploying machine learning-validated wearable loggers to track circadian melanopic light exposure alongside parametric measures of the trigeminal blink reflex. Additionally, they are evaluating functional MRI as a translational biomarker in canine models of inherited retinal degeneration to track cone-mediated geniculocortical responses and assess the impact of gene augmentation therapies.

papers.title: Daily light exposure habits of youth with migraine: a prospective exploratory study
papers.abstract: This prospective investigation utilized multi-channel wearable light loggers to characterize the 'visual diet'—specifically melanopic equivalent daylight illuminance (mEDI)—in a cohort of adolescents and young adults with migraine. Despite adherence to evening and nighttime light hygiene, participants frequently failed to meet recommended daytime mEDI targets (≥250 lux). Critically, a phase-delayed temporal profile of light exposure was identified in individuals with chronic migraine, where the diurnal peak of melanopic stimulation occurred approximately 60 minutes later compared to episodic cases. Quantitative analysis demonstrated a robust correlation between individual circadian delay in light exposure and monthly headache frequency, suggesting that the timing of retinal melanopic stimulation may be a biomarker or modulator of migraine disease burden in pediatric populations.
papers.authors: Carlyn Patterson Gentile, Ryan Shah, Blanca Marquez De Prado, Nichelle Raj, Christina L Szperka, Andrew D Hershey, Geoffrey K Aguirre

papers.title: Identifying chest-worn light logger adherence: a validation study
papers.abstract: To enhance the reliability of continuous light monitoring in clinical research, this study developed and validated a computational framework for assessing subject adherence to wearing the ActLumus light logger. A logistic regression model was trained using tri-axial accelerometry (movement and device orientation), photopic illuminance, and time-of-day variables as features. The model achieved high classification accuracy (AUC 0.93–0.94) in differentiating between active wear, non-wear, and appropriate nighttime removal states. When applied to an independent validation dataset of youth with migraine, the algorithm maintained robust performance, providing a standardized method for data cleaning and ensuring the integrity of longitudinal light-exposure metrics in neuro-ophthalmic research.
papers.authors: Carlyn Patterson Gentile, Adah Thomas, Ryan Shah, Blanca Marquez De Prado, Nichelle Raj, Christina L. Szperka, Geoffrey K. Aguirre

papers.title: A measure of the blink reflex to parametric variation of mechanical stimulation of the trigeminal nerve
papers.abstract: This study characterizes the stimulus-response properties of the human blink reflex using a novel parametric mechanical stimulation paradigm targeting the trigeminal somatosensory afferents. Electromyographic (EMG) recordings of the orbicularis oculi were obtained across a range of mechanical intensities, and the resulting response amplitudes were modeled using a sigmoidal Hill function. Quantitative results revealed substantial individual variability in absolute sensitivity; however, a consistent laterality effect was observed across participants, with significantly higher mechanical thresholds for the contralateral versus ipsilateral blink response. The findings suggest that the reflex circuit incorporates a stable neural gain mechanism that persists despite baseline differences in trigeminal sensitivity, providing a normative model for assessing sensory hypersensitivity in conditions like migraine.
papers.authors: Eric A Kaiser, Edda B Haggerty, Dena P Garner, Vatinee Y Bunya, Geoffrey K Aguirre

papers.title: Temporal sensitivity for achromatic and chromatic flicker across the visual cortex
papers.abstract: Using blood oxygen level-dependent (BOLD) fMRI and silent substitution stimuli, this research mapped the temporal sensitivity functions (TSFs) for post-receptoral pathways (LMS, L–M, and S-cone) across the human visual hierarchy. While peak temporal sensitivity increased from the lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) through the cortical visual areas, V1 exhibited a notable degree of normalization across eccentricity and post-receptoral channels relative to retinal and LGN inputs. Unexpectedly, area V1 showed minimal variation in peak sensitivity across eccentricity despite clear differences in spatial resolution. Analysis of carry-over effects and distributed pattern activity further revealed that high-frequency achromatic flicker (64 Hz) induces subtle neural adaptation in V1, even when the bulk BOLD response is negligible, highlighting the extensive filtering and amplification processes that shape human cortical vision.
papers.authors: Carlyn Patterson Gentile, Manuel Spitschan, Huseyin O. Taskin, Andrew S. Bock, Geoffrey K. Aguirre

papers.title: Cone-Driven, Geniculocortical Responses in Canine Models of Outer Retinal Disease
papers.abstract: This study evaluated the efficacy of functional MRI as a translational biomarker for measuring cone-mediated visual function in canine models of inherited retinal degeneration (PDE6B-RCD1, RPGR-XLPRA2, and NPHP5-CRD2). By employing cone-directed spectral modulations, the authors successfully isolated post-retinal responses in the LGN and visual cortex of wild-type and diseased animals. Quantitative fMRI metrics detected preserved luminance and chromatic responses in rod-loss models (RCD1) but identified significant attenuation or absence in cone-disease models (XLPRA2 and CRD2). Critically, the study demonstrated that NPHP5 gene augmentation therapy can restore cortical BOLD responses to luminance stimulation, establishing fMRI as a non-invasive, high-throughput tool for validating gene and cell-replacement therapies in veterinary and human translational vision science.
papers.authors: Huseyin O Taskin, Jacqueline Wivel, Gustavo D Aguirre, William A Beltran, Geoffrey K Aguirre

0234.name: Geoffrey Woodman
0234.bio: Geoffrey Woodman is a Professor of Psychology and the E. Bronson Ingram Chair of Neuroscience at Vanderbilt University, where they direct research on the neural basis of visual attention and memory. Woodman's laboratory employs a comparative approach, utilizing electrophysiology and behavioral measures in both humans and nonhuman primates to investigate how the brain selects and maintains information during complex tasks. They identify neural signatures of attentional selection and study the cognitive architecture of working memory through computational modeling and brain stimulation techniques. Their current work examines the interaction between sensory noise and cognitive deficits in neurotypical and clinical populations.
0234.research_direction: Dr. Woodman has recently been investigating the deep intersections between visual attention, working memory, and long-term memory. Their recent work explores whether the classic capacity limits of visual working memory can be computationally modeled as byproducts of long-term memory retrieval dynamics, while also theoretically re-evaluating the historical boundaries between working memory storage and top-down attentional control. Using EEG, they are examining how executive control circuits might unconsciously detect "hidden" long-term memory traces even when participants fail to explicitly recognize a visual stimulus. Additionally, Dr. Woodman studies how statistical regularities guide visual search, investigating how rapidly observers can update feature-based attentional sets when environmental probabilities shift and whether implicit spatial biases rely on the retrieval of integrated task episodes.

papers.title: Capacity not required: A long-term memory model that exhibits key signatures of working memory
papers.abstract: The authors utilize the Context Maintenance and Retrieval model (CMR-WM) to demonstrate that the behavioral signatures of visual working memory (WM)—specifically set-size effects and limited storage capacity—emerge naturally from the retrieval dynamics of long-term memory (LTM). By integrating an evolving temporal context into a unified LTM framework, the study simulates change-detection and continuous-report performance, showing that asymptotic capacity limits are a byproduct of item-to-context interference and competitive retrieval rather than a discrete, fixed-capacity buffer. These findings advocate for a re-examination of the traditional dichotomy between LTM and WM, suggesting that short-term maintenance phenomena can be parsimoniously explained through LTM contextual dynamics.
papers.authors: Sean M. Polyn, Geoffrey F. Woodman

papers.title: Executive control can query hidden human memories
papers.abstract: This study employs electroencephalography (EEG) and event-related potential (ERP) analysis to investigate the neural mechanisms underlying explicit recognition failures for stimuli stored in long-term memory. Analysis of the error-related negativity (ERN) reveals that executive control mechanisms can rapidly query and detect the presence of stored memory representations, even when participants fail to explicitly recognize the item (misses). The results suggest that memory traces remain physiologically accessible via a functional pathway independent of explicit retrieval mechanisms, implying that recognition failures often stem from explicit access bottlenecks rather than trace degradation, and highlighting a specialized role for frontoparietal control circuits in monitoring 'hidden' mnemonic content.
papers.authors: Chong Zhao, Keisuke Fukuda, Geoffrey F. Woodman

papers.title: Super rapid learning of new attentional sets
papers.abstract: The researchers utilized a probabilistic visual search paradigm to evaluate the speed at which humans update feature-based attentional priorities in response to shifting environmental regularities. Following an initial acquisition phase for color-probability mappings, the statistical regularities were scrambled to assess relearning rates. The findings demonstrate a 'super rapid' learning effect, where participants re-established new attentional sets significantly faster than their initial acquisition speed. This accelerated adaptation was modulated by the level of proactive interference from previous sets, indicating that the attentional system continuously and rapidly updates internal models of environmental priors to optimize perceptual selection in non-stationary contexts.
papers.authors: Seth A. Marx, Sisi Wang, Geoffrey F. Woodman

papers.title: How attention and working memory married and divorced, with Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance as the witness
papers.abstract: This theoretical review synthesizes several decades of research concerning the functional relationship between top-down attentional control and visual working memory (VWM). The authors trace the evolution of the field from early modular theories to the 'attentional template' hypothesis, which posited that VWM maintenance and attentional guidance are identical processes. Evaluating subsequent evidence of capacity dissociations and selection inefficiencies, the paper argues for a revised multi-state architecture of WM. It addresses contemporary debates on the capacity of the internal spotlight, the mechanisms of distractor suppression, and the functional partitions that distinguish representations maintained for storage from those actively guiding perceptual prioritization.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
papers.authors: Christian N. L. Olivers, Pieter R. Roelfsema, David Soto, Geoffrey F. Woodman

papers.title: Investigating memory episodes in location probability learning: Can altering response features reset spatial bias?
papers.abstract: This investigation assesses the episodic-retrieval account of implicit location probability learning (LPL) by examining whether learned spatial biases are dependent on the retrieval of integrated task episodes. Across two experiments, participants performed a visual search task where a frequent target location induced an attentional bias. The researchers manipulated motor-response requirements between training and test phases to determine if changing task-irrelevant response features would 'reset' the bias by disrupting episode retrieval. The results showed that spatial priorities remained robust despite motoric changes, suggesting that LPL-induced biases are predominantly driven by stimulus-location associations rather than integrated memory episodes that include specific motor outputs.
papers.authors: Xinger Yu, Geoffrey F. Woodman

0235.name: George A. Alvarez
0235.bio: George A. Alvarez is the Fred Kavli Professor of Neuroscience in the Department of Psychology at Harvard University and a visiting scholar at the Kempner Institute. Alvarez’s research investigates the computational constraints of the human visual system, with a focus on the mechanisms of attentional selection, visual working memory, and resource allocation. They employ a methodology that combines human psychophysics and neuroimaging with deep neural network (DNN) modeling to study how the brain processes visual information. Recent work by Alvarez focuses on the alignment between biological and artificial intelligence, using deep learning frameworks to model perceptual phenomena such as lightness illusions and contour integration.
0235.research_direction: Dr. Alvarez has recently been investigating the computational mechanisms underlying perceptual organization, using artificial neural networks as models to bridge human psychophysics and machine vision. Their recent work explores how visual systems integrate local elements into global structures, testing whether purely feedforward architectures can capture human-like contour integration and developing "visual anagram" stimuli to probe holistic, configural shape processing across different models. To better unpack the internal mechanics of these networks, they are also developing novel interpretability techniques to visualize the specific natural image features that drive individual unit activations and to isolate the functional role of feature inhibition. Furthermore, their research investigates how information is routed within Vision Transformers, applying mathematical decomposition to understand how these models exchange positional and semantic content to achieve long-range contextual processing.

papers.title: Bi-Orthogonal Factor Decomposition for Vision Transformers
papers.abstract: The authors propose Bi-orthogonal Factor Decomposition (BFD), a diagnostic framework for analyzing information exchange in Vision Transformers (ViTs) by disentangling token activations into orthogonal positional and content factors. By applying ANOVA-based statistical decomposition followed by Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) of the query-key interaction matrix, they uncover bi-orthogonal modes that mediate communication between tokens. Their results demonstrate that self-attention energy is primarily driven by content-content interactions, with heads specializing into distinct content-content, content-position, and position-position operators. The analysis further identifies that the superior holistic shape processing of self-supervised models like DINOv2 is attributed to intermediate-layer mechanisms that simultaneously preserve positional structure and enrich semantic content through long-range contextual interactions.
papers.authors: Fenil R. Doshi, Thomas Fel, Talia Konkle, George A. Alvarez

papers.title: A feedforward mechanism for human-like contour integration
papers.abstract: This study challenges the necessity of recurrent and top-down feedback for perceptual organization by demonstrating that purely feedforward deep convolutional neural networks (DCNNs) can emulate human-like contour integration. The authors show that ImageNet-pretrained architectures like Alexnet, when fine-tuned on contour detection tasks, replicate human psychophysical signatures including gestalt 'good continuation' and uncrowding effects. The research identifies two critical inductive biases supporting this capacity: a gradual progression of receptive field sizes across the model hierarchy and a learned sensitivity bias for gradually curved contours (~20°). These findings provide a computational existence proof that feedforward hierarchical processing is sufficient to implement complex mechanisms of perceptual grouping and organization.
papers.authors: Fenil R. Doshi, Talia Konkle, George A. Alvarez

papers.title: Visual Anagrams Reveal Hidden Differences in Holistic Shape Processing Across Vision Models
papers.abstract: The authors introduce 'Visual Anagrams,' a diagnostic benchmark consisting of object pairs that share identical local part statistics but differ in their global configural arrangements. They develop the Configural Shape Score (CSS) to quantify this holistic shape sensitivity across 86 pretrained vision models, finding that ImageNet accuracy and standard shape-vs-texture bias do not fully account for configural competence. Through attention ablation and representational similarity analysis, the study reveals that high-CSS models, such as self-supervised and language-aligned Vision Transformers, leverage long-range contextual interactions in middle-to-late layers to integrate local features into compositional shape representations. The results suggest that robust, human-like vision requires architectural frameworks that integrate local texture with global configural cues.
papers.venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2025)
papers.authors: Fenil R. Doshi, Thomas Fel, Talia Konkle, George A. Alvarez

papers.title: Understanding Inhibition Through Maximally Tense Images
papers.abstract: This research explores the functional role of feature inhibition in neural network vision models, investigating how these systems ensure images do not express specific features despite the inherent asymmetry of ReLU activation functions. The authors propose probing these mechanisms using 'maximally tense images' (MTIs)—stimuli designed to simultaneously drive high levels of excitation and inhibition for a target feature. They introduce two interpretability techniques: +/- attribution inversions, which decompose images into excitatory and inhibitory components, and the attribution atlas, which characterizes the global manifold of inhibitory responses. The study further examines the challenges posed by feature superposition, demonstrating how interfering features can produce attribution patterns that mimic inhibitory motifs.
papers.authors: Chris Hamblin, Srijani Saha, Talia Konkle, George A. Alvarez

papers.title: Feature Accentuation: Revealing 'What' Features Respond to in Natural Images
papers.abstract: The authors introduce 'feature accentuation,' a post-hoc interpretability method for visualizing the spatial and semantic drivers of neural unit responses in complex natural images. Unlike traditional feature visualization that generates synthetic patterns from noise, feature accentuation applies gradient-based optimization to natural image seeds to emphasize the specific attributes (e.g., textures, object parts) that drive a unit's activation. This approach generates naturalistic visualizations that localize relevant features and provide a high-resolution tool for assessing model-brain alignment. The method is used to synthesize targeted stimulus sets that systematically vary along model-specific encoding axes, enabling a more stringent test of the computational features driving neural responses in biological vision systems.
papers.authors: Christopher Hamblin, Thomas Fel, Srijani Saha, Talia Konkle, George A. Alvarez

0236.name: George R. Mangun
0236.department: Department of Psychology and Department of Neurology
0236.lab_name: Laboratory for the Neural Mechanisms of Attention
0236.bio: George R. Mangun is a Professor of Psychology and Neurology and the founding Director of the Center for Mind and Brain at the University of California, Davis. Their research focuses on the neural mechanisms of selective attention, specifically investigating how top-down signals from the frontal and parietal cortex modulate sensory processing in the visual system. Utilizing a multimodal approach that integrates high-density EEG/ERP with functional MRI, Mangun maps the spatial and temporal dynamics of attentional control and selection. Mangun is also a co-author of the textbook, 'Cognitive Neuroscience: The Biology of the Mind.'
0236.research_direction: Dr. Mangun has recently been investigating the neural dynamics and cognitive control mechanisms underlying various forms of visual and cross-modal attention. Their recent work explores how top-down anticipatory attention is organized hierarchically—from broad sensory dimensions to specific feature attributes—and probes the neural antecedents of self-generated, volitional shifts of attention in non-spatial domains like color. Using primarily EEG multivariate pattern analysis combined with fMRI, they are also examining unconscious preparatory signals that precede overt saccades during visual search, alongside investigations into how internal representations of targets and distractors are rhythmically sampled at theta frequencies within sensory memory. Additionally, Dr. Mangun is studying how the right-lateralized ventral attention network dynamically couples with sensory cortices to mediate attentional reorienting during auditory and visual expectancy violations.

papers.title: The Ventral Attention Network Mediates Attentional Reorienting to Cross-Modal Expectancy Violations: Evidence from EEG and fMRI
papers.abstract: This study employs a multimodal neuroimaging approach (integrated EEG and fMRI) to investigate the role of the right-lateralized Ventral Attention Network (VAN) in mediating attentional reorienting during violations of cross-modal sensory expectancy. Using an auditory-visual trial-by-trial cueing paradigm, the researchers observed that expectancy violations elicited significant increases in early-latency (approximately 100 ms) event-related potential (ERP) negative deflections across both auditory and visual modalities. fMRI and source localization identified recruitment of the right temporoparietal junction (TPJ) and inferior frontal gyrus (IFG) specifically during unexpected events. Furthermore, functional connectivity analysis demonstrated increased coupling between VAN nodes and modality-specific sensory cortices—the superior temporal gyrus for auditory violations and the fusiform gyrus for visual violations—suggesting that the VAN facilitates adaptive cognitive control by resolving sensory conflict via top-down modulation of bottom-up inputs.
papers.authors: Soukhin Das, Sreenivasan Meyyappan, Evelijne M. Bekker, Sharon Corina, Mingzhou Ding, George R. Mangun

papers.title: Hierarchical Organization of Human Visual Feature Attention Control
papers.abstract: Applying multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) to EEG alpha-band (8–12 Hz) oscillations, the authors tested the hypothesis that anticipatory feature-based attention is implemented via a hierarchical top-down control mechanism. Participants were cued to attend to either a broad feature dimension (color vs. motion) or a specific feature attribute (e.g., blue vs. green, or upward vs. downward motion). Decoding of preparatory neural activity revealed that dimension-level biasing significantly preceded attribute-level biasing, with the onset of the former occurring approximately 160 ms earlier (240 ms vs. 400 ms post-cue). These findings provide electrophysiological evidence that the frontoparietal attention network first biases broad sensory categories within the visual hierarchy before narrowing the focus of top-down signals to specific feature attributes to enhance target selection.
papers.authors: Sreenivasan Meyyappan, Mingzhou Ding, George R. Mangun

papers.title: Volitional Attention to Color: Breaking Willed Attention out of the Spatial Domain
papers.abstract: This research investigates the neurophysiological correlates of 'willed attention' (self-generated volitional shifts) in the non-spatial domain of stimulus color. Utilizing a trial-by-trial cueing design where subjects either followed instruction or freely chose a target color (orange vs. purple), the study employed support vector machine (SVM) decoding on EEG signals. While post-decision alpha-band (8-12 Hz) power and broadband voltage patterns significantly differentiated the chosen colors, the researchers found no pre-decision signals that predicted the participants' volitional choices. This result stands in marked contrast to established findings in willed spatial attention, where pre-decisional neural activity is predictive of subsequent shifts. The findings suggest that the neural antecedents of volitional control may not be domain-general but rather exhibit specific organizational differences when applied to non-spatial feature selection.
papers.authors: John G. Nadra, Grace Sullivan, George R. Mangun

papers.title: Unconscious Neural Activity Predicts Overt Attention in Visual Search
papers.abstract: The study explores the neural antecedents of overt attention—voluntary saccadic eye movements—during an unguided visual search in cluttered arrays. By applying SVM decoding to broadband and alpha-band EEG, the authors demonstrated that the direction of the initial saccade can be predicted up to two seconds prior to the search array's onset based on broadband activity. Interestingly, immediately preceding alpha-band power (within 1 second) was not predictive, which differentiates these overt shifts from willed covert spatial attention. The results suggest that overt visual search is preceded by early preparatory neural dynamics that are more characteristic of willed motor actions than the transient biasing associated with covert attention, highlighting a distinct role for long-lead unconscious neural activity in shaping complex visual search behavior.
papers.authors: John G. Nadra, Jesse J. Bengson, George R. Mangun

papers.title: Out-of-Phase Rhythmic Sampling of Internal Visual Target and Distractor Object Representations Correlates with Target Discrimination
papers.abstract: This study investigates whether rhythmic attentional sampling persists after the offset of visual stimulation, specifically within internal sensory memory. Participants performed an object-based attention task with a transient (50 ms) target overlaid by a distractor. Multivariate decoding of EEG activity revealed that the magnitudes of neural representations for both target and distractor objects oscillated at theta frequencies (4-8 Hz) for nearly one second after stimulus offset. Crucially, higher task performance (target discrimination accuracy) was significantly correlated with greater theta-band phase differences between target and distractor representations. These results indicate that the brain separately and rhythmically samples target and distractor representations in memory, and that the desynchronization of these sampling rhythms facilitates the resolution of representational competition.
papers.authors: Sean Noah, Sreenivasan Meyyappan, Mingzhou Ding, George R. Mangun

0237.name: George Sperling
0237.bio: Sperling is a Distinguished Professor at the University of California, Irvine, known for identifying iconic memory and developing the partial report paradigm to measure visual sensory storage. Their research integrates mathematical and computational modeling to investigate visual processes, including the three-systems theory of motion perception and the dynamics of spatial and feature-based attention. Recently, Sperling's work has expanded into measuring perceptual attention filters and exploring substance-invariant salience processing to explain how the brain extracts information from various visual stimuli.
0237.research_direction: Dr. Sperling has recently been investigating the computational function and capacity limits of topographic salience maps in the human visual system. Their recent work explores whether spatial and ensemble computations—such as judging distances, localizing centroids, and estimating numerosity—rely on substance-invariant processing, where the brain extracts featureless spatial coordinates independently of the specific luminance, chromaticity, or texture of the stimuli. To probe these mechanisms, they employ psychophysical partial-report paradigms featuring rapidly masked, multi-feature visual arrays combined with ideal detector analysis. Through these behavioral and computational methods, they are also examining the boundaries of parallel visual processing, specifically seeking to quantify how many concurrent salience maps an observer can maintain and what distinct sources of error constrain these representations in working memory.

papers.title: Salience maps for judgments of frontal plane distance, centroids, numerosity, and letter identity inferred from substance-invariant processing
papers.abstract: Topographic salience maps integrate multi-feature sensory inputs into continuous scalar salience values indexed by spatial coordinates (x, y). Beyond the conventional view that salience maps serve primarily to dictate action priority and attentional deployment, this study shows that they execute substance-invariant perceptual measurements analogous to physical calibration tools. Across a suite of psychophysical paradigms, observers performed four visual tasks: estimating frontal-plane spatial distance between two target tokens, computing the center of mass (centroid) of target arrays, estimating target numerosity, and identifying large alphabetic letters. The targets and distractors were systematically defined by luminance contrast, chromaticity, or grating texture orientation, including rigorous isoluminant configurations in the fovea and periphery to rule out luminance-channel contributions. Distance, centroid, and numerosity judgments exhibited strict substance invariance—performance was equivalent across homogeneous and heterogeneous feature compositions and remained intact under isoluminance, demonstrating that these metric evaluations operate solely over featureless spatial location coordinates represented within salience maps. In contrast, letter recognition was the sole task showing moderate performance facilitation with luminance information. These results establish that the primate visual system uses shared salience maps as low-dimensional coordinate representations for diverse spatial and ensemble computations independently of luminance pathways.
papers.authors: Lingyu Gan, George Sperling

papers.title: Deriving the number of salience maps an observer has from the number and quality of concurrent centroid judgments
papers.abstract: Topographic salience maps translate multi-channel visual feature inputs into scalar priority landscapes across the visual field. While observers can concurrently judge centroids of three intermixed dot colors, the upper capacity limit for parallel salience representations in the human brain has remained unresolved. Using an eleven-experiment partial-report paradigm, observers viewed tachistoscopic 300 ms presentations of 28 to 32 item arrays composed of M intermixed feature classes (with M spanning from 3 to 8), followed by a post-stimulus mask and a feature cue instructing the observer to localize the spatial centroid of only the cued feature set. Ideal detector analyses revealed that observers simultaneously sampled and pooled spatial coordinates from 12 to 17 individual items. Quantitative modeling of whether performance in an M-feature experiment could be predicted from performance in the corresponding (M-1)-feature baseline demonstrated that one observer maintained at least 7 concurrent salience maps, while two observers maintained at least 5. Computational decomposition of six potential error sources established that performance ceilings were not constrained by feature-based attentional filtering or motor execution noise, but primarily by channel capacity during multiplexed item-location encoding and working memory constraints during retention of calculated centroid coordinates.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Lingyu Gan, Peng Sun, George Sperling

0238.name: Gerrit Maus
0238.bio: Maus is a vision scientist at Magic Leap, Inc., where they apply principles of human perception to the development of augmented reality technologies. Previously, Maus served as an Assistant Professor at Nanyang Technological University and a postdoctoral researcher at UC Berkeley, focusing on how the brain compensates for sensory delays and discontinuities. Their research includes studies on motion extrapolation, the flash-lag effect, and the automatic recalibration of gaze direction following eye blinks. Maus utilizes an approach that combines psychophysics with neuroimaging techniques such as functional MRI (fMRI) and transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) to investigate the neural mechanisms of spatial and temporal vision.
0238.research_direction: Dr. Maus has recently been investigating the applied visual ergonomics of augmented reality systems, alongside fundamental research into anomalous motion perception. Their recent work in spatial vision explores how users tolerate binocular disparity artifacts in see-through head-mounted displays, utilizing visual search tasks and Nonius alignment to measure how vertical misalignment impacts sensory fusion, vertical vergence, and subjective discomfort. Additionally, they have been examining the Rotating Snakes illusion, using psychophysical motion cancellation paradigms to investigate how specific color-opponent signals, such as strictly luminance-controlled blue-yellow combinations, modulate the strength of perceived illusory motion.

papers.title: Eye posture and screen alignment with simulated see-through head-mounted displays
papers.abstract: Rendering virtual environments on near-eye head-mounted displays demands precise knowledge of display calibration, scene geometry, and ocular anatomy to prevent binocular disparity artifacts. In optical see-through augmented reality (OST-AR), binocular vertical misalignment (BVM) creates an incongruence between the unmediated, geometrically aligned real background and the misaligned virtual overlay. This study evaluated human tolerance to BVM during an active visual search task over random-dot stereograms while concurrently assessing subjective discomfort (via a visual discomfort questionnaire) and objective binocular posture (using Nonius alignment). Across varying degrees of vertical disparity and stimulus angular subtense, empirical results demonstrate that physiological compensation for vertical disparity is partitioned approximately evenly between sensory fusion and motor vertical vergence. Significant inter-individual differences in misalignment thresholds and symptom severity were observed, indicating that individualized calibration parameters are critical to mitigate asthenopia and maximize visual performance in see-through wearable systems.
papers.authors: Agostino Gibaldi, Yinghua Liu, Christos Kaspiris-Rousellis, Madhumitha S. Mahadevan, Jenny C. A. Read, Björn N. S. Vlaskamp, Gerrit W. Maus

papers.title: Blue-yellow combination enhances perceived motion in Rotating Snakes illusion
papers.abstract: The Rotating Snakes illusion evokes anomalous visual motion from static repeated asymmetric luminance profiles. Although chromatic variations—specifically combinations of blue and yellow—have been qualitatively reported to exacerbate this illusion, rigorous empirical verification under controlled luminance remained unestablished. Here, psychophysical nulling via a motion cancellation paradigm was employed to determine the point of subjective stationarity across blue-yellow (BY), red-green (RG), and achromatic greyscale configurations, with corresponding micropattern segments precisely luminance-matched across conditions. Results revealed a statistically significant main effect of color profile: the physical angular velocity needed to achieve perceptual stationarity was significantly higher for the blue-yellow stimulus relative to both the red-green and achromatic baselines, while the latter two exhibited comparable effect magnitudes. These quantitative findings provide direct empirical evidence that S-cone-opponent chromatic signals modulate the spatiotemporal contrast mechanisms that generate anomalous motion percepts.
papers.authors: Maiko Uesaki, Arnab Biswas, Hiroshi Ashida, Gerrit Maus

0239.name: Gi-Yeul Bae
0239.bio: Gi-Yeul Bae is an Assistant Professor in the Department of Psychology at Arizona State University and the principal investigator of the Visual Cognitive Neuroscience Laboratory. Bae’s research investigates the neural architectures of visual perception and memory, employing EEG decoding and psychophysics to track stimulus-specific information in the human brain. Bae develops computational models that examine how prior trial history and categorical frameworks introduce systematic biases into visual working memory. Their work aims to describe how the brain maintains a stable and coherent visual experience by integrating sensory inputs with internal goals and past experiences.
0239.research_direction: Dr. Bae has recently been investigating the mechanisms underlying serial dependence in visual perception and working memory, focusing on how prior stimulus history systematically biases current judgments. Their recent work explores the tension between attractive and repulsive serial dependencies, probing whether these history effects are rooted in low-level sensory encoding—such as visual adaptation—or if they emerge from higher-order, post-perceptual decisional dynamics. To disentangle these processing stages, they employ continuous mouse-tracking and delayed-estimation paradigms, manipulating factors like working memory maintenance and attentional distraction to determine how they dictate the direction of the bias. Additionally, they are examining how these short-term perceptual history effects interact with long-term categorical priors, such as cardinal orientation biases, to balance sensory sensitivity with perceptual stability.

papers.title: Is repulsive serial bias in visual perception driven by adaptation mechanisms?
papers.abstract: This study examines whether repulsive serial bias—the phenomenon where the reported perception of a stimulus is repelled by a task-irrelevant prior stimulus—is caused by low-level sensory adaptation mechanisms, such as those underlying the tilt aftereffect. By concurrently measuring repulsive serial bias in a location delayed-estimation task and adaptation-driven bias using an inducer stimulus, the researchers demonstrated that the two effects are uncorrelated. Furthermore, only repulsive serial bias was linked to a significant response time modulation and a curved mouse-tracking trajectory (starting with stronger repulsion and ending with reduced repulsion). These findings provide evidence that repulsive serial bias involves higher-order, post-perceptual decisional processes rather than solely reflecting sensory representation distortions during encoding.
papers.authors: Scott Janetsky, Kuo-Wei Chen, Gi-Yeul Bae

papers.title: Working memory flips the direction of serial bias through memory-based decision
papers.abstract: This research investigates how working memory (WM) maintenance determines the direction of serial bias in visual perception. Using an orientation delayed-estimation paradigm, the authors demonstrated that a typical repulsive serial bias can be flipped into an attractive serial dependence when a high-attentional-demand distracting task interrupts WM maintenance. Analysis of mouse-tracking response trajectories and reaction times revealed patterns inconsistent with a purely sensory-driven account. The results suggest that task-irrelevant preceding stimuli influence the decision-making process for new stimuli, and the direction of the resulting bias is contingent upon how stimulus information is maintained in WM, supporting the role of memory-based decisional dynamics in history-dependent perceptual biases.
papers.authors: Kuo-Wei Chen, Gi-Yeul Bae

papers.title: Cardinal bias interacts with the stimulus history bias in orientation working memory
papers.abstract: This study explores the interplay between cardinal bias (the tendency for orientation reports to shift away from horizontal and vertical axes) and serial history bias (the influence of the preceding trial's orientation). Through a series of orientation delayed-estimation experiments, the author found that the direction and magnitude of the cardinal bias are systematically modulated by the orientation of the stimulus presented on the prior trial. The findings demonstrate that these two types of biases do not simply operate in isolation but interact, suggesting they may share a common representational framework or decisional constraints within the working memory system. The results emphasize that working memory leverages both long-term categorical knowledge and recent perceptual history to optimize performance.
papers.authors: Gi-Yeul Bae

papers.title: Repulsive and attractive serial dependence: Balancing sensitivity and stability in visual perception
papers.abstract: This paper investigates the coexistence of attractive and repulsive serial dependencies in visual perception, proposing that they reflect a functional trade-off between maximizing sensory sensitivity (via repulsion/adaptation) and maintaining perceptual stability (via attractive integration). Utilizing orientation reproduction tasks and continuous mouse-tracking, the authors found that response trajectories often begin with a strong repulsive bias away from the prior stimulus that either attenuates or shifts toward attraction as the response progresses. These decisional dynamics suggest a hierarchical processing model where early-stage sensory adaptation is followed by late-stage decisional integration, allowing the visual system to adaptively weigh previous information according to task context and sensory noise.
papers.authors: Kuo-Wei Chen, Gi-Yeul Bae

papers.title: Decisional dynamics underlie attractive and repulsive serial dependence with delayed estimation
papers.abstract: The authors explore the computational and neural mechanisms governing the direction of serial dependence in delayed-estimation tasks. By scrutinizing mouse-tracking data and modeling response error distributions, this study tests whether serial biases stem from distortions in initial sensory encoding or from post-perceptual response-adjustment processes. The researchers found that attractive and repulsive biases exhibit distinct temporal signatures in the response trajectory, indicating that history-dependent effects are actively integrated into the decision-making process during the reporting phase. These results provide empirical evidence that decisional dynamics, rather than static representational shifts, play a central role in generating the complex history effects observed in visual working memory.
papers.authors: Kuo-Wei Chen, Gi-Yeul Bae

0240.name: Gideon Caplovitz
0240.bio: Gideon Caplovitz is a cognitive neuroscientist who investigates the neural mechanisms and principles underlying human visual experience, specifically how the brain integrates features such as form and motion into coherent percepts. Utilizing psychophysics, functional MRI (fMRI), and high-density electroencephalography (EEG), Caplovitz explores the spatiotemporal integrative processes of the visual system and the neural correlates of object-based attention. Their research employs visual illusions to isolate specific sensory mechanisms and includes the investigation of octopus cognitive processes to relate biological vision to the development of artificial intelligence.
0240.research_direction: Dr. Caplovitz has recently been investigating how contextual boundaries and spatial structures shape visual processing and cognition across multiple levels of the cognitive hierarchy. Using fMRI and retinotopic mapping, their recent work explores whether object-based attention spreads automatically across early visual areas, testing if this phenomenon is an obligatory neural process rather than a strategic behavior dependent on spatial uncertainty. In the domain of motion perception, they are leveraging computational modeling and novel psychophysical stimuli—such as the Flying Bluebottle illusion—to examine how moving background contexts distort the perceived trajectories of visual targets. Furthermore, they are probing how spatial structure influences higher-level event segmentation, evaluating the methodological and statistical rigor of the "doorway effect" to understand how physical environmental transitions might act as cognitive boundaries that disrupt memory retrieval.

papers.title: Invalid Trials Are Not Required to Observe Neural Correlates of Object-based Attention in Retinotopic Visual Cortex
papers.abstract: This research investigates whether the object-mediated allocation of attention is an obligatory, automatic process or a strategic behavior contingent on spatial uncertainty or the presence of invalidly cued targets. Using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and the known retinotopic organization of the human early visual cortex, the study measured blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) signal modulation at task-irrelevant, uncued locations within a cued object. Critically, the experiments employed a 100% valid cueing paradigm to eliminate strategic monitoring of non-cued locations. Statistically significant object-based attention (OBA) effects were observed in cortical areas V1, V2, and V3 during both 100% valid runs and runs containing invalid trials. The magnitude of these neural correlates was found to be comparable across conditions, providing strong evidence that object-based attentional spreading occurs automatically within the visual hierarchy and is not reliant on the inclusion of invalid trials in the experimental design.
papers.authors: Taissa K. Lytchenko, Marvin R. Maechler, Nathan H. Heller, Sharif Saleki, Peter U. Tse, Gideon P. Caplovitz

papers.title: New insights and a computational model for understanding induced motion revealed through novel variants of the Flying Bluebottle Illusion
papers.abstract: This paper explores the mechanisms of induced motion using the Flying Bluebottle Illusion, where a target's perceived trajectory is significantly distorted by the motion of surrounding context. The authors introduce the Dueling Orbit Illusion, a series of variants where a target moves in a circular orbit while surrounding inducers follow an offset orbital path. These stimuli reveal that the perceived orbiting motion of the target is 'pulled' and distorted in both direction and extent by the background motion. A straightforward computational model is proposed to quantify the magnitude of this contextual influence based on stimulus parameters. The findings suggest that induced motion reflects high-level integrative processes in the visual system and provide a predictive framework for understanding motion contrast and relative motion perception across diverse observer domains.
papers.authors: Ryan E. B. Mruczek, Gideon P. Caplovitz

papers.title: Reply to Francis: Replicability, false alarms, and walking through doorways
papers.abstract: In this peer-reviewed commentary, the author addresses methodological critiques regarding the robustness and replicability of the 'doorway effect'—the phenomenon where passing through a physical boundary impairs memory for recently acquired information. The reply analyzes the statistical validity of previous findings, addressing concerns related to false alarm rates and potential publication bias in the field. By examining the specific environmental conditions that trigger event segmentation, the author argues that environmental transitions act as cognitive boundaries that disrupt the continuity of mental representations. The paper emphasizes the necessity of rigorous experimental control in studying how spatial structure influences information processing and memory retrieval, ultimately defending the theoretical significance of physical boundaries in shaping cognitive architecture.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS)
papers.authors: Gideon P. Caplovitz

0241.name: Giovanni Federico
0241.department: Department of Education, Psychology and Communication Sciences
0241.lab_name: Laboratory of Experimental Psychology and Cognitive Neuroscience
0241.bio: Giovanni Federico is a cognitive neuroscientist and tenure-track Assistant Professor researching the neurocognitive foundations of physical reasoning and technological culture. Federico's work examines how the human brain processes tool affordances, distinguishing between semantic and sensorimotor pathways and exploring the cognitive mechanisms of technical reasoning. They utilize a methodology that integrates behavioral paradigms, eye-tracking, and neuroimaging techniques such as functional MRI and EEG. Federico’s current research investigates the evolution of technical abilities and the interaction between human cognition and technological change.
0241.research_direction: Dr. Federico has recently been investigating the cognitive neuroscience of technology, combining theoretical modeling and structural MRI to map the neural networks that support human technical reasoning and tool use. Their recent work explores how our cognitive strategies dynamically shift between mechanical and social brain networks when we interact with increasingly complex or opaque modern technologies. In the visual domain, they use high-resolution eye-tracking to examine how top-down causal reasoning and the functional affordances of objects guide gaze trajectories and visual exploration during scene perception. Additionally, their research spans into veterinary neurology, where they are investigating the pathophysiological mechanisms—specifically neurotrophic withdrawal—underlying adverse musculoskeletal and neurological side effects associated with anti-NGF pain therapies in osteoarthritic dogs.

papers.title: A neurotrophic withdrawal hypothesis for multisystem adverse events associated with anti-NGF therapy for canine osteoarthritis pain
papers.abstract: Therapies neutralizing nerve growth factor (NGF), notably the canine monoclonal antibody bedinvetmab and newly authorized agents such as izenivetmab, effectively attenuate osteoarthritic pain but are increasingly associated with pharmacovigilance reports documenting concurrent musculoskeletal, autonomic, and central neurological complications. While prevailing interpretations treat these diverse manifestations as unrelated background pathologies or reporting artifacts, this paper presents a unifying mechanistic perspective: systemic sequestration of NGF induces an iatrogenic state of neurotrophic withdrawal. Signaling through tropomyosin receptor kinase A (TrkA) and the p75 neurotrophin receptor (p75NTR) is essential not merely for nociceptive signaling but for sensory axon survival, autonomic regulation, lower urinary tract innervation, and skeletal repair mediated by calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP)-positive dorsal root ganglion (DRG) afferents. The authors formulate a 'dual-hit' pathophysiological model wherein sustained depletion of trophic support synergizes with increased mechanical joint loading permitted by effective analgesia, precipitating accelerated joint destruction, bone remodeling failure, and neuropathic decline, particularly in geriatric animals with attenuated homeostatic resilience.
papers.authors: Giovanni Federico, Alfonso Ilardi, Valerio Elia, Sergio Chieffi

papers.title: Growing Technological Opacity and the Social Brain
papers.abstract: While cumulative cultural evolution has long been assumed to impose escalating computational demands primarily on mechanical problem-solving faculties, recent cognitive neuroscience evidence reveals that growing technological opacity increasingly recruits the social brain. Over evolutionary history, artifacts have shifted from physically transparent implements to functionally opaque mechanisms, complex division-of-labor systems, and autonomous digital or computational agents. This theoretical framework posits that human cognition dynamically negotiates between two large-scale, intrinsically anticorrelated neural systems: the technical brain (anchored in the left inferior frontal gyrus and area PF within the inferior parietal lobule), specialized for deterministic mechanical causality, and the social brain (spanning the temporoparietal junction, temporal pole, and anterior medial prefrontal cortex), dedicated to mentalizing and agentic inference. As physical mechanisms become epistemically opaque, bottom-up perceptual cues and heightened causal uncertainty drive network switching, compelling humans to rely on transactive socio-technical expertise and to project intentional stances onto non-biological technological systems.
papers.authors: François Osiurak, Giovanni Federico

papers.title: Causal reasoning guides visual exploration
papers.abstract: Visual scene perception requires resolving contextual and functional relations among objects, particularly when environmental coherence is disrupted. Employing high-resolution eye-tracking during a free-viewing paradigm, this study evaluated whether oculomotor exploration under contextual violations is governed by implicit causal reasoning—the cognitive capacity to identify and simulate mechanical interactions. Observers viewed scenes depicting mechanical tools embedded in either congruent or incongruent settings, with stimuli segmented into functional effect-producing components and manipulable grasp handles. Spatiotemporal fixation trajectories and transition probability modeling across designated areas of interest revealed that participants prioritize the functional working end of tools to resolve affordances and systematically project gaze toward adjacent scene elements that could plausibly receive or mediate physical work. These findings establish that eye-movement allocation during object exploration reflects top-down causal and mechanical inference rather than low-level physical saliency or automatic grasp-related sensorimotor affordances.
papers.authors: Luigi Valio, Donatella Ferrante, Roberto Montanari, Maria Antonella Brandimonte, Giovanni Federico

papers.title: Toward a cognitive neuroscience of technology
papers.abstract: Addressing twelve peer commentaries on their target article, the authors synthesize a comprehensive research agenda for the cognitive neuroscience of technology. The revised framework refines the structural and functional taxonomy of the parietal lobes, delineating the technical reasoning core situated in left area PF from adjacent posterior parietal territories engaged in motor manipulation knowledge and conceptual transformations required for digital interfaces. The left inferior frontal gyrus (IFG) is characterized as a dual-function control node that simultaneously routes representations across specialized hubs and supplies executive scaffolding for sequential planning and action selection under high cognitive load. Furthermore, the synthesis integrates white-matter connectivity, reward and dopaminergic circuitry, and affordance hierarchies extending across physical, digital, and symbolic domains, establishing translational implications for cognitive aging, neurorehabilitation of apraxia, and human-technology adaptation.
papers.authors: Giovanni Federico, Ciro Rosario Ilardi, Maria A. Brandimonte, Paola Marangolo, François Osiurak

papers.title: Left area PF as a neural marker of technical reasoning
papers.abstract: Technical reasoning represents the neurocognitive capacity to deduce and manipulate mechanical relationships and physical principles, constituting an essential cognitive adaptation underpinning cumulative tool culture. Utilizing high-resolution 3 T structural magnetic resonance imaging in 75 healthy young adults (54 females; mean age = 20.92 ± 3.28 years), this investigation examined whether individual variability in psychotechnical problem-solving maps onto morphometric variation within inferior parietal cortex subregions. Voxel- and surface-based morphometry demonstrated that grey matter volume specifically within left area PF, localized to the supramarginal gyrus of the inferior parietal lobule, significantly predicts technical reasoning proficiency. This anatomical relationship remained robust after adjusting for total intracranial volume, demographic metrics, and personality factors. By contrast, control volumes in right prefrontal cortices tracked general fluid intelligence and abstract logical abilities without correlating with technical reasoning, validating left area PF as a structurally specialized technical hub supporting human physical cognition.
papers.authors: Giovanni Federico, Ciro Rosario Ilardi, Paola Marangolo, Chloé Bryche, Maximilien Metaireau, Alexandre Bluet, Mathieu Lesourd, Yves Rossetti, François Osiurak

0242.name: Gabriel Kreiman
0242.bio: Gabriel Kreiman is a Professor of Ophthalmology at Harvard Medical School and a researcher at the F.M. Kirby Neurobiology Center at Boston Children's Hospital. Kreiman’s research integrates high-resolution intracranial neurophysiology in the human brain with computational modeling and psychophysics to study how neural circuits encode, process, and transmit information. This work addresses the neuronal correlates of visual object recognition, memory formation, and the development of biologically-inspired artificial intelligence models. Their current projects focus on elucidating the mechanisms of visual cognition—such as pattern completion and context-dependent recognition—while building AI architectures that mimic human-like visual perception and learning.
0242.research_direction: Dr. Kreiman has recently been investigating the computational and neural mechanisms of visual processing across both biological and artificial systems. Their recent work explores human object recognition and rapid learning using invasive single-neuron and iEEG recordings, specifically probing how feedforward and top-down recurrent signals help the brain resolve visually ambiguous stimuli like minimally recognizable configurations. In animal models, they are studying inter-areal communication across the visual cortex to parse how shared neuronal variability is structured during both stimulus-driven and spontaneous states. Alongside this physiological work, their computational research tests high-level scene understanding in artificial intelligence by benchmarking how well vision-language models interpret graphical humor, while also developing efficient continual learning algorithms that mitigate catastrophic forgetting through shape-biased compositional feature replays.

papers.title: Single-neuron encoding of rapidly learned visual information reshapes human perception
papers.abstract: The study investigates the neurophysiological basis of rapid visual object recognition through single-neuron recordings in the human occipital (OC) cortex and medial temporal lobe (MTL). Utilizing a paradigm involving the recognition of degraded images, the authors demonstrate that neurons in both regions modulate their firing patterns to encode newly acquired visual information and drive perceptual shifts. Population decoding reveals that OC neurons exhibit increased processing latencies during the identification of learned images, which consequently delays response onsets in the MTL. These findings suggest that OC-mediated recognition following rapid learning involves extensive recurrent processing—potentially via higher-order neocortical feedback—independent of direct MTL feedback, providing mechanistic constraints for biologically plausible few-shot learning models.
papers.authors: Marcelo Armendariz, Julie Blumberg, Jed Singer, Franz Aiple, Jiye Kim, Nuria Dominguez-Iturza, Armin Brandt, Peter Reinacher, Andreas Schulze-Bonhage, Gabriel Kreiman

papers.title: HumorDB: Can AI understand graphical humor?
papers.abstract: This work introduces HumorDB, a curated dataset designed to evaluate the capacity of AI systems to interpret graphical humor, serving as a benchmark for complex scene understanding and high-level cognitive integration. The dataset includes diverse visual formats—including photos, cartoons, and sketches—and incorporates minimally contrastive image pairs to isolate humor-inducing features. Evaluation of state-of-the-art vision models and large vision-language models (VLMs) across classification, rating, and comparison tasks reveals a substantial performance gap compared to human benchmarks. Saliency and attention map analyses indicate that models often fail to localize the specific incongruities that elicit humor, suggesting that human-like humor understanding requires more robust architectures capable of contextual reasoning and bridging the gap between perception and abstraction.
papers.authors: Vedaant Jain, Felipe dos Santos Alves Feitosa, Gabriel Kreiman

papers.title: Neural correlates of minimal recognizable configurations in the human brain
papers.abstract: This research explores the neural substrates of pattern completion using minimally recognizable configurations (MIRCs) and their unrecognizable sub-parts (sub-MIRCs). Through invasive human neurophysiological recordings (iEEG), the authors show that successful MIRC identification is characterized by a dynamic interplay of feedforward and feedback signals between frontal and temporal cortices. Furthermore, the study finds that sub-MIRC recognition improves significantly following exposure to the original full objects, a process of rapid unsupervised learning reflected in modulated neural activity within the temporal cortex. These results are at odds with strictly feedforward architectures of visual recognition, highlighting the essential role of top-down signals from the frontal lobe in resolving visually ambiguous stimuli.
papers.authors: Antonino Casile, Aurelie Cordier, Jiye G. Kim, Andrea Cometa, Joseph R. Madsen, Scellig Stone, Guy Ben-Yosef, Shimon Ullman, William Anderson, Gabriel Kreiman

papers.title: Tuned compositional feature replays for efficient stream learning
papers.abstract: Addressing the challenge of catastrophic forgetting in online stream learning, the authors propose Compositional Replay Using Memory Blocks (CRUMB), a continual learning algorithm. CRUMB mitigates knowledge loss by replaying feature maps reconstructed from a codebook of trainable and re-usable 'memory blocks.' In convolutional neural networks (CNNs), these vectors are concatenated to compositionally approximate feature map tensors, allowing the model to store only memory block indices rather than raw images, reducing the memory footprint to 3.6%. The reconstruction mechanism biases the network toward shape-based features over texture, enhancing stability during sequential task learning. Empirical evaluation across seven benchmarks demonstrates that CRUMB significantly outperforms thirteen existing methods in both mitigating forgetting and computational efficiency.
papers.venue: IEEE Transactions on Neural Networks and Learning Systems (TNNLS)
papers.authors: Morgan B. Talbot, Rushikesh Zawar, Rohil Badkundri, Mengmi Zhang, Gabriel Kreiman

papers.title: Trial-by-trial inter-areal interactions in visual cortex in the presence or absence of visual stimulation
papers.abstract: This study investigates single-trial inter-areal communication within the visual cortex of mice and macaques. Using calcium imaging and extracellular neurophysiological recordings, the authors quantify the predictability of neuronal activity in one cortical layer or area based on the activity of another, distinguishing between stimulus-driven and non-stimulus-driven shared variability. The results demonstrate bidirectional interactions between L2/3 and L4 in mice and V1 and V4 in macaques, with the latter showing directional asymmetry. The research identifies a bimodal distribution of neurons: those primarily driven by visual input and those whose activity remains highly predictable during spontaneous states. These findings highlight the significance of non-visual shared variability and provide a framework for computational models that account for the transformations from sensory inputs to cortical encoding.
papers.authors: Dianna Hidalgo, Giorgia Dellaferrera, Will Xiao, Maria Papadopouli, Stelios Smirnakis, Gabriel Kreiman

0244.name: Gregory J. Zelinsky
0244.department: Department of Psychology, Department of Computer Science
0244.bio: Gregory J. Zelinsky is a Professor at Stony Brook University with appointments in the Departments of Psychology and Computer Science, specializing in the intersection of human vision and artificial intelligence. Zelinsky’s research focuses on the mechanisms of visual search, scene perception, and working memory, utilizing eye-tracking technology to record human oculomotor behavior. They integrate these behavioral data with image-based neurocomputational models to simulate and predict the spatiotemporal dynamics of attention and information selection. Their work aims to clarify how the brain represents object categories and manages visual guidance through the development of computational frameworks that mimic human visual processing.
0244.research_direction: Dr. Zelinsky has recently been investigating the computational and neural mechanisms underlying active visual perception, object recognition, and attention. Their recent work explores how the visual system maintains stable scene representations by using latent diffusion models and autoencoder architectures to test whether top-down generative processes support robust object recognition and the perception of peripheral details. In parallel, they are examining the neural control of visual search by applying time-series partial information decomposition to electrophysiological recordings from the primate superior colliculus. Through these diverse approaches, Dr. Zelinsky investigates how single neurons integrate competing cognitive signals—such as target guidance, bottom-up salience, and search history—to guide overt attention, and how the brain synthesizes foveal and peripheral inputs to construct a stable visual world.

papers.title: Generating metamers of human scene understanding
papers.abstract: This research introduces MetamerGen, a generative framework based on latent diffusion models designed to synthesize scene metamers that align with latent human scene representations. The model employs a dual-stream architecture utilizing DINOv2 self-supervised encoders to fuse sparse, high-resolution foveal features with low-resolution peripheral gist information. By conditioning image synthesis on behavioral fixation data, the authors evaluated the sufficiency of fixated information for scene understanding through a real-time same-different discrimination paradigm. The study demonstrates that high-level semantic features in the generated scenes are the primary predictors of perceptual equivalence (metamerism), providing a tool to investigate the information extracted and retained by the visual system during scene viewing.
