papers.venue: Accepted to the 2025 International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2025) / arXiv:2601.11675
papers.authors: Ritik Raina, Abe Leite, Alexandros Graikos, Seoyoung Ahn, Dimitris Samaras, Gregory J. Zelinsky

papers.title: Multiple patterns of selectivity in superior colliculus control visual search
papers.abstract: The primate superior colliculus (SC) is critical for visually-guided behavior, yet how it integrates multiple control signals like target guidance and search history remains debated. This study recorded single-unit activity from rhesus monkeys performing a multi-target search task and applied a novel time-series partial information decomposition (PID) analysis to characterize neural selectivity. The findings reveal a heterogeneous population of SC neurons exhibiting pure selectivity to target color or previous fixation, as well as mixed and dynamic selectivity where codes switch over the fixation period. These results suggest that the SC functions as a flexible cognitive control center that integrates feature-based attention and inhibitory tagging signals rather than acting as a simple static priority map.
papers.authors: Abe Leite, Hossein Adeli, Robert M. McPeek, Gregory J. Zelinsky

papers.title: Generating objects in peripheral vision using attention-guided diffusion models
papers.abstract: This study tests the hypothesis that the perception of a stable visual world is supported by the active generation of objects in the blurred periphery, guided by task-relevant information from fixations. The authors utilized a latent diffusion model conditioned on high-resolution image features extracted from locations corresponding to human behavioral fixations. Quantitative evaluation showed that human-fixation-driven conditioning significantly improved the fidelity of generated target objects in peripheral areas compared to random fixation baselines, as measured by sum of squared errors (SSE) in pixel space. The results indicate that active peripheral generation is category-specific and task-dependent, providing a computational mechanism for how the brain maintains object context despite peripheral information loss.
papers.authors: Ritik Raina, Seoyoung Ahn, Gregory J. Zelinsky

papers.title: The attentive reconstruction of objects facilitates robust object recognition
papers.abstract: The authors propose a neurocomputational model, Object Reconstruction-guided Attention (ORA), asserting that robust object recognition is facilitated by the top-down generative reconstruction of hypothesized objects. Built on an autoencoder architecture, ORA uses an encoder to produce latent object-centric representations and an iterative decoder to generate high-resolution reconstructions that serve as templates to bias feedforward feature routing. The model was benchmarked against standard CNNs using corrupted image datasets (MNIST-C and ImageNet-C), where it demonstrated superior robustness to noise and occlusion. Crucially, the ORA model's performance aligned more closely with human behavioral metrics, including reaction times and patterns of recognition errors, than purely feedforward architectures.
papers.authors: Seoyoung Ahn, Hossein Adeli, Gregory J. Zelinsky

papers.title: Evaluating theories of neural information integration during visual search
papers.abstract: This work applies time-series partial information decomposition (PID) to a dataset of recordings from the monkey superior colliculus (SC) during a multi-target visual search task to evaluate theories of information integration. The analysis sought to distinguish between different modes of neural coding: decision-variable selectivity (encoding priority/expected value), functional specialization (encoding specific task variables like previous fixation), and code-switching (temporal multiplexing). The results show that SC neurons employ a diverse array of these strategies to integrate target guidance, bottom-up salience, and inhibitory tagging signals. By quantifying unique, redundant, and synergistic information, the study reveals the SC as a specialized midbrain hub for the complex integration required to drive overt attention during search.
papers.authors: Abe Leite, Hossein Adeli, Robert M. McPeek, Gregory J. Zelinsky

0246.name: Guido Maiello
0246.bio: Guido Maiello is a Lecturer at the University of Southampton specializing in the neural and computational mechanisms of visual-motor integration. They utilize psychophysics, eye-tracking, functional MRI, and virtual reality to investigate how the human visual system facilitates actions like grasping and object manipulation in 3D space. Maiello's research examines how observers judge grasp quality and integrate multi-sensory cues—including shape, material, and depth—to plan and execute motor tasks. Their work also explores the impact of visual impairments on hand-eye coordination and the development of image-computable models for visual shape similarity.
0246.research_direction: Dr. Maiello has recently been investigating the visuomotor mechanisms that guide how humans grasp three-dimensional objects. Their recent work explores whether the fundamental principles of grasp selection, such as how we adjust our grip based on cues about an object's surface material and mass distribution, generalize from highly constrained two-digit tasks to naturalistic, multidigit grasping. By observing participants handle objects with varying physical properties under both restricted and unconstrained free-choice conditions, they are examining how sensory information and conflicting cues drive contact point selection and grip uncertainty. Ultimately, their research probes how well classic precision-grip paradigms reflect the complex, unconstrained hand movements that humans use to interact with the world.

papers.title: Does precision grip research extend to unconstrained, multidigit grasping?
papers.abstract: This study asks whether findings from the extensive precision-grip (thumb-index) grasping literature—such as sensitivity to object mass distribution and surface material—generalize to naturalistic grasps in which participants are free to use any number of digits. Participants grasped three-dimensional objects made of brass or wood under two conditions: a constrained precision-grip task and an unconstrained task in which any grip configuration was permitted. When unconstrained, participants rarely chose a strict two-digit precision grip, instead favoring multidigit grasps; nonetheless, in both grip conditions, contact points shifted toward the object's center of mass, and when material and mass-distribution cues conflicted, selection variability increased, indicating greater uncertainty about the optimal grasp. Critically, even when additional digits were recruited, participants placed the thumb and index finger at essentially the same locations used during precision grip, indicating the extra digits primarily served a stabilizing/support role. The results imply that core principles derived from precision-grip research—center-of-mass alignment and material sensitivity—extend to more naturalistic, unconstrained multidigit grasping.
papers.authors: Fabrizio Lepori, Frieder T. Hartmann, Kira I. Dehn, Manuela Chessa, Roland W. Fleming, Guido Maiello

0247.name: Guillaume S Masson
0247.department: Institut de Neurosciences de la Timone (INT)
0247.main_research_area: Visual motion processing and oculomotor control
0247.bio: Guillaume S. Masson is a neuroscientist and former director of the Institut de Neurosciences de la Timone (INT) who researches the neural mechanisms of visual motion perception and eye movement control. Masson’s work focuses on how the brain integrates and segments local motion signals to generate reflexive and pursuit oculomotor responses, often employing short-latency ocular following as a model system. Using a multi-scale approach that combines human psychophysics, non-human primate electrophysiology, and Bayesian computational modeling, Masson investigates how nonlinear interactions within cortical areas V1 and MT facilitate visual inference under uncertainty. Their current research explores the role of predictive signals and environmental statistics in shaping the spatiotemporal dynamics of sensory integration for active vision.
0247.research_direction: Dr. Masson has recently been investigating the computational and cognitive mechanisms underlying human visual motion processing and visually guided behavior. Their recent work explores how the visual system integrates or segments complex, multicomponent motion signals, aided by their development of novel, real-time generative models for synthesizing dynamic naturalistic textures like Motion Clouds. Additionally, they are probing the active, cognitive nature of smooth pursuit eye movements to understand how top-down predictive priors, target kinematics, and low-level image features like spatial frequency modulate oculomotor control. Finally, Dr. Masson is also applying information-theoretic frameworks to visual search, investigating how prioritizing sensory data compression might govern human perceptual decision-making and performance bottlenecks in complex scenes.

papers.title: DynTex: A real-time generative model of dynamic naturalistic luminance textures
papers.abstract: The study introduces DynTex, an open-source toolbox designed for the real-time synthesis of Motion Clouds (MCs), which are stochastic dynamic textures with parametrically controlled spatiotemporal statistics. MCs are characterized by their energy distribution in Fourier space, particularly across orientation, spatial frequency, and speed. The generative model employs a frame-by-frame autoregressive (AR) process to ensure temporal continuity and allows for precise manipulation of bandwidth parameters. By implementing the synthesis on GPU architectures, the authors achieve high-frame-rate rendering suitable for psychophysical and neurophysiological experiments. The paper demonstrates the toolbox's utility in bridging the gap between simple synthetic stimuli (e.g., gratings, dots) and complex natural videos, providing a calibrated method for probing hierarchical visual motion processing.
papers.authors: Andrew Isaac Meso, Jonathan Vacher, Nikos Gekas, Pascal Mamassian, Laurent U Perrinet, Guillaume S Masson

papers.title: Multicomponent motion is perceptually organised along distinct dimensions revealed by Distance Scaling and Forced Choice paradigms
papers.abstract: This research investigates the internal dimensionality and geometric organization of human visual motion processing when confronted with multiple localized frequency components. Using distance scaling and forced-choice psychophysical tasks, the authors map how the visual system integrates or segments overlapping motion signals based on their contrast and spatiotemporal frequency characteristics. The results indicate that motion components are supralinearly integrated when they align along a shared iso-velocity line in Fourier space, facilitating coherent object motion perception. Conversely, components are segmented when they differ significantly in mean scale or frequency, pointing to a flexible pooling mechanism that adapts to scene complexity. This study provides a quantitative framework for understanding the computational rules governing the transition between motion integration and transparency.
papers.authors: Andrew Isaac Meso, Jonathan Vacher, Nikos Gekas, Pascal Mamassian, Laurent U Perrinet, Guillaume S Masson

papers.title: Spatial frequency, not orientation, can be associated to speed statistics: Effects on pursuit eye movements
papers.abstract: This paper examines the specificity of visual priors for motion statistics in the human oculomotor system. Participants performed smooth pursuit eye movements to targets whose speed regularities were varied across experimental blocks. The study specifically tested whether the internal model underlying anticipatory pursuit and pursuit gain is associated with low-level image features such as spatial frequency or orientation. Oculomotor data revealed that anticipatory eye velocity and steady-state gain were selectively modulated by the spatial frequency content of the stimuli, matching the learned speed statistics, whereas orientation had no significant effect. These findings suggest that the brain's predictive models for motion are scale-dependent, likely reflecting the non-uniform distribution of speed statistics across different spatial scales in natural environments.
papers.authors: Cléo Schoeffel, Anna Montagnini, Guillaume S Masson

papers.title: Cognitive processes involved in smooth pursuit eye movements
papers.abstract: This work explores the higher-order cognitive influences on smooth pursuit eye movements, moving beyond the traditional view of pursuit as a purely reflexive behavior. The authors investigate how internal models of target kinematics, motion predictability, and task-relevant goals modulate oculomotor control. Utilizing behavioral metrics from tracking tasks and computational modeling, the study demonstrates that the pursuit system actively maintains specific retinal velocity and position 'errors' to facilitate visual processing, rather than merely attempting to minimize image slip. The findings emphasize the integration of bottom-up sensory signals with top-down predictive information, such as expected acceleration and target reappearance probabilities, to optimize tracking performance in dynamic environments.
papers.authors: Anna Montagnini, Laurent U Perrinet, Guillaume S Masson

papers.title: Prioritizing Compression Explains Human Perceptual Decisions in Visual Search
papers.abstract: This study proposes an information-theoretic account of human decision-making in visual search tasks. The authors hypothesize that the visual system employs a strategy aimed at prioritizing data compression to handle the high dimensionality of sensory input. By analyzing behavioral data from search experiments where target-distractor similarity and set size were systematically manipulated, the researchers show that accuracy and reaction time distributions are well-modeled by a framework that minimizes informational redundancy. The results suggest that perceptual bottlenecks in visual search are not solely due to limited neural capacity but represent an adaptive optimization for processing efficiency. This compression-based approach provides a unified explanation for set-size effects and search asymmetries in complex visual scenes.
papers.venue: 2024 IEEE International Conference on Image Processing (ICIP)
papers.authors: Andrew Isaac Meso, Anna Montagnini, Jason Bell, Guillaume S Masson

0248.name: Halely Balaban
0248.lab_name: Cognitive Dynamics and Adaptability Lab (CDA Lab)
0248.main_research_area: visual working memory and intuitive physics
0248.bio: Halely Balaban is an Assistant Professor of Cognitive Psychology and director of the Cognitive Dynamics and Adaptability Lab at The Open University of Israel. Balaban’s research examines the relationship between visual working memory and commonsense physical reasoning, focusing on how the mind maintains and updates representations of dynamic objects in visual scenes. Using a multi-method approach that integrates EEG, behavioral psychophysics, and computational modeling, Balaban has analyzed how intuitive physics guides tracking mechanisms and how mental simulation is constrained by serial capacity limits. Their work identifies bidirectional links between representational content and the pointer systems underlying human visual cognition.
0248.research_direction: Dr. Balaban's recent work explores the cognitive architecture of dynamic visual working memory and mental simulation. They have recently been investigating how visual working memory’s "pointer system" maintains stable indexes of external targets, using behavioral change-detection and electrophysiological markers to ask whether these representations are anchored by low-level spatiotemporal continuity or higher-level physical objecthood. Broadly, their research explores a theoretical dichotomy between abstract "physics" simulation and detailed "graphics" rendering in the mind, investigating how this architectural split might explain diverse phenomena ranging from dorsal-ventral stream specializations to cognitive processing in aphantasia. To probe the mechanics of this internal physics engine, they are utilizing novel imagined-object-tracking paradigms to determine whether humans extrapolate hidden motion trajectories serially or in parallel. Additionally, they are examining the functional role of the internal graphics system, questioning whether a lack of visual imagery might indirectly influence social reasoning through downstream changes in affective arousal.

papers.title: Working memory's pointer system is governed by physical objecthood, not spatiotemporal information
papers.abstract: To accommodate continuous changes in the environment, visual working memory (VWM) relies on an indexical pointer system that maintains a one-to-one mapping between internal online representations and external entities. When this mapping is invalidated, updating fails and VWM triggers a resetting process, which manifests behaviorally as an acute inability to detect salient changes in visible items. Through behavioral tracking and change-detection paradigms that manipulate trajectory continuity and surface features, this study investigates whether pointer assignment is dictated by continuous spatiotemporal coordinates or by higher-level physical objecthood. Resetting occurred specifically when the perceptual integrity of physical objects was disrupted—even under conditions where spatiotemporal continuity was held constant—demonstrating that VWM pointers are organized around physical objecthood rather than low-level spatiotemporal trajectories.
papers.authors: Halely Balaban

papers.title: Emotion may indirectly link rendering and social reasoning
papers.abstract: This article evaluates the functional significance of mental imagery in social cognition, addressing proposals regarding the impairments in autobiographical memory and interpersonal empathy observed in congenital aphantasia. The authors argue against a necessary, direct computational link between internal graphical rendering and high-level social reasoning algorithms. Instead, they hypothesize an indirect architecture mediated by affective arousal: rendered sensory images serve as inputs to downstream emotional activation networks, which subsequently modulate empathic responses and personal episodic recall. This indirect pathway reconciles why individuals with aphantasia show selective attenuation in emotional responses to purely verbal descriptions while exhibiting preserved reasoning competencies in broader social domains.
papers.authors: Halely Balaban, Tomer D. Ullman

papers.title: Physics versus graphics as an organizing dichotomy in cognition
papers.abstract: Drawing an analogy to the decoupled simulation pipelines of modern computational graphics and physics engines, this review proposes that human mental simulation is organized along a foundational dichotomy: physical simulation versus graphical rendering. Physical simulation constructs abstract, object-based representations to predict mechanical, dynamical, and spatiotemporal trajectories without necessitating image generation. In contrast, graphical rendering reconstructs detailed, coordinate-space pixel arrays for visual inspection and imagery. This architectural separation provides a unifying framework that accounts for diverse cognitive and neuroscientific phenomena, including dorsal versus ventral stream functional specializations, task performance preserved in aphantasic individuals during spatial reasoning, mental rotation mechanics, and the resource limits of attentive tracking.
papers.authors: Halely Balaban, Tomer D. Ullman

papers.title: Visual working memory's pointer system: Past, present, and future
papers.abstract: This review consolidates the empirical and theoretical landscape surrounding the visual working memory (VWM) pointer system—the core cognitive architecture providing dynamic, content-independent indexes between internal mental files and external targets. The authors review electrophysiological markers, notably the contralateral delay activity (CDA), to differentiate continuous item updating from the disruptive 'resetting' response triggered upon index invalidation. Key topics include the neurofunctional dissociation between content feature storage and content-free indexing, the primacy of objecthood over featural continuity in assigning indexes, mechanisms of information compression (object-unification versus grouping), and integration with intuitive physical priors.
papers.authors: Halely Balaban, Roy Luria

papers.title: The capacity limits of moving objects in the imagination
papers.abstract: Although multiple object tracking (MOT) during online perception supports simultaneous tracking of 3–4 items, the capacity boundaries of dynamic mental simulation remain largely unknown. Across nine pre-registered behavioral experiments (N = 313), an Imagined Objects Tracking (IOT) paradigm was deployed wherein participants observed ballistic animated trajectories that halted mid-flight, requiring them to mentally project unobserved physical motion to predict impact timing. While simulating one moving entity matched physical ground truth, tracking two imagined targets degraded performance, yielding response patterns that fit a Serial Model (updating one object at a time) rather than a Parallel Model. This single-object bottleneck persisted despite strong perceptual grouping cues, naturalistic occlusions, and simplified kinematics, indicating that trajectory extrapolation in the imagination operates serially.
papers.authors: Halely Balaban, Tomer D. Ullman

0249.name: Haluk Öǧmen
0249.bio: Haluk Öğmen is a Professor and Senior Associate Dean at the University of Denver’s Ritchie School of Engineering and Computer Science, where they direct the Perceptual and Cognitive Dynamics Laboratory. Öğmen’s research focuses on reverse-engineering the human visual system to analyze how the brain processes information across space and time, specifically through the study of visual masking and motion perception. By employing computational neuroscience and psychophysical methodologies, they investigate the neural mechanisms underlying non-retinotopic representations and the interaction between attention and sensory memory. Their technical work includes theoretical research on the microgenesis of conscious vision and the development of neural models that account for the temporal dynamics of human perception.
0249.research_direction: Dr. Öǧmen has recently been investigating a diverse range of visual and cognitive processes, spanning from the fundamental dynamics of working memory to applied clinical eye-tracking. In the domain of memory, their recent work explores how the spatial layout and set-size of visual arrays influence the latency and precision with which individuals update or actively remove obsolete items from visual working memory. They are also examining high-level object perception, using virtual reality and mental rotation paradigms to understand how geometric properties like bilateral symmetry and axes of elongation guide the visual system in establishing internal reference frames for unfamiliar shapes. Furthermore, Dr. Öǧmen is developing novel computational frameworks that apply persistent homology to eye-tracking data, investigating whether the topological structure of spatio-temporal scanpaths can serve as robust screening markers for neural disorders like dyslexia and ADHD.

papers.title: Spatial Layout Influences the Dynamics of Visual Working Memory for Both Categorical and Continuous Stimuli
papers.abstract: This investigation examines how the spatial configuration and set-size of stimuli modulate the temporal dynamics of visual working memory (VWM) updating and removal. Utilizing a modified partial-update paradigm, the study assesses the latency and precision of memory modification when specific items in a multi-item array are designated as no longer relevant. The findings indicate that the efficiency of the active removal process is not solely a function of item count but is significantly impacted by the spatial layout of the visual array. The research contrasts performance across categorical and continuous stimulus domains, demonstrating that spatial proximity and structural organization in the visual field dictate the rate at which internal representations are purged or updated to accommodate new sensory information.
papers.authors: Shaoying Wang, Srimant P. Tripathy, Haluk Öğmen

papers.title: Leveraging Persistent Homology of Eye Movements for Neural Disorder Screening
papers.abstract: This paper presents a novel framework for the automated screening of neurological and cognitive impairments by applying Persistent Homology, a method from topological data analysis (TDA), to eye-tracking data. Traditional feature extraction techniques often fail to represent the complex spatio-temporal dynamics of scanpaths and fixations across diverse tasks. The authors propose a methodology to extract robust topological features that capture the underlying structure of ocular behavior. When applied to datasets for dyslexia and ADHD, a shallow multilayer perceptron classifier using these spatio-temporal topological features achieved high sensitivity and specificity. The results demonstrate that topological invariants provide a powerful, task-independent signature for identifying abnormal eye movements associated with various neural disorders.
papers.authors: Dongcheng He, Shaoying Wang, Haluk Öğmen

papers.title: The roles of symmetry and elongation in developing reference frames
papers.abstract: This study systematically explores how geometrical properties, specifically bilateral symmetry and axes of elongation, facilitate the selection and development of perceptual reference frames for unfamiliar objects. Using a virtual reality (VR) environment to eliminate extraneous environmental cues, the researchers employed mental rotation and novel-shape recognition tasks to identify the stability of internal reference axes. Behavioral data revealed that subjects utilize the most symmetrical or elongated axis as a primary reference orientation. When both cues are present, the system employs a competitive 'winner-take-all' mechanism where elongation generally dominates symmetry. These findings support a canonical sensorimotor theory of object representation, suggesting that internal reference frames are dynamically established through the integration of ubiquitous geometrical invariants.
papers.authors: Dongcheng He, Haluk Öğmen

0251.name: Hannah Block
0251.bio: Hannah J. Block is an Associate Professor whose research characterizes the neurophysiological substrates of human sensorimotor control and multisensory integration. Utilizing transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), and robotic behavioral assays, Block’s lab investigates how the central nervous system weights and realigns visual and proprioceptive inputs during motor learning. Their current research examines the mechanisms of visuo-proprioceptive recalibration and the spatial representation of the body to understand how these sensory updates influence motor skill retention. This work aims to connect sensory perception and motor control research to inform clinical strategies for stroke rehabilitation and the development of assistive technologies.
0251.research_direction: Dr. Block has recently been investigating how the brain integrates visual and proprioceptive information to guide motor control and dynamically update body representation. Their recent work explores the behavioral mechanisms of visuo-proprioceptive recalibration, specifically asking how the motor system adapts to spatial cue conflicts of varying abruptness and whether explicit cognitive awareness of these sensory mismatches alters perceptual realignment. To map the neural substrates of these multisensory processes, they use non-invasive brain stimulation (TMS and cTBS) to probe how somatosensory, parietal, and frontal cortices communicate sensory updates to the motor cortex during precision skill learning. Additionally, they utilize resting-state fMRI to examine how individual differences in sensory weighting—whether a person relies more heavily on vision or proprioception—are intrinsically reflected in whole-brain functional connectivity networks.

papers.title: Frontal and Parietal Contributions to Proprioception and Motor Skill Learning
papers.abstract: This study evaluated the distinct roles of the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) and the supramarginal gyrus (SMG) in motor skill acquisition and proprioceptive processing during a spatially complex maze-tracing task. Using continuous theta-burst stimulation (cTBS) to induce transient focal inhibition, the research measured changes in movement accuracy and variability (RMSE) across various execution speeds on a Kinarm robotic manipulandum. While participants in all experimental conditions exhibited basic skill improvement, inhibition of the DLPFC or SMG selectively impaired the reduction of movement variability at high precision speeds. These results suggest that while low-level sensorimotor mechanisms support basic learning, higher-order proprioceptive regions in the posterior parietal cortex and cognitive control nodes in the frontal cortex are essential for managing the precision and complexity requirements of advanced motor skills.
papers.authors: Manasi Wali, Hannah J. Block

papers.title: Timing of responses to gradual and abrupt visuo-proprioceptive cue conflict with and without feedback
papers.abstract: The study investigated the temporal dynamics and magnitude of visuo-proprioceptive recalibration under gradual versus abrupt spatial offsets (70 mm) and analyzed the impact of performance feedback on these processes. Behavioral results indicated that although an abrupt conflict onset triggered near-instantaneous perceptual realignment, the final magnitude of recalibration reached a steady state comparable to that of a gradually introduced conflict. Furthermore, the presence of performance feedback significantly enhanced error-based motor adaptation in the indicator hand but did not appreciably shift the magnitude of perceptual recalibration in the target hand. These findings demonstrate that perceptual recalibration following a multisensory cue conflict is primarily driven by the magnitude of the discrepancy rather than the rate of onset, and that this process is largely distinct from the error-based mechanisms mediating motor adaptation.
papers.authors: Reshma Babu, Ramanpreet K. Matharu, Che-Wei Lo, Hannah J. Block

papers.title: Somatosensory cortex and body representation: Updating the motor system during a visuo-proprioceptive cue conflict
papers.abstract: This investigation explored the neural substrates through which multisensory body representation updates are communicated to the motor system. Utilizing transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) and continuous theta-burst stimulation (cTBS), the research established that short-latency afferent inhibition (SAI)—a marker of sensorimotor integration—is specifically modulated by proprioceptive recalibration during visuo-proprioceptive cue conflict. Experimental results showed that inhibiting the primary somatosensory cortex (S1), but not the primary motor cortex (M1), increased both proprioceptive variance and recalibration magnitude. These results support a model where multisensory updates to hand representation are conveyed via an S1-to-M1 pathway, suggesting that S1 activity reflects the outcome of higher-order multisensory computations rather than simple unisensory processing.
papers.authors: Jasmine L. Mirdamadi, Reshma Babu, Manasi Wali, Courtney R. Seigel, Anna Hsiao, Trevor Lee-Miller, Hannah J. Block

papers.title: Network dynamics for sensory prioritization: Functional connectivity related to individual sensory weighting of vision versus proprioception during upper limb control
papers.abstract: This research utilized resting-state functional MRI (rsfMRI) to examine how individual variations in sensory weighting—specifically the reliance on visual versus proprioceptive cues—are reflected in whole-brain functional connectivity. Using atlas-based and individually-localized regions of interest, the study quantified intrinsic connectivity between sensorimotor networks and other cortical nodes. The analysis revealed that individual sensory prioritization during upper limb tasks is significantly correlated with the strength of functional connectivity between sensorimotor regions and the default mode network (DMN). The results suggest that the DMN may facilitate the integration of unisensory signals with internal representations, thereby contributing to the unique sensory prioritization strategies observed across individuals during motor control.
papers.authors: Kess L. Folco, Artur Pilacinski, Hu Cheng, Sharlene D. Newman, Manasi Wali, Reshma Babu, Hannah J. Block

papers.title: The role of explicit knowledge in compensating for a visuo-proprioceptive cue conflict
papers.abstract: This study evaluated how conscious awareness of a spatial mismatch between visual and proprioceptive cues influences the magnitude of perceptual recalibration. Using a 70 mm forward shift of the visual cue, three groups were provided with varying levels of information, ranging from no awareness to explicit instructional and direct visual cues of the limb discrepancy. The findings indicated that explicit instructional knowledge alone was insufficient to override the brain's intrinsic belief in a 'common cause,' with recalibration magnitudes remaining largely consistent with uninformed controls. Significant reductions in recalibration were only observed when instructions were combined with redundant visual evidence of the mismatch, suggesting that the causal inference framework governing multisensory integration is robust against purely top-down cognitive instructions but sensitive to contradictory sensory evidence.
papers.authors: Anna Hsiao, Hannah J. Block

0252.name: Hans Op de Beeck
0252.bio: Op de Beeck is a Professor in the Department of Brain & Cognition and Dean of the Faculty of Psychology and Educational Sciences at KU Leuven. Their research investigates the neural mechanisms underlying visual object recognition and the representational plasticity associated with learning and expertise. Methodologically, the lab integrates human functional neuroimaging (fMRI) and psychophysics with rodent electrophysiology and computational modeling using deep artificial neural networks. Op de Beeck examines the topographic organization of the ventral visual stream and how neural representations are altered in neurodevelopmental disorders and following brain damage.
0252.research_direction: Dr. Op de Beeck's recent work explores the functional organization and representational dynamics of the human occipitotemporal cortex, focusing on how the visual system categorizes objects and processes written scripts. Using a combination of unsmoothed fMRI, fMRI-EEG fusion, and continuous behavioral tracking, they have recently been investigating the precise spatial topography and temporal emergence of object domains, probing how neural representations of animacy, taxonomy, and category selectivity support visual decision-making. Alongside theoretical arguments defending the fundamental role of discrete category selectivity over purely continuous semantic dimensions, their research examines the specialization of the visual word form area to determine its exact spatial and representational niche among other selective regions. Furthermore, they are studying the behavioral acquisition of orthography, using modified scripts like line-based Braille to test whether the visual system's processing of written language relies on specific low-level geometric features.

papers.title: Connecting the dots: Similar visual orthographic acquisition for Braille or line junctions
papers.abstract: This study investigates the hypothesis that line junctions, ubiquitous in natural environments and most scripts, are essential visual primitives for orthographic processing. Researchers compared the visual acquisition of traditional Braille (a dot-based script) with 'Line Braille,' a novel variant utilizing line junctions. Behavioral metrics and learning curves across multiple sessions revealed that the presence of line junctions provided only a marginal and temporary advantage during early training. These findings challenge the theory that the visual word form system is evolutionarily or developmentally tuned to line-based geometries, suggesting instead that the neural representation of scripts is primarily driven by linguistic status rather than specific low-level shape properties.
papers.authors: Filippo Cerpelloni, Olivier Collignon, Hans Op de Beeck

papers.title: Can category-selective cortex predict categorisation behaviour?
papers.abstract: The researchers employed a multivariate distance-to-bound (DTB) framework to evaluate whether neural activity in the occipito-temporal cortex (OTC) predicts human categorization performance. Using fMRI data alongside high-resolution behavioral measures—including reaction times and continuous mouse-movement trajectories—the study assessed responses in the fusiform face area (FFA), parahippocampal place area (PPA), and extrastriate body area (EBA). The analysis demonstrated that univariate signal strength within these category-selective patches is significantly correlated with behavioral indicators of decision-making, supporting the view that category-selective regions serve as the primary neural substrate for providing the evidence needed to solve visual categorization tasks.
papers.authors: Timothée Maniquet, Huangxu Fang, N. Apurva Ratan Murty, Hans Op de Beeck

papers.title: Representational dynamics of the main dimensions of object space: Face/body selectivity aligns temporally with animal taxonomy but not with animacy
papers.abstract: This investigation utilizes fMRI-EEG fusion and temporal searchlight decoding to map the representational geometry of the human ventral visual stream. By examining the hierarchical organization of animacy, animal taxonomy, and specific category selectivity (faces vs. bodies), the authors resolve the temporal unfolding of object space. The results indicate that while a coarse animacy distinction appears early, the more fine-grained representations of animal taxonomy and face/body selectivity emerge with synchronized temporal dynamics. This suggests that the occipitotemporal cortex (OTC) organizes object information through a complex interplay of semantic and structural dimensions rather than a strictly sequential feedforward hierarchy based on superordinate categories.
papers.authors: Gaëlle Leys, Chiu-Yueh Chen, Andreas von Leupoldt, J. Brendan Ritchie, Hans Op de Beeck

papers.title: In defense of categories
papers.abstract: In this theoretical commentary, the author critiques recent shifts toward defining occipitotemporal cortex (OTC) organization solely through behaviorally relevant dimensions. While acknowledging the utility of continuous semantic dimensions, the author argues that discrete category selectivity remains a fundamental organizational principle. The piece highlights that statistical comparisons between dimensional and categorical models are often biased by binarization. It asserts that categories provide essential explanatory power for the specific tuning properties, topographical layout, and developmental emergence of functional specialization in high-level visual areas that behavioral dimensions alone fail to capture.
papers.authors: Hans Op de Beeck

papers.title: The position of visual word forms in the anatomical and representational space of visual categories in occipitotemporal cortex
papers.abstract: The study maps the spatial and representational coordinates of word-selective subregions within the human occipitotemporal cortex at an individual-subject level, avoiding the limitations of spatial smoothing. By characterizing the location of the visual word form area (VWFA) relative to regions selective for faces, bodies, hands, numbers, and tools, the researchers analyzed the multidimensional arrangement of category selectivity. The findings demonstrate that while word selectivity occupies a reliable anatomical niche in the occipitotemporal sulcus, its representational similarity profile suggests a distinct specialization that integrates, yet remains dissociable from, the broader animate-inanimate organizational framework of the visual stream.
papers.authors: Ineke Pillet, Burak Cerrahoğlu, Ruben V. Philips, Chiu-Yueh Chen, Hans Op de Beeck

0253.name: Heather Lucas
0253.bio: Heather D. Lucas is an Assistant Professor at Louisiana State University whose research focuses on the neurocognitive mechanisms of episodic and relational memory. Lucas's work utilizes event-related potentials (ERPs) and eye-tracking to investigate how individuals navigate memory constraints and employ strategic behaviors during information gathering and encoding. Lucas examines these processes across the lifespan and in clinical populations, including individuals with traumatic brain injury and neurodivergent adults, to understand how neural and cognitive factors influence learning outcomes.
0253.research_direction: Dr. Lucas has recently been investigating the neurocognitive mechanisms of memory and semantic processing, exploring how encoding strategies adapt across varying affective states, task demands, and neurocognitive profiles. Using eye-tracking and event-related potentials, their recent work explores how the temporal dynamics of gaze support the construction of visual memories and whether visual working memory comparisons operate via isolated features or integrated objects. In the realm of episodic memory, they are examining whether acute anxiety—such as the threat of shock—impairs retention by disrupting semantic-organizational encoding strategies. Additionally, their research assesses learning and communication in autistic adults, specifically investigating the efficacy of retrieval practice paired with corrective feedback and how this population evaluates and assigns semantic meaning to manual gestures.

papers.title: The impact of threat of shock on memory for threat-irrelevant information: Evidence for a role of reduced semantic organization
papers.abstract: The mechanisms through which acute state anxiety modulates episodic memory encoding remain controversial, particularly with respect to threat-irrelevant, neutral stimuli. Across two experiments utilizing a threat-of-shock paradigm, this study investigated whether anticipatory anxiety degrades episodic retention by disrupting semantic-organizational encoding strategies. In Experiment 1, participants encoded and freely recalled lists of semantically unrelated neutral words under alternating conditions of shock threat versus safety. Threat blocks resulted in significantly diminished recall accuracy alongside reduced semantic clustering, quantified via a semantic path length metric that assesses vector distance across consecutively recalled words. In Experiment 2, semantically related word lists were used to control for block-order dynamics. Threat of shock again induced significant decrements in recall volume and elicited longer, less organized semantic path lengths. Crucially, mediation analyses confirmed that anxiety-induced shifts toward longer semantic path lengths mediated the negative relationship between autonomic physiological arousal (indexed via skin conductance responses) and downstream free recall performance. These findings indicate that attenuated semantic executive control serves as a key neurocognitive mechanism underlying the adverse effects of acute anxiety on declarative memory formation.
papers.authors: Felicia M. Chaisson, Christopher R. Cox, Amber M. Alford, Lauryn M. Burleigh, Steven G. Greening, Heather D. Lucas

papers.title: Examining the Roles of Retrieval Practice and Post-Retrieval Feedback in Learning Among Autistic Adults
papers.abstract: Retrieval practice robustly enhances declarative memory retention, with performance further optimized when followed by informative feedback; however, empirical evidence regarding the efficacy of retrieval-based learning and corrective feedback in autistic individuals has been lacking. In two experiments, the authors examined retrieval practice and post-retrieval feedback on associative memory in autistic and neurotypical adult cohorts. Participants encoded pairs of semantically unrelated words and subsequently reviewed them across practice conditions comprising retrieval practice with feedback, retrieval practice without feedback, or restudy. Learning modalities (auditory in Experiment 1; visual in Experiment 2) and practice formats (cued recall vs. four-alternative forced choice) were varied across experiments, with final retention assessed via cued recall. In both experiments, post-retrieval feedback yielded robust mnemonic benefits across both diagnostic groups, disproportionately benefiting items recalled incorrectly on initial practice. Additionally, Experiment 2 confirmed a significant testing effect—retrieval practice outperformed passive restudy even in the absence of feedback across autistic and non-autistic cohorts alike. These findings confirm that retrieval practice coupled with corrective feedback represents a highly viable and generalizable instructional strategy for autistic adult learners.
papers.authors: Brianna E. Cairney, Eileen Haebig, Heather D. Lucas

papers.title: Interpretations of meaningful and ambiguous hand gestures in autistic and non-autistic adults: A norming study
papers.abstract: Co-speech and silent manual gestures are integral to human communication, yet existing findings on how individuals on the autism spectrum process and assign semantic meaning to gestures remain equivocal. To provide a standardized, cross-population stimulus set, this study created and normed an open database of 162 silent gesture video clips comprising iconic, emblem, and ambiguous manual gestures. Equal cohorts of autistic (N = 40) and non-autistic (N = 40) adult raters evaluated each clip for semantic meaningfulness on continuous rating scales and provided open-ended, single-word descriptors. Ratings of meaningfulness exhibited exceptional concordance across diagnostic groups (r > 0.90 across all stimuli). Analysis of naming data, however, demonstrated greater naming variability and lexical dispersion among autistic participants compared to neurotypical peers. This indicates that perceived meaningfulness remains intact in autistic adults, and that group discrepancies in gesture tasks are more likely driven by lexical access or semantic selection processes rather than atypical core semantic gesture processing. The normed database and accompanying kinematic profiles provide an open-science resource for multimodal communication research.
papers.authors: Brianna E. Cairney, Stanley H. West, Eileen Haebig, Christopher R. Cox, Heather D. Lucas

papers.title: Dynamic interactions between memory and viewing behaviors: Insights from dyadic modeling of eye movements
papers.abstract: Visual memory representations are constructed through active oculomotor exploration, but the temporal trajectory over which specific gaze metrics support encoding within individual study epochs remains unclear. The authors applied structural equation modeling via dyadic path models to evaluate spatial reconstruction accuracy based on the temporal dynamics between scanpath entropy (spatial dispersion of gaze) and item-to-item saccadic transition frequency. Trials were partitioned into early and late temporal windows to model direct contributions to memory as well as indirect pathways where early-trial viewing cascaded into alterations of late-trial viewing. Across analyses, sustained low scanpath entropy throughout the entire trial predicted superior spatial memory precision. In contrast, the functional contribution of item-to-item transitions shifted across time: higher transition rates during early-trial viewing negatively predicted memory performance, whereas late-trial transition frequency positively predicted memory accuracy. Early oculomotor sampling patterns also indirectly mediated subsequent recall accuracy via downstream effects on late-trial exploration. Furthermore, individual differences in standardized memory ability predicted gaze effectiveness, with oculomotor dynamics partially mediating this relationship. The model demonstrated strong goodness-of-fit upon validation in an independent replication dataset, emphasizing that the chronological order and dynamic coordination of eye movements critically govern encoding success.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
papers.authors: Heather D. Lucas, Ana M. Daugherty, Edward McAuley, Arthur F. Kramer, Neal J. Cohen

papers.title: Behavioral and electrophysiological evidence for the flexible recruitment of feature- and object-based processing in visual working memory comparison
papers.abstract: The architectural debate regarding whether visual working memory (VWM) comparisons operate over integrated object tokens or isolated feature dimensions remains unresolved. Prior event-related potential (ERP) studies examining change detection have documented that the N200—an electrophysiological marker of VWM comparison—is modulated by both task-relevant and task-irrelevant attribute changes, suggesting an obligatory object-based processing bias. To determine whether VWM comparison can operate in a strictly feature-based mode, the authors introduced task constraints designed to isolate relevant features: an initial block containing purely task-relevant alterations followed by a second block featuring both relevant and irrelevant changes, alongside arrays manipulating within-display feature repetition. In Block 2, N200 amplitudes were selectively sensitive to task-relevant feature changes and remained unaffected by task-irrelevant alterations, regardless of intra-display repetition status, demonstrating isolated feature-based comparison processing. However, downstream behavioral performance and N200 latency metrics revealed that task-irrelevant variations were nevertheless processed when no relevant change was detected. These findings demonstrate that VWM comparison is computationally flexible and dynamically shifts between feature-based and object-based processing architectures depending on task goals and prior context.
papers.authors: Stephanie M. Saltzmann, Katherine C. Moen, Brandon Eich, Felicia M. Chaisson, Gaojie Fan, Rebecca R. Goldstein, Melissa R. Beck, Heather D. Lucas

0254.name: Heiko H. Schütt
0254.department: Department of Behavioural and Cognitive Sciences
0254.bio: Heiko H. Schütt is an Associate Professor at the University of Luxembourg specializing in the development of mechanistic models for visual perception and cognitive behavior. Their research integrates deep neural networks, Bayesian inference, and efficient coding to explain human visual processing, particularly regarding eye movements and object recognition in natural scenes. Schütt developed open-source computational toolboxes, including Psignifit 4 for psychometric function fitting and the rsatoolbox for representational similarity analysis. Their work focuses on creating models that bridge behavioral and neurophysiological data while advancing statistical methods for evaluating representational geometries.
0254.research_direction: Dr. Schütt has recently been developing advanced computational frameworks to bridge the gap between biological visual systems and artificial neural networks. Their recent work explores rigorous statistical tools for evaluating model-to-brain alignment, including an open-source Python toolbox for representational similarity analysis, generative models that disentangle signal from trial-to-trial noise in multivariate brain measurements, and novel Bayesian methods for comparing representational geometries. By probing how well current deep learning architectures capture human error patterns and cortical activity across the visual hierarchy, they investigate the biological plausibility of these artificial systems. Building on these neuro-computational intersections, they are also exploring ways to directly improve machine learning algorithms, such as designing new margin-based loss functions to enhance the out-of-distribution generalization and adversarial robustness of computer vision models.

papers.title: A Python Toolbox for Representational Similarity Analysis
papers.abstract: This work introduces rsatoolbox, an open-source Python implementation for Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA) designed to relate high-dimensional neural activity patterns to computational models. The toolbox incorporates a suite of recent methodological advances, including the use of cross-validated Mahalanobis distances (crossnobis) to provide unbiased estimates of representational dissimilarity matrices (RDMs) in the presence of noise. It further integrates advanced RDM comparators and rigorous statistical inference procedures, such as condition- and subject-level bootstrapping, to evaluate model-to-brain alignment. The software facilitates the evaluation of deep neural networks and other hierarchical models against multivariate data from fMRI, EEG/MEG, and large-scale electrophysiology.
papers.authors: Jasper J. F. van den Bosch, Tal Golan, Benjamin Peters, JohnMark Taylor, Mahdiyar Shahbazi, Baihan Lin, Ian Charest, Jörn Diedrichsen, Nikolaus Kriegeskorte, Marieke Mur, Heiko H. Schütt

papers.title: Disentangling signal and noise in neural responses through generative modeling
papers.abstract: In this paper, we propose the Generative Modeling of Signal and Noise (GSN) framework to solve the problem of separating condition-related signal covariance from trial-to-trial noise covariance in multivariate neural measurements. While traditional analyses rely on trial averaging, GSN explicitly models measured responses as the sum of samples from latent multivariate signal and noise distributions. By applying shrinkage estimators to the data covariance, GSN allows for more accurate characterization of the population-level representational geometry even in regimes with high noise or limited trials. We demonstrate that GSN provides superior estimates of signal distribution and improves the reliability of inferences regarding neural representations in both simulated and empirical fMRI datasets.
papers.authors: Kendrick Kay, Jacob S. Prince, Thomas Gebhart, Greta Tuckute, Jingyang Zhou, Thomas Naselaris, Heiko H. Schütt

papers.title: Bayesian Comparisons Between Representations
papers.abstract: This paper presents a formal Bayesian framework for quantifying the similarity between neural network representations based on the predictive distributions of linear readouts. It is argued that the prior predictive distribution serves as a comprehensive description of a model's inductive bias and generalization capability. By employing information-theoretic metrics such as the Jensen-Shannon distance or total variation distance between these distributions, the method induces pseudo-metrics for representations that account for uncertainty. This approach establishes a theoretical unification between disparate representational similarity metrics, connecting task-based linear probing with kernel-based measures like centered kernel alignment (CKA) and representational similarity analysis (RSA).
papers.authors: Heiko H. Schütt

papers.title: High Error Margin Loss: Improving Robustness and Generalisation by Overcoming Training Issues of Margin-Based Losses
papers.abstract: This study proposes the High Error Margin (HEM) loss as a robust alternative to the standard cross-entropy (CE) loss for training deep neural network classifiers. CE loss is susceptible to overconfidence and continues to update weights for well-classified samples, which can negatively impact adversarial robustness and out-of-distribution generalization. HEM loss is a variant of multi-class margin loss that avoids premature termination of gradient updates while curbing overconfidence. Extensive benchmarking across multiple architectures shows that HEM loss significantly improves performance in unknown class rejection, adversarial defense, and continual learning, while remaining competitive with CE on clean accuracy.
papers.authors: Michael W. Spratling, Heiko H. Schütt

papers.title: Integrating Vision: From Neuroscience to Artificial Intelligence
papers.abstract: This review synthesizes the current state of knowledge regarding the biological foundations of vision—spanning the retina, lateral geniculate nucleus, and cortical areas V1 through V6—with modern advancements in artificial neural networks (ANNs). We evaluate the extent to which deep neural networks serve as effective models for biological vision by analyzing their ability to predict human error patterns and multivariate neural signals. The article outlines a research program where failures in model-to-brain alignment drive the development of more biologically plausible architectures, such as those incorporating feedback connections and multisensory integration, to bridge the performance gap between artificial systems and the complexity of human perception.
papers.authors: Haoshan Ye, Heiko H. Schütt

0255.name: Heleen A. Slagter
0255.department: Department of Experimental and Applied Psychology
0255.bio: Heleen A. Slagter is a Professor of Cognitive Neuroscience at Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam and the Director of the Institute for Brain and Behavior Amsterdam (iBBA). Slagter's research investigates the neural mechanisms underlying cognitive functions such as selective attention and conscious perception, focusing on how these processes are modulated by mental training and prior experience. Utilizing EEG, fMRI, and computational modeling, they examine the plasticity of the predictive brain and how practices like meditation can alter information processing and self-awareness. Slagter has received VIDI and ERC Starting and Consolidator grants for this work.
0255.research_direction: Dr. Slagter has recently been investigating the dynamic interplay between visual attention, working memory, and motor planning, with a specific focus on how behavioral goals and environmental statistics shape sensory representations. Using EEG, eye-tracking, and interactive behavioral tasks, their recent work explores the "selection-for-action" framework to determine how prospective motor plans—such as the intent to manually grip a memorized object—alter visual feature spaces within working memory and influence an item's attentional salience. They are also studying spatial selective attention and proactive inhibitory control, employing visual search paradigms to ask how contextual volatility and viewer-dependent sensorimotor perspectives dictate an observer's ability to implicitly learn to ignore salient distractors. Additionally, Dr. Slagter has been examining the underlying mechanisms of sensory processing sensitivity, theoretically exploring whether predictive processing frameworks can explain heightened environmental reactivity through the increased precision-weighting of incoming sensory signals relative to internal priors.

papers.title: Grounding distractor inhibition in action control: Implicit distractor-location learning is viewer dependent
papers.abstract: This study challenges the traditional view of spatial selective attention as a purely sensory filter by investigating whether the suppression of irrelevant distractors is constrained by an agent's sensorimotor perspective. Across three experiments using an additional-singleton visual search task on a monitor positioned flat on a tabletop, the researchers manipulated the participants' standing positions to decouple world-centered coordinates from viewer-centered coordinates. The findings demonstrate that implicit distractor-location learning is fundamentally viewer-dependent when embedded in active behavioral contexts. This suggests that the mechanisms of distractor inhibition are not abstractly mapped to the environment but are instead integrated into the planning of how an agent samples information from their specific perspective, reinforcing a selection-for-action framework for inhibitory control.
papers.authors: Litian Chen, Freek van Ede, Chris Jungerius, Heleen A. Slagter

papers.title: Sensory processing sensitivity: theory, evidence and directions
papers.abstract: This theoretical review synthesizes the literature on sensory processing sensitivity (SPS), a trait characterized by heightened reactivity and deep processing of environmental stimuli. The authors propose a novel mechanistic account of SPS grounded in the predictive processing framework, hypothesizing that the brains of high-SPS individuals consistently assign higher precision to incoming sensory signals. This elevation in precision increases the weight of sensory evidence relative to internal priors, explaining the phenotypic manifestations of enhanced sensitivity. The article evaluates existing behavioral and neurophysiological evidence supporting this precision-weighting model and outlines future research trajectories to clarify the neurobiological basis of SPS and its relationship to other personality dimensions.
papers.authors: Corina U. Greven, MacKenzie D. Trupp, Judith R. Homberg, Heleen A. Slagter

papers.title: Action similarity warps visual feature space in working memory
papers.abstract: While visual working memory (VWM) is often studied as a passive storage system, this research investigates how prospective action plans retrospectively influence memory representations. Utilizing an interactive VWM task where participants reproduced bar orientations using specific manual actions (gripping or sliding), the study found that the similarity of intended actions adaptively distorted the stored visual information. Specifically, perceptually similar items were remembered as more distinct when they were associated with different action plans compared to when they were linked to the same action. Control experiments ruled out motor biases, indicating that the action plans caused a genuine warping of the sensory feature space in VWM. These results suggest that VWM flexibly optimizes representations to facilitate efficient and distinct behavioral outputs.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS)
papers.authors: Caterina Trentin, Luigi Falanga, Jannik Jeske, Christian N. L. Olivers, Heleen A. Slagter

papers.title: Action Planning Renders Objects in Working Memory More Attentionally Salient
papers.abstract: The study utilized EEG and eye-tracking to examine the neurophysiological basis of the interaction between visual working memory (VWM) and action planning. Participants memorized a shape and, in an action condition, planned to interact with it at a later test stage. During the retention interval, they performed an intermittent visual selection task. The results showed that VWM items associated with a future action plan exerted a stronger bias on eye gaze and elicited specific event-related potential (ERP) signatures: an enhanced posterior positivity contralateral (Ppc), indicating increased sensory saliency; an earlier distractor positivity (PD) component, reflecting expedited suppression; and heightened motor-region activity. These findings provide evidence for 'selection-for-action' in VWM, where the intent to act on a memorized object prioritizes its neural representation and increases its attentional weight.
papers.authors: Caterina Trentin, Chris Olivers, Heleen A. Slagter

papers.title: Reduced contextual uncertainty facilitates learning what to attend to and what to ignore
papers.abstract: This research investigates how environmental variability influences the ability to learn to ignore salient distractors. In a series of visual search experiments, participants were trained in environments with varying levels of contextual volatility. The results revealed that low contextual uncertainty significantly reduced attentional capture by salient color singletons. Critically, this reduction in capture generalized from familiar search displays to novel ones, suggesting that the benefit was not driven by specific contextual cueing (associative memory for particular displays) but rather by the development of generic predictions regarding task-relevant features and locations. The findings indicate that the statistical volatility of the learning environment is a key determinant in the acquisition of proactive inhibitory control and the modulation of bottom-up sensory drive.
papers.authors: Chris Jungerius, Sophie Perizonius, Heleen A. Slagter

0256.name: Hendrikje Nienborg
0256.bio: Nienborg is a Senior Investigator at the National Eye Institute and the head of the Visual Decision Making Section. Their research investigates the neural mechanisms that integrate sensory signals with cognitive factors such as attention, motivation, and prior knowledge to guide behavior. Using large-scale electrophysiological recordings, optogenetics, and computational modeling, their lab explores how cortical circuits process information from central and peripheral visual fields. Nienborg’s work examines how decision-related feedback is broadcast across the visual cortex and the influence of spontaneous movements on sensory encoding in primates.
0256.research_direction: Dr. Nienborg's recent work explores the complex interplay between visual processing, behavioral state, and perceptual decision-making across mammalian species. They have recently been investigating how non-visual signals shape early sensory representations, examining both species-specific differences in how spontaneous body movements modulate the primary visual cortex and how serotonergic circuits from the dorsal raphe nucleus regulate states of visual attention. In higher-order vision, their research tracks the real-time evolution of perceptual choices, using large-scale population recordings in the macaque parietal cortex to observe single-trial drift-diffusion dynamics. Additionally, Dr. Nienborg is working to develop more interpretable computational models of the early visual system, exploring how simplified convolutional neural networks can accurately capture stimulus invariance and complex feature selectivity across massive primate and rodent neural datasets.

papers.title: Is the impact of spontaneous movements on early visual cortex species specific?
papers.abstract: This review evaluates the evidence regarding species-specific differences in movement-related neural modulation within the primary visual cortex (V1). While rodent studies consistently report large, brain-wide gain changes and substantial variance in V1 activity driven by locomotion and orofacial behaviors, recent investigations in macaques and marmosets show minimal direct modulation. The authors discuss how these discrepancies may arise from differences in behavioral state, the impact of eye movements on retinal input, eccentricity-dependent effects, and slow neural drift. They propose a functional taxonomy for movement signals to facilitate standardized cross-species comparisons in active vision research.
papers.authors: Incheol Kang, Bharath Chandra Talluri, Jacob L. Yates, Cristopher M. Niell, Hendrikje Nienborg

papers.title: Decisions: Tracking the evolution of a single choice
papers.abstract: The authors discuss recent advancements in large-scale neural recording technologies that permit the direct observation of decision-related computations within single trials, moving beyond traditional trial-averaged analyses. Focusing on population activity in the macaque lateral intraparietal (LIP) area, the article highlights evidence that decision variables evolve toward a choice boundary in a manner consistent with drift-diffusion dynamics. This real-time resolution provides empirical support for the theory that decision-making involves the noisy integration of evidence over time, a mechanism previously difficult to resolve due to the high variability of individual neural responses.
papers.authors: Bharath Chandra Talluri, Hendrikje Nienborg

papers.title: Serotonergic neurons in the dorsal raphe regulate visual attention
papers.abstract: This study identifies the dorsal raphe nucleus (DRN) as a critical controller of visual attention via serotonergic signaling. Utilizing a behavioral model to track attention allocation in mice and simultaneous DRN fiber photometry, the researchers observed that serotonergic activity is suppressed during periods of focused attention on cued stimuli. Optogenetic activation of DRN-5HT neurons was sufficient to impair detection performance, while their inhibition enhanced it. Furthermore, serotonin levels in the visual cortex were found to decrease during active detection, establishing serotonin as a key neuromodulatory carrier of attentional state in the mammalian visual system.
papers.authors: Aashay Patel, Katsuhisa Kawaguchi, Lenka Seillier, Hendrikje Nienborg

papers.title: Towards a simplified model of primary visual cortex
papers.abstract: The authors demonstrate that deep convolutional neural network (CNN) models of the primary visual cortex (V1) can be substantially simplified without loss of predictive power. By recording responses from over 29,000 neurons in mouse V1 and analyzing existing monkey datasets, they show that a two-layer model can capture more than 70% of response variance. They introduce "minimodels" that fit individual neurons using shared lower-level filters, showing that these simplified architectures provide a more interpretable account of how biological neurons achieve stimulus invariance and complex feature selectivity compared to overparameterized deep networks.
papers.authors: Incheol Kang, Adam Lazere, Hendrikje Nienborg

0257.name: Hermann Bulf
0257.bio: Hermann Sergio Bulf is a developmental cognitive neuroscientist and Professor of Developmental Psychology at the University of Milano-Bicocca. Bulf’s research investigates the early development of perceptual and cognitive capacities in infants, focusing on visual statistical learning, biological motion detection, and face processing. They employ methodologies such as eye-tracking and neural entrainment (EEG) to examine how newborns and infants extract structural regularities from their environment and how early-life predispositions, such as the preference for social cues, influence subsequent cognitive growth. Additionally, Bulf explores the ontogenetic foundations of magnitude processing, specifically the spatial mapping of numbers and size in the preverbal mind.
0257.research_direction: Dr. Bulf has recently been investigating the early development of social cognition, visual attention, and pattern learning in both typical and atypical populations. Their recent work explores how the developing brain processes complex socio-emotional cues, using high-density EEG to examine how infants integrate action kinematics with facial expressions, and physiological measures to assess newborn attention to vocal prosody. Additionally, they are employing eye-tracking and visual habituation paradigms to study how toddlers and preschoolers—including those at high risk for autism—extract abstract visual rules and statistical regularities from their environment. Beyond early infancy, they are also testing how affective social experiences like ostracism influence the flexibility of spatial attention and gaze-cueing behavior throughout childhood and adulthood.

papers.title: The infant brain combines emotional information from faces and action kinematics
papers.abstract: Using high-density EEG, this study investigated the neural mechanisms by which 6-month-old infants integrate emotional valence across different visual modalities: action kinematics and facial expressions. Infants were presented with dynamic point-light displays of actions (arm movements) conveying happy or angry emotions, followed by static happy or angry faces. ERP analyses focused on the N290 and P400 components to assess early and late stages of emotion processing. Results demonstrated that while the N290 differentiated between happy and angry facial expressions regardless of the preceding action, the P400 was specifically modulated by the congruency between action kinematics and faces. Specifically, happy faces elicited a larger P400 when preceded by incongruent (angry) kinematics compared to congruent (happy) kinematics, suggesting that bodily kinematics provide a salient social context that biases the subsequent processing of facial affect in the developing brain.
papers.authors: Margaret Addabbo, Julia Mermier, Joanna Rutkowska, Marlene Meyer, Sabine Hunnius, Chiara Turati, Hermann Bulf

papers.title: Visual statistical learning and social attention in neurotypical, minimally speaking and speaking autistic preschoolers
papers.abstract: This research utilized eye-tracking to evaluate the relationship between visual statistical learning (SL), social attention, and spoken language abilities in autistic and neurotypical preschoolers. Minimally speaking autistic children, speaking autistic children, and neurotypical peers were tested on their ability to extract statistical regularities from visual sequences (transitional probability tracking) and their preference for social vs. non-social stimuli. Contrary to hypotheses of core deficits in these domains, participants across all groups exhibited significant evidence of statistical learning and a robust preference for social stimuli. Furthermore, within-group analyses revealed no significant correlation between SL performance or social attention indexes and standardized measures of expressive language (Mullen Scales and Vineland-II). These findings suggest that language acquisition atypicalities in autism may be independent of basic statistical learning and social orienting mechanisms in the preschool period.
papers.authors: Roberta Bettoni, Margaret Addabbo, Chiara Pezzana, David Vagni, Ermanno Quadrelli, Chiara Turati, Hermann Bulf

papers.title: Newborns' attention to socio-emotional prosodic cues from voices
papers.abstract: The study examined the relative contribution of socio-emotional and linguistic prosodic information in capturing neonatal attention during the first days of life. Using a non-nutritive sucking (NNS) paradigm, newborns were exposed to a nursery rhyme presented in three conditions: narrated by a female actress (high linguistic and socio-emotional cues), hummed by the same actress (high socio-emotional, low linguistic), and synthesized by a computer (low socio-emotional, high linguistic). Results showed a significant inhibition of sucking behavior—an index of heightened attention—in response to the hummed and narrated conditions compared to the synthesized voice. Additionally, prenatal exposure to maternal speech and music was positively correlated with the strength of the attentional response. These findings indicate that the neonatal brain is predisposed to orient toward the socio-emotional dimensions of vocal stimuli, with this sensitivity being shaped by intrauterine auditory experience.
papers.authors: Valentina Silvestri, Silvia Polver, Maria Lorella Giannì, Angelo Petrelli, Matteo Santini, Lorenzo Colombo, Hermann Bulf

papers.title: Ostracism affects children's behavioral reactivity and gaze cueing of attention
papers.abstract: This study explored the impact of self-experienced social exclusion (ostracism) on attentional processes and emotional reactivity in 6-year-old children, 10-year-old children, and adults. Participants engaged in an online ball-tossing game (Cyberball) where they were either included or ostracized, followed by a Posner-style gaze-cueing task. Results revealed that ostracism significantly modulated the gaze-cueing effect across all ages: ostracized individuals were slower to detect targets in incongruent locations compared to included participants, suggesting that social exclusion impairs the ability to flexibly reorient attention away from social signals. Behaviorally, both children and adults exhibited increased negative affect (disappointment) following ostracism. For 10-year-olds, ostracism also reduced target detection accuracy. The findings suggest that the cognitive and affective consequences of social exclusion on social signal processing emerge early in development and persist into adulthood.
papers.authors: Giada Basset, Alessia Testa, Chiara Turati, Ermanno Quadrelli, Hermann Bulf

papers.title: Learning and generalization of repetition-based rules in toddlers at high-risk for Autism Spectrum Disorder
papers.abstract: This study investigated visual rule learning (RL)—the ability to extract and generalize abstract repetition-based patterns (e.g., ABA)—in toddlers at high familial risk (HR) for Autism Spectrum Disorder compared to neurotypical (NT) controls. Using a visual habituation-dishabituation paradigm, toddlers were exposed to sequences of geometric shapes following specific repetition rules. While NT toddlers successfully discriminated familiar from novel rules, providing evidence for rule abstraction and generalization, the HR group showed significant impairments in extracting these high-order regularities. These results suggest that deficits in the early mechanisms of rule induction may be a marker of the broader social-communicative profile associated with autism, potentially hindering the acquisition of structured systems like language and social conventions.
papers.authors: Roberta Bettoni, Margaret Addabbo, Chiara Ghidina, Chiara Pezzana, David Vagni, Chiara Turati, Hermann Bulf

0258.name: Herwig Baier
0258.institution: Max Planck Institute for Biological Intelligence
0258.bio: Herwig Baier is a Director at the Max Planck Institute for Biological Intelligence, where they investigate the functional architecture of neural circuits governing animal behavior. Baier's research employs larval zebrafish as a transparent vertebrate model, integrating genetic engineering, calcium imaging, and optogenetics to map sensory-to-motor transformations. The laboratory established large-scale behavioral screens and developed the Zebrafish Brain Atlas to classify neuronal cell types and their synaptic connectivity. Their current work explores the circuit-level logic of spatial attention, social interactions, and the influence of evolutionary processes on behavioral programs.
0258.research_direction: Dr. Baier's recent work explores the molecular, functional, and evolutionary architecture of neural circuits in teleost fishes. By integrating single-cell RNA sequencing, multiplexed RNA hybridization, and two-photon calcium imaging, they are investigating how the anatomical position of genetically defined neurons in brain areas like the optic tectum and diencephalon shapes their diverse physiological roles. They have recently been examining how visual sensory information is transformed into specific ecological behaviors, tracing the photoneuroendocrine pathways that link intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells to camouflage responses, and using deep-learning-based pose estimation to compare binocular and monocular prey-capture strategies across divergent species.
