Beyond visuomotor systems, their research also probes the temporal regulation of complex behaviors, testing whether parent-offspring nest interactions in cichlids are guided by real-time social cues or hard-wired biological clocks.

papers.title: Transcriptomic neuron types vary topographically in function and morphology
papers.abstract: This study investigates the phenotypic uniformity of transcriptionally defined neuronal types in the zebrafish optic tectum. By integrating large-scale single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) with spatial mapping and functional two-photon calcium imaging, the authors demonstrate that neurons within a single transcriptomic cluster can manifest highly divergent morphological and physiological characteristics based on their anatomical position. The findings reveal that while transcriptomic identity provides a baseline molecular framework, extrinsic positional information significantly expands the functional repertoire of genetically related neurons, creating a spatially structured diversity that is not captured by gene expression levels alone.
papers.authors: Inbal Shainer, Johannes M. Kappel, Eva Laurell, Joseph C. Donovan, Martin W. Schneider, Enrico Kuehn, Irene Arnold-Ammer, Manuel Stemmer, Johannes Larsch, Herwig Baier

papers.title: Molecular delineation of a retina-dependent photoneuroendocrine pathway in zebrafish
papers.abstract: This research defines the neural circuit architecture mediating visual background adaptation (VBA), a camouflage response in which animals adjust skin pigmentation to match ambient brightness. The authors identifies intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells (ipRGCs) that express the transcription factor Onecut1 as the primary sensors for environmental light intensity. These cells provide direct axonal input to hypothalamic neurons producing melanin-concentrating hormone (MCH), which triggers skin lightening. Photic activation of this ipRGC-hypothalamic axis concurrently represses the pomca-dependent darkening pathway. The study delineates a discrete photoneuroendocrine switch that maps sensory irradiance to specific hormonal outputs, ensuring appropriate behavioral and physiological adaptation to light conditions.
papers.authors: Krasimir Slanchev, Eva Laurell, Irene Arnold-Ammer, Enrico Kuehn, Uyyashrinila Pandiarajan, Herwig Baier

papers.title: Diverse prey capture strategies in teleost larvae
papers.abstract: The study conducts a comparative neuroethological analysis of predatory behavior across six larval teleost species, including zebrafish, medaka, and four Tanganyikan cichlids. Utilizing high-speed videography and deep-learning-based pose estimation, the researchers quantified eye and tail kinematics during prey pursuit. The results demonstrate a profound evolutionary divergence in hunting strategies: while zebrafish and cichlids utilize a binocular strategy with eye convergence to fixate prey in the central visual field, medaka employ a monocular strategy with characteristic side-swing strikes and no convergence. This work reveals that even in closely related lineages, the visuomotor algorithms for predatory strikes have specialized according to distinct ecological and sensory requirements over 240 million years of evolution.
papers.authors: Duncan S. Mearns, Sydney A. Hunt, Martin W. Schneider, Ash V. Parker, Manuel Stemmer, Herwig Baier

papers.title: Intrinsic timing of brood care in shell-dwelling cichlids
papers.abstract: Investigating the temporal regulation of parental care in the shell-dwelling cichlid Lamprologus ocellatus, this study examines whether the emergence of offspring from the nest is driven by maternal cues or internal larval maturation. Through automated behavioral assays and timing-conflict experiments, the authors show that maternal and larval behaviors are synchronized by independent, hard-wired clocks rather than real-time social feedback. Mothers resist the premature emergence of fostered older larvae, while orphans adhere to a light-seeking phototactic transition precisely on day 9 post-fertilization. These results challenge traditional models of parent-offspring conflict, suggesting that brood care stages in this species are governed by intrinsic molecular timers that ensure coordinated transitions in life-history stages.
papers.authors: Ash V. Parker, Manuel Stemmer, Swantje Grätsch, Alessandro Dorigo, Oriol Rodriguez Ramirez, Abdelrahman Adel, Alex Jordan, Herwig Baier

papers.title: Genoarchitectonics of the larval zebrafish diencephalon
papers.abstract: This paper establishes a molecularly defined structural framework for the larval zebrafish diencephalon by integrating the expression of approximately 50 marker genes within the Max Planck Zebrafish Brain (mapzebrain) atlas. The authors utilize multiplexed RNA hybridization chain reaction (HCR) to delineate the alar and basal subdivisions of the diencephalic prosomeres (P1-P3), providing high-resolution boundaries for the thalamus, prethalamus, and pretectum. The resulting genoarchitectonic map identifies specific domains for glutamatergic, GABAergic, and diverse aminergic and neuropeptidergic populations. This work provides an objective anatomical foundation for localizing neural circuits and interpreting the evolutionary conservation of the vertebrate forebrain across species.
papers.authors: Mario F. Wullimann, Nouwar Mokayes, Inbal Shainer, Enrico Kuehn, Herwig Baier

0260.name: Holger Wiese
0260.bio: Holger Wiese is an Associate Professor at Durham University whose research examines the cognitive and neural architecture of face perception and person recognition. Utilizing high-temporal resolution electroencephalography (EEG) and event-related brain potentials (ERPs) such as the N250 and N250r, Wiese investigates how the human brain transitions from image-dependent unfamiliar face processing to image-invariant familiar face representations. Their work explores social biases in face memory, including the own-race and own-age effects, as well as neuro-cognitive changes in face recognition across the adult lifespan. Wiese’s recent investigations focus on the consolidation of newly learned identities and the specific visual information, such as color and contrast, encoded within long-term facial representations.
0260.research_direction: Dr. Wiese has recently been investigating the neural and cognitive mechanisms underlying human face recognition, utilizing the high temporal resolution of event-related potentials to map out the serial stages of identity processing. Their recent work explores how distinct perceptual operations—ranging from early structural encoding to long-term memory access and domain-general person knowledge—can be isolated using experimental manipulations like repetition priming and contrast negation alongside key neural markers such as the N170 and N250r. They are also probing the theoretical structure of facial memory, testing whether the visual system relies on static, eye-centered feature templates or idiosyncratic, experience-driven representations derived from a viewer's distinct perceptual history. Additionally, Dr. Wiese is examining individual differences in face recognition ability, correlating these precise neural signatures with standardized behavioral assessments to understand why people vary so substantially in their face identification effectiveness and efficiency.

papers.title: Event-Related Brain Potential Correlates of Face Processing: A High-Precision Replication and Individual Differences Study
papers.abstract: This study addresses the necessity for high-powered, high-precision replications of event-related potential (ERP) correlates in human face processing, focusing on the neural basis of substantial inter-individual variability. Utilizing a large cohort (N = 84) and a comprehensive battery of standardized behavioral tasks (including CFMT+ and GFMT2) alongside a custom-designed response time priming paradigm, the researchers quantified several key ERP markers: the P100 contrast effect, the N170 inversion and face-selectivity effects, and the image-independent N250r familiarity effect. The analysis evaluates the internal consistency and reliability of these components as indices for specific processing stages, examining their capacity to predict behavioral performance and characterize individual differences in both familiar and unfamiliar face identification effectiveness and efficiency.
papers.authors: Maria Ciocan, Lisa Gandlin, Milena M. Bojdo, Linda H. Lidborg, Holger Wiese

papers.title: EXPRESS: Representations for face recognition
papers.abstract: The authors challenge the 'essentialist' paradigm of facial identity representations, which assumes a static set of features defines a known individual. They argue that biologically plausible models must account for the statistical regularities and inherent variability of a perceiver's history of exposure to various facial identities. Integrating evidence from event-related potential (ERP) studies and computational simulations, the paper posits that identity recognition relies on idiosyncratic, viewer-specific representations derived from image sampling across diverse viewing conditions. This theoretical framework emphasizes that facial representations are dynamically formed and highly dependent on the observer's specific perceptual history, suggesting a shift away from traditional fixed-value models of familiar face recognition.
papers.authors: Bartholomew P. A. Quinn, Tsvetomila Popova, Poppy Green, Holger Wiese

papers.title: Neural correlates of familiar face recognition: Evidence in support of a serial model
papers.abstract: This research utilizes the high temporal resolution of event-related brain potentials (ERPs) to test the hypothesized serial architecture of face recognition, which moves from perceptual encoding to long-term identity access and finally to domain-general person knowledge. In Experiment 1, contrast negation was used to disrupt early structural encoding, evidenced by an enhanced N170, while familiarity-related differences at occipito-temporal sites emerged subsequently (approx. 200 ms). Experiment 2 demonstrated that preceding familiar face targets with identity-congruent name primes selectively modulated a later ERP window (300-400 ms). These findings corroborate a sequential processing chain where perceptual (N170), facial long-term (200-300 ms), and domain-general (300-400 ms) representations are activated in discrete, separable stages.
papers.authors: Milena M. Bojdo, Deni Zakriev, Maya Schipper, Maria Ciocan, Linda H. Lidborg, Holger Wiese

papers.title: The role of the eye region for neural correlates of familiar face recognition: The N250r reveals no evidence for eye-centred face representations
papers.abstract: To investigate whether the human face recognition system utilizes eye-centered identity representations, the authors analyzed the N250r—an ERP index of image-independent familiar face activation—using repetition priming. Participants viewed 'blur chimeras' where only specific regions (eyes or mouth) remained unfiltered in a spatially low-pass filtered face. While unfiltered eye regions in a blurred face elicited a clear N250r relative to fully blurred faces, Experiment 3 revealed a statistically equivalent N250r for unfiltered mouth regions. The results demonstrate that while detailed information from local features facilitates the activation of robust facial identity representations, this process is not specifically privileged for or optimized around the eye region, contradicting models of strictly eye-centered facial memory.
papers.authors: Bartholomew P. A. Quinn, Tsvetomila Popova, Poppy C. E. Green, Rupert Talfourd-Cook, Holger Wiese

0261.name: Hong XU
0261.department: School of Social Sciences, Division of Psychology
0261.bio: Hong Xu is an Associate Professor of Psychology at Nanyang Technological University. Their research characterizes the neural mechanisms underlying visual perception, with a focus on face processing and self-motion (heading) perception. Xu utilizes a methodology incorporating human psychophysics, eye tracking, EEG, and computational modeling to examine how sensory information is integrated and adapted across the cortical hierarchy. Their laboratory also conducts translational research applying vision science principles to virtual reality simulations and investigating the role of social cues in digital trust and fake news detection.
0261.research_direction: Dr. Xu has recently been investigating the early perceptual mechanisms and oculomotor dynamics underlying how humans process artificial or deceptive media. By manipulating ultra-brief stimulus durations and measuring eye movements like pupillometry and saccades, their recent work explores whether phenomena such as the Uncanny Valley effect and the detection of AI-generated deepfakes rely on rapid, bottom-up visual processing or require prolonged, serial feature inspection. In a related vein, they are also examining how physiological indices of cognitive load and arousal during media consumption might serve as markers for fake news discernment. Broadening their scope into applied human factors and public health, Dr. Xu further investigates how lifestyle and sociodemographic variables—such as sleep quality among occupational drivers or internet usage patterns in older adults—interact to influence real-world safety behaviors and psychological well-being.

papers.title: Detect AI-generated faces in a glance? Effect of stimulus durations on deepfake detection and eye movements
papers.abstract: This study evaluated human performance and oculomotor dynamics in the discrimination of hyper-realistic AI-generated deepfakes versus veridical facial images across varying temporal windows. Using a 2AFC task, 38 participants judged the veracity of 112 faces generated via Stable Diffusion (1.5 and XL 1.0), StyleGAN, and various face-swapping algorithms (e.g., DFDC) across stimulus durations of 16.67, 33.33, 50, 100, 500, and 1000 ms. Results analyzed via Generalized Linear Mixed Models (GLMMs) demonstrated that detection accuracy was significantly modulated by both generative algorithm type and viewing duration. While SD-generated and real images were reliably identified at ultra-brief exposures (>83% accuracy at 16.67 ms), StyleGAN and face-swapped images exhibited markedly lower discriminability (~7% and 20% respectively). Notably, face-swapping artifacts became significantly more detectable with prolonged exposure, suggesting that serial feature inspection aids in artifact identification, whereas StyleGAN detection did not benefit from increased temporal integration. Eye-tracking data revealed that real and face-swapped images elicited fewer fixations and saccades at durations exceeding 500 ms, while SD-generated images triggered more frequent saccades with higher amplitudes. Area of Interest (AOI) analysis indicated a persistent focus on the nasal region regardless of image authenticity, providing evidence for holistic processing strategies during deepfake evaluation.
papers.authors: Zihao Zhao, Mingzhi Lyu, Adams Wai Kin Kong, Hong Xu

papers.title: Fake News Detection through Eye-tracking Measures: A Preregistered Scoping Review
papers.abstract: This scoping review synthesizes empirical evidence from 25 studies (2017–2025) investigating the application of eye-tracking metrics as physiological indices of misinformation discernment. Following the PRISMA-ScR framework, the analysis identifies key oculomotor parameters, specifically fixation duration and pupillary response, as critical markers of the cognitive and affective load associated with news consumption. The review finds that while fixation metrics (e.g., dwell time on metadata) often correlate with analytical scrutiny, results remain inconsistent across studies due to high variability in stimulus complexity and platform design. In contrast, pupillary dilation emerged as a more robust and consistent indicator of the physiological arousal and cognitive effort triggered by deceptive content. The synthesis highlights a critical reliance on lab-based simulations and cognitive-centric theories, identifying significant gaps in the study of socio-cultural influences on gaze behavior. The findings suggest that pupillary dynamics and saccadic count can potentially serve as diagnostic signals for automated fact-checking systems by reflecting the transition between heuristic and systematic processing of media content.
papers.authors: Gabriel Rongyang Lau, Cameron Mavericks, Hong Xu

papers.title: A stimulus exposure of 50 ms elicits the uncanny valley effect
papers.abstract: This research investigated the temporal dynamics and early perceptual mechanisms underlying the Uncanny Valley (UV) effect through brief stimulus presentation. In Experiment 1, 41 participants rated human-robot hybrid faces on indices of attractiveness, eeriness, and humanness after exposures of either 50 ms (brief) or 3 s (prolonged). The results showed that the UV effect—characterized by a non-monotonic relationship between human-likeness and affinity—was elicited even at 50 ms, suggesting that the sensation of eeriness is accessible during early visual processing stages prior to deliberate cognitive evaluation. Experiment 2 utilized a two-alternative forced-choice (2AFC) task to assess the Categorical Perception Hypothesis, finding that while brief exposures significantly increased response variance and uncertainty in human-robot categorization, the most eerie faces were not the most difficult to categorize. These findings indicate that while categorical uncertainty and the UV effect can both be triggered by impoverished visual input, categorical conflict is likely not the primary causal driver of the UV phenomenon, pointing instead toward more rapid, bottom-up perceptual mechanisms.
papers.authors: Jodie Yam, Tingchen Gong, Hong Xu

papers.title: Assessing Risk Factors for Driving Safety: The Role of Sleep Quality and Driving Experience Among Occupational Bus Drivers in Singapore
papers.abstract: This study employed a multidimensional psychometric approach to identify sociodemographic and lifestyle predictors of risky driving behaviors among occupational bus drivers in Singapore. Utilizing a comprehensive battery including the Driver Behaviour Questionnaire (DBQ), the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), and the Driving Anger Scale (DAS), the research validated the internal reliability (Cronbach's α > .7) and construct suitability of these measures for the target population. Correlation analysis identified poor sleep quality as a primary risk factor, demonstrating significant positive associations with ordinary and aggressive violations, errors, and heightened driving anger. Conversely, weekly driving distance, used as a proxy for workload, showed negative correlations with risky attitudes, suggesting a potential role for experience in habituating drivers to urban stressors. Factor analysis revealed that while younger drivers were more prone to performance errors, older drivers exhibited more frequent cognitive lapses. The study provides a roadmap for targeted interventions focusing on sleep hygiene and stress management to mitigate on-road accidents in professional transportation sectors.
papers.authors: Xuehao Yang, Hong Xu

papers.title: Medical service satisfaction and depression among middle-aged and older Chinese adults: moderating role of distinct Internet-using patterns
papers.abstract: This study utilized data from the China Family Panel Studies (CFPS) 2020 (N = 4,523, age ≥ 45) to examine the relationship between medical service satisfaction and depressive symptoms, with a focus on the moderating effects of digital engagement. Depressive symptoms were quantified using the CES-D scale, while medical service satisfaction was assessed across multiple indicators. Regression analysis revealed that overall medical service satisfaction (OMSS) is a potent negative predictor of depression. Crucially, the study identified distinct Internet-using patterns that significantly modulate this association. Frequent use of the Internet for information retrieval (e.g., health-related searches) amplified the protective effect of medical satisfaction on mental health, whereas hedonic Internet use (e.g., gaming or entertainment) showed a weaker moderating effect. These results suggest that digital literacy and information-oriented Internet usage can serve as compensatory mechanisms for perceived healthcare quality, providing implications for public health strategies aimed at enhancing psychological well-being in aging populations through targeted digital interventions.
papers.authors: Lunxin Liu, Boya Liu, Jing Zheng, Lang Wang, Zhiliu Liao, Hong Xu

0262.name: Hong-jin Sun
0262.bio: Sun is an Associate Professor at McMaster University whose research explores the cognitive and neural mechanisms of human spatial perception and navigation. Utilizing immersive virtual reality technologies—including simulations of driving, biking, and walking—Sun investigates how visual spatial attention and visuospatial asymmetries are modulated by depth and distance in three-dimensional environments. Their work focuses on how behavioral relevance, semantic environmental information, and multisensory integration guide attentional prioritization in complex scenarios. Current research directions include examining the influences of depth on inhibition of return (IOR) and the interaction between top-down preparation and visual search in 3D space.
0262.research_direction: Dr. Sun has recently been investigating how spatial attention is dynamically modulated by motor actions, 3D spatial constraints, and behavioral relevance. Their recent work explores spatial orienting in naturalistic and 3D virtual environments—such as driving simulators—to examine how ongoing action planning and semantic context interact with reflexive attentional capture and classic phenomena like inhibition of return. Additionally, they are probing visual field asymmetries to test whether the demands of spatial localization versus feature discrimination alter the traditional "near advantage" for peripersonal space, and how manual proximity relates to downward attentional biases. Broadening their focus on cognitive control, Dr. Sun also utilizes EEG to investigate how the temporal proximity of immediate versus delayed rewards impacts resource allocation and cognitive flexibility during task-switching paradigms.

papers.title: Action planning can override exogenous cueing effects
papers.abstract: This study examines the interplay between endogenous attention mechanisms driven by action planning and exogenous spatial orienting, specifically focusing on the modulation of the inhibition of return (IOR) effect. Utilizing a virtual three-dimensional (3D) driving simulation, the researchers employed a modified cue-target paradigm where participants prepared a lane change (action planning) either before or during cue presentation. The results demonstrated that while robust IOR was observed in the absence of action planning, the preparation of a goal-directed movement significantly attenuated the IOR at action-relevant spatial locations, while sparing it at action-irrelevant locations. Controls for working memory load and pure endogenous orienting confirmed that the observed reduction in exogenous capture was specifically mediated by the prioritization of action-relevant sensory representations, suggesting that motor preparation can override reflexive attentional biases during dynamic stimulus interactions.
papers.authors: Noah Britt, Hong-Jin Sun

papers.title: Distribution of attention in three-dimensional space
papers.abstract: The universal applicability of the 'near advantage' in spatial attention—the phenomenon where targets in peripersonal space are detected more rapidly than those in extrapersonal space—is investigated across varying task demands. Through a series of three experiments utilizing 3D virtual environments, the researchers compared target localization (reaction time to onset) and target discrimination (identification of stimulus properties) across near and far depth planes. The findings revealed a task-specific reversal: while target localization exhibited a traditional near advantage, target discrimination produced a significant far advantage, with shorter reaction times and greater facilitation during near-to-far spatial orienting. These results challenge the notion of a monolithic attentional bias toward near space and support a model where attentional distribution along the z-axis is dynamically reconfigured by the computational requirements of the dorsal and ventral visual processing streams.
papers.authors: Noah Britt, Hanna Haponenko, Brett A. Cochrane, Bruce Milliken, Hong-Jin Sun

papers.title: Context-dependent modulation of spatial attention: prioritizing behaviourally relevant stimuli
papers.abstract: Human spatial attention is investigated as a function of semantic scene grammar and behavioral relevance within a simulated driving environment. Licensed drivers performed a peripheral cue-target localization task where the target, a roadside pedestrian avatar, was oriented either toward or away from the roadway. Attentional facilitation was significantly enhanced when the pedestrian’s orientation implied potential intersection with the vehicle's path (high behavioral relevance) compared to when oriented away. Critically, this orientation-specific selectivity vanished when 3D contextual cues were removed, when the observer's viewpoint was stationary, or when an inanimate control object was used. The findings suggest that attentional capture by peripheral stimuli is not merely a reflexive response to low-level features but is gated by internal models of context-specific behavior, reflecting the influence of overlearned expertise on the prioritization of environmentally relevant information.
papers.authors: Noah Britt, Jackie Chau, Hong-jin Sun

papers.title: The Impact of Immediate and Delayed Rewards on Task-Switching Performance
papers.abstract: The differential impact of reward temporal proximity on cognitive flexibility and attentional control was evaluated using a cue-based task-switching paradigm. Participants performed tasks involving immediate or delayed reward contingencies while event-related potentials (ERPs) were recorded. Behavioral data indicated that immediate rewards significantly reduced reaction times and enhanced performance accuracy in task repetition trials compared to delayed rewards; however, this facilitatory effect was absent in task-switching trials. Neurophysiological analysis revealed that immediate rewards elicited a significantly larger P300 amplitude during repetition trials, suggesting heightened allocation of attentional resources to the ongoing task. The results support the Expected Value of Control (EVC) theory, indicating that while rewards optimize attention during stable task states, the increased cognitive load of switching may saturate processing capacity, rendering reward-driven prioritization less effective.
papers.authors: Guang Zhao, Huijun Wang, Rongtao Wu, Zixin Zhao, Shiyi Li, Qiang Wang, Hong-jin Sun

papers.title: Lateral peri-hand bias affects the horizontal but not the vertical distribution of attention
papers.abstract: This study dissociates the effects of manual proximity (peri-hand space) from the robust lower visual field (LVF) attentional bias, often referred to as 'downward bias'. In two experiments, participants performed a spatial cueing target detection task while hand position was manipulated (lap vs. eye-level proximity to the display). Experiment 1 confirmed a significant downward bias in reaction times and cueing effects for targets in the LVF. Experiment 2 demonstrated that while positioning the dominant hand near the display induced a lateral peri-hand effect—altering the horizontal distribution of attention—it failed to modulate the magnitude of the vertical downward bias. These findings indicate that the attentional advantage for the lower visual field is a stable, hard-wired perceptual asymmetry that remains resilient to immediate changes in motor affordances or hand-related multisensory integration.
papers.authors: Noah Britt, Hong-Jin Sun

0263.name: Hongjing Lu
0263.bio: Lu investigates the mechanisms of human learning and reasoning by developing computational models that emulate human-level intelligence. Their methodology integrates theories from psychology and statistics with tools from computer vision, machine learning, and computational neuroscience to perform behavioral and fMRI-based investigations. Lu’s research identifies two principles of human inference: the application of generic priors to guide learning from sparse data and the manipulation of structured representations for complex tasks. Current projects in their lab focus on biological motion perception, action recognition, and the computational underpinnings of causal and analogical reasoning in both biological and artificial systems.
0263.research_direction: Dr. Lu’s recent work explores a diverse set of questions spanning visual cognition, social perception, and artificial intelligence. In the domain of biological motion and social vision, they are investigating the neural mechanisms underlying self-recognition from point-light displays using fMRI, alongside behavioral studies examining how individuals with schizotypal traits discriminate threats using complex naturalistic videos versus isolated kinematic cues. Their recent work also explores the mechanics of analogical and relational reasoning, examining how visuospatial scaffolds influence human visual category learning and using counterfactual tasks to probe whether large language models are capable of genuine abstract structural mapping. Furthermore, they have recently been applying natural language processing and agent-based modeling to investigate how the structural topology of decentralized social networks influences the semantic trajectory and causal language of collective beliefs.

papers.title: Network structure shapes consensus dynamics through individual decisions
papers.abstract: This study employs natural language processing and agent-based modeling to characterize the emergence and semantic trajectory of collective narrative beliefs within decentralized online social networks. By analyzing data from large-scale social network experiments, the researchers demonstrate that network topology fundamentally constrains the convergence of group consensus and the semantic orientation of communicative acts. An embedding-based narrative alignment metric revealed that fully connected networks prioritize the communication of causal antecedents and precursors, whereas locally connected topologies tend to emphasize event outcomes and effects. Although the presence of complex causal structures in source media can attenuate the influence of network topology by fostering deeper integration of prior background knowledge, structural connectivity remains a primary determinant of linguistic change. Participants in fully connected networks exhibited the most significant shift toward causal language in post-interaction narratives, suggesting that global connectivity optimizes the alignment of shared mental models regarding the causal structure of events.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS)
papers.authors: J. Hunter Priniski, Bryce Linford, Anna Hirschmann, Sai Krishna Venumuddala, Fred Morstatter, Nancy Rodriguez, P. Jeffrey Brantingham, Hongjing Lu

papers.title: Threat discrimination of real-world social interactions in schizotypal traits
papers.abstract: This research investigates the behavioral and computational mechanisms underlying threat detection deficits across the schizophrenia spectrum, focusing on a nonclinical sample (N=161) with varying schizotypal traits. The study utilized naturalistic video stimuli of social interactions, processed via deep-learning-based rendering to selectively isolate or parse social contextual information. Findings indicate that individuals with high scores on schizotypal personality traits—specifically suspiciousness and odd beliefs—demonstrate a significant decline in threat discrimination sensitivity when presented with rich social context. Conversely, these individuals showed enhanced threat detection performance when social cues were abstracted to basic body kinematics. These results suggest that the social cognition impairments characteristic of the schizophrenia spectrum, and to a lesser extent the autism spectrum, are driven by an inability to effectively integrate complex social context, leading to a reliance on low-level motion cues for threat appraisal.
papers.authors: Akila Kadambi, Sophia Baia, Elinor Yeo, Hongjing Lu

papers.title: Enhancing visuospatial mapping in relational category learning
papers.abstract: The acquisition of visual relational categories is theorized to depend on structured, compositional representations that explicitly encode role-filler bindings. However, the high cognitive overhead associated with analogical mapping over such representations often drives learners to rely on unstructured, feature-based exemplars, which significantly limits generalizability. This study investigated the efficacy of two visuospatial interventions—spatial categorization of exemplars and color-coded role highlighting—on the Synthetic Visual Reasoning Test (SVRT). Through a series of experiments, the researchers found that spatially segregating positive and negative instances significantly accelerated concept discovery, particularly when learning was scaffolded with an easy-to-hard problem sequence. In contrast, color-based role highlighting only facilitated learning when it provided unambiguous and nonredundant cues for structural alignment. The results suggest that specific environmental scaffolds can mitigate cognitive load and maintain the engagement of compositional reasoning mechanisms during relational category acquisition.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
papers.authors: Andrew J. Lee, Keith J. Holyoak, Hongjing Lu

papers.title: Evidence from counterfactual tasks supports emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
papers.abstract: This paper evaluates the emergent analogical reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs) against the hypothesis that their performance is a byproduct of training data mimicry. The authors employed 'counterfactual' reasoning tasks, including letter-string analogies with permuted alphabets and a novel 'Digit Matrices' task using permuted numerical sequences, designed to minimize similarity to existing training corpora. While standard GPT-4 performance degraded on these zero-shot counterfactual tasks, the study reveals that augmenting the model with a code execution interface—enabling precise list indexing and counting—allows it to achieve human-level proficiency. These results demonstrate that the previously reported failures of LLMs on counterfactual benchmarks are likely due to auxiliary processing bottlenecks, such as counting errors, rather than a lack of fundamental relational reasoning capacity. The findings support the existence of a generalized, emergent ability for abstract structural mapping in modern LLMs that extends beyond statistical retrieval.
papers.authors: Taylor W. Webb, Keith J. Holyoak, Hongjing Lu

papers.title: Self-Awareness from Whole-Body Movements
papers.abstract: This study utilizes human neuroimaging and multivariate pattern analysis to investigate the neural mechanisms underlying whole-body self-recognition from dynamic point-light displays. Despite the absence of first-person visual experience and the sparsity of biological motion signals, individuals can accurately identify their own actions. The researchers employed general linear modeling and representational similarity analysis (RSA) on fMRI data to dissociate brain regions specialized for self-processing. Results identified a distinct frontoparietal network, specifically including motor-related regions, that exhibits increased activation and finer-grained representations when observers view their own movements compared to those of others. These findings support common coding theories of action, suggesting that self-action recognition is mediated by a matching process that integrates visual input with prior motor and proprioceptive experience, rather than relying solely on visual template matching.
papers.authors: Akila Kadambi, Gennady Erlikhman, Micah Johnson, Martin M. Monti, Marco Iacoboni, Hongjing Lu

0264.name: Hsin-Hung Li
0264.bio: Li is an Assistant Professor at The Ohio State University and leads a research program focused on the neural and computational foundations of decision-making, attention, and working memory. Li's work utilizes a multi-methodological approach—combining psychophysics, eye-tracking, and functional neuroimaging (fMRI/EEG) with formal computational modeling—to understand how the brain represents information and handles uncertainty. Previously, they conducted doctoral and postdoctoral research at New York University, investigating the dynamics of neural population codes and the intersection of visual perception and metacognition. Their current research seeks to identify the mechanisms through which top-down cognitive processes modulate sensory inputs to guide adaptive human behavior.
0264.research_direction: Dr. Li has recently been investigating the neural mechanisms underlying working memory and decision-making, with a particular focus on how the human brain allocates limited cognitive resources and monitors representational uncertainty. Their recent work explores how metacognitive access to uncertainty is formatted in the brain, using EEG and fMRI alongside generative decoding models to examine whether visual memoranda and subjective values are maintained via probabilistic population codes that track trial-by-trial confidence. Additionally, they are probing how working memory precision is dynamically optimized to maximize behavioral utility, combining human neuroimaging with recurrent neural networks to understand how reward incentives, stimulus priors, and task priorities flexibly adjust neural response gain. Finally, Dr. Li’s research investigates information flow across the cortical hierarchy, assessing how top-down feedback signals from higher-order prefrontal and parietal networks govern visual resource allocation and propagate structured spatial memory drift errors during maintenance delays.

papers.title: Distinct oscillatory neural rhythms support representational precision and confidence in working memory
papers.abstract: Working memory permits the persistent maintenance of sensory information to drive adaptive action, yet its neural representations are inherently corrupted by stochastic noise. Effective decision-making thus necessitates that observers monitor the subjective uncertainty of stored representations. Employing scalp electroencephalography (EEG) during a spatial delayed-estimation working memory paradigm coupled with single-trial uncertainty judgments, this study investigated how oscillatory neural dynamics encode memory uncertainty. Inverted encoding-decoding modeling revealed that two dissociable frequency bands multiplex distinct forms of uncertainty. Mnemonic location information was reconstructed from delay-period alpha-band (8–13 Hz) activity, where the representational precision (the dispersion of the decoded posterior probability distribution) systematically predicted trial-by-trial reported uncertainty. In contrast, beta-band (13–30 Hz) activity carried a scalar, magnitude-dependent confidence signal characterized by sustained, slow dynamics that tracked uncertainty ratings across consecutive trials. These findings reveal a frequency-multiplexed neural dynamical architecture supporting introspective access to working memory.
papers.authors: Yang Di, Xingwei An, Hsin-Hung Li

papers.title: Probabilistic neural code supports metacognition in value-based decisions in the human brain
papers.abstract: Subjective value representations guide everyday decision-making but are inherently noisy, leaving judgments vulnerable to valuation uncertainty. Whether human observers maintain metacognitive access to value uncertainty and how such information is formatted across neural populations remain fundamental questions. By pairing a value bidding task with explicit uncertainty reporting and functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), this study evaluated whether subjective values are encoded probabilistically in cortex. Explicit trial-by-trial uncertainty ratings tracked behavioral valuation variance across choice items. Utilizing neural generative decoding models, full continuous probability distributions over subjective value were decoded from multivoxel response patterns within the ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) and the superior parietal lobule/intraparietal sulcus (SPL-IPS). Crucially, the dispersion of the decoded distributions predicted subjective uncertainty reports at the trial, item, and inter-individual levels, indicating that cortical populations multiplex subjective value and uncertainty via probabilistic population coding.
papers.authors: Ling Huang, Hui-Kuan Chung, Hsin-Hung Li

papers.title: Dynamics of working memory drift and information flow across the cortical hierarchy
papers.abstract: Working memory is supported by distributed cortical networks, but how memory representations drift across delays and propagate between hierarchical stages remains poorly understood. Using time-resolved multivoxel fMRI decoding during a spatial memory-guided saccade task, this study evaluated the spatiotemporal evolution of spatial memoranda across retinotopic field maps. Decoded representations in dorsal visual and parietal areas drifted progressively from the veridical stimuli toward the direction of subsequent behavioral motor errors, consistent with continuous attractor models. These behaviorally predictive neural drift errors surfaced earliest in higher dorsal stream areas (V3AB and IPS0) before emerging in primary visual cortex (V1). Interareal directional correlation analyses revealed that maintenance intervals were dominated by feedback information flow descending from higher-order areas to early visual cortex, whereas passive sensory stimulation exhibited feedforward-dominant signaling. These results show that top-down feedback propagates structured drift errors across the cortical hierarchy to generate memory inaccuracies.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Hsin-Hung Li, Wei Ji Ma, Clayton E. Curtis

papers.title: Efficient Allocation of Working Memory Resource for Utility Maximization in Humans and Recurrent Neural Networks
papers.abstract: Working memory is a limited, noisy resource that must be allocated dynamically to optimize behavioral utility. To assess whether human observers flexibly allocate memory precision according to expected reward incentives independently of attentional selection, participants performed an orientation delayed-estimation task following the acquisition of stimulus–reward contingencies. Memory precision, quantified by report variance, reflected both environmental stimulus priors (cardinal orientation biases) and reward incentives, with both factors increasingly stabilizing representations over longer delay durations, while systematic biases remained unchanged. A dynamic extension of efficient coding theory incorporating temporal decay and an objective function centered on expected utility accounted for these behavioral patterns. Furthermore, recurrent neural networks (RNNs) trained under matched conditions developed identical properties, showing lower representational variance for high-reward and high-probability orientations that amplified over time. Transfer learning demonstrated that recurrent connectivity is necessary for adapting resource allocation to shifting priors and reward schedules.
papers.venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems
papers.authors: Qingqing Yang, Hsin-Hung Li

papers.title: Neural mechanisms of resource allocation in working memory
papers.abstract: Under cognitive capacity limits, working memory resources are prioritized according to task relevance, but the neural mechanisms underlying multi-item resource allocation have remained poorly understood. Computational neuroimaging methods were developed to demix and decode blood oxygen level-dependent (BOLD) signals corresponding to simultaneously maintained items assigned different behavioral priorities. In striate (V1) and extrastriate visual areas, population response gain scaled with item priority: high-priority memoranda were decoded with lower uncertainty and reduced angular error compared to low-priority memoranda, and these neural fidelity differences predicted behavioral performance within and across participants. Trial-by-trial variance in prefrontal delay-period BOLD activity accounted for the gain and precision differences observed in early visual cortex. These findings delineate a top-down control mechanism wherein feedback signals from prefrontal cortex selectively adjust the gain of visual cortical representations to govern resource allocation in working memory.
papers.authors: Hsin-Hung Li, Thomas C. Sprague, Aspen H. Yoo, Wei Ji Ma, Clayton E. Curtis

0265.name: Hsin-I Liao
0265.bio: Hsin-I Liao is a Senior Research Scientist at NTT Communication Science Laboratories within the Human Information Science Laboratory. Their research focuses on decoding internal cognitive states, including preference formation, visual attention, and auditory salience, by analyzing implicit ocular behaviors such as pupillary dilation responses and microsaccades. Liao employs psychophysical methodologies to explore how these physiological markers reflect and participate in multisensory integration and attractiveness judgments. Liao earned their Ph.D. in Psychology from National Taiwan University and has collaborated with the Division of Biology at the California Institute of Technology.
0265.research_direction: Dr. Liao has recently been investigating the physiological correlates of attention and cognition, with a strong methodological focus on pupillometry and non-image-forming visual pathways. Their recent work explores how the pupillary light response can serve as an index for covert cross-modal attention—such as tracking auditory objects across varied visual luminance fields—and examines how top-down spatial attention interacts with pupillomotor pathways when stimuli are rendered unconscious through continuous flash suppression. Additionally, they are investigating how endogenous brain states govern temporal processing limits, utilizing real-time closed-loop pupillometry to test whether infraslow pupillary phase fluctuations predict a listener's capacity during an auditory attentional blink. Broadening their study of retinal inputs to cognition, Dr. Liao also uses silent substitution paradigms to isolate intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells (ipRGCs), exploring how these specific melanopsin-driven signals modulate working memory performance independently of traditional cone-mediated vision.

papers.title: Real-time tracking of pupil-phase fluctuations reveals state-dependent modulation of temporal attentional capacity
papers.abstract: Although baseline pupillary diameter is widely utilized to index autonomic arousal and central brain state, whether infraslow pupillary dynamics systematically govern the capacity limits of temporal attention remains unresolved. To address this, an auditory attentional blink paradigm requiring dual-target detection (T1 and T2) was implemented. In Experiment 1, trial-level regression demonstrated that successful second-target identification contingent on correct first-target identification (T2|T1) was associated with smaller pre-stimulus baseline pupil diameters. Furthermore, spectral decomposition isolating slow pupillary fluctuations (< 0.2 Hz) revealed that T2|T1 identification accuracy was systematically augmented during the pupillary dilation phase occurring within 0–2 seconds after a constriction trough. In Experiment 2, a closed-loop system deployed real-time pupillometry to trigger stimulus presentation locked to predefined phases of ongoing endogenous pupillary fluctuations, producing significant phase-dependent differences in T2|T1 detection performance. Linear mixed-effects modeling confirmed that this phase-dependent modulation remained robust after covarying for tonic baseline pupil size, indicating that infraslow brain-state phase dynamics govern temporal processing capacity beyond static arousal levels alone. These findings indicate that temporal attentional bottlenecks reflect dynamic, state-dependent processing limitations rather than invariant structural constraints.
papers.authors: Yuta Suzuki, Hsin-I Liao

papers.title: Pupillary responses to invisible brightness escape from attentional modulation
papers.abstract: Although the pupillary light response (PLR) has historically been categorized as a reflexive subcortical circuit tracking retinal irradiance, recent findings indicate modulation by perceived or attended brightness. Here, pupillary modulations to stimuli rendered phenomenologically invisible via continuous flash suppression (CFS) were evaluated alongside top-down attentional modulation. In Experiment 1, isolated bright and dark Gabor patterns presented under interocular suppression evoked significant, albeit attenuated, pupil constrictions and dilations, respectively, remaining invariant to feature-based attentional manipulations. In Experiment 2, spatial attention was directed to one of two competing Gabors using a sustained rapid serial visual presentation (RSVP) task. While spatial attention significantly modulated PLR amplitudes when targets were consciously visible, attentional modulation of the PLR was completely eliminated under interocular suppression. These findings demonstrate that unconscious luminance signals propagate through subcortical pupillomotor pathways, whereas spatial attentional gating of the PLR strictly depends on visual awareness, indicating a cortical-subcortical gating architecture in pupillomotor control.
papers.authors: Yung-Hao Yang, Hsin-I Liao

papers.title: Selective activation of ipRGC modulates working memory performance
papers.abstract: Intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells (ipRGCs) express melanopsin with peak sensitivity to short-wavelength light (460–480 nm) and project to non-visual brain structures regulating circadian rhythms, alertness, and cognition. While blue-spectrum illumination enhances working memory performance, whether these cognitive benefits stem from integrated signals across classic photoreceptors or direct ipRGC activation remained unknown. To isolate this mechanism, a silent substitution paradigm was implemented to selectively modulate ipRGC excitation while holding long-, medium-, and short-wavelength-sensitive (LMS) cone excitations constant at a metameric magenta chromaticity. Participants performed visual 1-back and 2-back working memory tasks under low- versus high-ipRGC illumination regimes. High-ipRGC excitation produced a statistically significant enhancement in 2-back hit rate, with no corresponding difference in the 1-back task, alongside reductions in subjective sleepiness and fatigue ratings. These results provide direct evidence that isolated ipRGC signaling, independent of subjective blue percepts or cone excitation differences, selectively modulates working memory and cognitive capacity.
papers.authors: Yuta Suzuki, Shigeki Nakauchi, Hsin-I Liao

papers.title: Seeing an Auditory Object: Pupillary Light Response Reflects Covert Attention to Auditory Space and Object
papers.abstract: Although attentional allocation across space and perceptual objects is well characterized in the visual domain, the operational mechanisms governing auditory selection remain less understood. Here, the pupillary light response (PLR) was utilized as an involuntary physiological index to probe auditory attentional shifts and the coupling between space- and object-based auditory attention. Across multiple experiments, participants covertly attended to spoken auditory streams positioned in visual spaces characterized by bright or dark backgrounds. The PLR systematically reflected the background luminance of the spatial location where the attended auditory object was situated, constricting for auditory sources aligned with bright visual fields and dilating for those aligned with dark fields. This pupillomotor modulation persisted regardless of whether auditory attention was directed via spatial (left vs. right) or non-spatial (e.g., talker gender) cues, and was invariant to presentation mode (dichotic headphones vs. free-field loudspeakers). Gaze position drift analyses confirmed that minor fixation deviations could not account for the effect, establishing that auditory object-based selection automatically constructs spatial representations that interact with oculomotor pupillary circuits.
papers.authors: Hsin-I Liao, Haruna Fujihira, Shimpei Yamagishi, Yung-Hao Yang, Shigeto Furukawa

0266.name: Hui Chen
0266.department: Department of Psychology and Behavioral Sciences
0266.bio: Chen is a Professor at Zhejiang University specializing in the cognitive neuroscience of visual processing. Their research examines the relationships between visual attention, working memory, and conscious awareness, specifically investigating how internal representations guide external selection. Chen identified the 'attribute amnesia' phenomenon and utilizes behavioral psychophysics, eye-tracking, and electroencephalography (EEG) to map these mental processes. Their work applies these findings to examine cognitive deficits in neurodevelopmental and psychiatric disorders such as autism and schizophrenia.
0266.research_direction: Dr. Chen's recent work explores the complex intersection of visual attention and working memory consolidation, frequently utilizing the attribute amnesia paradigm to understand how the brain selects and filters information. They have recently been investigating the basic mechanics of mnemonic encoding, questioning whether traditional spatial cueing costs actually reflect memory consolidation bottlenecks and testing whether voluntary saccades or prolonged fixations are sufficient to guarantee the robust storage of visual features. Beyond basic visual cognition, their research probes the developmental trajectory of memory selection by examining how young children and adults differ in their ability to actively inhibit attended but outdated visual information. Additionally, Dr. Chen applies these behavioral paradigms to clinical populations, mapping the temporal dynamics of attentional hyperfocusing and assessing the flexibility of expectation updating in individuals with schizophrenia.

papers.title: Testing the memory encoding cost theory using the multiple cues paradigm
papers.abstract: This study evaluates the memory encoding cost (MEC) theory, which suggests that the cognitive resources required to consolidate a spatial cue into working memory are the primary drivers of cueing costs in valid-invalid spatial cueing paradigms. Utilizing a multiple-cue methodology, the researchers assessed how varying the memory load of peripheral cues influences subsequent target reporting. The empirical results support the MEC account, demonstrating that behavioral invalidity costs scale with cue consolidation demands, thereby indicating that the traditional 'attentional resource' limit may be better characterized as a mnemonic consolidation bottleneck where the encoding of cues competes with the processing of targets.
papers.authors: Jian Li, Huixin Song, Xiaoqi Huang, Luo Chen, Mowei Shen, Hui Chen

papers.title: Attention, voluntary saccade, or long-term fixation: None of them confirms visual working memory consolidation
papers.abstract: The investigation explores whether directing foveal attention through voluntary saccades or prolonged fixation is sufficient to trigger the automatic consolidation of object attributes into visual working memory. Across four experiments employing a modified attribute amnesia paradigm, participants were required to gaze at masked locations to identify target singletons. Despite sustained foveation and successful target localization in pre-surprise trials, report accuracy plummeted in the surprise trial for both color and identity features. These results suggest a functional dissociation between saccadic selection and mnemonic consolidation, demonstrating that neither voluntary eye movements nor long-term fixations guarantee that attended information is robustly stored in working memory.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
papers.authors: Xuanxuan Cai, Enfu Sun, Zhongting Chen, Hui Chen

papers.title: Children exhibit superior memory for attended but outdated information compared to adults
papers.abstract: This research identifies a developmental reversal in cognitive selectivity, specifically regarding the mechanism of memory selection which filters attended but no-longer-relevant information. Using the attribute amnesia task with eye-tracking across five experiments, the study found that young children (ages 4–6) demonstrate significantly better recall for 'outdated' information compared to adults. While adults efficiently filter out information that becomes task-irrelevant after being attended, children appear to automatically encode this information into memory. These findings suggest that the active inhibitory processes required for memory selection are not fully developed in early childhood, leading to a broader but less efficient encoding strategy compared to the highly selective adult brain.
papers.authors: Yingtao Fu, Jie He, Mowei Shen, Hui Chen

papers.title: The dynamic process of hyperfocusing and hyperfiltering in schizophrenia
papers.abstract: The study investigates the temporal dynamics of cognitive selection in individuals with schizophrenia (PSZ), focusing on the contradictory findings of attentional deficits versus supranormal selection. Using a trial-based attribute amnesia paradigm, the researchers tracked how the selection of relevant features (hyperfocusing) and the suppression of irrelevant features (hyperfiltering) evolved over time. The results revealed that PSZ exhibit an initial phase of intensified attentional selection that rapidly decays, transitioning into a state of high distractibility. This dynamic model suggests that the core cognitive impairment in schizophrenia is not a simple lack of attention, but rather an unstable 'hyper-selective' state that fails to maintain its integrity over extended durations.
papers.authors: Jian Li, Bao-Liang Zhong, Dongsheng Zhou, Luo Chen, Enze Tang, Jiewei Zheng, Xiaoqi Huang, Huixin Song, Chenxiao Guan, Huiying Liu, Mowei Shen, Hui Chen

papers.title: Flexibility Retained: Unimpaired Updating of Expectations in Schizophrenia
papers.abstract: This study examines the flexibility of belief updating in patients with schizophrenia (PSZ), specifically their ability to adjust cognitive expectations following feedback. In a modified attribute amnesia task, participants were subjected to a surprise question regarding a previously ignored stimulus attribute. Both PSZ and healthy controls (HCS) exhibited significant and comparable improvements in report accuracy during subsequent control trials, indicating a rapid and effective updating of task-related expectations. The results provide robust evidence that, despite profound deficits in various cognitive domains, the core mechanisms for updating internal models in response to expectation violations remain largely functional in individuals with schizophrenia.
papers.authors: Jian Li, Luo Chen, Dongsheng Zhou, Enze Tang, Jiewei Zheng, Xiaoqi Huang, Bao-Liang Zhong, Chenxiao Guan, Huiying Liu, Mowei Shen, Hui Chen

0269.name: Ignacio Serrano-Pedraza
0269.department: Department of Experimental Psychology, Cognitive Processes and Speech Therapy
0269.bio: Ignacio Serrano-Pedraza is a Professor of Vision Science at the Complutense University of Madrid, where they direct the Laboratory of Visual Psychophysics. Their research utilizes human psychophysics and computational modeling to analyze the functional mechanisms of the human visual system, with specific focus on motion perception, spatial vision, and stereopsis. Serrano-Pedraza has investigated neuronal inhibitory mechanisms, such as center-surround antagonism, and their influence on motion discrimination and stereoscopic anisotropy. Their current work involves applying psychophysical findings to clinical research to identify biomarkers for sensory alterations in populations with schizophrenia, epilepsy, and depression.
0269.research_direction: Dr. Serrano-Pedraza has recently been investigating the spatiotemporal limits and neural architecture of binocular vision, with a particular focus on stereoscopic depth and motion perception. Their recent work explores the boundaries of stereoscopic orientation anisotropy, specifically probing how human visual sensitivity to vertical versus horizontal disparity corrugations varies across a broad range of spatial and temporal frequencies. To uncover the underlying mechanisms of these phenomena, they have been utilizing an individual differences approach alongside multivariate analysis to map out whether distinct orientation-selective and temporal-frequency-tuned channels drive the perception of 3D depth and frontoparallel stereomotion. Additionally, they are employing psychophysical cancellation paradigms and computational modeling to examine cross-scale center-surround motion interactions under binocular and dichoptic viewing conditions, aiming to delineate the early visual processing hierarchy of interocular gain control and binocular summation.

papers.title: Center-surround motion interaction between low and high spatial frequencies under binocular and dichoptic viewing
papers.abstract: This study examines cross-scale motion interactions using a center-surround spatial configuration, building on previous findings that static coarse-scale features impair the discrimination of moving fine-scale features. The researchers utilized a psychophysical cancellation speed metric to quantify the strength of these interactions across varied spatial frequencies, temporal frequencies, contrasts, and durations. Findings indicate that cancellation speeds follow bandpass tuning for spatial frequency and increase with temporal frequency up to 12 Hz. Results remained consistent under both binocular and dichoptic presentations, although the interaction was significantly more robust in the binocular condition. Computational simulations using a motion-sensing model suggest that the observed differences are accounted for by a processing hierarchy involving interocular gain control, binocular summation, and a subsequent cross-scale interaction stage.
papers.authors: Omar Bachtoula, Ignacio Serrano-Pedraza

papers.title: Spatiotemporal Characteristics of the Stereoscopic Anisotropy
papers.abstract: This research quantifies the spatiotemporal properties of the well-documented stereoscopic orientation anisotropy, where detection thresholds for vertical disparity corrugations are significantly higher than for horizontal ones. Using dynamic random-dot stereograms, the authors measured thresholds across a broad spatiotemporal range (0.05 to 0.8 cpd and 0 to 8 Hz). The results demonstrate that while disparity thresholds increase with temporal frequency following a low-pass characteristic, the magnitude of the anisotropy is greatest at low spatial frequencies and decreases as spatial frequency rises. Modeling indicates that the anisotropy is best explained by a global vertical shift in sensitivity, suggesting that while the underlying spatiotemporal weighting functions are similar for both orientations, there is an inherent processing disadvantage for vertical corrugations.
papers.authors: Ichasus Llamas-Cornejo, Ignacio Serrano-Pedraza

papers.title: Orientation mechanisms in stereoscopic vision: an individual differences approach
papers.abstract: Using factor analytic and principal component techniques, this study investigated the existence of orientation-selective mechanisms within the stereoscopic system. Disparity thresholds were collected from 37 participants for sinusoidal depth corrugations across seven orientations (0° to 90°) and three spatial frequencies (0.1, 0.4, and 0.8 cpd). While a strong anisotropy was observed at the lowest spatial frequency, the multivariate analysis revealed that thresholds for proximal orientations clustered together. These findings provide evidence for the existence of multiple disparity channels tuned to specific orientations, rather than a single broadly-tuned mechanism, supporting a more complex neural architecture for the processing of three-dimensional depth corrugations.
papers.authors: Ichasus Llamas-Cornejo, David H. Peterzell, Ignacio Serrano-Pedraza

papers.title: Temporal mechanisms in frontoparallel stereomotion revealed by individual differences analysis
papers.abstract: This study explores the neural architecture underlying temporal processing in frontoparallel (cyclopean) motion using an individual differences framework. Disparity thresholds for vertical and horizontal drifting sinusoidal corrugations were measured across seven temporal frequencies (0.25 to 8 Hz) in a sample of 34 participants. Thresholds remained relatively constant up to 1 Hz before increasing monotonically at higher frequencies. Principal component analysis and subsequent rotation (Varimax and Direct Oblimin) identified two distinct temporal factors: a low-frequency factor loaded at 0.25–2 Hz and a high-frequency factor loaded at 2–8 Hz. The moderate intercorrelation between these factors suggests the presence of two partially interdependent temporal mechanisms involved in the perception of frontoparallel stereoscopic motion.
papers.authors: Ichasus Llamas-Cornejo, David H. Peterzell, Ignacio Serrano-Pedraza

0270.name: Ikuya Murakami
0270.bio: Ikuya Murakami is a Professor at the University of Tokyo specializing in the psychophysics of human vision and the neural mechanisms of perception. Murakami’s research utilizes experimental psychophysics, eye-movement tracking, and functional neuroimaging to investigate how the brain processes visual motion, achieves perceptual completion, and integrates signals across sensory modalities. Their work includes studies on the temporal dynamics of the flash-lag effect and the role of physiological factors, such as microsaccades and melanopsin activation, in modulating visual sensitivity and the subjective experience of duration.
0270.research_direction: Dr. Murakami has recently been investigating the complex spatiotemporal dynamics of visual perception, utilizing psychophysics and magnetoencephalography (MEG) to probe the mechanisms underlying spatial localization and time estimation. Their recent work explores how motion-induced position shifts—such as the twinkle-goes and flash-grab illusions—interact with endogenous neural theta oscillations and high-level perceptual completion within the blind spot and behind occluders. They are also examining how temporal expectations and visual hierarchies shape conscious perception, specifically testing how rhythmic predictability modulates orientation repulsion and how spatial crowding distorts the perceived duration of visual targets. Additionally, they are investigating non-image-forming retinal pathways, probing how melanopsin activation by short-wavelength light within the optic disk influences baseline visual sensitivity and absolute light detectability across the broader visual field.

papers.title: Temporal dynamics of the twinkle-goes illusion and its relationship to neural theta oscillations
papers.abstract: The 'twinkle-goes' illusion describes an illusory overshoot in the perceived disappearance position of a moving stimulus when it vanishes against a dynamic noise background, likely mediated by delayed sensory evidence accumulation. This study quantified the temporal evolution of this positional shift using probe stimuli at varying spatio-temporal offsets. Experiment 1 revealed that the illusory displacement is minimal at the instant of physical stimulus offset and monotonically increases over a window of approximately 120 ms post-vanishing. Experiment 2 employed magnetoencephalography (MEG) to examine rhythmic modulation, demonstrating that the magnitude of the positional overshoot significantly correlates with the phase of pre-stimulus theta-band oscillations. These findings imply that visual motion prediction is a slow-paced process rhythmically updated in alignment with endogenous neural theta cycles.
papers.authors: Ryosuke Nakayama, Kaoru Amano, Ikuya Murakami

papers.title: The illusion of orientation repulsion is weakened in a temporally more predictable visual target
papers.abstract: Orientation repulsion, in which a target's perceived tilt is biased away from inducer orientations, reflects contextual inhibitory modulation in the visual cortex. This study investigated how temporal expectation influences the magnitude of this illusion. Experiment 1 demonstrated that multimodal rhythmic cues, which enhance temporal predictability, significantly reduce repulsion magnitude when the target appears at the expected onset. Experiment 2 showed that this reduction requires subjective awareness of the cue-target contingency. Experiment 3 isolated the hazard rate effect, finding that repulsion further diminishes as the conditional probability of target onset increases over time. The authors propose that heightened temporal expectation reduces perceptual latency, granting conscious access to a premature neural representation of the target before contextual inhibitory signals have fully evolved.
papers.authors: Tomoya Nakamura, Ikuya Murakami

papers.title: Flash grab effect within the regions of modal and amodal completions
papers.abstract: The flash-grab effect (FGE) causes a flashed stimulus to appear shifted in the direction of a reversing motion. This study examined the FGE within areas of perceptual completion: the natural blind spot (modal completion) and regions behind physical occluders (amodal completion). Using a perceptual matching paradigm, the researchers found that flashes presented adjacent to these completed regions were subjectively localized within the 'filled-in' or 'occluded' zones. Interestingly, the FGE was observed for bottom-to-inside shifts but absent for top-to-inside shifts in both completion types. The magnitude of the illusion was generally smaller than in control conditions with physical inducers. These findings suggest that motion-induced position shifts are integrated with high-level perceptual completion processes, and the visual system treats completed regions as valid spatial substrates for mislocalization.
papers.authors: Hoko Nakada, Yuya Seshita, Haruka Shimazaki, Sohei Kito, Tomoya Nakamura, Ikuya Murakami

papers.title: Perceived duration of visual stimuli contracts due to crowding
papers.abstract: This investigation utilized spatial crowding to dissociate low-level feature extraction from higher-level object recognition stages in duration perception. Using letter and Vernier stimuli matched for first-order physical properties, the study manipulated discriminability through lateral masking. Results indicated that stimuli rendered difficult to identify by crowding were perceived as having significantly contracted durations compared to uncrowded controls. Systematic experiments ruled out explanations based on low-level energy differences, cognitive response biases, or shifts in perceived onset/offset timing. These findings provide evidence for distributed timing mechanisms within the visual hierarchy, suggesting that time-sensitive neural structures are coupled with high-level feature integration and object recognition processes that are selectively impaired by peripheral crowding.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
papers.authors: Sofia Nagisa, Ikuya Murakami

papers.title: Illumination by short-wavelength light inside the blind spot decreases light detectability
papers.abstract: Despite the absence of rod and cone photoreceptors in the optic disk (blind spot), this region contains the photopigment melanopsin within intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells (ipRGCs). This study investigated whether melanopsin activation modulates absolute light detection thresholds. Using a psychophysical task, the authors found that illuminating the blind spot with blue light (short-wavelength) significantly impaired the detectability of a light stimulus presented in the normal visual field. This suppressive effect persisted immediately after the offset of the blind-spot illumination, suggesting a signaling pathway with sluggish kinetics consistent with melanopsin rather than intraocular scattering. No such effect was observed with red light. These data suggest that melanopsin activation in the optic disk contributes to the estimation of baseline neural noise, thereby modulating the sensitivity of the image-forming visual system.
papers.authors: Marina Saito, Kentaro Miyamoto, Ikuya Murakami

0272.name: Ilker Yildirim
0272.lab_name: The Cognitive and Neural Computation Lab (CNCL)
0272.bio: Ilker Yildirim is an Assistant Professor of Psychology at Yale University and directs the Cognitive and Neural Computation Lab. Yildirim's research utilizes a reverse-engineering approach to study how the human brain converts sensory signals into mental representations of objects, physical dynamics, and social agents. By integrating generative models, probabilistic programming, and deep learning, Yildirim develops computational theories that are evaluated using human psychophysical behavior and multi-area neural data. This work focuses on establishing an engineering-level account of visual cognition and its function in supporting reasoning and decision-making processes.
0272.research_direction: Dr. Yildirim has recently been investigating how the visual system employs internal generative models to perceive and predict complex scene dynamics. Their recent work explores the computational foundations of intuitive physics, utilizing simulation-based models to probe how humans visually estimate the properties of highly deformable materials—such as liquids and soft cloths—and how predictive "look-ahead" simulations help observers segment continuous physical events. Beyond physical dynamics, they are also examining multiarea object processing in the primate inferotemporal cortex, testing the hypothesis that neural representations in body patches operate as an "inverse graphics" engine to recover 3D object properties from 2D retinal inputs. Additionally, their research investigates the algorithmic mechanisms of dynamic visual attention, modeling how the brain strategically allocates limited perceptual computations on the fly during sustained goal-directed tasks like multiple object tracking.

papers.title: Computational models reveal intuitive physics and statistical cues separately contribute to the visual perception of liquids
papers.abstract: This research explores the computational foundations of liquid perception, contrasting high-level motion statistics with simulation-based intuitive physics. The authors introduce 'Ripple,' a generative model that infers liquid viscosity by mapping the latent physical processes governing the interaction between liquids, external forces, and rigid geometries. Across behavioral tasks measuring viscosity similarity judgments in qualitatively diverse scenarios (e.g., splashing versus pouring), Ripple explains significant unique variance in human performance that is not captured by task-specific deep neural networks or general-purpose video foundation models. These results demonstrate that human perception of mutable substances involves an internal model of physical causality that transcends discriminative image statistics.
papers.authors: Yuting Zhang, Wenyan Bi, Yuyang Miao, Ilker Yildirim

papers.title: Multiarea processing in body patches of the primate inferotemporal cortex implements inverse graphics
papers.abstract: This study investigates the computational architecture of stimulus-driven, multiarea processing within the primate inferotemporal (IT) cortex. The authors propose that the functional organization of IT body patches is optimized for 'inverse graphics'—a process of inferring 3D object properties from 2D retinal inputs. By modeling the processing hierarchy across IT nodes (specifically regions 38 and 46), the research shows that an inference network optimized for 3D shape recovery aligns significantly better with neural population representational dissimilarity matrices (RDMs) than traditional discriminative models. The findings suggest that IT cortex implementations reflect structure-preserving representations analogous to the reverse of a graphics-based generative model of image formation.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS)
papers.authors: Hakan Yilmaz, Aalap D. Shah, Ariadne Letrou, Satwant Kumar, Rufin Vogels, Ilker Yildirim

papers.title: Computational models reveal that intuitive physics underlies visual processing of soft objects
papers.abstract: Modeling the perception of soft objects, such as cloths, presents significant challenges due to their high-dimensional deformation spaces and complex internal structures. This paper introduces 'Woven,' a framework utilizing physics-based simulations to generate probabilistic representations of soft-object dynamics. The authors evaluate the model against human performance in visual matching tasks involving physical transformations like falling and waving. Woven captures the nuances of human stiffness estimation, including systematic successes and errors, outperforming standard deep neural networks and ablation baselines. These results indicate that the visual processing of deformable objects relies on internal generative models of intuitive physics to resolve 'explaining away' challenges inherent in dynamic scenes.
papers.authors: Wenyan Bi, Aalap D. Shah, Kimberly W. Wong, Brian J. Scholl, Ilker Yildirim

papers.title: Adaptive computation as a new mechanism of dynamic human attention
papers.abstract: The authors propose 'adaptive computation' as a mechanistic theory of dynamic human attention, formulated as a resource-rational allocation process. In this framework, attention is the on-the-fly distribution of limited perceptual computations based on their expected impact on task-specific decision outcomes. Using Multiple Object Tracking (MOT) as a benchmark, the model quantitatively predicts trial-level tracking accuracy, localization errors, and subsecond shifts in attentional focus. Notably, the approach accounts for both the subjective sense of cognitive effort and the prioritization of goal-relevant objects over visually salient distractors, providing a domain-general algorithmic explanation for the strategic deployment of limited computational resources in the brain.
papers.authors: Mario Belledonne, Eivinas Butkus, Brian J. Scholl, Ilker Yildirim
