papers.title: Temporal segmentation and "look ahead" simulation: Physical events structure visual perception of intuitive physics
papers.abstract: This research examines how physical event structures modulate the visual perception of intuitive physics through temporal segmentation and predictive 'look-ahead' simulations. Utilizing a dual-task paradigm, the authors show that human observers segment continuous physical dynamics into discrete events based on prediction error and causal transitions. Experimental data reveal that selective processing of objects is significantly attenuated at event boundaries relative to event middles, suggesting that the updating of internal event models imposes a transient computational bottleneck. The study supports a predictive processing account where the visual system structures perception by continuously simulating future physical states and segmenting inputs at points of maximum uncertainty.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
papers.authors: Tristan S. Yates, Shannon Yasuda, Ilker Yildirim

0274.name: Ione Fine
0274.bio: Ione Fine is a Professor of Psychology at the University of Washington who researches the adaptation of the human brain to long-term sensory deprivation, such as blindness and deafness. Fine uses functional MRI, psychophysics, and computational modeling to investigate the relationship between neural function and neuroanatomical structure. Their work includes the development of "virtual patients" to model and predict perceptual experiences produced by sight restoration technologies like retinal and cortical prostheses. Fine also characterizes the mechanisms of cross-modal plasticity and the limitations of experience-dependent recovery in high-level visual processing.
0274.research_direction: Dr. Fine has recently been investigating sensory plasticity, perceptual learning in prosthetic vision, and binocular signal processing in the early visual cortex. Their recent work explores cross-modal reorganization in early blindness, combining theoretical models of skill acquisition with psychophysics and computational modeling to understand whether auditory enhancements—like improved pitch perception—arise from reduced internal noise or sharper cortical tuning. Additionally, they are studying perceptual learning in sight recovery by using "virtual patient" simulations and gamified training to determine how well the visual system can adapt to and generalize the distorted neural population responses produced by visual prosthetics and optogenetics. Finally, they utilize fMRI and quantitative modeling to probe fundamental visual computations, mapping how dichoptic contrast signals from each eye are combined as they propagate across the V1–V3 hierarchy.

papers.title: Enhanced pitch perception in early blind individuals and musicians is due to reduced internal noise
papers.abstract: This study evaluates whether the behavioral advantage in pitch perception observed in early blind individuals and musicians stems from sharper cortical frequency tuning or reduced internal noise. Using a notched-noise task to assess peripheral frequency selectivity and a pitch discrimination task to probe cortical mechanisms, the researchers compared early blind and sighted cohorts matched for musical training. Results showed no significant differences in peripheral tuning. However, early blind individuals and musicians both exhibited superior pitch discrimination, which computational modeling attributed to lower trial-by-trial internal noise rather than narrower bandwidths of the underlying auditory filters. These findings identify internal noise reduction as a key mechanism of experience-dependent auditory plasticity.
papers.authors: Woon Ju Park, Jasmine Awad, Ione Fine

papers.title: Perceptual learning of prosthetic vision using video game training
papers.abstract: Electronic and optogenetic sight recovery technologies often fail to provide complementary firing in on- and off-center neural populations, resulting in distorted visual input. Using 'virtual patients'—sighted observers viewing simulated distorted population responses—this study examined whether gamified training (a custom variant of Fruit Ninja) facilitates more effective perceptual learning than standard object discrimination tasks. While both training groups showed significant performance improvements, the results indicated no significant transfer of learning from the video game to novel object recognition. This suggests that while humans can learn to interpret scrambled population responses, the resulting plasticity may be highly task-specific rather than generalizable across visual domains.
papers.authors: Rebecca B. Esquenazi, Kimberly Meier, Michael Beyeler, Drake Wright, Geoffrey M. Boynton, Ione Fine

papers.title: Dichoptic contrast integration across the human visual cortex hierarchy using functional MRI
papers.abstract: This investigation utilizes fMRI and continuous behavioral reporting to determine how contrast signals from each eye are integrated across the human visual hierarchy (V1–V3) under non-rivalrous viewing conditions. Participants viewed dichoptic gratings with independently modulated contrasts while their BOLD responses were recorded. A Minkowski mean model was used to characterize the integration rule. Results demonstrated that the integration exponent increased significantly across the hierarchy, moving from a near-averaging model in V1 toward a maximum-response (winner-take-all) model in V3. These findings suggest that the neural representation of binocular contrast undergoes a non-linear transformation as it propagates through the early visual cortex, aligning with the perceived maximum contrast at higher stages.
papers.authors: Kelly Chang, Xiyan Li, Kimberly Meier, Kristina Tarczy-Hornoch, Geoffrey M. Boynton, Ione Fine

papers.title: A unified model for cross-modal plasticity and skill acquisition
papers.abstract: This review proposes a unified hypothesis to explain cross-modal plasticity in early blind individuals by drawing parallels with the mechanisms of skill acquisition in sighted populations. Synthesizing the 'cortical recycling' theory and the 'metamodal' hypothesis, the authors argue that the reorganization of visual cortex for non-visual tasks is not a unique consequence of sensory deprivation but rather follows the same functional, algorithmic, and structural constraints that mediate the development of expertise and novel cognitive abilities. The paper suggests that the recruitment of visual areas (e.g., hMT+ for auditory motion) is driven by innate computational biases that are repurposed through competitive interactions during development to solve unique perceptual challenges.
papers.authors: Woon Ju Park, Ione Fine

papers.title: Editorial: Insights in visual neuroscience: 2023
papers.abstract: This research editorial synthesizes major recent advancements in visual neuroscience, emphasizing the interdisciplinary intersection of biology, clinical practice, and computational modeling. The work reviews current findings on the genetic and neural bases of color vision deficiencies and summarizes new perspectives on cortical plasticity. It highlights the shift toward understanding large-scale cross-modal reorganization in the blind through the lens of developmental flexibility and skill acquisition, providing a conceptual framework for how high-level cortical areas are repurposed following sensory loss to enhance the processing of remaining sensory inputs.
papers.authors: Benjamin Thompson, Vallabh E. Das, Ione Fine

0275.name: Ipek Oruc
0275.department: Department of Ophthalmology and Visual Sciences
0275.bio: Ipek Oruc is an Associate Professor at the University of British Columbia and director of the NOVA Lab, where they investigate the neural mechanisms of higher-level vision and object recognition. Oruc’s research integrates computer science, visual psychophysics, and neuroimaging to examine how the brain develops perceptual expertise for complex stimuli such as faces. They also study visual dysfunction in neurodevelopmental disorders like autism and conditions such as prosopagnosia to inform the development of rehabilitation paradigms. Additionally, Oruc applies deep learning and data science to create automated diagnostic tools and predictive models using retinal imaging.
0275.research_direction: Dr. Oruc has recently been investigating human visual perception and computational modeling across both naturalistic and clinical domains. Their recent work explores the mechanisms of face processing, specifically probing the "blur paradox" to understand how spatial scale and image degradation interact, while also using head-mounted cameras to quantify the atypical naturalistic "face diets" and viewpoint exposures of adults with autism spectrum disorder. In parallel, they are utilizing convolutional neural networks to advance neuroimaging methodologies, investigating how hierarchical CNN features can be mapped onto early and object-selective visual cortices to generate synthetic fMRI responses for novel stimuli. Furthermore, Dr. Oruc applies these deep learning and explainable AI techniques to clinical ophthalmology, analyzing retinal fundus images to determine whether diabetic retinopathy manifests with sexually dimorphic spatial patterns.

papers.title: The blur paradox: Better recognition at a distance
papers.abstract: Under conditions of significant visual degradation, specifically blur, an inverse relationship exists between image size and recognition accuracy, where smaller or more distant stimuli are more easily identified. This investigation utilized a face recognition protocol with high-resolution grayscale celebrity images subjected to physical holographic filters to replicate this 'blur paradox' in a naturalistic viewing context. Across two experiments, participants demonstrated superior identification performance for blurry faces at smaller angular sizes (approximately 1.7°) compared to larger sizes (4.8°). The findings indicate that recognition efficiency improves gradually as viewing distance increases, suggesting that scale-dependent mechanisms in the visual system favor coarser, lower-spatial-frequency features when fine-scale information is obscured by blur.
papers.authors: Caitlin Long, Lei Yuan, Claudia Wu, Ipek Oruc

papers.title: AI-Assisted identification of sex-specific patterns in diabetic retinopathy using retinal fundus images
papers.abstract: This research utilizes convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and explainable AI techniques to determine if diabetic retinopathy (DR) manifests with sexually dimorphic patterns in retinal fundus images. VGG16 models were fine-tuned on a curated dataset of nearly 3,000 images, matched for clinical confounders such as age, HbA1c levels, and disease severity. Saliency mapping via Guided Grad-CAM revealed that the diagnostic features identified by the AI varied by sex: classifications in female retinas were primarily driven by features in the macula, while male classifications relied on the optic disc and peripheral vasculature. These results suggest sex-dependent risk profiles for complications such as macular edema versus proliferative disease, potentially informing more personalized screening and diagnostic protocols.
papers.authors: Parsa Delavari, Gulcenur Ozturan, Eduardo V. Navajas, Ozgur Yilmaz, Ipek Oruc

papers.title: CNN-Extracted Features Generate Synthetic fMRI Responses to Unseen Images
papers.abstract: To address the limitations imposed by the scarcity and high cost of human neuroimaging data, this study introduces a method for generating high-fidelity synthetic fMRI responses using features extracted from convolutional neural networks (CNNs). By establishing hierarchical correspondences between CNN layers and biological visual areas—such as the early visual cortex (EV) and the lateral occipital cortex (LOC)—the model produces voxel-wise activity patterns for novel visual stimuli. Decoding experiments demonstrated that these synthetic datasets can effectively augment real fMRI data, achieving superior performance in image classification and reconstruction tasks. The high correlation between generated and observed responses supports the utility of CNN-based augmentation for advancing computational models of the human visual system.
papers.authors: Parsa Delavari, Leonid Sigal, Ipek Oruc

papers.title: Atypical daily visual exposure to faces in adults with autism spectrum disorder
papers.abstract: This study provides the first longitudinal empirical measurement of the 'face diet'—daily visual exposure to faces—in adults with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) using head-mounted cameras. Analysis of over 360 hours of first-person perspective footage revealed that individuals with ASD experience a 30% reduction in total face exposure compared to neurotypical controls. This deficit is primarily characterized by significantly less time spent viewing familiar faces. Furthermore, the qualitative nature of face viewing in ASD is atypical, involving greater viewing distances (resulting in smaller retinal images) and a bias toward profile views rather than frontal orientations. These results suggest that the development of face-processing expertise in ASD may be constrained by both a quantitative lack of exposure and a qualitatively distinct visual environment.
papers.authors: Todd Kamensek, Grace Iarocci, Ipek Oruc

0276.name: Irene Sperandio
0276.department: Department of Psychology and Cognitive Science
0276.bio: Irene Sperandio is an Associate Professor who investigates the neural mechanisms underlying size constancy and the integration of retinal and extra-retinal signals for perception and action. Utilizing a multimodal approach including functional MRI, electroencephalography (EEG), psychophysics, and kinematics, Sperandio explores how the primary visual cortex (V1) and higher-order cortical areas process object size relative to viewing distance. Their work employs visual illusions, such as the Ebbinghaus illusion, to examine the computational and neuroanatomical dissociations between the ventral and dorsal visual streams. Sperandio's research also addresses the developmental trajectories of visual perception and the characterization of anomalous perceptual experiences in clinical conditions such as psychosis.
0276.research_direction: Dr. Sperandio’s recent work bridges high-level visual perception, social cognition, and consciousness. They have recently been investigating the neural dynamics of spatial vision, utilizing fMRI, high-density EEG, and kinematic tracking to understand how early visual networks achieve size-distance constancy for perception and action, as well as how they mediate contextual phenomena like the Ebbinghaus illusion. In parallel, their research explores the physiological foundations of social-emotional processing, employing continuous flash suppression and facial EMG to trace pre-conscious autonomic reactions to emotional faces, and high-density EEG to examine how autobiographical memory shapes empathic neural resonance to others' physical pain. Furthermore, they are investigating the physiological correlates of altered states of consciousness, using pupillometry and subjective metrics to probe how rhythmic auditory stimulation modulates arousal, attention, and the complexity of visual imagery.

papers.title: Phenomenological and physiological correlates of altered states of consciousness induced by rhythmic auditory stimulation
papers.abstract: This study characterizes the induction of altered states of consciousness (ASC) through rhythmic auditory stimulation (RAS) using a multidisciplinary approach. Participants were exposed to drumming-derived rhythms—both perfectly regular loops and those containing natural micro-variations—while their ocular indices, specifically pupil diameter and eye blink rate, were continuously monitored via eye-tracking to index arousal and attention. Subjective experiences were quantified through structured questionnaires and evaluations of hallucinatory-like perceptual phenomena. The results confirmed that RAS reliably induces ASC compared to sensory restriction controls. While global ASC intensity was similar across rhythm types, micro-variable stimulation uniquely enhanced the structural complexity of visual imagery. Physiological data reflected dynamic shifts in attention, with the qualitative structure and intensity of the ASC experience being significantly modulated by the listener's level of musical expertise.
papers.authors: Nicola De Pisapia, Maria Laura Mencaroni, Giulio Velardo, Irene Sperandio

papers.title: Pre-conscious reactions to faces as the biological roots of emotion perception
papers.abstract: This investigation employs a continuous flash suppression (CFS) paradigm to determine whether emotional facial expressions trigger physiological responses prior to conscious access. By monitoring facial electromyography (EMG) of the zygomaticus major and corrugator supercilii, skin conductance level (SCL), and pupil diameter, the researchers compared reactions to fearful, happy, and neutral expressions during interocular suppression and after breakthrough to awareness. Fearful faces elicited significant pupillary dilation and increased corrugator activity even when visually suppressed, supporting the existence of a fast, subcortical threat-detection pathway involving the amygdala and superior colliculus. Furthermore, the magnitude of these pre-conscious responses correlated with individual levels of empathy and schizotypy, suggesting that social-cognitive traits are intrinsically linked to the autonomic resonance of emotional cues at a subconscious level.
papers.authors: Cecilia Dapor, Ronen Hershman, Daniela Ruzzante, Federica Meconi, Irene Sperandio

papers.title: Perspective matters: using past experiences to understand others' insensitivity to physical pain
papers.abstract: This research evaluates the role of autobiographical memory (AM) in mentalizing by investigating whether personal experience of an event is a prerequisite for empathic neural resonance. Using a pain decision task and high-density EEG, the study compared neural and behavioral responses to individuals with normal pain sensitivity versus those with clinical congenital insensitivity to pain. Event-related potential (ERP) analysis focused on the late P300 component, revealing that neural discrimination between sensitive and insensitive targets was associated with individual empathy traits. Multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) indicated that while AM reactivation can support empathy by allowing observers to use the self as a model, this strategy is flexibly inhibited when self-experience diverges from the target's state, shifting the mechanism toward active perspective taking for accurate social inference.
papers.authors: Federica Meconi, Marco Canducci, Sebastian Michelmann, Alessandro Grecucci, Irene Sperandio

papers.title: Network dynamics underlying alterations in apparent object size
papers.abstract: This study utilizes functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) combined with dynamic causal modeling (DCM) to investigate the effective connectivity within the visual hierarchy during the Ebbinghaus illusion. Despite constant retinal stimulation, the contextual manipulation of inducer size alters the perceived diameter of a central target circle. The analysis identified a cortical network comprising the primary visual cortex (V1) and the lateral occipital complex (LOC). DCM results demonstrated that the illusory effect is mediated by a combination of feedforward signaling from V1 to LOC and reciprocal feedback modulation from LOC to V1. These findings indicate that subjective size perception emerges from re-entrant processing and top-down modulation of early visual representations, rather than being determined solely by initial retinal signal processing.
papers.authors: Lihong Chen, Baoyu Wu, Haoyang Yu, Irene Sperandio

papers.title: Temporal features of size constancy for perception and action in a real-world setting: A combined EEG-kinematics study
papers.abstract: To investigate the neural chronometry of size-distance scaling, this study integrated high-density electroencephalography (EEG) with infrared motion tracking during manual estimation (perceptual) and reaching-and-grasping (action) tasks in a 3D environment. Using a paradigm where physical object size was scaled with distance to maintain a constant retinal angle, the researchers identified a positive visual evoked potential (VEP) at ~90 ms that reflected physical object size rather than retinal input. Kinematic results showed that peak grip aperture was precisely scaled to the physical dimensions of the targets, consistent with the preservation of grip constancy. These findings suggest that size-distance scaling operations occur at the earliest cortical stages of visual processing (~90 ms post-stimulus) and that the initial representation of size remains largely invariant to the specific task demands of the perception or action systems.
papers.authors: Simona Noviello, Saman Kamari Songhorabadi, Zhiqing Deng, Chao Zheng, Juan Chen, Angelo Pisani, Elena Franchin, Enrica Pierotti, Elena Tonolli, Simona Monaco, Louis Renoult, Irene Sperandio

0277.name: Isabel Gauthier
0277.main_research_area: Visual object recognition and perceptual expertise
0277.bio: Isabel Gauthier is a cognitive neuroscientist who researches the neural and behavioral mechanisms of visual object recognition and perceptual expertise. Gauthier uses novel objects, such as "Greebles," to demonstrate that category-specific neural responses in the fusiform face area can be recruited through experience rather than being strictly innate. Their methodology integrates high-resolution fMRI, event-related potentials (ERP), and psychophysics to investigate the plasticity of the human visual system. Gauthier’s current research focuses on quantifying individual differences in high-level visual abilities and exploring the relationships between domain-general recognition and ensemble perception.
0277.research_direction: Dr. Gauthier has recently been investigating individual differences in high-level visual cognition, anchoring much of their research around the psychometric construct "o," a domain-general capacity for subordinate-level object discrimination. Their recent work explores how this stable perceptual factor can be reliably measured and how it theoretically fits alongside broader cognitive constructs like general intelligence and visual memory. Using latent variable modeling and varied behavioral paradigms, they are assessing the extent to which "o" drives performance on diverse visual tasks, such as distinguishing authentic from AI-generated faces or binding object identities to episodic spatial locations. Additionally, their research probes the boundaries between domain-general and category-specific visual processing by testing for distinct, specialized perceptual mechanisms, such as an isolated food-recognition ability and its potential relationship to behavioral traits like food neophobia.

papers.title: Domain-general object recognition predicts human ability to tell real from AI-generated faces
papers.abstract: This study examines individual differences in the human capacity to distinguish GAN-generated (AI) faces from authentic ones. Utilizing latent variable modeling on a large sample, the authors assessed the predictive utility of the 'o' factor—a psychometrically defined measure of domain-general object recognition ability representing the shared variance between subordinate-level perception and memory. Results demonstrate that 'o' is a significantly stronger predictor of AI-face detection performance than either specialized face recognition ability or general intelligence (g). Systematic analysis of visual cues indicates that low-'o' individuals are disproportionately misled by specific generative artifacts, whereas high-'o' individuals exhibit more robust visual processing under these challenging conditions. The findings suggests that the ability to navigate novel, non-evolutionary perceptual challenges is grounded in a domain-general visual mechanism rather than artifact-specific knowledge.
papers.authors: Jason K. Chow, Rankin W. McGugin, Isabel Gauthier

papers.title: Is Domain-General Object Recognition Ability a Novel Construct?
papers.abstract: This review synthesizes the evidence for 'o'—the domain-general ability for subordinate-level object discrimination—and evaluates its position within established hierarchies of cognitive abilities, such as the Cattell-Horn-Carroll (CHC) framework. The authors argue that while 'o' shares conceptual overlap with visual memory and processing speed (Gs), it represents a distinct construct characterized by the precision of perceptual encoding across diverse object categories. By bridging the gap between vision science and psychometric research on individual differences, the review outlines how this stable perceptual factor accounts for variance in high-level vision that is independent of general intelligence (g) or category-specific expertise.
papers.authors: Conor J. R. Smithson, Isabel Gauthier

papers.title: Using scene proximity judgments to study food-specific recognition ability
papers.abstract: This investigation tests the existence of specialized visual mechanisms for prepared-food recognition by controlling for domain-general object recognition ('o') and scene-recognition abilities. The researchers developed outdoor scene-recognition tests to match the textural and chromatic complexity of food stimuli. Performance across food-matching and food-oddball tasks remained significantly correlated after regressing out variance from 'o' and scene-recognition, indicating a category-specific visual ability for food. Furthermore, this food-specific recognition variance was found to be a reliable predictor of food neophobia, suggesting that individual differences in the perceptual processing of food are uniquely tied to affective and behavioral responses to food items.
papers.authors: Conor J. R. Smithson, Yiming Lin, Isabel Gauthier

papers.title: Object recognition ability predicts episodic location memory, enhanced by meaningfulness
papers.abstract: The research explores whether the domain-general object recognition factor 'o' relates to episodic memory for spatial locations, which is extrinsic to object identity. Using a location-reproduction paradigm with stimuli varying in semantic meaningfulness, the study found that 'o' significantly predicts the precision of object-to-location binding. This relationship was found to be moderated by semantic content, with a stronger correlation observed for high-meaning objects. These results suggest that superior subordinate-level perceptual encoding, as captured by 'o', facilitates the integration of object identity with episodic context, challenging traditional boundaries between perceptual discrimination and associative memory processes.
papers.authors: Nurit Gronau, Conor J. R. Smithson, Isabel Gauthier

papers.title: Measuring object recognition ability: Reliability, validity, and the aggregate z-score approach
papers.abstract: This paper validates a brief, psychometrically sound measure of domain-general object recognition ability ('o') suitable for research contexts with time and sample constraints. The authors compared a latent variable modeling approach with an aggregate z-score approach using two diverse object recognition tests. Longitudinal data from 163 participants revealed that the aggregate 'o' measure is stable over time (test-retest r = 0.77) and highly representative of the latent factor (r = 0.93). The study demonstrates that this domain-general ability is highly reliable and distinct from general intelligence, perceptual speed, and low-level visual sensitivity, providing an efficient toolkit for future investigations into high-level visual cognition.
papers.authors: Conor J. R. Smithson, Jason K. Chow, Ting-Yun Chang, Isabel Gauthier

0279.name: Isabelle Boutet
0279.bio: Isabelle Boutet is an Associate Professor at the University of Ottawa and the Principal Investigator of the SCOPE Lab, where they investigate the cognitive and neural mechanisms of face perception across the human lifespan. Boutet’s research utilizes behavioral psychophysics, eye-tracking, and electroencephalography (EEG) to examine how individuals process socially relevant cues such as identity and emotional expression. A portion of their work focuses on cognitive aging, specifically how age-related sensory declines influence facial recognition and how familiarity affects visual scanning patterns. Additionally, Boutet analyzes the interpretation of emojis and non-verbal cues in digital contexts in the absence of face-to-face interaction.
0279.research_direction: Dr. Boutet has recently been investigating how emotional and social information captures visual attention and guides sociocognitive evaluations across different mediums. Their recent work explores the mechanisms of emotion-driven attentional capture, utilizing the emotion-induced blindness paradigm to test whether the disruptive effect of high-arousal images on top-down attention is modulated by affective value or bottom-up physical salience. In the domain of face perception, they are examining age-related shifts in emotion processing, combining behavioral recognition tasks with eye-tracking to determine whether emotion recognition deficits in older adults stem from altered early-stage visual sampling strategies or higher-order cognitive integration. Additionally, their research extends to digital emotional signaling, assessing how the use of positive and negative emojis in professional text communications influences social perceptions of sender competence and gender-specific appropriateness.

papers.title: Emojis at Work: The Effects of Emoji Use on Perceptions of Competence and Appropriateness
papers.abstract: This research investigates the sociocognitive impact of utilizing positive and negative emojis in text-based professional communications, specifically concerning the evaluation of sender competence and interactional appropriateness. Through simulated workplace instant messaging scenarios, the study demonstrates that the inclusion of negative emojis leads to a significant decrement in perceived competence and professional decorum across various message valences. While positive emojis can enhance competence ratings when accompanying neutral or positive text, they fail to offset the negative attributions associated with professional discord. The analysis also reveals gender-specific evaluative biases, where female recipients judged negative emotional signaling from female senders as particularly non-compliant with workplace display rules.
papers.authors: Erin L. Courtice, Megan Lawrence, Charles A. Collin, Isabelle Boutet

papers.title: Sex differences in the ability to recognise non-verbal displays of emotion: A meta-analysis
papers.abstract: This multilevel meta-analysis quantifies the magnitude and moderators of sex differences in humans' proficiency at identifying discrete emotional expressions across visual and auditory modalities. Synthesizing data from over 200 samples and 500 effect sizes, the study evaluates the robust 'female advantage' in emotion recognition. Quantitative analysis reveals a significant, though small-to-moderate, overall performance benefit for females. Crucially, the magnitude of this effect is moderated by variables including the specific emotional category (e.g., negative vs. positive valence), the sex of the individual portraying the emotion, the sensory modality of the stimulus, and the age of the participants, providing a comprehensive framework for understanding biological and social influences on affective processing.
papers.authors: Erin Leigh Courtice, Megan Lawrence, Collin Charles, Isabelle Boutet

papers.title: Perceptual Salience Does Not Influence Emotional Arousal’s Impairing Effects on Top-Down Attention
papers.abstract: The investigation explores the interplay between the emotional significance of visual stimuli and their physical salience using the emotion-induced blindness (EIB) paradigm. The study tests the hypothesis that the capacity of high-arousal images to capture attention and disrupt the processing of temporal targets is modulated by bottom-up perceptual features. Results indicate that while emotional arousal robustly impairs top-down attentional control, these interference effects are independent of the physical salience of the distractors. This suggests that the prioritization of emotional information in competitive visual processing is driven by affective value rather than physical contrast or luminosity, supporting a modular view of emotion-driven attentional capture.
papers.authors: Erin L. Courtice, Megan Lawrence, Collin Charles, Isabelle Boutet

papers.title: Emotion Processing in Late Adulthood: The Effect of Emotional Valence and Face Age on Behavior and Scanning Patterns
papers.abstract: This study employs a comprehensive experimental framework to examine age-related shifts in facial emotion processing, evaluating behavioral recognition accuracy alongside high-resolution eye-tracking data. Utilizing the FEAT stimulus set, which features both younger and older models, the investigation found that older adults consistently rate negative expressions as lower in negative valence and positive expressions as higher in arousal compared to younger cohorts. Despite a marked decline in recognition accuracy for negative emotional states in late adulthood, visual scanning patterns remained highly stable across generations, with both groups exhibiting a primary focus on the eye region. These findings suggest that the observed performance deficits in older adults are likely attributable to higher-order cognitive-affective integration rather than differences in early-stage visual sampling strategies.
papers.authors: Bozana Meinhardt-Injac, Nicole Altvater-Mackensen, Alexandra Mohs, Jean-Christophe Goulet-Pelletier, Isabelle Boutet

papers.title: Fostering Creativity Through Education: Lessons From the PISA 2022 Survey
papers.abstract: This paper provides a critical commentary on the PISA 2022 international assessment of creative thinking, which evaluated the generative and evaluative abilities of over 140,000 students across 60 countries. The authors analyze the methodological framework used to derive global creative thinking scores and identify significant limitations, particularly the tendency of aggregate scores to obscure individual profiles of creative strengths and weaknesses. By positioning the PISA results within broader cognitive space theories, the research explores how educational systems can better foster personally meaningful goals and self-expression. The findings suggest a need for more nuanced metrics that capture the diverse dimensions of creativity beyond standard divergent thinking tasks.
papers.authors: Jean-Christophe Goulet-Pelletier, Ophélie A. Collet, Paul T. Sowden, Sylvana M. Côté, Isabelle Boutet

0280.name: J. Anthony Movshon
0280.bio: J. Anthony Movshon is a visual neuroscientist and the founding Director of the Center for Neural Science at New York University. Movshon’s research investigates how neural circuits in the primate cerebral cortex encode and represent visual information, focusing on the mechanisms of motion and form perception. Using an approach that integrates single-unit electrophysiology, computational modeling, and psychophysics, Movshon applied neurometric functions to link neuronal firing rates to behavioral performance. Their current work explores the hierarchical processing of naturalistic textures and the developmental impact of abnormal early visual experience on cortical function.
0280.research_direction: Dr. Movshon's recent work explores how the primate ventral stream transforms simple visual features into sophisticated representations of complex forms, naturalistic textures, and object structure. In early visual cortex, their research investigates the computational mechanisms by which V1 and V2 neurons pool basic orientation and spatial frequency inputs to build selectivity for higher-order image statistics. They have recently been probing how these early cortical representations of naturalistic texture link to perceptual decision-making by recording from awake, behaving macaques during texture discrimination tasks. Further along the visual hierarchy, Dr. Movshon is studying area V4, utilizing image continua ranging from scrambled textures to natural photographs to understand how neural populations compute contrast-invariant codes and transition from local feature processing toward object-centric representations.

papers.title: Emergence of a contrast-invariant representation of naturalistic texture in macaque visual cortex
papers.abstract: The primate visual system must distinguish changes in stimulus dimensions like texture and contrast using population codes, as individual neurons are typically modulated by both. We investigated the neural representation of these dimensions by recording multiunit activity in macaque V1, V2, and V4 using texture images defined by naturalistic statistical structure (Portilla-Simoncelli model) and varying in contrast. We found that while contrast modulates activity across all three areas, sensitivity to naturalistic structure is absent in V1, present in V2, and most pronounced and heterogeneous in V4. Using linear population decoders, we demonstrated that V1 only represents contrast, while V2 and V4 represent both. Crucially, the V4 population provides a robustly contrast-invariant representation of texture, enabling the linear readout of naturalistic structure across varying contrast levels through a simple mechanism dependent on the diversity of neuronal tuning.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS)
papers.authors: Gerick M. Lee, Najib J. Majaj, Charlie L. Rodríguez-Deliz, Lynne Kiorpes, J. Anthony Movshon

papers.title: Responses of neurons in macaque V4 to object and texture images
papers.abstract: The transition from local feature processing to object-centric selectivity in the ventral stream is thought to first emerge in area V4, yet the specific computations remain unclear. We recorded from single units in awake macaque V4 using a stimulus continuum ranging from fully scrambled textures to original photographic images, constructed to preserve local statistics while destroying global shape and scene structure. Our results show that V4 populations reliably distinguish photographs from scrambled textures and exhibit a significantly larger dynamic range of responses for photographic images. We found that V4 sensitivity to photographic structure emerges slowly (~140 ms peak), suggesting the involvement of recurrent cortical mechanisms. Furthermore, V4 neural responses categorically separate photographic images from even slightly scrambled counterparts, a pattern well-predicted by the image-computable DISTS metric but not by simpler texture models.
papers.authors: Justin D. Lieber, Timothy D. Oleskiw, Laura Palmieri, Eero P. Simoncelli, J. Anthony Movshon

papers.title: Foundations of visual form selectivity for neurons in macaque V1 and V2
papers.abstract: We investigated the computational principles by which neurons in macaque V1 and V2 construct selectivity for complex visual forms from simpler inputs. Using a 'droplet' stimulus set—composed of sparse, randomly superimposed patches of localized contrast band-limited in orientation and scale—we recorded single-unit activity and fit the responses with a two-layer linear-nonlinear model. The model represents receptive fields as sparse combinations of subunits selective for orientation and spatial frequency. While V1 neurons exhibit tight tuning and simple subunit combinations, we identified a subpopulation in V2 that pools broadly across orientations to encode more complex features. The resulting 'afferent field' maps reveal that while these models explain a significant portion of variance for droplets and classical gratings, they are less effective at capturing selectivity for naturalistic textures, indicating that V2 employs additional nonlinearities to represent higher-order image statistics.
papers.authors: Timothy D. Oleskiw, Justin D. Lieber, Eero P. Simoncelli, J. Anthony Movshon

papers.title: Neuronal and Behavioral Responses to Naturalistic Texture Images in Macaque Monkeys
papers.abstract: The ability of primate visual area V2 to represent higher-order statistical structure in natural textures has been established in anesthetized subjects, but its direct link to perceptual behavior remains debated. We recorded single-unit activity in V1 and V2 of awake macaques performing a texture discrimination task along a continuum of naturalness. Neuronal sensitivity in V2 was significantly higher and more aligned with behavioral sensitivity than in V1, though individual neurons in both areas remained less sensitive than the animal's behavior. We observed that choice-correlated neural activity (choice probability) was inconsistent across monkeys and tasks, being present in only one of two monkeys for the texture task and untethered from neuronal sensitivity. These findings suggest that while V2 provides a more sophisticated representation of naturalistic structure than V1, the neural signals directly supporting texture perception and decision formation likely reside or are further refined in downstream extrastriate areas.
papers.authors: Corey M. Ziemba, Robbe L. T. Goris, Gabriel M. Stine, Richard K. Perez, Eero P. Simoncelli, J. Anthony Movshon

0281.name: Jack Gallant
0281.department: Department of Psychology and Helen Wills Neuroscience Institute
0281.bio: Jack Gallant is a cognitive neuroscientist who develops voxel-wise encoding models to characterize how the human brain processes naturalistic sensory and cognitive information. Using high-field functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and machine learning techniques, Gallant’s research maps the functional organization of the cerebral cortex during tasks such as movie watching and language comprehension. This work includes the creation of semantic atlases and the reconstruction of visual experiences from brain activity. Their current research focus involves refining these computational models to decode complex mental states and individual differences in brain representation.
0281.research_direction: Dr. Gallant's recent work explores how complex semantic and perceptual information is organized across the human cerebral cortex using fMRI and high-dimensional voxelwise encoding models during naturalistic tasks. They have recently been investigating the dynamic nature of these representations, testing how visual semantic tuning shifts when individuals transition from passive movie-watching to active virtual reality navigation. Their research also maps the distributed functional networks mediating ecologically valid spatial navigation, examines how abstract semantic relations are encoded independently of specific objects, and probes how personal experiences drive individual differences in conceptual processing during narrative listening. To better interpret these high-dimensional cortical maps, they are developing new machine learning techniques, such as sparse concept encoding models, to disentangle overlapping semantic features and accurately read out distinct neural tuning profiles from dense representations.

papers.title: Visual semantic tuning across the cortex shifts between tasks
papers.abstract: The investigation explores the dynamic modulation of visual semantic representations across the human cerebral cortex as individuals switch between naturalistic tasks with distinct behavioral requirements. Utilizing functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and high-dimensional voxelwise encoding models, the researchers compared cortical tuning profiles measured during passive movie-watching with those captured during an active virtual reality navigation task. Results demonstrate that task demands induce widespread and significant reconfigurations of semantic selectivity throughout the cortex, with the most pronounced shifts occurring in functional networks dedicated to navigation and spatial attention. Principal component analysis (PCA) of these tuning shifts indicates that active navigation systematically increases the neural representation of task-relevant object categories, such as vehicles and traffic signals. These findings suggest that the brain's semantic representational space is flexibly optimized to prioritize information critical for achieving specific behavioral goals.
papers.authors: Tianjiao Zhang, Jack L. Gallant

papers.title: Representations of semantic relations in the human cerebral cortex
papers.abstract: This research addresses the cortical organization of semantic relations (e.g., 'has-part', 'larger-than') and whether relational information is represented independently of the specific concepts being connected. Using fMRI, brain activity was recorded while six participants performed a relation-judgment task involving over one thousand relational pairs. Voxelwise encoding models were employed to map relational selectivity across the cerebral cortex. The results reveal that semantic relations are represented within the same distributed cortical regions that encode conceptual knowledge. Crucially, relational encoding was found to be independent of the specific concept pairs used in any instance, supporting an abstract representational framework. Voxel-level analysis indicates that most responsive sites exhibit preferential selectivity for single relations, suggesting that relational information is organized into functional maps similar to those of conceptual categories.
papers.authors: Catherine Chen, Xue L. Gong, Fatma Deniz, Daniel L. Klein, Jack L. Gallant

papers.title: A map of the cortical functional network mediating naturalistic navigation
papers.abstract: To delineate the human cortical architecture underlying naturalistic navigation, participants performed a complex taxi-driver task in an immersive virtual world while their brain activity was recorded using fMRI. High-dimensional voxelwise encoding models (VEM) were fitted to 28,134 perceptual, cognitive, and motor features to characterize the functional organization of the navigation system. The study identified a distributed network of 11 functionally distinct regions—comprising five prefrontal, three parietal, and three visual areas—that mediate active navigation. These regions are organized along functional gradients that map the transformation of low-level perceptual inputs through higher-order decision-making processes into task-specific motor outputs. This comprehensive map provides a unified account of the representational structure and functional properties of the brain's navigation circuitry under ecologically valid conditions.
papers.authors: Tianjiao Zhang, Emily X. Meschke, Jack L. Gallant

papers.title: Disentangling Superpositions: Interpretable Brain Encoding Model with Sparse Concept Atoms
papers.abstract: While dense feature spaces from artificial neural networks (ANNs) effectively predict brain responses, they suffer from 'superposition,' where multiple semantic features become entangled along correlated directions. This entanglement renders regression weights non-identifiable, precluding principled interpretation of voxel selectivity. This paper introduces the Sparse Concept Encoding Model (SCEM), which utilizes non-negative sparse dictionary learning to transform dense embeddings into a higher-dimensional, axis-aligned space of 'concept atoms.' By creating an interpretable semantic basis, SCEM enables direct readout of voxel tuning from model weights without compromising predictive accuracy. Applied to narrative-listening fMRI data, the SCEM successfully disentangled overlapping cortical representations for fundamental magnitudes—time, space, and number—while providing structured, interpretable maps of the distributed conceptual system.
papers.authors: Alicia Zeng, Jack L. Gallant

papers.title: Individual differences shape conceptual representation in the brain
papers.abstract: Traditional neuroimaging analyses often overlook person-specific variations in conceptual representation caused by unique experiences or disease. This study introduces a statistical framework to quantify and interpret individual differences in high-dimensional functional brain maps. Voxelwise encoding models were used to map conceptual representations in 24 participants listening to naturalistic narratives. The results reveal systematic and stable individual differences in cortical conceptual tuning despite exposure to identical stimuli. Inter-subject variability was found to be highest in cortical regions associated with social cognition, which are hypothesized to integrate sensory inputs with personal beliefs and subjective experiences. This framework provides a rigorous basis for a precision neuroscience approach to characterizing unique cognitive traits and monitoring cognitive disorders.
papers.authors: Matteo Visconti di Oleggio Castello, Tom Dupré la Tour, Jack L. Gallant

0282.name: Jacob Feldman
0282.department: Department of Psychology, Rutgers Center for Cognitive Science
0282.bio: Jacob Feldman is a Professor of Psychology and Cognitive Science at Rutgers University who specializes in the mathematical and computational modeling of human visual perception and concept learning. Feldman’s research investigates how the visual system utilizes principles of simplicity and Bayesian inference to organize image data and estimate the structure of the world. Their work addresses shape representation, perceptual grouping, and the Boolean complexity of human categorization. Currently, Feldman explores the probabilistic origins of compositional mental representations and information-theoretic frameworks for signal detection.
0282.research_direction: Dr. Feldman has recently been investigating how the human visual and cognitive systems extract structured representations from complex, continuous environments. Their recent work explores the computational mechanisms underlying biological motion perception, specifically examining how observers use dynamic shape, optic flow, and skeletal cues to categorize actions and infer emotions from point-light displays and naturalistic videos. Additionally, they are investigating the foundations of high-level cognition, using information-theoretic models to understand how humans form compositional mental representations and acquire probabilistically defined concepts based on their simplicity and compressive complexity. Finally, their research extends into applied perception and human-robot interaction, assessing how the specific geometry and path curvature of autonomous mobile robots influences human affective states during everyday encounters.

papers.title: Simplicity and complexity of probabilistically defined concepts
papers.abstract: Concept learning difficulty in humans is fundamentally linked to the complexity of the concepts being acquired. While this simplicity bias is well-documented in deterministic Boolean domains, this work investigates its manifestation in probabilistic concepts defined over continuous multi-dimensional feature spaces. Using a mixture-of-Gaussians framework, the study demonstrates that the spatial arrangement of mixture components significantly affects learning independently of statistical discriminability. The paper proposes an information-theoretic account centered on compressive complexity, where conceptually simple categories are characterized by their approximate reconstructibility from lower-dimensional feature projections, whereas complex concepts require high-fidelity representations of multi-feature combinations.
papers.authors: Jacob Feldman

papers.title: The role of dynamic shape cues in the recognition of emotion from naturalistic body motion
papers.abstract: Human observers possess a robust capacity to infer affective and emotional states from human body kinematics, even in the absence of facial or surface cues. This study evaluates the mechanisms of this inference by comparing classification performance across point-light displays (PLDs), stick figures, and motion-controlled stimuli. The results indicate that human emotion recognition relies heavily on skeletal representations of dynamic shape. Furthermore, the presence of explicit skeletal connectivity significantly enhances the reliability of emotion judgments, suggesting that the visual system processes biological motion through a medial-axis-based representational framework that facilitates the interpretation of non-rigid transformations.
papers.authors: Erika Ikeda, Nathan Destler, Jacob Feldman

papers.title: Effects of Mobile Robot Passing-Motion Path Curvature on Human Affective States in a Hallway Environment
papers.abstract: To ensure social acceptance of autonomous mobile robots (AMRs), navigation algorithms must generate trajectories that are perceived as comfortable by humans. This research examines how the curvature of an AMR’s path, modeled using Bézier curves, impacts human affective responses (pleasure and arousal) during hallway encounters. Through systematic manipulation of path geometry, the study reveals a nonlinear relationship between curvature and emotional state. Participants exhibited the most positive responses to paths with moderate curvature, while extremely straight or sharply curved trajectories were associated with increased physiological arousal and decreased subjective pleasure.
papers.authors: Benjamin Greenberg, Uriel González-Bravo, Jingang Yi, Jacob Feldman

papers.title: Human Action Classification from Naturalistic Videos
papers.abstract: This research explores the computational substrates underlying human action categorization in complex naturalistic scenes. By analyzing how human observers map optic flow and high-dimensional motion patterns to discrete action labels, the study identifies critical motion-based features used in classification. The findings connect low-level motion descriptors to mid-level skeletal shape models, demonstrating that action perception is subserved by a structured representational architecture that organizes dynamic visual input into biologically plausible kinematic categories.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the 47th Annual Meeting of the Cognitive Science Society
papers.authors: Uriel Gonzalez-Bravo, Jacob Feldman

papers.title: Probabilistic origins of compositional mental representations
papers.abstract: Mental representation typically involves the composition of complex concepts from discrete, simpler features, yet the ecological validity of this discrete architecture in a continuous probabilistic world remains unclear. This article develops an information-theoretic framework to quantify the fidelity and efficiency of featural representations relative to multidimensional environmental probability models. Compositionality is framed as an optimal solution that balances fidelity, simplicity, and robustness. The analysis demonstrates that the efficacy of compositional forms is dependent on the directional projection of features within the underlying probability space, providing a formal justification for the emergence of compositional structure in human cognition.
papers.authors: Jacob Feldman

0283.name: James Bisley
0283.bio: James Bisley is a Professor at UCLA whose research explores the neural mechanisms of visual attention, perception, and short-term memory. Their work focuses on the lateral intraparietal area (LIP) and its role as a priority map that integrates bottom-up sensory salience with top-down behavioral goals to guide eye movements. Utilizing single-unit electrophysiology, microstimulation, and reversible inactivation in animal models, Bisley’s laboratory investigates how the brain maintains spatial stability across saccades and how motion information is encoded. Beyond basic neuroscience, Bisley also contributes to translational research involving haptic feedback systems for robotic surgery and prosthetic applications.
0283.research_direction: Dr. Bisley has recently been investigating the neural mechanisms of oculomotor control alongside the development of bio-inspired haptics for telerobotic systems. In the visual domain, their recent work explores how the primate brain maintains perceptual stability across eye movements, using single-unit recordings and psychophysics to probe saccadic suppression, corollary discharge, and how the lateral intraparietal (LIP) area differentiates between voluntary saccades and reflexive gaze shifts. Beyond vision, their research extends into artificial tactile systems, combining high-resolution piezoresistive sensors with machine learning to extract complex spatiotemporal features and replicate human touch. Additionally, they are exploring how to integrate bio-inspired models of cutaneous mechanoreceptors into teleoperated surgical and ultrasound robots to restore real-time kinesthetic feedback during remote medical procedures.

papers.title: A roadmap and case study of haptic-enabled tele-ultrasound systems: From concept to clinical feasibility
papers.abstract: Telerobotic ultrasound platforms are increasingly explored to facilitate remote medical diagnostics in underserved areas, yet the absence of kinesthetic feedback remains a significant barrier to diagnostic efficacy. This research presents a comprehensive software and hardware framework utilizing a KUKA LBR iiwa robotic manipulator for haptic-enabled tele-ultrasound. The system implements a low-level control interface that achieves a real-time responsiveness with an average end-to-end latency of 3.6 ms. A bio-inspired haptic feedback model, which simulates the population responses of cutaneous mechanoreceptors, was integrated to provide surgeons with meaningful vibration and force cues. Empirical evaluations involving expert clinicians demonstrated that this bio-inspired feedback loop significantly enhanced the localization of anatomical structures within tissue phantoms compared to standard visual-only control.
papers.authors: Ouyang Qiangqiang, Juan Wu, Songping Sun, Saeid Nahavandi, James Bisley

papers.title: The Relationship Between Saccadic Suppression and Perceptual Stability
papers.abstract: The primate visual system maintains a stable perception of space despite the frequent and rapid shifts in retinal input caused by saccadic eye movements. While predictive remapping of receptive fields is a leading candidate for maintaining transsaccadic stability, the mechanism of saccadic suppression—the selective reduction in visual sensitivity—is also integral to the process. This study utilizes single-unit recordings and psychophysical paradigms to investigate how visual signals are integrated with non-visual oculomotor information (corollary discharge) during saccades. The results suggest that the brain actively prevents the decoding of self-generated visual motion by combining afferent signals with internal motor plans, effectively neutralizing the disruptive effects of global retinal shifts and facilitating a continuous, stable percept of the environment.
papers.authors: Koorosh Mirpour, James Bisley

papers.title: A Teleoperated Robotic System with Haptic Feedback for Soft Tissue Incision
papers.abstract: Minimally invasive robotic surgery often lacks haptic feedback, forcing surgeons to rely exclusively on visual cues, which can impair performance during complex procedures like soft tissue incisions. This study describes the design and implementation of a teleoperated system that incorporates a bio-inspired haptic algorithm modeling the firing patterns of cutaneous mechanoreceptors. The control architecture utilizes a master-slave hybrid scheme with a weighted quadratic program to compute inverse kinematics, allowing the system to maintain precision over uneven and delicate surfaces. In trials using phantom tissues, the integration of simulated cutaneous afferent activity improved the localization of underlying structures and the control of incision depth, demonstrating the utility of bio-inspired feedback in enhancing surgical accuracy.
papers.venue: Journal of Control, Automation and Electrical Systems
papers.authors: Facundo Garcia-Cardenas, Joao Fabian, Oscar E. Ramos, Ruth Canahuire, James Bisley

papers.title: Machine learning-coupled tactile recognition with high spatiotemporal resolution based on cross-striped nanocarbon piezoresistive sensor array
papers.abstract: Developing artificial tactile systems with human-like sensitivity and spatiotemporal resolution is essential for the next generation of robotic and prosthetic effectors. This study presents a high-density tactile sensor array fabricated using a cross-striped nanocarbon piezoresistive architecture. The sensor exhibits excellent sensitivity and stability across dynamic range constraints. A deep learning framework was trained on the high-dimensional spatiotemporal data generated by the array to perform complex feature extraction. The integrated system achieved superior performance in identifying subtle surface textures and complex 3D shapes. These findings suggest that the synergy of nanostructured sensing materials and advanced machine learning models can effectively replicate the sophisticated tactile processing found in biological systems.
papers.authors: Qiangqiang Ouyang, Chuanjie Yao, Houhua Chen, Liping Song, Tao Zhang, Dapeng Chen, Lidong Yang, Mojun Chen, Hui-jiuan Chen, Zhenwei Peng, James Bisley

papers.title: The representation of voluntary and reflexive fast eye movements in the macaque lateral intraparietal area (LIP)
papers.abstract: The lateral intraparietal area (LIP) is widely considered a priority map that integrates sensory and cognitive signals to guide goal-directed actions, yet its involvement in reflexive motor control remains controversial. This study investigates whether LIP neurons distinguish between voluntary saccades and reflexive fast eye movements, such as the fast phases of optokinetic nystagmus (OKN). By recording single-neuron activity in macaques, the researchers found that robust perisaccadic responses typical of voluntary eye movements were significantly attenuated or absent during reflexive fast phases. Conversely, LIP activity during OKN slow phases was found to reliably encode gaze position and stimulus motion direction through a generalized linear model (GLM). These results indicate that LIP is specialized for goal-directed sensorimotor integration rather than acting as a general oculomotor controller.
papers.authors: Koorosh Mirpour, James Bisley

0284.name: James Gordon
0284.institution: Hunter College, City University of New York
0284.main_research_area: Visual neuroscience of color and form
0284.bio: James Gordon is a Professor Emeritus in the Department of Psychology at Hunter College, where they investigate the neural mechanisms underlying the processing of color and form. Gordon’s research utilizes a combination of psychophysical techniques, such as hue scaling and chromatic adaptation, alongside physiological measures including visual evoked potentials (VEP) to map the development of parallel visual pathways from infancy to adulthood. Gordon has contributed to the creation of nonlinear models for human luminance contrast and the study of color-brightness interactions in the primary visual cortex. Their current work focuses on identifying specific visual processing deficits in pathologies such as schizophrenia, glaucoma, and autism to facilitate clinical diagnosis and potential intervention strategies.
0284.research_direction: Dr. Gordon has recently been investigating the early cortical mechanisms underlying human color and spatial vision. Their recent work explores how the primary visual cortex processes color not through isolated pathways, but by integrating cardinal chromatic and luminance signals with spatial frequency and form information. To probe these higher-order mechanisms, they utilize psychophysical scaling and chromatic visual evoked potentials (cVEPs) to examine phenomena such as the nonlinear effects of adjacent luminance contrast on the hue and saturation of short-wavelength (S-cone) patterns. Additionally, they have been researching the neurophysiological bases of the spatial contrast sensitivity function, employing tablet-based psychophysics and computational receptive field modeling to delineate the distinct contributions of magnocellular and parvocellular pathways across different spatial and temporal frequencies.

papers.title: Cortical processing of color: Chromatic visual evoked potentials
papers.abstract: This review analyzes human cortical color representation via chromatic visual evoked potentials (cVEPs), demonstrating that cortical color processing is primarily mediated by spatially-tuned neurons. Contrary to the strict segregation of cardinal color and luminance signals characteristic of the thalamic input (L-M and S pathways), cortical evoked responses indicate that the human visual cortex integrates these signals through higher-order color mechanisms. These mechanisms are responsive to a population-wide distribution of all combinations of cardinal directions, specifically within the primary visual cortex (V1). The findings challenge classical opponent-color theory by showing that color computation is intrinsically combined with spatial frequency and form processing, rather than being handled by isolated pathways. The study utilizes perceptual scaling of color saturation and high-density cVEP recordings to identify the relative contributions of single-opponent and double-opponent neuronal populations to pattern-based color perception.
papers.authors: Robert Shapley, Valerie Nunez, James Gordon

papers.title: Low luminance contrast’s effect on the color appearance of S-cone patterns
papers.abstract: This investigation examines the robust nonlinear interaction between low-level luminance contrast and color appearance for stimuli restricted to S-cone modulation. Utilizing equiluminant checkerboard patterns where short-wavelength-sensitive (S) cones are selectively activated, the study demonstrates that +S (purple-appearing) and -S (yellow-appearing) checks undergo significant hue and saturation shifts depending on the luminance of adjacent gray checks. Specifically, +S checks appear as highly desaturated lavender when surrounded by darker gray regions but shift toward purple when the surround is slightly brighter. Psychophysical paired comparisons and occipital visual evoked potentials (VEPs) confirm that these appearances are driven by early cortical nonlinearities. The results provide electrophysiological evidence that color perception is not derived from isolated chromatic pathways but from the integration of color and luminance contrast signals in the human posterior cortex.
papers.authors: Robert Shapley, Valerie Nunez, James Gordon

papers.title: The spatial contrast sensitivity function and its neurophysiological bases
papers.abstract: Evaluating contrast sensitivity across spatial frequencies (CSF) is essential for diagnosing the functional integrity of early visual pathways. In this investigation, spatial CSFs were acquired using a custom iPad-based platform and modeled using a difference of Gaussians (DoG) receptive field formulation to elucidate underlying neurophysiological mechanisms. Test-retest reliability across and within sessions was established in a cohort of 22 adult observers tested at five spatial frequencies spanning 0.41 to 13 cycles/degree under two temporal presentation durations (33 ms and 500 ms). The resulting CSF profile transitioned between bandpass and lowpass configurations depending on stimulus presentation duration. Electrophysiological and psychophysical cross-comparisons with macaque and human single-cell recordings indicate that contrast sensitivity above 1.5 cycles/degree—regardless of temporal duration—is governed by sustained mechanisms corresponding to parvocellular projections into primary visual cortex (V1). In contrast, sensitivity at the lowest tested spatial frequency (0.41 cycles/degree) is predominantly mediated by transient channels associated with magnocellular input to V1. Furthermore, DoG model fits confirm that the high-spatial-frequency attenuation of the CSF mirrors the receptive field center profile of the smallest parvocellular units, supporting the viability of consumer tablet devices for robust clinical psychophysics.
papers.authors: Vance Zemon, Pamela D. Butler, Michael E. Legatt, James Gordon

0285.name: James Herman
0285.bio: Herman investigates how primate visual perception and cognitive functions such as attention and decision-making emerge from coordinated activity between the cerebral cortex and subcortical regions including the superior colliculus and basal ganglia. Their research characterizes the neural mechanisms of learning-driven behavioral changes using a combination of high-density extracellular electrophysiology, psychophysics, and targeted neuronal perturbations. Recently, Herman’s work has integrated computational modeling, including recurrent vision transformers, to analyze the relationship between biological and artificial intelligence in how populations of neurons govern specific cognitive tasks.
0285.research_direction: Dr. Herman has recently been investigating the biological and computational mechanisms that drive visual attention and spatial prioritization. Their recent work explores how the macaque superior colliculus integrates distinct signals for physical salience, reward value, and goal-directed attention during covert and overt orienting tasks. Alongside neural recordings, they have been developing biologically inspired artificial intelligence models—specifically utilizing Recurrent Vision Transformers, working memory modules, and reinforcement learning—to simulate top-down attentional control and biased competition. Through these parallel approaches, they are examining how reward feedback and recurrent processing organize spatial attention in both primate sensorimotor circuits and artificial vision systems.

papers.title: Independent encoding of salience, value, and attention in primate superior colliculus
papers.abstract: The study investigates how the primate superior colliculus (SC) integrates signals of physical salience, reward value, and goal-directed attention. While some theories suggest the SC acts as a unified priority map, neural recordings from macaques performing a spatially cued orientation-change detection task alongside a saccade task revealed that these three factors exert independent influences. Single-neuron analysis and population-level linear classifiers demonstrated that representations of salience, reward, and attention do not generalize across categories, indicating a modular rather than a unified encoding scheme. These findings support a model where the SC flexibly routes information to guide distinct overt orienting and covert attentional behaviors based on behavioral context.
papers.authors: Matthew Murawski, James Herman

papers.title: A recurrent vision transformer shows signatures of primate visual attention
papers.abstract: This research introduces a Recurrent Vision Transformer (Recurrent ViT) that incorporates a capacity-limited spatial memory module and recurrent feedback to simulate top-down attentional control in primates. Unlike standard feedforward transformers, this architecture allows stored information and current visual inputs to jointly determine attention allocation. Trained via reinforcement learning on a cued orientation-change detection task, the model replicates key biological signatures of attention, including heightened detection accuracy and decreased reaction times for validly cued stimuli. Analysis of self-attention maps shows dynamic spatial prioritization and reactivation of cues before expected changes, while internal weight perturbations produce performance shifts comparable to those observed in the macaque frontal eye fields and superior colliculus.
papers.authors: Jonathan Morgan, Badr Albanna, James P. Herman

papers.title: A Neural Network Model of Visual Attention Integrating Biased Competition and Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: The authors present a neural network model of visual attention (NNMVA) that bridges the gap between AI self-attention and biological mechanisms of biased competition. The model utilizes self-attention from Vision Transformers (ViTs) to simulate competition between representations, coupled with Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) for working memory and an actor-critic reinforcement learning framework. By training the system solely on reward feedback during a cued orientation-change detection task, the model develops behavioral patterns typical of non-human primates, such as reaction time benefits and accuracy improvements for attended locations. The study demonstrates that reward-driven learning signals can sufficiently organize top-down feedback to guide attentional prioritization in a manner consistent with subcortical and cortical circuits.
papers.authors: Jonathan Mark Morgan, Badr Albanna, James P Herman

0286.name: James Hillis
0286.bio: James Hillis is a research scientist at Meta’s Reality Labs, where they apply vision science to the design of augmented and virtual reality systems. Hillis’s research includes multisensory integration, 3D shape perception via disparity and texture cues, and the development of computational models for perceptual quality metrics. Previously, Hillis served as an assistant professor at the University of Glasgow and conducted postdoctoral research at the University of Pennsylvania. They use psychophysical methods and computational modeling of human perception to study display performance and human-computer interaction in immersive environments.
0286.research_direction: Dr. Hillis has recently been exploring the perceptual and computational dynamics of vision within immersive augmented and virtual reality environments. Their recent work investigates how real-world environmental factors, such as spatial clutter, background luminance, and depth, impact the visibility of superimposed AR imagery by utilizing natural scene statistics derived from egocentric video to determine sensory requirements for display optimization. Alongside this applied research, they are studying the mechanisms of human eye movements during naturalistic 3D visual search. By comparing human gaze and fixation sequences collected in VR against resource-rational reinforcement learning models, Dr. Hillis is examining how biological and cognitive constraints drive the active allocation of visual attention in complex, dynamic scenes.

papers.title: Environment to Bits: What do AR Systems Need to Know About the Environment to Ensure High Quality Display Experience?
papers.abstract: Unlike conventional emissive displays on mobile devices that adjust brightness based strictly on ambient illuminance, optical see-through augmented reality displays superimpose virtual imagery directly onto physical environments, making visual target detection and legibility highly dependent on local background luminance, spatial clutter, depth structure, and relative motion. Using egocentric video captured during everyday activities, this work quantifies natural environment image statistics to evaluate background variability and determine the minimal environmental sensing required for perceptual optimization. The findings outline architectural considerations for sensor integration and display pipelines, emphasizing the need for synchronized environmental capture, real-time rendering adjustment, and psychophysical evaluation to ensure robust display visibility.
papers.venue: SID Symposium Digest of Technical Papers
papers.authors: James Hillis, Lili Zhang, Takahiro Doi, Xueyan Niu, Charlie S. Burlingham, Thomas E. Yerxa, Jasmine Jan, Romain Bachy, Kavitha Ratnam

papers.title: A Resource-Rational Account of Human Eye Movements During Immersive Visual Search
papers.abstract: Naturalistic visual search requires observers to sample visual information under stringent cognitive and biological constraints. This study formalizes visual search in complex 3D environments as a problem of bounded optimal information gathering, cast as a meta-level Markov decision process (meta-MDP) defined over latent visual representations extracted by a deep convolutional neural network. Reinforcement learning agents optimized to solve this meta-MDP converge toward an ideal observer policy previously formalized only for highly simplified visual arrays. When evaluated against human gaze and fixation sequences collected during immersive visual search tasks in virtual reality (VR), the resource-rational model exhibits close qualitative and quantitative alignment with human fixation behavior, demonstrating that naturalistic scanpaths reflect the rational allocation of limited internal computational resources.
papers.venue: Open Mind: Discoveries in Cognitive Science
papers.authors: Angela Radulescu, Bas van Opheusden, Frederick Callaway, Thomas L. Griffiths, James M. Hillis

0287.name: James J. DiCarlo
0287.department: Department of Brain and Cognitive Sciences
0287.main_research_area: visual object recognition and computational neuroscience
0287.bio: James J. DiCarlo is the Peter de Florez Professor of Neuroscience at MIT and an Investigator at the McGovern Institute for Brain Research. DiCarlo’s research focuses on reverse-engineering the neural mechanisms of human visual intelligence, specifically how the primate ventral visual stream enables object recognition. Through the integration of large-scale neurophysiology, machine learning, and neural perturbation, their lab develops neurally mechanistic computational models to explain how the brain transforms retinal images into invariant representations. DiCarlo also serves as the Director of the MIT Quest for Intelligence, coordinating interdisciplinary work at the intersection of natural and artificial intelligence.
0287.research_direction: Dr. DiCarlo has recently been investigating how image-computable artificial neural network models of the primate ventral visual stream can be leveraged to precisely predict and manipulate both neural activity and high-level visual perception. Their recent work explores using these sensory-computable models to design subtle, targeted visual stimuli that noninvasively drive specific population-level responses in the macaque inferior temporal cortex and intentionally shift human category percepts. Additionally, they are extending topographic deep neural networks to simulate the perceptual effects of direct causal interventions, such as microstimulation and optogenetic suppression, to evaluate mechanistic alignment with biological vision. Furthermore, their research probes the foundational optimization objectives of the visual system by testing whether models trained to estimate 3D spatial properties align with ventral stream representations as effectively as traditional object categorization models.

papers.title: Noninvasive precision modulation of high-level neural population activity via natural vision perturbations
papers.abstract: This study demonstrates that sensory-computable models of the primate ventral stream have reached a level of accuracy sufficient to drive predetermined activity patterns in high-level neural populations noninvasively.
