By applying perceptually subtle, model-guided perturbations to natural visual feeds, the researchers successfully modulated neural population activity in the macaque inferior temporal (IT) cortex. The experimental results showed a high quantitative alignment between the predicted neural effects and biological recordings, including the ability to inject experimenter-specified population patterns. These findings suggest that artificial neural network (ANN) models can now be used to design high-resolution, vision-based neural interventions that are potentially imperceptible to the subject.
papers.authors: Guy Gaziv, Sarah Goulding, Ani Ayvazian-Hancock, Yoon Bai, James J. DiCarlo

papers.title: Vision CNNs trained to estimate spatial latents learned similar ventral-stream-aligned representations
papers.abstract: Traditional modeling of the primate ventral stream has focused on object categorization as the primary optimization objective. This research explores the alternative hypothesis that the ventral stream may be optimized for estimating 3D spatial latents, such as object pose and position. Using synthetic datasets from a 3D graphics engine, the authors trained convolutional neural networks (CNNs) on various combinations of spatial and categorical tasks. They found that models optimized for only a few spatial latents achieved neural alignment scores with the primate ventral stream comparable to models trained on hundreds of object categories. The results indicate that internal representations for spatial estimation and categorization are highly similar, suggesting that the ventral stream's functional role may encompass a broader range of latent estimation tasks beyond simple recognition.
papers.authors: Yudi Xie, Weichen Huang, Esther Alter, Jeremy Schwartz, Joshua B. Tenenbaum, James J. DiCarlo

papers.title: The Quest for an Integrated Set of Neural Mechanisms Underlying Object Recognition in Primates
papers.abstract: This review provides a comprehensive perspective on the current state of SMART (sensory computable, mechanistic, anatomically referenced, and testable) models of the primate ventral visual stream. The authors evaluate how leading artificial neural network (ANN) models align with biological brain activity and behavioral recognition patterns. The article discusses the transition from conceptual models to image-computable systems that can predict image-by-image neural responses in the inferior temporal (IT) cortex. It identifies key frontiers in the field, including the need for better integration of recurrent processing, topographic constraints, and the development of models that capture the full variance of primate visual intelligence.
papers.authors: Kohitij Kar, James J. DiCarlo

papers.title: Do Topographic Deep ANN Models of the Primate Ventral Stream Predict the Perceptual Effects of Direct IT Cortical Interventions?
papers.abstract: Current topographic deep artificial neural network (TDANN) models have demonstrated the ability to capture the functional organization and response patterns of the primate ventral stream. This work extends these models by incorporating perturbation modules that simulate causal interventions such as microstimulation, optogenetic suppression, and muscimol inactivation. By evaluating these models against nine established benchmarks from the IT perturbation literature, the researchers found that TDANNs qualitatively predict the behavioral effects of neural interventions. However, the models currently exhibit quantitative misalignments, suggesting that while they are useful guides for causal hypothesis generation, further refinements in model architecture and topographic constraints are required for precise predictive accuracy.
papers.authors: Martin Schrimpf, Paul McGrath, Eshed Margalit, James J. DiCarlo

papers.title: Strong and Precise Modulation of Human Percepts via Robustified ANNs
papers.abstract: While standard artificial neural networks (ANNs) are sensitive to adversarial perturbations that do not affect human perception, this study demonstrates that robustified ANNs can guide the construction of low-norm image perturbations that strongly and precisely alter human category percepts. The researchers show that these robust models discover 'wormholes' in image space—subtle perturbations that shift a subject's perceptual state from one category to another semantically distinct category. By testing these perturbations on human observers, they found that contemporary ANN models of biological vision are now accurate enough to guide effective interventions in human perceptual states, bridging the gap between artificial and biological robustness.
papers.venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS) 36
papers.authors: Guy Gaziv, Michael J. Lee, James J. DiCarlo

0288.name: James W. Tanaka
0288.bio: James W. Tanaka is a Professor of Psychology at the University of Victoria and a Fellow of the Royal Society of Canada who investigates the cognitive and neural mechanisms underlying face and object recognition. Tanaka’s research examines the 'expertise hypothesis,' which posits that face-like holistic processing is a byproduct of perceptual experience, a concept demonstrated through the part-whole effect paradigm. This work extends to clinical and applied domains, including the development of digital interventions for children with autism and studies on the 'other-race' effect in social perception. Currently, their lab utilizes EEG, eye-tracking, and psychological embedding software like PsiZ to model how individuals represent complex visual categories and to track the temporal dynamics of face familiarity.
0288.research_direction: Dr. Tanaka has recently been investigating the perceptual mechanisms of person perception alongside distinct, applied applications of machine learning in clinical informatics. Their recent work explores early visual processing and holistic integration, using whole-person composite paradigms and rapid saccadic choice tasks with backward masking to determine whether face and body recognition relies on the initial feedforward sweep or late-stage decisional processes. In a separate applied domain, they are also investigating how electronic health records and longitudinal nursing assessments can be leveraged to improve clinical situational awareness. Specifically, Dr. Tanaka is exploring data engineering protocols and supervised machine learning frameworks to predict hospital-acquired infections and support proactive patient safety interventions.

papers.title: Attending to faces and bodies in person perception
papers.abstract: This study employs a whole-person composite paradigm to investigate the cognitive mechanisms underlying the integration of facial and bodily information in identity perception. Observers performed a sequential matching task using aligned or misaligned face-body composites, where they were cued to attend to one component while ignoring the other. Results demonstrated a robust congruency effect: identity judgments for the cued target were systematically biased by the identity of the task-irrelevant distractor. Critically, this interference effect persisted regardless of the spatial alignment between the face and body, providing empirical evidence that facial and bodily cues are integrated at a late-stage decisional level rather than during early perceptual holistic encoding. The findings suggest that person perception is an obligatory, additive process where it is difficult to isolate information from individual body parts.
papers.authors: Anna K. Lawrance, Nicholas J. Argument, Katelyn Forner, Eric Y. Mah, James W. Tanaka

papers.title: A Machine Learning Approach to Predict Health Care-Acquired Urinary Tract Infections From Electronic Nursing Documentation
papers.abstract: This research implements a supervised machine learning (SML) framework to enhance clinical situational awareness by predicting healthcare-acquired urinary tract infections (HAUTI) from longitudinal nursing records. The study evaluated multiple algorithmic architectures, including Logistic Regression, Random Forest, and Support Vector Machines, finding that the eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) model achieved the highest predictive performance. Analysis of feature importance revealed that nursing assessment variables—specifically metrics related to skin integrity, mobility, and neurological status—served as critical indicators for HAUTI risk. The results demonstrate the viability of using automated documentation analysis as a predictive tool to support nursing vigilance and improve patient safety outcomes in acute care settings.
papers.authors: Yaser Alqarrain, Abdul Roudsari, Karen L. Courtney, James W. Tanaka

papers.title: Fast saccades to faces during the feedforward sweep
papers.abstract: The current study utilizes a saccadic choice task combined with a backward-masking paradigm to test the hypothesis that face detection occurs during the initial feedforward sweep of visual processing. By using masks designed to selectively disrupt recurrent feedback signals while maintaining feedforward activation, the researchers measured minimum saccadic reaction times (SRT) for face and house categorization. The experiments revealed that ultra-fast, accurate saccades toward face targets were reliably elicited within a 110-160 ms post-stimulus interval, even under masking conditions that significantly diminished perceptual awareness. These findings indicate that the human visual system can initiate category-selective motor responses based on coarse, low-spatial frequency information processed during the first feedforward wave, prior to the integration of fine details through feedback mechanisms.
papers.authors: Alison Campbell, James W. Tanaka

papers.title: Improving Situation Awareness to Advance Patient Outcomes: A Systematic Literature Review
papers.abstract: A systematic evaluation of the evidence surrounding digital interventions designed to augment nursing situational awareness (SA) and its subsequent impact on hospital-acquired adverse events. The review synthesizes findings from studies utilizing electronic health record (EHR) dashboards and real-time monitoring systems at the point of care. Results indicate that while technological tools can improve level-1 (perception) and level-2 (comprehension) awareness, there remains a significant lack of standardized metrics and theoretical grounding for assessing level-3 awareness (projection of future states). The analysis concludes that future development must focus on theory-driven interface designs that align with clinical workflows to foster proactive rather than reactive clinical decision-making.
papers.authors: Yaser Alqarrain, Abdul Roudsari, Karen L. Courtney, James W. Tanaka

papers.title: Data Preparation for Supervised Learning: Improving Nursing Situation Awareness to Reduce Healthcare-Acquired Urinary Tract Infection
papers.abstract: This methodological paper details the data engineering protocols required to prepare heterogeneous nursing assessment datasets for training supervised machine learning models. Using the Cross-Industry Standard Process for Data Mining (CRISP-DM) framework, the study addresses common challenges in clinical informatics, specifically the management of missing data in electronic health records (EHR). The authors describe techniques for feature extraction and normalization of longitudinal nursing notes to predict healthcare-acquired urinary tract infections (HAUTI). The findings underscore that robust data preprocessing and the selection of context-relevant nursing variables are essential prerequisites for achieving reliable predictive accuracy in artificial intelligence applications for healthcare.
papers.venue: Studies in Health Technology and Informatics
papers.authors: Yaser Alqarrain, Abdul Roudsari, Karen L. Courtney, James W. Tanaka

0289.name: Jan R. Wiersema
0289.department: Department of Experimental Clinical and Health Psychology
0289.bio: Jan R. Wiersema is a professor at Ghent University whose research focuses on the neurocognitive underpinnings of developmental conditions such as autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and ADHD. Wiersema utilizes neurophysiological methodologies, including high-density EEG, frequency tagging, and fMRI, to investigate social perception, self-referential processing, and the mechanisms of self-other distinction. Their work explores how the visual and motor cortices represent complex social interactions and observed actions within visual scenes. Through leadership of the EXPLORA research group, Wiersema aims to identify neural biomarkers of social-cognitive challenges and characterize the dimensions of cognitive effort and uncertainty in clinical populations.
0289.research_direction: Dr. Wiersema has recently been investigating the cognitive, neural, and social mechanisms underlying autism and sub-clinical autistic traits. Their recent work explores self-referential processing across development, using EEG and event-related potentials to track the early sensory and later cognitive stages of responding to self-relevant stimuli, such as hearing one's own name or viewing self-associated shapes. In the visual domain, they are examining how non-social autism traits influence local-global spatial integration during the perception of biological motion using spatially and temporally scrambled point-light displays. Additionally, Dr. Wiersema is probing the interpersonal aspects of autism, testing whether perspective-taking relies on basic relational framing and investigating the "double empathy problem" to understand how communication dynamics are shaped by the neurological match between interaction partners.

papers.title: (Deictic) relational responding is not related to autism traits in the general population
papers.abstract: Based on Relational Frame Theory (RFT), deictic relational responding is hypothesized to be the functional core of perspective-taking and Theory of Mind (ToM), with autism-related social difficulties potentially stemming from deficits in these relational repertoires. This study evaluated the proposed association between deictic relating and autism traits in two experiments (N=134 and N=120) using a non-clinical sample. Participants' relational abilities were assessed using the Relational Ability Index (RAI), which measures simple, reversed, and double reversed deictic relations. Results demonstrated no significant correlation between Autism Spectrum Quotient (AQ) scores and performance on deictic relating or other RAI subscales. These findings challenge the RFT assumption that sub-clinical autism traits are linked to altered deictic relational responding, suggesting a need to reassess the role of basic relational operants in social-cognitive phenotypes.
papers.authors: Maura Nevejans, Jamie Cummins, Jan De Houwer, Emiel Cracco, Roeljan Wiersema

papers.title: Adults with autism's communication preferences with others with and without autism: A mixed-methods study
papers.abstract: This study examined the 'double empathy problem' by investigating whether autistic adults experience more effective social interaction within same-neurotype dyads versus cross-neurotype dyads. Using a mixed-methods design, 407 autistic adults completed a questionnaire evaluating 14 statements and six qualitative open-ended items concerning their communicative experiences. Quantitative analysis revealed that participants rated interactions with other autistic individuals as significantly easier and more effective across nearly all assessed dimensions, excluding body language. Qualitative themes identified a shared sense of mutual understanding, reduced social judgment, and a decreased requirement for social camouflaging or masking. These results support the theory that social interaction challenges in autism are context-dependent and influenced by the neurological match between partners rather than being purely inherent to the autistic individual.
papers.authors: Hannah De Laet, Annabel Nijhof, Roeljan Wiersema

papers.title: Evidence that non-social autism traits in the general population are correlated with spatial processing of biological motion
papers.abstract: Theoretical models of biological motion (BM) perception in autism suggest that social difficulties may arise from atypical processing of movement kinematics. This preregistered study (N=193) utilized spatial and temporal scrambling of point-light displays to investigate whether autism traits in a neurotypical population are associated with specific BM processing deficits. While no correlation was observed between total Autism Spectrum Quotient (AQ) scores and temporal scrambling effects, a significant correlation emerged between the 'attention to detail' subscale and the impact of spatial scrambling. This suggests that non-social autism traits are selectively linked to differences in local-global spatial integration required for the perception of global BM patterns, rather than to a general deficit in temporal motion binding.
papers.authors: Emiel Cracco, Danna Oomen, Jan R. Wiersema

papers.title: Intact Neural Responding to Hearing One's Own Name in Children with Autism
papers.abstract: Diminished behavioral responsiveness to the own name is a clinical hallmark of autism, yet its neurophysiological basis is poorly understood. This study recorded event-related potentials (ERPs) in children with autism (n=34) and neurotypical controls (n=33) during an auditory oddball paradigm featuring the own name, a familiar other's name, and an unknown name. Despite significant parental reports of reduced name responsiveness in the autistic group, ERP results showed a comparable enhancement of the parietal P3 component for the own name versus a close other's name in both groups. No diagnostic group differences or self-bias effects were found for the N1 or SON negativity. The results indicate that the neural mechanisms for detecting self-relevant auditory stimuli remain intact in school-aged children with autism, suggesting that their behavioral lack of responsiveness may be attributable to factors other than primary detection deficits.
papers.venue: Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders
papers.authors: Rachida El Kaddouri, Annabel Nijhof, Marcel Brass, Jan R. Wiersema

papers.title: Electrophysiological correlates of self-related processing in adults with autism
papers.abstract: This study investigated the temporal dynamics of the 'self-bias'—the cognitive prioritization of self-related stimuli—in adults with autism (n=32) and neurotypical controls (n=27). Utilizing a shape-label associative matching task while concurrently recording ERPs, the research aimed to determine whether autism-related processing differences occur at early sensory or later cognitive stages. Behaviorally, both groups exhibited equivalent self-prioritization effects. Electrophysiologically, early sensory processing, indexed by the N1 component, showed similar self-bias across groups. However, at later cognitive stages, the autism group exhibited a significantly reduced differentiation between self- and other-related stimuli, as evidenced by a diminished modulation of the parietal P3 component. These findings suggest that while early sensory detection of self-relevance is preserved in autism, later stages of cognitive evaluation and integration of self-related information are altered.
papers.authors: Letizia Amodeo, Judith Goris, Annabel D. Nijhof, Jan R. Wiersema

0290.name: Jan Theeuwes
0290.bio: Jan Theeuwes conducts research in cognitive neuroscience regarding stimulus-driven attentional capture and the interplay between top-down and bottom-up visual selection. Their work utilizes psychophysics, EEG, and fMRI to investigate how environmental statistical regularities and reward history automatically bias attention, challenging traditional dichotomies of attentional control. Theeuwes founded the Institute for Brain and Behavior Amsterdam (iBBA) and developed the 'Self-Explaining Roads' design principle for applied human factors. Additionally, they contributed to the development of the OpenSesame experiment software.
0290.research_direction: Dr. Theeuwes's recent work explores the complex interplay between top-down goals, physical salience, and selection history during visual search. Through behavioral paradigms, they are investigating the underlying mechanics of attentional capture, specifically testing whether feature search operates via discrete serial clusters rather than parallel sweeps, and examining how a feature's historical salience persistently disrupts top-down control. To understand the neural basis of these phenomena, their lab has recently been utilizing fMRI and combined SSVEP/ERP recordings to map the timing and neural loci of learned distractor suppression. Through this multimethod approach, they are investigating how statistical learning proactively modulates sensory gain in early visual cortex, as well as testing whether target enhancement and distractor suppression operate across distinct egocentric or object-centered spatial reference frames in dynamic environments.

papers.title: Beyond top-down: Feature search as a serial clump-wise process
papers.abstract: This research interrogates the traditional dichotomy between parallel and serial visual search modes by examining how observers utilize top-down feature templates to mitigate attentional capture. Contrary to models suggesting a broad-field parallel sweep for feature search, the experimental evidence indicates that the visual field is processed in discrete serial 'clumps' or clusters. The study suggests that even when observers adopt a specific feature search mode intended to suppress physically salient but irrelevant distractors, the underlying selection mechanism involves an iterative serial process rather than a comprehensive parallel scan, redefining the interplay between task-directed attention and stimulus-driven capture.
papers.authors: Jasper de Waard, Jan Theeuwes

papers.title: Learning Modulates Early Encephalographic Responses to Distracting Stimuli: A Combined SSVEP and ERP Study
papers.abstract: By integrating steady-state visual evoked potentials (SSVEPs) and event-related potentials (ERPs), this study investigates the temporal dynamics of distractor suppression driven by selection history. Utilizing an additional singleton paradigm with spatially predictable distractors, the authors found that statistical learning induces a proactive suppression of the high-probability distractor location. This was evidenced by a baseline reduction in SSVEP amplitudes at the learned location before search display onset, as well as modulated early ERP components (such as the PD). These findings support a sensory gating mechanism where the gain of early visual processing is adjusted proactively to filter out anticipated distractors.
papers.authors: Dock H. Duncan, Norman Forschack, Dirk van Moorselaar, Matthias M. Müller, Jan Theeuwes

papers.title: Proactive distractor suppression in early visual cortex
papers.abstract: This fMRI study examines the neural locus and timing of learned distractor suppression. Using an ROI-based analysis in early visual areas (V1-V3), the researchers analyzed BOLD responses in participants who learned that distractors frequently appeared in a specific spatial location. The results demonstrated spatially specific neural suppression at the high-probability distractor location, which was present during both search trials and omission trials (where no stimuli were presented). The existence of suppression in the absence of external visual input provides robust evidence for a proactive, top-down modulation of early visual cortex that leverages implicit spatial priors to optimize visual selection.
papers.authors: David Richter, Dirk van Moorselaar, Jan Theeuwes

papers.title: Object-Centered Spatial Learning in Dynamic Contexts: History-Driven Distractor Suppression and Target Enhancement
papers.abstract: This investigation explores the coordinate systems—specifically egocentric versus object-centered reference frames—underpinning visual statistical learning (VSL) for attentional control. Across a series of experiments using dynamic displays, the authors discovered a dissociation between target enhancement and distractor suppression. While target-based learning successfully transitioned to an object-centered frame, allowing for enhancement regardless of changes in the object's orientation or viewpoint, distractor suppression remained largely anchored to a retinotopic or egocentric spatial coordinate. These results imply that the mechanisms responsible for history-driven prioritization of targets and suppression of distractors operate through distinct representational levels in the human priority map.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
papers.authors: Yayla A. Ilksoy, Dirk van Moorselaar, Sander A. Los, Jan Theeuwes

papers.title: Secondary capture: Salience information persistently drives attentional selection
papers.abstract: The study introduces the concept of 'secondary capture' to describe the persistent influence of a feature's salience history on subsequent visual selection. The experiments show that items possessing features that were previously task-relevant or physically salient continue to capture attention even when those features are no longer relevant to the current search goal. This persistence indicates that salience information is deeply integrated into selection history, resulting in a residual bias within the attentional priority map that competes with contemporary goal-directed search templates and disrupts purely top-down control.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
papers.authors: Dock H. Duncan, Jan Theeuwes

0291.name: Jared Medina
0291.bio: Jared Medina is an Associate Professor at Emory University whose research characterizes how the human brain constructs and maintains representations of the body and surrounding space. Their methodology integrates single-case cognitive neuropsychology in brain-damaged populations with functional neuroimaging, non-invasive brain stimulation, and the development of multisensory illusions. Medina investigates the mechanisms of somatosensory plasticity, tactile spatial remapping, and the constraints governing embodiment and the sense of self.
0291.research_direction: Dr. Medina's recent work explores how the human brain integrates visual, tactile, and motor signals to construct body representations and guide movement. They have recently been investigating the neural mechanisms of sensorimotor compensation, using fMRI to examine how motor networks functionally reweight and rely on distinct cortical and subcortical pathways following extensive damage to the primary somatosensory cortex. Additionally, their research probes the flexibility of the body schema by utilizing mirror-box illusions to test whether physical anchoring or precise spatial mapping drives the subjective embodiment of supernumerary limbs. Finally, they are examining the psychophysical mechanisms underlying visuo-tactile interactions, applying signal detection theory to determine whether observing touch on another body part alters a viewer's genuine tactile sensitivity or simply shifts their top-down decision criterion.

papers.title: Reweighting of visuomotor areas during motor processing subsequent to somatosensory cortical damage
papers.abstract: While somatosensory inputs are essential for precise motor execution, the human neural network's response to primary somatosensory cortex (S1) damage remains under-investigated. Using fMRI, this study analyzed motor networks in two individuals (LS and RF) with extensive left S1 damage but preserved motor function. In patient LS, who had near-complete S1 hand area destruction, moving the contralesional hand induced increased activation in the ipsilesional putamen and significant deactivation in the contralesional cerebellum compared to controls. In contrast, patient RF, with a small spared region of S1, showed robust activation in that spared region during both movement and direct somatosensory stimulation. Furthermore, both patients exhibited heightened activation in the right middle occipital gyrus during contralesional hand movement. These results suggest a functional reweighting of the motor system following sensory loss, characterized by an increased dependence on subcortical action selection mechanisms in the putamen and potential inhibition of sensory prediction processes in the cerebellum, alongside a reliance on visual imagery.
papers.authors: Yuqi Liu, Elizabeth J. Halfen, Jeffrey M. Yau, Simon Fischer-Baum, Peter J. Kohler, Olufunsho Faseyitan, H. Branch Coslett, Jared Medina

papers.title: Anchoring to the hand, but not spatially distinct mappings, facilitates illusory supernumerary finger embodiment
papers.abstract: This research utilizes the 'Anne Boleyn illusion'—a mirror-box-induced perception of a sixth finger—to explore the constraints on supernumerary limb embodiment. Across several experiments, the study investigated whether illusory embodiment is driven by anchoring the supernumerary percept to the physical hand or by the existence of spatially distinct visual-to-proprioceptive mappings. Results indicated that the illusion is significantly facilitated when the illusory finger is perceived as physically attached (anchored) to the dorsum of the hand, rather than being spatially isolated. Mismatches in posture and elongated or curved finger forms did not abolish the illusion, suggesting that the body schema is remarkably flexible when integrating multisensory signals into empty space. These findings imply that physical connectivity to a recognized body part is a more critical constraint for illusory embodiment than anatomical realism or precise spatial alignment.
papers.authors: Isabel T. Folger, Jared Medina

papers.title: Viewed touch influences tactile detection by altering decision criterion
papers.abstract: Observation of touch on a body part has been shown to improve tactile detection on the observer's own body, often attributed to a vicarious somatosensory system. This study applied signal detection theory across three experiments to determine if this enhancement stems from increased perceptual sensitivity (d') or a change in the decision criterion (β). Participants performed a tactile detection task while viewing a hand being touched, approached by a finger, or a control stimulus. The results consistently demonstrated that viewing touch, or even observing a finger approaching the hand without contact, induced a liberal shift in the decision criterion (the observer became more likely to report touch) rather than a reliable increase in tactile sensitivity. These findings suggest that the 'visual enhancement of touch' is primarily a result of top-down shifts in tactile decision mechanisms rather than a boost to the underlying somatosensory signal.
papers.authors: Anupama Nair, Jared Medina

0292.name: Jarrod Lewis-Peacock
0292.bio: Lewis-Peacock investigates the neural mechanisms underlying cognitive control and the management of information within working memory. Their research utilizes neuroimaging techniques, such as multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) and real-time fMRI neurofeedback, to decode and manipulate mental representations in the human brain. Lewis-Peacock examines how the brain prioritizes, updates, and removes information from the focus of attention to support goal-directed behavior. Their work explores the intersection of memory and control, specifically how strategic shifts in attention and cognitive interventions influence long-term memory outcomes and the intentional forgetting of information.
0292.research_direction: Dr. Lewis-Peacock has recently been investigating the neural mechanisms of working memory, attentional control, and sensory representation using a combination of fMRI, EEG, and computational modeling. Their recent work explores how the visual system handles competing information, specifically examining the temporal dynamics of salient distractor suppression during search tasks and how perceptual similarity causes visual distractors to blend into working memory representations. They are also using neuroimaging to understand the interplay between memory systems, testing how the intentional suppression of active working memory content impacts the subsequent hippocampal encoding of new, long-term associations. Finally, their research bridges diverse sensory and cognitive domains by probing the distinct cognitive control strategies used to prioritize targeted items within visual working memory, while additionally utilizing multivariate decoding to map how the sensorimotor cortex represents kinesthetic features like amplitude and velocity during passive movement.

papers.title: Neural correlates of kinematic features of passive finger movement revealed by univariate and multivariate fMRI analyses
papers.abstract: This research employed high-resolution functional MRI combined with mass-univariate and multivariate pattern analysis to delineate the neural coding of kinesthetic parameters during robotic passive finger displacement. By utilizing parametrically modulated models of stimulus duration, the study demonstrated that BOLD activity in sensorimotor and subcortical regions is positively correlated with movement amplitude and negatively with velocity. Notably, extension movements evoked significantly higher activation in sensorimotor cortex than flexion movements. Multivariate decoding revealed that neural representational strength is significantly higher for movement amplitude and direction than for velocity, suggesting that the primary neural architecture for proprioceptive representation prioritize spatial displacement over movement speed.
papers.authors: Gustavo S. P. Pamplona, James Sulzer, Ewa Beldzik, Olivier Lambercy, Silvio Ionta, Roger Gassert, Jarrod A. Lewis-Peacock

papers.title: Rapid inversion of singleton distractor representations underlies learned attentional suppression
papers.abstract: This study utilized multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) of EEG data (N=40) to investigate the temporal dynamics of salient singleton distractor representations during visual search. The researchers identified two distinct representational phases: an initial bottom-up signal (100–200 ms) and a subsequent transformed signal (200–400 ms). Temporal generalization and representational similarity analyses revealed that the later phase was a neural inversion of the early signal within a shared representational subspace, where distractor spatial coding was reversed relative to target coding. The magnitude of this representational inversion predicted search efficiency (reaction times), providing evidence for a rapid top-down transformation mechanism that implements learned attentional suppression of salient distractors at the onset of search.
papers.authors: Ziyao Zhang, Jarrod A. Lewis-Peacock

papers.title: Maintenance suppression enhances subsequent associative learning
papers.abstract: This investigation utilized fMRI and directed forgetting protocols to examine how intentional suppression of information in working memory (WM) impacts the encoding of subsequent long-term memories. The findings demonstrate that actively suppressing the maintenance of recently learned associations significantly enhances the encoding fidelity of novel, subsequent information, particularly within the hippocampal CA1 subfield. Furthermore, maintenance suppression was found to bias retrieval-related neural activity, favoring the reactivation of more recently acquired associations over those previously suppressed. These results support an adaptive account of active forgetting, wherein suppression in WM serves to clear cognitive resources and optimize the hippocampal state for the acquisition of new, high-fidelity memory representations.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Ziyao Zhang, Jarrod A. Lewis-Peacock

papers.title: Signal Intrusion Explains Divergent Effects of Visual Distraction on Working Memory
papers.abstract: The authors developed a computational 'signal-intrusion' model, extending the Target-Confusability-Competition (TCC) framework, to provide a unified explanation for the varied behavioral costs of visual distraction in working memory, such as attractive biases, precision impairment, and increased guess rates. Across three delayed-estimation experiments (N=220), model comparisons indicated that sensory interference is best characterized by the integration of a target signal with an intrusive distractor signal. The model demonstrates that the likelihood of intrusion is a function of the perceptual similarity between the target and distractor, consistent with sensory-recruitment theories. This provides evidence that diverse mnemonic distortions arise from a single, similarity-dependent representational blending mechanism.
papers.authors: Ziyao Zhang, Jarrod A. Lewis-Peacock

papers.title: The consequences of strategic prioritization in working memory
papers.abstract: This study compared three common experimental approaches for inducing strategic prioritization in visual working memory—test-relevance cuing, rewarding, and refreshing—to determine if they share a common neural or behavioral mechanism. The results support a dual-mode theory of prioritization: a 'focused mode,' which utilizes the focus of attention for high-priority items, and a 'diffuse mode,' involving alternative resource-shifting processes. Test-relevance cuing was found to consistently engage the focused mode, whereas rewarding effects were more flexible, alternating between focused and diffuse modes. Refreshing did not appear to rely on the focus of attention. These findings reveal that strategic prioritization in working memory is not a monolithic process but relies on distinct cognitive control operations depending on task context.
papers.authors: Evie Vergauwe, Charlotte Hautekiet, Ziyao Zhang, Jarrod A. Lewis-Peacock

0293.name: Jason B. Mattingley
0293.department: Queensland Brain Institute and School of Psychology
0293.bio: Jason B. Mattingley is the Foundation Chair in Cognitive Neuroscience at the University of Queensland, holding a joint appointment between the Queensland Brain Institute and the School of Psychology. Mattingley's research investigates the neural architecture of selective attention, multisensory processing, and executive control to understand how the brain prioritizes sensory input and coordinates motor behavior. They employ a multimodal approach combining psychophysics, functional MRI, electroencephalography, and transcranial brain stimulation to probe cognitive functions in healthy adults and patients with neurological conditions. Mattingley's recent work focuses on the influence of neural oscillations on perception and the mechanisms of brain plasticity during learning and decision-making tasks.
0293.research_direction: Dr. Mattingley has recently been investigating how the visual system utilizes top-down expectations and prediction errors to process both simple visual features and complex real-world objects. Using high-temporal resolution EEG combined with multivariate pattern analysis and pupillometry, their recent work explores how predictive certainty—as well as the violation of distinct spatial and identity predictions—dynamically modulates the representational fidelity of sensory encoding, particularly under conditions of perceptual ambiguity. Beyond predictive coding, they are also examining the mechanisms underlying transsaccadic visual stability, specifically using psychophysics and computational modeling to understand how spatial attention is continuously allocated across rapid eye movements to maintain a stable, world-centered reference frame. Finally, Dr. Mattingley's research probes the computational architecture of perceptual decision-making, applying evidence accumulation models to test how the brain integrates dynamic motion signals from multiple discrete sensory sources.

papers.title: Expectation dynamically modulates the representational time course of objects and locations
papers.abstract: This study characterizes the temporal evolution of neural representations for stimulus identity ('what') and spatial location ('where') under varying conditions of predictive certainty. Utilizing rapid serial visual presentation (RSVP) of familiar real-world objects combined with multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) of high-temporal resolution electroencephalography (EEG), the researchers demonstrated that expectations regarding stimulus location exert a biphasic influence on representational fidelity. Specifically, location-based predictions resulted in an early attenuation of decoding accuracy between 160 and 238 ms post-stimulus, which subsequently transitioned into a significant enhancement of representational strength from 273 to 430 ms. In contrast, predictive cues for object identity consistently modulated representational fidelity in later processing windows (>250 ms), where unexpected stimuli exhibited reduced decoding accuracy relative to random baselines. These findings reveal that identity and location expectations operate via dissociable neurocomputational mechanisms, with spatial predictions specifically modulating the latent time course of sensory encoding.
papers.authors: Margaret Jane Moore, Amanda K. Robinson, Jason B. Mattingley

papers.title: Violated predictions enhance the representational fidelity of visual features in perception
papers.abstract: Testing core tenets of predictive coding theory, this investigation examined the perceptual and neural consequences of violated expectations in the human visual system. Participants performed a dual-report orientation discrimination task while pupil diameter was recorded as a physiological marker of surprise. Orientation stimuli were presented within statistically structured sequences to establish specific feature-based expectations. Behavioral results indicated that orientation information that violated local predictions led to significantly accelerated reaction times and increased report precision compared to expected or random conditions. Corresponding neural analyses suggested that these prediction errors result in an enhancement of representational fidelity in sensory cortex. The findings indicate that the visual system prioritizes unexpected feature information by increasing both its processing speed and the robustness of its neural representation, providing a mechanism for the rapid detection of environmental change.
papers.authors: Reuben Rideaux, Phuong Dang, Luke Jackel-David, Zak Buhmann, Dragan Rangelov, Jason B. Mattingley

papers.title: A computational account of transsaccadic attentional allocation based on visual gain fields
papers.abstract: The maintenance of a stable perceptual world requires the brain to coordinate shifts of spatial attention with rapid eye movements (saccades). This study investigated the precision of transsaccadic attentional allocation using a psychophysical paradigm in which observers monitored for orientation targets embedded in dynamic visual noise during goal-directed saccades. By recovering orientation-tuning functions through biologically constrained filters, the researchers found that attentional selectivity remains remarkably precise and is minimally perturbed by the execution of saccades. The authors developed a computational observer model based on visual gain fields, which accurately recapitulates the human behavioral data. The model demonstrates that a rapid estimation of spatiotopic object locations—rather than mere retinal remapping—enables the visual system to allocate attentional resources within a stable world-centered reference frame in near real-time, reconciling discrepancies between retinal and external spatial coordinates.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS)
papers.authors: William J. Harrison, Imogen Stead, Thomas S. A. Wallis, Peter J. Bex, Jason B. Mattingley

papers.title: Integrated Perceptual Decisions Rely on Parallel Evidence Accumulation
papers.abstract: While simple perceptual decisions based on isolated stimuli are well-understood, real-world behavior often necessitates the integration of information from multiple, discrete sensory sources. This study investigated the computational architecture of such integrative decisions using motion direction decoding and evidence accumulation modeling. The researchers compared serial models, where evidence is sampled from one source at a time, against parallel models, where multiple streams are processed simultaneously. Utilizing a biologically plausible motion filtering framework to analyze behavioral and neural responses, the study found robust evidence favoring parallel integration as the fundamental mechanism regulating multi-source perceptual decisions. These results suggest that the human brain optimizes decision-making by concurrently accumulating evidence from all task-relevant sensory inputs, rather than through a sequential or switching mechanism, thereby maximizing the rate of information gain.
papers.authors: Dragan Rangelov, Julia Fellrath, Jason B. Mattingley

papers.title: Expectation Modifies the Representational Fidelity of Complex Visual Objects
papers.abstract: This research addresses whether top-down expectations modulate the neural representational fidelity of complex, familiar real-world objects, particularly under conditions of perceptual uncertainty. Using electroencephalography (EEG) and multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA), the study quantified neural representations of high-fidelity and degraded object images that were either expected or unexpected based on learned statistical regularities. The results demonstrated that predictive cues sharpen the representational fidelity of visual objects, as evidenced by significantly increased decoding accuracy for expected stimuli compared to unexpected ones. Notably, these expectation-driven enhancements were evident across the visual processing hierarchy and played a causal role in resolving ambiguity for degraded visual input. The findings suggest that the human brain employs predictive coding to optimize object recognition by selectively modulating the evidence representational strength within cortical patterns of activity.
papers.authors: Margaret Jane Moore, Amanda K. Robinson, Jason B. Mattingley

0294.name: Jay Pratt
0294.bio: Jay Pratt is a Professor in the Department of Psychology at the University of Toronto who investigates the mechanisms of visual cognition and their role in guiding human action. Pratt's research focuses on how the brain selectively acquires information from the visual field and how this selection influences motor outputs, such as eye movements and limb reach. Methodologically, Pratt utilizes psychophysical testing, eye-tracking, and electrophysiological measures (EEG/ERP) to explore phenomena including attentional prioritization and inhibitory processes like inhibition of return. They also study the modulation of visual pathways by hand proximity.
0294.research_direction: Dr. Pratt's recent work explores the mechanisms underlying early attentional prioritization, visual search dynamics, and memory encoding. Utilizing paradigms like temporal order judgments, they have recently been investigating how diverse features—ranging from the physical stability and orientation of everyday objects to the uncanny valley of artificial faces and the semantic affective valence of written characters—compete for initial perceptual awareness. Within visual search, their research examines the rapid time course of attentional adaptation, using eye-tracking to parse whether search efficiency in the presence of novel distractors is driven primarily by proactive target-feature enhancement or reactive distractor suppression. Additionally, they are probing the intersection of selective attention and memory by testing whether the act of selecting a target from a search array triggers its obligatory encoding into visual working memory.

papers.title: "Not so intuitive" physics: Orientation supersedes stability in prioritizing attention
papers.abstract: This study employs a cueless temporal order judgment (TOJ) task to determine whether physical stability acts as a primary feature for attentional prioritization. Using various stimuli including common objects (traffic cones), novel objects, and simple lines, the researchers measured the point of subjective simultaneity (PSS) across multiple experiments. Results indicated that while stable canonical orientations of common objects captured attention, this effect was absent for unfamiliar objects. Crucially, vertical orientation—a frequent covariate of physical stability—was found to prioritize attention independently of stability itself. These findings suggest that the attentional system does not prioritize stability per se; rather, the perception of stability is an inferential process derived from lower-level visual cues such as upright orientation and familiarity.
papers.authors: Ece Yucer, Andrew Clement, Jay Pratt

papers.title: Rapid development of inhibitory effects in response to novel features: It's mostly target-feature enhancement
papers.abstract: This research examines the rapid onset and underlying mechanisms of the inhibition effect—where search efficiency improves in the presence of a singleton distractor. Using randomized mini-blocks and eye-tracking, the authors assessed how attentional adaptations to novel target and distractor colors develop over time. The study reveals that the inhibition effect (shorter reaction times and distractor avoidance) emerges as early as the second trial of a block, even when the distractor features are previously unseen. Gaze analysis demonstrates that this rapid adaptation is predominantly driven by target-feature enhancement (proactive guidance toward known target attributes) rather than reactive distractor-feature suppression, though evidence for distractor-specific suppression was observed following its initial presentation.
papers.authors: Zachary Hamblin-Frohman, Jay Pratt

papers.title: There is something eerie in rapidly perceiving faces
papers.abstract: As artificial faces and deepfakes become more prevalent, this study investigates whether the 'subjective eeriness' characteristic of the uncanny valley phenomenon results in specialized visual processing. Through a series of cueless temporal order judgment (TOJ) experiments, participants identified the perceived onset of faces that varied systematically in their levels of human-likeness and eeriness. The researchers utilized affective ratings to confirm stimulus placement within the uncanny valley. The results demonstrated that while faces in the uncanny valley elicit strong aversive reactions, eeriness itself is not the sole driver of early attentional prioritization. The findings suggest that the visual system's prioritization of faces is influenced by complex interactions between human-likeness and affective valence rather than a simple response to perceived eeriness.
papers.authors: Ece Yucer, Jay Pratt

papers.title: Examining visual prior entry of semantic affective valences: positive is biased over negative
papers.abstract: This study addresses whether semantic affective valences (positive vs. negative) influence early perceptual prioritization using a Temporal Order Judgment (TOJ) paradigm with Chinese characters to minimize low-level visual confounds. By measuring the Prior Entry Effect (PEE), the researchers evaluated the direct competition between emotionally charged semantic stimuli presented at varying Stimulus Onset Asynchronies (SOAs). The experiments revealed a consistent and robust bias for positive over negative semantic valences in early attentional engagement. Although the magnitude of this effect was smaller than those typically observed with facial stimuli, the results provide direct evidence that affective information extracted from semantic processing can modulate the initial time course of visual perception and attentional engagement.
papers.authors: Sihan He, Jay Pratt

papers.title: Selectively attended information is obligatorily encoded into visual working memory
papers.abstract: The authors test the selective-encoding hypothesis, which posits that the process of selecting an item from a search array leads to its mandatory encoding into visual working memory (VWM). Using a dual-trial paradigm, participants searched for a target either in isolation (target-alone) or among distractors (selection) on Trial 1, followed by a search task on Trial 2 where a color distractor could match the previous target. Experiments 1 and 2 showed that Trial 1 selection significantly increased subsequent distraction from matching features, an effect not seen in the target-alone condition. Experiment 3 demonstrated that this selection-driven capture was eliminated when VWM was filled to capacity. These findings establish a causal link between attentional selection and VWM, suggesting that VWM encoding is an obligatory consequence of selective attention.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
papers.authors: Zachary Hamblin-Frohman, Jay Pratt

0295.name: Jeffrey Allen Saunders
0295.bio: Jeffrey Allen Saunders is an Associate Professor in the Department of Psychology at the University of Hong Kong and directs the 3D Vision and Action Lab. Saunders' research investigates the computational processes and psychophysical principles governing human 3D perception and visuomotor coordination. This work includes studies on the integration of depth cues, such as texture and stereopsis, and how these factors inform the control of reaching and grasping movements. Additionally, Saunders examines the reliability of visual and nonvisual information in perceiving self-motion and heading, utilizing mathematical models to describe human behavioral performance.
0295.research_direction: Dr. Saunders has recently been investigating the role of vision in spatial orientation and postural control, utilizing virtual reality to study the mechanisms of cybersickness and how humans dynamically adjust visual cue weighting during continuous sensory perturbations. Their recent work also explores the interplay between bottom-up and top-down visual attention, employing rapid serial visual presentation and dual-detection tasks to examine phenomena like emotion-induced blindness and peripheral selective perception. Within this attentional research, they use oculomotor metrics, specifically microsaccade rates, alongside hierarchical Bayesian modeling to track dynamic shifts in a viewer's attentional state over time. Additionally, they probe broader cognitive and affective processes, investigating how mechanisms like self-reflective rumination and emotion reappraisal mediate the relationship between creativity and depressive symptoms.

papers.title: Knowing the upcoming distractor image or category can reduce the emotion-induced blindness effect from erotic images
papers.abstract: This research evaluates the efficacy of top-down cognitive interventions on the bottom-up attentional capture known as emotion-induced blindness (EIB). Utilizing a rapid serial visual presentation (RSVP) paradigm containing erotic and neutral distractors, the study implemented image-specific and categorical warnings to assess proactive interference reduction. Across three pre-registered experiments, results indicated that prior distractor foreknowledge significantly attenuated the EIB effect. Specifically, image-specific previews yielded a 77.6% reduction in attentional distraction, markedly outperforming categorical text warnings and same-category image previews, which provided roughly 35% reduction. These findings suggest that high-fidelity top-down information facilitates the formation of a negative template or primes distractor processing, enabling more efficient inhibition of emotionally salient task-irrelevant stimuli.
papers.authors: Ho Ming Chan, Jeffrey Allen Saunders

papers.title: Investigating visual weighting during postural control using virtual reality
papers.abstract: The study characterizes visual cue weighting in human postural stability using a continuous psychophysics approach. Participants maintained standing posture within a virtual environment subjected to continuous pseudorandom roll perturbations. To modulate visual uncertainty, the spectral composition of these perturbations was varied by adding higher-frequency oscillations (0.35 Hz or 0.70 Hz) to a baseline low-frequency signal (0.085–0.155 Hz). Spectral analysis of head kinematics revealed that increased visual uncertainty led to a systematic reduction in the physical response to low-frequency perturbations. The data support an optimal sensory integration model where visual weights are dynamically adjusted in response to cue reliability. The methodology further demonstrates that continuous psychophysics can effectively quantify sensory contributions to balance with short exposures that avoid inducing cybersickness.
papers.authors: Yingying Bei, Jeffrey Allen Saunders

papers.title: Modelling attention levels using microsaccade rates in response to vibrations in the peripheral field of vision
papers.abstract: This paper investigates the relationship between selective perception and attentional allocation across central and peripheral visual fields using oculomotor metrics. The researchers analyzed behavioral response accuracy and microsaccade rates during a dual-detection task involving vibrational stimuli in the periphery. A hierarchical Bayesian modeling approach was employed to estimate chronological changes in attention levels and their contribution to behavioral detection performance. Results indicated that temporal microsaccade rates serve as a sensitive indicator of attentional state, with specific directional dominance in the peripheral field influencing detection parameters. The findings provide a computational framework for evaluating visual attention in complex information displays and characterize the interplay between microsaccadic activity and peripheral sensory processing.
papers.venue: EAI Endorsed Transactions on Intelligent Systems and Machine Learning Applications
papers.authors: Minoru Nakayama, Sai Ho Yip, Jeffrey Allen Saunders

papers.title: Preregistered test of whether a virtual nose reduces cybersickness
papers.abstract: A common hypothesis in virtual reality research is that providing a stable visual reference, such as a virtual nose, can mitigate cybersickness by providing an internal rest frame. This study performed a high-powered, pre-registered replication to test this intervention. Participants experienced simulated self-motion via a head-mounted display, with motion sickness quantified using the Fast Motion Sickness (FMS) scale and the Simulator Sickness Questionnaire (SSQ). Bayesian analysis of the data revealed an effect size near zero (dz = -0.02, 95% CI [-0.37, 0.33]), with results strongly favoring the null hypothesis. The study concludes that the implementation of a virtual nose does not provide a general or effective reduction in motion sickness, contradicting previous low-powered reports and suggesting that its benefits are negligible in standard VR navigation contexts.
papers.authors: Sai Ho Yip, Adrian K. T. Ng, Henry Y. K. Lau, Jeffrey A. Saunders

papers.title: Relationship Between Creativity and Depression: The Role of Reappraisal and Rumination
papers.abstract: The investigation explores the cognitive mechanisms underlying the observed association between creativity and clinical/sub-clinical depression, specifically testing the roles of self-reflective rumination and reappraisal frequency. Across two cohorts (N=122 pilot; N=201 main), the study utilized self-reported creativity indices and standardized psychopathology measures. Path analysis revealed that while creativity and depression exhibited a weak positive correlation, this relationship was fully accounted for by self-reflective rumination as a common underlying factor. Reappraisal frequency, though generally associated with lower depression, did not significantly moderate or mediate the link between creativity and mood. The results suggest that the apparent link between creativity and 'madness' is largely driven by adaptive forms of ruminative thinking rather than deficiencies in emotional regulation strategies like reappraisal.
papers.authors: Chin Yui Lam, Jeffrey Allen Saunders

0296.name: Jeffrey D. Wammes
0296.bio: Jeffrey D. Wammes is an Assistant Professor at Queen's University who researches how learning and experience reorganize representational spaces in the brain to facilitate memory retrieval. Wammes utilizes functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), computational tools, and behavioral experiments to investigate the mnemonic benefits of active learning tasks, particularly the 'drawing effect,' and how these activities drive representational change in the hippocampus. Their research also examines the dynamics of attention, specifically analyzing how intentional and unintentional mind-wandering impact performance in laboratory settings and educational environments.
0296.research_direction: Dr. Wammes has recently been investigating the cognitive and neural mechanisms underlying memory encoding, visual learning, and attentional dynamics. A prominent line of their recent work explores the "drawing effect," utilizing behavioral paradigms and multi-dimensional experience sampling to decompose visual production into its motoric, elaborative, and visual feedback components to determine how the act of drawing alters ongoing thought and bolsters subsequent memory. They are also examining the temporal fluctuations of mind-wandering, seeking to identify objective behavioral signatures of attentional lapses—such as response time speed and variability—and testing whether targeted interventions like concurrent testing can sustain focus during continuous learning. Additionally, Dr. Wammes employs fMRI and cortical manifold analysis to investigate how implicit visual statistical learning reshapes whole-brain functional architecture, specifically mapping large-scale connectivity shifts between visual networks, attentional networks, and the medial temporal lobe.

papers.title: Visual Statistical Learning Alters Low-Dimensional Cortical Architecture
papers.abstract: This study utilized functional magnetic resonance imaging and cortical manifold analysis to examine how implicit visual statistical learning (SL) reorganizes whole-brain functional architecture. By projecting connectivity patterns onto a low-dimensional manifold, the researchers identified that associative learning is driven by a systematic expansion of visual cortical regions along a principal neural gradient, indicating increased modularity and reduced extrinsic communication. Conversely, regions within the dorsal attention network (DAN) exhibited contraction, signifying enhanced integration with higher-order association cortex. These large-scale reconfigurations were specifically localized to shifts in covariance between the visual-parietal axis and the perirhinal cortex (PRC), supporting a model where cortical regions reorganize during sequence extraction while the medial temporal lobe monitors prediction violations.
papers.authors: Keanna Rowchan, Daniel J. Gale, Qasem Nick, Jason P. Gallivan, Jeffrey D. Wammes

papers.title: Concurrent testing improves attention generally and selectively during video lectures
papers.abstract: This research explored 'concurrent testing' as a novel pedagogical intervention to mitigate mind wandering (MW) during online video lectures. In a large-scale study (N = 298), test questions were strategically embedded within lecture segments previously identified as having high baseline MW rates. Results demonstrated that concurrent testing significantly reduced the frequency of MW and increased the probability of on-task thought states compared to pre-lecture testing controls. This attentional benefit was most pronounced during targeted segments, effectively curbing the transient lapses in engagement that typically arise during extended video-based instruction. The findings suggest that the timing and strategic placement of retrieval practice can selectively modulate the temporal dynamics of learner attention.
papers.authors: Silvia Shiwei Zhou, Aidan G. Taylor, Amy Tuer, Selena Breithaupt, Si Pan, Jeffrey D. Wammes

papers.title: Drawing behaviour influences ongoing thought patterns and subsequent memory
papers.abstract: To elucidate the cognitive states underlying the mnemonic 'drawing effect,' the authors employed multi-dimensional experience sampling (mDES) to characterize the phenomenological features of ongoing thought during encoding. Participants encoded word stimuli by either drawing or writing while periodically describing their internal states across multiple dimensions. Behavioral results replicated the drawing-related memory advantage in free recall. Multivariate analysis of the mDES data revealed that drawing uniquely elicited thought patterns characterized by elevated visual imagery and semantic elaboration. Furthermore, the emergence of these visual-elaborative thought patterns was found to predict successful subsequent memory, suggesting that the act of drawing enhances retention by systematically shifting the drawer's internal cognitive landscape toward more robust, multi-modal representational states.
papers.authors: Silvia Shiwei Zhou, Keanna Rowchan, Brontë Mckeown, Jonathan Smallwood, Jeffrey D. Wammes

papers.title: Memory specificity through visual production: Multimodal recognition and source memory misattributions
papers.abstract: This investigation decomposed the mnemonic impact of visual production into its constituent motoric, elaborative, and pictorial components using old/new recognition and source memory paradigms. Participants engaged in Drawing, No Ink Drawing, Tracing, and Visualizing tasks designed to systematically isolate these features. While full drawing behavior maximized both recognition and source memory accuracy, the 'No Ink' condition—which preserves motoric and elaborative encoding without visual feedback—resulted in high general recognition but a significant increase in source memory misattributions. Specifically, participants frequently misidentified 'No Ink' items as 'Drawn' items, suggesting a hierarchy of multisensory components where motoric engagement drives recognition gains while visual feedback is essential for maintaining memory specificity and accurate source attribution.
papers.authors: Hala Rahman, Keanna Rowchan, Jeffrey D. Wammes

papers.title: Slow and steady: Speed and variance independently predict lapses in attention during rhythmic responding
papers.abstract: This study evaluated the behavioral signatures of attentional disengagement by analyzing response time (RT) dynamics during a rhythmic responding task. The researchers aimed to dissociate the predictive utility of mean RT (speed) and RT variability (coefficient of variation) for detecting mind-wandering episodes. Quantitative modeling of behavior during self-reported lapses revealed that both increased RT variability and global slowing of responses significantly correlated with off-task thought. Critically, speed and variance were found to provide independent predictive value, suggesting that lapses in attention manifest through dual behavioral pathways: a loss of rhythmic stability and a reduction in task-oriented processing speed. These findings establish robust objective markers for the moment-to-moment monitoring of attentional states.
papers.authors: S. Jalava, Jeffrey D. Wammes

0297.name: Jelena Ristic
0297.bio: Jelena Ristic is a Professor of Psychology at McGill University and directs the Laboratory for Attention & Social Cognition. Their research investigates the mechanisms of human attention and its intersection with social cognition, specifically examining how signals like eye gaze and facial expressions facilitate interpersonal communication. Employing a combination of electroencephalography (EEG), laboratory eye-tracking, and naturalistic mobile gaze monitoring, the lab studies the divergence between controlled and real-world social interactions. Their findings contribute to the understanding of the evolutionary development of social orienting and the role of attention in mediating group dynamics.
0297.research_direction: Dr. Ristic has recently been investigating how the human visual system processes social interactions, from the micro-kinematics of eye movements to the ensemble perception of small social groups. Using visual search paradigms, their recent work explores whether facing ensembles—ranging from dyads to larger collectives—are processed as unified Gestalt wholes driven by coarse orientation cues like head and body direction. In parallel, they are examining the spatiotemporal dynamics of social gaze in both laboratory and naturalistic settings. By leveraging dual mobile eye-tracking during live exchanges and high-resolution kinematic analysis of eye movements, Dr. Ristic tests how factors such as interpersonal familiarity, facial occlusion, and the underlying intentionality of a gaze shift influence mutual looking behavior and observer attention.

papers.title: The effects of familiarity and facial occlusion on social gaze dynamics in natural dyadic interactions
papers.abstract: This study utilized dual mobile eye-tracking technology to investigate the spatiotemporal dynamics of mutual gaze behavior during live dyadic interactions. Across two experiments, looking patterns were assessed as a function of interpersonal familiarity (strangers vs. friends) and visual facial occlusion (standard opaque face masks). Quantitative analysis of fixation proportions within ocular, perioral, and facial regions of interest revealed that reciprocal face-to-face looking remained exceptionally sparse, accounting for only 4–7% of the total interaction time. These results indicate that strengthening the social context through familiarity or weakening it via facial occlusion does not significantly modulate the low baseline prevalence of mutual looking in naturalistic exchanges, suggesting a robust constraint on bidirectional gaze signaling in ecological settings.
papers.venue: Canadian Journal of Experimental Psychology / Revue canadienne de psychologie expérimentale
papers.authors: Florence Mayrand, Mikayla Strandberg, Jelena Ristic

papers.title: Perceptual grouping of individuals in social triads
papers.abstract: This research tested the hypothesis that small social collectives in interactive orientations are processed as unified perceptual wholes rather than as independent agents. Utilizing a visual search paradigm, the study measured the efficiency of individuating a target person (defined by a specific hand gesture) embedded within facing (interactive) or non-facing (non-interactive) triads. Results demonstrated a significant search impairment for individuals situated within facing triads compared to non-facing ones. This observed 'grouping cost' suggests that facing configurations facilitate the perceptual integration of triads into a coherent ensemble, which in turn hinders the selective processing of constituent members. This provides empirical evidence that social communicative cues act as a Gestalt grouping principle in triadic structures.
papers.authors: Luowei Yan, Clara Colombatto, Jelena Ristic

papers.title: A perceptual advantage for social groups in interactive configurations
papers.abstract: Across three preregistered visual search experiments, this study examined whether the human visual system is preferentially tuned to detect social triads in 'core configurations'—where group members face one another. Participants localized facing groups among non-facing distractors or vice versa, with results yielding a robust search advantage for facing orientations. This effect persisted even when the search displays were inverted, a manipulation that typically disrupts holistic template-based processing. The findings suggest that the prioritization of interactive social groups is mediated by high-level sensitivity to coarse orientation-based cues (e.g., body and head direction) rather than fine-grained facial features, supporting the existence of a specialized perceptual mechanism for the rapid detection of small social units.
papers.authors: Clara Colombatto, Francesca Capozzi, Victoria Fratino, Jelena Ristic

papers.title: Search advantages for facing social groups reflect optimal interactive group sizes
papers.abstract: This investigation explored the boundary conditions of social perceptual grouping by manipulating the numerosity of facing groups in a visual search task. The researchers assessed the efficiency of detecting interactive (facing) vs. non-interactive (non-facing) groups ranging in size from dyads to octads. Results revealed a clear search advantage for facing configurations that was sharply constrained by group size: the effect was most pronounced for groups of two and three members and diminished significantly as group size exceeded five. This suggests that the visual system's capacity for ensemble triadic and dyadic processing is optimized for the small-scale social interactions that characterize the human evolutionary environment, rather than for the aggregate statistics of larger crowds.
papers.authors: Luowei Yan, Clara Colombatto, Jelena Ristic

papers.title: Intentional looks facilitate faster responding in observers
papers.abstract: This study addressed the mechanisms by which observers decode intentionality from subtle eye gaze dynamics. Participants viewed video clips of gazers whose shifts in focus were either autonomous (self-chosen) or commanded (computer-instructed). Observers were found to be significantly faster at predicting the direction of upcoming eye movements when the gazer's choice was intentional (Experiment 1) and showed enhanced orienting of attention at longer stimulus onset asynchronies (SOAs) in response to intentional vs. instructed looks (Experiments 2 and 3). High-resolution kinematic analysis of the eye region revealed that intentional shifts were preceded by specific motor signatures and pre-saccadic motion patterns. These findings indicate that the human visual system is adept at extracting mental state information from low-level motoric cues during social signaling.
papers.authors: Florence Mayrand, Sarah D. McCrackin, Jelena Ristic

0298.name: Jennifer K. E. Steeves
0298.department: Department of Psychology, Faculty of Health
0298.bio: Jennifer K. E. Steeves is a Professor and the Associate Vice President Research at York University and holds a York Research Chair in Non-Invasive Visual Brain Stimulation. Steeves examines how the human brain reorganizes in response to altered sensory input, such as early monocular enucleation, or to specific cortical lesions like those causing prosopagnosia. By integrating functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) with transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) and MR spectroscopy, they investigate the neural mechanisms underlying object, face, and scene perception. Their current work focuses on identifying biomarkers for brain plasticity and developing neuromodulation protocols to treat clinical conditions like visual hallucinations and visual snow syndrome.
0298.research_direction: Dr. Steeves has recently been investigating sensory neuroplasticity and the functional consequences of altered perceptual experience across several distinct domains. A major focus of their recent work explores the neural and psychosocial impacts of monocular enucleation, using fMRI population receptive field (pRF) mapping to examine topographic reorganization in early visual cortex, alongside survey-based methods to assess how the developmental timing of eye loss affects vision-related quality of life. Additionally, they are studying crossmodal plasticity by behavioral testing of how long-term musical training influences both social (face-voice) and non-social audiovisual recognition. Furthermore, their methodological research utilizes MRI-guided transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) over primary visual cortex to map individual differences in cortical excitability by quantifying the relationship between TMS-induced phosphene size, phosphene thresholds, and modeled electric field strengths.

papers.title: Enhanced voice recognition in musicians
papers.abstract: This study examined potential crossmodal enhancements in person and object identity recognition associated with musical training. Musicians and non-musicians performed a forced-choice recognition task using face-voice and car-horn stimulus pairs under unimodal (auditory only, visual only) and bimodal (audiovisual) conditions. Performance was measured as recognition sensitivity (d'). Results revealed that musicians possess significantly higher sensitivity for recognizing female voices compared to non-musicians, while no such expertise-related advantage was observed for non-social auditory stimuli (car horns). Sensitivity for voice recognition was positively correlated with both total years of musical training and current weekly practice hours. These results suggest that long-term musical experience facilitates auditory specialization and neuroplasticity in social cognitive domains, supporting a functional dissociation between the neural substrates of person-related and object-related auditory processing.
papers.authors: Allison J. Sletcher, Stefania S. Moro, Jennifer K. E. Steeves

papers.title: Timing of eye removal influences low-vision quality of life and self-perception of facial appearance in people with one eye
papers.abstract: This research investigated the psychosocial health outcomes of unilateral eye enucleation, specifically assessing the influence of developmental timing. Participants were categorized based on whether they underwent eye removal during infancy/early childhood (Early Monocular Enucleation, E-ME) or adulthood (Late Monocular Enucleation, L-ME). Psychosocial health was evaluated using the Low-Vision Quality of Life (LVQoL) questionnaire, the Negative Physical Self-Scale (Facial Appearance sub-scale), and the Hospital Anxiety and Depression scale. Findings demonstrated that L-ME participants reported significantly lower vision-related quality of life compared to binocular viewing controls. Within the enucleated groups, lower self-perception of facial appearance was strongly associated with diminished quality of life in the L-ME group but not the E-ME group. These data suggest that physiological and functional adaptations occurring during critical periods of postnatal visual development in E-ME individuals provide a psychosocial health advantage over those who experience late-life vision loss.
papers.authors: Aysha N. Kinakool, Stefania S. Moro, Jennifer K. E. Steeves

papers.title: Increased population receptive field size in early visual cortex following the loss of one eye
papers.abstract: The current fMRI study investigated the topographic organization and spatial representation of the primary visual cortex in adults following the loss of binocularity through early monocular enucleation. Population Receptive Field (pRF) mapping was conducted in areas V1, V2, and V3 using sweeping checkerboard stimuli.
