Quantitative analysis revealed that individuals with one eye possess significantly larger pRF sizes across all examined early visual regions compared to binocularly intact controls. Furthermore, an increased rate of pRF expansion with eccentricity was identified in the hemisphere contralateral to the remaining eye. These findings indicate a systematic shift in visual field representation, suggesting that the reduction of binocular input and the elimination of binocular competition early in development trigger large-scale sensory plasticity within the topographically organized visual cortex.
papers.authors: Matthew C. Macdonald-Dale, Stefania S. Moro, Diana J. Gorbet, Remy Cohan, Peter J. Kohler, Jennifer K. E. Steeves

papers.title: Quantifying phosphene size using MRI-guided transcranial magnetic stimulation to primary visual cortex
papers.abstract: This study established a standardized methodology for quantifying individual differences in the perception of TMS-induced phosphenes to assess visual cortical excitability. Using MRI-guided stereotaxic neuronavigation and a custom computer-based reporting tool, phosphene size was measured and analyzed in relation to phosphene thresholds (PT), scalp-to-cortex distance (SCD), and modeled electric field (E-field) strength in area V1. Perceived phosphene size was significantly negatively correlated with both PT and the peak electric field strength at the stimulation hotspot. No significant correlation was found between SCD and phosphene size, supporting the hypothesis that SCD does not adequately account for the biophysical properties of intervening tissues. These results demonstrate that subjective phosphene characteristics serve as reliable biomarkers for individual cortical response to neuromodulation, facilitating the optimization of TMS protocols for both research and clinical applications in vision.
papers.authors: Remy Cohan, Stefania S. Moro, Jennifer K. E. Steeves

0299.name: Jenny Bosten
0299.bio: Jenny Bosten is an Associate Professor of Psychology at the University of Sussex and Director of the Sussex Vision Lab, where they study the biological and environmental determinants of human color vision. Bosten’s research uses psychophysics, neuroimaging (fMRI, EEG), and genetic analysis to examine how phenotypic variations, such as anomalous trichromacy and putative tetrachromacy, influence individual perceptual experience. They investigate the ecological calibration of the visual system by analyzing natural scene statistics and characterize cortical representations of color through projects such as COLOURCODE and COLOURMIND. Bosten also applies vision science to clinical contexts, developing diagnostic tools for pediatric color vision deficiency and virtual reality-based assessments for patients with low vision.
0299.research_direction: Dr. Bosten has recently been investigating human color processing, bridging the gap between early cortical mechanisms and applied visual aids for anomalous trichromacy. Their recent work explores how cortical color mechanisms are tuned across different hue axes, utilizing steady-state visually evoked potentials (SSVEPs) and evaluating distinct EEG paradigms to measure nonlinear chromatic integration and spatial opponent processes. In parallel, they are examining the empirical and theoretical efficacy of multi-notch filters—such as EnChroma glasses—marketed to enhance color discrimination for individuals with red-green color vision deficiencies. By combining large-scale psychophysical testing with computational modeling of cone spectral sensitivities, Dr. Bosten evaluates how these optical interventions alter chromatic signals and functional color space volume.

papers.title: Tuning of cortical color mechanisms revealed using steady-state visually evoked potentials
papers.abstract: This research utilizes steady-state visually evoked potentials (SSVEPs) and electroencephalography (EEG) to investigate the transformation of chromatic signals within the human visual cortex. By employing isoluminant chromatic checkerboard stimuli and measuring the amplitude of intermodulation components (specifically I1), the authors quantified cortical color tuning functions across various hue axes. The study findings indicate that these cortical mechanisms are broadly tuned, with similar bandwidths observed for both cardinal and intermediate color directions. Furthermore, the tuning functions were found to be independent of the presence of perceptible spatial chromatic edges, suggesting that the measured responses originate from single-opponent neural populations in the early visual cortex rather than double-opponent ones.
papers.authors: Ana Rozman, Dylan J. Watts, Lucy Somers, Jenny Bosten

papers.title: Comparison of intermodulation and oddball methods for measuring human cortical color tuning functions using steady-state visually evoked potentials
papers.abstract: This study evaluates two distinct SSVEP-based EEG paradigms for characterizing the tuning of human cortical color mechanisms: an intermodulation (IM) component-based approach and a reverse oddball method. By recording neural responses to systematically varied chromatic stimuli, the researchers compared the effectiveness and signal-to-noise ratios of these techniques in resolving tuning bandwidths and peak amplitudes. The results demonstrate that while both methods are sensitive to cortical color representation, the IM method provides a more direct metric of nonlinear chromatic integration, whereas the oddball method is particularly effective at capturing the distinctiveness between discrete chromatic categories.
papers.venue: Journal of the Optical Society of America A (JOSA A)
papers.authors: Ana Rozman, Chris Racey, Jenny M. Bosten

papers.title: Empirical tests of the effectiveness of EnChroma multi-notch filters for enhancing color vision in deuteranomaly
papers.abstract: The authors conducted a large-scale psychophysical assessment of EnChroma multi-notch filters to evaluate claims regarding their ability to enhance color discrimination in individuals with red-green color vision deficiency (CVD). Eighty-six CVD observers and twenty-four controls were tested using the Ishihara plates and the Farnsworth-Munsell 100-Hue test. The study found no significant generalized improvement in chromatic discrimination performance when the filters were worn. Computational modeling of the chromatic signals corroborated these behavioral results, indicating that the filters enhance contrast for specific wavelengths while simultaneously reducing it for others, yielding no net expansion of the usable color space for deuteranomalous observers.
papers.authors: Lucy Somers, Anna Franklin, Jenny Bosten

papers.title: Predicted effectiveness of EnChroma multi-notch filters for enhancing color perception in anomalous trichromats
papers.abstract: Using a theoretical model of anomalous trichromatic cone spectral sensitivities, this paper quantifies the potential shifts in chromatic signals induced by EnChroma multi-notch filters. The researchers calculated expected changes in discriminability across the hue circle for various shifts in L- and M-cone peak sensitivities (delta lambda max). The modeling results indicate that the filters produce highly idiosyncratic effects that depend on an individual's specific degree of spectral overlap. While the filters may enhance specific red-green signals for some observers, they do not restore normal trichromatic color volume and can introduce novel chromatic distortions, suggesting they do not provide a functional cure for CVD.
papers.authors: Lucy Somers, Jenny Bosten

0301.name: Jeremy B Wilmer
0301.bio: Jeremy B. Wilmer is a Professor of Psychology whose research investigates the nature and origins of individual variation in human cognition, focusing on face recognition and visual perception. Wilmer utilizes large-scale, internet-based citizen science through platforms like TestMyBrain.org to examine the heritability and cognitive specificity of social-perceptual abilities. Their work extends into statistical cognition and data visualization, where they develop tools and practices, such as ShowMyData.org, to communicate individual-level data in scientific research. By using massive sample sizes and psychometric methodologies, Wilmer aims to map the architecture of the human mind through its variations.
0301.research_direction: Dr. Wilmer has recently been investigating how the human visual system extracts information from statistical graphics and how individual differences in face processing relate to social cognition. Their recent work explores the intersection of ensemble perception and data visualization, using spatial readout paradigms to test how accurately viewers estimate central tendencies from raw-data dot plots compared to explicitly marked summary statistics like bar graphs. To address systemic spatial misinterpretations such as "average-blindness," they are developing and evaluating novel plot formats designed to better align with the visual system's automatic statistical extraction mechanisms. Additionally, Dr. Wilmer has been leveraging massive citizen-science cohorts to psychometrically validate more inclusive, diverse measures of theory-of-mind, such as a multiracial update to the Reading the Mind in the Eyes Test. Utilizing these large-scale datasets, they are modeling how discrete visual abilities—specifically face perception and emotion recognition—independently predict traits associated with the broader autism phenotype.

papers.title: The Paradox of Certainty: When Graphed Ensembles Convey Averages Better than Graphed Averages
papers.abstract: This research critiques the ubiquitous graphical convention of presenting summary statistics, such as isolated mean markers, under the assumption that visual simplification enhances communicative accuracy. Using a novel drag-and-drop spatial localization paradigm, the study assessed viewers' precision in estimating average values across various plot formats, including standard bar graphs, line plots, and raw-data dot plots. The findings reveal a pervasive 'average-blindness' in summary-only visualizations, where participants systematically mislocated explicitly marked means as being biased toward the bar body or line segments. In contrast, participants exhibited 'ensemble-acuity,' extracting central tendency from raw-data ensembles with a degree of precision approaching formal confidence intervals. These results suggest that explicit statistical summaries paradoxically induce certainty-based errors by engaging ambiguous graphical conventions, whereas unsummarized data distributions facilitate more accurate automatic statistical extraction via the human visual system's ensemble processing mechanisms.
papers.venue: Journal of Vision (also published in Proceedings of the 47th Annual Meeting of the Cognitive Science Society)
papers.authors: Yang Wang, Timothy F. Brady, Sarah H. Kerns, Jeremy B. Wilmer

papers.title: Multiracial Reading the Mind in the Eyes Test (MRMET): An inclusive version of an influential measure
papers.abstract: This study details the psychometric development and validation of the Multiracial Reading the Mind in the Eyes Test (MRMET), a diverse and non-gendered replacement for the original Reading the Mind in the Eyes Test (RMET). The MRMET addresses critical limitations of its predecessor, specifically the Eurocentric stimulus set and the reliance on complex, gender-stereotyped vocabulary. Normed on a massive citizen-science cohort (N ≈ 60,000) via TestMyBrain.org, the paradigm was evaluated using item response theory and classical test theory. The MRMET demonstrated equivalent or superior internal consistency, improved item-level discriminability, and enhanced predictive validity for the Communication dimension of the broader autism phenotype (BAP) compared to the RMET. These findings establish the MRMET as a high-quality, psychometrically interchangeable, and more equitable tool for measuring theory-of-mind and social-cognitive abilities across diverse populations.
papers.authors: Heesu Ally Kim, Jasmine Kaduthodil, Roger W. Strong, Laura T. Germine, Sarah Cohan, Jeremy B. Wilmer

papers.title: Face perception and facial emotional expression recognition ability: Both unique predictors of the broader autism phenotype
papers.abstract: The degree to which discrete face-processing mechanisms associate with sub-clinical social traits remains a central question in cognitive neuroscience. This investigation utilized path analytic modeling to determine whether individual differences in face perception ability (measured via the CFPT) and facial expression recognition (measured via the RMET/MRMET) independently predict the broader autism phenotype (BAP). In a large-scale neurotypical sample, the study controlled for general verbal ability—a known correlate of expression identification—to isolate face-specific variance. The results indicated that both perceptual and affective face-processing skills significantly and uniquely predicted difficulties in the nonverbal communication dimension of the BAP. These findings provide evidence for a positive manifold of face-processing abilities and suggest that impairments in distinct visual mechanisms are fundamental, non-redundant contributors to the social-cognitive profile of autistic-like traits.
papers.authors: Gilles E. Gignac, Romina Palermo, Ellen Bothe, Dana L. Walker, Jeremy B. Wilmer

papers.title: Average-Blindness and Ensemble-Acuity: When Plotted Raw Data Conveys Averages Better Than Plotted Averages
papers.abstract: This work characterizes a systemic cognitive failure in graph interpretation termed 'average-blindness,' where observers consistently misperceive the location of explicitly marked averages in summary visualizations. Through a series of spatial readout experiments, the authors demonstrate that this error typically manifests as the 'Bar-Tip Limit' effect, wherein the mean is perceived as the outer boundary of the data distribution rather than its center. The study contrasts this with 'ensemble-acuity,' the visual system's robust capability to derive accurate summary statistics directly from unsummarized raw data points. By comparing estimation performance across bar, line, and ensemble plots, the research highlights a striking paradox: unsummarized data facilitates more precise central tendency estimation than explicit statistical markers, suggesting that current graphical standards may be suboptimal for conveying basic statistical information.
papers.authors: Yang Wang, Sarah H. Kerns, Timothy F. Brady, Jeremy B. Wilmer

papers.title: Star Mean: A new, intuitive, and accurate way to graph averages
papers.abstract: Mean-based bar graphs are prone to several severe and frequent misinterpretations, including the Bar-Tip Limit error (misperceiving the mean as an outer limit) and the Uniformity Fallacy (mistaking a distribution for uniform). This paper introduces 'Star Mean,' an alternative graphical format designed to re-center the mean as a salient balance point within a distribution. The study validates 'Star Mean' against standard summary plots using readout-based measurement to assess whether the new format improves the accuracy of viewers' mental models of the underlying data. Initial empirical results suggest that by visually anchoring the average away from container-like boundaries, 'Star Mean' effectively mitigates dichotomization biases and improves the estimation of both central tendency and overlapping variance, presenting a more transparent alternative for scientific communication.
papers.authors: Sarah H. Kerns, Jeremy B. Wilmer

0302.name: Jeremy M. Wolfe
0302.bio: Jeremy M. Wolfe is a cognitive scientist who developed the Guided Search model, which explains how preattentive feature information directs focal attention during visual search. Wolfe’s research examines the interplay between bottom-up stimulus-driven guidance and top-down observer-driven goals, recently resulting in the Guided Search 6.0 framework. Wolfe applies psychophysical methodologies to real-world scenarios such as cancer screening in radiology and threat detection in airport security. Their current research investigates the mechanisms behind the 'low prevalence effect' and 'inattentional blindness' in expert observers.
0302.research_direction: Wolfe and colleagues investigate the computational and psychological principles governing human visual foraging, hybrid search, and dynamic object tracking across the adult lifespan. They utilize the Marginal Value Theorem (MVT) and psychophysical paradigms to examine how observers optimize patch-leaving strategies and maintain environmental reward-rate representations amidst cognitive load and task interruptions. Through hierarchical Bayesian modeling and signal detection theory (SDT), the lab probes the mechanisms of target selection within Activated Long-Term Memory (aLTM), investigating how conceptual hierarchies and signal-strength factors limit awareness and modulate decision criteria in expert domains like medical image perception. Their research further characterizes the Low Prevalence Effect (LPE) and Prevalence-Induced Concept Change (PICC) to understand how statistical base rates and feedback influence the robustness of diagnostic thresholds.

papers.title: A common signal-strength factor limits awareness and precise knowledge of multiple moving objects across the adult lifespan
papers.abstract: The study investigates the psychophysical determinants of age-related declines in multiple identity tracking (MIT) and multiple object awareness (MOA) across the adult lifespan (ages 18–76). Utilizing hierarchical Bayesian modeling, the authors contrasted a single-process signal-detection model (characterized by a signal-strength parameter, d') against a dual-process framework that incorporates an additional high-threshold recollection parameter (R). The results demonstrate that a common signal-strength factor provides the most parsimonious explanation for tracking performance across all age groups, with d' exhibiting a linear decline as a function of age. These findings suggest that the primary constraint on dynamic tracking in older adults is a degradation in the sensitivity of spatiotemporal representations rather than a selective failure of discrete, recollection-based identity-location binding mechanisms.
papers.authors: Iris Wiegand, Igor S. Utochkin, Ava Mitra, Chia-Chien Wu, Jeremy M. Wolfe

papers.title: Mixed hybrid visual foraging is near optimal
papers.abstract: This research explores human patch-leaving strategies within the context of 'mixed hybrid visual foraging,' wherein observers must monitor and collect multiple instances of varied target types, including both specific items and categorical sets, across fluctuating patch densities. Evaluated against the Marginal Value Theorem (MVT), the study sought to determine if increased cognitive load and target heterogeneity disrupt the optimality of quitting decisions. Findings indicate that participants' patch-leaving behavior remained remarkably consistent and near-optimal across conditions of varying target specificity and memory set sizes. Despite absolute performance differences in collection rates, the robust adherence to MVT-based quitting rules suggests that human foragers utilize a generalized, rule-based decision mechanism that is resilient to the increased complexity of hybrid search environments.
papers.authors: Injae Hong, Jeremy M. Wolfe

papers.title: Effects of prevalence and feedback in the identification of blast cells in peripheral blood: expert and novice observers
papers.abstract: The investigation characterizes the interplay between perceptual expertise, target prevalence, and trial-by-trial feedback in a high-stakes clinical task: the identification of blast cells in hematological smears. Comparing medical professionals with trained novices, the study measured shifts in decision criteria and the magnitude of the Low Prevalence Effect (LPE). Both cohorts demonstrated a significant LPE when provided with accuracy feedback, although experts displayed greater robustness. Crucially, the absence of feedback induced a liberal criterion shift consistent with Prevalence-Induced Concept Change (PICC), although experts maintained a significantly more conservative baseline criterion. The results provide empirical evidence that professional expertise modulates, but does not eliminate, the impact of statistical base rates on the decision thresholds utilized in diagnostic medical image perception.
papers.authors: Wanyi Lyu, Jennifer S. Trueblood, Jeremy M. Wolfe

papers.title: Categorically distinct subsets allow flexible memory-selection in hybrid search
papers.abstract: This series of experiments examines the mechanisms of memory selection within Activated Long-Term Memory (aLTM) during hybrid visual and memory search. The authors investigated whether searchers can effectively partition a large memorized set into relevant subsets on a trial-by-trial basis using semantic vs. perceptual cues. Results demonstrate that partitioning based on semantic categories (e.g., conceptual object classes) allows for efficient, cost-free memory selection, whereas perceptual features (e.g., color) fail to support flexible memory narrowing. These findings imply that the internal organization of target templates in hybrid search is fundamentally structured by conceptual hierarchies, enabling rapid, context-dependent restriction of the memory search space during the prioritization of task-relevant items.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
papers.authors: Nurit Gronau, Makaela Nartker, Sharon Yakim, Igor S. Utochkin, Jeremy M. Wolfe

papers.title: No matter what you do, travel is travel in visual foraging
papers.abstract: This study assessed the resilience of human visual foraging behavior to different forms of task interruption and involuntary patch termination. Utilizing a patch-leaving paradigm governed by the Marginal Value Theorem (MVT), the authors examined whether external task-switching or forced travel resets the foraging state or if observers maintain a latent representation of the patch's instantaneous reward rate. Behavioral data from three experiments revealed that foraging strategies were largely preserved across interruptions, with observers resuming pre-interruption collection rates and maintaining optimal quitting thresholds. The results suggest that the cognitive resources dedicated to tracking environmental value in foraging are robust to temporary disruptions, indicating that foraging rules are integrated into a stable, long-term representational framework rather than being solely dependent on transient working memory.
papers.authors: Injae Hong, Grace Yan, Jeremy M. Wolfe

0303.name: Jessica Cantlon
0303.bio: Jessica Cantlon is the Ronald J. and Mary Ann Zdrojkowski Professor of Developmental Neuroscience at Carnegie Mellon University, where they investigate the evolutionary and developmental foundations of quantitative reasoning. Cantlon’s research employs functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and behavioral paradigms to compare numerical cognition across human infants, children, adults, and non-human primates. Cantlon identified conserved neural mechanisms in the intraparietal sulcus that support approximate magnitude estimation, indicating a biological continuity in mathematical intuition that predates symbolic language. Their recent work examines the neural overlap between visuospatial processing and early mathematical learning, addressing assumptions about gender differences in cognitive development.
0303.research_direction: Dr. Cantlon’s recent work explores the cognitive and neural foundations of numerical perception, spatial reasoning, and visual abstraction. Using fMRI in children and adults, they have recently been investigating how numerical and geometric representations develop, overlap, and respond to spatial training or environmental socialization within the parietal cortex. Beyond neuroimaging, their behavioral research examines quantity estimation in naturalistic scenes to understand how object segmentation and visual occlusion act as computational bottlenecks during numerical cognition in the wild. Additionally, they are evaluating how artificial neural networks compare to humans and non-human primates on visual match-to-sample tasks, probing how specific model architectures and training biases influence the capacity for relational and visual-semantic abstraction.

papers.title: Segmentation as a bottleneck in numerical cognition
papers.abstract: This research investigates the ecological validity of numerical perception by transitioning from traditional dot arrays to naturalistic visual scenes. Adult participants performed a non-symbolic number discrimination task across four stimulus regimes: standard dot arrays, noisy dot arrays, naturalistic photographs, and pseudo-naturalistic images with preserved object boundaries. Psychometric results revealed significant impairments in numerical precision and accuracy for naturalistic and pseudo-naturalistic arrays relative to controlled dot stimuli. Quantitative modeling indicated that accuracy decreases as a function of total object count specifically in naturalistic conditions, an effect robustly driven by object occlusion. These findings suggest that the computational overhead associated with object segmentation and boundary resolution in cluttered environments acts as a measurable bottleneck, constraining numerical cognition in the wild.
papers.authors: Lauren S Aulet, Jessica F Cantlon

papers.title: Intersection of spatial and numerical cognition in the developing brain
papers.abstract: We examined the neural architecture supporting the developmental overlap between numerical and visuospatial cognition using fMRI in children (ages 4-8) and adults. Participants engaged in numerical matching, geometric shape matching, and number line estimation (NLE) tasks. Whole-brain and ROI-based analyses identified early cortical specialization for both numerical and geometric properties in the parietal cortex. However, children demonstrated significantly greater conjunctive activation between these tasks across the intraparietal sulcus compared to adults. Critically, during NLE, children’s neural recruitment overlapped with both numerical and geometric substrates, whereas adult activity was confined to number-specific parietal regions. These results provide the first neurobiological evidence that early numerical magnitude processing relies on an integrated spatial-numerical representational system that bifurcates as a function of development and expertise.
papers.authors: Lauren S Aulet, Caroline M Kaicher, Jessica F Cantlon

papers.title: Artificial Neural Networks Reveal a Cognitive Continuum Toward Human Abstraction
papers.abstract: This work evaluates the extent to which artificial neural network (ANN) models capture the hierarchical and evolutionary trajectory of human abstract reasoning. We benchmarked over 200 pretrained architectures against behavioral data from non-human primates (macaques), indigenous Tsimane’ adults, and U.S. children and adults using three match-to-sample (MTS) tasks varying in abstraction: visual-semantic, regular shape, and relational reasoning. Our analyses revealed that as task demands required higher levels of relational abstraction, ANN decisions progressively diverged from adult human behavior, echoing patterns seen in non-human primates. However, representational similarity analysis (RSA) demonstrated a shared latent cognitive structure across all biological and artificial groups, indicating common underlying cognitive strategies. The degree of human-like alignment was significantly moderated by specific inductive biases, including model scale, architectural depth, and the presence of language-based supervision.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the Annual Meeting of the Cognitive Science Society
papers.authors: Wenjie Li, Margaret Henderson, Yonatan Bisk, Jessica Cantlon

papers.title: Cognitive and neural mechanisms of spatial learning and transfer in adults
papers.abstract: To differentiate between domain-specific and domain-general theories of spatial visualization development, we conducted a longitudinal fMRI training study in 60 adults. Participants underwent a nine-week spatial visualization intervention focused on mental rotation, with neural activity assessed pre- and post-training. Behavioral results demonstrated significant improvements in mental rotation and transfer to geometric reasoning. Neuroimaging analyses revealed that these gains were primarily coupled with localized changes in the parietal cortex (intraparietal sulcus) and premotor sensory-motor imagery circuits, while activity in prefrontal executive networks remained stable. These findings support the hypothesis that spatial learning is driven by the refinement of domain-specific spatial transformation mechanisms in the dorsal stream rather than general improvements in executive control.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the Annual Meeting of the Cognitive Science Society
papers.authors: Marissa Laws, Jessica Cantlon

papers.title: Plasticity, gender, and the environment during numerical and spatial development
papers.abstract: This study evaluates the impact of gender socialization and spatial environment on the development of numerical and spatial cognitive systems. We utilized fMRI to measure brain activity in 51 children (ages 4-8) during numerical magnitude comparison and geometric shape matching tasks. Multivariate and Bayesian analyses revealed widespread neural similarities between boys and girls in the recruitment of the math-responsive parietal network. Furthermore, localized brain activity during these tasks was unrelated to individual scores on gender category, socialization measures, or the complexity of the child's early spatial learning environment. These data challenge models of early biological or environment-driven gender divergence in foundational mathematical cognition and support the stability of core quantitative systems across early childhood development.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the Annual Meeting of the Cognitive Science Society
papers.authors: Marissa Laws, Jessica Cantlon

0304.name: Jessica K. Witt
0304.bio: Jessica K. Witt is a Professor of Psychology at Colorado State University whose research investigates the relationship between visual perception and motor capabilities. Witt examines the action-specific account of perception, utilizing empirical methodologies to demonstrate how factors such as physiological state, reachability, and performance success scale the perceived geometry of the environment. Their current research extends these principles to information visualization, applying psychophysical methods to the communication of uncertainty in datasets such as hurricane forecasts and medical risks. Witt’s work applies vision science to cognitive engineering, aiming to support decision-making through perceptually-aligned graphical representations.
0304.research_direction: Dr. Witt’s recent research bridges basic ensemble perception and applied data visualization to explore how visual information shapes human judgment. In applied domains, they have recently been investigating how dynamic visual formats can better communicate complex scientific data, spatial uncertainty, and accumulating risks to lay audiences. For example, their work evaluates how narrative visualizations influence risk perception and empirical trust in public health contexts, and tests how animated risk trajectories impact hurricane evacuation decisions compared to traditional static graphics like the cone of uncertainty. Additionally, in basic vision science, their recent work examines spatial ensemble coding, specifically testing how observers judge the spatial dispersion of simultaneously presented dot clusters and whether variability estimation biases are driven by stimulus set size rather than memory demands.

papers.title: Narrative visualizations: Depicting accumulating risks and increasing trust in data
papers.abstract: This study examines the efficacy of narrative visualizations in communicating cumulative risk, particularly in contexts like the COVID-19 pandemic where data may be perceived as counterintuitive by laypeople. Across two experiments, the researchers compare narrative visualizations against static graphics and affect-laden anecdotes. The results indicate that narrative visualizations, which explicitly depict the data-generating process and the accumulation of risk over time, mitigate the reduced concern often induced by static visualizations. Mediation analysis demonstrates that these visualizations enhance risk perception and trust by improving the user's perceived understanding of the data lineage, contrasting with anecdotes which increase concern through emotional mechanisms. The authors argue that narrative visualizations represent a distinct class of visual communication tools essential for conveying complex, surprising scientific information while maintaining empirical trust.
papers.authors: Madison Fansher, Logan Walls, Chenxu Hao, Hariharan Subramonyam, Aysecan Boduroglu, Priti Shah, Jessica K. Witt

papers.title: Variability of dot spread is overestimated
papers.abstract: Prior work has shown that observers overestimate the variability of ensembles of low-level (e.g., color, orientation) and mid-level (e.g., size) features when items are presented sequentially, leaving open whether this bias reflects a memory-related distortion tied to sequential presentation or a more general perceptual bias. This study tests whether the overestimation generalizes to static, simultaneously presented displays and to a spatial property—the perceived spread (dispersion) of a cluster of dots. Across experiments, participants judged the spatial variability of dot clusters containing different set sizes and consistently overestimated how spread out the dots were relative to their true spatial variability. The overestimation bias was reliably observed for smaller set sizes (10 and 20 dots) but was absent when set size increased to 50 dots, suggesting the bias is not simply a general overestimation of variability but depends on ensemble size, and that it is not solely attributable to memory demands from sequential presentation since it emerges even with simultaneous, static displays.
papers.authors: Jessica K. Witt, Mengzhu Fu, Michael D. Dodd

papers.title: Visualizing Uncertainty in Hurricane Forecasts with Animated Risk Trajectories
papers.abstract: This study evaluates an alternative to the widely used 'cone of uncertainty' (COU) for communicating hurricane forecast track uncertainty to nonexperts, motivated by evidence that the COU is frequently misread as implying that only locations inside its boundary are at risk. The authors developed 'animated risk trajectories' (ARTs)—sets of animated icons, each depicting one plausible storm path drawn from the forecast ensemble—and compared nonexperts' risk perception and evacuation decisions for towns at varying distances from the most likely track when forecasts were displayed as ARTs versus as a traditional COU. Relative to the COU, ARTs produced higher perceived risk for towns located outside the cone's boundary, better aligning perceived risk with the actual probabilistic forecast. Perceived risk under the ART format was further modulated by the animation's visual properties, including icon density and whether the distribution of trajectories was unimodal or bimodal. The findings support animated ensemble-based visualizations as a way to reduce a specific, consequential misinterpretation of hurricane forecast uncertainty.
papers.authors: Jessica K. Witt, Zachary M. Labe, Amelia C. Warden, Benjamin A. Clegg

0305.name: Jessica Montag
0305.bio: Jessica Montag is an Associate Professor of Psychology at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign and a faculty member at the Beckman Institute for Advanced Science and Technology. Montag’s research examines how linguistic and cognitive abilities emerge from experience, focusing on the relationship between environmental statistics, visual salience, and language processing. They utilize eye-tracking to investigate oculomotor behavior during reading and sentence production, alongside corpus analyses and naturalistic audio recordings to quantify language input. Montag’s work demonstrates how structural complexities in picture books and individual differences in text exposure shape syntactic development and vocabulary acquisition across the lifespan.
0305.research_direction: Dr. Montag's recent work explores the statistical and social structure of naturalistic language environments, particularly investigating how early linguistic input is shaped by shared picture book reading. Using a combination of caregiver surveys, daylong audio recordings, and novel corpus generation, they have been examining how factors like caregiver communicative strategies, the presence of older siblings, and the specific syntax of children's books influence an infant's exposure to diverse vocabulary. Their research also evaluates the mathematical modeling of these everyday language environments, specifically questioning how information-theoretic metrics like burstiness can accurately quantify the temporal clustering of words in developmental audio samples. Furthermore, Dr. Montag has recently been studying the visual and motor mechanics of reading, utilizing eye-tracking to investigate how saccadic behavior and oculomotor control continue to mature alongside reading expertise from late childhood into young adulthood.

papers.title: An Online Survey of Picture Book Reading Practices with Children Between the Ages of 0 and 30 Months
papers.abstract: This study characterizes the frequency and nature of at-home picture book reading practices for infants and toddlers (N=282 caregivers) in the United States. Quantitative analyses of survey data revealed that reading is a highly prevalent activity, with over 90% of families engaging at least weekly and nearly 70% reading daily. The investigation measured the distribution of verbatim text reading alongside a spectrum of extra-textual behaviors, demonstrating that both the quantity of reading and the specific communicative strategies employed vary significantly as a function of child age and emerging linguistic proficiency. The results provide high-resolution data on the variability of linguistic input children encounter during shared reading in early developmental stages.
papers.authors: Trisha N. Patel, Zeynep B. Marasli, Alyssa Choi, Jessica L. Montag

papers.title: A novel corpus of naturalistic picture book reading with 2-to-3 year old children
papers.abstract: The authors present a new, sharable corpus of naturalistic caregiver-child interactions recorded in home environments to elucidate the causal relationship between picture book reading and language outcomes. Analyses of the transcriptions indicate that while caregivers primarily read the provided book text, the resulting speech profiles—including mean length of utterance (MLU), lexical diversity, and conversational turn-taking—are significantly modulated by the syntactic and textual characteristics of the books. Comparative analyses against other conversational contexts in the CHILDES database demonstrate that book reading provides unique exposure to complex linguistic constructions and rare lexical items that are often absent in standard child-directed speech.
papers.authors: Anastasia Stoops, Mengqian Wu, In Ho Ted Jung, Jessica L. Montag

papers.title: The Applications and Limitations of the Burstiness Metric in Investigating the Temporal Distribution of Words in Child-Centered Audio
papers.abstract: This research evaluates the utility of the burstiness metric for quantifying the temporal dynamics of word occurrences within naturalistic, child-centered audio environments. Given that the temporal presentation of linguistic stimuli impacts acquisition, the study applies information-theoretic measures to daylong recordings to differentiate between periodic and bursty (intermittent) signaling patterns. The paper examines the mathematical constraints and performance of the burstiness metric when applied to finite event sequences in developmental corpora and discusses the implications of temporal non-uniformity for ecological models of language learning.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the Annual Meeting of the Cognitive Science Society
papers.authors: Zeynep Marasli, Jessica L. Montag

papers.title: The Role of Siblings on Infant Language Exposure in Daylong Audio Recordings
papers.abstract: Leveraging daylong audio recordings, this study investigates how family structure, specifically the presence of older siblings, influences the quantity and quality of linguistic input received by infants. The research quantifies the distribution of child-directed speech versus overheard adult-directed or sibling-directed speech. By analyzing these naturalistic distributional statistics, the authors test competing hypotheses regarding the 'birth order effect' and evaluate whether the increased density of overheard speech in multi-child households provides sufficient statistical regularities to support lexical and syntactic development despite potentially reduced direct caregiver engagement.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the Annual Meeting of the Cognitive Science Society
papers.authors: Maily Galindo, Jessica L. Montag

papers.title: Reading skill affects reading saccades well into late childhood
papers.abstract: This eye-tracking study examines the developmental trajectory of oculomotor parameters during naturalistic, multi-line reading in adolescents and young adults. Contrary to models suggesting adult-like oculomotor control by early adolescence, the findings demonstrate that saccadic length and velocity are significantly predicted by individual differences in reading expertise well into the teen years. The study found a persistent and tight coupling between reading fluency and saccadic behavior, indicating that the efficiency of eye movement patterns continues to be refined as lexical processing and text integration skills mature across the lifespan.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the Annual Meeting of the Cognitive Science Society
papers.authors: Anastasia Stoops, Jessica L. Montag

0307.name: Jiahui Guo
0307.institution: The University of Texas at Dallas
0307.department: Department of Psychology, School of Behavioral and Brain Sciences
0307.bio: Jiahui Guo is an Assistant Professor at The University of Texas at Dallas whose research explores the neural mechanisms of high-level perception, with an emphasis on face recognition and social cognition. Guo’s work utilizes naturalistic stimuli and functional neuroimaging to map individualized brain topographies and investigate how specialized cortical regions support visual tasks. By integrating computational modeling, deep neural networks, and neuropsychological assessments of populations such as those with prosopagnosia, Guo aims to develop models of human functional brain organization and its behavioral outcomes.
0307.research_direction: Dr. Guo has recently been investigating the fine-grained functional architecture of the human cortex using naturalistic fMRI paradigms and advanced computational modeling. Their recent work explores how idiosyncratic brain topographies, such as category-selective and retinotopic regions, can be precisely mapped and aligned across individuals using connectivity hyperalignment and generative neural tuning models. They apply these high-dimensional mapping techniques to probe the developmental origins of cortical organization, studying whether specialized functional connectomes can emerge in congenitally blind and deaf individuals devoid of typical sensory experience. Additionally, they have been examining the computational mechanisms of high-level vision by using representational similarity analysis to evaluate how well deep convolutional neural networks capture the neural and behavioral geometries of dynamic, naturalistic face processing.

papers.title: Shared connectome and organization in the human cortex irrespective of sensory experience
papers.abstract: This study employs a naturalistic movie-viewing paradigm (using adapted audio and video versions of 101 Dalmatians) to examine the extent to which the functional architecture of the high-level human cortex is dependent on sensory experience. By applying connectivity hyperalignment to functional MRI data from congenitally blind and deaf individuals, we demonstrate that category-selective functional topographies, particularly in the ventral visual pathway, develop and organize into a shared latent space regardless of prior visual or auditory input. Our findings reveal that the fundamental connectome organization associated with specialized processing is largely conserved across modalities, suggesting that the cortical infrastructure for high-level representations can emerge independently of specific sensory experiences.
papers.authors: Jiahui Guo, Francesca Setti, Ma Feilong, Davide Bottari, Maria Ida Gobbini, Pietro Pietrini, Emiliano Ricciardi, James V. Haxby

papers.title: Modeling naturalistic face processing in humans with deep convolutional neural networks
papers.abstract: This research evaluates the efficacy of deep convolutional neural networks (DCNNs) as computational models for the neural and cognitive processing of dynamic, naturalistic faces. Using a large-scale dataset of 707 naturalistic face video clips, we conducted representational similarity analysis (RSA) across DCNN layers, human behavioral arrangements, and fMRI-measured neural responses in face-selective regions. Results indicate that late-intermediate DCNN layers effectively capture categorical face attributes (e.g., age, gender, expression) that align with human behavioral and neural geometries. Conversely, the final fully connected layers, optimized for identity discrimination, show significantly weaker correlations with human brain and behavioral data, suggesting that current DCNN architectures do not fully replicate the mechanisms underlying human face individuation and dynamic feature processing.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS)
papers.authors: Jiahui Guo, Ma Feilong, Matteo Visconti di Oleggio Castello, Samuel A. Nastase, James V. Haxby, M. Ida Gobbini

papers.title: A normative database for specialized functional topographies
papers.abstract: We present a novel computational framework and a normative database designed to estimate individualized functional brain topographies using naturalistic movie stimuli. By utilizing connectivity hyperalignment (CHA) to map idiosyncratic functional architectures into a shared high-dimensional model, we can predict participant-specific, category-selective regions (e.g., face, place, and body-selective areas) from resting-state or naturalistic viewing data. Our methodology demonstrates that movie-based predictions achieve high fidelity, frequently exceeding the reliability of traditional functional localizer scans. This database serves as a resource for precisely localizing specialized cortical regions in individual brains across diverse datasets, facilitating the study of fine-grained functional organization and individual differences.
papers.authors: Jiahui Guo, Ma Feilong, Samuel A. Nastase, James V. Haxby, M. Ida Gobbini

papers.title: The Individualized Neural Tuning Model: Precise and generalizable cartography of functional architecture in individual brains
papers.abstract: We introduce the Individualized Neural Tuning (INT) model, a generative framework that characterizes brain functional architecture through a shared stimulus matrix and individual-specific neural tuning matrices. This model enables the precise mapping of individualized functional topographies, including category-selective regions and retinotopic maps, from high-dimensional neural responses to naturalistic stimuli. Our experiments demonstrate that the INT model accurately predicts individualized, fine-grained response patterns to novel stimuli and effectively quantifies inter-individual variability in functional organization. The model provides a robust solution for aligning idiosyncratic brain topographies into a common representational space while preserving individual-specific functional granularity.
papers.authors: Ma Feilong, Samuel A. Nastase, Jiahui Guo, Yaroslav O. Halchenko, M. Ida Gobbini, James V. Haxby

0309.name: Jian Chen
0309.department: Department of Computer Science and Engineering
0309.bio: Jian Chen is an Associate Professor in the Department of Computer Science and Engineering at The Ohio State University and directs the Interactive Visual Computing Lab. Chen’s research integrates vision science and human-centered computing to design immersive 3D visualizations and interactive metaphors for data exploration. They utilize cognitive and perceptual experiments alongside mathematical modeling to quantify how humans process global configurations, such as ensembles and gist, within large-scale datasets. This work is applied to neuroscience and brain imaging, focusing on the representation of spatially complex biological information.
0309.research_direction: Dr. Chen's recent work explores the intersection of human visual perception and machine visual intelligence, particularly focusing on how information is extracted from complex graphical displays. They have recently been investigating the visual literacy of artificial agents, comparing the chart-reading behaviors and ratio-estimation capabilities of CNNs and multimodal large language models against human benchmarks across varying data distributions. In parallel, their research examines the perceptual mechanics of visualization design, utilizing crowdsourced behavioral experiments to probe how low-level image statistics govern perceived visual complexity and testing how separable visual dimensions—such as paired length and texture—can optimize the display of high-dynamic-range 3D scientific data. Furthermore, Dr. Chen is studying expert visual search in applied clinical settings, combining extensive eye-tracking and interactive mouse-tracking data to model the visual navigation strategies, perceptual bottlenecks, and diagnostic errors of pathologists examining gigapixel medical images.

papers.title: A Rigorous Behavior Assessment of CNNs Using a Data-Domain Sampling Regime
papers.abstract: This research introduces a data-domain sampling framework designed to quantitatively assess the graphical perception capabilities of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). Focusing on ratio estimation tasks within bar charts, the authors evaluate CNN behavior across three critical dimensions: sensitivity to distributional shifts between training and test sets, stability under low-sample constraints, and comparative performance against human observational benchmarks. Analyzing 16 million trials from 800 CNN models and 6,825 human trials, the study demonstrates that CNN biases and performance levels are fundamentally governed by the distance between training and test distributions. The findings suggest that CNNs can achieve human-expert performance in visual decoding when the training domain is appropriately formalized, providing a reusable methodology for comparing human and machine visual intelligence.
papers.venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
papers.authors: Shuning Jiang, Wei-Lun Chao, Daniel Haehn, Hanspeter Pfister, Jian Chen

papers.title: What Makes a Visualization Image Complex?
papers.abstract: The authors investigate the factors influencing the perceived visual complexity (VC) of data visualizations through a large-scale crowdsourcing experiment involving 1,800 images and 349 participants. The analysis examines how 12 objective image-based metrics—spanning information-theoretic, clutter, color, and object-based measures—align with human complexity scores. Results indicate that perceived VC is modulated by both low-level image statistics, such as corner counts and distinct color frequencies, and high-level structural elements. Feature congestion, an information-theoretic metric capturing color and texture patterns, serves as a primary predictor for visualizations with high continuous stimuli, while edge density effectively predicts complexity in node-link diagrams. Furthermore, a non-linear "bell-curve" relationship was identified for text annotations: an initial increase in the text-to-ink ratio (TiR) reduces complexity by providing context, but excessive text eventually complicates the visual field.
papers.venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
papers.authors: Mengdi Chu, Zefeng Qiu, Meng Ling, Shuning Jiang, Robert S. Laramee, Michael Sedlmair, Jian Chen

papers.title: GPT-5 Model Corrected GPT-4V's Chart Reading Errors, Not Prompting
papers.abstract: We present a quantitative evaluation of zero-shot large language model (LLM) performance on chart reading tasks, comparing the agentic GPT-5 model against the multimodal GPT-4V. The study probes model capabilities using 107 visualization-based questions derived from the CHART-6 benchmark where GPT-4V previously failed. By analyzing the interplay between model architecture and prompt engineering, the results show that advancements in the underlying model (GPT-5) are the dominant driver of increased inference accuracy, whereas prompt variations yielded only marginal effects. The study quantifies the evolving visual literacy of artificial agents and highlights a significant narrowing of the performance gap between artificial models and human observers in complex graphical reasoning tasks.
papers.authors: Kaichun Yang, Jian Chen

papers.title: Eye-Tracking, Mouse Tracking, Stimulus Tracking, and Decision-Making Datasets in Digital Pathology
papers.abstract: Interpretation of giga-pixel whole-slide images (WSIs) remains a critical yet error-prone process in pathology, with diagnostic accuracy averaging approximately 70%. This work introduces PathoGaze1.0, a comprehensive behavioral dataset capturing the dynamic visual search and decision-making processes of 19 pathologists during cancer diagnosis. The dataset comprises 18.69 hours of eye-tracking (171,909 fixations), mouse interaction (1,867,362 events), and viewport navigation data (EMSVD) across 397 WSIs. By emphasizing ecological validity through the PTAH application-grounded testbed, the authors provide the multimodal evidence necessary to model inter-observer inconsistencies and search-related diagnostic errors. This resource facilitates the development of AI assistive tools and training protocols aligned with expert perceptual and interactive workflows in clinical pathology.
papers.authors: Veronica Thai, Rui Li, Meng Ling, Shuning Jiang, Jeremy Wolfe, Raghu Machiraju, Yan Hu, Zaibo Li, Anil Parwani, Jian Chen

papers.title: Evaluating Glyph Design for Showing Large-Magnitude-Range Quantum Spins
papers.abstract: This research addresses the challenge of visualizing quantum spin data characterized by high dynamic ranges through the empirical evaluation of bivariate glyph designs. Grounded in perception science theories—including integral and separable dimensions and preattentive scene features—the study investigates how pairs of visual channels influence task performance. Experimental results validate that bivariate glyphs encoded with highly separable dimensions, specifically length-color and length-texture pairs, significantly improve completion times and accuracy for comparison tasks. Key findings include a ranked order of separable variables for 3D glyph design and the identification of categorical representations within bivariate mappings as a mechanism to reveal global structures. This work contributes to the design of perceptually accurate representations for reveals patterns in large-scale scientific datasets.
papers.venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
papers.authors: Henan Zhao, Garnett W. Bryant, Wesley Griffin, Judith E. Terrill, Jian Chen

0310.name: Jiawei Zhou
0310.department: School of Ophthalmology and Optometry, Eye Hospital
0310.lab_name: Lab of Visual Deficits and Visual Rehabilitation
0310.bio: Jiawei Zhou is a Professor and Principal Investigator at Wenzhou Medical University, where they direct the Lab of Visual Deficits and Visual Rehabilitation and the Zhejiang-Canada Joint Translational Visual Cognition Laboratory. Zhou’s research focuses on the neural mechanisms of visual information processing and ocular dominance plasticity, specifically regarding amblyopia, strabismus, and myopia. Utilizing high-resolution 7T fMRI and psychophysical paradigms, Zhou investigates the dynamics of interocular suppression and sensory eye dominance to develop binocular treatments and perceptual learning protocols. Previously a postdoctoral researcher at McGill University, Zhou works in the fields of amblyopia treatment and visual rehabilitation.
0310.research_direction: Dr. Zhou has recently been investigating the mechanisms underlying binocular imbalance and exploring both traditional and emerging therapies for amblyopia across the lifespan. Their recent work surveys the evolving clinical landscape of amblyopia management, analyzing broad methodological shifts toward digitally mediated neuromodulation while also evaluating the optimal timing for conventional pediatric interventions like occlusion therapy. At the psychophysical level, they are assessing whether higher-order binocular functions, such as dynamic stereopsis, remain deficient in patients whose monocular visual acuity has already been successfully restored. Additionally, Dr. Zhou is testing novel, non-invasive paradigms to dynamically modulate interocular suppression and rebalance sensory eye dominance in adults, specifically examining the therapeutic potential of monocular contrast sensitivity perceptual learning and temporally modulated flicker during binocular rivalry.

papers.title: Research hotspots and trends of amblyopia treatment from 2015 to 2025: a bibliometric analysis
papers.abstract: A systematic bibliometric evaluation of amblyopia treatment trends between 2015 and 2025 was conducted using CiteSpace to analyze metadata from Web of Science Core Collection and PubMed. Analysis of 514 publications revealed a significant temporal shift from traditional occlusion therapies toward digital binocular interventions and perceptual learning paradigms. The study identifies a surge in clinical trials validating technologically-mediated neuromodulation therapies, with the United States and China emerging as the primary contributors to the evolving research landscape characterized by personalized and technologically optimized treatments.
papers.authors: Chenyan Zhou, Xiaoru Li, Xiaoliang Luo, Shuning Song, Lvchun Wang, Junpeng Huang, Xiaobing Zhang, Die Liu, Yong Chai, Jiawei Zhou

papers.title: Dynamic Stereopsis Is Abnormal in Treated Anisometropic Amblyopia
papers.abstract: This study assessed dynamic binocular disparity processing in anisometropic amblyopes who had achieved clinical visual acuity normalization (BCVA ≤ 0.1 logMAR) following successful patching therapy. Using lateral motion Gabor elements across a range of speeds (0.17–5.33°/s), the researchers quantified stereo sensitivity via a staircase method. Results demonstrated that while speed tuning profiles remained intact across all groups, treated amblyopes exhibited significantly attenuated dynamic stereo sensitivity compared to both emmetropic and non-amblyopic anisometropic controls, indicating that higher-level binocular deficits persist despite the restoration of monocular optotype acuity.
papers.authors: Yiya Chen, Yao Chen, Robert F Hess, Jiawei Zhou

papers.title: Monocular Contrast Sensitivity Visual Perceptual Learning Rebalances Adult Amblyopes’ Two Eyes
papers.abstract: The research investigated whether monocular contrast sensitivity visual perceptual learning (vPL) can rebalance interocular dominance in adults with binocular imbalances. Participants, including anisometropic amblyopes and myopic anisometropes, underwent a 10-day 2AFC contrast detection training regimen at 6 cpd using the amblyopic or non-dominant eye. Post-training psychophysical assessments revealed significant enhancements in monocular contrast sensitivity and a shift in the binocular balance point at both the trained and neighboring spatial frequencies. While visual acuity improved in both eyes, binocular summation ratios remained unchanged, suggesting that monocular vPL effectively modulates interocular suppression mechanisms to improve binocular fusion.
papers.authors: Wenman Lin, Zhifen He, Shiqi Zhou, Liuqing Weng, Liying Zou, Renhao Ye, Jinli Zhu, Fan Lu, Jiawei Zhou

papers.title: New advances in amblyopia therapy: early patching is more effective than extended optical treatment
papers.abstract: This clinical commentary evaluates recent evidence regarding the optimal timing for initiating occlusion therapy in pediatric amblyopia. Synthesizing data from contemporary trials, the authors argue that early commencement of patching (within weeks of refractive correction) yields superior visual outcomes compared to the traditional approach of extended optical treatment alone. The article emphasizes that immediate intervention leverages greater neuroplasticity in the developing visual system, recommending a shift toward more proactive management strategies in pediatric ophthalmology to improve long-term visual recovery.
papers.authors: Shiqi Zhou, Jiawei Zhou

papers.title: Effects of Monocular Flicker on Binocular Imbalance in Amblyopic and Nonamblyopic Adults
papers.abstract: To investigate the regulatory effects of temporal modulation on binocular balance, this study examined how monocular flicker influences initial eye dominance in amblyopic and nonamblyopic adults. Utilizing an onset binocular rivalry paradigm with varying temporal and spatial frequency parameters, the researchers demonstrated that high-frequency monocular flicker in the non-dominant eye effectively shifted the binocular balance toward the other eye, with the magnitude of the shift showing a clear dependence on temporal frequency. These findings suggest that monocular temporal flicker can dynamically adjust the net balance of interocular suppression, offering a potential non-invasive tool for regulating sensory eye dominance.
papers.authors: Yiqiu Lu, Liying Zou, Wenjing Wang, Ruyin Chen, Jia Qu, Jiawei Zhou

0311.name: jiayu Zhan
0311.department: School of Psychological and Cognitive Sciences
0311.bio: Jiayu Zhan is an Assistant Professor at Peking University's School of Psychological and Cognitive Sciences and the Institute for Artificial Intelligence. Their research examines the computational and neural mechanisms of visual cognition, specifically the representation and categorization of complex social stimuli such as faces and dynamic expressions. Zhan has developed frameworks to quantify task-relevant information within brain activity and contributed to the identification of a specialized third visual pathway for dynamic social perception. Their work also bridges cognitive neuroscience and artificial intelligence by investigating the grounding of abstract concepts and human values within large language models.
0311.research_direction: Dr. Zhan has recently been investigating the underlying cognitive and computational architectures of facial expression recognition. Their recent work explores whether the visual system processes facial action units and discrete emotion categories through parallel or sequential pathways by comparing multi-task and pipelined convolutional neural networks. To understand individual differences in emotion perception, they are also examining potential gender-based modulations in how facial affect is structured and processed. By combining high-fidelity 3D facial datasets with representational similarity analysis, their research bridges computational modeling and cognitive psychology to map the mechanistic frameworks driving how humans perceive emotion in faces.

papers.title: CoEmo: Modeling Cognitive Processes in Facial Expression Recognition through Action Units and Gender Perspectives
papers.abstract: This research examines the underlying cognitive architecture of facial expression recognition at the interface of computational modeling and cognitive psychology. Specifically, the study investigates whether facial action units (AUs) and discrete emotion categories are processed through parallel or sequential neural frameworks and evaluates potential gender-based modulations of these processes. By developing a high-fidelity 3D facial dataset with comprehensive AU amplitude and emotion annotations, the authors contrast parallel and sequential architectures implemented via multi-task learning and pipelined convolutional neural networks (CNNs). Performance metrics indicate that the parallel processing model (F1 = 42.9%) significantly surpasses the sequential model (F1 = 17.1%), corroborating the parallel processing hypothesis. Representational similarity analysis (RSA) further characterizes sex-specific representational structures: female emotion recognition demonstrates alignment with social-distance metrics between emotions, whereas male performance is uniquely driven by representations of anger. These results provide evidence for parallelism as a primary cognitive mechanism and reveal distinct gender-related differences in the neural representation of facial affect.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the 47th Annual Meeting of the Cognitive Science Society (CogSci 2025)
papers.authors: Shangjing Huang, Xiaoxue Gao, Jing Wang, Yuankun Fang, Jiani Zhang, Shiwei Qiu, Jialu Ouyang, Xiaolin Zhou, Fujia Wang, Jiayu Zhan

0312.name: Jifan Zhou
0312.department: Department of Psychology and Behavioral Sciences
0312.bio: Zhou is a Professor and doctoral supervisor at Zhejiang University, where their research focuses on the cognitive architecture of visual working memory (VWM) and its interaction with attentional mechanisms. Their work explores how mental representations in VWM guide visual search behaviors and the storage of dynamic relations between functional objects. Zhou also investigates phenomena such as attribute amnesia and the postdictive effects of choice on attention, applying interdisciplinary approaches that link cognitive psychology with artificial intelligence to model human information processing.
0312.research_direction: Dr. Zhou has recently been investigating the cognitive mechanisms underlying how we sample the visual environment and how we represent the viewpoints of others. In the domain of working memory, their recent work explores how individuals voluntarily balance relying on internal storage versus physically resampling the external world when faced with varying sampling costs and time pressures. Additionally, they are examining the architecture of spontaneous visual perspective-taking by using spatial judgment tasks to test whether our ability to automatically adopt another’s viewpoint reflects a genuine perceptual simulation or a rule-based heuristic inference grounded in naive optics. To further unpack these socio-perceptual processes, Dr. Zhou also investigates the specific causal cues that trigger perspective-taking, testing whether human-like action sequences—such as gazing at an object before reaching for it—are sufficient to induce this phenomenon even toward distinctly non-human agents.

papers.title: Regulating Memory Use: Individual Differences in Working Memory Capacity in Natural Tasks
papers.abstract: This study examines how individuals with different working memory (WM) capacities voluntarily regulate the balance between relying on internal memory versus re-sampling the external world, in tasks where memory use is not experimentally forced. Across two experiments (N = 120), participants completed a copying task and a change-detection task; Experiment 1 increased the cost of resampling the display to push participants toward greater reliance on internal storage, while Experiment 2 imposed time pressure to increase demands for consistent memory use across trials. Raising sampling cost increased overall memory use but did not amplify individual differences in WM capacity as measured by mean memory usage. Time pressure, by contrast, revealed a reliable link between WM capacity and the trial-to-trial consistency of memory use, with higher-capacity individuals showing more stable reliance on memory across sampling episodes. The findings indicate that WM capacity shapes voluntary memory regulation not primarily by increasing how much is remembered, but by governing how consistently memory use is deployed under varying task demands.
papers.authors: Xutao Zheng, Mowei Shen, Hui Chen, Jifan Zhou

papers.title: I'll believe it unless it's too absurd: Spontaneous visual perspective-taking as prior-based heuristic inference
papers.abstract: This work adjudicates between two competing accounts of spontaneous visual perspective-taking (VPT)—the ability to automatically represent what another agent sees—by testing whether VPT reflects genuine perceptual simulation of the other's viewpoint or a heuristic, symbolic inference grounded in naive optics. Across two experiments, participants performed a line-length judgment task that was irrelevant to another agent's perspective, while being given prior visual information from the agent's viewpoint that was either plausible, absent, or implausible given the scene geometry. A robust perspective-consistent bias emerged when the prior was plausible, no bias emerged when no prior was given, and only a weaker, partially attenuated bias emerged when the prior was implausible. This graded sensitivity to the plausibility of the agent's purported viewpoint—rather than an all-or-none simulation of the other's visual experience—supports the heuristic-inference account, in which spontaneous VPT arises from reasoning about naive optical plausibility rather than from reconstructing another's actual perceptual experience.
papers.authors: Xucong Hu, Yitong Zheng, Qinyi Hu, Hui Chen, Mowei Shen, Jifan Zhou

papers.title: Good to see you R2-D2: Inducing spontaneous perspective-taking towards non-human agents through human-like gaze and reach
papers.abstract: This study asks whether spontaneous visual perspective-taking (VPT), typically studied with human or human-like agents, can be induced toward clearly non-human-looking agents if those agents display human-like behaviors. Across four experiments, agents with non-human appearance were given combinations of two human-like actions—gazing toward an object and reaching for it—that are behaviorally diagnostic of perceiving and acting on the environment. Non-human agents elicited spontaneous perspective-taking effects when they exhibited both gaze and reach, but this effect depended critically on temporal order: perspective-taking was sustained only when gaze preceded reach, consistent with the causal structure in which visually guided reaching is the behavioral consequence of prior perception. The results indicate that human-like appearance is not necessary to trigger spontaneous VPT; rather, displaying causally ordered, human-like perception-action sequences is sufficient, suggesting VPT is driven by inferred behavioral/causal cues rather than by surface visual similarity to a human.
papers.authors: Xucong Hu, Haokui Xu, Hui Chen, Mowei Shen, Jifan Zhou

0313.name: Joan Danielle K. Ongchoco
0313.bio: Joan Danielle K. Ongchoco is an Assistant Professor at the University of British Columbia and the Director of the UBC Perception & Cognition Lab. Ongchoco's research focuses on the interface between perception and higher-level cognition, specifically investigating how the mind constructs discrete objects and events from continuous sensory input. They study the phenomenon of 'scaffolded attention' and how event segmentation influences various mental processes, including memory, decision-making, and the subjective experience of time. Their work utilizes psychophysical methods and computational modeling to explore how perceptual structures shape human thought and imagination.
0313.research_direction: Dr. Ongchoco's recent work explores how the human mind structures incoming visual and conceptual information, using both psychophysical paradigms and computational modeling to investigate phenomena ranging from time perception to bounded decision-making. In the visual domain, they have recently been examining how low-level luminance features drive "scaffolded attention" to produce everyday hallucinations on uniform grids, and whether the subjective time dilation caused by temporal oddballs spills over into the perception of subsequent events. Their research also investigates mid-level perceptual organization, probing whether the visual system automatically tracks and prioritizes unfinished spatiotemporal trajectories to create a "visual Zeigarnik effect." Beyond perceptual processing, Dr. Ongchoco uses frameworks like partially observable Markov decision processes to explore higher-level cognition, modeling how individuals adapt their deliberative thinking plans to complex reward structures and how agents navigate epistemically transformative shifts in their environments.

papers.title: Are you a visual “shader” or a “bolder”? Different visual routines create everyday hallucinations in “scaffolded attention”
papers.abstract: In scaffolded attention, observers inspecting regular, uniform grids spontaneously perceive illusory shapes and contours devoid of corresponding sensory input—a form of non-clinical, everyday hallucination. Observers typically report either subjective luminance and color modulations within grid cells ('shading') or illusory boundary tracing and accentuation along intersecting grid lines ('bolding'). Across 100 participants tested via an interactive grid paradigm, this study characterized the prevalence, phenomenology, and stimulus dependencies of these distinct visual routines. The qualitative nature of the hallucinated percepts was strongly contingent upon grid luminance polarity: 89% of hallucinating observers reported bolding on dark grids with light backgrounds, whereas only 36% reported bolding on light grids with dark backgrounds. These results demonstrate that low-level luminance contrast and figure-ground segmentation modulate the initial selection of either surface units or boundary networks, thereby governing the specific emergent visual routines that produce scaffolded attention.
papers.authors: Andrea S. Ying, Joan Danielle K. Ongchoco

papers.title: The spontaneous prioritization of "unfinishedness" in perception: A visual Zeigarnik effect
papers.abstract: The persistence of unfinished tasks in conscious thought and memory is known as the Zeigarnik effect, typically explained through high-level motivational commitments or goal representations. Across four psychophysical experiments (N = 120), this investigation evaluated whether incomplete visual structures are intrinsically prioritized during early- to mid-level perceptual processing independently of higher-level motivational factors. Observers tracked dynamic paths traveling through visual mazes from origin to destination while visual probes flashed briefly along each route, subsequently requiring metric spatial reproduction. Paths either traversed fully to the destination or halted abruptly prior to completion, rendering them visually unfinished. Despite the task irrelevance of event completion, spatial reproductions showed significantly higher precision on unfinished trials compared to completed trajectories. This spatial localization advantage persisted when controlling for low-level visual kinematics, terminal positions, and display configurations. These findings reveal a visual Zeigarnik effect, showing that the visual system automatically extracts event completeness and prioritizes unfinished spatiotemporal events during percept formation.
papers.authors: Joan Danielle K. Ongchoco, Kimberly W. Wong, Brian J. Scholl

papers.title: When New Experience Leads to New Knowledge: A Computational Framework for Formalizing Epistemically Transformative Experiences
papers.abstract: Epistemically transformative experiences (ETEs) are phenomenologically and epistemically distinctive events that impart knowledge an agent could not have acquired or accurately simulated through prior experience alone. Here, the distinction between epistemically transformative and non-transformative learning is formalized using partially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs). Using a simulated Flatland-style navigation task, learning efficiency was evaluated as an artificial agent transitioned from a two-dimensional grid space to either an expanded two-dimensional environment (epistemically non-transformative) or a three-dimensional domain (epistemically transformative). Under non-transformative conditions, behavioral policies and latent state spaces learned in initial environments transfer efficiently to accelerate reinforcement learning. In contrast, under transformative transitions, prior policy representations offer negligible benefit and require structural reorganization to acquire novel behavioral competencies. This computational architecture demonstrates how formal decision-theoretic and probabilistic frameworks can operationalize qualitative philosophical distinctions concerning epistemic change.
papers.venue: Open Mind: Discoveries in Cognitive Science
papers.authors: Joan Danielle K. Ongchoco, Isaac M. Davis, Julian Jara-Ettinger, L. A. Paul

papers.title: People's thinking plans adapt to the problem they're trying to solve
papers.abstract: In high-dimensional decision spaces where exhaustive evaluation is computationally intractable, decision-makers often exhibit a good-action bias by selectively simulating actions associated with high prior expected value. Across five preregistered behavioral experiments and computational simulations, this study tested whether deliberative simulation strategies flexibly adapt to task demands or reflect a rigid cognitive heuristic. When evaluating options in environments characterized by additive reward structures, participants preferentially simulated high-value alternatives (Experiments 1 and 2). However, when utility structures introduced critical minimum thresholds or catastrophic low-value risks, participants rapidly and adaptively redirected their deliberation toward low-value options (Experiments 3–5). Computational modeling shows that this problem-contingent shift in simulation priority is resource-rational, maximizing expected utility under bounded cognitive resources by sampling options that offer the highest reduction in outcome uncertainty.
papers.authors: Joan Danielle K. Ongchoco, Joshua Knobe, Julian Jara-Ettinger

papers.title: What's next?: Time is subjectively dilated not only for 'oddball' events, but also for events immediately after oddballs
papers.abstract: Subjective time is notoriously elastic, as demonstrated by the temporal oddball effect where low-probability stimuli embedded within a sequence of identical standards are perceived as lasting substantially longer than their objective duration.
