Across psychophysical reproduction experiments using sequential multi-colored visual stimuli with variable intervals, this study investigated the temporal boundary conditions of this perceptual dilation: whether subjective temporal distortion is strictly object-bound to the oddball or propagates downstream. The data show that subjective time dilation reliably occurs both for the oddball item and for the subsequent standard stimulus appearing immediately afterward. This forward temporal spillover demonstrates that oddball-induced dilation is not driven solely by enhanced retrospective encoding of the deviant stimulus, but reflects prospective attentional upregulation and temporal uncertainty regarding upcoming sequence dynamics that persist until post-oddball regularities are re-established.
papers.authors: Joan Danielle K. Ongchoco, Kimberly W. Wong, Brian J. Scholl

0314.name: Joan López-Moliner
0314.department: Department of Cognition, Development, and Psychology of Education
0314.lab_name: Vision and Control of Action (VISCA) Group
0314.bio: Joan López-Moliner is a Full Professor at the Universitat de Barcelona and a researcher at the Institute of Neurosciences (ubNeuro). Their research examines how the human visual system processes information for motor tasks, such as object interception or navigation, through computational modeling and optimal decision-making frameworks. Using psychophysics, 3D virtual reality, and eye tracking, López-Moliner investigates the integration of sensory feedback with internal priors—such as gravity—to explain the precision of human interceptive actions. Their current work focuses on motion-in-depth perception, optic flow, and the adaptation of perceptual systems to augmented and virtual realities.
0314.research_direction: Dr. López-Moliner’s recent work explores how the visual system processes motion, timing, and environmental priors to guide action under perceptual uncertainty. They have recently been investigating interceptive behaviors and Time-to-Contact estimation, using immersive virtual reality and eye tracking to test how humans balance online sensory inputs with internalized physical rules, such as gravity, when tracking and catching moving targets. In the domain of spatial navigation, their research examines how the brain interprets complex optic flow geometry, specifically exploring how the rotational retinal curl induced by gaze stabilization is utilized for heading estimation. Additionally, they are developing new computational and psychophysical approaches to quantify perceptual noise, seeking to characterize single-trial subjective uncertainty in time perception and to compare the underlying precision of smooth pursuit for lateral versus in-depth motion.

papers.title: Beyond the Focus of Expansion: Retinal curl as a functional signal for heading estimation
papers.abstract: This research challenges the prevailing Focus of Expansion (FOE) recovery paradigm in heading estimation, proposing instead that the visual system functionalizes retinal curl—the rotational flow component resulting from gaze stabilization—rather than treating it as a nuisance signal to be filtered. In a series of experiments using a large-scale virtual environment, stationary participants reported perceived heading while fixating on ground targets at various eccentricities, a behavior that induces sustained retinal curl. By employing real-time manipulations that intactly preserved, cancelled, or over-cancelled the foveal curl component, the study demonstrated that systematic heading biases are directly driven by the magnitude of retinal curl. The results were modeled using a feedback controller integrated with a ring-attractor neural network featuring gaze-contingent inhibition and a straight-ahead prior. These findings suggest that the brain exploits the inherent geometry of gaze stabilization to simplify navigation, utilizing retinal curl as a functional control signal rather than explicitly recovering the FOE from a filtered flow field.
papers.authors: Kontessa I. Zorpala, Joan López-Moliner

papers.title: The predictive outfielder: a critical test across gravities
papers.abstract: This study critiques traditional interception models, such as the Gaze-Angle Strategy, which rely on closed-loop heuristics coupling optic variables directly to locomotion without internalizing environmental dynamics. The authors propose a novel predictive model that integrates optic variables (e.g., elevation angle and expansion rate) with internalized physical constants—specifically gravity and target size—to continuously update estimates of a target's 3D landing position and remaining flight time. Utilizing an immersive virtual reality framework, the researchers manipulated simulated gravitational acceleration and ball size to create conditions where heuristic and predictive strategies produce divergent trajectories. The empirical findings, including the observed kinematic patterns and timing responses of the participants, aligned significantly better with the predictive strategy. This indicates that human interceptive behavior is guided by a prospective controller that utilizes internalized gravitational priors to compensate for sensorimotor delays and optimize spatial and temporal precision in catching tasks.
papers.authors: Borja Aguado, Joan López-Moliner

papers.title: A comparative analysis of perceptual noise in lateral and depth motion: Evidence from eye tracking
papers.abstract: This research evaluates the precision of visual speed perception for lateral and in-depth motion by characterizing observational uncertainty through smooth pursuit eye tracking. Applying a smooth pursuit model based on a Kalman filter and inverse optimal control theory, the study quantifies speed uncertainty across various motion dynamics, including random walk, linear, and nonlinear trajectories. While prior psychophysical discrimination tasks have frequently reported significantly higher thresholds for motion-in-depth compared to fronto-parallel motion, this work demonstrates that when velocity-based information facilitates position prediction, perceptual uncertainties for depth and lateral motion become largely consistent. The study distinguishes between additive and multiplicative noise components, identifying additive noise as the primary driver of uncertainty in both dimensions. These results challenge the assumption of a fundamental sensitivity deficit for motion-in-depth and reconcile the discrepancy between laboratory-based perceptual thresholds and the high precision exhibited in real-world visually guided actions.
papers.authors: Joan López-Moliner

papers.title: Quantifying uncertainty in time perception: A modified reproduction method
papers.abstract: This paper introduces a novel 'temporal bracketing' methodology designed to estimate subjective uncertainty in time perception on a single-trial basis, addressing the limitations of traditional methods that derive uncertainty from cross-trial variability. In this modified reproduction task, participants were instructed to indicate the start and end of a reproduced duration (ranging from 0.6 to 4.0 seconds) by controlling a key press, effectively defining a subjective temporal window. The study validates the bracket width as an efficient metric for temporal uncertainty, showing high correlation with traditional measures of precision. Quantitative analysis of the relative variability at the bracket boundaries suggests the presence of both additive and multiplicative noise components in the timing architecture. This methodological advancement provides a more granular tool for investigating the cognitive mechanisms of time perception, including the simultaneous timing of multiple intervals and the role of metacognitive uncertainty in temporal decision-making.
papers.authors: Jaume Boned, Joan López-Moliner

papers.title: Prediction of time to contact under perceptual and contextual uncertainties
papers.abstract: This study investigates how the human visual system integrates sensory and contextual information to estimate Time-to-Contact (TTC) under varying levels of uncertainty. Using an interceptive task involving simulated flyball trajectories, the researchers manipulated sensory uncertainty by varying target presentation duration and contextual uncertainty by varying the duration of an occlusion period. The analysis of eye-tracking data and manual interceptive errors revealed that high sensory uncertainty (brief presentation) induces a robust center bias in hand movements, suggesting an increased reliance on prior distributions of motion. However, this bias was effectively mitigated by longer presentation durations, even when followed by extended occlusion. The high degree of correlation between eye and hand movement accuracy across different uncertainty levels confirms that the predictive processes guiding these effectors utilize a common readout of motion information, effectively balancing online visual input with internalized priors to solve complex timing tasks.
papers.authors: Pamela Villavicencio, Cristina de la Malla, Joan López-Moliner

0316.name: Jocelyn Faubert
0316.bio: Jocelyn Faubert is a professor of visual perception and cognitive neuroscience at the Université de Montréal, where they direct a multidisciplinary research laboratory focused on human performance. Faubert’s work investigates the neural mechanisms of sensory-cognitive integration, specifically how aging, neurodevelopmental conditions, and traumatic brain injuries affect the processing of complex dynamic scenes. They developed the NeuroTracker system, a 3D multiple-object tracking technology used to assess cognitive load in clinical settings and modify mental performance in athletes. Their research methodology integrates psychophysical testing with immersive virtual reality environments, such as CAVE systems and EON Icube technology, to connect fundamental vision science with real-world applications.
0316.research_direction: Dr. Faubert's recent work explores a wide continuum of visual processing, from computational models of foundational pathways to applied perceptual-cognitive training. They have recently been developing neurophysiologically inspired frameworks to understand basic visual mechanisms, investigating how the retina de-multiplexes overlapping cone signals for color perception and how the dorsal pathway resolves complex biological motion using hierarchical Bayesian models. In parallel, they are utilizing behavioral paradigms like 3D-Multiple Object Tracking and deep learning analysis of large-scale EEG datasets to assess individual differences in perceptual-cognitive function, specifically probing how biological sex, athletic expertise, and neurological pathologies influence neurobehavioral baselines and learning rates. Furthermore, their research translates these perceptual models into clinical applications, exploring how age-related declines in predictive cognition and motion processing can inform the development of real-time, proactive fall prevention technologies for older adults.

papers.title: Critical role of EEG signals in assessment of sex-specific insights in neurological diagnostics via machine learning approach
papers.abstract: This study utilizes artificial deep neural networks to evaluate the detectability of biological sex within electroencephalogram (EEG) signals using extensive datasets of over 12,000 subjects. Applying balanced accuracy (BAcc) as a robust performance metric, the research demonstrates that although sex-related neural patterns are highly consistent and transferable across diverse populations, they play a negligible role as confounders in the machine-learning-based detection of neurological pathologies. The results suggest that sex-specific biomarkers, while prominent in EEG data, do not significantly bias the diagnostic accuracy for pathological states, providing critical insights for the development of equitable AI models in neurological disease prediction.
papers.authors: Mohammad-Javad Darvishi-Bayazi, Mohammad Sajjad Ghaemi, Irina Rish, Jocelyn Faubert

papers.title: The nature of multi-channel color perception from three photodetector types with wide overlapping spectral sensitivity bands
papers.abstract: This research introduces a neurophysiologically inspired physical model for the de-multiplexing of signals from three types of broadband retinal photodetectors (L, M, and S cones) characterized by significant spectral overlap. The framework implements fundamental retinal signal processing principles, specifically the contrast between photoreceptor signals and the ON/OFF antagonistic responses of the neural network, to redirect inputs into separate chromatic channels corresponding to red, green, blue, yellow, and white perception. The proposed method offers a computationally feasible alternative to traditional additive/subtractive models for simulating human-like color coding in spectroscopy and multichannel imaging applications.
papers.authors: Vasile Diaconu, Jocelyn Faubert

papers.title: “Extended Descriptive Risk-Averse Bayesian Model” a More Comprehensive Approach in Simulating Complex Biological Motion Perception
papers.abstract: A hierarchical Bayesian simulation model is proposed to represent the human visual system's dorsal pathway for processing complex biological motion, specifically the perception of soccer kick directions. By incorporating a disremembering strategy and mutual inhibition mechanisms between motion pattern detectors, the model successfully simulates the psychometric functions, angular thresholds, and reaction times of expert athletes. The findings underscore the critical role of rotational optic flow and motion cues, rather than dynamic form, in enabling the robust perception of biological movement from sparse point-light stimuli, matching human behavioral data with high precision.
papers.authors: Khashayar Misaghian, J. Eduardo Lugo, Jocelyn Faubert

papers.title: Immediate fall prevention: the missing key to a comprehensive solution for falling hazard in older adults
papers.abstract: This perspective article identifies a critical gap in geriatric fall prevention, arguing that current solutions lack the necessary predictive technology to intercept falls before impact. The authors propose a framework based on the breakdown of high-level predictive cognitive mechanisms and dorsal pathway motion processing in the aging brain. By utilizing computational models of biological motion perception, the paper advocates for the development of real-time anticipation-interception systems. Such technologies aim to close the gap between life expectancy and wellness expectancy by shifting the focus from post-fall detection to proactive, immediate prevention of hip fractures and related traumas.
papers.authors: Khashayar Misaghian, Jesus Eduardo Lugo, Jocelyn Faubert

papers.title: Gender comparison of perceptual-cognitive learning in young athletes
papers.abstract: This study examines sexual dimorphism in the baseline performance and learning rates of perceptual-cognitive skills in 72 young athletes and non-athletes using a 3D-Multiple Object Tracking (3D-MOT) paradigm. Results indicate that while male athletes achieve significantly higher initial absolute speed thresholds, the learning curves across five training weeks are similar for both sexes and both athlete/non-athlete status. The findings confirm that participating in competitive sports is associated with superior perceptual-cognitive function and suggest that while males may have higher temporal resolution of attention at baseline, the capacity for cognitive enhancement through training is consistent across genders.
papers.authors: Isabelle Legault, Jocelyn Faubert

0317.name: Jochen Triesch
0317.department: Department of Physics and Department of Computer Science and Mathematics, Goethe University Frankfurt
0317.bio: Jochen Triesch holds positions as a Senior Fellow at the Frankfurt Institute for Advanced Studies and a Professor at Goethe University Frankfurt, specializing in the self-organization of intelligent behavior. Triesch developed the 'Active Efficient Coding' framework, which provides a theory for the joint development of sensory coding and motor control in biological systems such as binocular vision. Their research integrates computational modeling, machine learning, and developmental robotics to study how neural circuits adapt through synaptic plasticity and how artificial systems can emulate human-like cognitive development. Triesch currently focuses on developmental artificial intelligence, spiking neural networks, and the mathematical principles governing neural competition for synaptic resources.
0317.research_direction: Dr. Triesch has recently been investigating the intersection of biologically inspired visual learning, embodied sensorimotor development, and synaptic network dynamics. Their recent work explores how biological constraints—such as active foveated vision, dynamic physical growth, and event-driven sensing—can drive autonomous motor skill acquisition and closed-loop oculomotor control in simulated infant models and fully spiking neural networks. Additionally, they are investigating how principles of mammalian visual processing might enhance artificial systems, probing how natural human gaze dynamics influence self-supervised object representation and how subcortical-like, long-range skip connections shape hierarchical compositionality in deep neural networks. At the synaptic level, their research also models the mechanisms of neuronal homeostasis, examining how local competition for shared molecular resources enables recurrent circuits to maintain stable activity across varying timescales.

papers.title: MIMo grows! Simulating body and sensory development in a multimodal infant model
papers.abstract: This study introduces MIMo v2, an expanded multimodal infant model implemented in the MuJoCo physics engine to facilitate the investigation of sensorimotor development. Unlike previous static embodiments, this version incorporates a dynamic growth module that modulates physical size, body mass, and joint actuation capabilities based on longitudinal pediatric data from birth to 24 months. The platform integrates bio-inspired features including a foveated visual system with age-dependent acuity scaling and stochastic sensorimotor latencies that simulate finite signal transmission speeds within the nervous system. The architecture is designed to support the autonomous acquisition of complex motor milestones, such as crawling and self-touch, providing a realistic in silico environment for modeling the co-development of body and mind.
papers.venue: 2025 IEEE International Conference on Development and Learning (ICDL)
papers.authors: Francisco M. López, Miles Lenz, Marco G. Fedozzi, Arthur Aubret, Jochen Triesch

papers.title: Homeostatic regulation across fast and slow timescales through aggregate synaptic dynamics
papers.abstract: The authors propose 'aggregate scaling,' a novel computational framework for neuronal homeostasis that models synapses as competitors for a shared pool of limited molecular building blocks. This approach addresses the discrepancy between the rapid timescales required for theoretical network stability and the slow kinetics of biological homeostatic plasticity (e.g., AMPA receptor trafficking). By integrating the competitive redistribution of these resources with Hebbian learning, the model achieves global stability and prevents runaway excitation in recurrent circuits. The resulting dynamics preserve essential physiological properties, including stable firing rates at homeostatic set-points and log-normal synaptic weight distributions, while reproducing experimental observations of slow-acting compensatory scaling during prolonged activity perturbations.
papers.authors: Petros Evgenios Vlachos, Jochen Triesch

papers.title: Hierarchical Residuals Exploit Brain-Inspired Compositionality
papers.abstract: This paper presents Hierarchical Residual Networks (HiResNets), a deep learning architecture inspired by the multi-level connectivity of the mammalian brain, specifically the direct skip connections from subcortical structures to various stages of the cortical hierarchy. By incorporating long-range residual connections between disparate hierarchical layers, the network is biased toward learning feature maps relative to compressed representations provided by skip links, thereby more effectively exploiting hierarchical compositionality. Experiments across several convolutional benchmarks, including modified ResNet-18 and ResNet-101 architectures, demonstrate that hierarchical residuals significantly improve classification accuracy and accelerate convergence. Analytical results suggest that these long-range projections facilitate more efficient semantic abstraction by providing richer gradient flow and structural priors.
papers.venue: European Symposium on Artificial Neural Networks, Computational Intelligence and Machine Learning (ESANN 2025)
papers.authors: Francisco M. López, Jochen Triesch

papers.title: A spiking neural network for active efficient coding
papers.abstract: The authors develop the first fully spiking implementation of the Active Efficient Coding (AEC) framework, utilizing asynchronous inputs from neuromorphic event-based cameras. The system consists of a two-layer spiking neural network (SNN) that learns to efficiently encode visual features (resembling simple and complex cells in V1) through unsupervised spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP) and homeostatic mechanisms. The population activity of the encoding layers generates an intrinsic reward signal based on coding efficiency, which drives a spiking reinforcement learning agent. This agent learns closed-loop oculomotor control, including visual tracking of translating objects and gaze stabilization on rotating stimuli, without external supervision or extrinsic rewards. This work demonstrates the feasibility of achieving self-calibrating, energy-efficient sensorimotor learning in fully neuromorphic architectures.
papers.authors: Thomas Barbier, Céline Teulière, Jochen Triesch

papers.title: Human Gaze Boosts Object-Centered Representation Learning
papers.abstract: This work investigates how the foveated nature of human vision and active gaze behavior influence the self-supervised learning (SSL) of visual representations. By simulating five months of egocentric visual experience using the Ego4D dataset and human gaze prediction models, the researchers extracted gaze-centered foveal crops to mimic the selective amplification of central visual information. Training a time-contrastive SSL model on these modified streams revealed that focusing on central vision significantly improves the formation of object-centered representations compared to uniform full-field training. The analysis demonstrates that the SSL model successfully leverages the temporal slowness inherent in gaze movements to disentangle foreground objects from backgrounds, providing a critical step toward bio-inspired unsupervised visual learning from natural egocentric data.
papers.authors: Timothy Schaumlöffel, Arthur Aubret, Gemma Roig, Jochen Triesch

0318.name: Jody C. Culham
0318.bio: Jody C. Culham is a Professor of Psychology and the Tier 1 Canada Research Chair in Immersive Neuroscience at Western University. Culham’s research investigates the neural mechanisms underlying visually guided actions, such as reaching, grasping, and tool use, using neuroimaging techniques including functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS). They utilize an immersive neuroscience framework to study brain function through 3D stimuli and naturalistic behaviors in virtual or augmented reality environments. This work focuses on the human parietal cortex and the specialized roles of the dorsal and ventral visual streams in real-world contexts.
0318.research_direction: Dr. Culham's recent work explores how the human brain processes visual, spatial, and social information under naturalistic, ecologically valid conditions. They have recently been using immersive virtual reality and fMRI to investigate how active visuomotor control and cortical representations are influenced by real-world features, such as gravitational kinematics during manual target interception and stereoscopic 3D depth cues during face viewing. Additionally, their research expands into social vision, employing fNIRS to examine how the temporal dynamics of the brain's mentalizing network are modulated by live, two-way conversations versus pre-recorded or avatar-based interactions. Across these distinct topics, Dr. Culham focuses on bridging the gap between reductionist 2D laboratory paradigms and the complex sensory and motor demands of the active, embodied observer.

papers.title: fNIRS reveals that live social interactions and visual realism influence neural responses
papers.abstract: Natural human social discourse requires active mentalizing and Theory of Mind (ToM) processing, yet social neuroscience has predominantly relied on static or pre-recorded stimuli. In this investigation, functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) was used to measure hemodynamic responses across core ToM nodes during two-way interactive conversations. The experimental paradigm systematically varied temporal dynamics (live versus yoked pre-recorded video interactions) and partner visual realism (real human versus an animated Apple Memoji avatar). Deconvolution modeling using finite impulse response functions revealed that pre-recorded conversations elicited significantly prolonged oxyhemoglobin (HbO) responses across regions of interest—including the left temporoparietal junction (lTPJ)—relative to live conversations, reflecting sustained cognitive and communicative effort. Furthermore, multivariate pattern classification in the right temporoparietal junction (rTPJ) dissociated neural responses to real human partners from those to avatars, an effect paralleled by eye-tracking metrics demonstrating a significant gaze preference toward the eye region of human versus avatar faces. These findings demonstrate that both real-time social presence and physical visual realism modulate the recruitment and spatiotemporal dynamics of the human mentalizing network.
papers.authors: Michaela Kent, Eva Deligiannis, Kevin M. Stubbs, Karsten Babin, Emma G. Duerden, Jody C. Culham

papers.title: Bringing Vision Science Closer to the Real World
papers.abstract: While reductionist laboratory paradigms and low-dimensional artificial stimuli have yielded substantial insight into early- and mid-level feature representations, characterizing the computational architecture of high-level visual cognition requires closer alignment with real-world complexity. This review delineates theoretical and methodological frameworks to bridge laboratory vision science and naturalistic environments. Key approaches include implementing rich, multi-attribute 3D stimuli and ethologically grounded tasks; employing immersive extended and virtual reality (VR) technologies that maintain veridical egocentric visual geometry, motion parallax, and stereoscopic disparity; acknowledging the human participant as an active, embodied agent engaged in continuous closed-loop sensorimotor control rather than a passive observer; integrating ecological goals shaped by evolution and ontogenetic development into biological and artificial neural network (ANN) models; and adopting multivariate analytical techniques that treat natural spatial and temporal scene variance as informative signal rather than confounding noise. Together, these strategies highlight how immersive neuroscience can advance models of human visual perception and visually guided action.
papers.authors: Jody C. Culham, Eva Deligiannis

papers.title: Binocular cues to 3D face structure increase activation in depth-selective visual cortex with negligible effects in face-selective areas
papers.abstract: Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) studies of human face processing typically use 2D planar images that lack stereoscopic binocular disparity cues. To test whether binocular 3D structural cues modulate cortical face representations, fMRI was acquired while participants viewed orthostereoscopically presented facial images configured with real-world viewing geometry across four conditions: veridical stereoscopic 3D, zero binocular disparity (2D), pseudoscopic 3D (reversed binocular disparity), and monocular 2D. In depth-selective occipitoparietal cortex—including areas V3A, V3B, IPS0, IPS1, and hMT+—stereoscopic 3D faces evoked significantly greater univariate blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) activation levels and distinctive multivariate response patterns compared to flat 2D faces. Conversely, ventral and lateral face-selective regions—including the occipital face area (OFA), fusiform face area (FFA), and posterior superior temporal sulcus (pSTS)—exhibited negligible modulation of activation magnitude or representational patterns by internal binocular disparity. These results demonstrate that while binocular facial geometry recruits dorsal depth-processing streams, category-selective representations within the ventral visual stream remain largely invariant to binocular disparity, validating 2D image proxies for ventral face network investigations.
papers.authors: Eva Deligiannis, Marisa Donnelly, Carol Coricelli, Karsten Babin, Kevin M. Stubbs, Chelsea Ekstrand, Laurie M. Wilcox, Jody C. Culham

papers.title: Target interception in virtual reality is better for natural versus unnatural trajectory shapes and orientations
papers.abstract: Human visual motion processing and interceptive motor control rely on internal forward models of physical kinematics, such as gravitational acceleration (g). Using an immersive virtual reality (VR) platform, this study evaluated how the spatial geometry and orientation of a moving target affect manual interception accuracy and timing. Human participants executed rapid punches to intercept a virtual sphere moving along trajectories that orthogonally varied in contour geometry (parabolic vs. triangular/tent) and orientation (gravitationally upright vs. inverted), while visual fixation was constrained to restrict trajectory presentations entirely to either the lower or upper visual field. Movement initiation times were significantly faster for trajectories adhering to natural gravitational physics (upright and parabolic), independent of visual field. Moreover, spatial error analysis demonstrated that movement endpoints deviated systematically along the predicted path of future target motion for upright orientations, indicating that prior expectations of natural gravitational kinematics modulate both visuomotor planning latency and predictive online trajectory correction.
papers.authors: Sofia Varon, Karsten Babin, Miriam Spering, Jody C. Culham

papers.title: Introduction to the special issue on Visual Cognition and Visuomotor Control: A tribute to Mel Goodale
papers.abstract: This introductory article reviews and synthesizes the collection of empirical studies and theoretical contributions comprising the special issue dedicated to Melvyn A. Goodale. The authors survey the contemporary legacy of the two-visual-streams framework, which posits functional segregation between ventral stream pathways underlying vision-for-perception and dorsal stream networks supporting online vision-for-action. Key thematic topics addressed across the issue include neuropsychological dissociations in visual form agnosia and optic ataxia, the sensorimotor role of haptic and proprioceptive feedback during real versus pantomimed grasp execution, neural substrates of size constancy and visual illusions across development and handedness, human echolocation processing in blind individuals, and the necessity of real-world tangible objects over pictorial displays in sensorimotor neuroimaging.
papers.authors: Jody C. Culham, Gavin Buckingham, Monika Harvey, Irene Sperandio, Ingrid S. Johnsrude

0319.name: Johan Wagemans
0319.bio: Johan Wagemans is a Full Professor at KU Leuven, where they lead the Laboratory of Experimental Psychology and direct long-term Methusalem projects focused on the psychology and neuroscience of visual perception. Wagemans’ research integrates principles of perceptual organization—including symmetry, grouping, and figure-ground segregation—with psychophysics, computational modeling, and neuroimaging. Their work investigates mid-level vision and how the brain constructs representations from complex stimuli. Wagemans applies these findings to the study of atypical perception in autism and the cognitive foundations of visual arts and aesthetics.
0319.research_direction: Dr. Wagemans has recently been investigating visual perception across highly diverse contexts, ranging from sensory deprivation to complex aesthetic appreciation. Their recent work explores the phenomenal and neurophysiological dynamics of the Ganzfeld effect, using immersive spaces, EEG, and eye-tracking to examine how unstructured multimodal input and low-level physiological triggers induce visual hallucinations and perceptual decays. Additionally, they are studying visual category learning and generalization in autism, utilizing artificial multidimensional stimulus spaces to map how autistic adults process visual feedback and prediction errors during novel categorization tasks. Finally, to advance empirical aesthetics, Dr. Wagemans has been developing carefully orthogonalized stimulus datasets of Western paintings, providing researchers with controlled tools to disentangle how artistic style, image content, and emotional valence independently drive aesthetic judgments.

papers.title: The Multifaceted Ganzfeld at the Crossroad Between Visual Perception and Consciousness: Behavioral, Neural and Qualitative Aspects
papers.abstract: This research characterizes the perceptual, phenomenal, and emotional dimensions of the Ganzfeld effect—a state of sensory homogeneity—using a comprehensive multi-methodological framework. By transitioning from traditional Ganzfeld goggles to an immersive Ganzfeld space, the authors assessed the induction of altered states of consciousness (ASCs) through co-registered electroencephalography (EEG) and eye-tracking. The study identifies specific behavioral markers, such as changes in ocular motility and blink rate, that correlate with the emergence of visual and auditory hallucinations. Quantitative questionnaire data and qualitative inductive content analysis of participant interviews reveal that the Ganzfeld environment elicits profound full-body experiences, including sensations of dizziness and imbalance, suggesting a systemic shift in the integration of prior expectations and incoming sensory noise within a predictive coding architecture.
papers.authors: Eleftheria Pistolas, Boris Quétard, Sucharit Katyal, Johan Wagemans

papers.title: Wave after wave: The suggestibility of noise in the experience of multisensory hallucinations under multimodal Ganzfeld stimulation
papers.abstract: The study investigates the frequency and thematic nature of hallucinations elicited by a multimodal Ganzfeld (MMGF) paradigm, combining homogeneous visual stimulation with three auditory noise conditions (no-noise, white-noise, and brown-noise). Utilizing a between-subjects design across laboratory and museum settings, the authors employed inductive content analysis to categorize hallucinatory experiences as unimodal, multisensory, or multimodal. While visual hallucinations were ubiquitous across conditions, the presence of brown noise—characterized by a power spectral density inversely proportional to frequency—specifically facilitated the emergence of water-related auditory and integrated multisensory hallucinations. These results indicate that the spectral profile of auditory noise acts as a suggestible prior that shapes the content of hallucinations, providing empirical evidence for the role of cross-modal integration in unstructured perceptual environments.
papers.authors: Eleftheria Pistolas, Liv Smets, Johan Wagemans

papers.title: Altered category learning and reduced generalization in autistic adults
papers.abstract: This study characterizes the behavioral and neurophysiological profiles of visual category learning and generalization in 38 autistic and 38 neurotypical (NT) adults using an artificial multidimensional stimulus space defined by curvature and aspect ratio. Behavioral results demonstrate that while autistic individuals eventually achieve categorical proficiency, they exhibit significantly slower acquisition rates and reduced accuracy when generalizing to novel stimulus sets. Electrophysiological (EEG) recordings revealed an attenuated N1 component in the right occipitotemporal cortex during early categorization, alongside heightened and delayed frontal activation following negative feedback, suggesting atypical feedback processing and increased sensitivity to prediction errors. Furthermore, the magnitude of the generalization deficit was quantitatively correlated with individual scores on the Intolerance to Uncertainty Scale, suggesting a link between perceptual learning strategies and clinical traits.
papers.authors: Jaana Van Overwalle, Stephanie Van der Donck, Birte Geusens, Bart Boets, Johan Wagemans

papers.title: And then there was light in the ganzfeld: clarifying the methods, experiences, and modulating factors of hallucinations and decays
papers.abstract: This paper provides a critical synthesis and refinement of the Ganzfeld literature, focusing on the terminology and dynamics of visual hallucinations and perceptual decays. Utilizing an immersive Ganzfeld space and a multi-method approach, the authors propose and validate a clear taxonomy for three distinct types of brightness and color decays: 'fade-out', 'black-out', and 'blank-out'. The research investigates the temporal dynamics of these phenomena and their relationship to low-level physiological triggers, such as blinks and eye movements (saccades and convergence). By disentangling these decaying experiences from emergent hallucinations, the study establishes a rigorous methodological foundation for future work investigating the neural correlates of sensory-deprived visual awareness and its relationship to higher-level top-down predictions.
papers.authors: Eleftheria Pistolas, Johan Wagemans

papers.title: Leuven Orthogonalized Art Data Set (LOAD): A Multidimensional Art Image Set for Aesthetic Appreciation Research
papers.abstract: To address the need for controlled stimulus sets in empirical aesthetics, the authors developed the Leuven Orthogonalized Art Data Set (LOAD), comprising 343 Western paintings. The dataset is specifically designed to orthogonalize several key dimensions known to influence aesthetic judgment: artistic style (ranging from Renaissance to Abstract Expressionism), content (human vs. non-human), and emotional valence. Through large-scale validation involving 50 participants per image, the researchers obtained multi-faceted ratings for pleasure, fluency, interest, liking, and familiarity. This structured resource enables researchers to disentangle the often-confounded interrelations between objective image properties and subjective aesthetic appraisals, facilitating more precise investigations into the cognitive and perceptual mechanisms underlying the appreciation of visual art.
papers.venue: Psychology of Aesthetics, Creativity, and the Arts
papers.authors: Yi Lin, Hans Op de Beeck, Johan Wagemans

0320.name: Johannes Burge
0320.bio: Johannes Burge is an Associate Professor of Psychology at the University of Pennsylvania who researches how the visual system performs tasks in natural environments. Burge utilizes psychophysics, natural scene statistics, and computational modeling to identify rules for transforming sensory signals into behavioral representations. Their work includes the development of Accuracy Maximization Analysis (AMA) for learning task-optimal filters and the investigation of depth perception cues such as defocus, disparity, and motion. By comparing human performance to ideal observer models, Burge examines how biological systems adapt to the statistical regularities of the natural world.
0320.research_direction: Dr. Burge has recently been investigating human depth perception and 3D motion processing by combining psychophysical experiments with natural scene statistics and computational modeling. Their recent work explores the "reverse Pulfrich effect"—a stereoscopic motion illusion driven by interocular blur differences—by examining how factors like clinical monovision corrections and low-light environments influence temporal processing delays. They are also investigating the limits of human stereopsis in the real world, using high-fidelity stereo databases and double-pass psychophysics to isolate how external nuisance variability in natural images constrains depth discrimination. Furthermore, to bridge natural scene statistics and early visual mechanisms, Dr. Burge is developing image-computable ideal observer models to study the normative principles governing local motion-in-depth estimation and to understand how feature-specific divisive normalization optimizes the neural encoding of binocular disparity.

papers.title: Monovision-induced motion illusions in presbyopic and non-presbyopic populations
papers.abstract: This study characterizes the prevalence and perceptual severity of the reverse Pulfrich effect—a 3D motion illusion caused by interocular processing speed asymmetries—within large cohorts of non-presbyopic (n=45) and presbyopic (n=17) individuals. Using a 2-interval forced-choice (2IFC) psychophysical paradigm, the authors induced interocular blur differences using both ophthalmic trial lenses (1.0D) and onscreen Gaussian blurring. Results indicate that monovision-induced misperceptions of depth are near-universal, appearing in 84% of the general population and 100% of the presbyopic group. Quantitative measurements reveal processing delays of several milliseconds, which translate into substantial misestimations of distance for moving targets, particularly at the high velocities associated with tasks such as driving.
papers.authors: Victor Rodríguez-López, Callista M. Dyer, Johannes Burge

papers.title: How distinct sources of nuisance variability in natural images and scenes limit human stereopsis
papers.abstract: This research investigates how external stimulus variability—a significant source of nuisance noise—constrains human stereo-depth discrimination in real-world environments. Utilizing a high-fidelity database of natural stereo-images with co-registered ground-truth distance data, the authors employed a double-pass psychophysical protocol to isolate the effects of luminance-contrast patterns and local-depth structure (disparity contrast). Analysis of decision-variable correlations reveals that stimulus-driven uncertainty accounts for a large fraction of total performance variance and induces strikingly consistent response patterns across different human observers. These findings demonstrate that perceptual limits in naturalistic viewing are governed more by specific image features than by internal neural noise, supporting the development of image-computable models for predicting human performance.
papers.authors: David N. White, Johannes Burge

papers.title: Decreases in overall light level increase the severity of the reverse Pulfrich effect
papers.abstract: Using a binocular 4f tunable lens system to independently manipulate retinal illuminance and retinal blur, this work quantifies how classic and reverse Pulfrich effects scale as a function of mean luminance. Experimental data collected across four orders of magnitude (0.2 to 12.8 cd/m²) demonstrate that interocular processing delays increase logarithmically with decreasing light levels. The results show that the temporal processing speed advantage of blurry over sharp images (the reverse Pulfrich effect) is exacerbated under low-light conditions. This interaction between luminance and blur suggests that individuals using monovision corrections may experience heightened 3D motion misperceptions in mesopic and scotopic environments, with significant implications for clinical practice and public safety.
papers.authors: Victor Rodriguez-Lopez, Benjamin M. Chin, Johannes Burge

papers.title: Optimal Estimation of Local Motion-in-Depth with Naturalistic Stimuli
papers.abstract: This study develops image-computable ideal observer models to explore the normative principles governing 3D motion estimation from binocular naturalistic video clips. The observers employ task-optimized spatiotemporal filters to extract motion cues—such as changing disparities and interocular velocity differences—and non-linearly decode latent motion variables from filter responses. The research identifies that the optimal filters are dictated by task-specific natural image statistics and that the decoding process requires quadratic response combination due to the jointly Gaussian nature of the filter response distributions. The model accurately reproduces counterintuitive human performance patterns, providing a computational link between natural scene statistics and the early visual system's processing of motion in depth.
papers.authors: Daniel Herrera-Esposito, Johannes Burge

papers.title: Feature-specific divisive normalization improves natural image encoding for depth perception
papers.abstract: The authors examine the functional role of divisive normalization in optimizing the encoding of binocular disparity from natural stereo-images. By comparing feature-specific (narrowband) and feature-independent (broadband) normalization regimes, they utilize Fisher information to measure encoding fidelity across large populations of binocular receptive fields. The analysis reveals that feature-specific normalization significantly enhances the precision with which disparity is represented, particularly as the number of neural units increases. Additionally, the study shows that the spatial frequency most useful for encoding varies systematically with disparity magnitude and stimulus size, matching known neurophysiological properties and providing a principled account of how normalization mechanisms are tailored to task-relevant natural stimulus properties.
papers.authors: Long Ni, Johannes Burge

0321.name: John A. Greenwood
0321.bio: John A. Greenwood is a Professor of Visual Perception at University College London whose research focuses on the mechanisms of spatial vision and object recognition. Greenwood examines 'visual crowding,' the disruptive effect of clutter on recognition, in both typical peripheral vision and clinical conditions such as amblyopia and nystagmus. Their methodology integrates behavioral psychophysics, eye tracking, and functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) to model how the brain encodes visual dimensions like motion, depth, and face identity. Currently, the lab investigates the computational topology of the visual field and the processes underlying visual imagery and hallucinations.
0321.research_direction: Dr. Greenwood has recently been investigating how spatial location and visual field properties shape higher-level visual processing, particularly face and object recognition. Using a combination of psychophysics and fMRI population receptive field (pRF) mapping, their recent work explores whether high-level face-selective regions inherit the spatial anisotropies and retinal position biases characteristic of early visual cortex. In parallel, they are developing targeted behavioral tests to characterize both sensory and cortical visual deficits in various clinical populations. Specifically, they are measuring visual crowding in pediatric retinal dystrophies using adaptive computerized tasks, while also employing fragmented-letter recognition paradigms to detect cortical visual loss in neurodegenerative conditions like posterior cortical atrophy.

papers.title: The perceptual and neural processing of familiar faces is shaped by the statistical regularities of real-world viewing
papers.abstract: This study investigates whether the cognitive and neural mechanisms of face recognition are influenced by the statistical regularities of facial feature placement in the visual field during central fixation. Psychophysical results demonstrate that familiarity judgments for familiar face halves (left/right or upper/lower) are significantly faster and more accurate when presented in typical (e.g., left half in the left visual field) compared to atypical locations. Corresponding fMRI data reveal that face-selective cortical regions—specifically the occipital face area (OFA) and fusiform face area (FFA)—exhibit significantly greater BOLD responses for familiar face halves in their typical spatial locations. These findings provide evidence for a visuospatial scaffolding model, where higher-level face representations are tuned to the consistent spatial statistics of real-world experience, contradicting the view that face identification is invariant to retinal position.
papers.authors: Bartholomew P. A. Quinn, David M. Watson, Kira Noad, Timothy J. Andrews, John A. Greenwood

papers.title: Elevated Visual Crowding in CRB1-Associated Retinopathies: Understanding Functional Visual Deficits Using Child-Friendly Computerized Testing
papers.abstract: This investigation characterizes functional visual deficits in individuals with CRB1-associated retinopathies, focusing on visual acuity and crowding—the disruptive effect of nearby clutter on object recognition. Using an adaptive, child-friendly computerized 'VacMan' task, thresholds were measured for both unflanked and flanked targets in participants with early-onset severe retinal dystrophy (EOSRD), Leber congenital amaurosis (LCA), and cone-rod dystrophy (CORD). Results indicate that both foveal acuity and crowding are significantly elevated in CRB1 patients compared to typical controls, with deficits largely independent of age or clinical phenotype. These findings demonstrate for the first time that CRB1 mutations produce cortical-level recognition impairments (elevated crowding) in addition to low-level sensory loss, establishing crowding as a robust outcome metric for future gene therapy trials.
papers.authors: Ana Catalina Rodriguez-Martinez, Vijay K. Tailor-Hamblin, Bethany E. Higgins, Pete R. Jones, Tessa M. Dekker, Robert H. Henderson, John A. Greenwood, Mariya Moosajee

papers.title: Common patterns of spatial selectivity in early visual cortex and face-selective brain regions
papers.abstract: The research employs population receptive field (pRF) mapping to determine if face-selective cortical regions (OFA, pFus, mFus) share the retinotopic anisotropies characteristic of early visual cortex (V1-V3). By presenting large-field bars containing upright or inverted faces, the study measured pRF size, density, and visual field coverage across polar angles. Results show that both early and high-level face regions demonstrate a greater number of pRFs and increased coverage along the horizontal (vs. vertical) meridian and in the lower (vs. upper) visual field. Additionally, pRF numbers in the middle fusiform area (mFus) were higher for upright than inverted faces, likely supporting the configural processing advantage. These results suggest that the spatial properties of specialized category-selective regions are built upon the fundamental sampling biases inherited from early visual cortex.
papers.authors: Anisa Y. Morsi, Hugo T. Chow-Wing-Bom, D. Samuel Schwarzkopf, Valérie Goffaux, Tessa M. Dekker, John A. Greenwood

papers.title: The Graded Incomplete Letters Test (GILT): a rapid test to detect cortical visual loss, with UK Biobank implementation
papers.abstract: Impairments in object recognition, such as those seen in posterior cortical atrophy (PCA), are often misattributed to ophthalmic conditions. We present the Graded Incomplete Letters Test (GILT), a psychophysical tool that measures the threshold for recognizing letters across parametrically varied levels of pixel fragmentation ('completeness'). Validated in the UK Biobank (n=2,359) and clinical cohorts, the GILT demonstrates that healthy adults maintain recognition at very low completeness levels, whereas patients with PCA show marked deficits even with minor degradation. With a sensitivity of 83-89% and specificity exceeding 94%, the test effectively differentiates cortical visual loss from typical Alzheimer’s disease and common eye conditions. The study highlights the utility of the GILT as a rapid clinical screening tool for identifying neurodegenerative damage to the higher-order visual hierarchy.
papers.authors: Keir X. X. Yong, Axel Petzold, Paul J. Foster, Andrew Young, Stephen Bell, Yuhan Bai, Alexander P. Leff, Sebastian J. Crutch, John A. Greenwood

papers.title: The resolution of face perception varies systematically across the visual field
papers.abstract: This study tests whether face perception varies systematically around the visual field or in an idiosyncratic fashion, as previously suggested. We developed a gender acuity test to measure the smallest face size required for reliable gender categorization in peripheral vision. In three psychophysical experiments, results consistently showed a horizontal-vertical anisotropy, with significantly better resolution along the horizontal than the vertical meridian, and a consistent advantage for the lower over the upper visual field. These spatial variations match the known properties of low-level vision and early visual cortex (e.g., cortical magnification and pRF density). The finding that face resolution follows these systematic patterns indicates that higher-level processing either passively inherits or actively maintains the characteristic spatial selectivity established in early vision.
papers.authors: Anisa Y. Morsi, Valérie Goffaux, John A. Greenwood

0323.name: John Jonides
0323.bio: Jonides is the Edward E. Smith Distinguished University Professor of Psychology and Neuroscience at the University of Michigan and co-directs the Functional MRI Laboratory. Their research examines the behavioral and neural architectures of working memory and executive control using methodologies such as functional MRI, PET, and transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS). Jonides has investigated the mechanisms of attentional capture, the dissociation between verbal and spatial working memory, and the relationship between cognitive control and fluid intelligence. Their current work focuses on the dysfunction of these mechanisms in clinical populations, including those with major depressive disorder and ADHD, and explores how environmental interventions like nature exposure may restore attentional resources.
0323.research_direction: Dr. Jonides has recently been investigating the precise mechanisms governing visual attentional capture and distractor suppression. Their recent work explores the foundational drivers of stimulus-driven capture, utilizing psychophysical paradigms to decouple abrupt onsets from low-level physical salience and forced-response saccade chronometry to map how target and distractor priority signals compete over milliseconds. Additionally, they are examining how the balance between early automated suppression and later reactive disengagement is modulated by internal cognitive states and individual differences. By combining eye-tracking metrics with pupillometry and thought-probing, Dr. Jonides investigates whether executive resource fluctuations like mind-wandering, or conditions such as ADHD, specifically impair initial oculomotor capture or the subsequent ability to rid the focus of attention of irrelevant information.

papers.title: Are abrupt onsets highly salient?
papers.abstract: This study interrogates the pervasive assumption that the prioritized attentional capture observed for abrupt onsets is a direct consequence of high physical salience. By employing a psychophysical oddball detection paradigm to explicitly quantify salience, the authors compared abrupt onsets with color singletons and color-singleton onsets. Results indicated that abrupt onsets actually exhibited the lowest levels of physical salience among the stimulus classes. Despite this lower salience, only onsets consistently captured attention in a visual search task, whereas color-based distractors were effectively suppressed. These findings suggest that physical salience is neither a necessary nor sufficient prerequisite for attentional capture by onsets, highlighting a dissociation between low-level feature contrast and attentional priority.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
papers.authors: Han Zhang, Esha Brar, A. Kane York, John Jonides

papers.title: Attentional capture by abrupt onsets: Foundations and emerging issues
papers.abstract: This theoretical review revisits the landmark research by Yantis and Jonides regarding the unique status of abrupt onsets in capturing visual attention. The authors evaluate the stimulus-driven capture framework in the context of contemporary evidence, identifying critical gaps in current understanding. The paper delineates several emerging issues for future research, including the requirement for increased spatiotemporal precision in measurement, the modulation of capture by selection history and longitudinal experience, and the contribution of individual differences to the balance between proactive and reactive control. The work calls for a conceptual refinement of visual attention theories to better account for the robust capture potency of dynamic onsets.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
papers.authors: Han Zhang, A. Kane York, John Jonides

papers.title: The temporal dynamics of visual attention
papers.abstract: Using a novel forced-response chronometric method, this study tracked the latent priority of visual attention as it evolves over milliseconds. Participants performed saccades toward targets while ignoring salient distractors at varying processing latencies. A computational model was implemented to characterize the asynchronous arrival of distractor and target priority signals. The results reveal that attentional bias shifts between distractor-ward and target-ward directions as a function of time. The authors propose two distinct mechanisms for distractor handling: a 'fast' mechanism that directly inhibits the expression of distractor signals and a 'slow' mechanism where target-driven signals eventually override earlier distractor-driven priority. These findings underscore the critical importance of temporal dynamics in theories of distractor suppression.
papers.authors: Han Zhang, Jacob Sellers, Taraz G. Lee, John Jonides

papers.title: Lingering on distraction: Examining distractor rejection in adults with ADHD
papers.abstract: This study investigated whether individuals with ADHD exhibit deficits in avoiding attentional capture or in reactively disengaging from distractors once captured. Adults with and without ADHD performed an additional-singleton search task while their eye movements were recorded. While both groups showed comparable initial oculomotor capture by salient distractors, individuals with ADHD exhibited a specific impairment in reactive rejection. Oculomotor metrics revealed that the ADHD group 'lingered' on distractors, characterized by a higher frequency of additional fixations and significantly longer dwelling durations before disengagement. These results suggest that ADHD is associated with a specific breakdown in the reactive processes required to rid the focus of attention of irrelevant information.
papers.authors: Han Zhang, Tessa R. Abagis, Clara J. Steeby, John Jonides

papers.title: How does mind-wandering affect distractor suppression?
papers.abstract: The authors explored whether the suppression of salient visual distractors is contingent upon the availability of executive resources. Fluctuations in attentional state were measured through thought-probes identifying mind-wandering and through pre-trial pupillometry as a proxy for arousal. Results showed that initial oculomotor suppression of distractors remained intact during mind-wandering and periods of low pupillary arousal, suggesting that early-stage distractor inhibition is an automated process likely driven by selection history. However, mind-wandering exacerbated distractor interference during later processing stages, leading to increased target looking times. The findings support a dual-stage model where initial oculomotor control is resource-independent, while subsequent task-relevant processing and disengagement require active attentional control.
papers.authors: Han Zhang, Kevin F. Miller, John Jonides

0324.name: John K. Tsotsos
0324.department: Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, Lassonde School of Engineering
0324.lab_name: Laboratory for Active and Attentive Vision (LAAV)
0324.bio: Tsotsos is a Distinguished Research Professor of Vision Science at York University and holds the NSERC Tier I Canada Research Chair in Computational Vision. They developed the Selective Tuning (ST) theory, a computational framework for visual attention that addresses the complexity of visual information processing through a hierarchy of winner-take-all mechanisms. Their research connects computational neuroscience and artificial intelligence, focusing on the integration of top-down attentional control with bottom-up sensory processing. Tsotsos also develops active vision systems for robotic navigation and object search.
0324.research_direction: Dr. Tsotsos has recently been investigating the mechanisms of active vision and spatial reasoning across both biological and artificial systems. Their recent work explores how humans dynamically coordinate gaze and posture to select optimal 3D viewpoints during real-world search, and they are leveraging these behavioral insights to design better training curricula for reinforcement learning agents in complex environments. At the neural level, they are probing the mechanics of color-form integration by computationally modeling how border ownership cells process equiluminant stimuli in the primate ventral stream. Furthermore, Dr. Tsotsos is examining both applied and theoretical limits of artificial visual systems, developing top-down, task-aware gaze prediction models for driving while critically evaluating the statistical unreliability and inherent biases of modern computer vision dataset construction.

papers.title: Real-world visual search goes beyond eye movements: Active searchers select 3D scene viewpoints too
papers.abstract: Traditional visual search paradigms often constrain observers to static 2D displays, thereby neglecting the high-dimensional viewpoint selection inherent in ecological settings. This study investigates the mechanisms of 3D active search using the Psychophysical Experimental Setup for Active Observers (PESAO) to track synchronized binocular gaze and head-neck kinematics in a physical workspace. Analysis of search-driven viewpoint selection reveals that observers actively optimize their viewing height and pose to resolve target-pose ambiguity and negotiate inter-object occlusions. While categorical accuracy remained robust throughout the task, search efficiency—quantified by response latencies, fixation counts, and locomotor distance—showed significant improvement, particularly in trials involving initially occluded targets. These results demonstrate that active vision involves a strategic integration of oculomotor and postural control to acquire optimal, informative views for 3D spatial reasoning.
papers.authors: Tiffany C. Wu, John K. Tsotsos

papers.title: Equiluminant Border Ownership Cells as a Missing Link in Color Form Perception
papers.abstract: This research identifies a putative sub-population of border ownership (BOWN) neurons that encode the 'figure' side of borders defined exclusively by equiluminant chromatic contrast. Drawing on neurophysiological evidence from primate areas V1 and V4, the authors propose a hierarchical mechanistic model to demonstrate how these equiluminant BOWN signals are synthesized within the ventral stream. Computational simulations indicate that these neurons exhibit high color selectivity and orientation tuning comparable to luminance-driven BOWN cells. The model suggests these cells function as a critical intermediary, transforming V1 chromatic edge responses into object-centered shape representations in V4, thereby bridging the gap in color-form integration theories.
papers.authors: Paria Mehrani, John K. Tsotsos

papers.title: Boosting Reinforcement Learning in 3D Visuospatial Tasks Through Human-Informed Curriculum Design
papers.abstract: While Reinforcement Learning (RL) has shown efficacy in structured environments, its performance on complex visuospatial reasoning tasks involving active observation remains limited. This work evaluates the capacity of deep RL frameworks, including Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) and imitation learning (BC/GAIL), to solve a 3D 'Same-Different' task. Initial results confirmed that end-to-end agents struggle to converge on optimal policies when confronted with the high-dimensional challenges of active viewpoint selection. However, by incorporating a human-informed curriculum—where the training regimen is strategically structured based on behavioral findings from real-world human psychophysics—agents successfully acquired the complex active observation strategies necessary for visuospatial problem-solving, underscoring the value of biologically-inspired curricula in the development of artificial general intelligence.
papers.authors: Markus D. Solbach, John K. Tsotsos

papers.title: SCOUT+: Towards practical task-driven drivers' gaze prediction
papers.abstract: Drivers' gaze allocation exhibits high variability during complex safety-critical maneuvers, such as intersection crossing, where top-down task demands override bottom-up saliency. Traditional saliency models often fail in these scenarios because they represent task context implicitly. SCOUT+ is proposed as a practical, task-aware architecture for gaze prediction that utilizes readily available geospatial data (GPS-derived maps and routes) to explicitly model driving objectives. Evaluated on the DR(eye)VE and BDD-A benchmarks, SCOUT+ significantly outperforms baseline bottom-up models and achieves performance parity with models requiring privileged ground-truth task labels. This research highlights the effectiveness of incorporating latent task-based priors from environmental mapping to enhance the predictive accuracy of driver monitoring systems in practical, real-time applications.
papers.authors: Iuliia Kotseruba, John K. Tsotsos

papers.title: Statistical Challenges with Dataset Construction: Why You Will Never Have Enough Images
papers.abstract: The generalization of deep neural networks (DNNs) from standardized computer vision benchmarks to safety-critical real-world applications is hindered by the statistical unreliability of current evaluation methodologies. This work presents a formal argument, supported by sampling theory, that the construction of a truly representative test set is mathematically and practically implausible for complex visual domains. The authors identify pervasive biases in existing datasets—including selection bias, geographical clustering, and availability bias—which violate the assumptions required for reliable statistical inference. Consequently, performance metrics derived from non-random holdout sets provide an incomplete and potentially misleading assessment of model robustness. The paper recommends that future validation protocols prioritize the verification of a model's internal decision-making logic and fault-tolerance over aggregate accuracy scores.
papers.authors: Josh Goldman, John K. Tsotsos

0325.name: John Maule
0325.bio: John Maule is an Assistant Professor at the University of Sussex and the lead of the Statistical Perception Lab. Their research explores the intersection of vision science and cognitive psychology, focusing on the ensemble perception of color and how individuals extract summary statistics from complex visual scenes. Maule investigates the 'visual diet' through hyperspectral imaging and image analysis to quantify how chromatic statistics influence perception, adaptation, and aesthetic preference. Additionally, their work examines neurodiversity in vision, specifically studying atypical color perception and adaptation in autistic populations using psychophysical and behavioral methodologies.
0325.research_direction: Dr. Maule has recently been investigating how real-world environmental statistics and lighting conditions shape human color perception across different contexts. Their recent work explores the concept of visual diet, using head-mounted cameras and behavioral psychophysics to examine how the chromatic statistics of diverse geographic locations influence color discrimination thresholds and aesthetic preferences. Alongside this environmental focus, they are exploring the developmental trajectory of color cognition, investigating how early infant perceptual biases interact with language acquisition to form categorical color representations. Additionally, Dr. Maule has been utilizing computational color-vision modeling and environmental spectral measurements to quantify how dynamic natural illumination—such as the dusk transition—and color vision deficiencies impact the luminance contrast and real-world visibility of sports equipment like pink cricket balls.

papers.title: Not So Pretty in Pink: Computational Modelling of Cricket Ball Visibility with Colour Vision Deficiency
papers.abstract: Approximately 9% of male cricketers have a color vision deficiency (CVD, i.e., protanomaly or deuteranomaly), and day-night Test cricket uses a pink ball that players anecdotally report as harder to see than the traditional red ball, particularly around dusk. This study computationally models how CVD affects the visibility of cricket balls of different colors under realistic match lighting. The authors measured the spectral reflectance of new and worn red and pink balls in the laboratory, and recorded spectral measurements of match backgrounds (pitch, grass, sightscreens, crowd, sky) and illumination across a day-night fixture at Lord's Cricket Ground, from daylight through dusk to floodlit night conditions. These measurements were combined with color-vision models to compute luminance contrast of each ball against its background for standard trichromatic observers and for observers with protanomaly or deuteranomaly. Ball visibility, as indexed by modeled contrast, was reduced for CVD observers relative to typical observers across conditions, with the pink ball showing particular vulnerability during the dusk transition, providing a mechanistic, image-based account of the reduced visibility reported by colorblind cricketers.
papers.authors: Peter M. Allen, Oliver R. Runswick, Luke Wilkins, David L. Mann, Matthew A. Timmis, John Maule

papers.title: Difficult at dusk? Illuminating the debate on cricket ball visibility
papers.abstract: This study quantifies how the visibility of cricket balls of different colors (red, white, pink) changes across the lighting transitions of a day-night match, addressing player reports that the pink ball used in day-night Test cricket is especially hard to see at dusk. The authors derived spectral reflectance from laboratory measurements of new and worn red, white, and pink balls, and paired these with spectral measurements of match backgrounds (pitch, grass, sightscreens, crowd, sky) and of illumination recorded during an actual day-night fixture at Lord's Cricket Ground, spanning natural afternoon daylight, the dusk transition, and floodlit night play. Combining these spectral measurements yielded estimates of ball-to-background luminance contrast across the match's lighting phases for each ball color. Contrast for the pink ball dropped disproportionately during the dusk transition relative to the red and white balls, providing a physical, illumination-based explanation for players' subjective reports that the pink ball is hardest to pick up specifically around dusk, rather than being uniformly less visible throughout a match.
papers.venue: Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport
papers.authors: John J. Maule, Robert Maguire, Matthew A. Timmis, Oliver R. Runswick, Luke Wilkins, David L. Mann, Stephen J. Dain, Jenny M. Bosten, Peter M. Allen

papers.title: Effects of visual diet on colour discrimination and preference
papers.abstract: This study examines the extent to which human color perception and aesthetic preferences are calibrated to the low-level chromatic statistics of the local visual environment ('visual diet'). Utilizing calibrated head-mounted cameras, the researchers characterized chromatic scene statistics for participants living in distinct environments: remote rainforest (Esmeraldas), urban Ecuador (Quito), and urban UK (Sussex). Although all environments exhibited a blue-yellow bias in chromatic distribution, the magnitude of this bias varied. Behavioral psychophysics revealed group differences in blue-yellow color discrimination thresholds that aligned with local environmental statistics, supporting a perceptual learning model rather than a fixed efficient coding framework. Conversely, while color preferences generally correlated with natural scene statistics, they did not specifically track local environmental variations and were influenced by cultural factors, challenging the hypothesis that aesthetic experience is purely a product of sensory calibration to the immediate environment.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences
papers.authors: Alice E. Skelton, John Maule, Simeon Floyd, Beata Wozniak, Asifa Majid, Jenny M. Bosten, Anna Franklin

papers.title: The Development of Color Perception and Cognition
papers.abstract: This review synthesizes the developmental trajectory of color vision and color cognition from infancy through childhood, integrating psychophysical, neural, and cross-linguistic evidence. It traces how basic chromatic discrimination emerges early in infancy and continues to be refined, and how this perceptual foundation interacts with the later acquisition of color language and categorical color cognition. The review addresses long-standing debates about the relationship between color perception and color language, including how the acquisition of color terms shapes categorical perception of hue and how universal versus culture-specific patterns of color categorization emerge over development, drawing on evidence from infant looking-time paradigms, cross-cultural and cross-linguistic comparisons, and studies of color preference. The authors argue for a framework in which early-developing perceptual biases (such as biases in color preference and discrimination) interact bidirectionally with later-acquired linguistic and conceptual color categories, jointly shaping the mature adult system of color perception and cognition.
papers.authors: John Maule, Alice E. Skelton, Anna Franklin

0326.name: John Serences
0326.bio: John Serences is a Professor and Chair of the Department of Psychology at UC San Diego, investigating how top-down behavioral goals and attentional factors modulate visual perception, memory, and decision-making. Their research utilizes functional MRI, electroencephalography (EEG), psychophysics, and computational modeling to examine population-level representations in the human brain. Serences employs quantitative neuroimaging techniques, including multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) and forward encoding models, to reconstruct feature-selective responses within the visual cortex. Their work provides evidence for the 'sensory recruitment' theory of working memory and characterizes how spatial priority maps in the parietal and frontal cortices coordinate the selection of relevant environmental stimuli.
0326.research_direction: Dr. Serences has recently been investigating the computational and neural mechanisms underlying visual working memory, selective attention, and scene perception. Utilizing continuous-report recall paradigms, their recent work explores whether working memory recruits early sensory representations that remain vulnerable to visual distractors, and investigates how inter-item similarity drives mnemonic compression to alter recall bias and precision. They are also using high-power longitudinal fMRI and multivariate pattern analysis to map the distributed neural locus and representational drift of working memory load signals across the visual hierarchy over time. Beyond memory storage, Dr. Serences is employing voxel-wise fMRI encoding models to test whether scene-responsive cortex is driven by explicit 3D geometric features or low-level 2D image statistics, while simultaneously using large-scale spiking neural network simulations to uncover the anatomical connectivity rules required for top-down feature-based attention.

papers.title: A 2D Gabor-wavelet baseline model out-performs a 3D surface model in scene-responsive cortex
papers.abstract: This study employs fMRI and voxel-wise encoding models to interrogate the representational format of scene-selective regions, including the Parahippocampal Place Area (PPA), Retrosplenial Complex (RSC), and Occipital Place Area (OPA). The researchers evaluated whether BOLD responses in these areas are better characterized by 3D geometric features (e.g., surface orientation and depth) or 2D image-level features (low-level Gabor-wavelet filters). Utilizing a stimulus set designed to dissociate these feature classes, variance partitioning analyses revealed that 2D Gabor-wavelet models account for significantly more variance across the scene-processing hierarchy than 3D models. The findings suggest that apparent 3D selectivity in scene-responsive cortex may emerge from correlations with 2D image statistics rather than the explicit encoding of 3D surfaces.
papers.authors: Anna Shafer-Skelton, Timothy F. Brady, John T. Serences

papers.title: Memory recall errors reflect interacting sensory and mnemonic representations
papers.abstract: Using a delayed-estimation orientation recall paradigm, the authors investigate whether visual working memory (WM) utilizes abstract codes or recruits early sensory representations. Psychophysical results demonstrate that recall precision is independently impaired by memorandum noise and the presence of feature-neutral distractors. Critically, distractors that share feature overlap with the remembered item induce systematic attractive biases, shifting memory reports toward the distractor's orientation. The magnitude of this attractive bias is further modulated by stimulus-level noise and behavioral relevance. These results provide evidence for a sensory recruitment model where WM maintenance involves feature-specific sensory-like population codes that remain susceptible to interference from incoming sensory inputs.
papers.authors: Holly Kular, John T. Serences

papers.title: Distributed and drifting signals for working memory load in human cortex
papers.abstract: This high-power longitudinal fMRI study (12 subjects, 144 total scanner-hours) evaluates the neural locus of visual working memory (VWM) load signals.
