While univariate BOLD activity showed localized, load-dependent increases in the intraparietal sulcus (IPS), multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) revealed that information regarding set size (0–4 items) is distributed throughout the visual hierarchy, including areas showing univariate decreases. Furthermore, the researchers observed significant representational drift in these load-sensitive neural patterns across sessions despite stable behavioral performance. These findings argue against a restricted locus of load signals in the posterior parietal cortex and instead support a dynamic, distributed population code for memory storage that is refined over time.
papers.authors: Kirsten C. S. Adam, Edward Awh, John T. Serences

papers.title: Near-random connections support top-down feature-based attentional modulations in early sensory cortex
papers.abstract: Employing large-scale spiking neural network simulations, the authors examine the architectural constraints required for top-down feature-based attention (FBA). The model features a hierarchical structure with sensory sub-networks and a higher-order control layer (e.g., prefrontal cortex) characterized by high-dimensional feature tuning. The simulations demonstrate that sparsely-connected, near-random reciprocal projections between layers can sustain targeted gain enhancements of behaviorally relevant features. This balance between randomness and structure supports global and precise FBA modulations in early sensory layers without requiring rigid point-to-point anatomical mapping or inducing spurious representations of irrelevant stimuli that could interfere with perception.
papers.authors: Sunyoung Park, John T. Serences

papers.title: Similarity-driven compression during encoding supports biased but more precise working memory
papers.abstract: This study investigates the mechanism of similarity-driven compression (or chunking) in visual working memory (VWM) using a continuous-report orientation task. Behavioral experiments demonstrate that increasing inter-item similarity during the encoding phase induces a systematic recall bias toward the ensemble mean of the stimuli. Paradoxically, this bias is accompanied by an increase in recall precision (i.e., reduced circular standard deviation), suggesting that the VWM system strategically reformats sensory inputs to exploit statistical regularities in the environment. This reformatting optimizes mnemonic stability and population-level fidelity at the expense of item-specific veridicality.
papers.authors: Janna Wennberg, John T. Serences

0327.name: Jonathan Cant
0327.bio: Jonathan Cant is an Associate Professor in the Department of Psychology at the University of Toronto Scarborough and directs the Cant Lab. Their research integrates functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and psychophysical behavioral methods to map the neural substrates of human visual perception and cognition. Cant investigates the functional organization of the ventral stream, focusing on how the brain distinguishes between object shape, surface-based cues such as texture and color, and complex scene ensembles. Their work also examines the interactions between these perceptual pathways and their role in producing adaptive behaviors within natural environments.
0327.research_direction: Dr. Cant's recent work explores the mechanisms and boundary conditions of ensemble perception, specifically how the visual system extracts summary statistics from complex stimuli like crowds of faces and natural scenes. Using methods ranging from rapid psychophysics and image reconstruction to EEG and multivariate pattern analysis, they have recently been investigating the temporal dynamics that separate the neural processing of isolated local elements from global ensemble representations. Their research also examines whether this rapid statistical averaging is purely automatic, probing how it is dynamically regulated by top-down factors such as structural context, selective attention, and action-driven motor planning. Furthermore, they are testing the domain-generality of these processes by asking if ensemble coding is strictly optimized for intrinsic visual properties—like spatial boundaries and facial expressions—or if it can flexibly encompass abstract, cross-modal features such as object weight and real-world size.

papers.title: Rapid ensemble encoding of average scene features
papers.abstract: This study evaluates the visual system's capacity for extracting summary statistical information from complex scene ensembles. Across five experiments, the authors demonstrate that participants can accurately and rapidly (within 125 ms) extract ensemble-level features, specifically average scene content (naturalness vs. manufacturedness) and spatial boundary (openness vs. closedness). These processes appear to function independently of visual working memory (VWM) resources. However, rotating the constituent scenes significantly disrupted the extraction of average orientation, suggesting that these global ensemble mechanisms are constrained by the diagnosticity of cardinal edge information typically found in upright natural scenes.
papers.authors: Vignash Tharmaratnam, Jason Haberman, Jonathan S. Cant

papers.title: Attention and stimulus structure interact during ensemble encoding of facial expression
papers.abstract: The study explores the interplay between attentional deployment and stimulus consistency in the synthesis of face ensemble representations. Using an image reconstruction paradigm based on similarity ratings, the authors recovered visual estimates of ensemble summaries. The results indicate that focused attention selectively enhances the neural representation of central faces within a crowd. Furthermore, the structural consistency of emotional valence between central and surrounding faces facilitates the fidelity of both local and global representations. However, the influence of the central face on the overall ensemble summary is most pronounced only when focal attention is directed toward a center face that conflicts with the surrounding emotional context, revealing a highly flexible relationship between attention and stimulus statistics.
papers.authors: Marco A. Sama, Moaz Shoura, Adrian Nestor, Jonathan S. Cant

papers.title: Examining the role of action-driven attention in ensemble processing
papers.abstract: This paper examines how action-driven attention—the prioritization of visual features relevant to motor planning—modulates the extraction of ensemble summary statistics. Participants performed an ensemble size-estimation task while concurrently preparing or executing reaching movements toward targets defined by specific features. The findings reveal that when action-relevant features (e.g., size) are congruent with the ensemble task requirements, they exert a biasing effect on the perceived average size of the ensemble. This effect was absent when the action-relevant feature was task-irrelevant, suggesting that ensemble processing is not purely automatic but is dynamically regulated by the motor system's attentional priorities.
papers.authors: Kristina Knox, Jay Pratt, Jonathan S. Cant

papers.title: The neural dynamics of face ensemble and central face processing
papers.abstract: Using multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) of electroencephalography (EEG) data, this study probes the temporal dynamics and informational basis of face ensemble perception. Stimuli varied parametrically in shape and surface properties. The results demonstrate that both visual dimensions contribute to ensemble encoding, with surface cues exhibiting a more dominant influence on the neural signal. Critically, the decoding of central faces was found to precede the decoding of the surrounding ensemble members. Moreover, the temporal profile of central face representations aligned closely with that of isolated single faces, whereas ensemble-level representations showed distinct temporal divergence, suggesting a bifurcation in the processing of local identity and global statistical summaries.
papers.authors: Marco Agazio Sama, Adrian Nestor, Jonathan Samuel Cant

papers.title: Testing the flexibility of ensemble coding: Limitations in cross-modal ensemble perception
papers.abstract: This study examines the flexibility of ensemble coding mechanisms by investigating whether the visual system can extract summary statistics from non-visual features (e.g., average weight, real-world size) associated with visual object stimuli. Across several experiments, participants were tasked with judging the average value of these abstract features for sets of objects. The results demonstrated that unlike low-level visual features (e.g., orientation, color), observers failed to accurately extract ensemble summaries for weight and real-world size upon initial exposure. These findings suggest significant constraints on the domain-generality of ensemble perception, indicating that rapid statistical averaging is primarily optimized for intrinsic visual properties rather than abstract cross-modal associations.
papers.authors: Greer Gillies, Keisuke Fukuda, Jonathan S. Cant

0328.name: Jonathan Flombaum
0328.bio: Jonathan Flombaum is an Associate Professor in the Department of Psychological & Brain Sciences at Johns Hopkins University and the director of the Visual Thinking Lab. Flombaum’s research focuses on the computational and representational constraints of human cognition, specifically the intersection of visual perception, attention, and memory. They investigate object persistence, multiple object tracking, and the role of categorical biases in visual working memory. By combining behavioral psychophysics with mathematical modeling, their work identifies how the mind utilizes core knowledge of physics and categorization to navigate the limitations of mental computation.
0328.research_direction: Dr. Flombaum's recent work explores how the visual system structures the representation of moving objects, specifically investigating whether circular and orbiting trajectories are processed as independent translating items or as composite, object-centered systems. Using multiple-object-tracking paradigms and psychophysical measurements of the motion-silencing illusion, they are examining how the underlying reference frames for rotational versus translational motion impact our ability to accurately track targets and detect local feature changes. Additionally, Dr. Flombaum has recently been investigating how sensory non-uniformities across the visual field affect the perceived timing of events. By leveraging rapid serial visual presentation (RSVP) tasks and gaze-contingent driving simulators, their research probes how stimulus eccentricity influences processing speed, judgments of visual simultaneity, and hazard detection latency in both foundational and applied contexts.

papers.title: The format of representation for objects in orbit: Composite and internally referenced
papers.abstract: This paper asks whether objects moving on circular ('orbiting') trajectories are represented as independent, translating items or as parts of a composite, internally-referenced system, analogous to points affixed to a rotating frame. Because a composite representation requires the visual system to reference each element's position both to an object-internal frame and to an external anchor, the authors predicted that tracking and localization should be harder for rotational motion than for translational motion matched on local kinematics. Across several multiple-object-tracking and localization experiments, participants showed selectively impaired performance for orbiting compared with translating targets, even when instantaneous speed and trajectory curvature were equated. The pattern held when only a single item had to be tracked through rotation, arguing against an account based purely on tracking load. The authors conclude that orbital motion recruits a structured, composite object representation rather than being processed as an ordinary translating object, extending accounts of object-file and object-centered representation to circular motion.
papers.authors: Qihan Wu, Jonathan I. Flombaum

papers.title: How does peripheral vision affect driver performance when passing on roads with lateral traffic conflicts? A simulated driving experiment
papers.abstract: This study characterizes driver perception across the visual field in the context of lateral traffic conflicts during highway navigation. Leveraging a gaze-contingent simulated scotoma and empirical driving data, the researchers modeled the relationship between stimulus eccentricity and hazard detection latency. The study demonstrates that processing speed non-uniformities across the visual field lead to systematic biases in perceived simultaneity and duration. These temporal discrepancies in peripheral vision are shown to influence how drivers integrate spatiotemporal information from multiple vehicles, suggesting that individual differences in the strategic control of eye fixations are primary determinants of hazard perception efficacy and overall driving safety.
papers.authors: Aditya Upadhyayula, Ian Phillips, Jonathan I. Flombaum

papers.title: The Motion-Silencing Illusion Depends on Object-Centered Representation
papers.abstract: Motion silencing is the phenomenon whereby otherwise salient changes in color, luminance, or shape become difficult to detect when the changing elements simultaneously translate or rotate. The authors developed a psychophysical method to quantify illusion strength continuously and used it to compare rotational and translational motion matched for local velocity at each element. Rotation produced a substantially stronger silencing effect than translation, even though both conditions were equated on instantaneous retinal motion energy at the location of each changing element. The authors argue that silencing arises from a failure to correctly attribute changes to their spatial locations, and that rotation exacerbates this failure because perceiving a rotating display relies on an object-centered representation in which each element's position must be referenced both to an internal, object-relative frame and to an external frame. This dual-reference requirement increases the difficulty of correctly binding a change to a location, producing greater silencing for object-centered (rotational) than for purely translational motion.
papers.authors: Qihan Wu, Jonathan I. Flombaum

papers.title: Eccentricity advances arrival to visual perception
papers.abstract: Building on well-documented eccentricity-dependent non-uniformities in retinal and early visual processing, this study asked whether such non-uniformities produce measurable differences in the perceived timing (rather than just the accuracy) of visual events across the visual field. In Experiment 1, observers fixated centrally while viewing a rapid serial visual presentation (RSVP) letter stream and judged which letter was simultaneous with a briefly flashed cue presented at varying eccentricities along the horizontal meridian; observers systematically reported earlier stream items as simultaneous with more peripheral cues than with central cues, indicating an illusory advance in perceived timing for peripheral stimuli. Experiment 2 conceptually replicated this eccentricity-dependent temporal misbinding, and Experiment 3 showed that the effect tracks absolute eccentricity rather than the relative spatial separation between the cue and the RSVP stream. The authors interpret the results as evidence that transient stimuli at eccentric retinal locations are processed and 'arrive' at perceptual awareness faster than foveal stimuli, providing direct behavioral evidence that spatial non-uniformities in visual processing speed translate into systematic distortions of perceived simultaneity.
papers.authors: Aditya Upadhyayula, Ian Phillips, Jonathan Flombaum

0329.name: Jonathan Touryan
0329.institution: U.S. Army DEBCOM Army Research Laboratory
0329.lab_name: Cognition and Neuroergonomics (CaN) Collaborative Technology Alliance
0329.bio: Jonathan Touryan is a senior research scientist within the Human Research and Engineering Directorate at the U.S. Army DEVCOM Army Research Laboratory. Touryan’s research focuses on the intersection of visual neuroscience and neuroergonomics, utilizing high-density electroencephalography (EEG), eye-tracking, and virtual reality to decode neural signatures of situational awareness and target detection in complex environments. Touryan contributed to the development of the Lab Streaming Layer (LSL) and large-scale data analysis frameworks to enhance human-autonomy teaming and brain-computer interface technologies. Touryan earned a PhD in the neurophysiology of vision from the University of California, Berkeley, and completed postdoctoral training at the Yale University School of Medicine.
0329.research_direction: Dr. Touryan has recently been investigating how to decode latent cognitive states and situational awareness during naturalistic visual search and spatial navigation. Their recent work explores the use of machine learning to analyze combined EEG, eye-tracking, and head-tracking data within immersive virtual reality, examining how oculomotor dynamics like saccade size relate to the temporal onset of neural object processing. In applied contexts, they are investigating expert visual strategies by comparing the attentional allocation of military personnel and civilians, alongside efforts to refine the algorithms used to classify 3D head movements during unconstrained viewing. Furthermore, their research extends into human-autonomy teaming, utilizing generative AI to model continuous performance dynamics and predict the temporal trajectories of operator errors during simulated driving tasks.

papers.title: Decoding target discriminability and time pressure using eye and head movement features in a foraging search task
papers.abstract: This research investigates the utility of synergistic eye and head movement metrics for inferring latent cognitive states during naturalistic visual search in virtual reality (VR). Participants performed a foraging task with varying levels of target-distractor discriminability and temporal constraints while wearing a head-mounted display with integrated eye tracking. Support vector machine (SVM) classifiers were utilized to decode task conditions based on gaze and head orientation features. Results demonstrate that a multimodal model integrating both eye and head movement characteristics significantly outperforms unimodal models in predicting target discriminability and time pressure, achieving higher classification accuracy by capturing the coordinated visuomotor dynamics inherent in unconstrained 3D environments.
papers.authors: Anthony J. Ries, Chloe Callahan-Flintoft, Anna Madison, Joseph Dankovich, Jonathan Touryan

papers.title: Human Performance Modeling Using Generative AI Principles
papers.abstract: The authors introduce a Generative Cognitive Modeling Tool designed to overcome the limitations of conventional performance models that offer only static assessments of operator state. Leveraging generative AI frameworks and large-scale simulated driving datasets, the tool models the continuous latent dynamics of human performance. The proposed architecture identifies and predicts cognitive states associated with driving errors up to 25 seconds before their occurrence, demonstrating that such errors are the result of predictable temporal trajectories rather than stochastic events. Additionally, the model characterizes how disruptions in these ongoing dynamics influence the voluntary utilization of autonomous driving aids, providing a novel methodology for assessing human-autonomy teaming.
papers.authors: Stephen M. Gordon, Vernon J. Lawhern, Jonathan Touryan

papers.title: Saccade size predicts onset time of object processing during visual search of an open world virtual environment
papers.abstract: This study employs deep convolutional neural networks to decode electroencephalographic (EEG) activity during active, closed-loop visual search within an immersive virtual environment. The research focuses on identifying the behavioral and environmental determinants of the variable latency of P300-analogous neural responses locked to fixation onsets. By constructing fixation-locked response profiles from decoded activity, the authors evaluate the influence of top-down and bottom-up factors, including fixation duration and stimulus salience. Findings reveal that saccade size is the most reliable predictor of response onset time, with large-magnitude saccades significantly reducing latency jitter. This suggests that oculomotor characteristics are critical for isolating neural signatures of object processing in naturalistic, free-viewing paradigms.
papers.authors: Stephen M. Gordon, Bianca Dalangin, Jonathan Touryan

papers.title: Evidence of elevated situational awareness for active duty soldiers during navigation of a virtual environment
papers.abstract: The research quantifies physiological and behavioral indicators of situational awareness (SA) by comparing active-duty service members with a civilian control group during a navigational search task in an open-world virtual environment. Participants searched for targets under dual-task conditions involving an auditory cognitive load. Active-duty individuals exhibited superior search performance and distinct oculomotor strategies, characterized by significantly higher peak saccade velocities and larger average saccade magnitudes. Neural analysis via CNN-based decoding of EEG (P300-like response) showed that military personnel allocated significantly more attentional resources to initial object fixations than to subsequent refixations, indicating a more efficient and expert-like strategy for information acquisition and environment scanning.
papers.authors: Leah R. Enders, Stephen M. Gordon, Heather Roy, Thomas Rohaly, Bianca Dalangin, Angela Jeter, Jessica Villarreal, Gary L. Boykin, Jonathan Touryan

papers.title: A Comparison of Head Movement Classification Methods
papers.abstract: This study evaluates the performance and reliability of several automated algorithms for classifying head movements in 3D virtual reality (VR) environments. Using data from participants performing a foraging task in a head-mounted display, the authors benchmarked automated classification methods against human-rater ground truth. The comparison focused on algorithm sensitivity to movement onset/offset times, peak angular velocity, and movement amplitude across varied motion profiles (e.g., pursuit vs. instantaneous targets). The findings identify specific biases in established classification techniques and offer design principles for researchers seeking to incorporate head-tracking data as an objective measure of behavioral state and visual exploration in immersive contexts.
papers.authors: Chloe Callahan-Flintoft, Emily Jensen, Jasim Naeem, Anna Madison, Anthony J. Ries, Jonathan Touryan

0330.name: Jonathan Victor
0330.bio: Jonathan Victor is the Fred Plum Professor of Neurology and Neuroscience at Weill Cornell Medicine and directs the Division of Systems Neurology and Neuroscience. Victor’s research integrates mathematical modeling and information theory with neurophysiology to investigate sensory processing within the visual and olfactory systems. They developed metric-space analyses for neural spike trains and conduct studies on how cortical networks represent visual textures and natural scene statistics. Additionally, Victor applies computational frameworks to examine large-scale brain dynamics and cognitive motor dissociation in patients with disorders of consciousness.
0330.research_direction: Dr. Victor's recent work explores the theoretical and geometric foundations of neural coding and visual perception. They have recently been investigating vision as a dynamic spatiotemporal process, examining how eye movements like saccades and drifts actively reformat spatial scenes into temporal luminance modulations rather than capturing static snapshots. In addition to this work on active vision, their recent research employs psychophysical ranking paradigms and multidimensional scaling to map the latent geometric spaces of perception, probing how internal representations transform from low-level visual features to hierarchically structured semantic categories. Furthermore, they are modeling neural coding through non-Euclidean geometry, framing neuronal spike trains as discrete trajectories within hyperbolic space to study the mathematical substrates of sequence encoding and temporal decision-making.

papers.title: Walks with jumps: a neurobiologically motivated class of paths in the hyperbolic plane
papers.abstract: This study introduces 'walks with jumps' within the hyperbolic plane (H²) as a formal mathematical framework for the representation of neuronal spike trains. In this model, a point moves at a constant velocity in a defined direction, punctuated by discrete, instantaneous jumps. This non-Euclidean representation exhibits a 'point of no return' property, which may serve as a geometric substrate for temporal decision-making processes that undergo progressive refinement. Due to the non-commutative nature of isometries in hyperbolic space, the endpoint of a walk encodes specific details of the temporal sequence of jumps (spikes) beyond a simple count. However, the researchers demonstrate that this encoding is degenerate, as disparate temporal patterns can map to identical endpoints. The paper employs the tools of hyperbolic geometry to analytically characterize these trajectories and their implications for neural coding.
papers.authors: Jason DeBlois, Eduard Einstein, Jonathan D. Victor

papers.title: The visual system does not operate like a camera
papers.abstract: The authors provide a formal rebuttal to the 'static camera' model of vision, which suggests that visual perception is primarily a product of static snapshot images captured during saccadic landings. They argue instead that vision is a fundamentally dynamic, spatiotemporal process driven by temporal luminance modulations. These modulations are actively generated by various classes of eye movements, including saccades, inter-saccadic drifts, and blinks. By summarizing contemporary evidence for active space-time encoding, the authors illustrate how the visual system reformats spatial scenes into temporal signals to achieve efficient information representation. The article addresses specific misconceptions regarding the utility of oculomotor transients and corrects inaccuracies in the interpretation of neural and psychophysical data within the camera-like viewpoint framework.
papers.authors: Michele Rucci, Ehud Ahissar, David C. Burr, Igor Kagan, Martina Poletti, Jonathan D. Victor

papers.title: The Geometry of Low- and High-Level Perceptual Spaces
papers.abstract: This research explores the geometric transformations of perceptual spaces along a representational gradient from low-level visual features to high-level semantic categories. Utilizing an efficient psychophysical ranking paradigm across five domains—ranging from scrambled textures to animal names—the authors applied non-metric multidimensional scaling to build latent representation models. The findings reveal that while all domains share a stable global geometry (typically requiring 5-7 dimensions with modest spherical curvature), their internal topological organization differs significantly. Specifically, semantic-dominated domains exhibit a 'tree-like' hierarchical structure that is absent in feature-dominated domains. This suggests that while the underlying geometric manifold of perception remains relatively invariant, semantic information imposes a distinct hierarchical arrangement on the represented points.
papers.authors: Suniyya Amna Waraich, Jonathan D. Victor

0331.name: Jonathan Winawer
0331.department: Department of Psychology and Center for Neural Science
0331.lab_name: Winawer Laboratory for Visual Perception and Neuroscience
0331.bio: Jonathan Winawer is a Professor of Psychology and Neural Science at New York University and directs the Winawer Laboratory for Visual Perception and Neuroscience. Winawer’s research characterizes the computational principles and biological constraints of the human visual system, examining how sensory pathways encode and transform information to support perception. They employ a multi-modal approach integrating psychophysics with neuroimaging techniques, including functional MRI (fMRI), magnetoencephalography (MEG), and intracranial electrocorticography (ECoG). Winawer’s work involves developing predictive models of cortical responses, mapping visual field organization, and investigating the neural mechanisms underlying temporal summation and perceptual adaptation.
0331.research_direction: Dr. Winawer has recently been investigating the spatial organization and functional dynamics of the human visual cortex using fMRI, population receptive field modeling, and psychophysics. Their recent work explores how spatial representations in early visual areas are dynamically restructured by top-down signals, specifically examining how memory feedback alters the spatial resolution of cortical tuning and how spatial attention proactively modulates baseline activity prior to stimulus onset. They are also probing the fundamental architecture of visual processing by investigating how spatial frequency preferences and cortical magnification covary across the V1 visual field map, as well as how spatial tuning and tolerance for visual noise evolve along the ventral stream during object recognition. Additionally, their methodological research addresses the challenges of remote data collection by developing online psychophysical tools that leverage visual crowding to strictly enforce central gaze fixation without the need for specialized eye-tracking hardware.

papers.title: Object recognition along the ventral stream: effects of visual noise
papers.abstract: The study employs fMRI and critical-band masking to investigate the biological basis of the ~1.5-octave spatial frequency band critical for human object recognition. By measuring BOLD responses from V1 through ventral temporal cortex (VTC) to band-pass noise and noisy natural images, the authors demonstrate a divergence between sensory tuning and recognition utility. While neural responses to noise alone widen from 2 octaves in V1 to 5 octaves in VTC, the bandwidth that limits image decoding remains conserved at ~2 octaves. These results imply that the recognition band reflects a readout constraint rather than an early sensory filter, with downstream areas like VTC exhibiting an 8-fold increase in noise tolerance to maintain stable recognition performance.
papers.authors: Ajay Subramanian, Ekin Tünçok, Jan W. Kurzawski, Najib J. Majaj, Denis G. Pelli, Jonathan Winawer

papers.title: EasyEyes: Crowded dynamic fixation for online psychophysics
papers.abstract: To address the challenge of gaze control in remote web-based experiments, the authors introduce 'crowded dynamic fixation,' a method that uses visual crowding and temporal modulation to ensure central fixation without specialized eye-tracking hardware. Participants are required to foveate and track a moving target amidst clutter, making it impossible to perform the task while peeking at peripheral stimuli. Laboratory and online validation using EyeLink trackers revealed that this technique reduces peeking behavior to 0% and maintains fixation accuracy within 0.6 degrees. The tool enables reliable measurement of eccentricity-dependent visual phenomena, such as crowding distances and acuity thresholds, in standard web browsers across large, diverse populations.
papers.authors: Fengping Hu, Joyce Y. Chen, Denis G. Pelli, Jonathan Winawer

papers.title: Feedback scales the spatial tuning of cortical responses during both visual working memory and long-term memory
papers.abstract: Using fMRI-based population receptive field (pRF) reconstruction, this research characterizes the spatial resolution of visual representations in early human visual cortex (V1–V3) during mnemonic maintenance and retrieval. The study compares the spatial tuning of feedforward sensory responses with that of top-down feedback signals generated during working memory and long-term memory tasks. Findings indicate that feedback-driven mnemonic activity exhibits significantly broader spatial tuning compared to direct perceptual encoding. This suggests that top-down modulation transforms visual information into a lower-resolution spatial format, potentially favoring representational stability or high-level integration over the fine-grained precision typical of sensory processing.
papers.authors: Robert Woodry, Clayton E. Curtis, Jonathan Winawer

papers.title: Unpacking the V1 map: Differential covariation of preferred spatial frequency and cortical magnification across spatial dimensions
papers.abstract: Using high-resolution fMRI and quantitative modeling in a large cohort (n=40), the authors investigate how preferred spatial frequency (SF) and cortical magnification (CM) covary throughout the human V1 visual field map. Both properties show marked asymmetries across polar angles, with higher resolution and surface area along the horizontal than vertical meridian. While the two properties exhibit proportional scaling as a function of eccentricity—consistent with retinal ganglion cell density constraints—this proportionality breaks down across polar angles. These results imply that cortical resource allocation for spatial resolution and surface area are subject to different organizational principles along distinct spatial dimensions, challenging simple constancy models of V1 organization.
papers.authors: Marc M. Himmelberg, Yuna Kwak, Marisa Carrasco, Jonathan Winawer

papers.title: Spatial attention selectively alters visual cortical representation during target anticipation
papers.abstract: This study utilizes concurrent fMRI and psychophysics to investigate how endogenous spatial attention proactively modulates activity in human visual cortex (V1–V3) prior to stimulus onset. The authors find that target anticipation induces a stimulus-independent baseline BOLD increase at cued locations and a corresponding decrease at uncued locations. These pre-target baseline shifts are highly predictive of subsequent behavioral performance gains at attended locations. The results demonstrate that top-down attentional mechanisms selectively restructure the cortical representational state to prioritize incoming information at specific visual field locations, illustrating a clear neural tradeoff in processing resources between attended and unattended space.
papers.authors: Ekin Tünçok, Marisa Carrasco, Jonathan Winawer

0332.name: Joo-Hyun Song
0332.department: Department of Cognitive, Linguistic, and Psychological Sciences
0332.bio: Song investigates the behavioral and neural mechanisms that integrate cognitive processes, such as attention and decision-making, with motor control. Their research employs a multi-methodological approach—including continuous action tracking, fMRI, and EEG—to examine how humans coordinate eye and hand movements within complex, dynamic environments. Song utilizes the reach-tracking paradigm to demonstrate how real-time motor trajectories reveal internal cognitive states and the continuous interplay between perception and action.
0332.research_direction: Dr. Song has recently been investigating the intricate interplay between continuous motor behavior and higher-order cognition, particularly focusing on how executive functions shape sensorimotor learning. Their recent work explores whether implicit motor adaptation is modulated by visual attentional demands and domain-specific working memory, as well as how emergent motor timing developed during physical actions influences perceptual temporal acuity. Additionally, they are leveraging continuous 3D reach tracking as a behavioral window into developmental social cognition. By measuring movement kinematics like initiation latency and trajectory curvature, Dr. Song is dissecting the distinct inhibitory control mechanisms—specifically conflict monitoring versus resolution—that underlie theory-of-mind inferences and selective trust in both children and adults.

papers.title: Automatic, but not autonomous: Implicit adaptation is modulated by goal-directed attentional demands
papers.abstract: This study examines whether implicit sensorimotor adaptation, traditionally viewed as an obligatory and resource-independent process, is sensitive to goal-directed attentional demands. Utilizing an error-clamp paradigm to isolate implicit learning from explicit strategies, human participants performed a reaching task while concurrently monitoring a rapid serial visual presentation for targets. Across two experiments, the researchers observed that dual-task interference did not attenuate learning; rather, performing the visual task enhanced implicit adaptation, particularly when response-contingent feedback was provided. Model-based analyses identified an increase in error sensitivity under dual-task conditions, while retention remained stable. These results are consistent with arousal-mediated modulation of cerebellar error processing and suggest that while implicit adaptation is automatic, its magnitude is contingent on the physiological and attentional state of the learner.
papers.authors: Joshua J. Liddy, Sean R. O’Bryan, Alexander Daskalopoulos, Joo-Hyun Song

papers.title: Emergent motor timing enhances time perception
papers.abstract: The study investigates how the stable temporal patterns developed during goal-directed actions, termed emergent motor timing, influence temporal precision in perception. Participants engaged in a self-paced throwing task where temporal consistency developed implicitly through repetitive practice. The experiment revealed a significant positive correlation between the stability of motor timing and performance on a subsequent perceptual time-interval discrimination task. These findings provide evidence for a shared representational primitive for timing across the sensorimotor and perceptual systems, suggesting that temporal acuity is shaped by the implicit development of spatiotemporal movement structures rather than isolated internal clock mechanisms.
papers.authors: Xinyu Yan, Se-Woong Park, Helene Serre, Dagmar Sternad, Joo-Hyun Song

papers.title: Manual reach tracking reveals distinct inhibitory processes in children’s and adults’ inferences about belief
papers.abstract: This research utilizes continuous 3D reach tracking to dissociate the inhibitory control mechanisms involved in social cognition, specifically theory-of-mind inferences, in children aged 4 to 6 and adults. By measuring initiation latency as an index of conflict monitoring and reach curvature as an index of conflict resolution, the study explored how participants respond to true versus false belief scenarios. The data indicated that conflict monitoring efficiency improves significantly with age, while the capacity for conflict resolution in action remained relatively stable. The results demonstrate that the cognitive demands of false-belief tasks are supported by dissociable inhibitory processes that exhibit distinct developmental trajectories.
papers.authors: David M. Sobel, David G. Kamper, Joo-Hyun Song

papers.title: Systematic modulation of sensorimotor learning by domain-specific working memory
papers.abstract: This paper investigates whether individual differences in sensorimotor adaptation are predicted by domain-specific visuospatial working memory capacity (WMc) or domain-general executive resources. Participants performed spatial and feature-based WMc assessments followed by three visuomotor rotation tasks designed to isolate explicit and implicit learning components. Results showed that visuospatial WMc specifically correlated with the magnitude of explicit re-aiming strategies across tasks. Paradoxically, higher visuospatial WMc was associated with reduced implicit adaptation in error-clamp conditions. These findings suggest that spatial working memory provides a domain-specific scaffold for explicit motor strategies and interacts with the implicit recalibration system in a manner not predicted by traditional additive models of motor learning.
papers.authors: Sean R. O'Bryan, Joshua J. Liddy, Joo-Hyun Song

papers.title: Distinct Inhibitory Control Mechanisms Underlie Selective Social Inferences
papers.abstract: Using a reaching-based choice task, this study dissociated the inhibitory mechanisms required for monitoring social conflict from those required for resolving it during selective learning tasks. Children (4–6 years old) and adults were required to evaluate information provided by human pointing cues versus non-social arrow cues that were either accurate or deceptive. Analyses of initiation latency revealed that human cues imposed higher conflict-monitoring demands than arrow cues across all age groups. However, the ability to resolve this conflict to produce a correct reaching response (measured via trajectory deviance) showed significant developmental improvement, suggesting that the maturation of selective trust is primarily driven by gains in conflict-resolution capacity rather than changes in the initial social-monitoring process.
papers.authors: David M. Sobel, David G. Kamper, Yuyi Taylor, Joo-Hyun Song

0334.name: Jorge Morales
0334.department: Department of Psychology; Department of Philosophy and Religion
0334.bio: Jorge Morales is an Assistant Professor of Psychology and Philosophy at Northeastern University and directs the Subjectivity Lab. Their research combines psychophysics, functional neuroimaging (fMRI), and philosophy to investigate conscious experience and visual perception. Morales examines how the mind constructs visual reality, focusing on the perception of absences, the representation of perspectival shape, and the mechanisms underlying metacognitive introspection. This work addresses the relationship between subjective mental states and their neural and computational foundations.
0334.research_direction: Dr. Morales has recently been investigating the representational and metacognitive architectures underlying both biological perception and artificial systems. In the domain of human visual cognition, their recent work explores whether predictive memory distortions like representational momentum extend beyond spatial motion to non-kinematic visual features such as brightness, proportion, and color saturation. They are also developing formal quantitative approaches to study subjective experience, examining how confidence ratings can be validly utilized in consciousness science and proposing an 'Introspective Signal Detection Theory' to model how observers detect internal phenomenal signals against sensory noise. Furthermore, they have been probing the internal mechanics of Large Language Models, testing whether these systems rely on propositional logic rather than quasi-perceptual formats for visual-spatial imagery tasks, and assessing whether models can be trained to introspectively report the hidden parameter weights driving their decisions.

papers.title: Artificial Phantasia: Evidence for Propositional Reasoning-Based Mental Imagery Within Large Language Models
papers.abstract: This research introduces the 'Artificial Phantasia' framework to evaluate whether Large Language Models (LLMs) solve visual-spatial problems via quasi-perceptual, iconic representations or through propositional logic. By subjecting models to tasks involving spatial transformations, the study demonstrates that LLMs emulate mental imagery behaviors using high-level linguistic descriptions and propositional reasoning rather than the image-like, sensory formats characteristic of biological cognition. These findings suggest a functional divergence in how spatial simulations are computationally realized in transformer architectures compared to human visual systems, contributing to theoretical debates on the representational format of mental simulation.
papers.authors: Morgan McCarty, Jorge Morales

papers.title: Representational Momentum Transcends Motion
papers.abstract: The study investigates whether representational momentum (RM)—a classic mnemonic distortion where the remembered position of a moving object is displaced in the direction of its motion—is a domain-general predictive principle. Across seven experiments, the authors provide evidence that predictive mnemonic distortions extend beyond kinematic spatial displacement to non-motion perceptual dimensions, including brightness, color saturation, and proportion. Conversely, the effect was found to be absent for changes in hue, indicating specific constraints on the visual system's automatic predictive architecture. The results suggest that the mind's automatic predictions shape memory across a wide range of perceptual domains, exposing the common computational mechanisms underlying perception and memory.
papers.authors: Dillon Plunkett, Jorge Morales

papers.title: Self-Interpretability: LLMs Can Describe Complex Internal Processes that Drive Their Decisions, and Improve with Training
papers.abstract: This paper investigates the 'self-interpretability' of Large Language Models (LLMs), specifically their ability to accurately quantify and report the internal parameters, such as attribute weights, that govern their decision-making. Utilizing fine-tuned GPT-4o and GPT-4o-mini models on multi-attribute decision tasks involving stochastic hidden preference vectors, the authors demonstrate that LLMs can faithfully report their own internal weighting schemes. Furthermore, the research shows that this capacity for introspective reporting can be systematically enhanced through targeted training and generalizes to novel decision domains, offering a potential pathway toward more transparent and verifiable AI systems.
papers.authors: Dillon Plunkett, Adam Morris, Keerthi Reddy, Jorge Morales

papers.title: Confidence in Consciousness Science
papers.abstract: This article defends the validity of confidence ratings as a methodological bridge for the scientific study of subjective experience. Addressing critiques that metacognitive reports are distinct from and potentially irrelevant to conscious character, the author argues that confidence and awareness are fundamentally linked via shared cognitive and neural architectures. The paper posits that confidence ratings possess objective anchors and correlate robustly with visibility judgments and neurophysiological markers of awareness. By framing confidence as a mechanistically grounded tool, Morales demonstrates how metacognition provides a rigorous and tractable framework for evaluating conscious states, countering philosophical skepticism regarding the reliability of introspective reports.
papers.authors: Jorge Morales

papers.title: Introspection Is Signal Detection
papers.abstract: The author proposes a formal architecture for the study of introspection termed Introspective Signal Detection Theory (iSDT), extrapolating the principles of classical Signal Detection Theory (SDT) from perception to the domain of self-monitoring. The framework models the reliability of introspective judgments as a function of 'mental strength'—a domain-general phenomenal magnitude representing the intensity of conscious experiences. Just as perceptual SDT models the detection of external stimuli against sensory noise, iSDT characterizes introspection as the detection of internal phenomenal signals. This quantitative framework allows for the calibration of introspective accuracy across varied contexts and provides a unified signal-processing paradigm for understanding the relationship between perception and metacognition.
papers.venue: The British Journal for the Philosophy of Science
papers.authors: Jorge Morales

0335.name: Jorge Otero-Millan
0335.department: Herbert Wertheim School of Optometry & Vision Science
0335.bio: Jorge Otero-Millan’s research focuses on the mechanisms of ocular motor control and their intersection with visual perception and vestibular integration. Otero-Millan investigates fixational eye movements, specifically microsaccades, and their role in maintaining visual stability during head and eye rotations across all three axes. Utilizing computational modeling, virtual reality, and eye-tracking, Otero-Millan develops methodologies to characterize nystagmus and other oculomotor abnormalities. Their research explores the application of these metrics as non-invasive diagnostic biomarkers for neurological and vestibular disorders such as Parkinson’s disease, vertigo, and concussions.
0335.research_direction: Dr. Otero-Millan has recently been investigating the intricate relationship between oculomotor dynamics, spatial perception, and vestibular function. Their recent work explores how active gaze behavior and structural eye constraints shape visual processing, using behavioral experiments and computational modeling to probe how eye movements influence heading perception during optic flow and how image saliency interacts with egocentric biases to drive free-viewing saccades. They are also examining the perceptual consequences of brainstem oculomotor adaptation, utilizing modified landmark tasks to measure whether sustained eccentric gaze holding induces subsequent distortions in spatial localization. Broadening their scope into clinical and methodological domains, they are evaluating how gravito-inertial cues modulate vibration-induced nystagmus in patients with vestibular loss, while simultaneously developing novel, hardware-free software protocols to precisely quantify end-to-end latency in gaze-contingent display systems.

papers.title: Horizontal saccade bias results from combination of saliency anisotropies and egocentric biases
papers.abstract: This study investigates the mechanistic etiology of the horizontal saccade bias in human free-viewing behavior, where eye movements are disproportionately executed along cardinal axes. By analyzing orientation anisotropies in saliency content across two large-scale eye-tracking datasets, the authors demonstrate that image-based saliency is the primary predictor of cardinal saccade prevalence. They implement a targeting model integrating allocentric saliency features with egocentric oculomotor biases to account for observed saccadic distributions and their persistence under image tilt conditions. The findings suggest that saccade generation strategies reflect an adaptive optimization to environmental regularities and the structural constraints of the human oculomotor system in an upright orientation.
papers.authors: Stephanie M. Reeves, Jorge Otero-Millan

papers.title: Distortion of perceived visual space after prolonged horizontal eccentric gaze holding
papers.abstract: The research evaluates the perceptual sequelae of oculomotor adaptation following sustained eccentric gaze holding, a process that triggers rebound nystagmus. Using a modified landmark task to measure spatial biases, the study identifies significant shifts in the internal representation of visual space following 40-degree gaze maintenance at extreme horizontal eccentricities. The results indicate that the adaptive mechanisms of the gaze-holding integrator do not merely affect motor output but also induce systematic, asymmetric distortions in spatial localization and distance sensitivity. These findings highlight a dependence of perceived visual space on the recent history of eye positions and the corresponding adaptive states of the brainstem neural circuitry.
papers.authors: Terence L. Tyson, Dennis F. Perez, Jorge Otero-Millan

papers.title: A method for measuring closed-loop latency in gaze-contingent rendering without extra equipment
papers.abstract: This paper presents a novel software-based methodology for quantifying the end-to-end (closed-loop) latency of gaze-contingent rendering (GCR) systems without requiring external specialized hardware. The protocol utilizes a dual-pupil simulation paradigm wherein a 'driver' stimulus following a pre-determined trajectory controls a 'follower' gaze-contingent stimulus. By cross-correlating the positions recorded through the system’s own eye tracker, the method isolates and quantifies temporal delays across sampling, rendering, and display stages. Validation against induced artificial delays confirms that the method precisely captures total system latency, including frame-to-frame variability, offering a standardized tool for high-precision vision research and virtual reality applications.
papers.authors: Matt D. Anderson, Emily A. Cooper, Jorge Otero-Millan

papers.title: Behavioral and Modeling Evidence that Eye Movements Bias Self-motion Perception
papers.abstract: The study characterizes the influence of active gaze dynamics on heading perception during visual self-motion (optic flow). Behavioral experiments manipulating gaze eccentricity and pursuit velocity revealed systematic heading estimation errors that scale with the magnitude and direction of eye rotation. The authors propose a Bayesian ideal observer model that incorporates eccentricity-dependent retinal motion noise, an underestimation of extra-retinal rotation signals, and a prior for straight-ahead motion. The model successfully reproduces human error patterns across multiple tasks, suggesting that natural gaze strategies, such as maintaining gaze near the optic-flow singularity, serve to mitigate inherent gaze-dependent perceptual biases during navigation.
papers.authors: Matt D. Anderson, Emily A. Cooper, Jorge Otero-Millan

papers.title: Amplification of vibration induced nystagmus in patients with peripheral vestibular loss by head tilt
papers.abstract: This study examines the modulation of skull vibration-induced nystagmus (VIN) by gravito-inertial cues in patients with unilateral vestibular loss (UVL). Utilizing a multisensory integration model, the authors hypothesize that the canal imbalance induced by high-frequency vibration is centrally misattributed as a 'virtual translation' due to incorrect computations of head orientation relative to gravity. Findings demonstrate that VIN magnitude is systematically dependent on head tilt, showing significant augmentation in affected-ear-down positions and attenuation in ear-up positions. These results provide insights into the central processing of ambiguous vestibular signals and suggest positional VIN as a refined bedside diagnostic metric for assessing vestibular tone and recovery.
papers.authors: Ari A. Shemesh, John C. Kattah, David S. Zee, Francisco Zuma e Maia, Jorge Otero-Millan

0336.name: Joseph DeGutis
0336.lab_name: Boston Attention and Learning Laboratory (BAL Lab)
0336.bio: Joseph DeGutis is a cognitive neuroscientist whose research focuses on the mechanisms and rehabilitation of attention and face perception. As the co-director of the Boston Attention and Learning Laboratory, DeGutis utilizes behavioral psychophysics, functional MRI, and non-invasive brain stimulation to characterize cognitive deficits and develop targeted interventions. Their work includes developing computer-based training paradigms for sustained attention and exploring the neural basis of developmental prosopagnosia. DeGutis’s current research aims to improve cognitive outcomes for individuals with traumatic brain injury, PTSD, and age-related neurodegeneration.
0336.research_direction: Dr. DeGutis’s recent work broadly explores the neural and cognitive mechanisms underlying face perception, sustained attention, and metacognition. A major focus of their research investigates developmental prosopagnosia, utilizing fMRI to map functional connectivity abnormalities within the face-processing network while also conducting behavioral studies to isolate specific face-name recollection deficits and quantify psychosocial impacts like social anxiety. Beyond person recognition, they have recently been examining the intersection of emotion and cognitive control, developing novel continuous performance paradigms to assess how negative emotional distractors capture attentional resources and influence subsequent memory encoding. Additionally, their clinical work probes global metacognitive biases in veterans with PTSD and depression, investigating whether the mismatch between objective cognitive performance and subjective confidence can serve as a marker of psychological health and be targeted through computerized cognitive training.

papers.title: Left hemisphere abnormalities in face-selective activation and functional connectivity in developmental prosopagnosia
papers.abstract: This neuroimaging investigation utilized fMRI to characterize the functional architecture of developmental prosopagnosia (DP) through passive face viewing and resting-state connectivity analyses in a sample of 34 DPs and 23 controls. The study identified significantly attenuated face-selective activation within the left fusiform face area (FFA) and the left occipital face area (OFA). Resting-state functional connectivity analyses further revealed widespread intra-network disruptions, with the most robust reductions localized to the connectivity between the right anterior superior temporal sulcus (aSTS) and the left FFA. These findings demonstrate that DP is associated with focal left-hemisphere neural abnormalities within the face-processing network rather than broad, non-selective cortical deficits.
papers.authors: Alison Campbell, Xian Li, David Rothlein, Michael Esterman, Joseph DeGutis

papers.title: Social Interaction Anxiety in Developmental Prosopagnosia: Prevalence, Severity, and Individual Differences
papers.abstract: This study quantified the prevalence and clinical severity of social anxiety in a cohort of 88 individuals with developmental prosopagnosia (DP) compared to 58 neurotypical controls. Assessment via the Social Interaction Anxiety Scale indicated that 44% of the DP sample exceeded the clinical threshold for probable social anxiety disorder, with symptoms predominantly linked to social mixing and interactions with unfamiliar individuals. Further psychometric modeling demonstrated that higher levels of extraversion and lower autistic traits served as significant moderators, reducing the severity of social anxiety symptoms. The results underscore the substantial psychosocial morbidity associated with congenital face blindness and highlight the role of personality factors in social adaptation.
papers.authors: Leah Kirsch, Travis C. Evans, Regan Fry, Alison Campbell, Joseph DeGutis

papers.title: Characterizing the effects of emotional distraction on sustained attention and subsequent memory: A novel emotional gradual onset continuous performance task
papers.abstract: The researchers developed and validated the 'emogradCPT,' a novel experimental paradigm designed to quantify the interference of exogenous emotional stimuli on endogenous sustained attention. Across three experiments, the introduction of negative background distractors during a neutral digit-discrimination task significantly impaired discrimination sensitivity (d') and increased reaction time variability relative to neutral or positive conditions. Post-task memory assessments revealed a robust mnemonic bias for negative distractors, which were remembered with higher accuracy than non-negative stimuli. These findings suggest that emotionally negative information selectively captures attentional resources, causing reliable disruptions in ongoing goal-directed performance and biasing subsequent memory encoding.
papers.authors: Michael Esterman, Sam Agnoli, Travis C. Evans, Audreyana Jagger-Rickels, David Rothlein, Courtney Guida, Carrie Hughes, Joseph DeGutis

papers.title: Face naming and recollection represent key memory deficits in developmental prosopagnosia
papers.abstract: This research characterized the specific face memory impairments in developmental prosopagnosia (DP) beyond perceptual deficits. Testing 69 DPs and 99 controls using ROC analysis of confidence-rated Old/New judgments, a remember-know paradigm, and a face-name associative task, the study revealed significant impairments in recollection and contextual memory. Crucially, the deficit in face-name association (proper name recall) remained robust even after statistically controlling for group differences in face perception. These results suggest that the core pathology of DP extends to hippocampal-dependent recollection mechanisms and the specific semantic binding required for person identity recognition.
papers.authors: Tanvi Palsamudram, Alison Campbell, Regan Fry, Bar Yosef, Leah Kirsch, Nicole D. Anderson, Mieke Verfaellie, Joseph DeGutis

papers.title: Negative global metacognitive biases are associated with depressive and posttraumatic stress disorder symptoms and improve with targeted or game-based cognitive training
papers.abstract: This study investigated global metacognitive bias—the mismatch between objective performance and subjective confidence—in veterans suffering from depression and PTSD. The cohort exhibited significant negative biases (underconfidence relative to actual performance) that correlated with symptom severity. Following 10 weeks of computerized cognitive training (either targeted or entertainment-based), these negative metacognitive biases showed significant improvement. Crucially, longitudinal modeling indicated that the reduction in negative bias was associated with significant decreases in clinical symptom severity, suggesting that metacognitive accuracy is a sensitive marker of psychological health and a viable target for cognitive remediation.
papers.authors: Sam Agnoli, Henry Mahncke, Sarah-Jane Grant, Zachary T. Goodman, William P. Milberg, Michael Esterman, Joseph DeGutis

0338.name: Joy Geng
0338.bio: Geng investigates the cognitive and neural mechanisms that govern how humans prioritize visual information based on behavioral goals and prior experiences. Their work characterizes the balance between the selection of task-relevant targets and the suppression of irrelevant distractors, proposing models such as "good-enough" attentional guidance to explain search efficiency. Methodologically, Geng integrates functional MRI, electroencephalography (EEG), eye-tracking, and psychophysics to map the dynamics of attentional templates and their impact on perception. Their lab currently explores how these processes operate in complex environments, including 3D contexts and virtual reality.
0338.research_direction: Dr. Geng has recently been investigating the flexible mechanisms underlying attentional control and target templates during visual search. Their recent work uses behavioral paradigms and fMRI with multivariate pattern analysis to explore whether preparatory templates strategically shift away from veridical features to maximize separability from distractors, and how they incorporate non-target associated information like scene context. Additionally, they are exploring spatial guidance in naturalistic scenes to understand how large semantic anchor objects provide deterministic spatial cues for locating targets. Finally, their research addresses how these selective attentional states and crossmodal multisensory processes impact downstream episodic memory, specifically examining phenomena like boundary contraction during spatial recall and the enhancement of environmental source memory.

papers.title: Preparatory attentional templates in prefrontal and sensory cortex encode target-associated information
papers.abstract: The efficacy of visual search is predicated on the maintenance of a target template in working memory to facilitate attentional guidance and match-decision processes. Traditionally, these templates are thought to encode veridical features of the target object; however, recent behavioral evidence suggests that non-target associated information, such as scene context, can also guide search. Using fMRI and multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA), we investigated the neural representation of such associated information within preparatory attentional control networks. Human participants learned specific face-scene category associations and performed a cued visual search task. While face-specific neural codes were decodable in the fusiform face area (FFA), superior parietal lobule (SPL), and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dLPFC) during the cue phase, they were absent during the preparatory delay. In contrast, category-level information for the associated scene was decoded in the ventrolateral prefrontal cortex (vLPFC) during the cue phase and persisted in the inferior frontal junction (IFJ) and parahippocampal place area (PPA) during the delay period. These results provide a novel demonstration that target-associated information from long-term memory can supplant veridical target features in the 'target template' to optimize sensory gain and guide selection during difficult visual search.
papers.authors: Zhiheng Zhou, Joy J. Geng

papers.title: Anchor objects guide spatial attention during visual search
papers.abstract: Naturalistic scene viewing involves the utilization of semantic and spatial regularities to optimize search efficiency. This study tested the hypothesis that 'anchor objects'—large, stationary entities that define the spatial layout of an environment—form a privileged class of semantic associates that provide deterministic spatial guidance for smaller target objects. In a series of RSVP search experiments, participants were primed with semantic anchors, non-anchor semantic associates, or unrelated control objects before identifying a target in either spatially congruent or incongruent positions. Results indicated that although all semantically related objects facilitated target identification (priming of identity), only anchor objects provided robust predictive spatial cues that significantly reduced reaction times and enhanced localization precision. These findings suggest that anchor objects are unique semantic associates that integrate identity and location information to constrain the attentional search space in complex environments.
papers.authors: Makayla Souza-Wiggins, Joy J. Geng

papers.title: Multisensory processing impacts memory for objects and their sources
papers.abstract: While multisensory integration is known to enhance recognition memory for individual stimuli, its impact on broader episodic memory components, such as neighboring objects and environmental source context, remains largely unexplored. Across three experiments, we examined whether encoding semantically congruent audiovisual signals benefits memory for adjacent purely visual objects and the environmental context in which they were presented. Our results showed that multisensory integration did not significantly improve the recognition of neighboring visual objects but markedly enhanced source memory for the environmental scene where the encoding occurred. These results indicate that multisensory processing plays a unique role in episodic memory formation by facilitating the binding of items to their context, demonstrating that the benefits of crossmodal signals extend beyond the individual objects to the global environmental representation.
papers.authors: Shea E. Duarte, Andrew P. Yonelinas, Simona Ghetti, Joy J. Geng

papers.title: Object-based attention during scene perception elicits boundary contraction in memory
papers.abstract: Boundary extension and contraction are characteristic memory distortions wherein the remembered spatial extent of a scene is larger or smaller than the original. We tested the hypothesis that selective, object-based attention during encoding serves as a critical driver of boundary contraction. Participants performed either a scene memorization task or a visual search task for specific objects within those scenes. Memory for the spatial boundaries was then quantified through drawing tasks and subjective ratings. We observed that the search task resulted in significantly greater boundary contraction than the memorization task. Furthermore, the likelihood of accurate object recall correlated with the degree of spatial compression, with attention to central targets leading to a loss of peripheral information. These findings suggest that the allocation of attention to specific objects within a scene constrains the spatial envelope in memory, resulting in a distinct contraction bias toward the attended object.
papers.authors: Elizabeth H. Hall, Joy J. Geng

papers.title: Task-adaptive changes to the target template in response to distractor context: Separability versus similarity
papers.abstract: Theories of attentional control typically characterize the target template as a veridical memory representation of target features. However, recent findings suggest that templates can shift 'off-veridical' when doing so increases the distinctiveness of the target relative to a linearly separable distractor context. This study investigated whether such shifts result from low-level perceptual biases (e.g., simultaneous contrast) or reflect a strategic, task-adaptive mechanism. Utilizing a two-dimensional search task (color and orientation), we independently manipulated the linear separability of color and the visual similarity of orientation. Results showed that the target color template only shifted away from distractors when the orientation dimension was highly similar and thus ineffective for guidance. When orientation was distinct enough to support search, color templates remained veridical. These data confirm that the attentional template is flexibly and adaptively configured, prioritizing features that most effectively distinguish the target from the current distractor context to maximize search performance.
papers.authors: Xinger Yu, Raisa A. Rahim, Joy J. Geng

0340.name: Jr. Rhea T. Eskew
0340.bio: Rhea T. Eskew, Jr. is a Professor of Psychology at Northeastern University. Eskew's research focuses on characterizing color detection and discrimination through quantitative models and psychophysical testing, with an emphasis on S-cone pathways and higher-order chromatic mechanisms. Their work includes investigating asymmetries in ON and OFF pathways, the role of cones in border distinctness, and the effects of light adaptation on response dynamics. Eskew is a Fellow of the Optical Society of America and served as the inaugural Robert M. Boynton Lecturer.
0340.research_direction: Dr. Eskew has recently been investigating the mechanisms of spatial color integration and surface completion, using parametric psychophysics to probe visual phenomena like neon color spreading and the Boynton illusion. Their recent work explores how high-contrast luminance boundaries capture and constrain low-contrast chromatic edges, and tests whether illusory color filling-in is governed by slow, diffusive processes or faster parallel mechanisms. Additionally, they are examining the suprathreshold perceptual scaling and contrast masking of visual increments and decrements to understand the asymmetries between visual channels. By employing Maximum Likelihood Difference Scaling (MLDS) and pedestal discrimination paradigms, Dr. Eskew seeks to characterize the distinct transducer functions and internal noise profiles that underlying ON and OFF pathways in both S-cone and achromatic vision.

papers.title: The Boynton Illusion: Chromatic edge attraction to a luminance contour
papers.abstract: The Boynton Illusion describes a phenomenon where the perceived location of a low-contrast chromatic edge is significantly biased by the presence of a nearby high-contrast luminance contour. This study employed a position judgment task to parametrically investigate this color spreading effect across S-cone, equiluminant red-green, and achromatic directions. Using a gap effect stimulus consisting of a bipartite box divided by a central contour, the researchers demonstrated a robust attraction effect of high-contrast boundaries on chromatic edges. When the chromatic test region was physically smaller than the demarcated area, the edge was perceived as being closer to the contour (filling-in); when it extended beyond the contour, the edge was similarly attracted (filling-out). Results showed that while S-cone and equiluminant red-green stimuli exhibited similar magnitudes of positional displacement, achromatic stimuli showed relatively smaller effects. These findings suggest that the visual system prioritizes suprathreshold achromatic contours to assign uniform surface attributes within demarcated regions, effectively using luminance boundaries to constrain chromatic integration.
papers.authors: Jingyi He, Yesenia Taveras-Cruz, Rhea T. Eskew, Jr.

papers.title: S cone increments and decrements: Nearly-linear perceptual scales and variable noise
papers.abstract: This research investigated the suprathreshold perceptual representation of S-cone incremental (S+) and decremental (S−) visual signals using maximum likelihood difference scaling (MLDS) and pedestal discrimination tasks. Contrary to previous findings in the achromatic domain which show strong asymmetries, the estimated perceptual scales for both S-cone polarities were found to be approximately linear and symmetric up to high contrast levels. However, a significant asymmetry was observed in the pedestal discrimination thresholds, which rose more steeply for S+ pedestals compared to S− pedestals, indicating stronger high-contrast masking in the S-ON pathway. To reconcile the linear perceptual scales with the non-linear discrimination thresholds, the authors proposed and validated a variable-noise MLDS model. In this model, internal noise in the S-cone pathways grows proportionally with the square root of the stimulus contrast, allowing for accurate prediction of forced-choice discrimination performance from scaling data and suggesting fundamental physiological differences in noise characteristics between S-ON and S-OFF pathways.
papers.authors: Yangyi Shi, Rhea T. Eskew, Jr.

papers.title: Psychophysics of neon color spreading: Chromatic and temporal factors are not limiting
papers.abstract: Neon color spreading (NCS) is an illusory phenomenon used to study surface completion and color filling-in. This study utilized a parametric psychophysical approach to evaluate the efficacy of cone-isolating and equiluminant stimuli in generating NCS for both incremental and decremental polarities. Experiment 1 demonstrated that once differences in base detection thresholds are controlled, all cone types and polarities generate NCS at approximately twice the detection threshold level, indicating that chromatic resolution rather than specific cone-opponent circuitry limits the effect. Experiment 2 measured the temporal contrast sensitivity functions for NCS using L-cone flicker modulations from 0.5 to 8 Hz. The results showed that NCS sensitivity remains constant or increases with higher temporal frequencies, providing strong evidence against models of NCS based on slow, diffusive filling-in processes. Instead, the data support the existence of relatively fast, parallel mechanisms underlying illusory surface completion that operate on similar timescales to low-level flicker detection.
papers.authors: Jingyi He, Ennio Mingolla, Rhea T. Eskew, Jr.

papers.title: Asymmetries between achromatic increments and decrements: Perceptual scales and discrimination thresholds
papers.abstract: Human perception of achromatic increments (A+) and decrements (A−) exhibits qualitative asymmetries, likely reflecting divergent processing in ON and OFF retinal channels. This study quantified these differences using maximum likelihood difference scaling (MLDS) and a fourfold 2-alternative spatial forced-choice (2SAFC) pedestal discrimination paradigm. The experiments revealed that A+ perceptual scales follow a modified Naka-Rushton transducer function, whereas A− scales are best described by a cubic function. Correspondingly, discrimination thresholds for A+ pedestals increased monotonically with contrast, while A− thresholds exhibited a non-monotonic 'dipper' function, initially increasing and then decreasing at high contrasts. The authors developed a unifying model where the pedestal discrimination threshold is inversely proportional to the derivative of the perceptual scale. This model accurately predicts the threshold-vs-contrast (TvC) functions from the scaling data, suggesting that the well-known asymmetries in brightness perception and contrast masking are manifestations of a shared underlying transduction mechanism constrained by the distinct statistics of ON and OFF visual pathways.
papers.authors: Yangyi Shi, Rhea T. Eskew, Jr.

0341.name: Juan Chen
0341.lab_name: Action Perception and Learning Lab (APL Lab)
0341.bio: Juan Chen is a Professor at the School of Psychology at South China Normal University and serves as the director of the Action Perception and Learning Lab. Chen's research investigates the neural and behavioral mechanisms of human perception and hand actions, focusing on the functional differences between the processing of 3D real-world objects and 2D images. Using a multimodal approach that includes fMRI, EEG, psychophysics, and kinematics, Chen examines size constancy in the visual cortex and the implicit plasticity of the dorsal visual stream. Their current work explores how visually guided motor training affects sensory encoding in the absence of conscious perceptual awareness.
0341.research_direction: Dr. Chen has recently been investigating the mechanisms of size constancy and size-distance scaling, focusing on how the perceptual and visuomotor systems compute object size under restricted viewing conditions. Their recent work explores the extent to which perceptual judgments and reach-to-grasp actions can integrate non-retinal depth cues, including auditory signals, explicit semantic distance knowledge, and internal priors about an object's canonical real-world distance. Additionally, they are probing the intersection of motor planning and sensory processing, using high-density EEG to examine how vergence eye movement planning modulates early cortical visual responses via motor-to-sensory efference copies. Finally, they are evaluating representational differences between planar images and tangible 3D objects, utilizing viewpoint adaptation paradigms to uncover how binocular disparity and stereoscopic depth cues influence the visual system's viewpoint invariance.

papers.title: Contribution of auditory distance cues to size constancy in perception and grasping in restricted viewing
papers.abstract: This research explored the integration of auditory distance cues into size-distance scaling computations for both perceptual judgments and motor control (grasping). Under conditions where visual distance information was severely restricted, results demonstrated that auditory distance cues significantly enhanced the accuracy of perceptual size estimates but failed to preserve size constancy for the motor system's grip aperture. However, following extensive auditory distance training, participants exhibited a moderate improvement in incorporating auditory cues into their reach-to-grasp movements. These findings suggest that while the neural mechanisms underlying grasping do not natively integrate auditory distance as effectively as proprioceptive or visual cues, the visuomotor system maintains sufficient plasticity to learn and utilize these non-visual signals for computing real-world object size.
