papers.authors: Chao Zheng, Gexiu Wang, Xiaoming Zhou, Jie Gao, Irene Sperandio, Melvyn A. Goodale, Juan Chen

papers.title: Effects of Vergence Eye Movement Planning on Size Perception and Early Visual Processing
papers.abstract: The study utilized high-density electroencephalography (EEG) and psychophysics to investigate how the motor command associated with planning a vergence eye movement (specifically, divergence) influences visual size processing and the earliest stages of cortical analysis. Participants were tasked with judging the size of stimuli presented during the preparation phase of a gaze shift from a near fixation point to a far screen. Results indicated that planning divergence led to an increase in perceived object size alongside a significant reduction in size sensitivity. Electrophysiological analysis revealed that the size-dependent modulation of the C1 component—peaking at approximately 80 ms and reflecting primary visual cortex activity—was effectively eliminated during the planning stage of the divergence eye movement. These results suggest that motor-to-sensory efference copies for vergence modulate visual signals at the earliest levels of the visual hierarchy.
papers.authors: Yichong Zhang, Xiaoqian Wu, Chao Zheng, Yuqing Zhao, Jie Gao, Zhiqing Deng, Xilin Zhang, Juan Chen

papers.title: Viewpoint adaptation revealed potential representational differences between 2D images and 3D objects
papers.abstract: This investigation examined the impact of three-dimensional depth information, particularly binocular disparity, on the neural representation of objects using a viewpoint adaptation paradigm. Researchers compared viewpoint aftereffects generated by 2D flat images against those produced by 3D stimuli, including both real tangible objects and stereoscopic images. Findings showed that adaptation to 3D stimuli induced significantly stronger viewpoint aftereffects for faces and kettles compared to 2D images. Through computational modeling, the authors demonstrated that these behavioral differences are best explained by broader neural tuning for viewpoints in 3D versus 2D object representations. This suggest that the inclusion of valid depth cues enhances the viewpoint invariance of the human visual system, indicating a fundamental difference in how the brain encodes real-world 3D structures compared to planar image projections.
papers.authors: Zhiqing Deng, Jie Gao, Toni Li, Yan Chen, BoYu Gao, Fang Fang, Jody C. Culham, Juan Chen

papers.title: The contribution of semantic distance knowledge to size constancy in perception and grasping when visual cues are limited
papers.abstract: This study evaluated whether purely cognitive or semantic knowledge of an object's egocentric distance can support size constancy in perception and action systems when sensory distance cues are unavailable. Under 'glow-in-the-dark' viewing conditions that minimized visual depth information, providing explicit verbal information regarding the target's distance led to a moderate improvement in size-distance scaling. Critically, this cognitive benefit was equivalent for both perceptual size judgments and the visuomotor control of grip aperture in reach-to-grasp tasks. These findings imply that unlike sensory cues (such as vergence or proprioception), which often demonstrate specialized preferences within the dorsal or ventral visual streams, semantic knowledge serves as a high-level cognitive prior that supports size-distance computations across both visual systems without a specific motor or perceptual bias.
papers.authors: Gexiu Wang, Chao Zheng, Xiaoqian Wu, Zhiqing Deng, Irene Sperandio, Melvyn A. Goodale, Juan Chen

papers.title: Internal representations of the canonical real-world distance of objects
papers.abstract: The researchers investigated whether the human cognitive system maintains stable internal representations of the 'canonical' real-world distance of objects (e.g., that an airplane is typically far and a pair of glasses is near) and how these representations bias size perception. Behavioral experiments established that participants provide consistent canonical distance ratings for objects even when images are presented in isolation. Priming and adaptation paradigms demonstrated that these internal distance representations automatically modulated the perceived size and distance of subsequently presented targets. Objects associated with a 'near' canonical distance were perceived as smaller than those associated with a 'far' canonical distance, even when their retinal image sizes were identical. This indicates that canonical real-world distance is an inherent attribute of object representation that serves as an automatic prior for size-distance scaling and constancy.
papers.authors: Yijin Wang, Jie Gao, Fuying Zhu, Xiaoli Liu, Gexiu Wang, Yichong Zhang, Zhiqing Deng, Juan Chen

0342.name: Jude Mitchell
0342.department: Department of Brain and Cognitive Sciences
0342.bio: Jude F. Mitchell is an Associate Professor in the Department of Brain and Cognitive Sciences at the University of Rochester. Their research investigates the neural mechanisms of selective attention and sensory processing, focusing on how internal brain states influence visual perception and oculomotor control. Mitchell utilizes the common marmoset as a model for visual neuroscience, leveraging its smooth cortical surface to employ techniques such as laminar electrophysiology and optogenetic circuit mapping. Their current work explores the physiological basis of foveal vision, trans-saccadic integration, and the roles of distinct neuronal classes in active visual behavior.
0342.research_direction: Dr. Mitchell has recently been investigating the behavioral, neural, and computational mechanisms of active vision and oculomotor control. Their recent work explores pre-saccadic attention in the marmoset model, using electrophysiological recordings in area MT and behavioral markers like post-saccadic smooth eye movements to understand how motion information is processed and integrated during saccade planning. They are also probing the ethological bounds of primate gaze by tracking head-eye coordination and oculomotor dynamics in freely moving marmosets during natural foraging tasks. Broadening their investigation to artificial systems, they are examining the computational utility of foveated vision to test how simulated biological resolution gradients, such as cortical magnification, influence self-supervised object learning in bio-inspired neural networks.

papers.title: Probing the limited oculomotor range of common marmosets (Callithrix jacchus)
papers.abstract: Using a wide-field-of-view head-mounted eye tracker and a behavioral arena designed for natural foraging, we characterized the oculomotor dynamics of freely moving marmosets. We demonstrate that while marmosets are often characterized as having a highly limited oculomotor range in head-fixed laboratory tasks, their physical range is significantly broader in ethological contexts. However, the animals consistently prioritize rapid head movements for gaze shifts, maintaining eye positions within a narrow central range to facilitate efficient target acquisition and stabilization. These results provide new constraints on models of primate active vision and head-eye coordination.
papers.authors: Oviya Mohan, Alexia Nelms, Amy Bucklaew, Dora Biro, Jude Mitchell

papers.title: Simulated Cortical Magnification Supports Self-Supervised Object Learning
papers.abstract: We investigate the computational utility of foveated vision by applying human-inspired models of foveation and cortical magnification to egocentric video datasets. Using a self-supervised learning framework, we trained bio-inspired neural networks on sequences transformed to reflect the varying resolution of the primate retina and primary visual cortex. Our results indicate that incorporating these biological resolution gradients consistently enhances the quality of learned semantic object representations. Specifically, the expansion of central features via cortical magnification improves object recognition and induces a more efficient trade-off between foveal detail and peripheral context during development.
papers.authors: Zhengyang Yu, Arthur Aubret, Gabriel Sarch, Jacob L. Yates, Shanna H. Coop, Jude Mitchell

papers.title: Pre-saccadic Neural Enhancements in Marmoset Area MT
papers.abstract: We investigated the neural correlates of pre-saccadic attention in the middle temporal (MT) area of common marmosets using a saccade foraging task. Electrophysiological recordings revealed that neurons with receptive fields containing the saccade target exhibited significant enhancements in firing rate and motion information content prior to saccade onset. These modulations were predominantly additive and multiplicative increases across the neuron's tuning curve, rather than selective feature-tuned enhancements. Our findings indicate that marmosets exhibit pre-saccadic neural enhancements comparable to those observed in macaques, supporting the marmoset as a robust model for studying the circuit mechanisms of active visual attention.
papers.authors: Shanna H. Coop, Jacob L. Yates, Jude F. Mitchell

papers.title: Pre-saccadic enhancement of target stimulus motion influences post-saccadic smooth eye movements
papers.abstract: This study examines the post-saccadic following response (PFR) in marmoset monkeys as a behavioral marker of pre-saccadic motion integration. We found that immediately following a saccade to a peripheral motion target, marmosets exhibit involuntary smooth eye movements that track the target's motion direction with low gain. This following response occurs even when the stimulus disappears during the saccade, indicating it relies on a predictive estimate formed during pre-saccadic selection. The gain of the PFR serves as a quantitative index of attentional selection among multiple stimuli, demonstrating that primates automatically recruit smooth pursuit mechanisms during the planning of saccadic eye movements.
papers.authors: Shanna H. Coop, Garrett W. Bunce, Yonatan T. Abrham, Amy Bucklaew, Jude F. Mitchell

0344.name: Julie D. Golomb
0344.bio: Julie D. Golomb is a Professor at The Ohio State University and director of the Vision and Cognitive Neuroscience Lab, where they investigate how the brain constructs a stable perceptual representation from dynamic visual input. Golomb’s research employs behavioral psychophysics, functional MRI, EEG, and eye-tracking to explore interactions between attention, memory, and perception. Their work indicates that the visual system primarily encodes spatial location in retinotopic coordinates during high-level processing and examines how attention is remapped across eye movements. Current research focuses on the neural mechanisms of feature binding and the spatiotemporal representations of three-dimensional visual space.
0344.research_direction: Dr. Golomb has recently been investigating the spatiotemporal dynamics of human visual perception, focusing heavily on how the visual system maintains stability across eye movements and constructs complex spatial representations. Their recent work explores trans-saccadic perception using psychophysics and fMRI, specifically examining how saccadic predictability mitigates postsaccadic feature interference and whether eye movements transiently disrupt high-level semantic processing of natural scenes. Additionally, they are probing the neural computations underlying higher-order visual representations, utilizing EEG-fMRI fusion and representational similarity analysis to track the transformation of 2D retinal inputs into 3D spatial percepts and to disentangle an object's real-world size from low-level retinal features. Finally, Dr. Golomb is leveraging these multimodal neuroimaging datasets to evaluate artificial neural networks, investigating how aligning computer vision models with human EEG activity can generate more biologically plausible artificial intelligence.

papers.title: Spatiotemporal predictability of saccades modulates postsaccadic feature interference
papers.abstract: This investigation explored whether the spatiotemporal predictability of saccadic eye movements mitigates the systematic feature interference and perceptual instability often observed during trans-saccadic remapping. Utilizing a postsaccadic feature report paradigm across two preregistered experiments, the authors manipulated the spatial and temporal certainty of upcoming saccades. While both spatial and temporal predictability enhanced overall task performance, spatial predictability specifically reduced 'swapping errors'—instances where participants erroneously reported features from the previous retinotopic location instead of the spatiotopic target. These findings demonstrate that high-level expectations regarding saccade targets facilitate the efficient remapping of spatial attention and the suppression of residual retinotopic traces, thereby maintaining perceptual stability across eye movements.
papers.authors: Tzu-Yao Chiu, Isabel Jaen, Julie D. Golomb

papers.title: Post-saccadic disruption of semantic category information in naturalistic scenes
papers.abstract: This study examines the impact of saccadic eye movements on the neural and behavioral processing of high-level semantic category information in complex naturalistic scenes. Utilizing a combination of psychophysical categorization tasks and fMRI multivoxel pattern analysis (MVPA), the researchers assessed scene processing at varying post-saccadic latencies. Behavioral results indicated a robust decline in categorization accuracy for images presented within 50 ms after saccade completion. Corresponding fMRI data revealed that neural representational integrity for scene categories in the parahippocampal place area (PPA) was significantly degraded during short post-saccadic intervals (0–100 ms) compared to longer delays (400–600 ms). These findings suggest that the transient disruption of visual processing following a saccade extends beyond low-level features to impair high-level semantic representations in the ventral stream.
papers.authors: Yong Min Choi, Tzu-Yao Chiu, Julie D. Golomb

papers.title: Unfolding spatiotemporal representations of 3D visual perception in the human brain
papers.abstract: This research investigates the neurocomputational mechanisms underlying the transformation of two-dimensional retinal inputs into three-dimensional spatial percepts. Employing a large-scale multimodal neuroimaging dataset (EEG and fMRI fusion) and representational similarity analysis (RSA), the authors characterized the spatiotemporal dynamics of multiple spatial features and coordinate systems, including Cartesian and Polar frameworks. While robust 2D spatial representations were detected early in the visual hierarchy, unique neural signatures for depth and integrated 3D features—such as 3D radius and 3D polar angle—emerged at later latencies and in higher-level cortical regions, including the parahippocampus. These results delineate a clear spatiotemporal trajectory of 3D spatial encoding, progressing from initial 2D mapping to complex, integrated 3D representations that support navigation and interaction.
papers.authors: Zitong Lu, Julie D. Golomb

papers.title: Achieving more human brain-like vision via human EEG representational alignment
papers.abstract: This study introduces Re(presentational)Al(ignment)net, a computational framework designed to enhance the neural alignment of computer vision models with human visual processing using non-invasive EEG recordings. By implementing a novel multi-layer encoding-based alignment paradigm, the authors modified the internal representations of the CORnet architecture to better approximate human neural activity patterns. Results demonstrate that ReAlnet significantly increases representational similarity to human EEG signals across diverse object categories and generalizes to unseen classes. Furthermore, cross-modal validation with fMRI data confirmed that these EEG-aligned models more closely resemble human cortical processing in multiple regions of interest (ROIs) compared to baseline models, providing a scalable method for developing personalized and brain-like artificial intelligence systems.
papers.authors: Zitong Lu, Yile Wang, Julie D. Golomb

papers.title: Human EEG and artificial neural networks reveal disentangled representations of object real-world size in natural images
papers.abstract: This study utilizes representational similarity analysis on the large-scale THINGS-EEG2 dataset and various artificial neural network (ANN) architectures to disentangle the neural encoding of object real-world size from retinal size and perceived depth. The researchers identified a pure, unconfounded representation of real-world size in the human brain that emerges at late temporal stages, following the processing of depth and retinal size. Comparable findings were observed across diverse ANNs (ResNet, CLIP, and Word2Vec), where real-world size information was predominantly represented in deeper, higher-level layers. These results suggest that real-world size serves as a stable and high-level dimension of object space that integrates both visual and semantic information across biological and artificial systems.
papers.authors: Zitong Lu, Julie D. Golomb

0345.name: Julie M. Harris
0345.bio: Julie M. Harris is a Professor of Psychology and Neuroscience at the University of St Andrews whose research investigates how the brain processes complex visual information to guide motor action. Their work utilizes psychophysical, behavioural, and computational techniques to explore binocular stereopsis, motion-in-depth, and the ecological principles of animal camouflage. Harris studies how the human visual system decodes three-dimensional signals and the application of these processes to tasks such as hazard perception in driving and visual communication in virtual environments. Previously, they held research positions at the Smith-Kettlewell Eye Research Institute and the Universities of Edinburgh and Newcastle.
0345.research_direction: Dr. Harris has recently been investigating the perceptual and cognitive processing of natural animal warning signals. Their recent work explores how receivers process salient aposematic patterns, using human behavioral tasks to examine the relationship between subjective metamemory judgments and objective image recognition. Additionally, they are developing computational models of the early avian visual system to quantify the population-level neural excitation triggered by these biological patterns, providing an objective, predator-centric framework for evaluating visual ecology. Beyond their core vision science research, Dr. Harris is also examining systemic academic research culture, exploring how metric-driven competition impacts collaborative science and evaluating qualitative frameworks designed to foster more inclusive and collegial environments.

papers.title: Natural warning signals unexpectedly shape human metamemory ratings but not image recognition success
papers.abstract: This study evaluates whether the salient patterns associated with aposematism provide a functional advantage in memory retention or recognition. Utilizing a database of Lepidoptera images, the researchers measured human metamemory ratings (judgments of learning) and objective recognition memory performance following single exposures. Although aposematic patterns elicited significantly higher metamemory ratings from observers compared to cryptic species, logistic mixed-effects modeling indicated no significant difference in objective hit rates between the groups. The findings suggest that while warning signals are subjectively perceived as more memorable, their primary evolutionary advantage may reside in perceptual processes and immediate distinctiveness rather than intrinsic memory-retention superiority. The study further identifies 'memorability' as a consistent image-level property that predicts recognition across observers regardless of aposematic status.
papers.authors: Federico De Filippi, Olivier Penacchio, Akira R. O'Connor, Julie M. Harris

papers.title: A computational neuroscience framework for quantifying warning signals
papers.abstract: The authors present a quantitative definition of animal warning signals based on the population activity they stimulate in a receiver's brain. A computational model emulating the early avian visual system was developed using artificial neurons with realistic receptive fields to process hyperspectral images of aposematic and undefended Lepidoptera. By defining a 'neural signature' of patterns through metrics of population-level neural excitation, the study demonstrates that warning signals drive significantly stronger and more distinct responses in the modeled predator's visual cortex compared to both natural scenes and non-defended prey. Cross-validation analysis showed the framework could correctly classify 87.2% of species, offering an objective tool for testing the evolution and functional design of animal signals through the lens of predator-centric neural computation.
papers.authors: Olivier Penacchio, Christina G. Halpin, Innes C. Cuthill, Paul George Lovell, M. Wheelwright, J. Skelhorn, C. Rowe, Julie M. Harris

papers.title: Foregrounding Positive Research Culture
papers.abstract: Synthesizing themes from the International Research Culture Conference 2023, this work analyzes the systemic impact of excessive competition on the academic research environment. The article argues that existing metrics for assessing research output often catalyze an overly competitive landscape that is detrimental to collaborative scientific endeavors and individual researcher wellbeing. The authors advocate for the implementation of inclusive, adaptable measurement frameworks that prioritize collegiality and knowledge sharing across different demographic groups. The paper specifically examines the erosion of academic values and the disproportionate distribution of service tasks, suggesting that institutional progress toward a positive research culture requires a shift from metric-focused competition to qualitative assessments of community engagement and ethical research practices.
papers.authors: Anne-Marie Craig, Julie M. Harris

0346.name: Jun-Yun Zhang
0346.department: School of Psychological and Cognitive Sciences
0346.bio: Jun-Yun Zhang is an Associate Professor at Peking University specializing in visual perception and cortical plasticity. Zhang developed the "double training" and "Training-Plus-Exposure" (TPE) paradigms, which demonstrate that perceptual learning can generalize across retinal locations and orientations. Using psychophysical methodologies, they investigate the mechanisms underlying visual crowding, rule-based learning, and top-down influences on sensory processing. This research also extends to clinical applications, focusing on the diagnosis and treatment of visual deficits in individuals with amblyopia.
0346.research_direction: Dr. Zhang's recent work explores the underlying neural mechanisms of visual perceptual learning, focusing heavily on the boundaries between stimulus specificity and broad generalization. To investigate how training transfers to untrained visual field locations or novel features, they deploy complex behavioral paradigms like double-training and training-plus-exposure across various texture and orientation discrimination tasks. Their research also probes the practice volume required for visual plasticity, specifically testing whether brief memory reactivation can substitute for intensive training regimes to drive perceptual gains. Broadening their scope into clinical vision, Dr. Zhang has recently been examining higher-order processing deficits in children with amblyopia by utilizing dynamic slit-viewing tasks to measure temporal contour integration.

papers.title: Double training promotes retinotopic transfer of category learning
papers.abstract: Traditional views distinguish perceptual learning, which is typically retinotopically constrained, from category learning, which is expected to generalize across the visual field. Recent studies have challenged this by demonstrating that information-integration (II) category learning can exhibit visual-field specificity. This study utilized a double-training paradigm to examine the transfer of II learning across retinal locations. Participants were trained on a categorization task using Gabor stimuli at a single peripheral location, and transfer was evaluated in the opposite visual hemifield. The results confirmed visual-field specificity but demonstrated that robust transfer could be enabled through simultaneous or subsequent passive exposure to an irrelevant contrast discrimination task at the untrained location. Conversely, performing the irrelevant task before category training failed to produce transfer. This order-dependent effect suggests that II category learning and perceptual learning share common mechanisms of location-specific plasticity and flexible transfer protocols.
papers.authors: Jun-Ping Zhu, Xin-Yu Xie, Cong Yu, Jun-Yun Zhang

papers.title: Brief memory reactivation may not improve visual perception
papers.abstract: Visual perceptual learning (VPL) typically requires a high volume of trials to achieve significant performance gains. Some research has suggested that brief memory reactivation, through a few trials daily, could trigger reconsolidation and yield improvements comparable to full-practice training. We investigated this claim using a texture discrimination task (TDT) and an expanded experimental design to compare reactivation, no-reactivation, and full-practice groups. While between-group comparisons initially showed significant improvements in the reactivation group, these were found to be comparable to those in the no-reactivation (test-retest only) group. Furthermore, within-group analyses demonstrated that intensive practice over three additional days provided significantly superior gains compared to both brief reactivation and simple test-retest. These findings indicate that traditional, intensive training protocols are essential for substantial perceptual improvements and that brief memory reactivation may not be an effective substitute.
papers.authors: Jun-Ping Zhu, Jun-Yun Zhang

papers.title: Temporal Contour Integration Deficits in Children With Amblyopia
papers.abstract: While spatial domain deficits in contour integration are well-documented in amblyopia, the impact on temporal contour integration is less clear. This study employed a slit-viewing task to investigate how children with amblyopia integrate visual fragments over time. Collinear Gabor elements were moved behind a narrow vertical slit, and detection accuracy for tilted contour paths was measured. We systematically varied slit width, orientation jitter, and stimulus velocity. Results indicated that amblyopic eyes (AEs) suffer from significant temporal contour integration deficits compared to fellow eyes (FEs) and normal controls, requiring significantly wider slits to maintain detection performance. These deficits were most prominent under high collinearity and moderate movement speeds. The severity of temporal deficits correlated with AE visual acuity but appeared independent of spatial contour integration deficits, suggesting amblyopia impairs higher-order temporal processing mechanisms in dorsal and ventral visual streams.
papers.authors: Yan-Ru Chen, Shu-Qi Jiang, Xiang-Yun Liu, Jun-Yun Zhang

papers.title: Feature variability determines specificity and transfer in multiorientation feature detection learning
papers.abstract: Perceptual learning is frequently specific to the trained stimulus feature, but multi-stimulus paradigms such as the training-plus-exposure (TPE) procedure have shown potential for generalization. This study examined the roles of roving and feature variability in a multi-orientation feature detection task where a target bar differed from background bars by 16°. Observers practiced with four target orientation search stimuli characterized by either low (5°) or high (45°) orientation deviation. We found that training with low feature variability led to significant performance improvements but failed to transfer to swapped target-background orientations. In contrast, training with high variability slowed the initial learning rate but enabled significant generalization. Furthermore, a modified TPE procedure involving passive exposure to high-variability orientations facilitated transfer for stimuli initially trained with low variability. These results suggest that high feature variability during training is a crucial determinant for enabling generalization in complex visual learning tasks.
papers.authors: Jun-Ping Zhu, Jun-Yun Zhang

papers.title: The Neural Mechanism of Perceptual Learning
papers.abstract: This review analyzes the neural processes mediating visual perceptual learning (VPL), focusing on the long-term performance enhancements resulting from systematic training. Historically, the orientation and location specificity of VPL have been interpreted as evidence of low-level plasticity in the primary visual cortex (V1). However, the emergence of training tactics like double-training and training-plus-exposure (TPE) has demonstrated complete learning transfer to untrained conditions, indicating the involvement of higher-level cognitive mechanisms. The paper evaluates competing theories, including the 'early cortical plasticity' model and the 'rule-based learning' or 'reweighting' models, which suggest improved readout of early sensory signals by higher-order decision units. We discuss how top-down feedback and task-relevant attention modulate these processes, reconciling specificity and transfer within a unified framework of neural plasticity.
papers.authors: Yan-Ru Chen, Yu-Wei Zhang, Jun-Yun Zhang

0348.name: Justin Halberda
0348.department: Department of Psychological and Brain Sciences
0348.bio: Justin Halberda’s research investigates the architectural links between visual perception, numerical cognition, and the development of language. Halberda characterizes the human 'approximate number system' (ANS), using psychophysical modeling to demonstrate how non-verbal magnitude estimation precision predicts symbolic mathematical performance across the lifespan. Their work employs methodologies such as change detection paradigms, multiple object tracking, and large-scale internet-based testing to probe the constraints of visual working memory and attentional selection. Additionally, Halberda explores the interface of vision and semantics by analyzing how the meanings of logical quantifiers are grounded in non-linguistic perceptual systems.
0348.research_direction: Dr. Halberda has recently been exploring the cognitive architectures underlying higher-order visual perception and early logical reasoning. In the domain of visual cognition, their recent work investigates how the visual system extracts and maintains magnitude information, using dynamic stimuli and rapid discrimination tasks to test whether numerosity adaptation survives non-retinotopic spatial displacement and whether observers automatically encode the extreme boundaries of magnitude sets alongside summary statistics. They are also probing the mechanisms of visual working memory, employing mixture-modeling to examine how individuals use internal generative models of their own perceptual precision to systematically structure their guesses when sensory evidence is absent. Additionally, Dr. Halberda’s developmental research investigates the foundations of early human thought, using novel decision-making paradigms to determine whether toddlers employ domain-general reasoning strategies—such as disjunctive inference and modal judgments of possibility—prior to formal language acquisition.

papers.title: Guessing reveals internal models of perceptual precision
papers.abstract: The present study characterizes the representational mechanisms governing guessing behavior in visual cognition and working memory. While traditional psychophysical models, such as Signal Detection Theory, treat guesses as stochastic noise or uniform distributions over feature space, the authors demonstrate through a mixture-modeling framework that human guesses are systematically structured. Results from multiple magnitude discrimination and continuous-report tasks reveal an 'anti-Bayesian' pattern where observers preferentially guess values they encode with the least precision. This complementary relationship between guessing and perceptual fidelity suggests that observers strategically leverage internal generative models of their own sensory noise and metacognitive knowledge of representational fidelity to guide decisions in the absence of evidence, reframing guessing as a theoretically informative behavior that expresses an individual's internal model of their own perceptual capacity.
papers.authors: Caroline Myers, Chaz Firestone, Justin Halberda

papers.title: Number adaptation survives spatial displacement
papers.abstract: This research investigates the spatial reference frames of numerosity adaptation, a higher-order visual feature localized to the intraparietal sulcus (IPS). Canonical adaptation effects for early visual features like orientation and color are typically retinotopically specific. Across six experiments using dynamic stimuli, the authors tested whether number adaptation travels with moving objects or remains anchored to retinal coordinates. Observers adapted to dot arrays within translating discs and were then tested with probes in varying spatial positions. The findings demonstrate that number adaptation persists despite spatial displacement, effectively binding to moving objects rather than fixed retinal locations. This result reveals a non-retinotopic form of adaptation that diverges from early visual processing, indicating that the visual system automatically extracts and maintains numerical information as a persistent, object-bound attribute during motion.
papers.authors: Caroline Myers, Chaz Firestone, Justin Halberda

papers.title: Logical Concepts of (Im)possibility Guide Young Children's Decision-Making
papers.abstract: The study examines the early developmental foundations of modal judgment—the cognitive capacity to distinguish between necessity, possibility, and impossibility—prior to the acquisition of modal language. Utilizing a novel decision-making paradigm with preschool-aged children (N = 96), the authors assessed participants' ability to recruit logical modal categories to guide one-shot rational decisions. Findings reveal that children as young as 34 months successfully navigate choices crossing logical boundaries (e.g., necessity versus possibility), whereas they struggle with intra-categorical probability comparisons (e.g., high versus low probability). These results suggest that the cognitive architecture for representing logical (im)possibility emerges spontaneously and independently of linguistic mastery or probabilistic reasoning, supporting the existence of a domain-general logical engine for modal inference in early childhood.
papers.authors: Nicoló Cesana-Arlotti, Sofia Jáuregui, Peter Mazalik, Shaun Nichols, Justin Halberda

papers.title: A continuity in logical development: Domain-general disjunctive inference by toddlers
papers.abstract: Disjunctive inference (A or B, not A, therefore B) is a fundamental logical reasoning strategy often observed in specific contexts like word learning. This study investigates whether this capacity represents a domain-general cognitive tool available to toddlers (aged 2.3–3.2 years). Using a comparative experimental design across three conceptually distinct domains—linguistic label mapping, social agent fact-learning, and physical outcome prediction—the researchers found consistent evidence of disjunctive reasoning. Toddlers systematically considered and rejected competitors to identify correct targets in all scenarios, regardless of the domain. The results provide evidence for a domain-general logical reasoning engine that operates before formal education or extensive experience with logical operators, suggesting a profound continuity in the architecture of logical thought throughout human development.
papers.authors: Nicoló Cesana-Arlotti, Justin Halberda

papers.title: Observers Efficiently Extract the Minimal and Maximal Element in Perceptual Magnitude Sets: Evidence for a Bipartite Format
papers.abstract: The Approximate Number System (ANS) is traditionally modeled as extracting summary statistics, such as the mean or total numerosity, from magnitude sets. This research explores whether the visual system also represents the extremes of such sets, specifically the minimal and maximal elements. Through a series of rapid discrimination tasks, the authors demonstrate that observers extract the bounds of a magnitude set with an efficiency that is independent of set size, mirroring the performance patterns observed in ensemble average extraction. These results provide empirical evidence for a bipartite representational format that encodes both the range and the distribution of magnitude sets. This format facilitates more sophisticated cognitive operations, such as range comparison and ordinal mapping, than simple averaging models allow, expanding our understanding of the representational content of the intuitive number sense.
papers.authors: Darko Odic, Tyler Knowlton, Alexis Wellwood, Paul Pietroski, Jeffrey Lidz, Justin Halberda

0349.name: Jutta Billino
0349.bio: Billino is an Associate Professor at Justus Liebig University Giessen investigating visual perception and sensorimotor control across the adult lifespan. They employ psychophysical methods, eye-tracking, and motion capture to examine the interaction and individual variation of sensory, motor, cognitive, and motivational mechanisms. Billino's research covers motion processing pathways, saccadic eye movement plasticity, and visuomotor adaptation in both healthy populations and clinical patients with cerebral lesions. They aim to identify mechanisms of functional aging and the factors involved in perceptual and motor preservation.
0349.research_direction: Dr. Billino has recently been investigating the intersection of cognitive aging, predictive processing, and sensorimotor control, alongside contributing to the structural development of clinical neuropsychology education. Their recent experimental work explores how prior knowledge and semantic expectation violations influence visual processing and memory across the lifespan, using virtual reality eye-tracking to study gaze guidance during active locomotion and assessing episodic memory for incongruent objects in naturalistic scenes. In the domain of motor control, they are also examining the cognitive response selection and temporal constraints of bimanual coordination by modeling reaction time distributions to varying spatial and symbolic cues. Additionally, their recent clinical policy papers address the practical challenges of integrating empirical research and clinical competencies into Germany's evolving neuropsychological psychotherapy training frameworks.

papers.title: In Theorie und Praxis: Wie Promotion und Gebietsweiterbildung in Neuropsychologischer Psychotherapie verbinden? – Spezifische Herausforderungen und Chancen für Promotionsvorhaben
papers.abstract: The transition to the reformed psychotherapist training legislation in Germany has formalized Neuropsychological Psychotherapy (NPPT) as an autonomous specialty area of psychotherapy practice, introducing significant structural ramifications for academic qualifications. This position paper analyzes the integration of doctoral research (Promotion) with specialty residency training (Gebietsweiterbildung) in NPPT at academic outpatient clinics. The authors evaluate systemic bottlenecks, including funding constraints, clinical supervision infrastructure, and research-practice reconciliation under current chamber regulations. They outline operational structural frameworks designed to harmonize rigorous empirical neurocognitive research programs with outpatient clinical qualification requirements, offering concrete strategies to cultivate clinical neuropsychologist-scientists and counter ongoing healthcare underprovision.
papers.authors: Patrizia Thoma, Mathias Klinghammer, Jutta Billino

papers.title: Violated expectations during locomotion through virtual environments: Age effects on gaze guidance
papers.abstract: Active locomotion demands dynamic attentional allocation between environmental information foraging and sensorimotor gait stabilization, a balance that older adults often recalibrate toward the walking ground. This study evaluated how predictive processing and expectation violations modulate gaze guidance during locomotion across adult aging. Healthy younger (n = 24, 18–38 years) and older adults (n = 24, 60–81 years) traversed a realistic virtual reality (VR) hallway rendered in Unity containing semantically expected and unexpected objects while eye movements were tracked at 120 Hz with an HTC Vive Pro Eye system. Participants also performed neuropsychological testing of executive functioning and motor control. Dwell times on unexpected objects were significantly elevated compared to expected objects across cohorts (t(23) = −5.35 and t(23) = −6.83, respectively). However, this effect was significantly more pronounced in older adults: while dwell times on expected objects were lower in older adults than younger adults (t(46) = 3.95, d = 1.14), dwell times on unexpected objects reached parity (t(46) = 0.10, d = 0.03). Dwell time allocation was significantly linked to executive cognitive control capacities rather than fine or gross motor performance. These results demonstrate that expectation violations powerfully commandeer overt attentional resources during locomotion, potentially exacerbating fall risk in older populations.
papers.authors: Sophie Meissner, Jochen Miksch, Lena Würbach, Sascha Feder, Sabine Grimm, Wolfgang Einhäuser, Jutta Billino

papers.title: Neuropsychologische Psychotherapie im Approbationsstudium – Quo vadis?
papers.abstract: The German Psychotherapy Training Reform (PsychThApprO) mandates that clinical neuropsychological concepts, diagnostics, and interventions be integrated into master's curricula and qualifying clinical placements (Berufsqualifizierende Tätigkeit III; BQT III). This article reviews the challenges German university departments confront in institutionalizing Neuropsychological Psychotherapy within constrained fiscal and personnel structures. Outlining pedagogical and organizational paradigms implemented across university clinics in Mainz, Bochum, and Giessen, the authors demonstrate how rotational models, video livestreaming of diagnostic intakes, supervised therapy sessions, and partnerships with accredited inpatient clinics can provide Master's students with clinical competencies in neurocognitive remediation, fostering sustained career paths into ambulatory neuropsychological healthcare.
papers.authors: Mathias Klinghammer, Patrizia Thoma, Jutta Billino

papers.title: Reaction time distribution analysis of bimanual movements with spatial and symbolic cues
papers.abstract: The preparation of asymmetric bimanual reaching movements (differing amplitudes) typically incurs a performance cost compared to symmetric movements, an effect known to be sensitive to the nature of the movement cues. This study employed ex-Gaussian distribution analysis (parameters μ, σ, and τ) to scrutinize the sensorimotor mechanisms underlying these costs in younger adults. Spatially cued movements exhibited a minimal asymmetric cost to μ (approximately 4.8 ms), indicative of inherent temporal coupling between limbs. Conversely, symbolically cued movements produced substantial increases in μ along with smaller increases in σ and τ. The findings suggest that asymmetric costs for symbolic cues are driven by a combination of stimulus-response translation overhead and temporal coupling, with the former being the dominant factor. The dispersion and skewness of the reaction time distributions (σ and τ) were uniquely affected by translation processes, highlighting the interplay between cognitive response selection and motoric constraints in bimanual coordination.
papers.authors: Jarrod Blinch, Catherine E. Gooch, Allison R. Clark, Bryce Murrin, Constanze Hesse, Laura Koroknai, Jutta Billino

papers.title: Aging attenuates the memory advantage for unexpected objects in real-world scenes
papers.abstract: Prior schema knowledge profoundly modulates episodic memory across the adult lifespan, yet how predictive scene schemas bias object representation in older age remains unresolved. A cohort of 23 younger (18–38 years) and 23 older adults (52–81 years) viewed 60 photographic scenes containing target objects that were either semantically congruent or incongruent with the context. In a surprise post-encoding assessment, object recognition discriminability and object-to-scene associative matching were evaluated. Although semantic expectancy violations conferred an overall recognition memory benefit in both cohorts, this memory advantage was significantly attenuated in older adults. Furthermore, older adults exhibited a pronounced schema-congruency bias when matching recognized targets to original scene backgrounds. These findings align with predictive coding models positing an increased prior weighting in senescence, demonstrating that heightened reliance on top-down semantic schemas diminishes the encoding benefit typically afforded by prediction errors.
papers.authors: Lena Klever, Jasmin Islam, Melissa Le-Hoa Võ, Jutta Billino

0350.name: K. Suzanne Scherf
0350.bio: Scherf investigates the developmental trajectories of visual and social-cognitive processes, focusing on how the brain’s functional specificity for face processing emerges from childhood through adulthood. Their research utilizes multimodal neuroimaging techniques, including functional and structural MRI and diffusion tensor imaging, alongside eye-tracking and behavioral paradigms to study typical development and neurodevelopmental conditions such as autism. Scherf examines the impact of pubertal maturation on the reorganization of neural circuits involved in social information processing during adolescence. Additionally, they oversee the design and evaluation of digital serious games intended to serve as social interventions for individuals with autism spectrum disorder.
0350.research_direction: Dr. Scherf’s recent work explores the developmental trajectory and individual variability of social visual perception, with a strong focus on face processing during adolescence and in autism spectrum disorder. They have recently been investigating how internalizing symptoms modulate early psychophysical discrimination thresholds for complex facial expressions, while also examining the developmental magnitude of the own-race bias in facial identity recognition. To understand individual differences in these mechanisms, their research probes the intra-individual stability of unfamiliar face memory across varying stimulus contexts using paradigms like the Cambridge Face Memory Test. Additionally, they are employing high-resolution eye-tracking to determine whether behavioral interventions alter macro-level social visual attention to dynamic gaze shifts in autistic youth, alongside methodological work evaluating the test-retest reliability of these adolescents' self-reported social functioning compared to parent evaluations.

papers.title: Ask autistic adolescents too: informant discrepancies and test-retest reliability in social behavior
papers.abstract: This study evaluated informant discrepancies and the temporal stability of self-reported social functioning in autistic youth compared to parent reports. Across two randomized controlled trials comprising 81 parent-adolescent dyads (ages 10–18), participants completed the Social Skills Improvement System (SSIS) rating scales across a 2- to 3-month interval. Test-retest reliability was established within the control cohorts (N = 40) using intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs) based on two-way mixed-effects models and Pearson correlations. Autistic adolescents demonstrated moderate test-retest reliability for both social competence and problem behaviors without systematic reporting bias for social skills, whereas problem behaviors exhibited regression-to-the-mean patterns. Baseline analyses across all dyads demonstrated weak inter-rater concordance and significant systematic divergence: autistic youth reported significantly higher social competence and fewer problem behaviors relative to parent evaluations, with the magnitude of disagreement increasing as adolescent-reported social competence scores rose. These results challenge assumptions regarding the unreliability of autistic self-report and support incorporating youth perspectives into multidimensional clinical assessments.
papers.authors: Hunter Mattern, Glenn I. Roisman, K. Suzanne Scherf

papers.title: Perceiving motivational signaling and complexity in facial emotion expressions: the role of internalizing symptoms
papers.abstract: This investigation tested whether internalizing symptoms modulate early, non-linguistic perceptual sensitivity to facial expressions varying along distinct signaling dimensions. Emerging adults (N = 123) performed an online psychophysical just-noticeable-difference (JND) staircase paradigm using stimuli from the Complex Emotion Expression Database, measuring discrimination thresholds required to distinguish expressive faces from neutral counterparts. Stimuli systematically crossed motivational direction (approach vs. avoid), structural complexity (basic vs. complex), and affective valence (positive vs. negative), with concurrent assessment of depression and anxiety symptomatology. Observers exhibited lower perceptual thresholds (greater sensitivity) for approach-oriented relative to avoidance-oriented expressions, but sensitivity was not systematically structured by complexity or valence. Elevated depressive symptoms did not predict perceptual discrimination thresholds across any expression subcategory, reflecting intact early sensory encoding of affect. Conversely, heightened anxiety symptoms specifically predicted decreased sensitivity (elevated thresholds) to anger and fear displays, implicating targeted disruption of early visual processing for threat-related expressions.
papers.authors: Myles N. Arrington, Lark Caboy, Jordan Sigler, Sara Silber, Lorah D. Dorn, Glenn I. Roisman, K. Suzanne Scherf

papers.title: Investigating the stability of individual differences in face recognition behavior
papers.abstract: While individual variability in unfamiliar face recognition is widely characterized as a stable, highly heritable cognitive trait, prevailing frameworks rely predominantly on between-subject variance across extreme performers rather than evaluating intra-individual stability across task contexts. To examine intra-individual reliability and consistency, emerging adults were assessed on two structurally matched paradigms of unfamiliar face memory differing primarily in stimulus target gender (the male CFMT+ and the female F-CFMT+). Although aggregate sample-level performance demonstrated strong rank-order stability (r = 0.71), significant intra-individual discrepancies emerged: 16.7% of participants exhibited divergent recognition accuracy between male and female tests exceeding 1 standard deviation. Moreover, high behavioral stability was disproportionately confined to individuals at the upper and lower performance margins. Participant demographic and psychometric covariates—including observer sex, age, and self-reported social skills—failed to account for this task-dependent variance, challenging unidimensional models of face recognition competence.
papers.authors: Myles N Arrington, K Suzanne Scherf

papers.title: How is race perceived during adolescence? A meta-analysis of the own-race bias
papers.abstract: Adolescence involves major neurodevelopmental reorganizations in social perceptual circuitry, often indexed by emerging behavioral biases in facial processing. This study examined the developmental trajectory and magnitude of the own-race bias (ORB) in identity recognition across adolescence (~10 to 22 years of age) through a Bayesian random-effects meta-analytic framework. Synthesizing 38 effect sizes across 16 empirical studies comprising 1,321 adolescent participants, the analysis tested hypotheses derived from perceptual expertise and social-cognitive models, which predict an age-dependent expansion of the ORB driven by cumulative disproportionate contact with own-race exemplars. The meta-analytic summary effect revealed a small, positive ORB (Hedges' g = 0.24) that remained stable across varying prior distributions and levels of analytical uncertainty. However, effect magnitude was not reliably moderated by chronological age or participant racial categorization, demonstrating that adolescent ORB expression does not follow simple linear accretion models of perceptual exposure.
papers.authors: Junqiang Dai, Jason W. Griffin, K. Suzanne Scherf

papers.title: Social visual attention as a treatment outcome: evaluating the social games for autistic adolescents (SAGA) intervention
papers.abstract: Difficulty decoding dynamic eye-gaze shifts is a hallmark feature of autism spectrum disorder (ASD) hypothesized to stem from atypical social visual attention (SVA). In this randomized controlled trial evaluating the serious game intervention Social Games for Autistic Adolescents (SAGA) versus standard-of-care controls, high-resolution eye tracking was acquired during an ecologically naturalistic Gaze Perception task to establish whether intervention-driven improvements in gaze decoding were mediated by increases in foveation toward faces and target referents. Contrary to mechanistic predictions, autistic participants in the serious game condition did not show preferential increases in proportional dwell time or fixation counts to faces relative to control participants; both arms exhibited modest gains in face-directed looking across test intervals. Furthermore, baseline SVA metrics failed to predict behavioral gaze-decoding accuracy at pre- or post-test. These findings demonstrate that therapeutic enhancements in social gaze interpretation occur independently of quantitative shifts in macro-level ocular engagement with facial features.
papers.authors: K. Suzanne Scherf, Jason W. Griffin, Charles F. Geier, Joshua M. Smyth

0352.name: Karen B. Schloss
0352.bio: Karen B. Schloss is an Associate Professor at the University of Wisconsin–Madison, where they direct the Visual Reasoning Lab and hold affiliations with the Wisconsin Institute for Discovery. Schloss’s research investigates the cognitive and perceptual processes that enable humans to derive meaning from visual features, particularly color semantics and aesthetics. They developed the Ecological Valence Theory, which explains human color preferences as a product of affective associations with objects and environments. Currently, Schloss employs psychophysical methods and virtual reality to study information visualization design and methods for making scientific communication more accessible.
0352.research_direction: Dr. Schloss has recently been investigating the perceptual and cognitive foundations of information visualization, focusing on how the human visual system extracts meaning from complex graphical displays. Their recent work explores the rules of visual semantics through their "Color Inference Framework," using behavioral and psychophysical paradigms to examine how observers dynamically map colors to abstract or concrete conceptual categories and how affective colormaps can balance emotional valence with high-frequency spatial resolution. Additionally, they are studying distinct perceptual illusions and cognitive heuristics that influence quantitative reasoning, such as testing how transparency and saturation drive "opaque-is-more" inferences and measuring figure-ground segregation errors caused by occlusion in multi-layer bar charts.

papers.title: Understanding the opaque-is-more bias and saturated-is-more bias for colormap data visualizations
papers.abstract: This study characterizes the perceptual underpinnings of magnitude inference from colormap visualizations, specifically focusing on the isolation of "opaque-is-more" and "saturated-is-more" biases. The researchers utilized a psychophysical paradigm to dissociate opacity effects by modulating saturation relative to background colors while maintaining a constant CIELAB lightness (L*) coordinate. Experimental results demonstrate that the opaque-is-more bias—the cognitive heuristic where higher opacity denotes greater data magnitude—persists independently of lightness variation. Furthermore, the work identifies a novel "saturated-is-more" bias and discusses the findings within the framework of applicability and combination principles, contributing to a mechanistic model of multi-bias integration in visual reasoning.
papers.authors: Melissa A. Schoenlein, Mouloukou Sidibe, Karen B. Schloss

papers.title: Affective Color Scales for Colormap Data Visualizations
papers.abstract: This research investigates the design of affective colormaps, addressing the conflict between emotional communication and spatial resolution requirements. Given that affective associations are often mediated by lightness contrast, monochromatic scales designed for emotional impact frequently fail to resolve high-frequency spatial data. The authors evaluated sixteen color scales varying in hue, chroma, and lightness, demonstrating that colormaps can be engineered to simultaneously preserve lightness contrast for spatial vision while effectively conveying targeted emotional valences. The study validates a "data-dependence hypothesis," showing that perceived affective meaning is significantly modulated by the frequency distribution of underlying data values, necessitating data-aware visualization design strategies.
papers.venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
papers.authors: Halle C. Braun, Kushin Mukherjee, Seth R. Gorelik, Karen B. Schloss

papers.title: Perceptual and Cognitive Foundations of Information Visualization
papers.abstract: This comprehensive review articulates the perceptual and cognitive architectures that facilitate the interpretation of information visualizations, organized into the domains of feature perception, semantic mapping, and world-based comprehension. The author posits that visualization efficacy depends on architectural alignment with internal neurocognitive constraints, specifically through semantically-resonant mappings defined by the "Color Inference Framework." Key topics include how observers utilize color-concept associations and systematic biases (e.g., dark-is-more) to infer data meaning, and the visual system's capacity for extracting global statistical summaries from complex displays. The work provides a theoretical basis for designing visualizations that minimize cognitive load and maximize communication efficiency.
papers.authors: Karen B. Schloss

papers.title: Beyond the Cloud: A Perceptual Illusion in Overlaid Bar Charts
papers.abstract: This work identifies and quantifies a novel perceptual bias, the "Beyond the Cloud" illusion, which occurs during the interpretation of overlaid bar chart displays. Through behavioral experimentation, the authors measured significant errors in observers' height estimations for underlying bars when they are partially occluded by semi-transparent overlays. The findings indicate that overlapping spatial boundaries and transparency interfere with fundamental visual processes of figure-ground segregation and contour integration within the visual system, leading to biased quantitative judgments. This research offers critical insights into the perceptual limitations of multi-layer data visualization and proposes specific design constraints to improve the accuracy of comparative visual assessments.
papers.authors: Wenxuan Zhao, Karen B. Schloss

papers.title: Color semantics in human cognition
papers.abstract: This article introduces the "Color Inference Framework" to model how observers derive meaning from colors in visual communication. The framework distinguishes between relatively stable color-concept associations and the dynamic, context-contingent process of color semantics, detailing the specific inferential operations used to resolve semantic conflicts when mapping sets of colors to conceptual categories. Empirical findings are reviewed to demonstrate that these inferences are robust and extend across both concrete and abstract conceptual domains, such as social and temporal categories. The paper argues that understanding the rules governing color-meaning inferences allows for the systematic design of more intuitive and interpretable information graphics.
papers.authors: Karen B. Schloss

0353.name: Karin James
0353.department: Department of Psychological and Brain Sciences
0353.bio: Karin Harman James is a Professor at Indiana University Bloomington where their research examines the intersection of sensori-motor experience and cognitive development. James utilizes functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (fMRI) to study how self-generated motor actions, such as handwriting and object manipulation, facilitate the functional specialization of the brain's visual systems. By studying both children and adults, James investigates the neural correlates of learning in domains like literacy and object recognition. Their research focuses on how bodily interaction with the environment shapes neural representation and perception.
0353.research_direction: Dr. James has recently been investigating the profound connections between fine motor action, visual perception, and cognitive development. Their recent work explores how active, self-generated movements—such as preschool children learning to write letters by hand or adults manually exploring novel 3D objects—facilitate the development of specialized neural reading circuits and robust visuo-haptic object representations. Additionally, they are examining the broader relationship between sensorimotor development and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) through the lens of embodied cognition. Using both psychophysical laboratory experiments and ecological classroom studies, Dr. James assesses how the physical and cognitive demands of different transcription modalities, like traditional handwriting versus digital typing, affect real-time information encoding in students with varying levels of inattention.

papers.title: A Classroom Study on Notetaking Modalities and Inattentive Attention‐Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder Symptoms
papers.abstract: This ecological classroom investigation evaluated the impact of self-selected notetaking modalities—specifically laptops, tablets, and traditional longhand—on academic performance in relation to inattentive Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) symptomology. Regression analyses of quiz data from a collegiate sample indicated a significant interaction between symptom severity and transcription medium: higher levels of inattentive ADHD symptoms were associated with diminished learning outcomes when utilizing manual handwriting, whereas performance was selectively facilitated by digital modalities. The findings suggest that the transcription-related motoric and cognitive load inherent to longhand notetaking may disrupt encoding efficacy in students with elevated inattentive traits, positioning digital tablets and laptops as effective compensatory tools for information retention.
papers.authors: Gabrielle A. Shimko, Emily R. Fyfe, Karin H. James

papers.title: The Relationship Between Motor Development and ADHD: A Critical Review and Future Directions
papers.abstract: This review provides a comprehensive synthesis of behavioral and neuroimaging evidence to examine the mechanistic link between motor developmental trajectories and the etiology of Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD). The authors argue that conventional theoretical frameworks often neglect the motor system as a foundational component of the disorder's functional impairment. By applying the principles of embodied development, the paper highlights how sensorimotor deficits—ranging from fine motor dexterity to gross motor coordination—are intrinsically coupled with cognitive dysregulation throughout early development. This perspective suggests that integrating motor-based assessments and interventions is crucial for advancing the diagnostic and therapeutic landscape of ADHD.
papers.authors: Gabrielle A. Shimko, Karin H. James

papers.title: The effects of notetaking modality and symptoms of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) on learning
papers.abstract: This experimental study examined the interaction between lecture notetaking modalities and ADHD symptoms to determine if digital transcription could mitigate the encoding deficits associated with slower handwriting speed (HWS). In a controlled laboratory setting, participants oversampled for ADHD diagnoses engaged in handwritten, typed, or no-note conditions while viewing standardized educational content. Performance on delayed recall assessments revealed that individuals with significant ADHD symptomology derived greater learning benefits from active transcription than from passive listening. The results further demonstrated that individual differences in HWS and sustained attention are critical moderators of notetaking efficacy, indicating that typing may serve as a beneficial alternative for students whose manual transcription speed limits real-time encoding.
papers.authors: Gabrielle A. Shimko, Karin H. James

papers.title: The importance of multisensory-motor learning on subsequent visual recognition
papers.abstract: This psychophysical investigation assessed the 'active advantage' in visual object recognition by comparing the effects of multisensory (visuo-haptic) manual exploration of novel 3D objects against passive observation. The study focused on how viewer-controlled viewpoint selection—specifically the prioritization of planar views where the major axis of elongation is perpendicular or parallel to the line of sight—contributes to the construction of robust structural representations. Experimental results showed that active manual control facilitates the selection of informative object orientations, leading to superior recognition accuracy and faster reaction times. The integration of haptic feedback during active encoding was found to further refine the internal 3D model, optimizing subsequent cross-modal and unisensory recognition performance.
papers.authors: Hellen Kyler, Karin James

papers.title: Learning to write letters and digits by hand in preschool
papers.abstract: This longitudinal research investigated the impact of graphomotor production on the development of literacy-related neural networks and symbol recognition in pre-literate children. By comparing handwriting to tracing and typing experiences, the study tracked the emergence of a specialized 'reading circuit' comprising visual and motor regions, including the lateral occipital and premotor cortices. Findings indicated that the physical production of symbol forms through handwriting provides unique sensorimotor contingencies that facilitate more robust symbol categorization and neural specialization compared to non-production modalities. The study emphasizes the critical role of self-generated manual action in establishing the functional connectivity necessary for early reading and writing proficiency.
papers.authors: Sophia Vinci-Booher, Deborah Zemlock, Susie Ju, Karin James

0354.name: Karl R. Gegenfurtner
0354.bio: Karl R. Gegenfurtner is a professor of psychology whose research examines the interactions between low-level sensory processing, higher-level visual cognition, and sensorimotor control. Gegenfurtner investigates color vision and eye movements, specifically how color contributes to object recognition and how visual information is used to guide motor behavior. Their methodological approach combines psychophysics and eye tracking with computational modeling and virtual reality to study perception in naturalistic environments. Currently, their work focuses on the neural representation of complex scenes and the mechanisms of color constancy through an object-oriented lens.
0354.research_direction: Dr. Gegenfurtner has recently been leveraging immersive virtual reality to investigate the metric structure of human color space and the computational mechanisms underlying color constancy in complex 3D environments. Their recent work explores how global illumination and local spatial contexts interact to shape human reflectance estimation, while simultaneously comparing human psychophysical performance against deep neural network models to test the impact of varying perceptual cues. Beyond color vision, they are examining the dynamic orchestration of naturalistic visuomotor behavior, specifically tracking how observers coordinate saccades, pursuit eye movements, and manual actions to minimize sensory uncertainty during continuous target-interception tasks. Additionally, Dr. Gegenfurtner is developing new methodological and data visualization tools, such as diagonal confidence intervals for scatter plots, to improve the accurate communication of within-subject experimental effects.

papers.title: Color discrimination in action: High-throughput measurement in immersive VR
papers.abstract: We developed an active sensing paradigm to bypass the temporal constraints of large-scale chromatic mapping by measuring discrimination thresholds within a color-calibrated immersive virtual reality (VR) environment. Using a 4-alternative forced-choice (4-AFC) odd-one-out task integrated into a rhythmic motor interaction framework, participants indicated chromatic targets in DKL color space via high-frequency manual slicing (approximately 1 trial per second). Psychophysical results replicated characteristic hue-chroma asymmetries, including lower thresholds for hue compared to chroma and quadrant-specific variations in the hue-chroma ratio. Validation against keyboard-based psychometric functions confirmed that the high-throughput motor engagement did not degrade the precision of threshold estimates, demonstrating that calibrated immersive VR provides a scalable and motivating platform for characterizing the metric structure of human color space.
papers.authors: Giulia Agosti, Jacob Hadnett-Hunter, Karl R. Gegenfurtner

papers.title: Colour Constancy: Colour Interaction between Local Surround and Illumination in Virtual Reality Scenarios
papers.abstract: This study utilized photorealistic virtual reality (VR) and Unreal Engine to investigate the interaction between global illumination and local chromatic surrounds in 3D scenes. Using an HTC Vive Pro Eye headset, observers performed a neutral-point matching task under five distinct illuminants across Indoor and Outdoor environments. Chromaticities were systematically manipulated in CIELAB color space to evaluate the contribution of local spatial context to reflectance estimation. Results demonstrated a significant attenuation of color constancy performance when the chromaticity vector of the illuminant was diametrically opposed to that of the local surround. These findings emphasize that robust color constancy is critically dependent on the spatial distribution and relative direction of chromatic signals within the scene, rather than global statistics alone.
papers.authors: Raquel Gil Rodríguez, Laysa Hedjar, Betül Kilic, Karl R. Gegenfurtner

papers.title: Human-Aligned Evaluation of a Pixel-wise DNN Color Constancy Model
papers.abstract: We performed a direct comparison between human psychophysical behavior and a pixel-wise Deep Neural Network (DNN) for color constancy within immersive VR. The model architecture comprised a ResNet-based U-Net pre-trained for surface reflectance estimation on synthetic imagery, followed by decoder-specific transfer learning on baseline VR scenes. To ensure comparative validity, model performance was assessed using the identical achromatic object selection task employed with human observers, rather than standard physical ground truth metrics. The DNN exhibited high alignment with biological performance, showing similar, condition-dependent declines in constancy when established perceptual cues—such as local surround contrast and spatial mean chromaticity—were selectively manipulated or removed, though maximum flux mechanisms had minimal impact on both systems.
papers.authors: Hamed Heidari-Gorji, Raquel Gil Rodriguez, Karl R. Gegenfurtner

papers.title: Keeping your eye, head, and hand on the ball: Rapidly orchestrated visuomotor behavior in a continuous action task
papers.abstract: We investigated the dynamic orchestration of saccadic, pursuit, and head movements during a continuous visuomotor interception task (Pong) on a mobile device. By monitoring sequential behavior under varying difficulty levels (e.g., target velocity and paddle size), we identified a task-contingent strategy where pursuit eye movements are selectively prioritized immediately preceding interception to provide high-fidelity motion information. Conversely, information-destabilizing events, including saccades and blinks, are systematically suppressed during critical action windows. This finely tuned orchestration, which correlates positively with interception accuracy, demonstrates how humans establish intuitive, goal-directed motor routines to minimize sensory uncertainty and optimize performance in evolving environmental demands.
papers.authors: Anna Schroeger, Alexander Goettker, Doris I. Braun, Karl R. Gegenfurtner

papers.title: Within-subject confidence intervals for pairwise differences in scatter plots
papers.abstract: We propose a frequentist method for the computation and graphical representation of within-subject confidence intervals (CIs) along the diagonal axes of scatter plots to illustrate pairwise differences in bivariate data. This technique addresses the limitations of standard vertical and horizontal error bars, which frequently obscure the correlational structure of paired observations and fail to support direct inference about differences in central tendency. Empirical validation via researcher surveys demonstrated that the simultaneous plotting of standalone effects and diagonal CIs significantly improves the accuracy and subjective certainty with which scientists interpret within-subject effects relative to the identity line. The proposed framework aligns visual representation with standard repeated-measures statistical analyses, reducing ambiguity in the communication of experimental results.
papers.authors: Alexander C. Schütz, Karl R. Gegenfurtner

0355.name: Kartik K Sreenivasan
0355.bio: Kartik K. Sreenivasan is an Associate Professor of Psychology at NYU Abu Dhabi who researches the neurobiological mechanisms supporting working memory and goal-directed behavior. Using a multimodal approach integrating fMRI, MEG/EEG, and transcranial magnetic stimulation, Sreenivasan examines the distributed and dynamic nature of mnemonic representations across the prefrontal and visual cortices. Their work investigates how the brain maintains information in the presence of interference and how parallel memory systems contribute to behavioral responses. Additionally, Sreenivasan explores the intersection of working memory with perception and cognitive control to understand the constraints and flexibility of human mental representation.
0355.research_direction: Dr. Sreenivasan has recently been investigating the neural architecture and large-scale network dynamics that support human visual working memory. Their recent work explores whether memory representations are stored as simple point estimates or as rich probability distributions that inherently embed uncertainty, using fMRI decoding to map cortical activity directly to behavioral precision. Additionally, they are examining how the brain maintains multiple sequential memory items over time, leveraging MEG and dimensionality reduction to test whether these items are retained through temporal neural replay or by transforming them into structured low-dimensional geometric subspaces. To understand the limits of memory fidelity, Dr. Sreenivasan also investigates the mechanisms underlying feature binding and swap errors, utilizing Dynamic Causal Modeling and oscillatory analyses to probe how alpha-band phase synchrony and directed feedback signals between frontoparietal and early visual cortices maintain cohesive object representations.

papers.title: Probabilistic working memory representations in human cortex guide behavior
papers.abstract: Current models of working memory (WM) fundamentally differ in how they conceptualize individual memory architectures. While information-sparse models treat memories as discrete point estimates without metacognitive components like uncertainty, information-rich models propose that memories are stored as probability distributions across feature space, inherently embedding uncertainty. We evaluated these theories by generating behavioral probability distributions from subjects' iterative reports of motion direction on single trials. Crucially, the unique characteristics of these behavioral distributions, such as single-trial asymmetry, were highly correlated with neural probability distributions decoded from fMRI activity patterns in the occipital and parietal cortices. These results indicate that individual memory representations in human cortex multiplex feature content and uncertainty, supporting information-rich models where complex probabilistic dynamics directly influence memory-guided behavior.
papers.authors: Ying Zhou, Clayton E. Curtis, Daryl Fougnie, Kartik K. Sreenivasan

papers.title: Neural Subspaces Encode Sequential Working Memory, but Neural Sequences Do Not
papers.abstract: The mechanisms underlying the maintenance of multiple items in working memory remain a subject of active debate, specifically regarding whether sequential items are retained through sequential neural replay (neural sequences) or via distinct low-dimensional organizational structures (neural subspaces). We analyzed broadband MEG data from human participants using multivariate decoding and dimensionality reduction techniques to adjudicate between these hypotheses. Our findings revealed low-dimensional, behaviorally relevant neural subspaces that organized memory representations during the retention period, whereas these structures were absent during stimulus encoding. Conversely, we found no evidence for sequential replay of memory items during the delay period. These results suggest that the human brain transforms temporal sequences into structured geometric patterns within low-dimensional representational spaces to support stable and efficient maintenance of multiple items.
papers.authors: Aniol Santo-Angles, Jiarui Yang, Ying Zhou, Wing Kwan Hannah Chu, Grace W Lindsay, Kartik K. Sreenivasan

papers.title: Alpha phase-coding supports feature binding during working memory maintenance
