papers.abstract: The ability to bind an object's individual features into a cohesive representation is a critical bottleneck in working memory (WM), yet the underlying neural mechanisms remain elusive. Using magnetoencephalography (MEG) in a task designed to induce binding (or swap) errors, we tested the hypothesis that feature binding is implemented through neural phase synchrony. We found that swap errors are characterized by a significant reduction in phase-locked oscillatory activity during the maintenance period, localized to a distributed network of sensorimotor, parietal, and visual areas. This reduction was driven by increased phase-coding variability in the alpha-band (8–12 Hz) rather than changes in power. These results, which align with biophysical attractor models of spiking neural networks, demonstrate that stable phase-locking serves as a primary organizational principle for maintaining the integrity of feature bindings in WM.
papers.authors: Mattia F. Pagnotta, Aniol Santo-Angles, Ainsley Temudo, Joao Barbosa, Albert Compte, Mark D'Esposito, Kartik K. Sreenivasan

papers.title: Effective connectivity of working memory performance: a DCM study of MEG data
papers.abstract: Visual working memory (WM) involves a large-scale network of frontal, parietal, and occipital regions, but the nature of the directed causal influences (effective connectivity) within this network and their relationship to behavioral outcomes are poorly understood. We utilized Dynamic Causal Modeling (DCM) on MEG data to measure connectivity during a multi-item delayed estimation task. We categorized trials into high-accuracy, low-accuracy, and swap errors using computational behavioral modeling. Results showed that WM maintenance is supported by performance-dependent configurations of feedforward and feedback signals. Specifically, low-accuracy trials were associated with disrupted feedback connectivity during early maintenance and disrupted feedforward connectivity in late delay. Swap errors, in contrast, showed consistently disrupted feedback signals from frontoparietal nodes to early visual cortex throughout the entire delay period, supporting a distributed model where large-scale network reconfiguration determines memory fidelity.
papers.authors: Aniol Santo-Angles, Ainsley Temudo, Vahan Babushkin, Kartik K. Sreenivasan

0356.name: Katharina Dobs
0356.bio: Dobs is a Professor of Applied Computer Science at Justus Liebig University Giessen and directs the Visual Cognitive Computational Neuroscience (VCCN) Lab. Their research integrates deep learning architectures with human behavioral and neuroimaging data to investigate the computational principles underlying visual recognition and the functional organization of the cortex. Dobs has conducted studies demonstrating that brain-like functional specialization, such as face-selective regions, emerges in artificial neural networks optimized for specific visual tasks. Their current research, supported by an ERC Starting Grant and a LOEWE Start Professorship, focuses on developing models to explain the organization of the human visual system into specialized domains.
0356.research_direction: Dr. Dobs has recently been investigating the computational and neural mechanisms underlying high-level perception by combining deep neural networks (DNNs) with neuroimaging techniques like fMRI, EEG, and MEG. A major focus of their recent work explores face processing, using task-optimized DNNs to probe the computational origins of the Other-Race Effect and face pareidolia, while also mapping the temporal dynamics of how prior scene context influences human face detection. Broadening their scope within the visual system, they are examining how human category-selective cortical regions might be driven by underlying multidimensional feature tuning rather than strict categorical boundaries. Furthermore, their research extends these NeuroAI approaches beyond vision, investigating how goal-driven artificial networks can be used to model the complex neural dynamics of the proprioceptive pathway.

papers.title: Prior Scene Context Shapes the Neural Dynamics of Face Detection
papers.abstract: This study characterizes how prior contextual expectations derived from scene layout modulate the temporal dynamics of face detection using electroencephalography (EEG) and multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA). Observers performed a face detection task on natural scenes containing a single face, which were preceded by either a faceless preview of the same scene or a neutral control. Behavioral results demonstrated significant facilitation in face localization speed and accuracy in the presence of contextual previews. Neurally, face-location decoding revealed that prior scene context allows representations to emerge significantly earlier, suggesting a rapid modulation of sensory-driven processing. Furthermore, time-frequency analyses identified a sustained preview advantage in induced oscillatory activity across alpha, beta, and gamma bands, while the absence of context elicited delayed, compensatory neural signals. These results indicate that even rapid face perception reflects an interaction between incoming sensory input and temporally distinct contextual prior knowledge.
papers.authors: Sule Tasliyurt-Celebi, Daniel Kaiser, Katharina Dobs

papers.title: Diverse Visual Experience Promotes Integrated Representations and Mitigates Bias in Deep Neural Networks for Face Perception
papers.abstract: This research investigates the computational origins of the Other-Race Effect (ORE) by analyzing how the diversity of training exposure influences representational geometry in deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs). By training CNNs on exclusively Asian faces, exclusively White faces, or a diverse mix of both, and comparing their performance to human behavioral data, the authors found that homogeneous training exposure spontaneously generates ORE-like recognition biases. Representational similarity analysis (RSA) revealed that these biases are associated with a lack of cross-group representational overlap. Conversely, networks trained on diverse face sets developed an integrated representational geometry with balanced discriminative performance across groups, which most accurately captured human behavioral benchmarks. These findings suggest that human recognition biases emerge as a consequence of optimizing neural representations to the specific statistical distributions of familiar groups and provide a framework for mitigating bias through diverse visual experience.
papers.authors: Elaheh Akbari, Katharina Dobs

papers.title: Human-like face pareidolia emerges in deep neural networks optimized for face and object recognition
papers.abstract: The authors explore the functional basis of face pareidolia—the perception of face-like patterns in inanimate objects—using task-optimized deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) as computational models. They tested whether pareidolia emerges from the visual system's simultaneous optimization for fine-grained face identification and generic object categorization. Comparing CNN internal representations to human behavioral signatures and neural dynamics measured via magnetoencephalography (MEG), the study found that only dual-task networks (trained on both face and object tasks) aligned with human neural responses. These networks initially represented pareidolia stimuli as similar to real faces, relying on shared features like eyes for classification. This suggests that face pareidolia is not a perceptual error but a byproduct of a broadly tuned face detection mechanism designed to support robust, high-performance face recognition within complex real-world environments.
papers.authors: Pranjul Gupta, Katharina Dobs

papers.title: Multidimensional feature tuning in category-selective areas of human visual cortex
papers.abstract: This work proposes a unifying framework for the functional organization of the human high-level visual cortex by reconciling categorical and dimensional perspectives. Utilizing a data-driven Bayesian non-negative matrix factorization (NMF) of fMRI voxel responses to thousands of natural images, the authors identified multiple interpretable representational dimensions within well-known category-selective areas (FFA, EBA, and PPA). They found that even highly selective voxels remain tuned to multiple, partially overlapping dimensions that encode subcategory features and cross-category distinctions. These dimensions form sparse subclusters within selective areas while also contributing to globally distributed feature-based maps across the visual cortex. The results suggest that category selectivity emerges from sparse tuning to a limited set of high-level dimensions, providing a more multifaceted and comprehensive account of how the brain encodes complex visual information than traditional categorical models.
papers.authors: Leonard E. van Dyck, Martin N. Hebart, Katharina Dobs

papers.title: Artificial intelligence meets body sense: task-driven neural networks reveal computational principles of the proprioceptive pathway
papers.abstract: This article highlights the application of task-driven deep neural networks to decode the computational logic of the proprioceptive system. By training artificial networks to solve motor control and musculoskeletal tasks, the authors show how these models can predict the complex neural dynamics of proprioceptive processing in both the cuneate nucleus and the primary somatosensory cortex. The study emphasizes that these normative models not only achieve high predictive accuracy of neural activity but also provide insights into the specific format of limb-state representations required for movement execution. Additionally, the paper discusses the translational potential of these biologically inspired encoders for neuroprosthetics, suggesting that understanding the goal-driven organization of proprioception is critical for restoring sensory feedback in brain-machine interfaces. This work advocates for the expansion of NeuroAI frameworks to include somatosensory and motor domains.
papers.authors: Leonard E. van Dyck, Frank Bremmer, Katharina Dobs

0357.name: Kathryn Bonnen
0357.bio: Assistant Professor Kathryn Bonnen investigates the neural computations and sensorimotor mechanisms supporting vision-guided behavior in naturalistic environments. Utilizing a combination of psychophysics, wearable eye tracking, and body motion capture, Bonnen characterizes how the brain integrates binocular and monocular cues for tasks such as 3D motion tracking and complex locomotion. Their work examines the relationship between natural scene statistics and the development of visual processing, employing computational models to link environmental properties with neural representations and behavioral outcomes.
0357.research_direction: Dr. Bonnen has recently been investigating naturalistic visual development and the sensory signals generated by self-motion. Their recent work explores infant visual diets and motor control in unconstrained settings, using head-mounted cameras to quantify everyday exposure to environmental statistics like cardinal orientations and the developmental timescales of head kinematics. Additionally, they are examining the computational principles of optic flow processing, asking how spatial anisotropies in visual sampling reflect adaptations to the physical geometry of an animal's habitat during navigation. Methodologically, Dr. Bonnen is also advancing continuous psychophysics, utilizing dynamic target-tracking paradigms and Bayesian observer frameworks to simultaneously estimate sensory noise, processing latency, and motor dynamics across diverse observer cohorts.

papers.title: Moving through everyday life: distinct developmental timescales for head-rotation magnitude and rotation efficiency in infancy
papers.abstract: While laboratory paradigms have documented the role of head kinematics in visual orienting and gaze stabilization during infant development, little is known about how head motor control evolves within unconstrained domestic settings. This study evaluated 383 hours of egocentric video recordings captured via head-mounted cameras from 88 infants ranging from 3 weeks to 29 months of age. Using a visual-odometry algorithm, the authors quantified rotational magnitude (comprising net and total head rotation across short temporal windows) and rotational efficiency (the directional coherence of head movement). Head-rotation magnitude exhibited substantial increases across the first year of life, reflecting expanding muscular strength and postural maturation. In contrast, rotational efficiency showed prolonged developmental gains persisting through 29 months. These divergent timescales indicate that the development of infant head control involves a progressive kinematic reorganization toward directional directness rather than a simple scaling of head movement amplitude.
papers.authors: Zachary J. Petroff, Rajat Kapgate, T. Rowan Candy, Linda B. Smith, Kathryn Bonnen

papers.title: The world through infant eyes: Evidence for the early emergence of the cardinal orientation bias
papers.abstract: Natural and built environments contain a pronounced anisotropic distribution of orientation energy, characterized by an overrepresentation of cardinal (horizontal and vertical) contours relative to oblique orientations aligned with the direction of gravity. In adults, this environmental structure is associated with enhanced perceptual sensitivity for cardinal orientations (the oblique effect). To test whether cardinal dominance characterizes human visual input prior to the establishment of mature postural control and gravitational alignment, the authors analyzed head-camera video recordings from 75 infants aged 1 to 12 months across two distinct environments (Indiana, USA and Tamil Nadu, India). Orientation energy was computed across multiple spatial frequency bands, including 0.5 cycles per degree. Even at 3 weeks of age, infants experienced a marked prevalence of cardinal contours, yielding an overall median cardinal-to-oblique ratio of 1.90 (bootstrapped 95% CI: 1.81 to 2.03) that remained stable across development and geographical setting. These results confirm that an anisotropic visual diet is present well before infants can reliably align their bodies with gravity, providing the sensory substrate necessary for experience-dependent tuning of visual cortical pathways.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Zachary J. Petroff, Swapnaa Jayaraman, Linda B. Smith, T. Rowan Candy, Kathryn Bonnen

papers.title: Continuous psychophysics: past, present, future
papers.abstract: Continuous target-tracking psychophysics has emerged as an innovative experimental paradigm that complements classical forced-choice psychophysical methodologies. Rather than gathering isolated, discrete responses over numerous repeated trials, continuous psychophysics requires participants to continually track dynamically changing stimulus properties (such as position in 2D or 3D space) using manual effectors or eye movements. Analyzing response trajectories with cross-correlation functions and Bayesian observer frameworks (e.g., Kalman filter modeling and optimal feedback control) permits simultaneous estimation of sensory noise, processing latency, and motor execution dynamics in a fraction of the testing time required by standard forced-choice protocols. The review synthesizes theoretical principles and practical applications of continuous psychophysics across spatial contrast sensitivity, motion-in-depth perception, and multisensory integration, while discussing its utility for non-traditional subject cohorts such as infants, pediatric patients, and individuals with visual impairments.
papers.authors: Johannes Burge, Kathryn Bonnen

papers.title: Motion vision: Fish swimming to see
papers.abstract: Self-motion generates dynamic optic flow fields across the visual epithelium, providing sensory information critical for navigation, speed regulation, and postural equilibrium across species. However, neural systems frequently sample optic flow with substantial spatial non-uniformities; for example, the optomotor response of larval zebrafish (Danio rerio) demonstrates prominent visual field anisotropies, preferentially relying on downward and lateral motion vectors. This commentary reviews computational modeling and behavioral experiments showing how spatial biases in optic flow sampling reflect an optimal adaptation to the physical geometry of natural habitats and the animal's locomotor state. By prioritizing visual field regions situated closest to stable environmental structures (such as riverbeds), animals maximize the signal-to-noise ratio of self-motion estimates while minimizing velocity ambiguities arising from compound translational and rotational movements.
papers.authors: Kathryn Bonnen

0358.name: Katja Fiehler
0358.bio: Katja Fiehler’s research investigates the neurocognitive mechanisms underlying the integration of perception and action, focusing on how sensory information facilitates goal-directed eye and hand movements. Their work explores the reference frames used for spatial coding, the role of predictive mechanisms such as efference copies in shaping sensory perception, and the interaction between sensorimotor processes, attention, and working memory. Utilizing a multimodal approach, Fiehler combines psychophysical experiments in virtual and real-world environments with kinematic motion tracking, functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), and electroencephalography (EEG). Current research directions include examining the adaptive nature of the human brain in complex environments and the mechanisms of tactile suppression during movement execution.
0358.research_direction: Dr. Fiehler has recently been investigating how the brain integrates multisensory information to guide perception, spatial navigation, and goal-directed action. Their recent work explores spatial representations, using virtual reality and psychophysics to ask how humans weigh optic flow cues during visually-induced self-motion (vection) and how landmark proximity versus semantic scene grammar shapes allocentric coding for memory-guided reaching. Additionally, they are probing the temporal dynamics of somatosensory feedback, employing EEG to track tactile suppression across different kinematic phases of a reach and testing how body orientation and gravitational reference frames influence haptic size estimation. Finally, their research examines the supramodal mechanisms underlying the sense of agency, specifically evaluating whether the sensorimotor temporal recalibration of delayed visual feedback transfers to auditory modalities.

papers.title: Temporal dynamics of early somatosensory processing in goal-directed actions
papers.abstract: This study employs 64-channel electroencephalography (EEG) to investigate the phase-dependent modulation of somatosensory evoked potentials (SEPs) during goal-directed reaching. The research specifically focuses on the P45 component, a short-latency marker of primary somatosensory cortex (S1) activity, in response to vibrotactile stimuli applied to the moving index finger. While psychophysical results indicate a general suppression of tactile sensitivity during reaching (tactile suppression), a selective recovery in detection thresholds occurs around the peak movement velocity (maximum speed). Correspondingly, the P45 amplitude is significantly attenuated during the acceleration and deceleration phases of movement but demonstrates a transient recovery at maximum speed. Correlation analyses demonstrate that reduced P45 magnitudes are predictive of higher perceptual detection thresholds, suggesting that early cortical gating in S1 dynamically calibrates sensory input to facilitate sensorimotor control according to real-time feedback requirements.
papers.authors: Elena Fuehrer, Dimitris Voudouris, Lisa K. Maurer, Katja Fiehler

papers.title: Spatial proximity and scene grammar: Shaping spatial representations for memory-guided actions in naturalistic environments
papers.abstract: This research examines how spatial proximity and cognitive-semantic structures (scene grammar) influence allocentric spatial coding within complex, naturalistic virtual reality (VR) environments. Using a memory-guided placement task involving imperceptible shifts of large, immovable 'anchors' (landmarks), the study quantifies the weighting of allocentric reference frames. Results confirm that anchors are utilized to construct spatial representations of manipulable local targets. The accuracy of these spatial representations is primarily modulated by the proximity between the anchor and the target, with minimal influence from the semantic congruency between the two. These findings indicate that in naturalistic scenes, spatial geometric factors like landmark proximity dominate over high-level semantic associations in determining the recruitment and precision of allocentric cues for motor planning.
papers.authors: Bianca R. Baltaretu, Melissa L.-H. Võ, Katja Fiehler

papers.title: The effect of vection on the use of optic flow cues
papers.abstract: This investigation assesses the relationship between visually-induced illusory self-motion (vection) and the processing of optic flow fields for spatial navigation. Through a series of psychophysical tasks, the study evaluates whether the subjective intensity of experienced vection modulates the gain and integration of visual flow information during heading and distance estimation. The research tests the hypothesis that top-down self-motion perception recalibrates the weighting of low-level visual motion signals in the absence of physical vestibular input. Quantitative results suggest that the strength of vection correlates with the precision of spatial updates, demonstrating a top-down influence on the calibration of the visual-vestibular interface for internal spatial representation during locomotion.
papers.authors: Matthew McManus, Katja Fiehler

papers.title: Haptic size perception is influenced by body and object orientation
papers.abstract: This study examines how gravitational and body-centric reference frames influence haptic object representation. Participants performed manual size-matching tasks while the orientations of the stimulus and the participant's body (e.g., body tilt) were systematically manipulated. The research identifies systematic perceptual biases in haptic size estimation that are significantly modulated by the alignment of the object's axes with the gravitational vertical. The findings indicate that haptic size perception is not localized to the tactile surface but is integrated with proprioceptive and vestibular signals to form representations within extrinsic spatial reference frames. This suggests that multisensory signals for body orientation are critical for calibrating somatosensory feedback during tactile exploration and feature estimation.
papers.authors: Matthew McManus, Laurence R. Harris, Katja Fiehler

papers.title: Recalibration of perceived agency transfers across modalities
papers.abstract: This research investigates the generalizability and cross-modal transfer of sensorimotor temporal recalibration (STR) and the sense of agency (SoA). In an adaptation paradigm, participants were exposed to systematic temporal lags between their motor actions (button presses) and visual feedback (Gabor patches). Following adaptation, participants performed simultaneity and agency judgments across visual and auditory modalities. The study found that while the recalibration of temporal simultaneity (point of subjective simultaneity, PSS) was modality-specific, the recalibration of the sense of agency transferred across modalities. These findings suggest that while low-level temporal timing mechanisms may be constrained by sensory modality, the sense of agency is governed by a high-level, supramodal mechanism that utilizes generalized causal predictions to maintain coherent action-effect attribution.
papers.authors: Belkis Ezgi Arikan, Kielan Yarrow, Katja Fiehler

0359.name: Katsumi Watanabe
0359.department: School of Fundamental Science and Engineering
0359.bio: Katsumi Watanabe is a Professor at Waseda University who investigates the mechanisms of human perception, cognition, and action. Their research utilizes psychophysics, functional brain imaging, and eye-tracking to examine interactions between explicit and implicit mental processes. Watanabe conducts research in crossmodal perception, social cognition, and the neural basis of decision-making. Their current work focuses on applying cognitive science principles to human-robot interaction and analyzing the psychological and behavioral effects of artificial intelligence and digital media.
0359.research_direction: Dr. Watanabe has recently been investigating a diverse range of topics spanning core visual psychophysics, cross-species social cognition, and affective psychology. In human vision, their recent work explores how the visual system evaluates kinematic naturalness using speed-altered point-light walkers, and examines whether spatial distortions like the Ebbinghaus illusion interact with judgments of visual numerosity and density. Beyond basic visual processing, they are also studying human-animal interactions by measuring how well observers can perceive canine emotions from isolated facial features and by quantifying affective forecasting biases in owners anticipating pet cognitive decline. Finally, their applied psychological research probes everyday emotional regulation across the adult lifespan, utilizing psychometric surveys to understand how stress and personality traits drive the distinct use of music versus alcohol as coping strategies.

papers.title: Age differences in alcohol and music consumption among Japanese nonproblem drinkers
papers.abstract: This study investigated the cross-sectional relationship between aging and the utilization of alcohol and music as emotional regulation strategies in a sample of 1,279 Japanese non-problem drinkers. Utilizing a comprehensive psychometric battery including the Drinking Motives Questionnaire-Revised (DMQ-R), Brief Music in Mood Regulation (B-MMR), and Cognitive Emotion Regulation Questionnaire (CERQ), the researchers observed that younger adults exhibited significantly lower alcohol consumption rates compared to older cohorts. Mediation analysis indicated that lower extraversion and a deficit in positive reappraisal strategies among younger participants were associated with elevated stress levels, which subsequently predicted the use of music for diversion. The results suggest that alcohol and music consumption function as complementary rather than alternative modes of affect regulation across the adult lifespan.
papers.authors: Naoki Kato, Shunji Oshima, Katsumi Watanabe

papers.title: Detecting unnaturalness in biological motion with altered playback speeds
papers.abstract: The study examined the visual system's sensitivity to kinematic inconsistencies in human motion by presenting point-light walker (PLW) stimuli with manipulated temporal scaling (altered playback speeds). Participants performed a sequential discrimination task to identify veridical versus speed-altered gaits. The researchers manipulated orientation (upright vs. inverted) and spatial configuration (intact vs. scrambled) to delineate the roles of global form and local motion cues. Findings demonstrated that observers could reliably detect kinematic unnaturalness above chance levels, even when translational speed was controlled. Notably, detection performance remained robust under inversion and scrambling manipulations, suggesting that the perception of kinematic naturalness in biological motion is primarily mediated by local motion signals rather than global configural processing.
papers.authors: Kan Misumi, Hiroshi Ueda, Yuichiro Nishiura, Katsumi Watanabe

papers.title: Anticipated, experiencing, and recalled emotional responses to dog cognitive dysfunction syndrome in Japanese dog owners
papers.abstract: This investigation quantified the affective forecasting bias regarding Canine Cognitive Dysfunction Syndrome (CDS) among future, current, and former caregivers of senior dogs in Japan (N = 342). Using an online survey instrument, the study assessed emotional responses to 11 specific CDS-related geriatric behaviors and five categories of caregiving stress. Results revealed a significant discrepancy in emotional valuation: prospective caregivers (owners of younger dogs) significantly overestimated the negative emotional distress of caregiving compared to the experienced affect reported by current senior dog owners or the recalled affect of former owners. Among the measured variables, psychological caregiving stress was found to be the most significant predictor of negative emotional intensity across all ownership stages.
papers.authors: Yu-Lin Liu, Aiko Murata, Katsumi Watanabe

papers.title: Reading emotions in dog eyes and faces by Japanese observers: A replication and extension study of Burza et al (2022)
papers.abstract: The researchers evaluated the cross-cultural generalizability of inter-species social perception by replicating and extending the findings of Burza et al. (2022) with a Japanese cohort (N = 342). Participants categorized presumed canine emotional states from static images of full faces or isolated eye regions across three dog breeds. Japanese observers identified emotions at rates significantly above chance in both conditions, with performance significantly enhanced by the presence of full facial context. The ability to interpret canine affect was found to be independent of dog ownership status and did not correlate with human emotion recognition proficiency, suggesting that cross-species emotion perception may rely on distinct cognitive mechanisms that are partially independent of intra-species social cognition.
papers.authors: Aiko Murata, Yu-Lin Liu, Katsumi Watanabe

papers.title: Ebbinghaus illusion changes numerosity perception independent of density perception
papers.abstract: This study investigated the interaction between the Ebbinghaus size illusion and the perception of visual numerosity and density. To decouple retinal angular size from perceived size, the researchers utilized a flash-lag paradigm where the size of surrounding contextual stimuli changed dynamically. Experiments tested whether the induced illusory increase or decrease in central disk area biased judgments of dot numerosity and distribution density. Quantitative results indicated that numerosity estimation remains invariant to the area inequalities induced by the Ebbinghaus illusion, suggesting that numerical processing is cognitively independent of perceived surface area. Furthermore, the magnitude of the Ebbinghaus effect itself was found to be predominantly modulated by retinal size rather than by dissociated perceived size.
papers.authors: Saki Takao, Katsumi Watanabe

0361.name: Keisuke Fukuda
0361.bio: Keisuke Fukuda investigates the cognitive and neural mechanisms of human information processing, focusing on the interplay between selective attention, visual working memory, and long-term memory. Fukuda integrates electrophysiological recordings, such as EEG and ERP, with behavioral experiments and computational modeling to analyze the temporal dynamics of neural networks. Their research examines the basis of individual differences in memory capacity and explores how metacognitive accuracy and memory distortions affect information retention and retrieval. By combining an individual-differences approach with neuroscientific techniques, Fukuda studies the biological constraints of the mind and investigates methods to optimize cognitive performance.
0361.research_direction: Dr. Fukuda has recently been investigating the mechanisms of visual memory, exploring how visual information is encoded into working memory, stabilized for long-term storage, and occasionally distorted. Their recent work explores the dynamics of visual working memory (VWM), specifically examining how internal prioritization modulates the vulnerability of VWM representations to proactive and retroactive interference from new perceptual inputs. They are also investigating the nature of intrinsic image memorability, combining behavioral paradigms with deep neural networks to probe which stimulus features drive mnemonic success and how memorable items capture spatial attention during encoding. Additionally, their research examines broader memory formation and error, utilizing EEG to unpack how repeated encoding opportunities build visual long-term memory, and testing whether top-down sensory predictions can generate robust false episodic memories for events that never actually transpired.

papers.title: Prediction-based false memory: Unconfirmed prediction can result in robust false memories
papers.abstract: This study explores the hypothesis that explicit predictions about future events can generate false memories independently of whether the predictions are verified. Across several experiments, participants made predictions about forthcoming stimuli, which were either subsequently presented, omitted, or directly contradicted. Results indicate that the mere act of predicting a stimulus is sufficient to induce robust false memories of its occurrence. These mnemonic distortions were resistant to visual rebuttal and persisted even when participants exhibited high accuracy for the items themselves. Further manipulations demonstrated that this prediction-based error is modulated by indirect forms of evidence and cannot be explained by simple action effects. The findings suggest that top-down predictive processing can fundamentally overwrite episodic representations, creating durable memories for events that never transpired.
papers.authors: Olya Bulatova, Keisuke Fukuda

papers.title: Working Memory Prioritization Changes Bidirectional Interactions With Perceptual Inputs
papers.abstract: The research investigates how the prioritization of representations within visual working memory (VWM) affects their vulnerability to proactive and retroactive interference during perceptual comparisons. Utilizing a double-serial retro-cue paradigm, observers prioritized one of two unfamiliar shape memoranda for comparison with a subsequent perceptual probe. The results revealed an asymmetrical effect of internal attention: while both retroactive and proactive biases were observed, only retroactive reports were modulated by prioritization. Reports of prioritized items were significantly more precise and showed reduced attractive biases toward the perceptual probe compared to unprioritized items. Conversely, reports for the perceptual probes were biased similarly regardless of memory priority. These findings indicate that internal attention enhances the stability of prioritized VWM content against interference from incoming sensory signals.
papers.authors: Joseph M. Saito, Frida Printzlau, Yvanna Yeo, Keisuke Fukuda

papers.title: Attend to compete or compete to attend: The possible role of attention in processing competing stimuli within visual working memory
papers.abstract: Visual stimuli vary in memorability, an intrinsic property that determines their likelihood of being successfully encoded into visual working memory (VWM). This study examines whether the competitive advantage enjoyed by memorable stimuli is driven by the preferential allocation of spatial attention. By combining a face VWM task with an incidental letter-report task, the authors measured the distribution of spatial attention over time. Data showed that spatial attention was not biased toward memorable stimuli immediately; instead, differences in attention allocation only emerged approximately 450 ms after stimulus onset. Furthermore, the VWM performance benefit for memorable items was only present when encoding time was sufficient for these attentional differences to manifest. These results suggest that memorable stimuli attract limited VWM resources via late-stage attentional prioritization rather than superior initial sensory encoding.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
papers.authors: Greer Gillies, Jonathan S. Cant, Keisuke Fukuda

papers.title: Deep neural network decodes aspects of stimulus-intrinsic memorability inaccessible to humans
papers.abstract: While humans show consistent patterns in which images they remember or forget, it is unclear whether this interindividual consistency is driven purely by stimulus-intrinsic properties or by shared extrinsic factors such as interstimulus similarity. This study compares human performance with ResMem, a deep neural network designed to decode image memorability. Across three experiments, the researchers demonstrate that ResMem effectively predicts memorability based on stimulus-intrinsic factors independent of extrinsic contextual influences. Crucially, the model was found to decode aspects of memorability that are largely inaccessible to human conscious awareness. These results confirm the multifaceted nature of memorability and establish computational methods for isolating intrinsic stimulus features that reliably drive mnemonic success across both biological and artificial neural networks.
papers.authors: Chong Zhao, Joie Kim, Tzu Hsuan Tang, Joseph M. Saito, Keisuke Fukuda

papers.title: Decomposing the multiple-encoding benefit in visual long-term memory: Primary contributions by the number of encoding opportunities
papers.abstract: Repeated exposure to visual information improves its subsequent retention in long-term memory (VLTM), a phenomenon known as the multiple encoding benefit (MEB). This research seeks to determine whether the MEB is driven by the total number of encoding opportunities, the cumulative number of items stored in visual working memory (VWM), or the frequency of successful retrievals. Using an experimental design that varied the number of objects and encoding events, and monitoring VWM load via EEG correlates (posterior alpha suppression and negative slow wave), the authors isolated the primary mechanism. The findings reveal that recognition performance increases as a direct function of the number of encoding opportunities, independent of VWM capacity utilization or retrieval success. This suggests that the mere repetition of encoding events is the critical factor in transitioning visual information from working memory to durable long-term storage.
papers.authors: Caitlin J. I. Tozios, Keisuke Fukuda

0362.name: Keith A. Schneider
0362.department: Department of Psychological and Brain Sciences
0362.bio: Keith A. Schneider is a Professor and the Director of the Center for Biomedical and Brain Imaging at the University of Delaware. Schneider investigates the functional architecture of the human visual system, with a technical focus on subcortical structures such as the lateral geniculate nucleus, pulvinar, and superior colliculus. Utilizing high-resolution functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and visual psychophysics, they examine how neural mechanisms of attention, perception, and awareness are implemented. Their current work explores temporal processing dynamics and the magnocellular hypothesis in clinical populations, investigating how subcortical abnormalities contribute to disorders like dyslexia.
0362.research_direction: Dr. Schneider's recent work bridges computational psychophysics and high-resolution neuroimaging to investigate the early neural and cognitive mechanisms underlying visual perception and decision-making. Using functional MRI, they have recently been examining early subcortical visual processing, specifically targeting the laminar subdivisions of the human lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) to parse the relative contributions of the magnocellular and parvocellular pathways during binocular rivalry. Additionally, their recent work explores the computational architecture of metacognitive uncertainty in perceptual decisions by developing a novel information-theoretic entropy model. By applying this mathematical framework to visual psychophysical tasks, Dr. Schneider investigates how spatial attention and explicit response biases influence latent decision parameters and subjective uncertainty profiles.

papers.title: An entropy model of decision uncertainty
papers.abstract: Characterizing metacognitive uncertainty provides critical insights into the computational architecture governing perceptual decisions, yet decision uncertainty has lacked an analytical functional parameterization comparable to signal detection theory models of choice accuracy. In this work, an information-theoretic framework is formulated wherein an observer's subjective uncertainty is modeled as the joint entropy incorporating both the entropy of the external sensory stimuli and the entropy of categorical response probabilities across the psychometric function. Establishing this functional form permits the recovery of latent internal decision parameters that cannot be deduced from choice distributions alone. Applying the model to visual psychophysical tasks demonstrates that spatial attentional cues alter decision uncertainty profiles distinctively compared to explicit instructional response biases, despite producing identical shifts in the point of subjective equality. These findings reveal that while different decisional mechanisms can yield divergent uncertainty distributions across perceptual tasks, they can nonetheless operate over shared underlying representational parameters.
papers.authors: Keith A. Schneider

papers.title: Neural Dynamics during Binocular Rivalry: Indications from Human Lateral Geniculate Nucleus
papers.abstract: During binocular rivalry, perception alternates between incompatible monocular inputs presented dichoptically, providing a model for visual awareness; however, the relative functional contributions of the magnocellular (M) and parvocellular (P) pathways in early subcortical visual structures remain unresolved. High-resolution functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) at 3T was employed to record blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) responses within the laminar subdivisions of the human lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) during spontaneous rivalry and a physically alternated replay control condition using achromatic stimuli to prevent chromatic opponent confounds. Although standard general linear model (GLM) parameter estimation showed elevated eye-specific modulation in M compared to P subdivisions during rivalry, an equivalent modulation occurred during the replay condition. Contrasting rivalry against replay by subtracting replay beta weights isolated rivalry-specific dynamics predominantly within the P subdivisions, whereas M subdivision modulation did not significantly exceed physical alternation. These results indicate that perceptual alternations during binocular rivalry are primarily governed by interocular competition localized within the parvocellular pathway of the human LGN.
papers.authors: Irem Yildirim, Keith A. Schneider

0363.name: Kelly Bijanki
0363.bio: Kelly Bijanki is an Associate Professor at Baylor College of Medicine and director of the Translational Neuromodulation Lab. Bijanki’s research utilizes invasive intracranial electrophysiology, including stereotactic electroencephalography (sEEG) and direct brain stimulation, to investigate the neural mechanisms of human affect and social cognition. They study the clinical application of deep brain stimulation for treatment-resistant psychiatric disorders by characterizing the causal roles of the cingulum bundle and amygdala in mood regulation and anxiolysis. Additionally, Bijanki examines the developmental trajectory of facial emotion perception and the neurophysiological signatures of emotion processing biases within fronto-temporal networks.
0363.research_direction: Dr. Bijanki has recently been investigating the spatiotemporal neural dynamics of emotion processing and the mechanisms of deep brain stimulation (DBS) for treatment-resistant depression. Using direct intracranial recordings (iEEG), their recent work explores how the brain's encoding of naturalistic facial affect develops from childhood to adulthood across temporal and prefrontal networks. They are also examining both behavioral and electrophysiological markers of depression, probing whether negative emotion processing biases and aperiodic (1/f) background neural activity can effectively track longitudinal symptom severity and predict DBS efficacy. Additionally, Dr. Bijanki is investigating how individual macroanatomical variations, such as cortical folding in the cingulate region, influence white matter connectivity to better understand how distinct neural networks are engaged during therapeutic neuromodulation.

papers.title: The representation of facial emotion expands from sensory to prefrontal cortex with development
papers.abstract: This developmental study utilizes intracranial electroencephalography (iEEG) to characterize the ontogenetic trajectory of neural encodings for facial affect from childhood (ages 5–10) to adulthood (ages 13–55). Utilizing multivariate pattern analysis on neural responses to naturalistic emotional stimuli in a short film, the researchers identified that while the posterior superior temporal cortex (pSTC) reliably encodes facial emotion throughout development, the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) only begins to significantly represent affective information post-childhood. This spatial expansion of emotion representation into higher-order social-cognitive prefrontal areas suggests a maturation of top-down emotional processing circuits that is absent in early childhood.
papers.authors: Xiaoxu Fan, Abhishek Tripathi, Kelly Bijanki

papers.title: Asymmetric cingulum bundle connectivity is modulated by paracingulate sulcus morphology
papers.abstract: This investigation defines the electrographic connectivity profile of the human cingulum bundle (CB) and evaluates the impact of macroanatomical variability in the paracingulate sulcus (PCS). Using intracranial single-pulse electrical stimulation (SPES) and stereotactic EEG (sEEG) to measure effective connectivity in patients undergoing epilepsy surgery evaluation, analysis of pulse-evoked potentials (PEPs) revealed significant hemispheric asymmetry characterized by leftward dominance. Critically, this asymmetry was modulated by PCS morphology: left CB connectivity was maximized in the presence of a left PCS, whereas right CB connectivity was prioritized in its absence. These results indicate that individual anatomical variations in the cingulate region fundamentally dictate the extent of white matter network engagement during therapeutic neuromodulation.
papers.authors: Isabel A. Danstrom, Joshua A. Adkinson, Meghan E. Robinson, Lu Lin, Atul Maheshwari, Ben Shofty, Garrett Banks, Mohammed Hasen, Sameer A. Sheth, Alica M. Goldman, Eleonora Bartoli, Sarah R. Heilbronner, Kelly R. Bijanki

papers.title: Affective bias predicts changes in depression during deep brain stimulation therapy
papers.abstract: This longitudinal study examines whether neurocognitive measures of affective bias can predict clinical outcomes in treatment-resistant depression (TRD) patients receiving deep brain stimulation (DBS). By assessing emotion recognition and affective processing alongside clinical monitoring via the Montgomery-Åsberg Depression Rating Scale (MADRS), the researchers found that baseline negative affective bias—the tendency to prioritize negative over positive valence—significantly predicted long-term symptomatic improvement following chronic subcallosal cingulate DBS. Furthermore, shifts in these behavioral biases during therapy were correlated with changes in clinical severity, suggesting that biomarkers of affective processing function can serve as objective proxies for titrating stimulation efficacy.
papers.authors: B. Cui, M. M. Mocchi, B. A. Metzger, P. Kalva, J. F. Magnotti, J. G. Fiedorowicz, A. Waters, C. K. Kovach, Y. Y. Reed, R. K. Mathura, C. Steger, B. Pascuzzi, K. Kanja, A. Veerakumar, V. Tiruvadi, A. Crowell, L. Denison, C. J. Rozell, N. Pouratian, W. Goodman, P. Riva Posse, H. S. Mayberg, Kelly R. Bijanki

papers.title: Aperiodic (1/f) Neural Activity Robustly Tracks Symptom Severity Changes in Treatment-Resistant Depression
papers.abstract: This study evaluates the utility of aperiodic (1/f) neural activity as a longitudinal biomarker for symptom fluctuations in treatment-resistant depression (TRD). Utilizing multi-month intracranial recordings from patients with deep brain stimulation (DBS) systems, the researchers analyzed the spectral properties of local field potentials (LFPs). Findings indicated that aperiodic features, specifically the spectral slope and offset, significantly correlated with depressive symptom severity across time, outperforming traditional periodic (oscillatory) band-power metrics. These correlations were most pronounced in prefrontal and amygdala-centered networks, providing evidence that aperiodic activity captures state-dependent changes in the excitation/inhibition balance associated with the pathophysiology of TRD.
papers.venue: Biological Psychiatry: Cognitive Neuroscience and Neuroimaging
papers.authors: Carl Hacker, Madaline M. Mocchi, Jiayang Xiao, Brian Metzger, Joshua Adkinson, Bailey Pascuzzi, Raissa Mathura, Denise Oswalt, Andrew Watrous, Eleonora Bartoli, Anusha Allawala, Victoria Pirtle, Xiaoxu Fan, Isabel Danstrom, Ben Shofty, Garrett Banks, Yue Zhang, Maria Armenta-Salas, Kourosh Mirpour, Sanjay Mathew, Jeffrey Cohn, David Borton, Wayne Goodman, Nader Pouratian, Sameer Sheth, Kelly R. Bijanki

papers.title: Brain mechanisms underlying the emotion processing bias in treatment-resistant depression
papers.abstract: This research utilizes stereotactic electroencephalography (sEEG) to investigate the spatiotemporal dynamics of the emotion processing bias in treatment-resistant depression (TRD). By comparing high-temporal resolution recordings from the amygdala and prefrontal cortex (PFC), the study identified a significant imbalance in bottom-up and top-down processing. TRD patients exhibited heightened amygdala activation to negative stimuli (bottom-up) and delayed, attenuated amygdala responses to positive stimuli associated with aberrant inhibitory signaling from the orbitofrontal cortex (top-down). Chronic deep brain stimulation was found to selectively modulate these dynamics by relieving abnormal top-down inhibition of positive information, thereby shifting the affective processing balance toward a more normative state.
papers.authors: Xiaoxu Fan, Madaline Mocchi, Bailey Pascuzzi, Jiayang Xiao, Brian A. Metzger, Raissa K. Mathura, Carl Hacker, Joshua A. Adkinson, Eleonora Bartoli, Salma Elhassa, Andrew J. Watrous, Yue Zhang, Wayne Goodman, Nader Pouratian, Kelly Bijanki

0364.name: Ken Nakayama
0364.lab_name: Whitney Laboratory for Perception and Action
0364.bio: Nakayama is an Adjunct Professor at the University of California, Berkeley, and previously served as the Edgar Pierce Professor of Psychology at Harvard University. Nakayama's research utilizes human psychophysics to investigate the mechanisms of mid-level vision, focusing on how the visual system constructs surface representations to bridge low-level features and high-level object perception. Their work on face recognition includes the identification of developmental prosopagnosia and the characterization of "super-recognizers" to explore the cognitive and genetic substrates of recognition. Additionally, Nakayama examines the integration of visual attention, motion processing, and visuo-motor coordination to understand the functional architecture of the human visual system.
0364.research_direction: Dr. Nakayama's recent work explores the intimate coupling between visual representation and motor execution, investigating how perceptual and abstract cognitive computations continuously leak into ongoing motor trajectories rather than following a rigid sequence of seeing, deciding, and acting. To probe the specific mechanisms of sensorimotor adaptation, they have recently been utilizing large-scale, web-based citizen science platforms to examine how expansive demographic and individual variables modulate implicit and explicit motor learning during visuomotor rotation tasks. Furthermore, their research investigates whether the explicit cognitive strategies used during these motor learning paradigms are subject to unconscious cultural biases by comparing spatial re-aiming behaviors across different global populations. Ultimately, by combining massive online behavioral datasets, cross-cultural paradigms, and theoretical synthesis, Dr. Nakayama is working to uncover the diverse cognitive and demographic factors that govern how humans dynamically calibrate their movements to visual feedback.

papers.title: Unconscious cultural cognitive biases in explicit processes of visuomotor adaptation
papers.abstract: This research investigates the degree to which cultural background modulates the cognitive strategies utilized during motor learning. Using a visuomotor rotation task with a verbal report paradigm, the study compared Norwegian and Japanese cohorts to quantify differences in explicit re-aiming strategies. Findings indicated that Japanese participants demonstrated a significant bias toward aiming at more deviant locations to counteract the visual perturbation, even following successful target acquisition. Despite these distinct explicit strategies, both groups exhibited similar behavioral metrics in terms of reach accuracy and implicit aftereffect magnitude. These results suggest that the explicit component of motor learning, as measured via self-report, is susceptible to unconscious cultural cognitive biases, challenging the assumption of universality in the mechanisms of sensorimotor adaptation across human populations.
papers.authors: Chiharu Yamada, Yoshihiro Itaguchi, Claudia Rodríguez-Aranda, Jonathan S. Tsay, Richard B. Ivry, Ken Nakayama

papers.title: Large-scale citizen science reveals predictors of sensorimotor adaptation
papers.abstract: Sensorimotor adaptation maintains precise movement calibration amidst biomechanical alterations and fluctuating environmental dynamics. Although conventional investigations conducted over the past century have successfully delineated distinct learning mechanisms via tightly controlled, small-cohort laboratory experiments, such paradigms remain severely constrained in interrogating the expansive set of individual and demographic variables modulating sensorimotor performance. Leveraging a web-based citizen science platform, this investigation acquired over 2,000 experimental sessions employing a visuomotor rotation task. This expansive corpus replicated canonical phenomena, reconciled discrepancies, and challenged longstanding assumptions within the learning and memory literature, while unveiling previously unrecognized demographic determinants that govern the distinct implicit and explicit processes subserving sensorimotor recalibration. The findings demonstrate how high-powered exploratory citizen-science architectures can critically augment standard hypothesis-driven laboratory paradigms within sensorimotor neuroscience.
papers.authors: Jonathan S. Tsay, Hrach Asmerian, Laura T. Germine, Jeremy Wilmer, Richard B. Ivry, Ken Nakayama

papers.title: Rethinking Vision and Action
papers.abstract: Motor execution constitutes a decisive evolutionary arbiter of individual and species survival, yet motor behavior has historically remained segregated from core psychological inquiry due to disciplinary compartmentalization and the classic tripartite heuristic of sequential processing (see → decide → act). Contemporary investigations into motor control have revealed substantial empirical anomalies that directly contradict this feedforward caricature, demonstrating a considerably more intimate coupling between visual representation and action execution. This review delineates behavioral and neurophysiological evidence showing continuous leakage of perceptual and abstract cognitive computations into ongoing motor trajectories, prompting detailed examination of three pertinent theoretical frameworks that challenge rigid sensory-motor boundaries and realign our understanding of visual processing in the service of action.
papers.authors: Ken Nakayama, Jeff Moher, Joo-Hyun Song

0365.name: Kenneth D. Miller
0365.bio: Kenneth D. Miller is the Peter Taylor Professor of Neuroscience and a principal investigator at the Zuckerman Mind Brain Behavior Institute at Columbia University, where they co-direct the Center for Theoretical Neuroscience. Miller's research utilizes mathematical and computational methods to investigate the circuitry and development of the cerebral cortex, with a specific focus on the primary visual cortex (V1). Miller developed the Stabilized Supralinear Network (SSN) model, which provides a framework for understanding nonlinear cortical integration and context-dependent modulation of neural responses. Their current work uses data-driven modeling to investigate principles of neural computation and the self-organization of cortical circuits.
0365.research_direction: Dr. Miller has recently been utilizing data-driven computational modeling to investigate the circuit-level mechanisms of contextual visual processing and neural decision-making. A major focus of their recent work explores center-surround interactions in the primary visual cortex using Stabilized Supralinear Networks (SSNs), specifically examining how different inhibitory interneuron subtypes and the integration of feedforward and feedback signals generate phenomena like surround suppression and inverse responses. Beyond early vision, they are studying the geometry of neural state spaces in macaque area LIP to model how recurrent competitive circuits shape evidence accumulation during motion discrimination tasks. To further support these population-level systems analyses, they are also developing transformer-based machine learning architectures designed to infer and stitch together unrecorded, multi-region brain dynamics across large-scale animal datasets.

papers.title: Characteristics and dynamical signatures of recurrent cortical circuits during context-dependent processing
papers.abstract: This study employs data-driven computational modeling to infer the circuit architecture of the mouse primary visual cortex (V1) during context-dependent sensory processing. By fitting spatially extended stabilized supralinear networks (SSNs) to the observed responses of excitatory (E), parvalbumin (PV), somatostatin (SST), and vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP) neurons, the researchers find that inhibitory stabilization is a dynamic process where the dominant inhibitory cell type affecting E-cells varies with stimulus parameters and spatial location. While PV-mediated stabilization is consistently required, the necessity for SST-mediated stabilization is stimulus-dependent. The analysis reveals that traditional uniform perturbations may fail to reveal paradoxical effects in certain inhibitory subtypes; instead, patterned perturbations are required to uncover the paradoxical response modes characteristic of inhibition-stabilized networks. Furthermore, the results demonstrate that recurrent excitatory connections and nonlinear input-output transformations are indispensable for reproducing cortical spatial response profiles, especially under conditions where feedforward thalamic inputs are weak.
papers.authors: Yue Kris Wu, Ho Yin Chau, Serena Di Santo, Kenneth D. Miller

papers.title: Inpainting the Neural Picture: Inferring Unrecorded Brain Area Dynamics from Multi-Animal Datasets
papers.abstract: The authors propose NeuroPaint, a transformer-based masked autoencoding architecture designed to reconstruct latent neural dynamics in unrecorded brain regions by exploiting the shared structure across large-scale multi-animal datasets. In typical high-density extracellular recordings (e.g., Neuropixels), only a subset of brain areas is sampled simultaneously. NeuroPaint leverages overlapping recorded regions across different sessions and animals to 'in-paint' missing activity through a cross-attention stitcher and temporal tokenization framework. Tested on both synthetic and large-scale empirical mouse datasets (e.g., the IBL brain-wide map), the model successfully infers single-neuron firing rates and inter-area interactions in unobserved regions. The results show that this approach significantly outperforms standard baselines like LFADS and enables population-level systems neuroscience analyses that transcend the physical limitations of single-subject recording sessions.
papers.authors: Ji Xia, Yizi Zhang, Shuqi Wang, Genevera I. Allen, Liam Paninski, Cole Lincoln Hurwitz, Kenneth D. Miller

papers.title: Stabilized Supralinear Network Model of Responses to Surround Stimuli in Primary Visual Cortex
papers.abstract: This research investigates the circuit mechanisms underlying visual center-surround interactions in primary visual cortex (V1) using the stabilized supralinear network (SSN) framework. The model accounts for three critical features of surround suppression: the suppression of both excitatory and inhibitory synaptic currents, the dominance of orientation-matched suppression (where surround suppression is strongest when the surround orientation matches the center orientation regardless of the cell’s preferred tuning), and feature-specific suppression observed in plaid stimuli. The authors demonstrate that a spatially two-dimensional SSN with strong local recurrent connectivity operates in an inhibition-stabilized regime that naturally reproduces these phenomena. The findings are further validated in a biologically realistic conductance-based spiking network, which also replicates the rapid decay kinetics of V1 activity following the silencing of thalamic inputs.
papers.authors: Dina Obeid, Kenneth D. Miller

papers.title: The geometry of the neural state space of decisions
papers.abstract: Through the analysis of large-scale population recordings from macaque area LIP during a motion-direction discrimination task, this study characterizes the geometric structure of decision-making in neural state space. Contrary to the standard drift-diffusion model (DDM) where evidence integration is viewed as a one-dimensional scaling of activity at choice targets, the data reveal that evidence accumulation occurs along adaptive, context-dependent directions on a curved decision manifold. The population activity undergoes a dynamical transition from sensory-driven deliberation to commitment, characterized by adaptive retinotopic shifts. The authors propose a mechanistic circuit model in which competitive interactions and self-excitation drive the 'winning' activity bump, transitioning the system from external-input-dominated to intrinsic-circuit-driven dynamics. The model’s predictions for how choice selectivity varies with trial speed are confirmed by single-trial and trial-averaged population analyses.
papers.authors: Mauro M. Monsalve-Mercado, Kenneth D. Miller

papers.title: Contextual modulation emerges by integrating feedforward and feedback processing in mouse visual cortex
papers.abstract: This study develops a unified circuit model of the mouse primary visual cortex (V1) to explain how feedforward and feedback signals are integrated to generate complex contextual modulations. Reanalysis of V1 data reveals that increasing the spatial extent of a visual stimulus leads to only a minimal increase in the total area of the responsive neural population, a finding that challenges existing feedforward models of surround suppression (SS). The proposed model suggests that SS in Layer 2/3 is inherited from Layer 4, while 'inverse responses' (size-tuned responses to luminance-matched 'holes' in full-field gratings) are driven by wide feedback connections from higher cortical areas. Cross-orientation surround facilitation is explained by the integration of these feedback-driven inverse responses with feedforward-driven classical receptive field activity, illustrating a multi-stage mechanism for contextual processing across the cortical hierarchy.
papers.authors: Serena Di Santo, Mario Dipoppa, Andreas J. Keller, Morgane M. Roth, Massimo Scanziani, Kenneth D. Miller

0366.name: Kevin Willeford
0366.institution: NOVA Southeastern University College of Optometry
0366.department: College of Optometry, Department of Optometric Sciences
0366.bio: Kevin Willeford is an Assistant Professor at Nova Southeastern University’s College of Optometry, where their research focuses on the neural mechanisms governing sensorimotor fusion and binocular vision. Willeford developed Limbus Segment Tracking (LST), a non-invasive image-processing method designed to quantify large-scale ocular rotations that traditional video-based eye trackers do not capture. Their work utilizes eye-movement analysis and visual evoked potentials (VEP) to investigate attentional processes, the quantification of aniseikonia, and the clinical evolution of ocular motility disorders. Willeford’s research also involves optimizing eye-tracking reliability by mitigating pupil-induced fixational drift and characterizing ocular duction patterns in both normal and strabismic populations.
0366.research_direction: Dr. Willeford's recent work spans visual cognition, ocular motor function, and optometric education. Specifically, they have recently been investigating the premotor theory of attention by testing whether exogenous spatial cueing and attentional orienting remain functional in patients with restricted eye movements (paralytic strabismus) during saccadic and manual response tasks. To improve the clinical assessment of these and other ocular motility disorders, their recent work explores novel protocols that use digital image processing and statistical indices to objectively quantify monocular and binocular duction patterns over longitudinal and cross-sectional timeframes. Additionally, Dr. Willeford is examining the development of clinical reasoning by analyzing how optometry students utilize performance feedback to adjust their metacognitive accuracy, resolution, and confidence judgments across various educational scales.

papers.title: Exogenous spatial attention is functional in paralytic strabismics
papers.abstract: This study challenges the strict interpretation of the premotor theory of attention, which suggests an obligate link between ocular motor execution and the allocation of spatial attention. The researchers employed two experiments to measure the effects of exogenous visual cues—designed to facilitate or inhibit attentional shifts—on the response latencies of both saccadic and manual (keypress) targets in patients with paralytic strabismus. By incorporating a no-cue control condition, the study quantified the presence and direction of cue-induced attentional modulation. Results indicated that all patients exhibited classic signatures of cue-target interactions, with faster responses to proximate targets and slower responses to distal targets across both eye and hand effectors. These findings support the hypothesis that premotor structures program attentional shifts in an effector-independent manner, maintaining functional exogenous orienting even when peripheral ocular motility is severely restricted.
papers.authors: Kevin T. Willeford, Robert M. McPeek

papers.title: A protocol to quantify cross-sectional and longitudinal differences in duction patterns
papers.abstract: The authors propose a novel clinical protocol to address the lack of established systems for objectively quantifying ocular duction patterns. The methodology integrates digital image processing with a statistical framework consisting of summary indices—specifically focusing on movement area and symmetry—to evaluate ocular motility. The protocol provides a global characterization of the motor field, allowing for the detection of monocular and binocular imbalances in synergistic muscle pairs. By establishing criteria for minimal detectable change (MDC), the researchers demonstrate the protocol's utility in evaluating both cross-sectional deviations from normative populations and longitudinal shifts indicative of pathological progression or therapeutic resolution. This systematic approach transforms subjective clinical observations into reliable, continuous biometric data suitable for tracking ocular motility disorders over time.
papers.authors: Kevin T. Willeford, Victoria Copel, Hua Rong

papers.title: Feedback Changes Metacognitive Accuracy Over Different Time Scales
papers.abstract: This study investigates how optometry students utilize metacognitive feedback to improve their self-assessment accuracy during a national board examination preparation course. Third-year students were required to make sequential retrospective confidence judgments regarding the probability that their answers to board-style questions were correct. Metacognitive accuracy was quantified using indices such as error (mismatch between average confidence and correctness), calibration, and resolution. These metrics were analyzed across item-by-item, single session, and course-wide time scales to determine if providing performance feedback could dynamically alter metacognitive accuracy. The results demonstrated that while feedback delivery over varied durations provided the potential for students to refine their calibration and resolution, the degree of improvement was highly variable, suggesting that individuals utilize metacognitive feedback in distinct ways during their clinical education.
papers.authors: Kevin T. Willeford, Nicole Patterson, Jamie Althoff

0369.name: Kirsten Adam
0369.bio: Kirsten Adam is an Assistant Professor at Rice University who investigates the cognitive and neural constraints that limit human attention and memory. Adam's research utilizes electroencephalography (EEG) and functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) to examine how the brain manages visual distractions and why individuals experience moment-to-moment fluctuations in performance. Their work focuses on visual working memory capacity, demonstrating how attentional lapses and stimulus history influence the representation of information in the early visual cortex.
0369.research_direction: Dr. Adam has recently been investigating the dynamic mechanisms and capacity limits of visual working memory, exploring how observers manage these strict cognitive bottlenecks. Their recent behavioral work explores whether memory retention can be optimized by aligning performance feedback with an individual's intrinsic capacity, and how observers might rapidly recruit visual long-term memory to bypass capacity limits during explicit stimulus repetitions. On a neural level, they are using fMRI and multivariate decoding to test whether memory load constraints stem from a localized parietal bottleneck or instead rely on distributed, drifting representational codes across the broader cortex. Additionally, they are investigating the true magnitude of attentional capture, utilizing single-trial surprise paradigms to measure how salient distractors disrupt visual search before observers have the opportunity to develop learned suppression strategies.

papers.title: Distributed and drifting signals for working memory load in human cortex
papers.abstract: While increases in working memory (WM) load reliably yield behavioral costs, whether the underlying neural constraints stem from a localized hub in the intraparietal sulcus (IPS) or are distributed throughout the cortex remains contentious. In a high-powered, pre-registered fMRI study (N = 12 observers; 12 scanner-hours each), participants completed a visual WM delayed-estimation task under variable load (0 to 4 items). Analyses replicated classical load-dependent monotonic increases in univariate BOLD activity within parietal cortex; however, systematic bidirectional univariate modulations—both signal increases and decreases indicative of population receptive field surround suppression—were also evident across early and high-level visual areas. Crucially, multivariate pattern analyses accurately decoded WM load across visual, parietal, and frontal cortices regardless of the sign of univariate changes, challenging models of an exclusive parietal bottleneck. Furthermore, significant representational drift in multivariate load-encoding patterns was detected across sessions, suggesting that cortical load codes undergo continual experience-dependent reorganization to support efficient storage.
papers.authors: Kirsten C. S. Adam, Edward Awh, John T. Serences

papers.title: Beyond routine maintenance: Current trends in working memory research
papers.abstract: Theoretical perspectives on working memory (WM) are evolving away from classical frameworks of static, persistent maintenance toward dynamic, flexible mechanisms of active cognition. Synthesized by the organizers of the 2024 Working Memory Symposium, this review evaluates emerging trends across four foundational themes: (1) expanding empirical investigations beyond conventional visual and verbal domains into cross-modal sensory systems to evaluate the generality of WM principles; (2) establishing the malleable and context-sensitive format of WM representations, which actively reformat to facilitate prospective motor planning and behavioral goals; (3) resolving how complex feature bindings, structural hierarchies, and modality-independent pointers (or object files) coordinate multi-item storage within capacity limits; and (4) illuminating shared computational and functional architecture between WM and related faculties, including selective attention, episodic retrieval, and executive control. The authors integrate current evidence regarding distributed sensory recruitment and dynamic population codes, outlining crucial benchmarks for developing unified models of active cognitive processing.
papers.authors: Kirsten C. S. Adam, Laura-Isabelle Klatt, Jacob A. Miller, Marlene Rösner, Keisuke Fukuda, Anastasia Kiyonaga

papers.title: Capacity-aligned feedback enhances visual working memory performance
papers.abstract: Because visual working memory (VWM) is sharply capacity-limited, previous research has evaluated performance feedback and reward incentives to improve retention, yet findings have been equivocal. This paper proposes an optimal strategy framework postulating that feedback is maximally beneficial when incentivized goals align with an individual's intrinsic capacity limits rather than encouraging unconstrained performance maximization. Across three whole-report behavioral experiments manipulating goal difficulty (1–5 items) under blocked and intermixed conditions, optimal group-level performance occurred when goals matched average human capacity (~3 items). In contrast, supra-capacity goals (e.g., remembering 5 items) triggered an overload effect that systematically increased attentional lapse rates (chance-level recall). Pre-registered individual-differences analyses in Experiment 2 confirmed that individual performance peaked when incentive targets matched each participant's measured capacity limit, accompanied by a quantifiable trade-off between metacognitive calibration and maximal memory retrieval.
papers.authors: Olga Kozlova, Kirsten C. S. Adam

papers.title: First encounters: Estimating the initial magnitude of attentional capture
papers.abstract: Attentional capture is routinely evaluated using repetitive paradigms where participants complete hundreds of visual search trials containing salient distractors, a design that can inadvertently establish secondary task-sets for proactive distractor suppression. To estimate capture magnitude in the absence of distractor experience, large web-based cohorts performed a shape search task containing a single surprise distractor-present trial (Exp. 1: N = 970; Exp. 2: N = 1,025 across four sparse blocks). Initial capture costs were 9- to 15-fold larger (~370–580 ms) than canonical multi-trial estimates (~30 ms). Furthermore, capture was strongly modulated by stimulus history: singleton distractors rendered in a previously unseen color produced substantially greater slowdown (~585 ms) than distractors rendered in colors previously encountered during distractor-absent search (~375 ms). Reaction time mixture modeling demonstrated that capture manifests as large delays on a subset of trials rather than a small, uniform shift across the full distribution, indicating that typical laboratory estimates severely underestimate initial distraction costs.
papers.authors: Kirsten C. S. Adam, Zi Yang, John T. Serences

papers.title: Behavioral signatures of the rapid recruitment of long-term memory to overcome working memory capacity limits
papers.abstract: Working memory and long-term memory are conventionally investigated in isolation using unrepeated abstract arrays to avoid long-term memory contributions. In contrast to incidental array repetitions, which typically fail to enhance visual working memory performance, this study evaluated whether explicit repetitions enable the rapid deployment of visual long-term memory (VLTM) to overcome working memory capacity limits. In two behavioral experiments using continuous whole-report color recall of 6- or 8-item displays, explicit array repetitions approximately doubled recall performance from baseline (~2.8 items) to over 5–6 items across eight repetitions, with substantial improvements emerging after a single repetition. Subsequent surprise recognition tests verified above-chance recognition of repeated arrays. Crucially, fine-grained inter-response time (IRT) analyses identified a distinctive temporal slowing after reporting 2–3 items that emerged exclusively for repeated arrays, providing a behavioral metric of chunk retrieval and demonstrating rapid synthesis between active working memory and episodic long-term traces.
papers.authors: Kirsten C. S. Adam, Chong Zhao, Edward K. Vogel

0370.name: Kohitij Kar
0370.lab_name: Visual Intelligence and Technological Advances (VITAL) Lab
0370.bio: Kohitij Kar is an Assistant Professor in the Department of Biology and a Canada Research Chair in Visual Neuroscience at York University. Kar’s research functions at the intersection of primate neurophysiology and artificial intelligence, focusing on the recurrent neural mechanisms underlying core object recognition in the ventral stream. Utilizing large-scale electrophysiology, behavioral assays, and deep learning, they develop computational models to analyze the relationship between biological and artificial vision. Their work investigates how these neural frameworks can be used to understand visual cognition and to model neurodevelopmental disorders such as autism.
0370.research_direction: Dr. Kar has recently been investigating the neural computations underlying high-level visual perception, focusing on how the primate inferior temporal (IT) cortex represents complex features like image memorability, facial expressions, and scene context. Their recent work explores the mechanisms of cortical plasticity and naturalistic object recognition by directly comparing behavioral and electrophysiological data from macaques with state-of-the-art artificial neural network models.
