Specifically, they are examining whether distinct visual dimensions—such as face identity versus expression, or categorical object features versus intrinsic image memorability—are multiplexed within shared neural subspaces or handled by dissociable circuits. To support these large-scale psychophysical and modeling efforts, Dr. Kar is also developing open-source, portable home-cage testing kiosks that facilitate high-throughput, low-stress behavioral experiments in nonhuman primates.

papers.title: Distinct contributions of memorability and object recognition to the representational goals of the macaque inferior temporal cortex
papers.abstract: This study evaluates whether image memorability—a metric describing the intrinsic likelihood of a stimulus being remembered—and object identity are represented through distinct or multiplexed neural mechanisms in the macaque inferior temporal (IT) cortex. By recording large-scale neural population activity during delayed match-to-sample object discrimination, the researchers characterized the neural geometry of these features. The results indicate that IT neurons exhibit specific tuning for memorability that is statistically dissociable from categorization-related signals. These findings suggest that the primate ventral stream is optimized not only for category-level discrimination but also for the representational prioritization of memorable stimuli, potentially facilitating downstream consolidation and cognitive processing.
papers.authors: Soroush Ziaee, Ram Ahuja, Sabine Muzellec, Ezgi Fide, R. Shayna Rosenbaum, Kohitij Kar

papers.title: Facial expression discrimination emerges from neural subspaces shared with detection and identity
papers.abstract: Deciphering the neural computations underlying high-level face perception, including detection, identity recognition, and expression discrimination, remains a core challenge in visual neuroscience. Using rhesus macaques to model human facial processing, this study employs electrophysiological recordings and computational modeling to analyze the representational structure of the ventral stream. The researchers found that facial expression information is not localized to modular circuits but emerges from distributed neural population activity. Specifically, expression discrimination is supported by neural subspaces that are shared with face detection and identity manifolds. This integrated representational geometry suggests that the primate visual system employs a unified manifold to multiplex various social and categorical dimensions required for robust face perception.
papers.authors: Maren H. Wehrheim, Shirin Taghian Alamooti, Hamidreza Ramezanpour, Kohitij Kar

papers.title: Hierarchical Optimization predicts Plasticity in the Macaque Inferior Temporal Cortex following Object Training
papers.abstract: This research investigates how task-specific plasticity in the macaque inferior temporal (IT) cortex supports the learning of new object discrimination tasks. By comparing IT neural activity in task-naive monkeys and those trained to perform specific discriminations, the authors observed that training increases object selectivity, linear separability, and object invariance. To provide a mechanistic account of these changes, the study utilized sensory-computable, mechanistic, architecturally referenced, and testable (SMART) artificial neural network (ANN) models of the ventral stream. Simulations demonstrated that gradient-based, performance-optimizing updates within a hierarchical visual model effectively predict the observed empirical changes in neural population metrics and behavioral performance, suggesting that hierarchical optimization is a viable model for cortical plasticity in adult primates.
papers.authors: Lynn K. A. Sörensen, James J. DiCarlo, Kohitij Kar

papers.title: Low-cost, portable, easy-to-use kiosks to facilitate home-cage testing of nonhuman primates during vision-based behavioral tasks
papers.abstract: The authors introduce and validate an open-source, portable kiosk system for high-throughput behavioral testing of nonhuman primates (NHPs) in their home-cage environments. This system allows for the execution of complex vision-based tasks, such as object discrimination, without the stressors associated with laboratory restraint or head fixation. Validation across rhesus macaques and marmosets revealed that behavioral metrics, specifically image-level accuracy signatures (B. I1), are highly consistent between in-lab and in-cage settings. The study demonstrates that this automated methodology significantly increases experimental data volume while maintaining the fidelity of psychophysical measurements, providing a scalable solution for large-scale behavioral and neural research in NHPs.
papers.authors: Hamidreza Ramezanpour, Christopher Giverin, Kohitij Kar

papers.title: The impact of scene context on visual object recognition: comparing humans, monkeys, and computational models
papers.abstract: This study quantifies the effect of scene context on object recognition by comparing the behavioral biases of humans and macaques with those of state-of-the-art computational models. Utilizing context-level (B. C1) and image-level (B. I1) behavioral signatures, the researchers observed that monkeys exhibit context-driven effects, such as congruency biases, that closely match human psychophysical patterns. However, standard feedforward artificial neural networks (ANNs) and neural responses recorded from the macaque IT cortex (which were not explicitly trained in context) failed to fully explain the shared behavioral variance between the two species. This identifies a critical explanatory gap in current models of the ventral stream regarding the integration of contextual and relational information during naturalistic object recognition.
papers.authors: Sara Djambazovska, Anaa Zafer, Hamidreza Ramezanpour, Gabriel Kreiman, Kohitij Kar

0371.name: Konstantinos Derpanis
0371.department: Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science
0371.bio: Konstantinos G. Derpanis is an Associate Professor at York University and a Faculty Affiliate at the Vector Institute, focusing on computer vision, human motion understanding, and temporal sequence analysis. Their research applies deep learning and probabilistic modeling to 3D human pose estimation, motion segmentation, and point tracking through occlusions. This work connects computational vision and vision science by using neural network architectures to model human lightness and illusion perception. Derpanis also conducts research on spatio-temporal representations and weakly supervised learning for sequence alignment in video datasets.
0371.research_direction: Dr. Derpanis has recently been investigating the internal representational structures of deep neural networks, developing unsupervised methods like sparse autoencoders to discover and align interpretable semantic concepts across varying architectures and network layers. Their recent work also extensively explores spatiotemporal feature learning, specifically probing whether video models and multi-modal large language models genuinely utilize dynamic motion cues or merely rely on static appearance biases for tasks like action recognition and pixel-level visual grounding. Additionally, they are researching generative multi-view 3D scene inpainting by employing diffusion models constrained by explicit geometric cues such as depth maps and shadow volumes. Across these domains, they utilize techniques ranging from mutual-information metrics to novel motion-centric benchmarks to systematically characterize and guide exactly what fundamental visual information modern vision models encode.

papers.title: Universal Sparse Autoencoders: Interpretable Cross-Model Concept Alignment
papers.abstract: The authors introduce Universal Sparse Autoencoders (USAEs), a novel framework designed to identify and align interpretable semantic concepts across multiple disparate pretrained deep neural networks. In contrast to conventional concept-based interpretability techniques that operate on a per-model basis, USAEs facilitate the discovery of a joint concept space capable of reconstructing and interpreting internal activations from multiple architectures simultaneously. This is achieved by training a single overcomplete sparse autoencoder (SAE) to minimize a shared objective across varying tasks and datasets, thereby capturing common factors of variation. Empirical results demonstrate that USAEs uncover semantically coherent universal concepts in vision models, spanning from low-level textures to high-level object parts. Furthermore, the framework enables novel applications such as coordinated activation maximization for multi-model visualization and analysis.
papers.authors: Harrish Thasarathan, Julian Forsyth, Thomas Fel, Matthew Kowal, Konstantinos G. Derpanis

papers.title: Geometry-Aware Diffusion Models for Multiview Scene Inpainting
papers.abstract: This work addresses the problem of 3D scene inpainting where input images from multiple viewpoints contain masked regions requiring consistent completion. The authors propose a geometry-aware conditional generative model that avoids the blurriness typical of radiance-field-based fusion methods by operating in a learned feature space. The methodology employs an autoregressive inpainting strategy, conditioning each new view on previously generated content while utilizing a multi-view depth estimator to gradually reconstruct scene geometry. Key geometric cues, including depth maps and shadow volumes, are rendered to provide explicit constraints on the diffusion process. The model demonstrates state-of-the-art performance on the SPIn-NeRF and NeRFiller benchmarks, notably maintaining multi-view consistency even in the few-view setting where traditional 3D fitting methods fail.
papers.authors: Ahmad Salimi, Tristan Ty Aumentado-Armstrong, Marcus A. Brubaker, Konstantinos G. Derpanis

papers.title: Quantifying and Learning Static vs. Dynamic Information in Deep Spatiotemporal Networks
papers.abstract: This paper presents a systematic approach to quantifying the degree of absolute static (appearance-based) versus dynamic (motion-based) information encoded within the hidden representations of deep spatiotemporal models. The methodology utilizes a novel sampling procedure to generate video pairs that isolate specific factors of variation, followed by a mutual-information-based metric to assess unit-wise bias across various layers and channels. Extensive evaluations across action recognition and video segmentation tasks reveal that many state-of-the-art models exhibit a significant bias toward static features. To mitigate this, the authors propose StaticDropout, a semantically guided dropout mechanism that selectively suppresses static-biased channels during training. Results show that balancing static and dynamic representations improves performance on datasets requiring temporal reasoning, such as Something-Something-V2.
papers.venue: IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence (TPAMI)
papers.authors: Matthew Kowal, Mennatullah Siam, Md. Amirul Islam, Neil D. B. Bruce, Richard P. Wildes, Konstantinos G. Derpanis

papers.title: PixFoundation 2.0: Do Video Multi-Modal LLMs Use Motion in Visual Grounding?
papers.abstract: The authors investigate the pixel-level visual grounding capabilities of video multi-modal large language models (MLLMs), specifically examining whether these models utilize temporal motion cues or rely primarily on static appearance. Identifying deficiencies in current benchmarks where single-frame analysis often suffices for motion-related queries, the paper introduces four motion-centric probing techniques and a new benchmark, MoCentric-Bench. These probes assess the model's ability to distinguish authentic motion from synthetic counterparts and its comprehension of temporal ordering. The findings indicate that current video MLLMs often fail at dense spatiotemporal grounding tasks when static shortcuts are removed. Simple motion-centric adaptation techniques are explored to improve performance, setting a new baseline for future research in dense video understanding and reasoning.
papers.authors: Mennatullah Siam, Matthew Kowal, Md Amirul Islam, Richard P. Wildes, Konstantinos G. Derpanis

papers.title: Visual Concept Connectome (VCC): Open World Concept Discovery and Their Interlayer Connections in Deep Models
papers.abstract: The Visual Concept Connectome (VCC) is proposed as an unsupervised methodology for elucidating the internal representational structure of vision models across multiple layers. Unlike prior concept discovery methods that are restricted to single-layer analysis, VCC reveals fine-grained semantic concepts and their weighted interlayer connections throughout the entire network depth. This approach enables a global analysis of network structure, characterizing the branching patterns and hierarchical assemblies of concepts. The authors use VCCs to perform a comparative study between CNNs and Transformers, demonstrating that Transformers exhibit higher levels of compositionality in deeper layers. Practical utility is shown through failure mode debugging, where VCCs are used to identify the specific layers and concept assemblies responsible for classification errors in image classification tasks.
papers.venue: IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR)
papers.authors: Matthew Kowal, Richard P. Wildes, Konstantinos G. Derpanis

0373.name: Kowa Koida
0373.department: Department of Computer Science and Engineering
0373.bio: Kowa Koida is an Associate Professor at Toyohashi University of Technology and directs the Visual Neuroscience Lab, focusing on the neural substrates of color perception and object recognition. Their research integrates primate electrophysiology, human psychophysics, and neurotechnology to examine how the cerebral cortex transforms visual stimuli into subjective experiences. Koida contributed to the development of high-precision tungsten microelectrodes and investigated how cortical microstimulation influences behavioral color judgment. Current research directions include mapping the functional structure of the lateral geniculate nucleus and examining how material properties like gloss and transparency affect three-dimensional shape perception.
0373.research_direction: Dr. Koida has recently been investigating the mechanisms of color vision through a combination of primate neurophysiology, human psychophysics, and methodological innovation. Their recent work explores the causal neural basis of color categorization by applying electrical microstimulation to color-tuned clusters in the macaque inferior temporal cortex during behavioral tasks. In parallel, they are examining human color assimilation phenomena—such as the watercolor effect—using eye-model simulations to determine how early optical factors like chromatic aberration drive hue and luminance dependencies. To further support these complex visual experiments, Dr. Koida has also been developing advanced electrophysiological tools, including a highly synchronized, single-PC recording system for awake behaving primates and a minimally invasive microelectrode marking technique to precisely align recording sites with postmortem histology.

papers.title: Digital Signal Processor Integrated Recording System for Visual Neurophysiology using a Single Personal Computer
papers.abstract: The authors present an integrated visual neurophysiology recording and experimental control system hosted entirely on a single personal computer interfaced with a digital signal processor (DSP) data acquisition (DAQ) chassis. The architecture partitions workloads between two coordinated instances of MATLAB: one executes Psychtoolbox routines for visual stimulus delivery and behavioral task control, while the DSP on the DAQ executes high-bandwidth neural digitization, online spike detection, and real-time data streaming. A secondary parallel MATLAB instance computes real-time peri-stimulus time histograms (PSTHs) and monitoring metrics, with inter-application variable synchronization sustained within a 1 ms latency boundary. Over 2,000 cumulative operational hours in awake macaque electrophysiology experiments, the single-PC system maintained millisecond-precision timing and high system stability without computational degradation.
papers.authors: Tatsuya Oikawa, Kowa Koida

papers.title: 色同化の色相依存性と輝度依存性をもたらす眼光学的要因 (Optical factors contributing to the hue and luminance dependency of color assimilation)
papers.abstract: Color assimilation is a visual phenomenon where a target's perceived color shifts toward that of its immediate surroundings, yet the relative influence of optical versus neural factors remains debated. This study employed human psychophysical experiments using stimuli modeled on the watercolor effect and corresponding eye-model simulations based on spectral optical transfer functions. The results identified a significant hue-dependent interaction between background luminance and the frequency of perceived assimilation; specifically, red inducers required higher background luminance while blue inducers required lower luminance for maximal effect. Quantitative analysis of simulated retinal images revealed that variations in luminance contrast at the retinal level, driven specifically by chromatic aberration and light scattering, accurately predict these hue-dependent shifts, suggesting that early-stage optical factors are primary determinants of color assimilation characteristics.
papers.venue: VISION (Journal of the Vision Society of Japan)
papers.authors: Natsumi Tsuji, Kei Kanematsu, Kowa Koida

papers.title: A Fine-Scale and Minimally Invasive Marking Method for Use with Conventional Tungsten Microelectrodes
papers.abstract: Achieving microscopic alignment between extracellular unit recording sites and postmortem histological architecture remains challenging due to the tissue disruption caused by conventional electrolytic lesioning. The authors present an electrolytic marking technique that generates fine-scale tungsten oxide deposits using standard tungsten microelectrodes. Delivering biphasic current pulses at intensities of 40–50 μA, comparable to typical intracortical microstimulation protocols, reliably produces discrete markings ranging from 10 to 100 μm matching the microelectrode tip diameter. The deposited tungsten oxide causes negligible histological damage, remains stable in cerebral tissue in vivo for over two years, and appears vividly red under dark-field microscopy following standard Nissl staining in mouse and macaque cerebral cortex.
papers.authors: Tatsuya Oikawa, Kento Nomura, Toshimitsu Hara, Kowa Koida

papers.title: Effect of microstimulation of the inferior temporal cortex on color judgment behavior
papers.abstract: To establish whether color-tuned neuronal clusters in the ventral visual stream causally mediate perceptual color categorization, electrical microstimulation was administered to the anterior inferior temporal cortex (AITC) in macaque monkeys performing a categorical color-choice task across 110 stimulation sites over 76 penetrations. Sites were distributed across the anterior middle temporal sulcus, targeting areas where color-selective multi-unit activity concentrates. Electrical microstimulation systematically displaced behavioral psychometric functions, primarily through horizontal shifts in chromatic threshold and reductions in psychometric slope. Behavioral modulation magnitude was spatially correlated with the density of physiological color tuning; however, the directional bias induced by microstimulation was negatively correlated with the chromatic preference of the multi-unit cluster at the stimulation site, demonstrating that artificial activation of localized AITC modules directly biases categorical color judgments.
papers.authors: Kowa Koida, Hidehiko Komatsu

0374.name: Krista A. Ehinger
0374.department: School of Computing and Information Systems
0374.bio: Krista A. Ehinger is an Associate Professor at the University of Melbourne whose research explores the interface between biological and artificial vision, focusing on scene recognition, visual search, and depth perception in naturalistic environments. Ehinger utilizes a methodology that integrates psychophysical experiments and eye-tracking with computational modeling techniques such as Bayesian inference and deep neural networks. Their work investigates how scene context and peripheral encoding facilitate navigation and object detection in both humans and machines. Ehinger has developed large-scale scene understanding databases and models for predicting human attentional allocation.
0374.research_direction: Dr. Ehinger has recently been investigating the intersection of human visual cognition and complex computational scene understanding. Their recent work explores the mechanisms of visual memory, specifically testing how similarity-based exemplar models can predict context-dependent memorability for high-dimensional, real-world object categories. In the realm of computer vision, they are developing AI models that simulate human amodal perception by using diffusion frameworks to iteratively resolve occluded object contours and depth ordering in densely packed scenes. They have also been probing the limits of artificial vision in higher-order cognitive tasks, such as evaluating how well multimodal large language models navigate multi-stage abstract visual reasoning. Furthermore, their applied computational research extends into complex physical and spatial reasoning, focusing on novel geometric and deep learning pipelines for analyzing 3D environments, including physics-based disassembly planning and subsurface infrastructure mapping.

papers.title: Tests of a Hybrid-Similarity Exemplar Model of Context-Dependent Memorability in a High-Dimensional Real-World Category Domain
papers.abstract: This research evaluates the efficacy of a hybrid-similarity exemplar model in predicting context-dependent recognition memory for high-dimensional visual stimuli, specifically geological rock samples. The model posits that recognition decisions are mediated by the integrated similarity of a test probe to stored exemplars, incorporating a mechanism where feature matching on highly salient, distinctive attributes modulates the self-similarity of items. Across experiments manipulating study list composition and encoding tasks (descriptive matching versus neutral instruction), the framework successfully captured fundamental benchmark phenomena, including variations in memorability driven by category size and feature distinctiveness. However, the model and several architectural extensions were unable to fully account for the observed stochastic variance in hit rates within target categories, suggesting that current high-dimensional feature representations may require more granular item-level refinement to fully explain visual memorability.
papers.authors: Robert M. Nosofsky, Adam F. Osth, Krista A. Ehinger

papers.title: Deep Learning and Geometric Modeling for 3D Reconstruction of Subsurface Utilities from GPR Data
papers.abstract: The study introduces a hybrid deep learning and geometric modeling pipeline for the automated 3D reconstruction of buried linear utilities from Ground Penetrating Radar (GPR) B-scan data. The architecture leverages deep neural networks—specifically evaluating YOLOv8, YOLOv11, and Mask R-CNN—to perform keypoint detection on hyperbolic signal reflections within real-world radargrams. Summit points detected by the model are aggregated via a 3D Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise (DBSCAN) algorithm to delineate utility trajectories, followed by RANSAC-based geometric fitting to finalize the 3D paths. The Mask R-CNN backbone achieved a superior keypoint F1-score of 0.822, and the integrated pipeline yielded an average 3D path Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) of 0.06m. This approach circumvents common limitations such as reliance on synthetic data or the processing of full 3D data volumes, providing a scalable solution for subsurface infrastructure mapping.
papers.authors: Peyman Jafary, Davood Shojaei, Krista A. Ehinger

papers.title: Beyond Perception: Evaluating Abstract Visual Reasoning through Multi-Stage Task
papers.abstract: This paper investigates the performance of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) on non-perceptual visual logic by introducing MultiStAR, a multi-stage benchmark for Abstract Visual Reasoning (AVR) based on the RAVEN dataset. MultiStAR decomposes the reasoning process into discrete stages, including primitive attribute identification, attribute comparison, and higher-order rule inference. To provide a more granular evaluation, the authors propose MSEval, a metric that accounts for the joint probability of correctness across all intermediate reasoning steps rather than terminal accuracy alone. Benchmarking 17 proprietary and open-source MLLMs reveals that while current models exhibit proficiency in basic perception, their performance significantly degrades at the rule detection and logical chain reasoning stages, highlighting a critical bottleneck in navigating multi-stage abstract dependencies.
papers.venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics (ACL Findings 2025)
papers.authors: Yanbei Jiang, Yihao Ding, Chao Lei, Jiayang Ao, Jey Han Lau, Krista A. Ehinger

papers.title: State-Based Disassembly Planning
papers.abstract: Addressing the computational bottlenecks in physics-based disassembly planning for complex 3D structures, this work proposes State-Based Disassembly Planning (SBDP). The approach prioritizes translational over rotational motion within a physics-based simulation to improve autonomy and search scalability for assemblies with high-dimensional motion constraints. The method utilizes novel Directional Blocking Graphs (DBGs) enriched with state information to model mechanical dependencies between components and introduces two specialized evaluation functions to optimize the search process. Validation on a benchmark of thousands of physically valid industrial assemblies demonstrates that SBDP significantly outperforms existing geometric and simulation-based state-of-the-art planners in terms of both success rate and computational efficiency.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence (AAAI)
papers.authors: Chao Lei, Nir Lipovetzky, Krista A. Ehinger

papers.title: Sequential Amodal Segmentation via Cumulative Occlusion Learning
papers.abstract: To facilitate class-agnostic scene understanding, this paper introduces a diffusion-based framework for sequential amodal segmentation that resolves both visible and occluded object regions along with their depth ordering. The model employs a cumulative occlusion learning strategy, where a cumulative mask representing previously segmented layers is used to condition the reverse diffusion process, effectively capturing aleatoric uncertainty in occluded regions. This architecture enables the system to iteratively refine object contours and resolve complex layering in densely packed visual scenes, simulating human amodal perception capabilities. Experimental results on the COCOA, KINS, and D2SA datasets demonstrate that the proposed model surpasses established baselines in segmentation fidelity and occlusion order accuracy for objects with uncertain categories.
papers.authors: Jiayang Ao, Qiuhong Ke, Krista A. Ehinger

0375.name: Krista Kelly
0375.department: School of Optometry and Vision Science
0375.bio: Krista Kelly is an Assistant Professor at the University of Waterloo and directs the Vision and Neurodevelopment Lab. Kelly's research examines the impact of atypical early-life visual experiences, such as amblyopia, strabismus, and pediatric cataracts, on brain development and functional skills. Utilizing psychophysics, binocular eye tracking, and motion capture for gait analysis, they investigate the mechanisms behind reading delays and motor coordination deficits in children. Their work focuses on identifying biomarkers for vision-related impairments and developing interventions to address functional outcomes for pediatric patients.
0375.research_direction: Dr. Kelly’s recent work explores the broad neurodevelopmental and sensorimotor consequences of amblyopia, conceptualizing the condition as a complex functional deficit rather than a simple loss of unilateral visual acuity. They have recently been investigating the real-world impacts of early abnormal visual experience by measuring reading fluency via rapid serial visual presentation (RSVP) paradigms and assessing eye-hand coordination during visually guided reaching tasks. To capture these phenomena, their research combines high-resolution eye-tracking to quantify fixational instability with kinematic motion capture to analyze saccadic and motor behavior in pediatric populations. Furthermore, Dr. Kelly examines both the broader health-related quality of life impacts of the disorder and the efficacy of modern interventions, specifically evaluating how contrast-rebalanced dichoptic therapies—such as specialized video games and movies—influence the recovery of stereoacuity and binocular function.

papers.title: Editorial: Development and neuroplasticity of the visual system, amblyopia and beyond
papers.abstract: This editorial introduces the Research Topic focusing on experience-dependent plasticity, structural remodeling, and functional reorganization in the mammalian visual system following abnormal early sensory experience. The compiled empirical and theoretical contributions demonstrate that amblyopia represents a complex neurodevelopmental condition extending well beyond unilateral visual acuity impairment to encompass profound deficits in binocular integration, interocular suppression, oculomotor stability, and eye-hand coordination. The editorial highlights emerging paradigms demonstrating that visual neuroplasticity persists well past classical critical periods, examining electrophysiological markers (such as binocular intermodulation responses) and dichoptic therapies designed to restore balanced binocular interaction and ameliorate sensorimotor dysfunctions.
papers.authors: Kevin R. Duffy, Alex S. Baldwin, Anna Kosovicheva, Benjamin Thompson, Krista R. Kelly

papers.title: Eye-hand coordination during visually-guided reaching in children with monocular deprivation amblyopia
papers.abstract: Monocular deprivation (MD) amblyopia resulting from a dense unilateral congenital or infantile cataract causes significant sensory and ocular motor impairment, yet its impact on kinematic eye-hand coordination remains inadequately characterized. In this study, 17 children aged 7–15 years with MD amblyopia and 41 age-matched normal controls performed rapid visually guided reaches to peripheral targets (±5° and ±10°) during binocular viewing while hand movements (LEAP Motion Controller) and binocular eye movements (EyeLink 1000) were recorded. Children with MD amblyopia exhibited lower primary saccade gain, decreased saccadic endpoint precision, and elevated frequencies of reach-related corrective saccades. Reaching kinematics were also disrupted, characterized by prolonged total movement duration, lower peak velocity, prolonged deceleration phases in the terminal approach, and lower pointing accuracy. Kinematic deficits were especially pronounced in participants with poorer visual acuity outcomes (≥0.7 logMAR), reflecting impaired online visual feedback utilization and deficient visuomotor compensation following early visual deprivation.
papers.authors: Krista R. Kelly, Mina Nouradanesh, Reed M. Jost, Christina S. Cheng-Patel, Eileen E. Birch, Serena X. Wang, James Y. Tung, Ewa Niechwiej-Szwedo

papers.title: Slow binocular reading during rapid serial visual presentation (RSVP) in children with amblyopia and the role of fixation instability
papers.abstract: Children with amblyopia exhibit marked reading speed deficits during binocular viewing, but whether this reflects fixation instability or increased inter-word saccades has remained unresolved. To isolate ocular motor contributors, sentence reading speed was evaluated under rapid serial visual presentation (RSVP)—which eliminates the requirement for saccadic navigation between words—in 32 amblyopic children and 30 control children aged 8–12 years. Exposure thresholds (log words per minute [WPM]) were determined using a 2-down 1-up staircase alongside video eye-tracking to quantify fellow eye (FE) and amblyopic eye (AE) bivariate contour ellipse area (BCEA). Amblyopic children read significantly slower than controls (2.75 ± 0.47 vs. 3.06 ± 0.40 log WPM) and exhibited elevated BCEA in both eyes. However, amblyopic children with preserved FE fixation stability (n = 11) demonstrated RSVP reading rates comparable to controls, whereas those with poor FE stability (n = 21) were significantly impaired. Eliminating inter-word saccades failed to normalize reading rates, demonstrating that fellow-eye fixational instability directly drives slow binocular reading in amblyopia.
papers.authors: Dorsa Mir Norouzi, Norah M. Nyangau, Yi-Zhong Wang, Lori M. Dao, Cynthia L. Beauchamp, David R. Stager Jr., Jeffrey S. Hunter, Krista R. Kelly

papers.title: Functional consequences of amblyopia and its impact on health-related quality of life
papers.abstract: Amblyopia affects up to 4% of the pediatric population and often produces lifelong visual dysfunction. While clinical management centers primarily on resolving high-contrast visual acuity loss in the amblyopic eye, broad functional consequences frequently persist. This comprehensive narrative review delineates recent advancements in assessing everyday functional impairments in amblyopia, including deficits in spatial contrast sensitivity, attentional allocation, processing speed, and reading fluency. Furthermore, the review outlines motor and systemic correlates, such as altered reaching and grasping kinematics, impaired manual dexterity, reduced physical activity, and adverse changes in body composition. The multidimensional degradation of health-related and vision-related quality of life (HRQoL) across social, emotional, and academic domains is summarized, emphasizing the clinical necessity of moving beyond acuity-only endpoints toward holistic, whole-person rehabilitation paradigms.
papers.authors: Krista R. Kelly, Yi Pang, Benjamin Thompson, Ewa Niechwiej-Szwedo, Carolyn D. Drews-Botsch, Ann L. Webber

papers.title: Baseline and outcome stereoacuity of children with anisometropic amblyopia undergoing dichoptic amblyopia treatment
papers.abstract: This study evaluated factors influencing pre-treatment and post-treatment stereoacuity and composite binocular function (BF) scores in children with anisometropic amblyopia receiving contrast-rebalanced dichoptic therapy. Data were pooled across 185 children aged 3–12 years participating in eight clinical trials employing dichoptic video games or contrast-rebalanced movies. Higher baseline stereoacuity and BF scores were associated with better baseline amblyopic eye visual acuity, milder interocular suppression, lower degrees of anisometropia, and anisometropia driven by astigmatism. Following therapy, superior stereoacuity and BF outcomes were correlated with better baseline binocularity, greater visual acuity gains, lower anisometropia, and astigmatic etiology. Children aged 3–6 years who achieved complete visual acuity restoration demonstrated significantly greater stereoacuity and BF recovery than those with residual amblyopia, highlighting that early dichoptic intervention supports meaningful stereoscopic recovery alongside visual acuity gains.
papers.authors: Eileen E. Birch, Reed M. Jost, Krista R. Kelly

0377.name: Kristina J. Nielsen
0377.department: Solomon H. Snyder Department of Neuroscience
0377.bio: Kristina J. Nielsen is an Associate Professor of Neuroscience at Johns Hopkins University who researches the neural circuits responsible for object recognition and motion perception. Nielsen's laboratory uses two-photon calcium imaging and high-density electrophysiology to map the functional transformations occurring between primary and higher-level visual cortical areas. By studying non-human primates and ferret models, Nielsen investigates how these representations emerge during development and the extent of adult plasticity. Their work aims to bridge the gap between pixel-level visual inputs and the invariant object representations formed in the brain.
0377.research_direction: Dr. Nielsen has recently been investigating the mechanisms that govern the development and computational organization of higher-level visual cortex. Their recent work explores the developmental timeline of motion processing, comparing the distinct sensory requirements for the emergence of direction selectivity in primary visual cortex versus higher-tier motion areas like PMLS. By examining these early network-level interactions, they are investigating how transient functional architectures challenge traditional, strictly feedforward models of cortical maturation. Alongside their developmental research, Dr. Nielsen is also exploring the computational principles underlying 2D and 3D shape perception in the mature primate ventral visual stream. Specifically, they are investigating how successive neural transformations across areas V1, V4, and inferotemporal cortex achieve critical objectives like dimensional compression and representational invariance to support stable object recognition.

papers.title: Early development of direction selectivity in higher visual cortex
papers.abstract: The computation of motion direction is an essential element of visual processing represented in both early cortical stages, such as primary visual cortex (V1), and higher-tier motion areas, such as middle temporal area (MT) in primates and posteromedial lateral suprasylvian (PMLS) cortex in ferrets. Tracking the developmental time course of directional tuning in the ferret visual pathway revealed that direction selectivity emerges earlier in PMLS than in V1, contradicting standard bottom-up hierarchical maturation models. While sensory experience influences direction selectivity across both cortical areas, the sensory requirements differ fundamentally: drifting gratings that provide coordinated spatiotemporal cues are necessary for the development of direction selectivity in V1, whereas spatially stationary flickering stimuli containing only temporal modulation are sufficient to induce direction selectivity in PMLS. These findings indicate that motion pathway maturation is governed by complex network-level interactions that do not depend strictly on feedforward drives from V1.
papers.authors: Dallas C. Khamiss, Augusto A. Lempel, Brandon R. Nanfito, Kristina J. Nielsen

papers.title: Development of Higher-Level Vision: A Network Perspective
papers.abstract: Whereas extensive neurodevelopmental research has mapped the mechanisms governing early visual processing through primary visual cortex (V1), the developmental principles shaping downstream extrastriate and higher-order visual cortex remain poorly understood. The conventional model presumes a sequential, feedforward maturation process that mirrors the hierarchical ordering observed in adult cortex. However, an evaluation of structural, physiological, and behavioral evidence across species indicates that the mature hierarchy arises from an evolving series of distinct, transient network configurations rather than simple incomplete variants of adult connectivity. Adopting an interactive, network-level perspective across multiple cortical stages will be necessary to resolve the biological rules governing higher visual development, uncover specific temporal windows of susceptibility to neurodevelopmental disorders, and design effective clinical interventions.
papers.authors: James A. Bourne, Radoslaw M. Cichy, Lynne Kiorpes, Maria Concetta Morrone, Michael J. Arcaro, Kristina J. Nielsen

papers.title: How Shape Perception Works, in Two Dimensions and Three Dimensions
papers.abstract: The primate ventral visual stream executes a succession of nonlinear transformations that convert retinal light patterns into high-level structural representations supporting 2D pattern recognition and 3D volumetric shape comprehension. This review outlines an integrative computational framework defining three primary objectives governing ventral stream coding: radical dimensional compression to facilitate transmission across white-matter tracts and enable compact mnemonic storage; explicit linear readouts allowing downstream circuits to directly access shape features for executive control; and representational invariance to preserve perceptual constancy across changes in size, orientation, illumination, and retinal position. Analyzing neural encoding across early visual cortex, intermediate area V4, and inferotemporal cortex (IT) demonstrates how successive receptive field transformations fulfill these computational objectives to yield detailed, stable object perception.
papers.authors: Kristina J. Nielsen, Charles E. Connor

0378.name: Kristina Visscher
0378.bio: Kristina Visscher is an Associate Professor in the Department of Neurobiology and Associate Director of the McKnight Brain Institute at the University of Alabama at Birmingham. Visscher's research utilizes functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), electroencephalography (EEG), and psychophysics to investigate how cognitive control mechanisms modulate sensory processing and adapt to environmental changes. A focus of their work is cortical plasticity following central vision loss, specifically exploring how the brain reorganizes to utilize peripheral vision in patients with macular degeneration. Visscher also leads efforts within the McKnight Brain Aging Registry to characterize neural network dynamics and cognitive health in the oldest-old population.
0378.research_direction: Dr. Visscher has recently been investigating how visual experience, sensory deprivation, and aging shape large-scale functional network connectivity and attentional mechanisms. Their recent work explores intrinsic connectivity plasticity in patients with macular degeneration, specifically examining how the loss of central vision and the compensatory use of a peripheral preferred retinal locus alter resting-state connections between early retinotopic cortex and higher-order category-selective visual areas. To isolate the behavioral drivers of these adaptations, they are also probing how peripheral vision training and simulated scotomas impact the spatially specific allocation of habitual, exogenous, and endogenous attention. Beyond visual cortex reorganization, Dr. Visscher examines broader functional brain architecture in cognitive aging, utilizing fMRI to investigate how network segregation and modularity relate to maintained processing speed in the oldest-old. Additionally, their research spans clinical interventions, as they are currently conducting randomized trials combining functional neuroimaging and ecological momentary assessment to test whether speed-of-processing cognitive training drives neural plasticity and improves real-world functional independence in older adults.

papers.title: Increased attentive use leads to more idiosyncratic functional connections
papers.abstract: This work explores how the frequency of attentive cortical engagement influences the variability of whole-brain functional connectivity (FC) patterns across individuals. The authors define a metric of 'idiosyncrasy' to measure the deviation of a region's FC profile from the population mean. In neurotypical subjects, foveal V1 representations—which support high-attention tasks—exhibited significantly higher idiosyncrasy compared to peripheral representations. In patients with macular degeneration, the cortical representation of the preferred retinal locus (PRL) showed a similar increase in idiosyncratic connectivity relative to both control regions and corresponding retinal locations in sighted participants. These results suggest that increased cognitive or attentive use of a specific sensory representation drives personalized neural reorganization, resulting in unique, snowflake-like connectivity architectures that are shaped by individual experience.
papers.authors: Pinar Demirayak, Leland L. Fleming, Paul Stewart, Rachel Chua, Kristina M. Visscher

papers.title: Network segregation is associated with processing speed in the cognitively healthy oldest-old
papers.abstract: The study investigates the relationship between large-scale functional network organization and cognitive performance in a rare cohort of healthy adults aged 85 and older (the 'oldest-old'). Utilizing a custom cortical parcellation optimized for the aged brain, the researchers calculated network segregation and modularity within the association system, specifically targeting the fronto-parietal (FPN), cingulo-opercular (CON), and default mode (DMN) networks. The analysis revealed that higher segregation within these association networks is strongly correlated with maintained processing speed and superior global cognition. These findings provide evidence for the dedifferentiation hypothesis, suggesting that the preservation of distinct, segregated functional systems is a hallmark of successful cognitive aging into the tenth decade of life.
papers.authors: Sara A. Nolin, Mary E. Faulkner, Paul Stewart, Leland L. Fleming, Stacy Merritt, Roxanne F. Rezaei, Pradyumna K. Bharadwaj, Mary Kate Franchetti, David A. Raichlen, Cortney J. Jessup, Lloyd Edwards, G. Alex Hishaw, Emily J. Van Etten, Theodore P. Trouard, David Geldmacher, Virginia G. Wadley, Noam Alperin, Eric S. Porges, Adam J. Woods, Ron A. Cohen, Bonnie E. Levin, Tatjana Rundek, Gene E. Alexander, Kristina M. Visscher

papers.title: The Everyday Function Intervention Trial (EFIT) protocol: A randomized clinical trial
papers.abstract: This article details the experimental design and methodology for the Everyday Function Intervention Trial (EFIT), a double-blind randomized clinical trial assessing cognitive training transfer to real-world outcomes. The protocol targets the enhancement of instrumental activities of daily living (IADL) and general functional independence in older adults through speed-of-processing training. A key innovation in this trial is the integration of ecological momentary assessment (EMA) via mobile devices to capture high-frequency behavioral data outside the laboratory. Furthermore, the protocol incorporates task-based and resting-state fMRI to identify neural biomarkers of plasticity and determine if specific changes in network connectivity mediate the relationship between cognitive intervention and improved everyday performance.
papers.authors: Lesley A. Ross, Courtney Fine, Abigail T. Stephan, Hye Won Chai, Ava McVey, Christine B. Phillips, Alyssa Gamaldo, Jacqueline Mogle, Nancy Dennis, Martin Sliwinski, Kristina Visscher

papers.title: Impact of Deprivation and Preferential Usage on Functional Connectivity Between Early Visual Cortex and Category-Selective Visual Regions
papers.abstract: The authors investigated intrinsic functional connectivity (FC) plasticity in individuals with late-stage macular degeneration (MD) to determine how sensory deprivation and compensatory input usage reorganize the visual system. Using resting-state fMRI acquired in total darkness, the study mapped connectivity between specific V1 retinotopic sectors (representing the central lesion, the peripheral preferred retinal locus [PRL], and non-preferred peripheral regions) and higher-order areas like FFA, PPA, and hMT+. Results indicated that all spared peripheral representations in V1, regardless of their status as preferred or non-preferred viewing loci, developed significantly stronger functional connections to the motion-selective area MT compared to sighted controls. These findings suggest that long-term central vision loss induces a broad reorganization of spared visual pathways that is not strictly localized to the areas receiving preferential behavioral use.
papers.authors: Leland L. Fleming, Matthew K. Defenderfer, Pinar Demirayak, Paul Stewart, Dawn K. DeCarlo, Kristina M. Visscher

papers.title: Constraining the Possible Mechanisms Underlying Performance Improvements Following Peripheral Vision Training
papers.abstract: This study evaluates whether the behavioral improvements seen after training with peripheral vision are caused by spatially specific enhancements in attentional allocation. Using a gaze-contingent simulated scotoma paradigm, the researchers probed three distinct types of attention: habitual, dynamic exogenous, and dynamic endogenous. Healthy participants underwent 10 days of training on visual tasks at a specified peripheral retinal location. Post-training assessments revealed that habitual attention improved specifically at the trained retinotopic location. In contrast, improvements in dynamic exogenous and endogenous attention were observed globally, occurring at both trained and untrained peripheral locations. This dissociation suggests that the primary driver of location-specific perceptual learning in peripheral vision is a shift in habitual attentional bias rather than a localized refinement of dynamic attentional control mechanisms.
papers.authors: Mandy Biles, Marcello Maniglia, Ishant Yadav, Kristina M. Visscher

0380.name: Krystel Huxlin
0380.bio: Krystel Huxlin is the James V. Aquavella Professor of Ophthalmology at the University of Rochester, where they investigate the capacity for repair and neuroplasticity in the damaged adult visual system. Huxlin’s research utilizes psychophysical training paradigms, non-invasive brain stimulation, and advanced perimetry to develop rehabilitation strategies for patients with cortical blindness resulting from stroke. In the field of physiological optics, they work on the development of non-surgical laser refractive index change (LIRIC). Huxlin also studies the molecular mechanisms underlying corneal wound healing and nerve regeneration.
0380.research_direction: Dr. Huxlin has recently been investigating the neuroplastic potential of the adult visual system following primary visual cortex (V1) damage, focusing on how visual retraining paradigms can facilitate functional recovery in cortically blind visual fields. Their recent work explores the spatial and temporal evolution of visual field defects after occipital stroke, using longitudinal perimetry data to benchmark spontaneous recovery and evaluate the accuracy of different clinical measurement instruments. They are also utilizing optical coherence tomography to determine whether targeted psychophysical training can provide patient-specific neuroprotection by halting trans-synaptic retrograde degeneration and retinal thinning following cortical insults. In a distinct line of ocular research, Dr. Huxlin is studying the metabolic mechanisms underlying corneal scarring, examining whether pharmacological manipulation of mitochondrial transport can remodel myofibroblasts and attenuate fibrosis after tissue injury.

papers.title: What V1 Damage Can Teach Us About Visual Perception and Learning
papers.abstract: This synthesis evaluates the neuroplastic potential of the adult visual system following primary visual cortex (V1) lesions, which typically result in contralateral homonymous visual field loss. We characterize the evolution of visual retraining paradigms, such as detection and discrimination tasks within cortically-blind fields, and review current evidence regarding the efficacy and generalizability of training-induced recovery. The work details the mechanistic insights provided by psychophysical and neuroimaging investigations, specifically addressing how cortical damage alters visual circuit architecture and how targeted behavioral interventions can facilitate functional relearning. Finally, we address the limitations and opportunities for optimizing vision restoration therapies in patients with stroke-induced cortical blindness.
papers.authors: Matthew R. Cavanaugh, Berkeley K. Fahrenthold, Krystel R. Huxlin

papers.title: Evolution of Visual Field Defects After Occipital Stroke: A Quantitative Analysis
papers.abstract: To establish a quantitative benchmark for the natural progression of homonymous visual defects, we performed a retrospective analysis of longitudinal Humphrey automated perimetry data from 532 occipital stroke patients. Utilizing metrics such as perimetric mean deviation (PMD) and deficit area across a range of 0 to 2986 days post-insult, we identified spontaneous improvements in approximately 77% of patients during the subacute phase (<6 months), with partial deficits exhibiting greater recovery than complete hemianopia. While perimetric measurements generally stabilized in the chronic period (>6 months), roughly half of the subjects showed fluctuations exceeding 1 dB in PMD. These findings define the temporal and spatial characteristics of spontaneous recovery, providing critical parameters for clinical assessments of restorative therapies in cortical blindness.
papers.authors: Elizabeth L. Saionz, Matthew R. Cavanaugh, Brent A. Johnson, Donald Harrington, Geoffrey K. Aguirre, Krystel R. Huxlin

papers.title: MAIA and Humphrey Perimetry Differ in Their Estimation of Homonymous Visual Field Defects
papers.abstract: This study quantitatively compared the estimation of visual deficit size, severity, and progression in participants with homonymous hemianopia using the Humphrey Field Analyzer (HFA) 10-2 and the Macular Integrity Assessment (MAIA) microperimeter. Analyses of reliable, monocular perimetry data from 60 adult patients post-occipital stroke revealed that HFA and MAIA provide well-correlated but systematically offset measurements of visual sensitivity. Specifically, MAIA consistently estimated significantly larger deficit areas and lower mean sensitivities compared to HFA. These discrepancies are likely driven by differences in photopic versus mesopic background luminance and fixation control mechanisms. The results suggest that diagnostic criteria for defining cortical blindness and monitoring progression must be instrument-specific to account for inherent differences in stimulus parameters and patient performance.
papers.authors: Bryan V. Redmond, Berkeley K. Fahrenthold, Jingyi Yang, Elizabeth L. Saionz, Matthew R. Cavanaugh, Krystel R. Huxlin

papers.title: Manipulating mitochondrial pyruvate carrier function causes metabolic remodeling in corneal myofibroblasts that ameliorates fibrosis
papers.abstract: Pathological corneal scarring is characterized by the differentiation of keratocytes into scar-forming myofibroblasts, a transition mediated by metabolic shifts. We investigated whether modulating mitochondrial pyruvate carrier (MPC) function could influence this profibrotic differentiation. Pharmacological inhibition of MPC with UK5099 in corneal fibroblasts stimulated a distinct metabolic remodeling profile, characterized by reduced mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation. This metabolic shift significantly downregulated the expression of alpha-smooth muscle actin (α-SMA) and suppressed the deposition of extracellular matrix proteins, effectively attenuating the myofibroblast phenotype. These data identify MPC-mediated pyruvate transport as a critical metabolic regulator of corneal fibrosis and suggest a novel pharmacological strategy for restoring corneal clarity following ocular injury.
papers.authors: Kye-Im Jeon, Ankita Kumar, Paul S. Brookes, Keith Nehrke, Krystel R. Huxlin

papers.title: Training in Cortically Blinded Fields Appears to Confer Patient-Specific Benefit Against Retinal Thinning
papers.abstract: Damage to the primary visual cortex (V1) initiates trans-synaptic retrograde degeneration (TRD), resulting in the progressive thinning of the ipsilesional retinal ganglion cell complex. We conducted a meta-analysis of optical coherence tomography (OCT) data from 48 participants with unilateral V1 stroke to evaluate whether visual restoration training impacts TRD progression. Longitudinal measurements of the macular ganglion cell-inner plexiform layer (GCL-IPL) and retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL) thickness demonstrated that while participants who trained in their intact hemifield exhibited continued retinal thinning, those who underwent direction discrimination training within their blind fields experienced a significant stabilization of GCL-IPL thickness over six months. This provides evidence that behavioral visual stimulation can serve as a neuroprotective intervention to halt the progression of trans-synaptic atrophy following cortical insult.
papers.authors: Berkeley K. Fahrenthold, Matthew R. Cavanaugh, Madhura Tamhankar, Byron L. Lam, Steven E. Feldon, Brent A. Johnson, Krystel R. Huxlin

0381.name: Lana M. Trick
0381.lab_name: DRiVE Lab (Driving Research in Virtual Environments)
0381.bio: Lana M. Trick is a Professor of Psychology at the University of Guelph and the director of the Driving Research in Virtual Environments (DRiVE) Lab. Trick’s research examines the mechanisms of visual attention and memory, focusing on how these operations change across the lifespan and in neurodivergent populations such as those with ADHD or autism. Using driving simulators, Trick investigates the impact of cognitive load, distraction, and vehicle technologies on collision risk and driver performance. Their work also provides data on spatial enumeration processes, including subitizing and multiple-object tracking, to identify the capacities and limitations of human visual processing.
0381.research_direction: Dr. Trick has recently been investigating the allocation of visual attention and cognitive resources across both applied transportation contexts and basic visual cognition paradigms. Their applied work uses high-fidelity driving simulators, eye-tracking, and physiological measures to explore how hazard perception and vehicle control are affected by internal states like unintentional mind-wandering, external cognitive loads such as complex audiobooks, and neurodivergent sensory processing in autistic drivers. Concurrently, their recent basic research utilizes dual-task paradigms to examine the cognitive architecture shared between multiple-object tracking (MOT) and visually guided touch. Specifically, they are testing whether spatial indexing mechanisms—such as those proposed by the FINST framework—compete for the same representational resources as the preparation and execution of reaching movements.

papers.title: Driving performance is better predicted by unintentional rather than intentional mind-wandering in high density traffic
papers.abstract: This study utilized a high-fidelity driving simulator to investigate the differential impact of intentional versus unintentional mind-wandering on performance across varying traffic densities. While mind-wandering was found to be more prevalent during low-demand driving conditions, unintentional attentional lapses emerged as the superior predictor of performance decrements in high-density traffic. Specifically, unintentional mind-wandering accounted for 14-18% of the variance in horizontal steering variability, velocity fluctuations, and hazard perception-response times. These findings support the executive failure theory of mind-wandering, suggesting that spontaneous shifts in attention under high cognitive load pose a significantly greater risk to driving safety than deliberate off-task thoughts.
papers.venue: Transportation Research Part F: Traffic Psychology and Behaviour
papers.authors: Heather E. K. Walker, Lana M. Trick

papers.title: EXPRESS: Multiple-object tracking and visually guided touch: Dual-task interference reveals distinct effects of target indexing and target report method
papers.abstract: Drawing on the FINST (FINgers of INSTantiation) framework, this research explores the cognitive mechanisms shared between multiple-object tracking (MOT) and visually guided motor actions. The experiment employed a dual-task paradigm where participants tracked moving targets while concurrently executing localized touches on items that changed color. By manipulating the target report modality—comparing effector-congruent touch reporting to effector-incongruent keyboard reporting—the study aimed to dissociate interference caused by shared indexing resources from that caused by action-plan overlap. Results indicated significant dual-task costs that were amplified when reporting and tracking utilized the same effector, providing evidence that the spatial indexing mechanism supporting target individuation in MOT is functionally linked to the preparation and execution of reaching movements.
papers.authors: Mallory Elizabeth Terry, Lana M. Trick

papers.title: Easy listening or driving distraction? The relationship between audiobook complexity level and driving performance on simple routes
papers.abstract: This experiment investigated whether the semantic and cognitive complexity of auditory secondary tasks affects driving performance during monotonous, low-traffic conditions. Participants operated a driving simulator while listening to audiobooks categorized by varying difficulty levels. The results showed that while driving speed remained stable, increased audiobook complexity led to significant impairments in several safety-critical metrics, including increased hazard response latencies, reduced headway distance to lead vehicles, and higher standard deviation of lateral position (SDLP). Additionally, participants demonstrated poorer recall for the content of complex audiobooks, suggesting that high-level auditory processing competes for a limited pool of central attentional resources even during relatively simple vehicle control tasks.
papers.venue: Transportation Research Part F: Traffic Psychology and Behaviour
papers.authors: Jessica M. Kespe, Lana M. Trick

papers.title: The impact of cognitive load on a lane change task (LCT) among male autistic individuals: A driving simulator study
papers.abstract: This research assessed how increased cognitive demand influences the driving behavior and physiological responses of autistic young adults during a standardized lane change task (LCT). Using eye-tracking and skin conductance measures within a simulator environment, the study compared high-functioning autistic participants with neurotypical controls. Autistic drivers exhibited elevated heart rates and distinctive gaze patterns characterized by reduced scanning of high-stimulus roadway regions under high-load conditions (e.g., performing a concurrent n-back task). While these drivers adopted more conservative steering strategies, they were less effective at adapting to dynamic task demands. The findings highlight the critical role of executive function and sensory processing in driving performance for this demographic, pointing toward the need for tailored interventions in driver rehabilitation.
papers.venue: Transportation Research Part F: Traffic Psychology and Behaviour
papers.authors: Wondwesen Girma Mamo, Wael Alhajyaseen, Kris Brijs, Lana M. Trick

papers.title: Action matters! Target report technique affects interference between visually guided touch and multiple-object tracking
papers.abstract: This study examines the role of action-plan overlap in the interference observed between multiple-object tracking (MOT) and visually guided touch. Participants performed a dual-task where they tracked 1–4 targets while responding to color changes by touching the affected items. The research manipulated the response modality used to report target locations at the end of each trial, comparing a touch-based report (maximal overlap with the primary action) to a keyboard-based report (minimal overlap). Data revealed that while the method of report did not impact single-task MOT, dual-task performance was significantly more impaired when reporting required the same effector as the tracking-related touches. These results suggest that performance decrements in MOT-action tasks are driven by both specific action-plan interference and a general competition for shared spatial indexing mechanisms.
papers.authors: Vanessa Amelio, Mallory Elizabeth Terry, Lana M. Trick

0382.name: Lars F Muckli
0382.bio: Lars F Muckli is a Professor of Visual and Cognitive Neurosciences and Director of fMRI at the University of Glasgow's Centre for Cognitive Neuroimaging. Muckli’s research examines the predictive processing framework, investigating how internal models and cortical feedback modulate sensory perception in the early visual cortex. They use high-resolution, layer-specific fMRI techniques at ultra-high fields (7T) to isolate top-down signals in the superficial layers of the primary visual cortex. Their work combines neuroimaging with computational modeling to identify the mechanisms by which the brain anticipates visual input and processes contextual information.
0382.research_direction: Dr. Muckli has recently been investigating how the primary visual cortex serves as a dynamic interface for predictive processing, focusing on how top-down contextual priors and sensory evidence are integrated in early sensory regions. Using ultra-high field 7T fMRI and multivariate decoding, their recent work explores the spatial and laminar organization of feedback to V1, probing whether top-down signals related to mental imagery, illusory contours, and natural scene context target distinct cortical depths or specific retinotopic subregions. They are also investigating whether cross-modal predictive feedback, such as auditory scene information projecting to early visual areas, operates independently of conscious visual experience by studying individuals with aphantasia. Additionally, Dr. Muckli is examining spatial phenomenology at the physiological blind spot using psychophysical methods to contrast competing predictions from Predictive Processing and Integrated Information Theory regarding the neural architecture of spatial consciousness.

papers.title: Protocol for investigating the warping of spatial experience across the blind spot to contrast predictions of the Integrated Information Theory and Predictive Processing accounts of consciousness
papers.abstract: This experimental protocol delineates a structured adversarial collaboration aimed at adjudicating between Integrated Information Theory (IIT) and Predictive Processing (PP) frameworks regarding the neural substrates of spatial phenomenology. The investigation focuses on the perceptual warping of space at the physiological blind spot, a region devoid of feedforward retinal input. According to IIT, the perceived spatial metric is determined by the underlying cause-effect structure of the cortical network; consequently, the lack of activatable units in the blind spot's ipsilateral representation should induce a measurable warping of subjective space. Conversely, PP accounts (including Active Inference and Neurorepresentationalism) hypothesize that hierarchical internal models dynamically accommodate structural anomalies through Bayesian inference, predicting that the perceived field remains coherent and non-warped. The protocol details psychophysical distance-matching tasks, blind spot mapping procedures, and quantitative metrics to be applied across data collection sites to test these divergent predictions.
papers.authors: Clement Abbatecola, Bernard Marius 't Hart, Belén M. Montabes de la Cruz, Lucy S. Petro, Cyriel M. A. Pennartz, Giulio Tononi, TWCF-INTREPID consortium, Lars F. Muckli

papers.title: Retinotopic biases in contextual feedback signals to V1 for object and scene processing
papers.abstract: This study characterizes the spatial organization of cortical feedback signals converging in the primary visual cortex (V1) during natural scene and object processing. Utilizing ultra-high field (7T) fMRI and multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA), we demonstrate that contextual feedback carries category-specific information that successfully generalizes across sensory modalities (e.g., auditory scene-to-visual generalization). Crucially, the spatial distribution of this feedback exhibits distinct retinotopic biases: scene-related feedback information preferentially projects to peripheral V1 locations, whereas task-relevant object information is optimally decoded from foveal subregions. These findings support a 'cognitive blackboard' model of V1, where higher-order cortical areas map abstract contextual and mnemonic priors onto the precise retinotopic coordinates of the early visual cortex to facilitate proactive inference and scene completion.
papers.authors: Matthew A. Bennett, Lucy S. Petro, Clement Abbatecola, Lars F. Muckli

papers.title: Priors, evidence, and memory: Dynamics of predictive processing in a hierarchical visual system
papers.abstract: This theoretical synthesis reviews the computational dynamics of hierarchical predictive processing in the human visual system, with a specific focus on the interplay between feedforward sensory evidence and internally generated priors. Drawing upon recent laminar fMRI data, the review delineates how the visual cortex integrates memory-driven predictions via feedback projections to specific laminae (deep and superficial layers). It argues that the primary visual cortex (V1) functions as a dynamic interface for evaluating the correspondence between sensory observations and proactively generated internal models of the environment. The paper discusses how the microcircuitry of the cortex enables the multiplexing of bottom-up sensory streams with top-down contextual modulation, effectively transforming the early visual cortex into a contextualized representation of the external world informed by previous experience.
papers.authors: Lars F. Muckli

papers.title: Decoding sound content in the early visual cortex of aphantasic participants
papers.abstract: The research investigates cross-modal feedback from auditory scenes to the early visual cortex (V1) in individuals with aphantasia, a condition characterized by the absence of conscious visual mental imagery. Using high-resolution fMRI and multivariate decoding, we assessed whether categorical information from natural sounds (e.g., forest or street scenes) is represented in V1 when participants are deprived of visual input. Despite the subjective lack of phenomenal imagery, sound content was successfully decoded from V1 activation patterns in aphantasic participants at levels comparable to control subjects with vivid imagery. These results demonstrate that content-specific cross-modal predictive feedback remains intact in the absence of conscious visual experience, suggesting that the neural architecture for predictive feedback to V1 is functionally independent of the mechanisms generating conscious visual mental images.
papers.authors: Belén M. Montabes de la Cruz, Clement Abbatecola, Roberto S. Luciani, Alice T. Paton, Johanna Bergmann, Petra Vetter, Lucy S. Petro, Lars F. Muckli

papers.title: Cortical depth profiles in primary visual cortex for illusory and imaginary experiences
papers.abstract: Employing 7T laminar fMRI, this study probed the mesoscale distribution of activation patterns in primary visual cortex (V1) during mental imagery and illusory perception (Kanizsa figures). Multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) revealed a distinct laminar dissociation: imagery-induced representations were predominantly localized to the deep cortical layers, whereas information regarding illusory contours was decodable primarily from the superficial layers. Furthermore, while illusory content shared representational information with perceptual content, imagery-induced signals did not generalize to either illusory or perceptual states. These results indicate that V1 microcircuits utilize different feedback pathways to integrate perception-related illusions and internally generated mnemonic imagery, highlighting the hierarchical organization of feedback signals in the human visual system.
papers.authors: Johanna Bergmann, Lucy S. Petro, Clement Abbatecola, Min S. Li, A. Tyler Morgan, Lars Muckli

0383.name: Laura Dugué
0383.bio: Laura Dugué is a Professor of Cognitive and Computational Neuroscience whose research examines the periodic nature of human perception and attention. Utilizing a multimodal framework that integrates EEG, MEG, fMRI, and transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), Dugué investigates how brain oscillations and traveling waves organize information sampling across the visual field. Their work provides causal evidence for the role of alpha and theta rhythms in attentional selection. This research is supported by the ERC-funded SAMPLING project and an appointment to the Institut Universitaire de France.
0383.research_direction: Dr. Dugué has recently been investigating the spatiotemporal dynamics of visual processing, focusing heavily on cortical traveling waves and the rhythmic nature of attention. Their recent work explores how both macroscopic and mesoscopic traveling waves propagate across the cortex, using non-invasive M/EEG, intracranial recordings, and computational forward-modeling to rigorously distinguish true global phase gradients from spatially constrained local activity. Additionally, they are examining the interplay between these spatial wave dynamics and top-down cognition, specifically investigating how endogenous attention might trigger perceptual traveling waves during binocular rivalry. Beyond spatial propagation, their research also probes the temporal dynamics of attentional sampling, using psychophysics and reverse correlation to understand how alpha and theta rhythms periodically reshape visual sensory tuning curves over time.

papers.title: The dominance of large-scale phase dynamics in human cortex, from delta to gamma
papers.abstract: This research characterizes the spatial spectral properties of cortical phase dynamics using high-density intracranial recordings (sEEG) across a spectrum of temporal frequencies from delta to gamma. The authors introduce a spatial spectral estimation method optimized for the non-uniform sampling geometry of sEEG electrode arrays. They demonstrate that the cortical surface is dominated by large-scale phase dynamics—specifically macroscopic traveling waves characterized by low spatial frequencies—where spatial power decreases monotonically as a function of spatial frequency. These findings suggest that local neural variability is embedded within a global spatiotemporal context, highlighting macroscopic waves as a fundamental scale for cortical integration and communication.
papers.authors: David M. Alexander, Laura Dugué

papers.title: Attention-induced perceptual traveling waves in binocular rivalry
papers.abstract: Utilizing a combination of human psychophysics and computational modeling, this study investigates the mechanisms of mesoscopic traveling waves in the human visual system during binocular rivalry. The authors demonstrate that perceptual waves, typically characterized by the propagation of dominance during rivalry, can be triggered by endogenous attentional modulation in the absence of exogenous physical triggers. They present a recurrent neural network model featuring mutual inhibition and attentional gain to simulate how focal attention initiates spatiotemporal phase gradients that propagate across retinotopic space. The results support the hypothesis that the brain's internal attentional systems leverage the same canonical neural computations as stimulus-driven processes to facilitate information transfer across the cortical surface.
papers.authors: João V. X. Cardoso, Hsin-Hung Li, David J. Heeger, Laura Dugué

papers.title: Locally Induced Traveling Waves Generate Globally Observable Traveling Waves
papers.abstract: This investigation addresses the interpretation of traveling waves (TWs) observed in non-invasive M/EEG recordings, specifically whether global sensor-level phase gradients reflect true macroscopic cortical waves or result from spatially constrained local activity. By combining source-space simulations with empirical MEG and EEG data, the authors demonstrate that locally induced TWs in the visual cortex are sufficient to produce apparent global propagation across the sensor array due to volume conduction and lead-field properties. They establish a quantitative framework for distinguishing between true global macroscopic waves and mesoscopic local dynamics, concluding that extracranial measures often reflect the spatial integration of local cortical activity into seemingly large-scale patterns.
papers.authors: Kirsten Petras, Laetitia Grabot, Laura Dugué

papers.title: Traveling Waves in the Human Visual Cortex: An MEG-EEG Model-Based Approach
papers.abstract: The authors develop a model-based analytical framework to identify and characterize oscillatory traveling waves in the human visual cortex using high-density M/EEG. By integrating a traveling wave propagation model with anatomical forward-modeling of the head, they estimate wave parameters including velocity, direction, and spatial frequency directly from sensor-level signals. Applying this methodology to empirical data recorded during visual tasks, they confirm that sensory-evoked activity exhibits consistent spatiotemporal phase offsets characteristic of mesoscopic traveling waves. This study demonstrates that integrating computational models of wave propagation with non-invasive electrophysiology can successfully resolve the fine-grained spatiotemporal dynamics of the human brain.
papers.authors: Laetitia Grabot, Garance Merholz, Jonathan Winawer, David J. Heeger, Laura Dugué

papers.title: Attention Rhythmically Shapes Sensory Tuning
papers.abstract: Using a high-powered psychophysical reverse correlation paradigm, the authors analyze the temporal dynamics of how voluntary attention reconfigures sensory representations. They find that attentional benefits to performance sensitivity (d') are not continuous but fluctuate rhythmically, with alpha-band (~12 Hz) oscillations predominating during sustained focus and theta-band (~6 Hz) oscillations during exploratory behavior. Crucially, reverse correlation reveals that these behavioral rhythms are underpinned by the periodic sharpening and broadening of sensory tuning curves. These results provide evidence that attentional sampling is a discrete, rhythmic process that periodically optimizes the quality of the sensory filter rather than a continuous gain-enhancement mechanism.
papers.authors: Laurie Galas, Ian Donovan, Laura Dugué

0384.name: Laura Lewis
0384.department: Institute for Medical Engineering and Science (IMES); Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (EECS)
0384.bio: Lewis develops multimodal neuroimaging technologies to investigate the neural and physiological mechanisms governing sleep and arousal states. Their research integrates fast fMRI, electroencephalography, and computational signal processing to characterize subsecond brain dynamics and the activity of deep subcortical circuits. Lewis identified synchronized cerebrospinal fluid flow during sleep, a process that facilitates metabolic waste clearance and brain maintenance. Their current work examines how these neural and fluid dynamics are modulated by sensory inputs and how they are altered in neurological and psychiatric disorders.
