0384.research_direction: Dr. Lewis has recently been investigating the intricate physiological connections between macroscopic neural rhythms, systemic hemodynamics, and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) dynamics across sleep and wakefulness. Their recent work explores how pulsatile waves of CSF—traditionally linked to brain waste clearance during sleep—behave during acute attentional lapses in sleep-deprived individuals, and how these vital fluid oscillations are impacted by neural and vascular changes in the aging brain. To capture these complex phenomena, they are advancing multimodal neuroimaging techniques, utilizing concurrent fast fMRI and EEG to decode subsecond brain states and developing biophysical models to directly quantify CSF flow velocities. Additionally, they are probing the fundamental temporal resolution of fMRI, examining how local vascular architecture in visual cortex influences our ability to accurately measure rapid neural events.

papers.title: Attentional failures after sleep deprivation are locked to joint neurovascular, pupil and cerebrospinal fluid flow dynamics
papers.abstract: This investigation delineates the systemic coupling between cognitive performance, neurovascular signaling, and glymphatic-like fluid dynamics during acute sleep deprivation. Utilizing concurrent fast fMRI and EEG, the authors demonstrate that momentary failures of attention are strictly synchronized with a multimodal state change encompassing broadband electrophysiological shifts, autonomic pupillary constriction, and pulsatile waves of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) flow. These CSF waves, which are typically characteristic of non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep, are found to intrude into the wakeful state during periods of attentional failure. The temporal dynamics reveal that CSF is expelled from the brain at the onset of a lapse and drawn back upon behavioral recovery, suggesting that attentional costs are fundamentally tied to a unified neuromodulatory circuit governing both high-level cognition and brain-wide fluid clearance.
papers.authors: Zinong Yang, Stephanie D. Williams, Ewa Beldzik, Stephanie Anakwe, Emilia Schimmelpfennig, Laura D. Lewis

papers.title: Brainwide hemodynamics predict EEG neural rhythms across sleep and wakefulness in humans
papers.abstract: The authors present a machine learning framework to decode continuous fluctuations of neural rhythms from whole-brain hemodynamic signals. Utilizing simultaneous EEG and accelerated fMRI data, they demonstrate that the power of alpha (8–12 Hz) and delta (1–4 Hz) rhythms can be predicted in held-out subjects with high fidelity. The results identify distinct and replicable fMRI network architectures associated with each rhythm: alpha power predictions were primarily driven by specialized networks in the arousal and visual systems, while delta power reflected more diffuse cortical patterns. This work indicates that high-frequency fMRI signals contain robust information about subsecond brain states and provides a generalizable computational approach for mapping the large-scale network architecture underlying distinct electrophysiological rhythms across sleep and wakefulness.
papers.authors: Leandro P. L. Jacob, Sydney M. Bailes, Stephanie D. Williams, Carsen Stringer, Laura D. Lewis

papers.title: Modeling dynamic inflow effects in fMRI to quantify cerebrospinal fluid flow
papers.abstract: This research introduces a quantitative framework for measuring cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) flow velocities using flow-sensitive fMRI. Recognizing that conventional fMRI inflow signals are qualitatively sensitive to fluid motion but lack physical units, the authors developed a dynamic biophysical model to simulate signal intensity as a function of time-varying flow velocities and RF excitation timing. The model was validated using human data and a physical flow phantom. To facilitate velocity estimation, they implemented a physics-based deep learning inversion of the forward model. The results show that this approach enables the direct quantification of pulsatile CSF velocities from fMRI data, transforming a traditional neuroimaging contrast into a quantitative tool for studying brain waste clearance and neurofluid dynamics.
papers.authors: Baarbod Ashenagar, Daniel E. P. Gomez, Laura D. Lewis

papers.title: The aging human brain exhibits reduced cerebrospinal fluid flow during sleep due to both neural and vascular factors
papers.abstract: Utilizing simultaneous fast fMRI-EEG, this study identifies significant reductions in sleep-dependent cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) flow within the aging human brain. Comparing healthy young and older adults, the authors found that large, low-frequency CSF pulsations during NREM sleep are significantly attenuated in older individuals. This decline is attributed to a combination of neural factors—specifically the reduction of frontal EEG delta power—and vascular factors involving impaired neurovascular coupling and reduced cerebrovascular reactivity. Moreover, the magnitude of these sleep-related fluid oscillations was found to be associated with gray matter atrophy in older adults. These results identify specific neurovascular targets for interventions aimed at preserving brain waste clearance in aging and neurodegenerative disease.
papers.authors: Sydney M. Bailes, Stephanie D. Williams, Baarbod Ashenagar, Joseph Licata, Massinissa Y. Bosli, Brandon J. Dormes, Hannah J. Yun, Dabriel Zimmerman, Alejandra Hernandez Moyers, David H. Salat, Laura D. Lewis

papers.title: The temporal specificity of BOLD fMRI is systematically related to anatomical and vascular features of the human brain
papers.abstract: This study investigates the spatial variability of the temporal specificity of BOLD fMRI signals, defined as the ability to resolve rapid neural events through the hemodynamic low-pass filter. Utilizing ultra-high-field (7T) fMRI and frequency-modulated visual stimuli, the authors mapped the frequency-dependent attenuation of BOLD responses in the primary visual cortex (V1) across a range of stimulus frequencies. They found that temporal specificity is not uniform but is systematically related to the anterior-posterior anatomical axis and local vascular architecture. Specifically, voxels within the calcarine sulcus preserved significantly higher response amplitudes (25%) at fast frequencies compared to those near the occipital pole (18%). These findings emphasize the necessity of accounting for local hemodynamic heterogeneity when interpreting the timing of subsecond neural dynamics in high-resolution neuroimaging data.
papers.authors: Daniel E. P. Gomez, Jonathan R. Polimeni, Laura D. Lewis

0386.name: Laure Pisella
0386.bio: Laure Pisella is a CNRS researcher at the Lyon Neuroscience Research Center (CRNL) who studies the neural substrates of human action and perception. Pisella’s work focuses on the role of the posterior parietal cortex in visuomotor integration and the mechanisms of optic ataxia, hemispatial neglect, and Bálint syndrome. Using clinical neuropsychology, eye-tracking, and prism adaptation, they investigate how the brain processes spatial information for motor control and maintains visual stability during trans-saccadic remapping. Their current research explores the influence of aging on the distribution of spatial attention and the competitive mechanisms underlying target selection in the visual periphery.
0386.research_direction: Dr. Pisella has recently been investigating how the dorsal visual stream integrates spatial, attentional, and peripheral inputs to guide motor action, spatial cognition, and reading. Their recent work explores visuomotor transformations in peripheral vision, utilizing gaze-contingent masking and spatial cueing paradigms to examine how pointing hypometria is modulated by covert attention, visual field loss, and specialized sensorimotor expertise like juggling. In clinical contexts, they are studying the real-world impact of visual crowding and stimulus eccentricity on functional visual acuity in patients with Posterior Cortical Atrophy. Additionally, their research evaluates visuo-attentional processing in developmental populations, developing novel visual search tools to detect simultaneous visual processing deficits associated with non-phonological dyslexia.

papers.title: Attentional modulation of peripheral pointing hypometria in healthy participants: An insight into optic ataxia?
papers.abstract: This study examines the integration of attentional signals within the visuomotor transformation of peripheral targets, with a focus on the systematic gaze-centered hypometric bias observed in optic ataxia (OA). Utilizing endogenous (central predictive) and exogenous (peripheral non-predictive) cueing paradigms, the researchers evaluated the influence of covert attention on pointing accuracy and endpoint variability in healthy adults and OA patients. Experimental results demonstrated that invalid endogenous cues significantly exacerbated pointing hypometria across all participants, whereas peripheral cues failed to produce a similar modulation. The findings suggest that the positional encoding of peripheral targets relies on a spatial calibration process within the superior parietal lobule and intraparietal sulcus (SPL-IPS) that is dynamically modulated by endogenous attentional orientation, providing evidence that the hypometric reaching characteristic of OA may stem from a deficit in attentional resolution at the point of action planning.
papers.authors: Tristan Jurkiewicz, Audrey Vialatte, Yaffa Yeshurun, Laure Pisella

papers.title: Validation of a screening test based on symbols visual search to detect visuo-attentionnal reading difficulties
papers.abstract: Aiming to identify visuo-attentional (VA) dyslexia, this research validates a novel psychophysical screening instrument that assesses simultaneous visual processing capacity. The test employs a visual search paradigm requiring participants to identify symbols (defined by the conjunction of separable features) against a background of distractors, which is contrasted with simpler color-based search tasks. Cross-sectional assessment of 2,015 children aged 3–11 and a longitudinal evaluation of 769 4th and 5th graders established the 'Temporal Gap'—the efficiency of symbol processing relative to color—as a robust predictor of orthographic reading speed and accuracy. The tool demonstrates high specificity for detecting dorsal stream-mediated VA fragilities that contribute to reading impairments independent of phonological processing deficits, supporting its utility for early risk detection in neurodevelopmental diagnostics.
papers.authors: Audrey Vialatte, Eric Chabanat, Agnes Witko, Laure Pisella

papers.title: Take Caution of Normal Visual Acuity in Posterior Cortical Atrophy!
papers.abstract: This clinical investigation analyzes the diagnostic insufficiency of standard foveal acuity measures in patients presenting with Posterior Cortical Atrophy (PCA). By comparing performance on Monoyer charts (single-line presentation) versus ETDRS charts (multi-line arrays) at distances of 2 and 4 meters, the authors quantified the differential effects of visual crowding and stimulus eccentricity. Findings reveal that while PCA patients frequently maintain normal acuity on isolated-line charts, they exhibit significant functional declines when confronted with high-density visual displays or closer viewing distances. This uncommon reduction in acuity at near distances significantly correlates with higher-order visual symptom scores (Q-ACP), emphasizing the necessity of combining varied optotype conditions to prevent misdiagnosis of PCA as primary ocular pathology.
papers.authors: Tristan Jurkiewicz, Maïté Formaglio, Sarah Verrecchia, Caroline Froment, Laure Pisella

papers.title: Impact of macular scotoma and tubular vision on oculomotor behavior and performance in visuospatial comparison tasks
papers.abstract: Employing gaze-contingent masking, this study delineates the specific roles of central and peripheral vision in visuospatial cognitive tasks. Participants performed a computerized version of the Elementary Visuo-Spatial Perception (EVSP) test under conditions of simulated macular scotoma or tubular vision. The absence of macular vision significantly impaired response accuracy across all spatial subtests (midline, orientation, and magnitude) and markedly reduced within-object exploration saccades. Conversely, simulated tubular vision primarily disrupted midline bisection judgments and decreased the frequency of alternation saccades between objects. These results indicate that the dorsal visual stream relies on macular inputs for fine perceptual discrimination and on peripheral inputs for global saccadic coordination and inter-object spatial comparison.
papers.authors: Hind Drissi, Tristan Jurkiewicz, Audrey Vialatte, Aarlenne Zein Khan, Laure Pisella

papers.title: Effect of juggling expertise on pointing performance in peripheral vision
papers.abstract: This study examines the influence of high-level motor expertise on the calibration of peripheral spatial representations and the precision of visuo-guided reaching. Expert jugglers and non-experts were evaluated in an open-loop peripheral pointing task to determine if the 'third eye' phenomenon—involving continuous monitoring of ball zeniths via horizontal covert attentional shifts—induces plasticity in the posterior parietal cortex. Quantitative analysis of pointing endpoints revealed that expert jugglers demonstrated significantly reduced gaze-centered hypometria, particularly within the upper visual field, when compared to the control group. This indicates that task-specific sensorimotor training in monitoring peripheral locations leads to a vertically asymmetrical improvement in the internal spatial maps used for coordinate transformation, reducing the characteristic biases of peripheral reaching.
papers.authors: Tristan Jurkiewicz, Ludovic Delporte, Patrice Revol, Yves Rossetti, Laure Pisella

0387.name: Laurence Harris
0387.bio: Laurence R. Harris is a Professor of Psychology and Director of the Multisensory Integration Laboratory at York University and conducts research within the Centre for Vision Research. Their research investigates how the brain synthesizes visual, vestibular, and somatosensory information to maintain a sense of self-motion, body orientation, and the "perceptual upright." Employing methodologies such as virtual reality, parabolic flights for microgravity simulation, and specialized apparatuses like the "Tumbling Room," Harris explores human adaptation to unusual gravitational and sensory environments. Their work extends to the temporal aspects of perception, examining how the brain synchronizes disparate sensory signals to create a unified experience of the world.
0387.research_direction: Dr. Harris has recently been investigating how the human brain integrates visual, vestibular, and gravitational cues to perceive spatial dimensions, self-motion, and the dynamics of the external world. Their recent work explores the pervasive influence of our internal model of gravity, using virtual reality, postural manipulations, and galvanic vestibular stimulation to determine how real-time gravito-inertial signals impact both the prediction of parabolic object trajectories and the perceived height of static objects. They are also probing the mechanisms of self-motion and orientation by applying continuous psychophysics to track the temporal dynamics of heading perception from optic flow, and by investigating whether visually simulated linear acceleration can induce an illusory sensation of body tilt. Additionally, their research systematically re-evaluates classic visual-oculomotor phenomena, utilizing modern psychophysical paradigms to test whether smooth pursuit eye movements genuinely alter perceived stimulus velocity in the Aubert-Fleischl effect.

papers.title: Evidence for a Vestibular Contribution to Object Motion Prediction
papers.abstract: This study investigates whether the human capability for predicting object motion in accordance with gravity relies on an internalized prior or real-time vestibular signals. Utilizing virtual reality to dissociate visual up from physical gravity, participants predicted the time-to-contact of ball stimuli following parabolic trajectories under simulated earth-normal (1g) and inverted (-1g) gravities. By testing subjects in upright and supine postures—the latter of which reorients the otolith organs relative to gravity—and employing disruptive galvanic vestibular stimulation (dGVS), the research demonstrated that altering vestibular input significantly increases estimated arrival times. These findings indicate that vestibular information regarding instantaneous body orientation is a critical component in the internal modeling of gravity-contingent object dynamics.
papers.authors: Björn Jörges, Laurence R. Harris

papers.title: Failure to Replicate the Aubert-Fleischl Effect
papers.abstract: The Aubert-Fleischl effect, a classic psychophysical observation where an object's velocity is perceived as slower during smooth pursuit than during fixation, was systematically re-examined using a modern speed discrimination paradigm. Participants compared the speed of a sphere cloud during active pursuit and gaze fixation. Across multiple experiments, the results failed to demonstrate the expected underestimation of speed during pursuit, with calculated points of subjective equality (PSEs) showing no significant difference between conditions. The study suggests that the effect may not be a fundamental property of the visual-vestibular-oculomotor system but rather a phenomenon sensitive to specific stimulus parameters such as dot density, peripheral cues, and experimental context.
papers.authors: Björn Jörges, Laurence R. Harris

papers.title: Can Visual Acceleration evoke a sensation of tilt?
papers.abstract: Applying Einstein’s equivalence principle to multisensory integration, this research explores whether visually simulated linear acceleration (linear vection) can be misinterpreted by the brain as a change in the gravito-inertial force vector, thereby inducing a perceived body tilt. Observers in a virtual reality environment were subjected to interaural visual acceleration while their perceived verticality was measured using the Ocular-Centric Rod and Frame Test (OCRFT) and subjective reports. The data confirm that visual acceleration signals can indeed evoke a sensation of tilt, indicating that visual self-motion cues are integrated into the central estimation of the direction of gravity, consistent with a Bayesian framework for orientation perception.
papers.authors: Björn Jörges, Nils-Alexander Bury, Meaghan McManus, Ambika Bansal, Robert S. Allison, Michael Jenkin, Laurence R. Harris

papers.title: Precision and Temporal Dynamics in Heading Perception Assessed by Continuous Psychophysics
papers.abstract: This research utilizes continuous psychophysics to quantify the temporal resolution and precision of heading estimation from visual optic flow. Participants continuously adjusted a joystick to track their perceived direction of self-motion within a 3D dot cloud that simulated varying headings over time. System identification techniques and cross-correlation analysis were applied to derive the sensorimotor latency and gain of the tracking response. The results indicate that the human visual system possesses a high-fidelity mechanism for estimating heading that can rapidly adapt to changes in optic flow, although the gain and precision are constrained by the temporal integration windows of the underlying neural circuits.
papers.authors: Björn Jörges, Ambika Bansal, Laurence R. Harris

papers.title: The Impact of Gravity on Perceived Object Height
papers.abstract: The study examines how the perception of an object's spatial dimensions, specifically vertical height, is modulated by the internal model of gravity. Using head-mounted displays to present virtual cylinders, participants performed height-judgment tasks while either standing upright or lying supine. The results showed that the perceived size of static objects is significantly biased by the direction of gravity acting on the observer's body. These systematic distortions suggest that the brain's representation of Earth's gravity serves as a pervasive spatial reference frame that scales environmental proportions, extending beyond its known role in dynamic motor control to fundamental aspects of static spatial vision.
papers.authors: Björn Jörges, Nils-Alexander Bury, Meaghan McManus, Ambika Bansal, Robert S. Allison, Michael Jenkin, Laurence R. Harris

0388.name: Laurent Madelain
0388.bio: Laurent Madelain is a Professor of Psychology at the University of Lille and serves as the Deputy Director of the SCALab research unit. Madelain’s research focuses on the operant control of human eye movements, specifically investigating how saccades and smooth pursuit are modulated by their consequences rather than acting solely as reflexive responses. Utilizing psychophysical methodologies and reinforcement paradigms, they explore the mechanisms through which motor patterns emerge from environmental contingencies and biological constraints. Madelain's current work examines the role of motor planning in contextual adaptation and the influence of reinforcement on sensorimotor variability and active vision.
0388.research_direction: Dr. Madelain has recently been investigating the plasticity and control of the oculomotor system, with a major focus on the mechanisms of saccadic adaptation. Their recent work explores how reactive saccades adapt to non-visual stimuli like auditory and tactile targets using double-step paradigms, specifically probing the rules of cross-modal transfer between vision and other senses, as well as testing which spatial or perceptual cues can effectively trigger contextual adaptation. Beyond sensorimotor recalibration, they are applying operant conditioning frameworks to study oculomotor decision-making, developing computational models to determine how reinforcement contingencies shape saccadic reaction time distributions. Additionally, Dr. Madelain is studying the mechanisms of eye guidance during natural reading, using real-time parafoveal magnification paradigms to investigate whether the perceptual span is fundamentally constrained by peripheral visual acuity drop-offs or central attentional limitations.

papers.title: Saccades adapt to visual and auditory stepping targets and display an asymmetrical pattern of cross-modal transfer
papers.abstract: This study investigated the cross-modal plasticity of reactive saccades by assessing the transfer of adaptation between visual and auditory modalities. Using a stepping-target paradigm, the authors demonstrated that saccadic gain can be adaptively modified in response to auditory target displacements, indicating that auditory-guided eye movements utilize plastic mechanisms similar to visual-reactive saccades. However, the study revealed a pronounced asymmetry in cross-modal transfer: adaptation induced by visual errors transferred extensively to auditory-reactive saccades, whereas auditory-induced adaptation showed negligible transfer to the visual domain. These findings imply that saccadic adaptation occurs at a sensorimotor stage where visual and auditory processing converge, yet the visual adaptive signals exert a broader influence on the oculomotor plant's generalized motor commands.
papers.authors: Ali Batikh, Valérie Gaveau, Muriel Panouillères-Moindrot, Denis Pélisson, Laurent Madelain

papers.title: Ineffective cues for contextual saccade adaptation
papers.abstract: This study evaluated the efficacy of nine distinct contextual cues—including first-step amplitude, starting location, target color, target shape, stimulus duration, auditory lateralization, symbolic indicators, and trial-sequence regularities—in driving contextual saccade adaptation via a modified double-step paradigm. While spatially relevant motor-related cues, such as the amplitude of the initial target displacement and the gaze-starting position, successfully induced simultaneous adaptation states for opposing intra-saccadic steps, purely perceptual cues failed to elicit significant gains. Notably, participants exhibited a functional dissociation, demonstrating high accuracy in explicitly reporting non-motor cues while remaining unable to utilize this information for sensorimotor adaptation. These results underscore selective constraints on oculomotor learning that prioritize motor-linked spatial cues over explicit perceptual awareness.
papers.authors: Maxime Martel, Laurent Madelain

papers.title: Parafoveal magnification visual acuity does not modulate the perceptual span in reading
papers.abstract: This research addressed whether the spatial extent of the perceptual span in reading is determined by the decline in visual acuity with retinal eccentricity or by attentional resource allocation. A parafoveal magnification (PM) paradigm was employed to compensate for acuity drop-off by magnifying text in the parafovea in real-time, equalizing the visibility of text across the visual field. Despite the enhanced visibility of parafoveal information, indices of reading performance—including fixation durations, saccadic amplitudes, and overall reading rates—remained stable compared to control conditions. The failure of PM to expand the perceptual span supports an attention-limited account of eye guidance in reading, indicating that the processing rate of visual information is constrained by central attentional capacities rather than peripheral sensory limitations.
papers.authors: Vasiliki Myrodia, Kevin B. Paterson, Timothy R. Jordan, Laurent Madelain

papers.title: Sensorimotor adaptation of reactive saccades to tactile targets and its transfer to visual targets
papers.abstract: To determine the locus of saccadic adaptation, this study investigated the adaptive control of eye movements directed toward tactile targets (vibrations on the participant's hand) and measured cross-modal transfer to visual saccades. Participants underwent a double-step adaptation protocol where tactile target locations were surreptitiously shifted during the saccade. Results indicated robust sensorimotor adaptation of tactile reactive saccades. Crucially, tactile-induced adaptation showed complete transfer to visual saccades of equivalent vectors, whereas visual-induced adaptation exhibited only partial transfer to the tactile modality. This significant transfer from a non-visual modality to the visual system provides evidence that saccadic adaptation is not exclusively a retinal-error-driven process but involves recalibration at an upstream sensorimotor stage where multisensory inputs are integrated into motor programs.
papers.authors: Ali Batikh, Valérie Gaveau, Eric Koun, Romeo Salemme, Alessandro Farnè, Denis Pélisson, Laurent Madelain

papers.title: Predicting changes in saccade latency distributions in a choice paradigm: A contingency discrimination model
papers.abstract: This study applied an operant framework to the study of saccadic reaction times (SRTs), probing whether the temporal allocation of saccades is governed by reinforcement contingencies. Participants performed a gaze-contingent choice task where SRTs were reinforced according to concurrent random-interval schedules. The authors developed the Contingency Discrimination Model (CDM), which predicts SRT distribution shifts based on the relative discriminability and payoff of different latency intervals. Experimental results showed that SRT distributions shifted systematically in accordance with the reinforcement rates, demonstrating that the oculomotor system dynamically adjusts response timing to maximize utility. The CDM successfully accounted for the observed variability and distribution shapes, supporting the view that saccadic initiation is a decisional process under the control of learned environmental regularities.
papers.authors: Raphaëlle Radenne, Laurent Madelain

0389.name: Laurie M. Wilcox
0389.department: Department of Psychology, Faculty of Health
0389.bio: Laurie M. Wilcox is a Professor in the Department of Psychology at York University and a core member of the Centre for Vision Research. As the York Research Chair in 3D Vision, Wilcox investigates the neural mechanisms underlying stereoscopic depth perception and surface interpolation using psychophysical methodologies. Their research addresses the role of disparity in 3D shape perception, the integration of depth cues in complex environments, and the evaluation of image quality in stereoscopic displays. Wilcox also serves as the Scientific Director of the Vision: Science to Applications (VISTA) program.
0389.research_direction: Dr. Wilcox has recently been investigating spatial perception and the integration of 3D depth cues, with a major focus on how these mechanisms operate within augmented and virtual reality environments. Their recent work explores how the visual system weighs ordinal monocular cues, such as occlusion, against metric binocular disparity when estimating egocentric distance, 3D surface relief, and object size. Using psychophysical methods alongside optical and video see-through head-mounted displays, they are systematically evaluating the perceptual conflicts and geometric distortions that arise from technological limitations, such as camera-eye misalignments and the improper rendering of physical occluders. Additionally, they have been applying this expertise in depth perception to aviation safety, utilizing high-fidelity flight simulators to investigate how individual differences in spatial cognition impact a pilot's susceptibility to dangerous distance and altitude misperceptions like the "black hole" illusion.

papers.title: Misperception of the distance of virtual augmentations
papers.abstract: The research investigates the integration of binocular disparity and monocular occlusion cues within augmented reality (AR) environments. The study specifically addresses the depth cue conflict that arises when virtual content is rendered at distances beyond a physical occluder but remains visible. Through a series of distance-matching psychophysical experiments conducted both within reach space (0.35–0.5 m) and beyond reach space (0.9–1.5 m), the authors quantify perceptual biases. Results indicate a consistent and significant underestimation of the egocentric distance of virtual targets when rendered beyond a physical surface. This underestimation error was found to be proportional to the target distance and persisted even when proprioceptive and reach-based feedback was provided, demonstrating that the ordinal information provided by occlusion dominates metric disparity signals in AR depth perception.
papers.venue: 2025 IEEE Conference on Virtual Reality and 3D User Interfaces (VR)
papers.authors: Domenic Au, Robert S. Allison, Iroshini Gunasekera, Laurie M. Wilcox

papers.title: The Role of Depth Cues in 3D Size Judgements
papers.abstract: This study evaluates how human observers integrate monocular and binocular depth cues to determine the perceived 3D size and relief of objects. Using naturalistic virtual environments, the researchers measured perceptual thresholds (Just Noticeable Differences, JNDs) and points of subjective stationarity (PSS) across different viewing conditions. The experiments were designed to test whether the visual system exhibits depth constancy by compensating for changes in viewing distance when determining shape and size. The results suggest that while stereopsis contributes significantly to the perception of surface relief in near space, size judgments for complex 3D shapes are heavily influenced by monocular pictorial cues as distance increases, leading to systematic distortions in perceived object volume when metric cues are limited or in conflict.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the 2025 ACM Symposium on Applied Perception (SAP)
papers.authors: Iroshini Gunasekera, Romina Abadi, Faruq Afolabi, Xue Teng, Robert S. Allison, Laurie M. Wilcox

papers.title: Occlusion Effects on Action Space Distance Perception in Augmented Reality
papers.abstract: This investigation examines the influence of simulated occlusion on the perception of absolute distance within the action space (defined as the region within 1.5 meters of the observer). Using an optical see-through head-mounted display (OST-HMD), the researchers manipulated the visibility of virtual objects relative to real-world occluders. The study quantifies how the absence of expected physical occlusion—a common limitation in current AR systems—distorts egocentric distance estimates. Quantitative analysis reveals that observers rely more heavily on ordinal depth cues than on metric binocular disparity when estimating distance in cluttered scenes. The findings underscore the critical role of correct occlusion rendering for maintaining spatial accuracy and facilitating natural user interactions in immersive AR applications.
papers.venue: ACM Symposium on Virtual Reality Software and Technology (VRST)
papers.authors: Iroshini Gunasekera, Romina Abadi, Faruq Afolabi, Xue Teng, Robert S. Allison, Laurie M. Wilcox

papers.title: Visual Illusions in Aviation: Simulating the Black Hole Phenomenon
papers.abstract: This research utilizes a high-fidelity flight simulator to investigate the 'black hole' illusion—a dangerous spatial disorientation phenomenon where pilots misperceive altitude and distance during night approaches. The study evaluates the effectiveness of a Level 2 Instrument Proficiency Check training device in eliciting this illusion and examines the role of individual differences, specifically gender and mental rotation ability, in susceptibility. Experimental data show that pilots frequently make shallow final approaches during simulated night flights compared to day flights, indicating a systematic altitude error. Critically, the study found that lower mental rotation scores were predictive of higher susceptibility to the illusion, and that traditional flight experience did not significantly mitigate the perceptual errors. The findings advocate for the inclusion of simulator-based training protocols to enhance pilot awareness of depth-related visual illusions.
papers.venue: Human Factors: The Journal of the Human Factors and Ergonomics Society
papers.authors: Arleen Aksay, Brittney Hartle, Robert S. Allison, Laurie M. Wilcox

papers.title: Geometric distortion on video see-through head-mounted displays
papers.abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive metrological framework for measuring and analyzing geometric distortions in video see-through (VST) head-mounted displays. The authors develop an experimental setup using inward-facing light-measuring devices and outward-facing cameras to compare digital distortions introduced by HMD optics with the geometric deviations present in the passthrough video content. The study investigates how camera misalignment relative to the observer's eye center (IPD mismatch) and depth distance in the 3D scene contribute to perceived spatial inaccuracies. Findings indicate that a dual-camera configuration is essential to minimize VST geometric distortion, as single-camera systems inherently fail to provide accurate perspective at multiple depth planes. The methodology provides a standardized approach for evaluating image quality and spatial fidelity in medical and industrial AR headsets.
papers.venue: Journal of the Society for Information Display (JSID)
papers.authors: Iroshini Gunasekera, Romina Abadi, Faruq Afolabi, Xue Teng, Robert S. Allison, Laurie M. Wilcox

0390.name: Leslie Carver
0390.bio: Leslie J. Carver is a Professor at UC San Diego who investigates the neural mechanisms underlying social cognition, memory, and reward processing during early development. Carver’s research utilizes event-related potentials (ERP) and longitudinal behavioral paradigms to study typically developing infants as well as those with or at risk for Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD). They focus on identifying neurophysiological markers of joint attention and predictive coding to evaluate the social motivation hypothesis and understand how early brain function shapes social trajectories.
0390.research_direction: Dr. Carver has recently been investigating the early development of infant perceptual and social-communicative processes, with a dual focus on multisensory integration and joint attention. Their recent work explores how young infants use dynamic visual motion trajectories to predict the precise timing of auditory consequences, employing remote looking-time paradigms to probe early intuitive physical reasoning about collision events. Additionally, they have been examining the developmental dynamics of shared focus in infants at an elevated familial likelihood for autism spectrum disorder. By applying high-density behavioral coding to naturalistic video recordings of caregiver-infant play, Dr. Carver investigates how these dyads utilize specific sensorimotor cues—such as face-following versus manual hand-following pathways—to successfully coordinate joint visual attention. Ultimately, their research seeks to uncover how subtle variations in early infant motor and perceptual systems might cascade into altered parent-infant social scaffolding and coordination.

papers.title: Infants Anticipate the Timing of Sounds From Dynamic Collision Events
papers.abstract: Dynamic visual motion regularly provides predictive sensory evidence that allows observers to forecast ensuing auditory consequences. This study examined whether infants between 4 and 5 months of age possess intuitive physical event representations enabling them to utilize dynamic visual trajectories to predict the precise temporal onset of collision sounds. In a moderated remote testing paradigm, looking times were assessed across two infant groups presented with an animated two-dimensional disk colliding with a barrier. One cohort observed alternating multimodal conditions manipulating audiovisual (AV) temporal congruence: an AV-synchronous condition where the auditory transient coincided with physical contact, and an AV-asynchronous condition where the auditory transient preceded collision. A second cohort viewed amodal visual control conditions in which the disk altered color either synchronously at barrier contact (visual color change; VCC synchronous) or asynchronously prior to contact (VCC asynchronous). Offline behavioral coding of looking times demonstrated that infants exhibited significantly increased fixation duration toward AV-asynchronous relative to AV-synchronous trials. This looking-time divergence was absent in the visual-only color-change control conditions. Additionally, infants displayed significantly longer looking times during AV-asynchronous events than during VCC-asynchronous events. These findings reveal that 4- to 5-month-old infants formulate precise temporal expectations regarding the alignment of kinematic collisions and resulting sounds, indicating that early crossmodal predictive frameworks operate to scaffold physical reasoning within multisensory environments.
papers.authors: Andrew Marin, Zara Fearns, Melanie Dratva, Lindsey J. Powell, Viola S. Störmer, Leslie J. Carver

papers.title: Parent-infant coordination of attention during object play in infants at elevated and low likelihood for autism
papers.abstract: This longitudinal investigation quantified the behavioral dynamics of joint attention (JA) using naturalistic video recordings of 9- to 12-month-old infants at high (FH+) and low (FH-) familial likelihood for autism spectrum disorder. By employing high-density offline coding of gaze and manual actions during home-based play, the study examined the sensory-motor pathways preceding the establishment of shared focus. Results indicated that while FH+ and FH- infant-parent dyads achieved comparable total durations of joint attention, the communicative cues utilized to reach coordination differed significantly. Parents of FH+ infants demonstrated an increased reliance on face-following pathways and engaged in more intensive monitoring behaviors to facilitate shared attention, suggesting that caregiver behavioral adaptations emerge in early infancy to compensate for subtle differences in infant motor or social engagement before formal diagnostic markers are evident.
papers.authors: Lauren M. Smith, Julia Yurkovic-Harding, Leslie J. Carver

papers.title: Multimodal pathways to joint attention in infants with a familial history of autism
papers.abstract: Joint attention (JA) is a foundational socio-communicative behavior emerging early in ontogeny that allows infants and adult caregivers to coordinate shared focus on an external referent. While disruptions in JA mediated by face-following pathways represent an early behavioral marker of autism spectrum disorder (ASD) detectable by 12 months, emerging evidence demonstrates that JA can also be successfully established via manual and hand-following pathways. This study examined the developmental dynamics of multimodal JA pathways in 6-, 9-, and 12-month-old infants with (FH+) and without (FH-) an elevated familial likelihood of ASD. Naturalistic caregiver-infant play interactions were recorded remotely in domestic settings and subjected to fine-grained offline behavioral coding of gaze directions and manual actions. The total cumulative duration of time spent in coordinated JA did not significantly differ between FH+ and FH- dyads. However, significant group differences emerged in the preparatory cues preceding JA episodes: caregivers of FH+ infants engaged in greater scaffolding behavior to establish triadic attention and relied more heavily on face-following than hand-following pathways relative to caregivers of FH- infants. These findings indicate that underlying infant motoric and sensorimotor variations alter the structure of multimodal interactive cues, suggesting that early motor differences can cascade into altered parent-infant social coordination.
papers.authors: Lauren M. Smith, Julia Yurkovic-Harding, Leslie J. Carver

0391.name: Leyla Isik
0391.lab_name: Isik JHU Computational Cognitive Neuroscience Lab
0391.bio: Leyla Isik is the Clare Boothe Luce Assistant Professor of Cognitive Science at Johns Hopkins University and directs a research program on the neural and computational basis of social vision. Isik's work examines how the human brain converts visual input into social representations, including the recognition of actions and complex social interactions. They employ a multi-disciplinary approach involving human neuroimaging with fMRI and MEG, behavioral psychophysics, and computational modeling such as deep neural networks and graph-based AI. Current research directions include studying the development of social perception in neurotypical and autistic populations and creating artificial intelligence systems designed to emulate human social intelligence.
0391.research_direction: Dr. Isik has recently been investigating the neural and computational mechanisms of high-level visual perception, focusing primarily on how the human brain processes faces and dynamic social interactions. Their recent work explores the functional architecture of the lateral visual stream, utilizing naturalistic movie viewing, fMRI-EEG fusion, and voxel-wise encoding to map the spatiotemporal hierarchy and early childhood development of social perception in regions like the superior temporal sulcus. To understand the precise computations driving these abilities, they are evaluating whether deep generative models utilize disentangled representations for face processing, and whether graph-based models tracking relational cues like gaze and physical contact can capture complex social scene understanding. Furthermore, they are systematically benchmarking hundreds of deep learning architectures against human neuroimaging and behavioral data to identify representational gaps between current artificial intelligence systems and dynamic human social vision.

papers.title: Early Neural Development of Social Interaction Perception: Evidence from Voxel-Wise Encoding in Young Children and Adults
papers.abstract: This study employs fMRI and voxel-wise encoding models to characterize the cortical maturation of social interaction perception in a developmental cohort of 122 children (ages 3–12) and 33 adults during naturalistic movie viewing. The movie was annotated with spatiotemporal features and high-level social categories, including motion energy, face presence, social interactions, and Theory of Mind (ToM) events. Results demonstrate that encoding models based on both low-level visual and high-level social features accurately predict brain activity in children as young as 3 years old. Crucially, social interaction representations in the superior temporal sulcus (STS) were found to be present early in childhood and attained adult-like functional profiles by age 7. These findings suggest that the specialized neural architecture for third-party social interaction perception develops rapidly and concurrently with basic visual systems like motion and face processing.
papers.authors: Elizabeth Jiwon Im, Angira Shirahatti, Leyla Isik

papers.title: Modeling dynamic social vision highlights gaps between deep learning and humans
papers.abstract: This research benchmarks over 350 deep learning architectures—including image, video, and language-aligned models—against human behavioral ratings and fMRI responses to naturalistic videos of complex multi-agent social interactions. While state-of-the-art vision models reach the noise ceiling in predicting ventral stream responses and low-level scene features, they exhibit significant deficiencies in matching human social interaction judgments and neural activity within the lateral visual stream. Although video-based models show an advantage in mid-level lateral regions and language models (leveraging human-annotated captions) better align with behavioral ratings, all tested models fail to capture the neural representations of dynamic social vision. The results identify a substantial representational gap in AI's ability to model the hierarchical processing and abstract representations required for dynamic social perception.
papers.authors: Kathy Garcia, Emalie McMahon, Colin Conwell, Michael F. Bonner, Leyla Isik

papers.title: Relational Information Predicts Human Behavior and Neural Responses to Complex Social Scenes
papers.abstract: Tracking relational visual cues is essential for human social scene understanding, yet these cues are often underutilized in computational models. This study evaluates two graph-based models—SocialGNN and RNN Edge—that explicitly incorporate relational signals such as gaze direction and physical contact. Benchmarking these models against human behavioral ratings and fMRI data from naturalistic and animated stimuli (PHASE dataset), the authors found that both models effectively predict social interaction judgments. Notably, the simplified RNN Edge model, which processes only relational temporal edges without node features, achieved performance comparable to much larger state-of-the-art vision transformers. Neurally, these relational models significantly outperformed node-centric models in predicting responses in the superior temporal sulcus (STS), providing evidence that the STS primarily represents structured relational information during social perception.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the Annual Meeting of the Cognitive Science Society
papers.authors: Wenshuo Qin, Manasi Malik, Leyla Isik

papers.title: A spatiotemporal hierarchy for social interaction perception in the lateral visual stream
papers.abstract: To characterize the spatiotemporal dynamics of social interaction perception, this study employs a regression-based fusion of fMRI and EEG data recorded during naturalistic movie viewing. The results delineate a functional hierarchy in the lateral visual stream, where posterior regions in the lateral occipitotemporal cortex (LOTC) process mid-level social action features and anterior regions in the superior temporal sulcus (STS) process increasingly abstract social content. Unlike the ventral stream's strict sequential processing, the lateral stream displays rapid, concurrent representation of both mid- and high-level features in anterior regions, with latencies consistent with rapid hierarchical computation. This study provides a comprehensive spatiotemporal map of the lateral social stream, suggesting it is optimized for high-speed, parallel processing of dynamic social relations.
papers.authors: Emalie McMahon, Elizabeth Jiwon Im, Michael F. Bonner, Leyla Isik

papers.title: Disentangled deep generative models reveal coding principles of the human face processing network
papers.abstract: This study investigates the computational principles of the human face processing network by testing the hypothesis that it employs a disentangled representation. Using deep generative models (Beta-VAE) to learn latent axes of variation from face images, the authors compared these representations to fMRI activity in the Occipital Face Area (OFA) and Fusiform Face Area (FFA). Encoding models based on disentangled latent variables significantly outperformed entangled ones, revealing that neural populations in the face network align with specific, statistically independent axes of facial variation. These results suggest that disentanglement serves as an organizing principle for high-level visual representations, enabling the brain to encode complex category-specific information through a structured and interpretable latent space.
papers.authors: Paul Soulos, Jean Daunizeau, Leyla Isik

0392.name: Li Zhaoping
0392.department: Werner Reichardt Centre for Integrative Neuroscience (CIN)
0392.bio: Li is a professor at the University of Tübingen and a department head at the Max Planck Institute for Biological Cybernetics. Li developed the V1 Saliency Hypothesis (V1SH), which posits that the primary visual cortex creates a bottom-up saliency map to guide exogenous visual attention. Their current research focuses on the Central-peripheral Dichotomy (CPD) theory, exploring how the brain manages an information bottleneck by specializing peripheral vision for gaze selection and central vision for object recognition. Li’s methodology integrates theoretical modeling with experimental techniques, including human psychophysics, fMRI, and electrophysiology in multiple species.
0392.research_direction: Dr. Zhaoping has recently been investigating the functional and neuroanatomical architecture of the visual system, with a major focus on the Central-Peripheral Dichotomy that distinguishes top-down foveal "seeing" from bottom-up peripheral "looking." Using a combination of psychophysical paradigms—such as trans-saccadic integration tasks and the reversed depth illusion—alongside clinical case studies of macular degeneration, their recent work explores the spatial constraints and temporal delays of recurrent feedback during object recognition and saccade targeting. To understand the neural implementation of these mechanisms, they are also examining how the conduction velocity of horizontal intracortical axons in primate V1 scales with distance to computationally synchronize contextual signals for the bottom-up saliency map. Additionally, their theoretical research extends the efficient coding principle to multisensory integration, modeling how cortical neurons might dynamically adapt their tuning to efficiently decorrelate complex, multi-source sensory inputs.

papers.title: Conduction velocity of intracortical axons in monkey primary visual cortex grows with distance: implications for computation
papers.abstract: This research investigates the neuroanatomical and physiological scaling of conduction velocities in horizontal intracortical axons within the primate primary visual cortex (V1). It addresses how these axons facilitate contextual modulations across spatially disparate classical receptive fields to integrate global scene properties. The work demonstrates that axonal conduction velocity is not fixed but increases with projection distance. This distance-dependent scaling is hypothesized to be a critical computational requirement for synchronizing the temporal arrival of contextual signals across multiple spatial scales, thereby maintaining the temporal coherence necessary for the V1 saliency map and subsequent visual inference tasks.
papers.authors: Li Zhaoping

papers.title: Testing the top-down feedback in the central visual field using the reversed depth illusion
papers.abstract: This study employs a psychophysical paradigm centered on the 'reversed depth illusion' in random-dot stereograms (RDSs) to evaluate the speed and efficacy of top-down feedback in foveal vision. In this illusion, contrast-reversing one eye's image causes a depth perception that is anti-correlated with the physical disparity due to initial feedforward V1 responses. By manipulating stimulus duration and signal-to-noise ratios, the author quantifies the temporal accumulation required for higher-level priors to overwrite the erroneous feedforward signal. The results indicate that even in the central visual field, corrective top-down feedback incurs a significant delay, supporting the Central-Peripheral Dichotomy (CPD) theory regarding the differential distribution of recurrent processing across the visual field.
papers.authors: Li Zhaoping

papers.title: Trans-saccadic integration for object recognition peters out with pre-saccadic object eccentricity as target-directed saccades become more saliency-driven
papers.abstract: The authors investigate the spatial constraints of trans-saccadic integration (TSI) during object recognition. Through a series of psychophysical experiments, they demonstrate that the performance benefit gained from integrating pre- and post-saccadic visual information decreases as the pre-saccadic eccentricity of the target increases. This attenuation in TSI is linked to the functional transition in oculomotor control: whereas saccades to central targets are guided by top-down task goals, those to more peripheral targets are increasingly dominated by bottom-up saliency signals generated in V1. These findings provide evidence that the mechanisms for high-fidelity trans-saccadic evidence accumulation are spatially bounded by the shift between the 'seeing' system of the fovea and the 'looking' system of the periphery.
papers.authors: Junhao Liang, Li Zhaoping

papers.title: Applying the efficient coding principle to understand encoding of multisensory and multimodality sensory signals
papers.abstract: This theoretical work extends the efficient coding (Infomax) principle—previously applied to monocular and binocular signal decorrelation in the retina and V1—to the broader problem of multisensory and multimodal integration. The proposed framework treats congruent and opposite sensory signals as independent, decorrelated components that optimize the information-theoretic representation of multi-source inputs. The model predicts specific neural tuning characteristics, such as the observed broader tuning widths in 'opposite' neurons compared to 'congruent' neurons in cortical areas MT and MST. It further explains how neural receptive fields dynamically adapt to the statistical regularities of sensory environments to provide a robust, general-purpose representation for subsequent object segmentation.
papers.authors: Li Zhaoping

papers.title: Looking with or without seeing in an individual with age-related macular degeneration impairing central vision
papers.abstract: This case study examines the functional partitioning of gaze guidance and perceptual recognition in a patient with age-related macular degeneration (AMD) that eliminated central vision. Consistent with the Central-Peripheral Dichotomy (CPD) theory, the patient remained capable of performing saliency-driven saccades to peripheral targets using the V1-mediated bottom-up saliency map ('looking'). However, the absence of a functional fovea prevented the recruitment of top-down feedback required for complex object recognition ('seeing'). The results provide clinical support for the hypothesis that peripheral vision is evolutionarily optimized for gaze targeting rather than high-fidelity visual decoding, highlighting the specialized role of V1 in guiding attention even in the absence of central vision.
papers.authors: Li Zhaoping

0393.name: Liad Mudrik
0393.department: School of Psychological Sciences and Sagol School of Neuroscience
0393.bio: Liad Mudrik is a researcher at Tel Aviv University who investigates the neural substrates and functional roles of conscious experience. Mudrik utilizes adversarial collaborations to compare theories of consciousness, such as Global Neuronal Workspace and Integrated Information Theory. Using psychophysics, EEG, and augmented reality, they explore how semantic knowledge shapes perception and whether consciousness is required for complex information integration and volition. Mudrik’s background in neuroscience and philosophy informs their work on the mind-body problem and the limits of unconscious processing.
0393.research_direction: Dr. Mudrik's recent work explores the boundaries of conscious awareness, with a strong focus on refining the methodological rigor of unconscious processing research. They have recently been developing novel psychophysical calibration methods to accurately estimate participant-specific subliminal thresholds, evaluating how trial-by-trial awareness reporting impacts unconscious response priming, and building large-scale meta-scientific databases to track how different visual suppression paradigms influence empirical outcomes. Beyond subliminal perception, their research investigates the cognitive penetrability of vision by probing whether high-level semantic priming can bi-directionally modulate low-level perceptual integration, such as the formation of illusory contours in the Kanizsa illusion. Additionally, they are examining the broader epistemological challenges of consciousness science, evaluating philosophical frameworks for attributing subjective experience to non-standard entities like artificial intelligence, animals, and neural organoids.

papers.title: The Subliminal Threshold Estimation Procedure (STEP): A calibration method tailored for estimating subliminal thresholds
papers.abstract: The empirical study of unconscious processing requires a precise balance between effective stimulus suppression and the preservation of sufficient signal strength to maintain sensitivity. Traditional psychophysical calibration methods, such as fixed-step staircases, are typically not optimized for identifying the 'upper subliminal threshold'—the maximal intensity at which a stimulus remains below the threshold of awareness for an individual. We introduce the Subliminal Threshold Estimation Procedure (STEP), a novel calibration framework designed to rigorously estimate these participant-specific thresholds. Computational simulations demonstrate that STEP markedly outperforms existing methodologies, which often exhibit significant threshold estimation error and low accuracy. Empirical validation across three experiments confirms STEP's utility in refining the methodological rigor of subliminal processing paradigms and establishing reliable conditions for the study of unconscious cognition.
papers.authors: Eden Elbaz, Itay Yaron, Liad Mudrik

papers.title: Training can enhance unconscious response priming on fast trials even when measuring consciousness on a trial-by-trial basis
papers.abstract: Assessing awareness through concurrent trial-by-trial reports can introduce a multi-tasking cost that potentially obscures subliminal effects in reaction time (RT) data. We investigated whether this interference can be mitigated through task familiarity and training across two experimental sessions. Participants were categorized into groups providing either offline (post-test) or online (per-trial) awareness reports. Initial results revealed significant RT delays in the online group, indicating a substantial multi-task cost; however, this cost was notably reduced following session-based training. Critically, we observed robust unconscious response priming specifically in rapid-RT trials, and the magnitude of this effect was enhanced by training. These findings suggest that while trial-by-trial awareness probes initially introduce task-switching noise, their disruptive influence on subliminal processing can be recovered through habituation to the reporting requirements.
papers.authors: Shai Fischer, Ofer Kahane, Amir Tal, Liad Mudrik

papers.title: The UnconTrust database for studies of unconscious semantic processing and attentional allocation
papers.abstract: The extent and robustness of unconscious processing remain highly contentious in cognitive science, largely due to significant methodological heterogeneity across published studies. We present the UnconTrust database, a systematic meta-scientific repository cataloging the paradigms, awareness measures, and outcomes of 426 experiments focused on unconscious semantic and attentional processing. This structured dataset enables researchers to evaluate how specific methodological parameters—such as suppression techniques (e.g., visual masking, continuous flash suppression) and types of statistical analysis—influence the reported findings. Accompanied by an interactive visualization platform, UnconTrust facilitates large-scale evidence synthesis and helps identify methodological sources of theoretical consensus versus empirical conflict in the field of subliminal cognition.
papers.authors: Maor Schreiber, Francois Stockart, Liad Mudrik

papers.title: Semantic priming modulates the strength and direction of the Kanizsa illusion
papers.abstract: Visual illusions are often cited as prime examples of cognitive impenetrability, suggesting they are immune to non-perceptual top-down processes. We revisit this claim in five experiments focused on the Kanizsa illusion, where illusory contours create a nonexistent shape from Pac-Man-like inductors. We hypothesized that semantic priming would modulate the holistic experience of the illusion. Results demonstrated that primes semantically related to the Pac-Man video game reduced the probability of perceiving the illusory shape, whereas primes indexing the illusory shape itself ('triangle') enhanced the illusion. These findings provide evidence for the cognitive penetrability of vision, suggesting that semantic knowledge and top-down predictions can bi-directionally modulate the strength and direction of low-level perceptual integration.
papers.authors: Nataly Davidson Litvak, Amir Tal, Liad Mudrik

papers.title: Extrapolating other consciousnesses: The prospects and limits of analogical abduction
papers.abstract: The attribution of consciousness to non-standard systems, including nonhuman animals, neural organoids, and artificial intelligence, requires a rigorous epistemological framework. We evaluate the argumentative structures behind such attributions, concluding that 'analogical abduction'—a form of reasoning that integrates analogical elements with inference to the best explanation (IBE)—provides the strongest justification for extrapolating consciousness from humans to non-standard entities. We argue that simpler forms of reasoning, such as the argument from analogy or IBE individually, fail to meet the necessary criteria for valid extrapolation. While analogical abduction offers a promising approach for the science of consciousness, we characterize the limits of this method given the current lack of consensus on a fundamental neural theory of subjective experience.
papers.authors: Niccolò Negro, Liad Mudrik

0394.name: Lihui Wang
0394.bio: Lihui Wang is an Associate Professor and Principal Investigator at Shanghai Jiao Tong University who researches the neural substrates of visual perception through the framework of enactive cognition. Wang’s work investigates how the interaction between the body and the environment shapes cognitive processes, focusing on the functional roles of eye-movement patterns in face recognition and emotional processing. By integrating multi-modal neuroimaging techniques such as fMRI, EEG, and MEG with machine learning, they develop diagnostic algorithms for psychiatric disorders and compare human embodied intelligence with artificial systems. Their recent research identifies dynamic representations of facial information in the human ventral pathway to characterize oculomotor-perceptual coupling.
0394.research_direction: Dr. Wang has recently been investigating the intricate relationship between oculomotor behavior, visual perception, and motor control using a combination of high-resolution eye-tracking, EEG, and MEG. Their recent work explores the functional architecture of active visual sampling, questioning whether macro- and micro-saccades share unified control mechanisms and how early sequential fixations coordinate the extraction of global-to-local information during face recognition. At the neural level, they are examining how the human ventral stream encodes these top-down oculomotor programs during visual exploration, as well as how reward incentives alter the temporal dynamics between sensory preparation and motor action selection. Furthermore, Dr. Wang is applying these foundational oculomotor paradigms to clinical populations, utilizing pro- and anti-saccade tasks to probe top-down inhibitory deficits and gaze hyperactivity in individuals with obsessive-compulsive disorder.

papers.title: Dynamic face-related eye movement representations in the human ventral pathway
papers.abstract: This study utilized magnetoencephalography (MEG) to investigate the neural representations of oculomotor trajectories in the absence of image perception. Participants performed a dot-tracking task on a uniform background where the stimulus motion replicated gaze patterns previously recorded during the free-viewing of faces and houses. Representational similarity analysis and multivoxel pattern decoding revealed that face-specific eye movement patterns are dynamically represented along the human ventral stream, including the orbitofrontal cortex (OFC), anterior temporal lobe (ATL), medial temporal cortex, and ventral occipitotemporal cortex. These results suggest that the ventral pathway encodes the structural motor programs associated with facial exploration, supporting a predictive coding framework where top-down categorical signals from the prefrontal and anterior temporal regions guide perceptual synthesis through oculomotor priors.
papers.authors: Zhongbin Su, Xiaolin Zhou, Stefan Pollmann, Lihui Wang

papers.title: Active action selection in reward-modulated visual perception
papers.abstract: Using an EEG-based cue-target paradigm, this research explored the temporal dynamics between reward-modulated sensory processing and motor selection. A non-informative cue indicated the availability of a monetary incentive, followed by a lateralized visual target requiring a manual response. Event-related potential (ERP) analysis demonstrated that reward enhanced neural activity in both the motor and visual cortices during the preparatory interval. Post-target, the motor cortex exhibited sustained reward-driven enhancement for both contralateral and ipsilateral hand responses, whereas the visual cortex showed an earlier and more transient modulation. These findings indicate that incentive-based modulation facilitates task-relevant information processing by reducing the selection latency in visual regions and maintaining prioritized preparatory activity in the motor system.
papers.authors: Tingjuntao Ni, Li Zhang, Lihui Wang

papers.title: Specified functions of the first two fixations in face recognition: Sampling the general-to-specific facial information
papers.abstract: This study characterized the functional specializations of the initial oculomotor fixations during the face recognition process. High-resolution eye-tracking revealed a central-to-divergent scanning hierarchy: the primary fixation (Fix I) typically anchors on the nasal bridge to facilitate coarse-grained global feature integration, while the subsequent fixation (Fix II) shifts towards discriminative local landmarks such as the eyes and mouth. Pattern classification analysis demonstrated that Fix II carries significantly higher mutual information regarding face identity than Fix I. The integration of the two fixations significantly improved identity decoding compared to individual gaze points, suggesting a synergistic oculomotor strategy where early global configuration is subsequently supplemented by local featural sampling for robust person identification.
papers.authors: Meng Liu, Jiayu Zhan, Lihui Wang

papers.title: Concurrent oculomotor hyperactivity and deficient anti-saccade performance in obsessive-compulsive disorder
papers.abstract: A clinical assessment was conducted to evaluate oculomotor control and inhibitory dysfunction in patients with obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) using pro-saccade and anti-saccade paradigms. The study quantified saccadic latency, gain, and directional error rates to determine the integrity of volitional gaze control. Results indicated that patients with OCD exhibit a characteristic pattern of oculomotor hyperactivity, marked by a significantly increased frequency of intrusive microsaccades during fixation. Furthermore, the OCD cohort displayed pronounced deficits in the anti-saccade task, characterized by elevated directional error rates and prolonged latencies. These findings suggest that OCD is associated with a specific breakdown in top-down inhibitory mechanisms over reflexive motor programs, likely reflecting dysregulation within the fronto-striatal oculomotor circuitry.
papers.authors: Zhenni Wang, Chen Zhang, Qihui Guo, Qing Fan, Lihui Wang

papers.title: Common structure of saccades and microsaccades in visual perception
papers.abstract: This research investigated the structural and functional continuity between macro-saccades and micro-saccades during active visual sensing. Through psychophysical experiments and high-frequency eye-tracking, the study assessed whether both classes of eye movements are governed by a unified control mechanism. Measurements confirmed that saccades and microsaccades follow the same amplitude-velocity main sequence relationship and are modulated by task-dependent cognitive load and stimulus complexity in a similar manner. The results provide evidence for a consolidated oculomotor framework where microsaccades represent a scaled-down version of saccades, both serving the identical function of active information sampling and target selection during visual perception.
papers.authors: Zhenni Wang, Radhakrishnan N. Meghanathan, Stefan Pollmann, Lihui Wang

0395.name: Lili Sahakyan
0395.bio: Lili Sahakyan is a Professor of Psychology at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, where they direct the Context, Memory, & Forgetting Lab and maintain affiliations with the Beckman Institute and the Neuroscience Program. Their research investigates the cognitive and neural mechanisms of human long-term memory, focusing on the strategic control of memory and the processes underlying intentional forgetting. Sahakyan utilizes functional MRI, EEG, and eye-tracking to examine how internal mental context and executive functions modulate memory retention and suppression. Their work also explores these memory control mechanisms in populations at risk for psychopathology, specifically investigating how schizotypy relates to episodic memory deficits.
0395.research_direction: Dr. Sahakyan has recently been investigating the cognitive and physiological mechanisms underlying intentional forgetting and relational memory. Their recent work explores the temporal dynamics and boundary conditions of motivated forgetting, using directed forgetting paradigms to test how stimulus meaningfulness, prior familiarity, and delayed testing might dissociate active cognitive inhibition from passive memory decay. In parallel, they have been utilizing high-resolution eye-tracking to examine encoding and retrieval strategies in associative memory, asking how visual fixation patterns and scanpaths contribute to phenomena like the cross-race effect in face-scene pairings. Additionally, Dr. Sahakyan uses pupillometry to track autonomic markers of cognitive control in real time, investigating whether trial-by-trial pupil fluctuations can index the mental effort required to intentionally forget natural scenes or the neurocognitive resources allocated to successfully bind items to their contexts.

papers.title: Encoding and retrieval eye movement patterns reveal cross-race effect in relational and item memory
papers.abstract: This study employs high-resolution eye-tracking to examine the mechanisms underlying the cross-race effect (CRE) within both item and relational (face-scene) memory frameworks. By quantifying fixation frequency, duration, and scanpath similarity during encoding and recognition, the researchers assessed whether the CRE results from differential encoding strategies or retrieval monitoring discrepancies. The findings indicate that while relational memory displays a robust CRE, the deficit is primarily mediated by distinct viewing patterns during the encoding phase and subsequent mismatch signals during the recognition of other-race faces, suggesting that the CRE is not a monolithic failure of face representation but an interplay of strategic allocation and memory strength.
papers.authors: Huiyu Ding, Jonathon Whitlock, Lili Sahakyan

papers.title: Pupil fluctuations signal intentional forgetting of natural scenes
papers.abstract: The investigation characterizes autonomic markers of motivated forgetting using an item-method directed forgetting (DF) paradigm with naturalistic scene stimuli. Utilizing pupillometry, the authors compared successfully forgotten items following a 'Forget' cue (active forgetting) with forgotten items following a 'Remember' cue (passive forgetting). Quantitative analysis revealed that active forgetting is associated with a significantly larger phasic pupil dilation during the post-cue window relative to passive forgetting. These results provide evidence that successful intentional forgetting is a cognitively demanding process that recruits distinct inhibitory control mechanisms, differentiating it from stochastic, passive mnemonic decay.
papers.authors: Huiyu Ding, Jonathon Whitlock, Lili Sahakyan

papers.title: Delayed testing in directed forgetting dissociates active and passive forms of forgetting
papers.abstract: This research evaluates the longitudinal persistence of the item-method directed forgetting (DF) effect by measuring recognition accuracy across immediate, 24-hour, and 4-day retention intervals. By fitting exponential forgetting curves to the behavioral data, the study dissociated the decay rates of 'Forget' (F)-cued items from 'Remember' (R)-cued items. The results demonstrated a significantly steeper forgetting trajectory for F-cued items compared to R-cued items across all delays. This accelerated rate of forgetting supports models of active inhibition or contextual unbinding, suggesting that the forget instruction facilitates a more rapid degradation of the item's mnemonic accessibility rather than merely reflecting a deficit in passive rehearsal.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
papers.authors: Jonathon Whitlock, Huiyu Ding, Ryan Hubbard, Lili Sahakyan

papers.title: The role of prior familiarisation and meaningfulness of verbal and visual stimuli on directed forgetting
papers.abstract: This series of experiments investigates the boundary conditions of directed forgetting (DF) by manipulating stimulus modality (verbal vs. visual), semantic significance, and episodic familiarity (through 0, 2, or 6 pre-exposures). The findings reveal a complex interaction: while episodic familiarization generally attenuates the magnitude of the DF effect for meaningful stimuli, semantically impoverished visual materials, such as fractals, exhibit resistance to intentional forgetting cues regardless of the degree of familiarity. These results suggest that the effectiveness of cognitive control processes in memory is constrained by the inherent representational strength and meaningfulness of the encoded information.
papers.authors: Yi-Pei Lo, Huiyu Ding, Jonathon Whitlock, Lili Sahakyan

papers.title: Trial-level fluctuations in pupil dilation at encoding reflect the strength of relational binding
papers.abstract: This study examines the physiological predictors of relational binding by monitoring task-evoked pupil responses during the encoding of associative word-picture pairs. Using a trial-level analytic approach, the authors found that variance in pupil size during learning predicted subsequent associative recognition performance and preferential viewing patterns during retrieval for the relational task, but did not predict performance for single-item recognition. The specificity of these findings to relational memory indicates that phasic pupillary fluctuations serve as a real-time index of the neurocognitive resources allocated to the binding of items to their context, rather than reflecting generalized arousal or item-specific memory formation.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
papers.authors: Jonathon Whitlock, Ryan J. Hubbard, Huiyu Ding, Lili Sahakyan

0396.name: Linda B. Smith
0396.department: Department of Psychological and Brain Sciences
0396.bio: Linda B. Smith is a Distinguished Professor at Indiana University who researches developmental cognitive science and vision. Smith's work utilizes a complex systems approach to examine the interdependencies between perceptual, motor, and cognitive development, focusing on how infants' active exploration structures their visual input. Through high-resolution egocentric data from head-mounted eye-trackers, they investigate the statistical regularities in the developmental environment that support visual object recognition and word learning. Their current research links human development with machine learning by modeling how sensory-motor experiences create pathways for cognitive acquisition.
0396.research_direction: Dr. Smith has recently been investigating the environmental inputs and developmental mechanisms that drive early learning across visual perception, language, and mathematical cognition. Their recent work explores the natural statistics of the infant visual diet, using egocentric head-mounted cameras and computational models to study how phenomena like high-contrast edge-simplicity biases and highly skewed, repetitive object views might provide a specialized training curriculum for the developing visual cortex and efficient object categorization. In parallel, they are examining the temporal dynamics of early language acquisition by tracking how spontaneous infant vocalizations couple with gross motor movements during free play. Broadening their scope to formal education, Dr. Smith is also investigating early mathematical cognition by exploring how relational learning interventions and systematic transcoding "smart errors" help young children acquire complex structural concepts like multidigit place value.
