papers.title: A solution to generalized learning from small training sets found in infant repeated visual experiences of individual objects
papers.abstract: This study addresses the developmental paradox where one-year-old infants exhibit robust category generalization despite extremely limited and skewed training data. Utilizing a corpus of 87 infant-perspective (egocentric) head-camera recordings captured during mealtimes, the authors quantified the visual statistics for eight early-learned object categories. The results reveal that infant experiences are highly non-uniform, dominated by repeated encounters with a single instance of a category. Graph-theoretic analysis of the similarity structure within these experiences identified a 'lumpy' manifold, characterized by high-density clusters of similar images interspersed with sparse, high-variability views. In computational experiments, the researchers demonstrated that artificial training sets mimicking this skewed, lumpy distribution—specifically by oversampling varied views of an individual object—enable machine learning models to achieve broad generalization to novel instances after minimal training exposures, outperforming traditional balanced datasets. These findings suggest that the natural statistics of infant environments provide a specialized curriculum for efficient representation learning.
papers.authors: Frangil Ramirez, Elizabeth Clerkin, David J. Crandall, Linda B. Smith

papers.title: Smart Errors in Learning Multidigit Number Meanings
papers.abstract: This longitudinal study investigated the emergence of place value (PV) concepts by focusing on 'smart errors'—mistakes in writing or transcoding multidigit numbers that reflect a partial, yet systematic, understanding of base-ten syntax (e.g., writing '10005' for '105'). Using a sample of 279 kindergartners, the authors employed network analysis to map the connectivity between informal numerical knowledge and formal symbolic representations. The results indicate that children who produced smart errors, such as expanded-form transcoding, showed significantly steeper growth trajectories in PV understanding and multidigit calculation skills by second grade compared to children who made unsystematic errors. This research suggests that such errors serve as valid indicators of latent structural knowledge and represent a critical transitional phase in the integration of verbal number names and Arabic numeral systems.
papers.authors: Corinne A. Bower, Kelly S. Mix, Gregory R. Hancock, Lei Yuan, Linda B. Smith

papers.title: Place Value Learning in Kindergarten
papers.abstract: The present study tests the hypothesis that kindergartners possess sufficient informal foundations to benefit from formal place value instruction, contrary to traditional developmental stage theories. The researchers conducted a randomized controlled trial involving 20 scaffolded lessons designed to engage relational learning mechanisms such as structure mapping and progressive alignment. Children in the experimental group received instruction that highlighted the multiplicative structure of base-ten units through repeated comparisons, while the control group engaged in standard single-digit arithmetic. Post-intervention assessments revealed that the instruction group made significantly greater gains in both approximate and precise understandings of multidigit notation. These findings provide empirical support for the effectiveness of leveraging relational learning regularities to accelerate mathematical development as children transition to formal schooling.
papers.authors: Kelly S. Mix, Corinne A Bower, Gregory R. Hancock, Linda B. Smith

papers.title: Infant vocal productions coincide with body movements
papers.abstract: This study explores the sensorimotor coupling between vocalizations and gross motor activity in infants aged 9 to 24 months. Utilizing high-resolution behavioral coding of vocal productions and head/hand movements, the researchers analyzed the temporal dynamics of multimodal activity during free play. The findings demonstrate that spontaneous infant vocalizations are not isolated events but are significantly coupled with synergistic co-activations of extraneous motor systems. Quantitative metrics showed that the temporal precision of these movement-vocalization couplings tightens as a function of age and the increasing recognizability of speech. This evidence supports a dynamic systems framework in which language development is deeply embedded within the maturation of the broader motoric system and the refinement of rhythmic, coordinated action patterns.
papers.authors: Jeremy I. Borjon, Drew H. Abney, Chen Yu, Linda B. Smith

papers.title: An edge-simplicity bias in the visual input to young infants
papers.abstract: The development of orientation-selective neurons in the primary visual cortex (V1) depends on the statistics of early visual experience. This study provides the first direct measurement of edge statistics in the infant visual diet by analyzing a large corpus of egocentric head-camera images from infants (3–6 months) and adults in naturalistic home environments. Computational analysis revealed a pervasive 'edge-simplicity' bias in infant visual input: images are dominated by sparse edge patterns with fewer distinct orientations and higher contrast compared to adult input. Specifically, over one-third of infant images met criteria for high edge simplicity, compared to less than one-tenth for adults. These simple patterns, often derived from architectural regularities like doors and corners, persist in the infant's view longer, creating a developmentally ordered curriculum that likely facilitates the maturation of sparse edge coding in the mammalian visual system.
papers.authors: Erin M. Anderson, T. Rowan Candy, Jason M. Gold, Linda B. Smith

0400.name: Lisa M. Oakes
0400.bio: Lisa M. Oakes is a professor in the Department of Psychology and the Center for Mind and Brain at the University of California, Davis. Oakes’s research investigates developmental cascades in infant mental abilities, specifically the integration of visual attention, memory, and categorization during the first years of life. Utilizing eye tracking, representational similarity analysis, and looking-time paradigms, Oakes examines how infants scan naturalistic scenes and whether their gaze is directed by physical salience or semantic meaning. Their work focuses on how early attentional mechanisms interact with environmental experience to influence long-term cognitive and perceptual development.
0400.research_direction: Dr. Oakes has recently been investigating the development of infant visual attention, exploring how emerging gaze patterns relate to underlying neural architectures and computational models of vision. Their recent work uses representational similarity analysis to compare infant fixations on natural scenes against adult fMRI data, while also testing how specific low-level image features—such as those extracted by graph-based visual salience models—guide oculomotor orienting during the first year of life. Beyond stimulus-driven mechanisms, they are exploring how environmental and social contexts shape spatial attention by measuring infant orienting across diverse global cultures and using head-mounted eye-tracking to probe how parents' multimodal spatial language structures their child's real-time looking behavior. Taken together, their research treats early attention as a dynamic developmental cascade, combining precise eye-tracking, computational saliency, and naturalistic observation to understand how infants actively select and process visual information across different contexts.

papers.title: Relating infant fixations to adult cortical activation patterns using the Natural Scenes Dataset
papers.abstract: This study employed representational similarity analysis (RSA) to evaluate the representational alignment between the spatial distribution of infant fixations (N=93, ages 5–7 and 10–12 months) and BOLD activation patterns derived from adult fMRI data within the Natural Scenes Dataset. Younger infants demonstrated gaze patterns that significantly correlated with neural activity in low-level ventral stream regions, whereas the eye movements of older infants and adults were more closely linked to mid-level cortical activations. These findings provide longitudinal and cross-sectional evidence for a developmental shift in visual attention from low-level feature sensitivity in early visual cortex to the utilization of increasingly abstract, higher-order representations coded in mid-level visual areas.
papers.authors: Brianna K. Hunter, John E. Kiat, Steven J. Luck, Lisa M. Oakes

papers.title: A cross-cultural analysis of infants' spatial attention on the infant orienting with attention (IOWA) task
papers.abstract: Visuo-spatial attention was assessed in a large, diverse sample of 6- to 9-month-old infants (N=568) from rural Malawi and suburban California using the Infant Orienting With Attention (IOWA) task. The investigation sought to determine whether basic attentional mechanisms are universal or context-dependent. While infants across both populations showed consistent cueing effects—specifically faster and more accurate saccades to targets following valid vs. invalid spatial cues—significant cross-cultural differences emerged in baseline performance. Malawian infants exhibited significantly longer fixation latencies but higher overall accuracy in target localization compared to US infants, suggesting that while the core attentional architecture is stable, local environmental factors modulate the temporal and precision parameters of gaze deployment.
papers.authors: Michaela C. DeBolt, Bess L. Caswell, Matthews George, Kenneth Maleta, Elizabeth L. Prado, Shannon Ross-Sheehy, Christine P. Stewart, Lisa M. Oakes

papers.title: Parents' multimodal spatial language structures infants' in-the-moment attention during spatial play
papers.abstract: Using head-mounted eye-tracking, this study investigated how caregivers' multimodal spatial inputs—combining spatial language, object labels, and deictic gestures—modulate the real-time visual attention of 9-month-old infants during puzzle play. Quantitative analyses of looking duration revealed that caregivers' production of spatial descriptors and object labels significantly prolonged infants' fixations on relevant objects compared to utterances without these categories. Furthermore, the efficacy of this verbal input was significantly enhanced when coupled with deictic gestures, such as pointing, which elicited the longest sustained looking episodes. The results indicate that multimodal parental scaffolding plays a critical role in structuring the infant's information-processing environment by directing and maintaining attention on task-relevant spatial properties.
papers.authors: Erim Kızıldere, Christian M. Nelson, Marianella Casasola, Katharine Graf Estes, Lisa M. Oakes

papers.title: The predictive ability of GBVS feature channels on infants' fixations of natural scenes
papers.abstract: The contribution of individual low-level stimulus dimensions to infant eye movements was evaluated by decomposing the Graph-Based Visual Salience (GBVS) model into orientation, color, and intensity feature channels. Gaze locations from infants (N=167) aged 4 to 12 months were recorded as they viewed naturalistic photographs. Using a map-averaging technique to compensate for infant eye-tracking calibration error, the study found that orientation was the primary predictor of the spatial distribution of fixations, and this effect became more pronounced with age. Exploratory analyses indicated that the predictive power of specific channels was moderated by visual clutter, suggesting that scene-level complexity constraints influence how physical salience guides attention during the first postnatal year.
papers.authors: Brianna K. Hunter, John E. Kiat, Shannon M. Klotz, Christian M. Nelson, Steven J. Luck, Lisa M. Oakes

papers.title: What have we learned about infant visual attention in the first 25 years of the 21st century?
papers.abstract: This theoretical review synthesizes the major conceptual and methodological advancements in the field of infant visual attention since 2000. It documents the transition from a hierarchical subcortical-to-cortical maturation model toward a dynamic developmental cascade framework that recognizes attention as an emergent property of interacting systems. Key innovations discussed include the application of high-precision eye-tracking, the use of head-mounted cameras to capture egocentric perspectives in naturalistic environments, and the development of computational models of saliency and scene semantics. The authors argue that these tools have shifted research focus toward understanding how infants' visual inputs change through active engagement and how environmental diversity shapes individual developmental trajectories.
papers.authors: Brianna K. Hunter, Erim Kızıldere, Shannon M. Klotz, Christian M. Nelson, Julie Markant, Lisa M. Oakes

0401.name: Lisa Renzi-Hammond
0401.department: Department of Health Promotion and Behavior, College of Public Health
0401.bio: Lisa Renzi-Hammond studies the functional relationships between sensory integrity, neurological health, and cognitive vitality across the human lifespan. Their research utilizes psychophysical, electrophysiological, and neuroimaging methodologies to investigate how visual function serves as a non-invasive biomarker for central nervous system health. Renzi-Hammond examines how dietary carotenoids, such as lutein and zeaxanthin, influence neural processing speed and protect against neurodegenerative diseases. They serve as the Director of the Institute of Gerontology and co-director of the Cognitive Aging Research and Education (CARE) Center, translating vision science into public health initiatives for dementia prevention and education.
0401.research_direction: Dr. Renzi-Hammond has recently been investigating the psychophysical effects of short-wavelength light filtration, specifically exploring how blue-light and high-energy visible (HEV) filtering lenses impact real-world visual function in both general and pseudophakic older adult populations. Using brightness matching paradigms and randomized cross-over designs, their recent work examines whether selective attenuation of blue light alters intraocular light scatter, glare disability, chromatic contrast, and overall visual comfort when viewing naturalistic scenes under bright illumination. In more foundational color vision research, they are also exploring the "hue-heat hypothesis," measuring how variations in stimulus luminance dynamically modulate the perceived psychological warmth of primary hues. Expanding into public health and gerontology, their recent interdisciplinary work additionally utilizes survey methodologies to investigate how well-being-oriented continuing education might mitigate systemic burnout and improve career sustainability for certified nursing assistants in long-term care facilities.

papers.title: Assessing certified nursing assistants' interest in well-being-oriented continuing education to improve job sustainability and career progression
papers.abstract: The study investigated the demand for and efficacy of continuing education (CE) modules focused on occupational well-being among certified nursing assistants (CNAs) to address the workforce crisis in long-term care facilities. Utilizing a cross-sectional survey methodology (N=221), participants were assessed via the Professional Fulfillment Index (PFI) alongside metrics for job satisfaction and perceived career progression. Statistical analysis revealed that while participants reported high overall satisfaction with their career choice, limited opportunities for vertical career mobility were significant predictors of systemic burnout (OR = 0.51) and diminished professional fulfillment (OR = 2.42). Findings emphasize that implementing CE programs targeting psychological resilience and structured career pathways can stabilize the direct care workforce by enhancing professional fulfillment and reducing attrition.
papers.authors: Anita M. Reina, Ashley N. Adawi Suker, Fiona Douglas, Kerstin Emerson, Ke'vOn T. Hamilton, Austin D. Dobbs, Curtis Harris, Jenay M. Beer, Lisa M. Renzi-Hammond

papers.title: Visual Function Under Bright Light Conditions Tested Using a Blue-Light Absorbing or Clear Lens in Pseudophakic Patients
papers.abstract: This study quantified the psychophysical benefits of blue-light filtering (BLF) spectral profiles on visual performance in pseudophakic individuals (N=25) who had previously received UV-only intraocular lens (IOL) implants. Using a single-masked, randomized cross-over design, researchers evaluated glare disability (GD), chromatic contrast (CC), two-point light thresholds, and dysphotopsia severity (spoke and snowball diameter) under broadband xenon illumination. The BLF test condition significantly improved CC and GD (P < 0.001) compared to the UV-only control. Furthermore, the lateral extent of snowballs and spoke-like photic phenomena was reduced by 24% and 19%, respectively. The data suggest that selective attenuation of short-wavelength light significantly mitigates intraocular light scatter, thereby enhancing functional vision and reducing dysphotopsia in geriatric patients post-cataract surgery.
papers.authors: Billy R. Hammond Jr., Jacob B. Harth, Lisa M. Renzi-Hammond

papers.title: The effects of a HEV‐filtering contact lens on the brightness of natural images
papers.abstract: This investigation evaluated whether high-energy visible (HEV)-filtering soft contact lenses influence the perceived brightness and clarity of naturalistic scenes under bright illumination. Employing a subject-masked, contralateral design (N=60), the study compared an HEV-filtering lens (attenuating 400–450 nm) against a clear control. Psychophysical endpoints included brightness matching of natural images and measurements of intraocular scatter using two-point light thresholds. Results demonstrated that the HEV-filtering lenses resulted in a statistically significant increase in subjective brightness and image contrast (P < .01). By reducing the impact of violet/blue scatter, the lenses improved the retinal signal-to-noise ratio, providing a mechanism for enhanced visual comfort and brightness perception in real-world environments.
papers.authors: Billy R. Hammond, John R. Buch, Patricia Martin, Wright Shamp, Jacob B. Harth, Cameron Wysocky, Lisa M. Renzi-Hammond

papers.title: Blue-Light Filtering Increases the Brightness of Natural Images in Pseudophakic Adults
papers.abstract: Evidence for the influence of blue-light filtering (BLF) on subjective brightness perception in the elderly is examined using a brightness matching paradigm with complex natural images. A cohort of forty pseudophakic participants (M = 71.15 years) viewed diverse natural stimuli through either a visibly clear control or a BLF spectral profile matched to common IOL designs. The BLF lens induced a consistent and significant ~17% increase in perceived brightness across all images (t[78] = -2.529, p = 0.007). This perceptual enhancement was independent of image contrast or chromatic variance, suggesting that BLF modifies the gain of the visual system's response to luminance, likely by reducing intraocular scatter and enhancing neural processing efficiency for broad-spectrum natural scenes.
papers.authors: Billy R. Hammond, Jacob B. Harth, Yaw Buabeng, Lisa M. Renzi-Hammond

papers.title: Increasing intensity directly increases the perceived warmth of primary colors
papers.abstract: The perceptual association between color appearance and temperature—often termed the hue-heat hypothesis—was tested by examining the influence of luminance on judgments of color warmth. Using four primary hues (Red, Yellow, Green, Blue), the study measured perceived warmth across a range of intensities. The results confirmed a robust between-colors effect where longer-wavelength stimuli were judged warmer regardless of intensity. Critically, a within-color effect was observed: increasing the intensity of any given color stimulus directly and significantly shifted the perceived temperature toward a warmer judgment. These findings demonstrate that color-temperature associations are not static properties of chromaticity but are dynamic responses modulated by the total energetic flux of the visual stimulus.
papers.authors: Billy R. Hammond, Colin R. Gardner, Billy R. Wooten, Lisa Renzi-Hammond

0402.name: Lisa S. Scott
0402.bio: Lisa S. Scott is a Professor of Psychology at the University of Florida and the director of the Brain Cognition & Development Lab. Scott’s research examines the neurobiological and behavioral mechanisms of visual attention, perception, and learning, with a focus on how early experience influences face and object recognition across the lifespan. Utilizing a multimodal approach including electroencephalography (EEG), event-related potentials (ERPs), and eye-tracking, Scott tracks the specialization of neural circuits and the acquisition of perceptual expertise. Their recent investigations include longitudinal studies of brain development and the visuocortical foundations of learning from infancy into childhood.
0402.research_direction: Dr. Scott has recently been investigating how early sensory and linguistic experiences shape the developing brain's prioritization of objects and faces during the first year of life. Their recent work explores the ways in which learned associations—such as pairing novel objects with verbal labels during short training sessions—drive competitive visuo-cortical responses, utilizing electrophysiological paradigms like event-related potentials and frequency-tagged steady-state visual evoked potentials (ssVEPs). Additionally, they are examining the early developmental trajectories of social vision, employing fast periodic visual stimulation to test how exposure to familiar versus unfamiliar racial groups influences neural face categorization and individual identity differentiation. To support rigorous investigation of these visual phenomena, Dr. Scott is also advancing field methodologies by establishing standardized best practices for infant eye-tracking and developing newly validated, highly controlled stimulus databases of diverse face images.

papers.title: Competitive Cortical Prioritization Emerges for Trained Objects across the First Year of Life
papers.abstract: This longitudinal and cross-sectional study employed frequency-tagged steady-state visual evoked potentials (ssVEPs) to determine how experience-driven cortical competition shapes object recognition during the first year of life. Parent-infant dyads across 6, 9, and 12 months of age engaged in storybook training where novel computer-generated objects were associated with distinct labels. During subsequent EEG recording, infants were concurrently presented with trained and novel objects flickering at 5 Hz and 6 Hz, respectively. Results revealed that although no visuocortical bias was evident at 6 months, by 9 and 12 months, neural responses were significantly enhanced for trained stimuli and suppressed for untrained competitors. These findings suggest that competitive neural interactions in the extrastriate cortex are modulated by experience and maturation, establishing a prioritized attentional template for learned object categories.
papers.authors: Maeve R. Boylan, Anna-Lena Tebbe, Jamie Newland, Jessica Sanches Braga Figueira, Andreas Keil, Lisa S. Scott

papers.title: Experience With Face Groups Impacts Face Processing, but Not Face Differentiation in 6- and 9-Month-Old Infants
papers.abstract: Utilizing a fast periodic visual stimulation (FPVS) EEG paradigm, this research examined the influence of racial group familiarity on neural face categorization and individual differentiation in 6- and 9-month-old infants. Visual stimuli consisting of familiar and unfamiliar race face groups, controlled for low-level image statistics, were presented at a base rate of 6 Hz, with individual identity changes occurring at a 1.2 Hz oddball frequency. A medial occipital 6 Hz response was significantly greater for familiar race groups compared to unfamiliar ones, a effect most pronounced in the 6-month-old cohort. Conversely, robust 1.2 Hz responses were observed across both age groups and all face categories, indicating that individual-level face differentiation is preserved despite emerging visuocortical biases toward familiar social groups. Topographical analyses further revealed that face differentiation responses become increasingly right-lateralized as a function of age.
papers.authors: Grace Wallsinger, Maeve R. Boylan, Jessica Sanches Braga Figueira, Ryan Barry-Anwar, Gabriella Silva, Andreas Keil, Lisa S. Scott

papers.title: Eye Tracking for Infant Populations: A Comparison of Methods and Best Practices
papers.abstract: This comprehensive review provides a technical comparison between screen-based and head-mounted eye-tracking methodologies specifically adapted for infant developmental research. The authors evaluate the relative spatial and temporal accuracy of these systems, the efficacy of various infant-centric calibration protocols, and the validity of common data quality metrics such as precision and robustness. Beyond comparing hardware, the paper establishes standardized procedures for experimental design, gaze estimation, and automated data processing. It offers a set of best-practice recommendations aimed at improving the reliability and cross-study comparability of oculomotor data in infant cognition and perception studies.
papers.authors: Julia Farrell Aukerman, Jamie Newland, Lisa S. Scott

papers.title: How labels shape visuo-cortical processing in infants
papers.abstract: The current investigation explored the extent to which brief linguistic associations can rapidly reshape the neural processing of visual objects in early development. During an approximately six-minute associative learning task, novel computer-generated stimuli were paired with either individual-level labels (e.g., proper names) or category-level labels. Event-related potentials (ERPs) were recorded to assess shifts in early and late neural signatures of perception in 6- and 9-month-old infants. The data demonstrate that even minimal experience associating objects with specific labels modulates the visuocortical response, supporting the hypothesis that early linguistic input serves as a powerful mechanism for shaping attentional prioritization and neural representation of the visual environment.
papers.authors: Maeve R. Boylan, Ece Kutlu, Jessica Sanches Braga Figueira, Bianca M. Garner, Ryan Barry-Anwar, Zoe Pestana, Andreas Keil, Lisa S. Scott

papers.title: Diverse Face Images (DFI): Validated for racial representation and eye gaze
papers.abstract: This paper introduces and validates the Diverse Face Images (DFI) database, a curated stimulus set designed to address the need for representative and controlled visual assets in social perception research. The database comprises high-resolution photographs of 64 individuals representing four major racial/ethnic categories (Black, White, Asian, and Hispanic/Latinx), with participants displaying both direct and averted gazes. Validation was conducted through an extensive behavioral study where adult raters provided subjective assessments of perceived race, gender, attractiveness, and gaze orientation. The resulting psychometric data confirm that the DFI database provides a robust, validated toolkit for investigating the neurocognitive mechanisms of face processing, racial bias, and joint attention.
papers.authors: Charisse B. Pickron, Alexia J. Brown, Caitlin M. Hudac, Lisa S. Scott

0403.name: Lotfi B. Merabet
0403.bio: Lotfi B. Merabet is a clinician-scientist and Professor of Ophthalmology at Harvard Medical School who investigates the mechanisms of neuroplasticity in response to vision loss. Merabet’s research characterizes how the brain's structural and functional architecture reorganizes following both ocular blindness and brain-based visual impairment. By employing neuroimaging techniques such as functional MRI and diffusion tensor imaging alongside behavioral tasks, Merabet explores how the visual cortex is recruited for non-visual processing and identifies the neural correlates of visual search deficits. Their current work focuses on translating these findings into rehabilitative strategies and assistive technologies designed to improve functional outcomes for individuals with visual disabilities.
0403.research_direction: Dr. Merabet has recently been investigating the behavioral and neural mechanisms underlying cerebral visual impairment (CVI), focusing on how early neurodevelopmental injury alters higher-order perceptual processing. To characterize these visual bottlenecks, their recent work explores individuals' capacity for endogenous visual mental imagery and their search efficiency during feature-conjunction tasks. Utilizing eye-tracking in naturalistic and dynamic virtual environments, they are also examining the relative influence of bottom-up low-level saliency versus top-down semantic cues on gaze and exploration behavior. Furthermore, by employing functional neuroimaging and resting-state connectomics, Dr. Merabet investigates the large-scale reorganization of visual brain networks in CVI, specifically probing alterations in structural integration and the differential recruitment of the dorsal and ventral visual streams during spatial processing.

papers.title: Assessing visual mental imagery abilities in cerebral visual impairment
papers.abstract: The investigation characterized the capacity for voluntary mental representation in individuals with cerebral visual impairment (CVI), evaluating how neurodevelopmental injury to retrochiasmatic visual pathways impacts endogenous visual simulation. Utilizing the Vividness of Visual Imagery Questionnaire (VVIQ) in conjunction with assessments of verbal IQ and clinical visual function, the study demonstrated that visual imagery vividness is significantly altered in the CVI population compared to neurotypical controls. These deficits in mental imagery persisted independently of baseline visual acuity, gestational status, or the presence of comorbid neurodevelopmental conditions such as autism spectrum disorder (ASD). The findings imply that impaired visual imagery constitutes a core feature of the CVI clinical profile, reflecting a disruption in the shared neural substrates underlying top-down imagery generation and bottom-up visual perception.
papers.authors: Claire E. Manley, John Ravenscroft, Lotfi B. Merabet

papers.title: Reorganization of integration and segregation networks in brain-based visual impairment
papers.abstract: This study utilized connectomics and resting-state functional connectivity (rs-FC) to map the large-scale reorganization of neural architecture in individuals with cerebral visual impairment (CVI). Through voxel-based morphometry (VBM) and link-level network analysis, the researchers identified significant structural and functional alterations, specifically finding reduced gray matter volume within the primary visual cortex (V1) and the intraparietal sulcus (IPS). Graph-theoretical metrics revealed a reorganization of the balance between network integration and segregation, evidenced by shifts in weighted degree and inter-areal connectivity across the visual hierarchy. These results quantify the impact of early neurological injury on the modular organization of the visual system and provide a neurophysiological framework for the complex visuospatial and perceptual deficits characteristic of brain-based visual impairment.
papers.authors: Ibai Diez, Carla Troyas, Corinna M Bauer, Jorge Sepulcre, Lotfi B Merabet

papers.title: Impaired Visuospatial Processing in Cerebral Visual Impairment Revealed by Performance on a Conjunction Visual Search Task
papers.abstract: The research quantified higher-order visuospatial processing deficits in cerebral visual impairment (CVI) using a feature-conjunction visual search paradigm. Subjects were required to identify a target defined by dual visual features (e.g., color and shape) presented among varying distractor set sizes (1 to 32 items). Quantitative performance was measured via reaction time (RT) as a function of set size, accuracy, and the resulting slopes and intercepts from the RT-x-set size linear function. Participants with CVI exhibited significantly higher RTs, lower accuracy, and significantly steeper search slopes compared to neurotypical controls, indicating a marked decrease in search efficiency and a greater reliance on serial processing. These findings validate conjunction search performance as a sensitive behavioral biomarker for the higher-order perceptual bottlenecks observed in the CVI population.
papers.authors: Claire E Manley, Corinna M Bauer, Peter J Bex, Lotfi B Merabet

papers.title: Visuospatial processing in early brain-based visual impairment is associated with differential recruitment of dorsal and ventral visual streams
papers.abstract: Utilizing functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and eye tracking, this study investigated the neural correlates of visuospatial processing during a naturalistic visual search task in individuals with cerebral visual impairment (CVI). Behavioral data confirmed search impairments in CVI, including prolonged reaction times and decreased gaze precision while tracking a human target in dynamic virtual environments. fMRI analysis revealed significant hypoactivation along the dorsal visual stream in CVI participants, supporting the hypothesis of dorsal stream dysfunction (DSD). Conversely, regions within the ventral visual stream exhibited hyperactivation in CVI compared to neurotypical controls, while activation in the early visual cortex (EVC) and prefrontal cortex remained comparable between groups. These results suggest that visuospatial deficits in CVI are associated with an atypical pattern of differential recruitment across the two processing streams, potentially reflecting impaired selective attention and uncoupled bottom-up ventral processing.
papers.authors: Zahide Pamir, Claire E Manley, Corinna M Bauer, Peter J Bex, Daniel D Dilks, Lotfi B Merabet

papers.title: Visual search patterns during exploration of naturalistic scenes are driven by saliency cues in individuals with cerebral visual impairment
papers.abstract: The study investigated the relative influence of bottom-up image salience and top-down image semantics on the visual search behavior of individuals with cerebral visual impairment (CVI). Gaze patterns were recorded during a target-directed search task in naturalistic scenes and compared to predictions from Graph-Based Visual Saliency (GBVS) and semantic models (Global Vectors for Word Representations combined with Linguistic Analysis of Semantic Salience). Individuals with CVI were significantly less likely to find targets and exhibited larger search areas and increased fixation counts compared to controls. Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) analysis demonstrated that the search strategies of CVI participants were more strongly associated with low-level saliency cues than semantic cues, whereas controls effectively utilized semantic information to guide search. These results indicate that CVI is characterized by a deficit in top-down semantic integration, leading to a stimulus-driven search profile.
papers.authors: Kerri Walter, Claire E Manley, Peter J Bex, Lotfi B Merabet

0406.name: Lucia Melloni
0406.institution: Max Planck Institute for Empirical Aesthetics
0406.department: Predictive Brain Department, Research Center One Health Ruhr
0406.lab_name: Neural Circuits, Consciousness, and Cognition Research Group
0406.bio: Lucia Melloni is a cognitive neuroscientist who investigates the neural and computational foundations of consciousness, perception, and memory. Melloni’s research examines how the brain utilizes predictive mechanisms to interpret sensory input and shape subjective experience through a multimodal approach that integrates invasive electrocorticography (ECoG), non-invasive MEG/EEG, and computational modeling. They coordinate large-scale adversarial collaborations designed to empirically arbitrate between competing theories of consciousness as part of an open science framework. Their work also explores the neuroethological aspects of experience, examining how memory and prediction contribute to the continuity of conscious life in real-world contexts.
0406.research_direction: Dr. Melloni’s recent work explores the neural mechanisms of consciousness and predictive processing across multiple sensory modalities. They have recently been spearheading large-scale adversarial collaborations using multimodal neuroimaging (fMRI, MEG, iEEG) to rigorously test competing predictions from dominant models of conscious visual perception, such as Integrated Information Theory and Global Neuronal Workspace Theory. Alongside these macro-level theoretical tests, their research investigates the precise temporal dynamics of visual awareness, utilizing Continuous Flash Suppression to probe how short- and long-term perceptual histories prime current subjective visibility versus objective discrimination. They are also investigating predictive coding in the auditory domain, mapping how the cortical hierarchy integrates "what" (content) and "when" (temporal) expectations during speech processing. Finally, their recent theoretical work seeks to broaden the study of subjective experience beyond neurotypical adults, proposing a neuroethological framework to investigate consciousness across evolutionary scales and non-verbal populations.

papers.title: Adversarial testing of global neuronal workspace and integrated information theories of consciousness
papers.abstract: This large-scale adversarial collaboration implemented a theory-neutral framework to adjudicate between the Integrated Information Theory (IIT) and Global Neuronal Workspace Theory (GNWT). Utilizing a sample of 256 human subjects, the study employed multimodal neuroimaging (fMRI, MEG, and iEEG) to test preregistered, divergent predictions regarding the neural correlates of conscious visual perception. Results demonstrated that conscious content could be decoded from visual, ventrotemporal, and inferior frontal cortices. Sustained neural activity in posterior regions correlated with stimulus duration, while content-specific frontal-visual synchronization was observed. These findings provide partial evidence for both theories while simultaneously challenging fundamental assumptions, specifically IIT’s claim regarding sustained posterior synchrony and GNWT’s emphasis on late prefrontal ignition events.
papers.authors: Cogitate Consortium, Oscar Ferrante, Urszula Gorska-Klimowska, Simon Henin, Rony Hirschhorn, Aya Khalaf, Alex Lepauvre, Ling Liu, David Richter, Katarina Bendtz, Tara Ghafari, Dorottya Hetenyi, Jay Jeschke, Csaba Kozma, Ole Jensen, Gabriel Kreiman, Huan Luo, Melanie Boly, Stanislas Dehaene, Christof Koch, Giulio Tononi, Michael Pitts, Liad Mudrik, Lucia Melloni

papers.title: Towards a neuroethological approach to consciousness
papers.abstract: This article proposes a shift in consciousness research towards a neuroethological framework, applying Tinbergen’s four questions: mechanism, ontogeny, adaptive value, and phylogeny. The authors argue that current research is excessively human-centric, primarily focusing on verbal reports in neurotypical adults. By shifting toward an ethological perspective, researchers can investigate consciousness as an evolutionary continuum shaped by ecological pressures. The review emphasizes the importance of integrating neurophysiological metrics with naturalistic behavior to explore conscious states in non-verbal populations, including infants and non-human animals, thereby providing a more robust foundation for identifying the universal biological principles of subjective experience.
papers.venue: Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences
papers.authors: Yuranny Cabral-Calderin, Julio Hechavarria, Lucia Melloni

papers.title: “What” and “when” predictions jointly modulate speech processing
papers.abstract: This study examined the hierarchical integration of 'what' (content) and 'when' (temporal) regularities in auditory speech processing using magnetoencephalography (MEG). By manipulating statistical regularities at syllable and pseudoword levels, the authors demonstrated that temporal predictability at slower time scales selectively enhanced mismatch responses to deviant pseudowords, whereas faster scales modulated responses to syllables. Source reconstruction localized these hierarchical interactions to a shared frontoparietal network. Dynamic causal modeling (DCM) revealed that the integration of congruent content and timing predictions is mediated by hierarchical gain modulation within this distributed cortical network, rather than distinct anatomical levels for each temporal scale.
papers.authors: Ryszard Auksztulewicz, Ozan Bahattin Ödül, Saskia Helbling, Ana Böke, Drew Cappotto, Dan Luo, Jan Schnupp, Lucía Melloni

papers.title: Unpacking the complexities of consciousness: theories and reflections
papers.abstract: This review synthesizes the current state of consciousness science, focusing on the lack of convergence among major neuroscientific theories. The authors analyze prominent frameworks, including Global Neuronal Workspace (GNW) and Integrated Information Theory (IIT), against the backdrop of results from recent large-scale adversarial collaborations. The paper identifies critical points of theoretical divergence, such as the necessity of prefrontal involvement and the nature of neural synchronization. By highlighting the limitations of current empirical benchmarks, the authors propose a roadmap for more precise theory testing, calling for the development of quantitative, theory-neutral protocols to bridge the gap between competing explanatory models of subjective experience.
papers.authors: Liad Mudrik, Melanie Boly, Stanislas Dehaene, Stephen M. Fleming, Victor A.F. Lamme, Anil K. Seth, Lucia Melloni

papers.title: What you saw a while ago determines what you see now: The effect and temporal dynamics of awareness priming on implicit behavior
papers.abstract: Using Continuous Flash Suppression (CFS), this study investigated awareness priming, defined as the modulation of current perceptual access by previous conscious experiences. The researchers found that prior conscious exposure to words significantly increased both the subjective visibility and objective discrimination of stimuli presented at the threshold of awareness. A distinct temporal dissociation was identified: short-term history (1-10 previous trials) primarily boosted discrimination accuracy, while long-term history (10-30 trials) selectively enhanced subjective visibility. These findings suggest that areas lower in the cortical hierarchy support objective performance over short intervals, whereas higher-order regions with broader temporal integration windows mediate conscious awareness over extended periods.
papers.authors: Zefan Zheng, Darinka Trübutschek, Shuyue Huang, Yongchun Cai, Lucia Melloni

0408.name: M.D. Rutherford
0408.bio: M.D. Rutherford is a Professor and Chair of the Department of Psychology, Neuroscience & Behaviour at McMaster University, where they hold a Canada Research Chair in Social Perception. Rutherford’s research investigates the developmental and evolutionary foundations of social cognition, focusing on how humans process visual social cues such as eye gaze, facial expressions, and biological motion. Using eye-tracking and psychophysical methodologies, Rutherford studies social perception in typically developing infants and the early identification of autism spectrum disorders. Their work examines the mechanisms of visual adaptation, animacy detection, and the ontogeny of specialized cognitive systems for social navigation.
0408.research_direction: Dr. Rutherford has recently been investigating the developmental trajectories of social attention and face perception, primarily using longitudinal eye-tracking to study how infant gaze patterns relate to later autism traits. Specifically, their research explores how early visual preferences for distinct facial features—such as looking at the eyes or focusing on the mouth during speech—interact with the downstream development of theory of mind and expressive language in both neurotypical and neurodivergent populations. Beyond developmental vision, their recent work employs reverse correlation paradigms to extract classification images of social categories, investigating the internalized visual and phenotypic stereotypes people hold about scientists. Additionally, they are investigating broader evolutionary psychology topics outside of vision, using computational natural language processing to identify linguistic markers of reproductive timing and life history strategies within large-scale social media corpora.

papers.title: Picture a scientist: classification images of scientists are perceived as White, male, and socially inept
papers.abstract: Applying a reverse correlation (RC) paradigm, this research visualized internalized mental representations of social categories including "scientist," "hero," "genius," and "person." In the first phase, participants (N=20) completed a two-image forced-choice task to generate composite classification images (CIs). Phase 2 involved 251 naive participants rating these CIs on valenced traits (e.g., sociability, communication, competence) and demographic characteristics (race, gender). Results indicated that the scientist CI was predominantly perceived as White and male, aligning with persistent vocational stereotypes. Notably, scientists were rated significantly more negatively than the other categories, particularly regarding unsociability and poor communication skills, suggesting that negative biases toward scientists may have been exacerbated by the sociopolitical climate of the COVID-19 pandemic.
papers.authors: Maheen Shakil, Hasan Siddiqui, M.D. Rutherford

papers.title: Face perception and social cognitive development in early autism: A prospective longitudinal study from 3 months to 7 years of age
papers.abstract: This prospective longitudinal study (N=153) tracked the development of face perception and social cognition from age 3 months through 7 years, comparing typically developing (TD) infants and those who later met criteria for autism spectrum condition (ASC). Utilizing five eye-tracking face tasks during the first year, findings revealed that attenuated visual attention to eyes and direct gaze significantly predicted atypical adaptive behavior (measured via Vineland scales) at 4 years and impaired theory of mind (ToM) at 7 years. Principal component analysis indicated that ASC infants exhibit less integrated processing of facial topography and eye-gaze cues, highlighting a developmental cascade where early social perceptual deviations underpin long-term deficits in childhood social functioning.
papers.authors: Xiaomei Zhou, Hasan Siddiqui, M.D. Rutherford

papers.title: Preference for Eyes Predicts Later Autism-Related Characteristics in Children with a Family History of Autism
papers.abstract: Investigating prospective markers of neurodivergence, this study employed infrared eye-tracking to monitor visual preference for ocular regions in infants with a familial history of autism. Longitudinal analysis revealed that a significant developmental decline in eye preference across the first year of life served as a robust predictor of subsequent autism-related behavioral characteristics in early childhood. These data suggest that the trajectory of selective social attention—rather than static cross-sectional performance—is a critical biomarker for identifying neurodevelopmental shifts during the sensitive period of early infancy in high-risk populations.
papers.authors: Esin Gurcan, M.D. Rutherford

papers.title: Linguistic Markers of Faster Life History Strategies among Teen Parents on Reddit: A Comparative Analysis
papers.abstract: Grounded in Life History Theory, this study examined linguistic signatures of reproductive timing and environmental unpredictability using a large-scale corpus of social media data. A sample of 15,591 Reddit posts from teen parents and non-parent controls was processed via WMatrix5 for semantic field analysis. K-cluster analysis of 232 semantic sub-classifications demonstrated that teen parents exhibit significantly higher linguistic homogeneity and reduced emotional variability compared to age-matched peers. These findings suggest that early parenthood is associated with linguistic patterns reflecting a faster life history strategy, characterized by specific attachment markers and redirected social investment, discernible through computational natural language processing.
papers.authors: Sophia Melanson Ricciardone, Vinícius Betzel Koehler, M.D. Rutherford

papers.title: Autism Impairs the Language Development Benefits of Infants' Looking to the Mouth
papers.abstract: This longitudinal investigation assessed the predictive utility of early social attention for expressive language development across varying autism traits. Eye-tracking at 9–12 months quantified visual fixation on the mouth region of speaking faces. In infants with low autism traits, mouth-looking positively correlated with expressive language proficiency; however, this relationship was significantly inverted for infants with moderate-to-high autism traits (ADOS-2 scores > 12.74). These results suggest that while audiovisual synchrony at the mouth facilitates language acquisition in neurotypical development, it does not provide comparable sociocommunicative support for children on the autism spectrum, indicating divergent mechanisms of speech processing.
papers.authors: Esin Gürcan, Keshvi Bhatt, M.D. Rutherford

0410.name: Manish Singh
0410.department: Department of Psychology; Rutgers Center for Cognitive Science (RuCCS)
0410.bio: Manish Singh is a Professor of Psychology and Cognitive Science at Rutgers University who investigates the computational and psychological foundations of human vision. Singh’s research focuses on how the brain constructs three-dimensional representations of objects and surfaces from two-dimensional retinal images, specifically examining part-based shape representations, skeletal models, and object completion. By integrating psychophysical experiments with probabilistic Bayesian modeling, Singh examines phenomena such as transparency, illusory contours, and the visual prediction of physical object behavior. Their work also addresses theories of perception, including the interface theory of perception and the evolutionary logic of perceptual systems.
0410.research_direction: Dr. Singh's recent work explores how the human visual system relies on geometric constraints and evolutionary priors to interpret dynamic, ambiguous scenes. Through psychophysical experiments using random-dot kinematograms and dynamic rotating stimuli, they have recently been investigating how the brain integrates local optic flow with global contour geometry to resolve figure-ground depth, and how it recovers 3D structure from non-rigid motion. Specifically, their empirical research asks how shape priors like convexity interact with texture accretion, and whether observers default to interpreting non-rigid transformations as biologically plausible, articulated rigid motions. Alongside these psychophysical investigations, Dr. Singh is exploring broader theoretical questions regarding the Interface Theory of Perception, analyzing how the evolutionary tuning of perceptual systems for survival fitness—rather than strict veridicality—might fundamentally constrain the representational scope of our scientific theories.

papers.title: Perception, Evolution, and the Explanatory Scope of Scientific Theories
papers.abstract: This work evaluates the Interface Theory of Perception (ITP) and its implications for the foundational constraints of scientific theorizing. ITP suggests that natural selection has not tuned perceptual systems for veridicality but has instead shaped them into species-specific 'interfaces' designed to optimize fitness-payoffs. The authors argue that this evolutionary trajectory imposes a conceptual and structural bottleneck on scientific understanding, as theories are inherently formulated within the data formats provided by these interfaces (such as spacetime and discrete objects). Consequently, the explanatory reach of any scientific theory is fundamentally delimited by the non-veridical nature of human perception, suggesting that objective reality remains largely outside the representational scope of our current theoretical frameworks.
papers.authors: Donald D. Hoffman, Manish Singh

papers.title: Perceptual Biases in the Interpretation of Non-Rigid Shape Transformations from Motion
papers.abstract: This study investigates the computational constraints and perceptual biases that govern the recovery of 3D shape from non-rigid motion. While structure-from-motion (SFM) research typically focuses on rigid objects, many ecological entities, such as biological organisms, undergo non-rigid transformations. Through psychophysical experiments using stimuli with dynamic length changes during rotation, the authors demonstrate a systematic bias in the human visual system toward interpreting non-rigid motion as part-wise rigid. Specifically, observers reinterpreted image-plane length changes as variations in the angular orientation of a rigidly attached part relative to a main body. The findings are modeled using a geometric framework that suggests the visual system prioritizes interpretations consistent with the biological constraints of articulated motion over mathematically possible but ecologically rare non-rigid deformations.
papers.authors: Ryne Choi, Jacob Feldman, Manish Singh

papers.title: Interaction of contour geometry and optic flow in determining relative depth of surfaces
papers.abstract: This research examines the integration of boundary geometry and texture motion in the perception of dynamic occlusion and figure-ground assignment. Utilizing random-dot kinematograms, the authors manipulated the speed profile of texture near a boundary (accretion/deletion) and the geometry of the occluding contour (convexity vs. concavity). The experiments reveal that contour geometry (specifically convexity) acts as a dominant cue that can override traditional depth-from-motion indicators, such as the speed-gradient and accretion/deletion of texture. The results indicate that the visual system employs a complex interaction between local optic flow signals and global contour shape to resolve depth ordering, suggesting a Bayesian-like integration where shape-priors (convexity) exert significant influence on the interpretation of ambiguous motion signals.
papers.authors: Ömer Dağlar Tanrıkulu, Vicky Froyen, Jacob Feldman, Manish Singh

0412.name: Margaret Livingstone
0412.bio: Margaret Livingstone is the Takeda Professor of Neurobiology at Harvard Medical School and studies the functional organization and development of the primate visual system. Livingstone’s research, conducted in collaboration with David Hubel, identified parallel processing pathways for color, form, and motion within the visual cortex. Their current work investigates the plasticity of the inferotemporal cortex, examining how early visual experience and learning influence the formation of specialized domains such as face-selective patches. Using functional MRI, single-unit electrophysiology, and behavioral modeling, Livingstone explores the biological basis of object recognition and visual perception, including the neurobiology of artistic illusions and developmental dyslexia.
0412.research_direction: Dr. Livingstone's recent work explores the functional organization, development, and temporal dynamics of high-level object representations in the primate ventral stream. Using macaque single-unit electrophysiology, they have recently been investigating the neural mechanisms of face processing, probing how face-selective neurons respond to illusory "pareidolia" stimuli to isolate part-based versus holistic encoding, and examining how early visual deprivation impacts the long-term plasticity of the face-patch system. Their research also leverages naturalistic paradigms to study dynamic visual coding, recording from primary visual and inferotemporal (IT) cortices during free viewing to understand how feature selectivity is integrated and maintained across saccadic eye movements. Additionally, they are mapping functional homologies between macaque and human visual cortices by comparing single-unit natural scene responses to human fMRI data, while utilizing deep neural networks to model how the millisecond-by-millisecond temporal evolution of individual IT responses might recapitulate the broader hierarchical progression of the visual system.

papers.title: Response dynamics in macaque ventral stream recapitulate the visual hierarchy
papers.abstract: The temporal evolution of feature selectivity in macaque inferotemporal (IT) cortex was examined using chronic multielectrode arrays, revealing a systematic progression from simple to complex representations over the course of a single stimulus response. Early neuronal responses were characterized by brisk, transient activity correlating with the initial layers of deep neural networks (DNNs) and showing a preference for simpler, part-based features. In contrast, late-phase responses were more sustained and exhibited higher correlations with deeper DNN layers, reflecting a shift toward complex, integrated feature selectivity. This temporal cascade was accompanied by an increase in population sparseness, supporting the hypothesis that local cortical microcircuits utilize recurrent processing to iteratively refine high-level object representations. These findings suggest that the temporal dynamics within a single cortical area can recapitulate the hierarchical progression of the entire ventral visual stream.
papers.authors: Will Xiao, Kasper Vinken, Margaret S. Livingstone

papers.title: Mapping macaque to human cortex with natural scene responses
papers.abstract: Establishing functional homology between primate species is traditionally hampered by the use of low-dimensional, category-specific stimuli and predefined functional labels. We present a data-driven alignment framework that maps functional correspondence between macaque and human visual cortex using high-dimensional neural responses to a large battery of 700 natural scenes. By directly comparing macaque single-unit electrophysiology with human fMRI BOLD signals, we identified a fine-grained functional alignment based on response pattern similarity. This hypothesis-agnostic approach revealed that macaque face patches correspond to more anterior regions in the human temporal lobe than previously suggested by standard functional landmarks. These results demonstrate that naturalistic stimulation can uncover shared organizational principles across species without assuming the specific representational tuning of individual cortical regions.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS)
papers.authors: Kasper Vinken, Saloni Sharma, Margaret S. Livingstone

papers.title: Face cells encode object parts more than facial configuration of illusory faces
papers.abstract: The neural basis of face pareidolia—the perception of illusory faces in inanimate objects—was investigated in macaque inferotemporal (IT) cortex using single-unit electrophysiology. While face-selective neurons exhibited robust responses to pareidolia stimuli, their activity did not correlate with human behavioral faceness ratings. Crucially, the selectivity was found to be driven by local, generic object parts (e.g., 'eye-like' features) rather than the global, face-like configuration typically required for human perception. Disrupting the configural arrangement did not significantly attenuate the response of these units, indicating that the neural code for 'face cells' in the macaque emphasizes local diagnostic features over holistic structure. This finding reveals a fundamental misalignment between the feature-based encoding strategies of high-level visual neurons and the holistic nature of human face perception.
papers.authors: Saloni Sharma, Kasper Vinken, Akshay V. Jagadeesh, Margaret S. Livingstone

papers.title: Early face deprivation leads to long-lasting deficits in cortical face processing
papers.abstract: The impact of early experience on the development of the primate face-patch system was evaluated by comparing typically reared macaques with those deprived of face exposure during the first year of life. While face-selective domains eventually emerged in IT cortex following late exposure, the fine-grained neural tuning of these regions remained significantly impaired. Neurons in face-deprived animals exhibited mixed selectivity for faces and hands, as well as reduced precision in encoding face identity, expression, and viewpoint compared to controls. These findings indicate that while higher-order visual cortex retains the plasticity to acquire category selectivity outside of the initial critical period, early experience is indispensable for the formation of the specialized, high-fidelity neural representations necessary for expert-level facial processing.
papers.authors: Saloni Sharma, Margaret S. Livingstone

papers.title: Feature-selective responses in macaque visual cortex follow eye movements during natural vision
papers.abstract: We recorded neural activity from macaque primary visual cortex (V1) and inferotemporal (IT) cortex during naturalistic free viewing to determine how feature selectivity is maintained across saccadic eye movements. While V1 responses were primarily driven by immediate retinal input and exhibited transient selectivity, IT neurons maintained stable representations of preferred visual features across the saccade cycle. Notably, high-level neurons in IT displayed a 'look-ahead' effect, where activity reflected the features of the upcoming fixation target prior to saccade completion. These results demonstrate that the ventral stream actively integrates visual information across saccades, facilitating the maintenance of a stable, object-centered perceptual world during natural oculomotor behavior, a process that is obscured in traditional passive fixation paradigms.
papers.authors: Will Xiao, Saloni Sharma, Gabriel Kreiman, Margaret S. Livingstone

0414.name: Maria Robinson
0414.bio: Robinson investigates the mechanisms of visual cognition and memory using computational modeling and mathematical psychology. Their research focuses on the architecture of visual working memory, employing signal detection theory to evaluate discrete-slot capacity models and analyze how memory fidelity evolves across timescales. Robinson also examines ensemble perception and the integration of sensory evidence into cognitive representations through quantitative frameworks. In the field of metascience, they contribute to the development of measurement practices and the evaluation of auxiliary assumptions in psychological theory assessment.
0414.research_direction: Dr. Robinson has recently been investigating the computational mechanisms underlying visual memory and perception by leveraging representational geometry to make zero-free-parameter predictions of human behavior. Their recent work explores how observers combine category-level gist with item-specific details, and whether perceptual similarity spaces—derived from both human judgments and deep neural networks—can a priori predict the precise distributions of visual working memory errors. They are also examining ensemble perception, utilizing similarity-based competition models to understand how observers encode and retain access to continuous feature distributions rather than mere summary statistics. Additionally, their research spans broader methodological and theoretical evaluations, including dissecting core versus auxiliary assumptions in classic models of working memory capacity and probing whether graph-theoretic measures of semantic networks reflect genuine individual differences or task-specific heuristics.

papers.title: Bridging Bayesian and representational theories of memory to predict memory bias
papers.abstract: Explaining how memory representations evolve necessitates understanding how observers combine category-level gist with item-specific details. This work investigates how these representations interact in visual memory by integrating a normative Bayesian framework with algorithmic representational models of gist and individual item storage. To test the architecture's capacity to predict gist-induced systematic memory distortions, human participants completed separate tasks quantifying item-specific and gist memory, alongside independent behavioral assessments of representational stimulus space to parameterize memory fidelity. By transferring these empirically constrained parameters into the model without fitting, the framework generated zero-free-parameter predictions for a third task in which item memory was distorted by category structure. The model quantitatively predicted complete error distributions—including the magnitude, direction, variance, and skewness of biases across stimulus offsets—demonstrating that fusing Bayesian inference with empirical representational geometry captures how noisy memory traces are combined across hierarchical levels of abstraction.
papers.authors: Anxin Miao, Timothy F. Brady, Maria M. Robinson

papers.title: The Target Confusability Competition ensemble model predicts full feature distribution reports
papers.abstract: Recent empirical findings demonstrate that visual observers retain access to continuous distributions of ensemble features rather than mere summary statistics, challenging standard pooling accounts of ensemble perception. This paper shows that the Target Confusability Competition (TCC) ensemble model directly accounts for these distributional report data at a process level. Without free-parameter tuning or post hoc adjustment, the model leverages similarity-based encoding and activation summation in continuous feature space to quantitatively predict observer response distributions across Gaussian, uniform, and bimodal color sets. These results demonstrate that psychophysically scaled feature-similarity integration naturally affords access to rich distributional information in ensemble perception without requiring distinct summary-statistic extraction mechanisms.
papers.authors: Timothy F. Brady, Chattarin Poungtubtim, Maria M. Robinson

papers.title: Predicting visual working memory errors with a priori measures of representational geometry from human and artificial systems
papers.abstract: A foundational goal in cognitive science is determining whether the geometry of mental representations can generate quantitative, a priori predictions of visual working memory errors. Using independent pairwise human perceptual similarity judgments alongside representational distance matrices extracted from pretrained deep convolutional and vision transformer neural networks, the representational geometry of novel face stimuli and fundamental visual dimensions (color, shape, orientation, and spatial location) was characterized outside of any memory paradigm. When coupled with a single-parameter decision rule, these network- and human-derived geometries predicted complete continuous report error distributions—identifying which specific exemplars yield higher confusability—without fitting memory response data. The framework transferred successfully across 30 novel face sets and diverse feature dimensions, consistently outperforming standard mixture models and circular tuning-function models while reducing free parameters, demonstrating that representational geometry provides an a priori, falsifiable bridge between perceptual encoding and memory failure.
papers.authors: Timothy F. Brady, Maria M. Robinson

papers.title: Zooming in on what counts as core and auxiliary: A case study on recognition models of visual working memory
papers.abstract: Theoretical evaluation in cognitive psychology often conflates core theoretical principles with auxiliary methodological assumptions. Through an in-depth reanalysis of influential change-detection studies and their direct replications supporting discrete-capacity ('all-or-none' slot) models of visual working memory, this article highlights pervasive vulnerabilities in theory assessment. The investigation reveals that critical operational and statistical auxiliary assumptions—including the diagnostic efficacy of model-comparison criteria and response-bias invariances across memory loads—were systematically violated or unverified in the original datasets. Once these auxiliary assumptions are addressed and diagnostic testing conditions are restored, continuous-resource signal detection models decisively outperform discrete-slot architectures. The work provides a formal taxonomic guide for dissecting core versus auxiliary assumptions across different modeling stages and contextualizes the findings within contemporary metascience and computational discovery.
papers.authors: Maria M. Robinson, Jamal R. Williams, John T. Wixted, Timothy F. Brady

papers.title: Local but not global graph theoretic measures of semantic networks generalize across tasks
papers.abstract: Graph-theoretic methods are increasingly deployed to quantify individual differences in semantic memory networks and link topological properties to complex cognitive traits like creative cognition. However, it remains unsettled whether observed network metrics reflect genuine individual variation in semantic structure or task-specific retrieval heuristics. Across four behavioral experiments evaluating weighted and unweighted semantic networks derived from multiple relatedness tasks, local graph-theoretic metrics (such as fine-grained nodal distance and local edge weights between specific concept pairs) exhibited robust generalizability and test-retest reliability across paradigms. Conversely, macro-level global topological metrics—including average clustering coefficients and characteristic path lengths—failed to show consistent cross-task stability. These findings indicate that while local connectivity faithfully captures individual differences in semantic representations, global network indices may largely reflect task-dependent strategic processes.
papers.authors: Maria M. Robinson, Isabella C. DeStefano, Edward Vul, Timothy F. Brady

0415.name: Marianne Maertens
0415.department: Institute of Computer Engineering and Microelectronics, Department of Computational Psychology
0415.bio: Maertens is a Professor of Computational Psychology at Technische Universität Berlin, where they investigate how the human visual system transforms retinal stimulation into perceptual categories. Their research examines the mechanisms of lightness, transparency, and edge perception to analyze the relationship between objective visual performance and subjective experience. By combining experimental psychophysics with computational modeling, Maertens develops image-computable theories regarding how the brain interprets complex visual scenes. Maertens previously held research positions at New York University and the Max Planck Institute for Human Cognitive and Brain Sciences and received the Emmy Noether and Heisenberg fellowships.
0415.research_direction: Dr. Maertens has recently been investigating the computational and physiological mechanisms underlying human edge sensitivity and early spatial vision. Their recent work explores how well standard linear-nonlinear filter bank models predict psychophysical edge detection across varying spatial frequencies and visual noise conditions. To address the dynamic nature of active vision, they are examining whether integrating involuntary fixational eye movements—specifically ocular drift—into spatiotemporal neural models improves predictions of pattern vision compared to traditional stationary frameworks. Additionally, they have been working to bridge the gap between simplified parametric stimuli, like Cornsweet edges, and real-world perception by testing human-generated line drawings as a metric for evaluating edge sensitivity within complex naturalistic scenes.

papers.title: Line drawings as a tool to probe edge sensitivity in natural scenes
papers.abstract: This study evaluates the utility of human-generated line drawings as a metric for assessing edge sensitivity within naturalistic visual environments, moving beyond the traditional reliance on simplified, parametric stimuli. Observers performed a contour-tracing task on natural images subjected to various types of two-dimensional visual noise. Using a signal detection theory framework, individual edge traces from noise-free conditions established a ground-truth signal to quantify performance in noisy conditions through metrics such as d-prime and response bias. Findings indicate that noise interference patterns in natural scenes mirror those observed in traditional psychophysical studies using Cornsweet edges, particularly for edges whose spectral profiles align with natural image statistics. This consistency suggests that mechanisms identified in controlled paradigms generalize to complex scenes, positioning line drawings as a high-fidelity tool for characterizing real-world visual behavior and individual variability in edge perception.
papers.authors: Lynn Schmittwilken, Anna L. Haverkamp, Marianne Maertens

papers.title: Ocular drift shakes the stationary view on pattern vision
papers.abstract: The role of involuntary fixational eye movements, specifically ocular drift, is investigated in the context of human edge sensitivity. While traditional spatial vision models assume stationary retinal input during fixation, ocular drift dynamically redistributes stimulus power, emphasizing high spatial frequency content. The authors combined empirical edge sensitivity data obtained under visual noise with neural modeling to test if incorporating drift improved model predictions. Analysis revealed that drift-induced spectral shifts align with the human contrast sensitivity function (CSF), leading to superior data fitting compared to stationary assumptions. Mechanistic modeling further demonstrated that standard multi-scale architectures may artificially compensate for the absence of drift by redistributing activity across spatial frequency channels. These results argue for a transition from purely spatial models to spatiotemporal frameworks that recognize the active nature of visual sampling during fixation.
papers.authors: Lynn Schmittwilken, Marianne Maertens

papers.title: Standard models of spatial vision mispredict edge sensitivity at low spatial frequencies
papers.abstract: The standard model of early spatial vision, which employs orientation- and spatial frequency (SF)-selective channels followed by nonlinear recombination, is tested for its ability to account for psychophysical sensitivity to high-contrast edges. Using a 2-alternative forced-choice (2-AFC) localization task, the authors measured sensitivity to Cornsweet edges (peak SFs: 0.5, 3, and 9 cpd) in the presence of broadband and narrowband noise. Although single- and multi-scale versions of the standard model successfully predicted performance in many conditions, significant and systematic deviations were observed for the lowest SF edges and in the presence of pink noise. These failures suggest that the standard linear-nonlinear filter bank architecture may lack necessary components for processing broadband, behaviorally relevant stimuli, potentially indicating a shift from contrast-based to luminance-based detection mechanisms at low spatial frequencies.
papers.authors: Lynn Schmittwilken, Felix A. Wichmann, Marianne Maertens

0416.name: Marieke Mur
0416.department: Department of Psychology; Department of Computer Science; Brain and Mind Institute
0416.bio: Mur is an Assistant Professor at Western University with joint appointments in the Department of Psychology and the Department of Computer Science. Their research integrates psychology, neuroscience, and artificial intelligence to study how the human brain transforms visual input into representations. Using high-field functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), psychophysics, and deep neural networks, Mur investigates the neural population codes and representational geometries that support object recognition. Mur contributed to the development of representational similarity analysis (RSA), a framework used to connect brain-activity patterns, computational models, and behavioral measures.
0416.research_direction: Dr. Mur has recently been investigating the functional organization and computational mechanisms underlying both high-level cognition and visual perception. Their recent work explores the spatial organization of the primate lateral prefrontal cortex, utilizing multi-electrode arrays and a novel Topographic Similarity Analysis framework to investigate how neural topographies adapt to shifting cognitive task demands. In parallel, they are employing deep neural networks trained on various object individuation tasks to probe whether classic perceptual phenomena, such as the face inversion effect, stem from domain-specific or domain-general processing mechanisms. To further uncover fine-grained cortical computations, Dr. Mur is also developing new high-resolution neuroimaging methodologies, testing frequency-tagged fMRI techniques to map stimulus-driven spatiotemporal neural dynamics in the human visual cortex.

papers.title: Toward task mapping of primate prefrontal cortex
papers.abstract: The lateral prefrontal cortex (LPFC) is characterized by its capacity to underpin a diverse array of cognitive functions, including inhibitory control, decision-making, and working memory. In contrast to neurons within sensory cortical regions, LPFC units demonstrate adaptive coding, where neural tuning dynamically reconfigures to represent task-relevant information across various domains. Such context-dependent responsiveness presents a significant challenge to conventional functional mapping methodologies. This article proposes a paradigm shift from stimulus-based mapping to 'task mapping' in the LPFC. We discuss the inherent structural and functional complexities of this region, such as integrative connectivity, dynamic tuning properties, and expansive spatiotemporal receptive fields. To address these, we introduce Topographic Similarity Analysis (TSA)—a framework derived from representational similarity analysis (RSA)—designed to detect and characterize functional topographies. We further discuss the capacity of TSA to identify the reorganization of neural topographies in response to learning and shifting task demands, and its potential extension to human high-field fMRI to delineate the cognitive dimensions of LPFC function.
papers.authors: Jinkang Derrick Xiang, Julio C. Martinez-Trujillo, Taylor W. Schmitz, Marieke Mur

papers.title: Frequency-tagged fMRI: A platform for fine-grained spatiotemporal analysis of cortical function
