papers.abstract: We introduce and validate frequency-tagged functional MRI (ft-fMRI) as a high-resolution technique for mapping neural dynamics by synchronizing oscillatory stimuli with stimulus-driven BOLD responses. Utilizing a dual-frequency tagging protocol at 3T and 7T, we dissociated fundamental, multiplexed, and nonlinear intermodulation frequency responses within the human visual cortex at the level of individual vertices. The analysis revealed robust temporal synchronization and fine-grained cortical topographies. Specifically, we identified spatially dissociable populations of vertices that encoded multiple frequencies simultaneously (multiplexed) and others exhibiting nonlinear intermodulation components, showing reproducible dynamics across experimental sessions. By bridging the spatiotemporal resolution gap between traditional fMRI and electrophysiology, ft-fMRI provides a powerful platform for investigating fine-grained cortical computations underlying perception and multisensory integration.
papers.authors: Geoffrey N. Ngo, Reebal W. Rafeh, Lyle E. Muller, Ali R. Khan, Ravi S. Menon, Taylor W. Schmitz, Marieke Mur

papers.title: The face inversion effect through the lens of deep neural networks
papers.abstract: This work evaluates the longstanding debate regarding whether the face inversion effect (FIE) is the result of domain-specific processing mechanisms specialized for faces or domain-general mechanisms associated with perceptual expertise in individuating stimuli. Using deep neural networks (DNNs) as computational models, specifically VGG-16, we examined the impact of different training regimes on the emergence of inversion effects. By training networks to individuate either faces or non-face objects (e.g., birds), we analyzed the similarity of representations in the penultimate layer for upright versus inverted images. The results demonstrate that face-like inversion effects observed for objects of expertise, traditionally cited as evidence for domain-general accounts, can arise from domain-specific optimization. The findings suggest that the behavioral signatures of human face perception are well-explained by optimization for individuation tasks and that the underlying computations may not be unique to the face domain.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences
papers.authors: Ehsan Tousi, Marieke Mur

papers.title: Task-specific topographic maps of neural activity in the primate lateral prefrontal cortex
papers.abstract: The functional organization of the lateral prefrontal cortex (LPFC) remains poorly understood, particularly regarding whether activity topographies are stable or adapt to varying task demands. We characterized the functional topography of LPFC neural activity in rhesus macaques using chronically implanted multi-electrode arrays while the animals performed three distinct cognitive tasks: oculomotor delayed response (ODR), visuospatial working memory (VWM), and context-dependent decision making (CDM). We applied Topographic Similarity Analysis (TSA) to quantify the similarity of task tuning across electrodes. Our findings reveal that functional maps of neural population activity are remarkably stable within a given task across multiple sessions but adapt dynamically between different tasks. The topography exhibited a spatial scale consistent with afferent LPFC input patterns and cortical columns. These results indicate that LPFC topographic maps provide robust neural codes for task specialization while maintaining the flexibility to reorganize for different cognitive requirements.
papers.authors: Jinkang Derrick Xiang, Megan Roussy, Benjamin Corrigan, Roberto A. Gulli, Rogelio Luna, Maryam Hasanzadeh Mofrad, Lyle Muller, Jörn Diedrichsen, Taylor W. Schmitz, Julio Martinez-Trujillo, Marieke Mur

0417.name: Marion Rouault
0417.bio: Marion Rouault is a Chargée de Recherche at the CNRS, based at the Paris Brain Institute (ICM), where they investigate the neurocognitive architecture of human metacognition. Rouault's research explores how individuals monitor their own cognitive processes, specifically focusing on the computational mechanisms that transform local confidence signals into global self-beliefs and self-esteem. Using behavioral psychophysics, computational modeling, and neuroimaging techniques such as fMRI and MEG, Rouault examines the functional roles of these signals in learning and decision-making. Their work also addresses the clinical implications of metacognitive efficiency in psychiatric disorders, aiming to characterize how self-evaluation impairments relate to mental health symptoms.
0417.research_direction: Dr. Rouault has recently been investigating the computational structure of metacognition, focusing on how humans evaluate their own cognitive performance across different levels of abstraction. Their recent work explores the relationship between local, trial-by-trial confidence judgments and broader, global self-performance estimates using psychophysical tasks across perceptual and memory domains. By employing hierarchical Bayesian modeling, they are examining whether specific metacognitive capacities—such as overall confidence biases versus the precise sensitivity to distinguish correct from incorrect decisions—function as stable, domain-general traits or domain-specific skills. Furthermore, they are applying these theoretical distinctions to applied, real-world contexts by investigating how metacognitive bias and sensitivity operate in physicians during complex medical decision-making.

papers.title: Physicians’ metacognition in medical decision-making
papers.abstract: This study addresses the widespread belief that physicians are prone to overconfidence in clinical settings, a factor often implicated in diagnostic errors. Using a controlled experimental framework, the authors distinguish between metacognitive bias—the absolute tendency to report high or low confidence—and metacognitive sensitivity—the precision with which confidence judgments differentiate between correct and incorrect outcomes. Fifty-two physicians completed a series of clinical case-vignettes involving headache diagnosis. The analysis revealed that while physicians exhibit a pronounced overconfidence bias, their underlying metacognitive sensitivity remains remarkably high, indicating that they possess significant insight into the accuracy of their individual decisions. These results suggest that medical errors may be driven by global calibration errors rather than an inherent lack of evaluative capacity.
papers.authors: Camille Lakhlifi, Rayan Kouzy, François-Xavier Lejeune, Nicolas Beuzon, Jérôme Mawet, Caroline Roos, Mehdi Khamassi, Benjamin Rohaut, Marion Rouault

papers.title: Isolating domain-specific and domain-general contributions to global confidence
papers.abstract: Human self-monitoring operates across a hierarchy of abstraction, ranging from local decision confidence to global self-performance estimates (SPEs). This investigation aimed to determine whether these hierarchical levels of metacognition are domain-specific or represent stable individual traits. Participants performed psychophysical tasks in memory and perceptual domains while providing trial-by-trial confidence ratings and periodic global performance assessments. Computational modeling demonstrated that metacognitive efficiency (M-ratio) is idiosyncratic to the task domain, showing no significant correlation across tasks. However, metacognitive bias was found to be a stable individual characteristic that generalizes across domains. These findings provide evidence for a dual-process model of self-belief formation, where domain-specific evaluative signals are integrated with domain-general dispositions to form stable global self-beliefs.
papers.authors: Sophie Bavard, Andrew McWilliams, Flora Chartier, Karim N’Diaye, Stephen M. Fleming, Marion Rouault

papers.title: A hierarchy of metacognitive capacities
papers.abstract: This research explores the neurocomputational structure of metacognition by bridging local, decision-level confidence with global, higher-order self-performance estimates (SPEs). By matching performance across memory and perceptual discrimination tasks, the authors examined how participants aggregate local confidence signals into broader evaluations of their own abilities. The results reveal a double dissociation in the hierarchy: metacognitive monitoring efficiency is highly domain-specific, while the general level of confidence (metacognitive bias) is stable across task types. By formalizing these relationships within a hierarchical Bayesian framework, the study elucidates how local inefficiencies may be buffered or amplified when forming global self-beliefs, with potential implications for the understanding of self-evaluation distortions in psychiatric and aging populations.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the Cognitive Computational Neuroscience (CCN) 2024
papers.authors: Sophie Bavard, Andrew McWilliams, Flora Chartier, Stephen M. Fleming, Marion Rouault

0418.name: Marisa Carrasco
0418.department: Department of Psychology and Center for Neural Science
0418.bio: Marisa Carrasco is the Julius Silver Professor of Psychology and Neural Science at New York University, where they investigate the relationship between the psychological and neural mechanisms of vision. Carrasco’s research utilizes human psychophysics, functional neuroimaging (fMRI), neurostimulation (TMS), and computational modeling to characterize how attention modulates early visual processing and alters the subjective appearance of stimuli. Their work distinguishes between endogenous and exogenous attention and documents how attentional mechanisms interact with sensory factors like spatial resolution and contrast sensitivity to shape perceptual performance.
0418.research_direction: Dr. Carrasco's recent work explores the complex interactions between covert attention, spatial perceptual asymmetries, and oculomotor dynamics. They have recently been investigating how spatial vision inherently varies around the visual field—such as through horizontal-vertical or vertical meridian asymmetries—and whether these intrinsic constraints differ across primate species or can be mitigated by visual adaptation and spatial cueing. In addition to spatial vision, their research examines whether the transient perceptual enhancements driven by exogenous attention, like apparent contrast boosts, are preserved when sensory representations are transferred into visual working memory. Finally, Dr. Carrasco investigates the temporal mechanisms of visual processing and sensory evidence accumulation by tracking how perceptual task difficulty and temporal expectations uniquely modulate pupillary responses and fixational eye movements, particularly microsaccades.

papers.title: Covert spatial attention is uniform across cardinal meridians despite differential adaptation
papers.abstract: The primate visual system manages limited bioenergetic resources through mechanisms of visual adaptation and covert spatial attention. Given that visual perception is heterogeneous across the visual field—exhibiting a horizontal–vertical anisotropy (HVA) and a vertical meridian asymmetry (VMA)—and that visual adaptation is more pronounced at the horizontal than the vertical meridian, this study investigated whether such differential adaptation modulates the efficacy of attention. Using an orientation discrimination task at isoeccentric cardinal locations, we manipulated endogenous (voluntary) and exogenous (involuntary) attention via informative central or uninformative peripheral cues, respectively. While adaptation significantly reduced contrast sensitivity more along the horizontal than the vertical meridian, mitigating the HVA, both types of attention enhanced performance at attended locations and impaired it at unattended locations to a uniform degree across all cardinal meridians. These results demonstrate that the compensatory potential of covert spatial attention is limited; it does not flexibly adjust to resolve intrinsic or adaptation-induced perceptual asymmetries around the visual field.
papers.authors: Hsing-Hao Lee, Marisa Carrasco

papers.title: Transient increases to apparent contrast by exogenous attention persist in visual working memory
papers.abstract: Exogenous attention is known to transiently enhance the perceived contrast of visual stimuli. According to the sensory recruitment hypothesis, visual working memory (VWM) maintenance utilizes the same early cortical infrastructure as online perception. We tested whether the attentional boost to apparent contrast is preserved when stimuli are encoded into VWM. Using a delayed contrast comparison task with exogenous pre-cues, we applied model comparisons to evaluate the persistence of attentional effects. Our findings reveal that the reflexive attentional increase in perceived contrast does not decay during the maintenance period but is instead stored as a persistent 'snapshot' in VWM. This result indicates that VWM representations are reformatted from the attentionally modulated perceptual state at the time of encoding, supporting theories of shared neural mechanisms between perception, attention, and memory maintenance.
papers.authors: Luke Huszar, Tair Vizel, Marisa Carrasco

papers.title: Opposite asymmetry in visual perception of humans and macaques
papers.abstract: Visual performance in humans is characterized by robust polar angle asymmetries, including superior sensitivity along the horizontal than vertical meridian (HVA) and along the lower than upper vertical meridian (VMA). We investigated whether the macaque monkey, the primary animal model for human vision, exhibits similar constraints using a two-alternative forced-choice motion direction discrimination task. While both species showed heterogeneous sensitivity around the visual field, they displayed a striking divergence in the vertical meridian asymmetry: whereas human observers exhibited the typical VMA with poorest sensitivity at the upper vertical meridian, adult macaques (Macaca nemestrina) revealed an inverted VMA, with their sensitivity being poorest in the lower vertical meridian. This species-specific inversion may reflect distinct evolutionary adaptations in visuomotor integration and highlights the necessity of accounting for polar angle dependencies when modeling primate visual systems.
papers.authors: Ekin Tünçok, Lynne Kiorpes, Marisa Carrasco

papers.title: Temporal attention and oculomotor effects dissociate distinct types of temporal expectation
papers.abstract: Temporal expectation, the probabilistic prediction of when an event will occur, relies on two distinct temporal structures: hazard rate (the increasing conditional probability of an event over time) and temporal precision (the variability of an event's onset). We investigated the interaction between these expectations and voluntary temporal attention at the behavioral and oculomotor levels. Our results demonstrate a dissociation in fixational eye movements: while hazard-based expectations were independently reflected in microsaccade dynamics, precision-based expectations only modulated oculomotor behavior when temporal attention was concurrently deployed. Furthermore, we identified perception–eye movement dissociations for both expectation types, although the performance benefits of attention consistently coincided with systematic modulations in microsaccade rates. These findings suggest that the brain utilizes distinct neural computations to integrate different temporal regularities for enhancing perceptual performance and maintaining fixational stability.
papers.authors: Aysun Duyar, Marisa Carrasco

papers.title: Eyes on hold: motion task difficulty jointly delays microsaccade and pupil responses
papers.abstract: Microsaccades and pupil diameter exhibit characteristic temporal profiles in response to task-relevant stimuli, typically involving a period of inhibition followed by a rebound. We investigated how task difficulty in a motion direction discrimination task (manipulated via cardinal vs. oblique directions and varying tilt offsets) modulates these dynamics. Psychophysical results showed that higher task difficulty led to more robust and prolonged microsaccade inhibition, resulting in significantly delayed rebounds. Concurrently, pupillary responses in more difficult conditions were characterized by both higher peak amplitudes and delayed peak latencies. The significant correlation between the timing of microsaccade rebounds, peak pupil dilation, and behavioral response times suggests that these oculomotor and autonomic signals are driven by a common neural mechanism for sensory evidence accumulation. These findings establish that the temporal dynamics of fixational eye movements and pupil responses serve as sensitive indices for the duration and intensity of perceptual decision-making processes.
papers.authors: Rania Ezzo, Bochen Song, Bas Rokers, Marisa Carrasco

0419.name: Mark B. Neider
0419.bio: Mark B. Neider is a Professor and the Interim Chair of the Department of Psychology at the University of Central Florida and directs the Applied Cognition and Aging Laboratory. Neider’s research examines the mechanisms of human perception and cognition in complex contexts, focusing on the interaction between attentional and memory systems. Neider utilizes methodologies such as high-fidelity driving simulation, virtual reality, eye tracking, and electroencephalography (EEG) to study behavior throughout the lifespan. Their work focuses on developing evidence-based training interventions and technological solutions intended to improve performance and safety in high-stakes environments.
0419.research_direction: Dr. Neider has recently been investigating the mechanisms of attentional guidance and distractor suppression using complex, naturalistic stimuli. Their recent work explores whether proactive inhibitory control extends beyond simple, low-level visual features to high-level object categories, probing the boundary conditions of this categorical suppression under varying set sizes and display complexities. Additionally, they are examining how the proportional distribution of multiple colors within real-world targets guides initial saccades, developing new computational tools to precisely quantify and manipulate these chromatic properties for rigorous experimental control. Finally, they have been applying these fundamental principles of visual search to human-computer interaction, using oculomotor tracking to investigate how visual characteristics like icon concreteness and complexity impact cognitive load and user performance.

papers.title: MATCH: A toolbox to assess the primary color of real-world objects and generate color-matching stimuli
papers.abstract: This research introduces Matching And Transforming Closely Hued objects (MATCH), a computational toolbox designed to facilitate the objective quantification and manipulation of chromatic properties in real-world stimuli for experimental psychology. Addressing the inherent limitations of subjective color labeling, MATCH integrates theoretical frameworks from visual cognition to provide high-precision metrics on color distribution and specific coordinates within a stimulus set. Across two validation studies, we demonstrated that stimuli generated by MATCH were perceptually more proximal to reference objects than those categorized by human observers. Further, a visual search experiment utilizing MATCH-generated distractors yielded data consistent with contemporary models of attentional guidance, confirming the toolbox's utility in providing rigorous control over chromatic variables in naturalistic search paradigms.
papers.authors: Jessica N. Goetz, Mark B. Neider

papers.title: Top-down categorical information can be utilized in distractor suppression
papers.abstract: The mechanisms of distractor suppression were investigated to determine if proactive inhibitory control extends beyond first-order visual features to high-level categorical information. Through three experiments, we replicated classical suppression effects using categorical objects rather than simple salience-based singletons. In Experiment 1, we established that categorical cues elicit behavioral benefits consistent with proactive suppression. Experiment 2 controlled for stimulus salience, revealing significantly attenuated response times (RTs) when a specifically cued distractor category was present in the display. Experiment 3 demonstrated the preservation of these effects within modified target sets. These findings suggest that the attentional system does not rely solely on target feature weighting but actively utilizes top-down categorical knowledge to inhibit task-irrelevant distractors.
papers.authors: Jessica N. Goetz, Mark B. Neider

papers.title: How robust is categorial distractor suppression? Assessing the impact of additional categories and increased set size
papers.abstract: This study evaluated the boundary conditions of categorical distractor suppression by increasing ecological complexity through the expansion of distractor categories and display set sizes. Across three experiments, participants performed a visual search task for specific target orientations embedded among categorical objects. We observed robust distractor suppression effects (faster RTs on trials containing cued distractor categories) when the number of categories was increased (Experiment 1) and when set sizes were moderately increased (Experiment 2). However, suppression effects were no longer significant when both category count and set size were simultaneously increased (Experiment 3). The results indicate that while categorical suppression is a robust mechanism in many contexts, its efficacy is constrained by task complexity, potentially leading observers to adopt alternative search strategies under high processing demands.
papers.authors: Jessica N. Goetz, Mark B. Neider

papers.title: Proportion of colour proportionally affects guidance in search for conjunction and real-world objects
papers.abstract: Traditional models of visual search often utilize simple, monochromatically defined stimuli, yet naturalistic objects frequently comprise multiple colors in varying ratios. We investigated how the proportional distribution of color features within an object modulates attentional guidance. In Experiment 1, we utilized color conjunctions with defined primary and secondary color proportions (e.g., 70-30 or 90-10). In Experiment 2, real-world objects were objectively classified via color histograms to establish dominant and subordinate chromatic components. Our results indicate that search is guided in parallel by multiple target colors, but the degree of guidance is strictly contingent upon the proportion of those colors. Specifically, target-matching primary colors elicited stronger initial saccadic guidance compared to secondary colors, demonstrating that the attentional system weights feature guidance proportionally based on the stimulus's internal feature distribution.
papers.authors: Jessica N. Goetz, Mark B. Neider

papers.title: Keep it real, keep it simple: the effects of icon characteristics on visual search
papers.abstract: This study addressed the conflicting evidence regarding the impact of icon concreteness, visual complexity, and distinctiveness on visual search performance in human-computer interfaces. We operationalized concreteness into three discrete levels: concrete (real-world object imagery), photorealistic (representative drawings), and abstract (no conceptual information). Using oculomotor tracking, we analyzed search and verification phases for icons varying in these dimensions. The results demonstrated that icons with high concreteness significantly facilitated search performance by enhancing target template matching. However, increased visual complexity was found to incur substantial identification costs, evidenced by prolonged verification times. The findings suggest that effective interface design should prioritize highly concrete yet visually simple icons to optimize user interaction and minimize cognitive load during search tasks.
papers.authors: Jessica N. Goetz, Mark B. Neider

0421.name: Mark D. Lescroart
0421.bio: Mark D. Lescroart is a neuroscientist and associate professor at the University of Nevada, Reno, specializing in the computational modeling of human visual perception. Lescroart’s research employs voxel-wise encoding models, fMRI, and deep neural networks to investigate how the brain transforms retinal input into representations of 3D scene structure, object geometry, and human actions. They have conducted studies on the neural encoding of medial axis structures and the identification of body-selective regions in the visual periphery. Their current research, supported by an NSF CAREER award, explores how task-related attentional states modulate visual representations and involves the development of the Visual Experience Database (VEDB).
0421.research_direction: Dr. Lescroart has recently been investigating the neural representations of complex visual features while advancing the computational tools used to study visual processing and behavior. Their recent fMRI work explores how the visual cortex encodes the identity and spatial location of human bodies during naturalistic viewing, utilizing voxel-wise encoding models to probe distributed feature topographies and investigate newly identified body-selective regions tuned to the visual periphery. Concurrently, they are developing methods to interpret deep neural network models of the visual system, creating image-computable frameworks that synthesize targeted "superstimuli" designed to selectively drive specific cortical responses. Alongside these neuroimaging efforts, Dr. Lescroart is also refining behavioral measurement methodologies by designing robust, deep learning-based eye-tracking systems that leverage synthetic data and advanced augmentation to precisely estimate gaze and pupil parameters under challenging real-world conditions.

papers.title: Novel Body-Selective Regions Responsive to Bodies Away from the Center of Gaze
papers.abstract: This study identifies two previously unidentified cortical regions in the human visual system that exhibit specialized selectivity for images of human bodies located in the visual periphery. Utilizing high-resolution 7T fMRI data from the Natural Scenes Dataset (NSD) and voxel-wise encoding models, the researchers localized the Ventromedial Body Area (VMBA) and the Medial Body Area (MBA). Unlike the well-known Extrastriate Body Area (EBA) and Fusiform Body Area (FBA), these regions—situated posterior to the parahippocampal place area (PPA) and superior to the retrosplenial complex (RSC) near the parieto-occipital sulcus—respond optimally to bodies viewed away from the center of gaze, suggesting a neural substrate for processing social and action-related information in the peripheral field.
papers.authors: Yu Zhao, Matthew W. Shinkle, Mark D. Lescroart

papers.title: Visualizing and Controlling Cortical Responses Using Voxel-Weighted Activation Maximization
papers.abstract: The authors introduce Voxel-Weighted Activation Maximization (VWAM), a technique for interpreting deep neural network (DNN)-based encoding models of the human brain. By mapping activations from multiple layers of a pretrained Inception V3 network to fMRI BOLD responses using linear regression, the method creates an image-computable model of the visual cortex. VWAM utilizes gradient-based optimization to synthesize stimuli that maximize predicted responses in individual voxels and entire regions of interest (ROIs). Validation in an fMRI study demonstrated that these generated 'superstimuli' reliably and selectively drive activity in both early and higher-level visual areas, providing a flexible framework for characterizing and modulating human cortical representations without the need for natively generative models.
papers.authors: Matthew W. Shinkle, Mark D. Lescroart

papers.title: LEyes: A lightweight framework for deep learning-based eye tracking using synthetic eye images
papers.abstract: LEyes is introduced as a novel, computationally efficient framework for gaze estimation that overcomes the bottleneck of manual data annotation by utilizing on-the-fly generation of synthetic eye images. This system adapts to various recording devices and incorporates physiologically accurate 3D eye models to simulate realistic variations in lighting and camera position. Evaluations across multiple public datasets show that LEyes-trained models frequently outperform conventional eye-tracking algorithms in identifying pupil centroids and corneal reflections. The framework offers a scalable solution for high-precision eye tracking in naturalistic contexts using low-cost hardware, effectively bridging the gap between simulated training environments and real-world application diversity.
papers.authors: Arnab Biswas, Mark D. Lescroart

papers.title: Voxelwise Modeling Reveals Selectivity for Body Part Identity and Location in BOLD fMRI Responses to Complex Naturalistic Stimuli
papers.abstract: This research investigates the representation of human body parts and their spatial locations in the lateral occipitotemporal cortex (LOTC) using a large-scale encoding model approach. The researchers employed a deep neural network (OpenPose) to parameterize the identities and positions of body parts across diverse stimulus sets, including natural movie clips and computer-rendered scenes. Regularized linear regression was used to fit these quantified features to BOLD fMRI signals. The findings reveal a complex, distributed pattern of tuning within LOTC that encompasses both the identity of body components and their retinotopic or relative coordinates, challenging simple modular accounts of body representation and providing evidence for a more integrated topography of body-related features in the human brain.
papers.authors: Matthew W. Shinkle, Mark D. Lescroart

papers.title: A framework for generalizable neural networks for robust estimation of eyelids and pupils
papers.abstract: This paper presents pylids, a deep learning framework designed to improve the accuracy and robustness of video-oculography under challenging imaging conditions. Built upon the DeepLabCut architecture, the model addresses the scarcity of labeled training data by leveraging algorithmic annotations from high-quality eye videos and employing domain-specific data augmentation, such as simulated reflections and occlusions. The authors demonstrate that the performance of the DNN can be predicted based on the distributional distance between training and test data. By implementing guided sampling strategies and data pruning, the framework achieves state-of-the-art results in pupil and eyelid localization while requiring significantly fewer training samples and enhancing generalization to real-world, noisy datasets.
papers.authors: Arnab Biswas, Mark D. Lescroart

0422.name: Mark Greenlee
0422.department: Department of Experimental Psychology and Methodology
0422.bio: Mark Greenlee is the Chair of Experimental Psychology and Methodology at the University of Regensburg and co-director of the institution's Magnetic Resonance Imaging Center. Greenlee’s research examines the neural mechanisms underlying human visual and vestibular processing, focusing on self-motion perception and visual-vestibular integration. Using high-field fMRI, EEG, and psychophysical techniques, Greenlee investigates cortical plasticity, population receptive field mapping, and the effects of training on visual crowding. Their work also includes the study of cognitive functions such as visual short-term memory, attention, and the neural correlates of perceptual filling-in.
0422.research_direction: Dr. Greenlee's recent work explores how the visual system encodes, maintains, and integrates information across diverse perceptual and cognitive contexts. They have recently been investigating early visual processing mechanisms by mapping the spatiotemporal parameters of the contour erasure effect and perceptual filling-in, while also exploring multisensory integration by testing how task-irrelevant, semantically congruent olfactory cues modulate visual search efficiency. In the domain of working memory, their research examines the precision of visual short-term memory for motion direction using random dot kinematograms, specifically modeling how action video game experience might alter neural resource allocation across different retention delays. Additionally, Dr. Greenlee leverages fMRI to study cognitive control in dynamic settings, measuring how the default mode network and posterior cingulate cortex respond to unpredictable technological errors and system-induced stress during task performance.

papers.title: Visual search performance depends on the congruency of olfactory sensations
papers.abstract: This research investigates the multisensory influence of olfaction on visual search efficiency in a cluttered environment. Utilizing a specialized four-channel olfactometer, participants were exposed to suprathreshold fruit odorants (lemon, apple, or strawberry) or neutral air while identifying target fruit images among distractors. The results demonstrate a significant performance benefit—characterized by higher accuracy and reduced response latencies—when the odorant was semantically congruent with the visual target. Conversely, incongruent odorants or neutral air did not facilitate search. Post-hoc analysis revealed that individual differences in baseline visual search capability moderated the effect: participants with lower initial performance derived the greatest benefit from congruent multisensory cues, while high performers exhibited disruption when exposed to incongruent sensations. These findings suggest that task-irrelevant olfactory inputs can dynamically modulate early visual processing and attention, effectively increasing the saliency of congruent visual targets.
papers.authors: Serena Castellotti, Marija Soldo, Tina Plank, Maria Michela Del Viva, Mark W. Greenlee

papers.title: The spatial and temporal properties of the contour erasure effect and perceptual filling-in
papers.abstract: The contour erasure effect is a perceptual phenomenon where flicker adaptation at an object's boundary causes the object to vanish and be replaced by the background. This study characterized the spatial and temporal parameters governing this effect using a two-alternative forced-choice (2AFC) paradigm following adaptation to flickering ring-shaped contours. The magnitude of adaptation was found to increase with stimulus eccentricity and flicker rate (reaching a plateau at 6 Hz), as well as with longer adaptation durations. Conversely, the effect diminished with increased interstimulus intervals and when adapter sizes exceeded the target dimensions. Size-tuning analysis revealed that adaptation was most potent when the adapter was slightly smaller than the target disk, indicating specific lateral interactions. The data suggest that contour erasure shares fundamental mechanisms with contrast adaptation and scotoma filling-in, likely originating in early visual areas within the magnocellular pathway.
papers.authors: Yih-Shiuan Lin, Chien-Chung Chen, Mark W. Greenlee

papers.title: Visual short-term memory in action and non-action video game players: A focus on short and long delay intervals
papers.abstract: This study examined the precision of visual short-term memory (VSTM) for motion direction in action video game players (AVGPs) versus non-action video game players (NAVGPs). Participants performed a continuous reproduction task for the direction of random dot kinematograms (RDKs) following short (0.5 s) or long (3 s) retention intervals. While AVGPs generally required fewer training blocks to achieve task proficiency, the primary focus was on the precision of memory representations across different delays. Applying a resource-rational model (RRM), the authors analyzed the trade-off between behavioral precision and neural encoding costs. The findings indicate that while NAVGPs showed significant precision decay at long delays due to a higher weighting of neural costs during encoding, AVGPs demonstrated more efficient resource allocation, maintaining stable and high-precision memory traces over extended intervals. These results suggest that long-term action video game experience facilitates more robust encoding and retention strategies in the visual system.
papers.authors: Andrea Pavan, Seyma Koc Yilmaz, Hulusi Kafaligonul, Julia Föcker, Mark W. Greenlee

papers.title: Dynamic modulation of the processing of unpredicted technical errors by the posterior cingulate and the default mode network
papers.abstract: Technostress arising from unpredicted system failures was investigated through functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) while participants solved arithmetic problems. Two types of spontaneous runtime errors were introduced: 'problem errors' (distorted stimuli) and 'feedback errors' (erroneous performance reports). Behavioral data indicated that these unpredicted events significantly elevated response times and error rates in subsequent trials. On a neural level, the occurrence of unexpected errors triggered increased blood oxygen level-dependent (BOLD) responses in the posterior cingulate cortex (PCC) and nodes of the default mode network (DMN), regions typically associated with monitoring internal states and environmental changes. The results suggest that the PCC plays a critical regulatory role in the human response to technological unreliability, coordinating the redistribution of cognitive resources to cope with system-induced stress and maintain task performance under dynamic environmental demands.
papers.authors: Zhiyan Wang, Markus Becker, Gregor Kondla, Henner Gimpel, Anton L. Beer, Mark W. Greenlee

0423.name: Mark J. Fenske
0423.bio: Mark J. Fenske is a Professor of Psychology at the University of Guelph and directs the Cognitive-Affective Neuroscience Lab. Fenske’s research investigates the neurocognitive interface of attention, emotion, and motivation, specifically how cognitive control mechanisms like inhibition influence the emotional evaluation of stimuli. Using functional MRI and psychophysiological measures, Fenske has found that the act of ignoring distractions can result in their subsequent affective devaluation. Their broader research program also addresses the cognitive and perceptual impacts of states such as boredom and the neural foundations of performance.
0423.research_direction: Dr. Fenske has recently been investigating the cognitive and affective dynamics of boredom, attention, and emotion regulation to understand how these traits influence everyday functioning and decision-making. Their recent work explores the psychological architecture of trait boredom proneness, specifically asking how it relates to maladaptive emotion regulation strategies and executive function impairments like poor attentional control and cognitive inflexibility. In educational contexts, they are using thought probes and episodic memory tests to examine whether spontaneous behavioral coping mechanisms, such as doodling versus structured note-taking, actually alter state boredom, mind-wandering, and information retention during academic lectures. Additionally, their research bridges cognitive psychology and clinical audiology by investigating how individual differences in boredom proneness and everyday attention failures shape the subjective severity of age-related hearing loss and subsequently influence a patient's likelihood of adopting hearing aids.

papers.title: Boredom Proneness Is Predicted by Difficulties in Emotion Regulation that Are Mediated by Corresponding Problems with Attention and Cognitive Flexibility
papers.abstract: The well-established links between boredom proneness and dysfunctional behaviors—including substance misuse, pathological gambling, and problematic smartphone engagement—have been hypothesized to reflect emotion-dysregulation mechanisms driving maladaptive coping with negative affect. However, empirical investigations clarifying how specific facets of emotion regulation relate to boredom proneness remain sparse. This investigation examined whether trait boredom proneness is predicted by maladaptive emotion-regulation strategies (specifically expressive suppression and rumination) and whether such relationships are underpinned by executive function impairments (attentional control, working memory, and cognitive flexibility). Undergraduate participants (N = 219) completed a comprehensive psychometric battery evaluating trait boredom proneness, emotion-regulation profiles, and perceived cognitive failures across attention, memory, and cognitive flexibility domains. Structural and mediation analyses revealed that generalized difficulties in emotion regulation significantly predicted boredom proneness, an effect that was partially mediated by self-reported attentional difficulties and diminished cognitive flexibility, but not by memory failures. Furthermore, individual propensities for expressive suppression and rumination positively predicted boredom proneness, whereas cognitive distraction showed no significant association. These findings highlight distinct cognitive-affective pathways through which executive dysfunction and maladaptive emotion regulation interact to heighten vulnerability to chronic boredom.
papers.authors: Natasha Vogel, Mark Fenske

papers.title: Note-taking for the win: Doodling does not reduce boredom or mind-wandering, nor enhance attention or retention of lecture material
papers.abstract: Although doodling and incidental motor fidgeting are traditionally categorized in educational settings as behavioral indices of inattention, recent proposals have framed them as functional coping mechanisms that may preserve performance by mitigating boredom and attenuating mnemonic deficits. To rigorously evaluate these competing hypotheses, two experiments (combined N = 222) assessed the influence of concurrent doodling on state boredom, attentional allocation, spontaneous mind-wandering, and episodic retention of lecture content. In Experiment 1, participants engaged in a repetitive auditory monitoring task while either performing structured doodling (shading geometric templates) or listening passively. In Experiment 2, participants listened to a 45-minute academic lecture assigned across four distinct conditions: structured doodling, unstructured (free-form) doodling, intentional note-taking, or a listen-only control. Throughout the lecture, intermittent thought probes measured real-time fluctuations in state boredom, mind-wandering, and focused attention, followed by an objective post-lecture comprehension test. Across both paradigms, doodling failed to alleviate state boredom or mind-wandering and conferred no benefits to sustained attention or information retention relative to control listening. In contrast, focused note-taking optimized cognitive engagement, generating significantly higher attentional focus and superior test scores alongside the lowest observed levels of state boredom and mind-wandering.
papers.authors: Emily Krysten Spencer-Mueller, Mark J. Fenske

papers.title: The Cognitive-Affective Hearing Aid Paradox: Boredom Proneness and Attentional Difficulties Predict Worse Age-Related Subjective Hearing but Lower Rates of Hearing Aid Adoption
papers.abstract: Untreated age-related hearing impairment significantly elevates risks for depressive symptoms, social isolation, and accelerated cognitive decline, yet adherence to rehabilitative intervention remains notably low. Although audiometric thresholds inform clinical severity, self-reported subjective hearing handicap is historically a stronger determinant of hearing aid acquisition. Building upon evidence that individuals high in trait boredom proneness and attentional lapses perceive hearing loss more negatively, this longitudinal investigation examined whether these cognitive-affective individual differences mediate the pathway between subjective auditory impairment and actual hearing aid adoption. Older adults (aged 50+) recruited from hearing-health clinics completed pure-tone audiometry alongside standardized self-report measures of hearing handicap, effortful exertion while listening, boredom proneness, and spontaneous mind-wandering, with device adoption tracked across a 5-year follow-up period. While boredom proneness and spontaneous mind-wandering did not independently predict device acquisition in direct univariate models, parallel mediation models demonstrated that both traits significantly mediated the relationship between subjective hearing handicap (as well as listening effort) and hearing aid purchase. Crucially, whereas heightened hearing handicap and listening strain increased the probability of device purchase, elevated boredom proneness and spontaneous mind-wandering functioned as suppression variables that predicted reduced rates of adoption, demonstrating a paradoxical barrier in hearing healthcare decision-making.
papers.authors: Alyssa C. Smith, Carolyn M. L. Crawford, Gurjit Singh, Mark J. Fenske

papers.title: Subjective Impact of Age-Related Hearing Loss Is Worse for Those Who Routinely Experience Boredom and Failures of Attention
papers.abstract: Despite demonstrable psychosocial and cognitive benefits associated with audiological interventions, many older adults experiencing presbycusis fail to pursue auditory rehabilitation. A critical contributor to low treatment uptake is the persistent discordance observed between objective pure-tone audiometric thresholds and subjective evaluations of auditory disability. This investigation tested whether individual differences in cognitive-affective vulnerability—namely trait boredom proneness and everyday attention failures—account for variance in the subjective burden of age-related hearing impairment. A clinical sample of older adults completed diagnostic pure-tone audiometry and self-report instruments quantifying hearing handicap (Hearing Handicap Inventory for the Elderly), subjective listening effort, boredom proneness, and spontaneous attentional lapses. Regression and mediation analyses revealed that individuals with greater susceptibility to boredom reported significantly more severe perceived hearing handicap and heightened listening strain. Crucially, parallel mediation demonstrated that this relationship between boredom proneness and subjective hearing handicap was mediated by individual differences in sustained task-focused attentional control, an effect that remained consistent regardless of the severity of objective audiometric hearing thresholds. These findings identify distinct neurocognitive-affective traits underlying subjective hearing distress that may inform clinical counseling and improve rehabilitation uptake.
papers.authors: Carolyn M. L. Crawford, Kalisha Ramlackhan, Gurjit Singh, Mark J. Fenske

0424.name: Mark W. Becker
0424.bio: Mark W. Becker is a Professor in the Cognition and Cognitive Neuroscience program at Michigan State University who investigates the mechanisms governing visual attention and its application to real-world tasks. Their research utilizes eye-tracking and psychophysical methodologies to explore how visual search is influenced by target prevalence, emotional stimuli, and individual differences in working memory. Becker has examined 'panic search'—where threat-related stimuli improve search efficiency for non-threatening items—and has conducted interdisciplinary studies on the efficacy of medical and nutritional labeling. Becker’s current work focuses on the processes guiding the allocation of attention and the cognitive factors that lead to errors in critical visual search environments.
0424.research_direction: Dr. Becker’s recent work explores the cognitive and oculomotor mechanisms that govern attentional guidance and target detection during visual search. They have recently been investigating how environmental regularities—such as target scarcity in the low-prevalence effect and implicit statistical contingencies—interact with goal-directed volitional control. Using behavioral search tasks, continuous dynamic displays, and eye tracking, their research examines whether factors like rare targets and salient distractors alter global search quitting thresholds, or if they instead modulate continuous evidence accrual and internal activation thresholds. Additionally, they are studying the functional components of preparatory attentional templates, specifically isolating how color and form information distinctively drive peripheral saccadic guidance versus post-fixation target verification.

papers.title: Guidance of attention by statistical learning when multiple guidance mechanisms compete
papers.abstract: Observers implicitly extract environmental statistical regularities to bias visual attention toward spatial coordinates and surface features correlated with target occurrence; however, empirical investigations have typically evaluated these statistical biases in isolation. In Experiment 1, a visual search paradigm tested whether human observers simultaneously acquire and implement dual independent regularities—one mapping target probability to a spatial quadrant and another to a surface color. The behavioral results demonstrated that both statistical regularities were acquired implicitly, exerting independent, additive influences on attentional guidance. Experiments 2 and 3 investigated how volitional goal-directed control interacts with implicit statistical learning by presenting endogenous feature cues while maintaining implicit spatial contingencies. Endogenous cuing along one feature dimension did not attenuate the implicit learning of contingencies in the other. Crucially, the deployment of statistical regularities was contingent upon the validity of volitional cues: statistical biases facilitated performance during neutral or valid cuing but were eliminated under invalid cues. These findings demonstrate that volitional control and statistical learning operate within an integrated hierarchical framework where volitional guidance takes precedence over implicit statistical biases during selection conflicts.
papers.authors: Mark W. Becker, Morgan Dodd, Tristan Janisse

papers.title: Reducing the low-prevalence effect with probe trials
papers.abstract: Target scarcity during visual search triggers an elevated miss rate termed the low-prevalence effect (LPE), presenting a persistent operational hazard in visual screening. Across four experiments, this study examined whether distributing artificial 'probe' trials—target-present trials paired with post-response feedback—effectively mitigates the LPE. Experiment 1 used a low-prevalence T-among-Ls search task and demonstrated that interleaved probe trials substantially attenuated target miss rates. Experiment 2 evaluated dual-target search (T and O targets among L and Q distractors) while manipulating the proportion of probe trials dedicated to each target; the observed probe benefit scaled strictly with the frequency of the probed target exemplar, showing minimal generalization to unprobed targets. Experiment 3 used eye tracking to dissociate whether probe trials shift trial-level quitting thresholds, alter item-evaluation decision criteria, or enhance attentional guidance. Gaze metrics demonstrated that probe trials selectively improved top-down attentional guidance toward features matching frequently probed targets, without altering quitting thresholds (number of inspected items) or conservative shifts in decision criteria. Finally, Experiment 4 showed that performance improvements persisted without explicit trial feedback, confirming that probe trials alleviate the LPE by shifting perceived target prevalence rather than reinforcing accuracy through feedback alone.
papers.authors: Mark W. Becker, Andrew Rodriguez, Derrek T. Montalvo, Chad Peltier

papers.title: Salient distractors influence information accrual rather than quitting threshold in visual search
papers.abstract: The addition of an irrelevant salient singleton to visual search arrays has previously been observed to increase target misses while accelerating target-absent reaction times, an effect typically interpreted as a reduction in the global quitting threshold. Across two experiments, this investigation demonstrates that this behavioral profile persists when the salient singleton shares no critical dimensions with background distractors, but reverses when the salient singleton shares orientation features with the search target, producing prolonged target-absent response times and reduced miss rates. This crossover effect contradicts a unitary quitting threshold explanation. Instead, the empirical patterns align with a drift-diffusion framework wherein a salient stimulus provides a rapid burst of evidence accumulation toward its associated decision boundary: when sharing target features, evidence accrues rapidly toward the 'target-present' boundary, whereas non-target salient features drive evidence toward the 'target-absent' boundary. This evidence-accrual account offers a parsimonious alternative to global threshold shifts and specifies the conditions under which salient singletons enhance or disrupt target detection.
papers.authors: Mark W. Becker, Jeff Moher, Derrek T. Montalvo, Andrew Rodriguez

papers.title: Activation thresholds, not quitting thresholds, account for the low prevalence effect in dynamic search
papers.abstract: The low-prevalence effect (LPE) describes the marked reduction in detection accuracy that occurs when search targets are rare. Standard visual search models attribute this deficit to lowered quitting thresholds, where observers abort search after inspecting fewer items on discrete trials. However, this quitting threshold account cannot directly explain performance in continuous monitoring tasks involving dynamic displays that lack discrete trial terminations. In Experiment 1, a 2 (display dynamic: continuous moving vs static) × 2 (target prevalence: 10% vs 40%) design demonstrated that while baseline detection was lower in dynamic displays, an LPE of equivalent magnitude occurred in both display types. In Experiment 2, participants searched for either of two targets (Ts and Ls) where prevalence was varied within-display (10% vs 40%), an arrangement eliminating trial-level quitting threshold adjustments even in static searches. Replicating Experiment 1, a pronounced LPE persisted across both static and dynamic modalities. These results demonstrate that the LPE in continuous and multi-target search is not governed by quitting thresholds, supporting instead an activation-threshold model wherein target infrequency raises the internal evidentiary threshold required for an attended item to trigger conscious detection.
papers.authors: Mark W. Becker, Andrew Rodriguez, Jeffrey Bolkhovsky, Chad Peltier, Sylvia B. Guillory

papers.title: Isolating the impact of a visual search template's color and form information on search guidance and verification times
papers.abstract: Visual search guidance relies on preparatory attentional templates, with pictorial cues consistently providing greater search benefits than linguistic text cues. However, pictorial cues provide both detailed structural form and chromaticity, leaving it ambiguous whether picture benefits arise from peripheral guidance via chromatic signals or spatial form resolution. Given that spatial visual acuity drops precipitously with retinal eccentricity while color discrimination remains relatively robust, high-fidelity form information may contribute minimally to peripheral oculomotor guidance. Using eye tracking across a 2 (cue modality: pictorial vs text) × 2 (color information: chromatic vs achromatic) factorial design, this study separated search guidance (latency and saccadic steps before target fixations) from target verification (post-fixation dwell time). Experiment 1 cued search targets using full-color images, grayscale images, color-descriptive text, or neutral text. Experiment 2 matched text cue font colors to the target's dominant hue. Oculomotor metrics demonstrated that high-fidelity form information predominantly improved target verification dwell times, whereas chromatic information drove efficient attentional guidance across the visual periphery, indicating distinct functional dissociations between form and color components within the search template.
papers.authors: Derrek T. Montalvo, Andrew Rodriguez, Mark W. Becker

0425.name: Markus Lappe
0425.bio: Markus Lappe is a Professor of General Psychology at the University of Münster who researches the computational and biological mechanisms of visual perception in relation to motor activity. Lappe’s work examines how the visual system integrates retinal information with eye movement signals for spatial stability and how humans utilize optic flow and biological motion for navigation and action recognition. By combining psychophysical experiments with quantitative computational modeling and neurophysiological data, Lappe explores the plasticity of perceptual space and the neural processes involved in perceiving the environment during active movement.
0425.research_direction: Dr. Lappe has recently been investigating the computational and behavioral mechanisms underlying optic flow processing, visual stability, and sensorimotor control. Their recent work explores how the visual system parses complex retinal flow to simultaneously estimate self-motion and track moving objects, including how configural biological motion cues from pedestrian crowds integrate into these global heading estimates. In the domain of active vision, they are examining the limits of spatial perception by using nonrigid motion stimuli to probe the functional links between smooth pursuit, catch-up saccades, and corollary discharge. Additionally, Dr. Lappe is modeling the spatial distribution of oculomotor learning across 2D population codes and utilizing varied feedback paradigms to understand how the brain continuously updates and optimizes saccadic motor planning in risky environments.

papers.title: The role of feedback for sensorimotor decisions under risk
papers.abstract: This study examines how varying feedback modalities and schedules influence the optimization of motor planning in risky environments, where the ideal aiming strategy is a function of an individual's motor variability. Participants executed saccades toward targets comprised of reward and penalty zones under conditions of error-based versus reinforcement feedback and trial-by-trial versus summary statistics. The results indicate that trial-by-trial reinforcement feedback is superior for facilitating optimal sensorimotor decisions, as it minimizes endpoint deviation and reduces loss-aversive biases. Conversely, summary feedback was associated with an incremental drift in internal aiming models, suggesting that high-frequency reinforcement signals are critical for the continuous calibration of the movement planning system.
papers.authors: Christian Wolf, Artem V. Belopolsky, Markus Lappe

papers.title: Flow parsing as causal source separation allows fast and parallel object and self-motion estimation
papers.abstract: We present a computational framework for flow parsing that treats the decomposition of retinal optic flow as a causal source separation task. The model utilizes heading likelihood maps to delineate flow components consistent with global self-motion from local perturbations caused by independent object motion. This probabilistic approach allows for the simultaneous estimation of the observer's heading, detection and localization of moving objects, and the recovery of scene-relative object velocity. Simulations demonstrate that this likelihood-based architecture effectively replicates human psychophysical performance, including the systematic biases in heading estimation observed when self-motion signals are confounded by moving distractors.
papers.authors: Malte Scherff, Markus Lappe

papers.title: Adaptation across the 2D population code explains the spatially distributive nature of motor learning
papers.abstract: This research introduces a population-based gain field model to explain the spatially distributive properties of oculomotor learning, characterized by the emergence of an adaptation field. The model implements sensorimotor transformations as error-driven modulations of 2D topographic maps representing visual input, motor output, and internal movement predictions (corollary discharge). By fitting the model to experimental data on saccade adaptation and target localization, we demonstrate that the radial shape, amplitude-dependent asymmetry, and spatial generalization of learning arise from distributive updates at the population level. Our findings indicate that learning is most extensive in the motor domain, whereas visual and corollary discharge representations show more localized plasticity.
papers.authors: Jana Masselink, Markus Lappe

papers.title: Inability to pursue nonrigid motion produces instability of spatial perception
papers.abstract: This study identifies a specific class of nonrigid visual motion—rotating vortices—that disrupts the maintenance of a stable spatial representation during eye movements. While these stimuli are accurately perceived during fixation, they prove impossible to track with smooth pursuit eye movements. Although catch-up saccades are precisely directed at the moving target, the stimulus appears to jump in space upon saccade landing, indicating a failure of the internal compensation mechanism for eye-movement-induced retinal displacement. These findings reveal that visual stability depends on motion processing mechanisms shared with the smooth pursuit system, and that saccadic compensation is functionally decoupled from the control of catch-up saccades.
papers.authors: Krischan Koerfer, Tamara Watson, Markus Lappe

papers.title: Limb articulation of biological motion can induce illusory motion perception during self-motion
papers.abstract: We investigate how the articulation of biological motion (the gait of point-light walkers) contributes to self-motion perception in crowded environments. The study examines the effects of mismatched limb articulation and translation—such as walking in place—on the perception of lateral crowd speed during simulated forward self-motion. Results show that articulation rate induces an illusory crowd speed percept that biases the observer's heading estimate. This effect is absent in spatially scrambled displays, indicating that the illusion is driven by configural, body-form-dependent articulation cues rather than local first-order motion. These findings suggest that the visual system integrates biological motion signals into the global optic flow analysis used for navigation.
papers.authors: Anna-Gesina Hülemeier, Markus Lappe

0426.name: Markus Meister
0426.bio: Markus Meister examines the principles of information processing within large-scale neural circuits, focusing on the mammalian retina and the superior colliculus. Their research utilizes high-density multielectrode arrays and optogenetic techniques to investigate how sensory inputs are transformed into behaviorally relevant neural representations. By integrating experimental findings with mathematical modeling, Meister aims to define a standard model for retinal computation and identify the circuit mechanisms behind rapid learning and task coordination.
0426.research_direction: Dr. Meister's recent work explores the computational principles of the nervous system across multiple scales, ranging from early visual circuits to spatial navigation algorithms and global cognitive constraints. Within visual neuroscience, they have recently been investigating how the retina parses scenes through parallel information channels and how the superior colliculus computes unified, feature-independent saliency maps to guide visual attention. Broadening into neuromorphic computation, their research examines how recurrent biological neural networks might solve complex spatial mapping and shortest-path navigation problems using local synaptic rules rather than extensive trial-and-error. Additionally, Dr. Meister is probing the fundamental informational bottlenecks of human brain architecture, exploring the mechanistic reasons why sequential cognitive control operates at a surprisingly low bandwidth despite our massive sensory input capabilities.

papers.title: The Standard Model of the Retina
papers.abstract: This comprehensive review synthesizes decades of retinal research into a unified framework designated as the "Standard Model" of early visual processing. The author posits that the retina decomposes the visual scene into approximately 40 parallel information channels, each represented by a distinct retinal ganglion cell type. These circuits perform specialized computations—including motion discrimination, edge orientation, and contrast adaptation—using a rectified subunit architecture wherein signals from photoreceptors are filtered by bipolar cells, rectified at the synapse, and spatially pooled by ganglion cells. The article characterizes the biophysical postulates of this model, its quantitative fidelity in predicting neural firing patterns from arbitrary light stimuli, and its status as a mature baseline for systems neuroscience. It further examines how this circuit diagram bridges molecular mechanisms with behavioral perception while identifying remaining gaps in our understanding of retinal connectivity.
papers.authors: Markus Meister

papers.title: Preference-independent saliency map in the mouse superior colliculus
papers.abstract: Using two-photon calcium imaging in awake mice, this study identifies a saliency map within the superficial superior colliculus (sSC) that functions independently of local neuronal feature preferences. The researchers demonstrate that conspicuous stimuli—defined by spatial contrast or motion against a background—elicit robust, synchronized activations in both excitatory and inhibitory populations, including neurons with negligible orientation or direction selectivity. This saliency-driven activity peaks at the receptive field center and is subject to long-range surround suppression extending up to 40 degrees. The response amplitude correlates precisely with the relative salience of the stimulus rather than its absolute physical parameters. These findings indicate that the sSC integrates disparate feature signals into a unified priority map to guide visual attention and orienting behaviors, a representation that persists even in the absence of cortical input.
papers.authors: Ruixiang Wu, Jinhuai Xu, Chunpeng Li, Zhaoji Zhang, Ya-tang Li, Markus Meister

papers.title: The unbearable slowness of being: Why do we live at 10 bits/s?
papers.abstract: This perspective addresses the fundamental informational bottleneck in human cognition, characterized by a behavioral throughput limit of approximately 10 bits/s despite a sensory input capacity exceeding 10^9 bits/s. The authors propose a dual-processing brain architecture comprising an 'outer' system capable of high-bandwidth parallel sensorimotor processing and an 'inner' system that distills this data into low-dimensional variables for sequential cognitive control. By analyzing diverse tasks such as competitive typing, Rubik's cube solving, and memory sports, the study quantifies this 10 bit/s speed limit and explores its implications for neural efficiency and evolutionary adaptation. The authors argue that the vast number of neurons in the cerebral cortex remains paradoxically large for such low-bandwidth behavior and suggest new research directions to identify the mechanistic constraints of this sequential, single-threaded cognitive architecture.
papers.authors: Jieyu Zheng, Markus Meister

papers.title: A Fast Algorithm for All-Pairs-Shortest-Paths Suitable for Neural Networks
papers.abstract: This paper presents a neuromorphic algorithm for the All-Pairs Shortest Path (APSP) problem that utilizes the analog computational properties of recurrent neural networks. The authors demonstrate that the shortest path distance matrix D for a directed graph with adjacency matrix A can be computed via matrix inversion as D_ij = ceil(log_gamma[(I - gamma*A)^-1]_ij) for a sufficiently small gain parameter gamma. The work establishes graph-theoretic bounds for this relationship and evaluates the 'R-distance' algorithm's performance across varied graph topologies and weighted edges. This method provides sub-cubic computational complexity for dense graphs and maps directly onto a biological neural circuit architecture where synaptic weights represent edge adjacencies and steady-state neuronal activations reflect geodesic distances.
papers.authors: Zeyu Jing, Markus Meister

papers.title: Endotaxis: A neuromorphic algorithm for mapping, goal-learning, navigation, and patrolling
papers.abstract: The authors propose 'endotaxis,' a biologically plausible neuromorphic algorithm that enables animals to navigate toward goals in structured, complex environments by repurposing ancient chemotactic circuits. The mechanism is implemented via a three-layer neural circuit: a 'point' layer for location encoding, a 'map' layer that learns topological adjacencies through recurrent connectivity, and a 'goal' layer that computes a virtual chemotactic gradient directed toward specific resources. Unlike reinforcement learning frameworks that require extensive trial-and-error, endotaxis facilitates rapid spatial learning and one-shot goal identification using local Hebbian rules. Simulations in varied labyrinths demonstrate that the algorithm efficiently computes shortest paths and supports complex behaviors such as patrolling and multi-target navigation, providing a mechanistic link between simple taxes and high-level cognitive mapping.
papers.authors: Tony Zhang, Matthew Rosenberg, Zeyu Jing, Pietro Perona, Markus Meister

0427.name: Marlene Behrmann
0427.bio: Marlene Behrmann is a cognitive neuroscientist specializing in the psychological and neural mechanisms of visual processing, including object, face, and word recognition. Behrmann’s research investigates how the brain transforms retinal signals into coherent percepts by integrating functional neuroimaging, psychophysics, and computational modeling. They study neurotypical populations and individuals with brain damage or neurodevelopmental disorders, such as autism and prosopagnosia, to examine cortical organization and plasticity. Recently, Behrmann’s work has focused on the developmental trajectory of hemispheric specialization and the structural connectivity of neural circuits underlying high-level vision.
0427.research_direction: Dr. Behrmann's recent work explores the functional architecture and neural resilience of the human visual system by investigating how it adapts to severe focal damage or large-scale cortical resections. They have recently been tracking longitudinal cohorts of patients who have undergone pediatric hemispherectomies or occipitotemporal resections, using functional MRI and psychophysics to understand whether a single structurally intact hemisphere can reorganize to support space- and object-based attention, as well as high-level category selectivity for faces, words, and objects. Additionally, their research investigates the network-level consequences of adult-onset visual agnosia through detailed, long-term single-case neuropsychological studies. By combining behavioral paradigms with multimodal neuroimaging—including representational similarity analysis and high-density EEG mapping of task-dependent oscillatory frequencies—they are evaluating both local processing deficits and remote neural disruptions to better understand how structural damage perturbs distributed object-recognition networks across the ventral and dorsal streams.

papers.title: Visual agnosia in the era of behavioral and neural investigations
papers.abstract: This longitudinal assessment of patient S.M. over thirty years evaluates the continuing efficacy of single-case neuropsychological methodology in the context of contemporary neuroimaging. By integrating behavioral psychophysics with structural and functional MRI (fMRI), the research explores the neural circuitry underlying integrative visual agnosia. While standard behavioral assays characterize the magnitude of visuoperceptual deficits and fMRI identifies the topography of the distributed object-recognition network, joint behavioral-imaging paradigms provide critical causal evidence regarding brain-behavior correspondences. The findings demonstrate that single-subject investigations, enhanced by high-resolution imaging, remain indispensable for elucidating the functional and structural architecture of the ventral and dorsal visual streams.
papers.authors: Marlene Behrmann

papers.title: Lesion-network mapping in task-dependent frequencies uncovers remote consequences of focal damage
papers.abstract: This study employs high-density electroencephalography (EEG) to characterize the temporal and spectral dynamics of transcallosal diaschisis in a patient with visual agnosia. Utilizing SilenceMap, a novel source-localization algorithm designed to detect regions of suppressed oscillatory power, the researchers analyzed task-dependent responses to intact and scrambled object stimuli. The results reveal a significant reduction in the slope of object-shape sensitivity within the lesioned right posterior temporal cortex across broad frequency bands (>4 Hz). Critically, the analysis identified contralesional diaschisis in homotopic regions of the structurally intact left hemisphere specifically within the theta band (4–8 Hz). These findings suggest that focal damage in the ventral stream induces remote, frequency-specific disruptions across the functional network, highlighting the value of spectral EEG fingerprints in precision neurology.
papers.authors: Alireza Chamanzar, Erez Freud, Pulkit Grover, Marlene Behrmann

papers.title: Space- and object-based attention in patients with a single hemisphere following childhood resection
papers.abstract: Using a modified Egly-Driver two-rectangle paradigm, this research evaluates the efficiency of space- and object-based attentional selection in patients who underwent childhood hemispherectomy. The study compares lateralization profiles and attentional shifting latencies between hemispherectomy patients and age-matched typically developing (TD) controls. Results indicate that while patients exhibit significantly longer reaction times (RTs) for invalidly cued targets, they remain capable of both spatial and object-based attentional benefits within a single hemisphere. This functional resilience suggests that the remaining hemisphere can reorganize to support attentional computations typically distributed across both hemispheres, though the absence of bilateral integration leads to suboptimal processing speeds compared to TD individuals.
papers.authors: Sophia Robert, Michael C. Granovetter, Marlene Behrmann

papers.title: Cross-sectional and longitudinal category-selectivity in visual cortex following pediatric cortical resection
papers.abstract: This investigation examines the developmental trajectory and stability of category-selective regions (face, place, object, and word) in children following unilateral cortical resection for epilepsy. By synthesizing cross-sectional and longitudinal functional MRI data, the study assesses the degree of functional reorganization within the structurally intact hemisphere. The analysis reveals that the remaining cortex maintains a robust and relatively typical topographic organization of category-selective maps despite the absence of contralateral input. While the system demonstrates significant neural resilience and categorical preservation, subtle differences in behavioral proficiency persist, indicating that the compensatory capacity of a single hemisphere for high-level visual recognition is substantial but may not fully achieve neurotypical levels.
papers.authors: T. T. Liu, M. C. Granovetter, A. M. S. Maallo, S. Robert, J. Z. Fu, C. Patterson, D. C. Plaut, Marlene Behrmann

papers.title: Functional Resilience of the Neural Visual Recognition System Post-Pediatric Occipitotemporal Resection
papers.abstract: This study evaluates whether a single hemisphere is sufficient to support visual stimulus individuation following pediatric occipitotemporal cortex (OTC) resection. Using fMRI localizers and a repetition suppression (RS) paradigm, the researchers quantified category selectivity (CS) and neural representations for faces, words, and objects in nine OTC resection patients, twelve control patients, and twenty-one healthy controls. Although univariate and multivariate neural signatures (derived from representational similarity analysis) in the structurally preserved hemisphere were indistinguishable from those of controls, the OTC resection patients showed significantly lower behavioral accuracy in face and object recognition. These findings suggest that while the neural architecture of the visual recognition system is highly resilient to early damage, bilateral OTC contributions are necessary for typical behavioral proficiency in high-level vision.
papers.authors: Michael C. Granovetter, Anne Margarette S. Maallo, Shouyu Ling, Sophia Robert, Erez Freud, Christina Patterson, Marlene Behrmann

0428.name: Martin A. Giese
0428.department: Section Computational Sensomotorics, Hertie Institute for Clinical Brain Research
0428.bio: Martin A. Giese is a Professor of Computational Sensomotorics at the University of Tübingen and leads a research section at the Hertie Institute for Clinical Brain Research and the Centre for Integrative Neuroscience. Giese’s research combines computational neuroscience and psychophysics to investigate the neural mechanisms underlying biological motion recognition and social perception. Their work involves the development of physiologically-inspired neural models and the use of computer animation to study how the brain represents body movements and facial expressions. This research applies these frameworks to clinical studies of movement disorders and social cognition deficits in psychiatric conditions.
0428.research_direction: Dr. Giese has recently been exploring the intersection of biological perception and deep learning, investigating how both natural and artificial visual systems process complex affective and spatial information. Using computer-animated dyads and high-fidelity 3D avatars generated via markerless motion capture, they are examining the perceptual mechanisms underlying social interactions, such as how human observers integrate emotional cues from multiple interacting agents and how the macaque visual system responds to varying levels of biomechanical realism. Their recent work also translates biological principles into machine vision, testing whether norm-referenced encoding strategies can enable highly data-efficient facial expression recognition across extreme morphological shifts, such as between realistic faces and cartoons.
