Additionally, they are investigating the internal mechanics of self-supervised Vision Transformers, probing how specialized elements like register and [CLS] tokens influence the coupling of local and global image semantics, while concurrently designing knowledge distillation frameworks to efficiently extract high-resolution dense features at lower computational costs.

papers.title: Facial expression recognition based on multi-domain norm-referenced encoding
papers.abstract: This study proposes a biologically-inspired neural mechanism to address the challenge of out-of-domain transfer in facial expression recognition, particularly when adapting models to unnatural morphologies like cartoon characters. The authors implement a norm-referenced encoding strategy where facial features are parameterized as deviation vectors relative to a domain-specific reference. By leveraging the principle that these relative deviations are preserved across distinct shape domains, the framework achieves extreme data efficiency, enabling successful adaptation to novel domains with as few as one training image. Evaluation on datasets featuring highly variable head shapes confirms the model's superior generalization and scalability compared to standard convolutional neural network benchmarks.
papers.authors: Michael Stettler, Alexander Lappe, Martin A. Giese

papers.title: Another BRIXEL in the Wall: Towards Cheaper Dense Features
papers.abstract: The research introduces BRIXEL, a knowledge distillation framework aimed at reducing the computational and memory overhead associated with generating high-resolution dense feature maps in vision foundation models like DINOv3. To circumvent the quadratic complexity of transformer architectures at high input resolutions, the method employs a student network that learns to upsample its own feature maps to match the fidelity of a high-resource teacher. Empirical results demonstrate that BRIXEL significantly outperforms baseline models on dense downstream tasks while maintaining lower input resolutions, providing a computationally efficient path to achieving fine-grained spatial feature representation.
papers.authors: Alexander Lappe, Martin A. Giese

papers.title: Register and [CLS] tokens yield a decoupling of local and global features in large ViTs
papers.abstract: This work investigates the emergence of high-frequency artifacts in the attention maps of self-supervised Vision Transformers such as DINOv2, identifying the model's tendency to repurpose patch tokens as implicit registers for global information as the underlying cause. While the integration of explicit register tokens cleans these attention maps, the authors demonstrate that this intervention induces a functional decoupling where global image semantics become isolated within the register tokens, losing their veridical correspondence with local features. The study further identifies similar decoupling effects for the [CLS] token in models lacking explicit registers, highlighting a critical trade-off between attention map interpretability and the integrative representation of visual information.
papers.authors: Alexander Lappe, Martin A. Giese

papers.title: MacAction: Realistic 3D macaque body animation based on multi-camera markerless motion capture
papers.abstract: The authors present MacAction, an end-to-end pipeline for synthesizing high-fidelity 3D macaque body animations using synchronized multi-camera markerless motion capture and deep pose estimation. The system utilizes sparse manual keyframe annotations to achieve the kinematic precision required for life-like full-body simulations with 86 joints. Behavioral validation using eye-tracking with rhesus monkeys revealed a body-based uncanny valley effect, where animals exhibited conspecific-like gazing behavior for high-fidelity avatars but reduced engagement for intermediate levels of realism, confirming the sensitivity of the primate visual system to biomechanical realism in social stimuli.
papers.authors: Lucas M. Martini, Anna Bognár, Rufin Vogels, Martin A. Giese

papers.title: Perceptual encoding of emotions in interactive bodily expressions
papers.abstract: This study explores how the human visual system perceptually integrates emotional signals from multiple interacting agents. Utilizing computer-animated dyads with independently manipulated emotional styles, the researchers demonstrate that the perception of an agent's emotion is systematically biased by the emotional context of its interaction partner. The results indicate that interacting emotional styles are jointly encoded by the brain rather than processed as independent signals, suggesting that the perception of social affect is fundamentally dependent on the interactive context and the relative alignment of emotional expressions between agents.
papers.authors: Andrea Christensen, Nick Taubert, Elisabeth M. J. Huis in 't Veld, Beatrice de Gelder, Martin A. Giese

0429.name: Martin Arguin
0429.lab_name: NeuroCVL - Laboratoire de neurocognition de la vision
0429.bio: Martin Arguin is a Professor at the Université de Montréal and a researcher at the Centre de recherche de l’Institut Universitaire de Gériatrie de Montréal (CRIUGM). Arguin investigates the cognitive and neural mechanisms of visual processing, focusing on shape perception, object recognition, and the spatiotemporal dynamics of attention during reading. They utilize psychophysics, EEG/ERP electrophysiology, and computational modeling to study visual function in healthy populations and individuals with neurological impairments. Their research examines the impact of aging on visual encoding and the development of optimized typography intended to improve reading performance in developmental dyslexia.
0429.research_direction: Dr. Arguin has recently been investigating the fine-grained temporal dynamics of visual word and object recognition. Their recent work explores how the visual system utilizes spatial frequency and spatial scale information over time, specifically questioning whether these visual features are processed via dissociable mechanisms with distinct temporal progressions. To probe these dynamics, they employ random temporal sampling—rapidly fluctuating signal-to-noise ratios during brief stimulus exposures—to generate classification images that map the behavioral oscillatory patterns of visual information extraction. Additionally, they are examining how healthy aging impacts these perceptual oscillations, utilizing Fourier-transformed efficiency data and machine learning classifiers to characterize age-related changes in temporal visual processing.

papers.title: Dissociation between the processing of spatial frequencies vs scale in visual word recognition
papers.abstract: This study investigates the theoretical and empirical independence of spatial frequency (SF) and spatial scale (SS) in visual word recognition. While these constructs are often treated as equivalent, the authors hypothesize they are processed via dissociable mechanisms. Across two experiments using random temporal sampling with 16 adult readers each, the researchers measured processing efficiency for words presented over 200 ms. Experiment 1, utilizing non-overlapping SF bandpass filters (1.2–9.6 cpd), revealed a 'fine-to-coarse' temporal progression, contradicting traditional 'coarse-to-fine' models. Experiment 2, which used Gaussian apertures of varying sizes (SS), demonstrated a 'global-to-local' processing order. The distinct temporal signatures for SF and SS suggest that orthographic recognition relies on separate perceptual channels for frequency and scale information.
papers.authors: Clémence Bertrand Pilon, Martin Arguin

papers.title: The processing of spatial frequencies through time in visual word recognition
papers.abstract: This investigation examined the temporal dynamics of spatial frequency (SF) usage during a 4-alternative forced-choice word reading task in 16 neurologically intact adults. Stimuli consisted of target words additively combined with white noise, where the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) was manipulated using a random temporal sampling function over a 200 ms duration. Four distinct SF bands were tested (center frequencies 1.2, 2.4, 4.8, and 9.6 cpd). Contrary to the coarse-to-fine hypothesis of object recognition, results demonstrated that higher SF ranges dominated the earliest stages of processing, followed by a shift toward lower SFs. Classification of individual data patterns using Support Vector Machine (SVM) algorithms indicated that the most distinctive SF signatures are captured when temporal processing efficiency is recoded into its Fourier transform, reflecting the oscillatory nature of visual information extraction.
papers.authors: Clémence Bertrand Pilon, Martin Arguin

papers.title: The oscillatory features of visual processing are altered in healthy aging
papers.abstract: The study compared temporal visual processing features between healthy young and elderly adults using random temporal sampling during object and word recognition. Over 200 ms stimulus exposures, target visibility was modulated by random SNR fluctuations. Classification images (CIs) were generated to map processing efficiency as a function of target onset time and SNR oscillation frequency (5–55 Hz). While both groups showed significant variations in efficiency related to temporal frequency content, the elderly group demonstrated altered perceptual oscillation patterns. An SVM classifier reached 100% accuracy in distinguishing participants by age group based on their Fourier-transformed CIs. These behavioral findings provide evidence that healthy aging significantly impacts the neural oscillatory mechanisms underlying visual recognition, manifesting as distinct temporal efficiency signatures.
papers.authors: Mélanie Lévesque, Martin Arguin

0430.name: Martin Eimer
0430.bio: Martin Eimer is a Professor of Psychology at Birkbeck, University of London, and serves as the director of the Brain and Behaviour Lab. Their research program utilizes event-related brain potentials (ERPs) and behavioral paradigms to study the cognitive and neural architecture of visual attention, visual search, and face perception. Eimer has characterized electrophysiological signatures of attentional selection, including the N2pc component, and investigated structural encoding processes associated with the N170 face-sensitive component. Their work focuses on the temporal dynamics of attentional control, the integration of multisensory information, and the neurocognitive basis of face recognition deficits such as developmental prosopagnosia.
0430.research_direction: Dr. Eimer has recently been investigating the real-time neural dynamics of top-down attentional control during visual search, primarily utilizing EEG markers such as the N2pc and Pd components. Much of their recent work explores the preparatory activation of attentional templates, using rapid serial probe presentation (RSPP) to track how observers dynamically switch priorities, incur target switch costs, and handle the capacity limits of maintaining multiple target features simultaneously. Additionally, they are investigating the mechanisms of signal suppression, asking whether proactive neural inhibition can be flexibly deployed against salient but unpredictable singleton distractors. Finally, their research aims to dissociate the underlying stages of selective visual processing by testing whether probabilistic expectations facilitate perception through early attentional biases or via later, post-selective encoding into working memory.

papers.title: Rapid Changes of Attentional Priorities in Visual Search: Tracking Covert Switches of Preparatory Attentional Templates in Real Time
papers.abstract: The dynamic reconfiguration of attentional priorities is a fundamental component of cognitive control, though the covert nature of template switches makes them difficult to quantify without overt behavioral cues. Utilizing a high-definition rapid serial probe presentation (RSPP) paradigm combined with EEG, this study tracked the real-time activation of preparatory attentional templates via the N2pc component. The findings demonstrate that observers can rapidly reassign feature-selective templates between early and late potential target onsets based on endogenous temporal expectations. Cued template switches revealed a temporary deactivation of the initial task set—resembling an attentional blink for templates—suggesting that reconfiguration involves a discrete neural transition rather than a continuous shift in preparatory bias.
papers.authors: Gordon Dodwell, Rebecca Nako, Martin Eimer

papers.title: Unpredictable singleton distractors in visual search can be subject to second-order suppression
papers.abstract: The signal suppression hypothesis suggests that attentional capture by salient distractors can be avoided through proactive inhibition. This study investigated whether such suppression is restricted to predictable feature values (first-order suppression) or can be applied to distractors with unpredictable features (second-order suppression). Using a multiframe letter-probe paradigm and measuring lateralized ERP markers (N2pc and Pd), the authors show that second-order suppression of unpredictable color singletons is achievable when the distractor and target features are sufficiently separated in feature space to avoid performance-hindering crosstalk. The results indicate that the mechanisms of distractor inhibition are not limited to static templates but can be deployed flexibly against unpredictable salient-but-irrelevant visual signals.
papers.authors: Brandi Lee Drisdelle, Alon Zivony, Martin Eimer

papers.title: The capacity limitations of multiple-template visual search during task preparation and target selection
papers.abstract: Efficient visual search is guided by mental representations of target features (attentional templates) that are activated during search preparation. This study evaluated the capacity limits of concurrent template maintenance by comparing single-color and three-color search using the RSPP paradigm and ERP (N2pc) measures. While results showed that observers can activate up to three color-specific templates in parallel when target identity is unpredictable, this multiple-template state incurred significant performance costs and attenuated the efficiency of attentional guidance (target N2pc). These findings suggest that mutual inhibitory interactions between co-activated templates impose a fundamental capacity limitation on the efficacy of top-down attentional control in visual search.
papers.authors: Anna Grubert, Ziyi Wang, Ella Williams, Mikel Jimenez, Roger Remington, Martin Eimer

papers.title: Target switch costs in visual search arise during the preparatory activation of target templates
papers.abstract: Switch costs in task-switching paradigms are typically attributed to the reconfiguration of stimulus-response mappings. This study investigated whether similar costs in visual search originate from the preparatory activation of target-defining templates. Utilizing the RSPP paradigm to measure N2pc components elicited by target-matching probes, the researchers tracked template activation states across target repetition and target switch trials. On repetition trials, templates were activated early (~800 ms prior to search onset). Conversely, on switch trials, template activation was markedly delayed, emerging only in the final 200 ms of the preparatory interval. These results provide direct electrophysiological evidence that target switch costs in search are mediated by the time required to neuraly reconfigure and activate new attentional task sets.
papers.authors: Anna Grubert, Ziyi Wang, Martin Eimer

papers.title: A dissociation between the effects of expectations and attention in selective visual processing
papers.abstract: It remains disputed whether probabilistic expectations facilitate perception through direct sensory modulation or via indirect attentional mediation. This research utilized a category-based RSVP task and electrophysiological markers (N2pc and P3) to dissociate these mechanisms. Categorical expectations were found to enhance target identification accuracy; however, they had no modulatory effect on the N2pc component, which serves as a biomarker for attentional engagement. These findings suggest that expectations facilitate perceptual awareness by lowering the threshold for encoding information into working memory at a late, post-selective stage, rather than by biasing the early mechanisms of attentional selection and engagement.
papers.authors: Alon Zivony, Martin Eimer

0431.name: Martin N. Hebart
0431.institution: Max Planck Institute for Human Cognitive and Brain Sciences
0431.department: Department of Medicine and Independent Research Group Vision and Computational Cognition
0431.bio: Martin N. Hebart is a computational neuroscientist who researches the latent representational dimensions underlying human object recognition and semantic knowledge. Hebart directs the Vision and Computational Cognition group and participates in the THINGS initiative, utilizing large-scale behavioral and neuroimaging datasets to map multidimensional spaces of visual perception. Their methodology integrates multivariate pattern analysis and representational alignment techniques to compare human neural representations with deep neural networks and artificial intelligence. Hebart’s current research investigates the transformational cascade from low-level visual input to high-level semantic reasoning and how these processes are altered in psychiatric conditions involving visual phenomena.
0431.research_direction: Dr. Hebart has recently been exploring the computational and neural architectures underlying human visual object representation and spatial vision. Their recent work investigates the representational alignment between deep neural networks and human behavior, developing high-throughput frameworks to probe the specific semantic and visual dimensions that drive perceived object similarity. In the human brain, they are studying how the ventral visual pathway multiplexes broad categorical domain knowledge with fine-grained, image-specific details across large naturalistic datasets. Additionally, their research investigates the spatial and predictive dynamics of early visual cortex, leveraging geometric deep learning to predict individual functional retinotopy directly from structural MRI and using functional imaging to examine how foveal V1 predictively encodes peripheral targets during saccade preparation.

papers.title: Predicting functional topography of the human visual cortex from cortical anatomy at scale
papers.abstract: The authors developed the deepRetinotopy toolbox, a geometric deep learning framework that predicts individual-specific functional topographic organization of the human visual cortex solely from structural MRI (T1-weighted) scans. Topographic mapping traditionally requires resource-intensive functional neuroimaging, but this model provides an efficient alternative that generates accurate retinotopic predictions (eccentricity and polar angle) across diverse datasets, scanners, and protocols. The utility of the predicted maps was demonstrated by automating individual visual area boundary delineation and by analyzing age-related changes in V1 organization across a sample of 11,060 anatomical scans, showing that large-scale functional organization is predictable from cortical anatomy alone.
papers.authors: Fernanda L. Ribeiro, Robert Satzger, Felix Hoffstaedter, Christian Bürger, Peer Herholz, David Linhardt, Noah C. Benson, D. Samuel Schwarzkopf, Alexander M. Puckett, Steffen Bollmann, Martin N. Hebart

papers.title: Dimensions underlying the representational alignment of deep neural networks with humans
papers.abstract: This study investigates the latent factors determining the representational alignment between deep neural networks (DNNs) and human mental representations using a shared-dimension comparison framework. While global scalar metrics like Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA) quantify alignment levels, they fail to specify the underlying features driving this similarity. By mapping DNN activations and human behavioral judgments onto a 49-dimensional interpretable space, the researchers identified a fundamental divergence in representational strategies: human judgments are predominantly organized by semantic and conceptual dimensions, whereas DNNs exhibit a heavy reliance on low-level visual properties. These findings emphasize that high predictive accuracy in DNNs does not guarantee human-like semantic processing and highlight the necessity for dimension-specific alignment evaluations.
papers.authors: Florian P. Mahner, Lukas Muttenthaler, Umut Güçlü, Martin N. Hebart

papers.title: A high-throughput approach for the efficient prediction of perceived similarity of natural objects
papers.abstract: The researchers present DimPred, a computational framework designed for high-throughput prediction of perceived object similarity from neural network activations. To overcome the combinatorial explosion of collecting human similarity judgments for large datasets, the approach maps DNN features onto 49 behaviorally-derived, interpretable representational dimensions using an L2-penalized regression model. Validation across five independent image sets showed that DimPred predicts behavioral ground-truth similarity with accuracies up to 0.898, consistently outperforming traditional RSA and feature-reweighted RSA methods. The results demonstrate that existing DNN representations are sufficient for automated sampling of behaviorally relevant similarity scores, facilitating large-scale alignment between computational models and human perception.
papers.authors: Philipp Kaniuth, Florian P. Mahner, Jonas Perkuhn, Martin N. Hebart

papers.title: Decoding peripheral saccade targets from foveal retinotopic cortex
papers.abstract: This study provides direct evidence of image-specific foveal prediction signals reaching the primary visual cortex (V1) during saccade preparation. Utilizing a gaze-contingent fMRI paradigm where peripheral saccade targets were removed before fixation, the authors demonstrated that stimulus identity could be decoded from the foveal retinotopic cortex despite the absence of direct foveal stimulation. Decoding sensitivity was specific to stimulus shape but not semantic category, suggesting a low-level feature-based feedback mechanism. Furthermore, fluctuations in foveal decodability covaried with activity in the intraparietal sulcus, identifying it as a candidate source for the feedback. These findings reveal a neural mechanism for trans-saccadic perceptual stability where foveal regions predictively represent upcoming visual inputs.
papers.authors: Luca Kämmer, Lisa M. Kroell, Tomas Knapen, Martin Rolfs, Martin N. Hebart

papers.title: The scope and limits of fine-grained image and category information in the ventral visual pathway
papers.abstract: The authors characterize the cortical organization of coarse-scale category versus fine-grained image-specific information in the human ventral visual stream using high-resolution fMRI and the large-scale THINGS database. Applying multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) to neural responses from 8,000 images, they identified distinct representational structures for semantic categories and individual exemplars. While category-selective regions (e.g., face- or place-selective clusters) exhibit clear domain-specific preferences, the study found they also encode extensive fine-grained information about individual images within and across categories. These results suggest a multidimensional representational architecture in high-level visual cortex where specialized modules are integrated into a broader, continuous representational landscape supporting diverse behavioral goals.
papers.authors: Markus W. Badwal, Johanna Bergmann, Johannes H.R. Roth, Christian F. Doeller, Martin N. Hebart

0432.name: Martin Rolfs
0432.bio: Martin Rolfs is a Professor of Experimental Psychology at Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin, where they lead the Active Perception and Cognition Lab and serve as a principal investigator in the Science of Intelligence (SCIoI) Cluster of Excellence. Rolfs's research examines mechanisms linking sensory processing to motor control, focusing on how eye movements, such as saccades and microsaccades, shape visual experience and attentional allocation. Their work addresses the predictive remapping of attention and the functional role of corollary discharge signals in maintaining visual stability. Using a combination of psychophysics, eye tracking, EEG, and computational modeling, Rolfs investigates how motor kinematics and the incidental sensory consequences of movement contribute to perception in active observers.
0432.research_direction: Dr. Rolfs has recently been investigating how the visual system maintains stability and extracts useful information despite the drastic sensory disruptions caused by saccadic eye movements. Their recent work explores the perceptual and functional roles of intra-saccadic visual signals, combining submillisecond video projection, EEG, and computational modeling to determine how high-speed retinal motion and saccadic smear contribute to object correspondence across eye movements. Additionally, they are probing the sensorimotor plasticity of active vision by examining how humans temporally recalibrate the perceptual binding between their saccades and delayed sensory consequences. Finally, their research also investigates pre-saccadic foveal prediction, utilizing gaze-contingent paradigms to understand how the fovea dynamically anticipates the features of salient peripheral targets before the eyes even arrive.

papers.title: Object continuity through invisible retinal motion at saccadic speed
papers.abstract: This study investigates the mechanisms of object correspondence across saccades by isolating high-speed retinal motion from extraretinal signals using submillisecond video projection. Utilizing a quartet motion display, a classic tool for studying long-distance object correspondence, the researchers demonstrated that even when motion speeds render the displacement invisible (visibility at chance levels), the retinal motion signals robustly bias object correspondence decisions. These results indicate that retinal motion alone, independent of motor corollary discharge, provides a sufficient signal for maintaining object continuity across the high-velocity image shifts induced by saccadic eye movements.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS)
papers.authors: Melis Ince, Carolin Hübner, Martin Rolfs

papers.title: Temporal recalibration to delayed visual consequences of saccades
papers.abstract: This research explores the plasticity of temporal binding between saccadic eye movements and their immediate sensory outcomes. Using a psychophysical paradigm where participants judged the temporal relationship between a horizontal saccade and a contingent high-contrast flash, the authors demonstrated significant temporal recalibration following exposure to systematic delays. Participants shifted their perceptual reports, increasingly judging post-saccadic flashes as occurring during the movement. The effect was robust across various visual contexts but significantly attenuated in a passive replay condition, emphasizing the critical role of active motor execution in the recalibration of sensorimotor contingencies.
papers.authors: Wiebke Nörenberg, Richard Schweitzer, Martin Rolfs

papers.title: Early visual signatures and benefits of intra-saccadic motion streaks
papers.abstract: The investigation explores the functional utility of intra-saccadic motion streaks using co-registered eye tracking and EEG. By implementing gaze-contingent target shifts that either preserved continuous motion streaks or presented discrete apparent motion, the study revealed that the presence of streaks facilitates gaze correction, as evidenced by reduced secondary saccade latencies. EEG decoding analyses indicated that post-saccadic target location information is extracted more effectively when streaks are present, with the target's trajectory being encoded in orientation-selective visual channels within 50 ms of saccade offset, suggesting a direct perceptual benefit of saccade-induced motion signals.
papers.authors: Richard Schweitzer, Thomas Seel, Jörg Raisch, Martin Rolfs

papers.title: The magnitude and time course of pre-saccadic foveal prediction depend on the conspicuity of the saccade target
papers.abstract: Continuing work on predictive foveal enhancement, this Research Advance employs a gaze-contingent orientation-discrimination task to probe the relationship between peripheral target salience and pre-saccadic foveal predictions. By parametrically varying the opacity (and thus the signal-to-noise ratio) of a peripheral orientation signal, the authors found that the magnitude of target-congruent foveal enhancement scales with target conspicuity. The temporal dynamics of this predictive signal exhibited an oscillatory modulation particularly pronounced under high-conspicuity conditions, suggesting that the feedback of target features to the foveal representation is a stimulus-dependent, dynamically evolving process reflecting sensitivity changes rather than decision bias.
papers.authors: Lisa M. Kroell, Martin Rolfs

papers.title: Saccadic omission revisited: What saccade-induced smear looks like
papers.abstract: This paper re-evaluates the phenomenon of saccadic omission by using tachistoscopic displays of natural scenes to make otherwise invisible saccade-induced smear perceptible to human observers. Through time-resolved psychophysical assessments, the authors identified a U-shaped temporal profile of perceived smear magnitude and orientation throughout the duration of a saccade. The findings show that visual features preserved in the smear are primarily low spatial frequencies and orientations parallel to the saccade trajectory. A computational motion-filter model based on saccadic velocity and contrast sensitivity functions successfully predicted the perceived smear, suggesting that omission stems from the natural filtering properties of the visual system rather than specialized suppression mechanisms.
papers.authors: Richard Schweitzer, Mara Doering, Thomas Seel, Jörg Raisch, Martin Rolfs

0433.name: Martin Szinte
0433.department: Institut de Neurosciences de la Timone (INT)
0433.lab_name: inVibe (Integration of Visual and Behavioral Diversity)
0433.bio: Martin Szinte is a CNRS researcher at the Institut de Neurosciences de la Timone (INT) who examines the links between visual perception and oculomotor behavior. Their research focuses on the mechanisms of visual stability and retinotopic remapping, investigating how the brain maintains a constant representation of the environment during eye movements. Szinte utilizes a multi-modal approach combining behavioral psychophysics, eye-tracking, and high-field (3T/7T) fMRI mapping. Szinte also contributed to the development of the Eye-Tracking-BIDS standard, an international initiative dedicated to standardizing eye-tracking data within neuroimaging frameworks to enhance scientific transparency and reproducibility.
0433.research_direction: Dr. Szinte has recently been investigating the functional neuroanatomy and spatial topography of the human oculomotor system using ultra-high-field fMRI. Their recent work explores how the cortical networks responsible for eye movements—such as the distinct subdivisions of the frontal and parietal eye fields—are spatially organized and functionally connected during saccadic and smooth pursuit tasks. Additionally, they are utilizing advanced deep learning frameworks, such as DeepMReye, to decode gaze position directly from BOLD activity rather than relying on standard optical tracking. Through these combined mapping and modeling approaches, they aim to characterize the multiplexed visuomotor architecture of the human brain and test the limits of extracting eye-tracking data purely from neural signals, even in the absence of visual input when participants' eyes are closed.

papers.title: Unveiling the Functional Architecture of Human Eye Fields
papers.abstract: The functional neuroanatomy of the human oculomotor network remains less characterized than its non-human primate counterpart. In this study, we utilized ultra-high-field resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data from 20 healthy participants to investigate the intrinsic connectivity of human eye fields. We mapped BOLD time-series correlations between retinotopic regions across the visual hierarchy and anatomical clusters in the parietal and prefrontal cortex, specifically targeting the medial, superior, and inferior branches of the precentral sulcus. These clusters, defined using the Glasser multimodal parcellation, encompassed the supplementary and cingulate eye fields, the frontal eye field, and the premotor eye field. By refining vertex selection to areas strongly activated during saccadic and smooth pursuit tasks, we identified consistent functional connectivity patterns. Specifically, our findings reveal robust coupling between oculomotor parietal clusters and three distinct prefrontal eye field subdivisions, providing a comprehensive anatomical-functional framework for the human oculomotor system.
papers.authors: Marco Bedini, Uriel Lascombes, Sina M. Kling, Guillaume S. Masson, Martin Szinte

papers.title: Distinct human eye fields unraveled by fMRI visual field and oculomotor mapping tasks
papers.abstract: While the frontal eye fields (FEF) in non-human primates are well-defined, the topography and subdivision of their human homologues remain debated. This study employed high-field fMRI and advanced modeling to comprehensively map the human eye fields. We localized cortical frontal and parietal regions during the execution of saccadic and smooth pursuit eye movements in a cohort of 20 participants. Our results demonstrate that the human eye fields are composed of multiple distinct visuomotor areas, each exhibiting unique profiles of activation and spatial organization. This organization challenges the traditional single-area view often extrapolated from monkey models and suggests a more complex, multiplexed architecture for the control of human gaze behavior. The study utilizes visual field mapping and oculomotor tasks to identify these regions with high spatial precision.
papers.authors: Uriel Lascombes, Sina Kling, Guillaume S. Masson, Martin Szinte

papers.title: Decoding eye closed gaze position using DeepMReye
papers.abstract: Monitoring gaze position is a critical component of many neuroimaging paradigms, yet standard eye-tracking techniques often fail during eyes-closed periods or in the absence of visual input. We explored the utility of DeepMReye—a deep learning framework for gaze decoding from fMRI signals—to track eye position during eyes-closed conditions. Participants performed a sequence of controlled gaze shifts to known spatial locations with both eyes open and closed, while undergoing fMRI. Although the DeepMReye network was primarily trained on conventional eyes-open calibration data, it successfully generalized to decode gaze position during eyes-closed intervals in the dark. These findings indicate that oculomotor signals encoded in the BOLD signal are sufficient for robust gaze tracking even without retinal stimulation, enabling gaze monitoring in total darkness or during sleep and imagery research.
papers.authors: Sina M. Kling, Uriel Lascombes, Matthias Nau, Guillaume S. Masson, Martin Szinte

0434.name: Martin Wiener
0434.bio: Martin Wiener is an Associate Professor at George Mason University and directs the STAR Lab, focusing on the neural foundations of time and space perception. Wiener’s research integrates functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (fMRI), Electroencephalography (EEG), and Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS) to investigate how the brain constructs temporal and spatial dimensions. Their work explores the intersection of vision and timing, specifically how image features like memorability and visual hierarchy clutter modulate perceived duration and memory encoding. By combining these neuroimaging techniques with computational modeling and psychophysics, Wiener aims to map the sensory and motor circuits that enable rhythmic processing, navigation, and decision-making.
0434.research_direction: Dr. Wiener has recently been investigating the cognitive and neural architectures that underlie human time perception across visual, auditory, and motor domains. Their recent work explores the motor system's active role in timing, using mechanically induced robotic tremors, EEG, and transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) to examine how movement noise and neural oscillator entrainment influence duration judgments and tempo matching. Additionally, they are probing the metacognitive aspects of sensorimotor timing, employing behavioral reproduction tasks and fMRI to uncover how individuals monitor their own temporal errors, integrate performance feedback, and utilize brain systems like the Default Mode Network to dynamically update internal timing standards. Finally, they have expanded their temporal investigations into high-level visual cognition, combining psychophysics with recurrent convolutional neural network models to test how an image's intrinsic memorability interacts with sensory processing speed to distort a viewer's subjective sense of time.

papers.title: Awareness of both global uncertainty and feedback in human time estimation
papers.abstract: This study investigates the metacognitive capacity of humans to monitor timing errors and the subsequent influence of feedback on temporal learning. Participants performed a temporal reproduction task across varying levels of global uncertainty and feedback conditions. The research specifically evaluated whether individuals could discern the direction of their timing errors and how these metacognitive judgments informed behavior on subsequent trials. Results indicated that humans maintain a robust self-awareness of temporal accuracy, utilizing error-direction information and performance feedback to dynamically update and refine their internal timing standards. Findings suggest that the degree of behavioral improvement is modulated by the perceived level of global uncertainty, supporting a Bayesian framework for metacognitive timing control.
papers.authors: Chetan Desai, Farah Bader, Martin Wiener

papers.title: A coupled oscillator model predicts the effect of neuromodulation and a novel human tempo-matching bias
papers.abstract: This research identifies a systematic tempo-matching bias in humans and provides a computational explanation via a phase-coupled oscillator model. Utilizing a novel beat-matching paradigm, the study observed that participants' matched frequencies were anchored toward the starting comparison frequency, leading to underestimation or overestimation of a 2 Hz target. EEG recordings demonstrated neural entrainment to both stimulus tempos, with phase synchronization increasing as the tempos converged. The phase-coupled oscillator model successfully replicated the behavioral shifts and predicted that increasing the coupling strength of the target oscillator would attenuate the bias. Causal evidence was provided by applying 2 Hz transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) over the supplementary motor area (SMA), which reduced the behavioral bias as predicted by the model.
papers.authors: Chloe Mondok, Martin Wiener

papers.title: Mechanically Induced Motor Tremors Disrupt the Perception of Time
papers.abstract: Using a robotic manipulandum (KINARM), this study investigates the 'tremors in time' hypothesis by testing how mechanically induced motor noise affects temporal precision. Human subjects judged auditory and visual durations while performing reaching movements subject to artificial tremors of varying frequency and amplitude. In accordance with a Bayesian cue-combination framework, the introduction of motor noise increased the variability of sensory duration estimates, as evidenced by significantly higher coefficients of variation (CV) for temporal judgments. High-frequency tremors, in particular, disrupted the ability to maintain precise timing estimates, suggesting that the motor system provides a distinct duration channel that is optimally integrated with exogenous sensory inputs to construct a final perceived duration.
papers.authors: Keri Gladhill, Rose De Kock, Weiwei Zhou, Wilsaan Joiner, Martin Wiener

papers.title: Memorability shapes perceived time (and vice versa)
papers.abstract: Across a series of psychophysical experiments, the researchers demonstrate a bidirectional link between image memorability and subjective time perception. Stimuli with higher memorability scores derived from the LaMem dataset were consistently perceived as staying on screen longer and were timed with greater precision than low-memorability images. Conversely, images with longer subjective durations were found to be more memorable in delayed recall tests. Applying a recurrent convolutional neural network (rCNN) model of the ventral visual system, the study found that more memorable images are processed with higher efficiency and faster speeds. This increase in processing speed predicts both the dilation and the sharpened resolution of perceived durations, suggesting that perceived time is a function of the rate of sensory evidence accumulation.
papers.authors: Alex C Ma, Ayana D Cameron, Martin Wiener

papers.title: Neuroimaging Signatures of Metacognitive Improvement in Sensorimotor Timing
papers.abstract: This fMRI study explores the neural substrates of metacognitive improvement in human sensorimotor timing using a 're-do' experimental design. Participants performed a temporal reproduction task for supra-second intervals (1.5–6 s) and were given the opportunity to repeat trials following feedback. Behavioral results showed significant reductions in error and enhanced precision on repeat trials. Neuroimaging analysis revealed that these metacognitive improvements are mediated by functional interactions between the Default Mode Network (DMN) and a canonical Timing Network (TN). The DMN exhibited increased BOLD activity during error monitoring and reproduction on repeat trials, while task-based connectivity between the TN and DMN was higher when participants integrated feedback to update their temporal estimates.
papers.authors: Farah Bader, Martin Wiener

0435.name: Martina Poletti
0435.department: Department of Brain and Cognitive Sciences
0435.bio: Martina Poletti is an Associate Professor at the University of Rochester who investigates the mechanisms of active vision and fine-scale oculomotor control. Poletti’s research demonstrates that visual perception and selective attention are non-uniform and modulated within the 1-degree foveola. Utilizing high-precision eye tracking and adaptive optics scanning light ophthalmoscopy, they examine how microscopic eye movements, such as microsaccades, are controlled to facilitate high-acuity tasks. Their research focuses on the interplay between sensory processing, motor behavior, and attentional allocation at the arcminute scale to study the perception of fine spatial details during active exploration.
0435.research_direction: Dr. Poletti's recent work explores the fine-scale perceptual and oculomotor dynamics of human foveal vision using high-precision eye tracking, adaptive optics, and gaze-contingent displays. They have recently been investigating the functional architecture of the foveola, probing how spatial summation, meridian asymmetries, and visual crowding vary topographically across this high-acuity region rather than acting as a homogeneous sensor. Their research also examines how central visual perception is actively modulated by microscopic fixational eye movements—such as ocular drift and microsaccades—and by the frequency-selective allocation of covert exogenous attention. Additionally, they are studying the plasticity of the adult oculomotor system, mapping how fixational drift and spatial targeting adaptively shift in patients navigating cortically induced blindness.

papers.title: Systematic arcminute-scale fixational offsets in patients with early visual cortex damage
papers.abstract: This research investigated whether stroke-related lesions in the primary visual cortex, resulting in cortically induced blindness (CB), influence fixational oculomotor control. Utilizing high-resolution eye tracking, the study revealed that CB patients demonstrate a subtle but systematic gaze offset (measuring only a few arcminutes) toward their blind hemifield during passive fixation tasks. This directional bias was found to dissipate during high-acuity central discrimination tasks, although fixational precision remained comparable to age-matched controls. Analysis of the underlying oculomotor dynamics indicated that while microsaccades showed no directional bias, ocular drift was significantly biased away from the blind field. These findings suggest that the adult oculomotor system dynamically adapts to asymmetric cortical injury, potentially implementing an attentional pointer or a compensatory rebalancing of visual drive.
papers.authors: Ashley M. Clark, Sanjana Kapisthalam, Matthew R. Cavanaugh, Krystel R. Huxlin, Martina Poletti

papers.title: Non-uniform signal pooling across the foveola
papers.abstract: The study utilized adaptive optics (AO) scanning light ophthalmoscopy and high-speed eye tracking to characterize spatial summation and lateral interactions within the human foveola. By correcting for monochromatic aberrations and retinal image motion, the researchers determined that Ricco’s area of complete summation encompasses multiple photoreceptors and remains largely unaffected by pre-neural factors, indicating that foveal acuity is primarily limited by post-receptoral neural pooling. The results demonstrate that signal pooling is non-uniform across the 1-degree foveal region, with distinct topographical variations in spatial summation and crowding zones. This evidence challenges the traditional conception of the foveola as a homogeneous high-resolution sensor and emphasizes the role of localized neural architecture in shaping central vision.
papers.authors: Krishnamachari S. Prahalad, Ashley M. Clark, Benjamin Moon, Austin Roorda, Pavan Tiruveedhula, Wolf Harmening, Alexander Gutnikov, Samantha K. Jenks, Sanjana Kapisthalam, Michele Rucci, Jannick P. Rolland, Martina Poletti

papers.title: Frequency-selective contrast sensitivity modulation driven by fine-tuned exogenous attention at the foveal scale
papers.abstract: This study explored the spatial frequency (SF) selectivity of covert exogenous attention within the high-acuity foveola. Using gaze-contingent displays and high-precision eye tracking to ensure precise attentional allocation, the authors measured contrast sensitivity across a range of spatial frequencies. The findings reveal that foveal exogenous attention selectively enhances contrast sensitivity for low- to mid-range spatial frequencies (4–8 cycles per degree, CPD), with negligible benefits for higher frequencies (12–20 CPD). These results indicate that, despite the foveola's capacity to resolve up to 30 CPD, the exogenous attention mechanism remains an inflexible system that prioritizes lower spatial frequencies, paralleling its behavior in the visual periphery.
papers.authors: Yue Guzhang, T. Florian Jaeger, Martina Poletti

papers.title: Asymmetries in foveal vision
papers.abstract: While visual field asymmetries are well-established in extrafoveal vision, they are typically presumed to be absent in the foveola. This investigation employed high-precision tracking and gaze-contingent stimulus presentation to test fine spatial discrimination at eight isoeccentric locations within the central 0.3 degrees of the fovea. The study found that horizontal-vertical meridian asymmetries (higher sensitivity along the horizontal) persist in the foveola. Crucially, the vertical meridian asymmetry was found to be reversed: unlike the periphery where the lower field is superior, sensitivity in the foveola was significantly higher for stimuli presented in the upper visual field. This discovery demonstrates that foveolar vision is not uniform and possesses unique perceptual structures that differ from the surrounding parafovea.
papers.authors: Samantha K. Jenks, Marisa Carrasco, Martina Poletti

papers.title: Oculomotor Contributions to Foveal Crowding
papers.abstract: This paper examines how fixational eye movements, specifically microsaccades and ocular drift, influence visual crowding within the central fovea. Crowding—the impairment of object recognition due to nearby distractors—is typically studied under the assumption of a static retinal image. By employing a retinal stabilization paradigm, the authors demonstrated that the natural jitter of the eye during fixation significantly modulates foveal crowding. The study found that while ocular drift generally improves uncrowded visual acuity, its effect on crowded stimuli is more complex, potentially exacerbating the spatial integration of target and flanker signals. The results suggest that the dynamic nature of the retinal input, driven by microscopic oculomotor activity, is a critical factor in the spatial bottlenecks of foveal perception.
papers.authors: Ashley M. Clark, Aaron Huynh, Martina Poletti

0436.name: Marvin Chun
0436.bio: Chun is the Richard M. Colgate Professor of Psychology at Yale University, where they investigate the neural substrates of visual attention, memory, and perception. Their research utilizes functional MRI and machine learning to decode brain activity, enabling the prediction of individual differences in cognitive performance through connectome-based predictive modeling. Chun’s work on contextual cueing demonstrates how implicit memory for environmental regularities guides spatial attention. They also conduct research on the functional architecture of the human visual system.
0436.research_direction: Dr. Chun's recent work explores the neural mechanisms underlying visual working memory (VWM) and cognitive control, primarily utilizing fMRI pattern decoding and whole-brain functional connectivity approaches. A major line of their research investigates how visual representations are maintained and transformed during memory delays in the occipitotemporal and posterior parietal cortices, examining whether perceptual features like shape and color are stored independently or interactively integrated. They are also studying how these brain networks resolve competing demands in VWM, using cross-decoding to ask how multiple items are represented simultaneously—such as through linear averaging mechanisms—and how sensory regions balance object identity stability with fluctuating attentional loads. Additionally, Dr. Chun has recently been applying connectome-based predictive modeling to characterize the large-scale network architecture of executive functions, probing how general cognitive control and specific sub-processes like inhibition and shifting map onto individual differences in the human connectome.

papers.title: Connectome-Based Predictive Models of General and Specific Executive Functions
papers.abstract: This study characterizes the unity and diversity of executive functions (EF) by applying Connectome-based Predictive Modeling (CPM) to whole-brain functional connectivity data. Utilizing fMRI datasets from the Human Connectome Project, the researchers developed neuromarkers to predict individual differences in task performance across the Flanker (Inhibition), Dimensional Change Card Sort (Shifting), and 2-back (Updating) paradigms. Results identified a common executive function factor represented by a dense functional connectome spanning the frontoparietal, default-mode, and dorsal attention networks. While the Updating-specific component demonstrated high cross-prediction with the general EF factor, specific models for Inhibition and Shifting exhibited more specialized connectivity profiles, supporting a hierarchical architecture of cognitive control in the human connectome.
papers.authors: Shijie Qu, Yueyue Lydia Qu, Kwangsun Yoo, Marvin M. Chun

papers.title: Interactive shape and color representation in visual working memory for colored objects in the human occipitotemporal cortex
papers.abstract: Using fMRI pattern decoding and cross-decoding techniques, this research investigated whether visual features such as shape and color are maintained independently or integrated within the human occipitotemporal cortex (OTC) during visual working memory (VWM). While these features are represented in a largely orthogonal and independent manner during initial perceptual encoding, the study found a significant drop in cross-decoding performance during the VWM delay period within shape-selective and ventral color areas. This finding provides the first evidence for interactive coding of shape and color in VWM, suggesting that sensory representations are actively transformed into a more integrated format to support efficient information storage and retrieval.
papers.authors: Yaoda Xu, Benjamin Swinchoski, JohnMark Taylor, Marvin M. Chun

papers.title: Representing Visual Objects, Attention, and Load in Human Occipito-temporal and Posterior Parietal Cortices
papers.abstract: This study explores the neural mechanisms by which the brain manages stability and adaptability in visual processing across varying task demands. Using fMRI pattern decoding, the authors examined the representational overlap of object identity, attentional priority, and cognitive load in the human occipito-temporal cortex (OTC) and posterior parietal cortex (PPC). Findings reveal that OTC maintains relatively invariant object representations despite fluctuations in attention and load, providing stability in identification. In contrast, PPC representations are highly adaptive and modulated by task context. The interaction between these regions facilitates a balance between maintaining object identity and flexibly responding to changing goal-directed demands.
papers.authors: Yaoda Xu, Marvin M. Chun

papers.title: Transformed Visual Working Memory Representations in Human Occipitotemporal and Posterior Parietal Cortices
papers.abstract: The sensory account of visual working memory (VWM) posits that the same neural representations are shared between perception and memory. This study tested this hypothesis by using fMRI cross-decoding to compare object representations when they served as VWM targets versus distractors, and during encoding versus the delay period. In both human occipitotemporal and posterior parietal regions, a significant drop or chance-level cross-decoding was observed between these states. These results indicate that VWM content is represented in a transformed state distinct from its initial perceptual trace, challenging the idea that sensory areas provide a passive, shared buffer for both perception and short-term retention.
papers.authors: Yaoda Xu, Marvin M. Chun

papers.title: Using fMRI representations of single objects to predict multiple objects in working memory in human occipitotemporal and posterior parietal cortices
papers.abstract: This research quantifies the relationship between neural representations of individual items and multi-object arrays within visual working memory (VWM). By analyzing fMRI response patterns in the occipitotemporal and posterior parietal cortices, the study demonstrates that the VWM representation for a pair of objects can be accurately modeled as the linear average of the representations for each item presented alone. This averaging relationship held even after accounting for the modulatory effects of task load. These results suggest that VWM capacity and representational space are governed by competitive interactions and a normalization mechanism that approximates the mean of individual component representations in high-level visual and parietal areas.
papers.authors: Yaoda Xu, Marvin M. Chun

0438.name: Mary Hayhoe
0438.lab_name: Vision, Cognition, and Action Virtual Reality Lab
0438.bio: Mary Hayhoe is a Professor of Psychology at the University of Texas at Austin and works in the field of active vision. Hayhoe utilizes virtual reality and motion-tracking technologies to study eye movements and visual perception during natural, goal-directed activities. Their research investigates the interplay between gaze control, working memory, and sensory-motor decision-making. This work demonstrates how task-specific demands and internal rewards dictate the allocation of visual attention in dynamic environments.
0438.research_direction: Dr. Hayhoe's recent work investigates the visuo-motor control loop in naturalistic environments, utilizing mobile eye-tracking, full-body kinematics, and 3D photogrammetry to study how foveal and parafoveal vision guide foothold selection and route planning on rugged terrain. They have recently been framing these visually guided actions as sequential decision-making under uncertainty, exploring how active gaze deployment can be formalized using Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes (POMDPs) and inverse reinforcement learning. Their recent research also examines the specific perceptual mechanisms of locomotion, employing head-mounted virtual reality and prism-rotation paradigms to disentangle how humans use the focus of expansion versus local retinal flow for steering and postural stability. Additionally, they are applying this emphasis on fine-grained, ecologically valid measurement to social cognition, investigating the micro-level gaze dynamics and interpersonal synchronization of parent-infant joint attention during unstructured play.

papers.title: The Role of Retinal Flow in Walking
papers.abstract: This study characterizes the influence of retinal flow patterns on goal-directed walking trajectories by employing a prism-rotation paradigm in a head-mounted virtual reality system. The researchers dissociated the focus of expansion (FOE) from visual direction to isolate their roles in steering behavior. Experiments involved manipulating the distribution of ground-plane and wall-plane texture to vary optic flow salience across different surfaces. Quantitative analysis of walking paths reveals that individuals rely heavily on local ground-plane motion statistics to maintain postural stability and coordinate foot placement. Prisms were found to induce lateral trajectory deviations primarily by activating a balance-preserving response to perturbed retinal flow in the lower visual field, suggesting that overground navigation is controlled by a complex integration of heading direction and gait-stabilizing motion cues rather than simple FOE-based heading detection.
papers.authors: Nathaniel V. Powell, Daniel Panfili, Youjin Oh, Jonathan S. Matthis, Mary Hayhoe

papers.title: Visual control of walking using terrain reconstructions
papers.abstract: The authors investigate the visuo-motor control loop during natural locomotion on rugged outdoor terrain by integrating high-precision photogrammetric 3D reconstructions with mobile eye-tracking and full-body kinematics. The research quantifies the spatial precision of gaze deployment relative to subsequent foothold selections across multiple steps and terrains of varying difficulty. Findings indicate that gaze is predominantly allocated to the ground plane one to two steps ahead, with fixations centered on potential footholds with a standard deviation of approximately 0.23 to 0.25 meters. The study demonstrates that while foveal vision is critical for the initial selection of stable footholds and the management of gait-induced instabilities, the parafoveal retina provides sufficient spatial information for maintaining heading and longer-term path planning. This suggests a hierarchical control mechanism where gaze serves both immediate motor execution and prospective route optimization.
papers.authors: Daniel P. Panfili, Karl Muller, Kathryn Bonnen, Mary M. Hayhoe

papers.title: Examining micro-level natural behaviour to improve generalizability in behavioural science: a case study of parent–child joint attention
papers.abstract: This research evaluates the generalizability of social-cognitive mechanisms by examining the micro-level dynamics of parent-infant joint attention in unstructured, naturalistic play settings. Utilizing high-frequency head-mounted eye tracking and multimodal behavioral analysis, the study characterizes the transition between social-engagement phases and their underlying attentional markers. The results reveal that joint attention is a highly contingent and emergent phenomenon, with gaze patterns and interpersonal synchronization being modulated by momentary task goals and sensory-motor constraints. The authors argue that traditional laboratory findings often fail to capture the high-dimensional variability and situational dependencies inherent in natural behavior. They propose a naturalistic framework that prioritizes the measurement of fine-grained behavioral regularities to build more generalizable theories of social interaction and cognitive development.
papers.venue: Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences
papers.authors: Chen Yu, Brianna E. Kaplan, Sara E. Schroer, Mary Hayhoe

papers.title: Computational elements of natural vision
papers.abstract: This article presents a theoretical synthesis that formalizes natural visually guided behavior as a problem of sequential decision-making under uncertainty, framing gaze control within the Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP) architecture. The authors summarize two decades of empirical observations to demonstrate that gaze deployment in complex tasks—such as navigation and manipulation—is governed by internal models that account for environmental uncertainty and energetic costs. The paper advocates for the use of active sampling models where agents optimize for long-term behavioral rewards. Furthermore, it highlights the potential of modular inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) to recover subjective rewards and discount factors from human behavioral trajectories, providing a computational framework for understanding how perception, cognition, and action are integrated in ecologically valid settings.
papers.authors: Constantin A. Rothkopf, Mary M. Hayhoe

papers.title: Approaches to understanding natural behavior
papers.abstract: The authors delineate a roadmap for the systematic investigation of vision in its natural context, moving beyond traditional stimulus-driven oculomotor research toward task-oriented behavioral paradigms. By leveraging 3D scene reconstruction and mobile eye-body tracking, they illustrate how natural behavior consists of sequences of decisions shaped by behavioral goals, energetic trade-offs, and environmental regularities. The paper details how complex, gait-induced retinal motion patterns are managed through predictive control and stabilization mechanisms. The researchers emphasize that natural visually guided actions should be analyzed as an integrated visuo-motor loop where the deployment of gaze is adaptively tailored to the statistical structure of the environment and individual motor noise, providing a formal approach to studying sensory-motor decisions in vivo.
papers.authors: Alexander Goettker, Nathaniel Powell, Mary Hayhoe

0439.name: Mary Peterson
0439.bio: Mary A. Peterson is a Professor Emerita at the University of Arizona whose research examines the neural mechanisms of visual perception and the organization of visual input into objects and backgrounds. Peterson’s findings show that high-level semantic knowledge and object memories influence early figure-ground assignment through reentrant processing, which contrasts with traditional hierarchical models. Utilizing psychophysics, EEG, and fMRI, Peterson investigates competitive inhibitory processes during object detection and the role of the perirhinal cortex in perceptual organization. Their current research examines how past experience, context, and unconscious knowledge shape conscious visual experience and attentional allocation.
0439.research_direction: Dr. Peterson has recently been investigating the mechanisms underlying figure assignment and object detection, challenging traditional feedforward models to explore how semantic meaning and cortical reentrant signals shape early visual organization. Their recent work utilizes bipartite displays and drift diffusion modeling to examine how top-down linguistic cues, structural priors like familiar parts versus holistic configurations, and dynamic visual exposure histories compete to resolve structural ambiguity. Additionally, they have been exploring theoretical vision science by evaluating the philosophical boundary between perception and cognition, specifically analyzing the roles of nonconceptual representation, iconicity, and adaptation. Finally, their research extends into applied visual cognition by investigating how stereoscopic depth and interactive viewing within virtual reality environments influence the formation of user mental models and subsequent decision-making processes.

papers.title: Ambiguity and Reentrant Processing in Object Detection
papers.abstract: This article critiques the traditional feedforward model of object detection, proposing a dynamical framework where multiple semantic interpretations are activated at high cortical levels prior to conscious perception. Empirical evidence is reviewed demonstrating that even unrecognized interpretations compete across borders to influence figure assignment. The author posits that object detection is not a terminal stage in a hierarchy but an iterative process mediated by reentrant signals that resolve semantic and structural ambiguity, suggesting that meaning is an intrinsic component of the detection mechanism.
papers.authors: Mary A. Peterson

papers.title: Semantic influences on object detection: Drift diffusion modeling provides insights regarding mechanism
papers.abstract: Applying drift diffusion modeling (DDM) to a figure-assignment task, this study elucidates the mechanisms through which linguistic semantics influence visual object detection. Using bipartite displays containing familiar objects, we manipulated label validity and superordinate category membership. DDM analysis revealed that valid labels primarily increased the drift rate (signal-to-noise ratio), particularly for upright objects. Conversely, invalid labels from the same superordinate category raised the decision threshold, indicating a higher requirement for evidence accumulation to resolve semantic conflict. These results favor a semantic network hypothesis over a low-level feature feedback model.
papers.authors: Jingming Xue, Robert C. Wilson, Mary A. Peterson

papers.title: Does exposure within an experiment affect the influence of familiar parts versus wholes on figure assignment?
papers.abstract: This investigation assesses whether the influence of familiar parts and holistic configurations on figure assignment is modulated by within-experiment exposure. Observers reported figural status for bipartite displays featuring upright, inverted, or part-rearranged (PR) familiar configurations. The findings demonstrate that inverted configurations act as stronger figural priors than PR versions, highlighting the role of inter-part connectivity. Furthermore, block-by-block analysis revealed that exposure within the experiment significantly increased the weight of familiar parts in figure assignment, suggesting that the visual system dynamically reweights part-based and holistic representations based on statistical regularities.
papers.authors: Colin S. Flowers, Mary A. Peterson

papers.title: Block on perceptual variation, attribution, discrimination, and adaptation
papers.abstract: In this critical analysis of Ned Block's theory of the perception-cognition boundary, we evaluate the roles of perceptual variation, attribution, and discrimination. We contest the singular representation requirement, arguing that perceptual categories can be nonconceptual while remaining functionally primitive. Integrating neuroscientific research on adaptation and perceptual constancy, the paper demonstrates that attribution and discrimination are codependent operations of the visual system. We argue against the necessity of 'core cognition' as an intermediate stage, proposing instead a unified account where perceptual capacities are fundamentally grounded in iconicity and non-propositional content.
papers.authors: Susanna Schellenberg, Andrew J. P. Fink, Carl E. Schoonover, Mary A. Peterson

papers.title: Virtual Reality, Mental Models, and Mindful Decision-Making
papers.abstract: This research explores how Virtual Reality (VR) affordances, specifically interactive viewing and stereoscopic depth cues, modulate the development of mental models and mindful decision-making. Through two lab experiments, we isolated the cognitive impacts of these features on information acquisition and perceived control. The results indicate that VR presentations significantly enhance the accuracy and robustness of users' mental models compared to traditional 2D displays. These high-quality mental representations were found to mediate an increase in mindfulness during decision-making tasks, suggesting that VR's immersive depth and interactivity have profound implications for cognitive architecture in digital environments.
papers.venue: Journal of the Association for Information Systems
papers.authors: Heshan Sun, Siyuan Li, Shih-Lun Tseng, Mary A. Peterson

0440.name: Maryam Vaziri-Pashkam
0440.department: Department of Psychological and Brain Sciences
0440.lab_name: Movement and Visual Perception Lab (MVP Lab)
0440.bio: Maryam Vaziri-Pashkam is a cognitive neuroscientist who investigates the neural and computational architectures supporting real-time interactions with objects and social agents. Using methodologies such as fMRI, body movement tracking, and machine learning, Vaziri-Pashkam examines how the human brain integrates visual information with motor control across the dorsal and ventral processing streams. Their research has identified object and action representations within the parietal cortex and compared these biological representations to artificial convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to evaluate models of the visual system. Currently, their work focuses on the neural mechanisms involved in action prediction, object affordances, and the extraction of shape features for grasping.
0440.research_direction: Dr. Vaziri-Pashkam's recent work investigates how the human visual system processes and attends to objects across diverse environments, bridging perception, attention, and action. Their behavioral research explores the varied cues that guide object recognition and search, utilizing object kinematograms to probe whether dynamic shape perception relies on configural processing, while also quantifying how the spatial predictability of objects in natural scenes influences top-down attentional guidance. They are also examining the plasticity of multisensory integration during manual interaction, specifically testing how observers combine familiar visual features like volume with newly learned associations to estimate object weight. At the neural level, their fMRI and theoretical work explores how object representations are modulated by task demands and attention—comparing models of tuning sharpening versus multiplicative gain in the visual cortex—and challenges classic dual-stream theories by investigating the parallel processing of object shape across both the ventral and dorsal pathways.

papers.title: Object Recognition from Dynamic Cues: Examining the Inversion Effect
papers.abstract: This study evaluates whether categorization performance based solely on dynamic motion cues is sensitive to stimulus orientation, analogous to the well-documented inversion effect in static vision. Utilizing object kinematograms—stimuli where object form is defined by motion cues isolated from static features—the researchers tested four animate and four inanimate categories. The findings demonstrate significant inversion effects for most animate categories (excluding reptiles) and, notably, for several inanimate categories like vehicles and balls. These results suggest that dynamic object recognition is orientation-dependent and utilizes configural processing mechanisms, informing the development of computational models that account for visual processing in dynamic environments.
papers.authors: Niloufar Faridani, Shifa Maqsood, Sophia Robert, Amirali Soltani Tehrani, Maryam Vaziri-Pashkam

papers.title: Judging object weights using familiar and newly learned cues: cue combination and individual differences
papers.abstract: The research investigates how human observers integrate established visual cues, such as object volume, with novel, newly learned associations to estimate mass during manual interaction. Through a series of experiments using containers with varied haptic and visual properties, the study assesses the efficiency of multisensory cue integration. Results indicate that while familiar cues are robustly combined to optimize perceptual precision, the acquisition and integration of novel cues are constrained by substantial individual variability and the required duration of sensorimotor training. The work delineates the plasticity and limits of the neural systems responsible for mapping visual features to physical object properties during action execution.
papers.authors: Amirali Soltani Tehrani, Niloufar Faridani, Maryam Vaziri-Pashkam

papers.title: Object Spatial Certainty and Attention: Quantifying Variability in Object Locations in Scenes
papers.abstract: This study characterizes how the variability and predictability of object locations within naturalistic scenes influence the deployment of visual attention. The authors developed an 'Object Spatial Certainty' index to quantify human priors regarding typical object-scene spatial associations. By manipulating target spatial predictability in search tasks, the researchers demonstrated that high spatial certainty significantly enhances the effectiveness of scene context in biasing attentional allocation. In contrast, increased variability in object location (low certainty) diminishes these contextual search benefits. These findings quantify the impact of spatial uncertainty on the efficiency of top-down attentional guidance in complex visual environments.
papers.authors: Niloufar Faridani, Amirali Soltani Tehrani, Maryam Vaziri-Pashkam

papers.title: Attention Modulates Human Visual Responses to Objects by Tuning Sharpening
papers.abstract: This functional MRI study investigates the neural mechanisms of object-based attention by examining how target-distractor similarity in representational space affects attentional modulation. Using stimuli from four object categories (human bodies, cats, cars, and houses), the researchers analyzed responses across V1 and several category-selective regions (LO, pFs, EBA, and PPA). The results reveal that the strength of the attentional bias toward a target decreases as the representational distance between the target and distractor is reduced. Computational simulations further demonstrate that this modulation is better explained by a tuning sharpening mechanism—where neural populations narrow their selectivity—rather than a multiplicative gain increase.
papers.authors: Narges Doostani, Gholam-Ali Hossein-Zadeh, Radoslaw Martin Cichy, Maryam Vaziri-Pashkam

papers.title: Two “What” Networks in the Human Brain
papers.abstract: This theoretical review challenges the classic Ungerleider-Mishkin dichotomy that divides visual processing into a dorsal 'where' pathway and a ventral 'what' pathway. The author synthesizes cross-species evidence of robust object shape and category selectivity within the dorsal pathway, specifically in the posterior parietal cortex. A comparative analysis of dorsal and ventral object representations identifies critical differences in their tolerance to image transformations and sensitivity to task demands, with dorsal regions exhibiting stronger task modulation and weaker tolerance. The article proposes that the human brain utilizes two distinct and parallel networks for processing object shapes, likely optimized for different behavioral goals such as action guidance versus object identification.
papers.authors: Maryam Vaziri-Pashkam

0441.name: Masataka Sawayama
0441.department: Graduate School of Information Science and Technology
0441.bio: Masataka Sawayama is an Associate Professor specializing in visual 'Shitsukan' (material perception), investigating how humans recognize complex surface qualities such as gloss, wetness, and translucency. Sawayama’s work integrates human psychophysics with computational modeling and deep neural networks to identify the image cues and neural mechanisms involved in material recognition. Their research also explores the intersection of computer vision and cognitive neuroscience, including the development of brain-decoding models and the analysis of semantic representations in the visual cortex.
0441.research_direction: Dr. Sawayama has recently been investigating the computational, neural, and behavioral mechanisms underlying "Shitsukan"—the visual perception of material qualities such as gloss, wetness, and translucency. Their recent work explores how the human visual system disentangles complex optical interactions, using psychophysical experiments and image decomposition algorithms to examine how color and luminance signals are efficiently coded to isolate material properties from object geometry. To understand the neural basis of these processes, they are comparing multi-unit activity in macaque visual cortices (V4 and IT) to deep neural networks, evaluating how task-specific objectives and multimodal supervision shape material representations in the primate ventral stream. Across these approaches, Dr. Sawayama examines how the visual hierarchy relies on diagnostic image statistics rather than full physical scene reconstruction to robustly estimate material attributes in natural environments.

papers.title: Revisiting Color Efficient Coding through Material Perception
papers.abstract: This study investigates the efficient coding of natural scenes by examining the redundancy in cone signals and early visual transformations. While classical theories emphasize the decorrelation of luminance and color signals (e.g., via PCA), the author notes that object material properties introduce significant redundancy between these channels due to complex optical interactions. Utilizing a median cut algorithm derived from computer graphics, this research proposes a novel decomposition method that enhances processing efficiency while isolating diagnostic features for material versus geometry. Behavioral psychophysical experiments indicate that color reduction via this algorithm significantly impairs material classification performance but leaves object recognition largely unaffected, implying that geometric structure remains accessible even in low-bit visual representations.
papers.authors: Masataka Sawayama
