papers.title: Correspondence between Monkey Visual Cortices and Deep Neural Networks reveals task-specific representations of material
papers.abstract: This study explores the alignment between neural representations in the macaque visual system and deep neural networks (DNNs) specifically for material perception. By analyzing multi-unit activity from the inferior temporal (IT) cortex and V4 while monkeys performed material-related tasks, and comparing these signals to various DNN architectures (including vision-language and purely vision-based models), the researchers evaluated how task-specific objectives influence representational similarity. The findings demonstrate that models trained with high-level semantic objectives or multimodal supervision exhibit higher correspondence with cortical responses in IT than models focused on low-level image features. This suggests that the primate ventral stream organizes material information based on task-relevant features and semantic category rather than simple visual statistics.
papers.authors: Takahiro Kawabe, Masataka Sawayama

papers.title: Human Visual Perception of Shitsukan
papers.abstract: This research chapter provides a comprehensive synthesis of human Shitsukan (material and quality) perception, focusing on the computational and psychophysical mechanisms used to estimate properties like gloss, wetness, and translucency. The authors argue that the estimation of these physical attributes is an inherently ill-posed problem because image formation depends on the nonlinear interplay of geometry, illumination, and material. They propose that the human visual system circumvents these complexities by relying on diagnostic image statistics and intensity gradient information rather than full physical reconstruction. The work reviews evidence for how different layers of the visual hierarchy—from early luminance histograms to higher-level semantic understanding—contribute to our robust experience of material qualities in natural environments.
papers.venue: Shitsukan—Understanding and Manipulating Material and Quality Perception (Springer Nature)
papers.authors: Shin'ya Nishida, Masataka Sawayama

0442.name: Mathew Diamond
0442.lab_name: SENSEx Lab (SISSA Explorations into the Neuronal foundations of Sensory Experience Lab)
0442.bio: Mathew Diamond is a Professor of Cognitive Neuroscience at SISSA, where they direct the SENSEx Lab and coordinate the PhD program in Cognitive Neuroscience. Diamond’s research investigates the neuronal algorithms underlying tactile perception, specifically examining how the rodent whisker system and human sensory pathways encode stimulus features such as texture, intensity, and duration. By integrating multi-channel electrophysiology, optogenetics, and psychophysics, their work characterizes the transformation of sensory signals into subjective percepts and explores the role of working memory and sensory history in decision-making. Diamond is a co-author of the textbook From Neuron to Brain.
0442.research_direction: Dr. Diamond's recent work explores the neural mechanisms of time perception alongside systemic demographic challenges in clinical neuroscience. In the domain of sensory processing, they have recently been using optogenetics, electrophysiology, and computational modeling in rodents to investigate how primary somatosensory regions and the dorsolateral striatum causally support the judgment of tactile stimulus duration and the temporal organization of behavior. At a theoretical level, they are developing Bayesian frameworks to test whether intrinsic neural fatigue and cellular heterogeneity allow neural circuits to adaptively encode sequences of time. Expanding beyond systems neuroscience, their diverse portfolio also includes survey-based research investigating the structural barriers, mentorship dynamics, and gender biases experienced by female neurosurgeons.

papers.title: Neural heterogeneity enables adaptive encoding of time sequences
papers.abstract: The mechanisms by which neural circuits represent time intervals on the scale of hundreds of milliseconds to minutes remain poorly understood. This study proposes a theoretical framework demonstrating that biological systems can leverage intrinsic neural fatigue—the decay of activity during persistent stimulation—to encode temporal intervals. By developing a Bayesian framework that incorporates parametrically heterogeneous stochastic dynamics with interval priors, the researchers predict timing information availability irrespective of the specific decoding mechanism. The results reveal a fundamental trade-off between the precision of representing the immediate preceding interval and the retention of information from earlier ones. Crucially, the model shows that cellular diversity is not merely a biological byproduct but a functional requirement for encoding sequences of time intervals, suggesting that neural heterogeneity plays a vital computational role in the formation of temporal memory.
papers.authors: Sebastian Reinartz, Arash Fassihi, Maria Ravera, Mathew E. Diamond

papers.title: Women in neurosurgery aim for recognition of merit, not tokenism: insights from an Italian survey
papers.abstract: Despite shifts in medical demographics, women remain underrepresented in neurosurgery, prompting debate over the drivers of this disparity. This investigation analyzed gender-related challenges using a 49-item survey administered to female members of the Italian Society of Neurosurgery. Analysis of 119 respondents revealed that personal motivation is the primary career driver, while mentorship is perceived as critical by nearly 70%. However, over half of the participants reported experiencing gender bias in residency and professional environments, with significant difficulties in reconciling familial responsibilities and professional advancement. Despite these obstacles, the majority of respondents expressed opposition to identity-based remedial measures such as gender quotas or segregated conference sections. Instead, the findings emphasize a collective demand for a merit-based system that ensures professional visibility and recognition irrespective of gender, placing the onus on scientific associations to eliminate structural biases.
papers.authors: Barbara Cappelletto, Rossella Rispoli, Paola Peretta, Laura Grazia Valentini, Debora Garozzo, Maurizio Fornari, Concetta Alafaci, Mathew E. Diamond

papers.title: Direct contribution of the sensory cortex to the judgment of stimulus duration
papers.abstract: While it is established that perceptual experiences of time often accompany sensory input, the causal role of primary sensory regions in timing computations remains controversial. This study employed optogenetic manipulation and electrophysiological recordings in rats to investigate the involvement of the vibrissal somatosensory cortex (vS1) in judging the duration and intensity of tactile vibrations. Optogenetic excitation of vS1 neurons was found to dilate the perceived duration of stimuli in one cohort of animals, while simultaneously amplifying the perceived intensity in another. This suggests that a single population of sensory cortical neurons multiplexes information for both stimulus features. A computational model based on integrated membrane currents successfully replicated the animals' choices, indicating that time perception is intrinsically linked to the same sensory processing pathways that encode physical stimulus attributes. The results identify the sensory cortex as a critical gateway in a distributed network for time perception.
papers.authors: Sebastian Reinartz, Arash Fassihi, Maria Ravera, Luciano Paz, Francesca Pulecchi, Marco Gigante, Mathew E. Diamond

papers.title: Reply Letter to: The dorsolateral striatum encodes a temporal basis for the organization of behavior
papers.abstract: This peer-reviewed correspondence addresses recent findings regarding the neural representation of time within the dorsolateral striatum (DLS). The authors respond to critiques of their previously proposed framework, which suggests that DLS activity provides a necessary temporal scaffold for the coordination of complex behavioral sequences. The discussion centers on the robustness of neuronal time-coding algorithms and the physiological relevance of striatal dynamics in rodents performing duration-based discrimination tasks. The letter refines the interpretation of how the striatum integrates sensory cortical drive to facilitate the organization of behavior across time, emphasizing the consistency of their temporal basis model with existing neurophysiological data.
papers.authors: Alessandro Toso, Sebastian Reinartz, Mathew E. Diamond

0443.name: Matteo Valsecchi
0443.bio: Valsecchi is an Associate Professor at the University of Bologna whose research examines the mechanisms of human visual perception and oculomotor control. Their work focuses on how the brain maintains a stable and continuous perceptual experience despite the resolution differences between foveal and peripheral vision and the interruptions caused by saccadic eye movements. Using psychophysics, eye tracking, and electrophysiological techniques such as SSVEPs, Valsecchi has investigated phenomena including saccadic suppression, transsaccadic integration, and the influence of prediction on peripheral appearance. Recent studies by Valsecchi explore the metacognitive aspects of vision, specifically analyzing confidence biases and the perceived uniformity of the visual field across eccentricities.
0443.research_direction: Dr. Valsecchi’s recent work explores the mechanisms of spatial attention, particularly investigating how the visual system uses statistical learning and habituation to suppress irrelevant distractors, such as luminance transients and color singletons, across both within-trial and across-trial timescales. They have also recently been examining the intersection of oculomotor circuitry and covert cognition by probing how cortical alpha oscillations measured via EEG relate to the covert tracking of moving peripheral targets, and whether fixational microsaccade dynamics can reliably index internal cognitive states like mind wandering during sustained vigilance tasks. Additionally, their research investigates visual metaperception across the visual field, questioning how metacognitive confidence biases—such as peripheral overconfidence—adaptively scale with varying eccentricities during natural scene categorization tasks.

papers.title: Attentional tracking reduces cortical alpha oscillations
papers.abstract: The premotor theory of attention posits that overt and covert attentional orienting recruit shared neural circuits and mechanisms, an assertion widely evaluated during shifts of spatial attention and gaze toward peripheral targets. Cortical alpha oscillations have previously been tightly coupled with overt smooth pursuit eye movements; however, how alpha dynamics relate to the covert tracking of moving visual targets in the periphery remains poorly understood. In this study, 16 human participants maintained central fixation while covertly tracking a visual target moving along the horizontal meridian across three velocities (2, 6, or 12 °/s) within the left or right visual hemifield, while concurrent electroencephalography (EEG) and eye-tracking recordings were obtained. Analyses demonstrated that occipitoparietal alpha power was systematically attenuated as observers covertly tracked targets positioned deeper in the visual periphery, irrespective of tracking velocity. These findings show that cortical alpha suppression indexes covert attentional allocation during visual motion tracking, demonstrating functional convergence between covert tracking and overt pursuit in support of the premotor theory of attention.
papers.authors: Songlin Qiao, Xuemei Xia, Jing Chen, Matteo Valsecchi

papers.title: Peripheral overconfidence in a scene categorization task
papers.abstract: Visual discriminability and spatial resolution decline markedly from the fovea to the peripheral visual field, yet empirical evidence regarding whether metaperception (perceptual confidence) accurately tracks these physiological differences remains contradictory. While peripheral underconfidence occurs during local orientation discrimination, overconfidence has been observed in coarse detection. Here, we tested whether peripheral overconfidence emerges in tasks aligned with the specialized global processing capacities of peripheral vision, specifically rapid natural scene categorization. Human observers performed a 2-alternative forced-choice scene categorization task using the artificial scotoma/window paradigm, followed by a 2-interval confidence forced-choice procedure (CFC) to quantify confidence bias and metacognitive sensitivity while matching task performance across eccentricities. Participants exhibited pronounced overconfidence in judgments informed by peripheral compared to central visual input. This demonstrates that visual confidence does not monotonically decrease with peripheral eccentricities, but instead adaptively reflects a metacognitive prior calibrated to the spatial-scale demands of the task and the functional specialization of the visual periphery for global scene analysis.
papers.authors: Nino Sharvashidze, Matteo Toscani, Matteo Valsecchi

papers.title: Is mind wandering reflected in microsaccade dynamics?
papers.abstract: Mind wandering entails an attentional decouple wherein internal cognitive processing shifts toward task-unrelated thoughts, precipitating lapses in sustained attention during daily life. Although several pupillometric and ocular metrics have been linked to task-unrelated thought, whether fixational microsaccade dynamics index the onset of mind-wandering states remains unresolved. Here, participants completed the Sustained Attention to Response Task (SART), a go/no-go vigilance paradigm susceptible to attentional drift. Microsaccadic rates were quantified across temporal epochs preceding commission errors (failures to withhold responding to rare no-go targets, indexing mind wandering) and compared against epochs preceding successful target withholds. Cluster-based permutation testing revealed a robust, significant depression in microsaccadic frequency in the time windows directly antecedent to commission errors relative to correct response inhibitions. Because fixational microsaccades are modulated by top-down mental effort and cognitive workload, this systematic deceleration in microsaccadic frequency demonstrates that periods of mind wandering reflect intense cognitive engagement in task-unrelated operations rather than neural quiescence or idling.
papers.authors: Matteo Valsecchi, Mario Dalmaso, Luigi Castelli, Eleonora Baldini, Giovanni Galfano

papers.title: Within-Trial and Across-Trials Habituation Mechanisms to Irrelevant Visual Transients
papers.abstract: Visual search efficiency improves when observers encounter repeated task-irrelevant feature singletons or luminance transients at fixed display locations across trials, a suppression effect attributed to attentional habituation. This study investigated whether analogous repetition benefits occur when irrelevant luminance transients repeat at an identical spatial location within an individual trial, and evaluated how this within-trial suppression interacts with across-trials habituation. Across four visual search experiments, distractor interference—quantified by response time costs and error rates—was significantly attenuated when four sequential luminance transients preceded the search target at a single location compared to single-transient presentations. Crucially, the magnitude of this within-trial repetition benefit was unaffected by manipulations of local and global across-trials transient probabilities, demonstrating the concurrent existence of functionally dissociable within-trial and across-trials habituation mechanisms. Furthermore, spatial transposition of the initial three transients substantially disrupted the repetition benefit, establishing that suppression is spatially specific rather than driven by general temporal warning signals or unspecific preparation.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
papers.authors: Matteo Valsecchi, Massimo Turatto

papers.title: Learning to resist distraction by spatially predictable luminance transients and color singletons: same or different mechanisms?
papers.abstract: Salient task-irrelevant visual stimuli, such as abrupt luminance transients or color singletons, involuntarily capture spatial attention during visual search. While statistical learning of regularities in distractor occurrence mitigates capture at high-probability locations (distractor-location effect), this spatial suppression typically impairs target processing when targets appear at that location (target-location effect) for feature singletons. In a series of visual search experiments, we investigated whether spatially predictable luminance transients and color singletons elicit identical suppression mechanisms. Replicating established singleton dynamics, spatial learning attenuated interference from both classes of distractors at high-frequency locations. However, learned spatial predictability for luminance transients yielded a robust distractor-location effect without producing a corresponding target-location suppression effect. Additionally, luminance-transient interference escalated with increasing target-to-distractor spatial distance. These dissociations indicate that learned attenuation of luminance-transient capture does not rely on static priority-map suppression, but instead operates through distinct habituation and spatial filtering mechanisms compared to color singletons.
papers.authors: Matteo Valsecchi, Massimo Turatto

0444.name: Matthew Davidson
0444.department: School of Psychology, Graduate School of Health
0444.main_research_area: Neuroscience of consciousness and active perception
0444.bio: Matthew Davidson is a cognitive neuroscientist and Lecturer at the University of Technology Sydney, where they are a member of the Behavioural Sciences and Technology research group. Davidson’s research examines the neuroscience of consciousness and active perception, specifically investigating how neural activity and subjective experience are influenced by natural movement. Using a combination of mobile electroencephalography (EEG) and virtual reality (VR), they study how perceptual sampling and multisensory integration are phase-locked to the human gait cycle. This research, supported by an ARC Discovery Early Career Researcher Award (DECRA), has been published in journals including Nature Communications, eLife, and PLOS Biology.
0444.research_direction: Dr. Davidson has recently been exploring the dynamic mechanisms of visual awareness, cross-modal metacognition, and the interplay between natural movement and sensory processing. Much of their recent work investigates unconscious visual processing through the development of a novel "tracking continuous flash suppression" (tCFS) psychophysical paradigm, which they use to test whether semantically complex or affective stimuli possess privileged access to conscious awareness. Beyond interocular suppression, they are utilizing EEG and multivariate pattern analysis to determine whether automatic, post-decisional neural error signals generalize across distinct sensory modalities, like vision and audition, to encode domain-general confidence. Additionally, their research examines how human locomotion shapes visual sampling, leveraging immersive virtual reality and fine-grained kinematic tracking to ask whether near-threshold perceptual sensitivity rhythmically fluctuates in phase with the biomechanical stride cycle.

papers.title: Priority access to awareness? A new 'CFS tracking' paradigm reveals no priority for fearful faces or a face inversion effect
papers.abstract: Continuous flash suppression (CFS) is widely used to investigate unconscious visual processing by quantifying the time required for a monocularly suppressed stimulus to break into conscious awareness (breaking CFS or bCFS). Stimuli possessing supposed biological or affective significance, such as fearful or upright faces, frequently yield shorter breakthrough latencies, which has been widely interpreted as evidence for priority access to consciousness or attenuated interocular suppression. In this study, the authors applied tracking CFS (tCFS), an adaptive psychophysical approach in which target contrast continuously ramps up until perceptual breakthrough (bCFS) and subsequently decreases until perceptual re-suppression (reCFS) across repeated transitions, thereby quantifying suppression depth directly in decibels of contrast. Evaluating upright and inverted faces displaying happy, neutral, and fearful expressions demonstrated that while bCFS contrast thresholds systematically differed across stimulus categories, reCFS thresholds exhibited corresponding parallel shifts. As a consequence, suppression depth (the ratio of breakthrough to re-suppression thresholds) remained entirely uniform across all facial expressions and orientations. These results show that differences in bCFS latencies reflect shifts in overall visibility and baseline contrast sensitivity rather than differential unconscious processing or privileged access to awareness.
papers.authors: David Alais, Lina Ye, Jacob Coorey, Matthew J. Davidson

papers.title: An Automatic Domain-General Error Signal Is Shared across Tasks and Predicts Confidence in Different Sensory Modalities
papers.abstract: The study of decision self-evaluation has predominantly focused on visual paradigms and explicit confidence ratings, leaving open whether metacognitive evaluations are encoded automatically and shared across sensory modalities. Using multivariate pattern analysis of electroencephalographic (EEG) data, the authors evaluated whether post-decisional neural signals cross-generalize between tasks and sensory modalities in the absence of explicit metacognitive prompts. Participants (N = 21) performed a speeded visual discrimination task with no requirement for confidence ratings, followed by an unspeeded auditory discrimination task where trial-by-trial confidence was reported. A linear multivariate classifier trained on post-response EEG epochs to discriminate errors from correct responses on the visual task successfully generalized to differentiate correct and error trials in the subsequent auditory task. This cross-modal generalization was absent for stimulus-locked EEG classifiers and uniquely predicted subjective confidence ratings on the auditory task. These findings demonstrate that post-response neural activity automatically encodes a domain-general metacognitive evaluation signal across distinct sensory modalities without requiring explicit self-report.
papers.authors: Matthew J. Davidson, Sriraj Aiyer, Nick Yeung

papers.title: A new 'CFS tracking' paradigm reveals uniform suppression depth regardless of target complexity or salience
papers.abstract: Standard continuous flash suppression (CFS) protocols rely on the latency to break suppression (bCFS) to infer unconscious visual processing, but this metric confounds suppression potency with differences in baseline contrast sensitivity. Here, the authors introduced tracking CFS (tCFS), a continuous psychophysical technique wherein monocular target contrast dynamically ramps up until breakthrough into conscious perception and then ramps down until returning to subjective suppression, yielding paired bCFS and re-suppression (reCFS) thresholds across repeated transitions. Evaluating diverse stimulus classes—including complex semantic images (faces, houses) and low-level visual patterns (linear gratings, phase-scrambled noise)—demonstrated that while bCFS thresholds varied significantly across categories, reCFS thresholds varied in lockstep, resulting in an invariant suppression depth across all stimulus types. Furthermore, manipulating the rate of contrast change systematically altered suppression depth in a manner quantitatively captured by a damped harmonic oscillator model of reciprocal inhibition and adaptation. These findings suggest that CFS is mediated by early, non-selective cortical suppression mechanisms and indicate that differential bCFS thresholds do not reflect selective unconscious processing of high-level semantic content.
papers.authors: David Alais, Jacob Coorey, Randolph Blake, Matthew J. Davidson

papers.title: Walking modulates visual detection performance according to stride cycle phase
papers.abstract: Although human walking feels continuous and smooth, locomotion imposes cyclic motor demands that may periodically influence sensory processing. To investigate whether locomotion modulates visual sensitivity, the authors continuously sampled near-threshold visual detection performance as participants walked unencumbered along a linear path in an immersive wireless virtual reality environment. Fine-grained kinematic tracking of the stride cycle revealed strong periodic modulations in detection accuracy, reaction times, and response likelihood at approximately 2 cycles per stride (~2 Hz) at the group level, with optimal perceptual performance consistently aligned with the swing phase of each step and perceptual decrements aligned with footfall. Group-level Bayesian prevalence analysis demonstrated that individual participants exhibited highly prevalent behavioral oscillations clustering in idiosyncratic frequency regimes of either 2 or 4 cycles per stride, locked in phase across observers. These results reveal that natural locomotion rhythmically entrains visual perception, aligning heightened sensory sampling with the mechanically stable swing phases of the gait cycle.
papers.authors: Matthew J. Davidson, Frans A. J. Verstraten, David Alais

papers.title: tCFS: A new 'CFS tracking' paradigm reveals uniform suppression depth regardless of target complexity or salience
papers.abstract: We introduce 'tracking' continuous flash suppression (tCFS), a novel psychophysical paradigm designed to measure the dynamic depth of interocular suppression with higher precision and lower variance than traditional breakthrough methods. In tCFS, participants use a motor response to continuously track the visibility of a target as its contrast is automatically adjusted based on whether it is currently dominant or suppressed. This allows for the simultaneous quantification of breakthrough thresholds (bCFS) and re-suppression thresholds (reCFS). Across multiple experiments using varied stimulus categories—including faces, houses, objects, and simple gratings—we found that while breakthrough thresholds vary significantly across categories, the calculated suppression depth is consistent. This uniform suppression depth suggests that once a stimulus is suppressed, the inhibitory influence exerted by the dominant mask is determined by local competitive interactions in the primary visual cortex that are blind to the higher-level complexity or categorical salience of the target image.
papers.authors: David Alais, Jacob Coorey, Randolph Blake, Matthew J Davidson

0445.name: Maurice Ptito
0445.department: School of Optometry; Department of Applied Mathematics and Computer Science
0445.bio: Maurice Ptito researches the development and functional plasticity of the visual system in humans and animal models. Their work addresses sensory substitution, specifically the use of the Tongue Display Unit to enable blind individuals to process spatial information through tactile pathways. Ptito employs neuroimaging and electrophysiological techniques, including diffusion MRI tractography, fMRI, and PET, to investigate how the brain reorganizes in response to congenital or acquired blindness. They currently hold the Harland Sanders Research Chair in Vision Science and investigate the neural mechanisms of cross-modal reorganization and spatial navigation.
0445.research_direction: Dr. Ptito's recent work explores the neural mechanisms of visual deprivation, with a dual focus on cross-modal plasticity and applied sensory substitution. To understand the fundamental rules of cortical reorganization, they have recently been using magnetoencephalography (MEG) in late-blind adults to map how tactile and auditory inputs reroute to the primary visual cortex, while also using electrophysiology in mouse models to probe the critical periods governing receptive field refinement. Alongside this basic neurobiology, their recent research investigates behavioral interventions designed to improve spatial cognition and navigational autonomy for visually impaired individuals. Through obstacle-course assessments and large-scale surveys, they are testing the efficacy of various assistive technologies, including finger-mounted vibrotactile travel aids, 3D-printed tactile maps, and multisensory indoor navigation systems tailored for comorbid populations with intellectual disabilities.

papers.title: Pathways of Cross-Modal Access to the Visual Cortex in Late Blindness
papers.abstract: This investigation utilizes magnetoencephalography (MEG) to characterize the neurophysiological pathways facilitating the rerouting of tactile and auditory information to the primary visual cortex (V1) in late-blind (LB) adults. By assessing neural response latencies and directed connectivity metrics (alpha-band Granger causality) following tactile finger stimulation and auditory cueing, the study demonstrates that LB individuals exhibit cross-modal recruitment of V1 with latencies comparable to those observed in congenital blindness. The findings suggest that the functional architecture supporting cross-modal plasticity remains latent and can be unmasked even after the completion of visual development, indicating that early visual experience does not preclude the establishment of non-visual thalamocortical or cortico-cortical inputs to the visual cortex.
papers.authors: Samuel Paré, James Isaac Lubell, Sylvain Baillet, Ron Kupers, Maurice Ptito

papers.title: International prevalence of tactile map usage and its impact on navigational independence and well-being of people with visual impairments
papers.abstract: This study reports on a large-scale international survey (N=1,262) investigating the utilization of tactile maps among people with visual impairments (PVI) and their subsequent impact on spatial cognition and quality of life. Quantitative analysis of survey responses from 40 countries reveals a significant correlation between tactile map experience and superior cognitive mapping performance, higher educational attainment, and increased self-reported well-being. Furthermore, participants with early exposure to tactile maps demonstrated a greater capacity for forming generalized spatial representations and a higher degree of navigational autonomy. The results emphasize the critical role of tactile cartography in overcoming the limitations of egocentric navigation and suggest that widespread implementation of 3D-printed tactile resources could significantly improve independence for the PVI population.
papers.authors: Maxime Bleau, Kopila Kafle, Min Wang, Soutongnoma Safiata Kabore, Jorge Luis Cueva-Vargas, Joseph Paul Nemargut, Maurice Ptito

papers.title: Technology and instructions to help people with blindness and intellectual disability manage indoor travel: a case series study
papers.abstract: This research evaluates a multisensory assistive technology intervention designed to facilitate independent indoor navigation for individuals suffering from the dual challenge of blindness and intellectual disability. The system integrates a customized sensory navigation platform with tailored instructional protocols to provide structured tactile and auditory guidance. Through a series of case studies, the investigators measured performance metrics including route recall, deviation frequency, and the reduction in human-guided assistance. The findings demonstrate that consistent use of the technology, coupled with behavioral training, enables users with significant cognitive and sensory impairments to navigate complex indoor environments with increased reliability and self-determination, addressing a critical gap in assistive technology research for comorbid populations.
papers.authors: Maxime Bleau, Samuel Paré, Ismaël Djerourou, Daniel-Robert Chebat, Ron Kupers, Maurice Ptito

papers.title: Enhancing navigation and obstacle avoidance with a vibrotactile device as secondary electronic travel aid
papers.abstract: This study assesses the efficacy of a finger-mounted vibrotactile sensory substitution device (SSD) as a supplemental electronic travel aid (ETA) for blind individuals during active navigation. Using a standardized obstacle course, the researchers evaluated user performance with the SSD used in conjunction with a traditional white cane compared to the cane alone. Metrics focused on the detection of extra-peripersonal obstacles and the avoidance of high-level hazards (e.g., objects at head height) that are undetectable by conventional canes. The integration of low-complexity vibrotactile feedback led to significant improvements in obstacle anticipation and a marked reduction in collisions, suggesting that secondary ETAs can effectively expand the sensory horizon of blind users and enhance safety in complex environments.
papers.authors: Carlos de Paz, Ana Belén Varas, David Travieso, Maxime Bleau, Ismaël Djerourou, Maurice Ptito

papers.title: Refinement but not maintenance of visual receptive fields is restricted by a critical period in mouse V1
papers.abstract: The study explores the temporal constraints of neuroplasticity in the mouse primary visual cortex (V1) by examining the developmental trajectory of receptive field (RF) refinement. Using electrophysiological recordings and controlled visual deprivation paradigms, the authors demonstrate that the precise tuning of RF properties depends on visual input during a specific post-natal critical period. Intriguingly, the findings reveal that while the absence of vision during this window prevents the acquisition of mature RF characteristics, the maintenance of refined RFs—once matured—is remarkably resilient to subsequent visual deprivation. This dissociation suggests that distinct molecular and circuit-level mechanisms govern the activity-dependent maturation versus the ongoing stability of cortical sensory representations.
papers.authors: Alper Vatansever, Ismaël Djerourou, Fabien C. Schneider, Maurice Ptito

0446.name: Maximilian Riesenhuber
0446.bio: Maximilian Riesenhuber is a Professor of Neuroscience at Georgetown University and Co-Director of the Center for Neuroengineering. Their research integrates computational modeling with human behavioral data, functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), and electroencephalography (EEG) to examine the neurocomputational mechanisms of object recognition and learning. Riesenhuber developed hierarchical, biologically plausible models of the visual cortex to show how neural populations extract invariant features from complex stimuli. Their current research investigates cross-modal sensory processing in vision, audition, and touch to translate biological insights into neuromorphic artificial intelligence and augmented cognition technologies.
0446.research_direction: Dr. Riesenhuber has recently been investigating the neural architecture of word recognition, specifically exploring how the brain constructs parallel visual and auditory processing hierarchies for written and spoken language. Using fMRI, MEG, and rapid adaptation paradigms, their recent work explores the functional dynamics of modality-specific lexicon hubs—such as the visual and auditory word form areas—examining how these regions assemble whole words from sublexical features and provide cross-modal scaffolding to one another. Beyond language, they are also investigating the neural mechanics of perceptual automaticity, tracking how extensive visual training with morphed stimuli might shift category representations from the prefrontal cortex down into the ventral occipito-temporal cortex to bypass executive processing bottlenecks. Additionally, their research probes metamodal sensory plasticity by testing whether translating speech into vibrotactile sensory substitution stimuli that match natural acoustic features can successfully recruit established auditory speech networks.

papers.title: Evidence for hierarchical representations of written and spoken words from an open-science human neuroimaging dataset
papers.abstract: Reading and speech recognition both require multi-tier hierarchical cortical processing that transforms sensory features into whole-word representations; however, the degree of organizational homology between the visual and auditory pathways remains incompletely characterized. To resolve lexical and sublexical representations across modalities, the authors performed parametric regression analyses on the Mother Of all Unification Studies (MOUS) open-science fMRI dataset (n = 204), assessing cortical responses to variations in whole-word frequency alongside sublexical unit frequency (bigrams and syllables) during reading and listening tasks. Analysis of the reading data demonstrated significant inverse correlations with lexical frequency in the visual word form area (VWFA) of the left mid-fusiform gyrus and with bigram frequency in posterior occipital cortex, confirming hierarchical orthographic encoding. In the auditory modality, spoken word frequency parametrically modulated BOLD responses in the left mid-superior temporal gyrus within the auditory word form area (AWFA), whereas syllable frequency selectively modulated activity in posterior superior temporal gyrus. Furthermore, cross-modal convergence was identified in the left inferior frontal gyrus, which correlated with both visual and auditory word frequencies. These findings indicate parallel posterior-to-anterior processing hierarchies within the anteroventral visual and auditory processing streams, progressing from sublexical structures to lexical hubs that connect to frontal language regions.
papers.authors: Suneel Banerjee, Kimberly Jin, Plamen Nikolov, Philip Cho, Vishnu R. Pendri, Lillian Chang, Srikanth R. Damera, Maximilian Riesenhuber

papers.title: Distinct cross-modal coupling between the written and auditory language networks during reading and spoken word processing
papers.abstract: The development of lexical representations in the visual word form area (VWFA) is hypothesized to be driven by top-down scaffolding from the auditory language system, particularly via putative lexical representations in the anterior superior temporal gyrus (the auditory word form area, AWFA). The authors examined functional responses and functional connectivity (FC) between individually localized VWFA and AWFA regions of interest (n = 18) during visual reading and spoken word perception, alongside MEG sensor-level and beamforming coherence analyses from the MOUS dataset. The fMRI results revealed marked cross-modal asymmetry: the VWFA responded selectively to spoken words and exhibited heightened functional coupling with the AWFA during auditory processing, whereas the AWFA showed no comparable recruitment or cross-modal connectivity during reading. MEG source analyses demonstrated significant signal coherence between the AWFA and VWFA emerging approximately 300 ms post-stimulus onset during spoken word comprehension. These findings elucidate an asymmetric cross-modal architecture wherein spoken language representations in the anterior temporal lobe provide direct scaffolding to ventral occipito-temporal reading circuits without reciprocal engagement during standard visual orthographic processing.
papers.authors: Lillian Chang, Philip Cho, Suneel Banerjee, Srikanth R. Damera, Laurie S. Glezer, Benson Stevens, Kimberly Jin, Plamen Nikolov, Maximilian Riesenhuber

papers.title: Extensive Experience Remodels Neural Task Circuitry to Escape the Frontal Bottleneck and Increase Automaticity of Categorization
papers.abstract: Standard models of perceptual categorization propose a two-stage hierarchy in which early sensory cortices represent physical shape features while prefrontal cortex (PFC) units encode task-dependent category boundaries. However, executive processing in the PFC creates a processing bottleneck that limits concurrent task execution. To examine how extended training alters this circuitry, human subjects completed over 30,000 categorization trials with parameterized morphed car stimuli across 5 to 10 weeks. Using longitudinal fMRI and EEG rapid adaptation paradigms, neural tuning and connectivity were tracked following initial acquisition (~4 hours) and extensive practice (~16 additional hours). Although category selectivity was initially confined to the PFC with shape tuning in the ventral occipito-temporal cortex (vOTC), extensive training induced an emergence of discrete category selectivity directly within the vOTC. Concurrently, vOTC showed marked reductions in functional connectivity with the PFC and enhanced coupling with motor output cortices. This functional disconnection from the prefrontal bottleneck directly predicted preserved categorization performance under dual-task interference, demonstrating that prolonged sensorimotor experience can physically bypass executive prefrontal circuits to achieve automated processing.
papers.authors: Patrick H. Cox, Clara A. Scholl, Marissa L. Laws, Nelson E. Jaimes, Xiong Jiang, Maximilian Riesenhuber

papers.title: Evidence for a Spoken Word Lexicon in the Auditory Ventral Stream
papers.abstract: A core premise of spoken language comprehension models is the existence of an auditory lexicon housing neural representations of complete spoken words, yet its anatomical locus has remained controversial. Drawing an architectural parallel to the visual word form area (VWFA) in reading, the authors used fMRI rapid adaptation (fMRI-RA) to probe whether the anterior superior temporal gyrus harbors an auditory word form area (AWFA) selective for individual spoken words. In 26 participants, adaptation profiles in response to pairs of real words, unfamiliar pseudowords, and experimentally trained novel words were evaluated. The putative AWFA demonstrated robust release from adaptation for single-phoneme substitutions that was indistinguishable from the release evoked by completely different words, confirming fine-grained neural tuning for specific real words rather than sublexical acoustic overlap. Furthermore, targeted phonological training with novel spoken words selectively sharpened neuronal tuning within this region. These findings locate the auditory word-form lexicon within the anterior superior temporal gyrus, illustrating that the auditory and visual ventral processing hierarchies employ convergent mechanisms for whole-word representation.
papers.authors: Srikanth R. Damera, Lillian Chang, Plamen P. Nikolov, James A. Mattei, Suneel Banerjee, Laurie S. Glezer, Patrick H. Cox, Xiong Jiang, Josef P. Rauschecker, Maximilian Riesenhuber

papers.title: Metamodal Coupling of Vibrotactile and Auditory Speech Processing Systems through Matched Stimulus Representations
papers.abstract: Sensory substitution technologies seek to compensate for sensory loss by translating information across modalities, but the neurocomputational principles governing whether non-native sensory inputs can access established cortex remain unclear. This study investigated whether matching the representational format of vibrotactile speech to the acoustic feature hierarchy of natural speech promotes the metamodal recruitment of auditory speech networks. Sighted, normal-hearing human participants were trained to identify words delivered through vibrotactile stimulation using either a vocoder-based algorithm (designed to match the spectrotemporal modulation patterns of acoustic speech) or an unaligned token-based mapping scheme. Pre- and post-training fMRI experiments revealed that only subjects trained on the vocoded algorithm exhibited recruitment of speech-selective regions in the superior temporal gyrus (STG) by vibrotactile input. Moreover, this condition was uniquely accompanied by strengthened functional coupling between primary somatosensory cortex and auditory speech areas. These findings demonstrate that representational alignment is critical for facilitating cross-modal functional reorganization, offering computational constraints for the design of neurobiologically grounded tactile speech sensory substitution systems.
papers.authors: Srikanth R. Damera, Patrick S. Malone, Benson W. Stevens, Richard Klein, Silvio P. Eberhardt, Edward T. Auer, Lynne E. Bernstein, Maximilian Riesenhuber

0447.name: Meenakshi Khosla
0447.bio: Meenakshi Khosla is an Assistant Professor in the Department of Cognitive Science at the University of California, San Diego. Khosla’s research operates at the intersection of artificial intelligence and computational neuroscience, focusing on the development of data-driven models to analyze information processing in the human brain. They use deep neural networks and functional neuroimaging (fMRI) to characterize structured neural representations in the visual cortex, including the identification of food-selective neural populations. Their work also involves building interpretable machine learning tools for large-scale brain mapping across sensory and cognitive domains.
0447.research_direction: Dr. Khosla's recent work explores the complex challenge of representational alignment, investigating how to meaningfully compare high-dimensional feature spaces across diverse artificial neural networks and the human brain. To achieve this, they have recently been developing sophisticated mathematical frameworks based on optimal transport—such as unbalanced soft-matching and hierarchical layer-to-layer couplings—which evaluate partial unit correspondences and resolve architectural mismatches between different systems. Applying these novel metrics, their research investigates how shared representational geometries evolve dynamically across model layers, learning stages, and out-of-distribution shifts in artificial vision networks. Additionally, they are probing the underlying nature of biological meaning by modeling the human language cortex with cross-modal, vision-based embeddings to evaluate the semantic abstractness and form-independence of cortical responses.

papers.title: Barycentric alignment for instance-level comparison of neural representations
papers.abstract: This work introduces a barycentric framework for representational alignment that explicitly quotients out nuisance symmetries, such as unit reordering and orthogonal transformations, to map neural activations into a universal embedding space. Unlike traditional set-level metrics (e.g., CKA or RSA) that aggregate similarity over entire stimulus distributions, this approach enables instance-level consistency measures to evaluate how individual stimuli cluster across model populations. The authors utilize this stimulus-specific analysis to identify input properties that predict representational convergence in vision and language models and to construct shared spaces for human cortical regions across individuals. The results demonstrate that post-hoc alignment of unimodal models can recover cross-modal semantic judgments comparable to contrastively trained vision-language systems.
papers.authors: Shreya Saha, Zoe Wanying He, Meenakshi Khosla

papers.title: Unbalanced Soft-Matching Distance For Neural Representational Comparison With Partial Unit Correspondence
papers.abstract: This paper presents an unbalanced soft-matching metric for comparing neural representations that accounts for partial unit correspondences and varying neuron counts between systems. By extending the soft-matching distance to a partial optimal transport setting, the authors relax strict mass conservation requirements, allowing certain units to remain unmatched. This provides a robust measure of alignment that avoids forced correspondences for low-quality or non-homologous features. The metric is shown to preserve correct matches under outlier noise in synthetic simulations and achieves higher alignment precision across homologous brain areas than standard soft-matching. This ability to partition units by match quality enables the identification of privileged representational axes within specific subpopulations of neurons.
papers.authors: Chaitanya Kapoor, Alex H Williams, Meenakshi Khosla

papers.title: Representational Alignment Across Model Layers and Brain Regions with Hierarchical Optimal Transport
papers.abstract: The authors propose Hierarchical Optimal Transport (HOT), a unified framework for the global alignment of high-dimensional representations in deep neural networks and biological systems. HOT jointly optimizes for soft, globally consistent layer-to-layer couplings and neuron-level transport plans, permitting representational mass from a source layer to be distributed across multiple target layers to handle architectural depth mismatches. This method produces a symmetric global alignment score and reveals smooth hierarchical correspondences across vision models, large language models, and human visual cortex recordings. By incorporating the global activation structure of the entire network, HOT provides more stable and interpretable comparisons than greedy or layer-independent matching techniques.
papers.authors: Shaan Shah, Meenakshi Khosla

papers.title: Bridging Critical Gaps in Convergent Learning: How Representational Alignment Evolves Across Layers, Training, and Distribution Shifts
papers.abstract: This research presents a large-scale systematic audit of representational convergence across dozens of vision models, evaluating alignment through affine-invariant linear regression, rotation-invariant orthogonal Procrustes, and unit-order-invariant soft-matching. The study demonstrates that representational convergence is primarily driven by shared input statistics and architectural biases, with alignment crystallizing within the first training epoch prior to task-performance plateaus. Furthermore, while early layers maintain tight alignment across out-of-distribution (OOD) shifts, deeper layers diverge in proportion to the severity of the distribution shift. These findings elucidate the evolution of representational universality during task optimization and have significant implications for the design of brain-like artificial systems.
papers.venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS)
papers.authors: Chaitanya Kapoor, Sudhanshu Srivastava, Meenakshi Khosla

papers.title: Modeling the language cortex with form-independent and enriched representations of sentence meaning reveals remarkable semantic abstractness
papers.abstract: This research investigates the semantic abstractness of the human language system by modeling neural responses to sentences using cross-modal and form-independent representations. The authors utilize vision foundation models to extract embeddings from synthetic images generated from sentence prompts, demonstrating that aggregating these vision-based representations rival large language models (LLMs) in predicting language cortex activity. Enhancing neural predictivity through the use of multiple paraphrases and the enrichment of sentence prompts with implicit commonsense context further improves encoding performance. These findings suggest that the human language cortex maintains highly abstract, form-independent meaning representations that transcend specific sensory modalities or linguistic surface forms.
papers.authors: Shreya Saha, Shurui Li, Greta Tuckute, Yuanning Li, Ru-Yuan Zhang, Leila Wehbe, Evelina Fedorenko, Meenakshi Khosla

0448.name: Megan A. K. Peters
0448.bio: Megan A. K. Peters is an Associate Professor of Cognitive Sciences at the University of California, Irvine, and a Fellow in the CIFAR Brain, Mind & Consciousness program. Peters' research investigates how the brain represents and utilizes uncertainty to support adaptive behavior and metacognitive evaluations, focusing on the computational mechanisms of conscious awareness. They employ a methodology combining psychophysics, functional neuroimaging, and computational modeling to characterize how biological and artificial systems monitor internal noise and model their environments. Additionally, Peters is a co-founder and board chair of Neuromatch, a nonprofit organization focused on education in computational neuroscience and artificial intelligence.
0448.research_direction: Dr. Peters has recently been investigating the computational and neural foundations of subjective experience, metacognition, and perceptual confidence. Their recent work explores how biological and artificial systems monitor their own decision-making, utilizing Signal Detection Theory to define normative strategies for confidence reporting and formalizing an "introspective psychophysics" to rigorously model subjective dimensions like vividness and urgency. To uncover the neural basis of these phenomena, they are testing whether specific EEG markers track evidence accumulation for subjective confidence, alongside developing novel deep learning autoencoders to isolate task-relevant representational geometries from complex fMRI and ECoG datasets. Furthermore, they are applying these metacognitive paradigms to artificial intelligence by evaluating how well Large Language Models internally monitor and linguistically communicate their own uncertainty relative to human benchmarks.

papers.title: Introspective psychophysics for the study of subjective experience
papers.abstract: This work formalizes a methodology for establishing subjective experience as a tractable empirical target by quantifying the mappings between environmental variables, neurobiological processes, and self-reported phenomenology. It posits that the historical view of introspection as an unreliable or unverifiable metric can be reframed by treating its inherent variance and non-linearities as features of canonic computational processes, analogous to the noise-driven foundations of Fechnerian psychophysics. The proposed framework, termed 'introspective psychophysics', provides a rigorous approach to modeling the generation of phenomenal dimensions—including urgency, vividness, clarity, and confidence—across both biological and artificial systems.
papers.authors: Megan A. K. Peters

papers.title: Task relevant autoencoding enhances machine learning for human neuroscience
papers.abstract: The study introduces Task-Relevant Autoencoder via Classifier Enhancement (TRACE), a deep learning architecture designed to isolate behaviorally-relevant, low-dimensional neural representations from high-dimensional neuroimaging data. TRACE addresses the challenge of overfitting in small-sample human neuroscience datasets by augmenting an unsupervised autoencoding bottleneck with a supervised classification loss focused on behavioral outcomes. The authors demonstrate that prioritizing features that drive task performance, rather than general variance, enables more effective identification of target neural patterns in fMRI and ECoG signals, facilitating the discovery of functionally relevant representational geometries.
papers.authors: Seyedmehdi Orouji, Vincent Taschereau-Dumouchel, Aurelio Cortese, Brian Odegaard, Cody Cushing, Mouslim Cherkaoui, Mitsuo Kawato, Hakwan Lau, Megan A. K. Peters

papers.title: Metacognition and Uncertainty Communication in Humans and Large Language Models
papers.abstract: This paper evaluates the metacognitive monitoring and uncertainty communication capacities of Large Language Models (LLMs) in comparison to human observers. Utilizing signal detection theory and metrics of calibration and sensitivity, the authors assess how LLMs report confidence and respond to task difficulty. While finding instances of alignment in metacognitive-like behaviors, the study identifies critical divergences in how models communicate internal uncertainty linguisticly versus trial-by-trial accuracy. The findings are discussed in the context of curiosity-driven information seeking and the development of calibrated metacognition to support robust human-AI collaborative decision-making.
papers.authors: Mark Steyvers, Megan A. K. Peters

papers.title: Optimal metacognitive decision strategies in signal detection theory
papers.abstract: This research provides a normative Signal Detection Theory (SDT) framework for deriving optimal type 2 (confidence) criteria based on distinct agentic objectives. The authors define formulae for ideal type 2 criterion placement under four optimization goals: maximizing type 2 accuracy, maximizing expected reward, calibrating confidence to objective accuracy, and maximizing the disparity between type 2 hit and false alarm rates. By applying these normative standards to behavioral data, the framework allows for the quantification of metacognitive biases and suboptimal strategy selection in human observers, distinguishing these effects from primary perceptual sensitivity.
papers.authors: Brian Maniscalco, Lucie Charles, Megan A. K. Peters

papers.title: Behavioral and neural measures of confidence using a novel auditory pitch identification task
papers.abstract: The study investigates the neural signatures of auditory metacognition using a novel pitch identification paradigm and simultaneous 32-channel EEG. Specifically, the authors test the hypothesis that the centro-parietal positivity (CPP) slope indexes the accumulation of evidence for confidence as well as for primary task performance. Results demonstrate that while CPP build-up rate tracks identification accuracy and reaction time, it fails to significantly covary with trial-by-trial confidence ratings. This finding suggests that the CPP slope may predominantly reflect first-order perceptual processing rather than the higher-order computations specific to subjective confidence in the auditory domain.
papers.authors: Tamara Tang, Jason Samaha, Megan A. K. Peters

0450.name: Megumi Kobayashi
0450.department: Department of Psychology and Human Studies
0450.bio: Megumi Kobayashi is an Associate Professor at Niigata University who researches the developmental trajectory of person recognition and face processing during infancy. Kobayashi utilizes behavioral preferential-looking methods and functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) to investigate how infants integrate facial and body cues to identify individuals. Their recent work examines the influence of environmental factors on visual development, including the impact of mask-wearing during the COVID-19 pandemic and the role of scenic context in shaping facial preferences.
0450.research_direction: Dr. Kobayashi has recently been exploring the early ontogeny of visual cognition, with a particular focus on how infants process faces and natural scenes. Their recent work investigates the experiential factors shaping face recognition, using visual preference paradigms to examine how restricted exposure to unmasked faces during the COVID-19 pandemic impacts an infant's visual specialization for maternal faces. Additionally, they are studying the intersection of object and scene perception by asking how coherent versus scrambled scenic contexts influence an infant's detection of upright faces during the first year of life. Beyond face processing, Dr. Kobayashi's research explores the early emergence of scene memory biases, using familiarization-novelty procedures to test whether classic phenomena like boundary extension and spatial extrapolation are operational in the visual system prior to the development of voluntary locomotion.

papers.title: Variations in face experiences during the COVID-19 pandemic affect infants' preference for their mother's face
papers.abstract: This study examined the impact of social environment alterations during the COVID-19 pandemic on the ontogeny of facial recognition in Japanese infants. Utilizing a simultaneous visual preference paradigm, the researchers assessed 5–8-month-old infants' preferences for maternal versus unfamiliar female faces under both masked and unmasked conditions. Group-level results indicated that infants from provincial regions (subject to less stringent restrictions) demonstrated a significant preference for their mother's face in both conditions. In contrast, infants raised in Tokyo (subject to prolonged state-of-emergency protocols) exhibited a significant preference for the maternal face only when both stimuli were masked. Individual-level regression analysis further revealed that the degree of maternal preference in the unmasked condition was positively correlated with the infant's cumulative exposure to unmasked faces in daily life. These findings suggest that early visual experience with visible facial configurations modulates the specialization of the face-processing system during infancy.
papers.authors: Megumi Kobayashi, Machi Sugai, So Kanazawa, Masami K. Yamaguchi

papers.title: Characteristics of boundary extension in 7- to 8-month-old infants
papers.abstract: This investigation explored the occurrence of boundary extension (BE)—a memory distortion wherein viewers remember more of a scene's periphery than was actually present—in 7- to 8-month-old infants. Using a familiarization-novelty preference procedure, the study tested whether infants exhibit typical memory biases for scene boundaries when presented with wide-angle and close-up views. The behavioral data provided evidence that 7-8-month-old infants demonstrate boundary extension, indicating that the cognitive mechanisms required for spatial extrapolation and the schema-driven construction of mental scenic representations are operational by late infancy. These results further suggest that scenic memory distortions are an inherent property of the visual memory system that emerges prior to the development of complex motor skills like voluntary locomotion.
papers.authors: Nanako Yamanaka, Megumi Kobayashi, Nobu Shirai

papers.title: The role of scenic context on upright face preference in infancy
papers.abstract: This research examined the developmental influence of scenic context on facial detection mechanisms during the first year of life. In a series of preferential looking experiments, 4–5-month-old and 6–7-month-old infants were presented with pairs of upright and inverted faces embedded within either intact or scrambled natural scenes. The results demonstrated a clear developmental shift: while younger infants (4–5 months) exhibited a robust upright face preference regardless of scenic coherence, older infants (6–7 months) only showed a significant preference for the upright face when it appeared in an intact, coherent scene. No significant difference was found in preferences for scenery alone. These findings suggest that by 6 months of age, infants begin to integrate global scenic spatial information into their face-processing systems, reflecting the emergence of adult-like contextual facilitation in person detection.
papers.authors: Megumi Kobayashi, So Kanazawa, Masami K. Yamaguchi

0451.name: Melchi M. Michel
0451.bio: Michel is an Associate Professor at Rutgers University who investigates the human visual system through the lens of probabilistic inference and ideal observer modeling. Their research examines how the brain integrates sensory data to form perceptual judgments, focusing on mechanisms of visual search, saccadic eye movements, and transsaccadic integration. By comparing human performance against mathematically optimal standards, Michel explores how observers exploit statistical regularities in both natural and artificial environments. Their work also extends to clinical domains, including the evaluation of visual performance in medical imaging and the development of training interventions for retinopathic patients.
0451.research_direction: Dr. Michel has recently been investigating the computational and physiological mechanisms that support visual perception in dynamic, uncertain conditions. Their recent work explores how human observers identify categorical targets despite high levels of within-category variability in stimulus contrast, size, and spatial position, using optimal Bayesian observer models to evaluate human information integration strategies. Additionally, they are investigating the temporal dynamics of visual sensitivity during rapid eye movements. To do so, they employ steady-state visually evoked potentials (SSVEPs) alongside computational simulations to isolate and measure the precise physiological markers of saccadic suppression in the human visual system.

papers.title: Target identification under high levels of amplitude, size, and position uncertainty
papers.abstract: This research investigates how human observers classify image patches into categorical targets under significant within-category variability across multiple dimensions, including amplitude (contrast), size, and spatial position. The authors treat the problem as categorical identification from a set of mutually exclusive categories, which are further partitioned into subcategories representing specific target configurations. By deriving a mathematically optimal Bayesian observer for this identification task, the study provides a baseline to evaluate human performance and information integration strategies. The findings reveal the computational mechanisms humans use to resolve high-dimensional uncertainty during target identification in complex visual environments.
papers.authors: Yelda Semizer, Melchi M. Michel

papers.title: Saccadic Suppression Measured by Steady-state Visual Evoked Potential
papers.abstract: Visual sensitivity is drastically reduced during the execution of rapid eye movements (saccades), a phenomenon termed saccadic suppression. While well-characterized in non-human primate neurophysiology and human psychophysics, human physiological markers of this suppression remain less clearly defined. This study utilizes steady-state visually evoked potentials (SSVEPs) to provide a physiological characterization of saccadic suppression in the human visual system. By presenting flickering stimuli at 40 Hz and measuring EEG responses, the authors recovered a suppression window that aligns with behavioral results. Computational simulations confirmed that the SSVEP amplitude accurately reflects the transient suppression of neural responses, providing an objective tool for studying the temporal dynamics of visual sensitivity during eye movements.
papers.authors: James P. Wilmott, Melchi M. Michel

0452.name: Melissa Beck
0452.bio: Melissa R. Beck is a Professor of Psychology at Louisiana State University and a member of the Multidisciplinary Institute for Neuroscience Discovery (MIND). Beck utilizes eye-tracking, behavioral psychophysics, and cognitive modeling to investigate how the human brain maintains stable visual representations across eye movements and shifts of attention. Their research examines change blindness, visual search efficiency, and the role of metacognition in perception. Beck applies cognitive science to applied domains, including the optimization of human-computer interfaces for aviation and the development of spatial reasoning training protocols for STEM education.
0452.research_direction: Dr. Beck's recent work explores the intricate cognitive and neural mechanisms connecting visual working memory, long-term memory, and visual search. They have recently been investigating how the prioritization of attentional templates in working memory influences distinct eye-movement phases—such as search initiation, scanning, and verification—during visual search in realistic scenes. Additionally, their research examines hybrid visual search, specifically asking how maintaining target templates in activated long-term memory interacts with visual working memory's capacity to process and store distractor information. To further unpack memory capacity limits, they are also utilizing electrophysiological markers like the N2pc and CDA to determine exactly which stages of visual working memory processing—encoding, maintenance, or comparison—benefit from perceptual grouping.

papers.title: Effects of template priority on working memory-guided search for real objects: evidence from eye-movements
papers.abstract: This research investigates how the prioritization of attentional templates in working memory (WM) influences different stages of visual search in realistic scenes. Utilizing eye-tracking to segment reaction times into initiation, scanning, and verification phases, the study compared performance for current versus prospective templates. The results demonstrated that template priority specifically facilitates the scanning and verification epochs—evidenced by fewer object fixations and reduced gaze duration on targets—but does not affect the latency of search initiation. These findings suggest that higher-priority templates are characterized by increased representational precision, which optimizes the matching process between external stimuli and internal memory representations during complex search tasks.
papers.authors: Hanane Ramzaoui, Melissa R. Beck

papers.title: Activated long-term memory and visual working memory during hybrid visual search: Effects on target memory search and distractor memory
papers.abstract: Hybrid visual search involves the simultaneous search of the environment and a memory set maintained in activated long-term memory (aLTM). This study explored the extent to which loading aLTM with target templates interferes with visual working memory (VWM) maintenance of distracting information. Across seven experiments, the authors measured distractor memory (via revisits and recognition) and target memory search (via dwell times and error rates). The data revealed that increasing the memory set size in aLTM does not directly impede VWM for distractors; however, the presence of a hybrid search task itself reduces VWM capacity by a fixed amount. These results support a model where VWM acts as a bottleneck for passing visual representations to aLTM for comparison rather than serving as the primary storage for search templates.
papers.authors: Stephanie M. Saltzmann, Brandon Eich, Katherine C. Moen, Melissa R. Beck

papers.title: Examining Perceptual Grouping on Stages of Processing in Visual Working Memory: An ERP Study
papers.abstract: Perceptual grouping, such as through feature similarity, is known to mitigate the capacity limitations of visual working memory (VWM). This Registered Report Stage 1 protocol details an electrophysiological investigation aimed at identifying the specific VWM stages—individuation encoding, maintenance, or comparison—where grouping benefits emerge. By recording Event-Related Potentials (ERPs) during a bilateral change-detection task with color repetition, the researchers utilize the N2pc to index attentional selection, the Contralateral Delay Activity (CDA) to measure memory load, and the N2/FN400 components to index comparison and decision-making processes. The study tests whether grouping leads to more efficient encoding/maintenance or if it prioritizes specific representations during the memory-percept comparison phase.
papers.authors: Hanane Ramzaoui, Melissa Beck

0454.name: Micaela Mitolo
0454.bio: Micaela Mitolo is a researcher at the University of Parma specializing in the neuroimaging and neuropsychology of aging and neurodegenerative disorders. Mitolo utilizes multimodal imaging techniques, including structural and functional MRI, proton magnetic resonance spectroscopy, and quantitative susceptibility mapping, to identify biomarkers for Alzheimer's disease and Dementia with Lewy Bodies. They investigate the neural correlates of visuospatial processing and the melanopsin retinal ganglion cell system, alongside the predictive value of sulcal morphometry in cognitive decline. This research also explores the relationship between sleep quality, gray matter atrophy, and functional connectivity in patients with mild cognitive impairment.
0454.research_direction: Dr. Mitolo has recently been investigating the neural substrates and clinical biomarkers of cognitive and sensorimotor deficits across various neurodegenerative and sleep disorders. A major focus of their recent work explores visuospatial and attentional impairments in Dementia with Lewy Bodies, combining task-based fMRI, eye-tracking, and kinematic pointing tasks to map the brain networks underlying phenomena like attentional fluctuations, visuomotor targeting errors, and early visual hallucinations. Beyond these visuoperceptual systems, they are also using magnetic resonance spectroscopy to examine neurometabolic alterations in the brainstems of patients with narcolepsy. Additionally, their research systematically evaluates how fluid biomarkers—such as blood-based proteins across the Alzheimer's disease continuum—correspond with distinct structural, functional, and microstructural MRI metrics.

papers.title: Sustained attention in dementia with Lewy bodies: a task-based fMRI study
papers.abstract: Patients with dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB) present with characteristic attentional fluctuations and sustained attention impairments, yet the specific task-related functional neuroanatomy underlying these deficits remains insufficiently understood. In this study, 30 DLB patients and 25 age-matched healthy controls (HC) were evaluated using comprehensive neuropsychological testing and a 3T functional magnetic resonance imaging protocol while executing an auditory Psychomotor Vigilance Task (PVT). DLB patients exhibited pronounced behavioral impairments during the PVT, marked by increased attentional lapses and significantly longer reaction times, alongside deficits in visuospatial cognitive domains. Task-based fMRI analyses demonstrated that DLB patients displayed significant blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) hypoactivation compared to HC in key posterior attention nodes, specifically the bilateral precuneus, cuneus, angular gyrus, and intracalcarine cortex. These results reveal distinct functional disruptions within posterior cortical networks mediating sustained attention in DLB, offering neurofunctional markers that illuminate the neural basis of cognitive fluctuations and provide targets for cognitive rehabilitation and neuromodulation.
papers.authors: Davide Braghittoni, Greta Venturi, Lucia Guidi, Elettra Capogna, Giovanni Sighinolfi, Luca Baldelli, Giulia Amore, Chiara La Morgia, Luisa Sambati, Annalena Venneri, Raffaele Lodi, Caterina Tonon, Micaela Mitolo

papers.title: Visuospatial performance and its neural substrates in Dementia with Lewy Bodies during a pointing task
papers.abstract: Dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB) involves sensorimotor and cognitive deficits that frequently overlap with other neurodegenerative syndromes, impeding timely differential diagnosis. This study implemented linear mixed-effects modeling and machine learning algorithms to examine kinematic parameters of pointing, saccadometry, and superior parietal lobule (SPL) volumetry to differentiate DLB patients from healthy elderly controls. DLB patients manifested significant motor impairments, including prolonged movement duration, larger endpoint pointing errors, and spatially modulated inaccuracies across visual targets. Eye-tracking demonstrated prolonged saccadic latencies, increased amplitudes, and prominent hypermetria, with directional modulation revealing disruption along visuomotor control streams. Structural MRI volumetry confirmed significant volumetric reduction of the SPL in DLB patients, particularly localized to the left hemisphere, which correlated inversely with pointing performance. A multimodal classifier integrating kinematic, oculomotor, and volumetric features reliably distinguished DLB patients from controls, highlighting the utility of combined sensorimotor and morphometric phenotyping.
papers.authors: Annalisa Bosco, Caterina Foglino, Lucia Guidi, Davide Braghittoni, Greta Venturi, Luisa Sambati, Luca Baldelli, Giovanna Calandra-Buonaura, Patrizia Fattori, Raffaele Lodi, Caterina Tonon, Micaela Mitolo

papers.title: Minor Visual Phenomena in Lewy Body Disease: A Systematic Review
papers.abstract: Minor visual phenomena (MVP), such as passage hallucinations, presence hallucinations, visual illusions, and pareidolias, are frequently reported across the Lewy body disease (LBD) continuum and often emerge during prodromal stages prior to fully formed complex visual hallucinations (VH). This systematic review evaluated the clinical presentation, prevalence, and pathophysiological underpinnings of MVP in LBD, focusing on their associations with VH and visuoperceptual/visuospatial deficits. Across 44 studies identified in PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, APA PsycInfo, and Cochrane Library, substantial methodological heterogeneity was observed, spanning semi-structured clinical interviews (e.g., NEVHI), standardized experimental batteries (such as the Noise Pareidolia Test), and qualitative reporting. The findings indicate that MVP exhibits high diagnostic specificity for LBD relative to Alzheimer's disease. Furthermore, pareidolic responses and sense of presence positively correlated with VH manifestations, and MVP severity was inversely associated with visuoperceptual abilities, implicating early visual pathway and integrative network disruptions in the emergence of these misperceptions.
papers.authors: Elettra Capogna, Virginia Pollarini, Alessia Quinzi, Lucia Guidi, Luisa Sambati, Maria Sasca Criante, Elena Mengoli, Annalena Venneri, Raffaele Lodi, Caterina Tonon, Micaela Mitolo

papers.title: Pons metabolite alterations in narcolepsy type 1
papers.abstract: Narcolepsy type 1 (NT1) stems from the selective neurodegeneration of hypocretin/orexin-producing neurons situated in the posterolateral hypothalamus that project diffusely into brainstem reticular nuclei. This study evaluated neurometabolic profiles in the pontine tegmentum of 21 NT1 patients and 20 age-matched healthy controls using single-voxel proton magnetic resonance spectroscopy (1H-MRS) at 1.5T. Relative concentrations of N-acetylaspartate (NAA), choline (Cho), and myo-inositol (mI) scaled to total creatine (Cr) were determined using LCModel. NT1 patients demonstrated significantly decreased pontine NAA/Cr (p = 0.007) and NAA/mI (p = 0.011) ratios relative to controls, reflecting localized neuronal/axonal compromise. NAA/Cr reductions in the pons correlated inversely with daytime somnolence measured by the Epworth Sleepiness Scale (p = 0.023). Pontine mI/Cr showed significant correlations with Multiple Sleep Latency Test parameters: an inverse correlation with mean sleep latency (p = 0.008) and a positive correlation with sleep-onset REM episodes (p = 0.027). Furthermore, CSF hypocretin-1 titers correlated positively with NAA/Cr (p = 0.039) and negatively with mI/Cr (p = 0.045) and Cho/Cr (p = 0.026), demonstrating the diagnostic and pathophysiological relevance of pontine 1H-MRS biomarkers in NT1.
papers.authors: Micaela Mitolo, Fabio Pizza, David N. Manners, Lucia Guidi, Annalena Venneri, Luca Morandi, Caterina Tonon, Giuseppe Plazzi, Raffaele Lodi

papers.title: Association between blood-based protein biomarkers and brain MRI in the Alzheimer's disease continuum: a systematic review
