papers.abstract: Blood-based protein biomarkers (BBMs) provide scalable, minimally invasive metrics of neurodegenerative pathology in Alzheimer's disease (AD), but their correspondence with in vivo structural, functional, and spectroscopic magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) markers warrants systematic synthesis across the disease spectrum. A systematic literature search conducted across PubMed and Web of Science identified 33 peer-reviewed studies investigating associations between core BBMs (plasma Aβ42, Aβ40, p-tau181, p-tau217, p-tau231, neurofilament light chain [NfL], glial fibrillary acidic protein [GFAP]) and MRI parameters from preclinical stages and subjective cognitive decline to mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and AD dementia. Hippocampal volume was positively associated with plasma Aβ42 and Aβ42/Aβ40 ratio, and negatively associated with Aβ40. Plasma p-tau181 and p-tau217 levels exhibited inverse correlations with temporal grey matter volume and neocortical thickness. NfL concentrations correlated inversely with diffusion tensor metrics of white matter tract integrity, whereas elevated plasma GFAP tracked increased myo-inositol values within the posterior cingulate cortex and precuneus. These findings confirm consistent biomarker-imaging couplings across preclinical and prodromal AD stages, underscoring the clinical value of multi-marker panels.
papers.authors: Micaela Mitolo, Gemma Lombardi, Riccardo Manca, Benedetta Nacmias, Annalena Venneri

0455.name: Michael A. Crognale
0455.bio: Michael A. Crognale is a Professor of Visual Neuroscience and Chair of the Department of Psychology at the University of Nevada, Reno. Crognale’s research investigates the physiological mechanisms of sensory processing, focusing on color vision, comparative visual capacities, and neural development across the lifespan. They utilize methodologies such as high-density electroencephalography (EEG), electroretinography (ERG), and adaptive optics scanning laser ophthalmoscopy (AOSLO) to examine visual function ranging from photoreceptor genetics to cortical attention. Their work is applied to the clinical diagnosis of color vision deficiencies and human factors in aviation visibility.
0455.research_direction: Dr. Crognale’s recent work explores the physiological and psychophysical mechanisms underlying human visual processing, with a strong focus on color vision and electrophysiological methodology. They have recently been investigating ways to optimize visual evoked potential (VEP) recordings, evaluating whether novel spatio-temporal stimulus variations or tripolar concentric ring EEG electrodes can better isolate and enhance cortical signals from sustained chromatic pathways. Their research also employs these VEP techniques alongside behavioral paradigms, such as multiple object tracking, to examine whether early chromatic and achromatic visual pathways are differentially susceptible to top-down attentional demand. Additionally, they are probing the neural computations of brightness induction by testing contrast gain control models in ON and OFF pathways, while concurrently developing and validating modern, tablet-based psychophysical platforms for high-throughput clinical color vision screening.

papers.title: Alternating pattern orientation or phase can increase the amplitude of the visual evoked potential
papers.abstract: The research evaluates the cortical response characteristics to pattern-reversal visual evoked potentials (VEPs), which typically yield robust signals for achromatic stimuli but attenuated responses for isoluminant chromatic stimuli. This attenuation is hypothesized to result from contrast adaptation within the sustained parvocellular and koniocellular visual pathways, which exhibit higher time-averaged contrast under reversal paradigms compared to pattern-onset paradigms. To address this, the authors implemented a novel stimulus protocol that modulates pattern orientation or phase in addition to luminance reversal to minimize steady-state adaptation. Findings demonstrate that these spatio-temporal modifications significantly increase the amplitude of the chromatic VEP, providing a methodological enhancement for electrophysiological studies of the sustained chromatic pathways in the human visual cortex.
papers.authors: Jawshan Ara, Alireza Tavakkoli, Michael A. Crognale

papers.title: Comparison of tripolar and traditional EEG recording of the visual evoked potential
papers.abstract: This study conducts a comparative performance analysis between traditional disc electroencephalography (EEG) and tripolar concentric ring electrodes (TCRE/tEEG) in the recording of pattern-reversal visual evoked potentials (VEPs). The authors characterized the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and noise profiles, finding that tEEG exhibits significantly enhanced robustness against non-physiological interference, particularly 60 Hz line noise and its harmonics, due to its inherent Laplacian spatial filtering properties. While the qualitative morphology of the VEP waveforms was preserved across both electrode types, systematic shifts in the latencies of primary peaks (N75, P100, N135) were observed, suggesting that the TCRE configuration isolates a more localized subset of the spatiotemporal neural generators involved in early visual processing.
papers.authors: Mackenzie V. Wise, Gideon P. Caplovitz, Gabriel Foster, Michael A. Crognale

papers.title: Application of the angular indication measurement and foraging interactive D-prime paradigms to tablet-based color vision testing
papers.abstract: The authors developed and validated a tablet-based platform for screening color vision deficiencies (CVD) using two advanced psychophysical paradigms: the Angular Indication Measurement (AIM) and the Foraging Interactive D-prime (FInD). The study benchmarked these automated paradigms against traditional clinical assessments, including the Farnsworth-Munsell 100-hue (FM-100) test and the Hardy-Rand-Rittler (HRR) plates. Using Spearman’s rho and linear mixed models to analyze total error scores (TES) and discrimination thresholds, the researchers demonstrated that these computer-based paradigms accurately categorize observers into superior, average, and deficient color discrimination groups. The findings support the use of mobile tablet technology as a reliable and high-throughput alternative to legacy clinical color vision testing methods.
papers.venue: Journal of the Optical Society of America A
papers.authors: Christabel Arthur, Jingyi He, Peter J. Bex, Jan Skerswetat, Michael A. Crognale

papers.title: Dependence of brightness induction on the contrast polarity of a disk–annulus stimulus
papers.abstract: This study investigates the neural computations underlying brightness induction by testing a model based on edge integration theory coupled with contrast gain control. Using a disk-annulus paradigm, observers performed brightness matches across varying annulus luminance levels. The data was used to construct achromatic color appearance matching functions (ACAMFs), which were found to be non-linear and well-modeled by second-order polynomial functions. The analysis revealed that brightness induction is highly dependent on the contrast polarity (increment vs. decrement) of the target disk relative to its annulus. These results support the existence of distinct gain control mechanisms for the ON and OFF pathways in the human visual system that regulate the strength of induction from luminance edges.
papers.venue: Journal of the Optical Society of America A
papers.authors: Osman Kavcar, Michael E. Rudd, Michael A. Crognale

papers.title: Pattern reversal chromatic VEPs like onsets, are unaffected by attentional demand
papers.abstract: The study examined the susceptibility of early chromatic and achromatic cortical processing to attentional modulation using visual evoked potentials (VEPs) and a multiple object tracking (MOT) distractor task. Participants were presented with pattern-reversal stimuli in CIE color space along isoluminant (L−M and S−(L+M)) and achromatic axes while performing varying levels of the MOT task. Frequency tagging and FFT analysis showed that while achromatic VEP amplitudes were significantly modulated by attentional demand—exhibiting a decrease in response during the distractor task—the chromatic VEP responses remained robust and invariant. These findings indicate that while top-down attention influences luminance-based spatial pathways in the primary visual cortex, the chromatic pathways are largely resistant to such attentional filtering.
papers.authors: Christabel Arthur, Osman B. Kavcar, Mackenzie V. Wise, Michael A. Crognale

0456.name: Michael A. Webster
0456.bio: Michael A. Webster is a Foundation Professor in the Department of Psychology and Director of the Center for Integrative Neuroscience at the University of Nevada, Reno. Webster’s research examines visual adaptation and how the human visual system recalibrates its sensitivity in response to changes in the stimulus environment and observer physiology, such as aging or ocular disease. They utilize a methodological approach integrating psychophysical experiments, computational modeling, and natural image statistics to study color constancy, image focus, and high-level perception, including facial recognition. Their work characterizes forms of adaptation across various visual domains and investigates how these processes function to optimize vision for specific ecological contexts.
0456.research_direction: Dr. Webster has recently been investigating the neural and perceptual mechanisms underlying human color vision, focusing on how the visual system adapts to environmental statistics and compensates for sensory deficits. Their recent work explores post-receptoral gain-control in anomalous trichromacy, using contrast adaptation aftereffects and achromatic locus mapping to probe how the brain recalibrates chromatic signals to overcome receptor-level sensitivity losses. Additionally, they are examining fundamental asymmetries in color space—such as non-uniformities in hue sensitivity and the sensory boundaries of the warm-cool dimension—by deploying visual search paradigms, behavioral matching, and frequency-tagged visual evoked potentials. Across these distinct topics, Dr. Webster is trying to determine how early in the cortical hierarchy our subjective color categories are instantiated and how these perceptual anchors relate to the ecological properties of the natural visual world.

papers.title: Asymmetries in hue measured behaviorally and with visual evoked potentials
papers.abstract: The perception of hue varies in its rate of change across different regions of color space, notably exhibiting higher sensitivity near yellow compared to green, yet the neural locus of these asymmetries remains poorly understood. We employed frequency-tagged visual evoked potentials (VEPs) and behavioral matching tasks to determine if these effects are present in early cortical representations. Using isoluminant chromatic gratings modulated sinusoidally in hue within the DKL cone-opponent plane, we recorded occipital responses to varying degrees of hue separation. Both VEP amplitudes and behavioral contrast-matching functions revealed significantly stronger responses for hue differences centered on the yellow quadrant of the chromatic plane. These findings suggest that the non-uniformities observed in hue categories and appearance are instantiated early in the cortical processing hierarchy rather than emerging as higher-order cognitive or linguistic inferences.
papers.authors: Jesse R. Macyczko, Osman B. Kavcar, Michael A. Crognale, Michael A. Webster

papers.title: Color contrast adaptation and compensation in color deficiencies
papers.abstract: Anomalous trichromacy stems from reduced spectral separation between L and M cone photopigments, resulting in attenuated L-M cone-opponent signals and diminished chromatic sensitivity. We investigated the physiological mechanisms of compensation for these deficits by measuring the strength of chromatic contrast adaptation. Observers adapted to high-contrast chromatic modulations, and the resulting shifts in color appearance were quantified via a nulling task. While deutan and protan observers exhibited significantly elevated contrast thresholds, the magnitude of their adaptation aftereffects far exceeded predictions based on their sensory sensitivity losses. This indicates a robust post-receptoral gain-control mechanism that recalibrates the visual system to the environmental color gamut, partially compensating for congenital receptor-level attenuation through neural normalization.
papers.authors: Fatemeh Basim, Erin Goddard, Yueran Yang, Michael A. Webster

papers.title: Warm versus cool colors and their relation to color perception
papers.abstract: The warm-cool dimension is a fundamental aspect of color experience, yet its sensory basis remains enigmatic. We examined the perceptual landmarks of the warm-cool division by having observers rate 36 hue angles across multiple lightness levels and estimate their unique and binary hue loci. The warm-cool boundary was highly stable across luminance variations and was oriented along an orange-red to cyan-blue axis in cone-opponent space. Projections into the CIELAB uniform color space revealed that the warm and cool peaks align with directions of minimal perceived saturation (chroma). These results suggest that the warm-cool dimension is tied to a distinct, early-stage asymmetry in color-opponent processing that may reflect an adaptation of the visual system to the specific chromatic statistics of the environment.
papers.authors: Jake Manalansan, Lorne A. Whitehead, Michael A. Webster

papers.title: Achromatic loci in normal and anomalous trichromats
papers.abstract: Achromatic stimuli like white or gray serve as neutral perceptual anchors that may reflect the visual system's alignment with environmental illumination. We mapped the size and orientation of the achromatic loci in both normal and anomalous trichromats using a high-resolution color-naming task across various background luminances. In normal trichromats, the achromatic region was typically restricted and biased along the blue-yellow axis. For anomalous observers, the achromatic categories were substantially expanded, reflecting their L-M sensitivity loss; however, the degree of expansion was significantly less than predicted by their threshold thresholds. This partial restriction of the achromatic range suggests a compensatory recalibration of chromatic signals at a level of processing where sensory inputs are mapped into stable perceptual categories of neutral and chromatic appearance.
papers.venue: Journal of the Optical Society of America A
papers.authors: Fatemeh Basim, Arsiak Ishaq, Jesse R. Macyczko, Erin Goddard, Vanessa Honson, Juno Kim, Kimberly A. Jameson, Michael A. Webster

papers.title: Visual search for warm and cool colors
papers.abstract: Uniform color spaces predict reduced sensitivity along the warm-cool axis, but whether this translates to differences in visual salience remains unclear. We utilized a visual search paradigm where observers located chromatic targets within variegated noise backgrounds defined by different chromatic axes. Search times were significantly slower when the target-background contrast varied along the warm-cool or blue-yellow directions compared to orthogonal magenta-green axes, confirming a selective loss of sensitivity to these specific directions in the cone-opponent plane. Despite the unique status of warm and cool categories in color experience and their ecological associations with objects and backgrounds, no significant difference in search speed was found between warm versus cool or blue versus yellow hues, indicating that the perceptual unique axis does not confer an inherent salience bias in complex visual arrays.
papers.venue: Journal of the Optical Society of America A
papers.authors: Jake Manalansan, Camilla Simoncelli, Michael A. Webster

0457.name: Michael Arcaro
0457.bio: Arcaro is an Assistant Professor at the University of Pennsylvania whose research explores how intrinsic neural architectures and sensory experiences interact to shape the organization of the primate visual system. Using multimodal approaches including fMRI, electrophysiology, and behavioral psychophysics, Arcaro’s work characterizes the development of topographic maps and functional domains from birth through adulthood. Their research includes identifying the necessity of early visual experience for the formation of face-selective domains and analyzing the comparative evolution of cortical expansion in humans versus other primates.
0457.research_direction: Dr. Arcaro has recently been investigating the developmental, evolutionary, and structural foundations of the primate visual system. Their recent work explores the subcortical scaffolding of high-level vision, using high-resolution fMRI and diffusion tractography in adults and neonates to examine how the pulvinar represents complex natural scenes and routes hierarchically organized, retinotopic projections to the visual cortex. To understand how functional topographies emerge and evolve, they are comparing population receptive field maps and cortical maturation trajectories between humans and macaques, investigating whether human-specific visual capabilities stem from the expansion of conserved architectures or the addition of novel cortical areas. Furthermore, Dr. Arcaro is probing the fine-scale structure-function relationships of the ventral stream, combining in vivo imaging with ex vivo histology to determine the specific laminar and metabolic microarchitectures that physically delineate functional modules like inferotemporal face patches.

papers.title: Processing of natural scenes in the human pulvinar
papers.abstract: This study characterizes stimulus feature representation in the human pulvinar using high-resolution 7T fMRI and naturalistic stimuli. Utilizing voxel-wise encoding models (population receptive field [pRF] analysis) across thousands of natural scenes, the research identifies distinct subregions within the pulvinar showing robust selectivity for body and face categories in the contralateral visual hemifield. Complementary functional connectivity analysis reveals these subcortical regions are precisely co-activated with homologous category-selective patches in the ventral stream during ecological viewing. The findings demonstrate that fundamental hallmarks of cortical organization—specifically functional modularity and hierarchical integration—are manifested within the thalamic pulvinar, challenging strictly cortico-centric models of high-level vision and recognition.
papers.authors: Daniel R. Guest, Emily J. Allen, Kendrick N. Kay, Michael J. Arcaro

papers.title: Humans have a longer period of cortical maturation across depth and hierarchy than macaques
papers.abstract: This comparative neuroimaging study employs the T1-weighted/T2-weighted (T1w/T2w) MRI ratio as an index of intracortical microarchitecture and myelination to evaluate developmental trajectories in humans and macaques. The results delineate a conserved 'inside-out' maturational sequence, where deeper cortical laminae demonstrate accelerated T1w/T2w increases and earlier developmental plateaus than superficial layers. This laminar progression is nested within a macro-scale hierarchical gradient that originates in sensorimotor areas and terminates in higher-order association cortex. While the topographic layout of these gradients is consistent across species, human cortical maturation is significantly protracted across all hierarchies and depths, providing an extended temporal window for the experience-driven refinement of neural circuits and cognitive adaptations.
papers.authors: Monami Nishio, Xingyu Liu, Allyson P. Mackey, Michael J. Arcaro

papers.title: Expansion of a conserved architecture drives the evolution of primate visual cortex
papers.abstract: To determine the structural mechanisms underlying human brain evolution, this research compares functional topography between humans and rhesus macaques using population receptive field (pRF) mapping. The data reveal that the massive expansion of the human visual system results primarily from the surface area enlargement of a conserved retinotopic map framework shared with other primates, rather than the de novo addition of novel functional areas. This expansion follows a non-uniform distribution, with the most significant increases localized to higher-order parietal and lateral temporal regions. Comparisons with neonates demonstrate that these species-specific areal proportions are already established at birth, suggesting that the architecture for human-characteristic perceptual and cognitive abilities is governed by intrinsic developmental programs.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS)
papers.authors: Emily E. Meyer, Marcelina P. Martynek, Sabine Kastner, Margaret S. Livingstone, Michael J. Arcaro

papers.title: An intrinsic hierarchical, retinotopic organization of visual pulvinar connectivity in the human neonate
papers.abstract: Through probabilistic tractography of diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) data, this study maps the structural scaffolding of the pulvino-cortical system in human newborns. Extensive white matter projections connecting the pulvinar to occipital, dorsal, lateral, and ventral streams are identified at birth. The connectivity patterns within the pulvinar exhibit sophisticated topographical motifs, including intra-areal retinotopic mapping and a preserved hierarchical organization across processing streams. Although the global architecture resembles the adult configuration, projections to the ventral visual cortex are quantitatively less mature, aligning with the extended developmental period of the object recognition pathway. These results indicate that the subcortical framework for high-level visual communication is pre-established at birth, likely scaffolding subsequent cortical specialization.
papers.authors: Vladislav Ayzenberg, Chenjie Song, Michael J. Arcaro

papers.title: Inferotemporal face patches are histo-architectonically distinct
papers.abstract: This investigation correlates functional specialization with underlying microanatomy by performing in vivo fMRI-guided localization of face patches followed by high-resolution ex vivo histology in the same rhesus macaques. Analysis of laminar profiles across the inferotemporal (IT) cortex indicates that face-selective domains possess unique histo-architectonic signatures, characterized by elevated cytochrome oxidase (CO) metabolic activity and specific myelin densities compared to adjacent non-selective tissue. In particular, the middle lateral (ML) patch demonstrates a unique neurochemical profile with heightened CO staining. These findings emphasize that functional modules in the ventral stream are grounded in distinct cellular and metabolic microarchitectures, and that individual-specific precision mapping is critical for detecting these structure-function relationships.
papers.authors: Hiroki Oishi, Vladimir K. Berezovskii, Margaret S. Livingstone, Kevin S. Weiner, Michael J. Arcaro

0458.name: Michael Beyeler
0458.department: Department of Computer Science and Department of Psychological & Brain Sciences
0458.bio: Michael Beyeler is an Associate Professor at the University of California, Santa Barbara, and directs the Bionic Vision Lab. Their research integrates computational neuroscience, artificial intelligence, and neuroengineering to develop visual neuroprostheses for individuals with blindness. Beyeler focuses on building biophysically grounded models of neural stimulation and using virtual reality testbeds to optimize prosthetic interfaces. This work utilizes multimodal data and machine learning to investigate and augment human visual perception.
0458.research_direction: Dr. Beyeler has recently been investigating the intersection of visual neuroprosthetics, assistive technology, and computational models of biological vision. Their recent work explores the real-world utility and user-centered design of bionic eyes and assistive tools, examining both the daily informational needs of blind individuals and how gamified psychophysical paradigms might improve perceptual testing for retinal prosthesis users. In addition to applied visual rehabilitation, they are probing fundamental visual-motor control mechanisms, utilizing immersive virtual reality to study predictive internal models for intercepting moving targets during visual occlusion. Finally, Dr. Beyeler is evaluating how well artificial intelligence models parallel biological vision by benchmarking reinforcement learning agents for their robustness to visual perturbations and their neural alignment with large-scale cortical recordings from the mouse visual system.

papers.title: Gamification Enhances User Engagement and Task Performance in Prosthetic Vision Testing
papers.abstract: This study evaluates the influence of gamification on the psychophysical assessment of retinal prosthesis recipients (n=3 Argus II users). By comparing standard clinical paradigms with gamified versions of circle localization and motion direction discrimination tasks—incorporating multimodal elements such as scoring, adaptive difficulty, and affectively framed auditory feedback—the researchers quantified performance via response precision and accuracy. Findings demonstrate that gamification significantly improves localization performance and reduces angular error, likely by mitigating the cognitive fatigue associated with repetitive testing; however, effects on motion processing were heterogeneous, suggesting that the impact of engagement-enhancing features is task-dependent and mediated by the intrinsic cognitive load of the perceptual task.
papers.authors: Lily M. Turkstra, Byron A. Johnson, Arathy Kartha, Gislin Dagnelie, Michael Beyeler

papers.title: Look, predict, intercept: Visual exposure seeds model-based control in moving-target interception
papers.abstract: This research investigates the control strategies underlying the interception of moving targets that undergo temporary occlusion using immersive virtual reality paradigms. In two experiments involving ambulatory interception (N=18) and shooting tasks (N=41), the study tests a hybrid control hypothesis. Participants maintained interception accuracy significantly above chance following target disappearance, with curved motor trajectories emerging only when visual information was withdrawn. These results support a two-stage, effector-invariant interception strategy where an initial period of visual exposure (approximately 1–1.5 s) is sufficient to seed a predictive internal model that sustains control in the absence of continuous optic flow input.
papers.authors: Lauren Tenaya Eckhardt, Anvitha Akkaraju, Tori N. LeVier, Justin M. Kasowski, Michael Beyeler

papers.title: Mouse vs. AI: A Neuroethological Benchmark for Visual Robustness and Neural Alignment
papers.abstract: To address the gap between the robust generalization of biological vision and the vulnerability of reinforcement learning (RL) agents to distributional shifts, this work introduces a bioinspired benchmark based on a visually guided foraging task in a 3D Unity environment. Agents are evaluated on two complementary tracks: (1) Visual Robustness, assessing behavioral generalization across ecologically realistic visual perturbations (e.g., fog, illumination changes); and (2) Neural Alignment, quantifying the ability of an agent's internal representations to predict large-scale calcium imaging recordings from over 19,000 neurons in mouse primary visual cortex (V1) and higher visual areas (HVA) via linear readouts.
papers.authors: Marius Schneider, Joe Canzano, Jing Peng, Yuchen Hou, Spencer LaVere Smith, Michael Beyeler

papers.title: Assistive technology use in domestic activities by people who are blind
papers.abstract: This mixed-methods study characterizes the informational needs and adaptive strategies of legally and totally blind individuals (N=16) during the performance of instrumental activities of daily living (iADLs) at home. Through semi-structured interviews and behavioral observations, the authors identify a prevalent preference for low-tech tactile systems over digital alternatives and a hierarchical problem-solving framework where digital assistant applications are typically utilized as a last resort. Key barriers to technology adoption include accessibility regressions in software updates and the challenge of precise object localization, suggesting that future assistive neurotechnologies must better integrate with the multimodal and user-specific nature of domestic workflows.
papers.authors: Lily M. Turkstra, Tanya Bhatia, Alexa Van Os, Michael Beyeler

papers.title: Aligning Visual Prosthetic Development With Implantee Needs
papers.abstract: This qualitative study evaluates the translational efficacy of current bionic eye technologies by reconciling the lived experiences of six visual prosthesis recipients (Argus II and Orion) with the expectations of six leading researchers. Thematic and statistical analyses reveal a significant discrepancy between predicted and actual device utilization, with implantees using their devices less frequently than researchers anticipated due to usability, reliability, and functional limitations. Implantees emphasized a critical demand for enhanced spatial resolution, intelligent software integration for task-specific assistance, and greater independent utility, advocating for a shift toward user-centered design in the development of next-generation visual neuroprostheses.
papers.authors: Lucas Nadolskis, Lily M. Turkstra, Ebenezer Larnyo, Michael Beyeler

0459.name: Michael Bonner
0459.bio: Michael F. Bonner is an Assistant Professor in the Department of Cognitive Science at Johns Hopkins University, where he directs the Bonner Lab. His research investigates the computational principles of the human visual system by integrating functional neuroimaging with deep neural network modeling. He focuses on characterizing the high-dimensional nature of cortical representations, challenging traditional low-dimensional theories of neural coding through advanced statistical techniques. His recent work explores the alignment between artificial and biological vision systems and the latent manifold structure that underlies individual differences in visual experience.
0459.research_direction: Dr. Bonner has recently been investigating the high-dimensional geometry of visual representations in the brain and the principles that govern representational alignment between biological and artificial vision systems. Using spectral analysis of fMRI responses to naturalistic movies and images, their recent work explores the fundamental organization of the visual hierarchy, probing whether neural populations rely on expansive, scale-free manifolds to encode both shared sensory inputs and unique individual visual experiences. Additionally, they are examining the computational drivers of brain-model similarity by comparing human and macaque neural data against large, diverse ensembles of deep neural networks. Specifically, Dr. Bonner investigates how latent dimensionality impacts model predictivity and tests whether brain-like visual processing is driven by universal regularities of natural scenes, massive experience-dependent training, or the inherent architectural inductive biases of untrained convolutional networks.

papers.title: High-dimensional structure underlying individual differences in naturalistic visual experience
papers.abstract: The research investigates the neural mechanisms by which unique subjective visual experiences are constructed from shared sensory inputs by analyzing the high-dimensional geometry of the human visual hierarchy. Utilizing spectral decomposition of fMRI responses acquired during naturalistic movie viewing, the authors demonstrate that idiosyncratic neural signatures are robustly maintained across several orders of magnitude of the latent eigenspectrum. This multidimensional representation, which is not captured by standard intersubject correlation (ISC) metrics, significantly predicts individual variance in subsequent memory recall, including the semantic richness and abstraction of narrative descriptions. The findings suggest that individual perception is mediated by information integration across an expansive, high-dimensional manifold in the visual cortex.
papers.authors: Chihye Han, Michael F. Bonner

papers.title: Universal scale-free representations in human visual cortex
papers.abstract: Utilizing the Natural Scenes Dataset, this study characterizes the large-scale population covariance of the human visual cortex to identify its fundamental organizing principles. By applying a spectral analysis to fMRI responses, the authors discovered that neural representations follow a consistent scale-free organization, with variance decaying as a power law across approximately four orders of magnitude of latent dimensions. This scale-invariant structure is highly conserved across individual subjects and across multiple regions of the visual hierarchy from V1 to V4. Furthermore, functional hyperalignment reveals that these high-dimensional dimensions are shared between brains, suggesting a universal spectrum of visual information that is systematically distributed across the entire representational manifold rather than confined to low-dimensional subspaces.
papers.authors: Raj Magesh Gauthaman, Brice Ménard, Michael F. Bonner

papers.title: Universal dimensions of visual representation
papers.abstract: This work addresses whether the representational alignment between deep neural networks (DNNs) and the human visual cortex is driven by specific optimization constraints, such as architecture and task objectives, or by universal features of natural image representation. By characterizing the universality of latent dimensions across an ensemble of hundreds of networks with diverse designs, the authors identified a common subspace of shared representational features. Comparative analysis with human fMRI data showed that the specific features which align most closely with cortical responses are those that are universal across artificial networks, independent of their individual task or architectural biases. This suggests that biological and artificial vision systems converge on similar high-dimensional geometries dictated by the statistical regularities of natural visual inputs.
papers.authors: Zirui Chen, Michael F. Bonner

papers.title: Convolutional architectures are cortex-aligned de novo
papers.abstract: The study investigates the role of architectural inductive biases in the emergence of cortex-aligned representations in neural networks, challenging the prevailing view that massive experience-dependent training is necessary for brain-model similarity. The authors demonstrate that untrained convolutional neural networks (CNNs) exhibit significant representational alignment with the ventral visual streams of humans and macaques 'de novo,' provided they incorporate specific architectural constraints: spatial dimensionality compression via pooling and feature-channel expansion. In contrast, scaling feature dimensionality in transformers or fully connected architectures failed to generate similar brain-like representations. The results suggest that the fundamental wiring of the visual cortex is closely mimicked by the architectural constraints of CNNs, allowing for brain-aligned processing even without learning.
papers.authors: Atlas Kazemian, Eric Elmoznino, Michael F. Bonner

papers.title: High-performing neural network models of visual cortex benefit from high latent dimensionality
papers.abstract: This study evaluates the 'compression hypothesis' in visual neuroscience, which posits that neural networks should reduce image representations to low-dimensional manifolds to achieve robust semantic invariance. By quantifying the latent dimensionality of numerous DNN models of the visual system, the authors demonstrate that, conversely, models with high effective dimensionality are superior predictors of neural activity in both human fMRI and macaque electrophysiology. Furthermore, high latent dimensionality was positively correlated with improved generalization performance when learning novel object categories. These results provide evidence that the visual cortex prioritizes high-dimensional sensory codes that preserve rich perceptual detail, challenging traditional views that emphasize low-dimensional representations as the goal of cortical visual processing.
papers.authors: Eric Elmoznino, Michael F. Bonner

0460.name: Michael Gaebler
0460.institution: Max Planck Institute for Human Cognitive and Brain Sciences
0460.bio: Michael Gaebler is a cognitive and neuroscientist who leads the Mind-Body-Emotion Group at the Max Planck Institute for Human Cognitive and Brain Sciences. Gaebler’s research focuses on the bidirectional relationship between mental states and peripheral physiology, specifically examining how brain-heart interactions influence emotional arousal, interoception, and sensory perception. They utilize high-density neuroimaging, including EEG and fMRI, alongside immersive virtual reality to develop naturalistic paradigms for investigating subjective experience in healthy and pathological populations. Gaebler’s work also explores the integration of digital health tools and ambulatory assessments to connect laboratory findings with real-world affective phenomena.
0460.research_direction: Dr. Gaebler has recently been investigating the intersection of emotion, interoception, and visual perception by leveraging immersive virtual reality (VR) to create highly naturalistic experimental environments. Their recent work explores how brain-body interactions—particularly the bidirectional coupling between cardiac rhythms and neural activity—shape subjective emotional arousal and the spatial perception of visual threats. To capture these complex dynamics, they employ simultaneous EEG and ECG to analyze physiological markers like heartbeat-evoked potentials, alongside developing novel open-source VR software for the continuous, real-time tracking of affective states. Furthermore, they are studying socio-visual processing in 3D space, using multivariate pattern analysis to decode how the brain simultaneously represents facial expressions and stereoscopic depth cues. Broadly, their research integrates these multimodal empirical approaches with theoretical models of dynamic "brain-body states" to understand the functional links between cardiovascular and mental health.

papers.title: EEG decodability of facial expressions and their stereoscopic depth cues in immersive virtual reality
papers.abstract: This study evaluated the feasibility of multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) for decoding affective and spatial information from high-density EEG data recorded in fully immersive virtual reality (VR). Participants were presented with virtual faces displaying four distinct emotional expressions (neutral, happy, angry, surprised) under both monoscopic (2D) and stereoscopic (3D) viewing conditions. Using time-resolved linear classifiers (logistic regression), the researchers demonstrated that EEG signals reliably differentiate facial expressions. Furthermore, the presence of binocular disparity elicited a distinct neural signature that was also decodable. Despite the added complexity of 3D depth, expression-specific neural representations remained robust and invariant across viewing conditions. Eye-tracking data confirmed that while gaze patterns reflect emotional content, they do not account for the observed neural decoding performance, supporting the use of VR-EEG for ecologically valid social neuroscience research.
papers.authors: Felix Klotzsche, Ammara Nasim, Simon M. Hofmann, Arno Villringer, Vadim Nikulin, Werner Sommer, Michael Gaebler

papers.title: Brain–body states as a link between cardiovascular and mental health
papers.abstract: This theoretical framework conceptualizes the bidirectional coupling between cardiac dynamics and neural activity through the lens of high-dimensional 'brain–body states.' Integrating principles from dynamical systems theory, the authors propose that the functional alignment of the central and peripheral nervous systems defines a state space where patterns of cardiovascular and brain activity traverse various attractors. These states are classified as micro-, meso-, or macro-states based on their temporal stability and reversibility, reflecting mechanisms ranging from transient neural interactions to long-term structural plasticity. The paper argues that persistent occupancy of dysfunctional state subspaces—characterized by altered interoceptive signaling or reduced heart rate variability—is a core feature of mental health conditions like depression and hypertension, offering a unified pathobiological perspective for psychosomatic medicine.
papers.authors: Arno Villringer, Vadim V. Nikulin, Michael Gaebler

papers.title: AffectTracker: real-time continuous rating of affective experience in immersive virtual reality
papers.abstract: To overcome the limitations of retrospective self-reports in naturalistic neuroscientific experiments, the authors developed 'AffectTracker,' an open-source Unity tool for continuous, real-time assessment of subjective valence and arousal. The tool utilizes an immersive controller interface allowing participants to navigate a two-dimensional affect grid while experiencing dynamic 360-degree virtual environments. Empirical validation across two multi-site studies demonstrated that AffectTracker provides high user experience and low cognitive interference compared to traditional methods. By capturing moment-to-moment fluctuations in affective experience, the tool enables more precise mapping between subjective feelings and time-varying physiological or neural signals (e.g., HRV, EEG), facilitating the study of emotional dynamics in complex digital scenarios.
papers.authors: Aurélien Fourcade, Francesca Malandrone, Lucy Roellecke, Anthony Ciston, Jeroen de Mooij, Arno Villringer, Sara Carletto, Michael Gaebler

papers.title: No cardiac phase bias for threat-related distance perception under naturalistic conditions in immersive virtual reality
papers.abstract: This pre-registered investigation tested the hypothesis that the timing of the cardiac cycle modulates the perception of spatial proximity to threatening stimuli. Participants in an immersive VR environment performed a pointing task to indicate the distance of briefly presented threatening (spiders) or non-threatening animals at different points in the cardiac cycle. Using Bayesian hypothesis testing on a large-scale dataset, the study found no evidence of a perceptual bias associated with cardiac systole or diastole, supporting the null hypothesis for interoceptive modulation of distance perception. These findings suggest that previously reported cardiac-phase-related biases in threat processing, often observed with static 2D stimuli, may not generalize to naturalistic, multimodal 3D environments where sensory integration requirements are more demanding.
papers.authors: Felix Klotzsche, Paweł Motyka, Aleksander Molak, Václav Sahula, Barbora Darmová, Conor Byrnes, Arno Villringer, Michael Gaebler

papers.title: Linking brain-heart interactions to emotional arousal in immersive virtual reality
papers.abstract: The study investigated how the brain's internal monitoring of the heart, indexed by the heartbeat-evoked potential (HEP), relates to conscious emotional arousal during a high-arousal naturalistic VR task. Participants experienced a simulated roller coaster while concurrent EEG and ECG data were recorded. Multivariate analysis of the HEP revealed that fronto-central HEP amplitudes were significantly modulated by the intensity of subjective arousal. Furthermore, higher arousal was linked to decreased EEG alpha power and changes in cardiac autonomic indices (HRV). The results provide evidence that interoceptive heart-brain interactions are dynamically adjusted in response to emotional intensity, suggesting that the neural representation of visceral signals is an integral component of the subjective experience of arousal in dynamic settings.
papers.authors: Aurélien Fourcade, Felix Klotzsche, Simon M. Hofmann, Alessandro Mariola, Vadim V. Nikulin, Arno Villringer, Michael Gaebler

0461.name: Michael H. Herzog
0461.department: Brain Mind Institute, School of Life Sciences
0461.bio: Michael H. Herzog is a Professor of Psychophysics at EPFL's Brain Mind Institute and directs the Laboratory of Psychophysics. Herzog’s research focuses on the spatio-temporal dynamics of human vision, specifically how global context and grouping mechanisms resolve visual crowding and feature integration. Herzog employs an interdisciplinary framework of psychophysical experiments, electrophysiology, and mathematical modeling to examine feed-forward models of visual processing. Their laboratory also investigates visual perception as a potential endophenotype for psychiatric conditions, notably schizophrenia, to identify biomarkers of neural dysfunction.
0461.research_direction: Dr. Herzog has recently been investigating the spatial and temporal mechanisms of visual crowding and unconscious feature integration, exploring whether these phenomena are governed by local feedforward pooling or global perceptual grouping. Using behavioral paradigms such as vernier arrays and sequential metacontrast, their recent work examines how mid-level scene organization and motion streams dictate which visual features are integrated into conscious percepts. Beyond fundamental visual psychophysics, their research explores perceptual and neural dynamics in clinical populations. Specifically, they are investigating how cataracts and surgical interventions impact higher-level visual functioning beyond standard acuity, and are utilizing EEG to examine whether oscillatory traveling waves can reveal Bayesian predictive coding deficits in schizophrenia.

papers.title: How are grouping and interference related in crowding?
papers.abstract: The mechanisms of visual crowding—the degradation of target perception in the presence of surrounding clutter—remain contested, particularly regarding whether interference stems from local feature pooling, lateral inhibition, or substitution. This study employed an array of lines with a central vernier offset to investigate how global grouping processes modulate these effects. Results indicate that participants' discrimination performance was minimally affected by a single pro-vernier flanker, contradicting predictions from standard pooling and substitution models. Conversely, increasing the number of pro- or anti-vernier elements significantly modulated thresholds. Notably, the study found a larger interference effect for flankers positioned closer to the fovea, an observation that violates the classic in-out anisotropy of crowding. These findings suggest that crowding is governed by complex spatial grouping mechanisms that are not adequately accounted for by existing feedforward pooling models.
papers.authors: Oh-Hyeon Choung, Nadia Ruethemann, Michael H. Herzog

papers.title: Visual Crowding
papers.abstract: Visual crowding, defined as the inability to recognize objects in clutter, is a fundamental bottleneck of visual information processing. While traditionally characterized as a local phenomenon arising from feature pooling in early visual areas, this review synthesizes evidence showing that crowding is a global and highly dynamic process. We discuss how overall stimulus configuration and perceptual grouping determine the spatial and temporal limits of crowding, involving both feedforward and feedback neural dynamics. The review highlights that crowding can be released by uncrowding when flankers are grouped away from the target, suggesting that mid-level vision and global scene organization are critical for object recognition across the entire visual field.
papers.authors: Lisa Schwetlick, Michael H. Herzog

papers.title: To what extent do cataracts and cataract surgery change perception?
papers.abstract: This longitudinal study investigated the impact of cataracts and subsequent surgical intervention on a comprehensive battery of visual functions beyond standard visual acuity (VA). We assessed 28 adults (aged 55–85) across multiple tasks, including orientation discrimination, visual search, and coherent motion (CMot), before and after bilateral cataract surgery. Pre-operative results showed that cataracts severely impaired most visual functions, except for coherent motion. Post-operatively, while VA and contrast sensitivity improved markedly, tasks requiring higher-level processing, such as visual search and reaction times, showed little to no improvement. Our findings indicate that while cataracts primarily degrade low-level signal quality, higher-level cognitive compensation may maintain some functions, and clinical assessments should extend beyond VA to fully capture visual health status.
papers.authors: Simona Garobbio, Hanna Zuche, Ursula Hall, Nina L. Giudici, Chrysoula Gabrani, Hendrik P. N. Scholl, Michael H. Herzog

papers.title: Oscillatory Traveling Waves Provide Evidence for Predictive Coding Abnormalities in Schizophrenia
papers.abstract: Within the framework of Bayesian predictive coding, schizophrenia is hypothesized to involve abnormal sensory inference driven by atypical encoding of prior beliefs. We utilized EEG to characterize brain rhythms as oscillatory traveling waves in patients and healthy controls. Results demonstrated that patients with schizophrenia exhibited stronger top-down alpha-band traveling waves during the resting state, potentially reflecting overly precise priors in the high-level hierarchy. Furthermore, stronger bottom-up alpha-band waves were observed in patients during a visual task, consistent with an increased signaling of sensory precision errors. These findings provide a spatial-temporal characterization of predictive coding deficits in schizophrenia and advance our understanding of the neurophysiological mechanisms underlying psychiatric symptoms.
papers.authors: Andrea Alamia, Dario Gordillo, Eka Chkonia, Maya Roinishvili, Celine Cappe, Michael H. Herzog

papers.title: Investigating the relationship between subjective perception and unconscious feature integration
papers.abstract: Visual perception requires the temporal integration of features over windows of unconscious processing lasting up to 450 ms. Using the sequential metacontrast paradigm (SQM), we examined whether this integration depends on subjective perceptual grouping. In two experiments, we found that the integration of a red anti-vernier with a preceding white vernier was contingent on whether participants perceived the anti-vernier as part of the same motion stream. When the anti-vernier was grouped separately from the stream, it was not integrated. These results suggest that feature integration is not a purely feedforward process but is modulated by high-level object-level representations and grouping mechanisms, highlighting a critical link between unconscious processing and conscious percepts.
papers.authors: Lukas Vogelsang, Maëlan Q. Menétrey, Leila Drissi-Daoudi, Michael H. Herzog

0462.name: Michael J Tarr
0462.bio: Michael J. Tarr is the Kavčić-Moura Professor of Cognitive and Brain Science at Carnegie Mellon University and investigates the computational and neural architectures underlying high-level visual perception. Tarr’s research focuses on how the primate brain transforms two-dimensional retinal inputs into representations of objects, faces, and scenes, emphasizing the role of perceptual expertise and learning. They employ a multi-disciplinary approach that integrates large-scale functional neuroimaging, such as the BOLD5000 dataset, with deep learning and generative AI models to bridge the gap between biological and artificial vision systems. Tarr’s current work explores the inductive biases of the human visual system and develops NeuroAI frameworks to map cortical semantic selectivity across the ventral visual pathway.
0462.research_direction: Dr. Tarr has recently been investigating the neural representations of complex, naturalistic visual environments by bridging human fMRI data with advanced deep learning architectures. Their recent work explores how the visual cortex processes both static semantic information and dynamic motion, utilizing vision transformers to map category-selective brain areas to specific spatial subregions in images and leveraging video diffusion models to decode optical flow directly from cortical activity. Additionally, they are developing scalable generative stimulus toolkits that produce highly parameterized novel objects to study perceptual learning, feature variability, and category acquisition in both biological and artificial vision systems. Beyond their experimental research, Dr. Tarr examines the evolving meta-scientific landscape of academic communication, evaluating how the rapid rise of preprints and algorithm-driven dissemination are transforming traditional peer review and scientific gatekeeping.

papers.title: Brain Mapping with Dense Features: Grounding Cortical Semantic Selectivity in Natural Images With Vision Transformers
papers.abstract: This research introduces BrainSAIL (Semantic Attribution and Image Localization), a novel voxel-wise encoding framework designed to link human cortical selectivity with spatially distributed semantic features in naturalistic visual scenes. By leveraging dense spatial representations from large-scale vision transformers (ViTs), the method extracts semantically consistent embeddings that bridge the gap between raw pixel data and neural activations. BrainSAIL employs a denoising distillation process to isolate specific image subregions that drive neural tuning patterns in category-selective areas, such as the fusiform face area and parahippocampal place area. The results demonstrate that incorporating dense semantic grounding provides a more granular and interpretable mapping of high-level visual representations in the human brain compared to whole-image embedding models.
papers.authors: Andrew F. Luo, Jacob Yeung, Rushikesh Zawar, Shaurya Dewan, Margaret M. Henderson, Leila Wehbe, Michael J. Tarr

papers.title: Reanimating Images using Neural Representations of Dynamic Stimuli
papers.abstract: The study presents BrainNRDS (Neural Representations of Dynamic Stimuli), a computational framework that explicitly disentangles static and motion-related representations as they are processed in the human visual cortex. Utilizing state-of-the-art video diffusion models (DragNUWA), the authors demonstrate that dense, object-level optical flow can be decoded directly from fMRI brain activity. The approach establishes that video-based encoders outperform traditional static image models in predicting neural responses to naturalistic dynamic stimuli. Furthermore, the decoded neural signals are shown to enable the realistic reanimation of static frames, providing insights into the distinct cortical pathways subserving spatial and temporal visual processing in motion-rich environments.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR)
papers.authors: Jacob Yeung, Andrew F. Luo, Gabriel Sarch, Margaret M. Henderson, Deva Ramanan, Michael J. Tarr

papers.title: The Oomplet dataset toolkit as a flexible and extensible system for large-scale, multi-category image generation
papers.abstract: This paper introduces the Oomplet Dataset Toolkit (ODT), an open-source generative stimulus engine designed for the high-throughput study of perceptual learning in biological and artificial systems. The toolkit generates 'Oomplets'—cartoon-like humanoid characters—parameterized across ten distinct feature dimensions, allowing for the creation of over 9.1 million unique stimuli with controlled categorical boundaries. Through behavioral validation, the authors show that human adults effectively discriminate categories based on varying subsets of these dimensions. The ODT provides a scalable and customizable alternative to internet-sourced image datasets, facilitating rigorous assessments of how visual complexity and feature variability influence category acquisition and representational development.
papers.authors: John P. Kasarda, Angela Zhang, Hua Tong, Yan Tan, Rui Wang, Timothy Verstynen, Michael J. Tarr

papers.title: Gatekeeping Without Peer Review
papers.abstract: This perspective analyzes the evolving landscape of scientific communication, focusing on the systemic shift toward rapid digital dissemination via preprints. The article examines how the traditional peer-review process serves as a centralized gatekeeping mechanism and contrasts this with emerging decentralized models where research impact is increasingly mediated by social media and algorithmic visibility. It evaluates the tradeoffs between the acceleration of scientific sharing and the risks associated with unvetted data, discussing the implications for institutional hiring, the preservation of scientific rigor, and the democratization of access to foundational research findings.
papers.authors: Michael J. Tarr

0463.name: Michael K. McBeath
0463.lab_name: PEARL Lab (Perception, Ecological Action, Robotics, and Learning Lab)
0463.bio: Michael K. McBeath is a Professor of Psychology at Arizona State University whose research explores the intersection of psychology, engineering, and perception-action. McBeath works on the Linear Optical Trajectory (LOT) model, which describes the navigational strategies used by humans and animals to intercept moving targets such as baseballs and frisbees. Their methodology utilizes computational modeling and psychophysical experiments to investigate multisensory object perception, auditory illusions like the Doppler effect, and the influence of natural regularities on empirical aesthetics.
0463.research_direction: Dr. McBeath's recent work explores the ecological and embodied grounding of perception across both auditory and visual domains. They have recently been investigating sound symbolism and psychoacoustic regularities, using cross-cultural recognition tasks and vocal mimicry paradigms to understand how fundamental acoustic features in speech, scat singing, and talking drums map onto linguistic meaning and environmental sounds. In the realm of embodied cognition, their research examines how sensorimotor feedback—such as rhythmic body movement or the facial muscle activation required to produce specific vowels—shapes observers' aesthetic evaluations of music and the crossmodal naming of emotional faces. Additionally, Dr. McBeath is investigating spatial allocation in vision, using image inversion paradigms to test whether vertical attention biases toward the tops of objects and bottoms of scenes are driven by fixed low-level visual features or by behaviorally relevant environmental affordances like gravity and interactivity.

papers.title: Yorùbá Speech Surrogacy with the Dùndún Talking Drum: Recognition Accuracy is a Function of Language Familiarity and Music Training
papers.abstract: This research evaluates the acoustic correspondence and perceptual intelligibility of the Nigerian dùndún talking drum as a surrogate for Yorùbá vocalizations in both speech and song. Utilizing a cross-cultural 2x2 experimental design, the study compared recognition performance across four groups: native Yorùbá versus American English speakers, further divided by musical expertise. Acoustical analyses confirmed that the dùndún precisely replicates microstructural temporal patterns, fundamental frequency (f0) contours, and intensity modulations characteristic of tonal language. Perceptual data demonstrated that while the drum maintains high surrogacy fidelity, identification accuracy is significantly moderated by linguistic familiarity and musical training. These findings support the conceptualization of drum languages as specialized cognitive platforms that exploit sound-symbolic regularities to facilitate tonal communication, highlighting the interplay between cultural expertise and universal psychoacoustic principles.
papers.authors: Kristina L. Knowles, K. Jakob Patten, Cecilia Durojaye, Babatunji O. Dada, Michael K. McBeath

papers.title: Scat Singing and Vocal Winging: Vowel Phoneme Timbre Dimensions Reflect Physical Natural Regularities
papers.abstract: The study investigates the ecological grounding of vowel phoneme timbre by exploring the mapping between spectral dimensions and perceptual biases. Using multidimensional scaling of similarity ratings for fundamental frequency-matched vowel stimuli, the research identifies two primary spectral dimensions: tone height (spectral centroid) and harmonicity (alignment of overtones). Experiment 2 reveals that participants utilize phonemes at spectral extremes (e.g., /i/ for high-frequency 8 kHz signals and /Ʌ/ for low-frequency 60 Hz signals) during vocal mimicry of non-speech auditory stimuli. Analysis of scat singing and spontaneous speech further validates that vowel phonemes possess characteristic f0 values correlating with their perceived tone height. The results demonstrate that the auditory system internalizes these natural acoustic regularities as perceptual biases, serving a functional role in source tracking and segregation during auditory scene analysis.
papers.authors: K. Jakob Patten, Michael K. McBeath

papers.title: When right side up is upside down: Vertical attention bias tracks interactive feature regularities in upright and inverted images
papers.abstract: This investigation examines the Vertical Attention Bias (VAB), which directs observers' attention toward the tops of objects and the bottoms of scenes, potentially reflecting the spatial distribution of behaviorally relevant affordances. Across two experiments utilizing triptych image paradigms, the study tested whether this bias is driven by low-level image features or higher-order ecological regularities. Results indicate that the VAB pattern—top-salience for objects and bottom-salience for scenes—effectively flips following stimulus inversion (180° rotation), although the effect magnitude is attenuated. These findings provide evidence that the bias is coupled to behaviorally relevant environmental invariants, such as gravity-constrained interaction zones, rather than fixed retinotopic locations. The data suggest a generic downward vantage tendency that optimizes the perceptual processing of interactive space and body-level affordances.
papers.authors: Matthew D. Langley, Madelaine T. Vu, Michael K. McBeath

papers.title: How music-induced movement impacts perception of emotional valence and intensity
papers.abstract: This study explores the sensorimotor grounding of musical aesthetics by investigating how physical engagement with music modulates the perception of emotional valence and intensity. Participants rated the affective qualities of musical excerpts while either remaining stationary or performing rhythmic movements that were either congruent or incongruent with the musical tempo. The results demonstrate that physical movement systematically enhances the perceived intensity of the music. Furthermore, congruent motor activity was found to facilitate more polarized emotional valence judgments, whereas incongruent movement tended to attenuate these effects. These findings support a Bayesian framework for cue integration, where interoceptive feedback from rhythmic motor activity serves as a prior that recalibrates the aesthetic and affective evaluation of auditory stimuli, confirming the robust role of embodiment in musical experience.
papers.authors: K. Jakob Patten, Mordecai J. Garcia, Michael K. McBeath

papers.title: Names with /i/ Suit Positive Faces: The Naming Paradigm
papers.abstract: Extending the articulatory feedback hypothesis and the 'gleam-glum' effect, this research investigates the sound-symbolic association between vowel phonemes and facial emotional valence. Utilizing a novel 'Naming Paradigm,' participants were tasked with selecting or generating first names for faces displaying varied emotional expressions. The study confirms a significant preference for names containing the high-front vowel /i/ (the production of which involves zygomaticus major muscle activation consistent with smiling) when naming positively valenced faces as opposed to negative or neutral ones. This preference persisted even during the generation of pseudo-words, suggesting that the embodied nature of speech production informs crossmodal mappings between phonological features and affective states. The results indicate that sound symbolism for valence is robust enough to influence the linguistic categorization and naming of social stimuli.
papers.authors: K. Jakob Patten, Michael K. McBeath

0464.name: Michael Pratte
0464.bio: Michael S. Pratte is an Associate Professor and Associate Department Head at Mississippi State University, where they direct the Perception and Cognitive Neuroscience Lab. Pratte's research integrates psychophysics, functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), and hierarchical Bayesian modeling to investigate the mechanisms of human vision and memory. They have studied visual working memory capacity, demonstrating that discrete limits exist when accounting for stimulus-specific variability, and have analyzed the sudden-death dynamics of iconic memory decay. Pratte's methodological work focuses on developing computational models and multivariate pattern analysis techniques to decode sensory representations and attentional selection from neural activity in the human visual cortex.
0464.research_direction: Dr. Pratte has recently been investigating the fundamental architecture of visual representations, focusing on whether perceptual and mnemonic processes operate along a continuous gradient or through discrete, all-or-none states. Their recent work explores visual working memory and perceptual grouping, utilizing change-detection tasks and global ensemble statistics to determine whether visual features can be stored independently of spatial locations and whether local feature segmentation occurs via discrete states. Additionally, they are examining the mechanisms of metacognition by using distinct psychophysical manipulations and continuous confidence reports to understand how subjective certainty relates to primary decision accuracy and the precision of sensory evidence. To support these theoretical inquiries, Dr. Pratte is also actively developing advanced computational tools, including open-source software packages that facilitate the application of hierarchical Bayesian mixture models to continuous reproduction data in cognitive science.

papers.title: Perceptual confidence has near perfect access to the existence of discrete representations, but only weak access to precision
papers.abstract: In the domain of perceptual decision-making, there is a significant theoretical debate regarding whether metacognitive confidence tracks a continuous strength of sensory evidence or discrete representational states. This study utilized a global motion direction estimation task coupled with continuous confidence reports to adjudicate between these accounts. Using hierarchical Bayesian mixture modeling, the authors analyzed response error distributions and their relationship to subjective confidence. The results demonstrate that while observers have near-perfect metacognitive access to whether a discrete representation of the stimulus was successfully formed (distinguishing detection from guessing), they exhibit remarkably weak sensitivity to the actual precision of those representations. This finding suggests that human perceptual confidence is primarily driven by the presence of all-or-none representational states rather than the qualitative fidelity of sensory information.
papers.authors: Marshall L. Green, Michael S. Pratte

papers.title: Features without their locations in visual working memory: Evidence from change-detection tasks
papers.abstract: This research investigates whether visual working memory (VWM) is fundamentally object-based, requiring features to be bound to spatial locations, or whether features can be stored independently. Across three change-detection experiments, including one utilizing articulatory suppression to control for verbal encoding, the authors measured memory capacity for colors, locations, and their conjunctions. The findings revealed that color capacity significantly exceeded conjunction capacity (color-location), indicating that many color representations were successfully maintained even when their associated locations were forgotten. Error analysis of location reports showed a predominance of swap errors with negligible random guessing, suggesting that feature-location binding is prone to failure while the feature identities themselves remain accessible. These results support a model of VWM where features can be represented and retrieved independently of their studied locations, challenging strict object-based storage theories.
papers.authors: Conne George, Michael S. Pratte

papers.title: bmm: An R package for Bayesian mixture modeling of continuous report data
papers.abstract: Quantitative research in visual working memory frequently employs mixture models to separate mnemonic components such as capacity, precision, and guessing rates. Standard maximum-likelihood estimation techniques often lack the flexibility to handle complex hierarchical structures or small trial counts typical of modern experimental designs. The authors present `bmm`, an R package built upon the `brms` and `Stan` frameworks that facilitates hierarchical Bayesian estimation of these models. The package utilizes a linear model syntax to allow researchers to vary model parameters across experimental conditions and groups while incorporating informed priors to enhance subject-level parameter recovery. The tutorial details implementation strategies for fitting these models to continuous reproduction data (e.g., color or orientation recall), offering a robust and accessible computational tool for the cognitive science community.
papers.authors: Yen-Chen Daniel Lin, Marshall L. Green, Michael S. Pratte

papers.title: Similarities and differences in the effects of different stimulus manipulations on accuracy and confidence
papers.abstract: The relationship between objective performance (accuracy) and subjective certainty (confidence) is a central problem in metacognition research. This paper examines how various stimulus manipulations—including changes in signal-to-noise ratio, exposure duration, and spatial frequency—differentially impact the primary decision process and the secondary confidence evaluation. Through a series of psychophysical experiments and computational modeling, the authors demonstrate that while certain manipulations produce correlated shifts in both accuracy and confidence, others create dissociations that reveal the limits of metacognitive sensitivity. The results highlight that confidence judgments are often influenced by stimulus-specific heuristics that do not perfectly align with the underlying sensory noise levels, suggesting that the mechanisms for estimating evidence quality are distinct from those mediating the initial perceptual choice.
papers.authors: Herrick Fung, Marshall L. Green, Michael S. Pratte

papers.title: Segmenting local features using global ensemble statistics is a discrete, all-or-none process
papers.abstract: Perceptual grouping and segmentation are often described as processes that accumulate evidence to a threshold. This study challenges that view by investigating whether the segmentation of local features based on global ensemble statistics occurs along a continuum or via discrete states. Observers performed a segmentation task involving regions defined by different orientation distributions. Modeling the resulting data with hierarchical Bayesian mixture models revealed that performance was best described by a two-state process: participants either successfully segmented the target regions with high precision or failed completely, appearing to guess randomly. There was no evidence for intermediate or 'fuzzy' segmentation states that varied with stimulus difficulty. These findings suggest that the integration of local features into a coherent global representation is a discrete, all-or-none operation within the visual system.
papers.authors: Marshall L. Green, Michael S. Pratte

0465.name: Michael S. Landy
0465.department: Department of Psychology and Center for Neural Science
0465.lab_name: Landy Laboratory for Vision and Action
0465.bio: Michael S. Landy is a Professor of Psychology and Neural Science at New York University, where they investigate the computational principles underlying human perception and action. Landy’s research focuses on sensory cue integration, specifically the development of ideal-observer models that characterize how the brain combines multiple sources of sensory information. Their methodology incorporates psychophysical experimentation, functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), and mathematical modeling. This work addresses topics such as texture segregation, depth perception, and sensory decision-making under uncertainty.
0465.research_direction: Dr. Landy has recently been investigating the computational mechanisms underlying metacognition and sensory adaptation across both visual and motor domains. Their recent work explores how the visual system computes perceptual confidence, using Bayesian ideal-observer models to test whether confidence judgments accurately track the increasing internal noise associated with peripheral eccentricity. In the motor domain, they are examining how humans integrate internal motor-execution cues with external visual feedback to evaluate action success during both implicit and explicit visuomotor adaptation. Additionally, their research investigates multisensory processing, probing how precision-based causal inference models can explain the brain's ability to temporally recalibrate to audiovisual timing discrepancies.

papers.title: Visual confidence accurately tracks increasing internal noise with eccentricity in peripheral vision
papers.abstract: The internal noise inherent to sensory representations necessitates robust metacognitive monitoring for optimal decision-making. This study addresses whether perceptual confidence accurately mirrors the escalation of internal noise associated with increasing eccentricity in peripheral vision. Using a normative Bayesian framework and an incentivized post-decision wagering task, we assessed spatial localization and orientation estimation across varying degrees of eccentricity. We modeled sensory noise based on perceptual response distributions and evaluated an ideal-observer model against several alternatives. Our results demonstrate that the Bayesian ideal-observer model consistently provided the best fit for confidence reports, indicating that the human visual system accurately tracks the spatial profile of internal noise in the periphery to generate well-calibrated confidence judgments.
papers.authors: Luhe Li, Michael S. Landy

papers.title: Implicit adaptation's effect on sensorimotor and motor confidence
papers.abstract: Sensorimotor adaptation is driven by both explicit strategic corrections and implicit, automatic recalibration. While explicit adaptation is known to decrease sensorimotor confidence, the impact of implicit adaptation on metacognitive judgments remains debated. We isolated implicit adaptation using an error-clamped visual feedback paradigm during a slicing reach task. Participants indicated their perceived hand direction and confidence levels through endpoint wagering. Although robust implicit adaptation and corresponding shifts in perceived reach direction were observed, these unconscious corrections did not systematically influence confidence judgments of motor awareness. These findings suggest a dissociation between the cues used for motor-awareness confidence and those used for sensorimotor goal-success confidence, implying distinct underlying computational mechanisms.
papers.authors: Marissa H. Evans, Jordan A. Taylor, Michael S. Landy

papers.title: Sensorimotor confidence during explicit motor adaptation
papers.abstract: This study investigates the integration of multisensory and motor-execution cues in determining sensorimotor confidence during adaptation to sudden sensory perturbations. Participants performed slicing reaches toward a visual target with their unseen hand while adapting to large shifts in visual feedback. We examined the temporal dynamics of adaptation and confidence to identify which cues—prospective (e.g., motor planning) or retrospective (e.g., sensory feedback)—most influence the evaluation of action success. Bayesian modeling revealed that observers incorporate error signals into their confidence judgments in a manner that parallels the adaptive update of motor plans, suggesting that sensorimotor confidence is computed using an internal representation of the motor system's current state of calibration.
papers.authors: Marissa H. Evans, Michael S. Landy

papers.title: Metacognition in Motion: The Interplay Between Motor Evidence and Visual Information in Shaping Sensorimotor Confidence
papers.abstract: This investigation examines the contribution of internal motor signals and external visual feedback to the detection of partial errors (subtle, endogenous motor corrections) and the associated sensorimotor confidence. Using electromyographic (EMG) recordings during a conflict task, we manipulated the visibility of visual conflict using supraliminal and subliminal primes. We observed that participants exhibited above-chance metacognitive efficiency in detecting partial errors, even when they remained unaware of the initial conflict. Confidence levels were systematically modulated by the amplitude of motor activation and the latency of correction. Our results indicate that internal motor evidence and external visual information are integrated to shape sensorimotor confidence, with a greater reliance on internal signals when external feedback is degraded.
papers.authors: Catherine Culot, Marissa H. Evans, Shannon M. Locke, Michael S. Landy

papers.title: Precision-based causal inference modulates audiovisual temporal recalibration
papers.abstract: The brain maintains stable temporal perception across sensory modalities by adjusting to timing discrepancies through temporal recalibration. We tested whether this process is governed by a multisensory causal-inference mechanism. Participants were exposed to varying audiovisual stimulus-onset asynchronies (SOAs) across multiple sessions. Consistent with causal-inference models, recalibration effects exhibited a non-monotonic relationship with adapter SOA, plateauing as discrepancies increased. We compared six observer models and found that a model incorporating both causal inference and modality-specific precision of signal arrival latencies best explained the observed nonlinearities and asymmetries. This suggests that the same inferential processes that manage multisensory integration on a single trial also mediate the long-term adaptation of cross-modal temporal biases.
