papers.authors: Luhe Li, Fangfang Hong, Stephanie Badde, Michael S. Landy

0467.name: Michael-Paul Schallmo
0467.bio: Michael-Paul Schallmo is an Assistant Professor in the Department of Psychiatry & Behavioral Sciences at the University of Minnesota. Their research utilizes a multimodal neuroimaging approach, including high-field functional MRI (7T), MR spectroscopy, and EEG, combined with behavioral psychophysics to investigate how psychiatric and neurological conditions alter neural processing in the visual system. Schallmo focuses on the functional and neurochemical foundations of visual dysfunction in populations such as those with schizophrenia, autism spectrum disorders, and visual snow syndrome. As an investigator for the Psychosis Human Connectome Project, Schallmo's work aims to identify objective biomarkers for sensory impairments and clarify the link between brain chemistry and perceptual organization.
0467.research_direction: Dr. Schallmo has recently been investigating the neural mechanisms of visual contextual processing and how these pathways are altered across various clinical and pharmacological states. Their recent work explores how fundamental visual functions, such as contrast surround suppression and contour integration, are affected in individuals on the psychosis spectrum and how these processes are modulated by serotonergic psychedelics like psilocybin. To examine these questions, they combine behavioral psychophysics with ultra-high field (7T) fMRI and magnetic resonance spectroscopy to probe excitation-inhibition dynamics, functional connectivity, and spatial coding across primary and higher-order visual cortices. Additionally, their research spans novel efforts to psychophysically quantify the perceptual characteristics of Visual Snow Syndrome and tests whether the aperiodic slope of resting-state EEG signals can be utilized as a non-invasive metric for assessing cortical glutamatergic tone.

papers.title: Aperiodic slope reflects glutamatergic tone in the human brain
papers.abstract: Non-invasive quantification of the cortical excitation-inhibition (E:I) balance remains a fundamental challenge in human neuroscience. This research investigated whether the aperiodic (1/f) exponent of the electroencephalography (EEG) power spectrum serves as a reliable proxy for neurochemical concentrations. By integrating resting-state EEG with ultra-high field (7T) magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS) in the medial occipital cortex, the study demonstrated that shallower (flatter) aperiodic slopes are significantly associated with higher concentrations of the excitatory neurotransmitter glutamate. Conversely, no significant relationship was found between the aperiodic slope and GABA levels. These results validate the aperiodic slope as a physiologically grounded, non-invasive metric for assessing excitatory tone in the human brain, providing a quantitative tool for investigating E:I dynamics across varying functional and clinical states.
papers.authors: Aislin A. Sheldon, Hannah R. Moser, Kamar S. Abdullahi, Karly D. Allison, Carter B. Mulder, Samantha A. Montoya, Scott R. Sponheim, Małgorzata Marjańska, Michael-Paul Schallmo

papers.title: Impaired Contour Object Perception in Psychosis
papers.abstract: Contour integration—the neural synthesis of fragmented visual elements into a coherent whole—is a well-documented deficit in schizophrenia. This study utilized a transdiagnostic framework to investigate whether these impairments are specific to schizophrenia or represent a broader feature of psychotic psychopathology (PwPP). Utilizing behavioral psychophysics and ultra-high field (7T) functional MRI, the researchers found significant contour discrimination deficits in PwPP, particularly those with schizophrenia, compared to healthy controls and biological relatives. Imaging data revealed hyper-responsiveness in the lateral occipital complex (LOC) and aberrant task-based functional connectivity between primary and higher-order visual regions. These neural abnormalities were contingent on the requirement to segment contours from background noise, suggesting that impaired suppressive mechanisms and disorganized connectivity underlie visual integration failure in the psychosis spectrum.
papers.venue: Biological Psychiatry: Cognitive Neuroscience and Neuroimaging
papers.authors: Rohit S. Kamath, Kimberly B. Weldon, Hannah R. Moser, Kamar S. Abdullahi, Philip C. Burton, Scott R. Sponheim, Cheryl A. Olman, Michael-Paul Schallmo

papers.title: Center-surround processing in psychosis
papers.abstract: As part of the Psychosis Human Connectome Project, this study explored the mechanisms of altered contrast surround suppression in individuals with psychotic psychopathology (PwPP). The researchers combined psychophysical testing, 7T fMRI, and 7T MRS to measure contextual modulation in the primary visual cortex (V1) and the lateral occipital complex (LOC). While V1 surround suppression strength was found to be comparable across groups, individuals with psychosis and their first-degree relatives exhibited significantly reduced suppression specifically in the LOC. Furthermore, multi-voxel pattern analysis (MVPA) indicated that the neural representations of spatial context in V1 are less reliable in PwPP. The findings suggest that while low-level gain control remains largely intact, higher-order contextual processing and the robustness of spatial coding are selectively disrupted in psychosis.
papers.authors: Samantha A. Montoya, Hannah R. Moser, Rohit S. Kamath, Li Shen Chong, Andrea N. Grant, Małgorzata Marjańska, Scott R. Sponheim, Stephen A. Engel, Cheryl A. Olman, Michael-Paul Schallmo

papers.title: Enhanced visual contrast suppression during peak psilocybin effects: Psychophysical results from a pilot randomized controlled trial
papers.abstract: Surround suppression is a fundamental visual property where the perceived contrast of a target stimulus is attenuated by its spatial context. This pilot, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial investigated the impact of the serotonergic psychedelic psilocybin on this process. During peak drug effects (25 mg), participants performed a contrast-matching psychophysical task. The results showed that psilocybin significantly enhanced the magnitude of contrast surround suppression compared to the niacin placebo, indicating a shift toward less veridical perception. The degree of suppression enhancement positively correlated with the intensity of subjective visual alterations. These findings provide evidence for the role of serotonin (likely 5-HT2A receptor) modulation in visual contextual processing and suggest that psychedelic states involve heightened sensitivity to surrounding context during object perception.
papers.authors: Link Ray Swanson, Sophia Jungers, Ranji Varghese, Kathryn R. Cullen, Michael D. Evans, Jessica L. Nielson, Michael-Paul Schallmo

papers.title: What does visual snow look like? Quantification by matching a simulation
papers.abstract: Visual Snow Syndrome (VSS) is defined by the persistent perception of flickering, pixelated noise throughout the visual field, yet quantitative characterization of this percept has been limited. This study introduced a novel psychophysical matching paradigm in which participants with VSS (n=31) adjusted a computer simulation to reflect their internal visual experience. The results provided a standard quantitative profile: visual snow elements were exceptionally small (diameter < 2 arcmin), highly dynamic (mean temporal frequency = 18.2 Hz), and perceived at low contrast (average RMS contrast = 2.56%) with low density (2.87%). High intra-observer reliability (ICC > 0.89) validates this simulation as a precise tool for characterizing VSS phenomenology, enabling objective symptom tracking and furthering research into the syndrome's neural origins.
papers.authors: Samantha A. Montoya, Carter B. Mulder, Karly D. Allison, Michael S. Lee, Stephen A. Engel, Michael-Paul Schallmo

0468.name: Michael. S. Beauchamp
0468.bio: Michael S. Beauchamp is a Professor and Vice Chair for Research in the Department of Neurosurgery at the University of Pennsylvania. Beauchamp’s research investigates the neural mechanisms of multisensory integration and visual perception, focusing on the combination of auditory and visual information during speech. Utilizing blood-oxygen-level-dependent functional magnetic resonance imaging (BOLD fMRI) and intracranial electroencephalography (iEEG), Beauchamp has identified the superior temporal sulcus (STS) as a hub for integrating complex sensory signals. Their current research involves developing computational models of multisensory perception and advancing brain-mapping techniques to assist patients with language and perceptual impairments.
0468.research_direction: Dr. Beauchamp’s recent work explores the neural, behavioral, and computational mechanisms of multisensory integration, focusing particularly on how visual facial movements influence auditory speech perception. Using high-density intracranial recordings (sEEG) in human patients, they have recently been mapping the fine-grained spatio-temporal dynamics of audiovisual fusion within the superior temporal sulcus. Their research also investigates the universal nature of multisensory illusions like the McGurk effect by comparing large-scale behavioral responses across diverse linguistic groups, including English, Mandarin, and Japanese speakers. To formalize the computations underlying this integration, they are testing whether deep neural networks and Bayesian causal inference models can replicate human patterns of cross-modal fusion and individual perceptual variability. Furthermore, they are evaluating the practical utility of visual speech cues by examining how well different types of AI-generated synthetic faces improve speech-in-noise perception compared to natural human facial dynamics.

papers.title: Stereoelectroencephalography Reveals Neural Signatures of Multisensory Integration in the Human Superior Temporal Sulcus during Audiovisual Speech Perception
papers.abstract: This study utilizes high-density stereoelectroencephalography (sEEG) recordings from 42 neurosurgical patients to resolve the spatio-temporal neural dynamics of the superior temporal sulcus (STS) and gyrus (STG) during speech processing. While the STG exhibits robust responsiveness to unisensory auditory phonological input, significant multisensory enhancement in the form of elevated high-gamma power was localized specifically to the posterior STS. By bypassing the hemodynamic lag and spatial averaging inherent in fMRI, the authors demonstrate that the STS serves as a specialized computational node for the integration of auditory speech and visual labial motion, whereas the adjacent STG functions primarily as an auditory processor without corresponding multisensory gain.
papers.authors: Yue Zhang, John F. Magnotti, Xiang Zhang, Zhengjia Wang, Yingjia Yu, Kathryn A. Davis, Sameer A. Sheth, H. Isaac Chen, Daniel Yoshor, Michael S. Beauchamp

papers.title: A Deep Neural Network Model of Audiovisual Speech Recognition Reports the McGurk Effect
papers.abstract: This research investigates the emergent perceptual properties of AVHuBERT (Audiovisual Hidden-unit Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers), a state-of-the-art deep neural network for speech recognition. The authors tested whether the model exhibits the McGurk effect, a hallmark of human audiovisual phonetic fusion. By systematically injecting stochastic noise into the DNN’s cross-modal fusion layers, the model's responses successfully recapitulated the full range of inter-individual variability in visual influence seen in humans. The findings suggest that high-performance transformer architectures trained on naturalistic audiovisual corpora can develop internal representational spaces and disparity thresholds that mirror human Bayesian causal inference in multisensory speech perception.
papers.authors: Haotian Ma, Zhengjia Wang, Xiang Zhang, John F Magnotti, Michael S Beauchamp

papers.title: The McGurk effect is similar in native Mandarin Chinese and American English speakers
papers.abstract: Addressing long-standing debates regarding the role of linguistic and cultural background in multisensory integration, this study employed a large-scale, standardized behavioral paradigm to compare susceptibility to the McGurk effect in native Mandarin Chinese and American English speakers. Utilizing identical, high-fidelity audiovisual stimuli and controlled experimental conditions, the researchers found no significant differences in the magnitude of visual influence between the two groups. The results indicate that the neural mechanisms governing the fusion of incongruent auditory and visual speech cues are robust to linguistic variations such as tonality and provide evidence for a universal computational architecture for audiovisual speech integration.
papers.authors: John F. Magnotti, Debshila Basu Mallick, Gan Feng, Bo Zhou, Wen Zhou, Michael S. Beauchamp

papers.title: The Noisy Encoding of Disparity Model Predicts Perception of the McGurk Effect in Native Japanese Speakers
papers.abstract: This study applies the Noisy Encoding of Disparity (NED) model—a Bayesian causal inference framework—to characterize the multisensory speech perception profiles of native Japanese speakers. By quantifying individual differences as parameters of sensory noise and prior probabilities for a common causal source, the model successfully predicts the varied susceptibility to the McGurk effect within the Japanese cohort. The findings challenge the traditional view that Japanese listeners are uniquely resistant to visual speech influence, demonstrating instead that their perceptual patterns are consistent with universal Bayesian integration principles governed by individual-specific noise levels in sensory encoding.
papers.authors: John F. Magnotti, Anastasia Lado, Michael S. Beauchamp

papers.title: Synthetic faces generated with the facial action coding system or deep neural networks improve speech-in-noise perception, but not as much as real faces
papers.abstract: The efficacy of synthetic visual speech in facilitating speech-in-noise (SiN) intelligibility was evaluated by comparing naturalistic talker videos against avatars generated via the Facial Action Coding System (FACS) and generative deep neural networks (DNNs). While both types of synthetic facial animation provided significant perceptual gains relative to auditory-only conditions, neither matched the substantial enhancement provided by real human faces. The study suggests that although current generative models capture broad labial movements, they lack the subtle, high-frequency spatio-temporal dynamics or non-rigid facial deformations critical for optimal multisensory perceptual benefits in challenging acoustic environments.
papers.authors: Yingjia Yu, Anastasia Lado, Yue Zhang, John F. Magnotti, Michael S. Beauchamp

0470.name: Michele Rucci
0470.department: Department of Brain and Cognitive Sciences
0470.bio: Michele Rucci is a Professor of Brain and Cognitive Sciences and Neuroscience at the University of Rochester and co-directs the Active Perception Laboratory. Rucci’s research investigates the intersection of sensory processing and motor behavior, specifically examining how microscopic eye movements such as drifts and microsaccades facilitate visual perception and neural encoding. Through the use of computational modeling, psychophysics, and high-precision eye tracking, Rucci has found that these fixational movements are components for high-acuity spatial vision rather than random noise. Their work addresses the theory of active vision by proposing that the brain utilizes oculomotor dynamics as an information-processing stage to decode the visual environment.
0470.research_direction: Dr. Rucci has recently been investigating how continuous oculomotor behaviors, ranging from fixational drift and microsaccades to blinks and smooth pursuit, actively shape early visual processing. Using high-resolution eye tracking and precise gaze-contingent displays, their recent work explores how the temporal luminance transients generated by these movements reformat spatial information on the retina. Specifically, they are studying how physical eye kinematics, such as blink mechanics or residual foveal jitter during visual tracking, dynamically filter visual input to alter contrast sensitivity across different spatial frequencies. Additionally, their research examines the underlying mechanisms of fine oculomotor control, probing the spatial and temporal factors that trigger corrective fixational saccades to maintain gaze.

papers.title: Residual Foveal Motion Facilitates Processing of Visually Tracked Objects
papers.abstract: Investigation into smooth pursuit eye movements reveals that failure to achieve perfect retinal stabilization serves a functional role in visual encoding. Reconstructing foveal motion through high-resolution tracking shows that residual retinal jitter during pursuit mirrors fixational eye drift. This motion implements a whitening strategy for natural images, equalizing luminance modulations across low spatial frequencies and shifting contrast sensitivity toward lower spatial frequencies relative to fixation. These results suggest that retinal motion during pursuit is an active strategy for encoding space in the joint space-time domain.
papers.authors: Bin Yang, Jonathan D. Victor, Michele Rucci

papers.title: What one sees depends on how far the eye has moved
papers.abstract: Saccade-induced luminance transients are shown to filter visual information according to spatial frequency rather than just retinal location. Analysis of magnitude-dependent saccade kinematics demonstrates that reduced saccade amplitudes selectively attenuate post-saccadic sensitivity to low spatial frequencies. This finding indicates that the spatiotemporal flow generated by saccades acts as a content-based selection mechanism, where the scale of gaze shifts determines the spectral content of the resulting neural representation, effectively shaping perception through the kinematic properties of eye movements.
papers.authors: Y. Howard Li, Michele A. Cox, Jonathan D. Victor, Michele Rucci

papers.title: Spatial and Temporal Factors Influencing Fixational Saccades
papers.abstract: The generation of microsaccades during sustained fixation is governed by a dynamic interaction of spatial gaze-centering and temporal release mechanisms. By employing a gaze-contingent procedure to localize the perceived visual center, the study demonstrates that fixational saccades provide precise error-correction for even minimal gaze displacements. The findings reveal that while these saccades are highly accurate in relocating gaze, their probability of occurrence and latency are modulated by current fixation error, reconciling competing theories of oculomotor control and suggesting fixational saccades serve a corrective function that can only be avoided for limited periods.
papers.authors: Jie Z. Wang, Claudia Cherici, Michele Rucci

papers.title: Consequences of eye movements for spatial selectivity
papers.abstract: The human visual system exploits the temporal luminance modulations generated by fixational eye drift to shape spatial tuning. Using precise gaze-contingent stimulus control, this research shows that contrast sensitivity follows the power of these induced modulations within specific temporal bands. Specifically, varying the speed of fixational drift has divergent effects on spatial sensitivity: enhancements at high spatial frequencies are coupled with sensitivity losses at low spatial frequencies. This demonstrates that spatial selectivity is a dynamic product of motor behavior rather than a fixed neural property, and that spatial tuning is not hard-wired but depends on fixational motion.
papers.authors: Janis Intoy, Y. Howard Li, Norick R. Bowers, Jonathan D. Victor, Martina Poletti, Michele Rucci

papers.title: Eye blinks as a visual processing stage
papers.abstract: Blinking is traditionally viewed as a visual interruption, yet high-resolution eye tracking and spectral analysis of visual input signals reveal it serves as a functional processing stage. The study shows that blink-induced luminance transients increase the power of retinal stimulation, specifically enhancing visibility at low spatial frequencies. This effect occurs irrespective of whether the transients are generated by active blinking or passive stimulation, indicating that blinks act as a computational component of a visual strategy to reformat spatial information into the temporal domain, effectively compensating for the loss in stimulus exposure.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS)
papers.authors: Bin Yang, Janis Intoy, Michele Rucci

0471.name: Michelle Greene
0471.bio: Michelle R. Greene is an Assistant Professor of Psychology at Barnard College who examines the neural and computational foundations of rapid visual scene perception. Greene’s research utilizes behavioral psychophysics, electroencephalography (EEG), and machine learning to study how humans and artificial intelligence systems extract semantic meaning from complex environments. Greene developed the Visual Experience Dataset—a head-mounted video and gaze-tracking corpus—and conducts NSF-funded research on the efficient coding of visual, structural, and conceptual scene features. Their current projects aim to bridge the gap between human visual cognition and computer vision models.
0471.research_direction: Dr. Greene has recently been investigating the computational and neural mechanisms of natural scene and object recognition, focusing on how bottom-up visual features, conceptual meaning, and top-down task goals dynamically shape perception. Their recent work explores the temporal and behavioral dissociation between structural visual complexity and semantic richness during rapid scene categorization, utilizing steady-state visual evoked potentials (SSVEPs) and perceptual behavioral paradigms to track how these dimensions unfold over time. They are also examining the profound role of behavioral relevance in visual processing, advocating for a naturalistic behavioral taxonomy to understand occipitotemporal organization while developing novel brain-guided convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to model how dynamic observer goals reshape spatiotemporal scene representations. Additionally, they use artificial systems to study the emergence of scale and viewpoint invariance, investigating how the statistical structure of a network's "visual diet" drives the development of object representations that mirror the human ventral stream.

papers.title: Divergent roles of visual structure and conceptual meaning in scene detection and categorization
papers.abstract: The rapid recognition of scene gist suggests an efficient visual processing mechanism, yet the factors determining the ease of scene understanding remain unclear. We investigate the dissociation between visual structure—quantified via image compressibility metrics—and conceptual richness—derived from human-generated semantic descriptions. Across four behavioral paradigms involving rapid scene detection and basic-level categorization, we demonstrate that high visual information content consistently impairs performance, indicative of a perceptual information bottleneck. Conversely, high semantic complexity selectively enhances early detection sensitivity (d') while having a minimal or nuanced impact on categorization accuracy. These results suggest a functional dissociation where structural complexity imposes processing costs, whereas semantic richness facilitates early perceptual access, possibly through top-down modulation of visual templates.
papers.authors: Sage Aronson, Maria S. Adkins, Michelle R. Greene

papers.title: Look to the behavior—but first, define it: toward a behavioral taxonomy of vision
papers.abstract: Current debates in visual neuroscience suggest that the functional organization of the occipitotemporal cortex is driven by behavioral relevance rather than rigid stimulus categories. However, the lack of a systematic behavioral taxonomy—an ontology of what humans actually do in real-world environments—limits the actionability of this hypothesis. I argue that the path forward requires leveraging naturalistic datasets that synchronize tasks, gaze tracking, and physical movement to identify the 'basic-level' actions of human behavior. By treating category-selectivity as a data-driven outcome of adaptive visual processing rather than a starting assumption, we can discover which ecological behaviors consistently recruit specific neural categorizations to support goal-directed actions.
papers.authors: Michelle R. Greene

papers.title: Visual and Semantic Scene Information: A Steady-State Visual Evoked Potentials Study
papers.abstract: Efficient coding theories propose that the visual system compresses redundant information to optimize processing. This study utilizes steady-state visual evoked potentials (SSVEP) to assess how structural (visual) and conceptual (semantic) information levels modulate objective scene recognition. We presented triplets of images designed to maximize similarity in one information dimension while minimizing it in others. Our findings reveal that the brain's neural signature for scene information evolves over time, with early responses tracking low-level image entropy and later components aligning with semantic complexity. This temporal progression underscores how the sparse code for scenes is flexibly adapted to suit the behavioral goals and information capacity limits of the mammalian visual system.
papers.authors: Skylar Stadhard, Sage Aronson, Michelle R. Greene

papers.title: Learning Invariant Object Representations in Deep Convolutional Neural Networks
papers.abstract: Deep convolutional neural networks (dCNNs) have achieved near-human accuracy in visual categorization, yet they often lack the robust viewpoint and scale invariance characterized by human vision. We evaluate the conditions under which dCNNs develop invariant object representations using a combination of synthetic and real-world image datasets. By analyzing the activation patterns across network layers, we investigate how the integration of diverse transformational data (the 'visual diet') affects the emergence of canonical versus non-canonical viewpoint sensitivity. Our results demonstrate that supervised training on ecologically representative viewpoints facilitates the development of representational geometries that mirror the human ventral stream, suggesting that environmental statistics are a primary driver of biological-like invariance in artificial systems.
papers.authors: William Davis, Michelle R. Greene

papers.title: Brain-guided Convolutional Neural Networks Reveal Task-Specific Representations in Scene Processing
papers.abstract: Although scene categorization is the primary benchmark for visual understanding, human observers perform a multitude of tasks within any environment. To investigate how task demands reshape scene representations, we developed a novel brain-guided convolutional neural network (CNN) where each layer was guided by time-resolved ERP responses recorded during object detection and scene affordance tasks. The network successfully predicted task-specific differences by leveraging image features that humans identified as crucial for each goal. Our activation map analysis revealed that the brain's spatiotemporal representation of local features evolves systematically from 244 ms to 402 ms post-stimulus, demonstrating that distinct image features emerge at different processing stages depending on the observer's goals.
papers.authors: Bruce C. Hansen, Michelle R. Greene, Henry A. S. Lewinsohn, Audrey E. Kris, Sophie Smyth, Binghui Tang

0473.name: Miguel Eckstein
0473.bio: Miguel Eckstein is a Professor at the University of California, Santa Barbara, and directs the Vision and Image Understanding Laboratory. Eckstein’s research integrates psychophysics, computational modeling, and neuroimaging techniques—including fMRI and EEG—to investigate the mechanisms of human visual search, attention, and face perception. Their work includes modeling human performance in complex tasks, such as medical image interpretation. Eckstein also develops bio-inspired computer vision systems to bridge the gap between human and machine intelligence.
0473.research_direction: Dr. Eckstein has recently been investigating the computational principles underlying visual search and attention, exploring whether the behavioral and neurophysiological hallmarks of human covert spatial attention can emerge naturally in feedforward convolutional neural networks trained for target detection. Their recent work also examines the psychophysics of oculomotor control during naturalistic search tasks, quantifying how observers integrate foveal gaze cues from social agents with peripheral scene context to guide targeted saccades. Additionally, they are studying applied medical image perception to understand how deep learning systems interact with human visual constraints, such as the limits of foveated search and cognitive load in 3D volumetric scans. In this clinical domain, their research leverages deep neural networks as model observers to predict expert radiologist performance and assess how hierarchical visual architectures learn to discount signal-like anatomical noise.

papers.title: Emergent neuronal mechanisms mediating covert attention in convolutional neural networks
papers.abstract: This study characterizes the internal representations of deep neural networks that develop human-like covert spatial selection through task optimization in noisy environments. By analyzing the activation patterns of over one million individual units, the authors identify emergent 'location-opponent' neurons that exhibit differential excitatory and inhibitory tuning to cued versus uncued locations. These findings suggest that the neurophysiological hallmarks of attention, such as gain modulation and spatial suppression, can arise as an emergent property of hierarchical visual architectures learning to maximize target detection sensitivity without explicit top-down feedback or specialized attention modules.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS)
papers.authors: Sudhanshu Srivastava, William Yang Wang, Miguel P. Eckstein

papers.title: The psychophysics of dynamic gaze-following saccades during search
papers.abstract: This research investigates the oculomotor control mechanisms and psychophysical constraints of gaze-following in naturalistic, dynamic visual search tasks. Utilizing video stimuli of social scenes, the authors quantify how foveal gaze information and peripheral scene context integrate to guide saccadic targeting. The results demonstrate that foveal gazer cues significantly reduce the spatial error of the first saccade towards goals at large eccentricities (~9 degrees) and that observers execute predictive, anticipatory saccades based on gazer head velocity before the movement's completion. The study elucidates how the brain integrates social cues with spatial constraints to optimize search efficiency in complex environments.
papers.authors: Srijita Karmakar, Miguel P. Eckstein

papers.title: Convolutional neural network model observers discount signal-like anatomical structures during search in virtual digital breast tomosynthesis phantoms
papers.abstract: This work evaluates the performance of convolutional neural network (CNN) model observers in replicating the search behavior of expert radiologists during digital breast tomosynthesis (DBT) interpretation. Unlike standard linear model observers, which are limited by local noise statistics, the CNN models demonstrated the ability to 'discount' or suppress responses to normal anatomical structures that possess target-like features (signal-like masses). This selective discounting allows CNN observers to more accurately predict human search sensitivity and specificity, providing a computationally efficient framework for optimizing 3D medical imaging protocols through the lens of human-centered computer vision.
papers.authors: Aditya Jonnalagadda, Bruno B. Barufaldi, Andrew D. A. Maidment, Miguel P. Eckstein

papers.title: Greater benefits of deep learning-based computer-aided detection systems for finding small signals in 3D volumetric medical images
papers.abstract: The authors assess the differential performance impact of deep learning computer-aided detection (CADe) systems on human search efficiency across 2D versus 3D volumetric medical imaging modalities. Utilizing digital breast tomosynthesis (DBT) and synthetic 2D mammography, the study finds that AI assistance provides a significantly greater boost to human d' in 3D search. This result is linked to the CADe's ability to mitigate intrinsic human search limitations, specifically the under-exploration of large 3D volumes caused by the foveated nature of the visual system and the high cognitive load associated with navigating through slice-based volumetric data.
papers.authors: Devi S. Klein, Srijita Karmakar, Aditya Jonnalagadda, Craig K. Abbey, Miguel P. Eckstein

papers.title: Emergent human-like covert attention in feedforward convolutional neural networks
papers.abstract: This paper presents evidence that feedforward convolutional neural networks (CNNs) spontaneously exhibit behavioral signatures of human covert attention when trained to optimize target detection in noise. Despite lacking explicit attentional feedback mechanisms, the networks demonstrate significant cueing effects, including increased sensitivity (d') and faster convergence at validly cued locations. The findings propose a normative account for the existence of covert attention, suggesting it is not necessarily a specialized neural module but a computational property that emerges as a solution to maximizing perceptual sensitivity in hierarchical visual systems.
papers.authors: Sudhanshu Srivastava, William Yang Wang, Miguel P. Eckstein

0475.name: Miki Uetsuki
0475.department: Department of Community Studies, College of Community Studies
0475.main_research_area: cognitive and visual processing of reading
0475.bio: Miki Uetsuki is an Associate Professor in the Department of Community Studies at Aoyama Gakuin University, specializing in experimental and cognitive psychology. Uetsuki's research examines the psychophysical and cognitive mechanisms underlying reading, with a focus on visual crowding effects and the temporal characteristics of sentence processing in Japanese scripts. They utilize methodologies ranging from psychophysical behavioral measurements to event-related potentials (ERPs) to investigate how dynamic visual information processing correlates with reading proficiency. Additionally, their work explores human information processing in clinical populations and the psychological impressions of 'textual prosody' in reading.
0475.research_direction: Dr. Uetsuki's recent work explores how top-down cognitive experience and social inferences shape visual perception and recognition. In the domain of reading, they have recently been investigating how acquired literacy modulates visual crowding, using psychophysical paradigms to test whether bidirectional reading experience in native Japanese readers influences spatial tuning and crowding reduction for alphabetic versus kana scripts across horizontal and vertical orientations. Expanding into high-level object and social perception, Dr. Uetsuki is also examining the visual and psychological cues humans use to accurately match handcrafted artifacts, such as cloth dolls, to their creators. To isolate these mechanisms, their recent work explores how matching performance changes when specific visual information is restricted—such as masking facial features or presenting rear views of the objects—and investigates the extent to which physical attributes, facial morphology, and inferred Big Five personality traits guide these complex perceptual judgments.

papers.title: Japanese readers show a crowding reduction even in vertically oriented strings of letters
papers.abstract: Visual crowding in letter strings degrades target recognition performance, yet this perceptual degradation is significantly attenuated for familiar letter strings relative to strings composed of arbitrary symbols. Although earlier investigations in readers of Latin script have shown that this crowding reduction is strictly constrained to horizontally aligned text, this study evaluated native Japanese readers who possess extensive, bidirectional literacy across both horizontal and vertical orthographic layouts. Psychophysical assessments demonstrated that Japanese readers exhibit significant crowding attenuation for alphabetic strings presented vertically as well as horizontally, indicating that acquired reading experience directly modulates the spatial tuning and directionality of letter-specific crowding reduction. Conversely, this attenuation failed to generalize to Japanese syllabic kana characters relative to symbol strings, indicating fundamental differences in the early visual processing mechanisms engaged by alphabetic versus moraic Japanese scripts.
papers.authors: Miki Uetsuki, Kazushi Maruya

papers.title: Effect of personality traits on matching dolls and their makers
papers.abstract: Prior investigations show that individuals can accurately link personal belongings, pets, and handcrafted artifacts to their owners or creators above chance levels; however, the precise visual and psychological mechanisms mediating this association remain poorly understood. Three experimental paradigms were conducted utilizing handcrafted cloth dolls produced by novice collegiate makers and standardized photographs of the makers. In Experiment 1, masking the periocular area of the dolls slightly reduced performance compared to unmasked baselines but retained statistically significant above-chance matching accuracy (χ²(1) = 5.44, φ = 0.19, p < 0.05), demonstrating that matching relies on features beyond the eye region. In Experiment 2, participants achieved above-chance matching accuracy even when presented solely with the dorsal (rear) perspective of the dolls, confirming the diagnostic utility of non-facial physical attributes. In Experiment 3, the influence of personality trait inferences was evaluated using the Big Five framework. While facial morphology dominated matching judgments when faces were visible, inferred personality congruence significantly predicted matching accuracy when facial information was visually occluded.
papers.authors: Miki Uetsuki, Misako Kimura

0476.name: Min-Shik Kim
0476.bio: Min-Shik Kim is a Professor in the Department of Psychology at Yonsei University and the director of the Yonsei Cognition Lab. Kim’s research examines the mechanisms of attentional control and the representation of visual information using computational modeling, psychophysics, and neuroscientific techniques. Their work investigates how executive working memory capacity influences visual search efficiency and the conditions under which memory contents capture spatial attention. Kim also studies object continuity, visual imagery, and the application of cognitive science within education and marketing contexts.
0476.research_direction: Dr. Kim's recent work explores the mechanisms governing visual attention and working memory, focusing on how feature-based, spatiotemporal, and contextual information guide visual selection. They have recently been investigating the role of feature-based filtering in prioritizing task-relevant stimuli, examining phenomena like the attentional boost effect during dual-task RSVP paradigms and visual search within the action effect paradigm. In the domain of visual working memory, their research probes how task-irrelevant spatial and temporal overlaps in sequential displays induce feature-location misbinding errors. Additionally, they are studying how implicit statistical learning shapes attentional guidance over time, specifically testing whether varying target search templates disrupt location probability learning and whether non-spatial, interpersonal social associations can effectively serve as contextual cues.

papers.title: Feature-based filtering determines object-based selection in the attentional boost effect
papers.abstract: This study examined the selection mechanisms underlying the attentional boost effect (ABE) through a dual-task paradigm involving background image memorization during a multi-featured target detection RSVP task. Experiment 1 demonstrated that distractors sharing a single feature with the target (target-match distractors) provided no memory advantage over target-nonmatch distractors, with both showing lower mnemonic performance than images paired with the target or baseline. Experiment 2 utilized color-color conjunctions to test if spatial configuration or feature overlap drives the effect; images paired with distractors containing all target features (both-match) exhibited memory enhancement comparable to the target itself. These results indicate that the ABE is an object-based selection process modulated by feature-based filtering rather than a pure temporal selection mechanism.
papers.authors: Juyeon Joe, Yoongeol Yang, Min-Shik Kim

papers.title: Spatiotemporal position overlap disrupts feature binding in visual working memory
papers.abstract: This research investigated the influence of task-irrelevant spatiotemporal relationships on feature-location binding within visual working memory (VWM). Across several experiments using sequential memory displays, the authors assessed misbinding errors when test probes shared spatial or temporal attributes with the original memoranda. The data revealed that feature misbinding occurred more frequently for items sharing either a spatial or temporal position, with no significant difference in error rates between the two. However, when stimuli were presented unilaterally, temporal overlap induced greater misbinding than spatial overlap, suggesting that temporal cues may take precedence over spatial information within a single hemifield. These results highlight the flexibility of the spatiotemporal reference frames used for object representation in VWM.
papers.authors: Juyeon Joe, Min-Shik Kim

papers.title: Attenuation of spatial bias with target template variation
papers.abstract: The study explored the impact of attentional template consistency on the acquisition of location probability learning (LPL) in visual search. Participants performed a search task where a target appeared with high probability in a specific quadrant. While a target-consistent group (fixed shapes) developed a robust and persistent spatial bias toward the frequent location, a target-variant group (randomly changing target shapes) exhibited significantly attenuated spatial bias. The findings suggest that the alternative use of varying attentional templates interferes with the emergence of long-term habitual spatial prioritization. The results imply that regularity-based spatial habits depend not only on the number of attentional shifts to a location but also on the search-relevant contextual consistency of the target template.
papers.authors: Injae Hong, Min-Shik Kim

papers.title: Feature-based selective attention operates during visual search in the action effect paradigm
papers.abstract: This study investigated whether feature-based selective attention mediates the allocation of priority in the action effect paradigm, where action planning influences subsequent visual search efficiency. Using a modified visual search task, the authors analyzed how the planning of specific motor responses modulates attentional weight toward stimuli sharing features with the intended action's consequences. The behavioral results indicated that simple action planning facilitates the allocation of attention to feature-matched targets, suggesting that the action effect is driven by a mechanism of feature-based filtering that prioritizes task-relevant information in a top-down manner during the early stages of visual selection.
papers.venue: The Korean Journal of Cognitive and Biological Psychology
papers.authors: Sori Jeong, Eunhee Ji, Min-Shik Kim

papers.title: Implicit learning of social information in contextual cueing
papers.abstract: This paper explores whether interpersonal social associations can serve as contextual cues to guide attention in visual search tasks. Moving beyond traditional spatial configuration cues, the experiments tested whether the implicit learning of target-distractor identity co-occurrences (social context) enhances search performance. The results demonstrated that participants successfully encoded the associations between specific target and distractor identities, leading to a significant reduction in reaction times when social contextual information was predictive. This suggests that the visual system can implicitly acquire and utilize social interpersonal schemas to facilitate attentional guidance, independent of the physical layout of the search display.
papers.authors: Lijeong Hong, Min-Shik Kim

0477.name: Ming Meng
0477.lab_name: Philosophy and Social Science Laboratory of Reading and Development in Children and Adolescents
0477.bio: Ming Meng is a neuroscientist specializing in the neural mechanisms underlying visual perception, attention, and mental representation. Utilizing functional MRI, psychophysical experiments, and computational modeling, Meng investigates how the brain decodes visual information both with and without conscious awareness. Their research explores the interplay between binocular rivalry and stereopsis, the lateralization of face processing, and the neural substrates of aphantasia. Meng has demonstrated that individuals lacking subjective mental imagery still exhibit stimulus-specific representations in early visual cortices, revealing a dissociation between neural encoding and conscious experience.
0477.research_direction: Dr. Meng has recently been investigating the mechanisms of early visual processing, with a primary focus on the dynamic interplay between binocular integration and interocular suppression. Their recent work explores how the visual system coordinates stereopsis and binocular rivalry over time, and how global contextual imbalances in binocular contrast influence local depth perception. Additionally, they are examining the neural hierarchy of attentional selection by using dichoptic multiple object tracking paradigms to isolate early monocular processing stages in dynamic scenes. Dr. Meng's research also probes the boundary between low-level sensory signals and conscious awareness, investigating how subliminal contrast changes drive perceptual breakthroughs during rivalry and whether widespread spatial phenomena, such as clockwise rotational biases, emerge from early sensory asymmetries or higher-level cognitive ambiguity resolution.

papers.title: Monocular advantage for multiple object tracking
papers.abstract: This study employs a dichoptic multiple object tracking (MOT) paradigm to investigate the neural processing hierarchy of attentional selection in dynamic visual scenes. By utilizing a task where target retinal projections are switched between eyes during tracking while maintaining perceptual continuity, the researchers demonstrated a significant monocular advantage, as evidenced by a substantial decrement in tracking performance—exceeding 40%—under interocular switch conditions compared to non-switch controls. These results suggest that attentional modulation in MOT operates at an early stage of visual processing, likely at or prior to the monocular layers of the primary visual cortex (V1), and potentially involves subcortical structures such as the lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN).
papers.authors: Guiping Zheng, Rong Jiang, Ke Zhou, Shuai Chang, Xinping Yu, Liqin Zhou, Ming Meng

papers.title: Breaking and restoring ocular balance: Temporal interactions in binocular rivalry and stereopsis
papers.abstract: This research explores the dynamic temporal coordination between binocular integration (stereopsis) and interocular suppression (binocular rivalry). Through a series of psychophysical experiments, the authors show that preceding episodes of binocular rivalry exert a suppressive aftereffect that significantly elevates subsequent stereo detection thresholds. Conversely, brief stereoscopic stimulation rebalances subsequent rivalry dynamics by reducing ocular dominance asymmetry and increasing the incidence of mixed percepts without affecting the alternation rate. These findings suggest that the early visual system employs a shared computational principle for regulating ocular balance, where binocular integrative and suppressive mechanisms reciprocally modulate one another to maintain unified visual awareness.
papers.authors: Rong Jiang, Ming Meng

papers.title: Increases versus decreases: Asymmetric effects of contrast changes during binocular rivalry modulated by awareness of perceptual switch
papers.abstract: This investigation examines how subconscious contrast dynamics influence perceptual selection during binocular rivalry. By comparing the effects of stimulus intensity increments and decrements on the breakthrough of suppressed stimuli, the study reveals a directional asymmetry: contrast increases lead to significantly faster breakthroughs into perceptual dominance compared to decreases. While increases consistently facilitate breakthrough relative to static baselines, the effect of contrast decreases is contingent upon the observer's awareness of interocular conflict. These findings indicate that the resolution of perceptual competition in the visual system is modulated by an interplay between subliminal sensory signals and top-down awareness-dependent mechanisms.
papers.authors: Changzhi Huang, Rong Jiang, Ming Meng

papers.title: Clockwise Bias in 2D Rotation: A Cognitive Rather Than Sensory Phenomenon
papers.abstract: The mechanisms underlying the pervasive clockwise (CW) bias in 2D rotation perception were evaluated across multiple visual awareness paradigms. Results from apparent motion tasks revealed a robust CW preference when stimuli reached awareness, whereas no such bias was observed during low-level interocular conflict in binocular rivalry or in breakthrough times from continuous flash suppression (b-CFS). Manipulations of stimulus ambiguity and input uncertainty further demonstrated that the bias emerges after stimuli reach conscious awareness. These results suggest that the CW preference is driven by higher-level cognitive processes involved in resolving perceptual ambiguity rather than by fixed low-level sensory asymmetries or motor response biases.
papers.authors: Rong Jiang, Ruo-Si Li, Ming Meng

papers.title: Contextual Binocular Imbalance Impairs Local Stereopsis
papers.abstract: This study investigates the impact of global binocular contrast distributions on the sensitivity of local stereoscopic processing. By manipulating the binocular contrast balance of the context surrounding a local stereo target, the researchers found that contextual binocular imbalance significantly elevates stereo detection thresholds. This inhibitory effect is further modulated by the collinearity between context and target stimuli and is consistently observed across both fused and rivalrous context conditions. The findings suggest that lateral connectivity and inter-regional gain control within the primary visual cortex (V1) play a critical role in integrating global contextual information with local disparity signals to determine depth perception sensitivity.
papers.authors: Rong Jiang, Shuai Chang, Xin-Ping Yu, Ming Meng

0478.name: Mingzhou Ding
0478.department: J. Crayton Pruitt Family Department of Biomedical Engineering
0478.bio: Mingzhou Ding is the J. Crayton Pruitt Family Professor at the University of Florida and utilizes engineering and computational approaches to investigate the neural foundations of cognitive functions. Ding applies Granger causality to neuroscience to provide a mathematical framework for assessing directional information flow and functional connectivity in brain networks. Their research integrates multimodal imaging techniques—including EEG, fMRI, ECoG, and local field potentials—to study visual spatial attention, emotional processing, and the dynamics of large-scale networks in healthy aging and clinical conditions such as Parkinson's disease. This work focuses on the technical development of signal processing methods and their application to understanding how the brain coordinates sensory input and top-down control.
0478.research_direction: Dr. Ding has recently been investigating the dynamic neural codes underlying visual attention, perceptual learning, and affective processing. Their recent work explores the mechanisms of spatial attention control, utilizing fMRI, EEG, and multivariate pattern analysis to uncover how internally driven "willed" attention differs from externally cued attention, and how anticipatory population-level patterns predict attentional benefits across the visual hierarchy. Additionally, they are examining the temporal constraints of visual processing by using EEG frequency tagging to probe how targets and emotional distractors are rhythmically sampled during perceptual competition. Beyond attention, Dr. Ding's research investigates how neural representations evolve over time, testing fatigue versus sharpening models during stimulus repetition in the primary visual cortex and using representational similarity analysis to map the high-dimensional geometry of emotional valence within the amygdala.

papers.title: Neural representation of emotional valence in human amygdala and surrounding regions
papers.abstract: This study employs high-resolution functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and representational similarity analysis (RSA) to characterize the neural encoding of affective valence within the human amygdala complex and adjacent subcortical structures. The research evaluates whether emotional valence—spanning from pleasant to unpleasant—is represented via unidimensional population codes or dissociable neural patterns. Our findings demonstrate that the amygdala represents the full spectrum of valence using distinct ensemble activity patterns that allow for robust decoding of affective categories. The representational geometry revealed a negative bias in amygdalar activity space, where aversive stimulus patterns occupied a more expansive manifold; notably, this bias was found to normalize following clinical interventions. These results establish the amygdala as a high-dimensional hub for affective evaluation, utilizing population-level neural patterns to discriminate between rewarding and threatening sensory information.
papers.authors: Ke Bo, Lihan Cui, Yujun Chen, Guanghui Zhang, Andreas Keil, Mingzhou Ding

papers.title: Neural Mechanisms of Willed Attention Control
papers.abstract: We contrasted the neural substrates of willed (internally generated) and instructed (externally cued) visual spatial attention control using fMRI and electroencephalography (EEG). While both attention types recruited the canonical dorsal attention network (DAN), willed attention—prompted by a choice cue—uniquely engaged a frontoparietal decision network involving the dorsal anterior cingulate cortex (dACC), anterior insula (AI), and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC). Using multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA), we successfully decoded the intended direction of attention from activity within this decision network prior to stimulus presentation. Furthermore, EEG analyses revealed that the power and phase of alpha-frequency (8-12 Hz) oscillations in the period immediately preceding the choice cue predicted both the subsequent attentional decision and the level of activation in the decision network, suggesting that spontaneous attentional shifts are significantly biased by ongoing, pre-cue intrinsic brain states.
papers.authors: Changhao Xiong, Qiang Yang, Sungkean Kim, Sreenivasan Meyyappan, Jesse J. Bengson, George R. Mangun, Mingzhou Ding

papers.title: Rhythmic sampling and competition of target and distractor in a motion detection task
papers.abstract: This study investigates the neural dynamics of rhythmic sampling and resource competition in a visual attention task using EEG and frequency tagging. Participants performed a motion detection task on a random-dot kinematogram (RDK) target flickered at 4.29 Hz, superimposed on emotional IAPS distractors flickered at 6 Hz. Moving-window multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) decoding was applied to the 6 Hz power patterns to index distractor processing, while the 4.29 Hz power tracked target processing. Results demonstrated that both target and distractor representations are sampled rhythmically at a delta frequency (~1 Hz). Critically, the relative phase between the target and distractor sampling time courses predicted behavioral performance: a phase difference near π (temporal separation within the sampling cycle) was associated with higher coherent motion detection rates, suggesting that temporal segregation of sampling cycles mitigates the detrimental effects of distraction.
papers.authors: Changhao Xiong, Nathan M. Petro, Ke Bo, Lihan Cui, Andreas Keil, Mingzhou Ding

papers.title: Stimulus Repetition Induces a Two-Stage Learning Process in the Primary Visual Cortex
papers.abstract: This research evaluates the competing fatigue and sharpening models of stimulus repetition by applying moving-window MVPA decoding and weight map analysis to fMRI data from the primary visual cortex (V1). Human subjects were passively exposed to 120 repetitions of oriented Gabor patches. The analysis identified a distinct two-stage learning trajectory in V1. The initial stage (Stage 1), comprising approximately the first twelve repetitions, was characterized by univariate repetition suppression and a decline in decoding accuracy to chance levels, aligning with the fatigue model's prediction of a non-selective reduction in neural response. In contrast, the subsequent stage (Stage 2) showed a progressive increase in decoding accuracy above chance as repetitions continued, supporting the sharpening model where representations become more distinct through long-term learning and selective reduction of irrelevant neural activity.
papers.authors: Lihan Cui, Ke Bo, Changhao Xiong, Yujun Chen, Andreas Keil, Mingzhou Ding

papers.title: Decoding Visual Spatial Attention Control
papers.abstract: We utilized multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) and a meta-analytic approach on two fMRI datasets to characterize the neural patterns of anticipatory spatial attention control across the visual hierarchy. The study evaluated both univariate BOLD activation and multivariate decoding accuracy in regions of interest (ROIs) during instructed and choice-based attention paradigms. Results revealed that while univariate activation increases were most pronounced in higher-order visual areas, MVPA decoding was significant across all visual cortical ROIs, with the highest decoding accuracies observed in lower-order areas like V1. Furthermore, individual differences in stimulus discrimination performance were more accurately predicted by decoding strength than by the magnitude of univariate signal changes, providing evidence that the information content of population-level neural patterns, rather than simple gain modulation, is a primary driver of attentional benefits.
papers.authors: Sreenivasan Meyyappan, Abhijit Rajan, Qiang Yang, George R. Mangun, Mingzhou Ding

0479.name: Miranda Scolari
0479.bio: Miranda Scolari is an Associate Professor in the Department of Psychological Sciences at Texas Tech University and the director of the Selective Attention & Perception Lab. Scolari’s research characterizes the neural and behavioral mechanisms that allow the human visual system to prioritize information within limited processing capacities, focusing on the functional architecture of the frontoparietal attention network. Using methodologies such as fMRI, transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), and pupillometry, Scolari investigates how top-down attentional gain is allocated to sensory neurons and how space- and feature-based selection mechanisms interact during perceptual decision-making. Their work further examines the representational sharpening of visual information and the intersection of selective attention with working memory and implicit learning processes.
0479.research_direction: Dr. Scolari has recently been investigating how cognitive control, attention, and learning dynamically shape human perception and behavior. Their recent work explores the neural basis of visual categorization, using fMRI and inverted encoding models to test how frontoparietal attention networks selectively sharpen early visual cortex representations of boundary-adjacent exemplars. Beyond visual plasticity, they are also examining the physiological and kinematic markers of cognitive exertion and error, employing pupillometry to track self-control depletion and motion capture to evaluate post-error slowing during complex reach-to-grasp actions. Additionally, they are probing the intersection of subjective visual experience and memory by asking whether individual differences in mental imagery vividness, including aphantasia, modulate mnemonic biases like the animacy advantage in free-recall tasks.

papers.title: Individual differences in mental imagery do not moderate the animacy advantage in memory
papers.abstract: The animacy advantage—the consistently observed mnemonic benefit for animate versus inanimate concepts—has been theorized to involve several underlying cognitive mechanisms, yet the specific role of mental imagery remains poorly understood. We investigated whether individual variability in the vividness of visual mental imagery, as assessed by the Vividness of Visual Imagery Questionnaire (VVIQ), modulates the magnitude of this effect. Across free-recall tasks, including a population of individuals experiencing aphantasia (the absence of voluntary mental imagery), the animacy advantage remained robust and was not moderated by subjective imagery vividness. Although manipulations of encoding effort improved overall recall performance, they did not interact with concept animacy. These findings suggest that the animacy advantage in memory does not depend on the generation of mental images but rather emerges from semantic or attentional mechanisms that operate independently of an observer's subjective imagery capacity.
papers.authors: Michael J. Serra, Julia N. Keiner, Nicolasa C. Villalobos, Abigail Kortenhoeven, Miranda Scolari

papers.title: The role of the frontoparietal attention network during rule-based categorization
papers.abstract: While recent evidence indicates that category learning is supported by representational sharpening within the early visual cortex, the source of this top-down sensory modulation is hypothesized to reside within the frontoparietal attention network. This neuroimaging study utilized topographic mapping of the intraparietal sulcus (IPS0–IPS5) to investigate its role in providing feature-selective control during rule-based categorization. Using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and generalized psychophysiological interaction (gPPI) analyses, we observed significant functional connectivity between topographic IPS subregions and the visual cortex during learning. Inverted encoding models (IEMs) further demonstrated that reconstructed orientation representations in posterior (IPS0/1) and middle (IPS2/3) IPS were significantly enhanced only when orientation was task-relevant. Anterior IPS (IPS4/5), however, exhibited generalized enhancement across rules. These results characterize a functional gradient within the parietal cortex that supports the selective biasing of sensory signals necessary for the acquisition of new category representations.
papers.authors: Shinyoung Jung, Sean R. O’Bryan, Miranda Scolari

papers.title: Post-error adjustments occur in both reaching and grasping
papers.abstract: Post-error slowing (PES), typically measured as a delay in reaction time following a mistake, has been widely documented in discrete cognitive tasks but remains under-explored in ecological motor actions. We investigated behavioral adaptations following errors in a complex reach-to-grasp task requiring selection between target and distractor locations. Kinematic analyses were employed to evaluate whether adjustments were restricted to pre-movement planning or extended into movement execution. Our results demonstrate that PES is not limited to reaction time delays but manifests as significant alterations in both the reaching and grasping phases, characterized by reduced peak velocities and elongated movement durations. These findings provide evidence for a global, intentional shift toward cautious motor control following an error, supporting a functional account of error reactivity rather than a purely interference-driven mechanism.
papers.authors: Joe Opdenaker, Jarrod Blinch, Miranda Scolari

papers.title: Changes in pupil size track self-control failure
papers.abstract: Ego-depletion describes the phenomenon where initial self-control exertion leads to subsequent performance decrements, yet the physiological underpinnings remain elusive. We employed pupillometry to investigate the role of attentional effort, mediated by the locus coeruleus-norepinephrine (LC-NE) system, in these effects. Participants performed high- or low-demand attention tasks followed by a common Stroop task. Analysis of tonic and phasic pupillary responses revealed that sustained pupil diameter (PD) was significantly elevated during self-control exertion and that this elevation persisted through the subsequent task, where it predicted reduced accuracy on incongruent trials. Serial mediation modeling confirmed that elevated sustained PD serves as a physiological marker for the depletion effect. These results suggest that self-control failures following exertion are linked to a maladaptive shift in the LC-NE system, providing a robust physiological account of the mechanisms underlying ego-depletion.
papers.authors: Sean R. O'Bryan, Mindi M. Price, Jessica L. Alquist, Tyler Davis, Miranda Scolari

papers.title: Category Learning Selectively Enhances Representations of Boundary-Adjacent Exemplars in Early Visual Cortex
papers.abstract: Successful categorization often requires the ability to make fine visual discriminations along continuous feature dimensions. We tested the hypothesis that category learning induces a representational sharpening of sensory populations specifically tuned to feature values near the learned category boundary. Using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and a theoretically motivated inverted encoding model, we quantified changes in population-wide orientation tuning as human subjects learned categories defined by either orientation or spatial frequency rules. Our results revealed that orientation representations in the early visual cortex (V1-V3) were significantly sharpened specifically for orientation rule learners. This enhancement was non-uniform across feature space, with the greatest representational sharpening observed for stimuli adjacent to the category boundary compared to those at the category centers. These findings support an efficient model of neural plasticity where sensory enhancements are selectively allocated to the most behaviorally relevant regions of feature space during the acquisition of category knowledge.
papers.authors: Sean R. O'Bryan, Shinyoung Jung, Anto J. Mohan, Miranda Scolari

0480.name: MiYoung Kwon
0480.lab_name: The Kwon Lab for Low Vision and Brain Research
0480.bio: MiYoung Kwon is an Assistant Professor at Northeastern University whose research explores basic and clinical vision science to understand how the human brain processes visual information under degraded or atypical sensory conditions. Kwon investigates the mechanisms of visual perception and brain plasticity in the context of aging and eye diseases such as glaucoma and macular degeneration. Utilizing an approach that includes psychophysics, functional neuroimaging (fMRI, EEG), eye tracking, and computational modeling, Kwon examines how the visual system adapts to sensory loss. Their research aims to uncover principles of visual reconstruction and develop strategies for the detection of vision loss and the enhancement of functional vision for individuals with visual impairments.
0480.research_direction: Dr. Kwon’s recent work explores how aging, neurodegenerative ocular diseases, and varied luminance conditions impact functional spatial vision and complex daily tasks. They have recently been investigating the trajectory of basic visual computations—such as contrast sensitivity, binocular summation, and surround suppression—across the healthy adult lifespan and in clinical populations with age-related macular degeneration and glaucoma. Using clinical psychophysics, including the quick contrast sensitivity function (qCSF) and computational modeling of sensory pooling, their research characterizes the underlying mechanisms of central visual field loss. Additionally, their recent work explores the specific challenges of low-luminance (mesopic) environments, using psychophysical paradigms and digital assessments to measure how rod-dominant lighting modulates cortical spatial integration and impacts reading performance across adulthood.

papers.title: Preserved Contrast Sensitivity in Early and Intermediate Age-Related Macular Degeneration and Marked Loss in Late Stage: ALSTAR2
papers.abstract: This cross-sectional study utilized the quick contrast sensitivity function (qCSF) method to evaluate spatial vision across different stages of age-related macular degeneration (AMD) within the ALSTAR2 cohort (n=586 eyes). The researchers quantified the area under the log CSF (AULCSF) and contrast sensitivity at discrete spatial frequencies, adjusting for age and lens status. The findings demonstrate that while AULCSF significantly decreases with age and disease progression, contrast sensitivity remains largely preserved in early and intermediate AMD relative to age-matched healthy controls. In contrast, late-stage AMD eyes exhibited a precipitous and statistically significant decline in qCSF metrics, suggesting that functional contrast loss is primarily characteristic of advanced macular degeneration rather than earlier clinical stages.
papers.authors: Cynthia Owsley, Liyan Gao, Lindsay Gooden, Tracy N. Thomas, Jiaxin Pu, Jason N. Crosson, Christine A. Curcio, Gerald McGwin, MiYoung Kwon

papers.title: Significant Age-Related Visual Declines but Preserved Binocular Summation of Contrast Sensitivity and Visual Acuity Across Adulthood
papers.abstract: To determine the longitudinal trajectory of binocular integration, this study measured monocular and binocular contrast sensitivity (CS) and high-contrast visual acuity (VA) in 292 normally sighted individuals (ages 18-87). Using Pelli-Robson and ETDRS charts, the authors calculated the binocular summation ratio (BSR) and performed model comparisons to elucidate the underlying pooling mechanisms. Despite linear age-related declines in absolute binocular sensitivity—approximately 37% for CS and 59% for VA—the BSR remained robust and stable throughout adulthood. Modeling results indicated that CS summation aligns with a near-quadratic summation rule, while VA summation is better described by a signal-averaging weighted linear model, suggesting that the cortical circuitry for binocular summation is resilient to senescent changes.
papers.authors: Boris Peñaloza, MiYoung Kwon

papers.title: Impact of Rod-Dominant Mesopic Conditions on Spatial Summation and Surround Suppression in Early Visual Cortex
papers.abstract: This investigation explored the reconfiguration of cortical spatial integration under mesopic (dim light) conditions, where both rod and cone photoreceptors contribute to the visual signal. Using psychophysical paradigms to measure contrast thresholds as a function of stimulus size, the researchers derived spatial summation curves to estimate the area of complete summation and the strength of surround inhibition. The results indicated that transitioning from photopic to rod-dominant mesopic conditions significantly expands the cortical spatial summation area and concurrently diminishes surround suppression. This suggests that the human visual system dynamically modulates its spatial pooling and gain control mechanisms to maximize photon capture at the expense of high-frequency spatial resolution in low-luminance environments.
papers.authors: Michaela Klimova, MiYoung Kwon

papers.title: Age-Related Changes in Mesopic Reading Vision Across Adulthood
papers.abstract: This study quantified changes in reading performance under mesopic (2 cd/m²) and photopic (220 cd/m²) luminance across the adult lifespan (n=157, ages 18-84). Parameters including maximum reading speed (MRS), critical print size (CPS), reading accessibility index (ACC), and reading acuity (RA) were measured using the digital MNREAD application. The analysis revealed a monotonic, linear decline in all reading metrics as a function of age under both conditions. Crucially, the deterioration of reading performance was significantly more severe under mesopic lighting, particularly for CPS and RA. These results establish normative age-indexed benchmarks for mesopic reading vision and emphasize the utility of low-luminance assessments for capturing the full extent of functional vision loss in the elderly.
papers.authors: Boris Peñaloza, Traci-Lin Goddin, David S. Friedman, Cynthia Owsley, MiYoung Kwon

papers.title: Impact of Glaucomatous Ganglion Cell Damage on Central Visual Function
papers.abstract: This review synthesizes recent psychophysical and neuroimaging research regarding the impact of glaucomatous retinal ganglion cell (RGC) loss on central visual perception. Challenging the traditional view of glaucoma as solely a peripheral vision disorder, the article highlights the prevalence of macular RGC damage in the early and moderate stages of the disease. It details how this structural neurodegeneration compromises fundamental computations such as contrast coding, spatial summation, and temporal integration in the central visual field. The review further examines how these low-level deficits propagate to disrupt complex functional activities, specifically reading and object recognition, and underscores the need for clinical assessments that characterize both central and peripheral vision to better predict quality-of-life outcomes.
papers.authors: MiYoung Kwon

0483.name: Monica D. Rosenberg
0483.lab_name: Cognition, Attention, and Brain Lab (CAB Lab)
0483.bio: Monica D. Rosenberg is an Associate Professor in the Department of Psychology at the University of Chicago and the Principal Investigator of the Cognition, Attention, and Brain Lab. Rosenberg’s research investigates the neural mechanisms underlying sustained attention and individual differences in cognition using functional MRI and machine learning. They utilize connectome-based predictive modeling (CPM) to identify whole-brain functional connectivity fingerprints that predict attentional states and traits from task-based and resting-state data. This work further examines the temporal dynamics of attention across the lifespan and its functional intersections with learning, memory, and clinical symptoms such as ADHD.
0483.research_direction: Dr. Rosenberg’s recent work explores the neural and cognitive dynamics of sustained attention, subjective mental states, and expectation violation across both controlled experimental tasks and naturalistic environments. Using multimodal behavioral paradigms and fMRI connectome-based predictive modeling, they have recently been investigating how continuous fluctuations in attention relate to long-term memory and whether heightened attentional states act as a selective "spotlight" or a global "floodlight" for processing concurrent sensory inputs. Their research also examines how time-resolved functional brain networks track second-to-second shifts in task engagement and momentary surprise during ecological activities like watching movies or sports. Finally, they are probing the cognitive basis of intrinsic brain organization by mapping how idiosyncratic, spontaneous streams of thought during resting-state fMRI correlate with functional connectivity patterns and predict trait-level behavioral differences.

papers.title: Sustained Attention Is More Closely Related to Long-term Memory Than to Attentional Control
papers.abstract: This study dissociates individual differences in sustained attention (SA) from attentional control/working memory (AC/WM) and long-term memory (LTM) using a multi-method approach. Through latent factor modeling of behavior from an audiovisual continuous performance task (avCPT) and executive function paradigms (Flanker, Simon, and change localization), the authors identified SA as a distinct cognitive factor. While correlated with AC/WM, the SA factor demonstrated more robust predictive associations with LTM performance. Functional MRI analyses using a pretrained connectome-based predictive model (CPM) confirmed this link, as neural signatures of sustained attention successfully predicted individual differences in out-of-scanner LTM retrieval but failed to predict AC/WM capacity. The results suggest that the neural and cognitive architecture of sustained attention is fundamentally more proximal to memory encoding and maintenance than to executive control mechanisms.
papers.authors: Chong Zhao, Anna Corriveau, Jin Ke, Edward K. Vogel, Monica D. Rosenberg

papers.title: Common brain network dynamics capture attention fluctuations in tasks and movies
papers.abstract: This research utilizes time-resolved functional MRI connectivity to investigate whether shared neural dynamics track attentional fluctuations across diverse sensory and cognitive contexts. By applying edge co-fluctuation time series analyses to data from participants performing auditory and visual continuous performance tasks (CPT) and engaging with naturalistic narratives (movies and podcasts), the authors identified consistent network-level deflections associated with both objective lapses in task performance and subjective shifts in engagement. The findings reveal a modality-general and context-independent functional network that captures second-to-second variability in sustained attentional states, demonstrating the generalizability of time-resolved connectomic models from controlled experimental settings to ecological viewing conditions.
papers.authors: Anna Corriveau, Jin Ke, Monica D. Rosenberg

papers.title: Ongoing thoughts at rest reflect functional brain organization and behavior
papers.abstract: The study probes the cognitive basis of resting-state functional connectivity (rsFC) by linking in-scanner subjective experiences with brain dynamics. Using an 'annotated rest' fMRI paradigm where participants verbally described and rated their thoughts after multiple rest intervals, the researchers found that within- and between-individual similarity in self-reported thought content significantly correlated with rsFC topography similarity.
