Furthermore, decoding models trained on these thought-based neural signatures generalized to a large independent cohort (N=908) from the Human Connectome Project, where the decoded rest-state mental patterns predicted trait-level individual differences in cognition and emotional health. These data indicate that 'intrinsic' functional brain organization is heavily influenced by ongoing, idiosyncratic mental streams, providing a mechanistic link between rest-state brain dynamics and behavioral traits.
papers.authors: Jin Ke, Taylor A. Chamberlain, Hayoung Song, Anna Corriveau, Ziwei Zhang, Taysha Martinez, Laura Sams, Marvin M. Chun, Yuan Chang Leong, Monica D. Rosenberg

papers.title: Sustained attentional state is a floodlight not a spotlight
papers.abstract: The authors evaluate competing models of attentional fluctuations—the 'selective spotlight' vs. the 'global floodlight'—by examining memory encoding for task-relevant and task-irrelevant information. In an online multimodal experiment involving simultaneous visual and auditory streams, participants responded to stimuli in a single target modality before undergoing a surprise recognition test for both modalities. Analysis revealed that successful memory for task-relevant items positively predicted memory for their task-irrelevant pairs within individuals, and no resource trade-off was observed across participants. These findings reject the hypothesis that increased sustained attention narrows focus via selective filtering; instead, they support a 'floodlight' model where heightened attentional states globally enhance information processing across all concurrent inputs regardless of task relevance.
papers.authors: Anna Corriveau, Anthony R. James, Megan T. deBettencourt, Monica D. Rosenberg

papers.title: Brain network dynamics predict moments of surprise across contexts
papers.abstract: This study identifies a common neural substrate for surprise—the psychological state triggered by expectation violation—across controlled and naturalistic settings. The authors developed a surprise edge-fluctuation-based predictive model (EFPM) using fMRI regional interaction dynamics from an adaptive learning task. The EFPM successfully generalized to predict momentary surprise in individuals watching suspenseful basketball games and in a third cohort viewing videos that violated psychological expectations. The model demonstrated superior generalizability compared to sliding-window functional connectivity, BOLD activation, and traditional behavioral metrics. These results suggest that belief-inconsistent surprise across distinct cognitive domains is mediated by shared, high-frequency functional network dynamics that can be translated into a unified neural space.
papers.authors: Ziwei Zhang, Monica D. Rosenberg

0484.name: Moreno I. Coco
0484.bio: Moreno I. Coco is an Associate Professor at Sapienza University of Rome and a research affiliate at I.R.C.C.S. Fondazione Santa Lucia. Coco's research integrates cognitive neuroscience with computational modeling to investigate the mechanisms of vision, language, and memory across the human lifespan. Utilizing eye-tracking and co-registered electro-physiology (fixation-related potentials), they explore how semantic knowledge and contextual information guide visual attention and information encoding. Their recent work focuses on the development of diagnostic tools by identifying early cognitive markers of neurodegeneration in prodromal stages of dementia.
0484.research_direction: Dr. Coco's recent work explores how high-level semantic context and perceptual features interact to shape visual attention, memory, and joint action. They have recently been investigating object-scene integration within naturalistic environments, utilizing normative database development and eye-tracking paradigms to determine how semantic consistency influences visual working memory binding in both healthy aging and mild cognitive impairment. In parallel, their research examines long-term visual memory fidelity, using deep neural network modeling to test how within-category conceptual interference and scene richness impact exemplar-level mnemonic discrimination. Expanding beyond individual cognition, they are also studying multimodal interpersonal coordination by co-registering eye movements and speech to map how collaborative task goals, such as joint visual search, drive gaze alignment in interacting dyads.

papers.title: Task goals constrain the alignment in eye-movements and speech during interpersonal coordination
papers.abstract: This study examines the modulation of interpersonal behavioral coordination by specific collaborative task goals, comparing route planning and visual search within dyads. By co-registering eye movements and speech while participants engaged with complex subway maps, the researchers utilized Cross Recurrence Quantification Analysis (CRQA) to quantify temporal couplings across modalities. Findings indicate that task-specific constraints significantly influence gaze alignment dynamics; route planning elicits higher baseline alignment, whereas successful visual search is characterized by an increase in gaze coordination toward the trial's end. The results suggest that the motor-cognitive systems governing vision and language organize complementarily to optimize joint performance under differing goal-directed pressures.
papers.authors: Alexia Galati, Rick Dale, Camila Alviar, Moreno I. Coco

papers.title: The Visual Integration of Semantic and Spatial Information of Objects in Naturalistic Scenes (VISIONS) database: attentional, conceptual, and perceptual norms
papers.abstract: The authors introduce VISIONS, a comprehensive image database comprising 1,136 naturalistic scenes accompanied by extensive normative data regarding their attentional, conceptual, and perceptual properties. Norms were collected from 185 participants across three levels of granularity: isolated critical objects, whole scenes, and objects embedded within scenes. The dataset provides metrics for semantic consistency, spatial plausibility, visual complexity, and name agreement, modeled to distinguish between low-level perceptual features and high-level knowledge-based contextual factors. This resource is designed to support ecologically valid investigations into the mechanisms of object-scene integration, visual search, and long-term memory.
papers.authors: Elena Allegretti, Giorgia D'Innocenzo, Moreno I. Coco

papers.title: Visual short-term memory binding and attentional processes during object-scene integration are preserved in mild cognitive impairment
papers.abstract: This research investigates the integrity of visual working memory (VWM) binding and its relationship with overt attention in younger adults, healthy older adults, and individuals with mild cognitive impairment (MCI). Utilizing an eye-tracking change detection paradigm with naturalistic scenes, the study manipulated object saliency and semantic consistency during encoding. Results demonstrated that semantically inconsistent objects consistently captured attentional prioritization across all groups. Crucially, despite overall performance differences, the fundamental mechanisms of VWM binding and object-scene integration remained preserved in individuals with MCI, suggesting that predictive semantic processes and attentional control are relatively resilient in the prodromal stages of neurodegeneration.
papers.authors: Elena Allegretti, Marika Mauti, Moreno I. Coco

papers.title: The upside of cumulative conceptual interference on exemplar-level mnemonic discrimination
papers.abstract: This study explores how within-category conceptual and perceptual interference affects the fidelity of episodic traces in long-term visual memory (LTVM). Through a series of experiments manipulating indices of cumulative conceptual interference—incorporating both categorical capacity and exemplar similarity—the authors evaluate the precision of object representations using a mnemonic discrimination task. Contrary to traditional views that interference uniformly degrades memory, the findings reveal that high cumulative interference at encoding can facilitate better discrimination between targets and similar lures. This suggests that the cognitive demands imposed by interference during learning may induce more distinctive representational patterns, enhancing pattern separation at the exemplar level.
papers.authors: Emma Delhaye, Giorgia D'Innocenzo, Ana Raposo, Moreno I. Coco

papers.title: Differential effects of intrinsic properties of natural scenes and interference mechanisms on recognition processes in long-term visual memory
papers.abstract: The authors examine the impact of intrinsic scene properties—specifically semantic and perceptual richness quantified via deep neural network (DNN) modeling—on recognition accuracy and metacognitive efficacy in long-term visual memory. The research analyzes the interference generated by categorical similarity during encoding and retrieval. Empirical results demonstrate that while perceptual information provides a memorability boost, semantic richness and category interference exert a dominant negative influence on recognition performance and response latencies. The study provides evidence for an integrative understanding of representational dynamics, where high-level semantic interference often overrides the benefits of low-level perceptual clarity in memory maintenance and access.
papers.authors: Anastasiia Mikhailova, Sophie Lightfoot, José Santos-Victor, Moreno I. Coco

0485.name: Moritz Wurm
0485.department: Department of Psychology and Cognitive Science
0485.bio: Moritz Wurm is a cognitive neuroscientist at CIMeC, University of Trento, where they investigate the neural basis of action recognition and understanding. Using fMRI and MEG combined with multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA), Wurm examines how the brain decodes actions across different levels of abstraction, from physical kinematics to conceptual meanings. Their work has identified roles for the lateral occipitotemporal and parietal cortices in representing the "physics of actions" and integrating action-object knowledge. Currently, Wurm focuses on characterizing the predictive mechanisms the brain uses to process dynamic visual events and social interactions.
0485.research_direction: Dr. Wurm's recent work explores the neural computations underlying how we perceive, predict, and understand the goal-directed actions of others. To investigate how the visual system anticipates continuous biological motion, they have recently been using magnetoencephalography (MEG) and dynamic representational similarity analysis to track the temporal hierarchy of predictive coding, testing how holistic postural priors and low-level kinematics guide our sensory forecasts. Additionally, their fMRI research utilizes cross-decoding paradigms to disentangle how distinct cortical networks encode the abstract physical mechanics of observed actions—such as how objects are separated or compressed—independent of the actor's raw bodily movements. Finally, they are investigating how these perceptual and mechanical representations bridge into semantic and higher-order mentalizing networks to allow observers to infer complex, hidden intentions from naturalistic behavior.

papers.title: Decoding the neural stages from action and object recognition to mentalizing
papers.abstract: Higher-level interpretation of observed behavior requires the binding of action concepts with semantic knowledge of persons and objects to infer mental states. Utilizing fMRI and crossmodal multiple regression representational similarity analysis (RSA) across video actions and written sentences, this study delineated the representational transitions between recognition systems and mentalizing networks. Inferring intentions engaged a modality-invariant, distributed set of lateral and medial frontoparietal and temporal cortices. Rather than exhibiting a strictly serial, feedforward architecture from action and object recognition streams into the mentalizing system, representational similarity structures showed substantial convergence. In particular, a left-lateralized core substrate comprising ventrolateral prefrontal cortex, inferior parietal cortex, and anterior lateral occipitotemporal cortex (LOTC) demonstrated joint representational sensitivity to conceptual action features, object identities, and inferred intention states, serving as a semantic bridging hub between perceptual-semantic pathways and higher-order mentalizing circuits.
papers.authors: Moritz F. Wurm, Seoyoung Lee

papers.title: Hierarchical priors enable neural prediction of perceived biological motion
papers.abstract: Visual perception of biological motion is hypothesized to rely on predictive mechanisms guided by internal generative models. Combining source-reconstructed magnetoencephalography (MEG) with dynamic representational similarity analysis (dRSA), this study quantified how distinct priors govern predictive representational geometry during biological motion perception. Under veridical viewing, cortical representations exhibited an inverted temporal predictive hierarchy, wherein high-level, viewpoint-invariant bodily kinematics were decoded prior to viewpoint-dependent postures and lower-level retinotopic motion. Disruption of holistic configurational priors via stimulus inversion selectively impaired high-level predictive encoding while sparing low-level dynamics. In contrast, disrupting kinematic transition dynamics via piecewise temporal scrambling completely suppressed predictive states, constraining cortical activity to a lagged, stimulus-driven processing regime. These findings establish that predictive encoding of naturalistic human motion relies on a tiered system of configurational and kinematic priors.
papers.authors: Ingmar E. J. de Vries, Floris P. de Lange, Moritz F. Wurm

papers.title: Decoding the physics of observed actions in the human brain
papers.abstract: Understanding goal-directed actions requires visual analysis of bodily movement kinematics together with mechanical inferences regarding the physical transformations imposed on target objects. In four fMRI sessions, participants viewed natural action videos, point-light displays (PLDs), pantomimed actions, and abstract geometric animations portraying physical state transformations. Cross-classification between real actions and abstract animations demonstrated that the anterior inferior parietal lobule (aIPL), predominantly in the right hemisphere, represents abstract action effect structures (e.g., separating or compressing) invariant to entity morphology and movement kinematics. Conversely, cross-decoding between natural actions and PLDs revealed that the superior parietal lobule (SPL) selectively processes bodily movement patterns devoid of visible object state changes. Lateral occipitotemporal cortex (LOTC) encoded both kinematic features and object transformation effects, demonstrating that parietal and temporal structures implement complementary mechanical representations during action observation.
papers.authors: Moritz F. Wurm, Doruk Yiğit Erigüç

papers.title: Action prediction relies on high-level holistic and low-level kinematics priors
papers.abstract: The human brain continuously generates predictions about future states to facilitate social coordination and interaction. This study utilized a novel dynamic representational similarity analysis (dRSA) framework applied to source-reconstructed magnetoencephalography (MEG) data from participants observing naturalistic biological motion (dance sequences). Under normal conditions, neural predictions followed a hierarchical organization where view-invariant body posture was predicted at the earliest latencies, while view-dependent kinematics and pixel-level motion were represented closer to real-time. Experimental disruption of high-level holistic priors through stimulus inversion selectively attenuated high-level predictions and shifted the representational latency of viewpoint-invariant features. Conversely, disrupting low-level kinematics via temporal piecewise scrambling eliminated motion prediction across all levels and significantly increased post-stimulus neural responses, consistent with the generation of large prediction errors. These findings provide evidence that biological motion perception is supported by an integrated hierarchy of long-term holistic expectations and short-term kinematic regularities.
papers.authors: Ingmar E. J. de Vries, Floris P. de Lange, Moritz F. Wurm

papers.title: Predictive neural representations of naturalistic dynamic input
papers.abstract: Adaptive interaction in dynamic settings demands continuous forecasting of incoming sensory input, yet neuroimaging paradigms have predominantly evaluated predictive processing using static or discrete event structures. Here, dynamic representational similarity analysis (dRSA) was developed to track the temporal emergence of feature representations from continuous input using time-varying multivariate models. Applied to source-space magnetoencephalography (MEG) during the observation of continuous dance movements, dRSA isolated both lagged sensory representations and forward-looking, predictive neural codes. Predictive neural representations revealed a hierarchical temporal architecture: abstract, high-level stimulus features were predicted across wider, earlier anticipatory temporal windows, whereas low-level visual kinematics were anticipated immediately prior to actual sensory arrival, demonstrating how the human brain dynamically forecasts continuous hierarchical input.
papers.authors: Ingmar E. J. de Vries, Moritz F. Wurm

0490.name: Máté Lengyel
0490.department: Department of Engineering (Cambridge); Department of Cognitive Science (CEU)
0490.bio: Máté Lengyel is a Professor of Computational Neuroscience who researches the mathematical and biological principles underlying learning and memory. Lengyel's work utilizes Bayesian approaches to statistical inference and reinforcement learning to characterize how the brain represents uncertainty and adapts to its environment. By combining normative theories with dynamical systems analysis of neural circuits, Lengyel connects behavioral goals with cellular and network mechanisms. They collaborate with experimentalists to validate these models using multi-unit recordings, human psychophysics, and functional neuroimaging.
0490.research_direction: Dr. Lengyel has recently been investigating the computational principles and circuit-level mechanisms that optimize neural representations across diverse cognitive domains. Their recent work explores how recurrent circuit architectures support robust sensory inference and working memory, investigating phenomena like stimulus-driven variability quenching in the visual cortex and the use of dynamic spatiotemporal coding trajectories rather than stable attractors for maintaining information. Additionally, they are examining how biological constraints, specifically neural noise and metabolic costs, shape the geometric structure of task representations in the prefrontal cortex to efficiently suppress irrelevant stimuli. To further analyze complex neural dynamics, Dr. Lengyel is also developing advanced machine learning frameworks—such as infinite Gaussian Process Factor Analysis and hierarchical successor representations—to discover time-varying neural manifolds in hippocampal populations and to model policy-independent spatial mapping during complex navigation.

papers.title: Hierarchical Successor Representation for Robust Transfer
papers.abstract: The successor representation (SR) provides a mechanism for decoupling environmental dynamics from reward structures, yet its utility is often hampered by policy dependence and poor scaling in complex topologies due to spectral diffusion. This study introduces the Hierarchical Successor Representation (HSR) to mitigate these issues by incorporating temporal abstractions into predictive features. By applying non-negative matrix factorization (NMF) to the HSR, the authors derive a sparse, low-rank state representation that encodes robust topological structures. This hierarchical approach enables policy-agnostic maps that facilitate highly sample-efficient transfer across multi-compartmental environments and improve exploration efficiency in large-scale, procedurally generated spaces.
papers.authors: Changmin Yu, Máté Lengyel

papers.title: Effects of noise and metabolic cost on cortical task representations
papers.abstract: This work characterizes how neural circuits optimize the representation of task-relevant stimuli while suppressing task-irrelevant information under biological constraints. Using task-optimized recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and mathematical analysis, the authors demonstrate that the emergence of specific representational geometries is governed by the interplay of neural noise and firing rate regularization (metabolic cost). High noise and metabolic constraints drive the circuit toward a minimal representational strategy. Comparing these computational findings with primate lateral prefrontal cortex (PFC) recordings reveals that neural activity during learning shifts toward this minimal geometry, utilizing activity-silent, sub-threshold dynamics to effectively ignore irrelevant inputs.
papers.authors: Jake P. Stroud, Michal Wojcik, Kristopher T. Jensen, Makoto Kusunoki, Mikiko Kadohisa, Mark J. Buckley, John Duncan, Mark G. Stokes, Máté Lengyel

papers.title: Discovering Temporally Compositional Neural Manifolds with Switching Infinite GPFA
papers.abstract: To overcome the limitations of standard Gaussian Process Factor Analysis (GPFA)—namely, fixed latent dimensionality and static factor contributions—this paper proposes 'infinite GPFA.' This Bayesian non-parametric extension utilizes an Indian Buffet Process (IBP) prior over the factor loading process to infer a potentially infinite set of latent factors and their time-varying activation identities. The model allows for the discovery of temporally compositional neural manifolds where distinct subsets of factors are expressed at different epochs. Through variational expectation-maximization and sparse Gaussian Process methods, the authors demonstrate the model's ability to identify task-contingent switching dynamics in hippocampal population activity during complex spatial navigation tasks.
papers.authors: Changmin Yu, Maneesh Sahani, Máté Lengyel

papers.title: The computational foundations of dynamic coding in working memory
papers.abstract: Classical models of working memory (WM) emphasize stable attractor-based maintenance, yet neural recordings often exhibit complex spatiotemporal dynamics. This review synthesizes theoretical evidence that dynamic coding is a principled computational feature rather than a byproduct of biological noise. By analyzing task-optimized neural networks, the authors show that dynamic trajectories are necessary for efficient information loading, robustness against interference, and high-dimensional readout. The study argues that dynamic coding represents an optimized solution for maintaining and manipulating information under realistic task demands and resource limitations, suggesting a significant revision to the canonical understanding of WM maintenance.
papers.authors: Jake P. Stroud, John Duncan, Máté Lengyel

papers.title: Response sub-additivity and variability quenching in visual cortex
papers.abstract: Stimulus-driven activity in the visual cortex is characterized by a universal reduction in neural variability (quenching) and sub-additive integration of multiple inputs. This review provides a unified framework for these phenomena by examining recurrent circuit dynamics. It highlights how Stabilized Supralinear Networks (SSNs)—circuits with power-law activation functions and excitatory-inhibitory balance—naturally account for the stimulus-dependent quenching of correlated noise and the gain-control mechanisms underlying sub-additivity. The authors discuss how these circuit-level properties support the brain's internal model of environmental statistics, facilitating robust and efficient sensory inference.
papers.authors: Robbe L. T. Goris, Ruben Coen-Cagli, Kenneth D. Miller, Nicholas J. Priebe, Máté Lengyel

0491.name: N. Apurva Ratan Murty
0491.bio: N Apurva Ratan Murty is an Assistant Professor of Cognition and Brain Science at the Georgia Institute of Technology and directs the Murty Lab. Murty’s research focuses on the intersection of biological vision and artificial intelligence to map the neural algorithms and codes associated with visual intelligence. By combining high-field functional MRI (3T/7T) and human electrophysiology with deep neural networks and generative AI, Murty develops models such as TopoNets to characterize the functional organization of the brain. Their work investigates category-selective brain regions and the neurobiological foundations of perceptual disorders, including agnosia and prosopagnosia.
0491.research_direction: Dr. Murty has recently been exploring the alignment between artificial neural networks and the human brain by developing biologically constrained models and rigorously probing their internal representational geometry. Their recent work investigates how imposing spatial wiring-length constraints during network training might serve as a domain-general principle for inducing brain-like topographic maps, examining whether such models naturally develop clustered selectivity for visual features, speech, and music. To evaluate the biological fidelity of these computational encoding models, they use targeted adversarial stimulus perturbations to probe whether artificial networks exhibit the same robust, localized coding axes measured in human fMRI responses. In parallel with this computational work, Dr. Murty is also mapping the functional neuroanatomy of high-level vision, specifically investigating how regions like the temporal pole might serve to bridge perceptual face recognition networks with higher-order social cognition.

papers.title: TopoNets: High Performing Vision and Language Models with Brain-Like Topography
papers.abstract: Cortical neurons in the mammalian brain exhibit topographic organization, where units with similar functional tuning are spatially clustered. Standard artificial neural networks (ANNs) typically lack this organization, and previous attempts to enforce topography have often resulted in significant task performance degradation. This work introduces TopoLoss, a novel training objective that facilitates the emergence of spatially organized functional representations without substantial loss in predictive accuracy. TopoNets, trained using this framework, demonstrate brain-like characteristics such as localized feature processing, reduced representational dimensionality, and increased parameter efficiency. Furthermore, these models show superior alignment with neural activity in the visual and language cortices compared to non-topographic baselines.
papers.authors: Mayukh Deb, Mainak Deb, N. Apurva Ratan Murty

papers.title: Targeted perturbations reveal brain-like local coding axes in robustified, but not standard, ANN-based encoding models
papers.abstract: While artificial neural network (ANN) encoding models have become the standard for predicting human fMRI responses, their reliability under targeted stimulus manipulations has not been extensively tested. We demonstrate that contemporary encoding models are unexpectedly fragile, exhibiting high sensitivity to small, imperceptible stimulus perturbations that reveal unreliable local coding directions. We show that a model's sensitivity to adversarial probes is a more effective discriminator for biological alignment than standard prediction accuracy. Critically, we find that robustified models—trained with adversarial robustification techniques—develop stable, brain-like local coding axes and spatially localized feature sensitivity that better capture the functional organization of the primate visual system.
papers.authors: Nikolas McNeal, N. Apurva Ratan Murty

papers.title: End-to-end Topographic Auditory Models Replicate Signatures of Human Auditory Cortex
papers.abstract: The human auditory cortex is topographically organized, featuring smooth tonotopic maps for frequency and modular regions specialized for speech and music. However, standard auditory neural networks do not inherently replicate this spatial structure. We present TopoAudio, a suite of end-to-end topographic auditory models trained using a cortical wiring-length constraint. These models maintain competitive task performance and fMRI predictivity while reproducing hallmark biological features, including smooth tonotopic and amplitude-modulation maps in early layers and spatially clustered selectivity for music and speech in higher-order layers. Our results suggest that spatial smoothness constraints represent a domain-general organizing principle for achieving biologically grounded representations in artificial systems.
papers.authors: Haider Al-Tahan, Mayukh Deb, Jenelle Feather, N. Apurva Ratan Murty

papers.title: Linking faces to social cognition: The temporal pole as a potential social switch
papers.abstract: This work explores the neural architecture of the human face-processing network and its integration with social cognition. Based on recent fMRI findings, we distinguish between the roles of the perirhinal cortex (PR) and the temporal pole (TP). While the PR is involved in face-specific perceptual identification, the TP serves as a critical person-identity node that links facial representations to social semantic knowledge and Theory of Mind networks. We argue that the TP acts as a functional 'social switch,' facilitating the transition from visual face recognition to complex social inference. This framework suggests that the TP is a key evolutionary adaptation for managing the high-dimensional social information processed by the primate brain.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS)
papers.authors: Alish Dipani, Nikolas McNeal, N. Apurva Ratan Murty

papers.title: Small-scale adversarial perturbations can expose differences between predictive encoding models of human fMRI responses
papers.abstract: ANN-based encoding models of the human visual system often achieve similar levels of voxel-wise predictive accuracy, making it difficult to distinguish between competing models using standard metrics. We propose adversarial sensitivity as a novel probe to characterize the local representational geometry and biological alignment of these models. By applying small-magnitude stimulus perturbations, we reveal significant vulnerabilities in contemporary encoding frameworks and demonstrate that robustness to adversarial probes is more effective than prediction score at identifying brain-like representations. Our results show that incorporating robustness constraints into encoding models yields internal features that more closely align with the localized coding strategies observed in the human visual cortex.
papers.venue: Proceedings of UniReps: Workshop on Unifying Representations in Neural Models (PMLR)
papers.authors: Nikolas McNeal, Mainak Deb, Apurva Ratan Murty

0492.name: Nancy B. Carlisle
0492.bio: Nancy B. Carlisle is an Associate Professor at Lehigh University and the director of the Carlisle Attention and Memory (CAM) Lab. Carlisle’s research investigates the neurocognitive mechanisms of top-down attentional control, specifically focusing on how working memory representations guide visual selection. A central component of their work involves the study of negative templates to examine the cognitive and electrophysiological processes that allow for the proactive suppression of distractors. Carlisle utilizes behavioral psychophysics, eye-tracking, computational modeling, and event-related potentials (ERPs) to characterize the flexibility of the human attentional system.
0492.research_direction: Dr. Carlisle’s recent work explores the mechanisms of proactive attentional suppression, focusing on how individuals utilize working memory representations to avoid distractors during visual search. They have recently been investigating negative attentional templates to determine whether their underlying visual working memory precision differs from positive target cues, and how the efficacy of these templates is influenced by state-based motivations like financial reward versus trait-level cognitive control efficiency. In addition to top-down cueing, their research examines the role of environmental regularities, comparing how explicit, memory-guided suppression relates to implicit learned suppression driven by selection history and individual distractibility. Furthermore, they are testing the broader interplay between top-down and bottom-up attention by exploring how explicit task goals might dynamically unlock implicit spatial statistical learning.

papers.title: Within-subject manipulations of proactive control do not change negative templates benefits: Exploring the effect of reward on negative and positive cues
papers.abstract: This investigation explored the influence of state-based proactive control, modulated through financial incentives, on the utilization of negative attentional templates during visual search. While trait-level proactive control capacity has been linked to the magnitude of negative cue benefits, the role of situational motivation remains unresolved. Participants completed a visual search task incorporating positive, negative, and neutral cues across high- and low-reward conditions. While search performance for positive templates significantly improved under high-reward conditions, no corresponding modulation was observed for negative templates. These findings suggest that the suppressive mechanisms engaged by negative templates are relatively resistant to within-subject state-based fluctuations in engagement and instead depend more fundamentally on trait-level proactive control efficiency.
papers.authors: Matthieu Chidharom, Matt Tong, Nancy B. Carlisle

papers.title: Why Are Some Individuals Better at Using Negative Attentional Templates to Suppress Distractors? Exploration of Interindividual Differences in Cognitive Control Efficiency
papers.abstract: This study examines the interindividual variability in the efficacy of negative attentional templates—working memory representations used to proactively suppress distractors. Utilizing a large-scale reanalysis of existing behavioral and eye-tracking datasets (N = 139), the authors tested whether proactive control efficiency, operationalized as reaction time (RT) variability (SD-RT), predicts the magnitude of search benefits following negative cues. The results demonstrated that individuals with higher proactive control (lower SD-RT) exhibited significantly larger RT benefits and made fewer first saccades to cued distractor items. These findings indicate that the ability to successfully implement a template for rejection is constrained by an individual's trait-level proactive control efficiency, accounting for the large variance in negative template use reported across the literature.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
papers.authors: Matthieu Chidharom, Nancy B. Carlisle

papers.title: Similar Quality of Visual Working Memory Representations between Negative and Positive Attentional Templates
papers.abstract: Central theories of attentional control posit that search templates are maintained in visual working memory (VWM). This study investigated whether the well-documented performance costs associated with negative templates (distractor cues) compared to positive templates (target cues) originate from differences in the precision of their underlying VWM representations. Across multiple experiments employing mixture modeling and recall-error standard deviation as metrics of representational quality, the results revealed no significant difference in VWM precision between negative and positive cues. These findings suggest that the relative inefficiency of suppression compared to selection is not a consequence of degraded representational quality in memory but likely reflects distinct downstream control processes involved in the guidance of attention during the search phase.
papers.authors: Matthieu Chidharom, Mahsa Zafarmand, Nancy B. Carlisle

papers.title: Distinct mechanisms of attentional suppression: exploration of trait factors underlying cued- and learned-suppression
papers.abstract: Proactive attentional suppression can be activated either through explicit top-down cues (cued-suppression) or through the implicit learning of environmental regularities (learned-suppression). This study utilized a within-subjects design to evaluate the relationship between these two mechanisms of suppression. Correlation analyses revealed no significant relationship between performance benefits derived from cued- and learned-suppression tasks. Furthermore, individual differences in cued-suppression magnitude were significantly associated with VWM capacity, whereas learned-suppression magnitude was linked to self-reported trait-level distractibility. These results provide evidence for the existence of heterogeneous proactive control mechanisms, where cued-suppression relies on explicit, memory-guided control and learned-suppression is driven by implicit mechanisms sensitive to selection history and distractibility traits.
papers.authors: Matthieu Chidharom, Nancy B. Carlisle

papers.title: Explicit attentional goals unlock implicit spatial statistical learning
papers.abstract: Spatial statistical learning typically facilitates attentional orienting toward high-probability target locations; however, such biases may conflict with the need for flexible, goal-directed selection. This study examined a goal-specific probability cueing mechanism to determine if implicitly learned spatial priority maps can be activated selectively based on the current target category. Across five experiments, participants learned distinct spatial distributions for different target categories and were tested on their ability to utilize these maps when cued with a specific category template. Participants demonstrated significant RT benefits when targets appeared at category-specific high-probability locations. These findings demonstrate that spatial priorities derived from statistical regularities can be dynamically unlocked by explicit attentional goals, revealing a sophisticated level of flexibility in how selection history and current goals interact.
papers.authors: Ziyao Zhang, Nancy B. Carlisle

0493.name: Nancy Kanwisher
0493.department: Department of Brain and Cognitive Sciences
0493.bio: Nancy Kanwisher is the Walter A. Rosenblith Professor of Cognitive Neuroscience at MIT and maps the functional architecture of the human brain using fMRI. Kanwisher identified and characterized specialized cortical regions, such as the Fusiform Face Area (FFA) for face processing and the Parahippocampal Place Area (PPA) for scene recognition. Their current research integrates intracranial recordings and deep neural networks to investigate the computational principles and developmental origins of these regions. This work examines the organization of the human mind into distinct, domain-specific processors for high-level perception and cognition.
0493.research_direction: Kanwisher is currently refining a modular-interactionist framework of human cognition, utilizing precision fMRI and the novel Efficient Multifunction fMRI Localizer (EMFL) to map the functional topography of domain-specific cortical regions. Her research investigates the neurocomputational "physics engine" within the frontoparietal network, employing multivariate fMRI decoding to demonstrate how the brain distinguishes physical ontologies—specifically "things" versus "stuff"—and runs forward simulations to predict future states like object collisions. Simultaneously, she explores the functional encapsulation of the core language system, arguing that deep narrative comprehension emerges from the systematic exportation of linguistic data to external systems for mental model construction. This work increasingly emphasizes human-specific methodologies, such as high-resolution intracranial recordings and deep neural networks, to bypass the limitations of comparative animal models in studying uniquely human faculties.

papers.title: What does it mean to understand language?
papers.abstract: This work advances a theoretical framework positing that the human core language system is functionally encapsulated and insufficient for deep narrative comprehension. The authors argue that language understanding requires the systematic exportation of information from the core left-hemisphere temporal and frontal regions to other domain-specific cortical systems. These external systems are recruited to compute situation-specific mental models, generate perceptual and motor simulations, and integrate linguistic input with long-term world knowledge and autobiographical memory. The paper synthesizes existing fMRI evidence to support this modular-interactionist architecture and proposes future experimental strategies to identify the neurocomputational pathways through which the language system interfaces with the broader cognitive landscape.
papers.authors: Colton Casto, Anna Ivanova, Evelina Fedorenko, Nancy Kanwisher

papers.title: An efficient multifunction fMRI localizer for high-level visual, auditory, and cognitive regions in humans
papers.abstract: The study introduces and validates the Efficient Multifunction fMRI Localizer (EMFL), a novel 14-minute paradigm designed to identify 14 major functional regions of interest (fROIs) in a single session. By presenting visual and auditory stimuli simultaneously, the EMFL efficiently localizes specialized regions including the fusiform face area (FFA), parahippocampal place area (PPA), extrastriate body area (EBA), visual word form area (VWFA), and lateral occipital complex (LOC), alongside the language network, theory of mind (ToM) regions, and the domain-general multiple demand (MD) system. Precision fMRI validation demonstrates that the EMFL reliably captures individual-specific functional topographies and response profiles comparable to those derived from standard unimodal localizers, significantly reducing required scan time for comprehensive functional mapping.
papers.authors: Ammar I. Marvi, Sam Hutchinson, Evelina Fedorenko, Rebecca R. Saxe, Frederik S. Kamps, Tamar I. Regev, Emily M. Chen, Nancy G. Kanwisher

papers.title: Dissociable cortical regions represent things and stuff in the human brain
papers.abstract: Investigating the neural basis of material perception, this study distinguishes the processing of 'things' (discrete, rigid, or non-rigid objects) from 'stuff' (continuous liquid or granular substances). Using fMRI and a series of dynamic video stimuli, the researchers identified robust double dissociations in both the ventral and dorsal visual pathways. Specifically, specialized sub-compartments within the lateral occipital complex (LOC) and the frontoparietal physics network (FPN) exhibited preferential selectivity for either object shape or substance fluidity and physical dynamics. The findings suggest that the human brain utilizes distinct mental algorithms and representational formats for different physical ontologies, analogous to the mesh-based and particle-based computations employed in artificial physics engines.
papers.authors: Vivian C. Paulun, Raghavendra Rao T. Pramod, Joshua B. Tenenbaum, Nancy Kanwisher

papers.title: Decoding predicted future states from the brain's “physics engine”
papers.abstract: This study evaluates the 'physics engine' hypothesis, which posits that a network of frontal and parietal brain regions (PN) runs forward simulations to predict physical events. Using multivariate fMRI decoding, the authors demonstrate that the PN abstractly represents object contact relationships, such as containment, support, and attachment, in a manner that generalizes across diverse visual scenarios. Crucially, the PN—but not primary visual or ventral temporal areas—exhibits anticipatory representational states that decode upcoming future contact events (collisions) before they occur. These findings provide empirical evidence that the PN implements a generative model of the physical world capable of predictive simulation to support intuitive physical reasoning and intervention planning.
papers.authors: R. T. Pramod, Elizabeth Mieczkowski, Cyn X. Fang, Joshua B. Tenenbaum, Nancy Kanwisher

papers.title: Animal models of the human brain: Successes, limitations, and alternatives
papers.abstract: This review assesses the role of comparative neuroscience in identifying the modular architecture of the human mind. The author highlights the significant contributions of animal models, such as the macaque face-patch system, in elucidating the mechanisms of specialized cortical regions. However, it underscores the fundamental limitations of non-human models for uniquely human cognitive functions, including syntax-based language processing, high-level theory of mind, and music perception. The paper advocates for a methodological shift towards human-specific approaches, emphasizing high-resolution intracranial recordings (ECoG) and the application of deep neural networks as computationally explicit alternatives for modeling specialized human-specific neural systems.
papers.authors: Nancy Kanwisher

0494.name: Naseem Al-Aidroos
0494.bio: Al-Aidroos investigates the cognitive and neural mechanisms that enable the brain to prioritize goal-relevant information within complex visual environments. Their research integrates behavioral measures, such as eye tracking and limb tracking, with neurophysiological techniques including EEG/ERP, pupillometry, and fMRI to study the optimization and failure of attentional control. Al-Aidroos examines how attention regulates functional communication between high-level and low-level regions of the visual cortex and the role of visual working memory in supporting these processes.
0494.research_direction: Dr. Al-Aidroos has recently been investigating how goal-directed attentional control settings influence both the initial capture of visual attention and its subsequent resolution. Their recent work explores the interplay between visual working memory and long-term memory in maintaining these attentional templates, specifically examining whether episodic long-term memory representations can directly guide spatial selection without active working memory mediation. By combining dual-task behavioral paradigms with electrophysiological markers like the N2pc component, they are probing the temporal dynamics of how rapidly memory-based templates can bias involuntary orienting during visual search. Furthermore, they are utilizing spatial cueing paradigms to map the spatial profile of attention immediately following capture, aiming to understand how the top-down relevance of a distractor dictates the spatial precision of attention at a newly selected locus.

papers.title: Attentional control settings determine not only what captures attention, but where attention goes once captured
papers.abstract: While goal-directed attentional control settings (ACSs) are known to modulate the initial capture of spatial attention by task-congruent stimuli, the impact of these settings on the subsequent resolution of attention remains under-investigated. This research examined whether the top-down relevance of a distractor influences the spatial allocation of attention following its capture. Utilizing a spatial cueing paradigm with specific distractor-target pairings, the study mapped the spatial profile of attention post-orienting. The experimental data indicate that ACS-matching cues not only facilitate more robust capture but also delineate a distinct spatial window of attention relative to non-matching cues. These findings suggest that attentional templates exert a continuous influence on the priority map, affecting both the triggering of selection and the subsequent spatial precision of attentional resolution at the selected locus.
papers.authors: Samantha Joubran, Anna Katzatchkova, Fatima Abboud, Naseem Al-Aidroos

papers.title: Control over attentional capture within 170 ms by long-term memory control settings: Evidence from the N2pc
papers.abstract: Observers configure goal-directed attentional control settings (ACSs) to prioritize the selection of task-relevant information. While ACS maintenance within visual working memory (VWM) is well-documented, the latency at which episodic long-term memory (LTM) representations can modulate spatial attention is less clear. This study employed the N2pc component—an electrophysiological marker of lateralized spatial selection—to investigate the temporal dynamics of LTM-based attentional guidance. In a modified Posner cueing paradigm featuring a 30-item episodic memory set, the results demonstrated that LTM-based ACSs significantly modulated N2pc amplitude within a 170 ms window post-stimulus. These results indicate that goal-relevant representations retrieved from LTM can rapidly reconfigure early sensory processing and bias involuntary orienting, challenging strictly serial models of the transition from long-term storage to active attentional templates.
papers.authors: Lindsay Plater, Maria Giammarco, Samantha Joubran, Naseem Al-Aidroos

papers.title: Assessing the role of long-term memory and visual working-memory attentional templates in guiding attentional capture and decision making
papers.abstract: The interaction between visual working memory (VWM) and long-term memory (LTM) in guiding visual search is frequently conceptualized as a transition of representations into an 'active' template state. This research utilized a dual-task paradigm to compare the functional efficacy of VWM-based and LTM-based templates in modulating attentional capture and search-related decision processes. By manipulating memory set sizes and maintenance durations, the study investigated whether LTM representations effectively guide attention without explicit VWM mediation. Behavioral indices, including capture costs and search efficiency slopes, demonstrated that while both systems guide selection, VWM-maintained templates offer significantly more robust suppression of non-matching distractors. The findings suggest that LTM-based guidance may rely on a reactive reinstatement mechanism that is functionally dissociable from the proactive maintenance characteristic of VWM templates.
papers.authors: Jessica M. Kespe, Niyatee Narkar, Naseem Al-Aidroos

0498.name: Neda Nategh
0498.department: Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering
0498.bio: Nategh investigates the neural mechanisms and computational algorithms that enable stable visual perception during active behavior, particularly during rapid eye movements. Their research combines multi-electrode array recordings in non-human primates with statistical modeling, such as time-varying generalized linear models, to decode how the brain processes dynamic visual information. By examining perisaccadic neural dynamics in extrastriate and prefrontal areas, Nategh’s work identifies how sensory memory and response enhancements bridge discontinuities in retinal input. Their current research aims to develop biologically-plausible frameworks for describing high-dimensional neural data to provide insights into both biological vision and artificial intelligence.
0498.research_direction: Dr. Nategh has recently been investigating the neural mechanisms underlying dynamic visual processing, with a primary focus on how spatial and temporal perception is altered during eye movements. Their recent work explores perisaccadic phenomena—such as spatial mislocalization and temporal compression—by recording from macaque extrastriate areas V4 and MT to map population spiking activity directly to single-trial perceptual reports. To capture these rapid, nonstationary shifts in spatiotemporal receptive fields, they are actively developing and deploying advanced computational frameworks, specifically time-varying generalized linear models. Beyond extrastriate cortex, they also investigate local inhibitory circuits in the early visual system, combining paired intracellular perturbations with multi-electrode array recordings to determine how individual retinal amacrine cells modulate feature sensitivity and response gain in ganglion cell networks.

papers.title: Limits of V4 perisaccadic firing rate modulations in explaining perceptual mislocalization
papers.abstract: The degree to which distinct visual sensory structures mediate the perceived coordinates of visual targets remains unresolved. To determine whether extrastriate area V4 drives shifts in spatial localization around the time of saccadic eye movements, perisaccadic mislocalization was probed using an integrated behavioral and neurophysiological paradigm in non-human primates, mapping single-trial perceptual reports directly to population spike rates in area V4. Monkeys exhibited characteristic perisaccadic mislocalization oriented counter to saccade trajectories. Extrastriate population responses were evaluated by calculating the center of mass of firing rates across probe positions for V4 units whose receptive fields bordered the saccade target. Although perisaccadic responses displayed vector shifts oriented toward the saccade target, trial-by-trial variance in shift magnitude did not correlate with perceptual displacement. These data indicate that receptive field displacements inferred from mean firing rate modulations in area V4 are insufficient to explain single-trial behavioral mislocalization, demonstrating that higher-order neural population dynamics or alternative representational codes are necessary to account for perisaccadic spatial perception.
papers.authors: Geyu Weng, Kelsey Clark, Behrad Noudoost, Neda Nategh

papers.title: A population readout of extrastriate activity reveals biased and smoothed temporal representations across saccades
papers.abstract: Perceived temporal intervals undergo transient compression and distortion perisaccadically, yet the circuit computations underpinning time representation during rapid gaze shifts remain poorly defined. To elucidate how perisaccadic temporal features are structured and decoded within extrastriate cortex, multi-electrode array recordings were gathered from macaque area MT and V4 populations during millisecond-precision visual probe stimulation alongside single-trial nonstationary statistical modeling. Decoded population readouts revealed that perisaccadic spikes systematically advance the decoded temporal profile of presaccadic receptive-field stimuli—biasing estimated onset times toward earlier latencies—while concurrently suppressing temporal sensitivity and degrading stimulus onset discrimination. Enforcing synthetic in silico perturbations demonstrated that the representational temporal bias directly causes the loss in temporal sensitivity. These results indicate that extrastriate ensembles adopt an adaptive encoding strategy prioritizing the most recent presaccadic input at the expense of temporal precision, highlighting a computational tradeoff between temporal resolution and perceptual continuity across saccades.
papers.authors: Adeleh Poursadegh, Maryam Zekri, Geyu Weng, Amir Akbarian, Kelsey Clark, Hossein Rabbani, Behrad Noudoost, Neda Nategh

papers.title: Neural correlates of perisaccadic visual mislocalization in extrastriate cortex
papers.abstract: Visual perception of spatial position exhibits significant distortion during saccades, a phenomenon known as perisaccadic mislocalization whose underlying neurophysiological mechanisms have remained elusive. By recording single-unit and multi-unit spiking activity across extrastriate cortex (areas V4 and MT) in four macaque monkeys during a visually guided saccade task with fine-grained visual probes, a statistical modeling framework was deployed to isolate time-varying spatiotemporal receptive field dynamics at millisecond resolution. Decoded model readouts successfully recapitulated behavioral spatial bias toward the saccade target and identified the precise underlying subcomponents of neuronal sensitivity. Crucially, the spatial bias was driven primarily by an emergent gain enhancement for probe stimuli positioned near the saccade target in neurons whose classical receptive fields were situated far from the target. These findings demonstrate that extrastriate networks transiently reallocate representational bandwidth toward the impending gaze endpoint, establishing that perisaccadic distortions emerge from targeted resource concentration supporting active foveation.
papers.authors: Geyu Weng, Amir Akbarian, Kelsey Clark, Behrad Noudoost, Neda Nategh

papers.title: Time-varying generalized linear models: characterizing and decoding neuronal dynamics in higher visual areas
papers.abstract: Cortical neurons in higher visual areas dynamically modulate their tuning properties in response to rapid interactions between feedforward sensory inputs and internal variables such as cognitive state, motor planning, and reward expectancy. Standard point-process generalized linear models (GLMs) offer an established framework for single-trial encoding and decoding of spike trains, but conventional formulations inherently assume temporal stationarity, rendering them incapable of capturing nonstationary receptive field shifts in higher visual circuits. This review synthesizes time-varying extensions of point-process GLMs engineered to resolve nonstationary tuning curves and multi-filter spatiotemporal sensitivity maps. We discuss how parameterizing time-varying kernels enables the decoding of transient perceptual representations, the dissection of specific physiological components driving behavioral changes, and the in silico manipulation of model filters to establish causal links between dynamic neural representations and visual behaviors.
papers.authors: Geyu Weng, Kelsey Clark, Amir Akbarian, Behrad Noudoost, Neda Nategh

papers.title: Modulation of input sensitivity and output gain by retinal amacrine cells
papers.abstract: The conventional canonical view of retinal processing relies on hierarchical, feedforward parallel pathways that sum visual features sequentially, leaving open how local inhibitory circuits implement contextual modulation across pathways. By deploying causal intracellular current injections into single amacrine cells paired with multi-electrode array recordings of ganglion cell populations in the salamander retina, an unsupervised dimensionality reduction and non-parametric modeling framework was developed to evaluate inhibitory influence on multi-dimensional visual stimulus spaces. Perturbing single amacrine cells unveiled two distinct functional classes of modulation: an input-pathway modulation that selectively adjusts the sensitivity and activation threshold of individual visual features within a ganglion cell, and an output modulation that divisively regulates the overall response gain across multiple features simultaneously. These findings establish distinct functional operations for amacrine cells in early visual processing, separating primary feature construction, contextual feature selection, and global retinal gain gating.
papers.authors: Neda Nategh, Mihai Manu, Stephen A. Baccus

0500.name: Nelson Cowan
0500.bio: Nelson Cowan proposed the 'embedded-processes model,' which defines working memory as an activated subset of long-term memory governed by a capacity-limited focus of attention. Their research focuses on quantifying the discrete limits of this focus—established as approximately three to four items in adults—and investigating how these constraints evolve throughout childhood development. Utilizing experimental psychology and neuroscientific frameworks, Cowan examines the interplay between selective attention, sensory storage, and the cognitive mechanisms underlying memory disorders. Their recent research extends into the relationship between consciousness and working memory architecture across the human lifespan.
0500.research_direction: Dr. Cowan's recent work explores the capacity limits, underlying architecture, and developmental trajectories of working memory. They have recently been investigating visual working memory constraints, using mixture modeling and diverse stimulus sets to test how attention limits the binding of complex object features and whether heterogeneous items can bypass domain-general memory bottlenecks. Their research also has a strong developmental focus, examining how children learn to use semantic elaboration strategies for serial order memory and tracking how metacognitive monitoring—our ability to judge our own memory accuracy—matures across the lifespan. Additionally, they are studying the interplay between immediate attention and long-term retention, such as how working memory capacity supports the statistical learning and segmentation of unfamiliar speech patterns.

papers.title: Colors, characters, locations, and shapes: The capacity of working memory for multiple, dissimilar sets of items
papers.abstract: This research evaluates the capacity constraints of working memory (WM) when maintaining heterogeneous stimulus sets (chromaticity, orthographic characters, spatial locations, and geometric shapes). Across two experiments (N = 181), researchers examined whether stimulus diversity allows for memory performance that transcends the fixed-capacity thresholds typically observed for unitary stimulus categories. While total array performance scaled with stimulus heterogeneity, the results indicated that the precision and recall of an initial three-item set were significantly attenuated by the inclusion of additional sets. The findings suggest a hierarchical pointer-indexing architecture where, despite the utilization of domain-specific resources, a domain-general bottleneck—likely involving the central focus of attention—constrains the number of discrete stimulus types that can be effectively indexed in parallel.
papers.authors: Luísa Superbia-Guimarães, Nelson Cowan

papers.title: Object- and feature-based working memory limits for pairs of complex objects and their development during the school years
papers.abstract: Evaluating object- versus feature-based constraints in visual working memory (VWM) development, this study uses complex stimulus pairs defined by four orthogonal features (color, orientation, shape, and internal texture). Through mixture modeling, the researchers decoupled variance attributable to stochastic attention lapses (unencoded objects) from incomplete feature-specific mnemonic resolution. Developmental trajectories across children (ages 8–12) and young adults demonstrate that while object-level selection increases, a primary mechanism for capacity improvement resides in the increased efficiency and independence of feature instantiation within attended objects. These results support a bifurcated encoding architecture involving an initial object-indexing phase followed by the independent, parallel binding of constituent features.
papers.authors: Chenye Bao, Yu Li, Nelson Cowan

papers.title: Children's use of semantic elaboration in immediate serial order memory
papers.abstract: This developmental investigation explores the efficacy of semantic elaboration strategies in facilitating serial order memory during the elementary school years. The researchers evaluated how constructing narratives or meaningful associations between items influences the retention of item-to-item bindings. The findings demonstrate that while younger children primarily rely on phonological maintenance, older children increasingly leverage semantic elaboration to scaffold working memory performance. The study indicates that the maturation of strategy deployment and the ability to utilize long-term memory schemas for associative binding are critical drivers in the developmental trajectory of serial order memory, effectively mitigating the constraints of purely phonological rehearsal.
papers.authors: Luísa Superbia-Guimarães, Reese Lavers, Maya Steiger, Kellen Hendrix, Bret Glass, Nelson Cowan

papers.title: Short- and long-term influences of repeated speech examples on segmentation in an unfamiliar language analog
papers.abstract: This study utilizes a cross-modal speech analog to examine the contribution of working memory (WM) to the statistical learning of linguistic segments. The paradigm presented overlapping auditory strings with varying repetition frequencies to simulate the parsing of fluent speech into words. Quantitative analysis revealed that although increased repetition frequency enhanced boundary detection and segmental parsing within immediate WM, these representations often failed to consolidate into robust long-term memory (LTM) traces without semantic integration. The findings suggest that phonological WM capacity provides a baseline for linguistic segmentation but is insufficient for long-term acquisition, highlighting the necessity of interaction between attention-based storage and higher-level semantic processes.
papers.authors: Neyla Sfeir, Dominic Guitard, Nelson Cowan

papers.title: A lifespan study of the confidence–accuracy relation in working memory and episodic long-term memory
papers.abstract: This research presents a large-scale lifespan investigation into the meta-cognitive calibration of subjective confidence and objective memory performance across working memory (WM) and episodic long-term memory (LTM) systems. Utilizing meta-d' and signal detection theory (SDT) metrics, the study analyzed whether the fidelity of memory monitoring matures at different rates for items within the focus of attention compared to those retrieved from episodic stores. Findings reveal that while young children exhibit absolute storage deficits, their ability to monitor accuracy in WM is functionally mature and comparable to adults. Conversely, meta-cognitive calibration for LTM displays a protracted developmental course, suggesting that monitoring the focus of attention is a fundamental capability that precedes the executive control required for episodic meta-memory.
papers.authors: Nathaniel R. Greene, Alicia Forsberg, Dominic Guitard, Moshe Naveh-Benjamin, Nelson Cowan

0501.name: Nelson Roque
0501.department: Department of Human Development and Family Studies
0501.bio: Nelson Roque is an Assistant Professor at Pennsylvania State University specializing in the intersection of cognitive aging, vision science, and digital health technology. Roque's research employs ambulatory assessment frameworks and mobile health platforms to investigate the dynamics of visual attention and cognitive performance in real-world settings. Using computational phenotyping and passive sensing, Roque examines how environmental exposures, such as air quality, and behavioral factors, including sleep and technology use, influence the progression of cognitive decline in older adults. Their work focuses on the development of digital biomarkers for the detection of neurodegenerative conditions through remote, high-frequency smartphone assessments.
0501.research_direction: Dr. Roque has recently been investigating the diverse behavioral and environmental determinants of cognitive aging. Their recent work explores how contextual dimensions of digital engagement—particularly the difference between cognitively active device use and passive screen time—impact memory and executive control across the adult lifespan. To improve how these behaviors are measured in real-world settings, they are examining the privacy concerns and public acceptability of using continuous mobile health sensors, such as GPS and wearable biometrics, for remote cognitive phenotyping. Furthermore, they are studying environmental risk factors for neurodegenerative disease by mapping demographic gaps in ambient air quality monitoring networks and evaluating the role of indoor airborne pollutants in dementia risk.

papers.title: Screen time in context: Toward a theoretical model of digital engagement across the lifespan
papers.abstract: Traditional operationalizations of digital behavior rely disproportionately on unidimensional aggregate duration ("screen time"), obscuring the multifaceted mechanisms through which digital engagement modulates cognitive and psychological outcomes across ontogeny. Grounded in Bronfenbrenner's bioecological systems theory, this framework introduces the construct of "virtual microsystems" to formalize the reciprocal, nested interactions occurring across proximate physical and digital environments throughout the lifespan. By analyzing empirical evidence spanning early childhood through late adulthood, the model articulates how five key contextual dimensions—modality of engagement (active vs. passive), functional objective, temporal placement and environmental situatedness, structural fragmentation of content (e.g., short-form algorithmic streams vs. long-form narrative media), and affective valence—differentially govern cognitive functioning and mental health trajectories. Consequently, this ecological paradigm underscores the imperative to transition from duration-centric metrics toward context-aware, ecologically valid measurement batteries and developmentally tailored digital policies.
papers.authors: Rinanda Shaleha, Nelson Roque

papers.title: The importance of accurate indoor air quality assessment in the aging and dementia population
papers.abstract: Given that older adults typically spend upwards of 80% of their daily lives in enclosed spaces, indoor air quality represents a critical yet undercharacterized environmental determinant of neurodegenerative vulnerability, particularly among populations at elevated risk for Alzheimer's disease and related dementias (ADRD). Existing environmental health thresholds and regulatory air-pollution standards remain disproportionately restricted to ambient outdoor monitoring networks, which fail to reflect the substantial intra-individual micro-environmental exposure heterogeneity within personal residences. This perspective emphasizes the urgent necessity of centering indoor airborne pollutant exposures—including fine particulate matter (PM2.5) and volatile organic compounds—within neurocognitive aging research and brain health policy frameworks, advocating for scalable, in-home longitudinal environmental monitoring paradigms to establish accurate exposure biology and mitigate cognitive decline.
papers.authors: Nelson A. Roque, H. Dean Hosgood, Charles B. Hall

papers.title: Acceptability of Active and Passive Data Collection Methods for Mobile Health Research: Cross-Sectional Survey of an Online Adult Sample in the United States
papers.abstract: The successful deployment of mobile health (mHealth) architectures and wearable phenotyping platforms for cognitive aging and clinical surveillance depends fundamentally on user perceptions of data governance, privacy preservation, and granular sensor acceptability. A cross-sectional survey was administered to a non-probability online sample of U.S. adults (N = 1,489; mean age = 35.5 years, SD = 12.0; 43.8% female; 76.2% non-Hispanic White; 99.3% smartphone owners) via Prolific and Qualtrics to systematically evaluate user willingness to share active and passive data streams across behavioral tasks, physical sensors, and digital metadata. Participants exhibited significantly higher willingness to share continuous passive biometric and health-relevant indicators, whereas streams possessing pronounced re-identification vulnerability or surveillance invasiveness—most notably continuous geospatial GPS logging and in-vehicle dashcam video—yielded the lowest acceptance. Crucially, end-user data governance emerged as paramount: 71.3% demanded comprehensive retrospective data deletion privileges, 64.5% endorsed stream-specific toggle controls, and 43.9% desired temporal-window erasure, while data dissemination to commercial health insurers (30.4%) or informal care partners (25.8%) faced substantial resistance.
papers.authors: Nelson Roque, John Felt

papers.title: From screens to cognition: A scoping review of the impact of screen time on cognitive function in midlife and older adults
papers.abstract: As digital device saturation extends across the adult lifespan, delineating the cognitive sequelae of screen-mediated behaviors in mature cohorts has become a vital epidemiological priority. Following PRISMA-ScR methodological protocols, a scoping review was conducted across PubMed and CINAHL (2018–2023) to synthesize observational and experimental evidence evaluating screen-based behaviors in relation to cognitive functioning among adults aged 40 years and older. Synthesizing data across 17 qualifying investigations revealed a pronounced functional dichotomy: cognitively active screen utilization (e.g., purposeful computer operations, search, problem-solving interfaces) demonstrated consistent positive associations with performance in episodic memory, executive control, and attentional domains. Conversely, cognitively passive digital engagement (principally prolonged sedentary television viewing) was correlated with heightened risk of global cognitive deterioration and steeper rates of verbal memory decrement. Furthermore, these domain-specific associations were systematically modulated by key covariates, including educational attainment, physical activity levels, sleep hygiene, and baseline technology literacy.
papers.authors: Rinanda Shaleha, Nelson Roque

papers.title: Identifying air quality monitoring deserts in the United States
papers.abstract: Environmental epidemiological models and air pollution health risk assessments depend heavily on the spatial infrastructure of ground-level regulatory air quality monitoring stations. Utilizing the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency's AirData directory (September 2024 vintage), longitudinal station operating records from 1957 to 2024 (spanning 20,815 cumulative historical stations and 4,821 concurrently active monitors) were analyzed alongside 2017–2021 American Community Survey demographic data and 2013 USDA Rural-Urban Continuum Codes to quantify spatial surveillance coverage. Nationwide, 1,848 counties—representing 58.8% of all U.S. counties, encompassing roughly 40% of the contiguous landmass, and housing approximately 50.7 million residents (15.3% of the total population)—were classified as 'air quality monitoring deserts' devoid of even a single operational monitoring sensor. Logistic modeling established that nonmetropolitan status, geographical concentration in the Midwest and South, lower educational attainment (proportion of adults aged ≥25 without a high school credential), elevated county poverty rates, primary industry employment (agriculture, forestry, fishing, mining), and higher proportions of Black residents were all significantly associated with increased odds of desert classification, whereas higher concentrations of working-age adults reduced these odds.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Nelson A. Roque, Hailey Andrews, Alexis R. Santos-Lozada

0502.name: Nestor Matthews
0502.department: Department of Psychology and Neuroscience Program
0502.bio: Nestor Matthews serves as Professor of Psychology and Chair of Neuroscience at Denison University, where they investigate the mechanisms of human sensory plasticity. Their research employs psychophysical methodologies to study perceptual learning, with a focus on how training affects sensitivity to visual motion, temporal order, and simultaneity. Matthews has documented the double dissociation of radial and rotational motion sensitivity and the ways in which global depth perception modulates local timing accuracy. Additionally, Matthews conducts comparative research on sensory expertise by examining populations such as professional drum corps performers to analyze the limits of temporal processing and cross-modal transfer between vision and audition.
0502.research_direction: Dr. Matthews has recently been investigating the perceptual mechanisms underlying how human observers extract structural and quantitative information from complex, everyday visual displays. Their recent work explores visual communication by examining how people learn to detect statistical patterns, such as main effects and two-way interactions, across different formats like 2 × 2 line and bar graphs. By employing trial-and-error classification tasks, they are testing how perceptual grouping and ensemble processing constrain a viewer's ability to recognize these numeric relationships. Additionally, Dr. Matthews is investigating the psychophysics of typographic environments by using signal detection paradigms to ask how observers estimate sentence length within full-page text arrays. Through spatial manipulations like text inversion and mirror-reversal, they aim to uncover the rapid visual heuristics—such as spatial anchoring and line-counting—that guide layout evaluation independent of explicit lexical processing.

papers.title: Learning to detect patterns in 2 × 2 graphs
papers.abstract: Effective visual communication and statistics pedagogy rely on observers' capacity to discern structured relationships within graphical displays. This investigation evaluated pattern detection in 2 × 2 graphs representing a continuous response variable across two bi-level predictor factors (Factor A on the abscissa and Factor B denoted by visual series markers). While previous research highlighted observers' verbal descriptions of main effects and interaction patterns, the perceptual grouping mechanisms underlying these judgments remained uncharacterized. In a preregistered trial-and-error classification task, 416 naive adults learned to categorize 2 × 2 line or bar graphs containing identical numeric data based on Factor A main effects, Factor B main effects, or two-way interactions. Line displays yielded significantly superior classification accuracy relative to bar charts for both interaction and Factor B configurations, whereas accuracy for Factor A main effects was uniformly poor across display formats. Additionally, participants trained on bar graphs frequently adopted an erroneous decision rule, reporting main effects only in the presence of an interaction; this classification bias was markedly reduced with line graphs. These results demonstrate that graph format and predictor assignment constrain the perceptual availability of statistical patterns through ensemble processing, informing visualization design and statistical literacy.
papers.authors: Nestor Matthews, Megan Lynn Broderick, Samantha Anne Kozlowski

papers.title: Omit needless words: Sentence length perception
papers.abstract: Textual brevity facilitates readability and information accessibility, but the psychophysical mechanisms that govern how human observers estimate sentence length remain largely uncharacterized. Applying signal detection theory paradigms, this study assessed sentence length discrimination among naive adult observers evaluating ecologically valid, full-page typographic layouts. Participants completed a two-alternative forced-choice task judging whether a bolded target sentence embedded within distractor prose contained more or fewer than 17 words.
