Findings indicated that observers discriminated target sentence length rapidly (median reaction times between 300 and 400 ms) and with high precision (~90% accuracy). Inverting the text array upside down yielded negligible latency penalties and minimal accuracy loss (90.7% correct for standard vs. 89.0% for flipped text), contrasting sharply with the robust inversion costs typical of orthographic reading and face recognition. Furthermore, observers systematically underestimated the length of mirror-reversed target sentences, a bias consistent with left-anchored scene syntax and left-to-right reading conventions. Error distribution analyses demonstrated that participants achieved high temporal and perceptual efficiency by employing a rapid text-line counting heuristic rather than explicit lexical enumeration, offering empirical support for line-based copy-editing strategies to reduce unnecessary phrasing.
papers.authors: Nestor Matthews, Folly Folivi

0504.name: Nicholas Gaspelin
0504.bio: Nicholas Gaspelin is an Associate Professor in the Department of Psychological Sciences at the University of Missouri and the director of the Attention and Distraction Lab. Gaspelin’s research examines the cognitive and neural mechanisms of selective attention, specifically the signal suppression account, which proposes that top-down inhibitory processes can prevent salient distractors from capturing attention. They utilize behavioral psychophysics, eye-tracking, and electroencephalography (EEG) to analyze event-related potential (ERP) components such as the N2pc and distractor positivity (Pd). Gaspelin’s current work investigates how implicit learning and selection history influence attentional guidance and the efficiency of suppression in complex visual environments.
0504.research_direction: Dr. Gaspelin's recent work explores the mechanisms of attentional control, specifically focusing on how the human visual system manages and proactively suppresses salient distractors. They have recently been integrating behavioral psychophysics, large-scale eye-tracking, and electrophysiology—particularly the N2pc component—to adjudicate between models of automatic attentional capture and the signal suppression hypothesis. Their research investigates how bottom-up physical salience interacts with top-down factors like task relevance, the spatial breadth of the attentional window, and experience-dependent learning to guide visual selection. Additionally, their recent studies probe the fundamental link between covert attention and overt gaze, examining whether presaccadic covert shifts are a mandatory prerequisite for programming accurate saccades in varying search environments.

papers.title: What can a half-million saccades tell us about distractor suppression?
papers.abstract: This investigation presents a high-powered pooled analysis of approximately 500,000 oculomotor responses from over 350 subjects to probe the underlying mechanisms of proactive distractor suppression. By examining the distribution and latency of saccades toward salient distractors across multiple experiments, the study evaluates the extent to which selection history and stimulus-driven salience interact to determine attentional guidance. The findings demonstrate that experience-dependent learning (selection history) significantly modulates the efficacy of proactive inhibition, ultimately supporting a hybrid framework of attention that reconciles top-down suppressive control with bottom-up salience-driven signals.
papers.authors: Kaitlyn N. Drennan, Nicholas Gaspelin

papers.title: Ignoring salient distractors inside and outside the attentional window
papers.abstract: The study adjudicates between the attentional window account and the signal suppression hypothesis regarding the automaticity of attentional capture. Using a shape-discrimination task to explicitly manipulate the breadth of the attentional window (focused vs. diffuse), the authors coregistered behavioral reaction times with the N2pc component—an electrophysiological marker of covert attentional allocation. Results indicated that salient distractors failed to elicit an N2pc or behavioral cost regardless of their position relative to the attentional window, suggesting that feature-based control mechanisms can prevent capture irrespective of spatial focus.
papers.authors: Xiaojin Ma, Steven J. Luck, Nicholas Gaspelin

papers.title: From capture to control: Initial capture increases learned suppression
papers.abstract: This study explores the hypothesis that the phenomenon of attentional capture by a salient distractor provides a critical error signal that drives the subsequent development of proactive suppression. By longitudinal tracking of behavioral and neural indices of capture and suppression, the research demonstrates that the magnitude of initial distraction predicts the robustness of learned inhibition in subsequent trials. These findings suggest that the cognitive system utilizes initial failures in attentional control as feedback to calibrate top-down suppressive mechanisms, transforming stimulus-driven capture into adaptive, proactive control.
papers.authors: Yue Zhang, Nicholas Gaspelin

papers.title: Is covert attention necessary for programming accurate saccades? Evidence from saccade-locked event-related potentials
papers.abstract: This research assesses the mandatory nature of covert attentional shifts prior to overt gaze movements using coregistered EEG and eye-tracking. The authors measured the presaccadic N2pc component—a neural index of covert selection—to determine if its presence is a prerequisite for saccadic accuracy. Results showed that the N2pc only preceded saccades under conditions of high distractor competition and was absent in simpler search environments. Crucially, neither the presence nor the amplitude of the presaccadic N2pc correlated with gaze precision, and multivariate decoding identified target locations well before saccade initiation even in the absence of an N2pc, suggesting gaze control is mediated by distinct presaccadic mechanisms.
papers.authors: Travis N. Talcott, John E. Kiat, Steven J. Luck, Nicholas Gaspelin

papers.title: Salience effects on attentional selection are enabled by task relevance
papers.abstract: This study investigates the interplay between bottom-up salience and top-down task relevance using color-contrast manipulations to define singleton salience. Initial psychophysical experiments confirmed that high-contrast singletons elicited stronger bottom-up signals, facilitating faster target detection. However, in a subsequent additional singleton paradigm where these singletons were task-irrelevant, both high- and low-salience distractors were effectively suppressed below baseline levels. These results demonstrate that the impact of physical salience on attentional selection is gated by task relevance, supporting the signal suppression hypothesis over models that posit automatic capture by highly salient stimuli.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
papers.authors: Yue Zhang, Nicholas Gaspelin

0506.name: Nicolò Cesana-Arlotti
0506.bio: Nicolò Cesana-Arlotti is an Assistant Professor of Psychology at Yale University and a faculty member of the Wu Tsai Institute, where they investigate the ontogenetic origins of logical reasoning. Their research focuses on the 'logic of thought,' examining how preverbal infants and children utilize logical operations such as disjunctive syllogism and quantification to support learning and decision-making. Using methodologies including high-resolution eye-tracking, pupillometry, and behavioral paradigms, Cesana-Arlotti has provided evidence that logical concepts emerge before the acquisition of language. Their work explores the computational interface between these logical resources and adult visual perception to analyze the continuity of domain-general reasoning throughout development.
0506.research_direction: Dr. Cesana-Arlotti has recently been investigating the foundational origins and automaticity of logical and modal reasoning across human development. Their recent work explores how preverbal infants and young children mentally represent concepts of possibility, necessity, and probability, using looking-time and interactive decision-making tasks to probe how early modal judgments guide physical and social expectations prior to language acquisition. Additionally, they are examining the domain-generality of early deduction, utilizing high-resolution eye-tracking to test whether toddlers spontaneously deploy disjunctive syllogism—or the process of elimination—across diverse cognitive contexts like word learning and action prediction. Furthermore, Dr. Cesana-Arlotti's research extends into adult visual cognition, measuring behavioral response times to determine whether these exact deductive inferences operate automatically and involuntarily during rapid visual scene processing.

papers.title: Irresistibly Logical: Automatic Logical Inferences in Visual Scene Processing
papers.abstract: The capacity for deductive inference pervades intuitive reasoning, yet its automaticity in non-linguistic perception remains unresolved. Across five behavioral experiments, this investigation tests whether disjunctive elimination occurs spontaneously and involuntarily during visual scene processing in adults. Observers viewed animations where an ambiguous item was sampled into a cup from a two-item set, after which one candidate appeared outside the cup. Participants exhibited significantly accelerated response times when revealed outcomes matched the deductively entailed identity compared to when they violated it. This inferential advantage persisted across repeated trials, even when the logically implied target contradicted prior statistical base rates (a 2:1 sampling bias favoring the alternative outcome). Furthermore, the effect facilitated rapid object classification and dissociated from non-logical spatiotemporal object-tracking heuristics, demonstrating that deductive inferences operate automatically and imperviously to probabilistic counterevidence within visual scene perception.
papers.authors: Nathaniel Braswell, Chaz Firestone, Nicolò Cesana-Arlotti

papers.title: Logical Concepts of (Im)possibility Guide Young Children's Decision‐Making
papers.abstract: Rational decision-making in stochastic environments depends on modal judgment: discriminating between states that are necessary, merely possible, or impossible. It has long been theorized that robust modal judgments emerge late in childhood, contingent upon mastering modal vocabulary. In two experiments, 96 children between 34 and 65 months old were tasked with assisting an agent to achieve a goal or prevent harm by interacting with apparatuses possessing distinct topological constraints. Preschoolers systematically chose the optimal course of action when options crossed qualitative, categorical modal boundaries (such as distinguishing impossible paths from possible or necessary outcomes). In contrast, children struggled when selections differed merely in continuous probability (e.g., distinguishing between 66% and 33% likelihoods). These results reveal that preschool children spontaneously deploy discrete logical modal concepts to direct instrumental decisions prior to the mastery of explicit modal language.
papers.authors: Nicolò Cesana-Arlotti, Sofia Jáuregui, Peter Mazalik, Shaun Nichols, Justin Halberda

papers.title: Core Logic: Fourteen-month-olds exclude physical possibilities that would make an agent irrational
papers.abstract: Human reasoning is distinguished by the capacity to perform abstract computations that integrate information across disparate cognitive domains. This research investigates whether preverbal infants possess the logical resources to integrate physical probability with expectations of social rationality. Across three preregistered experiments, the authors demonstrate that both adults and 14-month-old infants spontaneously employ disjunctive syllogism (A or B; not A; therefore B) to resolve ambiguity in social events. Specifically, infants were shown an agent reaching for a hidden object whose identity was ambiguous between two physical possibilities. Infants exhibited increased looking times when the agent's subsequent behavior was inconsistent with a logically inferred preference, suggesting they had eliminated impossible outcomes to deduce the agent's goal. These findings provide evidence for a domain-general 'core logic' that serves as a foundation for human thought, functioning independently of natural language and specific domain-restricted representations.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the 47th Annual Conference of the Cognitive Science Society (CogSci)
papers.authors: Zihan Wang, Nicolò Cesana-Arlotti

papers.title: The origin of the possible: 12-month-olds' understanding of certain, likely, and unlikely events
papers.abstract: The capacity for modal cognition—representing and reasoning about potentiality and necessity—is fundamental to human planning and prediction. This study investigates the developmental origins of these abilities by examining whether 12-month-old infants can represent modal categories (e.g., certainty vs. mere possibility) before the acquisition of modal language. Using two preregistered habituation experiments, the researchers tested infants' ability to distinguish between future physical outcomes based on their probability levels. In Experiment 1, infants were presented with events having 100% vs. 66% probability, while Experiment 2 tested 66% vs. 33% probability. The results indicate that 12-month-olds can distinguish between likely and unlikely outcomes, suggesting they possess the cognitive resources to mentally represent and compare multiple possible future states. These findings challenge minimalistic views of early probabilistic intuition and suggest that a proto-modal representational system for potentiality emerges early in the ontogeny of the mind.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the 47th Annual Conference of the Cognitive Science Society (CogSci)
papers.authors: Şeref Can Esmer, Nicolò Cesana-Arlotti

papers.title: A Continuity in Logical Development: Domain-General Disjunctive Inference by Toddlers
papers.abstract: While preverbal infants show looking-time signatures consistent with elementary deductions, it remains contentious whether such inferences represent domain-general logic or domain-specific heuristics, and whether they persist into early childhood. In this study, 36 toddlers aged 2.3 to 3.2 years were tested across three distinct cognitive tasks: novel word-to-referent mapping, agentive preference induction, and physical race outcome prediction. Using high-resolution eye tracking, toddlers displayed systematic oculomotor double-checking—shifting fixation to examine and reject an alternative candidate prior to settling on the target—across all three contexts. Toddlers executed these disjunctive inferences successfully prior to formal schooling and without relying on explicit logical language, providing robust evidence for an ontogenetically continuous, domain-general logic of thought operating across diverse representational domains.
papers.authors: Nicolò Cesana-Arlotti, Justin Halberda

0507.name: Nihong Chen
0507.department: Department of Psychology, School of Social Sciences
0507.bio: Nihong Chen is an Associate Professor at Tsinghua University and a Principal Investigator at the IDG/McGovern Institute for Brain Research. Chen’s research investigates the neural mechanisms of human visual perception, focusing on how perceptual learning and attention reshape the functional architecture of the visual cortex. Using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), and psychophysical modeling, they have characterized the cortical plasticity of areas like V3A and MT+ and explored the computational strategies the brain employs to resolve visual crowding. Chen’s current work examines how cortical population codes and multi-stage integration models facilitate object recognition in complex and ambiguous visual environments.
0507.research_direction: Dr. Chen has recently been investigating how the visual system integrates, filters, and learns sensory information across the early cortical hierarchy. Using techniques such as high-resolution fMRI, multivariate pattern analysis, and Dynamic Causal Modeling, their recent work explores the neural architectures underlying color-motion feature binding and the specific cortico-cortical interactions that support spatial attention. They are also examining the limitations and adaptability of peripheral vision, specifically testing computational pooling models of visual crowding and tracing changes in feedforward connectivity induced by perceptual learning. Additionally, their research probes the statistical learning of naturalistic textures by comparing human psychophysics with Deep Convolutional Neural Networks to better understand how visual representations adapt to environmental regularities.

papers.title: Multivariate Patterns of fMRI Activity in Human V2 Predict Feature Binding of Color and Motion
papers.abstract: This study investigates the neural architecture of feature binding using a steady-state misbinding illusion where color and motion signals are perceived incorrectly relative to their physical properties. Utilizing 7-Tesla fMRI and multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA), the researchers examined whether the human visual cortex codes for physical or perceived feature pairings. The results demonstrate that multivariate patterns of activity in the secondary visual area (V2), but not V1, significantly predict the perceived (misbound) combinations of color and motion. Additionally, direction-selective adaptation effects in V2 were found to be contingent on color and significantly correlated with the magnitude of psychophysical aftereffects across subjects, indicating that V2 is a critical site for the active binding of basic visual features into coherent objects.
papers.authors: Yan-Yu Zhang, Xilin Zhang, Nihong Chen

papers.title: Seeing in crowds: Averaging first, then max
papers.abstract: To delineate the pooling strategies underlying the visual crowding effect—a bottleneck in peripheral object recognition—this research measured the internal response distributions of human observers during an orientation discrimination task. In contrast to standard compulsory averaging models, human response patterns revealed that perceptual decisions under crowded conditions are better characterized by a non-linear two-stage model. This proposed 'Avg-Max' model posits an initial stage of local orientation signal averaging followed by a late-stage signed-max operation that selects the extreme response across items. These results suggest that the visual system employs a combination of linear integration and non-linear decision rules to optimize information extraction from cluttered peripheral environments.
papers.authors: Xincheng Lu, Ruijie Jiang, Meng Song, Yiting Wu, Yiran Ge, Nihong Chen

papers.title: Learning Improves Peripheral Vision Via Enhanced Cortico-Cortical Communications
papers.abstract: This study explores the neural plasticity induced by Preferred Retinal Location (PRL) training in normally sighted adults, which is known to alleviate crowding and enhance peripheral visual resolution. Employing functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) combined with effective connectivity analysis (Dynamic Causal Modeling), the researchers investigated changes in inter-areal communication before and after training. The results demonstrate that perceptual learning significantly enhances feedforward connectivity from the primary visual cortex (V1) to extrastriate regions (V2 and V3) specifically at the trained PRL. These findings provide neurobiological support for a reweighting theory of perceptual learning, suggesting that the visual system adaptively prioritizes task-relevant signal transmission along the cortical hierarchy to overcome resolution bottlenecks.
papers.authors: Yuwei Cui, Xincheng Lu, MiYoung Kwon, Nihong Chen

papers.title: A comparison of statistical learning of naturalistic textures between DCNNs and the human visual hierarchy
papers.abstract: This study compares the acquisition of high-order statistical regularities in naturalistic textures between human observers and Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (DCNNs). Using a psychophysical paradigm that targets specific image statistics, the researchers found that DCNNs replicate the human-like learning curves and performance improvements across various texture families. Computational analysis of the model's internal representations reveals that texture selectivity enhancement is hierarchically distributed, with more pronounced plasticity occurring in deeper convolutional layers (L4 and L5). These findings suggest that DCNNs can serve as effective digital twins for investigating the neural mechanisms of statistical learning and the cortical organization of natural scene encoding in the primate ventral stream.
papers.authors: Xincheng Lu, Ziqi Yuan, Yichi Zhang, Hailin Ai, Siyuan Cheng, Yiran Ge, Fang Fang, Nihong Chen

papers.title: Attention spotlight in V1-based cortico-cortical interactions in human visual hierarchy
papers.abstract: This investigation demonstrates the neural correlates of the 'attention spotlight' by analyzing the spatial distribution of signal transmission within the human visual cortex. Utilizing fMRI background connectivity analysis, the researchers mapped the interactions between retinotopic V1 and downstream areas (V2–V4) under focal and diffused attentional states. The data reveal that focal attention sharpens the spatial gradient of background connectivity, prioritizing signal transmission at attended locations relative to the surround. Dynamic Causal Modeling (DCM) further indicates that this attentional modulation involves both feedforward and feedback recurrent processing. These results characterize attention as a context-dependent filter that enhances the precision of information transmission across the early stages of the visual hierarchy.
papers.authors: Yanyu Zhang, Xilin Zhang, Xincheng Lu, Nihong Chen

0509.name: Niko A. Busch
0509.bio: Niko A. Busch is a Professor of Experimental Psychology who studies the neural mechanisms of visual perception, attention, and memory. Busch investigates how spontaneous brain oscillations, specifically in the alpha band (8–13 Hz), modulate cortical excitability and bias subjective perceptual experience prior to stimulus onset. Their methodology integrates electroencephalography (EEG) and psychophysics with a focus on open science, including leadership in the EEGManyPipelines project to assess the robustness of neuroimaging analysis. Current research in their laboratory examines rhythmic sampling in visual attention and the role of typicality in complex scene recognition.
0509.research_direction: Dr. Busch has recently been investigating the mechanisms that determine the capacity and rapid temporal decay of iconic memory. Using partial-report paradigms and computational modeling, their recent work explores how the fidelity of this ultra-brief sensory store is modulated by top-down spatial attention, pre-stimulus pupil-linked arousal, and spontaneous fluctuations in cortical excitability. In addition to early sensory traces, they are examining the neural and oculomotor correlates of covert spatial attention and visual working memory. By combining EEG and eye-tracking, they are investigating whether markers like alpha-band lateralization, contralateral delay activity, and microsaccades reliably track spatial orienting during tasks involving exogenous cues, and whether visual memories are actively maintained in retinotopic or screen-centered reference frames across saccades.

papers.title: Effects of spatial attention on iconic memory are primarily driven by costs rather than benefits
papers.abstract: Across two experiments using a partial-report paradigm, we investigated the modulation of iconic memory—an ultra-brief sensory store—by endogenous spatial attention. Using spatial pre-cues and variable display-to-cue onset asynchronies (SOAs), we modeled the temporal dynamics of information decay. We found that valid attentional cues did not significantly enhance performance relative to a neutral baseline at any SOA. Instead, the observed attentional modulation was driven almost entirely by substantial performance costs at invalidly cued locations. These results demonstrate that spatial attention influences the earliest measurable phase of iconic memory by shaping the initial sensory trace, primarily through the inhibitory suppression of task-irrelevant sensory input rather than the enhancement of attended representations.
papers.authors: Paul J.C. Smith, Niko A. Busch

papers.title: Spontaneous Alpha-Band Lateralization Extends Persistence of Visual Information in Iconic Memory by Modulating Cortical Excitability
papers.abstract: We examined the influence of ongoing pre-stimulus brain states on the capacity and persistence of iconic memory using EEG. Participants performed a partial-report task while spontaneous fluctuations in pre-stimulus alpha-band oscillations (8–13 Hz) were recorded. Results revealed that the degree of alpha-band lateralization—specifically, higher alpha power in the hemisphere ipsilateral to the target location—predicted significantly higher recall accuracy. Modeling of the iconic decay function showed that this effect was due to an increase in the initial availability of visual information at stimulus offset rather than a change in the decay rate. These findings suggest that trial-by-trial variations in cortical excitability at the moment of stimulus onset modulate the encoding of sensory information into the iconic store, independent of post-perceptual decision strategies.
papers.authors: Paul Justin Connor Smith, Niko A. Busch

papers.title: Pre-stimulus pupil-linked arousal enhances initial stimulus availability in iconic memory
papers.abstract: This study investigated how baseline physiological arousal, indexed by pre-stimulus pupil diameter, relates to the initial capacity and subsequent decay of iconic memory. Using a partial-report task with variable cue delays, we observed that larger pre-stimulus pupil sizes were associated with improved recall performance. Non-linear modeling of the iconic memory decay revealed that this arousal-linked benefit was specifically localized to the initial stimulus availability at the beginning of the maintenance interval. No relationship was found between pupil size and the rate of information decay. These results suggest that fluctuations in the locus-coeruleus-norepinephrine system modulate the gain of early sensory encoding, thereby determining the initial robustness of representations within the iconic memory store.
papers.authors: Paul J.C. Smith, Niko A. Busch

papers.title: Contralateral delay activity and alpha lateralization reflect retinotopic and screen-centered reference frames in visual memory
papers.abstract: We utilized EEG to determine whether visual working memory (VWM) representations are maintained in retinotopic (gaze-centered) or spatiotopic (screen-centered) reference frames. Participants memorized lateralized items and performed a saccade during the maintenance interval. We tracked two neural indices: the contralateral delay activity (CDA) and alpha-band lateralization. The CDA remained consistently lateralized relative to the stimulus's original retinotopic location, even following saccades that moved the location to the opposite hemifield. In contrast, alpha-band lateralization shifted to reflect the screen-centered coordinates after the saccade, regardless of memory requirements. These results indicate a functional dissociation where the CDA supports the active maintenance of information in a retinotopic frame, while alpha lateralization reflects spatiotopic attentional orienting or disengagement.
papers.authors: Wanja Alexander Mössing, Svea Christine Schröder, Anna Lena Biel, Niko A. Busch

papers.title: Alpha-Band Lateralization and Microsaccades Elicited by Exogenous Cues Do Not Track Attentional Orienting
papers.abstract: We investigated whether alpha-band lateralization and microsaccade directionality serve as reliable indices of the focus of attention during inhibition of return (IOR). While human participants exhibited a standard behavioral IOR effect—characterized by initial facilitation and subsequent response-time inhibition at exogenously cued locations—neural and oculomotor markers did not track this transition. EEG alpha activity lateralized toward the cue only during the behavioral facilitation phase and failed to re-lateralize during the inhibition phase. Concurrently, microsaccades were predominantly oriented away from the cue during the lateralization period. These findings challenge the view that alpha lateralization and microsaccades directly represent the covert focus of spatial attention, suggesting instead that they reflect the initial sensory processing of salient exogenous stimuli.
papers.authors: Elio Balestrieri, René Michel, Niko A. Busch

0510.name: Nikolaus Kriegeskorte
0510.bio: Nikolaus Kriegeskorte is a Professor of Psychology and Neuroscience at Columbia University and the Director of Cognitive Imaging at the Zuckerman Mind Brain Behavior Institute. Kriegeskorte specializes in cognitive computational neuroscience, developing deep neural network models that simulate the human visual system's ability to recognize objects and scenes. They developed Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA), a methodology that characterizes neural representations through their geometry to facilitate comparisons between brain activity, behavior, and computational models. Their current research focuses on integrating feedforward and recurrent processing in brain-inspired AI to investigate the inferential nature of biological vision.
0510.research_direction: Dr. Kriegeskorte's recent work explores how advanced machine learning architectures can elucidate human visual processing and the structure of neural population codes. They have recently been using transformer attention mechanisms and generative diffusion models as fMRI encoding frameworks, investigating how the brain dynamically routes high-level visual features and synthesizing optimal image stimuli to map novel categorical selectivities across the cortex. In addition to these large-scale mapping efforts, their research investigates the theoretical foundations of representational geometry, analyzing how measurement constraints like fMRI spatial pooling distort representational distances and developing topological extensions of Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA) to capture the invariant manifold structure of neural responses. Beyond visual neuroscience, their recent work explores human cognition at a collective scale, developing probabilistic models to infer objective truth from crowdsourced probability judgments while accounting for individual calibration biases.

papers.title: Transformer brain encoders explain human high-level visual responses
papers.abstract: Traditional linear encoding models frequently fail to account for the complex spatial and feature-routing properties inherent in high-level cortical visual processing. This research investigates how the attention mechanism from transformer architectures can model the dynamic routing of retinotopic visual features to category-selective brain regions. The authors propose the Transformer Brain Encoder (TBEn), an encoder-decoder framework utilizing a frozen vision transformer backbone and learnable ROI-specific queries. These queries aggregate information through cross-attention to predict fMRI responses during natural scene viewing. TBEn significantly outperforms alternative factored encoding methods in predictive accuracy across various datasets and modalities. Furthermore, the model offers intrinsic interpretability by visualizing the attention-routing signals that drive specific categorical regions, suggesting a mechanistic account of how the human brain routes visual content based on relevance.
papers.authors: Hossein Adeli, Sun Minni, Nikolaus Kriegeskorte

papers.title: In Silico Mapping of Visual Categorical Selectivity Across the Whole Brain
papers.abstract: Elucidating the functional specialization of the human cortex often requires experimenter-defined hypotheses, which may overlook novel selectivities. This paper presents an in silico framework for the data-driven discovery of visual categorical selectivity across the entire brain. The methodology utilizes an encoder-decoder transformer featuring a brain-region-to-image-feature cross-attention mechanism to nonlinearly map deep network features to fMRI activation patterns. By pairing this brain encoder with diffusion-based generative models and large-scale datasets (ImageNet, BrainDIVE), the researchers synthesize optimal stimuli that maximize activation within specific cortical parcels. The approach reveals regions with complex compositional selectivity for diverse semantic concepts, validated through rigorous in silico statistical testing on held-out data. This pipeline enables the generation of novel, data-driven hypotheses about functional selectivity to be subsequently tested in empirical fMRI studies.
papers.venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS)
papers.authors: Ethan Hwang, Hossein Adeli, Wenxuan Guo, Andrew Luo, Nikolaus Kriegeskorte

papers.title: When do measured representational distances reflect the neural representational geometry?
papers.abstract: The fidelity of representational distances estimated from sparse (neural recordings) or pooled (fMRI voxels) measurements to the ground-truth neural representational geometry is a fundamental concern in systems neuroscience. Using theoretical analysis and simulations, the authors demonstrate that while random sampling of individual neurons yields undistorted distances, measurement channels that average across neurons with non-negative weights introduce linear distortions. These distortions overweight the population-mean dimension and attenuate signal dimensions orthogonal to it. Crucially, the study proves that removing the pattern mean from measured responses recovers the ground-truth representational geometry exactly in expectation. These results provide a formal justification for the use of correlation distance in representational similarity analysis and emphasize mean-centering as a vital step for accurately relating neural data to computational models.
papers.authors: Veronica Bossio Botero, Nikolaus Kriegeskorte

papers.title: Collective inference of the truth of propositions from crowd probability judgments
papers.abstract: Aggregating human probability judgments offers a pathway to collective intelligence, yet is hindered by individual miscalibration and cognitive biases. This study investigates the inference of objective truth from a collection of graded confidence ratings using data from 376 participants judging 1,200 general-knowledge claims. The authors introduce unsupervised and supervised probabilistic models that jointly estimate the truth of propositions and individual subject parameters for accuracy and miscalibration. Findings demonstrate that accounting for individual calibration significantly enhances the accuracy of collective inference compared to simple majority voting or uncalibrated averaging. This computational framework provides a robust method for online communities and collaborators to pool distributed intelligence with a well-calibrated sense of uncertainty, potentially facilitating the identification of reliable information in social networks.
papers.authors: Patrick Stinson, Jasper van den Bosch, Trenton Jerde, Nikolaus Kriegeskorte

papers.title: The Topology and Geometry of Neural Representations
papers.abstract: Characterizing brain representations requires descriptions that distinguish functional regions while remaining robust to idiosyncratic noise and neuroanatomical differences. This paper proposes topological representational similarity analysis (tRSA), an extension of traditional RSA that moves beyond geometric descriptions (RDMs) to characterize the topology of neural population codes. Using summary statistics derived from persistent homology, tRSA captures how activity patterns 'hang together' at an intermediate scale, reflecting the underlying manifold structure. Evaluation using fMRI data and artificial neural network simulations shows that topological signatures are more invariant across individuals than geometric signatures while maintaining high sensitivity to the computational function of cortical regions and network layers. This framework enables researchers to calibrate comparisons between brains and models to be sensitive to geometry, topology, or a combination of both.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS)
papers.authors: Baihan Lin, Nikolaus Kriegeskorte

0511.name: Nikolaus Weiskopf
0511.bio: Nikolaus Weiskopf is the Director of the Department of Neurophysics at the Max Planck Institute for Human Cognitive and Brain Sciences and holds honorary professorships at Leipzig University and University College London. Weiskopf’s research focuses on the development of 'in vivo histology,' a technique using quantitative magnetic resonance imaging (qMRI) to non-invasively map the human brain's microstructure, including myelin and iron content. By integrating high-resolution MRI with biophysical modeling, Weiskopf studies cortical laminar architecture and fine-scale brain connectivity. Their work bridges the gap between macroscopic neuroimaging and microscopic anatomy to investigate the structural foundations of brain function and pathology.
0511.research_direction: Dr. Weiskopf has recently been advancing high-resolution quantitative magnetic resonance imaging to investigate the mesoscopic and microstructural organization of the human brain. Their recent work explores how to optimize ultra-high-field 7T MRI and accelerated multi-parameter mapping protocols to reliably capture fine-grained tissue properties for both basic research and clinical neuro-oncology. Applying these cutting-edge neuroimaging techniques to visual neuroscience, they are investigating the anatomical geometry of short association fibers that connect V1 and V2 to understand their structural role in maintaining retinotopic maps. Furthermore, their research examines the feasibility of extending closed-loop fMRI neurofeedback to the scale of individual cortical layers and columns, aiming to selectively target feedforward and feedback neural channels.

papers.title: High-resolution quantitative T2 mapping of the human brain at 7 T using a multi-echo spin-echo sequence and dictionary-based modeling
papers.abstract: The authors present a method for sub-millimeter isotropic quantitative T2 mapping of the human brain at 7 Tesla using a multi-echo spin-echo (MESE) sequence combined with dictionary-based signal modeling. To mitigate the sensitivity of ultra-high-field MESE to B1+ inhomogeneities and stimulated echo effects, they employ Bloch equation-based simulations to generate an Echo Modulation Curve (EMC) dictionary. This dictionary accounts for slice-selective excitation and refocusing profiles, as well as the effects of finite pulse durations. The resulting high-resolution T2 maps demonstrate high spatial fidelity and reduced bias compared to conventional mono-exponential fitting, providing a robust tool for investigating tissue microstructure and pathological changes in vivo.
papers.authors: Jochen Schmidt, Dvir Radunsky, Patrick Scheibe, Carsten Jäger, Noam Ben-Eliezer, Robert Trampel, Nikolaus Weiskopf

papers.title: Short association fibres form topographic sheets in the human V1–V2 processing stream
papers.abstract: This study employs high-resolution diffusion-weighted MRI at 7 Tesla to characterize the anatomical organization of short association fibers (SAF), or U-fibers, connecting the primary (V1) and secondary (V2) visual cortices. By integrating in vivo neuroimaging with post-mortem histological validation using polarized light imaging (PLI), the researchers demonstrate that SAF are not randomly distributed but are organized into precise, topographic sheets that maintain the retinotopic map between cortical areas. The findings reveal a highly consistent geometry of these connections across individuals, suggesting that SAF provide a fundamental structural scaffold for mesoscopic cortical communication and hierarchical information processing.
papers.authors: Fakhereh Movahedian Attar, Evgeniya Kirilina, Denis Chaimow, Daniel Haenelt, Christian Schneider, Luke J. Edwards, Kerrin J. Pine, Carsten Jäger, Katja Reimann, Andreas Pohlmann, João Periquito, Tobias Streubel, Robert Trampel, Siawoosh Mohammadi, Thoralf Niendorf, Markus Morawski, Nikolaus Weiskopf

papers.title: Closed-loop fMRI at the mesoscopic scale of columns and layers: Can we do it and why would we want to?
papers.abstract: The authors explore the theoretical and technical feasibility of extending closed-loop functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) paradigms, such as neurofeedback and Brain-Computer Interfaces (BCI), to the mesoscopic scale of cortical columns and layers. They analyze the impact of sub-millimeter voxel sizes on temporal signal-to-noise ratio (tSNR) and the precision of online signal extraction. The paper argues that targeting layer-specific activity (e.g., feedback vs. feedforward channels) could significantly enhance the efficacy of endogenous neuromodulation and provide deeper insights into the volitional control of fine-grained neural circuits, while identifying key challenges in prospective motion correction and real-time hemodynamic modeling at high fields.
papers.venue: Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences
papers.authors: Denis Chaimow, Romy Lorenz, Nikolaus Weiskopf

papers.title: A fast protocol for multi-center, multi-parametric quantitative MRI studies in brain tumor patients using vendor sequences
papers.abstract: The researchers developed and validated a time-efficient Multi-Parameter Mapping (MPM) protocol for 3 Tesla MRI scanners, utilizing standard product sequences (multi-echo gradient echo and EPI) provided by scanner vendors to ensure cross-site reproducibility. The 8-minute protocol enables the simultaneous quantification of longitudinal relaxation rate (R1), effective transverse relaxation rate (R2*), proton density (PD), and quantitative susceptibility (chi). Validation was performed using a multi-compartment phantom and five healthy volunteers scanned at different sites, followed by a clinical feasibility study in four patients with brain tumors. The results demonstrate that the protocol provides reliable and reproducible markers of the tumor microenvironment, facilitating its application in large-scale multi-center clinical trials.
papers.authors: Dennis C. Thomas, Ulrike Nöth, Katharina Johanna Wenger, Ralf Deichmann, Nikolaus Weiskopf

papers.title: Multi-parameter quantitative mapping of R1, R2*, PD, and MTsat is reproducible when accelerated with Compressed SENSE
papers.abstract: This study assesses the impact of Compressed SENSE (CS) acceleration on the reproducibility and reliability of quantitative Multi-Parameter Mapping (MPM) of the human brain. Using a 3 Tesla scanner, the authors compare standard acquisition protocols with CS-accelerated versions for mapping R1, R2*, proton density (PD), and magnetization transfer saturation (MTsat). They evaluate the Coefficient of Variation (COV) and perform Bland-Altman analysis across repeat scans to determine if acceleration introduces systematic biases or increases measurement noise. The results indicate that Compressed SENSE can significantly reduce acquisition time while maintaining high parameter stability, supporting the translation of quantitative in vivo histology to routine clinical research settings.
papers.authors: Kerrin J. Pine, Luke J. Edwards, Pierre-Louis Bazin, Robert Trampel, Nikolaus Weiskopf

0513.name: Nilsu Atilgen
0513.lab_name: Reading, Eye-movements, Attention and Digital Interfaces Lab (READ-lab)
0513.bio: Nilsu Atilgen is an Assistant Professor of Psychology at Bilkent University and a Scientific Consultant for The Readability Consortium. Their research examines the cognitive and perceptual mechanisms of reading, specifically focusing on how sensory constraints such as visual crowding and peripheral vision influence fluency. Atilgen utilizes psychophysical methods and eye-tracking to study how typographic variables and digital display settings affect reading performance for individuals with dyslexia and low vision. This work connects vision science with human-computer interaction to address digital accessibility and inclusive information design.
0513.research_direction: Dr. Atilgen’s recent work explores the intersection of reading performance, applied artificial intelligence, and visual accessibility. They have recently been examining how typographic variables, such as font face and character spacing, influence reading speed and comprehension in children to assess the potential of personalized text formats. In the domain of low vision, their research investigates text accessibility by developing optical character recognition pipelines that simulate visual acuity and contrast sensitivity deficits to evaluate how multimodal AI models process degraded text compared to human readers. Beyond visual perception, they also study motor-based statistical learning, utilizing typing-to-dictation paradigms to map how adults acquire novel orthotactic sequence constraints during language production. Furthermore, Dr. Atilgen evaluates human-AI interaction in applied reading contexts, employing psychophysical measures to probe the readability of AI-generated educational materials and assessing the safety of using large language models to simplify complex clinical radiological reports for patients.

papers.title: Statistical learning of orthotactic constraints: Evidence from typing
papers.abstract: This study characterizes the acquisition of orthotactic constraints—the statistical regularities governing letter sequences—within the motor modality of typing. Across three experiments using a typing-to-dictation paradigm, the researchers demonstrate that adult participants rapidly internalize novel first-order and complex second-order sequential rules through production. The findings reveal that while learners successfully acquire coda-based constraints, acquisition of onset constraints is less consistent, suggesting that the underlying mechanism for new sequencing rules relies on a chaining-type process rather than hierarchical representation. Critically, the study provides evidence that orthotactic learning is functionally independent of phonotactic learning, supporting the existence of domain-general incremental learning principles that operate across distinct modalities of language production.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
papers.authors: Nilsu Atılgan, Nazbanou Nozari

papers.title: VI-OCR: “Visually Impaired” optical character recognition pipeline for text accessibility assessment
papers.abstract: This paper introduces VI-OCR, a novel assessment pipeline designed to quantify text accessibility for individuals with low vision by integrating computer vision with human psychophysical models. The framework bridges the gap between state-of-the-art optical character recognition (OCR) and low-vision research by employing an image degradation module that simulates visual acuity and contrast sensitivity function (CSF) deficits. By comparing the performance of multimodal large language models (such as Qwen2.5-VL and GPT-4o) to human data on degraded text stimuli (including MNREAD and ETDRS charts), the authors identify specific failure modes in AI models, such as difficulties with extreme contrast reduction. The results support the feasibility of using VI-OCR as an objective, automated tool for evaluating the visibility of digital and physical text environments.
papers.authors: Qingying Gao, Roberto Manduchi, Pradeep Y. Ramulu, Nilsu Atılgan, Donald C. Fletcher

papers.title: Accuracy of Information and References Using ChatGPT-3 for Retrieval of Clinical Radiological Information
papers.abstract: This research evaluates the reliability of Large Language Models (LLMs) in clinical communication, focusing on the retrieval and simplification of complex radiological data for patient education. The study assesses ChatGPT-3.5 and GPT-4's performance in generating anatomically accurate summaries of MRI and CT scan reports and cross-references them against established medical literature. Quantitative analysis of user perceptions from two demographic cohorts—young adults and seniors—reveals high levels of perceived usefulness and trust in AI-simplified content. However, technical evaluation highlights significant risks associated with bibliographic hallucinations and the fabrication of clinical references, emphasizing the need for robust verification mechanisms before LLMs can be integrated into clinical patient-facing workflows.
papers.authors: Md Mamunur Rashid, Nilsu Atılgan, Jonathan Dobres, Ben D. Sawyer

papers.title: Humanizing AI in Education: A Readability Comparison of LLM and Human-Created Educational Content
papers.abstract: This investigation utilizes psychophysical measures to compare the readability of educational materials authored by human experts versus those generated by Generative AI (specifically ChatGPT-3.5). The study employed 300-word passages at an 8th-grade reading level, measuring objective metrics including reading velocity (words per minute) and comprehension accuracy, alongside qualitative assessments of familiarity, interest, and perceived quality. Results indicate that LLM-generated content achieved higher reading speeds and comparable comprehension scores relative to traditional human-authored texts. The findings suggest that AI-driven content creation can meet or exceed human standards for readability, offering a scalable method for personalizing instructional materials to individual reader needs.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the Human Factors and Ergonomics Society Annual Meeting
papers.authors: Md Mamunur Rashid, Nilsu Atılgan, Jonathan Dobres, Stephanie Day, Veronika Penkova, Mert Küçük, Steven R. Clapp, Ben D. Sawyer

papers.title: The Influence of Format Readability on Children’s Reading Speed and Comprehension
papers.abstract: This study examines how typographic variables—specifically font face and character spacing—modulate reading performance in a pediatric population (grades 3–5). Researchers manipulated eight distinct fonts (serif vs. sans serif) and three levels of character spacing (narrow, normal, wide) while measuring reading speed and comprehension through narrative text passages. Linear mixed-effects modeling revealed that passages presented in Roboto and Arial yielded significantly higher reading velocities at the group level. On an individual basis, students demonstrated substantial performance gains when matched with their personal 'best-fit' font variation, without observing a speed–comprehension trade-off. The results emphasize the importance of individualized typographic formatting in educational technology to support fluency and literacy development.
papers.authors: Stephanie L. Day, Nilsu Atılgan, Amy E. Giroux, Ben D. Sawyer

0514.name: Nitzan Censor
0514.department: School of Psychological Sciences and Sagol School of Neuroscience
0514.bio: Nitzan Censor is a Professor at Tel Aviv University investigating the neurobehavioral mechanisms underlying human perceptual and motor learning. Their research utilizes behavioral psychophysics, non-invasive brain stimulation, and functional neuroimaging to examine how skill-based memories are formed, modified, and consolidated within neural representation systems. Censor studies the temporal dynamics of memory reactivation and the role of offline consolidation in learning and memory modification. Their work also addresses the interaction between visual memory representations and computational models such as convolutional neural networks to decode the dynamics of human vision over time.
0514.research_direction: Dr. Censor's recent work explores the temporal dynamics, consolidation, and targeted modulation of both visual and emotional memories. Within visual processing, they have recently been investigating the evolution of visual memory representations over time using convolutional neural networks, as well as testing whether brief memory reactivations can allow highly specific visual perceptual learning to generalize to untrained spatial locations and features. In parallel, their research probes various mechanisms for down-regulating persistent, aversive visual memories and traumatic experiences. To address this, they employ behavioral directed-forgetting paradigms to examine how negative visual contexts interact with the top-down cognitive control of interleaved verbal information, alongside clinical approaches utilizing transcranial magnetic stimulation to disrupt the reconsolidation of reactivated traumatic memories in patients with PTSD.

papers.title: Hippocampal-network transcranial magnetic stimulation to target reactivated intrusive memories: A proof-of-concept study in PTSD treatment
papers.abstract: This proof-of-concept clinical investigation evaluates the therapeutic potential of non-invasive neuromodulation targeting the hippocampal-cortical network to mitigate intrusive traumatic memories in patients with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). Grounded in the memory reconsolidation framework, traumatic memories were briefly reactivated before the application of network-targeted transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) intended to disrupt the restabilization of the memory trace during its labile state. The research measures primary endpoints regarding the frequency and emotional distress associated with involuntary re-experiencing symptoms. The findings indicate that circuit-specific stimulation applied during the post-reactivation reconsolidation window can successfully attenuate the pathological strength and persistence of traumatic intrusive memories.
papers.authors: Or Dezachyo, Noga Yair, Noga Mendelovich, Niv Tik, Daniel S. Pine, Haggai Sharon, Ido Tavor, Yair Bar-Haim, Nitzan Censor

papers.title: Targeting memory of embedded positive verbal content indirectly modulates negative visual memory
papers.abstract: This study explores the indirect down-regulation of persistent negative visual memories by directly modulating interleaved positive verbal information using a list-method directed forgetting (DF) paradigm. Participants encoded sequences where positive words were embedded within negative pictorial contexts and were subsequently cued to either remember or forget the verbal content. The experimental results demonstrate that the intentional forgetting of positive verbal items significantly attenuated the mnemonic fidelity of associated negative visual context. Furthermore, an additional experiment showed that simple instructions to remember verbal content can indirectly reduce negative visual memory strength even in the absence of explicit verbal retrieval, suggesting that top-down verbal mnemonic control can be leveraged to regulate aversive emotional representations.
papers.authors: Stas Kozak, Taly Markovits, Noam Hacohen, Yair Bar-Haim, Nitzan Censor

papers.title: Brief memory reactivations enable generalization of offline visual perceptual learning mechanisms
papers.abstract: Visual perceptual learning (VPL) is typically constrained by high specificity to trained stimulus features and retinotopic locations, usually requiring extensive multi-day training. This investigation tests whether brief memory reactivations—consisting of only five trials—can trigger offline consolidation processes that facilitate learning generalization. Utilizing a texture discrimination task (TDT), the study demonstrates that brief reactivation of a previously consolidated memory not only maintains performance gains at the trained location but also promotes significant generalization to untrained visual field locations and stimulus orientations. These results point to a highly efficient, reactivation-induced plasticity mechanism that transforms specific procedural skills into flexible, generalizable representations, bypassing the limitations of standard practice-dependent plasticity.
papers.authors: Taly Kondat, Yuka Sasaki, Takeo Watanabe, Nitzan Censor

papers.title: Convolutional neural networks uncover the dynamics of human visual memory representations over time
papers.abstract: To investigate the temporal evolution of human visual memory representations, the authors applied a hierarchical computational framework utilizing convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to analyze the impact of distractor interference. By quantifying memory strength relative to distractors sharing varying degrees of similarity with targets across CNN layer depths, the researchers found that visual working memory initially utilizes a broad spectrum of distributed low-level and high-level representations. However, across delays of minutes to 24 hours (post-sleep), memory representations undergo a systematic transition toward high-level, semantic-heavy structures. This transformation reflects a qualitative shift in the neocortical and hippocampal systems, where detailed episodic visual features are integrated into abstract conceptual schemas over time.
papers.authors: Eden Zohar, Stas Kozak, Dekel Abeles, Maya Shahar, Nitzan Censor

papers.title: Memory modulation: Dominance of negative visual context over neutral verbal memory
papers.abstract: This research examines the limits of inhibitory memory control when neutral verbal items are encoded within high-arousal negative visual contexts. Employing a directed forgetting paradigm, the study found that the presence of negative visual context abolished the typical mnemonic advantage provided by 'remember' instructions relative to 'forget' instructions for interleaved words. Negative visual memories themselves proved highly persistent and resistant to indirect modulation across time, including after a 24-hour consolidation interval. These findings demonstrate the prioritized processing of aversive visual information, which overrides top-down control of neutral interleaved content and highlights the significant challenges of down-regulating traumatic or negative memories through standard cognitive-control mechanisms.
papers.authors: Stas Kozak, Noa Herz, Maya Tocker, Yair Bar-Haim, Nitzan Censor

0515.name: Nuttida Rungratsameetaweemana
0515.bio: Nuttida Rungratsameetaweemana is an Assistant Professor of Biomedical Engineering at Columbia University and the principal investigator of the Systems Intelligence Lab. Their research investigates the neural computations and coding schemes that facilitate adaptive cognitive processes, such as flexible decision-making, memory maintenance, and contextual information processing. By integrating biologically constrained recurrent neural networks with experimental data from human intracranial recordings and functional neuroimaging, Rungratsameetaweemana characterizes the mechanisms of goal-directed information transformation across the cortical hierarchy. Their work demonstrates that early sensory regions play an active, task-dependent role in shaping neural representations to support flexible behaviors.
0515.research_direction: Dr. Rungratsameetaweemana has recently been investigating the neural circuit mechanisms underlying working memory, cognitive flexibility, and top-down control across both biological and artificial systems. Using techniques ranging from fMRI representational similarity analysis to single-trial spiking data in neurosurgical patients, their recent work explores how dynamic top-down categorization rules reorganize sensory representations in the visual cortex, and how transient, cell-type-specific bursting supports information maintenance. To understand the computational principles of these cognitive processes, they are also probing recurrent neural networks to see how feedback pathways and disinhibitory signaling enable flexible context-dependent decision-making while mitigating representational biases. Finally, their research examines the intersection of neuroscience and artificial intelligence, testing whether transferring latent dynamics from human electrophysiological data can serve as a biological teacher signal to optimize artificial sensory and decision models.

papers.title: Neural heterogeneity shapes the temporal structure of human working memory
papers.abstract: The maintenance of information within working memory (WM) has traditionally been linked to persistent population activity, though continuous neural discharge is energetically demanding and often inconsistent with observed cortical heterogeneity. Utilizing single-trial spiking analysis of 902 neurons from 21 neurosurgical patients, we demonstrate that WM maintenance is supported by transient, burst-like coordinated activity rather than sustained firing. Cross-temporal decoding revealed localized generalization, with decoding accuracy scaling with the width of temporal windows, suggesting that apparent persistence emerges from temporally interleaved activity across the neural ensemble. A feature-based cell-type classifier identified pyramidal neurons as the primary carriers of content-specific information during burst events, while interneurons were strongly modulated by memory load and behavioral variables, indicating a flexible and metabolically efficient circuit substrate for information retention.
papers.authors: Daria Kussovska, Robert Kim, Nuttida Rungratsameetaweemana

papers.title: Feedback promotes efficient-coding while attenuating bias in recurrent neural networks
papers.abstract: While environmental regularities facilitate efficient-coding in human decision-making, non-uniform stimulus statistics often induce deleterious representational biases in artificial neural networks, compromising generalization. We investigated this trade-off using a three-layer hierarchical continuous-time recurrent neural network (ctRNN) trained on biased stimulus distributions. We found that the networks preferentially allocated representational resources to high-probability stimuli across the hierarchy, in line with efficient-coding principles. Critically, the selective ablation of top-down feedback connections magnified these biases and suppressed the representation of rare stimuli. These results suggest that while hierarchical models exploit statistical regularities for efficiency, feedback pathways are essential for regulating representational bias and maintaining the robust processing of low-probability inputs.
papers.authors: Holly Kular, Robert Kim, John Serences, Nuttida Rungratsameetaweemana

papers.title: Brain2Model Transfer: Training sensory and decision models with human neural activity as a teacher
papers.abstract: Transfer learning typically utilizes large pre-trained artificial models, but human neural activity provides a potentially superior source of low-dimensional, abstract representations optimized for sensorimotor tasks. We introduce Brain2Model Transfer (B2M), a framework where human electrophysiological data collected during sensory and decision-making tasks serves as a teacher signal for training artificial neural networks. We propose two strategies: Brain Contrastive Transfer, aligning network activations with neural signals via a contrastive objective, and Brain Latent Transfer, projecting task-specific latent dynamics via supervised regression. In applications including memory-based decision-making in RNNs and scene reconstruction in VAEs, B2M-guided models exhibited significantly faster convergence and higher predictive accuracy than those trained in isolation, demonstrating the utility of biological representations for enhancing artificial learning.
papers.authors: Tomas Gallo Aquino, Victoria Liu, Habiba Azab, Raissa Mathura, Andrew J Watrous, Eleonora Bartoli, Benjamin Y Hayden, Paul Sajda, Sameer A Sheth, Nuttida Rungratsameetaweemana

papers.title: Categorization dynamically alters representations in human visual cortex
papers.abstract: Human cognitive flexibility relies on the dynamic reconfiguration of selective attention to extract abstract features from complex stimuli based on varying goals. We examined the adaptation of sensory representations in the human visual cortex as participants categorized novel shapes according to different linear and non-linear boundaries. Using fMRI and representational similarity analysis (RSA), we found that task-specific categorization rules dynamically reorganize population-level codes to prioritize goal-relevant features. These findings demonstrate that sensory representations are not static but are actively sharpened by top-down constraints, providing a mechanistic link between task-dependent feedback and the flexible mapping of sensory inputs onto abstract behavioral categories.
papers.authors: Margaret M. Henderson, John T. Serences, Nuttida Rungratsameetaweemana

papers.title: Disinhibitory signaling enables flexible coding of top-down information
papers.abstract: The ability to map identical sensory inputs to different actions based on context is a hallmark of cognitive flexibility, yet its circuit-level implementation remains poorly understood. We investigated the role of disinhibitory signaling within recurrent neural networks (RNNs) performing context-dependent decision tasks. Our results indicate that disinhibitory pathways—specifically those involving interneuron-mediated gating—facilitate the flexible representation of top-down information by modulating the gain of specific neural populations. This mechanism enables the dynamic reorganization of representational manifolds, preventing interference between conflicting task mappings. We conclude that disinhibition serves as a fundamental computational substrate for hierarchical control and the implementation of context-aware behavioral flexibility.
papers.authors: Tomas G. Aquino, Robert Kim, Nuttida Rungratsameetaweemana

0516.name: Oakyoon Cha
0516.lab_name: DCANT Lab (Dynamic Cognition, Attention, & Neural Timing Lab)
0516.bio: Oakyoon Cha is an Assistant Professor of Psychology at Sogang University and director of the DCANT Lab, following a tenure as a faculty member at Sungshin Women's University. Cha’s research utilizes psychophysics, EEG, and computational modeling to investigate the mechanisms of visual awareness, with an emphasis on ensemble perception and perceptual rhythms. They examine how the human visual system summarizes complex information from large stimulus sets and how neural oscillations contribute to a continuous visual experience. Cha’s work also explores individual differences in object recognition and the underlying domain-general abilities involved in statistical visual processing.
0516.research_direction: Dr. Cha has recently been investigating visual ensemble perception, specifically expanding beyond basic summary metrics like mean and variance to explore how the visual system extracts categorical frequency statistics from complex, multidimensional stimuli. Their recent work uses behavioral covariance tasks with faces and novel geometric shapes to ask whether observers can reliably track the most prevalent category (the mode) and the number of distinct categories (diversity) through a domain-general ensemble mechanism. Alongside this research, they are developing computational methods to isolate the behavioral signatures of intrinsic neural rhythms from psychophysical duration data. By creating a modeling framework that fits rhythmic cumulative distribution functions to measurements like response times and binocular rivalry dominance phases, Dr. Cha aims to better decode discrete temporal periodicities, such as theta and alpha oscillations, directly from behavioral time courses.

papers.title: Categorical frequency judgments as effective ensemble judgments for object features
papers.abstract: Visual ensemble perception research has predominantly concentrated on univariate summary metrics, such as mean and variance, which often fail to account for the multidimensional complexity inherent in natural visual stimuli. This investigation examines whether categorical frequency statistics—specifically the mode (the most prevalent category within a set) and diversity (the number of distinct categories)—operate as viable ensemble representations for complex visual entities. In Study 1, the shared variance between mode identification and diversity discrimination across facial identities was evaluated, establishing that observers reliably track categorical distributions of facial identities. In Study 2, the evaluation of mode extraction was extended across disparate visual classes, specifically comparing facial identities with novel geometric silhouettes (blobs). The findings reveal significant shared behavioral covariance across categorical frequency tasks regardless of visual category, indicating that categorical summary statistics engage domain-general ensemble mechanisms that operate effectively across high-dimensional object features.
papers.authors: Oakyoon Cha

papers.title: Procedure for extracting temporal structure embedded within psychophysical data
papers.abstract: Although extensive neurophysiological evidence demonstrates that perceptual and cognitive processing is modulated by intrinsic neural rhythms (such as theta and alpha oscillations), isolating behavioral markers of these rhythmic dynamics from psychophysical data remains technically challenging. To resolve these methodological limitations, the authors introduce the Parametric Analysis of Temporal Structure (PATS) framework. PATS models duration data—such as response times and multistable perceptual dominance phases in binocular rivalry—by fitting a rhythmic cumulative distribution function (rCDF) that incorporates periodic sinusoidal modulations into standard cumulative distribution functions. The method quantifies the incremental variance accounted for by the oscillatory component relative to a non-rhythmic baseline and rescales fitted oscillation amplitudes accordingly. Psychophysical experiments and simulations indicate that PATS exhibits high statistical power and parameter stability even when applied to small sample sizes, establishing a robust computational pipeline for decoding discrete temporal periodicities in behavioral time courses.
papers.authors: Oakyoon Cha, Randolph Blake

0517.name: OH-SANG KWON
0517.institution: Ulsan National Institute of Science and Technology
0517.bio: Oh-Sang Kwon is an Associate Professor at UNIST whose research examines the computational principles of human perception and action. Kwon utilizes Bayesian modeling and psychophysical techniques to investigate how the brain integrates sensory signals with internal models of scene statistics to form inferences. They have modeled visual illusions as products of rational inference and developed accounts for the interaction between motion and position perception. Current research focuses on the effects of sensory history on perception and the cognitive and perceptual changes associated with aging.
0517.research_direction: Dr. Kwon has recently been exploring the computational and psychophysical mechanisms underlying visual, temporal, and multisensory perception. Their recent work investigates how the human visual system processes time and motion, ranging from how attentional event-termination cues might distort perceived duration to the low-level temporal filters that drive twinkle perception in luminance and chromatic flickering stimuli. They are also examining applied visual psychophysics, utilizing observer models to evaluate how display parameters like refresh rates and duty ratios interact with pursuit and fixation eye movements to generate motion artifacts. Across these diverse topics, Dr. Kwon utilizes normative modeling and artificial neural networks to probe complex perceptual judgments, including how prior visual context integrates with vestibular signals during heading estimation and how generative frameworks might explain the natural emergence of attractive and repulsive perceptual biases under sensory uncertainty.

papers.title: Environmental motion presented ahead of self-motion modulates heading direction estimation
papers.abstract: This study employs a normative computational framework to investigate how pre-movement visual context influences heading direction estimation in non-stationary environments. Using a novel paradigm on a motion platform, the authors demonstrated that environmental motion occurring immediately prior to self-motion significantly biases human heading perception. The results are explained by a contextual causal inference (CCI) model that optimally integrates vestibular and visual signals by accounting for the causal likelihood of environmental motion stability. The CCI model successfully predicts behavioral biases and variability by balancing the reliability of current sensory measurements against temporal contextual priors, outperforming alternative heuristic and winner-take-all architectures.
papers.authors: Liana Nafisa Saftari, Jongmin Moon, Oh-Sang Kwon

papers.title: Influence of Temporal Frequency, Duty Ratio, and Eye-Stimulus Dynamics on Motion Artifacts
papers.abstract: This research characterizes the complex interactions between display temporal parameters and eye movement dynamics that give rise to motion artifacts in electronic displays. Through psychophysical experiments and a normative observer model, the study evaluates how refresh rates and duty ratios modulate perceived discrepancies between sampled and continuous images. The findings reveal that while increased temporal frequencies consistently mitigate artifacts, the effect of duty ratio is highly sensitive to eye-stimulus dynamics—specifically whether the observer is in a pursuit or fixation state. The results provide quantitative constraints for display engineering to achieve perceptual indistinguishability between discrete and continuous motion stimuli.
papers.venue: SID Symposium Digest of Technical Papers
papers.authors: Chang-Yeong Han, Eun Cho, Hyosun Kim, Oh-Sang Kwon

papers.title: Temporal processing underlying transient twinkle perception in luminance and chromatic stimuli
papers.abstract: Transient twinkle perception (TTP) describes the detection of frequency transitions between sequentially presented flickering stimuli that are perceived as steady. This study contrasts monophasic Gaussian and bi-phasic temporal integration models to account for TTP across luminance and equiluminant chromatic conditions. Empirical results indicate that luminance-based TTP magnitudes are best explained by a bi-phasic temporal filter, whereas chromatic TTP aligns more closely with a monophasic Gaussian filter. These findings suggest that TTP is not a specialized perceptual mechanism but an emergent outcome of low-level visual temporal processing within the human visual system.
papers.authors: Chang-Yeong Han, Seonggyu Choe, Eun Cho, Hyo-sun Kim, Oh-Sang Kwon

papers.title: Attractive and Repulsive Perceptual Biases Naturally Emerge in Generative Adversarial Inference
papers.abstract: Human perceptual estimates exhibit a characteristic bias reversal, shifting toward prior expectations under high sensory uncertainty and away from them under high stimulus certainty. We propose Generative Adversarial Inference (GAI), an end-to-end learned network that unifies efficient coding and Bayesian inference. GAI utilizes a three-player adversarial game to learn latent representations and implicit posterior mappings from sensory inputs without handcrafted priors or likelihoods. The model spontaneously reproduces the full transition from attractive to repulsive biases and recovers Fisher information profiles predicted by efficient coding theory, providing a neurally plausible account of perceptual distortions.
papers.authors: Hyun-Jun Jeon, Hansol Choi, Oh-Sang Kwon

papers.title: An event-termination cue causes perceived time to dilate
papers.abstract: This study identifies the role of event-termination knowledge as a significant factor in temporal distortion. Using a time reproduction task featuring a rotating clock hand, the authors found that the presence of an explicit termination cue caused subjects to significantly overestimate the duration of the event (time dilation). Computational analysis based on an attention-theory-of-time perception revealed that the magnitude of dilation is not a function of total event duration or spatial distance, but rather the time the stimulus spends within a field of attention generated by the termination cue. These findings support an attentional gate model where the rate of temporal unit accumulation is modulated by localized attentional focus.
papers.authors: Seonggyu Choe, Oh-Sang Kwon

0518.name: Okihide Hikosaka
0518.bio: Okihide Hikosaka is an investigator at the National Eye Institute, where they head the Neuronal Networks Section within the Laboratory of Sensorimotor Research. Hikosaka’s research focuses on the neurophysiological mechanisms of the basal ganglia, specifically their role in controlling saccadic eye movements, habit formation, and reward-based decision-making. Utilizing electrophysiological recordings and optogenetic manipulations in non-human primates, Hikosaka’s work has identified parallel circuits that independently process stable long-term values versus flexible short-term reward associations. These findings regarding the lateral habenula and dopamine neuron diversity address mechanisms of motivational control and their relationship to neurological and psychiatric conditions such as Parkinson's disease and depression.
0518.research_direction: Dr. Hikosaka's recent work explores the intricate subcortical and basal ganglia circuits that govern value-based decision-making and oculomotor control in macaque monkeys. Utilizing single-unit recordings and pharmacological interventions, they have recently been investigating the specific roles of structures like the subthalamic nucleus and substantia nigra pars reticulata in mediating action facilitation and the reactive inhibition of planned saccades. Their research also examines how reward signals are converted into saccadic vigor within the superior colliculus, applying retrograde optogenetics to map how integrated sensorimotor commands from the frontal eye field converge onto these downstream midbrain targets. Furthermore, they are probing the broader motivational architecture of the brain by interrogating how regions like the periaqueductal gray continuously track reward expectancy during choice tasks, even in the face of unexpected omissions.

papers.title: Multiple groups of neurons in the superior colliculus convert value signals into saccadic vigor
papers.abstract: Saccadic eye movements toward high-value targets are characterized by increased vigor, including shorter reaction times and higher peak velocities.
