This study investigated the neuronal substrates of this modulation by recording from four distinct subtypes of superior colliculus (SC) neurons—visual, visuomotor, motor, and tonic—in macaque monkeys during a value-based saccade task. Findings demonstrate that object value positively modulates the activity of visual, visuomotor, and motor neurons. Using a temporal decomposition bootstrapping method, the researchers identified three distinct response phases: early visual (EVIS), late visual (LVIS), and pre-saccadic motor (PreSAC). Notably, value modulation was significant in the LVIS and PreSAC phases but absent during EVIS, suggesting that reward signals impact later visual processing and motor transformation rather than initial sensory encoding. Furthermore, the study identified a novel class of tonic neurons that decrease firing at object onset and remain inhibited through saccade execution, potentially facilitating movement via the disinhibition of other SC neuronal populations.
papers.authors: Atul Gopal, Whitney Griggs, Hidetoshi Amita, Okihide Hikosaka

papers.title: Beyond the Brake: the Subthalamic Nucleus Predominantly Facilitates Action in Non-human Primates
papers.abstract: The classical hyperdirect pathway model identifies the subthalamic nucleus (STN) as a primary source of action suppression. However, this study challenges that view through single-unit recordings in macaques performing a value-based choice task. Results indicate that approximately 89% of task-related STN neurons exhibit activity consistent with action facilitation rather than suppression. Cluster analysis identified three distinct populations, with two large facilitative clusters whose firing rates and response latencies predicted saccadic reaction times on a trial-by-trial basis. Only a minor third cluster showed activity consistent with action suppression. These results suggest a dual-function model in which the STN primarily facilitates desired actions, likely providing crucial excitatory drive to structures like the globus pallidus external segment (GPe), effectively reevaluating the STN's role in the oculomotor and cognitive control circuits of the basal ganglia.
papers.authors: Atsushi Yoshida, Richard J. Krauzlis, Okihide Hikosaka

papers.title: Retrograde Optogenetics Reveals Functional Convergence within a Corticotectal Pathway of Non-Human Primates
papers.abstract: The functional organization of prefrontal outputs to motor-related subcortical structures remains a point of contention in systems neuroscience. This study employed retrograde optogenetics in awake macaques to interrogate the corticotectal projection from the frontal eye field (FEF) to the superior colliculus (SC). Optical activation of this pathway evoked robust, contralateral saccades and specifically modulated reaction times, establishing its causal role in saccade generation. Opto-tagging of FEF neurons projecting to the SC identified a heterogeneous population of visual, visuomotor, and motor neurons. These diverse cortical outputs converged primarily onto motor-related neurons within the SC. The findings support a visuomotor convergence model where mixed prefrontal signals drive motor-selective subcortical targets, resolving the debate over whether prefrontal outputs carry pure motor commands or integrated sensory-motor signals.
papers.authors: Xuefei Yu, Atul Gopal, Ken-Ichi Inoue, Martin Bohlen, Genevieve Kuczewski, Marc A. Sommer, Hendrikje Nienborg, Masahiko Takada, Okihide Hikosaka

papers.title: Contribution of glutamatergic projections to neurons in the nonhuman primate substantia nigra pars reticulata for reactive inhibition
papers.abstract: Reactive inhibition, the rapid cancellation of an initiated motor plan, is essential for behavioral flexibility. Recording from the lateral substantia nigra pars reticulata (SNr) in macaques, this study found that individual SNr neurons exhibit bidirectional value coding, increasing activity during object rejection and decreasing activity during selection. Pharmacological blockade of glutamatergic inputs in the lateral SNr disrupted this inhibitory control, leading to impaired suppression of reflexive saccades and shortened reaction times for both high- and low-value objects. The results demonstrate that excitatory glutamatergic projections, likely originating from the subthalamic nucleus (STN), provide the necessary drive for SNr-mediated action suppression. This highlights a conserved basal ganglia mechanism where the SNr serves as an integration hub for facilitative and suppressive inputs to dynamically regulate motor output to the superior colliculus.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS)
papers.authors: Atsushi Yoshida, Okihide Hikosaka

papers.title: Periaqueductal gray passes over disappointment and signals continuity of remaining reward expectancy
papers.abstract: The periaqueductal gray (PAG) is typically known for its role in defensive and nociceptive processing, but its function in reward-based motivation is less clear. This study used single-neuron recordings in macaque monkeys to examine PAG activity during a task where expected rewards were occasionally omitted. Contrary to predictions of reward prediction error (RPE) signaling, PAG neurons did not encode disappointment or negative errors. Instead, they exhibited persistent activity that tracked the continuity of remaining reward expectancy throughout the trial. This suggests that the PAG provides a stable motivational representation that sustains goal-directed behavior despite transient negative outcomes, distinguishing its role from the more flexible value coding found in midbrain dopamine systems.
papers.authors: Hyunchan Lee, Okihide Hikosaka

0520.name: Oliver Layton
0520.bio: Oliver W. Layton is an Associate Professor of Computer Science at Colby College. Their research focuses on the neural mechanisms underlying human navigation and self-motion perception, combining large-scale dynamical neural modeling with psychophysical experiments to investigate how the primate brain processes optic flow. Layton developed the Competitive Dynamics model to simulate interactions between cortical areas such as MSTd, MT, and V1, exploring how these systems facilitate figure-ground segregation and world-relative object motion recovery. Their current work evaluates the efficacy of accuracy-optimized convolutional neural networks in modeling the primate dorsal stream and applies bio-inspired algorithms to autonomous navigation.
0520.research_direction: Dr. Layton's recent work investigates the neural and computational mechanisms underlying self-motion perception, focusing heavily on how optic flow is processed in the dorsal visual stream. Their research frequently compares artificial neural networks against biological benchmarks in primate cortical areas like MT and MSTd, exploring whether task-driven objectives—such as heading accuracy optimization—or unsupervised learning rules like autoencoding best capture true neurophysiological tuning. To probe the origins of these biological representations, they have recently been examining how architectural inductive biases, including ReLU-driven activation sparsity and biologically parameterized motion inputs, influence network robustness to sensory perturbations. Alongside these machine learning approaches, Dr. Layton employs human psychophysical experiments coupled with recurrent network modeling to study the temporal stability of heading perception, specifically testing how the visual system accumulates evidence and utilizes hysteresis to bridge dynamic disruptions in visual motion.

papers.title: For MSTd, Autoencoding is all you need
papers.abstract: While goal-driven artificial neural networks (ANNs) effectively account for functional representations across the primate ventral visual stream, their applicability to the dorsal visual stream remains unresolved. We examined how objective functions and architectural inductive biases affect neural alignment to the dorsal medial superior temporal area (MSTd), a cortical region selective for full-field optic flow patterns and implicated in self-motion perception. We benchmarked 54 feedforward and convolutional ANNs alongside Non-negative Matrix Factorization (NNMF) against neurophysiological tuning benchmarks in macaque MSTd. Models were trained on the TR360 optic flow dataset using either a supervised heading and rotation estimation task (accuracy-optimized) or an unsupervised reconstruction task (autoencoding), operating on either raw velocity vector fields or biologically parameterized middle temporal (MT) speed- and direction-tuned inputs. Across all evaluations (Earth Mover's Distance across 3D translation and rotation azimuth and elevation tuning distributions), accuracy-optimized ANNs failed to reproduce biological tuning, developing severe backward-azimuth biases. Conversely, linear autoencoders operating over MT-like motion afferents yielded state-of-the-art alignment with MSTd neurophysiology without requiring non-negativity or sparsity constraints. Furthermore, systematically varying hidden-layer capacity revealed that strong dimensionality reduction is not requisite for biological tuning alignment, suggesting that dorsal stream area MSTd is organized around unsupervised reconstructive representation rather than behavioral task-accuracy maximization.
papers.authors: Oliver W. Layton, Scott T. Steinmetz

papers.title: Artificial Neural Networks and the Visual System: A Brief History and Future Directions
papers.abstract: This review explores the historical and conceptual synergy between the architecture of artificial neural networks (ANNs) and the computational principles of the biological visual system. Over the past half-century, developments in ANN design have been deeply informed by neurophysiological findings, particularly the hierarchical organization of the primate visual cortex. The article traces this evolution from early models like the Neocognitron to contemporary convolutional neural networks (CNNs), which have demonstrated remarkable success in modeling response properties in the ventral stream. Conversely, the paper examines how these computational models now serve as powerful tools for generating testable hypotheses in visual neuroscience. Finally, the author discusses future directions for bridging the gap between biological vision and machine intelligence, emphasizing the potential for biologically inspired constraints to improve the robustness and interpretability of vision models.
papers.venue: VISION (The Journal of the Vision Society of Japan)
papers.authors: Oliver W. Layton

papers.title: ReLU, Sparseness, and the Encoding of Optic Flow in Neural Networks
papers.abstract: The rectified linear unit (ReLU) activation function is widely posited to promote biologically plausible, sparse population coding in deep neural networks. Here, we examined whether ReLU-driven activation sparseness improves the performance, robustness, and biological fidelity of multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) and convolutional neural networks (CNNs) optimized to estimate 3D translational and rotational self-motion from optic flow. Across 3,015 test stimuli in the TR360 benchmark, both CNNs and MLPs reliably decoded camera translation (within 5.5° MAE; 236.9°² MSE) and rotation (within 0.3°/s MAE; 0.2°²/s² MSE) irrespective of whether activations were rectified linear (ReLU) or non-sparse (e.g., ELU, GELU, tanh, linear). We systematically challenged the models across perturbed self-motion regimes, including additive random-direction noise, severe spatial subsampling (up to 99% vector dropout), and locally discrepant flow generated by independently moving objects. While ReLU architectures exhibited high lifetime and population sparseness, networks with continuous, non-sparse representations exhibited equivalent or superior robustness to noise and motion artifacts. Furthermore, profiling single-unit tuning preferences revealed that task accuracy optimization across all architectures induced pronounced, non-biological biases toward backward headings, indicating that neither task optimization nor ReLU-mediated sparsity is sufficient to account for biological optic flow representations.
papers.authors: Oliver W. Layton, Siyuan Peng, Scott T. Steinmetz

papers.title: Accuracy optimized neural networks do not effectively model optic flow tuning in brain area MSTd
papers.abstract: Goal-driven convolutional neural networks (CNNs) optimized for classification have proven remarkably successful at capturing receptive field properties in the ventral stream, but whether task-accuracy optimization accounts for tuning in the dorsal motion pathway remains undetermined. We evaluated how well accuracy-optimized CNNs trained to infer 3D observer translation and rotation from optic flow capture the neurophysiological response properties of neurons in dorsal medial superior temporal area (MSTd). CNN representations were contrasted with a classic unsupervised model based on Non-Negative Matrix Factorization (NNMF) applied to simulated middle temporal (MT) population responses. Although CNNs achieved high metric accuracy on novel optic flow stimuli (5.5° translation MAE; 0.2° rotation MAE; 236.9°² translation MSE), their hidden units exhibited distinct departures from primate MSTd neurophysiology, most notably a severe skew toward backward translation preferences. In contrast, the NNMF model successfully matched the 3D heading and rotation tuning distributions and peak discriminability observed in empirical MSTd recordings, despite showing lower decoding accuracy on compound translation-plus-rotation flows. Enforcing non-negative weights and sparse coding constraints within accuracy-optimized CNN architectures failed to recover biological MSTd tuning profiles, demonstrating that standard task-optimization objectives are insufficient to explain receptive field formation in primate MSTd.
papers.authors: Oliver W. Layton, Scott T. Steinmetz

papers.title: Temporal stability of human heading perception
papers.abstract: Accurate estimation of self-motion direction (heading) from optic flow requires balancing sensitivity to dynamic visual changes against resilience to transient sensory fluctuations caused by visual clutter or moving objects. We tested whether the primate visual system maintains heading estimates via temporal evidence accumulation and hysteresis. In psychophysical paradigms, human observers judged their final heading after experiencing simulated linear self-motion that underwent an abrupt direction switch (switch angles between 5° and 30°). Judgments exhibited systematic attractive biases toward the pre-switch trajectory, with bias magnitude increasing significantly when post-switch optic flow exposure was reduced from 500 ms to 250 ms. Inserting blank blackout intervals before, between, or after heading switches confirmed that heading representations persist across temporary cessations of visual input. Simulations using the Competitive Dynamics (CD) neural model of cortical areas MT and MSTd—which incorporates distance-weighted template pooling and recurrent competitive feedback—closely matched human judgment biases and temporal persistence without invoking ad hoc differential motion filters. These findings establish that recurrent network dynamics in MSTd provide the temporal inertia necessary to stabilize self-motion perception against momentary environmental noise.
papers.authors: Mufaddal Ali, Eli Decker, Oliver W. Layton

0521.name: Olivia S. Cheung
0521.bio: Cheung is an Assistant Professor who studies the neurocognitive mechanisms underlying high-level visual perception and the acquisition of perceptual expertise. They utilize a multimodal approach integrating behavioral psychophysics, functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), and computational modeling to examine how visual features and conceptual knowledge interact to represent categories such as faces, objects, and musical notation. Cheung’s research focuses on the neural malleability of the ventral stream, specifically exploring how experience and learning shape category-selective brain regions. Additionally, they investigate the influence of socio-emotional factors and implicit biases on visual recognition and holistic face processing.
0521.research_direction: Dr. Cheung's recent work explores the perceptual mechanisms and socio-cognitive factors underlying high-level face processing and rapid social evaluation. They have recently been investigating the mechanics of holistic face processing by isolating its distinct facilitatory and inhibitory components across classic behavioral paradigms. Additionally, their research examines how top-down influences, such as implicit social bias and intergroup contact, interact with bottom-up morphological cues to shape both the configural encoding of out-group faces and the appraisal of traits like trustworthiness. Finally, they are exploring how intrinsic facial morphology drives complex social inferences, using computer-generated models to test how features associated with masculinity and femininity influence judgments of politician competence and predictions of electoral success.

papers.title: Two faces of holistic face processing: Facilitation and interference underlying part-whole and composite effects
papers.abstract: Holistic processing, characterized by the obligatory perceptual integration of disparate facial features into a unified gestalt, is widely considered a defining hallmark of face perception. Established behavioral paradigms—specifically the part-whole task, the standard partial-design composite task, and the complete composite face task—are conventionally used to quantify these holistic effects. However, empirical discrepancies and weak or absent inter-task correlations across diverse populations and experimental manipulations have challenged the construct validity and theoretical coherence of a singular holistic mechanism. Here, the distinct contributions of facilitation and interference were isolated within the complete composite paradigm to evaluate their correspondence with performance in other tasks. Generalized linear mixed-effects modeling and individual differences analyses revealed that the holistic effect observed in the part-whole task was selectively associated with facilitation rather than interference in the complete composite task. In contrast, the holistic effect in the standard composite task correlated specifically with interference and showed no relationship with facilitation. These results demonstrate that conventional paradigms probe dissociable facets of holistic processing, establishing that partitioning holistic mechanisms into distinct facilitatory and inhibitory components is critical for understanding face perception.
papers.authors: Haiyang Jin, William G. Hayward, Olivia S. Cheung

papers.title: Implicit bias and experience influence overall but not relative trustworthiness judgment of other-race faces
papers.abstract: Facial trustworthiness evaluations are generated rapidly during first impressions; however, the degree of cross-racial consistency and the determinants of individual variation remain disputed. While normative consensus is widely reported, socio-cognitive factors—specifically negative implicit racial bias and deficient intergroup contact—have been linked to depressed trustworthiness appraisals for other-race faces. In this preregistered investigation, cohorts of White (N = 338) and Black (N = 299) observers completed a 200-face trustworthiness rating task (100 Black, 100 White faces), a race Implicit Association Test (IAT), and an intergroup contact inventory. Although absolute, overall trustworthiness ratings for other-race targets were significantly modulated by both implicit racial bias and contact experience, relative trustworthiness judgments (relative differences evaluated against own-race baseline ratings) remained highly concordant across observers irrespective of bias or contact levels. These findings demonstrate an operational dissociation wherein top-down socio-cognitive attitudes alter the absolute scaling of trustworthiness impressions, whereas bottom-up morphological cues driving relative approach-versus-avoidance determinations remain invariant across racial groups.
papers.authors: Olivia S. Cheung, Nathan J. Quimpo, James Smoley

papers.title: Effects of masculinity vs. femininity on competence judgement of politician faces and election outcome prediction
papers.abstract: Rapid visual inferences of competence from candidate photographs reliably predict real-world electoral victories, yet it remains debated whether these impressions stem from intrinsic facial morphology or extraneous photographic cues such as hairstyle, apparel, and posture. Across four preregistered experiments using counterbalanced designs, observers evaluated candidate competence on individual faces and forecasted electoral outcomes for winner–runner-up pairs. In Experiments 1 and 2, assessments were performed using unedited photographic portraits and standardized computer-generated face models reconstructed exclusively from candidate facial morphology, respectively. In Experiments 3 and 4, the synthetic facial stimuli were systematically manipulated along a masculinity–femininity continuum. Across Experiments 1 through 3, electoral victors elicited significantly higher competence ratings and higher predicted win probabilities than runners-up; this predictive effect was reversed or eliminated solely in Experiment 4, where winner facial morphology was feminized and runner-up morphology was masculinized. Across all conditions, perceived competence ratings remained robustly correlated with election outcome forecasts. These results confirm that facial morphological cues alone are sufficient to drive competence inferences and predict electoral success, and that masculine features reinforce stereotypical leadership impressions.
papers.authors: Olivia S. Cheung, Davit Jintcharadze

papers.title: The role of implicit social bias on holistic processing of out-group faces
papers.abstract: While perceptual expertise facilitates robust holistic processing of in-group faces, findings regarding holistic coding for out-group categories and its underlying determinants remain equivocal. This study investigated how out-group holistic processing magnitude—assessed across two distinct social categories (other-race and other-age)—is predicted by implicit social bias, individuating intergroup contact, and baseline in-group holistic processing capacity. Although participants exhibited substantial contact with the racial out-group but limited contact with the age out-group, implicit social bias emerged as a significant positive predictor of holistic processing for both other-race and other-age facial stimuli. Moderation analyses further revealed that the relationship between implicit bias and out-group holistic processing was selectively pronounced among observers possessing superior in-group holistic perceptual ability coupled with minimal experiential familiarity with out-group members. These findings indicate that top-down social evaluative biases interact with perceptual mechanisms to shape the configural encoding of out-group facial representations.
papers.authors: Wei Chen, Mahlet T. Kassa, Olivia S. Cheung

0522.name: Olivier Collignon
0522.bio: Olivier Collignon investigates the neurobiological foundations of multisensory perception and crossmodal plasticity. Their research explores how the human brain adapts to sensory deprivation, demonstrating that visual cortical regions in blind individuals can be functionally repurposed for auditory and tactile processing. By combining psychophysical methods with neuroimaging techniques like fMRI and M/EEG, Collignon identifies the computational principles governing brain reorganization and its potential for sensory restoration. Collignon serves as a Principal Investigator at the Crossmodal Perception and Plasticity Lab and is affiliated with the School of Health Sciences at HES-SO Valais-Wallis.
0522.research_direction: Dr. Collignon's recent work explores how the human brain integrates multisensory information and how early sensory experience dictates cortical development and cognitive mapping. Using fMRI, representational similarity analysis, and EEG frequency tagging, they have recently been investigating the mechanisms behind cross-modal processing, questioning how neural assemblies construct supramodal representations for numerosity, audiovisual speech phonology, and combined face-voice emotional expressions. Furthermore, their research probes the specific developmental role of visual input by examining early visual and ventral occipito-temporal pathways in patients with reversed neonatal cataracts, alongside studying how early or late blindness alters the physical mapping of interoceptive emotions. Ultimately, Dr. Collignon is examining the boundaries between inherent, modality-independent neural architectures and the plastic computational changes driven by sensory deprivation during sensitive periods.

papers.title: Brain Representation of Numerosity across the Senses and Presentation Formats
papers.abstract: This fMRI study investigates the neural coding of nonsymbolic and symbolic numerosity (quantities 2–5) across visual and auditory modalities and sequential versus simultaneous presentation formats. Using multivariate pattern decoding and representational similarity analysis (RSA) on human participants, the research identifies a posterior-to-anterior computational gradient within the dorsal processing stream. Early visual areas represent quantities based on sensory-specific attributes, while intraparietal sulcus (IPS) and frontal regions exhibit cross-modal alignment of numerical patterns, specifically for sequential presentations. The findings suggest that the brain's abstract representation of 'fiveness' is multifaceted, with temporal sequencing serving as a critical bridge for supramodal magnitude encoding, while simultaneous formats retain idiosyncratic neural geometries.
papers.authors: Ying Yang, Michele Fornaciai, Irene Togoli, Iqra Shahzad, Remi Gau, Alice Van Audenhaege, Filippo Cerpelloni, Olivier Collignon

papers.title: Impact of a transient neonatal visual deprivation on the development of the ventral occipito-temporal cortex in humans
papers.abstract: The study investigates how early visual experience influences the development of the human visual brain by examining a group of individuals who underwent cataract-reversal surgery following a short period of neonatal blindness. Using fMRI, the researchers demonstrate that while low-level visual feature encoding in the early visual cortex (EVC) is permanently impaired, categorical selectivity in the downstream ventral occipito-temporal cortex (VOTC) remains remarkably preserved. Interestingly, simulating cataracts in a control group led to disruptions in both EVC and VOTC, suggesting that the brain's developmental pathways differ under natural versus late-onset visual degradation. Deep neural network modeling further supported these findings, indicating that specific cortical regions and their associated computational roles have distinct sensitive periods for sensory input.
papers.authors: Stefania Mattioni, Mohamed Rezk, Xiaoqing Gao, Junghyun Nam, Zhong-Xu Liu, Remi Gau, Valérie Goffaux, Andrea I. Costantino, Hans Op de Beeck, Terri Lewis, Daphne Maurer, Olivier Collignon

papers.title: Phonological Representations of Auditory and Visual Speech in the Occipito-temporal Cortex and Beyond
papers.abstract: This study characterizes the neural representations of phonological information extracted from speech sounds and lip movements (visual speech). Using fMRI and individual functional localization of the word-selective ventral occipito-temporal cortex (word-VOTC) and the left superior temporal sulcus (lSTS), the authors demonstrate that both regions encode phonological features from both modalities. However, a divergence in coding schemes is revealed: while the lSTS integrates these signals into a unified, cross-modal representation, the word-VOTC maintains distinct, non-aligned geometries for auditory and visual phonemes. These results extend the known functional role of the word-VOTC beyond orthography and highlight a distributed network for multisensory phonology.
papers.authors: Alice Van Audenhaege, Stefania Mattioni, Filippo Cerpelloni, Remi Gau, Arnaud Szmalec, Olivier Collignon

papers.title: Visual experience shapes bodily representation of emotion
papers.abstract: The influence of visual experience on the interoceptive and exteroceptive mapping of emotions in the body is investigated by comparing early blind, late blind, and sighted individuals. Participants performed a naturalistic haptic task to identify perceived bodily changes associated with various affective states. Findings reveal that visual deprivation significantly alters these bodily maps: blind individuals report changes in mouth and hand areas as more relevant, whereas sighted individuals emphasize visceral sensations. Furthermore, the typical categorization of emotions along valence and arousal dimensions in bodily maps was absent in the blind group. These findings demonstrate that visual experience is a critical driver in the development of the conceptual and physical representation of emotions within the human body.
papers.authors: Giada Lettieri, Roberta P. Calce, Eléonore Giraudet, Olivier Collignon

papers.title: Intermodulation frequencies reveal common neural assemblies integrating facial and vocal fearful expressions
papers.abstract: Effective social interaction relies on integrating facial and vocal emotional cues. This study uses a multi-input EEG frequency tagging paradigm to identify neural populations that integrate fearful facial and vocal expressions. By identifying intermodulation frequencies—direct neural markers of multisensory integration—the researchers demonstrate the existence of shared neural assemblies that process combined face-voice emotional signals. These intermodulation responses provide evidence for a supramodal representation of fear that transcends individual sensory modalities, highlighting the brain's specialized architecture for efficient social communication through multisensory integration.
papers.authors: Francesca M. Barbero, Siddharth Talwar, Roberta P. Calce, Bruno Rossion, Olivier Collignon

0523.name: Paola Binda
0523.department: Department of Translational Research and New Technologies in Medicine and Surgery
0523.bio: Paola Binda is a neuroscientist who researches the physiological foundations of human visual perception and its interactions with cognitive and metabolic processes. Binda’s research in pupillometry demonstrates that pupil diameter serves as an index of high-level visual attention and cortical processing rather than a simple reflex. Their work utilizes ultra-high-field (7T) fMRI and psychophysics to investigate short-term ocular dominance plasticity and the role of subcortical structures like the pulvinar in visual stability. Binda leads the Pisa Vision Lab and the ERC-funded PUPILTRAITS project, which examines how individual variations in visual processing correlate with personality traits and physiological biomarkers.
0523.research_direction: Dr. Binda has recently been investigating the mechanisms and drivers of adult visual cortical plasticity, with a major focus on short-term ocular dominance plasticity. Their recent work explores how homeostatic shifts in eye dominance can be induced not only by traditional monocular deprivation, but also by introducing temporal visual-motor mismatches during active augmented reality tasks. To uncover the neural and physiological underpinnings of this plasticity, they are utilizing ultra-high field 7T fMRI to examine regulatory pulvinar-V1 connectivity, alongside high-resolution pupillometry during binocular rivalry to develop objective biomarkers of sensory gain changes. Additionally, they are investigating the broader neurometabolic modulation of visual cortical excitability, using combined MRS and EEG to measure how acute ketone supplementation alters the occipital excitatory-inhibitory balance and steady-state visual evoked potentials.

papers.title: Short-term monocular deprivation in healthy humans: a meta-analysis and new perspectives
papers.abstract: The authors present a comprehensive meta-analysis of over 150 datasets from 73 studies published since 2011, investigating the phenomenon of short-term ocular dominance plasticity in adult humans. The analysis confirms a robust and transient enhancement of the previously deprived eye's contribution to binocular vision following monocular patching, indicative of homeostatic plasticity in the adult visual system. The magnitude of this ocular dominance shift was positively correlated with the duration of deprivation and was consistently observed across different patching methodologies, including both translucent and light-tight occlusion. Furthermore, the study evaluates alternative monocular manipulations—such as image filtering, distortion, and suppression from awareness—which produce qualitatively similar plastic effects without traditional visual deprivation. These findings are discussed within the framework of predictive coding, suggesting that the adult visual system dynamically recalibrates monocular gain to maintain optimal information processing in response to altered environmental statistics.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences
papers.authors: Cecilia Steinwurzel, Giacomo Pennella, Claudia Lunghi, Paola Binda

papers.title: The pulvinar regulates plasticity in human visual cortex
papers.abstract: This study employs ultra-high field 7-Tesla functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) to elucidate the neural mechanisms underlying short-term ocular dominance plasticity in normally sighted human adults. The researchers demonstrate that a two-hour period of monocular deprivation induces a transient shift in perceptual eye dominance, which is mechanistically linked to a reduction in functional connectivity between the pulvinar and the primary visual cortex (V1). This connectivity decrease was found to be selective for the pulvinar-to-V1 directionality. Critically, across the participant cohort, the magnitude of the ocular dominance shift was negatively correlated with the strength of pulvinar-V1 connectivity, implying that individuals with stronger pulvinar influence over the sensory cortex exhibit reduced plasticity. The results support a revised model of adult cortical reorganization wherein modulatory signals relayed by the pulvinar act as a regulatory gate for the induction of short-term plasticity in early visual areas.
papers.authors: Miriam Acquafredda, Jan W. Kurzawski, Laura Biagi, Michela Tosetti, Maria Concetta Morrone, Paola Binda

papers.title: Monocular delay during visually guided actions is as effective as monocular deprivation in driving ocular dominance plasticity
papers.abstract: Short-term monocular deprivation, typically operationalized via eye-patching, induces a homeostatic shift in ocular dominance toward the deprived eye. This study reveals that a comparable plastic effect can be elicited without visual deprivation by introducing a temporal mismatch in the visual input. Participants engaged in a goal-directed visuomotor task (tower building) while the visual input to their dominant eye was delayed by 333 ms using an augmented reality setup. The results show that one hour of monocular delay during active action is as effective as traditional monocular deprivation in shifting ocular dominance toward the manipulated eye. Notably, this effect was absent when the delayed stimuli were viewed passively, suggesting that homeostatic plasticity in the adult visual system is gated by a cross-modal mismatch between visual and motor/proprioceptive signals rather than a simple reduction in monocular sensory drive.
papers.authors: Cecilia Steinwurzel, Giacomo Pennella, Maria Concetta Morrone, Giulio Sandini, Paola Binda

papers.title: Acute supplementation of beta-hydroxybutyrate increases visual cortical excitability in humans: a combined Electro-EncephaloGraphy and Magnetic Resonance Spectroscopy study
papers.abstract: This study investigates the neurometabolic and electrophysiological impact of acute ketosis on human visual cortical function. Using a combined approach of 7-Tesla Magnetic Resonance Spectroscopy (MRS) and Electroencephalography (EEG), the researchers assessed healthy volunteers before and after oral supplementation of the ketone body beta-hydroxybutyrate (βHB). The results demonstrated that βHB significantly increased the amplitude of steady-state visual evoked potentials (SSVEPs) and enhanced power in the resting-state alpha band (8–13 Hz). Concurrently, MRS measurements (MEGA-PRESS sequence) revealed a significant increase in occipital glutamate concentration, while GABA+ levels remained unchanged. The increase in glutamate was positively correlated with the enhancement of SSVEP amplitudes, providing evidence that acute βHB intake increases visual cortical excitability by modulating the excitatory-inhibitory balance within the occipital cortex.
papers.authors: Cecilia Steinwurzel, Maria Concetta Morrone, Ele Ferrannini, Francesca Frijia, Domenico Montanaro, Giuseppe Daniele, Paola Binda

papers.title: Pupillometry indexes ocular dominance plasticity
papers.abstract: This research introduces an objective physiological biomarker for ocular dominance plasticity by integrating high-resolution pupillometry with the paradigm of binocular rivalry. Adult participants underwent two hours of short-term monocular deprivation using a translucent patch. Perceptual dynamics were assessed before and after deprivation using a rivalry task where luminant disks (black vs. white) were presented monocularly. The results indicate that the amplitude of pupil-size modulations, which physiologically track the alternations in conscious perception during rivalry, increased significantly following deprivation. This increase in the depth of pupillary modulations corresponds with the behavioral shift in ocular dominance toward the deprived eye, reflecting an enhancement of the effective monocular signal strength. The study demonstrates that pupillometry can serve as an automatic and reliable index of adult homeostatic plasticity, correlating with subjective perceptual reports while providing an objective measure of sensory gain changes.
papers.authors: Miriam Acquafredda, Paola Binda

0524.name: Pascal Mamassian
0524.institution: French National Centre for Scientific Research
0524.bio: Pascal Mamassian is a CNRS Director of Research and the director of the Laboratoire des Systèmes Perceptifs at the École Normale Supérieure (ENS), PSL University. Mamassian’s research focuses on mid-level vision, examining the computational link between the detection of elementary image features and the conscious awareness of natural scenes. They utilize behavioral psychophysics and Bayesian probabilistic modeling to investigate 3D perception, motion, and the temporal dynamics of sensory integration. Their work centers on visual confidence and meta-perception, exploring the mechanisms through which observers evaluate the accuracy of their own perceptual decisions.
0524.research_direction: Dr. Mamassian has recently been investigating how the human visual system combines sensory evidence, prior expectations, and contextual cues to build robust perceptual and metacognitive representations. Their recent work explores the computational relationship between first-order perceptual decisions and confidence judgments, specifically asking how long-term priors and multisensory integration shape an observer's metacognitive access to sensory uncertainty. They are also examining mid-level visual processes, investigating how the brain achieves perceptual segmentation in complex natural scenes and how it estimates material properties like gloss through transmissive or transparent layers. Across these diverse domains, they employ advanced psychophysical difference-scaling methods and probabilistic generative modeling to map the underlying perceptual geometry that links physical stimulus variables to our subjective visual experience.

papers.title: Are we ready to tackle perceptual segmentation of natural scenes?
papers.abstract: Perceptual segmentation is a fundamental visual operation that partitions inputs into distinct objects, characterized by complex spatiotemporal dynamics. This work reviews the theoretical shift from classical feedforward feature detection to iterative Bayesian inference models, which posit that segmentation emerges through the integration of bottom-up sensory signals with top-down priors, such as spatial compactness and structural consistency. By examining human subjective segmentation maps for naturalistic images, the authors demonstrate that the tempo of perceptual choices reflects the iterative refinement process required to resolve ambiguity in natural scenes. The paper synthesizes recent advancements in machine learning algorithms and psychophysical experimentation to propose a unified framework for understanding how the visual system achieves robust perceptual organization in naturalistic environments.
papers.authors: Ruben Coen-Cagli, Pascal Mamassian

papers.title: Long-term perceptual priors drive confidence bias that favors prior-congruent evidence
papers.abstract: Bayesian models of perception typically assume that first-order decisions and metacognitive confidence judgments share the same precision-weighted integration of prior expectations and sensory likelihoods. This study investigates potential dissociations in the influence of low-level, long-term perceptual priors—specifically the slow-motion prior—on these two processing levels. Utilizing motion direction discrimination tasks, the researchers identify a persistent confidence bias toward prior-congruent evidence that remains significant even after accounting for objective perceptual performance. Computational modeling reveals that this behavior is best explained by a mechanism where the prior-congruent evidence serves as a supplementary metacognitive cue, decoupled from the posterior evidence used in the primary decision. These findings suggest that long-term perceptual priors exert a more profound influence on the metacognitive level than on initial perceptual inferences.
papers.authors: Marika Constant, Elisa Filevich, Pascal Mamassian

papers.title: Confidence judgements from fused multisensory percepts
papers.abstract: Optimal multisensory integration necessitates the precise estimation of unisensory uncertainty, but the accessibility of these individual uncertainty signals following bimodal fusion is poorly understood. Through temporal bisection tasks across visual, auditory, and audiovisual conditions, this study assesses the metacognitive ability to monitor unisensory validity after integration. The results demonstrate that once sensory information is integrated into a fused bimodal percept, human observers lose introspective access to unisensory cues, even when explicitly instructed to focus on a single modality. Generative modeling indicates that an integrative model, in which confidence is computed directly from the bimodal posterior, best captures the observed overconfidence and metacognitive susceptibility to incongruent cues. This suggests a critical loss of sensory-specific information between the stages of perceptual integration and metaperceptual evaluation.
papers.authors: Nicola Domenici, Pascal Mamassian

papers.title: Perceiving gloss through transparency
papers.abstract: Visual material perception involves disentangling an object's reflectance from illumination and intervening media properties. This study utilizes a maximum likelihood conjoint measurement (MLCM) paradigm to investigate how achromatic color shifts and luminance contrast compression, induced by transparent layers, modulate the perception of surface gloss. Through series of matching experiments, the researchers quantify the contamination of perceived specularity by the reflectance and absorption characteristics of the transparent medium. While results indicate a significant degree of gloss constancy, observers consistently overestimated gloss when objects were viewed through light-colored transparent layers. These findings suggest that the human visual system employs a heuristic weighting of contrast-dependent specular cues that is influenced by, but fails to fully compensate for, the optical properties of intervening transmissive materials.
papers.authors: Sabrina Hansmann-Roth, Pascal Mamassian

papers.title: Perceptual Scales Predicted by Fisher Information Metrics
papers.abstract: Perception can be modeled as a transduction process that maps physical variables onto internal psychological representations via perceptual scales. This work embeds the derivation of these scales within a probabilistic framework, establishing a theoretical relationship with the Fisher information of the underlying perceptual generative model. By conducting psychophysical difference-scaling experiments using both classical (spatial frequency, orientation) and naturalistic (texture interpolation) stimuli, the authors demonstrate that perceptual sensitivity is primarily constrained by the stimulus power spectrum. The findings show that the measured perceptual scale corresponds to the transduction function predicted by the generative model, offering a way to extend the concept of perceptual distance toward a full perceptual geometry of image representations.
papers.authors: Jonathan Vacher, Pascal Mamassian

0525.name: Patrick Bennett
0525.bio: Patrick J. Bennett is a Professor and Senior Canada Research Chair in Vision Science at McMaster University and co-directs the Vision and Cognitive Neuroscience Lab. Their research utilizes psychophysics, computational modeling, and electrophysiology to study the mechanisms of visual perception, with a focus on the effects of healthy aging and perceptual learning. Bennett applies ideal observer theory to establish benchmarks for human performance in tasks involving face and object recognition. Their current investigations examine how neural noise and changes in executive control relate to age-associated declines in visual processing and decision-making strategies.
0525.research_direction: Dr. Bennett has recently been investigating the mechanisms of visual motion processing and the temporal dynamics of perceptual learning. To understand age-related declines in motion perception, their recent work explores whether directionally selective visual mechanisms become more broadly tuned during senescence by measuring directional masking using drifting dot psychophysics. In a distinct line of research, they are examining the acquisition and durability of stimulus-specific perceptual learning. Specifically, Dr. Bennett uses complex, non-face texture identification tasks across varying retention intervals to determine exactly how many practice trials are required for the visual system to develop long-lasting, stimulus-specific enhancements.

papers.title: The effects of aging on directionally selective masking
papers.abstract: Age-related degradation of motion perception may stem from an expansion of the bandwidth of directionally selective visual mechanisms. To evaluate this hypothesis, directional masking was measured in younger and older adults across five psychophysical experiments. Experiments 1–3 quantified the contrast necessary to discriminate the direction of coherently drifting signal dots embedded within high-contrast mask dots, where the directional distribution of the mask dots was systematically manipulated using notch filters; directional selectivity was defined by the slope of the threshold-versus-notch function. Older adults exhibited elevated thresholds and reduced directional selectivity; however, scaling signal and mask contrast to multiples of each observer's unmasked motion discrimination threshold eliminated these age effects. Experiments 4 and 5 assessed direction discrimination thresholds by varying the proportion of coherently moving dots in masks composed of dots drifting in directions that differed across conditions. In these suprathreshold conditions, older observers continued to show increased discrimination thresholds and reduced directional selectivity. These findings support the hypothesis that directionally selective mechanisms become more broadly tuned during senescence.
papers.authors: Lia E. Tsotsos, Eugenie Roudaia, Allison B. Sekuler, Patrick J. Bennett

papers.title: The time course of stimulus-specific perceptual learning
papers.abstract: Perceptual task training can produce long-lasting, stimulus-specific performance enhancements. While rapid stimulus-specific learning emerging after just 105 practice trials has been observed in face identification, other visual tasks typically exhibit a much longer progression. This study investigated the acquisition dynamics and durability of stimulus-specific learning using unfamiliar, non-face texture stimuli across two sessions separated by either 24 hours (Experiment 1) or one week (Experiment 2). Observers performed a 1-of-10 texture identification task with varying amounts of Session 1 training (21, 63, 105, or 840 trials) and completed 840 trials in Session 2, where half of the participants maintained the trained textures and half transitioned to novel textures. In both experiments, stimulus-specific learning—operationalized as the accuracy difference between the identical and novel conditions—scaled as a linear function of the log-transformed number of Session 1 trials and achieved statistical significance after approximately 100 trials. The effect size of stimulus novelty did not vary between the 1-day and 1-week retention intervals, indicating that stimulus-specific perceptual learning for complex textures emerges continuously with practice, concurrently with task-general learning.
papers.authors: Patrick J. Bennett, Ali Hashemi, Jordan W. Lass, Allison B. Sekuler, Zahra Hussain

0526.name: Patrick Cavanagh
0526.bio: Patrick Cavanagh conducts research in visual neuroscience, specifically in the areas of visual attention, motion perception, and the intersection of art and science. Cavanagh utilizes discrepancies between perception and reality found in shadows and artistic depictions to examine how the brain reconstructs the visual world through inference processes. They identified that motion can distort the perceived position of objects, leading to theories regarding the neural representation of space. Their work also investigates 'visual language' and the mechanisms by which the brain compresses sensory information for communication with higher-order cognitive centers.
0526.research_direction: Dr. Cavanagh has recently been investigating how contextual dynamics, early visual processing, and physiological factors give rise to visual illusions of motion, position, and size. A major focus of their recent work explores the frame effect, where they manipulate frame kinematics, probe numerosity, and selective attention to understand how moving reference frames distort the perceived location of flashed targets. They are also examining the mechanisms behind classic apparent motion phenomena, using concurrent pupillometry and computational modeling to test whether reflexive pupil dilation triggers the peripheral drift illusion, and utilizing smooth pursuit paradigms to isolate the contour interactions driving the furrow illusion. Furthermore, their research investigates the spatial consequences of backward masking, specifically questioning how the spatiotemporal proximity of partially effective masks might interfere with boundary integration and cause the illusory shrinkage of visible objects.

papers.title: Following Randolph Blake's furrow further
papers.abstract: This study revisits the furrow illusion, where a vertically moving target's perceived trajectory is deflected by an oblique, static background grating. Psychophysical investigations reveal that the magnitude of the illusion is target-luminance dependent and is effectively abolished when observers perform smooth pursuit of a moving fixation point that stabilizes the target on the retina. The authors introduce a novel 'peep-hole' variant of the furrow stimulus, wherein the static grating is constrained within the target boundary; this version produces a significant directional shift that persists during tracking, suggesting that moving terminators at the target-contour intersections are the primary drivers of the perceived oblique path.
papers.authors: Anna Riga, Stuart Anstis, Ian M. Thornton, Patrick Cavanagh

papers.title: Pupil dilation underlies the peripheral drift illusion
papers.abstract: The researchers examine the physiological basis of the peripheral drift illusion (PDI), characterized by episodic apparent motion in static sawtooth luminance gradients. They hypothesize that the illusory motion is triggered by retinal luminance transients resulting from reflexive pupil dilation following eye movements or blinks. Concurrent pupillometry and behavioral reporting demonstrate that both the amplitude and the temporal duration of pupil dilation are significantly correlated with the reported duration of the illusory episodes. Computational simulations of pattern luminance modulation, using time-courses derived from observed pupillary dynamics, successfully generate the impression of motion, confirming the causal role of pupil-mediated retinal illumination changes in PDI.
papers.authors: George Mather, Patrick Cavanagh

papers.title: Illusory shrinkage of objects under backward masking
papers.abstract: This paper explores the secondary spatial consequences of backward masking when the mask is only partially effective and the target remains visible. Experimental results indicate that visible targets undergo a significant reduction in perceived size under these conditions. This 'illusory shrinkage' is shown to be a function of the spatiotemporal proximity between the target and mask contours, suggesting that masking signals interfere with the spatial integration of object boundaries at early stages of visual processing, leading to a constricted internal representation of the object's physical dimensions.
papers.authors: Sae Kaneko, Stuart Anstis, Patrick Cavanagh

papers.title: Deconstructing the frame effect
papers.abstract: The research decomposes the structural and dynamic components of the frame effect, wherein a moving frame shifts the perceived position of internal flashed probes. Across three experiments, the authors manipulated probe numerosity, frame kinematics, and spatiotemporal probe-frame offsets. Findings indicate that the presence of multiple internal probes amplifies the illusory shift, while the effect shows minimal accumulation over repeated motion cycles. Furthermore, oscillating frames induce more robust shifts than unidirectional frames, and the magnitude of the position shift is maximal near the frame's leading edge, highlighting the critical role of perceptual grouping and frame continuity in visual stabilization.
papers.authors: Mohammad Shams, Peter J. Kohler, Patrick Cavanagh

papers.title: Influence of frame and probe paths on the frame effect
papers.abstract: This study investigates the robustness of the frame effect across various frame and probe trajectory configurations. The illusory position shift is found to persist across diverse kinematic profiles, including nonlinear and circular paths, and remains undiminished by changes in frame shape or orientation during displacement. The results indicate that the effect is driven by the perceived rather than physical motion of the frame. Additionally, the study demonstrates that when multiple overlapping frames compete, the resulting position shift is determined by which frame is selectively attended. The effect is suppressed by the presence of static anchors or the use of continuous rather than flashed probes, underscoring the competition between moving and static reference frames.
papers.authors: Stuart Anstis, Patrick Cavanagh

0529.name: Pawan Sinha
0529.department: Department of Brain and Cognitive Sciences
0529.lab_name: The Sinha Lab for Developmental Research
0529.bio: Pawan Sinha is a Professor of Vision and Computational Neuroscience at MIT who investigates the biological and computational mechanisms underlying perceptual development and object recognition. Sinha founded Project Prakash, an initiative that restores sight to congenitally blind children in India to study how the brain interprets visual information after prolonged deprivation. Their research also explores neurodevelopmental disorders, advancing the hypothesis that autism is characterized by a deficit in sensory prediction. By combining experimental data from diverse populations with computational modeling, their laboratory investigates the processes that allow the human brain to transform sensory input into mental representations.
0529.research_direction: Dr. Sinha has recently been investigating the interplay between early sensory experience, neural plasticity, and perceptual development, prominently utilizing both computational models and unique clinical cohorts. Much of their recent work explores visual recovery in individuals who receive sight-restoring surgery late in life, using multi-parametric MRI to evaluate structural gray matter changes and longitudinal psychophysics to track the post-operative emergence of spatial hyperacuities. Alongside these empirical approaches, they employ deep neural networks to test the adaptive initial degradation hypothesis, probing how early sensory limitations like visual blur or color blindness interact with time-limited learning rates to shape robust, generalizable object representations. Expanding beyond fundamental visual development, their research also investigates predictive processing in autism, including the creation of validated psychometric tools to quantify everyday prediction challenges across sensory, motor, and social domains.

papers.title: Computationally Probing the Role of Time-Limited Neuronal Plasticity in Early Visual Development
papers.abstract: This computational study investigates the 'adaptive initial degradation' hypothesis using deep neural networks to determine whether time-limited plasticity serves an adaptive role during visual development. By modeling developmental plasticity as a monotonically decreasing learning rate, the researchers simulated the interaction between improving sensory fidelity (e.g., transition from blur to clear) and diminishing neural flexibility. The analysis revealed that restricted plasticity contributes to the stabilization of early-formed representations, particularly in lower hierarchical layers, and yields modest gains in overall task performance. These findings suggest that the decline of plasticity may facilitate the retention of features learned from early, low-fidelity inputs, which subserve robust perception later in development.
papers.authors: Marin Vogelsang, Lukas Vogelsang, Pawan Sinha

papers.title: Gray matter abnormalities in sight deprivation and sight restoration
papers.abstract: This research evaluates the structural plasticity of the human brain following the restoration of sight in congenitally blind individuals treated late in life. Using multi-parametric MRI, the study assessed gray matter integrity via measures of cortical thickness, curvature, and T1-weighted signal intensity (reflecting cortical myelin content). Despite significant white matter plasticity previously reported in this same cohort, longitudinal analyses following sight-restoring surgeries showed no statistically significant changes in gray matter metrics. These results indicate that structural adaptations to late-onset visual experience are predominantly confined to white matter pathways, suggesting that gray matter architecture may be less susceptible to large-scale structural reorganization after the closure of early sensitive periods.
papers.authors: Caterina A. Pedersini, Alessio Fracasso, Amna Dogar, Bas Rokers, Pawan Sinha

papers.title: The Status of Vernier Acuity Following Late Sight Onset
papers.abstract: This longitudinal study examines the recovery of vernier acuity—a spatial hyperacuity indicative of multi-unit cortical processing—in congenitally blind children from Project Prakash who received sight-restoring surgery late in childhood. By tracking both resolution and vernier acuities post-operatively, the researchers found that late-sighted individuals eventually achieve hyperacuity, where their ability to detect contour misalignments exceeds their ability to resolve closely spaced stimuli. However, the magnitude of this hyperacuity remains significantly lower than that of normally sighted controls. These results provide evidence of residual cortical plasticity for spatial integrative processing even after years of initial deprivation, while also highlighting the limitations of recovery late in development.
papers.authors: Lukas Vogelsang, Priti Gupta, Marin Vogelsang, Pragya Shah, Kashish Tiwari, Dhun Verma, Mrinalini Yadav, Sruti Raja, Suma Ganesh, Pawan Sinha

papers.title: Development of a Self-Report Measure of Prediction in Daily Life: The Prediction-Related Experiences Questionnaire
papers.abstract: The authors introduce the Prediction-Related Experiences Questionnaire (PRE-Q), a novel self-report tool developed using mixed methods and validated via Rasch modeling to quantify day-to-day prediction skills in adults. The study tested the validity of the measure across sensory, motor, and social domains in both autistic and neurotypical populations. Findings demonstrated that autistic individuals report significantly more difficulties with prediction-related tasks in daily life, aligning with theoretical models of autism as a disorder of predictive processing. The PRE-Q provides a psychometrically robust instrument for researchers and clinicians to assess functional prediction challenges and identify areas for targeted clinical support.
papers.venue: Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders
papers.authors: Amanda M. O'Brien, Toni A. May, Kristin L. K. Koskey, Lindsay Bungert, Annie Cardinaux, Jonathan Cannon, Isaac N. Treves, Anila M. D'Mello, Robert M. Joseph, Cindy Li, Sidney Diamond, John D. E. Gabrieli, Pawan Sinha

papers.title: Impact of early visual experience on later usage of color cues
papers.abstract: This study explores the teleological role of early color-degraded vision in the development of robust visual recognition. By assessing late-sighted individuals who gained vision in adolescence, the researchers found that these individuals rely excessively on chromatic cues for object recognition, whereas normally sighted children are robust to the removal of color. Computational simulations with convolutional neural networks suggest that the mature state of the late-sighted children's color system at sight onset leads to overfitting on chromatic features. In contrast, the neonatal visual system's initial color blindness forces the brain to learn luminance-based representations, which are inherently more robust and subserve generalizable object recognition later in life.
papers.authors: Marin Vogelsang, Lukas Vogelsang, Priti Gupta, Tapan K. Gandhi, Pragya Shah, Piyush Swami, Sharon Gilad-Gutnick, Shlomit Ben-Ami, Sidney Diamond, Suma Ganesh, Pawan Sinha

0530.name: Peter Bandettini
0530.bio: Bandettini co-led the development of functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) using blood oxygenation level-dependent (BOLD) contrast and introduced correlation analysis for functional mapping. Bandettini's research focuses on advancing the spatial resolution, temporal sensitivity, and interpretability of fMRI through ultra-high-field imaging of cortical layers and the development of multi-echo pulse sequences. Their current work explores the extraction of neuronal and physiological signatures from fMRI time series data to examine individual differences in brain connectivity and visual processing. Bandettini serves as the Director of the NIH Functional MRI Facility and is the current Editor-in-Chief of Aperture Neuro, having previously served as Editor-in-Chief of NeuroImage.
0530.research_direction: Dr. Bandettini's recent work explores the spatial and temporal boundaries of ultra-high-field (7T) fMRI to better isolate true neural activity from neurovascular noise. They have recently been investigating how to improve layer-specific functional imaging by suppressing macrovascular biases from respiration, alongside pushing the temporal limits of rapid multivariate decoding to capture visual object representations before the typical hemodynamic response peaks. Applied to visual perception, they are using these submillimeter fMRI techniques to probe the cortical layers of V1, examining the specific interplay between retinal signals and top-down feedback mechanisms that drive negative afterimages. Broadly, their methodological research also extends to critiquing standard fMRI statistical pipelines to help discover hidden, un-averaged topographic signal features, and designing cross-species, real-time pupillometry frameworks to track how spontaneous neuromodulatory arousal impacts cognition.

papers.title: The human brain mechanisms of afterimages: From networks to cortical layers
papers.abstract: By employing submillimeter-resolution 7T fMRI, this study interrogated the laminar-specific neurovascular underpinnings of negative afterimages within the primary visual cortex (V1). Utilizing a perception-matching paradigm to control for illusory content, the research demonstrated that while physically present stimuli evoke activation across superficial and granular layers, afterimages selectively recruit deep cortical laminae. Whole-brain analysis further revealed extensive engagement of visual sensory regions and salience networks, suggesting that the conscious perception of afterimages arises from an interplay between persistent retinal signals and top-down cortical feedback mechanisms.
papers.authors: Sharif Ismail Kronemer, Burak Akin, Micah Holness, A. Tyler Morgan, Laurentius Huber, Paul A. Taylor, Javier Gonzalez-Castillo, Daniel A. Handwerker, Peter A. Bandettini

papers.title: What are we missing? What are we assuming? The need to foster feature discovery tools to improve statistical models
papers.abstract: This commentary critically examines the methodological constraints of the Statistical Parametric Mapping (SPM) framework, emphasizing that model-driven assumptions and strict statistical thresholding often obscure idiosyncratic but biologically significant fMRI signal features. The author advocates for the implementation of 'feature discovery' tools and 'transparent thresholding' to enable the visualization of subthreshold topographic maps. It is argued that such exploratory methodologies are necessary to capture the high-dimensional, non-random variability in neurovascular signals that traditional multi-subject averaging and normalization pipelines typically discard, thereby facilitating new mechanistic insights into human brain organization.
papers.authors: Peter Bandettini

papers.title: Rapid decoding of neural information representation from ultra-fast functional magnetic resonance imaging signals
papers.abstract: Utilizing ultra-fast 7T fMRI with a repetition time (TR) of 125 ms, this research evaluated the temporal limits of information recovery from hemodynamic signals during naturalistic object viewing. By applying multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) to the high-frequency time series, the researchers demonstrated that object-category information can be decoded from the visual cortex within 2 seconds of stimulus onset, significantly preceding the peak of the canonical hemodynamic response function (HRF). The study further indicates that sparse decoding techniques, which prune large-vessel voxels from the input, can resolve rapid neural dynamics and mitigate the temporal blurring inherent in the neurovascular coupling.
papers.authors: Yoichi Miyawaki, Kenshu Koiso, Daniel A. Handwerker, Javier Gonzalez-Castillo, Laurentius Huber, Arman Khojandi, Yuhui Chai, Daniel Glen, Peter A. Bandettini

papers.title: Cross-species real-time detection of trends in pupil size fluctuation
papers.abstract: This study introduces rtPupilPhase, an open-source signal processing framework designed for the online detection of pupillary unrest phases as a proxy for central neuromodulatory state. Validated across human, macaque, and rodent datasets, the system identifies trends in pupillary dynamics that lag neural activity in the locus coeruleus and basal forebrain by approximately 100 ms. By enabling the real-time classification of physiological arousal states, the tool supports the development of closed-loop experimental paradigms and biofeedback systems intended to investigate the relationship between spontaneous arousal fluctuations and cognitive or perceptual performance.
papers.authors: Sharif I. Kronemer, Victoria E. Gobo, Catherine R. Walsh, Joshua B. Teves, Diana C. Burk, Somayeh Shahsavarani, Javier Gonzalez-Castillo, Peter A. Bandettini

papers.title: Improving laminar fMRI specificity by reducing macrovascular bias revealed by respiration effects
papers.abstract: This methodological investigation characterized the influence of respiration-induced physiological noise on the laminar specificity of fMRI signals at 7T. By analyzing depth-dependent sensitivity within BOLD and 3D VAPER (integrated VASO and perfusion) sequences, the researchers quantified macrovascular draining vein biases that preferentially contaminate superficial cortical layers during the respiratory cycle. The study proposes specific physiological noise regression strategies and the utilization of cerebral blood volume (CBV)-weighted contrasts to suppress these non-neuronal signals. These advancements improve the fidelity of microvascular mapping and the accuracy of inter-regional laminar functional connectivity estimates.
papers.authors: Yuhui Chai, A. Tyler Morgan, Daniel A. Handwerker, Linqing Li, Laurentius Huber, Bradley P. Sutton, Peter A. Bandettini

0531.name: Peter Bex
0531.bio: Professor Peter Bex conducts cross-disciplinary research at the intersection of basic visual neuroscience and clinical ophthalmology. Bex's laboratory utilizes computational modeling, psychophysics, and eye-tracking to examine how the human visual system processes dynamic, cluttered real-world environments compared to laboratory stimuli. A focus of their translational work is the development of objective, automated diagnostic tools—such as the Angular Indication Measurement (AIM) and Foraging Interactive D-prime (FInD)—to monitor the progression and remediation of visual function loss in patients with glaucoma, amblyopia, and macular degeneration. Through these tools, Bex seeks to optimize residual vision and develop rehabilitation strategies for blinding eye diseases.
0531.research_direction: Dr. Bex has recently been developing rapid, adaptive psychophysical methods to precisely quantify visual function in both healthy and clinical populations. Their recent work extensively utilizes novel behavioral frameworks, such as the FInD and AIM paradigms, to investigate a diverse array of visual phenomena including cone-isolating color discrimination and principal component-based face space sensitivity. A major focus of their research explores higher-order face processing, specifically investigating how spatial frequency distortions impact the face inversion effect and characterizing selective configural face deficits in individuals with cerebral visual impairment. Additionally, they are investigating the subjective dynamics of multistable perception, using unsupervised clustering to map continuous perceptual states and transition pathways during binocular rivalry to better understand the neural hierarchy of interocular competition.

papers.title: Which perceptual categories do observers experience during multistable perception?
papers.abstract: To delineate the phenotypic landscape of visual consciousness during binocular rivalry, the researchers utilized the InFoRM-Rivalry paradigm to capture continuous subjective reports across six a priori categories: two exclusive monocular states and four mixed configurations (superimposition and piecemeal). Unsupervised k-means clustering applied to data from 28 participants revealed a high dimensionality of experience, with an average of 10 ± 8 distinct perceptual clusters identified. These states mapped primarily onto exclusive and superimposed manifolds rather than piecemeal transitions, regardless of stimulus contrast. Hidden Markov modeling of transition pathways indicated that shifts occur most frequently between monocularly exclusive and binocularly superimposed categories. These findings suggest that interocular competition is mediated by hierarchical conflicts between monocular and binocular neural populations rather than a simple low-level reciprocal inhibition of monocular channels.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences
papers.authors: Jan Skerswetat, Peter Bex

papers.title: Facing distortion: Impact of spatial distortions on upright and inverted face identification
papers.abstract: This study investigates the spatial frequency tuning of face identification under conditions of geometric pixel-shifting distortion. Utilizing an adaptive staircase within the Foraging Interactive D-prime (FInD) framework, identification thresholds were measured for upright and inverted faces subjected to bandpass-filtered noise at peak frequencies ranging from 1 to 32 cycles/face. Results demonstrated a significant orientation-by-frequency interaction (F5,35 = 2.72, p = 0.0354): upright face recognition exhibited a characteristic asymmetric U-shaped tuning curve with maximum sensitivity at mid-spatial frequencies (4–8 cycles/face), whereas thresholds for inverted faces increased monotonically with frequency. Significant inversion effects were observed only at high frequencies (16 and 32 cpi). The finding that peak sensitivity correlates with configural eye spacing suggests that the face inversion effect is primarily driven by disruptions to eye geometry within specific high-frequency bands.
papers.authors: Bliss Cui, Peter Bex

papers.title: Novel color vision assessment tool: AIM Color Detection and Discrimination
papers.abstract: To address the limitations of existing clinical color vision tests, such as prolonged testing time and coarse diagnostic resolution, the authors developed the Angular Indication Measurement (AIM) paradigm, a response-adaptive, self-administered system for assessing cone-isolating detection and chromatic discrimination. AIM utilizes 4x4 grids of adaptively generated stimuli, where participants indicate the gap orientation of cone-isolating Landolt C optotypes (targeting L, M, and S-cone pathways) or chromatic edges in equiluminant space (discrimination along eight color directions). Evaluating 23 color-normal and 15 color vision deficient (CVD) participants, the study employed supervised Support Vector Machine (SVM) classifiers to categorize CVD subtypes. The AIM platform achieved classification accuracies comparable to the Rayleigh-match anomaloscope while significantly reducing testing duration compared to the Farnsworth-Munsell 100 hue test, establishing it as a precise tool for rapid phenotype profiling.
papers.authors: Jingyi He, Jan Skerswetat, Peter J. Bex

papers.title: Impaired face identity discrimination in individuals with cerebral visual impairment: a pilot study
papers.abstract: Higher-order perceptual deficits, particularly in face processing, are hallmark symptoms of cerebral visual impairment (CVI) but lack robust quantification. In this pilot study, face discrimination thresholds were measured in the 199-dimensional Basel Face Model (BFM) space using the Foraging Interactive D-prime (FInD) paradigm. Comparing eight CVI subjects to eight controls, the study found significantly elevated thresholds in the CVI group across both canonical and tilted orientations [t(13)=-3.439, P=0.004]. Crucially, discrimination performance did not correlate with visual acuity, and follow-up control experiments (N=23) confirmed that identity recognition is resilient to low-level resolution loss (digital blur). The results suggest that CVI involves a selective impairment in processing configural or principal component-based facial features, independent of primary visual pathway integrity and low-level visual deficits.
papers.authors: Kerri Walter, Claire E. Manley, Lotfi B. Merabet, Peter J. Bex

papers.title: A novel, rapid, quantitative method for face discrimination
papers.abstract: This research introduces a high-throughput, self-administered psychophysical method for quantifying face discrimination thresholds by integrating the Foraging Interactive D-prime (FInD) paradigm with the Basel Face Model (BFM). Across three experiments, the study quantified sensitivity to the 199 structural principal components of the BFM. Observers exhibited maximal sensitivity to the first 10 structural components. Experiments manipulating component combinations showed that thresholds were significantly lower for components in combination than alone [t(7) = 2.90, p = .023], consistent with probability summation and Euclidean distance models rather than superadditivity. The method’s robustness was validated through remote testing and rotation-invariant conditions, providing a rapid (approx. 25-second) and precise tool for measuring individual differences in face space discrimination across clinical and healthy populations.
papers.authors: Kerri Walter, Peter Bex

0532.name: Peter J Kohler
0532.bio: Peter J. Kohler is an Associate Professor in the Department of Psychology at York University and director of the Kohler Visual Neuroscience Lab. Kohler’s research focuses on mid-level visual processing, investigating how the human brain transforms early sensory signals into representations of symmetry, shape, and motion. Utilizing a combination of high-density steady-state EEG, functional MRI, and psychophysical modeling, Kohler characterizes the spatiotemporal dynamics of neural populations across topographically organized visual areas. Their current work explores the hierarchical organization of pattern regularity and the binocular integration mechanisms required for perceiving motion in depth.
0532.research_direction: Dr. Kohler's recent work explores how the human visual system utilizes foundational Gestalt cues to facilitate perceptual organization, with a specific focus on different classes of symmetry. Using visual search paradigms with multi-element arrays, they have recently been investigating how attentional deployment is differentially guided by targets defined by reflectional versus rotational symmetry. Furthermore, their research examines the interaction between this micro-level feature processing and macro-level spatial regularities. By testing observers on repeating, wallpaper-like lattice textures, they are probing the underlying computational mechanisms that govern how structural periodicity and visual symmetry interact to modulate attentional gating and overall search efficiency.

papers.title: Visual search efficiency is modulated by symmetry type and texture regularity
