papers.abstract: While symmetry serves as a foundational Gestalt cue facilitating perceptual organization and scene understanding, empirical work has predominantly focused on isolated reflectional symmetry. Here, visual search paradigms were employed to investigate how search efficiency is differentially governed by symmetry class (reflection versus rotation) and spatial regularity across repeating lattice textures. Observers searched for target elements embedded within multi-element arrays across varying set sizes, allowing quantification of search slopes (ms/item) as an index of serial versus parallel attentional deployment. Search slopes were significantly shallower for targets defined by reflectional symmetry compared to rotational symmetry, indicating higher processing efficiency and greater parallel extraction for mirror symmetry. Additionally, global lattice regularity significantly facilitated target detection relative to disordered configurations, demonstrating that macro-level structural regularity interacts with micro-level symmetry processing. These results reveal that the visual system recruits distinct computational mechanisms across different symmetry classes and that spatial periodicity in wallpaper-like visual textures fundamentally modulates attentional gating and perceptual efficiency.
papers.authors: Rachel Moreau, Nihan Alp, Alasdair D. F. Clarke, Erez Freud, Peter J. Kohler

0533.name: Peter Kok
0533.department: Department of Imaging Neuroscience, Queen Square Institute of Neurology
0533.bio: Peter Kok is a Professor of Cognitive Neuroscience and Sir Henry Dale Fellow at the UCL Queen Square Institute of Neurology, where they conduct research on the neural mechanisms of predictive coding. Kok’s work examines how the brain integrates prior knowledge and sensory input to shape visual perception, utilizing ultra-high field (7T) fMRI to study laminar-specific activity in the visual cortex. They also employ magnetoencephalography (MEG) to analyze the temporal unfolding of perceptual inferences and investigate the role of the hippocampus in generating top-down expectations. This research aims to characterize the computational architecture of the visual system and its implications for understanding perceptual disorders.
0533.research_direction: Dr. Kok has recently been investigating the neural and computational mechanisms underlying top-down perceptual expectations, exploring how internally generated predictions shape visual processing. Their recent work employs diverse methods—including magnetoencephalography (MEG), ultra-high-field (7T) layer-specific fMRI, and psychophysics—to understand how sensory templates are maintained prior to stimulus onset and how the brain distinguishes between veridical perception and internally generated false percepts. Specifically, they are examining the role of pre-stimulus alpha oscillations in holding visual predictions online and modeling how expectations about a stimulus's presence interact computationally with expectations about its specific content. Furthermore, they are mapping the precise anatomical pathways of these top-down signals, investigating how perceptual predictions are communicated via feedback channels from the hippocampus to the deep cortical layers to better understand both normal vision and perceptual disturbances.

papers.title: Contents of Visual Predictions Oscillate at Alpha Frequencies
papers.abstract: The mechanisms by which the human brain maintains endogenously generated perceptual templates online during the pre-stimulus interval remain a subject of active debate. In this study, we combined magnetoencephalography (MEG) with time-resolved multivariate decoding to examine the neural representations of cued sensory predictions. Participants performed a visual shape discrimination task where auditory cues signaled the identity of an upcoming stimulus. Frequency decomposition of the decoded shape-specific signals revealed significant oscillatory fluctuations specifically within the alpha band (10–11 Hz) prior to stimulus onset. Quantitative analyses demonstrated that the magnitude of this stimulus-specific alpha power was functionally linked to the behavioral efficacy of expectations on discrimination performance. These results indicate that perceptual predictions are encoded via alpha-band oscillations, providing a discrete neural mechanism for the active deployment of sensory templates in anticipation of incoming inputs.
papers.authors: Dorottya Hetenyi, Joost Haarsma, Peter Kok

papers.title: Shared and Diverging Neural Dynamics Underlying False and Veridical Perception
papers.abstract: While false percepts are generated internally, they often exhibit a phenomenological similarity to veridical perception, suggesting a convergence of underlying neural mechanisms. Using multivariate decoding of human MEG data, we investigated the overlap between these states across the stages of content discrimination and stimulus detection. We found that both high-confidence false percepts and veridical percepts are characterized by shared stimulus-like orientation signals and a common neural code for perceptual confidence. However, false percepts were uniquely distinguished by a significant increase in pre-stimulus high alpha/low beta power (11–14 Hz) arising from a parieto-occipital network. This suggests that while veridical and false inferences eventually utilize shared representational architecture, false percepts are driven by distinct pre-stimulus oscillatory dynamics that may reflect an over-reliance on top-down signaling.
papers.authors: Joost Haarsma, Dorottya Hetenyi, Peter Kok

papers.title: Communication of perceptual predictions from the hippocampus to the deep layers of the parahippocampal cortex
papers.abstract: The hippocampus is theorized to play a pivotal role in the generation of perceptual predictions, but the directional communication between hippocampal subfields and neocortex during prediction signaling remains poorly understood. Utilizing ultra-high-field (7-tesla) fMRI, we interrogated the medial temporal lobe (MTL) while auditory cues signaled upcoming visual shapes. We observed that shape-specific predictions in CA2/3 and the pre/parasubiculum were negatively correlated with stimulus-evoked neural patterns. Crucially, layer-specific informational connectivity analyses demonstrated that predictive communication between CA2/3 and the parahippocampal cortex (PHC) was confined to the deep cortical layers of the PHC, which typically receive feedback projections. These findings suggest that the hippocampus generates predictions through internal pattern completion and propagates these signals back to the neocortex via deep-layer feedback channels.
papers.authors: Oliver Warrington, Nadine N. Graedel, Martina F. Callaghan, Peter Kok

papers.title: How Layer-Specific fMRI Can Contribute to Understanding Perceptual Disturbances Across Psychiatric Disorders
papers.abstract: Perceptual dysregulation, a hallmark of various psychiatric conditions, is increasingly framed as a failure to optimally integrate endogenous signals (such as priors and imagination) with exogenous sensory inputs. In this review, we examine the utility of sub-millimeter laminar fMRI for identifying the circuit-level disruptions underlying these phenomena. Because feedforward and feedback signals are anatomically segregated into different cortical depths, layer-specific imaging allows researchers to test whether hallucinations result from excessive feedback or attenuated sensory drive. We synthesize current findings on depth-dependent neural activity in healthy and clinical cohorts, discuss the potential of pharmacological layer-fMRI in precision psychiatry, and evaluate the methodological advancements required to move beyond primary sensory regions into higher-order association cortices.
papers.authors: Joost Haarsma, Peter Kok

papers.title: Expectations about presence enhance the influence of content-specific expectations on low-level orientation judgements
papers.abstract: Perceptual expectations can be directed toward either the occurrence of a stimulus (presence) or its specific properties (content), yet their computational interaction is poorly defined. Through psychophysical experiments and Bayesian decision modeling across discovery and replication samples, we examined how these two forms of expectations influence perceptual inference. We found that expectations of stimulus presence acted as a regulatory gain mechanism for content expectations: orientation-specific biases on discrimination were significantly enhanced when a stimulus was anticipated to appear compared to when it was not. This modulation occurred for both veridical detections and confident false percepts. While presence and content expectations independently influenced confidence in stimulus detection, their interaction in shaping discrimination judgements suggests a hierarchical architecture in which the predicted presence of a stimulus gates the precision of its content-specific priors.
papers.authors: Joost Haarsma, Aaron Kaltenmaier, Stephen M. Fleming, Peter Kok

0534.name: Peter Neri
0534.bio: Peter Neri is a CNRS Director of Research at the École Normale Supérieure (ENS) in Paris and leads the Vision team within the Laboratoire des Systèmes Perceptifs. Neri’s research investigates the computational and neural mechanisms of human sensory processing, focusing on how the brain extracts structural features from complex natural scenes and noisy environments. By integrating high-resolution psychophysical reverse correlation techniques with quantitative system identification models, Neri characterizes the nonlinear transformations and ‘perceptual templates’ that underlie visual detection and discrimination. Their work aims to provide physiologically plausible accounts of how diverse sensory signals are processed to drive and control behavior across both visual and auditory domains.
0534.research_direction: Dr. Neri has recently been investigating sensory processing across species by bridging advanced computational modeling, ecologically relevant human psychophysics, and comparative behavioral research. In human vision, their recent work explores how the visual system extracts signals from complex naturalistic environments, developing mathematical frameworks that model perception as geometric operations on sensory manifolds while also evaluating robust reverse correlation methods to map human perceptual templates. Additionally, they are using immersive virtual reality to probe how local visual feature detectors dynamically adapt to global environmental statistics, such as the structural validity of cast shadows. Broadening their scope to cephalopod vision and behavior, Dr. Neri is examining complex signaling in cuttlefish, specifically investigating how these animals process visually driven, multimodal postural communication displays and how the temporal dynamics of their mantle patterns encode internal physiological states.

papers.title: Perceptual processes as charting operators
papers.abstract: This study develops a novel geometrical framework for modeling elementary sensory computations by recasting perceptual processes as charting operators. The author proposes a mathematical representation of perception as a distance-measuring operation over a structured sensory manifold, where classification involves determining proximity to target-present versus target-absent templates. This intrinsic geometry framework is shown to be sufficiently expressive to account for a wide range of empirical findings in human vision, including the properties of first-order and second-order perceptual kernels derived via system identification. By relating behavioral descriptors to notions of manifold flatness and curvature, the work offers a unified theoretical account of how the visual system extracts signals from noise through non-Euclidean metric operations.
papers.authors: Peter Neri

papers.title: Reverse Correlation of Natural Statistics for Ecologically Relevant Characterization of Human Perceptual Templates
papers.abstract: Psychophysical reverse correlation is the established methodology for estimating neuronal and perceptual receptive fields, but its validity is often challenged by the highly structured, non-Gaussian statistics of natural scenes. This research evaluates the efficacy of five distinct computational approaches—including regularized logistic regression and maximally informative dimensions (MID)—for retrieving human perceptual templates under ecologically relevant conditions. By applying these techniques to experimental data where the human observer approximates a template matcher to varying degrees, the authors demonstrate that optimization-based methods (minimizing loss or maximizing information) effectively characterize human sensory strategies in naturalistic backgrounds. The study identifies specific scenarios where simple covariance-corrected linear techniques yield misleading artifacts and provides a robust framework for interpreting template-matching behavior in the presence of complex environmental statistics.
papers.authors: Lorenzo Landolfi, Peter Neri

papers.title: Cuttlefish interact with multimodal “arm wave sign” displays
papers.abstract: While cephalopods are renowned for dynamic skin patterning, their use of stereotyped postural movements for social signaling remains poorly understood. This study introduces a previously undescribed communication display in two species, Sepia officinalis and Sepia bandensis, termed the 'arm wave sign'—a sequence of rhythmic undulations and postural shifts. Using non-invasive behavioral playback experiments, the researchers demonstrate that cuttlefish recognize these signs visually, showing significantly higher response rates to upright versus inverted displays, analogous to face-selective perception in humans. Furthermore, analysis of the mechanical waves generated by these movements suggests a multimodal signaling strategy where visual cues are integrated with mechanoreceptive vibrations detected via the lateral line or statocysts, providing evidence for the convergent evolution of complex social communication across divergent phyla.
papers.authors: Sophie Cohen-Bodénès, Peter Neri

papers.title: State-dependent dynamics of cuttlefish mantle activity
papers.abstract: The extraordinary visual appearance of the cuttlefish mantle is typically analyzed in the context of static camouflage, yet its temporal fluctuations may convey information about internal physiological states. This study develops specialized analytical tools to characterize pattern dynamics across different feeding states (satiated vs. hungry). The authors demonstrate that the temporal properties and fluctuation statistics of specific mantle components differ significantly between these states, even in the absence of measurable changes in the absolute magnitude of pattern expression. These findings indicate that cuttlefish skin encodes internal motivational variables through dynamic temporal patterning that is inaccessible to conventional static expression analyses, suggesting a sophisticated neural control system for state-dependent behavioral signaling.
papers.authors: Sophie Cohen-Bodénès, Peter Neri

papers.title: Human sensory adaptation to the ecological structure of environmental statistics
papers.abstract: Sensory adaptation is classically viewed as a local phenomenon constrained by the spatiotemporal bandwidth of specific detectors. Using immersive virtual reality to probe human visual discrimination within ecologically valid environments, this study demonstrates that the operation of local edge detectors is fundamentally shaped by slow, global statistical regularities, specifically the reliability of cast shadows. When shadows are ecologically consistent, local visual operators anchor their integration templates around object-level representations; however, as shadow reliability decreases, these operators disengage from object units and revert to image-feature-driven processing. These results reveal that sensory mechanisms are not strictly local but are instead highly integrated processors that dynamically adapt to the structural validity of environmental statistics to optimize feature extraction during natural behavior.
papers.authors: Peter Neri

0535.name: Peter U. Tse
0535.department: Department of Psychological and Brain Sciences
0535.bio: Peter Ulric Tse is a Professor of Cognitive Neuroscience at Dartmouth College, where Tse investigates the neural mechanisms underlying visual consciousness and volitional attention. Their research employs functional MRI, psychophysics, and neurophysiology to examine how the brain constructs subjective experience and manages top-down volitional mental operations. Tse developed the 'criterial causation' framework, which explores how informational causation is realized in physical neural circuits. Tse additionally conducts research on form-motion interactions, octopus cognition, and the neural basis of imagination.
0535.research_direction: Dr. Tse has recently been investigating the neural architecture of spatial cognition, using fMRI to map how attentional load and hemifield specificity are distributed across early visual and frontoparietal networks during multiple-object tracking. Their recent experimental work also explores spatial representation and motion-induced position shifts through psychophysics and eye-tracking, examining how external spatial reference frames influence illusions like the Flying Bluebottle and probing the dissociation between conscious perception and saccadic localization in the Frame Effect. Alongside this empirical research, they have been developing broad theoretical frameworks regarding the philosophy of mind and the evolution of human cognition. Specifically, their recent conceptual papers investigate the mechanisms of consciousness by proposing models of "criterial causation" as alternatives to intrinsic information theories, while also exploring how premotor neural circuits for manual object control may have been evolutionarily repurposed to support abstract human imagination.

papers.title: Hemifield Specificity of Attention Response Functions During Multiple Object Tracking
papers.abstract: This neuroimaging study employed functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) to delineate the cortical topography of Attention Response Functions (ARFs) within a multiple-object tracking (MOT) paradigm. Participants tracked varying quantities of targets (0–4) distributed across bilateral hemifields among identical distractors to isolate tracking load effects from sensory input. The results demonstrate a clear hierarchical dissociation in hemifield specificity: BOLD activity in early visual areas, including V3a and the hMT+ complex, was parametrically modulated primarily by the attentional load in the contralateral hemifield. Conversely, higher-order nodes of the dorsal attention network, such as the intraparietal sulcus (IPS) and superior parietal lobule (SPL), exhibited significant modulation by tracking load across the entire visual field. These findings suggest that attentional capacity limits are constrained by hemisphere-specific processing bottlenecks in early extrastriate cortex, while integrative frontoparietal systems support global attentional deployment.
papers.authors: Marvin R. Maechler, Eunhye Choe, Patrick Cavanagh, Peter J. Kohler, Peter U. Tse

papers.title: The Disencapsulated Mind: A Premotor Theory of Human Imagination
papers.abstract: This theoretical paper proposes a premotor theory of human imagination, arguing that the uniquely human capacity for creativity and abstract mental modeling arises from the 'disencapsulation' of previously modular sensory and motor cognitive domains. The author posits that neural circuits originally evolved for the premotor planning of sequential object manipulation (manual effector control) were reconfigured to support virtual operations over symbols and mental objects within an internal workspace. This retooling allows for both volitional and non-volitional mental simulations, analogous to the premotor theory of attention. The theory concludes that this evolutionary transition resulted in a fundamental bifurcation of human consciousness into a concrete form focused on physical perception and an abstract form dedicated to hypothetical mental models, which may explain both the roots of human creativity and the emergence of species-specific psychotic disorders.
papers.authors: Peter U. Tse

papers.title: New insights and a computational model for understanding induced motion revealed through novel variants of the Flying Bluebottle Illusion
papers.abstract: This study utilizes novel variations of the Flying Bluebottle and double-drift illusions to investigate the role of spatial reference frames and positional uncertainty in motion-induced position shifts (MIPS). In a series of psychophysical experiments, participants estimated the perceived trajectory of a drifting Gabor patch in the presence of stationary anchoring lines. The results demonstrate that anchors positioned within 1.5 degrees of visual angle (dva) of the motion path significantly attenuate the illusory position shift, with the effect magnitude scaling inversely with anchor distance. The authors propose a computational model where global motion integration is locally constrained by the nearest stable spatial landmark. These findings suggest that the human visual system dynamically recalibrates absolute position estimates by prioritizing relative location information from high-certainty external reference points, particularly when the moving target is viewed at high eccentricity.
papers.authors: Ryan E. B. Mruczek, Sharif Saleki, Patrick Cavanagh, Peter U. Tse

papers.title: Ontological conceptions of information cannot account for consciousness
papers.abstract: This conceptual analysis argues against ontological or 'intrinsic' theories of information, such as Integrated Information Theory (IIT), as sufficient frameworks for explaining consciousness. The author maintains that quantifying causal integration or mathematical structure fails to account for the qualitative, subjective nature of phenomenal experience. Instead, he advocates for a framework of 'criterial causation,' in which consciousness arises from the satisfaction of criteria realized in biological neural decoding systems. According to this view, information is not an inherent property of a physical state but is defined by how a system decodes inputs based on pre-set parameters. The paper concludes that an adequate account of consciousness must move beyond information-theoretic metrics to incorporate the mechanisms by which physical neural states realize intentional representation and downward mental causation.
papers.authors: Peter U. Tse

papers.title: Dissociation between perception and saccadic localization in the Frame Effect
papers.abstract: This research investigates the degree of dissociation between conscious perceptual awareness and motoric saccadic control using the Frame Effect—an illusion where a moving frame induces a substantial displacement in the perceived location of a static flash. Through a series of psychophysical tasks and high-resolution eye-tracking, the authors compared the magnitude of the illusory shift in perceptual judgments versus the shifts in saccadic landing positions. Across multiple experiments varying frame velocity and probe timing, the study found that perceived position shifts were approximately three times larger than the shifts observed in saccadic targeting. This constant dissociation suggests that the visual system maintains independent and non-overlapping spatial representations for conscious perception and the immediate control of motor action, adding novel evidence to the debate regarding the independence of vision-for-perception and vision-for-action streams.
papers.authors: Sharif Saleki, Eunhye Choe, Patrick Cavanagh, Peter Tse

0536.name: Petra Vetter
0536.bio: Petra Vetter is an Assistant Professor who investigates how the human brain integrates non-visual signals—such as auditory, emotional, and motor information—to shape visual perception. Vetter's work utilizes high-field fMRI with multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) and eye-tracking to demonstrate that the early visual cortex represents sensory content in the absence of retinal input or conscious awareness. They study neuroplasticity in congenitally blind individuals, examining how visual cortical areas are repurposed for spatial mapping through touch and audition. Vetter's research is supported by SNSF PRIMA and Consolidator grants and focuses on the mechanisms of cognitive penetration and cross-modal guidance of eye movements.
0536.research_direction: Dr. Vetter has recently been investigating how auditory information influences visual processing and oculomotor control, particularly when conscious visual input is absent or suppressed. Their recent work explores top-down feedback to the early visual cortex, using fMRI and multivariate pattern analysis to ask whether semantic sound categories and sound-symbolic speech—such as the "bouba-kiki" effect—elicit distinct neural representations in blindfolded listeners. Additionally, they employ continuous flash suppression and eye-tracking to examine how semantic audio-visual congruence interacts with visual awareness, testing whether matching sounds modulate detection sensitivity for biological motion or guide gaze toward unseen threat-related images. They also synthesize broad behavioral and neurophysiological evidence to delineate how both low-level acoustic properties and high-level semantic features of sound reflexively and voluntarily drive various eye movements.

papers.title: Decoding the “bouba-kiki” effect in early visual cortex
papers.abstract: Using high-resolution functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and multivoxel pattern analysis (MVPA), this study investigated whether sound-symbolic speech sounds—specifically the 'bouba-kiki' effect—elicit distinct neural representations in early visual cortex (EVC) without concurrent visual stimulation. Blindfolded participants performed shape judgments on 'round' (e.g., bouba) and 'spiky' (e.g., kiki) sound-symbolic words. Results demonstrated that neural activity patterns in V1, V2, and V3, as well as the right intraparietal sulcus and Broca's area, reliably distinguished between these sound-symbolic categories. Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA) further revealed that these neural patterns were significantly correlated with behavioral shape judgments, suggesting that sound symbolism manifests through distinct sensory-specific neural codes rather than solely as a high-level linguistic phenomenon.
papers.authors: Stefano Ioannucci, Carole Jordan, Anne-Sophie Carnet, Carolyn McGettigan, Petra Vetter

papers.title: Semantic audio-visual congruence modulates visual sensitivity to biological motion across awareness levels
papers.abstract: This research employed dynamic continuous flash suppression (CFS) to examine the impact of semantically congruent versus incongruent sounds on detection sensitivity (d') for biological motion. Participants were required to detect visual human actions (walking, rowing, sawing) while hearing matching or non-matching sounds. Results showed that for participants with low levels of visual awareness, semantically congruent sounds significantly increased sensitivity specifically to upright biological motion. No such facilitation was found for participants with high awareness or for inverted motion. These findings suggest that the influence of semantic auditory feedback on visual representations is inversely related to visual signal strength, facilitating perception primarily when visual awareness is minimal or absent.
papers.authors: Stefano Ioannucci, Petra Vetter

papers.title: Decoding semantic sound categories in early visual cortex
papers.abstract: This fMRI study applied multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) to activity in retinotopically defined early visual regions (V1-V3) to determine the degree of categorical specificity in non-visual feedback during blindfolded sound perception. Participants listened to 36 natural sounds organized into a semantic hierarchy (e.g., animate/inanimate; human/animal/vehicle/object). MVPA successfully decoded both broad superordinate and intermediate semantic categories from early visual cortex patterns, despite the absence of visual input. Pairwise classification demonstrated that human-produced sounds were represented more distinctively than other semantic categories. These results provide evidence that categorical and semantic auditory information is represented in early visual cortex, potentially serving as a top-down predictive signal for expected visual input.
papers.authors: Giusi Pollicina, Samuel A Müller, Polly Dalton, Petra Vetter

papers.title: Auditory guidance of eye movements toward threat-related images in the absence of visual awareness
papers.abstract: Using a combination of continuous flash suppression (CFS) and high-speed eye-tracking, the authors investigated whether threat-related sounds could facilitate oculomotor orienting toward semantically congruent visual stimuli suppressed from conscious awareness. Observers viewed suppressed images of cars (threat) and hands (neutral) while hearing matching or non-matching sounds (engine vs. finger-snapping). Analysis of gaze distribution revealed that threat-related engine sounds guided eye movements specifically toward 'unseen' car images, increasing fixation time at the target location compared to neutral control conditions. This suggests that semantically congruent, threat-related multisensory signals can bypass conscious awareness to prioritize oculomotor actions, likely via a subcortical circuit involving the superior colliculus and amygdala.
papers.authors: Junchao Hu, Stephanie Badde, Petra Vetter

papers.title: How the eyes respond to sounds
papers.abstract: This review synthesizes behavioral and neurophysiological evidence regarding the modulation of various oculomotor responses—including saccades, microsaccadic inhibition, smooth pursuit, pupil dilation, and eyeblinks—by auditory stimulation. The authors evaluate how both low-level acoustic properties and high-level semantic/linguistic features of sounds drive reflexive and voluntary eye movements. The review delineates the underlying neural architecture, focusing on the integration of auditory spatial and categorical information within the superior colliculus and its functional connectivity with the auditory and visual cortices. By contrasting auditory-evoked responses with purely visually-driven ones, the paper highlights the unique characteristics of multisensory oculomotor control and identifies critical open questions for future cross-modal research.
papers.venue: Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Junchao Hu, Petra Vetter

0537.name: Philip J. Kellman
0537.bio: Philip J. Kellman is a Distinguished Professor at UCLA and the Director of the UCLA Human Perception Laboratory, where Kellman investigates the mechanisms of visual interpolation, object formation, and cognitive development. Their research explores how human perceivers extract structure from motion and contours to achieve object unity, a framework known as unit formation. Currently, Kellman’s work examines the intersection of human vision and artificial intelligence, specifically evaluating how deep convolutional neural networks differ from biological systems in processing global shape and abstract relational properties. Kellman also develops adaptive learning technologies that apply principles of perceptual learning to the medical, aviation, and educational domains.
0537.research_direction: Dr. Kellman's recent work explores both the fundamental psychophysical mechanisms of shape abstraction and the applied dynamics of perceptual category learning. In the domain of mid-level vision, they have recently been investigating how the visual system groups discrete elements, such as dot arrays, into continuous global shapes by probing the local geometric constraints that dictate the perception of smooth curves versus angular corners. Parallel to this, their research examines the acquisition of perceptual expertise in complex visual domains like face identification and dermatological image classification. Using paired comparison paradigms and adaptive training software, Dr. Kellman is exploring how specific pedagogical variables—such as the real-time presentation of contrast trials to resolve individual learner confusions, or the manipulation of multi-category roles as targets versus distractors—drive representational change and optimize the extraction of discriminative visual features.

papers.title: Adaptively triggered comparisons enhance perceptual category learning: evidence from face learning
papers.abstract: The acquisition of perceptual categories is fundamental across both expert domains like medical image analysis and general tasks like face identification. Previous findings indicate that the direct contrast of examples from distinct categories facilitates learning, especially for highly similar classes. This study introduces and evaluates a dynamic learning system that employs adaptively triggered comparisons (ATCs). In this framework, the pedagogical software monitors for specific categorical confusions and immediately generates comparison trials requiring the discrimination of simultaneously presented items from those confused categories. Utilizing a face identification paradigm involving 22 unique identities, the researchers demonstrated that ATCs significantly improved learning efficiency and mastery attainment compared to both traditional single-item classification and non-adaptive comparison schedules. These results suggest that tailoring the presentation of contrasting exemplars based on individual learner performance significantly optimizes the differentiation of complex visual categories.
papers.authors: Victoria L. Jacoby, Christine M. Massey, Philip J. Kellman

papers.title: Shape from dots: A window into abstraction processes in visual perception
papers.abstract: This research investigates the mechanisms by which the human visual system transforms discrete, unconnected sensory elements into abstract shape representations. The study addresses why the visual system frequently perceives smooth curvilinear contours from dot arrays rather than simpler, more parsimonious polygonal connections. Through a series of psychophysical experiments, the authors demonstrate that shape perception from dots is governed by precise smoothness and curvature constraints. In Experiment 1, they identify the spatial relations among dot triplets that differentiate perceived corners from smooth curves, finding a critical boundary around 90°. Experiment 2 shows that these local geometric rules predict the perception of global shapes in more complex configurations. Finally, mental rotation tasks in Experiment 3 reveal that shapes perceived as smooth curves support more robust and efficient mental representations than those with high angularity. The findings suggest that the visual system automatically segments contours into constant curvature primitives to form economical, relational, and additive abstract representations.
papers.authors: Nicholas Baker, Philip J. Kellman

papers.title: Target vs. distractor: Does the role of a category in comparisons influence learning? Evidence from skin cancer classification
papers.abstract: Perceptual category learning often benefits from paired comparisons, where learners must differentiate between simultaneously presented items. This study examines whether the specific roles assigned to categories within these comparisons—either as the target to be identified or the distractor to be ignored—affect the resulting learning outcomes. In a dermatological classification task with medically naive participants, the researchers manipulated the frequency with which 10 skin lesion categories (both benign and malignant) appeared as targets versus distractors. Results indicated that categories consistently presented as targets achieved significantly higher learning gains than those frequently relegated to the distractor role. This disparity was most pronounced in conditions where certain categories never functioned as targets. The findings suggest that while comparisons are highly effective for extracting discriminative features, the active selection of a target category is a critical driver of representational change in multi-category perceptual learning.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the 46th Annual Meeting of the Cognitive Science Society
papers.authors: Victoria L. Jacoby, Christine M. Massey, Philip J. Kellman

0540.name: Philippe G. Schyns
0540.bio: Philippe G. Schyns is a Professor of Psychology and Director of the Institute of Neuroscience and Psychology at the University of Glasgow. Schyns developed the 'Bubbles' technique, a data-driven methodology designed to isolate the specific visual information—such as spatial frequency and orientation—that humans utilize for object, scene, and face categorization. Their research integrates computational modeling, psychophysics, and brain imaging (MEG and EEG) to decode the information-processing content of neural signals. Currently, their work utilizes generative models and Deep Neural Networks to examine the relationship between brain activity and cognitive computation in the representation and transmission of visual information.
0540.research_direction: Dr. Schyns's recent work explores the cognitive and neural mechanisms of social perception, specifically investigating how the brain processes dynamic facial movements for emotion categorization and how mental representations of these expressions vary across cultures in clinical psychiatric contexts. Using magnetoencephalography (MEG) and data-driven generative models of facial action units, they have recently been examining the broader neurocomputational stages of visual categorization to understand how the pre-frontal cortex guides the occipito-ventral pathway in reducing high-dimensional sensory inputs into task-specific visual manifolds. Beyond faces, their research probes the computational structure of natural scene perception, asking how low-level color and edge features support the rapid behavioral extraction of semantic gist independent of object identity. Additionally, they are applying their expertise in facial kinematics to applied computer vision, developing novel architectural frameworks that integrate 3D morphable models and generative adversarial networks to synthesize high-fidelity, real-time head avatars from monocular video.

papers.title: Reevaluating the assessment of nonverbal behavior in psychosis symptomatology: A call for cultural sensitivity
papers.abstract: This study critiques the assumption of cultural universality in facial expressions of emotion, specifically within the context of clinical assessments for psychosis. The authors argue that psychiatric evaluations of nonverbal behavior often rely on Western-centric models of emotional expression, which may lead to misdiagnosis or biased assessments in diverse populations. Using a data-driven approach to reconstruct mental representations of facial expressions across cultures, the research demonstrates that Western and Eastern observers utilize distinct sets of facial movements (Action Units) and dynamic eye activity to represent emotions and their intensities. The paper advocates for the integration of cross-cultural variability into clinical diagnostic frameworks to improve the precision of nonverbal behavioral analysis in psychosis.
papers.authors: Julianna M. Schuch, Danielle Pratt, Claudia Haase, Vijay A. Mittal, Philippe G. Schyns

papers.title: The brain computes dynamic facial movements for emotion categorization using a third pathway
papers.abstract: In this investigation, the researchers characterize the functional role of a proposed 'third pathway' for social perception, dedicated to processing biological motion. By employing a generative model of dynamic facial expressions based on Action Units (AUs) and recording neural activity via magnetoencephalography (MEG), the study isolates dynamic social signals from static facial identity features. Representational interaction analyses reveal that the bank of the superior temporal sulcus (bSTS) and the superior temporal gyrus (STG) selectively represent, communicate, and integrate diagnostic facial movements necessary for emotion categorization. Concurrently, the occipital cortex acts as a computational filter, suppressing task-irrelevant shape and texture information, thereby supporting an algorithmic account of how the brain transforms sensory inputs into social categorical decisions.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS)
papers.authors: Yuening Yan, Jiayu Zhan, Oliver G. B. Garrod, Robin A. A. Ince, Rachael E. Jack, Philippe G. Schyns

papers.title: SelfieAvatar: Real-time Head Avatar reenactment from a Selfie Video
papers.abstract: This paper introduces 'SelfieAvatar,' a novel computational framework designed for high-fidelity, real-time reenactment of head avatars using only monocular selfie video input. The architecture integrates 3D Morphable Models (3DMMs) with a StyleGAN-based generative backbone to synthesize animatable personal avatars. To overcome the limitations of traditional GAN-based reenactment, which often fails to capture fine-grained textures like hair and wrinkles, the authors propose a detailed reconstruction model utilizing mixed loss functions for foreground segmentation and avatar image generation. Quantitative and qualitative evaluations demonstrate that this approach achieves superior detail recovery and cross-reenactment performance with significantly less training data than state-of-the-art volumetric or purely image-based methods.
papers.venue: IEEE 19th International Conference on Automatic Face and Gesture Recognition (FG 2025)
papers.authors: Wei Liang, Hui Yu, Derui Ding, Rachael E. Jack, Philippe G. Schyns

papers.title: Pre-frontal cortex guides dimension-reducing transformations in the occipito-ventral pathway for categorization behaviors
papers.abstract: The research examines the neurocomputational stages by which the brain reduces high-dimensional visual inputs into lower-dimensional manifolds tailored for specific categorization tasks. Using source-space MEG, the authors tracked neural transformations as participants performed four distinct tasks (identifying facial expression, face gender, pedestrian gender, or vehicle type). The results delineate a three-stage process: (1) an initial high-dimensional stage (50–120 ms) where occipital regions represent both task-relevant and task-irrelevant features; (2) a transformation stage where the pre-frontal cortex (PFC) modulates the flow of information; and (3) a final stage where higher-order ventral and dorsal regions represent task-aligned low-dimensional manifolds. This identifies the PFC as a crucial controller of the dimensionality reduction required for flexible perceptual behavior.
papers.authors: Yaocong Duan, Jiayu Zhan, Joachim Gross, Robin A. A. Ince, Philippe G. Schyns

papers.title: Visual Memory for Natural Scenes
papers.abstract: This study seek to understand the computational structure of color and edge features that enable the rapid recognition of 'scene gist' without relying on component object identity. Utilizing the L*a*b* color space, the authors test the conditions under which chromatic cues and brightness information concur to support scene categorization. Behavioral experiments involving scrambled edge and color distributions reveal that high-level semantic information can be preserved in low-level visual features. The results suggest that semantic scene processing may begin earlier in the visual hierarchy than previously hypothesized, with low-level feature integration and scene segmentation occurring in parallel with, rather than strictly before, high-level semantic perception.
papers.authors: Xiaohan Hannah Guo, Jiayu Zhan, Andrew Webb, Philippe G. Schyns

0541.name: Phillip Guan
0541.bio: Phillip Guan is a research scientist at Meta Reality Labs Research, where they investigate the interface between human vision science and near-eye display architectures. Guan’s research focuses on perceptual requirements for immersive computing, specifically establishing thresholds for world-locked rendering, stereopsis, and eye-tracked distortion correction in virtual and augmented reality. Their work involves the quantification of visual discomfort through the identification of behavioral correlates and the development of adaptive psychophysical frameworks such as AEPsych. Guan received a PhD in Vision Science from the University of California, Berkeley, where their doctoral research focused on stereoscopic depth constancy and binocular vision.
0541.research_direction: Dr. Guan’s recent work investigates the intersection of human visual perception and computational rendering in head-mounted displays, focusing on how system design choices and inaccuracies impact spatial vision, user comfort, and rendering efficiency. Their recent work explores how system anomalies—such as geometric perspective errors and subthreshold visual-vestibular jitter—alter egocentric distance perception and induce visually induced motion sickness, utilizing applied psychophysics and the objective tracking of oculomotor dynamics. Additionally, they have recently been examining how physiological phenomena like saccadic suppression can be exploited to develop efficient gaze-contingent rendering techniques that reduce computational workloads without degrading perceived image quality. To support these complex human-in-the-loop experiments, Dr. Guan is also developing advanced statistical frameworks, such as mixed-likelihood Gaussian processes, to jointly model diverse streams of qualitative and quantitative perceptual data.

papers.title: Errors in Stereo Geometry Induce Distance Misperception
papers.abstract: The authors evaluate how systematic inaccuracies in the rendering and display pipeline of stereoscopic head-mounted displays (HMDs)—specifically misalignments between virtual render cameras and display centers of projection, or viewing positions eccentric to the designed eyebox—induce significant errors in egocentric distance perception. They propose a unified geometric framework to quantify the predicted magnitude and direction of depth misperceptions resulting from these perspective errors. Using a custom experimental platform utilizing a Meta Quest 3 with integrated eye tracking, the researchers conducted five psychophysical experiments to validate the model, demonstrating that geometric inaccuracies can lead to both under- and over-estimations of distance. Furthermore, they demonstrate that real-time visual feedback can be leveraged to drive dynamic visuomotor recalibration, effectively mitigating these perceptual biases.
papers.authors: Raffles Xingqi Zhu, Charlie S. Burlingham, Olivier Mercier, Phillip Guan

papers.title: Subthreshold Jitter in VR Can Induce Visual Discomfort
papers.abstract: This study investigates the impact of subthreshold visual-vestibular conflicts on user comfort during naturalistic, long-duration virtual reality usage. The authors first employed psychophysical methods to establish detection thresholds for sinusoidal jitter in the render pose, which creates anomalous perceived motion of world-fixed content. They then introduced subthreshold levels of this jitter to participants using a Meta Quest 3 HMD during 90-minute gameplay sessions. While traditional pre- and post-session Simulator Sickness Questionnaire (SSQ) scores failed to reveal significant differences, time-resolved Motion Illness Symptoms Classification (MISC) ratings demonstrated that even imperceptible geometric instabilities significantly increase visual discomfort over time. These results highlight the necessity of high-precision rendering pipelines and the importance of high-frequency symptom monitoring in ecologically valid VR research.
papers.venue: UIST 2025 (ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology)
papers.authors: Samuel J. Levulis, Kevin W. Rio, Pablo Ramon Soria, James Wilmott, Charlie S. Burlingham, Phillip Guan

papers.title: Mixed Likelihood Variational Gaussian Processes
papers.abstract: The researchers introduce a mixed likelihood variational Gaussian process (GP) framework designed to jointly model diverse data types—such as binary performance data, qualitative Likert-scale confidence ratings, and expert priors—within a single variational evidence lower bound (ELBO). This approach enables human-in-the-loop experimentation to leverage auxiliary information that traditional GP models typically ignore. The framework's utility is demonstrated across three diverse applications: accelerating active learning in a VR camera-geometry identification task by imposing prior constraints, improving the fidelity of haptic surface-roughness perception models by incorporating confidence scores, and enhancing preference learning in robotic gait optimization. The results indicate that incorporating multi-modal auxiliary signals significantly improves sample efficiency and model calibration in complex perceptual and optimization tasks.
papers.venue: NeurIPS 2025 (Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems)
papers.authors: Kaiwen Wu, Craig Sanders, Benjamin Letham, Phillip Guan

papers.title: Identifying Behavioral Correlates to Visual Discomfort
papers.abstract: To address the limitations and biases of subjective surveys in quantifying visually induced motion sickness (VIMS), the authors investigate objective behavioral indicators of discomfort in naturalistic virtual reality environments. Utilizing a specialized VR headset designed to induce significant pupil-swim distortion, the study demonstrates that eye-tracked dynamic distortion correction (ETDDC) significantly alleviates user discomfort during extended gameplay. By applying representational similarity analysis (RSA) to a high-dimensional set of 41 head and gaze metrics, the researchers identify specific changes in blink frequency and oculomotor dynamics that serve as sensitive behavioral correlates of subjective discomfort. This work establishes a foundation for the development of sensor-based, real-time discomfort monitoring systems in immersive displays.
papers.authors: David Tovar, James Wilmott, Xiuyun Wu, Daniel Martin, Michael Proulx, Dave Lindberg, Yang Zhao, Olivier Mercier, Phillip Guan

papers.title: Saccade-Contingent Rendering
papers.abstract: This paper presents a novel gaze-contingent rendering strategy for head-mounted displays that bypasses the need for high-precision, low-latency gaze tracking by exploiting temporal suppression of visual sensitivity during and after saccades. The technique utilizes the observation that spatial acuity is significantly reduced for several hundred milliseconds following a saccadic eye movement. Psychophysical experiments confirm that reducing image resolution during and immediately after saccades is indistinguishable from full-resolution rendering for users. The method was further validated on a high-density, 90 pixels-per-degree (PPD) headset under typical VR viewing conditions, demonstrating a viable performance optimization that significantly reduces rendering workload without introducing perceivable artifacts or requiring continuous foveal tracking.
papers.authors: Yuna Kwak, Eric Penner, Xuan Wang, Mohammad R. Saeedpour-Parizi, Olivier Mercier, Xiuyun Wu, T. Scott Murdison, Phillip Guan

0542.name: Pinglei Bao
0542.department: School of Psychological and Cognitive Sciences
0542.bio: Pinglei Bao is a Principal Investigator researching the neural mechanisms of high-level visual cognition, including object recognition, scene categorization, and contour segmentation. Bao integrates large-scale electrophysiological recordings using Neuropixels, functional MRI, and micro-electrical stimulation in human and non-human primate models. Their research characterizes the primate inferotemporal (IT) cortex by identifying a systematic map of 'object space' to explain the organization of visual representations across the cortical surface. Bao's current work focuses on bridging population-level dynamics and single-neuron activity while using deep learning frameworks to model transformations in the primate visual system.
0542.research_direction: Dr. Bao’s recent work explores the functional organization, representational dynamics, and evolutionary homology of the high-level visual cortex across humans and non-human primates. Using a combination of human neuroimaging and fMRI-guided Neuropixels recordings in macaques, they have recently been investigating how the inferotemporal (IT) cortex processes complex object features, focusing on the hierarchical integration of shape and texture alongside the developmental precursors of specialized domains like the visual word form area. Their research also examines cross-species representational alignment by developing large-scale electrophysiological datasets of macaque responses to natural scenes to benchmark against human fMRI data and modern computational vision models. Furthermore, Dr. Bao is exploring the cognitive flexibility of the human visual system, employing representational similarity analysis to map how spatial geometries in regions like the lateral occipital complex dynamically reorganize to differentiate position-independent visual working memory from spatially constrained active perception.

papers.title: Triple-N Dataset: Non-human Primate Neural Responses to Natural Scenes
papers.abstract: The Triple-N (Non-human Primate Neural Responses to Natural Scenes) dataset represents a large-scale extension of the human Natural Scenes Dataset (NSD) to macaque monkeys, aiming to facilitate cross-species comparisons of visual representations. Utilizing fMRI-guided high-density Neuropixels probes, activity was recorded from 59 sessions across 27 inferotemporal (IT) cortex sub-regions in five macaques as they viewed 1,000 richly annotated natural images shared with the human dataset. The dataset includes over 30,000 visually responsive units, including approximately 2,100 well-isolated single neurons, predominantly from category-selective regions (face, body, scene, and color patches). Analysis of the dataset demonstrates fine-grained examination of category selectivity and temporal response dynamics shaped by both intrinsic neuronal properties and stimulus features. Cross-species alignment using neuron-to-voxel correlations reveals a strong correspondence in representational structure between macaque firing rates and human BOLD responses, while benchmarking shows how visual feature models and large language models (LLMs) align with these biological neural spaces.
papers.authors: Yipeng Li, Wei Jin, Jia Yang, Wanru Li, Baoqi Gong, Xieyi Liu, Zhengxin Gong, Kesheng Wang, Zishuo Zhao, Jingqiu Luo, Pinglei Bao

papers.title: Spatial Reorganization of Object Representations in High-Level Visual Cortex Distinguishes Working Memory from Perception
papers.abstract: This study investigates the neural mechanisms by which the human visual system balances the requirements for veridical object perception and flexible visual working memory (VWM). Focusing on the lateral occipital complex (LOC) and intraparietal sulcus (IPS), the researchers utilized fMRI and representational similarity analysis (RSA) to compare representational formats during perception and mnemonic maintenance. While perception in the LOC is characterized by strong spatial constraints and contralateral bias, VWM maintenance involves a significant spatial reorganization where object representations decouple from their perceived positions. Specifically, the contralateral bias observed during perception is markedly reduced during the VWM delay period, accompanied by an enhanced ipsilateral representation of cued objects. These findings suggest that high-level visual areas dynamically reconfigure their representational geometry to support stable, position-independent memory maintenance, distinguish memory from ongoing sensory input, and facilitate flexible cognitive manipulation.
papers.authors: Wanru Li, Jia Yang, Pinglei Bao

papers.title: Parallel and Integrated Processing of Shape and Texture in Primate Inferotemporal cortex
papers.abstract: The primate inferotemporal (IT) cortex is essential for object recognition, processing fundamental components such as shape and texture. This study employed fMRI-guided Neuropixels recordings in macaques to examine the hierarchical organization of these feature representations. Results reveal a two-stage processing scheme: in the middle IT cortex, shape- and texture-selective neurons are organized into distinct, anatomically adjacent but minimally overlapping parallel pathways. In contrast, neurons in the anterior IT cortex exhibit integrated preferences for both shape and texture information, forming a unified object representation. This transition from feature decomposition in middle IT to feature synthesis in anterior IT provides a neural scaffold for constructing complex, view-invariant object concepts from elementary visual attributes.
papers.authors: Xieyi Liu, Yipeng Li, Wei Jin, Pinglei Bao

papers.title: The Homology and Development of the Proto-Word Area in Macaques and the Visual Word Form Area in Humans
papers.abstract: The origin of the human visual word form area (VWFA) is often attributed to the recycling of cortical regions previously tuned to specific visual statistics. This study utilized high-resolution fMRI mapping and single-unit recordings to identify a homologous 'proto-word area' in the macaque inferotemporal cortex. Despite the absence of literacy training, this region exhibited selective responses to visual forms that mimic the statistics of written language, such as high-frequency spatial components and specific curvature patterns. Longitudinal data from young macaques indicated that this selectivity is present early in development, suggesting that the VWFA in humans develops from an ancestral cortical scaffold inherently tuned to the orthographic-like properties of natural objects. These results support the hypothesis that cultural expertise co-opts pre-existing, evolutionarily conserved visual processing modules.
papers.authors: Jia Yang, Li Yipeng, Wenfang Zhang, Haoxuan Yao, Jingqiu Luo, Hongyu Li, Xiaoya Chen, Shiming Tang, Pinglei Bao

0543.name: Po-Jang (Brown) Hsieh
0543.bio: Po-Jang Hsieh is a faculty member in the Department of Psychology at National Taiwan University and directs the Brain & Consciousness Lab. Hsieh’s research utilizes functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) to investigate the neural mechanisms underlying visual awareness, attention, and the distinction between conscious and unconscious processing. Their findings demonstrate how neural activity patterns in the visual cortex predict subjective perceptual states and decision-making behaviors. Prior to this position, Hsieh held an assistant professorship at Duke-NUS Medical School and conducted postdoctoral research at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.
0543.research_direction: Dr. Hsieh has recently been exploring a diverse array of perceptual phenomena across both the visual and auditory domains, focusing on how the human brain constructs, integrates, and maintains complex sensory representations. Their recent work explores the limits of unconscious vision, utilizing fMRI and multivariate pattern analysis alongside discontinuous flash suppression to investigate how deeply suppressed dynamic faces and scenes are processed within the ventral visual stream. Beyond unconscious perception, they are investigating high-level geometric and temporal representations, combining fMRI and MEG to track how the visual system encodes "perspectival shapes"—the specific 2D proximal projections of rotated 3D objects—while also examining how visual information influences the intentional binding effect during multisensory audiovisual actions. Additionally, their research extends into auditory cognition and applied sensory neuroscience, utilizing fMRI adaptation to map the distributed cortical networks underlying melody transposition tolerance, and rigorously testing whether 40-Hz audiovisual gamma entrainment can successfully modulate visual thresholds and spatial working memory in healthy individuals.

papers.title: Decoding dynamic faces and scenes without awareness under discontinuous flash suppression
papers.abstract: This study employs an optimized psychophysical paradigm using discontinuous flash suppression to evaluate the extent of unconscious processing for complex visual stimuli. While conscious perception of faces elicited broad univariate BOLD activations in contrast to scenes, such activity was absent for interocularly suppressed, invisible stimuli. However, multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) revealed that both static and dynamic invisible faces could be successfully decoded from scenes within the occipito-temporal region. Specifically, region-of-interest (ROI) analyses identified that the bilateral fusiform face area (FFA) and occipital face area (OFA) contained sufficient information to differentiate dynamic invisible faces from scenes. These findings demonstrate that interocularly suppressed facial information undergoes deep processing within the ventral visual stream, underscoring the necessity of high-signal stimuli and sensitive analytical methods for extracting unconscious neural signals.
papers.authors: Yen-Ju Feng, Shao-Min Hung, Po-Jang Hsieh

papers.title: Visual information shows dominance in determining the magnitude of intentional binding for audiovisual outcomes
papers.abstract: This research investigated the intentional binding (IB) effect—the perceived temporal compression between a voluntary action and its sensory consequence—in multimodal (audiovisual) contexts using a modified Libet clock paradigm depicting a physical collision event. Experiment 1 explored whether IB for unimodal auditory events generalizes to multimodal audiovisual events and how the magnitude of binding is influenced by cross-modal integration. Results indicated that the IB effect was significantly attenuated in both audiovisual and unimodal visual conditions relative to the unimodal auditory condition. Experiment 2 decomposed the audiovisual stimulus to evaluate predictive models of IB magnitude. Findings confirmed that IB in audiovisual and visual-only conditions was equivalent and significantly weaker than in auditory-only conditions. Bayesian analysis provided moderate evidence for this equivalence, suggesting that visual information exerts a dominant influence on the magnitude of intentional binding for multimodal sensory outcomes.
papers.authors: De-Wei Dai, Po-Jang (Brown) Hsieh

papers.title: Melody transposition tolerance in the human cortex: An fMRI adaptation and MVPA investigation
papers.abstract: This study explored the neural basis of melody transposition invariance—the ability to recognize relational pitch representations despite absolute pitch shifts—using fMRI adaptation and multivariate cross-classification (MVCC). Univariate results identified clusters in the right superior temporal gyrus (STG) and left middle temporal gyrus (MTG) that exhibited adaptation to both identical and transposed-same melodies. Furthermore, searchlight and ROI-based MVCC analyses demonstrated that voxel-wise BOLD patterns in the bilateral precentral gyrus (PreCG), left inferior frontal gyrus (IFG), left inferior parietal lobule (IPL), right angular gyrus (AG), and right STG showed significant tolerance to transposition. These findings suggest that transposition-invariant melody representations are distributed across a cortical hierarchy, extending beyond early auditory regions to involve motor and parietal association cortices.
papers.authors: Yun-An Han, Po-Jang Hsieh

papers.title: Neural representations of perspectival shapes and attentional effects: Evidence from fMRI and MEG
papers.abstract: Utilizing fMRI and MEG, this study examined whether the human brain represents 'perspectival shapes'—the 2D projections unique to a specific viewing angle—distinctly from viewpoint-independent distal object properties. By analyzing neural activity patterns during the perception of rotated 3D circular and elliptical stimuli, the researchers tested whether the visual system maintains representations consistent with proximal geometry. Shape classifiers trained on basic shapes identified neural representations in the lateral occipital cortex (LOC) corresponding to perspectival shapes regardless of attentional state. Multimodal evidence suggests that these representations emerge approximately 200 ms post-stimulus. Furthermore, attention was found to modulate the spatial and temporal persistence of these representations, with perspectival signals propagating from the occipital to the temporal lobe under attended conditions, challenging models that assume proximal features are discarded during unconscious inference.
papers.authors: Yi Lin, Yung-Yi Hsu, Tony Cheng, Pin-Cheng Hsiung, Chen-Wei Wu, Po-Jang Hsieh

papers.title: Forty-Hertz audiovisual stimulation does not have a promoting effect on visual threshold and visual spatial memory
papers.abstract: Motivated by findings in neurodegenerative animal models, this series of five experiments investigated the efficacy of 40-Hz audiovisual entrainment for enhancing perceptual and cognitive performance in healthy human subjects. Participants were exposed to gamma-frequency stimulation via LED sources, computer screens, and auditory binaural beats. Outcomes across visual detection thresholds, spatial frequency sensitivity, and visual spatial working memory tasks showed no significant improvements in the 40-Hz groups compared to control groups. Bayesian analysis supported the null hypothesis across most comparisons. Notably, 40-Hz stimulation appeared to interfere with standard learning effects, as the practice-driven improvements typically observed in control groups were absent in the stimulation groups. The study concludes that short-term 40-Hz sensory entrainment is ineffective as a general cognitive or perceptual enhancer in healthy individuals.
papers.authors: Pin-Cheng Hsiung, Po-Jang Hsieh

0544.name: Preeti Verghese
0544.lab_name: Verghese Lab: Vision Research on Attention and Adaptation
0544.bio: Preeti Verghese is a Senior Scientist at the Smith-Kettlewell Eye Research Institute whose research investigates the neural mechanisms and behavioral strategies governing visual attention, spatial perception, and oculomotor control. Verghese explores how clinical populations, particularly those with age-related macular degeneration and amblyopia, adapt to vision loss through altered eye-movement patterns and the use of peripheral retina for tasks such as stereopsis and visual search. Utilizing a combination of psychophysics, eye tracking, and computational modeling, they examine the integration of binocular and monocular cues to understand depth perception and target tracking in both healthy and impaired visual systems. Recent research by Verghese focuses on the recovery of stereopsis and the development of rehabilitative interventions designed to optimize functional vision in individuals with central field loss.
0544.research_direction: Dr. Verghese has recently been investigating visual perception and oculomotor control, with a strong focus on spatial and dynamic vision in individuals with macular degeneration. Their recent work explores how central field loss impacts 3D perception by examining the Bayesian integration of binocular disparity and motion parallax, while also quantifying how smooth pursuit deficits, retinal slip, and the use of an eccentric preferred retinal locus compromise dynamic visual acuity and predictive motion extrapolation. In addition to this clinical focus, they are mapping the spatial distribution of stereoscopic sensitivity across visual eccentricities to re-evaluate traditional models of foveal dominance in stereopsis for both neurotypical and amblyopic populations. Furthermore, Dr. Verghese is developing novel frequency-tagged fMRI paradigms to investigate fine-grained spatiotemporal cortical dynamics, specifically targeting how selective attention modulates enhancing and suppressive neural synchronization across the human visual hierarchy.

papers.title: The best stereoacuity is rarely at the fovea
papers.abstract: This study evaluates the spatial distribution of stereoscopic sensitivity in amblyopic and neurotypical populations, challenging the traditional model of universal foveal dominance for stereoacuity. Using random dot stereograms with eccentricity-scaled targets, the researchers measured depth thresholds at the fovea and at eccentricities of 2.5°, 5°, and 10° along the horizontal and vertical meridians. Results demonstrated that 87.5% of amblyopic observers and 75% of neurotypical controls attained their optimal stereoacuity at extrafoveal locations. Attempts to elicit foveal superiority in controls by optimizing stimulus parameters for high-frequency discrimination failed in all but one participant. The strong correlation between the experimentally determined 'best locus' sensitivity and clinical stereoacuity scores suggests that standard tests may frequently capture extrafoveal stereoscopic capacity, with significant implications for the clinical diagnosis and computational modeling of binocular vision.
papers.authors: Ângela Gomes Tomaz, Adrien Chopin, Noelia Gabriela Alcalde, Dennis M. Levi, Preeti Verghese

papers.title: Cue combination for depth perception in macular degeneration: Motion parallax augments disparity
papers.abstract: This research investigates depth cue integration in individuals with central field loss (CFL) due to macular degeneration (MD), specifically examining whether the visual system follows optimal Bayesian rules to combine binocular disparity and monocular motion parallax. Using random-dot stimuli depicting horizontally oriented sine-wave corrugations in depth, the researchers measured discrimination thresholds for each cue in isolation and in combination. While MD participants exhibited significant impairments in disparity-based depth perception within their scotoma regions, motion parallax sensitivity remained relatively preserved. Quantitative analysis demonstrated that many individuals with MD retain the capacity for optimal cue integration, contingent upon the availability of residual disparity signals. The findings identify motion parallax as a critical compensatory signal that improves 3D scene interpretation and spatial navigation for patients with impaired central stereopsis.
papers.authors: Jade Guénot, Preeti Verghese

papers.title: Oculomotor challenges in macular degeneration impact motion extrapolation
papers.abstract: This study quantifies the impact of central field loss (CFL) on trajectory estimation using a predictive motion extrapolation task. Participants with macular degeneration (MD) and normally sighted controls viewing simulated scotomas judged the end-points of targets that vanished before reaching a goal. The study isolated the effects of three factors: sensory occlusion by the scotoma, eccentricity-dependent positional noise, and oculomotor instability associated with the use of a non-foveal preferred retinal locus (PRL). Performance was assessed during both steady fixation and smooth pursuit tracking. Findings indicate that while scotoma-induced target disappearance significantly degrades accuracy, the reliance on an eccentric PRL introduces substantial oculomotor noise that further compromises trajectory estimation during active tracking. Statistical modeling confirms that target eccentricity and the duration of occlusion are the primary determinants of extrapolation errors in MD.
papers.authors: Jason F. Rubinstein, Noelia Gabriela Alcalde, Adrien Chopin, Preeti Verghese

papers.title: Smooth pursuit deficits impact dynamic visual acuity in macular degeneration
papers.abstract: This investigation examines the impact of smooth pursuit eye movement deficits on dynamic visual acuity (DVA) in individuals with macular degeneration (MD). Using a scanning laser ophthalmoscope (SLO) to project moving annular targets that briefly transformed into Landolt C optotypes, the study measured pursuit gain and discrimination accuracy. Results showed that individuals with MD exhibit significantly lower smooth pursuit gain compared to age-matched controls, especially when tracking targets at the acuity limit. Critically, the magnitude of pursuit gain, rather than the retinal eccentricity of the target relative to the preferred retinal locus (PRL), was the primary predictor of Landolt C orientation discrimination. The study concludes that the primary driver of impaired dynamic vision in MD is the retinal slip caused by poor velocity matching, which results in motion blur and compromises the visibility of moving targets.
papers.authors: Natela M. Shanidze, Preeti Verghese

papers.title: Frequency-tagged fMRI: A platform for fine-grained spatiotemporal analysis of cortical function
papers.abstract: To characterize fine-grained spatiotemporal dynamics in human visual cortex, this study developed a frequency-tagged functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) approach designed to isolate neural population responses and their interactions. By modulating stimulus components at distinct temporal frequencies, the researchers analyzed the resulting BOLD oscillations to distinguish between in-phase (enhancing) and anti-phase (suppressive) neural synchronization. The paradigm was applied to investigate how selective attention modulates these mechanisms across the visual hierarchy (V1-hV4). Findings revealed that attentional selection homogeneously increases the amplitude of anti-phase oscillations across areas, suggesting a global suppressive field, whereas the modulation of in-phase oscillations increases progressively from V1 to hV4. This methodology provides a high-resolution platform for mapping the cortical distribution of attentional gain and suppressive neural interactions.
papers.authors: Spero Nicholas, Chuan Hou, Preeti Verghese

0545.name: Qasim Zaidi
0545.bio: Qasim Zaidi is a SUNY Distinguished Professor who investigates the neural mechanisms of human visual perception through psychophysics, computational modeling, and neurophysiology. Their research focuses on how the visual system decodes information such as color constancy, three-dimensional shape from texture, and the perception of material properties. Zaidi studies the functional architecture of the primary visual cortex and retinal ganglion cell wiring, using generative models to link neural filter transformations to perceptual phenomena like amblyopic distortions and visual illusions. Recent work by Zaidi utilizes connectomics and fMRI-guided recordings to explore color decoding and the dynamics of primate retinal circuits.
0545.research_direction: Dr. Zaidi has recently been investigating how the visual system integrates low-level sensory signals with higher-level spatial and geometric constraints to resolve ambiguities about 3D shape, motion, and form. Their recent work explores the perceptual tension between object rigidity and non-rigidity, utilizing rotating 3D stimuli and novel "anti-sensory" illusions to examine how global shape priors and feature-tracking mechanisms compete with local motion-energy signals from the early visual cortex. They are also investigating the high-level perceptual consequences of early cortical architecture, modeling how V1 population anisotropies distort optic flow to create illusory wobbling, alongside behavioral studies probing the implicit projective "mental geometry" observers use to infer 3D object poses from 2D images. Additionally, Dr. Zaidi utilizes dichoptic matching paradigms and a framework of "generative phenomenology" to model hallucinatory phantom forms in amblyopic vision, seeking to mathematically describe how altered receptive field structures affect spatial localization and form detection.

papers.title: Phantom Forms in Amblyopic Vision and what they reveal about the Generative Brain
papers.abstract: The authors employ 'Generative Phenomenology' to quantify and model the hallucinatory phantom forms reported by amblyopes viewing high-contrast sinusoidal gratings. Utilizing a dichoptic matching paradigm with computer-generated plaid patterns (linear sums of gratings), the researchers acquired high-fidelity 'perceptograms'—viewable records of the observers' internal perceptions. By analytically equating cortical signals generated by test gratings in the amblyopic eye (AE) with signals from matched perceptograms in the fellow eye (FE), the study derives AE cortical filters as linear transforms of standard V1 steerable filters. The resulting transformed filters accurately replicate the reported phantoms and reveal fundamental alterations in receptive field structure and output cross-correlations, providing a mechanistic explanation for deficits in form detection and spatial localization.
papers.authors: Akihito Maruya, Bhavatharini Ramakrishnan, Farzaneh Olianezhad, Jingyun Wang, Jose-Manuel Alonso, Qasim Zaidi

papers.title: Anisotropy of object nonrigidity: High-level perceptual consequences of cortical anisotropy
papers.abstract: This study demonstrates a novel high-level perceptual anisotropy where vertically rotating rigid objects are perceived as significantly more non-rigid than their horizontally rotating counterparts. The authors model this phenomenon by incorporating established population-level anisotropies of primary visual cortex (V1) neurons—specifically higher cell densities and narrower tuning widths for horizontal orientations—into optic flow computations. Kinematic gradients, including divergence, curl, and deformation, were derived analytically and through computational simulations. Findings reveal that these hardwired cortical anisotropies distort the resulting velocity fields such that vertical rotations align more closely with physical non-rigidity (wobbling) than horizontal rotations, suggesting that failures in 3D shape constancy are directly inherited from low-level neural population properties.
papers.authors: Akihito Maruya, Qasim Zaidi

papers.title: Perceptual transitions between object rigidity and non-rigidity: Competition and cooperation among motion energy, feature tracking, and shape-based priors
papers.abstract: The research investigates the visual system's resolution of conflicts between rigid and non-rigid interpretations of moving objects. Using rigidly connected rotating 3D rings that often appear to wobble independently, the authors demonstrate that perception is driven by the dynamic interaction between motion-energy mechanisms (extracting motion orthogonal to contours) and feature-tracking mechanisms (signaling rotational velocity). At high rotation speeds, motion-energy signals dominate, leading to illusory non-rigidity. Conversely, at slower speeds or when salient features are added, feature-tracking and shape-based priors promote veridical rigidity.
