CNN-based computational models confirm that motion-energy flow patterns are classified as non-rigid, while MT-like pattern tracking supports rigid rotation, highlighting the hierarchical integration of motion cues.
papers.authors: Akihito Maruya, Qasim Zaidi

papers.title: Complexity of mental geometry for 3D pose perception
papers.abstract: The authors explore the mental geometry utilized by humans to infer the 3D poses of objects within real scenes and pictorial representations. By analyzing observer judgments of object orientations relative to camera and viewer positions across various shapes and environmental contexts, the study finds that human performance is consistently predicted by a mental model aligned with projective geometry. The results suggest that the human visual system possesses an implicit 'mental geometry' that applies projective transformations to 2D retinal images to resolve spatial ambiguity. This geometric reasoning allows for robust pose estimation despite the absence of explicit 3D information, establishing a framework for understanding how the brain represents object orientations in a 3D coordinate system.
papers.authors: Crystal Guo, Akihito Maruya, Qasim Zaidi

papers.title: Anti-Sensory Visual Illusion
papers.abstract: This article describes a novel visual illusion where the perceived direction of spinning motion is diametrically opposed to the direction signaled by local sensory mechanisms. Using stimuli designed to produce conflicting local and global motion cues, the authors show that high-level shape-based priors and global motion integration can override direction-selective signals from the early visual cortex (V1/MT). This 'anti-sensory' effect provides evidence for a hierarchical dominance in the visual brain, where the perceived motion of an undivided object is constrained by global consistency and prior expectations of rigidity, effectively suppressing discordant local motion energy measurements.
papers.authors: Akihito Maruya, Qasim Zaidi

0546.name: Qi Chen
0546.bio: Qi Chen is a cognitive neuroscientist who uses computational modeling and multi-modal neuroimaging, including fMRI, EEG, and intracranial recordings, to study the neural mechanisms of human perception and cognition. Their research explores the dynamics of visual attention and perceptual inference, demonstrating how intrinsic alpha-band oscillations facilitate perceptual grouping and resolve ambiguity through predictive preactivation. Chen also investigates numerical cognition, reinforcement learning, and the functional organization of the frontoparietal and default mode networks in cognitive control and multisensory integration.
0546.research_direction: Dr. Chen has recently been investigating the large-scale neural dynamics underlying both fundamental cognitive processes and neurological disorders using multimodal techniques like intracranial EEG, fMRI, and targeted brain stimulation. Their recent work explores basic mechanisms of human cognition, probing the temporal coordination of motor planning across the motor cortex, the causal role of frontal theta oscillations in updating prediction errors during rule-switching, and the thalamocortical pathways that make auditory cues highly efficient for spatial attention. Beyond healthy cognition, they are actively applying network-level electrophysiology to clinical challenges, such as quantifying the reproducibility of brain oscillations across seizures to better map epileptogenic zones in patients with focal epilepsy. Additionally, their team is examining how resting cortical excitability and prefrontal task-based connectivity evolve during the transition from short-term to chronic insomnia.

papers.title: Cortical excitability and brain function in patients with insomnia: a pilot transcranial magnetic stimulation and functional near-infrared spectroscopy study
papers.abstract: This pilot investigation utilized a multimodal approach combining single-pulse transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) and functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) to delineate the neurophysiological characteristics of short-term insomnia disorder (SID) and chronic insomnia disorder (CID). Cortical excitability was quantified via resting motor threshold (RMT) assessments, while fNIRS measured concentrations of oxy-hemoglobin (Oxy-Hb) and functional connectivity (FC) during a verbal fluency task (VFT). Results demonstrated that SID patients exhibit significantly lower RMTs, indicating cortical hyperexcitability, alongside elevated hemodynamic responses in the bilateral dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC), left medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), and right temporal lobe compared to CID patients. Furthermore, RMT values were negatively correlated with Oxy-Hb changes in the left mPFC, suggesting that altered prefrontal activation and diminished task-related connectivity in CID may underlie the progression of the disorder.
papers.authors: Jiali Luo, Qi Chen

papers.title: Reproducibility of temporally evolving seizure patterns and network connectivity in focal epilepsy
papers.abstract: This study quantified the intra-patient stability of seizure dynamics across repeated episodes using stereo-electroencephalography (SEEG) data from 14 patients with drug-resistant focal epilepsy. The researchers evaluated the reproducibility of ictal waveforms, periodic power spectra (using the FOOOF algorithm to isolate periodic components), and within/between-region functional connectivity (Pearson correlation). Findings revealed that ictal signatures within the identified epileptogenic zone (EZ) were significantly more reproducible across seizures than those in propagation or non-involved zones. Specifically, spectral reproducibility in the beta band during the pre-ictal period emerged as a robust marker for the EZ, suggesting that highly stable neural oscillations are localized to the seizure onset zone and can facilitate accurate pre-surgical mapping.
papers.authors: Yaohong Wei, Wei Zhang, Sinclair Xingzhou Liu, Biao Han, Qi Chen

papers.title: Medial Frontal Theta Reduction Impairs Rule Switching via Prediction Error
papers.abstract: To establish the causal relationship between medial frontal cortex (MFC) activity and cognitive flexibility, this research integrated high-definition transcranial direct current stimulation (HD-tDCS), electroencephalography (EEG), and hierarchical Bayesian modeling. Participants performed a probabilistic reversal learning task while the researchers modulated MFC theta oscillations. The study found that anodal HD-tDCS significantly reduced both mid-frontal theta power and the magnitude of rule-level prediction errors (RPEs), as quantified by the 'Sync Model.' This attenuation of theta-encoded learning signals led to impaired rule-switching performance, evidenced by an increased number of trials required to adapt to rule changes. These findings demonstrate that MFC theta oscillations causally support behavioral flexibility by encoding the prediction errors necessary for rule-level updates.
papers.authors: Yifei Zhang, Feng Deng, Jiajun Liao, Tom Verguts, Qi Chen

papers.title: Earlier finish of motor planning in the premotor cortex predicts faster motor command in the primary motor cortex: Human intracranial EEG evidence
papers.abstract: This research employed human intracranial EEG (sEEG) to investigate the temporal coordination between the premotor cortex (PMC) and the primary motor cortex (M1) during voluntary movement. By analyzing neural oscillations and evoked potentials during reaching tasks, the team examined the chronometry of motor planning offsets and motor command onsets. The results indicate that the 'earlier finish' (termination of preparatory oscillatory activity) in the PMC reliably predicts the onset latency of motor commands in M1. These findings provide direct electrophysiological evidence for a serial-to-parallel transition in the motor hierarchy, where the conclusion of a planning phase in the premotor regions triggers the subsequent execution phase in M1.
papers.authors: Jing Xia, Deshan Gong, Biao Han, Qiang Guo, Yang Zhan, Gereon R. Fink, Silvia Daun, Qi Chen

papers.title: Superior Attentional Efficiency of Auditory Cue via the Ventral Auditory-thalamic Pathway
papers.abstract: This study investigated the neural mechanisms underlying the observation that auditory informative cues are often more effective than visual cues in guiding spatial attention. Across two experiments using fMRI and psychophysics, the researchers manipulated cue modality and prediction validity. Behaviorally, auditory cues yielded consistently larger reaction time (RT) benefits. Neurally, when bottom-up targets matched the prior predictions established by auditory cues, there was significant activation in the ventral auditory-thalamic pathway, specifically involving the medial geniculate nucleus. Conversely, prediction violations by auditory cues specifically engaged the ventral frontoparietal network (FPN). The findings suggest that the superior efficiency of auditory attention is subserved by specialized thalamo-cortical loops that optimize processing when sensory inputs align with top-down expectations.
papers.authors: Ke Wang, Ying Fang, Qiang Guo, Lu Shen, Qi Chen

0547.name: Quan Lei
0547.bio: Quan Lei is an Assistant Professor of Psychology at Wichita State University and the director of the Vision and Accessibility (VISA) Lab. Lei integrates psychophysics, eye tracking, and computational modeling to investigate visual processes such as attention, perception, and short-term memory. Their research applies these principles to accessibility for individuals with visual impairments, including the development of inclusive autonomous vehicle interfaces. Lei also identified the 'weak conquer the strong' illusion in visual numerosity, which demonstrates how contrast energy modulates perceived quantities.
0547.research_direction: Dr. Lei has recently been bridging basic visual psychophysics with applied human factors research, with a strong focus on accessibility for visually impaired populations. On the applied side, their recent work explores how varying indoor illuminance levels impact both the objective hazard-detection accuracy and subjective navigational confidence of low-vision individuals interacting with architectural features like stairs and ramps. They are also investigating the intersection of visual impairment and emerging technologies, surveying how the severity of a user's vision loss shapes their trust in autonomous vehicles and their preferences for specific multi-modal interface designs. Beyond these clinical and applied domains, Dr. Lei is exploring the fundamental mechanisms of visual quantity perception, utilizing computational modeling to test how normalized contrast energy might serve as the primary sensory substrate driving human numerosity judgments and their associated visual illusions.

papers.title: The Effect of Illumination on the Visibility of Steps and Ramps for People with Low Vision
papers.abstract: In indoor environments, inadequate visibility of architectural features such as stairs and ramps introduces substantial navigational hazards for individuals with low vision. This investigation evaluated the influence of varying indoor photopic illuminance on step and ramp identification in low-vision individuals and normally sighted control observers under simulated acuity reduction. Physical full-scale step and ramp configurations were set up within an enclosed room under three overhead photopic lighting conditions: 800, 80, and 8 lux. Participants performed a five-alternative forced-choice (5-AFC) target identification task and provided subjective confidence ratings on a 5-point scale, with visual acuity and Pelli-Robson contrast sensitivity measured concurrently across each illuminance level. Objective recognition accuracy remained statistically invariant across the 8 to 800 lux photopic range in both cohorts. In contrast, ambient illuminance exerted a significant effect on subjective confidence ratings among low-vision participants, who exhibited systematically elevated certainty with increasing lighting levels. Furthermore, regression analyses revealed that objective identification accuracy was best predicted by contrast sensitivity, whereas subjective judgment confidence was primarily predicted by visual acuity. These findings demonstrate that while indoor photopic illumination shifts do not impair objective hazard identification accuracy, higher illumination levels are necessary to preserve subjective perceptual confidence during low-vision mobility.
papers.authors: Quan Lei, Rachel Gage, Daniel Kersten, Gordon E. Legge

papers.title: Preferences of Individuals With Different Levels of Visual Impairment for Autonomous Vehicles
papers.abstract: This research investigates the nexus between the magnitude of visual impairment and user expectations regarding autonomous vehicle (AV) technology. A cohort of individuals with varying degrees of vision loss provided data through a structured survey focused on perceived safety, technological trust, and human-machine interface (HMI) requirements. Analysis revealed that while there is an overarching inclination toward Level 5 full automation, participants with less severe deficits exhibited significantly higher acceptance of lower-level automation compared to those with total blindness. Furthermore, although auditory and speech-based modalities were the universally preferred interaction methods, the data indicates that individuals with residual vision retain a strong desire for redundant visual feedback. These results emphasize the necessity of adaptive, multi-modal interface designs tailored to the specific functional vision of the end-user.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the Human Factors and Ergonomics Society Annual Meeting
papers.authors: Robert Beran, Yueh-Hsun Wu, Quan Lei

papers.title: Numerosity depends on normalized contrast energy: Review and square-root law model
papers.abstract: Judgments of visual numerosity for randomly distributed elements of static contrast depend systematically on the integrated contrast energy (CE) of the stimulus array. We present a computational framework demonstrating that the square root of contrast energy, √(CE), normalized by stimulus contrast amplitude, accurately fits human numerosity estimation across varied psychophysical tasks and extensive set sizes. The model shows that judged numerosity scales as a linear function of √(N) for element counts exceeding the subitization regime. This square-root dependency accounts for several well-documented perceptual phenomena: the pervasive underestimation in absolute numerosity estimation; contrast constancy (the invariance of perceived quantity across varying contrasts in segregated arrays); the 'weak outnumber strong' illusion in which higher-contrast items appear less numerous when intermingled with lower-contrast items; and psychometric discrimination thresholds and sensitivity between arrays containing N and M items. The close fit of this normalized contrast energy formulation across broad ranges, including regimes traditionally categorized under Weber's law, indicates that normalized contrast energy serves as a fundamental sensory substrate encoding visual numerosity.
papers.authors: Quan Lei, Adam Reeves

0548.name: Quoc Vuong
0548.department: School of Psychology and Biosciences Institute
0548.bio: Quoc Vuong is a Senior Lecturer at Newcastle University’s Biosciences Institute and School of Psychology. Vuong investigates the neural and cognitive mechanisms involved in multi-sensory perception, specifically how the brain integrates spatiotemporal information from vision, audition, touch, and pain for object and face recognition. They utilize a multi-modal approach combining psychophysics, functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), electroencephalography (EEG), and eye-tracking. Their work explores the development of visual expertise and the cortical networks supporting the perception of dynamic objects and communicative interactions.
0548.research_direction: Dr. Vuong has recently been investigating the visual processing of social and kinematic cues, alongside highly diverse interdisciplinary behavioral research. Within vision science, their recent work explores the critical spatiotemporal and object features required to recognize naturalistic egocentric actions, and utilizes fMRI to map how cortical networks incidentally process communicative biological motion from point-light dyads. They are also examining the developmental ontogeny of visual emotion perception, synthesizing behavioral and neurophysiological data to trace how infants and children learn to interpret bodily postures. Beyond core perceptual mechanisms, Dr. Vuong has recently expanded into applied psychology by investigating the potential hypoalgesic effects of human-horse interactions using acute ischemic pain models. Additionally, they are employing latent class choice models to understand how cognitive-affective consistency influences consumer decision-making regarding alternative fuel vehicles.

papers.title: Seeing Just Enough: The Contribution of Hands, Objects and Visual Features to Egocentric Action Recognition
papers.abstract: Visual action recognition is remarkably resilient in humans even under extreme spatial ambiguity and visual clutter characteristic of first-person camera perspectives. To determine the critical visual information supporting action understanding from an egocentric perspective, this study implemented a Minimal Recognizable Configuration (MIRC) paradigm alongside semantic segmentation and feature reduction using videos from the EPIC-KITCHENS-100 dataset. Across 474 identified spatial MIRCs, classification analysis revealed that successful categorization relies heavily on regions containing the manipulated object and predominant orientation signals, whereas the active hand contributed only marginally. Furthermore, temporal disruption via consecutive frame scrambling disrupted recognition in 73% of MIRCs. These findings indicate that localized high-level object features and spatiotemporal continuity jointly constrain the search space during naturalistic human action perception.
papers.authors: Filip Rybansky, Sadegh Rahmaniboldaji, Andrew Gilbert, Frank Guerin, Anya C. Hurlbert, Quoc C. Vuong

papers.title: Cognitive consistency and preferences for alternative fuel vehicles: A latent class model
papers.abstract: This research investigates the complex psychological underpinnings of consumer decision-making regarding alternative fuel vehicles (AFVs) through the lens of cognitive consistency. The authors utilize a hybrid latent class choice model incorporating the Hot Coherence (HOTCO) framework to evaluate how attitudinal and emotional appraisals modulate both behavioral class membership and specific attribute preferences. By analyzing stated choice data and psychometric survey responses from UK households, the study demonstrates that heterogeneity in instrumental preferences—such as purchase price, driving range, and operational costs—is systematically linked to the perceived coherence between prospective vehicle types and a consumer's internal cognitive-affective states. Findings indicate that respondents who exhibit high emotional and cognitive alignment with pro-environmental innovation represent a distinct latent class with significantly different utility parameters compared to more instrumentally-driven consumers.
papers.venue: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment
papers.authors: Cristian Domarchi, Elisabetta Cherchi, Quoc C. Vuong

papers.title: Impact of equine interactions on human acute pain perception: Two cross sectional studies
papers.abstract: Animal-assisted therapies have demonstrated efficacy in pain modulation, but evidence is primarily restricted to canine interventions. Across two cross-sectional studies, the hypoalgesic effects of structured human-horse interactions were examined using an acute ischemic pain model induced via sphygmomanometer cuff occlusion. In Study 1, participants (N = 70) were allocated to Equine-Assisted Psychotherapy (EAP), horse interaction without psychotherapy (HI), or a non-equine control condition. In Study 2, participants (N = 53) engaged in Equine-Assisted Learning (EAL) versus a control session. Both studies demonstrated statistically significant decreases in subjective acute pain ratings following horse exposure with medium-to-large effect sizes, while control cohorts showed no pain reduction. Thematic analysis revealed that heightened positive affect, somatic relaxation, and attentional distraction likely mediate this pain attenuation.
papers.authors: Gwyneth Doherty-Sneddon, Roberta Caiazza, Emilia Pawlowska, Quoc Vuong

papers.title: Incidental visual processing of spatiotemporal cues in communicative interactions: An fMRI investigation
papers.abstract: Interpreting communicative interactions requires parsing interpersonal spatiotemporal contingencies, even when social stimuli fall outside the primary focus of attention. Using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), this investigation evaluated the incidental cortical processing of communicative versus independent actions depicted via point-light dyads while participants completed an attention-demanding color-change detection task at central fixation. Facing direction was systematically manipulated (facing vs. non-facing) along with spatial scrambling of the point-light motion vectors. Incidental perception of communicative interactions elicited selective hemodynamic responses in the right anterior superior temporal sulcus (aSTS) strictly when dyads maintained facing orientation. Subtracting motion-scrambled controls isolated additional interaction selectivity across parietal cortex, the left amygdala, and cerebellar/brainstem structures, demonstrating that socially contingent biological motion is decoded automatically by distributed cortical networks.
papers.authors: Anthony P. Atkinson, Quoc C. Vuong

papers.title: The development of emotion processing of body expressions from infancy to early childhood: A meta-analysis
papers.abstract: Recognizing emotions from bodily kinematics and posture is fundamental to social competence, yet its ontogenetic trajectory remains less understood than facial emotion recognition. This meta-analysis systematically synthesizes empirical studies evaluating bodily emotion perception in typically developing infants and young children up to approximately 7.5 years of age. Synthesizing outcome measures encompassing behavioral discrimination accuracy, eye tracking, pupillometric arousal, facial electromyography (EMG), and event-related brain potential components (including N290, P400, Nc, and N300/N400 complexes), the synthesis traces early perceptual sensitivity to biological motion in the first months of life through to complex affective categorization in early childhood. The review delineates how visual experience with upper-body and limb configurations shapes developmental milestones and highlights methodological needs for naturalistic paradigms.
papers.authors: Quoc C. Vuong, Elena Geangu

0550.name: Rachel Denison
0550.bio: Rachel Denison is an Assistant Professor at Boston University whose research investigates the temporal dynamics of visual perception, attention, and decision-making. Denison uses a multi-methodological approach integrating psychophysics, eye tracking, fMRI, and MEG/EEG with computational modeling to characterize how the brain prioritizes information at specific moments in time. Their research includes the development of a dynamic normalization model of temporal attention and high-resolution functional mapping of the magnocellular and parvocellular pathways in the human lateral geniculate nucleus. Denison’s current work examines the mechanisms of voluntary temporal attention and how the brain incorporates uncertainty into perceptual choices and confidence judgments.
0550.research_direction: Dr. Denison has recently been investigating the temporal dynamics of visual attention, perception, and subjective awareness. Their recent work explores how voluntary temporal attention prioritizes sequential stimuli, using behavioral cueing paradigms and time-resolved MEG decoding to determine whether these perceptual enhancements rely on temporal competition and where task-relevant representations are amplified across the cortex. Additionally, they are examining the computational mechanisms of continuous vision by developing dynamic spatiotemporal normalization models and using probabilistic orientation tasks to test how stimulus history impacts perceptual precision and bias over extended timeframes. Finally, their research investigates the disconnect between visual performance and subjective experience, utilizing relative psychometric functions to probe the phenomenon of "subjective inflation" and understand how inattention differentially modulates sensory signals for objective discrimination versus perceived visibility.

papers.title: Voluntary temporal attention improves perception even in the absence of temporal competition
papers.abstract: This study employs a two-target temporal cueing paradigm to evaluate whether the behavioral enhancements associated with voluntary temporal attention are contingent upon temporal competition between sequential stimuli. By manipulating the presence of temporal competitors through the inclusion of single-target trials, the authors demonstrate that attending to a specific point in time significantly improves orientation categorization accuracy even for isolated targets. The magnitude of this attentional enhancement is comparable to that observed under conditions of temporal competition. These findings challenge models where temporal attention primarily functions to resolve representational conflicts (e.g., within visual working memory) and instead support a prioritization mechanism, such as neural gain in early visual areas, that operates prior to competitive processing stages.
papers.authors: Karen J. Tian, Jennifer A. Motzer, Rachel N. Denison

papers.title: When awareness outstrips performance: critical tests of subjective inflation under inattention
papers.abstract: Utilizing a novel 'relative psychometric function' framework, this research characterizes 'subjective inflation'—the phenomenon where unattended visual stimuli are perceived as having higher visibility despite lower or equated objective performance. By analyzing full psychometric functions for contrast and texture processing, the authors find that inattentional inflation is a robust effect for both threshold and suprathreshold stimuli, though suprathreshold inflation is specific to global stimulus visibility rather than task-relevant features. The study establishes a unifying mathematical principle: inattentional inflation arises when attention reduces the performance threshold more substantially than it reduces the visibility threshold, suggesting an asymmetry in how selective attention modulates sensory signals for objective discrimination versus subjective experience.
papers.authors: Karen J. Tian, Brian Maniscalco, Michael L. Epstein, Angela Shen, Olenka Graham Castaneda, Toshiyuki Kurosawa, Megan A. K. Peters, Rachel N. Denison

papers.title: A dynamic spatiotemporal normalization model captures perceptual and neural effects of spatial and temporal context
papers.abstract: This paper presents the Dynamic Spatiotemporal Normalization (DSTN) model, which generalizes the divisive normalization framework to integrated space-time processing for continuous vision. By implementing spatiotemporal receptive fields with history-dependent excitatory and suppressive drives, the model accounts for contextual modulations across both spatial and temporal dimensions. The DSTN model successfully reproduces a suite of empirical phenomena, including biphasic temporal receptive fields, nonlinear contrast response dynamics, subadditivity, response adaptation, and bidirectional contrast-dependent suppression. The results indicate that integrated spatiotemporal normalization is a fundamental computation underlying the processing of dynamic visual input and the emergence of contextual effects like backwards masking in neural populations and behavior.
papers.authors: Angus F. Chapman, Rachel N. Denison

papers.title: Perceptual Support for Temporal Normalization Across Hundreds of Milliseconds
papers.abstract: This research investigates the psychophysical signatures of temporal normalization using a probabilistic orientation estimation task. The authors evaluate how the presence of preceding or succeeding stimuli impacts the precision and bias of target orientation representations over intervals of hundreds of milliseconds. Using mixture modeling to analyze the resulting error distributions, they demonstrate that temporal context induces suppressive effects that manifest as reduced perceptual precision and systematic biases. These behavioral patterns provide direct perceptual evidence for a history-dependent gain control mechanism that operates across extended temporal windows in the human visual system, consistent with the computational principles of dynamic normalization where current neural responses are regulated by the integrated activity of recent stimulus history.
papers.authors: Michael L. Epstein, Sophie Kovacevich, Rachel N. Denison

papers.title: Temporal attention amplifies stimulus information in fronto-cingulate cortex at an intermediate processing stage
papers.abstract: Using magnetoencephalography (MEG) and time-resolved multivariate pattern analysis, this study investigates the neural substrates of voluntary temporal attention in a two-target temporal cueing task while controlling for temporal expectation. The authors decode stimulus-specific orientation information to track its representational evolution across the cortex. The results reveal that temporal attention selectively enhances the representation of the first target approximately 250 ms post-stimulus. This amplification occurs primarily within a fronto-cingulate cortical network—comprising the anterior cingulate and superior frontal cortex—rather than in early visual areas. These findings suggest that voluntary temporal attention facilitates sequential stimulus processing by selectively routing and amplifying task-relevant representations in high-level cortical hubs to mitigate temporal interference.
papers.authors: Jiating Zhu, Karen J. Tian, Marisa Carrasco, Rachel N. Denison

0551.name: Rachel Kelly
0551.bio: Rachel Kelly is a Principal Scientist at Exponent specializing in the intersection of cognitive neuroscience, perception, and human behavior. Kelly’s research focuses on human performance and safety, specifically investigating driver behavior, visibility, attention, and the neurophysiology of motor planning. They apply technical expertise in applied physiology to evaluate human interaction with complex systems, including the assessment of warning effectiveness and behavioral responses to risk communication. Kelly performs the design and execution of human subjects studies, focus groups, and usability evaluations for consumer and medical technology.
0551.research_direction: Dr. Kelly's recent work explores the safety and ergonomic impacts of immersive head-mounted virtual reality (VR) displays on developing pediatric populations. Specifically, they have recently been investigating how sustained, multi-day VR exposure affects short-term physiological, sensorimotor, and cognitive functioning in older children. To quantify these impacts, their research utilizes comprehensive pre- and post-exposure testing batteries to measure fundamental visual functions—such as stereoacuity, accommodation, and vergence facility—alongside postural stability, hand-eye coordination, and executive inhibitory control. By tracking these functional metrics as well as subjective reports of visually induced motion sickness and musculoskeletal discomfort, Dr. Kelly aims to establish quantitative benchmarks that can inform user-safety guidelines for children interacting with emerging immersive technologies.

papers.title: Effects of virtual reality use in children aged 10 to 12 years
papers.abstract: While immersive head-mounted displays (HMDs) are increasingly utilized by pediatric demographics for educational and gaming applications, empirical investigations regarding the safety and physiological impacts of sustained, moderate virtual reality (VR) exposure on developing populations remain limited. This study evaluated the short-term physiological, sensorimotor, and cognitive outcomes in children aged 10 to 12 years across four consecutive days of 60-minute VR gaming sessions. Standardized batteries assessed visual functioning (including monocular and binocular visual acuity, stereoacuity, accommodation, and vergence facility), visuomotor and hand-eye coordination, postural stability (center-of-pressure and sway metrics), and executive function indexed via an inhibitory control task, alongside subjective ratings of musculoskeletal discomfort and visually induced motion sickness (VIMS). Assessments administered before immersion on Day 1, immediately post-exposure on Day 4, and following a washout period on Day 5 demonstrated no clinically meaningful or statistically significant impairments in visual performance, postural control, or inhibitory capacity. Furthermore, self-reported visual and physical discomfort remained negligible throughout testing. These findings indicate that repeated moderate VR usage is well tolerated in late childhood without precipitating acute functional deficits, offering quantitative benchmarks to support pediatric ergonomics and user-safety guidelines.
papers.authors: Karol Silva, Nichole Breeland, Ashley M. Clark, Ilke Öztekin, Rachel L. Kelly

0552.name: Rachel Pye
0552.department: School of Psychology and Clinical Language Sciences
0552.bio: Rachel Pye is an Associate Professor in the School of Psychology and Clinical Language Sciences at the University of Reading and formerly served as the Head of Psychology for the University of Reading Malaysia. Pye’s research investigates the cognitive and perceptual mechanisms of literacy, focusing on dyslexia and reading development in monolingual and multilingual populations. They utilize behavioral methodologies and eye-tracking to evaluate the efficacy of visual and phonological interventions for reading difficulties and to measure individual differences in attentional speed. Pye's work also extends to pedagogical science, exploring the prevalence of neuromyths among educators and the optimization of assessment strategies in psychological education.
0552.research_direction: Dr. Pye has recently been investigating a diverse array of applied and fundamental questions across cognitive psychology, education, and clinical practice. In the domain of visual processing, their recent work explores whether post-target distractor intrusions during rapid serial visual presentation tasks can serve as a reliable behavioral index for individual differences in attentional latency. They are also examining reading and dyslexia in multilingual environments, specifically evaluating whether dynamic testing frameworks can successfully isolate true decoding deficits from mere language proficiency limitations across different alphabetic and morphosyllabic scripts. Broadening into educational and clinical structures, their research additionally evaluates the prevalence of neuroscientific misconceptions among educators, the psychological impact of high-stakes assessment reductions on university students, and structural treatment inequities for cognitive behavioral therapy patients who rely on language interpreters.

papers.title: Clients using interpreters wait longer and have poorer outcomes in Talking Therapies for Anxiety and Depression – a retrospective cohort study on waiting times and treatment outcomes
papers.abstract: Although NHS Talking Therapies for Anxiety and Depression (TTad) delivers evidence-based cognitive behavioural interventions across England, therapeutic inequities continue to impact patients from culturally and linguistically diverse communities. This retrospective observational cohort study investigated waiting periods and clinical recovery rates for clients receiving interpreter-mediated Step 3 Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT). Utilizing national routine service audit datasets from 177,340 clients accessing care during the 2022–2023 period, treatment trajectories were contrasted between clients requiring language interpreters and non-interpreter controls. Survival and comparative analyses demonstrated that individuals requiring interpreter assistance incurred significantly prolonged referral-to-treatment intervals. Clinical outcomes also exhibited significant disparities: reliable clinical improvement was attained by only 58.5% of interpreter-assisted clients compared to 69.2% of non-interpreter clients. Concurrently, rates of reliable recovery were marked at 32.5% in the interpreter group versus 44.5% in the standard delivery cohort. The findings indicate systemic delays and diminished therapeutic efficacy in interpreter-facilitated talking therapies, underscoring the need for tailored structural and clinical adaptations.
papers.authors: Taf Kunorubwe, Natalie Meek, Rachel Emma Pye

papers.title: The Understanding, Use and Prevalence of Neuromyths among Medical Students, Health Sciences Students and Educators in Malaysia
papers.abstract: Neuromyths are pervasive misconceptions regarding neurobiology and cognitive architecture that originate from oversimplified, distorted, or ungrounded interpretations of neuroscientific evidence. Within instructional settings, such misconceptions threaten pedagogical efficacy by misdirecting institutional and instructor resources away from empirically substantiated learning methodologies. This empirical study evaluated the prevalence and endorsement of neuromyths versus established neuroscientific facts across secondary educators, university faculty, and undergraduate students pursuing medical and healthcare degrees in Malaysia. Administering an opportunity-sampled questionnaire battery across these cohorts, results demonstrated high overall rates of neuromyth endorsement concordant with international baselines. Significant cross-cohort divergence was identified: higher-education faculty endorsed significantly fewer neuromyths relative to secondary teachers and tertiary students. Neuromyths pertaining to learning styles, hemispheric dominance ('left-brain/right-brain'), and Brain Gym exhibited the highest persistence. Furthermore, a significant positive correlation emerged between accurate neurofact endorsement and myth resistance, indicating that foundational scientific and neurobiological literacy provides a protective epistemic buffer against instructional neuromyths.
papers.authors: Rachel E. Pye, Madihah Rushaidhi, Jun Jie Lim, Y. L. Soo, Paul S. Hubbard

papers.title: Measuring individual differences in the speed of attention using the distractor intrusion task
papers.abstract: Quantifying individual variability in the temporal deployment of visual attention remains challenging, as traditional visual search response times (RTs) and search slopes suffer from low test–retest reliability and confounding motor or sensory factors. Here, the post-target distractor intrusion (DI) rate in rapid serial visual presentation (RSVP) is evaluated as a reliable psychometric index of attentional latency. When targets are briefly presented amidst rapid distractor streams, erroneous reports of the immediate post-target item (lag +1 intrusion) reflect delayed transient attentional facilitation, closely tied to delays in the electrophysiological N2pc component. Across three experiments and downsampling simulations, DI rates demonstrated robust within-session internal consistency (Cronbach's α > .85) and one-year test–retest stability (r > .90), achievable within approximately 50 trials (around 5 minutes of administration). Furthermore, individual DI propensities correlated systematically with attentional processing speed, while remaining dissociable from unrelated executive control indices, reading speed, and attentional blink magnitude. These findings support the DI paradigm as an efficient, highly reliable instrument for measuring individual differences in the speed of selective attention.
papers.authors: Alon Zivony, Claudia C. von Bastian, Rachel Pye

papers.title: High stakes in the assessment arms race: a mixed-methods analysis of reducing assessment in an undergraduate psychology programme
papers.abstract: Reducing programmatic assessment load is widely proposed to mitigate student stress and afford curricular space for slow scholarship and deep learning. However, both faculty and learners often resist reductions, perceiving continuous assessment as necessary for engagement or risk management. This quasi-experimental, mixed-methods investigation examined the institutional shift to a single 100% summative assessment per module across final-year optional undergraduate psychology modules at an international branch campus in Malaysia. Quantitative comparisons across four cohorts (2018/19–2021/22; two pre-reform and two post-reform) revealed no significant change in overall module academic achievement. Qualitative reflexive thematic analysis from focus groups showed heightened student anxiety regarding high-stakes, single-assessment designs, regardless of whether students had experienced the previous multi-assessment framework. Participants overwhelmingly favored a dual-assessment model on the basis of perceived procedural fairness, risk dispersion, and portfolio diversity. The study highlights that merely decreasing assessment frequency without addressing assessment design, authenticity, and student workload perceptions fails to deliver the educational benefits envisioned by slow scholarship models.
papers.authors: Rachel Pye, Lynnette K. Gnagi, Ainslie Bi Qi Chuah, Kai Li Chung

papers.title: Dynamic tests as a language-free method for assessing reading in a multilingual setting
papers.abstract: Diagnosing developmental dyslexia and evaluating reading ability in linguistically diverse environments, such as Malaysia, is complicated by simultaneous multilingualism and multiliteracy, where low performance on conventional literacy batteries may stem from limited language proficiency rather than underlying phonological or orthographic decoding deficits. This study explored the diagnostic utility of the Dynamic Testing paradigm—a test-teach-retest framework aimed at isolating learning potential from pre-existing linguistic competence. A sample of 59 multilingual Malaysian adults reading English, Bahasa Melayu, and/or Chinese completed a dynamic reading test alongside the Adult Reading History Questionnaire (ARHQ) and a lexical decision task (LDT). Dynamic test performance significantly predicted self-reported risk for reading difficulty on the ARHQ, while remaining independent of lexical processing speed on the LDT. Stratifying participants by primary script literacy into alphabetic (English/Bahasa Melayu) and morphosyllabic (Chinese) cohorts demonstrated equivalent overall performance across orthographic groups. However, dynamic test scores significantly predicted reading difficulty only among alphabetic readers. The findings indicate that while dynamic testing reduces linguistic bias in multilingual populations, orthographic typology influences its diagnostic validity.
papers.authors: Rachel E. Pye, Huey Hwa Chan

0554.name: Ralf M. Haefner
0554.department: Department of Brain and Cognitive Sciences
0554.bio: Ralf M. Haefner is an Associate Professor in the Department of Brain and Cognitive Sciences at the University of Rochester, where they investigate the computational and neural mechanisms of perceptual decision-making. Their research focuses on how the brain performs probabilistic inference, specifically exploring how population responses in the visual cortex represent internal beliefs about the external world. Utilizing normative mathematical models and machine learning, Haefner’s work tests the hypothesis that the brain implements inference through neural sampling from learned generative models. Their studies address the functional role of correlated variability and top-down feedback in shaping sensory representations during hierarchical motion perception and evidence integration.
0554.research_direction: Dr. Haefner has recently been exploring the computational principles underlying visual perception, framing both neural activity and behavior through the lens of Bayesian probabilistic models. Much of their recent work investigates how the visual system utilizes hierarchical causal inference to solve complex motion perception challenges, examining how human observers and single neurons in area MT integrate or segment moving stimuli, resolve center-surround interactions, and dynamically assign spatial reference frames. Beyond motion processing, they are also employing deep generative networks, such as variational autoencoders, to investigate the computational purpose of top-down cortical feedback in shaping hierarchical representations and noise correlations in early visual areas like V1 and V2. To support these theoretical efforts, their recent research explores novel methodological approaches, developing encoding-agnostic techniques to rigorously evaluate competing Bayesian models against neural population data without relying on rigid assumptions about how the brain represents probability distributions.

papers.title: Top-down perceptual inference shaping the activity of early visual cortex
papers.abstract: Cortical feedback is a ubiquitous feature of the visual hierarchy, but its computational purpose in task-independent processing remains poorly defined. We employed a hierarchical deep generative model based on the Variational Autoencoder (VAE) architecture to study how adaptation to the statistics of natural images determines hierarchical representations and top-down modulations. Our model replicates the known response properties of neurons in primary (V1) and secondary (V2) visual cortices, including the emergent nonlinear sensitivity of V2 populations to natural texture statistics. The results demonstrate that top-down interactions are an essential component of hierarchical inference, naturally explaining empirical signatures such as neural responses to illusory contours and the systematic, task-independent structure of noise correlations in early visual areas.
papers.authors: Ferenc Csikor, Balázs Meszéna, Gergő Orbán, Katalin Ócsai, Ralf M. Haefner

papers.title: Hierarchical motion perception as causal inference
papers.abstract: Accurate visual motion estimation requires the brain to select or construct an appropriate reference frame, a problem for which previous research has found conflicting retinotopic, egocentric, and object-centric evidence. We introduce a hierarchical Bayesian causal inference framework that maps retinal image velocities to perceived motion by dynamically inferring the causal connectivity of reference frames. The model utilizes a mixture prior comprised of a delta component at zero and a slow-motion Gaussian distribution, reflecting the physical reality of friction and stationarity within local reference frames. Through joint inference, the model achieves automated segmentation of visual inputs into recursive groups and perceives motion relative to the most probable hierarchical reference frame. Psychophysical results from human observers confirm the model’s predictions regarding how common velocity information drives reference frame assignment.
papers.authors: Sabyasachi Shivkumar, Gregory C. DeAngelis, Ralf M. Haefner

papers.title: Bayesian causal inference unifies perceptual and neuronal processing of center-surround motion in area MT
papers.abstract: Center-surround (CS) modulation is a ubiquitous computation across the sensory hierarchy, yet existing models based on divisive normalization fail to account for the full spectrum of observed center-surround motion effects. We propose that these neural and perceptual phenomena emerge from a single normative principle: Bayesian causal inference over the latent reference frame structure of visual motion. We derived predictions for the mean activity and trial-to-trial variability of single neurons across a 4D stimulus space of center and surround velocities. Our model shows that the observed heterogeneity of area MT neurons—including those encoding retinotopic motion and those encoding motion relative to inferred reference frames—can arise from this single inferential process. This framework resolves discrepancies in whether surround stimuli suppress or facilitate responses and identifies the conditions under which MT neurons exhibit relative motion coding.
papers.authors: Gabor Lengyel, Sabyasachi Shivkumar, Gregory C. DeAngelis, Ralf M. Haefner

papers.title: Causal inference predicts the transition from integration to segmentation in motion perception
papers.abstract: The brain relies on motion cues to segment visual scenes and infer causal relationships between objects, involving the integration or segmentation of local motion vectors. Hierarchical Bayesian causal inference has been proposed to model these computations, but its dependency on sensory uncertainty has remained largely untested. Using a hierarchical stimulus configuration, we demonstrate that the perceptual boundary between integration and segmentation in human observers shifts according to motion coherence (sensory uncertainty). Notably, we found that perceptual variability is maximized at this transition point, a hallmark prediction of the Bayesian model. These results provide evidence that the human visual system approximates normative causal inference to resolve ambiguity in motion grouping, challenging deterministic interpretations of motion repulsion effects.
papers.authors: Boris Penaloza, Sabyasachi Shivkumar, Gabor Lengyel, Gregory C. DeAngelis, Ralf M. Haefner

papers.title: A General Method for Testing Bayesian Models using Neural Data
papers.abstract: Testing Bayesian theories of brain function against neural data is difficult due to a lack of consensus on how posterior beliefs are implementationally encoded (e.g., neural sampling versus distributed distributional codes). We present a method that bypasses the need for explicit encoding assumptions by testing the representational similarity between model-derived posteriors and neural population responses. This approach evaluates whether the relationships between model posteriors for different stimuli match the relationships between the corresponding neural responses. We introduce a model comparison diagnostic based on the alignment of model and data when injecting noise into the prediction pipeline. Using simulated V1 data, we demonstrate that this method can rigorously dissociate and falsify Bayesian models that are otherwise behaviorally indistinguishable, providing a tool for evaluating competing theories of neural probabilistic computation.
papers.authors: Gabor Lengyel, Sabyasachi Shivkumar, Ralf M. Haefner

0555.name: Ralph G. Hale
0555.bio: Ralph G. Hale is an Associate Professor of Psychological Science at the University of North Georgia and the Associate Director of the Center for Teaching, Learning, and Leadership. Hale’s research focuses on the intersection of visual perception and memory, specifically examining the watercolor illusion, color spreading, and figure-ground organization. Using psychophysical paradigms and virtual reality environments, Hale investigates how luminance, contrast, and environmental context influence spatial perception and visual long-term memory accuracy. Hale is also a co-author of a cognitive psychology textbook and mentors undergraduate researchers.
0555.research_direction: Dr. Hale has recently been investigating how contextual information and cognitive framing shape human perception, attitudes, and biases. In their work most relevant to visual cognition, they explore how top-down semantic contexts modulate the recognition of facial expressions, specifically examining how congruent versus incongruent situational narratives influence the categorization of sensory emotion features. Their recent work also explores implicit egotism and cognitive biases by testing whether subjective preferences for self-associated stimuli, such as the "Birthday Number Effect," correlate with explicit self-esteem. Additionally, they are investigating applied psychological questions, such as how the specific framing of financial and career information affects undergraduate students' self-efficacy and attitudes toward pursuing graduate education.

papers.title: The power of perspective: How framing affects undergraduate student attitudes toward graduate school
papers.abstract: This study examined how specific framing and informational perspective influence undergraduate student perceptions and attitudes regarding graduate education. Participants were presented with varied informational contexts regarding graduate program requirements, financial implications, and career outcomes. The results indicate that the cognitive framing of graduate school prospects significantly modulates student self-efficacy and interest, suggesting that pedagogical and administrative communication strategies can be optimized to improve graduate school enrollment and student professional development.
papers.venue: Psi Chi Journal of Psychological Research
papers.authors: Hannah V. Hyman, Isaac R. Wright, Ralph G. Hale

papers.title: Replication: Influence of Context on Emotion Perception in Facial Expressions
papers.abstract: This research aimed to replicate the findings of Carroll and Russell (1996) regarding the modulation of facial emotion recognition by semantic context. Participants evaluated a 'fear' facial expression (Matsumoto & Ekman, 1988) presented within congruent (fear-inducing), incongruent (anger-inducing), or no-context scenarios. A one-way ANOVA (F(2, 42) = 38.50, p < .001, ηp² = .64) confirmed that incongruent context significantly diminished accuracy in identifying the universal expression compared to congruent and neutral conditions. These findings underscore that emotion perception is a constructivist process where top-down semantic information guides the interpretation of ambiguous sensory features.
papers.venue: Psi Chi Journal of Psychological Research
papers.authors: Danica A. Barron, Ralph G. Hale

papers.title: Revisiting the Birthday Number Effect, Subjective Preferences, and Self-Esteem in College Students
papers.abstract: The Birthday Number Effect (BNE) — the tendency for individuals to prefer numbers associated with their own birth date — was investigated in a college-age cohort (N=101) to evaluate its relationship with self-esteem. Results demonstrated a robust BNE (F(1, 97) = 17.85, p < .001, ηp² = .16), with women exhibiting a more pronounced effect than men. However, correlational analyses revealed no significant association between the magnitude of the BNE and explicit self-esteem (r(99) = -.02, p = .88), contrary to implicit egotism theories suggesting BNE serves as a proxy for self-regard.
papers.venue: Psi Chi Journal of Psychological Research
papers.authors: Courtney G. Nutt, Anna N. DiMassimo, Ralph G. Hale

0556.name: Randi Starrfelt
0556.bio: Randi Starrfelt is a Professor of Neuropsychology who researches the cognitive and neural mechanisms of visual object recognition, focusing on word and face processing. Starrfelt studies acquired and developmental disorders, such as pure alexia and prosopagnosia, to examine how specialized visual functions are organized and dissociated in the brain. Their methodological approach combines experimental psychology, clinical neuropsychology, and brain imaging to assess the effects of brain injury and neurodevelopmental conditions. Their current work explores the relationship between reading and face recognition, along with the qualitative experiences of individuals with face blindness.
0556.research_direction: Dr. Starrfelt has recently been investigating the cognitive and neural architecture of high-level visual recognition, with a primary focus on face processing and developmental prosopagnosia (DP). Their recent work explores the methodological complexities of defining and diagnosing DP, scrutinizing how varying psychometric cutoffs, assessment tools, and task demands shape our understanding of the disorder's prevalence and core deficits. To probe the domain-specificity of face recognition within the visual ventral stream, they are systematically assessing how facial processing relates to other complex visual categories. Specifically, they employ carefully matched behavioral paradigms to investigate the degree of functional independence between face recognition and visual word recognition, fine-grained object discrimination, and viewpoint-dependent topographical memory.

papers.title: Disentangling developmental prosopagnosia: A scoping review of terms, tools and topics
papers.abstract: This preregistered scoping review synthesizes evidence from 224 peer-reviewed studies to characterize the conceptual and methodological landscape of developmental prosopagnosia (DP) in adults. The analysis scrutinizes how DP is defined and classified, identifying significant heterogeneity in diagnostic procedures, with over 40 distinct assessment tools utilized across the field. The review focuses on core research themes including the role of holistic processing and the specificity of face processing deficits. Findings highlight a persistent lack of consensus regarding the foundational definition of DP and suggest that the field's heavy reliance on cognitive neuropsychological frameworks may have unnecessarily constrained its scope. The authors propose new research trajectories to address these inconsistencies and broaden the understanding of atypical face recognition development.
papers.authors: Erling Nørkær, Silvia Regina Gobbo, Tone Roald, Randi Starrfelt

papers.title: Comparing word and face recognition – An insoluble conundrum?
papers.abstract: This viewpoint article addresses the unresolved theoretical debate concerning the degree of independence between face and word recognition mechanisms within the visual ventral stream. The authors analyze existing neuropsychological and neuroimaging evidence for dissociations versus associations between these two stimulus categories. They argue that conclusions are frequently confounded by methodological choices, specifically the lack of comparable tests and the impact of varying task demands on results. By evaluating different diagnostic strategies—such as the comparison of the Cambridge Face Memory Test against single-word reading accuracy versus delayed matching paradigms—the paper demonstrates how experimental design and task sensitivity can bias the interpretation of performance, complicating the development of a definitive model of functional cerebral organization for complex visual categories.
papers.authors: Ro Julia Robotham, Randi Starrfelt

papers.title: The relation between face recognition and topographical processing in developmental prosopagnosia
papers.abstract: This empirical study investigates the association between face recognition deficits and topographical processing impairments in a sample of 30 individuals with developmental prosopagnosia (DP) and 27 matched controls. Participants were assessed on topographical perception and topographical memory using viewpoint-dependent landscape recognition tasks. While the DP group demonstrated preserved topographical perception, they exhibited significant impairments in topographical memory compared to controls. Utilizing multivariate analysis, the researchers established that face recognition and topographical memory abilities are statistically dissociable within this population. These findings suggest that while these functions frequently co-occur in DP due to the proximity of underlying neural substrates in the posterior cerebral cortex, they rely on distinct cognitive and neural mechanisms rather than a single shared process.
papers.authors: Christian Gerlach, Anders Petersen, Randi Starrfelt

papers.title: Evidence for a Classical Dissociation between Face and Object Recognition in Developmental Prosopagnosia
papers.abstract: This research evaluates the domain-specificity of face recognition in developmental prosopagnosia (DP) by controlling for the influence of visual similarity across stimulus categories. Using a simultaneous matching paradigm featuring faces and non-face objects (houses) with systematically manipulated degrees of perceptual similarity, the study compared 21 individuals with DP to 21 age-matched controls. Results demonstrate a classical dissociation at the group level: while DPs showed severe impairments in face recognition, their performance on demanding and sensitive object recognition tasks was within the normal control range. This evidence of selectively preserved object recognition contradicts findings from previous smaller-scale studies and provides strong support for the hypothesis that face recognition relies on specialized mechanisms that can be independently compromised in DP.
papers.authors: Christian Gerlach, Randi Starrfelt

papers.title: Class A, Class B. Is that the only chemistry? A commentary on DeGutis et al. (2023): What is the prevalence of developmental prosopagnosia? An empirical assessment of different diagnostic cutoffs
papers.abstract: This commentary critically examines a recent empirical evaluation of diagnostic cutoffs for developmental prosopagnosia (DP) and its implications for prevalence estimates. The authors discuss the theoretical consequences of adopting different clinical thresholds, specifically the 2SD cutoff on the Cambridge Face Memory Test (CFMT), and the use of supplemental diagnostic indicators like subjective self-report questionnaires and famous face tests. They scrutinize how psychometric properties, such as the correlation between different assessment tools, can bias the classification of individuals and the resulting prevalence data. The authors advocate for a more nuanced diagnostic framework that considers the underlying factor structure of face recognition ability and the potential for shared processing resources between faces and other object categories.
papers.authors: Christian Gerlach, Erling Nørkær, Randi Starrfelt

0560.name: Reinoud Bootsma
0560.department: Institut des Sciences du Mouvement Etienne Jules Marey (ISM)
0560.bio: Reinoud J. Bootsma is a Professor of Human Movement Science at Aix-Marseille Université and a senior member of the Institut Universitaire de France. Bootsma’s research focuses on the ecological approach to perception and action, specifically investigating how visual information like time-to-collision (tau) regulates motor control in tasks such as catching, hitting, and aiming. Utilizing kinematic analysis and dynamical systems modeling, Bootsma explores the underlying principles of information-movement coupling and Fitts' law. Their current research focuses on the study of joint action and social coordination, analyzing how behavioral patterns emerge from continuous visual couplings between multiple actors.
0560.research_direction: Dr. Bootsma's recent work explores the behavioral dynamics of perceptuomotor coordination and skill acquisition across a diverse range of contexts. They have recently been using a continuous ball-and-beam paradigm to investigate how individuals learn motor control under varying accuracy constraints, as well as how these individual movement capacities transfer into coordinated joint actions between dyads. In the realm of visually guided action, their research examines lateral manual interception, developing dynamical models to simulate realistic hand trajectories and testing how visual variables, such as target approach angles, induce specific kinematic biases and reversal movements. Additionally, their recent work broadens the scope of motor control to cultural evolution, using cross-cultural morphometric analyses of expert potters to investigate how community-specific motor habits inherently bias the physical shaping of artifacts.

papers.title: Interpersonal coordination in a ball-and-beam paradigm: Transfer of skill from solo action to joint action
papers.abstract: This study employs a manual ball-and-beam paradigm to investigate the emergence of interpersonal coordination in functional joint actions and the degree of skill transfer from solo to dyadic performance. Participants manipulated beam inclination to roll a ball reciprocally between targets. Findings indicate that dyads predominantly adopt an anti-phase coordination mode, characterized by a significant reduction in relative phase variability over practice. Critically, variables coupled to ball speed, such as the spatiotemporal parameters of beam motion, were robustly propagated from individual to joint settings, whereas variables related to ball accuracy showed only moderate transfer. The results suggest that while joint action is constrained by task goals, coordination patterns are influenced by the participants' individual perceptuomotor capacities.
papers.authors: Marijn S. J. Hafkamp, Remy Casanova, Reinoud J. Bootsma

papers.title: Toward an Operational Dynamical Model of Lateral Manual Interception Behavior
papers.abstract: The authors develop a dynamics-based phenomenological model of discrete movement for lateral manual interception, aimed at generating kinematically realistic hand trajectories. The model's pattern formation architecture integrates a Duffing stiffness function, which establishes a fixed-point attractor at the predicted target arrival location on the interception axis, with a hybrid Rayleigh-Van der Pol damping function. Upon parametrization for movement direction, amplitude, and duration, the model accurately reproduces observed variations in hand kinematics using a single set of four coefficients across multiple conditions. Furthermore, the model inherently accounts for speed-accuracy trade-offs, demonstrating its utility in capturing the underlying control laws of interceptive actions.
papers.authors: Danial Borooghani, Remy Casanova, Frank T. J. M. Zaal, Reinoud J. Bootsma

papers.title: Angle-of-approach and reversal-movement effects in lateral manual interception
papers.abstract: This investigation explores the influence of target trajectory incidence angles on the control of lateral manual interception, specifically evaluating the angle-of-approach (AoA) and reversal-movement (RM) effects. The AoA effect describes a bias in hand positioning toward the direction of target arrival, while the RM effect involves an initial hand movement in the target's direction before reversing toward the actual interception point. Results confirm both effects across various interception locations, with increased incidence angles and lower target speeds magnifying the RM effect's frequency and amplitude. The findings suggest that interceptive guidance relies on intermediate-order information—conceptually a partial integration of target position and velocity or a fractional-order derivative—rather than simple predictive or first-order strategies.
papers.authors: Simon Ledouit, Danial Borooghani, Remy Casanova, Nicolas Benguigui, Frank T. J. M. Zaal, Reinoud J. Bootsma

papers.title: Cultural attraction in pottery practice: Group-specific shape transformations by potters from three communities
papers.abstract: Applying a cross-cultural experimental framework, this study investigates the divergence of morphological features in ceramic vessels produced by expert potters from French, Hindu Indian, and Muslim Indian communities. Participants were tasked with reproducing unfamiliar model shapes to minimize the influence of existing repertoires. Morphometric analysis demonstrated that vessel variation was significantly higher between communities than within them, revealing community-specific biases in the morphogenetic path and final form. These results provide empirical support for the "cultural attraction" hypothesis, suggesting that stable cultural traits emerge from group-specific habits of fashioning clay and technical preferences rather than purely through selective transmission.
papers.authors: Tetsushi Nonaka, Enora Gandon, John A. Endler, Thelma Coyle, Reinoud J. Bootsma

papers.title: Perceptuomotor skill acquisition in a solo manual ball-and-beam task with varying accuracy requirements
papers.abstract: This research characterizes the behavioral dynamics of individual skill acquisition in a novel manual ball-and-beam task. Participants practiced controlling ball motion through beam inclination adjustments under varying target-width constraints (small, medium, and large). Learning was marked by a transition from freezing to freeing degrees of freedom, evidenced by an increased range of beam motion and strengthened correlation between beam and ball dynamics. Task-specific accuracy requirements significantly modulated the emergent control strategy: larger targets promoted continuous beam movement, whereas smaller targets necessitated discrete, corrective adjustments. The findings highlight the role of environmental constraints in shaping the acquisition and stabilization of perceptuomotor coordination.
papers.authors: Marijn S. J. Hafkamp, Remy Casanova, Reinoud J. Bootsma

0561.name: Remy Allard
0561.bio: Rémy Allard is an Assistant Professor at the School of Optometry at the Université de Montréal and a researcher at the Psychophysical Laboratory of Vision. Allard's research investigates the mechanisms underlying motion and contrast perception, specifically focusing on how these processes are influenced by healthy aging and retinal pathologies such as age-related macular degeneration. Utilizing psychophysical paradigms and computational modeling, they develop functional clinical tests to assess photoreceptor efficiency and improve the detection of ocular diseases. Their research also extends to the characterization of visual symptoms following traumatic brain injuries to optimize post-trauma rehabilitation strategies.
0561.research_direction: Dr. Allard's recent work explores the low-level limits and biological origins of visual processing, ranging from photoreceptor efficiency to clinical sensory anomalies. In one line of research, they have recently been investigating how to psychophysically isolate and measure the photon-detection efficiency of rods, using equivalent input noise paradigms and motion direction discrimination tasks to examine how quantal fluctuations limit scotopic and mesopic contrast sensitivity. Additionally, their recent work examines atypical visual processing in autism spectrum disorder by seeking to link perceptual deficits in global motion to early retinal function. By combining behavioral motion coherence thresholds with electroretinography (ERG) in autistic individuals and their family members, Dr. Allard is exploring whether these sensory differences stem from inherited, low-level physiological anomalies in the retina.

papers.title: Psychophysically measuring the efficiency of rods
papers.abstract: While equivalent input noise (EIN) paradigms using external luminance noise have successfully quantified the quantal absorption efficiency of retinal cone photoreceptors, functional psychophysical estimation of rod efficiency has remained unestablished. Here, an external noise paradigm was adapted to evaluate rod photon-detection efficiency in healthy human observers through a motion direction discrimination task. Contrast thresholds were quantified with and without spatiotemporally extended dynamic external noise across a wide continuum of luminance intensities, spatial frequencies, and temporal frequencies under monochromatic blue and red display conditions (the latter minimizing rod stimulation). Two stimulus geometries were evaluated: an eccentric Gabor patch situated at 20° eccentricity and a rotating sinusoidal annular grating at 10° eccentricity. In both configurations, within a restricted scotopic-to-mesopic luminance regime, equivalent input noise scaled inversely with background luminance—conforming to the square-root de Vries–Rose law—and exhibited spectral and temporal flatness characteristic of Poisson photon noise. Crucially, contrast sensitivity under these conditions was markedly superior for short-wavelength (blue) relative to long-wavelength (red) illumination at matched photopic luminances, confirming that contrast sensitivity was bottlenecked by quantal fluctuations within the rod photoreceptor mosaic. These results demonstrate that rod photon absorption efficiency can be isolated and measured psychophysically via motion contrast thresholds in external noise using short-wavelength stimuli within the photon-noise-limited regime.
papers.authors: Geneviève Rodrigue, Laurine Paris, Judith Renaud, Rémy Allard

papers.title: Global motion coherent deficits in individuals with autism spectrum disorder and their family members are associated with retinal function
papers.abstract: This research investigates the association between global motion perception deficits and retinal processing abnormalities in individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and their biological family members. By evaluating motion coherence thresholds alongside electroretinography (ERG) metrics, the study demonstrates that both ASD probands and their parents—particularly mothers—exhibit significantly elevated motion coherence thresholds. These perceptual deficits correlate with distinct retinal response alterations, specifically reduced amplitudes of the photopic negative response (PhNR) and increased peak latencies for retinal a- and b-waves. The results provide empirical evidence that sensory processing anomalies in autism may originate at the retinal level and follow a familial inheritance pattern, suggesting a low-level biological basis for some autistic traits.
papers.authors: Irene O. L. Lee, Dennis M. Fritsch, Maximilian Kerz, Dorothy Thompson, Maryam Rezaei, Daphné Silvestre, Marko Nardini, Arthur Trognon, Michelle McKerral, David Skuse, Rémy Allard

0562.name: Renate Rutiku
0562.bio: Renate Rutiku is a Principal Investigator and Group Leader at the Institute of Psychology, Jagiellonian University, researching the neurobiological foundations of conscious perception. Rutiku's work focuses on disambiguating the neural correlates of consciousness (NCC) from their precursors and consequences, specifically examining the role of cortical layer 5 pyramidal neurons in coupling the state and contents of consciousness. Utilizing a multi-modal approach including electroencephalography (EEG), transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), and psychophysics, they investigate the temporal dynamics of perceptual markers and how the brain integrates top-down predictions with sensory evidence. Rutiku currently leads a SONATA BIS project exploring integration across the perceptual hierarchy using neuroimaging and behavioral modeling.
0562.research_direction: Dr. Rutiku has recently been investigating the neural architecture of visual working memory and the electrophysiological markers of conscious awareness. Their recent work explores whether idiosyncratic microstructural properties of early retinotopic cortex, mapped via quantitative MRI, constrain working memory fidelity and drive characteristic visual field asymmetries. In parallel, they are examining the interplay between subjective awareness and objective discrimination to determine if working memory maintenance relies simultaneously on implicit item traces and consciously accessible ensemble statistics. Beyond the visual system, Dr. Rutiku evaluates auditory EEG markers—specifically figure-ground modulation and event-related potentials like mismatch negativity—to develop more sensitive oddball paradigms for detecting covert consciousness in unresponsive clinical populations.

papers.title: Visual field inhomogeneities and the architectonics of early visual cortex shape visual working memory
papers.abstract: The degree to which the primary visual cortex (V1) is indispensable for visual working memory (vWM) maintenance remains an active area of controversy. Addressing this question through an individual-differences framework, this study investigated whether idiosyncratic structural and microstructural properties of early retinotopic cortex—specifically those underlying visual field inhomogeneities such as polar angle asymmetries—account for behavioral variance in vWM. A cohort of 292 participants completed multiparametric mapping (MPM) quantitative MRI (qMRI) to derive four distinct microstructural parametric maps: magnetization transfer, proton density, longitudinal relaxation rate (R1), and effective transverse relaxation rate (R2*). In an independent session, participants performed an 8-item circular display object-identification vWM retention task designed to map visual field asymmetries. Psychophysical results replicated characteristic visual field inhomogeneities in vWM, notably manifesting an inverted vertical meridian asymmetry (VMA). Quantitative MRI region-of-interest analyses revealed robust relationships between behavioral VMA and multiple qMRI metrics within V1, substantiating the contribution of V1 microarchitecture to vWM capability. Furthermore, morphometric cortical thickness analyses associated left–right behavioral asymmetry with area V3 thickness. These observations support the sensory recruitment hypothesis by demonstrating that structural and microstructural variations within early visual cortices place systematic constraints on visual working memory fidelity.
papers.authors: Julia Papiernik-Kłodzińska, Simon Hviid Del Pin, Kristian Sandberg, Michał Wierzchoń, Marisa Carrasco, Renate Rutiku

papers.title: The Two Lives of Visual Working Memory: Evidence for Distinct Conscious and Unconscious Representations
papers.abstract: Visual working memory (vWM) is widely assumed to interface with subjective conscious awareness and mental imagery, yet standard psychophysical and computational frameworks frequently formalize it as an array of discrete, independent item traces. Here, the architecture of vWM was evaluated to determine whether maintenance relies on dual dissociation: an implicit memory trace alongside a consciously reportable, integrated ensemble representation. Across 216 participants performing an item change-detection task, subjective perceptual awareness ratings were recorded during the memory delay period while systematically manipulating ensemble statistics (mean item diameter and set size variability). A clear dissociation between subjective and objective metrics emerged: perceptual awareness systematically increased for configurations containing larger and more variable elements, whereas objective discrimination precision was optimized by smaller, low-variance stimuli. Nevertheless, subjective awareness remained predictive of accuracy, and erroneous responses displayed non-random systematic bias toward display statistics rather than uniform guessing. Furthermore, individual trait variations in imagery vividness, assessed via the Vividness of Visual Imagery Questionnaire (VVIQ), selectively modulated conscious awareness and estimation bias without altering objective accuracy.
