These findings suggest that vWM execution is jointly mediated by an implicit item-level trace and a consciously accessible, ensemble-structured representation.
papers.authors: Aleksandra Lipińska, Kinga Ciupińska, Renate Rutiku

papers.title: Figure-ground modulation as a marker of active auditory perception across levels of consciousness
papers.abstract: This research evaluates the utility of figure-ground modulation in the auditory domain as a robust neural marker for assessing conscious awareness. The study employs an auditory scene segregation paradigm to measure the brain's capacity to differentiate target sounds from complex backgrounds. Through a series of experiments involving healthy awake individuals, subjects during deep sleep, and patients with disorders of consciousness (DOC), the findings show that the figure-ground EEG marker is consistently elicited during wakefulness but vanishes during NREM sleep. In clinical populations, the sensitivity and specificity of this mid-level auditory marker for detecting covert consciousness significantly outperformed traditional ERP measures like Mismatch Negativity (MMN) and the P3b component, suggesting its potential as a diagnostic tool for patients who are behaviorally unresponsive.
papers.authors: Renate Rutiku

papers.title: Assessing mismatch negativity (MMN) and P3b within‐individual sensitivity—A comparison between the local–global paradigm and two specialized oddball sequences
papers.abstract: Although mismatch negativity (MMN) and the P3b event-related potential (ERP) are widely cited electrophysiological markers of sensory deviance detection and conscious cognitive processing, standard clinical protocols often demonstrate inadequate within-individual sensitivity in patients with disorders of consciousness (DoC). This investigation compared the diagnostic reliability and individual-level detection rates of the local–global auditory quintlet paradigm against two specialized oddball protocols: the multi-feature Optimum-1 paradigm (probing frequency, duration, intensity, and spatial location deviants) and a dedicated learning-oddball paradigm. High-density scalp EEG was recorded in 15 healthy adults completing all three protocols. Nonparametric cluster-based permutation analyses revealed that both the Optimum-1 and the local-effect contrast achieved 100% within-individual detection sensitivity (15/15 participants), whereas the P3b and the global-effect contrast exhibited lower individual sensitivity (14/15 and 13/15 participants, respectively). Group- and single-subject analyses demonstrated strong parametric concordance between the global effect and classical P3b waveforms, confirming the utility of the global contrast for indexing conscious stimulus evaluation. However, the early local effect departed markedly in timing and topography from canonical MMN, eliciting an earlier latency accompanied by a pronounced P3a deflection without significant inter-paradigm amplitude correlation. These findings demonstrate that while the local–global sequence robustly elicits the P3b, its local novelty component should not be conflated with classical MMN.
papers.authors: Renate Rutiku, Chiara Fiscone, Marcello Massimini, Simone Sarasso

0564.name: Richard J. Krauzlis
0564.bio: Richard J. Krauzlis is a Senior Investigator at the National Eye Institute who examines the neural mechanisms underlying visual attention, perception, and oculomotor control. Krauzlis's research characterizes the superior colliculus, demonstrating its role in the internal orienting of attention and goal-directed selection independent of its motor functions. Utilizing electrophysiological recordings and computational modeling in both non-human primates and mice, their laboratory investigates how subcortical circuits, including the basal ganglia, interact with the neocortex to govern flexible visual behaviors and perceptual decision-making.
0564.research_direction: Dr. Krauzlis has recently been investigating the critical role of subcortical circuits—particularly the superior colliculus and basal ganglia—in visual attention, decision-making, and rapid object detection. In nonhuman primates, their recent work explores the causal contributions of the superior colliculus to covert spatial attention using targeted optogenetic suppression, while also employing reversible cortical inactivation to determine whether short-latency midbrain responses to faces rely on early feedback from the primary visual cortex. In parallel rodent models, they are using electrophysiology to probe how learned behavioral relevance shapes neuronal markers of selective attention in the superior colliculus, and examining how distinct striato-collicular pathways bias visually guided perceptual decisions. Broadening their scope to human oculomotor control, they are also pairing novel broadband visual stimuli with computational modeling to understand how motion coherence across distinct spatial frequencies drives reflexive ocular-following responses.

papers.title: A distinct circuit for biasing visual perceptual decisions and modulating superior colliculus activity through the mouse posterior striatum
papers.abstract: We investigated the rodent posterior striatum (PS) to elucidate its functional role in visual perceptual behavior, as this region receives primary inputs from the visual cortex and thalamus but remains understudied in rodents. Utilizing anatomical tracing and optogenetic perturbations in mice performing a visual change-detection task, we found that the direct pathway originating from the PS is largely segregated from the dorsomedial striatum (DMS) direct pathway. Activation of PS D1-receptor-expressing medium spiny neurons (D1-MSNs) robustly biased visual decisions according to task context, temporal expectation, and reward probability. Furthermore, electrophysiological recordings revealed that PS and DMS direct pathways differentially modulate neuronal activity in the superior colliculus (SC), targeting distinct populations and exerting opposite functional effects. These results identify a novel basal ganglia circuit that operates in parallel with the DMS to control visually guided decision-making.
papers.authors: Kara K. Cover, Kerry Elliott, Sarah M. Preuss, Richard J. Krauzlis

papers.title: Neuronal features of visual attention in the mouse superior colliculus depend on learned behavioral relevance
papers.abstract: Visual selective attention is a refined cognitive process acquired through environmental interactions rather than being fully innate. To investigate the plasticity of attentional circuits, we recorded spiking activity from superficial and deep layers of the superior colliculus (SC) in mice trained on three distinct behavioral tasks that attributed different levels of relevance to the same visual stimuli. We found that several fundamental markers of attention-related modulation—including cue-evoked activity and phasic responses to near-threshold change events—were contingent upon the learned behavioral significance of the stimuli. These effects were most prominent in the deep SC layers. Our results demonstrate that the functional recruitment of SC circuits for selective attention is driven by experience and task-specific learning, shaping even stimulus-driven features usually considered immutable.
papers.authors: Lupeng Wang, Christian Quaia, Kerry Elliott, Kara K. Cover, Richard J. Krauzlis

papers.title: Optogenetic Manipulation of Covert Attention in the Nonhuman Primate
papers.abstract: To investigate the causal role of subcortical circuits in cognitive functions, we employed transient optogenetic suppression of the primate superior colliculus (SC) during a covert attention task. Monkeys were required to detect and report a stimulus change at a cued location via joystick release while ignoring distractors. We delivered brief light pulses (utilizing the Jaws opsin) to SC neurons with response fields matching the cued location. Suppression significantly impaired detection performance, specifically lowering hit rates and increasing perceptual thresholds in a spatially selective manner. Importantly, performance remained unaffected when the cue was outside the suppressed response field or when single stimuli were presented, confirming that the deficit was cognitive rather than sensorimotor or purely visual. These findings demonstrate that SC activity is necessary for the covert selection of signals used for perceptual judgments in primates.
papers.authors: Leor N. Katz, Martin O. Bohlen, Gongchen Yu, Carlos Mejias-Aponte, Marc A. Sommer, Richard J. Krauzlis

papers.title: Ocular-following responses to broadband visual stimuli of varying motion coherence
papers.abstract: We utilized novel broadband visual stimuli to investigate how motion coherence across different spatial frequency (SF) bands influences human ocular-following responses (OFRs). The stimuli consisted of synthesized vertical sine-wave gratings with SFs ranging from 0.0625 to 4 cpd. By manipulating which SF components drifted, we characterized the SF dependency of the underlying motion-processing mechanisms. We found that OFR magnitude is highly sensitive to the spectral distribution of motion signals. The experimental data were well-characterized by a computational model in which the total excitatory drive is determined by a SF-weighted sum of drifting components, scaled by a contrast normalization term that incorporates contributions from both drifting and static spatial frequencies across the broadband spectrum.
papers.authors: Boris M. Sheliga, Edmond J. FitzGibbon, Christian Quaia, Richard J. Krauzlis

papers.title: Short-latency preference for faces in primate superior colliculus depends on visual cortex
papers.abstract: We identified a population of visually responsive neurons in the primate superior colliculus (SC) that exhibit a category-selective preference for faces over other objects at remarkably short latencies (~30-40 ms). Given the speed of these responses, it was unclear whether they originated from a direct subcortical retinotectal pathway or required cortical processing. To test this, we performed reversible inactivation of the lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) or primary visual cortex (V1) to eliminate cortical input to the SC. Cortical inactivation abolished the face-selective responses in the SC, demonstrating that this short-latency preference is not purely subcortical. These results suggest that rapid cortical feedback to the SC enables the midbrain to participate in early face detection and subsequent eye-movement orientation toward socially relevant stimuli.
papers.authors: Gongchen Yu, Leor N. Katz, Christian Quaia, Adam Messinger, Richard J. Krauzlis

0565.name: Richard A. Abrams
0565.bio: Richard A. Abrams is a Professor of Psychological & Brain Sciences at Washington University in St. Louis and directs the Attention & Performance Lab. Abrams's research examines the cognitive and neural mechanisms governing visual attention and motor execution, specifically focusing on the coordination of eye and limb movements and the control of covert attentional shifts. Abrams has conducted work on attentional capture, inhibition of return, and the role of perceptual objects in guiding action. Their recent investigations explore the suppression of unpredictable visual distractors and how specific action-related goals modulate ensemble perception and visual search performance.
0565.research_direction: Dr. Abrams has recently been investigating the mechanisms of top-down attentional control and distractor suppression, focusing on how the visual system proactively ignores highly salient information. Their recent work utilizes visual search paradigms to develop bias-free psychophysical metrics for isolating true inhibitory processes from target enhancement, and to examine whether historically robust distractors like dynamic motion onsets can be actively suppressed. They are also studying visual statistical learning, employing rapid serial visual presentation (RSVP) and spatial transfer tasks to determine how learned regularities are mapped onto configuration-based reference frames and whether across-trial predictability can attenuate phenomena like emotion-induced blindness. Additionally, their research extends into embodied cognition, exploring how inherent sensorimotor asymmetries—such as handedness or the right-ear advantage—might subtly bias perceptual decision-making during auditory and spatial discrimination tasks.

papers.title: Avoidance of capture by motion onset
papers.abstract: This study investigates the extent to which the human attentional system can proactively mitigate the capture of attention by motion onset, a potent dynamic stimulus typically thought to be resistant to top-down suppression. While previous literature has established that observers can suppress static color singletons, the capacity to inhibit dynamic motion cues has remained controversial. Utilizing a visual search paradigm augmented with occasional probe trials, the researchers assessed the attentional priority of motion distractors. The results provide novel evidence that motion-onset capture can be effectively avoided, demonstrating that the suppressive mechanisms of the attentional system are more flexible than suggested by earlier feature-specific models and can extend to dynamic visual properties.
papers.authors: Jahnavi Nair, Xiaojin Ma, Richard A. Abrams

papers.title: Bias-free measure of distractor avoidance in visual search
papers.abstract: The authors propose and validate a novel psychophysical metric designed to provide a bias-free assessment of distractor suppression during visual search tasks. Traditional methods often conflate distractor-related inhibition with target-related enhancement, complicating the interpretation of attentional priority maps. By employing a modified search paradigm that dissociates these processes, the study evaluates the mechanisms by which salient distractors are ignored. The findings confirm that observers can proactively reduce the attentional weight assigned to irrelevant singletons, decreasing their priority below a neutral baseline. This suggests that distractor avoidance is a robust, independent inhibitory process rather than a secondary effect of target selection.
papers.authors: Xiaojin Ma, Richard A. Abrams

papers.title: Statistical learning of across-trial regularities weakens emotion-induced blindness
papers.abstract: This research explores whether the impairment of visual awareness known as emotion-induced blindness (EIB) can be modulated by the statistical regularities of an image stream. In a series of five experiments, the investigators introduced predictability into the timing of targets and the emotionality and physical appearance of distractors within a rapid serial visual presentation (RSVP) task. The data indicate that the simultaneous predictability of distractor emotionality and physical features is sufficient to eliminate the EIB effect. These results reveal that the attentional system can leverage across-trial statistical learning to proactively downweight the priority of task-irrelevant emotional stimuli, even when participants lack explicit awareness of the underlying regularities.
papers.authors: Jiaxin Xu, Jingjing Qian, Yani Liu, Xiaohui Zhu, Mengyu Zhou, Yanju Ren, Richard A. Abrams

papers.title: Transfer of statistical regularity in visual search
papers.abstract: This study examines the reference frames underlying visual statistical learning by testing the transfer of learned spatial regularities to new scene contexts. While observers can learn to bias their attention based on object-centered probabilities (e.g., targets frequently appearing at the top of an object), it remains unclear whether these priors are tied to specific objects or broader spatial configurations. The results demonstrate that learned regularities transfer to new locations in the absence of explicit objects, yet this transfer is significantly diminished when the global configuration of the search display is altered. The findings suggest that attentional priorities are represented in a configuration-based reference frame that integrates information about the spatial context and the interrelationships between scene elements.
papers.authors: Gabriel Siegel, Richard A. Abrams

papers.title: Sensorimotor faculties bias choice behavior
papers.abstract: Investigating the intersection of embodied cognition and decision-making, this study tests how internal sensorimotor asymmetries, such as handedness and the right-ear advantage, influence perceptual judgments. Participants performed an auditory click-discrimination task where they identified the dominant ear of stimulus presentation and responded via manual keypresses under congruent or reversed mappings. The data reveal that when sensory evidence is absent (free choice), decisions are strongly biased toward the side of the participant's dominant hand. Additionally, inherent asymmetries in the auditory system were found to skew choices toward the right ear. These findings demonstrate that seemingly abstract cognitive decisions are significantly constrained and biased by the functional properties of the body's sensory and motor systems.
papers.authors: Jan Kubanek, Lawrence H. Snyder, Richard A. Abrams

0567.name: Robert Allison
0567.department: Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science
0567.bio: Robert S. Allison is a Professor in the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science and a member of the Centre for Vision Research at York University. Allison’s research focuses on the psychophysics and computational modeling of stereoscopic depth perception, examining how the human visual system processes three-dimensional information in natural and virtual environments. They specialize in the measurement and analysis of eye movements, the integration of multi-modal depth cues, and the optimization of human-computer interfaces for virtual and augmented reality systems. Their work relates to the application of technologies in 3D cinema, flight simulation, and clinical vision science.
0567.research_direction: Dr. Allison has recently been investigating visually guided behavior in virtual environments, display fidelity assessment, and, in a distinct line of research, software security ecosystems. Within vision science, their recent work explores how observers integrate binocular disparity and summation with optic flow to parse motion during physical locomotion, as well as how visuomotor gain discrepancies and display latencies in head-mounted displays drive postural adaptation and cybersickness. They are also examining psychophysical methodologies for advanced displays, testing how different forced-choice and flicker paradigms influence the subjective detection of compression artifacts in stereoscopic 3D media. Broadening their scope into computational networks, they are additionally mapping how security vulnerabilities propagate through open-source software dependency chains and investigating the systemic latencies of patch mitigation.

papers.title: The effect of gain adaptation on perception and posture
papers.abstract: This investigation characterizes the calibration of self-motion perception and postural stability in response to visuomotor gain discrepancies within immersive environments. Utilizing active self-motion paradigms, the study quantifies the point of subjective stationarity (PSS), visuo-postural sway, and dark-period postural variability following exposure to non-unity gains between physical locomotion and virtual optic flow. The researchers found that while visuomotor adaptation significantly modulates postural sway responses to visual perturbations, the perceived stationarity (PSS) remains invariant to gain adaptation. This dissociation suggests that somatosensory feedback during active locomotion may insulate perceptual stability from the recalibration observed in the postural control system, implying independent mechanisms for postural and perceptual adaptation.
papers.authors: Xue Teng, Laurie M. Wilcox, Robert S. Allison

papers.title: The Ripple Effect of Vulnerabilities in Maven Central: Prevalence, Propagation, and Mitigation Challenges
papers.abstract: This research presents a large-scale empirical analysis of the security landscape within the Maven Central ecosystem, specifically focusing on the prevalence and propagation of vulnerabilities in software dependency networks. Leveraging vulnerability data from OSV.dev and enriched CVE aggregates, the study examines the topological distribution of risk across artifacts and their dependents. Findings reveal that vulnerabilities propagate rapidly through dependency networks and that artifact centrality does not correlate with reduced vulnerability risk. Furthermore, the analysis identifies significant latency in patch adoption, with high-severity vulnerabilities often remaining unmitigated for several years despite the availability of fixes, suggesting systemic friction in dependency management within open-source ecosystems.
papers.venue: 2025 IEEE/ACM 22nd International Conference on Mining Software Repositories (MSR)
papers.authors: Ehtisham Ul Haq, Song Wang, Robert S. Allison

papers.title: Binocular contributions to motion detection and motion discrimination during locomotion
papers.abstract: This study investigates the integration of binocular cues, including disparity and summation, in the processing of optic flow and the parsing of global motion during physical locomotion. By comparing psychophysical thresholds for motion detection and direction discrimination across stereoscopic, synoptic (binocular without disparity), and monocular viewing conditions, the authors isolate the specific contributions of binocular disparity and binocular summation to flow parsing. Experimental results demonstrate that binocular disparity significantly improves detection thresholds and reduces discrimination biases during simulated forward and backward self-motion. The findings indicate that the visual system effectively capitalizes on binocular disparity to resolve depth-dependent motion ambiguities during locomotion, enhancing the differentiation of self-generated optic flow from independent target motion.
papers.authors: Hongyi Guo, Robert S. Allison

papers.title: Subjective assessment of visual fidelity: Comparison of forced-choice methods
papers.abstract: This work evaluates psychophysical methodologies for determining visually lossless performance in display compression systems, with a specific focus on the ISO/IEC 29170-2 flicker paradigm. The study compares sensitivity to compression artifacts across flicker-based and non-flicker-based forced-choice protocols using high-dynamic-range stereoscopic 3D (S3D) stimuli and video sequences. Quantitative analysis reveals that the flicker paradigm yields significantly higher sensitivity (lower detection thresholds) compared to non-flicker methods. While providing a conservative estimate of visual fidelity, the results suggest that the flicker protocol may overestimate artifact visibility under naturalistic viewing conditions, highlighting a critical trade-off between experimental rigor and ecological validity in visual quality assessment for advanced display technologies.
papers.venue: Journal of the Society for Information Display
papers.authors: Domenic Au, Sanjida Sharmin Mohona, Laurie M. Wilcox, Robert S. Allison

papers.title: Testing the 'differences in virtual and physical head pose' and 'subjective vertical conflict' accounts of cybersickness
papers.abstract: This investigation adjudicates between two leading theoretical models of cybersickness: the 'Differences in Virtual and Physical head pose' (DVP) hypothesis and the 'Subjective Vertical Conflict' (SVC) theory. Using head-mounted displays with experimentally introduced display latencies, the study tracks participants' spatial and temporal head pose dynamics alongside reported sickness symptoms. The DVP model's predictive power is evaluated based on the spatial magnitude and fractal dynamics (DFA alpha values) of pose discrepancies, while the SVC model is assessed based on the angular mismatch between perceived and expected gravity vectors. The findings provide strong empirical support for the DVP framework, demonstrating that cybersickness severity is highly predictable from the statistical and temporal properties of the virtual-to-physical pose error.
papers.authors: Stephen Palmisano, Lance Stephenson, Rodney G. Davies, Juno Kim, Robert S. Allison

0568.name: Robert Desimone
0568.department: Department of Brain and Cognitive Sciences
0568.bio: Robert Desimone serves as the Director of the McGovern Institute for Brain Research and the Doris and Don Berkey Professor at MIT, where they investigate the neural mechanisms of selective attention and executive control. Desimone’s research characterizes how the brain manages information overload by utilizing synchronous neuronal firing to amplify relevant sensory signals while suppressing background distractions. By employing electrophysiology, MEG, and optogenetics in primate models, Desimone identified circuits in the prefrontal and extrastriate cortex that coordinate top-down attentional focus. These findings inform the development of treatments for brain disorders such as schizophrenia and autism.
0568.research_direction: Dr. Desimone's recent work has been investigating the neural circuitry of visual attention and working memory, as well as the broad functional architecture of the primate brain. Using multiunit laminar recordings and optogenetics in macaques, their research explores the link between covert spatial attention and microsaccades, and probes whether feature-based attention and visual working memory rely on shared or dissociable cortical subpopulations. At the macro-scale, they have recently been leveraging functional MRI to map large-scale human brain networks during naturalistic movie watching and to trace causal effective connectivity in the macaque sensorimotor system using combined fMRI and targeted electrical microstimulation. Additionally, their recent work investigates the basic electrophysiological signatures of the neocortex by characterizing "spectrolaminar motifs"—predictable gradients of local field potential power across cortical depth—to develop robust frequency-based tools for layer identification in neurophysiological recordings.

papers.title: Stimulus representations in visual cortex shaped by spatial attention and microsaccades
papers.abstract: This study demonstrates that fixational eye movements, specifically microsaccades (MSs), are fundamentally linked to the neural mechanisms of covert spatial attention in the primate visual system. Utilizing multiunit recordings from rhesus macaques (Macaca mulatta) across cortical areas V4 and IT, as well as the lateral pulvinar, the researchers found that the typical firing rate enhancements associated with spatial attention are only engaged following a microsaccade directed toward the attended stimulus. If the initial MS after an attentional cue is directed away from the target, the expected gain modulation is delayed until the subsequent target-directed MS occurs. Furthermore, stimulus decoding accuracy and the precision of tuning curves in V4 were significantly improved during intervals following target-directed MSs compared to those following MSs directed away from the target. These findings imply that microsaccades do not merely correlate with attention but serve to coordinate and amplify object processing in extrastriate cortex, providing a neural basis for active vision during periods of fixation.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS)
papers.authors: Karthik Srinivasan, Eric Lowet, Bruno Duarte Gomes, Robert Desimone

papers.title: Dissociable neuronal substrates of visual feature attention and working memory
papers.abstract: In this investigation, the authors challenge the hypothesis that visual working memory (WM) and feature-based attention rely on the same neural substrates within the primate brain. By performing simultaneous laminar recordings in macaque monkeys across a hierarchy of areas including MT, MST, LIP, and the lateral prefrontal cortex (LPFC), they characterized the neural signatures of motion-direction WM and feature-based attention. The results reveal that while both processes recruit similar cortical regions, they are represented by distinct neuronal populations and rely on different circuit mechanisms. Specifically, whereas feature attention consistently modulates the gain of sensory-driven responses, WM representations are maintained through distinct firing patterns in different subpopulations. Optogenetic inactivation of the posterior LPFC selectively impaired attentional modulation without abolishing the underlying WM representation, demonstrating a functional dissociation between the selection of incoming sensory information and the maintenance of internal representations.
papers.authors: Diego Mendoza-Halliday, Haoran Xu, Frederico A. C. Azevedo, Robert Desimone

papers.title: Functional architecture of cerebral cortex during naturalistic movie watching
papers.abstract: This research provides a comprehensive map of the human cerebral cortex's functional organization by analyzing high-resolution fMRI data from 176 subjects during 60 minutes of naturalistic movie watching. Utilizing a data-driven clustering approach, the authors identified a stable macro-architecture consisting of 24 functional networks, each specialized for distinct sensory or cognitive processes such as language, social interactions, and visual feature extraction. The study highlights the existence of three domain-general executive control networks that exhibit a robust 'push-pull' relationship with domain-specific sensory areas; these networks were most active during transitions between movie segments and least active when feature-specific networks were highly engaged. By mapping the cortex under naturalistic conditions rather than constrained tasks, the study reveals a more unified and ecologically relevant parcellation scheme that captures the dynamic interplay of large-scale brain systems.
papers.authors: Reza Rajimehr, Haoran Xu, Asa Farahani, Simon Kornblith, John Duncan, Robert Desimone

papers.title: Whole-brain effective connectivity of the sensorimotor system using 7T fMRI with electrical microstimulation in non-human primates
papers.abstract: To elucidate the causal pathways of the primate sensorimotor system, the authors combined ultra-high-field (7 Tesla) functional MRI with focal electrical microstimulation (EM-fMRI) in rhesus macaques. By stimulating functionally identified regions of the primary somatosensory cortex and measuring brain-wide BOLD responses, they mapped the effective connectivity of local cortical sites to distal subcortical and cortical targets. The results demonstrate a highly specific topographic organization of sensorimotor signals, revealing isomorphic mappings between the lateral prefrontal cortex and major processing domains. The findings suggest that effective connectivity, rather than just spontaneous correlations, provides a quantitative measure of the directional and causal interactions necessary for coordinated sensorimotor control. The study also validates an MRI-compatible, 3D-printable microdrive system for precise electrode positioning in high-field environments.
papers.authors: Rui Xu, Narcisse P. Bichot, Atsushi Takahashi, Robert Desimone

papers.title: A ubiquitous spectrolaminar motif across independent studies, including Mackey et al.'s own data
papers.abstract: This work serves as a comprehensive rebuttal and technical validation of the 'spectrolaminar motif' discovered in previous research (Mendoza-Halliday et al., 2024), which suggests a canonical distribution of local field potential (LFP) power across cortical layers. Addressing criticisms regarding the tool derived from this motif (FLIP/vFLIP), the authors introduce vFLIP2, an enhanced algorithm for frequency-based layer identification. By analyzing diverse datasets from multiple independent research groups, including those from critics, the study confirms that high-frequency gamma power peaks in supragranular layers while alpha-beta power peaks in infragranular layers across the primate cortex. The consistent localization of these gradients relative to histologically defined layers supports the existence of a universal electrophysiological signature for the six-layered anatomical motif of the neocortex, facilitating more accurate layer identification in laminar electrophysiology recordings.
papers.authors: Alex James Major, Ahmed Abdaltawab, Jessica M. Phillips, Tian Wang, Eric Kenji Lee, Maxwell J. Lichtenfeld, Chandramouli Chandrasekaran, Yuri B. Saalmann, Alexander Maier, Earl K. Miller, André M. Bastos, Robert Desimone, Diego Mendoza-Halliday

0569.name: Robert G. Alexander
0569.bio: Robert G. Alexander is an Assistant Professor of Psychology and Counseling and a cognitive neuroscientist specializing in the mechanisms of human vision. Their research utilizes high-resolution eye-tracking and psychophysical methods to quantify the oculomotor signatures of perceptual expertise in professional domains such as radiology and aviation. By modeling how experts search and interpret complex visual environments, Alexander develops scalable educational tools and diagnostic biomarkers intended to reduce human error and accelerate skill acquisition. Alexander's work also explores the intersection of fixational eye movements, clinical visual impairments, and the development of deep learning tools for modeling expertise.
0569.research_direction: Dr. Alexander’s recent work spans visual attention, clinical perception, and methodological rigor within the vision sciences. They have recently been investigating the neural and behavioral mechanisms of attentional allocation, combining fMRI and high-precision eye-tracking to probe spatial cueing, bottom-up saliency under varying levels of perceptual awareness, and gaze dynamics like joint attention and Troxler fading during picture viewing. In the clinical domain, their recent work explores sudden-onset cortically mediated visual impairments, utilizing psychophysics, oculomotor assessments, and neuroimaging to understand how focal cortical abnormalities can disrupt motion perception and object recognition in visual clutter. Furthermore, they have been actively working to improve scientific and educational practices by co-developing standardized minimal reporting guidelines to enhance the reproducibility of eye-tracking research and creating pedagogical tools to scaffold undergraduate laboratory training.

papers.title: Improving undergraduate research with a student progress tracker: A "white paper" introduction to our innovative teaching approach for making student accomplishments visible and accessible
papers.abstract: This work introduces the "Star Chart," a novel pedagogical instrument designed to scaffold the initial research laboratory experiences of undergraduate students. The tool facilitates the systematic tracking of progress by visually emphasizing and celebrating key research milestones, effectively making the developmental trajectory of emerging scientists visible and accessible. By providing a rewarding framework for growth, the approach aims to enhance research self-efficacy, foster a sense of institutional belonging, and accelerate the transition from novice trainee to independent investigator. The paper details the implementation of this teaching innovation within the Human Factors and Neuroscience lab and provides a framework for adoption by other faculty to improve equity and access in undergraduate research training.
papers.authors: Robert G. Alexander, Ola Abozid, Maryan Botlero, Yana Kostova, Ahaylee Rahman, Aziza Swift

papers.title: A case study of sudden-onset cortically mediated visual impairments in a 12-year-old
papers.abstract: This clinical case report describes a unique instance of persistent visual impairment in a 12-year-old male following a sudden onset in the absence of acute trauma. The patient exhibited akinetopsia-like symptoms, specifically characterized by an inability to perceive motion in complex dynamic scenes despite maintaining normal motion sensitivity for simple stimuli (e.g., Gabor patches). Psychophysical evaluations revealed a selective and significant deficit in object recognition within visual clutter, present in both moving and static displays. Oculomotor assessments identified slowed saccadic velocities and impaired smooth pursuit. High-resolution anatomical and functional MRI identified gray-white contrast blurring in the right lingual gyrus and focal FDG hypometabolism on PET, indicative of focal cortical dysplasia (FCD). The findings suggest that focal abnormalities in the ventral visual stream can manifest as subjective motion perception deficits by disrupting recognition-in-clutter mechanisms.
papers.authors: Jan W. Kurzawski, Robert G. Alexander, Nicolas M. Brunet, Orrin Devinsky, Fengping Hu, Stephen L. Macknik, Susana Martinez-Conde, Molla Nawsher, Bas Rokers, Timothy M. Shepherd, Ashwin Venkatakrishnan, Jonathan Winawer

papers.title: Why did Rubens add a parrot to Titian's The Fall of Man? A pictorial manipulation of joint attention
papers.abstract: This study employs high-precision eye-tracking to quantify how Peter Paul Rubens's artistic modifications to Titian's original composition of 'The Fall of Man' redirected viewer attentional dynamics. Rubens introduced critical changes to character gaze directions and added a chromatically striking red parrot, features hypothesized to alter joint attentional cues. Gaze analysis revealed that Rubens's version significantly restricted viewer interest to a narrower spatial distribution, specifically concentrating fixations on Eve's face as the dramatic nucleus. Furthermore, the parrot was found to intermittently undergo Troxler fading during sustained foveation of Eve's face due to its luminance equivalence with the peripheral foliage. This perceptual alternation, mediated by microsaccade rates, likely contributes to the perceived dynamism of the Baroque masterpiece compared to its Renaissance predecessor.
papers.authors: Robert G. Alexander, Ashwin Venkatakrishnan, Jordi Chanovas, Sophie Ferguson, Stephen L. Macknik, Susana Martinez-Conde

papers.title: Effect of stimulus-background contrast on visual search
papers.abstract: This investigation examines the impact of orientation contrast between foreground regions and background textures on the allocation of bottom-up visual attention. Utilizing a Posner cueing paradigm combined with functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), the study measured spatial cueing effects and BOLD signal modulation across early visual areas (V1–V4). Results indicate that when the target foreground is visible (aware condition), orientation contrast in distractors monotonically decreases both the cueing effect and the fMRI signal, supporting a 'Gradient' mechanism of attention. In contrast, under conditions of stimulus invisibility (unaware condition), attention follows a 'Winner-take-all' distribution. These findings demonstrate that the neural distribution of bottom-up saliency in the human visual hierarchy is critically dependent on perceptual awareness.
papers.authors: Robert G. Alexander, Gregory J. Zelinsky

papers.title: Minimal reporting guideline for research involving eye tracking (2023 edition)
papers.abstract: This consensus-based document establishes a standardized framework for the reporting of eye-tracking methodology in studies involving human or non-human primate participants. Developed over a three-year international community initiative, the guideline specifies minimum reportable items across key domains including apparatus specifications, calibration procedures (e.g., validation methods, drift checks), data quality metrics (e.g., spatial precision, accuracy, data loss), and the implementation of classification algorithms for fixations and saccades. By providing a structured checklist for researchers, the guideline aims to rectify prevalent gaps in methodological transparency, thereby enhancing the reproducibility and interpretability of gaze-based measures across diverse psychological and clinical applications.
papers.authors: Matt J. Dunn, Robert G. Alexander, Onyekachukwu M. Amiebenomo, Gemma Arblaster, Denize Atan, Jonathan T. Erichsen, Ulrich Ettinger, Mario E. Giardini, Iain D. Gilchrist, Ruth Hamilton, Roy S. Hessels, Scott Hodgins, Ignace T. C. Hooge, Brooke S. Jackson, Helena Lee, Stephen L. Macknik, Susana Martinez-Conde, Lee Mcilreavy, Lisa M. Muratori, Diederick C. Niehorster, Marcus Nyström, Jorge Otero-Millan, Michael M. Schlüssel, Jay E. Self, Tarkeshwar Singh, Nikolaos Smyrnis, Andreas Sprenger

0570.name: Robert L. Goldstone
0570.department: Department of Psychological and Brain Sciences
0570.bio: Robert L. Goldstone is a Distinguished Professor and Chancellor’s Professor at Indiana University and the director of the Percepts and Concepts Lab. Goldstone’s research focuses on the bidirectional interaction between perceptual and conceptual systems, specifically exploring how mental categories reshape sensory discrimination through mechanisms like unitization and differentiation. This methodology integrates human behavioral experiments with computational modeling, including neural networks and agent-based simulations. Goldstone also investigates collective behavior, examining how individual-level cognitive rules scale to produce emergent group intelligence and social coordination.
0570.research_direction: Dr. Goldstone has recently been investigating the mechanisms of perceptual learning, categorization, and grounded cognition across a variety of theoretical and applied contexts. Their recent work explores how the perceptual learning processes that refine categorical boundaries in high-stakes expertise—investigated through the real-world psychophysics of baseball umpire calls—might also generate suboptimal cognitive biases or representational overfitting in novel environments. Additionally, they are using the framework of grounded cognition to examine how spatial object affordances dynamically prime semantic language processing, as well as how interactive visual simulations can be leveraged to teach abstract statistical reasoning. Finally, their research tests how visual and conceptual scaffolds, such as discrete region boundaries on brain maps, systematically guide and bias human exploratory search strategies during scientific discovery tasks.

papers.title: Attentionally modulated motor-to-semantic priming: evidence from a property verification task
papers.abstract: This study investigates the interplay between sensorimotor activation and semantic processing through a motor-to-semantic priming paradigm utilizing a property verification task. Participants were exposed to graspable object primes featuring action-relevant components, such as handles, oriented either ipsilaterally or contralaterally to the response hand. Quantitative results indicate that property verification judgements for action-relevant descriptors were significantly facilitated by spatial compatibility between the handle orientation and the response side, whereas action-irrelevant properties showed no such modulation. These findings corroborate a grounded cognition model where the language and sensory-motor systems are tightly coupled, further suggesting that the activation of object affordances is not mandatory but is dynamically constrained by the agent's current conceptual focus and task goals.
papers.authors: Elisa Scerrati, Cristina Iani, Sandro Rubichi, Robert L. Goldstone

papers.title: Bias in perceptual learning
papers.abstract: The authors present a systematic taxonomic framework for analyzing bias in perceptual learning (PL), characterizing instances where long-term modifications to the perceptual system, typically adaptive for task-specific information extraction, result in suboptimal performance or deleterious externalities in novel or changing environments. They argue that PL-driven enhancements in sensitivity or dimensional weighting are inherently constrained by the training manifold and the observer’s idiosyncratic utility, leading to a form of representation-level 'overfitting.' This framework is used to explain how the same mechanisms responsible for perceptual expertise can manifest as harmful cognitive-perceptual biases, such as those observed in social categorization or task-induced insensitivity to relevant but non-trained features.
papers.authors: Madeleine Ransom, Robert L. Goldstone

papers.title: The psychophysics of home plate umpire calls
papers.abstract: Utilizing a massive longitudinal dataset of over 3 million pitch-level observations, this study models the decision-making processes of professional baseball umpires through a psychophysical lens to identify the determinants of ball and strike classification. The authors employ parametric logistic regression to map the subjective boundaries of the strike zone and quantify the impacts of systematic factors such as feedback, practice, and status-based biases (e.g., the 'Matthew Effect'). The results demonstrate that umpire skill is subject to significant perceptual learning and is influenced by latent cognitive priors, illustrating how high-stakes expertise is refined through a combination of environmental feedback and the psychological structure of categorical boundaries.
papers.authors: Kevin S. Flannagan, Brian M. Mills, Robert L. Goldstone

papers.title: How do students reason about statistical sampling with computer simulations? An integrative review from a grounded cognition perspective
papers.abstract: This integrative review synthesizes pedagogical research on the use of interactive simulations for teaching statistical reasoning, specifically contrasting traditional dual-process accounts with a grounded cognition framework. The authors evaluate empirical evidence regarding how simulations support 'statistical habits of mind' while simultaneously identifying persistent challenges students face in developing aggregate views of data or a process-based understanding of the law of large numbers. The review proposes that grounded cognition offers a more robust explanatory framework for these learning outcomes, emphasizing the bidirectional relationship between perception and conception, and suggests specific instructional design strategies—such as guided perceptual routines—to facilitate more robust, transferable conceptualizations.
papers.authors: Sebahat Gök, Robert L. Goldstone

papers.title: How do brain maps affect novices in a simplified scientific investigation task?
papers.abstract: This experimental study examines how extrinsic conceptual scaffolds—specifically the partitioning of the brain into discrete regions via 'brain maps'—modulate investigative trajectories in a simplified scientific discovery task. The authors demonstrate that novices exhibit a systematic search bias toward region boundaries, treating them as highly informative landmarks during exploratory hypothesis testing (lesioning) and signal identification. This 'boundary attraction' effect significantly influenced predictive performance, suggesting that the spatial and conceptual structure of scientific tools fundamentally biases the exploratory trajectories of researchers and can either facilitate or hinder discovery depending on the alignment of underlying signals with these conceptual boundaries.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the 46th Annual Conference of the Cognitive Science Society
papers.authors: Marina Dubova, Robert L. Goldstone

0571.name: Robert M. McPeek
0571.department: Department of Biological and Vision Sciences
0571.bio: Robert M. McPeek is a Professor at the SUNY College of Optometry whose research focuses on the neural mechanisms governing visual attention and the coordination of visually-guided actions, such as saccadic eye movements and reaching. McPeek investigates how the brain selects targets for action, specifically examining the functional roles of the superior colliculus and the frontal cortex in oculomotor selection and decision-making. Utilizing a combination of psychophysical studies, neurophysiological recordings, and causal interventions, their laboratory seeks to bridge the gap between neural activity and behavioral output in complex visual environments.
0571.research_direction: Dr. McPeek has recently been investigating the neural mechanisms that govern spatial attention, visual search, and saccadic eye movement planning across both human and non-human primate models. Using single-unit recordings in the macaque superior colliculus, their recent work explores how oculomotor priority maps integrate stimulus features and search history, specifically examining how target size influences the buildup of motor activity and how previously fixated locations are deprioritized via inhibitory tagging during sequential search. Additionally, they are testing the premotor theory of attention by measuring exogenous cueing effects in human patients with paralytic strabismus to determine whether spatial attention can still be robustly allocated to visual fields where eye movements are physically impossible. Altogether, their research probes how the visual system seamlessly bridges early sensory transient responses, spatial attentional allocation, and goal-directed motor execution.

papers.title: Physiological correlates of a simple saccadic-decision task to extended objects in superior colliculus
papers.abstract: We investigated the neural implementation of the 'size-latency effect,' wherein saccade initiation delay is modulated by the spatial extent of the target. Using a stochastic accumulator framework, we predicted that smaller targets should be associated with higher drift rates in the buildup of motor activity but, counterintuitively, higher thresholds for saccade initiation. Neurophysiological recordings from the macaque superior colliculus (SC) confirmed these predictions, showing that intermediate-layer SC neurons exhibit steeper activity accumulation and higher peak firing rates for smaller targets. Furthermore, we found that visual transient responses in the SC vary with target size and are strongly correlated with both motor buildup rates and saccadic latencies, suggesting that the size-latency effect is driven by early visual response modulations that are subsequently integrated into the saccadic motor command.
papers.authors: Baptiste Caziot, Bonnie Cooper, Mark R. Harwood, Robert M. McPeek

papers.title: Exogenous spatial attention is functional in paralytic strabismics
papers.abstract: The premotor theory of attention suggests an obligate linkage between the neural mechanisms for programming eye movements and the allocation of spatial attention. We tested this hypothesis in human patients with paralytic strabismus who were physically unable to execute saccades to specific regions of the visual field. Using an exogenous cueing paradigm, we measured the influence of peripheral visual cues on the latencies of both target-directed saccades and manual keypresses. Despite the inability to move the eyes into the paralyzed field, patients exhibited robust facilitation of response latencies for targets spatially proximate to cues and inhibition for targets appearing after longer cue-target onset asynchronies (inhibition of return). These results demonstrate that exogenous attentional allocation remains functional in the absence of movement execution capability, challenging theories that posit a necessary reliance of attention on intact motor output.
papers.authors: Kevin T. Willeford, Robert M. McPeek

papers.title: Inhibitory tagging both speeds and strengthens saccade target selection in the superior colliculus during visual search
papers.abstract: Efficient visual search under time pressure requires the oculomotor system to avoid re-inspecting previously searched locations, a process theoretically mediated by 'inhibitory tagging.' We recorded single-unit activity from the superior colliculus (SC) of rhesus monkeys during a multisaccade visual search task to quantify how previous fixation history modulates target selection. We found that SC neuronal activity was significantly reduced when a stimulus in the response field had been previously fixated compared to when it was novel. Crucially, this inhibitory modulation resulted in earlier and more robust discrimination of the next saccade goal by SC neurons. The magnitude of this effect was greater for targets than for distractors and declined as a function of time since the previous fixation. These findings indicate that the SC instantiates a priority map that incorporates search history to facilitate the rapid and efficient selection of sequential saccade goals.
papers.authors: Christopher Conroy, Rakesh Nanjappa, Robert M. McPeek

0572.name: Robert Volcic
0572.bio: Robert Volcic is an Associate Professor of Psychology at New York University Abu Dhabi exploring the mechanisms of human multisensory perception and sensorimotor integration. Their research examines how visual and haptic information are integrated to guide motor actions, such as reaching and grasping, within three-dimensional environments. By employing psychophysical experiments, movement tracking, and computational modeling, Volcic investigates the bidirectional relationship between active motor behavior and sensory processing. Current work focuses on understanding how the brain resolves sensory uncertainties using redundant cues and how physical interactions with the environment shape perceptual estimates.
0572.research_direction: Dr. Volcic has recently been investigating the spatiotemporal dynamics of sensorimotor integration, focusing on how the human motor system combines diverse sensory inputs to guide precise reaching and grasping movements. Their recent work explores how non-visual modalities—particularly auditory, proprioceptive, and haptic signals—are temporally weighted and utilized during both the preparation and online control of goal-directed actions. Additionally, they are examining the decay dynamics of haptic spatial memory, testing how postural reference frames support movement when real-time sensory feedback is withdrawn. Beyond non-visual guidance, Dr. Volcic is probing foundational debates in visuomotor control, such as evaluating spatial variability at goal attainment to test whether pointing actions adhere to Weber's law, and investigating how tool-mediated physical signals integrate with vision to optimize bimanual grasping kinematics.

papers.title: Bimanual Postural Similarity Facilitates Haptic Memory-Guided Reaching
papers.abstract: The decay of precision in memory-guided reaching is a well-established phenomenon in the visual domain, but its dynamics for haptically-defined spatial locations remain poorly understood. This research investigated reaching movements directed toward targets haptically encoded by the contralateral hand after variable temporal delays (2, 4, and 6 seconds). The introduction of a short delay significantly increased endpoint uncertainty compared to online conditions, highlighting the critical role of continuous haptic feedback. However, performance remained stable across longer delays, and accuracy was significantly enhanced when the final posture of the reaching limb closely matched the posture of the encoding limb. These results suggest that postural information from the sensing arm provides a stable, long-lasting reference frame that supports action guidance when real-time haptic input is withdrawn.
papers.authors: Ivan Camponogara, Robert Volcic

papers.title: Temporal Dynamics of Sensorimotor Integration for Auditory and Proprioceptive Target Information During Movement Preparation and Execution
papers.abstract: Reaching movements toward non-visual (auditory or proprioceptive) targets exhibit modality-dependent variability, yet the temporal evolution of these effects during planning and execution is unclear. This study analyzed reaching kinematics toward auditory, proprioceptive, and multisensory (audio-proprioceptive) targets to determine when modality-specific precision emerges. The findings reveal that endpoint variability patterns are established during the movement preparation stage and dictate subsequent online control strategies. Proprioceptive guidance consistently yielded higher motor precision than auditory guidance. In multisensory conditions, the motor system demonstrated a strong reliance on proprioceptive signals, with trajectories closely resembling unisensory proprioceptive reaches. These findings indicate that the planning stage sets the parameters for sensory weighting and that proprioception dominates the guidance of limb movements to non-visual spatial locations.
papers.authors: Ivan Camponogara, Robert Volcic

papers.title: The Contribution of Audition and Proprioception in Unisensory and Multisensory Target Reaching
papers.abstract: Goal-directed reaching toward non-visual targets relies on the integration of auditory and proprioceptive inputs, but the specific weighting of these modalities remains debated. This study quantified movement accuracy and precision (endpoint variability) toward auditory, proprioceptive, and combined audio-proprioceptive targets in 3D space. Results showed that proprioceptive target reaching was significantly more precise than auditory target reaching across both azimuth and depth dimensions. In multisensory trials, movement characteristics and precision levels closely mirrored those of the proprioceptive-only condition, demonstrating a high reliance on proprioceptive information for motor output. These results suggest that the central nervous system prioritizes proprioceptive inputs due to their superior spatial reliability, providing further evidence for the modality-specific nature of non-visual sensorimotor control.
papers.authors: Ivan Camponogara, Robert Volcic

papers.title: Actions obey Weber's law when precision is evaluated at goal attainment
papers.abstract: Weber’s law—the principle that sensory precision scales proportionally with stimulus magnitude—is frequently reported as violated in visually guided grasping actions, leading to theories of dissociated visual coding for action and perception. This study evaluated Weber’s law using a two-finger pointing task, analyzing spatial variability at the moment of target contact (goal attainment). Contrary to reports of dissociation, motor precision decreased proportionally with the distance between targets, strictly adhering to Weber's law. These findings suggest that the human visuomotor system relies on the same fundamental visual information as the perceptual system and that previously reported violations in grasping are likely due to biomechanical constraints or measurements taken during flight phases that do not represent the final motor goal.
papers.authors: Ivan Camponogara, Robert Volcic

papers.title: Tool-sensed object information effectively supports vision for multisensory grasping
papers.abstract: Tools allow humans to extend their motor capabilities, yet how tool-mediated sensory signals integrate with vision for action control is poorly understood. This study examined bimanual grasping performance when objects were held either with a mechanical grabber or directly with the hand. We observed that tool-mediated sensing facilitated movement performance—evidenced by earlier movement initiation and reduced peak grip aperture—in a manner equivalent to direct haptic sensing. Selective manipulation of object features revealed that positional information provided by the tool was sufficient to promote this multisensory advantage. These results indicate that the central nervous system processes tool-sensed inputs through established multisensory integration pathways, treating tool-mediated signals as functional extensions of the hand for the optimization of reaching and grasping kinematics.
papers.authors: Ivan Camponogara, Alessandro Farnè, Robert Volcic

0573.name: Roberto Caldara
0573.bio: Roberto Caldara is a Full Professor at the University of Fribourg, where Caldara directs the Eye and Brain Mapping Laboratory (iBMLab) and holds the Chair of Visual and Social Neuroscience. Their research focuses on the 'other-race' effect and the cross-cultural variability of facial expression perception, addressing the universality of human visual cognition. Through eye-tracking, electrophysiology (EEG), and functional neuroimaging (fMRI), Caldara investigates how cultural factors modulate the neural mechanisms and oculomotor strategies used to decode social information. This work includes the development of psychophysical frameworks to isolate the diagnostic features utilized during the spatiotemporal processing of dynamic facial signals.
0573.research_direction: Dr. Caldara has recently been investigating the perceptual and neural mechanisms underlying high-level face processing, with a particular focus on social categorization and emotion recognition. Their recent work explores the Other-Race Categorization Advantage (ORCA), utilizing a mix of visual noise psychophysics, EEG time-course analyses, and neuropsychological case studies of prosopagnosia to determine how the visual system extracts racial cues under degraded conditions and whether core face-network regions are strictly necessary for this rapid categorization. In parallel, they are examining the visual decoding of facial expressions, using computational eye-tracking frameworks to test whether idiosyncratic viewer "fixation fingerprints" generalize from static images to dynamic videos, while also measuring how facial movement impacts recognition thresholds amid visual noise. Furthermore, their methodological research seeks to clarify the functional overlap between distinct electrophysiological techniques, testing whether frequency-domain responses driven by fast periodic visual stimulation map directly onto traditional early event-related potentials like the N170 during face categorization tasks.

papers.title: Prosopagnosia and the role of face-sensitive areas in race perception
papers.abstract: This study investigates the functional necessity of core face-processing regions—specifically the right Occipital Face Area (rOFA) and left Fusiform Face Area (lFFA)—for the rapid extraction of racial information from faces. By testing patient PS, a case of pure acquired prosopagnosia with lesions in these areas, the authors examined the Other-Race Categorization Advantage (ORCA). PS exhibited a preserved ORCA, categorizing other-race faces faster than same-race faces, comparable to healthy controls. However, psychometric function analyses revealed that PS required significantly more visual signal intensity (signal-to-noise ratio) to identify racial categories in ambiguous morphed faces. These data suggest that while basic racial categorization remains resilient to damage in the core face network, the rOFA and lFFA are indispensable for processing fine-grained, high-level racial representations.
papers.authors: Pauline Schaller, Anne-Raphaëlle Richoz, Justin Duncan, Peter de Lissa, Roberto Caldara

papers.title: Cross-Validating the Electrophysiological Markers of Early Face Categorization
papers.abstract: The relationship between the N170 event-related potential (ERP) and the steady-state visual evoked potentials (SSVEPs) generated by fast periodic visual stimulation (FPVS) during face categorization remains a subject of methodological debate. This research concurrently recorded EEG signals using both transient ERP and FPVS paradigms to determine if FPVS frequency-domain responses serve as a proxy for the N170. Results demonstrated that the magnitude of the FPVS response does not directly correlate with isolated ERP components such as the P1 or N170. Instead, the FPVS frequency response was significantly predicted by peak-to-peak amplitude differences between the N170 and the subsequent P2 component. This evidence indicates that FPVS-based neural markers reflect higher-order integration across multiple processing stages rather than a singular, early face-sensitive categorization stage captured by the N170.
papers.authors: Fazilet Zeynep Yildirim-Keles, Lisa Stacchi, Roberto Caldara

papers.title: Idiosyncratic Fixation Patterns generalize across Dynamic and Static Facial Expression Recognition
papers.abstract: This investigation sought to determine whether the stable, idiosyncratic oculomotor strategies observed in static face recognition—termed "fixation fingerprints"—extend to the decoding of dynamic facial expressions of emotion (FEE). Utilizing the iMap computational framework to analyze fixation distributions, the authors compared the spatial sampling patterns of observers identifying static FEEs versus dynamic sequences that capture the temporal evolution of emotional signals. Despite the increased visual complexity and temporal variance of dynamic stimuli, observers maintained highly consistent and unique fixation strategies across both formats. These findings suggest that the internal representational models used to extract diagnostic social information from faces are remarkably robust to stimulus dynamics, reflecting a stable, viewer-dependent trait in visual social cognition.
papers.authors: Anita Paparelli, Nayla Sokhn, Lisa Stacchi, Antoine Coutrot, Anne-Raphaëlle Richoz, Roberto Caldara

papers.title: Recognizing facial expressions of emotion amid noise: A dynamic advantage
papers.abstract: To evaluate the ecological benefit of facial dynamics in social perception, this study employed a psychophysical approach to measure recognition thresholds for the six basic facial expressions under varying levels of visual signal intensity (0%–100% normalized phase and contrast). While young adults showed comparable recognition for static and dynamic expressions at full signal (except for high-dynamics expressions like happiness and surprise), a profound dynamic advantage emerged at lower signal intensities, peaking around 20%. The temporal unfolding of facial movements significantly lowered the sensory thresholds required for accurate expression decoding compared to static snapshots. These results demonstrate that the human visual system effectively integrates temporal cues to compensate for suboptimal viewing conditions, resolving the "ceiling effect" often reported in studies of dynamic emotion recognition in healthy populations.
papers.authors: Anne-Raphaëlle Richoz, Lisa Stacchi, Pauline Schaller, Junpeng Lao, Michael Papinutto, Valentina Ticcinelli, Roberto Caldara

papers.title: The speed of race
papers.abstract: The Other-Race Categorization Advantage (ORCA)—the phenomenon where observers categorize other-race faces faster than same-race faces—is hypothesized to stem from heightened sensitivity to early visual race signals. This study combined behavioral reaction-time measures with EEG to explore the neural correlates of ORCA under parametric visual degradation (random noise). Behavioral results revealed a specific threshold at low signal intensities where only other-race signals remained sufficient for categorization. Neurally, this sensitivity was reflected in early ERP components, with enhanced amplitudes for other-race stimuli observed in the P1, N170, and N250 peaks. The findings suggest that the ORCA is driven by a hierarchy of neural processes, starting with low-level perceptual saliency in the early visual stream, which facilitates the rapid categorization of faces belonging to less familiar ethnic groups.
papers.authors: Peter de Lissa, Pauline Schaller, Roberto Caldara

0574.name: Roland Fleming
0574.main_research_area: Visual perception of materials and objects
0574.bio: Roland W. Fleming holds the Kurt Koffka Professorship of Experimental Psychology at Justus Liebig University Giessen and serves as the Executive Director of the Center for Mind, Brain and Behavior, a collaborative research center involving the Universities of Marburg and Giessen and TU Darmstadt. Fleming’s research investigates how the human brain estimates physical and functional properties of objects, such as 3D shape, gloss, and material elasticity, from retinal images. To study these processes, their lab combines psychophysical experiments, computer graphics, and unsupervised deep learning to model the visual system’s method of disentangling environmental cues. Fleming’s recent work focuses on the neural representations of core material dimensions and the computational mechanisms that enable humans to predict physical events and guide motor actions.
0574.research_direction: Dr. Fleming's recent work explores the computational and perceptual mechanisms underlying how humans see materials, 3D shapes, and coherent objects. They have recently been investigating the core dimensions of material perception by combining large-scale psychophysics with deep neural networks to build image-based models that predict human judgments of complex surface properties like gloss. In parallel, their research examines how early image measurements, specifically V1 orientation fields, drive 3D shape-from-shading and predict human shape illusions under diverse lighting conditions. Additionally, they are re-evaluating classical theoretical challenges like the visual binding problem, probing whether the visual system simply exploits the rich statistical regularities of natural scenes rather than relying on dedicated feature-integration architectures.

papers.title: No free lunch with the binding problem
papers.abstract: This work presents a fundamental re-evaluation of the visual binding problem, challenging the traditional assumption that explicit feature-integration mechanisms are required for coherent object perception. Drawing on the success of deep neural networks in visual processing tasks without dedicated binding architectures, the authors argue that the visual system exploits the rich statistical regularities and inherent feature correlations present in natural scenes. The paper suggests that these statistical dependencies allow the brain to bypass the classical binding problem, implying that the specialized neural processes historically postulated in cognitive science may be less necessary for functional vision than previously thought.
papers.authors: Giacomo Aldegheri, Roland W. Fleming

papers.title: Material fingerprinting: predicting human perception of material appearance through psychophysical analysis and neural networks
papers.abstract: The authors introduce the 'visual fingerprint,' a perceptual representation framework that links high-dimensional image measurements of materials to sixteen human-understandable appearance attributes. Using a psychophysical dataset of 347 real-world materials and over 110,000 human ratings, the study maps perceptual attributes across diverse categories including wood and fabrics. By integrating multimodal deep neural network features (CLIP) with a multi-layer perceptron, the researchers developed a predictive model capable of accurately reproducing human judgments of appearance and similarity using as few as two image frames, providing an intuitive and interpretable approach to material representation for digital environments.
papers.authors: Jiri Filip, Filip Dechterenko, Filipp Schmidt, Jiri Lukavsky, Jan Kotera, Veronika Vilimovska, Roland W. Fleming

papers.title: Orientation fields predict human perception of 3D shape from shading
papers.abstract: This study identifies orientation fields, derived from the responses of orientation-selective populations in the primary visual cortex (V1), as the primary image measurement driving human 3D shape perception from shading. The researchers establish a robust statistical correspondence between image orientation fields and 3D surface curvature properties that generalizes beyond ideal specular reflections to common shaded objects. Through psychophysical experiments, they demonstrate that orientation-based models accurately predict specific human shape illusions occurring under varied lighting and the robustness of shape perception against image modifications that disrupt luminance-based cues, resolving long-standing questions about the neural inputs for shape-from-shading.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Celine Aubuchon, Romain Vergne, Steven A. Cholewiak, Benjamin Kunsberg, Daniel Holtmann-Rice, Steven W. Zucker, Roland W. Fleming

papers.title: Gloss discrimination: Toward an image-based perceptual model
papers.abstract: This research investigates the visual discriminability of surface gloss across variations in illumination, shape, and viewpoint to establish a perceptual standard for material appearance. Using human paired-comparison tasks and maximum likelihood difference scaling (MLDS), the study quantifies how distal scene variables influence the statistics of proximal image data and subsequent perceptual sensitivity. Findings reveal that human gloss discrimination is highly consistent across individuals and is effectively predicted by a straightforward visual differences predictor (VDP). This framework allows for the estimation of visual discriminability bounds for surfaces across a wide range of realistic viewing conditions, independent of physical specular reflectance parameters.
papers.authors: Jacob R. Cheeseman, James A. Ferwerda, Takuma Morimoto, Roland W. Fleming

papers.title: Core dimensions of human material perception
papers.abstract: The authors employ a large-scale data-driven approach to identify the foundational representational dimensions of material perception in humans. Analyzing thousands of similarity judgments using a multimodal deep neural network (CLIP), they identified 36 interpretable dimensions that organize material perception across a vast array of visual appearances. This low-dimensional embedding accurately captures single-trial similarity judgments and reduces the complexity of relating image features to external behavior. The study demonstrates that these data-driven dimensions provide a bridge between low-level image statistics and high-level semantic categories, allowing for comprehensive modeling of how the visual system represents the physical and functional properties of materials.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Filipp Schmidt, Martin N. Hebart, Alexandra C. Schmid, Roland W. Fleming

0576.name: Rosanne L. Rademaker
0576.bio: Rosanne L. Rademaker is a cognitive neuroscientist and Group Leader at the Ernst Strüngmann Institute for Neuroscience, where they investigate the neural mechanisms of human perception and visual working memory. Their research employs high-field fMRI, M/EEG, psychophysics, and computational modeling to examine how the brain maintains sensory representations in the absence of direct input. Rademaker contributed to the sensory recruitment theory by demonstrating that the early visual cortex simultaneously represents incoming sensory signals and mnemonic information through flexible neural codes. Their work also explores how memory representations transition from veridical sensory formats to abstract, categorical formats along the visual hierarchy to facilitate goal-directed behavior.
0576.research_direction: Dr. Rademaker has recently been investigating the neural architectures and representational formats that support visual working memory. Utilizing fMRI, EEG, psychophysics, and recurrent neural network modeling, their recent work explores how feature information—ranging from orientation to high- versus low-level motion speed—is maintained and transformed across the visual hierarchy during memory delays. Specifically, they are examining whether mnemonic traces in early visual cortex rely on active top-down feedback, while also investigating potential transitions in representational geometry from veridical sensory codes to categorical formats between perception and memory. Their research further probes the spatial reference frames—weighing retinocentric against allocentric coordinates—used to anchor and stabilize these visual features. Finally, they are critically evaluating the methodological limits of generative forward modeling for aggregate EEG data, questioning whether phenomena like model mimicry prevent the unambiguous inference of underlying neural tuning properties.

papers.title: Model mimicry limits conclusions about neural tuning and can mistakenly imply unlikely priors
papers.abstract: We evaluate the validity of generative forward modeling as an inferential tool for characterizing neuronal tuning distributions from non-invasive human electroencephalography (EEG) data. Focusing on a recent study attributing an orientation-specific anisotropy to natural image statistics, we demonstrate that model mimicry—the phenomenon where divergent population tuning schemes yield indistinguishable aggregate responses—prohibits the unambiguous adjudication between competing biological hypotheses. Through computational simulations, we show that previous reports of a vertical-horizontal anisotropy in orientation tuning may arise as a modeling artifact rather than a true physiological property, and we propose that current implementations of this framework are insufficiently constrained for such claims.
papers.authors: Michael J. Wolff, Rosanne L. Rademaker

papers.title: A gradual transition toward categorical representations along the visual hierarchy during working memory, but not perception
papers.abstract: This study delineates the divergent representational geometries of oriented grating stimuli during sensory perception versus visual working memory (VWM) maintenance using fMRI-based multivariate pattern analysis. While early visual cortex (EVC) exhibits a 'veridical' representational structure consistent with efficient coding of natural image statistics during perception, we observe a systematic shift towards 'categorical' representations—characterized by increased psychological similarity near cardinal axes and relative repulsion in oblique space—during the delay period. This categorical transformation intensifies along the cortical visual hierarchy (V1 through V3 and into IPS), suggesting a reformatting mechanism that segregates mnemonic content from sensory input to prevent interference and stabilize information for behavior.
papers.authors: Chaipat Chunharas, Michael J Wolff, Meike D Hettwer, Rosanne L Rademaker

papers.title: Top-down feedback can explain the existence of working memory traces in early visual cortex
papers.abstract: We investigate the neural mechanisms underlying the maintenance of working memory (WM) traces in early visual cortex (EVC), specifically adjudicating between top-down cortical feedback and short-term synaptic plasticity (STSP). Utilizing a biologically-constrained recurrent neural network (RNN) model, we demonstrate that top-down feedback from higher-order areas is sufficient to replicate two primary hallmarks of human WM performance: the flexible selection of target items from memory via attentional gating and the maintenance of representational integrity during salient sensory distraction. Our findings suggest that while STSP may contribute to passive storage, active top-down signals are the essential driver for the robust and task-relevant maintenance of visual information observed in sensory areas.
papers.authors: N. N. Krause, A. Compte, Rosanne L. Rademaker
