papers.title: Visual representations in the human brain rely on a reference frame that is in between allocentric and retinocentric coordinates
papers.abstract: To identify the coordinate system used for spatial and feature-based visual representations in the human brain, we utilized electroencephalography (EEG) while participants performed a delayed-estimation orientation task with manipulated head orientations (upright vs. 45° tilt). Multivariate cross-classification analysis was employed to distinguish between retinocentric (eye-centered) and allocentric (world-centered) coding. Orientation information was successfully decoded from both voltage signals and alpha-band power. Critically, we find that the neural code for orientation, both during stimulus processing and the memory delay, is maximized in an intermediate reference frame between retinocentric and allocentric coordinates, indicating that the human visual system employs a hybrid coordinate system for stable perception and memory.
papers.authors: Maria S. Servetnik, Michael J. Wolff, Chaipat Chunharas, Rosanne L. Rademaker

papers.title: Better performance when recalling speed from high-level compared to low-level motion
papers.abstract: We investigated the precision of speed recall in visual working memory for high-level versus low-level motion stimuli across a series of psychophysical experiments. Participants performed a delayed-estimation task for the speed of objects defined by either high-level attentional tracking (e.g., multiple object tracking) or low-level luminance-defined motion (e.g., drifting gratings). We found consistently superior recall precision for speeds derived from high-level motion sources, a performance benefit that persisted across varying stimulus durations and delay lengths. These results suggest that motion speed is not maintained as a monolithic feature; rather, the representational fidelity of temporal information is significantly influenced by the hierarchical level of the motion-processing pathway involved.
papers.authors: Giuliana Martinatti Giorjiani, Amit Rawal, Rosanne L. Rademaker

0577.name: Roy Luria
0577.bio: Roy Luria is a Professor at Tel Aviv University whose research focuses on the neural mechanisms of visual working memory and executive control. Their work uses electrophysiological measures, specifically the contralateral delay activity (CDA) event-related potential, to track the maintenance and filtering of visual information in real-time. Luria examines the processes of memory updating and the "resetting" of mental representations, focusing on how individual differences in capacity relate to attentional control. By combining high-temporal resolution EEG with behavioral psychophysics, they study how the brain manages and updates internal representations when presented with competing visual input.
0577.research_direction: Dr. Luria has recently been investigating the cognitive and neural architecture of visual working memory (VWM), with a major focus on the indexing mechanisms that track visual information over time. Their recent work explores the VWM "pointer system" using electrophysiological markers like the contralateral delay activity (CDA) to understand how the brain decides whether to incrementally update or completely "reset" object representations in response to dynamic events like occlusion, physical transformations, and top-down statistical contexts. Alongside these tracking mechanisms, they are examining the fundamental format of VWM storage using continuous response paradigms to determine whether multi-feature items are maintained as integrated object files or as independent features. Furthermore, their research probes the limits of memory capacity by asking how low-level perceptual similarities between stimuli govern whether mixing distinct visual categories enhances or interferes with overall memory performance.

papers.title: Visual working memory's pointer system: Past, present, and future
papers.abstract: This review synthesizes the theoretical framework of the visual working memory (VWM) pointer system, emphasizing the functional dissociation between representational content and the indexing mechanisms (pointers) that enable access. The authors detail the 'resetting' vs. 'updating' dichotomy, where environmental changes that invalidate the mapping between an item and its VWM pointer trigger a termination of the current representation and the allocation of a novel one. The work leverages findings from the contralateral delay activity (CDA) to establish the neural and behavioral signatures of these processes, discussing their implications for VWM chunking, pointer assignment, and the integration of intuitive physical expectations into memory maintenance.
papers.authors: Halely Balaban, Roy Luria

papers.title: Feature-based versus object-based representation in visual working memory
papers.abstract: Across five experiments, this study investigated whether multi-feature objects (e.g., color and shape) are maintained in VWM as independent features or integrated object files. Using a continuous response distribution divided into accuracy quintiles, the researchers calculated the area under the curve (AUC) to assess whether the precision of one feature correlated with the other. The findings consistently revealed a robust feature dependency across variations in stimulus type (triangles, polygons), encoding duration (300 ms, 1200 ms), and response paradigms (sequential, simultaneous). The results provide strong empirical evidence for an object-based storage model where all constituent features of an object are maintained in a dependent manner.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
papers.authors: Ayelet Ramaty, Roy Luria

papers.title: The effect of occlusion on the visual working memory pointer-system
papers.abstract: This research examines how the VWM pointer system manages object representations during occlusion. Monitoring the contralateral delay activity (CDA) as a neural marker for online maintenance, the study explored whether the 'resetting' process—typically induced by abrupt, visible changes—occurs when changes are occluded. Experiment 1 observed a decline in CDA amplitude during occlusion, while subsequent experiments utilizing brief occluders isolated an ERP response to sudden stimulus appearance that could be distinguished from the neural signatures of pointer resetting. The study clarifies how VWM maintains spatiotemporal correspondence and triggers representational updates when objects are temporarily hidden from view.
papers.authors: Shani Friedman, Roberto Dell'Acqua, Paola Sessa, Roy Luria

papers.title: The effect of context on pointer allocation in visual working memory
papers.abstract: This study tested the hypothesis that the VWM pointer system strategically adapts its operations based on the statistical context of environmental changes. Using a shape-change detection task, the researchers manipulated the probability of 'updating' (incremental modification of a representation) versus 'resetting' (discarding and re-encoding a representation). Neural results indicated that in a 'resetting-dominant' context, stimuli that would normally trigger an updating process instead induced a significant drop in CDA amplitude, a marker of pointer resetting. This demonstrates that the pointer system's decision to update or reset is not merely a reflexive response to stimulus change but is modulated by top-down expectations and task-level contextual probabilities.
papers.authors: Shani Friedman, Trafton Drew, Roy Luria

papers.title: The role of perceptual similarities in determining the asymmetric mixed-category advantage
papers.abstract: Investigating the 'mixed-category benefit' in VWM, this study explored why mixing certain categories (e.g., colors and shapes) enhances performance while others show limited or asymmetric gains. Through three change-detection experiments, the researchers measured sensitivity (d') to determine how low-level perceptual feature overlap affects memory capacity. Results showed that the mixed-category advantage was significantly diminished when categories shared basic visual features, suggesting that the interference preventing the benefit occurs at the perceptual feature-level. This indicates that low-level similarity, rather than high-level categorical distinctiveness, is the primary driver of the asymmetric advantages observed in mixed-category visual working memory arrays.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
papers.authors: Reut Peled, Roy Luria

0578.name: Roy Mukamel
0578.bio: Roy Mukamel is a Professor at Tel Aviv University and directs the Motor Cognition Laboratory. Their research investigates the neural integration of action and perception, specifically examining how voluntary motor commands modulate activity in sensory cortices and how the brain represents intentions. Using a multi-modal methodology that includes functional MRI, EEG, virtual reality, and human intracranial electrophysiology, Mukamel addresses questions regarding motor skill learning, intermanual transfer, and the mechanisms of self-generated sensory feedback.
0578.research_direction: Dr. Mukamel has recently been investigating the intricate relationships between motor actions, sensory expectations, and skill acquisition. Their recent work explores how active behavior modulates sensory processing, using EEG and behavioral paradigms to study how motor efference copies shape auditory sensory attenuation and whether the expected intensity of an outcome structurally influences physical action kinetics. They are also examining the mechanisms of experience-dependent plasticity, probing whether active physical tracing functionally enhances visual shape discrimination and how observational motor learning consolidates over time in the absence of sleep. To complement these behavioral and electrophysiological inquiries, Dr. Mukamel is additionally developing novel, model-free fMRI analysis frameworks that map functional brain properties using temporal signal consistency rather than relying on standard hemodynamic assumptions.

papers.title: What the visual system can learn from the non-dominant hand: The effect of graphomotor engagement on visual discrimination
papers.abstract: The research investigates whether the enhancement of visual discrimination through graphomotor activity (tracing graphemes) is a general motor property or is specific to the highly trained dominant hand. Utilizing unfamiliar shapes, the study assessed visual discrimination thresholds in 60 healthy right-handed participants before and after tracing or passive visual training. Results demonstrated that graphomotor engagement with the non-dominant hand produced visual learning gains comparable to those of the dominant hand and passive visual-only training. The lack of a significant behavioral advantage for motor engagement over purely visual protocols suggests that shape tracing primarily facilitates discrimination by focusing visual attention on critical features rather than through unique motor-sensory contributions. These findings align with a symbolic theoretical framework where basic shape feature acquisition for object recognition occurs through visual inspection, irrespective of fine motor proficiency or hand laterality.
papers.authors: Shlomit Ben-Ami, Batel Buaron, Ori Yaron, Kyle Keane, Virginia H. Sun, Flip Phillips, Jason Friedman, Pawan Sinha, Roy Mukamel

papers.title: Expectations and Motor Signals Shape Auditory Evoked Responses in an Independent Manner
papers.abstract: Sensory attenuation, the reduction in neural response to self-triggered stimuli, is traditionally attributed to motor efference copies, yet the interaction between these signals and predictive expectations remains contested. In this EEG experiment (n=30), participants were trained to associate specific motor (button press) or visual cues with auditory tones. Over eight repetitions of cue-tone pairing, the amplitude of the auditory N100 component significantly decreased as association strength (expectation) increased. Crucially, the attenuation of the N100 following motor cues remained constant across the learning phase and showed no interaction with repetition number. This indicates that while both top-down expectations and motor-related signals modulate sensory processing, they do so through distinct, independent neural pathways. The results suggest that the motor system provides a generalized suppressive signal for self-generated consequences that is not updated by specific experience-based contingencies.
papers.authors: Batel Buaron, Roy Mukamel

papers.title: A randomization-based, model-free approach to functional neuroimaging: A proof of concept
papers.abstract: Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) typically relies on model-based inferences (e.g., GLM) that assume specific hemodynamic response functions (HRF) and linear signal summation. This paper introduces TWISTER (Temporal consistency Within Individual Subject Through Experimental Randomization), a model-free framework for mapping functional brain properties. The approach utilizes a randomization scheme to create experimental runs where stimulus dimensions are either consistent or inconsistent across time. By measuring the temporal consistency of BOLD time-courses between runs using cross-condition correlations within individual voxels, the method performs statistical inference without a generative model of the measured signal. Proof-of-concept testing indicates that this units-of-entire-runs approach is robust to violations of additivity and shift invariance, offering a data-driven alternative to standard multivariate and univariate fMRI analyses.
papers.authors: Matan Mazor, Roy Mukamel

papers.title: High or low expectations: Expected intensity of action outcome is embedded in action kinetics
papers.abstract: Goal-directed actions are performed to achieve sensory consequences, but how the kinetics of these actions are shaped by the properties of expected outcomes is not well-defined. In three experiments (n=120), the study examined how expected intensity of an auditory or tactile stimulus influences the kinetics (applied force) of the triggering button press. The researchers found an inverse relationship: participants applied significantly more force when expecting a low-intensity stimulus compared to a high-intensity one, even when action kinetics and stimulus attributes were independent. This kinetic modulation was abolished in the absence of a causal link between action and consequence. Furthermore, no correlation was found between applied force and perceptual detection thresholds (d'), indicating that kinetic signals encode high-level contextual expectations without necessarily modulating early sensory sensitivity through efference-based feedback.
papers.authors: Batel Buaron, Daniel Reznik, Roy Mukamel

papers.title: Sequence-specific delayed gains in motor fluency evolve after movement observation training in the absence of early sleep
papers.abstract: The expression of delayed performance gains in motor skill learning is traditionally thought to require a period of sleep for consolidation, particularly for physical practice. This study investigates the necessity of sleep for the consolidation of observational motor learning using a finger-to-thumb opposition sequence (FOS) task. Participants observed videos of a specific FOS and were tested for delayed gains in motor fluency (speed) without an intervening sleep interval. Results revealed that sequence-specific speed improvements emerged offline several hours after the observational training session. These results suggest that the neural consolidation of motor information acquired through the action observation network follows a time-dependent trajectory independent of sleep, mirroring patterns observed in perceptual learning rather than the sleep-dependent consolidation typical of physical motor skill acquisition.
papers.authors: Rinatia Maaravi-Hesseg, Nadav Aridan, Roy Mukamel

0579.name: Ru-Yuan Zhang
0579.department: School of Psychological and Cognitive Sciences
0579.lab_name: Laboratory of Cognitive Computational Neuroscience and Neuroimaging (CCNN)
0579.bio: Ru-Yuan Zhang is a computational neuroscientist who investigates the mechanisms of human perception, learning, and decision-making using fMRI, psychophysics, and deep learning models. Zhang’s research focuses on how the brain represents sensory uncertainty and how top-down processes like attention warp neural manifolds to optimize population coding in the human visual cortex. By comparing artificial neural networks with biological systems, they reverse-engineer the principles of perceptual learning and abstract visual reasoning to analyze human intelligence. Their work also includes computational psychiatry, applying Bayesian inference and reinforcement learning models to characterize cognitive deficits in individuals with anxiety and depression.
0579.research_direction: Dr. Zhang's recent work explores the computational and geometric principles underlying visual processing, predictive cognition, and decision-making. Within sensory processing, they have recently been investigating how phenomena like top-down attention and visual perceptual learning optimize population codes, using high-dimensional frameworks to measure how neural manifolds transform within the visual cortex. Their research also extends into predictive dynamics, examining how the brain might use neural prediction errors to drive abstract visual reasoning and how rhythmic neural trajectories in both humans and recurrent neural networks support the temporal anticipation of sequential events. Furthermore, Dr. Zhang is applying computational psychiatry approaches to clinical populations, modeling how anxiety and depression disrupt probabilistic inference and alter evidence accumulation strategies during decision-making in volatile environments.

papers.title: Neural prediction errors as a unified cue of abstract visual reasoning
papers.abstract: This work addresses the computational disparity between human-level abstract visual reasoning (AVR) and the limitations of deep neural networks by proposing a framework grounded in predictive coding. The authors posit that neural prediction errors (PEs)—the discrepancy between incoming visual inputs and top-down relational expectations—serve as the fundamental signal for identifying and generalizing abstract rules. The proposed model integrates a Relational Network with a PE-driven feedback loop to iteratively evaluate rule hypotheses in tasks such as Raven’s Progressive Matrices. Evaluations on AVR benchmarks, including PGM and RAVEN, demonstrate that this architecture achieves state-of-the-art accuracy and exhibits robust zero-shot generalization to novel visual attributes, supporting a crucial role for PE in the biological implementation of analogical reasoning.
papers.venue: IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence (TPAMI)
papers.authors: Lingxiao Yang, Xiaohua Xie, Wei-Shi Zheng, Fang Fang, Ru-Yuan Zhang

papers.title: A neural geometry approach comprehensively explains apparently conflicting models of visual perceptual learning
papers.abstract: Visual perceptual learning (VPL) improves sensory discrimination through training, but the mechanistic basis—whether it arises from sharpened neural tuning, increased gain, or attenuated noise—remains a subject of debate. This study introduces a neural geometry framework that unifies these seemingly contradictory models by conceptualizing population responses as geometric manifolds in high-dimensional neural space. Through the analysis of multi-unit recordings from macaque areas V1 and V4 alongside human fMRI data, the authors demonstrate that VPL is characterized by a singular geometric transformation: the optimization of task-relevant manifold alignment relative to decision boundaries. This transformation effectively increases the Fisher information of the population code, providing a comprehensive explanation for how learning-induced changes at the single-neuron level manifest as improved behavioral performance.
papers.authors: Yuan-Ao Cheng, Mehran Sanayei, Xiaolong Chen, Ke Jia, Shurui Li, Fang Fang, Takeo Watanabe, Alexander Thiele, Ru-Yuan Zhang

papers.title: Sequential temporal anticipation characterized by neural power modulation and in recurrent neural networks
papers.abstract: The ability to anticipate the precise timing of sequential events is fundamental to adaptive sensory processing. This study investigates the neurocomputational substrates of temporal anticipation using a combination of human electroencephalography (EEG) and recurrent neural network (RNN) modeling. Behavioral data show that participants dynamically adjust their expectations based on rhythmic regularities. EEG analysis reveals that this anticipation is mediated by the modulation of oscillatory power in the alpha (8–13 Hz) and beta (15–30 Hz) bands, which systematically track the progression of temporal intervals. RNNs trained on the same task exhibit latent-state dynamics that parallel the human neural data, suggesting that the brain utilizes a dynamical systems mechanism where the velocity of neural trajectories within a specific manifold encodes temporal intervals and predicts upcoming events.
papers.authors: Xiangbin Teng, Ru-Yuan Zhang

papers.title: Attention improves population codes by warping neural manifolds in human visual cortex
papers.abstract: This study investigates how top-down attention optimizes sensory processing by applying a neural population manifold framework to high-resolution 7T fMRI data. The researchers measured cortical responses during diverse attentional tasks and quantified the geometric transformations of neural representations in the visual cortex. They discovered that attention induces a non-linear warping of the neural manifold in areas V1–V3, characterized by the expansion of representational space along task-relevant stimulus dimensions and the contraction of irrelevant ones. This manifold warping increases the separability of neural patterns and enhances decoding accuracy. The findings support a 'tuning change' model of attention and provide a quantitative geometric explanation for how attention refines population-level neural codes to improve perception.
papers.authors: Yu-Qi You, Shurui Li, Yu-Ang Cheng, Yuanning Li, Kendrick Kay, Ru-Yuan Zhang

papers.title: Individuals with anxiety and depression use atypical decision strategies in an uncertain world
papers.abstract: This computational psychiatry study examines the decision-making strategies of individuals with internalizing disorders (anxiety and depression) in volatile environments. Using a restless multi-armed bandit task and Bayesian hierarchical drift-diffusion models (HDDM), the authors identified a specific computational phenotype associated with these disorders. Individuals with high symptom severity exhibit 'atypical' strategies marked by over-estimation of environmental volatility and heightened sensitivity to negative prediction errors. This manifests as excessive switching behavior and narrower decision boundaries (lower threshold for evidence accumulation), leading to suboptimal reward harvesting. These results demonstrate how affective states disrupt probabilistic inference and bias the exploration-exploitation trade-off, providing quantitative markers for clinical diagnosis.
papers.authors: Zeming Fang, Mingli Zhao, Ting Xu, Yuanning Li, Huichun Xie, Ping Quan, Haiyan Geng, Ru-Yuan Zhang

0580.name: Ruben Coen-Cagli
0580.bio: Ruben Coen-Cagli is an Associate Professor who investigates the principles of neural computation and their relationship to perceptual experience. Coen-Cagli’s research integrates tools from computer vision, machine learning, and probabilistic neural coding to model how the primary visual cortex (V1) represents the statistics of natural images. Specifically, they explore how cortical population activity approximates probabilistic inferences, focusing on the role of contextual modulation and trial-to-trial response variability. Through a combination of normative computational modeling and experimental collaboration, their work aims to identify the mechanisms by which the brain resolves sensory ambiguity in complex natural environments.
0580.research_direction: Dr. Coen-Cagli has recently been investigating how the visual system leverages the statistical regularities of natural environments to perform efficient probabilistic inference. Their recent work explores perceptual organization, combining psychophysics, high-density EEG, and eye-tracking to model human scene segmentation as an iterative Bayesian process and to map how these segmentation dynamics are altered in individuals with autism. At the single-neuron and population levels, they are examining the primary visual cortex to understand how natural image statistics shape trial-to-trial response covariability and response sparseness, specifically testing whether cortical variability acts as an energy-efficient representational medium for sensory uncertainty. Furthermore, their research develops computational frameworks based on Fisher information to quantify how stimulus signals are selectively routed between distributed neural populations through low-dimensional communication subspaces.

papers.title: Natural scene segmentation dynamics reveal iterative Bayesian inference
papers.abstract: The primate visual system dynamically partitions complex retinal inputs into discrete perceptual entities, yet the computational underpinnings for naturalistic and ambiguous scenes remain inadequately characterized. Utilizing a novel psychometric paradigm to reconstruct subjective human segmentation maps, we identified spatiotemporal dynamics that deviate from standard static models. We propose that these dynamics are emergent properties of Iterative Bayesian Inference (IBI), wherein sensory evidence is recursively integrated with a spatial prior favoring object compactness. Empirical evidence confirms that the latency of segmentation is modulated by the degree to which local image statistics align with this spatial prior, accurately reflecting individual-specific biases. Our findings designate IBI as a fundamental computational substrate for perceptual organization, linking the temporal evolution of choices to the iterative refinement of probabilistic estimates.
papers.authors: Tridib K. Biswas, Jonathan Vacher, Sophie Molholm, Pascal Mamassian, Ruben Coen-Cagli

papers.title: A Multimodal Framework for Understanding Perceptual Segmentation of Natural Scenes In Autism
papers.abstract: Atypicalities in perceptual organization, specifically visual segmentation and integration, are central to the sensory phenotype of Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD), yet traditional studies frequently utilize oversimplified stimuli that fail to engage real-world processing dynamics. We introduced a multimodal framework integrating psychophysical tasks, high-density electroencephalography (EEG), and eye-tracking to characterize natural scene segmentation. By employing a forced-choice judgment task on pairs of cues in naturalistic images, we reconstructed individualized segmentation maps and quantified uncertainty. Our data reveals that individuals with ASD exhibit increased reaction time latencies and greater idiosyncrasy in their perceived object boundaries. Corresponding neural markers include delayed occipital event-related potentials and diminished global field power across critical stimulus-processing windows, while oculomotor signatures indicate broader and more exhaustive initial image exploration. This framework bridges behavioral idiosyncrasies with underlying neural and attentional dynamics in neurodivergent populations.
papers.authors: Darnell K. Adrian Williams, Tridib K. Biswas, Concetta Brusco, Sophie Molholm, Ruben Coen-Cagli

papers.title: Relating natural image statistics to patterns of response covariability in macaque primary visual cortex
papers.abstract: Characterizing the neural representation of natural scenes requires a normative account of trial-to-trial response covariability in the primary visual cortex (V1). We investigated whether the structure of V1 noise correlations reflects hierarchical probabilistic inference constrained by the statistical regularities of natural images. By deploying pairwise Gaussian Scale Mixture (GSM) generative models to capture the joint dependencies of oriented local features, we derived specific predictions for neural activity under the neural sampling hypothesis. Our recordings in macaque V1 demonstrate that the spatial arrangement of image features selectively modulates the magnitude and extent of neuronal correlations in a manner consistent with the width of the inferred posterior distributions. These results provide empirical evidence that cortical variability functions as a representational medium for uncertainty, reflecting a fine-grained adaptation to the ecological statistics of the visual environment.
papers.authors: Amirhossein Farzmahdi, Adam Kohn, Ruben Coen-Cagli

papers.title: Measuring stimulus information transfer between neural populations through the communication subspace
papers.abstract: Distributed neural computation relies on the selective transmission of sensory signals across populations via low-dimensional communication subspaces. We present a theoretical framework using linear Fisher information to quantify stimulus routing efficiency. By decomposing the information into components that are either aligned with or orthogonal to the communication subspace, we analyze how the alignment of the population activity covariance with the stimulus-tuning direction determines the fidelity of signal propagation. Our results demonstrate that stimulus selection and multiplexing across the cortical hierarchy can be achieved through the precise alignment of noise correlations and tuning gradients within these coding subspaces. This framework provides a rigorous metric for evaluating interareal interactions in population recordings and suggests mechanisms for flexible, context-dependent gating of sensory information.
papers.authors: Oren Weiss, Ruben Coen-Cagli

papers.title: A Unified Theory of Response Sparsity and Variability for Energy-Efficient Neural Coding
papers.abstract: The neural code in sensory systems is marked by high levels of sparseness and trial-to-trial variability, yet the functional relationship between these two motifs remains debated. We propose a normative framework based on the principle of information-cost efficiency (ICE) to unify these properties. By characterizing the mathematical equivalence between the coefficient of variation (CV) and response sparsity across various probability density functions, we demonstrate that both metrics are positive indicators of a system's energy-efficient encoding capacity. We implemented a CV-maximization algorithm to derive optimal linear-nonlinear operators for natural image statistics, which yielded filters that accurately replicate the spatial receptive field structures observed in the primary visual cortex (V1). Our results suggest that cortical variability and sparseness are not distinct signatures of noise or metabolic constraints, but rather are synergistic features of a representational strategy optimized for energy-efficient probabilistic inference.
papers.authors: Mingyi Huang, Ruben Coen-Cagli

0581.name: Ruggero Micheletto
0581.bio: Ruggero Micheletto is a Professor at Yokohama City University with research integrating solid-state physics, nanophotonics, and cognitive neuroscience. Micheletto's work in vision science utilizes experimental psychophysics and eye-tracking to investigate the critical fusion frequency of light stimuli and the cognitive effects of linguistic distortions on visual perception. Previously a visiting professor at the Harvard Visual Attention Laboratory, Micheletto has used scanning near-field optical microscopy (SNOM) for real-time biological imaging and developed sensory substitution systems like 'VisualSound'. Current research directions involve the mathematical modeling of neural networks and the study of spatiotemporal dynamics in optical semiconductor blinking.
0581.research_direction: Dr. Micheletto's recent work explores the optical and electronic stability of wide-bandgap semiconductors, primarily focusing on light emission dynamics in gallium nitride (GaN) materials. Specifically, they have recently been investigating the spatiotemporal mechanisms behind photoluminescence "blinking"—where microscopic light-emitting regions unexpectedly flicker—in quantum wells and nanopillar arrays to determine how crystalline defects, excitation wavelengths, and collective electronic interactions drive these optical instabilities. In parallel, their research uses computational modeling to examine how introducing various elemental impurities alters the fundamental electronic structure and carrier pathways within GaN crystals. Additionally, they are assessing how specific manufacturing techniques, such as ion implantation and thermal annealing, influence the formation of performance-limiting atomic defects in silicon carbide power devices.

papers.title: Time and Spatially Resolved Analysis of Single Quantum Well InGaN/GaN Photoluminescence Blinking at Multiple Sample Frequencies
papers.abstract: This study conducts a high-resolution spatiotemporal characterization of photoluminescence (PL) blinking in InGaN/GaN single quantum well (SQW) structures by employing variable sampling frequencies. The research identifies discrete flickering dynamics in localized emission regions, demonstrating that the intensity variations are frequency-dependent. The analysis suggests that these optical instabilities are driven by fluctuating carrier capture and emission processes at non-radiative recombination centers and trap states within the quantum well. The findings provide a quantitative framework for evaluating the impact of crystalline defects on the optical stability of wide-bandgap semiconductor devices.
papers.authors: Kotaro Oikawa, Mitsuru Funato, Yoichi Kawakami, Ruggero Micheletto

papers.title: The Electronic Properties of Magnesium, Zinc, Scandium, and Chlorine in Wurtzite GaN: An Ab Initio Study
papers.abstract: This investigation employs ab initio density functional theory (DFT) to model the electronic and structural characteristics of Mg, Zn, Sc, and Cl impurities in wurtzite gallium nitride (GaN). By calculating formation energies and thermodynamic transition levels for various charge states, the study determines the electrical behavior of these substitutional defects. The results indicate that Sc and Cl introduce deep-level states within the bandgap that can act as compensating centers, while Mg maintains its role as a shallow acceptor. This work establishes a theoretical basis for understanding how these specific dopants influence carrier concentrations and recombination pathways in p-type and n-type GaN.
papers.authors: Giovanni Alfieri, Elizabeth Buitrago, Ruggero Micheletto

papers.title: Comparison of the Spatial and Temporal Photoluminescence Dynamics in InGaN/GaN at 365 nm and 430 nm Excitation
papers.abstract: This research examines the photoluminescence (PL) dynamics of InGaN/GaN heterostructures under selective excitation of the InGaN quantum well (430 nm) compared to simultaneous excitation of the GaN barrier and the well (365 nm). Experimental data reveal that selective excitation drastically improves PL spatial uniformity and suppresses the occurrence of blinking sites. The analysis concludes that the injection of carriers from the barrier in the simultaneous excitation mode activates complex trap-mediated recombination pathways and energy transfer mechanisms that are primarily responsible for the observed localized optical instabilities and blinking phenomena.
papers.authors: Kotaro Oikawa, Ruggero Micheletto

papers.title: Correlated photoluminescence blinking phenomenon on InGaN/GaN nanopillar structures
papers.abstract: This work reports the discovery of spatially correlated photoluminescence (PL) blinking in InGaN/GaN nanopillar arrays. High-resolution optical mapping reveals that the temporal fluctuations of PL intensity in individual pillars are not independent but exhibit long-range synchronization. The authors propose a phenomenological model wherein the quantum confined Stark effect (QCSE) and carrier exchange among adjacent crystalline domains modulate the emission state of the nanopillars. The results suggest a collective electronic response to ultraviolet excitation, indicating that blinking is influenced by a macroscopic interaction across the nanopillar ensemble rather than isolated local defects alone.
papers.authors: Kotaro Oikawa, Koichi Okamoto, Mitsuru Funato, Yoichi Kawakami, Ruggero Micheletto

papers.title: The effects of different anode manufacturing methods on deep levels in 4H-SiC p+n diodes
papers.abstract: This investigation characterizes the formation and concentration of electrically active deep-level defects in 4H-SiC p+n diodes as a function of various anode fabrication protocols. Utilizing deep-level transient spectroscopy (DLTS) and Laplace DLTS, the study identifies point defects associated with ion implantation and the subsequent thermal annealing steps required for p-type activation. The findings quantify how specific processing parameters influence the density of carrier traps, which in turn affects minority carrier lifetime and leakage current characteristics. The study provides critical insights for optimizing the fabrication of high-performance wide-bandgap power electronic devices.
papers.authors: Giovanni Alfieri, V. K. Sundaramoorthy, Ruggero Micheletto

0582.name: Ruth Rosenholtz
0582.bio: Rosenholtz is a Principal Research Scientist at NVIDIA Research and maintains an affiliation as a Principal Research Scientist at MIT’s Department of Brain and Cognitive Sciences and CSAIL. Rosenholtz developed the "Texture Tiling Model," which characterizes peripheral vision as an encoding scheme using summary statistics within localized pooling regions. Their research indicates that many observed attentional limits are consequences of peripheral encoding constraints. Rosenholtz's current work focuses on applying these computational models to analyze visual tasks such as driving, visual search, and the design of information visualizations.
0582.research_direction: Dr. Rosenholtz has recently been investigating the fundamental role of peripheral vision and summary-statistic encoding in shaping human perception, proposing a major theoretical shift in how the field conceptualizes visual attention. Their recent work explores whether phenomena classically attributed to capacity-limited attentional bottlenecks—such as visual search asymmetries, conjunction search, and change blindness—might instead be explained by the lossy, feature-pooling mechanisms of the visual periphery. To bridge basic science and real-world application, they are examining how background clutter and heterogeneity impact visual search and saccade latencies in complex digital interfaces like video conferencing. Additionally, they have been evaluating the gap between biological and machine vision by developing new image datasets to test neural network robustness to simulated peripheral interference, while simultaneously investigating the minimal set of interpretable image statistics required to accurately model human texture perception and synthesis.

papers.title: Toward a paradigm shift in visual attention
papers.abstract: This article serves as the author's formal response to thirty expert commentaries on the theoretical crisis within visual attention research. The work synthesizes feedback to further clarify the proposed paradigm shift, which argues that many capacity-limited phenomena previously attributed to attentional bottlenecks are more parsimoniously explained by the lossy, summary-statistic encoding of peripheral vision. Rosenholtz differentiates between sensory information loss in the periphery and computational complexity limits on task-level decision processes. By integrating ideal observer models and mechanistic perceptual accounts, the paper advocates for a transition toward a task-centric theory of selection that resolves existing empirical anomalies without the need for traditional, ill-defined attentional constructs.
papers.authors: Ruth Rosenholtz

papers.title: The effect of background clutter on visual search in video conferencing
papers.abstract: This empirical study quantifies the deleterious impact of virtual background complexity and variability on visual task performance within multi-tile video conferencing (VC) environments. Utilizing eye-tracking methodologies, the researchers demonstrate that increased background heterogeneity and high feature congestion significantly prolong saccade latencies and degrade target detection accuracy for interface elements, such as speaker highlights and reaction icons. The results provide a quantitative behavioral link between basic peripheral vision models and the usability of complex digital communicative tools. The findings suggest that current VC interface designs are often sub-optimal for human peripheral processing and search mechanisms, advocating for the adoption of perceptually-optimized background designs to reduce cognitive load.
papers.authors: Yelda Semizer, Ruth Rosenholtz

papers.title: Attributing Statistics to Synthesis Quality in Correlation-Based Texture Models
papers.abstract: The study addresses the interpretability-performance tradeoff in texture representation by introducing a model that merges neuroscience-inspired multi-scale pyramid filters with pairwise correlation statistics. The researchers decompose texture information into hierarchical statistical families and utilize a self-supervised contrastive learning objective (InfoNCE loss) to rank their relative importance for synthesis fidelity. They demonstrate that a drastically reduced parameter set of approximately 100 interpretable statistics is sufficient to generate high-quality texture syntheses comparable to style-transfer methods based on deep neural networks. This work provides a transparent and efficient alternative to over-parameterized latent spaces, offering new insights into the statistical basis of human texture perception.
papers.venue: NeurIPS (Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems)
papers.authors: Vasha DuTell, Anne Harrington, Zeyu Yun, Mark Hamilton, Christian Koevesdi, Edward Adelson, Bill Freeman, Ruth Rosenholtz

papers.title: COCO-Periph: Bridging the Gap Between Human and Machine Perception in the Periphery
papers.abstract: This paper introduces COCO-Periph, a benchmark dataset designed to evaluate and narrow the divergence between biological and machine vision performance in the visual periphery. By transforming images from the Microsoft COCO dataset using a modified, computationally efficient Texture Tiling Model (TTM), the authors simulate the lossy summary-statistic encoding of human peripheral vision. Evaluations of state-of-the-art object detection architectures reveal that standard deep neural networks (DNNs) are significantly more susceptible to peripheral clutter than human observers. While training models on the COCO-Periph dataset improves their alignment with human behavioral performance, current architectures still fail to replicate the human-like robustness to peripheral interference, highlighting a fundamental gap in machine-vision modeling of task-level selection.
papers.authors: Anne Harrington, Vasha DuTell, Mark Hamilton, Ayush Tewari, Simon Stent, William T. Freeman, Ruth Rosenholtz

papers.title: Visual Attention in Crisis
papers.abstract: This target article presents a critical reassessment of the conceptual foundations of visual attention research, arguing that the field has entered a Kuhnian crisis due to numerous unexplained anomalies. Rosenholtz demonstrates that seminal phenomena traditionally attributed to selective attention mechanisms—including visual search asymmetries, conjunction search difficulty, and change blindness—are more accurately and parsimoniously explained by the structural loss of information in peripheral vision via summary-statistic encoding (e.g., the Texture Tiling Model). The author proposes a unifying theory where all perception results from performing a specific visual task, with performance limits dictated by decision complexity rather than a dedicated attentional bottleneck or gate, effectively rethinking visual attention from the ground up.
papers.authors: Ruth Rosenholtz

0583.name: Ryan Ash
0583.department: Department of Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences
0583.bio: Ryan Ash is a psychiatrist and neuroscientist who develops noninvasive neuromodulation technologies to treat disorders characterized by excessive neural circuit stability, such as autism and OCD. Ash utilizes transcranial ultrasound stimulation (TUS) and repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) to investigate how brain states, particularly visual spatial attention, regulate neuroplasticity in the human visual cortex. Their work combines high-density EEG, steady-state visual evoked potentials (ssVEPs), and computational electrophysiology to connect fundamental circuit neuroscience with clinical interventions for behavioral inflexibility. Previously a clinical scholar at Stanford University, Ash currently directs a translational research program focused on image-guided ultrasound technologies and neuroplasticity-based therapeutics.
0583.research_direction: Dr. Ash has recently been investigating human visual cortical plasticity and the methodological foundations of non-invasive deep-brain neuromodulation. Their recent work explores whether transcranial focused ultrasound stimulation (TUS) targeted at the lateral geniculate nucleus can causally modulate visual contrast detection and steady-state visual evoked potentials (SSVEPs). To ensure the rigor of these neuromodulation interventions, they are developing psychophysically validated auditory masking protocols to isolate true ultrasonic effects from bone-conduction acoustic confounds. Additionally, they are examining long-term potentiation-like neuroplasticity in the visual cortex, using SSVEPs to probe how stimulus-specific response potentiation is influenced by covert spatial attention and repeated multi-day sensory exposure. To support these longitudinal interventional paradigms, their research also evaluates the day-to-day stability of SSVEP contrast-response functions as reliable electrophysiological biomarkers.

papers.title: Effects of transcranial focused ultrasound stimulation to human lateral geniculate nucleus on visual perception and steady-state visual evoked potentials
papers.abstract: To determine whether transcranial ultrasound stimulation (TUS) can causally modulate deep sensory nuclei in the human brain, this investigation examined the functional consequences of pulse repetition frequency (PRF)—a critical parameter hypothesized to govern acoustic radiation force versus mechanical displacement mechanisms—targeted to the lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN). Neurotypical adult human participants (n = 25) underwent visual psychophysical testing coupled with scalp electroencephalography, combining contrast increment detection thresholds with steady-state visual evoked potentials (SSVEPs) driven by frequency-tagged contrast-sweep stimuli. Sonication was targeted to the left LGN or an ipsilateral control site using an MRI-guided, depth-steerable 4-element focused ultrasound transducer (free-water ISPPA = 68 W/cm², 10% duty cycle, across multiple PRFs) with individual acoustic simulations and calibrated white-noise masking to eliminate auditory co-stimulation confounds. Despite acoustic modeling confirming focal target engagement in the majority of subjects, active LGN stimulation elicited no statistically significant shifts in SSVEP amplitude, phase delay, or contrast increment detection accuracy. These null findings provide an important cautionary benchmark regarding the effect sizes and efficacy of online neuronavigated deep-brain TUS paradigms in human sensory circuitry.
papers.authors: Martin TW Scott, Patti N Limon, Morteza Mohammadjavadi, Benjamin R. Kop, Nai-Feng Chen, Eva A Feredoes, Vladimir Vildavski, Gerald R Popelka, Anthony M. Norcia, Kim Butts Pauly, Ryan T Ash

papers.title: Psychophysical validation of calibrated white-noise and tuned-noise auditory masks for transcranial focused ultrasound
papers.abstract: Acoustic side-effects generated through bone conduction and transducer housing resonance present a significant confound in transcranial ultrasound stimulation (TUS) experiments. To establish a rigorous framework for blinding participants during ultrasonic neuromodulation, the authors synthesized and calibrated auditory masking protocols against a highly salient sonication protocol (500 kHz fundamental frequency, 487.5 Hz pulse repetition frequency, 10% duty cycle, ISPPA = 68 W/cm²). Both wideband white noise and carrier-envelope spectrum-matched noise masks were calibrated for A-weighted decibel sound pressure levels using an artificial ear. Masking efficacy was quantified across 20 neurotypical adults using an adaptive QUEST+ staircase in a two-interval forced-choice (2IFC) detection task. Masking successfully attenuated active TUS detection to chance levels (<55% accuracy) in 17 of 20 subjects for white noise and 18 of 20 subjects for tuned noise. However, effective masking required intensities near clinical occupational safety limits, and spectrum-tuned masking offered no significant statistical benefit over white noise, demonstrating that bone-conducted TUS percepts do not strictly follow conventional air-conduction acoustic spectra and highlighting the necessity of formal masking calibration in TUS clinical trials.
papers.authors: Martin TW Scott, Patti N Limon, Gerald R Popelka, Kim Butts Pauly, Anthony M Norcia, Ryan T Ash

papers.title: Spatial Attention and Session Day Independently Modulate Human Visual Cortical Plasticity
papers.abstract: This study examines the role of covert endogenous spatial attention in modulating stimulus-specific response potentiation (SSRP), a form of non-invasive cortical neuroplasticity, within the human visual system. Utilizing 128-channel high-density EEG, the researchers recorded frequency-tagged steady-state visual-evoked potentials (SSVEPs) at 6 Hz and 7.5 Hz in response to contrast-reversing checkerboard stimuli. While SSRP induction (2 Hz reversal) was localized to a single hemifield, the resulting response potentiation was observed bilaterally, challenging the paradigm of strict input or retinotopic specificity in humans. Crucially, the magnitude of potentiation was significantly higher on the second session day compared to the first, demonstrating that human SSRP effects accumulate over repeated exposures. Spatial attention was found to have a modest enhancing effect on potentiation in naïve participants during their initial session, but this modulation was occluded by the more robust plasticity effects observed during the second session.
papers.authors: Patricia Naomi Limon, Anthony M. Norcia, Ryan Thomas Ash

papers.title: Stability of steady-state visual evoked potential contrast response functions
papers.abstract: Repetitive sensory stimulation paradigms have frequently been posited to induce long-term potentiation-like neuroplasticity in primary sensory neocortex. In this study, the authors tested the capacity of repeated contrast-reversal sweep steady-state visual-evoked potential (ssVEP) stimuli to drive neuroplastic changes, while assessing the longitudinal stability of the underlying contrast-response function. Twenty healthy participants completed four 20-trial blocks daily over four consecutive testing days, fixating on 9-Hz contrast-reversing sinusoidal luminance gratings (3 cycles/degree) that swept logarithmically between 5% and 80% contrast across 10-second trials. Electrophysiological analysis at the 18-Hz second-harmonic frequency revealed no systematic or significant amplitude modulation across intra-day blocks or across successive testing days, failing to replicate sensory-induced cortical plasticity under these stimulus parameters. In contrast, individual ssVEP contrast-response profiles demonstrated remarkable consistency, with low within-subject coefficients of variation across blocks (15%–20%) and across days (22%–25%), confirming that sweep-ssVEP protocols provide an exceptionally reproducible electrophysiological biomarker for longitudinal repeated-measures interventional trials.
papers.authors: Ryan T Ash, Kerry C Nix, Anthony M Norcia

0584.name: Sabrina Hansmann-Roth
0584.bio: Hansmann-Roth is an Assistant Professor at the University of Iceland who researches human visual perception using behavioral psychophysics and computational modeling. Their work investigates how the brain represents environmental statistical information through feature distribution learning (FDL) and the extraction of visual ensembles. Hansmann-Roth also explores the mechanisms of serial dependence and visual priming to determine how past experiences and internal uncertainty influence perceptual decisions. Additionally, their research addresses material perception by examining the cognitive and sensory factors involved in perceiving surface properties like gloss and lightness.
0584.research_direction: Dr. Hansmann-Roth has recently been investigating the computational mechanisms that drive systematic biases, memory representations, and metacognitive uncertainty in human vision. Their recent work explores how the visual system balances sensitivity and stability through history effects like serial dependence and sensory adaptation, utilizing continuous mouse-tracking and orientation reproduction tasks to untangle how these biases unfold temporally and adapt to environmental stability. In the domain of visual working memory, they are examining how observers reconstruct spatial and temporal sequence order, as well as how the relative noise between competing item representations dictates whether inter-item memory biases are attractive or repulsive. Additionally, they are probing the origins of metacognitive confidence, specifically investigating how distinct sources of perceptual uncertainty—such as internal stimulus noise versus task-specific boundary distance—uniquely shape classical confidence signatures like the folded-X pattern.

papers.title: Repulsive and attractive serial dependence: Balancing sensitivity and stability in visual perception
papers.abstract: The human visual system employs adaptation to enhance perceptual sensitivity and serial dependence to maintain stability, yet the interaction between these often-conflicting biases remains poorly understood. This study investigated the temporal dynamics of orientation reproduction using mouse-tracking to dissociate these effects. Trajectory analysis revealed a robust, early-stage repulsive bias away from the preceding stimulus orientation, characteristic of sensory adaptation. However, as the response unfolded, higher-order decision processes significantly mitigated this repulsion, leading to attractive biases (serial dependence) or diminished repulsion depending on the environmental context. These results suggest that the visual system actively balances sensitivity and stability by modulating sensory biases through late-stage decision mechanisms.
papers.authors: Elín Kara Celin, Sabrina Hansmann-Roth

papers.title: The role of sequence stability on serial dependence
papers.abstract: Perceptual judgments are frequently biased toward previously encountered stimuli, a phenomenon known as serial dependence that typically facilitates the perception of continuity. This investigation explored how environmental stability—specifically the constancy of non-target features—modulates these history effects. Participants performed orientation reproduction tasks on stimulus sequences where spatial frequency was either fixed (stable) or varied randomly (unstable). Stronger attractive serial dependence was observed in unstable environments compared to stable ones. This finding indicates that in stable contexts, predictive coding may sharpen neural representations and reduce the need for historical integration, whereas environmental uncertainty triggers greater reliance on past information to maintain a coherent representation of a single object.
papers.authors: Elín Kara Celin, Sabrina Hansmann-Roth

papers.title: Reconstruction of Temporal and Spatial Order Information
papers.abstract: This study examines the computational and cognitive mechanisms underlying the reconstruction of spatial and temporal order in visual memory. Utilizing psychophysical paradigms that require the simultaneous maintenance of item identity and sequential positioning, the researchers investigate how systematic biases in order memory arise from the interaction between spatial locations and temporal intervals. The findings characterize the limits of order reconstruction and demonstrate that the visual system employs structured heuristics to resolve ambiguities in the relative positioning of memorized items, suggesting that order representations are encoded with probabilistic uncertainty similar to low-level visual features.
papers.authors: Elín Kara Celin, Sabrina Hansmann-Roth

papers.title: Noise in Competing Representations Determines the Direction of Memory Biases
papers.abstract: Human visual working memory is subject to systematic inter-item biases where reported features are shifted toward or away from non-target items. We propose a normative 'demixing' model suggesting these biases are optimal when the brain disentangles overlapping memory signals. Simulations of an ideal observer predict that the direction of these biases (attraction vs. repulsion) is governed by the relative noise distribution between items rather than just absolute sensory noise. Across four color-memory experiments, we verified that targets with identical absolute noise levels exhibit contrasting bias directions depending on the noise level of the concurrent non-target. These results support signal disentanglement as a unifying computational explanation for history-dependent and inter-item memory biases.
papers.authors: Andrey Chetverikov, Sabrina Hansmann-Roth

papers.title: Stimulus reliability but not boundary distance manipulations violate the folded-X pattern of confidence
papers.abstract: Metacognitive confidence judgments are typically characterized by a 'folded-X' pattern, where confidence increases with accuracy on correct trials but decreases on errors as task difficulty diminishes. However, some conditions produce a 'double-increase' pattern where confidence rises for both correct and error responses. This study tested the hypothesis that the confidence signature depends on the specific source of uncertainty: stimulus reliability (signal noise) versus boundary distance (feature similarity to the decision criterion). Across orientation judgment experiments using Gabor patches and moving dots, results confirmed that stimulus reliability manipulations elicit the double-increase pattern, whereas boundary distance manipulations preserve the folded-X signature. This indicates that human confidence estimates are sensitive to whether uncertainty originates from internal sensory noise or task-specific feature similarity.
papers.authors: Elín Kara Celin, Sabrina Hansmann-Roth

0585.name: Sabrina Pitzalis
0585.department: Department of Movement, Human and Health Sciences
0585.lab_name: Laboratorio di Neuroimmagini (IRCCS Fondazione Santa Lucia)
0585.bio: Pitzalis is an Associate Professor who specializes in the functional organization of the human visual system, specifically the dorsal stream and its role in self-motion perception. Using wide-field stimulation fMRI, retinotopic mapping, and high-density electrophysiology (ERPs), Pitzalis identified human homologs for macaque visual areas such as V6, V6A, and PEc. Their research examines how the brain segregates object-motion from egomotion (optic flow) and the integration of visuospatial signals for the control of locomotion and posture. Pitzalis conducts research at the Santa Lucia Foundation (IRCCS) in Rome on the neural substrates of spatial attention and multimodal sensorimotor interactions.
0585.research_direction: Dr. Pitzalis has recently been investigating the dynamic interactions between cognitive processing and motor execution, focusing on how whole-body actions influence visual and preparatory brain states. Using high-density EEG, their recent work explores cognitive-motor trade-offs by varying the physical complexity of task responses—such as reaching, stepping, or walking—during visuomotor tasks to examine how the brain allocates its anticipatory and attentional resources. In parallel, they are using fMRI and wide-field visual stimulation to map the velocity-tuning profiles of the dorsal stream, specifically isolating how cortical networks process optic flow-driven self-motion compared to object-motion. Finally, their research extends these cognitive-motor paradigms into clinical domains, investigating how dual-task training and metabolic factors impact neurodegeneration and cognitive decline in aging populations with conditions like Type 2 diabetes.

papers.title: Effects of Walking on Anticipatory Brain Processing During a Concurrent Cognitive Task
papers.abstract: This study utilized high-density electroencephalography (EEG) to evaluate the impact of treadmill locomotion on the neural correlates of task anticipation during a visuomotor discriminative response task (DRT). Forty participants performed the DRT in both static standing and walking conditions, while background optic flow was manipulated to simulate realistic movement. Analysis centered on the motor-related Bereitschaftspotential (BP) and the cognitive prefrontal negativity (pN). Results demonstrated that walking facilitated both cognitive and motor preparation, characterized by enhanced ERP amplitudes and improved behavioral response speed and accuracy compared to the static condition. Although the presence of a background flow field further potentiated motor readiness, it introduced an increased cognitive load that attenuated accuracy. The findings support the multiple resources theory, suggesting that locomotion-induced cortical arousal enhances resource availability for preparatory integration, even during dual-task scenarios.
papers.authors: BiancaMaria Di Bello, Camilla Panacci, Sveva Montesano, Raffaele Costanzo, Luca Boccacci, Merve Aydin, Andrea Casella, Stefania Lucia, Francesca Strappini, Francesco Di Russo, Sabrina Pitzalis

papers.title: The impact of type 2 diabetes on aging cognitive functions: A narrative review of neuropathophysiological mechanisms and mitigating strategies
papers.abstract: This narrative review synthesizes the neuropathophysiological mechanisms through which Type 2 Diabetes (T2D) accelerates cognitive decline and heightens dementia risk in aging cohorts. The authors detail how chronic hyperglycemia, systemic and central insulin resistance, oxidative stress, and vascular dysfunction converge to induce structural brain changes and impair neural efficiency across critical cognitive domains, particularly memory and executive functions. The paper critically evaluates the efficacy of established and emerging therapeutic strategies, including pharmacological treatments and innovative non-pharmacological interventions like cognitive-motor dual-task training, aimed at counteracting metabolic-driven neurodegeneration and preserving cortical integrity in elderly patients.
papers.authors: Andrea Casella, BiancaMaria Di Bello, Merve Aydin, Stefania Lucia, Francesco Di Russo, Sabrina Pitzalis

papers.title: Electrophysiological indexes of the cognitive-motor trade-off associated with motor response complexity in a cognitive task
papers.abstract: The cognitive-motor trade-off in the human brain was investigated by manipulating the complexity of motor responses (keypress, reaching, and stepping) required during a cognitive discriminative response task. Using event-related potential (ERP) and behavioral analysis, the study examined resource allocation across early perceptual and late post-perceptual processing stages. Results indicated that increasing motor complexity significantly enhanced early sensory-attentional processing, as evidenced by larger P1 and N1 amplitudes. However, this was accompanied by a concurrent reduction in late cognitive control, with a marked attenuation of the P3 component in the whole-body movement (stepping) condition. A novel component, the N750, scaled positively with motor response difficulty. These findings confirm a motor-priority trade-off model, wherein the cortex prioritizes motor execution demands at the expense of late-stage cognitive evaluation.
papers.authors: Bianca Maria di Bello, Andrea Casella, Merve Aydin, Stefania Lucia, Francesco Di Russo, Sabrina Pitzalis

papers.title: Modulation of anticipatory brain activity as a function of action complexity
papers.abstract: This research explored the modulation of preparatory cortical states by the complexity of stimulus-driven motor actions. EEG was recorded from 19 volunteers performing a visual discriminative response task (DRT) with three levels of response complexity: simple keypress, keypress with arm-reaching, and keypress with reaching and stepping. The study targeted slow cortical potentials (SCPs), specifically the Bereitschaftspotential (BP), prefrontal negativity (pN), and visual negativity (vN). Data revealed that simple actions were characterized by maximal motor excitatory preparation in premotor areas and substantial prefrontal inhibitory control. In contrast, complex whole-body actions involving stepping shifted preparatory activation toward bilateral dorsomedial parieto-occipital regions, reflecting specialized sensory readiness for the incoming stimulus. These results suggest that the brain optimally reconfigures its anticipatory network based on the sensory-motor integration requirements of the planned effector sequence.
papers.authors: Andrea Casella, Bianca Maria Di Bello, Merve Aydin, Stefania Lucia, Francesco Di Russo, Sabrina Pitzalis

papers.title: Neural sensitivity to translational self- and object-motion velocities
papers.abstract: Using wide-field visual stimulation and event-related functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), this study characterized the velocity-tuning profiles of the human motion-sensitive cortical network for translational self-motion (simulated by optic flow) and object-motion. The investigation utilized individual surface-based brain mapping and representational similarity analysis (RSA) to assess the responsiveness of areas V6, hPEc, CSv, PIC, and MT+ to varying translational speeds. While nearly all egomotion-responsive regions were modulated by self-motion velocity, medial areas including V6 and hPEc exhibited heightened sensitivity to self-motion signals across a broad velocity range, supporting their role in ego-speed estimation. Lateral areas such as MT+ demonstrated a preference for object-motion signals. These findings suggest a functional segregation within the dorsal visual stream where medial and lateral subsystems differentially encode egocentric and environmental motion velocities during navigation.
papers.authors: Valentina Sulpizio, Alessandro von Gal, Gaspare Galati, Patrizia Fattori, Claudio Galletti, Sabrina Pitzalis

0587.name: Sam Ling
0587.bio: Sam Ling is an Associate Professor at Boston University and the Director of the Visual Neuroscience Lab, where they investigate the mechanisms the human brain employs to prioritize information within cluttered visual environments. Ling’s research combines psychophysics, functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), and computational modeling to characterize how attention modulates neural response properties. Their work focuses on divisive normalization, contrast adaptation, and the ways in which top-down and bottom-up processes alter early visual representations.
0587.research_direction: Dr. Ling has recently been investigating the functional organization and top-down modulation of the early human visual cortex using model-based fMRI. Their recent work explores how population spatial frequency tuning maps onto receptive field sizes to create scale-invariant visual representations, an effort supported by their development of open-source computational tools for estimating voxel-wise tuning profiles. Additionally, they are examining how voluntary attention dynamically reconfigures these basic sensory properties, mapping both the spatial spread of the attentional spotlight and how feature-based attention shifts spatial frequency preferences globally across the visual field. Finally, Dr. Ling's research explores the intersection of broader cognitive states and visual gain, measuring how task-induced arousal and pupil size modulate contrast response functions in early retinotopic areas.

papers.title: Spatial Frequency Tuning Follows Scale Invariance in the Human Visual Cortex
papers.abstract: This study evaluates the principle of scale invariance in the human visual hierarchy, testing the hypothesis that the resolution of spatial sampling remains constant relative to receptive field (RF) size. Utilizing model-based fMRI to measure voxel-wise population spatial frequency tuning (pSFT) and population receptive field (pRF) characteristics in visual areas V1, V2, and V3, the researchers characterized the relationship between peak spatial frequency (SF) preference and RF size. By introducing the 'Cycles Per Receptive Field' (CPF) metric, they demonstrated that the ratio between preferred SF and pRF size is constant across eccentricities and cortical areas. These findings provide direct empirical evidence that neural populations in early human vision exhibit scale-invariant organization, where SF preferences scale inversely with the spatial extent of the population's receptive field.
papers.authors: Emily Wiecek, Luis D. Ramirez, Michaela Klimova, Sam Ling

papers.title: The Population Spatial Frequency Toolbox
papers.abstract: The Population Spatial Frequency Toolbox (pSF-Toolbox) is an open-source MATLAB-based software package developed to standardize and facilitate the estimation of population spatial frequency tuning (pSFT) from functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data. The toolbox provides a comprehensive pipeline, including Psychtoolbox scripts for parametrically varying SF stimulus presentation and an estimation module that fits voxel-wise log-Gaussian models to blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) signals. Validated across multiple neuroimaging studies, the toolbox enables researchers to characterize the peak preference and bandwidth of neural populations across the visual field, supporting investigations into the influence of cognitive states and retinotopic organization on spatial resolution and feature processing.
papers.authors: Luis D. Ramirez, Feiyi Wang, Emily Wiecek, Lauren N. Vinke, Sam Ling

papers.title: Dynamic estimation of the attentional field from visual cortical activity
papers.abstract: This research introduces a novel fMRI-based computational framework for the dynamic estimation of the locus and spatial extent (spread) of the attentional field in the human visual cortex. Participants performed a character discrimination task on a white-noise annulus while covertly attending to cued regions of varying widths. By modeling BOLD signal modulations in retinotopic areas V1–V3, the study successfully recovered the spatial profiles of attentional deployment. The results demonstrate that while the center of the attentional field is tracked with high precision, the magnitude of the cortical spread consistently exceeds the physical width of the cue, reflecting a broadening of the attentional spotlight that scales with behavioral demands and spatial uncertainty.
papers.authors: Ilona M. Bloem, Leah Bakst, Joseph T. McGuire, Sam Ling

papers.title: Attention alters population spatial frequency tuning
papers.abstract: Using voxel-wise population spatial frequency tuning (pSFT) and fMRI, this study investigated how feature-based attention reconfigures the fundamental spatial response properties of neural populations in the early visual cortex (V1–V3). Participants were cued to attend to one of two competing letter streams defined by distinct spatial frequencies. To isolate the global spatial spread of feature-based attention, tuning changes were measured in a task-irrelevant hemifield. The findings reveal that attention induces significant 'attractive shifts' in population SF preferences toward the task-relevant frequency. This evidence suggests that voluntary attention dynamically reconfigures the tuning profiles of visuocortical populations to prioritize task-relevant spatial details across the entire visual field.
papers.authors: Luis D. Ramirez, Feiyi Wang, Sam Ling

papers.title: Heterogeneous effects of cognitive arousal on the contrast response in human visual cortex
papers.abstract: While arousal is known to modulate visual processing in animal models, its effect on human visuocortical responses remains poorly defined. This study utilized fMRI to measure contrast response functions (CRFs) in early visual areas (V1–V3) while participants' cognitive arousal was manipulated via easy versus difficult auditory arithmetic tasks. Although group-level analysis showed minimal overall modulation, subject-level analysis revealed robust and stable individual differences: some participants exhibited enhanced neural gain with increased arousal, while others showed suppressive effects or no change. These heterogeneous BOLD modulations were significantly correlated with arousal-induced changes in pupil size, suggesting that individuals may occupy different regimes of a non-monotonic, non-linear relationship between cognitive arousal and sensory gain.
papers.authors: Jasmine Pan, Louis N. Vinke, Joseph T. McGuire, Sam Ling

0588.name: Sami R. Yousif
0588.institution: University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill
0588.bio: Sami R. Yousif is an Assistant Professor at The Ohio State University and the director of the Spatial Cognition Lab, having previously served on the faculty at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. Yousif's research investigates the format of mental representations, specifically how the mind encodes visuospatial relations using polar coordinate systems and heuristics such as the 'additive-area' rule. By analyzing systematic errors in visual matching and estimation tasks, Yousif explores the latent structure of spatial thought and its development from childhood to adulthood. They earned a PhD in cognitive psychology from Yale University and completed postdoctoral training as a MindCORE Fellow at the University of Pennsylvania.
0588.research_direction: Dr. Yousif has recently been investigating the boundaries between visual perception, memory, and higher-level cognition using behavioral psychophysics. A major focus of their recent work explores the theoretical limits of sensory adaptation, systematically testing whether repulsive aftereffects serve as a reliable litmus test for perceptual representation by probing adaptation to imperceptible cognitive dimensions like monetary value and visual ensemble statistics like average size. In the domain of numerical cognition, they are examining the relativistic nature of number perception, testing how spatial context and item density systematically distort the visual system's quantity estimates through phenomena like the "crowd size illusion." Additionally, they are investigating temporal and mnemonic distortions, exploring how the structural repetition of visual items—and the resulting changes in memory strength—alters subjective estimates of temporal recency.

papers.title: Can we “see” value? Spatiotopic “visual” adaptation to an imperceptible dimension
papers.abstract: The current investigation challenges the traditional view that repulsive adaptation aftereffects serve as a definitive litmus test for perceptual representation. In a series of four psychophysical experiments, the researchers demonstrate that adaptation can be induced for an explicitly non-perceptual dimension: arbitrarily assigned monetary value. The study shows that this adaptation is spatiotopic (spatially indexed) and generalizes across stimulus formats, from Arabic numerals to coin displays. These findings suggest that either repulsive adaptation can occur for imperceptible cognitive dimensions or that adaptation aftereffects fail to reliably demarcate the joint between perception and post-perceptual thought, necessitating a re-evaluation of adaptation as a criterion for perceptual content.
papers.authors: Sam Clarke, Sami R. Yousif

papers.title: An Illusion of Time Caused by Repeated Experience
papers.abstract: This research identifies a novel temporal distortion termed the 'temporal repetition effect,' which contradicts the widely held heuristic that memory strength or vividness correlates with temporal recency. Across six experiments using an online research platform, participants viewed sequences of object images where certain targets were repeated. Although repetition significantly enhanced recognition memory and vividness, participants systematically remembered the initial presentation of repeated items as having occurred significantly further back in time than non-repeated items encountered at the same point. This robust illusion, which persisted even over a week-long delay, indicates that the internal representation of time is predictably distorted by the mnemonic structure of experience.
papers.authors: Brynn E. Sherman, Sami R. Yousif

papers.title: The “crowd size illusion” and the relativity of number perception
papers.abstract: The study introduces the 'crowd size illusion' to examine the relativistic nature of human number estimation. While dominant models of numerical cognition typically focus on the intrinsic properties of the set being enumerated, this research demonstrates that perceived number is heavily modulated by spatial context. Specifically, the presence of empty cells in a sparse grid leads to significant underestimation of the number of items, while full crowds result in overestimation. These bidirectional effects suggest that the visual system does not extract discrete quantity in an absolute manner but represents number proportionally and relativistically relative to the spatial structure or density of the surrounding environment.
papers.authors: Gabriel C. L. Waterhouse, Sami R. Yousif

papers.title: Ensemble size perception as a case study of the bounds of adaptation
papers.abstract: This paper investigates the purported ubiquity of repulsive adaptation aftereffects across all perceptually encoded dimensions. Using ensemble size (average vs. cumulative size) as a case study, the authors conducted four experiments to determine if observers adapt to the average size of dot arrays. Despite evidence from prior literature that average size is a perceptually represented feature, the current study found no evidence of adaptation to this dimension.
