The results suggest that adaptation is not a universal property of all perceptual representations, placing critical bounds on the adaptation enterprise and challenging theories that treat adaptation as an inevitable consequence of perceptual encoding.
papers.authors: Sam Clarke, Rachel Olugbusi, Sami R. Yousif

0589.name: Samuel McDougle
0589.bio: Samuel McDougle is an Assistant Professor at Yale University and directs the Action, Computation, and Thinking (ACT) Lab. McDougle's research investigates the cognitive and neural architectures of human learning, focusing on the intersection of high-level cognition and motor behavior. Using an approach that includes psychophysics, computational modeling, and fMRI, McDougle explores how the brain integrates explicit strategies with implicit adaptation to acquire motor skills and maintain behavioral control.
0589.research_direction: Dr. McDougle's recent work explores the intersection of cognitive representations, sensory feedback, and motor learning to understand how humans plan and adapt movements. Specifically, they have been investigating how visuomotor adaptation and goal-directed reaching are shaped by distinct formats of motor working memory, latent "mental graphs" that organize action selection, and the decoupling of visually perceived versus physical distance. Broadening beyond traditional motor execution, their research also examines the cognitive dynamics of reinforcement learning. Using fMRI and behavioral paradigms, they are studying how transient reward feedback automatically influences sustained attention, as well as mapping the human cerebellum's role in processing temporally sensitive reward prediction errors during non-motor tasks.

papers.title: Linking motor working memory to explicit and implicit motor learning
papers.abstract: This correlational study investigated the distinct contributions of motor working memory (MWM) representational formats to long-term visuomotor adaptation. By decomposing MWM into effector-independent (abstract) and effector-specific (limb-bound) codes, the researchers examined how these short-term information stores relate to explicit strategies and implicit sensorimotor learning. Findings revealed that individual differences in the fidelity of effector-independent MWM selectively predicted the degree of explicit visuomotor learning. Conversely, the fidelity of inferred effector-specific MWM was selectively correlated with the magnitude of implicit adaptation driven by sensory prediction errors. These results demonstrate that separate formats of motor information maintained in working memory serve as specialized precursors for distinct long-term motor learning systems, highlighting a novel cognitive-motor interface.
papers.authors: Hanna Hillman, Taylor N. McClure, Samuel D. McDougle

papers.title: The human cerebellum encodes temporally sensitive reinforcement learning signals
papers.abstract: While the cerebellum is traditionally associated with supervised motor learning, its role in non-motor reinforcement learning (RL) is increasingly recognized in animal models. This fMRI study isolated cerebellar RL signals in humans using an instrumental task lacking sensorimotor contingencies. Robust reward prediction errors (RPEs) and reward-processing signals were localized to cognitive regions of the cerebellar cortex, specifically Crus I and II, independent of oculomotor or physiological confounds. Crucially, these cerebellar signals exhibited high temporal sensitivity, becoming undetectable when reward feedback was delayed by more than one second—a constraint not mirrored in the ventral striatum or hippocampus. Connectivity analysis showed coactivation between these cerebellar regions and a prefrontal-striatal circuit (mPFC, lPFC, and caudate) during feedback, delineating a temporally constrained cerebellar contribution to cognitive reward processing.
papers.authors: Juliana E. Trach, Yiran Ou, Samuel D. McDougle

papers.title: Mental graphs structure the storage and retrieval of visuomotor associations
papers.abstract: This study explored how latent cognitive graphs structure motor representations and influence action selection in hierarchical visuomotor mapping. Participants learned mappings that either possessed or lacked an imposed structure linking stimulus features (e.g., color or shape) to intuitive motor partitions (e.g., hands and finger pairs). Analysis of transitional response times (RTs) provided evidence that retrieving motor responses from memory involved the systematic traversal of a structured mental graph. Forced-response paradigms corroborated these graph-like computations within individual trials, and these structured representations were found to persist even after extensive practice. The findings suggest that internal computations over structured memory topologies directly shape the preparation and execution of movements, extending the role of cognitive maps from abstract knowledge into the domain of motor control.
papers.authors: Juliana E. Trach, Samuel D. McDougle

papers.title: Rewards transiently and automatically enhance sustained attention
papers.abstract: Sustained attention naturally fluctuates between vigilant and lapsed states, but the automatic impact of reward on these fluctuations remains debated. Utilizing a hybrid paradigm that integrated a continuous performance attention task with a reinforcement learning (RL) task, the authors examined how reward feedback, decoupled from attentional performance, affects vigilance. Across three experiments (N=296), intermittent, attention-independent rewards were found to transiently boost vigilance on a sub-minute timescale, effectively buffering against attentional lapses. This enhancement was consistent even when rewards were passively received, whereas prediction error surprise did not reliably modulate attention. These results indicate a fundamental, automatic relationship where reward feedback enhances sustained attention through generic arousal or motivational pathways rather than task-specific incentives.
papers.authors: Juliana E. Trach, Megan T. deBettencourt, Angela Radulescu, Samuel D. McDougle

papers.title: Independent influences of movement distance and visual distance on Fitts' Law
papers.abstract: Fitts' Law formalizes the speed-accuracy tradeoff in goal-directed reaching as a function of movement distance (D). However, D typically confounds physical displacement with visually perceived distance. In this study, the authors decoupled these variables using a visuomotor gain adaptation paradigm to determine their independent influences on movement time (MT). Results demonstrated that both the physical distance of the effector and the visually perceived distance to the target independently contribute to MT, supporting a bivariate formulation of Fitts' Law. The relative weighting of these distance cues was context-dependent, shifting based on movement range restrictions and the fidelity of visual feedback. These findings suggest that early-stage motor planning integrates multi-modal sensory context to determine the temporal constraints of movement.
papers.authors: Naser Al-Fawakhiri, Samuel D. McDougle

0590.name: Sang Chul Chong
0590.lab_name: Vision, Cognition, and Consciousness Lab (VCC Lab)
0590.bio: Sang Chul Chong is a vision scientist at Yonsei University who investigates how the human brain processes complex visual scenes through ensemble perception and statistical representation. Chong’s research explores the intersection of focused attention and visual consciousness, utilizing binocular rivalry and psychophysical paradigms to examine how the visual system manages processing capacity. Methodologically, their work employs eye tracking, ERP, and computational modeling to study the metacognition of perceptual resolution and social perception. Chong completed doctoral studies under Anne Treisman at Princeton University and postdoctoral training with Randolph Blake at Vanderbilt University.
0590.research_direction: Dr. Chong has recently been investigating the dynamic interplay between attention, metacognition, and ensemble perception. Their recent work explores the boundaries of sustained attention and statistical learning, probing phenomena such as inattentional blindness to peripheral display transients and the impact of spatial organization and attentional scope on contextual cueing in visual search. They are also focused on the mechanisms of visual metacognition, examining whether confidence judgments track internal attentional states or the resulting sensory representations, while additionally testing how accurately anxious individuals monitor their own attentional capture by threatening faces. Furthermore, utilizing ensemble perception paradigms, Dr. Chong investigates social vision to understand how top-down expectations and prior beliefs about social likelihood systematically bias the perceptual estimation of demographic crowds.

papers.title: Effect of multi-refresh-rate method on user experience: sustained attention and inattentional blindness
papers.abstract: This study analyzed the perceptual and cognitive impact of a multi-refresh-rate display strategy on user performance and subjective experience. Utilizing a sustained attention paradigm, the researchers examined whether observers detected significant reductions in refresh rates within task-irrelevant peripheral regions. Experimental results indicated a high prevalence of inattentional blindness, as the majority of participants failed to notice peripheral temporal changes while centrally focused on the primary task. Furthermore, variable refresh-rate (VRR) configurations did not compromise sustained attention or task accuracy. Detection of peripheral shifts improved only under conditions of explicit task-relevance or top-down expectations, suggesting that centrally allocated attentional resources effectively gate the awareness of peripheral display transients to optimize energy consumption without degrading user experience.
papers.authors: Jieun Cho, Jeunghwan Choi, Cheongil Kim, Ji-Hye Park, Sang Chul Chong

papers.title: How location-based organization affects the extent of contextual cueing
papers.abstract: This research investigated how location-based spatial organization and attentional scope modulate the magnitude of contextual cueing in visual search. Across three experiments, the spatial distribution of distractors and the number of items processed simultaneously (attentional scope) were manipulated. The results demonstrated that the learning of spatial contexts and the subsequent facilitation of target localization are highly dependent on the organizational structure of the search display. Specifically, broader attentional windows facilitated more robust contextual cueing effects, suggesting that the visual system prioritizes global spatial regularities for statistical learning when attentional resources are distributed across a sufficient number of group members. These findings indicate that the spatial arrangement of elements and the observer's attentional breadth are critical determinants of contextual learning efficiency.
papers.authors: An Zheng, Sang Chul Chong

papers.title: When seeing follows believing: The role of social likelihood in demographic estimation
papers.abstract: This study explored how prior social expectations and internal models of social likelihood bias the perception and statistical representation of demographic crowds. Using ensemble perception tasks, the researchers investigated whether the presence of minority group members is systematically overestimated due to their perceptual salience and lower social likelihood. The findings revealed a robust bias toward overestimating minority proportions, a phenomenon designated as the 'illusion of diversity.' This effect is attributed to the enhanced encoding of unexpected social information and the prioritization of rare demographic features in visual awareness and memory. The study suggests that top-down social expectations can significantly distort the perceived demographic composition of an environment, potentially influencing social judgments and policy support.
papers.authors: Yoonseo Heo, Sang Chul Chong

papers.title: Product, not process: Metacognitive monitoring of visual performance during sustained attention
papers.abstract: This investigation probed the informational cues underlying metacognitive monitoring (confidence) of fluctuations in visual performance during task-induced lapses of sustained attention. By analyzing the relationship between subjective confidence judgments and objective performance metrics, the study tested whether metacognition tracks the neurocognitive states of the visual system (the 'process') or the resulting sensory quality of the target representation (the 'product'). Data from two experiments (N=40) revealed that metacognitive judgments were primarily driven by the clarity and strength of the perceived target rather than introspective access to internal attentional fluctuations or system stability. This suggests a product-based mechanism for visual metacognition, where confidence tracks the output of visual processing as a proxy for performance monitoring.
papers.authors: Cheongil Kim, Sang Chul Chong

papers.title: Metacognitive monitoring of attentional bias toward threat in anxiety
papers.abstract: This paper evaluated the accuracy of metacognitive monitoring regarding threat-related attentional capture and its relationship with trait anxiety. The researchers utilized a novel paradigm integrating average facial expression judgments with subjective estimations of attentional allocation toward angry versus neutral faces. Results confirmed a positive correlation between anxiety levels and the magnitude of objective attentional bias toward threat. Crucially, while high-anxiety individuals maintained an intact ability to monitor trial-by-trial fluctuations in attentional bias, they consistently underestimated their overall degree of bias. This specific deficit in global metacognitive calibration suggests that anxious individuals may fail to recognize the extent of their attentional capture by threat, potentially hindering the recruitment of necessary attentional control mechanisms for emotion regulation.
papers.authors: Cheongil Kim, Juyoen Hur, Jeong Hyeon Park, Sang Chul Chong

0591.name: Sang Wook Hong
0591.bio: Sang Wook Hong is a researcher at Florida Atlantic University's Stiles-Nicholson Brain Institute who examines the neural mechanisms underlying human visual perception and awareness. Using psychophysics and functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), Hong investigates how the brain constructs internal representations of color, motion, and facial expressions from sensory inputs. Their research utilizes binocular rivalry and continuous flash suppression to explore the limits of visual awareness and the interaction between top-down knowledge and bottom-up sensory processing. Hong’s work also includes the study of individual differences in interocular grouping and the influence of visual working memory on perceptual experiences.
0591.research_direction: Dr. Hong has recently been investigating the mechanisms underlying visual integration, motion processing, and memory across multiple levels of the visual hierarchy. Their recent work explores how the visual system groups fragmented information into coherent percepts, using transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) to probe the causal role of gamma oscillations in contour integration, and leveraging individual differences in binocular rivalry to untangle the mechanisms driving interocular grouping. In the domain of motion perception, they are utilizing fMRI with cross-stimulus multivariate pattern analysis to examine how dorsal stream areas like V3A and MT+ abstract global motion trajectories from low-level spatial forms. Additionally, Dr. Hong is investigating the functional overlap between active visual perception and short-term memory, employing psychophysical methods to understand whether the maintenance of visual features in the absence of retinal input relies on the reactivation of sensory-specific cortical areas.

papers.title: Gamma frequency transcranial alternating current stimulation over the visual cortex modulates contour integration
papers.abstract: The human visual system relies on contour integration to link spatially fragmented orientation signals into coherent object boundaries. Although neural oscillations in the gamma band have been correlated with perceptual grouping and feature binding, establishing their causal contribution to contour integration has remained elusive. In this study, healthy adult observers performed a four-element collinear Gabor detection task within a field of pseudo-randomly oriented and positioned distractor elements. Participants were allocated to 40-Hz gamma-band transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS), 7-Hz theta-band tACS (active control), or sham stimulation applied over early visual cortex across pre-stimulation baseline and active stimulation sessions. Linear mixed-effects modeling revealed a significant session-by-group interaction, demonstrating that 40-Hz gamma stimulation selectively enhanced contour detection performance relative to baseline, whereas neither theta-frequency nor sham stimulation induced reliable perceptual gains. These findings provide direct causal evidence that entraining occipital gamma oscillations facilitates the integration of spatially distributed local visual inputs into continuous perceptual contours.
papers.authors: Yosun Yoon, Sang Wook Hong

papers.title: Emergence of form-independent direction selectivity in human V3A and MT+
papers.abstract: A key challenge in visual motion perception is that translating objects produce heterogeneous local velocity vectors across an aperture, requiring the visual hierarchy to pool disparate motion signals into form-invariant representations of global trajectory. Using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) at 3T and multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA), blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) responses were recorded across visual areas V1 through V4, V3A, and MT+ while observers viewed drifting sinusoidal gratings and limited-lifetime random-dot motion arrays across linear and spiral paths. Within-stimulus classification confirmed robust direction decoding across all examined retinotopic cortical areas. However, cross-stimulus classification—training classifiers on one visual format and decoding direction in the other—demonstrated marked hierarchical divergence: early visual areas (V1–V3) failed to generalize, with V1 exhibiting sub-chance classification caused by motion streaks generated by drifting random dots that mimicked orthogonal gratings. In contrast, higher-order dorsal stream areas MT+ and V3A demonstrated significant cross-stimulus generalization across both linear and spiral trajectories, demonstrating that direction selectivity becomes abstracted from low-level spatial carrier form as signals ascend the human dorsal visual pathway.
papers.authors: Sang Wook Hong, Frank Tong

papers.title: The role of pattern coherence in interocular grouping during binocular rivalry: Insights from individual differences
papers.abstract: Interocular grouping during binocular rivalry occurs when complementary image components presented separately to each eye are bound into a singular, coherent percept. The extent to which this binding is driven by monocular lateral interactions preserving eye-of-origin information or by feedback-mediated global pattern coherence from higher cortical areas remains unresolved. To adjudicate between these mechanisms, an individual differences psychophysical design was employed to assess the temporal distribution of rivalry states under conventional rivalrous dichoptic stimulation versus interocularly coherent configurations (such as interleaved concentric rings and radial gratings). Observers exhibiting longer cumulative durations of interocularly grouped coherent percepts also demonstrated prolonged dominance of monocularly coherent images; conversely, observers susceptible to protracted piecemeal or mixed percepts in classic rivalry displayed proportionally longer durations of non-coherent percepts under interocular conditions. This reliable covariance across individuals indicates that global pattern coherence mechanisms predominate over eye-of-origin lateral connectivity in governing interocular grouping dynamics during binocular competition.
papers.authors: Yosun Yoon, Sang Wook Hong

papers.title: Shared mechanisms between short-term memory and perception: a case study
papers.abstract: This research investigates the functional and neural overlap between the maintenance of visual information in short-term memory and its active perception. Utilizing a case-study framework combined with psychophysical probes, the paper examines whether the neural substrates typically associated with the high-fidelity representation of visual features (such as color and form) are recruited identically during both the online perception of a stimulus and the subsequent short-term maintenance of that stimulus in the absence of retinal input. The results provide evidence for shared mechanisms, suggesting that memory representations may be sustained through the re-activation of sensory-specific cortical areas, effectively blurring the distinction between perceptual encoding and mnemonic storage.
papers.authors: Steven K. Shevell, Rebecca St. Clair, Sang Wook Hong

0592.name: Sang-Hun Lee
0592.department: Department of Brain and Cognitive Sciences
0592.bio: Lee is a Professor at Seoul National University who researches the neural mechanisms underlying human visual perception and decision-making. Lee specializes in the spatiotemporal dynamics of the visual cortex, utilizing psychophysics, functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), and computational modeling to study phenomena such as binocular rivalry and traveling waves of cortical activity. Their work explores the attractor dynamics of working memory and Bayesian accounts of belief updating, focusing on how the brain forms decision variables and how prior choices influence future perceptual estimates. Lee previously served as the chair of the Department of Brain and Cognitive Sciences and participated in the World Class University (WCU) initiative at SNU.
0592.research_direction: Dr. Lee has recently been investigating the computational and neural mechanisms that drive systematic biases in visual working memory and perceptual decision-making. Using human psychophysics, fMRI, Bayesian modeling, and recurrent neural networks, their recent work explores how categorical decisions actively warp the memory representations of visual stimuli through drift dynamics directed at discrete attractors. They are also examining how committing to a choice updates probabilistic beliefs within an abstract decision-variable space, testing how the granularity of these past decisions alters the trajectory of subsequent perceptual judgments. Alongside these temporal memory dynamics, Dr. Lee is investigating spatial vision, specifically asking how individual differences in the topographic maps of human early visual cortex contribute to perceptual anisotropies when observers estimate an object's spatial extent.

papers.title: Attractor dynamics of working memory explain a concurrent evolution of stimulus-specific and decision-consistent biases in visual estimation
papers.abstract: While humans rely on working memory (WM) to sustain sensory information for estimation, their performance is systematically biased toward a subset of stimuli (stimulus-specific bias) and toward their own prior categorical choices (decision-consistent bias). This study identifies drift dynamics directed at discrete attractors as the unifying neural mechanism for these estimation shifts. Utilizing human psychophysical data, fMRI recordings, and task-optimized recurrent neural networks (RNNs), the authors demonstrate that categorical decisions actively steer memory trajectories. This decision-driven modulation of the attractor landscape explains how stimulus-specific drift and decision-consistent attraction co-evolve during memory maintenance, warping representations in a manner consistent with observers' internal beliefs.
papers.authors: Hyunwoo Gu, Joonwon Lee, Sungje Kim, Jaeseob Lim, Hyang-Jung Lee, Heeseung Lee, Min Jin Choe, Dong-Gyu Yoo, Jun Hwan Joshua Ryu, Sukbin Lim, Sang-Hun Lee

papers.title: Belief updating in decision-variable space: More fine-grained choices attract future ones more strongly
papers.abstract: Perceptual decision-making involves the construction of abstract decision variables (DVs) that integrate sensory evidence with internal priors. The authors propose that committing to a decision triggers a Bayesian belief update within this DV space, where the choice restricts the probabilistic distribution of the DV to align with the selected category. This mechanism predicts a "granularity effect": decisions made with higher precision (finer granularity) exert a more robust attractive pull on subsequent trials. Through seven psychophysical experiments and Bayesian modeling, the study confirms that this attraction occurs in a modality-independent DV space, demonstrating how the human brain leverages the abstract nature of decisions to adapt to temporal regularities in the environment.
papers.authors: Heeseung Lee, Jaeseob Lim, Sang-Hun Lee

papers.title: Evidence for belief updating in decision-variable space: past decisions with finer granularity attract future ones more strongly
papers.abstract: This study investigates how the creation of mental spaces for decision variables (DVs) facilitates adaptive behavior by integrating cumulative knowledge with new sensory information. The researchers hypothesize that decision commitment granularizes the internal belief distribution by restricting it to states corresponding to the committed choice. They evaluate this through psychophysical paradigms and a unified Bayesian model, establishing that the resulting choice-attraction bias is modulated by the precision of previous categorical decisions. The findings highlight the role of abstract DV representations, which are distinct from sensory and motor spaces, in supporting flexible probabilistic inference across trials.
papers.authors: Heeseung Lee, Jaeseob Lim, Sang-Hun Lee

papers.title: Bounded contribution of human early visual cortex to the topographic anisotropy in spatial extent perception
papers.abstract: The accurate estimation of an object's spatial extent—the enclosed region it occupies—is vital for environmental interaction, yet the role of topographic representations in the early visual cortex (EVC) remains debated. This investigation examines individual differences in topographic anisotropy within human V1, V2, and V3 compared to perceptual reports. Results indicate a significant mismatch in bias direction: EVC anisotropy is primarily determined by stimulus radiality, whereas perceptual bias is driven by co-axiality (orientation). Despite this divergence, a substantial portion of the individual variance in radial and co-axial anisotropy is shared between EVC activity and behavior, suggesting that while perception relies on EVC spatial maps, an additional cortical mechanism is required to transform these topographic biases into stable perceptual estimates.
papers.authors: Juhyoung Ryu, Sang-Hun Lee

0594.name: Sarah Lamer
0594.bio: Sarah Lamer is an Associate Professor in the Department of Psychology at the University of Tennessee, Knoxville, and the director of the Social Perception and Cognition (SPĀC) Lab. Lamer’s research focuses on how sociocultural and environmental cues, such as spatial positioning and televised nonverbal patterns, facilitate the transmission of gender and racial stereotypes. Utilizing psychophysics, eye-tracking, and diffusion modeling, they investigate the social-cognitive mechanisms that lead to group-based biases and perceptual distortions. Lamer’s work, supported by the National Science Foundation, examines the 'angry crowd bias' and the developmental precursors of social inequality.
0594.research_direction: Dr. Lamer has recently been investigating how subtle statistical regularities in our cultural environments shape high-level social cognition and intergroup bias. Their recent work explores this through a "Cultural Snapshots" framework, quantifying naturally occurring cues in mass media—such as the spatial elevation of social groups or patterns of nonverbal behavior—and translating them into controlled experimental stimuli to test their causal impact on attitude formation. They have also applied this approach to linguistic framing, examining how assigning grammatical agency to sexual assault survivors versus perpetrators in news coverage influences moral judgments and victim-blaming. Additionally, Dr. Lamer has been studying the perceptual mechanisms underlying social evaluation, specifically investigating how the visual system utilizes ensemble coding to rapidly extract summary statistics from natural crowds to infer higher-order properties like group cohesion and unity.

papers.title: Survivors as Agents: How Linguistic Agency Impacts Support for Survivors and Perpetrators of Sexual Assault
papers.abstract: Contemporary news media increasingly employs supportive language toward women reporting sexual assault; however, psychological theories of morality indicate that assigning high agency to survivors relative to perpetrators may elicit unintended victim-blaming effects. We examined whether agentic framing asymmetries are culturally pervasive and functionally alter public blame attributions. Content analysis of 1,738 sentences drawn from 494 ideologically diverse news articles revealed a systematic linguistic pattern in liberal sources, wherein survivors were framed with greater grammatical and thematic agency than perpetrators. In a subsequent experiment with college participants (N = 1,238) exposed to manipulated news sentences where either the survivor or perpetrator was portrayed agentically, male participants exposed to survivor-agentic language attributed significantly less blame to the perpetrators than those exposed to perpetrator-agentic language. These findings demonstrate that conferring grammatical agency on survivors can inadvertently diminish perpetrator accountability and foster victim-blame.
papers.authors: Darla Bonagura, Jenae Bluhm, Clara Bunnell, Wen Lou, Sarah Ariel Lamer

papers.title: Ensemble perception in entitativity judgments of natural crowds
papers.abstract: Observers routinely extract visual summary statistics from groups of individuals, yet the computational connection between ensemble coding mechanisms and high-level social assessments of entitativity remains incompletely understood in unconstrained visual contexts. Across experiments using ecologically representative images of real-world crowds, we investigated whether the visual system capitalizes on ensemble coding to infer social group cohesion, coordination, and unity. Rather than relying on serial inspection of discrete faces or individual postures, perceivers rapidly synthesized distributed social signals into visual ensemble representations, which directly predicted perceived group entitativity. The results show that visual ensemble perception operates as a foundational mechanism for making rapid, macroscopic inferences about group agency and social cohesion.
papers.authors: Sarah Ariel Lamer, Spencer Dobbs, Lindsay Goolsby, Timothy D. Sweeny, Max Weisbuch

papers.title: Cultural snapshots: A method to explain cultural transmission of bias
papers.abstract: Elucidating the pathways through which social biases and stereotypes proliferate requires connecting macro-level cultural ecologies with micro-level cognitive mechanisms. We outline the conceptual architecture and empirical application of the Cultural Snapshots methodology for investigating the cultural transmission of bias. This approach integrates the systematic sampling and quantitative coding of naturally occurring covariations of nonverbal, spatial, and linguistic cues within widespread cultural media (such as television programming and print materials) with tightly controlled behavioral paradigms. We demonstrate how isolating and manipulating these ecologically valid cue regularities allows researchers to causally test how ambient cultural environments generate and reinforce implicit and explicit intergroup biases across development.
papers.authors: Kristin Pauker, Max Weisbuch, Sarah Ariel Lamer

papers.title: Social transmission of bias
papers.abstract: The authors propose and refine the 'Cultural Snapshots' framework to elucidate how social biases are transmitted through culturally pervasive environmental patterns. This review synthesizes research showing that collective social norms and individual implicit attitudes are often founded on subtle, frequently encountered cues in public social ecologies—such as the vertical spatial elevation of social groups or televised patterns of nonverbal emotion. By shifting focus from individual-level experiences to the systematic quantification of public representations, the authors demonstrate how these cultural regularities provide a continuous and often invisible route for the socialization of intergroup bias. The paper provides a comprehensive guide for researchers to identify, quantify, and experimentally manipulate ecologically valid stimuli to establish causal links between social environments and cognitive outcomes.
papers.authors: Kristin Pauker, Max Weisbuch, Sarah Ariel Lamer

papers.title: Tracing Pathways From Social Ecology to the Mind: A Cultural Snapshots Approach to Understanding Gender Stereotype Socialization
papers.abstract: The everyday social ecologies people encounter are saturated with covarying contextual cues and descriptive patterns that embody gender distinctions. Nevertheless, standard methodological paradigms evaluating how public representations of gender shape societal attitudes frequently preclude causal inference. We detail how the Cultural Snapshots framework provides an ecologically valid methodology to delineate the causal transmission of gender stereotypes. By first quantifying real-world statistical regularities across cultural materials (such as nonverbal behaviors, spatial positioning, or role allocations) and subsequently translating those regularities into controlled experimental stimuli, researchers can rigorously test how ambient ecological patterns shape social cognition. We present a procedural framework for implementing this methodology and review critical considerations for investigating gender role socialization across developmental trajectories.
papers.authors: Sarah Ariel Lamer, Gillian Michelle Preston, Darla Bonagura, Megan Ruskey

0595.name: Sarah Shomstein
0595.department: Department of Psychological and Brain Sciences
0595.bio: Sarah Shomstein is the Thelma Hunt Professor and Chair of the Department of Psychological and Brain Sciences at The George Washington University. Shomstein's research explores the functional and neural mechanisms of attentional selection, specifically investigating how the human brain prioritizes information based on spatial and object-level representations. By integrating behavioral psychophysics, eye tracking, and functional neuroimaging (fMRI), their work identifies the computational signals that modulate sensory processing in both healthy individuals and patients with focal brain damage. Shomstein currently serves as the Editor-in-Chief of the journal Attention, Perception & Psychophysics.
0595.research_direction: Dr. Shomstein has recently been investigating how high-level semantic knowledge automatically guides attentional allocation, even when that information is strictly task-irrelevant. Their recent work explores how the visual priority map is shaped by complex contextual relationships, using behavioral measures of search efficiency to probe semantic grouping among objects and the congruency between local targets and global scenes. Furthermore, they are extending traditional visual search paradigms into multisensory domains, examining how visual attention is continuously influenced by crossmodal cues, such as the degree of audiovisual semantic relatedness. In a distinct but related line of inquiry, they are also testing the underlying mechanisms of holistic processing, manipulating the statistical probability of stimulus congruency to determine whether phenomena like the face-composite effect reflect fixed perceptual templates or dynamically learned attentional strategies.

papers.title: Task-irrelevant semantic grouping influences attentional allocation
papers.abstract: This study examines the mechanism by which task-irrelevant high-level object semantics modulate attentional prioritization, specifically testing if this bias is mediated by perceptual grouping. Across experiments using color-defined low-level groups and semantically defined high-level groups (grayscale and color objects), the researchers observed that while traditional low-level grouping is limited by set size constraints, high-level semantic relatedness provides a significant search efficiency advantage for larger groups in complex color displays. These findings suggest that semantic meaning serves as a robust mid-level factor in the attentional priority map, influencing selection independently of low-level feature grouping.
papers.authors: Ellie R. Robbins, Joseph C. Nah, Dick Dubbelde, Sarah Shomstein

papers.title: Task-irrelevant semantic relationship between objects and scene influence attentional allocation
papers.abstract: The research investigates the extent to which task-irrelevant semantic associations between global scene contexts and local objects continuously influence attentional allocation. Using behavioral measures of processing efficiency, the authors demonstrate that semantic congruency between a scene and its constituent objects biases the distribution of attention even when semantic information is not requisite for the task. The strength of this attentional guidance was found to be directly predicted by the subjective magnitude of semantic relatedness, indicating that high-level contextual knowledge automatically and pervasively modulates the attentional priority map.
papers.authors: Joseph C. Nah, George L. Malcolm, Sarah Shomstein

papers.title: Predicting attentional allocation in real-world environments: The need to investigate crossmodal semantic guidance
papers.abstract: This perspective piece highlights a critical gap in attentional research, which has predominantly focused on unisensory (primarily visual) mechanisms. The authors integrate findings from spatial, feature, and object-based attention with emerging work on semantic guidance to argue that real-world attentional allocation is inherently multisensory. They propose a framework for crossmodal semantic guidance, where semantic meaning extracted from auditory or other sensory inputs dynamically interacts with visual representations to prioritize information in complex, naturalistic environments.
papers.authors: Kira Wegner-Clemens, George L. Malcolm, Sarah Shomstein

papers.title: Holistic processing is modulated by the probability that parts contain task-congruent information
papers.abstract: The authors investigate the nature of holistic processing (e.g., the face-composite effect) by testing whether it arises from fixed internal templates or dynamic attentional strategies shaped by context. By manipulating the statistical probability that task-irrelevant parts of a stimulus contain congruent or incongruent information, they found that holistic processing effects are significantly modulated by experienced congruency probabilities. These results favor an attentional account of holistic processing, suggesting that it is a learned strategy for prioritized information processing rather than a purely bottom-up perceptual mechanism.
papers.authors: Kim M. Curby, Lina Teichmann, Mary A. Peterson, Sarah Shomstein

papers.title: Search efficiency scales with audiovisual semantic relatedness in a continuous manner
papers.abstract: This study explores the continuous nature of semantic influence in crossmodal attention by varying the degree of relatedness between task-irrelevant sounds and visual target images. The researchers found that search efficiency—specifically reaction times in a visual search task—scales monotonically with the strength of audiovisual semantic relatedness. This finding indicates that semantic knowledge does not just influence attention in a binary fashion but provides a graded signal that guides attentional selection across sensory modalities, suggesting a robust cognitive mechanism for crossmodal semantic integration.
papers.authors: Kira Wegner-Clemens, George L. Malcolm, Sarah Shomstein

0596.name: Sarah Waugh
0596.department: Department of Optometry and Vision Sciences
0596.lab_name: Centre for Vision across the Life Span (CVLS)
0596.bio: Waugh is a Reader in Optometry and Vision Sciences and Co-Director of the Centre for Vision across the Life Span at the University of Huddersfield. They utilize psychophysical methodologies to investigate spatial vision and visual processing, focusing on visual crowding, Vernier acuity, and the mechanisms underlying amblyopia. Waugh’s research indicates that foveal crowding distance is a more effective predictor of reading ability in children than traditional visual acuity. They have also conducted research into the temporal frequency discrimination of central and peripheral vision and the clinical assessment of binocular vision and accommodation.
0596.research_direction: Dr. Waugh has recently been investigating applied color vision, focusing on how congenital color vision deficiency and optical degradations impact performance in occupational and clinical contexts. Their recent work explores the real-world consequences of red-green deficiencies, specifically assessing how they affect the diagnostic accuracy of optometrists identifying retinal lesions in fundus photographs. Additionally, they are conducting psychophysical experiments with tools like the Farnsworth-Munsell 100-Hue test and computerized discrimination tasks to determine whether commercial multi-notch optical filters truly enhance functional color perception for affected individuals. To further establish the reliability of standard occupational screening protocols, their research also examines how induced dioptric blur influences the false-positive rates of various diagnostic assessments, including small-aperture lantern tests and pseudoisochromatic plates.

papers.title: Effect of congenital color vision deficiency on the ability of optometrists to correctly identify lesions in ocular fundus photographs
papers.abstract: This clinical investigation evaluated the diagnostic performance of optometrists with congenital color vision deficiency (CVD) compared to those with normal color vision (CVN) when identifying retinal lesions in digital fundus imagery. Using a sample of 55 practicing clinicians, the study quantified detection accuracy across 12 fundus photographs containing various pathologies. Findings revealed that while older age generally correlated with decreased accuracy, clinicians with CVD, particularly younger ones, demonstrated significantly lower success rates than their CVN counterparts (p = 0.002). Furthermore, the application of EnChroma remediation filters failed to provide statistically significant improvements in lesion identification. The results suggest that X-linked CVD may constitute a professional disability in ophthalmic practice, supporting recommendations for early vocational screening and counseling.
papers.authors: Richard C. Trevino, Anna A. Tichenor, Susan Kovacich, Hin Cheung, Leticia Álvaro, João M. M. Linhares, Monika A. Formankiewicz, Sarah J. Waugh

papers.title: Impact of blur on clinical and occupational colour vision test results
papers.abstract: This study investigated the sensitivity of various clinical and occupational color vision assessments to dioptric blur, focusing on the potential for false-positive results. Using a cohort of color vision normal (CVN) and color vision deficient (CVD) observers, researchers applied varying levels of positive lens blur (up to +8.00 D) while measuring performance on the Ishihara plates, the Fletcher–Evans (CAM) lantern, and computerized tests (CAD and CCT). Results indicated that visual acuity degradation significantly compromised lantern test specificity, with failure occurring at blur levels as low as +1.00 D. In contrast, the Ishihara and computerized discrimination tests remained resilient to blur up to +8.00 D. These findings suggest that small-aperture color tests used in aviation and maritime settings are highly susceptible to refractive errors, necessitating careful control of patient refractive state during occupational screening.
papers.authors: Leticia Álvaro, Monika A. Formankiewicz, Sarah J. Waugh

papers.title: Evaluation of the Efficacy of Enchroma Filters for Correcting Color Vision Impairment
papers.abstract: This psychophysical study assessed whether commercially available multi-notch filters (EnChroma CX-14) effectively enhance chromatic discrimination and naming in individuals with red-green color vision deficiency. Experiments involved both CVN observers wearing simulation filters (Variantor) and CVD participants using compensation filters. Performance was measured via the ColorDx CCT-HD, Farnsworth-Munsell 100-Hue test, and a real-world color-sorting task. While simulation filters accurately mimicked protanopia in normal observers, the compensation filters did not significantly improve error scores or task completion speeds in CVD subjects. Data models suggested that while filters may increase contrast for specific hues, they simultaneously reduce discrimination for others, leading to no net gain in functional color perception. The study concludes that current optical remediation tools do not fully compensate for the underlying cone-opsin deficiencies.
papers.authors: Leticia Álvaro, João M. M. Linhares, Monika A. Formankiewicz, Sarah J. Waugh

0597.name: Sashank Varma
0597.department: School of Interactive Computing and School of Psychology
0597.bio: Sashank Varma is a cognitive scientist who integrates human experimentation with computational modeling to study forms of human intelligence. Varma investigates the cognitive mechanisms underlying mathematical and computational thinking, including the processing of abstract geometric and topological concepts. Their research examines the 'cognitive alignment' between humans and machine learning models, utilizing computer vision and large language models to explore whether AI developmental trajectories mirror human cognitive progression. This work aims to define the neuroarchitecture of perception and reasoning while addressing the educational implications of cognitive learning principles.
0597.research_direction: Dr. Varma has recently been investigating the intersection of artificial intelligence and human cognition, deploying neural networks and behavioral experiments to explore mathematical, spatial, and relational reasoning. A major focus of their recent work explores the developmental origins of mathematical concepts, using computer vision architectures like CNNs to test whether geometric sensitivity and mental number lines can be induced purely from natural visual experience rather than innate cognitive circuitry. In parallel, they are probing Large Language Models to study higher-order cognition, specifically investigating whether these models naturally develop adaptive, resource-rational problem-solving strategies under complexity constraints and how closely they replicate human biases in structural analogical reasoning tasks. Finally, Dr. Varma continues to study human numerical cognition directly, examining the robustness of classical anchoring heuristics during complex mathematical estimation and exploring whether feedback-driven calibration can successfully mitigate these cognitive biases.

papers.title: Are More Tokens Rational? Inference-Time Scaling in Language Models as Adaptive Resource Rationality
papers.abstract: This research investigates whether resource rationality—the optimization of performance under inherent computational constraints—emerges as a general property of inference-time scaling in Large Language Models (LLMs). The study employs a novel Variable Attribution Task (VAT) to systematically manipulate task complexity by varying the number of candidate variables and logical trials (e.g., XOR and XNOR functions). Performance is compared between instruction-tuned (IT) models that utilize chain-of-thought prompting and Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) optimized via reinforcement learning for strategic reasoning path discovery. The findings indicate that both model types demonstrate an emergent transition from brute-force search to human-like analytic strategies as task complexity increases, even in the absence of explicit cost-based rewards, suggesting that test-time computation scaling naturally induces adaptive resource-rational behavior.
papers.authors: Zhimin Hu, Riya Roshan, Sashank Varma

papers.title: Computer Vision Modeling of the Development of Geometric and Numerical Concepts in Humans
papers.abstract: This study evaluates the developmental alignment between computer vision (CV) architectures and the maturation of mathematical cognition in human children. Using the ResNet-50 architecture as a computational case study, the researchers analyze the progression of latent representations for geometric and numerical concepts across ImageNet training checkpoints. The results demonstrate developmental alignment for specific geometric and topological (GT) classes, such as Euclidean geometry and metric properties, where the model's performance improvements track the sensitivity trajectories observed in human children. Additionally, the research identifies the induction of a human-like mental number line (MNL), exhibiting characteristic distance and ratio effects, which suggests that abstract mathematical intuitions can be acquired through learning to categorize complex natural visual environments without specialized innate circuitry.
papers.authors: Zekun Wang, Sashank Varma

papers.title: Modeling Understanding of Story-Based Analogies Using Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Building on the seminal analogical reasoning studies of Gentner and Holyoak, this research provides a fine-grained evaluation of Large Language Model (LLM) alignment with human performance on story-based mapping tasks. The study first assesses the semantic latent space of models by determining whether BERT-based sentence embeddings effectively differentiate between structural analogical targets and surface-similar distractors. Second, the authors evaluate the impact of enhanced two-step generative prompting strategies designed to simulate human-like relational induction. By correlating item-level model accuracy with human data across a benchmark of story analogy problems, the study quantifies the extent to which state-of-the-art architectures (e.g., GPT-4, Llama 3) replicate the cognitive profiles and reasoning biases inherent in human analogical detecting and mapping.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the 47th Annual Meeting of the Cognitive Science Society (CogSci 2025)
papers.authors: Kalit Inani, Keshav Kabra, Vijay Marupudi, Sashank Varma

papers.title: Alignment of CNN and human judgments of geometric and topological concepts
papers.abstract: This study probes the cognitive alignment between deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and human sensitivity to geometric and topological (GT) concepts. Evaluated through a six-image odd-one-out task testing 43 concepts (e.g., topology, Euclidean geometry, symmetry), the performance of five architectures—including ResNet-18 and DenseNet—is compared against behavioral data from children and adults. The investigation assesses whether CNNs can serve as a sufficiency proof for the 'learning account,' which posits that mathematical concepts are induced from visual experience rather than supported by innate 'core knowledge' circuitry. The results show that while CNNs successfully model human sensitivity to classes like Euclidean geometry, they diverge significantly on geometric transformations, with specific architectures like DenseNet aligning most closely with the performance profiles of children aged 3–6 years.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the 39th AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence (AAAI 2025)
papers.authors: Neha Upadhyay, Vijay Marupudi, Kamala Varma, Sashank Varma

papers.title: Estimation of factorial expressions and its improvement through calibration: A replication and extension of Tversky and Kahneman (1973)
papers.abstract: This research replicates and extends the classic psychological study by Tversky and Kahneman (1973) regarding the estimation of factorial products (e.g., 1x2x...x8 vs. 8x7x...x1). The study investigates the robustness of the anchoring and adjustment heuristic by varying the presentation direction of factorial sequences and introducing a feedback-driven calibration phase. Participants provided quantitative estimates of factorial products, and the researchers measured the resulting systematic underestimation and the efficacy of calibration in mitigating these biases. The findings quantify the persistence of anchoring effects in complex numerical judgments and demonstrate that targeted calibration significantly enhances the accuracy and precision of human intuitions for computationally intensive mathematical growth functions.
papers.authors: Jeffrey K. Bye, Vijay Marupudi, Reba Koenen, Jimin Park, Sashank Varma

0598.name: Scott O Murray
0598.bio: Scott O Murray is a Professor of Psychology who researches the neural and computational mechanisms underlying human visual perception and attention. Utilizing high-resolution functional MRI (fMRI) and computational modeling, Murray characterizes how the visual cortex represents complex features such as shape, size, and lightness, exploring how contextual information and top-down attention modulate early sensory processing. A portion of their recent research focuses on neurodiversity, applying vision science frameworks to study altered cortical computations and excitation-inhibition balance in individuals with autism spectrum disorder. By linking large-scale brain activity patterns to perceptual behaviors, Murray’s laboratory aims to identify the principles of how the brain constructs a representation of the environment.
0598.research_direction: Dr. Murray's recent work explores the mechanisms of visual-spatial processing across both human cognition and artificial intelligence systems. They have recently been investigating why multimodal language models struggle with visual perspective-taking and mental rotation, evaluating these AI models against human developmental benchmarks and designing cognitively-inspired spatial representations to help them overcome egocentric biases. In human neuroimaging, their recent studies use high-field fMRI to examine how the cerebellum supports top-down covert spatial attention independently of bottom-up stimulus features. Additionally, they are probing the neural basis of sensory hypersensitivity in autism spectrum disorder, combining EEG and structural MRI to investigate how subcortical anatomy might drive atypical alpha-band oscillations during visual processing.

papers.title: Cognitively-Inspired Tokens Overcome Egocentric Bias in Multimodal Models
papers.abstract: Multimodal language models (MLMs) typically exhibit robust performance on semantic vision-language tasks but frequently fail in spatial reasoning scenarios that require the adoption of an external agent's visual perspective. The authors attribute this deficiency to a systemic egocentric bias inherent in propositional image representations. To address this, they propose 'perspective tokens'—specialized embeddings that integrate orientation information through either embodied body-keypoint cues or abstract mental rotation mechanisms. Implementing these tokens within a LLaVA-1.5-13B framework leads to significant accuracy improvements in level-2 visual perspective-taking (VPT) across several synthetic and naturalistic benchmarks, including Isle Bricks V2 and 3DSRBench, demonstrating that embedding analog-like spatial structures into the token space enhances allocentric reasoning.
papers.authors: Bridget Leonard, Scott O. Murray

papers.title: Why Multimodal Models Struggle with Spatial Reasoning: Insights from Human Cognition
papers.abstract: This study investigates the divergence between multimodal language models (MLMs) and human spatial cognition, focusing on the absence of dorsal-stream-like computations in artificial systems. While current models effectively fuse linguistic data with ventral-stream-like visual features, they lack the computational architecture necessary for visual-motor integration and mental rotation. Utilizing a visual perspective-taking benchmark derived from developmental psychology, the authors evaluate GPT-4o and find that its performance on tasks involving viewpoint shifts matches the developmental level of a two-year-old child. The findings suggest that existing MLMs rely on propositional representations that fail to support the analog transformations required for robust allocentric spatial reasoning.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the 47th Annual Meeting of the Cognitive Science Society (CogSci)
papers.authors: Bridget Leonard, Kristin Woodard, Scott O. Murray

papers.title: Stimulus-Independent Modulation of Cerebellar Neural Activity by Visual Spatial Attention
papers.abstract: The authors examine the role of the cerebellum in non-motor cognitive processes, specifically covert visual spatial attention, using high-field fMRI. By implementing a baseline-shift paradigm that isolates top-down attentional signals from stimulus-evoked responses, the study measures BOLD activity in cerebellar subregions during an orientation discrimination task. The results demonstrate that directed spatial attention modulates neural activity in the cerebellum independently of the physical properties or presence of the visual stimulus. This stimulus-independent activity suggests the cerebellum participates in maintaining top-down attentional priority maps, extending its functional repertoire beyond traditional motor control into the domain of visual cognitive regulation.
papers.authors: Brenda (Siyue) Qiu, Kristin M. Woodard, Bridget Leonard, Scott O. Murray

papers.title: Failures in Perspective-taking of Multimodal AI Systems
papers.abstract: Leveraging established methodologies from cognitive and developmental science, this research probes the spatial representation capabilities of state-of-the-art multimodal AI systems, specifically GPT-4o. The study distinguishes between Level 1 perspective-taking, which concerns object visibility, and Level 2, which requires determining how an object appears from a specific orientation. Experimental results indicate that while multimodal models exhibit competency in Level 1 tasks, they show a significant performance decrement in Level 2 tasks that necessitate mental rotation and spatial transformation. The authors conclude that spatial representations in current multimodal systems are predominantly propositional and lack the analog fidelity required to mirror human-like perspective-taking development.
papers.authors: Bridget Leonard, Kristin Woodard, Scott O. Murray

papers.title: Investigating the Relationship Between Alpha-Band Power and Subcortical Structure Volumes in Autism
papers.abstract: Atypical alpha-band (~10 Hz) neural oscillations have been linked to the sensory hypersensitivity and altered gain control observed in individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD). This study explores the neuroanatomical contributors to these oscillatory differences by combining EEG spectral analysis with structural MRI volumetry. The researchers quantified alpha amplitude across stimulus-driven and resting-state conditions and examined its correlation with subcortical volumes, including the thalamus and hippocampus. The findings reveal a significant diagnosis-by-hippocampal volume interaction, indicating that structural characteristics of subcortical regions may differentially modulate cortical alpha oscillations in autistic compared to neurotypical adults, providing a potential structural basis for atypical sensory behavior in ASD.
papers.authors: Daniela L. Seczon, Mark W. Pettet, Hannah M. Rea, Scott O. Murray

0599.name: Scott Steinmetz
0599.bio: Scott T. Steinmetz is a researcher at Sandia National Laboratories within the Center for Computing Research, where their work focuses on computational neuroscience and human-machine teaming. Steinmetz investigates the capacity of accuracy-optimized convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to model the primate dorsal stream, specifically analyzing optic flow tuning and self-motion perception in brain area MSTd. At Sandia, they also develop frameworks for "Trusted AI," examining how human operators calibrate trust in autonomous systems through performance characterization and transparency. Steinmetz earned a Ph.D. in Cognitive Science from Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute, where they conducted research on the attentional modulation of the pupillary light response.
0599.research_direction: Dr. Steinmetz has recently been investigating the computational principles underlying motion processing by using artificial neural networks to model the primate dorsal visual stream. Their recent work explores whether supervised self-motion estimation or unsupervised reconstruction objectives best capture the complex optic flow tuning properties of neurons in cortical area MSTd. In related machine vision research, they are examining how specific architectural constraints, such as the choice of activation functions and induced representational sparsity, impact a network's robustness and navigational accuracy when processing dynamic optic flow fields. Beyond visual neuroscience, Dr. Steinmetz is also developing operational maturity models to systematically evaluate and communicate the trustworthiness, transparency, and safety of complex artificial intelligence systems deployed in high-stakes environments.

papers.title: For MSTd, Autoencoding is all you need
papers.abstract: While task-driven artificial neural networks (ANNs) have successfully modeled functional properties within the ventral visual pathway, their ability to explain representations in the dorsal visual stream remains less established. This study investigates the degree to which distinct computational objectives and architectural constraints induce neural alignment with the dorsal medial superior temporal area (MSTd), a cortical region selective for complex optic flow patterns that underpin self-motion and heading perception. Evaluating 54 ANNs alongside non-negative matrix factorization (NNMF) against empirical neurophysiological optic flow tuning metrics in MSTd reveals a marked divergence: models optimized for task accuracy in self-motion estimation fail to reproduce biological tuning distributions, developing strong biases toward backward azimuths. Conversely, unsupervised autoencoders trained to reconstruct motion inputs from middle temporal (MT)-like representations consistently exhibit superior alignment with MSTd tuning preferences. Incorporating explicit non-negativity or sparsity constraints does not enhance and often degrades biological fidelity, and relaxing bottleneck compression constraints does not impair correspondence. These findings indicate that the functional tuning properties of area MSTd are best accounted for by unsupervised, reconstruction-oriented objectives rather than supervised self-motion estimation.
papers.authors: Oliver W. Layton, Scott T. Steinmetz

papers.title: The Trust Calibration Maturity Model for Characterizing and Communicating Trustworthiness of AI Systems
papers.abstract: The rapid deployment and increasing scale of artificial intelligence models hinder access to critical information needed to evaluate their dependability, elevating the hazard of inappropriate or unsafe utilization. To establish an operational framework for communicating and evaluating AI trustworthiness, the Trust Calibration Maturity Model (TCMM) is proposed. The TCMM systematizes trustworthiness characterization across five interdependent dimensions of analytic maturity: Performance Characterization, Bias & Robustness Quantification, Transparency, Safety & Security, and Usability. Each dimension is evaluated along defined ordinal maturity levels, enabling system developers, evaluators, and stakeholders to systematically calibrate user trust, define rigorous operational requirements, monitor developmental maturity, and pinpoint domain-specific research requirements. The model is demonstrated on two distinct operational tasks: querying large language models (ChatGPT) for critical decision-making determinations in nuclear science, and employing PhaseNet deep neural network ensembles to characterize and categorize seismic event sources.
papers.authors: Scott T. Steinmetz, Asmeret Naugle, Paul Schutte, Matt Sweitzer, Alex Washburne, Lisa Linville, Daniel Krofcheck, Michal Kucer, Samuel Myren

papers.title: ReLU, Sparseness, and the Encoding of Optic Flow in Neural Networks
papers.abstract: Visual optic flow provides essential sensory input for estimating self-motion kinematics in robotic navigation, particularly within GPS-denied environments. This study examines how different activation functions—specifically ReLU, leaky ReLU, GELU, and Mish—affect estimation accuracy, noise robustness, and internal representational characteristics in convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) trained on three-dimensional translational and rotational optic flow fields. Network architectures using ReLU and leaky ReLU activation functions achieve superior generalization accuracy on novel flow patterns, maintaining translational errors within 5.5° mean absolute error (MAE) and rotational errors within 0.3°/s MAE, while also displaying significantly enhanced resilience against sparse input fields and moving object distractors compared to smooth activation counterparts. Analysis of unit activity distributions confirms that the bounded zero regimes of ReLU and leaky ReLU promote high population-level sparsity, demonstrating that sparse latent representations are key to robust, accurate self-motion estimation from dynamic optic flow.
papers.authors: Oliver W. Layton, Siyuan Peng, Scott T. Steinmetz

papers.title: Accuracy optimized neural networks do not effectively model optic flow tuning in brain area MSTd
papers.abstract: Although supervised, accuracy-optimized convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have emerged as primary predictive models for neural representations in the primate ventral stream, their suitability for modeling the dorsal visual hierarchy remains unverified. This work assesses how well accuracy-optimized CNNs capture empirical optic flow tuning properties observed in dorsal area MSTd compared to non-negative matrix factorization (NNMF), an unsupervised linear decomposition technique known to capture MSTd response properties. While CNNs achieve high regression accuracy when estimating 3D translation and rotation from full-field retinal flow patterns, their single-unit tuning properties diverge fundamentally from biological neurons, including an abnormal preference bias toward backward self-motion azimuths and improper coordination of translational and rotational tuning axes. Imposing NNMF-like biological constraints—specifically non-negative synaptic weights and explicit sparse coding—fails to rectify this divergence and substantially reduces self-motion estimation accuracy on compound flow patterns. These results establish that task accuracy alone is insufficient to drive biological receptive field organization in the dorsal stream, pointing to distinct organizational principles governing motion-processing cortical circuits.
papers.authors: Oliver W. Layton, Scott T. Steinmetz

0600.name: Scott Watamaniuk
0600.main_research_area: visual motion perception and smooth pursuit
0600.bio: Watamaniuk investigates the human visual system's capacity to process motion information and its role in guiding oculomotor and manual responses. Using high-resolution eye tracking and psychophysical methods, their research explores the coordination of binocular eye movements and the attentional demands associated with smooth pursuit. This work demonstrates that the brain can generate independent motor commands for each eye, which addresses classical theories of unitary conjugate eye control and provides data on the causes of strabismus. Additionally, Watamaniuk examines the impact of complex visual environments and cross-modal interactions, such as moving sounds, on perceptual and motor performance.
0600.research_direction: Dr. Watamaniuk has recently been investigating the neural and computational mechanisms underlying oculomotor control, with a particular focus on the long-standing debate between unified and independent binocular eye movements. Their recent work explores whether complex gaze behaviors—such as frontoparallel smooth pursuit and "remarkable saccades" during asymmetric vergence—are driven by a single conjugate motor command or by independent monocular pathways, utilizing novel computational modeling alongside high-frequency binocular eye tracking during monocular occlusion paradigms. In a distinct line of research, they are also examining the dynamics of miniature fixational eye movements, including microsaccades and slow ocular drift. Specifically, they use high-resolution eye tracking to investigate how varied spatial stimulus configurations, such as isolated central anchors versus peripheral target arrays, modulate fine retinal-image stability and overall gaze dynamics.

papers.title: A new oculomotor model demystifies “Remarkable Saccades”
papers.abstract: Binocular motor control has long been conceptualized through Hering's law of equal innervation, which posits that binocular gaze shifts result from the linear summation of a unitary conjugate command and a unitary vergence command. However, evidence demonstrating temporal desynchronization between inter-ocular rotations during vergence tracking challenges the necessity of a unitary vergence controller, supporting Helmholtz's hypothesis of independent ocular control. Even so, strict monocular independence fails to account for 'remarkable saccades'—aberrant saccadic displacements executed by an eye that is already accurately foveating an aligned target during asymmetric vergence. To reconcile these mechanisms, the authors formulate the Hybrid Binocular Control (HBC) computational framework. HBC implements independent cortical pursuit controllers for each eye interacting with a centralized, conjugate saccade burst generator in the brainstem, entirely dispensing with a dedicated vergence drive. The architecture generates remarkable saccades as an emergent dynamical property and accounts for systematic behavioral variations when observers selectively attend to one ocular image via variable attentional gain modulation. The resulting simulations replicate the kinematic velocity and displacement trajectories of remarkable saccades and standard binocular saccade phenotypes, establishing how independent and conjugate oculomotor pathways coordinate without explicit vergence signals.
papers.authors: Stephen J. Heinen, Arvind Chandna, Devashish Singh, Scott N. J. Watamaniuk

papers.title: Misalignment of a covered eye reveals frontoparallel smooth pursuit is driven by multiple signals
papers.abstract: Oculomotor research on smooth pursuit traditionally presumes that a unitary command rotates both eyes synchronously for both conjugate and vergence tracking (Hering's Law). Although recent demonstrations of asynchronous inter-eye motion during vergence tracking challenged unitary vergence control, whether frontoparallel conjugate pursuit similarly involves independent ocular systems remains unclear. To address this, neurotypical observers tracked a 0.4° visual stimulus traversing a tangent screen horizontally under sinusoidal trajectories and pseudorandom step-ramp direction reversals (peak target velocities of 5°/s and 25°/s). Monocular infrared occlusion paired with high-frequency binocular eye tracking (EyeLink 1000+, 1 kHz) allowed simultaneous recording of both ocular trajectories under monocular visual feedback. During monocular fixation preceding motion onset, the occluded eye deviated in rotational position consistent with an individual's phoria. Crucially, during subsequent monocular pursuit, this static misalignment persisted, yet both the viewing and occluded eyes closely matched the target's translational velocity. These findings indicate that frontoparallel smooth pursuit is driven by dissociated neural control mechanisms: a global unitary conjugate motor drive that matches target velocity across both eyes, operating alongside independent monocular subsystems that maintain static ocular alignment.
papers.authors: Stephen Heinen, Devashish Singh, Caroline Ulep, Scott Watamaniuk

papers.title: Peripheral targets attenuate miniature eye movements during fixation
papers.abstract: Voluntary fixation of a visual target is continuously disrupted by miniature fixational eye movements, notably microsaccades and slow ocular drift. Although microsaccades prevent perceptual fading across static scenes, their abrupt displacements transiently perturb fine retinal-image stability. This study examined how target spatial configuration and retinal locus modulate fixational oculomotor dynamics. Healthy observers fixated three distinct stimulus geometries: an isolated central dot (0.2°), a virtual circular configuration defined by eight peripheral dots without a central foveal anchor, and a combined central-plus-peripheral array, while high-resolution eye tracking recorded eye movements. Peripheral fixation targets induced a pronounced attenuation in microsaccadic amplitude, decreasing excursion sizes by an average of 46.3% compared to isolated central fixation. In addition, peripheral targets significantly reduced drift velocity, thereby dampening overall retinal slip. Fixation stability, quantified by bivariate contour ellipse area (BCEA), did not differ significantly between central and peripheral arrays, demonstrating that peripheral visual references stabilize ocular gaze by selectively suppressing miniature intrusive eye movements without degrading spatial fixation performance.
papers.authors: Scott N. J. Watamaniuk, Jeremy B. Badler, Stephen J. Heinen

0601.name: Se-Bum Paik
0601.institution: Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology
0601.department: Department of Brain and Cognitive Sciences
0601.bio: Se-Bum Paik is a computational neuroscientist and Associate Professor at KAIST, where they direct the Cognitive Intelligence Laboratory. Paik’s research investigates the developmental principles underlying the functional architecture of sensory systems in both biological and artificial neural networks. By integrating theoretical neuroscience, computational modeling, and psychophysical experiments, Paik explores how cognitive functions and neural topographies, such as cortical orientation maps, emerge from spontaneous activity and structural constraints. Their work has demonstrated that visual capabilities, including face and object detection, can arise in untrained deep neural networks as a result of innate biological strategies for information processing.
0601.research_direction: Dr. Paik has recently been exploring how principles of biological development and neural constraints can be translated into computational models to understand robust perception and learning. Their recent work investigates how early developmental scaffolds—such as simulated prenatal spontaneous noise, progressive low-to-high resolution sensory maturation, and hard-wired early visual filters—might drive neural networks to form abstract, shape-based representations rather than relying on superficial texture shortcuts. Beyond architectural priors, they are also investigating biologically plausible synaptic mechanisms to address fundamental training challenges in deep learning. Specifically, using computational simulations and human psychophysics, they are studying whether neuromimetic metaplasticity can prevent catastrophic forgetting during continual learning, and how initial soft-alignment strategies might overcome the biologically unrealistic weight transport problem to allow for efficient credit assignment.

papers.title: Brain-Inspired Warm-Up Training with Random Noise for Uncertainty Calibration
papers.abstract: This study demonstrates a developmental 'warm-up' strategy using random noise to enhance the uncertainty calibration of deep neural networks, inspired by the spontaneous prenatal random activity in the mammalian brain. By pretraining networks with random inputs and stochastic labels before the onset of structured sensory experience, the authors demonstrate a significant reduction in Expected Calibration Error (ECE) and overconfidence across varied architectures, including ResNet and Vision Transformers. This bio-inspired initialization regularizes the latent space and reshapes the loss landscape, facilitating robust probabilistic inference without diminishing top-1 classification accuracy on standard benchmarks.
papers.authors: Jeonghwan Cheon, Se-Bum Paik

papers.title: Gradual sensory maturation promotes abstract representation learning
papers.abstract: In biological systems, sensory organs mature gradually, exposing the brain to progressively higher-resolution inputs. This research investigates the computational benefits of this sensory maturation using neural network simulations and human psychophysics. The authors show that a low-to-high resolution training curriculum promotes the emergence of abstract, shape-based representations and prevents 'shortcut learning' of superficial high-frequency textures. This developmental scaffold results in enhanced out-of-distribution generalization, improved robustness to domain shifts, and more disentangled latent representations compared to models trained on static, high-fidelity data.
papers.authors: Jeonghwan Cheon, Se-Bum Paik

papers.title: One-Time Soft Alignment Enables Resilient Learning without Weight Transport
papers.abstract: Addressing the 'weight transport problem' in biologically plausible deep learning, the authors propose 'One-Time Soft Alignment' (OTSA), which approximates error gradients without continuous forward-backward weight synchronization. By implementing a soft alignment of synaptic weights during the initialization phase, the model achieves credit assignment efficiency comparable to standard backpropagation on large-scale tasks like ImageNet. Spectral analyses reveal that OTSA facilitates smoother gradient flow and convergence to flatter minima, ensuring robust performance against weight quantization and stochastic hardware noise in neuromorphic implementations.
papers.authors: Jeonghwan Cheon, Jaehyuk Bae, Se-Bum Paik

papers.title: Neuromimetic metaplasticity for adaptive continual learning without catastrophic forgetting
