papers.abstract: This paper presents a neuromimetic metaplasticity framework inspired by human working memory to mitigate catastrophic forgetting in sequential learning. The model incorporates heterogeneous synapses with varying stability and plasticity, dynamically modulating individual learning rates based on synaptic importance to previous tasks. This mechanism allows the network to solidify critical weights while maintaining flexibility for new information, enabling effective class-incremental learning without extensive data replay or structural expansion. Benchmarking on Split-CIFAR and sequential tasks demonstrates that this adaptive plasticity model significantly outperforms traditional regularization techniques in stability and memory capacity.
papers.authors: Suhee Cho, Hyeonsu Lee, Seungdae Baek, Se-Bum Paik

papers.title: Hard-wired visual filters for environment-agnostic object recognition
papers.abstract: The study explores the hypothesis that innate, 'hard-wired' architectures in the early visual pathway provide a foundation for environment-agnostic perception. By replacing the initial layers of deep neural networks with fixed Gabor-like filters modeled after biological receptive fields (GbDNNs), the authors show that such architectures are highly resilient to significant domain shifts, such as transitions from photographs to sketches. The results indicate that fixed structural priors in early vision facilitate the encoding of global shape information while suppressing sensitivity to local textures and noise, offering a brain-inspired strategy for invariant object recognition across diverse environmental contexts.
papers.authors: Minjun Kang, Seungdae Baek, Se-Bum Paik

0602.name: Sean Polyn
0602.bio: Sean Polyn is an Associate Professor of Psychology and Psychiatry at Vanderbilt University and directs the Vanderbilt Computational Memory Lab. Polyn's research investigates the neural and cognitive dynamics of human episodic memory, specifically examining the organization and retrieval of recently acquired information. They employ a multi-tiered methodology combining mathematical modeling, such as the Context Maintenance and Retrieval (CMR) model, with behavioral experiments, fMRI, and EEG to track the mental search process. Their work utilizes multi-voxel pattern analysis to decode category-specific neural activity during memory tasks and extends into clinical applications, including the study of memory dysfunction in schizophrenia.
0602.research_direction: Dr. Polyn has recently been investigating the cognitive and computational mechanisms that govern how episodic memories are organized and retrieved, focusing heavily on free and serial recall paradigms. Their recent work explores the boundary conditions of the temporal contiguity effect—the tendency to recall events that occurred close together in time—and probes how the sequence of memory retrieval is dynamically influenced by competing factors like semantic relationships, task demands, and even the social contexts present during encoding. To formally understand these phenomena, they use computational modeling, specifically comparing and extending architectures like the Context Maintenance and Retrieval framework, to determine how internal temporal and semantic cues interact to guide memory search. By bridging rigorous behavioral experiments with these quantitative models, Dr. Polyn is working to isolate the precise computational components necessary to unify our understanding of human memory performance across distinct mnemonic tasks.

papers.title: Bridging CRU and CMR in free and serial recall: A factorial comparison of retrieved-context models
papers.abstract: This research executes a systematic factorial model comparison between the Context Retrieval and Updating (CRU) and Context Maintenance and Retrieval (CMR) architectures to determine the necessary computational components for simulating human performance in both free and serial recall paradigms. The study evaluates the integration of CMR-specific features, such as drifting temporal context and long-standing semantic associations, into the CRU framework. The results indicate that while CRU's mechanisms for item confusion and recall termination are critical for modeling the ordinal structure of serial recall, the incorporation of CMR's contextual dynamics is essential for capturing the organizational biases observed in free recall, leading to a hybrid model that effectively unifies these traditionally distinct memory tasks.
papers.authors: Jordan B. Gunn, Sean M. Polyn

papers.title: Contextual influences on the organization of recall for ambiguous homographs
papers.abstract: This study investigates how linguistic and communicative contextual factors influence the semantic processing and mnemonic organization of ambiguous homographs (e.g., 'sage'). Through four pre-registered behavioral experiments, the authors manipulated physical scenes, communicative goals, and the identity of simulated conversational partners during encoding. While global recall probability and homograph disambiguation were not consistently affected by these variables, the identity of the communicative partner significantly organized the recall sequences, with participants exhibiting a strong tendency to recall homographs associated with the same partner in contiguous succession. These findings suggest that social attributes of the encoding environment function as salient episodic contexts that are automatically reinstated to guide the retrieval of language-based memories.
papers.authors: Melissa J. Evans, Clair MinKyung Hong, Jordan B. Gunn, Lisa K. Fazio, Sean M. Polyn

papers.title: The modulation and elimination of temporal organization in free recall
papers.abstract: The authors examine the boundary conditions and flexibility of the temporal contiguity effect—a fundamental signature of memory search—across six free-recall experiments. By systematically varying semantic list structure, retrieval practice, list length, and retention intervals, the study characterizes the conditions under which temporal organization is either preserved, attenuated, or entirely eliminated. Results reveal that strong semantic relationships and specific task demands, such as prior retrieval of list items, can override the default temporal organization of episodic memory. Quantitative modeling using the Context Maintenance and Retrieval (CMR) framework demonstrates that these modulatory effects are lawfully predicted by competition between temporal and semantic retrieval cues within an internally maintained context representation.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
papers.authors: Min Kyung Hong, Jordan B. Gunn, Lisa K. Fazio, Sean M. Polyn

0603.name: Sebastian M. Frank
0603.bio: Frank is an Emmy Noether Group Leader at the University of Regensburg, where they investigate the neurobiological foundations of learning and brain plasticity across the human lifespan. Their research utilizes visual perceptual learning as a model to study how sensory experiences lead to neural adaptations, combining psychophysics with neuroimaging techniques such as functional magnetic resonance spectroscopy (fMRS). Frank has identified developmental shifts in inhibitory (GABAergic) and excitatory (glutamatergic) signaling, specifically focusing on how these neurochemical dynamics differ between children and adults during skill acquisition. Beyond vision, their work examines cross-modal plasticity and the integration of visual-vestibular cues within the human cortex.
0603.research_direction: Dr. Frank has recently been investigating the neural and neurochemical mechanisms that govern sensory filtering, attention, and perceptual learning. Using time-resolved functional magnetic resonance spectroscopy (fMRS), their recent work explores how dynamic fluctuations in excitatory (glutamate) and inhibitory (GABA) neurotransmitters in the visual and parietal cortices help the brain manage competing sensory inputs. Specifically, they are examining the role of parietal GABAergic inhibition in suppressing visual distractors during multiple object tracking, as well as investigating how changes in excitatory drive in early visual areas might prevent the maladaptive perceptual learning of salient but task-irrelevant stimuli. Broadening their focus beyond the visual system, Dr. Frank is also evaluating the cortical mechanisms underlying tactile perceptual learning, seeking to understand how representational commonalities in the primary somatosensory cortex and higher-order networks allow learning to transfer to untrained body parts.

papers.title: Goal-directed visual information processing with GABAergic inhibition in parietal cortex
papers.abstract: The successful tracking of target signals within a cluttered visual environment requires mechanisms that mitigate interference from distractors. Using time-resolved functional magnetic resonance spectroscopy (fMRS), this study analyzed the dynamic fluctuations of γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA) and glutamate in the parietal and visual cortices during a multiple object tracking task. Findings demonstrate that as attentional load increases, both neurotransmitters elevate in the parietal cortex, whereas only glutamate concentrations rise in the visual cortex. Crucially, a specific metabolic profile in the parietal cortex—characterized by a more pronounced increase in GABA and a concurrent smaller increase in glutamate—was predictive of superior tracking performance. Further control experiments indicated that this parietal GABAergic modulation specifically supports the suppression of distractors rather than the enhancement of targets, suggesting that parietal inhibition is a key neural mechanism for establishing robust, goal-relevant representations in the presence of visual competition.
papers.authors: Zhiyan Wang, Sinah Wiborg, Antonia Wittmann, Nina Beck, Susanna Hirschle, Dominik Aschenbrenner, Markus Becker, Sebastian M. Frank

papers.title: Suppression of task-irrelevant learning achieved through withdrawal of excitation in early sensory areas
papers.abstract: While the neural substrates of learning have been widely researched, the mechanisms that actively prevent learning from occurring for task-irrelevant signals are less understood. This investigation employed functional magnetic resonance spectroscopy (fMRS) to monitor excitatory (glutamate) and inhibitory (GABA) processing in early visual cortex while participants were exposed to task-irrelevant visual signals varying in perceptual salience. The behavioral data revealed that visual perceptual learning was significantly reduced for suprathreshold (salient) relative to near-threshold (weak) irrelevant signals. Neurochemically, this suppression was associated with a specific decrease in glutamate concentrations in early visual areas during exposure to salient irrelevant features, without corresponding changes in GABAergic inhibition. These results suggest that an early gating mechanism operates by withdrawing excitatory drive to filter out salient but irrelevant sensory information, thereby preventing maladaptive plasticity.
papers.authors: Markus Becker, Savanna Babu, Zhiyan Wang, Sebastian M. Frank

papers.title: Transfer of tactile learning to untrained body parts: emerging cortical mechanisms
papers.abstract: Tactile perceptual learning often exhibits specificity to the trained skin site, yet performance improvements sometimes transfer to untrained body parts. This review synthesizes classical findings and modern neuroimaging results to evaluate the cortical mechanisms underlying this phenomenon. While somatotopic proximity in the primary somatosensory cortex (S1) explains transfer between adjacent fingers, it fails to account for transfer between distant sites, such as the hand and the foot. The article discusses evidence for cortical coactivation, where stimulation of one body part evokes responses in the representation of another, and the role of latent representations or functional connections among S1 regions. It is proposed that transfer is not governed by a single mechanism but results from an interaction between representational commonalities in S1 and higher-order sensory and decision-making areas that modulate the integration and readout of tactile information.
papers.authors: Sebastian M. Frank

0606.name: Serra Favila
0606.department: Department of Cognitive, Linguistic, and Psychological Sciences
0606.bio: Serra Favila is an Assistant Professor at Brown University who researches the neural and computational mechanisms of human episodic memory. Favila examines how environmental contexts, task goals, and interactions between similar memories transform mental representations and influence behavior. Their research utilizes functional neuroimaging (fMRI), intracranial recordings, eye-tracking, and computational modeling. Favila studies how hippocampal differentiation and visual cortex reactivation resolve competition during memory-guided attention.
0606.research_direction: Dr. Favila's recent work has been investigating the cognitive and neural mechanisms of visual memory, alongside the representational alignment between human cognition and artificial intelligence. Using fMRI and population receptive field modeling, their research explores how early visual cortex supports rapid, single-exposure episodic memory through retinotopically tuned reactivation, and how hippocampal processes that resolve memory competition shape top-down sensory tuning during memory-guided visual search. In addition to human neuroimaging, they have recently been evaluating artificial neural networks to determine whether deep vision models naturally adopt the geometric properties of human psychological space, such as testing their adherence to Shepard’s universal law of generalization. Broadening this computational focus, their recent work also explores whether large language models spontaneously construct human-like, multi-step cognitive maps to navigate complex social networks.

papers.title: Hippocampal mechanisms underlying the resolution of competition in memory and perception
papers.abstract: Adaptive behavior requires the prioritization of relevant sensory cues and mnemonic contents alongside the selective suppression of mutually competing representations. This study tested whether hippocampal computations that mitigate mnemonic interference directly modulate the tuning and selectivity of sensory representations to facilitate attentional selection. Human participants completed a memory-guided visual search paradigm while undergoing functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) with concurrent eye tracking. Neural representations were quantified using multivariate pattern similarity analysis and population receptive field modeling. Hippocampal pattern differentiation between competing scene representations directly predicted the spatial precision and accuracy of memory-guided saccadic eye movements. Within early visual cortex, preparatory activation of target-associated locations predicted successful search performance, whereas preparatory reactivation of competitor locations precipitated interference-driven search errors. Crucially, the magnitude of hippocampal pattern differentiation was systematically coupled to the attenuation of competitor representations in visual cortex, enhancing the fidelity of top-down preparatory tuning. These findings demonstrate that hippocampal mechanisms that resolve memory competition coordinate with visual cortical representations to optimize sensory selection during goal-directed attention.
papers.authors: Serra E. Favila, Mariam Aly

papers.title: Humanlike representation of social networks in large language models
papers.abstract: Navigating complex social environments requires constructing cognitive maps that capture indirect, multistep relationship structures rather than relying solely on immediate pairwise associations. This investigation evaluated whether large language models (LLMs) spontaneously generate humanlike multistep abstractions of social networks. LLMs were evaluated on text-based relational reasoning and message-routing tasks across structured social graphs. Network representations and choice probabilities were modeled against formal graph-theoretic metrics, specifically comparing direct single-step associations to multistep diffusion models formalized by Katz communicability. LLM navigation decisions and error distributions systematically tracked human behavioral profiles and were superiorly characterized by Katz communicability relative to single-step models. Notably, this multistep structural bias persisted even in task environments where integrating multi-hop pathways was uninformative or detrimental to routing accuracy. These results indicate that multistep relational abstraction serves as an intrinsic inductive bias when LLMs process graph-structured social contexts, establishing computational parallels between artificial neural representations and biological cognitive mapping in social cognition.
papers.authors: Jae-Young Son, Daniel Carstensen, Serra Elizabeth Favila

papers.title: Early Visual Cortex Supports One-Shot Episodic Memory via Spatially Tuned Reactivation
papers.abstract: Canonical models of episodic recall hypothesize that memory retrieval depends on the reactivation of sensory representations within early sensory cortices (cortical reinstatement). However, empirical demonstrations in primary visual cortex have predominantly utilized overtrained associative pairs combined with explicit mental imagery prompts, leaving open whether cortical reinstatement supports rapid, single-exposure episodic encoding. Utilizing fMRI and population receptive field (pRF) modeling, cortical responses were measured in healthy human observers during single-trial encoding, foveal recognition, and spatial location recall of parafoveal objects. Areas V1, V2, and V3 exhibited reliable, low-amplitude mnemonic BOLD responses during both memory tests. Despite the central presentation of cues and the lack of explicit spatial demands during recognition, retrieved representations exhibited significant retinotopic spatial tuning aligned to the initially encoded parafoveal coordinates. The fidelity and spatial tuning amplitude of this spontaneous reactivation predicted successful memory recall. Furthermore, spatial receptive field modulation during initial encoding—characterized by localized response enhancement at the target coordinate and surrounding suppression—predicted subsequent retrieval success. These findings establish that a single perceptual experience is sufficient to induce retinotopically specific reactivation in early visual cortex, confirming its fundamental role in one-shot episodic memory retrieval.
papers.authors: Robert Woodry, Jonathan Winawer, Serra E. Favila

papers.title: Deep Vision Models Follow Shepard's Universal Law of Generalization
papers.abstract: Shepard’s (1987) universal law of generalization posits that the probability of generalization between stimuli decays as a concave function of their distance in psychological space. While this law is a fundamental principle of biological perception, its validity in artificial neural networks (ANNs) has not been extensively characterized. We evaluated 26 diverse deep vision models by comparing their embedding space distances to human similarity judgments for naturalistic images. Using non-metric multidimensional scaling (NMDS) to derive proxy psychological spaces, we found that internal representations across various model architectures and training paradigms robustly adhere to Shepard’s law, producing concave generalization gradients aligned with human psychological data. These findings suggest that modern deep vision systems naturally exploit representational geometries similar to those in human psychological space, with semantic features playing a critical role in facilitating this alignment.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the 47th Annual Meeting of the Cognitive Science Society
papers.authors: Daniel L. Carstensen, Serra E. Favila, Steven M. Frankland

0607.name: Shahin Nasr
0607.bio: Shahin Nasr is an Assistant Professor of Radiology at Harvard Medical School and a researcher at the Athinoula A. Martinos Center for Biomedical Imaging. Nasr’s research utilizes ultra-high field (7T) functional MRI, psychophysics, and electrophysiology to map the mesoscale architecture of the human visual cortex, including the columnar organization of features such as color, motion, and depth. They investigate the relationship between natural scene statistics and cortical organization, as well as the impact of developmental and neurodegenerative disorders, such as amblyopia and schizophrenia, on visual processing channels.
0607.research_direction: Dr. Nasr has recently been using ultra-high-field (7T) fMRI to map the functional architecture of the human visual system across multiple stages of cortical processing. At the mesoscale level in early visual cortex, their recent work explores sub-millimeter resting-state functional connectivity between individual ocular dominance columns to better understand intrinsic binocular circuitry. In higher-level vision, they are investigating how the brain processes naturalistic environments and ego-motion, specifically probing the functional tuning of a newly identified scene-selective region in the posterior intraparietal gyrus (PIGS) that responds to optic flow. Additionally, Dr. Nasr is examining clinical populations to determine how developmental visual disorders, such as amblyopia, alter these high-level spatial representations and disrupt parietal mechanisms involved in navigation.

papers.title: Unraveling the mesoscale resting-state functional connectivity of ocular dominance columns in humans using high-resolution functional MRI
papers.abstract: Using ultra-high field (7T) fMRI at sub-millimeter resolution, this study characterizes the resting-state functional connectivity (rs-FC) between ocular dominance columns (ODCs) in the human primary visual cortex (V1). By mapping ODC topography and assessing cortical depth-dependent co-fluctuations, the research demonstrates that ODCs sharing the same ocular preference exhibit significantly stronger selective functional connectivity compared to those with unalike preferences. This selectivity is more pronounced in the middle and superficial cortical layers, aligning with known horizontal projection patterns in non-human primates. The results suggest that the mesoscale functional architecture of V1 is reflected in intrinsic connectivity patterns, providing a potential non-invasive metric for assessing binocular circuitry integrity.
papers.authors: Marianna E. Schmidt, Iman Aganj, Jason Stockmann, Berkin Bilgic, Yulin Chang, W. Scott Hoge, Evgeniya Kirilina, Nikolaus Weiskopf, Shahin Nasr

papers.title: Decreased scene-selective activity within the posterior intraparietal cortex in amblyopic adults
papers.abstract: This neuroimaging investigation evaluates the impact of amblyopia on the functional organization of scene-selective cortical areas, specifically focusing on the recently discovered posterior intraparietal gyrus scene-selective (PIGS) area. Using task-based fMRI with naturalistic scene and object stimuli, the researchers found that amblyopic adults exhibit significantly reduced evoked responses within PIGS compared to neurotypical controls. In contrast, activity in other scene-selective regions, including the parahippocampal place area (PPA) and retrosplenial cortex (RSC), remained comparable between groups. The magnitude of activity reduction in PIGS correlated with clinical metrics of visual impairment and subjective visual function scores (VFQ-39), suggesting that amblyopia preferentially disrupts parietal mechanisms involved in processing ego-motion and navigation-relevant scene cues.
papers.authors: Sarala N. Malladi, Jan Skerswetat, Marianna E. Schmidt, Roger B. H. Tootell, Eric D. Gaier, Peter J. Bex, David G. Hunter, Shahin Nasr

papers.title: Selective Functional Connectivity between Ocular Dominance Columns in the Primary Visual Cortex
papers.abstract: This study develops and validates a methodological framework for quantifying fine-scale functional connectivity between neuronal ensembles in the human brain. Using high-resolution 7T fMRI, the authors quantify resting-state co-fluctuations between individual ocular dominance columns (ODCs) in V1. They demonstrate that ODCs belonging to the same eye (alike columns) are more strongly functionally interconnected than columns responding to different eyes (unalike columns). By applying partial correlation analysis to sub-millimeter voxels, the work bridges the gap between invasive animal tract-tracing studies and non-invasive human neuroimaging, establishing selective functional connectivity as a robust feature of the human mesoscale connectome.
papers.venue: International Workshop on Ophthalmic Medical Image Analysis (OMIA)
papers.authors: Iman Aganj, Shahin Nasr

papers.title: A previously undescribed scene-selective site is the key to encoding ego-motion in naturalistic environments
papers.abstract: Through a series of high-resolution 7T fMRI experiments, this research identifies a novel scene-selective region located in the posterior intraparietal gyrus (PIGS) of the human brain. The study characterizes PIGS by its selectively high response to scenes compared to other object categories and its specific tuning to ego-motion cues, such as optic flow, which are essential for navigation through naturalistic environments. PIGS is functionally and anatomically distinct from existing scene-selective regions like the occipital place area (OPA) and parahippocampal place area (PPA). The findings suggest that human scene perception relies on a specialized parietal module dedicated to encoding the observer's movement relative to the environmental layout.
papers.authors: Bryan Kennedy, Sarala N. Malladi, Roger B. H. Tootell, Shahin Nasr

0608.name: Shannon Ross-Sheehy
0608.bio: Shannon Ross-Sheehy is an Associate Professor of Psychology at the University of Tennessee Knoxville and directs the Infant Visual Cognition Lab. Ross-Sheehy investigates the co-development of visual attention and memory systems, focusing on how neural substrates support the emergence of visual-cognitive competency in infants and adults. Utilizing high-resolution eye-tracking, pupillometry, and dynamic field modeling, Ross-Sheehy examines individual differences in scanning efficiency and attentional phenotypes. Their research aims to identify early attentional biomarkers in typical and atypical populations, such as preterm infants, to predict long-term cognitive outcomes.
0608.research_direction: Dr. Ross-Sheehy has recently been investigating the developmental trajectory of visual short-term memory, focusing on how infants and adults build and maintain visual representations across multiple eye movements. Their recent work explores whether the developing visual system can preserve memory for sequentially fixated objects or encode peripheral items that fall outside of the immediate foveal fixation history. To examine these phenomena, Dr. Ross-Sheehy utilizes high-resolution eye tracking alongside fixation-contingent n-back change-detection paradigms across cohorts of infants and adults. By carefully measuring overt looking behaviors as participants scan multi-element arrays, they aim to uncover the core cognitive architecture that allows humans to integrate visual information over time and space during the first year of life and beyond.

papers.title: Visual Short-Term Memory Persists Across Multiple Fixations: An n-Back Approach to Quantifying Capacity in Infants and Adults
papers.abstract: Visual short-term memory (STM) serves as a core architecture for broader cognitive functions, undergoing substantial maturation across the first postnatal year. Although overt gaze fixation is tightly linked to memory encoding, it remains unresolved whether developing infants can preserve distinct representations across sequentially fixated stimuli or encode items outside their foveal fixation history. In this study, cohorts of 5-month-olds, 11-month-olds, and adults (n = 24 per cohort) completed a passive change-detection paradigm featuring an n-back fixation-contingent design. High-resolution eye tracking recorded overt looking behavior while subjects observed multi-element arrays of colored circles, testing memory for the immediately preceding fixation (one-back), the penultimate fixation (two-back), and unfixated array elements (change-other). Across all age groups, convergent evidence showed retention for up to two sequentially fixated objects (one-back and two-back), alongside moderate preservation of nonfixated peripheral items. Temporal permutation analyses further demonstrated that change-preference metrics were not artifacts of spatial perseveration or systematic location biases.
papers.authors: Bret Eschman, Shannon Ross-Sheehy

0609.name: Shaul Hochstein
0609.department: Department of Neurobiology, Alexander Silberman Institute of Life Sciences
0609.bio: Shaul Hochstein is a Professor Emeritus at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, conducting research that ranges from the biophysics of photo-transduction to the cognitive psychology of conscious perception. Hochstein co-developed the Reverse Hierarchy Theory (RHT), which suggests that conscious perception begins at high-level cortical areas and descends to low-level representations when detailed scrutiny is required. Their research utilizes psychophysics, electrophysiology, and computational modeling to investigate ensemble perception, the mechanisms of perceptual skill learning, and the neural substrates of subjective experience.
0609.research_direction: Dr. Hochstein has recently been investigating the pervasive mechanisms of ensemble perception, exploring how the human visual system extracts summary statistical representations from groups of items. Their recent work explores this phenomenon across multiple feature dimensions and presentation modes, comparing spatial arrays to rapid serial visual presentations (RSVP) to uncover the underlying mechanisms driving explicit, goal-directed averaging versus automatic, implicit summary extraction. Behaviorally, they are examining temporal integration in these processes, specifically testing how perceptual history and serial dependence bias the implicit encoding of current visual ensembles. On a neural level, they are using fMRI and multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) to map the neuroanatomical loci of ensemble processing, investigating whether ventral object-selective cortical regions like the lateral occipital complex (LOC) are responsible for representing these summary statistics.

papers.title: Neural Patterns Reveal Lateral Occipital Complex Representation of Ensemble Mean Orientation
papers.abstract: Ensemble perception designates the visual system's capacity to compute summary statistical representations from groups of similar elements, as exemplified by rapid perceptual averaging. Although well characterized at the psychophysical level, the underlying neuroanatomical locus of ensemble encoding remains debated. Drawing on the concept of 'ensemble files' analogous to object files, this study tested the hypothesis that ensemble orientation statistics are represented in ventral object-selective cortex, specifically the lateral occipital complex (LOC). Using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) with multivoxel pattern analysis (MVPA), 25 participants estimated the mean orientation of arrays of heterogeneous oriented bars and reported their estimates in an intermittent two-alternative forced-choice (2AFC) task. While early extrastriate retinotopic cortex (V3) and parietal regions exhibited modest, broadly tuned representations of the average orientation, the lateral occipital complex exhibited the strongest orientation-selective coding, with distinct voxel activity patterns reliably classifying ensemble orientation means in both ROI-based and searchlight decoding analyses. Crucially, decoding accuracy within the LOC significantly correlated with behavioral discrimination performance across participants, demonstrating that object-selective ventral cortex plays a functionally relevant role in representing ensemble statistics.
papers.authors: Noam Khayat, Merav Ahissar, Shaul Hochstein

papers.title: Comparing explicit and implicit ensemble perception: 3 stimulus variables and 3 presentation modes
papers.abstract: Ensemble perception enables observers to overcome visual processing bottlenecks by encoding summary statistics that define the gist of a scene. While ensemble statistics can be extracted both via explicit instructions and implicitly during orthogonal tasks, the degree to which these processes share underlying mechanisms is unresolved. This study systematically compared explicit and implicit ensemble processing across three visual feature dimensions (circle diameter, bar orientation, and disk luminance) and three presentation formats (spatial arrays, rapid serial visual presentation [RSVP] sequences, and spatio-temporal streams). In implicit trials, participants completed a 2AFC item recognition task, where recognition likelihood exhibited a characteristic Gaussian profile centered on the ensemble mean. In explicit trials, participants judged whether test probes deviated from the ensemble mean or selected which of two probes lay closer to the mean, yielding classic sigmoidal psychometric functions. Quantitative comparison revealed that explicit ensemble averaging consistently achieved significantly higher precision than implicit ensemble extraction across all feature domains, presentation modalities, and testing formats, supporting the existence of distinct readout mechanisms for explicit goal-directed averaging versus automatic implicit summary extraction.
papers.authors: Noam Khayat, Marina Pavlovskaya, Shaul Hochstein

papers.title: Perceptual history biases in serial ensemble representation
papers.abstract: Ensemble perception allows the visual system to synthesize multiple redundant objects into summary statistical percepts. While serial dependence—the attractive bias of current perception toward recent stimuli—has been documented for explicit mean estimation in static spatial arrays, its role during implicit extraction of temporally presented ensembles is unknown. In a series of experiments, observers viewed rapid serial visual presentations (RSVP) of six circles of varying diameters (100 ms per item, 100 ms ISI) followed by an implicit 2AFC recognition test between an item presented in the sequence and a novel foil. Performance was primarily driven by current-trial statistics, with false alarms systematically increasing for foils matching the current ensemble mean. Crucially, when probes were positioned equidistant from the current trial's mean to isolate past effects, observers exhibited significant attractive biases toward the ensemble mean of immediately preceding trials, as well as an attraction toward the global distribution mean across the entire experimental session. These findings establish that serial dependence operates even under implicit temporal ensemble processing, reflecting an integration across current percepts, short-term history, and global statistical priors.
papers.authors: Noam Khayat, Merav Ahissar, Shaul Hochstein

papers.title: The Pervasiveness of Ensemble Perception: Not Just Your Average Review
papers.abstract: This monograph reviews the empirical and theoretical foundations of ensemble perception, positing that statistical summarization is a foundational, ubiquitous property of human visual cognition rather than an auxiliary heuristic. The work synthesizes findings across perceptual domains, tracing the representation of low-level visual features (orientation, spatial frequency, size, luminance, motion direction) up to high-level semantic and social cues (facial identity, expression, gaze direction, crowd dynamics, and numerical values). The authors assess the neurocomputational architectures supporting statistical extraction, contrasting feedforward pooling mechanisms with recurrent reverse-hierarchy feedback circuits, and evaluating models of subsampling versus complete sample pooling. Furthermore, the volume details the functional utility of ensemble representations in overcoming working memory capacity constraints, mitigating attentional bottlenecks, driving visual search guidance, and providing perceptual continuity and stability across saccadic eye movements and temporal interruptions.
papers.authors: Jennifer E. Corbett, Igor Utochkin, Shaul Hochstein

0610.name: Shaun Wallace
0610.department: Department of Computer Science and Statistics
0610.bio: Shaun Wallace is an Assistant Professor at the University of Rhode Island and the director of the Human-Centered Experiential Technologies (HAX) Lab. Wallace’s research operates at the intersection of vision science, human-computer interaction (HCI), and systems, focusing on how personalized typographic formats affect digital readability for diverse populations. As the architect of the Virtual Readability Lab, they employ large-scale crowdsourcing and psychophysical methodologies to quantify the impact of font characteristics on reading speed and comprehension. Their work utilizes vision science principles to develop adaptive computational systems that tailor information presentation to an individual's visual processing capabilities.
0610.research_direction: Dr. Wallace's recent work explores the intersection of visual perception, reading accessibility, and human-computer interaction across diverse digital environments. To understand the perceptual and cognitive friction of reading, they have recently been using eye-tracking alongside psychophysical choice experiments to investigate how specific typographic features—such as stroke weight and inter-character spacing—interact with a reader's age, linguistic background, and neurodivergence to influence word-level reading difficulty. Beyond low-level reading processes, they are investigating how interface design and individual psychological profiles impact higher-level cognitive shortcuts, utilizing behavioral and physiological metrics to model susceptibility to confirmation bias in news feeds. Additionally, their research examines the dynamics of digital peer production, analyzing longitudinal field data to model how different extrinsic incentive structures and interactive visualizations motivate both paid and unpaid crowdworkers to accurately maintain complex datasets.

papers.title: Breaking Word Barriers: Predicting Word-Level Reading Difficulty in People with and without Dyslexia
papers.abstract: While conventional computational readability metrics predominantly assess text difficulty at aggregate passage or sentence levels, they fail to isolate lexical-level reading friction experienced by neurodivergent readers. This work presents a machine learning framework for predicting word-level reading difficulty across individuals with and without dyslexia. By combining gaze-derived behavioral indicators with multifaceted linguistic and typographic features—such as syllabic structure, phonetic regularity, lexical frequency norms, and orthographic neighborhood density—the models classify difficulty at fine granularity. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that incorporating personalized cognitive and linguistic profiles significantly improves the accuracy of word-level difficulty prediction, providing a basis for real-time, adaptive assistive interfaces tailored to individual reading barriers.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the 2026 ACM SIGACCESS Conference on Computers and Accessibility (ASSETS '26)
papers.authors: Maedeh Hosseinpour, Borano Llana, Yusra Suhail, Kushas Khadka, Shaun Wallace

papers.title: Attract & Engage Visitors with Insights to Maintain an Evolving Tabular Dataset: a Longitudinal Naturalistic Field Study
papers.abstract: Maintaining open-access, evolving tabular data often suffers from contributor attrition and data decay. This paper presents a multi-year naturalistic field investigation of Drafty (specifically Drafty CS Professors), an open crowd-curated knowledge repository indexing academic hiring and faculty records. The authors examine the mechanism of leveraging immediate, actionable domain-level data visualizations and insights as intrinsic incentives to attract visitors and convert passive consumers into active, uncompensated data editors. Longitudinal analysis of web telemetry, edit trajectories, and provenance logs demonstrates that direct presentation of aggregate insights promotes sustained engagement and yields high edit veracity, sustaining domain-specific tabular datasets without financial reward mechanisms.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction (CSCW 2026)
papers.authors: Shaun Wallace, Na Kyoung Lee, Zhengyi Peng, Talie Massachi, Long Do, Surbhi Rathore, Sarah M. Brown, Jeff Huang

papers.title: Personalizing Font Size Normalization: Linguistic Background Shapes Which Font Attributes Matter
papers.abstract: Typographic normalization of digital font size has historically relied on static geometric heuristics or general-population perceptual averages. This study investigates how perception of typographic scale varies as a function of chronological age and linguistic background. Utilizing a modified discrete choice experiment deployed to crowdworkers alongside a screen calibration method that converts on-screen pixels to physical centimeters, the authors quantified the perceptual weights assigned to diverse typographical properties. While vertical character height (x-height/cap-height) was the predominant factor overall, distinct systematic variations emerged: readers with a Chinese language background weighted stroke weight most heavily, adults aged 40 and older placed heightened importance on stroke weight and inter-character spacing relative to younger cohorts, and native speakers of languages featuring pronounced descenders (such as Arabic and Hindi) were markedly sensitive to character width. These findings provide empirical foundations for personalized font normalization algorithms tailored to cross-cultural and demographic requirements.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the 34th ACM Conference on User Modeling, Adaptation and Personalization (UMAP '26)
papers.authors: Yusra Suhail, Kushas Khadka, Borano Llana, Maedeh Hosseinpour, Shaun Wallace

papers.title: Towards Fair and Equitable Incentives to Motivate Paid and Unpaid Crowd Contributions
papers.abstract: Maintaining dynamic public tabular datasets depends on balancing contributions from paid crowdworkers and unpaid peer-production volunteers, yet empirical comparisons of their motivations and work quality in real-world settings remain limited. Analyzing nine years of historical editing traces from Drafty alongside an empirical discrete choice conjoint experiment, this work compares trade-offs among task attributes including compensation scale, latency, intrinsic interest, and prosocial contribution value. Unpaid volunteers demonstrated 1.9-fold higher accuracy than paid crowdworkers on obscure, hard-to-verify data and 1.5-fold higher accuracy on entries requiring domain expertise. The findings model latent utility structures across worker types and provide framework guidelines for hybrid crowdsourcing platforms that harmonize extrinsic incentives and intrinsic alignment to optimize dataset integrity.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the 2025 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI '25)
papers.authors: Shaun Wallace, Talie Massachi, Jiaqi Su, Dave B. Miller, Jeff Huang

papers.title: Assessing Susceptibility Factors of Confirmation Bias in News Feed Reading
papers.abstract: This study investigates the multi-faceted user and interaction factors that influence susceptibility to confirmation bias during news consumption on digital platforms. Utilizing an experimental paradigm where participants interact with news feeds, the researchers quantify the impact of personality traits, prior beliefs, and information presentation formats on biased selection and perception. The work employs behavioral metrics, including dwelling time and selection patterns, alongside physiological indicators to model confirmation bias vulnerability. The findings delineate specific psychological profiles more prone to confirmation bias and provide evidence for how interface design can either exacerbate or mitigate these cognitive shortcuts in high-volume information environments.
papers.venue: CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI '25)
papers.authors: Nattapat Boonprakong, Saumya Pareek, Benjamin Tag, Jorge Goncalves, Tilman Dingler, Shaun Wallace

0611.name: Sheng He
0611.department: State Key Laboratory of Cognitive Science
0611.bio: Sheng He is a cognitive neuroscientist researching the functional and neural mechanisms of human vision, focusing on visual attention and the limits of conscious awareness. Using psychophysical methods and high-field (7T) functional MRI, they characterize how the brain processes visual information from early cortical stages to high-level representations, including responses to stimuli below the threshold of awareness. Their work examines binocular rivalry, the resolution of visual competition, and the role of feedback signals in the human visual cortex. They currently investigate the mesoscale neural circuitry of the visual system and the integration of visual features into coherent perception.
0611.research_direction: Dr. He's recent work explores the top-down cognitive and neural mechanisms shaping visual perception, conscious awareness, and temporal processing using methods spanning psychophysics, MEG, and 7T fMRI. They have recently been investigating how the brain orchestrates visual attention, asking whether the posterior inferotemporal cortex serves as an integrative neural priority map and probing whether retrospective spatial attention can rescue suppressed visual stimuli into conscious awareness. Alongside this, their research examines time perception to determine whether cross-modal duration adaptation relies on objective physical timing or subjective perceptual experience, and maps how high-level stimulus complexity modulates gamma-band neural entrainment across both cortical and deep subcortical networks. Finally, their theoretical work evaluates the architectural gaps between biological cognition and machine learning to outline strategic directions for brain-inspired artificial intelligence.

papers.title: The distinct role of human PIT in attention control
papers.abstract: This study employs 7T high-resolution functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (fMRI) to investigate the human posterior inferotemporal cortex (hPIT) as a candidate for a neural priority map. Utilizing spatial attention paradigms across multiple feature domains (motion, color, and shape), the research demonstrates that hPIT exhibits robust attentional modulation that is independent of stimulus category but highly sensitive to attentional demands. Functional connectivity analyses reveal that hPIT acts as an integrative hub bridging the dorsal and ventral attention networks, facilitating the orchestration of endogenous and exogenous control signals to optimize behavioral responses to complex visual environments.
papers.authors: Siyuan Huang, Lan Wang, Sheng He

papers.title: Retrospective attention can trigger the conscious representation of invisible stimuli
papers.abstract: This research utilizes a retrospective cueing paradigm combined with continuous flash suppression (CFS) to explore the recovery of visual information from stimuli that failed to reach awareness at the time of presentation. The study provides behavioral and neural evidence that a retro-cue delivered after the offset of a suppressed stimulus can retroactively facilitate its access into conscious awareness. These findings indicate the existence of a high-fidelity, pre-conscious buffer or latent representation that remains accessible to top-down attentional selection for a brief temporal window, suggesting that attention can boost past sensory events into phenomenal awareness.
papers.authors: Lan Wang, Sheng He

papers.title: Duration adaptation depends on the perceived rather than physical duration and can be observed across sensory modalities
papers.abstract: By investigating duration adaptation effects through a series of psychophysical experiments, this study examines whether temporal adaptation is driven by objective physical duration or subjective perceptual duration. The results show that duration aftereffects from visual adapters align more closely with subjectively matched durations than with their physical lengths. Furthermore, the study identifies a cross-modal adaptation effect where adapting to a visual stimulus influences the perceived duration of a subsequent auditory stimulus, provided the subjective durations are matched. These findings suggest that duration is encoded at a modality-independent, high-level processing stage susceptible to top-down perceptual biases.
papers.authors: Hao Chen, Sheng He

papers.title: Characterizing Frequency Response Functions of Low-Level and High-Level Stimuli in the Human Brain
papers.abstract: This investigation characterizes the frequency-specific neural responses and entrainment elicited by varying levels of visual complexity (low-level checkerboard patterns vs. high-level faces and landscapes) flickering at 20, 30, 40, and 48 Hz. Using 7T fMRI and Magnetoencephalography (MEG), the study demonstrates that high-level stimuli trigger significantly broader temporal lobe activation and more effective gamma-band entrainment in deep brain structures, including the hippocampus, compared to low-level stimuli. The results indicate that stimulus representational complexity significantly modulates the efficiency of rhythmic neural drive throughout the human cortical and subcortical hierarchy.
papers.authors: Na Zhao, LiNan Shi, Sheng He

papers.title: Brain-inspired artificial intelligence research: A review
papers.abstract: Structured around David Marr’s three-layer framework (computational, algorithmic, and implementation), this comprehensive review analyzes the theoretical and functional intersections between cognitive neuroscience and artificial intelligence. The paper evaluates the divergence between biological cognition mechanisms and current machine learning architectures, identifying specific limitations in the realization of human-like intelligence in AI. It proposes eight strategic research directions, including bionic information processing, embodied intelligence, and collaborative perceptual-interpretive mechanisms, aimed at narrowing the structural and algorithmic gap between human brains and artificial systems.
papers.authors: Guoyin Wang, Huanan Bao, Qun Liu, Tiangang Zhou, Si Wu, Tiejun Huang, Zhaofei Yu, Cewu Lu, Yihong Gong, Zhaoxiang Zhang, Sheng He

0613.name: Shigeki Nakauchi
0613.department: Department of Computer Science and Engineering
0613.bio: Shigeki Nakauchi is a Professor at Toyohashi University of Technology who investigates the computational and neural mechanisms underlying visual perception, color vision, and material recognition. Nakauchi's research utilizes a multidisciplinary approach combining psychophysical experimentation, EEG brain activity analysis, and mathematical modeling to study how the human visual system interprets environmental stimuli. Nakauchi developed specialized optical filters for Color Universal Design that simulate color vision deficiencies to facilitate inclusive design practices. Their current work focuses on 'Shitsukan' (material) perception and the application of spectral imaging to visualize information typically invisible to the human eye.
0613.research_direction: Dr. Nakauchi has recently been investigating high-level visual and social perception, using continuous flash suppression to study the pre-conscious detection of ambiguous faces and adaptation paradigms to examine how the visual system explicitly encodes emotional variance within crowds. Their recent work also explores multimodal cognitive and behavioral mechanisms, investigating how spontaneous motor rhythms influence working memory for musical tempo and using immersive virtual reality to identify predictive kinematic cues—such as pedestrian waist rotation—for human-robot collision avoidance. Additionally, they are advancing applied optical engineering by developing novel spread-spectrum modulated lighting techniques to accurately capture fluorescence measurements in complex, ambient-light environments.

papers.title: Aftereffects of variance in the perception of facial expressions in crowds
papers.abstract: This investigation explored the neural representation of summary statistics in social perception by examining whether the human visual system adapts to the emotional variance within a crowd. Utilizing morphed facial stimuli spanning a happy-to-angry continuum, the researchers demonstrated that adaptation to high- or low-variance facial ensembles induces robust aftereffects, shifting subsequent variance perception in the direction opposite to the adaptor. These findings suggest that the visual system explicitly encodes the variance of facial expressions as a distinct social signal, allowing for the dynamic recalibration of perceived emotional diversity within group contexts.
papers.authors: Moe Kudaka, Sachiyo Ueda, Hideki Tamura, Tetsuto Minami, Shigeki Nakauchi

papers.title: How we remember music tempo: the role of spontaneous motor tempo in recall and preference
papers.abstract: This study examined the relationship between individual internal rhythms, specifically spontaneous motor tempo (SMT) measured via finger-tapping, and the memory and preference for musical tempo. Using linear mixed modeling of behavioral data from synchronization and recall tasks, the researchers found that SMT significantly biased recalled tempo only when an 8-second rehearsal interval was provided, and similarly influenced subjective tempo preference. These results indicate that motor-based internal clocks modulate the retrieval and maintenance of temporal information in the phonological loop of working memory rather than at the level of initial sensory processing.
papers.authors: Kyoko Hine, Yoshitomo Wakana, Shigeki Nakauchi

papers.title: Waist rotation angle as indicator of probable human collision-avoidance direction for autonomous mobile robots
papers.abstract: The research investigated the anticipatory cues utilized in human-robot collision avoidance in head-on scenarios through immersive virtual reality experiments. By analyzing kinematic data, the study identified the waist rotation angle as a critical postural indicator that reliably predicts intended avoidance direction significantly before lateral displacement occurs. Integration of this orientation cue into an autonomous mobile robot (AMR) navigation algorithm facilitated early avoidance maneuvers, which resulted in significantly higher subjective comfort and trust ratings among pedestrians compared to standard reactive avoidance models.
papers.authors: Tatsuto Yamauchi, Hideki Tamura, Tetsuto Minami, Shigeki Nakauchi

papers.title: Spread spectrum lighting for excitation-emission matrix measurements in ambient light environments
papers.abstract: This paper proposes a novel spread-spectrum lighting technique designed to facilitate accurate excitation-emission matrix (EEM) fluorescence measurements in field environments contaminated by ambient light. By modulating excitation sources with mutually orthogonal codes, the system effectively differentiates fluorescence signals from fluctuating background illumination through signal processing. Experimental evaluation demonstrated that the proposed modulation method reduces errors from time-variant ambient components to approximately 55-57% of those encountered using conventional subtraction methods, enhancing the accuracy of nondestructive fluorescence fingerprinting for industrial and quality assessment applications.
papers.authors: Kota Sadamoto, Shigeki Nakauchi

papers.title: Facial ambiguity and perception: How face-likeness affects breaking time in continuous flash suppression
papers.abstract: Utilizing continuous flash suppression (CFS), this study assessed the pre-conscious processing of ambiguous facial images, including binary Mooney faces and gray-scale controls. The breaking time (BT) into conscious awareness was measured for upright and inverted stimuli to test for orientation-dependent facilitation. The findings revealed that upright face-like stimuli broke suppression significantly faster than inverted or non-face stimuli, even when the image features were below the threshold for conscious identification. This provides psychophysical evidence for a specialized, orientation-tuned mechanism for rapid face detection that operates independently of conscious visual recognition.
papers.authors: Michael Makoto Martinsen, Kairi Yoshino, Yuya Kinzuka, Fumiaki Sato, Hideki Tamura, Tetsuto Minami, Shigeki Nakauchi

0614.name: Shin'ya Nishida
0614.department: Graduate School of Informatics, Department of Intelligence Science and Technology
0614.bio: Shin'ya Nishida specializes in human vision and the mechanisms of sensory information processing. Nishida’s research explores visual motion, time perception, and the perception of material properties, or "Shitsukan," to investigate how humans interpret the physical world. They employ a methodology that integrates psychophysics and neuroscience with information engineering, including computer vision and virtual reality. Their current work focuses on developing biologically plausible, image-computable models of vision and aligning human perceptual capabilities with machine learning systems.
0614.research_direction: Dr. Nishida's recent work explores the computational mechanisms underlying human visual perception, with a major focus on aligning biological motion processing with machine vision optical flow algorithms. They have recently been developing large-scale psychophysical benchmarks and dual-pathway neural network models to investigate how the visual system extracts both first- and second-order motion signals in complex, naturalistic environments. Beyond motion, their research probes the temporal dynamics of the visuomotor hierarchy by using continuous tracking paradigms to contrast spatial position tracking with feature-attribute tracking. Additionally, Dr. Nishida is investigating broader questions of perceptual organization and phenomenology, examining how global temporal correlations drive visual grouping and exploring how inattentional noise might generate the subjective illusion of uniform color across the peripheral visual field.

papers.title: Inattentional noise leads to subjective color uniformity across the visual field
papers.abstract: This research explores the psychophysical mechanisms behind the 'pan-field color illusion,' wherein observers perceive vibrant color throughout a scene despite the limited chromatic sensitivity of peripheral vision. Utilizing signal detection theory (SDT), the authors modeled the impact of visual attention on internal chromatic signal strength and stochastic variability. The empirical results and model fitting demonstrate that inattention to the peripheral visual field significantly elevates internal signal variance. This increased 'inattentional noise' raises the probability of internal signal excursions exceeding the color detection threshold, resulting in an illusory enrichment of peripheral chromatic phenomenology. These findings suggest that stochastic noise inherent in peripheral processing under inattentional conditions is a critical factor in achieving the subjective sensation of color uniformity experienced in naturalistic environments.
papers.authors: Lana Okubo, Kiyofumi Miyoshi, Kazuhiko Yokosawa, Shin'ya Nishida

papers.title: Human visual grouping based on within- and cross-area temporal correlations
papers.abstract: Perceptual organization in human vision involves mechanisms that spatially group and segment image regions based on local feature similarities, such as temporal correlations in luminance. To investigate whether these computations are global, the authors utilized a Vision Transformer (ViT)-based stimulus generation algorithm to precisely manipulate the 'temporal similarity structures' (correlations in luminance, color, and spatial phase) both within and across image regions. Psychophysical results from a temporal 2AFC task revealed that human segmentation performance is governed by the joint configuration of within-area and cross-area correlations. The strong alignment between human performance and graph-based computational model predictions suggests that human texture segmentation involves a global optimization process that integrates pairwise similarity cues across the entire visual field.
papers.authors: Yen-Ju Chen, Zitang Sun, Shin'ya Nishida

papers.title: Revealing temporal dynamics of the visuomotor system via continuous tracking of position and attribute
papers.abstract: This study employs continuous tracking psychophysics to characterize the temporal dynamics of the human visuomotor hierarchy. The researchers compared 'position tracking' (PT), which involves following a target's spatial trajectory, and 'attribute tracking' (AT), which requires reproducing continuous changes in a target feature such as luminance. By computing cross-correlograms (CCGs) to estimate temporal kernels, the study found that PT responses are faster and less sensitive to stimulus parameters than AT responses. Subsequent experiments demonstrated that AT's increased latency stems from the cognitive requirements of identifying attribute change directions and mapping them to arbitrary motor responses. Comparison with traditional reaction time metrics indicated that PT peak latencies correlate with simple reaction times, whereas AT latencies align with choice reaction times, highlighting distinct processing stages in feature-based vs. position-based motor control.
papers.authors: Yen-Ju Chen, Zitang Sun, Shin'ya Nishida

papers.title: Machine learning modelling for multi-order human visual motion processing
papers.abstract: Despite the success of deep neural networks in optical flow estimation, machine vision often fails to replicate human sensitivity to higher-order (second-order) motion features. The authors propose a dual-pathway recurrent graph network architecture designed to mimic the cortical V1-MT processing hierarchy. The model integrates a trainable motion energy sensor bank for first-order signals and a specialized sensing pathway utilizing 3D CNN blocks for nonlinear preprocessing to extract second-order signals. Training on naturalistic datasets with varied material properties revealed that the requirement to estimate object motion in complex optical environments (e.g., non-Lambertian surfaces with moving highlights) naturally drives the development of second-order motion mechanisms. The resulting model aligns with human psychophysical performance and physiological tuning while generalizing to multi-order motion phenomena in natural scenes.
papers.authors: Zitang Sun, Yen-Ju Chen, Yung-Hao Yang, Yuan Li, Shin'ya Nishida

papers.title: HuPerFlow: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Human vs. Machine Motion Estimation Comparison
papers.abstract: The alignment between machine optical flow algorithms and human motion perception remains largely unquantified in naturalistic contexts. The authors introduce HuPerFlow, a large-scale benchmark comprising approximately 38,400 response vectors collected via online psychophysical experiments across 2,400 locations in ten standard optical flow datasets. The data indicate that while human-perceived flow aligns with ground truth in spatiotemporally smooth regions, it exhibits systematic deviations and errors in complex environments influenced by specific stimulus properties. By evaluating several state-of-the-art computer vision algorithms against this human-perceived flow benchmark, the study uncovers unique characteristics of human motion phenomenology and provides a framework for developing AI models that are perceptually aligned with biological vision.
papers.authors: Yung-Hao Yang, Zitang Sun, Taiki Fukiage, Shin'ya Nishida

0615.name: Shinsuke Shimojo
0615.department: Division of Biology and Biological Engineering
0615.bio: Shinsuke Shimojo is the Gertrude Baltimore Professor of Experimental Psychology at Caltech and investigates the psychophysical and neural mechanisms underlying human perception and decision-making. Shimojo's research explores implicit brain functions, crossmodal integration, and the resolution of perceptual ambiguity using techniques such as fMRI, EEG, and transcranial brain stimulation. They study the 'social brain' through investigations into interpersonal synchrony and the neural correlates of 'team flow.' Their current work examines the dynamic interactions between predictive and postdictive neural processes and the influence of subliminal sensory information on conscious preference.
0615.research_direction: Dr. Shimojo has recently been investigating the computational mechanisms of crossmodal perception, applying Bayesian causal inference models to probe how the brain resolves sensory uncertainty using audiovisual illusions in low-vision populations and at the physiological blind spot. Their recent work also explores the role of intrinsic neural rhythms as individual cognitive fingerprints, using high-density EEG and hyperscanning to examine the oscillatory basis of spontaneous motor tempo and to map stable neural traits during real-time social cooperation. Additionally, they are investigating the temporal aspects of awareness and self-evaluation, testing whether subjective experiences like an athlete's predictive "sixth sense" are driven by genuine foresight or by postdictive memory reconstruction.

papers.title: A hierarchical trait and state model for decoding dyadic social interactions
papers.abstract: This study introduces a hierarchical trait-state framework to distinguish between stable, inter-individual neural signatures (traits) and transient, task-dependent neural modulations (states) during real-time social cooperation. Utilizing EEG hyperscanning within a "team flow" music-rhythm paradigm, the authors applied a two-stage dimensionality reduction pipeline consisting of non-negative matrix factorization (NMF) followed by linear discriminant analysis (LDA) to extract a seven-dimensional latent brain space. The results demonstrated a trait-state hierarchy characterized by macro-segregation of latent dimensions representing neural traits and micro-segregation representing task-states. Representational similarity analysis (RSA) established a significant mapping between these EEG latent dimensions and behavioral skill-cognition metrics, indicating that individual neural fingerprints determine the capacity for achieving collective flow states.
papers.authors: Qianying Wu, Shigeki Nakauchi, Mohammad Shehata, Shinsuke Shimojo

papers.title: Did you see the sound? A Bayesian Perspective on Crossmodal Perception in Low Vision
papers.abstract: The paper examines multisensory integration in low-vision populations through the lens of Bayesian Causal Inference (BCI). Employing the Double Flash Illusion across 24 visual-field locations, the authors determined that low vision does not induce a global amplification of audiovisual interactions. Instead, the magnitude of sound-induced visual percepts was strongly predicted by local visual reliability and flash-detection sensitivity. BCI modeling indicated that low-vision observers exhibited weaker and more variable alignment with Bayesian-optimal predictions, characterized by broader visual likelihoods. These findings suggest that the brain maintains perceptual stability in the presence of sensory degradation by re-weighting internal uncertainty parameters rather than fundamentally altering the underlying computational architecture of multisensory inference.
papers.authors: Ailene Y. C. Chan, Noelle R. B. Stiles, Carmel A. Levitan, Armand R. Tanguay Jr., Shinsuke Shimojo

papers.title: Bayesian Causal Inference Accounts for Multisensory Filling-In at the Blind Spot
papers.abstract: This research investigates the neuro-computational mechanisms of multisensory filling-in at the physiological blind spot using a variant of the sound-induced flash illusion (the 'AV rabbit'). By applying Bayesian Causal Inference (BCI) modeling to compare perception across the blind spot and visible control regions, the authors found that the phenomenological strength of the illusion was preserved despite the total absence of feedforward retinal input. However, modeling revealed systematic shifts toward broader visual likelihoods and flattened sensory priors at the blind spot location. The results suggest that the brain sustains perceptual continuity across retinal gaps by flexibly re-weighting internal uncertainty estimates within a stable, probabilistic causal-inference framework.
papers.authors: Ailene Y. C. Chan, Noelle R. B. Stiles, Carmel A. Levitan, Daw-An Wu, Armand R. Tanguay Jr., Shinsuke Shimojo

papers.title: Natural finger-tapping tempo reflects intrinsic neuropsychological characteristics
papers.abstract: This study evaluates whether an individual’s spontaneous motor tempo (SMT) represents an overt manifestation of an intrinsic neural oscillator. Employing high-density EEG during unconstrained and externally paced finger-tapping tasks, the authors identified that individual motor tempos align with the peak frequency of delta/theta-band oscillations in the primary motor cortex. Performance at the natural SMT was uniquely associated with attenuated frontal error-related negativity (Ne) and enhanced parietal alpha power and default mode network (DMN) activity, indicating a state of reduced cognitive control and increased neural relaxation. These findings suggest that natural motor tempo serves as a stable cognitive 'fingerprint' reflecting intrinsic rhythms of the human brain.
papers.authors: Sai Sun, Daw-An Wu, Mohammad Shehata, Takuya Akashi, Morimichi Furudate, Chao Zhang, Ken-Ichiro Tsutsui, Satoshi Shioiri, Shinsuke Shimojo

papers.title: Is Athletes' Sixth Sense Real, or a Postdictive Reconstruction?
papers.abstract: This study investigates whether the 'sixth sense' reported by athletes—specifically the perceived ability to predict game outcomes—represents a genuine prospective prediction or a postdictive memory reconstruction. In a study of 113 athletes utilizing pre- and post-game questionnaires, the researchers observed that over 60% of participants revised their remembered predictions to align with actual performance outcomes. Crucially, victors revised their predictions toward more positive expectations, while defeated participants shifted theirs toward negative ones. This outcome-dependent memory distortion suggests that athletes' intuitive foresight is predominantly a postdictive phenomenon, reflecting the reconstructive nature of memory in self-evaluation and the maintenance of a consistent narrative of agency.
papers.venue: International Journal of Sport and Health Science
papers.authors: Koji Kadota, Motoki Okumura, Shinsuke Shimojo

0617.name: Shlomit Yuval-Greenberg
0617.department: School of Psychological Sciences and Sagol School of Neuroscience
0617.bio: Yuval-Greenberg is an Associate Professor at Tel Aviv University investigating the relationship between the oculomotor system and cognitive processes such as visual perception, attention, and memory. Their research uses a multimodal approach, combining eye tracking with electroencephalography (EEG) and functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) to examine eye movements as biomarkers for temporal expectation and cues for memory retrieval. Yuval-Greenberg has characterized the link between pre-stimulus oculomotor inhibition and expectation deficits in ADHD and developed methods for identifying and suppressing ocular artifacts in EEG recordings. Their current work focuses on the neural mechanisms of visual awareness and the integration of motor and visual components in episodic memory.
0617.research_direction: Dr. Yuval-Greenberg's recent work explores how oculomotor dynamics and pupillary responses serve as continuous markers for a broad range of perceptual and cognitive processes. They have recently been investigating the interplay between active vision and mental storage, specifically asking how the ability to freely execute eye movements minimizes visual working memory load in favor of external environment resampling. Their research also probes the mechanisms of temporal expectation and attentional control, using prestimulus oculomotor inhibition to study how prior environmental noise influences temporal learning flexibility, while tracking post-stimulus saccadic rate modulation to assess age-related differences in reactive inhibition and top-down exploration. Additionally, they are examining whether tonic and phasic pupil fluctuations can track internal lapses in auditory sustained attention, and how an observer's higher-order interpretation of another person's mental state modulates the classically reflexive gaze-cueing effect.

papers.title: When exploration replaces storage: how eye movements shape visual working memory
papers.abstract: This research investigates the tradeoff between internal visual working memory (VWM) storage and external perceptual resampling during naturalistic visual exploration. Traditional VWM paradigms constrain oculomotor behavior, potentially overestimating reliance on mental storage. Utilizing a target-matching task (inspired by the game Dobble), the study contrasted a simultaneous-display condition allowing free eye movements with a sequential-display condition requiring manual switches. Results indicated that when visual information can be accessed via eye movements, participants strategically minimize VWM load in favor of frequent, low-cost environment resampling. Conversely, manual-switching costs prompted a shift toward higher VWM utilization. These findings suggest that the functional architecture of VWM is fundamentally shaped by the ease of oculomotor access, supporting a model where exploration replaces storage in ecological vision.
papers.authors: Rania Qais, Robert T. Knight, Shlomit Yuval-Greenberg

papers.title: Keeping an eye on attentive listening: Task-evoked pupil size unveils fluctuations in auditory sustained attention
papers.abstract: This study utilized pupillometry to track fluctuations in sustained attention during a demanding auditory task. By analyzing tonic and phasic pupillary dynamics, the researchers aimed to identify physiological precursors to attentional lapses. Results demonstrated a robust linear relationship between baseline (tonic) pupil diameter and performance metrics, including reaction time (RT) variability and error rates. Attentional lapses were significantly associated with reduced tonic pupil size and attenuated task-evoked (phasic) dilations. Furthermore, individual differences in sustained attention capacity were reflected in the stability of pupil size across the session. These findings establish pupillary responses as a sensitive biomarker for internal alertness and the maintenance of focus in the auditory domain, suggesting potential applications in real-time attention monitoring.
papers.authors: Yarden Dankner, Lilach Shalev, Shlomit Yuval-Greenberg

papers.title: The post-stimulus modulation of the saccade rate reflects inhibitory control and top-down exploration in young and aging populations
papers.abstract: This investigation explored how aging influences the temporal dynamics of the saccadic rate modulation (SRM) following the presentation of new visual stimuli. SRM typically involves an initial inhibition phase followed by a rebound. The study hypothesized that inhibition reflects midbrain-mediated reactive control, while the rebound reflects cortical top-down exploratory drive. Comparing young adults to an elderly cohort, findings revealed that aging specifically shortens the duration of the post-stimulus inhibition phase, indicating a decline in inhibitory control. Additionally, while younger participants showed a significant rebound modulation by stimulus familiarity (familiar vs. unfamiliar objects), this top-down exploratory signature was attenuated in the aging population. The results suggest that oculomotor rate metrics provide a differentiable index for assessing age-related declines in distinct cognitive and neural control mechanisms.
papers.authors: Orit Shdeour, Shlomit Yuval-Greenberg

papers.title: The interpretation attributed to observed gaze shifts affects their social-cueing effect
papers.abstract: This paper examines the flexibility of the gaze-cueing effect (GCE), the reflexive shift of attention triggered by observing another individual's gaze shift. In two preregistered experiments, the authors tested whether the GCE is sensitive to the observer's interpretation of the actor's mental state. Participants viewed videos of gaze shifts while performing a peripheral target detection task, with experimental groups primed to interpret the gaze as either an attentional shift toward an external object or an indicator of internal cognitive processing ('thinking'). The results showed that the GCE was significantly suppressed when gaze shifts were attributed to internal processing. These findings demonstrate that social-attentional mechanisms are not purely reflexive but are modulated by higher-order social-cognitive interpretations and contextual framing.
papers.authors: Amit Zehngut, Shlomit Yuval-Greenberg

papers.title: Exposure to temporal variability promotes subsequent adaptation to new temporal regularities
papers.abstract: The study investigated the impact of prior temporal context on the acquisition of new temporal expectations. Using the prestimulus oculomotor inhibition effect as a biomarker for temporal orienting, participants were initially exposed to either a fixed (low-variability) or a random (high-variability) temporal context before transitioning to a new fixed regularity. Computational modeling and behavioral data revealed that individuals previously exposed to temporal noise adapted significantly faster to the new regularity than those coming from a stable context. The researchers argue that high temporal variability prevents the cognitive system from overfitting to local statistics, thereby promoting learning flexibility and generalizability. This suggests that environmental noise plays a functional role in optimizing the mechanisms of temporal expectation formation.
papers.authors: Orit Shdeour, Noam Tal-Perry, Moshe Glickman, Shlomit Yuval-Greenberg

0618.name: Shruti Japee
0618.bio: Shruti Japee is a Senior Associate Scientist in the Laboratory of Brain and Cognition at the National Institute of Mental Health. Japee’s research examines the neural mechanisms of emotion processing, with a focus on how the brain perceives and responds to facial and body expressions. By employing neuroimaging modalities such as fMRI and MEG alongside behavioral tasks, Japee investigates the functional connectivity between visual areas like the superior temporal sulcus and subcortical structures like the amygdala.
