Their work aims to characterize the neural correlates of emotional attention and the individual differences that modulate social and affective perception.
0618.research_direction: Dr. Japee's recent work explores the behavioral and neural mechanisms underlying how we perceive facial expressions, examining both human and non-human primate models. Using psychophysics and fMRI in individuals with Moebius syndrome—a condition causing congenital facial paralysis—they have recently been investigating whether the ability to physically execute facial movements is necessary for typical visual sensitivity to emotions and activity in affective neural networks. Additionally, their research probes the representational architecture of face processing in awake macaques, testing whether the inferior temporal cortex is tuned to specific morphological features or broader socio-emotional contexts. They are also utilizing representational similarity analysis to compare primate face patches against task-optimized deep neural networks, asking whether facial identity and changeable expressions are processed via segregated anatomical streams or jointly encoded in the visual system.

papers.title: On the Role of Sensorimotor Experience in Facial Expression Perception
papers.abstract: Visual perception of conspecific facial expressions operates rapidly and with high fidelity, yet the extent to which this faculty depends causally on sensorimotor embodiment remains contentious. This article examines three theoretical frameworks linking facial motor execution to visual expression decoding: motor simulation theory, the facial feedback hypothesis, and clinical models of facial paralysis. Motor simulation posits that visual categorization is mediated by covert recruitment of premotor and somatosensory circuits, whereas the facial feedback hypothesis argues that afferent proprioceptive signaling from facial musculature dynamically modulates affective experience. Evaluating empirical psychophysical evidence from individuals with Moebius syndrome (MBS), who present with congenital bilateral facial palsy, reveals elevated perceptual detection thresholds specifically across happy, fearful, and angry facial displays despite intact performance on non-affective visual control tasks. Integrating these psychophysical outcomes with functional neuroimaging data showing altered engagement of the posterior superior temporal sulcus (pSTS) and amygdala, the author argues that facial sensorimotor experience developmentally calibrates sensitivity within cortical and subcortical face-processing pathways.
papers.authors: Shruti Japee

papers.title: Real Face Value: The Processing of Naturalistic Facial Expressions in the Macaque Inferior Temporal Cortex
papers.abstract: While canonical fearful facial expressions reliably drive blood oxygen level-dependent (BOLD) valence effects in primate inferior temporal (IT) cortex under laboratory conditions, rhesus macaques exhibit 'fear grins' across varied socio-emotional settings, questioning whether IT cortex is tuned to morphological facial action units or to contextual communicative signals. Awake macaques were scanned using monocrystalline iron oxide nanoparticle (MION) contrast-enhanced high-field fMRI at 4.7T while viewing conspecific expressions defined either by contextual affect (calm vs. threatening contexts) or by specific featural action units (neutral vs. prototypical fear grins), alongside human facial displays. Voxel-wise regression demonstrated that conspecific expressions defined by socio-emotional context drove significantly stronger valence modulation in IT cortex than stimuli selected strictly by morphological action units, whereas human expressions elicited minimal valence effects. A two-alternative forced-choice behavioral task corroborated that fear grins systematically differ in perceived pleasantness across communicative settings. These results demonstrate that macaque IT cortex represents emergent socio-emotional meaning rather than isolated geometric facial features.
papers.authors: Jessica Taubert, Shruti Japee

papers.title: Inability to move one's face dampens facial expression perception
papers.abstract: Embodied simulation models propose that recognizing the emotional expressions of others relies on covert motor mimicry and somatic feedback. To investigate whether congenital inability to execute facial movements impairs perceptual sensitivity to emotional expressions, a battery of psychophysical tasks was administered to individuals with Moebius syndrome (MBS)—a rare congenital cranial dysinnervation disorder characterized by sixth and seventh cranial nerve paralysis—and demographically matched neurotypical controls. Participants performed threshold detection tasks across static and dynamic facial and bodily expressions alongside non-emotional visual control tasks. While MBS individuals demonstrated preserved capacity to detect basic facial feature transformations (e.g., mouth aperture), they exhibited significantly elevated 50% detection thresholds for happy, fearful, and angry facial expressions. MBS participants further showed selective impairments in facial motion processing, while whole-body motion perception remained intact despite dampened extraction of affective information from body movements. Exploratory fMRI during expression matching demonstrated blunted activation within the posterior superior temporal sulcus (pSTS) and attenuated amygdala reactivity in MBS participants relative to controls, indicating that congenital facial immobility selectively impairs visual sensitivity to emotional expressions and alters corresponding affective neural networks.
papers.authors: Shruti Japee, Jessica Jordan, Judith Licht, Savannah Lokey, Moebius Syndrome Research Consortium, Gang Chen, Joseph Snow, Ethylin Wang Jabs, Bryn D. Webb, Elizabeth C. Engle, Irini Manoli, Chris Baker, Leslie G. Ungerleider

papers.title: Equivalent processing of facial expression and identity by macaque visual system and task-optimized neural network
papers.abstract: Dual-stream neurobiological models of face perception hypothesize anatomical and functional segregation between invariant identity recognition (traditionally mapped to the ventral stream) and changeable expression processing (attributed to the superior temporal sulcus). To characterize the representational architecture underlying identity and expression coding, awake rhesus macaques were imaged using high-field fMRI during exposure to a extensive database of conspecific faces systematically varying in facial identity and expression category (neutral, fearful, aggressive, and appeasing), alongside task-optimized deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs). Representational similarity analysis (RSA) and cross-validated multivariate pattern decoding revealed that facial identity and expression signals are jointly encoded across macaque face patches (including middle and anterior fundal/lateral face areas) rather than strictly segregating into separate anatomical routes. Furthermore, deep neural networks concurrently optimized for identity and expression categorization recapitulated the representational geometry and hierarchical layer progression observed across the macaque ventral face system, demonstrating convergent computational principles between primate visual cortex and task-constrained artificial networks.
papers.authors: Hui Zhang, Xuetong Ding, Ning Liu, Rachel Nolan, Leslie G. Ungerleider, Shruti Japee

0620.name: Shui'er Han
0620.bio: Shui'er Han is a vision scientist and researcher at the Institute for Infocomm Research (I2R) within Singapore's Agency for Science, Technology and Research (A*STAR). Han’s research focuses on the mechanisms of binocular vision and the impact of prior experience on sensory perception, specifically regarding dichoptic stimulation and continuous flash suppression (CFS). They have characterized the temporal frequency tuning of visual suppression and utilize techniques such as psychophysical modeling and Virtual Reality to examine visual awareness. Han's work involves translating vision science into applications, including vision multiplexing configurations for augmented reality devices and assistive technologies for the visually impaired.
0620.research_direction: Dr. Han's recent work explores a diverse array of topics spanning binocular vision, multisensory development, and artificial intelligence. They have recently been investigating the ecological validity and practical consequences of binocular rivalry, utilizing virtual reality to probe interocular suppression under naturalistic 3D occlusion geometries and assessing how visual conflict impacts navigation with augmented reality head-mounted displays. To further support interocular suppression research, they have developed open-source software for the precise spatiotemporal generation of continuous flash suppression stimuli. Additionally, they are examining the developmental trajectories of audio-visual temporal precision in children, as well as benchmarking commercial vision-language models against human normative datasets to evaluate the models' capacity for low- and high-level perceptual organization and visual reasoning.

papers.title: To what extent do VLMs visually reason like humans?
papers.abstract: The study systematically benchmarks the perceptual organization and visual reasoning capabilities of three leading commercial Vision-Language Models (VLMs)—GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, and Gemini 1.5 Pro—against human normative data. Utilizing a comprehensive battery of 51 tests derived from clinical and experimental frameworks, including the Birmingham Object Recognition Battery (BORB), the Leuven Perceptual Organization Test (L-POST), and the MindSet dataset, the researchers evaluated the models across low-, mid-, and high-level vision. Quantitative analysis revealed that while VLMs demonstrate human-competitive or superior performance in high-level object recognition tasks, they exhibit significant deficits in low-level perceptual tasks involving orientation, spatial position, and occlusion, properties that are trivial for biological vision systems.
papers.authors: Shui'er Han, Chui Mae Wong, Laura Arden-Gardner, Chuanchu Wang

papers.title: Binocular rivalry under naturalistic geometry: Evidence from worlds simulated in virtual reality
papers.abstract: This research investigates the external validity of binocular rivalry (BR) by examining whether interocular suppression persists under geometrically plausible conditions typical of natural vision. Using virtual reality (VR), the authors simulated a cue-rich 3D-corridor to present rival stimuli in layouts ranging from geometrically implausible (traditional laboratory setups) to plausible (simulating naturalistic monocular occlusion). Psychophysical tracking of perceptual fluctuations demonstrated that canonical BR alternations occur reliably regardless of geometrical plausibility or stimulus type (static vs. moving). 3D modeling further confirmed that interocular conflicts arising from occlusion are common in natural scenes, suggesting that the mechanisms of binocular rivalry are fundamental to everyday vision rather than being laboratory artifacts of dichoptic stimulation.
papers.authors: Shui'er Han, Randolph Blake, Celine Aubuchon, Duje Tadin

papers.title: The effect of visual rivalry in peripheral head-mounted displays on mobility
papers.abstract: This study evaluates the impact of vision multiplexing—the superimposition of augmented information over a natural field of view—on target visibility in peripheral head-mounted displays (HMDs). The authors compared three multiplexing configurations (unilateral opaque, unilateral see-through, and bilateral see-through) while varying target eccentricity, depth, and gaze behavior to simulate real-world mobility. Results indicated that unilateral configurations suffer from significantly reduced target detection rates due to binocular rivalry between the augmented display and the background scene viewed by the fellow eye. Conversely, bilateral see-through configurations, which minimize interocular conflict, yielded the highest visibility. These findings provide empirical recommendations for the design of optical vision aids and wearable displays to mitigate perceptual suppression during navigation.
papers.authors: Shui'er Han, Sujin Kim, Jae-Hyun Jung

papers.title: The development of audio–visual temporal precision precedes its rapid recalibration
papers.abstract: The authors investigate the developmental trajectory of multisensory temporal precision and rapid temporal recalibration in children (ages 5–11) and adults. By re-analyzing datasets across audio–visual, audio–tactile, and visual–tactile pairings, the study reveals that audio–visual temporal precision achieves adult-like levels before the emergence of rapid recalibration, which first appears around age 9. In contrast, rapid recalibration was found to be notably absent or significantly weaker in other cross-modal combinations across all age groups. These results suggest a developmental dissociation where temporal precision acts as a prerequisite for the maturation of malleable recalibration mechanisms, likely evolved to accommodate distance-dependent propagation delays between light and sound.
papers.authors: Shui'er Han, Yi-Chuan Chen, Daphne Maurer, David I. Shore, Terri L. Lewis, Brendan M. Stanley, David Alais

papers.title: CFS-crafter: An open-source tool for creating and analyzing images for continuous flash suppression experiments
papers.abstract: Addressing the need for standardized stimulus control in interocular suppression research, the authors present CFS-crafter, a point-and-click open-source toolbox designed for the creation and analysis of continuous flash suppression (CFS) stimuli. The tool allows researchers to precisely manipulate the spatiotemporal properties of Mondrian maskers and target images, which are critical determinants of suppression strength. CFS-crafter facilitates the matching of mask and target features, such as spatial frequency and orientation bandwidth, to optimize suppression depth. By providing a streamlined workflow for stimulus generation and Fourier-based image analysis, the software aims to improve the reproducibility and comparability of findings across basic and clinical vision science studies.
papers.authors: Guandong Wang, David Alais, Randolph Blake, Shui'Er Han

0621.name: Shuo Wang
0621.bio: Shuo Wang is an Associate Professor of Radiology and Neurological Surgery who investigates the neural mechanisms of social attention, face processing, and decision-making. Wang’s research utilizes a multimodal approach, integrating human single-neuron recordings, eye tracking, fMRI, and computational modeling to examine how the brain processes socially relevant stimuli. Their work characterizes atypical neural encoding and visual saliency in individuals with autism spectrum disorder to facilitate clinical interventions.
0621.research_direction: Dr. Wang has recently been investigating the neural dynamics underlying goal-directed visual attention and object recognition in both humans and macaques. Using large-scale intracranial electrophysiology and rare human single-neuron recordings, their recent work explores how distributed networks across the visual cortex, medial temporal lobe, and prefrontal cortex coordinate to support active vision during naturalistic free-gaze search tasks. Specifically, they are examining how cross-regional oscillatory synchronization and low-dimensional population trajectories integrate perceptual input with top-down task demands to guide attentional control. Additionally, their research probes the spatiotemporal encoding of visual, semantic, and intrinsic memorability features, mapping how high-dimensional object representations are computationally transformed into stable episodic memories.

papers.title: Computational neural dynamics of goal-directed visual attention in macaques
papers.abstract: This study employs large-scale neural population recordings from cortical areas V4, IT, OFC, and LPFC in macaque monkeys performing a free-gaze visual search task with naturalistic stimuli. The researchers identify distinct neural subspaces specialized for encoding category-specific task goals and stimulus features. By examining dynamics within an orthogonal subspace of the neural state space, the authors demonstrate that foveal attention enhances peripheral representations through increased pattern separation and context-dependent geometric reshaping. The findings reveal that pre-search cue-related activity predicts subsequent search efficiency and that low-dimensional population trajectories integrate task demands with perceptual input to coordinate goal-directed attention.
papers.authors: Jie Zhang, Nuttida Rungratsameetaweemana, Shuo Wang

papers.title: Characterization of the spatiotemporal representations of visual, semantic, and memorability features in the human brain
papers.abstract: Utilizing high-resolution intracranial electroencephalography (iEEG) from 5,143 channels, this research maps the spatiotemporal neural encoding of visual, semantic, and memorability features during object perception. The study demonstrates that while the ventral temporal cortex (VTC) processes all three attributes, they exhibit distinct temporal trajectories: visual features emerge first, followed by semantic and then memorability information. Cross-modal validation using 7T fMRI and single-neuron recordings from the medial temporal lobe (MTL) reveals that memorability is an intrinsic stimulus property encoded early in the visual hierarchy. The results further indicate that prefrontal cortex representations of memorability arise from the integration of VTC signals, suggesting an integrated computational pathway connecting perception and memory.
papers.authors: Yue Wang, Peter Brunner, Jon T. Willie, Runnan Cao, Shuo Wang

papers.title: Gamma synchronization between the medial temporal lobe and medial frontal cortex for goal-directed visual attention in humans
papers.abstract: The study investigates the long-range coordination between the human medial temporal lobe (MTL) and medial frontal cortex (MFC) using simultaneous single-neuron and local field potential (LFP) recordings. During a goal-directed visual search, the researchers identified target-dependent gamma-band synchronization (30–80 Hz) as a primary mechanism for attentional control. Specifically, the amygdala shows enhanced spike-LFP phase-locking with the dACC during goal maintenance (working memory), while dACC spiking synchronizes with MTL LFPs during target detection and decision execution. These findings delineate a functional circuit where task-dependent oscillatory synchronization facilitates the alignment of representational geometry across frontal and temporal nodes to support active vision.
papers.authors: Jie Zhang, Jing Xia, Huihui Zhou, Shuo Wang

papers.title: A neuronal code for object representation and memory in the human amygdala and hippocampus
papers.abstract: Through recordings of 3,173 single neurons in neurosurgical patients, this paper identifies a 'region-based feature code' for visual objects within the human amygdala and hippocampus. Unlike sparse category-selective coding, these neurons exhibit receptive fields in a high-dimensional semantic feature space, enabling the flexible representation of diverse stimuli. The study demonstrates that the strength of this region-based neural response during encoding predicts successful memory retrieval and parametrically tracks image memorability. These results provide a unified framework for how the medial temporal lobe (MTL) transforms high-level visual features into stable representations that serve as the building blocks for episodic and semantic memory.
papers.authors: Runnan Cao, Peter Brunner, Puneeth N. Chakravarthula, Krista L. Wahlstrom, Cory Inman, Elliot H. Smith, Xin Li, Adam N. Mamelak, Nicholas J. Brandmeir, Ueli Rutishauser, Jon T. Willie, Shuo Wang

papers.title: A human single-neuron dataset for object recognition
papers.abstract: This data descriptor provides a large-scale dataset of single-neuron activity recorded from the human amygdala and hippocampus of 15 neurosurgical patients. The resource includes spike-sorted unit activity and synchronized intracranial LFP data from 1,716 neurons across multiple experiments using ImageNet and Microsoft COCO stimuli. The dataset captures neural responses during passive viewing and memory tasks, providing unprecedented spatial and temporal resolution for investigating category selectivity, sparse coding, and representational transformations in the medial temporal lobe. The released data, including electrode localization in MNI space and behavioral metrics, is intended to facilitate the development and validation of biologically constrained computational models of human object recognition.
papers.authors: Runnan Cao, Peter Brunner, Nicholas J. Brandmeir, Jon T. Willie, Shuo Wang

0622.name: Simona Buetti
0622.bio: Simona Buetti is a Research Associate Professor at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign and co-directs the Vision Lab. Their research investigates the cognitive and neural mechanisms of visual attention and perception using behavioral psychophysics, eye-tracking, and computational modeling. Buetti’s research on parallel visual processing demonstrates that visual search efficiency is often governed by logarithmic reaction time functions rather than purely serial mechanisms. Their current work examines how target-distractor distinctiveness across multiple feature dimensions—such as color, shape, and texture—is integrated to guide attentional prioritization and how background complexity influences distractor rejection times.
0622.research_direction: Dr. Buetti has recently been investigating the mechanisms of attentional guidance during visual search, focusing on how the visual system integrates multiple feature dimensions—such as color, shape, and surface texture—to determine target distinctiveness. Their recent work employs behavioral-computational frameworks and eye-tracking to explore the temporal interplay between bottom-up physical salience and top-down goal-directed attention during early saccadic programming. Additionally, they are examining how explicit task instructions dynamically modulate the attentional weights assigned to specific feature channels during multidimensional parallel search tasks. Furthermore, they are exploring the quantitative relationship between search efficiency and perceptual similarity, testing psychophysical models like Target-Contrast Signal Theory to understand how representational distance in a given feature space governs overt search behavior.

papers.title: Toward a Better Understanding of Target Distinctiveness in Visual Search: How Color, Shape, and Texture Information Combine to Guide Search
papers.abstract: The current investigation employs a behavioral-computational framework to elucidate how visual distinctiveness signals from multiple feature dimensions—specifically color, shape, and surface texture—are integrated to drive attentional guidance in tridimensional visual search tasks. Across a series of experiments, we contrast distinctiveness combination rules observed in bidimensional searches (where color and shape combine collinearly, whereas shape and texture combine orthogonally) to predict search efficiency when targets differ from distractors along all three dimensions simultaneously. Results indicate that the human visual system dynamically reweights these dimensional signals based on their relative task utility, with tridimensional distinctiveness best modeled by a weighted orthogonal combination of color and shape/texture signals. These findings suggest that feature-based attention is flexibly allocated across feature channels to optimize search performance in ecologically complex environments.
papers.authors: Zoe Jing Xu, Alejandro Lleras, Simona Buetti

papers.title: Evaluating the contributions of top-down and bottom-up processing on eye movements during parallel visual search
papers.abstract: This study investigates the interplay between top-down goal-directed attention and bottom-up stimulus-driven salience using eye-tracking in a pseudo-realistic search environment. By manipulating target-distractor similarity and the presence of high-salience singletons, we quantified the selectivity of initial and subsequent fixations toward task-relevant versus physically salient items. Our results demonstrate that while high-salience distractors exert a robust bottom-up capture effect during free-viewing conditions, this capture is significantly attenuated under top-down search instructions. Crucially, the data reveal that early saccadic programming is characterized by a temporal 'limbo' where selectivity toward the target evolves as a function of saccade latency, confirming that even in parallel search paradigms, efficient eye-movement guidance requires the temporal accumulation of feature-based evidence to overcome initial salience-driven biases.
papers.authors: Howard Jia He Tan, Alejandro Lleras, Zoe Jing Xu, Yifan Ding, Simona Buetti

papers.title: Quantifying the relationship between search efficiency and perceptual similarity in color space across different efficient search tasks
papers.abstract: We systematically evaluate the mathematical relationship between perceptual similarity in color space and parallel visual search efficiency to test competing accounts of attentional guidance. Using a well-defined color wheel, we compared the Universal Law of Generalization with Target-Contrast Signal Theory (TCST) by measuring search slopes across varying target-distractor color distances. Results show that search efficiency is best predicted by a model where the contrast signal is indexed by the perceptual distance when distractor identity is unpredictable, whereas a Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR) model better accounts for performance when distractor features are known. The findings demonstrate that search performance is linearly constrained by the representational distance between target and distractor templates, providing a quantitative bridge between psychophysical color discrimination and overt search behavior.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
papers.authors: Alejandro Lleras, Zoe Jing Xu, Howard Jia He Tan, Yujie Shao, Simona Buetti

papers.title: Top-down instructions influence the attentional weight on color and shape dimensions during bidimensional search
papers.abstract: Utilizing a predictive modeling approach, this research examines how explicit top-down instructions modulate the integration of color and shape signals during bidimensional parallel search. Previous work established that these dimensions combine following a city-block (collinear) metric when both are expected to be useful. Here, we show that instructing participants to prioritize a specific dimension (e.g., 'search for red') significantly increases the attentional weight assigned to that dimension, thereby altering the resulting search efficiency in redundant displays. Our computational analysis reveals that while the underlying city-block architecture of signal integration remains stable, the specific coefficients (attentional weights) applied to each dimension are highly malleable to top-down task demands, demonstrating a sophisticated mechanism for optimizing the target-distractor contrast signal.
papers.authors: Zoe Jing Xu, Alejandro Lleras, Zixu Gavin Gong, Simona Buetti

0624.name: Simona Monaco
0624.bio: Monaco is a researcher at the Center for Mind/Brain Sciences (CIMeC) at the University of Trento and directs the MonACo Action and Cognition Lab. Their research examines the neural mechanisms involved in integrating multisensory information, such as visual, haptic, and auditory cues, to plan and execute goal-directed motor actions. Using high-field functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and behavioral measurements, Monaco investigates how action-specific intentions influence processing within the early visual cortex and parieto-frontal networks. Their methodology includes multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) and graph theory to decode cortical representations of object features and motor strategies across the dorsal and ventral visual streams.
0624.research_direction: Dr. Monaco's recent work explores the neural mechanisms underlying sensory-motor integration, object perception, and action planning. Using fMRI and multivariate pattern analysis, they have recently been investigating how object properties like size are represented in early visual and frontoparietal cortices during haptic exploration versus mental imagery. Their research also utilizes EEG and masked priming paradigms to study embodied cognition, specifically asking whether subliminally presented action verbs can automatically prime manual grasping circuits without conscious awareness. Additionally, Dr. Monaco is examining the clinical applications of these perceptual and motor frameworks, exploring how the dual-visual stream hypothesis can inform the use of non-invasive brain stimulation and targeted neuromodulation to enhance neurorehabilitation.

papers.title: Decoding haptic and imagined stimulus size in the human cortex
papers.abstract: This neuroimaging study employed multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) to investigate the neural representation of object size during haptic exploration and mental imagery. Functional MRI data from blindfolded participants performing haptic exploration or size imagery of three differently sized rings demonstrated that the primary visual cortex (V1) and occipital pole (OP) contain accurate decodable information regarding stimulus size during tactile exploration but not during imagery, suggesting that haptic V1 activity is not simply a product of visual imagery. In contrast, frontal and parietal regions, including the anterior and posterior intraparietal sulcus (aIPS, pIPS) and dorsal premotor cortex (dPM), as well as the multisensory lateral occipital tactile-visual area (LOtv), supported size representations across both haptic and imagery tasks. Psychophysiological interaction (PPI) analysis revealed that V1 and OP exhibit significantly stronger functional connectivity with ventral and dorsal visual stream areas during haptic tasks compared to imagery, indicating task-dependent modulation of early visual processing for object properties.
papers.authors: Samantha Sartin, Federica Danaj, Fabio Del Giudice, Juan Chen, Dietrich Samuel Schwarzkopf, Irene Sperandio, Simona Monaco

papers.title: Recent Trends in Physical Therapy Interventions and Neuromodulation Techniques to Improve Neurorehabilitation
papers.abstract: This comprehensive review examines current advancements in physical therapy and non-invasive brain stimulation (NIBS) for neurorehabilitation. The article evaluates the efficacy of traditional physical interventions alongside modern technologies such as Virtual Reality (VR), Brain-Computer Interfaces (BCI), and transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS). A particular focus is placed on the dual-visual stream hypothesis—the specialization of the ventral stream for perception and the dorsal stream for action—as a neuroanatomical framework for understanding motor recovery and cognitive rehabilitation. The authors synthesize recent findings on neuroplasticity, emphasizing how targeted neuromodulation can exploit the interactions between sensory pathways and the motor system to enhance outcomes in patients with stroke, traumatic brain injury, and neurodegenerative disorders. The review identifies critical research gaps and proposes future directions for personalizing neurorehabilitation protocols based on individual neuroplastic responses.
papers.authors: Patralika Nath, Debanjan Banerjee, Manas Ranjan Panigrahi, Priyanka Singh, Samantha Sartin, Mariagrazia Ranzini, Cristina Scarpazza, Simona Monaco

papers.title: Subliminal Semantic Processing of Grasping Actions: Evidence from ERP Measures of Action-Verb Priming
papers.abstract: This study utilized Event-Related Potentials (ERPs) to investigate whether subliminally presented action-related verbs can prime the neural mechanisms involved in manual grasping. Using a masked priming paradigm, participants were exposed to action verbs (e.g., 'grasp') or non-action verbs followed by a target action task. Electrophysiological results indicated that action verbs modulated early ERP components associated with semantic processing and motor preparation even when stimuli were presented below the threshold of conscious awareness. Specifically, priming effects were observed in the modulation of the N400 component and early motor-related potentials, suggesting that the motor system is sensitive to linguistically encoded action concepts through automatic, bottom-up activation. These findings provide evidence for the embodiment of language, demonstrating that semantic information about actions can penetrate motor planning circuits without explicit awareness of the linguistic cues.
papers.authors: Margherita Marchioro, Tommaso Currò, Davide Tabarelli, Simona Monaco

0627.name: Soojin Park
0627.bio: Soojin Park is a cognitive neuroscientist who investigates the neural mechanisms of high-level visual scene representation and its role in human navigation. Their research utilizes functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and behavioral psychophysics to explore how the brain's scene-selective network, including the parahippocampal place area (PPA) and occipital place area (OPA), encodes spatial boundaries and environmental navigability. Park’s work characterizes scene perception as a process that integrates visual features with the functional and spatial constraints of an observer's environment. Formerly an assistant professor at Johns Hopkins University, Park currently leads the Visual Cognitive Neuroscience Lab at Yonsei University.
0627.research_direction: Dr. Park has recently been investigating how the human brain constructs functional representations of spatial environments to support navigation and spatial awareness. Their recent work explores how scene-selective regions, such as the parahippocampal place area and occipital place area, integrate individual visual features like path direction and distance into coherent spatial units using fMRI and multi-voxel pattern analysis. Beyond purely visual dimensions, they are also examining how active navigational experience shapes scene processing, using virtual reality to test how action-based constraints—such as encountering invisible walls—alter neural and behavioral representations. Additionally, their research extends into cross-modal perception, investigating how the brain synthesizes visual and auditory cues to form supramodal representations of an environment's geometric size.

papers.title: A Scene with an Invisible Wall—Navigational Experience Shapes Visual Scene Representation
papers.abstract: This study investigates how active navigational experience influences the neural and behavioral representation of visual scenes, independently of physical visual features. Using a virtual reality (VR) paradigm, participants navigated environments where some scenes were freely traversable while others were blocked by an 'invisible wall,' despite appearing visually navigable. Behavioral results from a same-different judgment task demonstrated that participants perceived scenes with different navigational histories as more visually distinct than scenes with identical histories, even when visual similarity was controlled. Neuroimaging data using fMRI and multi-voxel pattern analysis (MVPA) revealed that the parahippocampal place area (PPA) successfully decoded the navigability of scenes based solely on prior experience. These findings indicate that the human visual scene-selective cortex integrates functional constraints derived from navigational experience into its perceptual representations, suggesting that scene processing is a constructive process shaped by action-based knowledge.
papers.authors: Shi Pui Donald Li, Jiayu Shao, Zhengang Lu, Michael McCloskey, Soojin Park

papers.title: Combined representation of visual features in the scene-selective cortex
papers.abstract: This research examines the neural mechanisms by which the human brain integrates separate visual dimensions—specifically path direction and navigational distance—to form complex scene representations. Using fMRI and multi-voxel pattern similarity analysis, the study investigated whether the occipital place area (OPA) and parahippocampal place area (PPA) represent these features independently or as integrated conjunctions. Stimuli consisted of artificial indoor scenes with varying path configurations (single vs. double paths, left vs. right directions, and near vs. far distances). Results showed that the OPA represents single-path scenes based on both direction and distance features. Critically, representations of double-path scenes were more similar to the average of their constituent single-path features than to unrelated configurations, suggesting an integrated feature approach. The findings provide evidence that the OPA serves as a critical substrate for binding navigationally relevant visual features into a coherent scene unit for guided locomotion.
papers.authors: Jisu Kang, Soojin Park

papers.title: Multi-modal Representation of the Size of Space in the Human Brain
papers.abstract: The study explores the neural substrates underlying the perception of spatial environmental properties, specifically the geometric size of indoor spaces, through visual and auditory modalities. Participants were presented with images and reverberant sounds depicting small and large indoor spaces during fMRI scanning. The researchers employed a cross-modal multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) to identify modality-specific and supramodal (modality-independent) representations. Results revealed that while primary sensory cortices represented size in a modality-specific manner, the angular gyrus and the right medial frontal gyrus exhibited modality-integrated representations, showing sensitivity to the congruency of size information across vision and audition. Furthermore, background functional connectivity analysis demonstrated increased coupling between sensory-specific and modality-integrated regions during multimodal processing. These results suggest that spatial size perception relies on a hierarchical network where sensory-specific inputs are integrated into a supramodal representation of the environment's physical scale.
papers.authors: Jaeeun Lee, Soojin Park

0628.name: Sophia Vinci-Booher
0628.department: Department of Psychology and Human Development
0628.bio: Vinci-Booher is an Assistant Professor of Educational Neuroscience at Vanderbilt University who investigates the neural mechanisms mediating the relationship between action and perception across the lifespan. Their research examines how manual communication tasks, such as handwriting and drawing, facilitate the development of brain systems for literacy and symbol recognition. Utilizing functional and diffusion MRI, Vinci-Booher characterizes functional and structural brain changes, including white matter tract development, that occur during intensive learning periods. This work aims to identify how sensorimotor experiences drive neural reorganization and impact long-term educational outcomes.
0628.research_direction: Dr. Vinci-Booher's recent work explores the mechanistic links between motor action, visual perception, and cognitive development, with a particular focus on how manual behaviors like handwriting shape the developing brain. They have recently been investigating how the tight contingency between motor output and visual feedback during symbol production facilitates the neural foundations of early literacy in children. To capture these fine-grained developmental dynamics, their research utilizes dense longitudinal MRI and diffusion tractography to ask how individual differences in baseline white matter microstructure predict specific trajectories of sensorimotor and visual learning. Additionally, they are mapping the structural maturation of distinct hippocampal subfields across childhood and early adulthood to determine how localized tissue changes support the broader emergence of associative memory and inference.

papers.title: Dense longitudinal neuroimaging reveals individual brain change trajectories
papers.abstract: This review delineates the dense longitudinal neuroimaging (DLN) framework as a precision methodology for capturing the high-frequency dynamics of human brain development and learning. By shifting from sparse, cross-sectional sampling to dense MRI acquisitions within abbreviated temporal windows, DLN allows for the precise estimation of nonlinear, individual-specific trajectories of structural and functional neural change. The authors demonstrate how this approach advances the mechanistic understanding of cognitive maturation, particularly highlighting the role of the motor system in visual development and the establishment of individualized biomarkers for learning progress.
papers.authors: Sophia Vinci-Booher, Xueying Ren, Kendrick Kay, Chen Yu, Franco Pestilli, James R. Booth

papers.title: Brain correlates of early writing development: The foundational role of production tasks in early childhood
papers.abstract: This work synthesizes behavioral and neuroimaging research to characterize the foundational role of manual production tasks, such as handwriting and drawing, in the emergence of early literacy. The authors examine the sensorimotor brain connections recruited during these tasks in pre-reading children and their progression into the specialized neural systems of literate adults. They argue that the tight contingency between motor output and visual feedback during production induces persistent brain changes that facilitate letter and symbol recognition, thereby grounding abstract linguistic representations in sensorimotor experience to support long-term educational outcomes.
papers.venue: Advances in Child Development and Behavior
papers.authors: Sophia Vinci-Booher, Gabrielle A. Shimko, Harper Marshall, Karin Harman James

papers.title: Associative white matter tracts selectively predict sensorimotor learning
papers.abstract: Utilizing a machine-learning model selection framework, this study investigates whether baseline white matter microstructure can selectively predict future learning outcomes in the sensorimotor domain. Adult participants underwent diffusion tractography to measure mean fractional anisotropy (FA) across major tracts before training in drawing novel symbols. Results revealed that microstructure in the left hemisphere posterior arcuate fasciculus (pArc) and superior longitudinal fasciculus 3 (SLF3) selectively predicted drawing-based learning rates, while the left mid-longitudinal fasciculus (MDLFspl) predicted visual recognition performance. These findings suggest that individual differences in anatomical connectivity provide a selective structural scaffold for distinct skill acquisition trajectories.
papers.authors: Sophia Vinci-Booher, Daniel J. McDonald, Elizabeth Berquist, Franco Pestilli

papers.title: Learning to write letters and digits by hand in preschool
papers.abstract: This developmental study assesses the impact of handwriting versus typing on the acquisition of letter and digit knowledge in preschool-aged children. Through a controlled intervention, the researchers demonstrate that manual symbol production leads to significant gains in letter naming, word decoding, and visual word identification, surpassing the outcomes of typing-based practice. The results highlight the critical role of visual-motor integration in the development of phonological recoding and orthographic representations, suggesting that handwriting serves as a fundamental pedagogical bridge for early academic skill development.
papers.authors: Sophia Vinci-Booher, Deborah Zemlock, Susie Ju, Karin James

papers.title: Development of human hippocampal subfield microstructure and relation to associative inference
papers.abstract: This investigation maps the microstructural maturation of hippocampal subfields—CA1, CA2/3, dentate gyrus (DG), and subiculum (SUB)—across a developmental span of 6 to 30 years. Using diffusion-weighted MRI, the authors characterized subfield-specific age-related trajectories, identifying unique nonlinear patterns for the DG and CA2/3. Microstructural properties of the DG were selectively associated with memory-based associative inference performance, whereas SUB tissue organization predicted perception-based inference, independently of chronological age. These findings suggest that the distinct cellular development of hippocampal subfields underlies the maturation of discrete mnemonic and inferential capabilities.
papers.authors: Sophia Vinci-Booher, Margaret L. Schlichting, Alison R. Preston, Franco Pestilli

0629.name: Stefan Pollmann
0629.department: Institute of Psychology (IPSY), Faculty of Natural Sciences
0629.bio: Stefan Pollmann is a Professor of Experimental Psychology who investigates the neural and behavioral mechanisms underlying visual attention and perception. Pollmann’s research focuses on contextual cueing in visual search, exploring how spatial configurations facilitate target detection through implicit learning and memory-guided saccades. Utilizing high-resolution functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), eye-tracking, and event-related potentials (ERP), they examine the plasticity of the visual system and compensatory strategies such as saccadic re-referencing in cases of central vision loss. This research addresses how top-down attentional weighting and bottom-up saliency signals interact within the human visual cortex to guide environmental exploration.
0629.research_direction: Dr. Pollmann's recent work explores the behavioral and neural mechanisms underlying visual attention, decision-making, and perceptual adaptation. Using fMRI, psychophysics, and high-resolution gaze tracking, they are investigating how the brain coordinates attentional shifts during visual search, specifically examining prefrontal cortex dynamics across varying display densities and the integration of local and global spatial regularities in contextual cueing. Additionally, their research has recently been probing the exploration-exploitation trade-off during probabilistic foraging, mapping the frontopolar signaling and computational heuristics that drive patch-leaving decisions in both humans and animal models. Finally, they are investigating neuro-cognitive and oculomotor adaptations to central vision loss, focusing on how individuals with bilateral macular degeneration reorganize their cortical pathways to develop new extrafoveal saccadic reference points.

papers.title: Neural and Perceptual Adaptations in Bilateral Macular Degeneration: An Integrative Review
papers.abstract: This integrative review synthesizes empirical evidence regarding the neuro-cognitive and oculomotor adaptations resulting from bilateral central vision loss (CVL). We investigate the mechanisms underlying the adoption of a Preferred Retinal Location (PRL) and the subsequent developmental trajectory of saccadic re-referencing to an extrafoveal reference point. Leveraging findings from fMRI, psychophysics, and gaze tracking, the authors delineate how scotoma morphology and cortical reorganization within the visual hierarchy constrain search efficiency. The synthesis indicates that while functional PRL adoption occurs rapidly, the transition from foveal to eccentric saccadic referencing is a protracted process, necessitating evidence-based training protocols for functional recovery.
papers.authors: Giulio Contemori, Sharavanan Ganesan, Natalia Melnik, Elena Azañón, Stefan Pollmann

papers.title: Prefrontal dimension change-related activation differs for visual search in sparse and dense displays
papers.abstract: Target-defining dimension changes in visual search typically recruit the left lateral frontopolar cortex (FPC). However, right-hemispheric recruitment has been observed in sparse displays characterized by inefficient, serial-like search. This fMRI investigation manipulated display density (sparse vs. dense) to reconcile these findings. We demonstrate that dimension changes in dense displays—which facilitate efficient search—invoke the canonical left lateral FPC response, whereas sparse displays trigger right-hemispheric prefrontal recruitment. These results suggest that the neural substrates for attentional reweighting are dynamically modulated by search efficiency and display complexity, resolving a notable discrepancy in the existing neuroimaging literature.
papers.authors: Nico Marek, Ninja K. Horr, Dragan Rangelov, Stefan Pollmann

papers.title: Differential patch-leaving behavior during probabilistic foraging in humans and gerbils
papers.abstract: Utilizing a cross-species comparative framework, we investigate the computational heuristics of patch-leaving decisions in humans and gerbils. Leveraging the Marginal Value Theorem (MVT) as a normative benchmark, the study contrasts reward-yield maximization models with incremental heuristic rules. Behavioral analysis indicates that human foraging decisions are primarily governed by an incremental mechanism contingent upon discrete reward capture events, a strategy optimized for variable reward distributions. Conversely, gerbils and a subpopulation of human observers exhibit sensitivity to instantaneous capture rates consistent with MVT predictions. These findings reveal divergent species-specific strategies for resolving the exploitation-exploration trade-off in depleting environments.
papers.authors: Lasse Güldener, Parthiban Saravanakumar, Max F. K. Happel, Frank W. Ohl, Maike Vollmer, Stefan Pollmann

papers.title: Behavioral Bias for Exploration Is Associated with Enhanced Signaling in the Lateral and Medial Frontopolar Cortex
papers.abstract: The frontopolar cortex (FPC) is critically involved in the high-level coordination of exploratory transitions during goal-directed behavior. In this fMRI study, we correlated BOLD signal dynamics with individual variability in exploratory bias during a probabilistic foraging task. Signal magnitude in both lateral and medial FPC subregions significantly predicted an observer's propensity for exploration. Furthermore, FPC activity encoded the relative evidence supporting the decision to abandon the current patch for alternative options. These results substantiate a functional role for the FPC in monitoring alternative behavioral trajectories and managing the strategic reallocation of cognitive resources in complex environments.
papers.authors: Lasse Güldener, Stefan Pollmann

papers.title: Contextual cueing—Eye movements in rotated and recombined displays
papers.abstract: This study utilizes high-resolution gaze tracking to investigate the relative contributions of global spatial configurations versus local target-distractor spatial relations to the contextual cueing effect. We analyzed attentional guidance in transfer displays featuring rotated or recombined distractor arrangements. The results demonstrate that both global configuration and local distractor-target relations independently facilitate search efficiency, with fixation patterns in the transfer phase mirroring those established during learning. This suggests that contextual cueing is mediated by a multifaceted and flexible oculomotor representation that integrates both local and global spatial regularities to guide attention in complex visual environments.
papers.authors: Lei Zheng, Nico Marek, Natalia Melnik, Stefan Pollmann

0630.name: Stefan Van der Stigchel
0630.bio: Stefan van der Stigchel is a Professor of Cognitive Psychology and the principal investigator of the AttentionLab, where their research examines the mechanisms of visual attention, eye movement control, and working memory. Utilizing a combination of psychophysics, eye-tracking, and neuroimaging techniques, they explore how the brain filters sensory information to construct a coherent awareness of the environment. Their work extends to clinical populations, investigating attentional deficits such as hemispatial neglect and hemianopia to improve neurorehabilitation strategies. Currently supported by an ERC Consolidator Grant and an NWO Vici grant, Van der Stigchel is a science communicator and author of several books on concentration and focus.
0630.research_direction: Dr. Van der Stigchel has recently been investigating the dynamic interplay between visual working memory (VWM) and external visual sampling. Their recent work explores how observers balance the cognitive effort of internal storage against the physical access costs of information gathering, utilizing naturalistic copy-tasks to map individual strategy phenotypes. Additionally, they are examining the temporal dynamics of VWM in self-paced environments, specifically questioning how unconstrained encoding durations and retention delays interact to determine memory stability. To index these covert cognitive processes, Dr. Van der Stigchel also incorporates physiological measures like pupillometry and microsaccadic biases, probing how oculomotor behavior can serve as a continuous readout for subjective mental exertion, visual capacity limits, and the spatial allocation of internal attention.

papers.title: Putting effort into task complexity
papers.abstract: This work critiques the theoretical proposal that task complexity can serve as a metric for identifying a unifying capacity limit in visual processing. The authors argue that such a framework must incorporate cognitive effort to avoid a systemic underestimation of capacity. Using pupillometry as a physiological readout of mental exertion, the paper posits that observers' capacity limits are not static but are modulated by the subjective investment of resources. It highlights that individuals frequently adopt effort-minimizing heuristics, such as selecting less effortful oculomotor strategies, which can mask the true architectural limits of the attentional system. The authors advocate for task designs that maximize participant effort to prevent a conceptual crisis in the measurement of visual processing capacity.
papers.authors: Damian Koevoet, Stefan Van der Stigchel

papers.title: Shifting reliance between the internal and external world: A meta-analysis on visual-working memory use
papers.abstract: This meta-analysis evaluates the strategic trade-off between the utilization of internal visual working memory (VWM) and external environmental sampling. Synthesizing data from 'copy-task' paradigms, the study quantifies the impact of external 'access costs'—such as the temporal or motoric demands of sampling—and individual VWM capacity on information-gathering behavior. The results demonstrate a robust, principled shift toward increased internal storage as the cost of external information acquisition rises. The findings suggest that humans exhibit a flexible cost-benefit optimization process, where the allocation of cognitive labor between internal and external stores is governed by the minimization of total energetic and cognitive effort.
papers.authors: Tianying Qing, Christoph Strauch, Leendert Van Maanen, Stefan Van der Stigchel

papers.title: The rise and fall of memories: Temporal dynamics of visual working memory
papers.abstract: This research investigates how the duration of visual encoding and the subsequent retention delay jointly determine the efficacy of visual working memory (VWM) in naturalistic, self-paced environments. Utilizing a cursor-directed aperture copying task, the authors tracked unconstrained viewing and placing behavior at the level of individual items. The results indicate that VWM representation strength builds up as a saturating function of viewing time, plateauing at approximately one second per item. Critically, longer encoding durations significantly increased the resilience of these memories against decay during extended delays. These findings emphasize the dynamic nature of VWM, where representational stability is titrated based on anticipated utilization intervals.
papers.authors: Andre Sahakian, Surya Gayet, Chris L. E. Paffen, Stefan Van der Stigchel

papers.title: Relying on the external world: Individuals variably use low- and medium-loading, but rarely high-loading, strategies when engaging visual working memory
papers.abstract: Using a 'Shopping Game' paradigm, this study characterizes individual variability in the strategic allocation of visual working memory (VWM) resources versus external sampling. The investigation finds that while distinct 'sampling' and 'remembering' phenotypes exist, participants generally avoid high-loading strategies that would approach their actual VWM capacity limits. This suggests that the distribution of cognitive labor is driven by the minimization of mental effort rather than the exhaustion of available capacity. The data reveal that individuals flexibly adjust their reliance on external resources in response to task-specific constraints and access costs, prioritizing effort optimization over maximal memory utilization.
papers.authors: S. Böing, B. de Zwart, A. F. Ten Brink, T. C. W. Nijboer, S. Van der Stigchel

papers.title: Microsaccade biases can reflect task-specific spatial memorization strategies
papers.abstract: This study explores the relationship between microsaccadic oculomotor biases and the allocation of internal attention within visual working memory (VWM). Participants performed a retro-cue paradigm requiring the prioritization of orientations stored at specific spatial locations. The results show that microsaccade directions are systematically biased toward the coordinates of prioritized items held in memory. Crucially, the presence and directionality of these biases were found to be contingent upon the specific representational strategies adopted for spatial encoding. The findings suggest that while microsaccades provide a physiological readout of internal attentional selection, they are sensitive to the task-specific format of spatial representations.
papers.authors: Samson Chota, Kabir Arora, J. Leon Kenemans, Surya Gayet, Stefan Van der Stigchel

0631.name: Stefania Bracci
0631.bio: Stefania Bracci is an Associate Professor at the University of Trento and a researcher within the Object Vision Group at the Center for Mind/Brain Sciences (CIMeC). Bracci’s research investigates the organizational principles of object representations in the human visual cortex, examining the interplay between visual features, conceptual categories, and action-related properties. Utilizing functional MRI, representational similarity analysis, and computational modeling with deep neural networks, they study the topographic mapping of tool and hand representations in the occipitotemporal cortex. Their work further explores how task context and experience shape neural representational spaces, comparing biological visual processing with artificial intelligence models.
0631.research_direction: Dr. Bracci’s recent work explores the functional and topographic organization of the human occipitotemporal cortex, specifically investigating how the visual system dissociates action-related object properties from surface visual features. Using fMRI, multivariate pattern analysis, and voxelwise encoding models, they have recently been examining how representations of diverse categories—such as tools, hands, bodies, and food—are spatially organized across the lateral and ventral visual streams. Their research asks whether behavioral action-relevance forms a fundamental spatial gradient in the lateral cortex, distinct from ventral regions optimized for identifying geometric, chromatic, or textural attributes. Additionally, their recent work investigates the utility of deep artificial neural networks as models of biological vision, probing whether current computational models can naturally capture these action-driven cortical maps and evaluating the broader epistemological tension between predictive and explanatory frameworks in cognitive neuroscience.

papers.title: Object dimensions underlying food representations in visual cortex
papers.abstract: Human occipitotemporal cortex (OTC) possesses two food-selective regions located in lateral and ventromedial cortex, yet whether they serve distinct computational roles remains poorly understood. This neuroimaging investigation evaluated whether food representations across these two regions reflect a dissociation between action-related properties and surface visual features. Using two functional magnetic resonance imaging experiments with controlled stimulus sets varying systematically across category (food versus non-food objects), shape, color, and ensemble configuration, multivariate pattern analysis revealed a functional dissociation. Lateral OTC encoded food alongside other manipulable objects, reflecting action-relevant dimensions shared across graspable items. Conversely, ventromedial OTC showed heightened sensitivity to surface attributes, specifically chromatic information and textural ensemble layout critical for food identification, rather than action-related features. These results demonstrate that lateral OTC structures food representations within an action-oriented feature space, whereas ventral OTC processes surface visual properties essential for classifying edible items.
papers.authors: Davide Cortinovis, Giulia Orlandi, Lotte van Campenhout, Stefania Bracci

papers.title: Encoding models uncover fine-grained feature selectivity for bodies, hands and tools
papers.abstract: Category-selective territories within primate occipitotemporal cortex (OTC) are typically described by broad categorical tuning, yet fine-grained feature selectivity within these domains remains incompletely understood. To resolve this, densely sampled fMRI responses from participants viewing 200 diverse images depicting whole human bodies, isolated hands, tools, and manipulable and non-manipulable inanimate objects were analyzed using artificial neural network (ANN)-based voxelwise encoding models. Ridge regression models revealed that distinct semantic and visual feature spaces differentially predict neural responses across ventral and lateral OTC subregions. While ventral areas prioritize geometric shape and surface visual attributes, lateral OTC regions selective for hands and tools exhibit shared tuning for action-relevant and effector properties that cannot be accounted for by low- or mid-level visual features alone. These results indicate that lateral category-selective areas implement specialized representations reflecting behaviorally relevant action dimensions.
papers.authors: Davide Cortinovis, Martin N. Hebart, Stefania Bracci

papers.title: Investigating action topography in visual cortex and deep artificial neural networks
papers.abstract: Category-selective clusters in the primate occipitotemporal cortex (OTC) are embedded within large-scale topographic organizational maps, such as animacy and real-world size. This study demonstrates that action-related properties serve as an additional fundamental organizing principle of human visual cortex topography. Utilizing functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) with stimuli spanning human body parts, tools, and other objects matched for low-level visual features, univariate and multivariate representational analyses identified an action-related gradient along the dorsal-to-ventral axis in lateral OTC, transitioning continuously across representations of whole bodies, hands, tools, and manipulable objects. In contrast, standard and topographic deep artificial neural networks (TDANNs) trained on object classification failed to reproduce this action-based cortical organization, despite capturing aspects of animacy and size topography. These findings reveal an action-driven organizing dimension in lateral visual cortex and highlight the necessity of action-oriented inductive biases in computational vision models.
papers.authors: Davide Cortinovis, Nhut Truong, Hans Op de Beeck, Stefania Bracci

papers.title: Tool Representations in Human Visual Cortex
papers.abstract: This review synthesizes decades of functional neuroimaging literature investigating how tool representations are organized across the human visual ventral stream. The evidence highlights a pronounced functional and spatial divergence between lateral occipitotemporal cortex (LOTC) and ventral occipitotemporal cortex (VOTC). While LOTC encodes both geometric shape and behavioral action properties—critically isolating objects serving as manual end-effectors (such as tools and hands) from other graspable items—VOTC predominantly processes visual surface properties, including texture and material. Tool-selective regions in LOTC interface with dorsal parieto-frontal motor circuits to mediate goal-directed interaction. Comparing these neural architectures with contemporary deep artificial neural networks reveals that current vision models, primarily optimized for category classification, struggle to extract action-relevant dimensions. The authors argue that OTC tool selectivity reflects a behaviorally grounded action code and propose constraints for developing ecologically valid computational models.
papers.authors: Davide Cortinovis, Marius V. Peelen, Stefania Bracci

papers.title: The scientific value of explanation and prediction
papers.abstract: In response to criticisms regarding deep neural network (DNN) models of biological vision, this commentary addresses the epistemological tension between explanatory and predictive models in cognitive neuroscience. While purely predictive benchmarking on image classification may obscure underlying visual mechanisms, strictly controlled laboratory experiments risk producing explanatory frameworks that fail to generalize to ecological visual behavior. The commentary argues that deep learning models provide a versatile computational testing ground for evaluating mechanistic hypotheses across diverse psychological and neurobiological phenomena. Achieving robust models of primate vision requires bridging predictive capacity and explanatory mechanistic rigor, reconciling experimental control with ecological generalizability.
papers.authors: Hans Op de Beeck, Stefania Bracci

0632.name: Stella F. Lourenco
0632.lab_name: Lourenco Lab: Vision, Cognition, and Development
0632.bio: Lourenco investigates the ontogenetic origins and computational mechanisms underlying spatial and numerical representation in humans. Their research explores how the brain processes general magnitudes—such as area, number, and time—and the extent to which these systems share a common magnitude-based framework or remain perceptually independent. Utilizing psychophysical paradigms, eye tracking, and fMRI, Lourenco maps the developmental trajectories of spatial reasoning and investigates how early visuospatial competencies support the acquisition of symbolic mathematical concepts. Additionally, their work examines the influence of evolutionary-based fears and social categories on perceptual calibration and spatial biases.
0632.research_direction: Dr. Lourenco's recent work investigates the developmental and perceptual foundations of visual cognition, exploring how fundamental visual features shape both object processing and high-level social evaluations. They have recently been examining intersectional face perception in young children, using speeded categorization and trait judgment paradigms to test whether perceptual tuning to facial dominance and face-space statistics underlies race- and gender-based stereotypes. In the domain of physical scene processing, their recent research asks whether intuitive physics, such as judging an object's stability, relies on complex mental simulations or simpler perceptual heuristics like geometric centroids. Additionally, they are probing the upper limits of early visual robustness by challenging preschoolers to identify sparse, rapidly masked object contours, comparing these human inductive biases directly against state-of-the-art deep neural networks.

papers.title: Perceptual Calibration in Intersectional Race and Gender Categorization Across Development
papers.abstract: This research investigates whether the developmental slowdown in categorizing the gender of Black women (intersectional invisibility) is a result of experience-based perceptual tuning or conceptual stereotyping. Utilizing a speeded gender-categorization paradigm with stimulus faces matched for dominance and masculinity/femininity, the study tested children (ages 5–10) and adults to identify the onset and nature of intersectional categorization asymmetries. Results indicated that children’s increased response times for Black female targets emerge around age 7, suggesting that the human visual system calibrates gender prototypes based on the statistical regularities of frequently encountered face populations rather than entrenched social biases. This developmental dissociation supports a perceptual-calibration account where intersectional difficulty reflects the adaptive tuning of face-space representations to environmental statistics.
papers.authors: Nikita Agarwal, Maia Mast, Stella F. Lourenco

papers.title: Fast and robust visual object recognition in young children
papers.abstract: This study evaluates the upper limits of visual recognition robustness in preschool children by challenging their ability to identify objects under sparse and disrupted viewing conditions at high temporal speeds. Children as young as 3 years old identified objects from sparse outlines and stimuli with perturbed or deleted contours at presentation durations of 100 ms (forward and backward masked). When compared to state-of-the-art deep neural networks (DNNs), children significantly outperformed models trained on equivalent volumes of visual data. The findings reveal that the human visual system achieves robust, high-speed invariant object recognition through developmental constraints and inductive biases that do not require the massive, varied training sets currently utilized in artificial intelligence, highlighting a fundamental gap between biological and machine vision.
papers.authors: Vladislav Ayzenberg, Sukran Bahar Sener, Kylee Novick, Stella F. Lourenco

papers.title: Facial dominance overrides gender in children's stereotypes about intelligence
papers.abstract: This investigation examines the perceptual roots of the gender-brilliance stereotype by testing whether children’s attributions of intelligence are driven primarily by facial dominance cues rather than gender categories. Across two experiments, children (ages 6–10) performed intelligence and prosociality judgments on face pairs manipulated for gender and perceived dominance. The data demonstrated that children consistently prioritized dominance over gender when selecting 'smarter' individuals, even when feminine faces were more dominant than masculine ones. This dominance-based heuristic persisted under divided attention, suggesting that an early-emerging association between dominance and intelligence serves as a precursor to, or even a foundation for, more explicitly learned gender-based stereotypes about intellectual ability.
papers.authors: Ryno Kruger, Stella F. Lourenco

papers.title: Children’s Decision-Making About Others Reflects Gender Stereotypes More Than Race: Evidence From a US Sample
papers.abstract: This study explores the developmental intersection of race and gender in social decision-making, specifically testing whether the intersectional biases observed in perceptual face processing extend to social evaluations. Children (N = 97, ages 4–9) evaluated gender-stereotyped clothing and activity preferences for unfamiliar Black and White targets. Behavioral results indicated that children relied heavily on gender-congruent stereotypes to form social preferences, rating targets more positively when they adhered to gender-typed norms regardless of race. Unlike perceptual tasks where Black females are often miscategorized or processed slower, social evaluations did not show significant intersectionality effects, suggesting that high-level social decision-making in middle childhood is dominated by binary gender schemas that generalize across racial groups.
papers.authors: Nikita Agarwal, Stella F. Lourenco

papers.title: Object geometry serves humans’ intuitive physics of stability
papers.abstract: The 'intuitive physics engine' account posits that humans judge physical stability via mental simulation; however, this research tests whether perceptual geometric features provide a sufficient alternative mechanism. Through a series of experiments, the authors manipulated object geometry (geometric centroid, height, and base width) and measured judgments of falling direction in children and adults. Human performance was compared to computational models based on geometric features and a deep convolutional neural network (ResNet-50). Results showed that human judgments were highly correlated with models of geometric centroids and matched the performance of the non-simulating DNN. These findings suggest that object geometry is a primary cue for stability judgments, supporting a perceptual account of intuitive physics that operates independently of complex internal simulations.
papers.authors: Yaxin Liu, Vladislav Ayzenberg, Stella F. Lourenco

0633.name: Stephen Adamo
0633.department: Department of Psychology; Department of Radiology & Imaging Sciences
0633.lab_name: Attention Detection And Medical Observation (ADAMO) Lab
0633.main_research_area: visual attention and medical image perception
0633.bio: Adamo is an Assistant Professor at the University of Arizona with joint appointments in the Departments of Psychology and Radiology & Imaging Sciences. Adamo directs the Attention Detection And Medical Observation (ADAMO) Lab, where their research investigates the mechanisms of visual search and cognitive errors in medical imaging contexts. Their work examines phenomena such as 'subsequent search misses' and 'satisfaction of search' to determine how expertise, artificial intelligence, and 3D imaging technology affect detection accuracy. Adamo utilizes behavioral testing, eye-tracking, and electroencephalography (EEG) to connect basic vision science with applied clinical outcomes.
0633.research_direction: Dr. Adamo has recently been investigating visual search processes in medical image perception, focusing heavily on the "subsequent search miss" (SSM) or "satisfaction of search" phenomenon. Their recent work explores how this multi-target search error manifests in breast cancer screening, specifically by comparing observer performance in traditional 2D mammography versus 3D volumetric digital breast tomosynthesis. To understand the underlying cognitive and perceptual mechanisms driving these secondary target omissions, they utilize realistic virtual breast phantoms and gaze metrics to manipulate spatial depth, target feature similarity, and presentation environments. Additionally, they are examining how varying levels of perceptual expertise—from visually untrained novices to board-certified radiologists—influence an observer's susceptibility to multi-target search errors in both planar and volumetric displays.

papers.title: Comparing the subsequent search miss effect between mammography and tomosynthesis
papers.abstract: This study evaluates the subsequent search miss (SSM) phenomenon—traditionally characterized as satisfaction of search—in breast imaging by comparing 2D full-field digital mammography against 3D digital breast tomosynthesis (DBT). Utilizing virtual breast anatomy synthesized with single or multiple embedded lesions, the investigation examines how volumetric slice progression and depth-based navigation influence observer omission errors following an initial positive detection. Behavioral performance and gaze metrics are assessed to determine whether the spatial uncoupling of overlapping tissue in DBT attenuates the cognitive resource depletion and attentional template biases that drive secondary lesion misses in conventional projection radiography.
papers.venue: Proceedings of SPIE 13928, Medical Imaging 2026: Image Perception, Observer Performance, and Technology Assessment
papers.authors: Brandon Eich, Lyndon Rakusen, Miguel Lago, Claudia Mello-Thoms, Stephen H. Adamo

papers.title: Dig a Little Deeper: Comparing 2D to 3D Search Performance When Looking for Multiple Breast Cancers
papers.abstract: The study quantifies visual search efficacy for multiple malignant targets in two-dimensional digital mammography compared to segmented three-dimensional digital breast tomosynthesis (DBT). Utilizing the VICTRE in-silico pipeline to generate realistic breast phantoms with controlled lesion placement, the experiment required observers to identify up to two masses per case. The results demonstrate that volumetric searching in DBT significantly improves detection rates for both solitary lesions and secondary abnormalities. Notably, the Subsequent Search Miss (SSM) effect was statistically significant in both search environments, with no evidence that the increased signal-to-noise ratio in DBT eliminates the psychological satisfaction of search error compared to standard 2D projections.
papers.authors: Lyndon Rakusen, Brandon Eich, Stephen Adamo

papers.title: Comparing multiple-target search performance and the satisfaction of search effect between 2D and segmented-3D search
papers.abstract: This investigation analyzes multiple-target visual search mechanics and the satisfaction of search (SOS) effect across simplified 2D planar arrays and segmented-3D volumetric displays. Observers completed visual search trials containing zero, one, or two targets across varying salience levels. Segmented-3D displays yielded significant performance benefits over 2D displays, including reduced false alarm rates, elevated target detection sensitivity for both isolated targets and secondary targets in dual-target displays, and elongated inspection times on target-absent trials. Critically, the robust SOS decrement detected in planar 2D conditions was completely absent in segmented-3D environments, demonstrating that depth-segmented visual presentation preserves secondary target identification accuracy.
papers.venue: Proceedings of SPIE 12929, Medical Imaging 2024: Image Perception, Observer Performance, and Technology Assessment
papers.authors: Stephen H. Adamo, Rachel Brem, Stephen R. Mitroff

papers.title: Assessing satisfaction of search in virtual mammograms for experienced and novice searchers
papers.abstract: This work characterizes satisfaction of search (SOS) errors in synthetic mammographic volumes across varying levels of observer experience, focusing on target feature concordance. Patient breast anatomy was modeled via the Open Virtual Clinical Trials (OpenVCT) framework and embedded with up to two simulated abnormalities consisting of masses and microcalcification clusters. Experienced readers (radiologists, fellows, and residents) and novice observers were evaluated on dual-target detection.
