While both cohorts exhibited substantial SOS error rates, target similarity differentially influenced detection across experience levels: novices were significantly more prone to miss a secondary abnormality when it was perceptually dissimilar from the initial finding, whereas experienced practitioners showed equivalent miss rates irrespective of inter-target similarity.
papers.authors: Stephen H. Adamo, Nelson Roque, Bruno Barufaldi, Joseph Schmidt, Claudia Mello-Thoms, Miguel Lago

papers.title: Comparing experts to novices: reduced satisfaction of search when searching with virtual breast tomosynthesis
papers.abstract: This study measures satisfaction of search (SOS) rates in 3D digital breast tomosynthesis (DBT) utilizing computer-generated breast volumes produced with the OpenVCT architecture. Novices (undergraduate students) and domain experts (radiology residents, fellows, and board-certified radiologists) inspected reconstructed tomographic volumes containing zero, one, or two masses. While baseline sensitivity for single-mass cases did not differ between cohorts, experts exhibited a marginally lower false alarm rate (19.5% vs. 29.1%), significantly superior correct rejection rates on normal anatomy (76.7% vs. 44.5%), and a substantial attenuation of SOS omission errors (14.2% vs. 30.7%), providing evidence that specialized perceptual expertise mitigates multi-target search errors in volumetric breast screening.
papers.venue: Proceedings of SPIE 12467, Medical Imaging 2023: Image Perception, Observer Performance, and Technology Assessment
papers.authors: Stephen H. Adamo, Bruno Barufaldi, Miguel Lago

0634.name: Stephen Engel
0634.bio: Stephen Engel is a Professor of Psychology at the University of Minnesota who researches the neural mechanisms of visual perception and cortical plasticity. Engel utilizes functional MRI (fMRI) to map retinotopic organization and color tuning in the human primary visual cortex. Their current research program employs psychophysics, EEG, and immersive virtual reality systems to study how the adult visual system adapts to environmental changes. This work aims to develop therapeutic interventions for clinical conditions such as macular degeneration and amblyopia.
0634.research_direction: Dr. Engel has recently been utilizing psychophysical adaptation paradigms to investigate visual processing across both clinical and neurotypical populations. Their recent work explores the cortical origins of visual snow syndrome by testing whether spontaneous flickering percepts are susceptible to motion aftereffects, while also using high-level adaptation to anti-bodies to determine if human body shapes are coded in a norm-referenced vector space. In addition to these adaptation mechanisms, they are exploring long-term visual plasticity by tracking how human chromatic sensitivity dynamically recalibrates to repeatedly encountered environmental color shifts. Furthermore, Dr. Engel is investigating low-vision rehabilitation, evaluating whether customizing the spatial remapping of text around simulated central scotomas can optimize word recognition and reading performance.

papers.title: Visual Snow Is Susceptible to the Motion Aftereffect
papers.abstract: The authors utilized motion adaptation paradigms to determine if the internal flickering percept in visual snow syndrome (VSS) originates within motion-selective cortical pathways. Participants with VSS and typically sighted controls adapted to high-contrast drifting Gabor patches. The study demonstrated that VSS observers experience a motion aftereffect (MAE) within their subjective 'snow' percept when viewing a blank screen. The duration of this aftereffect scaled monotonically with the duration of the adapter (ranging from 1.6 to 45 seconds), exhibiting a power-law relationship characteristic of normal visual adaptation. These results provide psychophysical evidence that the spontaneous neural activity driving VSS symptoms reaches or arises in cortical areas selective for motion, such as V5/MT.
papers.authors: Samantha A. Montoya, Anna J. Hillstrom, Karly D. Allison, Carter B. Mulder, Hannah R. Moser, Michael S. Lee, Michael-Paul Schallmo, Stephen A. Engel

papers.title: Identity-based coding of human body shapes
papers.abstract: The neural representational structure of human body identity was investigated using a high-level perceptual adaptation framework. Participants were adapted to 'anti-bodies'—stimuli featuring geometric properties precisely opposite to those of a specific target body relative to an average body shape. Adaptation to these anti-bodies systematically biased the perception of an average test body toward the target identity. Crucially, the magnitude of this identity aftereffect increased as a function of the geometric extremity of the adapter. These findings establish that body identity is represented within a high-dimensional, norm-referenced vector space centered on a mean prototype, paralleling the well-documented mechanisms for face recognition in the human visual system.
papers.authors: Xinyu Liu, Stephen A. Engel

papers.title: Customizing spatial remapping of letters to aid reading in the presence of a simulated central field loss
papers.abstract: This study evaluated personalized spatial remapping as a method to mitigate reading deficits caused by central field loss (CFL). The researchers mapped trigram letter recognition accuracy across the central visual field in observers with simulated scotomas of varying geometries (horizontal, vertical, and square). Based on these visibility 'heat maps,' different remapping trajectories—shifting occluded text to functional retinal regions—were tested in a word recognition task. The results confirmed the customization hypothesis: the efficacy of a specific remapping strategy (e.g., horizontal vs. vertical gap) depends significantly on the specific shape of the CFL. While horizontal gap remapping generally yielded superior word recognition, the data suggest that tailoring remapping paths to individual scotoma properties is essential for optimizing low-vision assistive technologies.
papers.authors: Colin S. Flowers, Gordon E. Legge, Stephen A. Engel

papers.title: Effect of environmental color changes on chromatic sensitivity
papers.abstract: This research investigates how the human visual system maintains color constancy and sensitivity following long-term exposure to altered spectral environments. The study specifically examined 'visual mode switching,' where observers learn to adjust their chromatic sensitivity rapidly when moving between different lighting conditions or using colored filters. By tracking changes in unique yellow settings and chromatic discrimination thresholds over extended periods of adaptation, the authors quantified the time course of neural gain control. The findings indicate that the visual system develops specialized adaptive states through experience, allowing for near-instantaneous recalibration to repeatedly encountered environmental color shifts, thereby optimizing perceptual stability.
papers.authors: Yanjun Li, Katherine E. M. Tregillus, Stephen A. Engel

0635.name: Stephen Heinen
0635.bio: Stephen Heinen is a Senior Scientist at the Smith-Kettlewell Eye Research Institute, where they investigate the neural circuitry governing smooth pursuit, fixation, and saccadic eye movements. Heinen’s research utilizes oculomotor behavior as a non-invasive probe into human cognitive processes, including decision-making and attention allocation. They have provided evidence for independent ocular control during binocular viewing, which challenges classical oculomotor theories such as Hering’s Law. This work aims to translate basic neuroscience into clinical applications for diagnosing and treating conditions like strabismus, macular degeneration, and various psychiatric disorders.
0635.research_direction: Dr. Heinen has recently been investigating the neural mechanisms underlying binocular coordination, consistently challenging classic frameworks like Hering's Law of equal innervation. Their recent work explores the tension between unitary conjugate commands and independent monocular control by using high-resolution binocular tracking and infrared occlusion to examine ocular asymmetries during visual fixation and frontoparallel smooth pursuit. To formally test these mechanisms, they are developing computational models that attempt to explain complex oculomotor phenomena, such as how "Remarkable Saccades" emerge during asymmetric vergence steps without relying on explicit unitary vergence signals. Additionally, their research investigates how the spatial layout of visual stimuli—specifically comparing standard central points to peripheral contours—modulates gaze stability by influencing the recruitment of miniature fixational eye movements like microsaccades and slow ocular drift.

papers.title: A new oculomotor model demystifies “Remarkable Saccades”
papers.abstract: Oculomotor research and strabismus management have long been guided by Hering's Law of equal innervation, which states that binocular control relies on the linear summation of unitary conjugate and vergence commands. However, observations of interocular temporal asynchrony during midline vergence challenge the necessity of a unitary vergence signal, favoring independent monocular control. Yet, independent control cannot account for 'Remarkable Saccades'—paradoxical saccadic displacements executed by an eye already aligned on target during asymmetric vergence steps. To resolve this discrepancy, the Hybrid Binocular Control (HBC) computational model was developed. HBC integrates independent monocular pursuit controllers that interact directly with a unitary brainstem conjugate saccadic generator. Without invoking an explicit vergence command, HBC generates Remarkable Saccades as an emergent property. Incorporating a variable attentional gain further captures idiosyncratic behavioral variations occurring when observers direct attention to one eye's image. The model closely reproduces kinematic profiles across saccadic classes, providing empirical predictions regarding cortical-brainstem interactions and asymmetric oculomotor dynamics.
papers.authors: Stephen J. Heinen, Arvind Chandna, Devashish Singh, Scott N. J. Watamaniuk

papers.title: Misalignment of a covered eye reveals frontoparallel smooth pursuit is driven by multiple signals
papers.abstract: Traditional frameworks of ocular tracking postulate that a single unitary motor signal rotates both eyes conjugately according to Hering's Law. Although asynchronous dynamics under monocular occlusion during vergence have disputed unitary vergence commands, the role of independent control during frontoparallel tracking remains less clear. Binocular eye movements were recorded at 1000 Hz using an infrared-pass occluder while neurotypical human observers tracked a 0.4° dot translating horizontally across a tangent screen under predictable sinusoidal and pseudorandom motion regimes (peak velocities of 5°/s and 25°/s). During monocular tracking, the covered eye maintained a steady positional offset (phoria) that originated during initial fixation. Crucially, despite this persistent misalignment, the occluded eye matched the instantaneous target velocity of the viewing eye throughout pursuit. These findings indicate that while an overarching conjugate motor command drives tracking velocity, independent monocular controllers regulate binocular positional alignment via visual feedback.
papers.authors: Stephen Heinen, Devashish Singh, Caroline Ulep, Scott Watamaniuk

papers.title: Asymmetric eye movements during fixation challenge Hering's Law of a unitary neural command
papers.abstract: Binocular coordination during visual fixation is widely presumed to follow Hering's Law of equal innervation, largely because classical studies recorded from only a single eye. To determine whether fixational eye movements (FEMs) are yoked or uncoupled, binocular fixation was recorded during both binocular viewing and monocular occlusion in neurotypical subjects. Fixational stability quantified via bivariate contour ellipse area (BCEA) demonstrated interocular asymmetry even during binocular viewing, demonstrating independent oculomotor control. Under monocular occlusion, BCEAs were significantly greater in covered eyes than in viewing eyes, and eyes with larger BCEAs displayed elevated slow drift velocity. In contrast to drift disconjugacy, microsaccades were consistently binocular; however, microsaccadic amplitudes were selectively increased in viewing eyes with larger BCEAs to remediate drift errors. These findings demonstrate that while microsaccades rely on a unitary conjugate mechanism, fixational slow drift is governed by independent monocular control channels.
papers.authors: Arvind Chandna, Devashish Singh, Scott N. J. Watamaniuk, Stephen Heinen

papers.title: Peripheral targets attenuate miniature eye movements during fixation
papers.abstract: Fixating an isolated central point is standard practice for stabilizing gaze in visual psychophysics and ophthalmic imaging; however, small foveated targets provoke microsaccades and slow ocular drift that perturb retinal image stability and divert attentional resources. To investigate whether peripheral boundaries can stabilize gaze without triggering foveally mediated saccadic intrusions, human fixational stability was evaluated using central targets, peripheral circular rings of varying radii, and combinations thereof. Isolating gaze control to peripheral contours substantially decreased microsaccade rates and diminished drift dispersion relative to foveal spot fixation, while maintaining central alignment accuracy. The suppression of fixational intrusions confirms that small foveal points compel unnecessary foveation commands that elicit miniature catch-up saccades. Utilizing peripheral spatial references optimizes retinal image stabilization by circumventing foveal saccadic recruitment.
papers.authors: Scott N. J. Watamaniuk, Jeremy B. Badler, Stephen J. Heinen

0636.name: Stephen Mitroff
0636.department: Department of Psychological and Brain Sciences
0636.bio: Stephen Mitroff is a visual cognition researcher whose work focuses on the individual differences and malleability of visual search, perception, and memory. Mitroff’s research program leverages large-scale datasets from mobile applications and applied performance tools to analyze human variability in complex visual tasks. By investigating cohorts including radiologists, airport security officers, and elite athletes, Mitroff explores how cognitive factors like fatigue and personality moderate performance in high-stakes environments. Their current work emphasizes identifying the underlying mechanisms of expert performance and developing training regimens to enhance visual-attentional capabilities.
0636.research_direction: Dr. Mitroff has recently been investigating the behavioral dynamics of cognitive control and visual attention, with a distinct focus on the temporal mechanisms surrounding human error. By utilizing large-scale, trial-by-trial response time data and continuous motor tracking—such as computer cursor trajectories—their recent work explores how phenomena like pre-error speeding and post-error slowing can be used to model latent attentional states and forecast visual search failures before they happen. They are also examining the underlying architecture of cognitive flexibility by testing whether adaptations for spatial attention-shifting and rule-based task-switching rely on shared or domain-specific cognitive resources. Furthermore, their broader research portfolio touches on applied clinical psychology, having recently tracked longitudinal fluctuations in obsessive-compulsive symptomatology among university populations in response to large-scale environmental stressors.

papers.title: Characterizing and predicting behavioral changes before and after errors
papers.abstract: This study analyzes high-resolution, trial-by-trial performance data to identify behavioral precursors and consequences of human error in cognitive tasks. By delineating response time distributions and accuracy in the trials immediately preceding and following a mistake, the authors characterize the phenomenon of pre-error speeding and the subsequent compensatory mechanism of post-error slowing. The findings demonstrate that these behavioral fluctuations are systematic and can be utilized within a computational framework to predict upcoming performance failures, providing insights into the dynamic adjustment of decision criteria and the maintenance of cognitive control.
papers.authors: Sarah B. Malykke, Audrey Siqi-Liu, Dwight J. Kravitz, Stephen R. Mitroff

papers.title: Computer cursor trajectories are predictive of upcoming success in visual search
papers.abstract: This research utilizes mouse cursor tracking to reveal the online dynamics of decision-making during visual search tasks. By recording continuous motor output, the study calculates time-resolved kinematic features, including trajectory length, dwell times on distractors, and velocity profiles. Machine learning models trained on these cursor kinematics were able to accurately distinguish between hit and miss trials significantly before the participant's response (up to 1000 ms prior). The results suggest that continuous motor data provide a high-fidelity, real-time measure of latent attentional states and can predict search errors more effectively than discrete aggregate metrics.
papers.authors: Audrey Siqi-Liu, Sarah Malykke, Kelvin S. Oie, Dwight J. Kravitz, Stephen R. Mitroff

papers.title: Increases in symptoms associated with obsessive-compulsive disorder among university students during the COVID-19 pandemic
papers.abstract: This longitudinal study evaluated the persistent mental health impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on university students by tracking self-reported obsessive-compulsive (OC) symptomatology. Utilizing a cohort-based design, researchers compared clinical metrics across pre-pandemic, peak-pandemic, and later-pandemic intervals. The analysis revealed a significant increase in the severity and prevalence of OC symptoms within the student population during and following the pandemic peak. The results highlight the need for a shift in university health services from preventive measures to active assessment and treatment of clinical-level obsessive-compulsive symptoms triggered by large-scale environmental stressors.
papers.authors: Michael E. Silverman, Samoni Nag, Alyssa Kalishman, Patrick H. Cox, Stephen R. Mitroff

papers.title: The time course of an error: Benefits of examining pre-error speeding and post-error slowing simultaneously
papers.abstract: Human performance surrounding errors is often marked by pre-error speeding and post-error slowing (PES), typically studied as isolated phenomena. This study leveraged a massive behavioral dataset to perform a unified analysis of the temporal dynamics leading up to and following errors. Using correlation matrices of trial-by-trial response times, the authors demonstrate that errors disrupt stable behavioral consistencies, which then gradually recover through the PES phase. The study argues that examining these pre- and post-error changes concurrently provides a more comprehensive narrative of performance monitoring and the re-establishment of cognitive control following task failure.
papers.authors: Sarah B. Malykke, Audrey Siqi-Liu, Kelvin S. Oie, Dwight J. Kravitz, Stephen R. Mitroff

papers.title: Domain-specific cognitive flexibility: Shift-readiness adaptations for task- and attention-switching are non-transferrable
papers.abstract: This study investigates whether cognitive flexibility adaptations are regulated by a domain-general mechanism or independent, domain-specific processes. Across five experiments, the authors implemented a paradigm that orthogonally manipulated the frequency of cued task switches (rule-based associations) and attention shifts (spatial prioritizing). The results indicated that the reduction in switch/shift costs observed in response to high-frequency contexts did not transfer across domains; adjustments in task-switching performance were independent of attention-shifting adaptations. These findings suggest that shift-readiness is guided by domain-specific probabilistic learning of contextual demands rather than a shared executive resource.
papers.authors: Audrey Siqi-Liu, Sarah B. Malykke, Kelvin S. Oie, Dwight J. Kravitz, Stephen R. Mitroff

0637.name: Steven Dakin
0637.bio: Steven Dakin is a visual neuroscientist who researches the neural mechanisms of human perception and the development of diagnostic technologies for vision disorders. Dakin utilizes psychophysical techniques, computational modeling, and functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) to study the integration of local features into global visual structures, particularly in peripheral vision and under conditions of visual crowding. Their work focuses on the clinical application of these methods, including the creation of eye-tracking tools and pediatric vision tests like the Auckland Optotypes to assess neurodevelopmental and psychiatric conditions such as autism and schizophrenia. Formerly a Professor at University College London’s Institute of Ophthalmology, Dakin directs research initiatives in New Zealand aimed at improving eye-health equity through digital screening technologies.
0637.research_direction: Dr. Dakin's recent work spans both basic visual psychophysics and the clinical translation of novel ophthalmic technologies, particularly exploring the utility of consumer-grade tablets for automated vision screening. They are currently investigating the accuracy of iPad-based eye-tracking across diverse oculomotor tasks to determine if relative eye velocity can serve as a reliable biomarker, such as using reflexive directed eye movements to objectively diagnose color vision deficiencies. In the realm of clinical treatments, their recent work evaluates the safety and feasibility of emerging interventions, including the use of dichoptic digital therapeutics—such as contrast-balanced movie viewing—to reduce interocular suppression in childhood amblyopia, as well as systematically assessing the longitudinal adverse event profiles of electronic retinal prostheses. Additionally, they have recently been probing the fundamental mechanisms of foveal visual crowding, testing whether high-frequency flicker adaptation can mitigate crowding effects and improve visual acuity for briefly presented targets independently of pupil dynamics or fixational eye movements.

papers.title: Diagnosing Colour Vision Deficiencies Using Eye Movements (Without Dedicated Eye-Tracking Hardware)
papers.abstract: This study evaluates the diagnostic utility of an unmodified tablet-based system for identifying colour vision deficiencies (CVD) through the analysis of reflexive directed eye movements (DEMs). Utilizing the infrared head-tracking and front-facing camera of an iPad, the authors recorded oculomotor responses to chromatic stimuli presented on pseudoisochromatic plates. By quantifying the red–green equiluminant point and equivalent luminance contrast, the system performed binary classification of protan and deutan defects against normal trichromats. The methodology yielded a sensitivity of 90.0% and a specificity of 91.3% compared to gold-standard anomaloscopy. These findings suggest that automated analysis of DEM gain and velocity can provide a cost-effective, objective alternative for CVD screening in populations where traditional psychophysical testing is challenging.
papers.authors: Aryaman Taore, Gabriel Lobo, Philip R. K. Turnbull, Steven C. Dakin

papers.title: Harms associated with retinal implantation of a stimulating electrode array to treat outer-retinal degeneration: a systematic review and meta-analysis of safety
papers.abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis synthesize safety outcomes and adverse events (AEs) associated with retinal prostheses used to manage profound vision loss in outer-retinal degenerations. The analysis incorporates data from 59 peer-reviewed articles representing 11 distinct devices, including the Argus II and Alpha IMS systems. Utilizing the McMaster tool to assess risk of bias, the researchers quantified the incidence and timing of serious adverse events (SAEs). A key quantitative finding from the meta-analysis is that SAEs follow a log-uniform distribution across the post-implantation follow-up period. This work provides a comprehensive safety profile of electronic vision prostheses, highlighting the critical need for standardized reporting of longitudinal harms to optimize clinical decision-making and future device engineering.
papers.authors: Luke E. Hallum, Steven C. Dakin

papers.title: Flicker adaptation improves acuity for briefly presented stimuli by reducing crowding
papers.abstract: The authors investigate the mechanism by which adaptation to high-frequency (60 Hz) flickering noise enhances visual acuity for transiently presented targets. Using a 4AFC tumbling-T task with masked stimuli, the study tested whether reported acuity gains stem from altered pupil dynamics, fixation stability, or a reduction in visual crowding. Results demonstrated a significant acuity improvement (~8.4%, 0.038 logMAR) specifically for crowded (flanked) optotypes, with no effect observed for isolated targets. The magnitude of this improvement was positively correlated with baseline susceptibility to crowding but showed no association with changes in pupil diameter or fixational eye movements. These results suggest that flicker adaptation specifically mitigates foveal crowding, likely by attenuating neural sensitivity to transient low-spatial-frequency components that otherwise mask high-frequency target features.
papers.authors: Selassie Tagoh, Lisa M. Hamm, Dietrich S. Schwarzkopf, Steven C. Dakin

papers.title: Feasibility of a new 'balanced binocular viewing' treatment for unilateral amblyopia in children aged 3–8 years (BALANCE): results of a phase 2a randomised controlled feasibility trial
papers.abstract: This phase 2a randomized controlled trial assessed the feasibility, safety, and preliminary efficacy of Balanced Binocular Viewing (BBV)—a dichoptic digital therapeutic—for treating unilateral amblyopia. BBV involves presenting contrast-balanced movie content to each eye to promote binocular integration and reduce interocular suppression. Participants (n=32) were randomized to BBV or standard occlusion therapy. Adherence to the BBV protocol was approximately 57%. While both groups showed improvements in Best Corrected Visual Acuity (BCVA), there was no significant difference in the reduction of interocular suppression (measured via a specialized 'ghosting' task) between treatments at 16 weeks. The study concludes that while BBV is safe, future phase 3 trials must address barriers to adherence and utilize multi-center recruitment to overcome significant participant attrition.
papers.authors: Annegret Hella Dahlmann-Noor, John A. Greenwood, Andrew Skilton, Daniel Baker, Mohamed Abbas, Emma Clay, Payal Khandelwal, Denise Dunham, Siobhan Ludden, Amanda Davis, Hakim-Moulay Dehbi, Steven C. Dakin

papers.title: (The limits of) eye-tracking with iPads
papers.abstract: This paper provides a rigorous performance benchmark of eye-tracking implemented on a consumer-grade iPad Pro (3rd gen) compared to a research-grade Tobii 4C infrared tracker. Across tasks including fixation, saccades, smooth pursuit, and optokinetic nystagmus (OKN), the authors quantified gaze estimation accuracy and precision. The iPad-based system, utilizing the ARKit framework for head and gaze tracking, exhibited a mean absolute error of 3.61°, significantly higher than the Tobii’s 0.75°. However, eye velocity metrics—specifically OKN gain—showed robust correlation between devices, indicating that software-only solutions on mobile hardware are viable for specific clinical applications where relative eye movement velocity is the primary biomarker. The study cautions against using such hardware for absolute gaze positioning or high-precision saccadic characterization without rigorous outlier removal.
papers.authors: Aryaman Taore, Michelle Tiang, Steven C. Dakin

0638.name: Steven J. Luck
0638.bio: Steven J. Luck is a Distinguished Professor at UC Davis specializing in the neurocognitive architecture of visual attention and working memory. Luck's research integrates behavioral psychophysics, eye tracking, and electrophysiological recordings to characterize the capacity limits of human cognition and the translational impacts of cognitive dysfunction in disorders such as schizophrenia. Luck authored a guide to event-related potential (ERP) techniques and developed the open-source ERPLAB Toolbox to standardize brain activity analysis. Luck's work extends to global training initiatives, including workshops designed to promote experimental standards in cognitive neuroscience.
0638.research_direction: Dr. Luck has recently been investigating the neural mechanisms of visual working memory, attention, and object recognition using advanced electrophysiological and computational methods. Their recent work explores how the visual system represents both complex, naturalistic scenes and highly familiar orthographic stimuli, utilizing EEG decoding alongside deep convolutional neural networks to model population-level sensory tuning. In clinical populations, they are investigating the underlying cognitive architecture of psychotic and mood disorders, applying hierarchical modeling to trial-by-trial EEG data to disentangle fundamental sensory precision deficits from fluctuating attentional lapses and dysfunctional aperiodic neural dynamics. Furthermore, Dr. Luck is actively refining electrophysiological methodologies, systematically evaluating how artifact correction and rejection strategies impact the performance of multivariate pattern analysis in EEG pipelines.

papers.title: A Population Vector Model of Visual Working Memory for Real-World Scenes
papers.abstract: This research introduces a computational framework—the population vector model—designed to simulate the neural storage of complex, naturalistic scenes in visual working memory (VWM). Moving beyond the discrete, artificial objects prevalent in VWM research, the model utilizes a deep convolutional neural network (CORnet) to estimate high-dimensional vectors of simulated firing rates across the ventral visual hierarchy, from V1 to the inferotemporal (IT) cortex. By characterizing scene representations as noisy population vectors, the study successfully predicts behavioral performance (accuracy and response times) in change detection tasks and the topographic scalp distribution of EEG activity during the maintenance period. Results indicate that abstract, IT-like representations account for significantly more variance in behavioral and neural outcomes than spatially detailed, V1-like features.
papers.authors: John Emmanuel Kiat, Steven J. Luck

papers.title: Assessing the impact of artifact correction and artifact rejection on the performance of SVM- and LDA-based decoding of EEG signals
papers.abstract: This study systematically evaluates how two common preprocessing strategies—ICA-based artifact correction and trial-based artifact rejection—influence the performance of multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) in EEG research. Using multiple datasets from the open-source ERP CORE, the researchers assessed decoding accuracy for support vector machines (SVM) and linear discriminant analysis (LDA). The findings demonstrate that artifact correction is a critical step for minimizing non-neural confounds (e.g., ocular artifacts) that can spuriously inflate decoding accuracy. In contrast, rejecting trials containing artifacts often fails to enhance, and can even degrade, classification performance due to the resulting reduction in training trial counts. The study provides methodological recommendations for optimizing the signal-to-noise ratio in EEG decoding pipelines.
papers.authors: Guanghui Zhang, Steven J. Luck

papers.title: Assessing Trial-by-Trial Electrophysiological and Behavioral Markers of Attentional Control and Sensory Precision in Psychotic and Mood Disorders
papers.abstract: This transdiagnostic clinical investigation utilizes hierarchical modeling to parse the cognitive components of visual perceptual discrimination in individuals with schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, and major depression. By analyzing trial-by-trial behavioral data and concurrent EEG recordings, the study distinguishes between 'lapses' in attentional control and the 'precision' of internal sensory representations. The results reveal that while clinical groups exhibit significantly higher lapse rates—correlated with specific pre-stimulus neural markers of attentional state—the underlying precision of sensory encoding remains relatively intact. These findings suggest that cognitive impairments in serious mental illness are primarily driven by fluctuating attentional control rather than a fundamental degradation of sensory processing capabilities.
papers.authors: Megan A. Boudewyn, Molly A. Erickson, Kurt Winsler, Deanna M. Barch, Cameron S. Carter, Michael J. Frank, James M. Gold, Angus W. MacDonald III, J. Daniel Ragland, Steven M. Silverstein, Andrew P. Yonelinas, Steven J. Luck

papers.title: Experience-dependent Changes in the Visual Processing of Letters: Evidence from Electroencephalography Decoding
papers.abstract: Investigating how long-term visual experience tunes early orthographic processing, this study utilizes EEG decoding to compare the neural representations of upright versus inverted letters. Multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) was applied to classify individual letter identities from topographic scalp voltage patterns across various retinal eccentricities. The findings demonstrate that individual letters can be decoded more accurately when presented in their familiar upright orientation, with these effects emerging as early as 90–110 ms within the P1 and N170 latency ranges. This early emergence of orthographic tuning supports the hypothesis that extensive reading experience optimizes ventral stream representations to enhance the extraction of structural sensory information for rapid character recognition.
papers.authors: Kurt Winsler, Steven J. Luck

papers.title: Dysfunctional Alpha Modulation as a Mechanism of Working Memory Impairment in Serious Mental Illness
papers.abstract: This study deconstructs the neural dynamics of visual working memory (VWM) deficits in patients with psychosis and mood disorders by differentiating between oscillatory alpha-band (8–13 Hz) power and aperiodic (1/f) EEG components. Through single-trial analysis of a VWM task, the researchers found that impaired memory performance is specifically linked to attenuated post-stimulus alpha suppression, a neural marker of memory encoding. Crucially, increased behavioral errors in patients were predicted by elevated pre-stimulus aperiodic activity rather than true oscillatory alpha power. This suggests that the VWM impairments observed in serious mental illness reflect a failure in the transition to an active encoding state and a broader breakdown in state-dependent preparation, rather than a simple defect in alpha-mediated sensory gating.
papers.venue: Biological Psychiatry: Cognitive Neuroscience and Neuroimaging
papers.authors: Molly A. Erickson, Megan A. Boudewyn, Kurt Winsler, Charlotte Li, Deanna M. Barch, Cameron S. Carter, Michael J. Frank, James M. Gold, Angus W. MacDonald III, John D. Ragland, Steven M. Silverstein, Andrew Yonelinas, Steven J. Luck

0639.name: Steven K Shevell
0639.department: Departments of Psychology and Ophthalmology & Visual Science
0639.bio: Steven K. Shevell is the Eliakim Hastings Moore Distinguished Service Professor at the University of Chicago, where they investigate the neural and psychophysical mechanisms underlying human color and brightness perception. Their research focuses on how the visual system resolves ambiguity in complex scenes, utilizing paradigms such as chromatic interocular-switch rivalry to dissociate retinal stimulation from perceived color experience. By combining psychophysical methods with neuroimaging techniques like fMRI and EEG, Shevell has demonstrated that perceptual color representations emerge in higher cortical areas, such as V4, rather than being determined solely by early retinal signals. Their recent work explores divisive normalization as a canonical computation for explaining context-dependent sensory processing and the perceptual grouping of ambiguous neural representations.
0639.research_direction: Dr. Shevell has recently been investigating how the visual system resolves conflicting sensory inputs during bistable and multistable perception. Their recent work explores the mechanisms underlying chromatic ambiguity, specifically asking how spatial and temporal contextual cues bias perceptual selection when the eyes receive competing color information. To understand why these conflicting signals sometimes resolve into identical percepts (interocular color grouping) and other times into maximally distinct ones (difference enhancement), they combine psychophysical measurements of interocular-switch rivalry with computational modeling. Through this approach, they are evaluating whether feature-tuned divisive normalization can provide a unifying framework to explain how competing neural populations dynamically reweight these ambiguous chromatic signals.

papers.title: Perceptual resolution of ambiguity: A divisive normalization account for both interocular color grouping and difference enhancement
papers.abstract: Visual perception typically constructs an unambiguous, coherent representation of the environment, even when retinal inputs admit multiple conflicting interpretations that induce competition among neural populations. In such bistable or multistable scenarios, spatial and temporal contextual cues bias perceptual selection. While previous work has demonstrated that multiple chromatically ambiguous regions can resolve synchronously to yield identical percepts (interocular similarity grouping) or maximally distinct percepts (difference enhancement), traditional rivalry models based on fixed stimulus strength cannot readily account for these divergent outcomes, particularly given the nonlinearities inherent to chromatic processing. This work demonstrates that a feature-tuned divisive normalization framework, wherein neural responses are pooled across the stimulus space to dynamically reweight competing chromatic signals, accounts for both interocular grouping and difference enhancement. Computational simulations and psychophysical measurements in interocular-switch rivalry confirm that divisive normalization provides a parsimonious, unifying mechanism governing opposite perceptual resolutions of chromatic ambiguity.
papers.authors: Jaelyn R. Peiso, Stephanie E. Palmer, Steven K. Shevell

0641.name: Suk Won Han
0641.bio: Suk Won Han is a Professor in the Department of Psychology at Chungnam National University and directs the Cognitive Neuroscience Unit. Han’s research investigates the neurocognitive mechanisms of visual attention, working memory, and cognitive control through functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and behavioral psychophysics. Their work examines the functional fractionation of stimulus-driven attention networks, the impact of working memory contents on attentional capture, and the neural bottlenecks that lead to dual-task limitations. Han previously conducted research as a postdoctoral scholar at Vanderbilt University and as a research professor at Chungbuk National University.
0641.research_direction: Dr. Han has recently been investigating the core mechanisms of visual attention and working memory, focusing on how cognitive control and task demands modulate distractibility. Their recent work explores the attentional window account, using psychophysical search paradigms to test how the breadth of spatial focus—specifically parallel versus serial processing—determines whether abrupt onsets, color singletons, or memory-driven distractors capture attention. They are also examining the temporal dynamics of visual working memory, testing how spatial and value-based cues presented during encoding or maintenance protect internal representations from perceptual interference. Furthermore, Dr. Han is translating these basic cognitive frameworks into social and clinical domains by investigating how variations in exogenous and endogenous attentional orienting relate to real-world social connectedness, self-regulatory behaviors, and social cue processing across the autism spectrum.

papers.title: Visual Attention Across the Autism Spectrum
papers.abstract: This review synthesizes findings on visual attentional orienting mechanisms in individuals with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) and those with high autistic-like traits (ALT). The study evaluates key psychophysical indicators, including exogenous and endogenous orienting, responses to social versus nonsocial cues, and the effects of cue validity. The meta-analysis reveals that while exogenous attentional capture remains largely intact in these populations, endogenous orienting—specifically the strategic utilization and interpretation of cues—exhibits significant impairment. Findings further suggest that social cue processing (e.g., gaze following) is highly dependent on experimental context and stimulus timing, supporting a dimensional rather than a purely categorical framework for understanding attentional variations across the spectrum.
papers.authors: Seonmi Yun, Suk-Won Han

papers.title: Prioritization mechanisms in working memory modulate perceptual interference
papers.abstract: The study investigated how different modes and timings of prioritization in visual working memory (VWM) interact with perceptual interference from task-irrelevant distractors (suffix effect). Across a series of experiments manipulating item priority via value-based or spatial cues presented either during encoding (precues) or maintenance (retrocues), the research found that prioritized items were susceptible to suffix interference only when high value was assigned before encoding. In contrast, prioritization during the maintenance phase or through spatial cues provided robust protection against irrelevant suffix items. These results suggest that the resilience of working memory representations to external distraction depends on the specific cognitive mechanisms employed to bias processing toward behaviorally relevant information.
papers.authors: Koeun Jung, Suk Won Han

papers.title: Color singletons are suppressed under serial search, but not abrupt onsets
papers.abstract: This research compared the attentional capture profiles of salient color singletons and abrupt visual onsets across various visual search modes. Findings indicated that while color singletons elicit significant attentional capture when search is conducted in parallel (broad attentional window), they are effectively suppressed during serial search modes involving a narrow, shifted attentional focus. Conversely, abrupt onsets consistently captured attention regardless of the search mode or attentional window size. These distinct patterns suggest that suppression mechanisms are generalizable to static singletons under serial demand but do not extend to abruptly appearing stimuli, which appear to bypass top-down attentional filtering mechanisms.
papers.authors: Hae Chan Jeong, Koeun Jung, Suk Won Han

papers.title: Interaction between attentional allocation, social connectedness, and problem behaviors: a brief review and pilot data
papers.abstract: The research investigated whether core cognitive processes, specifically basic attentional orienting, are predictive of real-world psychosocial functioning and maladaptive behaviors. Pilot data involving 30 participants assessed via a modified attentional cuing task, the Adult Self-Report (ASR), and the Sociotype Questionnaire (SOCQ) demonstrated a significant interaction between cuing effect magnitude and ASR scores. Individuals reporting higher levels of self-regulatory problem behaviors exhibited reduced benefits from attentional cues. Furthermore, a negative correlation was observed between ASR scores and SOCQ scores, suggesting that subtle deficits in basic attentional control networks may serve as a mechanistic link to difficulties in social connectedness and adaptive behavioral regulation in typical development.
papers.authors: Seonmi Yun, Suk Won Han

papers.title: The degree of parallel/serial processing affects stimulus-driven and memory-driven attentional capture: Evidence for the attentional window account
papers.abstract: This study tested the validity of the attentional window account by quantifying search seriality through a novel visual search paradigm. By manipulating task difficulty to induce either parallel or serial processing, the researchers measured the resulting capture by salient distractors and items matching working memory contents. Results showed that both stimulus-driven and memory-driven capture occurred only when the attentional window was wide enough to encompass multiple stimuli simultaneously (parallel search). When the task necessitated a narrow window shifted serially between items, capture effects were abolished. These findings provide critical empirical support for the hypothesis that the search mode and the breadth of the attentional focus are primary determinants of whether salient irrelevant information disrupts goal-directed performance.
papers.authors: Cheolhwan Kim, Nahyeon Lee, Koeun Jung, Suk Won Han

0642.name: Summer Sheremata
0642.bio: Summer Sheremata is a cognitive neuroscientist who investigates how the human brain processes and maintains visual information through the coordination of attention and short-term memory. Currently an Assistant Teaching Professor at Northeastern University and formerly an Assistant Professor at Florida Atlantic University, Sheremata utilizes functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and behavioral psychophysics to map visuotopic representations in the parietal and visual cortices. Their research focuses on the neural architecture of cognitive systems and how these mechanisms are impacted by aging and neuropsychiatric conditions, including Alzheimer’s disease, schizophrenia, and hemispatial neglect. By examining hemispheric asymmetries and sensory mapping, Sheremata aims to identify the specific brain networks that support daily visual interactions and their potential for clinical decline.
0642.research_direction: Dr. Sheremata's recent work explores the architectural limitations of visual short-term memory and the mechanisms underlying individual differences in memory capacity. They have recently been investigating how attentional control interacts with these memory limits, using continuous report paradigms and early visually evoked ERPs to determine whether low-capacity individuals suffer from a fundamental failure to filter distractors and override attentional capture during early sensory processing. Additionally, their research examines the spatial biases governing visual retention, utilizing gaze manipulations during change-detection tasks to test whether characteristic behavioral asymmetries in short-term memory operate in retinotopic or spatiotopic coordinates.

papers.title: When remembering less is more: Unfiltered items are associated with reduced memory fidelity in visual short-term memory
papers.abstract: Visual short-term memory (VSTM) exhibits capacity constraints that vary significantly across individuals and correlate with general cognitive metrics. This study investigated whether low-memory individuals' performance deficits stem from an inability to selectively encode only goal-relevant items, particularly when stimuli numbers exceed capacity. By varying set sizes in a change-detection paradigm and a continuous report task, the authors demonstrated that performance between low- and high-memory groups diverges specifically when memory limits are exceeded, even with task difficulty controlled. Mnemonic fidelity, as measured by the precision of representations in the continuous report task, was significantly reduced in low-capacity individuals under high load. These findings suggest that failing to filter irrelevant information leads to the storage of 'unfiltered' items, which subsequently degrades the quality and precision of the items maintained in memory.
papers.authors: Young Seon Shin, Summer L. Sheremata

papers.title: Human Variation in Overriding Attentional Capture
papers.abstract: The ability to ignore salient but irrelevant stimuli is a hallmark of goal-directed behavior, yet individuals vary in their susceptibility to attentional capture. This research utilized neurophysiological measures, specifically early visually evoked event-related potentials (ERPs) like the P1 and N1, to map the rapid reallocation of spatial attention following distractor onset. By comparing contralateral and ipsilateral ERP amplitudes, the authors indexed the degree to which attention was diverted by distractors. The results showed that individual working memory capacity strongly predicts the ability to override capture: high-capacity individuals successfully resisted distraction, while low-capacity individuals involuntarily reallocated spatial attention to irrelevant information. This suggests that the poor attentional control associated with lower memory capacity is linked to a fundamental failure to override capture during the earliest phases of sensory processing.
papers.authors: Young Seon Shin, Summer Sheremata

papers.title: Behavioral asymmetries in visual short-term memory occur in retinotopic coordinates
papers.abstract: Visual short-term memory (VSTM) acts as a crucial buffer bridging perceptual discontinuities across interrupted sensory inputs, yet it remains severely capacity-limited due to architectural bottlenecks in underlying cortical networks. VSTM performance exhibits characteristic spatial biases that mirror neural hemispheric asymmetries associated with the visual field locus of remembered targets. Because sensory representations across early visual cortex are organized retinotopically, we examined whether spatial biases in memory performance are similarly locked to a retinotopic frame of reference rather than spatiotopic coordinates. Memory fidelity was assessed using a whole-display color change-detection paradigm across visual field quadrants while observers maintained either central fixation or eccentric fixation to displace retinal coordinates relative to monitor space. VSTM performance biases systematically tracked the retinal locus of the visual stimuli regardless of absolute screen coordinate positioning. These results indicate that spatial asymmetries governing VSTM retention operate in retinotopic coordinates, demonstrating an intrinsic dependence of behavioral visual working memory limits on retinotopically organized visual representations.
papers.authors: Summer Sheremata, George L. Malcolm, Sarah Shomstein

0643.name: Surya Gayet
0643.bio: Gayet is an Assistant Professor in Experimental Psychology at Utrecht University and the principal investigator of the CAP-Lab. Their research investigates the neurocognitive mechanisms by which sensory input is transformed into conscious experience, focusing on the interplay between visual perception, attention, and working memory. Utilizing a multimodal approach including psychophysics, fMRI, and EEG, Gayet applies Rapid Invisible Frequency Tagging (RIFT) to track covert visuo-spatial attention. Their work explores how internal states—such as task goals, statistical learning, and mnemonic content—modulate neural responses to sensory information.
0643.research_direction: Dr. Gayet has recently been investigating the mechanisms governing early visual processing and the top-down factors that dictate which stimuli successfully reach conscious awareness. Using interocular suppression paradigms like breaking continuous flash suppression, their recent work explores how pre-conscious visual competition is modulated by prioritized visual working memory contents, fear-conditioned physiological arousal, and spatial statistical regularities. Beyond conscious access, they are also examining the architecture of working memory itself to determine whether recall precision is driven by passive environmental prevalence or active, goal-directed task relevance. Additionally, Dr. Gayet applies Bayesian modeling to multisensory integration, investigating how the human brain dynamically weights visual and auditory signals during spatial localization and motion prediction tasks.

papers.title: Using hearing and vision for motion prediction, motion perception, and localization
papers.abstract: This research investigates the multisensory integration of auditory and visual signals in the context of spatial reasoning and motion processing. Through a series of experiments, the authors assessed how observers utilize varying levels of sensory reliability to perform motion prediction (extrapolating a hidden trajectory), motion perception (judging velocity and direction), and precise spatial localization. By applying Bayesian modeling to behavioral data, the study quantifies the flexible weighting of modalities, demonstrating that the human brain optimizes spatial performance by dynamically adjusting to the informational utility of each sense. The results provide evidence for a highly adaptive multisensory system capable of resolving spatial uncertainty in dynamic environments.
papers.authors: Yichen Yuan, Nathan Van der Stoep, Surya Gayet

papers.title: The priority state of items in visual working memory determines their influence on early visual processing
papers.abstract: Observers maintained representations in visual working memory (VWM) while performing concurrent perceptual tasks to examine how prioritization modulates early visual processing, specifically conscious access and attentional allocation. Utilizing the breaking continuous flash suppression (b-CFS) paradigm, attentional capture, and visual search tasks, the study demonstrated that stimuli congruent with prioritized VWM content enjoy a robust perceptual advantage compared to non-prioritized content. Critically, non-prioritized memoranda still exerted a significant, albeit smaller, bias over VWM-unrelated stimuli. The findings suggest that VWM content is not uniformly active; instead, observers exert flexible top-down control to up- or down-regulate memory representations according to task-specific utility, thereby modulating the extent of their interference with sensory input.
papers.authors: Dan Wang, Samson Chota, Luzi Xu, Stefan Van der Stigchel, Surya Gayet

papers.title: Spatial statistical learning of task relevance, rather than stimulus prevalence, improves visual working memory recall
papers.abstract: This study dissociates the effects of environmental stimulus prevalence (how often a stimulus appears) and task relevance (how often it is probed) on the quality of visual working memory (VWM) representations. Participants performed an orientation recall task where the spatial distribution of targets followed specific statistical regularities. Results indicated that mere frequent appearance at a specific location did not improve recall precision or reduce error. Conversely, locations with high task relevance—those more frequently probed—yielded significantly higher recall precision and fewer categorical errors. These findings support a model where statistical learning in VWM is optimized for the anticipated utility of information for goal-directed behavior rather than the passive encoding of frequent environmental features.
papers.authors: Luzi Xu, Andre Sahakian, Stefan Van der Stigchel, Chris L. E. Paffen, Surya Gayet

papers.title: Statistical Learning Facilitates Access to Awareness
papers.abstract: The authors investigated whether the human visual system leverages statistical regularities in the environment to prioritize certain objects for conscious access. Using the breaking continuous flash suppression (b-CFS) paradigm, they found that probable objects (those frequently encountered during a learning phase) reached conscious awareness significantly faster than improbable objects. To exclude post-perceptual shifts in decision criteria, the researchers employed an accuracy-based b-CFS task with fixed presentation durations and a visual-masking paradigm, both of which confirmed higher localization sensitivity for probable objects. The study concludes that statistical learning modulates the pre-conscious competition for limited sensory resources, thereby facilitating the rapid perception of expected environmental information.
papers.authors: Luzi Xu, Chris L. E. Paffen, Stefan Van der Stigchel, Surya Gayet

papers.title: Physiological arousal underlies preferential access to visual awareness of fear-conditioned (and possibly disgust-conditioned) stimuli
papers.abstract: This research examines the relationship between physiological arousal and the prioritized access to awareness for emotionally salient stimuli. By employing a Pavlovian fear-conditioning paradigm combined with the breaking continuous flash suppression (b-CFS) technique, the study evaluated the breakthrough times of stimuli paired with aversive outcomes. Results demonstrated that conditioned fear stimuli enjoy faster access to conscious awareness compared to neutral stimuli. Critically, this perceptual prioritization was significantly correlated with measures of physiological arousal, such as skin conductance and pupillary dilation. The findings suggest that the preferential processing of threat-related information is mediated by an arousal-driven mechanism that enhances the competitive strength of these signals during interocular suppression.
papers.authors: Piotr Litwin, Paweł Motyka, Surya Gayet

0644.name: Susana T. L Chung
0644.bio: Chung’s research investigates the mechanisms of visual perception in individuals with normal and impaired vision, focusing on conditions such as age-related macular degeneration and amblyopia. Their work utilizes psychophysical methods, including signal detection theory and reversed-correlation, as well as neuroimaging techniques like functional MRI and Scanning Laser Ophthalmoscopy. By exploring the neural and optical limits of vision, Chung examines how the brain adapts to central vision loss through cortical plasticity. Their research aims to develop rehabilitative strategies, such as perceptual learning and oculomotor training, to improve reading speed and functional independence for patients with visual impairments.
0644.research_direction: Dr. Chung has recently been investigating a diverse array of topics spanning clinical low vision, oculomotor adaptations, and fundamental visual processing. Their recent work explores how eye movements interact with visual impairments, specifically examining oculomotor abnormalities in amblyopia and utilizing compensated gaze tracking to study the unique reading strategies of low-vision individuals using screen magnification interfaces. To advance clinical evaluation, they are developing automated computational pipelines that register structural optical coherence tomography (OCT) with functional microperimetry to map macular disorders, while also leveraging natural language processing to connect unstructured electronic medical records to clinical capabilities and patient sentiments. Furthermore, they are probing the neural mechanisms of basic visual perception, employing electroencephalography (EEG) paradigms to investigate the top-down and bottom-up cortical networks that drive contour integration.

papers.title: The impact of eye movements on amblyopic vision: A mini-review
papers.abstract: This review synthesizes current knowledge on oculomotor abnormalities in individuals with amblyopia, specifically addressing deficits in fixational stability, saccadic dynamics, and smooth pursuit. It explores how these dysfunctions constrain visual acuity and spatial processing, while evaluating the therapeutic potential of eye-movement training and the utility of oculomotor signatures as diagnostic criteria for classifying different types of amblyopia.
papers.authors: Dennis M. Levi, Susana T. L. Chung

papers.title: Unifying Structure and Function Towards a Comprehensive Macular Evaluation in Eye Disorders: A Multi-Modal Approach Using Microperimetry and Optical Coherence Tomography
papers.abstract: The study introduces an automated computational pipeline for the point-wise registration of structural optical coherence tomography (OCT) data with functional microperimetry maps. By aligning en face scanning laser ophthalmoscope (cSLO) images with OCT B-scans, the framework enables precise topographical mapping of retinal layer thicknesses relative to local perimetric sensitivity, facilitating a more rigorous characterization of macular pathology-function relationships across diverse cohorts, including patients with albinism and macular degeneration.
papers.authors: Rijul Saurabh Soans, Benjamin E. Smith, Susana T. L. Chung

papers.title: Reading with Screen Magnification: Eye Movement Analysis Using Compensated Gaze Tracks
papers.abstract: This investigation utilizes compensated gaze tracking—a technique that remaps oculomotor coordinates from a dynamic magnified viewport to a static document frame—to analyze reading strategies in low-vision users. The results characterize the idiosyncratic saccadic and pursuit patterns necessitated by the interaction between the eye and manual scrolling interfaces, highlighting the sensory and motor adaptations occurring under significant visual field constraint.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the 2024 Symposium on Eye Tracking Research and Applications (ETRA '24)
papers.authors: Seongsil Heo, Roberto Manduchi, Susana T. L. Chung

papers.title: Using Natural Language Processing to link patients' narratives to visual capabilities and sentiments
papers.abstract: This research evaluates a machine learning-based framework to extract and categorize clinical data from the unstructured narrative sections of electronic medical records (EMRs) for low-vision patients. By utilizing supervised natural language processing (NLP) models, the authors successfully mapped patient-reported visual difficulties to clinical measures and performed sentiment analysis to quantify the psychological impact of vision impairment, establishing a scalable method for data mining in ophthalmic research.
papers.authors: Dongcheng He, Susana T. L. Chung

papers.title: Cortical Dynamics during Contour Integration
papers.abstract: Employing a temporal decoupling paradigm and electroencephalography (EEG) to separate stimulus evocation from contour grouping, this study identifies the middle temporal N300 component as a primary marker of visual element integration. The analysis reveals that interhemispheric lateral frontal-posterior parietal and medial frontal-superior parietal networks provide the requisite bottom-up and top-down attentional modulation necessary for recurrent integration across the visual cortical hierarchy.
papers.authors: Dongcheng He, Angeline Yang, Daniel R. Coates, Haluk Ogmen, Susana TL Chung

0645.name: Susanne Ferber
0645.bio: Susanne Ferber investigates the cognitive and neural mechanisms mediating human visual awareness and the transition between perception and action. Their research employs a multimodal approach, integrating behavioral psychophysics with neuroimaging techniques such as fMRI and EEG, alongside neuropsychological studies of patients with spatial neglect and simultanagnosia. Ferber's work examines the limits of visual working memory, the role of attentional templates in search, and the neural representation of visual cognition. Formerly the chair of the Department of Psychology at the University of Toronto, Ferber currently serves as the head of the Department of Psychology at Carnegie Mellon University.
0645.research_direction: Dr. Ferber has recently been investigating the mechanisms of conscious visual awareness as well as the neural architecture of spatial-numerical representations. Using the breaking continuous flash suppression paradigm, their recent work explores how specific facial cues—particularly vertical and horizontal gaze orientations—influence the transition of a stimulus from non-conscious processing into conscious awareness. In a distinct line of cognitive neuroscience research, they are also examining the functional overlap between internal representations of abstract magnitude and physical space. Specifically, they use fMRI to map the neural correlates of the mental number line, investigating how frontoparietal and cerebellar networks are recruited during numerical interval bisection tasks compared to physical line bisection tasks.

papers.title: Enhanced awareness of faces with slight downwards gaze in the breaking continuous flash suppression paradigm
papers.abstract: This study utilized the breaking continuous flash suppression (b-CFS) technique to investigate how vertical and horizontal gaze orientations influence the transition of facial stimuli from non-conscious processing into conscious visual awareness. While previous research has established a privileged status for direct gazes over horizontal averted gazes, vertical gaze deviations have remained largely unexplored. Participants performed a detection task followed by a gaze discrimination task for faces with downward, upward, leftward, rightward, and direct gazes rendered initially invisible through interocular suppression. The results demonstrated that detection times were significantly shorter for faces with downward gazes compared to all other gaze types, including direct gaze. Notably, while downward gazes were detected most rapidly, they were associated with lower discrimination accuracy relative to other orientations. These findings indicate that downward-tilted gazes enjoy prioritised access to conscious awareness, though this enhanced detectability does not translate to superior feature-level discrimination during pre-conscious processing.
papers.authors: Mayuna Ishida, Masaki Mori, Yingying Huang, Susanne Ferber

papers.title: The Neural Mechanism of Number Line Bisection: A fMRI study
papers.abstract: This neuroimaging investigation explores the functional architecture of the mental number line (MNL) by comparing neural activity during numerical bisection tasks versus physical line bisection. While spatial neglect is often characterized by lateralized biases in both physical and numerical domains, the degree of overlap between these representations is debated. Using fMRI, the study maps the neural correlates of numerical magnitude estimation along a spatial axis. The findings highlight a specific involvement of the right parietal cortex and the cerebellum in mediating spatial-numerical associations. By contrasting the bisection of number intervals with physical segments, the research identifies a causal role for frontoparietal networks in the internal mapping of magnitude, providing evidence for a shared yet dissociable neural mechanism for processing spatial and numerical intervals.
papers.authors: Stefanie Jung, Hans-Otto Karnath, Susanne Ferber

0647.name: T Rowan Candy
0647.bio: T. Rowan Candy is a Professor of Optometry and Vision Science at Indiana University who researches the mechanisms of typical and atypical visual development in human infants. Candy’s work focuses on how the developing brain coordinates visual experience with oculomotor responses to inform the management of conditions such as amblyopia and strabismus. Using optical modeling, neuroscience, and experimental psychology, Candy investigates the interaction between sensory input and motor output during the critical period of development. Recently, their lab has used egocentric imaging to characterize the visual statistics of naturalistic infant environments to identify the inputs that drive neural plasticity.
0647.research_direction: Dr. Candy's recent work explores the postnatal development of human binocular vision and oculomotor control, focusing on how the developing visual system manages early sensory disruptions like optical blur. To understand the motor mechanisms underlying clinical conditions such as strabismus and amblyopia, they have recently been investigating how simulated anisometropia and bilateral defocus impact reflex vergence using Purkinje image tracking, while also examining the longitudinal stability of accommodative errors in amblyopic children using dynamic retinoscopy. In parallel, their research probes the sensory maturation of cortical depth perception, utilizing steady-state visual evoked potentials (SSVEPs) and dynamic random-dot stereograms to map the distinct developmental timelines of absolute versus relative retinal disparity processing from infancy through adulthood. Together, this research program seeks to clarify how early interocular differences and sensory-motor feedback loops shape both typical and atypical visual development.

papers.title: The Impact of Simulated Anisometropia and Bilateral Defocus on Reflex Vergence Responses of Children and Adults
papers.abstract: This study utilized computational simulation to investigate the effects of spherical defocus—both anisometropic (unilateral) and bilateral—on reflex vergence eye movements in 6–8 year-old children and adults. Using a haploscopic setup with eccentric photorefraction and Purkinje image tracking, the authors recorded ocular alignment responses to step changes in disparity and continuous tracking tasks under conditions of induced blur. Results demonstrated that while both age groups could execute vergence responses to large disparity steps with up to 2.0 D of defocus, unilateral defocus (simulated anisometropia) significantly degraded performance in continuous tracking tasks compared to bilateral defocus. In cases of anisometropia, the ocular motor system often reverted to version-like movements tracking the focused eye, highlighting the critical role of interocular retinal image similarity in maintaining binocular alignment and preventing the developmental onset of strabismus.
papers.authors: Clara Mestre, T. Rowan Candy

papers.title: The repeatability of accommodative accuracy in childhood unilateral amblyopia
papers.abstract: This longitudinal observational study examined the repeatability and stability of accommodative responses in children (aged 4–15 years) with and without unilateral amblyopia to understand the chronic defocus experienced during occlusion or penalization therapies. Monocular accommodative accuracy was assessed using modified Nott dynamic retinoscopy at three target distances (25, 33, and 50 cm) across multiple repetitions and two separate visits. Linear mixed-model analysis revealed that while amblyopic eyes exhibited significantly larger accommodative lags that scaled with stimulus demand and the severity of visual acuity loss, the range of these responses remained consistent (typically <0.75 D) within and across visits. These findings indicate that the increased retinal defocus associated with amblyopia is a stable characteristic of the amblyopic eye's motor performance, providing a constant signal to the developing visual cortex during monocular viewing.
papers.authors: Kristine Huang, Angela M. Chen, T. Rowan Candy

papers.title: Late Development of Sensory Thresholds for Horizontal Relative Disparity in Human Visual Cortex in the Face of Precocial Development of Thresholds for Absolute Disparity
papers.abstract: The authors employed steady-state visual evoked potentials (SSVEPs) and dynamic random-dot stereograms to delineate the developmental time course of cortical sensitivity to absolute versus relative retinal disparity. Sensitivity was compared across human infants (mean age 5.3 months), children (4.7 years), and adults (25.3 years). Electrophysiological recordings showed that absolute disparity sensitivity—linked to early V1 processing—reaches adult-like levels relatively early in development. In contrast, sensitivity to horizontal relative disparity, which requires higher-order extrastriate computations to extract 3D shape and depth, is significantly immature in both infants and young children, improving by approximately tenfold into adulthood. This protracted maturation is not attributable to immaturities in monocular contrast or blur encoding, suggesting a specific, long-term developmental window for the cortical mechanisms underlying relative disparity processing.
papers.authors: Anthony M. Norcia, Milena Kaestner, Yulan D. Chen, Caroline S. Clement, T. Rowan Candy

0648.name: T Scott Murdison
0648.bio: T. Scott Murdison is a Research Scientist at Meta Reality Labs Research studying the intersection of neuroscience, psychophysics, and immersive display technology. Their research examines oculomotor control, including smooth pursuit and saccadic eye movements, and how display properties such as temporal refresh rates and depth cues influence these behaviors. Murdison develops computational models to optimize gaze-based interaction and predict user performance based on eye-tracker specifications and environmental demands. Their work addresses perception-action dissociations in digital environments to inform the development of interfaces for augmented and virtual reality.
0648.research_direction: Dr. Murdison has recently been exploring the intersection of human visual perception and display engineering, specifically focusing on optimizing power consumption in augmented reality systems. Their recent work investigates the perceptual limits of brightness roll-off, a technique that leverages the natural decline of contrast sensitivity in the peripheral visual field by strategically reducing luminance at the edges of virtual foregrounds. Using stereoscopic simulations and haploscope-based psychophysics, they are examining how varying peripheral luminance reduction profiles and additive contrast ratios affect a user's perceived image quality when digital content is overlaid on real-world backgrounds. Alongside these behavioral measurements, Dr. Murdison utilizes analytical modeling to assess the theoretical energy-saving efficacy of these rendering techniques for next-generation head-mounted display architectures.

papers.title: Stereoscopic Brightness Roll‐Off in Augmented Reality
papers.abstract: The study investigates the perceptual and energy-saving efficacy of Brightness Roll-Off (BRO), a technique leveraging the human visual system's non-uniform contrast sensitivity across the visual field. Using stereoscopic AR simulations, researchers applied luminance reduction profiles to virtual foreground layers composited with real-world backgrounds across various additive contrast ratios (3:1, 6:1, and 9:1). Psychophysical evaluation using a haploscope demonstrated that peripheral brightness reduction has a negligible impact on perceived image quality and sensitivity, often performing better than predictions from established computational metrics. Analytical modeling suggests that implementing optimized BRO profiles can reduce display power consumption by 20% to 34% for microLED and LCoS display architectures, providing a viable strategy for enhancing battery efficiency in next-generation head-mounted displays without compromising the stereoscopic user experience.
papers.venue: Journal of the Society for Information Display
papers.authors: Domenic Au, Xiuyun Wu, Nava Aghdasi, Yuta Asano, T. Scott Murdison

0650.name: Taiki Fukiage
0650.department: Human Information Science Laboratory, Sensory Representation Research Group
0650.main_research_area: human visual perception and media technology
0650.bio: Taiki Fukiage is a Senior Research Scientist at NTT Communication Science Laboratories specializing in vision science and media engineering. Fukiage earned a Ph.D. from the University of Tokyo in 2015 and develops mathematical models of human visual information processing to optimize artificial displays, including AR and VR technologies. Their research includes visibility-based rendering techniques, the 'Deformation Lamps' projection system, and comparative analyses between human depth perception and deep neural network representations. Currently, Fukiage investigates how to align machine vision models with human perceptual biases to improve image naturalness and visual comfort.
0650.research_direction: Dr. Fukiage has recently been investigating human depth perception and visual processing by bridging psychophysics with computational models and advanced display technologies. Their recent work explores the alignment between artificial and biological 3D vision, using affine error decomposition to systematically compare the monocular depth biases and compression patterns of diverse deep neural networks against human perceptual judgments. In the realm of virtual and augmented reality, they are evaluating the critical temporal limits of gaze-contingent displays by probing how ultra-low-latency ocular parallax rendering affects binocular fusion and dynamic occlusion cues. Additionally, Dr. Fukiage is actively studying human-centric image rendering frameworks, testing how early-stage visual processing models—such as contrast sensitivity and spatial frequency—can be applied to optimize perceptual naturalness and visual comfort on non-ideal viewing surfaces.

papers.title: Accuracy Does Not Guarantee Human-Likeness in Monocular Depth Estimators
papers.abstract: While deep neural networks (DNNs) have reached or surpassed human-level performance on physical-based depth benchmarks like KITTI, the alignment of these models' latent representations with human perceptual space remains a significant challenge for robustness and interpretability. We systematically evaluated 69 state-of-the-art monocular depth estimation architectures, including supervised, self-supervised, and generative models, by comparing their error distributions with human perceptual judgments. Utilizing affine fitting to decompose depth prediction errors into interpretable components—specifically depth compression, scaling, shearing, and translation—we identified a distinct trade-off between model accuracy and human similarity. Our results demonstrate that higher performance on objective metrics does not necessarily result in error patterns that reflect human perceptual biases, highlighting a critical divergence between superhuman accuracy and human-like visual space representation.
papers.authors: Yuki Kubota, Taiki Fukiage

papers.title: Human-like monocular depth biases in deep neural networks
papers.abstract: Human 3D vision from monocular 2D inputs is characterized by systematic distortions, such as distance compression and viewpoint-dependent affine shifts. We conducted a large-scale psychophysical comparison between human depth perception and 64 diverse DNN architectures using a novel human-annotated dataset of natural indoor scenes. By applying an exponential-affine error decomposition framework, we found that both humans and highly accurate DNNs exhibit consistent biases, including depth compression and vertical visual field priors. Strikingly, the correlation between a model's depth estimation accuracy and its similarity to human error patterns suggests a convergence toward human-like heuristics as models improve.
