However, significant differences remain in ordinal depth perception within affine-invariant spaces, suggesting that DNNs may prioritize metric accuracy over the structural relationships preserved in biological vision.
papers.authors: Yuki Kubota, Taiki Fukiage

papers.title: Low-Latency Ocular Parallax Rendering and Investigation of Its Effect on Depth Perception in Virtual Reality
papers.abstract: Ocular parallax—the subtle change in retinal images caused by the rotation of the eye around its center—is a vital but often neglected depth cue in gaze-contingent displays. To investigate its contribution to visual perception under free eye-movement conditions, we developed a high-frequency (360 Hz) and ultra-low-latency (4.8 ms) ocular parallax rendering system featuring custom gaze-tracking at the eye's front nodal point. Psychophysical evaluations revealed that ocular parallax significantly improves binocular fusion in stereoscopic viewing, even when rendering latency is relatively high. Conversely, monocular depth perception through dynamic occlusion cues requires extremely low latencies (sub-20 ms) to remain stable. These findings establish critical temporal requirements for immersive gaze-contingent graphics and demonstrate the visual system's integration of extra-retinal signals with ocular parallax shifts.
papers.venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
papers.authors: Yuri Mikawa, Taiki Fukiage

papers.title: Human-centric Image Rendering for Natural and Comfortable Viewing—Image Optimization Based on Human Visual Information Processing Models
papers.abstract: Standard display technologies often fail to maintain image fidelity when projected onto non-ideal surfaces or viewed through semi-transparent see-through displays due to interference from background patterns and ambient light. We propose a human-centric rendering framework that optimizes displayed content by leveraging mathematical models of early-stage visual information processing, including multiscale frequency decomposition and contrast sensitivity functions. By prioritizing the reproduction of visual features to which the human visual system is most sensitive—such as specific spatial frequency bands and luminance contrasts—the proposed model maintains perceptual naturalness and visual comfort even when physical compensation for surface irregularities is constrained by hardware limitations. This approach facilitates consistent visual quality in ubiquitous display environments and augmented reality applications.
papers.authors: Taiki Fukiage

0651.name: Takeo Watanabe
0651.department: Department of Cognitive, Linguistic, and Psychological Sciences
0651.lab_name: Laboratory for Cognitive and Perceptual Learning
0651.bio: Takeo Watanabe is the Fred M. Seed Professor of Cognitive and Linguistic Sciences at Brown University and conducts research on the mechanisms of visual perceptual learning (VPL). Watanabe documented task-irrelevant perceptual learning, showing that the human brain undergoes sensory plasticity through exposure to subliminal or unattended stimuli. Utilizing methodologies such as fMRI, real-time neurofeedback, and magnetic resonance spectroscopy, their research investigates the roles of reinforcement signals, attention, and sleep in the consolidation and stabilization of visual memories. Watanabe examines how excitatory and inhibitory neurotransmitter balances within the visual cortex affect the window of brain plasticity and its susceptibility to interference.
0651.research_direction: Dr. Watanabe has recently been investigating the neural mechanisms and boundary conditions that govern visual perceptual learning (VPL) under diverse internal and cognitive states. Their recent work explores how physiological factors, such as hunger, and psychiatric conditions, like body dysmorphic disorder, reshape the specific fMRI networks recruited to process feedback and optimize visual performance. Additionally, they are using behavioral paradigms and functional magnetic resonance spectroscopy (fMRS) to examine how conscious awareness and task-relevance dictate learning trajectories, probing how the visual system suppresses excitatory signals for irrelevant features and determines whether sequential training sessions interfere with or facilitate one another. Finally, their research investigates the intersection of VPL and higher-order cognition, testing whether complex category learning relies on the same highly location-specific, retinotopic representations that characterize early visual plasticity.

papers.title: Motivational state determines error-sensitive learning modes in visual perceptual learning
papers.abstract: The present study employed functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) to investigate how internal physiological states, specifically fasting and satiety, influence the neural processing of feedback during orientation discrimination training. Behavioral results indicated that while both groups achieved significant visual perceptual learning (VPL), the fasted cohort demonstrated significantly improved post-error accuracy, reflecting heightened sensitivity to negative outcomes. Whole-brain analysis revealed a dissociation in task-related activity: fasting was associated with attenuated prediction-error signaling in the ventral striatum as performance stabilized, whereas satiety was linked to a progressive reduction in dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC) recruitment, suggesting a decreased reliance on top-down executive control. Furthermore, fasting selectively enhanced feedback-locked responses to incorrect trials within the dorsal anterior cingulate cortex (dACC) and primary visual cortex (V1), with these error-related activations correlating with individual learning magnitude. These findings suggest that hunger triggers an outcome-monitoring learning regime characterized by increased error sensitivity, while satiety favors a control-driven mode of performance optimization.
papers.authors: Dongho Kim, Zhiyan Wang, Masamichi Sakagami, Yuka Sasaki, Takeo Watanabe

papers.title: Conscious awareness determines whether a second learning session disrupts or facilitates earlier learning
papers.abstract: This research explores the role of conscious awareness in the phenomena of retrograde interference (RI) and retrograde facilitation (RF) within the framework of visual perceptual learning (VPL). Traditional models posit that successive training sessions disrupt the stabilization of initial learning traces, resulting in RI. However, this study demonstrates that when the trained visual features are subthreshold (5% motion coherence) and thus remain outside conscious detection, a second training session unexpectedly enhances performance on the first task, resulting in RF. This facilitative effect was abolished when training sessions were separated by a one-hour interval, suggesting it occurs only during the initial labile phase of consolidation. Conversely, when stimuli were suprathreshold (10% coherence), RI was observed as typical. The results indicate that a detection system associated with conscious awareness is responsible for transforming facilitative neural interactions between successive learning sessions into disruptive ones, providing a novel boundary condition for consolidation and interference models.
papers.authors: Patrick Bruns, Kazuhisa Shibata, Takeo Watanabe

papers.title: Excitatory signal processing in early visual areas based on task-relevance and perceptual salience modulates visual perceptual learning
papers.abstract: The study investigates the neural mechanisms that suppress learning for task-irrelevant visual information using time-resolved functional magnetic resonance spectroscopy (fMRS). While unsupervised learning typically facilitates the acquisition of frequently exposed features, visible task-irrelevant features often fail to induce visual perceptual learning (VPL). By measuring dynamic changes in the concentrations of glutamate (excitatory) and gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA; inhibitory) in early visual areas (V1/V2), the researchers found that exposure to suprathreshold task-irrelevant coherent motion led to a significant reduction in glutamate levels compared to near-threshold exposure. No significant modulation was observed in GABAergic inhibitory signaling. These results suggest the existence of a gating mechanism within the early visual cortex that selectively withdraws excitatory processing to suppress the representation and subsequent learning of salient but irrelevant environmental signals, thereby preventing the cluttering of perceptual memory with trivial information.
papers.authors: Zhiyan Wang, Masako Tamaki, Savanna Babu, Sebastian M. Frank, Markus Becker, Daiki Ogawa, Takeo Watanabe

papers.title: Learning of the same task subserved by substantially different mechanisms between patients with body dysmorphic disorder and healthy individuals
papers.abstract: This investigation utilized fMRI to determine whether individuals with body dysmorphic disorder (BDD) employ different neural plasticity mechanisms than healthy controls during visual perceptual learning of a face detection task. Participants underwent six days of behavioral training on a low-spatial-frequency (LSF) face detection task. While both groups achieved comparable levels of behavioral performance improvement, the neural substrates underlying this learning were fundamentally distinct. Healthy controls exhibited plasticity primarily within early visual areas and the fusiform face area (FFA), consistent with standard feature-based learning. In contrast, patients with BDD showed a recruitment of higher-level cortical regions and altered connectivity patterns, potentially reflecting the brain's adaptation to preexisting dysfunctions in visual processing circuits. These results challenge the assumption that low-level perceptual learning follows a universal neural pathway, demonstrating that psychiatric conditions can profoundly reshape the brain's strategy for achieving task optimization.
papers.authors: Zhiyan Wang, Qingleng Tan, Sebastian M. Frank, Yuka Sasaki, David Sheinberg, Katharine A. Phillips, Takeo Watanabe

papers.title: Category Learning Can Depend on Location-Specific Visual Representations
papers.abstract: While category learning is often considered a high-level cognitive process that generalizes across the visual field, this study provides evidence that information-integration (II) category learning is constrained by the same retinotopic specificity seen in visual perceptual learning. Using a double-training paradigm (training-plus-exposure), the researchers investigated whether the learning of II category structures at one peripheral location could transfer to an untrained location. Initial results showed strong location specificity with minimal transfer. However, when participants received simultaneous or subsequent passive exposure to an irrelevant task at the untrained location, robust transfer was achieved. This order-dependent facilitation suggests that II category learning relies on plasticity within early, location-specific visual representations rather than purely abstract, high-level associations. The findings demonstrate that the neural mechanisms of categorization and perceptual skill acquisition share fundamental computational principles regarding representational stability and transferability.
papers.authors: Luke Rosedahl, Takeo Watanabe

0653.name: Talia Konkle
0653.department: Department of Psychology and Center for Brain Science
0653.main_research_area: cognitive and neural organization of vision
0653.bio: Talia Konkle is a Professor of Psychology at Harvard University and an associate faculty member at the Kempner Institute, specializing in the functional architecture of the human visual system. Konkle’s research uses behavioral psychophysics, functional MRI, and computational modeling to map the representational geometry of high-level visual experiences onto the cortical surface. Their work investigates the large-scale topographic organization of object knowledge, specifically the roles of real-world size and animacy in shaping neural responses. Konkle also bridges biological and artificial intelligence by using deep neural networks to study the computational pressures that drive representation learning and cortical specialization.
0653.research_direction: Dr. Konkle has recently been investigating the computational principles and inductive biases that shape high-level visual representation in both human brains and artificial neural networks. Their recent work explores how varying deep learning architectures, contrastive self-supervised training objectives, and efficiency-robustness constraints influence a model's alignment with human fMRI data, particularly regarding the spontaneous emergence of category-selective regions in the ventral stream. Beyond large-scale model benchmarking, they are developing mechanistic interpretability tools, such as geometrically constrained sparse autoencoders, to extract stable and semantically plausible concepts from large vision models. In parallel, they are utilizing custom ultra-wide angle neuroimaging to probe immersive scene representation in the human cortex, examining how distinct visual areas integrate peripheral information during naturalistic, panoramic vision.

papers.title: Archetypal SAE: Adaptive and Stable Dictionary Learning for Concept Extraction in Large Vision Models
papers.abstract: This study addresses the inherent instability in Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) used for mechanistic interpretability, where stochastic training factors frequently result in inconsistent dictionary atoms. The authors propose Archetypal SAEs (A-SAE), a framework that constrains dictionary elements to reside within the convex hull of the activation data, thereby anchoring the learned features to the empirical distribution. This geometric constraint significantly enhances both the stability and semantic plausibility of extracted concepts. Evaluations utilizing novel metrics for identifiability and plausibility across diverse vision backbones demonstrate that a relaxed variant (RA-SAE) preserves state-of-the-art reconstruction fidelity while uncovering more robust and interpretable feature sets in large-scale vision models.
papers.authors: Thomas Fel, Ekdeep Singh Lubana, Jacob S. Prince, Matthew Kowal, Victor Boutin, Isabel Papadimitriou, Binxu Wang, Martin Wattenberg, Demba E. Ba, Talia Konkle

papers.title: A large-scale examination of inductive biases shaping high-level visual representation in brains and machines
papers.abstract: In an extensive computational benchmarking effort involving over 1.8 billion regressions and 50,000 representational similarity analyses, this research evaluates how various model architectures and training objectives influence alignment with the human visual system. By comparing 224 diverse deep neural networks, including CNNs and Vision Transformers, against large-scale fMRI data from the Natural Scenes Dataset, the authors find that qualitatively distinct architectures and task objectives (e.g., contrastive vision vs. vision-language alignment) achieve surprisingly similar levels of brain predictivity when other parameters are controlled. These findings suggest that the emergent representational geometry of high-level visual cortex is shaped more by the broad statistics of natural image diets than by specific architectural constraints or downstream task demands.
papers.authors: Colin Conwell, Jacob S. Prince, Kendrick N. Kay, George A. Alvarez, Talia Konkle

papers.title: Contrastive learning explains the emergence and function of visual category-selective regions
papers.abstract: This work reconciles modular and distributed coding accounts of human ventral stream organization using a contrastive self-supervised learning framework. The authors demonstrate that training deep convolutional neural networks with instance-level contrastive objectives on natural image datasets leads to the spontaneous emergence of units selective for faces, bodies, scenes, and words, even in the absence of explicit category supervision. Using a novel sparse positive encoding procedure, they show that these emergent model units accurately predict neural responses in corresponding category-selective regions (e.g., FFA, PPA, EBA). Furthermore, virtual lesions to these model units result in specific, dissociable deficits in categorization performance, providing a computational account of how domain-general contrastive pressures drive functional specialization in the primate visual system.
papers.authors: Jacob S. Prince, George A. Alvarez, Talia Konkle

papers.title: Immersive scene representation in human visual cortex with ultra-wide angle neuroimaging
papers.abstract: Traditional fMRI studies typically present visual stimuli within the central 10-15° of the visual field, failing to capture the panoramic 220° experience of natural vision. This study employs a custom-engineered ultra-wide angle display system capable of a 175° unobstructed view to investigate cortical representation under immersive conditions. Results indicate that scene-selective regions (PPA, RSC/MPA, and OPA) maintain their category preferences and spatial tuning even when central vision is occluded by an artificial scotoma, whereas face-selective regions (FFA) show distinct modulation patterns. The findings provide evidence that high-level scene areas are not merely driven by foveal biases but are fundamentally organized to integrate peripheral information for immersive environmental representation.
papers.authors: Jeongho Park, Edward Soucy, Jennifer Segawa, Ross Mair, Talia Konkle

papers.title: Manipulating dropout reveals an optimal balance of efficiency and robustness in biological and machine visual systems
papers.abstract: Applying the efficient coding hypothesis to the human visual hierarchy, the researchers investigate the tradeoff between high-dimensional informational efficiency and representational robustness. By parametrically varying the dropout rate (p) during the training of object recognition models, they systematically manipulate the dimensionality and correlation structure (eigenspectrum) of internal representations. They find that an intermediate dropout level (approx. 70%) optimizes robustness to simulated neural lesions and generalization. Crucially, comparisons with high-resolution 7T fMRI data from the Natural Scenes Dataset reveal that models at this optimal robustness point also exhibit the highest representational alignment with human occipitotemporal cortex, suggesting that biological vision is constrained by similar pressures toward low-dimensional, robust feature spaces.
papers.authors: Jacob S. Prince, Gabriel Fajardo, George A. Alvarez, Talia Konkle

0654.name: Tao Gao
0654.department: Department of Statistics and Department of Communication
0654.bio: Tao Gao is an Associate Professor at UCLA whose research focuses on the mechanisms of human intuitive social commonsense. By integrating psychophysical experiments with computational modeling, Gao investigates how humans perceive social concepts such as animacy, intentionality, and agency from sparse visual stimuli. Their work extends into the development of communicative artificial intelligence and robotics, aiming to implement human-like social reasoning to facilitate human-machine collaboration. Before this appointment, Gao completed a PhD in cognitive psychology at Yale University and a postdoctoral fellowship at MIT’s Center for Brains, Minds and Machines.
0654.research_direction: Dr. Gao has recently been investigating the computational and cognitive mechanisms underlying human social intelligence, focusing on how agents visually infer intentions, cooperate, and communicate in shared spaces. Their recent work explores how humans utilize an "Imagined We" framework to maintain joint commitment during complex, multi-agent tasks, and how we use Bayesian Theory of Mind to optimize sparse communication during collaborative efforts. They are also studying action understanding by examining how the visual system distinguishes communicative pantomimes from purely instrumental actions based on physical environmental affordances. Additionally, they are applying insights from human spatial reasoning and planning to artificial intelligence, exploring how large language models can guide autonomous agents to design and construct complex 3D architectures in open-world environments.

papers.title: Joint Commitment in Human Cooperative Hunting through an 'Imagined We'
papers.abstract: Human collective coordination requires agents to maintain joint commitment to a shared goal amidst fluctuating environmental pressures and alternative individual incentives. This study investigates the cognitive underpinnings of shared intentionality in a multi-agent hunting task using a combination of psychophysical experiments and computational simulations. We formalize joint commitment through an 'Imagined We' (IW) framework, where individual actors infer the intention of a supraindividual agent that treats all team members as its constituent body parts. By comparing behavioral data against a baseline reward-sharing model, we demonstrate that humans prioritize collective success over individual proximity to the prey, regardless of environmental stochasticity. Our findings suggest that the internal representation of a joint identity ('we') enables the persistent execution of shared plans and facilitates sophisticated social coordination in complex, multi-goal environments.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences
papers.authors: Ning Tang, Siyi Gong, Minglu Zhao, Jifan Zhou, Mowei Shen, Tao Gao

papers.title: Communicating Through Acting: Affording Communicative Intention in Pantomimes
papers.abstract: Human observers possess an intuitive capacity to distinguish communicative pantomimes from kinematically similar instrumental actions directed at environment modification. This research evaluates the cognitive mechanisms underlying this distinction, specifically contrasting the hypothesis of competition between instrumental and communicative intentions against a nested architecture hypothesis. Utilizing a video dataset of action-object pairs with varying linguistic frequency and visual affordance, we demonstrate a nonmonotonic relationship between situational support and perceived communicativeness. Experimental results reveal that 'partial affordance'—where the environment provides limited support for an instrumental goal—elicits the peak perception of communicative intent, whereas full or absent affordance weakens this interpretation. These findings imply that the human visual system employs a rationality principle to identify instrumental sub-optimality as a diagnostic signal for communicative agency.
papers.authors: Siyi Gong, Kaiwen Jiang, Jessica G. Li, Mireille Karadanaian, Ziyi Meng, Tao Gao

papers.title: A relevance model of human sparse communication in cooperation
papers.abstract: Efficient human collaboration relies on the sparse transmission of highly informative signals to align mental states under bandwidth constraints. We propose a computational framework for information selection based on a 'relevance' metric derived from decision-making theory and Bayesian Theory of Mind (ToM). In this model, an utterance's utility is defined by its capacity to improve a partner's expected reward in a shared task. We validated this approach in a multi-agent navigation environment where participants and AI agents coordinated to avoid environmental hazards. Our relevance model accurately predicts human signaling choices and significantly outperforms state-of-the-art large language models, such as GPT-4, in strategic information selection. The results suggest that human sparse communication is grounded in an 'Imagined We' perspective that optimizes collective utility through recursive mental state inference.
papers.authors: Kaiwen Jiang, Boxuan Jiang, Anahita Sadaghdar, Rebekah Limb, Tao Gao

papers.title: APT: Architectural Planning and Text-to-Blueprint Construction Using Large Language Models for Open-World Agents
papers.abstract: We introduce APT, a novel framework for autonomous agents that utilizes Large Language Models (LLMs) to perform complex architectural construction within open-world environments like Minecraft. Unlike prior methods relying on voxel-based diffusion or low-level skill sets, APT leverages the spatial reasoning and chain-of-thought (CoT) decomposition capabilities of LLMs to map high-level natural language instructions or visual references into structured 3D blueprints. The architecture integrates a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) memory pool and a self-reflection module, enabling agents to iteratively refine construction plans and correct errors through visual inspection. Experimental results demonstrate that APT can generate and execute creative designs, including functional multi-room structures and complex systems, representing a significant advancement in the development of open-ended, human-like problem-solving agents.
papers.authors: Jun Yu Chen, Tao Gao

papers.title: A Bayesian theory of mind approach to modeling cooperation and communication
papers.abstract: This review synthesizes recent progress in modeling human-unique social intelligence—specifically cooperation and communication—through the lens of an agency-based Bayesian Theory of Mind (ToM). We move beyond traditional individualistic models of agency to propose a shared-agency perspective, which accounts for how humans coordinate behavior and beliefs as a collective unit. By formalizing ToM as the inverse planning of mental states (beliefs, desires, and intentions) from observed actions, we illustrate how agents can resolve communicative ambiguity and establish common ground using sparse signals. We argue that non-linguistic contextual constraints, such as the shared visual environment, provide the necessary inductive biases for robust social coordination. The framework provides a computational architecture for developing AI systems endowed with human-like visual common sense and intuitive social reasoning.
papers.authors: Stephanie Stacy, Siyi Gong, Aishni Parab, Minglu Zhao, Kaiwen Jiang, Tao Gao

0655.name: Taosheng Liu
0655.lab_name: Neuroimaging of Perception and Attention Laboratory (NPAL)
0655.bio: Liu investigates the computational and neural mechanisms of visual selective attention, working memory, and perceptual decision-making. Their research employs a multimodal approach, integrating functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), electroencephalography (EEG), and transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) with behavioral psychophysics. A primary focus of Liu’s work involves examining how the brain prioritizes task-relevant information during sensory competition and how these selection processes guide subsequent actions and memory consolidation.
0655.research_direction: Dr. Liu has recently been investigating the neural mechanisms of feature-based attention, alongside the intersection of basic visual features and high-level emotion perception. Using EEG techniques like frequency-tagging and multivariate decoding, their recent work explores both the spatial dynamics and capacity limits of attentional templates, such as whether feature-based attention spreads globally to task-irrelevant locations during pre-stimulus preparatory periods and how the brain manages the representational costs of maintaining templates for multiple colors simultaneously. In a distinct line of behavioral research, they are also examining how color signals influence facial emotion perception across different cultures. Specifically, they are investigating whether fundamental visual-emotional mappings, like the association between red and anger, compete with or override bivalent cultural symbolisms during visual processing.

papers.title: Preparatory attention to visual features spreads globally
papers.abstract: This study investigates whether the global spread of feature-based attention (FBA) — which enhances neural responses to attended features across the entire visual field — occurs during the preparatory period before stimulus onset. Using EEG and frequency-tagging via flickering dot fields, the researchers measured frequency-specific visual-evoked responses in participants cued to attend to specific colors or motion patterns. Results demonstrated that preparatory attention to a specific feature significantly facilitated responses at task-irrelevant locations, even in conditions where the attended-side stimulus onset was delayed. These findings suggest that the global spread of FBA is an endogenous mechanism that biases feature processing in anticipation of incoming sensory inputs, supporting its functional role in guided visual search.
papers.authors: Melisa Menceloglu, Søren K. Andersen, Taosheng Liu

papers.title: Cost of maintaining attentional templates for multiple colors revealed by EEG decoding
papers.abstract: The research examines the behavioral and neurophysiological constraints of maintaining multiple feature-based attentional templates. Participants performed a color-coherence detection task with varying numbers of color cues (one, two, or three) while EEG was recorded. Multivariate decoding of target colors from posterior electrode signals revealed that decoding accuracy was significantly reduced when multiple colors were attended compared to a single color. Behavioral performance showed parallel declines in accuracy and reaction time for multi-cue trials. The robust correlation between neural decoding deficits and behavioral performance suggests that maintaining multiple active attentional templates incurs a significant capacity cost, effectively limiting the brain's ability to enhance sensory representations of multiple features simultaneously.
papers.authors: Melisa Menceloglu, Sari Sadiya, Susan M. Ravizza, Taosheng Liu

papers.title: Red Facilitates Anger Perception Across Cultures
papers.abstract: Color signals carry significant psychological meanings that influence emotional processing. This study examines the 'red-anger' association within cultures where red also carries positive connotations, such as joy and celebration in Chinese culture. Across three experiments, the researchers tested whether red activates both positive and negative associations simultaneously or if one dominates. Behavioral data consistently showed that red facilitated the perception of anger across both Western and Eastern participants, regardless of the racial profile of the faces or the perceptual salience of the background. These results support a 'competition hypothesis' where the red-anger association predominates in visual-emotion processing despite bivalent cultural symbolic links.
papers.authors: Lijing Guo, Hong-Jin Sun, Taosheng Liu

0656.name: Tatiana Aloi Emmanouil
0656.bio: Tatiana Aloi Emmanouil investigates the cognitive and neural mechanisms of human vision, focusing on the interactions between attention, awareness, and memory. Emmanouil’s research integrates behavioral psychophysics with neuroimaging and neurostimulation methods, such as fMRI, EEG, and TMS, to study how visual information is summarized and stored. Their work includes research on ensemble coding—the statistical representation of visual groups—and investigations into visual processing occurring outside the focus of conscious awareness. Emmanouil also examines the neural substrates of visual working memory and the functional roles of the primary visual cortex and posterior parietal cortex in perception.
0656.research_direction: Dr. Emmanouil’s recent work explores how the perceptual system integrates diverse streams of information to form rapid, global impressions. In the domain of visual cognition, they have recently been investigating the mechanisms of ensemble perception, specifically testing whether observers automatically extract summary statistics—such as the average color or orientation of an array—across both task-relevant and ignored feature dimensions. In parallel, their research examines multisensory social perception by exploring how visual facial signals and auditory vocal cues interact to shape rapid judgments of trustworthiness. Using behavioral paradigms with multimodal stimuli, they are investigating the relative weighting and mandatory integration of these bimodal channels to understand exactly which cross-modal features drive human trust in virtual and conversational agents.

papers.title: Perceptual averaging on relevant and irrelevant featural dimensions
papers.abstract: This research investigates the nature of summary statistical representations in the human visual system, specifically examining whether perceptual averaging occurs automatically across both task-relevant and task-irrelevant feature dimensions. Across four experiments, the study tests the hypothesis that observers recover and store a representation of the mean value of a feature set distributed across the optic array. By comparing reports of bar orientations and colors under varied task demands, the authors evaluate a Similarity Hypothesis against an Averaging Hypothesis. The results clarify the degree to which ensemble encoding depends on attentional control and the extent to which global attributes of irrelevant feature sets are processed and stored in memory.
papers.authors: Tatiana Aloi Emmanouil, Anne Treisman

papers.title: Beyond Face Value: Visual and Auditory Signals in Human and Machine Trust Judgments
papers.abstract: This study explores how bimodal visual and auditory cues interact to shape rapid human judgments of trustworthiness in the context of conversational agents. Using a behavioral experiment with 150 participants, the researchers manipulated face and voice stimuli across four trust congruence conditions to determine the relative weighting of each modality. Findings indicate that while both facial and vocal signals contribute significantly to first impressions, their integration is mandatory and resistant to instructions to ignore a specific channel. The paper analyzes the specific acoustic-prosodic and visual features that correlate with perceived trustworthiness and discusses the implications for designing multimodal virtual agents.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the 7th ACM Conference on Conversational User Interfaces (CUI 2025)
papers.authors: Natalia Tyulina, Yuwen Yu, Tatiana Aloi Emmanouil, Sarah Ita Levitan

papers.title: Understanding Linguistic and Visual Factors that Affect Human Trust Perception of Virtual Agents
papers.abstract: The authors investigate the interdisciplinary relationship between spoken linguistic cues and visual facial signals in the formation of trust toward virtual agents. Through a crowdsourced perception study, the research analyzes how users evaluate agent trustworthiness when presented with multimodal audio-visual pairs. The study identifies specific nonverbal behaviors and auditory signals that serve as indicators of trust, highlighting the importance of cross-modal consistency in interface design. The results suggest that multimodal factors interact in complex ways to influence user engagement and satisfaction, with implications for assistive robotics and psychological assessment tools.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the 6th ACM Conference on Conversational User Interfaces (CUI 2024)
papers.authors: Natalia Tyulina, Tatiana Aloi Emmanouil, Sarah Ita Levitan

0657.name: Teng Leng Ooi
0657.bio: Teng Leng Ooi is a Professor in the College of Optometry at The Ohio State University, where they investigate the mechanisms underlying binocular vision and 3D space perception. Ooi’s research focuses on how the brain integrates sensory visual information with cognitive factors and motor signals to guide actions in natural, virtual, and augmented reality environments. Ooi developed the 'Push-Pull' perceptual learning protocol and video game-based therapies aimed at reducing sensory eye dominance and restoring stereopsis in individuals with amblyopia and strabismus. Their work utilizes psychophysical methods and optical imaging to explore the neural circuitry of binocular rivalry and suppression.
0657.research_direction: Dr. Ooi has recently been investigating how the visual system constructs stable representations of 3D space and how oculomotor precision impacts visual function. Their recent work explores egocentric distance perception during observer locomotion, specifically examining how the brain uses an internal model of the ground surface—an "intrinsic bias"—to maintain spatial stability across egocentric and allocentric reference frames in cue-impoverished environments. In related behavioral studies, they are probing the temporal integration limits for binocular depth discrimination in the intermediate distance range, using asynchronous target paradigms to test how continuous ground textures facilitate local spatial coding. Furthermore, extending into clinical vision, Dr. Ooi has been utilizing High-Definition Optical Coherence Tomography (HD-OCT) to quantitatively map fixational positional errors and gaze instability in adult amblyopia, seeking to understand how the inability to maintain targets on the anatomical fovea drives visual acuity loss.

papers.title: Determining fixation accuracy with optical coherence tomography and its implication on visual acuity in amblyopia
papers.abstract: The present study employed High-Definition Optical Coherence Tomography (HD-OCT) to quantitatively assess fixational positional error and stability in adult observers with amblyopia compared to controls with normal binocular vision. By identifying the anatomical foveal location through line scan coordinates, researchers calculated the distance between the fovea and the scan center to define positional error. The results demonstrated that amblyopic eyes exhibit significantly greater positional error and higher fixation instability than fellow or control eyes. Crucially, multivariate regression analysis identified positional error as the primary significant predictor of visual acuity loss in amblyopia, suggesting that the inability to maintain the target on the foveal center is a more critical limiting factor for acuity than temporal instability of the gaze.
papers.authors: Maureen D. Plaumann, Wei Wei, Teng Leng Ooi

papers.title: Perception of distance during self-motion depends on the brain’s internal model of the terrain
papers.abstract: This research investigates how the visual system maintains a stable perception of egocentric distance during observer locomotion. Static observers in cue-impoverished environments rely on an 'intrinsic bias'—an internal model of the ground surface—to code distance. The authors tested whether this internal reference frame operates using an egocentric or allocentric (world-centered) system during self-motion. Results showed that when observers walked in darkness or under reduced-cue conditions, the intrinsic bias remained anchored to the home-base location rather than shifting with the body. This allocentric anchoring integrates with external depth cues to construct a stable ground reference frame, effectively solving the optical challenge of moving retinal images during translation by referencing a fixed internal model of the terrain.
papers.authors: Liu Zhou, Zijiang J. He, Teng Leng Ooi

papers.title: Factors Affecting Stimulus Duration Threshold for Depth Discrimination of Asynchronous Targets in the Intermediate Distance Range
papers.abstract: The study explores the temporal integration requirements for binocular depth discrimination within the intermediate distance range (2–25 meters), where spatial coding mechanisms differ from the near range (<2 m). Using a two-interval forced choice (2IFC) paradigm with asynchronous targets, the researchers found that depth discrimination thresholds significantly improve with increased stimulus duration and binocular viewing. Furthermore, the presence of a continuous, texture-defined ground surface substantially reduced the duration thresholds required for accurate depth perception. These findings support the sequential surface integration process (SSIP) hypothesis, suggesting that the construction of a reliable ground-surface representation is a prerequisite for localizing objects in the intermediate distance range.
papers.authors: Yiya Chen, Zijiang J. He, Teng Leng Ooi

0658.name: Tessa Dekker
0658.department: Institute of Ophthalmology and Experimental Psychology
0658.bio: Tessa Dekker is a Professor of Developmental Cognitive Neuroscience who researches how the human brain learns to perceive and interact with the world during development. Dekker's work explores the intersection of genetics, neural plasticity, and environmental experience to understand typical visual development and the impact of eye disease. By combining behavioral psychophysics with functional neuroimaging and computational modeling, Dekker characterizes sensory-motor integration. Their research evaluates mechanisms of sight recovery and neural adaptation following treatments such as gene therapy for inherited retinal diseases.
0658.research_direction: Dr. Dekker’s recent work explores how visual perception and cortical organization develop, age, and adapt to sensory loss. They have recently been investigating lifespan changes in visual processing, from mapping the developmental trajectory of foveal crowding in children to examining how older adults utilize top-down prior knowledge to resolve perceptual ambiguity and exhibit altered susceptibility to experimentally induced visual hallucinations. In parallel, their research examines hierarchical cortical plasticity in early visual areas following congenital sensory deprivation, such as rod-only vision in achromatopsia. To characterize visual function in these clinical populations, they are also developing novel model-based fMRI frameworks and population receptive field (pRF) mapping techniques to measure contrast sensitivity and map scotomas across the visual field without requiring stable fixation.

papers.title: The development of visual acuity and crowding reveals the slow fine-tuning of foveal vision
papers.abstract: The developmental trajectory of foveal spatial vision was quantified by measuring gap-size thresholds for orientation discrimination in both isolated and flanked (crowded) conditions across 119 children (ages 3–13) and 30 adults. While isolated foveal acuity matured early, reaching adult parity by age 5–6, foveal crowding—defined by the disruptive influence of surrounding clutter—remained significantly elevated in children until age 7–8. A meta-analysis of 13 studies further validated this protracted developmental timeline. Critically, foveal crowding in children exhibited the same target-flanker similarity selectivity observed in adult peripheral crowding, suggesting a shared cortical pooling mechanism that biases early vision toward scene-level summary statistics ('gist') over high-resolution local features.
papers.authors: John A. Greenwood, Marilia Kyprianou, Tessa M. Dekker

papers.title: Reduced susceptibility to experimentally-induced complex visual hallucinations with age
papers.abstract: To characterize lifespan changes in hallucinatory susceptibility, this study employed Ganzflicker (high-frequency flicker) and Ganzfeld (perceptual deprivation) to induce visual hallucinations in 44 healthy adults aged 19–79. Reports of complex hallucinations (structured objects and scenes) were significantly rarer in older adults compared to younger adults across both induction methods. This age-related reduction remained significant after controlling for potential mediators including visual acuity, contrast sensitivity, vividness of mental imagery, and memory inhibition. These findings indicate that decreased complex hallucination proneness is characteristic of typical aging, suggesting that the clinical manifestation of such phenomena in older populations may serve as an early biomarker for underlying neuropathology.
papers.authors: Oris Shenyan, Laura Haye, Georgia A. Milne, Matteo Lisi, John A. Greenwood, Jeremy Skipper, Tessa M. Dekker

papers.title: Mapping Visual Contrast Sensitivity and Vision Loss Across the Visual Field with Model-Based fMRI
papers.abstract: A model-based fMRI framework was developed to quantify contrast sensitivity across a 40° visual field without the constraint of stable fixation, facilitating assessment in patients with severe sight loss. By integrating large-field visual stimulation across various spatial frequencies and contrast levels with anatomical templates (Benson atlas) and population receptive field (pRF) mapping, the researchers estimated contrast sensitivity slopes in V1. Validation in normally-sighted participants demonstrated high individual-level reproducibility of sensitivity profiles across eccentricities and quadrants. This neuroimaging approach provides a robust method for mapping scotomas and characterizing the functional integrity of early visual cortex in both health and retinal disease.
papers.authors: Hugo T. Chow-Wing-Bom, Matteo Lisi, Noah C. Benson, Freya Lygo-Frett, Patrick Yu-Wai-Man, Frederic Dick, Roni O. Maimon-Mor, Tessa M. Dekker

papers.title: Hierarchical cortical plasticity in congenital sight impairment
papers.abstract: This fMRI study examined cortical reorganization and stability following lifelong rod-only photoreceptor input in individuals with congenital achromatopsia. Primary visual cortex (V1) showed no large-scale retinotopic remapping in response to foveal cone-input deprivation, maintaining structural markers of deprivation. However, plasticity was observed at the level of hierarchical read-out; connective field modeling revealed that higher-order visual area V3 significantly reorganized its sampling to integrate functional rod signals from V1. This pattern of input-level stability paired with downstream read-out plasticity suggests a robust hierarchical optimization strategy that maximizes the utility of available sensory information while preserving foundational cortical architecture.
papers.authors: Roni O. Maimon-Mor, Mahtab Farahbakhsh, Nicholas Hedger, Andrew T. Rider, Elaine J. Anderson, Geraint Rees, Tomas Knapen, Michel Michaelides, Tessa M. Dekker

papers.title: Protective effect of prior knowledge in ageing
papers.abstract: The robust utilization of top-down priors to resolve perceptual ambiguity in aging was investigated using two-tone images in younger (<40 years) and older (>60 years) adults. While older adults exhibited significantly lower baseline recognition accuracy for ambiguous stimuli—a deficit partially explained by age-related declines in visual acuity—they showed a comparable magnitude of perceptual reorganization (the 'Aha!' effect) when cued with original photographic information. These findings demonstrate that despite the degradation of bottom-up sensory input quality in later life, the hierarchical mechanisms integrating prior knowledge into visual inference remain functionally resilient, potentially acting as a compensatory strategy to preserve perceptual stability.
papers.authors: Georgia Milne, Oris Shenyan, Laura Haye, Matteo Lisi, Tessa Dekker

0660.name: Thomas B. Christophel
0660.lab_name: Distributed Cognition and Memory Group (DisCo Lab)
0660.bio: Thomas B. Christophel heads the Distributed Cognition and Memory Group at Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin, where their research focuses on the neural architectures supporting short-term information storage. Christophel utilizes high-resolution functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) to decode and map content-specific representations across the human brain. Their work demonstrates the distributed nature of working memory, showing that sensory, parietal, and frontal regions—such as the frontal eye fields—actively maintain mnemonic information. Currently, their research examines how these distributed neural codes are transformed and integrated to guide cognitive processes and decision-making.
0660.research_direction: Dr. Christophel has recently been investigating the neural and cognitive architecture of visuospatial working memory, focusing on how low-level visual features are maintained in the face of varying memory loads and distractors. Using functional neuroimaging and multivariate encoding models, their recent work explores how memory representations are distributed across the cortical hierarchy, examining the simultaneous use of high-fidelity sensory traces in early visual areas alongside more abstract, categorical, and semantic codes in frontoparietal regions. Additionally, they are probing the mechanisms of memory capacity and interference through behavioral paradigms, testing whether top-down strategies like attentional refreshing, cross-modal distribution, or the use of self-generated verbal labels can shield specific memory items from degradation. Through this combination of approaches, they seek to delineate how the human brain flexibly recruits distinct representational formats to optimize the ongoing storage of visual information.

papers.title: Sensory Modality- and Load-Dependent Changes across Cortical Working Memory Representations
papers.abstract: This neuroimaging investigation examines the cortical architecture supporting multi-item working memory maintenance, specifically assessing whether distributed representations in sensory, parietal, and frontal regions exhibit differential sensitivity to mnemonic load. Utilizing functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) with a cohort of 81 participants, the researchers manipulated effective visual load by varying the sensory modality of two concurrently maintained items (orientations versus auditory pitches). Multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) revealed that increased visual load specifically attenuated orientation-selective decodability in the early visual cortex (V1–V3), whereas representations in the intraparietal sulcus and superior precentral sulcus demonstrated greater resilience to interference. Computational simulations further indicated that the decline in decoding performance reflects a degradation of mnemonic pattern fidelity in posterior sensory regions. These findings support a shared-labor model where high-precision sensory codes in the occipital cortex are complemented by more robust, albeit lower-precision, representations in anterior cortical regions.
papers.authors: Vivien Chopurian, Simon Weber, Thomas B. Christophel

papers.title: Refreshing Boosts Memory But Does Not Protect It Against Interference
papers.abstract: This study evaluates the functional role of attentional refreshing—the prioritization of a representation within the focus of attention—in shielding working memory contents from interference. Utilizing a retro-cue paradigm to direct internal attention to specific items, the researchers quantified mnemonic performance following the introduction of visual distractors or novel memory items. Although the results demonstrate that refreshing significantly enhances the accessibility of cued representations, as evidenced by improved recall accuracy and attenuated response latencies, this prioritization benefit does not confer resistance to subsequent interference. The absence of a protective effect implies that refreshing strengthens existing mnemonic traces within a capacity-limited store but does not transition these representations into an interference-resistant format, challenging models that equate attentional prioritization with representational consolidation.
papers.authors: Andreea-Maria Gui, Vivien Chopurian, Alessandra S. Souza, Carsten Allefeld, Thomas B. Christophel

papers.title: Verbal encoding strategies in visuo-spatial working memory
papers.abstract: This research investigates the intersection of visuo-spatial working memory and linguistic encoding, specifically examining how self-generated verbal labels influence the maintenance of low-level visual features. In behavioral experiments, participants performed continuous orientation and location recall tasks followed by a naming task for the same stimuli. The study characterizes a diverse repertoire of labeling strategies and demonstrates that the utilization of specific spatial descriptors (e.g., cardinal terms) predicts systematic biases in mnemonic recall. Specifically, the use of cardinal labels was associated with Class 1 attraction biases toward cardinal axes, while uncertainty-related modifiers predicted Class 2 repulsion biases away from these axes. These findings suggest that visuo-spatial working memory recruits shared representational resources with verbal systems, where linguistic categorization actively shapes the format of visual information during maintenance.
papers.authors: Joana Pereira Seabra, Vivien Chopurian, Alessandra S. Souza, Thomas B. Christophel

papers.title: Modality-, feature-, and strategy-dependent organization of low-level working memory
papers.abstract: The present study explores the mechanisms underlying capacity limitations in working memory, focusing on whether interference between concurrently maintained items is primarily driven by shared sensory modalities or specific feature dimensions. Through behavioral experiments involving the continuous recall of orientations and auditory pitches, the authors demonstrate that cross-modal item sets (auditory-visual) exhibit significantly reduced interference compared to unimodal sets, even under constant load conditions. Analysis of strategy reports and performance patterns suggests that distinct mnemonic formats, such as categorical versus veridical codes, are selectively recruited based on feature type. These results provide evidence for a cortical organization wherein specialization for low-level features minimizes interference across modalities and highlight the role of strategic encoding in optimizing the maintenance of heterogeneous information.
papers.authors: Vivien Chopurian, Anni Kienke, Christoph Bledowski, Thomas B. Christophel

papers.title: Visuospatial working memory is cortically enabled through veridical, categorical and semantic representations
papers.abstract: This fMRI study (N=40) utilizes multivariate encoding modeling to delineate the concurrent representational formats underlying the maintenance of visuospatial information in the human brain. The researchers characterized orientation-selective activity across the cortical hierarchy, identifying a gradient of abstraction: early sensory regions represent stimuli in a veridical, high-fidelity format, while extrastriate, parietal, and frontal areas increasingly recruit categorical and semantic codes. Critically, cross-condition encoding models revealed that neural patterns in the visual cortex during the memory delay generalize to those evoked during a separate spatial language task. These results suggest that visual working memory is supported by a distributed network of simultaneous representations ranging from low-level sensory traces to abstract, semantic, and goal-directed formats.
papers.authors: Joana Pereira Seabra, Andreea-Maria Gui, Vivien Chopurian, Alessandra S. Souza, Carsten Allefeld, Thomas B. Christophel

0661.name: Thomas C. Sprague
0661.lab_name: Perception, Cognition, and Action Lab (PCA Lab)
0661.main_research_area: computational neuroimaging of vision and attention
0661.bio: Thomas C. Sprague is an Assistant Professor at the University of California, Santa Barbara, and the Principal Investigator of the Perception, Cognition, and Action (PCA) Lab. Sprague’s research investigates how top-down behavioral goals, such as visual attention and working memory, transform neural representations of sensory information across cortical networks. Using functional MRI, EEG, and computational techniques like inverted encoding models, they reconstruct and quantify the fidelity of these representations. Their work examines the neural architecture of priority maps and how the brain maintains stable information about the environment to support goal-directed actions.
0661.research_direction: Dr. Sprague has recently been investigating the neural mechanisms underlying visual attention and working memory, focusing on how these systems interact to flexibly prioritize sensory information. Their recent work explores how top-down feature-selective attention for dimensions like color or motion reweights stimulus representations across specialized retinotopic maps using fMRI and inverted encoding models. Additionally, they are examining the resilience of spatial working memory representations within visual and parietal cortex when confronted with salient, task-irrelevant visual distractors during maintenance. Finally, utilizing EEG, rapid frequency tagging, and behavioral paradigms, their research investigates how anticipating a stimulus's relevance proactively tunes early visual populations and whether specific feature dimensions held in working memory automatically drive incidental attentional capture during visual search.

papers.title: Attention Modulates Stimulus Representations in Neural Feature Dimension Maps
papers.abstract: This study employs fMRI and spatial inverted encoding models (IEMs) to investigate how feature-selective attention (e.g., color versus motion) reweights activation profiles across specialized retinotopic cortical regions, denoted as neural feature dimension maps. The research tests the hypothesis that these maps independently index the physical salience and behavioral relevance of stimulus features to guide attentional priority. Results demonstrate a critical dissociation: stimulus representations are selectively enhanced in color-selective regions (hV4/VO1/VO2) specifically when color is task-relevant, and in motion-selective regions (TO1/TO2) when motion is relevant. Furthermore, while attentional enhancement in color maps is spatially localized to the stimulus position, modulations in motion maps reflect a more global prioritization of the relevant feature dimension across the visual field.
papers.authors: Daniel D. Thayer, Thomas C. Sprague

papers.title: Retinotopic Spatial Working Memory Representations Are Not Affected by Task-irrelevant Visual Stimuli
papers.abstract: The authors examine the robustness of spatial working memory (WM) representations in the human brain against task-irrelevant visual interference during the maintenance interval. Utilizing BOLD fMRI and multivariate spatial IEMs, they reconstruct mnemonic representations in retinotopic visual and parietal cortical areas. Although a brief, salient visual interrupter stimulus drives robust transient univariate responses in early visual regions, the fidelity, amplitude, and spatial precision of the reconstructed WM targets remain largely unchanged. The study finds that stable spatial WM representations in these maps continue to predict the precision of behavioral recall regardless of the presence of the distractor, suggesting that retinotopic WM codes are inherently resilient to external visual drive or potentially maintained via parallel redundant systems.
papers.authors: Kelvin Vu-Cheung, Edward F. Ester, Thomas C. Sprague

papers.title: Anticipated Relevance Prepares Visual Processing for Efficient Memory-Guided Selection
papers.abstract: This research utilizes EEG and Rapid Invisible Frequency Tagging (RIFT) to determine how the anticipated relevance of a future stimulus influences top-down, memory-guided visual selection. Participants performed a task where they maintained an orientation in working memory and were cued to the relevance of upcoming probes. The findings reveal that anticipating a probe's relevance proactively enhances early visual responses at the expected spatial location (indexed by RIFT power) before the stimulus appears. Moreover, multivariate neural patterns indicate that memory-matching probes evoke more distinct and precise representations when they are known to be relevant, demonstrating that the visual system proactively tunes sensory populations to facilitate efficient memory-based comparison and selection.
papers.authors: Lasse Dietz, Kelvin Vu-Cheung, Edward F. Ester, Thomas C. Sprague

papers.title: Interactions between working memory and attention depend on remembered feature dimension
papers.abstract: The study investigates 'incidental capture,' where the contents of visual working memory (WM) automatically guide attention toward matching items in a search array, even when those items are task-irrelevant. By comparing color and motion feature dimensions, the authors identify a critical dissociation: while color WM consistently induces attentional capture toward matching distractors (slowing search for the actual target), motion WM does not produce similar interference. Behavioral results suggest that this difference arises because motion directions maintained in WM may be reformatted into a spatial coordinate system, thereby reducing competition with feature-based search processes. These results indicate that the influence of WM on attentional deployment is highly contingent on the representational format of the remembered features.
papers.authors: Daniel D. Thayer, Thomas C. Sprague

0662.name: Thomas M. Spalek
0662.lab_name: Spalek Laboratory of Attention, Memory and Perception
0662.bio: Thomas M. Spalek is a Professor of Psychology at Simon Fraser University and the director of the Spalek Laboratory of Attention, Memory and Perception. Spalek’s research examines the cognitive mechanisms of visual attention and memory, specifically investigating phenomena such as the attentional blink and inhibition of return. Using electroencephalography (EEG), transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), and high-fidelity driving simulators, Spalek addresses theoretical models of human information processing and their practical applications in real-world contexts. Their work includes collaborative research on re-entrant visual pathways and their role in conscious perception.
0662.research_direction: Dr. Spalek has recently been investigating the temporal dynamics and underlying mechanisms of selective attention, focusing on how cognitive control is modulated by both phasic alertness and emotional stimuli. Their recent work explores how non-informative warning cues prepare the visual system for perception and action, using behavioral tasks and computational modeling to determine how heightened alertness influences visual search efficiency and alters competition between neural evidence accumulators during response conflict. Additionally, they are examining how affective signals reshape attentional allocation, utilizing modified flanker paradigms with emotional faces to separate the distinct influences of perceptual saliency and emotional meaning. In this domain, their research seeks to understand how specific stimulus features, such as arousal and valence, differentially drive early and late stages of target facilitation and distractor interference.

papers.title: Happy and threatening faces differentially influence facilitation and interference over time
papers.abstract: The present study employs a modified flanker task to examine how happy and threatening facial expressions modulate focused attention across early and late task performance stages. Results from behavioral and distributional analyses reveal that neutral faces elicit standard flanker patterns—facilitation and interference—in the early stage, but only interference persists into the late stage. Critically, happy faces are found to selectively enhance early-stage facilitation while reducing interference, whereas threatening faces amplify early-stage interference and eliminate facilitation. These findings suggest that emotional signals reshape the dynamics of selective attention and processing efficiency over time rather than inducing static mean-level shifts in performance.
papers.authors: Kesong Hu, Yuhan Hu, Fangqing Liu, Qi Fan, Hongmin Xu, Regard M. Booy, Anna Maslany, Kristen M. Thompson, Thomas M. Spalek

papers.title: Phasic Alertness Impairs Cognitive Control by Amplifying Competition between Evidence Accumulators
papers.abstract: While phasic alertness typically enhances cognitive speed, it frequently disrupts cognitive control by increasing susceptibility to distracting information. This study proposes a biologically motivated account wherein phasic alertness provides a transient, evidence-independent neural input to the decision process. This input facilitates faster overall response times but simultaneously intensifies the competition between neural evidence accumulators. Through computational modeling and behavioral experiments, the researchers demonstrate that this increased competition specifically slows the resolution of response conflict, thereby explaining the deleterious effects of heightened alertness on decision-making and cognitive control.
papers.authors: Jeshua Tromp, Nadja Jankovic, Vincent Di Lollo, Thomas M. Spalek

papers.title: Readiness for Perception and Action: Towards a More Mechanistic Understanding of Phasic Alertness
papers.abstract: Warning stimuli induce a state of phasic alertness that readies the brain for imminent perception and action, yet the cognitive mechanisms through which this state facilitates processing remain debated. This work identifies fundamental computational and neurophysiological problems that must be solved for non-informative alerting cues to improve performance across diverse cognitive tasks. By delineating how phasic alertness interacts with top-down temporal expectations and stimulus-driven processing, the authors propose a research framework for building mechanistic and computational models of the neural underpinnings of human alertness.
papers.authors: Christian H. Poth, Nadja Jankovic, Vincent Di Lollo, Thomas M. Spalek

papers.title: Arousal and Valence Have Dissociable Effects on Responses to Schematic Emotional Faces
papers.abstract: This research investigates whether the observed behavioral asymmetries in response to emotional faces are driven by affective meaning or by differences in perceptual complexity. Using schematic faces in a flanker paradigm, the researchers manipulated stimulus-driven arousal (e.g., presence of eyebrows) and emotional valence. The experiments reveal that arousal and valence produce dissociable effects on reaction times and subjective evaluative ratings. High-arousal features like v-shaped eyebrows facilitate rapid detection but do not necessarily modulate flanker interference patterns, suggesting that perceptual saliency and emotional meaning affect face processing at distinct stages of evaluation and structural encoding.
papers.venue: Canadian Journal of Experimental Psychology / Revue canadienne de psychologie expérimentale
papers.authors: Regard M. Booy, Nadja Jankovic, Thomas M. Spalek

papers.title: Phasic alerting in visual search tasks
papers.abstract: The study examines whether non-informative alerting signals facilitate performance in visual search tasks of varying complexity. While simple search tasks involve detecting a single pop-out item, compound tasks require both detection and the identification of a specific target detail. Across five experiments that systematically varied the stimulus-onset asynchrony (SOA) between the alert and the search display, the findings demonstrate that phasic alertness facilitates performance across both search types. This suggests that the alerting effect is independent of the complexity of the selective attention process and instead reflects a general enhancement of the visual system's readiness for incoming information.
papers.authors: Nadja Jankovic, Vincent Di Lollo, Thomas M. Spalek

0663.name: Thérèse Collins
0663.bio: Collins is a Professor at Université Paris Cité and a researcher at the Integrative Neuroscience and Cognition Center (INCC). Their research investigates the mechanisms of visual perception and motor control, focusing on how the brain maintains a stable visual experience despite constant eye movements. Using psychophysics, eye-tracking, and electroencephalography (EEG), Collins explores topics such as trans-saccadic integration, serial dependence, and the impact of motor planning on perceptual processing. Their work provides technical analysis of how sensory information is transformed into stable internal representations of objects and scenes.
0663.research_direction: Dr. Collins has recently been investigating the mechanisms of serial dependence—the phenomenon where current perceptual estimates are biased by recent sensory history—to understand how the visual system maintains stability across time. Their recent work explores these history effects across multiple levels of processing, combining behavioral psychophysics with EEG and representational similarity analysis (RSA) to probe everything from low-level orientation perception to the categorization of complex objects and emotional facial expressions. Specifically, they are examining whether attractive and repulsive temporal biases operate over raw physical stimulus properties or higher-level categorical representations, even extending this framework to map the multidimensional geometry of abstract social stereotypes. By manipulating stimulus durations, report formats, and feature ambiguity, Dr. Collins aims to disentangle stimulus-driven sensory adaptation from decision-based memory traces, ultimately seeking to isolate the neural codes that integrate past perceptual experience with incoming sensory signals.

papers.title: Serial Dependence operates on categorical rather than physical representations: evidence from behavior and EEG
papers.abstract: Perceptual stability across continuous fluctuations in sensory input is hypothesized to rely on serial dependence (SD), an attractive bias pulling current perceptual estimates toward preceding visual history. This investigation tested whether SD operates over low-level physical stimulus properties or high-level categorical representations. Using facial morphs parameterized across prototypes expressing anger, fear, and sadness, an odd-one-out psychophysical task first confirmed the categorical perception of emotional expressions by yielding a behavioral representational similarity matrix (RSM). Observers then reproduced facial expressions of sequentially presented morphs via a continuous adjustment dial while 64-channel EEG was recorded. Behavioral psychophysical modeling revealed that attractive SD was tuned to subjective perceptual distance rather than physical stimulus differences. EEG representational similarity analysis (RSA) revealed that neural responses selectively encoded emotional ambiguity rather than discrete category membership, such that near-prototypical expressions across categories shared representational structures. Models integrating continuous feature tuning with categorical structures optimally predicted behavioral report biases. Moreover, neural activity sustained decodable traces of past stimuli, with the magnitude of attractive SD scaling with the divergence between memory-based representations and incoming feedforward sensory input.
papers.authors: Pierre Costa, Thérèse Collins

papers.title: Attractive and repulsive history effects in categorical and continuous estimates of orientation perception
papers.abstract: Perceptual judgments are shaped by sequential context, manifesting as either attractive serial dependence or repulsive adaptation. To isolate the mechanisms governing these competing history effects, orientation perception of Gabor stimuli was evaluated across manipulations of stimulus duration (50 ms vs. 500 ms), report format (continuous adjustment vs. 2AFC categorical clockwise/counterclockwise discrimination), and response frequency (sequential reports on every trial vs. alternating reports on every second trial). In continuous estimation, orientation reports demonstrated repulsive biases from the preceding stimulus at brief (50 ms) presentations, but switched to robust attractive biases toward both the previous stimulus and previous motor response at longer (500 ms) presentations, regardless of response frequency. In contrast, categorical discrimination tasks dissociated the source of history biases: observers consistently showed repulsive biases driven by the preceding stimulus orientation alongside attractive biases toward the previous categorical choice. Decision-induced attraction was amplified in sequential designs at small angular separations, whereas stimulus-driven repulsion persisted across all presentation durations and report schedules. Consequently, the net history effect was repulsive in alternating categorical designs and attractive in sequential paradigms, indicating distinct stimulus- and decision-level contributions to serial perceptual biases.
papers.authors: Mert Can, Thérèse Collins

papers.title: The neural representation of stereotype content
papers.abstract: According to the Stereotype Content Model, mental evaluations of social groups are structured along two foundational axes: warmth and competence. This study tested the functional independence and geometry of these axes by examining serial dependence (SD) during social evaluations while recording electroencephalography (EEG). Thirty-six human observers evaluated named social groups along warmth and competence dimensions across sequential trials. Behavioral analysis revealed significant attractive serial dependence, wherein current ratings were pulled toward recently evaluated groups, selectively modulated by relative proximity in the two-dimensional stereotype space. Representational similarity analysis (RSA) of event-related potential (ERP) topographies demonstrated distinct spatio-temporal signatures indexing warmth versus competence. Importantly, sequential bias patterns correlated with the underlying representational geometry of the multidimensional stereotype space rather than independent univariate axes. These findings establish that serial dependence extends beyond lower-level sensorimotor processing into high-level social cognition, revealing that sequential integration smooths representations across an integrated multidimensional semantic manifold.
papers.authors: Thérèse Collins, Emilie Zhu, Patrick Rateau

papers.title: The Representational Similarity between Visual Perception and Recent Perceptual History
papers.abstract: Despite continuous temporal noise, eye movements, and lighting shifts, human visual perception appears remarkably stable across time. Serial dependence—the attractive bias pulling current visual reports toward recently encountered stimuli—is hypothesized to serve as an integrative temporal filter that enforces perceptual stability. To determine the neural mechanisms of this process, 64-channel EEG was acquired while observers viewed prototypical visual objects (faces, houses, and cars) and ambiguous inter-category morphs. Observers demonstrated reliable behavioral attractive serial dependence toward previous trial exemplars. Time-resolved representational similarity analysis (RSA) revealed that stimulus-evoked neural responses contained decodable information regarding the preceding trial's object category. This memory trace was detected immediately at stimulus onset (0 ms latency), indicating that serial dependence is established by a pre-existing preparatory neural state before incoming sensory input is fully processed. However, cross-temporal representational similarity between the current sensory response and the residual trace of prior stimuli was not significant, demonstrating that although past visual experience biases current representations, memory reactivation and active perception rely on distinct neural codes.
papers.authors: Junlian Luo, Thérèse Collins

0664.name: Tijl Grootswagers
0664.department: MARCS Institute for Brain, Behaviour and Development; School of Computer, Data and Mathematical Sciences
0664.bio: Tijl Grootswagers is an ARC DECRA Senior Research Fellow focusing on the temporal dynamics of visual object recognition and the neural mechanisms of human perception. Grootswagers utilizes multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) and machine learning to decode information from time-series neuroimaging data, specifically EEG, MEG, and fMRI. Their research investigates how the brain transforms sensory inputs into conceptual representations and examines the relationship between neural coding and behavioral decision-making. Recently, their work has expanded to include the neural representation of AI-generated content and the development of open-source methodologies for neuroimaging analysis.
0664.research_direction: Dr. Grootswagers has recently been utilizing time-resolved neuroimaging, primarily EEG and MEG, alongside multivariate decoding to map the rapid spatiotemporal dynamics of human visual processing. Their recent work explores how the brain sequentially resolves the semantic and shape-based dimensions of object space, such as animacy and aspect ratio, and evaluates whether these temporal hierarchies naturally emerge within deep neural network models. Additionally, they are investigating how recurrent neural mechanisms support object recognition under illusory occlusion and tracking the precise timeline by which the visual system extracts sensory and affective information from observed tactile interactions. Alongside these theoretical questions, their research systematically tests the spatial redundancy of neural signals to determine how effectively low-density EEG arrays can be used to robustly decode complex visual features.

papers.title: Robust neural decoding with low-density EEG
papers.abstract: This study systematically evaluates the effect of electrode sensor density on the multivariate decoding of visual gratings (defined by orientation, contrast, spatial frequency, and color) and complex naturalistic images. By subsampling a 128-channel array into configurations of 96, 64, 32, and 16 electrodes, the researchers demonstrate that while classification sensitivity generally increases with higher density, statistically robust neural representations of both low-level features and high-level image categories remain decodable even with 16 channels. These results indicate a substantial degree of spatial redundancy in time-resolved neuroimaging signals and underscore the practical efficacy of low-density EEG for robust neural decoding in both laboratory and translational settings.
papers.authors: Ling Huang, Manuel Varlet, Tijl Grootswagers

papers.title: Mapping object space dimensions: new insights from temporal dynamics
papers.abstract: The research investigates the spatiotemporal evolution of object space in the human visual cortex, focusing on the orthogonal dimensions of animacy and aspect ratio (stubby vs. spiky). Using whole-brain EEG and representational similarity analysis (RSA) during a 5 Hz rapid serial visual presentation paradigm, the study reveals that information regarding aspect ratio is encoded earlier (~100 ms) and more transiently than categorical animacy information. Furthermore, by employing silhouette stimuli to mask internal textural details, the authors demonstrate that the availability of visual information directly modulates the hierarchy of these dimensions, with shape-based aspect ratio becoming the primary representational feature when textural cues are attenuated.
papers.authors: Alexis Kidder, Genevieve L. Quek, Tijl Grootswagers

papers.title: Rapid visual engagement in neural processing of detailed touch interactions
