papers.abstract: Utilizing multivariate EEG decoding and frequency-domain analysis, this paper maps the neural dynamics of visually perceived tactile hand interactions (e.g., stroking, pressing) from the Validated Touch-Video Database. The findings show that the brain rapidly encodes body cues (hand orientation, perspective) within 60 ms, followed by sensory touch details and valence around 110–160 ms. Higher-order affective evaluations, including arousal, threat, and vicarious pain, are clearly identifiable by approximately 260 ms. These processes are differentially mediated by oscillatory activity, where theta-beta bands (6–20 Hz) support early body-cue processing and delta-alpha bands (1–13 Hz) characterize the encoding of sensory and emotional-affective dimensions.
papers.authors: Sophie Smit, Almudena Ramírez-Haro, Genevieve L. Quek, Manuel Varlet, Denise Moerel, Tijl Grootswagers

papers.title: The neural processes of illusory occlusion in object recognition
papers.abstract: This study examines the role of recurrent neural dynamics in object recognition under occlusion by combining magnetoencephalography (MEG) with a paradigm involving illusory Kanizsa figures. By presenting partial objects that are either aligned or misaligned with illusory 'occluding' surfaces, the authors use multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) and RSA to show that the perceptual induction of illusory contours significantly modulates the neural representation of partially hidden objects. These results suggest that the 'filling-in' of missing visual information is supported by feedback mechanisms between higher-order perceptual grouping modules and primary visual feature extraction in the ventral stream.
papers.authors: Almudena Ramírez-Haro, Denise Moerel, Genevieve L. Quek, Manuel Varlet, Tijl Grootswagers

papers.title: Hierarchical Emergence Profiles of Human-Derived Dimensions are a Fundamental Property of Deep Neural Networks
papers.abstract: This research evaluates whether the hierarchical emergence of semantic object dimensions (e.g., animacy, size) observed in the human brain is a fundamental characteristic of deep neural networks (DNNs). Using RSA across various DNN architectures, including CNNs and Vision Transformers, the study demonstrates that human-derived object dimensions emerge in a specific hierarchical order across the model layers that aligns with the temporal dynamics observed in human neuroimaging data. This suggest that the specific representational hierarchy of object space is not unique to biological systems but is an emergent property of optimizing computational models for visual categorization tasks.
papers.authors: Flora Burger, Genevieve L. Quek, Manuel Varlet, Tijl Grootswagers

0665.name: Timothy Brady
0665.bio: Timothy F. Brady is a Professor in the Department of Psychology at UC San Diego and directs the Vision and Memory Lab. Their research explores how the visual system encodes and maintains information, focusing on the capacity and fidelity of visual working memory and long-term memory. Brady’s work indicates that visual memory capacity is not strictly fixed but scales with the meaningfulness of stimuli and examines how ensemble statistics facilitate the representation of complex scenes. Utilizing psychophysics, computational modeling, and neuroimaging techniques such as EEG, Brady investigates memory limits and structural representations in the human brain.
0665.research_direction: Dr. Brady has recently been investigating the computational and representational architecture of visual working memory, moving beyond uniform models to explore how memories operate as dynamic, noisy beliefs rather than static copies. Their recent work employs continuous report and serial reproduction paradigms to examine whether memory fundamentally relies on continuous resources, and how these representations are shaped by stimulus-specific attractors, serial dependence, and rich individual differences. Beyond working memory, they are exploring ensemble perception to understand how efficiently the visual system extracts summary statistics, such as average identity or emotion, from high-level face stimuli obscured by naturalistic occlusions. Additionally, Dr. Brady is systematically evaluating the methodological rigor of cognitive modeling across domains, testing the validity of auxiliary assumptions in memory recognition models and probing the psychometric reliability of graph-theoretic measures used to map semantic memory networks.

papers.title: Beyond Uniform Perception: Individual and Stimulus-Specific Differences in Visual Working Memory
papers.abstract: This study challenges the assumption of a uniform psychological space in visual working memory (VWM) by demonstrating that systematic error patterns are highly idiosyncratic and stimulus-specific. Utilizing a novel within-participant serial reproduction method, the researchers identified reliable attractors within color space that persist across individuals but exhibit significant inter-individual variance. The experiments reveal that both contextual biases—specifically serial dependence in single-item maintenance and inter-item repulsion in two-item tasks—are fundamentally constrained by these latent perceptual structures. The findings suggest that VWM performance is dictated by an interplay between universal regularities and rich individual differences in representational organization, necessitating a move beyond uniform models of mnemonic similarity.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
papers.authors: Isabella DeStefano, Edward Vul, Timothy F. Brady

papers.title: Ensemble Perception of Faces with Naturalistic Occlusions
papers.abstract: The visual system utilizes ensemble perception to extract summary statistics from redundant stimuli, but the impact of naturalistic occlusions remains under-explored. This research employed continuous report tasks where participants estimated the average identity or emotional expression of face sets partially obscured by surgical masks or sunglasses. Results indicate that while occlusion introduces a performance cost, the visual system successfully establish robust ensemble representations, maintaining accuracy significantly above chance. However, further experimentation revealed that this resilience is partially contingent on the visual system learning stimulus-specific features of the response space (the face wheel). The study concludes that ensemble extraction for high-level features remains efficient under naturalistic noise, supported by adaptive feature-learning mechanisms.
papers.authors: Hayden Schill Hendley, Natalia K. Pallis Hassani, Timothy F. Brady

papers.title: Zooming in on what counts as core and auxiliary: A case study on recognition models of visual working memory
papers.abstract: Theory assessment in cognitive science is often confounded by auxiliary assumptions that link core hypotheses to experimental methodologies. This paper re-evaluates the evidence for 'all-or-none' versus 'continuous resource' recognition models in visual working memory. Through a rigorous reanalysis of seminal datasets and their replications, the authors demonstrate that original model comparison metrics were non-diagnostic due to unchecked violations of auxiliary assumptions. By identifying and testing these latent constraints, the researchers find that continuous resource models consistently outperform all-or-none alternatives. The work provides a conceptual framework for identifying and testing the gamut of assumptions in theory assessment and argues for the necessity of signal detection-based measures in understanding mnemonic failure.
papers.authors: Maria M. Robinson, Jamal R. Williams, John T. Wixted, Timothy F. Brady

papers.title: Local but not global graph theoretic measures of semantic networks generalize across tasks
papers.abstract: This investigation assesses the psychometric reliability of graph theoretic analyses used to model individual differences in semantic network structure. Across four experiments, the researchers tested whether network metrics for simple concepts remain stable across diverse semantic relatedness tasks (e.g., free association vs. relatedness judgments). While local measures—such as node strength and edge weights—demonstrated robust generalizability across tasks, global structural metrics like the average clustering coefficient and shortest path length proved less reliable. Through large-scale recovery simulations, the study identifies boundary conditions for inferring latent semantic organization and provides methodological recommendations for utilizing network science to quantify individual differences in semantic memory.
papers.authors: Maria M. Robinson, Isabella C. DeStefano, Edward Vul, Timothy F. Brady

papers.title: Representation and computation in visual working memory
papers.abstract: This review synthesizes recent advancements in visual working memory (WM) through a computational lens, emphasizing the transition from simplistic 'slot' metaphors to frameworks defined by noisy representation and Bayesian inference. The authors argue that WM representations are not static copies of sensory inputs but dynamic beliefs that incorporate uncertainty and environmental regularities. By examining neural population coding and mathematical process models, the paper highlights how the system optimizes limited resources. The synthesis covers the relationship between capacity and fidelity, the neural mechanisms supporting maintenance, and the role of computation in bridging behavioral performance with implemented neurobiology.
papers.authors: Paul M. Bays, Sebastian Schneegans, Wei Ji Ma, Timothy F. Brady

0666.name: Timothy D. Sweeny
0666.bio: Timothy D. Sweeny is an Associate Professor at the University of Denver, directing the Visual Perception, Emotion, & Cognition (VPEC) Lab and the Developmental Cognitive Neuroscience Program. Sweeny’s research utilizes psychophysics to investigate how neural and cognitive mechanisms shape visual perception, focusing on ensemble coding—the process by which the brain compresses complex social information, such as crowd gaze and emotional expressions, into summary statistics. They examine how these perceptual processes influence social behavior and consciousness, collaborating with clinical psychologists to study visual processing in populations with anxiety and autism spectrum disorder. This work connects low-level vision and high-level social-emotional cognition to analyze how humans interpret collective social cues and navigate complex environments.
0666.research_direction: Dr. Sweeny has recently been investigating visual perception across a diverse range of phenomena, spanning from high-level social vision to low-level perceptual organization. Their recent work explores ensemble perception and emotion evaluation, specifically testing whether the visual system's negativity bias when categorizing expressions in face crowds is sensitive to short-term manipulations in threat prevalence. In the domain of geometric shape perception, they are examining how Gestalt grouping cues like common motion can dynamically distort judgments of an object's aspect ratio on a single-trial basis. Furthermore, their research investigates computational face synthesis by developing methods to disentangle and independently control specific demographic and emotional attributes within the latent spaces of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) to generate balanced, unbiased facial stimuli.

papers.title: Biased judgments of emotion are resistant to changes in the prevalence of anger
papers.abstract: Evaluations of emotional facial expressions are inherently subject to uncertainty due to the subtlety and nuance of affective cues. Previous work showed that observers exhibit a systematic bias toward interpreting expressions negatively—a tendency that is particularly amplified in group or crowd settings. While this flexible negativity bias is hypothesized to serve an adaptive, protective function rooted in long-term statistical learning of crowd-related threat, the degree to which it recalibrates in response to short-term shifts in threat prevalence remains uncharacterized. To investigate this, observers evaluated either individual isolated faces or four-face ensembles, categorizing expressions along a happiness–anger dimension across three experiments where anger prevalence was experimentally manipulated (75% versus 25% of trials). Replicating prior findings, participants displayed a robust anger bias that was selectively enhanced when judging crowds. However, anger bias magnitudes remained invariant across prevalence regimes, irrespective of whether statistical prevalence was acquired implicitly through exposure or explicitly instructed a priori. These findings indicate that while visual emotion interpretation biases are dynamically sensitive to contextual visual factors such as crowd context, they are remarkably resilient to short-term statistical alterations in affective base rates.
papers.authors: Delaney McDonagh, Timothy Sweeny

papers.title: Similarity in motion binds and bends judgments of aspect ratio
papers.abstract: While perceptual grouping based on Gestalt similarity of features is widely recognized to bind visual objects, whether emergent grouping conversely distorts the perceived visual properties of individual constituents dynamically on a single-trial timescale is less established. This study investigated whether common motion vectors dynamically induce attraction or repulsion in perceived geometric aspect ratio on a trial-by-trial basis. Observers were briefly presented with pairs of elliptical stimuli defined by coherent random-dot kinematograms embedded in dynamic noise displays, differing in their horizontal-to-vertical aspect ratios. Following stimulus offset, an arrow retro-cue indicated which target ellipse's aspect ratio observers were to reconstruct. Coherent dot motion within the two stimuli was manipulated to be either shared (promoting grouping by common fate) or opposing/dissimilar (disrupting grouping). When shapes shared identical motion trajectories, aspect ratio reproductions of the probed shape were systematically attracted toward the aspect ratio of the unprobed item. Conversely, when motion trajectories diverged, a repulsive perceptual shift was observed. These findings demonstrate that motion-based grouping dynamically modulates perceived shape geometry within brief temporal windows, revealing that the visual system rapidly imposes perceptual assimilation or contrast in accordance with momentary perceptual organization cues.
papers.authors: Görkem Er, Timothy D. Sweeny

papers.title: GANalyzer: Analysis and Manipulation of GANs Latent Space for Controllable Face Synthesis
papers.abstract: Although state-of-the-art Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) synthesize high-fidelity facial imagery, latent representations lack direct interpretability regarding the relationship between input noise vectors and resulting facial semantics. Furthermore, models like StyleGAN3 trained on uncurated, imbalanced corpora display severe sample skew—for example, synthesizing over 77% happy expressions versus approximately 3% angry expressions across 100,000 unconstrained generations, with intersections such as angry women or happy Black individuals comprising under 1% and 2% respectively. To resolve these limitations and facilitate fine-grained facial attribute control, this paper introduces GANalyzer, a framework designed to analyze and steer the latent manifold of pre-trained GANs. GANalyzer develops specific transformation mappings to disentangle and independently modulate targeted demographic and affective attributes, including facial expression, age, perceived gender, and race. By isolating entangled directional vectors within the latent space, the framework enables both identity-preserving facial attribute editing and feature-guided synthesis. The authors validate the approach across diverse facial modifications and release an open-source balanced photo-realistic facial benchmark dataset to address demographic and expressive representation deficits.
papers.authors: Ali Pourramezan Fard, Mohammad H. Mahoor, Sarah Ariel Lamer, Timothy Sweeny

0667.name: Timothy J. Andrews
0667.bio: Timothy J. Andrews is a Professor of Psychology whose research investigates the neural mechanisms through which the human brain transforms low-level retinal signals into high-level visual perceptions of objects, faces, and scenes. Utilizing functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), psychophysics, and computational modeling, Andrews’s work examines the functional organization of the visual cortex, specifically addressing the debate between modular and distributed representations of category-selective information. Their research includes studies on the holistic representation of facial identity, the neural correlates of binocular rivalry, and how structural and functional connectivity within the temporal lobes support the recognition of natural images. Furthermore, Andrews explores how idiosyncratic eye movements and neural responses correlate with individual differences in visual cognition.
0667.research_direction: Dr. Andrews has recently been investigating the perceptual and neural mechanisms underlying visual identity and natural object recognition. Their recent work explores how the visual system builds robust face representations, using behavioral paradigms like the vertical composite face effect to probe holistic processing across hemifields, and fMRI to test how long-term exposure to retinal spatial regularities shapes responses in core face-selective regions. Furthermore, they are studying the intersection of face perception and higher-order social cognition by employing naturalistic movie-viewing paradigms and testing individuals with developmental prosopagnosia to determine how narrative comprehension and non-visual conceptual knowledge guide face encoding in extended cortical networks. Beyond faces, Dr. Andrews is also utilizing large-scale stimulus databases and data-driven neuroimaging analyses to map the broader functional architecture of the human visual cortex, seeking to understand how the statistical properties of natural objects map onto continuous, graded cortical topographies.

papers.title: The perceptual and neural processing of familiar faces is shaped by the statistical regularities of real-world viewing
papers.abstract: This research explores how consistent spatial regularities in naturalistic face viewing (fixating centrally such that face halves consistently fall on specific retinal positions) impact the cognitive and neural mechanisms of identity recognition. Behavioral experiments demonstrated that participants were faster and more accurate at judging the familiarity of face halves (left/right or upper/lower) when they were presented in "typical" versus "atypical" visual field locations. Functional MRI results indicated that while response patterns in early visual areas (V1-V4) were governed by retinotopic position regardless of typicality, higher-level face-selective regions—specifically the occipital face area (OFA) and fusiform face area (FFA)—as well as non-visual person-processing regions, exhibited significant activation biases for typically positioned face parts. These results suggest that the neural representations supporting familiar face recognition are refined by long-term statistical exposure to the spatial configurations of faces in the environment.
papers.authors: Bartholomew P. A. Quinn, Timothy J. Andrews

papers.title: Differences in face recognition predict the understanding of events during natural viewing
papers.abstract: The study examines the functional role of face recognition in the comprehension of complex social narratives during natural viewing. By utilizing a movie-based paradigm, the researchers compared the narrative comprehension of individuals with developmental prosopagnosia (DP) to age-matched neurotypical controls. The findings revealed that DP individuals were significantly less effective at understanding the unfolding events of the movie than controls. Crucially, across the entire participant sample, individual variance in face recognition ability was a robust predictor of event comprehension scores. These results highlight the critical importance of identity recognition in synthesizing and interpreting socially rich, naturalistic narratives.
papers.authors: Kira N. Noad, Timothy J. Andrews

papers.title: A composite face effect for vertically divided faces
papers.abstract: This study investigates the existence of a vertical composite face effect (CFE) to evaluate whether holistic processing integrates information between left and right face halves across the visual hemifields. While the horizontal CFE (integrating top and bottom halves) is well-documented, the vertical counterpart is less understood. Using composite stimuli formed by aligning or misaligning the left and right halves of familiar and unfamiliar faces, the authors measured familiarity judgment performance. The results showed that recognition was significantly disrupted when halves were aligned compared to when they were misaligned, producing a vertical CFE of similar magnitude to the traditional horizontal effect. These findings provide evidence for a common holistic mechanism that integrates facial information from both hemispheres into a unified representation.
papers.authors: Bartholomew P. A. Quinn, A. Mike Burton, Timothy J. Andrews

papers.title: Conceptual knowledge shapes the neural representations of learned faces in non-visual regions of the brain
papers.abstract: This investigation utilizes a naturalistic viewing paradigm to determine how non-visual conceptual knowledge affects the neural encoding of newly learned face identities. Participants learned faces by watching a movie presented either in its original narrative sequence or a scrambled sequence to manipulate conceptual coherence while maintaining visual input. Following a consolidation period, fMRI was used to measure responses during a face recognition task. Results demonstrated that conceptual coherence at encoding significantly enhanced subsequent recognition and identity-specific neural patterns. This effect was localized in an extended network of non-visual regions associated with person knowledge rather than core face-processing areas, indicating that narrative and social context play a primary role in the development of robust face representations.
papers.authors: Kira N. Noad, David M. Watson, Timothy J. Andrews

papers.title: A data-driven analysis of the perceptual and neural responses to natural objects reveals organizing principles of human visual cognition
papers.abstract: Addressing the limitations of experimenter-defined object categories, this study employs a data-driven approach to map the functional organization of the visual cortex using a large, unbiased sample of natural objects from the THINGS database. The researchers applied partial least squares (PLS) regression to model the relationship between perceptual object properties and neural activity measured via fMRI. The model accurately predicted neural responses throughout the visual cortex using a small set of latent components. These components revealed smooth, graded topographies across the cortical surface that correspond to the statistical regularities of objects in the natural world (e.g., animacy, size, and category) rather than discrete modules, suggesting that the visual brain's architecture is optimized to represent the inherent variance of environmental stimuli.
papers.authors: David M. Watson, Timothy J. Andrews

0668.name: Timothy Vickery
0668.bio: Timothy Vickery is an Associate Professor at the University of Delaware whose research examines the functional and neural architecture of human visual cognition. Vickery’s work focuses on the interactions between visual perception, selective attention, and memory systems, utilizing behavioral psychophysics and functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI). Research topics include visual statistical learning and the distortion of spatial perception by objects and grouping. They also investigate the shared representational mechanisms between working memory and attentional control.
0668.research_direction: Dr. Vickery has recently been investigating the cognitive architectures underlying memory, perceptual prioritization, and strategic behavior. In the realm of visual cognition, their recent work explores the interaction between memory systems, using continuous reporting paradigms to test whether retrieving information from long-term memory must draw upon capacity-limited visual working memory resources. They are also examining the mechanisms behind the "self-prioritization effect" via shape-label matching tasks and computational modeling to determine whether enhanced performance for self-relevant stimuli is driven by automatic perceptual capture or by downstream associative and decision-making processes. Additionally, expanding into probabilistic reasoning, Dr. Vickery is studying human decision-making in simple zero-sum games to understand how players build internal opponent models and deploy heuristic strategies under uncertainty.

papers.title: Retrieval from long-term memory does not bypass working memory
papers.abstract: This study employs a continuous reporting paradigm to investigate whether information retrieved from long-term memory (LTM) can circumvent the capacity-limited visual working memory (VWM) system. Across two experiments, participants maintained color information at varying set sizes while performing LTM retrieval. Results demonstrate that LTM retrieval incurs significant fidelity costs to concurrent VWM representations, and VWM load conversely impairs the precision of LTM reports. These reciprocal interference effects suggest that retrieved LTM information must occupy VWM resources, supporting a unified resource model of short-term and long-term memory interaction rather than a bypass mechanism.
papers.authors: Michael K. P. Mugno, Timothy J. Vickery

papers.title: Opponent Models and Heuristic Strategies for Simple Games
papers.abstract: This research analyzes human strategic decision-making in simple zero-sum games through the lens of opponent modeling and heuristic adaptation. The paper explores how players construct internal representations of their opponents' patterns and utilize heuristic shortcuts to optimize performance under uncertainty. By fitting behavioral data to computational models of strategic interaction, the study quantifies the transition from simple Nash equilibrium strategies to more complex, adaptive opponent models that exploit suboptimal play, providing insights into the cognitive architectures of competitive game play and probabilistic reasoning.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the 46th Annual Conference of the Cognitive Science Society
papers.authors: Timothy J. Vickery

papers.title: Self-relevance effects and label choice: Strong variations in label-matching performance due to non-self-relevant factors
papers.abstract: This investigation critiques the 'self-prioritization effect'—the supposed automatic perceptual enhancement for self-relevant stimuli—by examining whether variations in label-matching performance are driven by non-perceptual factors. Using a shape-label matching paradigm, the study demonstrates that label choices and task-related objectives significantly modulate the observed benefits for self-associated shapes. Computational analysis of information uptake rates reveals that the prioritization is often an associative advantage in decision-making or memory integration rather than an automatic perceptual capture, suggesting that self-relevance effects are highly contingent on the specific cognitive demands of the label-matching task.
papers.authors: Gregory Wade, Timothy J. Vickery

0669.name: Tina Plank
0669.bio: Tina Plank is a vision science researcher at the University of Regensburg who examines the mechanisms of neuroplasticity in the adult visual system, specifically in response to retinopathologies such as macular degeneration. Plank uses functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), population receptive field (pRF) mapping, and psychophysical methods to study cortical reorganization and the development of preferred retinal loci in patients with central vision loss. Their research investigates how targeted perceptual learning and eccentric vision training modulate neural properties in the visual cortex to influence clinical outcomes like reading speed and visual acuity. Additionally, Plank explores multisensory integration and the effects of olfactory and auditory cues on visual perception.
0669.research_direction: Dr. Plank has recently been investigating adult neuroplasticity in the early visual cortex, focusing on how perceptual learning alters spatial tuning in peripheral vision. Their recent work explores the neural mechanisms underlying visual crowding and practice-dependent performance improvements using functional magnetic resonance imaging. By training participants on eccentric orientation discrimination tasks with flanking distractors, they examine whether behavioral improvements—such as reduced critical spacing and crowding anisotropy—are linked to localized changes in population receptive field properties. Ultimately, their research aims to uncover how early retinotopic areas, such as V1 and V2, functionally adapt in response to targeted visual training.

papers.title: Training-induced changes in population receptive field properties in visual cortex: Impact of eccentric vision training on population receptive field properties and the crowding effect
papers.abstract: This study evaluated whether practice-dependent visual perceptual learning on an eccentric vision task alters population receptive field (pRF) properties in early retinotopic cortex. Fifteen healthy adult participants underwent 3-Tesla functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) before and after completing a four-day behavioral perceptual learning protocol. The training task required gap orientation discrimination (up, down, left, right) of a Landolt C optotype presented at 6.5° eccentricity in the upper right visual field flanked by ring distractors arranged in radial or tangential configurations. Flanker distance was varied using an adaptive staircase to quantify critical spacing and radial-tangential crowding anisotropy. PRF parameters were mapped across eccentricities from 0.5° to 9° using drifting bar stimuli within dorsal and ventral subdivisions of V1 and V2, including the trained region of interest (tROI). Psychophysical results showed significant post-training reductions in critical spacing and crowding anisotropy indices (p = 0.009, Cohen's d = 0.79). PRF analyses revealed an overall 21% reduction in pRF size in the tROI (p = 0.005). Significant pRF size decreases were localized to both ventral V2 (contracting from 1.47° to 1.20°, p < 0.0000001) and dorsal V2 (contracting from 1.15° to 1.04°, p = 0.009), most prominently at eccentricities matching the trained visual field location (p < 0.001). Conversely, pRF estimates remained statistically unaltered in ventral V1 (p = 0.181) and dorsal V1 (p = 0.055). These outcomes demonstrate that visual perceptual learning of a crowding task selectively refines spatial tuning in extrastriate cortex (V2), underscoring training-induced adult neuroplasticity.
papers.authors: Maka Malania, Yih-Shiuan Lin, Charlotte Hörmandinger, John S. Werner, Mark W. Greenlee, Tina Plank

0670.name: Todd Zickler
0670.department: John A. Paulson School of Engineering and Applied Sciences
0670.bio: Todd Zickler is the William and Ami Kuan Danoff Professor of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science at Harvard University. Their research focuses on the mathematical and physical modeling of light-material interactions to extract structural and radiometric scene information from visual measurements. By integrating computer vision, applied optics, and human perception, Zickler develops imaging systems for applications in robotics, augmented reality, and generative AI. Zickler's work includes techniques in reflectance modeling, Helmholtz stereopsis, and the design of bio-inspired sensors that emulate the vision systems of organisms.
0670.research_direction: Dr. Zickler's recent work explores generative frameworks and computational geometry to solve inverse problems in visual perception and computational optics. They have recently been leveraging diffusion models to extract physical scene properties from 2D data, investigating how differential motion resolves perceptual ambiguities in joint shape and material estimation, and how scenes can be autonomously decomposed into occlusion-ordered, amodally-completed object layers. Alongside these generative approaches, their research investigates hardware-software co-design and low-level vision, creating systems that combine phase-only diffractive lenses with physics-guided networks for single-shot hyperspectral imaging, as well as developing geometry-aware neural architectures to robustly group boundaries and junctions in noisy environments. Additionally, their theoretical work examines the algebro-geometric foundations of distance geometry, exploring spatial reconstruction and source localization based purely on unlabeled range measurements.

papers.title: Generative Perception of Shape and Material from Differential Motion
papers.abstract: The authors propose a conditional denoising-diffusion framework (U-ViT3D-Mixer) that jointly infers multimodal distributions of surface geometry (normals) and material properties (albedo, reflectance) from short, three-frame video sequences of objects undergoing differential motion. By employing a pixel-space diffusion model trained on synthetic datasets, the system captures inherent perceptual ambiguities in static frames—such as convex/concave or matte/shiny bistability—and demonstrates that the incorporation of motion cues collapses these distributions toward accurate, veridical estimations. The architecture employs decoupled spatial, temporal, and channel-wise interactions to maintain efficiency at higher resolutions while leveraging 3D attention for global consistency.
papers.venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS)
papers.authors: Xinran Nicole Han, Ko Nishino, Todd Zickler

papers.title: CObL: Toward Zero-Shot Ordinal Layering without User Prompting
papers.abstract: This research introduces Concurrent Object Layers (CObL), a diffusion-based scene representation model that decomposes complex images into an occlusion-ordered stack of isolated, amodally-completed object layers. Utilizing Stable Diffusion as a geometric and semantic prior, CObL generates multiple object layers in parallel through inference-time guidance, ensuring that the composited results remain consistent with the input image. The model demonstrates zero-shot generalization from synthetic tabletop training data to real-world photographs, facilitating autonomous discovery of object-centric representations, including amodal completion and occlusion ordering, without requiring predefined object counts or user-provided masks.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF International Conference on Computer Vision (ICCV)
papers.authors: Aneel Damaraju, Dean Hazineh, Todd Zickler

papers.title: Grayscale to Hyperspectral at Any Resolution Using a Phase-Only Lens
papers.abstract: This study addresses the reconstruction of 31-channel hyperspectral images from a single-shot grayscale measurement using a minimalist system comprising a phase-only diffractive lens and a filterless panchromatic photosensor. The proposed method utilizes a conditional denoising diffusion model trained on local, shift-invariant patches to mitigate the severely ill-posed nature of the inverse problem. During inference, per-patch hyperspectral predictions are synchronized using global physics-based guidance derived from the optical system's wavelength-dependent point spread function (PSF). The framework enables high-resolution hyperspectral reconstruction and provides per-pixel uncertainty metrics that strongly correlate with spectral estimation errors.
papers.authors: Dean Hazineh, Federico Capasso, Todd Zickler

papers.title: Trilateration Using Unlabeled Path or Loop Lengths
papers.abstract: This paper provides an algebro-geometric analysis of the source localization problem based on unlabeled range measurements, specifically path or loop lengths. The authors investigate the conditions under which a configuration of points in d-dimensional space is uniquely determined by a set of scalar distances without combinatorial labeling. They prove that generic frameworks are strongly reconstructible from sufficiently rich sets of unlabeled measurements, extending classical results in distance geometry and global rigidity to more complex measurement ensembles. The work establishes that even without labeling, the association between measurements and combinatorial data can be recovered for generic point sets.
papers.authors: Ioannis Gkioulekas, Steven J. Gortler, Louis Theran, Todd Zickler

papers.title: Boundary Attention: Learning curves, corners, junctions and grouping
papers.abstract: The authors introduce a lightweight neural architecture that infers hierarchical boundary structures—including curves, corners, and junctions—using a novel 'boundary attention' mechanism. Unlike traditional edge detectors that produce binary raster maps, this model generates a high-dimensional, pixel-resolution field representing local geometric variables and spatial grouping. The model's geometry-aware local attention operation refines these variables over multiple scales, allowing it to detect faint boundaries in high-noise environments. By embedding an intentional geometric bias, the network generalizes from simple synthetic training data to complex, low-light photographic images without manual tuning of local scale or consistency parameters.
papers.authors: Mia Gaia Polansky, Charles Herrmann, Junhwa Hur, Deqing Sun, Dor Verbin, Todd Zickler

0671.name: Tom P. Franken
0671.bio: Tom P. Franken is an Assistant Professor in the Department of Neuroscience at Washington University School of Medicine, where they investigate the neural mechanisms of sensory inference. Franken’s research focuses on how the brain resolves sensory ambiguities to represent objects, with an emphasis on border ownership assignment in the visual cortex and sound localization circuits in the brainstem. Using a combination of multielectrode electrophysiology, computational modeling, and behavioral assays, their work aims to characterize the cortical and subcortical computations that support stable perception. Franken has described how feedback signals organize into columns in the primate visual cortex and how artificial neural networks replicate brain-like grouping signals to predict dynamic visual scenes.
0671.research_direction: Dr. Franken has recently been investigating the neural computations underlying scene perception and sensory processing, focusing particularly on how the visual system assigns foregrounds and maintains spatial stability across saccades. Using laminar multielectrode arrays in area V4 of awake macaques, their recent work explores the temporal dynamics and functional hallmark properties of border ownership signals and cortical grouping cells. Parallel to these neurophysiological experiments, they have been examining whether similar brain-like border ownership selectivities spontaneously emerge in artificial neural networks trained strictly on self-supervised natural video prediction. Extending their systems-level approach beyond vision, Dr. Franken also investigates cellular heterogeneity in the mammalian auditory brainstem, utilizing in vivo patch-clamp recordings to characterize the anatomical and physiological properties of neurons driving sound-offset responses.

papers.title: Grouping signals in primate visual cortex
papers.abstract: Visual scene perception remains remarkably stable despite frequent saccadic displacements of the retinal image. This perceptual continuity is thought to rely in part on border ownership (BOS) neurons in cortical area V2, which signal foreground surface assignment for hundreds of milliseconds after contextual cues are extinguished and transfer this assignment across saccades. Theoretical models propose that upstream BOS selectivity is established via feedback from downstream grouping cells that maintain persistent proto-object representations with short latencies, centripetal ownership preferences directed toward the receptive field center, and de novo remapping after saccades. Utilizing laminar multielectrode arrays in area V4 of awake, behaving macaques (Macaca mulatta), the authors identified a prominent population of neurons exhibiting these functional hallmark properties across all laminar compartments. These V4 units fired with response latencies sufficiently rapid to drive V2 BOS tuning via corticocortical feedback. Furthermore, these grouping cells displayed substantially weaker tuning for luminance contrast polarity than canonical BOS neurons, suggesting a functional dissociation wherein grouping units maintain the spatiotemporal continuity of segmented visual surfaces while BOS neurons integrate this spatial assignment with local surface feature properties.
papers.authors: Tom P. Franken, John H. Reynolds

papers.title: Brain-like border ownership signals support prediction of natural videos
papers.abstract: To parse visual scenes into structured objects, the primate visual cortex assigns borders to foreground surfaces via border ownership (BOS) selective neurons. Here, the authors investigated whether functional BOS signals can spontaneously emerge in an artificial neural network trained solely on self-supervised future-frame video prediction without explicit segmentation objectives or object annotations. Analyzing units within PredNet trained on natural video sequences from the KITTI dataset, responses were evaluated for classical receptive fields exposed to isolated luminance edges belonging to figures on opposing sides while manipulating edge orientation, spatial position, and contrast polarity. Both representation (R) and error (E) units in PredNet demonstrated pronounced BOS selectivity that was invariant to luminance contrast polarity and tolerant across contour orientations, reproducing key neurophysiological phenomena observed in primate V2 and V4. The proportion and amplitude of BOS units scaled progressively across the network hierarchy (L3 > L2 > L1 > L0). These results demonstrate that the objective of predicting natural visual dynamics provides sufficient computational pressure for the emergence of brain-like border ownership representations.
papers.authors: Zeyuan Ye, Ralf Wessel, Tom P. Franken

papers.title: Distinct cell classes in the superior paraolivary nucleus (SPN) region in the gerbil auditory brainstem revealed by in vivo physiological and anatomical characterization
papers.abstract: The superior paraolivary nucleus (SPN/SPON) of the mammalian superior olivary complex exhibits characteristic sound-offset responses driven by acoustic-evoked glycinergic inhibition, though in vivo synaptic dynamics and cellular heterogeneity have remained unresolved. Performing in vivo patch-clamp intracellular recordings and biocytin labeling in Mongolian gerbils (Meriones unguiculatus), 12 morphologically reconstructed neurons within and bordering the SPN were characterized across ultrastructure, intrinsic membrane properties, and responses to intracellular current injections and acoustic stimuli. The neurons segregated into three distinct physiological and anatomical classes: fast cells, which fired exclusively at the onset of depolarizing current steps, produced short-latency post-inhibitory rebound action potentials to hyperpolarizing current or sound offset, and showed dense somatic synaptic coverage; slow cells, which exhibited sustained firing during depolarizing steps, prolonged hyperpolarizing inhibitory decays, and sparse synaptic coverage; and uninhibited cells, which lacked prominent sound-evoked hyperpolarization and post-inhibitory rebound spiking. The findings indicate functional segregation where fast cells convey temporally precise offset timing to the inferior colliculus, whereas slow cells provide sustained inhibitory modulation to the cochlear nucleus.
papers.authors: Tom P. Franken, Philip X. Joris, Philip H. Smith

0672.name: Tomoyasu Horikawa
0672.bio: Tomoyasu Horikawa is a researcher at NTT Communication Science Laboratories specializing in the intersection of computational neuroscience and artificial intelligence. Horikawa’s work focuses on developing brain decoding methodologies that utilize deep neural networks to translate human brain activity, primarily from fMRI, into visual and linguistic representations. Their research includes 'mind captioning' and hierarchical image reconstruction, which aim to decode the content of dreams, mental imagery, and subjective perceptions into descriptive text and images.
0672.research_direction: Dr. Horikawa has recently been investigating how complex, subjective visual experiences and semantic representations can be decoded and externalized directly from human brain activity. Their recent work explores the neural representation of shitsukan—the multidimensional perception of material properties and textures—by mapping fMRI BOLD signals onto deep neural network feature spaces to continuously reconstruct visual imagery and illusory percepts using deep generative models. In addition to visual reconstruction, they have also been developing mind captioning frameworks that aim to translate nonverbal cortical activity from passive video viewing and mental recall tasks into structured natural language. By linking visual cortex representations to the latent spaces of deep language models, Dr. Horikawa is probing how the brain processes dynamic visual scenes, ultimately seeking to build a computational bridge between neural population codes and explicit descriptive text.

papers.title: Decoding Shitsukan in the Brain
papers.abstract: Characterizing Shitsukan—the multidimensional perception of material properties, surface texture, and realistic qualities of objects—requires representational frameworks beyond simple low-level image statistics or discrete verbal labels. This work presents a brain decoding framework centered on mid-level hierarchical visual features shared between the primate visual pathway and deep neural networks (DNNs). By establishing regression models that translate functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) signals into DNN feature spaces, brain activity is converted into intermediate computational representations. Pairing these decoded neural representations with deep generative models enables the continuous, high-fidelity reconstruction of visual imagery, illusory percepts, and material appearances directly from cortical activity patterns. This paradigm clarifies how population codes within ventral and higher visual cortex represent subjective material qualities and provides a quantitative computational basis for materializing internal visual experiences.
papers.venue: Shitsukan: Understanding and Manipulating Material and Quality Perception (Springer Nature)
papers.authors: Yukiyasu Kamitani, Misato Tanaka, Tomoyasu Horikawa

papers.title: Mind captioning: Evolving descriptive text of mental content from human brain activity
papers.abstract: While significant progress has been achieved in decoding language representations from human cortical activity, generating coherent, syntactically structured linguistic descriptions of complex mental content rooted in visual semantics remains an unresolved challenge. A generative decoding framework termed mind captioning is demonstrated to iteratively synthesize descriptive text reflecting neural semantic representations via latent feature vectors derived from deep language models (LMs). Linear regularized regression decoders were trained on human blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data acquired during passive viewing of dynamic, soundless video clips to predict the contextualized semantic representations of reference video annotations. Candidate text sequences were subsequently evolved and optimized through masked language model (MLM)-guided word replacement and interpolation to minimize discrepancy with brain-decoded semantic vectors. The optimization progressively produced well-structured descriptive captions accurately depicting perceived dynamic scenes, persisting even when the canonical fronto-temporal language network was systematically excluded from the decoder features. Crucially, the approach generalized to verbalizing internally recalled memory content during visual imagery tasks, illustrating an interpretive bridge between nonverbal cortical representations and structured natural language.
papers.authors: Tomoyasu Horikawa

0673.name: Tony Pansell
0673.lab_name: Eye movements and vision – Tony Pansell's research group
0673.bio: Tony Pansell is a Professor of Optometry at Karolinska Institutet whose research investigates the physiological mechanisms of eye movement control and visual function, with a focus on acquired brain injuries. Their work utilizes high-resolution eye-tracking and psychophysical methods to characterize binocular vision disorders, visuo-vestibular integration, and visual motion hypersensitivity in clinical populations. Pansell identifies objective biomarkers for neurological conditions, such as post-concussive syndrome and Parkinson's disease, while evaluating the efficacy of neuro-rehabilitative interventions like color filters and vision training.
0673.research_direction: Dr. Pansell has recently been investigating the multisensory mechanisms underlying human gaze stabilization and visual perception in both healthy and clinical populations. Their recent work explores how visual, vestibular, and proprioceptive inputs are weighted to maintain visual stability, utilizing high-resolution eye-tracking to measure ocular torsion during passive roll-plane body rotations. Additionally, they are examining the pathophysiological basis of visual symptoms following traumatic brain injury, using critical flicker fusion thresholds to assess low-level temporal resolution and perceptual noise in post-concussion syndrome. Finally, their research addresses clinical binocular integration, utilizing dichoptic psychophysics to investigate whether top-down attention can dynamically shift visual reference frames in patients experiencing binocular fusion failure.

papers.title: Temporal visual processing deficits in post concussion syndrome
papers.abstract: Post-concussion syndrome (PCS) frequently manifests as debilitating visual motion hypersensitivity. This study utilized psychophysical critical flicker fusion (CFF) threshold measurements across varying visual-field eccentricities to evaluate whether PCS is associated with alterations in low-level visual temporal resolution. Fifteen patients with persistent PCS and fifteen age-matched controls were assessed. Analysis via generalized linear mixed models, incorporating CFF variability as a covariate, demonstrated that CFF thresholds were significantly elevated in the PCS group, primarily driven by heightened internal neural noise (perceptual noise). These findings suggest a foundational deficit in low-level sensory processing in PCS, which likely necessitates compensatory gain upregulation within visual pathways, underpinning the clinical manifestations of motion sensitivity.
papers.authors: Davide Frattini, Mariagrazia Benassi, Tobias Wibble, Mattias Nilsson, Roberto Bolzani, Tony Pansell

papers.title: Attention can shift the reference eye under binocular fusion failure: A case report
papers.abstract: In healthy binocular vision, images from both eyes are typically integrated into a single 'cyclopean' percept. This case report investigates a 44-year-old patient with acquired binocular fusion failure following surgical resection of a cerebellar vermis hemangioblastoma, which resulted in multi-directional diplopia. Through a series of psychophysical experiments involving dichoptic and binocular viewing, the study demonstrates that the patient could voluntarily switch the reference eye for visual direction, anchoring perception to either the left or right eye. These shifts were independent of stimulus properties or response demands and could be modulated by top-down attention. The results suggest that when automatic cyclopean fusion mechanisms fail, the visual system can adapt to a single-eye reference frame that is flexibly controlled by attentional mechanisms, providing insight into the plastic nature of binocular integration.
papers.authors: Jiahao Wu, Tengfei Han, Qian Wang, Zaizhu Han, Jan Johansson, Gustaf Öqvist Seimyr, Tony Pansell

papers.title: Using Eye-tracking to Assess the Relative Importance of Visual and Vestibular Input to Subcortical Motion Processing in the Roll Plane
papers.abstract: This protocol describes a comprehensive methodology for quantifying the relative contributions of visual and vestibular systems to human gaze stabilization during roll-plane rotations. The procedure implements isolated optokinetic stimulation, motorized whole-body vestibular rotations in complete darkness, and combined visuovestibular trials. High-resolution video eye-tracking (Chronos Eye-Tracking Device) is used to record ocular torsion and head stability across three rotational and translational dimensions. Dynamic and static gains, slow-phase velocities, and nystagmus frequencies are quantified to establish sensory weighting. The protocol serves to elucidate sensory deficits in motion processing and provides a framework for identifying objective oculomotor biomarkers, such as the increased visual reliance observed in patients with concussions.
papers.authors: Tobias Wibble, Tony Pansell

papers.title: Human proprioceptive gaze stabilization during passive body rotations underneath a fixed head
papers.abstract: This investigation explored the existence of a human gaze-stabilizing torsional eye movement response triggered by proprioceptive neck activation in the roll plane. Thirteen healthy participants were subjected to passive body rotations while their heads were maintained in a gravitationally upright, fixed position using a mechanical sled and stabilization beam. Oculomotor responses were recorded via high-frequency eye tracking during trials conducted in darkness and while viewing a projected visual scene. Results showed that passive neck flexion induced significant ocular torsion (rotating in the opposite direction of the neck extension) exclusively when combined with a visual background. This response mimics a predictive head rotation intended to align the head with the body. The absence of this response in darkness suggests that proprioceptive gaze stabilization in humans is not an autonomous reflex but relies on multisensory integration with visual orientational cues.
papers.authors: Tobias Wibble, Tony Pansell

0676.name: Uri Hasson
0676.bio: Uri Hasson is an Associate Professor at the University of Trento and the Principal Investigator of the Information and Integration Lab at the Center for Mind/Brain Sciences (CIMeC). Hasson’s research investigates the neurobiological principles underlying language comprehension, the processing of statistical regularities, and how the brain manages uncertainty in both visual and auditory domains. Recently, their work has expanded into the field of neuroAI, focusing on the alignment between human cognitive representations and artificial neural networks, such as deep vision models and large language models. Hasson utilizes fMRI, EEG, and computational modeling to explore how the brain integrates complex information and generates predictions in real-world contexts.
0676.research_direction: Dr. Hasson's recent work explores the intersection of artificial and biological vision, investigating both the alignment of computational models with human visual processing and the physiological mechanisms of human eye movements. In the computational domain, they have recently been probing deep neural networks to understand how brain-inspired topographic constraints affect network robustness, and evaluating how isolating category-specific latent subspaces or generating alignment-importance heatmaps can better map artificial feature representations to human conceptual similarity judgments. Alongside this modeling work, their research investigates oculomotor behavior and neurophysiology in human participants. Specifically, they are developing continuous, high-precision psychophysical methods to quantify sighting ocular dominance during binocular viewing, while also utilizing resting-state fMRI to examine how long-term sensory deprivation alters the functional neural circuitry underlying eye movements in congenitally blind individuals.

papers.title: Beyond topography: Topographic regularization improves robustness and reshapes representations in convolutional neural networks
papers.abstract: This research investigates the influence of topographic constraints on the representational geometry and functional robustness of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). By imposing local spatial regularization on a penultimate-layer topographic grid, the authors demonstrate that such constraints significantly enhance the network's resilience to internal architecture and weight perturbations. The topographic regularization systematically reconfigures the latent feature space into a more brain-aligned spatial layout, suggesting that spatial organization is a critical inductive bias for developing robust, biologically-plausible artificial vision systems.
papers.authors: Nhut Truong, Uri Hasson

papers.title: Modeling Human Concepts with Subspaces in Deep Vision Models
papers.abstract: This study addresses the representational divergence between artificial vision models and human conceptual structures by identifying category-specific subspaces within Deep Neural Networks (DNNs). Using a supervised feature-pruning approach optimized to align with human similarity judgments for specific semantic domains (e.g., animals, food), the authors demonstrate that different categories utilize distinct, non-overlapping latent feature sets. These category-specific subspaces capture relevant human-like variance and provide a computational metric for evaluating the conceptual alignment and fidelity of AI-generated imagery.
papers.venue: ACM Transactions on Interactive Intelligent Systems
papers.authors: Anna Bavaresco, Nhut Truong, Uri Hasson

papers.title: Quantifying sighting dominance using on-display projections of monocular and binocular views
papers.abstract: The authors propose a high-precision, quantitative methodology for the assessment of sighting ocular dominance, grounded in a two-camera geometric model. The method utilizes a binocular alignment task on a digital display to identify the relative weighting of each eye's contribution to the fused percept by comparing perceived target projections under monocular and binocular viewing. The resulting continuous index demonstrates exceptional test-retest reliability (ICC = 0.96) and is influenced by physiological parameters such as interpupillary distance and phoria, revealing systematic nearly-balanced vision in specific individuals.
papers.authors: Giuseppe Notaro, Uri Hasson

papers.title: Explaining Human Comparisons Using Alignment-Importance Heatmaps
papers.abstract: This paper introduces the Alignment Importance Score (AIS) to quantify the contribution of individual DNN feature maps to the representational alignment with human similarity judgments. The researchers generate image-specific heatmaps that identify diagnostic visual regions for comparative tasks. While these AIS-based heatmaps largely correspond to traditional gaze-prediction saliency, they successfully identify non-salient features that are nonetheless critical for conceptual comparisons, providing a more granular understanding of human-like decision-making in vision models.
papers.authors: Nhut Truong, Dario Pesenti, Uri Hasson

papers.title: Neural networks associated with eye movements in congenital blindness
papers.abstract: This resting-state fMRI study investigates the preservation and reorganization of oculomotor-related neural circuitry in the absence of visual input. By extracting orbital echo-planar imaging (EPI) signals as a regressor, the authors demonstrate that congenitally blind individuals retain functional connectivity between eye-orbit signals and the motor cortex, although coupling with the visual cortex is significantly attenuated compared to sighted controls. The results reveal a moderate large-scale reorganization of functional networks and instances of interocular decoherence, detailing the impact of long-term sensory deprivation on the endogenous control of eye movements.
papers.authors: Cemal Koba, Alessandro Crimi, Olivier Collignon, Emiliano Ricciardi, Uri Hasson

0678.name: Valerie Goffaux
0678.bio: Valerie Goffaux is an F.R.S.-F.N.R.S. Research Associate whose work characterizes the neuro-computational mechanisms underlying human face perception. Goffaux’s research indicates that face recognition is tuned to horizontal orientations and relies on specific spatial frequency integration, which challenges traditional hierarchical models of vision. Using psychophysics, high-density EEG (frequency tagging), and fMRI, they investigate how the brain leverages natural contrast statistics and visual field anisotropies to achieve face categorization. Their current projects explore the functional link between early visual cortex selectivity and high-level face-selective regions, focusing on how radial biases and contextual modulations influence perceptual resolution.
0678.research_direction: Dr. Goffaux has recently been investigating the visual and informational mechanisms underlying human face perception, with a major focus on the computational role of horizontal orientation cues. By utilizing orientation-filtered stimuli, their recent work explores whether this tuning to horizontal facial features provides the primary gateway to structural and surface identity cues, enables view-tolerant recognition across different head angles, and operates within a retina- or face-centered spatial reference frame. Additionally, they are examining the mechanisms driving ultra-rapid saccades toward faces in peripheral vision, specifically testing if these oculomotor advantages depend on low-level retinotopic properties like radial orientation biases. Finally, Dr. Goffaux is also investigating the temporal dynamics of high-level vision by mapping the boundary conditions of serial dependence to understand how the similarity of consecutively viewed faces induces either attractive or repulsive perceptual biases.

papers.title: Dissociating retina- and face-centered reference frames of human face recognition
papers.abstract: The study investigates the spatial coordinate system (retina-centered vs. face-centered) that defines the horizontal orientation preference fundamental to human face identification. Observers were tasked with identity recognition of famous faces across various stimulus rotations (0°, ±45°, and ±90°) using orientation-filtered image content. By tracking recognition performance as a function of the orientation filter relative to both the retina and the face stimulus, the researchers tested whether the sensitivity peak shifts with rotation or remains anchored to the facial geometry. Results demonstrate that recognition sensitivity consistently peaks within the face-relative horizontal range regardless of stimulus orientation, providing evidence for a face-centered reference frame. However, the magnitude of this horizontal advantage was significantly attenuated at 90° rotations, indicating that the specialized mechanisms for face processing also exhibit a degree of dependency on the retina-centered coordinate system.
papers.authors: Hélène Dumont, Valérie Goffaux

papers.title: Between repulsion and attraction in serial biases: Replication of Chen and Cook (2021)
papers.abstract: This study replicates the findings of Chen and Cook (2021) to explore the boundary conditions of serial dependence in high-level face perception. Serial bias refers to the perceptual phenomenon where the judgment of a current stimulus is systematically biased by previously encountered stimuli. Specifically, face identity perception has been shown to exhibit attractive biases (current face perceived as more similar to the previous one) when successive identities are similar, and repulsive biases (current face perceived as more different) when they are dissimilar. The research systematically varies the identity similarity between consecutive trials to map the transition point from attraction to repulsion, assessing the robustness of these conflicting serial effects across individuals and quantifying their impact on the representation of facial identity in the human visual system.
papers.authors: Marius Grandjean, Louise Kauffmann, Alexia Roux-Sibilon, Valérie Goffaux

papers.title: Does radial bias contribute to fast saccades toward faces in the periphery?
papers.abstract: The research evaluates whether the ultra-rapid saccadic advantage for faces in peripheral vision is mediated by the low-level radial orientation bias, which facilitates processing of stimuli oriented radially relative to the fovea. Fifty participants performed a saccadic choice task (faces vs. vehicles) at 15° eccentricity along the horizontal (HM) and vertical meridians (VM). The study also independently quantified individual radial bias and the strength of horizontal tuning for face identity. While saccadic reaction times were faster on the HM than the VM, the magnitude of the face-specific saccadic advantage remained constant across meridians. These results demonstrate that the prioritized detection of faces in the periphery persists independently of retinotopic orientation biases, suggesting that low-level radial selectivity and high-level category-specialized mechanisms provide separate, additive contributions to rapid oculomotor responses.
papers.authors: Marius Grandjean, Louise Kauffmann, Alexia Roux-Sibilon, Valérie Goffaux

papers.title: The view-tolerance of human identity recognition depends on horizontal face information
papers.abstract: The study addresses the informational basis of view-tolerant face recognition by characterizing the orientation tuning of identity cues across varying yaws (+75° to -75°). Human recognition performance was tested using orientation-filtered face stimuli and compared against two computational model observers: a view-selective model (where optimal information shifts orientations with viewpoint) and a view-tolerant model (where horizontal cues are stable). Experimental results revealed that human observers remain robustly tuned to the horizontal orientation range regardless of the viewpoint, even when profile views contain higher physical energy at non-horizontal angles. These findings indicate that the horizontal structure of the face is the primary informational gateway for building invariant identity representations, likely due to the high diagnosticity of horizontal cues in frontal views and their unique stability across rotational changes in appearance.
papers.authors: Alexia Roux-Sibilon, Hélène Dumont, Vincent Bremhorst, Christianne Jacobs, Valérie Goffaux

papers.title: Horizontal face information is the main gateway to the shape and surface cues to familiar face identity
papers.abstract: This study investigates whether the human preference for horizontal orientation information in face recognition stems from this range's capacity to convey shape and surface reflectance cues. Using orientation-filtered images of familiar male actors, the researchers monitored identity recognition accuracy across natural, inverted, and contrast-negated conditions. Image inversion was used to disrupt 2D shape relations, while negation specifically impaired access to surface cues. Non-linear Bayesian mixed-effects models were employed to fit Gaussian orientation-tuning functions to the resulting performance decrements. Findings showed that both inversion and negation effects peaked sharply in the horizontal range with comparable tuning bandwidths and amplitudes. These results suggest that the horizontal bias in face identification is driven by this orientation's privileged role in carrying both primary sources of identity-diagnostic information: structural shape and surface pigmentation.
papers.authors: Helene Dumont, Alexia Roux-Sibilon, Valérie Goffaux

0681.name: Victoria Plaza
0681.department: Department of Basic Psychology (Departamento de Psicología Básica)
0681.bio: Victoria Plaza is a Professor in the Department of Basic Psychology at the Universidad Autónoma de Madrid and a member of the Cognition, Attention, and Learning Lab. Plaza’s research examines the cognitive mechanisms of associative learning, focusing on the application of the differential outcomes procedure to memory and discriminative learning in clinical populations such as those with Alzheimer’s disease and Down syndrome. They also utilize eye-tracking methodologies to investigate active vision, exploring how stimulus relevance and cognitive load influence fixation durations and strategic behavior during visual search tasks.
0681.research_direction: Dr. Plaza has recently been investigating how learning and memory shape both low-level visual processing and higher-level cognitive skill acquisition. Their recent work explores the dynamic adjustment of oculomotor strategies, using eye-tracking to examine how fixation durations and functional viewing fields evolve as individuals transition from exploratory to memory-guided visual search. Alongside this oculomotor research, they are investigating the Differential Outcomes Procedure (DOP), an expectancy-based learning paradigm that uses unique reinforcement contingencies to boost memory and task performance. Across several recent studies and meta-analyses, they evaluate how DOP training can improve the perceptual recognition of ambiguous emotional facial expressions, while also testing its broader translational potential for enhancing early phonological development in children and mitigating cognitive deficits in clinical populations.

papers.title: Dynamic Adjustment of Fixation Durations in Visual Search
papers.abstract: This study challenges the conventional assumption of a constant functional viewing field (FVF) size and processing duration by examining oculomotor scanning patterns across multiple visual search paradigms. Utilizing eye-tracking across three distinct experiments—a comparative search task, a repeated search task with varying targets, and a contextual cueing paradigm—we analyzed the modulation of fixation durations as a function of trial repetition and target identity. Results demonstrate a systematic decrease in the number of fixations required to localize targets over successive trials. Critically, fixation durations were significantly modulated by target-distractor status: search fixations exhibited increased durations while target-entry fixations decreased over repetitions. These findings suggest a dynamic, learning-driven adjustment of oculomotor strategies, potentially reflecting expansions in the FVF and optimized attentional resource allocation during the transition from exploratory to memory-guided search.
papers.authors: M Pilar Aivar, Laura Cepero, Miguel A. Vadillo, Victoria Plaza

papers.title: The Differential Outcomes Procedure improves the recognition of facial expressions of emotion: A systematic review and meta-analysis
papers.abstract: This meta-analytical review quantifies the efficacy of the Differential Outcomes Procedure (DOP) in enhancing the identification and categorization of emotional facial expressions. By pooling data from multiple experimental datasets, we evaluated the impact of trial-specific reinforcement contingencies on accuracy and reaction time metrics compared to Non-Differential Outcomes (NOP) controls. The analysis identifies robust medium-to-large effect sizes for improved facial recognition across diverse populations, including healthy adults and individuals with neurocognitive or neurodevelopmental disorders. Furthermore, the results indicate that the DOP's benefits are particularly pronounced under conditions of high task difficulty, such as the recognition of low-intensity or ambiguous emotional expressions. We discuss these effects in the context of expectancy-based learning mechanisms and their potential for clinical application in populations characterized by social-cognitive deficits.
papers.authors: Michael Molina, Antonia Hurtado, Mayte Rodríguez, Luis J. Fuentes, Victoria Plaza, Ángeles F. Estévez

papers.title: Aplicación del Procedimiento de Consecuencias Diferenciales como una estrategia pedagógica para estimular la Conciencia Fonológica y la Velocidad de Denominación en estudiantes prelectores
papers.abstract: This investigation explored the efficacy of the Differential Outcomes Procedure (DOP) as a pedagogical tool to enhance phonological awareness and rapid automatized naming (RAN) in a sample of pre-reading children (N=61, aged 5 years). Using a longitudinal experimental design, participants were trained under either DOP (where unique reinforcers were associated with specific phonological targets) or NOP conditions. Psychometric assessments revealed that children in the DOP group achieved significantly higher accuracy and increased processing speeds in phonological awareness tasks compared to those receiving non-differential reinforcement. The findings suggest that the prospective memory and expectancy mechanisms activated by the DOP facilitate the acquisition of early literacy-related cognitive skills, particularly in the Second Level of Transition, providing a viable strategy for ameliorating early reading difficulties.
papers.authors: Michael Molina, Antonia Hurtado, Mayte Rodríguez, Luis J. Fuentes, Victoria Plaza, Ángeles F. Estévez

papers.title: From Basic to Applied Science: The Case of the Differential Outcomes Procedure
papers.abstract: This high-level review synthesizes decades of research on the Differential Outcomes Procedure (DOP), tracing its evolution from animal associative learning paradigms to sophisticated cognitive interventions in humans. We evaluate the neurophysiological evidence supporting the role of the prospective memory system and the activation of specific outcome expectancies in bypassing traditional associative memory deficits. The review details the application of the DOP across the lifespan—from pediatric development to pathological aging—with a focus on its utility in enhancing medical treatment adherence and face recognition in Alzheimer's disease. Finally, we propose a translational framework for integrating DOP-based reinforcement into digital healthcare platforms to promote patient autonomy and mitigate cognitive decline in clinical populations.
papers.authors: Luis J. Fuentes, Victoria Plaza, Ana B. Vivas, Ángeles F. Estévez

0684.name: Viola Stoermer
0684.department: Department of Psychological and Brain Sciences
0684.bio: Stoermer is an Associate Professor at Dartmouth College where they direct the BrainStörmer Lab, focusing on the cognitive and neural architectures of human perception, attention, and memory. Their research employs a multimodal approach—including psychophysics, EEG, and fMRI—to investigate how the brain selectively prioritizes sensory information and the mechanisms by which attention shapes subjective visual experience. Stoermer examines the representational structures of feature-based and object-based attention, the capacity limits of visual working memory, and the cross-modal integration of auditory and visual signals.
0684.research_direction: Dr. Stoermer has recently been investigating how high-level semantic meaning and past experience shape the limits of visual cognition, such as exploring how real-world object recognition scaffolds feature storage in visual working memory. Their recent work also probes the flexibility of attentional tuning, using psychophysics and EEG to determine how feature-based attention can "zoom" in and out of specific color spaces depending on task demands. Furthermore, they are examining the neural dynamics of selection history to understand how incidentally learned statistical regularities dynamically adjust the breadth of category search templates and bias early sensory gain. Finally, their research extends into multisensory perception, investigating how congruent, complex auditory scenes help resolve visual ambiguity during object identification in noisy environments.

papers.title: Real-world Objects Scaffold Visual Working Memory for Features: Increased Neural Engagement When Colors Are Remembered as Part of Meaningful Objects
papers.abstract: This study challenges the 'fixed-capacity' model of visual working memory (VWM) by investigating the neural mechanisms through which semantic meaning enhances feature storage. Utilizing EEG-based frequency-tagging (SSVEP) and contralateral delay activity (CDA) metrics, the researchers measured neural signals during a color maintenance task. Findings revealed that colors integrated into recognizable real-world objects elicited significantly larger CDA amplitudes and exhibited more stable spatiotemporal neural patterns across parietal-occipital electrodes compared to colors in scrambled shapes. Additionally, a novel fronto-central ERP distinguished meaningful from scrambled object maintenance during both encoding and retention. These results suggest that conceptual knowledge provides an efficient representational scaffold that proactively increases the priority and robustness of feature-based representations in VWM, expanding capacity beyond low-level visual limits.
papers.authors: Yong Hoon Chung, Timothy F. Brady, Viola S. Störmer

papers.title: Zooming In and Out: Selective Attention Modulates Color Signals in Early Visual Cortex for Narrow and Broad Ranges of Task-Relevant Features
papers.abstract: The flexibility of feature-based attention (FBA) tuning was explored by examining whether neural gain modulations in early visual cortex can 'zoom' in and out of color space according to task demands. By recording frequency-tagged steady-state visual evoked potentials (SSVEPs) while participants attended to contiguous ranges of colors (30° or 60°), the study demonstrated that FBA effectively enhances signals in the early visual cortex for the entire attended range. However, the magnitude of neural enhancement was significantly attenuated for the broader color range compared to the narrow range. These results indicate that the granularity of feature-selective selection is constrained by a resolution-dependent gain mechanism analogous to the zoom-lens model of spatial attention, with limits arising at early sensory processing stages.
papers.authors: Mert Özkan, Angus F. Chapman, Viola S. Störmer

papers.title: Early Cortical Sensitivity and Speeded Target Selection Underlie Incidentally Learned Prioritization of Visual Features
