papers.abstract: This research characterizes the neural correlates of selection history in feature-based attention through an incidental learning paradigm. Using EEG to track the N2pc component and early visual evoked potentials, the authors found that feature values frequently encountered as targets elicited enhanced early sensory gain (P1/N1) and a significant latency shift in the N2pc, signifying accelerated attentional allocation. These modulations indicate that incidental experience with statistical regularities proactively biases the tuning of early visual-cortical filters and facilitates more efficient target selection by lowering perceptual thresholds. The magnitude of these neural changes strongly correlated with individual behavioral benefits, demonstrating that selection history shapes the flow of information across multiple stages of the neural processing hierarchy.
papers.authors: Kevin Ortego, Doug Addleman, Viola S. Störmer

papers.title: Attention to Object Categories: Selection History Determines the Breadth of Attentional Tuning During Real-World Object Search
papers.abstract: The impact of selection history on the breadth of attentional templates was assessed using five experiments involving real-world object search. Participants learned environmental statistics where either specific objects or multiple category exemplars were frequent targets. Behavioral psychophysics and set-size manipulations revealed that searchers narrowly tune attention to specific objects when experience is limited to a single exemplar but adaptively broaden their templates to entire categories (e.g., all cars) after encountering multiple category members. Eye-tracking and response time patterns confirmed that these experience-driven changes modulate attentional guidance itself rather than post-selective decision thresholds, demonstrating that the visual system flexibly adjusts the resolution of search templates based on recent selection history.
papers.authors: Douglas A. Addleman, Reshma Rajasingh, Viola S. Störmer

papers.title: Cutting Through the Noise: Auditory Scenes and Their Effects on Visual Object Processing
papers.abstract: This study explored the multisensory mechanisms of object recognition by testing how complex auditory environments influence visual interpretation under high noise conditions. Using a cross-modal priming paradigm where visual objects emerged through noise, the researchers demonstrated that semantically congruent auditory scenes significantly lowered perceptual thresholds for object identification and enhanced recognition speed. This facilitation extended to category-matched objects that were never explicitly heard, suggesting that high-level auditory information provides a semantic scaffold integrated into the visual processing pipeline. The results indicate that auditory context is integrated early enough to resolve visual ambiguity, underscoring the importance of cross-modal semantic congruency in supporting meaningful perceptual experiences in naturalistic settings.
papers.authors: Jamal R. Williams, Viola S. Störmer

0686.name: Vivian C. Paulun
0686.bio: Vivian C. Paulun is an Assistant Professor at the University of Wisconsin–Madison and directs the Paulun Lab. Paulun’s research investigates the computational and neural foundations of high-level vision, specifically how the brain infers physical properties of materials—such as stiffness, mass, and elasticity—from visual information. To explore these mechanisms, they employ a combination of psychophysics, functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), and computational modeling that incorporates physics-based simulations and generative engines. Previously, Paulun completed postdoctoral training at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, working jointly with Nancy Kanwisher and Josh Tenenbaum in the Department of Brain and Cognitive Sciences.
0686.research_direction: Dr. Paulun's recent work explores how the human visual system infers the latent physical properties of dynamic objects and materials. Using functional MRI, they have recently been investigating the neural architecture underlying substance perception, probing how the brain distinctly represents discrete objects ("things") versus non-solid, deformable materials ("stuff") across visual and frontoparietal networks. Additionally, their research examines "ensemble physics" through psychophysical paradigms to understand how observers estimate emergent properties, such as the mass of a large group of moving items, when tracking individual components is computationally intractable. Finally, they are studying the specific mental algorithms supporting these physical judgments, employing physics-based simulations and behavioral experiments to determine whether observers integrate multiple sensory cues or flexibly switch between single-feature motion heuristics to infer internal properties like elasticity.

papers.title: Dissociable cortical regions represent things and stuff in the human brain
papers.abstract: The human visual system fundamentally distinguishes between discrete objects ('things') and nonsolid materials ('stuff'), yet the neural architecture supporting substance perception is largely uncharacterized. Scanned with functional MRI while viewing naturalistic video sequences of rigid and non-rigid things alongside liquid and granular stuff, participants exhibited a double dissociation within both ventral and dorsal visual pathways. Specifically, the lateral occipital complex (LOC) displayed sensitivity to both rigid shapes and deformable materials, whereas the frontoparietal physics network (FPN) responded to both categories but showed a significant representational preference for things. These results indicate that the brain engages distinct mental algorithms for thing-like and stuff-like entities, paralleling the divergent simulation engines utilized in artificial physics systems.
papers.authors: Vivian C. Paulun, Raghavendra Rao T. Pramod, Joshua B. Tenenbaum, Nancy Kanwisher

papers.title: Ensemble Physics: Perceiving the Mass of Groups of Objects is More Than the Sum of Its Parts
papers.abstract: While intuitive physics research typically examines property inference for individual objects, humans frequently reason about large collections of items where tracking each discrete part is computationally intractable. This study investigates 'ensemble physics,' a hypothesized representational mode for groups of objects with emergent physical properties. Utilizing psychophysical tasks where observers judged the average mass of marbles falling onto a cloth, the authors found that participants' judgments were significantly more accurate than predicted by the aggregation of individual object estimates. This ensemble benefit suggests that the human visual system simulates sets of objects as collective units with emergent physical properties, rather than as simple sums of individual parts, providing a mechanism for efficient physical reasoning in complex scenes.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the Annual Meeting of the Cognitive Science Society (CogSci)
papers.authors: Vicente Vivanco, Joshua B. Tenenbaum, Vivian C. Paulun, Kevin A. Smith

papers.title: Humans switch between heuristics instead of combining cues when judging object properties from motion
papers.abstract: Inferring internal physical properties such as elasticity from visual motion is a computationally complex, ill-posed problem, as an object's trajectory depends on both its material properties and initial conditions (e.g., velocity, orientation). This study proposes a resource-rational model of elasticity perception based on the learned statistics of object motion. Using 100,000 physics-based simulations of bouncing cubes, the authors identified 23 motion features diagnostic of elasticity. Behavioral experiments demonstrated that human observers do not employ standard cue combination; instead, they rely on single-feature heuristics and switch between them flexibly depending on the information available in the stimulus (e.g., observation time). This heuristic-switching model explains both the robust accuracy of human perception and specific systematic illusions where sensory features diverge from physical ground truth.
papers.authors: Vivian C. Paulun, Florian S. Bayer, Joshua B. Tenenbaum, Roland W. Fleming

0687.name: Vivian M Ciaramitaro
0687.bio: Vivian M. Ciaramitaro is an Associate Professor whose research examines the development and mechanisms of multisensory integration, focusing on how visual and auditory information are processed from infancy through adulthood. Ciaramitaro’s work utilizes psychophysical techniques, eye-tracking, and electroencephalography (EEG) to investigate how attention and plasticity influence sensory perception and neural responses. They explore cross-modal correspondences, the impact of emotional states like social anxiety on perceptual biases, and the role of experience in shaping sensory thresholds. By quantifying behavioral changes alongside brain activity, their research aims to elucidate the cognitive and neural foundations of how humans navigate complex sensory environments across the lifespan.
0687.research_direction: Dr. Ciaramitaro has recently been investigating multisensory integration and perceptual biases across diverse domains, spanning early developmental crossmodal learning to high-level visual face adaptation. Their recent work explores how visual experience scaffolds multisensory associations in children, specifically asking how the quantity of prior audio-visual exposure influences both targeted haptic exploration strategies and the strength of audio-tactile sound-shape mappings like the Bouba-Kiki effect. In a distinct line of research, they are investigating the perceptual mechanisms underlying affective biases by using psychophysical adaptation paradigms with morphed facial expressions to determine how social anxiety alters sensory recalibration to positive versus threatening faces. Together, their research probes how both developmental sensory exposure and internal emotional states modulate the fundamental mechanisms of perception and crossmodal association.

papers.title: Four Trials Is Not Enough: The Amount of Prior Audio–Visual Exposure Determines the Strength of Audio–Tactile Crossmodal Correspondence Early in Development
papers.abstract: Successfully navigating cluttered environments requires the brain to integrate signals from multiple sensory modalities, often relying on crossmodal correspondences like the Bouba–Kiki effect. This study investigated whether the efficacy of audio-tactile (AT) correspondences in 6- to 8-year-old children depends on the quantity of prior audio-visual (AV) experience. In a controlled haptic exploration task where visual input was obstructed, children had to match nonsense sounds to the curvature of three-dimensional shapes explored via touch. Results indicated that while four trials of prior AV exposure were insufficient to enhance AT mappings, eight trials significantly strengthened the correspondence. Furthermore, a strong correlation was observed between individual AV association strength during exposure and subsequent AT association strength, suggesting that early multisensory learning is highly sensitive to the amount of specific visual experience.
papers.authors: Shibo Cao, Rong Tan, Vivian M. Ciaramitaro

papers.title: Altered mechanisms of adaptation in social anxiety: differences in adapting to positive versus negative emotional faces
papers.abstract: Social anxiety is associated with persistent negative perceptual biases, though the underlying cognitive drivers remain poorly defined. This research examined the hypothesis that social anxiety alters the fundamental mechanisms of sensory adaptation to emotional facial expressions. Using a psychophysical adaptation paradigm, the study quantified the point of subjective equality (PSE) along a morph continuum ranging from angry to happy faces. Results demonstrated that individuals with high social anxiety exhibited significantly weakened adaptation to threatening (angry) faces compared to happy faces, a discrepancy not observed in low-anxiety controls. This failure to adequately recalibrate to negative social stimuli may preserve heightened sensitivity to threat, reinforcing negative biases in social interaction.
papers.authors: Erinda Morina, Daniel A. Harris, Sarah A. Hayes-Skelton, Vivian M. Ciaramitaro

papers.title: Prior visual experience increases children's use of effective haptic exploration strategies in audio-tactile sound-shape correspondences
papers.abstract: This study investigated whether prior visual exposure to abstract shapes improves haptic (tactile) exploration strategies in children, thereby facilitating audio-tactile (AT) sound-shape associations. Utilizing video-recorded behavioral analysis of 6- to 8-year-olds, the researchers categorized five specific haptic strategies: effective (contour following, clawing, pinching, and poking) and ineffective (sweeping). The findings revealed that children with prior audio-visual experience transitioned to using more effective and efficient strategies, such as poking the protrusions of shapes, whereas those without visual experience relied on less effective, uncategorizable methods. This shift in manual strategy suggests that visual imagery or memory aids the motor system in targeted haptic scanning, explaining the developmental role of vision in establishing crossmodal connections between audition and touch.
papers.authors: Shibo Cao, Julia Kelly, Cuong Nguyen, Hiu Mei Chow, Brianna Leonardo, Aleksandra Sabov, Vivian M. Ciaramitaro

0688.name: Walter Scheirer
0688.department: Department of Computer Science and Engineering
0688.lab_name: Notre Dame Computer Vision Research Lab
0688.bio: Walter Scheirer is the Dennis O. Doughty Collegiate Professor of Engineering at the University of Notre Dame, where they investigate recognition across vision and language. Scheirer applies extreme value theory to visual recognition and develops formal theories for open set recognition to address the identification of unknown classes in unconstrained environments. Their methodology integrates visual psychophysics to bridge human and machine perception, aiming to increase the robustness of neural networks against novel or occluded stimuli. Additionally, Scheirer’s work involves media forensics and the study of biologically-inspired learning algorithms to create adaptive and ethically grounded artificial intelligence systems.
0688.research_direction: Dr. Scheirer has recently been investigating the boundaries of artificial intelligence and software ecosystems across computer vision, human-computer interaction, and the digital humanities. In the realm of machine perception, their recent work explores open-world learning paradigms—specifically how agents can continuously detect and adapt to novel concepts in non-stationary environments—as well as how augmented reality facial filters impact the accuracy and robustness of automated face recognition systems. They are also examining the ethical and sociological dimensions of software design, combining algorithmic auditing with philosophical frameworks to operationalize virtue ethics and evaluate user data autonomy in contemporary communication platforms. Additionally, they are developing computational methods for literary analysis, utilizing transformer-based sequence labeling to extract narrative structures and story grammar to facilitate more transparent semantic matching in complex texts.

papers.title: Do We Need Subsidiarity in Software?
papers.abstract: This research evaluates software ecosystems through the sociological lens of subsidiarity, investigating the balance between individual data autonomy and centralized technological intervention. Utilizing a bifurcated methodology comprising algorithmic data flow auditing and qualitative user interviews, the study quantifies the degree of centralization in contemporary communication platforms. Analysis reveals that platforms such as Slack and Discord exhibit significant subsidiarity violations via opaque data harvesting and limited user agency, characterizing the trade-offs inherent in surveillance capitalism.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the ACM CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI)
papers.authors: Louisa Conwill, Megan Levis Scheirer, Walter Scheirer

papers.title: A Comprehensive Evaluation Framework for the Study of the Effects of Facial Filters on Face Recognition Accuracy
papers.abstract: This study introduces a comprehensive framework for quantifying the impact of augmented reality (AR) facial filters on the accuracy of automated face recognition (FR) algorithms. The authors contribute a gender-balanced, controlled dataset of facial images and establish a principled filter selection methodology to evaluate effects from American (Snapchat, Instagram) and Chinese (Meitu, Pitu) social media platforms. By analyzing shifts in the genuine and impostor similarity distributions, the work highlights significant biometric performance degradation and proposes a detection-correction mechanism within the latent embedding space to restore model robustness against filtering artifacts.
papers.venue: IEEE International Joint Conference on Biometrics (IJCB)
papers.authors: Kagan Ozturk, Louisa Conwill, Jacob Gutierrez, Kevin Bowyer, Walter J. Scheirer

papers.title: Design Patterns for the Common Good: Building Better Technologies Using the Wisdom of Virtue Ethics
papers.abstract: This paper explores the integration of virtue ethics into the Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) lifecycle to facilitate the design of ethical technologies. The authors delineate a framework of 'Design Patterns for the Common Good,' drawing from Aristotelian and Thomistic philosophical traditions to operationalize virtues within technical requirements. By conducting a systematic analysis of the translation process from abstract moral concepts to concrete interaction design choices, the research provides practitioners with a rubric for developing software that actively supports societal well-being and mitigates exploitative technological structures.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the ACM CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI)
papers.authors: Louisa Conwill, Megan Levis, Karla Badillo-Urquiola, Walter J. Scheirer

papers.title: Open Issues in Open World Learning
papers.abstract: This review identifies and analyzes critical research gaps in the domain of Open World Learning (OWL), specifically addressing the challenges of novelty detection, characterization, and continuous learning in non-stationary perceptual environments. The authors organize eight fundamental open problems into three categories: Theory of Novelty, Agent Design, and Agent Evaluation. The paper explores the application of information theory to quantify epistemic risk and knowledge acquisition, advocating for a transition from closed-set paradigms toward agents capable of identifying and learning novel semantic concepts without performance degradation on previously learned tasks.
papers.authors: Steve Cruz, Katarina Doctor, Christopher Funk, Walter Scheirer

papers.title: Story Grammar Semantic Matching for Literary Study
papers.abstract: This research presents 'Story Grammar Semantic Matching,' a structured framework for quantitative literary analysis that utilizes narrative structural elements as feature representations for semantic matching. Departing from word co-occurrence models, the methodology employs a transformer-based (BERT) pipeline to perform sequence labeling of prose and epic poetry with story-element tags (e.g., character traits, setting changes). Semantic similarities and allusions are then detected by analyzing the alignment of these grammatical structures, providing a more transparent and explanatory feature space for digital humanities research than traditional dense vector embeddings.
papers.authors: Abigail Swenor, Neil Coffee, Walter Scheirer

0689.name: Ward van der Tempel
0689.bio: Ward van der Tempel is the CTO and co-founder of VoxelSensors, where they oversee the development of neuromorphic-inspired 3D perception systems. They earned a PhD in Electrical Engineering from Vrije Universiteit Brussel (VUB), with research at the ETRO department focusing on Current-Assisted Photonic Demodulators (CAPD) and Time-of-Flight (ToF) imaging. Van der Tempel's current work involves the Single Photon Active Event Sensor (SPAES), which utilizes attention-based selective data gathering for low-power, low-latency spatial awareness and gaze tracking in wearable AI. They also participate in the SPECTRE program, a collaboration between VoxelSensors and VUB focused on 3D sensing for robotics and human-device interaction.
0689.research_direction: Dr. van der Tempel has recently been developing advanced optical sensing hardware tailored for the strict power and latency budgets of wearable extended reality (XR) platforms. Their recent work explores high-precision eye tracking by designing compact optical architectures—such as folded Offner layouts—that capture and digitize Dual Purkinje Images, specifically tracking the reflection offsets between the anterior cornea and posterior lens. In parallel, they are investigating novel approaches to spatial perception and environmental depth-sensing by replacing traditional frame-based cameras with asynchronous, single-photon active event sensors combined with laser triangulation. Across these distinct domains, Dr. van der Tempel is examining how to extract robust, high-speed visual data under dynamic ambient lighting conditions without exceeding the minimal mechanical and power constraints of all-day head-mounted displays.

papers.title: Wearable DPI (Dual Purkinje Images) system with Offner optical layout for lightweight XR
papers.abstract: This work describes the design and integration of a compact eye-tracking system utilizing Dual Purkinje Image (DPI) detection specifically optimized for lightweight Extended Reality (XR) form factors. The system employs a specialized Offner optical layout to achieve high-resolution gaze tracking while maintaining a minimal mechanical footprint. By leveraging the specific reflection properties of the anterior cornea (P1) and the posterior lens (P4), the architecture demonstrates robust estimation of the optical axis relative to the visual axis. The paper details the implementation of these components within a wearable frame and presents quantitative analysis of tracking accuracy and latency in dynamic real-world environments.
papers.venue: Optical Architectures for Displays and Sensing in Augmented, Virtual, and Mixed Reality (AR, VR, MR) VII (SPIE AR | VR | MR 2026)
papers.authors: Boris Greenberg, Ward van der Tempel

papers.title: High-resolution eye-tracking via digital imaging of Purkinje images
papers.abstract: We present a novel methodology for high-precision eye tracking based on the digital acquisition and processing of Purkinje reflections. The system utilizes a folded optical path incorporating a Dilated Point Inception (DPI) inspired module to extract positional data from the first and fourth Purkinje images (P1 and P4). By employing a serialized data stream from a custom sensor architecture, the implementation achieves significant reduction in latency compared to traditional frame-based tracking methods. The study evaluates the tracking resolution and robust feature extraction under varying ambient light conditions, demonstrating the system's capability for integration into all-day wearable XR devices.
papers.venue: Optical Architectures for Displays and Sensing in Augmented, Virtual, and Mixed Reality (AR, VR, MR) VI (SPIE AR | VR | MR 2025)
papers.authors: Ruei-Jr Wu, Boris Greenberg, Ward van der Tempel

papers.title: Low-power, low-latency perception for XR
papers.abstract: Extended reality (XR) platforms require seamless blending of virtual content with the physical environment, placing stringent demands on underlying spatial perception systems to ensure robust operation under strict power and latency budgets. Conventional depth-sensing architectures struggle to concurrently deliver the necessary frame rates, low latency (sub-5 ms), and micro-power operation within target operating envelopes of up to 6 meters for environmental mapping and 1.5 meters for near-field interaction. To address these fundamental constraints, this paper presents an active event sensor (AES) framework utilizing Switching Pixels Active Event Sensors in conjunction with laser beam triangulation. By transitioning from traditional frame-based readout to sparse, asynchronous single-photon event detection, the architecture achieves high-speed temporal tracking and robust ambient-light immunity while slashing dynamic power consumption, establishing a viable pathway for persistent, low-power spatial awareness and natural interaction in wearable XR devices.
papers.venue: Optical Architectures for Displays and Sensing in Augmented, Virtual, and Mixed Reality (AR, VR, MR) IV (Proceedings of SPIE, Volume 12449)
papers.authors: Ward van der Tempel, Robert Collier, Kostas Pataridis, Ségolène Rogge, Arman Alaie, Jean-Sébastien Staelens, Mahmoud Shahin, Johannes Peeters, André Miodezky, Christian Mourad

0691.name: Weina Zhu
0691.bio: Weina Zhu is a Professor in the School of Information Science at Yunnan University, specializing in the cognitive neuroscience of visual perception. Zhu’s research investigates how the human brain processes sensory information within and outside of conscious awareness, utilizing continuous flash suppression (CFS) paradigms and psychophysical modeling. They employ methodologies including high-density electroencephalography (EEG/ERP), eye-tracking, and image processing to examine the temporal dynamics of vision, the 'closure-superiority effect,' and the role of neural oscillations in defining temporal integration windows. This work connects computational mathematics and vision science to characterize mechanisms underlying rapid object recognition and visual attention.
0691.research_direction: Dr. Zhu's recent work spans computational neuroscience, visual cognition, and artificial intelligence, with a primary focus on applying advanced deep learning to decode complex spatiotemporal data. Their recent research heavily explores brain-computer interfaces, developing novel hybrid architectures—such as Transformer-Mamba networks and multi-scale attention models—to extract motor imagery intentions from noisy, non-stationary EEG signals. In the realm of visual psychophysics, they have recently been investigating how environmental context impacts object recognition, utilizing techniques like continuous flash suppression to probe how scene consistency modulates category-specific target identification under both conscious and unconscious viewing conditions. Additionally, their diverse portfolio includes work on explainable natural language processing, exploring how chain-of-thought prompting in large language models can provide transparent, step-by-step reasoning for multilingual sentiment analysis.

papers.title: FA-STTM: A hybrid Transformer-Mamba network for motor imagery EEG classification
papers.abstract: The authors present FA-STTM, a novel hybrid architecture that synthesizes the global dependency modeling of Transformers with the linear-time complexity of Mamba-based state-space models (SSMs) to optimize motor imagery (MI) electroencephalogram (EEG) decoding. The framework utilizes a Transformer encoder to capture broad spatiotemporal correlations across EEG channels and temporal segments, while a Mamba-based decoder effectively handles long-range sequence modeling with significantly reduced computational overhead compared to quadratic attention mechanisms. Validated on the BCI Competition IV-2a and IV-2b datasets, the model demonstrates robust classification performance against signal non-stationarity and inter-subject variability, outperforming established convolutional benchmarks in cross-subject generalization and inference efficiency.
papers.authors: Mingjie Gao, Caicai Gao, Zifeng Yao, Weina Zhu

papers.title: EMSA: Explainable multilingual sentiment analysis models providing sentiment analysis across multiple languages
papers.abstract: This study introduces the Explainable Multilingual Sentiment Analyzer (EMSA), a novel natural language processing framework designed to enhance the interpretability of cross-lingual sentiment classification. Leveraging large language models (LLMs) and chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting, EMSA bifurcates the sentiment analysis task into an explicit reasoning phase and a final categorization phase. The reasoning module generates intermediate linguistic and contextual justifications, providing transparent logic for the subsequent sentiment label (positive, negative, or neutral). Evaluation on the Chinese financial GubaSenti dataset and the English SST benchmark indicates that EMSA achieves superior performance over traditional transformer-based encoders like RoBERTa and XLNet, particularly in handling domain-specific nuances and linguistic diversity while increasing user trust through verifiable explainability.
papers.authors: Li Zhao, Jinwei Zhou, Jinde Cao, Weina Zhu

papers.title: MIFNet: a Mamba-based interactive frequency convolutional neural network for motor imagery decoding
papers.abstract: To address the challenges of low signal-to-noise ratio and complex spatiotemporal dynamics in EEG-based motor imagery (MI), the researchers developed MIFNet, an interactive frequency convolutional neural network incorporating a Mamba temporal module. The architecture utilizes a non-overlapping frequency decomposition strategy to isolate task-relevant mu (8–12 Hz) and beta (12–32 Hz) rhythms. A specialized ConvEncoder fuses spectral-spatial features from these decomposed bands, while a selective state-space model (SSM) based on the Mamba architecture captures long-range temporal dependencies with linear complexity. Experimental results across BCIC-IV-2A and High-Gamma datasets show that MIFNet significantly enhances decoding accuracy and robustness by bridging the gap between localized feature extraction and global temporal modeling.
papers.authors: Luoqian Yang, Weina Zhu

papers.title: The role of scene context in object recognition: Timing and mechanisms
papers.abstract: This psychophysical investigation explores how environmental consistency modulates the temporal dynamics and underlying mechanisms of visual object identification. Utilizing a dual-paradigm approach involving plain 2-alternative forced choice (2AFC) and binocular continuous flash suppression (CFS), the study examines the 'scene consistency effect' under conscious and unconscious viewing conditions. Results indicate that upright, congruent backgrounds facilitate target categorization primarily in the early stages of visual processing. The findings reveal a category-specific sensitivity, where furniture targets demonstrate a more pronounced reliance on contextual regularities for identification compared to animal stimuli, suggesting that high-level semantic schemas and global scene gist selectively modulate lower-level feature integration and breakthrough times from suppression.
papers.authors: Mingjie Gao, Jan Drewes, Weina Zhu

papers.title: TMSA-Net: A novel attention mechanism for improved motor imagery EEG signal processing
papers.abstract: The authors propose TMSA-Net, an end-to-end deep learning framework featuring a Temporal-Multi-Scale-Attention (TMSA) module specifically engineered for motor imagery (MI) EEG decoding. The architecture addresses the inherent non-stationarity and subject-specific variability of brain signals by adaptively assigning importance weights to specific channel-wise frequency bands and temporal windows. By integrating a multi-scale convolutional backbone with this selective attention mechanism, the model enhances the discriminability of latent neural patterns associated with motor intent. Comparative evaluations on the BCI Competition IV dataset 2a, 2b and the OpenBMI dataset demonstrate that TMSA-Net achieves statistically significant improvements in kappa values and mean classification accuracy relative to standard EEGNet and DeepConvNet architectures.
papers.authors: Qian Zhao, Weina Zhu

0692.name: Weiwei Zhang
0692.lab_name: Cognitive Neuroscience of Perception, Attention, & Memory (COMPAM) Lab
0692.bio: Weiwei Zhang is a Professor in the Department of Psychology at the University of California, Riverside, and directs the COMPAM Lab. Zhang’s research focuses on the functional and neural mechanisms of visual working memory, specifically the discrete capacity and mnemonic precision of visual representations. This work includes the fixed-resolution model of working memory, which posits that visual information is stored in a limited number of discrete slots. Their current research utilizes Bayesian cognitive modeling, psychophysics, EEG, and fMRI to explore how factors such as top-down attention, emotional states, and physical exertion modulate the quality and retention of visual information.
0692.research_direction: Dr. Zhang has recently been investigating the dynamic interactions between visual working memory, temporal attention, and executive control across both fundamental and applied contexts. Their recent work explores the continuous interplay between cognition and action, using mouse tracking to determine how working memory templates bias evolving perceptual decisions, and combining EEG and fMRI to assess how physical exertion impacts memory maintenance and distractor filtering. Additionally, they are employing transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) to probe the role of prefrontal alpha oscillations during the attentional blink, while also using mixture modeling to examine how pattern separation abilities relate to the representational precision of both short- and long-term memory. Finally, Dr. Zhang is extending their focus to the real-world cognitive consequences of digital behavior, investigating the complex links between short-form video consumption, problematic social media use, and executive function.

papers.title: Mental cost of simple(st) physical exertion
papers.abstract: This investigation delineates the action-cognition trade-off by examining the impact of concurrent isometric physical load, specifically handgrip exertion, on a visual working memory (WM) task. Using a combination of psychophysics, electroencephalography (EEG), and functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), the study adjudicates between the resource-sharing account—positing a unified pool for motor and cognitive resources—and the control-cost account, which suggests that physical effort prioritizes executive control over memory retention. While physical exertion reliably degraded behavioral WM accuracy, EEG data revealed that the contralateral delay activity (CDA), a neural correlate of WM maintenance, was not attenuated by motor load. Instead, elevated physical effort significantly enhanced CDA amplitude in the presence of distractors, suggesting a failure in top-down filtering that leads to the unintended retention of task-irrelevant information. fMRI results localized this action-cognition interaction within a frontoparietal executive network, including the bilateral inferior frontal and posterior parietal cortices, rather than motor or primary sensory regions.
papers.authors: Weizhen Xie, Yoojeong Choo, Weiwei Zhang

papers.title: The Roles of Alpha Oscillations in Attentional Blink
papers.abstract: The study explores the neurophysiological contributions of alpha-band oscillations (8–12 Hz) to the attentional blink (AB) phenomenon using transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS). By applying alpha-tACS over the right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (rDLPFC) and examining frontoparietal phase synchronization, the researchers tested the suppression hypothesis (selective modulation of inhibitory control at intermediate lags) against the diffuse attention hypothesis (broad enhancement of task performance). Findings across two experiments demonstrate that alpha-frequency neuromodulation increased T2 detection accuracy following T1 across all temporal lags in a lag-independent manner. These results support the diffuse attention hypothesis, indicating that alpha oscillations coordinate large-scale neural networks to foster a broad attentional state that minimizes overinvestment of resources into distractors and the primary target, thereby facilitating the processing of subsequent stimuli.
papers.authors: Sahereh Varastegan, Weiwei Zhang

papers.title: The Relationship Between TikTok Usage and Executive Function Is Mediated by Problematic Social Media Use
papers.abstract: This study analyzes the cognitive consequences of short-form video consumption by modeling the relationship between TikTok usage frequency, problematic social media use (PSMU), and executive function (EF) performance. While preliminary analysis indicated a significant correlation between TikTok usage and EF dysfunction, subsequent mediation analysis demonstrated that this effect is fully explained by PSMU and comorbid mental health symptoms, including depression and anxiety. When accounting for the variance associated with generalized problematic engagement patterns, TikTok usage metrics lost their predictive power regarding cognitive impairment. These findings suggest that the cognitive deficits often attributed to specific digital platforms are actually consequences of systemic problematic usage behaviors and associated affective disorders rather than platform-specific architectural features.
papers.authors: Jessica Golding, Anya Rallison, Kyra Zhang, Aisha Awan, Francisco Romero, Jillia Lacbain, Samuel Lee, Sahar Momand, Lilian Azer, Weiwei Zhang

papers.title: Working Memory Guides Perceptual Decisions Through Fast Capture and Slow Drift
papers.abstract: Leveraging high-resolution mouse tracking, this research dissociates the temporal dynamics through which working memory (WM) templates modulate perceptual decision-making. Continuous cursor trajectories provided a granular readout of the competitive influence exerted by WM content on sensory processing, revealing two distinct mechanisms operating on different timescales. Initially, a fast, transient attentional capture component was observed, characterized by an early trajectory curvature toward the WM-matching stimulus. This was followed by a slower, sustained drift in the accumulation of decision evidence, which systematically biased the final perceptual report toward the remembered feature (the 'tinted lens' effect). This dissociation indicates that WM-driven top-down modulation is not a unitary process but consists of temporally separable components that integrate mnemonic priors into evolving perceptual judgments.
papers.authors: Hyung-Bum Park, Weiwei Zhang

papers.title: Discrimination of Mnemonic Similarity is Associated with Short-term and Long-term Memory Precision
papers.abstract: This research investigates whether the computational mechanism of pattern separation, typically operationalized as lure discrimination in the Mnemonic Similarity Task (MST), accounts for individual differences in the precision of both short-term (STM) and long-term memory (LTM). By applying a mixture modeling framework to responses in continuous-estimation tasks, the study decomposed memory performance into recall probability and mnemonic precision (the inverse of circular variability). Path analysis of data from 132 participants revealed that behavioral markers of pattern separation significantly correlate with the resolution of representations in both STM and LTM, regardless of the likelihood of successful retrieval. These findings challenge strength-based unitary memory models and suggest that a common neural mechanism, potentially mediated by hippocampal circuits, governs the fidelity of mental representations across multiple memory timescales.
papers.authors: Weizhen Xie, Tianye Ma, Sanikaa P. Thakurdesai, Inik Kim, Weiwei Zhang

0693.name: Weizhen Xie
0693.bio: Weizhen Xie is an Assistant Professor at the University of Maryland and a researcher affiliated with the National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (NINDS) at the NIH. Xie directs the Integrated Cognitive Neuroscience (ICON) Lab, where their research investigates the neural mechanisms underlying human visual memory and cognitive control across different timescales. Their work utilizes techniques including intracranial EEG, fMRI, and behavioral modeling to explore the role of the medial temporal lobe in memory precision and consolidation. Additionally, Xie examines how cognitive representations are modulated by physiological and psychological factors such as sleep, emotion, and physical exertion.
0693.research_direction: Dr. Xie's recent work explores the cognitive and neural mechanisms underlying the formation, maintenance, and fidelity of visual working memory (VWM). They have recently been investigating how environmental structure and prior knowledge—such as perceptual grouping regularities, semantic associations between real-world objects, and intrinsic image memorability—facilitate the efficient encoding of visual information. Using approaches ranging from EEG and representational similarity analysis to masking paradigms, their research examines whether these features optimize memory by increasing neural differentiation among items to reduce interference or by enhancing the speed of early perceptual encoding. Additionally, Dr. Xie is investigating the causal neural architecture of memory resolution, utilizing voxel-based lesion-symptom mapping in neuropsychological patients to determine the specific role of the medial temporal lobe and hippocampus in supporting high-precision VWM representations.

papers.title: Neural Differentiation Underlying Perceptual Grouping Benefits in Visual Working Memory
papers.abstract: This research employs electroencephalography (EEG) and representational similarity analysis (RSA) to investigate the neural mechanisms through which perceptual grouping regularities (e.g., proximity and similarity) enhance the efficiency of visual working memory (VWM). By comparing neural activity during the retention of grouped versus ungrouped stimuli, the study tests whether grouping leads to a compression of representations or an increase in neural differentiation between items. Findings demonstrate that grouped items elicit more distinct neural patterns within the VWM buffer, suggesting that perceptual organization facilitates the individuation and separation of mnemonic representations. This increased neural differentiation significantly correlates with behavioral recall precision, supporting a model where the brain leverages environmental structure to mitigate inter-item interference and optimize representational fidelity during maintenance.
papers.authors: Qianru Xu, Chaoxiong Ye, Weizhen Xie

papers.title: Medial temporal lobe lesions reduce visual working memory precision
papers.abstract: In this neuropsychological study involving 40 patients undergoing surgical resection for drug-resistant epilepsy, the authors investigate the causal necessity of the medial temporal lobe (MTL), specifically the hippocampus, for high-fidelity visual working memory (VWM). Utilizing voxel-based lesion-symptom mapping (VLSM) and behavioral modeling of recall responses, the researchers dissociated memory quality (precision) from memory quantity (recall success). Results revealed that hippocampal damage selectively increased recall variability, indicating a significant reduction in VWM precision, even after controlling for total brain lesion volume. Conversely, overall lesion volume predicted a decrease in the probability of recall success. These data indicate that the MTL is critical for preserving the fidelity of VWM representations through pattern separation mechanisms, challenging unitary models that treat memory quantity and quality as interchangeable facets of a single strength parameter.
papers.authors: Yoojeong Choo, Sanikaa P. Thakurdesai, Asbah Qadri, Oceane E. Fruchet, Samantha N. Jackson, Radhika Chatterjee, Sara K. Inati, Kareem A. Zaghloul, Weizhen Xie

papers.title: Semantic Associations Facilitate Visual Working Memory Formation for Real-World Objects
papers.abstract: This study examines how prior conceptual knowledge interacts with perceptual constraints to support the formation of visual working memory (VWM) for naturalistic stimuli. Across multiple experiments, semantic associations between objects in a visual display were quantified using natural language processing (NLP) models (e.g., GloVe word embeddings), while image similarity was controlled using features from convolutional neural networks (e.g., VGG-16). The results indicate that high semantic relatedness among to-be-remembered items significantly facilitates encoding and retrieval under brief presentation conditions. This benefit suggests that observers utilize pre-existing semantic scaffolds to group information effectively, thereby overcoming the processing bottlenecks associated with complex real-world objects. The findings emphasize the fundamental role of long-term semantic associations in optimizing the short-term maintenance of visual information.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
papers.authors: Xinchi Yu, Sanikaa P. Thakurdesai, Weizhen Xie

papers.title: Perceptual encoding benefit of visual memorability on visual memory formation
papers.abstract: The authors investigated the temporal dynamics of visual memorability—a stimulus-driven attribute reflecting consistent memory performance across individuals—in the development of visual short-term memory (VSTM). By manipulating stimulus presentation durations (100–500 ms) and applying post-perceptual masking, the study tested whether memorability effects emerge during early perceptual encoding or subsequent consolidation. Behavioral results showed that high-memorability face images were more likely to be successfully encoded into VSTM within 100–200 ms of stimulus onset. This early encoding advantage was resistant to masking and predicted long-term recognition performance 24 hours later. Electrophysiological markers (contralateral delay activity, CDA) corroborated that image memorability enhances the efficiency of transforming perceptual inputs into durable mnemonic representations during the initial encoding phase, rather than simply increasing maintenance capacity.
papers.authors: Chaoxiong Ye, Lijing Guo, Nathan Wang, Qiang Liu, Weizhen Xie

0694.name: William G. Hayward
0694.bio: William G. Hayward serves as Chair Professor of Psychology and Dean of Social Sciences at Lingnan University, focusing on cognitive psychology and neuroscience. Hayward’s research examines how the brain processes visual information for object and face recognition, alongside the mechanisms of visual attention. By utilizing behavioral techniques, eye-tracking, EEG/ERP, and fMRI, Hayward investigates individual differences in facial scanning and the cross-cultural factors that impact visual expertise. Their current work explores the development of face familiarity and the stability of perceptual scanning patterns over time.
0694.research_direction: Dr. Hayward has recently been investigating the perceptual and cognitive mechanisms underlying face perception, focusing heavily on holistic processing and social trait judgments. Their recent work explores the structural components of holistic face perception, utilizing the composite face paradigm to evaluate whether facilitation and interference operate as distinct mechanisms under varying spatial attention and expectation conditions. Additionally, they are examining how individual differences in idiosyncratic eye-movement strategies, modeled via Hidden Markov Models, interact with and modulate these traditional behavioral metrics of holistic processing. Broadening their focus to complex social judgments, Dr. Hayward is also investigating how transient facial cues, such as emotional expressions, interact with baseline facial ambiguity and observer expertise—including participant age and cross-race effects—to influence facial age estimation.

papers.title: The effect of emotional expression on age estimates is modulated by face age and participant age
papers.abstract: The present study investigated the influence of happy and angry facial expressions on age estimation accuracy, with a specific focus on the modulating roles of face age, observer age, and face race. In a series of experiments using Asian participants, findings demonstrated that young faces were perceived as significantly older when displaying happy or angry expressions compared to neutral expressions. This aging effect of emotional expression was intensified in older observers and was more pronounced for other-race (White) faces relative to own-race (Asian) faces. Conversely, for older facial stimuli, smiling did not significantly alter age estimates across any participant group. The results suggest that transient cues such as expression-related wrinkles are weighted more heavily in age judgments when baseline facial information is ambiguous or when observers have less expertise, as in the case of older or other-race faces.
papers.authors: Luyan Ji, Senrong Liao, William G. Hayward

papers.title: Facilitation and interference are asymmetric in holistic face processing
papers.abstract: Holistic processing is a defining characteristic of face perception, yet common metrics like the part–whole and composite face tasks often lack convergent validity. This research re-evaluates these paradigms by distinguishing between two components of holistic interdependence: facilitation (performance gains from congruent context) and interference (performance costs from incongruent context). Utilizing the complete composite face task, the study demonstrates that facilitation and interference are asymmetrically modulated by target location and cueing probabilities. Specifically, the processing of target facial halves is differentially impacted by task-irrelevant regions depending on spatial attention and expectations. These findings suggest that facilitation and interference represent distinct mechanisms rather than a unitary holistic process, offering a potential explanation for the inconsistent correlations observed between different traditional face-perception tasks.
papers.authors: Haiyang Jin, Luyan Ji, Olivia S. Cheung, William G. Hayward

papers.title: Association of idiosyncratic eye-movement patterns with holistic processing of faces as measured by the composite face effect and the face inversion effect
papers.abstract: This study examined the relationship between individual differences in gaze strategies and the magnitude of holistic face processing. Using Hidden Markov Models (HMM) to analyze eye-tracking data, participants were categorized into two distinct clusters: an upper-focused group (prioritizing the eye region) and a lower-focused group (targeting the face center). Behavioral results revealed that while both groups exhibited standard face inversion effects, their performance in the composite face task differed significantly based on scanning preference. The upper-focused group displayed a larger composite effect when matching upper facial halves compared to lower halves, whereas the lower-focused group showed similar effect sizes across both regions. These results indicate that idiosyncratic visual attention strategies directly modulate the measurement of holistic processing, suggesting that traditional holistic metrics are sensitive to an observer's preferred fixation patterns.
papers.authors: Nianzeng Zhong, Janet H. Hsiao, Guomei Zhou, William G. Hayward

0695.name: William H. Warren
0695.department: Department of Cognitive, Linguistic and Psychological Sciences
0695.bio: William H. Warren is the Chancellor’s Professor of Cognitive, Linguistic, and Psychological Sciences at Brown University and the director of the Virtual Environment Navigation Lab (VENLab). Warren’s research utilizes immersive virtual reality to investigate how visual information, such as optic flow and affordances, regulates human locomotion, spatial navigation, and collective crowd dynamics. By applying a dynamical systems framework, Warren models the emergence of complex social behaviors such as flocking and pedestrian interactions from local visual-motor rules. Recipient of the 2023 Ken Nakayama Medal in Vision Science, Warren integrates experimental psychology and computational modeling to study the ecological coupling between an organism and its environment.
0695.research_direction: Dr. Warren has recently been investigating the visual and cognitive mechanisms that govern human spatial navigation and self-organized collective behavior. A major focus of their recent work involves using high-fidelity pedestrian trajectories and information-theoretic modeling to reconstruct dynamic "visual influence networks" in walking crowds, exploring how visual occlusion, spatial positioning, and designated leaders drive emergent group coordination. Additionally, they are probing fundamental questions about spatial representation by testing human navigators in immersive, non-Euclidean virtual reality mazes to determine whether spatial knowledge is structured as a globally consistent metric map or a local place-to-place graph. Finally, their research applies these basic mechanisms to emergency egress scenarios, utilizing virtual reality and machine learning to model how individuals weigh competing environmental signage and social cues under strict time pressure.

papers.title: Navigators learn a local graph, not a global map
papers.abstract: This research assesses competing theoretical frameworks for human spatial representation, specifically contrasting the metric embedding of spatial information in a Euclidean mental map with local place-to-place metrics in a labeled graph. Utilizing an immersive virtual maze, two groups of participants learned a multi-corridor environment: one group navigated a metric-consistent Euclidean maze, while the other navigated an 'impossible' non-Euclidean maze containing globally inconsistent metrics (covert teleports). Pointing estimates in the non-Euclidean group were systematically biased by the clockwise or counterclockwise test sequence, violating the metric postulates of symmetry and additivity. These findings demonstrate that human knowledge of navigable space is stored as a labeled graph that preserves local metric properties rather than a globally consistent Euclidean coordinate system.
papers.authors: Marianne Strickrodt, Tobias Meilinger, Heinrich H Bülthoff, William H. Warren

papers.title: Visual Influence Networks in Walking Crowds
papers.abstract: The authors present a quantitative framework for reconstructing the dynamic visual influence networks that mediate collective behavior in human crowds. By applying information-theoretic measures and causal inference to high-fidelity pedestrian trajectory data, the study quantifies the directional influence and information transfer between individuals. The resulting networks reveal that the 'coupling strength' between neighbors is a sparse, directed function of distance and visual occlusion, rather than a fixed metric radius. This work identifies influential spatial positions within groups and demonstrates how the topology of visual networks facilitates emergent consensus and coordinated motion without a central plan or designated leader.
papers.authors: Kei Yoshida, Mario di Bernardo, William H. Warren

papers.title: Modeling competing guidance on evacuation choices under time pressure using virtual reality and machine learning
papers.abstract: This study investigates the decision-making process during emergency evacuations when participants are faced with competing sources of information, such as social cues (neighbor behavior) and environmental signage. Using a virtual reality (VR) paradigm to simulate high-stress evacuation scenarios, the researchers employed machine learning techniques, including Random Forest models, to quantify the relative weights of these information sources. The findings indicate that evacuation choices are governed by a 'social-affordance' trade-off, where high levels of time pressure and cognitive load shift individual decision strategies away from explicit architectural guidance toward social-heuristic cues (following others).
papers.authors: Yuxin Zhang, Max Kinateder, Xinyan Huang, William H. Warren

papers.title: AI-Powered Safe Egress Time Assessment for Complex Building Environments
papers.abstract: This paper develops an AI-driven framework for the estimation of Safe Egress Time (SET) in complex architectural infrastructures. By integrating empirical behavioral parameters derived from virtual reality experiments into machine learning-based pedestrian dynamics simulations, the authors provide more accurate predictions of evacuation efficiency than traditional hydraulic or agent-based models. The assessment framework specifically accounts for the effects of crowd density, visual occlusion, and architectural complexity on human locomotion and decision-making kinetics, offering a robust tool for evaluating fire safety and egress reliability in large-scale environments.
papers.authors: Yuxin Zhang, Max Kinateder, Anne Templeton, William H. Warren

papers.title: Simulating and quantifying the influence of covert and explicit leaders on human crowd motion
papers.abstract: This study explores how directional information propagates through a human swarm via 'covert' (unidentified) versus 'explicit' (visually identified) leaders. The researchers utilize the Self-organized Collective Motion (SCruM) behavioral model to simulate experimental trajectory data, treating leader motion as the input variable. Through the reconstruction of visual influence networks, the paper quantifies how explicit leaders alter network topology and increase the intensity of local interactions. The results demonstrate that leader influence depends on their spatial position relative to the visual field and the degree of visibility within the crowd network, clarifying the mechanisms of self-organized collective motion.
papers.venue: 12th International Conference on Pedestrian and Evacuation Dynamics (PED 2025)
papers.authors: Kei Yoshida, Sina Feldmann, William H. Warren

0696.name: William S. Tuten
0696.department: Herbert Wertheim School of Optometry and Vision Science
0696.bio: Tuten is an Assistant Professor who researches cellular-level mechanisms of human vision through optical engineering and psychophysical methods. They utilize adaptive optics scanning laser ophthalmoscopy (AOSLO) to correct for ocular aberrations, enabling the stimulation of individual photoreceptors in living subjects. Their research examines the relationship between retinal structure and function in healthy eyes and those with degenerative diseases. Tuten investigates how spatial and color perception are shaped by photoreceptor topography and post-receptoral circuitry.
0696.research_direction: Dr. Tuten’s recent work explores the precise relationship between the cellular topography of the retina and visual perception, heavily leveraging adaptive optics scanning laser ophthalmoscopy (AOSLO) to target individual photoreceptors. They have recently been investigating how local variations in the L/M cone mosaic and the spatio-temporal properties of brief stimuli influence both achromatic spatial detection and color appearance phenomena, such as shifts in the spectral locus of unique yellow. Their research also examines structural and functional plasticity in atypical retinal development, assessing how the abnormally high photoreceptor densities seen in conditions like Enhanced S-cone Syndrome affect spatial resolution. Additionally, they are probing the underlying physiological consequences of scanning-based microstimulation itself, working to characterize how the periodic raster-scanning delivery of AOSLO displays might asymmetrically recruit downstream ON and OFF retinal ganglion cell pathways.

papers.title: Local variations in L/M ratio influence the detection and color naming of small spots
papers.abstract: The relative distribution of long-wavelength-sensitive (L) and middle-wavelength-sensitive (M) cones varies significantly among individuals and determines how spectral information is sampled. This study utilized adaptive optics scanning laser ophthalmoscopy (AOSLO) to deliver small, brief narrowband increment stimuli (543 nm or 680 nm) to specific, spectrally classified cone locations in the human parafovea. We observed that sensitivity to 680-nm light, when normalized by 543-nm sensitivity, increased in direct correlation with the local proportion of L cones at the stimulated site. Detection performance was well-modeled by a simple achromatic summation (L+M) mechanism and by photoreceptor-level ideal observer analysis, indicating that small-spot detection primarily leverages non-opponent signals. Chromatic responses (categorizing flashes as 'red' or 'green') were less frequent than achromatic ones, though their probability increased with stimulus intensity and when the local L/M ratio approached unity. The proximity of short-wavelength-sensitive (S) cones did not significantly impact color naming for these stimuli.
papers.authors: Maxwell J. Greene, Vimal P. Pandiyan, Ramkumar Sabesan, William S. Tuten

papers.title: Asymmetric activation of retinal ON and OFF pathways by AOSLO raster-scanned visual stimuli
papers.abstract: Adaptive optics scanning light ophthalmoscopy (AOSLO) is a powerful tool for high-resolution retinal imaging and stimulus delivery, yet its periodic raster-scanning delivery mode—where each pixel is illuminated for only tens of nanoseconds every 33–40 ms—differs fundamentally from natural viewing. Using in vivo calcium imaging in non-human primates, we investigated the physiological consequences of this intermittent stimulation on retinal ganglion cell (RGC) pathways. Our results demonstrate that raster-scanning introduces a significant bias, exaggerating asymmetries between the ON and OFF pathways. At high light levels, this delivery method results in elevated baseline activity in ON-center RGCs and increased rectification in OFF-center RGCs. These findings suggest that the temporal characteristics of the AOSLO display can selectively recruit specific retinal circuits, a factor that must be accounted for when interpreting psychophysical and physiological data obtained via scanning-based microstimulation.
papers.authors: Sara S. Patterson, Maxwell J. Greene, Alexandra E. Boehm, John E. Vanston, William S. Tuten

papers.title: Enhanced S-cone Syndrome, a Mini-review
papers.abstract: This mini-review synthesizes recent structural and functional findings in Enhanced S-cone Syndrome (ESCS), a rare autosomal recessive retinal dystrophy caused by variants in the NR2E3 gene. The condition is characterized by the misdirection of rod precursors during retinal development, leading to an absence of rods and a dramatic increase in S-cone numbers. We review high-resolution imaging data acquired via adaptive optics scanning laser ophthalmoscopy (AOSLO) and optical coherence tomography (OCT) which reveal supernormal parafoveal cone densities. Crucially, we highlight findings that these elevated cone counts confer supernormal visual acuity within the S-cone pathway, suggesting that the human visual system can adapt to utilize abnormally high densities of a single photoreceptor type to achieve superior spatial resolution. The review also discusses clinical management and the implications of these findings for understanding retinal development and plasticity.
papers.authors: Yiyi Wang, Jessica Wong, Jacque L. Duncan, Austin Roorda, William S. Tuten

papers.title: Unique yellow shifts for small and brief stimuli in the central retina
papers.abstract: We investigated the spectral locus of unique yellow—the wavelength perceived as neither reddish nor greenish—for diffraction-limited flashes of varying size (<11 arcmin) and duration (<500 ms). Stimuli were delivered to the fovea and parafovea using an AOSLO to correct for ocular aberrations and monitor retinal stimulus position with cellular precision. We found that the wavelength of unique yellow shifted significantly toward longer wavelengths as stimulus size or duration decreased. In subjects with spectrally classified cone mosaics, we further examined the relationship between local L/M cone topography and these color shifts. The results showed that variations in unique yellow were not entirely predictable from the local L/M cone ratio alone, indicating that the transformation from photoreceptor activations to color appearance involves significant post-receptoral neural processing that is sensitive to the spatio-temporal properties of the stimulus.
papers.authors: Maxwell J. Greene, Alexandra E. Boehm, John E. Vanston, Vimal P. Pandiyan, Ramkumar Sabesan, William S. Tuten

0697.name: Wilma A Bainbridge
0697.bio: Wilma A. Bainbridge is an Associate Professor of Psychology at the University of Chicago and the director of the Brain Bridge Lab. Bainbridge's research investigates the relationship between perception and memory, specifically focusing on 'memorability' as an intrinsic stimulus attribute that influences memory performance across individuals. They utilize methodologies including functional MRI, computer vision, and deep learning models to predict memory retention and identify the neural signatures of visual representations. Their work also explores cognitive phenomena such as the Mandela Effect and the impact of aphantasia on mental imagery and recall.
0697.research_direction: Dr. Bainbridge’s recent work explores the intrinsic stimulus properties that drive memory, investigating how deep neural network models of image memorability can predict diverse phenomena ranging from early childhood memory development to social media virality. They have recently been expanding this construct beyond the visual domain, utilizing large-scale behavioral experiments to evaluate whether the memorability of human voices serves as a similarly consistent, quantifiable acoustic attribute across listeners. In addition to stimulus-driven encoding, their research examines the fidelity of internal visual representations, using drawing-from-memory paradigms to probe how detailed object memory and structural spatial memory differentially degrade over time. Furthermore, they are investigating the underlying neural mechanisms of mental imagery limits like aphantasia, using fMRI to map how functional connectivity between frontoparietal and visual processing networks shapes visual memory retrieval.

papers.title: Image Memorability Predicts Social Media Virality and Externally-Associated Commenting
papers.abstract: The authors examine whether image memorability, an intrinsic stimulus property quantified by the ResMem deep neural network, predicts viral engagement on Reddit. Analyzing a large-scale naturalistic dataset across three distinct timepoints, they demonstrate that higher memorability scores significantly correlate with increased comment counts and upvotes, even when controlling for high-level image categories using a ResNet-152 backbone. Natural language processing (NLP) of user discourse reveals that memorable images preferentially elicit abstract, neutral-affect, and externally-associated comments, suggesting that memorability fosters a unique cognitive pathway to virality distinct from emotional arousal. Analysis of ResMem's internal representations further indicates that semantic distinctiveness is a critical latent variable common to both memorability and social media engagement.
papers.authors: Shikang Peng, Wilma A. Bainbridge

papers.title: The memorability of voices is predictable and consistent across listeners
papers.abstract: This study establishes auditory memorability as a stimulus-driven attribute that is consistent across listeners, extending the memorability construct from the visual to the auditory domain. Using recognition memory data from over 3,000 participants listening to diverse speakers, the researchers found that specific voice clips and individual speakers are reliably remembered or forgotten across a population. Regression models incorporating low-level acoustic features (e.g., fundamental frequency) and high-level traits (e.g., dialect) significantly predicted memorability scores in out-of-sample cross-validations. These effects remained robust after accounting for subjective listener evaluations of voice attractiveness and distinctiveness, indicating that vocal memorability reflects an inherent, quantifiable property of human speech sounds.
papers.authors: Cambria Revsine, Esther Goldberg, Wilma A. Bainbridge

papers.title: The neural underpinnings of aphantasia: a case study of identical twins
papers.abstract: The researchers conducted a unique functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) case study of monozygotic twins—one exhibiting aphantasia and the other possessing typical mental imagery—to identify objective neural markers of the condition. While performing mental imagery and memory retrieval tasks, the aphantasic twin displayed significantly reduced visual information in memory representations compared to their sibling. This deficit was linked to lower functional connectivity between frontoparietal control networks and occipitotemporal visual processing regions. Despite these differences, imagery-like neural activity was still detectable at lower levels in the aphantasic twin, suggesting that aphantasia represents a quantitative spectrum of imagery capacity rather than a discrete, absolute absence of visual representation.
papers.authors: Emma Megla, Deepasri Prasad, Wilma A. Bainbridge

papers.title: Drawings reveal changes in object memory, but not spatial memory, across time
papers.abstract: Using a drawing-from-memory paradigm combined with crowdsourced scoring of hundreds of sketches, this study quantifies the degradation of visual memory across varying encoding durations and retention intervals. The findings reveal a functional dissociation between object and spatial memory systems: while object-specific features—such as the proportion of items recalled and their fine-grained details—are highly sensitive to the passage of time and encoding constraints, spatial memory for the relative configuration and placement of objects remains remarkably stable and accurate. The researchers demonstrate that object recall can be predicted by factors such as saliency, location, and semantic meaning, whereas the spatial scaffold of a scene is preserved, supporting theories of independent visual pathways for object identity and spatial context in long-term memory.
papers.authors: Emma Megla, Samuel R. Rosenthal, Wilma A. Bainbridge

papers.title: Children develop adult-like visual sensitivity to image memorability by the age of four
papers.abstract: This developmental study investigates the onset of adult-like sensitivity to image memorability in children aged 3 to 6 years. Utilizing a continuous recognition task and comparing behavioral performance against the ResMem neural network's predictions, the authors find that children's memory consistency for scene images significantly aligns with adult-like patterns by age four. This correlation is particularly pronounced following a long-term (1-week) delay, where ResMem scores served as the most effective predictor of child memory across the age range. The results suggest that the cognitive and perceptual mechanisms that prioritize certain visual information for memory encoding are intrinsically established early in childhood development and do not require extensive lifespan experience or learned semantic associations.
papers.authors: Xinyu Guo, Wilma A. Bainbridge

0698.name: Wilson Geisler
0698.bio: Wilson Geisler is a vision scientist specializing in the application of ideal observer theory and natural scene statistics to model human visual perception and behavior. Geisler’s research characterizes the limits of visual performance by combining psychophysical experiments with neurophysiological recordings from the primate visual cortex and computational modeling. Their work includes the study of statistical properties of natural images, eye movement strategies during visual search, and the development of normalization models for cortical neuron responses. Geisler currently holds the David Wechsler Regents Chair in Psychology at the University of Texas at Austin and is a member of the National Academy of Sciences.
0698.research_direction: Dr. Geisler has recently been investigating the computational mechanisms underlying perceptual grouping and texture segmentation in complex natural scenes. Their recent work explores how the early visual system might utilize natural scene statistics, Gestalt principles, and spatial proximity as a self-supervised training signal to parse arbitrary textures without explicit supervision. In parallel, they are examining visual search and target detection under high levels of extrinsic uncertainty, probing how human vision copes with unknown target amplitudes, spatial scales, orientations, and background contrasts. Across these domains, Dr. Geisler combines human psychophysical experiments with computational modeling to test how well biologically plausible mechanisms—such as divisive contrast normalization and heuristic decision rules—approximate the performance of Bayes-optimal ideal observers in noisy, naturalistic environments.

papers.title: Proximity as a Ground-Truth Proxy for Training Texture Discrimination and Segmentation
papers.abstract: Perceptual grouping and scene segmentation rely critically on early visual mechanisms that determine whether local image patches belong to the same or distinct texture categories without explicit supervision. This study demonstrates that spatial proximity serves as an effective self-supervised proxy for ground-truth same-different labels directly within arbitrary natural images. Under broad ecological constraints, spatial proximity discrimination (near vs. far) and texture discrimination (same vs. different) share mathematically equivalent decision boundaries when evaluated across identical feature spaces. This proximity proxy enables the unsupervised learning of optimal decision variables and bounds directly from natural image statistics, which can be further refined dynamically to the image statistics of individual scenes. Incorporating these proximity-derived decision bounds as the front-end to a hierarchical Bayesian observer (HBO) model successfully segments complex natural scenes composed of arbitrary textures without requiring external teacher signals or manual annotations.
papers.authors: Wilson S. Geisler

papers.title: Principles of Local and Global Grouping that Underlie Segmentation of Natural Texture Images
papers.abstract: Human visual segmentation exploits low-level grouping mechanisms that operate independently of high-level category recognition to initiate visual parsing and facilitate learning novel materials. A biologically plausible Hierarchical Bayesian Observer (HBO) model for texture segmentation is formulated based on natural scene statistics and Gestalt perceptual organization principles. The model incorporates five sequential stages: local similarity grouping with divisive contrast normalization, mutual similarity grouping (amplifying local similarity if neighboring patches correlate with an identical set of surrounding patches), transitive grouping (good continuation), confidence grouping (propagating clear evidence from patches far from decision boundaries to resolve ambiguous boundary regions), and global region grouping. The local similarity stage, trained for optimal accuracy via Bayesian decision processes, quantitatively matches human texture discrimination across retinal eccentricities. Across synthetic and natural textures with complex geometric layouts, the full HBO framework achieves robust segmentation under variations in surface tilt, depth slant, and non-uniform illumination.
papers.authors: Wilson S. Geisler, Abhranil Das

papers.title: Optimal visual search with highly heuristic decision rules
papers.abstract: In covert visual search, normative Bayesian decision rules integrate prior spatial distributions with local target detectability ($d'$) across candidate locations through non-linear log-likelihood pooling. Psychophysical measurements of covert search and cued detection for wavelet targets in Gaussian noise revealed that human accuracy marginally exceeded the theoretical predictions of an independent-noise Bayes-optimal decision rule, despite human foveal neglect (sensitivity attenuation at central fixation). Computational simulations reconcile this apparent paradox through three mechanisms: first, fixed, computationally parsimonious heuristic decision rules (such as max-type operations over unweighted or coarsely weighted responses) attain efficiency near that of the optimal Bayesian rule; second, foveal neglect selectively dampens performance only at the exact central coordinate; and third, positive spatial correlations among sensory noise pools reduce decision variable variance, elevating search performance above predictions derived from statistically independent sensory responses.
papers.authors: Anqi Zhang, Wilson S. Geisler

papers.title: Target identification under high levels of amplitude, size, orientation and background uncertainty
papers.abstract: Visual target detection in natural environments routinely contends with multiple simultaneous dimensions of extrinsic stimulus uncertainty. This work derives the Bayes-optimal decision rule and provides an efficient simulation method for categorization tasks spanning five concurrent dimensions of uncertainty: target amplitude, 2D orientation, spatial scale, background contrast, and spatial pattern. Human psychophysical performance was measured for detecting additive wavelet targets in white noise across wide parametric variations in target scale and orientation. Comparing human hit and correct-rejection rates against the ideal observer and biologically plausible model observers reveals that an energy- and scale-normalized maximum-response observer (SNN-MAX) closely approximates optimal Bayesian classification. These findings show that contrast- and energy-normalization mechanisms enable the early visual system to achieve near-optimal target identification across large parameter manifolds of extrinsic stimulus variation.
papers.authors: Can Oluk, Wilson S. Geisler

papers.title: Effects of target-amplitude and background-contrast uncertainty predicted by a normalized template-matching observer
papers.abstract: Under natural viewing conditions, visual target detection is challenged by concurrent variations in target amplitude and local background contrast. Human psychophysical detection was measured for sine-wave targets in white noise and natural scene backgrounds across wide parametric sweeps of contrast and amplitude under varying target prior probabilities (0.2 and 0.5). While standard template-matching (TM) observers collapse toward chance performance when target priors are low under high extrinsic uncertainty, model observers utilizing divisive contrast normalization (normalized template-matching, NTM) or dynamic criterion adjustment (DTM) preserve near-optimal discrimination.
