Comparison with empirical hit and correct-rejection rates indicates that human performance is significantly better predicted by the NTM observer than by the classical TM observer across noise and natural background conditions. This suggests that static local contrast normalization, rather than trial-by-trial cognitive criterion updating, provides the primary computational mechanism for mitigating simultaneous background contrast and target amplitude uncertainty.
papers.authors: Can Oluk, Wilson S. Geisler

0699.name: Winrich Freiwald
0699.bio: Winrich Freiwald is a neuroscientist who investigates the neural circuitry underlying face recognition, social cognition, and attention. By integrating functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) with single-cell electrophysiology, Freiwald co-discovered the primate 'face patch' system, a network of brain regions dedicated to processing facial identity and expression. Their work characterizes how these regions transform sensory inputs into invariant object representations and how they interface with circuits for memory and emotional processing. Currently, their research explores the computational principles of the visual system and the mechanisms by which the brain exerts attentional control over social and non-social stimuli.
0699.research_direction: Dr. Freiwald's recent work explores the neural mechanisms underlying primate facial communication, using high-density single-neuron and large-scale recordings to investigate how sensorimotor cortices coordinate voluntary and emotional facial gestures through temporal coding hierarchies and inter-areal synchrony. In human studies, they have recently been utilizing precision and multi-echo fMRI to probe high-level social cognition, specifically mapping how the temporal pole links face perception to personal identity and examining how the default mode network subdivides into parallel architectures for processing social versus spatial information. Additionally, their research investigates the neural substrates of symbolic computation, recording from the primate frontal cortex during complex drawing tasks to explore how the brain represents and recombines motor action primitives as discrete symbols.

papers.title: Facial gestures are enacted via a cortical hierarchy of dynamic and stable codes
papers.abstract: This study challenges the long-standing neuropsychological model of functional segregation between medial (emotional) and lateral (voluntary) facial control systems in the primate brain. Utilizing high-density single-neuron recordings across primary motor, premotor, and cingulate face-motor areas, the researchers demonstrate that both lateral and medial regions encode both voluntary and emotional gestures. The functional organization of this system is characterized by a temporal hierarchy: posterior regions utilize dynamic, transient codes to represent fine-grained facial kinematics, whereas anterior regions exhibit more temporally stable and persistent neural representations. This finding suggests that a distributed, parallel-projecting cortical network coordinates socially meaningful facial communication through a continuum of temporal coding stability rather than distinct functional pathways.
papers.authors: Geena R. Ianni, Yuriria Vázquez, Adam G. Rouse, Marc H. Schieber, Yifat Prut, Winrich A. Freiwald

papers.title: Neural synchrony links sensorimotor cortices in a network for facial motor control
papers.abstract: The production of complex facial gestures requires the precise coordination of multiple distributed cortical regions. This research employs simultaneous large-scale neuronal recordings to identify the role of inter-areal neural synchrony in facilitating communication across the facial motor network. The findings indicate that synchronized oscillatory activity across primary motor, premotor, and somatosensory nodes serves as a critical mechanism for integrating descending motor commands with real-time sensory feedback. This synchronization effectively links separate cortical modules into a unified functional network, enabling the high-fidelity generation of communicative facial gestures essential for primate social interaction.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS)
papers.authors: Yuriria Vázquez, Geena R. Ianni, Elie Rassi, Adam G. Rouse, Marc H. Schieber, Fatemeh Yazdani, Yifat Prut, Winrich A. Freiwald

papers.title: Parallel systems for social and spatial cognition reaching the cortical apex
papers.abstract: Using precision fMRI to map individual human brains, this study investigates the functional subdivision of the default mode network (DMN) across social and spatial cognitive domains. Participants performed visual perception, semantic judgment, and episodic simulation tasks involving familiar individuals and locations. The results reveal that high-level association cortex is organized into two distinct, parallel systems: one specialized for processing social content (people) and the other for spatial content (places). These systems exhibit a consistent, parallel anatomical arrangement across the frontal, parietal, and temporal lobes, suggesting that the DMN facilitates domain-specific relational modeling through duplicated neural architectures.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS)
papers.authors: Ben Deen, Winrich A. Freiwald

papers.title: Neural representation of action symbols in primate frontal cortex
papers.abstract: This work identifies a localized neural substrate for the symbolic representation of motor behavior in the primate brain. Utilizing a novel drawing task designed to test compositional generalization, the researchers recorded from multiple regions including the motor, premotor, and prefrontal cortices. They identified a specific neural population in the ventral premotor cortex (PMv) that represents action primitives as discrete 'symbols.' These neural representations exhibit the critical properties of symbolic computation: motor invariance across low-level parameters, discrete categorical structure, and systematic recombination into novel sequences. This provides empirical evidence for a neural implementation of the symbolic grammars hypothesized to underlie complex cognitive operations.
papers.authors: Lucas Y. Tian, Kedar U. Garzón, Adam G. Rouse, Mark A. G. Eldridge, Marc H. Schieber, Xiao-Jing Wang, Joshua B. Tenenbaum, Winrich A. Freiwald

papers.title: A familiar face and person processing area in the human temporal pole
papers.abstract: This study identifies a long-sought functional region in the human temporal pole (TP) dedicated to the recognition of familiar individuals. By employing multi-echo fMRI sequences to mitigate signal dropout caused by magnetic susceptibility artifacts, the researchers characterized a region that responds selectively to images of familiar faces over unfamiliar ones, objects, or scenes. Unlike standard face-selective areas in the perirhinal cortex (PR) that track visual features, this TP area is strongly modulated by abstract social cognitive tasks, such as semantic judgments and episodic simulation. The area is functionally coupled with the social cognition network, identifying it as a critical neural hub linking face perception to personal identity and social memory.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS)
papers.authors: Ben Deen, Gazi Husain, Winrich A. Freiwald

0700.name: Woon Ju Park
0700.bio: Woon Ju Park is an Assistant Professor in the School of Psychology at the Georgia Institute of Technology and directs the Cortical Resilience Lab. Park’s research examines the mechanisms of sensory processing and brain plasticity in typical and atypical populations, including individuals with autism spectrum disorder and visual impairments. They utilize behavioral psychophysics, computational modeling, and multimodal neuroimaging techniques, such as functional and quantitative MRI, to investigate how the brain adapts to varied sensory environments. Their work specifically explores how developmental experiences and sensory deprivation influence the neural encoding of visual and auditory information.
0700.research_direction: Dr. Park has recently been investigating the computational and neural mechanisms underlying sensory plasticity and cognitive capacity limits, focusing heavily on how internal neural noise shapes perception across diverse populations. Their recent work explores cross-modal reorganization in early blind individuals, using psychophysical reverse correlation and computational modeling to examine how visual deprivation and expert training alter auditory motion processing and pitch discrimination. Additionally, they are investigating the sensory-noise hypothesis of visual working memory, employing psychophysics and transcranial direct current stimulation to determine whether the fidelity of early visual encoding fundamentally constrains memory precision in both neurotypical individuals and patients with schizophrenia. Across these varied lines of inquiry, Dr. Park is working to establish a unified computational framework that models how cortical circuits optimize sensory processing, whether by repurposing visual motion-sensitive areas like the MT+ complex for auditory tasks or by modulating internal noise during skill acquisition.

papers.title: Enhanced pitch perception in early blind individuals and musicians is due to reduced internal noise
papers.abstract: This research investigates the mechanisms underlying the superior pitch perception typically attributed to early blind individuals. By comparing performance across tasks that engage either peripheral/subcortical frequency selectivity (notched-noise tone detection) or cortical pitch discrimination, the study demonstrates that blind individuals and sighted musicians exhibit parity with controls in peripheral tasks but significant enhancements in cortical discrimination. Computational modeling reveals that this behavioral advantage is driven by a reduction in internal noise within cortical processing circuits rather than sharper frequency tuning. These findings highlight optimized internal noise as a central mechanism of auditory plasticity resulting from both sensory deprivation and expert training.
papers.authors: Woon Ju Park, Jasmine Awad, Ione Fine

papers.title: Sensory Neural Noise as a Limiting Factor in Visual Working Memory Precision in Neurotypicals and Individuals with Schizophrenia
papers.abstract: The neural constraints on working memory (WM) capacity remain debated, with traditional accounts focusing on prefrontal cortex limitations. This study tests the sensory-noise hypothesis, positing that the fidelity of early sensory encoding fundamentally limits WM precision. Using psychophysical paradigms and computational modeling, the authors demonstrate that individual differences in internal sensory noise during visual perception predict visual WM capacity. Furthermore, the characteristic WM deficits in schizophrenia are linked to atypically elevated sensory noise. Causal evidence is provided through transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) to the visual cortex, which modulated internal noise levels and concurrently altered WM precision in patients, suggesting that sensory recruitment fidelity is a key determinant of WM function.
papers.authors: Woon Ju Park, Megan Ichinose, Gengshi Hu, Geoffrey F. Woodman, Duje Tadin, Sohee Park

papers.title: A unified model for cross-modal plasticity and skill acquisition
papers.abstract: This paper proposes a comprehensive computational framework to explain the convergence of compensatory plasticity in sensory-deprived populations and expert skill acquisition. The model posits that both phenomena arise from the reduction of internal noise and the optimization of neural representations in cortical circuits. By integrating principles of neural adaptation and task-dependent learning, the authors explain how the brain optimizes sensory processing in response to environmental demands or the absence of primary modalities. The framework reconciles disparate findings in the plasticity literature by demonstrating how specific task requirements and input statistics interact to drive either task-specific or generalized cortical reorganization.
papers.authors: Woon Ju Park, Ione Fine

papers.title: The perception of auditory motion in sighted and early blind individuals
papers.abstract: This study employs a psychophysical reverse correlation paradigm to determine whether auditory motion processing relies on spatiotemporally non-separable energy filters, similar to the visual system's area MT, or on spatiotemporally separable position-inference mechanisms. The findings indicate that both sighted and early blind individuals utilize separable filters, inferring motion direction by comparing sound locations at the onset and offset of a stimulus rather than detecting continuous motion energy. Early blindness was found to refine these auditory motion filters by shifting their peak sensitivity toward the stimulus boundaries, thereby enhancing discrimination performance without changing the fundamental computational strategy used by the auditory system.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Woon Ju Park, Ione Fine

papers.title: Do you hear what I see? How do early blind individuals experience object motion?
papers.abstract: This review evaluates the functional and structural reorganization of the auditory system following early visual deprivation, specifically focusing on the representation of moving objects. It synthesizes evidence from behavioral psychophysics and multimodal neuroimaging to describe the cross-modal recruitment of the human MT+ complex—a region typically specialized for visual motion—for auditory tasks. The authors argue that while the blind auditory system achieves superior spatial performance, its underlying computations are distinct from visual energy-based motion processing and remain constrained by the inherent spatiotemporal resolution of the auditory modality. The work details the neural mechanisms that support the construction of a coherent spatial environment through sound in the absence of sight.
papers.venue: Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences
papers.authors: Ione Fine, Woon Ju Park

0701.name: Xiaolan Fu
0701.bio: Xiaolan Fu is the Founding Dean and a Professor at the School of Psychology, Shanghai Jiao Tong University, and previously served as the Director of the Institute of Psychology, Chinese Academy of Sciences. Fu's research focuses on the neural and computational mechanisms of visual perception, attention, and emotion, specifically in the areas of affective computing and micro-expression recognition. They led the development of the CASME (Chinese Academy of Sciences Micro-expression) databases and developed methodologies for decoding masked facial expressions using electromyography (EMG) and deep learning. Fu’s current research integrates cognitive psychology and neuroscience to address challenges in mental health and human-computer interaction.
0701.research_direction: Dr. Fu's recent work explores the physiological and computational mechanisms of emotion recognition and face perception, utilizing tools ranging from facial electromyography (EMG) to deep learning frameworks integrated with facial Action Unit (AU) dynamics. They have recently been investigating how to objectively quantify the intensity and duration of subtle micro-expressions, as well as probing how naturalistic, within-person appearance variability across large-scale image datasets impacts social evaluations like trustworthiness and attractiveness. Broadening their focus to internal cognitive states, their research examines the decoupling of internal thought from external sensory processing, using EEG inter-trial phase coherence to track how task difficulty modulates mind wandering. Additionally, they are investigating the neural architecture of sensorimotor integration by conducting neuroimaging meta-analyses to map the predictive networks that govern sensory attenuation during self-initiated actions.

papers.title: Action Unit Enhance Dynamic Facial Expression Recognition
papers.abstract: This study introduces AU-DFER, a novel computational framework designed to optimize Dynamic Facial Expression Recognition (DFER) by integrating Action Unit (AU) expression knowledge as a source of objective physiological priors. The architecture extracts dynamic AU features to capture fine-grained facial muscle dynamics, addressing the inherent limitations of deep learning models that rely solely on holistic spatial features. By incorporating quantified AU-expression relationships, the model effectively mitigates data imbalance issues in large-scale datasets and enhances the recognition of subtle temporal transitions. Experimental validation on standard dynamic expression benchmarks indicates that this AU-enhanced approach significantly improves classification robustness and accuracy over existing state-of-the-art DFER paradigms.
papers.venue: ACM International Conference on Multimedia (ACM MM)
papers.authors: Feng Liu, Lingna Gu, Chen Shi, Xiaolan Fu

papers.title: Task difficulty modulates the effect of mind wandering on phase dynamics
papers.abstract: This investigation utilizes the thought-probe method and EEG inter-trial phase coherence (ITPC) analysis to examine how task difficulty moderates the decoupling of internal cognition from external sensory and motor processing. Across multiple experiments involving semantic classification and motor response tasks, the authors demonstrate that mind wandering (MW) significantly attenuates ITPC in low-demand tasks but fails to suppress phase dynamics in high-difficulty conditions. The results suggest that increased external task difficulty preserves the precision of neural entrainment to stimuli, thereby limiting the availability of cognitive-executive resources for internally-oriented thoughts. These findings provide empirical support for the Baseline model of cognition, indicating that phase coherence serves as a key neural mechanism mediating the reciprocal balance between internal mind wandering and external engagement.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS)
papers.authors: Zhengkun Long, Georg Northoff, Xiaolan Fu

papers.title: Could Micro-Expressions Be Quantified? Electromyography Gives Affirmative Evidence
papers.abstract: The authors present an objective, physiological approach to micro-expression (ME) quantification using facial electromyography (EMG). By analyzing the CASMEMG database, the study proposes the percentage of maximum voluntary contraction (MVC%) as a novel indicator for measuring ME intensity. Quantitative analysis reveals that MEs typically exhibit an intensity range of 7% to 9.2% MVC% and a duration of 307–327 ms, which are significantly lower than those of macro-expressions. Furthermore, behavioral and self-report data confirm that MEs are characterized by reduced controllability and conscious awareness. This research establishes a theoretical and empirical foundation for micro-expression mechanisms, offering fine-grained metrics for affective computing and clinical psychological applications.
papers.authors: Jingting Li, Shaoyuan Lu, Yan Wang, Xiaolan Fu

papers.title: Chinese Face and Body Dataset (CFBD): Lab and personal photos of the same individuals
papers.abstract: To address the lack of within-model variability in facial stimuli, the authors introduce the Chinese Face and Body Dataset (CFBD), a large-scale resource comprising 2,195 images of 117 Chinese models. The dataset uniquely pairs controlled laboratory photographs with naturalistic personal images donated by the subjects to represent authentic appearance variation. Psychometric evaluations of social traits (trustworthiness, attractiveness, and distinctiveness) indicate that within-person variance across images is comparable to or greater than between-person variance. The findings highlight the significant impact of image context on social evaluation, showing that personal photos are perceived as significantly more trustworthy and attractive than laboratory counterparts, thereby facilitating more robust research into face representation and identity learning.
papers.authors: Ying Hu, Ruyu Pan, Yaqi Xiao, Xiaolan Fu

papers.title: The neural network of sensory attenuation: A neuroimaging meta-analysis
papers.abstract: This study employs coordinate-based activation likelihood estimation (ALE) to conduct an exhaustive meta-analysis of 48 functional neuroimaging (fMRI and PET) studies investigating sensory attenuation—the phenomenon where self-initiated actions lead to reduced sensory intensity. The analysis identifies a critical inhibitory network encompassing the right superior temporal gyrus (rSTG), right middle temporal gyrus (rMTG), and right insula. Meta-analytic connectivity modeling (MACM) reveals a functional dissociation between a cerebellum-centered action prediction network and a temporal-parietal conflict detection network. The findings support an internal forward modeling framework where cerebellar predictions suppress reflexive sensory input in the STG/MTG, enabling the brain to distinguish between self-generated and externally-induced sensory consequences.
papers.authors: Jingjin Gu, Tatia Buidze, Ke Zhao, Jan Gläscher, Xiaolan Fu

0702.name: Xiaoqing Gao
0702.bio: Gao is an Associate Professor at the Center for Psychological Sciences at Zhejiang University, specializing in the neural and behavioral development of visual functions. Gao's research investigates how early visual experiences, such as congenital cataracts, shape the processing of socially relevant information like facial identity and expressions. Utilizing neuroimaging techniques including fMRI frequency tagging, EEG, and fNIRS, Gao explores the development of face-space representations and the neural mechanisms of visual object categorization. Their work characterizes both typical development and the effects of early visual deprivation to elucidate the plasticity of the human visual system.
0702.research_direction: Dr. Gao has recently been investigating a broad range of topics spanning visual perception, social cognition, and network neuroscience. Their recent work explores early visual and social processes, using frequency-tagging EEG paradigms to probe whether rapid color categorization operates independently of language, alongside behavioral tasks to examine how face familiarity shapes the development of perspective-taking in children. In addition to these perceptual and cognitive inquiries, they are utilizing resting-state fMRI to characterize time-varying whole-brain dynamics through measures like dynamic brain entropy and effective connectivity. Specifically, they are investigating how the temporal transitions between distinct neural complexity states relate to general cognitive abilities in healthy populations, as well as how these spontaneous network dynamics are disrupted in neurodevelopmental conditions such as ADHD and Tourette syndrome.

papers.title: Familiar faces facilitate perspective-taking in children
papers.abstract: This research investigates the developmental impact of face familiarity on children's social-cognitive processing using an adapted Director Task. Across three experiments, children aged 9 to 11 demonstrated significantly enhanced perspective-taking performance when interacting with a familiar peer compared to a stranger (Study 1). Critically, familiarity acquired specifically through social interaction, rather than isolated person-knowledge acquisition, was necessary to promote subsequent perspective-taking abilities (Studies 2 and 3). These results suggest that familiar social categories induce a 'socially prepared state' that facilitates the recruitment of mentalizing processes, linking perceptual familiarity to high-level social functioning during middle childhood.
papers.authors: Xuan Wu, Minjie Wen, Jie He, Xiaoqing Gao

papers.title: Abnormal brain entropy dynamics in ADHD
papers.abstract: This study employs dynamical brain entropy (dBEN) analysis, a measure of neural signal complexity and irregularity, to characterize atypical spontaneous brain activity in individuals with ADHD. Utilizing resting-state fMRI data and a sliding-window approach, the researchers identified distinct BEN states. Patients with ADHD exhibited an increased fractional window (FW) and mean dwell time (MDT) in a low-entropy state involving sensorimotor and visual networks, which positively correlated with clinical severity. Conversely, a high-entropy state involving the default mode and executive control networks showed reduced FW and MDT in the ADHD group. These findings indicate that abnormal whole-brain entropy dynamics underpin the pathophysiology of ADHD and may serve as robust diagnostic biomarkers.
papers.authors: Xiaoyang Xin, Shuangshuang Gu, Cuiping Wang, Xiaoqing Gao

papers.title: The brain entropy dynamics in resting state
papers.abstract: To explore the time-varying nature of neural complexity, this study derived dynamical brain entropy (dBEN) from the resting-state fMRI data of 812 healthy young adults in the Human Connectome Project. Using a sliding-window method and k-means clustering, the whole-brain functional networks were categorized into four reoccurring BEN states. Results revealed that the temporal properties of these states—specifically fractional window and mean dwell time—are significantly associated with general cognitive abilities, such as processing speed and cognitive flexibility. States characterized by lower entropy in executive control and default mode networks were particularly linked to higher cognitive performance, suggesting that the dynamic transitions between complexity states reflect the functional efficiency of the human brain.
papers.authors: Xiaoyang Xin, Jiaqian Yu, Xiaoqing Gao

papers.title: Rapid color categorization revealed by frequency-tagging-based EEG
papers.abstract: This study addresses the long-standing debate over the origins of color categories by utilizing a fast periodic visual stimulation (FPVS) paradigm combined with EEG. Observers viewed a standard color flickering at a rapid rate (6 Hz) while deviant oddball colors from either within or across linguistic categories were introduced periodically. Despite equating perceptual distances between stimuli, cross-category oddballs elicited significantly larger neural responses at the oddball frequency than within-category oddballs. These findings demonstrate that color categorization occurs rapidly and automatically in the visual system, supporting the existence of categorical representations that are independent of post-perceptual naming processes.
papers.authors: Mengdan Sun, Xiaoqing Gao

papers.title: Altered dynamic functional and effective connectivity in drug-naive children with Tourette syndrome
papers.abstract: This research investigates the neural basis of Tourette Syndrome (TS) by analyzing dynamic functional connectivity (dFC) and effective connectivity (EC) in drug-naive pediatric patients. Using resting-state fMRI and group independent component analysis, the study found that children with TS spend significantly more time in a hyperconnected network state and exhibit more frequent state transitions than typically developing children. Abnormalities were specifically localized to the default mode network (DMN), which showed increased degree centrality and altered causal influences on other networks. These dFC and EC alterations were significantly correlated with tic severity and executive dysfunction, suggesting that disrupted DMN dynamics are central to the pathophysiology of TS.
papers.authors: Lekai Luo, Yi Liao, Fenglin Jia, Haibo Qu, Yuting Lou, Yixuan Feng, Yufeng Zang, Jianhua Feng, Xiaoqing Gao

0703.name: Xuexin Wei
0703.bio: Xuexin Wei is a computational and theoretical neuroscientist who investigates the neural mechanisms underlying adaptive and intelligent behavior. By integrating normative modeling with bottom-up analysis of large-scale experimental data, Wei develops theories on sensory adaptation, perceptual biases, and neural manifold geometry. Wei's research applies the principle of efficient computation to understand how environmental structures and task demands shape neural representations in the domains of vision and navigation. Currently, Wei's lab focuses on bridging biological neural coding with deep learning to explore generalization and probabilistic inference in both brain and artificial systems.
0703.research_direction: Dr. Wei’s recent work explores the computational principles underlying neural coding, spatial navigation, and perceptual inference. They have recently been developing normative Bayesian frameworks to explain seemingly contradictory perceptual biases—such as reconciling prior-driven attraction with efficient coding-driven repulsion—while also investigating the mathematical identifiability of these observer models from behavioral data. At the neural level, their research investigates how cognitive maps might emerge from self-supervised predictive visual processing, alongside developing novel techniques like split-trial analysis to quantify information-limiting noise in large-scale population codes. Furthermore, Dr. Wei is investigating the computational alignment between biological and artificial vision, introducing new metrics grounded in signal detection theory to isolate and compare task-relevant decision strategies between deep neural networks and primate visual areas like V4 and IT.

papers.title: Split-trial analysis reveals the information capacity of neural population codes
papers.abstract: This research presents 'split-trial analysis,' a novel computational method designed to quantify information-limiting noise in neural populations without requiring the estimation of high-dimensional noise covariance matrices. By partitioning individual-trial population responses into multiple repeated virtual measurements, the technique disentangles noise shared across the entire population (the information-limiting component) from private, non-limiting noise. Extensive numerical simulations demonstrate that this approach significantly outperforms existing methods in terms of sample efficiency, accuracy, and robustness. The authors apply the method to diverse neurophysiological datasets, identifying substantial information-limiting noise in the mouse head-direction system, minimal limiting noise in the mouse V1 orientation code, and highly stable temporal structures of information limits in the macaque prefrontal cortex during saccadic tasks.
papers.authors: Dylan Le, Xue-Xin Wei

papers.title: Quantifying Task-relevant Similarities in Representations Using Decision Variable Correlations
papers.abstract: This paper introduces Decision Variable Correlation (DVC) as a principled metric for characterizing the similarity of decision strategies between biological neural systems and deep neural networks (DNNs). Grounded in signal detection theory, DVC quantifies image-by-image correlations between decoded decisions derived from internal neural representations in classification tasks, thereby isolating task-relevant information structure from general representational alignment. Analysis of monkey V4/IT electrophysiological recordings and DNNs reveals that while model-to-model similarity is high, model-to-monkey similarity is consistently lower and unexpectedly decreases as ImageNet-1k classification performance improves. Furthermore, the results show that neither adversarial training nor pre-training on larger datasets improves brain-alignment in these critical task-relevant dimensions, suggesting a fundamental divergence between biological vision and current image classification models.
papers.venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2025)
papers.authors: Yu (Eric) Qian, Wilson S. Geisler, Xue-Xin Wei

papers.title: Identifiability of Bayesian Models of Cognition
papers.abstract: This study addresses the critical problem of parameter identifiability when inferring Bayesian observer models from behavioral data. The authors analytically investigate whether the fundamental components of these models—prior beliefs, likelihood functions (constrained by encoding noise), and loss functions—can be uniquely recovered from experimental observations. They prove that under broadly applicable conditions, these components are identifiable without a priori knowledge, provided that behavioral measurements are collected across multiple levels of sensory noise. The theoretical framework is validated through simulations and applications to human orientation perception datasets, providing rigorous guiding principles for experimental design and the interpretation of normative models in cognitive science and neuroscience.
papers.authors: Michael Hahn, Entang Wang, Xue-Xin Wei

papers.title: Cognitive maps from predictive vision
papers.abstract: This study explores the computational link between predictive processing in the visual hierarchy and the emergence of spatial representations in the hippocampal-entorhinal system. By training self-supervised neural networks to predict future visual states or inputs within simulated environments, the authors demonstrate that hexagonal grid-like activity patterns naturally emerge in the model's latent units. This findings suggests that the 'canonical' grid cell representations used for spatial navigation can be derived from a more general objective of optimizing predictive accuracy in dynamic visual environments. The research provides a unifying perspective on how the brain's internal models of the world may be constructed through self-supervised learning on visual sequences.
papers.authors: Margaret von Ebers, Xue-Xin Wei

papers.title: A unifying theory explains seemingly contradictory biases in perceptual estimation
papers.abstract: Perceptual biases are often interpreted as evidence for disparate computational strategies, such as Bayesian attraction to priors or efficient coding-driven repulsion. This paper presents a normative Bayesian framework that reconciles these seemingly contradictory phenomena via an additive decomposition of perceptual bias into three distinct components: attraction to a prior, repulsion from regions with high encoding precision (Fisher information), and regression away from stimulus boundaries. The theory reveals a universal rule for predicting the direction and magnitude of biases based on limited neural resources and environmental statistics. This unified account is validated across multiple sensory domains, including the perception of orientation, color, and magnitude, offering a singular explanation for diverse behavioral regularities in human perception.
papers.authors: Michael Hahn, Xue-Xin Wei

0704.name: Yaffa Yeshurun
0704.department: Department of Psychology and the Institute of Information Processing and Decision Making (IIPDM)
0704.bio: Yaffa Yeshurun is a Full Professor at the University of Haifa who researches the spatial and temporal dynamics of visual attention. Yeshurun investigates transient, stimulus-driven attention, specifically demonstrating its capacity to enhance spatial resolution and its impact on perceptual performance. Their research methodology utilizes psychophysical tasks to examine the trade-offs between integration and segregation processes, as well as the effects of perceptual load and crowding on visual processing. Yeshurun's recent studies apply these findings to real-world scenarios, including attentional selection during driving and individual variability in internal noise.
0704.research_direction: Dr. Yeshurun has recently been investigating the spatial and temporal dynamics of visual processing, focusing on both spatial attention and temporal interference. Their recent work explores how temporal crowding and visual masking degrade performance across different timescales, using orientation estimation tasks and mixture-model analyses to characterize changes in encoding precision and signal-to-noise ratios. They are also examining whether temporal crowding is a strictly peripheral phenomenon or if it extends to foveal vision, utilizing long stimulus-onset asynchronies to probe the temporal limits required to form stable visual representations. Additionally, Dr. Yeshurun is conducting large-scale psychophysical studies coupled with hierarchical Bayesian modeling to investigate individual variability in the perceptual costs and benefits of spatial attention during peripheral precueing tasks.

papers.title: Large-scale examination of the benefit and cost of spatial attention and their individual variability
papers.abstract: This study conducted a high-powered psychophysical investigation into the behavioral dynamics of spatial attention using a large population sample to characterize individual differences in attentional costs and benefits. Utilizing an orientation-acuity task with peripheral precueing, the researchers measured performance enhancements at validly cued locations (benefits) and decrements at invalidly cued locations (costs). Hierarchical Bayesian modeling was employed to assess the reliability of these effects across participants and to explore correlations with other cognitive traits. The findings reveal substantial individual variability in the magnitude of spatial attention effects, suggesting that the efficiency of attentional prioritization is a stable idiosyncratic trait rather than a uniform cognitive capacity.
papers.authors: Felipe Luzardo, Yaffa Yeshurun

papers.title: Interference across time: dissociating short from long temporal interference
papers.abstract: The research differentiates between short-scale temporal interference (visual masking, <150 ms) and long-scale temporal interference (temporal crowding, 175-475 ms) using an orientation estimation task and mixture-model analysis. By systematically varying stimulus-onset asynchrony (SOA) and inter-item similarity, the study characterizes the mechanisms underlying performance degradation at different temporal scales. Findings indicate that long-interval interference primarily compromises target encoding precision, whereas short-interval interference predominantly impacts the signal-to-noise ratio. Despite both phenomena inducing substitution errors and showing attenuation with item dissimilarity, the distinctive patterns of SOA effects suggest that temporal masking and temporal crowding are mediated by discrete perceptual mechanisms.
papers.authors: Ilanit Hochmitz, Ahmad Abu-Akel, Yaffa Yeshurun

papers.title: Temporal Crowding With Central Vision Reveals the Fragility of Visual Representations
papers.abstract: This investigation examines whether temporal crowding—the impairment of target identification by temporally adjacent distractors—is restricted to the periphery or also occurs in central vision. Participants performed an orientation estimation task on central stimuli separated by stimulus-onset asynchronies (SOAs) of 200 ms and 400 ms. Mixture-model analyses revealed significant temporal crowding at the fovea, even with intervals as long as 400 ms, primarily characterized by a robust reduction in encoding precision. The similar magnitude of interference between central and peripheral presentations suggests that temporal crowding is not a consequence of low-level sensory resolution limits but likely involves higher-order visual processing areas, underscoring the slow temporal dynamics required to form stable visual representations.
papers.authors: Tomer Sahar, Yaffa Yeshurun

0705.name: Yalda Mohsenzadeh
0705.bio: Mohsenzadeh is an Assistant Professor at Western University and a faculty member at the Vector Institute, focusing on the intersection of human visual cognition and artificial intelligence. Their research employs multi-modal neuroimaging techniques, including fMRI, MEG, and EEG, alongside deep learning architectures to decode the spatiotemporal dynamics of the human brain during visual processing and memory formation. By examining the computational principles of biological vision, such as image memorability and robust perception, Mohsenzadeh aims to develop machines that emulate human-level performance and resilience.
0705.research_direction: Dr. Mohsenzadeh has recently been investigating the spatiotemporal neural dynamics of visual cognition alongside the development of applied computer vision frameworks. Their recent work explores how the human brain processes complex, naturalistic stimuli over time, using techniques like EEG-fMRI-MEG fusion, multivariate pattern analysis, and representational similarity analysis to study conscious rapid object recognition, the attentional blink, and audiovisual integration. Furthermore, they are employing deep neural networks to computationally model high-level cognitive phenomena, such as probing the distinct latent visual features that drive image memorability using unsupervised autoencoders. In the applied clinical domain, Dr. Mohsenzadeh is also designing computationally efficient, slice-based deep learning models to detect pathological anomalies in 3D brain MRI volumes.

papers.title: Efficient slice anomaly detection network for 3D brain MRI Volume
papers.abstract: This research introduces a computationally efficient anomaly detection framework for 3D brain MRI volumes that mitigates the memory-intensive requirements of traditional 3D convolutional neural networks. The proposed architecture employs a slice-based approach utilizing a triplet loss training objective to characterize the manifold of normal anatomical variability. By operating on 2D slices while preserving inter-slice spatial consistency, the model identifies pathological deviations as anomalies. Evaluation on T1 and T2-weighted brain volumes demonstrates that this methodology surpasses existing reconstruction-based models in detecting spatial anomalies, offering significant improvements in inference speed and reducing the necessity for complex post-processing of noisy reconstruction outputs.
papers.authors: Zeduo Zhang, Yalda Mohsenzadeh

papers.title: Modeling Visual Memorability Assessment with Autoencoders Reveals Characteristics of Memorable Images
papers.abstract: This study investigates the computational underpinnings of visual memorability using an unsupervised deep learning framework. The authors propose an autoencoder-based model, utilizing a VGG16 backbone, trained in a single-epoch regime to approximate human memory recall after a single exposure. The analysis reveals a significant positive correlation between the autoencoder's reconstruction error and human memorability scores, indicating that highly memorable images occupy distinct regions of the visual feature space that challenge standard compression algorithms. Furthermore, the distinctiveness of the latent representations was found to be a robust predictor of memorability. Interpretability analysis via Integrated Gradients (IG) identified specific visual characteristics that contribute to an image's intrinsic memorability within the model's latent space.
papers.authors: Elham Bagheri, Yalda Mohsenzadeh

papers.title: Neural processing of naturalistic audiovisual events in space and time
papers.abstract: Using a combination of fMRI and MEG data fusion alongside deep neural network (DNN) modeling, this study maps the spatiotemporal dynamics of multisensory integration for naturalistic audiovisual stimuli. The researchers utilized GIST descriptors for visual features, Cochleagram models for acoustic features, and GloVe word embeddings for semantic content to perform representational similarity analysis (RSA). The results demonstrate asymmetrical neural representations of early cross-modal interactions, with acoustic features exhibiting significant correlations in both auditory and early ventral visual regions. Searchlight analysis confirmed a hierarchical progression where early DNN layers align with primary sensory cortices and deeper layers correspond to higher-level associative regions, providing a comprehensive characterization of how naturalistic multisensory events are synthesized in the human brain.
papers.authors: Yu Hu, Yalda Mohsenzadeh

papers.title: Multivariate Pattern Analysis of EEG Reveals Neural Mechanism of Naturalistic Target Processing in Attentional Blink
papers.abstract: This paper investigates the neural mechanisms of the attentional blink (AB) phenomenon using high-temporal resolution EEG and multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA). Participants performed a rapid serial visual presentation (RSVP) task involving naturalistic target images. Decoding of the neural signals revealed that the 'blink' (failure to perceive the second target, T2) is primarily driven by a disruption in late-stage neural representations (200–500 ms post-stimulus) rather than a failure of initial sensory encoding. The study finds that while naturalistic stimuli evoke more robust and persistent neural signatures than simplified targets, they are still subject to the capacity-limited bottleneck of conscious processing. These findings clarify the temporal window where attentional resources are depleted during the processing of complex, real-world visual information.
papers.authors: Mansoure Jahanian, Marc F. Joanisse, Boyu Wang, Yalda Mohsenzadeh

papers.title: Unveiling the neural dynamics of conscious perception in rapid object recognition
papers.abstract: To delineate the temporal evolution of conscious object perception, this study integrates EEG recordings with representational similarity analysis (RSA) during a rapid visual presentation task. The researchers utilized a sliding-window decoding approach to track the emergence and maintenance of category-level neural information under varying levels of stimulus visibility. The findings highlight a hierarchical progression: initial low-level feature encoding occurs within 100 ms, followed by category-specific representations between 150 and 250 ms. The transition to conscious perception was uniquely associated with the sustained stability and recurrence of these neural representations in later processing stages, whereas non-consciously perceived stimuli were characterized by a rapid decay of categorical information.
papers.authors: Saba Charmi Motlagh, Marc Joanisse, Boyu Wang, Yalda Mohsenzadeh

0706.name: Yang Sun
0706.bio: Yang Sun is an Associate Professor at the College of Educational Sciences, Shenyang Normal University, specializing in the cognitive neuroscience of visual perception. Their research investigates the 'self-prioritization effect' and how social-referential information modulates sensory processing using psychophysical paradigms, event-related potentials (ERP), and functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI). Sun has researched neural compensatory mechanisms in the medial prefrontal cortex that preserve self-bias in aging populations and examined the modulation of early visual cortex activity by social significance. Their current work employs computational modeling to delineate the interactions between social cognition, attention, and sensory perception.
0706.research_direction: Dr. Sun's recent work explores how the cognitive system prioritizes self-referential visual stimuli, such as a person's own face or name. Using facial recognition tasks and the self-associative matching paradigm, they have recently been investigating the self-prioritization effect across unconscious, perceptual, and attentional stages of processing. Ultimately, their research asks how this robust perceptual advantage acts as a foundational attentional anchor to facilitate efficient information processing and navigation within complex social environments.

papers.title: Recognition Priority of Self-Related Information
papers.abstract: This study explores the cognitive prioritization of self-referential stimuli, such as personal names and faces, identifying a robust processing advantage across unconscious, perceptual, and attentional levels. Utilizing the self-associative matching paradigm and facial recognition tasks, the research demonstrates that individuals detect self-relevant information with greater sensitivity and significantly faster response times compared to non-self-related information. The findings indicate that the self-prioritization effect (SPE) serves as a foundational attentional anchor that facilitates efficient information processing and navigation within complex social environments.
papers.authors: Yufei Liu, Rui Wang, Yang Sun

0707.name: Yaoda Xu
0707.bio: Xu investigates the neural mechanisms underlying visual object representation and the adaptive nature of visual information processing in the human brain. Their research utilizes functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and multi-voxel pattern analysis (MVPA) to explore the functional roles of the posterior parietal and occipito-temporal cortices in visual working memory and decision-making. Xu examines how the brain manages capacity-limited visual processing and evaluates the similarities and divergences between primate vision and convolutional neural networks (CNNs).
0707.research_direction: Dr. Xu's recent work explores the functional organization and representational dynamics of the human visual system, particularly emphasizing the posterior parietal cortex and visual working memory. Using fMRI and multivariate pattern analysis, they are investigating how neural representations are actively transformed between perceptual encoding and mnemonic maintenance, as well as how the brain orthogonalizes concurrent information streams to prevent interference between targets and distractors. Beyond working memory, their recent research examines the computational and spatial principles driving the specialization of the dorsal, lateral, and ventral visual streams—such as the segregated processing of 3D versus 2D object properties—by integrating neuroimaging meta-analyses with self-supervised topographic artificial neural networks. Finally, they have recently been utilizing novel fMRI decoding techniques to measure non-linear mixed selectivity in humans, probing how task demands interact with object categories to dynamically reshape representational geometry across the visual hierarchy.

papers.title: Neural correlates of 3D versus 2D perception: An activation likelihood estimation meta-analysis
papers.abstract: This study utilized activation likelihood estimation (ALE) to conduct a coordinate-based meta-analysis of neuroimaging literature comparing 3D and 2D visual processing. The analysis aimed to identify consistent neural substrates involved in processing depth cues and solid object properties. Results indicated that while ventral stream areas show robust activation for both 2D and 3D stimuli, dorsal stream regions, particularly within the posterior parietal cortex (PPC) and along the intraparietal sulcus, demonstrate a preferential involvement in 3D perception. These findings support a neurocognitive framework where the dorsal pathway contributes uniquely to the perception of visuospatial attributes that afford interaction, rather than merely subserving motor control. The meta-analysis highlights a consistent recruitment of the lateral occipital complex (LOC) and multiple parietal foci in reconstructing 3D object identity from sensory input.
papers.authors: Luiza P. Volpi, Su Keun Jeong, Yaoda Xu

papers.title: Transformed Visual Working Memory Representations in Human Occipitotemporal and Posterior Parietal Cortices
papers.abstract: This fMRI investigation challenged the sensory recruitment account of visual working memory (VWM) by examining representational transformations between perception and mnemonic maintenance. By comparing neural patterns for targets and distractors during the same delay period, the study equated experimental conditions to isolate representational format. Multi-voxel pattern analysis (MVPA) and cross-decoding revealed significant representational shifts between perceptual encoding and VWM maintenance throughout the occipitotemporal (OTC) and posterior parietal (PPC) cortices. Specifically, PPC exhibited more invariant target representations compared to the more substantial transformations observed in OTC. These results suggest that VWM does not simply sustain sensory input but involves a task-driven selection and consolidation process, where goal-directed transformations are mediated by associative areas to optimize the retention of task-relevant information against interference.
papers.authors: Yaoda Xu

papers.title: A single computational objective can produce specialization of streams in visual cortex
papers.abstract: This computational study investigated the functional and spatial principles underlying the emergence of the dorsal, lateral, and ventral processing streams in the human visual cortex. Using a large-scale fMRI dataset (NSD) and a novel topographic deep artificial neural network (TDANN), the researchers tested whether stream specialization arises from distinct behavioral goals or a unified objective. The findings demonstrated that models optimized for stream-specific tasks (e.g., object detection vs. action recognition) failed to predict brain responses as accurately as a self-supervised TDANN trained on a single objective of learning general visual representations under local spatial constraints. The model successfully replicated the spatial segregation and functional differentiation of the three streams, suggesting that cortical organization is driven by the need to balance representational utility with the energetic costs of long-range wiring.
papers.authors: Dawn Finzi, Eshed Margalit, Kendrick Kay, Daniel L. K. Yamins, Kalanit Grill-Spector, Maryam Vaziri-Pashkam, Yaoda Xu

papers.title: The human posterior parietal cortices orthogonalize the representation of different streams of information concurrently coded in visual working memory
papers.abstract: The study employed fMRI pattern decoding to identify the neural geometry used by the human brain to maintain goal-directed representations during distraction. Across two experiments, the human posterior parietal cortex (PPC) was found to orthogonalize the representations of different information streams held in visual working memory (VWM), including targets versus distractors and multiple concurrent targets. This representational scheme allows for independent information readout and minimizes interference between task-relevant and task-irrelevant signals. While the occipitotemporal cortex (OTC) showed entangled representations during encoding, the PPC successfully maintained orthogonalized codes during the delay period. These results suggest that representation orthogonalization is a fundamental neural principle for managing capacity-limited processing and supporting adaptive visual behavior in multi-stream environments.
papers.authors: Yaoda Xu

papers.title: Using fMRI to examine nonlinear mixed selectivity tuning to task and category in the human brain
papers.abstract: Nonlinear mixed selectivity, characterized by interaction effects in neuronal tuning to multiple variables, is critical for flexible behavior but has primarily been studied using invasive electrophysiology. This study demonstrated the feasibility of measuring such effects noninvasively in humans using fMRI and a 'pattern difference decoding' technique. Participants performed different tasks (oddball vs. one-back) on the same object categories to equate attentional demands. The analysis revealed distributed multivariate interaction effects between object category and task context across early visual, ventral, and dorsal stream regions. The results show that nonlinear mixed selectivity modulates representational geometry, often through rotations in representational space, allowing the brain to form task-adaptive codes that facilitate efficient readout of goal-relevant information.
papers.authors: JohnMark Taylor, Yaoda Xu

0708.name: Yi Jiang
0708.department: Division of Cognitive and Developmental Psychology
0708.bio: Yi Jiang is a Professor and Principal Investigator at the Institute of Psychology, Chinese Academy of Sciences, directing the Vision and Attention Lab. Jiang utilizes psychophysics, functional MRI, and high-temporal-resolution EEG to study the neural mechanisms of visual perception, selective attention, and the boundaries of conscious awareness. Their research includes investigations into the subconscious processing of social signals, specifically how biological motion and facial expressions are encoded without explicit awareness. Jiang's current work examines the rhythmic nature of attentional sampling and the cross-modal integration of visual, vestibular, and olfactory cues in human perception.
0708.research_direction: Dr. Jiang's recent work explores the neurocognitive and evolutionary mechanisms underlying high-level visual perception, particularly how the visual system processes social and affective signals. Using methods ranging from human pupillometry to cross-species fMRI and single-unit electrophysiology, they are examining the involuntary physiological markers of empathy during pain perception across different demographic groups, as well as the genetic and neural pathways that support the rapid detection of fearful faces. In the domain of visual attention, their research utilizes EEG to investigate how conscious awareness regulates the speed and neural coordination of rhythmic information sampling within the frontoparietal network. Additionally, they have recently been studying fundamental perceptual algorithms by asking how internal priors for Earth's gravity influence global motion integration, and how distinct spatial grouping cues distort time and numerosity perception to test for shared magnitude representations.

papers.title: Automatic pupillary responses to pain perception in adults and children: The influence of race and autistic traits
papers.abstract: This study employs pupillometry to investigate involuntary psychophysiological responses to observed pain across developmental stages and social groups. The results demonstrate that both adults and children exhibit a robust increase in pupil diameter when viewing painful compared to neutral facial expressions, identifying a distinct autonomic arousal signature. Critically, this pupillary response is modulated by a racial in-group bias, manifesting specifically in response to same-race painful stimuli. Furthermore, the magnitude of the pupillary dilation effect towards in-group pain is negatively correlated with individual Autism Spectrum Quotient (AQ) scores, suggesting that autonomic empathic resonance is sensitive to both social group identification and autistic trait variance.
papers.authors: Ting Zhang, Shujia Zhang, Yi Jiang

papers.title: Visual awareness sharpens and accelerates attentional sampling through enhancing inhibitory neural modulation in the attention network
papers.abstract: Using a high-temporal-resolution cueing paradigm combined with the Chromatic Flicker Fusion (CFF) method to manipulate stimulus visibility, this research explores the role of consciousness in the rhythmic sampling of attention. Electroencephalography (EEG) and temporal response function (TRF) analyses reveal that while both visible and invisible cues trigger a rhythmic reset of connectivity within the frontoparietal attention network, visual awareness significantly optimizes the sampling process. Specifically, conscious cues accelerate the attentional sampling frequency (approximately 8 Hz versus 4 Hz) and enhance inhibitory alpha-band neural oscillations and top-down prefrontal-parietal coupling. These findings indicate that visual awareness acts as a regulatory mechanism that refines the speed and neural coordination of rhythmic information selection.
papers.authors: Fang Yang, Peijun Yuan, Li Shen, Ke Zhou, Sheng He, Yi Jiang

papers.title: Implied gravity promotes coherent motion perception
papers.abstract: This investigation examines the impact of an internal gravitational prior on the visual integration of local motion cues into global patterns. Using a motion coherence threshold task, the researchers measured the visual system's sensitivity to global motion conveying natural (1 g) versus reversed (−1 g) gravitational accelerations. The findings indicate that perceptual thresholds are significantly lower for motion consistent with Earth's gravity, regardless of the stimulus parameters or environmental frames of reference. This indicates that gravitational acceleration cues are inherently extracted and integrated into unified motion percepts, supporting the existence of an embodied cognitive model of gravity that facilitates motion processing in natural terrestrial environments.
papers.authors: Xiqian Lu, Bogeng Song, Shaoshuai Zhang, Shujia Zhang, Mei Huang, Ying Wang, Yi Jiang

papers.title: Symmetrical and asymmetrical distortions in time and numerosity perception induced by chunked stimuli
papers.abstract: The research investigates whether time and numerosity share a common magnitude representation by analyzing perceptual distortions induced by spatial chunking (grouping). Using collinearity, illusory contours (ICs), and biological motion (BM) as chunked stimuli, the study found that while collinearity produced symmetrical overestimation for both time and numerosity, ICs exclusively induced numerical underestimation and BM exclusively induced temporal overestimation. The lack of consistent correlation between these distortions across stimulus types suggests that temporal and numerical representations are partially dissociable and are differentially influenced by specific spatial and socio-biological grouping cues.
papers.authors: Zhichao Xue, Xiangyong Yuan, Yi Jiang

papers.title: Genetic and neuronal basis for facial emotion perception in humans and macaques
papers.abstract: This comparative study delineates the evolutionary and genetic substrates of facial emotion processing, specifically focusing on the detection of fear. Integrating twin-based behavioral genetics, functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), and macaque single-unit electrophysiology, the authors demonstrate that the rapid recognition of fearful expressions is a heritable trait in humans and is mediated by a specialized neural pathway tuned to low-spatial-frequency (LSF) information. The study reveals LSF-selective neuronal activity in the macaque amygdala and temporal cortex that corresponds to human behavioral and neural responses, providing evidence for a cross-species, genetically-determined system for the preconscious detection of social threat signals.
papers.authors: Li Wang, Bo Zhang, Xiqian Lu, Ruidi Wang, Jian Ma, Yujie Chen, Yuan Zhou, Ji Dai, Yi Jiang

0709.name: Ying-zi Xiong
0709.department: Department of Ophthalmology, School of Medicine
0709.bio: Ying-zi Xiong is an Assistant Professor of Ophthalmology at the Wilmer Eye Institute and the Principal Investigator of the XYZ Sensory Lab. Xiong’s research examines the mechanisms through which the human brain adapts to sensory impairments, focusing on how visual and auditory deficits affect spatial localization and daily functioning. Using psychophysical methods and multisensory modeling, they develop translational tools to improve digital accessibility and clinical assessment for individuals with low vision and dual sensory loss. Xiong’s current work includes the Vision Accessibility Initiative, which integrates computer vision and human-computer interaction to create assistive technologies for reading and independent navigation.
0709.research_direction: Dr. Xiong's recent work explores spatial perception and accessibility, focusing heavily on multisensory integration and the impacts of visual impairment. They have recently been investigating multisensory spatial orientation in low-vision populations, specifically probing how visual deficits alter the perception of straight ahead across visual, auditory, and proprioceptive channels. In parallel, their research examines the fundamental architecture of spatial attention by testing whether attentional resources for localizing azimuth targets are shared or modality-specific across vision and hearing. To advance applied accessibility, they are also developing automated assessment pipelines that merge human contrast sensitivity functions with optical character recognition and vision-language models to computationally simulate human reading performance under degraded acuity and contrast conditions.

papers.title: VI-OCR: “Visually Impaired” optical character recognition pipeline for text accessibility assessment
papers.abstract: The authors introduce VI-OCR, a text accessibility assessment pipeline that merges human contrast sensitivity functions (CSF) with optical character recognition to simulate human-like reading performance under specific visual deficits. Using a specialized image degradation module to model acuity and contrast sensitivity loss, the study benchmarks specialized OCR models and vision-language models (VLMs), including Qwen2.5-VL and GPT-4o, across three reading tasks: letter recognition (ETDRS), word recognition (MNREAD), and natural scene text recognition. While certain high-performing models accurately replicate human-like performance reductions, some models exhibit limited generalizability or overperform relative to human observers in low-contrast conditions. The results demonstrate the feasibility of using persona-based simulations to automate text visibility assessments for low-vision accessibility research.
papers.authors: Qingying Gao, Roberto Manduchi, Pradeep Y. Ramulu, Yingzi Xiong

papers.title: Dividing Attention Between Vision and Audition in Spatial Localization Tasks
papers.abstract: This study evaluates whether spatial attention resources for vision and audition are modality-specific or shared (cross-modal) during simultaneous localization. Participants with normal vision reported the azimuth of single visual or auditory targets, unimodal pairs (two visual or two auditory), or bimodal pairs (one visual and one auditory). Locating two simultaneous auditory targets resulted in significantly larger errors (mean = 28.28°) that scaled with spatial separation, whereas bimodal localization performance showed minimal attentional cost (mean = 16.07°). These results support the modality-specific hypothesis, indicating that spatial attention operates through separate channels for vision and audition, although the authors suggest that higher task difficulty might eventually reveal cross-modal constraints.
papers.authors: Taylor J. Knickel, Gordon E. Legge, Ying-zi Xiong

papers.title: Perception of Straight Ahead With Vision, Hearing, and Proprioception by Individuals With Low Vision
papers.abstract: This research investigates the perception of straight ahead (PSA), a fundamental spatial reference, in individuals with low vision. The authors tested 35 low-vision participants and 17 controls across visual, auditory, and proprioceptive modalities. Low-vision individuals demonstrated significantly increased biases and variability in both visual and auditory PSA, with visual deficits correlating strongly with binocular acuity and contrast sensitivity. The generalization of these biases to the auditory modality suggests a cross-modal impact of vision loss on sound localization. In contrast, proprioceptive PSA remained accurate and intact across all subjects, indicating that proprioception may serve as a critical compensatory mechanism for spatial orientation when visual and auditory cues are compromised.
papers.authors: Diamond Brunt, Gordon E. Legge, Donald C. Fletcher, Yingzi Xiong

0711.name: YiZhong Wang
0711.bio: YiZhong Wang is a visual physiologist and the Director of the Macular Function Laboratory at the Retina Foundation of the Southwest, and an Adjunct Assistant Professor in Ophthalmology at UT Southwestern Medical Center. Wang's research focuses on characterizing human shape perception, contour integration, and perceptual organization across the lifespan and in various ocular pathologies. They specialize in the development of functional biomarkers for diseases such as age-related macular degeneration (AMD) and amblyopia, recently integrating deep learning frameworks to automate the segmentation and analysis of retinal structures in optical coherence tomography (OCT) imaging.
0711.research_direction: Dr. Wang has recently been investigating how to improve the clinical assessment and monitoring of diverse visual disorders through both traditional psychophysics and modern computational methods. Their recent work explores the specific mechanisms underlying functional deficits in pediatric amblyopia, such as using rapid serial visual presentation (RSVP) to isolate how fixation instability affects reading speeds independently of saccadic eye movements. Beyond developmental vision, they are also working on remote monitoring tools for adult retinal diseases, testing the clinical validity of digital applications designed to track visual acuity, hyperacuity, and contrast sensitivity in patients with maculopathy. Additionally, Dr. Wang employs machine learning to optimize early risk-screening questionnaires for pediatric strabismus and amblyopia, reflecting a broader effort to integrate advanced predictive models with applied visual neuroscience.

papers.title: Fixation instability is associated with slow reading during rapid serial visual presentation (RSVP) in children with amblyopia
papers.abstract: This investigation utilized rapid serial visual presentation (RSVP) to assess whether oculomotor deficits in the fellow eye (FE), specifically fixation instability, contribute to the characteristic reduction in reading speeds observed in children with amblyopia. By employing RSVP to eliminate the requirement for inter-word saccades and return sweeps, we isolated the impact of steady-state fixation on temporal visual processing. Results indicated that amblyopic children maintained significantly lower reading rates compared to typically developing controls even in the absence of saccadic demands. Regression analyses revealed that FE fixation stability serves as a robust quantitative predictor of RSVP reading performance, suggesting that subtle binocular motor dysfunction fundamentally constrains functional vision in pediatric amblyopia.
papers.authors: Krista Kelly, Dorsa Mir Norouzi, YiZhong Wang

papers.title: Machine-learning development of a questionnaire for vision screening
papers.abstract: This study employed machine learning (ML) architectures to optimize a pediatric vision screening questionnaire designed to identify children at high risk for amblyopia and strabismus. By training supervised learning models on clinical data from extensive pediatric cohorts, the researchers isolated key behavioral and ocular symptoms that maximize diagnostic sensitivity and specificity. The ML-derived screening tool demonstrated significantly higher predictive value for identifying amblyogenic risk factors in primary care settings compared to standardized non-computational questionnaires. This validated instrument provides a scalable, automated approach to early ocular pathology detection by integrating complex clinical predictors into a simplified, high-accuracy screening format.
papers.venue: Journal of American Association for Pediatric Ophthalmology and Strabismus
papers.authors: Eileen Birch, Brooke Koritala, Reed Jost, Sarah Morale, Yi-Zhong Wang

papers.title: Remote Monitoring of Visual Function in Patients with Maculopathy: The Aphelion Study
papers.abstract: The Aphelion study was a prospective, single-arm clinical trial designed to validate the in-clinic precision and test-retest reliability of the myVisionTrack expanded version (mVTx) for the self-assessment of visual acuity (VA) and contrast sensitivity in subjects with various maculopathies. One hundred twenty-two participants performed four digital tests: tumbling E, Landolt C, shape discrimination hyperacuity (SDH), and contrast sensitivity. Analysis using Bland-Altman methods showed high agreement with gold-standard ETDRS charts, with the tumbling E test exhibiting a 95% limit of agreement of ±0.18 logMAR. These findings confirm that digital hyperacuity and VA assessments are accurate and repeatable, facilitating their deployment for remote longitudinal monitoring of disease activity between clinical visits.
papers.authors: Anthony Joseph, Mark Bullimore, Faye Drawnel, Marco Miranda, Zoe Morgan, Yi-Zhong Wang

papers.title: Editorial: Rising stars in visual neuroscience: 2022
papers.abstract: This peer-reviewed editorial provides a high-level technical synthesis of current paradigms in visual neuroscience, focusing on developmental plasticity and pathology. It reviews recent research advances in the mechanisms of amblyopia, the role of cortical adaptation following monocular deprivation, and the identification of structural biomarkers for retinal degenerations. The article highlights the transition toward integrating deep machine learning with traditional psychophysics to enhance the diagnostic precision of optical coherence tomography (OCT) and microperimetry. By spotlighting emerging investigators, the editorial outlines the trajectory of translational research aimed at sight-restoration therapies and the objective quantification of visual functional loss.
papers.authors: Kimberly Meier, Dorita H. F. Chang, Alexandre Reynaud, Krista Kelly, Dorsa Mir Norouzi, Yi-Zhong Wang

0712.name: Yonggang Shi
0712.department: Department of Neurology, Keck School of Medicine; Department of Biomedical Engineering; Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering
0712.bio: Yonggang Shi is a Professor at the University of Southern California and directs the Neuro Image Computing Research (NICR) group at the Stevens Neuroimaging and Informatics Institute. Shi’s work centers on developing computational solutions for brain mapping, specifically utilizing diffusion MRI and 3D shape analysis to model connectomes and structural connectivity. Their research includes the development of algorithms for reconstructing retinofugal visual pathways and investigating neuroanatomical biomarkers for Alzheimer's disease and visual restoration. Shi holds multiple appointments across neurology and engineering, applying methodologies such as Riemannian metric optimization and Laplace-Beltrami spectral analysis to characterize the human brain in health and disease.
0712.research_direction: Dr. Shi has recently been developing advanced computational neuroimaging frameworks to map brain pathology and microstructural organization, with a strong focus on Alzheimer’s disease and white matter tractography. Their recent work explores how to better capture the spatial progression and heterogeneity of Alzheimer's by modeling the topographic spread of tau proteins across the cortex, utilizing generative diffusion models to harmonize multi-site brain scans and correct for tracer-specific variations. Additionally, they are investigating multimodal fusion architectures that integrate structural MRI, tau PET, and clinical assessments to improve the automated diagnostic staging of cognitive decline. Alongside their disease-focused research, Dr. Shi is designing novel 4D autoencoders and conditional diffusion models to denoise and restore fiber orientation distributions in diffusion MRI, aiming to map accurate neural pathways even in brain regions that suffer from severe imaging distortions.

papers.title: Graphical modeling of cortical tau pathology topography for its subtyping in Alzheimer's disease
papers.abstract: To address the limitations of existing tau PET subtyping methods in managing the entanglement of disease stage and pathological heterogeneity, this study introduces a novel graphical modeling framework. The approach utilizes a Reeb graph representation to extract individual-level topographic features of tau accumulation on the cortical surface, focusing on the topology of critical points in the tau standardized uptake value ratio (SUVR) maps. A population-level graphical model is then derived from these cross-sectional patterns to encode spatiotemporal dependencies and identify robust pathological subtypes. Evaluation on synthetic data and large-scale tau PET cohorts (ADNI, A4, and ADAD) demonstrates that the proposed framework achieves superior generalization and higher discriminative power for preclinical cognitive performance compared to the event-based Subtype and Stage Inference (SuStaIn) model.
papers.authors: Jiaxin Yue, Xinkai Wang, John Ringman, Yonggang Shi

papers.title: Multistage Alignment and Fusion for Multimodal Multiclass Alzheimer's Disease Diagnosis
papers.abstract: This paper presents a multistage framework for the automated multiclass diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease (AD), mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and cognitively normal (CN) states. The method integrates structural MRI, tau PET, diffusion-based fiber orientation distributions (FOD), and cognitive MoCA scores. A specialized Swin-FOD architecture is employed to extract order-balanced features from spherical harmonic FOD coefficients, while MRI and PET features are aligned via a coarse-to-fine contrastive learning strategy. The multimodal fusion is further refined using TabPFN-based priors to capture complex feature relationships. On a cohort of 1,147 participants from the ADNI dataset, the model achieved a 73.21% classification accuracy, with Shapley analysis quantifying the contribution of each imaging and clinical modality to the diagnostic outcome.
papers.venue: Medical Image Computing and Computer Assisted Intervention – MICCAI 2025
papers.authors: Shuo Huang, Lujia Zhong, Yonggang Shi

papers.title: Tau PET harmonization via surface-based diffusion model
papers.abstract: Multi-site tau PET integration is complicated by tracer-specific binding properties and pattern variations that transcend simple intensity shifts. This work proposes a harmonization framework that combines surface-based data preprocessing with a conditional diffusion model to generate vertex-wise mappings between tau SUVR maps on the cortical surface. The generative model is designed to eliminate site-specific and tracer-specific artifacts while preserving biological individual variability. Using data from the ADNI and Health and Aging Brain Study-Health Disparities (HABS-HD) studies, the authors demonstrate that the diffusion-based mapping successfully produces harmonized SUVR maps with consistent pattern distributions across different PET tracers, facilitating more robust large-scale multi-site Alzheimer's research.
papers.venue: 2025 IEEE 22nd International Symposium on Biomedical Imaging (ISBI)
papers.authors: Jiaxin Yue, Jianwei Zhang, Lujia Zhong, Yonggang Shi

papers.title: Autoencoder for 4-Dimensional Fiber Orientation Distributions from Diffusion MRI
papers.abstract: The authors propose a 4D autoencoder architecture for the robust representation and denoising of fiber orientation distributions (FODs) in brain diffusion MRI. The FOD is modeled as a 4D signal defined across 3D spatial coordinates and spherical angular space, with angular components encoded via spherical harmonics. The autoencoder learns a high-fidelity latent manifold of physically plausible FOD profiles, enabling the restoration of corrupted FODs from sparse or low-quality acquisitions.
