Quantitative experiments on simulated and in vivo human datasets show that the 4D latent representation preserves fine-grained angular features more effectively than standard voxel-wise filtering, leading to significant improvements in the reconstruction of complex white matter fiber crossings and overall tractography reliability.
papers.venue: 2025 IEEE 22nd International Symposium on Biomedical Imaging (ISBI)
papers.authors: Shuo Huang, Lujia Zhong, Yonggang Shi

papers.title: Diffusion Model-based FOD Restoration from High Distortion in dMRI
papers.abstract: Susceptibility-induced echo-planar imaging (EPI) distortions in diffusion MRI frequently corrupt the reconstruction of fiber orientation distributions (FODs) in high-distortion regions such as the brain stem. This study introduces a generative restoration framework using conditional diffusion models to recover high-fidelity FODs. The framework utilizes volume-order encoding for spherical harmonic coefficients and cross-attention mechanisms to exploit inter-order dependencies. By conditioning the generative process on low-distortion neighboring regions and subject-specific anatomical templates, the model restores the geometric coherence of the FODs. Validation on UK Biobank data (n=1315) demonstrates that the method substantially reduces root mean square errors and angular peak errors, facilitating improved tractography performance in clinically significant brain stem regions.
papers.venue: Medical Image Computing and Computer Assisted Intervention – MICCAI 2024
papers.authors: Shuo Huang, Lujia Zhong, Yonggang Shi

0713.name: Yoshifumi Kitamura
0713.bio: Yoshifumi Kitamura is a Professor and Deputy Director at the Research Institute of Electrical Communication at Tohoku University and the Director of the Interdisciplinary ICT Research Center for Cyber and Real Spaces. Kitamura’s research investigates the technical and psychological dimensions of interactive content design, focusing on 3D user interfaces, virtual reality, and the transmission of non-verbal information. They have coordinated interdisciplinary projects, including the development of the DIEM-A database for analyzing cultural variations in emotional bodily expressions through motion capture and computer vision. Their work integrates sensory feedback and social neuroscience to develop technologies for remote human communication and spatial awareness.
0713.research_direction: Dr. Kitamura's recent work explores human-computer interaction across extended reality (XR) environments, physical-digital interfaces, and data visualization. They have recently been investigating how users physically interact with 3D spatial environments, designing novel bimanual VR controllers that restrict motion degrees of freedom to improve manipulation precision alongside passive haptic systems for high-fidelity surgical simulators. In the realm of behavior and human perception, their research examines how movement kinematics reflect underlying cognitive and affective states, utilizing spatial tracking in educational metaverse platforms and biological motion point-light displays to map cultural variations in emotional expression. Additionally, Dr. Kitamura is developing interactive focus-plus-context visualization interfaces to help researchers navigate complex confusion matrices and audit misclassification patterns in multiclass image recognition models.

papers.title: Objective Evaluation Metrics from Behavioral Logs in Metaverse-Based International Virtual Exchange: Total Movement Distance and Learners' Self-Reported Intercultural Understanding
papers.abstract: This research investigates the utility of quantitative behavioral logs as objective proxies for learning outcomes within metaverse-mediated international virtual exchanges. By extracting spatiotemporal data from VRChat session logs, the authors calculated 'Total Movement Distance' during student presentations as a behavioral indicator. Correlation analysis revealed moderate positive associations between physical movement metrics and learners' self-reported levels of active participation and the deepening of intercultural understanding. The findings suggest that passive behavioral tracking can provide scalable, objective insights into the effectiveness of educational interventions in immersive social platforms.
papers.venue: International Conference on Computers in Education (ICCE 2025)
papers.authors: Manato Abe, Masako Hayashi, Yoshifumi Kitamura

papers.title: SnapSteer: A Bimanual 3D Manipulation Interface with Limitable Motion Degrees of Freedom
papers.abstract: The SnapSteer framework addresses the precision limitations inherent in unconstrained six-degree-of-freedom (6-DOF) virtual object manipulation by introducing a bimanual constraint mechanism. The technique extends the conventional single-handed 'Robot Telekinesis' model by assigning a secondary VR controller the role of a motion-limiter. This allows users to dynamically restrict translational or rotational degrees of freedom (DOFs) along specific axes, enabling 'snapping' behavior for more accurate alignment tasks. Quantitative evaluations demonstrate that this coordinated bimanual approach significantly improves manipulation precision and reduces cognitive effort in complex three-dimensional spatial tasks compared to standard 6-DOF methods.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the 31st ACM Symposium on Virtual Reality Software and Technology (VRST 2025)
papers.authors: Yujian Fang, Manato Abe, Kazuyuki Fujita, Yoshifumi Kitamura

papers.title: VirtuEleDent: A Compact XR Tooth-Cutting Training System Using a Physical EMR-based Dental Handpiece and Teeth Model
papers.abstract: VirtuEleDent is a high-fidelity dental surgery simulator that utilizes a passive haptic approach to provide realistic tactile feedback without the bulk of active force-feedback hardware. The system integrates a physical 3D-printed dental model with a handpiece device equipped with electromagnetic resonance (EMR) and inertial measurement unit (IMU) sensors. This configuration enables precise six-degree-of-freedom tracking of the handpiece tip relative to the tooth anatomy, which is rendered in real-time within a mobile head-mounted display. Expert validation with licensed dentists indicated that the passive resistance provided by physical contact with the model significantly enhances training realism and haptic presence for complex tooth-drilling procedures.
papers.venue: 32nd IEEE Conference on Virtual Reality and 3D User Interfaces (IEEE VR 2025)
papers.authors: Yuhui Wang, Kazuki Takashima, Masamitsu Ito, Takeshi Kobori, Tomo Asakura, Kazuyuki Fujita, Guang Hong, Yoshifumi Kitamura

papers.title: ConfusionLens: Focus+Context Visualization Interface for Performance Analysis of Multiclass Image Classifiers
papers.abstract: ConfusionLens is a diagnostic visualization interface designed to facilitate the performance analysis of multiclass image classification models. To manage the high visual complexity of large confusion matrices, the system employs a focus+context technique that enables practitioners to interactively drill down into localized between-class confusion clusters while maintaining a global view of model performance. Controlled experiments demonstrate that the tool significantly reduces task completion times for identifying misclassification patterns and increases error-analysis accuracy. Further implementation of instance-level visualization extensions, developed based on expert feedback, suggests the interface is highly effective for auditing neural network failures and informing model refinement strategies.
papers.venue: ACM Transactions on Interactive Intelligent Systems (TiiS)
papers.authors: Kazuyuki Fujita, Keito Uwaseki, Hongyu Bu, Kazuki Takashima, Yoshifumi Kitamura

papers.title: Toward an Asian-based bodily movement database for emotional communication
papers.abstract: This research introduces the Diverse Intercultural E-Motion Database of Asian Performers (DIEM-A), a high-fidelity motion-capture repository aimed at correcting Western-centric biases in non-verbal communication research. The database includes 10,767 emotional movement recordings from 97 professional performers in Japan and Taiwan across 12 distinct emotional categories and multiple intensity levels. Perceptual experiments using biological motion (skeletal point-light displays) confirmed that human observers can reliably decode emotional valence from motion kinematics alone. The study highlights significant cultural variations in expressive intensity and movement dynamics, providing a standardized dataset for the development of cross-culturally robust affect recognition models and human-centric AI motion generators.
papers.authors: Miao Cheng, Chia-huei Tseng, Ken Fujiwara, Shoi Higashiyama, Abby Weng, Yoshifumi Kitamura

0714.name: Yoshiyuki Ueda
0714.department: Institute for the Future of Human Society
0714.bio: Yoshiyuki Ueda is an Associate Professor at Kyoto University's Institute for the Future of Human Society, where they investigate the cognitive and neural mechanisms underlying human attention, emotion, and social interaction. Ueda's research utilizes behavioral experiments, eye-tracking, and neuroimaging to examine how cultural contexts influence visual search and perceptual processes. Their research includes ensemble perception, facial expression adaptation, and the development of facial expression databases for psychological research. Their current work also encompasses the study of human-robot interaction and the psychological markers of social exclusion.
0714.research_direction: Dr. Ueda has recently been investigating a remarkably diverse array of psychological phenomena spanning visual cognition, human-robot interaction, and social behavior. In the visual domain, their recent work explores the boundary conditions of visuospatial memory—specifically how sequential focal attention enables Hebb repetition learning for spatial arrays—as well as the perceptual and neural mechanisms underlying face perception, norm-based coding, and social evaluation. Beyond fundamental vision and memory research, they are examining the cognitive and social dynamics of human-robot interaction, evaluating how a robot's conversational politeness and users' sequential cognitive appraisals shape technology acceptance and future engagement. Additionally, their behavioral research extends into health and social psychology, investigating how everyday interpersonal conflict and the dispositional need to belong interact to drive maladaptive outcomes like subclinical binge eating.

papers.title: Impact of politeness and performance quality of android robots on future interaction decisions: a conversational design perspective
papers.abstract: Across two scenario-based behavioral experiments, this study evaluated how an android robot's polite conversational register and behavioral conduct modulate users' subjective evaluations and willingness to engage in repeated interactions under conditions of successful task completion versus minor task failure, benchmarked against human agents. The empirical findings demonstrated that politeness significantly elevated overall interaction impressions and fostered optimistic expectations regarding future performance across both robotic and human interlocutors. Although the buffering effect of politeness on agent preference was attenuated for androids relative to humans following a failure, politeness preserved users' willingness to re-engage the robot by mitigating expectations of recurrence, underscoring the critical utility of polite conversational design in promoting resilient human–robot interaction.
papers.authors: Waka Saeki, Yoshiyuki Ueda

papers.title: Sequential model based on human cognitive processing to robot acceptance
papers.abstract: This work formulated a structured conceptual model of social robot acceptance grounded in the temporal dynamics of human cognitive processing. Moving beyond conventional static acceptance models, the proposed framework delineates how early sensory and morphological feature extraction (such as physical appearance and nonverbal cues) sequentially feeds into intermediate cognitive appraisals (including attributed intentionality, perceived competence, and social warmth), which in turn dictate affective evaluation and downstream behavioral adoption decisions. The model provides an analytical framework identifying the cognitive bottlenecks where interactive or communicative failures disrupt user trust and technology adoption trajectories.
papers.authors: Waka Saeki, Yoshiyuki Ueda

papers.title: Effect of interpersonal conflicts and the moderating effect of the dispositional need to belong on binge eating
papers.abstract: This investigation examined the relationship between acute interpersonal conflict stress and subclinical binge eating frequency, evaluating the moderating function of the dispositional need to belong (dNTB) across two empirical studies in non-clinical cohorts. Psychometric evaluations of everyday social conflict interactions and eating episodes demonstrated that relational strain significantly predicted elevated binge eating propensity. Furthermore, dNTB significantly moderated this dynamic: individuals exhibiting high dNTB demonstrated heightened vulnerability to compensatory overeating following interpersonal friction, indicating that high baseline relational affiliation motivation interacts with interpersonal stress to trigger maladaptive eating behaviors before reaching clinical diagnostic thresholds.
papers.authors: Michihiro Kaneko, Yoshiyuki Ueda

papers.title: Sequential processing facilitates Hebb repetition learning in visuospatial domains
papers.abstract: Across a series of behavioral experiments, this study examined the boundary conditions governing Hebb repetition learning in the visuospatial domain, testing whether long-term serial order representations emerge from spatial arrays. While repetition learning is robust in auditory-verbal domains, visuospatial learning often fails under simultaneous visual presentation. By enforcing sequential focal attention across discrete spatial locations, the paradigm elicited robust visuospatial Hebb repetition effects comparable in magnitude and rate to verbal memory consolidation. The results establish that serial attentional prioritization constitutes a critical early temporal bottleneck for chunking and transferring serial order information into long-term representations, demonstrating cross-modal functional invariance in repetition learning mechanisms.
papers.authors: Yoshiyuki Ueda, Tsung-Ren Huang, Zixin Shen, Chifumi Sakata, Su-Ling Yeh, Satoru Saito

papers.title: Editorial: Recent advances and future directions in facial appearance research
papers.abstract: This editorial synthesizes contemporary methodological advancements and theoretical paradigms in the study of facial appearance, perceptual representation, and social evaluation. It reviews evidence examining multidimensional face-space structure, norm-based visual coding, ensemble summary statistics, and adaptation-induced aftereffects across neurotypical and atypical populations. Furthermore, it outlines neuroimaging evidence regarding the engagement of object-selective ventral occipitotemporal cortex during the processing of facial distortions and highlights the neural and cognitive mechanisms translating facial attractiveness and social signals into long-term interpersonal attraction within ecologically valid experimental settings.
papers.authors: Yoshiyuki Ueda, Koyo Nakamura, Chihiro Saegusa, Ayahito Ito

0715.name: Yuanning Li
0715.lab_name: Computational Cognitive and Translational Neuroscience Lab (CCTN Lab)
0715.bio: Yuanning Li is an Assistant Professor at ShanghaiTech University who researches the neural mechanisms of high-level cognitive processes, including speech, language, and vision. Li's work uses intracranial electrophysiology (ECoG/iEEG) and functional neuroimaging to investigate how sensory and semantic information is represented across neural populations. By integrating statistical machine learning and deep neural networks, they develop computational models for neural encoding and decoding to support brain-computer interface (BCI) applications. Li completed a postdoctoral fellowship at UCSF focused on speech neurophysiology and a doctoral dissertation at Carnegie Mellon University concerning the human ventral visual pathway.
0715.research_direction: Dr. Li's recent work explores the neural mechanisms of naturalistic perception and the development of advanced brain-computer interfaces for speech decoding. Using intracranial recordings (ECoG) alongside deep learning frameworks, they have recently been investigating how to reconstruct high-fidelity and tonal speech directly from cortical activity while mapping the representational alignment between the human language network and self-supervised AI models. Broadening their focus to cross-modal sensory integration, they are also studying predictive coding phenomena, specifically asking how top-down linguistic contexts dynamically modulate neural responses in the early visual cortex. Complementing this cognitive neurophysiology, Dr. Li develops biologically inspired spiking neural networks that mimic mammalian brainstem mechanisms to perform computationally efficient spatial audio processing.

papers.title: ITD-aware Binaural Spiking Networks for Sound Source Localization
papers.abstract: The paper proposes a biologically inspired spiking neural network (SNN) architecture tailored for sound source localization (SSL) by specifically leveraging interaural time difference (ITD) cues, mimicking the processing mechanisms found in the mammalian brainstem. The model employs leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) neurons and local synaptic learning rules to extract azimuthal features from binaural audio. Evaluations in reverberant and high-noise environments demonstrate that the ITD-aware SNN achieves robust localization accuracy with significantly lower computational and power overhead compared to conventional deep neural network (DNN) architectures. This work underscores the efficacy of temporal spike dynamics in reproducing specialized auditory perception for neuromorphic applications.
papers.venue: IEEE International Conference on Acoustics, Speech and Signal Processing (ICASSP 2026)
papers.authors: Nanjun Ye, Li Fu, Yuanning Li

papers.title: High-Fidelity Neural Speech Reconstruction through an Efficient Acoustic-Linguistic Dual-Pathway Framework
papers.abstract: This research presents a high-performance brain-computer interface (BCI) system for decoding naturalistic speech from human intracranial electrocorticography (ECoG). The authors developed a dual-pathway framework that concurrently models acoustic prosody and linguistic intelligibility by aligning cortical features with the latent spaces of pre-trained self-supervised models (e.g., Wav2Vec 2.0) and high-fidelity generative decoders (e.g., HiFi-GAN and Parler-TTS). This transfer learning approach allows for high-fidelity speech synthesis using limited subject-specific neural recordings (~20 minutes). Perceptual and objective metrics indicate significant improvements in phoneme error rates and speech naturalness, demonstrating the potential for restoring intelligible communication with personalized voice characteristics.
papers.authors: Jiawei Li, Chunxu Guo, Chao Zhang, Edward F. Chang, Yuanning Li

papers.title: Predictive vision-language integration in the human visual cortex
papers.abstract: This study investigates the neural substrates of cross-modal semantic integration using human fMRI and intracranial electrophysiology. By applying deep learning-based encoding models (LLMs and Vision Transformers), the authors demonstrate that linguistic context modulates neural response patterns in the early visual cortex (EVC). The study identifies distinct neuronal populations in the ventral stream that undergo semantic-driven enhancement or suppression, consistent with a predictive coding framework where linguistic priors act as top-down signals to shape visual representations. Spatiotemporal analysis reveals that these cross-modal semantic interactions occur early in the processing hierarchy, suggesting that the visual cortex is dynamically reweighted by linguistic information during naturalistic perception.
papers.authors: Shurui Li, Zheyu Jin, Ru-Yuan Zhang, Shi Gu, Yuanning Li

papers.title: Optimizing Tonal Speech Decoding from Electrocorticography with a Multi-band Ensemble Network
papers.abstract: Decoding tonal languages like Mandarin for BCIs is complex because lexical meaning depends on fundamental frequency (F0) contours. This study introduces an ensemble neural network architecture designed to integrate features across multiple frequency bands of the electrocorticogram (ECoG), including both high-gamma power and lower-frequency spectral components. By optimizing the fusion of these multi-band features, the framework captures both the articulatory phonetics and the laryngeal dynamics associated with tone. Experimental results show a marked increase in syllable and lexical tone decoding accuracy compared to traditional single-band models, establishing a more effective approach for Mandarin-specific neural-to-speech decoding systems.
papers.venue: 12th Annual IEEE International Conference on Neural Engineering (NER 25)
papers.authors: Peixi Yu, Youran Mu, Zhenjie Wang, Daohan Zhang, Junfeng Lu, Yuanning Li

papers.title: Convergent representations and spatiotemporal dynamics of speech and language in brain and deep neural networks
papers.abstract: This paper quantifies the representational alignment between self-supervised deep neural networks (DNNs) and the human language network during natural speech perception. Utilizing high-density intracranial recordings (ECoG), the authors assessed the similarity between neural activity and the internal representations of speech (Wav2Vec 2.0) and text (GPT-2) models. They found that shared contextual components between the two modalities explain the majority of brain-model alignment in high-order temporal and prefrontal areas. The study further identified distinct spatiotemporal peaks: an early predictive signal (40ms pre-onset) in the mid-STG and a later acoustic-phonetic peak (200ms post-onset) in the posterior STG, providing a hierarchical map of how artificial and biological systems convergently process linguistic information.
papers.authors: Peili Chen, Shiji Xiang, Linyang He, Edward F. Chang, Yuanning Li

0717.name: Yuka Sasaki
0717.department: Department of Cognitive, Linguistic, and Psychological Sciences
0717.lab_name: Laboratory for Cognitive and Perceptual Learning
0717.bio: Yuka Sasaki is a Professor of Cognitive, Linguistic, and Psychological Sciences (Research) at Brown University and the sub-director of the Laboratory for Cognitive and Perceptual Learning. Sasaki investigates the neural mechanisms of human brain plasticity and the role sleep plays in the consolidation and stabilization of visual learning. Using an approach that combines psychophysics with polysomnography, fMRI, and magnetic resonance spectroscopy, they examine how excitatory and inhibitory neurotransmitter concentrations modulate learning during NREM and REM sleep. Sasaki's research describes how sleep stabilizes new perceptual skills against retrograde interference and explores the 'first-night effect' in human sleep architecture.
0717.research_direction: Dr. Sasaki's recent work explores the neural mechanisms governing perceptual learning and memory consolidation, with a distinct focus on how the human brain balances cortical plasticity and stability. They have recently been investigating how different sleep stages—namely NREM and REM—as well as environmental disruptions like the "first-night effect" uniquely modulate the excitation-inhibition (E/I) balance within sensory and prefrontal networks. By employing multimodal neuroimaging techniques such as polysomnography, EEG, and magnetic resonance spectroscopy (1H-MRS), their research tracks shifting in vivo neurotransmitter ratios of glutamate to GABA to understand how these dynamics facilitate the acquisition and long-term stabilization of new visual and temporal skills. Additionally, they are working to validate non-invasive electrophysiological markers of this cortical neurochemistry to better measure these continuous learning and consolidation processes in human subjects.

papers.title: Unconscious switching of dorsal and medial pathways for plasticity and stability during NREM and REM sleep
papers.abstract: This study identifies a dual-pathway prefrontal architecture that regulates visual perceptual learning (VPL) during sleep. Through longitudinal neuroimaging, the authors demonstrate that the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) and medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) contribute differentially to learning depending on sleep stage. During NREM sleep, the DLPFC-EVA (early visual area) pathway exhibits increased E/I balance, signifying heightened plasticity, which correlates with significant offline performance gains. Conversely, during REM sleep, the mPFC-EVA pathway demonstrates reduced E/I balance, signifying increased stability, which is linked to enhanced resilience against retrograde interference from subsequent learning. These results suggest that the human brain automatically alternates between dorsal and medial prefrontal circuits to improve and secure newly acquired visual skills without conscious awareness.
papers.authors: Takashi Yamada, Theodore LaBonte-Clark, Nitzan Censor, Takeo Watanabe, Yuka Sasaki

papers.title: Concurrent multimodal estimation of cortical excitation and inhibition shows that EEG-based estimates are linked to the ratio of glutamate to GABA
papers.abstract: This research validates several proposed electroencephalography (EEG)-based indices of the cortical excitation/inhibition (E/I) ratio by comparing them with direct neurotransmitter measurements obtained via 1H-magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS). By performing concurrent EEG and MRS in human subjects over the early visual cortex, the authors evaluated candidate algorithms, including those derived from neural mass models, 1/f spectral slope, and criticality theory. The findings reveal that a criticality-based algorithm analyzing temporal dynamics in the alpha band (functional E/I) exhibits the strongest correspondence with the Glutamate-to-GABA ratio at the between-subjects level. This study provides empirical support for using non-invasive EEG measures as a proxy for cortical neurochemistry in cognitive and clinical neuroscience.
papers.authors: Aaron Cochrane, Luke Rosedahl, Masako Tamaki, Takeo Watanabe, Yuka Sasaki

papers.title: First-night effect reduces the beneficial effects of sleep on visual plasticity and modifies the underlying neurochemical processes
papers.abstract: The investigation utilized a within-subject paradigm to explore how the first-night effect (FNE)—the transient sleep disturbance experienced in novel environments—impacts cortical plasticity and memory consolidation. Using polysomnography and 1H-MRS, the researchers quantified changes in the glutamate/GABA (E/I) ratio in the early visual areas (EVA) during sleep. Results demonstrated that the FNE significantly attenuated both overnight performance improvements in a visual perceptual learning (VPL) task and the learning-dependent increase of the E/I ratio typically observed during NREM sleep. These findings indicate that the vigilant state associated with a novel environment disrupts the fundamental neurochemical transitions in the sensory cortex required for successful sleep-dependent plasticity.
papers.authors: Masako Tamaki, Takashi Yamada, Tyler Barnes-Diana, Zhiyan Wang, Takeo Watanabe, Yuka Sasaki

papers.title: Shift in excitation-inhibition balance underlies perceptual learning of temporal discrimination
papers.abstract: This study examined the neuroplastic correlates of temporal perceptual learning (TPL) during an auditory sub-second interval discrimination task. Participants underwent five days of training while the excitation-to-inhibition (E/I) ratio was monitored via 1H-MRS in the right inferior parietal cortex (IPC) and the primary auditory cortex (A1). A significant elevation in the functional E/I ratio was observed in the right IPC during the early learning phase, which returned to baseline levels as timing precision reached an asymptote. No comparable neurochemical shifts were found in A1, suggesting that high-order parietal regions, rather than primary sensory areas, serve as the primary site for the acquisition and stabilization of temporal interval representations.
papers.authors: Rannie Xu, Edward G. Walsh, Takeo Watanabe, Yuka Sasaki

papers.title: Plasticity–stability dynamics during post-training processing of learning
papers.abstract: This review synthesizes recent findings on the neural mechanisms governing the transition between a plastic state optimized for learning and a stable state that resists interference. The authors propose a cyclical model of plasticity-stability dynamics where post-training processing modulates the cortical excitation/inhibition (E/I) balance in a task-specific manner. Training triggers a rapid increase in the E/I ratio (plasticity) within relevant sensory areas, followed by a decrease toward baseline levels during stabilization or a shift toward inhibitory dominance during hyperstabilization. The article highlights the stage-specific contributions of non-REM and REM sleep to these dynamics, with NREM facilitating plasticity-dependent gains and REM promoting neurochemical stabilization.
papers.authors: Takashi Yamada, Takeo Watanabe, Yuka Sasaki

0718.name: Zaghloul Kareem
0718.bio: Zaghloul serves as the Chief of the Surgical Neurology Branch and directs the Functional and Restorative Neurosurgery Unit at the National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke. Their research utilizes intracranial electrical recordings, including electrocorticography and single-unit microelectrode arrays, to investigate the neural mechanisms underlying human episodic memory, decision-making, and visual working memory. By utilizing clinical neurosurgical procedures such as epilepsy monitoring and deep brain stimulation, Zaghloul’s laboratory characterizes the spatiotemporal patterns of neural activity and neuronal spiking sequences involved in memory encoding and retrieval. Their work integrates computational modeling and signal processing to decode the functional organization of human cortical and subcortical networks and identifies how specific neural patterns are reinstated during recall and how the basal ganglia modulate cognitive circuits.
0718.research_direction: Dr. Zaghloul has recently been investigating the high-resolution neural dynamics that underlie human episodic memory, semantic representation, and cortical pathologies using intracranial EEG and micro-electrode recordings. Their recent work explores how precise, temporal sequences of single-unit spiking in the anterior temporal lobe encode visual categories and semantic information, and how top-down attention refines the fidelity of these neuronal sequences during memory encoding. At the broader network level, they are examining how sub-second fluctuations in functional connectivity form unique episodic memory traces, alongside probing the specific role of the parahippocampal cortex in consolidating scene-selective visual memories. Furthermore, Dr. Zaghloul investigates how these delicate representational codes are disrupted in clinical conditions, mapping how focal seizures entrain cortical spiking into rigid, spatiotemporally organized traveling waves.

papers.title: Attention to memory content enhances single-unit spike sequence fidelity in the human anterior temporal lobe
papers.abstract: The research utilizes single-unit recordings in the human anterior temporal lobe (ATL) to examine how top-down attentional prioritization of memory content modulates the temporal structure of neuronal activity. The authors identify that higher-level semantic information is represented by temporally organized sequences of spikes that occur repeatedly during word processing. Goal-directed attention directed at prioritizing specific items for memory significantly increases the fidelity and temporal consistency of these spike sequences during encoding. Furthermore, retroactive attentional cueing evokes the replay of these stereotypical sequences, suggesting that attentional mechanisms enhance the representational precision of semantic information by refining the temporal coordination of population spiking in the ATL.
papers.authors: Kelsey K. Sundby, Alex P. Vaz, John H. Wittig Jr, Samantha N. Jackson, Sara K. Inati, Kareem A. Zaghloul

papers.title: The role of the parahippocampal cortex in memory consolidation for scenes
papers.abstract: This study investigates the mechanistic contribution of scene-selective neocortical regions, specifically the posterior parahippocampal cortex (PHC), to the systems-level consolidation of visual episodic memories. Utilizing intracranial EEG (iEEG) and a rare clinical opportunity involving PHC resection, the researchers assessed category-specific memory deficits post-operatively. Results revealed a significant, time-dependent attenuation of visual memory specifically for scene stimuli following PHC lesioning, an effect not attributable to impairments in initial encoding. The findings suggest that the reactivation of stimulus-specific representations within specialized neocortical modules is a critical component of the consolidation process required to transform transient perceptual experiences into stable long-term representations in the medial temporal lobe.
papers.authors: Weizhen Xie, Susan G. Wardle, Jenna Langbein, Oceane Fruchet, Molly Baumhauer, Audrey Phan, Ai Phuong Tong, Shruti Japee, Sara K. Inati, Chris I. Baker, Kareem A. Zaghloul

papers.title: Dynamic patterns of functional connectivity in the human brain underlie individual memory formation
papers.abstract: Leveraging the high temporal resolution of intracranial EEG, this study identifies sub-second fluctuations in functional connectivity that subserve episodic memory formation. By quantifying phase-locked correlations between neocortical electrode pairs during a verbal paired-associates task, the authors found that successful encoding of specific word pairs is associated with unique, reproducible patterns of dynamic functional coupling. These stimulus-specific connectivity configurations are transiently established during encoding and significantly reinstated during successful memory retrieval. The data provide direct evidence that specific, dynamic configurations of the human functional connectome constitute the neural substrate for individual episodic memory traces.
papers.authors: Audrey T. Phan, Weizhen Xie, Julio I. Chapeton, Sara K. Inati, Kareem A. Zaghloul

papers.title: Focal seizures induce spatiotemporally organized spiking activity in the human cortex
papers.abstract: The study characterizes the impact of focal ictal activity on neural population coding by recording cortical multi-unit activity (MUA) in participants undergoing seizure monitoring. The researchers found that pathological discharges during focal seizures are accompanied by population spiking bursts organized into highly consistent and stereotyped temporal sequences. As seizures evolve, these spiking motifs diverge from baseline patterns and develop a pronounced spatial organization that corresponds to the propagation direction of ictal traveling waves. The results suggest that focal seizures entrain cortical spiking into rigid, spatially organized motifs, providing a neurophysiological mechanism by which seizures disrupt representational coding and drive clinical symptomatology.
papers.authors: Joshua M. Diamond, Julio I. Chapeton, Weizhen Xie, Samantha N. Jackson, Sara K. Inati, Kareem A. Zaghloul

papers.title: Neuronal sequences in population bursts encode information in human cortex
papers.abstract: This study investigates the information-bearing capacity of temporal spiking sequences in the human anterior temporal lobe (ATL) using micro-electrode array recordings during a visual categorization paradigm. The authors demonstrate that population spiking activity organizes into discrete bursts, where the specific temporal order of neuronal firing reliably encodes both stimulus categories and individual exemplars. This sequence-based code is separable from and complements traditional representations based on spike rates or latencies. These findings suggest that the human brain utilizes precise neuronal sequences within population bursts as a fundamental neural code for representing higher-order semantic information in the neocortex.
papers.authors: Weizhen Xie, John H. Wittig Jr, Julio I. Chapeton, Mostafa El-Kalliny, Samantha N. Jackson, Sara K. Inati, Kareem A. Zaghloul

0719.name: Zaifeng Gao
0719.department: Department of Psychology and Behavioral Sciences
0719.main_research_area: visual working memory and biological motion
0719.bio: Gao is a Professor of Psychology and Human Factors at Zhejiang University and investigates the cognitive and neural architectures of visual working memory. Their research focuses on the encoding and retention mechanisms of visual information, emphasizing complex dynamic events such as biological motion and object-based attention. Utilizing behavioral experiments, functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), and electroencephalography (EEG), Gao examines how attention and memory load interact during visual processing. Additionally, their work extends into human factors and human-AI interaction, exploring trust calibration and situational awareness in automated driving systems.
0719.research_direction: Dr. Gao has recently been investigating human cognition across a broad spectrum, ranging from the fundamental neural architecture of working memory to the complex dynamics of human-AI collaboration. In their foundational cognitive research, they use psychophysics and fMRI to explore the "event cache," probing whether the short-term maintenance of dynamic visual events relies on distinct neural networks—specifically within the cerebellum—compared to traditional static object storage. Concurrently, their recent work explores the psychological and sociotechnical dimensions of human-machine interaction, examining how manipulating an autonomous agent's perceived mind and agency influences human trust and cooperative behavior during joint decision-making tasks. Broadening this focus to systems design, they are also developing comprehensive human-centered AI frameworks to evaluate how natural gestural interfaces, shared situational awareness, and balanced authority distribution can optimize teaming between humans and intelligent systems.

papers.title: Event cache: An independent component in working memory
papers.abstract: This study characterizes the 'event cache' as a functionally discrete component of the human working memory (WM) architecture, distinct from traditional object-based storage. Utilizing a multi-methodological approach involving psychophysical experiments, confirmatory factor analysis (CFA), and functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), the research demonstrates that event maintenance relies on neural correlates separable from those of object storage. Results emphasize the essential role of the cerebellar network, specifically identifying the left cerebellum Crus I as a critical hub for the encoding and retention of event-based information. These findings challenge monolithic WM models by providing empirical evidence for an independent sub-component dedicated to event representation, which is not merely a byproduct of stimulus motion.
papers.authors: Hui Zhou, Jinglan Wu, Jiaofeng Li, Zhihe Pan, Jinying Lu, Mowei Shen, Tengfei Wang, Yuzheng Hu, Zaifeng Gao

papers.title: PATE Model: A 30-Year Review and Analysis of Gestural Interaction Research
papers.abstract: Through a systematic PRISMA-guided literature review of 197 articles published over three decades, this paper establishes the Person-Action-Target-Environment (PATE) model to synthesize the evolution of gestural interaction research. The analysis reveals a paradigm shift from technical functionality and performance metrics toward a human-centered user experience (UX) focus. The study identifies 40 discrete influencing factors categorized into 10 groups, and proposes four critical evaluative dimensions: efficiency, ease of use, subjective experience, and tolerance degree. This structured framework serves as a theoretical foundation for designing and evaluating natural user interfaces (NUIs) within complex sociotechnical contexts.
papers.authors: Xiaojiao Chen, Jiayi Zhang, Yuanxiu Zhao, Qi Chen, Bolin Chen, Nan Xu, Entong Jin, Yi Shen, Yu Tian, Mowei Shen, Zaifeng Gao

papers.title: Are Humans Willing to Cooperate with Robots? Decision-Making Effects in Human-Robot Cooperation from the Perspective of Mind Perception Theory
papers.abstract: This investigation applies mind perception theory to examine the psychological determinants of human-robot cooperation in collaborative decision-making environments. By manipulating the perceived agency and experience of robotic partners, the researchers quantify how the attribution of mental states modulates human cooperative behavior and trust. The study utilizes behavioral metrics to evaluate how anthropomorphic cues and perceived intentionality affect the strategic alignment of human participants during joint tasks. The findings suggest that mind perception serves as a critical mediator in human-robot teaming, providing a theoretical basis for enhancing the social intelligence and collaborative efficacy of autonomous agents.
papers.authors: Yuanxiu Zhao, Qihang Zhou, Jiaofeng Li, Zaifeng Gao

papers.title: An Intelligent Sociotechnical Systems (iSTS) Framework: Enabling a Hierarchical Human-Centered AI (hHCAI) Approach
papers.abstract: To address the limitations of technology-centered AI development—such as algorithmic bias and opacity—this paper introduces the Intelligent Sociotechnical Systems (iSTS) framework. This model extends traditional sociotechnical systems (STS) theory by incorporating the unique dynamics of autonomous intelligent agents. The authors propose a hierarchical human-centered AI (hHCAI) methodology that prioritizes human leadership and social fairness within the design lifecycle. By integrating technology, human factors, and ethical considerations, the framework provides a structured systems engineering approach to develop AI applications that are robust, explainable, and aligned with human values.
papers.venue: IEEE Transactions on Technology and Society
papers.authors: Wei Xu, Zaifeng Gao

papers.title: Human-Centered Human-AI Collaboration (HCHAC)
papers.abstract: This work redefines the human-intelligence relationship as a bidirectional partnership within a joint cognitive system (JCS). Moving beyond unidirectional automation, the paper proposes a Human-Centered Human-AI Collaboration (HCHAC) framework based on an Input-Mediator-Outcome (IMO) model. It synthesizes current research in human-AI teaming to identify critical mediators of collaborative success, including shared situation awareness, trust calibration, and authority distribution. A case study in autonomous vehicle navigation is presented to demonstrate the practical application of the HCHAC framework, highlighting how human-centered design principles enhance team-level performance and system resilience in complex operational domains.
papers.authors: Qi Gao, Wei Xu, Hanxi Pan, Mowei Shen, Zaifeng Gao

0721.name: Zeynep M. Saygin
0721.bio: Saygin investigates the neuroanatomical foundations of cognitive specialization, focusing on how structural connectivity fingerprints determine the functional organization of the cortex during early development. Their research employs multimodal neuroimaging techniques, including diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) and functional MRI, combined with longitudinal assessments and computational modeling. Saygin developed methods to predict the emergence of category-selective visual areas and linguistic networks in children using pre-existing structural markers. Their current research program focuses on developing predictive models for clinical outcomes and understanding brain plasticity following adverse experiences or neonatal brain trauma.
0721.research_direction: Dr. Saygin has recently been investigating the functional organization and development of specialized cortical networks, with a primary focus on how category-selective regions in the ventral temporal cortex (VTC) support rapid object recognition. Using precision fMRI, their recent work explores the developmental trajectory of functional specialization in early childhood—specifically mapping the dissociation between core language and domain-general cognitive networks—while also interrogating the visual, auditory, and attentional response profiles of the Visual Word Form Area. Beyond high-level vision and language mapping, Dr. Saygin is examining how heightened physiological arousal from specific auditory triggers (misophonia) impacts concurrent higher-order social perception and face memory. Additionally, they are actively evaluating the precise structural and functional network effects of emerging non-invasive neuromodulation techniques, utilizing multimodal MRI to compare transcranial photobiomodulation against magnetic stimulation.

papers.title: Pilot study comparing effects of infrared neuromodulation and transcranial magnetic stimulation using magnetic resonance imaging
papers.abstract: This within-subjects pilot investigation utilized multimodal magnetic resonance imaging to evaluate the neuromodulatory effects of 1064 nm transcranial photobiomodulation (tPBM) versus high-frequency transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) on the human somatomotor cortex. By analyzing both task-evoked fMRI during a motor task and resting-state structural and functional connectivity, the study found that while both tPBM and TMS significantly augmented activation within the left somatomotor region, tPBM uniquely induced trending enhancements in structural (fractional anisotropy) and functional connectivity between the primary motor cortex (M1) and nodes within the striatal-thalamic pathway. These preliminary results suggest that tPBM may exert superior influence on remote connected nodes within the somatomotor circuitry compared to TMS.
papers.authors: Sophia A. Bibb, Emily J. Yu, M. Fiona Molloy, John LaRocco, Patricia Resnick, Kevin Reeves, K. Luan Phan, Sanjay Krishna, Zeynep M. Saygin

papers.title: Leveraging ventral temporal cortex's primary role in object recognition
papers.abstract: This article discusses the fundamental role of category-selective regions within the ventral temporal cortex (VTC) in supporting complex human behavior and development. Challenging contemporary proposals to shift neuroimaging paradigms entirely toward behavioral relevance, the authors argue that the VTC's modular organization facilitates rapid, initial object recognition computations that occur on a faster timescale than goal-directed modulation. They posit that category selectivity serves as a critical foundation for VTC information processing and advocate for future research that explores how these specialized visual representations are transferred to and integrated with other cortical regions to facilitate flexible behavioral outcomes.
papers.authors: Kelly J. Hiersche, Zeynep M. Saygin

papers.title: Demystifying the Visual Word Form Area: Precision fMRI of Visual, Linguistic, and Attentional Properties of Ventral Temporal Cortex
papers.abstract: Employing precision functional magnetic resonance imaging, this study interrogated the functional response profile of the visual word form area (VWFA) in the left ventrotemporal cortex (VTC) across an array of visual categories and auditory linguistic tasks. The investigation revealed that the VWFA exhibits a unique responsiveness to auditory language compared to adjacent category-selective regions, yet these responses are substantially smaller than its activation to visual words and even non-preferred visual categories. Furthermore, the region did not demonstrate generalized sensitivity to attentional demand. These findings clarify that the VWFA is not an amodal language node but rather a specialized visual interface that maintains consistent category selectivity while integrating with the broader frontotemporal language network.
papers.authors: Jin Li, Kelly Hiersche, Zeynep M. Saygin

papers.title: The effect of misophonia on cognitive and social judgments
papers.abstract: This study explored the impact of misophonia—a heightened aversion to specific environmental sounds—on higher-order social and cognitive processing using a multi-phase behavioral paradigm with individualized auditory triggers. Participants with misophonia exhibited increased reaction times during gender-judgment tasks for faces paired with trigger sounds and subsequently assigned lower likeability ratings and showed degraded mnemonic recognition for those specific faces compared to control participants. These findings indicate that the distress and physiological arousal characteristic of misophonia impair concurrent cognitive and social functions, demonstrating that the adverse effects of trigger exposure generalize to social perception and memory encoding in affected individuals.
papers.authors: Heather A. Hansen, Andrew B. Leber, Zeynep M. Saygin

papers.title: Functional dissociation of the language network and other cognition in early childhood
papers.abstract: Utilizing precision fMRI in a pediatric cohort (ages 2–9), this study mapped the functional specialization and connectivity of the core language network and the domain-general Multiple Demand (MD) network. The results demonstrated a robust double dissociation between these systems in early childhood: the language network responded selectively to auditory sentences but not to spatial working memory load, while the adjacent MD network showed the inverse pattern. Longitudinal and cross-sectional analyses revealed that while functional language selectivity increases with age, the underlying connectivity fingerprints for these networks are stable and distinguishable very early in development, suggesting that innate or early-emerging structural connectivity scaffolds the subsequent functional maturation of specialized cognitive domains.
papers.authors: Kelly J. Hiersche, Eliana Schettini, Jin Li, Zeynep M. Saygin

0723.name: Zhong-Lin Lu
0723.lab_name: NYU-ECNU Institute of Brain and Cognitive Science
0723.bio: Zhong-Lin Lu is a Professor of Neuroscience at NYU Shanghai whose research integrates psychophysical experimentation, functional brain imaging, and computational modeling to investigate human perception and cognition. Lu developed the three-system theory of visual motion perception and the incremental reweighting model of perceptual learning. Their current work focuses on applying hierarchical Bayesian models to develop adaptive testing methods, such as the quick Contrast Sensitivity Function (qCSF), for diagnosing visual deficits in clinical settings. Lu also examines the neural mechanisms of attention and the rehabilitation of sensory impairments in individuals with amblyopia, myopia, and dyslexia.
0723.research_direction: Dr. Lu has recently been developing advanced computational frameworks and quantitative psychophysical paradigms to study both basic cortical architecture and applied visual function. In their neuroimaging work, their recent research explores ways to optimize fMRI-based retinotopic mapping, utilizing techniques like variational inference and Gaussian process regression to dramatically accelerate population receptive field (pRF) modeling and rigorously quantify spatial parameter uncertainty across visual areas. Parallel to this methodological work, they are actively investigating how age-related changes in multidimensional vision impact real-world behaviors. Specifically, their clinical studies use rapid psychophysical assessments of contrast sensitivity, visual acuity, and visual field maps to evaluate how challenging lighting conditions, such as mesopic environments and glare, affect simulated driving performance and safety in older adults.

papers.title: Uncertainty in population receptive field estimates revealed by variational qPRF
papers.abstract: This study introduces variational qPRF, a variational inference framework designed to quantify the posterior uncertainty of population receptive field (pRF) parameter estimates in fMRI. Traditional pRF modeling focuses on point estimates (position and size), which neglects the reliability of these parameters. By approximating the complex joint posterior distribution of the pRF model using a computationally efficient variational approach, the method provides a precise measure of parameter variance across the cortical surface. Validation using simulated and Human Connectome Project (HCP) datasets demonstrated that variational qPRF successfully recovers ground-truth uncertainty and reveals that pRF reliability varies significantly across visual areas and eccentricities, offering a robust statistical tool for assessing the fidelity of retinotopic mapping.
papers.authors: Sebastian Waz, Yalin Wang, Zhong-Lin Lu

papers.title: Quantification of retinotopic maps with a Gaussian process modeling
papers.abstract: The authors present a novel computational methodology to quantify the topological structure of retinotopic maps on the human cortical surface using blood oxygenation level-dependent (BOLD) fMRI signals. Addressing the challenges of low signal-to-noise ratios and limited spatial resolution that often lead to topological violations in standard population receptive field (pRF) modeling, the study implements three innovations: extended polar angle parametrization, the utilization of cortical anchor points, and a Gaussian process (GP) regression model for map estimation. Evaluation on 181 subjects from the Human Connectome Project (HCP) showed that the GP model significantly outperformed linear regression, reducing topological violations from 49.2% to 31.5% and improving generalization error, thereby establishing a more accurate objective foundation for delineating visual area boundaries.
papers.authors: Sebastian Waz, Zhong-Lin Lu

papers.title: Assessment of visual function under various lighting conditions in a cohort of active older drivers: dimensionality and principal metrics
papers.abstract: This clinical study explores the multidimensional nature of functional vision in active older drivers (n=20, mean age 70) by systematically evaluating visual acuity (VA), the contrast sensitivity function (CSF), and the visual field map (VFM) across photopic, mesopic, and mesopic-with-glare conditions. Using quantitative psychophysical procedures (qVA, qCSF, and qVFM), the researchers employed Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to identify the essential metrics for comprehensive vision assessment. Results demonstrated that while mesopic VA captured 47% of the total variance, a four-metric set was required to account for 90% of the variation. The findings underscore that traditional photopic acuity testing is insufficient for characterizing age-related declines in low-light and glare sensitivity, which are critical for nighttime driving safety.
papers.authors: Deyue Yu, Landon Perry, Thomas Kerwin, Jingzhen Yang, Zhong-Lin Lu

papers.title: qPRF: A system to accelerate population receptive field modeling
papers.abstract: This paper describes the qPRF (quick PRF) system, a high-performance software architecture designed to accelerate the computation of population receptive field (pRF) models in fMRI data analysis. pRF modeling is traditionally a time-intensive process, often requiring days for small cohorts. The qPRF system achieves a speedup factor exceeding 1,000 compared to conventional toolboxes by utilizing a specially designed searchable tree structure and an efficient search algorithm to optimize the five-parameter pRF model. Benchmarked against Human Connectome Project (HCP) data (181 subjects), qPRF demonstrated negligible differences in median variance explained (R²) while dramatically reducing processing time, facilitating the application of more complex visual neuroscientific models and large-scale clinical dataset analysis.
papers.authors: Sebastian Waz, Yalin Wang, Zhong-Lin Lu

papers.title: Visual Function and Driving Performance Under Different Lighting Conditions in Older Drivers: Preliminary Results From an Observational Study
papers.abstract: This observational study evaluated the correlation between psychophysical measures of visual function and high-fidelity simulated driving performance in drivers aged 60 and older. Participants underwent quantitative testing of visual acuity (VA), contrast sensitivity (qCSF), and visual field maps (qVFM) across photopic, mesopic, and mesopic-with-glare conditions. These metrics were analyzed alongside driving performance indicators, including average speed, standard deviation of lane position (SDLP), and reaction times. The results revealed that while photopic VA and CSF were associated with overall lane-keeping ability, mesopic-specific visual deficits and glare sensitivity were significantly stronger predictors of nighttime driving impairments and delayed reaction times, suggesting that non-standard vision tests are critical for identifying crash risks in the geriatric population.
papers.authors: Jingzhen Yang, Enas Alshaikh, Deyue Yu, Thomas Kerwin, Christopher Rundus, Fangda Zhang, Cameron G. Wrabel, Landon Perry, Zhong-Lin Lu

0724.name: Zhou Tiangang
0724.department: State Key Laboratory of Brain and Cognitive Science
0724.lab_name: State Key Laboratory of Brain and Cognitive Science
0724.bio: Zhou is a researcher at the State Key Laboratory of Brain and Cognitive Science, Institute of Biophysics, Chinese Academy of Sciences, where they investigate the neural mechanisms of visual cognition. Their work centers on the "global-first" theory of topological perception, which posits that the human visual system extracts global topological properties, such as the number of holes, as the primary units of object representation before processing local features. Using psychophysics, functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), and transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), Zhou examines the subcortical and cortical pathways involved in visual attention, object-based working memory, and the development of brain-inspired neural networks. Their research includes applying cognitive models to artificial intelligence and diagnosing mental disorders through dual-pathway fusion perceptual networks.
0724.research_direction: Dr. Zhou's research has recently been operating at the intersection of visual cognition, brain-inspired artificial intelligence, and advanced medical image analysis. In the realm of fundamental vision, their recent work explores the representational mechanisms of visual working memory, using psychophysical paradigms to investigate how the brain uses spatial and feature-based pointers to track objects during dynamic sensory updates. To bridge biological and artificial vision, they are developing dual-pathway convolutional neural networks that mimic the human visual system's global-to-local processing hierarchy to improve computer vision robustness. Finally, their applied neuroimaging research focuses on designing specialized deep learning architectures for clinical challenges, including frameworks for undersampled MRI reconstruction, fine-grained hippocampal segmentation, and multimodal fMRI integration for diagnosing psychiatric disorders.

papers.title: Unravelling the object-based nature of visual working memory: insight from pointers
papers.abstract: This research investigates the representational units of visual working memory (VWM) by evaluating the efficacy of the pointer system in maintaining object correspondence during information updates. Utilizing a repetition benefit paradigm across three psychophysical experiments, we manipulated spatial coordinates, chromaticity, and morphological features as candidate pointer cues. The results indicate that while spatial indexing provides a robust primary cue for the pointer system, distinct feature-based information (shape and color) can effectively reestablish object-to-pointer mappings in VWM. These findings corroborate an object-based flexible pointer model, suggesting that the VWM system integrates multi-featural indices to preserve continuity across successive sensory inputs, rather than relying exclusively on spatial placeholders.
papers.authors: Ning Wei, Jintao Song, Hongyi Zhang, Tiangang Zhou

papers.title: Bimodality Approach to Mental Disorder Diagnosis via Dual-pathway Fusion Perceptual Network
papers.abstract: To enhance the diagnostic classification of psychiatric conditions such as schizophrenia and autism spectrum disorder, this study proposes a dual-pathway fusion perceptual (DP-FP) network for multimodal neuroimaging analysis. The architecture incorporates a coarse perception module that derives weighted feature representations from functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) functional connectivity data using cosine similarity metrics. By employing a multi-stage attentional perception mechanism, the model effectively integrates complementary information across data modalities. Experimental validation on the COBRE and ABIDE datasets demonstrated superior performance, achieving 87.6% accuracy for schizophrenia detection. Gradient-based interpretive analysis was further utilized to localize discriminative brain regions contributing to the classification results.
papers.venue: 2024 IEEE International Conference on Bioinformatics and Biomedicine (BIBM)
papers.authors: Ruipeng Xu, Shuoqiu Gan, Feng Zhao, Zhentao Zuo, Tiangang Zhou

papers.title: Brain Cognition-Inspired Dual-Pathway CNN Architecture for Image Classification
papers.abstract: Mimicking the human visual system's global-to-local processing hierarchy, this paper introduces a dual-pathway convolutional neural network (CNN) designed to improve image classification and robustness. The architecture bifurcates visual processing into two parallel streams: an 'analogy' pathway modeled after the subcortical retinotectal system for extracting coarse-grained topological invariants and shape-based gist, and a 'detail' pathway emulating the cortical ventral stream for capturing fine-grained textural and edge features. A top-down modulation framework facilitates the integration of these distinct feature sets. The resulting 'CogNet' demonstrates significantly enhanced out-of-distribution generalization and improved resilience against adversarial attacks on standard computer vision benchmarks compared to monolithic CNN architectures.
papers.venue: IEEE Transactions on Neural Networks and Learning Systems
papers.authors: Songlin Dong, Chengli Tan, Zhentao Zuo, Yuhang He, Yihong Gong, Tiangang Zhou

papers.title: KDI-Net: dual-domain mapping network for undersampled magnetic resonance imaging reconstruction
papers.abstract: KDI-Net is introduced as a novel hybrid-domain deep learning framework for reconstructing high-fidelity images from undersampled k-space magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) data. The network architecture consists of three interconnected modules—K-Block, D-Block, and I-Block—which perform concurrent operations in the frequency and image domains to preserve data consistency. By leveraging the underlying sparsity of k-space signals through cross-domain mapping, the model effectively suppresses aliasing artifacts and restores fine structural details. Quantitative evaluation using PSNR and SSIM metrics on the AUTOMAP and Calgary Campinas datasets revealed that KDI-Net consistently outperforms single-domain reconstruction methods, providing over 8% improvement in accuracy and facilitating 2-fold acceleration in data acquisition.
papers.venue: 2024 International Conference on Image, Signal Processing, and Pattern Recognition (ISPP)
papers.authors: Haiyang Guo, Zhentao Zuo, Dengdi Sun, Tiangang Zhou

papers.title: CMG: Class and mask guided network for hippocampus and its subregions segmentation
papers.abstract: This study addresses the anatomical complexity and low-contrast challenges of hippocampal subregion segmentation in MRI by proposing a Class and Mask Guided (CMG) network. The model utilizes a dual-guidance strategy: a semantic branch ensures categorical consistency across axial slices, while a mask-guidance branch imposes spatial boundary constraints to minimize leakage into adjacent structures. To capture the long-range dependencies necessary for delineating fine-grained subregional boundaries, the CMG network incorporates a hybrid attention mechanism within its encoder-decoder structure. Benchmarking results indicate that the dual-guidance approach provides significant improvements in Dice similarity coefficients for automatic segmentation tasks compared to standard U-Net and transformer-based baselines.
papers.venue: 2024 International Conference on Image, Signal Processing, and Pattern Recognition (ISPP)
papers.authors: Zimu Wang, Zhentao Zuo, Dengdi Sun, Tiangang Zhou

0725.name: Ziad M. Hafed
0725.department: Werner Reichardt Centre for Integrative Neuroscience (CIN)
0725.bio: Ziad M. Hafed is the Professor of Active Perception at the University of Tübingen and leads the Physiology of Active Vision Laboratory. Hafed’s research examines the neural mechanisms through which visual perception and motor control interact, focusing on the generation and functional impact of microsaccades and other fixational eye movements. By employing high-resolution electrophysiology, reversible neural perturbations, and computational modeling in primate models, Hafed has analyzed the role of the superior colliculus in active vision and established that phenomena like saccadic suppression can originate as early as the retina. Their work connects sensory processing and oculomotor behavior to understand how the brain maintains stable visual representations during self-motion.
0725.research_direction: Dr. Hafed's recent work explores the active interplay between oculomotor control and visual perception, utilizing neurophysiological recordings and behavioral paradigms in non-human primates. They have recently been investigating the sensory and motor computations of the superior colliculus (SC), contrasting it with the primary visual cortex to understand how trial-by-trial neural fluctuations drive saccadic reaction times. Their research also closely examines fixational eye movements, probing how foveal microsaccades dynamically modulate extrafoveal covert attention and how short-latency microsaccadic inhibition is distinctly driven by visual versus auditory cues. Furthermore, they are examining the mechanisms underlying perceptual continuity across eye movements, mapping the spatial and contrast-dependent boundaries of perisaccadic visual mislocalization while exploring how foveal SC neurons might utilize corollary discharge to compute trans-saccadic prediction errors.

papers.title: Foveal action for the control of extrafoveal vision
papers.abstract: This study utilizes real-time retinal image stabilization and neurophysiological recordings within the primate superior colliculus (SC) to resolve the causal link between foveal oculomotor activity and extrafoveal visual sensitivity. By isolating foveal oculomotor state, the researchers demonstrate that the generation of microsaccades is sufficient to modulate extrafoveal sensitivity at eccentricities exceeding the microsaccade amplitude by a factor of 50. The findings indicate that fixational eye movements are an inherent component of the mechanisms underlying covert spatial attention, operating through stereotypical shifts in sensory processing that occur both pre- and post-saccadically.
papers.authors: Tong Zhang, Xiaoguang Tian, Tatiana Malevich, Matthias P. Baumann, Ziad M. Hafed

papers.title: Vision dominates sound in mediating classic cue-induced microsaccadic eye movement modulations in rhesus macaque monkeys
papers.abstract: Investigating the sensory-motor pathways responsible for short-latency saccadic inhibition, this research evaluates the relative potency of visual and auditory onsets in modulating the metrics and timing of microsaccades in rhesus macaques. The study demonstrates that visual signals exert a dominant influence over the topographic reorganization of the oculomotor program during reflexive ocular suppression. The results suggest that the visual pathways projecting to the midbrain and brainstem premotor networks are significantly more robust than auditory-motor pathways in mediating these rapid, cue-induced behavioral adjustments.
papers.authors: Tatiana Malevich, Matthias P. Baumann, Yue Yu, Ziad M. Hafed

papers.title: Much higher covariation with foveation timing by superior colliculus than primary visual cortical neuronal activity
papers.abstract: The study compares the degree to which trial-by-trial fluctuations in neuronal activity in the superior colliculus (SC) and primary visual cortex (V1) correlate with saccadic reaction time (SRT) variability. Using simultaneous recordings or matched paradigms, the authors found that V1 visual response properties show negligible covariation with SRT. Conversely, the SC exhibits strong trial-by-trial correlations between foveation timing and both visual response magnitude and pre-stimulus baseline state. These results indicate that the SC reformats sensory inputs into a motor-ready representation that directly predicts behavioral latency.
papers.authors: Carlotta Trottenberg, Yue Yu, Tong Zhang, Matthias P. Baumann, Tatiana Malevich, Shweta Prasad, Ziad M. Hafed

papers.title: Foveal neurons of the monkey superior colliculus signal trans-saccadic prediction errors
papers.abstract: Recording from foveal superior colliculus (SC) neurons, this work investigates the neural basis of perceptual stability across rapid eye movements. The study reveals that foveal neurons, which do not directly receive visual input from extrafoveal targets prior to a saccade, exhibit elevated reafferent responses when the post-saccadic foveal image is inconsistent with the pre-saccadic extrafoveal preview. This prediction-error signal, which scales with the degree of sensory discrepancy, suggests the SC utilizes a corollary discharge-based mechanism to detect trans-saccadic changes and maintain visual continuity.
papers.authors: Tong Zhang, Amarender R. Bogadhi, Ziad M. Hafed

papers.title: Two-dimensional perisaccadic visual mislocalization in rhesus macaque monkeys
papers.abstract: This research develops a flexible behavioral paradigm to map the two-dimensional landscape of perisaccadic visual mislocalization in macaques. The results show that the direction of the saccade significantly influences the pattern of mislocalization, with upward saccades eliciting particularly strong reverse mislocalization for probe flashes presented ahead of the saccade target. Additionally, the magnitude of these perceptual shifts is modulated by low-level image properties, including the spatial frequency and luminance contrast of both the saccade target and the visual probes.
papers.authors: Matthias P. Baumann, Ziad M. Hafed

0726.name: Zijiang He
0726.department: Department of Psychological and Brain Sciences
0726.main_research_area: visual space perception and binocular vision
0726.bio: Zijiang He is a Professor in the Department of Psychological and Brain Sciences at the University of Louisville, specializing in the mechanisms of three-dimensional space perception and visual cognition. Their research explores the ground-based spatial coding scheme and the visual system's "intrinsic bias," an internal model used for distance representation in environments with limited visual cues. Utilizing psychophysics, virtual reality, and the blind walking-gesturing paradigm, He investigates how the brain integrates surface information through the sequential surface integration process (SSIP) and manages path integration during self-motion. Additionally, their work on binocular rivalry and sensory eye dominance has resulted in the development of "push-pull" perceptual learning protocols for treating visual impairments like amblyopia.
0726.research_direction: Dr. He's recent work explores the mechanisms of 3D spatial vision, specifically focusing on how the human visual system establishes spatial reference frames to perceive absolute distance and localize objects on the ground plane. They have recently been investigating the rules of static depth perception, using psychophysical judgments to test how the brain utilizes proximal texture gradients to sequentially build a stable surface representation of intermediate distances. Additionally, their research probes dynamic spatial updating during self-motion, examining how active locomotor and passive vestibular signals support an allocentric path-integration system that tracks spatial displacement in the dark. Across both lines of inquiry, they aim to uncover how environmental depth cues and body-motion signals interact to anchor visual targets within a cohesive topographical map of the environment.

papers.title: Advantage of the foreground for absolute distance perception in the intermediate distance range
papers.abstract: This study examines the Sequential Surface Integration Process (SSIP) hypothesis, which proposes that the visual system represents the ground surface by prioritizing proximal information near the observer's feet. Using psychophysical distance judgments in environments with impoverished depth cues, the researchers demonstrated that presenting texture gradient information in a near-to-far sequence yielded significantly more accurate absolute distance judgments compared to a far-to-near sequence. The findings suggest that the visual system relies on proximal ground cues to establish a reliable surface reference frame, which is then used to integrate distal depth information into a global representation of the terrain for localizing objects in the intermediate distance range (2–25 m).
papers.authors: Lizhu Yan, Lingling Bai, Teng Leng Ooi, Zijiang He

papers.title: An allocentric human odometer for perceiving distances on the ground plane
papers.abstract: Accurate localization of stationary objects during locomotion persists despite continuous retinal image displacement induced by self-motion. The present study demonstrates that the human visual system resolves this perceptual challenge by implementing an allocentric spatial reference frame. Observers were evaluated on judged target locations following short-distance walking displacements from an initial home-base location. Consistent with an allocentric coordinate framework, psychophysical measurements revealed that the intrinsic bias—the default implicit representation of the ground plane utilized to localize dimly illuminated targets in the dark—remained anchored to the origin location rather than translating along with the observer's body. Furthermore, the path-integration mechanism mediating this spatial updating was capable of utilizing both active locomotor and passive vestibular translational signals. Crucially, this path-integration updating operated selectively along the horizontal ground plane while failing along the vertical axis, demonstrating an anisotropic human odometer for terrestrial space perception.
papers.authors: Liu Zhou, Wei Wei, Teng Leng Ooi, Zijiang J He

0728.name: Árni Kristjánsson
0728.bio: Kristjánsson is a Professor of Vision Science at the University of Iceland. Their research characterizes the cognitive and neural mechanisms of visual attention, search, and memory. They investigate attentional priming, visual foraging, and how the human brain learns and represents the statistical distributions of features in the environment. Their methodology integrates traditional psychophysics and eye-tracking with electroencephalography (EEG) and computational modeling. Current research directions include investigating serial dependence in perception and exploring sensory substitution through haptic feedback systems for prosthetic applications.
0728.research_direction: Dr. Kristjánsson has recently been investigating how the human visual system extracts statistical regularities from the environment to guide attention, eye movements, and continuous search behaviors. Their recent work explores how observers learn complex feature distributions, questioning whether summary statistics like the mean and variance of colors or orientations influence explicit ensemble judgments differently than they do implicit spatial priority maps. They are also studying the functional integration of these probabilistic representations into the oculomotor system by analyzing saccade dynamics, alongside computational modeling of how visual repetition priming operates under distinct, exclusionary attentional sets. More broadly, Dr. Kristjánsson focuses on understanding continuous, multi-target visual foraging, examining how working memory, prior search history, and probabilistic templates shape sequential target selection in ecologically valid contexts.

papers.title: Two routes to a target: Visual priming for direct and indirect attentional sets
papers.abstract: This study examines the computational mechanisms underlying repetition priming across distinct levels of attentional set complexity. The researchers contrasted 'direct' attentional sets (where the cue matches the target) with 'indirect' sets (where the target is defined by exclusionary cues). Modeling behavioral response-time series using dynamic ideal observer frameworks revealed a bifurcation in processing: while direct sets are mediated by a robust first-order memory mechanism linked to automatic feature-based facilitation, indirect sets exhibit significant processing costs and a lack of priming. These findings suggest that search under exclusionary guidance bypasses standard priming circuits, instead recruiting higher-level executive functions associated with rule-based task switching and the active maintenance of attentional templates in working memory.
papers.authors: Alexander Pastukhov, Malin Styrnal, Claus-Christian Carbon, Árni Kristjánsson

papers.title: Amplification from saliency affects explicit but not implicit ensemble representations
papers.abstract: This research characterizes the 'amplification effect'—the systematic bias of ensemble summary statistics toward salient items—by dissociating explicit and implicit levels of representation. Using an orientation adjustment task for explicit reports and a feature distribution learning (FDL) search paradigm for implicit reports, the authors assessed how task-irrelevant saliency (size) influences orientation ensembles. Results demonstrated a pronounced saliency-induced bias in explicit mean orientation judgments; however, implicit representations of the full feature distribution remained veridical and resistant to saliency interference. The dissociation indicates that the visual system maintains high-fidelity implicit statistical representations of environmental variability that are distinct from the weighted, summary-based heuristics used in explicit conscious reports.
