papers.authors: Aleksei U. Iakovlev, Vladislav A. Khvostov, Árni Gunnar Ásgeirsson, Igor S. Utochkin, Árni Kristjánsson

papers.title: Learning of the mean, but not variance, of color distributions cues target location probability
papers.abstract: The investigation explores the capacity of the human visual system to utilize higher-order statistical regularities in color ensembles to update spatial priority maps. In a series of probability-cueing experiments, target location likelihoods were associated with either the mean or the variance of distractor color distributions. While observers successfully learned associations between specific hues (means) and spatial 'rich' locations, leading to significant search facilitation, they failed to learn contingencies based on color variance. These results establish critical constraints on statistical learning, suggesting that while the visual system integrates first-order moments into flexible priority maps, it lacks the mechanisms to associate second-order distributional variance with spatial probability during visual exploration.
papers.authors: Philippe Blondé, Sabrina Hansmann-Roth, David Pascucci, Árni Kristjánsson

papers.title: How does color distribution learning affect goal-directed visuomotor behavior?
papers.abstract: This study evaluates the degree to which detailed probabilistic feature representations are integrated into the oculomotor system. Observers performed odd-one-out visual search tasks where distractor colors formed specific Gaussian or uniform distributions. By analyzing saccadic reaction times (SRT) and endpoint deviations, the authors found that while attentional orienting (indexed by SRT) accurately reflected the learned shape of the feature distribution, saccade endpoints—though sensitive to the distribution mean—failed to differentiate between distribution shapes. These results suggest a functional dissociation in the processing of statistical regularities: whereas early attentional selection is guided by detailed probabilistic templates, final oculomotor motor execution relies on a coarser representation of the environmental statistics.
papers.authors: Léa Entzmann, Árni Gunnar Ásgeirsson, Árni Kristjánsson

papers.title: Understanding human visual foraging: a review
papers.abstract: This comprehensive review synthesizes recent advancements in the study of human visual foraging, shifting the theoretical focus from isolated single-target search to continuous, multi-target sequential selection. The paper evaluates the roles of attentional templates, working memory load, and environmental statistics in determining selection strategies, such as the propensity to stick to a single target type versus switching. The authors integrate findings on how reward contingencies and previous search history (priming) shape foraging behavior, proposing that foraging serves as a more ecologically valid model of natural vision. The review argues for new frameworks that emphasize the dynamic, self-paced nature of real-world visual exploration over traditional trial-based paradigms.
papers.authors: Tómas Kristjánsson, Árni Kristjánsson

0730.name: Ömer Dağlar Tanrikulu
0730.bio: Ömer Dağlar Tanrikulu is an Assistant Professor in the Department of Psychology at the University of New Hampshire and directs the UNH Vision Lab. Tanrikulu’s research explores the computational foundations of visual perception, focusing on how the visual system organizes sensory input through perceptual grouping and depth perception. By integrating psychophysical methods with virtual reality simulations, they investigate the interaction between contour geometry and dynamic motion cues like texture accretion and deletion. Tanrikulu also examines the philosophical underpinnings of cognitive science, specifically regarding the probabilistic and Bayesian nature of mental representations in visual processing.
0730.research_direction: Dr. Tanrikulu has recently been investigating the cognitive and computational mechanisms that shape both high-level belief systems and foundational perceptual representations. Within the cognitive science of religion, their recent work explores how the mind processes, prefers, and transmits supernatural concepts, using theoretical frameworks of thought dynamics alongside computational image-choice paradigms to weigh the relative influence of ontological categories, social utility, and threat. Concurrently, they are examining how the brain encodes sensory uncertainty during perceptual decision-making. By employing psychophysical experiments and computational modeling, Dr. Tanrikulu investigates whether the visual system relies on complex Bayesian probability distributions or simple heuristics, testing the hypothesis that representational complexity dynamically adapts to specific task demands in a resource-rational manner.

papers.title: Integrating the Cognitive Science of Religion With the Dynamic Framework of Thought
papers.abstract: This theoretical work establishes a bridge between the core tenets of the Cognitive Science of Religion (CSR) and the dynamic framework of thought derived from cognitive neuroscience and psychology. The authors examine the intersection of these fields, specifically exploring how neuroscientific mechanisms of thought dynamics can provide a foundational basis for CSR theories regarding the mental processing of religious concepts. The paper argues that current findings in cognitive psychology and neuroscience regarding constrained versus spontaneous thought processes can be applied to explain the persistence and transmission of minimally counterintuitive (MCI) ideas and ontological categories within religious belief systems, thereby grounding cross-cultural religious patterns in established biological and cognitive regularities.
papers.venue: Journal of Theoretical and Philosophical Psychology
papers.authors: Shannon Fleming, Paul Robertson, Daniel Turek, Ömer Dağlar Tanrıkulu

papers.title: Testing the Relative Influence of Three Key Factors in Mind-Based Models of Religion: Template Categories, Utility, and Threat
papers.abstract: This study employs a computational image-choice paradigm to quantitatively evaluate the relative impact of three fundamental factors—ontological category templates, social utility, and threat—hypothesized to drive preferences in the Cognitive Science of Religion (CSR) framework. Contrary to some previous hierarchical models, the results indicate that category templates exert the most significant influence on mental preferences for religious or supernatural concepts. While threat detection and social utility also produce independent and significant effects on participant choices, their influence is secondary to the ontological classification of the stimulus. The findings challenge traditional hierarchical structures in CSR and provide empirically scaled measures of typicality, utility, and threat for future research into the cognitive evolution of religion.
papers.authors: Shannon Fleming, Paul Robertson, Daniel Turek, Ömer Dağlar Tanrikulu

papers.title: Beyond Suboptimality: Resource-Rationality and Task Demands Shape the Complexity of Perceptual Representations
papers.abstract: The authors address the debate between Bayesian theories of perception—which posit that sensory uncertainty is represented via complex probability distributions—and critics who cite suboptimal decision-making as evidence for simpler, non-probabilistic representations. They propose that suboptimality is not an inherent limitation of representational capacity but a resource-rational adaptation to task demands. Through three psychophysical experiments, the researchers progressively restricted the utility of simple heuristic strategies. Computational model comparisons revealed that participant behavior is best described by simple representations when task-solvable with minimal effort, but shifts toward complex, distributional representations when heuristic strategies become ineffective. These results suggest that perceptual representations are dynamically adapted to be as simple or complex as required by the task, establishing resource-rationality as a critical constraint for perceptual theory.
papers.authors: Andrew Jun Lee, Daniel Turek, Ömer Dağlar Tanrikulu

E001.name: Fred Rieke
E001.bio: Rieke researches the biophysical mechanisms of sensory signal processing, focusing on the operation of the visual system at the physical limits of photon detection. Their work combines quantitative electrophysiological experiments and computational modeling to examine the transduction of light by rod and cone photoreceptors and the processing of these signals by retinal circuits. Current projects in Rieke’s laboratory address the origins of biological noise in photoreceptors, the integration of rod and cone signals under mesopic conditions, and the parallel pathways that transmit visual information from the eye to the brain.
E001.research_direction: Dr. Rieke has recently been investigating the functional origins of visual processing, exploring how early nonlinearities and light adaptation within the photoreceptor transduction cascade dictate downstream spatial and temporal computations. To causally isolate these early biophysical dynamics from subsequent circuit transformations, their recent work employs invertible phototransduction models and customized stimulus clamps alongside intracellular recordings. Additionally, they are examining the specific microcircuit mechanisms—such as bipolar cell ribbon architecture, short-term synaptic plasticity, and targeted amacrine inhibition—that partition graded inputs into parallel sustained and transient pathways and drive dynamic spatial tuning in retinal ganglion cells. Finally, they are exploring the broader computational sophistication of the primate retina, synthesizing physiological and anatomical evidence to understand how conserved vertebrate microcircuits mediate advanced feature extraction and predictive motion encoding prior to cortical transmission.

papers.title: Spatially local inhibition and synaptic plasticity together enable dynamic, context-dependent integration of parallel sensory pathways
papers.abstract: Retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) are classically segregated into units sensitive strictly to luminance changes versus those enhanced by spatial structure. Mouse Off-transient alpha RGCs diverge from this standard taxonomy, exhibiting maximal spike responses to spatially homogeneous stimuli while being profoundly suppressed by fine spatial contrast. Using patch-clamp recordings and computational modeling, this study delineates two coordinated circuit mechanisms driving this spatial preference. First, inhibitory synaptic inputs recruit spatially finer subunits than excitatory inputs, causing the excitation-inhibition (E/I) balance to shift systematically with spatial scale. Second, feedforward excitatory synapses undergo marked short-term synaptic depression; relief of presynaptic inhibition upon transitioning from structured to homogeneous inputs promotes recovery of synaptic gain, substantially boosting excitatory drive. A spatiotemporal conductance-based model demonstrates how the interaction between localized amacrine cell inhibition and short-term synaptic plasticity generates this distinctive, context-dependent spatial tuning.
papers.authors: Qiang Chen, Fred Rieke

papers.title: Origin and functional impact of early nonlinearities in primate retina
papers.abstract: Standard receptive field models treat the outer retina as largely linear, attributing nonlinear subunits primarily to synaptic rectification at the inner plexiform layer between bipolar and ganglion cells. Here, intracellular recordings from horizontal cells, cone bipolar cells, and parasol RGCs in the primate retina demonstrate that significant nonlinear spatial integration originates in the outer retina. Sinusoidal contrast-reversing gratings evoke substantial frequency-doubled (F2) voltage modulations in horizontal and bipolar cells, approaching half the magnitude observed in parasol ganglion cells. Biophysical modeling and experimental manipulations establish that these nonlinearities stem from asymmetric kinetics and localized light adaptation within the cone phototransduction cascade rather than post-photoreceptor synaptic rectification alone. Incorporating outer retinal phototransduction nonlinearities into receptive field architectures markedly improves response predictions to natural movies and structured visual inputs.
papers.authors: Vyom Raval, Rachel Oaks-Leaf, Qiang Chen, Fred Rieke

papers.title: Filter, Detector, Predictor: The expanding repertoire of retinal computation in vertebrates
papers.abstract: The primate retina has traditionally been conceptualized as a relatively passive, high-fidelity spatial and chromatic filter structured around three core channels: parasol, midget, and small bistratified ganglion cells. Conversely, non-primate vertebrates are recognized for extensive retinal feature extraction, nonlinear processing, and motion computation. This review synthesizes physiological, anatomical, and high-density multi-electrode array evidence demonstrating that the primate retina comprises 20 to 30 distinct ganglion cell types exhibiting computational complexity comparable to non-mammalian and rodent models. The authors examine how historical reliance on spatially homogeneous, artificial stimuli obscured these specialized processing streams. They discuss how conserved vertebrate retinal microcircuits implement sophisticated operations in the primate visual stream, including object-motion selectivity, differential motion suppression, and predictive motion encoding prior to cortical transmission.
papers.authors: Michael B. Manookin, Fred Rieke

papers.title: Cone bipolar cell synapses generate transient versus sustained signals in parallel ON pathways of the mouse retina
papers.abstract: Divergence of cone photoreceptor signals into parallel bipolar cell pathways establishes the initial substrate for functional segregation in the visual system, notably separating sustained from transient ON alpha retinal ganglion cells (ON-S and ON-T RGCs). Combining whole-cell voltage-clamp electrophysiology, serial block-face electron microscopic reconstruction, and two-photon imaging of the glutamate reporter iGluSnFR, this work investigates the loci of kinetic diversification. Presynaptic type 5i, 6, and 7 ON cone bipolar cells exhibit indistinguishable, sustained voltage responses to light noise and steps. However, glutamate release onto RGC dendrites and post-synaptic excitatory synaptic currents are kinetically distinct. Pharmacological disruption of GABAergic and glycinergic amacrine feedback demonstrates that presynaptic inhibition is not required for this kinetic divergence. Instead, ultrastructural reconstructions indicate that differences in synaptic ribbon architecture and ribbon-associated vesicle pool dynamics at bipolar cell terminals mediate the transformation from common graded inputs to transient versus sustained outputs.
papers.authors: Sidney P. Kuo, Wan-Qing Yu, Prerna Srivastava, Haruhisa Okawa, Luca Della Santina, David M. Berson, Gautam B. Awatramani, Rachel O. L. Wong, Fred Rieke

papers.title: Predictably manipulating photoreceptor light responses to reveal their role in downstream visual responses
papers.abstract: Dissecting the specific computational roles of upstream versus downstream nonlinearities in neural pathways remains challenging when multiple nonlinear processes interact. This study introduces an experimental and computational methodology that utilizes an analytically invertible biophysical model of the rod and cone phototransduction cascades to synthesize light stimuli that predictably control photoreceptor outer-segment currents in mouse and primate retinas. By generating light waveforms that selectively compensate for photoreceptor light adaptation and kinetic changes (a light-adaptation clamp), the approach isolates phototransduction dynamics from downstream retinal circuit transformations. This tool enables causal investigations of how early sensory receptor adaptation dictates receptive field spatial integration, temporal filtering, and contrast encoding in postsynaptic interneurons and ganglion cell outputs.
papers.authors: Qiang Chen, Norianne T. Ingram, Jacob Baudin, Juan M. Angueyra, Raunak Sinha, Fred Rieke

E002.name: Stephen Baccus
E002.bio: Stephen Baccus investigates the circuit mechanisms through which the retina encodes and adapts to natural visual environments. By integrating large-scale multielectrode recordings with biophysically-inspired deep learning models, their lab characterizes the nonlinear transformations performed by retinal interneurons during processes like contrast adaptation and motion sensitivity. Baccus also explores ultrasonic neuromodulation as a high-resolution, non-invasive method for stimulating neural tissue. Their work focuses on identifying principles of neural computation that explain how the visual system compresses information while maintaining ethological relevance.
E002.research_direction: Dr. Baccus has recently been investigating the computational principles of the retina by bridging the gap between biological neural circuits and interpretable machine learning models. Their recent work explores how populations of retinal ganglion cells and interneurons process complex natural scenes, leveraging convolutional neural networks modified with realistic synaptic dynamics to study multiscale contrast adaptation. To better understand these encoding processes, they are developing novel deep learning frameworks for mechanistic interpretability, mapping the causal roles of hidden network units directly to the distinct functions of biological amacrine cells. Additionally, their research spans neural decoding and sensory representation, using information geometry to examine how the retina optimizes its discriminability in natural environments and building hybrid decoding architectures to reconstruct visual stimuli despite the stochastic drift of fixational eye movements.

papers.title: Causal Interpretation of Neural Network Computations with Contribution Decomposition (CODEC)
papers.abstract: The authors present CODEC, a framework for mechanistic interpretability that shifts the focus from correlational feature mapping to direct causal analysis of how hidden units drive network outputs. By decomposing the vector of neural contributions into sparse, low-dimensional modes, the method uncovers the hierarchical evolution of computations in image-classification and retinal encoding models. A key finding is the emergence of decorrelated positive and negative effects on the output in deeper layers, facilitating precise causal manipulation of network behavior. In the context of the retina, CODEC identifies the combinatorial logic of model interneurons that underpins dynamic receptive field properties.
papers.authors: Joshua Melander, Zaki Alaoui, Shenghua Liu, Surya Ganguli, Stephen Baccus

papers.title: Hybrid Where-What Neural Decoder: Approximating Bayesian Inference for Real-Time Spike-Train Reconstruction
papers.abstract: This work introduces a hybrid neural decoding architecture designed for real-time reconstruction of visual stimuli from retinal spike trains. The model approximates Bayesian inference by partitioning the decoding task into 'where' (spatial localization) and 'what' (feature identification) pathways, effectively handling the stochastic nature of fixational eye movements. By leveraging deep learning to mimic probabilistic computations, the decoder demonstrates superior performance in high-acuity tasks and provides a framework for understanding how the brain might integrate diverse population features to maintain a stable visual percept despite continuous image drift.
papers.authors: Lane McIntosh, Niru Maheswaranathan, Aran Nayebi, Stephen Baccus

papers.title: A mechanistically interpretable model of the retinal neural code for natural scenes with multiscale adaptive dynamics
papers.abstract: The researchers developed a three-layer convolutional neural network (CNN) modified with local recurrent synaptic dynamics to model the responses of salamander retinal ganglion cells to complex natural scenes. By integrating a linear-nonlinear-kinetic (LNK) component, the model captures multiscale contrast adaptation spanning several orders of magnitude in time. The internal units of the network are directly relatable to retinal interneurons, allowing for a mechanistic explanation of how specific synaptic pathways contribute to ethological retinal computations and predictive coding under naturalistic conditions.
papers.authors: Satchel Grant, Xuehao Ding, Dongsoo Lee, Heike Stein, Lane McIntosh, Niru Maheswaranathan, Stephen Baccus

papers.title: Adaptation of retinal discriminability to natural scenes
papers.abstract: Using methods from information geometry and generative machine learning, this study investigates how the discriminability of a salamander retinal ganglion cell population is optimized for natural visual environments. By analyzing the manifolds of natural stimuli and their corresponding neural representations, the authors show that the retina dynamically adapts its sensitivity to enhance information transmission, particularly for localized motion signals. Critically, the analysis refutes the idea that noise correlations are optimized to boost information; instead, they are shown to be a deleterious but inevitable consequence of the shared circuitry required for spatiotemporal adaptation.
papers.authors: Xuehao Ding, Dongsoo Lee, Joshua Brendan Melander, Stephen Baccus

papers.title: Classification and analysis of retinal interneurons by computational structure under natural scenes
papers.abstract: The paper presents a novel approach to the functional classification of mouse retinal amacrine cells using high-resolution optical recordings and interpretable machine learning. By fitting a two-layer convolutional neural network to responses elicited by natural movies, the authors successfully categorized diverse interneuron types based on their internal computational roles. The study demonstrates that model-defined interneurons correspond to distinct biological amacrine cell types, revealing the specific inhibitory pathways that modulate ganglion cell output to encode natural scenes.
papers.authors: Dongsoo Lee, Juyoung Kim, Stephen Baccus

E003.name: Botond Roska
E003.institution: Institute of Molecular and Clinical Ophthalmology Basel
E003.department: Faculty of Medicine and Faculty of Science
E003.lab_name: Human Retinal and Central Visual Circuits Group
E003.bio: Botond Roska is a neurobiologist who investigates the functional organization of retinal circuits and the development of optogenetic therapies to restore sight. Roska's research group maps the interactions of approximately 100 retinal cell types using viral-mediated circuit tracing, electrophysiology, and computational modeling. They developed cell-type-targeted optogenetic strategies to reactivate light sensitivity in blind retinas, which resulted in clinical applications of this technology in humans. Their current research explores human retinal architecture and the integration of sensory signals within central visual pathways to advance translational treatments for hereditary blindness.
E003.research_direction: Dr. Roska has recently been investigating visual processing across multiple stages of the visual pathway alongside developing translational therapies for retinal degeneration. At the basic circuit level, their recent work explores fundamental mechanisms of synaptic feedback and inhibition, using tools like two-photon calcium imaging, monosynaptic rabies tracing, and in vivo single-cell gene editing to probe pH-mediated horizontal-to-cone signaling, feature-selective tuning in thalamic interneurons, and homeostatic adaptation to excitatory-inhibitory imbalances in the visual cortex. Bridging fundamental neuroscience and clinical ophthalmology, they are also actively evaluating targeted interventions for vision restoration. Specifically, they utilize expansive arrays of human retinal organoids for high-throughput compound screening to identify neuroprotective pathways for vulnerable cone photoreceptors, while investigating the clinical potential of emerging mutation-independent strategies like optogenetics and precise genetic base editing.

papers.title: In vivo single-cell gene editing using RNA electroporation reveals sequential adaptation of cortical neurons to excitatory-inhibitory imbalance
papers.abstract: The researchers developed a highly efficient in vivo gene editing technique utilizing RNA electroporation to deliver CRISPR-Cas9 components to individual neurons. By knocking out GABA-A receptor β subunits in layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons of the mouse visual cortex, they investigated the homeostatic response to a total loss of fast inhibition. In vivo patch-clamp recordings demonstrated a two-stage sequential adaptation program: an immediate, transient reduction in the strength of excitatory synaptic inputs followed by a shift in intrinsic membrane properties that lowered input resistance. This compensatory mechanism ultimately prevented the edited neurons from generating action potentials, thereby isolating them from the cortical circuit.
papers.authors: Georg Kosche, Alex Fratzl, Martin Munz, Botond Roska

papers.title: The sodium-bicarbonate cotransporter Slc4a5 mediates feedback at the first synapse of vision
papers.abstract: This study identifies the molecular mechanism governing negative feedback from horizontal cells (HCs) to cone photoreceptors at the primary visual synapse. Using cell-type-specific genetic perturbations and two-photon calcium imaging, the authors established that the electrogenic bicarbonate transporter Slc4a5, selectively expressed in HCs, is essential for this feedback loop. The findings suggest an unconventional synaptic mechanism where light-induced changes in HC membrane potential modulate Slc4a5-mediated bicarbonate transport, subsequently altering the pH within the synaptic cleft. This extracellular pH shift modulates the conductance of cone calcium channels, providing a voltage-dependent inhibitory signal that shapes downstream visual processing.
papers.authors: Rei Morikawa, Tiago M. Rodrigues, Helene Marianne Schreyer, Cameron S. Cowan, Sarah Nadeau, Alexandra Graff-Meyer, Claudia P. Patino-Alvarez, Mohammad Hossein Khani, Josephine Jüttner, Botond Roska

papers.title: Individual thalamic inhibitory interneurons are functionally specialized toward distinct visual features
papers.abstract: The authors investigated the functional architecture of inhibitory interneurons in the mouse dorsolateral geniculate nucleus (dLGN) using single-cell-initiated monosynaptic rabies tracing and in vivo two-photon calcium imaging. Contrary to the view that these interneurons act as general multiplexors, the study demonstrates that individual interneurons are highly specialized, receiving inputs from specific subsets of retinal ganglion cells (RGCs). Using FRMD7 mutant mice, they showed that interneuron direction selectivity is causally linked to retinal input specialization. This functional tuning for specific visual features, such as motion and direction, is consistent across both the somatic and dendritic compartments, allowing for feature-selective inhibition within the thalamic circuit.
papers.authors: Fiona E. Müllner, Botond Roska

papers.title: Retinal Disorders
papers.abstract: This comprehensive review examines the current landscape of inherited and acquired retinal pathologies, detailing the biological underpinnings of photoreceptor degeneration and macular dysfunction. The article discusses recent progress in clinical translation, emphasizing the development of mutation-independent therapies such as optogenetic vision restoration and precise genetic interventions like adenine base editing. It also addresses the critical role of human retinal organoids and non-human primate models in bridging the gap between basic circuit neuroscience and clinical ophthalmology, while navigating the regulatory and safety requirements for emerging gene and cell-based therapies.
papers.venue: Cold Spring Harbor Perspectives in Medicine
papers.authors: José-Alain Sahel, Eyal Banin, Jean Bennett, Jacque L. Duncan, Botond Roska

papers.title: Cell type-focused compound screen in human organoids reveals CK1 and MAPK11 inhibition protects cone photoreceptor death
papers.abstract: Utilizing a high-throughput platform consisting of ~20,000 human retinal organoids with GFP-labeled cones, the researchers performed a targeted chemical screen of 2,707 annotated compounds to identify regulators of cone survival. Following a seven-day glucose starvation period that typically induces 40% cone loss, the screen identified specific inhibitors of Casein Kinase 1 (CK1) and MAPK11 as potent neuroprotective agents. Conversely, broad inhibition of Class I/II histone deacetylases (HDACs) and prolonged HSP90 inhibition were found to exacerbate cone death. This work establishes a database of cell-type-specific toxicity and identifies novel therapeutic pathways for preserving central vision in macular degeneration and related dystrophies.
papers.authors: Stefan E. Spirig, Valeria J. Arteaga-Moreta, Zoltan Raics, Susana Posada-Céspedes, Stephanie Chreng, Olaf Galuba, Inga Galuba, Isabelle Claerr, Steffen Renner, P. Timo Kleindienst, Adrienn Volak, Jannick Imbach, Svitlana Malysheva, Rebecca A. Siwicki, Vincent Hahaut, Yanyan Hou, Simone Picelli, Marco Cattaneo, Josephine Jüttner, Cameron S. Cowan, Myriam Duckely, Daniel K. Baeschlin, Magdalena Renner, Vincent Unterreiner, Botond Roska

E005.name: Thomas Euler
E005.bio: Thomas Euler is a Professor for Ophthalmic Research at the University of Tübingen, where Euler investigates the functional organization and computational principles of retinal microcircuits. Their research utilizes two-photon calcium imaging and electrophysiology to record light-evoked population activity in mouse and zebrafish models. Euler has characterized the functional diversity of retinal bipolar and ganglion cells and applies natural scene statistics to probe early visual processing. Additionally, their laboratory develops open-source scientific tools and investigates how retinal circuits are altered during neurodegeneration.
E005.research_direction: Dr. Euler has recently been investigating the computational principles and functional diversity of the mouse retina by leveraging large-scale two-photon calcium imaging and convolutional neural networks to model the responses of tens of thousands of retinal ganglion cells (RGCs). Their recent work explores how specific retinal microcircuits are tuned for ethologically relevant behaviors, mapping regional functional adaptations across the visual field and using computational modeling to discover how distinct RGCs detect environmental chromatic shifts. Additionally, they are investigating the physiological plasticity of these circuits, probing how neuromodulators like nitric oxide dynamically alter temporal response kinetics in targeted cell subsets. Finally, Dr. Euler is examining the resilience of these visual pathways in disease models, assessing how progressive photoreceptor degeneration heterogeneously alters the functional output of different RGC types over time.

papers.title: A large-scale dataset of functional mouse ganglion cell layer responses
papers.abstract: The authors introduce the ALL-GCL dataset, a high-throughput functional imaging resource containing two-photon calcium recordings from over 80,000 neurons in the mouse retinal ganglion cell layer (GCL). The dataset aggregates data from 139 experimental sessions collected over nine years using a standardized battery of visual stimuli, including full-field chirps and moving bars, to enable the probabilistic classification of neurons into 46 functional groups. The work quantifies the impact of experimental metadata, such as fluorescent indicator kinetics and recording configurations, on response consistency, providing a standardized benchmarking platform for system identification and convolutional neural network (CNN) modeling of retinal computation.
papers.authors: Dominic Gonschorek, Jonathan Oesterle, Thomas Zenkel, Federico D'Agostino, Chenchen Cai, Nadine Dyszkant, Klaudia P. Szatko, Florentyna Deja, Tom Schwerd-Kleine, Ryan Arlinghaus, Katrin Franke, Zhijian Zhao, Timm Schubert, Philipp Berens, Thomas Euler

papers.title: Photoreceptor degeneration has heterogeneous effects on functional retinal ganglion cell types
papers.abstract: This longitudinal study characterizes the functional impact of progressive rod and cone degeneration on the physiological output of the mouse retina using the rd10 mutant model. By employing large-scale two-photon calcium imaging and functional clustering, the authors assessed the light-evoked responsiveness of specific retinal ganglion cell (RGC) types as the disease progressed from early rod loss (P45) to near-complete photoreceptor depletion (P180). The findings reveal significant heterogeneity in functional resilience across RGC channels; On-pathway and specific orientation-selective RGCs displayed relative functional stability, whereas Off-pathway and direction-selective circuits demonstrated early physiological deterioration. These results indicate that retinal circuits undergo type-specific functional remodeling, which may inform the temporal window for neuroprotective interventions.
papers.authors: Nadine Dyszkant, Jonathan Oesterle, Yongrong Qiu, Merle Harrer, Timm Schubert, Dominic Gonschorek, Thomas Euler

papers.title: Task-specific regional circuit adaptations in distinct mouse retinal ganglion cells
papers.abstract: This paper explores the existence of regional microcircuit specializations across the nasotemporal axis of the mouse retina, focusing on sustained ON alpha (sONα) retinal ganglion cells. Utilizing dendritic calcium imaging and presynaptic glutamate sensors, the researchers identified a functional asymmetry where temporal sONα RGCs exhibit markedly stronger surround suppression and unique temporal kinetics compared to their nasal counterparts. Computational population models using an encoder-decoder framework demonstrate that these localized circuit adaptations are optimized for the detection of small, dark, high-velocity stimuli, effectively tuning the retinal output to support ethologically relevant behaviors such as prey capture (e.g., cricket hunting).
papers.authors: Jonathan Oesterle, Yanli Ran, Paul Stahr, Jason N. D. Kerr, Timm Schubert, Philipp Berens, Thomas Euler

papers.title: Nitric oxide modulates contrast suppression in a subset of mouse retinal ganglion cells
papers.abstract: The study investigates the neuromodulatory influence of nitric oxide (NO) on the visual feature representations encoded by mouse retinal ganglion cells (RGCs). Through a combination of two-photon calcium imaging and multi-electrode array (MEA) recordings, the authors found that NO selectively targets a subset of suppressed-by-contrast RGC types, significantly attenuating their temporal suppression and accelerating response kinetics while leaving spatial receptive field properties unaffected. Additionally, the study characterizes a significant baseline adaptational response change in approximately one-third of RGC types during prolonged ex vivo experiments, necessitating the use of a sequential-recording paradigm to isolate drug-induced neuromodulation from intrinsic physiological adaptation.
papers.authors: Dominic Gonschorek, Matías A Goldin, Jonathan Oesterle, Tom Schwerd-Kleine, Ryan Arlinghaus, Zhijian Zhao, Timm Schubert, Olivier Marre, Thomas Euler

papers.title: A chromatic feature detector in the retina signals visual context changes
papers.abstract: The authors identify a novel chromatic feature detection mechanism in the mouse retina that signals transitions in visual context, such as ground-to-sky shifts. By training deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) on large-scale RGC responses to natural movies and performing model-guided in silico stimulus optimization (Maximally Exciting Inputs, MEIs), the study predicted a specific chromatic selectivity in transient Suppressed-by-Contrast (tSbC) RGCs. Experimental verification confirmed that tSbCs are selectively activated by full-field switches between green and ultraviolet illumination, matching the chromatic statistics of natural horizon transitions. The results suggest that these cells provide a contextual reference signal to higher brain regions to facilitate state-dependent visual processing.
papers.authors: Larissa Höfling, Klaudia P. Szatko, Christian Behrens, Yuyao Deng, Yongrong Qiu, David A. Klindt, Zachary Jessen, Gregory W. Schwartz, Matthias Bethge, Philipp Berens, Katrin Franke, Alexander S. Ecker, Thomas Euler

E006.name: Greg Field
E006.main_research_area: retinal neural coding and circuit function
E006.bio: Greg D. Field is an Associate Professor in the Department of Ophthalmology at UCLA and holds the Joan and Jerome Snyder Chair in Vision Sciences. Field’s research focuses on the neural coding of the retina, specifically investigating how populations of retinal ganglion cells transform visual scenes into electrical signals transmitted to the brain. Utilizing high-density multi-electrode arrays, computational modeling, and mouse genetics, their lab characterizes the functional connectivity and signal processing of diverse retinal cell types. This approach aims to understand the principles of sensory processing and inform the development of therapies for vision restoration in degenerative conditions such as glaucoma and retinitis pigmentosa.
E006.research_direction: Dr. Field has recently been investigating the computational architecture of the retina, focusing on how diverse functional mosaics of retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) encode and transmit visual information to the brain. Their recent work employs large-scale multielectrode array recordings combined with novel phototagging and retrograde viral methods to link the physiological visual responses of specific RGCs to their distinct morphologies and downstream projection targets. In parallel, they are examining the fundamental circuit mechanisms that govern visual sensitivity, such as how GABAergic inhibition shapes the receptive fields and contrast preferences of direction-selective RGCs near the absolute threshold of vision. Furthermore, Dr. Field's research explores how these neural pathways are impacted by blinding diseases, assessing how post-synaptic circuit remodeling during progressive photoreceptor loss influences the temporal windows for effective gene therapy intervention in models of retinitis pigmentosa.

papers.title: Projection Targeting with Phototagging to Study the Structure and Function of Retinal Ganglion Cells
papers.abstract: This study details a novel methodology utilizing the retrograde viral vector AAV2retro to selectively deliver opsins and fluorescent markers to retinal ganglion cell (RGC) populations based on their central projections, specifically targeting the superior colliculus (SC). By employing phototagging coupled with large-scale multielectrode array (MEA) recordings, the researchers matched the physiological visual response profiles of SC-projecting RGCs to their specific morphologies and axonal destinations. The approach facilitates high-throughput characterization of retinorecipient circuits without requiring transgenic animal models, demonstrating its utility across species like rats and primates to resolve structural-functional relationships in the mammalian visual system.
papers.authors: Martin O. Bohlen, Andra M. Rudzite, Tierney B. Daw, Genevieve M. Kuczewski, Ergi Spiro, Cassie Hammond, Darienne R. Rogers, Antonio Gallego-Ortega, Suva Roy, Kimberly Ritola, Marc A. Sommer, Greg D. Field

papers.title: Information Processing in the Retina
papers.abstract: This technical review comprehensively delineates the computational architecture of the vertebrate retina, focusing on the transformation of optical inputs into parallel streams of spatio-temporal-chromatic information. The article synthesizes modern understanding of the synaptic interactions within the outer and inner plexiform layers, including lateral inhibition by horizontal cells and the complex modulatory roles of amacrine cells. Key metrics of retinal performance, such as quantum efficiency, gain control, and the limits of signaling near absolute visual threshold, are evaluated within the context of the retina's role as a sophisticated pre-processing engine for the central visual system.
papers.authors: Greg D. Field

papers.title: Information Processing: Ganglion Cells
papers.abstract: This article examines the functional diversity and physiological organization of retinal ganglion cells (RGCs), which constitute the primary output of the eye. It details the classification of RGCs into distinct functional 'mosaics' that tile the visual field to provide a complete and redundant representation of specific visual features. The discussion includes the biophysical mechanisms underlying receptive field structure, spike-timing precision, and the influence of correlated activity on the neural code. Furthermore, it addresses how these output channels are differentially affected during retinal degeneration, impacting the information transmitted to downstream targets like the lateral geniculate nucleus and superior colliculus.
papers.authors: Greg D. Field

papers.title: GABAergic Inhibition Controls Receptive Field Size, Sensitivity, and Contrast Preference of Direction Selective Retinal Ganglion Cells Near the Threshold of Vision
papers.abstract: The study investigates the circuit mechanisms regulating the absolute sensitivity and receptive field (RF) properties of direction-selective retinal ganglion cells (DSGCs) under scotopic conditions. Utilizing large-scale multielectrode array recordings and pharmacological blockade of GABAergic signaling, the authors found that superior-preferring ON-OFF DSGCs (s-DSGCs) exhibit unique physiological adaptations compared to other types. Specifically, GABAergic inhibition was identified as a critical regulator that restricts the RF size and determines the contrast preference of DSGCs at the threshold of vision. Removing this inhibition unmasked OFF responses in normally ON-responsive cells and reduced the sensitivity disparity between DSGC subtypes, highlighting a novel role for inhibitory interneurons in shaping parallel visual pathways during dark adaptation.
papers.authors: Suva Roy, Xiaoyang Yao, Jay Rathinavelu, Greg D. Field

papers.title: Late gene therapy limits the restoration of retinal function in a mouse model of retinitis pigmentosa
papers.abstract: This study evaluates the temporal window for effective gene therapy intervention in a rhodopsin-mutant mouse model of retinitis pigmentosa. By simulating therapeutic rescue at discrete stages of photoreceptor loss (25%, 50%, and 75% rod degeneration), the research team quantified the degree of functional recovery in the retinal circuit. Findings demonstrate that while early intervention (25-50% loss) successfully restores light-evoked signaling and receptive field organization in retinal ganglion cells, late-stage administration (75% loss) fails to recover robust visual output. This decline in efficacy is attributed to permanent remodeling of post-synaptic circuits and the loss of functional connections between cones and second-order neurons, emphasizing the critical importance of early diagnosis and intervention in degenerative blinding diseases.
papers.authors: Miranda L. Scalabrino, Mishek Thapa, Tian Wang, Alapakkam P. Sampath, Jeannie Chen, Greg D. Field

E007.name: Sheila Nirenberg
E007.bio: Sheila Nirenberg is a neuroscientist who works on the retina's neural code, the mathematical language used to transmit visual information to the brain. Their research involves implementing these codes into optogenetic-based prosthetic systems to bypass damaged photoreceptor cells and restore sight in patients with degenerative retinal diseases. By integrating computational modeling, gene therapy, and wearable computerized devices, Nirenberg developed a platform that stimulates ganglion cells with specific spatiotemporal patterns. Nirenberg is also adapting these biological coding principles to the development of machine vision algorithms and robotic sensory processing.
E007.research_direction: Dr. Nirenberg has recently been investigating clinical and computational approaches to vision restoration, particularly focusing on optogenetic gene therapies for retinal degenerative diseases like retinitis pigmentosa. Their recent work explores the clinical translation of these therapies, utilizing preclinical animal models to test viral vectors expressing high-speed opsins and employing computational modeling to evaluate opsin performance under natural, broadband ambient lighting. To support these biological interventions, they are developing comprehensive hardware and software platforms that dynamically convert visual stimuli into precise spatiotemporal light patterns designed to drive retinal ganglion cells and mimic the retina's natural neural code. Alongside this research in visual prosthetics, Dr. Nirenberg is also exploring broader neurodegenerative network dynamics, using modified maximum entropy models and graph neural networks to quantify disruptions in EEG functional connectivity associated with Alzheimer’s disease.

papers.title: Enhanced Functional Connectivity for EEG Classification with a Modified Maximum Entropy Model: a Case Study of Alzheimer's Disease
papers.abstract: The study proposes a novel framework for classifying Alzheimer's Disease (AD) by estimating brain functional connectivity (FC) using a modified maximum entropy model (MEM) optimized for EEG data. Traditional FC metrics often fail to capture the complex, higher-order statistical dependencies inherent in neural populations. By adapting the pairwise maximum entropy model to quantify spontaneous fluctuations in synchronization levels during eyes-closed resting states, the researchers derived robust graph-based biomarkers. These FC graphs were then utilized as inputs for a Graph Neural Network (GNN) to distinguish between AD patients and age-matched controls. Results indicate that cognitive dysfunction in AD is associated with significantly diminished synchronization fluctuations and altered mean connectivity levels across several frequency bands, particularly in the alpha sub-band. The model effectively reduces biases from volume conduction while enhancing the discriminability of network-level disruptions in the AD continuum.
papers.venue: 2025 47th Annual International Conference of the IEEE Engineering in Medicine and Biology Society (EMBC)
papers.authors: Kaidong Wu, Maksim Vakulenko, Boyuan Yan, Sheila Nirenberg, Peter E. Latham

papers.title: Theoretical prediction of broadband ambient light optogenetic vision restoration with ChRmine and its mutants
papers.abstract: This study employs computational modeling to evaluate the efficacy of the high-sensitivity microbial opsin ChRmine and its engineered variants for restoring vision under natural, broadband ambient light conditions. Unlike traditional opsins requiring high-intensity monochromatic LED stimulation, ChRmine exhibits significantly enhanced light sensitivity and a broad absorption spectrum. The authors simulated the photocurrent kinetics and firing responses of retinal ganglion neurons (RGNs) expressed with ChRmine, ReaChR, CoChR, and CatCh under diverse light sources including sunlight, halogen lamps, and RGB LEDs. The results demonstrate that ChRmine allows for RGN firing at irradiances as low as 1.2 nW/mm², enabling goggle-free vision restoration under pure white light. While broadband activation results in slower turn-off kinetics, high-fidelity spike trains were evoked up to 50 Hz, with the hsChRmine mutant extending this limit to 80 Hz. This theoretical framework provides a guide for the clinical translation of high-sensitivity optogenetic retinal prostheses capable of functioning in real-world lighting environments.
papers.authors: Himanshu Bansal, Gur Pyari, Sukhdev Roy, Boyuan Yan, Suresh Viswanathan, Scott E. Brodie, Sheila Nirenberg

papers.title: A clinically viable approach to restoring visual function using optogenetic gene therapy
papers.abstract: The researchers present preclinical safety and efficacy data for a novel optogenetic gene therapy (BS01) aimed at restoring vision in patients with advanced-stage retinitis pigmentosa (RP). The therapy utilizes an adeno-associated virus (AAV2) vector to express the high-speed, light-sensitive opsin ChronosFP in retinal ganglion cells. Efficacy was validated in rd1 mice using dose-dependent electroretinogram (ERG) responses and multi-electrode array recordings, demonstrating that the treated retinas could produce high-fidelity spike patterns matching the natural retinal code. Safety profiles were established in rats, non-human primates, and mice through long-term immunohistochemical analysis, cell counts, and ocular toxicology assays. The study found that ChronosFP-expressing vectors were well-tolerated and remained efficacious over a broad range of vector doses and stimulating light intensities without causing significant anatomical or electrophysiological damage to the inner retina, supporting the transition to human clinical trials (NCT04278131).
papers.authors: Boyuan Yan, Suresh Viswanathan, Scott E. Brodie, Wen-Tao Deng, Kirsten E. Coleman, William W. Hauswirth, Sheila Nirenberg

papers.title: An Engineering Platform for Clinical Application of Optogenetic Therapy in Retinal Degenerative Diseases
papers.abstract: The paper introduces a comprehensive hardware and software platform designed for the clinical testing, training, and rehabilitation of patients undergoing optogenetic gene therapy for blindness. The system addresses the limitations of standard ophthalmic equipment by integrating a high-intensity DLP-based light stimulator with real-time neural computation units. Key features include a specialized software application capable of generating diverse visual stimuli (e.g., gratings, moving objects, and natural scenes) and converting them into precise spatiotemporal light patterns that mimic the normal retinal output. Crucially, the platform incorporates adjustable geometrical mapping functions to account for the radial displacement between foveal cones and their corresponding ganglion cells. Experimental validation demonstrated the system's ability to achieve millisecond temporal resolution and spatial resolution up to 0.05°, sufficient for cellular-level stimulation in the central retina. This engineering platform provides the infrastructure necessary for customizing prosthetic parameters and assessing visual acuity, motion detection, and object recognition in a clinical setting.
papers.venue: IEEE Journal of Translational Engineering in Health and Medicine
papers.authors: Boyuan Yan, Sheila Nirenberg

E009.name: Dario Ringach
E009.bio: Dario Ringach is a Professor of Neurobiology and Psychology at UCLA. Their research focuses on the functional organization and computational principles of the primary visual cortex. Ringach developed reverse-correlation techniques to map the receptive fields of visual neurons and conducted studies on the temporal dynamics of orientation selectivity and population coding. Their recent work utilizes large-scale two-photon calcium imaging and theoretical modeling to investigate energy-efficient coding, the development of binocular circuitry, and the relationship between spontaneous and stimulus-driven cortical activity.
E009.research_direction: Dr. Ringach's recent work explores how the primary visual cortex encodes sensory information at the population level, with a major focus on how neural representations dynamically adapt to diverse environmental statistics. Using techniques like two-photon calcium imaging and high-density extracellular recordings in mouse V1, they are investigating the geometric properties of population response manifolds to uncover how contrast gain control and pattern adaptation integrate both stimulus intensity and prior predictability. They have also recently been examining the temporal evolution of energy-efficient sparse coding to understand how cortical networks optimize the trade-off between metabolic cost and representational fidelity immediately following stimulus onset. Additionally, their research includes developing novel computational frameworks, such as subspace reverse-correlation, to accurately map receptive fields during unconstrained free viewing by computationally accounting for the retinal image translations caused by continuous eye movements.

papers.title: Dynamics of energy-efficient coding in visual cortex
papers.abstract: Sparse coding theories suggest that cortical populations represent sensory information by utilizing a minimal number of active neurons, yet the temporal evolution of these representations is not well understood. This study utilizes large-scale population recordings in the mouse primary visual cortex (V1) to demonstrate that stimulus onset initially triggers a broad wave of cortical activation, which results in a transient decrease in population sparseness alongside a peak in mutual information. Subsequently, the representation is refined through competitive recurrent interactions that sustain high informational fidelity while the overall population activity declines and sparseness increases. These findings provide empirical support for a dynamic refinement process that optimizes the trade-off between energy expenditure and representational fidelity in the early visual system.
papers.authors: S. Amin Moosavi, Antonia Pastor, Alfredo G. Ornelas, Elaine Tring, Dario Ringach

papers.title: Subspace reverse-correlation estimation of receptive fields during free viewing
papers.abstract: Mapping the receptive fields of visual neurons during unconstrained behavior is complicated by retinal image translations caused by frequent eye movements. We present a novel computational framework that utilizes the phase-shifting properties of Hartley basis functions to directly model eye-position effects as translations in a subspace, bypassing the need for explicit retinal image reconstruction. This method employs a closed-form gradient for parameter optimization, significantly reducing computational overhead compared to traditional shifter-network approaches. In applications to high-density extracellular recordings from the mouse primary visual cortex, the technique enhanced the spatial resolution and sharpness of receptive field estimates by an average of 56% over naive methods, facilitating the study of cortical function during naturalistic viewing.
papers.authors: S. Amin Moosavi, Elaine Tring, Dario Ringach

papers.title: Contrast and pattern adaptation in visual cortex share a common gain control mechanism
papers.abstract: Sensory neurons in the primary visual cortex (V1) adapt their response properties based on both the average contrast and the statistical distribution of visual patterns in the environment. This study examines whether these two forms of adaptation rely on independent or shared neural mechanisms. Using two-photon calcium imaging, we show that the distribution of V1 population responses across various adaptation states can be consistently modeled by a zero-inflated log-normal distribution. Adaptation-induced changes primarily manifest as coordinated shifts in the probability of neuronal silence and the mean of the log-responses, while the response variance remains relatively invariant. These results suggest that contrast and pattern adaptation are mediated by a common gain control mechanism that shifts the population response manifold in a highly structured and predictable manner.
papers.authors: S. Amin Moosavi, Elaine Tring, Dario L. Ringach

papers.title: Contrast gain control is a reparameterization of a population response curve
papers.abstract: Cortical gain control allows the primary visual cortex to adjust its sensitivity to the prevailing contrast of the environment, but its effect on population-level representations remains unclear. We recorded the activity of large neuronal populations in mouse V1 across environments characterized by different contrast distributions. We find that the family of population responses to a fixed stimulus can be described by an invariant vector function of stimulus intensity, reparameterized by an environment-dependent gain factor. This geometric framework reveals that gain control acts as a coordinated scaling of the population response manifold, preserving the underlying structure of the representation across diverse environmental statistics. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the discriminability of contrast levels is proportional to the logarithm of their ratio, suggesting a robust implementation of Weber-Fechner scaling at the population level.
papers.authors: Elaine Tring, S. Amin Moosavi, Mario Dipoppa, Dario L. Ringach

papers.title: On the contrast response function of adapted neural populations
papers.abstract: The magnitude of neural activity in the primary visual cortex is influenced by both the physical intensity of a stimulus and its probability of occurrence within the sensory environment. To understand how these factors are integrated, we measured the responses of large populations in the mouse primary visual cortex across various adaptation states. We demonstrate that the vector magnitude of the population response is accurately described by a separable power law that factors both the stimulus contrast and its prior probability. Our findings show that these relationships arise naturally in populations where neurons are driven by Gaussian inputs with environment-modulated means. This study provides a normative quantitative link between environmental statistics and the state of cortical adaptation, suggesting that the cortex optimizes its representation based on stimulus predictability.
papers.authors: Elaine Tring, Mario Dipoppa, Dario L. Ringach

E010.name: Matteo Carandini
E010.bio: Carandini is a Professor of Visual Neuroscience researching the principles of neural computation and how populations of neurons represent sensory information. Carandini developed the divisive normalization model, which describes a computation used by the brain to regulate neuronal activity. Their research utilizes technologies such as high-density Neuropixels probes and widefield calcium imaging to map brain-wide activity during behavior, specifically investigating how non-visual signals like locomotion and arousal influence visual processing. As a co-director of the Cortexlab and a founding member of the International Brain Laboratory, Carandini coordinates the integration of experimental data with computational models to study the neural basis of perception and decision-making.
E010.research_direction: Dr. Carandini's recent work explores brainwide neural dynamics and large-scale visual coding while concurrently developing advanced technologies to record and manipulate these circuits. To more efficiently map the visual cortex, they have recently been engineering novel dynamic stimuli, such as high-contrast "Zebra noise," to rapidly probe population tuning properties alongside building optimized open-source pipelines for 3D volumetric two-photon calcium imaging. Beyond the visual system, they are utilizing high-density Neuropixels and newly integrated optogenetic probes to investigate how stable, brainwide sequences of neural activity propagate with fixed temporal delays across different sensory and behavioral states. Furthermore, their research combines large-scale electrophysiology with functional ultrasound imaging to examine the mechanisms of neurovascular coupling, specifically testing how global hemodynamic fluctuations are driven by distinct, opposing populations of neurons.

papers.title: Mapping the visual cortex with Zebra noise and wavelets
papers.abstract: The study introduces 'Zebra noise,' a novel dynamic visual stimulus generated via thresholded fractal Perlin noise, designed to efficiently probe the tuning properties of large neuronal populations. By applying an analytical framework based on Gabor wavelets, the authors demonstrate that this high-contrast, sharp-edged stimulus allows for the rapid characterization of multiple tuning parameters—including receptive field position, orientation preference, size, spatial frequency, and motion vectors—in thousands of neurons across the mouse primary and higher visual areas within 5 to 15 minutes of recording. Experimental results from two-photon calcium imaging indicate that Zebra noise elicites significantly higher response repeatability than traditional sparse noise or drifting grating stimuli, offering a high-throughput toolkit for mapping visual representations.
papers.authors: Sophie Skriabine, Maxwell Shinn, Samuel Picard, Kenneth D. Harris, Matteo Carandini

papers.title: Invariant activity sequences across the mouse brain
papers.abstract: This research identifies a stable, brainwide scaffold of neural activity sequences characterized by fixed temporal delays. Utilizing large-scale chronic Neuropixels recordings, the authors show that neurons across the entire mouse brain fire in characteristic 50-100 ms sequences where each neuron is coupled to the local population with a consistent delay that remains invariant over weeks. While the participation of individual neurons in these sequences depends on their sensory or behavioral tuning, the temporal structure itself is ubiquitous, stable during both spontaneous and evoked states, and synchronized across disparate brain regions. These findings suggest that invariant activity sequences constitute a canonical computational primitive shared across diverse neural circuits.
papers.authors: Célian Bimbard, Kenneth D Harris, Matteo Carandini

papers.title: Brainwide blood volume reflects opposing neural populations
papers.abstract: Combining functional ultrasound imaging (fUSI) with brainwide Neuropixels recordings, this study characterizes the neurovascular coupling underlying global hemodynamic fluctuations. The authors identify two distinct, opposing populations of neurons—those that increase versus decrease activity during arousal (e.g., whisking)—distributed throughout the mouse brain. These populations possess distinct hemodynamic response functions, and their summed contributions predict fluctuations in local blood volume significantly better than bulk neural activity. The relationship between neural dynamics and hemodynamics is found to be consistent across regions and brain states, including REM sleep, demonstrating that neurovascular coupling is driven by the coordinated activity of these opposing brainwide populations.
papers.authors: Agnès Landemard, Michael Krumin, Kenneth D Harris, Matteo Carandini

papers.title: Suite3D: Volumetric cell detection for two-photon microscopy
papers.abstract: The paper presents 'Suite3D,' an open-source pipeline optimized for the volumetric analysis of 3D two-photon calcium imaging data. Traditional plane-by-plane processing often results in redundant cell detection and loss of axial signal integrity; Suite3D circumvents this by implementing 3D rigid and non-rigid motion correction followed by 3D correlation-based neuron detection and volumetric segmentation. This approach improves the signal-to-background ratio, ensures cell unique identification across imaging planes, and operates over 20 times faster than previous volumetric frameworks. The pipeline's efficacy is validated using diverse datasets from conventional and advanced volumetric microscopes across multiple brain regions.
papers.authors: Ali Haydaroğlu, Tinya Chang, Andrew Landau, Michael Krumin, Sam Dodgson, Liad J Baruchin, Maria Cozan, Jingkun Guo, David Meyer, Charu Bai Reddy, Jian Zhong, Na Ji, Sylvia Schröder, Kenneth D Harris, Alipasha Vaziri, Matteo Carandini

papers.title: Neuropixels Opto: Combining high-resolution electrophysiology and optogenetics
papers.abstract: This work describes the development and validation of 'Neuropixels Opto' probes, which integrate 960 electrical recording sites with 28 spatially addressable photonic emitters (blue and red wavelengths) on a single 1 cm CMOS shank. The integration of high-density electrophysiology and optogenetics allows for the simultaneous recording of thousands of neurons and the precise manipulation of genetically-defined subpopulations. Validation experiments in the mouse cortex and striatum demonstrate the probe's ability to perform optotagging for cell-type identification and to silience or activate neurons at specific depths, providing a transformative tool for high-resolution circuit analysis in behaving animals.
papers.authors: Anna Lakunina, Karolina Z Socha, Alexander Ladd, Anna J Bowen, Susu Chen, Jennifer Colonell, Anjal Doshi, Bill Karsh, Michael Krumin, Pavel Kulik, Anna Li, Pieter Neutens, John O'Callaghan, Meghan Olsen, Jan Putzeys, Harrie AC Tilmans, Zhiwen Ye, Marleen Welkenhuysen, Michael Häusser, Christof Koch, Jonathan T Ting, Neuropixels Opto Consortium, Barun Dutta, Timothy D Harris, Nicholas A Steinmetz, Karel Svoboda, Joshua H Siegle, Matteo Carandini

E011.name: Kenneth Harris
E011.department: UCL Queen Square Institute of Neurology
E011.bio: Kenneth Harris is a Professor of Quantitative Neuroscience at University College London and co-directs the Cortical Processing Laboratory. Harris researches how large-scale populations of neurons in the cerebral cortex integrate sensory information with internal brain states to guide perceptual decisions. Their work in neurotechnology and data analysis includes the development of Neuropixels probes and Kilosort spike-sorting software. These tools are used for the high-density recording and characterization of thousands of individual neurons across multiple brain regions.
E011.research_direction: Dr. Harris has recently been investigating the computational principles of neural population coding in the primary visual cortex using large-scale Neuropixels and two-photon imaging. Their recent work explores how sensory inputs and behavioral states, such as locomotion, are differentially integrated across superficial and deep cortical layers, and probes the underlying dimensionality of neural activity to reconcile low-dimensional network dynamics with high-dimensional sensory responses. Additionally, they are examining how visuomotor training reshapes cortical stimulus representations, specifically investigating the dynamic mathematical transformations that might sparsen and orthogonalize population codes to aid downstream decision-making. To support these large-scale experimental aims, they are also developing novel analytical methodologies, ranging from recurrent neural network models for latent variable inference to accessible workflows that leverage reasoning large language models for complex scientific data exploration.

papers.title: High-dimensional neuronal activity from low-dimensional latent dynamics: a solvable model
papers.abstract: This work addresses the paradox between the theoretical hypothesis of low-dimensional latent dynamics in recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and experimental observations of high-dimensional neural population activity in the mammalian cortex. The authors present an analytically solvable RNN model where low-dimensional pre-activation dynamics generate high-dimensional post-activation activity through nonlinear neuronal activation functions, producing power-law covariance eigenspectra consistent with cortical data. They introduce the 'Neural Cross-Encoder' (NCE), a nonlinear latent variable identification method, to infer pre-activation dimensionality. Applying NCE to large-scale Neuropixels recordings from the mouse primary visual cortex, they find that while responses to drifting gratings and spontaneous activity are consistent with low-dimensional latents, responses to naturalistic stimuli remain high-dimensional even at the latent level.
papers.authors: Valentin Schmutz, Ali Haydaroğlu, Shuqi Wang, Yixiao Feng, Matteo Carandini, Kenneth D. Harris

papers.title: AIRUS: a simple workflow for AI-assisted exploration of scientific data
papers.abstract: This methodological note proposes AIRUS (AI Research Under Supervision), an iterative and accessible workflow leveraging 'reasoning' large language models (LLMs) to facilitate scientific data analysis. The framework enables researchers to utilize LLMs for generating scientific hypotheses, producing executable analysis code, interpreting computational results, and refining analytical approaches in successive cycles. The author demonstrates the efficacy of this human-in-the-loop AI system through two case studies: an analysis of synthetic datasets and a complex exploration of real-world electrophysiological data from the International Brain Laboratory. The workflow is designed to empower experimentalists lacking deep programming or AI expertise to perform sophisticated data exploration via a simple copy-paste interface between LLMs and cloud-based notebooks.
papers.authors: Kenneth D. Harris

papers.title: Functional Dissociation of Layers 2/3 and 5 in the Primary Visual Cortex
papers.abstract: Utilizing large-scale two-photon calcium imaging and high-density Neuropixels recordings, this study challenges the classical columnar hypothesis by demonstrating fundamental differences in how layers 2/3 and 5 of the mouse primary visual cortex (V1) integrate sensory and behavioral information. The researchers found that layer 2/3 activity is predominantly modulated by visual input and is desynchronized by locomotion, whereas layer 5 activity is more strongly influenced by movement and exhibits increased synchrony during motor action. Furthermore, spontaneous activity in layer 2/3 is lower-dimensional and dominated by a single coding dimension compared to the higher-dimensional activity in layer 5. These findings suggest a functional division of labor where superficial layers specialize in robust sensory representations for downstream cortical processing, while deep layers integrate sensory signals with behavioral context to guide motor output.
papers.authors: Timothy P.H. Sit, Célian Bimbard, Anna Lebedeva, Matteo Carandini, Philip Coen, Kenneth D. Harris

papers.title: Visual experience orthogonalizes visual cortical stimulus responses via population code transformation
papers.abstract: This study investigates how behavioral training alters stimulus representation in the mouse primary visual cortex (V1). By measuring orientation tuning in 4,000-neuron populations, the authors identified that training on a visuomotor task induces a specific mathematical transformation of population activity. This transformation selectively suppresses responses to motor-associated stimuli in neurons that otherwise fire at intermediate levels, resulting in the sparsening and orthogonalization of population codes. The degree of this transformation fluctuates trial-to-trial, suggesting it is driven by dynamic circuit mechanisms rather than static synaptic plasticity. While this orthogonalization does not enhance the performance of an optimal stimulus decoder, it significantly improves the accuracy of suboptimal decoders with inductive biases, suggesting that learning-induced plasticity in V1 facilitates the readout of task-relevant information by downstream neural circuits.
papers.authors: Samuel W. Failor, Matteo Carandini, Kenneth D. Harris

papers.title: Visuomotor association orthogonalizes visual cortical population codes
papers.abstract: The authors measured orientation tuning in large populations of mouse V1 neurons before and after training on a visuomotor task to determine if task demands reshape cortical codes. They observed that training results in a population-level sparsening and orthogonalization of neural representations for motor-associated stimuli. This effect was captured by a simple mathematical transformation where responses to task-relevant stimuli were suppressed in cells with intermediate-level firing. The strength of this transformation was found to vary across trials, indicating it arises from dynamic circuit states rather than fixed synaptic changes. The results suggest that the primary visual cortex undergoes a representational shift that specifically differentiates task-relevant stimuli, thereby aiding downstream decision-making systems.
papers.authors: Samuel W. Failor, Matteo Carandini, Kenneth D. Harris

E013.name: David Heeger
E013.department: Department of Psychology and Center for Neural Science
E013.bio: David Heeger is a Silver Professor at New York University who investigates the computations of neural circuits. Heeger developed the normalization model, a theory of neural processing that explains how neurons integrate and scale signals within the visual cortex. Their research focuses on establishing a theoretical framework for cortical function. Heeger utilizes methodologies including functional MRI, psychophysics, and computational modeling of neural dynamics.
E013.research_direction: Dr. Heeger has recently been investigating the computational principles and physiological dynamics underlying visual processing and attention. Their recent work explores how canonical cortical operations, particularly divisive normalization and inter-areal communication, can be mathematically modeled using stable recurrent neural circuits and contrastive learning frameworks to explain neural manifold geometry. Alongside this theoretical modeling, they are using high-temporal-resolution fMRI and MEG to track the anticipatory baseline shifts and stimulus-evoked gain changes associated with voluntary temporal attention in the human visual cortex. Additionally, they are behaviorally probing the limits of top-down attention by investigating how stimulus features like high relative speed influence phenomena such as inattentional blindness.

papers.title: Contrastive Self-Supervised Learning As Neural Manifold Packing
papers.abstract: This work introduces CLAMP (Contrastive Learning As Manifold Packing), a framework that interprets contrastive self-supervised learning through the lens of representational geometry and neural manifolds. In the primate visual system, stimulus categories are encoded as manifolds within the neural state space; CLAMP treats the optimization of these representations as a manifold packing problem, aiming to maximize class separability by minimizing overlap between high-dimensional clusters. The authors demonstrate that CLAMP ENDOWS hyperparameters with clear physical interpretations—akin to short-range repulsive particle systems—and produces structured representational geometries that improve classification accuracy and align with biological benchmarks for neural manifolds in the visual cortex.
papers.venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS)
papers.authors: Guanming Zhang, David J. Heeger, Stefano Martiniani

papers.title: Hierarchical Neural Circuit Theory of Normalization and Inter-areal Communication
papers.abstract: The authors propose a hierarchical recurrent neural circuit framework incorporating reciprocal connections and dynamic divisive normalization to model canonical inter-areal communication. The theory analytically derives power and coherence spectra for cortical hierarchies (e.g., V1–V2), predicting that increased stimulus contrast shifts spectral peaks to higher frequencies. Crucially, the model unifies 'communication-through-subspace' and 'communication-through-coherence' principles by demonstrating that high-coherence frequency bands characterize low-dimensional communication subspaces, enabling selective information transfer between brain regions. The model also shows that feedback from higher cortical areas modulates the gain and dynamics of lower areas in alignment with experimental observations.
papers.authors: Asit Pal, Shivang Rawat, David J. Heeger, Stefano Martiniani

papers.title: Unconditional stability of a recurrent neural circuit implementing divisive normalization
papers.abstract: This research provides a rigorous mathematical stability analysis of Oscillatory Recurrent Gated Neural Integrator Circuits (ORGaNICs), which are biologically plausible recurrent networks that dynamically implement divisive normalization. Using Lyapunov's indirect method, the authors prove that ORGaNICs exhibit unconditional local stability when the recurrent weight matrix is the identity. By characterizing the system as a set of coupled damped harmonic oscillators, the study derives an energy function that characterizes the circuit's computational objectives. These findings provide a normative principle for recurrent cortical dynamics and facilitate the training of stable, high-dimensional neurodynamical models.
papers.venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS)
papers.authors: Shivang Rawat, David Heeger, Stefano Martiniani

papers.title: Anticipatory and evoked visual cortical dynamics of voluntary temporal attention
papers.abstract: Using high-temporal-resolution fMRI and MEG, this study tracks the cortical dynamics of voluntary temporal attention in the human visual system. The results identify two distinct components of attentional modulation in areas V1–V4: an anticipatory increase in baseline neural activity occurring before stimulus onset and an evoked modulation of the stimulus-driven response. These findings suggest that temporal attention acts as a dynamic gain control mechanism, prioritizing sensory information at specific time points through a combination of pre-stimulus baseline shifts and subsequent response scaling, effectively reorganizing the temporal profile of visual processing.
papers.authors: Rachel N. Denison, Karen J. Tian, David J. Heeger, Marisa Carrasco

papers.title: The visible gorilla: Unexpected fast—not physically salient—Objects are noticeable
papers.abstract: This study re-examines the limits of human attention by probing the impact of stimulus speed on the phenomenon of inattentional blindness. Through a large-scale replication and extension of the classic 'invisible gorilla' experiment (n > 1,500), the authors demonstrate that high relative speed significantly increases the probability of noticing an unexpected object, regardless of its physical salience or task-relevance. The results suggest the existence of a prioritized 'sentinel' motion detection system in the primate brain that can override task-focused endogenous attention, suggesting that the visual system is evolved to detect fast-moving potential threats even during demanding cognitive tasks.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS)
papers.authors: Michael Karlovich, Wayne Mackey, David J. Heeger

E016.name: Serge Dumoulin
E016.institution: Royal Netherlands Academy of Arts and Sciences
E016.bio: Serge Dumoulin is the Director of the Spinoza Centre for Neuroimaging and holds professorships at Utrecht University and VU Amsterdam. Dumoulin’s research characterizes the functional architecture of the human visual system using ultra-high field (7T) fMRI, psychophysics, and biologically-inspired computational models. They developed the population receptive field (pRF) mapping technique to quantify the spatial response properties of neural populations non-invasively.
