Dumoulin’s recent work applies these computational approaches to the topographic representation of higher-order cognitive functions, such as numerosity, and the plasticity of visual maps in response to neurological and ophthalmological disorders.
E016.research_direction: Dr. Dumoulin has recently been investigating the spatiotemporal dynamics and canonical computations of the human visual system, primarily utilizing ultra-high-field 7T fMRI and population receptive field (pRF) modeling. Their recent work explores the fundamental properties of spatial vision, modeling neural contrast sensitivity functions across cortical eccentricity and examining how the spatial precision of attention actively shifts pRF tuning. In addition to high-resolution spatial mapping, they are developing multimodal frameworks that integrate fMRI with MEG to track the millisecond-scale feedforward and feedback flow of visual information across the cortical hierarchy. Broadening this computational focus to naturalistic and biological constraints, Dr. Dumoulin is also investigating how V1 represents perceptually relevant object boundaries in natural scenes and how algorithmic processes like divisive normalization are rooted in the specific chemoarchitecture of cortical neurotransmitters.

papers.title: The precision of attention controls attraction of population receptive fields
papers.abstract: This investigation probes the relationship between the spatial specificity of attentional allocation and the subsequent displacement of population receptive fields (pRFs) in the human visual system. Utilizing 7-Tesla functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), the researchers demonstrate that the magnitude of pRF attraction toward an attended locus is significantly modulated by the precision of the attention field—contrasting focused and distributed attentional states. They apply a Gaussian attention field model to characterize the observed spatial resampling, finding that higher attentional precision induces more substantial pRF shifts, particularly within the extrastriate visual hierarchy. The findings suggest that the degree to which the visual cortex reorganizes its spatial sampling is contingent upon the concentration of attentional resources.
papers.authors: Sumiya Sheikh Abdirashid, Tomas Knapen, Serge O. Dumoulin

papers.title: Non-invasive mapping of the temporal processing hierarchy in the human visual cortex
papers.abstract: This study introduces a novel computational framework that integrates the high-resolution spatial mapping of fMRI with the millisecond-scale temporal resolution of magnetoencephalography (MEG). By employing forward modeling to project fMRI-defined visual field maps (defined via pRF estimation) into MEG sensor space, the authors non-invasively quantify the temporal contributions of distinct cortical regions to stimulus-evoked brain activity. Their results establish a clear spatiotemporal hierarchy across the visual cortex, demonstrating that V1 accounts for the majority of early MEG signal variance before activity propagates through subsequent extrastriate field maps. The methodology provides a robust means for tracking the feedforward and feedback flow of visual information in the living human brain.
papers.authors: Katharina Eickhoff, Arjan Hillebrand, Tomas Knapen, Maartje C. de Jong, Serge O. Dumoulin

papers.title: Modeling neural contrast sensitivity functions in human visual cortex
papers.abstract: This work develops a quantitative pRF-based framework to model the neural contrast sensitivity function (nCSF) at the population level throughout the human visual system. By systematically varying stimulus spatial frequency and contrast during 7T fMRI, the authors evaluate how peak spatial frequency tuning and contrast gain parameters evolve as a function of eccentricity and across the visual hierarchy. The nCSF model effectively captures the nonlinear transition from sub-threshold activity to response saturation. The study reveals that peak spatial frequency preferences decrease with eccentricity and increase in complexity as signals progress through higher-level visual areas, providing a detailed map of the cortical factors limiting human visual performance.
papers.authors: Carlien Roelofzen, Marcus Daghlian, Jelle A. van Dijk, Maartje C. de Jong, Serge O. Dumoulin

papers.title: V1 neurons are tuned to perceptual borders in natural scenes
papers.abstract: This study employs a multimodal approach—incorporating 7T fMRI in humans, electrophysiological recordings in macaques, and computational modeling—to elucidate how the primary visual cortex (V1) represents perceptually relevant boundaries in natural environments. The researchers find that V1 neurons exhibit significantly enhanced responses to object-background borders compared to non-border patches, even when local features like orientation energy and contrast are matched. This border-selective tuning manifests as early as 50 ms after stimulus onset, indicating a rapid feedforward detection mechanism. A secondary, delayed phase of activity suggests further contextual modulation, collectively demonstrating that V1 architecture is inherently tuned to the structural features that define perceptual segments in natural scenes.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS)
papers.authors: Paolo Papale, Wietske Zuiderbaan, Rob R. M. Teeuwen, Amparo Gilhuis, Matthew W. Self, Pieter R. Roelfsema, Serge O. Dumoulin

papers.title: Computational model links normalization to chemoarchitecture in the human visual system
papers.abstract: The authors propose a neurocomputational bridge between the algorithmic operation of divisive normalization (DN) and the underlying chemoarchitectural landscape of the human visual cortex. Using ultra-high-field 7T fMRI, they estimate voxel-wise normalization parameters and compare these against receptor density maps. The study identifies a systematic correlation between normalization strength and the distribution of GABAergic and glutamatergic receptors and transporters across the visual hierarchy. These findings provide biological evidence that divisive normalization serves as a canonical neural computation that is deeply rooted in the cortical neurochemical environment, linking systems-level fMRI observations to the molecular organization of the brain.
papers.authors: Marco Aqil, Tomas Knapen, Serge O. Dumoulin

E017.name: Kendrick Kay
E017.bio: Kendrick Kay is an Associate Professor at the University of Minnesota’s Center for Magnetic Resonance Research (CMRR) specializing in the intersection of computational modeling and high-resolution functional MRI. Kay's research focuses on developing predictive encoding models to characterize how the human visual cortex represents naturalistic stimuli and facilitates perceptual decision-making. They have developed neuroimaging resources, such as the Natural Scenes Dataset (NSD), and statistical tools like GLMsingle for fMRI response estimates. Kay's current investigations use ultra-high-field (7T and 10.5T) imaging to resolve functional architectures across cortical layers and columns.
E017.research_direction: Dr. Kay's recent work explores the computational principles of visual processing through "intensive" neuroimaging, leveraging massive within-subject 7T fMRI datasets to build precise, voxel-level encoding models of individual brain function. To bridge species and spatial scales, they have recently been developing matched-paradigm resources that link human hemodynamic measurements with single- and multi-unit macaque electrophysiology. Their research also investigates how well computational models trained on naturalistic images generalize to out-of-distribution synthetic stimuli, such as parametrically controlled gratings and noise patterns. Furthermore, Dr. Kay is developing generative statistical frameworks to disentangle trial-level signal from noise to improve estimates of neural dimensionality, while also establishing theoretical models to probe how top-down behavioral task demands dynamically shape sensory tuning throughout the visual system.

papers.title: Integrating neuroscience across species and scales
papers.abstract: This perspective piece situates a newly introduced large-scale macaque electrophysiology resource (the Triple-N dataset) within the broader effort to integrate neural measurements obtained across species and spatial/temporal scales. The authors discuss how the Triple-N dataset was deliberately designed to match the stimulus set and experimental paradigm of the human 7T fMRI Natural Scenes Dataset, enabling direct comparison of macaque single/multi-unit responses with human hemodynamic responses to identical natural images. They argue that such matched-paradigm designs are essential for bridging the complementary strengths of invasive electrophysiology (fine temporal and spatial resolution) and noninvasive human neuroimaging (broad coverage, ecological and clinical relevance), and for building unified computational models of visual cortical processing that generalize across species and measurement modalities.
papers.authors: Ammar I. Marvi, Jacob S. Prince, Kendrick Kay

papers.title: A 7T fMRI dataset of synthetic images for out-of-distribution modeling of vision
papers.abstract: The authors introduce NSD-synthetic, a 7T fMRI dataset collecting responses from the same eight participants used in the Natural Scenes Dataset (NSD) to a new set of 284 synthetic images that are deliberately out-of-distribution relative to the naturalistic images in NSD. The synthetic stimuli include parametrically controlled gratings, noise patterns, and other non-naturalistic image classes, allowing researchers to probe how well encoding models trained on natural scenes generalize to stimulus statistics they were not trained on. The authors show that the fMRI responses to these synthetic images are highly reliable and carry robust stimulus-related information, and they demonstrate that comparing candidate brain-computational models on this out-of-distribution set reveals meaningful differences in generalization performance that are not apparent when models are evaluated only on in-distribution natural images from NSD.
papers.authors: Alessandro T. Gifford, Radoslaw M. Cichy, Thomas Naselaris, Kendrick Kay

papers.title: Disentangling signal and noise in neural responses through generative modeling
papers.abstract: The authors present Generative modeling of Signal and Noise (GSN), a statistical framework that models trial-level neural response data (e.g., fMRI voxel or unit responses across repeated stimulus presentations) as the sum of draws from an underlying signal distribution and an independent noise distribution. By explicitly estimating the covariance structure of signal and noise separately, GSN allows researchers to denoise downstream analyses such as principal components analysis, improving estimates of the effective dimensionality of neural population responses and the accuracy of representational similarity estimates. The authors validate GSN on both simulated data and empirical fMRI datasets, showing that it recovers known signal properties more accurately than conventional approaches that do not separate signal and noise, and they release an accompanying software toolbox to enable broad adoption of the method.
papers.authors: Kendrick Kay, Jacob S. Prince, Thomas Gebhart, Greta Tuckute, Jenelle Zhou, Thomas Naselaris, Heiko H. Schütt

papers.title: Principles of intensive human neuroimaging
papers.abstract: This opinion article distinguishes an emerging 'intensive' fMRI approach from the more familiar 'wide' (many subjects, little data each) and 'deep' (few subjects, many hours each) sampling strategies that have dominated recent large-scale human neuroimaging efforts. Intensive fMRI is characterized by extensive within-subject sampling of a specific cognitive or perceptual phenomenon, sufficient to support voxel-level computational modeling and detailed characterization of individual brain function rather than only group-level inference. The authors articulate a set of guiding principles for designing intensive neuroimaging studies—covering stimulus/task design, session structure, quality control, and model validation—and argue that this approach is particularly well suited to testing detailed, quantitative models of sensory and cognitive processing at the level of single voxels or small populations of neurons.
papers.authors: Eline R. Kupers, Tomas Knapen, Elisha P. Merriam, Kendrick N. Kay

papers.title: Tasks and their role in visual neuroscience
papers.abstract: This review argues that visual neuroscience has historically emphasized careful control and quantification of visual stimuli while under-theorizing the role of the observer's task in shaping sensory processing. Drawing on evidence for widespread task-dependent modulation of activity throughout the visual system—from early visual cortex through higher-order areas—the authors propose a conceptual framework for classifying tasks and formally incorporating them into computational models of vision. They discuss how task demands can alter tuning properties, gain, and even the effective dimensionality of visual representations, and they call for experimental and modeling paradigms that treat the task, not just the stimulus, as a first-class variable in understanding visual cortical computation.
papers.authors: Kendrick Kay, Kathryn Bonnen, Rachel N. Denison, Michael J. Arcaro, David L. Barack

E018.name: Nicholas Priebe
E018.bio: Nicholas Priebe is a Professor of Neuroscience at the University of Texas at Austin where they investigate the circuit-level mechanisms and computations underlying sensory transformations in the mammalian visual cortex. Using in vivo whole-cell electrophysiology, two-photon imaging, and computational modeling, Priebe explores how neurons integrate thalamic and cortical inputs to generate selectivity for features such as orientation, motion, and depth. Their research examines contrast-invariant tuning, cross-orientation suppression, and the impact of behavioral states, such as locomotion and arousal, on cortical representation. Current projects focus on how these sensory representations are modulated by internal goals and integrated across different visual areas to guide behavior.
E018.research_direction: Dr. Priebe's recent work explores the fundamental mechanisms of sensory encoding and network dynamics in the early visual system. Using techniques ranging from in vivo whole-cell recordings to large-scale two-photon calcium imaging and high-density Neuropixels, they are investigating how the primary visual cortex multiplexes spatial features alongside environmental context to maintain stable stimulus tuning across diverse luminance regimes. They have also recently been examining the biophysical origins of irregular neocortical spiking, probing how temporal fluctuations in sparse thalamic input and shifting timescales of network synchrony shape cortical response variability during spontaneous and sensory-driven states. Additionally, their recent methodological work involves developing novel modular chamber systems to facilitate chronic, multi-modal longitudinal recordings of neural population dynamics in the awake marmoset neocortex.

papers.title: Independent encoding of orientation and mean luminance by mouse visual cortex
papers.abstract: This study examines whether the mouse primary visual cortex (V1) concurrently represents spatial stimulus features and ambient luminance levels. Using large-scale two-photon calcium imaging, the researchers demonstrate that while individual V1 neurons maintain luminance-invariant orientation selectivity, the population-level activity retains a robust representation of mean luminance. Dimensionality reduction via dDR reveals that signals for orientation and luminance are encoded along orthogonal axes in the neural response space. This geometric arrangement allows for the independent readout of sensory features and environmental context, suggesting that V1 utilizes a multiplexed population code where stimulus information is distributed randomly across the ensemble to decouple feature representation from environmental irradiance.
papers.authors: Ronan T. O’Shea, Xue-Xin Wei, Nicholas J. Priebe

papers.title: Synchrony timescales underlie irregular neocortical spiking
papers.abstract: This research investigates the network-level mechanisms driving the characteristic high variability and near-Poisson spiking statistics of neocortical neurons. Through in vivo whole-cell dynamic clamp recordings and high-density Neuropixels electrophysiology, the authors demonstrate that intrinsic neuronal properties contribute negligibly to spiking irregularity. Instead, spiking variability is shown to emerge from weakly synchronous network drive. Crucially, the study identifies a shift in the timescale of this synchrony, which contracts from approximately 200 ms during spontaneous activity to 25 ms during sensory-driven states. This modulation in synchrony timescales provides a mechanistic account for the systematic reduction in response variability (Fano factors) observed during cortical activation.
papers.authors: Jagruti J. Pattadkal, Ronan T. O'Shea, David Hansel, Thibaud Taillefumier, Darrin H. Brager, Nicholas J. Priebe

papers.title: The fluctuation-based regime of thalamocortical circuitry
papers.abstract: The study addresses whether sparse thalamocortical (TC) projections can drive cortical responses despite having subthreshold mean excitation levels. By isolating thalamic inputs via optogenetic cortical silencing and utilizing whole-cell recordings in mouse V1, the authors quantified the relationship between thalamic drive and the action potential initiation threshold. They find that while the average thalamic-mediated depolarization is insufficient to reach the spiking threshold, transient trial-by-trial fluctuations in synaptic input provide sufficient current to evoke visually-driven action potentials. This identifies the primary visual cortex as operating in a fluctuation-driven regime, where the temporal variance of thalamic activity, rather than its mean level, determines cortical output.
papers.authors: Liam Jennings, David Hansel, Nicholas J. Priebe

papers.title: Neural Recording Chambers for Long-Term Access to Brain Tissue
papers.abstract: The authors present a novel modular chamber system designed for chronic, multi-modal neural recording in the marmoset neocortex. The design incorporates a low-profile base with interchangeable inserts that allow for high-resolution two-photon imaging, wide-field mesoscopic calcium imaging, and high-density electrophysiology (e.g., Neuropixels) within the same surgical preparation. The system permits repeated access to the underlying tissue for pharmacological or viral manipulations while ensuring a stable, long-term seal. Validation in awake primates demonstrates that the chamber maintains optical clarity and consistent electrophysiological yields over several months, facilitating longitudinal studies of neural population dynamics and state-dependent computations.
papers.authors: Jagruti J. Pattadkal, Nicholas J. Priebe

papers.title: Luminance invariant encoding in mouse primary visual cortex
papers.abstract: This study explores how V1 maintains orientation and spatial frequency selectivity despite the profound shifts in retinal output that occur during adaptation between scotopic (rod-mediated) and photopic (cone-mediated) regimes. By measuring population activity in the LGN and V1, the authors find that while thalamic responses reflect the altered receptive field structures and interneuronal correlations of retinal ganglion cells, V1 selectivity remains invariant to luminance changes. Computational modeling suggests that this cortical invariance is achieved through the convergence of parallel functional thalamocortical channels. The results indicate that V1 circuitry is organized to extract stable stimulus features, effectively compensating for the dynamic range-dependent shifts of the peripheral visual system.
papers.authors: Ronan T. O’Shea, Ian Nauhaus, Xue-Xin Wei, Nicholas J. Priebe

E024.name: Daniel Yamins
E024.department: Departments of Psychology and Computer Science
E024.bio: Daniel Yamins is an Associate Professor of Psychology and Computer Science at Stanford University whose research focuses on the intersection of artificial intelligence and neuroscience. Yamins develops performance-optimized deep neural networks that serve as models of primate visual and auditory systems, showing that task-optimized architectures can predict neural response patterns. Their research uses high-throughput neurophysiology, functional brain imaging, and large-scale data analysis to model the algorithms of the human brain. Yamins currently investigates how self-supervised learning and 3D scene understanding contribute to the functional organization of sensory pathways and works on methodologies for model-brain comparisons.
E024.research_direction: Dr. Yamins has recently been investigating how predictive and generative models can learn rich, physically grounded representations of the world across multiple sensory domains. Their recent work explores self-supervised 3D scene understanding, developing computational methods to extract object-centric 3D geometries, novel views, and depth from single images. Within dynamic vision, they are probing large-scale video prediction architectures to understand how these models can perform zero-shot optical flow and motion estimation through test-time inference and counterfactual reasoning. Beyond the visual domain, Dr. Yamins is applying similar autoregressive predictive frameworks to human speech, investigating how abstract auditory representations emerge in the cortex by training models on biologically inspired cochlear features.

papers.title: Unified 3D Scene Understanding Through Physical World Modeling
papers.abstract: The authors propose a unified autoregressive generative framework, termed Local Random Access Sequence (LRAS) modeling, for comprehensive 3D scene understanding from single monocular images. By utilizing local patch quantization and a randomly ordered sequence generation scheme, the model achieves structural consistency in novel view synthesis and depth estimation without relying on diffusion priors. The architecture treats spatio-temporal patches independently, allowing the model to integrate optical flow as a latent intermediate for complex 3D scene manipulation and object-centric reasoning. Quantitative evaluations demonstrate state-of-the-art performance in geometry-aware generation tasks and self-supervised depth estimation.
papers.authors: Wanhee Lee, Klemen Kotar, Rahul Mysore Venkatesh, Jared Watrous, Honglin Chen, Khai Loong Aw, Daniel LK Yamins

papers.title: Taming generative video models for zero-shot optical flow extraction
papers.abstract: This research investigates the capability of large-scale, frozen, self-supervised generative video models to perform zero-shot optical flow extraction without task-specific fine-tuning. The authors introduce 'KL-tracing,' a test-time inference procedure that probes a model's internal predictive distributions by injecting localized tracer perturbations into the input frame and computing the Kullback-Leibler divergence between the perturbed and unperturbed next-frame distributions. The study demonstrates that successful flow extraction requires specific architectural properties—namely distributional prediction, factorized latents, and random-access decoding—found in the LRAS architecture. The resulting zero-shot method matches or exceeds the performance of specialized flow models on benchmarks such as TAP-Vid DAVIS and Kubric.
papers.venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS)
papers.authors: Seungwoo Kim, Khai Loong Aw, Klemen Kotar, Cristobal Eyzaguirre, Wanhee Lee, Yunong Liu, Jared Watrous, Stefan Stojanov, Juan Carlos Niebles, Jiajun Wu, Daniel L. K. Yamins

papers.title: Self-Supervised Learning of Motion Concepts by Optimizing Counterfactuals
papers.abstract: The paper introduces Opt-CWM, a self-supervised framework for estimating motion and occlusion primitives from pretrained next-frame video prediction models. To circumvent the sim-to-real gap associated with synthetic training data, the authors formulate motion estimation as an optimization problem over counterfactual probes. By learning to generate optimal probes through a novel sparse-prediction objective, the model extracts dense correspondence information from the latent representations of base video models. Opt-CWM achieves state-of-the-art performance for zero-shot motion estimation on real-world videos, demonstrating the efficacy of counterfactual reasoning in self-supervised world modeling.
papers.venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS)
papers.authors: Stefan Stojanov, David Wendt, Seungwoo Kim, Rahul Mysore Venkatesh, Kevin Feigelis, Klemen Kotar, Khai Loong Aw, Jiajun Wu, Daniel LK Yamins

papers.title: Representing Speech Through Autoregressive Prediction of Cochlear Tokens
papers.abstract: The authors propose AuriStream, a biologically inspired two-stage framework for speech representation learning modeled after the human auditory hierarchy. In the first stage, raw audio is transformed into a time-frequency representation based on the human cochlea, which is then quantized into discrete 'cochlear tokens.' The second stage employs an autoregressive sequence model trained on these tokens to learn phonemic and lexical semantic features. AuriStream shows high predictive alignment with human auditory cortex responses and outperforms standard spectrotemporal filter-bank models. The model also generates interpretable audio continuations, providing insights into the emergence of abstract auditory representations from predictive objectives.
papers.authors: Greta Tuckute, Klemen Kotar, Evelina Fedorenko, Daniel L. K. Yamins

papers.title: Unsupervised 3D Scene Representation Learning via Movable Object Inference
papers.abstract: This work presents Movable Object Radiance Fields (MORF), an unsupervised method for learning object-centric 3D representations from single images of complex scenes. Inspired by developmental cognitive science, MORF learns to disentangle foreground objects and backgrounds into separate radiance fields by observing motion cues. The framework leverages a 2D movable object inference module pretrained on monocular video to supervise the discovery of 3D objects in static multi-view training scenes. During inference, MORF performs a single-pass extraction of 3D geometries and appearances, enabling high-quality 3D reconstruction and scene editing on diverse object categories without human-provided semantic annotations.
papers.authors: Honglin Chen, Wanhee Lee, Hong-Xing Yu, Rahul Mysore Venkatesh, Joshua B. Tenenbaum, Daniel Bear, Jiajun Wu, Daniel LK Yamins

E026.name: SueYeon Chung
E026.department: Department of Physics and Department of Applied Mathematics
E026.lab_name: NeuroAI and Geometric Data Analysis (NAIGDA) group
E026.bio: SueYeon Chung is a theoretical neuroscientist who researches geometric and physical principles underlying neural representations in biological and artificial systems. Chung develops mathematical frameworks using high-dimensional geometry and statistical physics to analyze how neural population structures facilitate information processing and task execution. Their work focuses on characterizing neural manifolds to understand transformations of representations across processing stages, relating brain science to artificial intelligence. Formerly an Assistant Professor at New York University’s Center for Neural Science, Chung leads a research program that constructs neurally-plausible network models and biologically-inspired learning rules.
E026.research_direction: Dr. Chung's recent work explores the high-dimensional geometry of neural population codes, investigating how the structural properties of these representations support biological perception and artificial learning. They have recently been utilizing analytical frameworks like manifold capacity theory and statistical mechanics to examine how diverse neuronal tuning shapes representational manifolds for optimal stimulus discrimination, and to assess the learning behavior of continuous neural decoders. Their research also probes the dynamics of feature learning and task generalization, tracking how shared latent structures influence the disentanglement of neural representations during network training. Additionally, they are investigating key methodological challenges in systems neuroscience, employing Random Matrix Theory to understand and correct the systematic biases that arise when estimating representational similarity from sparse neuronal recordings.

papers.title: Neural Population Geometry and Optimal Coding of Tasks with Shared Latent Structure
papers.abstract: This study presents an analytical framework connecting the high-dimensional geometry of neural population activity to the generalization capacity of linear decoders on tasks sharing a common latent architecture. The authors identify four fundamental geometric statistics—characterizing dimensionality, factorization, and correlation structures—that serve as the primary determinants of task performance. Using this theoretical basis, they demonstrate that optimal neural representations adaptively expand or compress latent variables depending on the volume of training data, a process that naturally produces the disentangled representations observed in neurophysiological recordings from the macaque ventral stream. The findings provide a formal link between the structural properties of population codes and their functional utility in multi-task learning environments.
papers.authors: Albert J. Wakhloo, Will Slatton, SueYeon Chung

papers.title: Spectral Analysis of Representational Similarity with Limited Neurons
papers.abstract: This work utilizes Random Matrix Theory to analyze the impact of finite neuron sampling on representational similarity metrics, specifically Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA) and Canonical Correlation Analysis (CCA). The researchers establish that limited neuronal recording systematically biases similarity estimates downward due to the phenomenon of eigenvector delocalization in the sample Gram matrix. They demonstrate that for populations exhibiting power-law spectra, the number of localized eigenvectors scales as the square root of the total recorded population size. To mitigate this bias, the paper introduces a spectral denoising method capable of inferring population-level similarity from sparse data, validated through both synthetic models and empirical neural datasets.
papers.authors: Hyunmo Kang, Abdulkadir Canatar, SueYeon Chung

papers.title: Statistical Mechanics of Support Vector Regression
papers.abstract: Applying the statistical mechanics of disordered systems, this paper investigates the average-case learning behavior of epsilon-insensitive Support Vector Regression (ε-SVR) within the context of continuous neural decoding. The analysis identifies a critical phase transition in training error at a specific capacity load and characterizes the double-descent phenomenon in generalization error. The authors show that the epsilon tolerance parameter functions as a regularizer that effectively modulates and shifts generalization peaks. These results extend the theory of maximum-margin classification to regression tasks, providing a quantitative method for assessing linear decodability in the presence of inherent neural response variability.
papers.authors: Abdulkadir Canatar, SueYeon Chung

papers.title: Feature Learning beyond the Lazy-Rich Dichotomy: Insights from Representational Geometry
papers.abstract: This research introduces a geometric framework to analyze the mechanisms of feature learning in neural networks, expanding beyond the conventional binary categorization of 'lazy' (random feature) and 'rich' learning regimes. By monitoring the evolution and untangling of task-relevant representational manifolds during training, the authors identify a diverse taxonomy of learning strategies and stages influenced by inductive biases and network architecture. The study provides new insights into how structured neural activity enables out-of-distribution generalization in artificial networks and offers a geometric perspective on the organization of feature-learning circuits in biological systems.
papers.authors: Chi-Ning Chou, Hang Le, Yichen Wang, SueYeon Chung

papers.title: Variations in Neuronal Selectivity Create Efficient Representational Geometries for Perception
papers.abstract: The authors investigate why neurons across species and sensory areas exhibit high diversity in tuning properties such as stimulus amplitude and bandwidth selectivity. Using a manifold capacity framework, they demonstrate that amplitude heterogeneity improves perceptual coding by increasing the separation between representational centroids, while bandwidth diversity acts to decorrelate the underlying representational subspaces. Simulations and analysis of macaque V1 data reveal that these distinct geometric transformations are complementary: amplitude diversity is more beneficial for fine discrimination tasks, whereas bandwidth diversity disproportionately improves stimulus identification. This work suggests that tuning diversity is a fundamental neural strategy for optimizing representational geometry for varied perceptual demands.
papers.authors: Sonica Saraf, J. Anthony Movshon, SueYeon Chung

E028.name: Surya Ganguli
E028.bio: Ganguli is an Associate Professor of Applied Physics at Stanford University and directs the Neural Dynamics and Computation Lab. Their research integrates principles from physics, machine learning, and neurobiology to examine how cognitive functions such as sensory perception, memory, and motor control result from the collective dynamics of neural circuits. In vision science, Ganguli developed deep learning frameworks to model retinal responses to natural scenes and investigated the mechanisms of core object recognition in the ventral visual stream. Their current work focuses on 'NeuroAI,' aiming to establish a theoretical foundation for artificial intelligence by drawing insights from biological neural networks and the statistical mechanics of learning.
E028.research_direction: Dr. Ganguli's recent work explores the fundamental dynamics of complex networks by applying tools from statistical physics and geometry to models of artificial intelligence, biological memory, and physical computing. In the realm of deep learning, they have recently been investigating the mathematical mechanisms of representation and generation, examining how inductive biases in diffusion models facilitate the creation of novel images and how geometric signal propagation dictates feature learning and trainability in deep transformers. Their research also explores the mechanics of associative memory, specifically modeling how rapid, short-term synaptic plasticity interacts with high-dimensional energy landscapes to prevent catastrophic forgetting in recurrent neural systems. Additionally, they are utilizing spin-glass theory to study unconventional optical computing platforms, mapping how energy landscapes dynamically deform to help Coherent Ising Machines solve complex combinatorial optimization tasks.

papers.title: Short-term plasticity recalls forgotten memories through a trampoline mechanism
papers.abstract: The authors investigate the dynamics of continuous-state Hopfield associative memory networks integrated with rapid, short-term associative synaptic plasticity. Utilizing the cavity method and dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT), they delineate the phase boundaries between the retrieval and spin-glass (forgetting) regimes across variables of neuronal gain and memory load fraction. The study uncovers a 'trampoline mechanism' in which transient neural activity patterns trigger rapid synaptic modifications that locally depress the high-dimensional energy landscape, effectively trapping the system in a stable fixed point near the stored memory. This mechanism facilitates the robust recall of patterns even when the network is loaded beyond the classical critical capacity, preventing catastrophic forgetting by stabilizing neural transients through reactive synaptic updates.
papers.authors: Martina Del Gaudio, Federico Ghimenti, Surya Ganguli

papers.title: An analytic theory of creativity in convolutional diffusion models
papers.abstract: This work establishes a mechanistic, predictive framework for understanding creativity in score-based diffusion models, reconciling the discrepancy between optimal score-matching theory (which predicts training data memorization) and empirical results showing novel image generation. By isolating the inductive biases of locality (finite receptive fields) and translational equivariance (convolutional parameter sharing), the researchers derive the 'equivariant local score' (ELS) machine. This fully analytic system reveals a 'patch mosaic' mechanism wherein diffusion models generate exponentially many novel samples by combinatorially reassembling local patches from the training distribution across varying scales and spatial positions. The theory quantitatively predicts the outputs of trained ResNets and UNets with median r^2 values exceeding 0.94 across multiple datasets, including CIFAR-10 and CelebA.
papers.authors: Mason Kamb, Surya Ganguli

papers.title: Geometric dynamics of signal propagation predict trainability of transformers
papers.abstract: This paper analyzes the forward signal and backward gradient propagation in deep, randomly initialized transformers by modeling token representations as an interacting particle system. The authors derive exact update equations for the ensemble-averaged geometry of these token configurations, identifying critical phase transitions between ordered (attractive) and chaotic (repulsive) regimes. By analytically calculating Lyapunov exponents for token angles and backpropagated gradients, they provide necessary and sufficient conditions for initialization hyperparameters—such as weight variance and residual branch strength—to avoid rank collapse and gradient instability. The findings demonstrate that the vanishing of these exponents at the start of training serves as a robust predictor for minimal test loss in deep transformer architectures.
papers.authors: Aditya Cowsik, Tamra Nebabu, Xiao-Liang Qi, Surya Ganguli

papers.title: Get rich quick: exact solutions reveal how unbalanced initializations promote rapid feature learning
papers.abstract: The researchers provide exact analytical solutions to the nonlinear learning dynamics of networks transitioning between lazy (kernel) and rich (feature learning) regimes. The theory identifies a set of conserved quantities determined by layer-specific initialization variances and learning rates that govern the geometry of parameter space trajectories. The analysis distinguishes between 'upstream' (early layer dominated) and 'downstream' initializations, demonstrating that unbalanced upstream initializations in nonlinear networks can significantly accelerate rich feature learning and enhance early-layer interpretability. These theoretical predictions are verified through experiments on CNNs and modular arithmetic tasks, showing reduced sample complexity and accelerated emergence of hierarchical structure during training.
papers.authors: Daniel Kunin, Allan Raventós, Clémentine Dominé, Feng Chen, David Klindt, Andrew Saxe, Surya Ganguli

papers.title: Geometric landscape annealing as an optimization principle underlying the coherent Ising machine
papers.abstract: This study employs statistical physics and spin-glass theory to characterize the optimization performance of the Coherent Ising Machine (CIM). By modeling the CIM as a network of optical parametric oscillators, the authors analyze the deformation of the high-dimensional energy landscape during laser gain annealing, which interpolates between gradient descent on soft-spin landscapes and discrete binary optimization. Using the cavity method and the Kac-Rice framework, they identify discrete phase transitions—from flat to rough to rigid—in the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick spin glass landscape. The research uncovers how the CIM exploits soft-modes in the landscape to navigate toward low-energy global minima while evading a proliferation of unaligned local minima, providing a theoretical foundation for unconventional computing in combinatorial optimization.
papers.authors: Atsushi Yamamura, Hideo Mabuchi, Surya Ganguli

E032.name: Thomas Naselaris
E032.bio: Thomas Naselaris is an Associate Professor in the Department of Neuroscience at the University of Minnesota and a member of the Medical Discovery Team on Optical Imaging and Brain Science. Naselaris's research focuses on the generative capabilities of the human visual system, employing high-field fMRI and voxel-wise encoding models to investigate how the brain represents natural scenes and mental imagery. They have developed mathematical frameworks for reconstructing visual experiences from human brain activity through neural decoding. Currently, Naselaris's work integrates deep learning with functional neuroimaging to examine the transformations between perceptual and mnemonic representations in the visual cortex.
E032.research_direction: Dr. Naselaris has recently been investigating the computational mechanisms underlying visual perception and mental imagery using ultra-high-field fMRI and deep neural networks. Their recent work explores the representational geometry of the human visual cortex, specifically examining how concept manifolds evolve across the cortical hierarchy to disentangle visual categories. They are also probing the complex neural relationship between perceived and imagined stimuli, quantifying how sensory activity patterns are transformed into internally generated mental images across different visual areas. Furthermore, to advance brain-computer interfaces, they are leveraging benchmark datasets and state-of-the-art generative AI to evaluate how robustly fMRI decoding models trained on natural vision can be generalized to reconstruct purely imagined scenes.

papers.title: Variation in the geometry of concept manifolds across human visual cortex
papers.abstract: The efficacy of linear read-outs from high-level visual cortex in classifying visual concepts depends on the representational geometry of concept manifolds—the sets of neural activity patterns encoding varied exemplars of a specific category. This study utilizes ultra-high-field 7T fMRI data from the Natural Scenes Dataset (NSD) and a brain-optimized deep neural network (GNet) to quantify how manifold geometry evolves across the cortical hierarchy. We show that improvements in few-shot linear classification accuracy in the brain are predominantly driven by increases in 'geometric signal' (the distance between manifold centers), rather than changes in manifold dimensionality or overlap. In contrast, classification improvements in deep neural network layers are driven by increases in effective manifold dimensionality. Our results reveal that the human visual cortex and task-optimized artificial networks employ divergent geometric strategies to achieve conceptual disentanglement, despite operating under similar computational constraints.
papers.authors: Ghislain St-Yves, Kendrick Kay, Thomas Naselaris

papers.title: A transformation from vision to imagery in the human brain
papers.abstract: While it is established that mental imagery reactivates the visual cortex, the precise relationship between activity patterns during perception and imagery remains debated. We introduce the concept of an 'imagery transformation'—a linear mapping that relates visual activity patterns to mental imagery patterns for the same stimuli. Analyzing 7T fMRI data across two independent datasets, we demonstrate that imagery is not merely 'weak vision' or a simple rescaling of perceptual activity. In early visual areas (V1-V3), imagery transformations involve a significant reduction in neural dimensionality and a reorientation of the representational subspace, with imagery dimensions explaining only 25–50% of visual variance. Conversely, in high-level visual areas, the transformation approximates an identity function, suggesting a transition from pure reactivation in higher stages to a more complex, lossy compression in earlier stages of the visual hierarchy.
papers.authors: Tiasha Saha Roy, Jesse Breedlove, Ghislain St-Yves, Kendrick Kay, Thomas Naselaris

papers.title: NSD-Imagery: A Benchmark Dataset for Extending fMRI Vision Decoding Methods to Mental Imagery
papers.abstract: We present NSD-Imagery, a high-resolution 7T fMRI benchmark dataset extending the Natural Scenes Dataset (NSD) to include neural responses during mental imagery of both simple geometric patterns and complex natural scenes. We evaluate a suite of state-of-the-art vision decoding models (including MindEye1, MindEye2, and Brain Diffuser) on their ability to generalize from seen images to internally generated mental images. Our results demonstrate that decoding performance on mental imagery is largely decoupled from seen-image reconstruction performance. Specifically, models utilizing simple linear decoding architectures and multimodal feature alignment generalize more robustly to mental imagery, whereas complex architectures tend to overfit the visual training distribution. These findings provide a critical resource for developing brain-computer interfaces intended for clinical applications where visual information is internally generated.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR)
papers.authors: Reese Kneeland, Paul S. Scotti, Ghislain St-Yves, Jesse L. Breedlove, Kendrick N. Kay, Thomas Naselaris

papers.title: fMRI vision reconstruction methods robustly generalize to mental imagery
papers.abstract: Recent breakthroughs in generative AI and large-scale neuroimaging datasets have enabled high-fidelity reconstruction of seen images from human fMRI activity. However, the extension of these methods to mental imagery remains a primary challenge for clinical brain-computer interfaces. We evaluate several leading vision decoding frameworks on fMRI activity measured while subjects imagined previously memorized stimuli. We demonstrate that these models generalize robustly to mental imagery, producing reconstructions that are consistently identified by naive human raters in forced-choice tasks. Quantitative analysis reveals that reconstruction quality is more dependent on the alignment between the training and test image distributions than on stimulus complexity. Notably, reconstructions of imagined natural scenes were identified with higher accuracy than reconstructions of much simpler perceived geometric stimuli, highlighting the role of naturalistic priors in current decoding methodologies.
papers.authors: Reese Kneeland, Ghislain St-Yves, Jesse Breedlove, Kendrick Kay, Thomas Naselaris

E033.name: Ian Charest
E033.bio: Ian Charest is an associate professor and Courtois chairholder in cognitive and computational neuroscience who investigates how the human brain processes high-level visual and auditory information. Charest’s research utilizes a multi-methodological approach that combines functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and magneto-electroencephalography (M-EEG) with computational modeling, including representational similarity analysis (RSA) and artificial neural networks. A focus of their work involves characterizing individual representational idiosyncrasies and understanding the interaction between vision and semantics during the recognition of natural scenes.
E033.research_direction: Dr. Charest has recently been investigating how the human visual system transforms sensory inputs into high-level, modality-agnostic conceptual representations. Their recent work explores the convergence of vision and language, using fMRI and representational similarity analysis to test whether the brain's encoding of natural scenes aligns with the complex relational spaces of large language models. Additionally, they are probing the time-resolved neural computations underlying face identification across the entire ability spectrum, from patients with acquired prosopagnosia to exceptional super-recognizers. By leveraging high-density EEG alongside deep neural networks and semantic embeddings, Dr. Charest seeks to map how individual differences in visual recognition emerge from the integration of early perceptual features and later-stage semantic information.

papers.title: High-level visual representations in the human brain are aligned with large language models
papers.abstract: This study investigates whether the complex visual information extracted by the human brain from natural scenes—including object interrelations and environmental context—is effectively modeled by the representational format of large language models (LLMs). Utilizing the 7T fMRI Natural Scenes Dataset (NSD), the authors demonstrate that LLM embeddings derived from scene captions successfully characterize neural activity across an extensive network of brain regions. Through controlled model comparisons, they show that the alignment between brain and model representations arises from the LLMs' capacity to integrate relational information beyond the sum of individual words. Furthermore, deep neural networks (DNNs) trained to map visual inputs into this caption-based semantic space exhibit greater brain-model similarity than traditional object-recognition models, suggesting that visuo-semantic transformation constitutes a fundamental objective of the human visual system.
papers.authors: Adrien Doerig, Tim C. Kietzmann, Emily Allen, Yihan Wu, Thomas Naselaris, Kendrick Kay, Ian Charest

papers.title: Representations in vision and language converge in a shared, multidimensional space of perceived similarities
papers.abstract: The research explores the hypothesis that human sensory systems transform inputs into a shared, modality-agnostic representational space where visual and linguistic information converge. Participants performed behavioral similarity judgments on natural scene images and their corresponding textual captions from the Natural Scenes Dataset (NSD). Representational similarity analysis (RSA) revealed that both visual and linguistic similarity structures not only converged at the behavioral level but also accurately predicted fMRI responses in a consistent network of mid-to-high-level visual brain regions. Furthermore, computational models trained to align images with LLM-based embeddings outperformed standard category-trained networks in capturing this shared behavioral similarity structure. These findings suggest that conceptual representations are grounded in a commonRelational code that reflects the stable structure of the environment, transcending the specific sensory modality of input.
papers.authors: Katerina Marie Simkova, Adrien Doerig, Clayton Hickey, Ian Charest

papers.title: Neural computations in prosopagnosia
papers.abstract: This investigation identifies the computational deficits underlying the loss of face identification ability in brain-lesioned patient PS, a classic case of acquired pure prosopagnosia. By collecting a large-scale dataset of high-density electroencephalography (EEG) and applying representational similarity analysis (RSA), the authors compared time-resolved brain representations against various computational models, including deep convolutional neural networks (DNNs) and semantic embeddings. The study revealed that PS's neural representations exhibited excessive generalization of early visual patterns, remaining more similar to early layers of visual DNNs than those of neurotypical controls. Crucially, PS showed significant representational deficits in high-level visual and semantic computations, particularly during the N170 and P300 processing windows. These results provide mechanistic evidence that impaired face recognition is linked to a failure in constructing abstract, high-level representational geometries within the ventral visual stream.
papers.authors: Simon Faghel-Soubeyrand, Anne-Raphaelle Richoz, Delphine Waeber, Jessica Woodhams, Roberto Caldara, Frédéric Gosselin, Ian Charest

papers.title: Decoding face recognition abilities in the human brain
papers.abstract: This study employs a data-driven approach to characterize the neuro-computational variations across the face recognition spectrum, ranging from typical recognizers to 'super-recognizers' (individuals with exceptional face identification skills). Using high-density EEG and multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA), the authors successfully decoded individual face recognition ability scores from just one second of brain activity with high accuracy. Comparisons with DNN models of vision and semantics indicated that super-recognizers exhibit enhanced mid-level visual computations at early latencies and richer semantic representations at later latencies (approx. 600–700 ms). These findings provide the first direct empirical evidence linking high-level semantic brain computations to individual differences in face recognition ability, suggesting that superior performance is supported by more robust integration of visual and conceptual features.
papers.authors: Simon Faghel-Soubeyrand, Meike Ramon, Eva Bamps, Matteo Zoia, Jessica Woodhams, Anne-Raphaelle Richoz, Roberto Caldara, Frédéric Gosselin, Ian Charest

E035.name: Tim Kietzmann
E035.bio: Tim C. Kietzmann is a Professor of Machine Learning at the University of Osnabrück's Institute of Cognitive Science. Their research integrates deep learning and cognitive neuroscience to characterize the neuro-computational principles of human vision, focusing on how recurrent neural networks model the dynamic transformation of sensory signals in the brain. By combining neuroimaging techniques like MEG, EEG, and fMRI with neuro-inspired artificial intelligence, Kietzmann investigates how biological systems derive representations from environmental regularities. Kietzmann previously held positions at the Donders Institute and the University of Cambridge, where they used connectionist models to explain cortical dynamics.
E035.research_direction: Dr. Kietzmann has recently been investigating the computational principles underlying active vision, using recurrent neural networks to explore how metabolic energy efficiency and self-supervised next-glimpse prediction might drive the emergence of brain-aligned scene representations and predictive remapping across saccades. Their recent work also explores the neural and cognitive drivers of human eye movement behavior, combining MEG and eye-tracking to investigate whether fixation durations during natural scene viewing are dictated by early sensory processing demands or downstream memory encoding requirements. Additionally, they are examining the role of biological learning trajectories in artificial intelligence, testing whether training computer vision models on a simulated human developmental visual diet can overcome typical AI texture biases and foster robust, human-like shape recognition. Finally, their research bridges neuroimaging and natural language processing by exploring generative neural decoding techniques that link fMRI responses directly into the latent semantic spaces of large language models for interactive, open-ended brain readout.

papers.title: Predictive remapping and allocentric coding as consequences of energy efficiency in recurrent neural network models of active vision
papers.abstract: The maintenance of visual stability across saccadic eye movements is hypothesized to depend on predictive mechanisms using efference copies to anticipate forthcoming foveal inputs. This study examines whether such sophisticated computations require hard-wired evolutionary scaffolds or can emerge from the fundamental constraint of metabolic energy efficiency. Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) were trained to minimize preactivation costs while processing sequences of natural image patches and saccadic oculomotor signals. Results demonstrate that targeted inhibitory predictive remapping and the transformation of egocentric retinal coordinates into an allocentric reference frame emerge autonomously from energy-efficiency optimization. These models self-organized into prediction and error units, mirroring hierarchical predictive coding architectures. Multi-scale temporal analyses via virtual lesioning revealed both rapid lateral predictive signals and slower evidence integration cycles. These findings suggest that complex neurophysiological remapping and spatial coding arise from simple physical principles of efficient information processing.
papers.authors: Thomas Nortmann, Philip Sulewski, Tim C. Kietzmann

papers.title: Predicting upcoming visual features during eye movements yields scene representations aligned with human visual cortex
papers.abstract: Effective visual intelligence requires unified scene representations that integrate localized snapshots into a coherent structure. We propose Glimpse Prediction Networks (GPNs), recurrent neural models trained to predict the high-level feature embeddings of forthcoming glimpses along human-like scanpaths using self-supervised learning. GPNs successfully internalize the co-occurrence statistics and spatial arrangement of scene components, and their recurrent variants integrate information over multiple saccades into a unified representation. Using the Natural Scenes Dataset (NSD), we demonstrate that GPN internal representations align significantly with human fMRI responses across mid-to-high-level visual cortex, particularly in ventral and dorsal stream areas. GPNs outperform semantic-supervised controls and match state-of-the-art vision models, indicating that next-glimpse prediction during active vision is a biologically plausible, self-supervised computational route to brain-aligned scene representations.
papers.authors: Sushrut Thorat, Adrien Doerig, Alexander Kroner, Carmen Amme, Tim C. Kietzmann

papers.title: Brain-language fusion enables interactive neural readout and in-silico experimentation
papers.abstract: Neural decoding has historically been limited to static, non-interactive mappings between brain activity and specific labels or reconstructions. We introduce CorText, a framework that integrates functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) neural activity directly into the latent semantic space of a Large Language Model (LLM). Trained on neural responses to naturalistic scenes, CorText facilitates open-ended natural language interaction with brain data, generating descriptive captions and answering nuanced queries based solely on neural input. The system demonstrates zero-shot generalization to novel semantic categories and enables in-silico cortical microstimulation experiments. By applying counterfactual prompts to neural activity, we observed consistent, graded mappings between brain states and generated language, shifting the neural decoding paradigm toward generative, flexible interfaces between neuroimaging data and linguistic output.
papers.authors: Victoria Bosch, Daniel Anthes, Adrien Doerig, Sushrut Thorat, Peter König, Tim C. Kietzmann

papers.title: Why we linger: Memory encoding, rather than visual processing demand, drives fixation timing on natural scenes – evidence from a large-scale MEG dataset
papers.abstract: We investigated the neural determinants of fixation duration using a large-scale active vision dataset (AVS) that includes magnetoencephalography (MEG), eye-tracking, and semantic scene captioning. Multivariate analysis of MEG source-space dynamics and artificial neural network (ANN) modeling revealed that fixation durations do not correlate with visual processing latency or ventral stream representational dynamics. Instead, fixation timing is positively correlated with predicted patch memorability and inclusion in natural language captions. Electrophysiological results show that longer fixations co-occur with increased theta-gamma phase-amplitude coupling in the hippocampus and frontal cortex. These findings suggest that the brain's decision to remain fixated is not constrained by early sensory processing bottlenecks but is actively driven by downstream requirements for stabilizing cortical representations during memory encoding.
papers.authors: Philip Sulewski, Carmen Amme, Martin N. Hebart, Peter König, Tim C. Kietzmann

papers.title: Adopting a human developmental visual diet yields robust, shape-based AI vision
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence systems typically exhibit a significant misalignment with human vision, characterized by a heavy reliance on texture over shape and vulnerability to image distortions. We introduce the Developmental Visual Diet (DVD), a training curriculum for computer vision models that simulates the trajectory of human visual maturation from infancy to adulthood. By progressively increasing the complexity and fidelity of visual input, models naturally develop a robust shape bias and human-level abstract shape recognition. DVD-trained architectures demonstrate superior resilience to image corruptions and adversarial noise compared to large-scale foundation models trained on orders of magnitude more data. These results provide evidence that robust, human-aligned AI vision can be achieved by optimizing the developmental learning trajectory rather than merely scaling dataset size, offering a resource-efficient route toward biologically plausible artificial visual systems.
papers.authors: Zejin Lu, Sushrut Thorat, Radoslaw M. Cichy, Tim C. Kietzmann

E037.name: Samuel Nastase
E037.bio: Samuel Nastase investigates the neural mechanisms underlying human communication and shared cognition using naturalistic stimuli such as narratives and cinema. Nastase employs computational techniques, including hyperalignment and intersubject correlation, to map high-dimensional representational spaces shared across individual brains. Their recent work focuses on integrating large language models with neuroimaging data to understand how linguistic structures facilitate the transmission of information during social interaction.
E037.research_direction: Dr. Nastase has recently been investigating the neural computations underlying naturalistic language comprehension and social cognition by interfacing human brain recordings with deep neural networks. Their recent work explores how the brain processes complex continuous stimuli, using large language models to predict ECoG and fMRI activity and examining whether specific transformer computations mirror functional hierarchies in the cortical language network. In addition to linguistic processing, they are studying higher-level social inference and action understanding, mapping how the default mode network represents mental states of the self versus others and investigating the representational geometry of observed human actions during natural vision. By leveraging Shared Response Models to align neural activity across individuals, their research seeks to isolate the shared information spaces and functional connectivity patterns that drive complex, real-world cognition.

papers.title: Aligning brains into a shared space improves their alignment with large language models
papers.abstract: This study demonstrates that large language models (LLMs) can effectively predict word-by-word neural activity recorded via electrocorticography (ECoG) during naturalistic speech comprehension. To overcome the limitations of electrode-level and subject-specific encoding models, the researchers utilized a Shared Response Model (SRM) to estimate a common information space across a cohort of participants listening to a 30-minute podcast. Projections into this shared response space significantly enhanced the predictive accuracy of LLM-based encoding models and allowed for the denoising of individual brain signals, resulting in a 37% mean improvement in encoding accuracy. These gains were localized primarily to the superior temporal gyrus and inferior frontal gyrus, suggesting that shared responses across individuals provide a more robust target for modeling the neural representations of language.
papers.authors: Arnab Bhattacharjee, Zaid Zada, Haocheng Wang, Bobbi Aubrey, Werner Doyle, Patricia Dugan, Daniel Friedman, Orrin Devinsky, Adeen Flinker, Peter J Ramadge, Uri Hasson, Ariel Goldstein, Samuel A. Nastase

papers.title: Shared functional specialization in transformer-based language models and the human brain
papers.abstract: The research investigates whether the circuit computations in Transformer-based language models correspond to specialized functional processes in the human brain. Rather than analyzing static word embeddings, the authors deconstructed the model's internal operations into specific 'transformations'—the computations that integrate context across words. Using fMRI data from subjects listening to naturalistic narratives, they verified that these transformation-based circuits account for substantial variance in the cortical language network. Crucially, the study found that specific attention heads within the Transformer architecture differentially predict neural activity in distinct brain regions, revealing a correspondence between artificial circuit specialization and cortical gradients of layer depth and contextual integration.
papers.authors: Sreejan Kumar, Theodore R. Sumers, Takateru Yamakoshi, Ariel Goldstein, Uri Hasson, Kenneth A. Norman, Thomas L. Griffiths, Robert D. Hawkins, Samuel A. Nastase

papers.title: Cortical language areas are coupled via a soft hierarchy of model-based linguistic features
papers.abstract: This work posits that regions within the human language network coordinate through shared subspaces of linguistic features. The researchers developed a model-based functional connectivity framework using three classes of embeddings—acoustic, speech, and high-level language—extracted from a unified neural network model. By applying this framework to naturalistic fMRI data of narrative comprehension, they identified a soft hierarchy of stimulus-driven connectivity. Early auditory regions were coupled via low-level acoustic and speech features, whereas higher-order lateral temporal and default-mode regions were primarily coupled through abstract linguistic features. These results suggest that feature-specific communication channels facilitate the integration of complex information across the cortical language network.
papers.authors: Ahmad Samara, Zaid Zada, Tamara Vanderwal, Uri Hasson, Samuel A. Nastase

papers.title: Hierarchical systems in the default mode network when reasoning about self and other mental states
papers.abstract: The study utilizes fMRI and multi-voxel pattern analysis (MVPA) to investigate how the default mode network (DMN) handles mental state inference for the 'self' compared to 'other' agents. Participants performed tasks requiring them to monitor their own internal states or the mental states of individuals depicted in videos. The results identified a functional hierarchy along the medial prefrontal cortex: ventral regions selectively decoded mental state patterns specific to the self, while dorsal regions and the posterior cingulate cortex represented general social reasoning processes applicable to both targets. These findings suggest that the social brain contains both specialized modules for self-reflection and general-purpose systems for modeling mental states.
papers.authors: Isaac R. Christian, Samuel A. Nastase

papers.title: Behaviorally-relevant features of observed actions dominate cortical representational geometry in natural vision
papers.abstract: This fMRI study examines the neural representational geometry of action understanding using dynamic, real-world video stimuli. The researchers compared the predictive power of behavioral models (judgments of an action's purpose and sociality) against semantic models and low-level visual feature models. They found that behavioral models of transitivity (action purpose) and sociality (social content) significantly outperformed visual and semantic models in predicting neural representations across much of the cortex. These behaviorally relevant action features explained unique variance not only in the traditional action observation network but also in ventral temporal regions, indicating that high-level behavioral dimensions are central to how the brain organizes information about dynamic social interactions.
papers.authors: Jane Han, Vassiki Chauhan, Rebecca Philip, Morgan K. Taylor, Heejung Jung, Yaroslav O. Halchenko, M. Ida Gobbini, James V. Haxby, Samuel A. Nastase

E038.name: Haim Sompolinsky
E038.department: Department of Molecular and Cellular Biology and Department of Physics
E038.bio: Sompolinsky works in computational neuroscience, applying principles from statistical physics and nonlinear dynamics to study the mechanisms of neural circuit function. They developed attractor network models for associative memory and the balanced state theory of neural networks, which provides a framework for understanding the variability of neuronal activity. Their research methodologies integrate statistical mechanics and disordered systems theory to investigate neural population coding, learning, and the dynamics of brain circuits. Currently, Sompolinsky focuses on the intersection of biological and artificial intelligence, employing geometric methods to study information processing in vision and language within deep neural networks.
E038.research_direction: Dr. Sompolinsky has recently been exploring the theoretical foundations of both artificial and biological neural networks through the lens of statistical physics. Their recent work investigates the mechanics of modern deep learning architectures, analyzing how transformers dynamically combine distinct attention pathways and calculating the capacity limits of high-dimensional learning models. They are also addressing the challenge of catastrophic forgetting in continual learning, modeling phase transitions in network training and developing brain-inspired gating mechanisms to inject specific event memories into large language models. Furthermore, in biological contexts, they are examining how highly disordered recurrent brain circuits manage to robustly represent continuous spatial and visual variables via attractor dynamics despite immense synaptic irregularity.

papers.title: Order parameters and phase transitions of continual learning in deep neural networks
papers.abstract: This research addresses the phenomenon of catastrophic forgetting in deep neural networks (DNNs) through the lens of statistical physics and optimal control theory. We define macroscopic order parameters that characterize the training dynamics of sequential task acquisition and identify critical phase transitions governing the trade-off between memory retention and novel feature integration. By utilizing exact equations derived via the dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT) framework, we quantify learning curves and representational drift across multiple training protocols. Our results establish a theoretical foundation for assessing the optimality of continual learning strategies, demonstrating how weight-space trajectories can be steered to minimize interference while maintaining performance in high-dimensional learning regimes.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS)
papers.authors: Haozhe Shan, Qianyi Li, Haim Sompolinsky

papers.title: Simplified derivations for high-dimensional convex learning problems
papers.abstract: Statistical-physics formalisms in theoretical neuroscience and machine learning often rely on complex replica-method derivations that can obscure the underlying physical mechanisms. In this work, we provide a unified analysis of high-dimensional convex learning problems using a concise cavity approach, circumventing the need for replica symmetry assumptions. We examine three canonical architectures: perceptron classification of discrete points, the classification of object manifolds, and kernel ridge regression. By framing these as a bipartite system involving interacting feature and datum variables, we derive exact results for classification capacity and generalization error. Additionally, we identify a fundamental symmetry in perceptron-capacity problems that justifies the use of simplified, non-rigorous methods to obtain correct theoretical bounds in the thermodynamic limit.
papers.authors: David G. Clark, Haim Sompolinsky

papers.title: Memorization and Knowledge Injection in Gated LLMs
papers.abstract: The sequential integration of discrete event memories into Large Language Models (LLMs) remains a significant challenge due to catastrophic forgetting and the limitations of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG). We introduce Memory Embedded in Gated LLMs (MEGa), a continual learning framework inspired by the brain's complementary learning systems. MEGa utilizes a gating mechanism to activate specialized low-rank weights (LoRA) dedicated to specific event memories, allowing for direct weight-space knowledge injection. Each memory is indexed by query embeddings that match stored representations during inference. Experiments on fictional and real-world event datasets demonstrate that MEGa significantly improves recall and question-answering performance compared to standard fine-tuning and context-based methods, while maintaining the stability of previously acquired knowledge.
papers.authors: Xu Pan, Ely Hahami, Zechen Zhang, Haim Sompolinsky

papers.title: Symmetries and Continuous Attractors in Disordered Neural Circuits
papers.abstract: We investigate the emergence of continuous-attractor dynamics in recurrent neural networks with high degrees of heterogeneity and disorder, addressing the gap between idealized theoretical models and biological circuit complexity. By applying an optimization principle to model mouse visual and navigational circuits, we demonstrate that quasi-continuous-attractor states can arise despite synaptic irregularity. We develop a statistical generative process that reproduces experimental tuning curves and show that a continuous symmetry in this process results in doublet degeneracy within the connectivity matrix spectrum as N scales. This spectral property reflects an underlying circular manifold topology, providing a mechanistic explanation for how disordered brain circuits represent continuous variables like head direction with high precision.
papers.authors: David G. Clark, L.F. Abbott, Haim Sompolinsky

papers.title: Dissecting the Interplay of Attention Paths in a Statistical Mechanics Theory of Transformers
papers.abstract: We develop a statistical mechanics theory to analyze Bayesian learning in deep multi-head self-attention networks, operating in the finite-width thermodynamic limit where width N and training samples P scale such that P/N is constant. Our theory reveals that the network’s predictor statistics decompose into a sum of independent kernels corresponding to distinct 'attention paths' through the layer hierarchy. We identify a 'task-relevant kernel combination' mechanism that dynamically weights these information pathways to optimize the total kernel for task labels, enhancing generalization performance beyond the standard infinite-width Gaussian Process (GP) limit. We validate our exact equations through synthetic and real-world sequence classification, demonstrating that our theory identifies redundant attention heads for efficient network pruning without performance loss.
papers.venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS)
papers.authors: Lorenzo Tiberi, Francesca Mignacco, Kazuki Irie, Haim Sompolinsky

E039.name: Martin Schrimpf
E039.department: School of Life Sciences and School of Computer and Communication Sciences
E039.bio: Martin Schrimpf is a Tenure-Track Assistant Professor at EPFL and head of the NeuroAI Lab, where their research integrates machine learning, neuroscience, and cognitive science. Schrimpf is an architect of the Brain-Score platform, an initiative designed to benchmark artificial neural networks against large-scale neural and behavioral datasets to identify brain-like computational architectures. Their work focuses on developing predictive models of the primate visual ventral stream and the human language network to identify the functional principles of natural intelligence. Currently, Schrimpf investigates the use of these brain models for clinical applications, including the development of visual prosthetics and diagnostic tools for neurological disorders.
E039.research_direction: Dr. Schrimpf has recently been investigating the alignment between artificial neural networks and the biological brain, using both vision and language models as computational analogs to study human cognitive architecture. Their recent work explores the primate visual ventral stream by evaluating how network scaling impacts brain-like representations and by utilizing topographic models to guide microstimulation aimed at causally steering visual perception. Additionally, they are probing the functional organization of linguistic processing by applying neuroscientific localization methods to identify causally relevant language networks within large language and vision-language models. By targeting specific artificial pathways—such as analogs of the visual word form area—they are testing causal hypotheses about developmental reading disorders like dyslexia and examining how formal linguistic competence relates to broader cognitive reasoning.

papers.title: Model-Guided Microstimulation Steers Primate Visual Behavior
papers.abstract: This research introduces a computational framework designed to causally model and steer neural activity in high-level cortical regions through microstimulation. The framework utilizes Topographic Deep Artificial Neural Networks (TDANNs) to replicate the spatial organization of cortical neurons and incorporates a perturbation module that translates electrical stimulation parameters into localized changes in neural activation. By integrating a mapping procedure to translate model-optimized stimulation coordinates to the macaque ventral visual stream, the authors demonstrate that microstimulation at sites predicted to be functional significantly influences perceptual choices in a visual recognition task. The work establishes that brain-aligned topographic models can effectively guide causal interventions in primates, potentially informing the design of visual prosthetics capable of evoking complex object-level percepts.
papers.authors: Johannes Mehrer, Ben Lonnqvist, Anna Mitola, Abdulkadir Gokce, Paolo Papale, Martin Schrimpf

papers.title: Inducing Dyslexia in Vision Language Models
papers.abstract: The authors utilize large-scale vision-language models (VLMs) as computational analogs to investigate the neural basis of developmental dyslexia, a disorder linked to hypoactivation in the visual word form area (VWFA). By employing neuroscientific localization paradigms to identify word-selective units within VLMs, the study evaluates the effects of targeted unit ablation on reading performance.
