The findings indicate that selective perturbation of these artificial VWFA analogs—but not random units—induces human-like reading deficits, specifically characterized by phonological impairments while preserving general orthographic and cross-modal linguistic processing. The study provides a mechanistic framework for simulating reading disorders and testing causal hypotheses regarding the functional organization of the visual word processing system.
papers.authors: Melika Honarmand, Ayati Sharma, Badr AlKhamissi, Johannes Mehrer, Martin Schrimpf

papers.title: From Language to Cognition: How LLMs Outgrow the Human Language Network
papers.abstract: This study benchmarks 34 training checkpoints across diverse model scales to analyze how alignment with the human language network (LN) evolves relative to linguistic competence. The results demonstrate that neural alignment primarily tracks the acquisition of formal linguistic competence—encompassing knowledge of core syntactic and compositional rules—which saturates early in the training trajectory. In contrast, functional competence involving world knowledge and reasoning continues to develop as models reach superhuman next-word prediction performance, leading to a divergence between model representations and biological neural activity. These findings suggest that the human language network primarily encodes formal linguistic structures and that current LLMs outgrow their brain-like processing characteristics as they surpass human-level proficiency.
papers.venue: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP)
papers.authors: Badr AlKhamissi, Greta Tuckute, Yingtian Tang, Taha Binhuraib, Antoine Bosselut, Martin Schrimpf

papers.title: Scaling Laws for Task-Optimized Models of the Primate Visual Ventral Stream
papers.abstract: Evaluating over 600 task-optimized architectures, this research characterizes the scaling laws governing the neural and behavioral alignment of artificial neural networks with the primate visual ventral stream. The authors find that while behavioral alignment with core object recognition performance scales consistently with increased compute, model capacity, and dataset size, neural alignment in visual areas V1 through IT exhibits significant saturation. Parametric power-law fitting suggests that optimal biological alignment is achieved by allocating a higher proportion of compute to dataset scale than to model parameters (approximately a 0.7:0.3 ratio). The results indicate that simple scaling of contemporary vision architectures is insufficient for improving models of internal brain representations, necessitating new strategies for brain-like modeling.
papers.authors: Abdulkadir Gokce, Martin Schrimpf

papers.title: The LLM Language Network: A Neuroscientific Approach for Identifying Causally Task-Relevant Units
papers.abstract: This paper applies neuroscientific localization methods to large language models to identify functionally specialized, language-selective units analogous to the human core language system. The authors establish the causal necessity of these units for linguistic performance by demonstrating that their targeted ablation significantly degrades language task accuracy, whereas random unit ablation does not. Furthermore, these selective units demonstrate higher representational alignment with human brain recordings than unselected units. The research also investigates the emergence of specialized modules for logical reasoning and social cognition, finding that while specialized units exist across architectures, their functional organization is significantly more heterogeneous than that of the language-selective network.
papers.venue: Conference of the Nations of the Americas Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics (NAACL)
papers.authors: Badr AlKhamissi, Greta Tuckute, Antoine Bosselut, Martin Schrimpf

E040.name: Andreas Tolias
E040.bio: Tolias is a Professor of Ophthalmology at Stanford University and directs a research program focused on the intersection of systems neuroscience and artificial intelligence. Their work utilizes large-scale neural recordings and machine learning to investigate the network-level principles of perceptual inference and decision-making. Tolias led the MICrONS project, which produced a functional connectomics dataset, and developed 'digital twins' to simulate biological brain computation. Their current research focuses on reverse-engineering biological algorithms to design AI systems that are interpretable, robust, and efficient.
E040.research_direction: Dr. Tolias has recently been exploring the functional organization and computational principles of the mammalian visual cortex by integrating large-scale neural recordings with deep learning and functional connectomics. Their recent work investigates how diverse visual features are encoded across the cortical hierarchy, probing phenomena such as the topographic organization of complex naturalistic features in primate area V4, bidirectional neural tuning strategies anchored by opposing features, and the asymmetric representation of color-opponency across the mouse visual field. To decode these complex representations, they employ artificial neural networks as functional "digital twins" to synthesize optimal stimuli for individual neurons, and they are developing foundation models of neural activity designed to predict responses to entirely novel stimulus domains. Furthermore, they are leveraging millimeter-scale structural and functional datasets to investigate the anatomical basis of cortical computation, examining how specific feature selectivities relate to underlying dendritic morphology and universal synaptic wiring rules.

papers.title: Deep learning-driven characterization of single cell tuning in primate visual area V4 supports topological organization
papers.abstract: This study employs a data-driven, deep-learning framework to investigate the functional organization of macaque visual area V4, a region selective for complex naturalistic features that are difficult to parameterize. By training convolutional neural network models to predict the spiking activity of over 1,200 single units, the authors synthesized 'most exciting images' (MEIs) using in silico activation maximization, which were subsequently validated through in vivo closed-loop experiments. The results reveal that V4 neurons exhibit highly structured selectivity for non-parametric features such as complex textures, curvatures, and eye-like motifs. Critically, contrastive clustering of these model-derived selectivities demonstrated that V4 neurons are organized into functional groups with shared feature preferences, providing evidence for a topographic or columnar organization of mid-level visual features across the cortical surface.
papers.authors: Konstantin F. Willeke, Kelli Restivo, Katrin Franke, Arne F. Nix, Santiago A. Cadena, Tori Shinn, Cate Nealley, Gabrielle Rodriguez, Saumil Patel, Alexander S. Ecker, Fabian H. Sinz, Andreas S. Tolias

papers.title: Dual-feature selectivity enables bidirectional coding in visual cortical neurons
papers.abstract: Challenging the classical 'feature detector' paradigm, this work identifies a dual-feature encoding strategy in the mammalian visual cortex where neurons are tuned to two distinct features—one activating and one suppressive—relative to a non-zero baseline firing rate. Leveraging deep learning-based 'functional digital twins' of V1 and V4 neurons in both macaques and mice, the researchers demonstrate that neuronal activity varies linearly along a low-dimensional axis anchored by these opposing preferred and non-preferred features. This bidirectional code structures stimulus representation across the population and is conserved across species, suggesting a fundamental computational strategy likely mediated by feature-selective inhibitory normalization that enhances representational expressivity within the cortical hierarchy.
papers.authors: Katrin Franke, Nikos Karantzas, Konstantin Willeke, Maria Diamantaki, Kandan Ramakrishnan, Hasan Atakan Bedel, Pavithra Elumalai, Kelli Restivo, Paul Fahey, Cate Nealley, Tori Shinn, Gabrielle Garcia, Saumil Patel, Alexander Ecker, Edgar Y. Walker, Emmanouil Froudarakis, Sophia Sanborn, Fabian H. Sinz, Andreas Tolias

papers.title: Foundation model of neural activity predicts response to new stimulus types
papers.abstract: We developed a foundation model of the mouse visual cortex by training a deep neural network on a massive corpus of neural activity recorded from multiple individuals. This model demonstrates unprecedented zero-shot generalization, accurately predicting neuronal responses to novel stimulus domains—such as coherent motion and noise patterns—that were absent from the training set. Beyond sensory response prediction, the model's latent functional embeddings serve as a 'functional barcode' that can be transferred to predict anatomical properties, including synaptic connectivity, dendritic morphology, and cell type classification within the MICrONS dataset. These findings establish that large-scale neural data can be used to build foundation models that capture universal principles of cortical computation and relate function directly to cellular anatomy.
papers.authors: Eric Y. Wang, Paul G. Fahey, Zhuokun Ding, Stelios Papadopoulos, Kayla Ponder, Marissa A. Weis, Andersen Chang, Taliah Muhammad, Saumil Patel, Zhiwei Ding, Dat Tran, Jiakun Fu, Casey M. Schneider-Mizell, Nuno Maçarico da Costa, R. Clay Reid, Forrest Collman, Nuno Maçarico da Costa, Katrin Franke, Alexander S. Ecker, Jacob Reimer, Xaq Pitkow, Fabian H. Sinz, Andreas S. Tolias

papers.title: Functional connectomics reveals general wiring rule in mouse visual cortex
papers.abstract: Utilizing the millimetre-scale MICrONS dataset, which combines in vivo calcium imaging with electron microscopy, we investigated the relationship between synaptic connectivity and functional tuning across the visual hierarchy. By applying a digital twin model to disentangle feature tuning from spatial receptive field overlap, we identified a universal 'like-to-like' wiring rule: neurons with similar feature selectivities are preferentially connected across different cortical layers and areas, including feedback pathways. We also discovered a higher-order connectivity principle where postsynaptic cohorts exhibit greater functional similarity than predicted by pairwise rules. Recurrent neural network simulations show that these connectivity motifs mirror those optimized for task performance, suggesting that structured, non-random connectivity is essential for robust sensory processing and efficient credit assignment in biological networks.
papers.authors: Zhuokun Ding, Paul G. Fahey, Stelios Papadopoulos, Eric Y. Wang, Brendan Celii, Christos Papadopoulos, Andersen Chang, Alexander B. Kunin, Dat Tran, Jiakun Fu, Zhiwei Ding, Saumil Patel, Lydia Ntanavara, Rachel Froebe, Kayla Ponder, Taliah Muhammad, J. Alexander Bae, Agnes L. Bodor, Derrick Brittain, JoAnn Buchanan, Daniel J. papers.title: Asymmetric distribution of color-opponent response types across mouse visual cortex supports superior color vision in the sky
papers.abstract: This study systematically maps the cortical representation of color in the mouse, revealing a pronounced functional asymmetry across the visual field. Using large-scale population imaging and unsupervised clustering of responses to chromatic noise, we show that over one-third of neurons in V1 exhibit color-opponency in their receptive field (RF) centers. This color-opponency is markedly concentrated in the posterior visual cortex, which encodes the upper visual field (the sky). The asymmetry is driven by a localized population of Green-On/UV-Off neurons, a cortical specialization that is absent in the retinal output. Computational modeling suggests that this uneven distribution of chromatic response types is optimized for the statistics of natural scenes to improve the detection of dark UV-absorbing objects against the sky, potentially serving as an ethological adaptation for aerial predator detection.
papers.authors: Katrin Franke, Chenchen Cai, Kayla Ponder, Jiakun Fu, Sacha Sokoloski, Philipp Berens, Andreas S. Tolias

E041.name: Matthias Bethge
E041.bio: Matthias Bethge is a Professor for Computational Neuroscience and Machine Learning at the University of Tübingen and the Director of the Tübingen AI Center. Their research integrates statistical inference, deep learning, and psychophysics to investigate principles of perceptual inference in both biological and artificial systems. Bethge’s work includes neural style transfer, saliency modeling with DeepGaze, and the development of the DeepLabCut framework for pose estimation. Currently, their laboratory focuses on the robustness of visual representations and the study of neural decision-making through the lens of lifelong learning.
E041.research_direction: Dr. Bethge has recently been investigating the training lifecycles and evaluation paradigms of multimodal foundation models, alongside the persistent challenge of generalization in models of human visual attention. Their recent work explores strategies for continual multimodal pretraining, specifically probing how techniques like temporal model merging and dynamic, concept-aware data sampling can help networks acquire new skills over time without suffering from catastrophic forgetting. To better measure these rapidly evolving vision-language networks, they are also developing dynamic, sample-level benchmarking frameworks designed to test open-ended and emergent capabilities rather than relying on static aggregate datasets. Finally, in the realm of human visual saliency, Dr. Bethge is examining why predictive models often fail to generalize across different datasets, seeking to mathematically isolate a network's core predictive capacity from dataset-specific spatial artifacts like center bias and fixation spread.

papers.title: Concept-Aware Batch Sampling Improves Language-Image Pretraining
papers.abstract: The authors propose shifting vision-language model (VLM) pretraining from traditional offline, concept-agnostic filtering to adaptive, online concept-based curation. They develop DataConcept, a large-scale repository of 128 million image-text pairs enriched with detailed concept annotations, including semantic tags, bounding boxes, and synthetic captions. Leveraging this data, they introduce Concept-Aware Batch Sampling (CABS), a framework that constructs training batches dynamically based on target concept distributions. Two specific strategies, CABS-DM (Diversity Maximization) and CABS-FM (Frequency Maximization), are demonstrated to significantly enhance zero-shot classification and image-text retrieval performance for CLIP and SigLIP models across 28 diverse benchmarks.
papers.authors: Adhiraj Ghosh, Vishaal Udandarao, Thao Nguyen, Matteo Farina, Mehdi Cherti, Jenia Jitsev, Sewoong Oh, Elisa Ricci, Ludwig Schmidt, Matthias Bethge

papers.title: Modeling Saliency Dataset Bias
papers.abstract: Despite the high performance of modern saliency models on individual benchmarks, they suffer from significant degradation (up to 40%) in cross-dataset evaluation. The authors show that a substantial portion of this inter-dataset gap is caused by dataset-specific biases rather than model capacity. They introduce a modular saliency architecture that pairs a dataset-agnostic multiscale encoder-decoder with a specialized module containing fewer than 20 dataset-specific parameters. These parameters account for interpretable factors such as center bias, fixation spread, and multi-scale spatial structure. By adapting these parameters using as few as 50 samples, the model effectively closes 75% of the generalization gap, achieving state-of-the-art results on the MIT300, CAT2000, and COCO-Freeview benchmarks.
papers.authors: Matthias Kümmerer, Harneet Singh Khanuja, Matthias Bethge

papers.title: ONEBench to Test Them All: Sample-Level Benchmarking Over Open-Ended Capabilities
papers.abstract: Traditional static benchmarks struggle to evaluate the rapidly evolving, open-ended capabilities of foundation models. To address this, the authors introduce ONEBench, a unified benchmarking paradigm centered on sample-level evaluation rather than fixed dataset metrics. This framework allows for a continuously expanding pool of atomic tests that can be dynamically aggregated to probe specific emergent skills. Through extensive evaluation of frontier large language and vision models, ONEBench identifies granular failure modes and tracks capability emergence more effectively than aggregate scores. The methodology employs a sample-efficient aggregation technique grounded in the Plackett-Luce model to provide robust model rankings.
papers.authors: Adhiraj Ghosh, Sebastian Dziadzio, Ameya Prabhu, Vishaal Udandarao, Samuel Albanie, Matthias Bethge

papers.title: How to Merge Your Multimodal Models Over Time?
papers.abstract: This work investigates temporal model merging, the sequential integration of expert models finetuned on a progression of tasks without access to the original training data. The authors propose the TIME (Temporal Integration of Model Expertise) framework to analyze the merging process across training initialization, deployment strategy, and specific merging algorithms like Task Arithmetic and Model Soups. Utilizing the FoMo-in-Flux benchmark for continual multimodal pretraining, the study evaluates these strategies across various model scales and task sequences. The results offer practical guidance on managing the stability-plasticity trade-off during the long-term lifecycle of multimodal foundation models.
papers.authors: Sebastian Dziadzio, Vishaal Udandarao, Karsten Roth, Ameya Prabhu, Zeynep Akata, Samuel Albanie, Matthias Bethge

papers.title: A Practitioner's Guide to Continual Multimodal Pretraining
papers.abstract: Current vision-language foundation models are typically trained in stationary settings, failing to account for the non-stationary nature of real-world data streams. This paper provides a comprehensive research testbed, FoMo-in-Flux, comprising 63 diverse datasets to study continual multimodal pretraining. The authors evaluate various adaptation and retention strategies, including parameter-efficient finetuning (e.g., LoRA, GaLore) and model merging techniques. The resulting guide offers key insights into maintaining model stability and plasticity, identifying that the combination of finetuning and model merging is particularly effective for managing long-horizon updates and mitigating catastrophic forgetting in multimodal systems.
papers.authors: Karsten Roth, Vishaal Udandarao, Sebastian Dziadzio, Ameya Prabhu, Mehdi Cherti, Oriol Vinyals, Olivier Hénaff, Samuel Albanie, Zeynep Akata, Matthias Bethge

E042.name: Thomas Serre
E042.department: Cognitive, Linguistic, and Psychological Sciences; Computer Science
E042.bio: Thomas Serre is a Professor of Cognitive, Linguistic, and Psychological Sciences and Computer Science at Brown University. Serre conducts research at the intersection of biological and artificial vision, focusing on the computational principles of the visual cortex. Their work investigates how recurrent and feedback circuitry support visual reasoning and perception. By developing brain-inspired deep learning architectures and cognitive benchmarks, Serre aims to quantify the alignment between human and machine vision to advance neuroscience and artificial intelligence.
E042.research_direction: Dr. Serre has recently been investigating the fundamental alignment—and growing divergence—between artificial deep neural networks and biological visual systems. Their recent work explores classic cognitive phenomena, such as how the brain binds independent features into coherent object representations and how observers dynamically track objects across severe appearance changes, testing mechanistic hypotheses like neural phase synchrony using novel complex-valued recurrent networks. Additionally, they have been probing the boundaries of human-like spatial intelligence by developing rigorous new benchmarks to evaluate 3D geometric reasoning and egocentric visual perspective-taking in machines. Across both basic science and applied clinical domains like histopathology, their research systematically investigates the trustworthiness of artificial vision, examining whether these models utilize robust morphological indicators or simply rely on deceptive, dataset-specific spurious correlations.

papers.title: Better artificial intelligence does not mean better models of biology
papers.abstract: While deep neural networks (DNNs) were initially characterized by increasing alignment with primate perceptual and neural data as they achieved higher performance on computer vision benchmarks, recent empirical evidence suggests this alignment has plateaued or diverged as models scale toward superhuman accuracy. The authors argue that this divergence indicates the emergence of visual strategies in artificial systems that differ fundamentally from the biological constraints of primates. By evaluating representational and functional alignment across three distinct benchmarks, they posit that engineering-driven optimization for large-scale internet data is insufficient for modeling biological vision. They propose that computational neuroscience must prioritize algorithms intrinsically grounded in biological visual principles rather than maximizing performance on standard AI benchmarks.
papers.authors: Drew Linsley, Pinyuan Feng, Thomas Serre

papers.title: Feature binding in biological and artificial vision
papers.abstract: This work reviews the classical 'property binding problem' in vision science, examining how the brain integrates features like color and motion into coherent object representations. The authors evaluate traditional modular theories of functional segregation against evidence from deep learning models and large-scale clinical lesion studies. They find that deep neural networks (DNNs) achieve state-of-the-art performance in complex visual recognition without utilizing the explicit binding mechanisms, such as temporal synchrony, historically hypothesized to be essential for biological vision. The review suggests that natural vision may instead rely on a distributed, covariance-based representational architecture, and it discusses how this perspective reconciles findings of specialization without the need for strict segregation in the primate visual cortex.
papers.authors: Pieter R. Roelfsema, Thomas Serre

papers.title: Tracking objects that change in appearance with phase synchrony
papers.abstract: The authors examine the computational hypothesis that neural synchrony serves as an attentional mechanism allowing biological visual systems to track objects as they undergo significant appearance transformations due to lighting, pose, or non-rigidity. They introduce the Complex-Valued Recurrent Neural Network (CV-RNN), a novel architecture where neural magnitude encodes feature identity and phase represents spatial coordinates, enabling the decoupling of location from appearance. Performance is evaluated using 'FeatureTracker,' a large-scale challenge testing the ability of observers to track appearance-morphing stimuli. While state-of-the-art feedforward and standard recurrent neural networks fail to maintain object identity under these shifts, the CV-RNN demonstrates human-like tracking capabilities, providing a computational proof-of-concept for phase synchronization as a neural substrate for dynamic object tracking.
papers.authors: Sabine Muzellec, Drew Linsley, Alekh Karkada Ashok, Ennio Mingolla, Girik Malik, Rufin VanRullen, Thomas Serre

papers.title: The 3D-PC: A benchmark for visual perspective taking in humans and machines
papers.abstract: Visual Perspective Taking (VPT)—the ability to reason about an agent's egocentric viewpoint within a 3D environment—is a critical component of human spatial intelligence that requires robust 3D scene processing. The authors introduce the 3D Perception Challenge (3D-PC) to evaluate whether emergent 3D analysis capabilities in deep neural networks (DNNs) are sufficient for VPT. The benchmark comprises three tasks: depth order estimation, basic VPT (VPT-basic), and a controlled task (VPT-Strategy) designed to eliminate heuristic visual shortcuts. Experiments involving 327 DNNs show that while models often exceed human performance in depth ordering, they fail significantly in VPT-basic. Furthermore, models fine-tuned on VPT-basic fail to generalize to VPT-Strategy, highlighting a persistent gap between artificial systems and human-like 3D geometric reasoning.
papers.authors: Drew Linsley, Peisen Zhou, Alekh Karkada Ashok, Akash Nagaraj, Gaurav Suhas Gaonkar, Francis Lewis, Zygmunt Pizlo, Thomas Serre

papers.title: Deceptive learning in histopathology
papers.abstract: The authors systematically evaluate the trustworthiness of visual strategies learned by deep neural networks (DNNs) in histopathological image analysis. Using a dataset of whole-slide images (WSIs) from lung adenocarcinoma, they compare DNN performance on tumor detection, tissue-of-origin identification, and molecular profiling of KRAS and EGFR mutations. While DNNs demonstrate robust and generalizable strategies for tumor localization, the study reveals that their success in molecular profiling is 'deceptive,' relying on spurious correlations between histological subtypes and specific mutations rather than direct morphological indicators of genotype. This finding is confirmed through failure to generalize to laser-capture microdissection datasets, emphasizing the necessity of interpretability frameworks to differentiate between reliable diagnostic tools and models exploiting dataset-specific biases.
papers.authors: Sahar Shahamatdar, Daryoush Saeed-Vafa, Drew Linsley, Farah Khalil, Katherine Lovinger, Lester Li, Howard T. McLeod, Sohini Ramachandran, Thomas Serre

E043.name: Yukiyasu Kamitani
E043.bio: Kamitani researches brain decoding, developing methodologies to translate functional MRI signals into specific contents of human perception and mental imagery. Their work utilizes deep neural networks and machine learning to map hierarchical neural representations onto visual features, facilitating the reconstruction of seen images, dreams, and subjective illusory experiences. Currently, Kamitani focuses on generative brain decoding and the development of brain-machine interfaces that combine computational neuroscience with artificial intelligence to study human cognition.
E043.research_direction: Dr. Kamitani has recently been investigating how rich perceptual experiences can be decoded and reconstructed from human neural activity using deep neural network representations and generative models. Their recent work explores a wide breadth of decoding applications, including translating fMRI signals into complex natural sounds and utilizing ECoG recordings for closed-loop, brain-machine visual image retrieval. Beyond single-subject paradigms, they are examining how to computationally align functional topographies to achieve inter-individual neural code conversion without relying on shared stimulus presentations. Furthermore, they have been probing the theoretical and methodological limits of these frameworks, investigating representational redundancy through input recovery techniques and critically assessing whether modern diffusion-based visual decoders extract genuine, stimulus-specific features rather than producing spurious generative hallucinations.

papers.title: Readout Representation: Redefining Neural Codes by Input Recovery
papers.abstract: This study challenges the conventional hierarchical-causal framework of neural encoding by proposing an informational 'readout representation' framework. The authors argue that neural codes should be defined by the information recoverable (read out) from features rather than their causal origin. Through empirical evaluation using feature inversion and input recovery in both biological and artificial neural networks, the research demonstrates that high-fidelity inputs can be reconstructed even from heavily perturbed mid-level features. This finding indicates that a single input corresponds to a broad, redundant region of the feature space. The authors introduce a novel 'representation size' metric to quantify representational redundancy and model robustness, offering a unified perspective on how neural systems maintain detailed, information-rich representations while undergoing abstraction.
papers.authors: Shunsuke Onoo, Yoshihiro Nagano, Yukiyasu Kamitani

papers.title: Inter-individual and inter-site neural code conversion without shared stimuli
papers.abstract: This research addresses the challenge of inter-individual variability in functional topographies by developing a neural code conversion method that does not require paired brain data from shared stimuli. The proposed method utilizes a content-loss-based optimization strategy that aligns brain activity patterns based on the discrepancy between stimulus contents represented in a shared latent space (deep neural network features). The approach achieves conversion accuracies comparable to methods using shared stimuli and enables high-quality inter-individual visual image reconstruction. The framework demonstrates robust performance across data collected at different sites and with limited training samples, providing a foundation for scalable neural data analysis and potential brain-to-brain communication protocols.
papers.authors: Haibao Wang, Jun Kai Ho, Fan L. Cheng, Shuntaro C. Aoki, Yusuke Muraki, Misato Tanaka, Jong-Yun Park, Yukiyasu Kamitani

papers.title: Natural sounds can be reconstructed from human neuroimaging data using deep neural network representation
papers.abstract: This study demonstrates the reconstruction of arbitrary natural sounds from human fMRI activity by mapping neural responses to the hierarchical features of deep neural networks (DNNs). The authors employ an audio-generative model (SpecVQGAN) and show that latent features decoded from the auditory cortex provide significantly better reconstruction fidelity than traditional spectrotemporal or modulation-based features. The framework successfully produces perceptually plausible sounds across diverse categories, as validated by both quantitative feature analysis and human subjective ratings. This work establishes a methodology for decoding complex, non-temporal auditory experiences from the relatively coarse temporal resolution of fMRI signals.
papers.authors: Jong-Yun Park, Mitsuaki Tsukamoto, Misato Tanaka, Yukiyasu Kamitani

papers.title: Spurious reconstruction from brain activity
papers.abstract: The authors perform a critical assessment of recent text-guided brain decoding methods that utilize large-scale datasets (e.g., Natural Scene Dataset) and diffusion models. They identify a phenomenon termed 'output dimension collapse,' where decoders become specialized to specific semantic clusters in the training set, leading to reconstructions that are primarily a result of category classification and generative hallucination rather than genuine stimulus-specific detail. Through formal analysis and UMAP visualizations of text features, the study reveals that these methods often fail to achieve true zero-shot generalization on novel datasets. The paper emphasizes the necessity of diverse training sets and compositional representations to ensure authentic, generalizable visual image reconstruction.
papers.authors: Ken Shirakawa, Yoshihiro Nagano, Misato Tanaka, Shuntaro C. Aoki, Kei Majima, Yusuke Muraki, Yukiyasu Kamitani

papers.title: Image retrieval based on closed-loop visual–semantic neural decoding
papers.abstract: This paper presents a brain-machine interface (BMI) for image retrieval using electrocorticogram (ECoG) signals recorded from the human visual cortex. The system decodes neural activity into a high-dimensional visual semantic space derived from DNN features, allowing for real-time, closed-loop control. Users are able to retrieve specific target images from a large-scale database by modulating their brain activity in response to visual feedback. The results demonstrate that semantic representations in the visual cortex can be voluntarily controlled and effectively decoded to externalize mental intentions, providing a robust framework for communication and image retrieval via neural signals.
papers.authors: Ryohei Fukuma, Takufumi Yanagisawa, Hidenori Sugano, Kentaro Tamura, Satoru Oshino, Naoki Tani, Yasushi Iimura, Hui Ming Khoo, Hiroharu Suzuki, Huixiang Yang, Masayuki Hirata, Yukiyasu Kamitani

E044.name: Grace Lindsay
E044.department: Department of Psychology and Center for Data Science
E044.bio: Grace Lindsay is an Assistant Professor at New York University who utilizes computational neuroscience, psychology, and machine learning to study neural information processing. Their research employs artificial neural networks as functional models of the visual system to investigate how attentional mechanisms modulate sensory processing and task performance. Lindsay evaluates the validity of analytical tools in systems neuroscience and develops computer vision applications for climate change mitigation, such as analyzing satellite imagery to track environmental transitions. They are also the author of 'Models of the Mind,' a book detailing the mathematical history and theoretical foundations of brain research.
E044.research_direction: Dr. Lindsay has recently been exploring the intersection of biological and artificial intelligence, investigating how systems neuroscience frameworks—such as Marr’s levels of analysis and neural population geometry—can be applied to reverse-engineer and interpret the internal representations of artificial neural networks (ANNs). Reciprocally, their recent work explores using ANNs as highly observable, mechanistic models to test how specific neural circuit alterations causally drive changes in task behavior. In the realm of embodied control, they are investigating whether biological inductive biases, like mammalian spinal cord circuitry, can be integrated into network architectures to improve the efficiency and adaptability of quadruped robotic locomotion. Additionally, their research touches upon applied computer vision, examining how multi-temporal input strategies and transformer architectures can best fuse temporal data to enhance the semantic segmentation of satellite imagery for environmental monitoring.

papers.title: Neural Circuit Architectural Priors for Quadruped Locomotion
papers.abstract: Learning-based approaches to quadrupedal locomotion typically employ generic multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) that lack biological inductive biases, requiring extensive data or reward engineering to achieve robust movement. This study introduces Quadruped NCAP, an artificial neural network architecture incorporating architectural priors derived from mammalian spinal cord and limb neural circuits, such as central pattern generators and afferent feedback loops. The results demonstrate that these biologically inspired priors enable significantly higher data and parameter efficiency than standard MLPs, achieving comparable performance with orders of magnitude fewer parameters. The model exhibits superior generalization across varied terrains and robotic body configurations, and notably, it facilitates direct deployment on a physical quadruped robot without the reliance on conventional sim-to-real transfer methodologies, highlighting the efficacy of nervous-system-inspired connectivity in embodied control.
papers.authors: Nikhil X. Bhattasali, Venkatesh Pattabiraman, Lerrel Pinto, Grace W. Lindsay

papers.title: Improving satellite imagery segmentation using multiple Sentinel-2 revisits
papers.abstract: The analysis of remote sensing data frequently employs computer vision models pre-trained on static datasets, which fail to exploit the temporal dimension provided by frequent satellite revisits. This work evaluates various multi-temporal input strategies for fine-tuning pre-trained models on satellite imagery, specifically targeting the semantic segmentation of power substations—a task critical for monitoring climate change mitigation efforts. Through extensive testing across multiple model architectures, the study finds that fusing temporal representations within the latent space of the model is markedly superior to traditional data augmentation or input-level stacking. Architecturally, a SWIN Transformer-based model outperforms both U-Net and standard Vision Transformer (ViT) variants. These results, verified on a building density estimation benchmark, provide a specialized framework for leveraging the temporal revisits inherent in satellite data to enhance the performance of deep learning models in environmental remote sensing.
papers.authors: Kartik Jindgar, Grace W. Lindsay

papers.title: Multilevel interpretability of artificial neural networks: leveraging framework and methods from neuroscience
papers.abstract: As artificial neural networks (ANNs) approach the complexity of biological brains, relating their high-dimensional internal structures to external task behaviors has become a significant challenge. This paper proposes a multilevel interpretability framework adapted from David Marr’s three levels of analysis—computation, algorithm, and implementation—to provide a structured approach for understanding intelligent systems. We review and organize a suite of analytical tools from systems neuroscience, including neural population geometry analysis, decoding probes, and causal circuit manipulations, which can be applied to ANNs. By mapping specific interpretability goals to these levels, the framework seeks to bridge the gap between architectural properties and behavioral outputs, clarifying the assumptions and priorities required to reverse-engineer both biological and artificial neural computations.
papers.authors: Zhonghao He, Jascha Achterberg, Katie Collins, Kevin K. Nejad, Danyal Akarca, Yinzhu Yang, Wes Gurnee, Ilia Sucholutsky, Yuhan Tang, Rebeca Ianov, George Ogden, Chole Li, Kai J. Sandbrink, Stephen Casper, Anna Ivanova, Grace W. Lindsay

papers.title: Grounding neuroscience in behavioral changes using artificial neural networks
papers.abstract: Connecting neural population activity to functional outcomes is a central goal of systems neuroscience, yet the conceptualization of 'function' remains varied. This review advocates for grounding this goal in the causal relationship between specific neural circuit changes and observable changes in behavior. Artificial neural networks (ANNs) are presented as a uniquely observable and controllable format for testing such hypotheses, as they utilize complex transformations to produce task-relevant behavior. By serving as mechanistic models, ANNs allow researchers to causally test whether a given neural modification is sufficient to produce an experimentally observed behavioral shift. Furthermore, the work highlights the utility of importing interpretability methods from the field of artificial intelligence to identify the specific neural features and representational geometries that drive task performance and behavioral dynamics.
papers.authors: Grace W. Lindsay

papers.title: Editorial overview: Computational neuroscience as a bridge between artificial intelligence, modeling and data
papers.abstract: This editorial overview examines the current state of computational neuroscience as a pivotal intermediary between the development of artificial intelligence, theoretical modeling, and the influx of high-resolution neural data. The transformative impact of new experimental methodologies, which enable the collection of massive, multi-modal datasets, has necessitated a shift from single-neuron models to population-level frameworks. The article synthesizes recent advancements in five key areas: machine learning for neuroscience, neurosciences for machine learning, neural computation principles, computational models of sensory-motor circuits, and novel data analysis methods. It emphasizes the 'neuroconnectionist' paradigm, where brain-inspired architectures are used to simulate complex cognition and behavior, and discusses how the synergy between interpretability in AI and systems neuroscience is providing new insights into the functional organization of the cortex.
papers.authors: Grace W. Lindsay

E045.name: Wieland Brendel
E045.institution: Max Planck Institute for Intelligent Systems
E045.bio: Wieland Brendel is an independent Group Leader at the Max Planck Institute for Intelligent Systems and a Hector-endowed Fellow at the ELLIS Institute Tübingen. Their research operates at the intersection of computational neuroscience and machine learning, with a focus on human and artificial perception through robust and interpretable models. Brendel identified the texture bias in ImageNet-trained convolutional neural networks and works on causal representation learning to increase model generalizability. They were awarded the 2023 German Pattern Recognition Award for work in the field of computer vision.
E045.research_direction: Dr. Brendel has recently been investigating the fundamental mechanisms underlying compositional generalization, representation learning, and interpretability in deep neural networks. Their recent work explores how artificial visual systems can achieve data-efficient, human-like perception, examining how generative frameworks might be necessary for models to correctly process novel combinations of known objects and backgrounds. To theoretically ground how models learn these composable abstractions, they are probing the mathematics of unsupervised disentanglement and refining contrastive learning theories to better reflect the complex latent variability introduced by practical data augmentations. Additionally, Dr. Brendel is investigating the broader behavior of large-scale models, developing automated perceptual metrics to evaluate per-neuron interpretability across massive vision architectures and examining how pretraining data distributions dictate generalization scaling laws in Large Language Models.

papers.title: Generation is Required for Data-Efficient Perception
papers.abstract: This work interrogates the hypothesis that machine visual systems require a generative component to emulate the data-efficient compositional generalization characteristic of human perception. The authors compare discriminative, encoder-only architectures against generative, decoder-based frameworks, formalizing the inductive biases necessary to resolve the inverse problem of recovering latent factors from high-dimensional manifolds. They demonstrate theoretically that while enforcing these structural constraints on encoders is typically intractable due to their dependence on the unknown geometry of out-of-distribution manifolds, they can be implemented effectively in generative models by constraining the decoder and performing inversion. The researchers propose efficient inversion mechanisms via gradient-based search and generative replay. Empirical validation on photorealistic image datasets reveals that generative methods significantly outperform non-generative counterparts in zero-shot compositional generalization, successfully mapping novel combinations of known objects and backgrounds with minimal training data.
papers.authors: Jack Brady, Bernhard Schölkopf, Thomas Kipf, Simon Buchholz, Wieland Brendel

papers.title: LLMs on the Line: Data Determines Loss-to-Loss Scaling Laws
papers.abstract: The authors systematically investigate loss-to-loss scaling laws in Large Language Models (LLMs), which quantify the relationship between pretraining losses and downstream task performance. While linear or power-law-like correlations between in-distribution and out-of-distribution losses are found to be persistent across diverse settings, the study reveals that the specific parameters of these scaling frontiers are heavily contingent on data distribution, model architecture, and optimization settings. By evaluating a broad spectrum of training configurations, the research identifies that data-centric interventions—specifically scaling the diversity and composition of the pretraining corpus—are the primary levers for shifting scaling laws. This study provides a comprehensive diagnostic framework for predicting model generalization and underscores the limitations of assuming universal scaling trends across heterogeneous training regimes.
papers.authors: Prasanna Mayilvahanan, Thaddäus Wiedemer, Sayak Mallick, Matthias Bethge, Wieland Brendel

papers.title: Interaction Asymmetry: A General Principle for Learning Composable Abstractions
papers.abstract: The paper introduces 'interaction asymmetry' as a theoretical foundation for unsupervised disentanglement and compositional generalization. This principle posits that the mutual interactions between components of the same latent concept are significantly more complex than the interactions between components of different concepts. The researchers formalize this through block-diagonality conditions on the higher-order derivatives (specifically (n+1)th order) of the generator mapping from the latent space to the observation space. They prove that interaction asymmetry is sufficient for recovering ground-truth latent factors and enabling zero-shot recombination of learned concepts. To implement these theoretical findings, the authors develop a Transformer-based Variational Autoencoder (VAE) featuring a novel attention-regularization term on the decoder to penalize inter-slot interactions. Experiments on synthetic datasets show that this approach recovers object-centric representations and achieves out-of-distribution generalization without explicit object-level supervision.
papers.authors: Jack Brady, Julius von Kügelgen, Sébastien Lachapelle, Simon Buchholz, Thomas Kipf, Wieland Brendel

papers.title: InfoNCE: Identifying the Gap Between Theory and Practice
papers.abstract: This research addresses the discrepancy between the theoretical foundations of Contrastive Learning (CL) and its empirical application, specifically focusing on the variability of latent factors during data augmentation. Existing identifiability proofs for the InfoNCE objective frequently rely on assumptions of isotropic noise or strictly invariant latent factors, which do not align with the non-uniform variance introduced by standard augmentations like aggressive cropping. The authors generalize CL theory to encompass anisotropic latent distributions, better capturing the continuum of variability observed in practice. They introduce the AnInfoNCE objective, which accounts for these non-uniform latent changes, and provide a formal proof of its identifiability under generalized Gaussian conditional distributions. Their findings suggest that theoretical guarantees for representation learning must be aligned with the actual latent geometry induced by augmentations to ensure robust factor recovery.
papers.venue: International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Statistics (AISTATS)
papers.authors: Evgenia Rusak, Patrik Reizinger, Attila Juhos, Oliver Bringmann, Roland S. Zimmermann, Wieland Brendel

papers.title: Measuring Per-Unit Interpretability at Scale Without Humans
papers.abstract: To circumvent the lack of scalability in human-centric interpretability evaluations, the authors propose the Mechanistic Interpretability Score (MIS), a fully automated computational metric for assessing the semantic consistency of individual units in deep vision models. MIS utilizes perceptual similarity metrics (LPIPS) to quantify whether the top-activating images for a specific neuron align with a consistent semantic concept, mimicking human psychophysical tasks. The researchers apply this metric to a massive meta-analysis of over 70 million units across 835 vision models, uncovering a consistent anti-correlation between a model's top-1 classification accuracy and its average per-unit interpretability. Additionally, the study tracks the longitudinal development of representational structures during model training and across architectural depths, demonstrating that MIS serves as a scalable proxy for human judgment in mechanistic interpretability research.
papers.authors: Roland S. Zimmermann, David Klindt, Wieland Brendel

E046.name: Felix Wichmann
E046.bio: Felix Wichmann is a Professor of Neural Information Processing at the University of Tübingen, where they investigate human perception through psychophysical experimentation and computational modeling. Wichmann’s work includes the statistical analysis of psychometric functions and the evaluation of deep neural networks as behavioral models of human vision. Their research integrates machine learning, Bayesian inference, and signal detection theory to study the connection between early spatial vision and high-level object recognition. Current projects in Wichmann's laboratory focus on "shortcut learning" in artificial systems, the role of shape versus texture in recognition, and the perceptual mechanisms underlying the detection of causality.
E046.research_direction: Dr. Wichmann's recent work explores the computational mechanisms underlying human visual perception by integrating behavioral psychophysics with biological and artificial neural network models. A major focus of their research investigates the validity of deep neural networks as models of the primate visual system, specifically probing how human and machine observers compare in their learning dynamics, error consistencies, and ability to generalize across varying stimulus durations and out-of-distribution image distortions. Alongside these human-machine comparisons, they have recently been advancing mechanistic models of early spatial vision. To this end, their work seeks to mathematically disentangle early sensory noise from late-stage decision noise using psychometric data, while also examining whether biologically inspired dendritic nonlinearities can account for classical spatial vision phenomena like plaid masking.

papers.title: Behavioral differences between humans and machines arise early in visual processing
papers.abstract: This study interrogates the validity of Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) as computational models of human visual perception by analyzing behavioral discrepancies in object recognition. While DNNs demonstrate high predictive accuracy for primate cortical neural activity, psychophysical experiments reveal significant error inconsistencies. The authors find that these behavioral misalignments between humans and machines originate at the earliest stages of visual processing. The research highlights that DNNs fail to exhibit human-like robustness and representational alignment, particularly when challenged with out-of-distribution stimuli. The findings suggest that current architectures lack the fundamental mechanistic principles of the primate ventral stream, necessitating a shift toward image-computable models that more accurately reflect the biological constraints of human early vision.
papers.authors: Thomas Klein, Wieland Brendel, Felix A. Wichmann

papers.title: Estimating the contribution of early and late noise in vision from psychophysical data
papers.abstract: This research addresses the longstanding challenge in psychophysics of disentangling the relative contributions of early-stage (e.g., photoreceptor) and late-stage (decision-level) inner noise in visual detection and discrimination. Utilizing noise propagation theory through a nonlinear model cascade, the authors develop a method to quantify these noise sources using only behavioral data. The analysis demonstrates that while threshold-only datasets require significant external noise to distinguish sources, the use of full psychometric functions allows for reliable quantification even in the absence of external noise. Quantitative estimates reveal that early visual processing substantially reduces retinal noise, with behavioral early noise levels found to be significantly lower than those predicted by theoretical models of cone photocurrents, such as ISETBio.
papers.authors: Jesús Malo, José Juan Esteve-Taboada, Guillermo Aguilar, Marianne Maertens, Felix A. Wichmann

papers.title: Plaid masking explained with input-dependent dendritic nonlinearities
papers.abstract: The standard linear-nonlinear cascade model of spatial vision fails to account for plaid masking, a robust perceptual phenomenon where contrast thresholds for a test grating are elevated by a masking grating. This study proposes the Intrinsically Nonlinear Receptive Field (INRF) model, which replaces traditional linear filters with input-dependent dendritic nonlinearities. By implementing biologically realistic neurons where dendritic integration is sensitive to the specific spatiotemporal properties of the stimulus, the model successfully predicts experimental plaid masking data that has eluded the standard model for over three decades. The results suggest that these critical nonlinearities may be operative as early as the retinal ganglion cells, providing a more accurate representation of early spatial vision mechanics.
papers.authors: Marcelo Bertalmío, Alexia Durán Vizcaíno, Jesús Malo, Felix A. Wichmann

papers.title: Error consistency between humans and machines as a function of presentation duration
papers.abstract: Assessments of behavioral alignment between human observers and Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) often utilize error consistency as a metric, yet the temporal constraints of human vision are frequently ignored. This paper systematically investigates how stimulus presentation duration (ranging from 8.3 ms to over 1000 ms) impacts error consistency across natural, lowpass-filtered, and noisy images. The authors demonstrate that although humans can perform 8-way object classification with single-frame (8.3 ms) exposures, increased presentation time significantly enhances both performance and behavioral alignment with ANNs. These findings suggest that fair human-machine comparisons must account for the time-dependent nature of human visual processing, particularly the role of recurrent cortical feedback in resolving difficult or corrupted visual inputs.
papers.authors: Thomas Klein, Wieland Brendel, Felix A. Wichmann

papers.title: Comparing supervised learning dynamics: Deep neural networks match human data efficiency but show a generalisation lag
papers.abstract: This paper investigates the learning dynamics of deep neural networks (DNNs) relative to human observers in a supervised object recognition task. While humans exhibit near-immediate generalization to novel categories, DNNs frequently demonstrate a 'generalization lag,' requiring significantly more exposure to achieve comparable robustness to image distortions. The authors utilize a systematic psychophysical paradigm to compare the data efficiency and representational divergence between the two systems. The results indicate that while DNNs can match human data efficiency in certain controlled environments, their failure to generalize rapidly to out-of-distribution examples highlights a fundamental difference in the underlying learning algorithms or inductive biases, pointing toward a divergence in representational strategy.
papers.authors: Lukas S. Huber, Fred W. Mast, Felix A. Wichmann

E055.name: Pieter Roelfsema
E055.bio: Pieter Roelfsema is a neuroscientist specializing in the cortical mechanisms of visual perception, attention, and conscious experience. Their research utilizes primate electrophysiology, human neuroimaging, and computational modeling to investigate the function of the early visual cortex as a 'cognitive blackboard' during tasks such as perceptual grouping. A focus of their current work involves developing high-channel-count cortical neuroprostheses intended to restore rudimentary vision in blind individuals via electrical stimulation. Roelfsema's research group examines how feedback and lateral connections modulate neuronal activity to represent task-relevant features and facilitate object-background segregation.
E055.research_direction: Dr. Roelfsema has recently been investigating the neural computations underlying primate vision alongside the development of advanced cortical neuroprostheses. Their recent work explores the representational architecture of the ventral stream, using large-scale multi-area spiking datasets and recurrent computational models to examine how modulatory feedback facilitates attentional object segmentation and figure-ground modulation. Applied to clinical neuroengineering, they are developing computational and signal-processing techniques for high-density visual implants, focusing on filtering out microstimulation artifacts and mapping retinotopic topography using spontaneous resting-state activity in both macaques and blind human patients. Broadening their scope into human cognitive neuroscience, they have also been utilizing intracranial single-neuron recordings to study how hippocampal concept cells track semantic identities and support conceptual continuity during language comprehension.

papers.title: An extensive dataset of spiking activity to reveal the syntax of the ventral stream
papers.abstract: The authors introduce the THINGS Ventral-stream Spiking Dataset (TVSD), a large-scale neurophysiological resource documenting the spiking activity of neuronal populations in macaque V1, V4, and inferotemporal (IT) cortex during the presentation of 25,000+ naturalistic images from the THINGS database. Utilizing high-channel-count electrode arrays, the study investigates the representational syntax of the ventral pathway, demonstrating that noise correlations scale with the similarity of neuronal tuning both within and across hierarchical levels. The dataset enables high-fidelity visualization of feature-tuning using deep convolutional neural networks and establishes a benchmark for evaluating the alignment between biological visual processing and computational vision models, providing a high-resolution map of object vision in the primate brain.
papers.authors: Paolo Papale, Feng Wang, Matthew W. Self, Pieter R. Roelfsema

papers.title: Large-scale mapping of artificial perceptions for neuroprostheses using spontaneous neuronal activity in macaque and human visual cortex
papers.abstract: To address the clinical bottleneck of mapping phosphene locations for high-density visual prostheses, this research presents NEUmap, a framework for topography reconstruction using spontaneous neuronal activity. By applying Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) to correlations in multi-unit activity (MUA) and local field potentials (LFP) recorded during resting-state, the authors demonstrated that the intrinsic functional connectivity of the visual cortex preserves its retinotopic structure. The methodology was validated in sighted macaques and successfully translated to blind human volunteers with cortical implants, providing a rapid, calibration-free technique for aligning electrode coordinates with the visual field without requiring external visual input.
papers.authors: Antonio Lozano, Xing Chen, Mike La Grouw, Beiyan Li, Feng Wang, Maureen van der Grinten, Cristian Soto-Sánchez, Alper Morales-Gregorio, Eduardo Fernández, Pieter R. Roelfsema

papers.title: Modulatory feedback determines attentional object segmentation in a model of the ventral stream
papers.abstract: This work examines how modulatory feedback signals implement attentional object segmentation within a recurrent model of the primate ventral stream. Integrating top-down modulatory connections that interact with feedforward feature processing, the model replicates physiological signatures of figure-ground modulation (FGM) and perceptual grouping. The authors show that these feedback mechanisms allow the network to selectively enhance object-consistent representations in early visual layers, facilitating robust segmentation in cluttered environments. Quantitative comparisons with macaque neurophysiology suggest that modulatory feedback is a critical computational primitive for solving the binding problem and directing object-based attention.
papers.authors: Paolo Papale, Jonathan R. Williford, Stijn Balk, Pieter R. Roelfsema

papers.title: Pronouns reactivate conceptual representations in human hippocampal neurons
papers.abstract: Utilizing intracranial single-unit recordings in the human hippocampus, the authors investigate the neural basis of pronoun-noun resolution during discourse comprehension. They identify a population of 'concept cells' that respond selectively to specific semantic identities (nouns) and demonstrate that these neurons are reactivated when subsequent pronouns refer back to those identities. This reactivation occurs rapidly and dynamically, supporting a model where semantic memory networks in the medial temporal lobe maintain conceptual continuity during language processing. The findings provide direct evidence for the integration of linguistic markers and stable conceptual representations at the single-neuron level.
papers.authors: Doris E. Dijksterhuis, Matthew W. Self, Jessy K. Possel, Johannes C. Peters, Erika C. W. van Straaten, Sander Idema, J. Christiaan Baaijen, Sandra M. A. van der Salm, Erik J. Aarnoutse, Nicole C. E. van Klink, Pieter van Eijsden, Simon Hanslmayr, Richard Chelvarajah, Florian Roux, Luca D. Kolibius, Victoria Sawlani, David T. Rollings, Stanislas Dehaene, Pieter R. Roelfsema

papers.title: Comparison of electrical microstimulation artifact removal methods for high-channel-count prostheses
papers.abstract: This technical study evaluates signal processing strategies for mitigating electrical microstimulation artifacts in high-channel-count cortical interfaces. The authors benchmarked local curve fitting (LCF), principal component analysis (PCA), and independent component analysis (ICA) on datasets recorded from multi-electrode arrays in macaques. Performance was assessed based on the fidelity of multi-unit activity (MUA) recovery and artifact suppression efficiency. Results demonstrated that PCA-based subtraction effectively handles the high spatial and temporal variability of artifacts across channels, enabling the extraction of clean neuronal responses during ongoing stimulation—a prerequisite for the development of adaptive, closed-loop visual neuroprostheses.
papers.authors: Feng Wang, Xing Chen, Pieter R. Roelfsema

E056.name: Caspar Schwiedrzik
E056.main_research_area: cognitive neurobiology of learning and perception
E056.bio: Caspar M. Schwiedrzik is a Professor of Cognitive Neurobiology at Ruhr University Bochum, where they investigate the neural mechanisms underlying learning and cognitive flexibility. Schwiedrzik utilizes a comparative approach that integrates electrophysiological recordings and functional neuroimaging in both humans and non-human primates to examine the interplay of feedforward and feedback signals within the visual hierarchy. Their research explores how the brain generates sensory predictions and how these top-down signals facilitate the learning of abstract models and identity recognition. By combining empirical data with computational modeling, Schwiedrzik seeks to identify the principles that allow cortical circuits to adapt to environmental changes and generalize across novel situations.
E056.research_direction: Dr. Schwiedrzik has recently been investigating the flexible neural representations that support visual recognition and learning across the primate ventral stream. Their recent work explores how changing task demands and top-down predictive contexts dynamically reshape neural representational geometries, utilizing intracranial electrophysiology in humans and fMRI in macaques to probe these transformations. In parallel, they are examining the mechanisms of visual perceptual learning through psychophysics and neural modeling, specifically questioning how non-linear mixed selectivity and task-irrelevant stimulus variability might help overcome traditional learning specificity to enable broader behavioral generalization. Furthermore, their research assesses fundamental principles of hierarchical visual coding by probing how low-level features like orientation re-emerge within high-level functional hubs of both the inferotemporal cortex and deep convolutional neural networks.

papers.title: Multiple task-demands flexibly optimize neural geometry in human ventral temporal cortex
papers.abstract: Utilizing intracranial electrophysiology in patients undergoing epilepsy monitoring, this study examined the neural underpinnings of behavioral flexibility during trial-by-trial task switching. Subjects performed three distinct tasks—individuation, categorization, and conceptualization—each requiring unique representational geometries for the same set of visual stimuli. Results indicated that neural representations do not undergo an immediate, cue-driven transformation; rather, task-specific geometries emerged incrementally over successive stimulus repetitions within a trial. The ventral temporal cortex was identified as the exclusive region exhibiting dynamic optimization of representational distances for all three tasks, with these gradual geometric refinements significantly predicting trial-level behavioral performance. These findings suggest that sensory cortices implement context-dependent optimization far earlier in the processing hierarchy than previously hypothesized.
papers.authors: Tarana Nigam, Andrea F. Campos-Pérez, Pierre Mégevand, Juan R. Vidal, Marcela Perrone-Bertolotti, Philippe Kahane, Thomas Thesen, Orrin Devinsky, Lucia Melloni, Caspar M. Schwiedrzik

papers.title: Re-emergence of orientation coding in primate IT cortex and deep networks reveals functional hubs for visual processing
papers.abstract: Contrary to the efficient neural coding hypothesis which suggests that low-level features are progressively discarded in higher cortical areas, this study quantified orientation representation across the ventral stream using fMRI and multivoxel pattern analysis in macaques. Robust orientation information was detected in the inferotemporal (IT) cortex, distributed specifically within functional 'hubs' characterized by multivariate responsiveness to multiple object categories (faces, bodies, objects) and enhanced connectivity with upstream areas (V1–V4). This phenomenon was replicated in deep convolutional neural network models, where hub-like units supported hierarchical processing of complex inputs. These results imply that orientation information in high-level visual areas arises as a computational byproduct of functional diversity and network connectivity rather than redundant feature encoding, facilitating integrative visual processing.
papers.authors: Behnam Karami, Tarana Nigam, Sandrin S. Plewe, Caspar M. Schwiedrzik

papers.title: Task-Irrelevant Phase but not Contrast Variability Unlocks Generalization in Visual Perceptual Learning
papers.abstract: While visual perceptual learning (VPL) often results in highly specific performance gains restricted to trained retinal locations, this study investigated whether task-irrelevant stimulus variability can induce generalization. Subjects practiced an orientation discrimination task where trial-by-trial variability was introduced in either spatial phase or contrast. The results demonstrated that randomizing spatial phase led to complete spatial generalization of learning to untrained locations, whereas contrast randomization did not. This dissociation suggests that the neural substrates recruited for plasticity are contingent upon the nature of the task-irrelevant noise; variability in features processed with invariance in higher-order areas allows the visual system to utilize representations that facilitate broader transfer and overcome traditional learning specificity.
papers.authors: Beyza Akkoyunlu, Caspar M. Schwiedrzik

papers.title: Predictions enable top-down pattern separation in the macaque face-processing hierarchy
papers.abstract: Using fMRI in macaques, this research examined how top-down predictive signals, derived from statistical learning of face sequences, modulate neural representational geometries in the ventral visual stream. The authors found that contextual predictions significantly enhance pattern separability and increase the dimensionality of neural activity patterns in early stages of the face-processing hierarchy (ML/MF). These lower-level areas dynamically inherited higher-order, invariant tuning properties from the top-level area (AM), effectively transforming their feedforward representations. These findings provide evidence that top-down predictive context reconfigures representational spaces throughout cortical hierarchies to optimize the distinction of facial identities and facilitate efficient recognition.
papers.authors: Tarana Nigam, Caspar M. Schwiedrzik

papers.title: Visual perceptual learning of feature conjunctions leverages non-linear mixed selectivity
papers.abstract: Learning to identify visual objects often necessitates the integration of multiple features. This study employed psychophysical experiments and neural modeling to investigate how the visual system achieves orientation-color conjunction learning. The results show that while conjunction learning can occur via linear combinations of pure feature information, the most efficient and rapid learning involves non-linear mixed selectivity. Furthermore, subjects who utilized mixed-selectivity representations during training demonstrated superior performance on an untrained 'exclusive or' (XOR) task months later. These results suggest that the primate brain utilizes high-dimensional, non-linear representational spaces to support the flexible acquisition and generalization of complex multi-feature visual concepts.
papers.authors: Behnam Karami, Caspar M. Schwiedrzik

E057.name: Jason Fischer
E057.department: Faculty of Psychology and Educational Sciences
E057.bio: Fischer’s research investigates the cognitive and neural architectures used to navigate and predict the behavior of physical environments, a capability termed intuitive physics. Using functional MRI, psychophysics, and computational modeling, Fischer characterized a "physics engine" in the brain located within action-planning regions such as the premotor cortex. Their findings demonstrate that physical simulations occur in real-time to support survival-critical interactions and can operate independently of vivid visual imagery. Additionally, Fischer’s work examines serial dependence, describing how the brain integrates past and present visual information to maintain a stable and continuous perceptual experience.
E057.research_direction: Dr. Fischer’s recent work explores the cognitive and neural mechanisms underlying intuitive physics, specifically investigating how the visual system represents and simulates physical dynamics. They have recently been examining whether humans possess a dedicated, unitary mental resource for predicting physical events—such as object stability and collisions—that functions independently of general working memory and spatial reasoning. Using psychophysical paradigms, their research also probes how latent physical properties might shape basic visual processing, such as testing whether an object's perceived mass alters its estimated velocity. Furthermore, they are bridging perception, action, and evolution by investigating how the brain's internal "physics engine" informs motor kinematics during action planning, while exploring whether the capacity to mentally simulate hidden trajectories using motion-sensitive cortical areas is a mechanism conserved across primate species.

papers.title: Visual simulation: Catching a glimpse of what's to come
papers.abstract: This work explores whether the capacity for visual simulation—internally representing physical events beyond immediate sensory input—is a uniquely human trait. Contextualizing recent evidence from non-human primate studies, the author discusses findings that macaques utilize mental simulation to solve complex physical problems, such as predicting hidden-object trajectories. These simulations recruit motion-sensitive cortical areas even in the absence of explicit visual cues, suggesting that generative internal models of physical dynamics are a conserved cognitive mechanism across species for anticipating environmental changes.
papers.authors: Jason Fischer

papers.title: Velocity—Not Perceived as Such: The Role of Object Mass in Velocity Estimation
papers.abstract: This research investigates the perceptual integration of object mass into velocity estimation, challenging the conventional view of velocity as an independent visual primitive. Using a 2-alternative forced-choice (2-AFC) psychophysical paradigm, the authors manipulated object size and apparent material density to vary perceived mass while holding physical speed constant. Results demonstrate a systematic bias where objects with higher perceived mass are consistently judged as moving slower. These findings suggest that the human visual system encodes motion using dynamics-informed variables, potentially momentum, rather than Newtonian velocity alone.
papers.authors: Abdul-Rahim Deeb, Jason Fischer

papers.title: A dedicated mental resource for intuitive physics
papers.abstract: The authors hypothesize that humans possess a specialized, unitary mental resource for physical inference that functions independently of other cognitive domains. To test this, they utilized a battery of psychophysical tasks capturing individual differences in predicting outcomes like rigid body stability and collision dynamics. Results revealed high cross-task correlations in performance that were well-explained by a singular intuitive physics factor. Crucially, this resource was dissociable from general spatial reasoning and working memory, suggesting a dedicated neural and cognitive architecture for modeling the physical world.
papers.authors: Alex Mitko, Ana Navarro-Cebrián, Sarah Cormiea, Jason Fischer

papers.title: Physical reasoning is the missing link between action goals and kinematics
papers.abstract: This article proposes a framework in which intuitive physical reasoning serves as the essential computational bridge between high-level action goals and the specification of motor kinematics. The author argues that the brain's 'physics engine' does not merely provide a baseline for perception but actively informs motor planning by modeling latent object properties like mass distribution and friction. This model explains why grasp selection and anticipatory force calibration depend on internal physical simulations rather than simple visual heuristics, integrating the physics engine directly into the first-person action control system.
papers.authors: Jason Fischer

E060.name: Rufin VanRullen
E060.institution: French National Centre for Scientific Research
E060.department: Centre de Recherche Cerveau et Cognition (CerCo)
E060.bio: Rufin VanRullen is a CNRS Research Director at the Centre de Recherche Cerveau et Cognition (CerCo) whose work spans computational neuroscience and artificial intelligence. VanRullen investigates the rhythmic nature of human vision, specifically examining how alpha and theta brain oscillations produce discrete "perceptual cycles" in attention and perception. Their current research, supported by an ERC Advanced Grant, focuses on developing brain-inspired AI architectures that incorporate the Global Workspace Theory and predictive coding principles. By combining psychophysical experiments with deep learning and EEG analysis, VanRullen seeks to characterize the neural dynamics that enable flexible and robust cognition.
E060.research_direction: Dr. VanRullen has recently been investigating the intersection of human cognitive architectures and artificial intelligence, focusing on how both brains and machines integrate diverse streams of information. Their recent work explores the utility of cognitively inspired computational frameworks, specifically examining how Global Workspace architectures and top-down attention mechanisms can facilitate robust, amodal representation learning across different sensory modalities. In human neuroimaging, they are using fMRI decoding combined with generative latent diffusion models to probe the compositionality of these representations, investigating whether the cortex employs algebraic, modality-invariant codes across visual perception, language, and mental imagery. Additionally, they are exploring biologically motivated approaches to the classic visual binding problem, testing whether complex-valued representations and Kuramoto phase-synchronization dynamics can enhance object-centric scene decomposition in deep neural networks.

papers.title: An Attention Mechanism for Robust Multimodal Integration in a Global Workspace Architecture
papers.abstract: Drawing on Global Workspace Theory (GWT) from cognitive neuroscience, this work introduces a top-down attention mechanism designed to select and integrate relevant modalities within a shared amodal workspace. The architecture addresses the bottleneck of flexible multimodal fusion by employing an attentional spotlight to prioritize specific input streams. Benchmarking on the Simple Shapes and MM-IMDb 1.0 datasets demonstrates that the inclusion of this attention mechanism significantly enhances robustness against modality-specific noise and corruptions. Additionally, the model exhibits robust cross-task and cross-modality generalization, positioning the workspace-based selector as a competitive alternative to contemporary multimodal attention frameworks while maintaining biological plausibility.
papers.authors: Roland Bertin-Johannet, Lara Scipio, Léopold Maytié, Rufin VanRullen

papers.title: Modality-Agnostic Decoding of Vision and Language from fMRI
papers.abstract: This study investigates the existence of modality-invariant neural representations by training modality-agnostic decoders to predict stimulus identity from functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (fMRI) signals. Using a novel large-scale dataset, SemReps-8K, which captures brain activity during image viewing, reading of text descriptions, and mental imagery, the authors demonstrate that visual concepts can be decoded regardless of the presentation modality. Searchlight analyses identify expansive cortical regions that support these amodal representations, suggesting that the human brain utilizes generalized semantic codes to integrate information across disparate sensory inputs and internal cognitive states.
papers.authors: Mitja Nikolaus, Milad Mozafari, Isabelle Berry, Rufin VanRullen

papers.title: Evidence for compositionality in fMRI visual representations via Brain Algebra
papers.abstract: This research explores the compositional nature of neural encoding through 'Brain Algebra,' a method of perturbing fMRI patterns to reflect conceptual modifications. By applying semantic vector perturbations (e.g., adding 'winter' or 'night' attributes) to baseline neural patterns and reconstructing the resulting images via generative latent diffusion models, the authors show that the brain's representational space supports systematic, algebraic combinations of concepts. The decoded outputs demonstrate predictable and meaningful perceptual shifts, such as modifying a scene's season or lighting while preserving core structural features.
