These results provide empirical support for an algebraic-like process governing the composition of abstract visual features in human cortical representations.
papers.authors: Matteo Ferrante, Tommaso Boccato, Nicola Toschi, Rufin VanRullen

papers.title: Enhancing deep neural networks through complex-valued representations and Kuramoto synchronization dynamics
papers.abstract: Motivated by the biological solution to the binding problem, this paper proposes 'KomplexNet,' a hierarchical convolutional architecture that utilizes complex-valued units and Kuramoto synchronization dynamics to facilitate object-centric representation. By leveraging angular phases to group features belonging to the same object, the model implements both feedforward and recurrent feedback mechanisms to induce phase alignment. Experimental evaluations on multi-object categorization tasks, including overlapping digits and noisy image datasets, reveal that phase-based synchrony significantly improves classification accuracy and robustness to Gaussian noise. The findings suggest that incorporating synchronization dynamics into artificial neural networks enhances their capacity for structured scene decomposition and out-of-distribution generalization.
papers.authors: Sabine Muzellec, Andrea Alamia, Thomas Serre, Rufin VanRullen

papers.title: Semi-Supervised Multimodal Representation Learning Through a Global Workspace
papers.abstract: This work evaluates a neural architecture inspired by the 'Global Workspace' (GW) for semi-supervised multimodal learning, aiming for more frugal and human-like knowledge acquisition. The system utilizes specialized, frozen unimodal encoders and decoders linked through a central latent workspace, with training driven by a self-supervised cycle-consistency objective. Across various vision-language pairings and datasets, the GW architecture successfully aligns disparate modalities with four to seven times less matched training data than standard supervised approaches. The resulting amodal representation proves highly effective for downstream classification, cross-modal retrieval, and robust transfer learning, demonstrating the functional utility of cognitively-inspired architectural bottlenecks.
papers.venue: IEEE Transactions on Neural Networks and Learning Systems
papers.authors: Benjamin Devillers, Léopold Maytié, Rufin VanRullen

E061.name: Jan Brascamp
E061.bio: Jan Brascamp is an Associate Professor at Michigan State University who investigates the neural mechanisms of interpretation and selection that transform sensory input into conscious visual experience. Brascamp uses psychophysics, functional MRI, and computational modeling to explore phenomena such as binocular rivalry and perceptual bistability. Their research indicates that the visual cortex can independently perform decision-making tasks during perceptual switches, which addresses traditional models of cortical hierarchy. Brascamp also examines pupillary responses and visual prediction anomalies as potential biomarkers for psychiatric conditions like schizophrenia.
E061.research_direction: Dr. Brascamp has recently been investigating the sensory and cognitive drivers of pupillary dynamics, probing whether pupil responses during isoluminant stimulation and bistable perceptual switches—tracked covertly via optokinetic nystagmus—reflect subcortical luminance mechanisms, cortical feature analysis, or task-related arousal. Their recent work also explores the representational limits of conscious visual perception by examining the fidelity of visual memory during slow change blindness, supported by their development of semi-automated computational tools to generate gradual, naturalistic stimulus changes. Additionally, they are investigating specific disruptions in cortical excitatory-inhibitory dynamics in clinical populations, utilizing visual adaptation paradigms like tilt aftereffects and negative afterimages to isolate distinct sensory processing phenotypes in schizophrenia spectrum and bipolar disorders.

papers.title: No evidence for a cortical origin of pupil constriction responses to isoluminant stimuli
papers.abstract: This study investigated the neural substrates underlying pupillary constriction in response to isoluminant visual stimuli—transients where local luminance changes occur without a net flux increase. While two competing hypotheses attribute this 'isoluminant constriction' to either subcortical luminance-based pathways or cortical feature-based processing, the researchers utilized orientation-tuned contrast adaptation to isolate cortical contributions. Across three psychophysical experiments, contrast adaptation failed to attenuate the constriction amplitude, with Bayesian analyses providing evidence in favor of the null hypothesis. These findings demonstrate that isoluminant pupil responses are largely independent of the cortical neural populations susceptible to contrast adaptation, suggesting that the response likely originates from subcortical mechanisms or early-stage luminance-processing channels.
papers.authors: Vasilii Marshev, Haley G. Frey, Jan Brascamp

papers.title: The pupil response to perceptual switches: What happens when you ignore them
papers.abstract: This research re-examines the functional significance of pupillary dilation associated with perceptual transitions in bistable vision, typically attributed to norepinephrine-driven arousal. The authors hypothesized that these dilations may be artifacts of task relevance rather than intrinsic to the perceptual switch, as transitions are usually actively reported. By employing an ambiguous structure-from-motion stimulus and identifying perceptual states via optokinetic nystagmus (OKN), the study dissociated switches from overt reporting behavior. The results showed that while task-relevant transitions elicited robust dilation, task-irrelevant switches did not, and instead exhibited transient constrictions. This suggests that the previously observed arousal-linked pupillary signals primarily reflect the cognitive demands of task execution rather than the endogenous mechanisms of perceptual selection.
papers.authors: Bobicheng Zhang, Vasilii Marshev, Jan W. Brascamp

papers.title: Memory representations during slow change blindness
papers.abstract: To investigate the representational failures underlying slow change blindness—the inability to detect gradual visual changes without transient disruptions—the authors explored whether observers maintain memory of the changing features. Using a color-morphing paradigm, the study identified two distinct memory components present during undetected changes: a high-fidelity but transient representation of the most recent stimulus states and a more durable but coarse-grained representation of the overall stimulus category. The findings indicate that slow change blindness occurs not because observers lack the necessary information, but because the maintained representations are either too fragile or too low in resolution to support a comparison process capable of detecting infinitesimal gradients of change.
papers.authors: Haley G. Frey, Lua Koenig, Ned Block, Biyu J. He, Jan W. Brascamp

papers.title: A novel, semi-automatic procedure for generating slow change blindness stimuli
papers.abstract: The authors present a semi-automated computational procedure for the rapid generation of stimuli designed to study slow change blindness. Recognizing the scarcity of standardized stimuli and the difficulty of assessing detection without inducing trial-specific expectations, the method utilizes image manipulation to create naturalistic changes that unfold over several seconds. Validation experiments confirmed that these stimuli reliably induce change blindness and allow for the precise, trial-by-trial assessment of detection thresholds and the spatial scale of awareness. This framework provides a standardized and scalable tool for investigating the representational limits of conscious visual perception.
papers.authors: Haley G. Frey, Lua Koenig, Biyu J. He, Jan W. Brascamp

papers.title: Stronger tilt aftereffects in individuals diagnosed with schizophrenia spectrum disorders but not bipolar disorder
papers.abstract: This clinical neuroscience study examined the specificity of enhanced sensory adaptation in schizophrenia by comparing tilt aftereffects (TAE) and negative afterimages across patients with schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, and healthy controls. While TAEs reflect cortical orientation-selective adaptation and lateral inhibition, negative afterimages rely on subcortical/retinal luminance-based mechanisms. Results revealed that significantly augmented TAE magnitudes were unique to the schizophrenia group and correlated with negative symptom severity, whereas bipolar disorder patients performed similarly to controls. These findings point toward a specific disruption in cortical excitatory-inhibitory dynamics and an oversensitivity to recent visual regularities as a distinct pathophysiological marker of the schizophrenia spectrum.
papers.authors: Katharine N. Thakkar, Steven M. Silverstein, Jessica Fattal, Jacqueline Bao, Rachael Slate, Dominic Roberts, Jan W. Brascamp

E062.name: Matthew Self
E062.bio: Matthew Self is a neuroscientist and Senior Lecturer at the University of Glasgow’s School of Psychology and Neuroscience, where they direct research into the neural mechanisms of visual perception and memory formation. Self's work focuses on the functional significance of top-down feedback and recurrent connections between the visual cortex, thalamus, and hippocampus. Using a cross-species approach, they employ high-density electrophysiology, such as Neuropixels in mice and intracranial recordings in neurosurgical patients, to investigate how the brain integrates contextual information and experience-based predictions. Self has recorded from the human lateral geniculate nucleus and characterized the laminar-specific effects of attention and figure-ground segregation in the primary visual cortex.
E062.research_direction: Dr. Self's recent work explores how contextual information, top-down feedback, and local circuitry shape neural representations across the early visual system. Using primate electrophysiology and cross-species fMRI, they are investigating how higher-order perceptual organization—such as border-ownership and natural image occlusion—drives functional feedback from extrastriate areas like V4 back to primary visual cortex to facilitate figure-ground segregation. In parallel, their research employs human psychophysics to examine how perceived 3D surface continuity and binocular disparity constrain contextual phenomena like orientation-tuned surround suppression. Additionally, Dr. Self has recently been probing the subcortical foundations of human vision, utilizing rare intraoperative microelectrode recordings from the lateral geniculate nucleus to characterize classical cellular receptive-field properties and investigate how local interneurons gate ascending retinal signals during eye closure.

papers.title: Effects of eye closure on the spiking activity of human lateral geniculate neurons
papers.abstract: Electrophysiological properties of the human lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN), the primary subcortical relay linking the retina to early visual cortex, remain largely uncharacterized at the cellular level. Extracellular unit recordings were acquired from microelectrodes implanted into the LGN of clinical patients undergoing stereotactic deep-brain surgery. Human LGN neurons exhibited classic primate receptive-field features, including circular ON/OFF subfields, red-green cone-opponent chromatic tuning concentrated in dorsal parvocellular laminae, and preferences for high temporal frequencies within ventral magnocellular layers. Units displayed marked monocular dominance. Monocular eyelid closure selectively attenuated spontaneous firing rates in broad-spiking putative principal relay neurons tuned to the closed eye, while concurrently increasing the discharge rates of narrow-spiking putative local interneurons. These findings indicate that local GABAergic interneuronal circuits actively gate ascending visual signals through the human thalamus during eye closure.
papers.authors: Matthew W. Self, Osvaldo Vilela-Filho, Sergio Neuenschwander, Hélio F. Silva-Filho, Lissa C. Goulart, Pieter R. Roelfsema

papers.title: Orientation-tuned surround-suppression is strongest within perceived 3D surfaces
papers.abstract: Perceived visual contrast is modulated by surrounding spatial context, as shown by orientation-tuned surround suppression (OTSS), where surrounds of identical orientation suppress target contrast more effectively than orthogonal surrounds. While OTSS is largely attributed to horizontal interactions in early retinotopic visual cortex, this study shows that suppression strength is strongly governed by perceived three-dimensional surface structure. Altering the binocular retinal disparity of the surrounding texture systematically attenuated OTSS relative to coplanar configurations, regardless of whether surrounds appeared in front of or behind the central test patch. Crucially, metric disparity differences did not solely account for suppression magnitude: suppressive interactions were strongest when center and surround were perceived as part of a single, continuous 3D surface, and substantially weaker when segmented into separate surfaces despite smaller metric depth separations. These psychophysical results indicate that contextual suppression is constrained to cohesive surface representations and support top-down feedback gating of horizontal cortical interactions based on perceptual scene organization.
papers.authors: Jessy K. Possel, Pieter R. Roelfsema, Matthew W. Self

papers.title: Border-ownership tuning determines the connectivity between V4 and V1 in the macaque visual system
papers.abstract: Cortical feedback connections between visual processing stages are extensive, yet the functional connectivity logic linking higher-order representations to lower-tier cortex remains unresolved. Feedback from extrastriate areas to primary visual cortex (V1) selectively amplifies responses to perceptual figures compared to backgrounds via figure-background modulation (FBM). A postulated origin for these modulatory signals is border-ownership (BO) selective neurons in mid-tier visual areas such as V4. Functional interactions between V4 and V1 cell populations were evaluated in macaques using spike-count noise correlations and intracortical electrical microstimulation. Inter-areal functional connectivity matched an asymmetrical wiring model: BO-selective V4 neurons provided positive feedback toward the receptive-field coordinates corresponding to their preferred figure location, and negative or suppressive feedback toward the opposing background direction. A model implementing this connectivity scheme successfully reconstructed empirical V1 FBM profiles across complex geometric shapes, demonstrating that border-ownership selectivity organizes functional feedback from V4 to V1.
papers.authors: Danique Jeurissen, Anne F. van Ham, Amparo Gilhuis, Paolo Papale, Pieter R. Roelfsema, Matthew W. Self

papers.title: The representation of occluded image regions in area V1 of monkeys and humans
papers.abstract: Spiking activity in primary visual cortex (V1) is driven by feedforward retino-geniculate inputs within the classical receptive field (RF) and modulated by surrounding context. Dissociating rapid contextual influences from feedforward excitation remains difficult during natural visual processing. To isolate pure contextual inputs, V1 multiunit activity was recorded in macaque monkeys viewing complex natural images where feedforward input to the RF was eliminated by an occluding mask, and compared against responses to unoccluded scenes. V1 neurons exhibited rapid and selective spiking responses to occluded scenes in the absence of direct visual RF stimulation. Linear classifiers successfully decoded scene identity from occluded V1 activity patterns, and population response vectors for occluded stimuli were predictable from unoccluded responses, demonstrating significant representational concordance between feedforward and contextual activity. Furthermore, cross-species representational similarity analysis (RSA) showed that monkey V1 electrophysiological responses to occluded scenes correlated strongly with human V1 fMRI activation patterns for the identical visual stimuli, demonstrating that long-range top-down feedback rapidly reconstructs scene information in retinotopic V1 representations across primates.
papers.authors: Paolo Papale, Feng Wang, A. Tyler Morgan, Xing Chen, Amparo Gilhuis, Lucy S. Petro, Lars Muckli, Pieter R. Roelfsema, Matthew W. Self

E063.name: Mauro Manassi
E063.bio: Mauro Manassi is a vision scientist whose research focuses on how the human brain organizes and stabilizes visual information to create a coherent perception of the world. Manassi examines serial dependence and 'continuity fields,' exploring how the visual system biases current perception toward the recent past to maintain temporal stability. Utilizing psychophysical paradigms and visual illusions, their research addresses fundamental mechanisms like visual crowding as well as applied domains such as medical image perception. Their current work investigates the spatiotemporal integration processes that allow the brain to smooth over discontinuous retinal inputs and manage environmental clutter.
E063.research_direction: Dr. Manassi's recent work explores how temporal context shapes visual perception, investigating the boundary conditions that determine whether recent visual stimuli produce attractive serial dependence or repulsive negative aftereffects. They are mapping these sequential biases across multiple domains, from testing the integrity of perceptual priors in schizophrenia using low-level orientation adjustment tasks to exploring how adaptation modulates high-level trait impressions like facial trustworthiness and dominance. Beyond temporal context, their research examines the automaticity of social vision, utilizing dot-probe paradigms to ask whether complex facial traits pre-attentively capture visual attention. Finally, Dr. Manassi has recently been investigating the fine-grained temporal dynamics of spatial vision, measuring the precise time course required for recurrent perceptual grouping mechanisms to successfully overcome visual crowding in cluttered scenes.

papers.title: Dynamics of vision: Grouping takes longer than crowding
papers.abstract: While feedforward models of visual processing characterize feature extraction as an almost instantaneous hierarchical progression, phenomena such as uncrowding suggest that global configuration and recurrent grouping mechanisms play a primary role in target recognition. This study investigated the temporal constraints of grouping by measuring Vernier offset discrimination thresholds across varying flanker configurations (Lines, Rectangles, and Cubes) and stimulus durations. Empirical results and LAMINART neural network simulations revealed that while strong crowding persists at 20-ms stimulus durations across all configurations, uncrowding effects—marked by lower thresholds for Cubes and Rectangles—emerge only at longer (160-ms) durations. Furthermore, a 20-ms preview of grouped flankers, but not isolated lines, successfully released the subsequent Vernier from crowding for time spans up to 1 second. These findings indicate that visual crowding is a dynamic, time-consuming process where grouping mechanisms must evolve over a minimum temporal threshold to dissociate target representations from flanking clutter.
papers.authors: Martina Morea, Michael H. Herzog, Gregory Francis, Mauro Manassi

papers.title: Time, space and feature similarity determine attractive and repulsive serial biases in trustworthiness impressions
papers.abstract: Perceptual processing is modulated by the recent history of visual stimulation through two competing effects: positive serial dependence, which promotes attractive biases toward previous stimuli, and negative aftereffects, which induce repulsive biases away from adapted features. This study mapped the boundary conditions of these biases in the social domain by investigating how first impressions of facial trustworthiness are affected by sequential trial parameters. We manipulated exposure duration to preceding faces, spatial proximity, and feature similarity to determine the direction and magnitude of the resulting biases. Our results indicate that short durations and high stimulus similarity/spatial overlap favor positive serial dependence, facilitating a stable and coherent social experience. In contrast, prolonged exposure and significant feature or spatial divergence favor repulsive negative aftereffects. These data provide a unified framework for understanding how the visual system integrates temporal context to balance perceptual stability with sensitivity during social trait evaluation.
papers.authors: Fiammetta Marini, Clare Sutherland, Linda Jeffery, Mauro Manassi

papers.title: Faces displaying dominance and trustworthiness do not automatically capture attention
papers.abstract: While social impressions such as dominance and trustworthiness are formed rapidly from facial cues, the automaticity of their attentional processing remains debated. Paralleling research on emotional expression, we investigated whether faces displaying these fundamental traits automatically capture attentional resources using a series of dot-probe experiments. Across naturalistic and computer-generated face stimuli, we found that neither high dominance nor high trustworthiness faces significantly prioritized attentional capture compared to neutral counterparts. These results suggest that trait-based associations do not exert the same level of pre-attentional influence as primary emotional signals. Our findings support a model where personality-based trait inferences are context-dependent and formed after initial attentional allocation, challenging the viewpoint that character-based impressions are extracted through spontaneous, bottom-up attentional mechanisms.
papers.authors: Fiammetta Marini, Clare A. M. Sutherland, Bārbala Ostrovska, Mauro Manassi

papers.title: Intact Serial Dependence in Schizophrenia: Evidence from an Orientation Adjustment Task
papers.abstract: Current theories of schizophrenia (SCZ) suggest that atypical perception in the disorder arises from a diminished reliance on perceptual priors, which would manifest as reduced serial dependence—the attractive bias of current percepts toward recent stimulus history. We tested this hypothesis in 26 SCZ patients and 27 healthy controls using a visual orientation adjustment task designed to measure the strength, temporal persistence, and feature tuning of serial dependence. Contrary to the reduced-priors hypothesis, SCZ patients exhibited robust and intact attractive serial dependence, with biases comparable in magnitude and tuning to those of healthy controls. These results demonstrate that the integration of prior stimulus information into current perception remains functional in SCZ across standard orientation reproduction tasks. The findings suggest that deficits in integrating temporal context in schizophrenia are not a generalized feature of the disease but may be restricted to specific cognitive or perceptual processing domains.
papers.authors: David Pascucci, Maya Roinishvili, Eka Chkonia, Andreas Brand, David Whitney, Michael H. Herzog, Mauro Manassi

papers.title: Negative aftereffects of face trait impressions are modulated by emotional expressions
papers.abstract: This study explored the dynamic nature of social trait evaluations by examining how judgments of facial trustworthiness and dominance are influenced by the preceding visual context of emotional expressions. Using anti-expression stimuli to isolate perceptual adaptation from semantic or conceptual priming, we investigated whether exposure to specific emotional states induces visual aftereffects on subsequent trait impressions. The results showed significant negative (repulsive) aftereffects, where prior exposure to facial expressions systematically biased following social impressions (e.g., adaptation to dominance led to neutral faces being perceived as less dominant). These findings indicate that the formation of social first impressions is not a static process but is deeply integrated with the perception of transient facial cues through visual adaptation mechanisms. The results highlight that temporal context and adaptation significantly shape the subjective experience of social traits in facial perception.
papers.authors: Fiammetta Marini, Clare A. M. Sutherland, Linda Jeffery, Sarah D. Maisey, Mauro Manassi

E064.name: Heiko Neumann
E064.bio: Heiko Neumann is a Senior Professor at the Institute of Neural Information Processing at Ulm University and leads the Vision and Perception Science group. Neumann's research uses neural modeling to investigate the computational principles of visual information processing in biological systems and artificial architectures. They study the dynamics of motion perception, object recognition, and visual attention, focusing on how hierarchical neural circuits integrate contextual information for task-relevant behavior. Neumann's theoretical findings are applied to domains including autonomous robotics, medical image analysis, and human-computer interaction.
E064.research_direction: Dr. Neumann has recently been investigating visual perception across both biological and artificial systems, exploring the mechanisms of object representation, feature extraction, and spatial understanding. Their recent work explores biologically plausible neurocomputational models of object-based attention, specifically examining how recurrent thalamo-cortical loops facilitate incremental binding during mental contour tracing. Alongside this biological modeling, they are investigating the underlying discrepancies between primate and machine vision by analyzing the network dynamics that cause deep learning architectures to favor texture biases over robust shape cues. Furthermore, their research extends into applied computer vision, where they are developing self-supervised algorithms for view-invariant feature matching in robotics, while also assessing multimodal deep learning strategies for human action recognition and scene perception in autonomous navigation.

papers.title: A model of thalamo-cortical interaction for incremental binding in mental contour-tracing
papers.abstract: This study introduces a mesoscopic neural dynamical architecture that elucidates the mechanisms of object-based attention and incremental binding. The model posits that perceptual grouping occurs via an attentional spreading process, where neurons representing bound object elements are 'tagged' by sustained activity enhancement. Mechanistically, the model integrates feedforward feature extraction with recurrent thalamo-cortical loops, proposed to involve pyramidal cell integration hubs. The architecture suggests that apical dendritic signals carrying contextual grouping information are gated by higher-order thalamic nuclei (e.g., the pulvinar) based on task-relevance, providing a biologically plausible implementation of the 'growth-cone' hypothesis for mental contour grouping. Model performance was validated against neurophysiological data on the speed and scale-invariance of contour labeling.
papers.authors: Daniel Schmid, Heiko Neumann

papers.title: Teaching deep networks to see shape: Lessons from a simplified visual world
papers.abstract: This research investigates the discrepancy between the strong shape-dependency of primate vision and the pervasive texture/color bias in deep convolutional neural networks (DCNNs). Using synthetic datasets with controlled feature distributions (e.g., rectangles, 'L' and 'T' shapes), the authors demonstrate that while standard architectures can learn shape features in isolation, they systematically default to simpler surface-level cues when available. Through neural tangent kernel (NTK) analysis, the study shows that this bias is driven by the dynamics of mini-batch gradient descent, where weight updates for diverse, sparse shape features are effectively suppressed by consistent, dense updates from low-level features. The findings suggest that reaching human-level shape robustness in artificial vision requires novel learning algorithms characterized by sparser and more local weight adaptations.
papers.authors: Christian Jarvers, Heiko Neumann

papers.title: Cycle-Correspondence Loss: Learning Dense View-Invariant Visual Features from Unlabeled and Unordered RGB Images
papers.abstract: The authors propose Cycle-Correspondence Loss (CCL), a self-supervised training objective for learning view-invariant dense visual descriptors from uncalibrated and unordered sets of RGB images. CCL leverages the principle of cycle-consistency to autonomously detect valid pixel-level correspondences between disparate viewpoints by performing confidence-weighted bidirectional predictions. Unlike previous methods requiring registered RGB-D sequences or multi-view consistency labels, CCL enables robust keypoint learning from a single moving camera. Evaluation on keypoint tracking and robotic manipulation tasks demonstrates that CCL outperforms existing self-supervised RGB baselines and approaches the accuracy of fully supervised methods in dense object-centric representation learning.
papers.venue: IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA)
papers.authors: David B. Adrian, Andras Gabor Kupcsik, Markus Spies, Heiko Neumann

papers.title: Application of Scene Perception and Object Detection Technology Based on Computer Vision in Autonomous Driving for Public Transportation Route Optimization
papers.abstract: This paper explores the integration of computer vision-based scene perception and Geographic Information System (GIS) data for dynamic route optimization in autonomous public transit systems. The proposed framework employs deep learning architectures for real-time object detection and semantic segmentation to perceive environment variations, such as traffic congestion and physical obstructions. By blending visual scene understanding with GIS-based topographic information, the system dynamically recalculates optimal transit paths. Simulation results in virtual city environments indicate significant reductions in travel latency and energy consumption compared to traditional fixed-route approaches, highlighting the potential for computer vision to improve the scalability and safety of intelligent urban infrastructure.
papers.authors: Peiqi Chen, Daniel Schmid, Christian Jarvers, Heiko Neumann

papers.title: Multimodal vision-based human action recognition using deep learning: a review
papers.abstract: This comprehensive review categorizes and analyzes recent advancements in multimodal human action recognition (HAR) using deep learning. The authors provide a taxonomy of fusion strategies across four levels: data-level, feature-level, decision-level, and hybrid fusion. The study evaluates how the integration of complementary modalities—such as RGB, depth, skeleton, and infrared data—enhances recognition accuracy and robustness compared to single-modality systems. Furthermore, the review explores the application of self-attention mechanisms and transformer-based architectures for distilling spatio-temporal features across heterogeneous data streams. It concludes by identifying key challenges in the field, including cross-dataset generalization and the computational complexity of real-time multi-stream inference.
papers.authors: Fatemeh Shafizadegan, Ahmad Reza Naghsh-Nilchi, Elham Shabaninia, Heiko Neumann

E065.name: Philipp Sterzer
E065.bio: Philipp Sterzer is a neuroscientist and psychiatrist whose research examines the neural mechanisms of visual perception and their disruption in psychiatric conditions. Sterzer uses functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), psychophysics, and computational modeling to investigate how the brain processes ambiguous sensory information and integrates prior expectations through predictive coding. Their work analyzes the pathogenesis of delusions and hallucinations in psychosis, framing these symptoms as alterations in hierarchical belief updating. Formerly the head of the Visual Perception Lab at Charité – Universitätsmedizin Berlin, Sterzer currently heads the Translational Psychiatry Lab at the University of Basel and maintains a clinical fellowship with the Berlin Institute of Health.
E065.research_direction: Dr. Sterzer's recent work explores the neurocomputational mechanisms of perceptual inference, specifically focusing on how the brain balances internal prior expectations with bottom-up sensory evidence. They have recently been investigating how disruptions in this predictive processing framework give rise to the psychosis spectrum, spanning from subclinical traits to clinical schizophrenia. To probe these dynamics, their research employs computational approaches like hidden Markov modeling alongside psychophysical paradigms such as bistable visual perception and auditory decision-making, often incorporating pharmacological manipulations like ketamine. Furthermore, they are working to bridge these computational theories with systems neuroscience, examining how prediction errors and the precision-weighting of sensory signals map onto specific cortical microcircuits to explain psychotic phenomena like hallucinations and delusions.

papers.title: N-methyl-d-aspartate receptor hypofunction causes recurrent and transient failures of perceptual inference
papers.abstract: This study employs a double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover design using the N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor (NMDAR) antagonist S-ketamine in healthy volunteers, alongside a case-control comparison with schizophrenia patients, to investigate the neurocomputational mechanisms of altered perceptual inference. Utilizing a two-state hidden Markov model (GLM-HMM) applied to a bistable perception paradigm with varying signal-to-ambiguity ratios, the researchers demonstrate that perception fluctuates between an 'internal mode' (stabilized by prior-driven predictions) and an 'external mode' (dominated by incoming sensory data). Results indicate that both pharmacological NMDAR hypofunction and clinical schizophrenia significantly shift the dynamic balance toward the external mode, suggesting that psychotic experiences may arise from transient, minute-long dissociations where sensory evidence is processed without the stabilizing influence of internal world models.
papers.authors: Veith Weilnhammer, Marcus Rothkirch, Deniz Yilmaz, Merve Fritsch, Lena Esther Ptasczynski, Katrin Reichenbach, Lukas Roediger, Philip Corlett, Philipp Sterzer

papers.title: Reduced weighting of short-term perceptual priors during auditory perceptual decision-making in psychosis-prone individuals
papers.abstract: This research investigates how subclinical psychosis proneness modulates the integration of implicit and explicit perceptual priors during auditory decision-making. Across two independent online experiments (N=197) using an auditory two-alternative forced-choice (2-AFC) task and hidden Markov modeling (HMM), the authors quantified serial dependencies (choice history bias) and explicit probabilistic cue weighting. The findings reveal that individuals with higher scores on schizotypal and delusional ideation questionnaires exhibit a reduced weighting of implicit perceptual priors and an increased reliance on sensory likelihoods. These data support a hierarchical predictive processing framework of psychosis, suggesting that a continuum of inferential alterations—characterized by a shift away from low-level priors toward bottom-up sensory evidence—underpins the psychosis spectrum from subclinical traits to manifest disorder.
papers.authors: Anna-Chiara Schaub, Anna-Lena Eckert, Stijn A. Nuiten, Veith Weilnhammer, Philipp Sterzer

papers.title: Predictive Processing: A Circuit Approach to Psychosis
papers.abstract: This comprehensive review integrates computational theories of predictive processing with recent systems neuroscience findings regarding cortical microcircuitry and the mechanism of action of antipsychotic drugs. The authors synthesize evidence from animal models and human neuroimaging to map specific predictive processing components—such as the generation and propagation of prediction errors—onto discrete cortical layers and interneuron subtypes (e.g., PV+ and SOM+ cells). They propose that the positive symptoms of psychosis, including hallucinations and delusions, emerge from the maladaptive precision-weighting of these prediction signals. The article argues for a circuit-based approach to translational psychiatry, suggesting that quantifying how pharmacological interventions modulate layer-specific error signaling can bridge the explanatory gap between molecular targets and psychiatric symptomatology.
papers.authors: Georg B. Keller, Philipp Sterzer

E066.name: Duje Tadin
E066.department: Department of Brain and Cognitive Sciences
E066.bio: Duje Tadin is a Professor and Chair of the Department of Brain and Cognitive Sciences at the University of Rochester and serves as the Interim Dean of the School of Arts & Sciences. Their research investigates the neural mechanisms of visual perception, focusing on motion processing, spatial suppression, and the limits of sensory integration. Tadin utilizes human psychophysics, computational modeling, and non-invasive brain stimulation to study how these processes are altered in clinical populations, including individuals with schizophrenia and autism. Tadin’s laboratory also develops neuro-rehabilitative strategies, such as virtual reality-based training, to improve visual function and recovery following cortical damage.
E066.research_direction: Dr. Tadin has recently been investigating how the visual system resolves interocular conflict under naturalistic viewing conditions. Their recent work explores whether the dynamics of binocular rivalry—traditionally studied using highly artificial laboratory arrangements—generalize to geometrically plausible, cue-rich 3D environments. Using head-mounted virtual reality, they are examining how the spatial and geometric consistency of rival images, such as their relative depths and scene locations, influences core rivalry dynamics like dominance durations and switching rates. Ultimately, they are working to determine whether the brain's handling of conflicting visual inputs is sensitive to the physical rules of coherent 3D scenes, aiming to validate classic rivalry paradigms as tools for understanding everyday binocular vision.

papers.title: Binocular rivalry under naturalistic geometry: Evidence from worlds simulated in virtual reality
papers.abstract: Binocular rivalry is typically studied by presenting two irreconcilable images separately to the two eyes, an artificial geometric arrangement in which two distinct objects appear to occupy the same physical location—a configuration rarely, if ever, encountered in everyday vision. This raises doubts about whether laboratory rivalry findings generalize to naturalistic binocular viewing. The authors used a head-mounted virtual reality system to embed classic rivalry stimuli within a geometrically plausible, cue-rich 3D corridor environment, parametrically varying the spatial plausibility of the rival images (e.g., placing them at congruent versus incongruent depths and locations within the simulated scene). They found that rivalry dynamics—including dominance durations and switching rates—were systematically modulated by the naturalistic geometric plausibility of the rival images, indicating that the visual system's resolution of interocular conflict is sensitive to whether the conflicting inputs are consistent with a coherent 3D scene, and supporting the external validity of binocular rivalry as a tool for studying everyday binocular vision.
papers.authors: Shui'er Han, Randolph Blake, Celine Aubuchon, Duje Tadin

E069.name: James Elder
E069.department: Department of Electrical Engineering & Computer Science and Department of Psychology
E069.bio: James Elder is the York Research Chair in Human and Computer Vision and the Director of the Centre for AI & Society at York University. Elder's research integrates psychophysical experiments with computational modeling to study the principles of biological vision for the development of machine vision systems. Their technical focus includes natural scene statistics, perceptual organization, and contour processing. Recent applications of this work include 3D urban awareness, socially-aware robotics, and intelligent systems for sustainable mobility.
E069.research_direction: Dr. Elder has recently been investigating robust object tracking and motion analysis across a variety of complex, dynamic real-world environments. Their recent work explores multi-target tracking in team sports, developing hierarchical graph-based frameworks that integrate domain-specific vision cues—such as pose-guided scene text recognition for jersey numbers and homography-derived ground-plane coordinates—to solve challenging long-term player association problems. In the context of urban infrastructure, they are examining how back-projecting 2D camera detections onto 3D ground planes can improve the robustness of vehicle trajectory classification across multiple viewpoints. Additionally, their research applies visual tracking to assistive robotics, investigating how real-time RGB-D sensor processing and kinematic modeling can enable semi-autonomous wheelchair convoys to safely follow dynamic targets through uncontrolled spaces.

papers.title: Towards long-term player tracking with graph hierarchies and domain-specific features
papers.abstract: This research introduces SportsSUSHI, a novel tracking framework designed to mitigate the challenges of player re-identification and tracklet reconnection in team sports analytics, where dynamic motion, occlusions, and appearance similarity often cause identity switches. The method utilizes a hierarchical graph-based architecture to solve the association problem across extended temporal gaps. It integrates domain-specific features, including jersey numbers recognized via a text-recognition pipeline, team classification through clustering, and ground-plane field coordinates derived from camera homography. Experimental validation on the SoccerNet dataset and a new high-resolution hockey tracking dataset demonstrates that the inclusion of these domain-specific cues significantly enhances long-term association accuracy over baseline motion-and-appearance models.
papers.authors: Maria Koshkina, James H. Elder

papers.title: Ground Plane Projection for Improved Traffic Analytics at Intersections
papers.abstract: This study investigates the advantages of back-projecting vehicle detections from infrastructure cameras onto a ground plane for behavioral analysis at urban intersections. Traditional traffic monitoring systems typically operate in the 2D image plane, which is susceptible to perspective distortion and scale variations. The proposed framework employs intrinsic and extrinsic camera calibration to transform tracked vehicle trajectories into real-world 3D coordinates. Results indicate that analyzing motion on the ground plane leads to more precise trajectory classification and turning movement counts. Furthermore, the paper demonstrates that a weak fusion strategy combining back-projected detections from multiple infrastructure cameras further improves tracking robustness and accuracy in complex intersection scenarios.
papers.venue: 2024 IEEE 27th International Conference on Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITSC)
papers.authors: Sajjad Pakdamansavoji, Kumar Vaibhav Jha, Baher Abdulhai, James H. Elder

papers.title: Robot Wheelchair Convoys for Assistive Human Transportation
papers.abstract: We present AirChair, a semi-autonomous robotic system designed to facilitate the transport of multiple individuals with mobility impairments using a leader-follower convoy paradigm. The system architecture allows a single human guide to lead a primary wheelchair, while subsequent vehicles autonomously track and follow the preceding unit. Each wheelchair is equipped with an RGB-D sensor for real-time target tracking and motion planning, utilizing a back-end visual filter to mitigate environmental noise and maintain kinematic constraints. The system incorporates a semi-autonomous control interface that enables human intervention for safety. Experiments conducted in uncontrolled real-world indoor and outdoor environments validate the effectiveness of the vision-based tracking and the robustness of the convoy behavior.
papers.venue: 2024 IEEE International Conference on Smart Mobility (SM)
papers.authors: Hélio Perroni Filho, Jenny Ren, Mohammad Akhavan, Yuqian Hou, Walleed Khan, Arian Haghparast, Julian Forsyth, Kimia Rajaeifar, Michael Jenkin, James H. Elder

papers.title: A General Framework for Jersey Number Recognition in Sports Video
papers.abstract: Jersey number recognition is framed as a specialized task within scene text recognition (STR) to support long-term player tracking. The authors introduce a new public hockey dataset and evaluate the adaptation of state-of-the-art STR models, such as PARSeq, to the sports domain. The proposed pipeline includes a binary classifier to identify legible frames and uses pose estimation to localize the torso region for number extraction. The study explores the generalizability of these models across different sports (hockey and soccer) and describes a method for consolidating single-frame predictions into tracklet-level labels. Quantitative results show that fine-tuning on domain-specific data yields high accuracy, achieving over 91% on hockey images and 87% on soccer tracklets.
papers.authors: Maria Koshkina, James H. Elder

E075.name: Frederick Kingdom
E075.department: Department of Ophthalmology and Department of Psychology
E075.bio: Kingdom's research explores the computational and psychological mechanisms linking early-stage feature detection, such as edge and orientation sensing, to intermediate-level visual processing of contours, textures, and surfaces. Their investigations encompass domains including color vision, stereopsis, and the perception of transparency and lightness, frequently utilizing natural scene analysis to examine environmental constraints on vision. Kingdom integrates psychophysical experimentation with mathematical modeling and image processing to map the underlying architecture of human visual perception. Additionally, they are a co-developer of the Palamedes toolbox, a software resource for the analysis of psychophysical data.
E075.research_direction: Dr. Kingdom's recent work explores several core mechanisms of low- and mid-level visual perception, with a major focus on modeling the sensory architecture of binocular combination. Specifically, they have recently been investigating how parallel binocular sum and difference channels mediate the detection, identification, and surround masking of monocular and dichoptic stimuli. Beyond binocular vision, their research examines the channel dependencies of visual working memory, testing how cognitive load and encoding duration interact with the chromatic and luminance content of natural scenes. Additionally, they are probing dynamic spatial processing by assessing how task demands shift the reliance on edge-based versus region-based cues in texture perception, while also investigating internal models of gravity by measuring visual sensitivity to the acceleration of falling objects.

papers.title: Detection and identification of monocular, binocular, and dichoptic stimuli are mediated by binocular sum and difference channels
papers.abstract: The research delineates the sensory architecture of binocular combination by assessing the detectability and identifiability of monocular, binocular (in-phase), and dichoptic (anti-phase) stimuli. Using a two-alternative forced-choice (2AFC) psychophysical paradigm with low-contrast luminance discs, the study finds that identification and detection thresholds for same- versus opposite-polarity stimuli are approximately equal. Conversely, monocular versus binocular identification is significantly impaired compared to detection. These results are modeled using a two-dimensional decision space whose orthogonal axes are defined by the outputs of parallel binocular sum (S+) and binocular difference (S-) channels. The findings confirm that the same binocular sum-and-difference circuitry mediates both the initial detection of visual stimuli and the perceptual encoding of interocular disparities.
papers.authors: Mark A. Georgeson, Hiromi Sato, Ronald Chang, Frederick A. A. Kingdom

papers.title: Visual working memory for natural scenes: the effect of chromatic, luminance and spatial frequency content
papers.abstract: This investigation examines the capacity and information-channel dependency of visual working memory (VWM) for naturalistic scene images. VWM performance was measured as a function of encoding duration and cognitive load across stimuli containing full chromatic/luminance information, luminance-only (isochromatic), or chromatic-only (isoluminant) signals. The study found that recall for isoluminant scenes was significantly degraded compared to luminance-containing counterparts. Furthermore, while Fourier phase scrambling of scene structure severely impaired recall under high cognitive loads, performance for full-color and luminance-only scenes was comparable except during ultra-brief encoding intervals. The data suggest that VWM for natural scenes primarily leverages spatial structure within the luminance channel, though chromatic signals provide a distinct advantage for visual encoding under severe temporal constraints.
papers.authors: Ben J. Jennings, Tzu-Wei Joy Tseng, Frederick A. A. Kingdom

papers.title: Task-dependent contribution to edge-based versus region-based texture perception
papers.abstract: The study evaluates the relative reliance on edge-based versus region-based mechanisms in texture perception across detection and orientation-discrimination tasks. Utilizing Gabor micropattern arrays modulated by sinewave (SN), square-wave (SQ), or cusp-wave (CS) profiles, the researchers measured threshold amplitudes across several spatial frequencies. Detection thresholds consistently followed the order SQ < SN < CS, indicative of region-based integration mediated by overall stimulus energy. In contrast, discrimination thresholds for orientation-modulated and contrast-variance-modulated textures followed an edge-based ordering (SQ ≈ CS < SN) at low spatial frequencies. The findings demonstrate that the visual system's utilization of edge versus region cues is not fixed but is dynamically reweighted based on specific task requirements.
papers.authors: Elena Gheorghiu, Cassandra Diggiss, Frederick A. A. Kingdom

papers.title: Surround masking reveals binocular adding and differencing channels
papers.abstract: The research utilizes a surround-masking paradigm to investigate the role of binocular sum (S+) and difference (S-) channels in binocular contrast detection. Observers performed detection tasks for monocular, binocularly correlated (in-phase), and binocularly anticorrelated (anti-phase) sinusoidal gratings in the presence of correlated or anticorrelated surround masks. The results demonstrate a significant interaction between target and mask ocularity: detection and summation are enhanced when target and mask exhibit opposite interocular phase relationships and reduced when they are congruent. The data are modeled using a dual-channel MAX(S+S-) model incorporating separately gain-controlled sum and difference channels, providing psychophysical evidence for these channels' involvement in adult human binocular summation.
papers.authors: Rinku Sarkar, Kiana Zanetti, Alexandre Reynaud, Frederick A. A. Kingdom

papers.title: A visual bias for falling objects
papers.abstract: This study examines human sensitivity to visual acceleration to characterize the internal model of gravity. Participants viewed simulated naturalistic scenes of a ball moving in various directions and judged whether the object appeared to accelerate or decelerate. The results revealed a significant up-down asymmetry in the point of subjective constant velocity (PSCV): downward-falling objects required significantly higher physical acceleration to be perceived as constant-velocity compared to upward-moving objects. This finding suggests a systematic visual bias that underestimates downward gravitational acceleration, supporting the hypothesis that the human visual system possesses an inherent prior for the consistent acceleration of falling objects.
papers.authors: Mai Huong Phan, Björn Jörges, Laurence R. Harris, Frederick A. A. Kingdom

E076.name: Anitha Pasupathy
E076.bio: Pasupathy investigates the neural mechanisms underlying visual object recognition and scene perception, focusing on the intermediate cortical area V4. Their research addresses boundary curvature as a basis for shape encoding in the primate brain, extending earlier edge-detection models to explain complex form representation. Utilizing multi-contact electrode recordings, reversible cortical inactivation, and computational modeling, Pasupathy's lab examines how the ventral visual stream processes partially occluded objects and encodes form and texture. Their work aims to bridge biological vision and deep convolutional neural networks to determine how the brain achieves scene segmentation and understanding.
E076.research_direction: Dr. Pasupathy has recently been investigating the functional architecture and representational principles of the primate mid-level visual cortex, specifically focusing on how areas V2 and V4 encode complex shapes, textures, and motion. Their recent work explores the spatial organization of these representations across cortical layers, leveraging high-density Neuropixels recordings and deep learning-based "digital twins" to ask whether mid-level regions maintain rigid columnar structures or transition to sparse, high-dimensional topological clusters. In addition to mapping functional topographies, they are actively examining the neural mechanisms of visual crowding by testing how stimulus salience and target-distractor interactions impact object segmentation in cluttered visual scenes. Furthermore, Dr. Pasupathy is advancing the methodological toolkit for non-human primate electrophysiology by evaluating and refining insertion techniques to achieve stable, chronic Neuropixels recordings in awake, behaving monkeys.

papers.title: Deep learning-driven characterization of single cell tuning in primate visual area V4 supports topological organization
papers.abstract: By integrating large-scale Neuropixels recordings with deep learning-based 'digital twins,' this research provided a data-driven characterization of neuronal tuning in area V4 using natural image statistics. The authors utilized a ResNet-50-based model to characterize the tuning of over 1,200 neurons and synthesize 'Most Exciting Images' (MEIs), which were then validated through in vivo recordings. Feature attribution analysis revealed that V4 neurons are organized topologically into functional groups selective for complex, naturalistic features such as specific curvatures, textures, and even eye-like attributes. These findings suggest that the functional architecture of V4 follows a topological principle in a high-dimensional feature space, closely mirroring the feature maps found in deep convolutional neural networks and providing a framework for mapping mid-level visual processing.
papers.authors: Konstantin F. Willeke, Katrin Restivo, Mohammad Bashiri, Polina Zamarashkina, Katrin Franke, Thomas Euler, Fabian H. Sinz, Anitha Pasupathy

papers.title: High-Density Recording Reveals Sparse Clusters (But Not Columns) for Shape and Texture Encoding in Macaque V4
papers.abstract: This study leveraged high-density Neuropixels probes to examine the laminar functional architecture of macaque area V4, specifically regarding shape and texture selectivity. Recording simultaneously across cortical layers in awake monkeys, the authors quantified the similarity of tuning manifolds between neighboring neurons. While primary visual cortex (V1) is characterized by rigid columnar organization, the results demonstrated that V4 exhibits only sporadic, fine-scale functional clusters (~20% similarity with neighbors) that do not form consistent columns across the depth of the cortex. The absence of a columnar structure suggests that V4's high-dimensional feature space, which integrates diverse inputs for complex object recognition, may preclude the development of the coarse-scale topographic maps seen in earlier visual areas.
papers.authors: Tomoyuki Namima, Erin Kempkes, Polina Zamarashkina, Natalia Owen, Anitha Pasupathy

papers.title: Functional clusters for shape, texture, and motion encoding in macaque V2
papers.abstract: Employing high-density Neuropixels recordings, the authors characterized the functional organization and representational basis of macaque area V2 for shape, texture, and motion. In contrast to the sparse clustering observed in area V4, area V2 exhibited fine-scale, dense functional clusters (~500 µm) for shape and motion stimuli, consistent with a columnar architecture. Representational modeling demonstrated that V2 responses are well-explained by local image statistics and linear combinations of orientation filters, whereas V4 responses require more complex, object-centered components. These results suggest a hierarchical transition in the ventral stream from the local feature-based columnar organization of V1/V2 to the sparse, high-dimensional object-based representation characteristic of V4.
papers.authors: Taekjun Kim, Rohit Kamath, Gaku Hatanaka, Tomoyuki Namima, Celeste Dylla, Wyeth Bair, Anitha Pasupathy

papers.title: Neural Correlates of Crowding in Macaque Area V4
papers.abstract: This research investigated the neurophysiological basis of visual crowding—the impairment of object recognition in cluttered displays—within macaque area V4. Using parametric shape arrays, the authors recorded single-unit activity to determine how distractors modulate target shape selectivity. The findings revealed that V4 neurons do not simply pool features from the target and distractors, as predicted by classic texture-pooling models. Instead, the magnitude of crowding was titrated by the relative salience of the target versus the distractors. Enhancing target salience through feature contrast or similarity-based grouping could alleviate suppressive interactions, reflecting a dynamical process where V4 preferentially encodes salient stimuli in a cluttered scene to facilitate object segmentation.
papers.authors: Taekjun Kim, Anitha Pasupathy

papers.title: Inserting a Neuropixels probe into awake monkey cortex: two probes, two methods
papers.abstract: Addressing the technical challenges of chronic high-density electrophysiology in non-human primates, this paper describes refined methodologies for implanting Neuropixels 1.0 probes into the awake macaque cortex. The authors compared two distinct insertion strategies: a traditional durotomy followed by probe insertion and a trans-dural approach. The study evaluated the impact of these methods on neuronal yield, signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), and probe longevity over multiple months. The results provide a practical framework for achieving stable, high-channel-count recordings in behaving monkeys, facilitating the longitudinal study of neural population dynamics and circuit-level processing in the primate brain.
papers.authors: Tomoyuki Namima, Erin Kempkes, Bob Smith, Lydia Smith, Amy L. Orsborn, Anitha Pasupathy

E080.name: Stella Yu
E080.bio: Stella X. Yu is a Professor of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science at the University of Michigan, conducting research at the intersection of computer vision, machine learning, and human perception. Yu’s work focuses on actionable representation learning, utilizing unsupervised and self-supervised methodologies to identify mid-level visual structures and hierarchical groupings from unlabeled data. By integrating structural inductive biases such as symmetry and geometric priors into deep learning architectures, Yu aims to develop artificial sensing systems modeled after biological vision. Their research extends to interdisciplinary applications in medical imaging, robotics, and data-driven scientific discovery.
E080.research_direction: Dr. Yu's recent work explores a diverse set of challenges across foundational visual representation learning, multimodal alignment, generative modeling, and embodied AI. They have recently been investigating novel approaches to self-supervised learning, examining how techniques like continuous next-embedding autoregressive prediction and hyperbolic embedding spaces can capture complex hierarchical structures and instance prototypicality without relying on discrete codebooks or manual labels. In the multimodal and generative domains, their research aims to ground long, detail-rich text descriptions to fine-grained visual features, while also leveraging denoising diffusion models to synthesize novel views from noisy remote sensing data like Synthetic Aperture Radar. Furthermore, they are extending visual perception into physical action by developing hierarchical reinforcement learning architectures that enable humanoid robots to integrate vision-based goal anticipation with low-level motor control for autonomous navigation on rugged, unstructured terrain.

papers.title: Aligning Forest and Trees in Images and Long Captions for Visually Grounded Understanding
papers.abstract: Large-scale vision-language models (LVLMs) typically perform alignment by matching holistic image features with global caption representations, often failing to process long, detail-rich descriptions accurately. This research introduces CAFT (Cross-domain Alignment of Forests and Trees), a hierarchical framework designed for fine-grained image-text representation learning without requiring dense pixel-level supervision. The architecture utilizes a fine-to-coarse visual encoder (CAST) coupled with a hierarchical text transformer that processes individual sentence-level units before fusing them into a whole-caption embedding. A dual-level alignment objective enforces consistency between global scenes while biasing correspondences between localized regions and specific sentences. This approach ensures that coarse semantic abstractions are grounded in fine-grained visual evidence, leading to state-of-the-art results on long-text retrieval benchmarks and the emergent discovery of visual parts through unsupervised scene parsing.
papers.authors: Byeongju Woo, Zilin Wang, Byeonghyun Pak, Sangwoo Mo, Stella X. Yu

papers.title: Noise-Tolerant Novel-View SAR Synthesis via Denoising Diffusion
papers.abstract: Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) is critical for all-weather, illumination-invariant remote sensing, yet the application of deep learning to SAR is limited by the scarcity of high-quality labeled datasets. While novel-view synthesis can provide data augmentation, intrinsic SAR artifacts such as multiplicative speckle noise and radiometric variability pose significant challenges for generative modeling. This study proposes a self-supervised framework for novel-view SAR synthesis based on denoising diffusion probabilistic models (DDPMs). The method employs co-domain augmentations operating on pixel magnitudes and integrates a multiplicative Rayleigh speckle model to simulate realistic sensor noise. By utilizing the iterative denoising process of diffusion models, the framework generates high-fidelity, multi-angle SAR imagery that is robust to noise, substantially improving the performance of downstream automatic target recognition (ATR) systems in label-constrained scenarios.
papers.venue: IEEE Transactions on Geoscience and Remote Sensing
papers.authors: Amir Rahimi, Stella X. Yu

papers.title: Next-Embedding Prediction Makes Strong Vision Learners
papers.abstract: Inspired by the success of generative pretraining in natural language processing (NLP), this work investigates whether analogous principles can be effectively applied to self-supervised visual representation learning. The authors introduce Next-Embedding Predictive Autoregression (NEPA), a framework where a transformer model is trained solely to predict the latent embeddings of future image patches conditioned on preceding ones. NEPA operates in a continuous embedding space using causal masking and a stop-gradient mechanism to prevent representational collapse, eliminating the need for discrete codebooks, pixel-wise reconstruction heads, or contrastive negatives. Experimental results on ImageNet-1k demonstrate that NEPA-trained Vision Transformers (ViTs) learn highly expressive and scalable representations that achieve competitive accuracy and demonstrate superior transferability to downstream semantic segmentation tasks on ADE20K compared to established baselines.
papers.authors: Sihan Xu, Ziqiao Ma, Wenhao Chai, Xuweiyi Chen, Weiyang Jin, Joyce Chai, Saining Xie, Stella X. Yu

papers.title: Let Humanoids Hike! Integrative Skill Development on Complex Trails
papers.abstract: Autonomous humanoid navigation on rugged, unstructured terrain requires the seamless integration of visual perception, high-level decision making, and low-level motor execution. This paper presents LEGO-H, a hierarchical reinforcement learning framework that enables camera-equipped humanoid robots to navigate complex hiking trails autonomously. The architecture features a temporal vision transformer that anticipates future local goals to guide locomotion, effectively unifying movement with goal-directed navigation. To facilitate the transfer of policies from simulation to reality, the framework utilizes latent representations of joint-movement patterns and hierarchical metric learning to improve the privileged learning scheme. Empirical evaluations on diverse simulated topographies demonstrate LEGO-H's ability to handle complex physical and environmental challenges without relying on predefined motion primitives.
papers.authors: Kwan-Yee Lin, Stella X. Yu

papers.title: Unsupervised Feature Learning with Emergent Data-Driven Prototypicality
papers.abstract: The authors propose an unsupervised representation learning framework that encodes both visual similarity and dataset-level 'prototypicality'—a measure of an instance's representativeness—within a unified embedding space. By leveraging the geometric properties of hyperbolic space (specifically the Poincaré ball model), the framework introduces HACK (Hyperbolic sphere pACKing), which maps unlabeled images to a set of uniformly distributed particles. In this non-Euclidean manifold, hierarchical structures and prototypicality emerge as a function of the optimization objective: typical instances are naturally mapped near the origin, while atypical ones occupy the boundary. This emergent property provides an efficient mechanism for unsupervised instance selection, optimizing sample complexity and enhancing model robustness and generalization capabilities for both typical and atypical samples.
papers.authors: Yunhui Guo, Youren Zhang, Yubei Chen, Stella X. Yu

E081.name: Nicholas Baker
E081.bio: Nicholas Baker is an Assistant Professor of Neuroscience in the Department of Psychology at Loyola University Chicago and directs the Human Perception Lab. Baker’s research examines the information processing systems that transform local visual contours into abstract shape representations, building upon Gestalt principles. Using psychophysical methodologies and computational modeling, Baker investigates the nature of shape abstraction in human vision and compares these processes to the mechanisms of deep convolutional neural networks (DCNNs). Their work identifies discrepancies between biological vision and artificial intelligence, specifically regarding the sensitivity of deep networks to global object configuration.
E081.research_direction: Dr. Baker's recent work explores the mechanisms underlying object shape perception and how human visual abstraction diverges from the representations learned by artificial neural networks. They have recently been utilizing carefully manipulated image sets to probe these human-network differences, testing how distinct systems process complex 3D shape cues, the configural spatial arrangement of object parts, and sparse "shape-from-dots" displays. In addition to this comparative work, their research investigates the cognitive architecture of the human visual system itself, employing psychophysics to examine whether global form and local contour statistics are handled by independent processing mechanisms. Furthermore, Dr. Baker studies spatial distortions like the object-based warping illusion to tease apart the relative perceptual contributions of high-level abstract objecthood versus low-level contour properties such as convexity and solidity.

papers.title: Three-dimensional shape cues affect human and artificial recognition systems differently
papers.abstract: Humans preferentially rely on object shape for recognition, whereas convolutional and transformer-based neural networks are comparatively biased toward local texture cues; prior demonstrations of this dissociation have relied mainly on shape defined by external, 2D silhouette contour. This study extends the comparison to shape information conveyed by internal contours, shading, and attached shadows—cues that are especially informative when objects are viewed from noncanonical, three-dimensional viewpoints. The authors generated large image sets (roughly 120,000 images) of texture-substituted objects rendered from many viewpoints, with and without shading and cast/attached shadows, and compared human and multiple deep network architectures on their ability to classify these images by shape versus texture. Humans substantially outperformed all tested networks at classifying objects by shape when rich 3D cues (shading, shadows, internal contours) were present, and the human advantage over networks was larger when shape was conveyed only by external contour than when full 3D shape cues were available, indicating that networks fail to fully exploit non-contour 3D shape information that humans readily use.
papers.authors: Mikayla Cutler, Luke Baumel, Julia Tocco, William Friebel, George K. Thiruvathukal, Nicholas Baker

papers.title: Is object-based warping solely object-based?
papers.abstract: Object-based warping is the illusion in which the perceived distance between two dots is overestimated when the dots are superimposed on a bounded object (figural) region compared with when they fall on background (ground) regions, taken as evidence that perceptual 'objecthood' per se stretches perceived space. This study tested whether objecthood alone accounts for the magnitude of the illusion or whether low-level image properties that typically co-occur with objecthood—such as contour solidity and convexity—independently contribute. By manipulating solidity and convexity while holding perceived objecthood constant (and vice versa), the authors found that these low-level contour properties significantly modulated warping magnitude beyond what could be explained by objecthood ratings alone. The results indicate that object-based warping is not purely a consequence of abstract object representation but is also driven by lower-level shape features, challenging a strictly object-based account of the illusion.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
papers.authors: Nicholas Baker, Ajola Vushaj, William Friebel, Joanna Yahng

papers.title: Shape from dots: A window into abstraction processes in visual perception
papers.abstract: The visual system spontaneously organizes sparse sets of discrete elements (dots) into coherent, abstract shape representations, a phenomenon that offers a tractable window into how perception constructs shape from minimal, non-contour information. This paper reviews and extends behavioral work on shape-from-dots displays, arguing that dot configurations are not merely interpolated into continuous contours but are represented via abstracted structural descriptions that capture global form while discarding much local positional detail. The authors relate human performance on shape-from-dots tasks to the representations learned by deep neural networks, arguing that human abstraction processes for sparse shape stimuli diverge from network representations in ways that parallel previously reported human-network differences for contour-defined shapes, and propose that shape-from-dots paradigms provide a useful benchmark for probing abstraction mechanisms in both biological and artificial vision systems.
papers.authors: Nicholas Baker, Philip J. Kellman

papers.title: Independent mechanisms for processing local contour features and global shape
papers.abstract: This paper investigates how the visual system extracts stable global shape percepts despite high variability in the local contour features (e.g., curvature, corner statistics) that compose an object's boundary. The authors propose and test a dual-mechanism account in which a global shape system encodes the low-frequency, large-scale form of an object's contour with high fidelity, while a separate local system encodes only coarse summary statistics of high-frequency contour variation rather than precise local feature values. Across several psychophysical experiments manipulating local contour perturbations while holding global shape constant (and vice versa), participants' shape discrimination and matching performance was consistent with accurate, detailed representation of global form but only approximate, statistical representation of local contour detail, supporting the existence of independent, functionally dissociable mechanisms for local and global shape processing.
papers.authors: Nicholas Baker, Philip J. Kellman

papers.title: Configural relations in humans and deep convolutional neural networks
papers.abstract: Deep convolutional neural networks (DCNNs) have been proposed as candidate models of human object perception, but prior work by the authors showed that DCNNs, unlike humans, show little sensitivity to global object shape. This study asks whether that limitation reflects a broader deficiency in representing configural relations—the relative spatial arrangement of an object's parts—beyond just global contour shape. Using stimuli in which part identities were held constant while their configural arrangement was systematically varied, the authors compared human and DCNN sensitivity to configural changes. Humans were highly sensitive to alterations in part configuration, readily detecting changes that preserved local part identity, whereas tested DCNNs showed markedly reduced sensitivity to the same configural manipulations, indicating that DCNNs' shape-processing deficits extend beyond global contour to a more general failure to represent relational, configural structure among object parts.
papers.authors: Nicholas Baker, Patrick Garrigan, Austin Phillips, Philip J. Kellman

E082.name: Zoe Kourtzi
E082.bio: Zoe Kourtzi is a Professor of Experimental Psychology and Computational Cognitive Neuroscience at the University of Cambridge and the head of the Adaptive Brain Lab. Kourtzi’s research integrates multimodal neuroimaging, including 7T fMRI, EEG, and MRS, with machine learning to investigate the neural mechanisms of brain plasticity and lifelong learning. They examine how humans translate sensory experiences into adaptive decisions and develop predictive AI-guided models for the early diagnosis of neurodegenerative diseases and mental health disorders. This work connects systems neuroscience with translational neuroinformatics in the study of vision science and clinical diagnostics.
E082.research_direction: Dr. Kourtzi has recently been investigating the neural mechanisms of adaptive plasticity alongside the development of AI-driven tools for early dementia prediction. In the realm of visual neuroscience, their recent work explores how the brain refines mental templates during perceptual learning, utilizing ultrahigh-field 7T fMRI, magnetic resonance spectroscopy, and transcriptomics to probe laminar-specific recurrent inhibition and neurogenetic markers of cortical reorganization. Concurrently, they are building unsupervised and predictive multimodal machine learning models that integrate structural MRI, longitudinal cognitive assessments, and biological markers to forecast Alzheimer's disease trajectories. Through these parallel tracks, Dr. Kourtzi seeks to bridge fine-scale neurochemical dynamics with macroscopic behavior while engineering scalable, interpretable prognostic algorithms for patient stratification in real-world memory clinics and clinical trials.

papers.title: AI-guided patient stratification improves outcomes and efficiency in the AMARANTH Alzheimer's Disease clinical trial
papers.abstract: This study demonstrates that an AI-guided predictive prognostic model (PPM) can enhance patient stratification in Alzheimer's disease (AD) clinical trials by mitigating the impact of patient heterogeneity. The researchers applied the PPM, which utilizes baseline biological markers (including β-amyloid, APOE ε4 status, and medial temporal lobe grey matter density), to re-evaluate the AMARANTH trial of lanabecestat, a BACE1 inhibitor previously deemed futile. The model successfully stratified participants into slow- and rapid-progression subgroups. While the original trial showed no significant effect in the total population, the AI-guided analysis revealed that lanabecestat significantly slowed cognitive decline by 46% in the subgroup of individuals at the earliest stages of cognitive impairment. These findings highlight the potential for AI-driven precision medicine to improve clinical trial efficiency and rescue efficacious treatments through refined patient selection.
papers.authors: Delshad Vaghari, Gayathri Mohankumar, Keith Tan, Andrew Lowe, Christopher Shering, Peter Tino, Zoe Kourtzi

papers.title: Neurogenetic phenotypes of learning-dependent plasticity for improved perceptual decisions
papers.abstract: This research investigates the link between brain-wide gene expression and macroscopic neuroimaging phenotypes of learning-dependent plasticity in the adult human brain. Combining functional connectivity (FC) analysis and quantitative multi-parameter mapping (MPM) of cortical microstructure, the authors demonstrate that training on a perceptual decision task (discriminating Glass patterns in noise) induces specific spatial variations in cortical gradients. These plasticity markers are significantly linked to the expression of genes associated with neuronal signaling and synaptic organization within visual and fronto-parietal networks. Furthermore, the study shows that anodal transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) targeted at the visual cortex during training enhances learning and modulates functional connections without altering microstructural organization.
