These results reveal neurogenetic phenotypes of plasticity, providing a cross-scale framework that bridges molecular mechanisms and macroscopic brain dynamics supporting adaptive behavior.
papers.authors: Liz Yuanxi Lee, Joseph J Ziminski, Polytimi Frangou, Vasilis M Karlaftis, Yezhou Wang, Boris Bernhardt, Varun Warrier, Richard A I Bethlehem, Zoe Kourtzi

papers.title: Recurrent inhibition refines mental templates to optimize perceptual decisions
papers.abstract: The authors investigate the neural mechanisms underlying the formation of mental templates for perceptual decision-making using ultrahigh-field (7-T) functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS). Focusing on orientation discrimination, the study demonstrates that perceptual training induces recurrent inhibition within the superficial layers of the visual cortex. Specifically, the findings reveal an increase in γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA)-mediated inhibition and enhanced discriminability of orientation representations in superficial layers (rather than middle or deep layers). Computational modeling suggests that these fine-scale functional and neurochemical interactions refine task-relevant internal templates, thereby optimizing the brain's capacity to translate sensory inputs into adaptive perceptual decisions. This work provides a mechanistic account of how laminar-specific cortical plasticity supports cognitive flexibility through experience.
papers.authors: Ke Jia, Mengxin Wang, Cecilia Steinwurzel, Joseph J. Ziminski, Yinghua Xi, Uzay Emir, Zoe Kourtzi

papers.title: Robust and interpretable AI-guided marker for early dementia prediction in real-world clinical settings
papers.abstract: This paper presents the development and validation of a robust, interpretable AI-guided marker for early dementia prediction, designed for real-world clinical applicability. The Predictive Prognostic Model (PPM) integrates routinely-collected, non-invasive data, specifically structural MRI and cognitive assessments. Validation across multiple international cohorts—including the ADNI research database and real-world memory clinic data from the UK and Singapore—demonstrated that the PPM predicts progression from mild cognitive impairment (MCI) to Alzheimer's disease (AD) with significantly higher sensitivity than current clinical standards. The derived individualized prognostic index achieved a hazard ratio of 3.42 compared to standard grey matter atrophy and cognitive scores. The model correctly identified 82% of individuals who progressed to AD and 81% of those who remained stable, offering a scalable tool for patient stratification and early intervention.
papers.authors: Liz Yuanxi Lee, Delshad Vaghari, Michael C Burkhart, Peter Tino, Marcella Montagnese, Zhuoyu Li, Katharina Zühlsdorff, Joseph Giorgio, Guy Williams, Eddie Chong, Christopher Chen, Benjamin R Underwood, Timothy Rittman, Zoe Kourtzi

papers.title: Unsupervised multimodal modeling of cognitive and brain health trajectories for early dementia prediction
papers.abstract: The study introduces an unsupervised multimodal trajectory modeling (MTM) approach to address the challenge of early dementia prediction in the absence of labeled clinical diagnoses. Utilizing a mixture of state-space models, the MTM framework learns to capture longitudinal changes in cognitive performance and invasive biological markers (e.g., β-amyloid levels and grey matter density). The model successfully stratifies individuals into clinically meaningful clusters based on their trajectories of cognitive and brain health, demonstrating superior reliability compared to models trained on baseline data alone. Crucially, the MTM generalizes from research cohorts to heterogeneous real-world patient data with missing observations. By deriving an individualized cognitive health index, the approach enables more precise prediction of Alzheimer's disease progression than conventional MRI or cognitive metrics, providing a cost-effective, data-driven solution for clinical prognosis.
papers.authors: Michael C Burkhart, Liz Y Lee, Delshad Vaghari, An Qi Toh, Eddie Chong, Christopher Chen, Peter Tiňo, Zoe Kourtzi

E083.name: Benoit Cottereau
E083.department: Centre de Recherche Cerveau et Cognition (CerCo)
E083.lab_name: SV3M (Spatial Vision in Man, Monkey and Machine)
E083.bio: Benoit Cottereau is a CNRS Research Director at the CerCo laboratory in Toulouse and the IPAL laboratory in Singapore, specializing in the mechanisms of spatial vision and 3D scene understanding. Their research combines human and non-human primate neuroimaging (fMRI, EEG, MEG) with psychophysical experiments and computational modeling. Cottereau focuses on the development of bio-inspired artificial vision systems, utilizing event-based cameras and spiking neural networks to model biological processes such as optic flow, binocular disparity, and symmetry perception. This work encompasses fundamental neuroscience, clinical applications for rehabilitating visual pathologies like macular degeneration, and the design of energy-efficient artificial intelligence for robotic navigation.
E083.research_direction: Dr. Cottereau has recently been investigating robust perception and computational modeling across both biological and artificial sensory systems, with a major focus on advancing event-based vision. Their recent work explores how to optimize event camera performance by developing physics-grounded models to remove optical artifacts like lens flares, alongside designing novel frameworks for cross-domain sensor adaptation and grounding natural language in asynchronous visual streams. In clinical visual neuroscience, they are using fMRI to map the motion-selective cortical network—including areas like the V5/MT+ complex and V3A—in patients with maculopathy, examining whether these high-level regions undergo functional reorganization following central vision loss. Expanding beyond the visual domain, Dr. Cottereau's research also utilizes spiking neural networks to investigate how temporal recurrence and lateral connectivity might serve as fundamental mechanisms for processing time-varying signals in the biological auditory system.

papers.title: Learning to Remove Lens Flare in Event Camera
papers.abstract: This work introduces E-Deflare, the first systematic framework for remediating lens flare artifacts in event-based vision systems. The authors establish a theoretical foundation by deriving a physics-grounded forward model that characterizes the non-linear suppression of event generation caused by internal reflections and scattering within optical lenses. To facilitate model training and evaluation, the E-Deflare Benchmark is presented, consisting of the large-scale E-Flare-2.7K synthetic dataset and the E-Flare-R real-world test set captured via a custom optical system. Empirical results demonstrate that modeling the suppression mechanism allows for superior restoration of asynchronous event streams, significantly improving the performance of downstream perception tasks in the presence of challenging optical artifacts.
papers.authors: Haiqian Han, Lingdong Kong, Jianing Li, Ao Liang, Chengtao Zhu, Jiacheng Lyu, Lai Xing Ng, Xiangyang Ji, Wei Tsang Ooi, Benoit R. Cottereau

papers.title: Temporal recurrence as a general mechanism to explain neural responses in the auditory system
papers.abstract: This research investigates the computational role of recurrent connectivity in spiking neural networks (SNNs) for reproducing the complex temporal dynamics observed in biological auditory neurons. The authors demonstrate that a parsimonious architecture incorporating temporal recurrence and lateral connections can effectively account for diverse neural response properties, including adaptation, frequency selectivity, and the distinction between transient and sustained firing patterns. Unlike traditional compartment-based models, this recurrent SNN approach leverages internal memory within the feedback loops to process asynchronous auditory signals across multiple timescales, suggesting that temporal recurrence is a fundamental mechanism for the biological representation of time-varying sensory information.
papers.authors: Ulysse Rançon, Timothée Masquelier, Benoit R. Cottereau

papers.title: Talk2Event: Grounded Understanding of Dynamic Scenes from Event Cameras
papers.abstract: The authors present Talk2Event, a novel benchmark for attribute-aware language-driven object grounding in event-based perception. Developed from real-world driving data, the benchmark includes over 30,000 referring expressions annotated with four key attributes: appearance, status, viewer-relative spatial positioning, and inter-object relational cues. To bridge the gap between asynchronous event streams and natural language, the study proposes EventRefer, a framework utilizing a Mixture of Event-Attribute Experts (MoEE) to dynamically integrate multimodal features. This attribute-centric approach facilitates spatially and temporally aware grounding, achieving substantial performance gains over state-of-the-art baselines in event-only, frame-only, and sensor-fusion settings.
papers.venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS)
papers.authors: Lingdong Kong, Dongyue Lu, Alan Liang, Rong Li, Yuhao Dong, Tianshuai Hu, Lai Xing Ng, Wei Tsang Ooi, Benoit R. Cottereau

papers.title: Motion processing in visual cortex of maculopathy patients
papers.abstract: This study characterizes the functional integrity of the motion-selective cortical network in patients with central vision loss due to maculopathy using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI). By utilizing translational random-dot kinematograms, the researchers mapped neural activity in a specialized network including the human V5/MT+ complex, areas V3A and V6, and peripheral subregions of the early visual cortex (V1–V3). The results show that maculopathy patients exhibit robust and comparable activation patterns to those found in control participants viewing stimuli with artificial scotomas. These findings indicate that the large-scale cortical organization of the motion processing system remains largely stable following the onset of a central scotoma, with no evidence of significant functional reorganization in these high-level visual areas.
papers.authors: Célia Michaud, Jade Guénot, Cynthia Faurite, Mathilde Gallice, Christophe Chiquet, Nathalie Vayssière, Isabelle Berry, Yves Trotter, Vincent Soler, Carole Peyrin, Benoit R. Cottereau

papers.title: EventFly: Event Camera Perception from Ground to the Sky
papers.abstract: The paper introduces EventFly, a framework designed to ensure robust cross-platform and cross-domain adaptation in event-based visual perception. The methodology addresses the challenge of domain shift encountered when deploying models across event sensors with varying resolutions, noise characteristics, and acquisition perspectives (e.g., ground-level vs. aerial). By unifying multi-modal visual grounding and modeling sensor-invariant asynchronous dynamics, EventFly facilitates effective adaptation to disparate hardware configurations. Comprehensive evaluations on large-scale benchmarks demonstrate that the framework achieves state-of-the-art performance in semantic scene understanding and object localization under significant shifts in perspective and sensor modality.
papers.venue: IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR)
papers.authors: Lingdong Kong, Dongyue Lu, Xiang Xu, Lai Xing Ng, Wei Tsang Ooi, Benoit R. Cottereau

E086.name: Elena Gheorghiu
E086.bio: Gheorghiu is an Associate Professor at the University of Stirling whose research examines the hierarchical mechanisms of human visual processing and the integration of features into representations like contours, textures, and 3D shapes. Their work investigates binocular vision, stereopsis, and symmetry perception, with a focus on how contextual modulation enhances contour detection through the suppression of surround textures. Using psychophysics, EEG/ERP, and computational modelling, Gheorghiu maps the relationship between initial feature extraction and higher-order perceptual organization. Gheorghiu was a co-winner of the 2007 Best Visual Illusion of the Year contest for the discovery of the 'Leaning Tower Illusion.'
E086.research_direction: Dr. Gheorghiu has recently been investigating the mechanisms of mid-level vision, focusing on how the human visual system extracts structural regularities and parses complex textures. Their recent work explores how the perceptual processing of visual symmetry interacts with other grouping cues, such as luminance polarity. By combining psychophysics with event-related potentials, specifically the Sustained Posterior Negativity, they are tracking how angular misalignments between symmetry and luminance axes modulate behavioral and neural processing costs. Additionally, they are investigating human texture vision using dense Gabor micropattern arrays and computational modeling to determine how top-down behavioral goals, such as target detection versus discrimination, dictate whether the visual system relies on localized edge-based boundary mechanisms or global region-based encoding.

papers.title: The interaction between luminance polarity grouping and symmetry axes on the ERP responses to symmetry
papers.abstract: While visual symmetry constitutes a salient ecological cue, its perceptual processing is susceptible to ambient illumination such as shading cast across its symmetry axis. This study evaluated the functional interplay between symmetry detection and luminance-polarity grouping and assessed how this interaction modulates the Sustained Posterior Negativity (SPN) component of Event-Related Potentials (ERPs). Stimuli comprised dot patterns displaying reflection, rotation, translation, or quasi-random noise configurations, with luminance polarity segregated across a grouping axis into bright and dark dot regions. Relative angular offsets between symmetry axes and polarity-grouping axes were varied at 0°, 30°, 60°, and 90°. Psychophysical measurement using a two-interval forced-choice (2IFC) detection task showed that co-axial alignment (0° offset) yielded higher accuracy than single-polarity displays for rotational and translational regularity (though not reflection) and significantly outperformed all misaligned angular separations across all symmetry classes. Electrophysiologically, the SPN dissociated topographically into an early parieto-occipital subcomponent tuned to luminance-polarity grouping and a subsequent late component over central electrode sites sensitive to pattern regularity. Increasing relative axis disparities revealed systematic distinctions between cardinal (0°, 90°) and oblique (30°, 60°) angular separations. Moreover, a polarity-grouping effect emerged in the SPN interval for pure noise arrays contingent on symmetry condition, highlighting top-down task set influences. These results demonstrate that luminance-polarity grouping facilitates regularity detection when symmetry is less immediately salient, but misaligned grouping axes concurrently impose behavioral and neural processing costs.
papers.authors: Benjamin Dering, Damien Wright, Elena Gheorghiu

papers.title: Task-dependent contribution to edge-based versus region-based texture perception
papers.abstract: Texture segregation experiments suggest that specific texture types are processed via edge-based mechanisms while others recruit region-based mechanisms; however, nominally edge-based textures recruit region-based encoding when the perceptual demand involves detection rather than segregation. This study investigated whether the nature of the behavioral task governs the recruitment of edge-based versus region-based mechanisms in human texture vision. Stimuli were dense arrays of pseudo-randomly positioned Gabor micropatterns featuring five distinct modulation classes—orientation modulation, orientation variance modulation, luminance modulation, contrast modulation, and contrast variance modulation (CVM)—tested at modulation spatial frequencies of 0.1, 0.2, 0.4, and 0.8 cpd. Waveform profiles included square-wave (SQ), sine-wave (SN), and a compound missing-fundamental (CS) waveform generated by subtracting a fundamental sinewave from an equal-amplitude square-wave. In a detection task, threshold modulation amplitudes obeyed the ordering SQ < SN < CS across all spatial frequencies, consistent with integration of overall stimulus modulation energy by region-based mechanisms. In contrast, for the orientation discrimination task at low modulation spatial frequencies and for CVM textures across all spatial frequencies, thresholds exhibited the ordering CS ≤ SQ < SN, diagnostic of localized edge-based boundary processing. Computational modeling using Difference-of-Gaussian (DoG) filter responses confirmed lower peak amplitude responses for detection than discrimination across all stimuli except CVM textures, establishing that behavioral task demands dictate whether texture processing relies on boundary edges or spatial regions.
papers.authors: Elena Gheorghiu, Cassandra Diggiss, Frederick A. A. Kingdom

E089.name: Doris Tsao
E089.department: Department of Molecular & Cell Biology; Helen Wills Neuroscience Institute
E089.bio: Doris Tsao is a neuroscientist who researches the primate visual system, specifically the mechanisms underlying object and facial recognition. Tsao identified the macaque 'face patch system,' a series of cortical regions dedicated to face processing, using fMRI-guided single-unit recordings. Their work characterized the neural code for facial identity as a linear projection onto specific shape and appearance axes to describe how high-level visual features are represented. Currently, Tsao’s research at UC Berkeley extends to 3D vision and the global organization of object space, employing a methodology that combines electrophysiology, functional imaging, and computational modeling.
E089.research_direction: Dr. Tsao has recently been investigating the neural computations and comparative architecture underlying visual object recognition, memory, and mental imagery across multiple mammalian species. Using high-density Neuropixels and single-neuron recordings, their recent work explores how distributed, axis-based population codes in the ventral temporal cortex support both the perception of external stimuli and the internal construction of mental images in humans. Additionally, they are examining the intersection of perception and long-term memory in the macaque visual system, specifically asking how inferotemporal neural populations temporally multiplex sensory features with face familiarity signals. To contextualize these mechanisms evolutionarily and developmentally, Dr. Tsao is also investigating the structural compression of the ventral stream hierarchy in tree shrews compared to primates, alongside contributing to large-scale MRI mappings of normative brain maturation and aging trajectories in macaques.

papers.title: A compressed hierarchy for visual form processing in the tree shrew
papers.abstract: The primate ventral visual stream is characterized by a multi-stage hierarchical organization that serves as a benchmark for deep neural network (DNN) models. This study investigates the universality of this architecture by mapping the large-scale functional organization of the visual system in the northern tree shrew (Tupaia belangeri), a close relative of primates. Using high-density Neuropixels recordings across multiple cortical and thalamic regions, we find that tree shrews possess a significantly compressed ventral-stream hierarchy. Notably, area V2 in the tree shrew already demonstrates high-level functions typically associated with the primate inferotemporal (IT) cortex, including a comprehensive representation of object space, robust decoding of individual identities, and the presence of highly face-selective neurons. These findings suggest that the core computational principles of visual object recognition are conserved across these mammalian orders but are implemented at an earlier stage of the visual hierarchy in smaller mammals.
papers.authors: Frank F. Lanfranchi, Joseph Wekselblatt, Daniel A. Wagenaar, Doris Y. Tsao

papers.title: A shared code for perceiving and imagining objects in human ventral temporal cortex
papers.abstract: While visual perception mechanisms are well-documented in animal models, the neural substrates of mental imagery remain elusive. This study utilizes single-neuron recordings from the human ventral temporal cortex (VTC) to evaluate the representational overlap between perception and volitional imagery. We demonstrate that approximately 80% of visually responsive neurons in the VTC utilize a distributed axis-based code to represent object identity, which can be leveraged to reconstruct perceived images and synthesize optimal stimuli. Crucially, when subjects were asked to imagine specific objects, roughly 40% of these axis-tuned neurons reactivated the same axis-based code used during perception. These results provide direct single-unit evidence for a generative model within the human visual system, where the same neural populations support both the external perception and the internal construction of visual reality.
papers.authors: Varun S. Wadia, Chrystal M. Reed, Jeffrey M. Chung, Doris Y. Tsao

papers.title: Brain Charts for the Rhesus Macaque Lifespan
papers.abstract: Reference standards for brain growth and aging are well-established for humans but remain sparse for non-human primates (NHPs). Here, we aggregate a large-scale dataset of 1,522 MRI scans from 1,024 rhesus macaques (Macaca mulatta) to generate normative growth charts spanning the lifespan. Using Generalized Additive Models for Location, Scale, and Shape (GAMLSS), we map non-linear trajectories for global and regional brain tissue volumes, cortical thickness, and surface area. Our findings reveal key developmental milestones, such as the peak growth rates of gray and white matter, and identify patterns of age-related atrophy. These charts provide a standardized framework for identifying neurodevelopmental abnormalities and facilitate cross-species translational comparisons by highlighting both conserved and divergent brain maturation patterns between rhesus macaques and humans.
papers.authors: Samuel Alldritt, Julian Sergej Benedikt Ramirez, Reinder Vos de Wael, Richard A. I. Bethlehem, Michael P. Milham, Ting Xu, Doris Y. Tsao

papers.title: Temporal multiplexing of perception and memory codes in IT cortex
papers.abstract: The neural mechanisms by which the brain distinguishes between sensory perception and long-term memory remain a fundamental question in neuroscience. We measured neuronal activity in the anterior medial (AM) and perirhinal (PR) face patches of macaque monkeys while presenting familiar and unfamiliar faces. We found that facial identity is represented via a distributed axis code, but the subspace occupied by familiar faces is distinct from that of unfamiliar faces. Specifically, the familiar face subspace underwent a late-latency distortion that increased the neural distance between familiar identities, enhancing discriminability. This memory-related transformation occurred within the same population of neurons encoding sensory features, but with different temporal dynamics. These results suggest that inferotemporal and perirhinal cortex employ a multiplexed code that enables the simultaneous representation of veridical visual perception and the enhanced discrimination of familiar individuals through a distinct, long-latency temporal channel.
papers.authors: Liang She, Marcus K. Benna, Yuelin Shi, Stefano Fusi, Doris Y. Tsao

E090.name: Radoslaw Martin Cichy
E090.lab_name: Neural Dynamics of Visual Cognition Group
E090.bio: Radoslaw Martin Cichy investigates the neural basis of human visual cognition, specifically the transformation of retinal signals into object representations. Cichy utilizes a framework that combines fMRI, M/EEG, and behavioral data with deep neural network modeling to resolve cortical dynamics in space and time. They developed representational similarity analysis and fusion techniques to map the hierarchical correspondence between biological and artificial vision systems. Cichy’s current work examines the interaction of vision with language and attention, as well as the development of visual representations in early childhood.
E090.research_direction: Dr. Cichy has recently been investigating the spatiotemporal dynamics of visual perception and semantic integration by combining multimodal neuroimaging (fMRI and EEG) with advanced computational encoding models. Their recent work explores how the visual system processes naturalistic inputs, specifically probing when and how the brain dynamically recruits recurrent feedback networks to resolve difficult object recognition tasks. To map these functional architectures, they are systematically leveraging vision-trained deep neural networks and large language models to track the time course of low-level visual features transforming into high-level semantic representations across the cortex. Broadening this focus on cross-modal processing, their research also examines predictive neural mechanisms, such as how the visual act of silent reading automatically elicits early auditory representations associated with an "inner voice."

papers.title: Auditory representations of words during silent visual reading
papers.abstract: This study investigates the neural substrates of the 'inner voice' experienced during silent visual reading. By recording high-density EEG while participants engaged with naturalistic narratives, the researchers employed computational encoding models to differentiate between auditory, visual, and semantic representations. The results demonstrate the existence of robust, time-resolved auditory representations that emerge prior to word onset and correlate significantly with the phonological sequence of the read text. These auditory-like neural patterns were not redundant with visual or semantic information and exhibited signatures of predictive processing, such as increased representational strength for words with low lexical predictability (unexpected words). The findings suggest distinct stages of neural prediction where early auditory features contribute to pre-word onset expectations, while later features are active post-onset.
papers.authors: Jiawei Li, Adrien Doerig, Radoslaw Martin Cichy

papers.title: In silico discovery of representational relationships across visual cortex
papers.abstract: This study introduces an 'in silico' discovery framework to map the functional and representational architecture of the human visual cortex. By systematically relating human fMRI responses to natural scenes to a large battery of deep neural networks (DNNs) optimized for various tasks, the researchers identified task-specific functional mappings. They demonstrate that category-selective units in these models recapitulate the representational signatures of human cortical regions (like the FFA and PPA), including preferences for real-world size, animacy, and spatial layout. This benchmarking approach provides a high-resolution view of how computational goals align with neural representations in the visual system.
papers.authors: Alessandro T. Gifford, Maya A. Jastrzębowska, Johannes Singer, Radoslaw M. Cichy

papers.title: The time course of visuo-semantic representations in the human brain is captured by combining vision and language models
papers.abstract: This research investigates the temporal dynamics of the human visuo-semantic processing hierarchy using high-density EEG and encoding models. By combining representations from vision-trained DNNs and large language models (LLMs), the authors predicted neural responses to naturalistic object images. They found that fusion models outperform unimodal ones, with vision DNNs explaining early, broadband signals related to perception and LLMs explaining later, low-frequency signals related to semantic integration. The study characterizes how visual and semantic information is uniquely and complementarily processed over time.
papers.authors: Boyan Rong, Alessandro Thomas Gifford, Emrah Düzel, Radoslaw Martin Cichy

papers.title: Adaptive recruitment of cortex-wide recurrence for visual object recognition
papers.abstract: The 'adaptive recurrence hypothesis' suggests that recurrent neural activity beyond the ventral visual stream is recruited when feedforward processing is insufficient. To test this, the authors compared fMRI and EEG responses to images categorized by their recognizability in feedforward DNNs. They found that for images difficult for feedforward models, the brain rapidly and transiently recruits parieto-frontal networks. This recruitment reconfigures ventral stream representations to achieve successful object recognition. The results support a flexible model of vision where the brain dynamically adjusts its computational resources based on input complexity.
papers.authors: Pablo Oyarzo, Johannes J.D. Singer, Kohitij Kar, Diego Vidaurre, Radoslaw M. Cichy

papers.title: Recurrence affects the geometry of visual representations across the ventral visual stream in the human brain
papers.abstract: Using a backward masking paradigm and multivariate analysis of EEG and fMRI data, the authors isolated recurrent processing in the human ventral visual stream. They found that recurrence shapes visual representations starting at ~100 ms in the early visual cortex (EVC) and occurring in two subsequent phases (~175 ms and ~300 ms) in the lateral occipital cortex (LOC). Comparing neural data with CNNs showed that recurrence shifts the feature format in LOC from mid-level to high-level. The effect is mediated by oscillatory activity in the theta, alpha, and beta frequency ranges, highlighting the mechanisms of recurrent visual activity.
papers.authors: Siying Xie, Johannes Singer, Bati Yilmaz, Daniel Kaiser, Radoslaw M. Cichy

E093.name: Kalanit Grill-Spector
E093.bio: Kalanit Grill-Spector is a professor of psychology whose research examines the neural mechanisms of visual perception and their maturation throughout the human lifespan. Grill-Spector developed the fMRI-adaptation technique to probe the functional properties of cortical neurons and conducted studies on the ventral temporal cortex's role in face and object recognition. Their laboratory employs multimodal neuroimaging and computational modeling, including deep neural networks, to investigate how structural connectivity and visual experience drive the development of specialized brain regions. This research focuses on the relationship between cortical organization and the behavioral improvement of recognition abilities from infancy to adulthood.
E093.research_direction: Dr. Grill-Spector has recently been investigating the developmental origins and computational principles that shape the structural and functional organization of the human visual system. Using longitudinal quantitative MRI, high-resolution diffusion imaging, and steady-state EEG in infants, their recent work explores how postnatal cortical folding progresses and whether innate white matter connectivity scaffolds the hierarchical emergence of category-selective visual representations. In parallel, they are utilizing topographically constrained deep artificial neural networks to test whether the macro-scale segregation of visual processing streams is driven by a unified computational objective that balances general representational learning with local spatial wiring costs. Furthermore, by integrating fMRI with spatiotemporal population receptive field (st-pRF) modeling, Dr. Grill-Spector is examining whether widespread visual phenomena like simultaneous suppression fundamentally arise from compressive nonlinearities across the cortical hierarchy rather than from top-down attentional competition.

papers.title: A single computational objective can produce specialization of streams in visual cortex
papers.abstract: The authors evaluate the computational origins of the segregation of human visual cortex into ventral, lateral, and dorsal processing streams. Utilizing the large-scale Natural Scenes Dataset (NSD) and Topographic Deep Artificial Neural Networks (TDANNs), they test whether task-specific behavioral demands (e.g., action vs. object recognition) or a unified architectural constraint drives this functional differentiation. They find that a self-supervised model optimized for representational learning while minimizing local spatial wiring costs—implemented via a correlation-based topographic loss—replicates the large-scale topography of the visual streams better than task-specialized models. The TDANN successfully predicts voxel-wise neural responses and the spatial organization of category-selective clusters and motion sensitivity across streams, suggesting that functional organization arises from a single principle of balancing general representation learning with local spatial constraints.
papers.authors: Dawn Finzi, Eshed Margalit, Kendrick Kay, Daniel L. K. Yamins, Kalanit Grill-Spector

papers.title: How infant brains fold: Sulcal deepening is linked to development of sulcal span, thickness, curvature, and microstructure
papers.abstract: Cortical folding continues postnatally as sulci deepen, yet the timeline and underlying mechanisms of this maturation are poorly understood. Through longitudinal structural and quantitative magnetic resonance imaging (qMRI) in infants from birth to one year of age, the researchers measured macroanatomical and microstructural maturation in primary and secondary sulci. They found that sulci emerging earlier in utero are deeper at birth and deepen at a slower rate postnatally than later-emerging sulci. Analysis of local depth reveals that deeper portions of sulci (fundi) exhibit higher curvature and higher microstructural density (R1 relaxation rate) compared to surrounding walls. Mean sulcal depth was found to be predicted by a weighted sum of sulcal span, thickness, curvature, and tissue microstructure, indicating that postnatal brain folding is a multifactorial process rather than being driven by a single mechanical force.
papers.authors: Sarah S. Tung, Xiaoqian Yan, Bella Fascendini, Christina Tyagi, Charleny Martinez Reyes, Keithan Ducre, Karla Perez, Ahmad Allen, Juliet Horenziak, Hua Wu, Boris Keil, Vaidehi S. Natu, Kalanit Grill-Spector

papers.title: White matter connections of human ventral temporal cortex are organized by cytoarchitecture, eccentricity, and category-selectivity from birth
papers.abstract: This study investigates whether the functional organization of the human ventral temporal cortex (VTC) is scaffolded by innate structural connectivity. Using custom baby-specific MRI coils and high-resolution diffusion imaging in neonates and infants (0-6 months), the authors mapped the probabilistic white matter connectivity profiles of the VTC. They found that connectivity is organized by cytoarchitecture, eccentricity biases, and category-selectivity from birth. Connectivity profiles of functional regions within the same cytoarchitectonic area are similar at birth and develop in parallel, characterized by increasing connectivity to the lateral prefrontal cortex and decreasing connectivity to lateral occipital and parietal regions. These results suggest that innate white matter connections provide a stable structural blueprint that precedes and likely constrains the development of functional category-selectivity in the human brain.
papers.authors: Emily Kubota, Xiaoqian Yan, Sarah Tung, Bella Fascendini, Christina Tyagi, Sophie Duhameau, Danya Ortiz, Mareike Grotheer, Vaidehi S. Natu, Boris Keil, Kalanit Grill-Spector

papers.title: The emergence of visual category representations in infants' brains
papers.abstract: The researchers characterized the development of neural representations for faces, limbs, corridors, characters, and cars using steady-state visual evoked potential (SSVEP) electroencephalography in infants aged 3 to 15 months. While robust visual responses over early visual cortex were present at 3-4 months, category-selective representations emerged hierarchically: face-selective responses were reliable by 4-6 months, while responses to limbs and corridors emerged around 6-8 months. Spatiotemporal multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) indicated that category distinctiveness increases significantly between 6 and 15 months, allowing for robust decoding of visual categories from neural signals. These findings suggest that category representations are learned at different rates during infancy, with categories of high ecological significance showing earlier neural specialization.
papers.authors: Xiaoqian Yan, Sarah Shi Tung, Bella Fascendini, Yulan Diana Chen, Anthony M Norcia, Kalanit Grill-Spector

papers.title: Rethinking simultaneous suppression in visual cortex via compressive spatiotemporal population receptive fields
papers.abstract: Simultaneous suppression, where neural responses to concurrent stimuli are lower than the sum of responses to individual stimuli, is often attributed to resource competition or attention. The authors propose a stimulus-driven computational account based on a compressive spatiotemporal population receptive field (st-pRF) model. Using fMRI, they show that suppression occurs in single voxels, varies with stimulus size and timing, and increases across the visual hierarchy. The st-pRF model, which integrates spatial and temporal information through compressive nonlinearities, successfully predicts simultaneous suppression across the visual system without requiring task-dependent competition. This suggests that suppression is a fundamental outcome of the spatiotemporal summation properties of receptive fields, with larger pRF sizes and stronger nonlinearities in higher-order areas driving greater suppressive effects.
papers.authors: Eline R. Kupers, Insub Kim, Kalanit Grill-Spector

E096.name: James Haxby
E096.department: Department of Psychological and Brain Sciences
E096.bio: James V. Haxby works in cognitive neuroscience and introduced multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) to functional neuroimaging to decode high-level visual representations. Haxby’s research challenged modular theories of brain organization by demonstrating that faces and objects are represented by distributed, overlapping patterns of activity in the ventral temporal cortex. Recently, their work has focused on the development of "hyperalignment," a computational framework that maps idiosyncratic individual brain topographies into a common high-dimensional representational space. This methodology utilizes naturalistic stimuli, such as movies, to model the shared functional architecture of the human brain and investigate individual differences in neural tuning.
E096.research_direction: Dr. Haxby has recently been advancing the methodological foundations of human neuroimaging to better capture the fine-grained functional architecture of the cortex. Their recent work explores how to map idiosyncratic neural tuning in individual brains, developing computational models that use naturalistic movie-viewing fMRI to pinpoint what visual features specific cortical locations respond to and how they are topographically arranged. Alongside this focus on individual differences, they are also building massive new cortical surface templates from thousands of structural MRIs to improve how functional data is aligned and compared across broad populations. Additionally, they have recently been documenting the historical evolution of the field, reflecting on the foundational early neuroimaging studies that initially mapped the ventral object and dorsal spatial vision pathways.

papers.title: The Laboratory of Brain and Cognition: A Lab Is Born
papers.abstract: In this invited historical essay, Haxby recounts the founding of the Laboratory of Brain and Cognition (LBC) at the National Institute of Mental Health, describing how he, Cheryl Grady, and Barry Horwitz approached Leslie Ungerleider in the late 1980s with a proposal to use PET measurements of regional cerebral blood flow to map the ventral 'object vision' and dorsal 'spatial vision' pathways in the human brain. The piece traces the intellectual and institutional circumstances that led to LBC's founding, situates the lab's early PET studies within the broader emergence of functional neuroimaging as a tool for testing psychological theories of visual cortical organization, and reflects on how those foundational studies shaped the subsequent trajectory of research on the functional architecture of human visual and object perception.
papers.authors: James V. Haxby

papers.title: A cortical surface template for human neuroscience
papers.abstract: Existing cortical surface templates used for aligning and comparing fMRI and other neuroimaging data across individuals are typically built from a few dozen structural brain scans, limiting how well they represent population variability in cortical folding and surface area. The authors introduce 'onavg,' a new cortical surface template constructed from openly available high-quality structural MRI scans of 1,031 individual brains—roughly 25 times more brains than prior standard templates—yielding more uniform vertex sampling of the cortical surface and better representation of anatomical variability. They show that surface-based analyses (including functional alignment and group-level statistical mapping) performed using the onavg template achieve improved anatomical correspondence and downstream analytic accuracy compared with commonly used legacy templates, and they release onavg as an open resource for the human neuroimaging community.
papers.authors: Ma Feilong, Guo Jiahui, M. Ida Gobbini, James V. Haxby

papers.title: The individualized neural tuning model: Precise and generalizable cartography of functional architecture in individual brains
papers.abstract: The authors introduce the Individualized Neural Tuning (INT) model, a fine-grained model of cortical functional organization designed to capture idiosyncratic neural tuning at the level of individual cortical vertices while remaining generalizable across stimuli and tasks. Unlike coarser parcellation- or network-level approaches, INT jointly models representational content (what features a cortical location responds to) and topographic organization (how those response profiles are arranged across the cortical sheet) at fine spatial grain. Using naturalistic movie-viewing fMRI data, the authors show that INT-derived individual tuning maps generalize across independent stimulus sets and outperform standard hyperalignment and anatomical-alignment approaches at predicting held-out neural responses, demonstrating that INT provides a precise and generalizable cartography of idiosyncratic functional brain architecture.
papers.authors: Ma Feilong, Samuel A. Nastase, Guo Jiahui, Yaroslav O. Halchenko, M. Ida Gobbini, James V. Haxby

E099.name: Alexander Todorov
E099.bio: Alexander Todorov investigates social perception, focusing on the cognitive and neural mechanisms involved in forming impressions from facial appearance. Their lab employs data-driven computational methods and generative adversarial networks to visualize the perceptual structures underlying social judgments. By synthesizing behavioral experiments with functional neuroimaging, Todorov’s research characterizes systematic biases inherent in human face evaluation and analyzes their impact on real-world outcomes such as electoral success and judicial decisions.
E099.research_direction: Dr. Todorov has recently been investigating the computational and behavioral mechanisms underlying high-level social perception, focusing primarily on how human observers extract complex traits and stereotypes from faces. Their recent work explores the interplay between shared, stimulus-driven visual features and idiosyncratic, observer-specific factors in facial evaluation, utilizing tools like natural language processing to map the high-dimensional space of spontaneous social impressions. To probe these mental representations, they are leveraging deep generative networks and reverse correlation to model individualized, context-dependent visual templates of social categories, while also employing these deep learning architectures to synthesize diverse, highly realistic pediatric face databases for developmental studies. Additionally, their broader research investigates statistical learning and decision-making, examining how humans calibrate future expectations and risk-taking behavior when trying to distinguish predictive signals from transparently stochastic noise.

papers.title: Capturing variability in children's faces: an artificial, yet realistic, face stimulus set
papers.abstract: To mitigate the critical underrepresentation and lack of phenotypic diversity in existing pediatric face databases, the authors utilized deep neural networks (specifically StyleGAN-based architectures) to synthesize the Artificial Child Face Database (ACFD), comprising 500 high-resolution, photorealistic images. The stimulus set encompasses a developmental range from ages 3 to 10 and represents 15 distinct ethnic and racial categories. Empirical validation by adult observers (N = 585) established the representativeness of the dataset across perceived age, gender, and ethnicity, as well as the high ecological validity of the synthetic stimuli. The ACFD provides a privacy-preserving and diverse resource for investigating the ontogeny of social perception and the early emergence of facial stereotyping.
papers.authors: Sophia Thierry, Stefan Uddenberg, Daniel N. Albohn, Alexander Todorov

papers.title: People calibrate future expectations to past performance when predicting transparently random events
papers.abstract: This research investigates the persistence of suboptimal belief updating in the context of transparently stochastic processes. Across five behavioral experiments (N > 12,000), participants predicted outcomes of fair coin tosses, which inherently follow a binomial distribution. Despite the absence of an objective signal, participants' subjective expectations of future task performance and subsequent risk-taking propensities were significantly modulated by their cumulative success rate in previous trials (b = 4.20–8.31). This failure to maintain base rate adherence suggests a fundamental human constraint in distinguishing stochastic noise from predictive signals, characterized as a form of spurious signal detection where individuals systematically update internal mental models based on chance-driven outcome performance.
papers.authors: Russell Roberts, Reid Hastie, Alexander Todorov

papers.title: Spontaneous Content of Impressions of Naturalistic Face Photographs
papers.abstract: Utilizing natural language processing and computer vision techniques, this study characterizes a high-dimensional taxonomy of spontaneous social impressions derived from unconstrained free-response descriptions of naturalistic facial stimuli (N = 4,526). The analysis reveals that while dimensions from standard low-dimensional frameworks, such as the Stereotype Content Model (warmth and competence facets), are highly prevalent, they are insufficient to capture the breadth of the impression space, which includes significant alternative dimensions like health and uniqueness. The results demonstrate that this expanded taxonomy achieves nearly 100% coverage of the descriptor set and provides significantly enhanced predictive utility for global evaluative valence and social decision-making compared to aggregated low-dimensional facets.
papers.authors: Gandalf Nicolas, Stefan Uddenberg, Alexander Todorov

papers.title: Individualized models of social judgments and context-dependent representations
papers.abstract: The authors describe a data-driven reverse correlation framework leveraging deep generative networks to visualize high-resolution mental representations of social stereotypes at the level of the individual observer. The methodology permits the construction of psychologically aligned, photorealistic models that capture idiosyncratic variance for complex social dimensions such as trustworthiness. Results demonstrate that these individualized models are psychometrically robust and sensitive to context-dependent representations—e.g., distinguishing between visual templates for a 'trustworthy' individual in the context of childcare versus financial services—validating that individual-level factors account for the majority of meaningful variance in high-level social judgment, whereas simple judgments like masculinity are adequately modeled by aggregate metrics.
papers.authors: Daniel N. Albohn, Stefan Uddenberg, Alexander Todorov

papers.title: Determinants of shared and idiosyncratic contributions to judgments of faces
papers.abstract: The study employs variance component analysis (VCA) to quantify the relative contributions of stimulus-level (shared) and observer-level (idiosyncratic) variance in facial evaluation. Findings indicate that shared variance dominates in judgments of directly observable, low-level physical attributes such as masculinity, whereas idiosyncratic variance is the primary driver for high-level evaluative judgments such as trustworthiness. The relative magnitudes of these components are moderated by the granularity of the response scale (dichotomous vs. multi-point Likert) and the phenotypic diversity of the stimulus set. Predictive modeling using machine learning identifies observer age as the most stable determinant of idiosyncratic variance in social impression formation, outperforming other demographic variables such as race or gender.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
papers.authors: Daniel N. Albohn, Joel E. Martinez, Alexander Todorov

E105.name: Jason Barton
E105.department: Departments of Medicine (Neurology), Ophthalmology and Visual Sciences, and Psychology
E105.lab_name: Human Vision and Eye Movement Laboratory
E105.main_research_area: higher visual and ocular motor function
E105.bio: Jason J. S. Barton is a Professor and Canada Research Chair at the University of British Columbia specializing in the neurology of visual perception and ocular motor control. Barton’s research investigates higher-level cortical processing using psychophysics, functional MRI, and studies of clinical populations with neurological deficits such as prosopagnosia and hemianopic dyslexia. Barton examines the mechanisms of face and word recognition, navigational orientation, and the volitional control of saccadic eye movements. Their current work also focuses on perceptual learning and rehabilitative programs designed to improve perceptual functions and reading plasticity in patients with cerebral lesions.
E105.research_direction: Dr. Barton has recently been investigating the cognitive and neural mechanisms underlying high-level visual expertise, particularly for faces and written words. Their recent work explores whether these domains share computational strategies by testing behavioral face- and word-superiority effects, and examines how specific task demands, such as lexical identification versus font perception, drive the hemifield lateralization of visual word processing. Additionally, they are probing the nature of face-processing deficits in acquired and developmental prosopagnosia by applying deep learning frameworks to classify abnormal eye-movement scanpaths and identify diagnostic ocular motor markers. Beyond expertise and face recognition, their research also assesses top-down visual generation, investigating how mental visual imagery for object properties is uniquely compromised alongside perceptual deficits in neurodegenerative conditions like posterior cortical atrophy.

papers.title: Face and word superiority effects: Parallel effects of visual expertise
papers.abstract: To evaluate shared computational strategies in the expert processing of faces and written words, this investigation developed a face-based analogue of the classic word-superiority paradigm. Across forty subjects, the study contrasted identification performance for letters embedded in whole words, pseudowords, or nonwords against feature identification within learned, unfamiliar, and scrambled face configurations. Results demonstrated a significant face-superiority effect—where facial features were identified more efficiently in the context of a structurally coherent face than in isolation or in scrambled arrays—paralleling the linguistic word-superiority advantage. Quantitative patterns of response latencies across both tasks were significantly correlated, supporting the hypothesis that visual expertise for faces and words relies on similar whole-object structural constraints or non-independent neural mechanisms.
papers.authors: Marko Chi-Wei Tien, Andrea Albonico, Jason J. S. Barton

papers.title: Reading words versus seeing font or handwriting style: a study of hemifield processing
papers.abstract: This tachistoscopic study investigated the cerebral lateralization of visual word processing by dissociating linguistic identification from the perception of stylistic script attributes. Subjects judged either word identity or script style (computer font vs. handwriting) for stimuli presented in the left or right peripheral visual fields. The results revealed a significant right-field advantage (reflecting left-hemispheric specialization) exclusively for word-identity matching, with no hemispheric bias observed for style judged across identical stimuli. This finding suggests that the lateralization of the visual word form network is primarily driven by the specific task requirements of lexical identification rather than the perceptual regularity or visual properties of the text itself.
papers.authors: Helena Ghorbani, Gülcenur Özturan, Andrea Albonico, Jason J. S. Barton

papers.title: Scanning faces: a deep learning approach to studying eye movements in prosopagnosia
papers.abstract: Utilizing an image-classification framework based on deep learning, this study identified diagnostic ocular motor markers in patients with acquired and developmental prosopagnosia. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) were trained on scanpath representations to classify subjects based on their fixation patterns during a face recognition task. The model achieved an AUC of 80% in discriminating acquired prosopagnosia from healthy controls, identifying anomalous fixation biases specifically toward the lower face and the right eye. In contrast, scanpaths in developmental prosopagnosia appeared as degraded versions of control behaviors rather than unique anomalous signatures. These findings highlight the utility of deep learning in detecting abnormal behavioral patterns in complex visual disorders where traditional hypothesis-driven statistical analyses have shown limited sensitivity.
papers.authors: Atlas Kazemian, Ipek Oruç, Jason J. S. Barton

papers.title: Visual imagery deficits in posterior cortical atrophy
papers.abstract: This study explored the integrity of mental visual imagery in posterior cortical atrophy (PCA), a neurodegenerative syndrome characterized by progressive perceptual and visuospatial dysfunction. Using a battery of objective, forced-choice questionnaires to probe imagery for specific object properties such as color and shape, the researchers assessed PCA patients and matched controls. The results demonstrated that PCA is associated with profound and often selective deficits in visual imagery across multiple domains. Although these deficits frequently coincided with perceptual impairments, dissociations were observed, suggesting that the neurodegenerative process in PCA affects the shared posterior neural circuitry required for both the bottom-up processing of visual inputs and the top-down generation of mental representations.
papers.authors: Connor D. Dietz, Andrea Albonico, Jeremy J. Tree, Jason J. S. Barton

papers.title: The 2024 Richardson Lecture: Prosopagnosia – A Classic Neurologic Deficit Meets the Modern Era
papers.abstract: This review synthesizes findings from three decades of research into acquired prosopagnosia, centering on five key observations that refine our understanding of the face-processing network. It outlines the functional and structural distinctions between apperceptive variants (linked to inferior occipitotemporal cortex) and amnestic variants (linked to anterior temporal lesions), and situates these deficits within broader clinical syndromes involving topographic orientation and color perception. The paper also reviews evidence for multi-category object recognition deficits in prosopagnosia and the modular separation of identity from other facial cues like expression. Finally, it discusses the therapeutic potential of perceptual training, framing the disorder as a critical model for investigating the plasticity and specialization of high-level visual cognition.
papers.authors: Jason J. S. Barton

E107.name: Russell Epstein
E107.main_research_area: cognitive neuroscience of vision and navigation
E107.bio: Russell Epstein is a Professor of Psychology at the University of Pennsylvania, where they direct the Epstein Lab and serve as the Director of Graduate Studies for the Department of Psychology. Epstein’s research characterizes the neural mechanisms supporting human scene perception, spatial navigation, and the formation of cognitive maps using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and behavioral psychophysics. Epstein identified the parahippocampal place area (PPA), and their ongoing work investigates how the brain integrates visual information with spatial memory to represent environmental landmarks and guide wayfinding across both physical and abstract domains.
E107.research_direction: Dr. Epstein has recently been investigating the neural and cognitive architecture that allows humans to navigate and construct mental maps of complex environments. Using large-scale virtual reality and high-resolution fMRI techniques like multivoxel pattern analysis, their recent work explores the underlying format of these cognitive maps, asking whether spatial representations rely on fixed Euclidean metrics, flexible topological graphs, or hierarchically nested subspaces. They are also examining how scene-selective networks, such as the parahippocampal place area and retrosplenial complex, integrate disparate panoramic visual inputs and distal landmarks into cohesive, world-centered spatial frameworks. Furthermore, their research probes how the brain encodes real-world metric distances across varying local and global scales, and searches for a continuous "neural compass" in the human cortex that tracks a navigator's facing direction during dynamic movement.

papers.title: Distinct Mechanisms for Panoramic and Landmark-Based View Integration in Human Place-Selective Cortex
papers.abstract: The construction of a unified cognitive map requires the integration of disparate perceptual views into a singular spatial representation. This study identifies two distinct neuroanatomical substrates mediating this integration: panorama-based integration (linking views from a common vantage point) and landmark-based integration (linking views of a distal landmark from multiple vantage points). Utilizing high-resolution fMRI and multivoxel pattern analysis (MVPA) in participants navigating a large-scale virtual city, we demonstrate that the retrosplenial complex (RSC) and regions within the medial and lateral parietal lobe—specifically the medial, lateral, and superior parietal place-memory areas—encode panoramic associations. In contrast, landmark-based associations are selectively represented within the parahippocampal place area (PPA). These findings establish a functional dissociation within the human scene-selective network between systems supporting observer-centered spatial reference frames and those anchoring the cognitive map to distal environmental features.
papers.authors: Linfeng Tony Han, Russell A. Epstein

papers.title: Cognitive maps for hierarchical spaces in the human brain
papers.abstract: Naturalistic environments are frequently organized hierarchically, with subspaces nested within larger spatial structures. This study investigated the neural representation of such hierarchical spaces using fMRI and a memory task requiring spatial judgments within and across nested environments (e.g., a building inside a courtyard). Behavioral performance revealed significant integration costs, with reduced accuracy and increased reaction times for cross-subspace trials. fMRI activity in the retrosplenial complex (RSC), occipital place area (OPA), and hippocampus correlated with these behavioral integration effects. Multivoxel pattern analysis (MVPA) provided evidence that these regions represent the hierarchical structure of the environment rather than a simple Euclidean framework. The results indicate that human cognitive maps represent nested spaces by dividing them into discrete subspaces and employing an active, resource-demanding cognitive process to integrate them into a coherent global representation.
papers.authors: Michael Peer, Russell A. Epstein

papers.title: A neural compass in the human brain during naturalistic virtual navigation
papers.abstract: Maintaining a consistent sense of facing direction (FD) is a prerequisite for efficient wayfinding, yet identifying the human equivalent of the rodent head direction system during naturalistic movement has remained elusive. We acquired 7T fMRI data while participants freely navigated a large-scale virtual reality city and applied voxel-wise encoding models to identify directional tuning. Reliable FD-selective tuning was discovered in clusters within the retrosplenial complex (RSC) and the superior parietal lobule (SPL). These directional representations were remarkably robust, generalizing across perceptually distinct versions of the city, spatially separated locations, and different behavioral task demands. Model weight analysis suggests that these regions encode heading relative to the principal axis of the environment. These results provide evidence for a neural compass in the human posterior–medial and superior parietal cortex that maintains a stable, world-centered sense of direction during dynamic navigation.
papers.authors: Zhengang Lu, Joshua B. Julian, Geoffrey K. Aguirre, Russell A. Epstein

papers.title: The format of the cognitive map depends on the structure of the environment
papers.abstract: This study addresses a fundamental debate in spatial cognition: whether the brain constructs a consistent Euclidean cognitive map across all settings or whether the map's format is contingent upon environmental features. Participants learned three virtual environments (open maze, closed maze, and teleport maze) that shared an identical topological graph structure but differed in the availability of distance and direction cues. Post-learning memory assessments demonstrated that environmental structure fundamentally shaped the accuracy and format of spatial representations. The open maze predominantly elicited accurate Euclidean representations, whereas the teleport maze resulted in graph-like representations. In the closed maze, significant individual variability emerged, with participants forming either Euclidean or graph-like maps. These findings suggest that the cognitive map is not a fixed internal model but a flexible representation whose format—Euclidean or topological—is determined by the structural affordances of the environment.
papers.authors: Michael Peer, Catherine Nadar, Russell A. Epstein

papers.title: Neural representations of real-world distances in the human brain
papers.abstract: A key function of the cognitive map is to represent the metric distances between locations in the environment. While the hippocampus is known to represent spatial distance, it is unclear how these representations are organized across different scales and reference frames. In this study, we utilized fMRI and representational similarity analysis (RSA) to examine neural patterns while participants performed a distance-judgment task for real-world locations. We demonstrate that the hippocampus and retrosplenial complex (RSC) encode metric distances between places in a scale-dependent manner. Specifically, the anterior hippocampus and RSC represented distances at a global scale (across the city), while the posterior hippocampus was more sensitive to local spatial relationships. Furthermore, these distance representations were found to be modulated by the navigational relevance of landmarks. These results highlight a distributed system for distance coding where the medial temporal lobe and posterior cingulate cortex represent the metric structure of the real-world environment across multiple spatial horizons.
papers.authors: Michael Peer, Russell A. Epstein

E109.name: Monica Castelhano
E109.bio: Castelhano is a Professor at Queen's University whose research investigates the cognitive mechanisms underlying visual attention, memory, and perception within real-world environments. They utilize eye-tracking and behavioral measures to analyze how initial scene representations, or "gist," facilitate eye-movement guidance during complex visual search tasks. Castelhano’s work on the surface guidance framework examines how spatial layout and object functional properties interact with semantic information to shape human visual cognition. Their recent studies integrate Virtual Reality to investigate these processes in three-dimensional, naturalistic spaces.
E109.research_direction: Dr. Castelhano has recently been investigating the mechanisms by which contextual priors and scene structure guide attention during naturalistic visual search. Their recent work explores how the precision of our spatial expectations—quantified as a continuous scale of object placement certainty—influences search behavior, while also examining how depth layouts interact with top-down knowledge, such as whether a bias for foreground objects modulates standard semantic consistency effects in complex scenes. Furthermore, they are developing computational frameworks to model these internal cognitive maps, testing whether spatial priors derived from Large Language Models and scene knowledge graphs can successfully approximate human eye-tracking and search patterns.

papers.title: Object spatial certainty as a measure of spatial variability and its influence on attention
papers.abstract: This study characterizes the inherent variability in object-scene spatial associations by introducing the Object Spatial Certainty (OSC) Index. Moving beyond binary categorical definitions of spatial constraints (fixed vs. variable), the authors developed a ranked index for 150 objects based on normalized participant ratings of expected placement within environmental regions. Experimental results from two visual search tasks demonstrated that objects with High Certainty (e.g., highly predictable positions like boots) exerted significantly stronger contextual guidance on attentional allocation compared to Low Certainty objects (e.g., plants). These findings suggest that the efficacy of scene-based priors in search guidance is a direct function of the precision of learned spatial associations, highlighting the necessity of continuous measures of spatial reliability in modeling naturalistic scene perception.
papers.authors: Karolina J. Krzyś, Carmel Avitzur, Carrick C. Williams, Monica S. Castelhano

papers.title: A Framework for Leveraging LLMs for Scene Analysis and Cognitive Processing
papers.abstract: This research presents a computational pipeline designed to integrate Large Language Models (LLMs) with cognitive vision tasks by leveraging LLM-based spatial priors for target localization. The proposed framework extracts a knowledge graph from scene imagery via automated object detectors and prompts an LLM to generate probabilistic distributions of target placement based on common-sense spatial reasoning. Benchmarking against human eye-tracking data, the authors demonstrate that LLM-derived priors effectively approximate human search strategies and fixation patterns. The study concludes that LLMs can serve as robust proxies for internal cognitive maps, bridging the gap between human-level scene understanding and high-level computer vision models for automated scene analysis and cognitive strategy modeling.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Computer Graphics and Interactive Techniques (PACMCGIT)
papers.authors: Catarina Moreira, Jeffrey Cockburn, Monica S. Castelhano

papers.title: Foreground bias: Semantic consistency effects modulated when searching across depth
papers.abstract: This investigation explores the interaction between depth-based prioritization—specifically the 'foreground bias'—and semantic scene context during object search in complex environments. Utilizing chimera scenes with semantically incongruous depth-plane contexts, the study assessed how target detection is influenced by depth position and semantic congruency. Behavioral results indicated a clear search advantage for foreground targets, characterized by reduced detection latencies and fewer fixations. Most significantly, the magnitude of the semantic consistency effect—the benefit of contextually congruent targets—was markedly attenuated for objects located in the foreground compared to those in the background. These results suggest that the prioritization of proximal space potentially bypasses or reduces the impact of higher-level semantic constraints, indicating a depth-dependent hierarchy in the application of contextual priors during visual search.
papers.authors: Karolina J. Krzyś, Louisa L. Y. Man, Jeffrey D. Wammes, Monica S. Castelhano

E110.name: Edward Silson
E110.department: School of Philosophy, Psychology and Language Sciences
E110.bio: Edward Silson is a Lecturer in Visual Perception and Cognition who investigates the neural mechanisms of human visual perception and its integration with memory systems. Silson utilizes high-resolution fMRI, population receptive field (pRF) modeling, and TMS to map the functional architecture of the visual cortex, focusing on scene-selective regions and the medial parietal cortex. They explore how cortical specializations for categories such as faces and places interact with long-term memory and how brain damage or retinal disease impacts these systems. Recently, Silson’s lab has employed EEG-fMRI fusion to characterize the top-down dynamics of mental imagery and the role of opponent visuospatial coding as an organizing principle of brain integration.
E110.research_direction: Dr. Silson has recently been investigating the spatiotemporal dynamics and spatial tuning of high-level visual representations across perception, memory, and mental imagery. Their recent work explores the degree to which complex category-selective computations—such as face processing, scene representation in the occipital place area, and the extraction of rapid navigational affordances—are scaffolded upon the underlying retinotopic organization of the early visual cortex. To resolve the temporal cascade of these systems, they are employing multimodal approaches like EEG-fMRI and MEG-fMRI fusion to track how neural representations of familiar people and places unfold during top-down visual recall. Additionally, they utilize population receptive field (pRF) mapping to examine how opponent visuospatial coding schemes within the medial parietal cortex mediate the interplay between internally oriented memory networks and externally driven visual perception.

papers.title: Early spatiotemporal dynamics of navigational affordance coding in the dorsal visual cortex
papers.abstract: The extraction of navigationally relevant signals, or affordances, from dynamic environments is a prerequisite for successful movement. Integrating fMRI, MEG, and behavioral data, this study demonstrates that navigational affordance information is computed rapidly within dorsal early visual cortex (EVC) prior to reaching higher-level scene-selective regions. Analyses revealed that affordance-related signals are detectable within ~110 ms post-stimulus onset. Contrary to previous models identifying the occipital place area (OPA) as the primary locus, whole-brain results pinpoint dorsal EVC as the critical site for affordance extraction. Furthermore, by varying scene presentation durations, the study showed that while these representations begin to emerge at 33–66 ms, they only become robust with durations exceeding 132 ms, revealing the emergent nature of navigational affordance coding.
papers.authors: Elisa Zamboni, Rebecca Lowndes, Richard Aveyard, Catriona L. Scrivener, Jessica A. Teed, Yumeng Ma, Antony B. Morland, Edward H. Silson

papers.title: Visual imagery of familiar people and places in category selective cortex
papers.abstract: Visual mental imagery is a complex process involving a distributed network of cortical regions. This study used an EEG-fMRI fusion approach to characterize the neural dynamics of category-selective mental imagery in the medial parietal cortex (MPC), ventral temporal cortex (VTC), and V1. Participants engaged in mental recall of personally familiar people and places. fMRI results replicated category-selectivity in MPC, VPMA, LPMA, and FFA during imagery. Multivariate decoding identified stimulus-specific information in VTC, whereas MPC represented information across categories more broadly. EEG-fMRI fusion revealed that peak activity in MPC and VTC occurred early and near-simultaneously during recall, with place-selective representations in VTC peaking earlier than those for people. Delayed fusion correlations in V1 suggested that imagery involves a top-down progression from category-selective regions to early visual cortex.
papers.authors: Catriona L. Scrivener, Jessica A. Teed, Edward H. Silson

papers.title: Opponent visuospatial coding structures responses during memory recall and visual perception in medial parietal cortex
papers.abstract: While perception and memory are known to share neural representations in early visual cortex, their interaction in the medial parietal cortex (MPC) is less understood. This study employed population receptive field (pRF) mapping to quantify visuospatial coding within category-selective memory regions of the MPC. The researchers observed robust signatures of both positive and negative (inverted) pRF response profiles. Crucially, the pattern of visuospatial coding—specifically the dissimilarity between positive and negative pRF timeseries—predicted the distinctiveness of neural responses during both internally oriented memory recall and externally oriented visual perception. These results indicate that MPC utilizes an opponent visuospatial coding scheme to structure interactions between mnemonic and perceptual processing systems at the cortical apex.
papers.authors: Catriona L. Scrivener, Edward H. Silson

papers.title: Retinotopy drives the variation in scene responses across visual field map divisions of the occipital place area
papers.abstract: The occipital place area (OPA) is a scene-selective region that spatially overlaps several retinotopic visual field maps, including LO1, LO2, V3A, V3B, and V7. Using fMRI and representational similarity analysis (RSA), this study tested whether these subdivisions contribute unique computations during scene processing. Neural responses to 96 complex scenes were found to be heterogeneous across the different maps. RSA testing of seven candidate models—encompassing scene content, expanse, distance, and navigational affordances—failed to explain this variation. Instead, the heterogeneity in scene representations was significantly correlated with the maps' distinct retinotopic profiles. These findings suggest that the functional specialization of OPA is primarily driven by its underlying retinotopic organization rather than a single, high-level scene property.
papers.authors: Catriona L. Scrivener, Elisa Zamboni, Antony B. Morland, Edward H. Silson

papers.title: Shared spatial selectivity in early visual cortex and face-selective brain regions
papers.abstract: The relationship between the spatial selectivity of high-level category-selective regions and the retinotopic organization of early visual maps (V1-V3) is a central question in visual neuroscience. This research utilized population receptive field (pRF) mapping with face stimuli to investigate the spatial tuning of face-selective regions, including the occipital face area (OFA) and fusiform face patches (pFUS and mFUS). The results demonstrate that spatial tuning in these category-selective regions is significantly aligned with early visual cortex organization, exhibiting consistent contralateral and foveal biases. This suggests that face-selective representations are scaffolded onto a conserved visuospatial framework shared with the early stages of the visual processing hierarchy, rather than emerging as amodal or spatially independent systems.
papers.authors: Ivan Alvarez, Benjamin de Haas, Edward H. Silson

E111.name: Christopher Baldassano
E111.bio: Christopher Baldassano is an Associate Professor at Columbia University where they direct the Dynamic Perception and Memory Lab. Their research utilizes functional MRI, behavioral experiments, and machine learning to investigate how the human brain segments continuous experiences, such as narratives and films, into discrete event representations. Baldassano examines the computational mechanisms by which prior knowledge and schematic scripts influence the encoding and retrieval of information to connect high-level vision and episodic memory. Their work uses naturalistic stimuli and data analysis to characterize the processes by which the brain constructs and updates internal models of the world.
E111.research_direction: Dr. Baldassano's recent work explores how the human brain structures continuous, naturalistic experiences to build lasting memory representations. Using methods like fMRI, Hidden Markov Models, and eye-tracking, they have recently been investigating the dynamics of neural event segmentation, specifically asking how the brain's temporal chunking of movies and audio narratives shifts in response to repeated exposure and top-down attentional goals. Additionally, their research probes the cognitive scaffolds of memory encoding, examining how stable neural representations of virtual spatial contexts and active predictive gaze behaviors facilitate the binding of new episodic details. To further support studies of naturalistic vision, they are also developing novel computational stimulus frameworks that use generative AI to systematically decouple low-level visual textures from high-level object semantics, enabling more precise investigations into feature binding and abstraction.

papers.title: Repeated Viewing of a Film Clip Changes Event Timescales in The Brain
papers.abstract: This study characterizes the plasticity of the brain's temporal event representations as experiences become familiar through repetition. Using fMRI, participants watched narrative film clips from 'The Grand Budapest Hotel' six times, and neural event segmentation was quantified across various timescales using Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) and searchlight-based pattern similarity. The results demonstrate that neural event dynamics are not static; while many regions exhibit stability, others undergo significant granularity shifts.
