Specifically, certain cortical areas developed finer-grained (more detailed) event boundaries, while others transitioned toward coarser, more generalized representations. Critically, the emergence of robust, coarse-scale event structure in the lateral occipital cortex and middle temporal gyrus was significantly correlated with subsequent memory for the narrative content, indicating that the hierarchical reorganization of event timescales supports the formation of durable episodic traces.
papers.authors: Narjes Al-Zahli, Mariam Aly, Christopher Baldassano

papers.title: Spatial contexts with reliable neural representations support reinstatement of subsequently placed objects
papers.abstract: This research investigates the neural properties that determine the effectiveness of spatial contexts as mnemonic scaffolds. Utilizing a 23-room virtual reality 'memory palace' and fMRI, the authors measured the 'reliability' of neural activity patterns for specific rooms—defined by stability and distinctiveness—prior to an object-placement task. Results indicated that spatial locations with highly reliable neural representations significantly enhanced the reinstatement of subsequently associated objects during recall. This effect remained robust even after controlling for the direct retrieval of the rooms themselves, suggesting that high-quality neural context representations facilitate superior binding of episodic details during encoding rather than simply improving context accessibility at retrieval. These findings propose that neural reliability can serve as a quantitative metric for auditing the utility of spatial scaffolds in memory.
papers.authors: Rolando Masís-Obando, Kenneth A. Norman, Christopher Baldassano

papers.title: Accurate predictions facilitate robust memory encoding independently from stimulus probability
papers.abstract: The cognitive benefits of prediction are often confounded with the statistical probability of the predicted stimuli. This study decoupled these factors using a novel board game paradigm combined with real-time eye-tracking to assess online predictive fixations. The findings reveal two dissociable mnemonic mechanisms: accurate predictions (verified via ocular gaze patterns) improve memory by enhancing encoding precision, enabling direct episodic retrieval that bypasses schematic reliance. In contrast, high stimulus probability facilitates memory through a reconstructive retrieval strategy, where schematic knowledge is utilized to generate and recognize probable outcomes. These results challenge traditional prediction-error models by showing that successful predictive alignment—not just unexpectedness—actively strengthens the fidelity of new memory representations.
papers.authors: Jiawen Huang, Eleanor Furness, Yifang Liu, Morell-Jovan Kenmoe, Ronak Elias, Hannah Tongxin Zeng, Christopher Baldassano

papers.title: Decoupling lower-level and higher-level visual features in naturalistic scenes
papers.abstract: Because low-level visual features (e.g., textures and patterns) naturally covary with high-level semantic categories (e.g., objects and scenes), isolating their distinct contributions to neural and behavioral responses remains a significant challenge. To address this, the authors introduced the SPOT (Scenes, Patterns, Objects, Textures) Grid, a stimulus framework that uses a Stable Diffusion generative model to factorially combine higher-level scene-object content with lower-level texture-pattern constituent features. Quantitative validation using state-of-the-art deep neural networks confirmed that higher-level representations remained invariant across diverse lower-level backgrounds and that lower-level features were represented consistently regardless of the semantic objects they composed. This resource enables precise manipulations of visual hierarchy to study feature binding and abstraction in naturalistic vision.
papers.authors: Zall Hirschstein, Mariam Aly, Christopher Baldassano

papers.title: Top-down attention shifts behavioral and neural event boundaries in narratives with overlapping event scripts
papers.abstract: Human event segmentation is typically attributed to sudden changes in the external environment, but this study explores how internal goals and schematic scripts modulate this process. Participants listened to 16 audio narratives that factorially nested social scripts (e.g., a marriage proposal) within location scripts (e.g., a restaurant). Using fMRI and Hidden Markov Models (HMMs), the authors demonstrated that top-down attentional focus—induced by assigning specific roles to listeners—significantly shifted the temporal location of neural event boundaries. Brain regions within the default mode network, specifically the angular gyrus, parahippocampal gyrus, and medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), tracked overlapping scripts but reconfigured their segmentation dynamics to prioritize goal-relevant information. These results indicate that the brain does not passively respond to environmental shifts but actively partitions experience based on current priorities.
papers.authors: Alexandra De Soares, Tony Kim, Franck Mugisho, Elen Zhu, Allison Lin, Chen Zheng, Christopher Baldassano

E112.name: Iris Groen
E112.bio: Groen is an Associate Professor and MacGillavry Fellow at the University of Amsterdam’s Informatics Institute, specializing in the intersection of cognitive neuroscience and computer vision. Their research examines the neural representation of real-world scenes and videos by employing human brain imaging techniques, including fMRI, EEG, and ECoG, alongside deep neural networks. Groen investigates how the human brain processes natural image statistics and extracts action affordances from the environment to understand the principles of biological vision. Through this interdisciplinary approach, they aim to develop bio-inspired models of perception and align artificial intelligence with human neural processing.
E112.research_direction: Dr. Groen has recently been investigating the computational principles of naturalistic vision by extensively comparing deep neural network representations to human brain activity. Much of their recent work explores the temporal dynamics of visual processing, utilizing large-scale benchmarking of diverse deep video architectures against fMRI and EEG data to probe how the visual system integrates dynamic information and categorizes actions over time. They are also examining the ecological and temporal properties of higher-level vision, using fMRI to understand how scene-selective regions encode locomotive action affordances and leveraging intracranial EEG to model short-term neural adaptation across the visual hierarchy. Additionally, Dr. Groen is developing novel computational frameworks that use generative diffusion models to systematically manipulate visual stimuli, allowing researchers to isolate the precise visuo-semantic properties that drive selective cortical responses.

papers.title: The Human Brain as a Dynamic Mixture of Expert Models in Video Understanding
papers.abstract: This research performs a large-scale benchmarking of model-brain alignment using over 100 static and temporally-integrative deep video architectures compared against dynamic electroencephalography (EEG) recordings of naturalistic video stimuli. We implement a novel Cross-Temporal Representational Similarity Analysis (CT-RSA) to evaluate the correspondence between time-unfolded model features and the millisecond-scale evolution of neural response patterns. Our analysis reveals a distinct shift in neural preference: posterior electrodes initially align with hierarchical static object representations before transitioning to mid-level, temporally-integrating action features that closely track the dynamic content of the video. In contrast, frontal electrodes exhibit alignment with high-level static action representations without fine-grained temporal correspondence. We conclude that the brain functions as a dynamic mixture of expert models, where state-space models and self-supervised pretraining offer superior alignment to intermediate temporal integration in the human visual system.
papers.authors: Christina Sartzetaki, Anne W. Zonneveld, Pablo Oyarzo, Alessandro T. Gifford, Radoslaw M. Cichy, Pascal Mettes, Iris I. A. Groen

papers.title: Representation of locomotive action affordances in human behavior, brains, and deep neural networks
papers.abstract: This study characterizes the neural basis of locomotive action affordance perception (e.g., walking, climbing, or swimming) by comparing human behavioral annotations, multi-voxel fMRI responses, and deep neural network (DNN) activations to diverse real-world scenes. We demonstrate that the human visual cortex, specifically within scene-selective regions, represents locomotive affordances as a unique representational space that is distinct from low-level image properties, object content, or global scene categories. Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA) of fMRI patterns shows that these affordance representations emerge independently of the observer's task. We find that while standard DNNs trained on object or scene classification capture some behavioral variance, they generally fail to align with the specialized neural representations of locomotive affordances. These results identify a novel class of ecological representations in the human brain dedicated to identifying action possibilities within the environment.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS)
papers.authors: Clemens G. Bartnik, Christina Sartzetaki, Abel Puigseslloses Sanchez, Elijah Molenkamp, Steven Bommer, Nikolina Vukšić, Iris I. A. Groen

papers.title: One Hundred Neural Networks and Brains Watching Videos: Lessons from Alignment
papers.abstract: We present the first large-scale benchmarking of 99 deep video models to assess their representational alignment with human brain activity recorded via fMRI during naturalistic video viewing. We systematically disentangle four factors—temporal modeling, classification task, architecture (CNN vs. Transformer), and training dataset—to determine their impact on brain scoring across multiple regions of interest (ROIs). Our results show that temporal modeling is critical for alignment to early visual areas, while optimization for action-recognition task spaces is essential for alignment to high-level cortical regions. We identify significant differences in layer-wise alignment patterns between CNNs and Transformers and observe a negative correlation between computational complexity (FLOPs) and alignment in semantic-processing regions, suggesting that more efficient models may better approximate the human visual system's representations.
papers.authors: Christina Sartzetaki, Gemma Roig, Cees G. M. Snoek, Iris I. A. Groen

papers.title: BrainACTIV: Identifying visuo-semantic properties driving cortical selectivity using diffusion-based image manipulation
papers.abstract: We introduce Brain Activation Control Through Image Variation (BrainACTIV), a framework that leverages pretrained diffusion models to manipulate reference images to maximize or minimize activity in target human cortical regions. Unlike standard brain-optimized image synthesis methods that generate isolated samples, BrainACTIV produces controlled image variations that allow for fine-grained identification of the visuo-semantic properties driving selective neural responses. We demonstrate that this method effectively modulates predicted fMRI responses and aligns with established category preferences in specialized ROIs (e.g., faces, bodies, and places) while maintaining structural similarity to the original image. Furthermore, we show how BrainACTIV can accentuate subtle representational differences between regions selective for the same category, offering a robust tool for hypothesis-driven neuroscientific stimulus generation.
papers.authors: Diego García Cerdas, Christina Sartzetaki, Magnus Petersen, Gemma Roig, Pascal Mettes, Iris I. A. Groen

papers.title: Temporal dynamics of short-term neural adaptation across human visual cortex
papers.abstract: Using time-varying intracranial electroencephalography (iEEG), we investigate how neural adaptation patterns vary across the human visual hierarchy in response to naturalistic image categories with varying durations and repetition intervals. We identify two distinct signatures of short-term adaptation: response decay to sustained stimuli and repetition suppression. We find that higher visual areas in the ventral- and lateral-occipitotemporal cortex exhibit significantly slower adaptation and recovery dynamics compared to early visual areas (V1-V3). To account for these hierarchical differences, we implement an augmented delayed divisive normalization (DN) model with category-dependent input scaling. The model successfully predicts neural response time courses across the hierarchy, suggesting that area-specific normalization dynamics and category selectivity are the primary computational drivers of temporal adaptation in the human visual system.
papers.authors: Amber Marijn Brands, Sasha Devore, Orrin Devinsky, Werner Doyle, Adeen Flinker, Daniel Friedman, Patricia Dugan, Jonathan Winawer, Iris I. A. Groen

E113.name: Hugo Spiers
E113.bio: Hugo Spiers is a Professor of Cognitive Neuroscience at UCL whose research investigates how the brain constructs neural representations of space to support navigation, memory, and future planning. Spiers co-led the 'Sea Hero Quest' project, which utilized a mobile game to collect navigation data from millions of people worldwide to benchmark cognitive decline and Alzheimer’s risk. Their experimental methodology integrates high-resolution neuroimaging, virtual reality, and computational modeling to map the functional roles of the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex in complex spatial tasks. Current research directions involve environmental neuroscience and neuroarchitecture, focusing on how built environments and urban design influence human spatial behavior and neural dynamics.
E113.research_direction: Dr. Spiers has recently been investigating the cognitive and neural mechanisms underlying real-world spatial navigation across diverse populations and environments. Their recent work explores how expert navigators, such as London taxi drivers, mentally plan routes across vast urban networks, using response latencies and computational models to test if they utilize hierarchical neighborhood boundaries and non-sequential planning strategies at complex junctions. Additionally, they are utilizing massive global datasets from virtual reality gaming to assess how factors like education impact wayfinding across the lifespan, and whether digital spatial metrics can accurately predict physical, real-world navigation competency in older adults. Finally, Dr. Spiers is employing fMRI to examine the intersection of spatial mapping and neuroaesthetics, investigating how regions like the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex process both the structural complexity and subjective visual pleasantness of architectural spaces.

papers.title: Brain Dynamics during Architectural Experience: Prefrontal and Hippocampal Regions Track Aesthetics and Spatial Complexity
papers.abstract: This fMRI investigation explores the neural mechanisms underlying spatial and aesthetic processing during navigation within architectural environments. Utilizing first-person perspective video stimuli of diverse urban and indoor spaces, the researchers identify a functional dissociation in the BOLD response: the ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) is significantly modulated by the aesthetic valence (pleasantness) of the environment and task focus on valence, whereas the parahippocampal and hippocampal regions track the spatial complexity of the layout and the environmental memorability. Furthermore, the study identifies that computational curvature and specific qualitative attributes, such as fascination and coherence, engage distinct subregions of the visual and spatial mapping systems (e.g., lingual gyrus and cuneus), suggesting an integrated neural architecture for the evaluation of built environments.
papers.authors: Lara Gregorians, Zita Patai, Pablo Fernandez Velasco, Fiona E. Zisch, Hugo J. Spiers

papers.title: Education Is Positively and Causally Linked With Spatial Navigation Ability Across the Lifespan
papers.abstract: Utilizing a massive dataset from the citizen science mobile application 'Sea Hero Quest' (n = 397,162), this study quantifies the relationship between formal educational attainment and wayfinding performance across 38 countries. The analysis demonstrates a robust positive correlation between education level and navigation efficiency, with effect sizes (Hedge's g) increasing in older age groups and for tasks of higher spatial complexity. By controlling for multivariate sociodemographic factors and examining cross-national variation, the authors provide evidence for a causal or supportive link where education acts as a protective or enhancing factor for spatial cognitive capacity throughout the lifespan. The results highlight how environmental and socioeconomic factors modulate the development and preservation of the brain's internal navigation systems.
papers.venue: Open Mind: Discoveries in Cognitive Science
papers.authors: Antoine Coutrot, Rogier A. Kievit, Stuart J. Ritchie, Ed Manley, Jan M. Wiener, Christof Hölscher, Ruth C. Dalton, Michael Hornberger, Hugo J. Spiers

papers.title: Predicting real-world navigation performance from a virtual navigation task in older adults
papers.abstract: This study assesses the predictive utility of virtual reality (VR) based cognitive assessments for evaluating real-world navigational competency in older adults. By comparing digital wayfinding metrics from a mobile task with performance on a naturalistic navigation test in an unfamiliar physical urban setting, the researchers observed that VR performance significant predicts real-world success. Digital indices such as trajectory efficiency and goal-directedness were correlated with physical wayfinding accuracy, even after adjusting for general cognitive status and individual differences in familiarity. The research underscores the potential of scalable digital tools to benchmark spatial cognitive function against population-level norms (n > 280,000), facilitating the identification of early cognitive decline in naturalistic contexts.
papers.authors: Sarah Goodroe, Pablo Fernandez Velasco, Christoffer J. Gahnstrom, Jan Wiener, Antoine Coutrot, Michael Hornberger, Hugo J. Spiers

papers.title: Expert navigators deploy rational complexity-based decision precaching for large-scale real-world planning
papers.abstract: The research investigates how human expertise facilitates planning in vast state-spaces (over 26,000 streets) by examining the internal route-planning dynamics of licensed London taxi drivers. Utilizing response latencies as a proxy for cognitive inference time, the authors demonstrate that expert planners do not rely on a standard sequential tree-search. Instead, they exhibit 'decision precaching,' a mechanism characterized by the prioritization of mental sampling at critical, high-uncertainty street junctions during the initial phases of journey construction. Computational modeling reveals that this prioritization follows normative metrics of complexity reduction, where navigators sample remote states to simplify the global planning problem, providing real-world evidence for complexity-driven inference within internal cognitive models.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS)
papers.authors: Pablo Fernandez Velasco, Eva-Maria Griesbauer, Iva K. Brunec, Jeremy Morley, Ed Manley, David C. McNamee, Hugo J. Spiers

papers.title: London taxi drivers exploit neighbourhood boundaries for hierarchical route planning
papers.abstract: This study examines the hypothesis that humans utilize hierarchical representations to solve navigation problems in complex urban environments. By testing the ability of licensed London taxi drivers to generate street-by-street route plans from memory, the authors analyzed the temporal dynamics of journey construction. Findings reveal that response times are significantly modulated by regional neighborhood boundaries; selection latencies were notably higher when crossing boundaries compared to within-cluster transitions, an effect that persisted regardless of graph-theoretic network distance. These data provide empirical evidence for a clustered mental representation of large-scale space, suggesting that experts leverage topological boundaries to implement a computationally efficient hierarchical search strategy.
papers.authors: Eva-Maria Griesbauer, Pablo Fernandez Velasco, Antoine Coutrot, Jan M. Wiener, Jeremy G. Morley, Ed Manley, Hugo J. Spiers

E114.name: Thomas Wolbers
E114.bio: Thomas Wolbers investigates the neurocognitive mechanisms of spatial navigation and their vulnerability to aging and neurodegeneration. Utilizing immersive virtual reality, high-field functional MRI, and computational modeling, Wolbers’ laboratory has identified age-related declines in entorhinal grid cell representations and head-direction signals in the human thalamus. Their research extends from the mapping of the brain's navigation circuit to the development of VR-based diagnostic markers and behavioral interventions. These applications are designed to enhance memory consolidation and address cognitive decline in clinical populations.
E114.research_direction: Dr. Wolbers has recently been investigating the neural and computational mechanisms of human spatial navigation, with a particular focus on how these networks degrade during healthy aging and early Alzheimer's disease. Their recent work explores how the brain synthesizes multimodal spatial inputs, using ultra-high field fMRI to ask whether regions like the retrosplenial cortex maintain cue-specific or abstract neural representations of discrete visual landmarks and continuous self-motion cues. To pinpoint the computational drivers of navigational decline, they are combining immersive virtual reality tasks with mechanistic models to isolate specific sources of error in path integration and head direction tracking, such as spatial "memory leak" or synaptic noise. Furthermore, Dr. Wolbers is utilizing high-resolution neuroimaging to examine how advancing age alters the brain's ability to compute and anchor spatial maps to environmental boundaries.

papers.title: Path integration impairments reveal early cognitive changes in subjective cognitive decline
papers.abstract: Path integration (PI), the computational process of updating one's spatial position using self-motion cues, is fundamentally dependent on the entorhinal-hippocampal network, which exhibits pathological changes in the earliest stages of Alzheimer's disease (AD). This study employed an immersive virtual reality (VR) navigation task and a hierarchical Bayesian computational model to evaluate PI performance in individuals with subjective cognitive decline (SCD) and healthy controls. Behavioral data demonstrated that individuals with SCD exhibit significantly greater PI errors, which the modeling analysis attributed specifically to an increased 'memory leak' (the progressive decay of internal position estimates over distance). Other sources of error, such as velocity gain misestimates and sensorimotor reporting noise, did not significantly differ between groups. These findings suggest that decomposed PI metrics, particularly memory leak, may serve as a sensitive behavioral marker for presymptomatic neurodegeneration in the AD spectrum.
papers.authors: Vladislava Segen, Md Rysul Kabir, Adam Streck, Jakub Slavik, Wenzel Glanz, Michaela Butryn, Ehren Newman, Zoran Tiganj, Thomas Wolbers

papers.title: How human aging disrupts the head direction network: evidence from VR experiments and mechanistic models
papers.abstract: The head direction (HD) system provides a fundamental neural compass for navigation, yet its stability and fidelity across the human lifespan remain poorly understood. This study combined immersive VR behavioral experiments with mechanistic ring-attractor modeling to investigate how aging affects human orientation tracking. Behavioral assessments revealed that older adults exhibit significantly increased orientation errors and reduced angular precision compared to younger controls. Computational modeling of the HD network indicated that these age-related deficits are consistent with increased synaptic noise and the attrition of network units (neuronal loss). These results provide the first behavioral and computational evidence that normative aging compromises the precision of the human neural compass, potentially contributing to broader navigational impairments in late adulthood.
papers.authors: Matthieu Bernard, Jonathan Shine, Andrej Bicanski, Thomas Wolbers

papers.title: Altered Coding of Environmental Boundaries in Human Aging: An fMRI Study
papers.abstract: Environmental boundaries are critical spatial cues that anchor cognitive maps, supporting stable spatial orientation and location memory. Using high-resolution functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and a virtual object-location memory task, we investigated the neural representation of environmental boundaries in young and older adults. Behaviorally, both groups exhibited higher precision for locations near boundaries, but this effect was significantly attenuated in older adults, who showed a steeper decline in accuracy as distance from boundaries increased. fMRI analyses revealed that aging is associated with significantly altered univariate and multivariate neural coding of boundary proximity and geometry within the parahippocampal and entorhinal cortices. These findings suggest that age-related spatial memory deficits are partially driven by a reduced ability to compute and maintain stable, boundary-anchored spatial representations.
papers.authors: Vladislava Segen, Matthias Stangl, Jonathan Shine, Thomas Wolbers

papers.title: Representational similarity analysis reveals cue-independent spatial representations for landmarks and self-motion cues in human retrosplenial cortex
papers.abstract: The formation of a unified cognitive map requires the integration of diverse spatial inputs, such as discrete visual landmarks and continuous self-motion cues (optic flow). While previous adaptation-based fMRI studies found cue-specific coding, the existence of abstract, cue-independent representations in the human brain remains an open question. We applied representational similarity analysis (RSA) to ultra-high field (7T) fMRI data recorded during a virtual navigation task. Results demonstrated that the retrosplenial cortex (RSC) contains neural population codes for spatial locations that generalize across both landmark and self-motion conditions. These stable representations were primarily driven by the navigator's subjective position estimates rather than objective coordinates. This evidence positions the human RSC as a critical neural substrate for the synthesis of multimodal sensory signals into abstract, high-level spatial representations.
papers.authors: Xiaoli Chen, Ziwei Wei, Thomas Wolbers

papers.title: Repetition Suppression Reveals Cue-Specific Spatial Representations for Landmarks and Self-Motion Cues in the Human Retrosplenial Cortex
papers.abstract: Successful navigation relies on distinct cognitive mechanisms for processing environmental landmarks and tracking self-motion. Whether these navigational modes recruit shared or separate neural representations in the human brain is unresolved. Using ultra-high field 7T fMRI and a novel repetition suppression paradigm in desktop virtual reality, we investigated the neural coding of spatial locations derived from landmarks versus visual self-motion cues (optic flow). We identified adaptation-based allocentric positional coding in the retrosplenial cortex (RSC) for both cue types. However, multi-voxel activation patterns for these locations were cue-specific and did not generalize between conditions. These findings demonstrate that the human RSC can maintain distinct, cue-dependent neural maps of the same physical space, providing insight into the parallel processing of multimodal spatial information.
papers.authors: Xiaoli Chen, Ziwei Wei, Thomas Wolbers

E119.name: Janice Chen
E119.bio: Janice Chen is an Assistant Professor at Johns Hopkins University who investigates the neural mechanisms underlying the construction and retrieval of complex, real-world episodic memories. Their research utilizes naturalistic stimuli such as movies and narratives combined with functional neuroimaging and pattern analysis techniques to characterize how mnemonic and sensory systems interact. Chen has conducted studies on neural reinstatement and shared neural representations across individuals during the processing of continuous, semantically rich information.
E119.research_direction: Dr. Chen has recently been investigating how the human brain segments, encodes, and reactivates continuous, naturalistic experiences to form episodic memories. Using fMRI data collected during continuous movie-viewing and narrated recall, their recent work explores how transient shifts in multivoxel activity patterns across the cortical hierarchy correspond to the perceived salience of event boundaries. They are also applying clustering and hidden Markov modeling to understand how the default mode network utilizes a core set of reactivatable neural states to represent abstract situational models, such as high-level actions and social-affective narrative dimensions. Expanding beyond passive perception, their research investigates the role of active agency in memory organization, employing interactive narrative paradigms to examine how volitional choice shapes and personalizes idiosyncratic memory structures compared to generic semantic frameworks.

papers.title: A core set of neural states underlying naturalistic memory reactivation in the posterior medial cortex
papers.abstract: This research utilizes fMRI data from movie encoding and narrated recall tasks to delineate a discrete set of prototypical neural states in the posterior medial cortex (PMC) that support episodic reactivation. By applying k-means clustering and hidden Markov modeling to multivoxel activity patterns, the authors identified a common set of approximately 16 neural states that are reliably stimulus-locked across individuals and reactivated during internal recollection. These identified states were found to be significantly associated with high-level actions and social-affective dimensions of the narrative stimuli, suggesting that the posterior default mode network employs a spatially organized, generalizable code for representing situational models and abstract event information.
papers.authors: Yoonjung Lee, Hongmi Lee, Janice Chen

papers.title: Agency personalizes episodic memories
papers.abstract: This study examines the role of agency and volitional choice in the organization of naturalistic episodic memories. Participants engaged with interactive 'choose-your-own-adventure' narratives where their decisions either dictated or were yoked to the trajectory of story events. While high causal and semantic centrality facilitated recall across all conditions, individuals with high agency exhibited significantly more idiosyncratic and personalized memory structures. Their recollections were characterized by a shift away from normative semantic associations, as indicated by decreased predictability from sentence embedding models, suggesting that self-directed control personalizes memory by prioritizing self-relevant information and idiosyncratic associative structures over generic narrative frameworks.
papers.authors: Xian Li, Nicole Kim Ni, Savannah Born, Ria Jacqueline Gualano, Iris Lee, Buddhika Bellana, Janice Chen

papers.title: The Relationship between Event Boundary Strength and Pattern Shifts across the Cortical Hierarchy during Naturalistic Movie-viewing
papers.abstract: The authors investigated how the perceived salience of event boundaries modulates neural activity shifts across different levels of the cortical processing hierarchy. By measuring transient changes in multivoxel activity patterns (cortical boundary shifts) during naturalistic movie-viewing, they found that boundary strength—quantified by cross-participant agreement—linearly predicts shift magnitude in short-timescale sensory regions, such as early auditory and visual cortex. In higher-level regions like the default mode network, stronger boundaries were associated with enhanced temporal alignment of neural transitions across hierarchical levels. Furthermore, hippocampal responses were maximal at event boundaries where shifts were most synchronized across the hierarchy, supporting the role of cross-level alignment in episodic encoding.
papers.authors: Yoonjung Lee, Janice Chen

E121.name: Moshe Bar
E121.bio: Moshe Bar is a cognitive neuroscientist and former director of the Gonda Multidisciplinary Brain Research Center at Bar-Ilan University and the Cognitive Neuroscience Laboratory at Harvard Medical School. Bar’s research focuses on the "proactive brain" framework, exploring how the brain utilizes memory and contextual associations to generate top-down predictions that facilitate visual recognition and guide behavior. Utilizing neuroimaging methods such as fMRI and MEG, Bar investigates the neural substrates of scene perception, mind-wandering, and creativity. Their current work applies these cognitive principles to clinical neuroscience by examining how thought progression and predictive mechanisms are altered in mood disorders like depression.
E121.research_direction: Dr. Bar has recently been investigating the shared cognitive and neural mechanisms underlying spontaneous thought, creativity, and curiosity. Their research explores theoretical frameworks that liken internal mental simulation to mammalian play, mapping how the default mode network interacts with executive systems to regulate the balance between exploratory novelty-seeking and focused exploitation. Additionally, they have been translating these cognitive dynamics into clinical applications, testing whether gamified digital interventions that induce rapid, broadly associative thought progression can successfully disrupt ruminative thinking in depression. Their recent work also extends into computational modeling, developing neurally constrained frameworks to examine the circuit-level mechanisms driving context-dependent fear extinction and memory relapse.

papers.title: Spontaneous thought as play: the value of fictional goals in the default mode network
papers.abstract: This review proposes a novel functional framework for spontaneous thought (ST) by drawing a formal analogy to mammalian play. ST, predominantly mediated by the default mode network (DMN), is characterized by the internal simulation of non-utilitarian, 'fictional' scenarios. The authors argue that these simulations serve as a training ground for the cognitive system, enhancing the brain's predictive capacity and facilitating the generation of novel plans and ideas that extend beyond immediate contextual demands. This mechanism is posited to underpin human intelligence and contribute significantly to affective stability and mental well-being.
papers.authors: Gaia Molinaro, Moshe Bar

papers.title: ConFER: A Neurally Constrained Computational Model of Context-Dependent Fear Extinction Recall and Relapse
papers.abstract: The authors introduce ConFER, a computational framework based on neural circuit constraints designed to explain context-dependent fear extinction and the mechanisms of relapse. The model incorporates distinct pathways for cue and contextual information processing, integrating valence-specific stimulus representations within the basolateral amygdala (BLA). By simulating competing associations, the model accounts for phenomena such as fear renewal and spontaneous recovery. Notably, ConFER predicts that counterconditioning provides superior resilience against relapse compared to standard extinction protocols across diverse contexts.
papers.authors: Shreya K. Rajagopal, Einat Levy-Gigi, Einav Sudai, Moshe Bar

papers.title: Facilitating Thought Progression to Reduce Depressive Symptoms: Randomized Controlled Trial
papers.abstract: In this randomized controlled trial, the efficacy of a digital health intervention targeting ruminative thinking—a hallmark of depression—was investigated. The intervention utilizes a gamified mobile platform designed to induce 'thought progression' (FTP) through exercises that promote rapid, semantically broad, and associative cognitive styles. Clinician-led evaluations using the Montgomery-Åsberg Depression Rating Scale (MADRS) revealed that participants in the FTP group experienced significantly greater symptom reduction compared to the waitlist control. These improvements were sustained at 4 weeks post-trial, supporting the hypothesis that modulating the dynamics of associative processing can effectively alleviate depressive symptoms.
papers.authors: Shai-Lee Yatziv, Paola Pedrelli, Shira Baror, Sydney Ann DeCaro, Noam Shachar, Bar Sofer, Sunday Hull, Joshua Curtiss, Moshe Bar

papers.title: A shared novelty-seeking basis for creativity and curiosity: Response to the commentators
papers.abstract: In this response to commentaries on the Novelty-Seeking Model (NSM), the authors refine their theory by addressing issues of conceptual ambiguity, neural fractionation, and developmental trajectories. They clarify the role of top-down and bottom-up dynamics within the State of Mind (SoM) framework and discuss how different cognitive pathways might lead to distinct subtypes of curiosity and creativity. The authors specifically address the possibility of functional fractionation within the default mode network (DMN) and executive control network (ECN), which may support the transition between episodic simulation and semantic evaluation during creative and exploratory tasks.
papers.authors: Tal Ivancovsky, Shira Baror, Moshe Bar

papers.title: A shared novelty-seeking basis for creativity and curiosity
papers.abstract: This target article posits that curiosity and creativity are not distinct cognitive faculties but rather different manifestations of a single novelty-seeking mechanism (NSM). The authors provide a comprehensive synthesis of behavioral and neuroscientific data, demonstrating that both constructs are similarly influenced by memory, attention, and reward systems, and share a common neural substrate involving the interplay between the default mode network (DMN), salience network (SN), and executive control network (ECN). The specific expression of the NSM is regulated by the individual's 'state of mind' (SoM), which dictates the balance between exploratory and exploitatory cognitive modes.
papers.authors: Tal Ivancovsky, Shira Baror, Moshe Bar

E122.name: Elissa Aminoff
E122.bio: Elissa Aminoff is an Associate Professor of Psychology at Fordham University and the director of the Vision and Memory (VAM) Lab. Aminoff’s research investigates the psychological and neural mechanisms of high-level visual perception, specifically how it interacts with memory and contextual associations. They employ a multi-method approach combining neuroimaging (fMRI, EEG, MEG), computational modeling, and psychophysics to explore scene understanding and object processing. This research characterizes scene-selective brain regions and the involvement of these areas in processing the associations evoked by complex visual environments.
E122.research_direction: Dr. Aminoff has recently been investigating distinct questions across high-level visual neuroscience and cognitive gerontology. Within vision science, their recent work explores the representational geometry of scene-selective and object-selective visual cortex using fMRI and representational similarity analysis. Specifically, they are examining how the individual objects embedded within complex natural scenes shape neural response patterns both within and across semantic scene categories. In a separate line of behavioral research, they have also been studying the aging mind by investigating how a person's subjective age impacts their objective and subjective cognitive functioning. Using survey data and formal statistical mediation models, they are working to identify the intermediary psychological pathways, such as depressive symptoms and self-rated health, that link self-perceived aging to cognitive performance in older adults.

papers.title: Examining Mediators of the Relationship Between Subjective Age and Cognition
papers.abstract: Although empirical work has established robust associations linking subjective age—the self-perceived age that an individual experiences relative to chronological age—to cognitive functioning, the intermediary pathways mediating this relationship remain largely undercharacterized. This investigation evaluated the predictive utility of subjective age on both objective cognitive performance and subjective cognitive assessments, specifically testing depressive symptomatology and self-rated health (SRH) as potential statistical mediators. Leveraging cross-sectional secondary survey data collected from a cohort of 247 community-dwelling adults aged 50 years and older, hierarchical linear regression analyses and formal mediation models were estimated. An older subjective age was significantly associated with decrements across subjective cognition metrics, with depressive symptoms and self-rated health operating as significant partial mediators of these associations. Given the clinical malleability of depressive affect and perceived health status, these factors provide tractable behavioral targets for interventions designed to preserve perceived cognitive vitality in aging adults.
papers.venue: GeroPsych: The Journal of Gerontopsychology and Geriatric Psychiatry
papers.authors: Karen L. Siedlecki, Veronika Kobrinsky, Elissa Aminoff

papers.title: Scene-selective brain regions respond to embedded objects of a scene
papers.abstract: Visual scenes are structurally defined by their embedded objects and associated affordances, yet high-level cortical processing of scenes has historically been conceptualized in functional opposition to object processing. Utilizing human functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data from the large-scale BOLD5000 dataset, this study examined whether constituent objects predict neural representational geometry across 1,179 unique natural scene exemplars distributed across 18 semantic scene categories. Representational similarity analyses of embedded object composition were conducted both across distinct semantic categories and among exemplars within identical scene categories. Neural response patterns across both scene-selective and object-selective visual cortex were significantly predicted by embedded object identities, with this effect manifesting as equally or more pronounced within scene-preferring regions. In particular, object composition explained significantly more variance when evaluating scenes within the same semantic category than across categories. These results indicate that the computational profile of scene-selective cortex directly encompasses the encoding of constituent objects, suggesting that functional specialization in higher visual cortex reflects processing demands deployed during interaction with stimulus arrays rather than categorical segregation by stimulus class.
papers.authors: Elissa M. Aminoff, Tess Durham

E125.name: Miriam Spering
E125.department: Department of Ophthalmology and Visual Sciences
E125.bio: Miriam Spering is an Associate Professor at the University of British Columbia and director of the UBC EyeLab, specializing in the neural mechanisms of visual-motor control. Their research utilizes eye movements as a model system to investigate how the human brain transforms sensory signals into coordinated motor responses. By integrating visual psychophysics with high-resolution eye tracking and motion capture, Spering examines the intersection of perception and action in healthy populations, athletes, and clinical groups. Their investigations focus on identifying the sensorimotor signals underlying decision-making and developing ocular biomarkers for neurodegenerative and psychiatric conditions, such as Parkinson's disease.
E125.research_direction: Dr. Spering has recently been investigating the tight link between visual motion processing and continuous motor actions, primarily using smooth pursuit, ocular following, and manual interception paradigms. Their recent work explores how sensory uncertainty, complex visual motion features, and multisensory cues influence the continuous execution and rapid inhibition of these high-speed sensorimotor responses. In addition to mapping the shared mechanisms of motion integration between perception and action, they are utilizing perception-action dissociations to study how the oculomotor system can track subliminal stimuli outside of conscious awareness. Furthermore, Dr. Spering is examining the clinical applications of these pathways, assessing how specific eye movement deficits can serve as objective biomarkers for basal ganglia dysfunction in Parkinson's disease.

papers.title: Visual factors that determine sensory uncertainty in rapid interceptive hand movements
papers.abstract: Human manual interception and the accompanying smooth pursuit eye movements are fundamentally constrained by the reliability of visual motion signals, determined here through independent manipulations of presentation and occlusion durations. Using a simulated flyball paradigm, this study demonstrates that truncated target presentation durations lead to a significant center-of-distribution bias in hand interception endpoints, indicative of increased reliance on internal priors under conditions of high sensory uncertainty. Conversely, while long occlusions also degrade performance, short occlusion durations effectively resolve the center bias, provided that sufficient initial motion evidence was accumulated. Trial-by-trial correlations between oculomotor tracking accuracy and interception spatial/timing errors suggest that predictive mechanisms for both eye and hand movements operate on a unified readout of target motion information from the motion integration system.
papers.authors: Abibat A. Akande, Philipp Kreyenmeier, Miriam Spering

papers.title: Perception-action dissociations as a window into consciousness
papers.abstract: Experimental paradigms that reveal qualitative dissociations between perceptual reports and motor actions offer a robust methodology for identifying the neural correlates of conscious and unconscious processing. This perspectives article synthesizes evidence showing that human eye movements, particularly smooth pursuit, can accurately track stimulus motion even when the observer lacks conscious awareness of the motion direction due to binocular rivalry or flash suppression. Such dissociations demonstrate that the oculomotor system possesses a lower sensitivity threshold for certain motion signals than the perceptual system, accessing information that remains subliminal to phenomenal awareness. These findings highlight the functional autonomy of specific sensorimotor pathways and suggest that oculomotor responses provide a more nuanced indicator of visual processing than report-based measures alone.
papers.authors: Marisa Carrasco, Miriam Spering

papers.title: Shared Mechanisms Drive Ocular Following and Motion Perception
papers.abstract: This study characterizes the dynamics of neural motion integration in humans by comparing perceptual direction estimates with short-latency ocular following responses (OFR) to complex moving plaid stimuli. By systematically varying the contrast ratio between the two component gratings, the authors demonstrate that both eye movements and perceptual judgments exhibit an initial bias toward the high-contrast component direction before transitioning to pattern-based motion tracking as integration progresses. This temporal evolution of behavioral responses parallels the physiological shift from component- to pattern-tuning observed in direction-selective neurons within primate area MT. The presence of significant trial-by-trial correlations between tracking performance and perceptual reports further suggests that perception and the OFR utilize a common motion integration stage, establishing the OFR as a reliable behavioral proxy for neural integration dynamics.
papers.authors: Philipp Kreyenmeier, Romesh Kumbhani, J. Anthony Movshon, Miriam Spering

papers.title: Smooth pursuit inhibition reveals audiovisual enhancement of fast movement control
papers.abstract: Rapid sensorimotor control, such as the inhibition of ongoing smooth pursuit eye movements during target interception, utilizes multisensory signals to optimize performance in dynamic environments. Observers were tasked with suppressing pursuit as a target reached a hit zone, while congruency and timing of auditory motion cues were varied. The results indicate that auditory motion signals congruent with the visual target significantly improve both the latency and spatial precision of pursuit inhibition, reducing stop-signal delays and spatial variability. This cross-modal enhancement suggests that the low-level oculomotor circuitry responsible for fast motor decisions integrates auditory and visual information to enhance movement stability, confirming that multisensory integration facilitates the execution of high-speed motor control and reactive inhibitory processes.
papers.authors: Philipp Kreyenmeier, Israt Bhuiyan, Megan Gian, Hiu Mei Chow, Miriam Spering

papers.title: Eye movements in Parkinson's disease: from neurophysiological mechanisms to diagnostic tools
papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) provides a critical clinical model for investigating the role of basal ganglia-thalamocortical circuitry in oculomotor regulation. This review delineates how dysfunction in the hyperdirect, direct, and indirect pathways manifests as hallmark oculomotor deficits, including prolonged saccadic latencies, reduced gain, and impaired smooth pursuit maintenance. The authors synthesize recent advances in utilizing these eye movement metrics as objective, non-invasive digital biomarkers for phenotyping disease progression and monitoring response to therapeutic interventions such as dopaminergic medication and deep brain stimulation. While current evidence suggests that eye movements lack the specificity required for standalone diagnosis, their integration into high-dimensional longitudinal datasets alongside other clinical indicators represents a promising avenue for precision neurology in movement disorders.
papers.authors: Chrystalina A. Antoniades, Miriam Spering

E129.name: John M. Henderson
E129.bio: John M. Henderson is a Professor of Psychology at UC Davis whose research examines the acquisition and manipulation of visual information from complex environments to guide behavior. Utilizing a multimodal approach including eye-tracking, fMRI, and computational simulations, Henderson investigates the cognitive processes underlying scene perception, reading, and visual memory. Their current research focuses on the role of semantics in gaze control, specifically through the development of 'meaning maps' to quantify how knowledge-based importance drives visual attention. Henderson also studies the neural correlates of fixation durations and the interaction between vision and language during naturalistic tasks.
E129.research_direction: Dr. Henderson has recently been investigating how high-level semantic meaning guides visual attention, perception, and memory within complex naturalistic scenes. Their recent work explores the underlying mechanisms of scene guidance using data-driven meaning map methodologies and advanced vision-language transformers to computationally quantify local scene semantics. By employing paradigms such as change detection flickering and scene inversion, they are assessing how observers prioritize top-down semantic informativeness versus bottom-up visual saliency when parsing local objects and global scene gist. Furthermore, they are examining how reliance on these semantic schemas evolves across the lifespan, probing spatial recall in older adults to test whether scene knowledge compensates for episodic memory decline, and tracking infant gaze to characterize the developmental transition toward meaning-driven attentional control.

papers.title: Scene inversion impairs activation of scene-object semantic bias
papers.abstract: This study examines the top-down mechanisms of gist-activated scene-object semantic bias in parsing complex naturalistic environments. Utilizing a brief presentation paradigm with upright and inverted scenes, the researchers assessed how global semantic structure modulates the activation of expectations for semantically consistent versus inconsistent objects. Findings reveal that scene inversion significantly attenuates and delays the activation of these biases. Furthermore, the results highlight a hierarchical processing advantage, where superordinate-level semantic biases are activated earlier and exhibit greater robustness than basic-level biases, providing evidence for the functional priority of global scene gist in driving local semantic associations.
papers.authors: Alan Z. Lu, John M. Henderson

papers.title: DeepMeaning: Estimating and Interpreting Scene Meaning for Attention Using a Vision-Language Transformer
papers.abstract: The authors introduce DeepMeaning, a computational framework leveraging the Contrastive Captioner (CoCa) vision-language transformer to quantify local scene semantics and their influence on attentional guidance. By mapping image-text embeddings from a model trained on large-scale datasets, the framework estimates patch-level meaning and decomposes these representations into four primary semantic dimensions: object density, figure-ground organization, interaction potential, and local context consistency. Results indicate that these dimensions collectively account for over 50% of the explainable variance in human meaning ratings and fixation density, demonstrating that multimodal transformers can effectively serve as interpretable models for scene-based cognitive guidance.
papers.authors: Taylor R. Hayes, John M. Henderson

papers.title: Meaning maps predict reaction time in change detection
papers.abstract: Investigating the role of high-level semantic representations in visual change detection, this research employs a data-driven meaning-map methodology within a classic flicker paradigm. Across two experiments, the authors demonstrate that changes occurring in regions of high semantic informativeness (local meaning) are detected significantly faster than those in low-meaning regions, an effect that persists after statistically controlling for low-level image saliency. The observed semantic advantage was markedly reduced under scene inversion, suggesting that the visual system prioritizes the comparison of semantic features maintained in working memory for detecting environmental modifications.
papers.authors: Alan Z. Lu, Aditya Upadhyayula, John M. Henderson

papers.title: How schema knowledge influences memory in older adults: Filling in the gaps, or leading memory astray?
papers.abstract: This investigation explores the complex dynamics of schema-congruency effects on episodic memory in the context of cognitive aging. Using a spatial recall task for target objects in congruent or incongruent scene locations, the authors contrast compensatory and impairment-based accounts of age-related schema reliance. The findings demonstrate that increased schematic influences on spatial memory in older adults are statistically mediated by declines in recollection-based memory processes. The data suggest that schema knowledge serves as a compensatory scaffold when precise episodic details are unavailable, with recollection acting as a primary mechanism capable of overriding schematic bias in both young and older populations.
papers.authors: Michelle M. Ramey, Andrew P. Yonelinas, John M. Henderson

papers.title: The role of local meaning in infants' fixations of natural scenes
papers.abstract: The study characterizes the developmental trajectory of semantic influences on visual attention by evaluating the impact of local meaning on the fixation patterns of infants aged 4 to 12 months. Controlling for physical saliency and center bias through meaning-map and saliency-map comparisons, the researchers found that infants increasingly prioritize semantically informative scene regions for fixation as they mature. This provides the first empirical evidence for an age-related shift from predominantly feature-driven (bottom-up) attentional control to more meaning-driven (top-down) guidance during the first year of life, aligning infant scene-viewing behavior with adult-like cognitive priorities.
papers.authors: Lisa M. Oakes, Taylor R. Hayes, Shannon M. Klotz, Katherine I. Pomaranski, John M. Henderson

E131.name: Doug Munoz
E131.department: Biomedical and Molecular Sciences, Psychology, and Medicine
E131.bio: Douglas P. Munoz is a Professor at Queen’s University and the founding director of the Queen’s Centre for Neuroscience Studies. Munoz's research investigates the neural circuitry governing saccadic eye movements, pupillary responses, and blinking, with a focus on the roles of the cerebral cortex, basal ganglia, and superior colliculus. By integrating behavioral neurophysiology, neuroimaging, and high-resolution eye-tracking, their laboratory develops quantitative metrics to evaluate sensory, motor, and cognitive brain functions. Their work focuses on translating these findings into clinical applications, specifically establishing eye-tracking biomarkers for the early diagnosis and progression monitoring of neurological and psychiatric disorders, including Parkinson’s disease and Alzheimer’s disease.
E131.research_direction: Dr. Munoz has recently been investigating the fundamental kinematics and strategic control of the human oculomotor system across the lifespan, including the characterization of a pupillary "main sequence" and the optimization of spontaneous blink timing under varying cognitive loads. Their recent work also explores the clinical utility of multimodal eye-tracking metrics—encompassing pro- and anti-saccades, pupillary responses, and blinks—as non-invasive biomarkers to detect prodromal Parkinson’s disease and predict the future onset of severe motor symptoms like freezing of gait. Additionally, they are investigating the neural basis of gaze control during naturalistic behavior, combining single-unit recordings in the primate superior colliculus with computational saliency models to understand how visual features and midbrain activity dictate saccade timing and fixation durations during the free viewing of dynamic scenes.

papers.title: Learning to Blink Strategically Is Crucial to Performance in a Predictable Saccade Task and Varies Across the Lifespan
papers.abstract: This longitudinal cohort study (N=703, age range 5–91 years) characterizes the ontogenetic development and age-related decline of strategic blink modulation during a predictable oculomotor task. Using video-based eye tracking during an interleaved pro- and anti-saccade paradigm, we quantified the temporal distribution of spontaneous blinks relative to critical task intervals. We demonstrate that participants optimize blink timing by suppressing blinks during periods of high visual and cognitive load—specifically prior to and during the execution of antisaccades—and increasing blink probability during non-critical task phases. The capacity for this temporal optimization follows a non-linear trajectory across the lifespan, peaking in early adulthood. Crucially, we found that participants with poorer inhibitory control (higher antisaccade error rates) exhibited significantly reduced blink adaptation, suggesting that the strategic regulation of blinks shares common neural mechanisms with top-down oculomotor control and executive function.
papers.authors: Isabell C. Pitigoi, Donald C. Brien, Heidi C. Riek, Blake K. Noyes, Rachel Yep, Olivia G. Calancie, Ryan H. Kirkpatrick, Brian C. Coe, Michele Morningstar, Douglas P. Munoz

papers.title: The relation of eye movements to the occurrence of freezing of gait in Parkinson's disease
papers.abstract: This prospective longitudinal study, conducted as part of the Ontario Neurodegenerative Disease Research Initiative (ONDRI), investigated whether quantitative oculomotor metrics could predict the onset of freezing of gait (FOG) in Parkinson’s disease (PD). PD patients who were initially FOG-negative underwent biennial eye-tracking and clinical assessments. Analysis revealed that patients who progressed to FOG within the follow-up period exhibited baseline abnormalities in the antisaccade task, specifically increased saccadic reaction times and elevated direction error rates, compared to those who did not develop FOG. These oculomotor deficits, alongside increased upper limb rigidity, preceded the clinical emergence of gait freezing, suggesting that dysfunction in shared neural circuits—likely encompassing the mesencephalic locomotor region and frontostriatal pathways—underlies the pathogenesis of both oculomotor and gait initiation impairments in PD.
papers.authors: Juan Fernandez-Ruiz, Heidi C. Riek, Donald C. Brien, Brian C. Coe, David A. Grimes, Anthony E. Lang, Connie Marras, Mario Masellis, Richard H. Swartz, Brian Tan, Malcolm A. Binns, Stephen R. Arnott, the ONDRI Investigators, Douglas P. Munoz

papers.title: Main Sequence of Human Luminance-evoked Pupil Dynamics
papers.abstract: We report a detailed characterization of the motor kinematics and non-linear properties of the human pupillary light reflex. By systematically varying background luminance levels, we identified a non-linear relationship between luminance and steady-state pupil diameter that is effectively linearized through logarithmic scaling. We describe a pupillary 'main sequence'—a highly stereotyped, non-linear relationship between peak constriction velocity and peak diameter change—that is conserved across individuals and lighting conditions, analogous to the main sequence observed in saccadic eye movements. While we observed substantial trial-by-trial and across-participant variability in response metrics, resting pupil diameter was positively correlated with pupil gain. These findings provide a robust empirical framework for the quantitative analysis of pupil dynamics in basic science and clinical applications, highlighting conserved kinematic constraints in autonomic motor control.
papers.authors: Jonathan D. Coutinho, Jeff Huang, Philippe Lefèvre, Gunnar Blohm, Douglas P. Munoz

papers.title: Saliency Response in Superior Colliculus at the Future Saccade Goal Predicts Fixation Duration during Free Viewing of Dynamic Scenes
papers.abstract: To elucidate the neural correlates of saccade timing during naturalistic behavior, we recorded from single neurons in the primate superior colliculus (SC) while monkeys freely viewed dynamic videos. We integrated neurophysiological data with a computational saliency model to determine how visual saliency and SC activity at a future saccade goal influence the preceding fixation duration. Our results show that visual saliency at the goal—primarily motion and edge features—inversely correlates with fixation duration. Neurons in both the superficial (SCs) and intermediate (SCi) layers of the SC exhibited discharge rates that predicted the timing of saccade initiation. Furthermore, SCs neurons showed significantly higher activation during sequences of consecutive short fixations, providing evidence for concurrent saccade processing within the midbrain oculomotor circuit during free viewing of complex, dynamic environments.
papers.authors: Jessica Heeman, Brian J. White, Stefan Van der Stigchel, Jan Theeuwes, Laurent Itti, Douglas P. Munoz

papers.title: Multimodal oculomotor assessment reveals prodromal markers of Parkinson's disease in non-manifesting LRRK2 G2019S mutation carriers
papers.abstract: This study utilized a comprehensive multimodal oculomotor battery to detect early physiological markers of neurodegeneration in non-manifesting carriers of the LRRK2 G2019S mutation (LRRK2-NM), a prodromal cohort for Parkinson's disease (PD). We quantified saccadic performance, pupillary responses, and blink behaviors during an interleaved pro- and anti-saccade task in LRRK2-NM participants, idiopathic PD patients, and healthy controls. LRRK2-NM carriers exhibited subtle but distinct impairments in antisaccade latency and blink suppression patterns that resembled the deficits observed in established PD. These findings indicate that quantitative assessment of oculomotor and pupillary control can identify subclinical neurological dysfunction prior to the manifestation of classic motor symptoms, supporting the role of eye-tracking as a sensitive, non-invasive biomarker for monitoring disease progression in genetic forms of Parkinsonism.
papers.authors: Heidi C. Riek, Naomi P. Visanji, Isabell C. Pitigoi, Daniel G. Di Luca, Laura Armengou-Garcia, Nazish Ahmed, Julia E. Perkins, Donald C. Brien, Jeff Huang, Brian C. Coe, Anthony E. Lang, Douglas P. Munoz

E136.name: Tirin Moore
E136.bio: Tirin Moore is the Ben Barres Professor of Neurobiology at Stanford University and an Investigator of the Howard Hughes Medical Institute. Moore’s research investigates the neural circuits integrating visual perception with motor control, particularly the mechanisms of selective attention and gaze control in primates. This work identifies a causal link between prefrontal cortical activity in the frontal eye fields and the modulation of visual signals in the extrastriate cortex. Moore’s laboratory uses neurophysiological methods, including large-scale, high-density electrophysiological recordings and pharmacological perturbations, to examine the circuit-level logic of cognitive functions.
E136.research_direction: Dr. Moore's recent work explores the neural mechanisms underlying working memory, object permanence, and contextual visual processing across the primate visual and prefrontal cortices. They have recently been investigating how cognitive representations—such as the identity of occluded objects, abstract sensorimotor mapping rules, and mnemonic information—are sustained dynamically through neuronal ensemble coordination and transient functional connectivity. Using high-density electrophysiological recordings and targeted cortical inactivations, their research also examines how top-down signals from areas like the frontal eye field and feedback-driven interlaminar pathways shape contextual modulation in early visual cortex. To support these investigations, they are developing computationally efficient, real-time spike sorting frameworks for large-scale probe arrays like Neuropixels to enable advanced closed-loop neurophysiological experiments.

papers.title: A System for Live Sorting of Neuronal Spiking Activity from Large-scale Recordings
papers.abstract: We present the Live Sorting System (LSS), a computationally efficient framework for the real-time isolation and quantification of single-neuron spiking activity from large-scale, high-density electrophysiological arrays such as Neuropixels. LSS facilitates closed-loop neurophysiological experiments by leveraging the Kilosort4 template-matching architecture to establish initial waveform profiles, which are then used to assign incoming data batches (50 ms) via the SpikeGLX API. Benchmarking in macaque visual cortex demonstrates that LSS-derived post-stimulus time histograms (PSTHs) and visual response tuning curves are statistically indistinguishable from those produced by rigorous offline sorting. Furthermore, online population decoding using LSS significantly outperforms conventional voltage-thresholded methods and achieves parity with offline decoding performance.
papers.authors: Shreyas Muralidharan, Calvin Leng, Lucas Orts, Ethan Trepka, Shude Zhu, Matthew Panichello, Donatas Jonikaitis, Jacob Pennington, Marius Pachitariu, Tirin Moore

papers.title: Ensemble Coding of Hidden Objects in Visual Cortex
papers.abstract: This study investigates the neural substrates of object permanence within the dorsal extrastriate cortex of macaque monkeys. While population firing rates encoded the spatial trajectory of stimuli during occlusion, information regarding object identity within individual neuronal firing rates typically decayed to chance levels before the conclusion of the trial. However, identity information was robustly preserved within the spatiotemporal coordination of neuronal populations. Specifically, the structure and strength of pairwise cross-correlations among neurons within local ensembles reliably signaled the identity of hidden objects, independent of mean firing rate fluctuations. These results suggest that visual cortical circuits sustain representations of non-visible objects through ensemble-level coordination, even in the absence of direct retinal input or persistent single-unit spiking.
papers.authors: Shude Zhu, Danielle A. Lopes, Stephen Niño Cital, Tirin Moore

papers.title: Robust encoding of stimulus–response mapping by neurons in visual cortex
papers.abstract: We examine whether behavioral modulation of sensory cortical activity represents stimulus selection or abstract sensorimotor mapping rules. Monkeys performed tasks requiring the conversion of a remembered visual cue into specific oculomotor responses governed by alternating rules. We show that neurons in area V4 robustly encode the stimulus-response mapping rule during the memory-delay period, signaling the preparation of appropriate motor outputs rather than simply the sensory details of the memorandum. Furthermore, this motor-related delay activity was significantly diminished following the local inactivation of the frontal eye field (FEF). These findings indicate that visual cortical activity is modulated by top-down prefrontal signals to represent abstract behavioral variables, challenging the classical view that sensory areas are restricted to representing low-level stimulus attributes.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS)
papers.authors: Donatas Jonikaitis, Ruobing Xia, Tirin Moore

papers.title: Intermittent rate coding and cue-specific ensembles support working memory
papers.abstract: The classical model of working memory posits that memorandum-specific information is sustained by persistent neuronal spiking activity. By recording from large populations of lateral prefrontal neurons on single trials, we demonstrate that mnemonic information is intermittent, characterized by rapid transitions between coordinated 'On' and 'Off' states. During 'Off' states, single-neuron firing rates return to spontaneous levels and selectivity is lost; however, information remains decodable from the patterns of functional connectivity among neuronal ensembles. These results reconcile the controversy between 'persistent activity' and 'activity-silent' models by demonstrating that working memory relies on a hybrid mechanism where intermittent periods of rate coding coexist with information maintained in the transient synaptic structure of neuronal ensembles.
papers.authors: Matthew F. Panichello, Donatas Jonikaitis, Yu Jin Oh, Shude Zhu, Ethan B. Trepka, Tirin Moore

papers.title: Dependence of contextual modulation in macaque V1 on interlaminar signal flow
papers.abstract: Utilizing high-density Neuropixels probes, we investigated the laminar microcircuitry in macaque V1 underlying border ownership (Bown) modulation, a form of contextual integration involving nonclassical receptive field (nCRF) interactions. We quantified temporally precise cross-correlations to assess functional interactions among neurons across cortical layers during CRF and nCRF stimulation. Our results reveal that the magnitude of Bown modulation is reliably predicted by the proportion of interlaminar information flow originating from feedback/horizontal layers (layers 1–3 and 5/6) and targeting canonical input layers (layer 4C). This finding suggests that contextual modulation in V1 is dynamically regulated by the strength of feedback-driven interlaminar signaling, providing a functional logic for how top-down and horizontal inputs are integrated into local laminar processing.
papers.authors: Shude Zhu, Yu Jin Oh, Ethan B. Trepka, Xiaomo Chen, Tirin Moore

E140.name: Eckart Zimmermann
E140.bio: Eckart Zimmermann is a Professor of Perceptual Psychology at Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf, where they investigate the mechanisms underlying visual stability and spatial perception. Zimmermann’s research focuses on how the brain maintains a representation of the environment during retinal shifts caused by saccadic eye movements. Utilizing psychophysical methods, eye-tracking, and fMRI adaptation, they study spatiotopic coding, the role of efference copies in sensory attenuation, and the repulsive aftereffects of visual adaptation. Their work also addresses numerosity perception and the processes by which motor actions, such as walking, calibrate the visual perception of distance.
E140.research_direction: Dr. Zimmermann has recently been investigating how the visual system maintains spatial stability and updates predictions during self-generated movements. Their recent work explores the mechanisms of visuospatial constancy and saccadic omission, using techniques like immersive virtual reality and high-precision motion tracking to isolate the contributions of oculomotor corollary discharge and active head movements to spatial remapping. In parallel, they are examining how sensory attenuation and temporal predictability influence serial dependence, questioning how the brain dynamically weights recent perceptual history to interpret self-produced versus external stimuli. Finally, Dr. Zimmermann applies these computational frameworks to neurodiversity, probing whether individuals with high autistic traits exhibit altered sensorimotor predictions, mis-calibrated internal forward models, or an inflexible updating of perceptual priors during dynamic tasks.

papers.title: Reduced prediction updating shapes serial dependence in autistic traits
papers.abstract: This study utilized an immersive virtual reality penalty-kick paradigm to investigate the computational architecture of serial dependence in dynamic contexts and its alteration in individuals with high autistic traits. By introducing trial-by-trial prediction errors via lateral displacements of a disappearing ball, the authors demonstrated that individuals with elevated autistic traits exhibit significant prediction deviations, indicative of mis-calibrated internal forward models. Crucially, these individuals showed an inflexible and heightened reliance on priors, failing to down-weight them even when sensory distortions were maximized. This rigidity in prediction weighting suggests a failure in the dynamic updating of internal models in response to feedback, rather than a primary perceptual deficit, with domain experts exhibiting contrasting, perturbation-resistant stabilization strategies.
papers.authors: Antonella Pomè, Michael Wiesing, Eckart Zimmermann

papers.title: Disrupted sensorimotor predictions in high autistic characteristics
papers.abstract: This research investigates the role of oculomotor corollary discharge (CD) in visual stability and its impairment in neurodiversity. Using a saccadic omission task involving high-frequency gratings that become visible only during saccade-induced retinal motion, the study quantified how autistic traits affect the prediction of sensory consequences. Results indicate that individuals with high autistic quotient (AQ) scores display unselective habituation to intra-saccadic motion, attributed to imprecise CD/efference copy signals. The inability to accurately forecast and discount self-produced sensory input leads to impaired spatial updating and broad suppression generalization. These findings support a model where sensory sensitivities in autism are linked to a failure in maintaining visuospatial constancy through precise sensorimotor predictions.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS)
papers.authors: Antonella Pomè, Eckart Zimmermann

papers.title: Serial dependencies for externally and self-generated stimuli
papers.abstract: This study characterizes the interaction between sensory attenuation and serial dependence in visuospatial localization. Through a series of psychophysical experiments, the authors assessed how the attenuation of self-generated stimuli, driven by temporal predictability, modulates the magnitude of serial biases. The data reveal that temporal predictability consistently induces sensory attenuation, which in turn increases the reliance on recent perceptual history. The strength of the serial dependence effect was found to be contingent on the relative uncertainty between consecutive trials, with stronger biases occurring when the prior trial’s stimulus was more certain (less attenuated) than the current one. This suggests that the brain dynamically weights past experiences based on their relative precision to optimize the interpretation of self-produced versus external stimuli.
papers.authors: Clara Fritz, Antonella Pomè, Eckart Zimmermann

papers.title: Active head movements contribute to spatial updating across gaze shifts
papers.abstract: This investigation quantifies the contribution of head-related motor signals to the recalibration of internal spatial representations. Utilizing head-mounted displays and high-precision motion tracking, the researchers analyzed spatial updating during active gaze shifts involving simultaneous eye and head rotations. By manipulating the visual velocity gain relative to head displacement, the authors were able to isolate the role of vestibular and proprioceptive feedback. The findings demonstrate that active head movements are a primary driver of visual space remapping, indicating that the mechanisms of visuospatial constancy incorporate motor plan information from the entire gaze-control hierarchy, including head-in-space commands, rather than relying exclusively on oculomotor efference copies.
papers.authors: Manuel Bayer, Eckart Zimmermann

papers.title: Prediction of sensorimotor contingencies generates saccadic omission
papers.abstract: Addressing the neural basis of saccadic suppression, this work proposes that saccadic omission is a consequence of habituation to learned sensorimotor contingencies. Over several experimental sessions, participants were exposed to systematic intra-saccadic displacements, creating a predictable relationship between eye movements and retinal motion. The study found that such exposure leads to a selective reduction in the visibility of the anticipated intra-saccadic stimulation. This habituation is highly specific to the predicted motion parameters and depends on the integrity of the motor planning signal (efference copy). The results suggest that the brain actively omits predictable sensory disturbances through a dynamic calibration of internal models, facilitating perceptual stability across saccades.
papers.authors: Antonella Pomè, Nadine Schlichting, Clara Fritz, Eckart Zimmermann
