E141.name: Melvyn A. Goodale
E141.department: Department of Psychology; Department of Physiology and Pharmacology
E141.bio: Melvyn A. Goodale is a Distinguished University Professor Emeritus at Western University and co-proposed the "two-visual-systems" hypothesis, which dissociates the ventral stream for object perception from the dorsal stream for the visual control of action. Goodale’s research utilizes functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and kinematic behavioral analysis to investigate the neural pathways underlying visual processing in both healthy individuals and patients with neurological damage. Their work demonstrates how the brain separates conscious visual experience from the unconscious motor programming required for interacting with the physical world.
E141.research_direction: Dr. Goodale's recent work explores the functional dissociation between vision for perception and vision for action, extending their foundational "Two Visual Systems Hypothesis" across a wide range of behavioral and neuroimaging contexts. They have recently been using kinematic tracking and psychophysical measures to investigate whether the classic dorsal-ventral separation holds during size constancy tasks and size-contrast illusions, while also examining how these perception-action dynamics might differ between left- and right-handed individuals or be supported by feedforward networks in visual form agnosia (Patient DF). Beyond visually guided grasping, their research explores cross-modal sensory substitution by investigating whether expert blind echolocators experience the material-weight illusion to see how acoustic echoes inform motor and perceptual predictions. Finally, they are investigating higher-level visual processing by developing new analytical frameworks to decouple systematic response bias from true perceptual precision in facial age estimation tasks for both human observers and artificial intelligence systems.

papers.title: Separating error from bias: A new framework for facial age estimation in humans and AIs
papers.abstract: The authors identify a fundamental methodological confound in existing facial age estimation literature, where the standard Mean Absolute Error (MAE) metric conflates precision with systematic response bias (directional over- or under-estimation). By introducing a novel 'MAE-Unbiased' (MAE-Us) framework that isolates the variance of estimates from the chronological-age-bias (CAB) effect, the researchers re-analyzed large-scale human and AI datasets. The findings demonstrate that both biological and artificial systems are significantly more accurate than previously estimated when bias is decoupled from error, and that the perceived decline in accuracy for older and younger faces is largely an artifact of response bias rather than a precision deficit.
papers.authors: Tzvi Ganel, Yarden Mazuz, Daniel Algom, Melvyn A. Goodale

papers.title: The Two Visual Systems Hypothesis: New challenges and insights from visual form agnosic patient DF
papers.abstract: This comprehensive review updates the longitudinal record of patient DF, whose visual form agnosia provided foundational evidence for the functional dissociation between the ventral 'perception' and dorsal 'action' streams. The paper addresses recent theoretical challenges, confirming that DF’s preserved grasping dexterity relies on feedforward visuomotor networks in the dorsal stream rather than atypical haptic or online feedback loops. The study provides new neuroimaging evidence characterizing the progression of DF’s dorsal-stream lesions and surrounding atrophy, which explains her selective impairments in peripheral reaching while reinforcing the core tenets of the Two Visual Systems Hypothesis (TVSH).
papers.venue: Neuropsychologia (Special Issue: A Tribute to Mel Goodale)
papers.authors: Robert L. Whitwell, A. David Milner, Melvyn A. Goodale

papers.title: Size constancy in perception and action
papers.abstract: The study examines the neurocomputational mechanisms underlying size constancy—the ability to perceive object size as invariant despite variations in retinal image size with viewing distance. Utilizing a combination of psychophysical judgments and kinematic recordings of grasping movements, the researchers investigate how different modalities (visual, auditory, and proprioceptive) contribute to the scaling of object metrics in the ventral and dorsal streams. The paper highlights a persistent dissociation where visuomotor scaling (grip constancy) often shows superior accuracy compared to perceptual size estimates under impoverished viewing conditions, supporting the distinct metric requirements of vision-for-perception and vision-for-action.
papers.venue: Neuropsychologia (Special Issue: A Tribute to Mel Goodale)
papers.authors: Robert L. Whitwell, Irene Sperandio, Gavin Buckingham, Melvyn A. Goodale

papers.title: Weight perception and the material-weight illusion in expert human echolocators
papers.abstract: This research explores the limits of sensory substitution by investigating whether expert blind echolocators experience the material-weight illusion (MWI) through acoustic echoes. Using self-generated mouth clicks, participants assessed the material and weight of objects presented at various distances. The study demonstrates that expert echolocators can extract material properties from echoes to inform their weight expectations, yet they exhibit a modified or attenuated MWI compared to the visual MWI in sighted individuals. These results suggest that while echolocation can recruit 'visual' cortical areas like the lateral occipital complex, the integration of echo-based material cues for motor and perceptual predictions follows a unique cross-modal profile.
papers.venue: Neuropsychologia (Special Issue: A Tribute to Mel Goodale)
papers.authors: Gavin Buckingham, Jennifer L. Milne, Caitlin Byrne, Melvyn A. Goodale

papers.title: Revisiting the effect of visual illusions on grasping in left and right handers
papers.abstract: The researchers investigated whether the classic perception-action dissociation observed in right-handers generalizes to left-handed individuals using the Ponzo size illusion. While right-handers exhibited resistance to the illusion in both hands, left-handers showed significant sensitivity to the visual context when grasping with their dominant left hand, while their non-dominant right hand remained refractory. This asymmetry suggests that the 'automatic' visuomotor control mechanisms of the dorsal stream may be more tightly coupled with ventral-stream perceptual representations in the dominant hand of left-handers, potentially reflecting differences in hemispheric specialization or greater cognitive monitoring of action execution in this group.
papers.authors: Tzvi Ganel, Melvyn A. Goodale

E143.name: J. Randall Flanagan
E143.department: Department of Psychology and Centre for Neuroscience Studies
E143.bio: Flanagan’s research examines the cognitive, computational, and neural mechanisms involved in the planning, control, and learning of human actions, specifically object manipulation. Using methodologies such as robotic interfaces, eye-tracking, and functional magnetic resonance imaging, Flanagan analyzes how the brain integrates sensory feedback with internal models to predict and adapt to environmental dynamics. Their work addresses eye-hand coordination and the predictive nature of gaze behavior during tool use and manual interaction. Current research investigates the whole-brain dynamics of sensorimotor adaptation and the manifold structures within the cerebellar-cortical network that underlie motor reinforcement learning.
E143.research_direction: Dr. Flanagan has recently been investigating the intricate coordination of eye and hand movements during complex, goal-directed actions. Their recent work explores how the sensorimotor system allocates gaze during manual tasks, examining phenomena such as "gaze anchoring"—where saccades to new targets are inhibited until a primary reach is confirmed successful via visual or haptic feedback—and how the visual system manages competing demands when individuals must simultaneously manipulate objects and monitor stochastic events in their environment. Using gaze tracking and multi-target reaching paradigms, they are also studying how the brain coordinates oculomotor and limb control policies to gather strategic visual information and resolve target uncertainty when facing competing reach goals. Additionally, Dr. Flanagan investigates the effector-independent nature of sensorimotor memory by testing whether rapid, reflexive corrective responses—such as the vertical force adjustments made when lifting unexpectedly heavy objects—transfer between hands.

papers.title: Gaze-related functions driving gaze anchoring in reaching
papers.abstract: This study examines the phenomenon of 'gaze anchoring,' wherein saccadic eye movements toward a secondary target are inhibited until a primary reaching movement attains its objective. Using a multi-target reaching paradigm involving visual and haptic feedback manipulations, the research demonstrates that gaze remains foveated on the reach target until confirmation of success is received through either visual occlusion offsets or haptic contact signals. The results indicate that the duration of gaze anchoring is contingent upon the availability of sensory evidence confirming target acquisition, while planning for subsequent oculomotor responses can proceed concurrently with the manual action.
papers.authors: Jolande Fooken, Nethmi H. Illamperuma, J. Randall Flanagan

papers.title: Adaptive Gaze and Hand Coordination while Manipulating and Monitoring the Environment in Parallel
papers.abstract: The coordination of eye and hand movements was investigated in scenarios requiring simultaneous object manipulation and environmental monitoring. Using a dual-task paradigm where participants used either fingertips or tools to deposit a ball into a slot while detecting stochastic visual events, the study found that gaze is selectively allocated to critical sensorimotor control points, specifically contact events. Participants adapted by learning the temporal statistics of the monitoring task, adjusting the timing of their manual actions to minimize visual competition. The findings suggest that the sensorimotor system intelligently integrates environmental probabilities to optimize gaze allocation during parallel demands.
papers.authors: Jolande Fooken, Roland S. Johansson, J. Randall Flanagan

papers.title: Adaptation of the gain of the corrective lifting response in object manipulation transfers across the hand
papers.abstract: Skillful manipulation relies on rapid corrective responses to perturbations, such as the increased vertical force generated when an object is heavier than predicted. This study tested whether the adaptation of the gain of this corrective lifting response—the rate of force increase—generalizes between hands. Participants repeatedly lifted a light object that was occasionally replaced by a heavier 'catch' object, leading to a trial-by-trial increase in response gain. Results demonstrated that this gain adaptation transfers to the untrained hand on the first trial after switching, indicating that the sensorimotor memory updating the gain of reflexive corrective responses is maintained in an effector-independent coordinate system.
papers.authors: Michael R. McGarity-Shipley, Jason P. Gallivan, J. Randall Flanagan

papers.title: Gaze Behaviour Reveals Flexible Encoding of Competing Reach Goals Under Conditions of Target Uncertainty
papers.abstract: When planning reaches toward uncertain targets, the brain must manage multiple potential action goals. This research utilized gaze tracking to probe the internal representation of competing reach plans. Participants performed rapid reaching movements where the final target was one of several potential candidates. Gaze behavior revealed that the system does not simply average potential targets but flexibly encodes them by either tracking the spatial centroid of the distribution or biasing toward specific high-probability options. The findings suggest that oculomotor and limb control policies are coordinated to resolve uncertainty by prioritizing information gathering at strategic locations during the early phase of movement.
papers.authors: Anouk J. de Brouwer, M. J. Carter, L. C. Smail, Daniel M. Wolpert, Jason P. Gallivan, J. Randall Flanagan

E144.name: Eli Brenner
E144.bio: Eli Brenner is a researcher at the Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam whose work focuses on the intersection of visual perception and motor control. Brenner investigates how the brain utilizes distinct visual cues, such as position and velocity, to guide goal-directed movements like grasping, reaching, and hitting moving targets. Their methodology combines laboratory psychophysics with naturalistic studies to examine human interaction with dynamic environments. Currently, Brenner’s research explores the mechanisms of sensorimotor adaptation, the role of eye movements in locomotion, and the impact of sensory uncertainty on human action.
E144.research_direction: Dr. Brenner's recent work explores the interplay between visual information, cognitive expectations, and sensorimotor control during goal-directed actions. They have recently been investigating the kinematics of complex behaviors, examining how gaze is dynamically allocated between obstacle avoidance and grasp planning during walking, and how top-down expectations influence arm movements and ocular tracking. Their research also probes the mechanisms of online motor correction, questioning how hand trajectories are adjusted temporally and spatially to intercept jumping targets of varying speeds. Additionally, they are studying active vision and sensory substitution by testing how sensorimotor congruency impacts search efficiency through restricted foveal apertures, and identifying the minimal directional and temporal cues required to accurately guide the hand toward invisible targets.

papers.title: How a target’s speed influences the extent to which the time or place at which it is intercepted is adjusted
papers.abstract: This research evaluates the sensorimotor control policies governing the interception of moving targets, specifically determining whether corrective adjustments to hand trajectories prioritize spatial endpoint modification or temporal modulation. Using a paradigm where targets underwent abrupt jumps along their path at varying velocities, the authors analyzed how the central nervous system compensates for prediction errors. The findings indicate that while the absolute temporal magnitude of adjustments remains independent of target speed, the relative contribution of timing to error reduction is significantly enhanced at higher velocities, reflecting the increased spatial impact of temporal shifts for faster-moving stimuli. This suggests that the impact of timing adjustments scales with target kinematics rather than being dictated by a fixed temporal correction limit.
papers.authors: Giorgia Bertonati, Monica Gori, Jeroen B. J. Smeets, Eli Brenner

papers.title: Congruency between viewers' movements and the region of the display being sampled speeds up search through an aperture
papers.abstract: This study investigates the mechanisms underlying visual search efficiency within restricted foveal apertures, focusing on the role of sensorimotor congruency between manual inputs and visual feedback. Across multiple experiments, participants localized targets while either controlling the motion of a viewing aperture over a static display or moving the search display beneath a static aperture. The results demonstrate significant search acceleration only when the mapping between manual displacement and aperture sampling corresponds to intuitive egocentric expectations. Inverting these mappings eliminated the performance benefit, suggesting that spatial updating and memory for searched locations are optimized when sensory feedback aligns with self-generated motor commands and prior expectations of environmental interaction.
papers.authors: Emily M. Crowe, Danai T. Vorgia, Eli Brenner

papers.title: Guiding the Hand to an Invisible Target
papers.abstract: This research quantifies the minimal informational requirements for effective sensorimotor guidance in reaching tasks lacking direct visual target availability, aimed at informing the development of haptic assistive technologies. The study systematically manipulated the resolution of direction, distance, and time-to-arrival information provided to participants through visual cues in the absence of a visible target. Performance metrics, including reaching precision and path efficiency, suggest that motor control is highly resilient to coarse-grained temporal and distance information. However, reach performance is significantly more sensitive to the precision of directional cues. These findings provide critical design parameters for optimizing low-bandwidth sensory substitution devices and tactile bracelets for the visually impaired.
papers.authors: Marcin Furtak, Eli Brenner

papers.title: Gaze when walking to grasp an object in the presence of obstacles
papers.abstract: The paper examines the spatio-temporal dynamics of gaze allocation during a complex task requiring coordinated locomotion and manual interaction. By tracking eye movements as participants navigated a path containing both floor and tabletop obstacles to reach a target cup, the researchers assessed the distribution of foveal attention relative to task constraints. Quantitative analysis reveals that gaze is predominantly directed toward the primary locus of manual interaction—the target object—well before physical contact, while potential obstacles along the walking path are largely navigated using peripheral vision and spatial representations held in memory. The results indicate that high-resolution foveal processing is prioritized for planning precise grasp kinematics rather than path navigation or obstacle avoidance.
papers.authors: Dimitris Voudouris, Eli Brenner

papers.title: Methods matter: Exploring how expectations influence common actions
papers.abstract: This study investigates how high-level cognitive expectations and prior knowledge influence the execution of common goal-directed motor actions. Utilizing an experimental framework that varied the predictability of target behavior, the authors analyzed the kinematics of arm movements and the associated ocular tracking strategies. The research highlights that the influence of expectations on motor behavior is heavily modulated by the specific experimental methodology employed, such as the timing of cues and the consistency of stimulus presentation. The findings suggest that the integration of top-down expectations into sensorimotor control is a dynamic process that accounts for environmental reliability to optimize movement planning and online adjustments.
papers.authors: Andrea Ghiani, David Mann, Eli Brenner

E145.name: Jeroen Smeets
E145.bio: Jeroen Smeets is a Professor of Human Movement Sciences at Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam, specializing in the computational and experimental analysis of sensorimotor control. Their research focuses on the integration of visual information for goal-directed actions, specifically within the domains of interception, prehension, and the influence of perceptual illusions on motor performance. Smeets developed mathematical models of grasping and investigated the distinctions between perceptual and motor processing pathways. Their work examines how humans manage neural delays through continuous online corrections and the flexible use of sensory cues in dynamic environments.
E145.research_direction: Dr. Smeets has recently been investigating the mechanisms of online visuomotor control, motor adaptation, and spatial perception. Their recent work explores how the motor system integrates continuous visual feedback during goal-directed actions, using methods like brief visual occlusions and stochastic target perturbations to measure visual processing latencies and the strategic scaling of mid-flight corrective vigor. Beyond real-time movement control, they are studying reward-based motor learning across the lifespan to understand how differing success rates and binary feedback frequencies shape motor adaptation. Additionally, they are examining the multisensory nature of spatial vision by testing how whole-body orientation relative to gravity influences the weighting of egocentric versus allocentric reference frames during visual length judgments.

papers.title: Intercepting moving targets: does the visuomotor latency depend on whether one taps on the target or slides through it?
papers.abstract: This research evaluates the temporal characteristics of the human visuomotor control loop across different terminal constraints of an interceptive task. Participants were required to either tap a moving target, necessitating a reduction in terminal velocity, or slide through its trajectory to maintain momentum. By introducing stochastic spatial and temporal perturbations to the target, the investigators quantified the effective visuomotor latency from the onset of corrective motor responses. The findings clarify whether the intended interaction at the movement endpoint—stationary contact versus continuous motion—modulates the speed of visual processing for online trajectory control.
papers.authors: Eli Brenner, S. Bom, Jeroen B. J. Smeets

papers.title: Enforcing a high success percentage interferes with reward-based motor learning
papers.abstract: This study investigates the information-theoretic versus motivational effects of reward frequency in reinforcement-based motor adaptation across a developmental cohort (ages 7–58). Participants performed a circle-drawing task involving the scaling of movement radius based solely on binary auditory feedback. Two groups were maintained at either a 50% (moderate) or 80% (high) success rate through dynamic adjustment of target boundaries. While high success was hypothesized to bolster motivation, results indicated no significant group difference in self-reported engagement. However, the moderate success group demonstrated superior motor adaptation, suggesting that learning is optimized when binary feedback provides maximal entropy and that frequent failures are essential for updating internal models.
papers.authors: Katinka van der Kooij, Nina M. van Mastrigt, Moira van Leeuwen, Maaike van der Horst, Joyce E. Burger, Jeroen B. J. Smeets

papers.title: Do people only adjust ongoing movements vigorously when it is advantageous to do so?
papers.abstract: This investigation tests the strategic flexibility of visuomotor gains in online control, specifically whether the characteristic increase in vigor of late-stage corrections is an obligatory feature of the motor system. Participants responded to jittering targets where the task-relevant benefit of high-vigor corrections was systematically manipulated. By modeling acceleration profiles and response gains to target displacements, the authors demonstrate that online feedback gains are tuned according to the precision requirements and specific costs of error. The results suggest that the motor system actively scales the intensity of online corrections based on the instantaneous task-specific utility of precision.
papers.authors: Eli Brenner, Melissa L. Vlasblom, Ivo Rap, Jeroen B. J. Smeets

papers.title: Very briefly hiding the hand impedes goal-directed arm movements
papers.abstract: This experimental study quantifies the impact of brief visual occlusions and increased sensorimotor delays on the guidance of reaching movements. Participants navigated a cursor toward sequential targets under varying conditions of cursor visibility and temporal lag. The findings demonstrate that even millisecond-scale increases in average information delay, caused by hiding the cursor, significantly degrade reaching efficiency by increasing total movement time. Importantly, the research identifies that the temporal fraction of visibility is a more critical determinant of performance than the discrete update frequency, supporting a control model predicated on the quasi-continuous integration of recent visual feedback.
papers.authors: Eli Brenner, Jeroen B. J. Smeets

papers.title: The influence of body orientation on length judgements
papers.abstract: This study explores how whole-body orientation relative to the gravitational vector influences the perception of spatial extents. Utilizing a length-matching paradigm, participants estimated object lengths while positioned in various orientations, such as upright and supine. The data characterize whether spatial judgments are primarily anchored to an egocentric (body-fixed) frame or an allocentric (gravitational) frame. The results reveal systematic biases in perceived length as a function of body tilt, suggesting that multisensory integration of visual, vestibular, and somatosensory cues for size perception involves a complex weighting of reference frames that is sensitive to observer orientation.
papers.authors: Federica Scarpellini, Jeroen B. J. Smeets

E147.name: Sabrina Rossit
E147.bio: Rossit is an Associate Professor at the University of East Anglia who researches the neural mechanisms of human perception, motor control, and spatial attention. Their work focuses on how these processes are affected by stroke and brain injury, specifically visual neglect. Rossit uses functional MRI (fMRI), lesion-symptom mapping, and eye-tracking to develop and test interventions such as the c-SIGHT and EyeFocus neurorehabilitation trials. This research program relates cognitive neuroscience and clinical practice to study recovery outcomes for survivors of brain disease.
E147.research_direction: Dr. Rossit has recently been investigating the interplay between visuospatial attention and motor action across both healthy and clinical populations. Their recent work explores the visuomotor and functional consequences of stroke-induced visual neglect, examining how specific spatial reference frames—such as egocentric versus allocentric neglect—predict long-term recovery trajectories, and how these attentional deficits disrupt peripheral and bimanual reaching. In neurologically healthy individuals, they are studying spatial processing across different environments and lifespans, utilizing cancellation and line bisection tasks to assess aging effects on extrapersonal (far-space) attention, while also probing whether object affordances are preferentially processed in the lower visual field to facilitate reaching and grasping. Additionally, their methodological work advocates for increased transparency in the field, outlining practical frameworks for integrating preregistration and open science practices into the unique logistical challenges of neuropsychological patient research.

papers.title: Peripheral and bimanual reaching in a stroke survivor with left visual neglect and extinction
papers.abstract: This single-case investigation characterizes the visuomotor profile of a stroke survivor (E.B.) presenting with isolated left visual neglect and extinction in the absence of primary motor deficits. Utilizing a motion-tracking reaching paradigm, the study identifies a classical optic ataxia field effect, where reaching accuracy was significantly compromised for targets in the neglected contralesional peripheral visual field, irrespective of the reaching hand. Additionally, bimanual coordination tasks revealed a disproportionate movement time cost during incongruent reaching maneuvers compared to age-matched controls. These findings provide evidence that lateralized attentional deficits following posterior parietal damage frequently co-occur with specific visuomotor impairments in peripheral and bimanual reaching, suggesting overlapping neural substrates for spatial attention and the dorsal stream's control of action.
papers.authors: Ethan Knights, Robert D. McIntosh, Catherine Ford, Gavin Buckingham, Stéphanie Rossit

papers.title: Recovery of visuospatial neglect subtypes and relationship to functional outcome six months after stroke
papers.abstract: This longitudinal cohort study evaluated how acute egocentric and allocentric neglect phenotypes predict long-term recovery and functional independence in a sample of 400 stroke survivors. Standardized assessments (Oxford Cognitive Screen) were administered acutely and at six months post-stroke. Results demonstrated that while egocentric neglect followed a proportional recovery trajectory, allocentric neglect displayed a non-proportional pattern, with chronic patients failing to show expected rates of improvement. Multiple regression models revealed that initial allocentric neglect severity was a unique and significant predictor of poor functional outcomes (Stroke Impact Scale) at follow-up, whereas egocentric severity did not significantly improve the model's predictive power. These results highlight the clinical necessity of differentiating neglect reference frames to improve prognostic accuracy and target rehabilitation more effectively.
papers.authors: Helen Morse, Laura Biggart, Valerie M. Pomeroy, Stephanie Rossit

papers.title: Is there a lower visual field advantage for object affordances? A registered report
papers.abstract: The handle compatibility effect—characterized by faster responses when an object's handle orientation matches the responding hand—is often used to support affordance theories of object representation. This registered report systematically investigated whether this effect is modulated by the vertical visual field (VF) of stimulus presentation. Across two high-powered experiments (N=68 each), we found that the handle compatibility effect was absent in the upper VF and was not replicable when purely spatial compatibility was controlled. However, a robust compatibility effect was observed uniquely when stimuli were presented in the lower VF. These findings indicate that object affordances are sensitive to the functional relevance of the lower visual field for reaching and grasping actions, supporting a model where affordance-based visual processing is grounded in the suitability of an object for immediate motor interaction.
papers.authors: Annie Warman, Allan Clark, George L. Malcolm, Maximillian Havekost, Stéphanie Rossit

papers.title: Aging effects on extrapersonal (far-space) attention: cancellation and line bisection performance from 179 healthy adults
papers.abstract: While visuospatial attention is traditionally studied in near-space (peripersonal), most everyday tasks occur in far-space (extrapersonal). This study established lifespan normative data for far-space attention using computerized cancellation and line bisection tasks in 179 healthy adults (18–94 years). Analysis revealed that advanced age is associated with significantly slower search speeds and diminished search organization quality, although line bisection accuracy remained preserved across the age groups. A consistent leftward spatial bias (pseudoneglect) was observed in both tasks. The study provides age-graded norms for clinical assessment and demonstrates that extrapersonal attentional systems exhibit distinct age-related changes and sex differences (with faster processing in males) that may dissociate from peripersonal mechanisms.
papers.authors: Helen Morse, Amy A. Jolly, Hannah Browning, Allan Clark, Valerie Pomeroy, Stéphanie Rossit

papers.title: Practical routes to preregistration: A guide to enhanced transparency and rigour in neuropsychological research
papers.abstract: Preregistration is a core component of open research aimed at increasing transparency and minimizing publication bias by documenting study plans prior to data collection or analysis. However, neuropsychology faces unique challenges in implementing these practices due to rare clinical populations and intensive data collection requirements. This guide, developed by the British Neuropsychological Society Open Research Group, maps three primary routes to preregistration: repository-based, published protocols, and Registered Reports. We analyze the balance between methodological rigour and pragmatic flexibility required for clinical samples. By signposting specific resources and journal policies, the article provides a framework for neuropsychologists to adopt more robust open science practices while navigating the logistical constraints of neurological patient research.
papers.authors: Richard J. Binney, Laura J. Smith, Stephanie Rossit, Nele Demeyere, Gemma Learmonth, Elena Olgiati, Ajay D. Halai, Elisabeth Rounis, Jonathan Evans, Nicola M. J. Edelstyn, Robert D. McIntosh

E149.name: Stephen H. Scott
E149.department: Department of Biomedical and Molecular Sciences
E149.bio: Stephen H. Scott is a Canadian neuroscientist and engineer specializing in the neural and computational foundations of voluntary motor control. Scott developed the Kinarm robotic system, a tool used to investigate transcortical feedback pathways and quantify sensorimotor impairments in clinical populations. Their research methodology integrates primate neurophysiology and human behavioral experiments, utilizing optimal feedback control (OFC) theory to interpret how the brain processes sensory information to manage limb biomechanics. Scott's current work focuses on the intersection of robotics and brain-machine interfaces to facilitate the assessment and rehabilitation of neurological disorders such as stroke.
E149.research_direction: Dr. Scott has recently been investigating the neural, biomechanical, and computational mechanisms underlying goal-directed motor control. Their recent work explores how the primary motor cortex integrates proprioceptive and visual feedback to execute rapid reach corrections, and how physical factors like limb biomechanics and muscle co-contraction shape these neural control strategies. At the behavioral level, they are examining eye-hand coordination to understand how spatial predictability and response urgency differentially drive oculomotor and limb kinematics during dynamic visual interception tasks. Furthermore, their translational research utilizes robotic exoskeletons paired with uncertainty-aware deep learning to assess and classify subtle motor impairments in stroke and transient ischemic attack patients.

papers.title: Optimizing Stroke Detection Using Evidential Networks and Uncertainty-Based Refinement
papers.abstract: Traditional clinical evaluations of post-stroke neurological deficits often lack the sensitivity required to detect subtle impairments or monitor recovery effectively. In this study, we utilized the Kinarm Exoskeleton to record high-fidelity kinematic data from 337 stroke survivors and 368 healthy controls across three standardized motor tasks. We implemented a deep learning framework incorporating evidential neural networks to perform binary stroke classification while concurrently estimating aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty. By refining the training process with the most certain samples and excluding the top 10% of uncertain test cases, we increased the sensitivity for identifying motor deficits in minimally impaired stroke patients (those with normal scores on the Chedoke-McMaster Stroke Assessment) from 0.55 to 0.75. Additionally, the model was successfully extended to detect impairments in patients with transient ischemic attacks (TIA), achieving a classification accuracy of 0.92 and highlighting the clinical utility of uncertainty-aware robotic assessments.
papers.venue: IEEE Transactions on Neural Systems and Rehabilitation Engineering
papers.authors: Faranak Akbarifar, Sean P. Dukelow, Albert Jin, Parvin Mousavi, Stephen H. Scott

papers.title: Agonist-antagonist muscular co-contraction improves rapid corrective responses
papers.abstract: While muscle co-contraction is typically associated with increasing limb impedance to resist physical disturbances, its potential role in facilitating neural feedback responses remains poorly understood. We investigated how pre-perturbation agonist-antagonist co-activation modulates the control of the upper limb following mechanical loads. Utilizing a robotic exoskeleton, we quantified motor performance during a target recapture task under varying levels of voluntary co-contraction. Our results demonstrate that even low levels of co-contraction significantly enhance performance, resulting in faster and more accurate corrective responses compared to relaxed baseline states. Critically, significant kinematic differences between conditions were only observed after the initial 50 ms following perturbation onset, suggesting that the benefits of co-contraction are not primarily due to intrinsic muscle stiffness but rather reflect a priming of the central nervous system for rapid, task-dependent feedback control.
papers.authors: Daniel P. Armstrong, Kevin J. Deluzio, Stephen H. Scott

papers.title: Rapid eye and hand responses in an interception task are differentially modulated by context-dependent predictability
papers.abstract: Interacting with moving objects in unpredictable environments requires precise coordination between oculomotor and limb control systems. We examined eye-hand coordination in a rapid interception task where participants used a virtual paddle to catch a moving target that could suddenly 'jump' to a new location. We manipulated both jump certainty (frequency of target shifts) and response urgency (timing of the jump). High certainty about target perturbations led to significantly shorter reaction times for both eye and hand responses. Increased response urgency further reduced hand reaction times and increased movement vigor, whereas eye responses showed non-monotonic reaction time changes and invariant vigor. The weak correlation found between eye and hand response latencies suggests that although these systems likely share early sensorimotor processing of visual perturbations, they are modulated by separate task-specific control signals to meet the unique constraints of each motor system.
papers.authors: Jolande Fooken, Parsa Balalaie, Kayne Park, J. Randall Flanagan, Stephen H. Scott

papers.title: Toward biologically realistic models of the motor system
papers.abstract: This perspective advocates for the development of mechanistic, biologically realistic computational models of the motor system that unify motor behavior, limb biomechanics, and neurophysiology. We argue that the observed preference distributions of primary motor cortex (M1) neurons for specific movement directions and mechanical loads are not arbitrary but reflect optimal control solutions constrained by the physical properties of the motor effector, including limb geometry, intersegmental dynamics, and the force-velocity properties of biarticular muscles. By incorporating these bottom-up biomechanical features, models can more accurately predict the complex neural dynamics observed in M1 and other sensorimotor regions. The article highlights that just as large-scale language models have improved our understanding of neural language processing, the next generation of motor control theories must leverage detailed physical simulations to decode the functional architecture of the mammalian nervous system.
papers.authors: Stephen H. Scott

papers.title: Rapid Online Corrections for Proprioceptive and Visual Perturbations Recruit Similar Circuits in Primary Motor Cortex
papers.abstract: The primary motor cortex (M1) is a critical hub for processing sensory feedback to generate rapid goal-directed corrections, but the degree to which different sensory modalities are integrated within M1 circuits is unclear. We recorded single-neuron activity in M1 while rhesus macaques performed a reaching task that involved either mechanical loads (proprioceptive perturbations) or visual shifts of the hand and target. Our data show that the vast majority of M1 neurons are sensitive to both proprioceptive and visual feedback, eliciting strikingly similar population-level neural trajectories in response to both perturbation types. While we identified a small subpopulation of neurons that responded uniquely to specific modalities, the overall findings demonstrate that M1 circuits primarily integrate diverse feedback signals into a common representational space to support unified sensorimotor control. This suggests that the cortical substrate for rapid movement correction is highly convergent across visual and somatosensory inputs.
papers.authors: Kevin P. Cross, Douglas J. Cook, Stephen H. Scott

E150.name: Bijan Pesaran
E150.bio: Bijan Pesaran is the Robert A. Groff Professor of Neurosurgery at the University of Pennsylvania, where Pesaran investigates the neural mechanisms of multiregional communication and decision-making. Their research employs large-scale electrophysiological recordings and computational modeling to understand how distributed brain networks coordinate behaviors such as eye-hand movements. Transitioning from a background in theoretical physics to systems neuroscience, Pesaran developed techniques for decoding local field potentials and spiking activity to create brain-machine interfaces. Pesaran's current work focuses on engineering neurotechnologies and therapies for neurological disorders by mapping and controlling large-scale brain circuits.
E150.research_direction: Dr. Pesaran has recently been investigating the large-scale neural dynamics underlying complex motor and cognitive behaviors, ranging from naturalistic eye-hand coordination to top-down attentional control. Their recent work explores how distributed brain networks orchestrate flexible actions, examining phenomena such as inter-regional rhythmic synchronization during unconstrained looking and reaching, the role of prefrontal beta oscillations in suppressing salient visual distractors, and bilateral cortical coordination during human speech production. To rigorously track these fast-paced network interactions, they are developing advanced computational tools, including novel statistical frameworks designed to decode the exact temporal onset of task-relevant signals across both single-unit spikes and local field potentials. Additionally, they are advancing high-precision neurotechnologies by building multimodal surgical workflows that merge structural MRI with two-photon imaging to enable cellular-resolution mapping and highly targeted electrode placement in the primate brain.

papers.title: Speech motor commands are coordinated across both hemispheres of the human brain
papers.abstract: The traditional view of human speech motor control emphasizes a dominant left-hemisphere specialization. However, using high-resolution intracranial recordings and micro-electrocorticography (μECoG) across both hemispheres, this study demonstrates that motor commands for speech are bilaterally coordinated. The researchers identified synchronized neural activity in the ventral motor cortex of both hemispheres during syllable production. Using advanced decoding models, they found that speech features could be reconstructed from both hemispheres, though with distinct temporal dynamics. The findings suggest a bilateral network for speech production, where the two hemispheres share motor-command information to achieve the rapid, precise coordination required for vocalization, challenging the strictly lateralized model of language-related motor functions.
papers.authors: Stavis, K., Cogan, G. B., Armenta-Salas, M., Wingel, K., Choi, J. S., Dovonon, A., Viventi, J., Pesaran, B.

papers.title: Cellular-Resolution Image-Guided Localization in the Primate Brain
papers.abstract: Accurate localization of specific neural populations is critical for systems neuroscience and the development of high-precision neurotechnologies. This study introduces an image-guided surgical workflow that combines cellular-resolution two-photon imaging with structural MRI to localize functional brain regions in the rhesus macaque. The methodology leverages a custom-designed cranial window and localized fluorescent markers to register cellular-scale functional maps (e.g., orientation preference in visual cortex) onto macroscopic brain atlases. The authors quantify the registration accuracy and demonstrate that this multimodal approach significantly reduces error in electrode placement compared to standard stereotaxic techniques. This technique enables the targeted interrogation of specific cortical circuits defined by their cellular response properties in large animal models.
papers.venue: 46th Annual International Conference of the IEEE Engineering in Medicine and Biology Society (EMBC)
papers.authors: Stefanowicz, J., Choi, J. S., Wingel, K., Haggerty, J., Charles, A. S., Pesaran, B.

papers.title: A likelihood framework to decode the timing of information in spiking and LFP activity
papers.abstract: Traditional neural decoding methods often focus on 'what' information is present rather than 'when' it emerges relative to behavior. This paper presents a novel statistical likelihood framework designed to estimate the latency and temporal dynamics of information encoding within multimodal neural signals, specifically single-unit spikes and local field potentials (LFPs). The model utilizes a point-process likelihood for spikes and a Gaussian likelihood for spectral LFP features to identify the onset of task-relevant signals. Applying this to recordings from the posterior parietal cortex during reaching tasks, the authors show that LFP oscillations in the beta band provide earlier movement-related information than spike rates. This framework offers a robust tool for characterizing the sequential activation of neural populations across distributed networks during decision-making and motor planning.
papers.authors: Khazali, M. F., Dean, H. L., Hagan, M. A., Wong, Y. T., Pesaran, B.

papers.title: Neural signatures of behavioral transitions during naturalistic eye-hand coordination
papers.abstract: While coordination between looking and reaching is well-studied in structured tasks, the underlying neural dynamics during unconstrained, naturalistic behavior remain less clear. This study employs large-scale neural recordings from parietal area LIP and premotor area PMd in macaques performing a free-reaching task in a 3D environment. The authors utilize a hidden Markov model (HMM) to identify discrete behavioral states and their associated neural signatures. They report that transitions between looking and reaching states are marked by transient bursts of gamma-frequency coherence between LIP and PMd. Quantitative analysis reveals that the strength of this inter-regional coherence predicts the timing of coordinated movement initiation. These results suggest that rhythmic synchronization serves as a mechanism for the flexible coupling of independent motor systems during complex, self-timed behavior.
papers.authors: Shewcraft, R. A., Qiao, S., Garwood, I. C., Pesaran, B.

papers.title: Top-down control of exogenous attentional selection is mediated by beta coherence in prefrontal cortex
papers.abstract: The lateral prefrontal cortex (LPFC) is essential for prioritizing goal-directed (endogenous) signals over salient (exogenous) distractions, but the circuit mechanisms of this top-down control are unresolved. This research identifies a specific subpopulation of visual-movement (VM) neurons in the macaque LPFC that selectively encodes the conflict between salient distractors and reward-guided targets. Using spectral analysis, the authors demonstrate that top-down suppression of the distractor is mediated by high-power 'beta bursts' (15-25 Hz). These beta oscillations were found to be coherent with VM neuron spiking specifically during successful distractor inhibition. The study proposes a 'channel modulation' hypothesis, where beta-frequency dynamics in the prefrontal cortex act as a gate to suppress sensory-driven inputs, thereby enabling the maintenance of goal-directed focus during attentional conflict.
papers.authors: Dubey, A., Markowitz, D. A., Pesaran, B.

E151.name: Richard A. Andersen
E151.department: Division of Biology and Biological Engineering
E151.bio: Richard A. Andersen studies the neural mechanisms of sensory-motor integration and movement planning within the posterior parietal cortex (PPC). Andersen identified "gain fields," a computational principle that allows the brain to transform visual information into various coordinate systems by integrating sensory stimuli with eye and body position signals. Their laboratory develops cognitive-based brain-machine interfaces that decode intentional signals from the PPC of paralyzed patients to control robotic limbs and computer cursors. Andersen currently utilizes machine learning and neuroimaging techniques to develop neural prosthetics for the restoration of functions such as speech and coordinated reaching.
E151.research_direction: Dr. Andersen has recently been investigating the neural dynamics of motor intention, action perception, and multisensory integration using high-density intracortical microelectrode arrays in humans with tetraplegia. Their recent work explores how the frontoparietal network differentiates between executing and visually observing actions, and how continuous visual feedback shapes population-level motor cortex activity during ongoing tasks. To advance bidirectional brain-computer interfaces, they are examining how visual context affects the perceived timing of artificial tactile sensations delivered directly to the somatosensory cortex via microstimulation. Furthermore, Dr. Andersen's applied research tests the real-world feasibility of these implants, investigating everything from decoding complex bimanual motor imagery for steering physical vehicles to tracking the multi-year material degradation and functional performance of chronic electrode arrays.

papers.title: Hierarchical and Context-Dependent Encoding of Actions in Human Posterior Parietal and Motor Cortex
papers.abstract: This electrophysiological study investigates the neural substrates of action understanding by recording from the motor cortex (MC) and superior parietal lobule (SPL) in two human participants with tetraplegia during action intention and observation. Utilizing high-density microelectrode arrays, the researchers characterized a functional dissociation in frontoparietal geometry: whereas MC dynamics are specialized for goal-directed motor intention with minimal mirror-like overlap during observation, SPL maintains shared population-level representations for both executed and observed actions. Critically, the recruitment of observed-action codes in SPL is modulated by a context-dependent gating mechanism, appearing only when the observed stimuli are behaviorally relevant to the task. These findings support a hierarchical organization where SPL provides a flexible interface between perception and internal goal states, while MC remains focused on movement execution, challenging reflexive motor mirroring models.
papers.authors: Vasiliki Bougou, Jorge Gamez, Emily R. Rosario, Charles Liu, Kelsie Pejsa, Ausaf Bari, Richard A. Andersen

papers.title: Duration-modulated neural population dynamics in humans during BMI controls
papers.abstract: This research evaluates the autonomous dynamical systems hypothesis of motor cortex (MC) function during closed-loop brain-machine interface (BMI) control in humans. By analyzing MC population dynamics across varied task durations—ranging from rapid ballistic movements to sustained target acquisition—the study demonstrates that MC activity does not purely follow internal trajectories initialized at the start of movement. Instead, during extended-duration BMI control, MC population dynamics exhibit 'pauses' in state-space, sustaining specific activity patterns until the behavioral goal is attained. This deviation from autonomous behavior suggests that MC dynamics are significantly driven by continuous external inputs, such as visual feedback and persistent volitional intent, rather than being strictly governed by internal initial conditions and local circuitry.
papers.authors: Fei Yin, Charles Guan, Tyson Aflalo, Jorge Gamez, Kelsie Pejsa, Emily Rosario, Charles Liu, Ausaf Bari, Richard A. Andersen

papers.title: Visual context affects the perceived timing of tactile sensations elicited through intra-cortical microstimulation: a case study of two participants
papers.abstract: Investigating the multisensory integration of artificial tactile feedback, this study assesses how visual context influences the perceived timing of sensations elicited via intracortical microstimulation (ICMS) of the primary somatosensory cortex (S1). In two tetraplegic participants, the researchers quantified the temporal binding window for ICMS and visual cues, finding that perceptual simultaneity is biased by the ecological realism of the visual environment and the current amplitude of the stimulation. Simultaneous neural recordings from microelectrode arrays in S1 revealed that this region represents visual information associated with the ICMS context. The findings indicate that effective somatosensory brain-machine interfaces (BMIs) must account for temporal misalignments and environmental context to achieve naturalistic sensory integration and embodiment.
papers.authors: Isabelle A. Rosenthal, Luke Bashford, David Bjanes, Kelsie Pejsa, Brian Lee, Charles Liu, Richard A. Andersen

papers.title: Control of a commercial vehicle by a tetraplegic human using a bimanual brain-computer interface
papers.abstract: This paper presents the first implementation of a bimanual intracortical brain-computer interface (BCI) for the volitional control of a full-sized commercial vehicle in real-world environments. Utilizing 192-channel microelectrode recordings from the motor cortex (MC) and posterior parietal cortex (PPC) of a participant with tetraplegia, the system decodes complex bimanual motor imagery to separate steering and velocity functions. The participant successfully operated a Ford Mustang Mach-E through both virtual simulations and physical obstacle courses, achieving reaction times and steering accuracy statistically equivalent to a motor-intact control group. The study establishes the safety and feasibility of high-dimensional BCIs for safety-critical, real-world mobility tasks, moving beyond traditional laboratory-constrained applications.
papers.authors: Xinyun Zou, Jorge Gamez, Meghna Menon, Phillip Ring, Chadwick Boulay, Likhith Chitneni, Jackson Brennecke, Shana R. Melby, Gracy Kureel, Kelsie Pejsa, Emily R. Rosario, Ausaf A. Bari, Aniruddh Ravindran, Tyson Aflalo, Spencer S. Kellis, Dimitar Filev, Florian Solzbacher, Richard A. Andersen

papers.title: Quantifying physical degradation alongside recording and stimulation performance of 980 intracortical microelectrodes chronically implanted in three humans for 956-2130 days
papers.abstract: This longitudinal study characterizes the material and functional stability of 980 intracortical microelectrodes chronically implanted in three human participants for durations up to 2130 days. Using scanning electron microscopy (SEM) of explanted Neuroport arrays, the authors compared the degradation of Platinum (Pt) and Sputtered Iridium Oxide Film (SIROF) tips. SIROF electrodes demonstrated twice the likelihood of recording neural activity (measured by signal-to-noise ratio) compared to Pt, despite exhibiting greater physical degradation. The analysis identifies silicon core erosion, occurring after tip metal damage, as a critical failure mechanism. Furthermore, 1 kHz impedance was found to significantly correlate with physical damage, recording quality, and stimulation performance, identifying it as a robust in vivo biomarker for electrode interface degradation in long-term BCI implants.
papers.authors: David A. Bjånes, Spencer Kellis, Robert Nickl, Brian Baker, Tyson Aflalo, Luke Bashford, Srinivas Chivukula, Matthew S. Fifer, Luke E. Osborn, Breanne Christie, Brock A. Wester, Pablo A. Celnik, Daniel Kramer, Kelsie Pejsa, Nathan E. Crone, William S. Anderson, Nadar Pouratian, Brian Lee, Charles Y. Liu, Francesco V. Tenore, Loren Rieth, Richard A. Andersen

E152.name: Tamar Makin
E152.department: Medical Research Council Cognition and Brain Sciences Unit
E152.bio: Tamar Makin is a Professor of Cognitive Neuroscience at the University of Cambridge and the leader of the Plasticity Lab at the MRC Cognition and Brain Sciences Unit. Their research investigates the neural mechanisms of brain plasticity, specifically how the brain represents the body and adapts to changes such as limb loss or the integration of augmentative technologies. Using neuroimaging, psychophysics, and bioengineering, Makin has demonstrated the persistence of latent limb representations in the brain following amputation. Their current work focuses on motor augmentation, exploring how the human brain can be harnessed to control and embody artificial body parts to enhance physical capabilities.
E152.research_direction: Dr. Makin has recently been exploring the neurocognitive mechanisms underlying how the adult human brain represents, adapts to, and integrates both missing and artificial body parts. Using longitudinal fMRI, they are investigating the limits of cortical plasticity in the primary sensorimotor cortex, specifically tracking whether neural body maps reorganize or remain stable following arm amputation. Their recent work also examines motor learning and skill generalization during the use of supernumerary robotic limbs, testing how users acquire abstract control over augmentative devices like a toe-controlled extra thumb. Furthermore, they are studying the neurocognitive pathways for artificial touch, investigating the extent to which the central nervous system can use natural, intrinsic mechanical feedback from wearable devices to construct distinct cortical representations and guide intuitive haptic interfaces.

papers.title: From Restoration to Augmentation: New Approaches to Haptic Feedback for Artificial Limbs
papers.abstract: While conventional somatosensory restoration for prosthetic devices typically targets established neural pathways at the cortical, peripheral, or cutaneous levels, the integration of haptic feedback into augmentative supernumerary limbs presents a unique challenge due to the absence of innate sensory channels. This review examines a paradigm shift from artificial stimulation to the exploitation of intrinsic haptic signals—mechanical cues naturally generated at the physical interface between the wearable device and the user's skin. The authors argue that by optimizing device materials and wearable architecture to amplify these latent tactile transmissions, it is possible to provide intuitive and interpretable sensory information. This approach potentially facilitates neural embodiment and precise motor control of augmentative technologies without disrupting existing somatosensory functions, offering a scalable pathway for integrating supernumerary degrees of freedom into the human sensorimotor hierarchy.
papers.authors: Lucy Dowdall, Celia Foster, Tamar R. Makin

papers.title: Stable cortical body maps before and after arm amputation
papers.abstract: This study employs a longitudinal functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) framework to investigate the extent of cortical plasticity in the adult primary sensorimotor cortex (S1) by tracking three individuals from the pre-operative stage through a five-year post-amputation period. By directly comparing the representational topographies of the biological hand with those of the phantom hand and the lips across four to five sessions, the research identifies a remarkable preservation of digit-specific cortical maps. Multivariate pattern analysis and center-of-gravity (CoG) quantification demonstrate that the deafferented hand territory is not colonized by adjacent facial representations, nor does the representational structure of the missing digits undergo significant degradation or reorganization. These findings provide definitive evidence against the prevailing 'maladaptive plasticity' model of large-scale cortical reorganization following limb loss, instead highlighting the profound stability of adult somatosensory topographies and the persistence of the missing limb's neural signature.
papers.authors: Hunter R. Schone, Roni O. Maimon-Mor, Mathew Kollamkulam, Malgorzata A. Szymanska, Craig Gerrand, Alexander Woollard, Norbert V. Kang, Chris I. Baker, Tamar R. Makin

papers.title: Motor Learning Outside the Body: Broad Skill Generalisation with an Extra Robotic Limb
papers.abstract: The functional utility of supernumerary robotic technologies is contingent upon the capacity for generalized motor skill acquisition that transcends specific training contexts. This research utilized a seven-day training protocol to evaluate how participants learned to operate the 'Third Thumb,' a hand-worn robotic digit controlled via pressure sensors under the toes. Behavioral assessments were conducted to evaluate motor transfer across diverse task demands, altered body postures, and novel controller-effector configurations. The results demonstrated robust skill generalization, indicating that the central nervous system develops abstract, effector-independent motor policies for augmentative devices, analogous to motor equivalence in biological handwriting. Although training significantly reduced cognitive load and enhanced the subjective sense of agency, a persistent preference for biological effectors was observed, suggesting that additional neurocognitive factors beyond skill acquisition and embodiment influence the real-world adoption of motor augmentation.
papers.authors: Maria Molina-Sanchez, Lucy Dowdall, Giulia Dominijanni, Viktorija Pavalkyte, Clara Gallay, Edmund da Silva, Dani Clode, Tamar R. Makin

papers.title: Developing a Sensory Representation of an Artificial Body Part
papers.abstract: This investigation explored the neural and perceptual mechanisms underlying the integration of a wearable robotic digit into the human somatosensory system. Behavioral data indicated that participants intuitively utilized intrinsic mechanical feedback—tactile cues originating from the physical interaction between the device and the hand—to perform complex perceptual tasks with an efficiency comparable to state-of-the-art artificial feedback systems. Longitudinal functional neuroimaging (fMRI) identified the rapid emergence of a distinct, topographically organized cortical representation for the robotic digit within the somatosensory hierarchy. Following extensive sensorimotor training, this artificial representation underwent refinement, exhibiting increased representational similarity to the neural patterns associated with biological digits, which correlated with increased subjective embodiment. These findings suggest that the human brain can autonomously extract and integrate natural feedback to construct a coherent sensory representation of a supernumerary limb, facilitating technological embodiment through existing plasticity mechanisms.
papers.authors: Lucy Dowdall, Maria Molina-Sanchez, Giulia Dominijanni, Edmund da Silva, Viktorija Pavalkyte, Ema Jugovic, Matteo Bianchi, Fumiya Iida, Dani Clode, Tamar R. Makin

papers.title: A neurocognitive pathway for engineering artificial touch
papers.abstract: Artificial haptics presents a transformative potential for integrating physical and virtual environments, yet its efficacy is constrained by the neurocognitive interplay between the somatosensory system and engineered inputs. This perspective delineates the relationship between sensory feedback fidelity and the cognitive load required for effective interface operation. The authors propose a paradigm shift in neurotechnology design, moving from strict physiological biomimicry toward a framework of behavioral and cognitive congruence that aligns with the human brain's sensory, motor, and cognitive processing hierarchies. By accounting for the dynamic, context-dependent nature of multisensory integration and leveraging both explicit and implicit learning mechanisms, next-generation haptic interfaces can support more intuitive motor skill acquisition and sensory integration. This approach emphasizes the need for technologies that afford alternative solutions to user needs while maintaining compatibility with the user's underlying neurocognitive architecture.
papers.authors: Ilana Nisky, Tamar R. Makin

E153.name: J. Douglas Crawford
E153.bio: J. Douglas Crawford is a Research Professor and Canada Research Chair in Visuomotor Neuroscience at York University. Crawford’s research investigates the neural mechanisms underlying visuospatial memory and sensorimotor transformations for coordinated eye, head, and hand movements in three-dimensional space. Utilizing a multimodal approach that includes fMRI, MEG, transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), and neurophysiological recordings, their work explores how the brain updates internal representations of visual goals during self-motion. Crawford examines the 3D geometry of the gaze system and the role of the posterior parietal cortex in integrating target and effector information for reach planning.
E153.research_direction: Dr. Crawford has recently been investigating the neural networks and computations that underlie goal-directed motor behaviors like reaching, grasping, and eye movements. Their recent work explores how the brain integrates diverse streams of information—such as egocentric and allocentric spatial reference frames, or top-down auditory instructions combined with bottom-up visual cues—to dynamically plan these complex actions. To map these visuomotor transformations, they employ human fMRI coupled with graph theory analysis, alongside non-human primate neurophysiology and computational modeling. Specifically, they are examining how large-scale cortical networks functionally reorganize to support transsaccadic spatial constancy, and how distinct neural recording scales in the frontal eye fields capture the nuanced spatial and cognitive signals required for memory-guided gaze control.

papers.title: Modular Integration of Auditory Instructions and Visual Cues into the Cortical Reach Network
papers.abstract: This study employs an event-related fMRI paradigm and graph theory analysis (GTA) to investigate the cortical integration of 'bottom-up' visual stimulus attributes (spatial location) and 'top-down' auditory instructions (grip orientation) for goal-directed prehension. The researchers identified two distinct functional modules: an Occipital-Parietal-Somatomotor network responsible for mapping visual object properties into the reach plan, and a Temporal-Frontal-Somatomotor network for integrating verbal instructions into the grasp plan. Findings indicate that cue presentation order significantly modulates network topology, where the module corresponding to the initial cue tends to dominate recruitment in the contralateral motor cortex. Machine learning classification further demonstrated that modular network features effectively decode cue order, suggesting a flexible and order-dependent mapping of multisensory inputs to achieve effective motor integration.
papers.authors: Gaelle N. Luabeya, Ada Le, Amir Hossein Ghaderi, Lina Musa, Simona Monaco, Erez Freud, J. Douglas Crawford

papers.title: Spatial task instructions and global activation trends influence functional modularity in the cortical reach network
papers.abstract: Utilizing graph theory analysis (GTA) on fMRI data, this research examines how explicit task instructions (egocentric vs. allocentric) and global activation trends influence the modular organization of the human reach network. During egocentric reaching, nodes clustered into four bilateral modules spanning occipital-parietal, inferior parietal-lateral frontal, superior temporal-inferior frontal, and inferior occipital-temporal-prefrontal regions. Allocentric instructions significantly increased modular integration and hub recruitment within the superior temporal and inferior frontal nodes. The study concludes that whereas task-specific instructions drive intermediate and local network properties—such as increased modular communication between the ventral and dorsal streams—global activation trends associated with motor planning facilitate overall network integration and synchrony.
papers.authors: Lina Musa, Amirhossein Ghaderi, Ying Chen, J. Douglas Crawford

papers.title: Saccades influence functional modularity in the human cortical vision network
papers.abstract: This study investigates the dynamic reorganization of the human cortical vision network during active gaze shifts using fMRI and graph theory analysis. Under static fixation conditions, the network exhibits a clear modular structure consisting of a bilateral parietofrontal dorsal module and two lateralized occipitotemporal ventral modules. However, when horizontal saccades necessitate visual comparisons across the object, these lateralized ventral modules functionally integrate into a single bilateral sub-network. This integration is mediated by 'between-module' connectivity hubs in the lateral intraparietal cortex and dorsomedial occipital areas, indicating that the human visual system's modular organization is adaptively modified to support transsaccadic feature comparison and spatial constancy.
papers.authors: George Tomou, Bianca Baltaretu, Amir Hossein Ghaderi, J. Douglas Crawford

papers.title: Neural integration of egocentric and allocentric visual cues in the gaze system
papers.abstract: This review synthesizes recent neurophysiological and behavioral findings to explain how the primate brain integrates egocentric (body-centered) and allocentric (landmark-centered) visual information for optimal gaze control. The paper details specific cellular mechanisms within the prefrontal cortex, particularly the frontal eye fields (FEF) and supplementary eye fields (SEF). It describes the transformation of visual responses toward landmark-centered coordinates, the simultaneous maintenance of conflicting spatial codes during memory delays, and the eventual reintegration of these multiplexed signals in the motor burst for saccade generation. Furthermore, the review highlights that deep convolutional/multilayer perceptron network models replicate these neural population dynamics, suggesting that weighted integration emerges as a computational necessity for stable goal-directed behavior.
papers.authors: Vishal Bharmauria, Serah Seo, J. Douglas Crawford

papers.title: Multiunit Frontal Eye Field Activity Codes the Visuomotor Transformation, But Not Gaze Prediction or Retrospective Target Memory, in a Delayed Saccade Task
papers.abstract: Comparing the spatial coding of single-unit (SU) and multiunit (MU) activity in the frontal eye fields (FEF) of head-unrestrained monkeys, this study tracks the spatiotemporal progression of sensorimotor signals during memory-guided saccades. Using a model-fitting technique, the authors demonstrate that while MU activity reliably captures the fundamental eye-centered target (Te) to gaze (Ge) transformation, it fails to represent more nuanced cognitive signals such as predictive gaze codes in initial visual responses or retrospective target memory in final motor responses. These findings suggest that MU recordings can serve as a robust biomarker for healthy visuomotor transformations, though SU activity remains essential for characterizing subtle cognitive and predictive modulations of sensorimotor behavior.
papers.authors: Serah Seo, Vishal Bharmauria, Adrian Schütz, Xiaogang Yan, Hongying Wang, J. Douglas Crawford

E154.name: Paul Gribble
E154.bio: Paul Gribble is a Professor at Western University whose research examines the neural and computational mechanisms of human motor control and learning. Gribble investigates how the brain coordinates multi-joint movements and the role of sensory plasticity within the somatosensory cortex in acquiring motor skills. Their work includes studies on motor learning through visual observation, specifically how the brain maps observed actions onto its own motor system. This research employs a combination of human behavioral experiments, computational modeling, and neuroimaging techniques such as EEG and peripheral nerve stimulation.
E154.research_direction: Dr. Gribble's recent work explores the neural and behavioral mechanisms of human motor learning, combining computational modeling and psychophysical experiments to understand how the sensorimotor system controls movement. To advance this computational work, they have recently been developing MotorNet, an open-source framework that integrates recurrent neural networks with realistic biomechanical limb models to investigate how neural population dynamics navigate musculoskeletal constraints. Using these tools, their recent research models the neural state-space mechanisms underlying "savings"—the phenomenon where prior physical experience accelerates a person's re-adaptation to mechanical perturbations. In parallel human behavioral studies, Dr. Gribble is exploring observational motor learning, specifically probing the temporal durability of motor representations formed simply by watching others adapt to altered physical environments. Alongside these scientific inquiries, their recent scholarship also provides methodological frameworks for designing academic lab websites to improve digital science communication and resource management.

papers.title: A Context-Free Model of Savings in Motor Learning
papers.abstract: The mechanisms by which prior exposure to mechanical or visuomotor perturbations facilitates accelerated adaptation upon re-encounter—a phenomenon known as savings—remain a subject of active debate. This study utilized MotorNet, a computational framework for training recurrent neural networks (RNNs) to control a biomechanically realistic human upper-limb model, to investigate the neural substrates of savings. RNNs were trained on a center-out reaching task across four phases: baseline, adaptation to a velocity-dependent curl force field (FF), washout, and re-adaptation. The networks exhibited robust behavioral signatures of savings even in the absence of explicit contextual cues signaling the perturbation state. Savings magnitude was positively correlated with the dimensionality of the neural control space (network size). Analysis of RNN activity identified a persistent shift in preparatory neural states that remained following behavioral washout. Causal validation was achieved by delivering targeted perturbations to RNN hidden unit activity: displacements in the direction of the identified shift enhanced savings, while opposite-direction perturbations reduced or eliminated the effect. These results suggest that savings is supported by motor memory retention within a high-dimensional neural state space and can occur independently of strategic or cognitive learning components.
papers.authors: Mahdiyar Shahbazi, Olivier Codol, Jonathan A. Michaels, Paul L. Gribble

papers.title: How to design your academic website
papers.abstract: This technical commentary provides a methodological framework for the design and implementation of academic laboratory websites, which function as both public-facing portals for research dissemination and critical internal infrastructures for resource management. The author details essential architectural components, including indexed publication databases, research theme summaries, and digital laboratory manuals. The guide evaluates various deployment strategies, ranging from legacy content management systems to contemporary static site generators and automated hosting platforms. The discussion emphasizes the strategic importance of maintaining a persistent and accessible digital presence to facilitate trainee recruitment, foster academic networking, and ensure the long-term documentation of a laboratory's scientific contributions within its specialized domain.
papers.authors: Paul L. Gribble

papers.title: Durability of Motor Learning by Observing
papers.abstract: While visual observation of others' movements is known to engage the observer's sensorimotor system and support motor learning, the temporal stability of the resulting internal models is not well defined. This study utilized force channel probe trials in an upper-limb force-field reaching task to compare the retention of adaptation acquired through either direct physical practice or action observation. Participants were tested at multiple delays ranging from 1 minute to 24 hours post-exposure. While physical practice induced robust motor adaptation that was sustained at all time points with minor decay at 24 hours, observation-induced adaptation was significantly less stable, showing measurable decay by 1 hour and becoming undetectable at 24 hours. These findings indicate that although observation can update feedforward neural control of muscle activation, the resulting visually acquired representations of movement dynamics are more transient than those formed through physical experience, suggesting a limited temporal window for the efficacy of observational motor learning in skill acquisition.
papers.authors: Natalia Mangos, Christopher J. Forgaard, Paul L. Gribble

papers.title: MotorNet: a Python toolbox for controlling differentiable biomechanical effectors with artificial neural networks
papers.abstract: The integration of artificial neural network (ANN) controllers with physiologically realistic biomechanical effectors has been constrained by the non-differentiable nature of existing musculoskeletal modeling tools. We introduce MotorNet, an open-source Python framework designed to train RNNs to control differentiable biomechanical effectors. MotorNet provides a library of models, including point masses and multi-joint limbs driven by Hill-type muscle models with non-linear dynamics. The platform's differentiable architecture allows for the end-to-end optimization of control policies using backpropagation through time (BPTT), offering a faster and more stable alternative to standard reinforcement learning algorithms. Validation experiments confirmed that networks trained within MotorNet replicate core neurophysiological findings, such as the emergence of directional tuning in motor cortical units and the ability to adapt to external mechanical loads. MotorNet provides a scalable, standardized environment for investigating the complex relationships between neural population dynamics, sensorimotor feedback, and the physical constraints of the musculoskeletal system.
papers.authors: Olivier Codol, Jonathan A. Michaels, Mehrdad Kashefi, J. Andrew Pruszynski, Paul L. Gribble

E155.name: Constanze Hesse
E155.bio: Constanze Hesse is a Professor of Psychology at the University of Aberdeen and leads the Grasper Lab investigating the cognitive and sensory mechanisms underlying human motor control. Hesse’s research utilizes psychophysical experimentation and motion tracking to examine how visual information, material properties, and environmental constraints influence the planning and execution of reaching and grasping movements. Their work addresses the dorsal and ventral visual streams through studies on multisensory perception and clinical neuropsychology, including research with patients possessing visual agnosia. Hesse is currently exploring natural behavior in virtual reality environments and investigating how the affective or emotional properties of objects modulate motor avoidance strategies.
