E155.research_direction: Dr. Hesse has recently been investigating the complex interplay between visual perception, cognition, and motor execution across a diverse range of goal-directed behaviors. Their recent work explores how spatial cues, such as binocular disparity, and affective object properties, like perceived danger, influence the kinematics of obstacle avoidance during reaching and stepping in both physical and simulated environments. They are also examining the mechanisms underlying fine motor control, leveraging maximum grip aperture measurements during the grasping of exceptionally small objects to test competing theories of visuomotor size representation. Furthermore, Dr. Hesse is investigating cognitive and low-level visual influences on perception, specifically probing whether motor expertise shapes the visual discrimination of static action scenes and how image features like color saturation dissociate explicit psychological evaluations from implicit motor approach biases.

papers.title: Fading appetite: Desaturation of food images reduces cravings but not approach biases
papers.abstract: The present study investigated the dissociation between explicit evaluative processes and implicit motivational responses to food cues by manipulating image saturation. In the first experiment, the investigators analyzed the impact of partial and complete (grayscale) desaturation on explicit cravings and perceived palatability for both perishable and preserved food items. Results indicated a significant attenuation of self-reported cravings and palatability as saturation decreased, with larger effect sizes observed for perishable items, suggesting a reliance on chromaticity as a freshness cue. Conversely, Experiments 2 and 3 employed a stimulus-response compatibility (SRC) task to measure approach biases. Despite the reduction in explicit evaluations, robust approach biases were maintained across all saturation conditions and food categories. These findings demonstrate a divergence between attentional/evaluative sensitivity to low-level perceptual features and motivational approach responses, which appear primarily driven by reward associations rather than basic stimulus saliency.
papers.authors: Daniela Ruseva, Martin Giesel, Constanze Hesse

papers.title: From discomfort to danger: Exploring how affective obstacle properties influence avoidance in stepping
papers.abstract: This research explores how perceptual affective evaluations—specifically unpleasantness, dangerousness, and painfulness—modulate motor avoidance strategies during obstacle navigation. In Experiment 1, participants stepped over obstacles covered in varying textures (stones of different sizes and densities) while visual uncertainty was manipulated via monocular and binocular viewing. Lead minimum foot clearance (MFC) increased under monocular conditions but normalized with practice; however, obstacle unpleasantness did not systematically modulate MFC. In Experiment 2, obstacles featured either smooth or spiky (metal stud) surfaces. Results demonstrated significantly higher MFC for spiky obstacles. Hierarchical regression analysis revealed that perceived dangerousness, rather than unpleasantness, was the critical predictor for crossing step length after controlling for other affective ratings. The study concludes that while affective properties modulate avoidance parameters, the effect is highly stimulus-specific and contingent on perceived risk rather than general discomfort.
papers.authors: Zhong Jian Chee, Martin Giesel, Constanze Hesse

papers.title: Obstacle avoidance of physical, stereoscopic, and pictorial objects
papers.abstract: To investigate the transferability of motor training from simulated to natural environments, this study compared obstacle avoidance behavior across physical objects and closely matched 2D (pictorial) and 3D (stereoscopic) images. Using a pre-test post-test paradigm, participants performed reaching movements over obstacles of varying heights. Initial findings showed that participants significantly underestimated height-dependent safety margins when interacting with 3D stereoscopic images compared to physical counterparts. Crucially, after brief exposure to physical obstacles, the avoidance performance for 3D images became statistically indistinguishable from physical object avoidance, whereas no such calibration occurred for 2D images. These results highlight the necessity of binocular disparity cues for naturalistic hand movements in personal space and suggest that motor calibration in virtual environments relies on egocentric distance estimates refined through physical interaction.
papers.authors: Martin Giesel, Daniela Ruseva, Constanze Hesse

papers.title: No evidence for top-down expertise effects on action perception in sprinters using static images
papers.abstract: This study tested the perceptual resonance hypothesis, which suggests that motor expertise facilitates the visual processing of actions. Sprinters and non-athlete controls participated in a psychophysical discrimination task using a staircase procedure to identify differences between static video frames of walking and sprinting starts. The frames were presented either sequentially (temporal task) to evaluate representational momentum or simultaneously (spatial task). Contrary to predictions that athletes would exhibit superior discrimination or larger representational momentum for expert actions, the results showed no significant performance differences between groups in either task or condition. Post-hoc analyses indicated that observed variances were better explained by task order effects. These findings provide no evidence that motor expertise modulates action perception in the absence of dynamic kinematic information, challenging the extent of top-down expertise effects in static visual scenes.
papers.authors: Róisín Elaine Harrison, Martin Giesel, Constanze Hesse

papers.title: Grasping tiny objects
papers.abstract: The reliability of maximum grip aperture (MGA) as a proxy for object size representation in the visuomotor system was investigated using extremely small cuboids (0.5 to 5 mm). The study aimed to differentiate between the perception-action model (PAM), the digits-in-space (DIS) hypothesis, and biomechanical constraint accounts. While manual estimation apertures (MEA) consistently scaled with object height and adhered to Weber’s law, MGAs for grasping showed inconsistent scaling for objects below 5 mm, and the corresponding just-noticeable differences (JNDs) remained constant across stimulus magnitudes. The dissociation between estimation and action for small-scale targets, alongside the failure of grasping JNDs to scale with size, provides empirical support for the DIS hypothesis. The findings suggest that grasping is controlled by the positional trajectories of individual digits rather than a holistic perceptual size estimate, particularly when targets approach the hand's biomechanical limits.
papers.authors: Martin Giesel, Federico De Filippi, Constanze Hesse

E156.name: Volker Franz
E156.department: Wilhelm Schickard Institute for Computer Science
E156.bio: Volker Franz is a Professor of Experimental Cognitive Science at the University of Tübingen and leads the Experimental Cognitive Science research group. Their research examines human visual information processing, focusing on the interaction between sensory input and motor control in tasks such as grasping and object recognition. Franz conducts empirical evaluations of the 'two visual systems' hypothesis by using visual illusions to test functional similarities between perception and action pathways. Additionally, Franz works on neuroscientific methodology, specializing in statistical rigor, confidence interval estimation, and the development of software such as the Optotrak Toolbox for kinematic analysis.
E156.research_direction: Dr. Franz's recent work explores the computational mechanisms of perceptual decision-making and metacognition, developing novel mathematical frameworks to quantify accumulated evidence from confidence ratings and using information theory to measure metacognitive ability without traditional parametric assumptions. They have also been investigating the physiological signatures of predictive processing, utilizing pupillometry to track how the arousal system responds to structural violations of statistical regularities across auditory and visual domains. Additionally, their research critically examines classic theories of visual processing architectures, utilizing large-scale replications of behavioral benchmarks like Garner interference to test the hypothesized dissociation between the dorsal visuomotor action and ventral perception streams.

papers.title: Accumulated evidence as an additive performance measure based on confidence ratings
papers.abstract: Traditional evidence accumulation frameworks, such as drift diffusion models, typically treat the accumulation process as a latent variable that is only indirectly accessible. This research introduces a direct, additive metric for quantifying accumulated evidence by integrating a participant's choice with their reported confidence levels. Derived from the mathematical principles of Sequential Probability Ratio Tests (SPRTs), this measure defines evidence as the signed logarithmic odds of calibrated confidence ratings. A primary advantage of this formulation is its additivity; for instance, evidence gathered in one stimulus interval can be summed with evidence from a subsequent interval to represent the total evidence. This property allows researchers to estimate the magnitude of evidence accumulated during intermediate, unobservable periods of a task, providing a more transparent view of the dynamics of perceptual decision-making.
papers.authors: Sascha Meyen, Lin Lin, Carina Schrenk, Volker H. Franz

papers.title: Modality-general sensitivity of pupil responses to regularity violations
papers.abstract: Pupil dilation responses (PDRs) are established physiological indicators of arousal and surprise in response to environmental fluctuations, yet their consistency across different sensory modalities remains under-explored. This study investigated PDRs during the presentation of auditory (tones) and visual (dots) sequences characterized by varying degrees of statistical regularity. The results reveal a robust cross-modal similarity: transitions from structured, regular patterns to stochastic, random patterns consistently elicited significant pupil dilation, while the inverse transitions (random-to-regular) did not. These findings suggest that the pupil-linked arousal system is specifically sensitive to the violation of internal statistical models—signaling a discrete 'reset' of expectations—and that this mechanism operates as a domain-general process across the auditory and visual systems.
papers.authors: Hamit Basgol, Florian Raab, Peter Dayan, Volker H. Franz

papers.title: Violation of auditory regularities is reflected in pupil dynamics
papers.abstract: The human brain maintains internal predictive models of the environment, updating or resetting them when sensory input deviates from expected regularities. This study utilized pupillometry to investigate the physiological signatures of model violations in the auditory domain. Participants listened to tone sequences while performing a distractor task to maintain attention. Transitions from regular to random patterns, as well as shifts between distinct regular patterns, induced significant pupil dilation responses (PDRs). In contrast, transitions from random to regular patterns failed to elicit PDRs, suggesting a gradual updating of model parameters rather than a discrete reset. These results support the hypothesis that PDRs reflect locus coeruleus-norepinephrine (LC-NE) activity associated with a discrete shift in the internal representation of environmental statistics.
papers.authors: Hamit Basgol, Peter Dayan, Volker H. Franz

papers.title: Reviewing evidence for the perception-action model from Garner interference
papers.abstract: The Perception-Action Model (PAM) argues for a functional dissociation between ventral (perception) and dorsal (action) visual streams, with Garner interference often cited as a benchmark. Specifically, it is widely assumed that perceptual tasks are subject to Garner interference whereas visuomotor actions, such as grasping, are immune. This study challenges this dissociation through two high-powered, improved replications and a comprehensive literature review. The experimental data showed much smaller Garner interference effects in manual size estimation than previously reported, and the systematic review indicates that the purported immunity of motor actions to such interference is not consistently supported across the literature. The authors conclude that existing Garner interference evidence is insufficient to justify a strict ventral-dorsal separation in visual processing.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
papers.authors: Kriti Bhatia, Angela Osenberg, Markus Janczyk, Volker H. Franz

papers.title: Information-theoretic measures of metacognition: Bounds and relation to group performance
papers.abstract: Metacognitive ability, or Type 2 performance, is typically quantified using Signal Detection Theory (SDT) measures like meta-d', which rely on specific distributional assumptions regarding noise in confidence ratings. This paper develops a non-parametric alternative based on classical information theory, measuring the information that confidence reports transmit about the accuracy of individual predictions. The authors derive rigorous upper and lower bounds for this transmitted information and introduce Relative Metainformation (RMI) as a normalized measure. Simulations and empirical data demonstrate that RMI effectively decouples Type 2 from Type 1 performance. Furthermore, the study shows that in optimal ensemble classification settings, the collective accuracy of a group is directly determined by the RMI values of its individual members, establishing RMI as a critical predictor for collaborative decision-making outcomes.
papers.authors: Sascha Meyen, Frieder Göppert, Carina Schrenk, Ulrike von Luxburg, Volker H. Franz

E157.name: Heiner Deubel
E157.department: Department of Psychology, Chair of General and Experimental Psychology
E157.bio: Deubel is an emeritus professor of psychology whose research focuses on the functional relationship between visual attention, perception, and the control of motor actions such as saccades and reaching. Deubel demonstrated the obligatory coupling of attentional selection to the goal of upcoming eye movements, a finding that supports the 'selection-for-action' framework of cognitive control. Their methodologies involve behavioral psychophysics and eye-tracking to investigate how the brain maintains visual stability and spatial constancy despite frequent eye movements. Additionally, their work explores transsaccadic memory, predictive remapping, and the mechanisms by which perceptual learning generalizes across different retinal locations through active exploration.
E157.research_direction: Dr. Deubel has recently been investigating the tight coupling between motor systems, visual attention, and memory. Their recent work explores how the preparation of concurrent saccadic eye movements and manual reaches impacts the maintenance of spatial information in visual working memory, asking whether these distinct effectors draw from a shared attentional resource or utilize independent selection mechanisms. Additionally, they are examining transsaccadic perceptual learning to understand how active visual exploration affects feature tuning and spatial generalization when targets shift across different retinal coordinates. To support these inquiries, Dr. Deubel has also been developing novel psychophysical methods, such as embedding test signals within continuous, dynamic 1/f noise to map the spatiotemporal distribution of covert and presaccadic attention without biasing the observer with sudden luminance transients or discrete object boundaries.

papers.title: Independent Effects of Eye and Hand Movements on Visual Working Memory
papers.abstract: The maintenance of information within visual working memory (VWM) is known to be susceptible to interference from both saccadic eye movements and manual reaching. This investigation utilized a multi-tasking paradigm involving simultaneous effector movements to determine whether these motor systems share a common attentional resource pool or operate via independent mechanisms. Participants were tasked with maintaining spatial locations in VWM while executing either single or concurrent eye and hand movements toward various goals. Quantitative results demonstrated that VWM performance was independently reduced by each effector's movement preparation, without the synergistic or competitive trade-offs that would characterize a shared resource model. The findings suggest that effector-specific attentional selection circuits, likely involving distinct frontoparietal feedback loops, independently prioritize and stabilize spatial representations in VWM.
papers.authors: Nina M. Hanning, Heiner Deubel

papers.title: Perceptual learning across saccades: Feature but not location specific
papers.abstract: Perceptual learning is conventionally characterized by tight retinotopic and feature specificity, traditionally assessed while observers maintain steady central fixation. However, natural visual exploration relies on rapid saccadic eye movements that project target objects across differing retinal coordinates. Here, human observers were trained to saccade to a peripheral oriented grating and discriminate an intraduration orientation change occurring during the eye movement. Training induced robust transsaccadic perceptual learning that was strictly feature-tuned, showing no transfer to an untrained orientation. In contrast to fixation-based learning, orientation training transferred entirely to an untrained visual hemifield location. Three control experiments confirmed that this cross-location generalization is contingent upon active saccade execution, as training without saccades eliminated the transfer. Furthermore, learning at the trained location generalized to an untrained fixation task, whereas transfer to the untrained location did not. These findings demonstrate that transsaccadic perceptual learning operates via a dual mechanism involving a location-specific presaccadic component and an active, saccade-driven mechanism that provides flexible spatial generalization.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Lukasz Grzeczkowski, Zhuanghua Shi, Martin Rolfs, Heiner Deubel

papers.title: A dynamic 1/f noise protocol to assess visual attention without biasing perceptual processing
papers.abstract: Traditional psychophysical investigations of visual attention deploy discrete, localized test items to quantify perceptual sensitivity across space and time. However, the transient presentation of these localized probes introduces luminance transients and structural landmarks that inevitably bias the spatial and temporal distribution of attention. To resolve this methodological confound, this work introduces a novel psychophysical protocol that embeds orientation-filtered test signals directly into a seamless, full-screen dynamic 1/f ('pink') noise background. Because probe signals are integrated into the continuous texture without introducing distinct object boundaries or temporal onset transients, observer expectations and perceptual allocation remain uncontaminated. The utility and sensitivity of the protocol were verified across both covert spatial attention and presaccadic attention tasks, demonstrating that it reliably captures the spatial distribution, temporal dynamics, and performance costs and benefits of visual attention across the visual field.
papers.authors: Nina M. Hanning, Heiner Deubel

E158.name: Daniel Wolpert
E158.bio: Daniel Wolpert is a Professor of Neuroscience and Vice-Chair of the Department of Neuroscience at Columbia University's Zuckerman Institute. Wolpert’s research explores the computational principles governing how the brain plans and controls movement through Bayesian decision theory and internal models. Their work examines how the central nervous system integrates sensory signals with prior knowledge to compensate for biological noise and uncertainty. Wolpert's current research focuses on the 'COIN' (COntextual INference) model, investigating how the brain uses contextual cues to segment, store, and retrieve a repertoire of motor memories.
E158.research_direction: Dr. Wolpert has recently been investigating the computational principles of sensorimotor control, particularly how practice schedules and contextual inference govern multitask learning and memory consolidation. Their recent work also explores the intersection of movement and cognitive development, using functional neuroimaging and behavioral metrics to examine the relationship between early sensorimotor variability and cognitive trajectories in young children with autism spectrum disorder. Furthermore, to overcome the limitations of traditional lab-based studies, they are developing open-source virtual reality platforms that utilize precise kinematic tracking to conduct remote, ecologically valid behavioral experiments. By integrating theoretical modeling with pediatric fMRI pipelines and modern WebXR technologies, Dr. Wolpert aims to build a comprehensive picture of how human motor systems adapt and function in both typical and atypical populations.

papers.title: Curriculum effects in multitask learning through the lens of contextual inference
papers.abstract: The structure of practice, or curriculum, significantly dictates learning outcomes across sensorimotor, perceptual, and cognitive domains. Multitask learning often reveals a fundamental trade-off between the speed of acquisition and long-term stability; for instance, blocked training typically accelerates initial acquisition but degrades long-term retention compared to interleaved practice—a phenomenon paralleling catastrophic forgetting in artificial neural networks. We present a unifying computational framework based on contextual inference to reconcile these effects. This model suggests that the brain treats curriculum as a latent variable, integrating task transition dynamics, environmental contextual cues, and observation noise. By framing multitask learning as an inference problem over task contexts, the framework explains how structured curricula facilitate perceptual learning while interleaved schedules promote robust motor memory consolidation through the prevention of erroneous context switches.
papers.authors: Sabyasachi Shivkumar, Máté Lengyel, Daniel M. Wolpert

papers.title: Protocol to investigate sensorimotor features in young children with autism using functional and resting-state fMRI data from the NIMH Data Archive
papers.abstract: This protocol details a standardized methodology for extracting and analyzing sensorimotor biomarkers in toddlers and young children diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) using large-scale neuroimaging datasets. Leveraging functional and resting-state fMRI data from the National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH) Data Archive, the procedure outlines specific preprocessing pipelines designed to handle the high motion artifacts typical in pediatric and ASD populations. The protocol focuses on identifying atypical neural signatures within the primary motor cortex and cerebellum that correlate with quantitative behavioral measures of motor variability. By standardizing the integration of neurobiological and behavioral datasets, this method facilitates the identification of early sensorimotor features that differentiate ASD subtypes and their respective cognitive trajectories.
papers.authors: Katia Denisova, Daniel M. Wolpert

papers.title: Sensorimotor variability distinguishes early features of cognition in toddlers with autism
papers.abstract: While movement plays a vital role in social connectivity, the relationship between early sensorimotor features and atypical cognition in autism remains under-researched. We performed a comprehensive analysis of quantitative and observation-based movement metrics in over 1,000 toddlers with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) stratified by intelligence quotient (IQ). Our findings reveal that toddlers with lower-IQ ASD exhibit significantly altered sensorimotor features and diminished gross motor milestones compared to their higher-IQ counterparts. Conversely, higher-IQ ASD toddlers displayed sensorimotor profiles indistinguishable from typically developing controls, suggesting that higher cognitive ability may confer resilience against motor control disruptions. These results suggest that atypical sensorimotor functioning is a core characteristic of lower-IQ ASD subtypes and emphasize the potential for tailored interventions targeting sensorimotor learning mechanisms in early childhood.
papers.authors: Kristina Denisova, Daniel M. Wolpert

papers.title: Ouvrai opens access to remote virtual reality studies of human behavioural neuroscience
papers.abstract: We introduce Ouvrai, an open-source platform designed to facilitate high-fidelity remote behavioral experiments using modern virtual reality (VR) hardware. Capitalizing on the high spatial and temporal resolution of six-degree-of-freedom kinematic tracking in consumer VR devices, Ouvrai enables the design of sophisticated browser-based experiments using WebXR technologies. The system streamlines the workflow from experiment creation to deployment, integrating directly with cloud databases and crowdsourcing platforms like Prolific and Amazon Mechanical Turk. Through three distinct motor learning validation experiments, we demonstrate that Ouvrai can reliably replicate laboratory-based findings in remote settings, significantly lowering the barrier to entry for large-scale, ecologically valid studies of human sensorimotor and cognitive function.
papers.authors: Evan Cesanek, Sabyasachi Shivkumar, James N. Ingram, Daniel M. Wolpert

E159.name: Andrew Pruszynski
E159.bio: Andrew Pruszynski is an Associate Professor at Western University and holds the Canada Research Chair in Sensorimotor Neuroscience. Their research examines the neural computations underlying motor control and sensory perception, focusing on how the nervous system integrates tactile and proprioceptive feedback to facilitate skilled reaching and object manipulation. Pruszynski has shown that rapid motor reflexes exhibit goal-dependent characteristics previously attributed to voluntary control, and that peripheral tactile neurons process geometric features like edge orientation. Pruszynski’s laboratory utilizes high-density electrophysiology, robotic Kinarm perturbations, and computational modeling to map the population dynamics of motor circuits during active behavior.
E159.research_direction: Dr. Pruszynski’s recent work explores the neural computations underlying sensorimotor control, investigating both the peripheral mechanics of active touch and the cortical dynamics of reaching and motor planning. On the sensory side, they have recently been examining how active fingertip scanning velocities influence tactile edge orientation discrimination to understand the signaling capacities of peripheral somatosensory neurons. In the motor domain, their research uses high-density neural recordings in primates and human neuroimaging to probe how motor circuits balance stable representations of limb posture with the rapid state transitions required for movement, and how these regions integrate probabilistic sensory expectations to prepare for sudden mechanical perturbations. Furthermore, they are investigating the cognitive and computational mechanisms of motor sequence learning, utilizing continuous reaching paradigms to disentangle how the brain predicts upcoming targets and optimizes movement trajectories without inevitably incurring additive reaction time penalties.

papers.title: Speed-dependent modulation of tactile edge orientation discrimination
papers.abstract: This study quantified the effect of active scanning velocity on the human capacity for edge-orientation discrimination. Participants moved their fingertips across parallel and non-parallel edge pairs while matching scanning speeds to visual cues ranging from 5 to 180 mm/s. Findings indicate that while natural scanning speeds average approximately 29 mm/s, orientation discrimination performance is significantly optimized at slower speeds (5 mm/s) and substantially degraded at higher velocities (90 and 180 mm/s). This behavioral modulation corresponds to the signaling limits of first-order tactile neurons, suggesting that active movement strategies are calibrated to leverage the velocity-dependent information capacity of the peripheral somatosensory system.
papers.authors: Vaishnavi Sukumar, J. Andrew Pruszynski

papers.title: Compositional neural dynamics during reaching
papers.abstract: Using high-density neural recordings in non-human primates and a reaching task designed to dissociate reach direction from final limb posture, this work characterizes the compositional structure of neural population dynamics in M1 and PMd. The results reveal three fundamental components: a posture subspace containing fixed points for specific arm configurations, rotational dynamics that transition the state between these fixed points to drive movement, and a condition-independent shift dimension representing trial progression. This geometric organization allows the motor cortex to maintain a representation of limb posture while simultaneously generating the dynamics required for control, providing a framework for how the brain resolves posture-dependent mechanical complexities during reaching.
papers.authors: Mehrdad Kashefi, Jonathan A. Michaels, Rhonda Kersten, Jonathan C. Lau, Jörn Diedrichsen, J. Andrew Pruszynski

papers.title: Sensory expectations shape neural population dynamics in motor circuits
papers.abstract: This research investigates how the motor system incorporates probabilistic sensory expectations into preparatory activity and corrective responses. Utilizing Neuropixel recordings in macaques and fMRI in humans, the authors demonstrate that prior to a mechanical perturbation, motor and somatosensory circuits adopt a preparatory state where the neural population geometry linearly encodes the probability of future perturbation directions. Upon perturbation onset, a condition-independent signal triggers a rapid state transition, producing corrective responses that initially reflect these expectations. Recurrent neural network modeling reveals that this architecture emerges only when specific sensory input is integrated with a generalized trigger signal, supporting the view that motor control relies on the proactive manipulation of sensory feedback loops.
papers.authors: Jonathan A. Michaels, Mehrdad Kashefi, Jack Zheng, Olivier Codol, Jeffrey Weiler, Rhonda Kersten, Paul L. Gribble, Jörn Diedrichsen, J. Andrew Pruszynski

papers.title: Sequence preparation is not always associated with a reaction time cost
papers.abstract: The study challenges the canonical view that increased reaction time (RT) for longer motor sequences reflects the computational cost of sequential preparation. By independently manipulating sequence length, target acquisition requirements, and spatial ambiguity, the researchers show that observed RT increases are fully explained by the ambiguity in selecting the initial target. When this selection ambiguity is eliminated, RT remains constant regardless of sequence length, even though kinematic analyses confirm the sequence was prepared in advance. These findings suggest that the motor system can plan multiple future reaches in parallel without an additive temporal penalty at initiation.
papers.authors: Armin Panjehpour, Mehrdad Kashefi, Jörn Diedrichsen, J. Andrew Pruszynski

papers.title: Motor Sequence Learning Involves Better Prediction of the Next Action and Optimization of Movement Trajectories
papers.abstract: This investigation disentangles the 'what' (sequence content) and 'how' (execution optimization) components of motor sequence learning using a continuous reaching paradigm. By varying the visibility of upcoming targets, the study found that learning in hidden-target conditions is driven by improved prediction of future locations, whereas learning in full-visibility conditions involves the optimization of movement trajectories and increased smoothness. The resulting motoric representations were found to be effector-specific and encoded contextual information across sequences of four or more movements. The data demonstrate that motor sequence learning involves the development of specialized representations that refine trajectory dynamics beyond simple associative anticipation.
papers.authors: Mehrdad Kashefi, Jörn Diedrichsen, J. Andrew Pruszynski

E161.name: Sabine Kastner
E161.department: Department of Psychology and Princeton Neuroscience Institute
E161.bio: Kastner investigates the neural mechanisms underlying visual perception, attention, and awareness through a comparative translational framework involving humans and non-human primates. Their research utilizes a multi-modal approach that integrates functional neuroimaging, diffusion tensor imaging, and intracranial electrophysiology to map large-scale cognitive networks. A significant focus of this work involves elucidating the role of the thalamus in regulating cortical communication and exploring the rhythmic temporal dynamics of attentional selection. Additionally, Kastner examines the development of these cognitive functions in children and characterizes their disruption following focal brain lesions.
E161.research_direction: Dr. Kastner's recent work explores the neural circuit dynamics underlying visual spatial attention and cognitive control, focusing on how large-scale cortical and thalamocortical networks rapidly communicate. Using cross-species intracranial electrophysiology and microstimulation in humans and macaques, they have recently been investigating the specific roles of diverse neural signatures, such as how alpha-band oscillations gate target enhancement versus distractor suppression and how thalamic pulvinar burst firing causally drives cortical attention states. They are also examining how transient, high-frequency activity bursts facilitate fast, long-range information transfer between sensory and associative brain regions during behavioral tasks. Broadly spanning from historical scholarship on the foundational dual-pathways of primate visual cognition to modern computational methods, their recent work also includes the development of automated, geometry-free spike-sorting algorithms designed to robustly track single-neuron activity despite electrode drift in large-scale recordings.

papers.title: High-frequency bursts facilitate fast communication for human spatial attention
papers.abstract: This investigation delineates the neural substrates of rapid, large-scale information transfer between sensory and associative cortical regions during cognitive control. Utilizing high-density human intracranial electrophysiology (iEEG) and spiking neural network simulations, the researchers identify high-frequency activity bursts (HFAbs) as discrete temporal windows of synchronized population firing that mediate fast, long-range communication. These bursts are elicited by sensory cues and targets and exhibit dynamic phase-coupling with low-frequency oscillations. Crucially, the magnitude of cue-evoked HFAbs and their transient decoupling from slow rhythms serve as robust predictors of behavioral accuracy. Network-level synchronization analysis reveals functionally specialized cue- and target-activated subnetworks that operate with a lead-lag temporal organization, where cue-related activity facilitates state transitions in target-related networks to guide behavior.
papers.authors: Kianoush Banaie Boroujeni, Randolph F. Helfrich, Ian C. Fiebelkorn, J. Nicole Bentley, Peter Brunner, Jack J. Lin, Robert T. Knight, Sabine Kastner

papers.title: Causal role for pulvinar burst firing in thalamo-cortical attention control
papers.abstract: This study characterizes the causal influence of specialized thalamic firing modes—specifically burst and tonic firing—on the regulation of large-scale cortical networks and attentional performance in macaques. Using an Egly-Driver covert attention paradigm combined with simultaneous recordings and electrical microstimulation (EMS), the researchers demonstrate that pulvinar burst firing (BF) is dynamically modulated by attentional demands and predicts task accuracy. BF events were uniquely associated with the reconfiguration of population-level neural codes in the lateral intraparietal area (LIP). EMS targeted at the pulvinar successfully triggered bursts that enhanced target detection sensitivity and increased cortical spike-field synchronization. The extent of behavioral facilitation correlated with the strength of burst recruitment, establishing pulvinar bursts as a causal driver of moment-to-moment control over cortical dynamics and cognitive outcomes.
papers.authors: Rober Boshra, Michael Harris, Kacie Dougherty, Melissa Berg, Britney M. Morea, Henry J. Alitto, Mario C. Rodriguez, W. Martin Usrey, Sabine Kastner

papers.title: KIASORT: Knowledge-Integrated Automated Spike Sorting for Geometry-Free Neuron Tracking
papers.abstract: The paper introduces KIASORT (Knowledge-Integrated Automated Spike Sorting), an advanced framework for the high-fidelity isolation of single-unit activity from large-scale extracellular recordings. To overcome common limitations such as electrode drift, channel noise, and nonlinear waveform distortions, KIASORT utilizes channel-specific classifiers trained in a hybrid linear-nonlinear feature space integrating PCA and UMAP. This geometry-free approach enables independent, per-neuron tracking across the recording duration without assuming rigid probe layout or cluster stability. Validation via biophysical simulations and analysis of primate striatum and mouse cortex data shows that KIASORT effectively compensates for heterogeneous, neuron-specific drift that standard methods fail to resolve, significantly increasing the yield of high-quality units while maintaining real-time computational efficiency.
papers.authors: Kianoush Banaie Boroujeni, Thilo Womelsdorf, Sabine Kastner

papers.title: Differential neural mechanisms underlie cortical gating of visual spatial attention mediated by alpha-band oscillations
papers.abstract: This study utilizes intracranial electrocorticography (ECoG) in epilepsy patients to delineate the divergent alpha-band (8–14 Hz) oscillatory mechanisms facilitating target enhancement and distractor suppression. The results identify a spatiotemporal dissociation during the cue-target interval: dorsal intraparietal areas contralateral to the attended hemifield exhibit sustained alpha desynchronization (enhancing sensory processing), while ventrolateral extrastriate areas ipsilateral to the attended side show sustained alpha synchronization (suppressing irrelevant processing). Functional connectivity and Granger causality analysis reveal that attended locations benefit from enhanced interareal feedforward and feedback communication via cross-frequency coupling between alpha and high-frequency activity. In contrast, interareal interactions are suppressed at unattended locations, where intra-areal interactions are prioritized. These findings suggest that the brain employs distinct, complementary alpha-mediated dynamics to gate sensory information efficiently within the visual hierarchy.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS)
papers.authors: Xiaofang Yang, Ian C. Fiebelkorn, Ole Jensen, Robert T. Knight, Sabine Kastner

papers.title: From Cells to Circuits, from Vision to Cognition, from Monkeys to Humans: Leslie Ungerleider's Pioneering Neuroscience
papers.abstract: This retrospective review evaluates the landmark contributions of Leslie Ungerleider to cognitive neuroscience, particularly her formulation of the dual-pathway model of visual processing. The article traces the development of the 'What' and 'Where' framework from its foundations in rhesus macaque lesion and tract-tracing studies to its validation and refinement through human functional neuroimaging. Key topics include the defining of the functional topography of the visual cortex, the neural substrates of object and face recognition, and the implementation of biased competition mechanisms in selective attention. By emphasizing a rigorous translational methodology that bridges anatomy, physiology, and behavior across primate species, the review contextualizes Ungerleider's lasting impact on modern theories of cortical organization and multi-modal research strategies.
papers.authors: Chris Baker, Sabine Kastner

E167.name: Stefan Treue
E167.bio: Stefan Treue investigates the physiological mechanisms of visual perception and attention in the primate brain. Utilizing extracellular recordings in macaque monkeys and human psychophysical experiments, Treue examines how top-down cognitive signals modulate sensory processing in cortical areas such as the middle temporal (MT) and medial superior temporal (MST) regions. Treue proposed the feature-similarity gain model, which describes how attention multiplicatively increases the gain of neurons selective for attended visual features across the entire visual field. Their research was recognized with the Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz Prize, and Treue currently serves as the Director of the German Primate Center, where they advocate for transparency and ethics in animal research.
E167.research_direction: Dr. Treue has recently been investigating the neural and cognitive mechanisms underlying visual perception, attention, and decision-making across both human and non-human primates. Their recent work explores the functional anatomy and network dynamics of top-down spatial attention in macaque area MT, utilizing pathway-selective optogenetics to probe frontal eye field (FEF) projections and examining how phase-amplitude coupling of neural oscillations coordinates selective sensory information routing. In human subjects, they are examining the real-time dynamics of perceptual decision-making to understand how social context and dyadic interactions influence an individual's confidence and accuracy during continuous perceptual reports. Alongside this fundamental research, they are advancing primate experimental methodology and animal welfare by developing novel frameless 3D camera-guided neuronavigation systems for precise electrode targeting and by studying the intrinsic value of agency and cognitive enrichment through contrafreeloading behaviors.

papers.title: Confidence over competence: Real-time integration of social information in human continuous perceptual decision-making
papers.abstract: Human perceptual judgment is highly sensitive to social context, yet the real-time dynamics of how individuals integrate ongoing social cues remain poorly understood. This study employs a novel continuous perceptual report (CPR) paradigm with peri-decision wagering to monitor accuracy and confidence in human dyads. While social interaction led to a significant increase in reported confidence across most participants, there was no corresponding improvement in average perceptual accuracy compared to solo performance. Quantitative modeling reveals a mutual convergence of both confidence and accuracy within dyads, which effectively subsidizes the performance of less competent partners at the expense of better-performing individuals. These findings demonstrate that real-time social information integration in continuous decision-making is asymmetrically biased toward confidence alignment rather than competence optimization.
papers.authors: Felix Schneider, Antonino Calapai, Roger Mundry, Raymundo Báez-Mendoza, Alexander Gail, Igor Kagan, Stefan Treue

papers.title: Pathway-selective optogenetics reveals the functional anatomy of top-down attentional modulation in the macaque visual cortex
papers.abstract: Top-down spatial attention is a fundamental mechanism for prioritizing relevant sensory information, with the frontal eye field (FEF) identified as a primary source of this modulation. However, the specific functional role of direct FEF-to-MT projections remains debated. By implementing pathway-selective optogenetic silencing of FEF axonal terminals within extrastriate area MT in behaving rhesus macaques, we show that this direct feedback circuit mediates roughly one-third of the total attentional modulation observed in MT neurons. Critically, this pathway contributes both to the enhancement of responses to attended targets and the suppression of responses to distractors, without impacting the purely sensory components of the neuronal responses. These results establish the direct FEF-MT projection as a causal anatomical substrate for the gain modulation that characterizes spatial attention.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS)
papers.authors: Janina Hüer, Pankhuri Saxena, Stefan Treue

papers.title: Using camera-guided electrode microdrive navigation for precise 3D targeting of macaque brain sites
papers.abstract: Achieving precise and repeatable localization of specific cortical and subcortical sites is critical for systems neuroscience. We introduce a novel frameless neuronavigation system for awake macaque monkeys that utilizes a multi-camera setup to track infrared-reflective markers on the animal and the microdrive in real-time. This method enables the calculation of flexible 3D trajectories without the constraints of traditional stereotaxic frames. Validation experiments using MRI-detectable iron deposits and pilot electrophysiological recordings demonstrate a targeting precision of less than 0.5 mm. The system facilitates more accurate and flexible longitudinal recordings across diverse brain regions, significantly enhancing the capability to explore the functional organization of the primate brain.
papers.authors: Max Arwed Crayen, Igor Kagan, Moein Esghaei, Dirk Hoehl, Uwe Thomas, Robert Prückl, Stefan Schaffelhofer, Stefan Treue

papers.title: Contrafreeloading and the value of control over visual stimuli in Japanese macaques (Macaca fuscata)
papers.abstract: The phenomenon of contrafreeloading—where animals choose to work for resources that are also available for free—suggests that agency and environmental control provide intrinsic value. Using a touchscreen-based multiple-choice interface, we examined contrafreeloading behavior in Japanese macaques. Despite the absence of food or fluid restriction, monkeys consistently engaged in cognitive tasks to obtain rewards rather than relying solely on freely provided alternatives. The animals displayed stable task preferences and high levels of proficiency, indicating that cognitive enrichment via interactive platforms can enhance animal welfare by providing opportunities for competence and environmental mastery. These results argue for the implementation of automated cognitive tools as a scalable strategy for promoting the psychological well-being of captive non-human primates.
papers.authors: Lauren C. Cassidy, Anahita Nazari, Pinar Yurt, Ralf R. Brockhausen, Stefan Treue

papers.title: Coupled oscillations orchestrate selective information transmission in visual cortex
papers.abstract: Effective routing of sensory signals to higher-order associative areas is hypothesized to be gated by the phase-amplitude coupling (PAC) of local field potential (LFP) rhythms. We recorded single-unit activity and LFPs from area MT in rhesus monkeys performing a motion discrimination task to investigate the link between network-level dynamics and individual neuron firing. Our analysis reveals that beta-band (15–25 Hz) oscillations, representing local population activity, exert a unidirectional gating influence on the firing of single neurons and high-gamma (60–120 Hz) activity. The strength of this coupling is highly predictive of the subjects' behavioral performance, suggesting that low-frequency oscillations serve as a top-down orchestration mechanism that selectively regulates the transmission of relevant sensory information to downstream areas.
papers.authors: Mohammad Bagher Khamechian, Mohammad Reza Daliri, Stefan Treue, Moein Esghaei

E168.name: Nilli Lavie
E168.department: Department of Psychology and the Institute of Cognitive Neuroscience
E168.bio: Lavie is a professor of cognitive neuroscience who developed the 'Load Theory of Attention and Cognitive Control' to address the early versus late selection debate. Their research utilizes a combination of psychophysics, functional neuroimaging (fMRI), and transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) to investigate the neural mechanisms of information processing capacity. Lavie's work demonstrates how perceptual load and executive control determine the extent of distractor interference, impacting visual awareness and task performance. Currently, their research extends these frameworks to individual differences in attention and the application of cognitive load principles to real-world environments such as driving and clinical disorders.
E168.research_direction: Dr. Lavie’s recent work explores the neural and behavioral mechanisms underlying selective and sustained attention across healthy, developmental, and clinical populations. A major focus of their research investigates how perceptual load modulates distractor suppression, using techniques like frequency-tagged EEG and event-related potentials to examine attentional dysfunction and cross-modal orienting in individuals with post-stroke fatigue. They have recently been tracking the natural fluctuations of sustained attention, measuring midfrontal theta oscillatory dynamics to differentiate periods of stable cognitive performance from those vulnerable to errors. Broadening the ecological validity of their research, Dr. Lavie also translates these attentional frameworks to real-world settings by testing whether laboratory metrics can predict classroom distractibility in adolescents and by developing computational clustering methods to map naturalistic gaze distributions in dynamic driving environments.

papers.title: Increased neural responsiveness to distractors irrespective of perceptual load explains attention deficit in post-stroke fatigue
papers.abstract: This study evaluates the neurophysiological mechanisms of attentional dysfunction in post-stroke fatigue (PSF) through the framework of Load Theory. Thirty-two chronic stroke patients performed a selective attention task across low, medium, and high perceptual load conditions while neural activity was quantified using frequency-tagged EEG (steady-state visually evoked potentials; SSVEP) at a 10 Hz distractor flicker frequency. Behavioral results indicated that Fatigue Severity Scale-7 (FSS-7) scores predicted significant response slowing that was exacerbated by increased perceptual load. Electrophysiological data revealed that higher fatigue severity was specifically associated with increased 10 Hz power in response to task-irrelevant distractors regardless of the task's perceptual load during the later phases of each trial. These findings suggest that PSF involves a pervasive deficit in distractor suppression and sensory attenuation that is present irrespective of overall task demands.
papers.authors: Annapoorna Kuppuswamy, Anthony Harris, William De Doncker, Adrian Alexander, Nilli Lavie

papers.title: Oscillatory dynamics of sustained attention states
papers.abstract: The research delineates the neural oscillatory dynamics underlying fluctuations between periods of stable performance ('in-the-zone') and periods of heightened variability and error susceptibility ('out-of-the-zone') during the gradual onset continuous performance task (gradCPT). Using a sample of thirty young adults, the study identified these states via reaction time (RT) variance time courses. EEG analysis demonstrated that 'out-of-the-zone' states—characterized by reduced perceptual sensitivity (A') and increased commission errors—were associated with a significant decrease in midfrontal theta (4–7 Hz) power approximately 400 ms around stimulus transitions. Furthermore, intra-individual variability in midfrontal theta power predicted behavioral stability, while individual differences in theta variability were associated with RT variability and commission error rates, identifying midfrontal theta as a marker for attentional control stability.
papers.authors: Rodolfo Solís-Vivanco, Louise Barne, Anthony Harris, Xin Liu, Nilli Lavie

papers.title: Applying Information Theory Divergence to Unsupervised Clustering of Driving Gaze Distribution
papers.abstract: This paper presents a computational method for characterizing driver visual attention using unsupervised clustering based on information-theory divergence. Naturalistic driving gaze samples were transformed into a 'vocabulary' of patterns by representing multi-second segments as stationary distributions using Gaussian Mixture Models (GMMs). A divergence-based clustering algorithm was applied to these GMMs to categorize gaze distributions across diverse driving environments. The efficacy of the method was validated by calculating the mutual information between resulting gaze clusters and specific driving scenarios, such as approaching and crossing junctions. The approach offers a robust framework for quantifying situational awareness and the spatial-temporal distribution of attention in complex, dynamic automotive settings without requiring manual labeling of gaze fixations.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the Human Factors and Ergonomics Society Annual Meeting
papers.authors: Ron Moshe Hecht, Omer Tsimhoni, Andrea Braunshtain, Nilli Lavie

papers.title: Sustained selective attention in adolescence: Cognitive development and predictors of distractibility at school
papers.abstract: This developmental study examined the maturation of sustained and selective attention and their predictive value for real-world classroom inattention in 162 participants across early, middle, and late adolescence and adulthood. Using an irrelevant distractor paradigm with varied perceptual load, the study found that sustained attention—quantified as the coefficient of variation (CV) of reaction times—continued to develop throughout late adolescence. In contrast, selective attention (the modulation of distractor interference by perceptual load) reached maturation earlier. Both laboratory indices of response variability and selective attention interference were identified as significant unique predictors of classroom distractibility latent factor scores, even when controlling for cognitive aptitude and lesson interest, establishing the ecological validity of these laboratory-derived attention metrics.
papers.authors: Michael H. Hobbiss, Nilli Lavie

papers.title: Influence of Perceptual Load on Attentional Orienting in Post-Stroke Fatigue: A Study of Auditory Evoked Potentials
papers.abstract: The investigation examined how visual perceptual load modulates the bottom-up orienting response to unanticipated auditory stimuli in twenty-four chronic post-stroke fatigue (PSF) patients. Participants completed a three-tone auditory oddball task (target, standard, and novel tones) embedded within a visual search task of either low or high perceptual load. Event-related potentials (ERPs), specifically N1, P3a, and P3b components, were measured via EEG. Behavioral results showed increased response latencies in noise conditions for high-fatigue patients. Electrophysiological analysis revealed that high visual perceptual load significantly attenuated the P3a amplitude—a marker of involuntary attentional switching—in response to novel auditory stimuli in PSF patients. The findings suggest that the clinical experience of PSF is linked to a reduced neural capacity for managing competing attentional demands, manifesting as an attenuated orienting response under high load.
papers.authors: William De Doncker, Adrian Alexander, Anthony Harris, Annapoorna Kuppuswamy, Nilli Lavie

E170.name: John Duncan
E170.department: MRC Cognition and Brain Sciences Unit
E170.lab_name: Brain mechanisms of attention and control
E170.bio: John Duncan is a cognitive neuroscientist who researches the neural mechanisms of selective attention and fluid intelligence. Duncan co-developed the biased competition framework of visual attention and identified the multiple-demand (MD) system, a frontoparietal network involved in organizing goal-directed thought. Their research integrates functional neuroimaging, neuropsychology, and single-cell electrophysiology to analyze how the brain partitions complex cognitive tasks into structured attentional episodes. Duncan’s recent work explores the relationship between these cortical control systems and the processes of human reasoning and problem-solving.
E170.research_direction: Dr. Duncan has recently been investigating the neural architecture and dynamics of the multiple-demand (MD) system, focusing on how the primate brain supports flexible cognitive control and goal-directed behavior. Using high-resolution fMRI and multivariate analyses in humans, their recent work explores the fine-grained functional topography of the prefrontal cortex, mapping how domain-general control regions interdigitate with category-selective visual patches and testing whether these MD networks preferentially encode abstract task rules over specific stimulus properties. Alongside this human imaging research, they are utilizing single-neuron and population recordings in non-human primates to examine how extended frontal networks hierarchically decompose complex spatial problems into manageable sub-goals and dynamically update internal models based on reinforcement feedback. To bridge these lines of inquiry, their research also employs cross-species neuroimaging to directly compare human and macaque brains, seeking to characterize the evolutionarily conserved anatomical blueprints that allow primates to integrate incoming sensory signals into an actionable cognitive workspace.

papers.title: Cognitive control networks in human and macaque
papers.abstract: This research utilizes high-resolution functional magnetic resonance imaging and multimodal cortical parcellation to perform a direct cross-species comparison between the human multiple-demand (MD) system and homologous networks in the macaque brain. While the human MD system is well-characterized as a distributed architecture for integrating task-relevant information into mental models for action selection, its macaque counterpart has lacked systematic comparative validation. The study reveals a highly conserved topographic organization of domain-general control regions across species, suggesting that the distributed workspace for flexible cognitive control is an evolutionarily ancient feature of the primate brain.
papers.authors: Valentina Mione, Freja Holm Kristensen, Moataz Assem, Soren Kyllingsbaek, Mark J. Buckley, Daniel J. Mitchell, John Duncan

papers.title: Neural dynamics in ventrolateral prefrontal cortex underlie learning from feedback
papers.abstract: The study investigates the neurophysiological basis of adaptive behavior by recording single-neuron and population activity from the ventrolateral prefrontal cortex (vlPFC) in non-human primates during a spatial learning task. By analyzing neural trajectories as monkeys updated their behavior based on reinforcement, the authors demonstrate that vlPFC populations dynamically encode feedback outcomes and task-state transitions. These findings indicate that the vlPFC serves as a critical computational node for transforming reinforcement signals into updated internal task representations, thereby bridging past experience with future action selection.
papers.authors: Runhao Lu, Mikiko Kadohisa, Makoto Kusunoki, Daniel J. Mitchell, Alexandra Woolgar, Mark J. Buckley, John Duncan

papers.title: Category-biased patches encircle core domain-general regions in the human lateral prefrontal cortex
papers.abstract: Leveraging high-resolution multimodal MRI data from the Human Connectome Project (HCP), this study delineates the fine-grained functional topography of the lateral prefrontal cortex (PFC). The investigators identify specialized patches selective for faces, places, tools, and body parts that are systematically interdigitated with domain-general multiple-demand (MD) regions. Crucially, these category-selective patches are found to encircle the MD core without overlapping it. This recurring motif of interdigitated domain-specific and domain-general circuits suggests an organizational principle that facilitates the integration of specialized sensory signals into a common cognitive workspace.
papers.authors: Moataz Assem, Sneha Shashidhara, Matthew F. Glasser, John Duncan

papers.title: Neural dynamics of an extended frontal lobe network in goal-subgoal problem solving
papers.abstract: This study explores the hierarchical representation of complex tasks by recording from a broad frontal network—including the vlPFC, dmPFC, dPM, and insula/orbitofrontal cortex—as monkeys solved multi-step spatial mazes. The data reveal significant functional heterogeneity in the encoding of task components across the multiple-demand (MD) network: the vlPFC primarily represents sensory inputs and current states, the dmPFC maintains stable representations of global goals, and the dPM facilitates rapid movement selection. These results provide evidence for a distributed yet specialized framework within the frontal lobe that supports the hierarchical decomposition of goals into sub-goals.
papers.authors: Valentina Mione, Jascha Achterberg, Makoto Kusunoki, Mark J. Buckley, John Duncan

papers.title: Task and stimulus coding in the multiple-demand network
papers.abstract: Applying multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) to high-resolution fMRI data, the authors examine the representational content of the human multiple-demand (MD) system during various executive tasks. The findings indicate that core MD regions exhibit robust discrimination of distinct task-related operations—such as rule-switching and working memory—while showing significantly lower sensitivity to the categorical properties of the stimuli involved (e.g., faces vs. objects). This dissociation suggests that the MD network is functionally prioritized for encoding the abstract structure and control requirements of a task rather than the perceptual details of task-relevant stimuli.
papers.authors: Sneha Shashidhara, Moataz Assem, Matthew F. Glasser, John Duncan

E174.name: Laurent Itti
E174.department: Thomas Lord Department of Computer Science
E174.bio: Laurent Itti is a Professor of Computer Science, Psychology, and Neuroscience at the University of Southern California and the director of the iLab. Itti developed computational frameworks for visual saliency and bottom-up attention that simulate the neural mechanisms biological systems use to prioritize visual stimuli. Their research connects computational neuroscience and machine vision, focusing on scene understanding, eye-movement control, and the role of Bayesian surprise in perception. Itti’s recent work applies neuromorphic algorithms to real-time gaze prediction and uses eye-tracking behavior as a diagnostic tool for identifying neurological disorders.
E174.research_direction: Dr. Itti's recent work explores a diverse range of topics spanning biologically inspired deep learning, robotic visual navigation, and generative model forensics. They have recently been investigating how to improve network optimization by mimicking the non-linear computational properties of biological dendrites, alongside developing visual reinforcement learning architectures capable of lifelong learning without catastrophic forgetting. In the realm of embodied vision, their research aims to enhance sim-to-real transfer for navigating physical robots by translating first-person camera streams into latent Bird’s Eye View world models, supported by their curation of massive, multi-modal outdoor datasets for fine-grained 3D perception. Additionally, Dr. Itti is examining the geometric structure of generative AI systems, utilizing Riemannian manifolds to map model-specific artifacts and create robust metric fingerprints for detecting synthetic media.

papers.title: Riemannian-Geometric Fingerprints of Generative Models
papers.abstract: This work introduces a formal geometric framework for generative model (GM) attribution by defining fingerprints and artifacts within the context of Riemannian geometry. To overcome the limitations of Euclidean distance metrics in high-dimensional feature spaces, the authors propose learning Riemannian metrics from data, effectively characterizing GMs on non-Euclidean manifolds. The methodology utilizes geodesic distances and a kNN-based Riemannian center of mass to represent and analyze model-specific artifacts across diverse architectures and modalities, including vision and vision-language models. Empirical results across 27 distinct model architectures demonstrate significant improvements in attribution accuracy and cross-dataset generalization compared to previous Euclidean methods, facilitating robust identification of synthetic data in both white-box and black-box deployment scenarios.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF International Conference on Computer Vision (ICCV)
papers.authors: Hae Jin Song, Laurent Itti

papers.title: Perforated Backpropagation: A Neuroscience Inspired Extension to Artificial Neural Networks
papers.abstract: The authors propose 'Perforated Backpropagation,' a novel optimization paradigm that mimics the non-linear computational properties of biological dendrites within deep neural network architectures. The method extends the standard artificial neuron unit by introducing 'Dendrite Nodes' that are trained to minimize the residual error of the original neurons after an initial convergence phase. By freezing these nodes and re-optimizing the primary network parameters using integrated feedback signals, the system achieves hierarchical feature coding more representative of biological neural systems. Experiments using PyTorch across multiple vision and language domains, including EMNIST and SNLI datasets, demonstrate that the inclusion of dendrite-inspired nodes enables up to 90% model compression and accuracy improvements of up to 16% over original baseline architectures.
papers.authors: Rorry Brenner, Laurent Itti

papers.title: USCILab3D: A Large-scale, Long-term, Semantically Annotated Outdoor Dataset
papers.abstract: This paper presents USCILab3D, a comprehensive multi-modal outdoor dataset curated over 12 months using a teleoperated mobile robot equipped with a five-camera rig and a 360-degree LiDAR. The dataset comprises 1.4 million point clouds and 10 million images covering diverse environmental, weather, and lighting conditions across 229 acres. Automated labeling using state-of-the-art foundation models provides semantic annotations for 267 distinct object categories. The repository includes precise 3D reconstructions, pose-stamped trajectories, and multi-view imagery, specifically designed to address gaps in fine-grained semantic 3D vision. Benchmarking results for novel view synthesis and semantic segmentation demonstrate the dataset's efficacy in facilitating robust 3D perception and robotic navigation research in complex real-world settings.
papers.venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS) Datasets and Benchmarks Track
papers.authors: Kiran Lekkala, Henghui Bao, Peixu Cai, Wei Zer Lim, Chen Liu, Laurent Itti

papers.title: Bird's Eye View Based Pretrained World model for Visual Navigation
papers.abstract: This paper introduces a world model architecture that enhances the sim-to-real transferability of visual navigation agents through a latent Bird's Eye View (BEV) representation. The system employs a perception module pretrained on unlabeled video and trajectory data from the CARLA simulator to translate first-person view (FPV) RGB streams into egocentric BEV embeddings. Temporal dynamics and observation uncertainty are managed via a Mixture Density LSTM and anchor image-based state checking. The frozen pretrained model enables zero-shot deployment on physical differential drive robots, significantly accelerating reinforcement learning and goal-based planning in unseen environments. Results indicate that BEV representations provide a more robust and transferable latent space for navigation compared to direct FPV-based latent models.
papers.authors: Kiran Lekkala, Chen Liu, Laurent Itti

papers.title: Evaluating Pretrained models for Deployable Lifelong Learning
papers.abstract: The authors establish the DeLL (Deployment for Lifelong Learning) benchmark to evaluate the scalability and resource efficiency of visual reinforcement learning systems in continual learning scenarios. The proposed architecture integrates a task-mapper based on Few-Shot Class Incremental Learning (FSCIL) with an encoder pretrained on curated datasets. This modular design allows the system to recognize new tasks and load corresponding policy parameters without catastrophic forgetting or extensive computational overhead. Evaluated on the Atari 2600 suite, the system demonstrates superior performance in retaining knowledge across expanding task sequences and high efficiency in deploying to novel RL environments with minimal fine-tuning and reduced memory footprints.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Winter Conference on Applications of Computer Vision (WACV)
papers.authors: Kiran Lekkala, Eshan Bhargava, Yunhao Ge, Laurent Itti

E175.name: Eyal Seidemann
E175.department: Department of Neuroscience and Department of Psychology
E175.bio: Eyal Seidemann is a Professor of Neuroscience and Psychology at the University of Texas at Austin and directs the Seidemann Lab. Seidemann's research investigates the neural basis of visual perception and decision-making by combining widefield optical imaging with electrophysiology and optogenetics in alert macaque monkeys. Their work involves characterizing spatiotemporal population dynamics in the primary visual cortex and developing computational decoding models to predict psychophysical performance from neural signals. Seidemann's current research focuses on the real-time monitoring and manipulation of cortical circuits to elucidate the causal relationship between population-level activity and visual behavior.
E175.research_direction: Dr. Seidemann has recently been investigating the nonlinear temporal dynamics of neural population responses in the primary visual cortex using widefield optical imaging techniques in alert macaques. Their recent work explores how different mesoscopic neuroimaging modalities, including voltage-sensitive dyes and novel genetically encoded voltage and calcium indicators, capture distinct aspects of underlying neural activity. By developing dynamic gain-control models, they are seeking to reconcile the disparate temporal profiles of these macaque optical signals with macroscopic human fMRI and ECoG data. Furthermore, they are examining how these rapid, population-level computations at the columnar and retinotopic scales account for natural scene processing and specific perceptual phenomena, such as the behavioral impairments observed during visual similarity masking.

papers.title: Fast neural population dynamics in primate V1 captured by a genetically-encoded voltage indicator
papers.abstract: This study presents the first successful chronic widefield imaging of a genetically encoded voltage indicator (GEVI), specifically 'pAce', within the excitatory neurons of the primary visual cortex (V1) in alert macaque monkeys. The researchers utilized this technology to evaluate nonlinear neural dynamics triggered by visual stimuli with various temporal waveforms and contrast levels. Quantitative comparisons with signals from genetically encoded calcium indicators (GECIs) and synthetic voltage-sensitive dyes (VSDs) demonstrated that GEVI imaging captures significantly faster response transients and tracks higher temporal frequencies. Furthermore, GEVIs exhibited responses at lower stimulus contrasts than GECIs. The authors proposed a simple nonlinear model to relate these different indicators, supporting the hypothesis that GEVI signals represent the summation of local membrane potentials while GECI signals reflect temporally filtered spiking activity. This methodology enables the measurement of neural population responses at the scale of orientation columns in head-unrestrained primates when integrated with lensless imaging systems.
papers.authors: Jingyang Zhou, Yuzhi Chen, Matt Whitmire, Pin Kwang Tan, Jimin Wu, Ashok Veeraraghavan, Jacob T. Robinson, Wilson S. Geisler, Vincent A. Pieribone, Eyal Seidemann

papers.title: Disparate nonlinear neural dynamics measured with different techniques in macaque and human V1
papers.abstract: Diverse neuroimaging modalities offer varying spatial and temporal resolutions, complicating efforts to relate neural dynamics across different methods. This research compares the nonlinearity of neural dynamics measured using widefield voltage-sensitive dye imaging (VSDI) and genetically encoded calcium indicators (GECI) in macaque V1 against fMRI and electrocorticography (ECoG) data from human V1. Utilizing visual stimuli with diverse temporal profiles, the study found that stimulus-evoked VSDI and GCaMP responses in the macaque are surprisingly near-additive over time. This finding contrasts with the pronounced sub-additive dynamics previously observed in human visual cortex. To resolve these discrepancies, the authors developed a simple yet flexible delayed normalization model. This gain-control model successfully captures the distinct dynamics across different measurement techniques and species, suggesting that dynamic gain control functions as a canonical computation within neural processing circuits.
papers.authors: Jingyang Zhou, Matt Whitmire, Yuzhi Chen, Eyal Seidemann

papers.title: Neural correlates of perceptual similarity masking in primate V1
papers.abstract: Visual detection performance is significantly impaired when a target orientation closely matches the orientation of its background, a phenomenon known as similarity masking. This study investigated whether nonlinear computations in the primary visual cortex (V1) account for this perceptual effect. Using voltage-sensitive dye imaging (VSDI) in behaving macaques, the researchers measured population responses at both retinotopic and columnar scales. They discovered that V1 responses exhibit two distinct temporal phases: an initial transient phase where target-evoked signals are paradoxically enhanced by target-background similarity, and a subsequent phase where responses are suppressed in a manner consistent with behavioral masking. Integration of these two phases revealed that overall V1 activity at the columnar scale correlates with the behavioral masking effect. The findings are explained by a dynamic population gain-control model, supporting the role of V1 nonlinear mechanisms in natural scene processing and visual detection tasks.
papers.authors: Spencer Chin-Yu Chen, Yuzhi Chen, Wilson S. Geisler, Eyal Seidemann

E177.name: Klaus Oberauer
E177.bio: Klaus Oberauer is a Professor of Cognitive Psychology at the University of Zurich, specializing in the computational and functional architecture of human cognitive capacity. Oberauer proposed a three-level framework of working memory that distinguishes between the focus of attention, a region of direct access for maintaining ad-hoc bindings, and activated long-term memory. Their research utilizes a synthesis of behavioral experiments, eye-tracking, and formal computational modeling—specifically interference-based and Bayesian models—to investigate the mechanisms of information binding and retrieval. Current work by Oberauer explores the interactions between working memory and long-term memory, the nature of visual working memory representations, and the advancement of formal theory development in psychological science.
E177.research_direction: Dr. Oberauer's recent work explores the mechanistic architecture and capacity limits of working memory, frequently utilizing computational approaches like connectionist architectures and multinomial process tree modeling. They have recently been investigating how features and items are structurally bound together in memory, asking how semantic similarity influences serial recall and whether multi-element units are stored as integrated representations or independent pairwise bindings. Their research also examines the filtering and updating mechanisms of working memory, specifically probing whether briefly processed distractors can be prevented from encoding and whether the deliberate removal of irrelevant items enhances memory by freeing cognitive capacity or reducing proactive interference. Additionally, their recent theoretical work bridges the gap between procedural working memory and action control, exploring how stimulus-response bindings are represented, updated, and retrieved to guide goal-directed behavior.

papers.title: Semantic representations in working memory: A computational model
papers.abstract: This research provides a comprehensive mechanistic account of semantic knowledge's influence on verbal working memory (WM) by extending a connectionist architecture for immediate serial recall. The model incorporates semantic representations through a tagging mechanism that facilitates the selective encoding of categorical features shared among list items, allowing for the retrospective encoding of shared features. This architecture successfully captures semantic similarity effects, including the facilitation of order memory and the characteristic patterns of transposition errors—whereby items migrate more frequently toward the positions of semantically similar items—challenging existing models that conceptualize similarity primarily as a source of interference or reduced discriminability.
papers.authors: Benjamin Kowialiewski, Klaus Oberauer

papers.title: Can We Process Information Without Encoding It Into Working Memory?
papers.abstract: This study evaluates the limits of attentional filtering in working memory, specifically addressing whether information that must be briefly processed for a task, but is not intended for maintenance, can be selectively excluded from encoding. Utilizing a complex-span task with pre-cue, retro-cue, and distractor-free control conditions, the authors employed a Memory Measurement Model (M3) to quantify the memory strength of item and binding representations. The results demonstrate that processed distractors are retained in WM with comparable strength regardless of whether they were identified as irrelevant prior to or following the processing stage, suggesting that information requiring a processing operation cannot be selectively filtered during WM encoding.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
papers.authors: Chenyu Li, Gidon T. Frischkorn, Klaus Oberauer
