papers.title: Bindings for Action: Bridging the Gap Between Theories of Procedural Working Memory and Action Control Research
papers.abstract: This theoretical work synthesizes the Binding and Retrieval in Action Control (BRAC) framework with the procedural working memory (WM) model to advance a unified theory of human action control. The authors argue that both frameworks describe goal-directed behavior through analogous binding mechanisms—event files in BRAC and stimulus-response/item-context bindings in procedural WM. By extending the procedural WM model to simulate characteristic empirical findings in action control research, such as stimulus-response binding effects and their subsequent retrieval dynamics, the paper proposes an integrated computational framework for how procedural information is represented, updated, and retrieved to manage tasks.
papers.authors: Gidon T. Frischkorn, Isabel Courage, Hannah Dames, David Dignath, Christina U. Pfeuffer, Moritz Schiltenwolf, Andrea Kiesel, Klaus Oberauer

papers.title: The benefit of removing information from working memory: Increasing available cognitive resources or reducing interference?
papers.abstract: This investigation seeks to distinguish whether the 'removal benefit' in working memory—the enhanced memory for remaining items after discarding irrelevant ones—is caused by the reduction of proactive interference or the liberation of general cognitive resources. Through several experiments manipulating removal timing (immediate versus delayed), the authors found that removal failed to significantly reduce interference from the to-be-forgotten items. Instead, removal consistently improved memory for the item-location bindings of information encoded after the removal process. These findings provide evidence that the removal mechanism proactively facilitates performance by freeing up capacity rather than retroactively attenuating interference between stored representations.
papers.authors: Chenyu Li, Gidon T. Frischkorn, Hannah Dames, Klaus Oberauer

papers.title: A multinomial model-based analysis of bindings in working memory
papers.abstract: This study employs multinomial process tree (MPT) modeling to adjudicate between four theoretical accounts of unit integration in working memory: unitization, unitization-with-element-failure, pairwise-binding, and a hybrid model. Participants performed cued recall of multi-element units (triplets of items) in three experiments. Model comparisons revealed that the hybrid model—which posits both an integrated unit representation retrieved in an all-or-none manner and supplemental independent pairwise bindings—best explained the observed response distributions. The analysis also rejected the hypothesis that nonspatial item bindings are necessarily mediated through shared spatial locations, supporting a hierarchical, multi-level structure for bindings in WM.
papers.authors: Suaad Said Al Hadhrami, Lea M. Bartsch, Klaus Oberauer

E178.name: Bradley Postle
E178.department: Department of Psychology and Department of Psychiatry
E178.bio: Bradley Postle is a Professor of Psychology and Psychiatry at the University of Wisconsin–Madison who investigates the cognitive and neural foundations of human visual cognition, focusing on working memory, attention, and consciousness. Postle proposes that working memory is an emergent property of the brain, resulting from the coordinated recruitment of sensory and motor systems rather than a distinct storage buffer. Their laboratory utilizes a multi-methodological approach—including fMRI, EEG, and transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), often in simultaneous combinations—alongside multivariate computational modeling to examine the dynamic representation and prioritization of information in the mind.
E178.research_direction: Dr. Postle has recently been investigating the neural mechanisms and representational architectures that govern visual working memory. Their recent work explores the dynamic control of mnemonic information, using high-density EEG and single-pulse TMS to probe how the brain actively clears outdated items, resolves processing conflict between internal memory maintenance and external perception, and stabilizes representational precision via posterior beta-band oscillations. Additionally, they are investigating the spatial and geometric organization of working memory using fMRI and recurrent neural networks. Specifically, their research examines how early visual and parietal cortices divide the labor of encoding sensory content versus maintaining structural context—such as temporal order—while dynamically adjusting the priority status of held items.

papers.title: EEG Correlates of Active Removal from Working Memory
papers.abstract: This research identifies the neurophysiological substrates of volitional information clearance from visual working memory (WM). Using an ABC-retrocuing paradigm and high-density EEG, the authors evaluated the 'hijacked adaptation' hypothesis, which posits that active removal is mediated by top-down gain modulation of stimulus-specific perceptual circuits. Analysis of oscillatory dynamics revealed that the initiation of active removal is indexed by enhanced anterior-to-posterior traveling waves in the alpha and beta bands. Furthermore, the functional consequence of this operation was a significant reduction in the excitability of perceptual circuits tuned to the discarded item, as evidenced by attenuated event-related potentials (ERPs) to task-irrelevant 'pings' and a shift in the familiarity landscape estimated via Target Confusability Competition (TCC) modeling.
papers.authors: Jiangang Shan, Bradley R. Postle

papers.title: Temporal Dynamics and Representational Consequences of the Control of Processing Conflict between Visual Working Memory and Visual Perception
papers.abstract: This study characterizes the regulatory mechanisms managing processing conflict between concurrent visual working memory (VWM) maintenance and external visual discrimination. By integrating reinforcement-learning models with EEG, the researchers dissociated preparatory and reflexive control signals. Preparatory control was reflected in pretrial frontal-midline theta power, which predicted the fidelity of the VWM representation. Conversely, encountering unexpected mnemonic-perceptual conflict elicited a left-frontal positivity, serving as a control prediction error. This error triggered reflexive suppression of the conflicting perceptual representation, leading to below-baseline decoding of the discriminandum and a subsequent repulsive serial bias on VWM recall, illustrating the dynamic reconfiguration of neural resources to mitigate cross-modal interference.
papers.authors: Chunyue Teng, Jacqueline M. Fulvio, Mattia Pietrelli, Jiefeng Jiang, Bradley R. Postle

papers.title: Single-pulse TMS affects working-memory performance via posterior beta-band oscillations
papers.abstract: The causal link between posterior cortical oscillations and visual working memory (VWM) behavior was investigated using single-pulse transcranial magnetic stimulation (spTMS) coupled with EEG. Stimulating either the intraparietal sulcus (IPS) or early visual cortex (EVC) during the delay period revealed that spTMS-induced fluctuations in beta-band (13–30 Hz) power—rather than alpha-band activity—predicted trial-by-trial variance in VWM precision. The findings suggest that posterior beta oscillations are functional signatures of the representational stability and accessibility of items in VWM. This study provides evidence that perturbing specific frequency-dependent states in the dorsal visual stream can systematically modulate mnemonic readout, underscoring the role of beta dynamics in the maintenance of high-fidelity visual representations.
papers.authors: Jacqueline M. Fulvio, Saskia Haegens, Bradley R. Postle

papers.title: Representing context and priority in working memory
papers.abstract: This investigation explores how the brain dissociates first-order ordinal context from second-order priority status in working memory (WM). Through recurrent neural network (RNN) simulations and reanalysis of human fMRI and EEG datasets, the authors found that these two properties recruit distinct representational geometries. Ordinal context, which remains stable across a trial, is encoded by segregating item representations into orthogonal subspaces. In contrast, the dynamic prioritization of items is achieved via shifts within specific manifolds or strata inside these subspaces. The results indicate that while priority-based transformations are sensitive to behavioral efficiency and are prominent in early visual areas, context-based segregation is a more fundamental structural property of the dorsal visual stream used to organize mnemonic content.
papers.authors: Quan Wan, Adel Ardalan, Jacqueline M. Fulvio, Bradley R. Postle

papers.title: Investigating the roles of visual and parietal cortex in representing content versus context in visual working memory
papers.abstract: This research employs functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) to delineate the distinct neuroanatomical substrates responsible for encoding stimulus identity (content) and the contextual parameters (e.g., temporal order or spatial position) that organize information within visual working memory (VWM). Utilizing a design that systematically varies the mnemonic load and contextual demands, the authors observed that while early visual cortex (EVC) maintains high-resolution representations of sensory content, the intraparietal sulcus (IPS) is selectively involved in representing the contextual scaffold. The study demonstrates that parietal regions facilitate the binding of sensory features to their respective trial contexts, a process essential for the flexible prioritization and selective retrieval of items from a capacity-limited WM system.
papers.authors: Chunyue Teng, Bradley R. Postle

E180.name: Paul Bays
E180.bio: Paul Bays is a Professor of Computation and Cognition at the University of Cambridge, where they direct the Computational Cognition Group. Bays's research utilizes visual psychophysics, mathematical modeling, and eye-tracking to investigate how the brain constructs and maintains internal representations for goal-directed behavior. This work focuses on the resource-based limits of visual working memory, arguing that memory fidelity is constrained by neural noise rather than discrete storage slots. Additionally, their research characterizes the computational principles of feature binding, Bayesian efficient coding, and the predictive attenuation of self-generated sensory inputs.
E180.research_direction: Dr. Bays has recently been investigating the computational principles governing how the human brain encodes sensory information and allocates limited cognitive resources across modalities. Their recent work explores the dynamics of visual working memory, utilizing continuous analogue report tasks to isolate internal representational noise from motor execution errors and to examine how memory precision is impacted by varying set sizes, temporal delays, and intrinsic motivational states. Beyond visual cognition, they are also probing sensorimotor predictions and haptic perception, applying Bayesian efficient coding and probabilistic frameworks to investigate classical phenomena like the size-weight illusion and the mechanisms of sensory attenuation during self-touch.

papers.title: Divisive attenuation based on noisy sensorimotor predictions accounts for excess variability in self-touch
papers.abstract: The investigators delineate a computational framework to account for the systematic overestimation of target forces observed in tactile force-matching paradigms involving self-generation. By integrating sensory attenuation mechanisms driven by efference copy-based forward models, the study reconciles the discrepancy between direct manual reproduction and indirect adjustment via motor control. The model distinguishes between perceptual, mnemonic, and predictive noise components, demonstrating that self-generated tactile reafference exhibits heightened trial-to-trial variance. These findings provide empirical and theoretical support for a divisive scaling of sensory signals rather than a fixed subtractive offset, emphasizing the probabilistic nature of sensorimotor predictions in modulating haptic perception and isolating a pure measure of attenuation strength from nearly 500 participants.
papers.authors: Nicola Valè, Ivan Tomić, Zahara Gironés, Daniel M. Wolpert, Konstantina Kilteni, Paul M. Bays

papers.title: Intrinsic rewards guide visual resource allocation via reinforcement learning
papers.abstract: This research explores the influence of intrinsic motivational states on the allocation of limited-capacity visual resources. Utilizing continuous reproduction tasks for motion direction, the authors manipulated observers' perceived efficacy through deceptive performance feedback and variations in stimulus reliability. Results indicate that the visual system prioritizes the encoding of stimuli associated with lower levels of subjective uncertainty, effectively weighting internal representations by their perceived reliability (intrinsic reward). This prioritization strategy was formally modeled by augmenting a neural normalization framework with a reinforcement learning rule, where intrinsic reward signals cumulatively modulate resource gain. Crucially, this bias led to a deviation from the globally optimal error-minimization strategy, suggesting that intrinsic rewards can paradoxically impair task-wide representational fidelity by causing resource allocation to deviate from objectivity.
papers.authors: Ivan Tomić, Rodrigo Raimundo, Paul M. Bays

papers.title: Dynamics of variability and bias in working memory
papers.abstract: This research addresses the contested relationship between memory load and temporal decay in the maintenance of visual working memory (VWM). By combining data from six novel experiments with a meta-analysis of seven previously published datasets, the authors assessed the independent and interactive effects of set size and retention interval on the precision and systematic bias of feature reports. The analysis reveals that the variance of the error distribution increases with both the quantity of stored items and the duration of the delay, with a significant multiplicative interaction suggesting that higher memory loads accelerate the stochastic diffusion of stored representations over time. Conversely, stimulus-specific biases in the feature space remained invariant across changes in load and delay, indicating that while representational fidelity is subject to dynamic, resource-limited degradation, the underlying structural attractors in psychological space are stable over the timescales of working memory maintenance.
papers.authors: Ivan Tomić, Sebastian Schneegans, Paul M. Bays

papers.title: Weight illusions explained by efficient coding based on correlated natural statistics
papers.abstract: A normative computational theory for the Size-Weight Illusion (SWI) and Material-Weight Illusion (MWI) is proposed, grounded in the principles of Bayesian efficient coding. The model posits that the precision of haptic mass encoding is optimized to match the empirical joint distribution of mass and volume encountered in the natural environment. By analyzing the bivariate log-normal distribution of everyday liftable objects, the author demonstrates that the resulting non-uniformity in mass discriminability (Fisher information) leads to systematic estimation biases when decoded via a Bayesian framework. Specifically, the 'anti-Bayesian' overestimation of weight for smaller or denser objects is shown to be a predictable outcome of likelihood repulsion induced by the gradient of encoding precision. The framework quantitatively fits human weight-ratio estimates and explains the adaptability of weight illusions to altered environmental statistics.
papers.authors: Paul M. Bays

papers.title: Dissecting the components of error in analogue report tasks
papers.abstract: This methodological study systematically decomposes the sources of error in continuous analogue report tasks used to assay the fidelity of sensory and mnemonic representations. By varying the geometric parameters of the response interface—including color wheel diameter and chroma radius—alongside traditional manipulations of storage load and maintenance delay, the authors isolated representational variance from motor and decisional noise. The results show that set size effects exert a powerful influence on response variability even in the absence of a retention interval, while factors associated with manual precision and the scaling of the response space have negligible impacts. These findings provide a quantitative validation of the analogue report paradigm as a high-fidelity probe of internal representational states, while clarifying that the majority of reported variance reflects internal stochastic noise rather than peripheral execution errors.
papers.authors: Ivan Tomić, Dagmar Adamcová, Máté Fehér, Paul M. Bays

E181.name: Wei Ji Ma
E181.department: Department of Psychology and the Center for Neural Science
E181.bio: Wei Ji Ma is a Professor of Neural Science and Psychology whose research investigates the computational principles underlying human decision-making, perception, and memory. Ma developed Bayesian models of sensory processing and introduced the concept of probabilistic population codes to describe how the brain represents uncertainty. Their current work utilizes human behavioral experiments and mathematical modeling to explore resource rationality in visual working memory and the mechanics of multi-step planning in complex environments. Ma’s methodology integrates computational cognitive science with neuroimaging and electrophysiology to connect algorithmic theories with their biological implementations.
E181.research_direction: Dr. Ma's recent work explores the computational and cognitive principles underlying human planning, reward processing, and neural representation. They have recently been investigating the mechanics of goal-directed behavior, using computational process models to understand how humans utilize backward reasoning through subgoal spaces and how environmental uncertainty influences planning effort. Additionally, their research examines the mechanisms of decision-making by assessing how individual temporal discounting rates model real-world procrastination, and by testing whether dopaminergic neurons utilize information-theoretic efficient coding schemes to represent stochastic reward distributions. Finally, their recent theoretical work seeks to establish unifying frameworks to clarify foundational concepts of neural representation, aiming to rigorously map common analytical tools like representational similarity analysis to specific computational dimensions.

papers.title: Reward prediction error neurons implement an efficient code for reward
papers.abstract: The study formalizes the efficient coding of reward signals by deriving optimal population-level representations for stochastic reward distributions. Utilizing extracellular recordings from dopaminergic reward prediction error neurons (RPENs) in macaques and mice, the authors demonstrate that neuronal response properties—including the distribution of tuning function midpoints, the relationship between threshold and gain, and the adaptive scaling of slopes—align closely with the predictions of an information-theoretic efficient code. These results provide a unifying framework that links the principles of sensory efficient coding with distributional reinforcement learning in the reward system.
papers.authors: Heiko H. Schütt, Dongjae Kim, Wei Ji Ma

papers.title: Temporal discounting predicts procrastination in a real-world task
papers.abstract: This investigation examines the cognitive drivers of procrastination by tracking the continuous work progress of participants in a naturalistic, long-term reading task. Moving beyond traditional self-report measures and simple completion times, the study utilizes a high-resolution metric of procrastination based on the temporal profile of effort. The findings reveal a significant positive correlation between individual temporal reward discounting rates and the magnitude of task initiation delay, providing quantitative empirical evidence that procrastination can be modeled as a resource-rational trade-off mediated by the hyperbolic or exponential devaluation of future rewards.
papers.authors: Pei Yuan Zhang, Wei Ji Ma

papers.title: Backward reasoning through AND/OR trees to solve problems
papers.abstract: This research explores the computational mechanisms of human subgoaling and backward reasoning in goal-directed problem solving. The authors propose that these cognitive processes are implemented as a search through a subgoal space structured as an AND-OR tree, a architecture derived from early artificial intelligence research. Validated using behavioral data from the Tower of London and Rush Hour tasks, the results show that a single-parameter process model based on AND-OR tree search accurately characterizes human move sequences and subgoaling patterns, outperforming standard heuristic search models in capturing the underlying complexity of discrete planning.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the Annual Meeting of the Cognitive Science Society
papers.authors: Jeroen Olieslagers, Zahy Bnaya, Yichen Li, Wei Ji Ma

papers.title: Uncertainty affects planning effort, but not plans
papers.abstract: This paper investigates how human planning strategies adapt to different forms of environmental stochasticity, specifically reliability, volatility, and controllability. Across multiple experimental conditions, the study finds that increased uncertainty leads to a systematic reduction in planning effort, quantified by shorter initial response times and reduced search depth. Computational process modeling suggests that while human agents dynamically adjust their computational budget in response to the expected utility of planning in noisy environments, the qualitative structure of the resulting plans remains remarkably stable, indicating an adaptive balance between cognitive resource costs and reward maximization.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the Annual Meeting of the Cognitive Science Society
papers.authors: Jordan Lei, Wei Ji Ma

papers.title: Clarifying the conceptual dimensions of representation in neuroscience
papers.abstract: The authors propose a formal, information-theoretic framework to unify and clarify the concept of 'representation' in neuroscience. By defining four fundamental conceptual dimensions—sensitivity, specificity, invariance, and functionality—they provide a rigorous basis for evaluating neural coding hypotheses. The work demonstrates how established analytical techniques, including representational similarity analysis (RSA), encoding and decoding models, and causal interventions, can be mapped onto specific information-theoretic quantities. This framework serves as a tool for integrating disparate experimental results across studies and clarifying the evidentiary standards for representational claims.
papers.authors: Stephan Pohl, Edgar Y. Walker, David L. Barack, Jennifer Lee, Rachel N. Denison, Ned Block, Florent Meyniel, Wei Ji Ma

E186.name: Earl Miller
E186.department: Department of Brain and Cognitive Sciences
E186.bio: Earl K. Miller is the Picower Professor of Neuroscience at MIT, where their research investigates the neural mechanisms underlying executive brain functions such as attention, working memory, and rule learning. Miller developed the integrative theory of prefrontal cortex function and identified mixed selectivity in neurons, which allows for multifunctional neural representations. Their laboratory uses multi-electrode neurophysiology and computational modeling to study how oscillatory dynamics, specifically interactions between gamma and beta frequencies, coordinate top-down control across cortical networks. Currently, this research explores how large-scale neural dynamics enable the organization of thought and action in both healthy and disordered brains.
E186.research_direction: Dr. Miller has recently been using intracortical electrophysiology in non-human primates to investigate the neural dynamics underlying flexible cognition, working memory, and consciousness. Their recent work explores the functional role of cortical oscillations, examining how frontal theta traveling waves structure the readout of visual working memory, how spatial patterns of rhythmic activity might compartmentalize contextual information, and how distinct frequency bands coordinate the interhemispheric handoff of visual targets during active tracking. In the realm of value-based decision-making, they are analyzing prefrontal population activity to understand how neural representational geometry and subspace transformations support the parallel evaluation and subsequent selection of choice options. Additionally, Dr. Miller has been investigating the foundational mechanisms of unconsciousness by measuring how pharmacologically diverse general anesthetics impact the dynamical stability of cortical states.

papers.title: Neural subspace reorganization reflects value-based decision making
papers.abstract: Value-based decision making necessitates the parallel maintenance and comparative evaluation of multiple choice options and their respective reward values. This study performed bilateral recordings from the lateral prefrontal cortex (LPFC) in non-human primates tasked with sequentially processing option-value pairs. Analysis of neural representational geometry revealed that upon decision commitment, the chosen and unchosen options were transformed into mutually orthogonal subspaces, with a significant expansion of the representational volume for the chosen option. Post-decision, the chosen option's representation rotated into a stable subspace dedicated to the prescribed motor action, regardless of its temporal order in the sequence. This decision-driven reorganization of neural subspaces suggests a mechanism that facilitates a robust and interference-free readout of the selected behavior.
papers.authors: Huidi Li, Nikolaos Chrysanthidis, Scott L. Brincat, Jonas Rose, Earl K. Miller

papers.title: Similar destabilization of neural dynamics under different general anesthetics
papers.abstract: While diverse classes of general anesthetics act on different molecular pathways, they all culminate in a shared state of unconsciousness, suggesting a convergent neurodynamical signature. This study utilized intracortical electrophysiology and dynamical stability analysis to examine the effects of propofol, ketamine, and dexmedetomidine on cortical state in non-human primates. Despite their distinct pharmacology, all three agents induced a similar destabilization of cortical population dynamics. This loss of stability was characterized by elongated recovery periods following sensory perturbations and an associated shift toward high-amplitude, low-frequency power in the delta, theta, and alpha bands. The degree of instability strongly correlated with behavioral measures of consciousness, identifying cortical destabilization as a fundamental mechanism for anesthetic-induced loss of responsiveness.
papers.authors: Adam J. Eisen, Alexandra G. Bardon, Jesus J. Ballesteros, Andre M. Bastos, Jacob A. Donoghue, Meredith K. Mahnke, Scott L. Brincat, Jefferson Roy, Yoshitoyo Ishizawa, Emery N. Brown, Ila Fiete, Earl K. Miller

papers.title: Working memory readout varies with frontal theta rhythms
papers.abstract: Sensory attention is known to be rhythmically gated by cortical oscillations, yet whether internal cognitive processes like working memory (WM) readout are similarly structured remains unclear. This research shows that the phase of theta-frequency (3–6 Hz) oscillations in the frontal eye field (FEF) predicts the efficacy of information readout from WM. In non-human primates performing a change-detection task, behavioral performance fluctuated according to the local field potential (LFP) theta phase at the moment of probe onset and the target's location in retinotopic space. The data suggest that a theta traveling wave moves across the FEF's retinotopic map, effectively 'scanning' stored WM representations. Theta phase was coupled with both neuronal spiking and beta-band (12–20 Hz) activity, indicating a mechanism for the rhythmic modulation of cognitive readout.
papers.authors: Hio-Been Han, Scott L. Brincat, Timothy J. Buschman, Earl K. Miller

papers.title: Oscillatory control of cortical space as a computational dimension
papers.abstract: The capacity for flexible cognition relies on the brain's ability to incorporate contextual information to guide behavior. We evaluated the 'Spatial Computing' hypothesis, which posits that context organizes neural processing through specific spatial patterns of oscillations. Recordings from the prefrontal cortex in non-human primates during a context-dependent task revealed that sensory and rule-related information is compartmentalized into distinct cortical patches defined by their oscillatory profiles. These results suggest that the brain utilizes the spatial organization of cortical rhythms as a computational dimension to gate the flow of information and maintain distinct task-relevant representations, providing a mechanism for the rapid and flexible reconfiguration of neural networks.
papers.authors: Zhen Chen, Scott L. Brincat, Mikael Lundqvist, Robert F. Loonis, Melissa R. Warden, Earl K. Miller

papers.title: Evidence for an active handoff between cerebral hemispheres during target tracking
papers.abstract: Each cerebral hemisphere is primarily specialized for processing information within the contralateral visual hemifield, yet we perceive moving objects as a continuous and unified experience. This study investigated the neural coordination required for this interhemispheric transfer by recording from the prefrontal cortex as primates tracked targets moving across the vertical meridian. While beta (15–30 Hz) and gamma (30–80 Hz) rhythms primarily encoded sensory features, alpha (10–15 Hz) and theta (4–10 Hz) dynamics mediated the transfer process. Alpha power and spiking activity anticipated the target's movement between hemifields, while theta power registered the successful completion of the handoff. These findings support an 'active handoff' model where rhythmic 'handshaking' between hemispheres ensures seamless information flow and prevents representational loss during cross-hemifield transitions.
papers.authors: Matthew B. Broschard, Jefferson E. Roy, Scott L. Brincat, Meredith K. Mahnke, Earl K. Miller

E187.name: Timothy Buschman
E187.department: Department of Psychology, Princeton Neuroscience Institute
E187.bio: Timothy Buschman is an Associate Professor at the Princeton Neuroscience Institute where their research investigates the neural mechanisms underlying cognitive control, attention, and working memory. Buschman utilizes a multi-species approach integrating large-scale electrophysiology in non-human primates with optical imaging and optogenetics in rodents to examine how cognition emerges from the dynamic interaction of neural networks. Their findings characterize the divergent roles of prefrontal and parietal regions in top-down and bottom-up attention, as well as the low-dimensional subspaces that route information to guide flexible behavior. This work aims to develop computational models of brain function and provide insights into the dysfunction associated with neuropsychiatric and neurodevelopmental disorders.
E187.research_direction: Dr. Buschman has recently been investigating the neural architecture that supports cognitive flexibility, abstract decision-making, and top-down control. Their recent work explores how the brain dynamically routes information across distributed networks by organizing high-dimensional population activity into shared, low-dimensional "neural subspaces." Using large-scale electrophysiology and widefield calcium imaging in both mice and non-human primates, they are probing how animals use these geometric population codes to compose complex sensorimotor tasks and flexibly update attentional templates during visual search. Additionally, Dr. Buschman is studying how individual variations in the moment-to-moment expression of cortex-wide spatiotemporal activity motifs relate to global functional connectivity and distinct behavioral phenotypes.

papers.title: Building compositional tasks with shared neural subspaces
papers.abstract: This study demonstrates that cognitive flexibility is achieved through the reuse of low-dimensional 'neural subspaces' that represent sensory features and motor actions across different behavioral contexts. Monkeys were trained to alternate between three tasks with overlapping categorical and motor requirements. Population-level recordings from the lateral prefrontal cortex, parietal cortex, and striatum revealed that task-relevant variables (e.g., color, shape, and response direction) are encoded within stable subspaces that are shared across tasks. During task performance, neural activity transforms representations from a sensory-specific subspace into a common motor subspace. Flexibility arises as animals iteratively update internal task beliefs based on reward feedback, which then selectively gates the engagement of the appropriate shared subspaces. These results suggest a compositional neural architecture where complex behaviors are assembled from modular representational components.
papers.authors: Sina Tafazoli, Flora M. Bouchacourt, Adel Ardalan, Nikola T. Markov, Motoaki Uchimura, Marcelo G. Mattar, Nathaniel D. Daw, Timothy J. Buschman

papers.title: Multiplexed subspaces route neural activity across brain-wide networks
papers.abstract: The mechanisms by which the brain dynamically routes information across distributed networks to support cognitive flexibility are explored using mesoscale calcium imaging and high-density electrophysiology (Neuropixels) in mice. The researchers identified that brain regions interact through 'multiplexed subspace networks,' where distinct dimensions of neural activity within a single area are functionally coupled to different, overlapping sets of other regions. Information routing is controlled by the alignment of local population activity with these specific subspace dimensions; shifting the geometry of a representation within a region's high-dimensional activity space selectively engages different brain-wide networks. This geometric mechanism allows the brain to reconfigure communication channels on a moment-to-moment basis without structural rewiring.
papers.authors: Camden J. MacDowell, Alexandra Libby, Caroline I. Jahn, Sina Tafazoli, Adel Ardalan, Timothy J. Buschman

papers.title: Differences in the expression of cortex-wide neural dynamics are related to behavioral phenotype
papers.abstract: This research investigates the neural basis of individual differences in behavior by analyzing cortex-wide spatiotemporal motifs of activity in mice using widefield calcium imaging. The study found that while a small set of approximately 14-16 motifs explains the majority of variance in neural activity across all individuals (both 'typical' and 'atypical' neurotypes), individuals differ significantly in the frequency with which they express specific motifs. These variations in the sampling of low-dimensional dynamics explain a substantial portion of the variance in global functional connectivity and specific behavioral phenotypes. These findings suggest that behavioral diversity and neuropsychiatric symptoms may result from changes in the control processes that select and express specific large-scale neural patterns over time.
papers.authors: Camden J. MacDowell, Brandy A. Briones, Michael J. Lenzi, Morgan L. Gustison, Timothy J. Buschman

papers.title: Learning attentional templates for value-based decision-making
papers.abstract: Attentional templates—internal representations of task-relevant features—are critical for filtering sensory input. To investigate how these templates are learned and updated, monkeys were trained on a visual search task requiring the repeated acquisition of new templates. Recordings from the prefrontal and parietal cortex revealed that templates are represented in a structured geometric manner, where perceptually similar templates exhibit similar neural population codes. Learning occurs through an incremental shift in the neural representation toward rewarded features. Crucially, the attentional template transforms diverse stimulus features into a common value representation, allowing a unified decision-making mechanism to deploy attention regardless of the specific template identity. This work defines the neural mechanisms for the flexible control and reward-based learning of attention.
papers.authors: Caroline I. Jahn, Nikola T. Markov, Britney Morea, Nathaniel D. Daw, R. Becket Ebitz, Timothy J. Buschman

papers.title: Cognitive neuroscience: How the brain navigates abstract task spaces
papers.abstract: This peer-reviewed dispatch analyzes how biological systems utilize abstract task representations to facilitate rapid generalization to novel environments. It discusses recent empirical findings regarding the neural construction of abstract task spaces, focusing on how the brain maps sensory inputs and behavioral goals onto structured internal manifolds. The commentary evaluates the role of the prefrontal cortex in representing relational structures and suggests that such abstract representations are essential for overcoming the limitations of trial-and-error learning, thereby supporting complex decision-making and cognitive flexibility in both humans and non-human primates.
papers.authors: Sina Tafazoli, Adel Ardalan, Timothy J. Buschman

E191.name: Masud Husain
E191.department: Nuffield Department of Clinical Neurosciences and Department of Experimental Psychology
E191.bio: Masud Husain is a Professor of Neurology and Cognitive Neuroscience at the University of Oxford, where their work bridges the Nuffield Department of Clinical Neurosciences and the Department of Experimental Psychology. Husain’s research integrates clinical neurology with experimental neuroscience to investigate the mechanisms governing human attention, working memory, and motivated decision-making. By employing brain imaging and behavioral paradigms, they examine how these cognitive processes are impaired in conditions such as Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease, and stroke. Their research has challenged static models of working memory capacity, demonstrating instead that it is a resource that can be dynamically allocated based on task demands.
E191.research_direction: Dr. Husain's recent work explores the cognitive, computational, and neural mechanisms underlying decision-making, motivation, and visual working memory in both healthy aging and clinical populations. To understand attentional control, they have recently been investigating how visual distractors are filtered during memory encoding versus maintenance, utilizing delayed reproduction paradigms and mixture-modeling to quantify parameters like memory precision and misbinding in Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease. Additionally, their research investigates the neuroeconomic computations driving active information sampling and effort-based decision-making, probing how humans weigh potential rewards against physical effort costs and environmental uncertainty. By integrating drift-diffusion modeling, neuroimaging, and focal lesion studies, Dr. Husain examines how structural and functional disruptions in specific neural pathways—such as the hippocampus and frontoparietal networks—manifest clinically as severe apathy, altered valuation strategies, and impaired patient insight across various neurodegenerative and psychiatric disorders.

papers.title: Active information sampling in health and disease
papers.abstract: This review synthesizes the behavioral, neural, and computational substrates of active information gathering, conceptualized as a neuroeconomic optimization process wherein the brain evaluates the cost-benefit trade-offs of acquiring evidence to resolve uncertainty. The authors delineate the role of frontoparietal, limbic, insular, and striatal circuits, alongside the modulatory influence of catecholaminergic systems (norepinephrine, dopamine, and serotonin), in governing sampling strategies. The work highlights how disruptions in these mechanisms manifest transdiagnostically across clinical phenotypes, including schizophrenia, obsessive-compulsive disorder, and Parkinson’s disease, providing a framework for developing novel computational assays and targeted neurobiological interventions for psychiatric and neurological conditions.
papers.authors: Bahaaeddin Attaallah, Pierre Petitet, Masud Husain

papers.title: Self- versus caregiver-reported apathy across neurological disorders
papers.abstract: The study systematically quantifies the apathy reporting discrepancy (ARD) in 335 patients across various neurological diagnoses, including frontotemporal dementia (bvFTD and semantic variants), Parkinson’s disease, Alzheimer’s disease, and autoimmune encephalitis. Utilizing the Apathy-Motivation Index (AMI) and its caregiver counterpart (AMI-CG), the findings reveal that caregiver-rated apathy consistently exceeds patient self-reports across all clinical groups. This discordance is most pronounced in disorders characterized by impaired insight and anosognosia, such as bvFTD, and is significantly predicted by neuropsychological deficits in memory and verbal fluency. These cognitive impairments account for approximately 11.2% of the variance in caregiver ratings, suggesting that behavioral inertia and failure to recall motivated actions contribute to the reporting gap.
papers.authors: Sijia Zhao, Anna Scholcz, Matthew A Rouse, Verena S Klar, Akke Ganse-Dumrath, Sofia Toniolo, M John Broulidakis, Matthew A Lambon Ralph, James B Rowe, Peter Garrard, Sian Thompson, Sarosh R Irani, Sanjay G Manohar, Masud Husain

papers.title: Working memory filtering at encoding and maintenance in healthy ageing, Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease
papers.abstract: This investigation utilizes a delayed reproduction paradigm and mixture-modeling to dissociate the impact of distractors presented during the encoding versus maintenance phases of visual working memory (VWM) in Alzheimer’s disease (AD), Parkinson’s disease (PD), and healthy aging. While healthy elderly controls and PD patients demonstrate relatively preserved filtering efficacy across both phases, AD patients exhibit selective impairments in filtering irrelevant material during the maintenance period. Quantitative metrics of memory precision, target detection, misbinding, and guessing indicate that AD-related deficits are driven by increased stochastic noise and target detection failures. Structural neuroimaging reveals that whole hippocampal volume significantly correlates with filtering performance specifically during the maintenance delay, but not during the initial encoding phase.
papers.authors: Sofia Toniolo, Robert Udale, Verena Svenja Klar, Maria Raquel Maio, Bahaaeddin Attaallah, George K Tofaris, Michele T Hu, Sanjay G Manohar, Masud Husain

papers.title: Apathy and effort-based decision-making in Alzheimer's disease and subjective cognitive impairment
papers.abstract: The research characterizes motivational deficits in Alzheimer’s disease (AD) and subjective cognitive impairment (SCI) through an effort-based decision-making (EBDM) framework combined with drift-diffusion modeling (DDM). Patients with AD demonstrate reduced sensitivity to physical effort costs that correlates with executive dysfunction, whereas SCI participants exhibit elevated self-reported apathy associated with diminished effort sensitivity and augmented resting-state functional connectivity between the nucleus accumbens and the frontoparietal network. The findings suggest that while both AD and SCI involve disruptions in the valuation of effortful actions, the underlying psychological mechanisms and neural circuit anomalies are dissociable, with SCI apathy specifically linked to hyper-responsivity to uncertainty and altered ventral striatal connectivity.
papers.venue: Alzheimer's & Dementia: Diagnosis, Assessment & Disease Monitoring
papers.authors: Bahaaeddin Attaallah, Sofia Toniolo, Maria Raquel Maio, Masud Husain

papers.title: The role of the human hippocampus in decision-making under uncertainty
papers.abstract: Employing a lesion-deficit model in individuals with autoimmune limbic encephalitis, this study evaluates the necessity of the hippocampus for value-based decision-making under conditions of uncertainty. Across four experiments involving trade-offs between reward, physical effort, and uncertainty, hippocampal damage was found to selectively blunt behavioral sensitivity to reward and effort changes only when decisions involved uncertainty. Sensitivity to these attributes remained intact in uncertainty-free contexts, and the degree of blunted reward sensitivity under uncertainty correlated significantly with the severity of hippocampal atrophy. These results establish a context-sensitive role for the hippocampus in prospective valuation and the stabilization of preferences during decision-making tasks characterized by probabilistic outcomes.
papers.authors: Bahaaeddin Attaallah, Pierre Petitet, Rhea Zambellas, Sofia Toniolo, Maria Raquel Maio, Akke Ganse-Dumrath, Sarosh R. Irani, Sanjay G. Manohar, Masud Husain

E196.name: Igor Utochkin
E196.bio: Igor S. Utochkin is a Staff Research Scientist at the University of Chicago’s Institute for Mind and Biology and a member of the Awh-Vogel Lab. Utochkin’s research examines the cognitive and neural mechanisms of ensemble perception, focusing on how the visual system summarizes statistical information from groups of objects. They have developed computational models, such as the population response model, to explain the interaction between summary statistics and individual item representations in visual working memory. Their work utilizes behavioral psychophysics and signal-detection analysis to investigate how attention, feature similarity, and task requirements affect visual search and memory capacity.
E196.research_direction: Dr. Utochkin has recently been investigating the cognitive and computational mechanisms underlying ensemble perception and visual change detection. Their recent work explores how the visual system extracts statistical summaries from multi-item displays, using electrophysiological markers to ask whether this processing occurs automatically or requires dedicated attentional resources. They are also examining the representational boundaries of ensemble selection to determine whether rapid visual averaging operates on early, preattentive features or relies on fully bound objects. Complementing this experimental research, Dr. Utochkin applies multidimensional signal detection theory to model how observers integrate sensory evidence across complex displays, and they have recently developed advanced pedagogical resources for teaching psychophysics and computational modeling.

papers.title: The role of attention in basic ensemble statistics processing
papers.abstract: This study examines whether ensemble representations, typically viewed as a mechanism to bypass attentional capacity limits, actually necessitate attention for their formation. Using orientation ensembles, the authors employed two ERP markers: the P3 component to measure conscious change detection in attended stimuli and the visual mismatch negativity (vMMN) to assess automatic sensory discrimination in unattended stimuli. In Experiment 1, where observers actively reported orientation mean changes, a robust P3 response was elicited. In Experiment 2, where attention was diverted to a central task and the ensembles were task-irrelevant, no significant vMMN was observed in response to mean orientation shifts. These electrophysiological findings indicate that ensemble discrimination is not an automatic process and requires dedicated attentional resources.
papers.authors: Anton Lukashevich, Heida Maria Sigurdardottir, Nikita Kydriavstsev, Igor Utochkin

papers.title: A signal-detection account of item-based and ensemble-based visual change detection: A reply to Harrison, McMaster, and Bays
papers.abstract: This article challenges the conclusion that ensemble statistics play a limited role in visual change detection. While previous research suggested that sensitivity to global changes in four-item sets rarely exceeds the threshold predicted by an optimal summation model of individual signals, this reply argues that optimal summation itself is a form of ensemble-based decision-making. By applying multidimensional signal detection theory (SDT), the authors demonstrate that when observers must evaluate a multi-item display, evidence from all items is integrated before being compared against a decision criterion. Experimental results show that the statistics of the entire memory set influence performance even when only a single item is probed at test, suggesting that ensemble information is intrinsically used during optimal summation rather than being a separate, auxiliary memory source.
papers.authors: Daniil Azarov, Daniil Grigorev, Igor Utochkin

papers.title: What is the basis of ensemble selection?
papers.abstract: The authors investigate the representational basis of ensemble perception, specifically asking which types of visual information allow the visual system to select and summarize a relevant subset of objects intermixed with distractors. Across four experiments using orientation averaging, they tested three levels of representation: basic features, preattentive object files (unbound feature lists), and full-fledged bound objects. The results showed that ensemble selection is highly effective when defined by a unique basic feature (e.g., color) and moderately effective for preattentive object files (conjunctions shared with distractors). However, performance dropped to chance when selection required access to exact feature relationships in spatially bound objects. These findings suggest that the visual system's capacity for rapid statistical summary is restricted to early-stage, preattentive visual representations.
papers.authors: Vladislav A. Khvostov, Aleksei U. Iakovlev, Jeremy M. Wolfe, Igor S. Utochkin

papers.title: A problem case set for teaching psychophysics and psychophysical modelling
papers.abstract: This pedagogical article introduces an advanced instructional resource for teaching quantitative methods in vision science and cognitive psychology. The author presents a curated set of educational problems and pre-generated datasets centered on psychophysical data analysis and modeling. The resource is designed to move beyond basic introductory concepts by requiring students to develop and test computational models of perception, attention, and decision-making. By engaging with these research-oriented problems, students gain a deeper understanding of the theoretical underpinnings of psychophysical testing and the practical application of signal detection and population coding frameworks in modeling human performance.
papers.authors: Igor S. Utochkin

E197.name: Jennifer E. Corbett
E197.bio: Jennifer E. Corbett is a vision scientist specializing in the cognitive and neural mechanisms of ensemble representation and visual averaging. Corbett’s research examines how the visual system extracts statistical summaries, such as the mean and variance of features, to represent complex scenes and support perception across eye movements. They have investigated the functional role of these summary statistics in visual search, their influence on visually guided action, and differences in ensemble processing in clinical populations. Recent work by Corbett includes a synthesis of the pervasiveness of ensemble perception and the development of frameworks to optimize user performance in 3D environments.
E197.research_direction: Dr. Corbett's recent work broadly explores how the visual system compresses complex environments into statistical summaries to circumvent severe processing bottlenecks. Using psychophysical tasks and computational modeling, they have recently been investigating the underlying mechanisms of ensemble perception, specifically questioning how item saliency affects explicit versus implicit feature representations and whether these same low-level perceptual averaging processes ultimately drive higher-level economic and moral judgments. In a parallel line of collaborative vision research, their work tests whether pooling independent binary decisions from just two observers can enhance early visual processing and optimize rare target detection in applied settings. Additionally, they are investigating spatial cognition and sensorimotor compatibility, examining how the alignment of spatial reference frames between users and displays influences task performance and the preference for y-axis inversion in 3D interfaces.

papers.title: Why axis inversion? Optimizing interactions between users, interfaces, and visual displays in 3D environments
papers.abstract: This research investigates the cognitive and sensorimotor factors underlying the preference for y-axis inversion in 3D digital environments, such as those found in video games and laparoscopic surgery simulators. By synthesizing findings from human factors, ergonomics, and cognitive psychology, the study identifies critical methodological inconsistencies in previous literature that hinder a unified understanding of control-interface mappings. The authors propose a modular 'general purpose' framework to evaluate how inverting controller inputs and visual perspectives influences task performance across different movement goals. The framework is applied to common laparoscopic procedures to demonstrate its utility in assessing and predicting sensorimotor compatibility effects, concluding that performance optimization requires a task-specific alignment of spatial reference frames between the user and the display.
papers.authors: Jennifer E. Corbett, Jaap Munneke

papers.title: A Crowd of Two: Independent Collaboration Improves Target Detection
papers.abstract: The 'wisdom of crowds' effect is typically associated with large groups, but this study examines whether independent collaboration between just two experts can improve detection of rare targets in complex visual scenes, such as medical anomalies in mammograms or weapons in security baggage scans. Across two psychophysical experiments, the researchers demonstrate that averaging binary detection judgments from a pair of observers significantly increases diagnostic accuracy by 10–22% compared to individual performance. This facilitation results from a reduction in both misses and false alarms. Critically, the benefit of collaboration is maximized when individuals with the most dissimilar baseline perceptual profiles are paired, suggesting that independent errors cancel out to enhance collective sensitivity and overcome individual capacity limits in early visual processing.
papers.authors: Jennifer E. Corbett, Jaap Munneke

papers.title: Amplification from saliency affects explicit but not implicit ensemble representations
papers.abstract: This study dissociates the mechanisms underlying explicit and implicit ensemble representations by examining the 'amplification effect,' where salient items disproportionately bias the perceived average of a group. Observers viewed sets of lines varying in orientation and size (saliency). Explicit representations were measured via mean orientation adjustments, while implicit representations were assessed using Feature Distribution Learning (FDL) in an odd-one-out visual search task. Results revealed that while explicit reports were strongly biased toward salient items, implicit representations of the entire feature distribution remained unaffected by saliency. These findings support a population-coding model of ensemble perception where implicit processes maintain a high-fidelity representation of the full distribution, whereas explicit access is limited to a biased summary statistic generated through attentional weighting.
papers.authors: Aleksei Iakovlev, Vladislav Khvostov, Árni Gunnar Ásgeirsson, Árni Kristjánsson, Jennifer E. Corbett

papers.title: The Pervasiveness of Ensemble Perception: Not Just Your Average Review
papers.abstract: This monograph offers a comprehensive synthesis of contemporary research on ensemble representations—the visual system's ability to compress groups of similar objects into summary statistical descriptors like mean, variance, and range. The authors argue that ensemble encoding is a fundamental, inherently necessary component of human perception used to circumvent the brain's strict capacity bottlenecks for detail. The work reviews theoretical frameworks such as Reverse Hierarchy Theory and discusses the cortical underpinnings of statistical summaries. It highlights how ensemble perception operates both explicitly and implicitly to provide a stable 'gist' of complex visual scenes, suggesting that the visual system prioritizes global context over individual item representations to maintain a continuous and complete sense of the environment.
papers.authors: Jennifer E. Corbett, Igor S. Utochkin, Shaul Hochstein

papers.title: Psychological value theory: the psychological value of groups
papers.abstract: This research develops and tests Psychological Value Theory (PVT) to explain how the human visual and cognitive systems assign subjective value to groups of items or individuals. Through a series of six experiments involving sacrificial moral dilemmas and economic goods, the authors demonstrate that the perceived value of a group is primarily governed by a perceptual averaging process rather than a summation of individual member values. Computational modeling reveals that group valuations are highly sensitive to individual differences and salient high-value items (attentional capture) but disproportionately insensitive to group size. These findings provide a novel psychophysical account of human decision-making biases, suggesting that complex moral and economic judgments rely on the same fundamental ensemble-coding mechanisms as low-level visual perception.
papers.authors: Jaap Munneke, İlker Duymaz, Jennifer E. Corbett

E198.name: Andrey Chetverikov
E198.lab_name: Bergen Laboratory for the Study of Decision, Intuition, Consciousness, and Emotion (DICE)
E198.bio: Andrey Chetverikov is an Associate Professor of Cognitive Psychology at the University of Bergen, where they investigate the computational and neural foundations of visual perception. Chetverikov's research explores how the brain represents environmental variability and uncertainty, using "feature distribution learning" to analyze how observers approximate internal probability distributions of stimulus ensembles. By integrating Bayesian modeling with psychophysics and functional MRI, they examine the mechanisms behind perceptual and mnemonic biases, specifically how the visual system decodes noisy sensory signals. Their current work focuses on refining normative models of inter-item biases and the representation of motion and orientation features in the human visual cortex.
E198.research_direction: Dr. Chetverikov has recently been investigating the mechanisms of serial dependence, focusing on how previous visual encounters create attractive or repulsive biases in current perceptual estimates. Their recent work explores these dynamics through behavioral experiments, response trajectory analysis, and computational modeling to test frameworks capable of explaining both bias polarities within a single process. Specifically, they are examining how the active maintenance and cue-based prioritization of stimuli within visual working memory interact with these sequential effects. Additionally, they are engaging with the conceptual foundations of vision science, evaluating how flexible definitions of visual attention guide research into sensory uncertainty and optimal information prioritization.

papers.title: Between repulsion and attraction in serial biases: Replication of Chen and Bae (2024)
papers.abstract: This study replicated recent findings by Chen and Bae (2024) regarding serial dependence in pointing direction estimation. The original research identified a repulsive serial bias in delayed direction estimation that transitioned to an attractive bias when a distracting Stroop task was introduced during the retention interval. This investigation utilized PsychoPy-based behavioral testing and response trajectory analysis to validate these effects. The results corroborated the sign-switching phenomenon while uncovering significant, stable individual differences in bias polarity and magnitude. Critically, response trajectory data revealed that attractive-bias trials often exhibited an attractive sign from the very first frame of response initiation, whereas overall response executions were predominantly repulsive. These findings challenge monolithic Bayesian integration models of serial dependence and support the necessity of unified computational frameworks, such as the Demixing Model, capable of accounting for both attractive and repulsive contextual biases within a single process.
papers.authors: Juni B. Akselberg, Sara B. Cardona, Mikkel Dybvad, Lise Martine Karlstad, Malin Langemyr, Ingrid A. Mellingsæter-Jokic, Mats K. K. Moe, Amalie C. Solvang, Andrey Chetverikov

papers.title: Attention is doing just fine! Just don't take it too seriously
papers.abstract: This article addresses the conceptual 'crisis' in visual attention research proposed by Rosenholtz (2024). The authors argue that while the field lacks a singular, rigid definition of 'attention,' the existing loose conceptualization has been highly productive in guiding neuroscientific and psychophysical investigations into how the brain prioritizes and gathers environmental information. They highlight significant progress in understanding attentional sets, template-based selection, and the integration of peripheral vision constraints. The paper cautions against over-definition, which may restrict theoretical growth, and instead advocates for treating attention as a general descriptive category, similar to 'perception' or 'memory.' It emphasizes that many supposedly 'attentional' failures are better understood as optimal responses to sensory uncertainty or constraints imposed by the hierarchical organization of the visual system.
papers.authors: Árni Kristjánsson, Andrey Chetverikov

papers.title: Visual working memory prioritization modulates serial dependence beyond simple attentional effects
papers.abstract: This investigation explored how the prioritization of items within visual working memory (VWM) influences serial dependence (SD) using a combination of behavioral experiments and computational modeling. While previous theories suggest that SD is primarily driven by low-level adaptation or attentional selection during encoding, this study examined whether maintenance-related prioritization (induced via pre- and post-cues) independently modulates the sign or magnitude of the bias. The results demonstrated that tasks requiring active maintenance of a prior stimulus amplified attractive serial dependence, particularly with extended retention periods. However, when multiple items were held in memory, prioritization of one item over another did not significantly alter the strength of SD compared to non-prioritized items. These results suggest that while VWM maintenance is a critical component of SD, simple attentional gain modulation is insufficient to explain the contextual biases observed between sequential representations, supporting normative accounts like the Demixing Model.
papers.authors: Ekaterina Andriushchenko, Andrey Chetverikov, Gianluca Campana

E202.name: Michael A. Cohen
E202.department: Department of Psychology and Program in Neuroscience
E202.bio: Michael A. Cohen is an Assistant Professor of Psychology and Neuroscience at Amherst College and a Research Scientist at the McGovern Institute for Brain Research at MIT. Cohen’s research investigates the cognitive and neural limitations determining which environmental information reaches conscious awareness, examining the functional architecture of the visual system as a bottleneck for information processing. By combining psychophysics with neuroimaging methods such as fMRI and EEG, Cohen characterizes the bandwidth of perceptual experience and the distinctions between neural correlates of awareness and post-perceptual processes. Cohen received the 2024 Vision Sciences Society Young Investigator Award for research on how prior knowledge and neural representation shape the capacity of human vision.
E202.research_direction: Dr. Cohen's recent research investigates the fundamental limits, structure, and neural mechanisms of visual awareness. Using EEG and no-report visual masking paradigms, they have recently been working to isolate the true electrophysiological signatures of conscious perception from the post-perceptual cognitive processes typically required to make a task report. Their recent work also explores the capacity of this awareness, utilizing gaze-contingent virtual reality and inattentional blindness tasks to examine whether scene familiarity and prior knowledge can expand the bandwidth of information that reaches consciousness. Furthermore, Dr. Cohen has been investigating the architectural nature of conscious access, applying continuous reproduction tasks and psychophysical modeling across phenomena like the attentional blink and iconic memory to test whether visual information enters awareness along a graded continuum or in a discrete, all-or-nothing fashion.

papers.title: Neural signatures of visual awareness independent of postperceptual processing
papers.abstract: This study employs electroencephalography (EEG) and a no-report visual masking paradigm to dissociate neural activity associated with perceptual awareness from preconscious sensory encoding and postperceptual processes (e.g., task reporting). By parametrically varying the stimulus onset asynchrony (SOA) between face stimuli and masks in linear steps (17, 33, 50, 67, and 83 ms), the researchers observed a nonlinear, bifurcated increase in subjective visibility. Electrophysiological results identified a fronto-central event-related potential (ERP), termed the N2 (~250-300 ms), that closely mirrored this bifurcated psychometric function. Crucially, while report-based conditions showed late sustained signals like the P3b and temporal generalization of decoding, these task-related markers disappeared in the no-report condition, whereas the N2 persisted. These findings suggest that the primary neural substrate of consciousness emerges earlier than predicted by cognitive theories and is independent of explicit report.
papers.authors: Michael A. Cohen, Cole Dembski, Kevin Ortego, Clay Steinhibler, Michael Pitts

papers.title: Familiarity Alters the Bandwidth of Perceptual Awareness
papers.abstract: The authors investigate whether prior knowledge and familiarity with a scene can expand the bandwidth of perceptual awareness, potentially explaining the discrepancy between experimental evidence of sparse perception (e.g., inattentional blindness) and the intuitive sense of a rich visual world. Using a gaze-contingent virtual reality (VR) paradigm and an inattentional blindness task, observers were presented with real-world scenes that were either familiar or novel. Results demonstrated that observers were significantly more sensitive (higher d') and less conservative (lower criterion c) at detecting drastic peripheral alterations when the scenes were familiar. These findings challenge the 'filling-in' hypothesis—which suggests prior knowledge merely constructs a subjective sense of detail—and instead indicate that familiarity actually increases the amount of information that reaches conscious awareness.
papers.authors: Michael A. Cohen, Skyler Sung, Zaki Alaoui

papers.title: Perceptual Awareness Occurs Along a Graded Continuum: No Evidence of All-or-None Failures in Continuous Reproduction Tasks
papers.abstract: This research addresses the fundamental debate of whether information enters conscious awareness in a discrete, all-or-nothing fashion or along a continuous, graded scale. Using four distinct paradigms known to manipulate visual awareness—the attentional blink, backward masking, the Sperling iconic memory task, and retro-cuing—the study compares the fit of discrete 'mixture models' against a continuous signal detection framework (Target-Contrast-Contrast or TCC model) that accounts for psychophysical scaling. Formal model comparisons across all experiments and re-analyses of prior literature consistently favored the continuous model. The data suggest that even when perception is severely challenged, information reaches awareness at varying levels of precision rather than being completely absent or present, supporting a graded view of perceptual experience.
papers.authors: Michael A. Cohen, Jonathan Keefe, Timothy F. Brady

E203.name: Jason Haberman
E203.bio: Jason Haberman is an Associate Professor of Psychology at Rhodes College who researches ensemble perception, a heuristic that allows the visual system to represent information via summary statistics. Haberman’s work uses psychophysical methods to examine how the brain extracts average features—such as orientation, size, or facial expression—from groups of objects. Their current research investigates the intersection of vision science and social cognition, specifically examining the perception of social status and self-representation. Haberman previously held a postdoctoral position at Harvard University and completed their doctoral studies at the University of California, Davis.
E203.research_direction: Dr. Haberman's recent work explores how our daily visual diet shapes high-level face perception and the internal representation of identity. Specifically, they have recently been investigating how extensive exposure to mirror-reversed faces—such as those routinely encountered in mirrors and digital technologies—impacts subjective evaluative judgments of aesthetic appeal and perceived self-resemblance. By combining perceptual adaptation paradigms with horizontal orientation manipulations of both self-portraits and images of familiar peers, their research isolates the role of canonical viewing perspectives in face evaluation. Ultimately, they seek to understand the underlying mechanisms of how asymmetric, orientation-dependent visual experiences dynamically modulate our internalized representations of highly familiar faces.

papers.title: A reflection on faces seen under mirror reversal
papers.abstract: A substantial portion of visual exposure to human faces, particularly one's own, is mediated by digital technologies that often present a mirror-reversed perspective relative to direct physical viewing. To investigate how disparities in visual diet modulate subjective evaluative judgments, observers were presented with photographs of their own facial likeness that were either horizontally flipped (mirror-reversed) or displayed in true orientation (non-reversed). Using a 2 × 2 factorial design, perceptual adaptation to reversed versus non-reversed stimuli was systematically manipulated alongside image orientation. Participants evaluated both perceived self-resemblance and aesthetic appeal (pleasantness), subsequently completing the identical task using photographic likenesses of familiar close peers. Results demonstrated that non-reversed self-portraits were judged as significantly less representative of self-identity and elicited lower pleasantness ratings than mirror-reversed depictions. Conversely, this effect was absent when evaluating close peers, for whom non-reversed depictions constitute the canonically familiar orientation, and perceptual adaptation elicited asymmetric evaluative shifts. Experiment 1A was independently replicated seven years later. These findings indicate that technological exposure constructs an internalized yet adaptable visual self-representation that becomes disrupted when unfamiliar vantage points accentuate intrinsic facial asymmetries.
papers.authors: Jordan Suchow, Malerie McDowell, Jessica Huang, Jason Haberman

E210.name: John A. Solomon
E210.department: Department of Optometry and Visual Science
E210.bio: Joshua A. Solomon is a Professor of Visual Psychophysics at City, University of London, where they investigate the mechanisms of human visual perception through technical psychophysical and computational methods. Solomon’s work focuses on ensemble perception and summary statistics, specifically characterizing how the visual system extracts global features from crowded or noisy stimulus arrays. Their research employs signal detection theory and stochastic observer models to analyze texture segregation, motion detection, and the role of attention in visual sensitivity. Currently, Solomon examines the dynamics of information accrual in change detection and the probabilistic nature of evidence integration in oculomotor control.
E210.research_direction: Dr. Solomon's recent research investigates the architecture of sensory evidence integration and the computational mechanisms of visual feature detection. Specifically, they have recently been probing whether perceptual judgments and oculomotor preparation—such as saccadic eye movements—rely on a shared sampling mechanism or parallel, temporally distinct streams of sensory evidence during states of dynamic uncertainty. Alongside this sensorimotor research, their recent work explores the low-level visual channels responsible for detecting spatial modulations in dot density and luminance contrast. By employing a signal-detection framework and measuring psychophysical thresholds, they are working to model how monocular and binocular mechanisms process and integrate these distinct visual signals.

papers.title: Author Response to Brenner & Smeets
papers.abstract: In this technical response, the authors address critiques concerning the dissociation between perceptual and oculomotor evidence integration. They maintain that perceptual decisions and motor preparation, specifically saccadic eye movements, utilize temporally distinct streams of sensory evidence. The response clarifies that the observed lack of correlation between perceptual judgments and oculomotor errors in their original tasks supports a parallel-processing architecture rather than a common sequential sampling mechanism for both effectors, particularly under conditions of dynamic sensory uncertainty.
papers.authors: Matteo Lisi, Michael J. Morgan, Joshua A. Solomon

papers.title: Monocular and binocular mechanisms detect modulations of dot density and dot contrast
papers.abstract: This study employs a signal-detection framework to investigate the visual mechanisms responsible for detecting spatial modulations in dot density and luminance contrast. By measuring detection thresholds for these features in isolation and in various phase-aligned combinations, the researchers demonstrate a significant summation effect: thresholds for in-phase modulations of both features were substantially lower than for either feature alone. A quantitative model is proposed, incorporating monocular and binocular channels with specific gain and noise parameters to account for the integration of density and contrast signals in human psychophysical performance.
papers.authors: Kristina Zeljic, Michael J. Morgan, Joshua A. Solomon

E214.name: Barbara Anne Dosher
E214.bio: Barbara Anne Dosher is a cognitive scientist specializing in the mathematical modeling of human information processing, focusing on visual perception, attention, and memory. Dosher develops formal models such as the Perceptual Template Model (PTM) and the Integrated Reweighting Theory (IRT) to quantify how the brain filters external noise and enhances signal quality during task performance. As a Fellow of the National Academy of Sciences, Dosher investigates the mechanisms of perceptual learning and experience-dependent plasticity. Their research explores how training optimizes the decoding of visual information from early representations to decision-making units.
E214.research_direction: Dr. Dosher has recently been investigating the computational and behavioral mechanisms underlying visual perceptual learning and spatial attention. Their recent work explores how observers improve at multi-alternative identification tasks—specifically spatial frequency and orientation judgments—by examining how varying levels of informational feedback accelerate learning and how training generalizes across task-irrelevant visual features. To computationally account for these behavioral phenomena, they are developing robust hierarchical Bayesian frameworks for classic psychophysical models, such as the perceptual template model (PTM) and augmented Hebbian reweighting models. By combining these advanced parameter-estimation techniques with external noise paradigms, Dr. Dosher aims to isolate core attentional mechanisms and pinpoint how sensory readouts are reweighted trial-by-trial during visual decision-making.

papers.title: Hierarchical Bayesian augmented Hebbian reweighting model of perceptual learning
papers.abstract: The augmented Hebbian reweighting model (AHRM) has been widely applied to account for collective observer behavior in perceptual learning paradigms, but characterizing individual trial-by-trial learning dynamics within a unified statistical framework has historically been limited by severe computational tractability issues. To address this, the authors introduce the hierarchical Bayesian augmented Hebbian reweighting model (HB-AHRM), which jointly infers hyperparameter and parameter posterior distributions across population, observer, and testing tiers. To circumvent the prohibitive burden of simulation-based parameter estimation, an approximated likelihood approach was implemented via feature engineering and linear regression alongside PyTensor GPU acceleration, accelerating parameter estimation by roughly 20,000-fold relative to conventional simulation methods. Compared against an unpooled Bayesian inference procedure (BIP), the HB-AHRM achieved substantially reduced parameter posterior uncertainty and superior out-of-sample predictive accuracy for individual empirical learning curves across distinct training accuracy and feedback regimens.
papers.authors: Zhong-Lin Lu, Shanglin Yang, Barbara Anne Dosher

papers.title: Transfer of visual perceptual learning over a task-irrelevant feature through feature-invariant representations: Behavioral experiments and model simulations
papers.abstract: Perceptual learning is traditionally characterized by sharp specificity to trained stimulus attributes, but the degree to which learning generalizes across variation in task-irrelevant dimensions remains unresolved.
