Observers completed multi-session training in eight-alternative forced-choice (8AFC) identification paradigms using Gabor stimuli with response feedback under high external noise and zero-noise conditions: either orientation identification across multiple task-irrelevant spatial frequencies or spatial-frequency identification across multiple task-irrelevant orientations. Training on orientation identification with a single spatial frequency yielded broad transfer across untrained spatial frequencies (with mild specificity emerging only at the highest frequency), whereas spatial-frequency training transferred completely across all orientations. To explain these generalization patterns, the authors extended the identification integrated reweighting theory (I-IRT) into an expanded model (eI-IRT) that incorporates feature-invariant representations alongside feature-tuned representations. Simulations confirmed that Hebbian reweighting of feedforward readouts from both feature-tuned and feature-invariant channels to decision units quantitatively accounts for the empirical cross-feature transfer.
papers.authors: Jiajuan Liu, Zhong-Lin Lu, Barbara Dosher

papers.title: Informational feedback accelerates learning in multi-alternative perceptual judgements of orientation
papers.abstract: The vast majority of visual perceptual learning studies have evaluated two-alternative forced-choice paradigms, leaving open the degree to which performance gains in higher-dimensional tasks depend on the informational specificity of external supervision. Observers were trained on an eight-alternative forced-choice (8AFC) peripheral orientation identification task with Gabor stimuli across three contrast levels in high external noise under three feedback protocols: response feedback (RF; indicating the true stimulus class), accuracy feedback (AF; indicating only binary correctness), or no feedback (NF). While modest unsupervised learning emerged even under NF, the rate and magnitude of learning scaled systematically with informational content: RF accelerated threshold reduction, providing an additional benefit of approximately 2 standard deviations relative to unsupervised training. The full trajectory of proportion-correct learning curves and evolving identification confusion matrices were quantitatively captured by the identification integrated reweighting theory (I-IRT), demonstrating that augmented Hebbian reweighting rules flexibly exploit graded supervisory feedback signals during multi-alternative visual decision-making.
papers.authors: Jiajuan Liu, Zhong-Lin Lu, Barbara Anne Dosher

papers.title: Learning spatial frequency identification through reweighted decoding
papers.abstract: Although perceptual learning has been extensively documented in spatial orientation and contrast discrimination, evidence for plasticity in spatial-frequency judgments remains sparse, particularly in absolute multi-alternative identification. Observers were trained over multiple sessions on an eight-alternative forced-choice (8AFC) spatial-frequency identification task in peripheral vision using Gabor targets presented at low, medium, and high contrasts embedded in external noise, followed by noiseless transfer assessments. Training with full response feedback yielded significant improvements across all contrast levels (mean accuracy rose from 31.16% to 38.72%) and systematic contrast threshold reductions at both trained retinal locations. To model the underlying computational architecture, the authors introduced the identification integrated reweighting theory (I-IRT), combining an early sensory representation module with tuned spatial frequency and orientation filters feeding into competitive decision units. Model fits demonstrated that learning in absolute spatial-frequency identification reflects the optimized reweighting of feedforward readout connections to decision mechanisms rather than alterations in early sensory channel tuning.
papers.authors: Barbara Dosher, Jiajuan Liu, Zhong-Lin Lu

papers.title: Hierarchical Bayesian perceptual template modeling of mechanisms of spatial attention in central and peripheral cuing
papers.abstract: The perceptual template model (PTM) and external noise paradigm isolate three core mechanisms of visual attention: stimulus enhancement, external noise exclusion, and multiplicative noise reduction. Traditionally, PTM parameters are estimated independently per subject using maximum likelihood or separate Bayesian methods, which lack population-level pooling and require high trial counts. The authors formulated a three-level hierarchical Bayesian perceptual template model (HBPTM) that unifies trial-by-trial data across population hyperparameters, individual subject parameters, and experimental cuing conditions. Applied to psychophysical data from endogenous (central) and exogenous (peripheral) spatial precuing tasks in four-alternative pseudo-character identification, HBPTM accurately dissociated attentional mechanisms while dramatically reducing posterior parameter variance through shrinkage. Extensive simulation studies across varying participant sample sizes and trial budgets demonstrated that HBPTM consistently outperforms unpooled Bayesian inference, offering superior estimation accuracy and parameter stability in low-trial psychophysical regimes.
papers.authors: Zhong-Lin Lu, Barbara Anne Dosher

E216.name: Kazuhisa Shibata
E216.department: Laboratory for Human Cognition and Learning
E216.lab_name: Laboratory for Human Cognition and Learning
E216.bio: Shibata serves as the Team Leader of the Laboratory for Human Cognition and Learning at the RIKEN Center for Brain Science. Their research focuses on the neural mechanisms of visual perception, learning, and decision-making through a combination of psychophysics, functional MRI, and computational modeling. Shibata has used decoded fMRI neurofeedback (DecNef) to demonstrate that inducing specific activity patterns in the early visual cortex can drive perceptual learning without external stimuli. Their recent investigations explore the neurochemical factors, such as the ratio of excitatory to inhibitory neurotransmitters, that facilitate the stabilization and consolidation of newly acquired visual skills.
E216.research_direction: Dr. Shibata has recently been exploring the neural mechanisms underlying perceptual learning, memory consolidation, and higher-order cognition. Using behavioral paradigms alongside fMRI and EEG, their recent work investigates visual perceptual learning by examining whether task-irrelevant natural scenes can bypass early attentional suppression, and how conscious awareness dictates whether subsequent sensory exposures disrupt or facilitate initial memory traces. Beyond sensory processing, they are studying how extensive practice optimizes the high-dimensional neural geometry of task representations in frontoparietal networks to enable behavioral automaticity. Additionally, their research probes broader cognitive phenomena, including how temporal reporting constraints impact metacognitive efficiency in decision-making and how memory-based heuristics might drive logical reasoning fallacies.

papers.title: The order of task decisions and confidence ratings has little effect on metacognition
papers.abstract: This Registered Report investigates the potential impact of reporting order—specifically whether task decisions (D) precede or follow confidence ratings (C)—on metacognitive efficiency (meta-d'/d'). Utilizing both perceptual (motion discrimination) and memory (recognition) tasks, the study controlled for task accuracy and learning effects to isolate the influence of temporal and motor-preparatory factors. Empirical results demonstrate that metacognitive efficiency remains robust across various reporting sequences (D→C, C→D, and concurrent reporting), suggesting that the generation of confidence signals is largely independent of the motor-preparatory processes associated with the primary task decision.
papers.authors: Julian R. Matthews, Narumi Sugihara, Sofia Nagisa, Hiroki Ohashi, Kazuhisa Shibata

papers.title: The role of memory in affirming-the-consequent fallacy
papers.abstract: This study examines the neurocognitive basis of the 'affirming-the-consequent' logical fallacy within the context of transitive inference. Using fMRI and behavioral modeling, the researchers demonstrate that the fallacy arises from a memory-based heuristic where individuals unknowingly prioritize the memorized transitive relations over logical deduction. Neural evidence indicates that activation in the hippocampus and posterior parietal cortex during the encoding phase predicts the likelihood of committing the fallacy during the retrieval phase. The findings suggest that this logical error is a byproduct of efficient memory consolidation rather than a fundamental deficit in deductive reasoning capacity.
papers.authors: Yoko Higuchi, Ethan Oblak, Hiroko Nakamura, Makiko Yamada, Kazuhisa Shibata

papers.title: Unsupervised visual learning is revealed for task-irrelevant natural scenes due to reduced attentional suppression effects in visual areas
papers.abstract: The role of unsupervised exposure in visual perceptual learning (VPL) is investigated using natural scene images versus artificial control stimuli. Behavioral data reveal that prolonged exposure to task-irrelevant natural scenes induces robust VPL for orientational features, a phenomenon not observed with higher-order statistics-lacking artificial images. fMRI results indicate that natural scene features evade the top-down attentional suppression typically exerted by the primary task in V1 and V2. This suggests that the complex statistical structure of natural scenes permits unsupervised learning to occur by bypassing the brain's attentional gating mechanisms, thereby facilitating representational changes in early visual cortex.
papers.authors: Takeo Watanabe, Yuka Sasaki, Takuro Zama, Julian R. Matthews, Daiki Ogawa, Kazuhisa Shibata

papers.title: Practice reshapes the geometry and dynamics of task-tailored representations
papers.abstract: Using high-density EEG and representational similarity analysis (RSA), this study characterizes how extensive practice over multiple days optimizes the neural geometry of task representations. The researchers identify a transition from high-dimensional, compositional representations to stabilized, context-specific conjunctive subspaces. These task-tailored neural states integrate task-critical features nonlinearly while abstracting over redundant dimensions, effectively taming the dimensionality of the control representation. The stabilization and temporal alignment of these conjunctive states in the prefrontal and parietal cortices are shown to predict individual gains in behavioral automaticity and reduced switch costs.
papers.authors: Atsushi Kikumoto, Kazuhisa Shibata, Takahiro Nishio, David Badre

papers.title: Conscious awareness determines whether a second learning session disrupts or facilitates earlier learning
papers.abstract: This research explores the interaction between memory consolidation and conscious awareness in sequential visual perceptual learning. Utilizing a dual-session training paradigm with interleaved orientations, the study demonstrates that the stability of initial learning depends on whether the second stimulus is consciously perceived. When the second session involves sub-threshold (unconscious) exposure, it facilitates the consolidation of the first session's memory. Conversely, supra-threshold (conscious) exposure results in retrograde interference, disrupting the initial memory trace. These results highlight a gating role of consciousness in determining the fate of neural plasticity and memory stabilization in the human visual system.
papers.authors: Patrick Bruns, Kazuhisa Shibata, Takeo Watanabe

E217.name: C. Shawn Green
E217.bio: C. Shawn Green is the Mark and Ilene Laufman Family Professor and Chair of the Department of Psychology at the University of Wisconsin–Madison, where they direct the Learning and Transfer Lab. Green’s research investigates the computational and neural mechanisms of human learning, with a focus on how experience with complex environments, such as action video games, can drive improvements in perception and attention. They utilize psychophysical testing, cognitive training paradigms, and modern media to study the factors that determine the rate of learning and the extent to which acquired skills generalize to novel tasks. Green also serves as the Editor-in-Chief of the Journal of Cognitive Enhancement and applies their findings to domains including motor learning and educational practice.
E217.research_direction: Dr. Green's recent work explores the mechanisms and optimization of cognitive training, with a particular focus on how video game mechanics influence learning, skill transfer, and executive function. They have recently been investigating the broad cognitive benefits of action video games, questioning how enhanced attentional control might facilitate a generalized ability to extract environmental statistics and learn novel tasks. Additionally, their research critically evaluates the psychometric validity of traditional planning metrics, such as the Tower of London, and tests whether custom-designed mini-games can provide a more cohesive stealth assessment of goal-directed behavior. To address the practical challenge of participant dropout in longitudinal studies, they are also examining how motivational frameworks—such as manipulating performance feedback and deploying multidimensional dynamic difficulty adjustment—can optimize long-term task engagement and skill progression.

papers.title: Modeling Skill Progression in Children Through Novel Multidimensional Probabilistic DDA
papers.abstract: This research introduces a novel methodological architecture for cognitive control training within a video game environment, utilizing a multidimensional probabilistic Dynamic Difficulty Adjustment (DDA) system. Unlike conventional DDA, which typically modulates a single parameter, this framework adapts multiple task features in real-time based on individual player performance to maintain the 'zone of proximal development.' Data from a player cohort demonstrated skill stabilization after approximately 30-45 minutes of gameplay per module, with the system subsequently preserving engagement through controlled difficulty variability—a feature hypothesized to facilitate the transfer of skills to novel situations. The architecture provides a modular, configurable blueprint for developing personalized computerized cognitive training tools.
papers.venue: International Conference on Games and Learning Alliance (GALA 2025)
papers.authors: Angela Pasqualotto, Marios Fanourakis, Zeno Menestrina, Mor Nahum, Daphne Bavelier, C. Shawn Green

papers.title: Evaluating planning through play: Exploring the use of mini games to assess planning abilities
papers.abstract: This study evaluates the psychometric utility of custom-designed mini games for the 'stealth assessment' of planning—the cognitive capacity to formulate and execute goal-directed sequences. Addressing the low inter-task reliability observed in traditional planning assessments such as the Tower of London, the research tested four planning-centric mini games alongside a non-planning control and a battery of standard cognitive metrics. Results revealed that the mini-game paradigms demonstrated significantly higher inter-correlations than traditional measures, suggesting they tap into a more cohesive and unified planning construct. Two specific mini games emerged as robust indices of planning proficiency with minimal contamination from processing speed, offering a multifaceted and ecologically valid alternative to conventional laboratory tasks.
papers.authors: Emma G. Cunningham, Daphné Bavelier, C. Shawn Green

papers.title: Rethinking planning metrics: An analysis of common measurements of planning abilities
papers.abstract: The authors provide a rigorous individual-differences analysis of traditional planning tasks, including the Tower of London, the Zoo Map test, and the Traveling Salesperson Problem, across an original sample and a pre-registered replication. Despite their shared conceptual label, associations between these tasks remained negligible and statistically unstable between samples. Comparison with adjacent cognitive constructs revealed that planning tasks often correlated more strongly with external measures of processing speed than with each other. These findings suggest that current psychological measurements of planning do not reflect a singular underlying skill, necessitating a critical re-evaluation of planning as a unified cognitive construct in research and clinical assessment.
papers.authors: Emma G. Cunningham, Daphné Bavelier, C. Shawn Green

papers.title: Applications of Expectancy-Value Theory in Promoting Motivated Behavior in Cognitive Training
papers.abstract: This study applies Eccles’ expectancy-value theory (EVT) to address the challenge of participant persistence in long-term cognitive training regimens. By providing participants with experimental feedback designed to manipulate their perceived baseline skill and rate of improvement, the researchers measured the impact on sustained task engagement. The findings demonstrated that feedback emphasizing significant improvement was more effective at promoting long-term persistence than feedback indicating high initial performance without growth. The results suggest that participants utilize local performance trajectories to calculate their expectancy of success, providing a framework for optimizing feedback and motivational scaffolding in behavioral interventions.
papers.authors: Lauren E. Anthony, Aaron Cochrane, Victoria Klaas, Cameron A. Hecht, C. Shawn Green

papers.title: Learning and Transfer: A Perspective From Action Video Game Play
papers.abstract: This perspective piece synthesizes a body of literature documenting the broad cognitive benefits associated with action video game (AVG) play, a phenomenon that challenges the typical specificity of training-induced learning. The authors propose that the mechanism driving this wide-scale transfer is the enhancement of attentional control, which facilitates the rapid acquisition of task-relevant statistics and environmental regularities. Rather than direct transfer of specific skills, AVG play is theorized to promote 'learning to learn'—an increased rate of learning on novel, untrained tasks. The article discusses the theoretical implications for brain plasticity and the practical potential for leveraging AVG-inspired mechanics in the design of next-generation pedagogical and rehabilitative tools.
papers.authors: Daphne Bavelier, C. Shawn Green

E225.name: Maria Concetta Morrone
E225.department: Department of Translational Research on New Technologies in Medicine and Surgery
E225.bio: Morrone is a Professor of Physiology who investigates the functional architecture and plasticity of the mammalian visual system. Their work combines psychophysics, ultra-high field functional magnetic resonance imaging (7T fMRI), and electrophysiology to explore mechanisms of motion perception, visual stability across saccades, and multisensory integration. Morrone has researched how the brain maintains a stable spatial representation during eye movements and the role of the pulvinar in gating adult cortical plasticity. Their current research focuses on the development of the human visual system and the application of neuroimaging to study metabolic and physiological markers of cortical excitability.
E225.research_direction: Dr. Morrone's recent work explores the active neural mechanisms that underlie visual stability, perceptual memory, and short-term cortical plasticity. They have recently been investigating how the visual system maintains continuous perception across saccades and serial stimulus presentations, using psychophysics and high-temporal resolution EEG to probe how alpha and beta-band neural oscillations help carry short-term perceptual priors. Additionally, their ultra-high field 7T fMRI research examines the circuitry of adult neuroplasticity, specifically exploring how subcortical structures like the pulvinar regulate shifts in ocular dominance following short-term monocular deprivation. To further unpick the fine temporal details of early visual processing, they are also employing continuous behavioral tracking paradigms to analyze the real-time dynamics of cross-orientation inhibition among orientation-tuned populations in the human visual cortex.

papers.title: Serial dependence in face-gender classification revealed in low-beta frequency EEG
papers.abstract: This research employs high-temporal resolution EEG and multivariate classification to investigate the neurophysiological substrate of serial dependence in human face perception. By presenting sequences of intermingled male, female, and androgynous faces, the authors demonstrate that gender information from the previous stimulus can be decoded from the neural response to the current stimulus. This memory reactivation occurs selectively in low-beta frequency (14–20 Hz) oscillations, with female and male priors being carried at approximately 14 Hz and 18 Hz, respectively. The accuracy of these neural representations significantly correlates with individual psychophysical biases, suggesting that intrinsic rhythmic activity in the beta band maintains short-term perceptual priors to stabilize face perception.
papers.authors: Giacomo Ranieri, David C. Burr, Jason Bell, Maria Concetta Morrone

papers.title: Following the Tradition of the Italian School of Visual Science: Intellectually Challenging but also Incredibly Exciting
papers.abstract: This autobiographical review synthesizes the author's extensive contributions to visual neuroscience, situated within the historical context of the Italian school of vision. The work provides a comprehensive overview of the fundamental mechanisms of the mammalian visual system, including the development of motion processing in infants, the induction of short-term cortical plasticity via monocular deprivation, and the active mechanisms preserving visual stability during saccadic eye movements. By integrating psychophysics, electrophysiology, and ultra-high field (7T) fMRI, the author explores how the human brain maintains spatiotemporal continuity and constructs robust representations of the world despite constant ocular motor interruptions.
papers.authors: Maria Concetta Morrone

papers.title: Recent, but not long-term, priors induce behavioral oscillations in peri-saccadic vision
papers.abstract: This study examines the role of neural oscillations in the integration of pre-saccadic information with current sensory signals to maintain a continuous percept during eye movements. Using a psychophysical paradigm with Gabor stimuli presented around the time of saccades, the researchers identified that orientation judgments are biased by both short-term (1-back) and long-term (central tendency) priors. Crucially, the bias induced by short-term priors oscillated rhythmically at alpha frequencies (~9.5 Hz) in synchrony with saccadic onset, while the regression toward the mean remained temporally stable. These findings suggest that the alpha rhythm serves as a mechanism for communicating recent perceptual memory across saccades to ensure visual stability, whereas long-term memory is mediated by distinct, non-oscillatory circuitry.
papers.authors: Xin-Yu Xie, David C. Burr, Maria Concetta Morrone

papers.title: The pulvinar regulates plasticity in human visual cortex
papers.abstract: Using ultra-high field (7T) fMRI, this investigation reveals that the pulvinar plays a critical regulatory role in adult visual cortical plasticity induced by short-term monocular deprivation. The study found that a two-hour period of monocular patching leads to a shift in ocular dominance in V1, which is accompanied by a specific reduction in functional connectivity from the pulvinar to the early visual cortex. This connectivity change was selective for the pulvinar-to-V1 directionality and negatively correlated with the magnitude of the ocular dominance shift across participants. These results support a model where subcortical modulatory signals from the pulvinar gate the reorganization of early visual processing in the adult brain, challenging the view that such plasticity is purely intrinsic to the cortex.
papers.authors: Miriam Acquafredda, Jan W. Kurzawski, Laura Biagi, Michela Tosetti, Maria Concetta Morrone, Paola Binda

papers.title: Investigating cross-orientation inhibition with continuous tracking
papers.abstract: This paper utilizes a continuous tracking paradigm to analyze the high-resolution dynamics of cross-orientation inhibition (XOI) in human observers. Participants tracked the horizontal movement of a narrow vertical grating while exposed to uniform backgrounds, parallel masks, or orthogonal masks. Spectral and cross-correlation analyses of the tracking trajectories revealed that orthogonal masks reduce the gain of the tracking response in a divisive manner, consistent with known neurophysiological gain-control mechanisms. In contrast, parallel masks exerted a subtractive influence on the response. The study demonstrates that continuous tracking is a highly sensitive behavioral tool for characterizing the inhibitory interactions and temporal dynamics of orientation-tuned neuronal populations in the human primary visual cortex.
papers.authors: Pierfrancesco Ambrosi, David Charles Burr, Maria Concetta Morrone

E226.name: Merav Ahissar
E226.department: Department of Psychology and the Edmond & Lily Safra Center for Brain Sciences
E226.bio: Ahissar developed the Reverse Hierarchy Theory of perception and learning, which posits that perceptual learning is a top-down driven process proceeding from high-level generalizations to low-level sensory details. Ahissar's research utilizes behavioral psychophysics, Bayesian computational modeling, ERP, and fMRI to investigate mechanisms of skill acquisition and the neural basis of individual differences. They developed the 'poor-anchoring' theory of dyslexia, which suggests that reading disabilities stem from the rapid decay of perceptual memory traces rather than sensory deficits alone. Their current research, supported by an ERC Advanced Grant, examines the computational and neural constraints affecting the acquisition of communicative skills in populations with dyslexia and autism.
E226.research_direction: Dr. Ahissar's recent work explores how the brain integrates immediate sensory traces and long-term environmental statistics to form perceptual priors, utilizing behavioral paradigms, electroencephalography (EEG), and Bayesian modeling. They have recently been investigating how these statistical learning and memory mechanisms diverge in neurodevelopmental conditions, specifically examining whether dyslexia is characterized by a rapid decay of perceptual memory and whether autism spectrum disorder involves an overweighting of accumulative prior knowledge. To probe these questions, their research employs auditory frequency discrimination tasks to assess whether perceptual biases are driven by top-down predictive coding or bottom-up sensory integration, while also tracking neural markers like feedback-related negativity to evaluate performance monitoring and feedback sensitivity in autism. Furthermore, their theoretical work investigates the broader architectural mechanisms of perception, modeling how neural hierarchies might convert continuous, analog sensory signals from the physical world into the discrete, digital mental representations required for interpersonal communication.

papers.title: Rapid decay of perceptual memory in dyslexia
papers.abstract: The mechanistic underpinnings of developmental dyslexia are re-examined through the lens of perceptual learning and expertise acquisition. Integrating behavioral, electrophysiological (neural adaptation), and computational modeling evidence, the authors propose that dyslexia is fundamentally characterized by an accelerated decay of perceptual memory traces for both speech and non-speech regularities. This rapid trace decay prevents the efficient accumulation of environmental statistics, leading to reduced complexity in the formation of perceptual categories and a diminished learning slope for linguistic expertise. Paradoxically, this deficit causes the performance gap between dyslexic and neurotypical individuals to widen as cumulative exposure to stimulus regularities increases.
papers.authors: Ayelet Gertsovski, Merav Ahissar

papers.title: Digital–Analog Perceptual Duality
papers.abstract: This work formalizes a mapping between the classic mind-body duality and the distinction between 'brain-world' (BW) and 'brain-brain' (BB) interaction domains. BW interactions are defined as analog, continuous motor-sensory loops where neural systems interface with physical substances. Conversely, BB interactions represent inter-individual mental communication, which is inherently digital and discrete, relying on categorization to overcome bandwidth limitations. The authors provide a review of neural architectures, such as neuronal phase-locked loops (NPLLs), that perform the non-invertible transformations between analog sensory input and digital mental representation. They conclude that the perceived gap between physical and mental processes emerges from these unidirectional transformations within neural hierarchies.
papers.authors: Ehud Ahissar, Daniel Polani, Merav Ahissar

papers.title: The different roles of learning recent and accumulative statistics
papers.abstract: This review examines how humans integrate immediate temporal regularities (recent statistics) with long-term distributional knowledge (accumulative statistics) during perceptual inference. Utilizing Bayesian frameworks, the authors characterize the weighting of these information sources across neurodevelopmental conditions. Neurotypical perception is characterized by a flexible balance: fast updating of internal models in response to recent changes and stable reliance on accumulative statistics in invariant environments. In contrast, dyslexia is marked by an overweighting of the immediate past due to fast prior decay, while autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is associated with an overweighting of accumulative statistics, leading to slower updating of expectations and reduced social interactive flexibility.
papers.authors: Aviel Sulem, Merav Ahissar

papers.title: Reduced monitoring of task performance is an effective biomarker of autism
papers.abstract: This study utilizes electroencephalography (EEG) and behavioral modeling to evaluate performance monitoring and feedback sensitivity in autism spectrum disorder (ASD). Using a two-tone pitch discrimination task with choice-contingent feedback, the researchers tracked the feedback-related negativity (FRN), an ERP component localized to the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC). Results revealed that a clear FRN was absent in more than half of the ASD cohort, while present in nearly all neurotypical controls. Behaviorally, ASD participants exhibited diminished post-error response slowing and reduced online adjustment based on task difficulty. These findings suggest that impaired ACC-mediated monitoring of internal and external feedback is a robust biomarker for the reduced behavioral flexibility characteristic of autism.
papers.authors: Nathaniel J. Zuk, Yarden Weiss, Athena Akrami, Merav Ahissar

papers.title: Frequency-Specific Contributions to Auditory Perceptual Priors: Testing the Predictive-Coding Hypothesis
papers.abstract: This investigation tests the computational architecture of auditory perceptual priors by adjudicating between top-down predictive coding and bottom-up memory-based integration. By analyzing recency biases in a high-trial-count frequency discrimination task, the authors demonstrated that perceptual priors are frequency-specific and persistent across intervening task-irrelevant stimuli. Crucially, the bias was independent of the subjective percept of the preceding trial, indicating that priors are constructed from low-level sensory traces rather than being generated via high-level top-down predictions. These results support a bottom-up model of statistical learning where the brain's internal priors emerge directly from the temporal integration of recent sensory inputs.
papers.authors: Itay Lieder, Aviel Sulem, Merav Ahissar

E227.name: Dov Sagi
E227.bio: Dov Sagi is a Professor in the Department of Brain Sciences at the Weizmann Institute of Science, specializing in the psychophysics of human vision and the plasticity of sensory systems. Sagi developed the texture discrimination task (TDT), which demonstrated that adult visual performance can be enhanced through practice. Their research utilizes psychophysical methodologies and computational models, such as signal detection theory and the drift-diffusion model, to investigate lateral interactions in the visual cortex, spatial integration, and the role of context in orientation estimation. Currently, Sagi examines how sensory adaptation interacts with learning generalization and investigates the mechanisms of serial dependence in perceptual decision-making.
E227.research_direction: Dr. Sagi's recent work explores the temporal and network dynamics underlying visual awareness, specifically focusing on the phenomenon of motion-induced blindness. They have recently been investigating whether the sudden perceptual disappearance of salient targets during this phenomenon operates as a noisy excitable system characterized by abrupt state transitions, autonomous suppression trajectories, and obligatory refractory periods. To probe these mechanisms, their research employs psychophysical experiments that use dynamic, rotating mask patterns to deliver localized spatiotemporal perturbations to parafoveal targets. By measuring how these periodic visual sweeps trigger suppression and influence the timing of subsequent perceptual reappearance, Dr. Sagi aims to understand how fluctuations in visual awareness are governed by the interplay between external sensory triggers and intrinsic neural circuit states.

papers.title: Motion-induced blindness as a noisy excitable system
papers.abstract: In motion-induced blindness (MIB), salient visual stimuli intermittently vanish from visual awareness when surrounded by a moving mask pattern, though the precise temporal and network mechanics remain incompletely characterized. This study investigated whether the temporal dynamics of MIB exhibit the canonical properties of a noisy excitable system, which is defined by abrupt state transitions triggered by suprathreshold perturbations, autonomous stimulus-independent trajectory completions, and obligatory recovery phases. Psychophysical experiments tested observers with dynamic masks consisting of rotating radial bars configured with a central gap around a parafoveal luminous target, delivering periodic spatiotemporal perturbations to the target perimeter. The sweep of mask elements adjacent to the target locus frequently triggered abrupt perceptual suppression, confirming spatial locality. Consistent with excitable state kinetics, the duration of perceptual invisibility was decoupled from subsequent bar sweeps traversing the field during the suppressed epoch and demonstrated negligible dependence on global mask configuration. Following perceptual reappearance, a robust refractory interval spanning 0.5 to 2 seconds was observed during which further suppressive events could not be triggered. These findings indicate that MIB reflects the behavior of an excitable neural circuit where the mask acts as a perturbing trigger while subsequent perceptual suppression and recovery trajectories are governed by intrinsic network states.
papers.authors: Mikhail Katkov, Alexander Cooperman, Noya Meital-Kfir, Dov Sagi

E228.name: Uri Polat
E228.department: School of Optometry and Vision Science, Faculty of Life Sciences
E228.bio: Uri Polat is a Professor at Bar-Ilan University and Head of the School of Optometry and Vision Science, specializing in the mechanisms of visual perception and neuroplasticity. Polat conducted research on perceptual learning, demonstrating that targeted training with Gabor stimuli and lateral masking can improve visual function in adults with amblyopia. Their research investigates spatial interactions, visual crowding, and the temporal properties of visual processing to develop non-invasive clinical interventions for conditions such as presbyopia. Polat's work integrates psychophysical methodologies with clinical applications to explore the brain's capacity to compensate for blurred retinal input through cortical reorganization.
E228.research_direction: Dr. Polat's recent work explores the spatiotemporal dynamics of early visual processing, particularly investigating how spatial context and presentation time shape the boundaries of the human perceptive field. Using psychophysical paradigms like Gabor-based lateral masking and temporal truncation, they have recently been examining how foveal crowding affects basic feature discrimination and how these contextual interference effects are exacerbated by the aging visual system. Their research also probes the limits of binocular summation, testing how top-down observer awareness and spatial flanker configurations modulate interocular integration. Additionally, they investigate the neural mechanisms of neuroplasticity, exploring how sensory adaptation and the functional overlap of inhibitory cortical networks drive the generalization of perceptual learning across distinct visual tasks.

papers.title: Foveal crowding increases with age under limited viewing conditions
papers.abstract: This study explores the interaction between senescence and foveal crowding across the adult lifespan. Using a psychophysical letter identification paradigm with eccentric-flanker spatial configurations, researchers assessed visual acuity under varying temporal constraints in a cohort of 33 participants aged 20–89. Results indicate that while foveal crowding remains stable under sustained viewing, temporal truncation (40 ms) unmasks a significant age-related elevation in crowding susceptibility, characterized by a steeper decline in spatial resolution (visual acuity) and prolonged reaction latencies. These findings suggest that the degradation of temporal processing speed in the aging visual system exacerbates contextual interference at the fovea, even when isolated visual acuity remains largely intact.
papers.authors: Noah Rappeport, Maria Lev, Uri Polat

papers.title: Foveal crowding modifies a target’s properties under a brief presentation time
papers.abstract: Investigating the impact of foveal crowding on chromatic and achromatic information processing, this study employed a dual-task paradigm requiring both orientation identification and color discrimination of a central target letter (black vs. red). Psychophysical measurements revealed that temporal constraints (20–40 ms) significantly degrade both identification accuracy and chromatic sensitivity within the foveal region, with performance recovery occurring as the stimulus duration extends to 120 ms. The potentiation of these deficits by backward masking suggests that foveal crowding under brief temporal regimes shares underlying mechanisms with visual masking, likely transitioning from early sensory interference to higher-order integrative bottlenecks in the parvocellular stream.
papers.authors: Ziv Siman-Tov, Maria Lev, Uri Polat

papers.title: What Factors Affect Binocular Summation?
papers.abstract: This research evaluates the robustness of binocular summation (BS) and its modulation by spatial context and observer awareness. Utilizing Gabor-based lateral masking paradigms with varying target-flanker configurations (collinear vs. orthogonal) and separations (2λ, 3λ), the study manipulated presentation times (40–200 ms) and stimulus uncertainty via trial intermixing with stereoscopic shutter glasses. Findings indicate that when sensory awareness of the stimulated eye is minimized through intermixed presentations, BS factors approximate the theoretical √2 (1.41) limit, suggesting that top-down awareness and stimulus predictability play critical roles in the stability of interocular integration and the suppression of monocular inputs in spatial interaction tasks.
papers.authors: Marzouk Yassin, Maria Lev, Uri Polat

papers.title: Generalization in perceptual learning across stimuli and tasks
papers.abstract: This study investigates the neural mechanisms of learning transfer between visual tasks by examining the generalization of perceptual improvements from a backward-masked texture discrimination task (TDT) to a Gabor-based contrast detection (CD) paradigm. By manipulating stimulus consistency and sensory adaptation during training, the authors demonstrate that learning generalization occurs when the training and testing regimens engage convergent neural substrates, specifically those involving inhibitory lateral interactions and spatiotemporal masking. The results imply that the specificity of perceptual learning is governed by the functional overlap of the cortical networks recruited for stimulus processing, where increased adaptation enabled the transfer of learning to other tasks limited by similar sensory inhibitory processes.
papers.authors: Ravit Kahalani-Hodedany, Maria Lev, Dov Sagi, Uri Polat

papers.title: Dynamics of the perceptive field size in human adults
papers.abstract: This investigation quantifies the spatiotemporal characteristics of the perceptive field (PF) in the adult human visual system, identifying it as the fundamental unit of visual processing. Utilizing lateral masking experiments with Gabor patch triplets, the study mapped the spatial range of facilitatory and inhibitory contextual interactions as a function of target-flanker separation and stimulus duration (40–200 ms). The results characterize the PF's dynamic extent, revealing how spatial integration thresholds and the magnitude of lateral interactions shift under varied temporal constraints. These quantitative mappings elucidate the functional architecture of integrative units in the visual cortex, providing a model for how the system reconciles local contrast and orientation within specific spatial and temporal envelopes.
papers.authors: Marzouk Yassin, Maria Lev, Uri Polat

E229.name: Ladan Shams
E229.bio: Ladan Shams is a Professor of Psychology, BioEngineering, and Neuroscience at UCLA and directs the Multisensory Processing Lab. Their research investigates the computational principles and neural mechanisms of multisensory perception, examining how the brain integrates sensory modalities to form representations and facilitate learning. Shams has conducted work on the sound-induced flash illusion and the application of Bayesian Causal Inference models to explain sensory integration and recalibration. Their current research includes investigating top-down cognitive influences on perception and developing behavioral methods for assessing and remediating cognitive decline.
E229.research_direction: Dr. Shams has recently been investigating the computational principles underlying multisensory integration alongside the perceptual and physiological drivers of emotional experience. Their recent work heavily explores Bayesian Causal Inference (BCI), examining how the brain integrates audio-visual signals across multiple dimensions—such as time and numerosity in the sound-induced flash illusion—and evaluating the critical role of unisensory precision in these cue-weighting processes. To facilitate this computational research, they are developing open-source Python toolboxes that allow researchers to standardize the modeling of multisensory behavioral data. Beyond multisensory processing, they are also examining the intersection of perception and affect, investigating how visual features like color and saturation modulate the emotional valence of naturalistic scenes and exploring the autonomic psychophysiological markers of music-induced emotion.

papers.title: Crossmodal interaction of flashes and beeps across time and number follows Bayesian causal inference
papers.abstract: This study advances the Bayesian Causal Inference (BCI) framework into a multidimensional domain by investigating how the brain integrates temporal onset disparities and numerosity cues. Utilizing a parametric sound-induced flash illusion (SiFI) paradigm with varying audiovisual disparities, the authors demonstrate that the probability of signal integration is a joint function of asynchrony and numerical conflict. The proposed multidimensional BCI model exhibits high predictive accuracy across the stimulus space, suggesting that the human brain performs hierarchical causal inference by assessing congruency across multiple signal features to adjudicate between common-cause and independent-cause hypotheses.
papers.authors: Haocheng Zhu, Yiyang Zhang, Ulrik Beierholm, Ladan Shams

papers.title: Psychophysiological Correlates of Emotion During Music Perception
papers.abstract: This research examines the psychophysiological substrates of music-induced affect through an exploratory structural equation modeling (SEM) approach. Participants rated subjective valence and arousal while listening to unfamiliar instrumental excerpts, during which metrics including high-frequency heart rate variability (HF HRV), skin conductance levels (SCL), and respiration rates were quantified. Statistical analysis revealed that while HF HRV, SCL, and respiratory frequency exhibited significant correlations with subjective arousal, valence was specifically associated with HF HRV and the range of skin conductance responses (SCR). These results suggest that specific autonomic markers can objectively track distinct dimensions of emotional experience in music perception.
papers.venue: 2025 IEEE Signal Processing in Medicine and Biology Symposium (SPMB)
papers.authors: Charlotte Kelly, Amir Jahanian Najafabadi, Ladan Shams

papers.title: The effects of color and saturation on the enjoyment of real-life images
papers.abstract: The investigators analyzed how chromatic information and saturation levels modulate the affective evaluation of naturalistic scenes across the valence spectrum. Utilizing images from the International Affective Picture System (IAPS), the study found that the presence of color amplifies the perceived intensity of both positive and negative valence, increasing pleasantness for favorable images and unpleasantness for aversive ones. Furthermore, a non-linear relationship between saturation intensity and pleasure ratings suggests distinct computational mechanisms for the processing of chromatic presence versus saturation magnitude. These valence-dependent interactions remained significant after controlling for low-level features such as luminance and overall colorfulness.
papers.authors: Chenyang Lin, Sabrina Mottaghi, Ladan Shams

papers.title: BCI Toolbox: An open-source python package for the Bayesian causal inference model
papers.abstract: The BCI Toolbox is introduced as a comprehensive Python-based software package for implementing and analyzing Bayesian Causal Inference models in behavioral research. The package facilitates quantitative modeling of multisensory data through a graphical user interface (GUI) and modular functions for Monte Carlo simulations and model fitting (MLE and SSE). The authors validated the framework's reliability through rigorous parameter recovery testing, demonstrating its capacity to accurately estimate generative parameters such as common-cause priors and sensory likelihood variances. The toolbox utilizes Variational Bayesian Monte Carlo (VBMC) for parameter optimization, aiming to standardize the application of BCI theory to diverse experimental paradigms.
papers.authors: Haocheng Zhu, Ulrik Beierholm, Ladan Shams

papers.title: The overlooked role of unisensory precision in multisensory research
papers.abstract: This article addresses a critical methodological gap in multisensory integration studies: the systematic neglect of unisensory precision (the inverse of sensory noise) in determining integration outcomes. By re-evaluating normative Bayesian frameworks, the authors demonstrate that trial-to-trial or individual fluctuations in sensory reliability significantly impact cue weighting and the inference of causal structure. The piece advocates for the rigorous quantification of unisensory uncertainty as a prerequisite for testing models like Bayesian Causal Inference, highlighting how variations in sensory 'currency' across modalities fundamentally bias the weighting of visual and auditory signals.
papers.authors: Haocheng Zhu, Ulrik Beierholm, Ladan Shams

E230.name: Marc Ernst
E230.bio: Marc O. Ernst is the Chair of Applied Cognitive Psychology at Ulm University, where they investigate the computational principles underlying how the human brain integrates information from sensory modalities like vision, touch, and audition. Ernst’s research demonstrates that humans combine sensory cues in a statistically optimal, Bayesian fashion to minimize perceptual uncertainty. Their work utilizes psychophysical experiments, virtual reality, and mathematical modeling to explore perception-action loops, the role of prior knowledge in sensory processing, and the development of multisensory integration. Before joining Ulm, Ernst held positions at Bielefeld University and the Max Planck Institute for Biological Cybernetics.
E230.research_direction: Dr. Ernst's recent work explores the mechanisms of multisensory integration, sensorimotor control, and the development of spatial cognition following early visual deprivation. They have recently been investigating how sight restoration from congenital cataracts impacts visuomotor integration, measuring postural sway and optic flow sensitivity in patients while also evaluating if targeted audiovisual-motor training can improve spatial localization and navigation. In parallel, their research probes the computational rules of multimodal fusion, using psychophysical paradigms and biological modeling to test whether the brain integrates dynamic sensory signals primarily through transient intensity changes rather than sustained magnitude responses. Furthermore, they are studying object interaction dynamics, utilizing precision grip tasks to determine how the motor system estimates an object's center of mass and updates internal models of material density during goal-directed grasping.

papers.title: Postural stability and optic flow sensitivity following sight restoration from congenital bilateral cataracts
papers.abstract: This study examined the utilization of vision for postural stabilization and self-motion perception in individuals whose sight was surgically restored following years of congenital bilateral cataract deprivation. By quantifying postural sway in eyes-open versus eyes-closed conditions and under various radial and translational optic flow patterns, the researchers assessed the maturation of visuomotor integration. Findings indicate that cataract-treated individuals exhibit significantly higher postural sway than typically sighted controls and demonstrate a reduced ability to leverage visual information for balance stabilization. Furthermore, the sensitivity to illusory self-motion cues from optic flow was less pronounced in the treated group, suggesting that early visual experience is a critical determinant for the development of internal models that map optic flow to sensorimotor control, though partial recovery is possible with time post-surgery.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences
papers.authors: Irene Senna, Priscilla Balestrucci, Sophia Piller, Dennis Wiebusch, Marc O. Ernst

papers.title: Multisensory integration operates on correlated input from unimodal transient channels
papers.abstract: The mechanisms underlying the integration of dynamic multisensory signals remain poorly understood, particularly regarding the relative contributions of sustained versus transient neural responses. This paper proposes a computational framework based on the Multisensory Correlation Detector (MCD), a biologically inspired model analogous to the Hassenstein-Reichardt correlator. Through psychophysical experiments and modeling, the authors demonstrate that multisensory integration selectively operates on unsigned transient channels—signaling changes in intensity—rather than sustained channels encoding absolute magnitude. The MCD model successfully accounts for a wide range of perceptual phenomena, including temporal order judgments (TOJs), simultaneity judgments (SJs), the McGurk effect, and causality perception, suggesting that temporal correlation between unimodal transients is the primary driver of multimodal fusion in the human brain.
papers.authors: Cesare V. Parise, Marc O. Ernst

papers.title: Grasping new material densities
papers.abstract: Effective goal-directed actions like grasping require internal models of object mass distribution to minimize torque and ensure stability. This study investigated how humans estimate the center of mass (CoM) when interacting with novel objects composed of multiple materials with different densities (e.g., steel and PVC). Using a precision grip task, the researchers tracked grasp point selection over successive trials. Results showed that initial grasps were consistently biased toward the objects' geometric centers, indicating a reliance on shape cues rather than material priors. However, participants rapidly adapted their grasp locations toward the true CoM within several trials. The learning exhibited partial transfer across different mass distributions, suggesting that the motor system learns the relative density ratios of materials. Notably, torque minimization acted as a primary driver for adaptation, though the recalibration of the internal model was often incomplete.
papers.authors: Wendy J. Adams, Sina Mehraeen, Marc O. Ernst

papers.title: Multisensory training improves the development of spatial cognition after sight restoration from congenital cataracts
papers.abstract: Congenitally blind individuals typically display deficits in spatial representation and mobility that persist even after sight-restoration surgery. This study assessed the efficacy of a 5-day multisensory training program designed to associate audiovisual feedback with bodily movements in Ethiopian children treated for cataracts. Utilizing a longitudinal psychophysical approach, the researchers measured performance in visual/auditory localization and spatial bisection tasks. The training led to rapid and significant improvements in space representation and navigation speed, with treated participants reaching performance levels comparable to typically sighted controls in several metrics. These findings suggest that the lack of early visual calibration can be partially compensated for by targeted sensorimotor training, highlighting the lifelong plasticity of the human brain's spatial processing circuits.
papers.authors: Irene Senna, Sophia Piller, Chiara Martolini, Elena Cocchi, Monica Gori, Marc O. Ernst

E232.name: Uta Noppeney
E232.department: Donders Centre for Neuroscience, Biophysics Department
E232.lab_name: Multisensory Perception, Learning and Attention Group
E232.bio: Uta Noppeney is a Professor of Systems Neuroscience who investigates how the human brain integrates sensory inputs to form perceptions and guide behavior. They apply normative Bayesian frameworks to model multisensory causal inference and reliability-weighted cue integration across cortical hierarchies. Noppeney combines psychophysics and computational modeling with neuroimaging techniques such as fMRI, MEG, and EEG to characterize the neural dynamics of decision-making, learning, and attention. Their work explores these multisensory computational principles in healthy individuals across the lifespan and in clinical populations, such as those with neuropsychiatric disorders.
E232.research_direction: Dr. Noppeney’s recent work explores the neural and computational mechanisms underlying multisensory perception, specifically investigating how the brain weights and combines auditory, visual, and bodily signals based on principles of Bayesian causal inference. They have recently been utilizing fMRI, multivariate EEG, and psychophysics to ask whether these hierarchical cue-combination and arbitration processes are disrupted in specific populations, such as healthy older adults and individuals with schizophrenia. Additionally, their research probes the temporal dynamics of sensory integration, using neurostimulation (tACS) and individual EEG profiles to determine how the frequency of parietal alpha oscillations dictates the temporal binding window and influences the conscious sense of body ownership. Finally, they are expanding this focus on cross-modal correspondence into machine learning by developing and validating large-scale, annotated video datasets designed to train deep neural networks on audiovisual action recognition.

papers.title: Parietal alpha frequency shapes own-body perception by modulating the temporal integration of bodily signals
papers.abstract: This study investigates the mechanistic role of parietal alpha oscillations in the temporal binding of self-related sensory signals and the resulting sense of body ownership. Utilizing a combination of psychophysics, individual alpha frequency (IAF) quantification via EEG, and transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS), the authors demonstrate that the frequency of parietal alpha oscillations both predicts and causally modulates the temporal binding window (TBW) and perceptual sensitivity in body ownership and visuotactile simultaneity judgment tasks. Computational modeling further links IAF to the precision of asynchrony information within a hierarchical Bayesian causal inference framework. The findings establish that parietal alpha-band dynamics regulate the temporal parsing and integration of multisensory bodily inputs, thereby constraining the conscious experience of body ownership.
papers.authors: Mariano D'Angelo, Ugo Giulio Pesci, Jan-Mathijs Schoffelen, Uta Noppeney

papers.title: Multisensory perceptual and causal inference is largely preserved in medicated post-acute individuals with schizophrenia
papers.abstract: This investigation utilized an audiovisual sound-induced flash illusion paradigm combined with multivariate EEG and Bayesian Causal Inference (BCI) modeling to determine whether schizophrenia disrupts the computational or neural mechanisms of multisensory arbitration. By comparing normative BCI models against approximate solutions, the researchers assessed the ability of medicated individuals with schizophrenia to weight sensory signals by their relative reliabilities and infer the underlying causal structure of multisensory events. Despite clinical hypotheses of integration deficits, the results demonstrated that the core computational mechanisms and neural dynamics of perceptual and causal inference are largely preserved in this patient cohort, exhibiting comparable behavioral and electrophysiological profiles to age-matched healthy controls.
papers.authors: Tim Rohe, Klaus Hesse, Ann-Christine Ehlis, Uta Noppeney

papers.title: Audiovisual integration is preserved in older adults across the cortical hierarchy
papers.abstract: This study utilized functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and a spatial ventriloquist task to assess how healthy aging affects the neural hierarchies supporting multisensory perception. Employing Bayesian Causal Inference (BCI) modeling of BOLD responses, the researchers mapped the transformation of sensory signals from independent unimodal representations in primary cortices to integrated and causal-inference-weighted estimates in the intraparietal sulcus and superior temporal sulcus. The findings reveal that older adults retain the normative computational principles of reliability-weighted cue combination and causal inference, maintaining a preserved hierarchical architecture for multisensory integration despite general age-related sensory declines.
papers.authors: Sophie A. Jones, Uta Noppeney

papers.title: Audiovisual Moments in Time: A large-scale annotated dataset of audiovisual actions
papers.abstract: The authors present Audiovisual Moments in Time (AVMIT), a dataset consisting of 57,177 videos from the Moments in Time (MIT) corpus, each human-annotated for the presence and prominence of audiovisual action events. This resource addresses the need for high-quality, verified multimodal data in the training of deep neural networks (DNNs). Using Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) and pre-computed feature embeddings, the study demonstrates that training exclusively on AVMIT-filtered audiovisual actions significantly enhances recognition accuracy and performance on supervised audiovisual correspondence (SAVC) tasks. The dataset facilitates more robust cross-modal learning by providing a curated test set and clear labels for temporal and semantic alignment between audio and visual streams.
papers.authors: Michael Joannou, Pia Rotshtein, Uta Noppeney

papers.title: Alpha oscillations and temporal binding windows in perception: A critical review and best practice guidelines
papers.abstract: This article provides a systematic review and meta-analysis of the alpha temporal resolution hypothesis, which posits that the frequency of individual alpha oscillations determines the temporal window for integrating and segregating sensory inputs. Synthesizing evidence from 27 experiments spanning unimodal and multisensory paradigms, the authors identify significant interpretational challenges arising from methodological inconsistencies and decisional biases. The paper proposes a rigorous set of best-practice guidelines—emphasizing the use of signal detection theory and experimenter-independent analysis—to standardize the assessment of how alpha-band dynamics causally contribute to the temporal parsing of the sensory environment.
papers.authors: Jan-Mathijs Schoffelen, Ugo Giulio Pesci, Uta Noppeney

E234.name: Christoph Kayser
E234.department: Department for Cognitive Neuroscience, Faculty of Biology
E234.bio: Christoph Kayser is a Professor and Chair for Cognitive Neuroscience at Bielefeld University, where they investigate the neural mechanisms underlying multisensory integration and perceptual decision-making. Their research utilizes magnetoencephalography (MEG), electrophysiology, and computational modeling to determine how the brain combines information from different sensory modalities, such as vision and audition, to enhance perception in complex environments. Kayser’s work explores the functional role of neural oscillations in sensory tracking and the contribution of motor-auditory interactions to speech intelligibility. Additionally, their recent studies examine the alignment of physiological processes like respiration and oculomotor behavior with cognitive and sensory-motor events.
E234.research_direction: Dr. Kayser has recently been investigating how internal bodily rhythms and oculomotor signals continuously shape sensory processing across both visual and auditory domains. Their recent work explores whether the natural respiratory cycle and transient autonomic arousal—indexed by pupillometry and modified via breathwork—modulate visual cognitive performance, bistable perceptual switching, and the strength of EEG-based neural representations. In the auditory domain, they are probing the sensorimotor coupling between the eyes and ears by examining how saccade directions and eye-movement-related eardrum micro-oscillations influence spatial hearing. Furthermore, they are testing the controversial concept of auditory "perceptual cycles" by evaluating whether human hearing sensitivity and reaction times systematically fluctuate in low-frequency rhythmic patterns.

papers.title: Sound lateralization Ability is affected by saccade direction but not Eye Movement-Related Eardrum Oscillations (EMREOs)
papers.abstract: This investigation evaluated whether eye-movement-related eardrum oscillations (EMREOs)—micro-oscillations of the tympanic membrane that synchronize with saccades—functionally influence auditory spatial perception. EMREOs are hypothesized to reflect middle ear muscle activity that could potentially align visual and acoustic spatial reference frames. Human participants performed sound lateralization tasks (free-field and in-ear) with stimuli presented at varying latencies relative to saccade onset to sample different EMREO phases. No significant modulatory effects were found for perceptual sensitivity (d'), response bias, or reaction times as a function of the EMREO phase or amplitude. However, lateralization performance was significantly shaped by the spatial congruency between the saccade and the acoustic target. These results suggest that while saccade-related motor signals influence hearing, the specific mechanical oscillations of the eardrum captured by EMREOs have negligible perceptual impact on auditory spatial discrimination.
papers.authors: Nancy Sotero Silva, Felix Bröhl, Christoph Kayser

papers.title: Spontaneous perceptual reversals are accompanied by systematic changes in pupil size but not respiration phase
papers.abstract: The study explored the physiological coupling between autonomic rhythms and the dynamics of bistable perception using a Necker cube task. While previous models have suggested that the respiratory cycle might gate endogenous perceptual switches, this research analyzed spontaneous reversals in relation to both respiratory phase and pupil diameter. The findings indicated that perceptual transitions are consistently preceded by systematic pupil dilations, reflecting transient surges in arousal and cognitive load. Conversely, circular statistical analysis showed no systematic relationship between the phase of the spontaneous respiratory rhythm and the occurrence of perceptual reversals. These results demonstrate a dissociation where autonomic arousal, as indexed by pupil size, is intrinsically coupled with multistable perceptual dynamics, whereas the respiratory cycle does not exert a direct temporal gating influence on spontaneous endogenous switching.
papers.authors: Lisa Stetza, Christoph Kayser

papers.title: Effects of Short-Term Breathwork on Respiration and Cognition
papers.abstract: This research investigated the immediate behavioral and physiological impacts of brief (one-minute) voluntary breathing interventions. Participants performed four distinct breathing protocols (fast/slow frequency and varied I/E ratios) prior to a visual emotion discrimination task. Although the breathwork successfully induced shifts in subsequent respiratory parameters such as frequency and inhalation-exhalation ratios, these changes did not translate into sustained enhancements in discrimination accuracy or reaction times across the task blocks. However, a transient improvement in reaction times was observed immediately following all breathing practices, suggesting a short-lived facilitation of attentional alertness or sensorimotor responsiveness. The results indicate that while even very brief periods of consciously controlled respiration can transiently influence cognitive performance, these effects are ephemeral and do not lead to long-term improvements in sensory-cognitive efficiency.
papers.authors: Lena Hehemann, Lisa Stetza, Christoph Kayser

papers.title: Mixed evidence for the rhythmicity of auditory perceptual judgements in humans
papers.abstract: Addressing the controversy surrounding 'perceptual cycles' in audition, the authors systematically probed for rhythmic fluctuations in behavioral performance across multiple auditory tasks. Using binned linear models and trial-based analytical approaches, the study examined periodicities in sensitivity (d'), bias, and reaction times within the 2–8 Hz range while monitoring eye movements and dual-task interference. Rhythmic effects were found to be paradigm-specific and often restricted to individual ears, rather than being a universal feature of auditory processing. The presence of these signatures was modulated by attentional requirements and oculomotor activity. These findings challenge the notion of a universal rhythmic mode of hearing and suggest that behavioral periodicities in audition are contingent on specific sensorimotor constraints and top-down task demands.
papers.authors: Cécile Fabio, Christoph Kayser

papers.title: Evidence That Respiratory Phase May Modulate Task-Related Neural Representations of Visual Stimuli
papers.abstract: This study investigated the neurophysiological basis of respiratory-modulated cognitive performance by analyzing task-related neural representations in the human brain. EEG and respiratory signals were recorded during emotion and shape discrimination tasks, and a multivariate representation-centered framework using linear discriminant analysis (LDA) was employed to quantify sensory evidence. The results showed that both behavioral outcomes and the strength of neural representations (classifier evidence) were significantly modulated by the respiratory phase at stimulus onset. Specifically, neural signatures carrying task-relevant information (peaking ~300–200 ms prior to the response) were enhanced during specific respiratory phases, particularly near the transition to expiration. These findings provide evidence that respiration directly gates the quality of stimulus-specific neural encoding, supporting the role of respiratory rhythms in structuring sensory-cognitive brain representations.
papers.authors: Lisa Stetza, Lena Hehemann, Christoph Kayser

E235.name: Henrik Ehrsson
E235.bio: Ehrsson is a Professor of Cognitive Neuroscience at Karolinska Institutet, focusing on the multisensory processes that underpin the perception of the bodily self. Their research characterizes the neural mechanisms and computational principles by which the brain integrates visual, tactile, and proprioceptive signals to produce the experience of body ownership and self-location. Utilizing experimental paradigms such as the rubber hand illusion and virtual reality, Ehrsson employs functional neuroimaging and psychophysics to map the cortical networks responsible for bodily awareness. Their work investigates the relationship between multisensory integration and consciousness, with applications in neuroprosthetics and the treatment of psychiatric disorders.
E235.research_direction: Dr. Ehrsson has recently been investigating the neurocomputational and multisensory foundations of the bodily self, primarily using bodily illusions like the rubber hand and body-swap paradigms. Their recent work explores how rhythmic neural oscillations act as temporal sampling mechanisms, using high-density EEG to test how parietal alpha and beta frequencies constrain the temporal binding windows for integrating visuotactile and somatosensory signals into a coherent sense of body ownership. Additionally, they are studying the intersection of sensory integration and conscious access, applying drift-diffusion models to masked-priming tasks to determine whether bodily self-perception fundamentally requires conscious awareness of sensory evidence. Finally, their research examines the broader perceptual and cognitive consequences of altered body representation, testing how induced bodily disownership impacts the structural stability of a person's psychological self-concept, and how incorporating an artificial limb dynamically shifts the spatial localization of thermal pain, a phenomenon known as nociceptive drift.

papers.title: Beta oscillations support somatosensory temporal integration for body ownership
papers.abstract: This research investigates whether the temporal resolution of purely somatosensory integration for body ownership is governed by rhythmic neural oscillations, analogous to the role of alpha rhythms in visuotactile integration. Utilizing a robotic psychophysical paradigm of the somatic rubber hand illusion, the study recorded high-density EEG during self-touch to determine individual peak frequencies. Computational and statistical analyses demonstrate that beta-band (13–30 Hz) oscillations in the primary somatosensory and posterior parietal cortices, rather than alpha, constrain the temporal binding window of tactile and proprioceptive signals. Lower individual beta frequencies were significantly predictive of wider somatosensory temporal windows and reduced sensitivity to somatosensory asynchrony, suggesting that beta oscillations serve as a frequency-specific gating mechanism for integrating non-visual bodily signals into a coherent sense of self.
papers.authors: Mariano D'Angelo, Renzo C. Lanfranco, Marie Chancel, H. Henrik Ehrsson

papers.title: Parietal alpha frequency shapes own-body perception by modulating the temporal integration of bodily signals
papers.abstract: The study explores the neurophysiological constraints on the temporal integration of visual and tactile signals that generate the experience of body ownership. By combining EEG with psychophysical measurements during the rubber hand illusion, the authors show that individual alpha peak frequency (APF) in the posterior parietal cortex correlates with the width of the temporal binding window (TBW). Using a Bayesian causal inference model, it is demonstrated that faster alpha rhythms facilitate narrower TBWs and more precise discrimination of visuotactile synchrony, which in turn modulates the likelihood of inferring a common cause for multisensory bodily signals. These findings establish that parietal alpha oscillations act as a temporal sampling mechanism determining the resolution of the multisensory bodily self.
papers.authors: Mariano D'Angelo, Renzo C. Lanfranco, Marie Chancel, H. Henrik Ehrsson

papers.title: Conscious awareness, sensory integration, and evidence accumulation in bodily self-perception
papers.abstract: This paper investigates the relationship between multisensory integration and conscious access in the context of the bodily self. Utilizing a masked-priming version of the rubber hand illusion and a drift-diffusion model (DDM) of evidence accumulation, the research demonstrates that conscious awareness of multisensory stimuli is a requisite for the elicitation of body ownership. The results show that multisensory congruency significantly increases the drift rate, accelerating the accumulation of sensory evidence toward a conscious threshold. These findings suggest that body ownership perception is not a pre-conscious process but rather an emergent property where multisensory integration and conscious awareness are intrinsically coupled, supporting a model where the bodily self is a constant presence in conscious experience.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS)
papers.authors: Renzo C. Lanfranco, Sucharit Katyal, August Hägerdal, Xiaole Luan, Victoria Nos, H. Henrik Ehrsson

papers.title: Bodily disownership is associated with self-concept fragmentation
papers.abstract: This study examines the hypothesis that the pre-reflective multisensory representation of the bodily self provides a structural scaffold for the narrative self-concept. Through a series of experiments using a body-swap illusion to induce a sense of disownership of the participant's own physical body, the researchers quantified changes in self-concept clarity and semantic self-association coherence. The data reveal that inducing bodily disownership leads to a significant reduction in the perceived stability and consistency of personality traits and self-descriptors. Quantitative psychometric analysis suggests that disruptions in the physical sense of ownership impair the integrity of the psychological self, indicating that the bodily self is fundamental for maintaining a unified and non-fragmented self-concept.
papers.authors: Pawel Tacikowski, H. Henrik Ehrsson

papers.title: Feeling pain from a rubber hand: Nociceptive drift in the rubber hand illusion
papers.abstract: This research demonstrates the dynamic remapping of nociceptive space during the rubber hand illusion. The authors describe a novel phenomenon termed 'nociceptive drift,' where painful thermal stimuli delivered to the participant's physical hand are perceived as originating from a rubber hand that has been perceptually integrated into the bodily self. Experimental results indicate that this spatial shift of pain perception occurs specifically during synchronous multisensory stimulation and is positively correlated with the subjective magnitude of hand ownership. The findings suggest that the brain's internal representation of the body's safety margins and the localization of nociceptive signals are updated to include external objects that are successfully incorporated into the multisensory body representation.
papers.authors: Sara Coppi, Karin B. Jensen, H. Henrik Ehrsson

E236.name: Charles Spence
E236.bio: Spence heads the Crossmodal Research Laboratory at the University of Oxford, investigating how the human brain integrates information across various sensory modalities to form perceptual experiences. Their research utilizes psychophysical methodologies to explore the role of attention in multisensory processing, including a study on how auditory cues modulate the perceived freshness of food that received an Ig Nobel Prize. Spence’s current work focuses on gastrophysics—the science of multisensory food design—and the application of crossmodal insights to human-computer interaction, automotive safety signals, and environmental well-being through "sensehacking."
E236.research_direction: Dr. Spence's recent work explores the psychological mechanisms of multisensory perception, bridging crossmodal audiovisual mapping, food psychology, and human-computer interaction. They have recently been investigating how low-level acoustic features—such as timbre and spectrotemporal evolution—drive cross-cultural associations between complex music and abstract visual imagery or representational concepts using psychophysical matching tasks. In the culinary domain, their recent work explores the intersection of food and emerging technologies by probing "visual hunger" in response to AI-generated versus authentic food photography, alongside modeling the behavioral determinants of user trust in AI-assisted cooking systems. Furthermore, they are investigating the broader sociological dimensions of taste, utilizing structured psychometric tasting sessions to examine how demographic factors influence the perception and acceptance of intercultural fusion cuisine.

papers.title: Intercultural Dialogue Begins at the Dining Table: A Unilateral Kosovo Perspective on Turkish–Kosovar Fusion Cuisine
papers.abstract: This research investigates the psychological and sociological dimensions of fusion cuisine within the framework of gastrodiplomacy, specifically analyzing Turkish-Kosovar culinary integration. Through a series of structured tasting sessions conducted in Prizren and Pristina involving 451 participants, the study utilized psychometric questionnaires with 5-point Likert-type scales to evaluate preferences and metaphorical conceptualizations of fusion dishes.
