Quantitative analysis revealed that the acceptance of intercultural culinary fusion is significantly moderated by demographic factors, indicating that successful gastrodiplomatic initiatives must account for group-specific variability in the perception of culinary 'otherness' and the dialectical processes of cultural assimilation.
papers.authors: Ceyhun Uçuk, Çağın Çevik, Onurcan Arman, Charles Spence

papers.title: When and Why Do Users Trust AI in the Kitchen? A Hybrid Modelling Approach to the Adoption of AI-Assisted Cooking
papers.abstract: This study evaluates the determinants of trust and adoption of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in domestic culinary contexts using a hybrid modeling approach that integrates Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM) and a Zero-Inflated Poisson Regression Mixture Model. Based on data from 380 UK participants, the model identifies two distinct latent classes: 'Engagers' and 'Avoiders'. Trust is established as the critical predictor of adoption intention, significantly influenced by perceived accuracy, general attitudes toward AI, and AI anxiety. Behavioral analysis demonstrates that AI adoption is highly context-dependent, with significantly higher acceptance for analytical, resource-optimizing tasks (e.g., utilizing leftover ingredients) compared to socially-situated culinary activities.
papers.authors: Giovanbattista Califano, Tianyi Zhang, Charles Spence

papers.title: Exploring auditory morphodynamics: Audiovisual associations in sound-based music
papers.abstract: This investigation explores the perceptual mechanisms underlying crossmodal associations between abstract visual imagery and contemporary sound-based music, such as spectralism and electronic-glitch music. In an online psychophysical procedure (N=152), participants matched six musical excerpts to ad hoc generated abstract black-and-white images. Statistical analysis showed high inter-subject consistency, suggesting that these associations are mediated by a shared set of implicit perceptual criteria rooted in Gestalt and morphodynamic features. Factors such as smoothness, continuity, numericity, symmetry, and spectrotemporal evolution were identified as primary drivers of these correspondences, supporting a model where crossmodal associations in experimental music are driven by low-level isomorphic features rather than high-level semantic associations.
papers.authors: Riccardo Wanke, Alessandro Ansani, Nicola Di Stefano, Charles Spence

papers.title: Audiovisual associations in Saint-Saëns' Carnival of the Animals: A cross-cultural investigation on the role of timbre
papers.abstract: This cross-cultural empirical study examines how timbral characteristics influence the matching of complex musical stimuli to representational concepts, specifically using movements from Saint-Saëns' 'The Carnival of the Animals'. The researchers assessed whether participants from diverse cultural backgrounds consistently associate specific instruments and their acoustic properties (e.g., spectral centroid and temporal envelope) with particular animal subjects. The findings demonstrate that timbral cues provide critical crossmodal information that facilitates the recognition and categorization of representational musical themes, indicating that timbre serves as a primary mediator in the formation of complex multisensory associations and the cross-cultural invariance of representational music perception.
papers.authors: Nicola Di Stefano, Alessandro Ansani, Andrea Schiavio, Suvi Saarikallio, Charles Spence

papers.title: Assessing the visual appeal of real/AI-generated food images
papers.abstract: This paper presents two experiments investigating human discrimination and preference for AI-generated (DALL-E 3) versus authentic food photography across a continuum of food processing levels. Results indicate that while participants can relatively easily identify AI-generated images of ultra-processed foods, they consistently rate AI-generated visuals as significantly more appetizing than real photographs when the image source is undisclosed. This preference is driven by AI-driven optimization of features like symmetry, glossiness, and perceived energy density. Crucially, the disclosure of an image's AI origin attenuates its perceived appeal, highlighting a 'trust paradox' in digital food marketing. The study discusses these findings in relation to 'visual hunger' and its potential impact on consumer expectations and sustainability efforts.
papers.authors: Giovanbattista Califano, Charles Spence

E238.name: Monica Gori
E238.bio: Monica Gori is a Senior Scientist and Principal Investigator of the Unit for Visually Impaired People (U-VIP) at the Istituto Italiano di Tecnologia. Gori’s research integrates psychophysics, computational modeling, and engineering to investigate the development of multisensory integration and spatial cognition in sighted and visually impaired individuals. Gori formulated the 'cross-sensory calibration' hypothesis, which proposes that vision is used to calibrate other senses like hearing and touch for spatial tasks. Their work has led to the development of assistive technologies, including the ABBI (Audio Bracelet for Blind Interaction), and has been supported by an ERC Starting Grant (MySpace) and ERC Proof of Concept grant.
E238.research_direction: Dr. Gori has recently been investigating multisensory integration, focusing specifically on how early visual experience scaffolds the spatial and temporal calibration of the other senses. Their recent work explores these developmental trajectories by comparing sighted and congenitally blind individuals across a variety of psychophysical and neurocomputational paradigms, from audio-tactile spatial localization to the assessment of temporal integration windows. Beyond probing how the brain constructs cross-modal maps without sight, they are also examining how visually impaired children develop interceptive motor skills when relying entirely on compensatory auditory and tactile motion cues. Within typical visual processing, they are studying serial dependence in time perception, using interval reproduction and discrimination tasks to determine whether temporal perceptual biases are driven by task-specific mechanisms or generalized working memory. Furthermore, Dr. Gori translates this sensory research into applied assistive technology, developing and evaluating AI-powered smart canes equipped with vision-language models and haptic feedback to enhance spatial awareness and autonomous navigation for blind users.

papers.title: Space Impacts Temporal Processing via a Visual-Dependent Spatially Organized Neural Architecture
papers.abstract: The brain's ability to establish temporal relationships between multisensory stimuli is challenged by asynchronies, necessitating a degree of tolerance to form coherent representations. Within the framework of implicit causal inference, this study hypothesizes that spatial parameters modulate temporal resolution, as stimuli sharing a common spatial origin are more likely to be merged. Psychophysical data from sighted and congenitally blind participants demonstrate that sighted individuals show increased temporal tolerance (wider windows of asynchrony) for auditory-tactile stimuli in somatotopic or spatiotopic congruence, a phenomenon notably absent in blind individuals. A bioinspired neurocomputational model suggests that this interaction is mediated by a spatially organized synaptic architecture whose development is contingent upon visual experience, indicating that without vision, spatial alignment is not conceptualized as a prior for temporal processing.
papers.authors: Maria Bianca Amadeo, Cristiano Cuppini, Alessia Tonelli, Carolina Tammurello, Walter Setti, Claudio Campus, Sabrina Signorini, Elena Cocchi, Margherita Bonino, Francesca Tinelli, Paola Camicione, Massimiliano Serafino, Monica Gori

papers.title: The Development of Audio-Tactile Spatial Integration: Unraveling Vision's Contribution
papers.abstract: While vision is traditionally viewed as the dominant sense for spatial perception, its role in calibrating the refinement of other modalities remains unclear. This study examines the developmental trajectory of audio-tactile spatial integration in sighted and blind children using a localization task. In sighted subjects, tactile spatial precision stabilizes earlier than auditory precision, with statistically optimal bimodal integration (aligning with Maximum Likelihood Estimation predictions) emerging only in late childhood (after 12 years of age). In contrast, blind children exhibit superior unimodal sensory precision from an early age but show minimal developmental improvement in multisensory integration. These findings suggest that optimal cross-modal spatial map construction requires a late developmental window and is critically dependent on visual experience to scaffold the integration process.
papers.authors: Alessia Tonelli, Irene Senna, Maria Bianca Amadeo, Walter Setti, Nicola Domenici, Sabrina Signorini, Elena Cocchi, Giuseppina Giammari, Sandra Strazzer, Francesca Tinelli, Paola Camicione, Massimiliano Serafino, Monica Gori

papers.title: The study of multisensory interception for interaction with objects and others in visually impaired children
papers.abstract: Interception involves goal-directed motor actions to interact with moving objects and serves as a vital bridge between motor coordination and social engagement. In pediatric development, these skills facilitate environmental exploration and social play, but in children with visual impairments (VI), the lack of visual motion cues disrupts this developmental cascade. This review synthesizes findings on interceptive skills across typical and atypical development, discussing how alternative sensory pathways (auditory and tactile) may compensate for visual loss. The authors identify significant limitations in current literature, such as low ecological validity and a lack of longitudinal modeling, and propose future research directions involving immersive virtual reality and multisensory training to support motor and social rehabilitation in the VI population.
papers.authors: Tommaso Bartolini, Martina Riberto, Helene Vitali, Mark T. Wallace, Monica Gori

papers.title: SnapStick: Merging AI and Accessibility to Enhance Navigation for Blind Users
papers.abstract: Effective navigational aids for the blind must provide detailed environmental awareness while maintaining low cognitive load. SnapStick is an assistive system that integrates a smart cane, bone-conduction audio, and a mobile application utilizing the Florence-2 Vision-Language Model (VLM). The platform performs on-device real-time scene narration, semantic object recognition, text-to-speech reading, and bus route identification. Evaluation by blind participants using the System Usability Scale (SUS) revealed high satisfaction and 94% task accuracy. The findings demonstrate that fusing advanced computer vision models with purpose-driven haptic and auditory interfaces can significantly enhance autonomous navigation, safety, and environmental understanding for individuals with visual impairments.
papers.authors: Shehzaib Shafique, Gian Luca Bailo, Silvia Zanchi, Mattia Barbieri, Walter Setti, Giulio Sciortino, Carlos Beltran, Alice De Luca, Alessio Del Bue, Monica Gori

papers.title: Exploring the role of serial dependence in visual time perception
papers.abstract: Serial dependence is an active perceptual bias that maintains continuity by merging current sensory input with information from the recent past. While established in features like orientation and numerosity, its role in temporal processing is less understood. This study evaluated serial dependence in visual timing using temporal interval duration discrimination and reproduction tasks. Significant attractive serial biases were observed in both tasks, confirming that recent history influences time perception. However, the lack of correlation between individual bias magnitudes across tasks and the absence of a relationship with working memory capacity (Corsi test scores) suggest that serial dependence in the temporal domain is mediated by task-specific perceptual mechanisms rather than a centralized mnemonic buffer.
papers.authors: Jessica Bertolasi, Davide Esposito, Anna Vitale, Monica Gori

E239.name: Mark Wallace
E239.department: Department of Psychology; Department of Hearing and Speech Sciences
E239.bio: Mark T. Wallace is a neuroscientist and the Louise B. McGavock Chair of Neuroscience at Vanderbilt University, where they investigate how the brain synthesizes information across sensory modalities such as vision, hearing, and touch. Wallace’s research employs a multidisciplinary approach involving animal neurophysiology, human psychophysics, and neuroimaging techniques like fMRI and EEG to map the neural substrates of multisensory processing. Their work focuses on the development and plasticity of multisensory circuits and how these processes are altered in clinical conditions, including autism spectrum disorder and schizophrenia. Wallace has characterized the multisensory temporal binding window and its role in shaping perception and behavior across the lifespan.
E239.research_direction: Dr. Wallace has recently been exploring the mechanisms of sensory and multisensory processing, with a primary clinical focus on autism spectrum disorder. Their human research employs psychophysics and EEG—such as free-response audiovisual localization and mismatch negativity oddball paradigms—to investigate spatial integration and sensory prediction in autistic individuals, while also developing methodological frameworks to improve the inclusion of underrepresented, high-support-needs populations in sensory literature. Beyond clinical cohorts, they are investigating the low-level psychophysical determinants of auditory motion perception in macaque models to test whether auditory motion tracking relies on spatial displacement or continuous velocity cues. Additionally, their recent basic research utilizes transgenic mouse models to characterize the sensorimotor and behavioral phenotypes associated with specific, autism-linked genetic mutations affecting dopaminergic pathways.

papers.title: Intact Audiovisual Spatial Integration in Autistic Children
papers.abstract: This empirical study investigates multisensory spatial processing in autistic children (ages 7-17) using a free-response audiovisual localization task. Despite prior evidence of temporal binding window alterations in ASD, results indicated that autistic and non-autistic children exhibit similar accuracy and integration gains in the spatial domain. Exploratory cluster analyses further delineated relationships between clinical traits—such as motor functioning and social communication—and spatial localization performance, suggesting that spatial integration remains functionally intact despite other sensory processing differences.
papers.venue: Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders
papers.authors: Sarah G. Vassall, Ingrid Shragge, Hari Srinivasan, William J. Quackenbush, Mark T. Wallace

papers.title: Recommendations for Increasing Sample Diversity in Autism Research: Lessons from Multisensory Studies
papers.abstract: This systematic review assesses the demographic composition of participants in the multisensory autism literature, specifically examining representation across the spectrum of cognitive and support needs. The analysis demonstrates a profound bias toward high-functioning, low-support-needs individuals, which limits the ecological validity and generalizability of multisensory integration findings. The authors propose a framework for methodological and recruitment adaptations aimed at including high-support-needs (HSN) individuals, emphasizing the necessity of inclusive research to better understand the mechanistic link between sensory processing and core autism features.
papers.venue: Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders
papers.authors: Sarah G. Vassall, Ingrid Shragge, Hari Srinivasan, William J. Quackenbush, Mark T. Wallace

papers.title: Minimal Differences in Auditory and Visual Oddball Tasks in Autism: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
papers.abstract: The current meta-analysis evaluated the efficacy of oddball paradigms, specifically the mismatch negativity (MMN) ERP component, in detecting differences in sensory prediction between autistic and typically developing cohorts. Through a systematic review of auditory and visual oddball studies, the authors quantified effect sizes for deviance detection across modalities. The results revealed no significant group-level differences in MMN amplitude or latency, suggesting that MMN does not reliably serve as a biomarker for prediction deficits in ASD and that observed effects may stem from individual heterogeneity.
papers.venue: Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders
papers.authors: Sarah G. Vassall, William J. Quackenbush, Mark T. Wallace

papers.title: Contribution of displacement, duration, and velocity on auditory motion direction perception in macaque monkeys
papers.abstract: The study utilizes a non-human primate model (macaque) to investigate the low-level determinants of auditory motion direction perception. By systematically varying stimulus duration, velocity, and displacement in a direction-judgment task, the researchers found that displacement cues exerted the most significant influence on motion sensitivity. These results suggest that primate auditory motion processing likely relies on a 'snapshot' mechanism—inferring motion from sequential spatial locations—rather than the continuous velocity-selective integration characteristic of the visual system.
papers.authors: Adriana M. Schoenhaut, Ramnarayan Ramachandran, Mark T. Wallace

papers.title: Sex-Specific, Intermediate Behavioral Phenotypes in Heterozygous Dopamine Transporter Mutant DAT T356M Mice
papers.abstract: This study characterizes the behavioral phenotype of mice heterozygous for the DAT T356M mutation, a de novo variant identified in individuals with autism. While homozygous mutants show profound behavioral alterations, the heterozygous mice (DAT T356M+/-) provide a model for complex polygenic inheritance. Both male and female heterozygotes displayed spontaneous hyperactivity in novel environments but retained normal habituation, presenting an intermediate phenotype that suggests a gene-dosage effect on dopaminergic-mediated locomotor control and sensorimotor behavior.
papers.authors: E. Harris, K. C. Paffenroth, A. A. Tienda, F. E. Harrison, Mark T. Wallace

E240.name: Jean Vroomen
E240.bio: Jean Vroomen is a Professor and Head of the Department of Cognitive Neuropsychology at Tilburg University. Vroomen's research focuses on multisensory perception, specifically regarding the integration of auditory and visual signals during speech processing and temporal recalibration. Utilizing behavioral experiments and electroencephalography (EEG), they investigate these mechanisms across various populations, including infants, children, and clinical groups such as individuals with autism or schizophrenia. Vroomen’s work also examines the neural correlates of affective salience and the electrophysiological markers of predictive coding in sensory integration.
E240.research_direction: Dr. Vroomen’s recent work explores the behavioral and neural mechanisms underlying multisensory integration and perceptual adaptation, with a strong focus on how auditory and visual signals combine during speech and social perception. Using behavioral paradigms and electroencephalography (EEG), they have recently been investigating how visual cues, such as a speaker's head orientation or lip movements, calibrate auditory speech processing, especially when speech sounds are acoustically distorted or phonetically ambiguous. Beyond speech perception, their research examines holistic multimodal social processing, asking how distinct sensory streams—like facial shape, vocal pitch, and linguistic content—interact to shape complex subjective judgments like perceived trustworthiness. Additionally, they are applying these sensory and social paradigms to diverse developmental populations, using electrophysiological markers to investigate whether mechanisms of face processing and multisensory learning differ among typical individuals, those with dyslexia, autistic children, and children with high intellectual giftedness.

papers.title: A behavioral and electrophysiological investigation of the effect of horizontal head viewing angle on audiovisual speech integration
papers.abstract: This study examines the impact of a speaker's horizontal head orientation (ranging from 0° frontal to 100° side-back) on the behavioral and neural markers of audiovisual (AV) speech integration. Using consonant-vowel syllable identification tasks in both quiet and noisy environments, the researchers measured reaction times and event-related potentials (ERPs), specifically the N1 and P2 components. Behavioral results showed that head rotation reduces integration efficiency but does not eliminate it. Electrophysiological analysis revealed a functional dissociation between temporal and phonetic integration: visual-induced suppression of the auditory N1 (representing temporal prediction) was maximal at 45° and significantly attenuated at profile orientations, whereas suppression of the P2 component (representing phonetic integration) remained consistent across all viewing angles. These findings suggest that phonetic integration is more robust to changes in spatial perspective than temporal predictive mechanisms.
papers.authors: Jeroen J. Stekelenburg, Martijn Baart, Jean Vroomen

papers.title: Electrophysiological correlates of selective speech adaptation
papers.abstract: Selective speech adaptation (SSA) refers to the phenomenon where prolonged exposure to a specific phoneme temporarily decreases sensitivity to that sound, biasing the perception of ambiguous stimuli toward the unexposed category. This study utilized electroencephalography (EEG) to delineate the cortical time-course of SSA. Participants were adapted to Dutch vowels /e/ or /ø/ and then classified tokens from an ambiguous continuum. Behavioral data showed strong adaptation effects (>90% shift). Multi-variate pattern analysis (MVPA) and cluster-based permutations identified late differential EEG responses beginning approximately 575 ms post-stimulus onset. These deviations were localized to the left superior temporal gyrus (STG), indicating that the perceptual resolution of phonetic ambiguity driven by adaptation involves higher-order cortical processing stages rather than early, pre-attentive sensory gating.
papers.authors: Jeroen J. Stekelenburg, Jakob Limpens, Martijn Baart, Jean Vroomen

papers.title: Perceptual adaptation to noise vocoded speech by lipread information: No difference between dyslexic and typical readers
papers.abstract: The study investigates whether adults with developmental dyslexia (DD) exhibit deficits in lipread-induced perceptual adaptation to acoustically distorted speech. Participants were trained on Dutch words processed via six-channel noise-vocoding while seeing the speaker's articulatory movements (audiovisual) or a still face (auditory-only). Results indicated a significant 'lipread boost' in word recognition accuracy for both groups. Crucially, as listeners adapted to the vocoded signal over time, the rate and magnitude of adaptation in the auditory-only test blocks did not differ between dyslexic and typical readers. These findings challenge the hypothesis that dyslexia is characterized by a generalized failure in multisensory perceptual learning and suggest that the mechanisms for utilizing visual speech to recalibrate auditory representations remain intact in this population.
papers.authors: Faezeh Pour Hashemi, Martijn Baart, Jean Vroomen

papers.title: The multimodal trust effects of face, voice, and sentence content
papers.abstract: This research explores how social cues from multiple modalities—vocal pitch, facial width-to-height ratio (fWHR), and linguistic content—interact to shape perceived trustworthiness. Female participants rated the trust of voices speaking neutral or romantic sentences while being exposed to faces where fWHR was systematically manipulated. The findings show that sentence content is a dominant predictor of trust that extends into the multimodal domain. Furthermore, mean vocal pitch and facial fWHR served as significant indicators of trust, with cross-modal interactions demonstrating that task-irrelevant visual features (face shape) influence the evaluation of auditory stimuli (voice trust). This suggests that trust assimilation is a holistic process where sensory cues are integrated across channels even when some information is non-pertinent to the immediate task.
papers.authors: Isar Syed, Martijn Baart, Jean Vroomen

papers.title: Electrophysiological markers for social processing in early childhood in autism and intellectual giftedness
papers.abstract: This paper investigates neural markers of social cognition in children, specifically contrasting populations with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) and High Intellectual Potential (HIP). The study focuses on the N170 event-related potential (ERP), a well-established marker for face processing and social perception. By comparing the latency and amplitude of the N170 in response to social and non-social stimuli, the researchers evaluate its potential as a differential diagnostic tool. The results aim to clarify whether atypicalities in social ERP components are specific to autistic traits or if they manifest similarly in children with exceptional cognitive abilities who may exhibit social-behavioral overlaps. This work provides insight into the neurophysiological boundaries between different developmental trajectories in social information processing.
papers.authors: S. Kluin, T. van Laarhoven, M. I. van den Heuvel, J. Vroomen

E241.name: Fiona Newell
E241.department: School of Psychology and Trinity College Institute of Neuroscience (TCIN)
E241.bio: Newell is a Professor of Experimental Psychology at Trinity College Dublin whose research explores the behavioral and neural principles of multisensory integration. They examine how the human brain processes information from sensory modalities, such as vision, audition, and haptics, to facilitate object recognition, scene perception, and social interactions. Using psychophysical experiments and neuroimaging techniques including fMRI and EEG, Newell investigates perceptual changes across the lifespan and the mechanisms underlying conditions like synaesthesia. Their recent projects leverage virtual reality and neuroaesthetics to study human preferences and develop interventions for age-related cognitive decline.
E241.research_direction: Dr. Newell has recently been investigating multisensory integration, spatial perception, and object categorization across diverse developmental and aging populations. Their recent work explores the temporal precision of audio-visual binding in older adults using the Sound-Induced Flash Illusion, examining how this sensory efficiency is modulated by aging trajectories, sex differences, and nutritional status. They are also studying the neural and behavioral mechanisms of object recognition, using fMRI to map how the brain discriminates object authenticity based on material properties, and testing whether bimodal spatial cues aid in learning novel shape categories. Additionally, they are investigating the developmental dependencies of spatial processing by comparing susceptibility to haptic and visual illusions in sighted versus congenitally blind children to determine whether these amodal mechanisms require early visual experience.

papers.title: Visual categorisation of images of familiar objects based on their authenticity: an fMRI study
papers.abstract: This neuroimaging study investigates the cortical mechanisms underlying the discrimination of object authenticity (real vs. fake/plastic) using fMRI. Participants categorized images of familiar objects where authenticity was defined by subtle surface material properties. Behaviorally, subjects demonstrated high precision in identifying real versus plastic items. Functional imaging data revealed that images of real objects elicited significantly greater BOLD responses in the paracentral lobule, the left pre/postcentral gyrus, and the mid-cingulate cortex compared to their fake counterparts. These results suggest that the perception of object authenticity involves the recruitment of a distributed network that integrates visual-perceptual features with sensorimotor and semantic knowledge, rather than being restricted to early stages of the ventral visual stream.
papers.authors: Grace A. Gabriel, Cristina Simões-Franklin, Georgia O'Callaghan, John Stapleton, Fiona N. Newell

papers.title: Generalisation to novel exemplars of learned shape categories based on visual and auditory spatial cues does not benefit from multisensory information
papers.abstract: This study examines whether multisensory (audio-visual) information enhances the formation and generalization of novel object categories. In two experiments, participants learned to categorize novel objects defined by spatial parameters using visual-only (geometric shape), auditory-only (spatially defined soundscapes), or bimodal cues. While categorization successfully generalized to novel exemplars across all learning modalities, there was no evidence of a multisensory enhancement effect; bimodal performance did not significantly exceed that of the most reliable unimodal condition. The findings suggest that categorical representations are primarily driven by the most informative single sensory modality rather than a synergistic integration of redundant spatial cues, providing critical constraints on models of multisensory category learning.
papers.authors: Alan O'Dowd, Rebecca J. Hirst, Martina A. Seveso, Eimear M. McKenna, Fiona N. Newell

papers.title: EXPRESS: Susceptibility to spatial illusions does not depend on visual experience: evidence from sighted and blind children
papers.abstract: This research investigates the ontogeny of visuo-spatial illusions by comparing sighted children with congenitally blind children. Using a battery of illusions (including extent and size variants) explored through visual, haptic, and bimodal modalities, the study assessed whether susceptibility is a product of learned environmental regularities or innate neural mechanisms. Sighted children showed susceptibility across modalities and ages. Critically, congenitally blind children were also susceptible to illusions of extent via haptic exploration, indicating that early visual experience is not a requisite for these illusory spatial perceptions. The results support the existence of amodal, potentially innate spatial processing mechanisms in 'visual' brain regions that operate independently of prior visual input.
papers.authors: Sarah Cooney, Corinne A. Holmes, Giulia Cappagli, Elena Cocchi, Monica Gori, Fiona N. Newell

papers.title: Nutrition is associated with differences in multisensory integration in healthy older adults
papers.abstract: Utilizing data from a large cohort (N = 2,693) of older adults from The Irish Longitudinal Study on Ageing (TILDA), this study investigates the association between habitual diet and the temporal precision of multisensory integration. Precision was quantified using the Sound-Induced Flash Illusion (SIFI) across multiple stimulus onset asynchronies (SOAs). Participants with higher daily consumption of fruit and vegetables exhibited significantly greater temporal precision (lower SIFI susceptibility) at longer SOAs. In contrast, high intake of products high in fat, sugar, and salt (FSS) was associated with reduced temporal precision. These findings demonstrate that nutritional status is linked to low-level neuro-perceptual efficiency, suggesting a sensory-level mechanism for the protective effects of diet on cognitive aging.
papers.authors: Alan O'Dowd, Deirdre M. A. O'Connor, Rebecca J. Hirst, Annalisa Setti, Rose Anne Kenny, Fiona N. Newell

papers.title: Is a sex difference in audio-visual temporal precision consistent across age groups? An update on Hernández et al. (2019)
papers.abstract: This study re-evaluates sex differences in the temporal binding window of multisensory integration across the lifespan in a large sample (N = 3,479) of older adults. Performance on the Sound-Induced Flash Illusion (SIFI) was analyzed to measure audio-visual temporal precision. Results confirmed that females generally show higher precision at short SOAs (70 ms). However, at longer SOAs (150 ms and 230 ms), a significant age-by-sex interaction revealed that younger-old females (ages 50–64) were more susceptible to the illusion than age-matched males, a difference that disappeared in older cohorts. These results indicate that sex and age interact non-linearly to influence multisensory temporal processing, necessitating more nuanced models of sensory aging.
papers.authors: Alan O'Dowd, Rebecca J. Hirst, Annalisa Setti, Rose Anne Kenny, Fiona N. Newell

E242.name: Virginie van Wassenhove
E242.bio: Van Wassenhove is a Director of Research at CEA and heads the Cognition & Brain Dynamics lab within the Cognitive Neuroimaging Unit at NeuroSpin. Their research investigates the neurobiological underpinnings of temporal cognition and multisensory integration, focusing on how the brain encodes durations and sequences to construct experiences of time. Van Wassenhove utilizes neuroimaging techniques, including magnetoencephalography (MEG) and electroencephalography (EEG), to analyze the role of neural oscillations in predictive coding and information parsing. Their work characterizes the influence of alpha oscillations on perceptual priors and explores the impact of environmental factors, such as isolation, on subjective temporal maps. Current investigations integrate behavioral psychophysics with computational models to define the functional brain dynamics involved in timing and postdiction.
E242.research_direction: Dr. van Wassenhove's recent work explores the neurocognitive and psychological mechanisms underlying our subjective experience of time. Using neuroimaging techniques like MEG and EEG, they have recently been investigating how oscillatory dynamics—particularly alpha-band power—index temporal working memory load and support the automatic, unattended encoding of duration. Their research also tests how psychological time intersects with sensory processing, utilizing neural decoding and cognitive modeling in temporal oddball paradigms to examine whether an internal clock is driven by sensory features like motion and stimulus novelty. Broadening into behavioral and ecological domains, they are investigating the phenomenological distinction between perceived duration and the felt passage or "speed" of time, testing how cognitive load, virtual and real-world contexts, and visual event density differentially distort these separate facets of temporal experience.

papers.title: Alpha power indexes working memory load for durations
papers.abstract: This magnetoencephalography (MEG) study investigates the neural signatures of temporal working memory by orthogonalizing the number of discrete durations (item load) from the total elapsed sequence duration. The researchers demonstrate that temporal reproduction precision is primarily constrained by item load rather than absolute duration, with parieto-occipital alpha (7–13 Hz) and beta (15–30 Hz) oscillatory power providing a decodable index of working memory maintenance. Specifically, increased alpha power in parieto-occipital regions predicted greater precision in subsequent temporal reproduction, supporting the theory that alpha oscillations serve as a universal, domain-general mechanism for indexing working memory load, extending even to abstract, non-spatial temporal information.
papers.authors: Sophie K. Herbst, Izem Mangione, Charbel-Raphaël Segerie, Richard Höchenberger, Tadeusz Kononowicz, Alexandre Gramfort, Virginie van Wassenhove

papers.title: Spontaneous oscillatory activity in episodic timing: an EEG replication study and its limitations
papers.abstract: This EEG investigation extends previous findings regarding the role of spontaneous alpha oscillations in episodic timing—the automatic, unattended encoding of temporal intervals. Utilizing a retrospective duration estimation paradigm with unexpected probes, the study confirms a linear relationship between the relative duration of alpha bursts during quiet wakefulness and subjective temporal reports. However, the robustness of this neural marker is significantly modulated by experimental context; the predictive link is attenuated by mental fatigue and the adoption of endogenous temporal expectation strategies. Furthermore, the inclusion of immersive virtual reality environments was found to disrupt the correlation between alpha dynamics and retrospective timing, suggesting that episodic timing mechanisms are highly sensitive to contextual shifts and strategic monitoring.
papers.authors: Raphaël Bordas, Virginie van Wassenhove

papers.title: Separating sensory from timing processes: a cognitive encoding and neural decoding approach
papers.abstract: Applying an information-theoretic framework to temporal cognition, this study utilizes EEG, ACT-R cognitive modeling, and machine-learning-based neural decoding to test whether psychological time reflects sensory information flow. Through a temporal oddball paradigm, the authors investigate how sensory adaptation, novelty, and motion influence the rate of a hypothetical internal clock. The findings demonstrate that subjective timing performance is contingent upon both intrinsic temporal mechanisms and non-temporal sensory factors, where 'clock speed' effectively maps onto the magnitude of cortical sensory processing. Notably, motion stimuli were shown to tune the internal clock rate, providing a computational link between sensory decoding magnitude and perceived duration distortions.
papers.authors: Christina Yi Jin, Anna Razafindrahaba, Raphaël Bordas, Virginie van Wassenhove

papers.title: Distinctive features of experiential time: Duration, speed and event density
papers.abstract: This study dissociates two fundamental facets of temporal experience—subjective duration and the felt passage of time—by manipulating event density within naturalistic video sequences during a temporal bisection task. Quantitative results reveal that increased event density concurrently induces a subjective dilation of duration and an acceleration of the perceived passage of time. Crucially, participants exhibited significantly faster reaction times when judging the speed of time compared to estimating its duration. These diverging effects suggest that while duration estimation may rely on event-based accumulation, the felt passage of time is scaled by the rate of change in the environment, indicating the operation of discrete neurocognitive mechanisms for different experiential temporalities.
papers.authors: Marianna Lamprou-Kokolaki, Yvan Nédélec, Simon Lhuillier, Virginie van Wassenhove

papers.title: Cognitive effects on experienced duration and speed of time, prospectively, retrospectively, in and out of lockdown
papers.abstract: Exploiting an online dataset collected during the COVID-19 pandemic, this research examines the impact of parametric cognitive load (manipulated via 1-back and 3-back tasks) on prospective and retrospective temporal judgments. The analysis identifies a dissociation between duration estimation and the felt speed of time, noting that increased cognitive demand differentially modulates these metrics depending on whether attention is explicitly directed toward time (prospective) or diverted (retrospective). Furthermore, social isolation during lockdown selectively altered temporal phenomenology, and the study identifies a consistent inverse relationship where shorter perceived intervals are associated with an accelerated felt passage of time, highlighting the complex interplay between working memory capacity and subjective temporal experience in ecological settings.
papers.authors: Cyril Nicolaï, Maximilien Chaumon, Virginie van Wassenhove

E243.name: David Burr
E243.department: Department of Neuroscience, Psychology, Drug Research and Child Health
E243.bio: David Burr is Professor Emeritus of Physiological Psychology at the University of Florence, focusing on human vision and multisensory neuroscience. Burr's research investigates visual stability, specifically regarding saccadic suppression and the compression of space and time during eye movements. Burr also identified a specialized 'number sense' for non-symbolic numerosity perception across various sensory modalities and actions. Their work utilizes Bayesian frameworks to model perceptual processes, including theories on the 'hypo-priors' characteristic of autistic perception.
E243.research_direction: Dr. Burr's recent work explores how the visual system adaptively integrates information across space and time to optimize perception amidst sensory noise. They have recently been investigating visual crowding in peripheral vision, testing whether phenomena like color and orientation crowding function not as low-level resolution bottlenecks, but as flexible Bayesian integration processes that can occasionally improve perceptual precision. Their recent research also examines temporal continuity and structure in vision, exploring the mechanisms of serial dependence and utilizing frequency-tagged pupillometry to track how the visual system implicitly learns temporal statistical regularities without conscious awareness. Furthermore, they are actively studying the mechanisms underlying the Approximate Number System, employing dual-task psychophysics to disentangle whether numerosity biases, such as the connectedness illusion, are driven by fundamental perceptual grouping or by covert attentional capture.

papers.title: Pupillometric signature of implicit learning of statistical regularities
papers.abstract: This study employs a frequency-tagging pupillometric paradigm to identify biomarkers of implicit statistical learning involving temporal regularities in sequential arrays. Participants were exposed to numerosity-based pairings that occurred at a specific repetition frequency (1 Hz) while performing a task that diverted attention from the numerical features. Despite lack of conscious awareness of the underlying structure, pupillary responses significantly synchronized with the repetition frequency within three minutes of exposure. Findings indicate that the pupil responds to global statistical properties (numerosity or digit identity) rather than local features, suggesting that implicit learning mechanisms can extract and track higher-order environmental structure independently of directed attention.
papers.authors: Paola Binda, Chiara Terzo, Marco Turi, David C. Burr

papers.title: Reply to: Failure to replicate a superiority effect in crowding
papers.abstract: In this reply to Ozkirli et al. (2025), the authors defend their discovery of a 'superiority effect' in crowding, where judgements of target attributes (such as orientation) can become more precise in the presence of similar flankers. They argue that the failure to replicate this effect likely stems from differences in experimental parameters or the sensitivity of the measurement techniques employed. The paper reinforces the conceptual model that crowding is not merely a low-level resolution bottleneck but may result from an active, flexible integration process that optimizes visual recognition by pooling redundant signals from targets and flankers when they are highly consistent.
papers.authors: Guido Marco Cicchini, Giovanni D'Errico, David Charles Burr

papers.title: Color crowding considered as adaptive spatial integration
papers.abstract: The study investigates whether color crowding in peripheral vision follows Bayesian principles of flexible integration. Participants tracked the perceived hue of targets flanked by radially arranged distractors. Results demonstrate that target hues were strongly biased toward those of the flankers, particularly for targets with low purity (low reliability). Counterintuitively, the presence of identical flankers significantly reduced just-noticeable differences (JNDs) compared to unflanked conditions, indicating a flanker-induced gain in precision. These findings support the theory that crowding arises from an adaptive system that optimally integrates peripheral information to improve perceptual reliability, rather than reflecting a fundamental failure of object recognition.
papers.authors: Guido Marco Cicchini, Giovanni D'Errico, David C. Burr

papers.title: Serial Dependence in Perception
papers.abstract: This comprehensive review synthesizes recent research on serial dependence—the assimilative bias where current perceptual judgments are attracted toward recent stimuli. The authors argue that this phenomenon is a hallmark of generative perception, which stabilizes visual experience over time amidst inherent sensory noise and ambiguity. Drawing on Bayesian inference and predictive coding frameworks, the paper details how high-level cortical priors incorporate past experience and feed back to modulate early sensory areas. The review maps the manifestation of serial dependence across various domains, including orientation, numerosity, and face gender, highlighting its role in maintaining perceptual continuity and processing efficiency.
papers.authors: Guido Marco Cicchini, Kyriaki Mikellidou, David Charles Burr

papers.title: Perceptual grouping, not covert attention, drives the connectedness effect in the ANS
papers.abstract: The 'connectedness illusion'—where dots joined by lines appear less numerous than isolated dots—is a cornerstone piece of evidence for the role of object segmentation in the Approximate Number System (ANS). This study tests whether the effect is caused by perceptual grouping or by connected items capturing covert attention. Participants performed a dual-task involving go/no-go target detection and numerosity estimation. While connected arrays were consistently underestimated, detection performance (reaction times and accuracy) showed no attentional bias toward the connected pairs. These findings suggest that the connectedness effect is driven by fundamental visual segmentation processes into perceptual units rather than attentional capture.
papers.authors: Antonella Pomè, Giovanni Anobile, Guido Marco Cicchini, David Burr

E244.name: John Foxe
E244.lab_name: Frederick J. and Marion A. Schindler Cognitive Neurophysiology Laboratory
E244.bio: John J. Foxe is a translational neuroscientist serving as the Chair of the Department of Neuroscience and Director of the Del Monte Institute for Neuroscience at the University of Rochester. Foxe’s research focuses on identifying endophenotypic biomarkers for neurodevelopmental and psychiatric disorders, with a primary emphasis on autism spectrum disorder and schizophrenia. Utilizing high-density electrophysiology (EEG), structural and functional neuroimaging (fMRI), and psychophysical methods, Foxe investigates how the brain processes and integrates multisensory information. Their work aims to link these neural markers to underlying genotypes to better understand the biological mechanisms of disease and inform the development of targeted therapeutic interventions.
E244.research_direction: Dr. Foxe has recently been investigating the neurophysiological and structural underpinnings of altered sensory, motor, and cognitive processing in autism. Their recent work employs a diverse methodological toolkit—including high-density EEG, fMRI, diffusion-weighted imaging, and mobile brain-body imaging (MoBI)—to map distinct neuro-behavioral dynamics across multiple modalities. Specifically, they are exploring the temporal dynamics of top-down neural feedback during visual contour integration, pre-attentive tactile temporal perception using somatosensory mismatch negativity paradigms, and the neural resource competition that occurs when balancing simultaneous locomotive and cognitive demands. Furthermore, their research investigates how autism symptom severity relates to multisensory integration during naturalistic audiovisual speech perception, while also probing foundational, in vivo differences in gray matter neurite cytoarchitecture across the brain.

papers.title: Associations between symptom severity in autism and functional neuroimaging measures of audiovisual speech perception
papers.abstract: This investigation utilized functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) to evaluate the neurophysiological associations between autism symptom severity and multisensory speech integration during naturalistic narrative perception. The researchers quantified blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) signal activity and audiovisual (AV) gain in a cohort of participants to test the hypothesis that previously identified deficits in complex social speech processing correlate with the Calibrated Symptom Severity (CSS) index derived from the ADOS. While multisensory enhancement was observed in the canonical semantic network and extralinguistic regions such as the bilateral amygdala, autistic individuals demonstrated atypical frontal activations in regions that typically show task-induced de-activation in neurotypical controls. These findings suggest that higher symptom severity is associated with altered Default Mode Network (DMN) disengagement and the recruitment of compensatory frontal circuitry to resolve social-communicative demands during continuous audiovisual streams.
papers.authors: Lars A. Ross, Victor A. Del Bene, Sophie Molholm, John J. Foxe

papers.title: A symphony of functioning: exploring the interplay of cognition, movement, and visual demands in adolescents on the autism spectrum using mobile brain-body imaging (MoBI)
papers.abstract: Employing Mobile Brain-Body Imaging (MoBI), this study characterized the neuro-behavioral dynamics of dual-tasking in adolescents on the autism spectrum. High-density electroencephalography (EEG) and 3-dimensional kinematic tracking were used to monitor event-related potentials (ERPs) and gait parameters while participants performed cognitive tasks during treadmill walking. The paradigm investigated how the introduction of locomotive demands induces competition for neural resources and affects the amplitude and latency of sensory-motor ERP components. Results indicated that maintaining task accuracy in the ASD group required a significantly more widespread reallocation of cortical resources compared to neurotypical peers. This indicates that the neural substrates for locomotive and cognitive control are more heavily interleaved in autism, such that motor processing demands significantly exacerbate the recruitment of executive control networks.
papers.authors: Paige R. Nicklas, Lisa N. Cruz, Carol Terilli, Erin K. Bojanek, Pierfilippo De Sanctis, Edward G. Freedman, Sophie Molholm, John J. Foxe

papers.title: Autism is associated with in vivo changes in gray matter neurite architecture
papers.abstract: This study leveraged Restriction Spectrum Imaging (RSI) of high-resolution diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) data from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) study to characterize gray matter neurite architecture in vivo. The researchers quantified metrics of restricted diffusion—including total neurite density (TND), restricted normalized directional diffusion (RND), and restricted normalized isotropic diffusion (RNI)—across cerebellar, limbic, and neocortical networks. Significant cytoarchitectural anomalies were localized to the cerebellum and specific cortical regions, providing in vivo evidence for the narrow cell mini-columns and variable neuron density patterns previously identified in post-mortem histology. These results suggest that RSI-derived metrics of neurite density can serve as reliable physiological biomarkers for the neurobiological phenotyping of autism.
papers.authors: Zachary P. Christensen, Edward G. Freedman, John J. Foxe

papers.title: It’s all in the timing: delayed feedback in autism may weaken predictive mechanisms during contour integration
papers.abstract: This research investigated the temporal dynamics of feedback-dependent visual processing in autism using a contour integration paradigm. High-density visual-evoked potentials (VEPs) were recorded from children with ASD and neurotypical controls to measure the "illusory contour (IC) effect," an electrophysiological component indexing top-down statistical predictions conveyed from higher-order visual areas to primary sensory cortex. While the amplitude of the IC-effect and early feedforward signals (P1 and N1) did not differ significantly between groups, the onset of the feedback-dependent IC-effect was delayed by 21 ms in the ASD group. This temporal lag indicates that feedforward afference predominates for a significantly longer duration in autism, potentially limiting the influence of top-down priors and contributing to the characteristic local-processing bias in visual perception.
papers.authors: Emily J. Knight, Ted S. Altschuler, Sophie Molholm, Jeremy W. Murphy, Edward G. Freedman, John J. Foxe

papers.title: Somatosensory temporal sensitivity in adults on the autism spectrum: A high-density electrophysiological mapping study using the mismatch negativity (MMN) sensory memory paradigm
papers.abstract: This study employed a high-density electrophysiological somatosensory mismatch negativity (sMMN) paradigm to evaluate pre-attentive sensory memory and temporal discrimination in adults on the autism spectrum. Researchers used a tactile oddball task featuring duration-based deviants to assess whether atypical somatosensory reactivity in ASD stems from foundational deficits in temporal perception. Analyses of the sMMN component and behavioral d-prime (d') scores revealed no significant differences in temporal discrimination between autistic and neurotypical groups. However, exploratory analyses identified subtle modulations in the N1 and P220 amplitudes, suggesting that while the neuro-computational mechanisms of temporal somatosensory discrimination are largely conserved, broader cortical reactivity to tactile inputs is significantly altered in autistic adults.
papers.authors: Emily L. Isenstein, Edward G. Freedman, Sophie Molholm, John J. Foxe

E245.name: Salvador Soto-Faraco
E245.department: Departament de Tecnologies de la Informació i les Comunicacions
E245.bio: Soto-Faraco is an ICREA Research Professor who heads the Multisensory Research Group at Universitat Pompeu Fabra’s Center for Brain and Cognition. Soto-Faraco's research examines the cognitive and neural principles governing how the brain integrates information across sensory modalities, including vision, audition, and somatosensation. Using a combination of psychophysics, neuroimaging techniques such as EEG and fMRI, and non-invasive brain stimulation, they investigate the interplay between top-down attention and multisensory binding. Their current work explores perception in naturalistic, real-world environments to connect laboratory-based findings with ecological validity.
E245.research_direction: Dr. Soto-Faraco has recently been investigating the mechanisms of multisensory integration and rhythmic sensory stimulation to understand how they shape foundational cognitive capacities, such as visual working memory limits and long-term episodic memory encoding. Their recent work also explores atypical sensory and social processing in autism, utilizing EEG, eye-tracking, and pupillometry to probe how autistic adults integrate naturalistic audiovisual speech cues and allocate attention toward biological motion. Additionally, they are characterizing the fine-grained temporal dynamics of spatial cognition by using single-trial EEG analyses to map how transient bursts of frontal theta and parietal alpha oscillations align with critical milestones during virtual navigation.

papers.title: Multisensory Integration of Naturalistic Speech and Gestures in Autistic Adults
papers.abstract: The presence of visual speech cues and co-speech gestures typically facilitates auditory comprehension in adverse listening conditions. This study utilized EEG and naturalistic social stimuli to reveal that while neurotypical individuals exhibit non-linear alpha-band oscillatory suppression during audiovisual integration, autistic adults display an additive neural processing pattern. Despite these divergent neural signatures, both groups achieved comparable behavioral benefits from multisensory cues in a speech-in-noise task. The findings suggest that the autistic brain utilizes alternative compensatory pathways to integrate auditory and visual linguistic information, maintaining functional parity with neurotypical individuals in real-world communicative settings.
papers.authors: Magdalena Matyjek, Sotaro Kita, Mireia Torralba Cuello, Salvador Soto-Faraco

papers.title: Preference for Social Motion in Autistic Adults
papers.abstract: Atypical social attention, specifically a reduced looking preference for biological versus geometric motion, is a proposed biomarker for autism in childhood; however, its persistence into adulthood and the underlying cognitive mechanisms remain understudied. Through a combination of gaze tracking and pupillometry, this research found that autistic adults exhibit a significantly reduced spontaneous preference for social stimuli compared to neurotypical adults, who maintain a robust social bias. Elevated pupil dilation and faster responses to social motion in the autistic group suggest higher cognitive load and physiological arousal during social processing, indicating that lifelong differences in the salience of social cues characterize the autism spectrum.
papers.authors: Magdalena Matyjek, Nico Bast, Salvador Soto-Faraco

papers.title: Single-trial characterization of frontal theta and parietal alpha oscillatory episodes during spatial navigation in humans
papers.abstract: Conventional analyses of navigation-related brain activity often rely on trial-averaged power, which can obscure the transient nature of oscillatory signals. This study employed a single-trial analysis of human EEG data recorded during a virtual navigation task to isolate discrete episodes of frontal theta and parietal alpha oscillations. The results indicate that these rhythmic activities occur in transient bursts rather than sustained states and are specifically phase-locked to critical navigational milestones, such as turns and goal approaches. These findings suggest that discrete oscillatory episodes, rather than continuous rhythms, are the functional units of neural activity supporting spatial cognition in humans.
papers.authors: Mireia Torralba-Cuello, Angela Marti-Marca, M. S. Pápai, Salvador Soto-Faraco

papers.title: Crossmodal semantic congruence and rarity improve episodic memory
papers.abstract: Multisensory semantic congruence is known to improve short-term memory performance, but its influence on long-term episodic retrieval is less well defined. This research examined how the interaction between audiovisual semantic congruence and stimulus rarity at the time of encoding influences subsequent memory recall. Across multiple experiments, it was demonstrated that semantically congruent multisensory events are remembered significantly better than incongruent or unimodal ones, with the benefit being most pronounced for rare or distinctive stimuli. These findings highlight that the salience and semantic consistency of a multisensory event during acquisition are critical determinants of its long-term episodic storage and later retrieval success.
papers.authors: Pau Alexander Packard, Salvador Soto-Faraco

papers.title: Sensory stimulation enhances visual working memory capacity
papers.abstract: Visual working memory (vWM) is a capacity-limited cognitive system essential for high-level information processing. Building on previous research using transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS), this study investigated whether rhythmic visual and auditory sensory stimulation could non-invasively expand vWM capacity. Across six behavioral experiments, it was found that sensory entrainment at both 4 Hz and 7 Hz led to robust improvements in vWM capacity, particularly for individuals with lower baseline storage limits. Because these effects were not accompanied by changes in pupillary markers of arousal, the results point toward a specific modulation of the temporal sampling windows underlying working memory storage, rather than a general increase in cognitive alertness.
papers.authors: Indre Pileckyte, Salvador Soto-Faraco

E246.name: Michael N. Shadlen
E246.bio: Michael N. Shadlen investigates the neurobiological underpinnings of decision-making as a framework to understand cognitive processes such as reasoning and planning. Their research focuses on how the brain accumulates and integrates sensory evidence to reach a categorical commitment, emphasizing the role of the lateral intraparietal area (LIP) and the computational principles of the speed-accuracy tradeoff. Utilizing single-neuron electrophysiology in non-human primates, behavioral psychophysics, and computational modeling, Shadlen identifies how neural circuits transform visual signals into volitional actions. Their current work explores the scalability of these decision mechanisms to address complex cognitive operations, including memory-based choices and the neural basis of confidence.
E246.research_direction: Dr. Shadlen’s recent work explores the cognitive and neural mechanisms of decision-making, specifically focusing on how evidence is sequentially accumulated over time to drive choices. In the perceptual domain, they have recently been investigating how human observers incorporate the cost of deliberation time to optimize speed-accuracy tradeoffs, while also using simultaneous population recordings in the parietal cortex to directly observe single-trial stochastic evidence accumulation. Their research extends into preferential choice, using eye-tracking and functional neuroimaging to examine how visual attention interacts with evidence integration and whether subjective values are dynamically constructed during deliberation rather than retrieved as static preferences. Additionally, they are probing the circuit-level implementation of cognitive flexibility, employing two-photon calcium imaging and optogenetics in mice to understand how motor cortex networks dynamically reconfigure to map sensory inputs to context-dependent actions.

papers.title: Behavioral Signatures of Post-Decisional Attention in Preferential Choice
papers.abstract: This study evaluates the causal role of visual attention in preferential choice by testing models that propose a multiplicative interaction between gaze duration and subjective value during the evidence accumulation process. Through a secondary analysis of eye-tracking data from food-choice experiments, the authors examined predictions concerning the increased informativeness of the final fixation in high-value contexts and the allocation of attention during choices that conflict with stated preferences. Finding no empirical support for these causal predictions, they propose a post-decisional model wherein gaze behavior reflects a commitment state reached once the decision variable has achieved a termination bound. This framework explains observed gaze-cascade effects and the influence of overall item value on response latencies without requiring an attentional bias in the stochastic integration of evidence.
papers.authors: Ariel Zylberberg, Ian Krajbich, Michael N. Shadlen

papers.title: Incorporation of a Cost of Deliberation Time in Perceptual Decision Making
papers.abstract: This research investigates how decision-makers incorporate the cost of time to optimize the speed-accuracy tradeoff during sequential evidence accumulation. Utilizing a random-dot motion discrimination task with human participants, the authors manipulated deliberation costs by introducing a subtle time-pressure penalty. Behavioral data were modeled using a bounded drift-diffusion process, revealing that participants adjust their termination criteria by adopting collapsing bounds that decline as a function of time. A novel computational analysis demonstrates that the rate of bound collapse increases under higher time-cost conditions, representing an adaptive strategy that approximates an optimal reward-rate policy by balancing the marginal utility of additional information against the temporal costs of continued deliberation.
papers.authors: Shinichiro Kira, Ariel Zylberberg, Michael N. Shadlen

papers.title: ALM enables contextual decision-making via dynamic reconfiguration of local circuits
papers.abstract: The paper explores the neural implementation of flexible stimulus-response contingencies in the anterior lateral motor cortex (ALM). Using a mouse olfactory delayed match-to-sample paradigm where context odors dictate the behavioral mapping of subsequent test odors, the authors employed two-photon calcium imaging to identify distinct neuronal sub-populations encoding context, stimulus identity, and motor choice. They identified a subset of 'contingency neurons' displaying dual selectivity that effectively gate the transformation of sensory inputs into directional motor outputs. Optogenetic silencing during the context and delay intervals confirmed that ALM activity is causally necessary for configuring the appropriate behavioral mapping, suggesting that cognitive flexibility in the motor cortex is achieved through the dynamic reconfiguration of local circuit connectivity rather than abstract rule representation.
papers.authors: Jia Shen, Nuttida Rungratsameetaweemana, Prayshita Sharma, Darcy S. Peterka, Herbert Zheng Wu, Michael N. Shadlen

papers.title: Value construction through sequential sampling explains serial dependencies in decision making
papers.abstract: This study proposes a sequential sampling framework to account for serial dependencies in value-based decisions, challenging the assumption that subjective values are stable retrieved quantities. The authors argue that value is constructed during deliberation through a process of memory querying and evidence accumulation. By analyzing choice patterns and reaction times in preferential choice tasks, they demonstrate that item values fluctuate based on decision history—a process termed revaluation. A drift-diffusion model incorporating temporally correlated evidence samples shows that these dynamic value updates predict choices and ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) BOLD signals more accurately than models based on static preferences, providing a unified account of both decision speed and choice-induced preference changes.
papers.authors: Ariel Zylberberg, Akram Bakkour, Daphna Shohamy, Michael N. Shadlen

papers.title: Direct observation of the neural computations underlying a single decision
papers.abstract: By performing simultaneous population recordings from the lateral intraparietal area (LIP) during a motion discrimination task, the authors provide the first direct characterization of the stochastic drift-diffusion process at the single-trial level. Utilizing population decoding and state-space analysis, they isolate a scalar decision variable (DV) that represents the integral of noisy momentary evidence. This signal, which is undetectable in trial-averaged firing rates, is shown to predict the variability in both choice and reaction time on individual trials. The findings elucidate a parsimonious neural architecture where a specific subset of target-selective neurons represents the accumulated evidence (the integral), while direction-selective neurons represent the integrand, confirming that population-level stochastic diffusion is the physical driver of decision variability.
papers.authors: Natalie Steinemann, Gabriel M. Stine, Eric M. Trautmann, Ariel Zylberberg, Daniel M. Wolpert, Michael N. Shadlen

E247.name: Joshua I. Gold
E247.department: Department of Neuroscience, Perelman School of Medicine
E247.bio: Joshua I. Gold is a Professor of Neuroscience at the University of Pennsylvania, where Gold directs the Gold Lab and co-directs the Computational Neuroscience Initiative. Gold's research investigates the neural mechanisms of decision-making, specifically focusing on how the brain integrates uncertain sensory evidence with prior experience through inference and learning processes. To explore these functions, their laboratory employs a multidisciplinary approach that combines human psychophysics and pupillometry with non-human primate electrophysiology and computational modeling. This work aims to characterize the biological principles of belief updating and cognitive arousal to identify how adaptive behaviors are optimized within dynamic and complex environments.
E247.research_direction: Dr. Gold has recently been investigating the computational and neural mechanisms that drive perceptual decision-making and evidence accumulation in dynamic environments. Their recent work explores how the brain processes complex or uncertain sensory information, asking how observers weight correlated visual signals, incorporate simplicity biases during Bayesian inference, and use sensory adaptation in area MT to flexibly integrate evidence over time. They are also examining the distinct neural circuits that govern anticipatory response times, utilizing human intracranial recordings to map the independent neural signatures guiding choice commitment versus motor execution. Additionally, their research investigates how physiological readouts like pupillometry can be leveraged to track the underlying brainstem and neuromodulatory dynamics associated with arousal, uncertainty, and belief updating during these behavioral tasks.

papers.title: How Occam’s razor guides human decision-making
papers.abstract: Human decision-making often adheres to Occam’s razor, preferring simpler over complex explanations for uncertain evidence. Using a novel deep neural-network architecture and preregistered psychophysical experiments, we demonstrate that simplicity preferences in humans align with formal Bayesian model selection principles. Specifically, human choices reflect sensitivities to four theoretically grounded geometric complexity terms: dimensionality, boundary, volume, and robustness. Crucially, these simplicity biases persist in humans even when they are maladaptive to the task's specific reward structure, contrasting with artificial neural networks that can optimize away such biases. This suggests that the brain's preference for parsimony is an inherent, integrated feature of the inference process rather than a transient strategic adjustment.
papers.authors: Eugenio Piasini, Shuze Liu, Pratik Chaudhari, Vijay Balasubramanian, Joshua I. Gold

papers.title: Normative evidence weighing and accumulation in correlated environments
papers.abstract: In naturalistic decision-making, sensory observations are frequently correlated, requiring the brain to adjust the weight of evidence to avoid redundancy and maintain accuracy. We tested human participants on a visual-discrimination task where the degree of pairwise correlation between observations varied across trials without explicit cues. Participants demonstrated the ability to adapt to these changes with minimal training, producing decisions consistent with an approximately normative weighing and accumulation process. While choice accuracy remained robust across correlation conditions, response times (RTs) exhibited subtle suboptimalities, suggesting a systematic underestimation of the true correlation magnitude in the evidence-integration process. These findings highlight the computational robustness of the brain's evidence-accumulation mechanisms in handling complex, non-independent signal structures.
papers.authors: Nathan Tardiff, Jiwon Kang, Joshua I. Gold

papers.title: Human response times are governed by dual anticipatory processes with distinct neural signatures
papers.abstract: Anticipatory behavior is a key driver of response efficiency, yet its neural implementation remains poorly understood. Utilizing intracranial electroencephalography (iEEG) in neurosurgical patients, we dissociated two distinct anticipatory mechanisms that guide behavior during a sensory-motor task with variable foreperiod delays. One process influences the commitment to a choice, reflected in premature false alarms, while the second optimizes the speed of execution, reflected in response time (RT) reductions. We identified distinct neural signatures for these processes: choice-related anticipation was associated with low-frequency power changes in the prefrontal cortex, whereas execution-related anticipation was linked to distinct oscillatory patterns in motor regions. These results establish a dual-process framework for anticipation, mediated by spatially and functionally distinct neural circuits.
papers.authors: Ashwin G. Ramayya, Vivek P. Buch, Andrew G. Richardson, Timothy H. Lucas, Joshua I. Gold

papers.title: Sensory adaptation supports flexible evidence accumulation during perceptual decision making
papers.abstract: The flexibility required for decision-making in dynamic environments is often attributed to adaptive 'leaks' in the evidence accumulation process. We investigated whether such flexibility also arises from adjustments at the sensory encoding stage. We recorded single-unit activity in the middle temporal (MT) area of monkeys performing a direction-discrimination task with varying temporal stability in the stimulus environment. Monkeys adjusted their accumulation dynamics in a manner consistent with an adaptive leak dependent on temporal context. These behavioral changes were parsimoniously accounted for by stimulus-specific sensory adaptation within MT neurons, which was found to be independent of pupil-linked arousal. These results reveal a novel contribution of sensory adaptation to the flexibility of perceptual decision processes, shaping the quality of evidence available for downstream integration.
papers.authors: Kara D. McGaughey, Joshua I. Gold

papers.title: Pupil size as a window on neural substrates of cognition
papers.abstract: Cognitively driven pupil size modulations serve as a vital non-invasive proxy for brain state and information processing. This review delineates the specific contributions of three primary neural systems to pupillary dynamics: the pretectal olivary nucleus (PON), which mediates the pupillary light reflex under cortical control; the superior colliculus (SC), which governs orienting responses to salient stimuli; and the locus coeruleus (LC)-norepinephrine system, which links arousal to high-level cognitive computations like uncertainty and belief updating. We discuss how these substrates integrate sensory and cognitive signals and provide a framework for using pupillometry to infer the underlying neural circuit dynamics during learning and decision-making tasks, while highlighting critical caveats for future physiological interpretations.
papers.authors: Kara D. McGaughey, Joshua I. Gold

E249.name: Stephen M. Fleming
E249.department: Department of Experimental Psychology and Institute of Cognitive Neuroscience
E249.bio: Stephen M. Fleming is a Professor of Cognitive Neuroscience at University College London and leads the MetaLab, where their research focuses on the computational and neural basis of self-awareness and conscious experience. By integrating psychophysics, functional neuroimaging (fMRI/MEG), and Bayesian modeling, Fleming has developed frameworks for understanding how the brain monitors and evaluates its own cognitive processes. Their work examines the mechanisms of metacognition and confidence across domains such as visual perception and decision-making, while also investigating the clinical implications of metacognitive distortions in psychiatric and neurological conditions.
E249.research_direction: Dr. Fleming has recently been investigating the computational and neural mechanisms of metacognition, reality monitoring, and mental state attribution. Using approaches from computational psychiatry, their recent work explores how trial-by-trial confidence integrates into global self-beliefs in anxiety and depression, and how specific components of cognitive-behavioral therapy alter distinct parameters like metacognitive efficiency and reward sensitivity. In the visual domain, they are examining how fronto-parietal networks and sensory representational strength in the fusiform gyrus allow the brain to discriminate internally generated mental imagery from externally driven perception. Additionally, they are probing human-AI interaction by measuring how lay attributions of phenomenal consciousness and intelligence to large language models influence human trust and advice-taking behavior in decision-making tasks.

papers.title: A neural basis for distinguishing imagination from reality
papers.abstract: This study demonstrates that the discrimination between internally generated mental imagery and externally driven sensory perception is mediated by the integrated magnitude of sensory signals within the fusiform gyrus. Neural activity fluctuations in this mid-level visual area significantly predict trial-level confusions between real and imagined stimuli, while functional interactions with a fronto-parietal reality-monitoring network support the execution of binary reality judgments. These findings delineate a cortical mechanism for reality testing based on the readout of sensory representational strength.
papers.authors: Nadine Dijkstra, Thomas von Rein, Peter Kok, Stephen M. Fleming

papers.title: The influence of mental state attributions on trust in large language models
papers.abstract: This research investigates the impact of folk-psychological attributions of mental states on human trust and advice-taking behavior when interacting with Large Language Models (LLMs). Utilizing a preregistered experimental paradigm (N=410), the authors assessed subjective ratings of LLM consciousness and mentality alongside an advice-weighted decision-making task. Bayesian computational modeling demonstrated that while attributions of cognitive intelligence strongly facilitate trust and advice acceptance, attributions of phenomenal experience and consciousness are either uncorrelated or negatively associated with the degree of behavioral revision following LLM input, suggesting a decoupling of perceived intelligence and perceived sentience in human-AI collaboration.
papers.authors: Clara Colombatto, Jonathan Birch, Stephen M. Fleming

papers.title: Distorted learning from local metacognition supports transdiagnostic underconfidence
papers.abstract: This work characterizes the computational mechanisms underlying the persistence of low self-efficacy in anxiety and depression despite veridical performance. Across two large-scale samples, the authors distinguish between 'local' trial-specific confidence and 'global' long-run self-performance estimates during an experimental manipulation of external feedback. Computational results indicate that while global confidence remains responsive to external feedback valence, individuals high in anxious-depressive symptomatology exhibit a selective attenuation in the sensitivity of global self-beliefs to instances of high local confidence.
