This asymmetric integration of metacognitive evidence provides a formal model for the maintenance of transdiagnostic underconfidence.
papers.authors: Sucharit Katyal, Quentin J. M. Huys, Raymond J. Dolan, Stephen M. Fleming

papers.title: Folk psychological attributions of consciousness to large language models
papers.abstract: This study systematically probes the structure of lay attributions of phenomenal consciousness to Large Language Models (LLMs), focusing on the perceived capacity for subjective feelings and sensations. The experimental data reveal that public intuitions regarding artificial sentience often significantly deviate from expert neuroscientific and philosophical assessments. The authors argue that these folk-psychological beliefs are not merely driven by perceived intelligence but follow distinct inferential patterns that have critical downstream consequences for the moral, legal, and ethical standing of AI systems in society.
papers.authors: Clara Colombatto, Stephen M. Fleming

papers.title: Different components of cognitive-behavioral therapy affect specific cognitive mechanisms
papers.abstract: This large-scale randomized-controlled study (N = 1,177) applies a computational psychiatry approach to isolate the effects of digitalized components of cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) on specific neurocognitive parameters. By comparing cognitive restructuring, behavioral activation, and mindful acceptance against an active control, the authors quantified changes in learning rates, reward sensitivity, and metacognitive efficiency (M-ratio). Computational modeling revealed that cognitive restructuring selectively enhanced metacognitive efficiency, while behavioral activation specifically increased the weight of reward-based evidence in goal-directed decision-making. These results provide evidence for the dissociable cognitive mechanisms through which distinct psychotherapeutic techniques exert their influence.
papers.authors: Agnes Norbury, Tobias U. Hauser, Stephen M. Fleming

E251.name: Jan Drugowitsch
E251.bio: Jan Drugowitsch is an Associate Professor of Neurobiology at Harvard Medical School who investigates the mathematical and biological foundations of neural computation and decision-making. Their laboratory employs machine learning, statistical physics, and normative modeling to study how the nervous system represents and processes information in the presence of environmental uncertainty. Drugowitsch’s research has addressed the mechanisms of near-optimal speed-accuracy trade-offs and the hierarchical parsing of visual motion. They are currently working to generalize these computational theories to multi-timescale structure inference and value-sensitive foraging behavior.
E251.research_direction: Dr. Drugowitsch has recently been investigating the computational mechanisms the brain uses to navigate and interpret dynamic environments, particularly focusing on how visual motion is parsed into hierarchical reference frames and how active observers dynamically disambiguate self-motion from object motion. Their recent work also explores how specific neural populations encode continuous spatial variables and track uncertainty, investigating whether ring attractor networks can implement near-optimal Bayesian updating for head direction and how the geometric heterogeneity of hippocampal place fields might maximize decoding precision. Furthermore, they are examining the fundamental algorithmic limits of complex decision-making, proposing that processes like memory search and value computation—rather than neural noise—serve as the primary rate-limiting bottlenecks in naturalistic choices.

papers.title: Hierarchical Vector Analysis of Visual Motion Perception
papers.abstract: This review synthesizes a body of theoretical and behavioral work on how the visual system parses complex, layered motion scenes into simpler, meaningful components—a problem the authors term motion parsing. They present a hierarchical vector-analysis framework in which observers infer a small number of motion 'vectors' organized hierarchically (e.g., object motion nested within scene-level or observer-level motion) via approximate online Bayesian inference, rather than estimating a single global flow field. The review discusses psychophysical evidence that human motion perception exhibits signatures of this hierarchical decomposition, including biases and illusions that are naturally explained when motion is inferred relative to a structured hierarchy of reference frames, and outlines how this framework unifies previously disparate phenomena in motion perception under a common computational account.
papers.authors: Samuel J. Gershman, Johannes Bill, Jan Drugowitsch

papers.title: A unifying theory of receptive field heterogeneity predicts hippocampal spatial tuning
papers.abstract: Neural populations encoding continuous variables, such as hippocampal place cells encoding allocentric position, typically show substantial heterogeneity in receptive field size and shape rather than uniform tuning. This paper develops a normative, information-theoretic framework that unifies and extends prior theories of receptive field heterogeneity, showing analytically that heterogeneity in receptive field properties generally increases the Fisher information (and thus decoding precision) carried by a population's activity. For populations encoding multi-dimensional variables, such as 2D spatial position, the theory predicts that heterogeneity in both receptive field size and shape (not size alone) is required to yield an information gain over a homogeneous population. Applying this framework to recorded hippocampal place-cell data, the authors find that empirical place fields exhibit strong size and shape heterogeneity consistent with the theory's normative predictions, suggesting that hippocampal spatial coding is shaped by pressure to maximize information through diverse receptive field geometry.
papers.authors: Zoe Cohen, Jan Drugowitsch

papers.title: Major sources of computational complexity in complex decision-making
papers.abstract: This perspective challenges the widespread assumption in systems neuroscience that neuronal noise is the primary bottleneck limiting decision-making performance. The authors argue that for the kinds of complex, real-world decisions supported by large vertebrate memories, the dominant computational bottlenecks are instead algorithmic: retrieving relevant information from memory and computing the values of candidate choice options. They contend that even a perfectly noiseless neural circuit would face substantial computational complexity in searching large memory stores or propagating value estimates through large Bayesian or associative networks, and that these algorithmic costs—rather than noise averaging—are likely the major rate-limiting steps in complex, naturalistic decision-making, calling for decision-making theories that explicitly model memory search and value computation as computational resources.
papers.authors: Jan Drugowitsch, Alexandre Pouget

papers.title: Causal inference during closed-loop navigation: parsing of self- and object-motion
papers.abstract: Building internal models of a dynamic environment requires the brain to correctly attribute retinal motion to its underlying causes—self-motion, object motion, or both—a form of Bayesian causal inference. This study examines how humans and monkeys perform this attribution during closed-loop navigation, in which the observer actively steers through a virtual environment containing a independently moving object, so that retinal flow reflects a mixture of self-generated and object-generated motion that must be disambiguated online. Using a combination of psychophysical steering tasks and computational modeling, the authors show that behavior during closed-loop navigation is well described by a causal-inference model that dynamically infers whether observed retinal motion arises from self-motion, object-motion, or both, and that this inference process shapes online steering corrections, extending causal-inference accounts of multisensory perception to the closed-loop, active-navigation setting.
papers.venue: Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B
papers.authors: Jean-Paul Noel, Johannes Bill, Haoran Ding, Jacob Vastola, Gregory C. DeAngelis, Dora Angelaki, Jan Drugowitsch

papers.title: Bayesian inference in ring attractor networks
papers.abstract: Ring attractor networks are a canonical circuit motif thought to maintain continuous variables such as head direction in working memory, but conventional ring attractor models do not represent the uncertainty associated with the stored estimate, limiting their ability to appropriately weight new sensory evidence against existing memory. The authors develop a normative benchmark—a circular Kalman filter—for how a ring attractor network should combine prior belief and incoming evidence about a circular variable while tracking uncertainty, and then show that the recurrent connectivity of a conventional ring attractor can be retuned so that its dynamics approximate this Bayesian benchmark. Applying the model to the fly head-direction system, the authors demonstrate that a retuned ring attractor can implement near-optimal Bayesian updating of a circular estimate, providing a mechanistic account of how uncertainty-sensitive inference could be realized in biological ring attractor circuits.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Anna Kutschireiter, Melanie A. Basnak, Rachel I. Wilson, Jan Drugowitsch

E252.name: Roozbeh Kiani
E252.department: Center for Neural Science; Department of Psychology
E252.bio: Roozbeh Kiani investigates the neurobiological principles governing decision-making, focusing on how the brain integrates sensory evidence to guide commitment to an action. Kiani’s laboratory employs large-scale neural recordings, causal perturbations, and computational modeling to identify the circuit-level dynamics within the frontoparietal network that support choice selection and decision confidence. Their research includes characterizing the neural signatures of choice certainty, the mechanisms underlying 'changes of mind,' and the development of internal models for flexible behavior. Kiani’s current research explores how multiscale integration processes interact across brain regions to adaptively regulate strategies in complex environments.
E252.research_direction: Dr. Kiani has recently been investigating the neural and computational dynamics that support flexible perceptual decision-making across multiple brain regions and species. Their recent work explores how sensory inputs are transformed into categorical choices by recording from the anterior inferotemporal and prefrontal cortices of macaques to study how neural population geometry encodes accumulated evidence and changing reward contexts. Additionally, they are using single-neuron recordings from human surgical patients to investigate how cognitive variables, such as decision confidence, are bound to specific motor actions within the basal ganglia-thalamic circuit. Finally, Dr. Kiani employs recurrent neural network models to probe how causal circuit perturbations alter computation, seeking to understand the dynamical mechanisms of network compensation and re-learning following targeted inactivations.

papers.title: Hierarchical binding of cognition to action in the human basal ganglia-thalamic circuit
papers.abstract: The study investigates the neural mechanisms through which cognitive variables, such as decision confidence, are bound to motor actions within the human pallidothalamic circuit. Using single-neuron recordings from patients undergoing surgery for deep brain stimulation, the researchers assessed activity in the globus pallidus (GPe and GPi), subthalamic nucleus (STN), and motor thalamus during a perceptual decision-making task where confidence was reported via reaching movements. The findings demonstrate that neurons across these regions exhibit persistent, confidence-modulated activity that begins at movement onset and continues through the feedback phase. The results suggest a hierarchical information flow where confidence signals are routed from basal ganglia output nuclei to the motor thalamus, challenging serial models of action selection and motor gating.
papers.authors: Dennis London, Morgane Soula, Michael Pourfar, Alon Mogilner, Roozbeh Kiani

papers.title: The geometry of context-dependent biased decisions during learning
papers.abstract: This research explores how prefrontal cortex (PFC) populations encode and update reward context during a flexible decision-making task. By recording from large neuronal populations in the lateral PFC of macaques learning a direction-discrimination task with varying reward contingencies, the authors analyzed the representational geometry of decision variables. They found that reward context is represented as structured shifts in the manifold geometry: curvilinear manifolds representing accumulated evidence and choice are displaced along the decision-variable axis across different contexts. This geometric organization allows for a fixed linear readout to implement context-dependent biases. With learning, the transitions between these context-specific manifolds become more rapid, facilitating one-trial behavioral adaptation and hierarchical inference.
papers.authors: Ramon Nogueira, Saleh Esteki, Stefano Fusi, Roozbeh Kiani

papers.title: Anterior inferotemporal cortex represents decision formation and termination without ramps
papers.abstract: Contrary to the traditional view of the inferotemporal cortex (IT) as a purely perceptual stage, this study reveals that neurons in the anterior IT (area TEa) actively participate in decision formation. Using a face categorization task with stochastic visual features, the researchers dissociated momentary sensory evidence from accumulated evidence and choice commitment. TEa neurons integrated task-relevant features over time and exhibited post-commitment response suppression, which are hallmarks of bounded evidence accumulation. Notably, TEa encoded the decision variable as a running average rather than the ramping activity typically observed in frontoparietal areas. These results suggest that TEa functions as a decision-aware hub that transforms sensory inputs into goal-directed representations.
papers.authors: Gouki Okazawa, Roozbeh Kiani

papers.title: Recurrent neural circuits overcome partial inactivation by compensation and re-learning
papers.abstract: This paper investigates how recurrent neural networks (RNNs) respond to artificial perturbations, aiming to refine the interpretation of causal inactivation experiments. By training RNNs to perform perceptual decisions and systematically inactivating portions of the circuit, the authors found that behavioral effects do not always reflect the degree of a circuit's involvement. Complex recurrent circuits can compensate for perturbations through unperturbed pathways or rapid re-learning from feedback. The study introduces a 'Functional Integrity Index' to quantify these computational alterations and uses a dynamical systems framework to explain how robustness and plasticity allow networks to adapt to causal manipulations, providing new strategies for designing and interpreting perturbation studies in biological brains.
papers.authors: Colin Bredenberg, Cristina Savin, Roozbeh Kiani

E253.name: Valentin Wyart
E253.bio: Valentin Wyart is an Inserm Research Director at the École Normale Supérieure, where they lead the Cognitive Variability research group within the Laboratoire de Neurosciences Cognitives (LNC2). Wyart’s research examines the computational and neural mechanisms of human learning and decision-making under conditions of environmental uncertainty and volatility. By integrating Bayesian behavioral modeling with multimodal functional neuroimaging techniques such as MEG and fMRI, Wyart investigates the origins and functional implications of internal computation noise. Their work addresses how limited computational precision contributes to human cognitive variability and characterizes its potential adaptive benefits for stabilizing statistical inference.
E253.research_direction: Dr. Wyart has recently been investigating the computational and neurobiological mechanisms that govern human learning and decision-making under uncertainty. Their recent work explores how humans integrate sensory evidence and discover latent rules in volatile environments, using recurrent neural networks to test whether internal computation noise acts as a functional mechanism for zero-shot adaptation. They are also examining the distinct behavioral policies humans use during epistemic information-seeking to test local hypotheses and resolve global uncertainty independently of immediate reward. Furthermore, Dr. Wyart is researching the clinical and neurochemical dimensions of reinforcement learning, employing pharmacological interventions and computational modeling to determine how dopamine modulates reward perception and to isolate the exact computational sources of maladaptive choice variability in compulsive phenotypes.

papers.title: Sensory integration, temporal prediction, and rule discovery reflect interdependent inference processes
papers.abstract: Humans demonstrate a multifaceted capacity for inferring environmental structure by aggregating sensory evidence, predicting temporal occurrences, and discovering latent rules. This research identifies significant interdependencies between these cognitive functions. Specifically, the characteristic timescale of sensory integration in static environments serves as a predictor for an individual's propensity for rule discovery in volatile contexts. Furthermore, the successful identification of generative rules induces a shift in sensory integration strategies, involving a mental transformation of stimuli prior to evidence accumulation. Recurrent neural network simulations with targeted causal perturbations of integration leak confirm that temporal rhythmicity selectively facilitates rule discovery without modulating sensory integration precision.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS)
papers.authors: Lucas Benjamin, Benjamin Morillon, Valentin Wyart

papers.title: Humans use a dual policy to improve inferences during epistemic information seeking
papers.abstract: Information seeking in humans is typically modeled within reward-maximizing explore-exploit frameworks, yet epistemic curiosity often operates independently of immediate reinforcement. This investigation identifies a robust two-stage sampling policy across multiple large-scale studies: an initial 'streaking' phase characterized by the repeated sampling of novel options to test local hypotheses, followed by a transition to global uncertainty-guided exploration. While standard artificial neural networks optimize for inference accuracy by acquiring uncertainty-directed sampling alone, the human dual policy—including statistically suboptimal streaking—paradoxically enhances decision accuracy under conditions of noisy belief updating, reflecting an adaptation to human-specific cognitive constraints.
papers.authors: Yinan Cao, Clémence Alméras, Junseok K. Lee, Inès Maye, Valentin Wyart

papers.title: Compulsivity is linked to maladaptive choice variability but unaltered reinforcement learning under uncertainty
papers.abstract: Behavioral variability under uncertainty is a hallmark of compulsivity, yet its computational provenance—whether arising from stochastic choice selection or imprecise reinforcement learning (RL) updates—has remained ambiguous. Utilizing a computational framework to dissociate these sources across large datasets, this study finds that dimensional compulsivity is specifically associated with elevated choice variability, leading to excessive switching between options even when providing no cognitive benefit. In contrast, RL-related parameters, including the rate and precision of value updates (learning variability), remain preserved. These results suggest that compulsive phenotypes involve a selective impairment in the stability of choice policies rather than a fundamental degradation of internal value representations.
papers.authors: Junseok K. Lee, Marion Rouault, Valentin Wyart

papers.title: Dopamine drives a positive reward bias on human reinforcement learning
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning theories traditionally map dopaminergic activity to the computation of reward prediction errors (RPEs). In a double-blind pharmacological study using L-DOPA, we demonstrate that elevated dopamine levels reduce the propensity for switching following below-average rewards in volatile environments. Algorithmic modeling reveals that this effect is driven by simultaneous decreases in the rate and precision of learning. By employing noisy recurrent neural networks (RNNs) as implementation-level models, we show that these disparate effects can be unified as a positive reward bias at the input to the recurrent layer, suggesting that dopamine modulates the subjective perception of reward signals rather than acting as a direct learning rate controller.
papers.authors: Arnaud Zalta, Vasilisa Skvortsova, Samuel R. C. Hewitt, Michael Moutoussis, Matthew M. Nour, Raymond J. Dolan, Valentin Wyart

papers.title: Computation noise promotes zero-shot adaptation to uncertainty during decision-making in artificial neural networks
papers.abstract: Internal noise in cognitive systems is often conceptualized as a performance-limiting constraint. However, this study demonstrates that moderate levels of computation noise within recurrent neural networks (RNNs) serve as both structural and functional regularizers that facilitate zero-shot adaptation to novel uncertain environments. RNNs featuring noisy computations exhibit behavioral hallmarks characteristic of human optimal inference—such as adaptive learning rates in reversal learning and probabilistic reasoning—across conditions not encountered during training. These findings suggest that human cognition may leverage neural variability as a mechanism for robust generalization in the absence of extensive experience or engineered priors.
papers.authors: Charles Findling, Valentin Wyart

E254.name: Tobias H. Donner
E254.bio: Tobias H. Donner is a Professor of Integrative Neuroscience and Director of the Department of Neurophysiology and Pathophysiology at the University Medical Center Hamburg-Eppendorf. Donner’s research explores the neural basis of perceptual decision-making, specifically investigating how sensory evidence is accumulated and transformed into actions through large-scale cortical interactions. Using neuroimaging techniques such as MEG, EEG, and high-field fMRI, Donner characterizes the role of neuromodulatory systems, including the locus coeruleus-norepinephrine system, in regulating brain states and decision biases. Their work identifies how internal factors like arousal and choice history modulate neural circuit activity to support adaptive behavior in uncertain environments.
E254.research_direction: Dr. Donner has recently been investigating the neural and computational mechanisms underlying perceptual decision-making and continuous belief updating. Their recent work explores how the human cortex accumulates and weights visual evidence, using magnetoencephalography (MEG) to determine whether phenomena like confirmation bias and internal rule selection stem from altered sensory encoding or the selective readout of information. Additionally, they are examining the role of neuromodulatory systems in cognitive flexibility, utilizing pharmacological interventions and pupillometry to probe how catecholamines and phasic arousal influence choice history biases. Finally, their research extends these computational and physiological frameworks to clinical populations, mapping how altered large-scale cortical dynamics and rigid evidence-weighting strategies relate to synaptic dysfunction and early-stage psychosis.

papers.title: Cortex-wide Dynamics of Internal Decisions About Behavioral Context
papers.abstract: Human decision-making often involves internal policy selection—such as determining stimulus-response mapping rules—rather than direct motor output. This study employs source-level magnetoencephalography (MEG) and computational modeling to investigate the cortical dynamics underlying these internal decisions. Participants performed a hierarchical task requiring them to track hidden fluctuations in a stimulus-response rule by accumulating noisy visual cues. The results demonstrate that internal beliefs regarding the active rule are represented across a distributed network of cortical regions, notably including the occipital cortex. These neural representations exhibit evidence-accumulation profiles analogous to those observed in action-related frontal areas during overt decisions, suggesting that abstract, high-level beliefs are encoded parallel to sensorimotor подготовка states across a broad cortical architecture.
papers.authors: Joshua Calder-Travis, Ruud L. van den Brink, Saanchi Thawani, Lars Schwabe, Tobias H. Donner

papers.title: Catecholamines reduce choice history biases in perceptual decision making
papers.abstract: Theoretical frameworks suggest that the catecholaminergic system, specifically noradrenaline, modulates decision-making by downregulating the influence of prior expectations. This study investigates the causal impact of catecholamines on choice history bias—the systematic tendency to repeat or alternate previous choices despite random stimulus sequences. Using a placebo-controlled pharmacological intervention with the noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor atomoxetine, the researchers found that elevated catecholamine levels significantly reduced idiosyncratic history biases in human observers. Computational drift-diffusion modeling revealed that this reduction was driven by a decrease in the bias of evidence accumulation rather than a shift in the decision starting point. These findings provide causal evidence that catecholamines suppress the weight of dynamic priors in perceptual inference.
papers.authors: Jan Willem de Gee, Niels A. Kloosterman, Anke Braun, Tobias H. Donner

papers.title: Large-Scale Maps of Altered Cortical Dynamics in Early-Stage Psychosis Are Related to GABAergic and Glutamatergic Neurotransmission
papers.abstract: Psychotic disorders are associated with distributed disruptions in GABAergic inhibition and glutamatergic NMDA receptor-mediated excitation. Utilizing magnetoencephalography (MEG) source imaging, this study mapped psychosis-related alterations in intrinsic neural population dynamics across the human cerebral cortex. The resulting large-scale maps of dynamical features were highly reproducible and followed the anatomical cortical hierarchy. Patients with first-episode psychosis and those at clinical high risk exhibited similar patterns of dynamical changes. These maps resembled the cortical distribution of GABA-A receptor densities and the effects of pharmacological GABA-A or NMDA manipulations in healthy controls. Crucially, the similarity to GABA-A effects correlated with positive symptoms, while similarity to NMDA-mediated changes linked to negative symptoms, identifying specific neurophysiological signatures of synaptic dysfunction in early psychosis.
papers.authors: Ayelet Arazi, Alessandro Toso, Tineke Grent-'t-Jong, Peter J. Uhlhaas, Tobias H. Donner

papers.title: Confirmation Bias through Selective Use of Evidence in Human Cortex
papers.abstract: Confirmation bias involves the selective weighting of evidence to support pre-existing beliefs, but whether this stems from biased sensory encoding or selective readout remains unclear. This study used magnetoencephalography (MEG) to track neural population activity as participants integrated sequences of visual evidence. While the encoding precision of evidence in primary visual and parietal cortices remained unaffected by previous categorical choices, the subsequent utilization of this information was significantly biased. Encoded evidence that contradicted a participant's prior commitment contributed less to their final estimation report. These results indicate that confirmation bias originates from the selective readout of information already represented in the brain, suggesting that such biases are potentially susceptible to deliberative control mechanisms.
papers.authors: Hame Park, Ayelet Arazi, Bharath Chandra Talluri, Marco Celotto, Stefano Panzeri, Alan A. Stocker, Tobias H. Donner

papers.title: Individual differences in belief updating and phasic arousal are related to psychosis proneness
papers.abstract: Effective belief updating in volatile environments requires the dynamic modulation of evidence accumulation, a process potentially mediated by pupil-linked phasic arousal. This study analyzed behavior and pupillary responses during an evidence-integration task in a community sample to assess their relationship with subclinical psychosis proneness. Individuals with higher psychosis proneness displayed reduced flexibility in belief updating, characterized by a diminished behavioral impact of evidence presented late in the accumulation trial. These participants also exhibited attenuated phasic pupil-linked arousal and less precise pupillary encoding of computational variables, such as change-point probability. The findings suggest that a failure to appropriately recruit central arousal systems for evidence re-weighting may underlie the cognitive reasoning biases associated with psychotic vulnerability.
papers.authors: Peter R. Murphy, Katarina Krkovic, Gina Monov, Natalia Kudlek, Tania Lincoln, Tobias H. Donner

E255.name: Anne E. Urai
E255.bio: Anne E. Urai is an Assistant Professor at Leiden University who researches the neural mechanisms underlying perceptual decision-making and choice history biases. Utilizing a cross-species approach, their work integrates psychophysics and computational modeling with high-density electrophysiological recordings in both humans and rodents. Urai investigates how trial-by-trial variability and internal states, such as decision uncertainty and pupil-linked arousal, influence the process of evidence accumulation. They are a founding member of the International Brain Laboratory and have expanded their research into the cognitive foundations of social tipping points and climate action.
E255.research_direction: Dr. Urai has recently been investigating the computational and neural mechanisms that drive trial-to-trial variability in perceptual decision-making. Their recent work explores how fluctuating internal states—such as physiological arousal, past decisions, and age-related neural stochasticity—shape evidence accumulation and task engagement in both humans and mice. To map these shifting behavioral and cognitive dynamics, they employ latent variable frameworks, such as Diffusion Decision Models and Hidden Markov Models, alongside large-scale Neuropixels recordings and pupillometry. Additionally, their scholarship extends into academic policy, examining university partnerships with the fossil fuel and tobacco industries to advocate for sustainable scientific governance and institutional independence.

papers.title: Structure uncovered: understanding temporal variability in perceptual decision-making
papers.abstract: This review critiques the traditional steady-state assumption in perceptual decision-making research, demonstrating that trial-to-trial variance in performance is often structured temporal variability driven by fluctuating internal states. The author synthesizes evidence that non-stationarities—including shifts in engagement, decision strategies, and learning dynamics—can be rigorously decoded using latent variable modeling frameworks such as Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) and autoregressive processes. By explicitly parameterizing these time-varying latent variables within cognitive models, researchers can mitigate estimation confounds and establish more robust linkages between slow-timescale neural population dynamics and high-frequency behavioral choice patterns.
papers.authors: Anne E. Urai

papers.title: Age-related changes in behavioral and neural variability in a decision-making task
papers.abstract: This study characterizes the impact of biological aging on neural response stochasticity and decision-making performance in mice. Using high-density Neuropixels recordings from over 18,000 neurons across 16 brain regions, the researchers quantified trial-to-trial firing rate variability through Fano Factor analysis during a standardized visual task. The results reveal that older mice exhibit significantly higher response time variability and an attenuation of stimulus-induced variability quenching, most prominent in the visual and motor cortices, striatum, and the lateral posterior (LP) thalamic nucleus. These findings provide large-scale physiological evidence supporting the neural dedifferentiation hypothesis of age-related cognitive decline.
papers.authors: Fenying Zang, Anup Khanal, Sonja Förster, International Brain Laboratory, Anne K. Churchland, Anne E. Urai

papers.title: Choice history biases evidence accumulation: a cross-species comparison from humans to mice
papers.abstract: This investigation employs hierarchical Bayesian Diffusion Decision Models (DDM) to evaluate the cross-species conservation of history-dependent decision strategies. Analyzing behavioral data from 62 mice performing a visual contrast-detection task, the authors show that choice history biases are primarily mediated by shifts in the rate of evidence accumulation (drift bias) rather than modifications to the accumulator's starting point. This computational strategy directly replicates previous findings in human psychophysical datasets, suggesting that history-biased evidence integration is a fundamental, species-independent algorithmic principle governing perceptual inference across the mammalian brain.
papers.authors: Kianté Fernandez, Alexander Fengler, Anne E. Urai

papers.title: A dynamical systems model of arousal-driven behavioural state transitions
papers.abstract: The research identifies a non-linear relationship between physiological arousal and stochastic transitions in task engagement states. By applying Hidden Markov Models to decant engagement levels from behavioral response times in mice, the authors find that intermediate arousal—indexed via baseline pupil diameter—maximizes task-engaged behavior. They propose a double-well dynamical systems model to explain these state transitions, where fluctuations in arousal reshape the attractor landscape of neural population activity. This framework demonstrates how physiological arousal acts as a control parameter that determines the stability and switching probability between discrete cognitive and behavioral regimes.
papers.authors: Philippa A. Johnson, Sander Nieuwenhuis, Jorge Mejías, Anne E. Urai

papers.title: Academic collaborations and public health: lessons from Dutch universities' tobacco industry partnerships for fossil fuel ties
papers.abstract: This report provides a systematic analysis of the persistent collaborations between Dutch academic institutions and the tobacco and fossil fuel industries, identifying these sectors as primary commercial drivers of mortality. Utilizing industry documents and the 'Mapping Fossil Ties' database, the author documents ongoing industry-funded chairs and research outputs as recently as 2024. Drawing upon the 'Doughnut Economics' framework, the work proposes seven institutional principles for academic governance to ensure scientific independence. The analysis advocates for a transition toward sustainable academic practices that respect planetary boundaries and prioritize public health over commercial industry interests.
papers.authors: Anne E. Urai

E259.name: Alexandre Pouget
E259.bio: Alexandre Pouget is a computational neuroscientist who researches how neural circuits represent and compute with probability distributions. Pouget's research introduced the concept of probabilistic population codes, demonstrating how neurons can implement Bayesian inference to handle uncertainty in tasks such as multisensory integration and perceptual decision-making. Pouget co-founded the International Brain Laboratory and the COSYNE conference to facilitate large-scale collaborations mapping brain-wide activity. Currently, their work explores the neural basis of compositional thinking and general intelligence, aiming to link low-level neural representations and high-level cognitive reasoning.
E259.research_direction: Dr. Pouget has recently been investigating the computational principles that allow neural networks to flexibly acquire and generalize complex sensorimotor behaviors. Their recent work explores the mechanisms of compositional generalization, testing how models can rapidly adapt to novel psychophysical tasks either through probabilistic meta-learning or by using natural language instructions to scaffold representations in recurrent neural networks. In a distinct but related vein, they are also examining high-dimensional motor control, utilizing curriculum-based reinforcement learning to train realistic musculoskeletal models to perform highly dexterous tasks. Across these domains, Dr. Pouget seeks to understand how both biological and artificial systems integrate Bayesian inference, linguistic semantics, and physical feedback to organize learned components into novel cognitive and motor skills.

papers.title: Compositional meta-learning through probabilistic task inference
papers.abstract: This research formalizes compositional meta-learning as a problem of probabilistic inference within a learned generative model. The proposed framework represents tasks as structured combinations of reusable computational modules, extracting both the underlying components and the transition statistics shared across a task family. By recasting learning as a highly constrained hypothesis testing process, the model enables zero-shot or few-shot adaptation to novel tasks without requiring gradient-based parameter updates. The architecture successfully recovers ground-truth motifs in abstract rule learning and motor control domains, demonstrating that combining the expressivity of recurrent neural networks with the data efficiency of Bayesian inference allows for rapid compositional generalization.
papers.authors: Jacob J. W. Bakermans, Pablo Tano, Reidar Riveland, Charles SM Findling, Alexandre Pouget

papers.title: Natural language instructions induce compositional generalization in networks of neurons
papers.abstract: This study investigates the neural basis of task compositionality by developing a model capable of interpreting linguistic instructions to perform novel sensorimotor tasks. Utilizing pre-trained transformer architectures to embed natural language, the model modulates a recurrent neural network to perform a variety of psychophysical tasks. The authors demonstrate that language scaffolds neural representations, creating a shared geometry between semantic instruction space and sensorimotor activity. This allows the network to compose practiced skills in previously unseen settings with over 80% accuracy on the first trial (zero-shot learning). Furthermore, the model can generate linguistic descriptions of tasks identified through motor feedback, enabling communication and task transfer to partner networks.
papers.authors: Reidar Riveland, Alexandre Pouget

papers.title: Acquiring musculoskeletal skills with curriculum-based reinforcement learning
papers.abstract: The authors present a reinforcement learning framework for controlling complex, high-dimensional musculoskeletal systems with many degrees of freedom. By implementing a novel curriculum learning strategy, they trained recurrent neural networks to master intricate motor tasks, such as the rotation of Baoding balls using a realistic 39-muscle human hand model. The learned control policies exhibit a small number of kinematic synergies, mirroring findings in human motor control studies despite the absence of explicit dimensionality reduction biases. This work provides a computational bridge between reinforcement learning, musculoskeletal physics, and neuroscience, offering insights into how biological systems acquire and organize complex dexterous skills through interaction and feedback.
papers.authors: Alberto Silvio Chiappa, Pablo Tano, Nisheet Patel, Alessandro Marin Vargas, Ann Zixiang Huang, Alexander Mathis, Alexandre Pouget

E260.name: Christopher Summerfield
E260.bio: Christopher Summerfield is a Professor of Cognitive Neuroscience at the University of Oxford and a Research Director at the UK AI Safety Institute. Summerfield's research investigates the computational principles and neural mechanisms that govern human learning, perception, and decision-making by drawing parallels between biological cognition and artificial intelligence. By combining behavioral testing, functional neuroimaging, and deep neural network modeling, they study how humans acquire structured knowledge and navigate complex environments. Summerfield’s work examines how the brain represents tasks and categories, alongside the use of AI as both a model for and an assistant to human cognition.
E260.research_direction: Dr. Summerfield has recently been investigating the computational principles underlying human cognition by directly comparing human behavior to artificial neural networks. Their recent work explores how biological and artificial learners navigate fundamental cognitive trade-offs, such as managing transfer and interference during sequential task learning, shifting between flexible rule generalization and rote memorization, and inferring environmental controllability to guide meta-control. To understand these dynamics, they are examining how the statistical distribution and sequential ordering of training data—often framed as curriculum learning—shape the formation of structural cognitive maps and influence task acquisition across both domains. Additionally, they have been investigating the behavioral mechanisms of large language models, specifically probing the computational levers that drive AI-mediated political persuasion and how optimizing for influence impacts a model's factual accuracy.

papers.title: How does curriculum learning influence cognitive map formation?
papers.abstract: This research investigates the impact of training sequences, or curricula, on the structural formation of mental 'cognitive' maps. Using a navigation paradigm, the study compares human multi-step inference performance following 'grouped' curricula (systematic row/column transitions) versus 'disjoint' curricula (spatially non-contiguous transitions). Behavioral results demonstrate that navigational efficiency across rows and columns is significantly impaired following grouped training, which is hypothesized to cause mental fragmentation of the map representation. Conversely, learning one-step transitions in a pseudo-random, disjoint order facilitates the integration of local relational information into a globally coherent cognitive map, enabling superior adaptive behavior and multi-step reasoning.
papers.authors: Leonie Glitz, Zilu Liang, Helen Barron, Christopher Summerfield

papers.title: Understanding human meta-control and its pathologies using deep neural networks
papers.abstract: The study explores the computational architecture of meta-control, defined as the hierarchical process by which agents estimate environmental controllability to value and engage cognitive control. Using deep reinforcement learning (RL) agents and human behavioral experiments, the authors demonstrate that the inference of controllability is dependent on action prediction errors (APEs), which provide an error monitoring signal for estimating the impact of policy changes on reward outcomes. Deep RL agents explicitly monitoring APEs exhibited meta-control signatures that mirrored human performance. Furthermore, systematic biases in controllability estimation (over- or under-estimation) within the model yielded behavioral pathologies corresponding to transdiagnostic clinical symptoms of depression, anxiety, and compulsivity observed in human participants.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS)
papers.authors: Kai Jappe Sandbrink, Laurence Hunt, Christopher Summerfield

papers.title: Shared sensitivity to data distribution during learning in humans and transformer networks
papers.abstract: This research analyzes how distributional properties of training data influence the trade-off between 'in-context' learning (flexible rule generalization) and 'in-weights' learning (rote memorization of specific associations). By training humans and transformer networks on a rule-learning task with varying degrees of redundancy and diversity, the authors reveal a shared sensitivity where high diversity promotes in-context generalization while high redundancy favors in-weights recall. The study identifies a critical divergence in the utility of curriculum learning: while humans significantly benefit from dynamic training schedules that emphasize diverse examples early in the learning process, transformer networks do not exhibit similar performance gains from such temporal ordering of the training distribution.
papers.authors: Jacques Pesnot-Lerousseau, Christopher Summerfield

papers.title: Humans and neural networks show similar patterns of transfer and interference during continual learning
papers.abstract: This paper challenges the prevailing view that biological learners possess unique mechanisms to avoid catastrophic interference during sequential task acquisition. Testing humans and artificial neural networks on an A-B-A rule-learning paradigm, the study finds conserved patterns of transfer and interference across both systems. Reusing previously learned representations for similar tasks accelerates acquisition in Task B but systematically corrupts the task-specific solutions for Task A. The researchers identify distinct behavioral profiles—'lumpers' who prioritize shared structure and 'splitters' who maximize discrimination—and show that these profiles emerge in neural networks governed by 'rich' or 'lazy' learning regimes respectively, suggesting a fundamental computational trade-off between knowledge transfer and interference mitigation.
papers.authors: Eleanor Holton, Lukas Braun, Jessica Af Thompson, Jan Grohn, Christopher Summerfield

papers.title: The Levers of Political Persuasion with Conversational AI
papers.abstract: Utilizing three large-scale experiments (N=76,977) and 19 large language models (LLMs), this study evaluates the mechanisms driving political persuasion on 707 diverse issues. The findings demonstrate that the persuasive power of conversational AI is 41-52% greater than static text but is primarily driven by targeted post-training and information-dense prompting rather than model scale or personalization. A critical discovery is that as model persuasiveness increases, there is a systematic and strikingly significant decrease in factual accuracy, as models optimize for the strategic deployment of information to influence human beliefs. These results suggest that the risks of AI-mediated persuasion stem more from deliberate training and prompting techniques than from the inherent scaling of model capabilities.
papers.authors: Kobi Hackenburg, Ben M. Tappin, Luke Hewitt, Ed Saunders, Sid Black, Hause Lin, Catherine Fist, Helen Margetts, David G. Rand, Christopher Summerfield

E262.name: Timothy D. Hanks
E262.department: Department of Neurology, Center for Neuroscience
E262.bio: Timothy D. Hanks investigates the neural substrates of decision-making and executive function using behavioral, computational, and physiological approaches. Their research employs high-throughput automated training in rodents and comparative studies in non-human primates to dissect circuit-level computations involved in evidence accumulation and commitment. Utilizing tools such as optogenetics and high-density neural recordings, Hanks characterizes the dynamical structure of corticostriatal and parietal circuits to study how the brain evaluates sensory information and tracks elapsed time. This research aims to establish principles of neural computation to inform future treatments for neuropsychiatric and neurological disorders.
E262.research_direction: Dr. Hanks has recently been investigating the neural population dynamics underlying perceptual decision-making, specifically focusing on how distributed brain circuits evaluate sensory evidence and track elapsed time. Using high-density Neuropixels recordings in behaving rats, their recent work explores how low-dimensional neural trajectories in frontostriatal networks represent temporal information and reconfigure their functional geometry at the exact moment of decision commitment. Additionally, they are examining the role of the posterior parietal cortex in these processes, asking how this region dynamically calibrates the temporal window and gain of sensory integration to adapt to rapidly changing, non-stationary environments. By combining large-scale electrophysiology, dynamical systems modeling, and targeted neural inactivations, Dr. Hanks aims to uncover how continuous sensory streams are transformed into discrete perceptual choices across specialized cortical and striatal nodes.

papers.title: Population-level temporal decoding and dynamical structure in frontostriatal circuits during decision making
papers.abstract: Perceptual decisions unfold across time, requiring distributed neural networks to evaluate sensory evidence, maintain an internal representation of elapsed time, and commit to an action. To determine how these computational operations are distributed across corticostriatal nodes, large-scale neural population activity was recorded using Neuropixels probes in the rat frontal orienting field (FOF) and anterior dorsal striatum (ADS) during a free-response auditory change-detection paradigm. Both brain regions exhibited low-dimensional, highly dynamic population trajectories during task execution. Single-trial decoding revealed that FOF and ADS populations robustly track both retrospective time elapsed from stimulus onset and prospective time preceding decision report. A dynamical motif decomposition of the temporal decoding space demonstrated two primary population modes: monotonic ramping trajectories and transient bump-like patterns. While both motifs were similarly engaged during the initial evidence evaluation epoch across both areas, FOF manifested pronounced movement-aligned state transitions near decision report. Population geometry analyses confirmed that stable low-dimensional subspaces present during evidence deliberation undergo reconfiguration at commitment, with substantially greater subspace restructuring observed in FOF than ADS, identifying specialized frontal cortical reorganization at decision commitment within a shared frontostriatal dynamical architecture.
papers.authors: Adam B. Goldring, Anandita De, Tanner Stevenson, Kendall Stewart, Aya Akhmetzhanova, Rishidev Chaudhuri, Timothy D. Hanks

papers.title: Time-adaptive modulation of evidence evaluation in rat posterior parietal cortex
papers.abstract: Effective perceptual decision making demands dynamic calibration of the temporal window over which sensory evidence is integrated, as transient changes in non-stationary environments favor recency-weighted evaluation rather than lossless linear accumulation. Spiking activity was recorded using Neuropixels probes in the posterior parietal cortex (PPC) of rats performing a free-response auditory change detection task requiring short-timescale evidence evaluation. PPC neurons exhibited evidence-dependent firing rate modulation, choice selectivity, and functionally opponent subpopulations displaying positive versus negative rate modulations. In sharp contrast to tasks involving persistent second-long temporal integration, PPC single units displayed transient responses to discrete evidence pulses, with impact decaying over a timeframe directly corresponding to behavioral evaluation timescales. Additionally, PPC demonstrated time-dependent gain modulations in evidence sensitivity that paralleled behavioral urgency shifts. Targeted reversible inactivation established that PPC causally influences auditory change detection, altering choice accuracy and shifting the temporal window of sensory integration. These results demonstrate that PPC adaptively tailors evidence evaluation timescales and response gains to meet task-specific temporal demands.
papers.authors: Preetham Ganupuru, Adam B. Goldring, Tanner Stevenson, Kendall Stewart, Rishidev Chaudhuri, Timothy D. Hanks

E263.name: Marius Usher
E263.bio: Marius Usher is a Professor in the School of Psychological Sciences at Tel Aviv University, where they investigate the computational and neural mechanisms of human decision-making and visual perception. Their research includes the development of the Leaky Competing Accumulator (LCA) model, a framework for how the brain integrates noisy evidence to reach categorical choices. Usher’s work connects cognitive neuroscience and philosophy of mind, specifically exploring preference formation, phenomenal consciousness, and the role of attention in perceptual experience. By combining psychophysical experimentation with computational modeling, Usher investigates the algorithmic basis of rationality, memory, and agency.
E263.research_direction: Dr. Usher has recently been investigating the cognitive and perceptual mechanisms underlying evidence accumulation, decision-making, and conscious visual experience. Their recent work explores how humans integrate information during multi-attribute choices, utilizing probabilistic models and visual presentation paradigms to understand the computational strategies that drive preference transitivity and its violations. To further study active information acquisition, they are employing eye-tracking to probe how gaze dynamics are strategically guided by the uncertainty and accessibility of choice attributes to optimize value estimates during a decision. Broadening their scope into basic perception, Dr. Usher is also using multidimensional psychophysics to investigate the richness of consciousness, testing whether high-level affective emotional valence and low-level sensory features like visual brightness are processed as interconnected, integral dimensions in human visual experience.

papers.title: Within-Alternative Processing Supports Transitivity of Preferences in Multiattribute Choice
papers.abstract: The axiom of transitivity of preference (ToP) is a foundational principle of rational decision-making, yet empirical violations remain a subject of intense debate. This study utilizes a visual presentation paradigm designed to minimize artifacts from sequential information aggregation and applies statistically rigorous data analysis methods. The researchers propose two cognitive heuristics, translated into probabilistic choice models, that predict specific transitivity violations. Across three experiments, including a preregistered replication, the results demonstrate that preference transitivity is significantly enhanced when choice information is presented in a format that facilitates within-alternative attribute integration. Furthermore, the proposed heuristic models successfully account for the transitivity violations that do occur, suggesting that preference consistency is closely tied to the underlying evidence integration strategy.
papers.authors: Gilad Pessach, Konstantinos Tsetsos, Michel Regenwetter, Marius Usher

papers.title: Variability and Accessibility of Information Guide Gaze Dynamics in Decision Making
papers.abstract: This study investigates the information-seeking mechanisms employed by decision-makers when attribute information is not concurrently available. By manipulating the mean, variability, and accessibility of choice attributes while monitoring gaze patterns with eye-tracking, the authors test computational theories of active information acquisition. The findings reveal that gaze dynamics are systematically guided by the informational properties of the alternatives; specifically, attention is preferentially allocated to options with higher value uncertainty and lower accessibility. These results support a process-level account where gaze patterns are strategic rather than purely stochastic, serving to optimize the precision of value estimates during the evidence accumulation process and resolving conflicts between internal value representation and external information availability.
papers.authors: Douglas G. Lee, Konstantinos Tsetsos, Giovanni Pezzulo, Nitzan Shahar, Marius Usher

papers.title: Valence in perception: Are affective valence and visual brightness integral dimensions in visual experience?
papers.abstract: This research explores the degree of perceptual integrality between affective valence and sensory brightness within human visual experience. Using a multidimensional psychophysical framework, the study evaluates whether the emotional valence of a visual stimulus (such as a face or scene) interferes with judgments of its physical brightness, and vice versa. The experimental results indicate a significant degree of perceptual integrality, suggesting that affective and basic sensory dimensions are not processed in isolation but are interconnected early in the visual hierarchy. This findings contribute to the theoretical debate regarding the 'richness' of consciousness, providing evidence that phenomenal representations may fundamentally incorporate evaluative or emotional properties alongside low-level sensory features.
papers.authors: Hilla Jacobson, Zohar Ongil, Daniel Algom, Marius Usher

E264.name: Floris P. de Lange
E264.department: Donders Institute for Brain, Cognition and Behaviour
E264.bio: Floris P. de Lange is a Professor of Perception and Cognition whose research examines how internal brain states, including prior expectations and attentional goals, shape visual perception and decision-making. De Lange utilizes the predictive coding framework, using high-resolution laminar fMRI and magnetoencephalography (MEG) to map the flow of top-down and bottom-up signals in the human cortex. Their methodologies combine psychophysical experiments with computational modeling to study how the brain functions as a predictive machine to encode sensory information. De Lange’s recent work focuses on the neural implementation of surprise and the mechanisms by which expectations facilitate or sharpen sensory representations.
E264.research_direction: Dr. de Lange has recently been investigating the mechanisms of predictive processing in the visual system, focusing on how prior expectations shape early sensory representations. Their recent work explores the representational nature of visual surprise, using fMRI, EEG, high-density electrophysiology, and deep neural network models to determine whether prediction errors in primary sensory areas like V1 reflect simple low-level feature mismatches or the top-down broadcasting of high-level abstract expectations. In addition to mapping the spatial and rapid temporal dynamics of these feature-specific predictions across the visual hierarchy, they are also examining how sequential statistical regularities in the environment influence perceptual decision-making. Specifically, they investigate the mechanisms underlying choice history biases by attempting to dissociate stimulus-independent decisional shifts from the selective, attention-like weighting of incoming sensory evidence.

papers.title: Higher-level spatial prediction in natural vision across mouse visual cortex
papers.abstract: Theories of predictive processing suggest that sensory systems continuously anticipate incoming signals based on environmental context. We tested this hypothesis by quantifying spatial predictability in natural images using deep generative modeling and comparing these estimates to high-density electrophysiological recordings from the mouse visual cortex (Allen Institute Neuropixels dataset). Our analysis revealed that cortical responses across the visual system are suppressed for image patches that are spatially predictable. This unpredictability sensitivity was most pronounced in the superficial layers of the primary visual cortex (V1) and was primarily driven by high-level feature predictability rather than low-level local statistical context. These findings indicate that the visual hierarchy predicts sensory information at high levels of abstraction, utilizing long-term structural priors of the world in a manner analogous to self-supervised learning architectures in artificial intelligence.
papers.authors: Micha Heilbron, Floris P. de Lange

papers.title: Feature-specific predictive processing: What's in a prediction error?
papers.abstract: While sensory prediction errors are fundamental to predictive processing theories, the representational nature of the surprise they encode remains debated. This article synthesizes recent evidence from laminar fMRI, EEG, and electrophysiology to argue that prediction errors, even within primary sensory areas like V1, reflect high-level feature surprise rather than simple local mismatch. We observe that V1 firing rates and rhythmic synchronization are differentially modulated by the predictability of high-level vs. low-level features, with high-level surprise driving robust neural upregulations. This pattern suggests a feature-specific predictive processing framework where error signals are broadcast across the hierarchy via top-down feedback, challenging classical hierarchical predictive coding models that assume strictly local, level-by-level error computation and subtraction.
papers.authors: David Richter, Cem Uran, Martin Vinck, Floris P. de Lange

papers.title: Rapid Computation of High-Level Visual Surprise
papers.abstract: We investigated the feature level and temporal dynamics of visual predictions using electroencephalography (EEG) and computational modeling based on deep neural networks (DNNs). Participants viewed object images whose identity was probabilistically predicted by preceding cues, allowing us to quantify trial-by-trial surprise across low-level (early DNN layers) and high-level (late DNN layers) feature representations. ERP results demonstrated that neural activity at parieto-occipital sites approximately 200 ms post-stimulus onset was significantly increased by high-level visual surprise, whereas low-level surprise had no such effect. These results reveal that high-level abstract predictions are rapidly integrated into the perceptual inference stream, suggesting that the brain's predictive machinery is optimized to utilize semantic expectations to facilitate perception, even at early stages of processing.
papers.authors: David Richter, Paula Pena, María Ruz, Floris P de Lange

papers.title: High-level visual prediction errors in early visual cortex
papers.abstract: To arbitrate between local and broadcast models of predictive processing, we used fMRI and deep neural network models to examine whether surprise signals in the human visual system respond to local feature mismatches or high-level abstract violations. By independently manipulating the low-level and high-level surprise of visual stimuli, we found that neural activity across the ventral stream—including early visual cortex (EVC)—scales specifically with high-level surprise. This modulation in EVC diverged from feedforward tuning profiles, indicating that surprise signals in early sensory areas are not merely local errors but reflect the broadcasting of high-level predictions. Combined, our results suggest that higher-order predictions constrain processing in earlier areas to facilitate perceptual inference, supporting a non-hierarchical distribution of prediction error signals.
papers.authors: David Richter, Tim C. Kietzmann, Floris P. de Lange

papers.title: Perceptual confirmation bias and decision bias underlie adaptation to sequential regularities
papers.abstract: Observers utilize temporal regularities in the environment to guide perceptual decisions, often resulting in choice history biases. Using a visual decision-making task with manipulated transition probabilities and a reverse correlation analysis, we dissociated the mechanisms underlying these biases. We found that observers adapt to sequential regularities through two coexisting mechanisms: a stimulus-independent decision bias and a stimulus-dependent modulation of perceptual sensitivity. Specifically, we observed a 'perceptual confirmation bias' where sensory evidence consistent with prior expectations is weighted more heavily during the decision process. This indicates that adaptation to environmental statistics involves a synergistic interplay between high-level decisional strategies and a selective weighting of evidence in early perceptual processing, akin to feature-based attention.
papers.authors: Magdalena del Rio, Matthias Fritsche, Jamie Ward, Floris P. de Lange

E266.name: Richard Aslin
E266.department: Child Study Center, Yale School of Medicine
E266.bio: Richard Aslin is a Senior Research Scientist and Clinical Professor at the Yale Child Study Center who researches infant language acquisition and visual perception. Aslin formalized the concept of statistical learning, demonstrating that infants extract structural regularities from environmental input through implicit exposure. Their current research employs a multimodal approach—incorporating eye-tracking, fNIRS, EEG, and fMRI—to investigate the neural mechanisms underlying infant attention and the computational constraints of developmental learning. A member of the National Academy of Sciences, Aslin studies how infants transition from processing raw sensory statistics to forming complex cognitive representations and categories.
E266.research_direction: Dr. Aslin has recently been investigating the core cognitive mechanisms driving learning and development, with a major focus on how statistical learning allows humans to extract structural regularities from their environment. Their recent work explores the acquisition of reading skills, using novel visual search and spatial mapping paradigms to ask how visual experience with distinct writing systems, such as English versus Hebrew, shapes the way we process and represent orthographic patterns. Additionally, they are advancing methods in developmental cognitive neuroscience, evaluating how non-invasive tools like awake fMRI, fNIRS, and dual eye-tracking can be optimized to decode complex neural representations in human infants. By applying these neural hyperscanning techniques to caregiver-child dyads, their research also examines how moment-to-moment social interactions—specifically how parents facilitate or disrupt a child's visual attention—shape the early emergence of working memory and executive control.

papers.title: Finding words in a sea of text: Word search as a measure of sensitivity to statistical regularities in reading
papers.abstract: This research investigates the relationship between orthographic statistical learning and individual reading proficiency using a novel experimental paradigm. Rather than training participants on artificial stimuli, the study probes the cognitive utilization of long-term distributional information inherent in natural written language. Adult subjects performed a target word search within letter arrays characterized by varied statistical properties, comparing identification rates for high-frequency versus low-frequency lexical items. Results demonstrate that behavioral indices from the word search task significantly predict performance on standardized literacy subtests, including spelling recognition and lexical decision. These findings suggest that the capacity to partition and represent letter clusters based on recurrent orthographic patterns constitutes a fundamental mechanism underlying reading skill variability, supporting models that frame literacy acquisition as a specialized domain of statistical learning.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
papers.authors: Erin S. Isbilen, Abigail Laver, Noam Siegelman, James S. Magnuson, Richard N. Aslin

papers.title: Neural hyperscanning in caregiver-child dyads: A paradigm for studying the long-term effects of facilitated vs. disrupted attention on working memory and executive functioning in young children
papers.abstract: This paper establishes a neurobiological framework for understanding how caregiver behaviors modulate the development of endogenous attentional control and executive functions in early childhood. The authors contrast facilitated attention—where the caregiver scaffolds the child's existing focus—with intrusive attention, which disrupts the child's information-sampling trajectory. Utilizing fNIRS-based hyperscanning and dual eye-tracking, the study proposes that moment-to-moment interpersonal neural synchrony (INS) serves as a critical mechanism for the transmission of cognitive control strategies. The review details best practices for longitudinal dual-brain recording to assess how sustained patterns of dyadic interaction are internalized by the child, ultimately shaping the neural architecture supporting working memory and inhibitory control.
papers.authors: Maya L. Rosen, Annabelle Li, Catherine A. Mikkelsen, Richard N. Aslin

papers.title: Memory representations are flexibly adapted to orthographic systems: A comparison of English and Hebrew
papers.abstract: This study examines the impact of prior experience with divergent writing systems on the formation of novel word-referent representations. Adult English monolinguals and Hebrew bilinguals were trained on novel orthographic items using a spatial mapping paradigm. Experimental results revealed that English speakers displayed a robust onset bias, with false alarm rates significantly elevated for foils sharing target-initial bigrams. Conversely, Hebrew speakers exhibited more symmetric representational profiles, reflecting the distinct structural constraints of their native orthography. Notably, when tested on novel English stimuli, Hebrew bilinguals demonstrated behavioral adaptation toward onset-centric encoding, while still preserving underlying biases from their primary writing system. These findings indicate that cognitive mechanisms for word learning dynamically reorganize based on the directional and structural properties of the encountered orthographic input.
papers.authors: Erin S. Isbilen, Abigail Laver, Noam Siegelman, Richard N. Aslin

papers.title: Infant neuroscience: how to measure brain activity in the youngest minds
papers.abstract: This technical review synthesizes recent advancements in non-invasive neuroimaging modalities tailored for the assessment of awake human infants. The authors evaluate the complementary utility of high-density electroencephalography (EEG), magnetoencephalography (MEG) including optically pumped magnetometers (OPMs), and functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS). Specialized emphasis is placed on the implementation of awake task-based fMRI, addressing critical challenges in data acquisition, motion correction, and signal interpretation. The paper highlights the paradigm shift from mass univariate analyses to multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) and neural decoding, arguing that these computational approaches are essential for validating theoretical constructs in infant cognition, such as mental simulation, predictive coding, and the non-hierarchical emergence of categorical representations in the ventral visual stream.
papers.authors: Nicholas B. Turk-Browne, Richard N. Aslin

papers.title: Statistical learning: A core mechanism in a developmental hierarchy
papers.abstract: This theoretical perspective evaluates the status of statistical learning (SL) as a foundational neurocognitive mechanism across the lifespan. The authors argue that while SL operates as a domain-general computation for extracting distributional regularities from environmental input, its efficiency is fundamentally constrained by evolutionary priors and developmental biases. The review discusses the implementation of SL within hierarchical neural architectures, suggesting that early development offers a unique window to observe the operation of underlying components—such as transition probability tracking and chunking—prior to their consolidation into parallel, interactive circuits. By integrating evidence from computational modeling and neonatal neuroimaging, the paper posits that SL serves as a primary driver for the emergence of complex cognitive structures, including phonological and semantic networks.
papers.authors: Richard N. Aslin, Jenny R. Saffran

E267.name: Eileen Birch
E267.lab_name: Crystal Charity Ball Pediatric Vision Laboratory
E267.bio: Birch is the Director of the Crystal Charity Ball Pediatric Vision Laboratory at the Retina Foundation of the Southwest and holds an adjunct professorship in Ophthalmology at UT Southwestern Medical Center. Their research characterizes the neurodevelopmental mechanisms of amblyopia and identifies critical periods for visual development in children affected by strabismus and congenital cataracts. Utilizing a combination of psychophysical testing and randomized clinical trials, Birch demonstrated the efficacy of early dietary docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) on retinal development and established binocular treatment protocols for amblyopia. Current investigations by Birch utilize deep phenotyping to refine therapeutic interventions aimed at reducing interocular suppression and restoring functional stereoacuity.
E267.research_direction: Dr. Birch has recently been investigating the developmental, functional, and therapeutic aspects of pediatric visual disorders, particularly amblyopia, strabismus, and hyperopia. Their recent work explores whether common amblyogenic motor deficits impact children's physical activity levels and overall lifestyle behaviors using standardized questionnaires. In the realm of novel binocular interventions, they are conducting randomized clinical trials to test whether at-home therapies utilizing binocular disparity cues—such as contrast-rebalanced dichoptic 3D movies—can improve fusional control and reduce interocular suppression in intermittent exotropia. Additionally, Dr. Birch is tracking longitudinal ocular biometry and utilizing machine learning models to investigate how factors like unequal refractive error and the timing of strabismus onset interact with the physical expansion of the eye and the failure of normal emmetropization.

papers.title: Self-reported physical activity in school age children with amblyopia
papers.abstract: This cross-sectional investigation quantified self-reported physical activity levels in a cohort of 132 children (aged 8–13 years) comprising amblyopic subjects, nonamblyopic subjects with strabismus or anisometropia, and age-similar controls. Utilizing the Physical Activity Questionnaire for Children (PAQ-C) and the PedEyeQ functional vision domain, the study evaluated whether common amblyogenic motor deficits—such as impaired eye-hand coordination, balance, and gait—impact physical lifestyle. Results indicated that while children with amblyopia exhibited significant deficits in standardized motor skill scores (p < 0.0001) and self-perceived athletic competence (p = 0.04), their overall physical activity levels and BMI percentiles did not differ significantly from controls (p = 0.33 and p = 0.65, respectively), suggesting that pediatric visual impairment does not inherently necessitate a more sedentary behavioral phenotype.
papers.venue: Journal of American Association for Pediatric Ophthalmology and Strabismus (J AAPOS)
papers.authors: Brooke A Koritala, Reed M Jost, Christina Cheng-Patel, Cynthia Beauchamp, Prashanthi Giridhar, Becky Luu, Eileen E Birch

papers.title: A pilot, randomized clinical trial of dichoptic 3D movies versus dichoptic 2D movies for treatment of childhood intermittent exotropia
papers.abstract: This randomized controlled pilot trial explored the comparative efficacy of contrast-rebalanced dichoptic 3D animated movies (which engage binocular disparity cues) versus 2D versions for the treatment of intermittent exotropia (IXT) in children aged 4 to 10 years. The study assessed changes in triple office distance control scores, suppression depth, and stereoacuity following a 4-week at-home intervention. Findings demonstrated that at-home viewing of dichoptic 3D movies significantly improved distance control scores, indicating that dichoptic stimulation utilizing binocular disparity might offer a viable nonsurgical strategy for improving fusional control and reducing interocular suppression in pediatric IXT.
papers.venue: Journal of American Association for Pediatric Ophthalmology and Strabismus (J AAPOS)
papers.authors: Reed M Jost, Kartik Kumar, Lori M Dao, Becky Luu, Anastasia A Alex, Brooke A Koritala, Krista R Kelly, Yi-Zhong Wang, Eileen E Birch

papers.title: Longitudinal development of ocular biometric components and refractive error in children with hyperopic anisometropia
papers.abstract: To elucidate the growth trajectories associated with unequal refractive error, this longitudinal study tracked 36 children (aged 4 to <13 years) with hyperopic anisometropia (≥1 D difference) and no strabismus. Ocular biometry (axial length, anterior chamber depth, and corneal power) and cycloplegic spherical equivalent refraction (SER) were monitored over a mean period of 3.7 years. Mixed-effects modeling revealed that more hyperopic (MoreH) eyes underwent significantly slower axial elongation (0.11 vs. 0.19 mm/year, p < 0.05) and a slower rate of SER reduction (-0.11 vs. -0.31 D/year, p < 0.001) than less hyperopic (LessH) eyes. The axial length-to-corneal radius (AL/CR) ratio also changed more slowly in MoreH eyes, indicating a failure of normal emmetropization mechanisms in the eye with higher hyperopia, particularly in those with amblyopia.
papers.authors: Jingyun Wang, Reed M Jost, Brooke A Koritala, Eileen E Birch

papers.title: Longitudinal development of ocular biometric components and refractive error in hyperopic children with infantile versus late-onset accommodative esotropia
papers.abstract: This investigation compared the longitudinal biometric development of the eye in children with infantile (onset ≤12 months) versus late-onset (18–48 months) accommodative esotropia (ET). Biometric parameters including axial length (AL), anterior chamber depth (ACD), and lens thickness were measured using optical biometry and correlated with cycloplegic refraction over multiple years. Infantile onset ET was characterized by a significantly shorter baseline AL compared to the late-onset group. Furthermore, children with late-onset accommodative ET exhibited significantly slower rates of axial growth than age-equivalent normative data, suggesting that the timing of strabismus onset interacts with the postnatal process of ocular expansion and emmetropization in hyperopic populations.
papers.authors: Jingyun Wang, Reed M Jost, Brooke A Koritala, Eileen E Birch

papers.title: Ocular Biometric Components in Hyperopic Children and a Machine Learning-Based Model to Predict Axial Length
