papers.abstract: Recognizing the limitations of standard linear models in describing complex ocular growth, this study assessed biometric components in 212 hyperopic children (+1 to +10 D) across three age cohorts (3–5, 6–8, and 9–11 years). Cross-sectional analysis demonstrated that hyperopic axial growth is frequently compensated by concurrent reductions in corneal power. A machine learning-based classification and regression tree (CART) model was developed to predict axial length (AL) using spherical equivalent (SEQ), age, and sex. The CART model identified critical SEQ thresholds (3.94 D and 7.06 D) and achieved superior predictive accuracy (mean absolute error = 0.60) compared to traditional linear regression (MAE = 0.76), providing a data-driven tool for estimating biometric growth in highly hyperopic pediatric patients.
papers.authors: Jingyun Wang, Reed M Jost, Eileen E Birch

E268.name: James A. Bourne
E268.lab_name: Section on Cellular and Cognitive Neurodevelopment
E268.bio: James A. Bourne is a Senior Investigator and Chief of the Section on Cellular and Cognitive Neurodevelopment at the National Institute of Mental Health. Bourne's research characterizes the maturation and plasticity of the primate visual system using a multidisciplinary cell-to-system approach that integrates anatomy, in vivo imaging, and behavioral tasks. A primary focus of their work is the role of thalamocortical circuits, particularly the pulvinar nuclei, in establishing functional brain systems and their vulnerability to developmental perturbations. By examining these circuits, Bourne aims to elucidate the neurodevelopmental substrates of disorders such as schizophrenia and autism, building on their previous work regarding the hierarchical development of cortical areas like the middle temporal area.
E268.research_direction: Dr. Bourne has recently been investigating the evolutionary and developmental dynamics of primate-specific neural circuits, with a particular focus on how higher-order thalamocortical pathways involving the pulvinar support visual processing and complex cognition. Their recent work explores the protracted postnatal maturation of prefrontal cortical networks in marmosets, utilizing molecular profiling and immunohistochemistry to track the unique developmental trajectories of specific inhibitory interneuron populations. Within the visual system, they are examining the functional organization of the pulvinar to understand how it routes subcortical visual inputs across the cortex, modulates attention, and scaffolds the early development of the dorsal stream. To facilitate these circuit-level investigations, Dr. Bourne is also developing open-source, in-cage testing platforms that combine automated touchscreen cognitive assays with wireless neural recordings in freely behaving nonhuman primates.

papers.title: Developmental dynamics of marmoset prefrontal cortical SST and PV interneuron networks highlight primate-specific features
papers.abstract: The primate prefrontal cortex (PFC) exhibits a notably protracted postnatal developmental trajectory, which is integral to the progressive emergence of sophisticated executive functions and cognitive control. Central to this maturational process are GABAergic inhibitory interneurons, specifically the parvalbumin-expressing (PV+) and somatostatin-expressing (SST+) subtypes, which serve as critical regulators of cortical circuit synchronization, temporal precision, and synaptic plasticity. This investigation utilizes the common marmoset (Callithrix jacchus) to characterize the postmigratory development of these interneuron populations across multiple PFC regions, including granular (8aD, 8aV, 9, 46) and dysgranular (11, 47L) areas. Quantitative immunohistochemical and molecular profiling of PV, SST, the chloride transporter KCC2, and high-frequency firing-associated ion channels (Kv3.1b and Nav1.1) revealed that PV+ interneuron maturation extends significantly into adolescence. This process is marked by a progressive upregulation of specific ion channels and the late-stage consolidation of perineuronal nets (PNNs). In contrast, SST+ interneurons demonstrate a unique postnatal decline in density, a pattern that diverges from established rodent models. These findings provide a high-resolution developmental framework for understanding the primate-specific choreography of inhibitory circuit refinement and highlight potential windows of vulnerability relevant to the etiology of neurodevelopmental disorders such as schizophrenia and autism.
papers.authors: Nafiseh S. Hosseini Fin, Adrian Yip, Jack T. Scott, Leon Teo, Jihane Homman-Ludiye, James A. Bourne

papers.title: CalliCog is an open-source cognitive neuroscience toolkit for freely behaving nonhuman primates
papers.abstract: Traditional cognitive neuroscience in nonhuman primates (NHPs) often necessitates significant human intervention, including animal transport and physical restraint, which can introduce stress and limit experimental throughput. To address these constraints, we developed CalliCog, an open-source and scalable automated platform for in-cage behavioral testing in small primate species like the common marmoset (Callithrix jacchus). The system employs modular operant chambers integrated directly into home-cage environments, utilizing a low-cost hardware architecture and a flexible web-based application for task administration and automated progression. We demonstrated the toolkit's efficacy by training behaviorally naive marmosets on a pipeline of touchscreen-based cognitive assays, including novel discrimination, reversal learning, and delayed matching-to-sample tasks. Animals achieved task proficiency within a 2-week timeframe without human handling. Furthermore, the platform facilitates the precise synchronization of behavioral data with wireless electrocorticography (ECoG) or electrophysiological recordings, allowing for the characterization of neural correlates during complex cognition in an ethologically relevant, freely behaving context.
papers.authors: Jack T. Scott, Bruno L. Mendivez Vasquez, Brian J. Stewart, Dylan D. Panacheril, Darren K. J. Rajit, Angela Y. Fan, James A. Bourne

papers.title: Evolution and development of specialized primate thalamocortical circuits
papers.abstract: This comprehensive review examines the specialized organizational principles and developmental trajectories of thalamocortical connectivity in primates, with a particular focus on higher-order nuclei such as the pulvinar. Unlike rodent models where primary sensory pathways predominate, the primate brain is characterized by a massive expansion of multimodal associative circuits that link the thalamus with the prefrontal and posterior parietal cortices. We analyze the mechanisms of axonal pathfinding across forebrain boundaries, the early innervation of the cortical subplate, and the reciprocal influence of thalamic activity on cortical arealization. The review highlights how primate-specific evolutionary innovations, such as the emergence of the medial pulvinar (Pm) and the granular layer of the prefrontal cortex, have created unique network configurations that handle sophisticated cognitive and social functions. We discuss evidence that perturbations in the maturation of these specific thalamocortical motifs during sensitive windows of development may serve as the primary substrate for the pathophysiology of psychiatric illnesses, including schizophrenia and autism spectrum disorders.
papers.venue: The Cerebral Cortex and Thalamus (Oxford Academic)
papers.authors: David A. Leopold, James A. Bourne

papers.title: Visual Processing in the Pulvinar
papers.abstract: The pulvinar complex represents the largest and most neurochemically diverse thalamic nucleus in the primate brain, acting as a critical multimodal association hub that routes information across the visual cortical hierarchy. This review details the functional organization of the pulvinar, contrasting the 'core' retinotopically organized regions of the inferior pulvinar (PI) with the more 'matrix'-like, expansive connectivity of the lateral (PL) and medial (PM) subdivisions. We examine the driving and modulatory roles of pulvinar neurons, their integration of subcortical inputs from the superior colliculus and retina, and their involvement in complex behaviors such as directed attention and saccadic planning. Special emphasis is placed on the developmental maturation of the pulvino-cortical pathway, proposing that transient retinopulvinar projections to the middle temporal (MT) area provide a vital scaffold for the early establishment of the dorsal stream. The article concludes by discussing the clinical implications of pulvinar dysconnectivity, which is frequently implicated in the development of cognitive and perceptual deficits observed in neurodevelopmental conditions.
papers.venue: The Cerebral Cortex and Thalamus (Oxford Academic)
papers.authors: Angela Y. Fan, James A. Bourne

papers.title: CalliCog: an open-source cognitive neuroscience toolkit for freely behaving nonhuman primates
papers.abstract: The study of primate cognition remains primarily restricted to specialized laboratories due to the intensive labor and specialized infrastructure required for behavioral training. To democratize access to these models, we present CalliCog, a scalable, open-source, in-cage operant platform designed for freely behaving experiments in small NHPs such as marmosets. CalliCog features modular operant chambers that interface with home-cages, utilizing a centralized 'executive' computer to autonomously govern task progression across multiple subjects. By employing automated protocols for touchscreen training, we demonstrate that naive marmosets can rapidly acquire rule-based behaviors, including discrimination and working memory tasks, without human intervention. The system's architecture also permits the integration of wireless neural recordings, enabling the exploration of circuit dynamics during naturalistic behaviors. This toolkit aims to lower technical and financial barriers to NHP research, facilitating more broad-scale investigation into the neural foundations of cognition and their disruption in disease states.
papers.authors: Jack T. Scott, Bruno L. Mendivez Vasquez, Brian J. Stewart, Dylan D. Panacheril, Darren K. J. Rajit, Angela Y. Fan, James A. Bourne

E270.name: Angela Chen
E270.bio: Angela M. Chen is a Professor at the Southern California College of Optometry at Marshall B. Ketchum University, specializing in the diagnosis and management of pediatric vision disorders. Their research focuses on binocular vision anomalies, including strabismus, amblyopia, and accommodative insufficiency, through the use of multi-center randomized clinical trials. Chen serves as a primary clinical investigator for National Eye Institute-supported studies within the Pediatric Eye Disease Investigator Group (PEDIG) and the Convergence Insufficiency Treatment Trial (CITT-ART). Their work evaluates the effectiveness of vision therapy, optical interventions such as overminus lenses, and the repeatability of accommodative accuracy in children with unilateral amblyopia.
E270.research_direction: Dr. Chen's recent work broadly explores the assessment and management of pediatric binocular vision and accommodative disorders, alongside global public health and neuro-optometric rehabilitation. Using tools like open-field autorefraction and longitudinal clinical trials, they have recently been investigating habitual accommodative responses to retinal defocus in children with astigmatism, the long-term refractive impacts of overminus lens therapy for intermittent exotropia, and the efficacy of structured vergence therapies for convergence insufficiency. Furthermore, their research maps the clinical evidence surrounding various optical and rehabilitative interventions for oculomotor disorders in pediatric and adult patients recovering from mild traumatic brain injury. Additionally, they are evaluating global public health initiatives by measuring knowledge acquisition and retention among community health workers trained to identify and triage common childhood visual impairments in low-resource settings.

papers.title: Scoping review: Intervention for ocular motor disorders in children and adults with mild traumatic brain injury
papers.abstract: This scoping review maps and appraises the current clinical evidence for interventions targeting ocular motor disorders following mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI). The analysis evaluates outcomes for treatment modalities including watchful waiting, vestibular rehabilitation, neuro-optometric vision therapy (vision rehabilitation), and optical interventions such as prisms or tints. Synthesizing data from over 20 years of research, the study assesses the efficacy of these strategies in pediatric and adult cohorts, highlighting significant methodological variability and risk of bias across existing studies. The findings emphasize the requirement for standardized diagnostic criteria and high-quality randomized controlled trials to establish evidence-based protocols for post-concussion oculomotor management.
papers.authors: Angela M Chen, Aaron D Salzano, Allegra P Burgher, Lynn D Greenspan, Tiong Peng Yap, Jacqueline Theis, Su-Hsun Liu, Mitchell Scheiman, Tawna L Roberts

papers.title: Knowledge acquisition and retention when implementing public health awareness training on common pediatric eye conditions in Thailand
papers.abstract: This prospective evaluation assesses the effectiveness of a targeted public health training module designed to enhance the identification of common pediatric ophthalmic conditions (including refractive error, strabismus, and leukocoria) by community health workers in Thailand. The study measures knowledge acquisition and long-term retention using pre- and post-training assessments. Results demonstrate that the curriculum significantly improved workers' diagnostic recognition and triage competence, supporting the feasibility of integrating vision screening protocols into community-based primary care frameworks to reduce childhood visual impairment in low-resource settings.
papers.authors: Fountane Chan, Mani Woodward, Michael Parappilly, Yichen Fan, Saron Tedla, Ratipark Tamornpark, Jamie Anderson, Chalitar Chomchoei, Manassawin Kampun, Fartima Yeemard, Buathanya Srikua, Elizabeth White, Allison Summers, Angela Chen

papers.title: Accommodative responses in children with high and low levels of astigmatism
papers.abstract: This investigation examines accommodative performance in children (aged 3 to <10 years) with uncorrected astigmatism to challenge the assumption that they focus at the circle of least confusion. Using open-field autorefraction (WAM-5500) during a near-viewing task (33 cm), refractive states were measured and responses were classified relative to the anterior and posterior focal planes. The findings indicate that most children with astigmatism preferentially accommodate toward the anterior focal plane, resulting in significant accommodative lags in both principal meridians. These results clarify the habitual pattern of retinal defocus experienced by children with uncorrected astigmatism and its potential impact on emmetropization and amblyopia risk.
papers.authors: Jennifer X Haensel, Angela Chen, Susan Anne Cotter, Aparna Raghuram, Vivian M Manh, Lisa A Jordan, Tawna L Roberts

papers.title: Refractive Error Change and Overminus Lens Therapy for Childhood Intermittent Exotropia
papers.abstract: This randomized clinical trial extension evaluated the longitudinal (36-month) impact of overminus spectacle therapy on refractive error progression in children aged 3 to 10 years with intermittent exotropia (IXT). Participants were initially randomized to a protocol of -2.50 D overminus spectacles for 12 months followed by a weaning phase. The study primary outcome was the change in spherical equivalent refractive error from baseline to 3 years. Although an initial myopic shift was observed in the overminus group during active treatment, the analysis demonstrated that the rate of myopic progression over the full 36-month period did not significantly differ between the overminus and non-overminus cohorts, suggesting that the therapy does not induce long-term exacerbation of myopia in IXT patients.
papers.authors: Angela M Chen, Sergul A Erzurum, Danielle L Chandler, Amra Hercinovic, B Michele Melia, Amit R Bhatt, Donny W Suh, Marilyn Vricella, John W Erickson, Aaron M Miller, Justin D Marsh, Marie I Bodack, Stacy R Martinson, Jenna R Titelbaum, Susan A Cotter

papers.title: Effectiveness of vergence/accommodative therapy for accommodative dysfunction in children with convergence insufficiency
papers.abstract: As a secondary analysis of the Convergence Insufficiency Treatment Trial – Attention and Reading Trial (CITT-ART), this study evaluated the specific efficacy of office-based vergence/accommodative therapy (OBVAT) for improving accommodative function. Children aged 9 to 14 years with symptomatic convergence insufficiency and co-existing accommodative dysfunction (reduced amplitude or facility) were assessed. Outcome measures included monocular accommodative amplitude (push-up method) and accommodative facility (±2.00 D flippers). OBVAT resulted in statistically significant and clinically meaningful improvements in both accommodative amplitude and facility compared to placebo therapy, demonstrating that the accommodative subsystem can be effectively remediated through structured vision therapy protocols in this population.
papers.authors: Angela M Chen, Tawna L Roberts, Susan A Cotter, Marjean T Kulp, Lori T Sinnott, G Lynn Mitchell, Mitchell Scheiman

E271.name: Ben Deen
E271.bio: Ben Deen is an Assistant Professor in the Department of Psychology at Tulane University and a Faculty Associate of the Tulane Brain Institute. Deen's research utilizes high-resolution fMRI, intracranial recordings, and behavioral psychophysics to map the functional organization of the human brain, specifically regarding social perception and memory. By employing awake infant fMRI techniques, Deen identified that category-selective regions in the visual cortex are functional by four months of age. Their current investigations focus on the neural networks of the superior temporal sulcus and the parallel systems for social and spatial reasoning within the brain's association cortex.
E271.research_direction: Dr. Deen's recent work explores the functional and behavioral architecture of social cognition, specifically investigating how the primate brain processes, represents, and remembers other individuals. Using precision and multi-echo fMRI to overcome regional signal artifacts, they have recently been mapping how transmodal association areas and the Default Mode Network systematically segregate the processing of social agents from spatial environments. Their neuroimaging research investigates the specific anatomical pathways that bridge visual perception and conceptual memory, probing regions like the medial temporal lobe and the temporal pole to understand how the brain links familiar face recognition to high-level mental state attribution. Complementing this functional mapping and anatomical atlas development, they are also examining naturalistic social memory by designing novel behavioral paradigms that evaluate how humans encode and retain complex narrative details about people's traits, actions, and social ties over time.

papers.title: Developing a behavioral measure of social memory from narrative video
papers.abstract: Interpreting and predicting the behavior of others relies extensively on representations stored in long-term memory, such as traits, habits, and relationship histories. However, empirical instruments evaluating individual differences in naturalistic social memory remain scarce. This study designed and psychometrically assessed a novel behavioral measure evaluating memory for rich narrative content using the pilot episode of the television drama 'Friday Night Lights'. Following stimulus presentation, participants completed an extensive battery of multiple-choice items testing recall of characters' actions, direct statements, internal mental states, enduring traits, and social ties at multiple retention intervals. Memory performance across specific episodic event attributes (actions, statements, and mental states) exhibited high intercorrelation, supporting an integrated, unified social memory construct. Whereas performance for granular event details exhibited standard temporal decay, memory for higher-order abstract social attributes remained stable across delays. The task achieved moderate split-half reliability and demonstrated convergent validity through significant positive correlations with standardized verbal episodic memory and face-name association tasks, while establishing discriminant validity through an absence of correlation with perceptual face identity recognition memory.
papers.authors: Taylor Marcus, Didi Ross, Roma Kolluru, Ben Deen

papers.title: The MTL200: a surface-based, probabilistic atlas of the medial temporal lobe
papers.abstract: The primate medial temporal lobe (MTL) encompasses cortical regions surrounding the hippocampal formation—including the temporopolar cortex (TPC), entorhinal cortex (ERC), perirhinal cortex (PRC), and parahippocampal cortex (PHC)—that serve as essential transmodal gateways between neocortical sensory systems and declarative memory circuits. Existing anatomical atlases are predominantly volumetric, lack representation of TPC, or are constrained by small sample sizes, limiting surface-based analysis of neuroimaging data. Here, the authors introduce the MTL200: an open-resource, surface-based probabilistic atlas of human TPC, ERC, PRC, and PHC derived from manual annotations in 200 individual participants based on macroscopic sulcal boundaries matching cytoarchitectonic divisions. Probability maps and maximum-probability discrete labels were established in fsLR surface space alongside standard MNI152 volumetric space. Split-half cross-validation analyses confirmed high spatial consistency and reliability across the cohort. Furthermore, resting-state fMRI seed-based functional connectivity analyses revealed significant region-by-network interactions, demonstrating that the delineated MTL cortical subdivisions possess dissociable functional connectivity fingerprints with distinct large-scale neocortical networks.
papers.authors: Ian Faul, Adya Agarwal, Stephen Graziose, Andrew Nwacha, Janis Park, Anisah Sahibul, Katie Tong, Ben Deen

papers.title: Parallel systems for social and spatial cognition reaching the cortical apex
papers.abstract: This study tested the hypothesis that high-level human cognitive capacities for understanding social agents versus spatial environments are mediated by separate, parallel cortical networks. Using precision fMRI in individual subjects, blood-oxygen-level-dependent responses were mapped during visual perception, semantic trait judgments, and episodic simulation tasks targeting personally familiar people, familiar environments, and objects. The investigations uncovered two segregated, domain-preferring subnetworks within association cortex and the default mode network (DMN), spanning the medial prefrontal cortex (MPFC), medial parietal cortex (MPC), temporoparietal junction (TPJ), and superior frontal gyrus (SFG). In each major anatomical sector, person-selective and place-selective regions displayed consistent spatial adjacency and strong domain preference that persisted invariant to task modality. Intrinsic resting-state functional connectivity analyses revealed preferential within-domain network coupling. When mapped against the principal unimodal-to-transmodal cortical hierarchy, social and spatial processing streams remained segregated all the way to the cortical apex, incorporating distinct regions that form direct anatomical pathways to the hippocampal formation.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Ben Deen, Winrich A. Freiwald

papers.title: A familiar face and person processing area in the human temporal pole
papers.abstract: Human behavioral capabilities reveal specialized processing advantages for personally familiar faces over unfamiliar ones, yet identifying a dedicated familiar face region in the human temporal pole (TP) has long been impeded by severe magnetic susceptibility artifacts. Implementing multi-echo fMRI data acquisition and precision surface-based coregistration tailored to minimize signal loss, this study identified an area in human TP that responds selectively to visually presented familiar faces over unfamiliar faces, common objects, and scenes. In contrast to the adjacent perirhinal cortex (PR) and downstream ventral temporal face areas, the familiar face patch in TP was strongly recruited across diverse non-perceptual social cognitive tasks, including trait judgments, episodic simulation, and theory of mind reasoning. In addition, resting-state functional connectivity demonstrated that whereas PR preferentially couples with the ventral visual face stream, the TP region exhibits selective functional coupling with the broader default mode network subserving mental state attribution, establishing human TP as a critical link between visual face representations and high-level conceptual person memory.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Ben Deen, Gazi Husain, Winrich A. Freiwald

papers.title: Specialized Networks for Social Cognition in the Primate Brain
papers.abstract: This review synthesizes behavioral, electrophysiological, neuroimaging, and anatomical data across human and nonhuman primates to outline the functional architecture supporting social cognition. The authors examine the hierarchical organization of specialized cortical networks across three essential domains: face perception, dynamic social interaction analysis, and theory of mind mental state attribution. In the ventral stream, face-selective patches exhibit progressive coding principles spanning viewpoint-tuned individual units up to view-invariant identity representations. In the superior temporal sulcus (STS) and connected parietal areas, distinct circuits systematically parse social agent interactions. At the summit of the cortical hierarchy, regions within the default mode network (DMN)—including medial prefrontal, temporoparietal, and lateral temporal cortices—segregate into domain-specific subnetworks that run parallel to networks supporting nonsocial spatial computations. These comparative findings illustrate that modular domain-specific organization is not limited to sensory peripheries but is a defining architecture of transmodal association areas across the primate social brain.
papers.authors: Ben Deen, Caspar M. Schwiedrzik, Julia Sliwa, Winrich A. Freiwald

E272.name: Takao Hensch
E272.department: Department of Molecular and Cellular Biology
E272.bio: Takao Hensch identifies the biological mechanisms governing critical periods of brain development, specifically within the visual system. Their research integrates molecular, cellular, and systems neuroscience to demonstrate how specific inhibitory GABAergic circuits trigger the onset of these plastic windows, while molecular factors like perineuronal nets close them. Using mouse models and in vivo electrophysiology, Hensch’s laboratory investigates how early sensory experiences shape neural architecture and how these processes are altered in neurodevelopmental disorders. Their current work examines the potential to reopen plasticity in the adult brain to treat conditions such as amblyopia, autism, and mental illness.
E272.research_direction: Dr. Hensch has recently been investigating the biological mechanisms that govern the timing and limits of neural plasticity across the lifespan. Their recent work explores the markers and triggers of developmental critical periods, using EEG and visual evoked potentials to examine whether early exposure to general anesthesia accelerates visual circuit maturation in human infants, and investigating transient gamma-band oscillations as a potential biomarker for critical period onset in mice. Beyond early development, they are also probing the temporal constraints of adult visual plasticity, specifically asking how repetitive sensory stimulation and NREM sleep interact to consolidate cortical rewiring. Additionally, their research applies these principles of circuit balance to broader clinical and cognitive challenges, investigating how early life stress impacts dopamine-mediated visual attention and sleep architectures, and testing whether electromagnetic stimulation can drive neural recovery after a stroke by modulating the brain's metabolic and redox states.

papers.title: Frequency-specific electromagnetic modulation of brain redox state precedes cortical activity in stroke recovery
papers.abstract: The rehabilitation of neural function following ischemic stroke is contingent upon the restoration of metabolic homeostasis and circuit excitability within perilesional tissue. This study evaluates the efficacy of frequency-specific electromagnetic field (EMF) stimulation in modulating cortical states in a rodent model of cerebral ischemia. Utilizing real-time optical monitoring of NADH/NAD+ ratios alongside electrophysiological recordings, the authors demonstrate that EMF-induced shifts in the brain's redox potential occur significantly earlier than the recovery of stimulus-evoked cortical responses. These results establish that metabolic and redox rebalancing is a primary mechanism driving the neuroplastic effects of electromagnetic interventions, suggesting that redox-state dynamics serve as a predictive biomarker for functional recovery and therapeutic efficacy in stroke rehabilitation.
papers.authors: Henry Hing Cheong Lee, Shira Reznik Balter, Nathaniel W. Hodgson, Ana Parabucki, Batsheva Weisinger, Yaron Segal, Glen M. Doniger, Esther Shohami, Takao K. Hensch

papers.title: General anesthesia in early infancy accelerates visual cortical development
papers.abstract: Postnatal maturation of GABAergic inhibitory circuits is known to trigger the onset of critical periods for cortical plasticity in mammalian models. This investigation assesses whether exogenous potentiation of the GABA system via clinical general anesthesia (GA) alters the pace of human neurodevelopment. Through longitudinal visual evoked potential (VEP) recordings in a cohort of 93 infants, the study reveals that prolonged or repeated GA exposure (primarily sevoflurane and propofol) in the first six months of life leads to a premature maturation of VEP waveforms. This acceleration suggests that early exposure to GABA-active anesthetics may serve as an artificial trigger for critical period onset, potentially disrupting the typical windows of sensory plasticity and impacting the lifelong establishment of excitatory-inhibitory circuit balance in the human brain.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS)
papers.authors: Laurel J. Gabard-Durnam, Sarah A. McCormick, Ellen Underwood, Alice Tao, Isabelle Kim, Siobhan Coffman, Lindsay Benster, Maria Graziano, Charles A. Nelson, Charles B. Berde, Laura Cornelissen, Takao K. Hensch

papers.title: Rapid and cumulative adult plasticity in the mouse visual cortex
papers.abstract: Experience-dependent remodeling of the mature visual system can be elicited by repetitive sensory stimulation, yet the temporal constraints and consolidation mechanisms of adult plasticity remain poorly defined. This study utilizes flash-evoked visual potentials (VEPs) to characterize the induction and stabilization of response potentiation in the adult mouse primary visual cortex (V1). The researchers identified two distinct temporal phases: a rapid, within-session increase in VEP magnitude and a cumulative, multi-session potentiation across days. Mechanistic analysis indicates that while both phases require NMDA receptor-mediated signaling, the consolidation of cumulative plasticity is specifically dependent on NREM sleep. These findings provide a robust framework for understanding how sensory experience and sleep-dependent offline processing interact to regulate the boundaries of adult brain plasticity.
papers.authors: Hiroyuki Miyamoto, Emi Mazaki, Yuichi Makino, Q. Fang, T. Hamada, Youichi Handa, Takao K. Hensch

papers.title: Sleep-sensitive dopamine receptor expression in male mice underlies attention deficits after a critical period of early adversity
papers.abstract: Early life stress (ELS) is associated with long-term cognitive and emotional deficits, yet the circuit-level mechanisms remain largely unknown. This study identifies a neonatal critical period (P2–P9) in mice where fragmented maternal care induces a persistent imbalance in dopamine receptor expression within the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC). Adult male offspring exhibited significantly elevated D2R and suppressed D4R expression, which correlated with impaired performance in visual attention tasks and disrupted sleep architecture, including heightened NREM fragmentation and elevated hypothalamic orexin. These attention deficits were acutely rescued in adulthood by pharmacological restoration of D2/D4 signaling in the ACC. The findings establish a sleep-sensitive dopaminergic pathway as a critical mediator of the sex-specific cognitive consequences of early adversity.
papers.authors: Yuichi Makino, Nathaniel W. Hodgson, Emma Doenier, Anna Victoria Serbin, Koya Osada, Pietro Artoni, Matthew J. Smith, Dennis M. Twomey, Susan B. Mierau, Charles A. Nelson, Michela Fagiolini, Takao K. Hensch

papers.title: A transient neuronal oscillation signals the critical period for visual cortical plasticity
papers.abstract: The transition into windows of heightened neural plasticity, known as critical periods (CPs), is fundamental for the refinement of sensory circuits. This study demonstrates that a transient peak in gamma-band (40 Hz) EEG power serves as a robust biomarker for the open CP state in the primary visual cortex of mice. This oscillatory signature is acutely induced by sensory deprivation and is contingent upon the maturation of parvalbumin-positive (PV+) inhibitory interneurons, which facilitate the E-I circuit balance necessary for plastic rewiring. The identification of this gamma-band signal provides a non-invasive tool for monitoring the onset and closure of sensitive periods in brain development and may assist in the early detection of neurodevelopmental disorders characterized by deviant plasticity timing.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS)
papers.authors: Kathleen B. Quast, Rebecca K. Reh, Maddalena D. Adamo, Sameer C. Dhamne, Alexander Rotenberg, Michela Fagiolini, Takao K. Hensch

E273.name: Robert Hess
E273.bio: Robert Hess is a Professor of Ophthalmology at McGill University and Director of the McGill Vision Research Unit, focusing on the neurobiology of human vision and cortical plasticity. Their research integrates psychophysical experiments with computational modeling and multimodal neuroimaging, including fMRI and MEG, to investigate mechanisms of spatial, temporal, and motion perception. Hess has conducted research on binocular suppression and contour integration, resulting in the development of dichoptic digital therapeutics for amblyopia. Their current work explores the modulation of the adult visual cortex through non-invasive brain stimulation techniques to assist functional recovery in patients with visual impairments.
E273.research_direction: Dr. Hess has recently been investigating the mechanisms and treatments of binocular vision disorders, with a primary focus on amblyopia and stereopsis. Their recent work explores active therapeutic interventions for amblyopia—such as dichoptic visual training and non-invasive cortical stimulation—that specifically target interocular suppression to restore binocularity. To probe the neural underpinnings of this condition, they are combining flash suppression paradigms with steady-state visual evoked potentials to isolate the striate and top-down extrastriate contributions to amblyopic suppression. Furthermore, Dr. Hess has been examining the phenomenon of stereo-anomaly in healthy populations, utilizing digital psychophysics to dissociate basic binocular disparity detection from higher-order depth polarity discrimination.

papers.title: Towards a principled and efficacious approach to the treatment of amblyopia. A review.
papers.abstract: Current amblyopia management is undergoing a paradigm shift based on the understanding that binocular dysfunction, specifically interocular suppression, is the primary deficit rather than a secondary consequence of monocular acuity loss. This review evaluates the clinical transition from passive occlusion (patching) to active therapeutic interventions designed to restore binocularity. Specialized protocols involving dichoptic visual training, non-invasive cortical stimulation, and contrast-rebalanced stimuli are examined for their potential to leverage adult neuroplasticity. The analysis suggests that targeting the suppressive inhibitory networks directly provides a more effective and durable recovery of visual function, necessitating a re-evaluation of visual acuity as the gold standard for treatment endpoints.
papers.authors: Robert F Hess

papers.title: Stereo-anomaly is found more frequently in tasks that require discrimination between depths
papers.abstract: This study investigates the high variability in reported prevalence of 'stereo-anomaly' (defective stereopsis despite healthy vision), which ranges from 2% to 30%. Using a digital psychophysical battery, the researchers dissociated performance on disparity detection versus disparity discrimination (polarity judgment) tasks. In a cohort of 228 normally sighted individuals, 98% successfully completed detection-based trials, while only 69% reached criteria for discrimination. This suggests that a significant subset of the population possesses the neural circuitry to detect binocular disparity but lacks the higher-order processing required to correctly assign depth polarity (crossed vs. uncrossed), clarifying the nature of stereo-deficiency in the general population.
papers.authors: Alex S. Baldwin, Seung Hyun Min, Sara Alarcon Carrillo, Zili Wang, Ziyun Cheng, Jiawei Zhou, Robert F. Hess

papers.title: Flash Suppression Reveals an Additional Nonvisual Extrastriate Contribution for Amblyopic Suppression
papers.abstract: Anomalous binocular interactions in amblyopia were examined using a flash suppression paradigm combined with steady-state visual evoked potentials (ssVEPs). Thirteen adult amblyopes and matched controls performed behavioral tasks while cortical activity was recorded at occipital (Oz) and frontal locations. Results indicated that while interocular differences in subjective acuity were profound in amblyopes, occipital ssVEP responses did not show significant interocular differences at low spatial frequencies. However, flash suppression latencies were significantly extended when the amblyopic eye attempted to suppress the fellow eye. Crucially, specific frontal ssVEP modulations were observed, suggesting that amblyopic suppression involves a nonvisual extrastriate contribution likely related to top-down attentional control or selective inhibition.
papers.authors: Dave Saint-Amour, Laura Lefebvre, Clémence Bertrand Pilon, Robert F. Hess

E274.name: Zsuzsa Kaldy
E274.bio: Zsuzsa Kaldy is a Professor of Psychology at the University of Massachusetts Boston and the director of the Early Minds Lab. Kaldy’s research investigates the developmental trajectory of visual attention and visual working memory, specifically how infants and young children encode and maintain object representations. Using eye-tracking and pupillometric methodologies, they examine the intersection of cognitive effort and attentional focus in early learning processes. Their work integrates behavioral paradigms with developmental neuroscience to characterize typical development and the cognitive profiles of individuals with neurodevelopmental disorders such as autism spectrum disorder.
E274.research_direction: Dr. Kaldy has recently been investigating the development of visual working memory and executive function, with a major focus on how children strategically deploy cognitive resources. Their recent work explores the sampling-remembering trade-off using naturalistic paradigms, such as virtual shopping games, to measure how young children balance internal memory maintenance against cognitive offloading when the effort required to access external visual aids changes. Alongside these behavioral trade-offs, they are examining the mechanisms of proactive interference in visual working memory, using pupillometry to track the real-time cognitive effort required to manage trial-irrelevant item-location bindings during encoding and retrieval. Additionally, their research investigates broader environmental drivers of cognitive development, utilizing quasi-experimental meta-analyses to isolate how formal classroom schooling shapes the maturation of executive functions independently of chronological age.

papers.title: How Much Do You Remember When It's up to You? Measuring Memory Use Without Response Bias in Young Children
papers.abstract: This study utilized the 'Shopping Game' paradigm to investigate naturalistic visual working memory (VWM) utilization in children aged 4.5 to 7 years, specifically disentangling capacity limits from strategic memory deployment. By varying the accessibility costs of an external shopping list, the researchers quantified the context-dependent trade-off between environmental sampling and internal mnemonic maintenance. Results demonstrated that children dynamically adjust their reliance on external resources; as the cost of re-accessing the list increases, participants exhibit significantly higher internal memory load and application, suggesting that early cognitive control mechanisms are capable of optimizing resource allocation based on subjective effort and environmental constraints.
papers.authors: Candice Koolhaas, Erik Blaser, Zsuzsa Kaldy

papers.title: School changes minds: A meta-analysis shows that schooling modestly improves children's executive functions
papers.abstract: This meta-analysis synthesized 33 effect sizes from 12 studies (N ≈ 1,611; ages 4.5 to 9) to quantify the specific contribution of formal schooling to the development of executive functions (EF). Employing the school entry cut-off quasi-natural experiment, the study differentiated between maturation-driven and education-driven gains. A random-effects model revealed a small but statistically robust schooling effect (g = 0.24), indicating that the structured, goal-oriented environment of the classroom provides a significant boost to EF beyond chronological age. This finding offers a quantitative benchmark for the malleability of pediatric cognitive control and highlights the role of environmental demands in accelerating the maturation of neural circuits subserving EF.
papers.authors: Jamie Donenfeld, Mahita Mudundi, Erik Blaser, Zsuzsa Kaldy

papers.title: How attention and working memory work together in the pursuit of goals: The development of the sampling-remembering trade-off
papers.abstract: This theoretical opinion article proposes a resource-rational framework for understanding the developmental integration of selective attention and working memory (WM) in goal-directed behavior. The authors move beyond capacity-constrained models to describe a dynamic 'sampling-remembering trade-off,' where an agent's allocation of cognitive effort is dictated by the relative costs of external sampling versus internal maintenance. The proposed dynamic feedback model predicts that as the neurobiological constraints on WM and executive control relax throughout childhood, individuals will demonstrate an increasing propensity to favor internal retention over environmental re-sampling, reflecting a shift toward more efficient, goal-relevant information processing strategies.
papers.authors: Erik Blaser, Zsuzsa Kaldy

papers.title: The Extended Mind in Young Children: Cost-Dependent Trade-Off Between External and Internal Memory
papers.abstract: This cross-cultural investigation (US and China, N = 141) examined the developmental origins of 'cognitive offloading' in children aged 5 to 8 years. Participants performed a virtual shopping task where access to an external memory aid (a list) was parametrically manipulated via temporal delays (0–4 s). Results indicated that children exhibit a sophisticated sensitivity to access costs, reducing the frequency of external resource revisits and increasing the duration of internal encoding as delays increased. This cost-dependent strategic shift demonstrates that the 'extended mind'—the functional integration of external information with internal memory—is a robust feature of cognitive architecture that is established early in development and operates across diverse cultural contexts.
papers.authors: Yibiao Liang, Erik Blaser, Jia Ying Yi, Liyang Sai, Zsuzsa Kaldy

papers.title: The resolution of proactive interference in a novel visual working memory task: A behavioral and pupillometric study
papers.abstract: This study investigated the behavioral and pupillometric indices of proactive interference (PI) resolution in visual working memory (VWM) for item-location bindings. Utilizing a naturalistic paradigm that mixed PI and No-PI trials within blocks to minimize strategic encoding shifts, the researchers assessed the impact of previously encoded, trial-irrelevant information on current retrieval. Results showed a robust PI effect on VWM accuracy. While task-evoked pupillary responses—a real-time marker of cognitive effort—reliably predicted individual differences in encoding effort, they did not consistently reflect the specific effort of interference resolution at retrieval. This suggests that PI in VWM may be resolved via relatively implicit mechanisms when explicit strategic control is constrained.
papers.authors: Jamie Donenfeld, Erik Blaser, Zsuzsa Kaldy

E275.name: Lynne Kiorpes
E275.department: Center for Neural Science and Department of Psychology
E275.bio: Lynne Kiorpes is a Professor of Neural Science and Psychology at New York University and the Dean of the Graduate School of Arts and Science. Kiorpes investigates the neural mechanisms underlying the postnatal development of visual function and the pathophysiology of amblyopia using macaque monkey models. By integrating quantitative psychophysical methods with physiological and anatomical techniques, Kiorpes explores how early abnormal visual experience disrupts the maturation of visual pathways, particularly in extrastriate cortical areas. Their research characterizes the relationship between behavioral immaturities and neural responses with the goal of informing therapeutic interventions for developmental vision disorders.
E275.research_direction: Dr. Kiorpes has recently been investigating the neural mechanisms underlying the postnatal development of visual perception, using macaque monkey models to track how the visual system matures. Their recent work explores the development of global form and texture processing by pairing longitudinal psychophysical testing—such as radial frequency and naturalistic image discrimination tasks—with electrophysiological population recordings across the ventral visual stream. Specifically, they are examining whether the protracted, years-long refinement of spatial vision behavior is primarily constrained by the maturation of mid-level sensory representations in extrastriate areas like V4, or by the delayed development of downstream readout networks. Alongside this normative developmental research, Dr. Kiorpes is investigating the neurophysiological basis of experimental strabismic amblyopia to understand how signal transmission from the amblyopic eye is altered in dorsal stream regions like area MT, and how these neural changes disrupt temporal integration and motion perception.

papers.title: Neural Sensitivity to Radial Frequency Patterns in the Visual Cortex of Developing Macaques
papers.abstract: This study investigates the neural substrates of global form perception development by recording neuronal population activity in areas V1, V2, V4, and the posterior inferotemporal cortex (PIT) of young macaque monkeys (19–54 weeks) and an adult control. Using radial frequency stimuli—circular patterns with sinusoidal radial modulations—the researchers employed population decoding to evaluate whether improvements in behavioral sensitivity observed in early life are limited by the maturity of extrastriate representations. Findings reveal that while V1 neurons lack sensitivity to these global form patterns, populations in area V4 encode radial frequency stimuli maturely by 4–6 months of age. Because behavioral performance continues to refine long after these neural representations have stabilized, the results suggest that the primary bottlenecks for the development of shape perception reside in processing stages downstream of V4 rather than in the mid-level visual cortex itself.
papers.authors: Charlie L. Rodríguez Deliz, Gerick M. Lee, Brittany N. Bushnell, Najib J. Majaj, J. Anthony Movshon, Lynne Kiorpes

papers.title: Developmentally stable representations of naturalistic image structure in macaque visual cortex
papers.abstract: To determine whether postnatal improvements in form vision derive from developmental changes in mid-level visual cortical areas, this study analyzed neuronal and behavioral responses to synthetic texture stimuli containing naturalistic higher-order statistics versus spectrally matched noise. Longitudinal psychophysical testing showed that behavioral sensitivity to naturalistic structure reaches half-maximum at approximately 25 weeks of age. In contrast, multiunit neural sensitivity in areas V2 and V4 remained remarkably stable from the earliest recording point (20 weeks) through 56 weeks and into adulthood. Neural sensitivity was highest in V4 and significantly lower in V1. The observed dissociation between stable neural representations in the ventral stream and protracted behavioral maturation suggests that the limiting factors for texture perception development lie in the capacity of downstream circuits to effectively read out or integrate these stable sensory signals.
papers.authors: Gerick M. Lee, Charlie L. Rodríguez Deliz, Brittany N. Bushnell, Najib J. Majaj, J. Anthony Movshon, Lynne Kiorpes

papers.title: Development of radial frequency pattern perception in macaque monkeys
papers.abstract: This behavioral study characterizes the developmental trajectory of global shape sensitivity in macaque monkeys (aged 2 months to 10 years) using radial frequency (RF) stimuli. Utilizing a novel four-choice oddity task alongside traditional two-alternative forced-choice paradigms, the researchers measured discrimination thresholds for circular targets with sinusoidal radius modulations. Results indicate that RF pattern perception is present as early as 2 months postnatal, with sensitivity steadily improving well beyond the first year of life. Macaques exhibited higher sensitivity for patterns with higher radial frequencies (higher concentrations of curvature and orientation cues), matching the hyperacuity maturation patterns seen in humans. The study establishes a comprehensive behavioral benchmark for the protracted maturation of contour integration and global form processing in primates.
papers.authors: Charlie L. Rodríguez Deliz, Gerick M. Lee, Brittany N. Bushnell, Najib J. Majaj, J. Anthony Movshon, Lynne Kiorpes

papers.title: Responses to visual motion of neurons in the extrastriate visual cortex of macaque monkeys with experimental amblyopia
papers.abstract: Researchers characterized the representation of visual motion in the dorsal stream by recording single-unit responses in area MT and adjacent extrastriate regions of awake, fixating macaque monkeys with experimental strabismic amblyopia. Behavioral assessments confirmed substantial contrast and motion sensitivity deficits in these subjects. Neurophysiological results demonstrated a severe reduction in binocularity and a significant decrease in the number of neurons driven by the amblyopic eye compared to the fellow eye. While neurons driven by the amblyopic eye maintained qualitatively normal receptive field structures, they exhibited higher response variance and reduced evidence of temporal integration of upstream motion signals. The findings suggest that the primary driver of motion perception deficits in amblyopia is the reduction in the total number and strength of neuronal signals transmitted through the amblyopic eye to the extrastriate cortex.
papers.authors: Tom J. Van Grootel, Ramanujan T. Raghavan, Jenna G. Kelly, J. Anthony Movshon, Lynne Kiorpes

E276.name: Kang Lee
E276.department: Department of Applied Psychology and Human Development
E276.bio: Lee is a Tier 1 Canada Research Chair specializing in the developmental neuroscience of social cognition, specifically the mechanisms of face processing and the emergence of moral behaviors such as deception. Their research utilizes behavioral paradigms, eye-tracking, and neuroimaging techniques including fMRI, fNIRS, and EEG to examine how children perceive social categories and develop honesty. Lee is the co-inventor of Transdermal Optical Imaging (TOI), a contactless technology that employs machine learning to extract physiological data from facial blood flow patterns. Their work in vision science contributed to legal reforms in Canada regarding the standards for child witness testimony.
E276.research_direction: Dr. Lee has recently been investigating the cognitive, behavioral, and social factors that underlie cheating and moral transgressions in early childhood. Their recent work explores how individual traits and self-regulatory mechanisms, such as verbal intelligence, parent-reported conduct problems, and task-oriented persistence, relate to a young child's propensity to cheat during simulated academic assessments and unsupervised games. To understand the real-time dynamics of dishonesty, they are employing naturalistic paradigms to track whether specific nonverbal micro-behaviors—such as smiling or face-covering—can distinguish cheaters from non-cheaters during challenging tasks. Furthermore, they are testing social interventions to foster moral integrity, examining whether explicit interpersonal signals of trust can causally influence a child's likelihood of behaving honestly.

papers.title: Smiling, face covering, and rhythmic body rocking in children who cheat versus do not cheat
papers.abstract: This study analyzed the behavioral dynamics and nonverbal expressive markers of school-aged children (N=120, ages 4–7) during a challenging mathematical assessment to differentiate between honest and dishonest actors. By contrasting baseline expressive behaviors with critical test trials, the researchers identified that participants who engaged in cheating exhibited a significant elevation in smiling frequency during the test phase compared to non-cheaters. Notably, face-covering behavior emerged as a longitudinal predictor of dishonesty, manifesting throughout the experimental session and appearing even before children had an explicit opportunity for transgression. Rhythmic body rocking failed to yield significant discriminative utility. These results suggest that specific micro-behaviors and their temporal dynamics can serve as cues for identifying the precursors and correlates of cheating in early development.
papers.authors: Liyuzhi D. Dong, Kanza Batool, Catherine Ann Cameron, Kang Lee

papers.title: Bidirectional negative relation between young children's persistence and cheating
papers.abstract: This research utilized a cross-lagged experimental design to examine the reciprocal association between task-oriented persistence and academic cheating in 200 Han Chinese children aged 3 to 6 years. Study 1 demonstrated that situational persistence, rather than global trait persistence, was negatively correlated with the propensity to cheat in an unsupervised game environment. Study 2 confirmed these findings and further established a bidirectional negative relationship: while higher initial levels of situational persistence mitigated subsequent cheating behavior, the act of cheating itself predicted a significant decline in future task persistence. These findings elucidate the dynamic interplay between self-regulatory mechanisms and moral conduct during the critical preschool years.
papers.authors: Li Zhao, Junjie Peng, Kang Lee

papers.title: Cheating in childhood: Exploring the link between parental reports of problem behaviors and dishonesty on simulated academic tests
papers.abstract: Evaluated the predictive association between parent-reported behavioral disturbances and objective measures of academic cheating in school-aged children (N=439, ages 4–12). Using standardized psychiatric screening tools—specifically the Child Behavior Checklist (CBCL) and the Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire (SDQ)—the study monitored correlates of dishonesty across six simulated online assessments. Hierarchical regression analysis demonstrated that higher scores on the Conduct Problems subscale of the SDQ uniquely and significantly predicted cheating behavior, even after controlling for demographic variables such as age, gender, and ethnicity. In contrast, total CBCL scores and other SDQ subscales were not uniquely predictive, suggesting a specific link between early conduct-related phenotypes and moral transgressions in academic contexts.
papers.authors: Kaitlyn Wilson, Kanza Batool, Tz-Yu Duan, Catherine Ann Cameron, Kang Lee

papers.title: Young children with higher verbal intelligence are less likely to cheat
papers.abstract: This study explored the cognitive underpinnings of early childhood dishonesty by examining the unique roles of verbal and performance-based intelligence. In a sample of children (mean age = 5.73 years), the researchers administered a naturalistic cheating paradigm alongside standardized IQ assessments. Bootstrapping hierarchical logistic regression revealed that children with higher Verbal IQ scores were significantly less likely to engage in cheating behavior, a relationship that persisted after controlling for age, sex, and Performance IQ. Conversely, neither Performance IQ nor Total IQ scores demonstrated a significant independent relationship with cheating. The findings suggest that advanced verbal abilities may enhance a child's capacity for moral self-regulation or facilitate the cognitive integration of social norms, whereas non-verbal cognitive capacity does not appear to serve as a significant protective factor against dishonesty.
papers.authors: Li Zhao, Wenjin Sun, Kang Lee

papers.title: Trusting young children to help causes them to cheat less
papers.abstract: Through five pre-registered experimental studies (total N=328, mean age = 5.94 years), this research explored whether the interpersonal signaling of trust can causally induce honesty in kindergarteners. The experimental manipulation involved an adult either explicitly trusting children with a small task (e.g., safeguarding house keys) or withholding such a social signal before an unsupervised assessment of counting accuracy. Across all studies, children who received the trust-based message exhibited significantly lower rates of cheating compared to control participants. These findings provide robust experimental evidence for the reciprocity of trust in early childhood and suggest that fostering an ethos of trust serves as a potent social mechanism for internalizing and reinforcing moral integrity in developmental populations.
papers.authors: Li Zhao, Haiying Mao, Paul L. Harris, Kang Lee

E279.name: Glen Prusky
E279.lab_name: Laboratory for Visual Disease and Therapy
E279.bio: Glen Prusky is a neuroscientist whose research investigates the mechanisms of adaptive change and experience-dependent plasticity within the visual system. Prusky developed OptoMotry, a standardized virtual reality-based methodology that utilizes the optokinetic reflex to quantify visual thresholds in non-verbal subjects, ranging from rodent models to children with cerebral visual impairment. Their work integrates cellular, electrophysiological, and behavioral techniques to develop therapeutic interventions, including cell-based retinal transplantations and rehabilitative visual experiences for brain injury and stroke recovery. Currently, Prusky focuses on translating these psychophysical assessments into clinical tools to monitor and stimulate visual recovery in pediatric populations with neurological disorders.
E279.research_direction: Dr. Prusky has recently been developing objective, automated methods to assess spatial visual function in both hard-to-test clinical populations and animal models. Their recent work explores how to better quantify visual deficits and recovery trajectories in children with brain injury or cortical visual impairment by utilizing high-resolution eye-tracking, gamified Bayesian assessments, and AI-driven saliency modeling to measure contrast sensitivity, gaze kinematics, and the impact of environmental clutter. Concurrently, they are investigating the basic physiological substrates of spatial vision in mice, employing optokinetic tracking to map how isolated rod, cone, and intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cell populations drive spatial frequency resolution across varying luminance levels. By bridging basic retinal neurobiology with innovative pediatric psychophysics, their research aims to establish scalable, quantitative frameworks for diagnosing and monitoring complex visual system pathologies.

papers.title: A Novel Eye Tracking–Based Gamified Assessment of Contrast Sensitivity Function in Children: Prospective Development and Reliability Study
papers.abstract: Traditional psychophysical assessment of the contrast sensitivity function (CSF) in pediatric populations is constrained by the subjective nature of standard behavioral reports and the limited attentional capacity of young children. We developed an Eye Tracking–Based Gamified Contrast Sensitivity Function (ETGCSF) tool that utilizes automated gaze-contingent detection coupled with an adaptive Bayesian algorithm to objectively estimate contrast thresholds. In a prospective study of preschool-aged children, the ETGCSF demonstrated high test-retest reliability and significantly improved testing efficiency compared to standard methods. Our findings suggest that integrating eye-tracking with gamified reinforcement enables high-resolution spatial vision profiling in previously untestable or non-verbal pediatric populations, providing a scalable diagnostic tool for early detection of ocular and neurological visual pathologies.
papers.authors: Yunsi He, Yijing Zhuang, Lei Feng, Xuanyu Xu, Ying Deng, Moruomi Li, Yangfei Pang, Ying Yao, Wentong Yu, Zixuan Xu, Yusong Zhou, Yudan Zhong, Qiuying Li, Qingqing Ye, Junpeng Yuan, Yun Wen, Jinrong Li, Scott W. J. Mooney, Nazia M. Alam, Glen Prusky

papers.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI)-enabled Saliency analysis of Eye Tracking in Cerebral/Cortical Visual Impairment (SET-CVI)
papers.abstract: Cerebral/Cortical Visual Impairment (CVI) is often exacerbated by environmental clutter, yet quantifying this effect has historically relied on qualitative clinical observations. We employed generative artificial intelligence to conduct saliency modeling on eye-tracking data from children with CVI viewing complex naturalistic scenes. By correlating gaze kinematics with algorithmic metrics of scene saliency and clutter, we identified distinct patterns of visual search inefficiency and increased visual fatigue associated with high-complexity stimuli. The results demonstrate that AI-driven saliency analysis can objectively differentiate CVI-specific processing deficits from neurotypical gaze behavior, offering a quantitative framework for characterizing functional vision and optimizing rehabilitative strategies in brain-injured children.
papers.authors: C. Van Hove, Claudia Damiano, Nofar Ben Itzhak, Nazia M. Alam, Scott W. J. Mooney, Glen Prusky

papers.title: Luminance-dependent spatial visual function of adult mice with genetic alterations of photoreceptor activity
papers.abstract: To elucidate the contributions of discrete photoreceptor populations to spatial vision across the light-intensity spectrum, we measured optokinetic tracking (OKT) thresholds in mice with genetically isolated cone, rod, or intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cell (ipRGC) pathways. We characterized spatial frequency resolution and contrast sensitivity across a broad range of ambient luminance. Our results map the distinct luminance boundaries of rod- and cone-mediated spatial vision and demonstrate that spatial frequency thresholds are dynamically modulated by ambient light levels. These data provide a comprehensive characterization of the luminance-dependent operating range of the murine visual system and identify the physiological substrates underlying spatial visual behavior in scotopic, mesopic, and photopic environments.
papers.authors: Nazia M. Alam, Cara Altimus, Robert M. Douglas, Glen Prusky

papers.title: Quantitative patterns of visual impairment and recovery in children with brain injury
papers.abstract: Pediatric brain injury results in complex visual deficits that are often poorly quantified due to comorbid cognitive and communicative impairments. We utilized the 'Visual Ladder,' a gaze-based interactive software program, to longitudinally measure eye movement kinematics, visual field symmetries, and contrast sensitivity in a cohort of hospitalized children with diverse brain injuries. Our analysis identifies distinct diagnostic clusters of visual impairment based on objective psychophysical metrics and characterizes specific trajectories of functional recovery over time. These findings indicate that automated, high-resolution eye-tracking assessments can overcome the limitations of subjective clinical evaluations, providing a robust evidence base for the prognosis and management of pediatric cortical visual impairment.
papers.authors: Scott W. J. Mooney, Nazia M. Alam, Matthew J. Sciarabba, Kieran R. Sheldon, Glen T. Prusky

E280.name: Karthik Shekhar
E280.department: Department of Chemical and Biomolecular Engineering
E280.bio: Shekhar is the John F. Heil Jr. Professor at UC Berkeley, directing a research program at the intersection of neuroscience, genomics, and biophysics. Their work employs high-throughput single-cell transcriptomics and statistical machine learning to characterize the molecular diversity of neuronal types in the retina and visual cortex. Shekhar investigates how neural circuits develop and evolve across vertebrate species, and how sensory experience and electrical activity refine neuronal identity. Additionally, the Shekhar lab develops theoretical models to understand the electrochemical dynamics and diffuse charge transport at biological membrane interfaces.
E280.research_direction: Dr. Shekhar's recent work explores the molecular diversity, development, and biophysics of sensory systems across multiple scales. Using comparative single-cell transcriptomics, they have recently been investigating the evolutionary divergence of vertebrate photoreceptor types and examining how spontaneous cholinergic retinal waves shape the transcriptomic identity of developing retinal ganglion cells. Their recent research also extends beyond the visual system to explore how sensory experience and deprivation influence the transcriptomic maturation and plasticity of neuronal cell types in the developing somatosensory cortex. Furthermore, Dr. Shekhar investigates the fundamental physical principles of bioelectric signaling, utilizing computational and theoretical models to understand how localized ion channel currents drive spatiotemporal ionic reorganization and transient electric fields at biological membrane interfaces.

papers.title: Comparative transcriptomic insights into the evolution of vertebrate photoreceptor types
papers.abstract: To investigate the molecular diversification and potential evolutionary orthology of vertebrate photoreceptor types, we performed comparative single-cell and single-nucleus transcriptomic profiling across six vertebrate species, including zebrafish, lizard, and human. We identified conserved gene expression signatures defining the ancestral rod and four single cone types (red, green, blue, and UV). We further characterized the molecular identity of tetrapod double cones, identifying specific markers for their principal and accessory members. Integrative analysis suggests that double cone members likely diverged from ancestral red cones, and reveals that transcriptomic variation among cone subtypes correlates with their spectral sensitivity order. Conversely, rods were found to be highly distinct from all cone types, suggesting an evolutionary divergence that predates the spectral diversification of cones.
papers.authors: Dario Tommasini, Takeshi Yoshimatsu, Teresa Puthussery, Tom Baden, Karthik Shekhar

papers.title: Cholinergic waves have a modest influence on the transcriptome of retinal ganglion cells
papers.abstract: Spontaneous cholinergic retinal waves are essential for the refinement of visual circuits, yet their role in regulating the transcriptomic identity of retinal ganglion cell (RGC) types has remained unclear. Utilizing single-cell RNA sequencing to profile RGCs from wild-type and wave-disrupted (beta2-nAChR-knockout) mice during the first postnatal week, we assessed the extent of activity-dependent transcriptional regulation. We found that the absence of cholinergic waves resulted in relatively minor transcriptomic shifts compared to the substantial changes observed during normal postnatal development. Our analysis identified approximately 238 genes with type-specific differential expression, including the potassium leak channel Kcnk9 (TASK3). These findings suggest that the effects of spontaneous activity on RGC maturation are primarily mediated through post-transcriptional or local synaptic mechanisms rather than large-scale gene regulatory remodeling.
papers.authors: Rachana Deven Somaiya, Matthew A. Po, Marla B. Feller, Karthik Shekhar

papers.title: Molecular states underlying neuronal cell type development and plasticity in the postnatal whisker cortex
papers.abstract: We assembled a developmental transcriptomic atlas of the mouse whisker somatosensory cortex (wS1), identifying 45 molecularly distinct neuronal types. By comparing the maturation of wS1 and the primary visual cortex (V1) between postnatal days 12 and 22, we observed a conserved compositional shift in layer 2/3 (L2/3) glutamatergic neurons. Unlike in V1, where vision is required for this transition, full-face whisker deprivation in wS1 did not significantly impact the maturation of transcriptomic cell identities or subclass-specific gene programs. However, an acute, one-day competitive whisker deprivation protocol triggered robust, subclass-specific upregulation of activity-dependent genes within the corresponding barrel columns. Our results indicate that while the basal molecular maturation of wS1 neuronal types is largely experience-independent, these cells retain the capacity for rapid transcriptomic plasticity in response to sensory perturbations.
papers.authors: Salwan Butrus, Hannah R. Monday, Christopher J. Yoo, Daniel E. Feldman, Karthik Shekhar

papers.title: Spatiotemporal dynamics of ionic reorganization near biological membrane interfaces
papers.abstract: We present a theoretical and computational framework to investigate the spatiotemporal evolution of ionic diffuse charge layers at the interfaces of biological membranes. Traditional models of neural signaling often simplify membranes and electrolytes as equivalent RC circuits, neglecting the localized nature of ion fluxes and the resulting transient electric fields. Using matched asymptotic expansions of the Poisson-Nernst-Planck (PNP) equations, we model the multiscale coupling between nanometer-scale screening layers and micrometer-scale bulk electrolyte transport under conditions of uniform and localized ionic pumping. We identify three distinct spatial regimes of signal propagation—near-field, monopolar, and far-field—and show that localized pumping generates long-ranged electric fields that propagate in-plane with speeds significantly faster than bare diffusion. These findings suggest that transient ionic reorganization may play an unappreciated role in fast biological signaling.
papers.authors: Hyeongjoo Row, Joshua B Fernandes, Kranthi K Mandadapu, Karthik Shekhar

papers.title: Electrochemical response of biological membranes to localized currents and external electric fields
papers.abstract: This study analyzes the transient electrochemical response of a lipid membrane-electrolyte system subjected to localized transmembrane currents, emulating ion channel activity, and external electric fields. By applying matched asymptotic expansions to the Poisson-Nernst-Planck (PNP) equations, we derive analytical expressions for the transmembrane potential across multiple time and length scales. We show that the system's response partitions into distinct temporal regimes, ranging from rapid interfacial charging to long-term steady-state behavior. Our model demonstrates that the presence of electrodes and the finite thickness of the lipid bilayer fundamentally alter the charging dynamics compared to a bare electrolyte. At sufficiently long times, the system converges to an equivalent circuit description analogous to classical cable theory, providing a microscopic foundation for understanding the propagation of bioelectric signals in confined physiological geometries.
papers.authors: Joshua B Fernandes, Hyeongjoo Row, Kranthi K Mandadapu, Karthik Shekhar

E281.name: Elizabeth Spelke
E281.bio: Elizabeth Spelke is a researcher in cognitive development who formulated the core knowledge theory, which posits that infants possess innate systems for representing objects, agents, and number. Their methodology utilizes behavioral tasks, such as habituation and looking-time paradigms, to map the cognitive foundations of human knowledge. Spelke’s current research focuses on how these systems interact with language and symbolic thought to facilitate capacities for formal mathematics and abstract reasoning.
E281.research_direction: Dr. Spelke's recent work explores the developmental origins and boundary conditions of foundational cognitive systems across social, mathematical, and perceptual domains. Using anticipatory looking and reaching paradigms, they have recently been examining early social evaluation to determine how pre-verbal infants and toddlers use interactive cues like imitation or the physical costs of a task to infer social affiliations and identify prosocial helpers. In the domain of numerical cognition, their research investigates the representational formats of mathematical knowledge by testing whether domain-specific arithmetic skills acquired in real-world market environments successfully transfer to abstract, school-based learning contexts. Additionally, they are evaluating broader theoretical frameworks of the developing mind, synthesizing interdisciplinary perspectives on innate "core knowledge" systems and reviewing how historical ecological approaches to perception continue to influence the study of biological and artificial intelligence.

papers.title: Children's arithmetic skills do not transfer between applied and academic mathematics
papers.abstract: This field investigation evaluated the transferability of arithmetic competence between vocational and academic domains in children working in market environments in India (n = 1,436). The experimental results demonstrated that while these children effectively executed complex mental arithmetic during real-world transactions and in contextualized verbal problems, they exhibited a significant failure in solving isomorphic arithmetic problems when presented in the abstract format standard to school-based curricula. Conversely, a control group of non-working school children (n = 471) performed more accurately on abstract problems but failed to solve applied market-math problems. These findings underscore a critical lack of transfer between intuitive, domain-specific arithmetic acquired through practice and formal, symbolic mathematical systems, suggesting that educational curricula must bridge these disparate representational formats.
papers.authors: Abhijit V. Banerjee, Swati Bhattacharjee, Raghabendra Chattopadhyay, Esther Duflo, Alejandro J. Ganimian, Kailash Rajah, Elizabeth S. Spelke

papers.title: Infants use imitation but not comforting or social synchrony to evaluate those in social interactions
papers.abstract: To identify the specific social cues diagnostic of affiliation and prosocial value in early development, this research presented pre-reaching infants with dyadic social interactions involving imitation, comforting, or social synchrony. Utilizing anticipatory looking and manual reaching paradigms, the studies tested whether infants use these cues to predict future social approach and to form social preferences. The results indicated that while infants robustly used imitative behavior to infer social relationships and preferred imitators over non-imitators, they did not make similar inferences or display preferences based on comforting or synchronized movements. These findings suggest that imitation serves as a privileged cue in the core social cognition system for representing social relationships and evaluating social partners.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the 47th Annual Meeting of the Cognitive Science Society (CogSci 2025)
papers.authors: Ashley Thomas, Rebecca Saxe, Elizabeth S. Spelke

papers.title: Toddlers prefer agents who help those facing harder tasks
papers.abstract: This study investigated whether 16-month-old toddlers (N = 94) utilize cost-benefit analysis in their social evaluation of third-party helping actions. Across three experiments, the researchers tested whether toddlers differentiate between helpers based on the physical costs faced by the beneficiaries, distinguishing between agent-general costs (task difficulty) and agent-specific costs (individual competence). The findings reveal that toddlers selectively prefer agents who provide aid to individuals facing higher costs, whether due to the inherent difficulty of the task or the limited abilities of the beneficiary. This provides evidence that early social-evaluative mechanisms are integrated with naive utility calculus, allowing toddlers to prioritize prosocial actors who provide help where the need—defined as the required physical work—is greatest.
papers.venue: Open Mind: Discoveries in Cognitive Science
papers.authors: Brandon M. Woo, Shari Liu, Hyowon Gweon, Elizabeth S. Spelke

papers.title: Response to commentaries on What Babies Know
papers.abstract: In this comprehensive synthesis of current developmental cognitive science, the author addresses twenty-five critical commentaries on the core knowledge framework.
