The discussion evaluates the ontogenetic origins of domain-specific concepts, the interplay between iconic and propositional representational formats in the infant mind, and the distinct computational structures of numerical and social cognition. The author refines the definition of core systems as automatic, unconscious mechanisms that occupy a middle ground between low-level perception and high-level explicit belief, while evaluating new interdisciplinary methods—from computational modeling to neuroimaging—that probe the boundary conditions and combinatorial properties of these innate cognitive systems.
papers.authors: Elizabeth S. Spelke

papers.title: Eleanor Jack Gibson: A Life in Science
papers.abstract: This review provides a comprehensive analysis of Eleanor Gibson's scientific contributions to the fields of perception, learning, and developmental psychology. The article discusses Gibson’s challenge to behaviorist and Helmholtzian paradigms through her development of an ecological approach to perception, which emphasizes the active discovery of environmental affordances. It evaluates her pioneering experimental methods, including the 'visual cliff' and studies of perceptual differentiation, and discusses how her unified science of perception continues to influence modern research on the development of intelligence in biological and artificial systems. The author situates Gibson's work within the history of psychology and highlights its role in the shift toward a representational, information-based understanding of the developing mind.
papers.authors: Elizabeth S. Spelke

E283.name: John-Dylan Haynes
E283.department: Bernstein Center for Computational Neuroscience Berlin
E283.main_research_area: cognitive neuroscience and mental state decoding
E283.bio: John-Dylan Haynes is a Professor at the Bernstein Center for Computational Neuroscience Berlin and Director of the Berlin Center for Advanced Neuroimaging. Haynes's research focuses on decoding mental states from human brain activity using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA). Their work on the neural prediction of volitional decisions demonstrates that intentions can be decoded from brain signals several seconds before reaching conscious awareness. Haynes's current research explores the boundaries of brain-reading technology, the neural correlates of consciousness, and the ethical implications of neurotechnology.
E283.research_direction: Dr. Haynes has recently been investigating the neural representation and temporal dynamics of visual memory, focusing heavily on how the early visual cortex maintains information. Their recent fMRI and multivariate decoding work explores visual working memory to understand whether mnemonic representations remain purely sensory or undergo neural reformatting during prolonged maintenance, sensory distraction, and across individuals with differing mental imagery vividness. Additionally, they are investigating the micro-timing of early perceptual extraction, using partial-report paradigms to quantify the exact cue-readout latencies of iconic memory traces. To better probe these complex visual feature spaces, Dr. Haynes is also developing new methodological pipelines that utilize latent diffusion models to synthesize highly controlled, psychophysically validated naturalistic image stimuli.

papers.title: Neural dynamics of visual working memory representation during sensory distraction
papers.abstract: This study employs functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) to investigate the resilience of visual working memory (VWM) representations under sensory interference. By re-analyzing high-resolution data from a delayed recall task involving oriented gratings, the researchers demonstrate that stimulus-specific information remains decodable from early visual cortex (V1–V3) even when perturbed by high-contrast distractors. The results reveal that VWM representations undergo dynamic population-level transitions, shifting between sensory-like and distractor-resistant formats. This suggests that the human visual system leverages high-dimensional neural subspaces to multiplex incoming sensory input and stable mnemonic content, ensuring representational fidelity across the delay period.
papers.authors: Jonas Karolis Degutis, Simon Weber, Joram Soch, John-Dylan Haynes

papers.title: Synthesis and perceptual scaling of high-resolution naturalistic images using Stable Diffusion
papers.abstract: The authors present a methodological pipeline for the generation and psychophysical validation of high-resolution, naturalistic stimulus sets using latent diffusion models (specifically Stable Diffusion XL). To address the challenge of controlling semantic and physical properties in naturalistic scenes, the study employs a systematic text-to-image synthesis approach to create image continua. Critically, these stimuli are validated using maximum likelihood difference scaling (MLDS) to ensure that the Euclidean distances within the model's latent space correspond to human perceptual distances. This framework provides a rigorous tool for neuroimaging and vision research requiring fine-grained control over complex, photorealistic visual feature spaces.
papers.authors: Leonardo Pettini, Carsten Bogler, Christian F. Doeller, John-Dylan Haynes

papers.title: Temporal dynamics and readout latency in perception and iconic memory
papers.abstract: Using a partial-report paradigm with variable inter-stimulus intervals (ISIs) and cue timings, this study examines the micro-timing of information extraction from the iconic memory trace. The researchers quantify the 'cue-readout latency'—the temporal delay between the physical onset of a selection cue and the initiation of information transfer from the sensory buffer into a reportable state. Empirical findings indicate a readout latency of approximately 10–30 milliseconds. The results demonstrate that the observed decay of available information prior to physical stimulus offset is primarily an artifact of neural transmission delays (SLT and SLC), offering a revised model of the transition from perceptual encoding to sensory memory decay.
papers.authors: Karla Matić, Issam Tafech, Peter König, John-Dylan Haynes

papers.title: Visual working memory representations of naturalistic images in early visual cortex are not sensory-like
papers.abstract: Testing the sensory recruitment model of working memory, this investigation compares the neural representational format of naturalistic object-scenes during perception and mnemonic maintenance. Using fMRI-based multivariate cross-decoding, the study demonstrates that while early visual areas (V1–V3) contain stimulus-specific information throughout the delay period, the representational geometry in the later delay significantly diverges from the sensory format observed during encoding. These findings suggest that visual working memory involves a 'sensory reformatting' process, where mnemonic information is transformed from a purely sensory-like state toward a more stable or abstract representational code robust to temporal decay.
papers.authors: Leonardo Pettini, Carsten Bogler, Karla Matic, Kai Görgen, Christian F. Doeller, John-Dylan Haynes

papers.title: Working memory signals in early visual cortex are present in weak and strong imagers
papers.abstract: This study evaluates whether the recruitment of early visual cortex (EVC) for working memory depends on the vividness of individual mental imagery. Participants stratified into 'weak' and 'strong' imagers (including individuals with aphantasia) performed a delayed orientation-discrimination task during fMRI. Multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) revealed that orientation information was decodable with comparable precision from EVC in both groups, regardless of subjective imagery vividness. Furthermore, the fidelity of these sensory-like neural signals was equally predictive of behavioral performance in both weak and strong imagers, suggesting that VWM recruitment of sensory areas is a general mechanism dissociable from phenomenal imagery experience.
papers.authors: Simon Weber, Thomas Christophel, Kai Görgen, Joram Soch, John-Dylan Haynes

E284.name: Marius Peelen
E284.bio: Marius Peelen is a Professor of Visual and Cognitive Neuroscience and a Principal Investigator at the Donders Institute. Peelen investigates the neural mechanisms that enable efficient object and scene perception in naturalistic environments, bridging the gap between low-level visual processing and higher-order cognitive functions. Utilizing multivariate neuroimaging techniques such as fMRI and MEG alongside behavioral psychophysics, Peelen examines how top-down factors—including attention, expectations, and episodic memory—shape cortical representations. Recent work by Peelen focuses on the predictive nature of the visual system and the competitive interactions between external sensory input and internal cognitive processes like visual imagery.
E284.research_direction: Dr. Peelen's recent work explores how the visual system leverages environmental context to guide attention and facilitate object recognition in naturalistic scenes. Using techniques like fMRI, EEG, and multivariate decoding, they are investigating how 3D scene geometry and familiar "object constellations" generate predictive signals that dynamically update visual representations across time, even during periods of occlusion. Their research also examines the neural mechanisms of contextual guidance during real-world visual search, specifically asking whether preparatory activity in the object-selective visual cortex forms attentional templates tuned to the actual search targets or to spatial "anchor" objects. Additionally, Dr. Peelen has recently been probing the bottom-up processing of social stimuli, utilizing large-scale inattentional blindness paradigms to determine whether the human visual system possesses an inherent, attention-free sensitivity for upright human bodies.

papers.title: Dynamic context-based updating of object representations in the visual cortex
papers.abstract: This study employed functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) to demonstrate that the visual cortex dynamically updates object-level representations using predictive signals derived from the three-dimensional (3D) geometric structure of the surrounding scene. The researchers found that visual cortical representations of objects were significantly enhanced when their rotation was congruent with the viewpoint changes of the scene context. Furthermore, multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) revealed that the predicted orientation of objects could be decoded from activity in the visual cortex even during periods of complete occlusion. These findings indicate that the visual system maintains and updates latent object features via predictive contextual information to support perception in dynamic, naturalistic environments.
papers.authors: Giacomo Aldegheri, Surya Gayet, Marius V. Peelen

papers.title: The timecourse of inter-object contextual facilitation
papers.abstract: This investigation utilized electroencephalography (EEG) and multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) to characterize the temporal dynamics of 'object constellations'—familiar configurations of contextually associated objects. By assessing the neural representation of objects' real-world size as a proxy for recognition, the authors demonstrated that the visual system integrates information across multiple objects starting approximately 200 ms post-stimulus. Representational similarity analysis revealed that high-level representations of large and small real-world objects were significantly more robust when objects were presented in contextually associated pairs (e.g., chair and table) compared to isolated silhouettes. These results suggest that inter-object co-occurrence statistics facilitate visual processing by producing qualitatively distinct, integrated representations of familiar object groups.
papers.authors: Genevieve L. Quek, Alexandra Theodorou, Marius V. Peelen

papers.title: A body detection inversion effect revealed by a large-scale inattentional blindness experiment
papers.abstract: Using a large-scale, single-trial inattentional blindness paradigm (N = 13,539), the authors identified a robust 'body detection inversion effect' indicating specialized bottom-up sensitivity to the upright human form. The study found that silhouettes of people were detected significantly more frequently than silhouettes of plants, and upright person silhouettes were noticed more often than inverted ones despite identical low-level visual features. This preference for upright configural social cues persisted in the absence of top-down attention or explicit expectations, suggesting that the human visual system is inherently tuned to the upright human body to facilitate rapid social detection and perception.
papers.authors: Marco Gandolfo, Marius V. Peelen

papers.title: The neural basis of visual search in scene context
papers.abstract: This review synthesizes recent neuroimaging evidence to describe the neural substrates of contextual guidance during visual search in real-world scenes. The author argues that the object-selective visual cortex (OSC) plays a central role in mediating multiple types of contextual influences, including spatial regularities and semantic associations. The paper details how scene context triggers preparatory activity in the OSC that serves as a context-dependent 'attentional template,' biasing sensory processing toward task-relevant locations and features. Evidence from fMRI, MEG, and TMS demonstrates that these contextual signals are causally necessary for efficient object identification and that they facilitate visual search through interactions between the ventral stream and higher-level control regions.
papers.authors: Marius V. Peelen

papers.title: Attentional guidance through object associations in visual cortex
papers.abstract: This study addressed whether preparatory neural activity in the visual cortex represents the search target itself or the 'anchor' objects that provide spatial guidance in structured environments. Using functional MRI and eye-tracking, the researchers demonstrated that initial fixations were consistently directed toward target-associated anchor objects. Multivariate pattern analysis revealed that preparatory activity in the lateral occipital complex (LOC) and the right intraparietal sulcus (IPS) primarily represented the features of the guiding anchor object rather than the target category. These findings suggest that the visual system's 'attentional template' adaptively prioritizes contextual information over target features to facilitate efficient guidance in naturalistic visual search.
papers.authors: Maëlle Lerebourg, Floris P. de Lange, Marius V. Peelen

E286.name: Shinji Nishimoto
E286.bio: Nishimoto is a Professor at Osaka University and a Principal Investigator at the Center for Information and Neural Networks (CiNet). Their research focuses on the quantitative modeling of human brain activity evoked by naturalistic stimuli to investigate the neural basis of perceptual and cognitive functions. Nishimoto has worked on reconstructing dynamic visual experiences from fMRI signals and developing brain-decoding techniques using deep learning and generative models. Their current projects involve building high-dimensional encoding models to examine how the brain represents information across diverse modalities, timescales, and internal states.
E286.research_direction: Dr. Nishimoto has recently been using advanced deep neural networks, including large language models and generative AI, as frameworks to map how the human brain represents complex information across diverse sensory domains. Their recent work explores the hierarchical organization of semantics during naturalistic experiences, investigating how distributed cortical networks process multi-modal movie features, musical attributes, and spontaneous conversational dialogue. Additionally, they are benchmarking the spatiotemporal limits of visual decoding by formally comparing large-scale image representations across fMRI, MEG, and EEG recordings. Finally, their research examines the representational geometry of various cognitive tasks to isolate which neural functional architectures are universal across individuals and which remain highly idiosyncratic.

papers.title: A Quantitative Benchmark of Visual Information in Human Brain Recordings Across fMRI, MEG, and EEG
papers.abstract: This research establishes a formal quantitative benchmark for evaluating the representational information content across functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), magnetoencephalography (MEG), and electroencephalography (EEG) under identical experimental conditions. Utilizing the large-scale THINGS image database consisting of 1,854 object categories, the authors employ a unified decoding and encoding pipeline to assess the representational fidelity of each modality. The findings delineate a clear efficiency-precision trade-off: fMRI exhibits the highest spatial specificity and asymptotic decoding accuracy (reaching ~87%) for categorical representations, whereas MEG and stimulus-level aggregated EEG (group-level structure) demonstrate superior efficiency in capturing hierarchical visual features within short measurement intervals. This framework provides a principled basis for cross-modal comparison and modality selection based on the spatiotemporal scaling properties of visual neural representations.
papers.authors: Taisei Hara, Yoshito Masai, Shinji Nishimoto

papers.title: Text-to-music generation models capture musical semantic representations in the human brain
papers.abstract: This study investigates the functional correspondence between generative music models and the human auditory system by reconstructing heard musical stimuli from fMRI signals. Using the MusicLM framework and joint music-text embeddings (MuLan), the authors develop voxel-wise encoding models to map high-level musical semantics—such as genre, instrumentation, and mood—onto cortical activity. Results demonstrate that music-specific deep neural network (DNN) features provide significantly higher predictive accuracy for activity in the primary auditory cortex and superior temporal gyrus compared to general auditory models. Furthermore, the researchers achieve high-fidelity music reconstruction through retrieval-based decoding and latent conditioning of the MusicLM generator, indicating that the brain's internal representations of musical meaning are hierarchically aligned with the feature extraction mechanisms of state-of-the-art generative AI.
papers.authors: Timo I. Denk, Yu Takagi, Takuya Matsuyama, Andrea Agostinelli, Tomoya Nakai, Christian Frank, Shinji Nishimoto

papers.title: Conversational content is organized across multiple timescales in the brain
papers.abstract: Using fMRI hyperscanning of interacting dyads, this paper explores the neural architecture of language production and comprehension during spontaneous, interactive dialogue. By applying encoding models based on contextual word embeddings from large language models (LLMs), the authors quantify the linguistic coupling between speakers and listeners across broadly distributed cortical networks. The research identifies a timescale-dependent functional organization: shorter linguistic units (words and sentences) engage overlapping neural populations for production and comprehension, while longer-range discourse structures and narrative contexts recruit distinct, specialized systems. These findings suggest that the human brain dynamically adapts its representational strategy to facilitate mutual understanding across varying hierarchical levels of conversational meaning.
papers.authors: Masahiro Yamashita, Rieko Kubo, Shinji Nishimoto

papers.title: Cortical representational geometry of diverse tasks reveals subject-specific and subject-invariant cognitive structures
papers.abstract: This investigation examines the variability and invariance of cognitive representational geometry in the human cortex across 25 diverse tasks using fMRI. By integrating inter-subject correlation (ISC) and representational similarity analysis (RSA), the authors quantify the consistency of the abstract 'cognitive structure'—defined by the relational distances between task-evoked activity patterns. While primary sensory and higher-order visual regions exhibit high inter-subject invariance, the representational geometry in the fronto-parietal association cortex is found to be significantly individualized. Despite this person-specific variability, the idiosyncratic cognitive structures are robust enough to allow for 100% accurate subject identification from multi-task neural data, revealing a fundamental duality between shared functional backbones and highly individualized cognitive control systems.
papers.authors: Tomoya Nakai, Rieko Kubo, Shinji Nishimoto

papers.title: Unveiling Multi-level and Multi-modal Semantic Representations in the Human Brain using Large Language Models
papers.abstract: To map the hierarchical organization of semantic information in the human brain, this study utilizes fMRI recordings from participants viewing 8.3 hours of naturalistic movie stimuli. The authors employ Large Language Models (LLMs) to extract multi-level latent representations corresponding to speech content, visual object categories, and narrative story context. Voxel-wise encoding models demonstrate that LLM-derived features significantly outperform traditional semantic models, particularly in modeling the high-level background narrative. The research reveals a systematic cortical distribution of semantic selectivity: speech information is localized in temporal language networks, visual objects in the ventral stream, and story-level context in the default mode network, underscoring the necessity of multi-modal and multi-level modeling to understand how the brain constructs coherent narrative experiences.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the 2024 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP)
papers.authors: Yuko Nakagi, Takuya Matsuyama, Naoko Koide-Majima, Hiroto Q. Yamaguchi, Rieko Kubo, Shinji Nishimoto, Yu Takagi

E287.name: Umut Güçlü
E287.bio: Umut Güçlü is a Principal Investigator at the Donders Institute for Brain, Cognition and Behaviour, focusing on the integration of neuroscience and artificial intelligence. Güçlü’s research utilizes deep learning and in silico connectionism to develop computational frameworks for neural encoding and decoding, often referred to as 'brain reading' and 'brain writing.' They have worked on the reconstruction of perceived natural images from brain activity using generative adversarial networks and the characterization of feature complexity gradients in the human visual system. As an ELLIS Scholar, Güçlü’s work involves simulating and emulating in vivo neural computation to investigate the synergy between biological and machine intelligence.
E287.research_direction: Dr. Güçlü's recent work explores advanced neural encoding and decoding frameworks aimed at reconstructing naturalistic visual perception from brain activity. They have recently been investigating how biologically grounded spatial priors, such as retinotopic maps and receptive field organization, can be integrated into computational models to better map the relationship between complex sensory stimuli and neural responses across both human fMRI and macaque multi-unit activity. Their research also examines how state-of-the-art generative algorithms, including diffusion models and GANs, can be explicitly constrained by these spatial and temporal neural dynamics to drive high-fidelity, space-time-resolved reconstructions of dynamic images and videos. Additionally, Dr. Güçlü probes the functional alignment between artificial and biological visual hierarchies by evaluating how novel attention mechanisms and feature-disentangled latent spaces capture the distinct computational representations of different cortical areas.

papers.title: Neural encoding with affine feature response transforms
papers.abstract: This study introduces Affine Feature Response Transforms (AFRT), a methodology designed to integrate neuroscientifically grounded spatial priors into linearizing encoding models that characterize the mapping from sensory stimuli to neural activity. Standard encoding frameworks often overlook the intrinsic retinotopic organization of the brain, which can compromise model efficiency and the biological interpretability of the learned feature mappings. AFRT addresses this by formalizing the feature response through affine transformations that respect the spatial topology of the cortex. When applied to high-dimensional neuroimaging datasets, AFRT demonstrates improved predictive performance for voxel-level responses and provides more coherent representations of receptive field characteristics, thereby enhancing the functional alignment between artificial feature spaces and biological neural hierarchies.
papers.authors: Lynn Lê, Nils Kimman, Thirza Dado, Katja Seeliger, Paolo Papale, Antonio Lozano, Pieter Roelfsema, Marcel van Gerven, Yağmur Güçlütürk, Umut Güçlü

papers.title: Inverse receptive field attention for naturalistic image reconstruction from the brain
papers.abstract: This research presents a novel neural decoding paradigm for the high-fidelity reconstruction of naturalistic images and videos from functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data by leveraging the functional organization of neuronal receptive fields. The proposed Inverse Receptive Field Attention mechanism explicitly exploits spatial priors derived from retinotopic mapping to constrain the latent representations of image-to-image transformation networks. By integrating these spatial mappings into a generative modeling pipeline, the framework significantly improves the structural and semantic accuracy of visual reconstructions compared to baseline models. The approach demonstrates that incorporating biologically inspired spatial attention allows for the recovery of complex, dynamic visual experiences from large-scale, single-participant neuroimaging datasets with unprecedented detail.
papers.authors: Lynn Lê, Thirza Dado, Katja Seeliger, Paolo Papale, Antonio Lozano, Pieter Roelfsema, Yağmur Güçlütürk, Marcel van Gerven, Umut Güçlü

papers.title: MonkeySee: Space-time-resolved reconstructions of natural images from macaque multi-unit activity
papers.abstract: This paper presents a convolutional neural network (CNN)-based decoder architecture designed to reconstruct naturalistic images from multi-unit activity (MUA) recorded via Utah arrays in macaque cortical areas V1, V4, and IT. The authors investigate the differentiation of neural readout characteristics across the visual hierarchy, demonstrating that the CNN-based technique effectively captures region-specific representations. A key contribution is the development of a space-time-resolved decoding framework that leverages the high temporal resolution of MUA to capture the dynamics of visual processing. Additionally, the introduction of a Learned Receptive Field (LRF) layer allows the model to dynamically organize neural inputs into 2D spatial representations during training, significantly enhancing both the fidelity of the reconstructions and the structural interpretability of the decoding process.
papers.authors: Lynn Le, Paolo Papale, Katja Seeliger, Antonio Lozano, Thirza Dado, Feng Wang, Pieter Roelfsema, Marcel van Gerven, Yağmur Güçlütürk, Umut Güçlü

papers.title: PAM: Predictive attention mechanism for neural decoding of visual perception
papers.abstract: This work introduces Predictive Attention Mechanisms (PAMs), a novel task-driven architectural component for neural decoding that optimizes the integration of neural signals across the cortical hierarchy. Unlike standard self-attention mechanisms that compute input-input relationships, PAMs learn optimized 'output queries' during training that specifically target neural responses most relevant for reconstructing the latent features of generative models. This approach facilitates the dynamic allocation of attention across diverse brain regions based on their functional relevance to the reconstruction task. Validated on both macaque multi-unit activity and human fMRI datasets, PAM-enhanced decoders demonstrate superior performance in mapping brain activity to the latent spaces of generative adversarial networks and diffusion models, yielding high-precision reconstructions of perceived naturalistic stimuli.
papers.authors: Thirza Dado, Lynn Le, Marcel van Gerven, Yağmur Güçlütürk, Umut Güçlü

papers.title: Brain2GAN: Feature-disentangled neural encoding and decoding of visual perception in the primate brain
papers.abstract: This study characterizes the alignment between high-level neural representations in the macaque visual cortex and the feature-disentangled latent spaces of contemporary generative adversarial networks (GANs) and diffusion models. By analyzing multi-unit activity (MUA) recorded during a passive fixation task involving naturalistic images and faces, the authors compare the neural encoding efficacy of StyleGAN's z- and w-latents alongside language-contrastive CLIP representations. Mass univariate encoding analyses reveal that disentangled w-latent features significantly outperform conventional latents in predicting cortical responses, particularly in higher-level visual areas. Leveraging these feature-disentangled representations, the authors implement a multivariate decoding pipeline that achieves state-of-the-art spatiotemporal reconstructions of visual perception, underscoring the critical role of disentanglement in modeling biological visual processing.
papers.authors: Thirza Dado, Paolo Papale, Antonio Lozano, Lynn Le, Feng Wang, Marcel van Gerven, Pieter Roelfsema, Yağmur Güçlütürk, Umut Güçlü

E289.name: Gemma Roig
E289.lab_name: Computational Vision and Artificial Intelligence (CVAI) Lab
E289.bio: Gemma Roig is a Full Professor at Goethe University Frankfurt and leads the Computational Vision and Artificial Intelligence lab. Roig’s research integrates computer vision with cognitive neuroscience to develop brain-inspired AI architectures and uses deep neural networks as models for predicting human brain activity and behavior. They investigate representational alignment, multimodal learning, and invariant object recognition, utilizing data from MRI and EEG to benchmark machine intelligence against human perception. Before joining Goethe University, Roig held research and faculty positions at the Singapore University of Technology and Design and the MIT Center for Brains, Minds and Machines.
E289.research_direction: Dr. Roig has recently been investigating the intersection of artificial and biological vision, exploring how deep neural networks can be aligned with human neuroimaging data to better understand visual processing. Their recent work utilizes fMRI and EEG data both to model the hierarchical representations of the primate ventral stream and to test whether biological inductive biases can improve artificial robustness against adversarial attacks. To accelerate this research, they are developing open-source computational frameworks that automate representational similarity analysis between spatial or temporal brain responses and a wide library of AI architectures. In parallel, Dr. Roig is probing fundamental challenges in computer vision generalization, investigating how segmentation models handle severe visual degradations and utilizing mechanistic interpretability to detect and mitigate spurious shortcut learning in Transformers.

papers.title: Net2Brain: a toolbox to compare artificial vision models with human brain responses
papers.abstract: This work presents Net2Brain, an open-source Python framework designed to integrate diverse deep neural network (DNN) architectures into cognitive neuroscience research workflows. The toolbox provides an automated pipeline for downloading standard neuroimaging datasets—such as the Natural Scenes Dataset (NSD) and the BOLD Moments video dataset—and extracting hierarchical activations from a library of over 600 models, including vision-only, multimodal, and large language models (LLMs). Comparison between artificial and biological representational spaces is facilitated through built-in functionalities for representational similarity analysis (RSA), ridge-regression-based encoding models, and variance partitioning. The framework enables high-throughput benchmarking of brain-model alignment across the human visual hierarchy, supporting the systematic investigation of how different architectural components and training paradigms approximate cortical processing.
papers.authors: Domenic Bersch, Martina G. Vilas, Sari Saba-Sadiya, Timothy Schaumlöffel, Kshitij Dwivedi, Christina Sartzetaki, Radoslaw M. Cichy, Gemma Roig

papers.title: Cognitive Neural Architecture Search Reveals Hierarchical Entailment
papers.abstract: Addressing the debate between hierarchical and 'shallow' theories of the primate ventral stream, this research employs evolutionary neural architecture search (NAS) to evolve convolutional neural network (CNN) topologies optimized for alignment with human fMRI data. The study demonstrates that when architectures are evolved to maximize representational similarity with later regions of the ventral pathway (such as the inferior temporal cortex), they naturally develop structured representational hierarchies. Notably, these evolved architectures achieve higher brain-alignment scores than standard pretrained models even when using random weights. Furthermore, the identified brain-aligned architectures perform competitively on supervised image classification tasks, suggesting that the hierarchical structure required for biological alignment provides a powerful inductive bias for generalizable visual intelligence.
papers.authors: Lukas Kuhn, Sari Saba-Sadiya, Gemma Roig

papers.title: Beyond Data Augmentations: Generalization Abilities of Few-Shot Segmentation Models
papers.abstract: This paper introduces a novel evaluation paradigm termed 'half-shot learning' (HSL) to assess the robustness of few-shot semantic segmentation (FSS) models under severe data degradations. The authors propose a highly augmented testing suite where support images are subjected to aggressive cropping, occlusion, and transformation to simulate realistic perception challenges. Experimental results expose significant performance gaps in state-of-the-art FSS models when processing partially viewed objects. To mitigate these shortcomings, the work proposes the integration of spatial and channel-wise attention modules, demonstrating that enhancing the model's internal sense of 'objectness' through targeted attention mechanisms improves generalization to unseen categories in degraded support contexts.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the 20th International Joint Conference on Computer Vision, Imaging and Computer Graphics Theory and Applications (VISAPP)
papers.authors: Muhammad Ahsan, Guy Ben-Yosef, Gemma Roig

papers.title: Efficient Unsupervised Shortcut Learning Detection and Mitigation in Transformers
papers.abstract: Shortcut learning, where models rely on spurious or task-irrelevant features, remains a critical barrier to deploying robust AI in high-stakes environments. This work proposes a mechanistic interpretability framework to detect and mitigate such shortcuts in Transformer architectures without the need for manual bias annotations. The method identifies attention heads and feature subspaces that encode non-robust correlations by analyzing their impact on model decisions across diverse data partitions. An unsupervised decorrelation strategy is then applied to the latent space to suppress these identified shortcuts. Validation across multiple datasets, including medical diagnostics, shows that the framework significantly enhances worst-group accuracy and out-of-distribution generalization while maintaining computational efficiency on standard hardware.
papers.venue: IEEE/CVF International Conference on Computer Vision (ICCV)
papers.authors: Lukas Kuhn, Sari Sadiya, Jorg Schlotterer, Florian Buettner, Christin Seifert, Gemma Roig

papers.title: Limited but Consistent Gains in Adversarial Robustness by Co-training Object Recognition Models with Human EEG
papers.abstract: This study evaluates whether incorporating biological inductive biases from human neural responses can improve the reliability of artificial neural networks against adversarial perturbations. Using a dual-task learning framework, ResNet-50 models were co-trained to perform image classification while simultaneously predicting human EEG signals recorded during natural image viewing. The investigation focuses on the temporal dynamics of brain-model alignment, finding that networks successfully mimicking human representational patterns—particularly those occurring roughly 100ms post-stimulus in the parieto-occipital sensors—exhibit statistically consistent improvements in robustness against FGSM and PGD attacks. These results suggest that the representational geometry of the human visual system captures robust features that are inherently missing in purely supervised machine learning models.
papers.authors: Manshan Guo, Bhavin Choksi, Sari Sadiya, Alessandro T. Gifford, Martina G. Vilas, Radoslaw M. Cichy, Gemma Roig

E290.name: Hee-Yeon Im
E290.bio: Hee-Yeon Im is an Assistant Professor in the Department of Psychology at the University of British Columbia and the Principal Investigator of the Interactive Mind and Movement Lab. Im’s research investigates the neurocognitive mechanisms mediating the interaction between visual perception and goal-directed motor actions across typical and atypical development. Utilizing multimodal neuroimaging techniques such as magnetoencephalography (MEG) and functional MRI alongside psychophysics, they examine how the brain organizes visual inputs to guide task-relevant behaviors in various social and physical environments.
E290.research_direction: Dr. Im has recently been investigating the neural and cognitive mechanisms underlying visuomotor adaptation and goal-directed action. Their recent work explores how sensorimotor recalibration matures across childhood, using precise kinematic tracking and magnetoencephalography (MEG) to isolate the developmental trajectories of feedforward predictive planning versus online feedback-driven motor corrections. Beyond typical development, they are examining how deficits in fluid reach-to-grasp integration can serve as diagnostic behavioral markers of dorsal stream dysfunction in patients with cerebral visual impairment (CVI). Additionally, their research probes the fundamental boundaries of implicit sensorimotor learning by testing how concurrent goal-directed attentional demands, such as visual search tasks, modulate supposedly autonomous motor adaptation processes.

papers.title: Developmental changes in MEG oscillatory activity during visuomotor adaptation: Differential maturation of feedforward and feedback-related mechanisms
papers.abstract: Visuomotor adaptation—the sensorimotor recalibration of reach trajectories using visual discrepancy signals—matures continuously throughout childhood, yet the precise electrophysiological dynamics governing this ontogeny remain insufficiently elucidated. Whole-head magnetoencephalography (MEG) was recorded in children (6–12 years) and adults executing reaching movements toward targets under an abrupt 45° cursor rotation. Cortical oscillatory power was segregated into two distinct kinematic phases: the pre-peak velocity interval (dominated by feedforward predictive control) and the post-peak velocity deceleration interval (dominated by online feedback-driven correction). While both cohorts successfully adapted reaching trajectories, adult participants demonstrated superior accuracy, higher velocity, and decreased temporal variance. During the feedforward phase, children exhibited reduced pre-movement beta synchronization and attenuated post-stimulus beta desynchronization across motor, parietal, and occipital cortices compared to adults, reflecting immature predictive internal modeling. Concurrently, children showed prolonged, elevated prefrontal theta power following target display, consistent with enhanced reliance on executive supervisory mechanisms. In contrast, oscillatory divergences between age cohorts narrowed substantially during the deceleration window, suggesting that feedback-mediated trajectory correction matures closer to adult levels earlier than feedforward motor preparation. Stronger brain-behavior coupling between cortical oscillations and adaptation metrics in children highlights ongoing neurodevelopmental specialization.
papers.authors: Minsu Song, Alexander J. Cook, Advitya Hajela, Deborah E. Giaschi, Hee-Yeon Im

papers.title: Speed and Accuracy of Movement During Visuomotor Adaptation Are Still Developing in School-Age Children
papers.abstract: Visuomotor adaptation serves as a fundamental mechanism for acquiring and refining motor competencies during development. Although children as young as age five can compensate for rotational visual perturbations, the kinematic and temporal characteristics distinguishing pediatric adaptation from mature performance remain incompletely specified. Kinematic parameters—including onset latency, movement duration, velocity profiles, and directional error curves—were contrasted between adults (19–45 years) and school-aged children stratified into younger (6–8 years) and older (9–12 years) groups during reaching tasks under visual rotation. Adults and older children exhibited exponential reductions in angular error characteristic of cognitive feedforward re-aiming integrated with implicit calibration, whereas younger children demonstrated a linear error reduction profile with prolonged onset latencies, reflecting heavier dependence on slower feedback mechanisms. Furthermore, while terminal endpoint accuracy asymptotically approached adult levels by the end of training blocks across all cohorts, movement velocity and temporal stability remained immature in school-age children, indicating divergent developmental timetables for speed versus spatial accuracy optimization in sensorimotor recalibration.
papers.authors: Alexander J. Cook, Deborah E. Giaschi, Hee Yeon Im

papers.title: Impaired reach-to-grasp integration identifies cerebral visual impairment (CVI) in children and adults
papers.abstract: The authors identify the temporal and sensory dissociation between reaching and grasping components as a behavioral hallmark of Cerebral Visual Impairment (CVI). Using frame-by-frame kinematic analysis of goal-directed movements toward 3D targets, the study demonstrates that both pediatric and adult CVI cohorts rely significantly more on offline or static preplanned hand-shaping strategies compared to typically-sighted controls, who display fluid online integration of the reach and grasp. These deficits, consistent with a primary dysfunction of the dorsal visual stream, persist even when visual feedback is available. The research introduces a composite Reach-to-Grasp Integration (RGI) score that robustly differentiates CVI patients from healthy controls, providing a potential diagnostic screening tool for identifying visuomotor coordination impairments resulting from cortical brain injury rather than ocular damage.
papers.authors: Candace J. Burke, Mia W. Nevin, Denver Grimm, Jenni M. Karl, Melissa Aziz, Ahad Zafar, Deborah Giaschi, Hee-Yeon Im

papers.title: Automatic, but not autonomous: Implicit adaptation is modulated by goal-directed attentional demands
papers.abstract: This study challenges the traditional characterization of implicit sensorimotor adaptation as a resource-independent, fully autonomous process by examining its sensitivity to concurrent goal-directed attentional demands. Using a visuomotor rotation paradigm with clamped visual feedback, the researchers evaluated implicit adaptation while participants simultaneously performed a conjunction search task within a rapid serial visual presentation (RSVP) stream. Results indicated that performing the secondary task initially enhanced the rate of implicit adaptation relative to a single-task control, with response-contingent feedback sustaining this facilitation. Model-based analyses suggested that divided attention elevated error sensitivity. These findings demonstrate that while implicit adaptation operates outside voluntary control, it remains susceptible to modulation by the physiological and attentional state of the observer, suggesting it is automatic but not autonomous from broader cognitive processes.
papers.authors: Joshua Liddy, Sean O'Bryan, Alexander Daskalopoulos, Joo-Hyun Song, Hee-Yeon Im

E291.name: Nicole Rust
E291.bio: Rust is a Professor in the Department of Psychology at the University of Pennsylvania, focusing on the neural and computational mechanisms of visual object recognition and memory. Their research group combines behavioral experiments, large-scale neural recordings, and machine learning to examine how neurons in the inferotemporal cortex encode image memorability and familiarity. As a Simons Foundation Pivot Fellow, Rust applies systems neuroscience to investigate the biological basis of human emotion and mood. Rust also works on applying complex-systems frameworks to brain research, specifically regarding the challenges of treating psychiatric and neurological disorders.
E291.research_direction: Dr. Rust's recent work explores the neural computations underlying visual recognition memory, primarily using electrophysiological recordings and computational modeling of the macaque ventral visual stream. They are investigating how the brain transforms high-fidelity visual representations into signals of familiarity, specifically examining mechanisms like repetition suppression and representational sharpening in the inferotemporal cortex to understand how primates distinguish previously seen objects from highly similar novel distractors. Their research also asks how the brain integrates object identity with spatial context across the inferotemporal and perirhinal cortices to support the formation of cohesive visual episodes. Additionally, Dr. Rust has recently been exploring the broader methodological link between single-unit spiking and local field potentials, investigating how successful translation between these recording modalities depends on whether neural variables like image memorability and object category are encoded through overall population response magnitudes or distributed spatial patterns.

papers.title: Neural representations of visual memory in inferotemporal cortex reveal a generalizable framework for translating between spikes and field potentials
papers.abstract: Translating neurophysiological findings across species and recording modalities requires a systematic understanding of the relationship between single-unit spiking activity and aggregate measures like local field potentials (LFPs), particularly high-gamma activity (HGA; 50–150 Hz). In this study, neural responses were simultaneously recorded from macaque inferotemporal (IT) cortex during a single-exposure visual recognition memory task. The results demonstrate that HGA and spiking activity are strikingly aligned for neural variables encoded via a population response magnitude scheme, such as image novelty, recency, and memorability. Conversely, variables encoded as distributed patterns of activity across the population, such as object category, exhibit misalignment between spikes and HGA. By evaluating these findings against a broad set of existing literature, the authors propose a generalizable framework stating that the success of spike-to-LFP translation depends on whether the underlying variable is encoded through magnitude or pattern-based neural codes.
papers.authors: Catrina M. Hacker, Simon Bohn, Brett L. Foster, Nicole C. Rust

papers.title: Sharpened visual memory representations are reflected in inferotemporal cortex
papers.abstract: Visual recognition memory allows primates to distinguish previously encountered images from highly similar novel ones. This study investigates the neural underpinnings of this specificity in the macaque ventral visual stream. While repetition suppression—a reduction in firing rates for familiar stimuli—is a common correlate of memory, the authors demonstrate that a model of 'representational sharpening' better accounts for behavioral patterns. In this model, repetition selectively reduces responses to non-optimal features, thereby refining the population tuning. Electrophysiological recordings in the inferotemporal (IT) cortex and the hippocampus (HC) revealed that neural analogs of behavioral sharpening emerge in both regions. The findings suggest that IT cortex contributes significantly to shaping memory fidelity during the transition from visual processing to mnemonic storage, rather than this process being exclusively driven by hippocampal pattern separation.
papers.authors: Barnes G. L. Jannuzi, Catrina M. Hacker, Simon Bohn, Travis Meyer, Margaret L. Hay, Nicole C. Rust

papers.title: Resolving a paradox about how vision is transformed into familiarity
papers.abstract: A central paradox in systems neuroscience is the coexistence of highly selective representations for object identity in inferotemporal (IT) cortex with the coarse, non-selective signals of repetition suppression associated with visual familiarity. This study employs large-scale neural recordings and computational modeling to determine how the brain transforms IT population activity into a familiarity signal that preserves high visual specificity. The authors find that familiarity is not a global property of the population but is instead derived through a specific weighted linear readout of IT activity. This readout mechanism allows the brain to leverage the diverse selectivity of IT neurons to support recognition memory behavior, successfully predicting an individual's ability to distinguish an original image from visually similar distractors.
papers.authors: Simon Bohn, Catrina M. Hacker, Barnes G. L. Jannuzi, Travis Meyer, Margaret L. Hay, Nicole C. Rust

papers.title: The visual representation of things in places
papers.abstract: The primate brain must integrate information about object identity with spatial context to support visual episodes. This paper investigates how the ventral visual stream, specifically the inferotemporal (IT) and perirhinal (PRH) cortices, represents objects within their environmental backgrounds. Using neural recordings from rhesus macaques, the study quantifies the degree to which neural representations are modulated by 'place' (spatial background) and 'thing' (object identity). The findings indicate that while IT cortex primarily maintains a representation focused on object identity with modulation by position, PRH exhibits a more integrated coding scheme. This suggests that PRH facilitates the 'tagging' of objects with their environmental context, a computation essential for the formation of visual memories that link specific items to particular locations.
papers.authors: Travis Meyer, Barnes G. L. Jannuzi, Nicole C. Rust

E292.name: Christopher Niell
E292.department: Department of Biology and Institute of Neuroscience
E292.bio: Christopher Niell is a Professor at the University of Oregon who investigates the neural circuits underlying visual perception and behavior. Niell's research group utilizes methodologies including two-photon calcium imaging and high-density extracellular recordings to analyze the functional organization of the visual system. Their research established that behavioral states, such as locomotion, modulate sensory processing in the primary visual cortex. Niell’s current research explores visual processing during naturalistic ethological tasks and examines the neural architecture of the octopus brain to study the evolution of visual systems.
E292.research_direction: Dr. Niell has recently been investigating the neural dynamics of active vision, focusing on how naturalistic movements and active sensing shape visual processing in freely moving mice. Using high-density extracellular recordings and precision behavioral tracking, their recent work explores how regions like the primary visual cortex and the superior colliculus integrate visual input with distinct motor signals, such as head kinematics, eye position, and high-dimensional orofacial behaviors. Furthermore, they are examining the neuromodulation of these active circuits, specifically testing how serotonergic psychedelics alter natural visual sampling and state-dependent cortical activity. Extending beyond mammalian models, Dr. Niell is also investigating the evolutionary molecular basis of vision in cephalopods, mapping novel dopaminergic and cholinergic receptor networks in the octopus optic lobe to understand the independent origins of computations like lateral inhibition.

papers.title: Orofacial behaviors, not eye movements, govern neural activity in mouse visual cortex
papers.abstract: This research investigates the primary drivers of non-visual neural activity within the mouse primary visual cortex (V1), challenging the assumption that oculomotor signals are the dominant modulatory input as seen in primates. Utilizing large-scale extracellular recordings in freely moving mice alongside deep-learning-based video tracking (Facemap), the study decouples eye movements from high-dimensional orofacial behaviors such as whisking and sniffing. The researchers demonstrate that orofacial dynamics account for a significantly larger fraction of neural variance in V1 compared to eye position or saccades, even in total darkness. Furthermore, although eye movements are temporally correlated with orofacial actions, they possess minimal unique predictive power for neural activity. These results suggest that state-dependent orofacial motor signals are the fundamental source of movement-related modulation in the rodent visual system.
papers.authors: Dylan M. Martins, Emmalyn S. P. Leonard, Cristopher M. Niell

papers.title: Neural dynamics in superior colliculus of freely moving mice
papers.abstract: This study employs high-density Neuropixels recordings to characterize the laminar-specific neural dynamics of the superior colliculus (SC) in mice during naturalistic exploration. By integrating neural activity with precision tracking of head and eye kinematics, the authors identify a functional split between the superficial (sSC) and deep (dSC) layers. Neurons in the sSC are primarily visually driven, exhibiting a coarse-to-fine processing sequence following gaze-shifting saccades, whereas dSC neurons represent the motor components of orienting behaviors, remaining active in darkness and correlating more strongly with head rotation than with eye movement. The findings establish the SC as a sophisticated hub for active vision, where distinct laminar circuits independently process visual-evoked and motor-derived signals to guide ethological behavior.
papers.authors: Shelby L. Sharp, Jhoseph Shin, Dylan M. Martins, Keaton Jones, Cristopher M. Niell

papers.title: The impact of the serotonergic psychedelic DOI on active vision in freely moving mice
papers.abstract: The authors investigate the effects of the serotonergic psychedelic DOI (2,5-dimethoxy-4-iodoamphetamine), a 5-HT2A receptor agonist, on the neural circuits of active vision in freely moving mice. Using V1 extracellular recordings and simultaneous behavioral tracking, they find that while DOI increases the frequency of active sampling behaviors, it does not alter their fundamental kinematic structure. However, the drug induces a net suppression of visually-evoked activity in V1, with effects varying significantly across cortical layers. A critical finding is the dissociation between the impact of DOI on responses to natural gaze shifts versus flashed sparse noise stimuli during head-fixation, suggesting that the disruption of sensory processing by psychedelics is highly dependent on stimulus predictability and the statistics of the visual input.
papers.authors: Rolf J. Skyberg, Christopher W. Fields, Dylan M. Martins, Cristopher M. Niell

papers.title: Novel dopaminergic neurotransmission in the Octopus visual system
papers.abstract: Focusing on the octopus optic lobe, this study identifies the molecular and neurochemical basis of visual signaling in a brain that evolved independently from vertebrates. Through single-cell RNA sequencing and heterologous expression of ligand-gated ion channel genes from Octopus vulgaris, the researchers characterize two novel ionotropic receptors: DopC1, a dopamine-gated cation channel, and AChRB1, an acetylcholine-gated anion channel. Dopamine application is shown to stimulate robust neural activity in DopC1-expressing layers, indicating a role in excitatory neurotransmission. Meanwhile, AChRB1 facilitates inhibitory input to dopaminergic amacrine cells. This circuit motif, combining inhibitory cholinergic and excitatory dopaminergic signals, suggests that octopus amacrine cells perform lateral inhibition computations analogous to those of the vertebrate retina, despite using entirely different neurochemical substrates.
papers.authors: Amy Courtney, Ruth Styfhals, Marie Van Dijck, Jan Boulanger, Lotte Geenen, Marion Lanoizelet, Ian Hardege, Maximillian Lassnig, Anna M. Jansson, Janna Gehler-Rahman, Eduardo Almansa, Herbert A. Obenhaus, Eve Seuntjens, William R. Schafer, Judit R. Pungor, Cristopher M. Niell

papers.title: Natural visual behavior and active sensing in the mouse
papers.abstract: This technical review synthesizes current knowledge on how active sensing and natural behaviors format visual input in the mouse. The authors emphasize that head and eye movements are critical variables in cortical visual processing, modulating V1 activity and shaping neural computations in ways that traditional head-fixed paradigms cannot capture. They highlight findings that V1 neurons are enhanced by head movements in a luminance-dependent manner and that the superior colliculus provides essential top-down gain control for defensive behaviors like escape or freezing. The paper argues that the mouse visual system is optimized to extract ethologically relevant features—such as looming objects or prey localization—through active sensing, and calls for a paradigm shift toward studying vision during free movement to reveal the true computational principles of the brain.
papers.authors: Rolf J. Skyberg, Cristopher M. Niell

E294.name: Andrea Benucci
E294.department: School of Biological and Behavioural Sciences
E294.lab_name: Laboratory for Neural Circuits and Behavior
E294.bio: Andrea Benucci is a neuroscientist who investigates the computational principles of sensory processing and visual perception. Benucci's research integrates large-scale neural recordings, such as two-photon imaging and high-density electrophysiology, with patterned optogenetic manipulations and artificial neural network modeling. They developed automated, high-throughput behavioral platforms that standardize mouse training for complex visual tasks to facilitate the study of population-level neural dynamics. Their recent work focuses on the plasticity of cortical representations and how non-visual signals, including motor-related inputs, are integrated within the visual hierarchy to support perceptual stability and decision-making.
E294.research_direction: Dr. Benucci investigates the large-scale cortical population dynamics that support visual perception, decision-making, and sensorimotor integration in the mouse brain. Their recent work explores how the visual system encodes natural image statistics, using widefield calcium imaging and psychophysics to examine how primary and higher-order visual areas represent complex textures within low-dimensional neural manifolds. They have also recently been utilizing recurrent neural networks to study the geometry of perceptual decision-making, specifically investigating how distributed choice signals in the posterior cortex are dynamically disentangled from concurrent sensory and motor representations during visual discrimination tasks. Additionally, Dr. Benucci is studying how these multi-area networks are modulated by internal states like arousal, employing advanced Bayesian modeling to uncover how multifaceted movement and sensory signals interact across the cortex during active behavior.

papers.title: Regularizing hyperparameters of interacting neural signals in the mouse cortex reflect states of arousal
papers.abstract: Cortical networks concurrently represent and nonlinearly integrate pervasive movement-related signals alongside sensory inputs, yet regularizing the spatiotemporal interaction kernels between such multifaceted behavioral signals poses significant inferential challenges. Applying an Automatic Locality Determination (ALD) Bayesian regularization framework to widefield calcium recordings in GCaMP6s mice, we modeled the second-order, quadratic interaction kernels between saccadic eye movements and body movements across the posterior cortex during a visual discrimination task. We observed that the estimated ALD hyperparameters governing kernel smoothness, scale, and spatial locality systematically vary across individual animals in proportion to the magnitude of signal interactions, the variability of visual responses, and overall trial-to-trial variance. These hyperparameter fluctuations strongly track internal cognitive states, demonstrating significant positive correlations with pupil diameter variations as a physiological metric of arousal and attentional engagement. Consequently, regularizing hyperparameters inferred from generalized linear models serve as an objective readout of behavioral and cognitive states shaping cortical population dynamics.
papers.authors: Dmitry R. Lyamzin, Andrea Alamia, Mohammad Abdolrahmani, Ryo Aoki, Andrea Benucci

papers.title: Efficient coding of natural images in the mouse visual cortex
papers.abstract: The computational mechanisms by which ventral visual areas extract and encode naturalistic texture statistics to drive perception remain insufficiently understood. Using psychophysical paradigms in mice, we demonstrate that rodents can accurately discriminate natural textures from spectrally matched synthesized noise scrambles as well as differentiate across distinct texture families. Widefield calcium imaging across the visual cortex in untrained mice revealed that the secondary visual area (LM) demonstrates markedly greater selectivity for natural textures than primary visual cortex (V1), driven by higher-order statistical features parameterized via the Portilla–Simoncelli model. Textures are embedded in distinct low-dimensional neural subspaces whose distances correlate directly with stimulus statistical divergence and behavioral discriminability. These neural manifolds are significantly more compact in LM than in V1, yielding enhanced linear decoding performance. These findings identify texture perception in mice and provide an empirical link connecting natural image statistics, cortical subspace geometry, and perceptual discriminability in accordance with efficient coding principles.
papers.authors: Federico Bolaños, Javier G. Orlandi, Ryo Aoki, Akshay V. Jagadeesh, Justin L. Gardner, Andrea Benucci

papers.title: Distributed context-dependent choice information in mouse posterior cortex
papers.abstract: Choice signals across posterior cortical networks are commonly intertwined with concurrent sensory and motor activations, limiting understanding of their functional role in decision computations. We conducted mesoscale calcium imaging across the posterior cortex of mice performing an invariant visual orientation discrimination task designed to minimize mnemonic, motor, and novel sensory confounds. Choice signals defined an independent decision variable distributed across multi-area networks, with substantial representation along the ventral visual stream. This choice subspace remained nearly orthogonal to co-occurring sensory and motor representation dimensions and was systematically modulated by discrimination difficulty and attentional engagement. Training recurrent neural networks (RNNs) directly on empirical choice behavior yielded an equivalent decision variable whose low-dimensional trajectories matched the context-dependent dynamics of the cortical data. These findings reveal a distributed, context-dependent decision variable in the posterior cortex suited for flexible inference computations during dynamic task engagement.
papers.authors: Javier G. Orlandi, Mohammad Abdolrahmani, Ryo Aoki, Dmitry R. Lyamzin, Andrea Benucci

E295.name: Alessandra Angelucci
E295.bio: Angelucci investigates the anatomical organization and functional properties of neuronal circuits within the visual cerebral cortex to understand the mechanisms of visual perception. Their research employs optical imaging, array electrophysiology, optogenetics, and neuroanatomical tracing to map the connectivity of feedforward and feedback pathways. Angelucci’s work examines how these circuits integrate contextual information and modulate parallel processing streams between cortical areas such as V1 and V2. Their laboratory also develops computational neural network models to simulate cortical computations and explores the role of inhibitory interneuron subtypes in sensory processing.
E295.research_direction: Dr. Angelucci has recently been investigating the laminar microcircuitry of the primate primary visual cortex (V1) alongside the development of advanced neurotechnologies to probe these networks. Their recent work explores how specific cortical layers and inhibitory cell types, such as parvalbumin-expressing interneurons, govern fundamental computations like orientation tuning and the spatial surround modulation of neural response variability. To enable precise mechanistic studies in non-human primates, they are evaluating viral-mediated strategies for the selective genetic targeting of these GABAergic populations. Furthermore, they are validating the functional efficacy and acute tissue biocompatibility of the Utah Optrode Array, aiming to optimize this high-density penetrating device for large-scale, depth-resolved optogenetic stimulation.

papers.title: Size tuning of neural response variability in laminar circuits of macaque primary visual cortex
papers.abstract: This study employs laminar multi-electrode array recordings in macaque primary visual cortex (V1) to investigate how the spatial extent of visual stimuli modulates the trial-to-trial (Fano factor) and shared (spike-count correlation, $r_{sc}$) response variability across cortical layers. The researchers show that while stimuli matched to the receptive field (RF) size ubiquitously quench variability compared to the pre-stimulus baseline, the recruitment of the RF surround results in layer-specific modulations of variability. Specifically, in infragranular layers, stimulation of the near surround further reduces both individual and shared variability compared to RF-center stimulation alone, whereas this quenching is less pronounced in supragranular layers. These findings suggest that surround modulation stabilizes network dynamics through laminar-specific circuit mechanisms involving intrinsic and feedback connectivity.
papers.authors: Lauri Nurminen, Maryam Bijanzadeh, Alessandra Angelucci

papers.title: Cortical Response to Acute Implantation of the Utah Optrode Array in Macaque Cortex
papers.abstract: The authors conducted a systematic evaluation of the acute neuroinflammatory and structural biological responses to the implantation of the Utah Optrode Array (UOA)—a high-density 10x10 penetrating glass shank array with integrated micro-LEDs—within the macaque visual cortex. By varying shank diameter, surface texture, tip geometry, and insertion pressure, the study quantified microglial and astrocytic activation alongside neuronal viability. The results indicate that UOA designs featuring smaller shank diameters, smooth surface finishes, and rounded tip geometries minimize mechanical trauma and reactive gliosis. While higher insertion pressures led to greater tissue compression, they had a limited impact on the immediate inflammatory response. These data provide essential parameters for optimizing the biocompatibility and chronic stability of large-scale optogenetic interfaces in non-human primates.
papers.authors: Adrián Villamarin-Ortiz, Christopher F. Reiche, Frederick Federer, Andrew M. Clark, John D. Rolston, Cristina Soto-Sánchez, Eduardo Fernandez, Steve Blair, Alessandra Angelucci

papers.title: Laminar-specific control of response gain and orientation-tuning by parvalbumin-expressing inhibitory interneurons in primate visual cortex
papers.abstract: This work characterizes the laminar-specific role of parvalbumin-expressing (PV+) inhibitory interneurons in the computation of orientation tuning within the marmoset primary visual cortex (V1). By integrating laminar extracellular recordings with bidirectional optogenetic manipulations of PV+ cells, the researchers demonstrate a fundamental functional divergence between cortical depths: in granular layers, PV+ cells execute linear divisive/multiplicative gain control, whereas in extra-granular layers, they implement orientation-tuned nonlinear suppression that sharpens the orientation preference of pyramidal neurons. Computational modeling indicates that these effects arise from PV-mediated regulation of neuronal spiking thresholds in granular layers and input noise modulation in extra-granular layers, establishing a framework for understanding cell-type-specific inhibitory computations in the primate cortex.
papers.authors: Amin Vafaei, Andrew M Clark, Alireza Khadir, Weifeng Dai, Frederick Federer, Alessandra Angelucci

papers.title: Laminar specificity and coverage of viral-mediated gene expression restricted to GABAergic interneurons and their parvalbumin subclass in marmoset primary visual cortex
papers.abstract: The study evaluates a viral-mediated strategy to achieve cell-type-specific genetic access to GABAergic interneurons and the parvalbumin (PV) subclass in the primate visual cortex, which has historically been a challenge in non-human primate research. Utilizing adeno-associated virus (AAV) vectors containing Dlx distal enhancers, the authors characterized the laminar distribution, specificity, and transduction coverage of gene expression in marmoset area V1. Histological analysis demonstrated high selectivity for inhibitory populations across all cortical layers, with robust expression in PV+ neurons. These findings establish a viable methodological platform for high-resolution, cell-type-specific interrogation of cortical microcircuits in large-brained species using optogenetic and imaging techniques.
papers.authors: Frederick Federer, Julie Balsor, Andrew Ingold, David P. Babcock, Jordane Dimidschstein, Alessandra Angelucci

papers.title: An Optrode Array for Spatiotemporally Precise Large-Scale Optogenetic Stimulation of Deep Cortical Layers in Non-human Primates
papers.abstract: This paper describes the development and in vivo validation of the Utah Optrode Array (UOA), a 10x10 penetrating glass shank interface integrated with a micro-LED backplane for large-scale, depth-resolved optogenetics in non-human primates. The device allows for independent and simultaneous photostimulation of deep and superficial cortical layers over a 4x4 mm area. Through electrophysiological validation in macaque V1, the authors demonstrate the array's ability to drive neural activity with high spatiotemporal precision while maintaining negligible thermal effects. The UOA facilitates the investigation of hierarchical processing and long-range connectivity in the primate brain and serves as a prototype for high-resolution visual cortical prostheses.
papers.authors: Andrew M. Clark, Andrew Ingold, Christopher F. Reiche, David Cundy, Julie L. Balsor, Frederick Federer, Niall McAlinden, Yiyuan Cheng, John D. Rolston, Lars Rieth, Martin D. Dawson, Keith Mathieson, Steve Blair, Alessandra Angelucci

E296.name: Marlene Cohen
E296.bio: Marlene R. Cohen is a Professor of Neurobiology at the University of Chicago, investigating how neuronal populations encode sensory information to guide behavior. Cohen’s research examines visual attention, specifically how it modulates noise correlations between neurons to affect the fidelity of the population code. Using high-density multi-electrode electrophysiology and computational modeling, their lab characterizes the relationship between large-scale neural dynamics and perceptual decisions. Their current work focuses on identifying the neural principles of cognitive flexibility and exploring translational applications related to attention disorders and neurodegeneration.
E296.research_direction: Dr. Cohen has recently been investigating how neural population dynamics and representational formatting drive complex perceptual and cognitive behaviors. Using macaque electrophysiology, targeted microstimulation, human psychophysics, and computational modeling, their recent work explores whether low-dimensional correlated variability acts as a functional communication channel rather than merely acting as detrimental sensory noise. They are also examining how distinct cortical areas, such as MT and dlPFC, uniquely format sensory and reward information to serve specialized roles in decision-making. Furthermore, their research probes the physiological substrates of one-shot visual memory in area V4, the circuit mechanisms guiding the integration of novel cross-modal cues, and how entangled neural manifolds create performance costs during cognitive task switching.

papers.title: Behavioural and neuronal insights into multisensory combination of unpracticed cues
papers.abstract: The integration of diverse sensory signals weighted by their respective reliability is fundamental to adaptive decision-making. While practiced cues often demonstrate near-optimal Bayesian integration, the circuit mechanisms underlying the combination of unfamiliar, cross-modal stimuli remain poorly understood. This study employs large-scale human psychophysics and targeted electrical microstimulation in macaques to investigate integration strategies for novel visual (motion direction) and auditory (location) cues. The results reveal that within-modality visual cues are combined near-optimally, whereas cross-modal combinations frequently exhibit winner-take-all (WTA) dynamics. Causal manipulations show that within-modality integration is supported by weighted averaging in the visual cortex, while association areas like the prefrontal cortex (PFC) mediate WTA behavior. These findings suggest a circuit-level distinction between unimodal and multisensory processing mechanisms.
papers.authors: Keon S. Allen, Douglas A. Ruff, Marlene R. Cohen

papers.title: Neuronal signatures of successful one-shot memory in mid-level visual cortex
papers.abstract: High-capacity visual recognition memory requires neurons to encode and durably represent images after a single exposure. This research evaluates potential neural signatures of successful recognition—such as repetition suppression, sparse coding, and population response consistency—by recording from area V4 populations in macaques performing a temporally extended recognition task. While multiple signatures were observed, behavioral success was primarily predicted by sparse coding (specifically rare, high-firing events) during initial exposure and population response consistency during the retrieval phase. Furthermore, recognized images evoked accelerated neuronal dynamics, indicative of pattern completion. These results suggest that mid-level visual cortex provides the necessary physiological substrates for one-shot memory, serving as a critical node in distributed recognition networks.
papers.authors: Grace F. DiRisio, Cheng Xue, Marlene R. Cohen

papers.title: Guided by Noise: Correlated Variability Channels Task-Relevant Information in Sensory Neurons
papers.abstract: Low-dimensional correlated variability across sensory neurons is typically characterized as noise that limits information encoding. However, its consistent link to perceptual behavior suggests it may have a functional role. This study utilizes circuit modeling and neural population recordings across multiple brain regions and behavioral tasks to demonstrate that the dominant axis of shared variability consistently aligns with task-relevant stimulus features and intended action plans. The work proposes that shared variability reflects a communication channel for task-critical signals rather than detrimental noise. Causal evidence from microstimulation confirms that changes in the projection of neural activity onto the shared variability axis reliably predict behavioral biases, suggesting that downstream decoders utilize this variability as an informative signal for guiding behavior.
papers.authors: Ramanujan Srinath, Yunlong Xu, Douglas A. Ruff, Amy M. Ni, Brent Doiron, Marlene R. Cohen

papers.title: Linking neural population formatting to function
papers.abstract: Although sensory and behavioral information is often widely decodable across different cortical regions, brain areas exhibit clear functional specialization. This study posits that an area's function is defined by its representational 'formatting'—the specific way distinct information types are combined—rather than the presence of the information itself. Comparing the middle temporal area (MT) and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC) in macaques, the authors show that while both areas encode motion and reward, MT represents them separably while dlPFC integrates them to reflect decision outcomes. Microstimulation reveals that MT influences choices in a graded, sensory-biased manner, whereas dlPFC stimulation induces winner-take-all behavior. These findings support a modular framework where different areas flexibly reformat representations to meet specific behavioral objectives.
papers.authors: Douglas A. Ruff, Sol K. Markman, Jason Z. Kim, Marlene R. Cohen

papers.title: Task interference as a neuronal basis for the cost of cognitive flexibility
papers.abstract: Cognitive flexibility allows primates to switch between tasks, yet this ability incurs performance costs under uncertain conditions. Integrating human psychophysics, macaque electrophysiology, and artificial neural network (ANN) modeling, this study identifies 'task interference' as the neuronal basis for these costs. Performance decrements are driven by the persistence of task-irrelevant stimulus representations and the entanglement of neural codes for unrelated features. Unlike standard ANNs optimized for accuracy, biological networks and behavior-mimicking models exhibit these representational overlaps. The results suggest that the brain's inability to perfectly segregate competing task-relevant and irrelevant neural manifolds imposes a fundamental constraint on cognitive flexibility, potentially providing a mechanistic explanation for cognitive limitations in both health and psychiatric disorders.
papers.authors: Cheng Xue, Sol K. Markman, Ruoyi Chen, Lily E. Kramer, Marlene R. Cohen

E297.name: Adam Kohn
E297.department: Dominick P. Purpura Department of Neuroscience
