E297.bio: Adam Kohn is Professor and Chair of the Dominick P. Purpura Department of Neuroscience at the Albert Einstein College of Medicine, with additional appointments in the departments of Ophthalmology and Visual Sciences and Systems & Computational Biology. Kohn’s research examines the mechanisms by which cortical neuronal populations encode visual information and the processes governing communication between distinct brain areas. Using multielectrode array recordings, computational modeling, and psychophysics, their laboratory investigates how sensory adaptation and correlated variability influence neural representations and perceptual outcomes. Kohn defined the 'communication subspace' that mediates inter-areal signaling and explored the role of rhythmic synchronization in the visual hierarchy.
E297.research_direction: Dr. Kohn has recently been investigating how mid-level visual features are processed and transformed across the early primate visual hierarchy, specifically focusing on areas V1 and V2. Using high-density electrophysiological recordings in macaques, their recent work explores the representational geometry of neural populations to understand how the dimensionality of responses to complex, naturalistic textures shifts between cortical stages. They are also examining the temporal dynamics of these representations, probing how visual adaptation to higher-order image statistics alters neuronal sensitivity and population-level sensory encoding. Furthermore, Dr. Kohn is investigating the neural correlates of bottom-up visual salience, testing whether "pop-out" signals for distinct textures emerge inherently in early visual cortex or are dynamically induced by recent stimulus history.

papers.title: Adaptation with Naturalistic Textures in Macaque V1 and V2
papers.abstract: This study characterizes how prolonged exposure to naturalistic textures affects neuronal sensitivity and selectivity across the primate visual hierarchy, specifically in V1 and V2. Unlike prior work using simplified stimuli, the researchers employed synthetic textures and spectrally matched noise to determine if adaptation effects are locally generated or inherited from earlier stages. The findings demonstrate that while V1 responsivity is suppressed by both texture and noise adapters, V2 neurons exhibit a stimulus-specific reduction in responsivity dependent on the higher-order image statistics to which they are inherently selective. Quantitatively, texture information encoded by both single-unit and population-level activity was reduced post-adaptation in both regions, challenging the hypothesis that adaptation consistently optimizes sensory encoding for feature discrimination.
papers.authors: Aida Davila, Adam Kohn

papers.title: The representational geometry for naturalistic textures in macaque V1 and V2
papers.abstract: The research investigates the transformation of texture representations between primary (V1) and secondary (V2) visual cortex by analyzing the representational geometry of neuronal populations. Using high-density Neuropixel recordings in macaques, the authors found that population responses to naturalistic textures are significantly lower dimensional in V2 compared to V1. This dimensionality reduction is accompanied by a more systematic alignment of object manifolds representing different texture instantiations, facilitating superior discriminability for novel, out-of-sample textures. Conversely, responses to gratings were higher dimensional in V2, suggesting that the observed geometric shift is specific to the complex statistical structure of naturalistic stimuli. The results indicate that the visual system constructs a low-dimensional embedding of texture features to enhance representational robustness and generalization.
papers.authors: Abhimanyu Pavuluri, Adam Kohn

papers.title: Assessing neuronal correlates of salience and their adaptability with naturalistic textures in macaque V1 and V2
papers.abstract: This work explores whether neural correlates of bottom-up visual salience, or 'pop-out' responses, exist for complex naturalistic textures in areas V1 and V2. The study utilized multi-patch displays where a target texture was surrounded by distractors differing in either low-order or high-order image statistics. The authors observed minimal evidence for spontaneous pop-out modulation in either area for texture-defined salience. However, they found that brief adaptation to the distractor textures could induce significant pop-out responses in V2, but not V1. These results suggest that the neural mechanisms defining bottom-up attention are highly malleable and are dynamically updated based on recent stimulus history to prioritize novel or distinct environmental features.
papers.authors: Aida Davila, Adam Kohn

E299.name: Edward Callaway
E299.main_research_area: neural circuit mapping and visual processing
E299.bio: Edward Callaway is a neuroscientist at the Salk Institute who developed the monosynaptic rabies virus tracing technique for mapping direct synaptic connections between specific cell types. Callaway's research focuses on the organization and function of neocortical circuits, specifically investigating how neuronal populations in the visual cortex process and integrate sensory information. By integrating viral tracing, single-cell transcriptomics, and in vivo physiological recordings, their lab identifies the circuit-level mechanisms underlying visual perception and cortical computation. This work describes the architectural principles of the brain and investigates how circuit disruptions contribute to conditions such as autism and schizophrenia.
E299.research_direction: Dr. Callaway has recently been investigating the fine-scale architecture and transcriptomic identity of visual circuits across multiple species. Their recent work explores how cortico-thalamo-cortical pathways route feedforward and reciprocal communication between the primary visual cortex and higher visual areas via the pulvinar. They are also mapping local cortical microcircuits by coupling monosynaptic rabies tracing with single-nucleus RNA sequencing to determine the highly specific synaptic wiring rules of genetically defined excitatory and inhibitory cell subclasses. Furthermore, their methodological research seeks to refine how visual system data is acquired and interpreted, investigating new metrics to resolve thin laminar boundaries in macaque V1 using Neuropixels probes and evaluating potential anatomical biases in retrograde rabies tracing efficiency.

papers.title: Complementary Organization of Mouse Driver and Modulator Cortico-thalamo-cortical Circuits
papers.abstract: This study elucidates the fine-scale organizational principles of transthalamic pathways in the mouse visual system by mapping inputs to pulvinar neurons projecting to five distinct higher visual areas (HVAs). Utilizing intrinsic signal imaging for precise areal boundary definition and projection-specific monosynaptic rabies tracing, the authors characterized the distribution of corticothalamic (CT) inputs. The results reveal that 'driver' inputs from layer 5 (L5) CT neurons in primary visual cortex (V1) provide the primary drive to all pulvinar→HVA projections, supporting a parallel feedforward relay model that adheres to the 'no-strong-loops' hypothesis. Conversely, 'modulator' inputs from layer 6 (L6) CT neurons exhibit a reciprocally biased organization, originating predominantly from the HVAs targeted by the pulvinar neurons. These findings establish a definitive map of the dual hierarchical and reciprocal architecture of cortico-thalamo-cortical circuits.
papers.authors: Rachel M. Cassidy, Angel V. Macias, Willian N. Lagos, Chiamaka Ugorji, Edward M. Callaway

papers.title: Transcriptomic Cell Type Specificity of Local Cortical Circuits
papers.abstract: The authors present Single Transcriptome Assisted Rabies Tracing (START), a novel neurotechnology that couples monosynaptic rabies tracing with single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) to resolve synaptic connectivity at transcriptomic resolution. By applying START to mouse primary visual cortex (V1), the study maps the presynaptic inhibitory inputs to five layer-specific excitatory neuron subclasses (L2/3, L4, L5 IT, L5 ET, and L6). While connectivity at the major subclass level (Pvalb, Sst, Vip, Lamp5) broadly follows established patterns, the high-throughput transcriptomic readout identifies specific rules for finer genetically defined subtypes. Notably, Sst Chodl neurons are identified as highly enriched inputs to layer 6 excitatory cells, and VIP subtypes are found to split into functionally distinct populations that either avoided or preferentially targeted excitatory neurons. This work demonstrates that local cortical wiring motifs are dictated by refined transcriptomic identities.
papers.authors: Maribel Patiño, Marley A. Rossa, Willian Nuñez Lagos, Neelakshi S. Patne, Edward M. Callaway

papers.title: High-Resolution Laminar Identification in Macaque Primary Visual Cortex Using Neuropixels Probes
papers.abstract: This research evaluates the utility of high-density Neuropixels electrode arrays (20-μm vertical spacing) for the identification of cortical laminae in macaque primary visual cortex (V1). The authors demonstrate that conventional current source density (CSD) analysis of local field potentials (LFP) lacks the necessary spatial resolution and consistency to reliably delineate the thin sublayers of V1, such as layer 4A. To overcome these limitations, they developed a set of high-resolution metrics derived from action potential (AP) frequency band signals, including unit density, AP power spectra, local coherence, and spike waveform features (spread, duration, and peak-trough ratio). These metrics enabled the precise detection of laminar borders and the assignment of recorded neurons to distinct layers receiving parallel LGN inputs (magnocellular, parvocellular, and koniocellular), providing a practical framework for high-density electrophysiology in primate neocortex.
papers.authors: Li A. Zhang, Peichao Li, Edward M. Callaway

papers.title: Postsynaptic cell type and synaptic distance do not determine efficiency of monosynaptic rabies virus spread measured at synaptic resolution
papers.abstract: This study investigates the biological and anatomical factors influencing the efficiency of retrograde transsynaptic spread of glycoprotein-deleted rabies virus (RVdG) in mouse V1. Using a specialized rabies vector expressing both postsynaptic (PSD95-GFP) and presynaptic (SynPh-RFP) fluorescent markers, the authors directly measured the 'synaptic fraction'—the proportion of a starter cell's total excitatory postsynaptic densities that were successfully labeled with inputs. The data reveal that RVdG spread efficiency (approximately 40% under the tested viral titers and parameters) is independent of the starter cell type (comparing excitatory neurons to Sst+ and Vip+ inhibitory interneurons) and is not biased by the distance of synaptic contacts from the postsynaptic soma. This finding suggests that while rabies-mediated tracing is incomplete, the labeling of input networks is not systematically skewed by postsynaptic cell identity or synaptic location on the dendritic arbor.
papers.authors: Maribel Patiño, Willian N. Lagos, Neelakshi S. Patne, Paula A. Miyazaki, Sai Krishna Bhamidipati, Forrest Collman, Edward M. Callaway

papers.title: Multimodal cortical neuronal cell type classification
papers.abstract: This work establishes a comprehensive framework for the classification of cortical neurons by integrating high-throughput single-cell transcriptomics with anatomical and projection-based datasets. The authors define a consensus taxonomy for the mouse neocortex comprising approximately 56 transcriptomic excitatory types—categorized into intratelencephalic (IT), extratelencephalic (ET), and corticothalamic (CT) subclasses—and 60 inhibitory types including Pvalb, Sst, Vip, and Lamp5/Sncg populations. The article highlights the specific gene regulatory programs and epigenetic signatures (e.g., single-nucleus DNA methylation and chromatin accessibility) that correlate with distinct long-distance projection targets. It further evaluates the efficacy of linking these molecular clusters to functional and structural circuit properties, providing a roadmap for systematic cell-type characterization in mammalian brain atlases.
papers.venue: Pflügers Archiv - European Journal of Physiology
papers.authors: Xiaoyi Mao, Maribel Patiño, Will N. Lagos, Neelakshi Patne, Edward M Callaway

E300.name: Marla Feller
E300.department: Department of Molecular and Cell Biology; Department of Neuroscience
E300.bio: Feller investigates mechanisms governing the assembly and functional organization of neural circuits within the developing retina. Their research focuses on retinal waves, which are patterned spontaneous activity bursts in immature retinas that facilitate the wiring of connections to the central visual system. Using two-photon excitation microscopy, electrophysiology, and anatomical techniques, Feller’s lab explores how these activity patterns shape direction-selective circuits and the morphology of glial cells. Current projects also examine the role of intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells and the impact of early light-driven signals on nascent retinal networks.
E300.research_direction: Dr. Feller's recent work investigates the developmental mechanisms that establish precise connectivity in early visual circuits, focusing heavily on the assembly of direction-selective networks in the retina. They have recently been exploring how structured spontaneous activity, specifically early retinal waves, guides both the morphological outgrowth of starburst amacrine cells and the axis-specific synaptic wiring of direction-selective ganglion cells. To disentangle the interplay between activity-dependent and hardwired developmental programs, their research incorporates two-photon calcium imaging, dual whole-cell recordings, and subtype-specific transcriptomic screening to hunt for molecular cues that instruct asymmetric synaptogenesis. Furthermore, their recent work explores methodological advancements in functional imaging, including the engineering of a combined two-photon and single-photon microscopy platform to simultaneously track calcium transients and near-infrared neurotransmitter sensors.

papers.title: Retinal waves shape starburst amacrine cell dendrite development through a direction-selective dendritic computation
papers.abstract: This study demonstrates that starburst amacrine cells (SACs) utilize direction-selective dendritic computations to decode the spatiotemporal biases of spontaneous retinal waves during early development. Prior to the onset of vision, mouse retinal waves exhibit a nasal propagation bias that simulates forward optic flow. Using two-photon calcium imaging and morphological reconstructions, the authors show that SAC dendrites oriented in the nasal direction exhibit enhanced calcium transients and accelerated outgrowth relative to other quadrants. This developmental process depends on the early maturation of intrinsic dendritic properties, including electrical compartmentalization and spatiotemporal summation, which translate network-level activity patterns into asymmetric structural maturation. The findings establish that nascent dendritic computations can instruct spatially precise morphological refinement during the assembly of neural circuits.
papers.authors: Miah N. Pitcher, Aanica S.B. Gonzales, Raul Habib, Marla Feller

papers.title: Adapting a two-photon scanning microscope for simultaneous single-photon imaging of an infrared dopamine sensor
papers.abstract: The authors developed a novel optical configuration for two-photon scanning microscopes that enables the concurrent detection of two-photon-generated visible fluorescence and single-photon-generated near-infrared (nIR) fluorescence. By coupling the nIR signal into a single-mode optical fiber that functions as a confocal pinhole, the system achieves superior optical sectioning and background suppression for nIR nanosensors. The effectiveness of this platform was validated through simultaneous imaging of dopamine release and calcium transients in the retina, as well as a comparative evaluation of genetically encoded GRAB-DA indicators and carbon nanotube-based nIRCat sensors in the striatum. This methodology provides a framework for multi-modal functional imaging across widely separated spectral channels on a single scanning platform.
papers.authors: Matthew Tarchick, Franklin Caval-Holme, Ben Smith, Petra Mocellin, Markita Landry, Natsumi Komatsu, Marla B. Feller

papers.title: Activity-dependent development of synaptic circuits mediates direction selectivity in an axis-specific manner
papers.abstract: This research investigates the role of Stage II cholinergic retinal waves in the assembly of direction-selective (DS) retinal circuits. In beta2-nAChR knockout mice lacking these waves, the authors find a profound deficit in horizontal direction selectivity, whereas vertical direction selectivity remains functionally intact. Through dual whole-cell recordings and calcium imaging, they demonstrate that the loss of horizontal DS is caused by a specific failure in the maturation of asymmetric GABAergic synaptic connectivity between starburst amacrine cells and horizontal-preferring direction-selective ganglion cells (DSGCs). Conversely, vertical-preferring DSGCs establish tuned inhibitory inputs via activity-independent mechanisms. The results indicate that the maturation of different DS axes within the same functional family of neurons is governed by distinct, axis-specific developmental programs.
papers.authors: Karina Bistrong, Rachana Deven Somaiya, Eugene Y. Liang, Benjamin E. Smith, Marla B. Feller

papers.title: Differential Expression Analysis Identifies Candidate Synaptogenic Molecules for Wiring Direction-Selective Circuits in the Retina
papers.abstract: To identify the molecular cues directing synapse specificity, the authors conducted a transcriptomic screen of genetically identified direction-selective ganglion cell (DSGC) subtypes during the peak of asymmetric synaptogenesis (Postnatal Day 10). By performing RNA sequencing on nasal-preferring and ventral-preferring DSGCs, the study isolated differentially expressed genes encoding cell surface and secreted proteins. These candidates are hypothesized to mediate the precise and stereotyped wiring between radially symmetric starburst amacrine cell (SAC) processes and DSGC dendrites. The analysis reveals a transcriptional logic underlying the emergence of asymmetric inhibition, identifying a diverse set of synaptogenic factors that likely instruction circuit assembly independently of sensory experience.
papers.authors: Joshua M. Tworig, Robert D. Morrie, Karina Bistrong, Rachana D. Somaiya, S. Hsu, J. Liang, K. G. Cornejo, Marla B. Feller

papers.title: Mapping the retina onto the brain
papers.abstract: This review provides a comprehensive analysis of the topographic and functional organization of retinofugal projections in the mammalian visual system. It examines how the spatial and feature-selective information from retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) is preserved and transformed as it maps onto subcortical targets like the lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) and superior colliculus (SC). The authors discuss the cooperative roles of molecular gradients (e.g., ephrins) and spatiotemporally structured retinal waves in the activity-dependent refinement of these maps. The review also explores the divergence of over 40 RGC types into parallel processing channels that serve specific visual behaviors, offering a synthesis of the mechanisms that establish the structural and functional connectivity of the early visual pathway.
papers.venue: Cold Spring Harbor Perspectives in Biology
papers.authors: Daniel Kerschensteiner, Marla B. Feller

E301.name: John Maunsell
E301.bio: John Maunsell studies the physiological mechanisms underlying visual perception and attention. Maunsell's research utilizes electrophysiological recordings from single neurons in behaving primates and mice to determine how cognitive factors modulate sensory representations in the visual cortex. This work indicates that attention increases the gain of neuronal responses without altering stimulus selectivity, enhancing the signal-to-noise ratio for attended information. Maunsell’s laboratory currently employs optogenetic tools and computational analysis to investigate how specific cortical layers and cell classes contribute to perceptual sensitivity and behavioral decision-making.
E301.research_direction: Dr. Maunsell's recent work explores the neural circuitry underlying visual spatial attention, perceptual sensitivity, and sensory encoding across both cortical and subcortical pathways. Using sophisticated behavioral paradigms and optogenetics in macaques, they have recently been investigating whether activity in structures like the superior colliculus and the locus coeruleus noradrenergic system reflects targeted enhancements in perceptual sensitivity rather than downstream decision criteria, motor biases, or general arousal. Additionally, their research examines the causal readout of parallel early visual systems, utilizing optogenetic inhibition in mice to untangle the relative behavioral contributions of the primary visual cortex versus the superior colliculus during specific contrast and luminance detection tasks. Finally, they are probing the fundamental computational rules of visual processing by modeling how receptive field location and spontaneous activity influence cortical normalization dynamics in the macaque middle temporal area.

papers.title: Neuronal normalization in monkey MT is an intensity-weighted average
papers.abstract: Cortical normalization is a canonical computation that preserves stimulus selectivity by adjusting neuronal responses relative to the activity of the surrounding population. This study demonstrates that in the macaque middle temporal (MT) area, normalization strength varies significantly across the receptive field (RF) and is poorly described by standard models. We propose an intensity-weighted normalization framework where stimulus intensity is the product of contrast and a location-specific RF weight. This model accounts for cross-neuronal variability in normalization and accurately predicts the systematic increase in contrast sensitivity observed at central RF locations. Furthermore, we show that spontaneous activity serves as a measurable excitatory drive that contributes to the normalization pool in a manner equivalent to external visual stimuli.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS)
papers.authors: Chery Cherian, John H. R. Maunsell

papers.title: Neuronal modulation of the superior colliculus associated with visual spatial attention represents perceptual sensitivity, independent of perceptual decision and motor biases
papers.abstract: While the superior colliculus (SC) is known to play a critical role in visual attention, it remains debated whether its activity reflects perceptual sensitivity (d') or non-sensory factors such as decision criteria or motor intent. Using a behavioral paradigm that independently manipulates monkeys' perceptual decisions and motor requirements, we find that SC firing rates are strongly modulated by spatial attention in a way that aligns with perceptual sensitivity. These neuronal modulations remained invariant despite large shifts in perceptual decision criteria and were not correlated with trial-by-trial motor execution. The results indicate that SC activity represents the heightened perceptual sensitivity characteristic of attentional states, rather than reflecting downstream decision-making or motor preparation processes.
papers.authors: Supriya Ghosh, John H.R. Maunsell

papers.title: Locus coeruleus norepinephrine contributes to visual-spatial attention by selectively enhancing perceptual sensitivity
papers.abstract: The noradrenergic system of the locus coeruleus (LC) is traditionally associated with non-specific arousal, yet its specific role in selective spatial attention is less clear. We recorded from LC neurons in rhesus monkeys performing a cued spatial attention task and found that LC activity is selectively modulated by the focus of attention, particularly during the processing of contralateral stimuli. Optogenetic activation of LC neurons during sensory selection improved behavioral performance by selectively driving perceptual sensitivity (d') rather than altering motor criteria or general arousal levels. These findings demonstrate that LC-derived norepinephrine provides a targeted neuromodulatory signal that enhances the sensory representation of attended locations to improve perceptual performance.
papers.authors: Supriya Ghosh, John H. R. Maunsell

papers.title: Stimulus-dependent differences in cortical versus subcortical contributions to visual detection in mice
papers.abstract: Primary visual cortex (V1) and the superior colliculus (SC) are early visual processing centers, but their relative causal contributions to different visual features are poorly understood. We employed optogenetic white-noise inhibition and reverse correlation to estimate the neuronal-behavioral kernels (NBK) for contrast and luminance detection in mice. Results show that detection of contrast changes depends on the earliest stimulus-evoked spikes in both V1 and SC. Conversely, luminance change detection relies primarily on SC activity, with V1 showing no significant behavioral weight for this feature. These findings reveal a stimulus-dependent dissociation in how cortical and subcortical pathways are read out to guide visual behavior, suggesting that certain low-level features bypass cortical requirements for detection.
papers.authors: Jackson J. Cone, Autumn O. Mitchell, Rachel K. Parker, John H. R. Maunsell

E302.name: Greg Horwitz
E302.bio: Gregory Horwitz investigates the neural mechanisms of visual perception and decision-making, focusing on the cortical processing of color and spatial vision. Horwitz’s research integrates high-density electrophysiological recordings using microfabricated electrode arrays with viral gene delivery and optogenetic techniques to manipulate cell types in the primate visual system. By combining these neurophysiological approaches with psychophysical threshold measurements and computational modeling, the Horwitz Lab examines the relationship between retinal signaling and behavioral perception. Their research specifically addresses how chromatic and spatial contrast are integrated within the primary visual cortex (V1).
E302.research_direction: Dr. Horwitz has recently been investigating how the primate brain processes complex visual features and executes rapid motor commands, while concurrently advancing genetic tools for precise neural circuit manipulation. Their recent work explores how complex cells in the macaque primary visual cortex integrate luminance and chromatic contrast, using closed-loop electrophysiology to compare these biological receptive fields with spatial feature representations in deep artificial neural networks. Moving from sensory input to motor output, they are also examining the cerebellar control of eye movements, utilizing closed-loop optogenetic perturbations of Purkinje cells to probe the real-time internal feedback models that guide ongoing saccades. To facilitate these highly specific, circuit-level interrogations in non-human primates, Dr. Horwitz has been characterizing the cellular tropism of specialized viral vectors designed to selectively target distinct subclasses of cortical inhibitory interneurons.

papers.title: Preferential transduction of parvalbumin-expressing cortical neurons by AAV-mDLX5/6 vectors
papers.abstract: Viral vectors bearing cell type-specific cis-regulatory elements provide a critical methodology for targeting and functionally interrogating neuronal subclasses in the non-human primate brain. In this study, the cellular tropism of adeno-associated viral (AAV) vectors expressing fluorophore reporters under the regulation of an 862-bp murine Dlx5/6 intergenic enhancer-promoter construct was evaluated in adult cortex. Vectors were administered via intracortical microinjections into the primary and extrastriate visual cortex of two macaque monkeys (Macaca mulatta), the prefrontal cortex of two additional macaques, and the sensorimotor cortex of three rats. Quantitative post-mortem fluorescence immunohistochemistry revealed that transgene expression was predominantly restricted to GABAergic interneurons, exhibiting high selectivity for parvalbumin-expressing (PV+) interneurons across cortical layers and species. Conversely, calretinin-positive (CR+) cortical interneurons demonstrated minimal to negligible transduction. These findings indicate that AAV-mDLX5/6 vectors exhibit substantial subclass bias rather than unbiased pan-GABAergic tropism, likely reflecting the differential activity of distal-less homeobox transcriptional regulatory machinery across distinct interneuron developmental lineages.
papers.authors: Padideh Yazdan-Shahmorad, Shane Gibson, Joanne C. Lee, Gregory D. Horwitz

papers.title: Closed-Loop Optogenetic Perturbation of Macaque Oculomotor Cerebellum: Evidence for an Internal Saccade Model
papers.abstract: Accurate execution of rapid saccadic eye movements is widely thought to require an internal forward model encoded in the cerebellum that estimates oculomotor plant dynamics and compares instantaneous eye displacement against target command in real time. To probe the causal role and temporal operating regime of this putative feedback loop, closed-loop optogenetic excitation was delivered to Purkinje cells (P-cells) within the oculomotor vermis (OMV, lobules VIc/VII) of rhesus macaques during horizontal saccades. Brief laser pulses (10–30 ms) were triggered contingent on online saccade detection at discrete delays (0, 10, 20, or 30 ms after initiation) in animals transduced with AAV-L7-ChR2. Optical stimulation induced dysmetria whose magnitude, trajectory curvature, and deceleration profile were systematically contingent upon stimulus onset timing, saccade duration, and initial eye velocity. Perturbations applied early in long-duration saccades produced substantial hypometria or hypermetria depending on target vector and hemifield, whereas identical pulses delivered near saccade termination yielded negligible endpoint errors. Computational simulations of an internal feedback loop incorporating a local cerebellar integrator successfully accounted for these parametric kinematic alterations, providing empirical support that the primate oculomotor vermis computes an internal feedback signal that shapes ongoing saccade trajectories on a millisecond timescale.
papers.authors: Robijanto Soetedjo, Gregory D. Horwitz

papers.title: Color and luminance processing in V1 complex cells and artificial neural networks
papers.abstract: Visual object boundary segmentation relies heavily on the spatial concurrence of luminance gradients and chromatic transitions in natural scenes. To elucidate how cortical receptive fields represent multi-attribute spatial contrast, the tuning of phase-invariant complex cells in macaque primary visual cortex (V1) was compared to corresponding spatial-phase-invariant convolutional units in deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) trained on ImageNet categorization. In awake macaques, single-unit V1 responses to drifting luminance and cone-contrast gratings were characterized using automated closed-loop isoresponse measurements and multidimensional quadratic receptive field modeling. The observed isoresponse surfaces revealed a dichotomy: complex cells were either tuned purely along luminance/achromatic axes or exhibited ellipsoidal/hyperbolic isoresponse geometries indicating joint, nonlinear sensitivity to both luminance and chromatic contrast, while units selective solely to chromatic contrast were exceptionally rare. An analogous non-uniform distribution of spatiochromatic selectivity emerged among phase-invariant pooling units in the second layer of feedforward CNNs. These comparative results indicate that the selective representation of joint chromatic-luminance boundaries without an isolated chromatic-only complex representation provides an optimal computational basis for illumination- and contrast-polarity-invariant object recognition.
papers.authors: Luke M. Bun, Gregory D. Horwitz

E304.name: Gregory C. DeAngelis
E304.department: Department of Brain and Cognitive Sciences
E304.bio: Gregory C. DeAngelis is the George Eastman Professor at the University of Rochester, where they investigate the cortical circuits mediating 3D vision, motion perception, and multisensory integration. DeAngelis employs a multidisciplinary approach combining primate neurophysiology, psychophysics, and computational modeling to study how the brain processes binocular disparity and optic flow for navigation. Their research identifies the functional roles of the middle temporal (MT) and medial superior temporal (MST) areas in depth perception and self-motion. Currently, DeAngelis explores how the brain utilizes causal inference and eye-movement signals to distinguish object motion from self-motion in complex environments.
E304.research_direction: Dr. DeAngelis has recently been investigating how the visual system accurately computes 3D scene structure and independent object motion during self-motion. Their recent work explores the neural mechanisms underlying optic flow parsing, examining how dorsal stream areas like MT and MSTd integrate viewing geometry and global retinal motion to disentangle an observer's own eye and head movements from scene-relative object dynamics. To probe these questions, they employ a combination of human psychophysics, single-unit and population recordings in awake macaques, and recurrent neural network modeling. Additionally, they have recently been developing innovative behavioral methodologies, such as online Bayesian reward algorithms, designed to isolate and preserve the true subjective perceptual biases of animals during motion discrimination tasks without inadvertently training those biases away.

papers.title: Flexible computation of object motion and depth based on viewing geometry inferred from optic flow
papers.abstract: Perceiving 3D scene structure and object motion during self-motion requires the brain to account for the visual consequences of eye and head movements. Standard models of visual compensation for eye rotations typically utilize vector subtraction, but these fail in natural viewing geometries where the eye simultaneously translates and rotates. This study introduces a theoretical framework for computing object motion and depth in generalized viewing geometries. Human psychophysical results demonstrate systematic perceptual biases when specific viewing geometries are simulated by optic flow, occurring automatically without training. Computational modeling using recurrent neural networks suggests that these adaptive computations may be mediated by neurons in area MT whose joint tuning for retinal and eye velocity is modulated by the inferred viewing geometry.
papers.authors: Zhe-Xin Xu, Jiayi Pang, Akiyuki Anzai, Gregory C. DeAngelis

papers.title: Seeing a Three-Dimensional World in Motion: How the Brain Computes Object Motion and Depth During Self-Motion
papers.abstract: This comprehensive review examines how the visual system extracts 3D environmental structure and object motion from dynamic 2D retinal projections during observer movement. While self-motion generates global optic flow that complicates scene analysis, it also provides essential cues such as motion parallax and perspective changes. We propose an integrated computational framework that unifies optic flow parsing, depth from motion parallax, and coordinate transformations. The review details the neural implementation of these processes within the dorsal stream, emphasizing how areas MT and MSTd perform complex, joint inferences to disentangle self-motion, scene-relative object movement, and the 3D layout of the world.
papers.authors: Zhe-Xin Xu, Gregory C. DeAngelis

papers.title: Rewarding animals based on their subjective percepts is enabled by online Bayesian estimation of perceptual biases
papers.abstract: Investigating the neural basis of biased perception in animals is complicated by the fact that choice behavior is shaped by reward feedback, which can lead animals to learn strategies that compensate for their intrinsic perceptual biases. To preserve these biases during neurophysiological recordings, we developed an online Bayesian method to estimate an animal's subjective percept in real time. By utilizing an informative prior and multiple stimulus contexts to dissociate perceptual from decision-related biases, our method updates the reward boundary trial-by-trial to align with the animal's biased percept. Validation in macaque monkeys performing a motion discrimination task confirms that this approach prevents animals from learning to compensate for their biases, ensuring that reports reflect true subjective experience.
papers.authors: Yelin Dong, Gabor Lengyel, Sabyasachi Shivkumar, Akiyuki Anzai, Grace F. DiRisio, Ralf M. Haefner, Gregory C. DeAngelis

papers.title: A neural mechanism for optic flow parsing in macaque visual cortex
papers.abstract: To perceive object motion relative to the world during self-motion, the brain must discount the global retinal image motion (optic flow) caused by the observer's own movement. A hypothesized mechanism for this is optic flow parsing, where background flow is globally subtracted from the retinal motion of objects. We provide the first neural evidence for this process by training macaque monkeys to discriminate object direction in the presence of radial optic flow. Monkeys exhibited perceptual biases consistent with flow parsing, and single-unit and population recordings in area MT revealed that neural activity is systematically biased by peripheral optic flow. These effects have a substantial neural latency and cannot be explained by surround suppression or choice-related activity, suggesting area MT represents scene-relative object motion.
papers.authors: Nicole E. Peltier, Akiyuki Anzai, Rubén Moreno-Bote, Gregory C. DeAngelis

papers.title: Viewing geometry drives flexible perception of object motion and depth
papers.abstract: Visual perception is an active process involving eye and head movements that produce complex retinal image motion. To accurately represent the 3D world, the brain must decompose this motion into components caused by self-motion and those caused by object motion in the world. We present a theory that links the computation of motion and depth with the observer's inferred viewing geometry. Psychophysical experiments show that humans exhibit novel perceptual biases when different viewing geometries (e.g., pure rotation vs. rotation plus translation) are simulated by optic flow. These biases occur automatically and are well-predicted by our theoretical framework. Recurrent neural network models trained on these tasks show neural response patterns similar to area MT, suggesting that the visual system automatically infers viewing geometry to flexibly attribute image motion to either self-motion or 3D structure.
papers.authors: Zhe-Xin Xu, Jiayi Pang, Akiyuki Anzai, Gregory C. DeAngelis

E305.name: Dora E. Angelaki
E305.department: Center for Neural Science; Tandon School of Engineering (Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering)
E305.bio: Dora E. Angelaki is a neuroscientist who investigates how the brain integrates multisensory signals, such as visual and vestibular cues, to support spatial orientation, navigation, and decision-making. Angelaki’s work utilizes engineering-inspired computational frameworks, including Kalman filters and Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes (POMDP), to model how neural populations represent latent variables and update internal beliefs during naturalistic foraging tasks. They also explore the breakdown of these neural computations in conditions such as autism, focusing on the interplay between sensory evidence and internal model-driven behavior. A member of the National Academy of Sciences, Angelaki has conducted research on heading perception and the representation of inertial motion within cortical and subcortical circuits.
E305.research_direction: Dr. Angelaki has recently been investigating the neural and computational mechanisms underlying spatial navigation, belief updating, and sequential decision-making. Their recent work explores how the brain tracks latent spatial variables during virtual navigation tasks, examining phenomena such as how active locomotion predictively stabilizes head-direction ring attractors in mice and whether unconstrained eye movements actively support spatial working memory in primates. They are also investigating the role of the prefrontal cortex in higher-order cognition, using large-scale electrophysiology and computational modeling to understand how dynamic neural networks maintain context-invariant representations across varying optic flow environments and drive strategic planning during long-term foraging. Additionally, their research probes the physiological basis of altered Bayesian inference, utilizing brain-wide recordings in distinct autism mouse models to test whether prior expectations are inflexibly updated relative to incoming sensory evidence.

papers.title: Active locomotion predictively rescues head direction attractor dynamics in head-fixed mice
papers.abstract: The research investigates the impact of head-fixation, a common experimental constraint inducing vestibular-proprioceptive conflict, on the brain's internal compass within the anterodorsal thalamic nuclei (ADn). Utilizing large-scale neurophysiological recordings and ring-attractor modeling, the authors demonstrate that head restraint disrupts canonical population-level correlations and off-ring manifold dynamics during periods of immobility. Crucially, the coherent ring attractor state predictively recovers approximately 550 ms prior to the onset of locomotion, even in the absence of physical head rotation or translational vestibular feedback. These findings suggest that motor efference copies or anticipated re-afferent signals are sufficient to stabilize the head direction network, indicating that the system operates as a state-dependent predictive estimator rather than a passive integrator.
papers.authors: Alexandr Pak, Janna Aarse, Heng Wei Zhu, Jean-Paul Noel, Simón Carrillo Segura, André A. Fenton, Dora Angelaki

papers.title: Belief embodiment through eye movements facilitates memory-guided navigation
papers.abstract: This study examines the functional role of oculomotor signals as a cognitive resource for spatial inference and working memory. Using a closed-loop 'firefly' navigation task, the authors show that humans and macaques physically track latent task variables, specifically the relative distance to an invisible spatial goal, through gaze behavior. A recurrent neural network model incorporating tuned connectivity between oculomotor and evidence-integrating frontoparietal circuits (area 7a) successfully recapitulated these behavioral strategies and better predicted posterior parietal cortex activity than task-optimized models. The results establish that unconstrained eye movements facilitate the maintenance of internal beliefs during navigation, supporting an embodied cognition framework for spatial computations.
papers.authors: Akis Stavropoulos, Kaushik J. Lakshminarasimhan, Dora E. Angelaki

papers.title: A common computational and neural anomaly across mouse models of autism
papers.abstract: Leveraging high-yield rodent psychophysics and brain-wide extracellular recordings (over 53k units in 150 brain areas), this research tests the hypothesis that autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is characterized by an inflexible update of Bayesian priors. In three monogenetic mouse models of ASD (Fmr1, Cntnap2, and Shank3B), the authors identified an under-weighting of sensory evidence relative to prior expectations. Neurally, this deficit was marked by a shift in prior encoding from sensory to frontal cortices. Frontal populations in ASD mice lacked prediction-error responses to statistically surprising stimuli and exhibited a bias toward encoding the prior mean, suggesting a convergent neurophysiological phenotype across distinct genetic instantiations of the disorder.
papers.authors: Jean-Paul Noel, Edoardo Balzani, Luigi Acerbi, Julius Benson, The International Brain Laboratory, Cristina Savin, Dora E. Angelaki

papers.title: Context-invariant beliefs are supported by dynamic reconfiguration of single unit functional connectivity in prefrontal cortex of male macaques
papers.abstract: The study probes the cortical mechanisms that maintain stable belief representations across varying environmental contexts. Macaques performed a path integration task while optic flow density was manipulated on a trial-by-trial basis. While population-level decoders for task-relevant latent variables generalized across sensory contexts in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC) and area 7a, single-unit functional connectivity (noise correlations) underwent significant remapping. Specifically, the dynamic reconfiguration of fine-grain statistical dependencies in dlPFC was found to be necessary for Maintaining context-invariant population codes. These findings suggest that the brain establishes flexible functional subnetworks to support stable cognitive representations despite volatile sensory inputs.
papers.authors: Jean-Paul Noel, Edoardo Balzani, Cristina Savin, Dora E. Angelaki

papers.title: Dorsolateral prefrontal cortex drives strategic aborting by optimizing long-run policy extraction
papers.abstract: The authors explore the neural basis of strategic planning in macaques during a continuous virtual foraging task. Animals were observed 'strategically aborting' trials—forgoing immediate low-value targets to maximize their global, session-long reward rate. This behavior was accurately captured by modular actor-critic reinforcement learning models that optimize long-term value functions. Large-scale neurophysiological recordings revealed that population dynamics in the dlPFC, but not area 7a or MSTd, encoded the decision to abort immediately upon offer presentation. This identifies the dlPFC as a specialized policy module that integrates task state and long-run value to optimize sequential decision-making in naturalistic environments.
papers.authors: Jean-Paul Noel, Ruiyi Zhang, Xaq Pitkow, Dora E. Angelaki

E307.name: Christopher C. Pack
E307.bio: Christopher C. Pack is a Professor at the Montreal Neurological Institute-Hospital, where their research focuses on the neural mechanisms underlying visual perception and sensorimotor integration. Pack’s laboratory utilizes microelectrode recordings and computational modeling to investigate how the cerebral cortex encodes visual motion, particularly within cortical areas such as MT and V4. Pack's work examines the role of traveling waves in integrating sensory and motor signals during eye movements, as well as the impact of brain plasticity and non-invasive electrical stimulation on neural circuit function. This research aims to establish a quantitative understanding of the neural code to develop therapeutic interventions for neurological disorders affecting vision.
E307.research_direction: Dr. Pack has recently been investigating the neural mechanisms underlying visual perception, decision-making, and neuromodulation in the primate brain. Their recent work explores how sensory populations are read out during shape and motion discrimination tasks, using targeted pharmacological inactivation in visual areas V4 and MT to parse causal feedforward signals from top-down decision-related feedback. Alongside these behavioral readout studies, they are mapping the feature-selective properties and context-dependence of corticocortical feedback circuits from area MST to MT using causal microstimulation and paired single-unit recordings. Furthermore, they have been evaluating the fundamental neurophysiological mechanisms of non-invasive brain stimulation, recording individual neurons in alert macaques to uncover how techniques like temporal interference and transcranial electrical stimulation influence exact spike timing and target long-range axonal projections.

papers.title: Decision signals in the absence of spiking activity in primate visual cortex
papers.abstract: This study dissociates causal and feedback components of choice-related neural fluctuations by analyzing local field potentials (LFPs) in macaque area MT during a motion discrimination task. Using pharmacological silencing with muscimol to eliminate local spiking activity, the authors demonstrate that choice probability (CP) in the high-gamma band (70–150 Hz) is abolished, characterizing it as a feedforward, causal signal. In contrast, decision-related signals in the low-gamma (30–70 Hz) and lower frequency (5–30 Hz) bands persist despite the absence of local spiking, indicating they reflect non-causal feedback or multiplexed trial-history information rather than feedforward sensory output.
papers.authors: Yueyue S. Hou, Liu D. Liu, Christopher C. Pack

papers.title: Inactivation of primate area V4 reveals inductive biases in visual learning
papers.abstract: To investigate the readout mechanisms supporting object recognition, this research utilized reversible pharmacological inactivation of feature-selective domains in area V4 while macaque monkeys performed shape discrimination tasks. Despite stimulus identity being decodable from population activity across various domains, behavioral impairments were restricted to preferred stimuli that evoked maximal firing rates. These results reveal a strong inductive bias favoring a 'simple' scalar readout of total population activity over an optimal population code. This simplicity bias facilitates efficient learning on ecologically relevant timescales but results in suboptimal information extraction from the sensory representation.
papers.authors: Pooya Laamerad, Matthew R. Krause, Daniel Guitton, Christopher C. Pack

papers.title: Brain stimulation preferentially influences long-range projections in primates
papers.abstract: The cellular targets of transcranial electrical stimulation (tES) were examined using single-unit recordings in alert non-human primates. Neurons were categorized by waveform kinetics into regular-spiking, fast-spiking, and putative long-range axonal projections. Findings demonstrate that putative axons exhibit significantly greater susceptibility to entrainment by weak electric fields than somatic populations. This suggest that non-invasive neuromodulation primarily influences the 'edges' (connectivity) of cortical networks rather than local nodes, suggesting that the efficacy of brain stimulation is driven by the modulation of long-range projection fibers.
papers.authors: Pedro G. Vieira, Matthew R. Krause, Pooya Laamerad, Christopher C. Pack

papers.title: Feature selectivity of corticocortical feedback along the primate dorsal visual pathway
papers.abstract: Simultaneous recordings and causal microstimulation were employed to map the stimulus-selective properties of feedback from area MST to area MT in the macaque dorsal pathway. Functional connectivity analyses revealed that inhibitory feedback occurs more frequently between neurons with mismatched stimulus preferences, though the magnitude of suppression is maximal for neurons with similar preferences. Furthermore, the feedback influence is contrast-dependent, providing robust suppression during high-contrast visual stimulation and transitioning to excitation under low-contrast conditions, supporting a context-dependent gain control mechanism.
papers.authors: Yavar Korkian, Nardin Nakhla, Christopher C. Pack

papers.title: Temporal interference stimulation disrupts spike timing in the primate brain
papers.abstract: The neurophysiological mechanisms of temporal interference (TI) stimulation were evaluated in alert macaques via single-neuron recordings. The study establishes that TI primarily modulates spike timing and phase-locking rather than average discharge rates. However, the requirement for high-frequency carrier waves and amplitude-modulated waveforms reduces the entrainment efficacy of TI by approximately 80% relative to conventional tACS. These findings suggest that while TI can non-invasively target deep brain structures, its primary therapeutic utility may lie in desynchronizing pathological oscillations rather than imposing new exogenous rhythms.
papers.authors: Pedro G. Vieira, Matthew R. Krause, Christopher C. Pack

E308.name: Nikolaus F. Troje
E308.bio: Nikolaus F. Troje is a Professor at York University and holds the Canada Research Chair in Reality Research, where they direct the BioMotion Lab. Troje’s research investigates how the brain transforms sensory input into perceptual representations, focusing on biological motion and the extraction of social information from human movement. Utilizing 3D motion capture, computational modeling, and virtual reality, Troje explores the mechanisms of multi-sensory integration and the psychophysics of person perception. This work connects biology, psychology, and computer science to study how humans recognize identity, intent, and emotion through visual and kinematic cues.
E308.research_direction: Dr. Troje has recently been investigating human visual perception, sensorimotor integration, and physiological arousal across both natural and immersive environments. Their recent work extensively explores virtual and mixed reality, utilizing behavioral and physiological measures—including transcranial magnetic stimulation and electrodermal activity—to examine how head-mounted displays impact spatial perception, the integration of binocular disparity and motion parallax, and autonomic responses to simulated stressors. In addition to this work on spatial and applied perception, they are modeling basic oculomotor dynamics by attempting to characterize a normative main sequence for the human pupillary light reflex under varying luminance conditions. Furthermore, they are investigating the visual processing of animate agents, using direction-discrimination paradigms to test how the orientation and structural salience of biological motion point-light walkers influence early motor preactivation and response priming.

papers.title: Covariation of corticospinal excitability and the autonomous nervous system by virtual reality: the roller coaster effect
papers.abstract: This research investigates the physiological interplay between the central motor system and the autonomic nervous system (ANS) during immersive virtual reality (VR) exposure. Utilizing a simulated roller coaster paradigm, the study assessed corticospinal excitability through motor evoked potentials (MEPs) induced by transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) and monitored autonomic arousal via electrodermal activity (EDA). The results demonstrate a significant positive covariation between the magnitude of MEPs and sympathetic activation during high-intensity VR segments. These findings suggest that VR can act as a potent stressor that effectively modulates motor system excitability through autonomous pathways, providing a foundation for non-motor neurorehabilitation strategies aimed at inducing specific physiological states.
papers.authors: Sidney Grospretre, Siavash Eftekharifar, Anne Thaler, Adam O. Bebko, Nikolaus F. Troje

papers.title: Main sequence of human luminance-evoked pupil dynamics
papers.abstract: This study establishes a normative 'main sequence' for the human pupillary light reflex, analogous to the well-known saccadic main sequence. By systematically varying the intensity and duration of luminance stimuli, the researchers characterized the lawful relationship between the peak constriction velocity and the total amplitude of the pupil response. The analysis reveals that human pupil dynamics follow a highly predictable power-law scaling across a wide range of stimulus conditions. These results provide a comprehensive quantitative framework for modeling pupillary control mechanisms and offer a sensitive metric for identifying physiological or pathological deviations in autonomic and visual processing.
papers.authors: Anne Thaler, Konrad Kording, Douglas James Cook, Gunnar Blohm, Nikolaus F. Troje

papers.title: Relating visual and pictorial space: Integration of binocular disparity and motion parallax
papers.abstract: The research addresses the categorical distinction between visual and pictorial spaces by examining how the integration of binocular disparity and motion parallax specifies spatial properties. The study proposes a unified geometrical model where the transformation from a 3D environment to a perceptual space is defined by relief depth scaling and isotropic rotations (pictorial distortions). Experiments using exocentric pointing tasks in virtual reality validated that binocular disparity primarily determines distance and 3D shape, whereas motion parallax is essential for specifying the allocentric direction of objects. The findings demonstrate that perceptual spaces are best categorized by the specific visual cues available rather than the display medium.
papers.authors: Xiaoye Michael Wang, Nikolaus F. Troje

papers.title: Visual perception and user satisfaction in video see-through head-mounted displays: a mixed-methods evaluation
papers.abstract: This investigation presents a comprehensive analysis of the perceptual fidelity and user experience of video see-through (VST) head-mounted displays. Using a mixed-methods design, the study compared quantitative performance on depth perception and motor coordination tasks with qualitative user feedback across multiple HMD architectures. The findings indicate that while higher sensor resolution significantly enhances performance in reading and fine manipulation, temporal latencies and artifacts such as waveguide non-uniformity and color fringing negatively impact presence and user satisfaction. The study establishes critical trade-offs between hardware resolution and temporal consistency for the development of high-fidelity mixed-reality systems.
papers.authors: Jessica de Souza, Siavash Eftekharifar, Anne Thaler, Adam O. Bebko, Nikolaus F. Troje

papers.title: Response priming with inverted biological motion
papers.abstract: The study explores early motor preactivation processes using biological motion (BM) stimuli within a response-priming paradigm. Specifically, it investigates how the orientation of point-light walkers influences motor priming effects in a direction-discrimination task. The results show that while upright BM primes produce robust facilitatory effects on subsequent motor responses, inversion significantly attenuates or reverses these effects. This suggests that the early processing of animate agents relies on orientation-sensitive visual filters that are specifically tuned to the gravity-defined kinematics of terrestrial locomotion. The findings highlight the importance of high-level structural salience in modulating low-level motor system activity.
papers.authors: Thomas Hutcheon, Hominy McMahon, Clara Retzloff, Calum Tinker, Dorita H. F. Chang, Nikolaus F. Troje

E309.name: Deborah Giaschi
E309.department: Department of Ophthalmology and Visual Sciences
E309.bio: Deborah Giaschi is a Professor at the University of British Columbia and a principal investigator at the BC Children's Hospital Research Institute. Giaschi's research program investigates the neural mechanisms underlying the typical and atypical development of motion perception, stereopsis, and visuomotor coordination. Utilizing a multimodal approach that includes child-friendly psychophysics, functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), and magnetoencephalography (MEG), they characterize how cortical maturation is disrupted in disorders such as amblyopia and developmental dyslexia. Their current work focuses on translating these neuroscientific insights into binocular treatment strategies, including the use of customized video games and virtual reality to improve visual outcomes.
E309.research_direction: Dr. Giaschi has recently been investigating the underlying neural mechanisms and clinical treatments for developmental visual disorders, particularly amblyopia and strabismus. Their recent work explores the etiology of broad-spectrum visual deficits in these populations, using psychophysical methods to determine whether elevated motion coherence thresholds stem from low-level fixational instability or primary cortical deficits. Additionally, they are evaluating the efficacy of novel dichoptic video game therapies for reducing interocular suppression and restoring binocular functions like stereoacuity and motion-defined form perception. To support this translational shift from traditional monocular occlusion to binocular protocols, their research also examines the large-scale functional brain networks mediating visual attention, aiming to identify sensitive neuroimaging and psychophysical biomarkers that can reliably predict treatment outcomes and individualize clinical care.

papers.title: Poor fixation stability does not account for motion perception deficits in amblyopia
papers.abstract: This study examined whether elevated motion coherence thresholds in individuals with amblyopia are a secondary consequence of fixational instability or reflect primary cortical processing deficits. Fixation stability and global motion direction discrimination were measured at slow (1 deg/s) and fast (30 deg/s) speeds in adults with a history of unilateral amblyopia and healthy controls. While participants with amblyopia exhibited significantly elevated coherence thresholds for slow speeds in both the amblyopic and fellow eyes, and demonstrated greater bivariate contour ellipse areas (BCEA) indicating reduced fixation stability, there was no significant correlation between fixation stability metrics and perceptual thresholds. These findings suggest that motion perception impairments in amblyopia derive from neural deficits within motion-sensitive cortical areas rather than degraded retinal input caused by unstable fixation.
papers.authors: Kimberly Meier, Simon Warner, Miriam Spering, Deborah Giaschi

papers.title: Evaluation of motion perception and binocular vision following dichoptic treatment for amblyopia
papers.abstract: This investigation evaluated the efficacy of a video game-based dichoptic treatment (Vivid Vision) for restoring motion perception and binocular function in 21 participants with various etiologies of amblyopia. Pre- and post-treatment assessments measured monocular visual acuity, motion-defined form orientation discrimination, and global motion direction coherence thresholds, alongside binocular metrics such as stereoacuity and interocular suppression (contrast balance index). Following an 8-week training regimen, significant mean improvements were observed in amblyopic-eye visual acuity and motion-defined form perception, as well as fellow-eye global motion perception. Reductions in interocular suppression were noted in 43% of participants, though stereoacuity gains were limited to 14%, indicating that dichoptic protocols can effectively mitigate certain monocular and binocular deficits in a subset of patients.
papers.authors: Akosua Kesewah Asare, Cindy S. Ho, Hee Yeon Im, Deborah Eileen Giaschi

papers.title: Large-scale functional networks underlying visual attention
papers.abstract: This literature review synthesizes current knowledge on the large-scale neural architectures that mediate visual attention, focusing on the dynamic coordination between the dorsal and ventral attention networks (DAN and VAN). The authors evaluate the roles of the frontoparietal and salience networks in modulating sensory processing through top-down and bottom-up mechanisms. The paper highlights recent advancements in neuroimaging that reveal how these functional connectomes undergo reconfiguration during attentional shifts and discusses the implications of network-level dysfunction in developmental disorders such as amblyopia and dyslexia. By integrating findings from functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and electrophysiological studies, the review provides a comprehensive framework for understanding how distributed cortical nodes collaborate to prioritize visual information.
papers.authors: Alexander J. Cook, Hee Yeon Im, Deborah E. Giaschi

papers.title: A vision scientist walks into a clinic with the goal of improving treatment outcomes for amblyopia and strabismus
papers.abstract: In this Davida Teller Award lecture article, the author discusses the translation of visual neuroscience research into clinical practice for the management of amblyopia and strabismus. The paper reviews the evidence for broad-spectrum visual deficits beyond simple acuity loss, including motion perception, contour integration, and eye-hand coordination. It argues for a paradigm shift in treatment from monocular occlusion to binocular protocols that target the underlying neural suppressive mechanisms. The author highlights the necessity of using sensitive psychophysical and neuroimaging biomarkers to predict surgical and therapeutic outcomes, ultimately aiming to develop more individualized and effective treatment strategies for children with developmental visual disorders.
papers.authors: Deborah Giaschi

E312.name: Ari Rosenberg
E312.bio: Rosenberg’s research examines the hierarchical neural circuits and computations through which the brain reconstructs three-dimensional object representations from two-dimensional retinal inputs. Their lab integrates high-density neuronal recordings in non-human primates, human psychophysical experiments, and computational modeling to quantify 3D orientation selectivity and sensorimotor transformations. Investigations focus on the integration of monocular and binocular cues, multisensory processing for spatial constancy, and the characterization of canonical neural computations, such as divisive normalization, to study the neurodevelopmental basis of autism.
E312.research_direction: Dr. Rosenberg has recently been investigating how the mammalian visual system reconstructs three-dimensional space and motion from two-dimensional retinal inputs. Using multi-area electrophysiological recordings and computational modeling in behaving macaques, their recent work explores the hierarchical computations that transform 2D retinal velocities into 3D motion trajectories across cortical areas such as MT and FST. Additionally, they are examining the spatial organization and sensorimotor integration of the dorsal stream, probing how areas like V3A and CIP multiplex 3D visual features like surface tilt with decision-related choice activity and oculomotor motor plans. Broadly, Dr. Rosenberg is synthesizing cross-species mechanisms of 3D vision, outlining how distinct cortical subnetworks combine binocular stereopsis and monocular cues to encode object pose, surface orientation, and global scene layout for spatial cognition and goal-directed behavior.

papers.title: The Richness of Vision in the Mammalian Brain: Neural Codes for Visual Perception and Behavior in Three Dimensions
papers.abstract: Although systems neuroscience frequently evaluates visual representations using planar two-dimensional stimuli, navigating and interacting with objects in naturalistic environments requires neural adaptations tailored to three-dimensional (3D) space. This review synthesizes cross-species discoveries regarding mammalian neural adaptations for 3D visual perception. While binocular disparity tuning has been thoroughly mapped across primate visual cortex, comparable depth-sensitive receptive field architectures have now been discovered in non-primate models including tree shrews and rodents, despite species-specific anatomical and optical constraints. In humans, noninvasive population receptive field mapping now links disparity-sensitive cortical populations directly to stereoscopic depth judgements. At intermediate and higher stages of the primate ventral stream, 3D object representations are synthesized through the integration of binocular disparity and pictorial monocular cues, while the dorsal stream carries out coordinate frame transformations that yield object pose, surface orientation, and 3D motion tuning invariant to gaze angle. This comparative analysis highlights general neural coding principles underpinning 3D vision, providing foundational insights necessary to understand spatial cognition and guide the design of vision neuroprosthetics.
papers.authors: Ari Rosenberg, Holly Bridge, Charles E Connor, Jason M Samonds, Seiji Tanabe, Kristine Krug

papers.title: Differential clustering of visual and choice- and saccade-related activity in macaque V3A and CIP
papers.abstract: Cortical circuits across sensory and motor areas typically aggregate into functional clusters to minimize axonal wiring costs and facilitate local computations. Along the primate dorsal pathway, areas V3A and the caudal intraparietal area (CIP) form a hierarchical interface where 3D visual features, decision-related choice activity, and saccadic motor signals converge, frequently within individual neurons demonstrating mixed selectivity. Extracellular recordings were obtained from simultaneously isolated neuronal pairs in macaques performing an eight-alternative forced-choice 3D planar tilt discrimination task across multiple depths to evaluate spatial clustering across functional domains. Statistically significant clustering was present in both areas across all three domains; however, domain-specific differences emerged across the hierarchy. Visual feature selectivity and saccade direction tuning clustered significantly more tightly in V3A than in CIP, whereas choice-related activity was clustered significantly more strongly in CIP than in V3A. Furthermore, the degree of clustering did not depend on whether neurons exhibited mixed selectivity. These results suggest a functional architecture wherein V3A prioritizes within-domain processing of sensory and oculomotor signals, while CIP emphasizes cross-domain integration to bridge perception and goal-directed action.
papers.authors: Zikang Zhu, Byounghoon Kim, Raymond Doudlah, Ting-Yu Chang, Ari Rosenberg

papers.title: Hierarchical computation of 3D motion across macaque areas MT and FST
papers.abstract: Extracting 3D motion trajectories from 2D retinal velocities is essential for interceptive and avoidant behavior. To determine how and where primate visual circuits perform this computation, neuronal activity was recorded simultaneously from macaque middle temporal area (MT) and its downstream partner in the fundus of the superior temporal sulcus (area FST) during a 3D motion discrimination task isolating stereoscopic and monocular perspective cues. By dissociating true 3D trajectory tuning from local 2D planar motion responses, the electrophysiological data revealed a hierarchical transition: robust selectivity for 3D motion in depth was widespread among FST neurons (~37%) but largely absent in MT neurons (~8%), whose activity primarily reflected 2D retinal velocity components. Computational feedforward modeling showed that cue-invariant 3D motion selectivity in area FST can be constructed by selectively integrating the outputs of 2D direction-selective MT afferents, resolving controversies regarding MT's role in motion-in-depth processing and establishing FST as a key site for 3D motion representation.
papers.authors: Lowell W Thompson, Byounghoon Kim, Bas Rokers, Ari Rosenberg

papers.title: Neuronal Representations Supporting Three-Dimensional Vision in Nonhuman Primates
papers.abstract: Recovering a coherent, 3D model of the external world from ambiguous, shifting 2D retinal projections is a classic inverse problem solved by primate visual circuits. This review examines how the nonhuman primate visual system carries out this transformation across specialized pathways within the dorsal ('where') and ventral ('what') processing streams. Each stream contains specialized subnetworks tuned to distinct 3D visual parameters—including surface slant and tilt, object contour in depth, 3D motion vectors, and global scene layout—by combining binocular stereopsis with monocular cues such as perspective, texture gradients, and motion parallax. Computational differences across channels impose distinct information-limiting constraints on 3D perception. Furthermore, convergent physiological and neuroimaging evidence points to area V3A as a crucial branchpoint from which multiple 3D-fugal processing streams diverge toward parietal and temporal regions. The evolutionary enlargement of area V3A in humans relative to nonhuman primates may underlie enhanced 3D spatial cognition and manual dexterity.
papers.authors: Ari Rosenberg, Lowell W Thompson, Raymond Doudlah, Ting-Yu Chang

E319.name: Anya Hurlbert
E319.bio: Anya Hurlbert is a Professor of Visual Neuroscience who researches the physiological and computational mechanisms of human color perception, specifically color constancy. Their work employs psychophysical experimentation, computational modeling, and neuroimaging to investigate how the brain stabilizes object color across varying illuminants and the impact of individual differences on these processes. Hurlbert's current research also includes developing lighting technologies for health and applying machine learning to retinal OCT imaging for the early diagnosis of neurodegenerative diseases. They hold degrees in physics, physiology, and medicine, and co-founded the Institute of Neuroscience at Newcastle University.
E319.research_direction: Dr. Hurlbert's recent work explores how complex spectral and temporal illumination properties interact with human color perception and natural scene understanding. A major focus of their research investigates the interplay between color constancy and object appraisal, using immersive, spectrally tunable lightrooms to test how near-metameric and chromatic lighting shifts affect the perceived naturalness, ripeness, and quality of real-world food stimuli. They have also recently been examining the temporal dynamics of natural daylight, combining large-scale spectral measurements with psychophysical discrimination tasks to probe human visual sensitivity to chromaticity and color temperature changes over time. Furthermore, their research extends these ecological illumination principles to higher-level scene perception, analyzing historical paintings to understand how human observers utilize broad image statistics like contrast, brightness, and hue distribution to decode depicted time-of-day cues.

papers.title: Near-metameric illumination changes affect visually perceived food attributes
papers.abstract: This study evaluates the impact of near-metameric illumination modulations on the subjective appraisal of 3D naturalistic food stimuli. By isolating chromaticity-preserving spectral variations (metamers) in an immersive lightroom environment, the authors demonstrate that changes in surface color appearance alone, absent of contextual or illuminant color shifts, significantly modulate perceived food attributes such as ripeness, healthfulness, and purchase intention. Psychophysical data indicates that both hue and saturation shifts in the object's appearance under metameric light drive positive attribute ratings, with the specific directional effects varying across distinct food categories and individual observers.
papers.venue: Journal of the Optical Society of America A
papers.authors: Ilgin Cebioglu, Monaly Mistry, Ruben Vasey, Anya Hurlbert

papers.title: Perceived food quality under metameric vs. chromatic illumination changes
papers.abstract: Investigating the interplay between color constancy and perceived food quality, this research contrasts the effects of metameric and chromatic illumination shifts on real fruit stimuli. Utilizing a spectrally tunable lightroom, the authors presented trichromatic observers with objects under neutral metamers (CCT ~6500K) and broadband chromatic illuminants (2000K and 10000K). Results from calculated Positive Attribute Scores (PAS) reveal that while metameric modulations influence quality perception through changes in object color appearance, chromatic shifts can impact perceived quality independently of fruit color appearance, which is largely maintained through color constancy mechanisms.
papers.authors: Ilgin Cebioglu, Paul Nuttall, Nick Pollard, Laurence Potts, Anya Hurlbert

papers.title: Physical and perceptual measurements of temporal dynamics in natural daylight
papers.abstract: This work quantifies the spectral and temporal dynamics of natural daylight through an extensive dataset of directional light field samples (4512 spectra). The authors identify a consistent tripartite daily profile characterized by rapid chromatic transitions during dawn and dusk—following the daylight locus—and relative stability during the midday period. Psychophysical discrimination experiments reveal a perceptual asymmetry in chromaticity change detection, where observers exhibit higher sensitivity to cooler CCT shifts (~1.2 ΔE/s) compared to warmer ones (~2 ΔE/s). Findings suggest that natural rates of daylight change generally remain below human visibility thresholds (~0.4 ΔE/s), facilitating the perceptual stability of natural scenes.
papers.authors: Cehao Yu, Ruben Pastilha, Anya Hurlbert

papers.title: Tuning light to make fruit look natural: Memory colours, metamers and illumination modulation
papers.abstract: Addressing the relationship between memory colors and lighting design, this study explores the optimization of illumination spectra for the naturalistic depiction of fruit. The authors investigate how spectral modulation—specifically concerning metamers and spectral 'jaggedness'—influences naturalness judgments and the alignment of fruit color with established memory color prototypes. Results indicate that naturalness judgments encompass a range of correlated color temperatures but skew toward higher color fidelity illumination. Crucially, spectral jaggedness (the degree of spectral power distribution variation) was found to correlate negatively with perceived naturalness across all tested fruit categories.
papers.authors: Yesesvi Somayaji Konakanchi, Anya Hurlbert

papers.title: Time-of-day perception in paintings
papers.abstract: This study explores the encoding of temporal illumination cues in 17th–20th century Western European paintings. Through online and laboratory rating experiments, the authors demonstrate that human viewers reliably decode the depicted time of day from the image statistics of artworks. High 'morningness' ratings were found to correlate with increased brightness, contrast, and saturation, while 'eveningness' associated with lower saturation and brighter yellow/darker blue hues. A predictive linear model derived from principal components of image statistics explained 76% of the variance in time-of-day perception, suggesting that artists successfully tap into fundamental daylight-derived chromatic assumptions held by the human visual system.
