papers.authors: Cehao Yu, Mitchell J. P. Van Zuijlen, Cristina Spoiala, Sylvia C. Pont, Maarten W. A. Wijntjes, Anya Hurlbert

E321.name: Hannah Smithson
E321.main_research_area: human visual perception and neural mechanisms
E321.bio: Hannah Smithson investigates the neural and perceptual mechanisms of human vision, focusing on color and material perception. Smithson’s research utilizes high-resolution retinal imaging via adaptive optics scanning laser ophthalmoscopy (AOSLO) to link individual photoreceptor activity with visual performance in the living eye. By combining psychophysical experimentation with computer-rendered stimuli, they examine how the visual system achieves perceptual constancy and processes properties such as gloss, roughness, and translucency. Smithson also directs interdisciplinary initiatives that apply computational and optical analysis to historical medieval scientific texts regarding color and light.
E321.research_direction: Dr. Smithson has recently been investigating the complexities of human color vision and retinal physiology, spanning from the physical properties of environmental light to the cellular structure of the eye. Their recent work explores the computational challenges of material and color perception, using computer graphics and hyperspectral maps to understand how observers utilize the spatial geometry of specular highlights and the directional variations of natural lighting to estimate illuminants and resolve surface metamerism. At the physiological level, they are mapping the genetic and structural diversity of the human retina by quantifying ethnicity-related variability in L-cone spectral sensitivity and testing the feasibility of tracking the photoreceptor mosaic during extended sessions via adaptive optics scanning laser ophthalmoscopy (AOSLO) without pharmacological pupil dilation. Additionally, they are employing hyperspectral imaging to characterize how mixed-illuminant indoor environments stimulate all five human photoreceptor classes, investigating the chromatic regularities that may drive seasonal and short-term light adaptation.

papers.title: Investigating ethnicity-related variability in the human L-cone spectral sensitivity function
papers.abstract: This study quantifies inter-individual and inter-ethnic variances in the spectral sensitivity of long-wavelength-sensitive (L) cones. By integrating psychophysical measurements with genetic profiling of the OPN1LW gene, specifically the Ser180Ala polymorphism, the researchers evaluated how demographic and ethnic factors influence peak spectral sensitivity (lambda_max). The investigation aims to refine standard cone fundamentals to better represent the natural diversity of retinal photopigments across diverse human populations.
papers.authors: Allie C. Schneider, Takuma Morimoto, Michelle E. McClements, Robert E. MacLaren, Hannah E. Smithson

papers.title: When the brightest is not the best: illuminant estimation from the geometry of specular highlights
papers.abstract: This research evaluates the 'brightest is white' heuristic in human color constancy, which posits that the visual system estimates illuminant chromaticity based on the highest luminance pixel in a scene. Utilizing computer-rendered stimuli with controlled surface textures and varying specularity, the authors demonstrate that operational color constancy remains robust even when specular highlights fall on dark textural regions and do not constitute the brightest elements. The results suggest the visual system utilizes the spatial geometry and structural regularities of highlights—specifically their alignment with surface curvature—to disentangle material reflectance from illumination spectra.
papers.authors: Takuma Morimoto, Robert J. Lee, Hannah E. Smithson

papers.title: Quantifying CIE alpha-opic signals in the indoor built environment
papers.abstract: The study provides a comprehensive spectral and chromatic characterization of mixed-illuminant indoor 'built' environments, where artificial lighting and natural daylight interact. Using hyperspectral imaging, the authors calculate alpha-opic signals for the five human photoreceptor classes (L, M, S cones, rods, and melanopsin ipRGCs) across a typical office setting. Findings indicate that indoor environments exhibit statistical regularities in chromatic variation similar to those found in naturalistic scenes, primarily driven by daylight ingress, which may support both short-term and seasonal adaptational processes.
papers.venue: Journal of the Optical Society of America A
papers.authors: Samuel Ponting, Ruth Kelly Waskett, Manuel Spitschan, Hannah E. Smithson

papers.title: How many surfaces can you distinguish by color? Real environmental lighting increases discriminability of surface colors
papers.abstract: This paper investigates how directional variations in natural environmental illumination influence chromatic discriminability. By applying computer-graphics simulations to measured hyperspectral illumination maps, the authors quantify the resolution of illuminant metamerism for trichromatic and dichromatic observers. The results show that the directional complexity of real-world light allows for the disambiguation of over 80% of metameric surface pairs simply through changes in surface tilt, thereby effectively increasing the volume of distinguishable surface colors relative to uniform illumination conditions.
papers.authors: Takuma Morimoto, João M. M. Linhares, Sérgio M. C. Nascimento, Hannah E. Smithson

papers.title: Extended-period AOSLO imaging in the living human retina without pupil dilation: a feasibility study
papers.abstract: This study assesses the feasibility of longitudinal high-resolution retinal imaging using an adaptive optics scanning laser ophthalmoscope (AOSLO) without pharmacological mydriasis. By monitoring six participants over 1.5-hour sessions with concurrent visual stimulation, the authors modeled the dynamic relationship between natural pupil diameter and image metrics such as sharpness and contrast-to-noise ratio. The findings demonstrate that cellular-scale resolution of the photoreceptor mosaic is reproducible and stable across extended sessions, validating the use of AOSLO in scenarios where pupil dilation is contraindicated or undesirable.
papers.authors: Jiahe Cui, Maria Villamil, Allie C. Schneider, Penelope F. Lawton, Laura K. Young, Martin J. Booth, Hannah E. Smithson

E322.name: Christoph Witzel
E322.bio: Christoph Witzel is an Associate Professor at the University of Southampton and directs the Soton Colour Lab. Witzel’s research employs psychophysics, behavioral experiments, and mathematical modeling to investigate the subjective reality of color, focusing on mechanisms of color constancy, categorical perception, and the evolution of color naming across languages. They have published findings on the memory color effect and evidence challenging color-opponent theories of afterimages in favor of cone-adaptation models. Witzel’s work also explores multisensory integration through geomagnetic sensory augmentation and examines the cognitive impacts of generative artificial intelligence.
E322.research_direction: Dr. Witzel has recently been investigating the physiological, computational, and linguistic mechanisms that shape human color perception. Their recent work explores the low-level origins of complementary color afterimages, using large-sample psychophysics to test whether these phenomena are driven by photoreceptor-level cone adaptation or subcortical opponent mechanisms. Beyond early visual processing, they examine human expectations regarding relational color constancy, utilizing hyperspectral imaging and naturalistic scenes to assess how observers model surface chromaticity shifts under changing illuminants. Additionally, their research probes the interplay between sensory input and semantic knowledge in color categorization, using artificial neural networks to evaluate how color spaces emerge from visual or linguistic training, and comparing the cognitive organization of color terms between red-green dichromats and typical trichromats.

papers.title: The non-opponent nature of colour afterimages
papers.abstract: This psychophysical investigation challenges the prevailing theory that complementary color afterimages arise from cone-opponent neural mechanisms. By systematically measuring perceived hue and chroma across a diverse set of chromatic inducers, the study demonstrates that afterimage appearance aligns precisely with a quantitative model of adaptation at the photoreceptor level (cone contrasts) rather than the subcortical opponent stage. Results from three experiments, involving both large-sample behavioral testing and high-resolution psychophysical replication, indicate that three distinct peaks in afterimage intensity correspond to cone-excitation singularities. These findings establish that negative afterimages are primarily driven by nonlinear adaptation in the cone photoreceptors, offering a unifying explanation for previously contradictory phenomena in color science.
papers.authors: Christoph Witzel

papers.title: Exploring the categorical nature of colour perception: Insights from artificial networks
papers.abstract: This study employs artificial neural networks to investigate the emergence of color categories and their relationship to human perception. Using an 'odd-one-out' paradigm, the performance of unimodal vision networks (e.g., ResNet, VGG) and multimodal vision-language models (e.g., CLIP) was compared against human psychophysical data. The research reveals that human-like color categorization emerges most robustly in models trained on semantic visual tasks, such as object recognition, even in the absence of explicit linguistic input. While unimodal models explain a significant portion of human categorical patterns, vision-language models demonstrate superior alignment with human naming consistency. The results support a dual-origin hypothesis where categorical perception is a language-independent representation that is further refined by linguistic color terms during development.
papers.authors: Arash Akbarinia, Christoph Witzel

papers.title: Colour expectations across illumination changes
papers.abstract: This research explores human prior expectations regarding surface color shifts under naturally occurring and artificial illumination changes. Through a series of psychophysical tasks using naturalistic scenes and hyperspectral imaging, the study assesses whether observers possess internal models of how chromaticity coordinates shift when the spectral power distribution of the illuminant varies. Findings indicate that while human expectations lack precise colorimetric accuracy, they align with the general direction of color shifts observed in nature. The study demonstrates that relational color constancy is supported by the stability of cone-excitation ratios and that prior knowledge of surface color identities helps disambiguate reflectance from illumination, particularly under broadband lighting conditions.
papers.authors: Hamed Karimipour, Christoph Witzel

papers.title: Color blindness and semantic knowledge: Cognition of color terms from elicited lists in dichromats and normal observers
papers.abstract: Using the elicited lists method, this study investigates the semantic structure of color terms in individuals with red-green color vision deficiencies (protanopia and deuteranopia) compared to normal trichromats. The analysis focused on psychological salience (CSI), term adjacency, and the formation of cognitive clusters based on universalist and evolutionary hypotheses. Results showed that all participant groups, including dichromats, exhibited a highly similar semantic memory structure, starting with cardinal primary terms followed by achromatic and derived clusters. Despite significant sensory deficits, color-deficient observers acquired nearly identical semantic knowledge about color relationships, suggesting that the development of a linguistic color lexicon relies heavily on cultural transmission and social communication rather than exclusively on low-level chromatic sensitivity.
papers.authors: Humberto Moreira, Leticia Álvaro, Julio Lillo, Christoph Witzel

E323.name: Takehiro Nagai
E323.department: Department of Information and Communications Engineering
E323.bio: Takehiro Nagai is an Associate Professor at the Institute of Science Tokyo, where their research examines the psychological and computational mechanisms of human color and material perception. Nagai investigates how the visual system interprets surface qualities such as glossiness, translucency, and texture through psychophysical experimentation and image analysis. Their work addresses higher-level chromatic mechanisms and the top-down cognitive factors that influence material recognition in diverse environments. Previously, Nagai conducted postdoctoral research at the University of California, San Diego, and held faculty positions at Toyohashi University of Technology and Yamagata University.
E323.research_direction: Dr. Nagai's recent work explores the spatial, temporal, and cognitive mechanisms underlying human color and material perception. Using rigorous psychophysical paradigms, they have recently been investigating how the visual system might reference internal models of physical reflectance limits to determine luminosity thresholds in natural scenes, while also characterizing the temporal dynamics of chromatic and achromatic discrimination sensitivities immediately following sudden drops in ambient luminance. Their research additionally examines how broader spatial and cognitive contexts shape color vision, specifically testing how field of view extent modulates color constancy and how selective attentional load differentially impacts the evaluation of near-threshold versus suprathreshold chromatic differences. To facilitate this complex behavioral research, Dr. Nagai is developing specialized software pipelines that bypass default GPU color-management, enabling precise, laboratory-grade colorimetric and photometric stimulus control for experiments in immersive virtual reality environments.

papers.title: Optimal colors can predict luminosity thresholds in natural scenes
papers.abstract: Luminosity thresholds mark the perceptual boundary at which an object transitions from appearing as a reflecting surface to a self-luminous source. This research evaluates the hypothesis that the human visual system determines these thresholds by referencing internal models of the theoretical physical limits of surface reflectance (optimal colors) under a given illumination. Utilizing psychophysical tasks within naturalistic scenes, the authors demonstrate that observers' luminosity judgments align significantly with the boundaries of the physical color gamut. These findings suggest that an internal representation of chromatic constraints guides the visual system's capacity to infer material properties and lighting conditions.
papers.authors: Killian Duay, Takehiro Nagai

papers.title: Attention plays a greater role in judging large color differences than small ones
papers.abstract: The study investigates the differential impact of selective attention on the perception of small versus large chromatic differences. Using a dual-task psychophysical design, the researchers compared color discrimination performance under conditions of full versus divided attentional load. Results reveal that while near-threshold color discrimination remains relatively robust to attentional modulation, the evaluation of large, suprathreshold chromatic differences is significantly impaired when cognitive resources are diverted. This asymmetry suggests that the processing of large chromatic distances recruits higher-level, capacity-limited cognitive mechanisms—potentially involving categorical or memory-based representations—that are distinct from the early, autonomous stages of color processing.
papers.venue: Journal of the Optical Society of America A
papers.authors: Kashi Li, Takehiro Nagai

papers.title: Impact of field of view on color constancy in virtual reality
papers.abstract: This research examines how the extent of the visible field of view (FOV) modulates the degree of color constancy in immersive virtual environments. Participants performed achromatic adjustment tasks using a head-mounted display (HMD) under various simulated global illuminants while the FOV was systematically manipulated. The data demonstrate a significant positive correlation between FOV size and color constancy indices, indicating that the visual system integrates chromatic signals from the periphery to establish a more stable estimate of the scene illuminant. The study highlights the critical role of large-scale spatial context and scene statistics in chromatic adaptation and perceptual stability.
papers.venue: Journal of the Optical Society of America A
papers.authors: Killian Duay, Takehiro Nagai

papers.title: VR HMD color calibration and accurate control of emitted light using Three.js
papers.abstract: This article details a specialized software framework for high-precision colorimetric and photometric control in virtual reality using the Three.js library. The authors propose a methodology to bypass default GPU-based tone-mapping and color-management routines, enabling linear control of pixel-level luminance and chromaticity. By implementing custom shaders and unlit materials, the proposed pipeline allows researchers to present psychophysical stimuli defined in CIE coordinates with laboratory-grade accuracy. Photometric validation across multiple HMD models confirms that this framework meets the rigorous requirements for vision science research involving color and material perception.
papers.authors: Killian Duay, Yoko Mizokami, Takehiro Nagai

papers.title: Luminance and chromaticity discrimination sensitivities right after an abrupt decrease in background luminance
papers.abstract: This study characterizes the temporal dynamics of visual discrimination sensitivity following a sudden reduction in ambient luminance. Psychophysical thresholds for luminance and chromatic (L-M and S-cone) modulations were measured at discrete intervals immediately after a step-down in background luminance. The results show a sharp, transient reduction in sensitivity across all post-receptoral channels, followed by a non-linear recovery process. Notably, luminance gain-control mechanisms were found to stabilize faster than chromatic pathways, highlighting the distinct temporal constraints of achromatic and chromatic adaptation during the early phases of dark adaptation.
papers.authors: Minwoo Son, Takehiro Nagai

E324.name: Maria Olkkonen
E324.bio: Olkkonen is a docent of cognitive neuroscience at the University of Helsinki who investigates the computational and neural mechanisms underlying perceptual constancy. Their research examines how the human visual system constructs stable representations of color and material properties by integrating sensory signals with prior knowledge and memory. Olkkonen utilizes psychophysics, functional MRI (fMRI), and Bayesian computational modeling to characterize how the brain resolves internal noise and environmental variation. They also serve as a principal color scientist at Microsoft Finland, focusing on color perception in applied contexts such as augmented reality.
E324.research_direction: Dr. Olkkonen has recently been investigating how contextual and statistical information shapes visual perception, particularly in the domains of color and high-level object processing. Using psychophysical approaches like adjustment-to-neutral paradigms, their recent work explores whether background chromaticity directly modulates the low-level processing of facial expressions or whether it merely introduces high-level response biases. Additionally, they are examining the mechanisms of ensemble perception by testing how continuous hue distance versus categorical color boundaries influence the visual system's ability to extract the mean color of targets embedded among distractors. Broadening their methodological scope, Dr. Olkkonen has also been developing novel tools for applied perception research, notably creating an "AR-in-VR" simulation toolbox that allows scientists to systematically manipulate and study the perceptual impact of augmented reality display artifacts—such as color non-uniformity, additive blending, and geometric distortion—within controlled virtual environments.

papers.title: Does background color influence the perception of facial expression? Adjustment to neutral expression by Caucasian and Japanese participants
papers.abstract: This research investigates whether the chromaticity of a background, specifically reddish hues associated with anger, modulates the perception of facial expressions. Utilizing an adjustment-to-neutral paradigm, the study assessed participants of two ethnicities (Finnish and Japanese) who manipulated face image continua (angry-neutral-happy) across four background conditions: red, high-chroma red, green, and gray. The results demonstrated that when task-related response biases were minimized through the adjustment method, background color exerted no significant effect on the perceived neutral point. These findings suggest that previously reported interactions between background color and facial emotion are likely attributable to high-level associative or criterion biases rather than low-level perceptual modulation of expression processing.
papers.venue: Journal of the Optical Society of America A (JOSA A)
papers.authors: Tarja Peromaa, Kaisa Tiippana, Kun Qian, Maria Olkkonen

papers.title: Ensemble percepts of colored targets among distractors are influenced by hue similarity, not categorical identity
papers.abstract: The authors examine the capacity of the visual system to extract ensemble statistics, specifically the mean hue, from target distributions interspersed among distractor elements. The study tested whether the presence of a color category boundary between target and distractor distributions facilitates the segmentation and integration of ensemble signals. Psychophysical results showed that observers could selectively estimate target mean hues, but the presence of distractors introduced substantial noise and systematic perceptual biases. Critically, noise increased as the chromatic similarity between target and distractor hues grew, while the presence of a categorical boundary provided no measurable benefit to ensemble extraction. The findings indicate that hue ensemble segregation is driven by continuous chromatic distances rather than categorical labels.
papers.authors: Lari S. Virtanen, Toni P. Saarela, Maria Olkkonen

papers.title: AR-in-VR simulator: A toolbox for rapid augmented reality simulation and user research
papers.abstract: This paper presents the 'AR-in-VR Simulator,' a Unity-based software framework designed to simulate the visual artifacts and physical constraints of augmented reality (AR) head-mounted displays within a virtual reality (VR) environment. The toolbox allows researchers to systematically manipulate and evaluate display parameters—including field of view, luminance and color non-uniformity, and geometric distortion—to conduct controlled perceptual experiments without the hardware limitations of current optical see-through devices. The study characterizes the simulator's pipeline, which involves compositing virtual 'real world' scenes with AR content using additive blending, and evaluates the efficacy of this platform for benchmarking user performance and qualitative experiences across diverse AR display configurations.
papers.authors: Jacob Hadnett-Hunter, Benjamin Lundell, Ian Ellison-Taylor, Michaela Porubanova, Tapani Alasaarela, Maria Olkkonen

E325.name: Sophie Wuerger
E325.bio: Sophie Wuerger was a visual neuroscientist who researched the neural mechanisms underlying human color perception and the geometry of color space models. Utilizing a combination of psychophysics, electroencephalography (EEG), and functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), Wuerger investigated how chromatic signals from the retina are translated in the brain and how color constancy is maintained across the human lifespan. Their research addressed fundamental vision science and applied fields, including the development of computational appearance models, multisensory integration, and 3D skin-printing technologies.
E325.research_direction: Dr. Wuerger has recently been investigating the fundamental mechanisms of human contrast sensitivity and color vision, from developing comprehensive computational models that incorporate spatiotemporal and chromatic variables to compiling massive multicultural spectral databases of human skin phenotypes. Their applied psychophysical research explores supra-threshold contrast perception in optical see-through augmented reality, probing how the visual system processes image visibility when environmental light washes out physical contrast displays. In the clinical neuroimaging domain, they are employing fMRI and diffusion tractography to trace how primary open-angle glaucoma alters structural white matter and functional BOLD signals along color-opponent pathways in the LGN and V1. Additionally, their recent work delves into multisensory integration, using temporal-order judgment paradigms to examine how the perception of audio-visual simultaneity dynamically recalibrates based on the visual intensity of preceding stimuli.

papers.title: The International Skin Spectra Archive (ISSA): a multicultural human skin phenotype and colour spectra collection
papers.abstract: This paper introduces the International Skin Spectra Archive (ISSA), a comprehensive multicultural resource comprising 15,256 spectral and colorimetric records derived from 2,113 subjects across eight countries. The archive utilizes a standardized measurement protocol for human skin phenotype data collected between 2012 and 2024, facilitating the systematic study of biological, cultural, and environmental influences on skin color variability. The dataset provides high-resolution spectral reflectance data (360–780 nm) alongside CIE colorimetric parameters, structured by ethnicity, age, gender, and anatomical body location to support advanced research in computer vision, dermatology, and anthropological science.
papers.authors: Yan Lu, Kaida Xiao, Michael Pointer, Ruili He, Sicong Zhou, Ahmed Nasseraldin, Suchitra Sueeprasan, Cheng Gao, Changjun Li, Ali Sohaib, Yuanyuan He, Yoko Mizokami, Mengmeng Wang, Esther Perales Romero, Faraedon Zardawi, Lesley Gill, Ningfang Liao, Sophie Wuerger

papers.title: Supra-threshold Contrast Perception in Augmented Reality
papers.abstract: This research investigates the discrepancy between physical and perceived contrast in optical see-through augmented reality (OST-AR) displays, where environmental light often severely reduces available physical contrast. Utilizing a high-dynamic-range multi-focal haploscope, the authors conduct psychophysical experiments to evaluate the mechanisms of background discounting and supra-threshold contrast perception. The findings demonstrate that enhanced perceived contrast in AR environments is primarily explained by supra-threshold contrast models—wherein sensitivity increases with luminance—rather than the perceptual discounting of the real-world background. A generalized contrast matching model is developed to accurately predict image visibility and preserve perceived contrast across fluctuating ambient conditions.
papers.authors: Dongyeon Kim, Maliha Ashraf, Alexandre Chapiro, Rafał K. Mantiuk, Sophie Wuerger

papers.title: Analysis of the BOLD signal along colour-opponent pathways in LGN and V1 and Microstructural Alterations of the Optic Radiation in POAG and OHT Patients
papers.abstract: This study employs functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) to investigate neural processing alterations in patients with primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG) and ocular hypertension (OHT). By analyzing the blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) signal in the lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) and primary visual cortex (V1) in response to cone-opponent chromatic stimuli, the authors identify specific functional deficits within the geniculostriate pathway. Additionally, diffusion tractography revealed microstructural alterations in the white matter of the optic radiation, which significantly correlated with clinical indicators of visual field loss and light sensitivity thresholds.
papers.authors: Joanne L. Powell, Laura M Parkes, Anshoo Choudhary, Sophie M Wuerger

papers.title: castleCSF — A contrast sensitivity function of color, area, spatiotemporal frequency, luminance and eccentricity
papers.abstract: The authors present castleCSF, a unified analytical model of the human contrast sensitivity function (CSF) that incorporates spatial frequency, temporal frequency, chromatic modulation direction, background luminance, eccentricity, and stimulus area. The model was trained and validated using a consolidated database from 18 psychophysical studies, achieving a high level of predictive accuracy (3.59 dB error) across a broad parameter space. By isolating and characterizing the achromatic and chromatic mechanisms within a post-receptoral framework, castleCSF provides a robust tool for predicting visual performance and perceptual quality in display engineering and image processing applications.
papers.authors: Maliha Ashraf, Rafał K Mantiuk, Alexandre Chapiro, Sophie Wuerger

papers.title: Perceived Audio-Visual Simultaneity Is Recalibrated by the Visual Intensity of the Preceding Trial
papers.abstract: This study examines the rapid recalibration of audio-visual simultaneity perception as a function of stimulus intensity. Through a series of temporal-order judgment (TOJ), simultaneity judgment (SJ), and simple reaction-time (RT) tasks, the authors demonstrate that the point of subjective simultaneity (PSS) shifts based on the visual intensity of the stimulus in the preceding trial. These findings suggest that the human visual system dynamically recalibrates its perception of timing to compensate for intensity-dependent processing latencies in central arrival times, although the effect is task-contingent and appears more robust in TOJ paradigms than in SJ tasks.
papers.authors: Ryan Horsfall, Neil R Harrison, Georg F Meyer, Sophie M Wuerger

E326.name: Andrew Stockman
E326.bio: Stockman is the Steers Chair of Investigative Eye Research at the UCL Institute of Ophthalmology and directs the Colour & Vision Research Laboratories. Their research focuses on the psychophysical and physiological foundations of human color vision, specifically cone spectral sensitivities, temporal sensitivity, and light adaptation mechanisms. Stockman developed standardized physiologically-based color-matching functions and the CVRL database. Their work integrates visual psychophysics with molecular genetics to investigate how specific genetic defects affect visual processing speeds and sensitivity in normal and clinical populations.
E326.research_direction: Dr. Stockman has recently been investigating the extensive physiological variability in human color vision and how to account for it in modern colorimetry. Their recent work explores individual differences in cone spectral sensitivities across the lifespan by combining psychophysical color-matching experiments on multi-primary LED trichromators with advanced physiological modeling of lens density, macular pigment, and cone opsin shifts. Through this approach, they are examining how inter-observer variability drives metamerism failures with narrow-band displays and whether utilizing individualized color-matching functions can optimize cross-media color reproduction. In a distinct line of applied research, they are also testing how dynamic, light-based manipulations of visual processing speed during athletic training might influence dynamic visual acuity and visuomotor reaction times in professional sports.

papers.title: Importance of individual differences in cone spectral sensitivities and color matching functions and how to correct for them: tutorial
papers.abstract: This tutorial provides a rigorous examination of the spectral sensitivities of human long-, middle-, and short-wavelength-sensitive cones and their linear transformations into color matching functions (CMFs). The paper details the derivation of average physiological observer models and analyzes the significant inter-observer variability that characterizes the population. This variance—driven by genetic shifts in cone opsin λmax and fluctuations in the optical densities of the lens, macular pigment, and cone photopigments—leads to systematic observer metamerism failures, which are exacerbated by the narrow-band spectra of modern LED displays and lighting. The tutorial reviews advanced colorimetric standards and the implementation of individualized colorimetry as quantitative solutions to enhance color reproduction accuracy.
papers.venue: Journal of the Optical Society of America A
papers.authors: Andy Rider, Andrew Stockman

papers.title: Individual color matches and cone spectral sensitivities in 100 observers of varying age
papers.abstract: To quantify population-wide variability and age-dependent changes in human color vision, this study characterized the L-, M-, and S-cone spectral sensitivities of 100 observers across an age range of 8 to 80 years. Using a multi-primary LED-based visual trichromator, the researchers measured psychophysical color matches to a reference white. Individual cone fundamentals were derived by optimizing physiological parameters within an extended CIEPO06 framework, accounting for individual differences in macular and lens optical densities, photopigment densities, and λmax shifts of the cone opsins. Quantitative analysis revealed that older cohorts exhibit markedly higher inter-observer variability in their matches. The resulting mean data suggest a consistent 3 nm bathochromic shift in the M-cone peak and higher macular pigment density relative to the CIEPO06 standard observer.
papers.authors: Keyu Shi, Ming Ronnier Luo, Andy Rider, Siyuan Song, Tingwei Huang, Andrew Stockman

papers.title: Light‐based manipulation of visual processing speed during soccer‐specific training has a positive impact on visual and visuomotor abilities in professional soccer players
papers.abstract: This study evaluates a novel sport-specific vision training intervention that utilizes dynamic light modulations to perturb visual processing speed during athletic drills. A 6-week longitudinal protocol was implemented with professional soccer players, involving technical technical exercises under light-based speed manipulations. Longitudinal outcome measures included dynamic visual acuity (DVA), recognition time, peripheral identification accuracy, and various reaction time metrics. Post-intervention results demonstrated significant improvements in DVA and significant reductions in both sensory and motor components of choice reaction time. These findings suggest that high-speed light perturbations can enhance the efficiency of neural pathways involved in rapid visual processing and motor execution in elite athletes.
papers.authors: P. Rodrigues, J. Woodburn, A. J. Bond, A. Raisi, A. T. Rider, Andrew Stockman

papers.title: Individual Color Matching Functions and Application in Cross-media Color Reproduction
papers.abstract: The efficacy of individualized color matching functions (CMFs) in cross-media color reproduction was investigated to address failures in observer metamerism. Five observers utilized a multi-primary LED trichromator to generate personalized CMFs based on the extended CIEPO06 physiological model. These custom CMFs were then utilized in cross-media matching experiments involving a specialized display system. The results indicated that individual CMFs predicted visual matches with a precision approximately four times greater than standard CIE 1931 2° and 1964 10° colorimetric models. This research highlights the urgent need for personalized colorimetric frameworks to achieve superior consistency in high-fidelity color reproduction across different media and device types.
papers.authors: Siyuan Song, Ming Ronnier Luo, Tingwei Huang, Andrew Rider, Andrew Stockman

papers.title: Individual differences in color matches and cone spectral sensitivities in 51 young adults
papers.abstract: This study establishes high-resolution constraints on the variability of human cone spectral sensitivities in a cohort of 51 young adults. Using a 13-primary LED trichromator, observers performed color matches to a 7500 K white reference across both 2° and 10° visual fields. A CIELAB-based adjustment methodology (L*, a*, b*) was employed to minimize intra-observer variance. Individual physiological parameters—including macular and lens optical densities and spectral peaks for the L- and M-cone photopigments—were extracted by fitting the CIEPO06 standard model to the match data. The findings corroborate a 3 nm shift in the M-cone photopigment peak toward longer wavelengths and identify higher macular pigment density than the standard model, providing a refined dataset for individual difference modeling in vision science.
papers.authors: Keyu Shi, Ming Ronnier Luo, Andrew T. Rider, Siyuan Song, Tingwei Huang, Andrew Stockman

E328.name: Yoko Mizokami
E328.bio: Mizokami is a Professor at Chiba University's Graduate School of Informatics and directs the Vision Science Laboratory. Their research employs psychophysical techniques and image statistics to investigate human visual information processing, specifically color constancy and visual adaptation to natural environments. Mizokami has published on the perception of material properties (shitsukan), including the relationship between lighting and the visual appearance of skin color and texture. Their work applies these findings to color engineering, universal design for color vision diversity, and the evaluation of lighting environments.
E328.research_direction: Dr. Mizokami's recent work explores the complex visual perception of both human faces and material surfaces, specifically investigating the mapping between physical optical properties and subjective appearance. A major focus of their research examines facial skin coloration, using asymmetric color-matching and psychophysical paradigms to understand how variations in pigments like melanin and hemoglobin influence perceived brightness and social impressions of health and attractiveness. They are particularly interested in how these perceptual judgments deviate from objective CIELAB colorimetry and how they are significantly modulated by cross-cultural differences and task instructions. In addition to facial perception, Dr. Mizokami has recently been investigating material gloss and specular reflection. This branch of their work utilizes high-resolution optical apparatuses to map surface normal vectors and Bidirectional Reflectance Distribution Functions (BRDF), aiming to quantify spatial gloss unevenness and create novel frameworks for the digital archiving of complex specular variability.

papers.title: Quantifying Skin Color Appearance in Human Faces and Textured Skin Patches
papers.abstract: This research investigates the relationship between objective colorimetric measurements and perceived facial skin color through asymmetric color-matching experiments in CIELAB space. Using a stimulus set comprising 160 Caucasian and Chinese faces alongside isolated textured skin patches, the study analyzed perceptual shifts from colorimetric averages across different ethnicities and viewing contexts. Results indicate that perceived appearance deviates systematically from physical measurements: facial matches were consistently lighter and less chromatic than the ground truth, whereas matches for skin patches were lighter and more chromatic. Despite these deviations, linear models based on CIELAB means accounted for over 95% of the variance in observer matches, providing a robust framework for quantifying facial color appearance in technological and medical imaging.
papers.authors: Yan Lu, Kaida Xiao, Yoko Mizokami

papers.title: Gloss Archiving with Normal Vectors
papers.abstract: This study proposes a novel framework for the digital preservation of material gloss by integrating high-resolution surface normal vector distributions with gonio-reflectance measurements. Recognizing that conventional imaging fails to capture the complex specular variability of materials, the authors developed a method to archive surface texture and gloss characteristics simultaneously. By mapping microscopic surface orientations and specular intensity distributions, the methodology allows for the accurate reproduction of material appearance in virtual environments. The approach was validated using various glossy samples, demonstrating its efficacy in documenting and reconstructing material properties that are traditionally difficult to digitize with standard 2D or 3D scanning techniques.
papers.authors: Shinichi Inoue, Yoshinori Igarashi, Shota Tsuneyasu, Yoko Mizokami

papers.title: Cross-cultural comparison of the influence of skin-color change on facial impressions
papers.abstract: This cross-cultural investigation explores the impact of intra-individual skin color variations—specifically those driven by hemoglobin and melanin concentrations—on the formation of social impressions such as attractiveness, health, and preference. Using facial images of Japanese, Chinese, Thai, and Caucasian subjects, the study employed psychophysical surveys to quantify how hue shifts affect observer ratings. The findings reveal significant geographic and cultural disparities: East Asian observers generally associated reddish skin tones with positive attributes, while Caucasian observers tended to favor yellowish tones. These results emphasize that the relationship between facial coloration and social judgment is not universal but is shaped by the observer's cultural background and visual environment.
papers.authors: Yuanyuan He, Hiromi Sato, Yoko Mizokami

papers.title: Analysis of Gloss Unevenness and Bidirectional Reflectance Distribution Function in Specular Reflection
papers.abstract: The authors developed a specialized measurement apparatus with an angular resolution of 0.02° to quantify gloss unevenness, defined as the spatial intensity distribution of reflected light within a specular highlight. The study analyzed the physical relationship between gloss unevenness and the Bidirectional Reflectance Distribution Function (BRDF) across various materials, including mirrors, plastics, and inkjet papers. Results demonstrated that the magnitude of gloss unevenness peaks at reflection angles close to the full-width at half-maximum (FWHM) of the BRDF. This finding allows for a more precise physical definition of gloss unevenness and suggests that specular variability is a critical factor, alongside maximum intensity and highlight spread, in determining material appearance.
papers.authors: So Nakamura, Shinichi Inoue, Yoshinori Igarashi, Hiromi Sato, Yoko Mizokami

papers.title: Relationship between brightness perception and skin color influenced by experimental method
papers.abstract: This study examines how different experimental instructions—specifically direct 'appearance matching' versus holistic 'brightness judgment'—affect the perceived brightness of human skin. Utilizing stimuli with constant lightness but varying hue angles in CIELAB space, the researchers measured the perceptual boundary where skin appears 'too bright' or 'too dark.' The results show that the influence of hue on brightness perception is task-dependent and culture-specific: Japanese observers perceived reddish skin as significantly brighter than yellowish skin of identical lightness, a trend that was absent in Thai and Chinese observer groups. This suggests that the visual system's integration of chromatic and luminance cues for faces is modulated by both the specific judgmental criteria and the ethnic background of the observer.
papers.authors: Yuanyuan He, Hiromi Sato, Chanprapha Phuangsuwan, Kitirochna Rattanakasamsuk, Yoko Mizokami

E329.name: Sérgio Nascimento
E329.bio: Sérgio Miguel Cardoso Nascimento is an Associate Professor in the Physics Department at the University of Minho, where they conduct research within the Colour Science Laboratory. Nascimento’s work explores the intersection of human visual perception and the physical properties of light, focusing on color constancy, spectral imaging, and the statistical properties of colors in natural and artistic scenes. They have used hyperspectral imaging to quantify visual information and have integrated neural network architectures to develop automated diagnostic tools for color vision deficiencies and virtual restoration of historical paintings. Nascimento’s current research investigates how atmospheric scattering and natural lighting variations modulate color discrimination and aesthetic preferences in human observers.
E329.research_direction: Dr. Nascimento’s recent work explores the deep connections between human color perception and the statistical properties of natural environments. They have recently been using hyperspectral imaging and eye-tracking to investigate visual ecology, probing how gaze dynamics efficiently sample a scene's global chromatic statistics to feed individual cone photoreceptors and support color constancy. Their research also leverages these natural scene statistics to derive ecologically optimal color sets for perceptual modeling, and to examine how the inherent orientation of environmental color gamuts influences visual discrimination for red-green dichromats. Additionally, their applied and psychophysical work bridges multiple domains, ranging from developing rapid, neural network-assisted screening tools for color vision deficiencies to investigating how top-down cognitive factors, such as formal art education, modulate innate human color preferences.

papers.title: Rapid test for detecting red–green color vision deficiencies using a neural network-assisted color-naming task
papers.abstract: This study describes and evaluates an expedited digital diagnostic for red-green color vision deficiency (CVD) based on a categorical color-naming task integrated with a neural network (NN) classifier. A total of 56 participants—comprising normal trichromats, dichromats, and anomalous trichromats—performed a naming task on 182 chromatic samples drawn from natural scenes using 11 basic color categories. A sequential NN architecture was employed to analyze response patterns for observer classification and screening. Results indicate that high diagnostic precision, with sensitivity and specificity levels of 97% and 99% respectively, can be achieved using an optimized subset of only 20 diagnostically informative colors. The methodology demonstrates that computational analysis of categorical naming responses can reliably detect congenital color vision loss in under two minutes, offering a cognitively simple alternative to traditional psychophysical threshold measurements.
papers.authors: José A. R. Monteiro, Dora N. Marques, João M. M. Linhares, Sérgio M. C. Nascimento

papers.title: Eye movements efficiently expose single cone photoreceptors to global scene color statistics
papers.abstract: This research investigates how human gaze dynamics sample the chromatic statistics of natural environments to support robust color perception and constancy. By integrating eye-tracking data with hyperspectral scene radiance maps, the authors characterized the 'spectral diet'—the cumulative spectral signals received by individual L, M, and S cone photoreceptors during fixations and saccades. The analysis demonstrates that human eye movements are effectively tuned to rapidly sample the global chromaticity of a scene, exposing individual cones to a representative distribution of the environment's color statistics within short temporal windows. This optimized sampling strategy provides the neural mechanisms of color constancy with a stable representation of the ambient light, thereby facilitating efficient adaptation to varying environmental illuminants.
papers.authors: Takuma Morimoto, Luna Wang, Kinjiro Amano, David H. Foster, Sérgio M. C. Nascimento

papers.title: Optimal color sets to represent the colors of natural scenes by k-medoids clustering
papers.abstract: Traditional color systems like Munsell and the Natural Color System (NCS) provide uniform chromatic sampling but often fail to account for the non-uniform distribution and statistical biases of natural environments. In this work, the authors utilize a diverse hyperspectral image dataset of natural scenes to derive small, optimized sets of representative colors using a k-medoids clustering algorithm. The performance of these ecologically derived sets was evaluated against standard systems by measuring their capacity to minimize representation error across the natural color gamut. The findings reveal that k-medoids-based sets provide significantly higher representational accuracy for a fixed number of samples, suggesting they provide a more valid basis for psychophysical experiments and digital color modeling in naturalistic contexts.
papers.venue: Journal of the Optical Society of America A
papers.authors: José A. R. Monteiro, Dora N. Marques, João M. M. Linhares, Sérgio M. C. Nascimento

papers.title: Color preferences of Western females with art education
papers.abstract: This investigation explores how formal aesthetic training modulates biological color preference biases within a Western cohort. A psychophysical experiment was conducted with 95 observers, comparing females with university-level art education to a control group of art novices. Participants rated 46 physical samples from the Natural Color System (NCS) on a biphasic scale. While the novice group exhibited typical patterns—favoring high-chroma blues and disliking dark yellows—art-educated females demonstrated a significantly more uniform preference distribution across the hue and lightness spectrum. Specifically, the educated group showed a reduction in the typical overrating of red-purple hues, suggesting that systematic training in the visual arts promotes a more balanced evaluative framework that overrides innate chromatic biases.
papers.venue: Journal of the Optical Society of America A
papers.authors: Patrícia M. H. Oliveira, João M. M. Linhares, Claudia Feitosa-Santana, Sérgio M. C. Nascimento

papers.title: How the orientation of the color gamut of natural scenes influences color discrimination in red-green dichromacy
papers.abstract: This study evaluates the impact of natural scene chromatic statistics on the discriminative capacity of observers with red-green dichromacy. Using hyperspectral imagery, the authors simulated discrimination tasks where the chromatic axes of natural scenes were rigidly rotated within the CIELAB space. The analysis tested whether the alignment of a scene's dominant chromatic axis with a dichromat's confusion lines affects overall discriminability. The results demonstrate that the inherent orientation of colors in natural environments is biased in a direction that optimizes discrimination for red-green deficient vision compared to rotated or randomized chromatic distributions. This suggests a form of ecological resonance where the statistical regularities of the visual environment partially mitigate the perceptual information loss caused by the absence of a cone class.
papers.authors: Ruben Pastilha, Andreia E. Gomes, João M. M. Linhares, Sérgio M. C. Nascimento

E330.name: Paul Martin
E330.main_research_area: Primate color vision and retinal circuitry
E330.bio: Paul R. Martin is a Professor of Experimental Ophthalmology who researches the functional architecture of the primate visual system, focusing on the retinal and subcortical pathways mediating color, form, and motion perception. Martin’s work utilizes high-resolution neuroanatomical tracing, electrophysiology, and connectomic reconstruction to identify specific visual channels, including investigations into the role of 'thorny' and 'tufted' retinal ganglion cells. Martin has characterized the koniocellular pathway and the physiological mechanisms of chromatic sensitivity in the lateral geniculate nucleus. Their current research involves the connectomic mapping of the human fovea and the study of retinal circuit resilience to transsynaptic degeneration following cortical lesions.
E330.research_direction: Dr. Martin's recent work explores the structural and functional organization of the primate visual pathway, ranging from the physiological basis of color perception to the developmental interdependency of retinal and cortical circuits. To understand the neural substrates of chromatic vision, they have recently been investigating how early cone wiring and lateral geniculate nucleus pathways give rise to color opponency, working to reconcile these physiological responses with psychophysical perception. Their research also compares primate and rodent models to map retinal circuit architecture, examining how specialized foveal adaptations and neuro-glial interactions support visual processing and homeostasis. Additionally, Dr. Martin is studying cell-type-specific vulnerability during early development, using marmoset models to quantify how lesions in the primary visual cortex drive retrograde transsynaptic degeneration across distinct retinal ganglion cell populations like midget and parasol cells.

papers.title: Retinal ganglion cell circuits and glial interactions in humans and mice
papers.abstract: This comprehensive review synthesizes contemporary findings on the divergent and convergent architectures of retinal ganglion cell (RGC) circuits in primate and rodent models. The authors contrast the high-density, low-diversity RGC populations of the human fovea—dominated by midget and parasol pathways specialized for high-acuity and chromatic vision—with the high-diversity, lower-density RGC tiling observed in the mouse retina. The paper further evaluates the critical role of neuro-glial interactions, specifically involving Müller cells and microglia, in modulating RGC survival, synaptic plasticity, and homeostasis. It highlights that while transcriptional profiles of glia are largely conserved across species, their spatial density and functional specialization in the primate fovea represent significant evolutionary adaptations for specialized visual processing.
papers.authors: Kang-Chieh Huang, Ulrike Grünert, Paul R. Martin

papers.title: Color opponency: tutorial
papers.abstract: In this expert-level tutorial and discourse, the authors reconcile psychophysical and physiological definitions of color opponency in the primate visual system. The paper detail the neural substrate of chromatic antagonism, beginning with the selective and non-selective cone wiring in the outer retina that initiates the 'red-green' (L-M) and 'blue-yellow' [S-(L+M)] opponent channels. The authors critically evaluate the discrepancies between perceived unique hues and the cone-opponent axes defined by lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) neurons. Technical discussion includes the application of heterochromatic flicker photometry and relative-phase light modulation to isolate specific opponent responses, while considering the impact of slow inhibitory versus rapid excitatory inputs on the spectral tuning of parvocellular and koniocellular pathways.
papers.venue: Journal of the Optical Society of America A
papers.authors: Steven K. Shevell, Paul R. Martin

papers.title: Transsynaptic Degeneration of Retinal Ganglion Cells Following Lesions to Primary Visual Cortex in Marmosets
papers.abstract: This study quantified the age-dependent vulnerability of retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) to retrograde transneuronal degeneration following unilateral lesions of the primary visual cortex (V1) in the common marmoset (Callithrix jacchus). Utilizing RBPMS labeling for total RGC density and specific markers (CaMKII and GABA_A receptors) for non-midget populations, the authors found that RGC loss in the central 5 mm of the fovea was approximately twofold higher when cortical injury occurred at 2 postnatal weeks compared to 4 or 6 weeks. While midget-pathway cells exhibited severe degeneration, widefield and parasol cells (CaMKII-positive) demonstrated significant resilience. These results demonstrate that the window of highest susceptibility to transsynaptic RGC loss is restricted to the first six postnatal weeks, suggesting critical interdependency between retinal and cortical circuits during early development.
papers.authors: Tanin Sepehrisadr, Nafiseh Atapour, Alyssa K. Baldicano, Marcello G. P. Rosa, Ulrike Grünert, Paul R. Martin

E331.name: Maureen Neitz
E331.bio: Neitz is a Professor and the Ray H. Hill Endowed Chair in Ophthalmology at the University of Washington, where they specialize in the molecular genetics and neurobiology of the visual system. Neitz’s research identifies genetic variants in human cone photopigments that contribute to color vision deficiencies, nearsightedness, and age-related macular degeneration. This work includes research in gene therapy and the use of viral vectors to treat color blindness in adult non-human primates. Neitz's current work focuses on applying genomic techniques, such as long-read sequencing and droplet digital PCR, to develop diagnostic tools for early risk detection and therapeutic interventions for inherited retinal disorders.
E331.research_direction: Dr. Neitz has recently been investigating the neurobiological and genetic mechanisms underlying refractive development, specifically focusing on the contrast theory of myopia. Their recent work explores the hypothesis that retinal contrast signaling, rather than optical blur or hyperopic defocus, acts as the primary driver of axial eye growth via peripheral ON- and OFF-midget bipolar cell circuits. Alongside mapping this retinal circuitry, they are examining the relationship between genetic variability in cone opsins and myopia risk to understand how altered light absorption might mimic low contrast and impact growth-driving signals. Furthermore, they are evaluating clinical interventions based on these mechanistic models, specifically investigating how Diffusion Optics Technology spectacle lenses utilize light-scattering elements to selectively modulate peripheral retinal contrast and inhibit myopic progression.

papers.title: The Predictive and Explanatory Power of the Contrast Theory of Myopia
papers.abstract: The contrast theory of myopia posits that every cone in the peripheral human retina connects to a specific ON- and OFF-midget bipolar cell circuit that functions as a contrast detector, where the integrated activity of these cells directly drives axial eye growth. According to this model, lowering retinal contrast—specifically at the spatial frequencies to which peripheral midget bipolar cells are most sensitive (approximately 3–4 cyc/deg)—serves to inhibit the signal for axial elongation. This theory provides a neurobiological basis for emmetropization via dopaminergic amacrine cell signaling and supports the superior efficacy of Diffusion Optics Technology (DOT) lenses, which modulate contrast while preserving the high spatial frequencies necessary for central foveal vision, over traditional peripheral defocus interventions.
papers.authors: Jay Neitz, Maureen Neitz

papers.title: Diffusion Optics Technology (DOT): A Myopia Control Spectacle Lens Based on Contrast Theory
papers.abstract: This review evaluates Diffusion Optics Technology (DOT) spectacle lenses, which utilize thousands of light-scattering elements to reduce retinal image contrast as a method of slowing myopia progression. Unlike conventional 'blur' theories that suggest the eye grows to minimize hyperopic defocus, the 'contrast theory' proposes that the retinal contrast signaling pathway itself is the primary driver of refractive development. The article discusses how genetic variability in cone photopigments can cause inefficient light absorption, mimicking low contrast and driving axial growth. It further elaborates on the design of DOT lenses to mimic natural outdoor contrast levels, thereby down-regulating the retinal growth signals that dominate in high-contrast urban environments.
papers.authors: Jay Neitz, Maureen Neitz

papers.title: Clarification on the understanding of contrast theory in relation to the article “ON and OFF receptive field processing in the presence of optical scattering”: comment
papers.abstract: This technical clarification addresses potential misrepresentations of contrast theory regarding the differential involvement of ON- and OFF-retinal pathways in myopia. The authors argue that peripheral visual signals are the dominant mediators of refractive development and that accommodation in young hyperopic eyes serves to increase contrast on the peripheral retina, thereby stimulating growth. The comment elucidates that nucleotype polymorphisms in opsin genes are major determinants of common myopia risk and that optical scattering inhibits axial elongation by lowering the time-averaged contrast signaled by the retina, effectively counteracting the growth-driving signals generated by high-contrast stimuli.
papers.authors: Jay Neitz, Maureen Neitz

E332.name: Jay Neitz
E332.bio: Neitz is the Bishop Professor of Ophthalmology at the University of Washington and co-director of the Neitz Lab. Their research integrates molecular genetics with primate psychophysics to investigate the biological mechanisms underlying color perception and retinal disease. Neitz demonstrated the restoration of trichromatic vision in adult monkeys via gene therapy, a study concerning neural plasticity in the adult visual system. Currently, their work focuses on the 'contrast theory' of myopia and the development of spectacle lens technologies designed to mitigate the progression of nearsightedness.
E332.research_direction: Dr. Neitz's recent work explores the foundational retinal circuitry of primate color vision, using techniques like 3D connectomics and adaptive optics calcium imaging to map synaptic inputs to midget ganglion cells and investigate their diverse tuning to non-cardinal chromatic axes. They have also been translating this psychophysical and genetic expertise into accessible clinical diagnostics, developing rapid, field-ready tools for detecting red-green color vision deficiencies utilizing artificial neural networks and calibrated smartphone displays. Additionally, their research investigates the neurobiological mechanisms of myopia, examining how manipulating retinal contrast signaling pathways through novel optical interventions might regulate axial eye growth and aid in emmetropization.

papers.title: Rapid test for detecting red–green color vision deficiencies using a neural network-assisted color-naming task
papers.abstract: This study details the development of an optimized diagnostic screening protocol for congenital red-green color vision deficiency (CVD) by integrating a high-speed psychophysical color-naming task with an artificial neural network (ANN) classifier. The ANN model was trained on hue-naming response patterns from a large cohort of observers with genetically characterized cone photopigments to recognize phenotype-specific errors. The system effectively discriminates between normal trichromacy, protanomalous, and deuteranomalous phenotypes with high diagnostic sensitivity and specificity. The methodology provides a computationally efficient, intuitive screening tool that maintains robustness across varying display calibrations and serves as a rapid alternative to time-intensive clinical tests like the Nagel anomaloscope or the Farnsworth-Munsell 100-Hue test.
papers.authors: José A. R. Monteiro, Dora N. Marques, João M. M. Linhares, Sérgio M. C. Nascimento, James A. Kuchenbecker, Maureen Neitz, Jay Neitz

papers.title: iPhone-based anomaloscope for accessible, accurate color vision testing
papers.abstract: This work characterizes a digital Rayleigh-matching diagnostic platform implemented on a mobile smartphone to provide accessible and precise color vision assessment. The application utilizes the iPhone’s high-bit-depth display and luminance control to simulate the primary stimuli of a Nagel anomaloscope, allowing users to define their red-green mixture matching range against a calibrated yellow reference. Validation was conducted via genetic genotyping of the OPN1LW and OPN1MW opsin genes, achieving 100% diagnostic accuracy in differentiating protan and deutan defects and identifying the severity of anomalous trichromacy versus dichromacy. The findings demonstrate that modern calibrated mobile displays can achieve the diagnostic fidelity required to replicate laboratory-grade anomaloscope performance in diverse clinical and field settings.
papers.venue: Journal of the Optical Society of America A
papers.authors: Dragos Rezeanu, James A. Kuchenbecker, Maureen Neitz, Jay Neitz

papers.title: Amacrine cell inputs to OFF midget ganglion cells in macaque retina
papers.abstract: Utilizing serial block-face scanning electron microscopy (SBFSEM) and 3D connectomic reconstruction, this study maps the synaptic architecture of OFF midget retinal ganglion cells (mRGCs) in the macaque parafovea. Ten OFF mRGCs were fully reconstructed within a high-resolution retinal volume to identify their presynaptic bipolar and amacrine cell inputs. The results demonstrate that OFF mRGCs receive robust excitatory glutamatergic input from both invaginating midget bipolar cells and multiple diffuse bipolar cell types. Furthermore, the analysis revealed a complex inhibitory network provided by wide-field GABAergic and bistratified glycinergic amacrine cells. These findings provide a comprehensive anatomical substrate for understanding how the parvocellular pathway integrates spatial and spectral signals to mediate high-acuity form and color vision.
papers.authors: David W. Marshak, Andrea S. Bordt, Emma R. Yang, Joel N. Yearick, Marcus Mazzaferri, James A. Kuchenbecker, Judith Mosinger Ogilvie, Sara S. Patterson, Jay Neitz

papers.title: Cone-Opponent Ganglion Cells in the Primate Fovea Tuned to Non-Cardinal Color Directions
papers.abstract: This research investigates the functional diversity of foveal retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) and their tuning to chromatic stimuli using adaptive optics calcium imaging and large-scale multi-electrode recordings in the macaque eye. Beyond the well-known cardinal blue-yellow and red-green opponent axes, the study identifies populations of RGCs tuned to non-cardinal color directions, specifically L vs. M + S and M vs. L + S opponency. These non-canonical RGCs exhibit irregular spatial and chromatic receptive field structures not previously described. The findings suggest that the retinal output provides a much more diverse chromatic representation than typically assumed in hierarchical color vision models, with significant implications for how the primary visual cortex (V1) decodes hue information.
papers.authors: Tyler Godat, Kendall Kohout, Keith Parkins, Sara Patterson, Maureen Neitz, Jay Neitz

papers.title: Diffusion Optics Technology (DOT): A Myopia Control Spectacle Lens Based on Contrast Theory
papers.abstract: This article reviews the neurobiological and optical foundations of the 'contrast theory' of myopia and evaluates its application in the development of Diffusion Optics Technology (DOT) spectacle lenses. Unlike traditional theories prioritizing hyperopic defocus or peripheral blur as the primary drivers of axial eye growth, contrast theory posits that the overstimulation of retinal contrast signaling pathways, specifically peripheral midget bipolar cells, facilitates axial elongation. The DOT lens utilizes thousands of light-scattering elements to induce a mild reduction in retinal image contrast without compromising central visual acuity. Clinical data from the multi-year CYPRESS trial are synthesized to support the hypothesis that contrast modulation represents a more physiologically relevant signal for emmetropization than focus-based interventions alone.
papers.authors: Jay Neitz, Maureen Neitz

E333.name: Mark Fairchild
E333.department: Integrated Sciences Academy, College of Science
E333.bio: Mark D. Fairchild is a Professor whose research focuses on the psychophysical modeling of color appearance and the human visual system's response to high-dynamic-range (HDR) imagery. They developed the iCAM image appearance framework, contributed to the CIECAM02 color appearance model, and authored the textbook 'Color Appearance Models.' Fairchild’s technical work investigates chromatic adaptation, observer metamerism, and the development of LMS-based fundamental lightness and brightness scales. Currently, their research explores individual differences in color perception and the application of colorimetric measurement to complex natural stimuli, including vegetation and viticulture sensory evaluation.
E333.research_direction: Dr. Fairchild has recently been investigating how spatial contexts, environmental lighting, and individual physiological differences shape human color perception. Through psychophysical matching and scaling experiments, their recent work explores how contextual factors—such as stimulus size in high-dynamic-range displays, mixed ambient illumination, and simultaneous contrast—alter perceived brightness and chromatic adaptation. Parallel to this, they are examining individual variability in color vision to develop physiologically grounded color spaces and personalized color-matching functions that account for variations in macular and lens pigmentation. By bridging psychophysics with computation, they aim to systematically integrate these spatial, environmental, and observer-specific parameters to update standard color appearance frameworks like CIECAM16 for high-fidelity visual reproduction.

papers.title: Changes in Displayed Brightness/Lightness with Stimulus Size
papers.abstract: This study quantifies the influence of stimulus field-of-view (FOV) on the perceptual scaling of brightness and lightness in high-dynamic-range (HDR) display environments. Through a series of psychophysical experiments comparing 1° and 10° stimuli, the authors identify a consistent positive size effect where perceived brightness increases with the visual angle of the stimulus. This effect magnitude is shown to be a function of the target lightness level relative to the background but remains invariant across variations in chromaticity (hue and saturation). A revised CIECAM16 computational framework is proposed that integrates size-specific scaling parameters to improve the predictive accuracy of color appearance models for large-format HDR imagery.
papers.venue: Journal of Imaging Science and Technology
papers.authors: Saeedeh Abasi, Luke Hellwig, Dale Stolitzka, Mark D. Fairchild

papers.title: Chromatic Adaptation in Displays: The Influence of Ambient Environment
papers.abstract: This research examines the complex mechanisms of mixed chromatic adaptation in display systems as a function of the ambient viewing environment. Psychophysical data were gathered to evaluate the combined influence of ambient illuminance, surround chromaticity, and display luminance on the steady-state adaptation of observers. The investigation identifies a significant non-linear interaction between background and surround conditions that is not captured by existing models. Two computational frameworks are proposed—utilizing local adaptation weighting and global scene factors—which demonstrate improved predictive performance for perceptual color shifts in mixed-illumination display contexts.
papers.authors: Eddie Pei, Susan P. Farnand, Mark D. Fairchild

papers.title: Derivation and evaluation of fundamental hue scales
papers.abstract: The authors develop and evaluate the Fundamental Hue Scales (FHS), a physiologically-grounded color appearance framework derived directly from cone-fundamental LMS tristimulus values. FHS establishes distinct one-dimensional scales for hue appearance (quadrature) and hue discrimination, addressing the computational complexity and non-uniformity inherent in empirical XYZ-based models. Experimental verification through intermediate hue matching tasks demonstrates that the FHS architecture achieves superior linearity and perceptual spacing. By basing the model on cone sensitivities, the framework facilitates individualized colorimetric assessments by allowing for the integration of observer-specific lens and macular pigment density parameters.
papers.authors: Saeedeh Abasi, Mark D. Fairchild

papers.title: Extending CIECAM16 to account for simultaneous contrast
papers.abstract: This research addresses the systematic inaccuracies in the standard CIECAM16 model regarding the simultaneous contrast (SC) effect, where local induction from a background alters a stimulus's perceived color attributes. Through psychophysical assessment of induction magnitude across varied achromatic and chromatic surrounds, the authors derive a set of induction-dependent adjustment parameters. These parameters are integrated into the CIECAM16 architecture to modulate cone-response compression and lightness-dependency stages. Validation against experimental data indicates that the extended model significantly reduces prediction errors for the SC effect, providing a more robust model for scene-dependent color appearance.
papers.authors: Eddie Pei, Susan P. Farnand, Mark D. Fairchild

papers.title: Individual color matching functions from cross-media color-matching experiment
papers.abstract: The authors investigate the impact of human physiological variability on color matching using a novel cross-media matching paradigm. By matching broadband physical pigments, synthesized via Kubelka–Munk modeling, to digital display primaries, the study enables the empirical measurement of individual color matching functions (CMFs). Results reveal significant failures of the CIE 1931 standard observer in predicting matches for individual categorical observers, particularly those with distinct macular and lens pigmentation. The study proposes a method for deriving personalized CMFs and introduces a metric for quantifying observer metamerism failure potential, emphasizing the necessity of individual observer models in high-fidelity reproduction.
papers.authors: Che Shen, Mark D. Fairchild

E337.name: Trafton Drew
E337.main_research_area: visual attention and medical image perception
E337.bio: Drew investigates the neural underpinnings and practical consequences of human attentional and memory limitations within the domain of medical image perception. Their research utilizes a multimodal approach combining electroencephalography (EEG), eye-tracking, and behavioral metrics to analyze how experts such as radiologists navigate complex visual information. Drew has demonstrated inattentional blindness in expert observers, showing that specialists can miss salient anomalies when engaged in focused search tasks. Their work currently focuses on developing interventional methods to reduce diagnostic errors and mapping the electrophysiological correlates of hybrid search processes involving both visual space and memory.
E337.research_direction: Dr. Drew has recently been investigating the cognitive and neural mechanisms underlying both foundational visual search and real-world perceptual expertise. In the realm of basic visual cognition, their recent work explores how observers integrate visual working memory and long-term memory during complex hybrid search using electrophysiological markers like the CDA and FN400, as well as how predictive cues drive early quitting behaviors in target detection. Concurrently, they are examining the nature of professional visual expertise by studying specialists such as radiologists, pathologists, and architects. By utilizing eye-tracking, gaze-contingent viewing paradigms, and pupillometry, they investigate whether phenomena like holistic visual processing are domain-specific and how physiological signals track cognitive load across different levels of clinical training.

papers.title: Electrophysiological Correlates of Visual Memory Search
papers.abstract: In natural environments, humans frequently engage in hybrid search tasks that require simultaneous visual scanning and memory retrieval for multiple target items. Across three event-related potential (ERP) experiments, the respective roles of visual working memory (VWM) and long-term memory (LTM) were assessed during the memory search stage of hybrid search. Experiments 1 and 2 demonstrated that both the contralateral delay activity (CDA), an electrophysiological index of VWM storage load, and the frontal-central FN400 component, reflecting LTM familiarity and retrieval, increased monotonically as a function of memory set size (target load). These modulations demonstrate that both VWM maintenance and LTM retrieval actively sustain memory search, even when target load exceeds standard VWM capacity limits. In Experiment 3, manipulating the categorical similarity between target items and distractors revealed that the CDA and FN400 were modulated by memory set size only when distractors were categorically similar to targets. This dissociation suggests that categorically dissimilar distractors are rejected prior to triggering active retrieval, illuminating the interactive contributions of VWM and LTM representations during multi-target search.
papers.authors: Lauren H. Williams, Iris Wiegand, Mark Lavelle, Jeremy M. Wolfe, Keisuke Fukuda, Marius V. Peelen, Trafton Drew

papers.title: Cue relevance drives early quitting in visual search
papers.abstract: Although salient task-irrelevant distractors are known to induce premature search termination (early quitting) and cause observers to miss targets, it remains unclear whether task-relevant salient cues produce comparable early quitting behavior on trials where the cues fail to indicate the target. Human observers performed a challenging visual search task under distinct cueing contingencies. In a high-predictive condition, a salient cue correctly denoted the target on the majority of target-present trials, whereas in a low-predictive condition, the cue was unreliable and frequently produced false positives. Contrasted against a no-cue control baseline, observers in the high-predictive cue condition exhibited pronounced early quitting on false-positive cue trials, characterized by elevated miss errors and significantly reduced response latencies on target-absent trials. In contrast, low-predictive cues produced no evidence of early search termination. These findings demonstrate that false-positive salient cues precipitate early search abandonment only when they possess high predictive value, providing important operational constraints for computer-aided detection (CAD) environments where artificial cueing aids may occasionally misdirect human visual search.
papers.authors: Jeff Moher, Anna Delos Reyes, Trafton Drew

papers.title: Pathologist pupil dilation reflects experience level and difficulty in diagnosing medical images
papers.abstract: Digital whole-slide imaging enables continuous, non-invasive logging of oculomotor and pupillometric metrics during histopathological diagnostic reasoning.
