Pupillary dynamics index mental workload, arousal, and locus-coeruleus-regulated transitions between exploratory and exploitative attentional regimes. In this study, eye-tracking and pupillometry data were collected from 89 pathologists evaluating a standardized set of digital whole-slide breast biopsy cases. Both tonic (sustained baseline) and phasic (event-related transient) pupillary responses were analyzed against pathologist clinical experience, subjective case difficulty ratings, and consensus diagnostic accuracy. Trainees and less experienced pathologists exhibited significantly greater overall tonic pupil dilation across cases relative to board-certified attending specialists, reflecting greater global cognitive strain. In addition, transient phasic pupil dilation reliably scaled with subjective case complexity and diagnostic ambiguity, showing pronounced enlargement on difficult and discordant cases. These results confirm that pupillometric signals track both professional expertise and real-time cognitive processing load, highlighting the utility of physiological metrics for diagnostic monitoring and adaptive clinical decision support.
papers.authors: Trafton Drew, Catherine E. Konold, Mark Lavelle, Tad T. Brunyé, Kathleen F. Kerr, Hannah Shucard, Donald L. Weaver, Joann G. Elmore

papers.title: Visual expertise is more than meets the eye: an examination of holistic visual processing in radiologists and architects
papers.abstract: The holistic visual processing (HVP) model posited in perceptual expertise research suggests that experts process information over wider spatial extents coupled with distinct gaze dynamics to facilitate search speed and detection accuracy. To test whether HVP reflects a domain-general cognitive strategy or domain-specific adaptation, eye tracking and detection sensitivity (d') were quantified in two professional expert groups—radiologists and architects—alongside naive observers. Participants searched for subtle domain-specific targets in architectural computer-rendered perspective scenes and malignant pulmonary nodules in single-view posteroanterior chest radiographs under both unrestricted and gaze-contingent viewing (GCV) conditions that masked peripheral visual input. Radiologists demonstrated superior perceptual sensitivity (d') and were selectively impaired by peripheral occlusion during radiograph interpretation, whereas architects exhibited behavioral advantages during perspective image search without showing the typical elongated saccadic amplitude predicted by standard HVP theory. These findings demonstrate that visual expertise does not transfer across unrelated domains and suggest that expert search configurations are tailored to specific domain demands rather than a uniform, universal holistic visual strategy.
papers.authors: Spencer Ivy, Taren Rohovit, Jeanine Stefanucci, Dustin Stokes, Megan Mills, Trafton Drew

E339.name: Christian Olivers
E339.department: Department of Experimental and Applied Psychology, Faculty of Behavioural and Movement Sciences
E339.bio: Christian Olivers is a Full Professor of Visual Cognition whose research examines the functional and neural interactions between visual attention, working memory, and multisensory perception. Olivers investigates the 'attentional template,' specifically how representations stored in working memory guide selective vision and prioritize task-relevant environmental stimuli. Their work includes the development of the 'Boost and Bounce' theory of temporal attention and studies on the attentional blink and visual search using behavioral psychophysics, eye-tracking, and EEG. Currently, Olivers focuses on the dynamics of target representations in complex, multi-target search environments and the role of retinal eccentricity in selection biases.
E339.research_direction: Dr. Olivers has recently been investigating how visual cognition fundamentally changes across the visual field, with a strong focus on the processing differences between central and peripheral vision. Their recent work explores how retinal eccentricity influences perceptual and cognitive mechanisms like serial dependence, spatial attention limits, and the retinotopic-to-global spatial generalization of visual working memory, utilizing tools such as psychophysics and EEG impulse-response decoding. Additionally, they are examining how simulated central versus peripheral vision loss alters oculomotor dynamics and spatial orientation during naturalistic visual search in gaze-contingent virtual reality environments. Broadening the scope of their research into applied human factors, Dr. Olivers is also testing how information design principles and enhanced pictograms can be used to improve the comprehensibility of real-world public safety warnings.

papers.title: Serial dependence is stronger for peripheral than for central vision
papers.abstract: This research investigated the spatial tuning and eccentricity-dependent characteristics of serial dependence—the attractive bias that causes current perceptual judgments to be pulled toward recently encountered stimuli. Across three experiments employing an orientation adjustment task, the authors demonstrated that while serial dependence is robustly present at both foveal and peripheral locations, the magnitude of the bias increases significantly with retinal eccentricity. These results support a late-stage mechanism for history-dependent perceptual stabilization, suggesting that the visual system increasingly relies on temporal regularities to reduce sensory uncertainty, which is inherently elevated in the periphery due to coarser sampling and lower signal-to-noise ratios.
papers.authors: Guven Kandemir, Christian N. L. Olivers

papers.title: Selective attention and eccentricity: A comprehensive review
papers.abstract: This review provides a systematic synthesis of the interactions between selective attention and the non-homogeneous sensory architecture of the human visual field. It specifically addresses the 'peripheral attention deficit'—the decline in attentional efficacy for enhancing contrast sensitivity and spatial resolution as stimuli move further from the fovea. The paper evaluates whether this deficit arises from neurophysiological constraints such as cortical magnification or represents a distinct bottleneck in the deployment of attentional priority. By integrating findings from psychophysics, neuroimaging, and computational models, the review proposes a framework for how endogenous and exogenous attention mechanisms are dynamically optimized to compensate for peripheral sensory degradation.
papers.authors: Christian N. L. Olivers

papers.title: Comprehensibility and effectiveness of adapted beach safety flag designs
papers.abstract: This study evaluated whether public safety at open water locations can be improved by redesigning internationally standardized beach safety flags using clarified pictograms based on human factors and information design principles. The researchers compared public comprehension and behavioral compliance intentions for existing flag sets versus two alternative designs that integrated pictograms while maintaining standard color codes. Results from a large-scale online questionnaire (N=465) indicated that the pictogram-enhanced flags nearly doubled the level of correct hazard identification and significantly increased self-reported intentions to comply with safety warnings, demonstrating that evidence-based graphical modifications can mitigate the low intrinsic comprehensibility of current global safety standards.
papers.authors: Fenne D. Roefs, Bernard Korte, Martin Hoogslag, Christian N. L. Olivers

papers.title: The effects of simulated central and peripheral vision loss on naturalistic search
papers.abstract: Using gaze-contingent simulations within a 3D virtual reality supermarket environment, this experiment examined how central versus peripheral vision loss differentially impacts performance in a naturalistic visual search task. By quantifying navigational efficiency, oculomotor dynamics (including fixation duration and saccadic amplitude), and target verification times, the study found that peripheral vision loss was significantly more detrimental to search efficiency than central loss. Specifically, the absence of peripheral input disrupted the ability to localize targets and maintain spatial orientation during large-scale navigation, emphasizing that peripheral processing is critical for navigating and orienting within complex, immersive three-dimensional scenes.
papers.authors: Kirsten Veerkamp, Daniel Müller, Gwyneth A. Pechler, David L. Mann, Christian N. L. Olivers

papers.title: When do peripherally encoded memories generalize in visual working memory?
papers.abstract: This work investigated the neural dynamics and temporal progression of spatial generalization for items stored in visual working memory (VWM) from the retinal periphery. Utilizing EEG combined with impulse-response decoding techniques, the researchers tracked whether memory representations remain retinotopically anchored to their original encoding coordinates or transform into spatially global codes. The findings revealed that neural representations transition from location-specific to spatially and temporally generalized states early in the maintenance interval (approximately 400 ms post-encoding). Crucially, this abstraction occurred prior to the selection of a response-relevant item, indicating that VWM undergoes a dynamic transformation from sensory-bound traces to output-oriented, generalized representations during retention.
papers.authors: Guven Kandemir, Christian N. L. Olivers

E341.name: Melissa Võ
E341.bio: Melissa Võ investigates "scene grammar," the semantic and syntactic rules governing the organization of objects in real-world environments. Using eye-tracking, EEG, and immersive virtual reality, they examine how these internal representations guide attention and affect the efficiency of visual search. Võ's work addresses how "anchor objects" provide spatial context for locating smaller targets and how the brain processes inconsistencies in scene structure. Currently, their lab focuses on the developmental trajectories of scene knowledge and the implementation of these cognitive constraints into computational models of vision.
E341.research_direction: Dr. Võ’s recent work explores how the human visual system extracts meaning from real-world environments, focusing heavily on the interplay between local object features and global scene context. Using methods that range from controlled psychophysics to generative adversarial networks (GANs), they are investigating the specific roles that structural "anchor objects" and global ensemble statistics play in driving rapid scene categorization, perceived realism, and functional scene understanding. Their research also probes how top-down semantic scene regularities penetrate early perception to influence the representational fidelity of fine-grained, continuous object states. Additionally, Dr. Võ has recently been examining the intersection of goal-directed attention and memory, leveraging eye-tracking and electrophysiology to uncover the cognitive and neural mechanisms behind the "search superiority effect" during visual search tasks.

papers.title: Flexible usage of object and global scene information during human scene categorization
papers.abstract: This study evaluates the relative contribution and temporal integration of local object-based signals and global ensemble features (texture statistics) during rapid scene gist extraction. Through a series of psychophysical experiments involving controlled presentation durations, stimulus eccentricity, and spatial frequency masking, the authors demonstrate that while both information streams facilitate categorization with similar efficacy, human observers exhibit a systematic bias toward prioritizing object-level cues early in the processing pipeline. The results suggest a flexible, non-hierarchical mechanism where the visual system dynamically reweights local and global features based on their diagnostic value and spatial availability, rather than strictly following a global-to-local processing order.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
papers.authors: Sandro L. Wiesmann, Melissa L.-H. Võ

papers.title: Incidental Encoding of Objects during Search Is Stronger Than Intentional Memorization due to Increased Recollection Rather Than Familiarity
papers.abstract: The search superiority effect describes the enhanced mnemonic retention of objects identified as search targets compared to those encoded through intentional memorization. This study utilizes signal detection theory and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis, alongside event-related potentials (ERPs) and eye-tracking, to determine whether this benefit is driven by quantitative memory strength or qualitative differences in recognition processes (recollection vs. familiarity). Behavioral results from a remember-know paradigm demonstrate that visual search significantly boosts recollection rates for target objects, with no observed difference in familiarity compared to explicit memorization. Electrophysiological data revealed that while both tasks elicited the FN400 (familiarity) and Late Parietal Component (LPC, recollection), the LPC amplitude failed to predict memory performance specifically for searched items, suggesting that incidental encoding during goal-directed behavior utilizes neuro-cognitive pathways distinct from traditional laboratory-based memorization.
papers.authors: Jason Helbing, Dejan Draschkow, Melissa L.-H. Võ

papers.title: The role of anchor objects in scene function understanding
papers.abstract: This study tests the hypothesis that anchor objects—large, stable entities that predict the spatial layout and identity of smaller local objects—serve as the primary units for accessing functional scene schemas. Using action-matching and lexical decision task (LDT) priming paradigms, the researchers manipulated the presence of action-relevant anchors (REL), action-unrelated anchors (UNREL), and random non-anchor objects (RAND). Results show that matching performance and priming effects are significantly attenuated upon the removal of action-relevant anchors, while remaining relatively robust when unrelated objects are removed. These data suggest that scene function identification is hierarchically organized around specific anchor objects, and that global contextual information alone is insufficient to support high-level functional understanding in the absence of these key structural elements.
papers.authors: Lea Alexandra Müller Karoza, Sandro L. Wiesmann, Melissa L.-H. Võ

papers.title: Scene consistency enhances state representations of real-world objects
papers.abstract: While top-down scene context is known to facilitate high-level object categorization, its impact on the precision of fine-grained perceptual features remains under-explored. This research investigates how scene consistency influences the representation of continuous object states (e.g., the fill level of a container or the articulation angle of a tool) using the JURICS stimulus set. Across three experiments using a continuous report task, the authors found that participants exhibited significantly greater estimation errors for object states when targets were presented in contextually inconsistent scenes compared to consistent ones. These findings demonstrate that semantic scene regularities penetrate early perceptual processing, enhancing the fidelity of state-specific representations beyond simple identity recognition.
papers.authors: Yuri A. Markov, Melissa Lê-Hoa Võ

papers.title: Anchor objects drive realism while diagnostic objects drive categorization in GAN generated scenes
papers.abstract: Utilizing scenes synthesized by Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), this research dissociates the roles of anchor objects (which provide structural scene grammar) and diagnostic objects (which provide semantic identity) in scene understanding. By correlating human behavioral performance with high-level features extracted from deep neural networks (DNNs), the study reveals a functional double dissociation: perceived realism is primarily driven by the presence of anchor objects and high-level latent features within the DNN hierarchy, whereas scene categorization performance depends almost exclusively on diagnostic object information. These results indicate that the human visual system independently processes structural regularities and semantic category labels, with categorization remaining resilient even in the presence of low-realism artifacts.
papers.authors: Aylin Kallmayer, Melissa L.-H. Võ

E342.name: Beatriz Gil-Gómez de Liaño
E342.department: Departamento de Psicología Social y Metodología
E342.lab_name: Atención Visual y Memoria de Trabajo a lo largo de la Vida (Visual Attention & WM Lifespan Lab)
E342.bio: Beatriz Gil-Gómez de Liaño is a Professor at the Universidad Autónoma de Madrid who researches the functional interactions between visual attention and working memory. Their work utilizes experimental psychophysics, eye-tracking, and fMRI to investigate cognitive mechanisms in tasks such as hybrid visual foraging and rapid serial visual presentation (RSVP). Gil-Gómez de Liaño studies the development of these systems across the lifespan, including typical and atypical trajectories in children and clinical populations such as patients with traumatic brain injuries. Their recent projects, including the ForageKid and Hyperfocus initiatives, model the cognitive architectures underlying search behavior to develop interventions for attentional improvement.
E342.research_direction: Dr. Gil-Gómez de Liaño has recently been investigating the mechanisms underlying complex visual search and multi-target foraging, with a particular focus on how these processes evolve across human development. Their recent work explores how observers decide when to stop searching—known as patch-leaving behavior—by modeling whether spatial organization metrics, such as inter-target distance and scanpath patterns, can accurately predict quitting thresholds in static and dynamic environments. To understand the temporal dynamics of these strategies, they are tracking how search organization unfolds over the course of a trial and assessing how these behaviors differ between young children and adults during basic feature versus complex conjunction search. Additionally, they are probing the developmental trajectories of inattentional blindness, leveraging cognitive assessments and classical search paradigms to uncover how the maturation of executive control and attention influences an observer's susceptibility to missing unexpected, salient stimuli.

papers.title: One factor to bind them all: visual foraging organization to predict patch leaving behavior with ROC curves
papers.abstract: Determining quitting thresholds represents a fundamental problem in visual search paradigms such as radiological screening and security baggage inspection. This investigation evaluates the predictive capacity of spatial organization indices—specifically the best-r metric, mean intertarget distance (mean ITD), proximity to the nearest adjacent target (PAO), and intersection rate (IR)—as optimal criteria governing patch-leaving decisions during multi-target visual foraging amidst distractors. In a cohort of 29 adults tested across static and dynamic foraging tasks, combined with secondary analyses of diverse lifespan foraging datasets, Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curve modeling demonstrated that spatial organization indices consistently outperform conventional animal-derived intake rate metrics in classifying human quitting behavior. Crucially, combining spatial organization metrics and classical intake rates within a single unitary latent factor yielded maximal predictive power, establishing scanpath organization as a critical determinant in modeling optimal patch departure decisions.
papers.authors: Marcos Bella-Fernández, Manuel Suero Suñé, Alicia Ferrer-Mendieta, Beatriz Gil-Gómez de Liaño

papers.title: The time course of visual foraging in the lifespan: Spatial scanning, organization search, and target processing
papers.abstract: In non-exhaustive visual foraging, observers search a display for an undetermined subset of targets among distractors before choosing to leave the patch. While spatial scanning and organization metrics have been established in exhaustive cancellation paradigms, their temporal evolution in non-exhaustive dynamic foraging across development remains poorly characterized. Here, spatial organization metrics—including best-r, mean intertarget distance (mean ITD), PAO, intersection rates, and Bayesian spatial parameters—were applied to evaluate foraging dynamics in a cross-sectional cohort of 279 observers aged 4 to 25 years during feature and conjunction foraging under free giving-up time. The analyses demonstrate that younger observers deploy significantly less organized scanpaths, and feature foraging exhibits greater organization than conjunction foraging. Furthermore, organization decreases as display set size increases and degrades systematically across the duration of search within a patch, indicating that impending search termination is indexed by an organization decline that signals patch-leaving rules.
papers.authors: Marcos Bella-Fernández, Manuel Suero Suñé, Beatriz Gil-Gómez de Liaño

papers.title: Attentional development can help us understand the inattentional blindness effect in visual search
papers.abstract: Inattentional blindness (IB) occurs when an observer fails to notice a salient, unexpected visual event while engaged in an attentionally demanding primary task. To determine how developmental differences in attentional and executive mechanisms modulate IB, an unexpected critical stimulus was embedded within an ongoing visual search protocol administered to 277 participants aged 4 to 25 years. Participants were assessed with the Continuous Performance Test (CPT/K-CPT) for attentional functioning, the Reynolds Intellectual Screening Test (RIST) for general cognitive capacity, and classic visual search metrics (hit rate, reaction times, search slopes, and intercepts). A robust developmental effect was identified: younger children aged 4 to 8–9 years demonstrated substantially heightened IB rates (spanning 60% to over 90%) relative to older cohorts, whereas IQ proxies and basic task performance did not predict IB susceptibility. These findings indicate that the ontogeny of visual attention and executive control networks directly governs susceptibility to inattentional blindness.
papers.authors: Beatriz Gil-Gómez de Liaño, Chiara Castelletti, Elena Perez-Hernandez, María Quirós-Godoy, Jeremy M. Wolfe

E343.name: Todd Horowitz
E343.department: Behavioral Research Program, Division of Cancer Control and Population Sciences
E343.bio: Todd S. Horowitz is a cognitive psychologist and Program Director at the National Cancer Institute, managing research portfolios at the intersection of cognitive neuroscience and cancer control. Previously an Assistant Professor at Harvard Medical School and Associate Director of the Visual Attention Laboratory at Brigham and Women’s Hospital, Horowitz conducts research on visual search, multiple object tracking, and attentional mechanisms. Their work focuses on applying vision science to medical image interpretation and developing neuroscience-based approaches to cancer-related cognitive impairment. Horowitz utilizes psychophysical and experimental paradigms to investigate how human perceptual and cognitive limitations impact diagnostic performance in clinical settings.
E343.research_direction: Dr. Horowitz has recently been investigating the mechanisms of visual search and attentional control across both foundational cognitive paradigms and applied clinical contexts. Their recent work explores strategies to optimize human search performance, testing interventions such as temporalizing spatial displays through rapid serial visual presentation and using high-prevalence "probe" trials to mitigate target misses in low-prevalence screening tasks. In addition to developing updated theoretical frameworks that bridge classic feature search with real-world, multi-target foraging, they are probing the broader biological and systemic correlates of executive function. Specifically, Dr. Horowitz is examining the multivariate genetic architecture linking attentional control to psychopathology, alongside translational efforts to standardize clinical trial designs, cognitive assessments, and behavioral interventions for cancer-related cognitive impairment.

papers.title: Reducing the low-prevalence effect with probe trials
papers.abstract: The low-prevalence effect (LPE) describes the consistent decrease in target detection rates as signal frequency declines in visual search paradigms. This investigation explored the utility of 'probe' trials—periodic high-prevalence instances accompanied by immediate performance feedback—to mitigate these detection failures. In a series of experiments using T-among-L spatial configuration tasks, the inclusion of probe trials significantly modulated observer decision criteria without necessitating a shift in quitting thresholds. Results suggest that the probe-driven benefit is primarily mediated by an increase in perceived target prevalence, which subsequently enhances top-down attentional guidance. Eye-tracking data further indicated that these interventions bias guidance toward specific target features rather than increasing the overall number of items inspected, although the benefit demonstrated limited generalizability to non-probed target categories.
papers.authors: Sarah A. Becker, Andrew Rodriguez, Derrek T. Montalvo, Chad Peltier, Mark W. Becker, Todd S. Horowitz

papers.title: Presenting segmented images in a rapid serial visual presentation stream improves search accuracy
papers.abstract: Standard visual search performance is often limited by inefficient oculomotor behavior and peripheral clutter, particularly under time-constrained conditions. This study evaluated whether segmenting complex search displays into a temporal stream using rapid serial visual presentation (RSVP) could improve detection accuracy. In five experiments, observers searched for categorically defined targets in both simple Landolt C arrays and complex naturalistic scenes. RSVP presentation yielded significantly higher detection sensitivity (d') and a more liberal response criterion compared to static full-image viewing. The performance gain was attributed to the elimination of time-wasting eye movements and the maximization of processing time for individual image segments. These findings suggest that temporalizing spatial search can bypass traditional attentional bottlenecks in high-stakes screening tasks.
papers.authors: Krystina Diaz, Mark W. Becker, Chad Peltier, Jeffrey B. Bolkhovsky, Todd S. Horowitz

papers.title: The National Cancer Institute clinical trials planning meeting to address gaps in observational and intervention trials for cancer-related cognitive impairment
papers.abstract: The National Cancer Institute (NCI) convened a clinical trials planning meeting to synthesize current evidence and identify methodological requirements for advancing research on cancer-related cognitive impairment (CRCI). The expert panel focused on defining specific phenotypes of CRCI in non-central nervous system (non-CNS) cancer survivors and developed recommendations for longitudinal study designs and the integration of diverse biomechanisms, including neuroimaging and inflammatory biomarkers. The report outlines priorities for Phase II/III clinical trials evaluating both pharmacological (e.g., donepezil, methylphenidate) and behavioral interventions (e.g., cognitive training, physical activity). Key initiatives include standardizing remote cognitive assessments and broadening inclusion criteria to capture heterogeneous patient populations, with the goal of validating treatments for persistent cognitive symptoms across oncology care settings.
papers.venue: Journal of the National Cancer Institute (JNCI)
papers.authors: Michelle C. Janelsins, Kathleen Van Dyk, Sheri J. Hartman, Thuy T. Koll, Christina K. Cramer, Glenn J. Lesser, Debra L. Barton, Karen M. Mustian, Lynne I. Wagner, Patricia A. Ganz, Peter D. Cole, Alexis Bakos, James C. Root, Kristina Hardy, Allison Magnuson, Robert J. Ferguson, Brenna C. McDonald, Andrew J. Saykin, Brian D. Gonzalez, Jeffrey S. Wefel, David A. Morilak, Saurabh Dahiya, Cobi J. Heijnen, Yvette P. Conley, Alicia K. Morgans, Donald Mabbott, Michelle Monje, Stephen R. Rapp, Vinai Gondi, Catherine Bender, Leanne Embry, Worta McCaskill Stevens, Judith O. Hopkins, Diane St. Germain, Susan G. Dorsey, Todd S. Horowitz

papers.title: From Features to Foraging: Current Developments in Visual Search by Human Observers
papers.abstract: This major theoretical review synthesizes over a century of visual search research, tracing the transition from single-target feature searches to complex multi-target foraging paradigms. It provides a critical analysis of the 'two-stage assumption'—the dichotomy between preattentive parallel processing and attentive serial processing—arguing that standard reaction time (RT) slopes of set size often fail to capture the nuances of attentional deployment. The review examines the impact of target prevalence on detection errors and decision criteria, the mechanics of hybrid search involving both visual and working memory components, and the influence of individual variability. By integrating findings from medical image perception and professional screening tasks, the paper advocates for search models that better account for the continuous, interactive nature of real-world visual behavior.
papers.authors: Todd S. Horowitz

papers.title: Molecular genetic influences on attentional control and other executive processes and their links with psychopathology in the AFFECT study
papers.abstract: Attentional control (AC) is an essential component of executive functioning, yet its genetic architecture and relationship with psychopathology remain poorly understood. This study performed a large-scale multivariate genomic characterization of AC and general executive function using data from over 20,000 individuals. We identified two dissociable latent genetic factors: a broad factor influencing Common Executive Function (CEF) and a narrow factor specific to Attentional Control. While both factors showed significant heritability, they exhibited distinct patterns of genetic overlap with cognitive and clinical outcomes. AC was uniquely linked to polygenic liability for specific psychiatric conditions, such as ADHD, independent of general executive function. These results suggest that attentional control is influenced by a specialized shared polygenic architecture, emphasizing the need for more granular cognitive phenotyping in neuropsychiatric research.
papers.authors: Justin D. Tubbs, Travis T. Mallard, Maria Dalby, Yunxuan Jiang, Younga H. Lee, Karmel W. Choi, Tian Ge, Niels Plath, Lene Hammer-Helmich, Julie M. Granka, 23andMe Research Group, Andrew D. Grotzinger, David Hinds, Jordan W. Smoller, Joshua W. Buckholtz, Todd S. Horowitz

E344.name: Carly Leonard
E344.bio: Carly J. Leonard is an Associate Professor at the University of Colorado Denver and directs the Laboratory for Integrative Vision. Leonard’s research characterizes the interactions between perceptual and attentional mechanisms to understand how internal goals and prior experiences shape visual behavior. Using psychophysics, eye-tracking, and electrophysiological techniques (EEG/ERP), they investigate individual differences in oculomotor control and the neural mechanisms of visual selection. Leonard also examines cognitive dysfunction in schizophrenia, focusing on how attentional filtering and inhibitory mechanisms contribute to hyperfocusing and working memory deficits.
E344.research_direction: Dr. Leonard has recently been investigating the interplay between early visual processing, oculomotor dynamics, and individual differences in perception. Their recent work explores how the visual system guides spatial attention during complex tasks, using eye-tracking and EEG to examine how early sensory accrual and target selection signals influence saccadic latency during visual search for contour integration targets. Additionally, they are studying individual variability in higher-level social vision, utilizing psychophysics to determine whether differences in point-light biological motion perception within the autism phenotype reflect domain-general spatio-temporal processing or domain-specific mechanisms. Finally, their broader cognitive research investigates the psychological and neurobiological mechanisms of mental and physical effort, examining how neural circuitry regulates cost-benefit arbitration and the behavioral aftereffects of effort expenditure.

papers.title: Trying in the 21st century: An introduction to the special issue on effort
papers.abstract: This editorial introduces a special issue investigating the psychological and neurobiological mechanisms of mental and physical effort. Moving beyond classical conceptualizations that treat effort as a unitary construct or an epiphenomenal subjective state, the authors synthesize recent advances across psychophysics, computational modeling, and functional neuroimaging that dissociate anticipatory effort valuation from its online subjective perception. The included contributions examine how striatal, anterior cingulate, and dopaminergic circuitry regulate cost-benefit arbitration in health and in clinical conditions marked by motivational impairment, such as depression and schizophrenia. Furthermore, the work highlights the multifaceted nature of effort expenditure, detailing its post-execution cognitive aftereffects on subsequent risk-taking and task engagement.
papers.authors: Carly J. Leonard, John D. Salamone, Michael T. Treadway

papers.title: Individual differences in first saccade latency predict overt behaviour during search for a contour integration target
papers.abstract: During natural visual search, saccadic gaze shifts are guided by extrafoveal perceptual organization mechanisms that extract structural contours from background noise. This experiment examined individual differences in oculomotor parameters while participants searched for a closed-contour target composed of collinear Gabor patches embedded within randomly oriented Gabor distractors. Eye-tracking recordings revealed pronounced between-participant variability in initial saccade latency, which significantly correlated with first-saccade accuracy and the overall count of fixations required to find the target. Intra-individual trial-by-trial variations exhibited analogous relationships, although the extent to which prolonged latency enhanced search performance differed across observers. The findings are framed in terms of the temporal demands of recurrent cortical processing and individual variation in the capacity to flexibly distribute the spatial extent of visual attention.
papers.authors: Carly J. Leonard

papers.title: An investigation of individual differences in biological motion perception within the autism phenotype
papers.abstract: Perception of biological motion represents a foundational component of social perception that exhibits notable variance across the broader autism spectrum. This study investigated individual differences in the detection and discrimination of kinematic point-light displays of human biological movement in relation to dimensional autistic traits. By evaluating visual psychophysical thresholds alongside self-reported autistic traits, the investigation clarified whether atypical biological motion sensitivity reflects domain-general spatio-temporal motion processing differences or domain-specific social-cognitive mechanisms. The results offer quantitative constraints on developmental and perceptual models characterizing how individual variation in low- and mid-level visual processing relates to behavioral phenotypic variation.
papers.authors: Jessica M. Lister, Carly J. Leonard

papers.title: Early visual modulation and selection predict saccadic timing during visual search: An ERP study
papers.abstract: Saccadic eye movements depend upon both an initial period of visual information accrual and a subsequent selective decision determining gaze trajectory, yet their respective influences on saccadic latency remain disputed. In this electrophysiological investigation, human observers performed visual search for a contour integration target while electroencephalography (EEG) and electrooculography (EOG) tracked posterior cortical activity and saccadic onsets. Epochs were segmented into fast, intermediate, and slow saccadic latency tertiles. Slower saccades exhibited markedly attenuated occipital N1 amplitudes compared to intermediate and fast tertiles, indicating impoverished target selection signals. In contrast, the preceding posterior P1 component was significantly augmented on slow saccade trials relative to intermediate saccades, reflecting heightened sensory evidence accrual. These ERP patterns indicate that saccadic delays can emerge when the visual system encounters sensory overload, providing evidence that integrates models of information accumulation and spatial priority selection.
papers.authors: Ryan V. Ringer, Carly J. Leonard

E347.name: Stanislas Dehaene
E347.main_research_area: Cognitive neuroscience of consciousness and literacy
E347.bio: Stanislas Dehaene investigates the neural architecture underlying high-level human functions, particularly reading, mathematics, and consciousness. Dehaene characterized the 'visual word form area' in the ventral visual stream and identified the 'number sense' in the intraparietal sulcus, illustrating how education repurposes evolutionarily older cortical circuits. Using functional neuroimaging (fMRI, M/EEG), experimental psychology, and computational modeling, their research explores the transition from subliminal to conscious processing. This work currently focuses on the Global Neuronal Workspace Theory and the neural codes governing hierarchical symbolic representations in the human brain.
E347.research_direction: Dr. Dehaene's recent work explores the neural and cognitive architectures underlying distinctly human abilities, particularly reading, mathematics, and geometric perception. By combining high-resolution 7T fMRI, MEG, and convolutional neural networks, they have recently been investigating how the ventral visual stream transforms early retinotopic inputs into the abstract, ordinal letter codes required for visual word recognition. Their research also probes how the brain parses geometric regularities like symmetry and parallelism, contrasting standard visual object recognition mechanisms against symbolic "Language-of-Thought" models to isolate uniquely human shape perception networks. Broadening their focus to mathematical cognition, they are using behavioral datasets and semantic embeddings to map the conceptual architecture of mathematical knowledge, while simultaneously conducting massive longitudinal studies to track how early schooling environments drive the emergence of math gender gaps.

papers.title: From retinotopic to ordinal coding: Dissecting the cortical stages of visual word recognition
papers.abstract: This study utilizes 7-Tesla functional MRI and magnetoencephalography (MEG) to delineate the cortical transformation of visual word representations along the human ventral stream. The research identifies a hierarchy where early visual areas (V1-V4) primarily encode retinotopic letter positions, whereas higher-order regions, specifically the visual word form area (VWFA), transition to an invariant ordinal letter-position code. MEG time-course analysis reveals that retinotopic signals for word and letter position manifest between 60 and 200 ms, followed by the emergence of abstract ordinal representations in the 220–450 ms window. These findings elucidate the spatiotemporal dynamics by which the brain converts sensory visual input into structured prelexical orthographic codes.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS)
papers.authors: Aakash Agrawal, Stanislas Dehaene

papers.title: Rapid emergence of a maths gender gap in first grade
papers.abstract: A massive 4-year longitudinal study involving 2,653,082 French schoolchildren examined the emergence of gender disparities in mathematics. While boys and girls demonstrated nearly identical performance levels at the start of primary school, a significant gender gap favoring boys appeared within four months of schooling and expanded to an effect size of roughly 0.20 after one year. This trend was robust across different socioeconomic levels and school types. By leveraging near-orthogonal variations in age and schooling, the authors conclude that the gap is driven by the schooling environment rather than chronological age, highlighting the first year of primary education as a critical period for the entrenchment of sociocultural math stereotypes.
papers.authors: P. Martinot, B. Colnet, T. Breda, J. Sultan, L. Touitou, P. Huguet, E. Spelke, G. Dehaene-Lambertz, P. Bressoux, S. Dehaene

papers.title: A geometric shape regularity effect in the human brain
papers.abstract: This research combines fMRI and MEG in adults and six-year-olds to investigate the neural correlates of human geometric perception. The study identifies two distinct brain systems: an evolutionarily ancient occipitotemporal network for visual object recognition, well-modeled by feedforward convolutional neural networks (CNNs), and a specifically human dorso-frontal system that encodes discrete geometric regularities such as symmetry and parallelism. These symbolic representations appear approximately 150 ms post-stimulus and are better predicted by a 'Language-of-Thought' model than by visual hierarchies. Geometric regularity was found to modulate activation in mathematical processing regions, including the intraparietal sulcus and inferior temporal cortex, suggesting that abstract geometry engages a symbolic mode of perception.
papers.authors: Mathias Sablé-Meyer, Lucas Benjamin, Cassandra Potier Watkins, Chenxi He, Maxence Pajot, Théo Morfoisse, Fosca Al Roumi, Stanislas Dehaene

papers.title: Mapping and modeling the semantic space of math concepts
papers.abstract: The authors map the global semantic structure of mathematical concepts by analyzing behavioral similarity judgments for the 1,000 most frequent math terms in French and English. Using distributed semantic embeddings (GloVe) and behavioral data, the study demonstrates that approximately 50% of human judgment variance is explained by co-occurrence statistics. The analysis reveals that mathematical expertise, quantified by education level, modulates the familiarity and hierarchical entanglement of concepts. The resulting database provides a comprehensive map of mathematical space, incorporating lexical frequency, age of acquisition, and semantic connectivity to delineate the cognitive architecture of mathematical knowledge.
papers.authors: Samuel Debray, Stanislas Dehaene

papers.title: Cracking the neural code for word recognition in convolutional neural networks
papers.abstract: This computational study utilizes convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to investigate how the visual system is 'recycled' for reading. By retraining ImageNet-initialized networks on word recognition, the authors analyze the emergence of reading-specific units. The findings show a hierarchical transition from retinotopic feature detection to ordinal position coding, achieved through specialized 'space bigram' units that detect letter identities relative to word boundaries (blank spaces). The proposed architecture provides a mechanistic account for the emergence of invariant word recognition in the visual word form area (VWFA) and successfully predicts human behavioral patterns and neurophysiological data.
papers.authors: Aakash Agrawal, Stanislas Dehaene

E348.name: Laurent Cohen
E348.bio: Laurent Cohen is a Professor of Neurology at Sorbonne University and a clinical neurologist at the Pitié-Salpêtrière University Hospital. Cohen co-directs the PICNIC Lab at the Paris Brain Institute, where their research investigates the neural architecture underlying high-level cognitive functions such as language, reading, and calculation. Cohen identified the Visual Word Form Area (VWFA) and co-developed the Triple-Code model of numerical cognition with Stanislas Dehaene. Their current research utilizes functional neuroimaging and neuropsychological methods to explore cortical plasticity and the reorganization of the visual system in response to sensory deprivation and the acquisition of expertise.
E348.research_direction: Dr. Cohen's recent work explores the neural mechanisms bridging auditory, visual, and linguistic processing, with a particular focus on how the brain translates spoken language into visual text. Using functional MRI and diffusion-weighted imaging, they have recently been investigating ticker-tape synaesthesia—a phenomenon where auditory speech triggers vivid orthographic imagery—to map the structural and functional pathways linking phonological networks to the Visual Word Form Area. Their research also examines the cross-modal dynamics of visual language perception, employing neuroimaging and eye-tracking to assess how deaf and hearing individuals visually attend to and integrate manual gestures and lip-reading during Cued Speech. Additionally, they are investigating extreme variations in human cognition through neuropsychological case studies, evaluating how autobiographical hypermnesia impacts a person's capacity for mental time travel and episodic simulation.

papers.title: Bridging speech and sight: white matter anatomy in ticker-tape synaesthesia
papers.abstract: This study employs diffusion-weighted magnetic resonance imaging (DWI) and probabilistic tractography to investigate the structural neuroanatomy of ticker-tape synaesthesia (TTS), a condition where auditory speech triggers vivid orthographic mental imagery. Analysis of 17 synesthetes versus matched controls revealed a selective increase in streamline density within the left-hemispheric temporoparietal white matter. Specifically, hyper-connectivity was localized in the posterior segment of the arcuate fasciculus (pAF), bridging the supramarginal and superior temporal gyri with the ventral occipitotemporal reading network. These findings suggest that augmented anatomical pathways at this interface enhance the top-down phonological-to-orthographic translation that characterizes the TTS phenotype.
papers.authors: Romain Delsanti, Fabien Hauw, Romain Lahbari, Florence Bouhali, Laurent Cohen

papers.title: Autobiographical hypermnesia as a particular form of mental time travel
papers.abstract: This neuropsychological case study evaluates the phenomenon of autobiographical hypermnesia through a comprehensive assessment of mental time travel (MTT) across various temporal distances. Utilizing both objective and subjective metrics, the researchers analyzed the patient's capacity for autonoetic consciousness during the retrieval of past personal episodes and the episodic simulation of future events. The results demonstrate a global enhancement of episodic simulation capabilities that extend across both retrospective and prospective dimensions. The findings provide evidence that hyperthymesia involves a fundamental amplification of the neurocognitive systems supporting mental projection within personal temporality.
papers.authors: Valentina La Corte, Pascale Piolino, Laurent Cohen

papers.title: Seeing speech: Neural mechanisms of cued speech perception in prelingually deaf and hearing users
papers.abstract: This functional MRI investigation delineates the neural substrates of Cued Speech (CS) perception, comparing prelingually deaf experts, hearing experts, and naive controls. While silent lip-reading and CS sentences recruited common perisylvian language hubs across all groups, deaf expert users exhibited unique BOLD activation in the left Visual Word Form Area (VWFA) during the processing of isolated manual gestures. Expertise was further associated with a leftward functional lateralization in the lateral occipital cortex. The study concludes that CS provides a cross-modal pathway to core language processes, with manual gestures being integrated into the reading network and temporal language regions through specialized visual processing strategies.
papers.authors: Annahita Sarré, Laurent Cohen

papers.title: Tracking eye gaze during cued speech perception
papers.abstract: This eye-tracking study examines the oculomotor strategies employed by deaf and hearing users during the perception of Cued Speech (CS), a manual-labial communication system. By recording fixations during the presentation of words, pseudowords, and sentences, the researchers found that all participants focused predominantly on the speaker's lips and perioral region. However, deaf experts displayed a distinct pattern of gaze lateralization, optimizing the acquisition of simultaneous phonological information from both labial configurations and manual gestures. The findings reveal the specialized visual attention mechanisms developed to support phonological decoding in the absence of auditory input.
papers.authors: Annahita Sarré, Laurent Cohen

papers.title: Subtitled speech: the neural mechanisms of ticker-tape synaesthesia
papers.abstract: The researchers utilized fMRI to identify the functional neuroanatomy underlying ticker-tape synaesthesia (TTS), focusing on the processing of normal speech, reversed speech, and pseudowords. Ticker-tape synesthetes exhibited significant over-activation in the left perisylvian language network and the Visual Word Form Area (VWFA) compared to control subjects when hearing phonologically structured auditory stimuli. These results provide empirical support for the hypothesis that TTS arises from an atypical functional organization of the literacy system, characterized by an exaggerated top-down flow of information from phonological processing centers to orthographic representational areas in the ventral visual stream.
papers.authors: Fabien Hauw, Benoît Béranger, Laurent Cohen

E349.name: Jonathan Grainger
E349.main_research_area: Visual word recognition and orthographic processing
E349.bio: Jonathan Grainger is a CNRS Research Director at Aix-Marseille University who researches the cognitive and computational foundations of visual word recognition and orthographic processing. Grainger developed the Multiple Read-Out Model (MROM) and conducted research on letter-position coding and the open-bigram representation of printed words. Utilizing behavioral priming, eye-tracking, and electrophysiological techniques, their work maps the transition from low-level visual features to complex linguistic structures. Grainger's recent projects examine the application of these mechanisms to sentence-level reading and investigate the cross-species evolutionary foundations of sequential memory and orthographic-like processing.
E349.research_direction: Dr. Grainger has recently been investigating the perceptual and cognitive mechanisms underlying language processing across both visual and auditory domains. Their recent work explores how the brain encodes the identity and spatial position of words during reading, using behavioral paradigms to test how visual cues like word length and flanking letters influence parallel word recognition. They are also examining the sentence superiority effect to determine whether the enhanced visual identification of words within grammatical sequences is driven by rapid syntactic extraction or top-down predictive guessing. Additionally, their research investigates temporal order encoding in auditory speech comprehension, specifically probing how transposing phonemes or whole words disrupts processing under varying speech rates and structural constraints.

papers.title: Flanking letter effects are orthographic effects and not visual effects: evidence from same-different matching
papers.abstract: This study evaluates whether the facilitation of target word processing by related flanking letters (e.g., 'RO ROCK CK') is mediated by low-level pre-orthographic visual features or abstract orthographic representations. Using a simultaneous same-different matching task, the researchers compared the magnitude of flanker effects using letter strings versus non-orthographic symbol strings. Significant facilitatory effects were observed for orthographic stimuli but were entirely absent for symbol-based targets and flankers. These findings provide evidence that the pooling of information from flanking stimuli into a central processing channel is a specific property of the orthographic system, supporting models where multi-word reading involves the parallel activation of location-invariant orthographic features.
papers.authors: Stéphanie Massol, Jonathan Mirault, Jonathan Grainger

papers.title: Does predictability modulate the sentence superiority effect? Perhaps – but not as one might predict!
papers.abstract: The sentence superiority effect (SSE) describes the finding that single words are identified more accurately when embedded in grammatically correct sequences compared with ungrammatical re-orderings of the same words. This research investigated whether the SSE is driven by post-lexical guessing by manipulating target word predictability (cloze probability), cross-validated with Large Language Model (LLM) word-in-context probabilities. Participants identified target words at specific positions within briefly presented 5-word sequences using a post-cued partial report paradigm. While predictability enhanced overall identification in grammatical sentences, it did not significantly modulate the magnitude of the SSE. This lack of interaction suggests that the SSE reflects rapid, parallel syntactic and semantic category extraction rather than slow inferential guessing processes.
papers.authors: Stéphanie Massol, Jonathan Mirault, Stéphane Dufau, Jonathan Grainger

papers.title: Are Transposed-Phoneme Effects Observed When Listening to Sentences?
papers.abstract: This research investigates whether the transposed-phoneme effect—a phenomenon where nonwords containing transposed phonemes are difficult to reject as nonwords—persists during auditory sentence comprehension. Participants performed a speeded grammatical decision task on five-word auditory sequences where ungrammaticality was introduced by transposing two phonemes within a word (e.g., 'the pacle was clean'). In contrast to the robust transposed-word effects typically observed in sentence reading and listening, the results revealed no significant transposed-phoneme effects. This indicates that lexical and phonotactic constraints in a sentence context are sufficiently strong to prevent the perceptual confusion of phoneme order, suggesting that phonological encoding is significantly more precise than word-order encoding during auditory sentence processing.
papers.authors: Sophie Dufour, Jonathan Mirault, Jonathan Grainger

papers.title: Transposed-Word Effects in the Auditory Modality Also Occur With a Slow Speech Rate
papers.abstract: Using an auditory grammatical decision task, this study tested whether reducing the speech rate—thereby enhancing the precision of temporal word-order encoding—would attenuate transposed-word (TW) effects, similar to the reduction observed in visual reading when words are presented serially. Despite the significantly slowed presentation rate, the experiments revealed robust TW effects in both response latencies and error rates. These findings indicate that auditory word-order encoding flexibility is less dependent on bottom-up temporal noise than visual encoding is on spatial noise. The results suggest that auditory TW effects are primarily driven by top-down, global sentence-level representations rather than local serial position encoding.
papers.authors: Sophie Dufour, Jonathan Mirault, Jonathan Grainger

papers.title: The impact of relative word-length on effects of non-adjacent word transpositions
papers.abstract: This study investigates the role of word length as a coarse visual cue for word position coding during sentence reading. While adjacent word transpositions show no word-length effects, the researchers hypothesized that length cues would be utilized when positional uncertainty increases for non-adjacent words. Using a speeded grammatical decision task with 5-word sequences, the results showed that transposed-word effects (TWE) were significantly larger when non-adjacent transposed words shared the same length compared to different lengths. This modulation supports parallel processing models of reading, demonstrating that the brain utilizes coarse visual information to map word identities to spatial locations when high-precision foveal input is unavailable for parafoveal words.
papers.authors: Yun Wen, Jonathan Grainger

E350.name: Marc Brysbaert
E350.bio: Marc Brysbaert is a Professor of Psychology at Ghent University whose research centers on the cognitive and neural mechanisms of visual word recognition and reading. Brysbaert developed the SUBTLEX word frequency norms and examines hemispheric lateralization in language processing, including the split-fovea theory. Their research utilizes a combination of behavioral megastudies, eye-tracking, and neuroimaging to investigate how lexical variables influence language acquisition and bilingualism. Brysbaert currently focuses on integrating big data and open science methodologies to improve the reliability and reproducibility of psycholinguistic benchmarks.
E350.research_direction: Dr. Brysbaert's recent work explores the large-scale mechanics of visual word recognition and psycholinguistic methodology, increasingly at the intersection of human behavior and artificial intelligence. They have recently been utilizing large language models as "virtual participants" to simulate human reaction times in lexical decision tasks and to generate massive norming databases for stimulus features like concreteness, familiarity, and age of acquisition. Conversely, their research investigates how well these same language models perform against human baselines on standardized vocabulary tests to systematically benchmark AI lexical competence. Alongside this AI-focused research, they are compiling extensive crowdsourced datasets to examine how affective dimensions—such as valence and discrete emotions—impact word processing speed, while advancing the field's statistical rigor through methodological guidelines on applying linear mixed-effects models to better account for complex participant and stimulus variance.

papers.title: Updating the German Psycholinguistic Word Toolbox with AI-Generated Estimates of Concreteness, Valence, Arousal, Age of Acquisition, and Familiarity
papers.abstract: The study generated psycholinguistic estimates for approximately 185,000 German words using the GPT-4o-mini large language model. Five critical word features—concreteness, valence, arousal, age of acquisition (AoA), and familiarity—were estimated and validated against existing human-rated behavioral norms and datasets. Statistical validation through Spearman correlations demonstrated that AI-generated familiarity estimates significantly outperformed traditional corpus-based word frequency measures in predicting human performance on lexical decision tasks and vocabulary benchmarks. The resulting dataset serves as a comprehensive resource for experimental control in German linguistic and cognitive research.
papers.authors: Javier Conde, Gonzalo Martínez, María Grandury, Carlos Arriaga, Juan Haro, Sascha Schroeder, Florian Hintz, Pedro Reviriego, Marc Brysbaert

papers.title: Simulating lexical decision times with large language models to supplement megastudies and crowdsourcing
papers.abstract: This research investigates the utility of fine-tuning Large Language Models (LLMs) to predict human reaction times (RTs) in visual word recognition tasks. By fine-tuning GPT-4o-mini on a seed set of 3,000 words from an existing megastudy, the authors demonstrated that the model could accurately generate RT estimates for the remaining lexical items in the corpus, achieving high correlations with empirical human data. The paper discusses specific applications for this 'virtual participant' methodology, including filling gaps in sparse megastudy data, verifying experimental designs through simulation, and optimizing stimulus selection for subsequent human behavioral experiments.
papers.authors: Gonzalo Martínez, Javier Conde, Pedro Reviriego, Marc Brysbaert

papers.title: Applying Mixed-Effects Models in Research on Second Language Acquisition: A Tutorial for Beginners
papers.abstract: This methodological tutorial addresses the limitations of traditional ANOVA-based analyses (F1 and F2) in second language acquisition (SLA) research, advocating for the adoption of linear mixed-effects (LME) models. The guide provides a step-by-step framework for implementing LME in the user-friendly jamovi software using the GAMLj package. It emphasizes the handling of crossed random effects for both participants and stimuli, the advantages of modeling unbalanced data without loss of power, and the specific considerations for effect size calculation and power analysis in L2 learning contexts.
papers.authors: Marc Brysbaert

papers.title: Establishing vocabulary tests as a benchmark for evaluating large language models
papers.abstract: This study proposes the use of human vocabulary assessments as a rigorous benchmark for evaluating the linguistic competence and lexical coverage of large language models (LLMs). The performance of seven state-of-the-art models, including GPT-4 and Llama 2, was assessed using two standardized vocabulary test formats across English and Spanish. The findings revealed that while models perform exceptionally well on common lexical items, they exhibit significant and unpredictable gaps in low-frequency and specialized vocabulary knowledge. The authors advocate for the inclusion of these linguistic benchmarks to complement existing domain-specific and task-oriented evaluation metrics.
papers.authors: Gonzalo Martínez, Jessie S. Barrot, Javier Conde, Elena Merino-Gómez, Beatriz Bermúdez-Margaretto, José Alberto Hernández, Pedro Reviriego, Marc Brysbaert

papers.title: Ratings of valence, arousal, happiness, anger, fear, sadness, disgust, and surprise for 24,000 Dutch words
papers.abstract: To facilitate large-scale research on the interplay between emotion and language, this study compiled a comprehensive database of affective norms for 24,000 Dutch words. Using a crowdsourcing approach, word-level ratings were collected for the primary affective dimensions of valence and arousal, alongside six discrete emotion categories (happiness, anger, fear, sadness, disgust, and surprise). Regression analyses on lexical decision times confirmed that emotional variables significantly predict word processing speed, with a facilitator effect for positive words. The dataset includes additional psycholinguistic controls such as word frequency, length, and concreteness to support multi-variable modeling of lexical processing.
papers.authors: Laura J. Speed, Marc Brysbaert

E351.name: Elizabeth Schotter
E351.lab_name: Eye Movements and Cognition Lab (EMaC Lab)
E351.bio: Elizabeth Schotter is an Associate Professor at the University of South Florida who researches the neuro-cognitive mechanisms of language comprehension and production. Schotter utilizes eye-tracking, electroencephalography (EEG), and co-registration techniques to study how visual perception and linguistic experience influence word recognition and oculomotor control. Their research explores parafoveal processing, the sign superiority effect in deaf signers, and the computational modeling of lexical identification during natural reading. Schotter's current work links saccadic behavior to cognitive-linguistic processing through the coupled analysis of eye movements and neural language signals.
E351.research_direction: Dr. Schotter has recently been investigating the cognitive and neural mechanisms of reading, focusing on how visual and linguistic information is integrated across successive fixations. Their recent work explores the depth of parafoveal processing, utilizing eye-tracking, EEG, and co-registered methods to understand how peripheral orthographic cues and top-down semantic expectations influence word-skipping decisions and foveal word recognition. Additionally, they are examining the distinct visual strategies of different reader populations, investigating how skilled deaf readers leverage expanded leftward perceptual spans and contextual constraints to optimize oculomotor control and overall reading efficiency. Furthermore, their research probes the functional heterogeneity of language processing in the brain, asking how individual proficiencies in spelling and reading comprehension distinctly modulate event-related potentials in response to semantic and orthographic anomalies.

papers.title: Parafoveally perceived orthographic cues facilitate foveal semantic processing: Evidence from event-related potentials
papers.abstract: This electrophysiological investigation examined whether orthographic features extracted during parafoveal preview influence subsequent lexico-semantic integration in the fovea. Utilizing an RSVP-with-flankers paradigm combined with a parafoveal masking manipulation, the study recorded event-related potentials (ERPs) to assess N400 responses to expected words, orthographically related neighbors, and non-neighbor anomalies. Results indicated that parafoveal N400 responses were primarily modulated by orthographic similarity, with larger amplitudes elicited by non-neighbors. Crucially, the foveal N400 magnitude was significantly reduced when orthographic violations had been previously detected in the parafovea, suggesting that the detection of orthographic cues outside of direct fixation facilitates the subsequent stage of foveal semantic processing.
papers.authors: Brian Nestor, Ayah Elaboudi, Sara Milligan, Elizabeth R. Schotter

papers.title: Individual differences in sub-components of the N400: Sentence constraint effects vary by reading comprehension ability while orthographic expectancy violation effects vary by spelling ability
papers.abstract: This study explored the functional heterogeneity of the N400 ERP component by investigating how individual linguistic proficiencies modulate its sub-components. Neural responses were measured during the reading of sentences containing expected words, unexpected words (low cloze), or orthographically related (OR) anomalies. Correlation analyses revealed a dissociation in the neural markers of linguistic skill: reading comprehension ability was uniquely associated with the magnitude of contextual support effects, whereas spelling proficiency specifically predicted the magnitude of N400 responses to orthographic expectancy violations. These findings provide evidence for a multiple-generator account of the N400, characterizing it as a composite response where distinct sub-processes of semantic retrieval and orthographic identification are differentially impacted by a reader's specific skill set.
papers.authors: Sara Milligan, Ayah Elaboudi, Brian Nestor, Elizabeth R. Schotter

papers.title: Identifying text-based factors that contribute to the superior reading efficiency of skilled deaf readers: An eye-tracking study of length, frequency, and predictability
papers.abstract: Skilled deaf readers frequently demonstrate greater reading efficiency than hearing counterparts, characterized by faster reading rates and increased word skipping. This eye-tracking experiment investigated the influence of word length, lexical frequency, and contextual predictability on eye-movement control in reading-matched deaf and hearing adults. Deaf readers exhibited significantly higher skipping probabilities and shorter gaze durations than hearing readers. While both groups showed comparable sensitivity to lexical frequency, deaf readers' skipping decisions were more strongly influenced by word length and sentence-level predictability. The results suggest that deaf readers leverage visual and contextual cues more effectively during parafoveal processing to optimize saccadic targeting and reading speed, reflecting a qualitatively distinct strategic approach to text processing.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
papers.authors: Frances G. Cooley, Karen Emmorey, Emily Saunders, Grace Sinclair, Casey Stringer, Elizabeth R. Schotter

papers.title: Parafoveal N400 effects reveal that word skipping is associated with deeper lexical processing in the presence of context-driven expectations
papers.abstract: This study employed the co-registration of eye movements and EEG to investigate the depth of linguistic processing underlying word-skipping decisions. By manipulating the orthographic and phonological properties of parafoveal previews within varying levels of sentence constraint, the researchers extracted fixation-related brain potentials (FRPs) time-locked to the pre-target word. Analysis of trials where the target was skipped revealed a robust parafoveal N400 effect for semantically incongruous previews lacking phonological overlap, but this effect was contingent upon high contextual constraint. These findings indicate that skipping is not merely a product of low-level visual heuristics but can reflect extensive lexical identification supported by top-down expectations, suggesting a 'hedged-bet' mechanism in oculomotor control during reading.
papers.authors: Sara Milligan, Milca Jaime Brunet, Neslihan Caliskan, Elizabeth R. Schotter

papers.title: Deaf readers use leftward information to read more efficiently: Evidence from eye tracking
papers.abstract: The spatial extent and functional utility of the leftward perceptual span were examined in deaf signers and hearing adults using a gaze-contingent moving window paradigm. While rightward spans (word identification and perceptual spans) were similar across groups, deaf readers demonstrated a significantly expanded leftward span of approximately 10 characters, compared to only 4 characters in hearing readers. Importantly, the magnitude of the leftward span in deaf readers was positively correlated with their standardized reading comprehension scores. These results suggest that deaf readers more effectively monitor and process text to the left of fixation, likely facilitating the integration of previously read information and more efficient error recovery, which contributes to their overall superior reading rates.
papers.authors: Casey Stringer, Frances G. Cooley, Emily Saunders, Karen Emmorey, Elizabeth R. Schotter

E352.name: Jason Yeatman
E352.department: Graduate School of Education; Department of Psychology; Division of Developmental and Behavioral Pediatrics
E352.bio: Jason Yeatman is an Associate Professor at Stanford University with joint appointments in the Graduate School of Education, the Department of Psychology, and the School of Medicine. Yeatman’s research integrates vision science, computational neuroscience, and education to investigate how the brain's reading circuitry—specifically the Visual Word Form Area and white matter connections—develops in response to learning. As director of the Brain Development and Education Lab, Yeatman utilizes neuroimaging and the Rapid Online Assessment of Reading (ROAR) platform to study brain plasticity in typically developing children and those with dyslexia. Their current research focuses on how targeted behavioral interventions reshape neural circuits to design personalized literacy programs for diverse learners.
E352.research_direction: Dr. Yeatman has recently been investigating the neural and cognitive foundations of reading development and dyslexia, tracking how educational experiences shape the developing brain. Specifically, their research uses functional and diffusion MRI to ask whether neural signatures—such as the functional organization of the Visual Word Form Area and the microstructural properties of the arcuate fasciculus—are persistent developmental traits or highly plastic features that change in response to reading interventions. At the perceptual level, they are deploying psychophysical paradigms to isolate specific visual processing bottlenecks in dyslexia, testing whether reading struggles stem from deficits in exogenous spatial attention or slower temporal rates of visual encoding. To facilitate this research at a population scale, their recent work also explores the development of rapid, browser-based computerized adaptive testing platforms to precisely measure reading proficiency and phonological awareness in children outside the traditional laboratory environment.

papers.title: The balance between stability and plasticity of the visual word form area in dyslexia
papers.abstract: This longitudinal neuroimaging study assesses the functional evolution of the Visual Word Form Area (VWFA) in children with dyslexia undergoing reading intervention compared to neurotypical controls. Utilizing functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), the research explores whether the structural and functional anomalies characteristic of dyslexia represent plastic or persistent neural traits. Results indicate that while intensive pedagogical training promotes a significant increase in the spatial extent and responsivity of the VWFA, inherent differences in the broader functional landscape of the ventral occipitotemporal cortex (VOTC) remain, suggesting that certain neural signatures of dyslexia are enduring functional traits despite behavioral gains.
papers.authors: Jamie L. Mitchell, Maya Yablonski, Hannah L. Stone, Mia Fuentes-Jimenez, Megumi E. Takada, Kenny A. Tang, Jasmine E. Tran, Clementine Chou, Jason D. Yeatman

papers.title: ROAR-CAT: Rapid Online Assessment of Reading ability with Computerized Adaptive Testing
papers.abstract: This study presents the design and psychometric evaluation of ROAR-CAT, an unproctored, browser-based assessment of single-word reading proficiency that integrates Item Response Theory (IRT) and Computerized Adaptive Testing (CAT). By leveraging a calibrated bank of lexical items derived from 1,960 participants, the tool adaptively estimates a participant's latent reading ability with high precision. Validation across 32 school classrooms demonstrates that the approximately 3-minute ROAR-CAT yields scores that correlate strongly (r = 0.73 to 0.89) with traditional, proctored oral reading assessments, offering an efficient and scalable method for large-scale literacy monitoring.
papers.authors: Wanjing Anya Ma, Adam Richie-Halford, Amy K. Burkhardt, Klint Kanopka, Clementine Chou, Benjamin W. Domingue, Jason D. Yeatman

papers.title: Development of the arcuate fasciculus is linked to learning gains in reading
papers.abstract: Investigating the neuroplasticity of human white matter, this longitudinal study analyzes diffusion MRI (dMRI) data and reading achievement in a cohort of 340 children over a four-year period. The research employs longitudinal growth modeling to determine whether microstructural properties of the arcuate fasciculus act as stable predictors or dynamic correlates of learning. The findings reveal that within-individual changes in the diffusion properties of the left arcuate fasciculus—but not control white matter tracts or mathematical growth—are specifically linked to individual gains in reading proficiency, providing robust evidence for a model where white matter connectivity is dynamically sculpted by educational experience.
papers.authors: Ethan Roy, Emily M. Harriott, Tin Q. Nguyen, Adam Richie-Halford, Ariel Rokem, Laurie E. Cutting, Jason D. Yeatman

papers.title: Rapid online assessment of reading and phonological awareness (ROAR-PA)
papers.abstract: The authors present the development and validation of the Rapid Online Assessment of Reading-Phonological Awareness (ROAR-PA), a digital, self-administered measure for assessing phonological processing in young children. Through a series of validation studies involving students from Pre-K through 4th grade, the assessment demonstrates high internal consistency (α = 0.96) and strong concurrent validity with standardized clinical instruments like the CTOPP-2 (r = 0.80). Furthermore, implementation in public school classrooms confirms the tool's effectiveness as a scalable and predictive screener for early literacy development that can be administered without a test proctor.
papers.authors: Liesbeth Gijbels, Amy Burkhardt, Wanjing Anya Ma, Jason D. Yeatman

papers.title: Children with dyslexia show no deficit in exogenous spatial attention but show differences in visual encoding
papers.abstract: This research addresses the longstanding debate regarding the contribution of visual processing deficits to dyslexia by examining the relative roles of spatial attention and visual encoding speed. Using a multi-alternative forced-choice (mAFC) psychophysical paradigm, the study compares children with dyslexia to age-matched controls. The data demonstrate that although children with dyslexia show normal exogenous spatial attention orienting, they exhibit significantly slower visual encoding rates. These results suggest that reading difficulties are primarily associated with a reduced efficiency in the temporal encoding of visual information into short-term memory rather than a general deficit in the allocation of spatial attention.
papers.authors: Mahalakshmi Ramamurthy, Alex L. White, Jason D. Yeatman

E353.name: Kathleen Rastle
E353.bio: Kathleen Rastle is a Professor of Cognitive Psychology who investigates the mental and neural processes underlying reading acquisition and skilled word recognition. Rastle’s work employs a multi-methodological approach, including behavioral experiments, neuroimaging, and computational modeling, to understand how the brain extracts and represents orthographic, phonological, and morphological information. This research includes contributions to the development of the Dual-Route Cascaded model and analysis of how the statistical regularities of writing systems influence the neural pathways involved in literacy.
E353.research_direction: Dr. Rastle has recently been investigating the cognitive and statistical mechanisms underpinning reading and literacy development across diverse languages and populations. Using a combination of behavioral paradigms, computational modeling, and corpus analyses of children's books, their recent work explores how surface-level orthographic regularities shape how developing and adult readers learn to parse morphological word parts, as well as how compositional meanings are automatically activated during the visual recognition of Chinese compound words. They are also examining reading in applied everyday contexts, employing eye-tracking to measure how children allocate visual attention to same-language subtitles during video consumption.
