Furthermore, Dr. Rastle is investigating the macro-level factors impeding global literacy goals, analyzing large-scale educational datasets to evaluate how a lack of foundational phonics and word-decoding skills constrains broader reading comprehension in low- and middle-income nations.

papers.title: Morpheme knowledge is shaped by information available through orthography
papers.abstract: This investigation employs the morpheme interference paradigm with a cohort of skilled adult readers to evaluate competing definitions of affixal experience. The findings indicate that the acquisition of morphological knowledge is predominantly driven by exposure to lexical items in which affixes are orthographically identifiable without requiring specialized linguistic analysis. This constraint excludes numerous linguistically complex words while admitting 'morphological false alarms' (e.g., -er in corner), which are shown to actively interfere with the refinement of affixal representations. The results suggest a statistically-driven learning mechanism for morphology based on surface-level orthographic regularities rather than underlying linguistic structure.
papers.authors: Maria Korochkina, Holly Cooper, Marc Brysbaert, Kathleen Rastle

papers.title: Morphology in children's books, and what it means for learning
papers.abstract: This study provides a comprehensive quantification of morphological information across a corpus of 1,200 popular children's books to elucidate how morphological parsing abilities develop through naturalistic text exposure. The analysis reveals that the acquisition of affixal knowledge is challenged by the limited diversity of unique lexical stems per affix and the prevalence of orthographic patterns that mimic morphemic structures, potentially inducing erroneous morphological segmentation. A theory of affix learning is proposed that emphasizes the impact of these input-level constraints on the development of lexical decomposition strategies in developing readers.
papers.authors: Maria Korochkina, Kathleen Rastle

papers.title: Where Do Children Look When Watching Videos With Same-Language Subtitles?
papers.abstract: This eye-tracking study investigated the allocation of visual attention in 127 British children (ages 6–8) during exposure to videos containing same-language subtitles. The results demonstrate that children distribute approximately 20% of their total viewing time to the subtitle region, with gaze allocation increasing as a function of chronological age and standardized reading fluency. These findings quantify the extent of incidental orthographic processing during audiovisual consumption and provide a baseline for evaluating the potential of subtitled media as a supplementary tool for literacy development in early primary education.
papers.authors: Anastasiya Lopukhina, Walter J. B. van Heuven, Rebecca Crowley, Kathleen Rastle

papers.title: Compositional processing in the recognition of Chinese compounds: Behavioural and computational studies
papers.abstract: This research explores whether the visual recognition of Chinese compound words involves the routine activation of compositional meaning, a process previously primarily documented in Germanic languages. Utilizing a distributional semantics-based computational model (CAOSS), the authors quantified the semantic consistency and ease of constituent integration for Chinese compounds. Behavioral experiments revealed that these computationally derived metrics significantly predicted performance in sensibility judgment and lexical decision tasks for both familiar compounds and novel combinations. The study demonstrates that compositional processes are automatically engaged during Chinese reading, suggesting that statistical learning of constituent functions underpins compound recognition across disparate writing systems.
papers.authors: Cheng-Yu Hsieh, Marco Marelli, Kathleen Rastle

papers.title: Global literacy goals constrained by inadequate foundational decoding skills for pupils in low- and middle-income countries
papers.abstract: Through a large-scale analysis of standardized literacy assessments across 43 low- and middle-income countries, this study examines the factors impeding progress toward global literacy targets. The data reveal a widespread 'learning crisis,' where the majority of students in late primary education exhibit nearly zero performance on foundational word-decoding tasks. The results indicate that the absence of basic phonics-based decoding proficiency represents the primary obstacle to achieving literacy, as students who cannot decode individual words are unable to transition to reading for comprehension. The authors argue for a fundamental shift in educational policy to prioritize the early acquisition of foundational decoding skills.
papers.authors: Megan Crawford, Nosheen Raheel, Maria Korochkina, Kathleen Rastle

E354.name: Manuel Carreiras
E354.institution: Basque Center on Cognition, Brain and Language
E354.bio: Manuel Carreiras is the Scientific Director of the Basque Center on Cognition, Brain and Language (BCBL) and an Ikerbasque Research Professor. Their research utilizes neuroimaging methodologies, including fMRI, MEG, and EEG/ERPs, to examine the cognitive and neural foundations of language processing. Carreiras focuses on the mechanisms of visual word recognition, sentence comprehension, and the neuroplasticity associated with bilingualism and literacy. Their current work explores the cortical rhythms involved in language perception and the clinical applications of neuroimaging in studying language-related neurodegeneration and brain gliomas.
E354.research_direction: Dr. Carreiras has recently been investigating the neural mechanisms underlying language acquisition and visual language processing across highly diverse populations. Their recent work explores the architecture of visual word recognition, using functional neuroimaging and multivariate techniques to map how the reading network transitions from perceiving basic visual letter forms to accessing abstract semantic meaning. To test the flexibility and universality of these processes, they are employing masked priming and EEG to examine whether early orthographic coding is consistent across morphologically distinct languages like Arabic, and whether skilled deaf readers develop alternative neural strategies to read without auditory-phonological input. Expanding beyond traditional reading paradigms, they are also utilizing MEG to investigate how the brain tracks the rhythmic visual kinematics of sign language, alongside fNIRS to study early cortical adaptations to multisignal speech environments in bilingual infants.

papers.title: Alternative strategies of orthographic processing: the case of skilled deaf readers
papers.abstract: This investigation utilizes a combination of single-word recognition and masked priming paradigms alongside electroencephalography (EEG) to delineate the orthographic processing mechanisms in skilled deaf readers compared to hearing controls. Focusing on the pillars of letter identity and letter position, the research examines whether high reading proficiency in the absence of auditory-phonological input is supported by alternative neural strategies. Results demonstrate that deaf readers exhibit accelerated reaction times and distinct neurophysiological signatures during letter identity analysis, regardless of visual-orthographic form (e.g., case or visual similarity). These findings identify specific compensatory orthographic strategies in the deaf population that bypass traditional phonological-to-orthographic mappings to achieve efficient lexical access.
papers.authors: Sendy Caffarra, Brendan Costello, Noemi Fariña, Jon Andoni Duñabeitia, Manuel Carreiras

papers.title: Cortical tracking of sign language: The role of language knowledge in tracking of different articulators
papers.abstract: Utilizing magnetoencephalography (MEG) and 3D kinematic motion tracking, this study investigates the neurophysiological entrainment (cortical tracking) of brain activity to the rhythmic articulatory movements of sign language. The researchers quantified brain-signal coherence in the delta frequency band (0.5–2.5 Hz) while proficient signers and sign-naive controls observed semi-spontaneous narratives. While low-level tracking in occipital regions was comparable between groups, proficient signers demonstrated significantly enhanced cortical tracking in the right temporal cortex, specifically for linguistically salient facial and manual articulators. These results provide evidence that cortical tracking is a cross-modal linguistic feature modulated by language-specific expertise and long-term neuroplasticity.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS)
papers.authors: Chiara L. Rivolta, Mikel Lizarazu, Brendan Costello, Manuel Carreiras

papers.title: From perceiving words to reading: Neural multivariate representations of sublexical vs. lexico-semantic processing during word-reading
papers.abstract: This study employs functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) to dissociate the neural topographies of sublexical and lexico-semantic information during visual word recognition. By analyzing fine-grained activation patterns, the authors mapped the transition from form-based orthographic processing to abstract semantic representation within the reading network. The findings localized distinct multivariate signatures for sublexical variables (e.g., orthographic consistency) and lexico-semantic features (e.g., word frequency, semantic richness) in the ventral occipitotemporal cortex (vOTC) and left inferior frontal gyrus (LIFG). The data support a hierarchical model of word reading where the vOTC and LIFG play specialized roles in the multidimensional extraction of meaning from visual input.
papers.authors: Abraham Sánchez, Pedro M. Paz-Alonso, Manuel Carreiras

papers.title: Are the early stages of orthographic processing universal? Insights from masked priming with Semitic words
papers.abstract: To evaluate the universality of the initial phases of visual word recognition, this research utilized the masked priming paradigm within the unique templatic morphological framework of Arabic. Across two lexical decision experiments (yes-no and go/no-go), the study measured the magnitude of facilitation from nonword primes that shared orthographic but not morphological (root/pattern) properties with targets. Significant orthographic priming effects were observed, indicating that early-stage letter-position coding and orthographic abstraction are fundamentally universal and resistant to language-specific morphological constraints. These findings challenge models suggesting language-dependent weighting of linguistic domains and support a universal computational architecture for early orthographic processing.
papers.authors: Sami Boudelaa, Manuel Perea, Manuel Carreiras

papers.title: Functional Brain Adaptations During Speech Processing in 4-Month-Old Bilingual Infants
papers.abstract: Using functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS), this research identifies the neural correlates of early bilingual exposure during the critical window of language acquisition in 4-month-old infants. The study compared cortical responses to forward and backward speech stimuli in Spanish-Basque bilinguals and Spanish monolinguals. Results revealed distinct functional brain adaptations in bilingual infants, characterized by significantly increased hemodynamic activity in bilateral inferior frontal and temporal regions, contrasting with the left-hemispheric specialization observed in monolinguals. These findings demonstrate that dual-language environments induce rapid neuroplastic changes in the perisylvian network, facilitating the development of a more flexible neural system for multi-signal speech processing.
papers.authors: Borja Blanco, Monika Molnar, Irene Arrieta, César Caballero-Gaudes, Manuel Carreiras

E356.name: Victor Kuperman
E356.bio: Victor Kuperman is a Professor and Canada Research Chair in Psycholinguistics at McMaster University and holds an associate membership in the Department of Psychology, Neuroscience & Behaviour. Their research integrates oculomotor monitoring, behavioral experimentation, and computational modeling to investigate the cognitive processes underlying visual word recognition and sentence comprehension. Kuperman examines the impact of morphological complexity, individual differences in literacy, and the effects of aging on linguistic processing. By utilizing large-scale eye-tracking corpora and norming studies, Kuperman develops probabilistic models of visual comprehension to analyze how reader-level and text-level variables interact during naturalistic reading.
E356.research_direction: Dr. Kuperman has recently been investigating the cognitive mechanisms of reading across diverse writing systems, as well as the relationship between natural language production and psychological well-being. Using eye-tracking methods, their recent work explores both universal and script-specific oculomotor behaviors during text reading, leading large-scale initiatives to build multilingual gaze datasets that examine how visual and cognitive processing are affected by distinct formats like logographic characters or vertical text directionality. Beyond oculomotor research, they are also developing extensive written corpora—ranging from the life stories of older adults during the pandemic to wartime testimonies from civilians—to uncover how lexical and syntactic complexity might serve as markers for cognitive decline, resilience, and trauma. By integrating high-resolution gaze metrics with quantitative linguistic profiling, their research bridges visual processing and computational linguistics to better understand how we extract meaning from text and how written language reflects our underlying mental states.

papers.title: Dataset on cognitive and social well‑being of older adults around the COVID-19 pandemic: The CoSoWELL corpus of written life stories, release 2
papers.abstract: This publication details release 2 of the Cognitive and Social Well-Being (CoSoWELL) corpus, an expanded longitudinal repository of naturalistic language production from Canadian older adults (aged 60 and above). The dataset integrates linguistic features, such as lexical and syntactic complexity metrics derived from written life stories, with longitudinal psychometric assessments of loneliness, depression, and cognitive functioning (measured via MoCA scores) across multiple phases of the COVID-19 pandemic. This resource enables researchers to apply quantitative linguistic methods to model the interplay between socio-demographic factors, pandemic-related stressors, and the preservation of cognitive and social health in aging populations.
papers.authors: Aki-Juhani Kyröläinen, Marc-Antoine Paul, Victor Kuperman

papers.title: Wave 2 of the Multilingual Eye-Movement Corpus (MECO): New text reading data across languages
papers.abstract: This paper presents the Wave 2 expansion of the Multilingual Eye-Movement Corpus (MECO), a large-scale international collaboration providing standardized eye-tracking data for naturalistic text reading. The current release adds datasets from 654 participants across 13 languages, including underrepresented scripts such as Hindi, Traditional Mongolian, and Serbian, bringing the corpus total to 21 languages. The database pairs high-resolution gaze metrics (e.g., skip rates, fixation durations) with comprehensive participant-level cognitive profiles, including measures of print exposure (ART) and decoding speed. By providing standardized benchmarks and multi-lab replication samples, MECO Wave 2 facilitates robust cross-linguistic evaluation of universal and script-specific reading processes.
papers.authors: Noam Siegelman, Sascha Schroeder, Yaqian Borogjoon Bao, Cengiz Acartürk, Niket Agrawal, Lena S. Bolliger, Jan Brasser, César Campos-Rojas, Denis Drieghe, Dušica Filipović Đurđević, Sofya Goldina, Romualdo Ibáñez Orellana, Lena A. Jäger, Ómar I. Jóhannesson, Anurag Khare, Nik Kharlamov, Hanne B.
