M. Sá, Andrea Santana-Covarrubias, Irina Sekerina, Heida M. Sigurdardottir, Anna Smirnova, Priyanka Srivastava, Elisangela N. Teixeira, Ivana Ugrinic, Kerem Alp Usal, Karolina Vakulya, Ark Verma, João M. M. Vieira, Denise H. Wu, Jin Xue, Sunčica Zdravković, Junjing Zhuo, Laoura Ziaka, Victor Kuperman

papers.title: No wrap-up effect in Chinese reading: Evidence from eye movements
papers.abstract: This study utilized eye-tracking to investigate the sentence-final wrap-up effect—a phenomenon where processing time increases at syntactic boundaries—in simplified Mandarin Chinese reading. By manipulating the sentence position (medial vs. final) and character visual complexity of target words, the experiment demonstrated that words at the end of sentences were processed at equivalent or faster rates than medial words across primary eye-movement metrics (e.g., gaze duration and total reading time). Furthermore, characer visual complexity did not significantly modulate these effects. These findings provide evidence for a highly incremental processing model in logographic scripts and challenge the cross-linguistic generalizability of theoretical accounts grounded in the study of alphabetic languages.
papers.authors: Jin Xue, Yaqian (Borogjoon) Bao, Dongcheng Xie, Guangpu Chen, Victor Kuperman

papers.title: The eye movement database of passage reading in vertically written traditional Mongolian
papers.abstract: This paper introduces a specialized eye-tracking corpus capturing the naturalistic text reading behavior of 66 native readers of traditional Mongolian script, a unique vertical writing system. Extending the Multilingual Eye Movement Corpus (MECO), the dataset includes gaze metrics for 12 passages comprising 2,592 word tokens. The study provides standardized benchmarks for word frequency and length effects, alongside high-resolution temporal and spatial gaze records. As one of the few large-scale behavioral resources for a vertical script, this corpus enables critical cross-linguistic comparisons to distinguish between universal reading mechanisms and script-specific processing demands related to vertical directionality and Mongolian morphology.
papers.authors: Yaqian Borogjoon Bao, Xingshan Li, Victor Kuperman

papers.title: The narratives of war (NoW) corpus of written testimonies of the Russia-Ukraine war
papers.abstract: The Narratives of War (NoW) corpus is a newly established linguistic resource containing written testimonies from approximately 1,500 Ukrainian civilians collected between 2022 and 2024. The corpus integrates short personal narratives (provided in Ukrainian and English translations) with participant-level demographic data and psychometric scores from assessments of PTSD symptoms and moral injury. By applying systematic linguistic analysis to this trauma-related dataset, researchers can identify diagnostic markers and integrative complexity patterns that characterize the psychological states and resilience of non-combatant populations during active military conflict, facilitating broad research into the intersection of language, trauma, and survival.
papers.authors: Serhii Zasiekin, Larysa Zasiekina, Emilie Altman, Mykhailo Hryntus, Victor Kuperman

E357.name: Johannes Ziegler
E357.department: Centre de Recherche en Psychologie et Neurosciences (CRPN)
E357.bio: Johannes Ziegler is a Research Director at the CNRS and head of the Laboratoire de Psychologie Cognitive at Aix-Marseille University, specializing in the cognitive and neural substrates of literacy acquisition. Ziegler co-developed the Psycholinguistic Grain Size Theory, a framework for understanding cross-linguistic differences in reading development and dyslexia. Their research utilizes large-scale computational modeling, such as the Dual Route Cascaded (DRC) and CDP+ architectures, to simulate visual word recognition and the effects of orthographic depth on phonological decoding. Currently, Ziegler’s work focuses on integrating neuroimaging with digital pedagogical interventions to enhance reading fluency and support children with learning disabilities.
E357.research_direction: Dr. Ziegler has recently been investigating the cognitive, neural, and computational mechanisms underlying reading and language processing. Their recent work explores the relationship between domain-general statistical learning and online linguistic prediction, using fMRI and behavioral reaction-time tasks to probe how both typical readers and individuals with dyslexia anticipate semantic and syntactic regularities. In parallel, they are utilizing computational modeling to test how complex network models of reading aloud can be optimized and generalized using highly limited datasets, while also employing training paradigms to uncover how readers implicitly learn the morphological structure of novel words. Finally, their behavioral research examines the semantic grounding of abstract concepts, testing whether the representations of non-concrete words are fundamentally anchored in our internal social and emotional experiences.

papers.title: Modelling a complex cognitive system with limited data: Optimization and generalization in a computational model of reading aloud
papers.abstract: This computational study assesses the generalization capabilities of the Connectionist Dual-Process (CDP) model of reading aloud when optimized using highly constrained datasets. While complex connectionist architectures are typically assumed to require large-scale empirical corpora for robust parameter estimation, the authors demonstrate that CDP maintained quantitative predictive accuracy on independent validation sets even when trained on small-scale datasets (N < 300). Through sloppy parameter analysis, a low-dimensional parameter subspace was identified that governed the majority of the model's quantitative behavior. The results indicate that the structural constraints of the cognitive architecture effectively mitigate overfitting, enabling the analysis and understanding of complex reading systems even in data-scarce conditions, such as those characterizing clinical or developmental cohorts.
papers.authors: Conrad Perry, Marco Zorzi, Johannes C. Ziegler

papers.title: Neural Networks for Semantic and Syntactic Prediction and Visual-Motor Statistical Learning in Adult Readers With and Without Dyslexia
papers.abstract: This fMRI investigation explores the neurocomputational relationship between domain-general statistical learning (SL) and linguistic anticipation in typical readers and individuals with developmental dyslexia. Utilizing a predictive reading task alongside a visuo-motor Serial Reaction Time (SRT) task, the researchers mapped the distinct neural circuits mediating semantic and syntactic facilitation. The findings revealed specific group differences in the left precentral gyrus and right anterior insula during predictive processing. Notably, a significant correlation between SRT performance and linguistic prediction was observed in dyslexic readers, recruiting a network of inferior frontal and subcortical regions. This suggests that statistical learning mechanisms may facilitate neurocompensatory strategies in reading-impaired populations by leveraging environmental regularities for top-down processing.
papers.authors: Elisa Gavard, Valérie Chanoine, Franziska Geringswald, Jean-Luc Anton, Eddy Cavalli, Johannes C. Ziegler

papers.title: The Role of Social and Emotional Experience in Representing Abstract Words
papers.abstract: Across seven behavioral experiments, this study examines the multidimensional representational space of abstract concepts, specifically testing whether social and emotional experiences provide the semantic grounding for non-concrete words. Using lexical decision and semantic categorization paradigms, the authors quantified the impact of socialness and emotional valence on word recognition latencies. The results demonstrate that positive emotional valence and social relevance significantly facilitate processing, with emotional states serving as a primary organizational principle. Experimental evidence from affective priming suggests that abstract semantic representations are instantiated through internal affective and social experiential features rather than purely symbolic or linguistic relations, supporting a multi-modal embodied framework for abstract cognition.
papers.authors: Daria Goriachun, Kristof Strijkers, Núria Gala, Johannes C. Ziegler

papers.title: Semantic and Syntactic Predictions in Reading Aloud: Are Good Predictors Good Statistical Learners?
papers.abstract: The present study evaluates the proposed link between domain-general statistical learning (SL) and online linguistic prediction during vocal production. Participants performed a predictive reading task measuring semantic and syntactic facilitation effects, as well as multiple SL assessments (VSL, ASL, and SRT). While the results confirmed robust facilitation of reading onset latencies by both semantic and syntactic contexts, no consistent correlations were found between linguistic prediction efficiency and performance on non-linguistic SL measures. These findings challenge the view that the exploitation of statistical regularities in language is driven by a unitary, domain-general substrate, suggesting instead a more dissociated architecture for linguistic versus non-linguistic pattern extraction and prediction.
papers.authors: Elisa Gavard, Johannes C. Ziegler

papers.title: The effect of constituent frequency and distractor type on learning novel complex words
papers.abstract: This study investigates the implicit acquisition of morphological knowledge by examining how the frequency of constituent morphemes and the nature of orthographic competition influence the lexicalization of novel complex words. Skilled readers were trained on pseudowords composed of novel stems and suffixes, with the researchers manipulating the frequency of occurrence for individual morphemic subunits. The data reveal a complex pattern of facilitatory and inhibitory effects: first-constituent frequency facilitated learning only when distractors promoted learning of that component, whereas second-constituent frequency effects were dependent on distractors favoring the second component. These results indicate that morphological decomposition and integration into the mental lexicon are dynamically modulated by the statistical properties of the input and the distribution of distractors during word acquisition.
papers.authors: Elisabeth Beyersmann, Jonathan Grainger, Stéphane Dufau, Colas Fournet, Johannes C. Ziegler

E358.name: Erik Reichle
E358.bio: Erik Reichle is a Professor of Cognitive Psychology at Macquarie University specializing in the computational modeling of the cognitive, perceptual, and motor processes underlying skilled reading. Reichle developed the E-Z Reader model, a serial-attention framework that simulates eye-movement control by integrating word identification, visual attention, and saccadic programming. Their research methodology combines computer simulations with eye-tracking and neuroimaging data to investigate how reading processes vary across different writing systems and digital formats. Reichle’s current research extends these models to examine the "eye-mind link" and the neurocognitive mechanisms involved in complex visual information processing.
E358.research_direction: Dr. Reichle has recently been investigating the cognitive and oculomotor mechanisms underlying reading across diverse scripts, media, and stages of learning. Their recent work explores how bottom-up perceptual features and top-down linguistic expectations interact to guide eye movements, utilizing eye-tracking to probe spatial letter encoding in the parafovea and predictability effects in non-alphabetic scripts like Chinese. Additionally, they are employing computational modeling alongside eye-movement data to examine how the temporal spacing of visual exposure influences the acquisition and memory consolidation of new written word forms. Beyond basic oculomotor control, Dr. Reichle also investigates how the specific cognitive and perceptual affordances of digital reading formats—such as reading on tablets versus paper—alter attentional allocation and higher-level comprehension monitoring in both developing children and adult readers.

papers.title: Examining the effects of character and word predictability in Chinese reading
papers.abstract: This study evaluates the relative utility of character-based versus word-based cloze metrics in explaining predictability effects during the reading of Chinese, a script characterized by meaning-bearing characters and the absence of explicit word boundaries. Utilizing eye-tracking methodologies and the boundary paradigm, the research assesses how top-down contextual expectations and bottom-up perceptual information interact during foveal and parafoveal processing. Survival analysis of fixation durations and word-skipping probabilities suggests that while both graded and lexical prediction mechanisms appear to operate in tandem, character-based metrics are often as effective as word-based metrics in capturing oculomotor control patterns. These findings contrast with those observed in alphabetic scripts and highlight the role of sub-lexical linguistic features in Chinese reading architecture.
papers.authors: Jin Tian, Lili Yu, Roslyn Wong, Erik Reichle

papers.title: Eye Tracking and Simulating the Spacing Effect During Orthographic Learning
papers.abstract: This research investigated the influence of temporal spacing on the acquisition of new written word forms (orthographic learning) using a combination of eye-movement monitoring and computational simulations. Adult readers encountered sentences containing novel pseudowords under either spaced or massed conditions. While massed exposures resulted in shorter total reading times during the acquisition phase, offline post-tests demonstrated a significant spacing advantage in retention. Simulations using the E-Z Reader model, modified with a processing deadline mechanism, suggests that the spacing effect originates from attenuated attentional processing of massed items. The association between longer initial fixations and subsequent higher accuracy in orthographic identification tests points to the intersection of oculomotor control and memory consolidation in reading development.
papers.authors: Signy Wegener, Anne Castles, Elisabeth Beyersmann, Kate Nation, Hua-Chen Wang, Erik D. Reichle

papers.title: Reading from Paper, Computers, and Tablets in the First Grade: The Role of Comprehension Monitoring
papers.abstract: The study examines the impact of different reading media (paper, computer, and tablet) on the reading comprehension and metacognitive monitoring of children in their first year of formal education. By utilizing an inconsistency-detection paradigm, the researchers assessed the efficacy of comprehension monitoring—the ability to identify semantic contradictions within a text—across platforms. Results indicate that while literal comprehension was generally stable across media, the medium significantly influenced the calibration of performance and the identification of distant versus local inconsistencies. The findings suggest that the cognitive and perceptual affordances of digital devices may alter the allocation of attentional resources and text-level processing strategies even in developing readers.
papers.authors: Elena Florit, Pietro De Carli, Antonio Rodà, Lucia Mason, Erik Reichle

papers.title: Letter Identity and Position Coding in the Parafovea
papers.abstract: Across four experiments, this research examined the flexibility of coding letter identity and position information for words located in the parafoveal region (2°–5° from fixation). Using a modified same–different match task with transposed- and substituted-letter strings, the study investigated how retinal eccentricity and visual field impact lexical processing before foveal fixation. Results demonstrated a robust right-visual-field (RVF) advantage for word identification and showed that the detection of letter transpositions interacts significantly with eccentricity. Specifically, initial-letter transpositions were more readily detected in the LVF, while final-letter transpositions were better detected in the RVF. These findings challenge serial models of reading restricted to foveal word identification and suggest more complex spatial encoding of upcoming text in the parafovea.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
papers.authors: Aaron Veldre, Lili Yu, Sally Andrews, Erik D. Reichle

papers.title: Dynamic reading in a digital age: new insights on cognition
papers.abstract: This review synthesizes recent cognitive and psycholinguistic research regarding how the mental processes supporting the reading of static text are adapted for dynamic digital environments, such as handheld e-readers and smartphones. The paper evaluates the interplay between visual-oculomotor constraints and higher-level cognitive factors, highlighting the 'screen-inferiority effect' and the adaptation of reading strategies in response to multimodal and hypertextual contexts. By discussing the metacognitive and motivational influences on digital reading behavior, the authors propose a framework for how readers strategically adjust attention and lexical representation construction when engaging with dynamic text formats, offering insights for leveraging technology to optimize reading efficiency.
papers.authors: Sixin Liao, Lili Yu, Jan-Louis Kruger, Erik Reichle

E359.name: Simon Liversedge
E359.lab_name: Perception, Cognition and Neuroscience Research Group
E359.bio: Simon Liversedge is a Professor of Cognitive Psychology whose research utilizes eye-tracking and psychophysiological methodologies to examine the cognitive processes involved in reading and visual cognition. Liversedge investigates parafoveal processing and the effects of linguistic properties on oculomotor control across alphabetic and non-alphabetic scripts, such as Chinese. Their recent work employs the co-registration of eye movements and fixation-related potentials to integrate behavioral and neural data for the study of lexical identification.
E359.research_direction: Dr. Liversedge’s recent work explores the cognitive and oculomotor mechanisms of reading, primarily using eye-tracking and gaze-contingent display paradigms to study the dynamics of parafoveal processing. They have recently been investigating how the spatial extent of the perceptual window is modulated by foveal processing load and the structural familiarity of multi-word sequences, particularly in Chinese text. Their research also spans developmental and clinical populations, exploring the longitudinal emergence of orthographic, phonological, and semantic information extraction in children, while also assessing how adults with developmental dyslexia encode letter positions outside of central fixation. Additionally, they are investigating the limits of attentional selectivity by testing how cross-modal auditory distractors, such as background speech, disrupt eye movement control during complex reading tasks.

papers.title: Exploring effects of foveal load and preview restrictions for single and multiple parafoveal words in Chinese reading
papers.abstract: This study utilized the gaze-contingent boundary paradigm to investigate the modulation of parafoveal information extraction by foveal lexical processing load (manipulated via pre-target word frequency) in Chinese reading. Two experiments varied the extent of parafoveal preview (from zero to three characters and full preview) for target regions consisting of either a single multicharacter word or multiple constituent words. Findings indicated that increased foveal load (processing low-frequency pre-targets) significantly restricted the spatial extent of parafoveal processing, as evidenced by attenuated preview benefits and altered saccadic targeting for upcoming text. These results demonstrate that foveal processing difficulty dynamically constricts the perceptual window and are discussed in relation to the Foveal Load Hypothesis and the Multi-Constituent Unit (MCU) hypothesis.
papers.authors: Manman Zhang, Zhichao Zhang, Fang Li, Xuejun Bai, Chuanli Zang, Simon P. Liversedge

papers.title: Primary task demands modulate background speech disruption during reading of Chinese tongue twisters: an eye-tracking study
papers.abstract: Through eye-tracking, this research examined the breakdown of attentional selectivity during cross-modal distraction while reading Chinese tongue twisters. The study assessed how focal task demands (semantic acceptability versus noncharacter detection) influenced susceptibility to meaningful and meaningless background speech. Meaningful speech selectively hindered semantic integration—increasing regressive saccades and re-reading fixations—specifically when the primary task required semantic processing. Furthermore, the typical word frequency effect was delayed in the presence of speech. These findings provide robust evidence for the interference-by-process account, where the degree of distraction is determined by the overlap between the cognitive operations of the primary task and the automatic processing of the auditory distractor.
papers.authors: Zhu Meng, Guoli Yan, John E. Marsh, Simon P. Liversedge

papers.title: Development of orthographic, phonological and semantic parafoveal processing in Chinese reading
papers.abstract: This developmental eye-tracking study characterized the longitudinal emergence of different types of parafoveal processing in Chinese-speaking children (Grades 2–5) and adults. Using the boundary paradigm, the researchers manipulated orthographic, phonological, and semantic preview information for upcoming target words. Results revealed that orthographic parafoveal processing is established early in reading development, appearing by the second grade. Conversely, phonological and semantic preview benefits emerged more slowly, only becoming reliable in the third or fourth grades. The data suggest a developmental trajectory in which the extraction of orthographic codes serves as a prerequisite mediator for the subsequent activation of phonological and semantic representations in the parafovea.
papers.venue: The Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology
papers.authors: Min Liu, Sainan Li, Zhu Meng, Yongsheng Wang, Chuanli Zang, Guoli Yan, Simon P. Liversedge

papers.title: Parafoveal Processing and Transposed-Letter Effects in Developmental Dyslexic Reading
papers.abstract: This experiment investigated the flexibility of letter position encoding in the parafovea among adult readers with developmental dyslexia. Eye movements were monitored during a gaze-contingent boundary paradigm that manipulated parafoveal previews (identical, transposed-letter, or substituted-letter). While dyslexic readers effectively extracted letter identity information, they exhibited a marked deficit in sensitivity to transpositions involving the first two letters of upcoming words compared to skilled controls. These results indicate that developmental dyslexia is associated with underspecified or 'noisy' orthographic representations in the parafovea, leading to less robust letter position encoding during the early stages of word identification in fluent reading.
papers.authors: Julie A. Kirkby, Rhiannon S. Barrington, Denis Drieghe, Simon P. Liversedge

papers.title: Parafoveal processing of Chinese four-character idioms and phrases in reading: Evidence for multi-constituent unit hypothesis
papers.abstract: This study tested the Multi-Constituent Unit (MCU) hypothesis by investigating whether familiar multi-word sequences are processed as integrated lexical entries during natural Chinese reading. Eye movements were recorded using the boundary paradigm to compare parafoveal processing for four-character idioms versus literal, non-idiomatic phrases. Results showed a whole-unit preview benefit for high-frequency idiomatic expressions, where the entire four-character string was processed as a single unit. In contrast, literal phrases exhibited character-based processing. The findings provide empirical evidence that highly familiar multi-word sequences are stored and processed as unified lexical representations, facilitating more efficient oculomotor control and parafoveal pre-processing.
papers.authors: Chuanli Zang, Shuangshuang Wang, Xuejun Bai, Guoli Yan, Simon P. Liversedge

E360.name: Adrian Staub
E360.department: Department of Psychological and Brain Sciences
E360.bio: Adrian Staub is a Professor of Psychological and Brain Sciences at the University of Massachusetts Amherst and directs the UMass Eyetracking Lab. Staub's research investigates the real-time cognitive mechanisms of language comprehension, focusing on how word recognition and syntactic parsing operate during reading. Using eye-tracking and EEG co-registration, Staub explores how lexical predictability, word frequency, and grammatical structures influence oculomotor control and neural processing. Additionally, their work examines the role of visual attention and perceptual inference in the detection of linguistic errors, such as word transpositions and function word omissions.
E360.research_direction: Dr. Staub's recent work explores the cognitive and oculomotor mechanisms underlying language comprehension, primarily using large-scale eye-tracking corpora and behavioral paradigms to study how readers process written text. They have recently been investigating how word predictability and linguistic context influence reading behavior, testing formal models like Surprisal theory to determine if a word's statistical probability can account for all variations in reading difficulty. Their research also probes the fine-grained visual and cognitive processes involved in natural reading, examining whether readers use global sentence meaning or local word-transition statistics to overlook word-transposition errors, and questioning whether function and content words trigger inherently distinct fixation and skipping behaviors when basic visual features like word length are controlled. Additionally, their recent work evaluates methodological rigor within the field by analyzing how cognitive psychology researchers approach formal statistical power and sample size justifications in their experimental designs.

papers.title: Sample size and its justification in the Journal of Memory and Language
papers.abstract: This analysis scrutinizes current practices regarding sample size determination and formal power justification within articles published in the Journal of Memory and Language. The study evaluates the prevalence of explicit power analyses, the use of heuristic-based sample sizing, and the reporting of sensitivity analyses. Findings suggest that while there is an increasing trend toward justifying sample sizes, many studies still rely on conventional targets without formal consideration of expected effect sizes or the statistical power of the specific experimental designs used.
papers.authors: Adrian Staub

papers.title: Predictability in Language Comprehension: Prospects and Problems for Surprisal
papers.abstract: This review synthesizes the empirical evidence for Surprisal theory, which posits that incremental processing difficulty is determined by the negative log probability of a word given its preceding context. Technical assessment of the literature indicates that two core predictions are supported: the absence of specific costs for prediction violations (facilitation without inhibition) and a logarithmic relationship between predictability and reading time. However, the 'causal bottleneck' hypothesis—claiming surprisal accounts for all lexical and syntactic difficulty—is challenged by effects of low-frequency words and garden-path recovery that appear independent of conditional probability.
papers.authors: Adrian Staub

papers.title: The function/content word distinction and eye movements in reading
papers.abstract: This investigation re-evaluates the oculomotor differences between function and content words by controlling for length, frequency, and predictability across large-scale eye-tracking corpora. Standard accounts suggest function words are skipped more frequently due to their unique linguistic status. However, the results demonstrate that once lexical variables are statistically equated, skipping rates are comparable. Notably, function words exhibit slightly longer first-fixation and gaze durations, a finding that contradicts traditional models of automated function word processing and suggests that their integration into the syntactic framework may impose distinct processing costs.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
papers.authors: Adrian Staub

papers.title: Readers do not strongly rely on full-context information, but might utilize local word statistics, when 'correcting' word transposition errors in text
papers.abstract: This study tests whether rational inference over a noisy channel explains the failure to notice transposed-word (TW) errors. Experiment 1 manipulated global cloze probability to determine if context-driven semantic expectations modulate error detection rates, finding no reliable effect. Experiment 2 manipulated local 4-gram frequencies of the transposed sequence, finding that error detection was primarily sensitive to local n-gram statistics rather than global sentential fit. The results suggest that the 'correction' of transpositions in the post-lexical buffer is driven by local word-to-word transition probabilities rather than high-level rational integration of the intended message.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the 46th Annual Conference of the Cognitive Science Society
papers.authors: Kuan-Jung Huang, Adrian Staub

E361.name: Jon Andoni Duñabeitia
E361.bio: Jon Andoni Duñabeitia is a Full Professor and Director of the Nebrija Research Center on Cognition (CINC). Duñabeitia's research investigates the neurobiological and cognitive substrates of multilingualism, literacy, and visual word recognition across the human life cycle. Using experimental paradigms involving eye-tracking, virtual reality simulations, and behavioral psycholinguistic tasks, Duñabeitia examines how environmental factors and cognitive load modulate linguistic processing and executive control. Their current research integrates digital health technologies to develop predictive biomarkers for cognitive health and early neurodevelopmental interventions.
E361.research_direction: Dr. Duñabeitia has recently been investigating how to bring greater ecological validity and technological accessibility to psycholinguistic and cognitive research. Their recent work explores visual word recognition in dynamic environments, using high-fidelity virtual reality driving simulators to test how perceptual stressors like simulated weather impact the speed of lexical access during movement. They are also conducting methodological assessments of affordable technologies, examining the reliability of extracting core eye-movement reading metrics at extremely low sampling rates and validating immersive 3D setups for classic mental chronometry paradigms. In more applied domains, Dr. Duñabeitia is testing the far-transfer effects of multidomain computerized cognitive training on real-world driving safety, while simultaneously exploring how acoustic and singing-based vocal biomarkers might be integrated into digital health platforms to screen for neurodegenerative and psychiatric conditions.

papers.title: Listening to the Mind: Integrating Vocal Biomarkers into Digital Health
papers.abstract: This perspective explores the diagnostic utility of vocal biomarkers, derived from acoustic features (e.g., jitter, shimmer, pitch, and speech rate) and linguistic patterns, for identifying early indicators of neurodegenerative and psychiatric conditions. The authors propose the novel integration of singing-based assessments into digital health frameworks, arguing that melodic structures may engage broader neural networks than conventional speech, thereby increasing screening sensitivity for populations with cognitive or linguistic impairments. The article emphasizes the requirement for standardized machine learning architectures to facilitate the translation of these non-invasive vocal signatures into reliable clinical monitoring tools and personalized healthcare interventions.
papers.authors: Irene Rodrigo, Jon Andoni Duñabeitia

papers.title: Word recognition during movement under simulated weather conditions
papers.abstract: This research utilizes high-fidelity Virtual Reality (VR) to examine the impact of environmental stressors—specifically simulated sunny versus rainy weather—on visual word recognition in a dynamic driving context. Participants performed naming and identification tasks on orthographic stimuli presented via road signs during virtual navigation. Quantitative results confirmed the persistence of the word frequency effect under environmental disfluency; however, rainy conditions significantly increased response latencies. This negative effect demonstrated a progressive temporal accumulation, suggesting that adverse meteorological factors induce perceptual fatigue and diminish visual adaptation, thereby independently modulating the speed of lexical access during movement.
papers.authors: Francisco Rocabado, Natasha Alonso-Bernal, Jon Andoni Duñabeitia

papers.title: Transforming language research from classic desktops to virtual environments
papers.abstract: This study validates the migration of standard psycholinguistic behavioral paradigms from traditional 2D desktop monitors to immersive 3D virtual reality (VR) environments. By matching visual angles and response collection methods across platforms, the researchers conducted a lexical decision task to compare mental chronometry metrics. The results successfully replicated the robust lexicality effect in both environments, with no statistically significant differences in reaction times or error rates between VR and PC setups. These findings establish VR as a reliable and valid modality for behavioral data collection in language research, enabling the study of linguistic processing within naturalistic and ecologically valid spatial contexts.
papers.authors: Francisco Rocabado, Laís Muntini, Omar Fahmi Jubran, Thomas Lachmann, Jon Andoni Duñabeitia

papers.title: How low can you go? Tracking eye movements during reading at different sampling rates
papers.abstract: This methodological investigation assesses the reliability of cognitive markers in reading research when captured at sub-optimal temporal resolutions. The authors recorded eye-movement data at 2000 Hz and systematically downsampled the signal to simulate lower sampling rates (ranging from 30 to 125 Hz) typical of low-cost, consumer-grade hardware. The analysis demonstrates that core effects, such as the influence of word frequency on fixation duration, remain detectable even at significantly reduced frequencies provided that sample sizes are sufficiently powered. The study offers a quantitative benchmark for researchers utilizing affordable eye-tracking technologies, defining the limits of diagnostic sensitivity for sentence processing metrics.
papers.authors: Bernhard Angele, Zeynep Gunes Ozkan, Marina Serrano-Carot, Jon Andoni Duñabeitia

papers.title: The effects of cognitive training on driving performance
papers.abstract: This randomized controlled trial investigates the far-transfer effects of an 8-week, multidomain computerized cognitive training (CCT) program on real-world driving safety and performance. Utilizing a high-fidelity driving simulator, young adult participants were evaluated on various operational metrics before and after the intervention. Mixed-design ANOVA revealed a significant interaction between time and group, with the training cohort exhibiting a marked reduction in traffic infractions and enhanced hazard response efficiency compared to a passive control. These findings suggest that targeted stimulation of executive functions, including inhibition and spatial attention, can effectively improve performance in complex, safety-critical tasks like driving.
papers.authors: Jose Luis Tapia, David Sánchez-Borda, Jon Andoni Duñabeitia

E362.name: Julie Fiez
E362.department: Department of Psychology and Department of Neuroscience
E362.main_research_area: cognitive neuroscience of language and learning
E362.bio: Julie A. Fiez is a cognitive neuroscientist who investigates the neural mechanisms underlying speech, reading, and learning. Utilizing multimodal techniques such as functional neuroimaging (fMRI/PET), intracranial recordings, and behavioral testing, Fiez explores how the brain processes orthographic and phonological information during visual word recognition and working memory. Fiez's research examines the non-motor roles of the cerebellum and basal ganglia, specifically their contributions to error-correction and reinforcement learning systems. Currently, they work to bridge basic neuroscience and education by developing interventions that aim to optimize the acquisition of reading and mathematical skills.
E362.research_direction: Dr. Fiez has recently been investigating the neurocognitive architectures that support complex symbolic skills, specifically focusing on mathematical cognition and reading. Their recent work explores how the brain processes numbers, utilizing lesion-symptom mapping in stroke patients to map the distinct neural substrates—such as the intraparietal sulcus and core language regions—that govern precise versus approximate numeracy. Alongside this, they are studying the cognitive and neural demands of literacy by having typical adults, struggling readers, and cerebellar stroke patients learn to decode novel artificial orthographies. Through a combination of fMRI, lesion studies, and behavioral paradigms, their research probes how structures like the cerebellum and domain-general systems like the multiple demand network scaffold the complex phonological decoding required for early literacy acquisition.

papers.title: Lesion-symptom mapping reveals differential relationships between language and precise versus approximate numeracy
papers.abstract: Using Support Vector Regression Lesion-Symptom Mapping (SVR-LSM) in a cohort of 104 left-hemisphere chronic stroke survivors, this study evaluated the neuroanatomical dissociation between approximate and precise numerical processing and their respective overlaps with the language network. Precise numeracy was significantly correlated with aphasia severity and localized to the inferior frontal gyrus (IFG), angular gyrus (AG), and posterior temporal regions, as well as subcortical structures like the caudate and thalamus. In contrast, approximate numeracy demonstrated minimal correlation with language deficits and relied on the intraparietal sulcus (IPS), precentral gyrus, and anterior fusiform gyrus. These findings suggest that while precise mathematical operations recruit components of the core language system, magnitude approximation operates via an independent neural substrate.
papers.authors: Erin Duricy, Corrine Durisko, Julie A. Fiez

papers.title: The role of intraparietal sulcus in numeracy: a review of parietal lesion cases
papers.abstract: This systematic review synthesized evidence from 27 single-case studies involving focal left parietal lesions to characterize the causal necessity of the intraparietal sulcus (IPS) across four numeracy domains: Approximation, Calculation, Ordinality/Cardinality, and Transcoding. The analysis revealed that IPS damage is consistently associated with specific deficits in numerical approximation and magnitude estimation, supporting the Triple Code Model's assertion of an IPS-based analog magnitude representation. However, IPS involvement was not found to be universally critical for all numerical tasks, reinforcing a model of dissociable neural circuits for distinct facets of mathematical cognition within the parietal lobe.
papers.authors: Erin Duricy, Corrine Durisko, Julie A. Fiez

papers.title: Established and Emergent Reading Skills in Adults with Cerebellar Stroke: Evidence of Phonological Alexia
papers.abstract: This investigation utilized a dual-component assessment strategy, consisting of static lexical decision and dynamic artificial orthography training, to characterize reading impairments in patients with chronic cerebellar stroke. Results demonstrated that cerebellar damage significantly disrupts phonological decoding, evidenced by impaired non-word reading and a reduced ability to acquire new grapheme-phoneme correspondences in a novel script. Notably, nearly 40% of the patient sample met the clinical criteria for phonological alexia. The findings provide evidence that the cerebellum contributes to the assembly and application of phonological codes essential for both established and emergent reading processes, independent of primary motor articulation deficits.
papers.authors: Anna Chrabaszcz, Julie A. Fiez

papers.title: Contributions of the multiple demand network to emergent and skilled reading
papers.abstract: This fMRI study employed an artificial orthography (AO) paradigm in proficient adult readers to contrast the neural systems supporting emergent versus skilled reading. Emergent reading (decoding a novel script) elicited robust activation in the Multiple Demand (MD) network, specifically the left inferior-frontal junction, bilateral intraparietal sulcus, and anterior insula, alongside the traditional reading network in the left occipito-temporal cortex. While substantial spatial overlap was observed between emergent and skilled reading networks, the MD network showed task-dependent recruitment that declined as reading fluency increased. The results suggest that the MD network provides domain-general scaffolding to support the cognitively demanding process of phonological assembly during early literacy acquisition.
papers.authors: Anna Chrabaszcz, Kailee Lear, Corrine Durisko, Julie A. Fiez

papers.title: Phonological decoding and orthographic learning in poor and typical adult readers
papers.abstract: This study examined whether deficits in phonological decoding efficiency constrain orthographic acquisition in adults with chronic reading difficulties. Using a series of orthographic learning tasks (spelling, identification, and lexical decision) in both English and a novel artificial orthography, researchers found that poor readers achieved near-ceiling accuracy in learning new grapheme-phoneme mappings but exhibited a persistent fluency gap compared to controls. Crucially, poor readers' orthographic learning performance was comparable to typical readers under matched exposure conditions, suggesting that while phonological decoding efficiency bottlenecks fluency, it does not fundamentally prevent the formation of accurate orthographic representations.
papers.authors: Anna Chrabaszcz, Kailee Lear, Corrine Durisko, Julie Fiez

E363.name: Ken Pugh
E363.department: Yale Child Study Center; Department of Linguistics
E363.bio: Kenneth Pugh is a cognitive neuroscientist specializing in the neurobiological foundations of language and literacy development. Pugh utilizes functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and other multimodal neuroimaging techniques to delineate the cortical networks involved in typical reading and developmental dyslexia. Their research examines the functional connectivity and neuroplasticity of the literate brain, investigating how pedagogical interventions and environmental factors modulate circuitry for word recognition and phonological processing. As the Director of the Yale Reading Center and President of Haskins Laboratories, Pugh integrates genetic, behavioral, and neuroimaging data to develop models of reading disabilities and individual differences in learning.
E363.research_direction: Dr. Pugh has recently been investigating the neural mechanisms underlying behavioral improvements following reading interventions across both pediatric and adult populations. Their recent work explores how targeted reading treatments induce neuroplastic changes, utilizing electrophysiological and neuroimaging methods to track shifts in structural connectivity and functional brain architecture. Specifically, they are studying whether intervention-driven behavioral gains are linked to the normalization of canonical left-hemisphere reading networks or to the compensatory recruitment of right-hemisphere, frontal, and subcortical regions. Ultimately, their research seeks to map the heterogeneous neural indices of reading recovery to better understand how behavioral interventions physically shape white matter integrity and cortical activation patterns.

papers.title: Electrophysiological indices of reading intervention response: A systematic review
papers.abstract: This comprehensive review synthesizes 39 neuroimaging investigations to elucidate the relationship between behavioral improvements following reading interventions and concurrent neuroplastic changes. The analysis reveals evidence of altered neural activation, structural connectivity, and functional architecture within the canonical left-hemisphere reading circuitry, as well as compensatory recruitment of right-hemisphere, frontal, and subcortical regions. While individualized studies demonstrate specific patterns of normalization or compensation—such as increased left inferior frontal gyrus engagement or enhanced white matter integrity—a formal meta-analysis of longitudinal activation changes across a subset of eight studies failed to yield statistically significant global effects, highlighting the high degree of heterogeneity in neural response patterns across different pediatric and adult cohorts.
papers.venue: Advances in Child Development and Behavior
papers.authors: Brittany Lee, Nicole Landi, Kenneth R. Pugh

E364.name: Bruce McCandliss
E364.bio: Bruce McCandliss is a researcher in developmental cognitive neuroscience who investigates how educational experiences in literacy and mathematics transform the human brain. McCandliss’s research focuses on the neural mechanisms of reading acquisition and mathematical cognition, utilizing functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), diffusion tensor imaging (DTI), and high-density EEG to track experience-dependent plasticity. They examine the development of the visual word form area and use steady-state visual evoked potentials (SSVEP) to study the temporal dynamics of visual word recognition. Currently, McCandliss directs the Educational Neuroscience Initiative at Stanford, where they conduct longitudinal studies and school-based interventions to connect laboratory findings with classroom practice.
E364.research_direction: Dr. McCandliss has recently been investigating the neural and cognitive mechanisms underlying early academic learning, with a strong focus on how children's visual systems adapt to process text. Their recent work heavily utilizes steady-state visual evoked potentials (SSVEPs) to track how the developing brain becomes specialized for recognizing orthographic structures, such as familiar letter combinations and newly learned visual word forms. They are specifically exploring how cortical response latencies and experience-driven visual plasticity relate to individual differences in reading fluency and real-world classroom instruction. Beyond reading, their research expands into math cognition by developing high-resolution, tablet-based paradigms to probe the trial-by-trial cognitive dynamics of arithmetic fluency across childhood and adolescence. To anchor these neurocognitive metrics in authentic learning environments, Dr. McCandliss is pioneering research-practice partnerships that embed EEG laboratories directly within elementary schools, bridging the gap between basic visual neuroscience and everyday educational practice.

papers.title: Steady-state EEG captures how elementary classroom instruction drives plasticity for novel visual words
papers.abstract: This longitudinal study evaluates the influence of classroom instruction and exposure frequency on neural word representations in early readers. Utilizing steady-state visual evoked potentials (SSVEP) and a two-week 'learning sprint' model co-designed with teachers, the authors contrasted high-frequency words, medium-frequency words, and pseudowords. Results indicate that 4 Hz cortical responses are sensitive to corpus-based word frequency estimates. Critically, newly acquired low-frequency words (frequency <1 per million) taught in the children's own classrooms elicited cortical responses nearly identical to those evoked by long-term high-frequency words. Furthermore, 1 Hz neural responses associated with new vocabulary learning predicted individual variations in reading-related skills, specifically word decoding and rapid automatic naming (RAN), demonstrating the causal impact of authentic instructional practices on cortical plasticity.
papers.authors: Fang Wang, Elizabeth Y. Toomarian, Radhika S. Gosavi, Blair Kaneshiro, Anthony M. Norcia, Bruce D. McCandliss

papers.title: Cortical latency predicts reading fluency from late childhood to early adolescence
papers.abstract: Traditional EEG and ERP measures of visual word recognition timing often suffer from low signal-to-noise ratios and poor individual-level reliability. This research implements a novel SSVEP phase-based modeling approach to derive precise cortical latency estimates for visual word form processing. Analysis of 68 typically developing readers (ages 8–15) revealed a mean latency of approximately 170 ms for four-character strings, with individual latencies showing exceptionally high internal consistency (r = 0.94). These latencies remained stable across word-form manipulations (words, nonwords, and pseudofonts) but decreased linearly with age. Significantly, individual cortical latency was a robust predictor of single-word reading efficiency and sentence-level comprehension fluency, a relationship partially mediated by single-word naming speed.
papers.authors: Fang Wang, Quynh Trang H. Nguyen, Blair Kaneshiro, Anthony M. Norcia, Bruce D. McCandliss

papers.title: Tablet-based arithmetic fluency assessment reveals developments in math cognition and math achievement from childhood to adolescence
papers.abstract: While arithmetic fluency is typically assessed using aggregate paper-based scores, this study introduces a tablet-based paradigm capable of capturing trial-by-trial response times and error rates across diverse experimental contrasts. Testing 824 students in grades 3 through 7, the authors distinguished between 'common' single-digit problems (e.g., 5 + 3) and 'exceptional' problems (e.g., 4 + 4, 2 + 1). Although students exhibited higher absolute fluency on exceptional problems, performance on common problems was a superior predictor of standardized math achievement scores and mediated the link between socioeconomic status and academic outcomes. The results demonstrate that tablet-based assessments can reveal distinct cognitive dynamics and speed-accuracy tradeoffs that evolve as a function of age and overall mathematical proficiency.
papers.authors: Ethan Roy, Mathieu Guillaume, Amandine Van Rinsveld, Project iLead Consortium, Bruce D. McCandliss

papers.title: Emerging Insights From a Research-Practice Partnership Approach to Educational Neuroscience
papers.abstract: The translation of neuroscientific discovery into educational practice is often hindered by the physical and conceptual separation of research labs and schools. This commentary provides a comprehensive case study of the Brainwave Learning Center (BLC), a research-practice partnership (RPP) that co-locates a state-of-the-art EEG laboratory within an elementary school. The authors examine programmatic innovations, including specialized liaisons and the active involvement of students and teachers as collaborators. By analyzing the iteratively emerged values of this model, the paper offers a framework for building sustainable educational neuroscience ecosystems that prioritize ecological validity and collaborative inquiry into child development and learning.
papers.authors: Elizabeth Y. Toomarian, Radhika S. Gosavi, Lindsey R. Hasak, Madison Bunderson, Bruce D. McCandliss

papers.title: Progress in elementary school reading linked to growth of cortical responses to familiar letter combinations within visual word forms
papers.abstract: This longitudinal study investigates the neural internalization of statistical regularities in print (visual word form structure) over two years of elementary schooling. Using high-density EEG and frequency-tagged SSVEP, the authors measured cortical responses to three levels of print: coarse tuning, sublexical orthographic structures (familiar letter combinations), and whole word representations. Findings reveal that neural sensitivity to sublexical word form structures nearly doubled in amplitude and became increasingly left-lateralized over the developmental period. Critically, longitudinal decreases in the magnitude of these neural responses were uniquely linked to improvements in rapid automatic naming (RAN) of letters, suggesting that reading fluency development is predicated on the brain's rapid specialization for visual word form regularities.
papers.authors: Fang Wang, Blair Kaneshiro, Elizabeth Y. Toomarian, Radhika S. Gosavi, Lindsey R. Hasak, Sofia Moron, Quynh Trang H. Nguyen, Anthony M. Norcia, Bruce D. McCandliss

E365.name: Guinevere Eden
E365.lab_name: Center for the Study of Learning
E365.bio: Eden is a Professor in the Department of Pediatrics at Georgetown University and the Director of the Center for the Study of Learning. They use structural and functional magnetic resonance imaging to investigate the neural mechanisms underlying reading development and developmental dyslexia. Eden applied fMRI to the study of dyslexia, focusing on how the brain's visual and auditory systems support literacy acquisition. Their research examines the impact of sensory experience on brain plasticity and identifies neurobiological markers of reading remediation in children and adults.
E365.research_direction: Dr. Eden's recent work explores the structural neuroanatomy of language and cognitive development, utilizing large-scale pediatric neuroimaging datasets to study phenomena like dyslexia, bilingualism, and ADHD. They have recently been investigating how early dual-language acquisition shapes gray matter volume and cortical thickness, probing whether bilingualism interacts with executive function and neurodevelopment in children with and without ADHD. Their research also characterizes the distinct neural correlates of language proficiency versus language balance, while systematically re-evaluating the robustness of classical morphological markers of developmental dyslexia. Across these domains, Dr. Eden places a strong emphasis on methodological rigor, explicitly testing how structural MRI findings are influenced by different analytical pipelines like FreeSurfer and CAT12, varying spatial atlases, and global volume scaling.

papers.title: A Discovery and Replication Study of Dyslexia Does Not Reveal Reproducible Gray Matter Volume Differences
papers.abstract: Two decades of structural neuroimaging have reported gray matter volume (GMV) reductions in developmental dyslexia (reading disability, RD) within left perisylvian language regions. However, widespread methodological concerns have emerged regarding small sample cohorts, liberal statistical thresholding, and inadequate control of total intracranial volume and demographic confounders. To evaluate the robustness of these morphometric findings, a discovery and replication design was implemented in 262 children from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study. Voxel-based morphometry (VBM) conducted in SPM failed to replicate RD-associated GMV reductions across the discovery and replication cohorts, with more conservative statistical correction yielding negligible group differences. Parallel surface-based morphometric analyses in FreeSurfer likewise revealed non-converging profiles between cohorts. Full-factorial VBM interaction analyses confirmed significant divergence between datasets. Notably, omitting global GMV as a covariate eliminated this divergence while artificially magnifying RD group differences, indicating that classical GMV signatures of dyslexia are highly sensitive to analytic pipelines and global volume scaling rather than representing stable morphological markers.
papers.authors: Alison K. Schug, Iria S. Gutierrez-Schieferl, Guinevere F. Eden

papers.title: Associations between brain structure and both language proficiency and language balance in early bilinguals
papers.abstract: Neuroimaging investigations into bilingualism frequently examine either language proficiency or language balance (the degree of disparity between competencies across two languages), but rarely evaluate both dimensions simultaneously despite substantial shared variance. This whole-brain morphometric study assessed gray matter volume (GMV) and cortical thickness (CT) in 46 early Spanish–English bilingual adolescents (mean age = 16.7 years). Non-dominant language proficiency exhibited a significant positive correlation with GMV in the right angular gyrus (BA 39) extending into the superior temporal gyrus (BA 22). Language balance also correlated positively with right angular gyrus GMV and negatively with GMV in the left postcentral gyrus (BA 1), cerebellar lobule IX, and right superior occipital gyrus (BA 18); however, these associations were abolished after statistically controlling for language proficiency. Neither language metric demonstrated significant associations with CT. These results indicate that neuroanatomical correlates of language balance are primarily driven by underlying proficiency and localize outside canonical perisylvian language cortex.
papers.authors: Mia R. Coutinho, Edith Brignoni-Pérez, Nasheed I. Jamal, Guinevere F. Eden

papers.title: Are executive function and neuroanatomy in ADHD modulated by bilingualism?
papers.abstract: Bilingual language experience and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) independently impact executive function (EF) and the morphometry of frontoparietal and subcortical networks. Leveraging data from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study, this study investigated whether bilingualism differentially moderates EF performance and brain structure in children with ADHD. Early Spanish–English bilingual and English monolingual children with and without ADHD were evaluated using 2 × 2 factorial models across behavioral EF batteries, voxel-based morphometry for gray matter volume (GMV), and vertex-wise cortical thickness (CT). Factorial ANOVAs revealed widespread main effects of language experience on GMV and CT across multiple cortical and subcortical regions, whereas diagnostic status influenced GMV across select regions without impacting CT. Crucially, left thalamic GMV displayed independent, additive effects—exhibiting volume reduction in ADHD relative to neurotypical controls alongside volume enlargement in bilinguals relative to monolinguals—without significant interaction effects across any anatomical or behavioral metric, demonstrating that dual-language acquisition does not modulate the neural substrates of ADHD.
papers.authors: Anushka Oak, Iria S. Gutierrez-Schieferl, Guinevere F. Eden

papers.title: Neuroanatomical differences in early bilingual and monolingual children
papers.abstract: Prior investigations into the structural brain differences associated with early bilingualism have produced inconsistent results, largely due to small sample cohorts, adult-skewed demographics, and a predominant reliance on gray matter volume (GMV) rather than cortical thickness (CT). Drawing from the ABCD Study, this investigation compared early Spanish–English bilingual and English monolingual children (N = 1,209) closely matched on age, pubertal stage, biological sex, handedness, socioeconomic status (SES), and nonverbal reasoning. Whole-brain voxel-based morphometry identified bidirectional GMV differences across all lobes. Vertex-wise CT analyses similarly demonstrated widespread differences, with bilinguals displaying greater CT in regions within left inferior frontal, parahippocampal, and occipital cortices, as well as right superior temporal cortex, alongside more extensive regions of reduced CT across all lobes bilaterally. Parcel-wise CT comparisons showed close concordance with vertex-wise results when utilizing a fine-grained atlas (Destrieux), but diverged under coarser anatomical parcellation (Desikan–Killiany). Furthermore, SES significantly interacted with language status to modulate CT, indicating that bilingual neurodevelopmental variations depend heavily on morphometric metric, atlas scale, and environmental context.
papers.authors: Mia R. Coutinho, Guinevere F. Eden

papers.title: Agreement between FreeSurfer and CAT12 Cortical Thickness Measurements: A Discovery and a Replication Study in Children/Adolescents
papers.abstract: Automated estimation of cortical thickness (CT) from T1-weighted MRI is widely performed using surface-based reconstruction in FreeSurfer or voxel-based projection in the Computational Anatomy Toolbox (CAT12). To resolve conflicting findings regarding absolute and relative consistency between these packages, this investigation utilized discovery (N = 58) and replication (N = 301) pediatric cohorts aged 6–16 years. In both samples, mean whole-cortex and parcel-wise CT values (Desikan–Killiany atlas) exhibited strong positive correlations between pipelines. However, absolute measurement scales diverged systematically: FreeSurfer generated significantly lower CT estimates than CAT12 across the entire cortical mantle and in ≥94% of individual parcels across both cohorts. Inter-pipeline convergence was further modulated by chronological age, empirical image quality metrics, and MRI vendor platform. These systematic discrepancies demonstrate that while relative intra-cohort rank orders are largely preserved, absolute CT magnitudes derived from FreeSurfer and CAT12 are not directly interchangeable in developmental populations.
papers.authors: Cameron C. McKay, Marissa Laws, Gabrielle-Ann A. Torre, Ashley S. VanMeter, Guinevere F. Eden

E366.name: Marco Marelli
E366.bio: Marco Marelli is a Full Professor at the University of Milano-Bicocca’s Department of Psychology, specializing in the cognitive and computational mechanisms of language processing. Marelli's research focuses on the representation of meaning in the semantic system, exploring how linguistic information interacts with perceptual and motor domains through multimodal models. Utilizing vector space modeling, eye-tracking, and behavioral experiments, they investigate word recognition and the acquisition of novel word meanings. Marelli directs the ERC-funded project 'BraveNewWord,' which applies computational linguistics to study semantic learning in adult speakers.
E366.research_direction: Dr. Marelli has recently been investigating how human semantic memory, language processing, and visual attention are grounded in real-world sensory regularities. Their recent work explores this multimodal grounding by using computational models and deep neural networks to quantify how our visual environments—such as the spatial distances between objects in natural scenes or the statistical frequency of large-scale image tags—shape word recognition and conceptual structure. Beyond visual-semantic links, they are examining the auditory domain by mapping the objective acoustic resemblance between spoken words and environmental sounds to assess linguistic iconicity. Additionally, their research probes how deep-learning-derived similarity metrics predict human visual search efficiency in complex ecological images, and how sub-lexical statistical patterns can drive false memory formation for entirely novel words.

papers.title: SemanticScape: A Distributional Model of Concepts Grounded in Distance Patterns between Objects
papers.abstract: This work introduces a novel distributional semantic model (DSM) that constructs conceptual representations by aggregating spatial arrangement data from naturalistic visual scenes. Leveraging the ViSpa (Vision Spaces) dataset, the authors calculate high-dimensional vectors based on the distance patterns between co-occurring objects within individual images. This spatiocentric grounding approach allows for the quantification of conceptual proximity based on physical world regularities. The model's validity is demonstrated through its superior ability to predict human semantic relatedness judgments and lexical decision latencies, providing a robust computational account of how experiential visual structure informs the human semantic system.
papers.authors: Andrea Gregor de Varda, Marco A. Petilli, Marco Marelli

papers.title: False memories from nowhere: Humans falsely recognize words that are not attested in their vocabulary
papers.abstract: The present study investigates whether false memory formation in the Deese-Roediger-McDermott (DRM) paradigm can occur for novel linguistic strings (pseudowords) lacking prior lexical representation. The authors utilized a distributional semantic model architecture that decomposes strings into character n-grams to calculate semantic similarity between stimuli. Participants were tasked with memorizing lists of related pseudowords followed by a recognition test. Results indicate that both veridical and false recognition rates are significantly modulated by the distributional overlap between the target strings and the studied items. This indicates that human memory is highly sensitive to the semantic patterns elicited by sub-lexical regularities, even when the stimuli have never been previously encountered.
papers.authors: Daniele Gatti, Marco Petilli, Michela Marchetti, Tomaso Vecchi, Giuliana Mazzoni, Luca Rinaldi, Marco Marelli

papers.title: Cracking arbitrariness: A data-driven study of auditory iconicity in spoken English
papers.abstract: This research challenges the traditional view of linguistic arbitrariness by assessing the pervasiveness of auditory iconicity (onomatopoeia) in the English vocabulary. The authors developed a novel data-driven framework that embeds spoken lexical items and environmental sounds into a shared auditory manifold using short-time Fourier transforms and convolutional neural networks (CNNs) trained on sound classification and speech recognition. By measuring the objective acoustic resemblance between words and their referents, the study finds that imitation-based systematicity is a widespread mechanism across various semantic categories rather than a peripheral phenomenon. The derived similarity indexes were empirically validated against human iconicity judgments.
papers.authors: Andrea Gregor de Varda, Marco Marelli

papers.title: Visual search and real-image similarity: An empirical assessment through the lens of deep learning
papers.abstract: Integrating attention research with computer vision, this study investigates the predictive power of similarity principles on human search efficiency within complex ecological scenes. Utilizing deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to extract hierarchical visual features, the authors modeled the search surface by quantifying target-distractor (TD) and distractor-distractor (DD) similarities. Behavioral results indicate that human search performance improves as TD similarity decreases and DD similarity increases. The findings demonstrate that these computationally derived similarity metrics, based on real-world image features, effectively predict search latencies and suggest that TD and DD similarities influence different levels of the visual processing hierarchy.
papers.authors: Marco A. Petilli, Francesca Maria Rodio, Fritz Günther, Marco Marelli

papers.title: The Flickr frequency norms: what 17 years of images tagged online tell us about lexical processing
papers.abstract: This paper introduces large-scale visual frequency norms derived from nearly two decades of image metadata on Flickr.com to evaluate the role of visual experience in word recognition. By extracting tag frequencies from millions of naturalistic images, the authors established a proxy for the frequency with which concepts are visually encountered in daily life. Analysis of psycholinguistic datasets reveals that visual frequency is a significant predictor of lexical decision and word naming latencies, providing unique explanatory power even after accounting for linguistic co-occurrence frequency and imageability ratings. The results underscore the importance of multimodal experiential grounding in the computational modeling of the mental lexicon.
papers.authors: Marco A. Petilli, Fritz Günther, Marco Marelli
